### Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library—complete, uniform, convenient, economical—of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III;**

a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared from the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest care; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all the works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating the material treated below; expanded by works that are doubtful or apocryphal, but which possess some authority or influence in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes:

the first, of subjects, by consulting which one may see at a glance whatever each of the Fathers has written on any given topic; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture, and in what places in their works they have done so.

A most accurate edition, and one easily to be preferred to all others, if one weighs the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, uniform and consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

# Preface Concerning Saint Gregory the Great’s Commentary on the First Book of Kings

Since Peter Gussanvillaeus judged that this distinguished work ought to be denied to the most holy Doctor, and since the same opinion has seemed right to certain learned men, we ought to express our judgment concerning it before it is again published.

### I

There are altogether three opinions concerning the author of this Commentary.

The first holds that Gregory the Great must be regarded as its true and indisputable author. This opinion has been followed by all who, during approximately the last hundred and fifty years—with the sole exception of Gussanvillaeus, the latest of them all—have labored to publish the works of that eminent Doctor. For the earlier editors included this Commentary among the Gregorian writings as the genuine offspring of so great a Father. Almost all learned men, both among our own writers and among heterodox authors, who have drawn up a catalogue of the holy Doctor’s works support their judgment. Among these, William Cave deserves particular mention in his literary history of ecclesiastical writers, which was published not long ago.

### II

The second opinion, wholly opposed to the first, is that of Peter Gussanvillaeus, who entirely removes this Commentary from the catalogue of Gregory’s works, although—something that must not be concealed—he has nevertheless retained Gregory’s name in the Gussanvillaean edition.

That most fair-minded man nevertheless admits that this commentary on the First Book of Kings is thoroughly worthy of Gregory. He sufficiently indicates this in the words with which he concludes his critical judgment and decision:

> If only we could vindicate so devout and holy a work for Saint Gregory, without compromising the truth.

### III

The third opinion, lying almost midway between the other two, holds that the celebrated Commentary was collected and pieced together by Claudius, later abbot of the monastery of Classe, from homilies delivered by Saint Gregory on the First Book of Kings.

Most learned men incline to this opinion, especially Thomassinus, *De disciplina Ecclesiae*, part II, book II, chapter 28, section 2, and Louis Ellies du Pin, *Bibliotheca nova Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum*, volume IV, or the sixth century, under Gregory the Great.

We shall proceed most safely along this middle path, guided especially by Gregory himself. For in book XII, indiction 5, letter 24, he writes the following to John the subdeacon:

> Moreover, because my once most beloved son Claudius had heard me say certain things about Proverbs, the Song of Songs, the Prophets, and also the books of Kings and the Heptateuch—things which, because of my weakness, I could not commit to writing—he himself dictated them according to his understanding, so that they might not perish through forgetfulness, intending to bring these same materials to me at a suitable time, so that they might be dictated more accurately.  
>   
> When he had read them to me, I found that the sense of my words had been altered in a very unhelpful way. Therefore it is necessary that, without any excuse or delay, your Experience go to his monastery, have the brothers assemble, and make them bring together, in complete truthfulness, however many sheets concerning various Scriptures he has brought forward. Receive them and send them to me as quickly as possible.

From this it is clear that Saint Gregory expounded certain passages from the books of Kings not in writing but orally; that Claudius both took down and arranged these materials, but did not everywhere grasp the sense of his teacher Gregory, and indeed did not reproduce his style; and that the holy Doctor did as much as he could to prevent these materials from being brought into public view, ordering that all copies be brought to him so that they might be corrected at leisure. Whether he actually carried this out, we shall explain in its proper place.

### IV

From these facts it is easy to understand what characteristics and signs belong to Claudius’s compilation, by which it may be recognized and distinguished from any other work. Since it is woven from Gregory’s own words and thoughts, it ought to breathe his style, represent his teaching and his method of interpreting Sacred Scripture, and display his practice of turning it toward moral and allegorical meanings. Yet Claudius may sometimes, perhaps because his memory failed, have been compelled to supply something of his own; and this alone was enough for our Gregory almost to repudiate the offspring.

Let us imagine some celebrated preacher of the divine word who had delivered an elegant discourse on repentance, which a notary had hastily excerpted, and which the preacher later heard after it had been printed and released publicly. He reads it and compares it with the autograph. He observes that the subject of the discourse is the same, its division into various sections the same, its proofs—whether drawn from Sacred Scripture or from reason—the same, and its transitions not dissimilar. Almost everywhere the words are the same, and the manner of speaking nearly identical. Yet in certain places he notices that the discourse has been dislocated and is less coherent. Here an obsolete expression occurs; there he encounters a passage of Sacred Scripture incorrectly explained; elsewhere one of the holy Fathers is praised in place of another; here virtue is depicted in darker colors and with a rougher brush.

These things would certainly be enough for the orator to reject the work as spurious and publicly complain that the discourse he had composed had been corrupted and adulterated.

Gregory speaks in almost the same way about his homilies on the First Book of Kings and on other portions of divine Scripture when they have been taken down less accurately. Let us now see whether the Commentary on the First Book of Kings under discussion exhibits the characteristics and signs that, as we have said, ought to be found in Claudius’s compilation.

### V

Certainly no one who has read this work attentively and compared it especially with the books of the *Moralia* will deny that it breathes Gregory’s style and manner of speech. Since Gussanvillaeus denies this, it must now be demonstrated.

It is characteristic of Gregory to unfold the sentences of Sacred Scripture that he is expounding with remarkable variety, presenting at one moment the literal sense, at another the typological, allegorical, or moral sense. Anyone who does not observe this in the Commentary must be said to be blind.

Indeed, here as in Gregory’s other exegetical treatises, every verse of the sacred book is handled by precisely the same method: it is twisted, turned back, and pressed until absolutely all the nourishment and flavor it contains is extracted.

### VI

As regards diction and the construction of sentences, Gregory delights in a certain inverted arrangement of words, with frequent transpositions and, as it were, hyperbata. We gave many examples in the Preface to the books of the *Moralia*, from which we select a few to present here.

In book XXXI of the *Moralia*, section 4:

> For we know how cruelly that rhinoceros—namely, the earthly ruler—formerly raged against the Lord.

The expected order would be: “For we know with what cruelty that rhinoceros formerly raged,” and so forth.

In Homily 8 on Ezekiel, section 27:

> In which saying it is shown how the mind of blessed Jacob burned with desire for Jesus.

The expected order would be: “In which saying, how the mind of blessed Jacob burned with desire for Jesus is shown.”

In Homily 32 on the Gospels:

> For while it is established that the kingdom of heaven belongs to the reprobate …

The expected order would be: “For while it is established that …”

In book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 2:

> So that they might recognize from how great a perfection Benedict, while still a boy, had begun the grace of his way of life.

The expected order would be: “from how great a perfection Benedict, while still a boy, had begun …”

Who, then, would deny that these examples are entirely similar to what we read in book I of the Commentary, chapter 2, section 10?

> Let us now see with what praises of her fruitfulness holy Church boasts in the voice of Hannah.

Another writer would say: “Let us now see with what praises of her fruitfulness holy Church boasts …”

And in section 12:

> But when strength clothes them, it is pleasant to behold how strong he made them.

It would seem that the sentence ought to say: “But it is pleasant to behold how strong he made them, when …”

See also book V, chapter 2, section 18:

> Gather together how terribly you ought to fear almighty God, and how devoutly you ought always to serve him.

We shall refrain from reporting further examples.

Gregory almost always proceeds in sentences with two members, as it were two feet, ending in corresponding ways. This too can be observed in our commentator on the First Book of Kings by anyone who merely greets his work at the threshold.

### VII

Gregory not infrequently uses deponent verbs—in the terminology of the grammarians—in a passive sense, especially the verb *venerari*, “to be venerated,” as was abundantly demonstrated in the general Preface.

We find the same usage in the Commentary, for example in book IV, chapter 4, section 35:

> The later he is seen—the Shepherd in public—the more devoutly he is venerated;

that is, “he is worshiped and honored.”

And in section 51:

> Therefore they claim that they are endowed with the spirit of wisdom or prophecy, not so that they may be venerated, but so that they may be heard.

The holy Doctor often uses the verb *innotescere* to mean “to make known,” as in Homily 1 on the Gospels, section 1:

> It makes known what blows will precede the approaching end of the world;

that is, “it shows.” The same usage occurs a hundred times in the *Dialogues* and frequently in the Letters.

The author of the Commentary also often uses it in this sense, for example in book I, chapter 2, section 16:

> Which also gives birth to conception when it becomes known to those nearby …

And in chapter 3, section 8:

> For neither Moses nor Elijah could possess this outstanding strength, so that, while incomparable signs were being made known …

See also book II, chapter 2, section 11:

> Yet it then became known that he had blessed his own in this way.

Gregory also uses the verb *debere* in a manner almost peculiar to himself, as the following examples will make clear.

In book XI, letter 33, he writes to Marianus:

> And therefore it seems to me that your Fraternity ought to come to me before the summer season;

that is, “should come.”

In the same letter:

> And I, who see myself close to death, ought to pass into your hands;

that is, “should pass.”

In letter 34 of the same book:

> That is, four hundred solidi ought to have been set aside separately;

and shortly afterward:

> We wish your Fraternity to distribute …

instead of “may distribute.”

In Homily 17 on the Gospels:

> So that they ought to lick from that same rock of salt.

The verb *debere* must be understood in the same sense in book I of the Commentary, chapter 3, section 14:

> Because they had received all the Scriptures, so that they ought to find in them the sacraments of the divine Incarnation;

that is, “so that they might find.”

And in book II, chapter 2, section 20:

> So that they themselves ought to punish no one;

which means the same as “so that they might punish no one.”

Gregory often takes *adversitas* not in a passive but in an active sense, that is, as the action of those who oppose us. On this matter, consult book II of the *Moralia*, section 51, and the note on that passage, where we confirm the point with many testimonies.

One might also have added what we read in book III of the *Pastoral Rule*, admonition 16, or chapter 15:

> What are meant by the clouds moved by the wind, unless the adversities of wicked people?

That is, “the attacks and assaults of wicked people who oppose us.”

The same meaning occurs in book V of the Commentary, chapter 1, section 15:

> Because our holy preachers are crowned with a greater victory when they endure the adversities of their neighbors;

that is, “the adversities inflicted by their neighbors.”

Those accustomed to Gregory’s style know how frequently, when speaking of Christ, he uses the antithesis of the adverbs *super* and *inter*, “above” and “among,” as in book XV of the *Moralia*, section 20:

> The Only-Begotten of the Most High Father, since he is God above all things, became man among all things.

Similar examples occur in book XVI, section 37; Homily 7 on Ezekiel, section 19; Homily 23 on the Gospels; and elsewhere.

In the same way the author of the Commentary writes in book I, chapter 1, section 4:

> Because, he says, he who was born among all things shone above all things.

I shall refrain from adducing other examples.

Those who are not strangers to turning over and reading Gregory’s works know that the verb *reformare* frequently occurs there with a meaning almost unknown to other writers, or at least used by very few.

In book XXII of the *Moralia*, chapter and section 1:

> Lest the mind fall into despair, he restores it to hope through the remembrance of its virtues.

And in section 9 of the same book:

> He restores to him the understanding that he had lost.

The same meaning occurs almost twice at the very beginning of the *Moralia*, and in book II on Ezekiel, Homily 7, at the end:

> He restores the soul to hope.

In the Commentary, not far from the beginning—namely, book I, chapter 1, section 20—we read:

> For he arose because he restored his spirit to the urgency of preaching.

In Gregory’s writings, especially in the *Dialogues*, one reads to the point of weariness: “the habit of a holy way of life.” The writer of the Commentary likewise makes this expression familiar. Read especially book IV, chapter 4, section 18.

### VIII

Gregory commonly designates the author of the Book of Ecclesiasticus by the name “a certain wise man,” as in book XXVII of the *Moralia*, section 53:

> Through a certain wise man it is said: “Like ice in clear weather …”

And in book XXXIII, section 23:

> Hence it is said through a certain wise man: “Do not say, ‘The Lord’s mercies are many.’”

See also book VII, section 45, and book XX, section 51.

In precisely the same way, the commentator and interpreter of the First Book of Kings, in book V, chapter 4, section 2, praising Ecclesiasticus chapter 2, says:

> Hence it is rightly said through a certain wise man: “My son, when you approach the service …”

Finally, Saint Gregory is accustomed to quote entire words and sentences from the Rule of Saint Benedict, as we demonstrated in book I of his *Life*, chapter 3, section 6. We shall immediately show that this also applies to the author of the Commentary.

### IX

As regards doctrine, it is almost the same as Gregory’s own.

[Note: [Col. 0011] The general Preface demonstrated that all these doctrinal points are supported in Gregory’s works.]

The divinity of Christ is strongly asserted in book I, chapter 3, sections 4, 5, and following. The mystery of the Incarnation is excellently explained in book I, chapter 1, section 3.

For the real presence of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist, the unbloody sacrifice of the New Law, and the priesthood of the Christian religion, read book II, chapter 1, section 14, and book III, chapter 4, section 31.

For the vision of God granted only to the citizens of heaven—a point Saint Gregory often proves—see book I, chapter 1, section 4.

For Penance, confession of sins, satisfaction, and priestly absolution, consult book III, chapter 5, sections 13 and 14.

Following Gregory’s practice, the author of book IV, chapter 4, section 13, combines the three holy women into one Mary Magdalene.

What Gregory asserts concerning Christ alone, namely, that among human beings he was free from the devil’s servitude, this writer teaches in book III, chapter 5, section 9:

> What, then, is the hand of the Philistines, unless it is that power of the demons by which they lead souls dead in sin to eternal punishments? From this hand of the Philistines alone he had been free who said: “The prince of this world is coming, and in me, etc.”

[Col. 0013]

These points seem almost to demonstrate that the author of the Commentary under discussion was none other than Gregory himself. Nevertheless, certain features occur, whether in style of expression or in doctrine, that do not at all resemble Gregory and indicate otherwise.

### X

1. The preface of the Commentary departs from Gregorian simplicity; for it seems swollen with figures and excessively luxuriant.

2. The Commentary itself is sprinkled with certain words that occur nowhere in the genuine works of the holy Doctor, such as:

- *terrenitas*, “earthliness,” book II, chapter 2, section 27;
- *sonoritas praedicationis*, “the sonority of preaching,” book IV, chapter 4, section 27;
- *carnalitas*, “carnality,” book IV, chapter 5, section 40, and book V, chapter 4, section 14;
- *horribilitas*, “horribleness,” book III, chapter 5, section 9;
- *vaneglorius*, “vain-glorious,” book V, chapter 4, section 8;
- *granditudo*, “greatness,” book VI, chapter 2, section 25.

3. Most important, the author of the Commentary sometimes seems to depart from Gregory’s doctrine, especially concerning free will, to which he attributes too much.

As though only the beginnings of faith and holiness came from God and the rest from us, he says in book III, chapter 5, section 20:

> Because good desires are supplied to us through divine grace; but we advance the gifts of grace toward victories in virtue through the exertion of free will.

Yet he is not consistent with himself. For in book IV, chapter 2, section 9, moving toward the opposite extreme, he teaches that sinners are sometimes unable to rise from sin even when they wish to do so:

> Because, through imitation of the Shepherd, the reprobate fall into the servitude of sin, and even when they wish to do so they cannot be released from its yoke.

He confirms this somewhat farther below, in section 10:

> You gradually descend into knowledge of the evil imitation; but you cannot at all freely abandon the examples of its wickedness to which you freely submit yourselves. For everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin [John 8:35]. Therefore those whom sins rule by their own power cannot free themselves from their yoke. For they often come to the Lord with prayers; they ask to be freed, but they cannot be heard. For divine judgment deals with them in such a way that those who, when they could, did not wish to avoid evil cannot avoid it when they wish to do so; and those who freely rush into foreknown evils cannot flee from evils once experienced.

He speaks no less harshly in book VI, chapter 2, section 5, although we cannot deny that the same words are found in part III, chapter 15, or admonition 16, of the *Pastoral Rule*.

They can indeed be explained in an entirely sound sense as referring to sinners who, bound by an evil habit, can scarcely break its chains even if they profess that they wish to do so.

Furthermore, in book II, chapter 1, section 6, he seems to grant the saints after death only rest and security, not glory. This conflicts with Gregory, especially *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 25.

Among the blemishes of this Commentary one may note the teaching found in book V, chapter 2, section 15, and elsewhere, that formerly—that is, under the ancient law—it was not only lawful but commanded to hate one’s enemies.

He does not understand this of certain peoples whom God had commanded to be destroyed because of idolatry and other crimes, but of any enemies whatsoever. He wrongly interprets Christ’s words:

> It was said to the ancients, “You shall love … and you shall hate your enemy” [Matthew 5:27].

Christ’s words do not refer to a commandment of the old law, but to a false interpretation of the law devised by the teachers of the Jews, who were corrupting the word of God.

Therefore, although it may seem necessary to admit that the Commentary under discussion is Gregory’s work, it must nevertheless not be denied that it was interpolated by Claudius, his disciple, and corrupted in certain respects. Nor was it subsequently corrected by the holy Doctor, who certainly would not have left these blemishes untouched.

Certainly, after the above-mentioned letter had been written—book XII, letter 24—Gregory, afflicted by so many illnesses and distracted and tormented by so many cares, scarcely had the leisure to examine a work of such magnitude and bring it back to the anvil. Hence his decision was to bury it in perpetual darkness.

Nor should it for that reason be despised. If it is cleansed of the few blemishes we have indicated, it will be able to compete in excellence with the finest works of so great a master.

### XI

“Why, then,” you will ask, “did its first author consider rejecting it, and oppose its being brought into public view as far as he could?”

We reply that its interpolation itself provided sufficient reason for rejecting it. The principal explanation, however, must be sought in Gregory’s profound modesty and humility of spirit. These were so great that he could scarcely bear his works, whatever they might be, to be read and published.

On this matter the letter mentioned above should be read in full.

Certainly, in the *Life of Publius Vergilius Maro* by Tiberius Donatus, we read that when the poet felt himself weighed down by illness, he repeatedly and urgently asked for his writing chests, intending to burn the *Aeneid*. When this request was refused, he ordered in his will that it be burned as an uncorrected and unfinished work.

Would anyone therefore think so poorly of the *Aeneid* as to judge that it ought to be committed to the flames? The same must be said of our Commentary.

Let this, then, be our judgment concerning the work.

We hold that it arose from homilies delivered by Saint Gregory on the First Book of Kings and collected by Claudius, his disciple, and that it was published with some blemishes, attributable chiefly to lapses of memory.

Now we must report, in all fairness, the devices by which Father Gussanvillaeus attempts to overthrow this opinion.

### XII

1. Gregory, who frequently identifies his genuine works, is everywhere silent about this one.

2. There is profound silence concerning it among all writers, whether contemporaries, near-contemporaries, or even those of a much later age.

Yet Gregory clearly speaks, at the place already cited, of homilies delivered by him, taken down by Claudius, and later arranged in the form of a Commentary.

Nor is it surprising that those who in some fashion wove together bundles of Gregory’s sentences—Paterius, Tajus, Alulfus, or those who reviewed the holy Doctor’s works—did not remember this Commentary.

First, copies of it were always exceedingly rare and therefore less well known. Gussanvillaeus himself admits that he made every effort, but in vain, to find a copy in France, Belgium, England, Rome, Venice—where nevertheless he thinks it was first printed in 1537—and Strasbourg, where, according to Gesner’s testimony in the *Bibliotheca*, it appeared together with the *Pastoral Rule* in 1496.

Second, even if some of the writers mentioned possessed a copy, they may have wished to comply with Gregory, who did not approve it, and therefore judged that nothing should be excerpted from it and that it should be omitted from the catalogue of Gregory’s works.

Nevertheless, Ratherius, a monk of Lobbes and later bishop of Verona, who flourished around the year 928, quotes something from this Commentary while writing *On Contempt of the Canons* (*Spicilegium Acherianum*, volume II, part I, shortly before the end), in these words:

> Let us hear Gregory: “The cause of the ruin of the people is bad priests.”

These words are found in book II, chapter 2, at the verse:

> And he said to them: “Why are you doing such a thing?”

We must not conceal the fact that almost the same words occur in part I, chapter 2, of the *Pastoral Rule*. But in place of “the cause of ruin,” and so forth, the *Pastoral Rule* has “the snare of ruin.” From this it is clear that Ratherius was attending to the earlier passage rather than the later one.

There is no doubt that if it were possible to search diligently through the shelves of all libraries and read unpublished books, many other testimonies concerning this Commentary would be available to us.

Gussanvillaeus also insists that the *Exposition on the Song of Songs*, attributed to Gregory, was passed over in silence by all writers and especially by Paterius. Yet in the genuine and uncorrupted Paterius whom we shall publish, there is an important passage from this *Exposition*, as we shall at some point demonstrate in the notice [see below].

But let us proceed with the refutation of Gussanvillaeus’s objections.

### XIII

The learned man maintains that the author of the Commentary uses the Vulgate version of Sacred Scripture, whereas Gregory uses the Italic and Hieronymian versions; and he believes that this is sufficient to establish the distinction between the two writers.

Unfortunately, this method of proof failed the otherwise learned man. For he says that the holy Doctor quoted the following testimony only four times, in book I of Kings, chapter 15:

> “Were you not, when you were little …”

But it is found in none of the places assigned by Gussanvillaeus.

Moreover, only one’s eyes are needed to understand that our writer did not always use the Vulgate version; indeed, he departs from it very frequently.

At the very beginning we read:

> There was a certain man from Ramatha.

The Vulgate has *from Ramathaim*.

The Commentary has:

> Son of Jeroboam.

The Vulgate has:

> Son of Jeroam.

The Commentary has:

> Sons of Thau.

The Vulgate has:

> Sons of Tohu.

In the Commentary, verse 4 reads:

> And he gave Phenenna and her sons and daughters …

The Vulgate has:

> And he gave Phenenna his wife and all her sons and daughters portions.

It seems unnecessary to pursue the remaining examples.

From Habakkuk, chapter 3, the following is quoted in the Commentary, book I, chapter 3, section 4:

> Lord God, my strength, establish my feet in completion, and set me upon the heights, so that I may conquer in his glory.

This differs entirely from the Vulgate version.

Further below, many passages from Psalm 97 are quoted in a form wholly different from that in which they are read in the Vulgate.

In book I, chapter 1, section 10, Psalm 85 is quoted:

> And they shall worship before you, Lord, and they shall honor your name.

The Vulgate has:

> And they shall glorify your name.

In chapter 2, section 47, instead of:

> And my cup is intoxicating,

which is found in Psalm 22 of the Vulgate, there appears:

> And my intoxicating cup.

But in so clear a matter we would waste time by lingering.

I do not, however, deny that certain passages from Sacred Scripture are read here differently from the way they are found in Gregory’s other works.

Claudius, taking these materials down hurriedly, could not reproduce them with such fidelity that he would not err by even a single syllable in presenting the testimonies of Scripture.

On the other hand, we have observed many passages in this Commentary that have been transmitted differently from the way they ought to be read. This may perhaps have moved Saint Gregory to reject the work as adulterated.

It is worthwhile to point these passages out here, lest they provide an occasion for error.

At the end of book I, chapter 1, verse 28 of chapter I of the First Book of Kings is read:

> I commended him to the Lord;

but it should read:

> I lent him to the Lord.

In book II, chapter 4, this verse from chapter III is quoted:

> His eyes—those of Eli—had grown dim, and he could not see. The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel …

It is corruptly presented as:

> He could not see the lamp of God before it went out.

No version supports this reading. Nevertheless, Bede, Rabanus Maurus, Angelomus, and the false Eucherius read it in this way, perhaps carried away by Gregory’s authority because they had seen his name prefixed to this Commentary.

This is indeed a very strong argument that these writers knew the work. For from what earlier writer could they have derived this defective reading of Scripture?

In book V, column 306, we read:

> Thus he appeared to the post;

where it should read, as in the Vulgate:

> Both of them appeared to the post.

But this is a fault of the copyists, not of the author. For in explaining this verse he says:

> What does it mean that Jonathan is said to appear to the Philistines with his armor-bearer?

Therefore he read:

> Both of them appeared.

Further below, too, we read:

> Thus both of them appeared …

Let us proceed with the remaining objections of Gussanvillaeus.

### XIV

“Nor,” he says, “does the style itself have a Gregorian character, although in certain respects the author tried to imitate it; and this perhaps provided the occasion for the error.”

But how different it is from Gregory’s style will be demonstrated by reading the *Homilies on Ezekiel* alone. The proof is brief indeed, but weak, since it rests solely on the opponent’s testimony, unsupported by any examples—especially if the passages we have produced to the contrary are read again.

“But what more is there to say?” Gussanvillaeus asks. “If the author’s words are carefully weighed, it will appear clearer than daylight that he was some monk, since he frequently speaks about monks and the governance and discipline of monasteries.” He proves this with several arguments.

### XV

We willingly concede the force of these arguments. But what do they establish against the opinion we defend?

Does Gussanvillaeus deny that Gregory was a monk and abbot of monks, and therefore that it was incumbent upon him frequently to speak about monastic discipline?

If what this writer says about the monastic life is compared with the Rule of Saint Benedict, there will scarcely be room for doubt that he was devoted to observing that Rule.

For in column 78 we read:

> With the fervor of a novice,

which is found in chapter 1 of Saint Benedict’s Rule.

Near the beginning of column 93 appears:

> In the evil of disobedience, death prevailed;

words that allude to the following in chapter 2 of the Rule of Saint Benedict:

> Then at last the punishment for the disobedient shall be death itself prevailing over them.

In column 95, while discussing obedience, the author seems to have before his eyes what Saint Benedict teaches about that virtue both in chapter 5 of the Rule and in chapter 7.

In book IV, chapter 4, section 17, we read:

> Let them not readily impose the most narrow path of the way of life upon those who are newly approaching it;

words drawn almost verbatim from chapter 58 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Indeed, there can be no doubt that Saint Benedict is being praised when he says:

> Therefore the excellent teacher of that same most narrow life, an instructed disciple of the highest truth, commands, saying: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God.” And again: “Let hard and difficult things be announced to him, by which one goes to God, so that he may know what he is entering.”

Almost the same words appear in chapter 58 of the Rule.

From these considerations there also arises a substantial conjecture: Gregory did not deliver homilies on the books of Kings to the people, as Gussanvillaeus gratuitously imagines, but to the monks subject to him, and only during the period when, after returning from the royal city, he enjoyed greater leisure in the monastery. His son, or rather his foster son and disciple, Claudius, took care to record them.

### XVI

The controversy concerning the author of the Commentary having been settled, a few points concerning the work itself remain to be observed.

That it is mutilated, at least in some small degree, is clear from the fact that in book I, chapter 2, section 3, the writer mentions an explanation of the name “Helcana” given above, although no such explanation is found anywhere.

We suspect that a lacuna lies between sections 4 and 8 of chapter 1 of book I. There the text passes from the explanation of the words:

> From Ramatha Sophim, from Mount Ephraim,

to the following:

> He had two wives;

with the intervening material omitted, including:

> And his name was Helcana, son of Jeroboam, son of Heliu, son of Thau, son of Sup.

Not the slightest trace of these matters is found in the Commentary.

Many passages concerning Hebrew names occur that could have been illustrated with notes. But the material that suggested itself for discussion could scarcely have been contained within the limits prescribed for these notes.

Moreover, those who wish to be instructed about such matters will never read this Commentary; they will consult Origen and Jerome instead, especially their books on Hebrew names and on the locations and names of Hebrew places.

For the rest, in speaking of Jerome in note b to the preface, column 2, we carelessly let slip what we said about a Book of Samuel expounded by him. For those among our own scholars who are diligently laboring to publish the works of this holy Doctor deny that the *Exposition of the Book of Samuel* belongs to Jerome.

But this had not yet been published when we arranged our materials for the new edition of Gregory’s works.

### XVII

What has been contributed by our work in this edition must now be briefly explained. Since it was not possible for us to obtain a manuscript copy of any codex containing this Commentary, despite applying every diligence, we have reviewed it against the better editions, especially the Gilotian and Vatican editions. With their help we have removed not a few errors and restored some omissions. At times, moreover, where all the printed editions were faulty, we did not hesitate to correct them. Thus, in Book I, chapter 1, section 1, the text formerly read: “afflicting this man . . . through the hands of the wicked,” where without doubt it should read “fastening him,” and this is the reading we have adopted. Likewise, in Book II, chapter 1, section 2, the text formerly read, “his eyes had clung to his eyes”; but the sequence of the discourse shows that *osculis* (“kisses”), rather than *oculis* (“eyes”), should be read, as it now is. Whenever, however, we have determined only by conjecture how a corrupt passage ought to be corrected, we have been content to enter in the margin the reading that seemed better to us.

We have also, following our custom, divided the chapters—being rather long—into several sections by adding numbered marks. In the notes placed beneath the page, we have either presented variant readings or illustrated certain passages of the Commentary. May the reader be able to gather and taste the excellent and delightful fruits of our truly arduous labor.

It is unnecessary to say anything here about the exposition of the *Song of Songs*, which will follow this Commentary, or about the other works subsequent to it, since we have prefixed individual prefaces or notices to each. Yet in the preface to the Exposition of the *Song*, the testimony of Saint Columbanus ought not to have been omitted. He lists it among the works of Saint Gregory, together with the *Book of the Pastoral Rule* and the Homilies on Ezekiel, as may be seen in Columbanus’s letter included among the Gregorian letters (Book IX, final letter).

[Col. 0017]

## THE SIX BOOKS OF VARIOUS EXPOSITIONS BY SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT, ROMAN PONTIFF, ON THE FIRST BOOK OF KINGS, ALSO CALLED SAMUEL (C, G, S)*

### Prologue

[Col. 0017A] 1 After the books of Moses and Joshua son of Nun, and Judges, [Note: [Col. 0017C] The First Book of Kings, or Samuel, is the ninth book in the canon if the book of Ruth is distinguished from the Book of Judges. But if the history of Ruth is regarded as an appendix to the Book of Judges, it is the eighth.] the First Book of Kings appears as the eighth or ninth book in the canon of the Holy Scriptures. Yet because this book, like most of the volumes of sacred discourse, has not so far been expounded by the teachers of the holy Church, some of the simpler-minded suppose that it is not mystical and that the Spirit says nothing more elevated in it because it appears to narrate things more plainly according to the letter. But if they were to read what the holy teachers have said in other books of exposition, they would discover how immense is the depth of this history also. For very often, in their expositions, what is said here plainly according to the letter is shown to be exceedingly difficult according to spiritual understanding; and they openly imply that they understand much more sublimely what is contained in sacred history than what they read outwardly on its surface. It is plain according to the letter that Elkanah the Ephrathite is described as having had two wives (1 Sam. 1:1–2); that Eli the priest, while weakened by affection and released from the severity of correcting his sons, falls from his seat and dies with his neck broken (ibid. 4:18); and that King Saul refused to obey God in destroying the Amalekites (1 Sam. 15:9), but not long afterward lost both his life and his kingdom (1 Sam. 31:5). But these matters, plain indeed as they seem to the simpler-minded, the holy teachers, in order to grasp their meaning in a way worthy of their sublimity, did not seek their interpretation in the simplicity of the letter, but in the flight of allegory. Hence, when Saint Augustine (City of God, Book XVII, chapter 4) read historically of Elkanah’s two wives, he looked through the level surface of the reading to its spiritual height and explained that one bore the type of the Synagogue, while the other prefigured the holy Church. Saint Jerome likewise (Against the Pelagians, Book I, chapter 8; and Against Jovinian, Book I, chapter 10) understood the deaths of Eli the priest and Saul as placed in sacred history not merely to terrify disobedient rulers by the punishment they suffered, but also to signify, through the rejection of former and transgressing rulers, the destruction of the ancient Law and priesthood. The sacred history of Kings, then, must not be thought empty of spiritual mysteries merely because it has not been expounded sequentially by venerable fathers. Rather, it is all the higher and deeper because, like the vast expanse of an immense river, it could be drawn from in exposition at any small point, and, after filling their vessels, it continues to flow onward through the force of its fullness toward filling others each day. When, therefore, they drew certain things from this sacred history to strengthen their works, but passed over its fullness, hidden in the secrecy of its sublimity, what else did they appear to do than take something from an immeasurable stream to offer to the thirsty minds of the faithful? 3

2. We too follow their practice in the present work. We approach this immense history in order to open its meaning, yet we do not dare undertake to expound it in its entirety. In this, however, we differ from the venerable fathers mentioned above: we do not select and expound scattered passages from different places, as they did, taking up not some portion of this sacred history in sequence but scattered testimonies that they could explain for the instruction of the faithful. [Note: [Col. 0019D] Gilotian edition: “they ought to have had.”] Trusting, therefore, in the help of almighty God, we propose to explain the book from its beginning up to the anointing of King David, so that by this short portion now before us we may discover whether we ought to proceed further in exposition. For many, while making extravagant plans, can never become executors of their own undertaking—especially since an interpreter of sacred discourse resembles a man standing on a high watchtower, while sacred Scripture resembles a vast forest. A man situated on high, even if he surveys the immensity of the woodland with keen vision, sees the mountain summits, the ends of the hills, and the tall trees that appear to meet one another at a certain level, but does not notice how great the valleys and how broad the plains lie hidden in between. Yet if he begins to walk through what seemed to him a short distance, he suddenly realizes that, although he thought he had seen everything, very much remains that he had not seen. Hence the overconfident traveler is often deceived, and completes his journey all the more dangerously because, after the day has ended on the road, the darkness of night overtakes him—although he had imagined that he would cover even part of the day’s journey within what seemed a short stretch.

Thus, while we contemplate the meaning of sacred history at a certain summit of its senses, by the grace of almighty God we observe, as it were from a height, the lofty crowns of a dark forest. But when those same meanings begin to be examined and unfolded more subtly, they generate others in ever greater number. Thus, beneath the whole forest that appears to have been surveyed at the surface, the hollows of valleys and the expanses of Mount Matinus lie concealed and unseen. [Note: [Col. 0019D] Mount Matinus is in Calabria. Horace, *Epode* 16:

[Col. 0020D] “. . . when

the Po shall wash the peaks of Matinus.”]

We therefore proceed more safely if we measure what we see in such a way that we also reckon that we must traverse what we shall see as we advance. Accordingly, while proposing to explain a small part of this immense history, we bring the course of our journey to an end nearby, within the limits of our weakness—distrusting the slenderness of our talent no less than we are frightened by the depth of the sacred volume.

3. First of all, however, I have thought it necessary not so much to instruct as to implore the reader not to measure the weight of sacred history by the emptiness of my exposition, because divine utterances must never be assessed according to the abilities of their interpreters. They are not to be despised merely because they are not examined subtly; nor are they lofty and venerable merely because they are expounded eloquently and with subtlety. For there is one kind of excellence that is held in such esteem among the wise of this world as far as distinguished minds are able to exalt it. Sacred Scripture, however, because it is divinely inspired, surpasses even the distinguished talents of human beings by as much as distinguished human beings are inferior to God; and in its spiritual sublimity they perceive nothing except what is revealed to them by the goodness of the divine condescension itself.

Let no one, therefore, be so perfect in its knowledge that he cannot progress further, because every human advance remains beneath the height of the divinity that inspires it. Hence the Psalmist says of the Lord: “He covers his upper regions with waters” (Ps. 103:3). For if, under the name of “waters,” those profound heavenly understandings of the angels are signified, and God is said to cover the height of sacred discourse with waters, it is plainly established that a human being is always inferior to that reality whose lower regions alone are revealed to him. For this reason Moses also commands that whatever remains of the lamb be burned with fire (Exod. 12:10), because the sacred Scriptures, which were given so that the Redeemer might be known, are to be revered on account of their sublimity even when they are not understood.

Thus, even if nothing I say is valued, it must nevertheless be valued that this sacred Scripture, which is unworthily expounded by me, speaks many good and sublime things to the one to whom almighty God chooses to disclose its secrets. Sacred Scripture was so wonderfully fashioned by almighty God that, although it may appear to have been expounded in many ways, it nevertheless possesses secrets by which it preserves what is hidden; for it is almost never expounded in such a way that more does not remain for daily exposition. Through this incomprehensibility, almighty God has, in his great providence, taken account of human mutability. For, so that what is known may not become cheap, Scripture has been arranged so wonderfully that it is known without being exhausted, and is read with greater delight the more it is learned each day; while it continually reveals new things, it gives sweeter pleasure.

4. The history of Kings, therefore, since it was composed by the same Spirit by whom the other volumes of Holy Scripture are known to have been composed, must not be thought inferior in mysteries to those books to which it is not inferior in the authority of its title. All its writers are reported to have been prophets; when they recount historical events, they signify spiritual realities; they speak of outward things and intimate inward ones; they set forth earthly matters in order to accomplish heavenly purposes. Hence the First and Second Books of this same history are attributed to the prophet Samuel, so that from the title of the author it may be understood that the history he writes is not so much history as prophecy: its letter is simple and true, yet exceedingly lofty and deep because of the multiplicity of its hidden meanings.

We, however, take from such great weight only what we can bear according to the measure of our smallness. For although it is pleasant on the surface of the letter, higher in the allegory of its types, useful for instructing morals, and clear in the examples it presents, I decline, in each individual passage, both to assert the historical meaning, to unfold the typological meaning, to apply the moral meaning, and to set forth examples—although, with the Lord’s help, I shall expound some passages under one meaning and others under several.

[Col. 0020D] This is especially so because I have decided to devote myself to writing in these times, when, as the minds of certain ecclesiastical men are sunk in the old preoccupation with worldly aims, they judge new studies of writing to be superfluous precisely because they do not fail to recognize that the old works of venerable teachers abound. They would indeed be refuted by reason, unless they openly displayed the mark of slander on their faces. For those who despise new works as new, why do they disdain the old works they approve, being sated with worldly cares? Scripture aptly describes many of them under a single designation when it says: “A sated soul tramples the honeycomb” (Prov. 27:7). The honeycomb contains new honey. It is as though Scripture said: “When one is fed too immoderately on concern for earthly things, one does not rejoice in the fresh sweetness of the Scriptures, which ordinarily gives great pleasure.”

But since they find no old commentaries on this sacred history, they act more rightly if they embrace the work of our labor with the same charity with which it is offered for the benefit of the little ones of the holy Church, and if, instead of the annoyance of criticism, they offer the support of their prayers to us who labor in the profound depths of Scripture as in a most high sea. In this way they make the fruit of our sweat their own: by loving us out of kindness, they turn it to an increase of their eternal reward. They also make their own the fact that, after so many ages, this Scripture—so closed and unexplained—is brought to the common understanding, and that the little ones of the holy Church, while receiving the splendor of the new religion within the coverings of the Old Scripture, are assisted in the advancement of their devotion.

5. But because different testimonies concerning this history are found expounded in the various works of the holy Fathers, the reader should note that sometimes I follow their interpretations in my exposition, while at other times I labor to unravel the history in another way. Thus the work I undertake in the hope of divine inspiration may be strengthened by the authority of the ancient Fathers and may not be tedious to the reader, since, among the old things he knows, it presents him also with new things he does not know.

I am sometimes driven necessarily to this statement of interpretations, because if the venerable Fathers had explained in sequence everything they touched upon in part, they could not possibly have maintained the same sequence of discourse that they appear to have followed. When, therefore, I pass over the interpretations of the holy Fathers, I do so sometimes from necessity and sometimes for convenience: I remove tediousness from the reader, and, when I examine everything in sequence, many matters arise from the intervening passages that do not permit me to follow their interpretations.

In this work I earnestly ask the reader not to judge the words by comparison with the eloquence of the Church’s learned orators, but to weigh the meaning of the interpretations according to the principles of ecclesiastical discipline. For although, in accordance with God’s prohibition, I do not know how to plant a grove in his house (Deut. 16:21), I do not in any respect abandon the rule by which Holy Scripture is faithfully expounded.

[Col. 0022A] Yet wherever the learned reader finds something less pleasing, let him consider that, while I—a foreign sailor—undertake a spiritual history deep with lofty meanings, as though I were facing the storms of a great sea, it is hardly blameworthy if the helm of my speech is not guided beautifully when the foaming crests of the waves rush upon me, often forcing even the most skillful pilot to release the tiller.

Likewise, a devoted farmer entering a wooded field does not lay out straight lines for his furrows if he has not first repeatedly cut through it by turning back the plowshare; for ease never follows a skill if no habit of cultivation appears to have preceded that same expertise in plowing. Nor should anyone judge the plainness of the history by this standard. Often we reach the secrets of spiritual meanings with greater difficulty the farther away we see the entrance to those secrets situated in the plainer letter; and we are unable to touch its heights precisely because the step from which we think to touch them is lower.

For what is the understanding of divinity but a certain ineffable summit of loftiness? And since almighty God is recognized through the Scriptures, what is that same sacred Scripture but a kind of step that one climbs in order to reach that sublimity? Whenever, then, the history is plainer but its meaning is higher, what else does this signify but that this sublimity has a step from which it cannot easily be reached? If, therefore, the reader notices something unbecoming even in the explanation of the plainer history, he may grant pardon all the more readily insofar as he recognizes with greater reason that, while we do not advance beyond what is plainly visible toward those sublime things, we easily falter.

[Col. 0022C] I therefore explain the earlier parts of the book individually under both meanings, since they contain both the mysteries of the holy Church and the conduct of the elect person devoted to the pursuit of a good life. In this way, when we recognize the principles of the new faith in the actions of the ancients, we may also derive from them the edification of our own conduct. And because, in the salvation of the faithful, faith precedes works, we first set forth the typological meaning as a solid foundation, upon which the structure of the entire work undertaken may be placed or which may be followed by the moral or historical exposition.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0021]

### 5. CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0021D]

**(1 Sam. 1:1.)** There was a certain man from Ramatha Sophim, from the hill country of Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, son of Jeroboam, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephrathite.

1. Whom, then, does this man signify for us if not our Lord and Redeemer, who appeared in the weakness of our flesh yet did not subject that same weakness of the nature he assumed to the allurements of a more indulgent life? A man (*vir*) is so called from strength (*virtus*). But the human being created in paradise waged war with the apostate angel, yet did not take care to resist him through the strength conditionally granted to him. He was created strong, but was feebly subjected to the enemy; he was not a man by his own encounter, but by gift. Thus he was made strong in such a way that, once human nature had been condemned, it could not prevail against its victorious enemy unless the One who existed above human beings assumed it.

Our Creator, therefore, became our combatant. Whether he was a man is known if he is considered through the strength he displayed. He assumed our nature, and when it conquered in him, it restored the nobility with which it had been created; what had been made strong yet weak in Adam became weak yet strong in the Redeemer (Matt. 4). While he was fasting, the tempter came to him in the desert, renewed the weapons of his ancient victory, and hurled darts of gluttony, exaltation, and pride against him; but he found him resisting him in every respect.

The man, therefore, was manifested through victory: he overcame the apostate angel, already a strong victor, yet displayed to him not the power of his divinity but the weakness of his humanity. The prophet Jeremiah, contemplating this man, says: “A woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). Zechariah points him out, saying: “Behold the man: ‘The East’ is his name” (Zech. 6:12). Blessed Peter the apostle, preaching him to the Jews, says: “Jesus the Nazarene, a man approved by God among you through mighty deeds, wonders, and signs—him, delivered up according to the predetermined plan and foreknowledge of God, you fastened to the cross by the hands of the wicked and killed” (Acts 2:22–23). Hence Cleopas, speaking with the same Redeemer on the road, says: “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet, mighty in deed and word” (Luke 24:19).

He was a man who, in this world, expelled the ancient enemy from the Church and, dying, bound him in hell. And because the One who by dying weakened the powers of hell opened for us, by rising again, the way to eternity, he showed us the greatness of his power not only by living but also by dying and rising again. Since, therefore, our Redeemer is known to have performed great works of power through the humanity he assumed, the one who signifies him in type is rightly said to have been a man.

2. But we must ask why he is called “one man.” For if this “one” refers to number, it seems superfluous: each person is one and not two. Nor can we suppose that holy Samuel, who wrote these things, began pointlessly in opposition to the custom of the writers of the holy Church. When the writer of the Book of Job introduced the life of blessed Job as an example for the faithful, he began as follows: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job” (Job 1:1). Likewise, when the Evangelist Luke proclaimed at the beginning of his Gospel the praises of the righteous priest, he said: “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a priest named Zechariah” (Luke 1:5). The former did not say, “There was one man,” nor did the Evangelist say, “There was one priest.”

What, then, does it mean that the chosen prophet, contrary to the practice of writers, began with such an opening? Because he was not only a writer but also a prophet, he knew of whom the history spoke; and he knew whom the person spoken of historically signified. What the history narrates here contrary to ordinary historical usage, it expresses, in accordance with the practice of catholic faith, in the understanding of allegory. Hence, through this new manner of expression, the whole Church confesses together that Christ is one God and man. It therefore says: “There was one man,” because it was speaking of the God-man, affirming his divinity and humanity and showing more openly that there is not one person for the Word who assumes and another for the man who is assumed, but one and the same person of God and man. This unity may, however, appropriately be referred to the excellence of his dignity. For although the holy Church has had no other Redeemer, it has had certain men distinguished by the display of virtue. When he is therefore called “one,” he is shown to be incomparable.

3. He had no equal: by an excellent life and word he provided for the human race, and by a singular gift he was able to bestow the gifts of Redemption. Hence Paul says: “Receiving the abundance of grace, gift, and righteousness, they will reign in life through the one Jesus Christ” (Rom. 5:17). Rebuking the Jews with reference to the dignity of his excellence, he says: “If I had not done among them the works that no one else has done, they would not have sin” (John 15:24). The Psalmist, contemplating the excellence of his beauty, said: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips” (Ps. 44:3). Isaiah, bearing witness to the singular good of Redemption in him, says: “Truly he himself bore our sicknesses, and he carried our iniquities” (Isa. 53:4). The eternal Father likewise displayed his singular dignity, crying out from magnificent glory: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17; 17:5; 1 Pet. 2:17).

He was the one man of whom Peter confessed: “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). Paul asserts the greatness of his excellence, saying: “The Lord exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2:9). And because the excellence of his virtue surpasses not only elect human beings but also all the blessed angels, Paul, preaching him to the Hebrews, says: “Since he is the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his substance, and sustains all things by the word of his power, having made purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having become as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’? And again: ‘I will be his Father, and he will be my Son’?” (Heb. 1:3–5). He is rightly called “one man,” then, because no one can be compared with him. But now that we have recognized how great he is, let us hear where he was from.

4. **From Ramathaim-zophim, from the hill country of Ephraim.** Ramatha, Sophim, and Ephraim are Hebrew names. The first, in our language, means “completed vision”; the second, “watchtower”; and the third, “fruitful” or “bearing fruit.”

What is “completed vision” if not the perfect knowledge of almighty God? The teacher of the Gentiles indicates this completed vision when he says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, just as I also have been fully known” (1 Cor. 13:12). And what is meant by “watchtower” if not the sublimity of the angels? A watchtower is chosen on high for clearer vision. Ramatha Sophim is therefore rightly named, because the perfect knowledge of our Creator can be possessed only by those blessed citizens who dwell in that heavenly sublimity. The radiance of eternal light in its fullness is seen not in the lowliness of our present exile but from the state of eternal exaltation.

Hence Ramatha Sophim is rightly said to be situated on Mount Ephraim. For what is Mount Ephraim if not heaven? It is a fruitful mountain, continually producing the flowers of eternal beauty and the fruits of unfailing joy. Ramathaim and Zophim are rightly said to be situated on Mount Ephraim, because that eternal vision of almighty God and that height of the blessed citizens are not possessed on earth but in heaven.

Indicating that he is from Ramatha, he says: “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father” (John 10:15). Again he says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27; Luke 10:22). He was from the watchtower—that is, from the heights—when, rebuking the Jews, he said: “You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world” (John 8:23). He was from Mount Ephraim when he said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51). John the Baptist, affirming that he was from Mount Ephraim, says: “He who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3:31). Hence the Psalmist says: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven” (Ps. 18:7). Hence the teacher of the Gentiles says: “The second man is from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47).

The man, therefore, who is said to have been one is declared to have come from Ramatha Sophim, from the hill country of Ephraim, because the one who was born among all others and shone above all appeared so great on earth because he came from heaven. He was from Ramatha Sophim because, although he shone here incomparably, the greatness of his excellence is grasped only where his perfect knowledge is displayed to the eternal citizens.

Here he had been seen in the excellence of his virtue, when someone said: “What we have seen and heard, and our hands have touched, concerning the word of life” (1 John 1:1). But because he had not seen the greatness of his excellence, he promises it to us in Ramatha, saying: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

5. The name of this mountain can also signify the ever-blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God. She was indeed a mountain, because by the dignity of her election she surpassed the height of every chosen creature. Is Mary not a lofty mountain? In order to reach the conception of the eternal Word, she raised the summit of her merits above all the choirs of angels, even to the throne of divinity.

Foretelling the preeminent dignity of this mountain, Isaiah says: “In the last days, the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2). She was a mountain on the summit of the mountains because Mary’s height shone above all the saints. For just as “mountain” signifies height, so “house” signifies habitation. She is appropriately called both mountain and house: having been illumined by incomparable merits, she prepared a sacred womb for the Only-Begotten of God, in which he might recline. Mary would not be a mountain on the summit of the mountains if divine fruitfulness had not raised her above the height of the angels. Nor would she be the house of the Lord if the divinity of the Word had not lain in her womb through the humanity he assumed.

She is rightly called a fruitful mountain, for from her the best fruit—that is, the new human being—is generated. The prophet, looking upon her as beautiful and adorned in the glory of her fruitfulness, says: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1). Rejoicing in God because of the fruit of this mountain, David says: “Let the peoples give you thanks, O God; let all the peoples give you thanks. The earth has yielded its fruit” (Ps. 66:6). The earth yielded its fruit because the Virgin gave birth to him, having conceived not through material action but through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:35).

The Lord says to the same king and prophet: “From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11). Isaiah says: “The fruit of the earth will be exalted” (Isa. 4:2). For the one whom the Virgin bore was not only a holy man but also mighty God. At the greeting of Elizabeth, it is said to the same blessed Virgin concerning this fruit: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42).

Mount Ephraim is therefore rightly named after her, because, as she was raised up by the ineffable dignity of divine generation, in her fruit the withered shoots of human nature bloom again. The man, therefore, came from Ramatha Sophim, from Mount Ephraim, because the one who by the power of his divinity created the angels assumed the form of humanity from the flesh of the exalted Virgin.

And because through the humanity he assumed he wished to be born not from unbelievers but from believers, it follows: “The son of Jeroboam, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph.”

6. Four fathers’ names are given, because when the Lord assumed flesh from the faithful people, he had as fathers in respect of his humanity those whom the glory of an equal number of principal virtues illumined. Hence the divine promise is addressed not to some unbeliever but to faithful Abraham: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Hence the Evangelist Matthew, tracing the order of his generation, says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1). Hence he himself speaks to the Samaritan woman, saying: “Salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22). Hence Paul says: “To them belong the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises; to them belong the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:4–5).

These four names appropriately designate them because they possessed prudence in the knowledge of things; justice, by which they desired to order rightly what they had come to know; fortitude, by which they were able to carry out the good things they desired; and temperance, through which they accomplished everything with discretion.

7. It follows: **An Ephrathite.** But why is he said to be an Ephrathite if he is said to be from Mount Ephraim? The answer is clear according to the letter: someone could be from Mount Ephraim without having been born from the tribe of Ephraim. He is therefore called an Ephrathite so that the one shown by his place of origin may also be recognized by the stock of his descent.

Since Ephrathite means “fruitful,” this is rightly attributed to the person of the Redeemer, who is proclaimed by the prophecy of the Psalmist: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which yields its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1:4). Appearing in the fullness of time determined beforehand, he turned the flowers of heavenly teaching into the fruits of the elect; and all those from the human race whom he joined to himself he brought forth, as it were, as fruits for eternity. In this passage, while the life of the Redeemer is described, the destruction of the devil is also secretly indicated. For he was from Mount Ephraim, yet was not an Ephrathite: he fell from heaven, but the evil tree did not produce good fruit.

**(Verse 2.)** He had two wives: the name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second was Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.

8. What is signified by Peninnah if not the Synagogue? And what is signified by Hannah if not the holy Church? Peninnah is reported to have had children because, when our Redeemer appeared in the flesh, he found, through the Law he had given and through the prophets he had sent, children born in the faith of the Synagogue. Hannah, however, had no children because the holy Church, then newly established and recently joined to her heavenly bridegroom, was not yet giving birth through preaching. Hence the voice of the same bridegroom says to her in the *Song*: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts” (Song 8:8).

Or certainly she is said to have had no children not because of inequality of age but because of the sterility of barrenness. What, then, is Hannah’s barrenness if not the hardening of Judea? Since she could not turn the hard hearts of the Jews to faith in the Redeemer, she was truly barren.

It should be noted, however, that Peninnah, who is said to have given birth first, is called the second wife. The Synagogue first brought forth children in faith, but nevertheless was inferior in dignity to the holy Church. She was therefore the second wife not in the timing of the marital union but in the inequality of privilege.

It follows:

**(Verse 3.)** That man went up from his city on appointed days to worship and to sacrifice to the Lord, the God of hosts, at Shiloh.

9. For what spiritual city of the Redeemer could there have been other than Sacred Scripture? This city, to be sure, bestowed upon its citizens as many defenses as it had precepts, and provided them with as many weapons as it had counsels of salvation. But what did it mean for our Redeemer to ascend, except that, in the form of his humanity, he revealed the heights of his divinity? And because he is recognized in Sacred Scripture, he is rightly said to ascend from his own city. The appointed days are the promises concerning him set forth in the holy Scriptures. They are called days because they shine for the elect so that they may know him. They are also appointed days because we know that they were set down by the ancient Fathers in that same sacred word.

For Moses foreshadowed the day of his ascent when he said: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, and you shall listen to him as to me” (Deut. 18:18). He likewise appointed the day when he said: “The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:10). Appointing the day of this ascent, Micah said: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means the least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall go forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel” (Mic. 5:2). Hence Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14).

For as many promises concerning him as there are in the Law and the Prophets, so many appointed days of his ascent do we contemplate. For he ascended, as it were, on the appointed days when he said to the Jews: “Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life, because they are the ones that bear witness to me” (John 5:39). Again he says: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (ibid., 46). Thus he ascended on the appointed days because, by appearing, he displayed the signs of the promises that he had placed in the holy Scriptures.

The appointed days may also be understood as the promised splendors of miracles at his coming. The prophet Isaiah, observing these appointed days, says: “Say to the fainthearted: ‘Take courage, and do not fear; behold, our God will bring vengeance and recompense; God himself will come and save us.’ Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; then the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be opened” (Isa. 35:4–6).

But since we have recognized the appointed days of the Redeemer’s ascent, let us see whether he ascended on them. When John asked whether they were awaiting him or another, he answered through the disciples whom he sent, saying: “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the poor are evangelized; and blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me” (Luke 7:19). Thus he ascended on the appointed days: in order to drive the darkness of ancient error from the hearts of his elect, he shone forth with the splendors of so many promised miracles.

But he ascended to worship and to sacrifice, because he wished to be known for this purpose: that by dying he might redeem those whom he had taught by living. He worshiped, because, as an example to the elect, he presented himself wholly humble and abject before God the Father through obedience. He sacrificed, because he who had given us examples of humility by living handed himself over to God the Father as an offering and victim upon the altar of the cross, and redeemed by dying those whom he had taught by living. He knew that both were greatly necessary to us, and therefore he did not provide one without the other.

For when he had been born in Bethlehem of Judah, Herod sought him deceitfully in order to kill him (Matt. 2:13). But if the Redeemer had died then, he would indeed have sacrificed and not worshiped: he would have become a victim by dying, but he would not have taught by living those whom he had to free by his death. And if, while teaching us by living, he had refused to die, he would certainly have worshiped and not sacrificed.

Therefore, in order to worship, he fled into Egypt from the king who was persecuting him; and in order to sacrifice, he rebuked Peter when Peter tried to dissuade him, saying: “Get behind me, Satan, for you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men” (Matt. 16:23). Indicating that he would worship, he says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). Again he says: “I always do the things that please him” (John 8:29).

Indicating also that he would sacrifice himself, he says: “For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, and I will take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:17–18). And shortly before: “I am the good shepherd, who lays down my life for my sheep” (ibid., 11). Paul, contemplating his sacrifice, says: “He handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant aroma” (Eph. 5:2).

He therefore ascended to worship and to sacrifice, because he manifested himself through so many miracles for this purpose: to instruct us by words and examples, and by dying to overcome our death.

10. But it should be noted that when the Ephrathite is said to ascend in order to sacrifice, the almighty God to whom he sacrifices is called the God of hosts. Why is this understood to have occurred, except because through the Redeemer’s death not one Jewish people alone but all the nations were being redeemed? For what are the faithful multitudes of the nations except the army of almighty God?

The Psalmist, exhorting these armies to rejoice at the triumph of their king, says: “All you nations, clap your hands; shout to God with a voice of exultation” (Ps. 46). Again, observing them assembling, he said: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, Lord, and shall glorify your name” (Ps. 85:9).

He is therefore called the Lord of hosts because, through the Lord’s death, not only is elect Judea gathered, but all the nations are brought into the service of almighty God. As they lead faithful ranks strengthened with the weapons of the virtues against hidden enemies, they reach the heavenly kingdoms through the glory of triumph.

11. The place of the sacrifice is also specified, since it says: “In Shiloh.” Shiloh is interpreted as “sent” or “mission.” What else is signified by this mission except the command of obedience entrusted by the supreme Father to his only-begotten Son? What else is meant by his being said to sacrifice in Shiloh except that he gave himself to death in no other way than the Father had commanded?

He would not have sacrificed in Shiloh if he had died otherwise than as he had been commanded by the Father. Hence he said through himself: “As the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14:31). Paul says likewise: “He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8).

In Shiloh, therefore, he both worshiped and sacrificed, because both by living and by dying he did the will of his Father.

It continues:

**(Verse 3.)** “There were there two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, priests of the Lord.”

12. Concerning these men it is rightly asked why they are called priests of the Lord, when shortly afterward they are reported to be sons of Belial [Note: [Col. 0029D] In another reading, “are reported.”].

But if this question about the sons of Eli is asked simply according to the literal sense, the answer is easy: they were called priests of the Lord at a time when the priests of idols were designated by the names of false gods. Therefore, when they are called priests of the Lord, they are distinguished from the worshipers of idols by the marks of faith. These words praise their faith, not their life, because they practiced wickedness in their conduct but did not err concerning faith in the Creator.

This, however, may also suitably be applied to the leaders of Judea at the time of the divine Incarnation. They are reported to have been two priests, and this very fact is not related to praise of virtue but to the condemnation of cunning. Hence the Lord himself threatens them, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful outwardly but within are full of the bones of the dead” (Matt. 23:27).

13. But what does it mean that they are said to have been there? If Shiloh—that is, “mission”—signifies the command of the supreme Father, how were the leaders of Judea there, since they did not honor him to whom the command had been entrusted by receiving him, but expelled and killed him?
