Yet they were there because, although they acted savagely in bringing about the Lord’s death, they did not obtain through that savagery what they intended by their violence; rather, they fulfilled the plan of the eternal Father in the death of his only-begotten Son. Their plan was to hand him over to death so that the people might not be able to believe in him. But he who had his persecutors as helpers in carrying out the paternal command entrusted to him rose again after dying, and the whole world believed in him.

The sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were therefore there—that is, in the mission—because our Redeemer, in order to fulfill the will of his Father, had the leaders of the Jews as his supporters, although they themselves did not think that they were supporting the one whom they did not fear to kill.

Hence it continues:

**(Verse 4.)** “The day came, and Elkanah sacrificed, and he gave portions to Peninnah and to her sons and daughters.”

14. What day do we believe this to be except the day that Isaiah established by the testimony of Sacred Scripture, saying: “He shall be led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7) [Note: [Col. 0030D] In another reading: “Before his shearer he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth.”]?

The day came when the brightness of the promised oracle revealed the time of the Lord’s Passion. Then Elkanah sacrificed, because our Redeemer offered himself to the eternal Father in the sacrifice of our absolution through the death of the cross. Then he gave portions to Peninnah and to her sons and daughters, because he brought back to the joys of paradise the elect of Judea whom he found among the dead. Their portions are the gifts of everlasting joys.

Hence the Psalmist, choosing the place of his inheritance, says: “May my portion, Lord, be in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6).

Peninnah and her sons and daughters are rightly named separately in the distribution of the portions. Peninnah signifies the teachers of Judea; her sons signify its stronger hearers, while her daughters designate its weaker subjects. The mother, sons, and daughters are therefore mentioned separately because, on account of the differing merits of the ancient elect, their rewards were not equal.

It continues:

**(Verse 5.)** “But to Hannah he gave one portion, sorrowful, because he loved Hannah.”

15. Why was he not sorrowful when he gave portions to Peninnah, her sons, and her daughters, but is said to have been sorrowful when he gave one portion to Hannah?

What else is Hannah’s one portion except the temporal affliction of the holy Church? He gave her this portion when he said: “Truly, truly, I say to you, you shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice; you shall be sorrowful” (John 16:20). He gave her this portion when he commended Paul to Ananias, saying: “Go, for this man is a chosen vessel for me, to carry my name before the nations, and kings, and the children of Israel. For I shall show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts 9:15–16).

Hence that same teacher of the nations glories in receiving this portion, saying: “I complete in my body what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ” (Col. 1:24). Again he says: “I bear the marks of Jesus in my body” (Gal. 6:17). He also says: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (ibid., 14).

He had received one portion from the Bridegroom who had determined to glory in the cross alone. Therefore, when Elkanah gave portions to Peninnah, he was not sorrowful, because our Redeemer, after the triumph of death, joyfully restored the elect of the synagogue to the joys of paradise. But he gave Hannah her portion sorrowfully, because he could not fail to suffer with her, whom he was leaving as the companion of his death and heir of the cross. Hence, when Stephen was suffering, Jesus is reported to have stood with the heavens opened (Acts 7:55). His standing means that he shared in Stephen’s suffering.

16. As for what follows, that he loved Hannah, either matter may properly be understood as the cause of the other. Whether one takes him to have been sorrowful because he loved Hannah, or to have given her one portion for this reason, the interpretation is sound.

For if he had not loved her, he would not have wished to share in her sufferings. Why, then, is she led out of Egypt, except because she is invited to suffering? Yet lands flowing with milk and honey are promised to her.

Therefore, when he is said to give her one portion, he is rightly said to love her, because our Redeemer, although he assigned the labor of his cross to the holy Church, established for her exceedingly greater gifts of recompense in heaven.

Describing the growth of this suffering, he adds:

**(Verses 6–7.)** “But the Lord had closed her womb. Her rival also afflicted her and harassed her greatly, so much so that she reproached her because the Lord had closed her womb.”

17. The Lord closed the womb of the holy Church because, by his supreme judgment, the rejected people of the Jews could not bring forth children in the faith of our Redeemer. Her rival afflicted her, because the synagogue raged against her with threats and reproaches. But against the one whom neither threats nor insults had broken, she also inflicted punishments by torture.

She is therefore rightly said not merely to have been afflicted but to have been greatly harassed, because rejected Judea stirred itself against the elect Church with the terror of threats and struck her with blows. Hence, concerning Saul, who was then persecuting her, it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to Damascus, so that if he found any men of this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem” (Acts 9:1–2).

He who breathed threats and murder was plainly not only afflicting the Church, whom he wrongly regarded as his rival, but also harassing her. For he confesses that he had been her rival, saying: “You have heard of my former way of life in Judaism: how beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it, and advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers” (Gal. 1:13–14).

And because Judea fell into such a depth of condemnation that it rejoiced in being cast away by God’s eternal judgment, it is added: “So much so that she reproached her because the Lord had closed her womb.” For she still considered it a great thing that she would not prevail in turning to the faith.

Thus, as though the prophet marveled at the magnitude of her blindness, he says: “She is weighed down by such a darkness of error that she insults the good because she herself can no longer become good.”

Because the holy Church grieved for her as she perished, it follows:

**(Verse 7.)** “But Hannah wept.”

18. She also uttered the lament of her sorrow, saying: “There is great sorrow for me and continual pain in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom. 9:2–3).

And because she received no joy from their conversion, it follows:

**(Verse 7.)** “And she did not take food.”

She would have taken food if she had received the refreshment of joy from the complete conversion of Judea. Hannah therefore wept and did not eat, because she who grieved over perishing Judea received no joy from its salvation.

But the food of joy that is not given to the holy Church from the conversion of the Jews is offered through the Bridegroom’s exhortation. For although the reprobate do not receive the words of her preaching, those words are not without the reward of recompense. Almighty God rewards even what is offered to the reprobate without benefiting them; and what they inflict upon his elect preachers through adversity, he weighs for them as profit in the recompense of his just judgment.

Hence it is fittingly added:

**(Verse 8.)** “Then Elkanah her husband said to her: ‘Hannah, why are you weeping? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart afflicted? Am I not better to you than ten sons?’”

19. As though, through the consolation of inward inspiration, the Redeemer were saying to the teacher’s mind: “You complain in vain over the loss of the profit of preaching, since you receive a more abundant fruit precisely because you extend the affection of charity even to your enemies. You grieve over what ought to have made you rejoice.”

And because he himself is the reward of the elect, he asks: “Am I not better to you than ten sons?”

Hannah would have borne ten sons if the primitive Church had brought forth in faith the people of the Jews, placed under the Ten Commandments of the Law. And because some benefit others through preaching while displeasing the Creator in many ways, it is shown by reason that her husband is better for Hannah than ten sons.

The question about why she weeps may also signify the destruction of Judea. It is as though he said: “She is being mourned uselessly, since she is not pardoned even through the prayer of the righteous.”

When he then asks: “Why do you not eat?” the joy arising from the conversion of the Gentiles is plainly indicated. It is as though he said: “Since you must give birth to the whole world, you do not fail to rejoice without cause that the one who has been cast away does not abandon the darkness of error.”

It continues:

**(Verses 9–10.)** “Then Hannah arose, after she had eaten and drunk in Shiloh, while Eli the priest was sitting on a chair before the doors of the temple of the Lord; and, being bitter in spirit, she prayed to the Lord, weeping abundantly.”

20. What did it then mean for the holy Church to eat except to receive food of consolation through divine exhortation? And what did it mean for her to drink except to rejoice in the sweetness of inward consolation poured into her?

For if food strengthens and drink gladdens, we take food when, seeing the eternal rewards, we are strengthened amid adversities. And it is as though we drink after eating, because when the mind of the elect has strengthened itself through meditation on eternal goods [Note: Gilot: “is strengthened by their fruit.”], it rejoices all the more abundantly amid the great adversities it endures, the more clearly it sees the greater rewards laid up in heaven in return for great labors.

Made bold by this heavenly refreshment, it renews its strength, so that it despises earthly things all the more firmly as the love of heavenly things exalts it.

Hannah is therefore rightly said to have arisen after she had eaten and drunk. She arose because she reformed her mind for the urgency of preaching.

21. Because the Jewish people still possessed the rites of sacrifices, the honor of legal instruction, and the exalted dignity of the high priesthood, Eli the priest is said to have sat on a chair. Yet because he could offer this instruction of the Law not spiritually but carnally, he sat not inside the temple but before the doors of the temple.

For what is the temple of the Lord except the spiritual understanding of the holy Scriptures? The doors of the temple are the Law and the Prophecy. Hence the Lord appeared transfigured on the mountain in the midst of Moses and Elijah (Matt. 17:3; Luke 9:30), because the splendor of his divinity is perceived when his mysteries are sought not in the letter that kills (2 Pet. 1) but in the spiritual meaning of the Law and the Prophecy.

Eli therefore sat before the doors of the temple—that is, outside—because the teachers of the synagogue had been expelled from the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures, yet they possessed the authority of teaching and the dignity of leadership in the overthrow of the people subject to them.

Hannah, however, is written to have wept with a bitter spirit.

22. Since we have referred Hannah’s drinking to the joy of the holy Church, how can she be said to have wept with a bitter spirit when she is shown to rejoice?

It may reasonably be understood that contemplation of the heavenly reward had lifted her toward rejoicing, while compassion for rejected Judea stirred her to bitterness of spirit. Caught amid the storms of great persecution, she rejoiced when heavenly rewards were revealed to her, but she fell into bitterness when she saw the formerly elect people perishing.

Hence she is described as praying and weeping abundantly, so that through the gift of such great affection she might obtain the salvation of her people from the Lord.

The whole passage may also be understood in another way. In Shiloh—that is, in the ministry to which she was sent—she ate, because, although she could not win the entire Jewish people, she nevertheless converted many of them to faith in the Redeemer through preaching.

Thus, when Peter preached, five thousand men believed on one day (Acts 4:4), and three thousand on another (Acts 2:4) [Note: [Col. 0033D] Bernard says the same in *The Book on Loving God*, chapter 11, cols. 597–598 of the new edition.].

And because what we drink can be swallowed more easily than what we eat, Hannah ate and drank because she converted some with difficulty and others with ease through preaching. For at Peter’s preaching mentioned above, several thousand believed in a single moment, whereas Paul did not believe until he had violently opposed those very preachers with threats and murder.

After Hannah had eaten and drunk in Shiloh, she arose because, in order to remove from Judea those who were predestined to eternal life, she prepared herself for preaching to the Gentiles.

But what kind of child she desired to bear is shown by what is added:

**(Verse 15.)** “And she made a vow, saying: ‘Lord of hosts, if you will look upon and see the affliction of your handmaid, and remember me and not forget your maidservant, and give your servant a male child, I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head.’”

23. Why does Hannah ask the Lord for a male child except because those whom the holy Church desires to bear through preaching she wishes to be strong in evangelical perfection?

In comparison with evangelical perfection, those works of the Law that appeared strong were not strong but weak. There it was commanded: “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy” (Lev. 19:18). But in the Gospel the Lord commands: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44).

There [Note: [Col. 0033D] Something seems to be missing here. It may perhaps be read: “There the impurity of fornication is cut away from the body; here, as a mark of strength, etc.,” so that the distinction between the Evangelical and Mosaic Laws may be shown.] the impurity of fornication is cut away from the body; here, as a sign of the strength of one’s conduct, as though by a male child, unclean thought is also cut away from the heart: “Whoever,” he says, “looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

Thus the synagogue, which brought forth the Jewish people through the weakness of its commandments, did not bear a male child but rather a female. When Hannah therefore asks the Lord that a male child be given to her, what else is she seen to desire except to bring forth through the Gospel such people as appear strong both in outward bodily purity and in inward charity?

24. And because the order of preachers does not seek human glory from the conversion of the Gentiles, it is added: “I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life.”

One gives a son to the Lord when one claims none of the praise for oneself from the one whom one has brought forth through preaching. One gives him to the Lord throughout all the days of his life when one ascribes nothing to one’s own favor from the virtues by which a subject advances through improvement under obedience.

The days of the elect subject’s life are the holy virtues that illuminate his soul by shining within it, so that it does not grow dark on the way to the heavenly homeland through the night of vices.

25. But the perfect order of a preacher, while scorning to receive praise from the profit of preaching, does not seize the temporal goods of his subjects by coveting them. Hence it is rightly added there: “And no razor shall come upon his head.”

When a razor comes upon the head, it cuts the hair. What is signified by the hair, which is superfluous to the body, except the abundance of earthly substance? And what is signified by the razor except the greed of wicked shepherds?

The razor cuts the head of the child who has been born when the goods of subjects are seized through the greed of preachers. Hence the prophet says to sinful Judea: “Her shepherds are wolves in the evening; they leave nothing for the morning” (Zeph. 3:3).

Shepherds become wolves in the evening because, as this age grows dark and declines toward its end, they do not fear to seize the goods of their subjects. They leave nothing for the morning because, while they long for temporal things, they do not reserve for themselves rewards to be given when the coming judgment dawns.

Micah likewise condemns them, saying: “The prophets who lead my people astray, who bite with their teeth and preach peace; and if anyone gives nothing into their mouths, they consecrate war against him” (Mic. 3:5).

The prophets lead the Lord’s people astray when reprobate preachers confuse the judgments of their hearers. They announce peace while biting with their teeth because, in the appetite of their rapacity, as they look upon the earthly gifts of the wicked, they promise them security in divine forgiveness.

They consecrate war against those who give nothing into their mouths because they frighten even the just with strict judgments when those people do not provide them with earthly goods according to their desire.

Such men place a razor upon the child’s head when, under the pretext of charity, they preach heavenly things in order to take earthly things away through greed.

That the holy Church does not possess this razor for the plunder of her subjects, the distinguished teacher shows in himself when he says: “I seek not the gift, but I seek the fruit” (Phil. 4:17). Again he says: “The one who proclaims the Gospel should live from the Gospel. But I have not made use of this right” (1 Cor. 9:14–15).

For he who does not concern himself to receive from his subjects what is necessary for sustenance plainly shows with what greatness of contempt for the world he rejected shameful profits and illicit gifts.

Thus, when Hannah vows that no razor shall come upon her son’s head, she openly signifies the character of the holy Church, which brings the elect to eternal life through preaching but never takes away their temporal goods through avarice.

But because this is said while Hannah is still making her vow and has not yet given birth, it is fittingly added:

**(Verse 12.)** “And it came to pass, while she multiplied her prayers before the Lord, that Eli watched her mouth.”

26. What did it mean for the holy Church to multiply her prayers before the Lord out of the desire to give birth except to persist in constant prayers for the conversion of the synagogue? And what did it mean for the Jewish priesthood to watch her mouth except to lie in wait for the preaching of the holy Church?

He watched her mouth because he eagerly sought to criticize the sound preaching of the faith. She is rightly said to have had her mouth watched while she was multiplying her prayers, because he sought to harm her more craftily the more he recognized the greatness of her desires in the urgency of preaching.

Indeed, he would not have watched her mouth but attended to it if he had wished to hear the preaching of our faith for the benefit of his salvation.

It continues:

**(Verse 13.)** “Now Hannah was speaking in her heart, and only her lips were moving, while her voice was not heard at all.”

27. What else is the heart of the holy Church except the devoted and instructed blessedness of the faithful that exists within her?

Hannah spoke in her heart because the preaching of the holy Church benefited only those who were destined by divine predestination to be enlightened by the true light.

What, then, is the movement of the lips except the advancement of signs in holy preachers? Although their lips seemed to speak outwardly and to remain below, when they gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and life to the dead, they certainly displayed great movements of merit.

Hence that great lip of the holy Church, although it seemed to remain below while speaking—for she was humble not only in word and conduct but also exalted in the power of signs—raised the movement of its activity even to heaven, saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

Eli therefore saw only Hannah’s lips moving and did not hear her voice at all, because the Jewish priesthood marveled at the works of the apostles but was not advanced toward salvation by their preaching [Note: [Col. 0035D] In the printed editions: “The Jewish priesthood marveled at the works of the apostles but was not advanced by their preaching,” and so forth. We have been unable to retain that reading.].

Hannah’s voice was therefore not heard because, although the holy Church was marvelous through the display of signs, when she spoke the words of preaching she kindled outsiders to love of the Redeemer.

But what does Eli think of her, since he does not understand her?

It continues:

**(Verse 13.)** “Therefore Eli considered her drunk.”

28. We recognize this also according to the historical account in the Acts of the Apostles, because on the days of Pentecost the holy apostles were thought to be drunk when, having received the fullness of the Holy Spirit, they spoke of the mighty works of Christ in every language (Acts 2:4).

Spiritually, however, the holy Church is considered drunk because Judea does not think that she asserts what is true, but rather that she preaches heretical and false things. Yet she was drunk not through drinking error but through being filled with the Holy Spirit.

Drunkenness is accustomed to change the heart and estrange the mind. But the one who had entered houses shortly before, terrifying the faithful with threats and tearing them apart with killings, now proceeded with a changed heart, proclaiming that the Jesus whom he had persecuted was truly the Son of almighty God (Acts 9:5, 20).

Hence, boasting that he had lost the madness of his former state, he says: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man; but I received mercy because I acted ignorantly” (1 Tim. 1:13). Testifying that he had received another heart, he says: “But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Cor. 2:16).

Therefore he preached all the more attentively because in the mind of Christ he had received the force of a greater love.

But while the holy Church loved ardently, while she preached with confidence what she loved, the priesthood of the Jews treated her words as a burden of impatience rather than as the sweetness of devotion.

Hence it follows:

**(Verse 14.)** “And he said to her: ‘How long will you remain drunk?’”

And because he attempted to impose silence upon her, he added:

**(Verse 14.)** “Put away for a little while the wine with which you are soaked.”

29. Hannah would have put away the wine with which she was soaked if the holy Church, overcome by the threats of the Jews, had grown lukewarm in the fervor of preaching. And because they sought to remove the sense of preaching from her by force, Hannah is ordered to put away her wine for a little while.

Did Eli not then command Hannah to put it away when the leaders of the Jews, after having beaten the apostles, ordered them not to speak any longer in the name of Jesus? [Note: [Col. 0037D] Gilot has: “but they who …”]

But because they refused to put away the wine with which they were soaked, they answered: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). And again: “We cannot not speak of what we have seen and heard” (ibid., 4:20).

But because the holy Church preserved the virtue of gentleness amid words of freedom, it follows:

**(Verse 15.)** “By no means, my lord.”

30. She called him “lord,” to whom she was rendering the ministry of preaching; but, while calling him lord, she denied that she was drunk, so that in humility she might submit to the higher order and in truth oppose the false accusation.

Calling him lord, she honored him; denying that she was drunk, she showed with sufficient humility what she was not.

The accusation of drunkenness may also be understood in another way with regard to the holy Church. While she devoted herself to the ministry of evangelical preaching, while she advanced from the profit of believers into great public glory, the priests of the Jews did not think that she was seeking the summit of eternal goods but rather desiring the glory of earthly exaltation.

Thus, when she is called drunk, she is reproved for having overturned the state of her mind, setting aside heavenly things and seeking earthly ones.

31. But she who despised the world’s fleeting goods says: “By no means, my lord.”

For I am an exceedingly unhappy woman. It is as though she said: “You think that I desire the happiness of the fleeting world, but I see myself as all the more unhappy the farther away I recognize the joys of my happiness to be from here. Because I believe that I shall be happy there, I consider myself very unhappy here, insofar as I desire no glory for myself.”

The holy Church is called a woman because of her fruitfulness, and exceedingly unhappy because of her strength, since she was to give birth to the world through the word and could not perfectly despise the world’s glory unless heavenly love strengthened her with wondrous fortitude.

Or she was exceedingly unhappy because she grieved greatly over the destruction of her people.

The wise Solomon, marveling intensely at her, says: “Who shall find a strong woman?” (Prov. 31:10).

Here it should also be noted that she does not say, “I am an unhappy woman,” but “I am exceedingly so.” For she was exceedingly unhappy because no charm of the world pleased her.

Or certainly she declares herself exceedingly unhappy because she remembers that, through the merit of the first sin, she was expelled from the joys of eternal life, to which she cannot return except through the many tribulations of this life. For she would not be exceedingly unhappy if she could return to the lost joys of paradise without present tribulation.

Hence Paul, showing the unavoidable misery of this great unhappiness, says: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21).

Thus, as though the holy Church were responding to the Jewish priesthood that disparaged her, she says: “You ascribe to me a kingdom in the happiness of the present age, but my kingdom is that which is reached only through the affliction of great tribulation.”

It follows:

**(Verse 15.)** “I have drunk neither wine nor anything that can cause drunkenness.”

### 32

For she did not drink wine, because she did not seek temporal profits from the ministry of preaching. She did not drink anything else capable of intoxication, because she did not allow the desire of the flesh to overthrow her into the fall of vices. According to the preceding interpretation, she did not drink wine because she had no heretical perversity in her nourishment. She would have drunk something else capable of intoxication if, deceived by eloquence of speech, she had become puffed up. But because she taught the truth with right intention, she adds:

> **(Verse 15.) “But I poured out my soul in the sight of the Lord.”**

### 33

To pour out one’s soul in the sight of the Lord is to preach, solely for the love of the Creator, the knowledge of God’s word conceived in the mind. The soul is poured out when the understanding of God’s word, naturally implanted within, is made known for the benefit of its hearers. Whoever preaches the word of God for human approval, whoever preaches it for earthly advantage—because some other consideration is sought from preaching—that word is not brought forth from the soul in the sight of the Lord. Hence the teacher of the nations also declares:

> “For we are not like the many, adulterating the word of God, but as from sincerity, but as from God, before God we speak in Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:17).

Anna, therefore, poured out her soul in the sight of the Lord, because holy Church, perfected in the summit of every virtue, uttered words of great eloquence in instructing the faithful, yet desired to please God alone through the words of her life. She further commends this ministry of preaching, saying:

> **(Verse 16.) “Do not think your handmaid to be like one of the daughters of Belial, for from the abundance of my pain and grief I have spoken until now.”**

### 34

It is as though she said: “She who speaks to you of the goods of eternal life does not deserve to be despised as an idolater.”  
[Note: Gilot and Vatican manuscripts: “idolater.”]

She also asserts that she is his handmaid, so that from the name of her ministry he may recognize that she desires to serve him for eternal gains. It follows:

“For from the abundance of my grief and pain I have spoken until now.”

It is as though she were speaking more openly and saying: “Recognize from this that I have nothing from an evil spirit, because I come to speak from the great punishment of persecution, and I do not abandon the urgency of preaching, overcome by any punishment.”

Anna’s pain may also be referred to the affection of holy Church, and her grief to her passion. She spoke from an abundance of pain because, out of compassionate feeling, she uttered the word of preaching to the Jewish people as they were perishing.

[Note: “pain” (*doloris*) is absent in the printed editions; yet its necessity is clear from the sense alone.] Paul indicates this when he says:

> “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie; my conscience bears witness with me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart. For I myself could wish to be accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Romans 9:1–2 and following).

But the one who indicates that he speaks from an abundance of pain also shows from what abundance he speaks:

> “From the Jews I received five times forty lashes less one; three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned” (2 Corinthians 11:24).

Holy Church, patiently enduring adversity and humbly displaying the power of her innocence and truth, persuaded certain priests of Judea by speaking the good of her preaching. Hence it is added:

> **21 (Verse 17.) Then Eli said: “Go in peace; may the God of Israel grant you the petition that you asked of him.”**

### 35

Earlier, Eli opposed Hannah with insults when she was praying; afterward, however, her devotion pleased him. What does this mean except that the Jewish priesthood, through some ministers of its office, opposed the Church as she preached, while through others it eventually consented to the truth of our acknowledged faith? Of those who opposed it, it is said that they had the apostles flogged and ordered them not to speak further in the name of Jesus (Acts 5:40). Of those who consented, Luke likewise records:

> “A great multitude of priests obeyed the faith” (Acts 6:7).

Eli, therefore, prayed for Hannah’s fruitfulness when that great multitude of priests, obeying the faith, desired the number of the elect to be increased through the preaching of holy Church. He wished her to go in peace because he desired her to obtain the fruit of preaching without the pain of suffering. And because holy Church found favor in their desire, it follows:

> **(Verse 18.) “Would that your handmaid might find favor in your eyes.”**

It is as though she said: “May the work of my ministry be followed, in accordance with your desire, by the grace of divine dispensation.” It follows:

> **(Verse 18.) “And the woman went on her way, and ate and drank, and her face was no longer changed in different directions.”**

### 36

The woman went on her way because holy Church preached the word of faith to the Gentiles. The apostles also say this in threatening the Jews:

> “Since you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).  
> [Note: Gilot: “you have made yourselves.”]

She is rightly called a woman when she departs, because through the preaching of the Redeemer she was to produce among the Gentiles the fruit of great fertility. She ate and drank, yet her face was no longer changed in different directions, because she gained great profits from the conversion of the Gentiles, but found among the Gentiles also the persecution that she had suffered in Judea.

Explaining in what order she departed, he says:

> **(Verse 19.) “And they rose in the morning, and worshiped before the Lord; then they returned and came to their house, in Ramah.”**

### 37

What does it mean that earlier the woman Hannah alone is mentioned in the singular—“The woman went on her way”—but now the plural is used—“They rose in the morning”—unless it is so that she may be understood to have gone down with her husband?

Since the husband of holy Church is the Redeemer of the human race, who had already ascended into heaven when he left Judea, buried in the darkness of its unbelief, how can what is now said of Hannah and her husband Elkanah—that they rose together in the morning and returned together to their city—be understood in the type of Christ and the Church?

We have already said that the city of Ramah signifies the heavenly homeland. How, then, does this apply to holy Church, who, as soon as she ceased preaching to the Jews, did not ascend immediately to the heavenly homeland?

[Note: Gilot and Vatican manuscripts: “does not ascend.”] Yet when the Lord, rising from the dead, speaks through teachers sent to preach, saying:

> “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20),

it is not absurd to understand holy Church as rising and returning with him. For he who never abandons his elect through his spiritual presence remains with those who stand and departs with those who depart.

We have said that Ramah signifies the heavenly homeland, but we have not said that it can signify nothing else. What else, then, does it signify in this place except the fulfillment of prophecy in the calling of the Gentiles? Ramah is interpreted as “completed vision,” as we have already said. What, then, is the calling of the Gentiles, now fulfilled, except the completed vision of the prophets?

For the prophet asserted a vision, but not a completed one, when he proclaimed what he had seen as still future:

> “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord” (Psalm 85:9).

Again he promises:

> “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all the nations shall serve him” (Psalm 71:15).

The completed vision, therefore, is rightly called the promise of the prophets, because, with God as its author, all the nations believed in the Redeemer of the human race according to their prophecies.

Hannah is said to rise in the morning with her husband because holy Church passed over to the Gentiles with the word of preaching at the rising of the inner light. Or she rises in the morning because she left Judea in the night of unbelief. She also rises in the morning because she found a prosperous path in the conversion of the Gentiles.

She worshiped before the Lord because, in the rejection of the Synagogue, she reverenced the incomprehensible judgment of almighty God. She worshiped and departed because, when she withdrew from preaching to her own people solely by the ordering of almighty God, she obeyed the divine judgment, although she could not penetrate it by understanding.

She returned worshiping because she resolved to fulfill the ministry of preaching in the calling of the Gentiles, yet sought the proper manner of that preaching in heavenly contemplation. For it is the task of preachers to return to the light of divine contemplation. From there they draw the light by which they shine for the reverence of the faithful and pour it, through their speech, into the minds of their hearers.

Hence the excellent preacher is first lifted up to the secrets of the third heaven, and then is said to arrange earthly matters; entering the secrets of paradise, he receives words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak (2 Corinthians 12:2), so that outwardly he may discern and speak usefully.

Hannah, therefore, is remembered as having returned because, while holy Church arranged earthly matters, she was instructed in the contemplation of God—to which she often returns—concerning how those earthly matters should be arranged. Finally, she came to her house because she was able to establish herself in the devotion of her hearers once she had learned, by returning above, how to approach them.

The devotion of the Gentiles built the house of holy primitive Church. While she founded that house in them, she inhabited it with vigilant care. This house is described as established in the completed vision, because it could not be founded before the time foretold by the prophets for her calling had arrived.

It follows:

> **(Verses 19 and 20.) “Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the Lord remembered her. And it came to pass after the circuit of days that Hannah conceived and bore a son.”**  
> [Note: “Her” is absent in Gilot and the Vatican manuscripts. “And it came to pass,” etc., is also omitted; since the following verse explains it, we have judged that it should be appended here.]

### 38

Elkanah knew Hannah his wife when our Redeemer looked upon the appointed time for calling the Gentiles. As he poured the grace of heavenly love into the womb of the new bride, namely holy Church, he generated from her a new offspring of the faithful.

For he seemed not yet to know her when the Holy Spirit prevented the preachers who wished to cross into Asia (Acts 16:6). Hence, when he sent his disciples to preach in Judea, the Truth himself forbade them, saying:

> “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matthew 10:5).

When Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, then the Lord remembered her, because the Gentiles seemed to have come into remembrance before God when holy Church, joined to the Word of God by the grace of love, was visited for salvation.

What else does “the circuit of days” signify in this passage except the manifestation of the divine will displayed through the innumerable rays of the Holy Spirit? As it presents countless splendors of heavenly disposition to the minds of preachers suspended in contemplation, the circuit of time holds them enclosed, as it were, like many days.

The circuit of days preceded Hannah’s conception because the Word of God is not infused into holy Church for teaching until the rays of heavenly disposition have been more fully recognized by her. She conceived and bore a son because those whom she brings forth in the faith of the Redeemer are strengthened by a new manner of life.

> **(Verse 20.) “And she called his name Samuel, because she had asked him from the Lord.”**

### 39

Samuel is interpreted as “his name is God.” Whom, then, does Samuel more fittingly signify for us than the order of preachers who was called to the faith from the Gentiles?

Because he is strong in conduct, exalted in power, and because, when a special sign of divine grace is seen in him, devoted crowds of hearers are led to revere his preaching, his name is rightly declared by this designation. Hence the Lord says to Moses:

> “I have appointed you as a god to Pharaoh” (Exodus 7:1).

Again, in the Law, while forbidding insult, he says:

> “You shall not revile the gods” (Exodus 22:28).

It should be noted that the one whose name is called “God” was a son, not a daughter, because pastoral dignity, when weighed down by weak conduct, is not adorned by the splendor of so lofty a name.

Since, therefore, the order of teachers, promoted from the Gentiles to the ministry of evangelizing, was not unequal to the excellence of its dignity through the grace of its merits, it is rightly said:

> “She called his name Samuel, because she had asked him from the Lord.”

It should also be noted that here something is said to be “asked” which he obtained by asking. Thus the reason is plainly shown why Hannah’s firstborn is designated by so great a name. It is as though he said: “She gave him such a great name because the one born by heavenly gift was great through the grace of his merits.”

But to show with what care his provident mother nurtured him, it follows:

> **(Verses 21 and 22.) “His husband Elkanah went up, and all his household, to sacrifice the solemn sacrifice and fulfill his vow; but Hannah did not go up. For she said to her husband: ‘I will not go until the infant is weaned.’”**  
> [Note: “Infant” is absent in Gilot and the Vatican manuscripts.]

### 40

What is the solemn sacrifice except that offering of love by which holy Church is joined to her Creator in eternal contemplation?

Elkanah went up to it when our Redeemer, already triumphing over death and overcoming the darkness of our weakness, raised to heaven the flesh he had assumed for our salvation. His whole household went up with him because he raised the former elect of the Synagogue to the height of immortality.

He sacrificed the solemn offering when he presented himself in heaven to the eternal Father through the substance of glorified flesh, and made the nature of the angels rejoice not only over our redemption but also over their restoration.

Hannah is invited to this solemn offering because holy Church, through the spiritual exhortation of her heavenly Bridegroom, is kindled by daily desires of love toward the eternal contemplation of divine glory. Yet she refrains from ascending in order to nurse her son, because she patiently endures a delay of her own glory so that she may benefit Christ’s little ones here.

Was not that mother invited to the sacrifice of this solemn offering who said:

> “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23)?

But she who is drawn by the desires of love toward the sight of her Bridegroom should say whether she is willing to nurse her son:

> “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1:24).

She also indicates with what nourishment she fed the Corinthians, saying:

> “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3:2).

To nurse the little ones of holy Church is for pastors to nourish the hearts of weak or simple hearers with the food of plainer Scripture. To them the same excellent teacher says:

> “I determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2).

### 41

Infants are weaned when the little ones of holy Church receive growth both in spiritual instruction and in good conduct, and no longer seek the plainer things of sacred speech but its profound mysteries.

A weaned infant is brought so that he may appear before the Lord when, through the exhortation of preachers, every subordinate who is making good progress is adorned with good works. For one who is brought so that he may appear is carried not merely to see but also to be seen.

Since at the end many will hear from the Lord, “I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12), Samuel is said to appear in the sight of the Lord because the elect and humble subordinate, while perfectly despising present things, is by no means rejected when the final Judge arrives.

Those whom the world keeps fixed in love of itself do not appear in the sight of the Lord. For those who desire to be seen as eminent in the honor of passing things act through pride so that they may never be seen as honorable by the one before whom alone they ought to appear.

Hence the chosen king, placed at the summit of worldly affairs, begs not to be deceived by the flower of the world, saying:

> “Do not cast me away, O Lord, from your face” (Psalm 50:13).

Hannah therefore promises both to wean her son and to bring him so that he may appear before the Lord, because holy Church teaches the elect subjects whom she instructs to despise present things perfectly, to do good, and to hasten toward eternal goods through humility.

It should be noted that he is said to be brought from the place of weaning who is declared to appear in the sight of the Lord, because there is no small distance in the spiritual journey when, from what we learn through heavenly instruction, we advance toward the practice of perfect action.

Since one must never cease pursuing the same good work, it follows:

> **(Verse 22.) “And let him appear there continually.”**

### 42

We continually appear there from which we never depart. To appear continually in the sight of the Lord is not to obscure the beauty of good conduct with any darkness of life. For whoever does not fall into any illicit act never leaves the secrecy of the divine gaze. Divine goodness looks upon such a person as though he were placed in the light, because in the judgment of its election it does not regard the darkness of sins that it has condemned.

Therefore Hannah declares that she will not ascend to sacrifice the solemn offering until the infant is weaned, because holy Church proposes to guard her children as long as she can become certain of their perfection, namely, that they will not afterward depart from the goodness they have received.

The ascent to the solemn offering may, however, be referred to the height of holy preaching. For it is written through the Prophet concerning her husband’s ascent:

> “He ascended upon the cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm 17:11).

The Lord ascended upon the cherubim because he ascends into the lofty minds of his preachers and establishes there the height of his knowledge. He flies upon the wings of the winds because, before their spiritual eyes, he lifts himself by the breath of the Holy Spirit to the height of wondrous understanding.

> “He made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17:12),

because he conceals the sublimity of his majesty from the reprobate.

> “But around him was his tabernacle” (ibid.),

because to those whom he elevates through sublime gifts he also manifests the glory of his majesty.

### 43

It is fitting that, when Elkanah’s ascent is asserted, his whole household is said to have ascended, because he holds as household members and friends those whose minds he surpasses in the height of his contemplation.

What, then, is the solemn sacrifice of Elkanah—that is, of our Redeemer—except that ineffable inner love of instruction in the hearts of his saints? For each of them finds ineffable delight in the fact that the sublimity of the Redeemer, once revealed, teaches him so sublimely.

Hannah therefore denies that she will ascend with her husband until she nurses her son, because holy Church avoided touching upon lofty matters in preaching as long as she recognized that her inexperienced hearers, like little children, were entirely unable to grasp them.

Hence, in the very beginnings of holy Church, milk was offered, as it were, to Hannah’s still-small son through the writings of the three evangelists—Matthew, Luke, and Mark. In writing the history of the Lord’s humanity, they treated only briefly of his divinity.

But when the people of the Church grew and advanced toward the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age (Ephesians 4:13), those for whom drinking milk was no longer sufficient sought to be fed with solid food.

Thus mother Church was compelled to ascend, so that she herself might also become a cherub and draw near to the Redeemer flying above her; she took up wings, held him who walked upon them in the height of the mysteries, and drew from his majesty what she might give as nourishment to the one who sought it.

Consequently, when the evangelist John was asked by the brethren, he surpassed not only human but also angelic things, transcended all created realities, and preached the Only-Begotten whom he had been worthy to see in the bosom of the Father, saying:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

Hannah therefore ascended when holy Church raised herself so sublimely into the height of divine preaching. She also sacrificed the solemn offering when, from knowledge of the divinity, she kindled in the hearts of her hearers a flame of wondrous devotion.

The solemn offering was an incomparable utterance and a singular offering of devotion. She brought her son into the sight of the Lord when she impressed perfect knowledge of the supreme divinity upon the hearts of her hearers.

Since this knowledge of God must be held not only by faith but also by confession, and since we are not permitted either to remain ignorant of or to keep silent about what we believe and confess, the weaned child who is brought to the house of the Lord is declared to remain continually in the sight of the Lord.

It follows:

> **(Verse 23.) “And her husband Elkanah said to her: ‘Do what seems good to you; remain until you have weaned him.’”**

### 44

What does it mean that Hannah’s decision is strengthened by the authority of her husband, except that the purpose of holy Church is not presumed upon by human judgment but proceeds from the divine?

Whatever holy Church wished to arrange among the nations subject to her, she considered valid only when she had learned from the judgment of inner truth what ought to be arranged.

And because:

> “We have an advocate with the Father” (1 John 2:1),

who intercedes for us, he adds and says:

> **(Verse 23.) “And I pray that the Lord may fulfill his word.”**

### 45

What is the word that is asserted to be fulfilled except the predestined conversion of the Gentiles?

Because we are reconciled to God through his blood, he prays for the fulfillment of the word, through whose intercession our salvation is completed. To pray for it also means that, in the humanity he assumed, he continually presents himself to the eternal Father for our salvation. By not ceasing to offer himself in this way, he opens the way for our reception into life.

Since she perfected the counsel of his disposition by seeking it out, it is appropriately added:

> “The woman therefore remained and nursed her son until she weaned him.”

Then it follows:

> **(Verse 24.) “And after she had weaned him, she brought him with three calves, three measures of flour, and a flask of wine; and she brought him into the house of the Lord at Shiloh.”**

### 46

What, then, is signified here by a calf except the resolve to imitate the life of the perfect?

It is a calf when the intention of a person making progress arises in his heart; it is an ox when, through the strength of virtue, it is brought to the affection of a great manner of life.

Here it must be carefully asked why not one calf but three are said to have been brought to the tabernacle. The child is carried in three calves to indicate the form of those who are instructed for the ministry of preaching.

The perfect teacher watches over both the conversion of sinners and the preservation of the righteous. Like a laborer of the supreme master of the household, he places both oxen under the plow, so that he may not only watch over those who stand lest they fall, but may also raise up those who have fallen so that they may stand.

But whoever has two oxen in his care for his subjects, if he is to be perfect, should yoke a third ox in divine contemplation. Thus he may open the hearts of his neighbors with an undivided yoke, speaking as though plowing, and may continually stretch himself toward the vision of his Creator through the singular strength of love.

Samuel is therefore brought to the house of the Lord with three calves when every person making good progress resolves to benefit his neighbors through the labor of preaching and to cleave to the Creator’s inner vision through the secret of quiet.

Since the inexperienced mind can never properly accomplish this, he is also offered with three measures of flour. When loaves are made from flour, the preparation of nourishment is completed. But because the offering consists not of loaves but of measures of flour, it shows that one proposes the good devotion of teaching, not that one provides the benefit of the teaching itself.

A measure of flour therefore signifies the preparation of holy preaching. The child is brought with three measures of flour because, when we propose to preach, we prepare the word of knowledge for sinners unto conversion, for the righteous unto perseverance, and for ourselves unto heavenly contemplation.

Or, certainly, one measure is—as we have said—for the conversion of the sinner, another for the discipline of the married person, and a third for the outstanding purity of the celibate. They are called “measures” because of the measure of discretion. Hence blessed Paul also says:

> “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment” (Romans 12:3).

### 47

That the chosen order of preachers possessed this not through the frivolity of vanity but through the power of good intention is indicated by what follows. [Possibly: “chosen from the Gentiles.”] It follows:

> “And a flask of wine.”

The virtue of good intention is the love of God, which is poured out in the hearts of the elect through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

This gift of love is rightly represented by the name of wine because it takes possession of the mind and alienates it from earthly affections, so that it has no intention directed toward the world but is inflamed to desire heavenly things alone.

Yet to indicate the beginning rather than the perfection of this virtue, it is shown to have been a flask of wine, not a cup. For we place in a flask what we will at some time serve in a cup.

Hence the one who had tasted the perfection of heavenly love confessed to almighty God, saying:

> “You have anointed my head with oil, and my cup, making me drunk, how excellent it is!” (Psalm 22:5).

Samuel is therefore shown to have been offered in a flask of wine because, when each of the elect is prepared for the ministry of evangelical preaching, he proposes to expend the good of that preaching not for the vain ambition of this world but solely for love.

He is brought with calves for the resolve of strength, with measures of flour for the doctrine of the word, and with a flask of wine for the intention of love.

### 48

He teaches where these beginnings of virtue are to be perfected when he adds:

> “And she brought him into the house of the Lord at Shiloh.”

The house of the Lord is rightly understood as holy Church, which is said to be situated at Shiloh. Shiloh is the place where the ark of God is said to have remained.

What else, then, does Shiloh signify in this passage except the tradition of the old Law? For it contains, as it were, the ark of God, since it displays the carnal letter outwardly while holding spiritual knowledge enclosed within its secrets.

What, then, does it mean that the house of the Lord is said to be situated at Shiloh except that holy Church is understood to be founded in the mystery of Scripture as in a place?

Samuel is said to be brought there and offered there because outside holy Church there is no place where the merits of the virtues may grow and reach the summit of perfection.

But when it is asserted that he himself was brought, the reason for the delay is also mentioned when it is added:

> **(Verse 24.) “But the child was still very young.”**

For if he had not then been very young, so that he could approach on his own, there would have been no need for him to be brought by another.

It follows:

> **(Verse 25.) “And they sacrificed the calf and presented the child to Eli.”**

### 49

Earlier it was said of Hannah alone:

> “And after she had weaned him, she brought him with her.”

Now, however, it is said of Elkanah and Hannah together:

> “And they sacrificed the calf and presented the child to Eli.”

The calf was sacrificed when Samuel was brought and presented. If Elkanah was there both when he was led and when he was offered, why was it not said, “They brought him with them,” just as it says, “They sacrificed and presented”?

But because we have referred these things to the Church and to Christ, nursing and bringing belong to the Church, while offering and sacrificing belong both to the Church and to Christ.

The Church applies herself to the word of preaching, but does not herself provide those to whom she gives instruction with the power to fulfill the work. She presents the letter of Scripture by speaking, but she can give the good itself to those who ask only together with her Bridegroom.

The calf is sacrificed when divine grace is poured into the heart of one who asks for good things, so that he may joyfully expend in the practice of good works the good that he has resolved upon and determined.

The calf is sacrificed because the victim of a good purpose is received by almighty God through the offering of a devoted mind, provided that what the mind presents to him by making a vow is wholly slaughtered for God through gladness.

The Lord speaks of this sacrifice of the calf in the Gospel:

> “If you, although evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will my heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Matthew 7:11; Luke 11:13).

Paul says:

> “Whoever sows with blessings will also reap with blessings. Let each person give as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:6–7).

What does “to determine in the heart” mean except to propose something after deliberation? When he says “he determined,” he is, as it were, asserting that the calf was brought. But when he adds, “not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver,” he explains how the calf that was brought is sacrificed.

Calves are therefore brought when we prepare ourselves by proposing to undertake difficult things; the calf is sacrificed when the deliberated good purpose is offered to God with great devotion.

Both—that is, the man and the woman—are said to sacrifice the calf because the same gladness is displayed to the faithful subjects by the preacher’s voice and propagated in their hearts by divine grace.

They sacrifice the calf together when divine grace coincides with human preaching in the heart of a subject who is making good progress.

Three calves are brought because, when we resolve to bring help to those who have fallen and to those who stand, and to provide assistance for our own protection, these concerns are three in relation to the work, but one in the offering.

They are three because they are exercised toward ourselves and our neighbors with different considerations and at different times; but they are one calf because they are proposed together, offered to God with equal devotion, and share one gladness, with no other.

### 50

It follows:

> “And they presented the child to Eli.”

In Eli are represented not only the persons of the ancient teachers but also their teaching.

What, then, does it mean that the child Samuel is presented to Eli except what is plainly understood: whoever strives to benefit others by preaching ought to write not only new things but also old things?

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel by way of a parable:

> “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matthew 13:52).

Samuel is presented to Eli when the mind of a subject making good progress is instructed in the knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, so that in the books of the ancients he may read the letter that kills but also understand it according to the Spirit who gives life.

Thus he receives what sounds outwardly, recognizing, beyond the sound of the elements, what the Spirit sounds inwardly. He possesses the new things for faith, but whenever necessary he brings forward the ancient Scriptures for the confirmation of the New Testament.

He will then be able to defend the new things when he recognizes their rationale from the old.

Samuel is therefore plainly said to be presented to Eli, because only the person who does not ignore the rationale by which the old things are to be understood preaches the new things sufficiently.

Since we cannot understand those ancient Scriptures without a teacher, and since a teacher accomplishes nothing by teaching us if what he speaks outwardly is not infused into our hearts by divine grace, the mother did not present the child alone but with her husband.

To the one to whom she hands over the son, Hannah identifies herself with the word of proclamation, saying:

> **(Verse 26.) “I beg you, my lord, as your soul lives, I am that woman who stood here before you.”**

### 51

Hannah stood before Eli because holy Church did not collapse under any persecution from the teachers of the synagogue. It is as though the Church, boasting before the leaders of the Synagogue, said:

“Because I endured the adversities you inflicted upon me undefeated, I was able through the Gospel to bring the world to birth for God. For if, overcome by punishments, I had submitted myself to the old order, I would never have brought forth for the Redeemer a new offspring of so many nations.”

Because she speaks humbly, she calls him “Lord” in supplication. Since she desires that the pledge of eternal life be given to her through faith in the Redeemer, she says:

> “As your soul lives.”

But she who boasted that she had stood before him spoke great things about herself. And because she had spoken those great things humbly, not proudly, she immediately referred them to the praise of almighty God, saying:

> **(Verse 27.) “I prayed, and the Lord granted me the petition that I asked of him; therefore I too have commended him to the Lord.”**
52. Divine grace grants sons to holy Church for this purpose: that she may instruct them in the doctrine of truth, adorn them with good morals, watch over them with devout care, make them perfectly turn away from evil, and prepare for their eternal homeland an ample supply of good works. These are indeed duties of pastoral ministry, but the chosen preacher distrusts his ability to fulfill them by his own strength. Since, then, he can neither beget anyone through the Gospel by his own power nor safeguard those whom he begets, it is rightly said now through Hannah, as a figure of the Church: “I prayed, and the Lord granted me the petition for which I asked him. Therefore I too have entrusted him to the Lord, for all the days that he shall be entrusted to the Lord.” For he begs that he may be able to beget; and so that those whom he obtains through prayer may persevere in holy conduct, he likewise commends them to almighty God in his prayers. And because he never ceases from those same prayers, he says that he commends the son to God for all his days. To commend a son to the Lord for all one’s days is to supplicate him for the salvation of those whom one begets throughout the whole period of this life. The days during which we are commended to the Lord signify the times of the present life. In those days we need the aids of divine protection all the more powerfully as we are attacked by the more grievous temptations of wicked spirits.

But because in many books one reads not *commendatus* (“commended”) but *commodatus* (“lent”), this too is not without a sound meaning. For sons are lent by Mother Church during this life. Whatever we lend, we expect it to be returned to us, relying on the good faith of the recipient. The days, moreover, are the splendors of spiritual virtues. On those days Hannah’s son is lent to the Lord, because holy Church offers her chosen ones to him in the brightness of the virtues, so that afterward almighty God may present them to her in the splendors of rewards, for the increase of her eternal joy. It should also be noted that he is said to be commended for all the days, so that nothing may be lacking in him from what is to be possessed through spiritual conduct; the chosen preacher will not be able to receive him in eternal life as darkened in any respect.

It follows:

> (Verse 28.) And they worshiped the Lord there.

We too, as members of holy Church, when through the writings of the Old Testament we submit ourselves to the worship and commandment of the Creator [Note: [Col. 0049D] In Guss. and Vatic., “is submitted.”], worship the Lord there, because we hold the faith of the ancient Fathers and exercise that same faith through love in good works.

# CHAPTER II

[Col. 0049B]

We have brought forward these matters from the beginning by way of typological exposition; now let us seek our instruction in the same historical words through their moral significance.

> (I Kings I, 1.) “There was a certain man,” he says, “from Ramathaim-zophim.”

1. In this one man, what is more appropriately signified than each new despiser of the world? He is called a man because he is strong in purpose; but “one” because he is singular in love. He is a man because by great virtue he despises all present things; but he is one because he desires to enjoy only the vision of almighty God. Whoever perfectly despises earthly things is a man through strength; but if he does not ardently desire to see his Creator, he is not “one” in intention. The perfection of the man, therefore, is set forth in the proclamation of unity, so that one who powerfully despises the world may not divide his mind, but may gaze only upon heavenly things and sigh for those eternal joys that arise from the vision of the Creator.

Such indeed was the one who, confessing God, said: “What remains for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. LXXII, 25). Again he says: “Your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. XXVI, 8). For he who desired nothing on earth was certainly a man; but he who desired nothing either in heaven or on earth apart from God himself, who, having spurned everything, sought only his face, proved himself not merely a man but also “one.”

The Lord speaks of this unity in the Gospel concerning Martha, saying: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary” (Luke X, 41–42). [Col. 0049D] Speaking of the perfect number of believers, Luke likewise says: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV, 32). They had one heart because, through the intention of reason, they looked upon the Creator alone; they had one soul because, through the affection of love, they desired to see his face alone.

Hence the loving Prophet reflects within himself, saying: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI, 2). To obtain this unity, Truth, teaching, says: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 33).

[Col. 0050A]

2. This also concerns us, because we who, having renounced the world, have sought the solitude of a more secluded life are called monks. *Monos* is Greek; in Latin it means “one.” We are inscribed with this title of our name so that the sound of our designation may disclose to us the height of our dignity, and our mind may raise itself all the more ardently toward the vision of the Creator as it carries, as if displayed upon its forehead, the sublimity of the glory in which it ought always to remain.

But the sublimity of divine love is bestowed upon true elect persons only within the Catholic Church. Properly, then, the man who is called “one” is said to have been from Ramatha-zophim, from Mount Ephraim. *Ramatha*, as I have already said, is a Hebrew name, but in Latin speech it means “consummated vision.” This designation certainly suits holy Church, which was foreseen anciently by the prophets but established at the end of the ages in faith in the Redeemer. Holy Church is therefore called “consummated vision,” because through the Redeemer of the human race she was raised to the summit of religion, though formerly she had been seen only through the spirit of prophecy.

She is described as having been built at Zophim on Mount Ephraim (above, at the beginning of the allegorical exposition), because she is exalted in the highest contemplation of God and fruitful in spiritual virtues. *Zophim* means “watchtower” or “lookout”; *Ephraim*, “fruitful.” These names properly disclose the position of holy Church, which is high not only in the intention of vision but also in the excellence of her conduct.

By these names, too, the madness of heretics and the barrenness of other wicked persons are condemned. The former, because they depart from the straight path of faith, do not possess lofty contemplation; the latter, because they see what they ought to do rightly but always refuse to do it, possess a watchtower, as it were, but do not attain the mountain of virtues through an excellent life.

Holy Church, because she is exalted in Zophim—that is, in lofty contemplation—glories, saying: “Our way of life is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20). And because she has been established on the mountain of virtues through the fruit of good works, rejecting the crushed faith of the reprobate, she says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. II, 20, 26). Again, preaching, she says: “While we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Gal. VI, 10).

The man, therefore, who is called “one” is remembered as being from Mount Ephraim, because despising earthly things and desiring heavenly things benefits only the one who keeps himself within holy Church through the Catholic faith.

It follows:

[Col. 0050D]

> (Verse 1.) “And his name was Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph.”

3. We also explained this name above [Note: [Col. 0050D] No explanation of this name occurs above.], since from the Hebrew language it would be translated into ours as “fervor of God.” This name of the man certainly suits the order of the spiritual exposition. For one who is called “one man” must necessarily be reckoned as proceeding from the fervor of God. Who could either despise temporal things or love heavenly things without divine grace? Divine grace must indeed precede him, so that, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, the more ardently he loves what is highest, the more powerfully he despises what is lowest.

Four names of fathers are also written in the order of his genealogy, because those who believed in that same Redeemer of the human race throughout every part of the world through the writings of the four Evangelists were begotten in the faith of the Redeemer through their preaching.

He is also called an Ephrathite. One who comes from Mount Ephraim and is an Ephrathite is not barren in fertile land. For many within holy Church are counted by the name of faith, yet produce no fruits of action. When they come forth from the Church, they are considered, as it were, to be from a fruitful mountain; but because they themselves have no fruit of good works, they are not Ephrathites.

He is from Mount Ephraim but is not an Ephrathite who unlearns the Catholic faith in the Church but does not offer works worthy of the faith. To such people Truth threatens in the Gospel, saying: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI, 34). Again, under the figure of the fig tree, commanding the farmer of holy Church to remove the unfruitful soul, he says: “Cut it down; why should it occupy the ground?” (Luke XIII, 7). John the Baptist likewise threatens, saying: “Now the axe is laid to the root of the tree. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III, 10; Luke III, 9).

He had shown that those people were from Mount Ephraim but not Ephrathites, concerning whom Truth says in the Gospel by way of a parable: “He will destroy those evil men evilly and lease his vineyard to other farmers who will render its fruit to him in its seasons” (Matt. XXI, 41).

The man from Mount Ephraim, then, is called an Ephrathite because whoever among us holds the Catholic faith within holy Church, while casting away earthly things through the fervor of affection and loving heavenly things, must also be separated from the earthly things he despises by the labor of good works and prepared for the heavenly things he loves. Thus, because being in the Church without doing good works does not contribute to attaining the good of eternal salvation, the man who is said to be from Mount Ephraim is also remembered as having been an Ephrathite.

4. Hence he is described as having two wives, because he is joined to the active life through the fruitfulness of good works and to the contemplative life through love of inward delight. For this reason Phenenna is said to have had sons, but Hannah no sons. For what are the sons of the active life except the fruits of good works? And what is meant by Hannah’s having no sons except that immature contemplation does not quickly obtain the joys of inward contemplation that it has already begun to love?

The sons of the contemplative life are the joys of inward vision. But the mind that is beginning to contemplate eternal things reaches the enjoyment of them with greater difficulty insofar as it does not attend to their beauty. Who, then, can rejoice in the glory of a beauty that he does not see?

The mind that newly raises itself to contemplation of eternal goods rises toward them all the more slowly because it does not quickly lay aside the familiar darkness of its humanity. For while it cannot cast worldly cares away from itself, it carries dust, as it were, in its eyes, so that it cannot see what it desires to see.

The dust must first be removed from the eye, and then the eye must be refreshed. Dust is removed when all the images of corporeal things are taken away from the mind’s intention; the eye is refreshed when, through the practice of continuous meditation, that same intention of the mind is lifted toward eternal things. When, through long habit, it has learned to dwell in heavenly things, it gains purity through that same long habituation, so that, seeing eternal things more clearly, it may rejoice more fully in their glory.

Hannah is therefore said not to have had sons, so that not only the imperfection of one who is beginning may be signified, but also the loftiness of the contemplative life. For it is situated at a great summit of merits and cannot easily be possessed in the joy of its fruitfulness.

Hence Jacob desired Rachel as his wife (Gen. XXIX, 18 ff.), but Leah was first substituted for her, so that, in order to obtain Rachel’s beauty, the number of seven years might be doubled in service to his father-in-law. The lover of the contemplative life desires to attain it quickly in the abundance of eternal joy; yet the giver of all gifts, the Spirit, does not grant it quickly, lest he despise it as something cheap once it has been obtained, if its attainment is presented to him easily according to his wish. Rather, he enjoys it more sweetly and guards it more carefully the more difficultly he earns it.

Therefore it follows:

> (Verse 3.) And that man went up on appointed days to worship and sacrifice to the Lord of hosts at Shiloh.

5. He went up on appointed days because he gradually advances in the splendors of eternal vision. For what are those manifestations of inward light except the days of the chosen mind? They are appointed days because, by divine ordinance, they are arranged for those established in spiritual progress; they are also appointed days because we cannot be admitted into their brightness whenever we wish, but only when we are raised up by divine favor.

Sometimes he receives us into contemplation of inward light; at other times he allows us to fall even to the point of preferring the darkness of our humanity. He raises us, as it were, on appointed days, because he does not continually disclose the loveliness of inward light but reveals it according to the periods of his own ordering.

Our days, therefore, are those in which we are received into great splendors when the beauty of inward glory is revealed to us. They are called appointed days because enjoying the innermost light depends not on our striving but on divine favor.

Often, after prolonged silence, persistent supplications, and frequent sighs, we beg that the glory of inward light be opened to us, yet we are not found worthy to be received into its loveliness. Often we do nothing of the sort in desire for it, but divine grace suddenly precedes us, raises us from the depths of our weakness, carries us into heavenly things, and unexpectedly shows us the glory of its light.

We ascend, then, on appointed days because we cannot be raised into contemplation of heavenly things by our own striving but only by divine ordering. The days of ascent are also called days because, when we do not enjoy that lofty light, we are below; and when we are taken up into its high vision, we recognize how low we had been lying before the hour of our assumption.

Then we displease ourselves in what we were, but please ourselves in what we are, because the mind, already absorbed by love of heavenly things, rejoices in the light it enjoys and rejects all earthly things with profound horror.

Hence blessed Peter, when he is taken up the mountain, when he is overshadowed by a bright cloud, and when the glory of the transfigured Savior is shown to him, says: “It is good for us to be here, Lord” (Matt. XVII, 4). For because by the gift of almighty God he is now deemed worthy to be present at sublime things [Note: [Col. 0053D] Gilot., “to be present.”], he loves there an incomparable good beyond words, and, on account of its beauty, condemns all passing things as foul.

6. But what does it mean that this same man is said to ascend from his city? What else is a city than the stronghold of those dwelling together? And what is this city except the perfect guardianship of a heart fortified by vigilance? Like cohabiting citizens, it protects them with lofty walls, because, while it diligently watches over the virtues that must be guarded, the crafty enemy does not disturb their inward peace.

The wise man commanded us to remain in this city when he said: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. IV, 23). The Lord likewise commands his disciples, saying: “But you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV, 49).

We sit in the city when, through daily concern, we rest in the defense of inward guardianship. As we sit there, we are clothed with power from on high, because, already prepared as a dwelling place for the Holy Spirit, we are raised through his grace into contemplation of heavenly glory.

In this statement, then, that the Ephrathite man is said to ascend from his city, what else is indicated than the fault of our negligence? We wish to search out heavenly things through contemplation, yet we possess neither the guardianship of our heart nor even of our body.
