Often we look indecently, listen to idle things, speak excessively, and take sleep and food not for the body’s restoration but for the use of pleasure.

Thus, when we wish to examine obscure matters, behold heavenly things, leave our darkness, and taste the sweetness within, we are repelled from that secret place all the more deservedly as we more negligently scatter the strengths of our fortification. Ascending is now more difficult for us in proportion as, having fallen back upon ourselves, we have not taken care to raise ourselves into the height of vigilance by erecting the fortifications of the heart.

Let the man therefore ascend from his city, so that one who desires to advance through inward contemplation may order his outward senses, govern his mind, and, as one received into lofty fortifications, await until heavenly illumination visits him. Whoever now watches in readiness for the ascent of the appointed days becomes worthy of the guardianship of purity, so that he may be visited more frequently by divine favor.

But when he is said to ascend, the reason for his ascent is also mentioned, when it is added: “To worship and sacrifice to the Lord of hosts at Shiloh.”

7. Whoever is lifted to the summit of divine contemplation looks upon all things there in the light that illuminates him: both what may wondrously terrify him and what may ineffably delight him. For as that supreme vision opens itself to the chosen mind, it mercifully displays both the unfathomable abyss of God’s judgments and the abundance of his goodness, so that it casts the beholder down in great fear and raises him up in immense joy.

He is cast down by terror so that he may abandon the state of worldly affection; he is soothed by joy so that he may desire more ardently what he begins to taste beforehand of the Creator’s goodness.

He worships when, having considered the immensity of almighty power, he submits himself to the Creator in such a way that he is not lifted up against spiritual conduct by the impulses of carnal desire. In worshiping he sacrifices, because the more humbly he prostrates himself in divine veneration, the more sweetly he is refreshed by the delight of that supreme brightness.

To worship, then, for one who ascends, is to submit to almighty God with the great reverence of chaste love; to sacrifice is to be ineffably delighted by the sweetness of divine light. For the chosen mind consecrates itself to God as a spiritual sacrifice when, in that ineffable joy of its elevation, the fire of divine charity kindles it more ardently.

The devotion to God of each chosen person is therefore displayed under the Ephrathite man: he is said both to worship and to sacrifice, because the chosen mind desires to behold heavenly things in such a way that, advancing through spiritual vision, it both crushes the entire state of carnal life and receives the fullness of eternal joy.

Even if someone in the flesh is not taken up to this height of supreme contemplation, nevertheless, insofar as concerns that spiritual conduct into which he advances through the ascent of contemplation, before he advances he is in a certain sense carnal. For this itself is almost carnal: being unable, through the height of vision, to separate oneself from attention to corporeal things.

8. But so that human audacity’s rashness may be restrained, he is first said to worship and afterward to sacrifice. The ascent of the contemplative is properly ordered if it begins from fear. What else is fear than the preordained purification of the chosen mind as it passes over to contemplate divine glory?

He deserved to gaze upon the rays of divine light more purely insofar as, cast down by stronger fear, he is presented more purified to the inward vision of Majesty [Note: [Col. 0054D] Gilot., “will deserve.”].

Thus the conduct of this Ephrathite is shown outwardly to us so that it may reasonably demonstrate what must be done inwardly by those striving toward perfection. Therefore, while we desire to be sprinkled with the brightness of supreme glory, let us fix the daring of our presumption in this passage through fear, so that the more reverently we fear almighty God, the more perceptively we may see the glory of his goodness.

The greatness of this fear is sometimes also inflicted upon the chosen mind after the display of joyful vision. When this happens, it does not happen in order to purify the mind for the vision of glory but to guard it from pride. Hence Peter, James, and John first saw the glory of the transfigured Lord; afterward, struck with fear, they fell, lest, becoming proud, they should lose what they had deserved to see after being humbly raised up (Matt. XVII, 2 ff.).

Sometimes, therefore, worship precedes sacrifice; sometimes sacrifice precedes worship—but this occurs by divine ordering, not through our striving. The Ephrathite man is described as having ascended so that he might first worship and afterward sacrifice, because the order is perfect when we are lifted from the reverence born of fear of divine severity to the joyful contemplation of Majesty.

Yet divine clemency sometimes so exhilarates chosen minds by pouring in its sweetness that it does not lead them into the greatness of fear. Hence it follows:

> (Verse 4.) Then the day came, and Elkanah sacrificed.

9. Why does he say, “The day came, and he sacrificed,” and not, “He worshiped and sacrificed,” except because, as I said above, we are often raised by divine favor to behold the glory of divine brightness in such a way that at that time we are troubled by no consideration mingled with judgments?

Although the chosen soul never attends almighty God without great reverence, nevertheless it sacrifices, as it were, and does not worship, when it enjoys the bliss of that supreme joy in such a way that it is not shaken by any prostration of fear.

She had come into this disposition who said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I, 1). What disposition of fear does she display who desires to be kissed? It is also written concerning Moses: “For he spoke with God as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend” [Note: [Col. 0055D] Gilot., “with his friend.”] (Exod. XXXIII, 11). For, as if the day had come, Sacred Scripture shows him sacrificing in such a way that no worship of fear had prostrated him.

Here I observe that he is said to ascend “to worship and sacrifice,” yet when the day came he is not said to have worshiped and sacrificed, but only to have sacrificed. There are therefore some days on which we ascend in order to worship and sacrifice; there is another day which, when it comes, causes us to sacrifice.

When we are suspended by our own striving in meditation on divine things, these are like the appointed days of our ascent, because we behold certain rays of spiritual light, appoint certain stages for ourselves, and are raised from the depths of our humanity to a certain height. But since nothing is accomplished in these meditations without divine grace, and since we cannot succeed either in instilling fear into ourselves or in presenting the sweetness of divine delight, they are indeed days of ascent on which we determine to worship and sacrifice, yet on them we neither worship nor sacrifice.

Another day comes, and we sacrifice, because we are suddenly sprinkled with the light of divine grace and receive an ineffable abundance of love from the glory of his Majesty. This day, then, is not one of those days but follows them. For although we cannot receive this abundance of divine grace by our own ordering, we shall never deserve it unless we take every care to remain in spiritual brightness by meditating, reading daily, praying, and dwelling upon such spiritual things as lie within our power.

The day is said to have come in order to signify heavenly favor, because when it visits chosen souls, this is not within our power but arises from divine goodness.

It follows:

> (Verses 4 and 5.) And he gave portions to Phenenna, and to her sons and daughters. But to Hannah he gave one portion, sadly, because he loved Hannah.

10. The sons of Phenenna are the counsels of the holy mind that grow through the practice of piety in the active life. These sons receive portions with their mother when counsels of piety grow rich in good works through devotion, for the splendor of heavenly grace.

Indeed, the pious mind, the more loftily it is raised in divine contemplation, extends itself the more devotedly in holy action. The portions of this mother and her sons are the preparations for holy works.

But Hannah is given one portion, sadly, because through contemplation she desires heavenly things and, as long as she is hindered in this vale of time and does not obtain the heavenly things she loves, she has the nourishment of refreshment only in tears. She keeps herself fasting whenever, remembering that she has been cast away from eternal joys, she cannot weep.

She therefore receives one portion from the sad man because she is never refreshed according to her desire except when she is satisfied by weeping. The Ephrathite man gives it to her sadly; when he gives Phenenna her portion, he is not sad, because he rejoices in the preparation of good works. But as long as what he loves is delayed, he does not rejoice in heavenly joys.

He had certainly given this portion to Hannah who, seeing himself excluded from eternal goods, spoke, saying: “My tears have been my bread day and night, while they say to me every day: Where is your God?” (Ps. XLI, 4).

But the imperfection of one who is beginning is signified when the Ephrathite’s one wife is said to afflict and greatly distress the other. For no conflict of wives is assigned to the perfect person, since firm experience has already taught him to arrange distinctly the necessity of work and the intention of contemplation. He possesses both wives as if in peace when he neither assigns the times of work to contemplation nor disturbs the leisure of contemplation through the intention of work.

> (Verse 6.) Her rival also afflicted her and greatly distressed her, so that she reproached her because the Lord had closed her womb.

11. Hannah is afflicted by her rival when an immoderate devotion to good works disturbs the repose of inward vision. She is afflicted when the one who is shown to be nobler is placed before her; and she is greatly distressed because the contemplation of the chosen mind is constricted when one who desires to be in contemplation of sublime things expands himself excessively in the works of the active life.

For *angere* means “to constrict.” The vision of the mind is constricted when, hindered by the occupations of works, it is not at all expanded in that immensity of inward light. And because she is said to be greatly distressed, it should be noted that immoderate concern for good works also harms contemplation considerably.

Phenenna greatly distresses Hannah because, when the mind is excessively devoted to the active life, it is very difficult for it, once occupied in arranging earthly matters, to rise powerfully into the vision of heavenly things.

Phenenna also reproaches her as if she were barren, because, while we quickly produce the fruits of good works from the active life and cannot easily reach the joys of inward contemplation, this life appears barren when, in our inexperience, we despair of its fruitfulness.

Thus, while we love Phenenna for her fruitfulness, Hannah is afflicted, distressed, and marked with the reproach of barrenness, because the less we restrain our concern for good actions with the discretion we ought to exercise, the more difficult we make the purity of contemplation, since we do not retain the nobler life with outstanding diligence.

But because she has begun to ascend to higher things, if she is strong in her purpose, she endures such temptations and does not despair. She leans upon the heights of contemplation she has begun to pursue and scorns consolation from the food of action, since she has desired to delight in the Creator’s appearance alone.

Accordingly, it is aptly added:

> (Verse 7.) But Hannah wept and did not take food.

12. In weeping, the ardent desire for divine contemplation is shown; in the rejection of food, contempt for passing joy [Note: [Col. 0057D] Other editions: “contempt.”]. The mind that desires inward things with fervent longings weeps and takes no food when it rejects the blandishment of earthly joy and, with persistent sighs, longs for the loveliness of heavenly light to be poured into it.

He was rejecting this food who said: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. LXXVI, 3). But he who disdained to take the food of consolation from the delight of created things says that he found the banquets of his delights in the Creator alone: “I remembered God, and I was delighted” (ibid., 4).

He was urging his weeping wife toward these banquets when he said: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall still confess him, the salvation of my countenance and my God” (Ps. XLII, 5).

This exhortation is also recognized here, since her husband asks why she weeps, why she does not eat, and why she has an afflicted heart. It is as if he said: “Why are you saddened by not possessing the perfection of contemplation? If you do not obtain it in your inexperience, you will obtain it as you advance.”

Hence she who, afflicted by her rival, refused to eat, ate when encouraged by her husband; for she who, by wiser counsel, despises what is below has the perfection of contemplation in hope, although she does not yet possess it in the strength of experience [Note: [Col. 0058D] Other editions: “who despises what is below by the counsel of the elder.”].

The joy of renewed hope is almost food for contemplation that is failing and collapsing. At the voice of her husband, therefore, Hannah is refreshed when the intention of contemplation, shaken by temptation, is roused by the one who has begun to love her toward hope of her progress.

Having taken food, she rose, poured out prayers to almighty God, and vowed to him a male child, if she should deserve to receive one from him.

13. He vows a son born to almighty God who seeks the joy of contemplation as the fruit of the mind, not as a source of empty praise. But carnal superiors are often accustomed vehemently to oppose those earnest in their desire for contemplation; for they think that those who seek a more secluded life act all the more ineptly the more they themselves are ignorant of the power of inward sweetness.

If they sometimes rage against spiritual subjects in harsh words, they must be calmed by the most humble reasoning. For if they irrationally rise up against those acting rightly, reverence for the superior order requires that they be honored even when they exceed the bounds of reason.

Holy Scripture aptly represents both groups—the carnal superiors and the spiritual subjects—in Eli and Hannah. While Eli was sitting before the doors of the Lord’s temple and Hannah was praying, Eli watched her mouth and called her drunk. But she, patiently enduring the insults, displayed humility in her reply together with the truth of her reasoning. She asserted that, as his handmaid, she was speaking out of great pain and sorrow; she not only calmed his mind raging against her, but also turned it toward prayer for obtaining the fruit of her desire.

14. But since we have discussed these final matters according to the historical sense, we shall not act improperly if we investigate our instruction in the words of sacred history somewhat more subtly. If, then, the order of events is considered, she first ate and drank; afterward she was bitter in spirit, prayed to the Lord while weeping copiously, then made a vow and multiplied her prayers. What does Hannah’s multiplication of prayers signify except that perfection of the elect to which the excellent Teacher exhorts us when he says: “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. 5:17)? For no one except the perfect person can pray without ceasing. To pray without ceasing is always to attend upon the Creator through the affection of supplication. But one who is still weighed down by the weakness of imperfection does not beseech the Lord without ceasing, because even during the time of prayer the mind slips away from his presence through distraction.

It is rightly said that the holy woman made a vow before multiplying her prayers, because unless someone presents himself wholly as a heavenly being through the rigor of his purpose, he is drawn away from the affection of supplication all the more frequently as, through the mind’s instability, he turns in a circle toward worldly concerns and is not held before the Lord by vigilant custody. But the mind of the elect can devote itself to a spiritual purpose and to heavenly joys if it has already learned to weep copiously; if, through the abundance of its tears, it has learned to taste the sweetness above; and if, occupied in the joy of that inner refreshment of its own, it disdains to look back upon earthly things. Thus Hannah is plainly described as having wept copiously before making her vow, because no one can present himself wholly as a heavenly being in this way, by forgetting earthly things, unless, kindled by great tears, he has learned to receive the sweetness of inward delight as the consolation of a mind already dead to the world.

And because this consolation of tears is not received in the joy of the soul unless one first afflicts oneself through the bitterness of compunction, and pierces with the goad of salutary sadness whatever joy within oneself still lives from the passing world, Hannah is reported to have wept first in bitterness of spirit and thus to have been able to weep copiously. Solomon aptly indicates this when he says: “The stranger does not share in the joy of the heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul” (Prov. 14:10). The stranger is one who still directs the purpose of his delight toward external goods. Such a person is not admitted into the joy of the embittered heart, because no one can experience inward gladness unless he takes care perfectly to despise what is external.

But we must further note that she is reported to have risen before all these things, and that before she rose she had eaten and drunk. What is the food of the elect soul except, in the words of Truth, “every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4)? And what is it for the soul to rise except to raise itself to the condition of heavenly purpose? Thus she is said to have risen before she was bitter in spirit, and to have eaten and drunk before she rose, because the elect soul cannot grieve over the misery of the present life unless it stretches itself toward those things it has lost in heaven; nor does it raise itself toward those highest things if it fasts from the nourishment of sacred Scripture. Therefore, in order to rise, we eat and drink, because we are lifted to the height of heavenly love when we are strengthened by the profounder and clearer meanings of sacred Scripture.

Then, if we rise, we acquire bitterness of heart, because, while we are carried upward through love, the things below offer us no blandishments of joy but the harshness of affliction. From bitterness of spirit we now ascend to the streams of tears, because when we are pierced by continual and powerful compunction, we are able to weep more abundantly over the evils we encounter in this valley of tears, over those to come that we fear, and over the eternal goods that we have lost.

From there we proceed to the secrets of the vows that are to be made, because when the abundance of tears buries us beneath everything that delights outwardly, it displays us to heavenly eyes as though we had become wholly heavenly beings; and we make vows in which eternal goods please us in such a way that our mind does not defile itself with anything earthly or carnal. Then the multiplication of prayers follows our progress, because we seek eternal things in prayer with greater willingness, frequency, and urgency, insofar as we already draw breath in the consolation of future goods alone.

“In the morning they worship, and they return to their own city.”

15. After the multiplication of prayers, to worship in the morning with Hannah his wife is to preserve the virtue of humility amid the great gifts of the virtues. And because the soul, still weighed down by the burden of this corruption, cannot remain longer in that sublime vision, they are appropriately reported to have returned to their own city.

When the elect soul is driven away from contemplation of God because of the burden of its weakness, it ought to have built structures of defense, so that, having fallen back upon itself, it may hold itself on high, from where it may rise again without difficulty to that same height of inward love. This is also said by the prophet under the figure of Jerusalem, concerning the elect soul: “Stand upon the heights and see the gladness that will come to you from your God” (Baruch 4:36; 5:5). It is as though he said: Although you cannot remain continually in contemplation of God, do not allow yourself to be cast down to the depths, so that from the lofty towers of your guardianship you may climb without difficulty to contemplate the one you desire.

She returns to her own city, Ramah, when, driven away from the vision of the divine Majesty, she remains fixed in contemplation of the holy angels. But when she cannot prevail to think about that more subtle nature—that is, the angelic nature—if she returns in meditation to the blessed martyrs or to other elect persons who have already been received into eternity, then, because she thinks about their perfect glory, she is undoubtedly received into her own city: the one who is forbidden to remain in the heights is nevertheless permitted to dwell there. The city of Ramah is rightly called her own, because whatever she loves familiarly she undoubtedly believes to be hers. He knew that this city was his who said: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. 5:1).

[Note: [Col. 0059D] “But eternal in the heavens” is absent in Gilot.]

Again he says: “Jerusalem, which is above, is our mother” (Gal. 4:26). But whoever cannot return to that sublime city should nevertheless return to his own city, Ramah; and whoever is cast down from that highest place should be held in the vision of this Church, which still journeys below but shines with the radiance of a sublime life. From here he will be able to return again to behold the splendor of the lofty and true light, insofar as he does not allow that understanding—which the burden of the flesh draws back from the secret place of inward light—to be cast down to the lowest things of earth.

[Note: [Col. 0060D] Vaticanus: “does not cast it down to weakness.”]

16. What is it, then, that Hannah conceives and gives birth to after the cycle of days, except that contemplation, once raised to the beauty of the Creator, does not receive the joy of perfect devotion? She is therefore said to have conceived and given birth after the cycle of days, because, while contemplation is habitually snatched up to heavenly things, it receives in the vision of the heavenly light the gift of the fecundity it desired.

The cycle of days is the infusion of divine light. This light is enclosed within its circuit by many days when it illumines the mind with a single radiance but reveals the rays of its splendor to it in stages of dispensational manifestation, until it grasps a more perfect joy from a fuller manifestation.

Or certainly Hannah conceives after the cycle of days because, as long as the inexperience of contemplation shakes the mind’s gaze in the circle of mutability, the mind itself does not rise to receive the full joy of inward Majesty. Days pass, as it were, in a circle when the mind of one beginning raises itself to the summit of contemplation, but the radiance of the light it has perceived scarcely keeps it, still moist with dew and wandering, fixed in its own brightness. Thus she conceives after the cycle of days because the soul is first led from the whirl of its changeability into the strength of stability; and when, through practice, it has learned to stand fixed in contemplation, it apprehends the joy of perfect devotion in the fruit of its fecundity. It also gives birth to what it has conceived when it makes its neighbors aware of the glory of the heavenly Majesty.

17. The boy who has been born is brought to the tabernacle with three calves, because we ought to give thanks to the supreme Trinity for the abundance of the spiritual gift. Concerning these calves the prophet, beseeching the Lord, says: “Take away all iniquity, and receive what is good, and we will repay the calves of our lips” (Hos. 14:3). It is as though he said: For the abundance of your gifts we will offer sacrifices of praise through the service of our lips.

The boy is brought to the house of the Lord to be offered when the progress of a sacred mind is revealed to the teachers of the holy Church, so that, when it is examined in the discussion of the wise, it may in no way be stained by the deception of the crafty enemy. The house of the Lord may also signify the eternal homeland. Exulting over this, the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5).

The boy is brought to the house of the Lord when the elect mind is raised on high and strives to give thanks to almighty God for all in which it makes spiritual progress, recognizing that the gifts of its advancement have been bestowed upon it by him. It is rightly said that one calf is sacrificed when three are reported to have been brought, because although the Trinity of persons is sung in the divine praises by the confession of the faithful, the inseparable unity of those same persons is proclaimed.

But what kind or what extent of praise is there if it is not devout? Accordingly, three measures of flour are aptly joined to the same number of calves, so that we may be satisfied through devotion with what we say with our mouths in the praises of God. For he offers a calf without flour who utters words in praise of God but, with a wandering mind, does not attend to what he says.

But if, while uttering words in praise or prayer to God, we become joyful, then, by mingling joy with understanding, we join a jar of the wine that gladdens the human heart to the flour. This is clearly indicated by the one who says in his longing: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Ps. 66:7–8). He led three calves to the tabernacle who, in praising God and repeating the name of his divinity, set forth the distinct properties of the persons. But when he says “may they fear,” not “may they fear them,” but “may they fear him,” the one who brought three calves plainly sacrificed one.

And because he mixed flour with the calves and wine with the flour, he exults, saying: “To him I cried with my mouth, and I exulted beneath my tongue” (Ps. 65:17). For when he cried out, he led a sacrificial calf, as it were, to be offered; but he could not exult under his tongue if he did not understand the lofty words of his prayer. Thus, when he cried out, he understood what he cried out; and when he exulted in the offering to almighty God, he had not only a calf but also measures of flour and a jar of wine. Therefore the calf, flour, and wine are the praise of God, the understanding of praise, and the devout joy of the mind.

But why are a measure and a jar named in the offering to God, unless because they are names of measures? Paul also explains what this indicates spiritually when he says: “Each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that” (I Cor. 7:7).

[Note: [Col. 0061D] In Gilot, “his own” is lacking.]

Here Truth likewise says: “They will give into your lap a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing” (Luke 6:38). Sacred Scripture commands us to preserve this measure, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0061D] Where is this found in sacred Scripture? Perhaps Ecclesiasticus 3:22, where we read, “Do not seek what is too high for you,” which signifies the same thing.]

“Do not lift a burden above you.”

The elect soul must take great care to offer these three things to almighty God with the fervor of pious devotion and with zeal for manifest truth. Hence Hannah’s son is also said to have been offered to the priest. We do the same if, as we advance in holy conduct and already fruitful minds bring forth the fruit of spiritual joys, we bring before the examination of our superiors everything that is generated within us from heavenly contemplation.

And because elect men do not abandon the good of their humility amid sublime gifts, it follows:

(Verse 28.) “And they worshiped the Lord there.”

18. They worship the Lord in the house of the Lord who raise themselves with lofty minds to contemplation of the heavenly homeland, but through humility prostrate themselves before almighty God and are raised so sublimely with their whole heart in the power of the Spirit. We have touched on these matters briefly, not in their historical order but in summary, expounding their historical or moral meaning, so that we may investigate somewhat more fully, according to a moral and typological explanation, the words of the spiritual song that follows.

CHAPTER III

(II Kings 2:1.) “And Hannah prayed and said: ‘My heart has exulted in the Lord.’”

1. We have already shown that the type of the holy Church lies hidden in the person of Hannah. After the boy has been born, she declares that she exults in the Lord, because she did not swell with empty pride over having drawn the gentile people to faith in the Redeemer; rather, she fixed the purpose of her joy in him from whom she had received the gifts of her fecundity.

In these words she indicates the character of her joy in such a way that she simultaneously reveals the cause of that same exultation. The barren woman wept; the mother giving birth exulted, thereby foreshadowing the conduct of the holy Church. She grieves that she has been cast from the joys of paradise into this valley of tears, but she patiently bears the hardships of her exile for the sake of winning souls. She is accustomed to exult only in this: that, amid the misery of the time by which she is oppressed, the losses of the heavenly homeland may be restored through the glory of her fecundity, as the elect are multiplied.

Therefore she says: “My heart has exulted in the Lord,” because she has obtained the fruit of her purpose. Here it must be noted that she is said to have prayed what she utters in triumph. For it was stated above: “And Hannah prayed and said: ‘My heart has exulted in the Lord.’” But since she is understood to ask God for nothing, why is she said to have prayed? Because the holy woman knew through the spirit of prophecy that this would happen, earnestly desired it to happen, and speaks both in exultation and in prayer. She exulted in certainty about what was to come, earnestly desiring that what she knew through the revelation of the mystery should happen.

The holy Church likewise recalls, proclaims, and prays for divine benefits by loving and venerating them, because outwardly she carries out in speech what inwardly she desires with marvelous longing to take place, and she venerates what has taken place with great devotion. Therefore she says: “My heart has exulted in the Lord,” because she does not turn the gifts she receives for the fruit of eternal joy toward temporary gladness.

It follows:

[Col. 0062D] (Verse 1.) “And my horn has been exalted in my God.”

2. What is Hannah’s horn except the power of the holy Church? This horn wondrously raised itself when the Son of God, through the humanity he assumed, made himself a participant in our nature. The horn of the holy Church was therefore exalted in that humanity in which our nature now shines, raised above the angels.

But in asserting this God and Savior to be uniquely her own, the holy Church subtly displays the rejection of the Synagogue. Our horn, then, has been exalted in our saving God, because the sublimity of ecclesiastical power has been raised for us in the humanity of the Redeemer. Hence it is said of the same Redeemer through Zechariah: “He has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant, just as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets” (Luke 1:69–70). In reporting that her horn has been exalted, she subtly indicates that previously she had possessed a horn that had not been exalted.

The holy Church had a horn before the Redeemer’s coming, because in the patriarchs and prophets she had received from God both an upright order of life and the power to correct those who sinned. Yet she did not have an exalted horn, because, although she could live justly, she could not return to the joys of paradise without the Redeemer’s presence.

Now, however, the horn of the holy Church has been exalted, since we have received the Redeemer of the world who has come. Through his grace we can not only live rightly but also pass into the joys of paradise, because he has now died and risen for us; through his death death itself has perished, and paradise has opened itself to his faithful.

Our horn, then, has been exalted in our God, because, now that the grace of the Holy Spirit has been poured out upon the multitude of the elect, we see the image of the Redeemer impressed upon them: those who despise all earthly things, flee the pleasures of the flesh, and abandon their possessions shine with a power all the higher, since the holy Church did not possess such great emblems of virtue in the multitude of former times.

Our horn has been exalted in our saving God, because “as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12). Our Savior wished to exalt this horn when he said: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and upon all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19). Again he declares: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). Again he promises: “You will sit upon thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (ibid., 19:28).

Let Hannah therefore say: “My horn has been exalted in my God,” so that the glory of the holy Church may be signified—the Church that receives the singular summit of power from the presence of the Redeemer.

And because she is now extended throughout the whole world, although once she was distressed by persecutions within Judea, it follows:

(Verse 1.) “My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies.”

3. Who else are to be understood as the enemies of the Church except the Jews? Over them she has an enlarged mouth, because she now moves the tongues of all the gentile peoples who have become faithful against their unbelief. The mouth of the holy Church has been enlarged because she is spread throughout the whole world; and while she teaches all nations through the preaching of truth, she reproves the folly of the Jews as though with an enlarged mouth.

And because she was able to do this because she joyfully received the Redeemer of the world who came in the flesh, she explains the cause of her enlarged mouth, saying:

(Verse 1.) “Because I have rejoiced in your salvation.”

4. We have already learned who God’s salvation is. Concerning him Isaiah also prophesies, saying: “All flesh will see the salvation of God; all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of God” (Isa. 52:10; Ps. 97:3).

In our language, Jesus is called “Salvation” (*Salutaris*). Concerning him Habakkuk also promises himself joy, saying: “I will rejoice in God my Jesus” (Hab. 3:18). Behold: in the words of the ancient Jews, the Lord Jesus is affirmed to be God. Yet now the Jews await a Savior whom they by no means believe to be God.

Perhaps the Jews try to reject this in their own speech, and, while they interpret Jesus as “Savior,” understand “God the Savior” to mean not the person of the Only-Begotten but the Father. Nevertheless, in the same passage something follows by which the person of the Only-Begotten is demonstrated more clearly: “Lord God,” he says, “my strength, establish my feet in completion, and set me upon the heights, that I may overcome in his glory” (ibid., 19).

Behold, he speaks to God, saying: “Set me upon the heights.” But because he says, “I shall overcome in his glory,” the one of whom he speaks is certainly another. Who, then, is the one of whom he speaks except the Only-Begotten Son of God, whom he believes to be not only true man but also God?

Thus, when he speaks to God, saying, “I will rejoice in God my Jesus, and I will overcome in his glory,” he demonstrates not another God but another person of God. These are the arguments of the holy Church; these are her invincible assertions, spread throughout the whole world against the unbelief of the Jews.

The holy Church therefore has an enlarged mouth over her enemies, because now, by God’s authority, she is known everywhere, and from this the unbelief of the Jews is refuted. Let those who deny God’s Salvation hear the cause of her enlarged mouth, and let them be struck by the joy of our Salvation as by an argument for their own confusion. They can be struck, but they do not wish to cease from their blasphemies.

The world has now received God’s Salvation; all flesh has seen it, but the Jew does not believe, because, as I have said, he awaits a Savior who is not God. Let them therefore hear the prophet’s curse: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. 17:5). The Jews trust in a man, since they refuse to believe in the Redeemer while they await Antichrist at the end of the world.

To their confusion the Psalmist proclaims: “All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of God” (Ps. 97:3). It is as though he were confounding the unbelief of the Jews by saying: Why do you postpone your visions into the future? The one you await has already come; the one you had as promised has already appeared to all the ends of the earth. When you closed your eyes, he passed by; indeed, you have become so blind that such a great light stood before you and you did not see it.

“Therefore, shout joyfully to the Lord, all the earth; sing and exult and sing psalms. Sing psalms to our God on the lyre and with the voice of a psalm, with wrought trumpets and the voice of a horn. Shout joyfully in the presence of the Lord the King. Let the sea and its fullness be moved, the world and all who dwell in it. The rivers will clap their hands together; the mountains will exult before the face of the Lord” [Note: Gilot reads “will have exulted before the face of the Lord.”] “because he has come, because he has come to judge the earth” (ibid. 4 ff.).

It is as though he said: Because they are weighed down by such immense blindness that they have not deserved to see at all, rejoice all the more abundantly, you who have seen. But to show how wondrous and ineffable the joy should be, he piles up signs of rejoicing, saying: “Shout joyfully, sing, and sing psalms.” Desiring also to indicate the celebration of joy, he enumerates its instruments, saying: “Sing psalms to the Lord on the lyre, and on the lyre and with the voice of a psalm, with wrought trumpets and the voice of a horn; shout joyfully in the presence of the Lord the King.”

What does “in the presence of the King” mean except “in the knowledge of the Redeemer”? But he explains by how many this solemnity of joy should be celebrated, saying: “Let the sea and its fullness be moved, the world and all who dwell in it.” O unhappy Judea! The ends of the earth have seen the salvation of God; all the earth, moved, shouts joyfully; the whole world rejoices; the rivers clap their hands; the mountains exult. But the impious hearts of the Jews do not believe and are struck by the punishment of their envy in the darkness of their blindness.

Yet the one whom they do not fear to blaspheme the holy Church commends more earnestly, saying:

(Verse 2.) “There is none holy like the Lord.”

5. In the description of the Redeemer, everything incomparable is signified. The true Redeemer is shown precisely by this: that in everything said for his glory no one is compared with him. For he redeemed all, and he surpasses all.

This is rightly said against Judea, which despises the Redeemer with all the greater boldness because it remembers having had many men who shone with great praise for holiness. Hence, when reproaching the man born blind after his healing, they say: “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he is from” (John 9:28–29). Again they glory and say: “We are Abraham’s seed, and we have never been slaves to anyone” (John 8:33).

But Moses was a man, Abraham was a man, and Christ was a man. Nevertheless, Moses and Abraham were taken up for speech with God, whereas Christ was taken up into divinity. They were taken up for ministry; he, as the Only-Begotten, was taken up for kingship. Hence he says: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15).

“There is none holy like the Lord.” Sacred Scripture also testifies to this, saying: “In him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:9). Hence John says: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16).

“There is none holy like the Lord.” For in the assertion that he is Lord, the excellence of his holiness is commended. But the Jews assert that Christ, whom they await, is a mere man, and yet they believe that he will be their Lord and uniquely holy. The Psalmist, however, rejecting them, exhorts us to the joy of faith, saying: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness. Enter into his presence with exultation; know that the Lord himself is God” (Ps. 100 [Vulg. 99]:1–3).

They call him Lord who is not God. Therefore we should shout joyfully; we should serve with gladness, since we have such a Lord—one who is also truly believed to be God and who has confirmed by incomparable miracles the majesty of divinity that he asserted in himself. Those who deny his invisible divinity should therefore believe on the basis of his manifest works.

But how wondrous is that holiness which sanctifies sinners! Hence he says of the sinful woman: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). Recognizing this excellence of holiness, the woman suffering from the flow of blood said: “If I touch even the fringe of his garment, I shall be saved” (Matt. 9:21). But who would have confirmed her faith if the effect of her faith had not become manifest? For as soon as she touched his garment, the flow of blood stopped.

“There is none holy like the Lord,” therefore, because whoever was able to become holy received from him the gift by which he could be holy. The holy Church indicates this in the following words, turning to the same Redeemer out of her overflowing love:

(Verse 2.) “For there is none other beside you.”

6. “Holy” is understood. There would be someone holy beside him if anyone could possess the spirit of sanctification without the gift of the Only-Begotten. But who would dare assert this of human beings, when it is not at all established even concerning angels? For it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 33:6). The Word of the Lord is the Only-Begotten Son of God. The evangelist John identifies him when he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). If, then, even angels are believed to have been sanctified in the Son, it is much more firmly believed of human beings that they cannot find the grace of sanctification outside him.

7. This may also be understood without supplying any omitted word. When, therefore, she says, “There is none other beside you,” what else is signified in the Redeemer except the unchangeability of the divine essence? Hence he says to the blaspheming Jews: “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8:58). In Genesis he likewise reveals the same thing to Moses, saying: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14).

For the Only-Begotten God, to be means never to be otherwise. This state is as far removed from all mortals as it is clearly known that they are changed in many ways at every moment. This may also pertain to the condition of righteousness, because for the elect, to be means to remain in God through righteousness.

And because the Only-Begotten is God, there is no one outside him, since none of the elect exists except in him. If this is referred to his divinity in such a way that the understanding of his humanity is by no means excluded—for no one can be righteous who does not possess faith in the divine Incarnation—then the Jews are struck by each of these words. By despising the Redeemer, they await Antichrist, who is plainly proved not to be God.

Hence it is said through blessed Job: “Let his companions dwell in his tabernacle, he who is not” (Job 18:15). The tabernacle of Antichrist is the love of unbelief, by which he contradicts faith in the Redeemer. The Jews now remain in this tabernacle, because, while they lovingly inhabit the condition of their unbelief, they fight against the Redeemer.

They are also reported to be companions of him “who is not,” because in their purpose they assist the devil, who, having fallen from love of that supreme essence, immediately lost true being. For him “not to be” means being unable to return through participation in love to that supreme and blessed essence.

And because the Jewish people possessed not only the arduous way of life of their ancient fathers but also the display of miracles as an occasion for increasing their arrogance, it is added:

(Verse 2.) “And there is none mighty like our God.”

8. It is as though he were restraining Judea in its empty boasting, saying: Those whom you assert to have accomplished great things were mere men; the one whom I proclaim was not only a holy man but also powerful God. When strength is considered, excellence is indicated, because all human strength is utterly weak in comparison with divinity.

Yet in this passage the assertion of divinity does not prove the excellence of the work; rather, the incomparable nature of the strength demonstrates the truth of the divinity. It is as though he said: It is known that he uttered what is true because he confirmed by incomparable works the divinity that he asserted in himself. Hence he says of himself: “If I had not done among them the works that no one else has done, they would not have sin” (John 15:24).

Now the works themselves must be examined. Moses divided the sea (Exod. 14:12); Elijah divided the river (IV Kings 2:8); our Lord Jesus walked upon the sea (Matt. 14:24). What is more splendid: to provide a people crossing the dry bed of the deep with a road, or to make the very surface of the sea into a road? Those men, because they were weighed down by the burden of their humanity, needed a solid path through the depths on which to proceed. But the one who is known to have assumed the weakness of human nature into the height of divinity was borne over the waters by his own power.

Moses obtained the radiance of his face from converse with the Lord (Exod. 34:29); Joshua fixed the sun through his prayers (Josh. 10:12–13). But because Jesus is God, he shone before his disciples with the power of the sun. The children of Israel could not gaze upon Moses’ face; those who were worthy to see the glory of Jesus fell down, so that you might plainly recognize that what humanity passed over into was divine.

To him, while those men stood beside him on the mountain, the eternal Father said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 17:5–6). And therefore, in comparison with him, what is Elijah, who shut the heavens so that it would not rain and opened them so that it would rain (III Kings 17:1), when Jesus, with the heavens opened, presented the Father as witness to his divine generation?

“There is none mighty like the Lord,” therefore, because whatever virtue Moses was able to display, the Lord himself accomplished; Jesus, however, displayed everything wondrously by his own power, because he was also Lord of Moses.

For it was not Moses but the Lord who rained manna upon the people traveling through the wilderness (Exod. 16:13 ff.). It was not Moses but the Lord who went before the people by the pillar of fire at night and of cloud by day (ibid., 14:19). It was not Moses but the Word that came to him who brought water from the rock (ibid., 17:6). It was not Moses but the Lord who supplied the flying creatures to those who desired them (ibid., 16:17).

Hence the Lord restrains the Jews who glory in the strength of their fathers, saying: “It was not Moses but my Father who gave you bread from heaven” (John 6:32).

For this reason the Psalmist, not pointlessly exalting Moses but laudably extolling the Lord, says: “He performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the plain of Tanis; he divided the sea and led them through, and made the waters stand as in a wineskin. He led them by a cloud during the day and all night by the light of fire. He brought water from the rock and led waters down like rivers. He commanded the clouds from above and opened the doors of heaven; he rained manna upon them for food, and rained flesh upon them like dust and winged birds like the sand of the sea” (Ps. 78:12 ff.).

But the Lord Jesus, incomparably mighty, did not appear through another’s power but through his own. Hence, powerful in himself, he commands the paralytic and says: “I say to you, rise” (Matt. 9:6). It is also written: “All who touched him were healed of whatever sickness they had” (Mark 6:56). And again: “Power went out from him and healed them all” (Luke 6:19).

Neither Moses nor Elijah could possess this distinctive sign of strength: that, while incomparable signs were made known, they should most clearly designate the coming of the Only-Begotten. Therefore the Synagogue is rightly condemned to perpetual silence when it follows:

(Verses 3.) “Do not multiply lofty words. Let ancient things depart from your mouth.”

9. As if he were saying: “While you behold things incomparably new, you extol the deeds of the ancients in a blameworthy manner.” For those things had gone before as though they were a shadow. But now the true faithful devoutly adore these works of our Redeemer, because what was there veiled by the concealment of the mystery became manifest at the Redeemer’s coming: it had awaited the body of truth that was to be revealed. Therefore, if the old things are compared with the new, they are not old, because, understood in the Holy Spirit, they do not admit any oldness. Concerning that Spirit who renews all things, the Psalmist prays, saying: “Send forth your spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. CIII, 30).

The old things, then, are old when they are compared with the Redeemer’s works; but when we bring those former things forward spiritually to confirm these latter ones, they are renewed by the same Spirit by whom we understand them. Therefore, when holy Church reproves the Jews for their account of ancient things, what else is it indicating except that they understand the spiritual deeds of the Fathers carnally? For the Synagogue rises against holy Church with all the more rashness as it proudly exalts the knowledge of the Law and the Prophets—a knowledge which it learned had been divinely inspired in its fathers but materially displayed to itself.

Hence it follows: “Do not multiply lofty speech, boasting.” And so that they may cease to swell with pride, he adds, saying: “Let old things depart from your mouth.” For those things are already old to it which, as I have said, are not understood through the renewing Spirit. It is therefore as if he were saying: “It is fitting that you be silent concerning the account of those things whose new and splendid meanings you do not know. Even if you understand them subtly, they ought not to provide you with the swelling of arrogance, because God is the Lord of knowledge.”

The Redeemer of the human race, since he is the Word of the supreme Father, is certainly Lord of all knowledge. Isaiah spoke lofty and great things; Jeremiah spoke great things. Yet they would surely have said nothing if the Lord of knowledge had not disclosed these kinds of knowledge to them before they spoke. Hence, too, the books of the prophet Isaiah frequently read: “The word that came to Isaiah the prophet.” The book of Jeremiah likewise frequently says: “The word that came to Jeremiah the prophet.”

John, beholding this Word, the Lord of knowledge, in the highest bosom of the supreme Father, said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1). Therefore Paul, indicating that our Redeemer is the Lord of knowledge, says: “For in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II, 9).

When he therefore says, “Let old things depart from your mouth,” because God is the Lord of knowledge, what else is he saying except openly to show the Synagogue, by a clear argument, that it ought to be silent all the more carefully because it does not know not only what the things it says are, but also from whom they come? As if he were saying: “The knowledge which you assert belonged to your fathers ought to have given you arrogance all the less, since it belonged not to them but to the only-begotten Son of God—and you do not understand that very knowledge.”

He therefore says: “Let old things depart from your mouth,” so that the Jews may in no way corrupt what they are unable rightly to understand. He says, “God is the Lord of knowledge,” so that what they truly prove to be God’s they may not deceitfully ascribe to human beings.

But while Judaea is reproved for words of boasting, because she is pierced by no fear, torments are also announced to her concerning the hidden movements of the hearts of the faithless. For it follows:

**(Verse 3.) “And thoughts are prepared for him.”**

10. As if he were saying: “He whom you do not fear to blaspheme will be the judge not only of your tongue but also of your heart.” Hence through Isaiah he also threatens, saying: “I am coming to gather their works and their thoughts” (Isa. LXVI, 18). Here, too, the Lord threatens through Moses, saying: “Are these things not stored up with me and sealed in my treasuries?” (Deut. XXXII, 34).

And because these words command the Synagogue to be silent, let us now see with what praises of her fruitfulness holy Church glories in Anna’s voice. For he adds:

**(Verse 4.) “The bow of the mighty has been overcome.”**

11. What is the bow of the mighty except the deceitful savagery of the Jews? For from concealment, as though from a bow, they had inflicted a wound on the Redeemer, whom they killed by the hands of the Gentiles. But the bow of the mighty has been overcome, because he who died from their wound rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sent the promised Holy Spirit to his disciples. Hence it follows:

**(Verse 5.) “And the weak have been girded with strength.”**

12. By the term “strength,” the power of the Holy Spirit is indicated. Thus, when promising this same Spirit to his disciples, the Lord also said: “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV, 49). The grace of the Holy Spirit is rightly called strength, because when the elect receive it they become strong against all the adversities of this age.

But who are the weak mentioned here except the apostles? Yet they were weak when the bow of the mighty was being drawn, not when they were clothed with power from on high. For it is written of them at the hour of the Lord’s arrest that, “leaving the Lord, they all fled” (Matt. XXVI, 56). Was Peter not then exceedingly weak, when he feared the voice of the questioning servant girl and denied the Redeemer (ibid., LXIII, 74)?

The bow of the mighty had already been overcome, the savagery of the Jews had been annihilated, because the Redeemer had risen after conquering death; and yet the apostles, still weak, feared the mighty who had been overcome, behind closed doors (John XX, 19). But when strength clothed them, let us observe how strong it made them. For the Holy Spirit came upon them with a sudden sound and changed their weakness into the power of marvelous love (Acts II, 22 ff.).

They began, now clothed with strength, to preach Christ—men who had not been ashamed to flee and hide from their persecutors’ threats, and who had feared the words of women but now shattered the authority of rulers with freedom. Strength conquered fear; it overcame terrors, threats, and slaughter. Those whom it clothed by its coming it adorned in the heavenly warfare with the insignia of wondrous courage, so that amid scourging, slaughter, and insults they did not fear but rejoiced.

For it is written of them, now clothed with this strength: “The apostles went forth rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts V, 41). Hence, while preaching, they say: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials” (James I, 2).

Rightly, therefore, it is said: “The bow of the mighty has been overcome, and the weak have been girded with strength.” For the Redeemer first rose from the dead, then went up to heaven, and sent the Holy Spirit to his disciples. First the bow of the mighty had to be overcome, and afterward the weak had to be girded with strength. Hence it is also written: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII, 39).

13. Here it should be noted that this is spoken against Judaea, which despises the Redeemer’s miracles all the more proudly because it recognizes him dead amid his sufferings. He therefore says: “The bow of the mighty has been overcome, and the weak have been girded with strength.” It is as though he were answering the Synagogue, which slanders the Redeemer’s death, saying: “Do not despise the fact that he was able to die; rather, marvel that, having died, he rose again and by rising overcame the savagery of your people.”

And because he demonstrates this as something past, he speaks to her not only by announcing it but also by taunting her. As if he were reproaching her in her futile insolence, saying: “What did it profit you to kill one whom the snare of death could not hold? You killed him so that the whole world would not follow him; but for this very reason the whole world follows him, because he proved himself to be truly the Son of God by redeeming the human race through dying, by showing himself alive through rising again, by ascending into heaven, and by sending the promised Holy Spirit to his disciples.”

And because, on account of the merit of its unbelief, the Synagogue was rejected from participation in the promised grace, holy Church, reproaching it for this very thing, adds:

**(Verse 5.) “Those who were formerly full have hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry have been filled.”**

14. Who were formerly full except those who possessed knowledge of God before the other peoples? Who, then, should be understood as those formerly full other than the Jews, who had been instructed in faith in the Creator almost from the very beginning of the world?

They hired themselves out for bread. For what does “bread” signify here except the mysteries of the divine Incarnation? The place where bread is found is sacred Scripture. Hence the bread that came down from heaven says to those ignorant of how to find it: “Search the Scriptures, because they are the ones that bear witness about me” (John V, 39).

They therefore hired themselves out for bread because they had received all the Scriptures, so that in them they ought to have found the mysteries of the divine Incarnation. But when the bread came, the Synagogue—which had hired itself out for bread—left the place in which it ought to have found the bread it had sought. It had the Scriptures, as I have said, for recognizing the Redeemer; yet it rejected him who had come according to the Scriptures.

The hungry, therefore, have been filled, because those among the Gentiles who believed, while reverently receiving the mysteries of the divine Incarnation, possess heavenly food for inward delight. They are called hungry because, before the Redeemer’s coming, cast down by the hunger of unbelief, they had no food of spiritual refreshment. Or certainly they are called hungry because they receive the sweetness of spiritual food with great eagerness.

But those who were full and hired themselves out for bread should hear whom they were awaiting: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI, 33, 41 ff.). But because they did not deserve to recognize him, they answered: “Is this not the son of Joseph? How does he say, ‘I have come down from heaven’?” (Luke IV, 22; John VI, 42).

Yet he, who knew all things, prophetically declared that the hungry would come to recline at his banquet of delight, saying: “Amen, I say to you, many will come from east and west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, but the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matt. VIII, 11–12).

Those who were full, therefore, hired themselves out for bread, but the hungry are filled, because the children of the Synagogue had the nourishment of faith concerning the Redeemer’s future Incarnation in the holy Scriptures; but now, after they have been cast aside, while the Gentiles truly believe in him, they receive the mysteries of his divinity and humanity in the innermost refreshment of delight.

15. Since the eminent Teacher says: “All ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink—for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 3–4), it may reasonably be concluded that those people ate but were not filled, whereas these ate and were filled.

This is rightly said by holy Church against the Synagogue, so that those who are under grace may be shown to surpass by wondrous elevation those who are under the Law. For what was it for them to hire themselves out for bread except to seek in sacred Scripture the mysteries of the Redeemer who was to come?

Each of them indeed ate but was not filled, because he believed in the future Incarnation of the supreme Only-Begotten but did not see it present. To eat meant for him to retain the divine Incarnation sweetly in the desire of his mind; not to be filled meant not to see the presence he desired.

But the weak, who were to be girded with strength, heard from the bread by which they were filled the proclamation of their fullness: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. Amen, I say to you, many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. XIII, 16–17).

Those who desired to see were already eating the bread of inward delight through desire; but because they could not see, they had the joy of desire without the fullness that comes through enjoyment. For although Scripture says: “You gave them bread having every sweetness and every flavor” (Wis. XVI, 20), this is to be understood as being received by them in the way it could be known—as something known to them through faith and desired through the longing of love.

Therefore, those who were girded with strength are preferred to the Synagogue glorying in its first fathers, [Note: [Col. 0071D] Vaticanus and Gilot: “are brought forward.”] so that when the new and lofty summit of the elect is seen, it may no longer glory vainly.

And because the food of life is never removed from the banquet of holy Church, indicating both future and past things, he says:

**(Verse 6.) “Until the barren woman has borne many, and she who had many children has grown weak.”**

16. Who is the barren woman except holy Church, as we have already explained more fully above in the figure of Anna? What, then, is it for the hungry to be filled until the barren woman bears except to possess the bread of life until the end of the world? He himself also promises this, saying: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

For those whom holy Church brings forth are none other than the hungry. Therefore, while she bears, the hungry are filled, because until the end of the world she generates children for God; and while they believe that the Redeemer has come in the flesh, they eat the bread of life that they desire and are filled with its abundance.

But while the barren woman bears many, she who had many children grows weak. The Synagogue’s becoming weak means that it can no longer bear children through the institution of the old Law. For she who lost faith in her former husband now bears children for the devil and not for God.

It is rightly said, “She who had many children,” because, while instructing the people subject to it in the truth of the Scriptures to desire the advent of the coming Redeemer, it bore children from the embrace of the heavenly Bridegroom. But now she who had children has grown weak and has no children. She offers the Scriptures to her hearers, but because she denies the Redeemer, she never generates children for God. She is therefore said to have grown weak because spiritual fruitfulness is denied her.

And because both the Synagogue’s rejection and the Gentiles’ election occurred according to God’s incomprehensible judgment, it follows:

**(Verses 6–8.) “The Lord puts to death and gives life; he leads down to the underworld and brings back. The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and exalts. He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dungheap, so that he may seat him with princes and grant him the throne of glory.”**

17. It is as though he were answering someone astonished at the rejection of such an elect people, saying: “Why do you seek a rationale for things which supreme Reason performs incomprehensibly?” The eminent Teacher, reproving this kind of questioning, also says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to its maker, ‘Why did you make me this way?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. IX, 20–21).

It is therefore as if he were saying: Since the Lord of all is rightly recognized, let us understand that his work—in Judaea’s rejection as well as in the Gentiles’ election—is to be venerated, not scrutinized.

The Lord puts to death because, by an incomprehensible judgment, he separates the formerly elect people of the Jews from knowledge of the truth and condemns them forever. He gives life because, for a time, he receives the Gentiles through faith into knowledge of his only-begotten Son, and leads them eternally to contemplate his glory.

He leads down to the underworld because, by his strict judgment, avenging Gehenna receives for eternal punishment those who, through the fault of unbelief, separate themselves from veneration of the Redeemer. He brings back from the underworld because he receives the Gentile people as they devoutly approach faith in his Son—a people for whom the immense darkness of error was like a deep prison of the abyss.

He makes poor and makes rich because he strips rejected Judaea of spiritual virtues, while adorning elect Gentiles with both the price of faith and the splendors of good works.

He is also said to humble and exalt. For the Synagogue, by withdrawing from the Redeemer, laid down the heights of its exalted position; while holy Church, by venerating the Redeemer, rose from the depths of unbelief where it had lain cast down into the height of right faith and the loftiness of Christian authority.

Therefore, because Judaea despised the Son of God, the Gentiles deserved him; rightly, the former is believed to have been humbled and the latter exalted.

It follows: “Raising the needy from the dust and lifting the poor from the dungheap, so that he may seat him with princes and grant him the throne of glory.”

18. The needy and the poor signify the Gentile people, who are said to be raised from the dust and lifted from the dungheap because, when they are received into faith in the Redeemer, both their lesser and their more serious sins are forgiven.

Because dust is easily shaken off, while dung horribly stains and defiles, dust signifies lesser sins and dung more serious sins. It is also fittingly said that the needy is raised from the dust and the poor lifted from the dungheap. The former lay asleep in sins from which they could be raised by the lightest touch of grace. The latter lay in sins because, having fallen into more serious offenses, they needed the hand of great assistance.

But now let us hear to what summit the needy who is raised from the dust, and the poor who is lifted from the dungheap, are exalted.

**19. “So that he may seat him with princes and grant him the throne of glory.”**

Who are the princes designated here except the holy apostles? Concerning these princes, it is said to God through the Psalmist: “You will appoint them princes over all the earth; they will remember your name, O Lord” (Ps. XLIV, 17–18).

What does it mean that the poor man sits with princes except that the order of preachers, chosen from the Gentiles, holds in holy Church the summit of apostolic authority? He sits with princes because from the throne of heavenly teaching he offers the doctrine of salvation. He holds the throne of glory because he spreads the fragrance of a good reputation by which he surpasses others in dignity.

Or certainly he holds the throne of glory and sits with princes because he shines with the honor of exalted position and flashes with miracles. But he who is raised to such a lofty dignity indicates how he ought to use it when he adds:

**(Verse 8.) “For the hinges of the earth belong to the Lord, and he has set the world upon them.”**

20. The hinges of the earth are the ends of the earth. By the name “hinges,” he wished to designate those chosen preachers who came from the Gentiles. They are called the ends of the earth because they are produced, so to speak, from a lowly and despised Gentility.

These hinges are said to belong to the Lord because of the mortification of their own will. They belong to the Lord because they seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ. Yet when they are said to belong to the Lord, a singular holiness in them is indicated.

Let those who belong to the Lord observe that the world is placed above them, not beneath them. For what is designated by the name “world” except the fullness of the faithful subject to holy Church? God placed the world upon the hinges of the earth because preachers are appointed over holy Church for this purpose: to relieve the weakness of the faithful and to carry even the feeble toward the heavenly homeland, like a burden placed upon them. [Note: [Col. 0073D] Guss.: “are appointed.”]

They should not therefore always regard themselves as superior, but sometimes as subject, so that they may preside over the discipline by which vices are restrained, while in their own estimation and in the obedience of service they may often be beneath those over whom they are preeminent in the care of governance.

And because the burdens borne by preachers are great, he adds:

**(Verse 9.) “He will guard the feet of his saints.”**

21. As if he were saying: “They would collapse beneath such immense burdens if the Lord did not guard their feet.” The feet of his saints are the affections of their minds. They are guarded by the Lord because grace of marvelous devotion is poured into them, by which they bear so great a burden gladly.

The Lord is said to guard the feet of his saints because they would flee from the mass of such a weight if the love infused from above did not make what was intolerably heavy light for them.

The steadfast condition of strength may also be signified by the name “feet.” The Lord guards the feet of his saints when he strengthens them with marvelous fortitude, so that they do not fall beneath such immense burdens.

And because he is said to guard not one foot but feet, what are we to understand in the two feet of the saints except strength and humility? To avoid falling, we stand upon both feet.

Those who preside over faithful flocks encounter, on the way by which they journey toward the heavenly homeland, sometimes prosperity and sometimes adversity. Prosperity itself, because it arouses elation in the mind, strongly assaults it toward a fall. Nevertheless, so that the chosen soul may not fall from the mountain, it strives to stand on one side with the foot of strength and on the other stands with the foot of humility.

It would maintain a firm position amid both kinds of temptation if it stood with such solid humility that no prosperity lifted it up and no adversity cast it down.

What, then, does it mean when it says, “He will guard the feet of his saints,” except that every human virtue is weak without the Creator’s help? Our humility is weak: when it is caressed by the favor of prosperity, it is overthrown by the impulse of foolish joy. Our strength is weak: when it is struck by adversity, it is easily overcome.

We are crushed by sorrows and enervated by joys when almighty God abandons us to ourselves, not when he grants the help of his protection. He therefore says: “He will guard the feet of his saints,” because almighty God assists our weakness in bearing the burdens of those subject to us, so that neither adversities wear us down nor joys lead us astray.

Our feet are guarded by the Lord when, strengthened by divine assistance, we despise the joys that meet us in the world, fear no adversities, bear hardships gladly with steadfast patience, and restrain our exalted spirit from empty delight with unshaken humility.

22. The feet of the saints may also be understood as faith in and love of the Redeemer. With these feet they walk when, believing in him through faith, the faithful follow him in love.

He was asking that these feet be guarded for him by the Lord when he prayed, saying: [Note: [Col. 0075D] In his song it reads, *ἐν τῇ ᾠδῇ* (“in the song”); but someone could have read *ἐν τῇ αὐγῇ*, “in splendor.”] “Set me upon the heights, so that I may conquer in his brightness” (Hab. III, 19).

He is set upon the heights to whom the Redeemer’s divinity is revealed. He conquers in his brightness because, while he is illumined by the rays of the Redeemer’s glory, [Note: [Col. 0076D] Vaticanus and Gilot: “by the rays of his love.”] all the temptations of the evil spirit are destroyed.

He keeps his feet set upon the mountain who is lofty through contemplation of the truth and is inflamed with love for the one he believes to be the only-begotten Son of the supreme Father.

Peter had been set upon the heights when, confessing the Lord, he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Immediately he heard: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 16–17).

Founded upon faith and inflamed with love, he also preached the one whom he loved. Rightly, therefore, concerning the reprobate it is added:

**(Verse 9.) “And the impious will be silent in darkness.”**

23. Who are the impious understood here except the Jews, who are strangers to the piety of true faith and stained with the Redeemer’s death? Of them it is rightly said: “They will be silent in darkness,” because the saints, set upon the heights, confess the Redeemer of the world in eternal praises, whom they behold in the splendor of divine majesty.

The impious are therefore silent in darkness because the Jews do not preach the Redeemer for the reason that the ineffable brightness of his divinity does not illumine them. For it is written: “Let the impious be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. XXVI, 10).

Beholding them condemned to these darknesses, John says: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John I, 5). Hence David, not wishing but prophesying, says: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and make their back always bent down” (Ps. LXVIII, 24).

The impious are therefore silent in darkness because, even if the Jews utter the words of divine Scripture in praise of God, by denying the Son they offer no service of their voices to God the Father. For he is silent toward God who, while praising the Father, keeps silent about the praise of the Only-Begotten.

But the one whom they despise as crucified they will fear when he comes as judge. Hence it is also added:

**(Verses 9–10.) “For a man will not be strengthened by his own strength; his adversaries will fear the Lord.”**

24. Now he is hard in unbelief and strong in error, and he does not fear boldly to blaspheme the one whom he refuses to believe is God. For now he cannot be conquered as though he were a man; but then he will not be strengthened as a man, when the one who was crucified through their plots is seen in his own majesty.

Then his adversaries will fear, when they see all things moved by the power of the crucified one, when they see everything subjected to his judgment, and when through the lofty heavens they hear the thunderous judgments of their eternal condemnation. Hence it follows:

**(Verse 10.) “And over them he will thunder in the heavens.”**

25. Who are designated here by the name of the heavens except the holy apostles? To these heavens, promising the glory of their exalted position, the Lord says: “You will sit upon thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28).

Indicating the thunder of these heavens to the Jews, the Lord says: “They themselves will be your judges” (Luke XI, 19). He will therefore thunder over the impious Jews in the heavens because they will hear terrifying judgments of their condemnation from the holy apostles. By their judgment they will receive the sentence of eternal death from those whom they had afflicted with persecutions while they humbly preached the blessings of eternal life.

And because these things ought to be understood of the final judgment, it follows:

**(Verse 10.) “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth.”**

26. What are the ends of the earth except the final events of this world? The Lord judges the ends of the earth so that no matter may remain unpunished or without reward under his equitable sentence; for when he brings all things to their conclusion in judgment, he leaves nothing requiring examination untouched.

**(Verse 10.) “Then he will exalt the horn of his Christ.”**

27. When he receives all the elect into the eternal contemplation of his Only-Begotten, so that he may preside over them with that eternal and ineffable Majesty—though, while they lived as pilgrims in this present life, they were not with him. [Note: [Col. 0076D] Gilot and Vaticanus: “was not.”]

Then he will exalt the horn of his Christ, when the Redeemer’s exalted position is seen in its own height. John speaks of this exaltation: “We shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2).
