The power, or kingdom, of our Lord Jesus Christ is always equal; but he is said then to be exalted when we shall be such as to be able to behold his exalted nature. For whatever the human mind can now imagine concerning that exaltation is utterly nothing in comparison with the glory in question.

For it is written of it: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. LXIV, 4; I Cor. II, 9).

First, therefore, dominion is given to Christ; afterward his horn will be exalted, because the height of his exaltation is seen when our nature too is raised from the depths of its corruption, when by rising again it receives the integrity of its renewal, by which it can contemplate the Redeemer’s lofty light.

[Col. 0076D] 28. But if someone wishes “horn” to be understood as kingdom, the holy Church is signified by the kingdom of Christ. This horn will certainly be exalted, because our lowliness will be brought to equality with the angels. Hence the Lord also says of the elect in the Gospel: “They will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. XXII, 30).

Concerning this exaltation of his horn he says again: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (ibid. XIII, 43). The horn of Christ will therefore be exalted because holy Church will be raised up in the eternal contemplation of its Redeemer. She who is now oppressed in this valley of misery by the punishment of her abasement will then, after death has been swallowed up and she has been renewed, be lifted up to the summit of eternal joy.

But we have already presented these things in a typological explanation; it remains that in the following book we express them morally.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0077]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0077A]

1. In the preceding book, while we were examining the text of sacred history morally, we placed Anna’s fruitfulness in the perfection of supreme contemplation. For to conceive in the mind is to rejoice ineffably in the contemplation of almighty God; to give birth is not to be able to conceal the marks of the love conceived in the mind.

But what is it for a woman who has given birth to sing except to proclaim with true praises the Creator whom she loves ineffably? Therefore she says:

**(I Sam. II, 1.) “My heart has rejoiced in the Lord.”**

2. She who ate and drank, who possessed a bitter spirit, who wept abundantly, who made a vow—because the mind that can worthily praise almighty God is the mind that has reached the heights of his love through worthy struggles—learned through long practice to despise all things.

While rejecting every created thing from her attention, she rejoices all the more in the vision of eternal majesty insofar as the appearance of no creature can retain her in love of itself. Therefore she says: “My heart has rejoiced in the Lord,” because, having despised all things, she loves him alone.

He had come to this affection who said: “What remains for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. LXXII, 25). Rejoicing in God, he says: “Your face, O Lord, your face I will seek” (Ps. XXVI, 3). Hence the bride in the Song of Songs asks, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I, 1).

When she therefore says, “My heart has rejoiced in the Lord,” what else does she declare except that she has clung to the kisses of the one whom she ardently loves? [Note: [Col. 0077D] This should undoubtedly be read in this way, not *oculis* (“with the eyes”), as some other printed editions have it.]

She alone says this because she has learned by experience what power love possesses in the bridegroom’s chamber. Illumined by every victory over the passions and raised to the summit of the virtues, she reached that height from which, through the joy of wondrous devotion, she placed her heart in God with exultation.

And because she says “my heart,” what else did she assert except the freedom of her mind? The reprobate do not possess their own hearts, because the devil possesses them. Hence it is said concerning the traitor: “When the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, Simon Iscariot’s son, to betray him” (John XIII, 2). For if Judas, and not the devil, possessed his own heart, he himself would have placed good in it rather than the devil placing evil.

In contrast, the chosen man says: “I carry my soul in my hands” (Job XIII, 14). For what else is the hand of the elect except the power of inward freedom? What, then, is it to carry the soul in one’s hands except to retain the glory of inward freedom under one’s own power?

Whenever, therefore, we commit serious sins, we do not possess our own heart. Hence Jeremiah also reproaches the Jewish people in their serious wrongdoing, saying: “Hear, foolish people, you who do not have a heart” (Jer. V, 21). Again, another prophet, turning to God, confesses, saying: “Your servant has found his heart” (II Sam. VII, 27).

She therefore says: “My heart has rejoiced in the Lord,” in order to assert the freedom of the mind, without which she could not worthily praise God.

It follows:

**(Verse 1.) “My horn has been exalted in my God.”**

3. In the horn, the intention of the elect mind is signified. It is wonderfully lifted up when, rejoicing, it reaches the one who stands above all things. Hence she asserts that her horn has been exalted not in anything else but in God.

Whoever loves transient goods has an intention that is depressed, not exalted, because it is fixed below, where it is placed by desire. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. VI, 21; Luke XII, 34).

The Lord wished to exalt our horn when he said: “Lay up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (Matt. VI, 20, 33). Those whose horn was exalted were the ones to whom Paul conformed himself when he said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20).

But if someone loves only heavenly things and does not know how to taste that sweetness of inward delight, although he may be greatly exalted, he has not reached the summit of this exaltation. He is exalted by this elevation who, progressing through increases in virtue, has attained the height of supreme contemplation—not only so as to love heavenly things perfectly, but also so that, in the perfection of love, he may rest in the contemplation of almighty God alone.

He has his horn exalted in God who enjoys a lofty vision of the inward light, in which he glories with a certain familiar singularity. Therefore she does not say, “in our God,” but “in my God.” For she calls him “mine” whom she loves familiarly and uniquely.

He had reached this dignity of divine familiarity who said: “You are my God, and I will confess to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you” (Ps. CXVII, 28). Hence Isaiah, rebuking unbelievers, says: “Is it too little for you to trouble human beings, that you also trouble my God?” (Isa. VII, 13). 

She whose horn is raised up in God by such exaltation therefore confesses him as her God in a unique manner, because that supreme infusion of divine sweetness exalts the mind, makes it receptive to him, and renders it profoundly familiar with him.

It follows:

**(Verse 1.) “My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies.”**
### 4

Who are the enemies of the chosen mind except the evil spirits? What, then, is it to have a mouth enlarged over one’s enemies, except to reject all the suggestions of the evil spirits through the exceedingly abundant generosity of grace infused into oneself? For he has a narrow mouth who is unable, through the consideration of reason, to oppose all the deceits of the evil spirits. The mouth of the mind is its reason, and to speak is to deliberate. The mouth is filled when the mind’s reason, through the grace infused into it, is raised to the contemplation of the highest truth [Col. 0079A]. To be filled for it is to be imbued with the illumination of the highest truth. There it learns both what it should desire eternally and what it should despise temporally. And because the highest truth is love, the chosen soul is raised by the subtlety of truth, and is inflamed by love for the reality it has learned; and the more fervently the force of love implants this teaching within it, the more strictly it observes it.

Although evil spirits suggest evil things to this soul, they are put to shame by the opening of its enlarged mouth, because, instructed in the truth of supreme wisdom and kindled by the torches of the highest love, it now possesses immense wisdom as a light against the suggestion of error, and also ineffable charity against the pomp of this world when it is offered to it. In the immensity of that light it sees what it should reject, but through the power of supreme charity it loves to reject the foolish things it recognizes. Through wisdom it censures the evils suggested to it, but through the strength of charity it condemns what it has detected.

Thus it enlarges its mouth over its enemies, because from the abundance of reason it deliberates much against the demons; and it destroys their objections all the more keenly because, in the heights, it recognizes that by which it may reject the evils suggested to it. Hence, immediately indicating the reason, she says:

**(Verse 1.)** “Because I have rejoiced in your salvation.”

### 5

This is plainly as though she were saying: “Because my horn has been exalted in my God.” To rejoice in God’s salvation is precisely to have one’s horn exalted in one’s God. This is not understood of just any joy in salvation, but of that most perfect joy with which the chosen and perfected soul rejoices in the Bridegroom after the manner of a bride. Concerning this joy David earnestly begs, saying: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit” (Ps. 50:14).

Thus she who boasts that she has an enlarged mouth over her enemies is described as having first rejoiced in God’s salvation, because that blessed mind will be able powerfully to reject the suggestions of the evil spirits which, through contemplation, has been sublimely taken up into the divinity of the Redeemer and has received from him both greatness of wisdom and fullness of charity. She proclaims him with worthy praises, saying:

**(Verse 2.)** “There is none holy like the Lord; indeed, there is no other besides you, and there is none strong like our God.”

### 6

By these words of Anna, every chosen soul cries out in praise to the Redeemer concerning what it believes it has received from him as a gift. But from this order of devout confession the sequence is indicated by which we attain the same gifts that she has set forth in order. The Lord is therefore declared holy and strong: by him we are sanctified, led to rest, and glorified.

We receive sanctification from the Lord through the power of regeneration; “to be,” that is, to receive rest from the mutability of this corruption, at the end of our exile; and strength in the triumph of the resurrection. We attain the first of these gifts in the present life, when the soul of each chosen person is in the flesh, while both are still engaged in the struggle of works. We attain the next in the soul alone, apart from the flesh, after the life of the flesh, when the soul has already been taken up from the labors of this life. We attain the last in flesh and soul, when both have already been renewed through the glory of eternity.

He is therefore first called holy, because, through the grace of the saving bath of regeneration, the love of God is poured into the hearts of the regenerate. Through this grace we are prepared for the goods of our eternal homeland, so that when this life passes away in the course of its allotted time, that life may receive us—a life whose joy the souls of the elect, departing from here, may possess without fear of death.

Next, “to be” is ascribed to him, because, secure concerning the day of our consummation—that is, the splendor of the final resurrection—we await it while, in the gift of the rest we have received, we learn not to fear the examination of the final judgment but to await the joy of the promised glory.

Finally, he is declared strong, because in the joy of the future resurrection our weaknesses are strengthened when the flesh rises from the dust. Yet when the same dust of our flesh has been transferred into the glory of perpetual incorruption, it does not return again to the misery of its frailty.

It should also be noted that in these three stages we are led from one to the next; but when one begins to possess what one had not possessed, one does not lose what one possessed before. For when we are led from sanctification to rest, and from the soul’s repose to the strength of eternal incorruption, the sanctification of charity is increased for us in that rest, and both rest and love grow exceedingly in the resurrection.

Each soul, therefore, beholding its Creator joined to it through love amid such great gifts, should say in Anna’s words how greatly it savors the gift of perfect regeneration and the power of love. Let it say: “There is none holy like the Lord.” Let it say how much better for it is the gift of the promise of rest at the hour of its departure: “There is no other besides you.” Let it say how excellent and pleasing to it is its final renewal, in the joy of its perfected spirit and glorified flesh. Let it say: “And there is none strong like our God.”

It should also be noted that Anna speaks these words in a song of prayer. For the chosen mind to ask for such things in song is to desire such great gifts with joy. To ask is, for it, to desire; and to sing is to rejoice. Yet it becomes evident how vigorously she reproaches hidden enemies when she so joyfully beholds the gifts of her dignity. For she continues and says:

**(Verse 3.)** “Do not multiply lofty words, boasting; let ancient things depart from your mouth.”

The evil spirits speak lofty and ancient things when they suggest to the faithful that the high things which appear in this age should be desired. Therefore he who has already learned to exalt his horn in God, who has learned to be held in the joy of Majesty [Col. 0080D], despises with reproach whatever is offered to him by the seductions of this passing age, saying: “Do not multiply lofty words, boasting; let ancient things depart from your mouth.” It is as though he were speaking openly and saying: “The things offered to me displease me in proportion as, through desire, I see other things which greatly please me.”

### 8

This statement plainly applies to one who is already recognized as fit for the ministry of preaching. It can also appropriately be understood as directed against arrogant intellectuals and against negligent professors of holy life. One speaks loftily in boasting who boasts that, through the knowledge he has received, he understands sublime things. One speaks ancient things who, setting aside the words of Sacred Scripture, occupies himself with worldly speech.

Thus it is said to the arrogant: “Do not speak lofty things while boasting.” These words show that he does not prohibit the manner of speech but the disposition of the intention. It is as though he were saying openly: “Speak lofty things, but refrain from boasting about what is called lofty.” Hence Paul also devoutly admonishes his disciple, saying: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11:20). He did not say, “Do not speak loftily,” but “Do not be high-minded.” Likewise here it is not said, “Do not speak lofty things,” but “Do not speak while boasting,” because sacred utterances are to be sought more deeply; yet the more deeply one advances in seeking them, the more one ought to restrain oneself from the arrogance of empty glory by guarding humility.

It is also said to those who speak idly: “Let ancient things depart from your mouth.” The words of the world are ancient, because while the mind of the speaker is fixed on them through its intention, it is stripped of the beauty of its devotion. The reason why those people ought not to speak lofty things while boasting, and why ancient things ought to depart from their mouth, is demonstrated by what follows:

**(Verse 3.)** “Because God is the Lord of knowledge.”

Let the knowledgeable and arrogant person hear, then, that he is not himself the lord of knowledge, but God. He could rightly boast if the one who made him swell with pride through knowledge were not almighty God but he himself. Let us also hear, when we speak the words of the world, that God is the Lord of knowledge.

The minds of the elect are now renewed by knowledge not only of the New Testament but also of the Old. For the one who said, “Behold, I make all things new” (Isa. 43:19), has come. Since, therefore, we possess so many new things that we can speak, we can by no means speak ancient things without guilt. Let ancient things therefore depart from our mouth, so that, when the guilt of condemned antiquity is also restrained from our speech, we may pass into the beauty of the new human being.

But if we disregard this, let us hear:

**(Verse 3.)** “And thoughts are prepared by him.”

As though terrifying us by comparison, with the lesser guilt understood, he says: “From this let those who speak idly consider how much they ought to fear the guilt of speech, if the one against whom one sins by speaking also preserves the excesses of thoughts for examination at his judgment.” Let the arrogant hear likewise what follows:

**(Verse 4.)** “The bow of the mighty has been overcome, and the weak have been girded with strength.”

### 11

We have already said in the allegorical exposition that the unclean spirits are designated by the name “mighty.” Since they fell by growing proud of their heavenly glory, they are appropriately set before exalted teachers as a warning, so that the teachers may think humbly of themselves in proportion as they behold even angels fallen from heavenly glory through the desire for empty glory.

We also remember that our Redeemer did this with his exalted disciples. When they boasted that the demons were subject to them, they immediately heard from him: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10:18).

The bow of the mighty is therefore the pride of the evil spirits. They are called mighty either because they thought great things of themselves or because they overcome the human race through the force of great temptations. When impious intention drew this bow, it sought to shoot the arrows of its malice against its own Creator. “I will set my throne,” its prince said, “in the north; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14).

But the bow of the mighty was overcome, because God resisted the pride of the apostate spirits, cast them down from heaven, and stripped them of the glory conditioned upon their virtue, so that in the fallen angels humanity might learn what it should fear. For what will happen to a bronze vessel if God does not spare even golden ones filled with the stench of pride? Hence Peter also says in his Epistle: “God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but, having dragged them down with the chains of hell, he delivered them to Tartarus, reserving them for judgment” (2 Pet. 2:4).

It is as though a chosen and humble preacher were saying to the proud: “To make you cease from exaltation, look upon the punishments of the condemnation owed by angels like you—namely, fallen angels.”

### 12

Presenting those whom they ought to imitate, he says: “And the weak have been girded with strength.” If evil angels are called mighty because of the evil presumption of their self-esteem, the name “weak” rightly applies to the blessed spirits, who presume nothing of themselves and, in perpetual humility, are subject to the virtue of their Maker.

“The weak have been girded with strength,” because, by the merit of voluntary submission, the holy angels are joined to their Creator by the bond of inward love. The name “girding” appropriately suits them, because anyone who is girded is held on every side by the belt with which he is girded. Those most blessed spirits have likewise been so established in eternity that they can never fall away from it.

Hence an angel is sent to Daniel preaching in Babylon and is described as girded with a belt of gold (Dan. 10:5). Hence John saw in the Apocalypse an angel with a golden belt around his breast. The same blessed spirits rose from the merit of humility into the glory of love; and because they possess that glory in the embrace of eternity, they possess it without fear of losing it. They are ineffably glorious, but they can never lose that ineffable glory.

Therefore, let the arrogant person cease boasting and hear: “The bow of the mighty has been overcome.” And so that the condemned guilt of pride may advance in humility, it is said to him: “The weak have been girded with strength.” Strength is bestowed on the weak when, by the merit of submission, the power of heavenly charity is infused into the meek.

We are also girded when we are prepared for the ministry of the word. It is therefore fitting that the weak, girded with strength, are placed before those who boast in lofty speech, because those spirits who are sent into ministry for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation were humble before they were girded for ministry. Their weakness is mentioned first, and afterward the girding with strength.

Paul indicates that these spirits are girded for us when he says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14). The prophet also speaks of them: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him” (Dan. 7:10).

It is as though he were saying: “First recognize what you are, and then prepare yourselves for the salvation of others, because the work of preaching is properly fulfilled when the preacher who is exalted in word strives to be humble in ministry.”

But because he reproves proud and arrogant preachers in his speech, he adds:

**(Verse 5.)** “Those who were full before have hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry have been satisfied.”

### 13

Those who were full before are those who, while taking in the food of pride as nourishment for the mind, are unable to receive the delights of holy virtues, as though they were already full of food. Yet they hire themselves out for bread, because in the Scriptures they understand, they think that, according to the greatness of their wisdom, they receive the spiritual gifts of the virtues.

But they cannot be satisfied, because they can in no way add the gifts of the Holy Spirit to their fullness of arrogance. For “the spirit of discipline flees deceit and does not dwell in a body full of sins” (Wis. 1:5). It is also written: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5:5). In vain, therefore, do those desire to receive the things of God who, by their pride, make the giver of gifts hostile to them. They cannot be satisfied because they do not attain the gifts of spiritual graces.

But who are the hungry except those empty of the foods of vices and fasting from pride? The hungry, therefore, have been satisfied because holy men, endowed with the stronghold of humility, receive the lofty gifts of the virtues precisely because they do not think highly of themselves. Through the good of humility they become dwelling places of the Holy Spirit; and by receiving him as he remains within them, they are filled more fully with his gifts.

Hence the Lord also says through the Prophet: “Upon whom does my spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). The hungry are therefore greatly satisfied, because the Holy Spirit rests upon the humble in the fullness of his gifts.

### 14

This can also appropriately be said against negligent ministers of the sacred altar and reckless receivers of the Lord’s body. Those who were full before are full of the food of vices, and they hire themselves out for bread because they prepare the body for the reception of the Eucharist. They eat but cannot be satisfied, because, although they receive the sacrament with their mouth, they are not at all filled with the power of the sacrament.

They therefore fast from that sacramental power because they had been filled beforehand. Those who carry in their mind the crimes with which they had filled themselves do not receive the fruit of salvation in eating the saving offering. None are satisfied except the hungry, because those who fast perfectly from vices receive the divine sacraments in the fullness of their power.

And because even chosen men cannot be without sin, what remains except that they strive daily to be emptied of the sins with which human frailty never ceases to stain them? For one who does not daily empty out what he has done wrong, even if the sins he accumulates are small, is gradually filled in soul, and those sins rightly deprive him of the fruit of inward satisfaction.

Paul indicates that we must empty ourselves of this fullness when he says: “Let a person examine himself, and so eat from that bread and drink from the cup” (1 Cor. 11:28). What does “examine” mean here except to present oneself as approved and pure for the Lord’s table, after emptying oneself of the wickedness of sins?

Concerning those who are full he adds: “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” Therefore, since we sin daily, let us daily hasten to the lamentation of repentance, because this is the one virtue that empties out what guilt gathers in the belly of the soul.

Then truly the hungry are satisfied, because the more diligently we are cleansed by the lament of repentance, the more abundant a fruit of divine grace we receive in spiritual nourishment. Since this satisfaction of the elect extends to the end of the world, he continues and says:

**(Verse 5.)** “Until the barren woman has borne many, and she who had many children has grown weak.”

### 15

Who is designated by the name “barren woman” except the one of whom Paul speaks, saying: “The Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4:26–27)? A little later he applies Isaiah’s prophecy to her, saying: “For it is written: ‘Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband’” (Isa. 54:1).

But how is Jerusalem—the holy society of the blessed angels—understood as barren, when, according to the meaning of her name, she is fruitful in perpetual joy from the eternal vision of peace? Yet if she is the mother of chosen human beings, she was indeed barren when the human race perished in Adam. She was unable, as it were, to give birth when she lost, through the suggestions of the fallen spirit, the one in whom she ought to have extended the womb of her fruitfulness.

The weak are girded until the barren woman gives birth, because we need the powerful ministry of humble angels until all those predestined to life from the human race have been gathered, even to the end of the world. “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather his elect from the four winds” (Matt. 24:31; Mark 13:27).

They are then to be sent to gather those for whose salvation they are sent daily now, because they will not gather into the kingdom anyone except those to whom they now offer assistance through the strength of their girding. The hungry are also satisfied until the end of the world.

It is fittingly said that this barren woman bears “many,” because not all human beings but only the elect are brought to eternal joys. She is also appropriately said to give birth because through the ministry of the angels we are taught to seek heavenly things, so that we may be able to attain their blessings.

But when this barren woman gives birth, she who had many children grows weak, because, in proportion as the heavenly kingdoms receive richer gains of the elect through the ministries of the angels, the children of this Babylon are diminished. She is, as it were, weak in childbirth because, through the disordered love of passing things, she can no longer give birth to children as she usually did.

For the heavenly kingdoms are now preached everywhere; and when the minds of the faithful love what they hear and seek it also through good conduct, Babylon is, as it were, constricted in childbirth. Our mother Jerusalem gives birth throughout the world to those whom Babylon, with the exhausted womb of perdition, was accustomed to bear for hell.

Yet the strength of those who are girded is attributed not to them but to the one by whom they are girded. Thus it is appropriately added:

**(Verse 6.)** “The Lord puts to death and gives life.”

### 16

In these words the order should also be noted. He is first said to put to death and afterward to give life, because unless we cease to love the world, we cannot live for God through love, as John attests when he says: “Whoever loves the world does not have the love of the Father in him” (1 John 2:15).

Hence the one who remembered that he had been put to death and given life, cast down and raised up, said: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). He was alive, but not with the life of the world, because he said: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

It is not, therefore, one of those who are girded, but the Lord, who puts to death and gives life. To be put to death and given life is to desire nothing present and to desire eternal things. He explains to whom thanks for these gifts must be rendered when he says: “The Lord puts to death and gives life.”

Hence the preacher to the nations, mentioned so often already, says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7). He explains by what order almighty God works these things in the elect, saying:

**(Verse 6.)** “He leads down to the underworld and brings back.”

### 17

To put to death, he leads down to the underworld; and to give life, he brings back from the underworld. For almighty God to lead down to the underworld is to terrify sinners’ hearts through consideration of eternal torments. For him to bring back from the underworld is to raise the minds of penitents who are terrified and mourning their sins toward the hope of unfailing life.

We cease to sin when, through heavenly grace softening our hearts, we fear future torments. We are brought back from the underworld when, visited by inward consolation, we draw breath toward the hope of pardon through the lament of repentance.

The Lord is therefore appropriately said to lead down to the underworld and to bring back, because human hardness is neither shaken by fear nor raised by love through the preaching of a merely human being. If it belonged to teachers to put to death all whom their preaching touched, those people would cease to sin; and if it belonged to them to give life, all who heard heavenly things from them would immediately be kindled by the love of their inward affection to seek them with every effort.

But now, although eternal punishments are often threatened to sinners, and although heavenly goods that they can attain are preached to them, they neither fear the punishments nor desire the joys. Let us therefore cry out in praise of God in Anna’s words, attributing also to him the fact that some make progress through those preachers, and let us say: “The Lord puts to death and gives life.”

The Lord therefore leads down to the underworld and brings back, because those can fear future torments and those can love heavenly joys in whom the mercy of God works inwardly through the words that a human being speaks outwardly.

There is a means by which each person may recognize whether he has already been led down to the underworld and brought back: if he has died to the world and lives for heaven. For if he is chosen, he makes progress. Concerning this progress he adds:

**(Verse 7.)** “The Lord makes poor and enriches.”

### 18

The rich of this world boast of their abundant possessions because, by the profound and incomprehensible judgment of God, heavenly goods have been hidden from them. The Lord therefore makes people poor because, while he discloses eternal goods to the elect, they regard themselves as poorer in proportion as they see that they have been driven away from true riches.

Hence that king who was exceedingly wealthy in the possessions of the world, because the Lord had shown him true riches, cried out to him, saying: “Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor” (Ps. 24:16). The prophet Jeremiah, expressing in himself the illumination of every chosen person, says: “I am a man who sees my poverty” (Lam. 3:1).

To make someone poor for the Lord, therefore, is to stir the minds of the elect, through contemplation of everlasting goods, to despise all visible things. But to the one to whom he reveals the highest things, he also indicates that those same highest things must be sought for a longer time at the price of labor. He should therefore say that the one who makes poor also enriches, because, while we receive knowledge of heavenly goods from almighty God, we also receive from him the strength to strive for them with worthy labor.

He adds fittingly:

**(Verse 7.)** “He humbles and raises up.”

### 19

For in contemplating heavenly things they see how lowly they are on earth; yet, in that same lowliness of temporal poverty, through God’s grace they raise themselves on the wings of their merits to the joys of eternal life. Thus they receive humility in their estimation of exile, but sublimity in their preparation for holy action.

He continues:

**(Verse 8.)** “He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung, so that he may seat him with princes.”

### 20

Dust is the subtle deliberation of an illicit thought, which makes foul the mind in which it settles. For what is designated by dung except the foul audacity of an offense already committed? [Note: Guss. and Gilot. read: “and the audacity of an offense already committed are signified” (perpetrataque flagitii audacia designantur).] Hence the prophet, looking upon the life of carnal people buried in the filth of evil conduct, says: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:17).

The gifts of God are therefore counted in an appropriate sequence in the conversion of the sinful. The needy is first raised from the dust, and afterward the poor from the dung, because first the unclean deliberation is cut away from the heart, and afterward the guilt is removed from the action.

It is also appropriately said that the needy is raised from the dust and the poor lifted from the dung, because one who deliberates inwardly about wicked things sleeps away from the contemplation of justice, while one who commits unlawful acts outwardly lies in iniquity through action.

And because he now gains trophies over the evil spirits together with the mighty, he explains what the needy who has been raised and the poor who has been lifted merits, saying: “So that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory.”

### 21

To sit is the posture of one who triumphs. Hence in the Apocalypse of John the Lord shows the dignity of our victory, saying: “Whoever conquers, I will grant him to sit on my throne, just as I conquered and sat with my Father on his throne” (Rev. 3:21).

Paul also, contemplating this, counts the gifts of our raising and sitting among the praises of God, saying: “He raised us up with him and made us sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Eph. 2:6).

The princes sit with him because those who, with his help, restrain the powers of the evil spirits possess, in their triumph over them, the dignity of sitting over those whom they rule by the power presiding over them. The princes also sit with him because, although they are seen to stand bodily amid the misery of this passing life, they nevertheless possess with the Redeemer, in the heights, the seat of their merits; and they are not separated even in this valley of defilement from conformity to his glory.

The needy and poor in possessions are also those who, for the sake of the Gospel, abandoned everything they could have possessed in the world. To be able to sit with the princes, they must be raised from the dust and lifted from the dung.

For what are the praises of the tongue, and what are the insignia of passing dignities, except dust? By their flattering they soil the mind and blind it to true splendors. And what are perishing riches and transitory possessions, except dung to those who love eternal things? They are dung when holy souls hold them in contempt through humility, not when they pursue them out of desire.

Hence Solomon, looking upon the rich man of the world saddened by the loss of temporal goods, says: “The slothful person is to be stoned with the dung of oxen” (Ecclus. 22:2). It is as though he were saying: “He suffers blows of sorrow from that which the person who desires to labor for eternal life despises as dung.”

Paul says: “I have suffered the loss of all things and consider them as dung, that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3:8).

The needy is therefore raised from the dust and the poor lifted from the dung when the mind, renouncing the world, tramples on whatever used to please it—human praise, the honors of dignities, and abundance of possessions—while it looks toward the eternal things alone, which alone it ardently loves.

For the mind to be raised and lifted is to despise with inward sublimity those things it abandons bodily. For it to sit with princes is to share, through the joy of eternal rest, in the citizens of the heavenly homeland.

He then holds the throne of glory because, presiding so sublimely, he never ceases from the praises of his Creator. Admiring this throne of glory, the Psalmist says to the Lord: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5). Isaiah proclaims this seat of glory, saying: “Joy and gladness will be found in it, thanksgiving and the voice of praise” (Isa. 51:3). The holy Tobias likewise reveals it, saying: “Its streets will be paved with every precious and pure stone, and Alleluia will be sung throughout all its lanes” (Tob. 13:22).

But let the poor who has been rescued consider what follows, because he is not brought immediately to the sitting of the princes and to the throne of glory as soon as he has been raised:

**(Verse 8.)** “The hinges of the earth belong to the Lord,” he says, “and he set the world upon them.”

### 22

Since sinners are designated by the name “earth” in sacred Scripture, the hinges of the earth can appropriately be understood as those through whom the world revolves by means of foolish desires and leads people from one thing to another.

When, therefore, we behold converted sinners, let us burst forth into praise of the Creator in these words of Anna. For at that time we say, in effect, in other words: “By his grace those who were long held on the wheel of passing things through desire for the world have now begun to belong to the Lord.”

And when, having abandoned the seductions of secular life, they bravely endure powerful temptations, let us say: “He set the world upon them.” For he set the world upon them when it had previously been beneath them. They now bear it as a burden of temptations, although it once served them, as though subject to them, by flattering them while they reclined in pursuit of its delights and pleasures.

And because those who had great enjoyments in the world experience great temptations from it, it is added:

**(Verse 9.)** “He will guard the feet of his holy ones.”

### 23

These words reveal the help and favor of divine protection in such a way that they also signify the grave dangers of temptation. It is as though he were saying: “They endure such great temptations from the world to which they had clung that only the one who cannot abandon his faithful in tribulation is sufficient to help them.”

To guard the feet of his holy ones is to strengthen, through grace, the shaken affections of the elect so that they do not fall in temptation. Hence the prophet, who had been wavering toward a fall yet had been preserved by the Lord, said: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had nearly slipped” (Ps. 72:2). Again: “I was pushed and overturned so that I might fall, but the Lord received me. The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation” (Ps. 117:13–14).

Concerning the weakness of the enemies he adds:

**(Verse 9.)** “And the impious will be silenced in darkness.”

### 24

What does it mean that, when the Lord is said to guard the feet of the holy, the silence of the impious is mentioned, except that we are not driven into the fall of sin unless the perverse temptations of the evil spirits are suggested to us?

When, therefore, the Lord guards our feet, the impious are silent in darkness, because while we are protected by divine grace, the unclean spirits cannot give us the voice by which they would hurl us headlong. They are silent in darkness because they possess the darkened hearts of the reprobate, and they do not dare to advance from that obscurity toward us.

He explains why he guards the feet of the holy, saying:

**(Verse 9.)** “Because a man will not be strengthened by his own strength.”

### 25

It is as though he were saying: “He holds him for this reason: they could not stand without him.” For even if a man is recognized as virtuous, he fears falling in his own strength; he does not possess stability of strength [Note: Perhaps statum roboris, “stability of strength,” should be read, as below: “may not have stability of strength but a fall of weakness.”]; and he falls by desiring unlawful things as often as his inward footsteps are abandoned by the Lord who holds him.

Was he not a man to whom it was sung in the chorus of maidens: “Saul has struck down a thousand, and David ten thousand” (1 Sam. 18:7)? Yet when he was left amid the burdens of his own strength, he fell, driven into the guilt of his flesh, and learned through experience that a man in himself does not possess stability of strength but a fall of weakness.

Fearing relapse, he therefore asks the one by whom he must be held to stability, saying: “Do not utterly forsake me” (Ps. 118:8). Let no one deceive himself as though he could find in himself the strength to stand. Even if we often overcome great battles against hidden enemies, and if, by rejecting their suggestions, we pursue them as though they had been put to flight, it is not we whom the spirits fear at that moment, but the one whom they see and dread in us.

Or certainly, if they fear us also, they fear us precisely because they see that we have been taken up into the strength of divine grace. Thus it is appropriately added:

**(Verse 10.)** “The adversaries of the Lord will fear him, and over them he will thunder in the heavens.”

### 26

We are heavens when we are raised into the height of the divine grace presiding over us. We have thunder against his adversaries when, with the powerful voices of holy desires, we strike down everything that is breathed against us by their suggestion. For whatever thunder strikes, it kills.

The thunders of the heavens are therefore the perfect desires of the elect. They come forth with a terrifying sound, as it were, from the height of the heavens when they strike the evil spirits from that summit of the mind over which almighty God presides, so that, through love for the one presiding over it, the mind easily overcomes whatever hostile boldness might have been stirred to battle by the one suggesting evil.

But since the Redeemer warns us, we know that “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22). We have also learned from the same Lord’s promise that “whenever the sinner turns, he will be saved” (Ezek. 18:21).

At the end of her song, therefore, Anna should add and say what may terrify the sinner, and say what may make the righteous more cautious:

**(Verse 10.)** “The Lord,” she says, “will judge the ends of the earth.”

27. He does not say “the earth,” but “the ends of the earth.” For the ends of the earth are those who have closed the final span of their life in the perpetration of sin. But one who sins and corrects what he has done is earth because of his sin, yet is not the end of the earth, because although by his wrongdoing he has cast down the heights of his redemption, he rises from the depths of his downfall before judgment. He has wept for what he did, and he awaits the Judge who is to come with the greater joy because, through repentance, he himself bears within himself the lashes of retribution for his earthly condition. Since, then, the Lord judges the ends of the earth, the sinner who has turned back to the Lord should not be afraid, whether he is at the beginning or midway through his course. Since, likewise, the Lord judges the ends of the earth, the righteous person, having begun the practice of righteousness, should not presume. For if sudden death overtakes him while he is still slipping from that equity from which he can fall, because guilt closes in upon his final moments, he is judged according to the law governing the ends of the earth. It follows:

> **(Verse 10.) And he will give power to his king, and will exalt the horn of his Christ.**

28. Since above we have referred this passage to the Redeemer, we likewise do not alter that interpretation in the order of this exposition. For he is our peace, who made both one (Ephesians 2:14). He is also the cornerstone (1 Peter 2:4–6), in whom, as both walls of the elect are joined together, the structure of the eternal city is established. Let our discourse therefore retain its accustomed manner, so that, once the moral and allegorical understanding of the sacred song has been set forth, both may converge in him whom we believe by faith and merit through our conduct.

## CHAPTER II

For the divine word continues and says:

> **[Col. 0090A] (Verse 11.) And Elkanah went to Ramah, to his house.**

1. We have shown that this man signifies the Redeemer of the human race; Hannah, his wife, signifies the Church; the boy Samuel, the people of the Gentiles who believe; and the city of Ramah, the heavenly homeland. What, then, does it mean that after his wife’s song Elkanah is said to have gone to his own city of Ramah, since Hannah sang her song to God after the boy had been born, and the Redeemer ascended to heaven before the holy Church had begotten the Gentile people in faith?

This question is raised only by those who are known to understand merely the bodily presence of our Lord. For did Paul not have with him then the one who had ascended to the Father, when he said, “Or do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3)? He likewise declares: “We speak as from God, before God and in Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:17).

What, then, does it mean that he was sometimes present to the holy Church through the grace of his gift, and sometimes withdrew from her as part of the dispensation of testing? He was present so that, in the gathering of the Gentiles, she might pour forth abundantly the words of life; but at times he concealed himself from her as though absent, so that, when the gift of the word had been withdrawn, she might learn what she was without his presence.

Thus, after the end of the song, it is said: “Elkanah went to his house,” because the holy Church proclaims sublime things from his presence, while he who withdraws himself from mortals as part of his dispensation continually manifests himself to the eternal citizens. His house is the eternal fellowship of the heavenly citizens, which the Lord inhabits by loving, filling, and joining himself to it. He goes there when he leaves Hannah, because he who salutarily withdraws himself from us while we are still making progress continually joins and manifests himself to the perfected and completed citizens of the eternal homeland, since those who have already been tested no longer need to be tested through his absence.

It is therefore appropriately said after Hannah’s song: “Elkanah went to his house,” because the holy Church, which teaches such lofty things to the elect, is always abandoned by the pious dispensation of the Lord, and likewise does not always possess those lofty things to teach. Many hear the words, detest their former wickedness, and resolve upon works of a corrected life; but when they cease to hear, they return to iniquity as though they had never heard those words of life.

The Gentile people, the hearer of the holy Church, were devoted to hearing and ready to act. Appropriately, therefore, it follows:

> **(Verse 11.) But the boy Samuel was ministering in the presence of the Lord, before the face of Eli the priest.**

2. It is as though he were plainly saying: From what he had heard, he strove to please almighty God. He is appropriately called a boy because, although he had undertaken great things for the defense of our faith, he was still new in that generation of faith. And because he offered pleasing service to almighty God, he was a minister in the presence of the Creator. For the one whom divine favor willingly regards in the offering of his service is in the presence of the Lord.

Fearing greatly to be cast out from this presence of the Lord, someone prays, saying: “Do not cast me away from your face” (Psalm 50:13). Desiring likewise to be received there with intense longing, he considers the delay of his coming and says: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41:3). Hence Elijah glories and says: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand” (1 Kings 17:1).

Samuel, therefore, was a minister in the presence of the Lord because the Gentile people were highly acceptable to almighty God in the service of the new religion. By this wording the rejection of Judea is also hinted at secretly, since only Samuel, in whom the faithful people of the Gentiles is represented, is said to minister before the Lord. He alone, therefore, was in his presence, because the Jewish people had plainly ceased to please him.

The Lord speaks of both matters through Malachi. Indicating the rejection of Judea, he says: “I have no pleasure in you, and I will not accept an offering from your hand” (Malachi 1:10). But after expelling Jewish faithlessness from his presence, he adds whom he would gladly regard, saying: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every place a pure offering is offered to my name” (ibid., 11).

Yet we must carefully consider the statement: “Before the face of Eli, Samuel ministered to the Lord.” The order of the ancient teachers, seeing from afar through the spirit of prophecy the ministry of the preachers of the holy Church, recognized and proclaimed in advance the conversion of the Gentile people, their love for the Redeemer, and their reverence in his service.

He knew that this people would be devoted to the Lord’s service, for he said: “All the kings of the earth shall adore him; all the nations shall serve him” (Psalm 71:11). Hence Haggai says: “The one desired by all the nations will come, and the glory of the house of the Lord will be filled” (Haggai 2:8). Hence Isaiah says: “There will be a root of Jesse, and he who will rise up to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope” (Isaiah 11:10; Romans 15:12). Hence the Psalmist says: “Praise the Lord, all nations, and praise him together, all peoples” (Psalm 116:1). Hence the patriarch Jacob says: “He himself will be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis LIX, 10).

Before the face of Eli, therefore, the boy Samuel was a minister of the Lord, because what the Gentile people would later possess as worthy of God, the order of the ancient teachers foresaw through the spirit of prophecy. And immediately he adds concerning those who had been rejected:

> **(Verses 12–13.) Now the sons of Eli did not know the Lord, nor the priestly office toward the people.**

3. “They were,” is to be understood. For who else are the sons of Eli than the Israelites according to the flesh, who knew the sacred Scripture handed down by their fathers, yet did not know the one whom Scripture had promised?

Truth itself rebukes them in the Gospel, saying: “Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56). And again: “If you believed Moses, you would certainly believe me also, for he wrote about me” (ibid. 5:46).

They did not know the Lord, therefore, because they rejected the Redeemer who came in our flesh. Hence through Isaiah he complains, saying: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me” (Isaiah 1:3). It is as though he said: “I opened to him long beforehand, through the prophets, the ways of my incarnation, yet he did not receive what I had promised when it was presented.”

For this reason they also did not know the priestly office toward the people. They would have recognized the priestly office if they had proclaimed that the one promised by the Law and the prophets had already come for the redemption of the human race. Since they not only did not believe in him but also raged against him through persecution, they neither knew the Lord nor understood the priestly office toward the people.

Their wickedness would nevertheless have been less if the one who refused to proclaim the Redeemer’s coming for the benefit of those beneath him had at least feared to harm them. It follows, therefore:

> **67 (Verses 13–14.) But whenever anyone sacrificed a victim, the priest’s boy would come while the meat was being boiled; he had a three-pronged fork in his hand, and he would thrust it into the basin, kettle, pot, or cauldron, and whatever the fork brought up he would take for the priests.**

4. What does it mean to sacrifice a victim, except to offer to almighty God a confession of true faith? And what are the vessels in which the flesh is boiled during the sacrifice except the minds of the faithful?

When they believe that Christ Jesus, the man who is the Mediator between God and human beings, is the true Only-Begotten of the supreme Father, flesh is surely being boiled in them, so that it may be sacrificed to God through the service of their deepest devotion.

Who else is the priest’s boy except the people subjected through service to the faithless pastors of the Synagogue? He is appropriately called a boy because, preferring to hold fast to the weakness of the Law according to the letter, he refused to grow into a perfect man through the Gospel.

But what does it mean that he is assigned to carry out the seizure of food? And what does it mean, again, that in the violence he inflicted he is said to hold a three-pronged fork?

The food of the elect soul is the person of the Redeemer. This food is boiled in sacred vessels when, through the heat of the Holy Spirit, it is prepared in the minds of the elect for the sweetness of nourishment. Flesh is boiled when, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, we both firmly believe and effectively confess that the Lord’s humanity was assumed into the nature of divinity.

Hence through Moses he indicates that the flesh of the Paschal Lamb is to be eaten, saying: “You shall not eat anything from it raw, or boiled in water” (Exodus 12:9). To eat it raw is to believe our Redeemer to be merely human, apart from the grace of the Holy Spirit. It is boiled in water when the essence of the Redeemer is sifted through human wisdom.

The Jews, therefore, eat it raw; heretics eat it boiled in water. The former deny his divinity; the latter, through human wisdom, empty the mysteries of both his divinity and his humanity.

The priest’s boy is sent to take away the food of the faithful because the Jewish people, expelled from faith in the Redeemer, strove intensely to remove the love of that faith from the hearts of the faithful. He is appropriately said to have held a three-pronged fork in his hand, so that he might prevent the portion of flesh that he could pierce from being cooked after it had been drawn out.

The fork in the boy’s hand is the persecution of the Jewish people against the holy Church. And because he attempted to harm the faithful through flattery, punishments, and terrors, the fork rightly had three prongs. It is aptly said that whatever the fork brought up the priest’s boy took for the priests, because it was a great feast for wicked leaders if the crowd of their flattering or enraged agents could overthrow someone whom they had recognized as standing firm in the heights of our faith through his confession.

It follows:

> **(Verses 14–15.) Thus they did to all Israel who came to Shiloh, even before the fat was burned.**

5. Fat is the inner richness in which that devotion of mind is expressed by which the minds of the elect are joined to their Creator in more perfect love. They rightly sacrifice after the flesh has already been boiled, because no one can rise to the height of charity unless he first loves the mysteries of the incarnate divinity in which he believes.

To believe through the Holy Spirit that the humanity of the Lord Jesus was assumed into divinity, so that it may be sacrificed to God, is to boil the flesh. Before the fat was burned, therefore, the boy strove to seize the flesh from all Israel, because the agents of the Synagogue thought to overthrow the new confessors of Christ before perfect charity united them to almighty God.

The words of the sacred history itself indicate this more clearly, for it says: “While the meat was being boiled.” These words suggest not the completion of the boiling but its preparation. The order of this wicked exaction is shown by what follows:

> **(Verse 15.) The priest’s boy would come and say to the one sacrificing, “Give me meat, so that I may boil it for the priest; for I will not accept cooked meat from you, but raw.”**

6. He would give raw meat to the boy who, before his persecutors, asserted the pure humanity of Christ; and the boy would boil it for the priest because, through the fire of malice, the Jewish people thought this was what their leaders would gladly receive as nourishment for their minds.

The priest’s boy came and asked for raw meat when the Jewish people, serving the letter of the Law, urged the faithful to deny the Redeemer’s divinity. Coming, therefore, he says: “I will not accept cooked meat from you, but raw,” because he was unwilling even to hear that the one whom he had compelled the faithful to confess as a mere human being was God.

The importunity of this people is shown when the sacrilegious words are repeated in the wicked exaction. For it follows: “I will not accept cooked meat from you, but raw,” because he very much desired to hear of Jesus the Lord and our Redeemer not as Lord and human being, but only as a mere human being.

Yet those whom he tested as though they were imperfect in their understanding of the flesh, he found to be perfect. For those whom he compelled to deny the Redeemer’s divinity refused not only to deny the Redeemer themselves, but also labored to draw their compellers toward life. Hence it follows:

> **(Verse 16.) And the one sacrificing would say to him, “Let the fat first be burned today according to the custom, and then take for yourself as much as your soul desires.”**

7. He attempts to turn away the one asking for raw meat with a beastly appetite by promising him cooked meat at will. It is as though the holy Church were answering the badly hungry Jews and, in place of the simple humanity which they desired to devour, promising them the food of divinity, saying: “First allow that understanding which you are to have for the nourishment of life in the Holy Spirit to be boiled.”

Did the priest’s boy not ask for raw meat then, when, after the Lord had enlightened the man who had been born blind, it was said to him: “Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner” (John 9:24)?

What does “Give glory to God” mean except: “Do not ascribe the praises of your healing to this man, because he is not God”? And when he is asserted to be a sinner, he is denied not only to be God but also to be a righteous human being.

He refused to provide him with the raw meat he was asking for and offered him cooked meat, because the man who insistently asserted him to be the author of his salvation demonstrated, from the sign of such a great wonder that had been shown, that he was not merely a holy man but the true God.

But when the people had begun, having lost reason, to follow beasts, they insistently demanded that raw meat be served to them. For it follows:

> **(Verse 16.) “Now you will give it; otherwise I will take it from you by force.”**

It follows:

> **(Verse 17.) For the sin of the boys was very great before the Lord.**

And he adds the reason why this sin was shown to be great, saying:

> **(Verse 17.) “Because they drew people away from the sacrifice of the Lord.”**

**69** 8. It is recognized as a very great sin when it is not erased by tears of repentance. Seeing this very great sin of the Synagogue, the prophet says: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point” (Jeremiah 17:1).

Or certainly, the sin was very great before the Lord because it drew others into sin. Hence it adds: “Because they drew people away from the sacrifice of the Lord.” They drew people away from the sacrifice because they prevented the hearts of the weak from advancing to the confession of the true faith.

It should be noted that those who are drawn away from the sacrifice are called “people,” because if they had persisted in the true confession of our faith, the divine word would have marked them with the title “sons of God.” To them the Lord says through the Psalmist: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’; but you will die like human beings” (Psalm 81:6–7).

It follows:

> **(Verse 18.) But Samuel was ministering in the presence of the Lord, a boy girded with a linen ephod.**

9. Linen is known to be finer than woolen cloth. Samuel is appropriately said to have been clothed in a linen ephod, through whom the order of priests chosen from the Gentiles is signified.

For, in comparison with the life prescribed by the Law, the new conduct of the Gospel is the fineness of linen. There, something animal was commanded; there, everyone from whom no seed of offspring was left in Zion was cursed. But in the New Testament, because everything is finer, whoever follows its commands is adorned as though with a more delicate linen garment.

There, abstinence from marriage is condemned; here it is honored with marvelous praise. There, priests beget children carnally; here they produce the fruit of spiritual offspring all the more abundantly because they cannot suffer the losses to chastity that may arise through the good of marriage.

It is fitting that, when Samuel’s garment is explained, it is said to have been linen, so that it might openly display the glory of the new priesthood, which would shine with the radiance of a new chastity. But when Samuel is said to be a minister in the presence of the Lord, he is remembered as girded with a linen ephod, because divine service is properly offered when the person offering it is not defiled by the filth of carnal pleasure; and the gift of ministry is acceptable to God when, through the purity of holy conduct, the person of the minister is pleasing to God.

And because he was progressing in the beginnings of his newness, it further follows:

> **(Verse 19.) And his mother made him a little tunic, which she brought to him whenever she went up with her husband to sacrifice the solemn sacrifice to the Lord.**

10. To sacrifice a victim to the holy Church is to kindle the hearts of her hearers with love of the Creator through the words of preaching. Samuel is therefore said to have been brought a small garment because, while he was still advancing through the growth of his newness, he received from the Church, suited to his smallness, tokens of righteousness by whose splendor he might shine.

It follows:

> **(Verse 20.) And Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife, saying, “May the Lord give you offspring from this woman, in place of the thigh that you entrusted to the Lord.”**

11. Since good teachers of the ancient people are also represented in the person of Eli the priest, he is understood to have blessed Elkanah and his wife because the order of those ancient teachers foresaw the spiritual union of Christ and the holy Church, and proclaimed with devotion that the offspring of those chosen ones would one day be worthy of heaven.

Although this happened long beforehand, it became known that he had then blessed them in this way when, after the grace of our redemption had been revealed, every believer could understand that our ancient fathers had foretold so many good things concerning this renewal.

And so that the order in which this took place might be understood, it is added:

> **(Verse 20.) And they went to their own place.**

12. For the holy Church to go with her husband to her own place is sometimes to flee the troubles of the active life and to devote herself through contemplation to the joys of the life above.

That mother had left the boy for a time—the one who said: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). Was she with the boy when the power of love lifted that outstanding teacher to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2–4)? Was she then with the boy when he was received into paradise, heard words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak, and was carried away to his own place, since he says: “We have no lasting city here, but we seek the one that is to come” (Hebrews 13:14)?

But although she went with her husband to her own place, maternal affection compelled her to return to her son. For she said: “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1:24).

It follows:

> **(Verse 21.) Therefore the Lord visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters.**

**[Col. 0096A]** 13. The more perfect members of the holy Church are signified by the three sons, who are known always to have done brave deeds for faith in the Trinity. But if the holy Church gave birth only to the perfect, our weakness could not reach the rewards of eternal life.

The weakness of two daughters therefore follows the strength of the sons, because although the holy Church has brought forth strong members against the proud enemy of the human race, even her weaker members are led to the joys of the eternal homeland through the two commandments of charity.

And because whoever had begun at that time to be instructed for priestly ministry did not always remain in the beginnings of his newness, it follows:

> **(Verse 21.) And the boy Samuel grew great in the presence of the Lord.**

14. Here we must pay close attention to the fact that Samuel is called both a boy and one who had grown great. Moreover, when he is said to have grown great, this praise of his virtue is said to have been possessed not in the presence of human beings but in the presence of the Lord.

Why, then, is he called a boy? Because he had been raised to the height of perfection. Samuel is therefore called both a boy and one who had grown great in the presence of the Lord because the new order of preachers, although it reached the height of an eminent way of life, did not lose the virtue of its humility.

To grow great before God would not have benefited him if he had ceased to be a boy, because, once humility had been lost, he could not please almighty God by the loftiness of his conduct.

Indeed, those who were casting out demons from the possessed in the name of Jesus had already grown great; but because they had lost the good of their childhood, Truth rebuked them, saying: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10:18). Again, he declares: “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3).

Because, then, the life of the new preachers is both lofty in merit and level through humility, Samuel is appropriately said to have grown great and to have been a boy. And because they are highly acceptable to God in both respects, he is said not simply to have grown great, but to have grown great in the presence of the Lord.

It follows:

> **(Verse 22.) Now Eli was very old, and he heard all that his sons were doing throughout Israel, and how they slept with the women who watched at the door of the tabernacle.**

15. In the person of Eli, not only the ancient priesthood but also the teaching of the ancient fathers is represented, because, by presiding in spiritual dignity, he received the duty of instructing through saving preaching those for whom he offered acceptable sacrifices to the Lord.

What does it mean that Eli is said to be old, except that, in the hearts of the reprobate Jews, the force of the heavenly commandments had grown weak?

Eli was young so long as sacred Scripture retained the force of great authority among the elect of the Synagogue, because it had received the promises of the coming Redeemer and awaited him with great desire. Eli therefore grew old when Judea lost its devotion to observing the promise, so that it might see before itself the Redeemer desired by its fathers, proving himself through miracles, and yet, utterly blind amid such great light, doubt the presence of the truth.

He is also said to have been very old so that it might plainly be shown that every force of faith had withered in the Synagogue. Indeed, if Eli was very old, we must say that he lived in utter weakness. For what did it mean then for the old man of Scripture to live except to furnish the Synagogue with a very weak breath of faith?

He could be very old and still live while the hearts of the Jews wavered, so that they neither believed the Lord Jesus to be the true Redeemer nor openly condemned him as a blasphemer. The evangelist John shows the weakness of this old age, saying: “Some were saying, ‘He is good’; others, ‘No, but he is deceiving the crowds’” (John 7:12). Hence the Jews themselves, revealing the cunning of their craft, say: “How long will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (ibid. 10:24). Again they say: “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you” (Matthew 12:38).

16. But Eli, being very old, heard all that his sons were doing throughout Israel. He certainly “heard” these things because he knew them. What we know, we keep enclosed within the halls of memory. But when the sacred writings are consulted, they bring forth in public all the faithlessness of the Jews written within them and display it as though it had long been preserved in memory.

Amos attributes this knowledge of hearing, as it were, to Eli when he says: “The Lord God does nothing without revealing his word to his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7). Hence Habakkuk confesses to the only-begotten God, saying: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, and I was terrified; you will become known in the midst of the two living creatures” (Habakkuk 3:1, according to the interpretation of the Septuagint).

For the ancient teachers of the Synagogue, to hear beforehand of the crimes of the sons is to know them in advance. What he knew beforehand, he explains, for he says: “All that his sons were doing throughout Israel, and how they slept with the women who watched at the door of the tabernacle.”

To sleep with Jewish women is to be defiled by various heresies. These women are rightly said to watch at the door of the tabernacle. For what is the door of the tabernacle except the letter of the spiritual Law?

While the Jews understand sacred Scripture according to the letter alone, they established heresies there, at the very place from which they could have entered into the secret of the true faith. For just as one enters the interior of the tabernacle through the door, so through the letter of sacred Scripture one enters into spiritual knowledge of the Redeemer.

Because Judea is deceived through its observance of the letter, the women are said to watch at the door, not inside the tabernacle. And because the Jews contradict our Redeemer throughout all the Scriptures, it is not said that there was one woman, but many.

The sons of Eli do these things for themselves, because, according to the prophet’s word, “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:4, 20). But they are said to do them throughout Israel because, while the leaders perish in the night of their error, their inferiors are enveloped in the blindness of that darkness.

The sons of Eli therefore sleep with the women because the reprobate Jews are polluted by the admixture of their heresies until the end of the world. They also sleep because, although they are overwhelmed by the deepest night of their error, they are nevertheless to be awakened by Elijah to faith in the Redeemer at the end of the world (Matthew 17:11).

It follows:

> **(Verse 23.) And he said to them, “Why are you doing such things, the very evil things that I hear from all the people?”**

17. Behold, Eli was old, yet he spoke sharply, because the power of sacred eloquence, although it is lacking in the hearts of the reprobate, nevertheless carefully investigates the sins of the Jews before those who understand rightly.

Examining them with severity, he says: “Why are you doing such things, the very evil things that I hear from all the people?” By asking, “Why are you doing this?” he plainly shows that they were plunging into the night of heresy without the discernment of reason.

He says that they themselves had done the very evil things he heard, and asserts that those evil things came from all the people. What does this mean except that the whole Jewish people had fallen into the depths of heresies? The reprobate priests were the cause of that fall. Hence Hosea, prophesying, says: “The evil priests are the cause of the people’s ruin” (Hosea 5:1).

The people beneath them fell because they strove to imitate their falling leaders. When he says, “the very evil things that I hear from all the people,” the words should be understood to mean that the things were being done by the people, not merely reported by them. It is as though he said: “Why are you doing the evil things that I hear are being done by all the people?” Immediately indicating more clearly what he had said, he adds:

> **(Verse 24.) “Do not, my sons; it is not a good report that I hear about you, so that you make the people of the Lord transgress.”**

18. In what way would the people of the Lord transgress the commandments if they slept with women? But because this happened to them figuratively, it plainly prefigured what was to occur at the time of the Lord’s Incarnation.

When priests sleep with women, their subjects transgress the Lord’s commandments, because, while the leaders are defiled by the admixture of heresies, the reprobate multitude of the subject Synagogue is plunged into the same foulness.

He therefore says: “Why are you doing such things, the very evil things that I hear from all the people?” This is as though he said: “You sin all the more gravely because you defile the whole people more shamefully through your crime.”

Something similar is also said through the prophet: “From Dan,” he says, “the snorting of his horses and chariots is heard” (Jeremiah 8:16). In that passage it should not be understood that he reports a sound heard from Dan, but that he himself, raging with chariots and horses, produces the very sound that is heard.

Here we should also note that the one who reported hearing evil things from all the people added words of gentle affection, saying: “Do not, my sons; it is not a good report that I hear about you, so that you make the people of the Lord transgress.”

Eli both rebuked sharply and admonished gently, because the Scripture of the ancient fathers, while denouncing the error of the Jewish people, rebukes it and, with kindly affection, calls it from the night of that error to the day of true faith.

He calls them sons so that they may recognize that they ought to be heirs of the paternal promise and may receive the Savior of the world with all the greater devotion because they know that his promise was made to their fathers.

But wishing to turn them back from the audacity of sin, he adds the reason:

> **(Verse 25.) “If a man sins against another man, God can be reconciled with him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?”**

19. To sin against one man is for one human being to act perversely against another. What, then, does it mean when he says, “God can be reconciled with him,” except that such sins were light in comparison with those that the Jews were contemplating committing against the Son of God?

They were sinning against God because the one whom they were plotting to kill had shown in the clearest light of miracles that he was God. The Lord himself demonstrates this when he says: “If I had not done among them works that no one else has done, they would not have sin” (John 15:24). To show the implacability of God the Father, he adds: “But now they have no excuse for their sin, because they have seen and hated both me and my Father” (ibid.).

It is therefore as though he said: “By whose prayer can that sin be forgiven which is committed against the very one who forgives? Who will entreat almighty God for one who condemns the coeternal Only-Begotten to death?” He would say nothing more plainly if he confessed: “This one whom you persecute as though he were merely human is also God.”

The law of reason therefore demands that the one who persecutes the Creator be deprived of forgiveness. But divine mercy guides the strictness of reason. It reveals the equity of the law, but it did not maintain the force of the declaration in the execution of the promulgated law.

For it had been decreed with the rigor of equity that no prayer could attain the obtaining of pardon; yet, where no human prayer was sufficient, the mercy of the Redeemer was not lacking. Every human intercessor who might pray for transgressions is removed; but where no human being was sufficient, God himself, made human, became the merciful intercessor.

For, suspended on the cross, he prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXII, 34). God was therefore reconciled with those who had sinned against God, not through another’s prayer but through his own.

Yet God was not reconciled with all, but with some. Some of the Lord’s persecutors were converted when the apostles preached; the rest perished. Luke records the former, saying: “The number of them became five thousand” (Acts 4:4). Concerning the reprobate it follows:

> **(Verse 25.) And they did not listen to the voice of their father, because the Lord willed to kill them.**

[Note: [Col. 0093D] Gilot. and Vatican: “the Lord, by whom the one who had been born blind was enlightened.”]

[Note: [Col. 0093D] The same witnesses, and “because.”]

[Note: [Col. 0094D] Guss.: “from the sign of such great wonder that had been shown.”]

[Note: [Col. 0094D] In the Vulgate, “they drew back.”]

[Note: [Col. 0095D] Perhaps “and grew great” should be added; the words that follow in the exposition seem to pertain more to this phrase than to “boy,” “boy” being the reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0097D] Another witness: “we recognize.”]

[Note: [Col. 0098D] Guss. omits “crimes.”]
