[Note: [Col. 0099D] Perhaps “overcame” or “conquered” should be read, although all printed editions read “leads.”]

[Note: [Col. 0099D] Gilot. and Vatican: “did not maintain the force in the execution of the promulgated law.”]

20. Through the prophet the Lord declares: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII, 23; and XXXIII, 11). How, then, is it consistent for him to wish to kill the sinner and yet not to desire the sinner’s death? But in the testimony just cited what reveals the truth follows: “but that he should turn and live.” For he who wishes the sinner to live so that he may turn, if divine foreknowledge knows that he will not turn, kills him. The Lord therefore wills to kill those whom he foreknows will refuse to turn. For he is declared merciful and just when the Prophet pleads: “Lord,” he says, “deliver my soul; our God is merciful and just” (Ps. CXIV, 5). Through mercy he awaits the conversion of sinners; through justice he condemns those who have not turned. Through mercy he wills sinners to turn and live, but through justice he wills to punish those who have refused to turn; mercifully he does not save unless they are willing, and justly he condemns those who are unwilling.

When, therefore, he is said to wish to kill, the extreme and irreformable wickedness of sinners is revealed—a wickedness voluntarily punished by the execution of divine justice. We see even the most compassionate judges in secular affairs act in this way: they would wish no one to offend, so that they themselves would have to punish no one; but when the wicked boldly commit crimes, they voluntarily punish those whom they would much rather have punished for not committing the offenses that deserved punishment.

In contrast, this is perceived here: he does not say, “Because they refused to hear the voice of their correcting father,” but, “They did not listen because the Lord wished to kill them.” Yet whoever rightly considers the equity of the divine judgment thinks it makes no difference whether someone is killed or is left in that crime in which he is destroyed by eternal rejection. It is as though he said: “So great was the magnitude of their guilt that, although they received the signs of conversion, they could in no way rise from the pit of their death; and those who had drunk the sea of God’s wrath had, as an increase of their condemnation, not only the punishment of the sin they had committed but also the added vengeance for despising the preaching.”

But why should we marvel at this as something past, when we see it happening even now: Eli warning his sons, while the Lord wishes to kill them? What else does Holy Scripture daily suggest to the Jews than the darkness of their error? It does not proclaim the Redeemer through hidden and spiritual meanings in such a way that it does not plainly display his incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. Nor are they so irrational that they fail to see that such excellent blessings belong to the Redeemer; yet they are blind, hearing that the signs promised to their fathers have shone forth in the Redeemer and not believing. They are therefore blind, not merely by seeing the promises, but by not believing what has been brought to pass. [Note: Perhaps it should read: “not merely by not seeing the promises.”] Why do they not hear the warning voice of Scripture, unless it is because the Lord wishes to kill them? Yet it is no wonder if they perish by the judgment of the one whose Only-Begotten they sought to kill.

For, by the strictness of profound justice, judgment is being exercised against the Jewish people: they hear daily the admonitions of life through the speaking Scriptures, yet they themselves do not believe the Scriptures that admonish them. But after rejecting Jewish unbelief, he explains by what successes the order of holy preachers prevails among the Gentiles, saying:

**(Verse 26.)** “But the boy Samuel advanced and grew, and was pleasing both to God and to men.”

21. He advanced through the gain of preaching and grew through the increase in the number of ministers. For the Apostle [Note: “Paul” is added in Gilot and Vatican.] boasts of his progress, saying: “From Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum I have filled the Gospel of Christ” (Rom. XV, 19). Luke also mentions the manner of his growth, saying: “As the number of the disciples increased, there arose a murmuring of the Greeks against the Hebrews, because their widows were being neglected in the ministry” (Acts VI, 1). And shortly afterward: “They chose,” he says, “Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Prochorus, and the others” (ibid., 5). They set these before the apostles, and, after praying, laid hands upon them.

Again, concerning the progress of these new preachers it is written: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5).

22. But what is said must be examined carefully: “He was pleasing both to God and to men.” A teacher is pleasing to men when he presents himself to his subjects as worthy of reverence and adorned with good morals; but he is pleasing to God when he avoids boasting vainly about his good conduct and desires to earn the praise of God alone.

He therefore says, “He was pleasing both to God and to men,” because some preachers display an appearance of holiness that they do not possess. Although these please men, they displease God. Thus, as a type of the new and chosen preacher, Samuel is now said to have been “pleasing both to God and to men.” They present themselves as worthy of reverence to their subjects and offer purity of intention to God.

He had indeed sought to please men who said: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (II Cor. II, 15); and again: “I have become all things to all people, that I might save all” (I Cor. IX, 22). He also taught his hearers to please men, saying: “Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles, as I also please all people in all things, not seeking what is useful to me but what is useful to many” (I Cor. X, 32–33). But the one who had indicated that he pleased men commends purity of heart, saying: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I, 12).

“HE WAS PLEASING BOTH TO GOD AND TO MEN.” The new order of preachers displayed itself outwardly to its hearers as worthy of reverence, for imitation, and inwardly as acceptable to God through the innocence of its will. It follows:

**(Verse 27.)** “A man of God came to Eli.”

23. What is expressed by this man of God except that venerable company of the holy apostles? He is called a man of God because of the excellence of his holiness: he exercised, with an equal height of virtue, the summit of the order that he had ascended in presiding over the whole world. He came to Eli when he approached the priests of the Synagogue to announce its rejection. It follows:

**(Verses 27, 28.)** “And he said to him: ‘Was I not plainly revealed to your father’s house when it was in Egypt, in the house of Pharaoh, and did I not choose him from all the tribes of Israel as my priest, that he might go up to my altar, burn incense to me, and carry the ephod before me? And I gave to your father’s house all the sacrifices of the sons of Israel?’”

24. Since Judaea is rejected by divine judgment, the strictness of that judgment is shown to have been imposed with marvelous equity. First, the gifts previously bestowed upon Eli are enumerated, so that, when the almighty God is shown to be so benevolent a giver, it may be recognized how justly he strikes the one who despises him.

He asserted that he had revealed himself to his father’s house, so that it could have no excuse of ignorance. He also teaches that he had granted him knowledge of this same revelation in Egypt, so that Eli might in no way suppose that he had obtained it through his own merits. It is as though he plainly said: “There I made myself known to him, where he could have forgotten me and did not know how to remember me.”

And lest the gift of divine knowledge itself seem perhaps small to the reprobate, he is said to have been taken from the other tribes of Israel and raised to the summit of the priesthood. It is as though he said: “I preferred him to those among whom he was not superior but equal.”

25. It should be noted that three things are signified in the exercise of that priesthood. “That he might go up,” he says, “to my altar, burn incense to me, and carry the ephod before me.”

What else is shown in this altar than that stone which the patriarch Jacob raised as a memorial (Gen. XXVIII, 18)? And what other stone is represented than the one Paul proclaims in praise of the faithful, saying: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone” (Eph. II, 20)?

Eli’s father was therefore chosen by the Lord for the priesthood so that he might go up to the altar, because the order of the ancient teachers presided over the people entrusted to it for this purpose: to proclaim the restoration of the human race that was to come at the Redeemer’s arrival. He burned incense because he united the hearts of his hearers through desire to the one whom he proclaimed as the future Redeemer. He also carried the ephod because he furnished the desire of so great an expectation with the adornment of a worthy manner of life.

He would have burned incense and not carried the ephod if he had kindled the hearts of his hearers with longing for the coming Redeemer while differing from him through the deformity of an immoral life. And because the almighty God sought the truth of religion, not its outward appearance, before himself and not before the people, he is said to have commanded him to carry the ephod before him. To carry the ephod before the Lord is to seek, from innocence of life, the reward of divine goodness alone.

These words are plainly spoken against Eli as a reproach. He did not go up to the altar because, when the priesthood presided over the Synagogue in the time of revealed truth, he did not proclaim to the peoples entrusted to him the one who had shone forth as the Redeemer of the human race through such a multitude of signs. He did not burn incense to God because he stirred up the people to persecute him, not to love him. He also scorned to carry the ephod before the Lord because he did not shine with any true religious devotion. For although that adornment of life displayed certain marks of moral respectability, it arose from a false outward appearance, not from an intention of charity.

Thus the Lord also reproves this very thing in them, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful to men outwardly but within are full of the bones of the dead” (Matt. XXIII, 27).

But since he would seem to have bestowed less upon one to whom he had provided so many spiritual gifts unless he had also supplied temporal ones, it is added: “And I gave to your father’s house all the sacrifices of the sons of Israel.” As though he were openly bringing this charge against him [perhaps: “repeating it”], he says: “I failed him in nothing. I bestowed the heights of spiritual honor and power, and supplied an abundance of earthly prosperity for temporal use.”

But let us now hear with what force he investigates the audacity of his transgression, as he enumerates the gifts bestowed so reasonably. For it follows:

**(Verse 29.)** “Why do you kick away my victim and my offerings, which I commanded to be offered in the temple?”

26. Why does the judge ask “Why,” except one who investigates insistently? And the one who is reproved for having kicked away God’s victim and offerings is judged to have done him injury without any rational purpose. [Note: Gilot and Vatican read: “is shown” (indicatur).] It should be noted that he speaks in the plural: “Why did you kick away my victim?” so that what is said may appear to apply not only to Eli but also to his sons.

Wild animals commonly repel with a kick those that cling to them. What other victims were there for the faithful than to persist in the praises of their Redeemer, to proclaim that Christ Jesus had died for the salvation of the world, and, by rising again, had restored life to the human race? And what other offerings did they have except continually to present thanksgiving to the almighty God for the many benefits bestowed upon them?

Eli’s sons kicked these away because, in rejecting the new preaching, they did not follow the counsel of reason through the sacred writings but the impulse of brute ferocity. Truth wished to recall them from irrational savagery to the purpose of rational counsel, saying: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and they bear witness about me” (John V, 39).

Hence it is also said here: “Which I commanded to be offered in the temple.” In the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets, it had been written concerning the Lord’s passion and resurrection and the condition of the universal Church. The leaders of the Synagogue therefore kicked away the Lord’s victim and offerings that had been commanded to be offered in the Lord’s temple, because they tried not to examine the preaching of the holy Church by the authority of Holy Scripture but to condemn and reject it solely through the violence of their ferocity.

For if they had consulted the commandments of God in the sacred utterances with an enlightened mind, they would have received as divinely sent to them the holy preachers whom they violently cast away. But the one who reproves Eli’s sons—that is, the ancient teachers of the lesser order—for irrational ferocity also accuses the father himself of negligence, saying:

**(Verse 29.)** “You honored your sons more than me.”

27. As though openly reproving him, he says: “They rejected, and you honored those who rejected.” He honored his sons more than God because, while disregarding their manifest deeds when they were exposed, he provided them with temporal profits. Hence he adds:

**(Verse 29.)** “So that you might eat the first portions of every sacrifice of mine.”

28. By these words he seems to accuse the higher order of teachers, who consented to the Redeemer’s death because they feared losing the profits of the ancient offerings. Thus, after consulting with the Pharisees, they said: “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John XI, 47–48). And again: “You see that we accomplish nothing; behold, the whole world has gone after him” (ibid. XII, 19).

He therefore honored his sons so that they might eat, because he fell silent concerning the purpose of preaching, lest, while affirming the truth of the new offering, he should no longer have the ancient things available for the extravagance of his pleasure.

Since he has therefore explained the magnitude and character of the offense, let us now see with what equity of judgment he indicates the measure of punishment. For he adds:

**(Verse 30.)** “Therefore the Lord God of Israel says: Speaking, I spoke that your house and the house of your father should minister before me from now and forever. But now, far be this from me.”

29. As though striking him with an open and appropriate sentence, he says: “You honored your sons so that you might eat the first portions of every sacrifice; therefore the rights to the first portions are taken away from you, because they were honored unworthily.”

For what does it mean to say, “Far be it from me that your house should minister before me,” except: “I cast you down from the height to which the rights of the first portions belonged”? He was therefore seized by a marvelous execution of justice: from the very source where he greedily desired to consume the first portions, he was made to fast from receiving them.

For he allowed the Redeemer to die lest he lose the profits of the priesthood, but the Redeemer gained from the triumph of death the means by which he destroyed the benefits of the ancient sacrifice.

He says: “Speaking, I spoke that your house and your father’s house should minister before me; but now, far be this from me.” As though in plainer words he said: “I frequently warned you so that you might stand at such a height of dignity, but now you are not what I desired you to be.”

Because this is spoken concerning the rejection of the Jewish people, what follows concerns the order of the new preachers:

**(Verse 30.)** “But whoever glorifies me, I will glorify.”

30. We already behold the glory of those who glorify him, because the preachers of the holy Church sing the praises of the almighty God with great splendor of life and rejoice in presiding over the whole world. Behold, the entire Gentile world is now prostrate at the feet of the priests, and it boasts that it possesses in heaven as its patrons those to whom it rejoices to submit itself through obedience.

The Lord therefore glorifies those who glorify him, because he raises those from whom he daily receives devoted praises to the honor of the whole world. Is it not the glory of being glorified to remain on earth and close heaven? To live an ordinary human life and to display to one’s subjects, through the authority of power, the heavenly seats above?

Peter glorified the Lord when he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 16). But the Lord glorified the one who glorified him, answering: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (ibid., 19).

But concerning the rejected reprobates of the Jews it is added:

**(Verse 30.)** “But those who despise me will be without honor.”

31. They despise him because they in no way believe that he is the Redeemer of the world. Concerning them Truth itself complains in the Gospel, saying: “But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying: ‘We do not want this man to reign over us’” (Luke XIX, 14).

We already see their lack of honor [Note: Gilot and Vatican read: “we see their nobility.”], because they are proscribed both by lineage and by condition. They are without honor by lineage because they heard from Truth itself: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII, 44). They are also without honor by condition because, having lost their freedom and kingdom, they are oppressed by perpetual servitude to the nations.

But he shows the order of their punishments more clearly, saying:

**(Verse 31.)** “Behold, days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there will be no old man in your house.”

32. He is already without an arm, because the one who lost the temple and tabernacle no longer extends his hand to offer the ancient sacrifice. And because he was speaking to Eli—that is, to the chief priests of the Synagogue—he threatens to cut off not only his arm but also his house, clearly signifying the universal destruction of the ancient rite and teaching us to understand that what we now see accomplished in the new age was arranged in ancient times.

The Lord cut off both his arm and his house because he entirely removed both the chief priests of Judaea and the lesser priests from the ancient sacrifice. Hence it is appropriately added: “So that there will be no old man in your house.” The old men are to be understood as the priests, whose office is exercised with the great gravity of moral dignity and is not relieved from the weight of religion by any childish frivolity.

His arm and the arm of his father’s house were therefore cut off so that there would be no old man in his house, because the rite of the ancient priesthood vanished in such a way that no one at all remained who could sacrifice according to the ancient custom. For after the Redeemer of the human race offered himself for our sins according to the new manner of sacrifice, the priesthood according to the ancient custom ceased.

But the one who bears the loss of the priesthood he has lost suffers the torment of a greater punishment through the pain of envy. Therefore it is added:

**(Verse 32.)** “And you will see your rival in the temple, amid all the prosperity of Israel.”

33. He sees his rival within the temple because he himself has already been cast outside. For who else is the rival of the ancient priesthood than the order of the new preachers? As they strive through living and teaching to equal the efforts of the ancient and chosen fathers, they rightly emulate Eli’s good qualities in goodness. Hence Paul admonishes: “Let all of you emulate what is good in goodness” (Gal. IV, 18).

What else is meant by the prosperity of Israel except the felicities of this passing age, in which Israel according to the flesh greatly rejoiced? He therefore sees his rival amid all the prosperity of Israel because he sees the preachers of truth in the holy Church enjoying happiness, both in the abundance of their possessions and in the height of their dignity.

The fact that he is said to see him in the temple is also explained by a more profound understanding. His rival is in the temple amid all prosperity because the order of preachers arranges everything that serves it from the happiness of this age in contemplation of eternity. It follows:

**(Verse 33.)** “Nevertheless, I will not altogether remove a man from my altar.”

34. He would altogether remove a man from his altar if he admitted no one to the unity of our faith. He did not therefore remove him altogether, because although he rejected the reprobate priests of the Synagogue, he mercifully led many of them to knowledge of himself. Luke mentions them in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “A great number of priests were obedient to the faith” (Acts VI, 7).

They were found worthy of so great and new a ministry because they were unwilling to remain with the lost in their old condition. But since the Jewish priesthood had, for the torment of its envy, not only the chosen preachers from the Gentiles but also those who came to faith from Judaea, it follows:

**(Verse 33.)** “But so that your eyes may fail and your soul may languish.”

35. He did not altogether remove a man from his altar also for this reason: so that Eli’s eyes might fail and his soul languish. For he did not wish to admit the chosen from Judaea to the ministry of the new preaching, so that, when they had been removed, guilt might hold the reprobate for punishment.

Eli’s eyes failed when he heard, through the mouths of the preachers, the supreme priesthood proclaiming the truth of the faith and did not recognize it. His soul also languishes because, through the punishment of his rejection, it withered when he lost the grace of the Holy Spirit. It follows:

**(Verse 33.)** “And the greater part of your house will die when it reaches manhood.”

36. Manhood is the time of the Lord’s Incarnation, which the Apostle indicates when he says: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Gal. IV, 4–5).

What, then, were the commandments of Judaea except certain lessons of infancy? The same Apostle also indicates the time of this childhood, saying: “When we were children, we were enslaved under the elements of this world” (ibid., 3).

She therefore died at manhood, because, in the fullness of time, she raged against the Redeemer of the world and pierced herself with the sword of unbelief. It is rightly predicted that not the whole house but the greater part of the house would die, because some among them believed in the Redeemer.

Adding a cause of greater sorrow, he says:

**(Verse 34.)** “And this will be a sign for you concerning what will happen to your two sons, Ophni and Phinehas: both will die on one day.”

37. We have shown above that in Eli’s two sons the twofold order of the ancient priesthood is signified. They died on one day because they came together in the death of the Redeemer.

The death of the priests is appropriately remembered as a sign of the house that was to die, because when the shepherds perish, the flock must necessarily follow into the same destruction. And because they were deceived by false reasoning, they are said to die in the daytime. Blessed Job speaks of the falsity of that day, saying: “They walk in darkness as in light” (Job XXIV, 17).

But the one who expelled the old prepared the new priesthood. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 35.)** “And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest.”

38. When Eli’s sons had died, the Lord raised up a faithful priest for himself, because, after the leaders of the ancient people had been extinguished in unbelief, he chose the elect to undertake the ministry of our redemption.

He is called one who was assumed as faithful because the old priesthood, which he succeeded, was rejected through unfaithfulness. And because the faith of this priest is attributed to him as praise—a faith that works through love—the works of that love are indicated by the words that follow. For it follows:

**(Verse 35.)** “Who will act according to my heart and my soul.”

39. By expressions drawn from the parts of the human body, the ineffable divine substance wished to signify something that must not be understood literally of God. He therefore said: “Who will act according to my heart and my soul.”

This does not mean that the incorporeal and uncircumscribed substance of God possesses a heart and soul. Rather, he speaks to human beings as one human being speaks to another, so that, through what a person recognizes upon hearing his words, he may clearly understand what God also wills.

This could have been said more simply: “Who will do my will.” And he explains the reward of the work, saying:

**(Verse 35.)** “And I will build him a faithful house.”

40. What other house is meant here except the eternal homeland? Concerning this house the Lord says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV, 2).

This house is now said to be built because it is prepared through the actions of a devout life. Nevertheless, human work is unworthy to merit it unless the grace of the merciful God brings this about. Thus, when the building of the house is mentioned, the Lord rightly promises to build it for him, because human strength fails in so great a task unless it is divinely assisted.

Hence Paul says: “It is God who works in me both to will and to accomplish” (Phil. II, 13). Again he says: “It is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16).

He promised to build this house when he said: “I go to prepare a place for you, and I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be” (John XIV, 2–3).

But because he was to follow the grace that called him devoutly through the freedom of his will, it is added:

**(Verse 35.)** “And he will walk before my Christ all his days.”

41. For each of the elect, to walk before Christ is to behold oneself always in the presence of the Redeemer and to do what one knows to be acceptable to him. Or certainly, he walks before Christ who, in everything he does, always looks toward him and directs the uprightness of his life toward the one whom he recognizes as having come, through the humanity he assumed, to shape the likeness of the elect.

Yet Judaea is not to be abandoned forever in the darkness of its blindness, because it is said through the prophet: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. X, 22). Hence Paul says: “A partial blindness has happened in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel may be saved” (Rom. XI, 25–26). [Note: Gilot and Vatican read “will be” (fiet).] He therefore subsequently shows this visitation of Judaea, saying:

**(Verse 33.)** “But it will happen that whoever remains in your house will come to have prayer offered for him.”

42. Judaea then asks that the Lord be prayed for on its behalf, when, after the elect from the Gentiles have already been gathered, it recognizes the darkness of its blindness; when, through the priests of the almighty God, it desires him to be offered through confession of the Holy Trinity. For, in its former old condition, it does not presume to merit heavenly joys, but, having received the faith of the Redeemer after its conversion, it also extends that faith through preaching to others who are to be converted.

It is also rightly added:

**(Verse 33.)** “That he may offer a silver coin.”

Silver signifies the divine utterances, because it is said through the Prophet: “The utterances of the Lord are utterances tested by fire, silver tried in the fire” (Ps. XI, 7).

Judaea then expends this silver in the praises of God when it openly proclaims our faith, which, while placed in unbelief, it formerly opposed. And because it imitates through compassion the same Redeemer whom it proclaims in love, it is added:

**(Verse 33.)** “And a cake of bread.”

Bread signifies the one who said of himself: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI, 51). The cake of bread is the Redeemer’s flesh afflicted by suffering. Beholding this afflicted bread, the Prophet says: “Surely he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our pains” (Isa. LIII, 4).

And because a certain wise man says: “If you sit at the table of a powerful man, attend wisely to what is placed before you, for you must prepare similar things” (Prov. XXIII, 1–2, according to the Septuagint), Judaea then offers the cake of bread and the silver coin when it proclaims our Redeemer through open confession and, for love of the one whom it proclaims, does not refuse to endure torments from the unbelieving.

Because it takes great delight in this imitation of the passion and refreshment of sweetness, it follows:

**(Verse 33.)** “And let him say, ‘Let me go, I beg you, to one priestly portion.’”

44. “Let me go,” he says, as though he were saying: “Do not reject me as infamous and stained with the blood of the Redeemer’s death.” He also begs that one priestly portion be granted to him, because he desires to be joined to the true priests, so that he may share in the joys of those whose offerings he longs to imitate by offering himself.

Hence, explaining his desire for refreshment, he says:

**(Verse 33.)** “That I may eat a morsel of bread.”

Here it should be noted that he is said to possess a cake of bread in the devotion of offering, but a morsel in the desire to eat. Why, then, is not the cake of bread but the morsel desired for eating? And why is not the morsel but the cake said to be offered?

But because the morsel is made round, and roundness itself is in a certain way recognized as having neither beginning nor end, the eternity of the Redeemer is rightly signified by the morsel of bread.

We can offer the cake of bread, but not the morsel, because we can imitate the Lord’s passion by dying or by afflicting the flesh, but we do not possess within ourselves the eternity that we may present before his sight. And the morsel, not the cake, ought to be ours in the perfection of desire, because we who follow the Redeemer of the human race temporally by sharing his suffering desire to possess him in the heavenly homeland no longer mortal or suffering, but eternal and reigning.

The one who desires to offer the cake of bread therefore says: “That I may eat a morsel of bread,” because those converted from Judaea desire to possess our Redeemer in the eternity of refreshment. Here they have imitated his passion for the strenuousness of warfare, not for the reward of recompense.

# CHAPTER III

1. We have passed through this explanation of the sacred history in its typological sense so that, in the same words of the sacred history, we may seek something belonging to moral understanding.

Thus the boy Samuel is asserted to be a minister in the presence of the Lord; yet this ministry is said to be offered to the Lord not absolutely but before Eli’s face. By these words the perfection of ministry is not shown but humility.

For Eli’s face is the exercise of each instructor’s judgment. He ministers to the Lord before the face of his teacher who, in carrying out his ministry, does not follow the reasoning of his own judgment but walks along the path of work that is foreseen for him through the knowledge of his master.

For all perfect men, taught by God (John VI, 45; Isa. LIV, 13), are ministers in the presence of the Lord, but they are not his ministers before the face of a human being, because the divinity within them itself teaches how they are also to be ordered outwardly in life, morals, and doctrine.

Hence, by the praise of the Father’s oracle, it is promised to the Redeemer’s forerunner: “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke I, 76).

He is described as going before the face of the Lord because in his ministry he was not going to follow the judgment of a superior human being but the inspiration of divinity.

Samuel is therefore said to minister to the Lord before Eli’s face so that all who are subject may learn by his example to strive to please their Creator in their ministry in such a way that they do not presume to do anything contrary to the judgment of their superiors.

For when one is asserted to be the Lord’s minister before the face of his instructor, if through pride he despises going before that instructor’s face, he does not exist as a minister in the presence of the Lord. He is shown to be ignorant of the almighty One, whom he scorns to please through the judgment of the one whose authority he subjected himself to in order to please him.

Hence Eli’s sons are said both to be sons of Belial and not to know the Lord, and the office of priests toward the people is also mentioned. They are called sons because they are subjected to spiritual fathers for instruction.

But when they proudly despise following the counsels of those same fathers, they are rightly called sons of Belial, because they become imitators of the apostate spirit who fell from heaven through pride. They know the Lord all the more disastrously the more arrogantly they claim knowledge of him.

Thus it comes about that they do not know more perilously what they ought to know, because, thinking that they know it, they do not take care to learn while ignorant. And because they cannot love the invisible Creator whom they do not know, they dissipate, through their desire for visible things, the very ministries of God that they usurp for themselves.

Hence those who are reported as priests who do not know the Lord are also said not to know the priests’ office toward the people.

2. To disclose the causes of their reproach, a boy of the ignorant priest is said to come to every one making an offering with a three-pronged fork and violently demand raw meat. In these words, three kinds of gluttony are noted in the greed of his rapacity.

For the boy whose practice was to come before the meat was cooked in order to use violence in taking it could not wait for the proper hour of refreshment; and the one for whom the meat was sought did not know how to use simple foods. Moreover, by refusing cooked meat and demanding raw meat, he scorned to eat that same meat according to the common preparation.

But if the wickedness of the servants served the pleasure of the priests, why is the very great sin said to have been not that of the priests themselves but of the boys, even before the Lord?

By the same words, however, the greater guilt of the priests is revealed. For the one who asserts that the sin of the lesser men was very great before the Lord understood that the iniquity of the greater had grown into an accumulation of condemnation. The magnitude of the offense is nevertheless asserted not only because of the desire for unlawful food but also because of the violence of rapacity.

### 3

But the divine discourse returns to the account of the chosen boy, so that in him we may consider more attentively not what is to be rejected, but what is to be imitated. Accordingly, he is said to be girded with a linen ephod and to be in the presence of the Lord. What, then, is signified by the linen ephod if not the brightness of continence? We are girded with this ephod when we are held on every side to the purity of chastity, when no part of soul or body is released from the discipline of the law, through which we might dissipate ourselves into the darkness of lust.

Such a minister is therefore in the presence of the Lord, because he is not deceived concerning the hoped-for vision of almighty God, whom he serves with such great brightness of self-restraint. To this boy, as he ascended with her husband to offer the solemn sacrifice, his mother is said to have brought a small tunic. The mother ascends with her husband when the preacher’s mind, through foreknowledge of the inward Bridegroom, raises itself to contemplate those sublime joys of eternity. Then indeed he offers a solemn sacrifice, because, while he is joined to the Creator through the ineffable sweetness of that love, festive devotion is presented upon the heavenly altars.

And then she brings a small tunic, because, although through the great grace of inward visitation the pastor’s soul is lifted to heavenly things, he must nevertheless impose the precepts of conduct upon the little ones not according to the measure of his own subtle understanding, but according to their strength. Hence Moses, returning from the mountain with the immense radiance of his face, veiled his face so that the people might be able to look upon him (Exod. XXXIV, 33).

Let the one who is a spiritual mother therefore bring a small tunic to her son, so that she may prescribe for the still-small ones certain elementary and straightforward things, and not impose upon them the burden of her own strength. For those who can overcome the enemy through lesser deeds often fall amid great works. Hence David, advancing into battle against the strongest of the Philistines, laid aside his breastplate, shield, and all the implements of war; and he who could not move against the enemy under their weight struck him down with a single stone from his sling (I Sam. XVII, 39–40 and following).

That mother had ascended to offer a solemn sacrifice who said: “I know such a man, who was caught up into paradise” (II Cor. XII, 4). But from such greatness she did not bring a large garment for the little ones, because she says: “He heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak” (ibid.). Again: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III, 2). Let the mother therefore bring a small tunic to her little son, and let the measure of the garment be extended according to the size of the body, so that, while he fights with the virtue of a disciplined way of life, the enemy may not overthrow him beneath an unequal burden of weapons.

### 4

And because God multiplies the gains of converts for the preacher through the pastor’s discerning devotion to his charge, Hannah is said to have been visited by the Lord and, through the grace of the divine gift, to have merited the fruitfulness of sons and daughters.

She bears sons when she wins them through the word—those through whom she gives the seeds of preaching to others. She bears daughters when she recalls to the service of almighty God minds which, although they are not suited to preaching, nevertheless diligently nourish the seed of God’s word received from preachers; and these daughters, as though giving birth later, produce it through good works as an example to their neighbors.

But because Samuel is first said to have been girded with a linen ephod, and afterward the mother’s fertility may reasonably be understood in the plurality of her children, this can signify what we see happening daily: namely, that through the good reputation of the chosen disciples the master’s gains of converts increase. Hence, after the birth of brothers and sisters, Samuel is also said to have been magnified before the Lord, because those who turn the hearts of their neighbors to the service of almighty God through examples of devout conduct are already great in the Lord’s sight.

### 5

A great fear is impressed upon us, because Eli is condemned for the fault of his sons, although no personal sins of his are mentioned. For good subjects, living well is sufficient for salvation; but for superiors, their own life is not sufficient. Indeed, he is very old who always strives to live irreproachably. Hence it is also written: “For old age is honorable, not that which is of long duration, nor reckoned by number of years; for the senses of a human being are gray hairs, and an unblemished life is the age of old age” (Wis. IV, 8).

But some excel in living well who possess none of the authority that governance requires. For although they strive to rouse their subjects to perform good deeds, they are ashamed, through zeal for righteousness, to oppose those who are committing faults. Even if they sometimes come forward to rebuke them, they do more harm than good by speaking, because they do not confound their obstinacy with appropriate severity.

Eli heard of the crimes of his sons and of how they slept with the women at the entrance of the tabernacle. As though beginning with a harsh denunciation arising from his authority, he declared that he had heard of their very evil deeds from all the people. But although he ought to have pursued the faults he had exposed, he softened them with the words that followed, saying: “No, my sons.” In this designation of kinship it is clear how far he differed from the Lord’s will, because he called “sons” those whom the divine discourse had earlier declared to be sons of Belial—that is, sons of the evil spirit—saying: “Moreover, the sons of Eli were sons of Belial.”

[Note: Something seems to be missing here; what is read in verse 22—“how they slept,” and so forth—ought to have preceded this.]

To sleep with women is to sin securely and without fear of future vengeance. The women are worldly desires, which are rightly said to keep watch at the entrance of the tabernacle, because they lie in wait for those striving toward entry into the kingdom of heaven.

But whoever follows the desires of the world in such a way that he is often terrified by consideration of divine fear is indeed defiled with the women, but does not sleep with them; for although he slips by transgressing, he does not rest in his crimes through security. One who sleeps with the women is therefore not to be honored by the title of kinship, because those who, having already cast away the fear of God, are obstinate in their crimes must not be rebuked with a lighter correction. Otherwise they may think that the sin in which they fall is a light matter, since what is proclaimed with authority does not sound grave to them.

But lax pastors commonly bring forward certain arguments of reason amid the soothing remedies of their words. Hence Eli is also said to have spoken:

**(Verse 25.)** “If a man sins against another man, God can be appeased on his behalf; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?”

### 6

To sin against another person is for human beings to harm one another in matters that pass away. But to sin against God is to take away from him those things that he created for eternity. Therefore, whoever draws either his own soul or that of another faithful person into sin is convicted of sinning against God, because he attempts to take away from him what is his own.

This sin is shown to be so much graver in proportion as a worthy intercessor for its absolution is found more rarely. For under the question, “Who will pray for him?” it is not said that the remedies of repentance are thereby denied to such people, but that the deeper wounds of sins are healed with greater difficulty.

### 7

Yet this can be understood as having been said for the reason that the priests are being rebuked. A man sins against another man when someone commits a fault whose correction belongs to the judgment of a superior human being. Since the sins of subject people, which concern priests, are wiped away through the prayers of those priests, when a priest falls into sin there is no superior person whose prayers can atone for him.

The Truth itself also intimates this, saying: “If the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted?” (Matt. V, 13). Let him therefore say, “Who will pray for him?”—as if he were saying: Who remains as his intercessor when the one who was ordained to intercede for others casts himself headlong through transgression?

By this the greatness of the fault is shown, because many of them are cast by the Lord into the darkness of an impenitent heart and do not recover their senses through any human exhortation. Therefore what follows appropriately says:

**(Verse 25.)** “They did not listen to the voice of their father, because the Lord wished to kill them.”

### 8

The boy Samuel, however, is said both to make progress and to grow, and to please both God and human beings, so that the diligence of the chosen hearer may be represented. He directs his efforts along the path of a righteous life toward the heavenly homeland while he grows strong for greater things.

Hence the Psalmist says: “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXIII, 8). Progress in conduct, therefore, is growth in merits; pleasing God and human beings is the perfection of completed maturity.

And because conduct belongs to works, while merit proceeds from charity, those hearers make progress but do not grow who perform good works out of a desire for vanity and do not possess charity. We therefore make progress and grow if, through more exalted conduct, we are raised up by better works and, from that same elevation of works, direct our attention solely toward the joys of eternity.

To please both God and human beings is a great virtue, because we often offend our neighbors through our good work if we do not perform those same good deeds with great caution. Therefore the person pleases both God and human beings who is cautious in the good work he devotes to the service of almighty God—who takes care to please God in such a way that he does not offend anyone through God’s service.

### 9

And because this is said of Samuel while he is still a boy and placed under another’s instruction, the life of those living in common is taught through him. For some who live in common in sacred places, under the guise of great activity and with the fervor of recent conversion, desire to devote themselves to their own pursuits; the less useful they are to their brothers who share their dwelling, the less pleasing they are.

The chosen Samuel is therefore set before those living in common as a model, and they are shaped by him. Each of them pleases God and human beings when he is useful to his brothers and devoted to God. Let them therefore care for themselves in such a way that they do not neglect what belongs to their neighbor, so that through kindness they may please those who are with them below, while cautiously displaying to the heavenly eyes, through the devotion of their strength, the vigor of that strength, lest they crush the hearts of the weak as they hasten upward through the force of their own power.

### 10

The man of God is described as having come to Eli. He was about to deliver the severity of the divine sentence, and he carefully enumerated how many gifts God had bestowed upon him. And because at last he announces the punishment of the vengeance he deserved, what else does this signify but that the faults of pastors are judged more precisely? Not only do their sins aggravate the punishment of retribution for them, but so do the gifts that have been granted.

Again, because he repeats those same gifts one by one, he indicates something more serious: each gift contributes to the torment, since each is proved to have been badly preserved. For the person who pollutes the brightness of the pastoral dignity with the stains of wicked action keeps the gifts of almighty God badly within himself.

Hence Eli is appropriately reproved for having cast the Lord’s gifts and sacrifices away with his foot. The foot is that part of the body with which we touch the earth. In this lower part of the body, therefore, the soul’s inclination is represented by which earthly things are desired.

### 11

And because, as some have thought, sacrifices were accustomed to be offered for an achieved or anticipated victory, and gifts to be given to friends, what else are represented by sacrifices and gifts but the vows of those still making progress and the devotions of the perfect in the praises of almighty God?

When we make progress through the temptations of hidden enemies, as we prepare virtue for conflict with them, we hold sacrifices in the praises of almighty God. But when the battles brought against us have already been conquered, and we give thanks to almighty God for the victory achieved, we likewise sacrifice victims to that same Lord.

Those who offer him the affection of familiar love expend gifts upon him as upon a friend. Gifts, then, are the affections of charity, by which the hearts of the chosen burn with desire for their Creator.

And because, when a ruler pursues earthly things, he harms many who are engaged in spiritual conflict and many others who are just beginning to aspire upward, he casts away God’s sacrifices and gifts with his foot, because by the example of his wickedness he drives away the efforts of both groups.

The sacrifices are cast away because often the labor of spiritual warfare is abandoned by inexperienced soldiers of Christ when the leaders of the Christian campaign appear to pursue bodily ease in the repose of earthly allurements. The gifts are cast away with the foot because the affections of charity grow cold in the minds of many who already desire heavenly things when they see their superiors seeking the heavenly homeland with no desires of love, but lying bound by bodily coldness among the lowest pleasures.

Some of these people even bestow spiritual honors in a carnal manner and assign to kinship what is owed to merit. They would certainly fear the guilt of their presumption if they carefully considered what the Lord complains of concerning Eli the priest:

**(Verse 29.)** “You honored your sons more than me, so that you might eat the first portions of every sacrifice of my people Israel.”

### 12

He honors sons and relatives more than the Lord who chooses persons for sacred orders not on the basis of upright conduct, but out of love of kinship. The sons are said to have been honored for the purpose of eating the first portions of the sacrifice because carnal superiors bestow the heights of spiritual honor upon carnal relatives so that they may be enriched with ecclesiastical resources and heap up an abundance of wealth in the high position of the order.

They do not care what sort of people come to the spiritual ministry, but only that they may advance in temporal dignity those whom they embrace with carnal affection. He is therefore accused of having honored sons—but wicked sons, who ought not even to be regarded as close because of carnal kinship if they do not shine through the conduct required by ecclesiastical teaching.

But those who advance the reprobate are shown to confound the very order of promotion, since he reports that the sons were honored for the purpose of eating the first portions of the sacrifice. A priest does not preach in order to eat; rather, he ought to eat in order to preach. Paul also indicates this, saying: “The one who announces the Gospel should live by the Gospel” (I Cor. IX, 14).

Again he says: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing” (I Cor. IX, 9; I Tim. V, 18; Deut. XXV, 4), so that the preacher of holy Church may provide food for his body for the purpose of being able to bear the labor of preaching.

Those who advance relatives, therefore, are proved to pervert the proper order of promotion, since they do so not with the ministry as their aim, but with dignity as their objective. They certainly would not do this if they did not love themselves and their relatives carnally in the spiritual heights.

But if they understand Eli’s rejection, let them also fear the judgments of their own guilt. For the divine voice says: “You honored your sons more than me, so that you might eat all the first portions of my people Israel.”

**(Verse 30.)** “Therefore says the Lord God of Israel: Speaking, I spoke that your house and the house of your father should minister in my presence forever. But now—far be this from me.”

### 13

Behold, Eli is removed from the height of dignity by the divine sentence. He is convicted of having honored wicked sons for the sake of eating the first portions, so that the preachers of holy Church may understand that if they knowingly entrust spiritual ministries to the reprobate out of carnal love, they have fallen, through the equity of the inward Judge, from the height in which they appear outwardly to stand.

And because he subsequently added:

**(Verse 30.)** “But whoever glorifies me, I will glorify him,”

### 14

he subtly indicates that they had also been dishonoring him through their audacity. Paul also reproaches them for this very thing, saying: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Rom. II, 24).

Because they stain the beauty of the dignity they have received with the filth of a wretched reputation, they certainly dishonor the Lord. He is rightly driven from the summit of honor who injures the one by whom he is proved to have been honored.

In contrast, he affirms by a general promise, saying: “But whoever glorifies me, I will glorify him.” A pastor glorifies God when he shines out as an example of good works for the imitation of the faithful; when from the eminence of governance he radiates with the great light of an excellent way of life; when, as a mirror for sacred orders, he does not accept the persons of reprobate ministers, but chooses for the pattern of the subject flock those whom no one who looks to imitation is offended by, because he follows the true light in them.

The Truth himself speaks to such people, saying: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

The Lord glorifies those who glorify him because what the chosen pastors of holy Church outwardly bear from the glory of their position, they receive inwardly from the grace of divine goodness; and the honor by which they are exalted in human eyes they earn through worthy devotion from the generosity of inward Majesty.

In contrast, he complains that the glory of those who dishonor him is not bestowed by him, saying: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. VIII, 4). They reign from themselves and not from the choice of supreme ordination, because they are not divinely called to the glory of ecclesiastical dignity, but are brought to it through ambition.

The Lord does not know them because, through the judgment of inward equity, he rejects them. It is therefore as though he were saying: Even if the honor they possess appears to be mine, they did not deserve it through service; they seized it through ambition. Hence he adds:

**(Verse 30.)** “But those who despise me will be ignoble.”

### 15

It is as though he were speaking openly, saying: Although they display the nobility of dignity under the pretext of religion, they are nevertheless ignoble, because through the loftiness of their life they do not correspond to the excellence of the glory they possess.

But because all this is promised in the expression of the future tense, it may appropriately be referred to the merit of the retribution to come. Concerning this John says: “When he appears, we shall be like him” (I John III, 2). The evangelist Mark likewise declares: “Then they will see the Son of Man coming with great power and glory” (Mark XIII, 26).

When he asserts that he will glorify those who glorify him, he clearly promises them the glory of his likeness. The Lord glorifies those who glorify him because he rewards with eternal exaltation those who now shine within holy Church in the eyes of the chosen through examples of good works.

But those who despise him will be ignoble because they do not deserve to be received into the glory of the chosen. For since, through their reprobate conduct, they now wear the image of the fallen angels, they will then be ignoble with him when they are joined to him in inward punishment.

The Prophet, contemplating the glorification of the former and the ignobility of the latter, says:

“Let the holy ones exult in glory; let them rejoice upon their beds. The exultations of God are in their throats, and two-edged swords are in their hands, to execute vengeance upon the nations, rebukes among the peoples, to bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron shackles.”

The Lord glorifies those who glorify him because the humble chosen rejoice with him in eternal glory. Since they receive the splendor of glorification from the manner of their own conduct, they are said to rejoice upon their beds in the glory they have attained.

But those who despise him are struck with perpetual ignobility, because the kings and nobles of the nations are bound for punishment with iron—that is, eternal—bonds. The kings and princes of the nations are the proud and glorious superiors of carnal people.

They will then be ignoble when they are bound with iron chains, because those who now raise themselves up temporarily against the little ones are restrained by eternal punishment both from the brilliance of honor and from the boldness of their tyranny. Hence it is also added here:

[Col. 0117A] **(Verse 31.)** “Behold, the days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house.”

[Note: Gilot and the Vatican manuscript read “will come.”]

### 16

The arm of one who despises is temporal strength. And because, by transgressing, he went out from the household of the supreme Father, he has already begun to have the fallen angel as his father, apart from heavenly glory. His father’s house, therefore, is the society of subjects that favors him in evil. Concerning these he says above: “You honored your sons more than me.”

The arm of the despiser and the house of his father are cut off when, at the intervention of bodily death, the superior and his subjects alike lose the violence of their tyranny. He is then without an arm, because he can no longer exercise violence in the oppression of the little ones.

Hence the equity of the eternal Judge decrees: “Bind his hands and feet and throw him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXII, 13).

Nor will there be an old man in his house. The house of the condemned person is hell. Old age, however, is true maturity of wisdom. There will therefore be no old man in his house, because no counsel of salvation can be found in hell. Hence holy Scripture urges us toward works of true wisdom, saying: “Whatever your hand can do, do it with all your strength, for there is neither reasoning, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld, where you are hastening” (Eccl. IX, 10).

Paul says likewise: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 2). There will therefore be no old man in the house of the despiser, because whoever possesses sound wisdom has prepared a dwelling for himself not in hell, but in heaven.

That despiser also sees, to increase his punishment, his rival in the temple amid all the prosperity of Israel. The temple of God is the heavenly homeland, concerning which the Prophet also says: “The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven” (Ps. X, 4).

Israel, which is interpreted as “seeing God,” signifies that blessed multitude of angels concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 10). The prosperity of Israel is the everlasting joy of those blessed spirits.

The despiser will therefore see his rival in the temple, because the reprobate preacher, already condemned, recognizes that the order of the humble is now rejoicing in heavenly places. All the prosperity of Israel is granted to this rival; for it is written: “God will be all in all” (I Cor. XV, 28).

All the prosperity of Israel signifies all that God is for those most blessed citizens. For although that eternal essence—namely, the highest and simple Good—is in itself one and simple, nevertheless, because through the revelation of his Majesty he satisfies all the desires of those blessed spirits, the distinguished Doctor shows that he is this for them.

Therefore he carefully does not proclaim that God is all in himself, but all in all, because he who ineffably exists as one and simple Good in his own nature is as many goods to all the good as all of them are filled with joys from the contemplation of his glory.

All the prosperity of Israel is therefore granted to the rival because the order of the humble elect is received among the choirs of angels, to be satisfied eternally by the joys of divine contemplation. He is rightly said to be the despiser’s rival because God’s chosen—even from proud and negligent preachers—receive exhortations to good instruction.

Hence the Lord commands, saying: “Do everything they tell you, but do not act according to their works” (Matt. XXIII, 3). Paul likewise says: “Be zealous for the good among all in what is good” (Gal. IV, 18).

But since Scripture says: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. XXVI, 10), it seems contradictory that those condemned in hell should be understood to see those rejoicing in heaven.

Yet since “seeing” also pertains to knowledge, he sees his rival in the temple because, although the wicked person is held bound by the punishments of hell, he does not doubt that the humble elect—whom he does not see with his eyes—are present in heaven amid the joys of the angels.

It should also be noted that it is said twice: “There will be no old man in your house,” because the condemned person is instructed toward salvation neither by the experience of the punishments he possesses, nor by knowledge of another’s happiness, nor by the experience of the punishments he does not possess.

Sometimes, however, the elect are born as sons through the teaching of reprobate pastors. The guilt of those pastors does not hold these elect bound, because they follow the exhortations of his good preaching that they hear, and not the perverse works that they see. Hence it follows:

**(Verse 33.)** “Nevertheless, I will not completely remove from you a man from my altar.”

### 17

The men are those who shine from the height of a demanding way of life. It is therefore as though he were saying: For this reason I do not remove them from my altar, because they are men. In accordance with the merit of their conduct, strength and the loftiness of authority are preserved for them.

Hence, through the Prophet, the Lord proclaims decrees of equity, saying: “The soul that sins shall itself die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son” (Ezek. XVIII, 20).

The Lord would justly remove from him a man from his altar if the son bore the iniquity of his father. But precisely because the chosen hearer is seen in glory, punishment is heaped upon the reprobate teacher. Therefore it follows:

**(Verse 33.)** “But let your eyes fail and your soul waste away.”

### 18

His eyes fail because he is confounded by the life of one who has perfected what he taught through his exhortation. His soul also wastes away because he is compelled to grieve more abundantly when he recognizes that the good he taught is flourishing in his subjects through the glory of their reward, while he himself did not care to practice it.

In these words it should also be noted that the one who promises not to remove a man completely from his altar is indicating that the person he receives is found rarely. For the reprobate teacher has more hearers who follow the evil things they do than the righteous things they teach. Hence here too a large part of his house is said to die in the age of manhood.

### 19

The age of manhood is the time for administering the priesthood. The imitator of a reprobate teacher is brought to the age of manhood when he is promoted to the height of sacred order. When he reaches that age, he dies, because whoever approaches such a ministry unworthily, or lives in it unworthily, is condemned.

Hence Paul, mentioning the Lord’s body and blood, says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI, 29). They die in the age of manhood because they perish through presumption and the audacity of a higher ministry.

From this, then—from this very point—let those who are rash draw back, and let them not desire to undertake the burdens of so great a ministry, but fear them. For the one who is foretold to die when he reaches manhood lives until he reaches it; plainly, the weak and those unequal to so great a ministry, if they consider the measure of their weakness, have a place in holy Church in which they may live while guarding themselves.

Hence through Moses the Lord declares: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Exod. XIX, 12; Heb. XII, 20). This is also why, when Lot went out from Sodom, he refrained from ascending the mountain and withdrew to the little city of Zoar (Gen. XIX, 20 and following), lest, while still little, he should strive toward higher things, stumble upon manhood, and die.

We leave Sodom when we avoid the fires of burning desire. We do not immediately ascend to lofty places because we do not touch the summit of a higher ministry, measuring and considering our own weakness, lest, if we disdain to keep to the measure of our weak age, we who have lived as little ones should die in the age of manhood.

As a sign of the house that was to die, both sons of Eli are foretold to die on one day. We have said that these sons signify those who are promoted to sacred orders by carnal relatives, not with the intention of administering the order, but for the glory of worldly dignity.

Both therefore die on one day because they perish in their desire for worldly happiness. Secular glory, reverence of honor, the power of high office, the brilliance of dignity, the multitude of attendants, and the abundance of possessions loved in a worldly manner constitute a day—but a day that kills.

### 20

Let the sons of Eli therefore hear that both die on one day. Those who love the happiness of a passing life after receiving the pastoral height have an intention of joy but a result of lamentation; a purpose in the exultation of life, but an arrival in the sorrow of death. They hasten toward death whenever they rejoice vainly in temporal happiness.

The Apostle also proves this when he mentions the apostate widow, saying: “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (I Tim. V, 6). He said that she dies on this day when he showed that pleasures are the cause of the widow’s death.

But the death of the sons would be less evil if it did not itself become the cause of another’s death. Hence they are foretold not simply to die, but to die as a sign of the house that is to die, because when those who imitate the reprobate teacher nearby fall into the same precipice, the followers are added to the ruin of those whom they follow.

Let those who love temporal happiness because of the office of the height they have assumed hear this and fear the greatness of their guilt. They are worthy of a punishment all the more severe because they plainly see that they do not die alone from the vanity they love: while they drink death under the pretext of worldly joy, they pass the poison of their drink on to the multitude of those who follow them.

These words may also communicate to reprobate teachers the brevity of the present life. They die on one day because, when they reach the end of this life, what they lived is seen to have been altogether brief. Hence a certain wise man says: “The joy of the hypocrite is like a point” (Job XX, 5). Again, blessed Job speaks of the lovers of this world, saying: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld” (ibid. XXI, 13).

But when the reprobate have been snatched away for punishment, wise and chosen pastors are raised up for the care of the Lord’s flock. Therefore he adds:

**(Verse 35.)** “And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest.”

### 21

The Lord raises up a faithful priest for himself because, plainly, the highest office requires for its care one who not only understands rightly, but also ministers faithfully. He will then be able to minister rightly when he recognizes the measure of his ministry from sacred eloquence.

Hence, when a faithful priest is promised, he is said to act according to the heart and soul of almighty God. For what are the heart and soul of God if not his sacred Scripture? With the heart we think toward deliberation, while with the soul we are moved toward love.

Therefore, because in sacred eloquence we recognize the counsels of almighty God and find there the love with which he loved the human race, that eloquence reasonably signifies his heart and soul.

Almighty God therefore chooses as his priest for his ministry the one who acts according to his heart and soul, because no other person is worthy of so great an order except one who has learned his will from sacred eloquence and, through devotion to charity, applies what he has learned to the benefit of his neighbors.

But what is said must still be observed attentively:

**(Verse 35.)** “According to my heart and soul.”

### 22

For certain precepts are found in sacred Scripture which are indeed commanded by God’s dispensation, but not by God’s love. If the priest who is promised as one to be raised up were to fulfill these, he would act according to God’s heart but not according to his soul, since he would have translated into works the counsel of the divine dispensation rather than a commandment of love.

Were those commands not matters of God’s dispensation concerning which he says: “I gave them statutes that were not good” (Ezek. XX, 25)? And when the Pharisees disputed with the Truth himself concerning the granting of a bill of divorce, they heard: “Moses gave you the law because of the hardness of your hearts” (Matt. XIX, 8).

Since those precepts arose from the dispensation of his counsel, whoever made use of those same precepts acted according to the Lord’s heart, but not according to his soul. For the commandment of heart and soul is the one of which it is said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XV, 12). For he embraces through love what he commands through counsel.

Again he says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke VI, 27). Again he commands, saying: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.”

These and similar commandments are the commandments of God’s heart and soul, because through revelation this is shown to be the secret of his counsel, which is received in his sight through the testing of charity.

A faithful priest is therefore recognized by this sign: namely, whether he acts according to God’s heart and soul. He is truly faithful if he follows not the permission of God’s dispensation, but the commandments of love.

But because he is not chosen without purpose, but for the gain of the subject people, he adds and says:

**(Verse 35.)** “And I will build for him a faithful house.”

23. The priest’s house is the vast community in which the people subject to him dwell. This house is indeed built for him as a faithful house by the Lord, because it is raised up by divine inspiration for the pursuit of obedience. An unfaithful house is that association of subjects which daily receives the preaching of a good ruler, yet does not intend to obey him through the earnest practice of good works. It is recognized as an unfaithful house because the money of God’s word, entrusted to it through the ministry of its preacher, is squandered through a prodigal life, and what is committed to it for the profit of the enterprise is not found at all when the account must be rendered. Thus the Lord builds a faithful house for a good preacher when the hearts of the people subject to him are divinely prepared to obey his voice, so that it may not only guard what is deposited in it from the talent of the word, but also bring it, multiplied by abundant profit, to the table of eternal reception. It should be noted that the faithful house is said to be built by the Lord, so that the preacher may not vainly boast of the good conduct of the people subject to him. It should also be noted that the Lord raises up a priest faithful to himself, so that the hearts of those subject to him may not presume to attribute to their own merits the fact that they are governed by an excellent ruler. It should further be noted that the priest whom the Lord raises up is called faithful to him, whereas the house that he builds for him is said to be faithful to that priest; for the preacher owes obedience to God, while the subject owes obedience to his superior. Yet a superior rightly walks before his subject when Truth itself appears to guide every path of his life. It follows:

**(Verse 35.)** “And he shall walk before my Christ all his days.”

24. Christ of the Lord is the Redeemer of the human race. Since he is believed already to have ascended into heaven, he is now seen by his faithful not with bodily eyes but with the mind. He therefore walks before him all his days who does nothing on the impulse of a sudden thought. For in order to place upright steps outwardly in his actions, inwardly he looks toward Christ, whom through contemplation he carries in his heart. But because he is still speaking to the reprobate shepherd, he adds:

**(Verse 36.)** “It shall come to pass that whoever remains from your house will come to have prayer offered for him.”

25. Someone is said to remain from his house because a large part of it is reported to die. From the house of the reprobate shepherd remains the person whose consciousness of sin does not extinguish his hope of obtaining forgiveness. He therefore remains because the burden of his conscience is lightened by the purpose of repentance and the hope of attaining life. He comes to have prayer offered for him, and in repentance hastens to God, from whom he departed by sinning. He comes to have prayer offered for him because one who has made himself unworthy of God requires a worthy intercessor, so that he may be cleansed through the prayers of another, since he is recognized as unable to cleanse himself through his own prayers. Hence the blessed James also admonishes us, saying: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James 5:16). Again: “The continual prayer of the righteous is very powerful.” But prayer is effective for the person who, while restraining himself from the impurity of sin, restores himself to the likeness of God, from which he stripped himself by sinning. Hence it is also added here:

**(Verse 36.)** “To offer a silver coin.”

26. The image of the Lord is engraved on a coin, so that it may be recognized as belonging to the one by whom it is ordered to be formed. The coin therefore signifies the likeness of God. Hence in Genesis he says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26). And because from sacred Scripture we recognize the image and likeness of God, to which we are to be restored, the coin is said to be silver. Therefore the person who comes away from the path of sin so that prayer may be offered for him must offer a silver coin, because it profits him nothing that he is pierced with remorse through repentance, or that he confesses with tears, if inwardly he is not recognized as shining with the beauty of a good will, uncorrected and unreformed, with the light of God’s image.

The image and likeness of God consists in hating evil with renowned hatred and loving God with perfect love. Hence, seeing that the splendor of the divine likeness had perished from the human race, the Prophet looks toward the one who came from heaven with the glorious light of our restoration, saying: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity” (Psalm 44:8). Then, considering himself renewed into the form of perfection through contemplation of him, he says: “I have hated the wicked, and I have loved your law” (Psalm 118:113).

Therefore, the person who comes from the house of the reprobate through confession, and who in humility asks that the Lord be entreated for him, must take every care to offer a silver coin, so that, having received the radiance of a good will, he may perfectly hate the evil he has done and love with undivided affection the good he has neglected. Hence the decrees of reconciliation are proclaimed by the judgment of the righteous Judge. “On whatever day or hour,” he says, “the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezekiel 18:21, 27).

The sinner’s conversion, however, does not consist in the humility of confession, but in the renewal of the inner person: when the sinner, now corrected by divine inspiration, is displeased by the evil he loved and pleased by the good he hated. For there are some who accuse themselves of wickedness and crime but do not correct the perversity of their will. Such people are not believed to have turned to the Lord, because true conversion is not understood as residing in the mouth but in the heart. To convert means to turn completely. The sinner’s true conversion therefore occurs when both our persons are brought back to the good pleasure of our Creator: when our flesh is restrained from committing crime through hatred of iniquity, and when our mind is extended toward the intention of good action through love of righteousness.

But because there are some within the Church who come to the satisfaction of repentance only at the end of their lives, and the judgment of Truth says:

[Note: [Col. 0123D] The sense of these words is also found at Ezekiel 33:12.]

“Whenever the sinner turns, he lives,” some people commonly ask at length whether those who have committed sins throughout the greater part of their lives and accuse themselves of having acted wickedly only at life’s end immediately find life after the death of the flesh.

To this it must be said that, by the power of conversion, the magnitude of the crime is erased. The power of conversion is the affection of love infused into the heart through the visitation of the Holy Spirit. It is written of this same Spirit:

[Note: [Col. 0123D] This is found nowhere in these exact words in sacred Scripture. At 1 John 2:2 we read: “He is the propitiation for our sins.” The holy Fathers often praise many things that they merely cite from memory.]

“For he himself is the forgiveness of sins.”

For when he graciously visits the hearts of the elect, he powerfully cleanses them from every impurity of sins.
