As soon as he has poured himself into the mind, he ineffably arouses it to hatred of sins and vices and to love of virtues. He immediately causes it to hate what it loved and ardently love what it had hated, and to groan deeply over both: it remembers that it damnably loved the evils it now hates and hated the good it now loves.

For who would dare say that anyone visited by the grace of the Holy Spirit could perish, even if weighed down by the entire burden of sins? Since, then, the sinner is converted at no hour except the hour in which he is illumined by the Holy Spirit, what remains but that, just as he abandons the death of sin by execrating it, so he may live the life of righteousness to which he turns with longing?

He is received into life immediately after death if, at his conversion, he receives such a fire of love that it can consume in his soul every accumulated rust of sin. Hence it is said of the sinful woman: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). Hence the same Truth, hanging on the cross, says: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid., 23:43).

At the end of life, therefore, only those repent beneficially who, through an inward visitation, perfectly love the good and hate the evils they had loved. Yet if they cannot grieve sufficiently for the iniquities they have committed, they nevertheless live in the hour in which they are converted. For those who possessed the perfection of a good will in confessing their sin pass after death through the purifying punishment of sin into life, if they did not possess a sufficient power of love to erase their sins. Hence Paul says: “They will be saved, as though through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:15). But the sinner who has merited being saved there through fire should here, through the affliction of the flesh, complete what he recognizes to be lacking in the power of his love.

**(Verse 36.)** “And a twisted loaf of bread.”

[Col. 0123D]

27. The name “bread” sometimes signifies nourishment in earthly delight. Thus the prophet Jeremiah, recalling the people of corrupt Judah in their worldly appetite, says: “All her people groan” (Lamentations 1:11), “seeking bread.” The converted sinner therefore twists bread when he tortures his former pleasure through the affliction of repentance. To twist bread is to afflict the flesh for the pleasure previously committed.

Therefore, whoever desires to pass into salvation without the torment of fire should offer, together with the silver coin, a twisted loaf of bread, so that the person who abandons sins through a good will may utterly extinguish them through a strong affliction of the flesh. He was offering a silver coin who, having already recovered the likeness of God, condemned what he had done by confessing it, saying: “My wounds have become foul because of my foolishness” (Psalm 37:6). And again: “I am bent down and humbled exceedingly.”

But he who feared that the silver coin would not suffice for his offering took care to add a twisted loaf of bread. For he confesses and says: “I roared because of the groaning of my heart” (ibid., 9). A roar indicates weeping of great sorrow in the affliction of the penitent. Joining this twisted bread to the silver coin, he himself also says: “For I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin” (ibid., 19). To think upon one’s sin is to impose upon one’s former pleasure an affliction of the flesh proportionate to it.

He therefore twisted bread to be offered who, declaring the crimes he had committed, considered how he might erase them. And because the desire for praise sometimes steals upon penitents from the austerity of their way of life, the intention of the truly converted sinner is indicated by what follows:

**(Verse 36.)** “And let him say: ‘Dismiss me, I beg you, to one of the priestly portions.’”

28. The priestly portion of each person is the eternal reward of the elect. For all God’s elect are his priests, because they continually serve the one to whom they offer their ministry and never cease to offer sacred gifts. Hence they also say, rejoicing in the kingdom: “You redeemed us for God by your blood, and made us a kingdom and priests for our God” (Revelation 5:9–10).

To say to the converted sinner, “Dismiss me, I beg you, to one of the priestly portions,” is to expect from the austerity of life and repentance only a portion of eternal blessedness: namely, to find the security of delight, possessing it in perpetual enjoyment and never afterward dragging along the tortures of repentance. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 36.)** “That I may eat a morsel of bread.”

29. If bread is understood in sacred Scripture as delight, a morsel of bread is unfailing enjoyment of eternal life. Of this delight the prophet says: “Joy and gladness shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise” (Isaiah 51:3). Again, seeing guests invited to the table—not to twisted bread but to a morsel—he says: “Everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain joy and gladness” (ibid., 35:10).

Hence the Psalmist, speaking in the voice of the chastened penitent, says: “You have made known to me the paths of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence; delights are in your right hand forever” (Psalm 15:10). The paths of life are the afflictions of repentance, by which the sinner is led from the abyss of his condemnation to the heavenly homeland, while he voluntarily suffers for the iniquities he has committed.

Thus, when he indicates that he has been chastened as a sinner, he presumes to say: “You are the one, Lord, who restored my inheritance to me” (Psalm 15:5). And again, trusting, he says: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell” (ibid., 10).

The paths of life become known to the sinner when the afflictions of repentance are divinely revealed to him—when, namely, with an enlightened mind, he considers what bitterness of life he should set against each delight of his former fault. He glories that he is filled with joyous gladness in the presence of almighty God,

[Note: [Col. 0125D] “They glory” is read erroneously in all our printed editions.]

because he is refreshed by the manifest satiety of divine contemplation. Though for a time he is pierced by repentance in the left hand of present life, in the right hand of eternal life he is satisfied with delights forever.

Therefore, the person who offered a twisted loaf of bread is brought to eat a morsel, because the person who tortures harmful pleasures through love of the heavenly life prepares for himself perpetual refreshment at the banquet of eternal joy. It follows:

**CHAPTER IV**

**(1 Samuel 3:1.)** “Now the boy Samuel ministered to the Lord before Eli.”

1. It is shown that at this point he has repeated what was mentioned above concerning the elect boy, where he says: “Now the boy Samuel was the minister in the sight of the Lord, before the face of Eli.” To minister to the Lord before Eli is the same as to be the Lord’s minister before the face of Eli. And because, with the Lord’s help, we expounded this more fully there, we do not linger at all over repeating its exposition. But because the divine word speaks both here and there, it is shown that it did not do so without a useful reason.

For the sake of avoiding the reader’s weariness, we pass over the explanation, but state the reason for the repetition for his benefit. Some subjects, still inexperienced and obeying the teaching of the rulers of the holy Church, obey; but when they make somewhat greater progress through their manner of life, they do not remain in the same humility of obedience. Such people are well represented spiritually by Hagar, Sarah’s maidservant, who, when she saw that she had conceived by Abraham, her husband, despised her mistress (Genesis 16:5).

Hagar conceives when the subject’s reprobate mind believes that it is progressing either through the acquisition of knowledge or through the practice of a way of life. She is said, while pregnant, to have despised her mistress because the subject, having now advanced, disdains to submit through obedience to the will of the superior who presides over him. Yet she who despises her mistress is still called a maidservant, because proud subjects are weak through their arrogance and do not attain to the number of God’s children.

Samuel’s progress is explained because it was said above: “Now the boy Samuel was progressing

[Note: [Col. 0126D] In Gussanville, “and was growing and was pleasing both to God” is omitted.]

and growing and was pleasing both to God and to human beings” (1 Samuel 2:18). The height of conduct with which he passed through these three stages has been explained above. Since, then, he is now also remembered as ministering before his teacher, what does this mean except that he offers elect hearers an example, so that the more they progress toward a higher life, the more they may never forget to preserve the good of obedience? For they truly progress if, in proportion to the height of their merits, they strive both with the strength of their works and with the virtue of humility.

2. There is another point here that should be noted: Samuel is shown ministering to the Lord before Eli precisely when Eli is rebuked by the Lord for the negligence of his sons. Some subjects, while considering the measure of their own strength, prefer to be severe judges of their superiors rather than devoted hearers. Because they are accustomed to magnifying and examining the lives of their superiors, if they notice in their conduct even stains of a lesser fault, they refuse to submit to their commands through obedience.

But they would truly be strong if they humbly bore in their elders what they considered weak. For before God the person is recognized as great in merit who submits to one in a good command, even when that person does not appear venerable in some respect. For Eli is rebuked by the open sentence of God for the fault of negligence he committed, yet the boy of the Lord, Samuel, is remembered as ministering to the Lord before him. Thus he may gather within himself what sort of person he is who despises his superior for a lesser fault, if Samuel submitted to Eli in obedience—Eli whom almighty God rejected with such strictness in his judgment.

But because Eli is reproved for having greatly honored himself above subjects who were sinning, the dignities of the sacred orders themselves must be carefully considered. The ruler should honor a sinful subject only after correcting him; the subject, however, should not despise his superior even when he recognizes himself as righteous and the superior as a sinner. The eternal Judge has entrusted the judgment of subjects to the rulers of the holy Church, but has reserved those same rulers for his own examination.

This very fact—that they are reserved for God’s judgment—should be greatly feared by rulers, for they must prepare accounts of their life and teaching with all the greater care the wiser the Judge is whom they must face. Nor should they fear only his future judgment in the life to come, as though it were set at a distance, lest he who is present everywhere strike the unwary from nearby. Negligent shepherds, seeking to escape the punishment of future vengeance, reckon on long spans of the present life as a postponement of punishment; but the Judge who is everywhere present imposes repentance nearby, first withdrawing from them the light of contemplation and then snatching them away through death to torments.

Hence, concerning this same Eli, who shortly afterward dies with his neck broken, it is added:

**(Verse 1.)** “In those days there was no manifest vision.”

[Col. 0126D]

3. When a ruler despises doing what he knows ought to be done, strict judgment is carried out against him: he is made unable to see what must be done because he refused to fulfill what he saw. Manifest vision does not belong to a negligent shepherd but to one who loves. Hence Truth itself says: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

The brightness of manifest vision is the revelation of the truth that is loved. If this truth is displayed on account of the merit of love, it is most justly concealed from those who are sluggish in good works, because the sign of love is not in the affection of the mind but in the pursuit of good action. Hence in the Gospel the Lord first said: “Whoever has my commandments and does them is the one who loves me” (ibid.).

Since, therefore, the darkness of inner vision is incurred through negligence in action, it is most fitting that, when the priest is rebuked for contempt of the commandments, the concealment of vision is remembered. It follows:

**(Verse 1.)** “And the word of the Lord was precious.”

4. So far as the truth of the sacred history is concerned, he used “precious” to mean rare. The word was therefore precious because, since those who perceived the highest things through contemplation were rare, those who could frequently proclaim good things in speech could not be numerous.

We see this happening now also in the holy Church. Since many desire the glory of honor because of the reverence owed to high office, and neglect the ministries of the sacred order, they cannot proclaim to the peoples subject to them the highest things they are unable to see. Thus the word is recognized as precious in their household, because those whose superiors do not seek the heavenly things they should say out of desire, but the earthly things they should do, hear exhortations to good preaching only rarely.

Sacred Scripture marks such people when it says: “Mute dogs unable to bark” (Isaiah 56:10). It did not say “unwilling,” but “unable,” because, while they love the glory of the world with all their heart, all their soul, all their mind, and all their strength, they would like to say sublime things to the people, so that they might also obtain glory from the sublimity of their words.

Mute dogs therefore want to bark but cannot, because, while they ponder earthly things with a perverse heart, they grasp by no revelation the hidden truths they might bring forth. But because what is precious is usually guarded with great care, the statement “There was no manifest vision” may be referred to the negligence of carnal superiors.

5. What is added—“And the word of the Lord was precious”—refers to the ardent zeal of good subjects. Faithful subjects, even if they do not have someone who frequently proclaims heavenly things to them from the treasury of sacred Scripture, embrace with extraordinary devotion whatever they have occasionally been able to learn and guard it as something ineffably precious. Through good works they deposit it in heaven, where thieves capable of taking it away never approach.

Hence in the Gospel, concerning the buyer of the good pearl, it is said: “Having found one precious pearl, he gave all his possessions and bought it” (Matthew 13:46). When, therefore, the word of the elect is described as precious in a time of concealed vision, the praises of the subjects are announced, because they are to be praised with the greater glory the more that good which was lost from a higher place has remained below through the perfection of great love.

Through their good conduct it often comes about that the vision which had been concealed is revealed, so that those who devoutly guard the smallest things may know what they should do in greater matters also. Hence it is added:

**(Verses 2–4.)** “Now it happened one day that Eli was lying in his place, and his eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished. But Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was. And the Lord called Samuel.”

[Col. 0128A]

6. The boy Samuel is called by the Lord whenever the secrets of divine counsel are revealed to humble subjects, and they acquire, through the merit of their humility, the light of contemplation that exalted preachers lose as the recompense of their pride. It should be noted, however, that this is shown to have happened on a certain day,

[Note: [Col. 0127D] Vaticanus: “since Eli was lying in his place as well.”]

on which Eli is reported both to have been lying in his place and to have been unable to see. He is called in the daytime who, for his own salvation and that of others, is lifted up to learn the secrets of heavenly wisdom.

By contrast, Solomon received wisdom at night, so that the darkness of the time might indicate that he would not receive that same wisdom perseveringly (1 Kings 3:5, 12). This may also be understood in another way, because Eli’s darkness is mentioned. By specifying the day, the greatness of his blindness is revealed, for he certainly had great darkness who did not see in the daytime.

Now also, if we look to the state of the Church, there is a universal grace of light. The one who, scattering the rays of true brightness, would say, “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness” (John 8:12), has come. And because the glory of his inner splendor is ineffable, it is not said of this day or that day, but “on a certain day,” of which indeed there is no brightness; but the greatness of its brightness is unknown. [Would it not be better: “brightness is”; “but the greatness of its brightness,” etc.?]

The Shepherd therefore suffers great darkness if the one who is known by his office to be the eye of the Church does not possess the vision of such great light by grace. Hence Truth itself shows the darkness of this same eye to be great, saying: “If your eye is evil, how great will the darkness be!” (Matthew 6:23).

But he now indicates where such great darkness arises, for he says: “He was lying in his place.” The place of the preacher has the duty of standing, not lying down. Hence the Lord himself provides a model for preachers, saying: “I am among you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). To stand in the midst of the brethren is to offer oneself as an example to one’s juniors through a laborious way of life.

Standing therefore pertains to the labor of action and to the necessity of battle. Hence the commander of the spiritual struggle gives this command: “Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth” (Ephesians 6:14). And because lying down belongs to one who is at rest, the person who is remembered as lying in the place of battle and labor is reproved for following the tepidity of rest.

Standing also belongs to the righteous. Hence Paul says: “For by faith you stand” (2 Corinthians 1:23). Lying down therefore also pertains to negligence in a more relaxed way of life. Eli lies in his own place when a reprobate preacher rests in the seat of the righteous through a lapse into depravity.

The eyes of one lying in his place grow dim because those who occupy the height of pastoral office but do not carry out works of virtue, instead immersing themselves in the indulgences of a more relaxed life, cannot see the highest things. The lamp of God is no longer called this in praise of truth, but as an insult of mockery. For one who is called the lamp of God and is said to be unable to see is rather mocked by the very title with which he is designated.

In true praise of the righteous it is said: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35). He poured forth in speech the radiance of the true light which he had imbibed through love. The carnal preacher is also called a lamp by virtue of his office but blind in intention: he holds the dignity of providing light, but fixes his mind in the darkness of vanity.

7. His complete perversity is signified by the fact that it is not said “he did not see,” but “he could not see.” Hence, mentioning the evil tree, the Lord says: “A bad tree cannot produce good fruit” (Matthew 7:18).

The “lamp of God” cannot see when the person who presides in pastoral dignity is weighed down by such dense worldly love that he is raised to the vision of inner brightness by no inspiration of grace—when, having been cast away by God’s just indignation, he is left in the blindness of his own darkness, never again to be visited through the infusion of heavenly light.

It is rightly said: “Before it was extinguished.” Not to see is the punishment of the sinner who is still living in this world; but to be unable to see is the condition of the impious person who has died and been condemned to eternal punishment in the other world. Hence, by the judgment of the Creator, he is commanded to be shut outside in the darkness, so that he may never again be brought back to the sight of the light.

Therefore, when the reprobate preacher, still living in this world, is said to have been unable to see before the lamp was extinguished, he is compared with the impious person already condemned forever in blindness. The lamp is extinguished when the shepherd dies. Or certainly the lamp is extinguished because, when the reprobate preacher perishes through the death of the flesh, whatever appeared to shine in him loses the glory of his high office, and he remains like the mere casing of a lamp without light, while the person who is stripped entirely of every worldly splendor is compelled to be preserved for eternal judgment.

Before, therefore, the lamp of God is extinguished, he cannot see, because he possesses the merit of future condemnation through the eternity of his blindness and yet still shines before human beings through the splendor of the dignity he has received.

**(Verse 3.)** “But Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was.”

8. It is rightly said that the reprobate superior was not sleeping but lying down, while the subject who was a boy and elect was not lying down but sleeping, because “sleeping” is sometimes understood in a good sense, whereas “lying down” is almost always understood in a bad one. Hence the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2).

In the boy’s sleep, therefore, rest from evil action is signified for every elect subject. He sleeps in the temple, and where the ark is, who, occupied with heavenly desire and meditation on sacred Scripture, does not turn his attention to things belonging to perversity.

Some sleep in the temple but do not sleep in the place where the ark of God is, because some simple people rest through love in heavenly contemplation but do not know how to meditate on the hidden things of sacred Scripture.

Samuel, however, who is said to sleep not only in the temple but before the ark of God, signifies learned and elect subjects alike. As they more frequently draw the flames of their love from sacred Scripture through meditation, they are raised more deeply toward desire for the heavenly homeland. They choose the innermost parts of the temple for sleep, as it were, being separated all the farther from the public sphere of earthly activity the more secretly they are hidden through meditation in the sanctuary of inner vision.

**(Verse 4.)** “And the Lord called Samuel.”

9. For God’s calling is to awaken someone through the force of greater grace. The Lord calls the sleeper because he awakens those who rest from earthly concerns to an increase of heavenly knowledge. While we remain anxiously watchful over outward things, we do not perceive inward and spiritual realities.

The rejection of earthly care is therefore our preparation for receiving heavenly grace, because the divine gift is poured more abundantly into the elect the purer the mind has become through the guardianship of inner meditation. It follows:

[Col. 0130B]

**(Verses 4–9.)** “And the Lord called Samuel,” he says. “He answered and said: ‘Here I am.’ And he ran to Eli and said: ‘You called me, for here I am.’ He said: ‘I did not call you, my son; go back and sleep.’ And he went and slept. And the Lord again called Samuel. He arose and went to Eli and said: ‘Here I am, for you called me.’ He answered: ‘I did not call you, my son; go back and sleep.’ Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord, nor had the word of the Lord yet been revealed to him. And the Lord added and called Samuel a third time. He arose and went to Eli and said: ‘Here I am, for you called me.’ Then Eli understood that the Lord was calling the boy, and he said to Samuel: ‘Go and sleep; and if he calls you again, you shall say: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.”’”

10. What, then, does it mean that almighty God makes his call known with such art that the mind of the one called is held back from recognizing the caller; that, hearing God, he thinks this man is his teacher; that God sends forth the call but conceals its purpose; that he allows him to go to his teacher, return so often to the repose of sleep, and yet does not permit the sleeper to rest?

Could it be that the one who called whomever he wished to know his secrets was able to call with a voice like Eli’s but not with the voice he wished? Could the one who called whenever he wished not immediately disclose the reason for his calling? Could the one who wished to awaken him so that he might hear do so only by means of the teacher, without being able to teach him how he ought to hear?

In this matter almighty God employs a great dispensation, so that the hearts of the elect may be taught by a twofold instruction: on the surface of the history, subjects may see the good they should follow, namely obedience; and superiors may perceive hidden mysteries that, through examination, lead them to the light of understanding.

But what I think should be said first is that the boy, who thought that the Lord speaking was his teacher, heard a bodily voice. God therefore spoke to the boy not through himself but through an evangelical spirit,

[Note: [Col. 0129D] Perhaps it should read “through an angelic spirit”; and shortly afterward: “He moved an outward voice through an angelic spirit, but …”]

because he who is not confined by bodily form is not restricted to the sound of a voice by a bodily instrument. This also suited the boy’s capacity to hear. For although the merits of a subject at the beginning of his progress are great, since he is recognized as not yet being in perfection but still advancing in his way of life, he does not attain to that speech by which almighty God speaks through himself.

Almighty God himself—the supreme and unbounded Spirit—speaks spiritually to great and spiritual men when, through spiritual speech, he indicates to their minds both what they should do and what they should know how to say. He therefore moved an outward voice through an evangelical spirit, but the Creator Spirit indicated what he wished through the presence of his grace.

Calling him by a voice, while he was thought to be Eli, he remained hidden in his identity, so that the boy would run to his teacher; and when the boy heard that he had not been called, his error showed how great was the height of virtue on which he stood. The boy, then, humbly subject to a human being and exalted to the arduous height of obedience, approached when called and returned when commanded. What else does this provide for us as an example but the form of the highest obedience?

[Col. 0131B] **11.** True obedience neither scrutinizes the intention of superiors nor distinguishes among commands, because the person who has subjected the whole judgment of his life to another rejoices in this alone: that he carries out whatever is commanded him. For whoever has learned perfectly to obey does not know how to judge, because he considers it the only good to obey commands.

Yet in the glory of his perfect way of life, our own life is put to shame. For behold, we have resolved to advance under the leaders of the Christian army toward our heavenly homeland, but even when we are ordered to perform different tasks at different times, we murmur. Who could restrain himself from murmuring, who could control his anger, if he heard himself called twice and three times, yet learned from the caller’s reply that he had not been called at all? [Col. 0131C] We endure, to be sure, the darkness of our sluggishness because we do not see with what splendor the good of such virtue will answer with its reward.

There is, indeed, one good that restores life: if the evil of disobedience was sufficient to bring about death. If, then, death prevailed in the evil of disobedience, we are restored to life as often as we obey. Thus the boy Samuel is neither offended when he is called nor when he is dismissed, because he did not wish to discern the disposition of the one calling or dismissing him; he knew how to rejoice in this alone, that he had obeyed. And since rising pertains to labor, while returning pertains to the rest of sleep, what else is signified except that both prepare life for us, provided that the obedient person weighs in what he does nothing but the good of obedience?

A command must be valued for this alone: that it is the command of a superior; and whoever carries out the good of obedience ought to consider not the task imposed, [Col. 0131D] but the fruit. For in order to merit the joys of eternal life, what is sought is not the quality of the task but the putting to death of one’s own will and the execution of another’s will. Hence Paul says: “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God” (1 Cor. 7:19).

Therefore, in the sight of almighty God, neither tasks belonging to labor nor those belonging to rest are small if they can prepare eternal life for the obedient. Whoever, then, is subject to another’s authority should consider only this: that whatever is enjoined upon him according to God is a very great and lofty gain for the mind, since it prepares life as the reward of recompense. By contrast, let the disobedient consider that the first parent of the human race fell from the joys of paradise not through theft, robbery, adultery, or murder, but through disobedience concerning the forbidden fruit (Gen. 3:6). It is therefore rightly concluded that if commands of superiors, which seem small, when despised separate people from inward joys, then even the smallest things, when performed, prepare life.

**12.** Therefore, if the energetic practitioner of communal life and devout rival of those who serve God together with him desires to obtain a greater recompense of eternal merit through the good of obedience, let him recognize that he excels in this alone: if, more than others, he has subjected his own will to the judgment of his superior. For neither the great gains of fasting nor the disciplines of an austere life are to be highly valued by Christ’s devoted soldiers when a superior commands otherwise.

The refreshment enjoined by a superior is of greater merit than fasting undertaken by one’s own decision. Whoever restores his body at another’s command, though unwillingly, earns through his devotion the reward of fasting and acquires a greater recompense by eating. God therefore called the boy, but with a voice resembling that of his master, so that he might clearly indicate the manner of his speech. He concealed the reason for the call, so that he might show how exalted the chosen boy was in the humility of obedience. He allowed him to go to his teacher, so that he might offer the service of his devotion. He permitted him to return to the rest of sleep, so that we might clearly understand that we must not despise even what is least. He awakened him repeatedly, so that he might reveal the one whom he wished to place in the company of the elect, since even the persistence of commands would not weary him. Through the one who was destined to be rejected, he taught him how he ought to listen, so that we might clearly know [Col. 0132C] that the commands of superiors are to be revered even when the superiors themselves do not lead praiseworthy lives. Their teaching, which can become contemptible to the proud because of their wicked conduct, makes humble hearers attain the heights of divine intimacy.

**13.** But since the text continues, “Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord,” although above he is said to minister to the Lord, what is said appears highly contradictory, since he could not have failed to know the one whom he served. For who could serve one whom he does not know? Yet what follows makes clear how what sounds contradictory is to be understood in a fitting and rational sense: “Nor had the word of the Lord yet been revealed to him.” By this it is plainly indicated that the one whom he knew through love and service he did not know through the revelation of his word.

He had not yet heard him calling in this manner, although he testified that he knew him both by the devotion of his service and by the power of his love. But this is appropriately understood of the life of the faithful. Many make good progress under another’s instruction: at the beginning of their new life they offer their services to almighty God, yet through the purity of contemplation they do not reach the vision of his inward beauty. When, on account of the merit of their submission, they also receive the gift of divine contemplation and through inward experience understand it, they recognize that they had not yet known the one whom they served.

Jacob aptly represents this. As he traveled to receive a wife, he saw the Lord after the labor of his journey, in the repose of sleep; but when he awoke from sleep, he said: “Truly, the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it” (Gen. 28:16). He could not have doubted that the Lord was there before he slept, since he perceived that the Lord was everywhere. But because he then learned to know him more perfectly, he declared that he had been unaware of him because he had not previously recognized him with such intimacy.

The road by which one travels to a wife signifies the devoted intention of obedience, by which one desires to attain the fruitfulness of inward charity. Jacob therefore sleeps on the road when the faithful subordinate, conqueror of the evil spirit’s treachery, is received through the labor of obedience into the rest of inward vision. He will then confess that he has come to know the Lord, because, as he marvels at the beauty of the inward light to which he has newly been admitted, the experience of the beauty revealed to him shows him how much he previously did not know.

By faith, as by report, we know God; but through the love of contemplation, the one who became known to us through report is revealed as though by an exhibition of his presence. Appropriately, therefore, the subordinate who advances through obedience is said to have previously been unaware of the Lord when he is led to the heights of contemplation. For the one who had previously appeared through report as though unknown, and not through presence as though known, is found as though in the reality of his presence.

**14.** But since it is separately said, “He did not yet know the Lord, nor had the word of the Lord yet been revealed to him,” the passage may be understood more subtly. For in one and the same inward contemplation of God, wondrous love is poured into the contemplative from the fruit of such glory, and great awe arises from the revelation of the hidden word.

Some therefore know the Lord and receive the revelation of his word, because they are filled with extraordinary sweetness from the infusion of such great charity, which they continually draw from experience, and because they are instructed in great wisdom through the revelation of the word. Others know the Lord but do not receive the revelation of the Lord’s word. These are simple people, yet men perfected by a great way of life. In contemplating the glory of divine contemplation, they receive an ineffable sweetness of love, but they do not reach the height of his revealed word, because they have been admitted to the order of lovers, not to the height of preaching. The word is indeed revealed to them so that they may love it, but it is hidden from them so that they may not preach it.

Appropriately, then, it is said of the one who is raised to the ministry of preaching: “He did not yet know the Lord, nor had the word of the Lord yet been revealed to him.” In this way, by indicating what the novice does not yet possess, the text plainly shows with what gifts a preacher ought to be enriched. [Col. 0133D] For one who has not yet received that power of intimate love certainly does not know in his presence the almighty Lord whom he knows by faith as though by report. If he loves him ardently but does not yet know through the Spirit how to examine the secrets of the mysteries, he already knows the Lord, but he has not attained the revelation of his word.

Concerning the obedient boy, the text immediately adds:

**(Verse 9.)** “So Samuel went and slept.”

**15.** The boy is sent forth already instructed in knowledge of divine speech when the chosen subordinate is prepared, by the counsel of his superior, to learn spiritual things. For him to sleep means to rest in the desire for eternal life. That is, when the soul thirsts solely for heavenly things, all present realities are held in disdain, so that the more diligently everything bodily is driven away from its purpose, the more abundantly it may be filled with love of invisible things.

It should be noted that he is now commanded four times to return to the rest of sleep. For while we use this world negligently with regard to visible things, we remain vigilant in deed, speech, and thought. We are therefore commanded to sleep three times, so that through rest from work, silence of the mouth, and rejection of superfluous thoughts we may be prepared for knowledge of heavenly things. The fourth time we are sent to sleep when, with the permission of our superiors, we are commanded to cease even from useful service, so that, hindered by no anxious concern, the mind may gather itself wholly for the contemplation of heavenly vision.

**16.** It should also be noted that the Lord awakens the resting boy without Eli’s knowledge; yet, once awakened, he does not disclose the reason for his call unless Eli gives the command. For he raises chosen subordinates by hidden inspiration toward desire for the heavenly homeland, but he does not permit them, without their superiors’ consent, to be called through rest toward the homeland they love.

Since, therefore, each time the boy is called he is allowed to go to his teacher, what else is signified except that the desires of subjects, inspired by God himself, are submitted to the judgment of their superiors? The work of a subordinate, inspired by God, is recognized as pleasing to God when it is carried out at the command or with the permission of a superior.

The boy is therefore called four times by the Lord, and four times the teacher commands him to rest in sleep, because through divine inspiration we are inflamed with love for the more hidden life toward moderation in work, silence of speech, rejection of inward anxiety, and cessation from service; yet we are forbidden to fulfill the desires of our love without the permission of our superiors. The Lord calls and keeps silent about the reason for the call, so that, with the teacher’s permission, he may disclose himself to the subordinate who has been called. For after calling, God kept silent while the boy had not been bidden to listen; when the human teacher gave the command, the God who called disclosed the reason for his call. The text continues:

**(Verses 9–11.)** “So Samuel went and slept in his place. And the Lord came and stood, and called as he had called the second time, ‘Samuel.’ And Samuel said, ‘Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.’ And the Lord said to him.”

**17.** Since these words speak of the incorporeal and invisible divine substance in terms known to pertain to a body, they must necessarily be understood rationally. For where could the one who is everywhere come? How can one who is not formed as a bodily substance be said to stand and speak?

Yet all these expressions are placed by that substance, which dictates everything, as words adapted to our poverty, through which we may rise to understand the mysteries of its activity. The Lord’s coming means that he touches the hearts of the elect by the presence of his grace. His standing means that, by the gift of that same grace which remains, he retains the minds he touches through the gift of his unceasing grace. His calling means that he awakens the chosen mind to an increase of greater grace.

The Lord comes but does not stand when the hearts of the negligent are touched by grace, yet they do not persevere in the affection and love of the grace that touches them. He is like one who comes as though present but departs without standing, when, touched by divine grace, they suddenly resolve to do good, but, immediately abandoned, give up the intention of that same good resolution.

If the passage is referred to the power of contemplation, the Lord comes and stands when he suddenly touches the hearts of the elect through grace and does not suddenly abandon those whom he has touched, so that by coming he may visit, by standing confirm, and, having shown himself for the joy of the mind he loves, may not depart before that mind has been satisfied by living in him. But since he is said to stand, his eventual departure is indicated. For although he sometimes satisfies chosen souls for a little while through his revelation, he withdraws the sweetness of his presence so that they may desire what has been withdrawn more ardently.

The Lord therefore comes, visiting; he stands, showing himself gently; he calls, awakening the soul to love of the glory he has displayed through the most ardent desire. Hence, too, the boy, awakened so many times, is called again by name. Calling by name signifies the affection of great love and intimacy. Thus he also speaks to Moses, saying: “I know you by name” (Exod. 33:12, 17).

The name of the one called is therefore repeated when the mind of the one who sees is received into great intimacy with the inward Majesty and is lifted by powerful desires toward love of the one who calls it, so that nothing besides what it hears may please it, and it may continually desire to linger in the joy of its hearing.

Hence the text adds openly: “Samuel said, ‘Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.’” Whoever said “Speak” concluded that he had no alternative. For he seems to say in plainer words: “I replied, ‘Speak,’ because I could not reply otherwise.” For what else can the mind desire when it has been taken up into the joy of the speaking Majesty?

To say “Speak” to God in the mind is to desire always to hear that ineffably sweet speech. He says “Speak” because he would wish the Lord never to be silent. Hence it is added: “For your servant hears,” as though he were saying: “I desire to enjoy eternally what I receive through the experience of inward affection.”

He therefore asks the Lord to speak because he desires him never to be silent within his inward affections, lest the one who is lifted up by such sublime exultation while the Lord speaks should, when he is silent, be cast down into the narrow confines of condemned humanity. For if, while he speaks, we are taken up from the darkness of our corruption, when he becomes silent toward us by withdrawing grace, we are brought under the power of those same darknesses.

Rightly, then, raised to so great a height, he says to the Lord, “Speak,” because he delights in the joy of inward hearing to the same degree that nothing delights him in outward things; and the more eagerly he wishes to remain with the one speaking to him, the more willingly he would never wish to be cast down into his weakness.

**18.** Moreover, when, by God’s authorship, we say to the Lord, “Speak,” we say it because he grants it. Yet we cannot express with what affection the more perfect elect say this to him, because what belongs to desire, being ineffable, cannot be expressed in rational speech.

Peter aptly conveys this affection. When he stood beside the transfigured Lord on the mountain and saw his face shining like the sun and his garments white as snow, he said: “It is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tents here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matt. 17:4; Luke 9:33). For the one who says, “It is good for us to be here,” would, if he could, have wished never to be cast down from that vision of such glory.

When Peter says, “Lord, it is good for us to be here,” and Samuel says, “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears,” the words are different, but the affections are equal. Peter’s words on the mountain, with the Lord transfigured, signify what Samuel signifies when the Lord comes, stands, and calls him a second time.

Although Peter is reproved by the Evangelist as though he did not know what he was saying, this does not appear contrary to the sense just given. The Evangelist reproves not Peter’s affection but his judgment: having been taken up with the Lord into glory apart from others, he desired to remain there forever and did not want the Lord to descend into the disgrace of the cross for the sake of the common redemption.

He therefore did not know what he was saying, but he loved ardently what he saw, because he saw such a great good that it could not possibly be loved otherwise. Thus, although Peter is rightly reproved, he is also reasonably forgiven, because he was overcome by love through enjoyment of such Majesty.

Nevertheless, when Peter is accused of ignorance about what he said, the cause of that ignorance is also recalled. For the Evangelist adds: “For they were terrified with fear.” The ineffable beauty of the inward Majesty, when it graciously reveals itself, sometimes shakes the chosen mind with wondrous fear, lest, if the spirit that advances it does not restrain it with the bridle of fear, it leap from the greatness of the vision into elation.

In one and the same vision of revealed glory, the goodness of the Redeemer is seen ineffably to caress, and his justice ineffably to terrify, so that the more sweetly the goodness of God’s regard nourishes the mind of the one who sees, the more fearfully consideration of his justice makes it cautious lest it be satisfied in vain.

Thus, when Samuel is raised to intimacy with divine speech, he is told not joyful things about the progress of the elect but dreadful things about the downfall of the great. [Note: [Col. 0135D] Gilot: “dreadfully announced.”] For the text continues:

**(Verse 11.)** “And the Lord said to Samuel: Behold, I am doing a deed in Israel, which, whoever hears, will make both his ears tingle.”

**19.** Among sublime gifts, the chosen mind is restrained from elation all the more cautiously when, through the justice of almighty God, it sees even those rejected who appeared to be supported by more exalted gifts. Hence, concerning the word that the Lord threatens to accomplish, the ears of those who hear are said to tingle.

The ears of the body tingle when they are struck by an intolerable sound. When a shout is poured into the ear beyond its capacity for hearing, the sound rejected by the ear’s narrowness is turned into ringing, because, while the voice hisses through the chambers of the ears, having been poured in all at once, it does not enter inwardly.

For the ears of the mind, an intolerable shout is the rejection of some great preacher. The magnitude of the outpoured cry is not grasped because, while the exalted gifts granted to a rejected preacher are recalled, the judgment of divine justice by which he is cast out remains unknown. The magnitude of the voice poured out is therefore turned into ringing of the ears, because, although the judgment by which it occurs is not grasped by the mind’s attention, hearts are shaken with fear as it is weighed through prolonged reflection.

Just as ears ring from the sound of a great voice shut within, so the hearts of the righteous tremble at the rejection of great men when that rejection is long considered.

Both ears are said to ring: the right and the left. Since eternal life is signified by the right and the present life by the left, and since we hear what is said through the ear, what do we understand by the left ear except the intention of pious action, and by the right ear except the intention of heavenly vision?

Both ears of the hearer therefore ring because, when the ruin of eminent men is displayed, the intention of the elect is disturbed in both respects: with fearful hearts they raise themselves to contemplate eternal things, and they do not order temporal affairs without great dread.

He who said to the Lord, “Your justice is like the mountains of God; your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7), had experienced this ringing of the ears. The mountains of God signify the great and chosen men. These mountains of God are made equal to his justice when they fulfill his arduous commands in action. Yet the divine judgments are a great abyss, because, although what holy men do appears right in their eyes, they cannot know what it is like before the eyes of almighty God.

They therefore continually do the good they are capable of doing, yet fear that abyss of judgments thundering above them, because their hearts are shaken by the great terror of the Lord’s word, which they hear concerning his deeds.

Appropriately, it is said that only the ears of those who hear will tingle. For the Gospel likewise admonishes us: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8). Those who keep watch with their whole attention over what lies outside do not know this ringing of fear, because they do not sufficiently consider the height of the divine judgments over them.

But behold: the judgments’ sentences are repeated with what sharpness against the one who refused to consider the subtle judgments of God over him. For the text continues:

**(Verses 13–14.)** “For I have told him that I would judge his house forever because of the iniquity, since he knew that his sons were acting disgracefully and did not correct them. Therefore I swore to the house of Eli that the iniquity of the house of Eli would not be expiated forever by sacrifices or offerings.”

**20.** Since the sentence of just severity is often tempered by clemency, this is a judgment of great strictness, where the sentence of punishment is reaffirmed by repetition. Earlier, he had foretold it to Eli when, through the man of God, whose name was suppressed, he announced the sentence of his downfall. Since he now again swears that he will do the same, he repeats the judgment of condemnation.

Here it should also be noted that the one who did not correct his sons when they acted wickedly is reproved for committing an iniquity that could never be expiated by sacrifices or offerings. What, then, will be the severity directed against one’s own iniquity, if negligence regarding the care of another is an irremediable fault? If the sins of subjects, when left uncorrected, bind us under an unending guilt, by what punishments does the audacity of our own iniquity bind us?

Rightly, then, the ears of the hearer tingle, because the minds of the elect who consider this attentively tremble at such great strictness. Rightly the ears of the hearer tingle at this, because it contains an immensity of outcry that chosen hearts scarcely endure.

The right ear of the hearer rings because, although each person, by the merit of his perfection, raises himself to contemplate heavenly things, he nevertheless does not trust in the height of his life. The left ear also rings because, although someone possesses the gift of knowledge by which he can order temporal affairs perfectly, he has no confidence in the perfection of his ministry.

Amid sublime gifts they hear the word, from whose cry both ears suffer ringing; and under it they do not cease to be afraid for as long as this life of uncertainty continues. Hence the text appropriately adds:

**(Verse 15.)** “Samuel slept until morning.”

**21.** He sleeps until morning who rests in the conduct of the good work he has begun until the splendor of the Redeemer who is to come appears. He sleeps until morning who, throughout the entire night of the present life, waits through the purpose of begun righteousness for the brightness of the promised Redeemer to shine upon him for the joy of deserved recompense.

He heard the promised word in Israel, from which his ears do not cease to ring, because from the justice of God, whose severity he had seen, he drew the spirit of fear; under its weight he cannot awaken to love of the world.

But perhaps he is said to sleep until morning because of the ringing of the right ear. The right ear rings because, while the perfect lover of the inward life doubts concerning the perfection of contemplation, he desires more and more to advance in the lofty way of life he has begun.

Yet as long as we are in this mortal flesh, evil spirits lie in wait for those who strive toward the heights. To draw them away from the vision of inward glory, they gather fabrications of futile thoughts and set them before their inward eyes.

It is therefore aptly said: “Samuel slept until morning.” The temptation of unclean spirits is night; whoever sleeps until morning does not open his eyes throughout the night. He therefore sleeps in the night who disdains to look upon the fabrications of demons during temptation.

He also sleeps throughout the whole night because he is not overcome by the darkness of temptation but endures it manfully until, through the coming of grace, he is visited by the light of heavenly brightness. Then he awakens as though at morning, because after the darkness he rejoices in the delight of the light poured back upon him.

At that point he opens his eyes as though awakening, because he gladly looks upon the light with which he is sprinkled—the one who did not care to look upon the darkness brought against him. This is the effect of the ringing of the right ear: the person who relies upon heavenly things disdains to see what is rejected, and he demonstrates the certainty of his progress by not losing through open and violent battles what he advances in peace.

The text continues:

**(Verse 15.)** “And he feared to tell Eli the vision.”

**22.** He feared to tell him what the Lord had shown him, so that he might restrain the rashness of human audacity by the force of discipline. Some people are so headlong that they easily rush into criticizing their superiors and do not fear to threaten future punishments because of their errors.

Such people, plainly, do not know the custom of sacred Scripture and have never truly heard the Lord speaking to them. For those to whom almighty God, speaking, discloses the punishments of their superiors fear to tell them what they have heard.

Let those who criticize their superiors therefore consider how thoughtlessly they rush forward and fear the depths of their own fall. If those to whom almighty God speaks are afraid to speak to their superiors, with what terror ought those to whom God has not spoken at all to conceal themselves beneath the silence of their tongues?

Samuel’s fear therefore does not indicate servile terror but the reverence owed to pastoral dignity. Even if a negligent preacher deserves rebuke and threats on account of his own guilt, the loftiness of his office demands reverential fear.

The text continues:

**(Verse 15.)** “And he opened the doors of the house of the Lord.”

**23.** What does it mean that the one who was afraid to speak unlocked the doors of the house of the Lord, except that he was not ashamed to obey even though he feared to disclose the sad news? It was said above: “Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was.” The boy who is said to have slept in the temple of the Lord and now to open its doors is shown to have had an assigned ministry, namely, to open and close the doors at the proper hours.

Thus, although he was afraid to disclose the vision, he opened the doors of the house of the Lord and showed reverence toward his teacher in two ways: by carrying out his ministry and by guarding his speech. How strictly he maintained this restraint in speaking is shown if what follows is carefully considered. For the text immediately adds:

**(Verses 16–18.)** “Then Eli came to Samuel and said, ‘Samuel, my son.’ He replied, ‘Here I am.’ And he questioned him: ‘What is the word that the Lord spoke to you? I beg you, do not hide it from me. May God do this to you, and add this also, if you hide from me any of the words that were spoken to you.’ So Samuel told him all the words and did not hide anything from him.”

**24.** The fact that he is said to have been compelled to speak with such persistent adjuration declares that he had been bound by a strict obligation of silence. And because some subordinate persons ordinarily keep silent not to preserve purity but out of stubborn insolence, Samuel displays the form of the chosen subordinate: he remained silent reverently, but, once ordered to speak, he feared to remain silent.

Thus he shone with a twofold light of conduct: he kept silent through the virtue of filial fear, yet by speaking he sought the usefulness of speech.

The text continues:

**(Verse 18.)** “And he replied: ‘It is the Lord; let him do what is good in his eyes.’”

**25.** Whoever considers Eli’s reply more simply than he should thinks that Eli responded both correctly and humbly. For, as it is heard outwardly, what could he have said more humbly? He heard his own rejection and offered himself to the threatening God—or rather, to the God proclaiming the sentence of his rejection—for him to do whatever he wished.

But if this humility in his reply is examined closely, it is not true humility. True humility is recognized as that which accompanies the good of obedience in carrying out the commands of a superior. He would truly have been humble if he had offered himself for correction of the fault for which he was reproved.

Perhaps he would have been more truly humble if, once reproved, he had not merely replied but had imposed correction upon his wicked sons; if even then he had persisted in pastoral zeal and punished the crimes of the depraved priests with deserved retribution.

When he says, “It is the Lord; let him do what is good in his eyes,” he is therefore recognized as having declared his choice more openly than he gave a response of humility. For he preferred to incur the causes of God’s threats rather than condemn his sons for the iniquities they had committed.

How many imitators of Eli still exist—people who hear almighty God threatening them daily through sacred Scripture, yet are afraid to displease human beings, do not fear to incur the threats of divine anger, and, while fearing human enmities as though they were irreconcilable, trust in God’s mercy even while sinning!

**26.** Disordered confidence may have a place in the vengeance of almighty God, but it cannot obtain pardon. For an uncorrected sinner who persists in the purpose of his guilt, what is it to say of God who threatens him, “It is the Lord; let him do what is good in his eyes,” except to trust disorderly in the most orderly mercy of God?

He trusts rightly in the mercy of almighty God who corrects through repentance what he has done wrong by sinning and wipes it away through tears. To sin and presume upon the clemency of God the Creator is to expose oneself to the sea of his justice. Likewise, not to wipe away committed sins through repentance and yet to presume upon God’s mercy is to offend against the judgment of his strictness.

When Eli’s life is portrayed as the form of rejected preachers, not only the fault of his fall is shown but also the security of his precipitous guilt. He could have appeased the greatness of divine indignation through the fear of repentance; but because he neglected what he heard, he incurred what he deserved.

**27.** Almighty God is just in equity, yet he is believed to be even more abundant in compassion. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “His mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9). This is why, through the prophet Jonah, he proclaimed threats of destruction to the Ninevites, yet spared the punishment of the city’s overthrow when they repented (Jonah 3:1 and following).

This is also why the punishment of death was promised to King Hezekiah through the oracle of the prophet (2 Kings 20:1 and following; Isa. 38:1 and following). But because the king, fearing death, afflicted himself before the Lord with tears of repentance, he did not find the death by which he was to die with the one whom he feared.

Earlier, the Lord had asserted that he had spoken so that the house of Eli and his father might minister before him forever. [Note: [Col. 0139] Gilot and Vatican read: “he asserted that the Lord had spoken to him.”] But the one who had spoken good things concerning one who acted well changed the sentence concerning a house that had now become rejected, saying: “But now, far be this from me” (1 Sam. 2:30). If almighty God withdraws promises of good because those to whom he made them have changed for the worse, how much more does he withdraw the fulfillment of threats when he sees those to whom he declared punishment for their committed iniquities conducting themselves well?

What, then, are we to say to this, who sin daily yet remain secure in the bondage of our guilt? This very fact—that we do not grasp the strictness of divine justice—is greatly to be feared by us. For behold: the one who is cast out by divine indignation on account of the guilt of negligence is said to have been troubled by no fear.

But since we know the rejection of the rejected preacher as a matter for fear, let us hear of the progress of the elect. For the text continues:

[Col. 0141B] **(Verse 19.)** “And Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him.”

**28.** If this is read historically, it indicates that the boy Samuel grew in bodily age. But if, as with the other passages, we seek its meaning through spiritual inquiry, the Lord is described as being with the one who is said to have grown.

He grows who advances in the age of the mind toward the perfect man. Hence it is said through the Prophet concerning the elect who advance: “They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83:8). Paul likewise says: “Until we all arrive at a perfect man, at the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13).

Yet some grow in virtues and fall through elation. These seem to grow, but the Lord is not with them, because, by thinking highly of themselves, they cast out from themselves the one whom, while advancing in virtues, they could have had with them through humility.

Alternatively, if “grew” is understood of external dignity, the Lord is said to be with him because many are devout in a humbler rank, but when they suddenly reach the summit of dignity, they abandon their former works together with humility.

Samuel therefore both advances and, while advancing, has the Lord with him, so that he might represent the conduct of chosen preachers. When they obtain gifts and dignities by which they may benefit others, they do not neglect to please God in themselves; and from the very source from which they multiply the gifts they have received for others, they display within themselves the good that they desire to spread among others by speaking.

Hence the text adds:

[Col. 0141D] **(Verse 19.)** “And none of his words fell to the ground.”

29. The preacher’s word falls to the ground when it is cheapened by the preacher’s reprehensible conduct. Hence Truth’s voice says: “It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by people” (Matt. 5:13). It must be noted that the text says that none of his words fell to the ground, so that the preacher is clearly permitted to do nothing that he is permitted to condemn. For whatever he forbids to be done, if he himself does it, the word falls to the ground: while he who speaks it despises it, those who hear it do not reverence it.

The Lord was forbidding any word to fall to the ground when, speaking of negligent preachers, he explained the consequence of their negligence, saying: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (ibid. 5:19). The preacher does not loosen even the least commandment when his word falls to the ground through none of all his words. When it is said that no word fell to the ground from all Samuel’s words, whose character does Samuel signify except those who are rightly great both in preaching and in conduct in the kingdom of heaven?

Thus none of his words falls to the ground, because everything that the perfect preacher of the holy Church says in lofty terms is also proclaimed by him through an exalted way of life. Like someone placed upon a lofty watchtower, he instructs the wise by his word and shows the simple by his deeds the path by which they ought to enter their eternal homeland. Hence it follows:

> (Verse 20.) And all Israel, from Dan even to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord.

30. What are signified by Dan except the simple, and by Beersheba except the wise? Samuel is recognized as the Lord’s faithful prophet from Dan to Beersheba when the life of the chosen preacher is set before the simple as an example of salvation, and the mysteries of holy Scripture are revealed to the wise through his teaching.

Since Beersheba is interpreted as “the seventh well,” Beersheba can signify not only the wise but also the righteous. For what is the seventh well except the grace of the sevenfold Spirit? The life of sinners is represented by Dan, because through the ancient prophet it is said: “Let Dan be a serpent on the way, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s heel, so that its rider falls backward” (Gen. 49:17).

Thus Samuel is known as the prophet of the Lord from Dan to Beersheba when the life and teaching of the chosen preacher are revered by sinners and by the righteous alike: so that the fallen may see in him the good by which they may correct themselves through repentance, while the good may marvel at the height of life toward which they may grow stronger each day by advancing. It follows:

> (Verse 21.) And the Lord continued, so that he appeared at Shiloh.

31. Earlier, concerning the time of the reprobate shepherd, it is said: “In those days there was no manifest vision.” When the excellent preacher is therefore revealed through sacred eloquence, the Lord is said to appear again, because knowledge of the divine counsel—which is hidden from the reprobate—is disclosed to the elect as a reward for their purity.

If even human counsels are entrusted only to intimates, is the almighty God to be thought willing to reveal the secrets of his ordering to his enemies? First, therefore, the life of the righteous teacher is proclaimed; then it is said that the Lord continued so that he might appear, because the manifestation of divine light flees from the reprobate and hypocrites, while it opens itself to the elect and to pure hearts. Hence the true light itself, speaking, illuminates us and says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

Thus he continued so that the Lord might appear because he saw the eye of his preacher to be pure. But when it says, “so that he appeared at Shiloh,” it indicates that he appeared there on another occasion. Since it stated where he appeared, lest one believe that he appeared to Eli, it next identifies the person to whom he appeared, saying:

> (Verse 21.) For the Lord had revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh, according to the word of the Lord.

32. He revealed himself to Samuel when he disclosed to him the secret of his counsel concerning the rejection of the reprobate preacher. This is asserted to have happened according to the word of the Lord, so that what had been said not long before to Eli through the man of God may also be understood to have been fulfilled historically: “I will raise up for myself a faithful priest who shall act according to my heart and my soul, and he shall walk before my Christ all his days” (1 Sam. 2:35). And again: “You shall see your rival in the temple, amid all the prosperity of Israel” (ibid. 2:32).

If we examine this according to the spiritual understanding, how does the Lord continue so that he may appear to the elect, except because he who wondrously terrifies his elect by contemplation of his justice also ineffably soothes them by the manifestation of his glory? He who, appearing as the just one, shakes the hearts of the saints with terror “continues so that he may appear” when the sweetness of his mercy is poured back into the terrified heart.

This is why he did not always appear to Moses in fire, but at one time in fire and at another time in a cloud. In fire there is the terror of judgment. Hence, concerning the second coming of our Redeemer, the Psalmist says: “Fire shall go before him, and a mighty storm around him” (Ps. 49:3). In the cloud, however, the protection of mercy is expressed, because the Lord, promising his elect the consolation of that protection, says: “Then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud” (Mark 13:26; Luke 21:27).

The Lord therefore appears in fire and cloud to those journeying through the desert, because in this pilgrimage of exile he sometimes terrifies the minds of those contemplating him by his justice, yet raises them up when cast down by fear through the soothing comfort of his protection. The Lord thus appeared to Samuel and continued so that he might appear, because he who is seen by the minds of the elect in the fire of terror is also presented in the cloud of sweetness.

He had seen the vision of fire within, who announced it outwardly, saying: “Holy and terrible is his name” (Ps. 110:10). Wishing likewise to show him seen in fire, he says: “Come and see the works of the Lord, terrible in his counsels over the children of men” (Ps. 65:5). But he who appeared to him in fire continued so that he might appear, because he also offered him, from the cloud, the sweetness of his glory and delight. Therefore the one who had been terrified, now filled with joy, said: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. 30:20). Marveling likewise at the added appearance, he says: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart” (Ps. 72:1).

[Col. 0144A] 33. But what follows must be carefully considered: “According to the word of the Lord.” We must therefore know the word of the Lord before we can deserve to attain the Lord’s appearance, lest an unjust and indiscriminate vision of fire and cloud not only fail to show us the perfection of the heavenly journey but drive us toward the drowning of error.

Origen, wishing to see the Lord appearing without the word of the Lord, beheld the vision of the cloud in a disorderly manner [Note: [Col. 0143] Gregory discusses the same matter in Book 34 of the *Moralia*, no. 38; see the notes.], because he shuddered at the appearance of fire. For while denying or diminishing God’s justice and preaching his excessive clemency, he asserted that he would spare not only all condemned human beings but would also at some time free the reprobate angels from eternal punishment.

Novatian, however, loved looking upon the vision of fire more intensely. By declaring the justice of almighty God to be unrelenting, he removed from sinners every remedy of hope for obtaining pardon and of repentance. The Lord therefore appeared neither to Novatian nor to that other man, because neither of them perceived the almighty Lord according to what is discerned through the truth of sacred eloquence.

The Lord appears according to the word when he reveals himself to the mind in a manifestation that the faith of sacred Scripture does not reject. Hence it aptly follows:

> (Verse 21.) And Samuel’s word came throughout all Israel.

34. The word of the heretics does not come. Novatian’s word was that the just God never spares the faithful who have fallen once. Origen’s word was that the merciful Lord does not permit any rational creature to perish through eternal damnation. But because sinners who turn to the Lord do not perish, while angels who have fallen once and sinners who have died in their sin are never saved, the word of the heretics does not come.

Samuel’s word therefore came throughout all Israel, because the preaching of Catholic men is fulfilled—preaching that is rightly recognized in the truth of sacred eloquence. It must be noted that the word is said to have come from the one to whom the Lord is said to have added his vision, because the preaching of that person is true to whom the terror of divine justice is shown in such a way that the abundance of God’s goodness is not concealed: so that the truth seen terrifies the mind of the beholder, while the goodness displayed does not permit the terrified mind to fall into despair; and so that it presumes upon goodness to the extent that it does not rush into the audacity of transgression.

These discussions in the second book of the present work may suffice, so that, as we prepare to begin what follows with a new opening, our zeal for speaking may also be renewed through devotion.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0143]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0143D]

1. When we were diligently seeking how the meaning of sacred history might correspond to the conduct of the elect, we deferred returning, in exposition, to the course of the allegory. To supply what we appear to have omitted, therefore, the question arises: What does it mean that, while Samuel is said to minister to the Lord before Eli, the word of the Lord is described as precious?

As was said above, Samuel signifies the preachers of the holy Church, while Eli signifies the elect fathers of the Old Testament. The boy Samuel therefore ministered to the Lord before Eli when the new order of teachers preached faith in the Redeemer. Paul speaks of this ministry, saying: “Since I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I glorify my ministry” (Rom. 11:13). Again he says: “Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they ministers of Christ? So am I” (2 Cor. 11:22).

To minister to the Lord, then, is to undertake the labor of preaching. Samuel is said to have rendered this ministry to the Lord before Eli because whatever the new order of preachers asserted concerning the religion of the new faith, it strengthened by the authority of the ancient Fathers.

Samuel ministered to the Lord when the new preacher asserted, saying: “For I say that Christ Jesus was a minister of the circumcision for the sake of God’s truth, but that the Gentiles should glorify God for his mercy” (Rom. 15:8). In order also to perform before Eli the ministry that he offered to the Lord, he added: “As it is written: ‘Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and praise him together, all you peoples’” (Ps. 116:1).

And to restrain himself more closely before Eli in the ministry of the Lord, he added: “For Isaiah says: ‘There shall be the root of Jesse, and he who rises up to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles shall hope’” (Rom. 15:12; from Isa. 11:10).

The boy Samuel ministered to the Lord when Peter asserted the glory of the Lord’s Resurrection, saying: “Jesus the Nazarene, a man approved by God among you by signs and wonders, whom you killed, handed over through the hands of the wicked; God raised him from the dead on the third day by predetermined counsel, since it was impossible for him to be held by the pains of hell” (Acts 2:22 ff.).

2. But he also performed before Eli the ministry that he offered to the Lord, because he added, saying: “For David says: ‘You will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption’” (Acts 2:27; Ps. 16:10).

Samuel is therefore aptly said to minister to the Lord before Eli, because the elect preachers of the holy Church, while raising up the standing of the new faith through their preaching, confirmed by the authority of the ancient Fathers what they attempted to establish by reason.

[Col. 0145D] 3. At that time, moreover, the word of the Lord is said to have been precious. A precious thing cannot be bought for a small price. The price by which God’s word is bought is the labor of holy action. We buy, as it were, the thing we wish to possess at a price when, through the word of preaching that we receive, we offer the labor of good works.

The word was precious at that time because it was not given for merely any labor of works, when everyone who killed the buyer of the word thought that he was rendering service to God. The buyer of the word therefore required a great price at that time, because the one who had come to torment for what he believed could not preserve the word of faith without great labor.

That was the time when the word being bought exhorted people not by a figurative moral type but by the explicit command of speech [Note: [Col. 0145] Corruptly in Gilot and the Vatican edition: “of figurative mortality” (*typo figuratae mortalitatis*).], saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross daily and follow me” (Matt. 16:24). Again he says: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (ibid. 10:37). And: “Whoever does not renounce everything that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

Thus, when Samuel’s ministry is asserted, the word of the Lord is said to be precious, because clearly, at the beginning of the faith, those who believed the teachers preaching eternal life must be understood to have expended the works of great labor for the word of faith they had received.

And because the Jewish people had already lost the light of divine knowledge, it follows:

[Col. 0146B] > (1 Sam. 3:1.) In those days there was no manifest vision.

4. His vision would indeed have been manifest if he had believed in the Redeemer whom he had heard had come for his visitation. Concerning this blindness of theirs it follows:

> (Verse 2.) Now it happened that Eli was lying in his place, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished.

Eli’s vision is not manifest, because the priesthood of the Jews is buried in the blindness of its faithlessness. Eli therefore lies in his place, because he possesses the letter of the law, yet in the law and the prophets he does not possess the standing of light but the downfall of blindness.

The place of Eli—that is, of the Jewish preacher—is the sacred law. Since the Jewish priesthood still possesses sacred Scripture, it is in its place. And because, not knowing the power of sacred Scripture, it is not raised to the standing of faith, it is said to be not standing in its place but lying there.

Since it has also been cast down until the end of the world, it is said to be unable to see the lamp of God. Thus, although the Jews receive each day so many exhortations to preach from the holy Church, and although they do not believe even when defeated by so many affirmations of the holy faith, what else do we read about them in sacred Scripture—and also learn through experience—except that they have been cast down, not only so that they do not see, but also so that they cannot see?

Therefore the apostles, considering it useless labor to address those who could not see, say in their Acts: “Since you have judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

But although Eli is reported to be unable to see, he is called the lamp of God.
