For the ministry of the Synagogue was the lamp of God when it shone in the elect Fathers both through the light of true preaching and through the promise of the Redeemer who was to come. Yet this lamp could not be seen while Samuel was ministering, because, at the time of the new preaching, the teaching authority of the Synagogue incurred the punishment of perpetual rejection.

5. It must be noted that the text does not say that it could not shine, because it still bears the light of sacred Scripture for our sake, although it does not understand what it bears. Hence it is said to be unable to see before it was extinguished.

It is not yet extinguished, yet it cannot see, because, as I have already said, it bears the light but does not attend to it. It exists before it is extinguished, for as long as it shines. And because sacred Scripture is not taken away from it until the end of the world, if it does not see before it is extinguished, it is extended to the end of the world in blindness.

But if its being lit refers to the zeal of faithlessness, it cannot see for that very reason: because it is not extinguished. For if it were to extinguish the fire of faithlessness in its mind, once the zeal of impiety had been removed, it would open the eyes of its mind to the pleasing light of true faith.

But while it is said to be unable to see, it is declared an unworthy lamp, and another, worthy to see what is worthy, is sought. For the text continues:

[Col. 0147B] > (Verse 3.) But Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of the Lord was, and the Lord called Samuel.

6. Once Eli’s blindness had been confirmed, the Lord called Samuel, because, after the priesthood of the Jews had been condemned, he took up the new order of preachers into a greater grace.

But the one who explained whom he called also showed from where he called him, since he said that Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark was. The temple of God is the place where God dwells. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven” (Ps. 10:5). Paul identifies this place, saying: “God’s temple is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17).

The temple of God is therefore the soul of each of the elect. The temple in which the ark of God is stored is the mind in which the mysteries of divine eloquence are preserved through understanding.

What else, then, does sleeping in the temple mean except to persist in vigilant self-examination through the guarding of one’s attention? Samuel was sleeping in the temple of God because each preacher of the new grace, while perfectly despising everything that belongs to the world, rested in the innermost watchfulness of his elect mind. And because he had been instructed in the mysteries of divine Scripture, he slept in the temple where the ark was.

7. It must be noted that the text does not say “he slept” but “he was sleeping,” because he strove not to preserve this same watchfulness of mind in passing but to maintain it through enduring perseverance.

Samuel’s sleep therefore signifies the perfect contempt of the world in the teacher’s mind. The preacher sleeps in the temple when, having entirely rejected worldly anxiety, he conceals himself in his mind through consideration of spiritual matters.

Peter had chosen the repose of this sleep when he said: “It is not right for us to abandon the word of God and serve tables” (Acts 6:2). Jethro the Midianite likewise justly rebuked his kinsman Moses, saying: “You are being consumed by foolish labor; but hear my words, and the Lord will be with you. Stand before the people in the matters that concern God, so that you may bring their concerns before him” (Exod. 18:18–19).

Paul also calls the Corinthians back to the sleep of the temple, saying: “There is certainly already a fault among you, that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer fraud?” (1 Cor. 6:7). He had observed that those whom the business of lawsuits occupied could not sleep in the temple of God, because it withdrew them from spiritual meditation.

He is therefore said to have been called by the Lord while sleeping in the temple, because that teacher was taken up to know divine secrets who, through the attention of his heart, dwelt not in outward matters but in inward ones. It follows:

> (Verses 4–5.) And he answered and said: “Here I am.” And he ran to Eli and said: “You called me.” He said: “I did not call you, my son; return and sleep.”

8. Why did he who heard the Lord calling him run to Eli, except because he thought he had been called by Eli? And since we are following the order of the typological explanation, how can Eli be understood to speak when God is speaking to the boy?

Whatever our ancient Fathers said in the holy Scriptures is attributed to Eli’s speech. Since they did not speak from themselves, but God spoke through them whatever he willed, the voice heard in the holy Scriptures is recognized as God’s voice, although it is uttered through Eli.

The boy, because he ran to Eli while God was speaking, evidently heard a voice that God made similar to Eli’s voice. What, then, does it mean that the voice of divine speech does not differ from Eli’s voice, except that he himself also utters speech through the ancient Fathers?

Eli’s voice is recognized as God’s because whatever the elect Fathers say through sacred eloquence they received not from themselves but from the Lord. Hence throughout nearly all the speech of the prophets the phrase is repeated: “Thus says the Lord,” so that we understand the voice resounding through the prophet’s oracle to belong not to a speaking human being but to God who commands.

9. At times God speaks through Scripture; at times through hidden inspiration. He speaks through hidden revelation when the Spirit discloses to the elect mind either what must be done or what must be taught.

When Samuel heard the Lord calling him, he ran to Eli because the chosen order of preachers of the holy Church sought in sacred eloquence the character of what it had learned through God’s revelation. The rule of right understanding is expressed in the books of sacred Scripture, because the divine counsels were explained there by our venerable Fathers, who possessed the Holy Spirit.

Samuel, called so many times by the Lord, ran to Eli [Note: [Col. 0147D] Gilot.: “Samuel, now so often called by the Lord.”], because the order of preachers consulted the sayings of the ancient Fathers about everything it had learned through spiritual revelation, so that it believed something had finally been revealed to it by the Lord only when it recognized that it differed in no way from what it read in sacred Scripture.

For the person who does not know how to examine in the clear truth of sacred Scripture the nature of what he gathers through hidden contemplation is easily deceived. Hence the Apostle warns: “Satan transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14). How, then, are false things discerned in the brightness of true light?

Samuel therefore runs to Eli whenever he is called by the Lord, because holy preachers, lest they be deceived in their innermost contemplation by the appearance of false light, examine the manner of hidden revelation in the open truth of sacred Scripture.

10. The matter itself requires us to ask how it is appropriate for Eli to say, “I did not call you, my son.” Our Fathers, who speak through sacred eloquence to the new preachers, do not call them but indicate the character of their inner revelation.

To call is to awaken the minds of God’s elect through the inspiration of his grace. The ancient Fathers speak through sacred Scripture, but they cannot awaken the hearts of their hearers through the inspiration of divine grace.

When sacred eloquence is consulted and indicates that it cannot itself give the gift of spiritual grace [Note: [Col. 0149D] Guss.: “judge”], it excuses itself, by Samuel’s authority, as Eli, as it were, through certain words. Yet it can indicate how the gift it cannot give must be acquired. Hence Eli’s voice says to Samuel: “Return and sleep.”

11. What does Eli’s command that the called boy return to sleep mean except that he shows preachers how to prepare themselves to receive the gift of inner grace through the quiet of the mind?

It must be noted that he says: “Return.” Samuel returns when the chosen preacher returns from meditation on sacred eloquence to the secret of inner contemplation. Having returned, he slept, because he rested in attentive inner contemplation.

Here too it must be noted that Samuel is called three times by the Lord and three times is again commanded by Eli to sleep.

12. What does this mean except that we have learned from Truth itself as teacher that there are three degrees of love? “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matt. 22:37).

But what do we take the heart to mean except counsel? And what the mind except the will? What, finally, is signified by strength except the affection of love? And through counsel, what else do we investigate except certainty of truth? Through the will, what do we love except that we greatly desire good things? Through affection, what do we seek except the enjoyment of true joy?

Through the degrees of love we are raised to the highest things when truth is revealed through the counsel of our heart, true goodness is granted to the will of the mind, and spiritual and true joy is given to the affection of our strength through the infusion of divine grace.

13. Samuel was therefore called three times by the Lord because, while the order of preachers of the still-inexperienced Church extended itself toward higher pursuits, it sought truth through the reasoning of counsel, goodness through the choice of the will, and true joy through the purpose of affection.

He likewise approached Eli three times when called, because concerning every desire of his he consulted sacred Scripture with the haste of meditation. He also heard three times that Eli had not called him, because through meditation he learned that our Fathers handed down sacred writings to us for our instruction; yet they cannot themselves give us spiritual gifts.

What else does “I did not call you” mean except “I did not give you the desire for spiritual gifts”? For if sacred Scripture, or any of its writers, conferred spiritual gifts, all who read sacred eloquence and all who listened to interpreters of sacred Scripture would be adorned with spiritual gifts.

But now, when many read sacred Scripture and listen to preaching teachers, and after the effort of reading and the exhortation of preaching some remain in the former coldness of their vices while others, through grace, burn with love for holy virtues, it is plainly evident that the order of venerable Fathers shows us the gifts of the virtues through the Scriptures they published, but that the love of the virtues they commend is granted to us by the Creator alone.

Hence James piously admonishes us, saying: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17). Paul likewise says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

What else, then, does “I did not call you” mean except to show through open instruction that the raising of the faithful soul toward heavenly desires is generated solely by the infusion of divine grace?

Since Samuel is called three times by the Lord and three times commanded by his teacher to return to sleep, he indicates how those three degrees of love are acquired.

Since we have associated understanding with the heart, and understanding desires to find truth, great sleep is necessary, lest the lover awaken before the sought-for truth is found. Let the boy therefore return and sleep, so that the one who desires to find the light of truth may, through repose, take care not to admit the darkness of errors into himself.

Let him also sleep a second time, so that he may offer the service of love to almighty God with his whole mind, and so that the good things he loves may not be disguised by any veil of evil but may be loved with pure simplicity. Since this can be recognized only through great subtlety of discernment, the boy called by the Lord is commanded by Eli to return and sleep.

For if he neglects sleeping in order to ascend this degree of love, he does not obtain the virtue he desires. Although, with God’s inspiration, we can already love good things, unless we judge carefully, in great mental repose, what the good things we desire actually are, we do not acquire them.

Samuel is therefore sent to sleep three times, because the new order of preachers is admonished to love with its whole strength. And because we have referred strength to affection, while the mind’s affection is perfected through spiritual joy, Samuel possessed the great repose of sleep.

When the order of preachers learned spiritual matters with certainty through repose, it did not receive, under the appearance of true joy, a joy foreign to the truth. For, just as it often rejoices vainly concerning other virtues, the mind of one who contemplates often rejoices vainly concerning progress in contemplation.

Samuel therefore slept again, because if the order of teachers did not carefully watch itself in contemplation, it might sometimes suppose, through vain rejoicing, that it was rejoicing in true joy.

He slept the first time because, while directing his mind toward truth that had to be known, he rejected every error with great subtlety of counsel. He slept the second time because, when he learned to love the Creator with his whole mind, he resolved within himself, in great quiet, not to mix any reprehensible thing with the good things he desired.

He slept the third time so that, while receiving the highest joy from divine contemplation, he might be able, after considered reflection, to reject empty gladness.

And because this is said of Samuel while he was still advancing, it aptly follows:

> (Verse 7.) Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord, nor had the word of the Lord yet been revealed to him.

14. At that time the order of preachers did not know the Lord with the perfection to which it later advanced [Note: [Col. 0151] Gilot.: “Now the order of preachers did not know him with the perfection [it later attained].”].

Or perhaps he is said not to know the Lord for this reason: he did not yet disclose to weak and inexperienced hearers the lofty and profound things that he knew. Thus, to those who wished to know the day of the Lord’s coming, Truth says things that he knew in their entirety but did not wish to disclose: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Mark 13:32).

What does it mean that the Son, who knows all things, does not know the day of judgment, except that, among everything he knew, although he knew the day, he did not know it in order to speak of it, while he did know its time and character?

John the Baptist, who knew the Lord perfectly, likewise sent disciples to him as though he did not know him, saying: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” (Luke 7:20).

Samuel preached as though he did not know the Lord when the evangelist Matthew, passing over the Redeemer’s divinity, began with his humanity alone, saying: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1 ff.).

But Samuel certainly knew the Lord, and the word of the Lord had been revealed to him, when John, taking up his divinity and explaining it at a lofty level, said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

He did not know the Lord when Paul spoke, saying: “I have become all things to all people, so that I might save all” (1 Cor. 9:22). Since he became weak to the weak, and a little one to little ones, and all things to all people, he surely became ignorant even with the ignorant.

To use the language of that same ignorance, he says to the Corinthians: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (ibid. 2:2).

For among the wise he both knew the Lord and had his word revealed. Hence he says: “But we, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, as though by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18). Again he says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect—not the wisdom of this world or of the rulers of this age—but we speak God’s wisdom, hidden in a mystery” (1 Cor. 2:6).

Again he preaches the Lord whom he knew, saying: “Although he is the splendor of his glory and the likeness of his substance, and sustains all things by the word of his power, having made purification for sins, he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high, having become as much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?” (Heb. 1:3–5).

He is therefore said not to know the Lord, not through ignorance of knowledge but under the pretext of simplicity. It follows:

[Col. 0152A] > (Verse 9.) Eli therefore understood that the Lord was calling the boy.

15. For if he had not understood, he would never have supplied him with counsels of salvation through sacred eloquence. He understood, that is, he foresaw. Whatever the almighty God determined to do in the building of the future Church, he revealed to the ancient Fathers through the holy spirit of prophecy.

For through the prophet Amos it is said: “The Lord God does nothing without revealing his word to his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7). What else had he understood except the calling of the new preachers, who said: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them rulers over all the earth” (Ps. 45:17)?

But to the one whose calling he understood, he also supplied counsel, saying:

[Col. 0152B] > (Verse 9.) Go and sleep, and if he calls you thereafter, you shall say: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.”

16. Enough, I think, has now been shown concerning Samuel’s sleep as signifying the repose of inward meditation. This sleep is prescribed to Samuel by Eli because the teacher is instructed through sacred discourse to devote himself to contemplating inward mysteries. But what does it mean that whenever Samuel is called, he is each time sent back to sleep, and yet he is still by no means commanded to say to God, “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears”? There he is ordered to sleep, but not to speak; here, however, when sleep is enjoined as an act of obedience, permission to speak is also given.

There, too, when he is sent back to sleep, he is not told, “Go,” but “Return”; here, likewise, he is by no means told “Return,” but “Go.” What does such great variation in the commands signify? [Col. 0152C] We recognize this variation more clearly if we attend to what Samuel’s sleep signifies in this passage. Since we referred the earlier kinds of sleep to the testing of the gifts of holy love (above, nos. 11–12), what does it mean here for Samuel—that is, for the new preacher—to sleep, except to possess those same gifts, already tested and known, in the repose of security?

Thus, appropriately, he was previously not told “Go,” but “Return”; now, however, he is told not “Return,” but “Go.” For the one who was still examining was ordered to return, so that in the tranquility of his mind he might examine another gift—he who had already recognized another gift in that same repose of mind. But because he had now tested everything through examination, he is told “Go,” since he was now sent forth with secure purpose to possess what he had come to know. [Col. 0152D] Why, then, is sleep first commanded without speech, but now sleep together with speech, except because it was not permitted to say, “Speak,” unless one were certain through true knowledge that the one speaking inwardly was God addressing the mind? Therefore it is not said to the one still examining, because unless he has perfectly discerned the one speaking within, he ought not yet to desire or receive spiritual speech as something certain.

To say to God within the mind, “Speak,” is to receive his inward inspiration securely. This consequently belongs to one who knows perfectly, not to one who is still testing; for before the judgment of inward examination, divine speech is not tested, and what is unknown to us as coming from God is not received as certain and known. [Col. 0153A] It is therefore said to Samuel, “Go and sleep,” because when the order of holy preachers had learned spiritual gifts through the testing provided by sacred discourse, it came to know them through the instruction of that same Holy Scripture, so that it might rest in those gifts through love all the more securely the more clearly it had understood their power.

He was also commanded to say to God when he called, “Speak, Lord.” For he had been taught through devotion to sacred speech not only devoutly to hear the Lord speaking through the grace of inward visitation, but also, when he was silent, to implore him with great desires to deign to speak.

> **(Verse 9.)** So Samuel went and slept in his place.

17. The preacher of the holy Church has as many places as he has advances in life. Thus, consecrating the places of his progress with divine praises, blessed Job says: “At each of my steps I will declare him” (Job 31:37). He is not now stationed in the place of examination, but certainly in that of knowledge, when he is raised to higher things. For the preacher’s place is the certain knowledge of things to be known. Concerning condemned preachers the Lord says: “They held my law but did not know me” (Jer. 2:8).

Samuel therefore slept in his place when the order of spiritual teachers retained knowledge of spiritual things with certainty of truth. But the degree to which he advanced is shown, because it is immediately added:

> **(Verse 10.)** Then the Lord came and stood.

18. Since the Lord is said not to return but to come, the abandonment of Judea and the visitation of the holy Church are signified. Hence he is said not only to come, but also to stand. In reference to his visitation of Judea, [Note: [Col. 0153D] Gilot indicates that he came in order to appear.] he declares that he came, saying: [Col. 0153C] “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). But when he came, he did not stand, because he abandoned the one who despised the good of salvation. Hence he also threatens the rulers of the Synagogue, saying: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (ibid., 23:38). Again, announcing this, he says: “Amen, I say to you, the kingdom will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

The Lord therefore came to Samuel and stood, because he once took up the preachers of the holy Church and thereafter does not depart from them, preserving them through the guardianship of his grace. For he had come to Samuel when, presenting new preachers to the world, he said: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature; whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:15–16).

But if the Lord who comes must stand, let him say: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). The Lord therefore came not to depart, but to stand, because he chose new ministers of the faith, whom he protects until the end of the world as they succeed one another as his inheritance of holy virtues.

But let us hear what he adds: he comes by grace to visit, and stands by persevering in the unchangeability of his choice.

> **(Verse 10.)** And he called, as he had called the second time, “Samuel, Samuel.”

19. He called a second time because he bestowed upon him a twofold office in the ministry of preaching: by driving back the pride of the Synagogue, he was to crush it, and by calling the humility of the Gentiles to its fulfillment, he was to raise it up. Or certainly he is called a second time because he is roused for the destruction of the old person and the building of the new.

He was called once when he was instructed through the Spirit how he might wipe away sins and vices from the hearts of sinners; he was called a second time when God instructed him through the teaching of inward mastery that, once the structure of impiety had been destroyed in the minds of converts, he ought to raise up a new edifice of holy virtues.

Since the order of holy preachers both gladly learned this instruction and devotedly offered itself for obedience, the text continues:

> **(Verse 10.)** So Samuel said: “Speak, Lord, [Col. 0154B] for your servant hears.”

20. To hear God speaking is to fulfill his commands in one’s works. In contrast, Truth itself says to the condemned in the Gospel: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason you do not hear is that you are not of God” (John 8:47).

But to the one who hears he adds what he wishes to disclose; for it follows:

> **(Verse 11.)** And the Lord said to Samuel: “Behold, I am doing a deed in Israel, which whoever hears will have both ears ringing.”

And, explaining the same word, he said:

> **(Verses 13 and 14.)** “For I told him that I would judge his house forever because of the iniquity, since he knew that his sons were acting disgracefully and did not rebuke them. Therefore I swore concerning the house of Eli that the iniquity of his house would not be expiated forever by sacrifices or offerings.”

21. What else is signified by these words than the rejection of the Jews, already explained so many times? The preacher’s house is the multitude of the people subject to him, whom he inhabits as though possessing them, while he preserves them through the care of his solicitude.

The house of Eli, therefore—that is, the former priesthood—was Judea. While he cultivated it through a reprobate way of life, he made it unclean with the stains of his wickedness. He saw his sons acting disgracefully because the high priesthood saw the priests of the lower order raging against the Redeemer; yet it did not rebuke them, nor did it restrain them by any authority from shedding so great a quantity of blood.

Therefore, by divine threat, it is promised that his house will be judged forever. For God’s judgment is condemnation. It is judged forever, therefore, because it is decreed to perish by eternal punishment. And because this occurs through God’s eternal retribution, he is said to have affirmed under oath that the iniquity of Eli’s house would not be expiated forever by prayers or offerings. We plainly see this fulfilled, because the Jewish people persist in the obstinacy of their faithlessness.

For what is the present hardness and blindness of a people once so chosen except the oath of divine retribution? He confined himself under eternal death as a punishment he deserved who did not hesitate to drive eternal life to temporal death. But [Col. 0155A] he says that he had foretold this under oath because what he had earlier revealed to their predecessors concerning Judea’s rejection became known to the succeeding teachers of the holy Church: what is now said to Eli through Samuel had previously been said to him through the man of God.

The text continues:

> **(Verse 15.)** Samuel slept until morning.

22. Why is Samuel’s sleep described so attentively in sacred discourse? Since he is said to have repeated his sleep four times already, anyone who believes that this was not spoken spiritually by the Spirit of God is very foolish. Even if he is correctly understood to have slept so many times according to the historical truth, this is written so that allegorical meanings may be brought forth from the truth of the letter.

What, then, does this fifth sleep of Samuel signify? Since we referred the first sleep to the pursuit of truth, the second to the testing of true action, the third to the exploration of true joy, and the fourth to the enjoyment of perfection that had been found, tested, and known, the fifth kind of sleep is referred to the careful planning of speech.

Samuel therefore slept for the fifth time because the order of preachers, although it had learned the truth through the counsel of the heart, had chosen good through the will of the mind, had received true joy through the affection of virtue, and had rested securely in the exalted virtues through the certainty of the blessedness it had found and known, nevertheless could not preach to its subjects what it had come to know within itself without the careful administration of profound counsel.

Often a teacher has within himself what he should preach, but cannot preach what he has in the manner he ought, because although he has learned from the Lord’s revelation what he should say, he does not know the manner in which it should be presented to the people. Samuel therefore slept again because the order of preachers arranged within itself, with great attentiveness and repose, how it might avoid scattering uselessly the seed of God’s word that it had gathered through fruitful contemplation.

For while a preacher is compelled to consider what and how much to say, and when to speak; what he should say to everyone together, and how he should admonish some separately—because he employs the great repose of holy meditation—Samuel is very appropriately said to sleep again as a type of the new preachers.

For him to sleep at that time is to arrange the manner of speaking with a tranquil mind. To awaken is to leave the repose of meditation and go forth to speak. And because he does not awaken rationally until he has arranged what must be said, the text continues: “Until morning.”

Morning is the teacher’s perfect knowledge, in his mind, of how to proclaim the word. Hence the Prophet rebukes rash teachers, saying: “It is useless for you to rise before the light” (Ps. 126:2). They rise before the light who do not sleep until morning but awaken uselessly, because they utter the word fruitlessly, having learned through no meditation how it ought to be proclaimed.

Therefore he also shows them the proper counsel, saying: “Rise after you have sat,” so that, by meditating in repose, they may gather the word which, through the labor of speech, they may scatter not uselessly [Col. 0156A] but for the gain of their hearers.

The text continues:

> **(Verse 15.)** And he was afraid to tell Eli the vision.

23. What was he afraid of, except what he had learned by sleeping? For the one who orders the word through meditation determines by reason when he should also speak the word.

Samuel saw the vision, but was afraid to tell it to Eli, because the order of teachers in the holy Church saw Judea’s deserved rejection and feared to confront it with that rejection before the time of its own rejection. Hence it rather exhorts Judea to the remedy of repentance, saying: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized” (Acts 2:38).

For this reason it is added:

> **(Verse 15.)** He opened the doors of the house of the Lord.

24. What other house of the Lord is there than the holy Church? [Note: [Col. 0155D] Gilot: “And what are the doors of this house of the Lord that Samuel opened, when the order of preachers, as people hastened toward the unity of the true faith, …” [Col. 0156D]] And what are the doors of this house except spiritual virtues? Samuel opened the doors of the house of the Lord when the order of preachers, as people hastened toward the unity of the true faith, disclosed the gifts of spiritual virtues.

The doors of the house seemed closed when the virtues of the holy Church were unknown. It is fitting, however, that when Samuel feared to tell Eli the vision, he is remembered to have opened the doors of the house of the Lord, because before the order of preachers announced Judea’s manifest rejection, it opened the hidden things of spiritual virtues to those hastening toward the faith while it urged them to repentance.

For the one who feared to speak what he had seen at the time of mercy announced the vision of justice at the time when justice was to be demanded, saying: “Because you have made yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:45).

From this reasoning a question arises, since Samuel is said to have disclosed the vision to Eli more through Eli’s prayer and imprecation. For the text continues:

> **(Verses 16–18.)** Then Eli came to Samuel and said: “Samuel, my son.” He answered: “Here I am.” And he asked him: “What is the word that the Lord spoke to you? I beg you, do not hide it from me. May God do these things to you, and add these things, if you hide from me any of the words that were spoken to you.” So Samuel told him all the words, and did not hide anything from him.

25. How did the one who carried out the divine sentence learn the vision of his own rejection, when he heard it not so much from one who threatened as from one compelled by prayers and an imprecation? Those who ask this question should first understand that we are examining these matters not according to the letter, but according to their spiritual and typological meaning.

In this passage, Eli’s coming refers neither to bodily movement nor to an affection of the Jewish priesthood’s mind; nevertheless, for Eli to come meant that he, a rational creature of God, appeared to the preachers. He came, therefore, when he was seen in human nature and moved the hearts of the teachers to pity. [Note: [Col. 0156D] Another reading: “to compassion” (*miserendum*).] Eli’s coming, then, is not an approach of mind or body in the old people, but an appearance of human condition.

Or perhaps his coming consisted in the fact that he had been chosen from all peoples for the worship of God. He also called him “son,” he who is regarded by the one remembered to have been the founder of the holy Church among the elect Fathers. He therefore calls him “son” not as an expression of affection, but as a manifestation of lost dignity.

And because he is seen in the darkness of blindness, he is said to have asked that the vision be disclosed to him. For Eli’s entreaty means that, in view of their common nature, he provoked the minds of the preachers to mercy. He also added a curse to his entreaties, because the order of preachers, observing the Jewish priesthood placed in such misery, feared to anger the almighty Lord if it did not aid it by its word.

Hence it is appropriately added: “Samuel told him all the words, and did not hide anything from him.” He disclosed everything he had seen, so that, hearing what he deserved, the magnitude of his fear might turn him toward the earnest pursuit of divine mercy. [Col. 0157B] He disclosed all the Lord’s words to him so that, recognizing that he had been cast down in his old condition, he might hasten through tears of repentance toward renewal in the true faith.

He replied:

> **(Verse 18.)** “It is the Lord; let him do what is good in his eyes.”

26. What else is more clearly recognized in these words than the faithlessness of the Jewish people? For the one who calls the almighty God “Lord” still believes that he is serving him.

When the Jewish people is informed of its rejection by the teachers of the holy Church, it says: “It is the Lord; let him do what is good in his eyes.” Since it believes that it pleases God through the former institution, it is by no means afraid of the threats of the holy Church.

As though Jewish faithlessness were asserting in a clearer voice, and were saying to the preachers of the holy Church who threatened it: “Your threats inspire us with no fear, because we believe that we are serving in the matter of faith the one whose grace you proclaim that we have abandoned.”

When, therefore, he adds, “Let him do what is good in his eyes,” he mocks the teachers of the holy Church rather than offering himself to the divine judgment. As though he were speaking with another intention and saying: “He does not do anything of that kind to us, because the one whom you propose as our avenger is our Lord.”

The text continues:

> **(Verse 19.)** Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him.

27. Why is Samuel said to have grown after he had explained the vision to Eli, except because the order of our teachers, after rejecting the sons of the Synagogue by its word, found greater glory of reverence among the Gentiles?

He grew because the one who had previously confined himself to one nation through the ministry of the word later spread the renown of his holiness and teaching throughout the whole world. Hence the Psalmist says: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5). Again, speaking to the holy Church, he says: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you will appoint them rulers over the whole earth” (Ps. 44:17).

He therefore grew when he shone throughout the whole world. The Lord is also said to have been with him, because everything that gave off the fragrance of holiness, everything that shone brightly through the word, received this from the presence of the Redeemer, whom he had with him.

For although Paul penetrates by his word not only weak and earthly things but also the highest and heavenly things, he obtains this power of speech from the one whom he declares to be with him, saying: “Do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). [Note: [Col. 0157D] Perhaps one should read “who speaks in me,” as it stands in the Greek source and in the versions. Hence Gregory, explaining this passage, adds below: “For the one who spoke in him was with him.” [Col. 0158D]]

He gives off a fragrance throughout the world through his life, but he draws the fragrance of life from the one whom he displays, saying: “We are the good odor of Christ in every place” (ibid., 2:15). John indicates that everything comes from the Redeemer’s presence, saying: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16).

When Samuel is therefore said to have grown, the Lord is remembered to have been with him, because when the order of teachers shone throughout the whole world with the grace of great holiness and teaching, it could appear so great because the one who did not abandon it when it was placed in the world was with it.

The text continues:

> **(Verse 20.)** And all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord.

28. These names of places designate the whole of Judea. What, then, is designated in the whole of Judea except the whole Church? All Israel therefore recognizes that Samuel is the prophet of the Lord, because everyone who is faithful believes that the order of holy preachers speaks truth concerning the future.

The office of a prophet is both to proclaim future things and to reveal hidden things. The preachers of the holy Church exercise the ministry of prophecy when they detect hidden vices in the mind, disclose the secrets of spiritual virtues, bring the hidden meanings of the Holy Scriptures into common knowledge, and promise the future joys of the heavenly homeland to the faithful elect.

Samuel is therefore recognized by all Israel as a faithful prophet of the Lord, because one who does not place faith in the teachers of the holy Church cannot see the almighty Lord by faith.

And because the same glory of divine knowledge remained in the holy Church that had revealed itself to the first teachers, it is added:

> **(Verse 21.)** And the Lord continued to appear in Shiloh.

29. Shiloh is interpreted as “sent.” And because he sends them into the ministry of preaching until the end of the world, the Lord appears in Shiloh, because he shows himself more clearly through those by whom he discloses to others the glory of his light.

It is rightly said, “He continued to appear,” because those to whom the brightness of divine light is poured are continually chosen. Hence he adds the reason why he asserts that the vision was heard, saying:

> **(Verse 21.)** For the Lord had revealed himself to Samuel.

30. He continues to appear because the Lord who had revealed himself reveals himself again and again, and does not withdraw the gift of his manifestation from the holy Church, which he has not ceased to display to her from her beginning.

But although the Lord is said to have revealed himself to Samuel, it is not stated how often he continued to appear, because the holy Church is led onward until the end of the world, and preachers preside over it who proclaim the lofty joys of eternity from the depths of earthly existence, in proportion as they behold the highest things they proclaim in the height of God’s manifestation.

This appearance is said to have taken place according to the word of the Lord. What, then, is the word of the Lord except the promise of the Redeemer? He therefore continued to appear according to the word of the Lord because he does not cease to display the truth of his promise.

The word of the Lord in the continuation of his appearance is: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

The text continues:

> **(Verse 21.)** And Samuel’s word came to all Israel.

31. A word is recognized as having come when the promise of our preachers is fulfilled. The promise of the word is joy that will remain without end.

Samuel’s word therefore came to all Israel because the whole multitude of the holy Church attained the joy of eternal blessedness, and what is now promised to it in faith by its holy preachers is displayed to it in the heavenly kingdoms through the reality of the thing itself.

The word of the teachers in the promise made to the faithful is: “Everyone who believes in him will not perish, but will have eternal life” (John 3:15). Or certainly the word of the teachers in the promise of rewards is: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9).

Samuel’s word therefore came to all Israel, [Col. 0159C] because whoever believes the holy preachers—both when they urge a religious way of life in the present and when they promise eternal joys to the righteous—passes, by dying in the flesh, to the eternal joys that he awaited through holy living.

Hence the one in whose faith he had promised affirms, saying: “Amen, I say to you, heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Mark 13:31).

Or certainly Samuel’s word has already come to all Israel because, through the effect of divine retribution, the general rejection of the Jews is known to have been fulfilled. Explaining more fully the manner in which that word came to all Israel, he says:

## CHAPTER II

> **(1 Samuel 4:1–3.)** Israel went out to meet the Philistines in battle and encamped beside the Stone of Help. The Philistines, meanwhile, came to Aphek and drew up their battle line against Israel. When the battle had begun, Israel turned its back, and in that battle about the countryside four thousand men were struck down. And Israel returned to the camp.

1. Blessed Paul shows that the battles are spiritual when he urges the camp of the holy Church to victory, saying: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

Concerning these battles he also gives counsel for obtaining victory, saying: “Take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one, and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (ibid., 6:16–17). [Col. 0160A]

Peter likewise exhorts us, saying: “Be diligent and watchful in prayers, because your adversary the devil prowls about, seeking someone to devour; resist him, firm in faith” (1 Pet. 4:7; 5:8).

Thus, when the battles of the Israelites are reported according to the letter, inward and spiritual realities are signified. The Philistines are interpreted as “those falling by a cup,” and by this name the reprobate angels are expressed, because through a more abundant draught of pride they lost their position in eternal life.

For them, to fall as though by a cup was to take in the drink of pride without any hesitation or delay in withdrawing from it. What is drunk is easily consumed. Concerning the prince of these fallen ones, as though he were a drinker, the Lord says: “He did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44). He collapsed as though from drink: intoxicated by the swiftness of his pride, he did not stand even for a moment in the truth in which he had been created.

2. But it must be carefully asked how Israel according to the flesh is understood to go out to battle against these fallen ones. No one fights with one who has been subjected to him. How, then, is the Jewish people—subject to malignant spirits through unbelief—said to go out against them in battle?

It is nevertheless said to fight, not in the reality of strength, but in the deception of its own estimation. In the reality of strength it has been defeated by the malignant spirits; yet, while it preserves the traditions of the ancient Fathers, it believes that it is engaged in combat with malignant spirits.

Hence it is bound all the more tightly under the chains of its captivity, the more that the cunning of those spirits suggests to it confidence in a freedom it does not possess. For the crafty adversaries proclaim, through hidden suggestions, the strength of a false freedom, so that it may not notice the darkness oppressing it and so that they may possess it, already deceived, all the more securely because it does not take care to be released from the bonds of unbelief by which it is held through believing in our Redeemer.

It should also be noted that the rejected people is described in the words: “Israel went out.” It went out rightly at the time when it abandoned the memorials of the sacred faith. Hence John says concerning those who had strayed from the mysteries of Holy Scripture: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19).

For Israel according to the flesh to go out, therefore, is to pass beyond the boundaries of the right faith through error. But because they do not cease to await another Christ, they encamp beside the Stone of Help.

Israel is therefore rightly said to have turned its back, because it is also said to have gone out. For if it had remained within, it could not have been defeated, since, if it had preserved itself within the fortifications of faith, it would have defeated the armed forces of error.

And because it is overcome by deception, the Philistines are said to have drawn up their battle line at Aphek. To draw up a battle line for malignant spirits is to arrange arguments of deception in the unwary hearts of the Jews.

But when the battle began, Israel turned its back, because, fearing death, it did not resist the malignant spirits. For those fleeing from battle turn their backs to the enemy so that, by resisting, they may not die.

Since the Jews tremble to die if they believe in the Redeemer, they do not resist, so that they may live; they do not believe in the Redeemer so that they may be saved in the ancient circumcision. They would resist the malignant spirits if they held the weapons of their strength in faith in our Redeemer.

But they flee so that they may not die, and because they flee, they die. For the pursuing enemy kills the fugitive all the more easily because the one struck down in flight does not resist the sword of the victor threatening him.

Hence, in the same battle, four thousand of the Jews are remembered as having been struck down. Who are these four thousand except those who refused to receive the truth of the four Gospels? They are said to die in the fields because they remain amid the expanses of their errors.

And because they still by no means abandon the hiding places of their error, Israel is said to have returned to the camp. For, as I have already said, it still believes that it is engaged in battle with the malignant spirits, although it obeys their will rather than opposing it.

3. Since a cup is also understood in a good sense, the preachers of the holy Church can be understood as those who fall by a cup. Concerning this cup the Prophet boasts, saying: “You have anointed my head with oil, and my inebriating cup—how splendid it is!” (Ps. 23:5).

The inebriating cup is the abundant grace of the Holy Spirit, which is appropriately called a cup because, in a moment, the hearts of the elect are intoxicated by its fullness. Hence it is said concerning the first shepherds of the holy Church: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting” (Acts 2:2).

By this cup the preachers fall, because, while they abundantly receive the grace of the Holy Spirit, they completely abandon the condition of carnal life. Every day they fall by this cup like excessive drinkers, because although carnal impulses sometimes raise them up to commit sins, once they have been intoxicated by the Spirit’s power they are not found remaining in a state of sin.

Since the Jewish people has a battle of faith with these Philistines, the carnal Israel goes out daily to the field of battle.

4. The preachers of the holy Church can also be understood under the name of the Philistines because, through God’s mercy, they were led from the error of the Gentiles to the grace of faith. Israel turned its back while fighting with them because it does not resist the Spirit who speaks through the mouths of the preachers.

Israel went out to battle against the Philistines when the Jews resisted Stephen as he preached and debated the reasonableness of our faith. [Col. 0161D] But while fighting, it turned its back because it could not prevail in debate. For it is said in the Acts of the Apostles concerning those who turned their backs: “They could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke” (Acts 6:10).

For the Israelites to be struck down is to be separated from a life of unbelief. They are also rightly said to die in the fields; for the fields of battle are the flourishing understandings of sacred discourse.

The thousands of Israelite fighters are therefore assigned as having been struck down in the fields because those who were converted from Judea through the ministry of the holy preachers believed in the Redeemer of the human race through the teachings of the Holy Scriptures.

Four thousand are remembered as having been struck down because they embraced the same authority of sacred discourse from the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the Gospel.

But while some are blinded, others return to the camp, because some from Judea have been led through the ministry of preachers to knowledge of the Redeemer, while the fullness of that people opposes the assertions of the holy Church all the more boldly the more deeply it has been cast into the darkness of its unbelief and is not led to the light of truth.

For it to return to the camp is to persist in opposition. And because they accuse those who had believed as fools, defeated by no adequate argument, the text continues:

> **(Verse 3.)** The elders of Israel said: “Why has the Lord struck us today before the Philistines?”

5. Here the question is not an inquiry but a complaint of astonishment. In their astonishment, therefore, they ask about the blow, because they were unable to attain the reasoning by which they saw people of their religion receive faith in the Redeemer.

It should also be noted that those who ask in astonishment are said to be the elders of Israel, because the proud, who glory in their own wisdom, could by no means attain knowledge of divine mysteries. Hence, in the Gospel, the Lord says to the Father: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25).

They complain that they have been struck because, when they saw the ancient custom of the Law being abolished through those who had believed, they thought that certain wounds of a blow, inflicted upon them by God’s incomprehensible judgment, should be proclaimed in their common grief.

But since they complain that others have fallen, the text shows by what counsel they prepare themselves to resist:

> **(Verse 3.)** “Let us bring to ourselves from Shiloh the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and let it come into our midst, [Note: [Col. 0161D] Vatican manuscript: “and let it save us from the hand of our enemies.”] and let it save us from the hand of our enemies.”

The text immediately adds what their intention was in forming this plan:

> **(Verse 4.)** So the people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts, who sits above the cherubim.

6. This is certainly Israel’s counsel and action [Note: [Col. 0161D] Gussanville reads “*Israelitis*” (“of the Israelites”) for “*Is­raelis*” (“of Israel”).] in its battle against those falling by a cup, but it is an unheard-of counsel and action, because it is not the counsel and action of Israel according to the Spirit, but of Israel according to the flesh—namely, not [Note: [Col. 0162D] Perhaps one should read “of one wishing to see God,” or rather “of one not truly seeing God, but … considering himself to see him.”] of one who sees God, but of one who imagines that he sees the God whom he despises.

For what is “sending to Shiloh” except returning to the law of Moses, to whom the Lord says: “Come, I will send you to Pharaoh” (Exod. 3:10)? What is “bringing the ark of the Lord” except, by recalling them, bringing forward the mysteries of the old Law in order to reject the truth of the new faith?

And because they do not allow any of their own people to be ignorant of this knowledge of the Law, the ark is commanded to be brought into their midst. What does their statement “And let it save us from the hand of our enemies” mean except that, while they stubbornly defend the old things, they reject the new, and place their hope of salvation in this: that they cannot be drawn to the reasoning of the true faith through the efforts of good preachers?

Because, therefore, they boast that they possess the truth of divine knowledge through the old Law, they affirm that the same ark, which they command to be brought for their salvation, belongs to the Lord of hosts. And because they imagine themselves to excel in incomparable knowledge of that Law, when the ark is said to be brought, it is declared to belong to the Lord of hosts who sits above the cherubim.

> **(Verse 5.)** When the ark had arrived, all Israel shouted with a great cry.

7. Because they babble in reproach of the holy Church about the fact that they receive knowledge of the Law according to the flesh, without displaying any rational account. For those who are said to have shouted and to have said nothing thereby plainly express what they do: while they strive to speak spiritual things according to the flesh, they indeed have shouting in their loquacity, but they do not have the reason of truth. They say many things with their voice, but, speaking without reason, they harm the elect of the holy Church in no way; and, while the Synagogue speaks within itself, it is shaken by empty devotion, because the holy Church is not moved by its words. Hence it is very appropriately reported that only the earth resounded. The earth is now called Judea—not because it bears fruit for God, but on account of its carnality—for, plainly, since it refused to receive faith in the Redeemer, it entirely lost heavenly conduct. Yet, while it is shaken by its own shouting, it rejoices in the opinion by which it regards itself as fearsome to the preachers of the holy Church.

**(Verse 6.)** And the Philistines heard the sound of the shouting and said: “What is this shouting in the camp of the Hebrews?”

8. The Philistines hear the sound of the earth and the shouting of the camp because those who have been refreshed in the holy Church by the cup of the Holy Spirit recognize both Judea’s loquacity and the empty devotion of its unbelief. And because they hold their estimation in contemptuous derision, it is added:

**(Verses 6–7.)** And they learned that the ark of the Lord had come into the camp, and the Philistines were afraid, saying: “God has come into the camp,” and they groaned.

It is said ironically that the ark had come into the camp of the Hebrews, and that those fallen by the cup were afraid and groaned, because the sacraments of the ancient Law are carnally expounded by the carnal defenders of the Synagogue for the battle against the holy Church. For they argue about something which, if they perceived it according to the Spirit of God, could have made them truly terrifying to their enemies, if they had any. Thus, when those fallen by the cup are said to have been terrified and to have groaned, Scripture does not reveal the passions of minds in holy preachers, but mocks Jewish argumentation—which is recognized to be the more contemptible and worthy of laughter the more the Jewish people received from the Lord a spiritual Law for spiritual conduct, yet did not heed in the spirit what it had received through the gift of the Spirit. Therefore, adding the words of the same Jewish derision, they say:

**(Verse 8.)** “Woe to us! There was no such rejoicing yesterday or the day before.”

And because they are to be derided still more abundantly, they add:

**(Verse 8.)** “Who will deliver us from the hand of these exalted gods?”

9. It should be noted that those are derided by the designation “gods” who, departing from the faith of the ancient fathers, trust that they exist in the truth of faith and among the number of the sons of God. They claim that the proclamations of divine praise spoken by the Prophet apply to themselves, when the Lord declares: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” (Psalm 81:6). If, then, all Israelites according to the flesh are called gods merely by a false designation, the “exalted gods” of the same Jewish estimation are the Jewish sages according to that estimation’s falsehood. And because the learned men of the Synagogue come to engage the holy Church, they themselves are derided by the voice of the holy preachers—those who glory in a power of teaching that they do not possess. And because they pride themselves on the ancient conduct of the fathers of old, words of mockery are appended:

**(Verse 8.)** “These are the gods who struck Egypt with every plague in the wilderness.”

10. They would indeed be such, if they illuminated the nobility they derive from their carnal origin with the virtues of right faith. But now, because through carnal descent they are sons of those whose virtues they do not possess, they are mocked with contrary words concerning the loss of those virtues’ succession: “These,” they say, “are the gods.” As though the order of our teachers were openly rejecting the sages of the Jews in derision, saying: “They boast that they are the fleshly sons of great men, but they do not attain the nobility of faith belonging to those whose lineage makes them proud.” They are therefore gods by succession of lineage; but because they are not such by imitation of virtue, when they are said to be those who shone in virtue, they are mocked rather than praised. And because the teachers of the holy Church regard their assertions as worthless, it follows:

**(Verse 9.)** “Take courage and be men, Philistines, lest you serve the Hebrews as they served you.”

11. Against the empty assertions of the Jews, the teachers of the holy Church prepare nothing new that is stronger, because they consider worthless whatever the Jews falsely assert concerning contempt for the Redeemer. They would take courage against their encounter and contend with something like manly strength if they feared that the defenses of their assertions might be broken by wiser men arguing rationally. It is as though he said: “We need seek nothing subtle or sharp against their objections, since they offer nothing at all subtle or frightening, but only weak and contemptible things.” Yet, as I have said, although the preachers of the holy Church prepare nothing new against the Jews’ empty words, they nevertheless repel the attack of the Synagogue’s defenders by whatever means they can, with the plain and humble reasoning of our true faith. Hence it is added:

**(Verses 10–11.)** So the Philistines fought, and Israel turned away, each one to his tent; and there was a very great slaughter, and the ark of God was captured. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, also died.

12. The Philistines—that is, those fallen by the cup—fight when the teachers of the holy Church, carrying the standard of the catholic faith, meet the Jews who attack them. Israel turns away because in every disputation the Jews’ cunning is overcome. To turn away from them means that they are unable to oppose their adversaries with equal strength. Yet one who turns away while fighting is still in the battle, though fleeing; and although he is failing in strength, he does not abandon the desire to inflict harm. Such, then, is all Israel after its repulse. It flees because it is not sufficient to answer the teachers of the holy Church; but while fleeing it would still resist, because, defeated and confounded, it would desire to have something with which it might oppose the truth by which it has been conquered.

Thus, when Israel is said to have turned away, it is carefully added: “Each one to his tent.” The tent of each Israelite is a heart enclosed and fortified by unbelief. Since, therefore, defeated by the preachers of the holy Church, they return to the hiding places of their error, each one, fleeing from the battle, returns to his own tent. And because all this is said concerning the fulfillment of Samuel’s word—that is, concerning the threat against the primitive Church—it is stated that a very great slaughter took place. This slaughter may suitably be understood, according to the reader’s judgment, both as a spiritual striking and as a material one.

13. Concerning their spiritual striking, the Lord says to the disciples sent out to preach: “Whoever does not receive you when you go out from the house or city, shake the dust from your feet. Amen, I say to you: it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city” (Matthew 10:14). Again he says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16).

He also indicates a great material striking when he speaks to Jerusalem, saying: “The days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart, and they will press you in on every side, and your children with you, and they will cast you down to the ground, and they will not leave in you a stone upon a stone” (Luke 19:43–44). Likewise, as he proceeded toward his passion, in his gracious concern for the women who sympathized with him and mourned, he said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children. For behold, days will come in which they will say: ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed.’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains: ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills: ‘Cover us.’ For if they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?” (Luke 23:28 and following).

These words plainly signify both the death and the captivity inflicted upon the Jewish people by the Roman commanders Vespasian and Titus. It was then that a great slaughter took place, when, with the Jewish people massacred, the city was both captured and overturned; when, in vengeance for the divine blood, the people fell by the hostile sword, and those who were able to escape the blade endured the punishment of eternal captivity.

The magnitude of this slaughter is declared concerning Israel, which had already turned away, because the Jewish people were defeated and rejected by the teachers of the holy Church before they were conquered, killed, and led into captivity by the Roman army. For they could be conquered, killed, and led into temporal captivity for this reason: they had not accepted the security of eternal freedom offered to them by the teachers of the holy Church.

But this same slaughter was also decreed against ancient Israel through the profound dispensation of divine goodness, so that the ark of God might be captured by the Gentiles, and the understanding of the divine sacraments might be received by the faithful of the holy Church under a spiritual interpretation all the more securely because they could see that nothing remained in Judea to display them according to the flesh. For, by God’s will, the ancient people lost the city, the temple, and the old ark of the covenant, so that the new people of the holy Church might recognize the mystery of the true and new sacrifice more fully, seeing that, with new things appearing among the Jews, the old had utterly failed.

The ark of God is therefore said to have been captured by the Philistines because, after the practice of the ancient Scripture had been destroyed, the Gentiles faithfully receive its sacraments according to the truth of the spirit. The one who captures the ark of God is the one who grasps the mysteries of divine knowledge in sacred discourse through the truth of understanding and with the devotion of the mind. But once the ark has been captured, the two sons of Eli immediately die, because the priests of both the greater and the lesser order no longer live in the office of the ancient sacrifice. Those who have entirely ceased to offer sacred things are said to die. It follows:

**(Verses 12–13.)** But a man of Benjamin, running from the battle line, came to Shiloh on that day, with his garment torn and dust scattered over his head. When he had come, Eli was sitting on a seat, looking toward the road. When that man entered, he announced the news to the city, and the whole city wailed.

14. What is signified by this man who flees from the battle line, if not that part of the Jewish people which, coming to knowledge of the Redeemer, abandoned Jewish unbelief? His running means that he ceased from the perversity of his error with the speed of devotion. Because he resolved to do brave deeds in confessing the Redeemer, he was a man. He runs from the battle on the very day on which he was defeated, because with the illumination of faith by which he abandoned the darkness of unbelief, he approached to preach the truth he had come to know.

Hence he is also said to have come to Shiloh **[Note: Alternatively, “who.”]**, because he is sent to preach. He tore his garment because he stripped off the old man; he scattered dust over his head because he did not become proud in any way of the splendor of the new man with which he clothed himself. The torn garment pertains to the beauty of holy conduct; the scattering of dust pertains to the esteem of humility.

Since, therefore, holy preachers need neither purity of life without humility nor humility without holy conduct, the man who, as a type of the teachers, came to announce Israel’s destruction both tore his garment and scattered dust over his head. He carried dust scattered over his head when, speaking to the Lord, he said: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Genesis 18:27). The Prophet likewise spoke with dust scattered over his head when he pleaded, saying: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Psalm 102:15). He too had torn his garment who, confessing, said: “You tore my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Psalm 29:12).

15. But while the humility of the ecclesiastical preacher is commended, the pride of the Jewish teacher is likewise expressed, since Eli is said to sit upon a seat. In this passage Eli signifies not high priests but the teachers of the Law in the Synagogue. What does it mean that he sits upon a seat, if not that he is proudly exalted by his learning? And what does it mean that he looks toward the road, if not that, while he proudly receives the Scriptures, he contradicts the one by whom he ought to have gone to the eternal homeland?

The way of salvation is the one that declares of itself: “I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life” (John 14:6). He therefore looks not toward the way but against the way, because he does not recognize the Redeemer, whom he contradicts.

And it is fitting that the father is said to sit upon a seat after the death of his sons, because the Synagogue has no one who sacrifices according to the ancient custom, yet still has those who teach according to the ancient custom. And because it was instructed for service through learned teachers, when the one who sacrificed had ceased but the one who taught still remained, the sons are appropriately reported dead while the father sits upon a seat.

But when the multitude of the Synagogue heard the announcement of the Redeemer, it experienced not joy but sorrow. Hence, after the man came from the battle and announced the capture of the ark, the whole city is said to have wailed. Since this sadness reached even the teachers, it follows:

**(Verse 14.)** And Eli heard the sound of the shouting and said: “What is this sound of tumult?”

16. Tumult is the shouting of the people when it is confused—when, without discipline in listening, many speak at once and a great murmur arises without any display of reason. Thus, when Eli heard the city’s wailing, he said: “What is this sound of tumult?” For the teaching authority of the Synagogue, with its unbelieving subjects grieving over the preaching of Jesus Christ, wished to hear the cause of their grief but perceived not a reasoned answer, only the confusion of complaint.

Yet, so that he could not have the excuse of ignorance—the man who had come from circumcision to the ministry of ecclesiastical preaching disclosed to him the truth of the matter. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 14.)** But he hastened, came, and announced it to Eli.

But because Eli immediately died after receiving the announcement from the approaching man, what sort of hearer he was is made known next:

**(Verse 15.)** Now Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his eyes had grown dim, and he could not see.

17. He would have been of perfect old age if, by living, he had completed the number of one hundred years. Since two years are visibly lacking from that number, what else does this mean except that he would have possessed perfect maturity if he had recognized the twofold mystery in the incarnation of our Redeemer—namely, true divinity in his humanity and true humanity in his divinity?

But now, because he correctly understands much concerning the ancient Law and very much concerning the heavenly commandments, he is ninety-eight years old. And while he believes that God could be born through the flesh from a Virgin, yet denies that the nature of humanity was assumed into his divinity, he does not reach one hundred years.

Hence he rightly dies when he hears the man’s report, because, without faith in the Redeemer, the good things he knows, along with the others, do him no benefit. And because, by the profound and incomprehensible judgment of God, the blindness of ignorance is inflicted upon his mind, he is remembered as having grown dim-sighted and as having been unable to see. It follows:

**(Verse 16.)** And he said to Eli: “I am the one who came from the battle; I am the one who fled from the battle line today.”

18. It was as though he remembered having been in battle when he said: “You have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it, and advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers” (Galatians 1:13–14).

But he came from the battle who says: “I was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor, but I received mercy because I acted in ignorance” (1 Timothy 1:13). What else, then, is it for a Jew to flee from the battle line than to separate himself from the error of unbelievers? And what is it to come from the battle than to announce to others the good of right faith?

To flee belongs to one who fears; to come, to one who wills. Here, because he is first said to have come from the battle and only afterward to have fled from the battle line, although unbelief is abandoned before truth is preached, this is not surprising. For the statement that he later says he fled from the battle line does not follow the order in which the events occurred, but refers to the certainty of the statement he first made. This is also demonstrated according to the historical order, since, unless he had first fled from the battle line, he could not possibly have come from the battle.

19. But we, who seek spiritual meanings even in events that happened carnally among the Jews, should attend to the man whom we introduced speaking a little earlier. The Church heard that the one who had once persecuted began to evangelize, as it is written of him already evangelizing: “When he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples, and they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple” (Acts 9:26).

Again, when the Lord appeared to the disciple Ananias at Damascus, he said: “Rise, go to the street called Straight, and seek in the house of Judas a man named Saul of Tarsus, and lay your hand upon him, so that he may receive his sight” (ibid., 11–12). He immediately replied to the Lord, saying: “Lord, I have heard from many how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem, and he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who invoke your name” (ibid., 13–14).

When he preached to the Jews the one whom he had been accustomed to attack with threats and slaughter, he was plainly coming from the battle. But while all the disciples were afraid to join him as he preached, they doubted that he had fled from the battle line.

He was coming from the battle when, after the Lord had called him and cast him down upon the ground, he was told: “Rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you must do” (ibid., 7). But Ananias did not believe that he had fled from the battle line; he reported to the commanding Lord the evils he had done to the saints in Jerusalem and the authority he had received.

Therefore, to demonstrate truthfully to Ananias that he had come from the battle and had fled from the battle line, the Lord commanded him, saying: “Go, for this man is a chosen vessel for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel” (Acts 9:15).

It should be noted that on the day when he announced these things, he asserted that he had come from the battle and had fled from the battle line. They flee in the day because, as the Truth bears witness: “The one who is in darkness does not know where he is going” (John 12:35). It is also written: “Those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who are drunk, are drunk at night” (1 Thessalonians 5:7).

And because, in the example of the blessed Apostle Paul, we have begun to see a man fleeing from the battle line, let us attend to the fact that he flees in the day. It was night when he drew up the battle line against the holy Church, when, having received letters from the chief priests for Damascus, he hurried there, breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples (Acts 9:1–2).

But the one who prepared war at night fled in the day, because on the road a light from heaven suddenly shone around him, cast him down to the ground, and terrified him with indescribable fear, so that he might recognize the darkness of his immense error and fight in the daylight on behalf of the Church against which he had been waging war at night.

He therefore fled in the day whom the brightness of the Redeemer, revealed from heaven, surrounded so that he might abandon the night of unbelief. What, then, does it mean that he confesses that on the day on which he fled from the battle line he came from the battle? It signifies the intention of right preaching.

Some flee from the battle line on one day but come from the battle on another, because they abandon their former errors out of love for eternal life, but, when they are taken up into the ministry of preaching, they seek temporal rewards from the eloquence of their preaching. They therefore come on a day other than the day on which they fled: they are upright in conduct but perverse in their intention of preaching.

The holy preachers, however, who through the grace of our Redeemer believed from circumcision, came from the battle not on another day but on the very day on which they had fled from the battle line. For they obtained both gifts in the splendor of heavenly love: the truth of conduct together with the preaching of the word.

And because the teaching authority of the Jews, although not with the intention of learning the truth, nevertheless wished, out of curiosity, to hear the assertions of the holy preachers, it follows:

**(Verse 16.)** He said to him: “What has happened, my son?”

20. Under the description of one person he speaks to all, because he saw the people of his nation whom he had once instructed in the teaching of the Law. Or perhaps he called him “son,” not out of affection, but through the flattery of cunning, so that he might more easily capture him by deception, demonstrating that he loved him with paternal affection.

He therefore calls him “son” from whom he desires to learn what had happened, so that, in return for the great honor of the flattery, the man might distort the sequence of the truth. The honor of the appellation, then, refers not to love but to cunning.

But the man who rejected the favor of the praise offered to him openly declared the truth. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 17.)** But the one who announced the news answered: “Israel fled before the Philistines, and a great ruin occurred among the people. Moreover, your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, have died, and the ark of God has been captured.”

21. The fleeing man announced what he had learned by experience. What, then, does it mean that he asserts that Israel fled, if not that he steadfastly affirms that, while the Jewish people retain the meaning of the Law carnally, they cannot resist the spiritual teachers of the holy Church in debate?

And what does it mean that he proclaims that a great ruin occurred among the people, if not that he confirms that all who rejected the word of faith from the Jewish people perished by eternal death?

And what does it mean that Eli’s two sons are reported dead, if not that both orders of the ancient priesthood are said to have failed?

And what does it mean that he says the ark of God was captured, if not that he asserts that the knowledge of the divine sacraments was taken away from the Jews and faithfully grasped by the Gentiles? For now, by the calling grace of God, the divine mysteries are known by faithful Gentiles. It follows:

**(Verse 18.)** When he had named the ark of God, Eli fell backward from his seat beside the doorway; and, his neck broken, he died.

22. Why is it that Eli does not fall from his seat after hearing of Israel’s flight, after being told of the people’s ruin, or after being informed of the death of his sons, but, once he learns of the capture of the ark, both falls from his seat and loses his life?
