But because, as we have said, Eli signifies the Jewish sages and teachers of the Law, he did not fall from his seat when he heard of Israel’s flight, because he regarded as insignificant the fact that the simple children of the Synagogue were overcome in preaching by the teachers of the holy Church.

He did not fall when the people’s ruin was reported, because, when he heard that those who die in Judaism were perishing, he was not at all frightened. He did not fall when the death of his sons was announced, because, even when the cessation of both priestly orders was brought before him, he did not cease to be proud.

But when the capture of the ark was reported to him, he fell, because, seeing that the sacraments of his Scripture were deeply and spiritually known by the preachers and faithful of the holy Church, he no longer dared to be proud of his learning in sacred discourse, since he understood it only carnally.

He therefore falls from his seat because, once spiritual understanding is known, he does not presume to be proud of carnal teaching. But because he hears truths preached sublimely and does not believe them, he is confounded and not saved: he falls and dies.

He falls from his seat because he ceases to be exalted by his teaching. But he dies as he falls because, although defeated by reason, he is nevertheless not deemed worthy, by the judgment of that same reason, to attain eternal joys.

23. In this matter it should be noted that the one who dies as he falls falls beside the doorway. What does it mean that he falls beside the doorway, if not that, while he wanders blind, he stumbles against the Redeemer? He declares concerning himself: “Whoever falls upon this stone will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Matthew 21:44). He also says of himself: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and out and find pasture” (John 10:9).

Eli therefore died beside the doorway because the teaching authority of the Synagogue perished for this reason: it offended against the Redeemer. He fell there where he sinned. As he fell, he also broke his neck. In the neck the swelling of temporal power is signified. He therefore dies with his neck broken who is condemned because of the greatness of his unbelief, after losing royal power.

24. The letter of sacred Scripture may also be signified by the doorway. For we are led as if through a doorway into the courts of the eternal temple when, through the letter of sacred discourse, we are raised to allegorical and spiritual understanding. Within, the king is also seen, because the promised Redeemer of the human race is found in the spiritual understanding of sacred Scripture.

Eli therefore fell dead beside the doorway because the teaching authority of the Synagogue perished for this reason: in spiritual Scripture it sought the Redeemer of the human race, who had been promised in the spirit, not spiritually but carnally.

He died beside the doorway because he perished concerning that which he understood—the spiritual promise of the Redeemer—not according to spiritual understanding but according to the plain wording of the historical account.

And because through the study of his teaching he presided for a long time over Judea, which did good not from love but avoided evil from fear, it follows:

**(Verse 18.)** For he was old and advanced in years, and he judged Israel for forty years.

25. He was old and advanced in years through the length of time. He ruled for forty years through fear of the commandments of the Law. The number forty pertains to sinners. Hence the season of Lent has also been consecrated in the holy Church with the same number of days, so that we may strive through repentance to wipe away the sins we commit.

The number forty is completed from ten and four. And because, by sinning, we transgress the Decalogue of the divine Law, while we derive the capacity for sinning from the fourfold composition of the elements from which we consist, we are contained under the number forty for as long as we remain in sin.

Eli therefore judged Israel for forty years because the teaching authority of the Synagogue displayed the severe discipline of the Law to the subject people as a matter of fear, so that, through fear, it might hold in the state of righteousness the material of human condition, fragile through desire.

But now Eli is dead; now he lies beside the doorway with his neck broken. Nevertheless, the poison of his perverse teaching remains in his offspring. The one who does not believe among the Jewish sages has already been judged; but because minds conceive the seeds of perversity through his instruction, those who are born as children of his teaching do not abandon the madness of his unbelief. Hence it is added:

**(Verses 19–20.)** Now his daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and near to giving birth. When she heard the news that the ark had been captured, that her father-in-law had died, and that her husband had died, she bent down and gave birth, for sudden pains rushed upon her. At the very moment of her death, the women standing beside her said: “Do not be afraid, for you have borne a son.” But she did not answer or pay attention.

26. Who was Eli’s daughter-in-law except the Jewish people, subject to rejected priests? Because through their preaching it had received in its mind the seeds of unbelief, it was pregnant. And because it too was considering pouring out the evil it had conceived, it is said not only to have been pregnant but also to have been near giving birth.

What does it mean that, after hearing of the capture of the ark and the death of her father-in-law and husband, she is said to have given birth, if not that the remnant of the Jewish people, while recognizing that the spiritual sacraments of Scripture had passed over to the instruction of the Gentiles and seeing that the sages of the Synagogue had perished together with both priestly orders, did not cease to pour out in speech the seeds of its heresy, which it had conceived?

To give birth means to disclose the perversity one has conceived by speaking of it to others. And because she preaches what is rejected, she is remembered as bending down when she gives birth. Those who speak heavenly things give birth without bending down, as it were, because they raise the hearts of their hearers to the pursuit of good works in the uprightness of faith.

She therefore gives birth bent down when she asserts perverse things, because by speaking she brings this upon herself: the more attentively she speaks, the more deeply she is cast into the abyss of her condemnation. Thus she is rightly said to die while bending down to give birth. She dies in giving birth because she is condemned for the merit of her blasphemy.

And because she does not foresee the torments of her death, sudden pains are said to rush upon her. Sudden pains are the unexpected afflictions of death. The pains rush suddenly when the punishments of eternal retribution confront the Jewish people, who now, placed in contempt of the truth, do not fear them.

Because it supposes that it passes into eternal life by dying for the observance of its ancestral traditions, it then falls into sudden pains when it begins to endure torments it had not expected. It should also be noted that it is said of the dying woman: “Sudden pains rushed upon her,” because, while she is driven toward the end of life through the sufferings of the flesh, the scourges of pain begin to rush upon her temporally, by which her impiety is punished with eternal vengeance.

And because, with their end near, the rejected minds of the Jews encourage one another in unbelief, “At the very moment of her death, the women standing beside her said: ‘Do not be afraid, for you have borne a son.’”

She bore a son because she instructed a people that was hard in wickedness and unconquerable. But who are the women standing beside her except minds bound by an equal order of impiety? They stand not in the truth and uprightness of faith but in religious presumption and boasting.

For this reason they encourage her not to fear, because she has borne a son: so that she may be all the less afraid to die in the ancient tradition when she sees that those whom she instructed through her teaching have also become hardened and unconvertible in it.

But while she is compelled by an even greater pain within herself, she regards as worthless whatever others have achieved through her instruction. Hence it is added: “She did not answer or pay attention.” For when she begins to experience the bitterness of eternal pain, she takes no pleasure in having presided over others temporally.

Or certainly, she does not rejoice over the child who has been born because the one begotten by her instruction is seen in captivity. Hence it is added:

**(Verses 21–22.)** And she called the child Ichabod, saying: “The glory of the Lord has departed, because the ark of God has been captured.”

27. The ark is captured because now, by God’s providence, the sacraments of sacred Scripture are retained by true believers with the capacity of true understanding. And the glory of Israel has departed because, after it fell away from true religion, it ceased to give off the fragrance of a good reputation.

Yet it is rightly said not that Israel’s glory perished but that it was transferred, because the reputation for religion that it lost passed over to the Gentiles. The glory was transferred because in the holy Church the fragrance of true religion is diffused; founded upon faith in the Redeemer, it holds the gift of the Holy Spirit as a pledge of the eternal splendor it awaits.

For this reason she refuses to rejoice over the son who has been born: because, seeing that her former glory has passed over to the Gentiles, she laments that she has given birth to captivity. She also names the child from the transfer of glory, because he continually represents, as if by a name placed before him, the impiety in which she remains.

The fact that the mother gives him his name can also plainly make clear what we see: he received his name from the one from whom the merit of his impiety came.

## CHAPTER III

**(1 Samuel 5:1–3.)** Now the Philistines took the ark and carried it from the Stone of Help to Ashdod. The Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the temple of Dagon. When the people of Ashdod rose the next day, they found Dagon lying face down on the ground before the ark.

1. What does it mean that the ark is carried away from the Stone of Help, unless that the heralds of truth remove the mysteries of Scripture from him whom the Jews await under a false conception—that is, from Christ? For when they turn the testimonies of Holy Scripture toward knowledge of the true Redeemer, they take the ark away from him in whom the Jews had placed the hope of their assistance. And because the mysteries of the faith are entrusted to the Gentiles, the ark of God is brought to Azotus.

The ark is then carried into the temple. What, therefore, was the temple of Dagon except each unbelieving soul, once defiled by the superstition of idolatry? And what does the image of Dagon signify except the whole superstition of idolatry? What else, then, was it to bring the mysteries of the faith into the hearts of the Gentiles than to carry the ark of God into the temple of Dagon? For the ark was set up beside Dagon, as it were, when the preachers of Holy Church warned the Gentiles to examine, in order to test the truth of the faith, both the preaching they were hearing and the errors of the idolatry they maintained.

It was therefore fitting that on the following day the Azotians found Dagon lying face downward on the ground before the ark. Azotus had one day in the hearing of the preaching of truth, and another in the knowledge of the faith. On the first day, then, the ark of God is set beside Dagon, because, in hearing the preaching of the Redeemer, they detect the darkness of their ancient error. On the following day, when they rise, they find Dagon lying face downward on the ground before the ark, because, in their knowledge of the truth, idolatry has also lost its standing.

Hence, when Dagon’s fall is asserted, he is appropriately described as lying face downward on the ground. He falls before the ark because, through knowledge of the divine mysteries, his nature is revealed. But he lies face downward on the ground because, with God now acknowledged as its author, he has no image of pretended reasoning to present to the sight of the faithful. For whoever lies face downward on the ground presses his face into the earth. By the face of an image, however, the pretense of reason is expressed. To lie face downward on the ground, therefore, is to be wholly unable to deceive those who have come to know the truth by the frauds of one’s pretense.

Nevertheless, so that the Gentiles might recognize the truth more certainly, they attempted with increasing care to examine both the reasoning about our faith that they had heard and the ancient custom of their superstition. Accordingly, it follows:

*(Verse 3.)* “They took Dagon and restored him to his place.”

2. That is, in the temple where the ark of God had been placed. What, then, is it to restore Dagon to his place except, in view of the truth of the spiritual sacraments already recognized, to investigate carefully the position of idolatry? And because the more subtly the error of idolatry is examined, the more truly it is condemned, the text continues:

*(Verse 4.)* “And rising again at dawn, they found Dagon lying on his face before the ark of the Lord.”

They rise again at dawn because, now certain of the goodness they have heard, they raise themselves toward its love with deliberate resolve. The first day, therefore, is the day of testing; the next, of knowledge; and the third, of deliberate certainty already attained and of the profession offered. Since this day dawned for the enlightened minds of the converts in the splendor of a perfect and consummated faith, it follows:

*(Verse 4.)* “But the head of Dagon and the two palms of his hands had been cut off upon the threshold. Only Dagon’s trunk remained in its place.”

[Col. 0174C]

3. What else is Dagon—that is, the head of idolatry—than the devil himself, the beginning of every iniquity? And what are his hands’ palms except all the works of idolatry? Dagon therefore lost his head because, through the worship of idols, evil spirits cease to reign in the hearts of the Gentiles. His hands’ palms were also cut off because sacrifices are nowhere offered to empty idols. And because his deformity is everywhere seen by all the faithful, Dagon’s trunk is said to have remained in its place.

His head and hands are said to have been cut off and placed upon the threshold because whoever enters the true faith is commanded to reject the beginnings of the devil’s persuasion and to renounce all the works of that same Satan. These things were therefore placed on the threshold so that those entering might trample them underfoot; for no one can truly be faithful who does not intend both to oppose the wicked counsels of the evil spirit and to resist his iniquitous works.

For whoever avoids crushing Dagon’s head and hands, even if he appears to be numbered among the faithful, is shown to be an idolater in a certain sense. For in the service of demons, not only external sacrifices but also wicked desires are offered by their worshipers. Whoever, then, has been received into knowledge of the true faith but has not been removed from impure desires and wicked works—because he scorns to strike Dagon’s head and hands—offers to the evil spirit, whom he scorns in the offering of ritual ceremonies, an offering through the uncleanness of his inner desire and his outward life. Therefore it is added:

[Col. 0175A]

*(Verse 5.)* “For this reason the priests of Dagon do not tread upon the threshold to this day.”

4. Those who do not tread upon the threshold thereby show that they are Dagon’s priests. In these words we must carefully observe that he did not say “the threshold,” but “upon the threshold,” so that we may understand that Dagon’s head and hands must be trampled—those parts reported to have been cut off upon the threshold.

The priests do not tread upon the threshold because they avoid crushing his severed hands and head with their feet. Dagon’s priests remain to this day because there are still those who sacrifice to the ancient enemy through impure desires. They refuse to tread upon the threshold of the temple because they resist neither unclean suggestions nor evil works. They are therefore Dagon’s priests because, although they do not bow down before idols made by human hands, they nevertheless bend themselves through wicked deeds before the images of their desires. It follows:

*(Verse 6.)* “The hand of the Lord was heavy upon the Azotians.”

5. The hand of the Lord is the power of divine authority. Since the beginnings of paganism are represented by the Azotians, what does it mean that the hand of the Lord is said to have grown heavy upon them? He made his hand heavy upon Azotus when, by the power of his might, he moved the hearts of the Gentiles toward conversion. For when, through inward inspiration, he revealed to them the force of eternal death, he struck the minds of the nations with marvelous terror over the iniquities they had committed.

Therefore, when the hand of the Lord is said to have grown heavy and the Azotians are reported to have been killed, this heaviness of the hand is understood in the multiplication of converts. For the Gentiles’ death consisted in their separation from unbelief. To be slain by the hand of the Lord is to attain knowledge of the same true faith, not through human ministry but through divine power.

The hand of the Lord was therefore light upon Azotus when, through a few ministers of the faith, only a few were abandoning the error of paganism. Hence the Lord urges ministers of the word to pray, as though for the hand to grow heavier, saying: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few; ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” (Matt. 9:38). It is as though he said: “He separates a few from unbelief through a few ministers, as though with a light hand; ask him to multiply the ministers, so that he may, as it were, make his hand heavy through the multitude of converts.”

The manner of the killing is also explained: whoever is said to die by this killing is reported to have been bitten by mice in the more private part of the buttocks when he went out to relieve his bowels. Literally, a single blow is presented here; but in the typical interpretation it is doubled. For according to the literal meaning, both the heaviness of the Lord’s hand and the bite of the mice pertain to the effect of the same death: the hand of the Lord is said to grow heavy upon the Azotians so that they might be killed by the bites of mice.

6. Since, however, we have recognized spiritually two deaths—one by which sinners die to righteousness through sinning, and another by which the righteous rise from the sins in which they had lived through repentance; one that enters human hearts at the devil’s persuasion, and another that the power of almighty God brings about—we must therefore attend spiritually to both deaths in this passage.

The death by which sinners rise from sins through repentance is signified when it says: “The hand of the Lord was heavy upon the Azotians.” But the death by which the Gentiles showed themselves servants to uncleanness and iniquity is signified when they are said to have been bitten by mice and killed.

A mouse is an unclean animal, forbidden by the Law to be eaten (Lev. 11:29). What, then, are signified by mice except demons? And what is it to be bitten by mice except to be torn by the punishment of sin? They were bitten by mice when they went out to relieve their bowels. What, then, is relieving the bowels except, by the completion of sin, to bring forth the stench of a wretched reputation?

Whoever therefore goes out to relieve his bowels is killed by the bite of mice, because whoever, by sinning, extends himself into the knowledge of others through the example of wickedness is also held for eternal death by the grave bondage of demons. They are said to have been struck in the more private part of the buttocks because every sinner receives a wound in the part of his soul that he bends toward the pleasure of sin.

When, therefore, the hand of the Lord grows heavy upon Azotus, he is said to have been struck by mice because, when the Gentiles were converted from unbelief through the preaching of the teachers of eternal life, they came to know the death of sins to which they had been bound by the persuasion of demons.

For the Azotians to be bitten after the Lord’s hand has grown heavy is, after knowledge of the true faith, not to submit to demons but, through the illumination of faith, to perceive the stench of the sins by which they had offered themselves to the punishment of death. They were, as it were, bitten at the moment when they recognized the bites of their sins. It follows:

*(Verse 7.)* “When the men of Azotus saw such a plague, they said: ‘Let the ark of God not remain with us, for his hand is hard upon us and upon Dagon our god.’”

7. When they saw temples destroyed, sacrifices cease, wives divided from husbands and husbands from wives, sons separated from parents and fathers from sons, what else could they think but that the hand of the Lord was hard both upon themselves and upon their superstition? But what happened next follows:

*(Verse 8.)* “And they sent and gathered all the satraps of the Philistines. The men of Gath replied: ‘Let the ark of God be taken around.’”

8. It is said that they gathered the satraps of the Philistines, but it is not said why they gathered them. Yet since the satraps are said to have replied and to have given the advice that the ark should be taken around, it is plainly understood that they had been summoned to give counsel concerning the ark.

Who, then, are the satraps of the Philistines except the chosen preachers of the Gentiles? Satraps are called rulers. Of these rulers the Psalmist says: “The princes of the peoples have gathered together with the God of Abraham” (Ps. 46:10). By “peoples,” nations are signified. Whoever therefore joined the name of peoples to that of princes plainly designated those of whom he speaks as the satraps of the Philistines.

These princes of the peoples came together with Abraham’s God when the preachers proclaimed, for the salvation of the nations to be converted, the word that almighty God was breathing inwardly into them as desire. For there was, as it were, a marvelous concord between God and the princes in the hearts of the Gentile hearers, since they received both the reasoning of right preaching from the holy preachers and the fruit of good will from the Lord.

Since those who had said, “Let the ark of God not remain with us,” are recognized as adversaries, how do those sending them gather the princes? To send and gather the princes is to stir the minds of the holy preachers to the urgency of preaching, because preaching had to be more earnest where the hearts of the Gentiles were more deeply immersed in error.

Hence the distinguished teacher boasts that he chose a nobler victory over untamed enemies, saying: “From Jerusalem and all around as far as Illyricum I have fulfilled the Gospel of Christ; and I have made it my ambition to preach the Gospel, not where it had already been proclaimed, lest I should build on another’s foundation” (Rom. 15:19–20).

The princes were therefore summoned not by desire but by the error of unbelievers, when they judged that they could gain greater profit for God precisely where the darkness of error was carried higher by the breath of pride. The urgency of holy preaching is therefore also signified when it says: “The men of Gath replied: ‘Let the ark of God be taken around.’”

Some say, “Let the ark of God not remain with us”; others say, “Let it be taken around.” What is it to take the ark of God around except to preach publicly the mysteries of the true faith? The ark remains with those who embrace through love the sacraments of the true faith that they hear. But those who say, “Let the ark not remain with us,” desire the preaching of the faith to be turned away from them.

The satraps, therefore, say the opposite: “Let the ark of God be taken around,” because they preached the divine mysteries more earnestly to those whom grave error had inflamed with hatred of the truth. And because great gains of this kind were also brought into the heavenly kingdoms through the ministry of the holy preachers, it follows:

*(Verse 9.)* “As they were taking it around, the hand of the Lord brought about a very great slaughter in each city, and he struck the men of every city, from the least to the greatest; and the protuberant parts of their buttocks rotted.”

9. The ark is taken around when the mysteries of the faith are preached openly and without fear. And because innumerable people were converted at the beginnings of the faith, a very great slaughter is reported to have occurred in each city. Likewise, because not only the simple but also the wise were converted, the same slaughter is said to have extended from the least to the greatest.

But through the same striking, their protuberant parts are reported to have rotted. For the rotting of the protuberant parts of the buttocks means the complete destruction of the passage of sin in its accustomed discharge of foulness. Someone is rightly said to have been struck whose protuberant parts rot, because there are some who, after the purity of conversion, become entangled again in their former filth of wrongdoing.

Their protuberant parts do not rot at all because they bend back toward the accustomed flow of sins through wicked works. The one rebukes those who, through an incomplete striking, have been only imperfectly healed and have fallen back into their former foulness, calling them “a dog returning to its vomit, and a washed sow returning to wallow in the mud” (Prov. 26:11; 2 Pet. 2:22).

For he was, as it were, striking them so that their protuberant parts might rot when, thrusting in the sword of the word, he said: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” (Rom. 6:12).

10. Through the statement of the Azotians, “Let the ark not remain with us,” the perversity of those among the same Gentiles who heard the word of faith but refused to believe because they were not predestined to eternal life may also be signified.

For the satraps to take the ark of God around was for his holy preachers to withdraw the word of truth from them and reveal the mysteries of the faith to those who were worthy. The ark was therefore taken around because the sacraments of our faith were removed from the knowledge of some and revealed to others.

Hence, when it was taken around, a very great slaughter is reported to have occurred in each city, because wherever they carried the word of faith, the grace of conversion multiplied. And because wherever they preached there were among the believers some who were not predestined to eternal life, it follows:

*(Verses 10–11.)* “They sent the ark of God to Ekron. When the ark of God came to Ekron, the Ekronites cried out, saying: ‘They have sent the ark of God to us to kill us and our people.’ So they sent and gathered all the satraps of the Philistines, who said: ‘Send away the ark of the Lord to its proper place.’”

11. As we have said, the satraps are understood as the holy preachers. The Ekronites, whose name is interpreted as “sterile,” represent the unconvertible Gentiles. They gave the preachers the counsel that the ark should be sent away, so that, if they refused their salvation through the divine preaching, they would at least not obstruct the faithful who were journeying with the sacraments of the faith toward their eternal homeland.

The proper place of the ark—that is, of the divine sacraments—is recognized as being wherever whatever is now said about almighty God through the mystery of Scripture is later revealed to us in open knowledge. He knew the ark’s proper place who said: “No longer shall each man teach his neighbor and each his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jer. 31:34). John likewise promises, saying: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

12. The Ekronites cried out: “They have sent the ark of God to us, to kill us and our people.” The satraps give counsel, saying: “Send away the ark of the God of Israel, so that it may not kill us along with our people.” Who are the people of whom the satraps—that is, the rulers—say, “so that it may not kill us along with our people”? Who are these people except the Christian people? The rulers therefore say: “Send away the ark of the God of Israel, that it may return to its place.” It is as though they said: “Do not prevent us from attaining the merit of eternal life by that from which you fear death.”

But in adding, “so that it may not kill us along with our people,” they confound by this answer the hearts of the reprobate Gentiles in their error, since these men declare that they escape death through that by which the others fear to die. The holy preachers also remove the ark of God, because, when spiritual things are disclosed to contemptuous persons, condemnation is incurred by the indiscreet preacher if those same divine mysteries are abandoned to the faithless—not to be imitated, but to be mocked and [perhaps: trampled underfoot].

[Note: [Col. 0179D] Perhaps one should read *conculcanda* (“to be trampled underfoot”). Certainly *concludenda* (“to be shut up”) means nothing here. The sense is best if one reads *conculcanda*. Moreover, what the writer says here is confirmed by this Matthean testimony: “Do not give what is holy,” etc., “lest they turn and trample them underfoot.”]

For it was not so much the satraps as the Lord of the satraps who gave the command, as it were, for the ark to be transferred, saying: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine, lest they turn and trample them under their feet” (Matt. 7:6). Again he says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10:23). Thus they remove the ark lest they die, because they hide spiritual things from contemptuous persons, lest those who rashly disclose them be punished for their lack of discernment because of those persons’ contempt.

But because the ark is commanded to be sent away from the Ekronites, this surely indicates what I said before: during a time of persecution, holy preachers were exhorted that the Ekronites themselves should believe; but sometimes, if they would not receive the word of life, that they should not obstruct those who did receive it; and that, if they themselves did not take up the way of salvation for fear of torments, they should not impede those who would not cease to hasten toward the heavenly kingdoms either through threats or punishments. It follows:

*(Verse 12.)* “For there was fear of death in every city, and the hand of the Lord was very grievous indeed.”

How this is to be understood with reference to outward persecution has been explained above. It follows:

*(Verse 12.)* “Moreover, the men who had not died were struck in the more private part of the buttocks, and the wailing of each city went up to heaven.”

13. We need not speak here of the striking of the buttocks, since we have spoken of it above, unless something different were being said here. What, then, does he mean when he says, “Moreover, the men who had not died were struck”? Surely those who had died ought not again to have been bitten as punishment for the ark? And when the cry of those struck is said to have gone up to heaven, it could sufficiently have been shown that he was speaking of the living and not the dead. For the cry of dead men could not rise to heaven.

But since above we referred the striking of the buttocks to the recognition of sins, there are indeed men who have not died. For those are men who have resolved to do brave deeds for the eternal life that they desire. But men have not yet died when they intend great things and nevertheless do not at all weigh their past evils with the sorrow of compunction. They are therefore bitten by mice in order that they may die, because they recall the ways in which they wickedly fell and believe that, by their past deeds, they have deserved the loss of eternal life. Since they are men, they do not despair of God’s mercy; and since they are bitten in order to die, they do not exalt themselves over their beginning to become great.

14. Their cry indeed rises to heaven because almighty God mercifully receives the groans of converts. And because at the time of the Gentiles’ conversion there was a great rush to the faith, the cry is said to have risen not from some one city but from many cities. Thus the prophet prays in the person of the universal Church, saying: “Give heed to my prayer; from the ends of the earth I have cried to you” (Ps. 60:2–3). Showing that the cry of one crying from the ends of the earth had risen to heaven, he says: “From his holy temple he heard my voice, and my cry entered before him into his ears” (Ps. 17:7). Therefore, when each city is said to have cried to heaven, the universal repentance of conversion is commended.

But if the striking is referred to conversion and the cry to the devotion of divine praise, we read in the mysteries of Scripture precisely what we see. For in the praises of almighty God every city cries out, because the whole world does not keep silence concerning the Redeemer’s proclamations; it does not preach them secretly, but praises them with the jubilation of ineffable joy. What else was he doing than exhorting all cities to cry out when he said: “All nations, clap your hands; shout to God with the voice of exultation, for God is most high and terrible, a great king over all gods” (Ps. 46:2–3)? Again he admonishes: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; serve the Lord in gladness” (Ps. 99:2). Again, he expresses both the plague of the biting mice and the cry of the cities, saying: “Let the whole earth be moved at his presence; say among the nations that the Lord has reigned” (Ps. 95:9–10). For he had first said: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (ibid., 1).

The movement of the earth pertains to the sorrow of repentance; singing to the Lord, or proclaiming among the nations that the Lord has reigned, pertains to the task of preaching and to the devotion of divine praise. The cry of each city rises to heaven because throughout the world both the truth of preaching and the praises of devotion are proclaimed by the faithful of Holy Church, and through the acceptance of divine condescension they are raised to the height of the heavenly hearing.

## CHAPTER IV

*(1 Kings 6:1.)* “The ark of the Lord was therefore in the land of the Philistines for seven months.”

1. What do these seven months signify except the whole duration of the present life? Although the Azotians and Ekronites cried, “Let the ark of the God of Israel be taken around, and let the ark of God not remain with us,” the truth of the holy history nevertheless says—so that we may recognize the type of Holy Church—that the ark of God was in the land of the Philistines for seven months. Therefore it was not the will of evil and impious men, but God’s dispensation, that was fulfilled in the salvation of the Gentiles. The wicked have now been removed from paganism; those who persecuted Christ’s confessors have now died; and yet the ark of God is not taken from the land of the Philistines, because the divine sacraments are preserved among the Gentiles, intoxicated by the cup of the Holy Spirit, through diligent care.

It is fittingly said to have been there for seven months, because the mysteries of the holy Scriptures will endure with Christ’s faithful until the end of the world. But whoever has grasped the mysteries of that same Holy Scripture through the grace of inward charity is concerned not with the place in which the ark is temporarily left, but with the place in which it is established eternally. Hence it is added:

*(Verse 2.)* “And the Philistines summoned priests and diviners, saying: ‘What shall we do with the ark of God? Tell us how we may send it back to its place.’”

2. Who are those who consult priests and diviners except the faithful of Holy Church, who desire to hold without error the way of eternal salvation? And who are the priests and diviners except the preachers of Holy Church? They are priests on account of the offering of the sacrament, and diviners through the ministry of preaching. For these two qualities meet in the person of a pastor if he possesses both holiness of life and learning in wisdom, because he is appointed both to cleanse the sins of those subject to him and to drive away the darkness of errors by the light of preaching.

Therefore, the pastor of Holy Church who possesses holiness of life but does not possess the power of divine preaching is a priest indeed, but not a diviner. Likewise, if he possesses eloquence of speech without holiness of life, though he appears to be a diviner, he is not at all adorned with the honor of the priesthood, because by earthly conduct he tramples upon what he preaches loftily. But those who ask about the ark’s place and about sending the ark of God back summon both priests and diviners, because those who love the joys of the life to come through knowledge of divine preaching seek, for counsel concerning salvation, neither carnal wise men nor religious pastors who are excessively simple.

Thus they summon priests and diviners because they entrust themselves to those who, through their exalted knowledge, show them the uprightness of the heavenly way and who, through purity of life, are fitting intercessors with almighty God for those subject to them. They ask about sending the ark back to its place because they desire, from the knowledge of the Scriptures that they receive in the mysteries of words, to pass to the perfect knowledge of God in eternity. For the ark is sent back, as it were, when this small knowledge is fulfilled through the passage of the present life. And in its own place we behold the glory of the revealed ark of God when, with unveiled face, we contemplate the form of the divine majesty beyond the lofty coverings of figures. Of this return of the ark to its place the prophet says: “No longer shall one man teach his neighbor, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; from the least to the greatest they shall know me” (Jer. 31:34). John likewise promises, saying: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

But let us now consider what counsel the priests and diviners give those who ask about sending the ark back. For it follows:

*(Verse 3.)* “What did they say? ‘If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it away empty, but return to it what you owe for the sin; then you will be healed, and you will know why his hand does not withdraw from you.’”

[Col. 0182B]

3. What is an empty ark except divine knowledge without good works? To send back an empty ark is to bear no fruit of good works from knowledge of the spiritual sacraments. The ark is sent back empty when the mind of one coming to the faith already desires to pass into the eternal contemplation of God, yet does not trouble itself to labor in good works in this life.

The voice of the preachers therefore commands that, when the ark is sent away, it not be released empty, so that no faithful person who fails to multiply good works may presume to believe that he will pass into the eternal knowledge of almighty God.

The ark is not sent away empty if what is owed to it for sin is returned. What is owed to the ark for sin except the affliction of devoted repentance? Here we must note that he is speaking to those who were bitten by mice. For who are bitten by mice except those who, placed in the illumination of the Catholic faith, recall that they acted wickedly either before or after attaining knowledge of that same faith?

The one who committed no crimes before the grace of regeneration and preserved the gift of regeneration by a worthy way of life owes something to the ark, certainly, but does not owe it anything for sin. He is compelled to return the fruit of good works through knowledge of the divine word, but he is not driven to make satisfaction through repentance for the debt of crimes that he has rejected.

Those who are still being bitten should therefore return to the ark what they owe for sin, so that, in memory of their crimes, they may restore to almighty God a humble offering of repentance. Then they are healed, because the wound of conscience is closed when the afflicted mind is raised through repentance to the security of hoping for pardon.

Then they also know why the hand of the Lord does not withdraw from them, because they understand the benefit of compunction—or the good of afflicted flesh—when they rejoice ineffably in confidence in divine forgiveness.

For what is the pain of repentance except the distress of a wound inflicted by demons? The convert was, as it were, sighing in the pain of a still sharply piercing wound when he said: “I have turned in my anguish, while the thorn is fastened in me” (Ps. 31:4). What does “anguish” signify except the affliction of repentance? Yet he says that he has turned in that anguish while he feels the thorn’s piercing. It is as though he said: “While I am bitten by the recollection of my crime, I do not cease to return what is owed to the ark.”

The thorn is fastened when, by the dispensation of almighty God, the soul of the converts is inflamed to tears by the recollection of its crimes. The debt owed to the ark is paid when the measure of lamentation is extended according to the character of the crime; when, after prolonged tears, the light of inward consolation is poured into the mind long afflicted, and by divine gift it is relieved of the inner weight of the blow; when almighty God, through the grace of his inspiration, draws near to the purified mind and gladdens it with confidence in the forgiveness it has obtained—the confidence he supplies from the grace of his presence.

The person is healed from the blow, as it were, when, through the grace of the forgiveness poured out, the magnitude of the pain is removed from the afflicted mind of the penitent.

4. Hence, in the same psalm, the one who was turning in anguish while the thorn was being fastened addresses almighty God, the author of his healing, with joy, saying: “You are my refuge from the distress that has surrounded me, my joy” (Ps. 31:7).

He calls the exceedingly grievous hand of the Lord “distress.” Paul also speaks of this striking by the grievous hand, saying: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8:26). Whoever therefore indicates that he has found refuge and joy from the Lord amid distress makes clear that he has been healed from the blow of inward pain by the joy of divine forgiveness.

Again, while still grieving, he confesses, saying: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done what is evil in your sight” (Ps. 51:6). But because he presumes upon healing, he says: “You will make me hear joy and gladness, and the humbled bones will rejoice” (ibid., 8).

The debt owed to the ark is returned for sin when sinners are afflicted by knowledge of Holy Scripture and strive through suffering to wipe away the faults they acquired through the pleasure of the flesh. They are healed when, the measure of affliction now completed, they are raised by the help of inward consolation into confidence in divine forgiveness.

Hence the Psalmist says: “You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us tears to drink in due measure” (Ps. 80:6). He gives the drink of tears according to measure because, although the sinner is moved to compunction for his guilt by inward inspiration from God, he is also raised from that compunction’s affliction by the same God who consoles him.

Therefore the Lord says through Moses: “I kill and I make alive; I strike and I heal” (Deut. 32:39). He strikes and heals because those whom he wounds through compunction he cures through the security of forgiveness.

It is rightly said to those who have already been healed: “And you will know why his hand does not withdraw from you.” Before he heals, they cannot know why the hand of the Lord does not withdraw from them; for they understand the good of repentance when, in a heart already purified, they recognize the grace of the Holy Spirit and desire the gifts of divine forgiveness, over which they rejoice with ineffable exultation.

He had seen the cause of the Lord’s hand, already healing, by which it had not withdrawn from affliction, in those who express the exultation of the stricken when they speak to God, saying: “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy; we have rejoiced and taken delight throughout the days in which you humbled us, the years in which we saw evil” (Ps. 90:14–15).

They had, as it were, received mourning during the night of repentance; but in the morning—that is, when the brightness of divine favor appeared—they rejoiced together because they had been filled with mercy. They assert that they took delight in the days during which they had been humbled. Through the gift of healing, they are shown to know why the heaviness of the Lord’s hand had not withdrawn from them.

But because the princes are still said to advise that what is owed for sin be returned to the ark, while what is owed is not explained, the text adds:

(Verses 4–5.) They answered, saying: “What is it that we must return for the offense?” They answered them: “According to the number of the provinces of the Philistines, you shall make five golden anuses (ani) and five mice, because there has been one plague for you and for your rulers. And you shall make likenesses of your anuses and likenesses of the mice that devastated the land, and you shall give glory to the God of Israel, if perhaps he may lighten his hand from you, from your gods, and from your land.”

### 5

What does it mean that five likenesses of anuses and an equal number of likenesses of mice are commanded to be made according to the number of the provinces, and that in this way the debt owed to the ark is paid? Certainly, if these things are weighed in the Jewish manner according to the lowliness of the letter, they ought not merely to be despised, but are not even worthy of hearing. Yet he receives them appropriately who understands that, the baser they sound according to the letter, the more useful they are according to their spiritual meaning. For the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration this entire sacred history was written, would never bring forth such lowly matters if, in the secret of this lowliness, he did not signify certain great and exceedingly precious mysteries.

Hence the outstanding teacher confesses, saying: “All these things happened to them figuratively; but they were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). The deeper meaning must therefore be sought by the spirit precisely to the degree that, in the letter’s exposed flesh, what is spoken appears lowly. What, then, are the likenesses of the anuses and the images of the mice? And since above we have referred these matters both to demons that tempt and to members exposed to the foulness of sins, with what meaning are the likenesses of anuses and mice gilded?

The debt owed to the ark for sin is certainly paid well when the likenesses of the anuses and mice are fashioned from gold. In the likeness of an anus, a member that emits foulness is seen; nevertheless, because it is a likeness and not the reality, it is already stained by no stench. And because it is made of gold, this surely suggests that the appearance of deformity is changed through the splendor of beauty.

A converted sinner therefore makes a likeness of an anus when he recalls to memory the foulnesses of sin with which he had polluted his members. To fashion a likeness of an anus is to recollect with a repentant heart the shamefulness of one’s members, which had recently been sinning. He does not therefore fashion an anus itself, but a likeness of an anus: he washes his members from the foulnesses of sin, yet does not cease to recall the sins to which he had subjected those same members.

The likeness of a tumor is seen to be made from gold because the shamefulness of sins is worn away for the price of eternal salvation. Or perhaps the likenesses of anuses are made by remembering them and gilded by weeping: for by recalling what we have done, we form them; and while we mourn our offenses more attentively, we gild our members with the splendor of righteousness.

A likeness, rather than the reality, of an anus is seen because the sinner gazes upon the disgrace of his deformity when he not only refrains from practicing evil deeds by committing them, but also deeply grieves that he committed them in the past.

Five anuses, however, are commanded to be made because the satisfaction of all the Gentiles collectively is prescribed. Hence it is carefully noted: “According to the number of the provinces of the Philistines.” Why are there five provinces of the Philistines, unless the carnal life of the Gentiles is signified? Because they devoted the five bodily senses not to the praise of the Creator but to carnal life, the provinces of the Philistines are expressed by the number five.

They are commanded to make five golden anuses so that they may feel compunction concerning all the senses; and because all have sinned, they are therefore to restore all their members to the splendor of the life above—members that they polluted with every kind of disgrace through the allurements of the flesh. For the radiance of the heavenly way of life is shown in gold, since John says of the heavenly city: “The city itself was pure gold, like pure glass” (Rev. 21:18).

The members are therefore gilded when a body deformed by the earthly and muddy foulness of desire is changed into the splendor of eternal life—when, that is, through the beauty of holy conduct, what was filthy with the stench of sins in its pursuit of worldly pleasure begins to shine. Blessed Paul urged his hearers toward this gilding, saying: “Just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and to iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness for sanctification” (Rom. 6:19).

And as though compelling them to look upon the likenesses of anuses, he added: “What fruit, then, did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death.” The likenesses of anuses are therefore made for shame: certainly, we recall the stains of our foulness so that we may be ashamed of those same stains. But they are gilded for security: for while we cover our deformity with the splendor of the heavenly life, we await the scrutiny of the divine judgment with a certain confidence.

### 6

The mice also, which devastated the land, are commanded to be made of gold, because the unclean spirits that suggest the pleasures of corruption to our flesh are likewise recalled for the sake of our justification. For what is it to make likenesses of mice except to recall the victories that wicked spirits have won over us? Yet the likenesses of mice are also gilded when we sigh because we have been broken by their strength. For while we lament that we were defeated by their deceits, we certainly possess golden likenesses of mice when we no longer hold the demons’ past counsels as an indulgence in our deeds, but as an object of contempt and rejection.

The likenesses of mice are therefore made of gold because the demons’ former deceits advance us toward the splendor of a good life. We are already that much more humble insofar as our members shine through the splendor of the heavenly way of life; and we ourselves, who now perform deeds of strength with the help of almighty God, see that we had been overthrown by the deceits of unclean spirits.

The fact that they give this counsel to many also reveals its rationale, for they say: “Because there has been one plague for you and for your rulers.” They seem to say openly: “Because all of you were subjected to sin, it is necessary that you prepare your hearts together for the pursuit of a better life.” Hence Paul also says: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3:23).

### 7

And in order to commend more earnestly the resolve to improve one’s life, they repeat it insistently, saying: “You shall make likenesses of your anuses and of the mice that devastated the land, and you shall give glory to the God of Israel, if perhaps he may lighten his hand from you, from your gods, and from your land.”

To give glory to God after making the likenesses just mentioned is not to glory vainly in oneself because of the pursuit of good works or the esteem of humility, but to devote everything that is done to the praises of almighty God.

And since they say, “If perhaps he may lighten his hand from you” (1 Sam. 6:5), what else is understood in this word of uncertainty except that the reconciliation of criminals is shown to be difficult? Hence Jonah also says: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive?” (Jonah 3:2 [citation as printed]).

Therefore, since it is said, “If perhaps he may lighten his hand,” we ought to be moved to tears of repentance with great strength. For if those who practice severe penance scarcely find confidence of salvation, when can the negligent be saved? Yet although this difficulty of reconciliation is held in the estimation of penitents, it is by no means found with almighty God. For while the Ninevites humbled themselves through severe penance as though reconciliation were difficult, they easily merited the mercy of almighty God.

And when the people prostrated themselves before God in sharp lamentation through the voice of the prophet Joel, they surely brought it about that he who seemed difficult to appease might lighten his anger. For immediately it is written of him: “The Lord was jealous for his land and spared his people” (Joel 2:18).

The hand is therefore lightened when the mind, deeply pierced by repentance, is raised by divine inspiration toward the gift of the mercy it has obtained. And because, as I have said, at the beginning of the nascent Church there was both a general conversion of sinners and a general reconciliation of those who were converted, the hand of God, which is said to be lightened, is declared to be lightened both from the hearers and from their gods and from their land.

By the gods are signified exalted and wise men. For the Lord also says to Moses: “I have appointed you as a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1). And the commandment of the Law likewise prescribes: “You shall not revile the gods” (Exod. 22:28).

By the land, however, the life of the simple is expressed: while they receive the preaching of their superiors as rain from heaven falling upon them, they bring forth, from the watering of the word, the fruit of good works. The hand of the Lord is therefore lightened from the gods and from the land when both the wise and the simple are restored to certainty concerning divine forgiveness, either by hidden and spiritual consolation or by the judgment of preachers.

Hence the one who, a little earlier, had urged the members to be gilded, saying, “Present your members as slaves to righteousness for sanctification” (Rom. 6:19), as though pronouncing the judgment of the Lord’s lightened hand, says: “But now, having been freed from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit for sanctification, and the end is eternal life” (ibid., 22).

Again, marveling at those converted from the deformity of a worse life and seeing in them the complete splendor of gold, he said: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). Again, praising his own, he says: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. 2:15).

When, therefore, the likenesses of tumors and mice have been made from gold and glory has been given to God, the hand of the Lord is lightened: for after the mourning of repentance, after the improvement of life and the humility of one’s estimation, sinners are restored to the full mercy of almighty God.

And because all these things are still commanded through counsel—and some subjects devoutly fulfill the counsel of preachers, while others despise it—those who exalt the good through praise because of the splendor of a good life are stirred against the proud by the force of rebuke. For it follows:

(Verses 6.) “Why do you weigh down your hearts, as Egypt and Pharaoh did?”

### 8

A person weighs down his heart like Egypt and Pharaoh when, already possessing knowledge of sacred speech and understanding the wounds of his sins, he nevertheless does not direct his mind toward the true joys of the future life through improvement of conduct and the bitterness of repentance.

He is therefore rightly compared to the Egyptians in the heaviness of his heart. Egypt is indeed said to mean “darkness.” What, then, is understood by the name Egypt except the multitude of angels fallen from the heavenly seats? And what is designated in Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, except the devil himself, the author of darkness?

Those who evade repentance are therefore rightly compared to Egypt and Pharaoh in the weighing down of their hearts. For once the reprobate angels had fallen from the heavenly realm, they neither recover love for the blessedness they lost nor can they ever repent of the pride they committed.

When holy preachers therefore inveigh against shameless sinners with sharp reproof, they bring forward the likeness of Egypt and Pharaoh, so that their hearers may rush all the more readily toward satisfaction, recognizing that by refusing to repent they are like the condemned angels. Hence they press them insistently toward fulfilling the counsel, adding:

(Verses 7–9.) “Take, then, and make one new cart, and yoke two milch cows to the cart, upon which no yoke has been placed, and shut up their calves at home. Then take the ark of the Lord and place it on the cart, and put the golden vessels that you are returning to him for the offense in a box beside it, and send it away to go. And you shall watch; and if it goes up by the road toward Beth-shemesh, along the way to its own border, then he has inflicted this great evil upon us. But if not, we shall know that his hand did not touch us, but that it happened by chance.”

### 9

What is designated by the name of the cart except either the entire holy Church together or the soul of each individual believer? The wheels of this cart are surely the two Testaments. For when the holy Church, or any chosen mind instructed through the Old and New Testaments, relies upon them for eternal life, it is carried to its appointed place as though on wheels set high above the ground.

But the cart is commanded to be made new, so that whoever desires to reach eternal joys may be clothed, through the commandment of love, with the splendor of the new person. The Lord commanded this cart to be renewed, saying: “This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 15:12). Hence Paul commands, saying: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new person, who was created according to God” (Eph. 4:23). Addressing the Romans, he says: “Not in revelry and drunkenness, not in strife and jealousy, not in beds and licentiousness, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:13).

He therefore makes a new cart who both rightly understands the two Testaments and, clothed in the splendor of holy conduct, stretches himself toward heavenly desires.

### 10

The wheels on which this cart travels may also signify the twofold desire of each of the elect. Whoever, with God’s help, now endures the present life as the hardship of a pilgrimage desires to reach future blessedness for this reason: that he may become free from suffering and immortal—so that by one desire he may leave behind the misery he dreads, and by the other may never lose the blessedness he seeks.

The cows, however, are holy preachers. Because they are distinguished both by the twofold commandment of charity and by begetting souls of converts into a new way of life, they are rightly represented both by the number two and in the feminine gender.

The calves are earthly desires. When the cows draw the cart, they shut the calves up at home: for while they provide chosen believers with leadership toward the heavenly homeland, they prevent those desires that suggest a reprobate life from proceeding to action. They shut up the calves when they crush proud desires within the conscience at the very beginning of their suggestion and do not allow them to advance into action.

Hence cows upon which no yoke has been placed are said to be sought for drawing the cart: preachers must be provided for chosen believers who are subject to no burdens of crime and no authority of the devil’s power. Of this yoke the prophet says: “The yoke shall rot before the oil” (Isa. 10:27).

The order of the meanings appropriately agrees with the order of the words. Even if they are free from hostile domination, it is necessary that they always remain wary concerning their future way of life. The cows are therefore both without a yoke and yet have their calves shut up at home: holy preachers rule hostile spirits by the power of virtue, but they do not withdraw their attention from subduing depraved desires, since in this life they cannot possess perpetual security regarding the holiness with which they see themselves adorned.

And because the grace of divine knowledge is opened more broadly to such persons, the ark of the Lord is appropriately commanded to be taken up and placed upon the cart. The command that the ark be placed upon the cart for its hearers signifies this: that in the holy Church we find several orders of leaders. Since some possess greater prerogative than others, they also receive authority to command [Note: [Col. 0189D] He seems here to be referring to the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 1, where we read the same thing in abbreviated form.] at the height of a higher order.

When, therefore, the ark of the Lord is commanded to be brought back, it is said to be placed upon a new cart: for the person who proceeds rightly toward the eternal homeland with knowledge of spiritual mysteries does not abandon what he has learned from sacred Scripture through the beauty of a new way of life.

### 11

The golden vessels that have been returned to the ark for the offense are commanded to be placed beside it. He calls “golden vessels” those things he mentioned above, saying: “You shall make likenesses of your anuses and of the mice.” In these vessels, we said, the memory of sins and temptations is signified.

What, then, does it mean that above he described them as likenesses of anuses and mice, but now called them golden vessels? There the subject was what had to be paid to the ark for sin; here, however, the subject is the ark’s release. Why, then, are these same objects expressed by a more honorable name except because sins that have not been wiped away by the tears of repentance must be looked upon and mourned more attentively in their deformity, whereas those that have already been washed away by great tears are not to be regarded attentively or contemplated in their deformity, but are to be considered at times as an exercise of humility?

It is as though in the mind of the penitent who grieves bitterly there were a likeness both of an anus and of mice, whenever, in order to grieve more attentively, he gathers before the eyes of his mind the accumulated mass of sin. But when, already made secure in some measure concerning the remission of his sins through great and prolonged tears, he begins to hasten toward the heavenly homeland with the swift pace of a great way of life, he sees vessels that are already golden, as it were: for he sees sins not as things by which he had regarded himself bound, but as things he may devote to the praises of almighty God.

The same vessels are rightly placed in a box beside the ark. For if the ark signifies the secret of divine knowledge, the vessels are hung at its side: while the height of divine knowledge lifts the mind upward, our past weaknesses must be recalled to memory as an exercise of humility. They must not therefore be placed before the ark, lest, while we look too excessively upon our weaknesses, we be unable to rise toward heavenly things. It is clear, then, that they are hung at the side so that we may freely look upon what is above and, when it is useful, recall our weaknesses to the eyes of the mind.

### 12

What does it mean that they are commanded: “And send it away to go”? The ark is sent away when the instructed minds of subjects are permitted by their rulers to live freely, so that they may hasten toward the eternal homeland no longer under the command of another, but according to the judgment of their own reason.

It must therefore be held so that it may be placed upon the cart; once placed upon it, it is also sent away [Note: [Col. 0189D] Here he seems to be attending to the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 1, where we read the same thing in abbreviated form.]: for permission to order their own lives must not be granted to chosen subjects by their superiors before they have received instruction in spiritual doctrine and acquired a firm habit of good works.

Freedom of life is rightly granted neither to simple subjects who live well nor to learned but weak ones. The former can be deceived by the crafty adversary all the more easily because they have not learned through spiritual instruction how to detect his snares. The latter preserve the good of their instruction with greater difficulty because, although instructed, they see the tempter’s traps and are unable to avoid their bonds.

The ark is therefore appropriately sent away when the cart upon which it is to be placed has first been made, and when the golden vessels owed for sin have been hung at its side. The life of a subject living freely can then be secure when he has learned through long practice to preserve the renewal of the inner person; when, through purity of life, he has grasped the loftiness of divine instruction; and when, amid sublime gifts, he does not neglect to recall humbly the things he remembers having done wrongly at some time.

Since this freedom of life is bestowed upon good subjects solely for the pursuit of heavenly love, the reason for sending the ark away is appropriately added: “to go,” he says. It is as though he also said in other words: “They are to be permitted to live more freely for this one purpose, that they may advance more swiftly toward the heavenly homeland.”

But because some subjects are perfect according to human judgment, both in conduct and in knowledge, but not according to divine judgment, the diligence of good rulers must ensure that they do not entirely abandon their care of them even when those subjects think that they have been released from that care. Rather, with pious shrewdness, they should examine how those who have now been set free live, since they had known more fully the good qualities of their submission.

Hence it is added: “And you shall watch; and if it goes up by the road toward Beth-shemesh, along the way to its own border, then he has inflicted this great evil upon us. But if not, we shall know that his hand did not touch us, but that it happened by chance.”

### 13

Beth-shemesh, as we have already said, is interpreted as “house of the sun.” The preachers watch the ark after it has been sent away, to see whether it proceeds by the right road toward Beth-shemesh: for when subjects are released to their own judgment, superiors must investigate whether they turn the good of freedom toward progress on the heavenly journey.

It must also be carefully noted that the ark then rightly ascends toward Beth-shemesh when it does not abandon the road of its border by walking along it. Our borders are the chosen who have gone before us. Those are called neighbors who have possessions arranged beside one another. The borders of the elect, therefore, are the perpetual coheirs of the eternal kingdom. For they dwell as though in possessions arranged beside one another: summoned into the fellowship of the same eternal homeland, they have received by lot the rights of an eternal inheritance from the one and same majesty of the Creator.

Or they are called borders for this reason: because when the elect pass from good conduct to the joys of everlasting life, those who live rightly in this world are near to the citizens of heaven.

What, then, is the road of the neighboring borders except temporal affliction? The Lord himself demonstrates this road to Beth-shemesh, saying: “Narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7:14). He commends it again when, rebuking the disciples, he says: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe, was it not necessary that Christ should suffer and so enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:25–26). Hence Paul says: “Through many tribulations it is necessary for us to enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22).

The ark is therefore directed toward Beth-shemesh when it is seen to ascend by the road of the neighboring borders: for that person makes truer progress in the heavenly way of life who seeks to reach eternal joys not through worldly pleasures but through afflictions of the flesh and adversities of the world.

But because the ark is said not merely to go but to ascend after it has been sent away, a higher road is indicated for subjects released into freedom. They do not walk rightly by the road of Beth-shemesh if they do not progress daily from good things to better things. To ascend in the merits of virtues is to progress daily toward better things.

When the ark is rightly led toward Beth-shemesh, however, they attribute the great evil they suffered to the works of almighty God. They call that striking a great evil of which it was earlier written: “The hand of the Lord was against each of the cities with a very great slaughter.” And because we have referred that same slaughter both to the conversion of the Gentiles and to the salutary compunction of faithful sinners, when the ark proceeds rightly toward Beth-shemesh, that great evil which had occurred is indicated to have come from God: for the end of each of the elect shows what the preacher’s mind should recognize concerning their first works.

### 14

For if they fail at the end, it is clearly understood that their good beginnings were not from the Lord. Hence it is added: “But if not, we know that his hand did not touch us, but that it happened by chance.”

What is the hand of the Lord except the only-begotten Son of the eternal Father? Those are not touched by the hand of the Lord who are separated from their former way of life not by the inspiration of the divine Word but by a sudden decision of their own heart. They certainly fall away from the goodness they began all the more quickly because they did not know beforehand with what strength they would have to carry out what they had resolved: to enter the eternal homeland by the narrow way.

It is therefore appropriately said: “It happened by chance.” For what happens by chance occurs suddenly and without counsel or foresight. When, therefore, those who appeared to have converted after departing from the love of the world or from unbelief return to the wickedness of their former life, it is clearly understood that they were separated from their former way of life not by the hand of the Lord, as they seemed to have been struck down, but by an accidental event.

It follows:

(Verses 10–11.) They did this in this manner: taking two cows, they yoked them to the cart, shut up their calves at home, and placed the ark of God upon the cart, together with the box containing the golden mice and the likenesses of the anuses.

Since these matters have been explained more fully above, let us now see what the ark’s journey itself contains concerning spiritual instruction. For it follows:

(Vers. 12.) The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh and proceeded by one road, going forward and lowing; they did not turn aside either to the right or to the left.

### 15

To go straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh is, in the pursuit of heavenly perfection, to maintain the affliction of the flesh through the virtue of discernment. The cows do not proceed straight if discernment is not preserved in the affliction of the flesh.

Indeed, when the flesh is afflicted beyond measure, that same flesh, utterly weakened, is unable to provide help to the spirit. And if it is not afflicted sufficiently, while it grows proud it disdainfully refuses, like an untamed creature, to serve the mind as though it were free.

Therefore, when the cows are said to go straight along the road of Beth-shemesh, it is rightly added: “They did not turn aside either to the right or to the left.” To turn aside to the right is to persist immoderately in the virtue of abstinence: we abandon the road through a good that appears to be good when we pursue the necessary virtue of abstinence in such a way that we withdraw other forms of assistance from the flesh. To turn aside to the left is to indulge the flesh too abundantly. For we deviate from the road of Beth-shemesh through the fault of open laxity when we lead the flesh through luxuries, although we know that the road to paradise has been laid out through affliction.

### 16

And because there is no sincerity in a sparing way of life if the simplicity of good works does not agree with the purity of intention, it is carefully expressed: “They proceeded by one road.” A person proceeds by one road when he preserves in a right intention the virtue he displays in a good work.

In contrast, it is said of every reprobate: “Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two roads” (Ecclus. 2:14). The sinner enters the land by two roads when what he does appears to belong to God, but inwardly he retains a worldly intention in everything religious that he displays outwardly.

The Lord indicates that his elect walk by one road when he says: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6:22). Hence Paul says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). Hence David says: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14).

The cows therefore proceed by one road toward Beth-shemesh because the elect, hastening toward the eternal homeland, do good outwardly but do not seek worldly rewards from those same good works.

### 17

What does it mean that the same cows are said to proceed while going forward and lowing? They are said to go forward because holy men continually do good; but they low because they cannot extinguish carnal desires within themselves without great daily tribulation.

Lowing belongs to the labor of taming the flesh; going forward belongs to perseverance in good will. While the flesh is forced to restrain carnal movements contrary to its nature, it lows, as it were, while walking, because it is prevented from fulfilling its own desires.

These two things are fittingly described in the progress of the saints: going forward and lowing. For although, as they hasten toward the heavenly homeland, their desire is intensely earnest, they nevertheless possess an unconquerable endurance of labor.

Of these cows going forward it is said through Ezekiel: “They did not turn back as they went” (Ezek. 1:12). Paul also expresses the lowing of the cows and its cause when he says: “I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:23–24).

The cows therefore low, but they proceed: holy men, although the temptations they endure are great, nevertheless do not abandon the road to the heavenly homeland. They proceed, yet they low: although they hasten toward heavenly things with great desires, they obtain progress on the heavenly journey not from the rest of peace but from the triumph over temptation.

It follows:

(Vers. 12.) But the rulers of the Philistines followed as far as the borders of Beth-shemesh.

### 18

What are the borders to which it is necessary for superiors to follow the advancing ark of God, and beyond which it is not appropriate for them to proceed in the ark’s company? If we understand these borders as instruction in sacred speech and good works, this does not appear contrary to the meaning.

These borders of Beth-shemesh are the limits of the princes who follow when each superior has become perfect over his subjects in the measure of his knowledge of sacred speech and in the practice of good works. A pastor becomes secure concerning his subject when he already perceives spiritual things carefully and embraces with the strength of good works what he has discovered through reason.

These borders are called the borders of Beth-shemesh because, while they graciously receive God’s instructed workers, they introduce them into contemplation of the heavenly homeland. They are borders because they receive the worthy into contemplation and drive out the unworthy. The unlearned, if they presume to raise themselves to contemplate heavenly things more subtly, go astray through error rather than grasp the light of truth. And unless someone first performs good works, he ensures that he will never find the radiance of inward vision that he desires.

Hence the Lord, as though sending lovers of the contemplative life toward the borders of Beth-shemesh, says in the Gospel: “Whoever has my words and does them is the one who loves me; whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21). By saying that he will manifest himself only to those who love him, and that those love him who keep his commandments, he clearly teaches that he grants the light of his hidden vision only as a reward for good works.

It follows:

(Vers. 13.) Now the people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley.

### 19

Who can more fittingly be understood as the people of Beth-shemesh than those who are already perfect men in the sublimity of contemplation? For they are, as it were, of the house of the sun: having rejected all earthly things, they are illuminated by the splendors of the true light.

They are of the house of the sun who, already buried to the whole world, burn with the flame of an extraordinary love to behold the glory of their Creator. They ascend to their city in two ways: they are led to the glory of the heavenly homeland both now through contemplation and, at the end, through the reality of glory. Now they fly to the house of the sun by contemplation; but what they now behold through the purity of the mind, they will then grasp as the reality of eternal reward through present joy.
