The ark of God is therefore brought to Beth-shemesh when the chosen mind is raised to eternal joys either through the height of contemplation or through the assumption of reward.

Since we cannot know the ark’s eternal and ineffable dwelling, let us hear what is said about this dwelling, which we know. What does it mean that the people of Beth-shemesh harvest wheat in the valley except that those devoted to the contemplative life gather the delights of inward refreshment in the virtue of humility?

In sacred speech, a valley signifies the estimation of the humble, as the Psalmist testifies when he says of the Lord: “You send forth springs in the valleys” (Ps. 103:10). For he pours the infusion of heavenly grace into minds ordered through humility.

The people of Beth-shemesh therefore harvest wheat in the valley because, while devoting themselves to contemplation, they perceive heavenly things more clearly through the merit of humility and bind together sheaves of joy for the sweeter refreshment of their minds. For wheat bread is both whiter in appearance and more pleasing in taste.

### 20

Yet perhaps, while we are still placed in this life, we do not take bread but harvest ears of grain; in that heavenly life of blessedness, however, we shall eat not ears but bread.

In this life, when we are raised to contemplate eternal things, we strive to grasp likenesses of heavenly realities from these lowly and visible things, so that, in the words of the outstanding teacher, “we may understand the invisible things from the creation of the world through the things that have been made visible” (Rom. 1:20).

Hence that true Bethsamite, a household member of the rejoicing Sun of righteousness, says: “You have delighted me, Lord, in your creation, and I shall rejoice in the works of your hands. How greatly your works have been magnified, Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep” (Ps. 91:5–6).

But while we receive the joys of invisible things through visible realities, we still hold wheat, as it were, among the chaff. Then we shall have pure wheat, or bread made from wheat. For when death has already been swallowed up and, in eternal life, we see the Redeemer more clearly with unveiled face, we shall no longer need the cases of likenesses in order to know him.

It is therefore rightly said of the people of Beth-shemesh that they harvested wheat in the valley: although perfect men receive, through the merit of humility, the sublimity of heavenly contemplation, they cannot reach the contemplation of the pure substance of almighty God to such a degree that they no longer harvest the refreshment of their minds, as it were, among the chaff.

The goodness of this humility is signified when it is added:

[Col. 0194D] (Vers. 13.) And raising their eyes, they saw the ark of God.

### 21

They lift up their eyes, because, since they do not think highly of themselves, they are, in their own estimation, as though on level ground. They lift up their eyes, because they contemplate those whom divine grace deems worthy to behold, set on the heights of the summit of merit. But, while lifting up their eyes, they see the ark, because the more humbly they abase themselves in their own estimation, the better they are able to recognize the good qualities of their neighbors.

That Truth itself, which by its very presence abandons the hearts of the proud, also conceals from them those gifts which it bestows upon the humble, so that, as though utterly blinded, they no longer see even the sun spread over the earth, although they have ceased to see the rays of its brightness in heaven.

But because we have referred the return of the ark of God to the purpose of the contemplative life, the lifting of the eyes may also appropriately be referred to the practice of discerning spirits. The Bethsamites lift up their eyes when they examine with subtle scrutiny the gifts of those who come to them with the intention of a more secluded life; when, with attentive minds, they investigate whether the purpose of the higher life, which they seek by approaching it, is being pursued with a right and vigorous intention. To lift up their eyes, then, means for them to examine more profoundly the spirit of beginners.

But, while lifting up their eyes, they look upon the ark of God, because, when they examine their conversions more closely, they discover that they shine with the grace of spiritual virtues. And because they rejoice through affection for those whose good qualities they have come to know, it is fittingly added:

> **(Verse 13.) And they rejoiced when they had come.**  
> [Note: Gilot: “when they had seen.”]

It continues:

> **[Col. 0195B] (Verse 14.) And the cart came into the field of Joshua the Bethsamite and stood there.**

### 22

If Bethsames is interpreted as “house of the sun,” the house of the sun is the heavenly city. Here Joshua the Bethsamite signifies the Redeemer of the human race, not so much by a typological figure as by his very name and dignity. For *Joshua* means “savior” in our language. And the Lord says of himself: “The Son of Man has come to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10). Hence also Joseph is promised in a dream through an angel: “He himself will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

He also reveals himself to be a Bethsamite when he says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41). Hence John the Baptist says: “He who comes from heaven is above all” [Col. 0195C] (John 3:31).

What, then, is the field of Joshua the Bethsamite, if not the loveliness of the contemplative life? For there the greenness of grasses, the fragrances of spices, and the varied beauty of flowers are perceived, because, the more clearly that heavenly fellowship is contemplated, the more pleasantly there is displayed to the eyes of contemplatives what flowers incorruptibly among the angels, what flourishes unfadingly among the saints, and what gives forth an inviolate fragrance among virgins.

It is rightly said that this same field belongs to the Savior, because the more privately the lovers of the contemplative life conduct themselves, the more pleasing and familiar they are to our Redeemer. The cart also comes into the field of Joshua the Bethsamite when an elect mind, separated from the concerns of the world, directs itself solely toward heavenly things; when it already enjoys the loveliness of heavenly vision, because it scorns to look upon earthly things through love.

And it should be noted that this cart was said shortly above to have been new, because a mind loosened from the oldness of crimes certainly does not deserve to be received into such glory.

### 23

But the more secluded life has delights in the loveliness of vision and has immense labor in the vigor of combat, because we attain divine rewards through triumph and preserve them by fighting vigorously. Thus, concerning the cart that comes into Joshua’s field, it is rightly added: “And it stood there.”

To stand belongs to the guarding of battle, not to the repose of peace. The cart stood in the field because, although the mind already dwells by seeing and loving that lovely and ever-green homeland above, it cannot preserve what it delightfully possesses through the love of vision without the anxious vigilance of unceasing care.

Yet the human mind, placed in so great a struggle, would certainly fail if he who strengthened human weakness in his divinity did not provide it the assistance of his presence. Therefore, explaining the reason why the cart was able to stand in the field, he added:

> **(Verse 14.) For there was a great stone there.**

### 24

The great stone is understood to be the Redeemer of the human race. Concerning this stone the Psalmist says: “This stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 117:22). [Note: “this” is absent in Gilot.] The distinguished teacher likewise praises him, saying: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20), “in whom you also are built up like living stones” (1 Peter 2:5).

It is indeed called a great stone because it is proclaimed to possess incomparable strength. Thus, when the cart is said to have come and stood in the field, it is added: “There was a great stone there,” so that the hidden mysteries might signify that those devoted to the contemplative life are able to preserve gifts so immense because, by grace, they are near him from whom they received those same gifts.

It continues:

> **(Verse 14.) And they cut up the wood of the cart, and placed the cows upon it as a burnt offering to the Lord.**

### 25

What is the wood of the cart of the ark of God, if not the teachings of Holy Scripture and the examples of the righteous? The Bethsamites cut up the wood when the leaders of the more secluded life open the meanings of Scripture more subtly to the minds of those subject to them, and when they present the more excellent examples of the Fathers for imitation, so that the flame of heavenly love may burn more fervently in their hearts, the fuel for its fire being supplied more quickly, as it were, by the cut wood.

The wood of the cart signifies that the mind, renewed by the grace of God, retains these things in its memory. Concerning such wood the holy lawgiver decrees, saying: “There must always be fire on my altar; the priest shall feed it, supplying wood each morning, every day” (Leviticus 6:12).

But because the wood is said to have been cut, this more clearly indicates that those seeking the purity of the contemplative life should have revealed to them not common matters from sacred Scripture, but everything that is higher and more excellent, so that they may lift themselves more powerfully toward what is above, the more they delight in the nobler goods they hear.

Hence it is also rightly added: “Because they placed the cows upon it as a burnt offering to the Lord.” A *holocaust* means a burnt offering. When, therefore, the wood is cut and burnt offerings are made by placing the cows upon it, this signifies that those who receive the extraordinary teachings of Scripture with devoted minds extend themselves toward heavenly desires all the more deeply, and that nothing in them is left unconsumed by the flame of divine love.

At that time the teacher must take care that religious subjects contemplate lofty things and yet do not retain a lofty opinion of themselves, lest, as they advance higher through seeing the highest things, they fall through pride and are dashed down more dangerously. Hence it is also added here:

> **[Col. 0197A] (Verse 15.) But the Levites took down the ark of God and the chest that was beside it, in which were the golden vessels, and placed them upon the great stone.**

### 26

“Levites” is interpreted as “those who have been taken up.” Who, then, are the Levites, if not those so strengthened by divine grace that they can never be abandoned by the Holy Spirit?

The Levites take down the ark when perfect preachers admonish their subjects not to become inflated by spiritual knowledge. They also take down the chest with the golden vessels when they admonish them concerning the splendor of their life, so that they may think more humbly of themselves, since each of them has learned that our Redeemer has already reached the reward of his exaltation precisely because he did not think highly of himself in vain.

Thus it is rightly recorded that the ark was taken down and the golden vessels placed upon the great stone, because those who have more frequently learned to recall the greatness and humility of the Redeemer are better able to think humbly of themselves amid sublime gifts.

The one who wished to take down the ark of God and place it upon the great stone was the one who said: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus. Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in human appearance; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

But those who sacrifice to God, through the ministry of preaching, the offering of love from the hearts of their subjects also present from their own minds the very excellent gifts of offerings. Hence it is added:

> **(Verse 15.) But the men of Bethsames offered burnt offerings and sacrificed victims to the Lord on that day.**

### 27

On what day, if not that on which they placed the cows upon the wood of the cart as a burnt offering to the Lord? What, then, is that day if not the illumination of divine preaching?

On that day the Bethsamites offer burnt offerings to the Lord; on that day they sacrifice victims—when they cut the wood and place the cows upon it as a burnt offering to the Lord—because the holy preachers, by the light of the word with which they shine upon their subjects, also provide themselves the service of vision for the uprightness of the heavenly journey. They offer themselves to almighty God all the more freely, despising lowly things through the power of love, as they see that their hearers have already been joined to him in great intimacy.

But because the Bethsamite men are reported not only to have offered burnt offerings but also to have sacrificed victims, the spiritual offering of perfect men is signified. They offer burnt offerings when, through the ascent of contemplation, they are joined to almighty God with ineffable affection. But they join victims to the burnt offerings, because they attribute the good of such great joy not to their own merits but to divine goodness.

He offers a burnt offering without victims who is already joined to heavenly things in great delight but does not, through the virtue of humility, rule over the hidden impulses of rising pride. In the offerings of the perfect, therefore, burnt offerings and victims are described as coming together, because they are worthy both to enjoy divine sweetness and, in everything by which they now make themselves wholly heavenly, to remain strangers to pride.

> **[Col. 0198A] (Verse 16.) And the five lords of the Philistines saw this, and returned to Ekron on that day.**

### 28

The lords of the Philistines, as I said above, are the chosen preachers of the Gentiles. They are contained in the number five because they preside over either beginners in the faith or the carnal, in order to restrain the five bodily senses.

These men accompany the cart with the ark of God because they continue to attend with solicitude to disciples already instructed and progressing toward the practice of the spiritual life. But when the cart reaches the field of Joshua and the cows have been sacrificed, they return to Ekron, because, once they have considered their perfection, they no longer investigate the paths of their conduct.

They return to Ekron because they turn toward the conversion of others. For *Ekron* means “sterile” in our language. Those who lack either faith or good conduct are likewise sterile.

When the princes are said to have returned, it is rightly added: “On that day,” because, unless they recognized in them the brightness of such great perfection, they would not have returned from their solicitude with the certainty of security.

It continues:

> **(Verses 17–18.) These are the golden tumors which the Philistines returned as a guilt offering: one from Ashdod, one from Gaza, one from Ashkelon, one from Gath, and one from Ekron. And the golden mice, according to the number of all the cities of the Philistines, of the five provinces, from the fortified city even to the unwalled village, and to Abel the Great, upon which they placed the ark of the Lord, which remained until that day in the field of Joshua the Bethsamite.**

### 29

What all these things signify has been explained at length above. But why is it that, when the ark is commanded to be given what is owed for sin, five golden tumors and five mice are named together, whereas, when what was owed is said to have already been returned, the individual cities are reported to have returned one each separately?

They are named together above because the adornment of all the members was being shown together in the exchange of good works. Here, however, when the debt owed to the ark is described as having been returned, it is carefully shown that the individual cities offered one golden tumor and one mouse each, so that the converted sinner might understand that he must abandon his sins once and for all and no longer seek them through his habitual perversity.

The individual cities return individual tumors and mice when converted sinners, once their sins have been cleansed by the tears of repentance, do not repeat them. Hence sacred Scripture also admonishes, saying: “Do not repeat a word in prayer” (Sirach 7:15).

He repeats a word in prayer who has attempted to cleanse his sins through prayers but nevertheless does not cease committing other sins for which he must pray. Such a person does not offer one tumor and one mouse to God for his offense, because, although he is pierced with compunction in repentance, he multiplies the foulnesses that he confesses to God and presents before him.

When the cities or provinces of the Philistines are described as having returned one tumor and one mouse each, what else does this signify if not the perfection of true conversion? A person is perfectly converted when, having once mourned what he did wrongly, he does not repeat what he would have to mourn again.

He therefore offers one tumor and one mouse for sin who so grieves past offenses that he perfectly guards against future ones.

And because this pattern of conversion must be observed in the holy Church by the wise and the unlearned, by the strong and the weak alike, it is rightly said that this repayment of the debt extended from the fortified city to the unwalled village. For no one established within the holy Church is free to sin, and for no one is it harmless to commit evil. Therefore the Lord threatens through the prophet, saying: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:4).

The fortified cities are minds surrounded by the instruction of Holy Scripture. The unwalled villages are simple minds. Thus not only do the individual cities return one golden tumor, but the villages do so as well, so that whoever, by God’s agency, is converted to a religious life, having already washed away his foulness, may not again be defiled.

And because no one is so holy that he does not possess in himself some foulness for which he must grieve, the repayment of this debt extends even to Abel the Great, upon which they had placed the ark of God.

*Abel* is interpreted as “mourning.” This was evidently the name of the stone upon which they had placed the ark of God. But this name certainly suits our Redeemer, because, although he had no sins of his own for which to grieve, he cleansed our sins through daily prayers and tears.

There are also perfect men in the holy Church, joined to that supreme stone through the perfection of love. For he was united to this stone who said: “Nothing separates me from the love of Christ” (Romans 8:35). Let us hear how he paid the debt owed by the ark: “Previously,” he says, “I was a blasphemer and a persecutor” (1 Timothy 1:13). Again, confessing, he says: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 15:9).

It should also be noted that the debt owed by the ark is said to extend to the stone which is recorded as remaining in Joshua’s field until that day and upon which the ark of God is remembered as having been placed. What else do we understand by this than what we see in the holy Church: that even those satisfy God for their guilt who have not only been rescued from sins by God’s grace but have also been taken up into his tabernacle through the great heights of holy virtues?

It continues:

> **[Col. 0199C] (Verse 19.) But the Lord struck down some of the men of Bethsames because they had looked upon the ark of the Lord; and he struck down seventy men of the people and fifty thousand of the common people.**

### 30

Who are the Bethsamites who were struck down, if not heretics deceived by false contemplation? They were Bethsamites not in truth but in presumption. When, therefore, they presumed to see the ark upon the stone, they were struck down, because, when they unworthily examined the mysteries of the Lord and our Redeemer, they were crushed by the snares of eternal condemnation through the deceit of their own error.

But what is meant by the fact that seventy men of the people were struck down, while fifty thousand of the common people were struck down? Since the designation “people” also includes the nobles of the cities, whereas the common people are the remainder of the populace without nobles, this may be understood as follows: some of the heretics stood out among the others as nobles, and perished through error alone despite the purity of their works; the rest, following the rusticity of the common people, were darkened by error in faith and by the filth of evil action.

Hence some are expressed by the number fifty and others by the number seventy: the former completed the crimes conceived through the five bodily senses; the latter, while falsely attributing to themselves the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit, were overwhelmed by the eternal darkness of blindness.

And because true believers were saddened by their being struck down, it follows:

> **(Verse 20.) And the Bethsamites said: “Who can stand in the presence of this holy Lord God?”**

It is as though true but simple believers were saying: “If such wise men and philosophers are deceived in the knowledge of supreme Truth, when can the unlearned and simple come to know it?” Yet, even if they distrust their own measure, they do not doubt that the gift of divine knowledge is present in the Church. Therefore it is added:

> **(Verse 20.) “And to whom will he ascend from us?”**

### 31

The Lord ascends from us when what is hidden from us concerning knowledge of him is preached through the voice of the elect faithful. His ascending from us, as it were, means revealing to lofty hearts through humility what he has concealed from the simpler or weaker concerning eternal contemplation.

What, then, does it mean to say, “To whom will he ascend from us,” if not to seek a worthy teacher who will preach divine things without straying from the way of truth?

If we seek the historical sense in these words as well, we understand clearly that those who died because they saw the ark of the Lord were evidently unworthy of that vision. Rightly, then, those who see them struck down say: “Who can stand in the presence of this holy Lord God?” For if those who are unworthy die by seeing, how can those who handle it live?

In the holy Church, the Bethsamites are reprobate priests and ministers of the sacred altar who have died, because they belong to the house of the sun of justice by the dignity of their ministry, not by the virtue and grace of holiness.

They are Bethsamites because through the office of sacred offering they conduct themselves in the house of God. But they are to be struck with a harsher condemnation because they dare not merely to see the sacred mysteries but to handle them; because they no longer merely look upon the ark of the Old Testament but, surpassing everything, unworthily thrust themselves upon the body and blood of the Redeemer. Paul indicates that such people are struck down when he says: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11:29).

True believers say: “Who can stand in the presence of this holy Lord God?” They consider the height of so great an administration and fear the dignity of so great a sacrament. But while they fear undertaking the office of so great a thing, they seek more worthy persons who can perform it. Hence it follows: “And to whom will he ascend from us?”

As though humbly avoiding the sacred mysteries, they say: “Since we are struck down by our weak manner of life, ministers must be sought from a higher life; those whose elevated conduct raises them to the highest sanctification of virtues can stand before God through the office of such an offering.” [Note: Gilot and Vatican manuscripts: “since we are struck down not by a weak manner of life.”]

It continues:

> **(Verse 21.) Therefore they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying: “The Philistines have returned the ark of the Lord; come down and bring it up to yourselves.”**

### 32

*Kiriath-jearim* means “their city.” What is the city of the saints if not that Jerusalem which is above? Who are its inhabitants if not perfect men, separated from the love of the world by an elevated way of life? One of them, more effective than the others, says: “Our way of life is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

Messengers must be sent to these men so that they may receive the ark of God, because, when priests are being chosen, holy men must not only be accepted but also invited.

And it should be noted that the more exalted men are told through messengers: “Come down and bring it up.” They come down because they obey. They would not come down if, with a proud mind, they refused to provide what fraternal love demands of them. They are truly exalted when they do not withdraw themselves from Christ, when they do not reject what fraternal judgment imposes upon them.

Hence it is fittingly added:

## CHAPTER V

> **(1 Samuel 7:1.) Therefore the men of Kiriath-jearim came and brought up the ark of the Lord, and carried it into the house of Abinadab on the hill.**  
> [Note: We have judged that this passage, omitted in the other printed editions, ought to be restored, since it is expounded below as though it had already been introduced.]  
> **And they consecrated Eleazar his son, so that he might guard the ark of the Lord.**

### 1

*Abinadab* is interpreted as “my willing people”; *Gibeah* as “exalted.” And certainly the ark of God should be entrusted to such people.

A willing people is one whom good will alone draws to practice the works of virtue, whom necessity does not compel to fulfill God’s commands. Blessed Paul praises such people under one description, saying: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

What is the house of a willing people if not the stronghold of holy love? For one could not be willing in the ministry of virtues if he did not build for himself a dwelling place of love. This house is recognized as being situated in Gibeah, that is, in an exalted place, because by the height of charity we are lifted toward heavenly things.

Or certainly the house is in an exalted place because charity is preferred to all virtues. Indicating the height of this exaltation, Paul says: “I show you a still more excellent way. If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 12:31; 13:1).

But what does it mean that they consecrate Eleazar to guard the ark of God? We know this, certainly, from the practice of the holy Church: an elected minister first receives the blessing of consecration from the highest-ranking men before he undertakes the ministry of offering.

Since Eleazar means “help of God,” it is evidently shown that God’s ministers must not only be consecrated but also examined as to what kind of people they are before being promoted to this same order of consecration.

Who are the “help of God” if not those who, in their ministry, cooperate with divine grace, and whom the favor of almighty God visits inwardly, while they themselves confirm that grace by living and teaching well through their outward ministry? Hence they say, not without glorying together with Paul: “For we are God’s helpers” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

These men, exceedingly strong in conduct, learned in knowledge, fervent in love, and steadfast in endurance, not only do not need another’s help but are able, wherever they go, to assist others.

It is therefore rightly said: “They consecrated Eleazar so that he might guard the ark.” For those who still need the assistance of others should not be promoted to help others.

It is likewise rightly said that this same Eleazar was the son of Abinadab, because the person chosen for the ministry of preaching, placed in imitation of the saints, ought to derive from love all the assistance that he provides.

### 2

But because above we said that the cart signifies Sacred Scripture, while the ark signifies its spiritual knowledge, and that the chosen cows may signify elect souls, the fear of the Bethsamites—which we showed to be present among the elect in the offering of the sacrament—may also be referred to the burden of leadership.

No lesser holiness is suitable for instructing souls than for offering sacred mysteries. For this reason the Bethsamites are said to have been struck down, because many live as subjects who die as leaders.

The ark of God also has an external beauty. If a weak minister looks upon it not for spiritual veneration but for secular desire, he certainly does not live. The cause of their being struck down is therefore rightly explained when it is said: “Because they saw the ark of God.”

For what does “they saw” mean if not that, by seeing its glory, they desired it? Now, by God’s agency, the glory of the holy Church is abundant throughout the world. Since this glory is desired in a worldly manner by reprobate priests, the Bethsamite men die by looking outwardly upon the ark of God.

They do not desire its spiritual honor for the inner glory of virtues; rather, they desire to seize the splendor of the ark of God and to carry the magnificence of ecclesiastical leadership, in the flower of worldly life, amid their own adornments.

The ark of God is also looked upon outwardly to one’s destruction when wicked leaders, overcome by the external appearance of those subject to them, are drawn into carnal desire.

The men who look upon a great multitude of desire struck down by the weapon of fear say: “Who can stand in the presence of this holy Lord God?”

He stands in the presence of God who is strong in the order of the divine ministry. To stand signifies strength; to minister signifies service. Thus he is said to stand in the presence of God who arranges the order of the heavenly office in the height of worthy conduct, who is deceived in the ministry he exercises by no appetite for ecclesiastical honor and overcome by no carnal desire.

But because such capable ministers are rarely found, they rightly say: “Who can stand in the presence of this holy Lord God?” And because they entrust so great a burden—the burden of Christ’s little ones—to stronger men, they add: “And to whom will he ascend from us?”

How they sent to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, how they carried the ark of God into the house of Abinadab, and how they consecrated Eleazar, we do not alter, since it has been explained above.

> **(Verse 2.) And it came to pass that, from the time the ark of God remained in Kiriath-jearim, the days were multiplied.**

If we attend to the historical account, the days of the ark’s residence were multiplied because it remained there for a long time. Hence it is added:

> **(Verse 2.) For it was the twentieth year.**

Explaining why this multiplication of days has been introduced, he adds:

> **(Verse 2.) And all Israel rested after the Lord.**

That rest in the ancient people is to be understood not as the rest of good works but as the rest of good devotion. For it follows:

> **[Col. 0203B] (Verse 3.) But Samuel said to the whole house of Israel: “If you return to God with all your heart, remove the foreign gods from your midst, the Baals and the Ashtaroth; prepare your hearts for the Lord, serve him alone, and he will rescue you from the hand of the Philistines.”**

### 3

How were those who had not removed foreign gods from their midst resting after the Lord, except by good will? If all these matters are investigated spiritually, the days of the ark’s residence are multiplied.

But it remains in Gibeah; it remains in the custody of Eleazar, because, when the care of faithful souls is entrusted to religious preachers, the perfection of religion, supplied through exalted teaching, is fulfilled by devotion to good works.

Hence it is reported that the twentieth year was then approaching. If the number ten signifies the perfection of the ancient Law, what does twenty signify if not the more splendid religious life of the New? The number twenty is ten doubled. This number is perfected in the conduct of the elect when, through love, they avoid what the Law forbids and fulfill the sublime commandments of the Gospel.

### 4

But because we have referred the ark’s journey to the perfection of the contemplative life, the ark of God remains in Kiriath-jearim when the educated minds of contemplatives perfect the gift of their own learning in the delight of the heavenly brightness revealed to them.

The ark of God now remains there for twenty years because elect souls, raised to the summit of inward exaltation, possess the number ten in the perfection of knowledge and the number twenty in heavenly delight.

The multiplication of days may also be referred to the increase of spiritual virtues. Therefore, when the reason why the days are multiplied is expressed more explicitly, it is said to be the twentieth year, because the more abundantly the elect minds of contemplatives are nourished by heavenly contemplation, the more fully they are illumined by the splendors of spiritual virtues.

### 5

What, then, does it mean that all Israel is said to rest after the Lord in the twentieth year, if not that the sublimity of the perfection of the elect consists not in the strength of good works but in the virtue of contemplation?

To rest after the Lord is to hold fast to the imitation of our Redeemer with unconquerable love. Whoever has not learned, through contemplation, to love vigorously the ineffable joys of that heavenly city can more easily be cast down into love of the world; he therefore does not rest after the Lord.

Thus, when the ark remains in Kiriath-jearim and the days are multiplied, all Israel rests after the Lord, because, while the knowledge of the elect mind is raised into experience of heavenly delight, while the splendors of spiritual virtues are gathered together for it from the glory poured forth in abundance, it can persevere in holding to the imitation of the Lord all the more steadfastly. Once illumined by immense brightness, it cannot feel those darknesses that would separate it from the true light.

Hence it is rightly said that the one who rests after the Lord is called Israel, namely, “seeing God,” because the more deeply the contemplative is carried away into divine things, the less he is overcome by human things, which he powerfully restrains.

### 6

But because, by God’s agency, we have followed his ark as it journeyed to the place of his exaltation, let us consider with what diligence a preacher should attend to the correction of his subjects.

For it follows: “And Samuel said to the whole house of Israel: ‘If you return to the Lord with all your heart, remove the foreign gods from your midst.’”

What does Sacred Scripture customarily call foreign gods if not demons dwelling in idols made by human hands? We have said that new preachers of the holy Church are signified in Samuel.

Rightly, therefore, he commanded the whole house of Israel to remove foreign gods from its midst, because, among Gentiles approaching the faith, the order of preachers required not only the truth of a right journey but also the condemnation of ancient superstition. It would profit them nothing to profess and worship the truth, or to serve it, unless they had first abandoned and detested what was false.

Whoever is now placed within the holy Church by faith but rebels against God through wicked action must likewise be admonished to remove foreign gods from his midst. For even if he detests idols made by human hands, he nevertheless submits to the commands of demons through evil action.

He casts foreign gods away from his midst who is converted to God in such a way that he never again venerates unclean spirits through evil works.

### 7

These words of exhortation may also signify the pursuit of a more guarded life. For what is “in our midst” if not our heart?

There are some who, in their activity in the world, are defiled through weakness of heart by the habitual practice of evil thoughts. They continually do good things but never cease to think reprehensible thoughts.

Because as many demons rest in their hearts as there are unclean desires, they are urgently admonished to remove foreign gods from their midst, so that they may offer almighty God not only uprightness in action but also the glory of inward purity.

Hence it is fittingly added: “And prepare your hearts for the Lord.”

A person prepares his heart for the Lord when he not only separates his mind from unclean thought but also illumines it with the splendors of holy thoughts and virtues, so that, as though idols had been cast down and shattered, he may make himself a temple of God, raising there a seat for divine grace where he has not permitted wicked spirits to remain through the evil desires subject to them.

It is therefore rightly said first that the Israelites should remove foreign gods from their midst, and then that they should prepare their hearts for God, because the proper order of an initiated religious life is that each person should first reject what is evil and then draw near to almighty God with the zeal of a good intention.

Finally, it is necessary that the person who has already offered God the purpose of good will and the purity of a clean heart should express in upright good works what he has resolved inwardly by living well.

Therefore it follows:

> **“And serve God alone.”**
8. For he serves the Lord alone who does not mingle evil deeds with good works. For whoever does good in such a way that he does not abandon evil does not serve God alone, since he offers obedience to the evil spirit, whose will he does not fear to fulfill. Hence it happens that even while doing good he does not serve God, because he who is believed to have created the whole human being does not deem it fitting to have him share him with his adversary. Thus the Truth himself declares: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24). Hence Paul, inquiring, says: “What participation has righteousness with iniquity, or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share has the faithful person with the unbeliever, or what agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Cor. 6:14–15).

We are therefore commanded to serve the Lord alone, so that we who, with God’s help, have already begun to do good in order to obtain forgiveness for our sins may mix no evil with those same good deeds. For we are released from the bondage of our sins when the good works that we perform for their remission are not contaminated by evil. Speaking to the penitent who are devoted to him, the preacher says: “If you return to the Lord with all your heart, remove the foreign gods from among you, and serve God alone.” It is as though he said: You will then be able to be freed from sins when you do not defile by subsequent crimes the good of heart and deed that you offer to God for your release. Therefore, promising this, he says: “And he will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines.”

9. Whom else are the Philistines designated to be in this passage but evil spirits? They, intoxicated in an instant by the cup of their pride, fell from their state of glory through their swelling arrogance. What, then, is the hand of the Philistines except that power of the demons by which they lead souls dead in sin to eternal torments? From this hand of the Philistines alone was he free who said: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30). Hence Paul says: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23). Again he says: “We too were children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

O how great a gift is this promise: “He will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines”! For only he was free from this hand who committed no sin. From it all of us are delivered contrary to our merit. Hence Paul also says: “Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption of his righteousness, because of the redemption of former offenses, in the forbearance of God, to demonstrate his righteousness at the present time, so that he himself might be just and the justifier of the one who is from the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 3:24–26). Again he says: “By grace you have been saved” (Eph. 2:8).

It is as though he said: He will deliver you from the power of evil spirits, so that, as cruel enemies are driven from the road, when the death of the flesh intervenes you may more securely attain the eternal joys you desire. Great things, therefore, were promised by the one who taught great things through his commands, so that the greatness of the gift might incite strength for the labor. For it is a great thing to serve the Lord alone—that is, to do good persistently and not mingle evil with good works. But O how much greater it is, in the passage through this life, not to encounter the power of bloodthirsty spirits, to see no horrors along the way, to meet no hostile opposition, to escape eternal punishments, to experience the protection of our Deliverer, to lose the momentary light of the world and suddenly find the ineffable brightness of eternity!

Let those who desire to be delivered from the hand of the Philistines hear, then—let them hear: “Prepare your hearts for the Lord, and serve him alone,” so that here each may strive to gather for himself what will keep him from encountering there the hands of so many enemies, and so that those may pass securely into life who, among the treasures of their salvation that they gather here by living well, carry no works of death. The conduct of the elect is indicated by what follows:

**(Verse 4.)** “Then the children of Israel removed Baalim and Astaroth from among themselves, and served the Lord alone.”

10. It is the custom of the elect that, when they receive the exhortations of divine preaching, they are inflamed to undertake the good action they have heard about. For the reprobate frequently hear the words of God, but nevertheless propose no good works in accordance with those same words. They remain sluggish in their actions because, cast away from the divine light, they do not see through inward contemplation the glory of almighty God, whose words they hear.

Those who obey are therefore rightly called the children of Israel: the more clearly they behold his majesty revealed, the more devotedly they are recognized as obeying his commands. But because he is speaking to the converted, let us hear what he sees still lacking in them. For it follows:

**(Verses 5–6.)** “Samuel said: Gather all Israel at Masphath, so that I may pray to the Lord for you. And they gathered at Masphath.”

11. Masphath means “observation” or “contemplation.” Blessed Paul explains this observation when he says: “Now we see through a mirror in a mystery” (1 Cor. 13:12). To observe, then, is for us to contemplate eternal goods from the height of the Scriptures. We observe, as it were, what we already know through the truth of faith, although we do not yet see it with unveiled face.

For sinners who have been converted to assemble at Masphath means to trust, through the mind’s intention, in the mercy of almighty God. Yet they should presume upon God’s mercy in such a way that they do not neglect to erase through repentance what they remember having wickedly done. Hence it is immediately added there:

**(Verse 6.)** “They drew water and poured it out before the Lord.”

12. What does drawing water mean except bringing forth streams of tears from the profound contrition of a repentant soul? We draw water, as it were, when, considering how deeply we have fallen through iniquity, we weep. We pour out this water before the Lord if, when we are pierced by repentance, we do not seek worldly approval from the tears of that contrition, but only the fruit of divine reconciliation.

But while the mind is pierced by weeping, it is also necessary that the flesh, which was subject to pleasures, be afflicted. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 6.)** “And they fasted on that day.”

13. The day of a sinful soul is the hope of obtaining forgiveness through the promise of the divine word. Hence through the prophet the Lord promises, saying: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 18:32; 33:11). On that day, therefore, those fast who wear down their flesh through repentance, because in the light of hope they believe without doubt that they will attain forgiveness.

Yet this penitential affliction is suitable for erasing sins only when it has been imposed by the judgment of a priest, when, after examining the acts of those who confess, he assigns them a burden of affliction proportionate to the measure of their crime. Thus it rightly follows:

**(Verse 6.)** “And they said: We have sinned against you, O Lord. And Samuel judged the children of Israel at Masphath.”

14. A priest judges at Masphath when he does not follow human judgment but divine judgment; when, in everything that must be arranged, he raises himself into lofty contemplation and orders the judgment of his subjects according to what he recognizes as equitable in heavenly vision. Hence it is that in almost every matter Moses consults the Lord in the tabernacle of the covenant (Exod. 33:8), because the preacher of holy Church ought to behold the truth in intimate contemplation, so that he may be able to order the life of his subjects outwardly without reproach.

He can then more truly retain sins and remit them when, in the secret place of contemplation, he hears the Lord speaking what he himself is to say. Hence, after rising from the dead, the Lord first breathed upon the faces of the disciples and afterward granted authority to forgive and retain sins (John 20:21, 23), clearly showing that one who does not possess that contemplation of the mind ought not to be judge of souls.

For the Lord’s breathing upon the faces of preachers who are elect is his revealing to them, through the Holy Spirit, the inner and hidden paths of spiritual judgment. Hence Paul says: “The spiritual person judges all things” (1 Cor. 2:15). Again, commending the abundance of divine grace, he says: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (ibid., 12).

But one who has the spirit of this world cannot judge his subjects at Masphath, that is, in contemplation. Since he does not penetrate inward things through the spirit, he wanders outwardly in the cases he examines, guided by the spirit of the world. Thus it is rightly said that Samuel judged the children of Israel at Masphath, because holy preachers, in judging their subjects, determine nothing outwardly except what is revealed to them inwardly by divine inspiration.

But when good subjects submit themselves to the judgment of their superiors, they provoke the anger of spiritual enemies against themselves more intensely. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 7.)** “And the satraps of the Philistines went up against Israel.”

15. After the foreign gods had been removed, the fast completed, and the scrutiny of judgment exercised by the preacher, the rulers of the Philistines go up against Israel. For when we advance toward a higher life, evil spirits, who always envy those who act well, become more hostile to us. And because they desire to bring us down from the height of an innocent life, they are said to ascend.

For evil spirits to ascend means for them to raise themselves up to assault hearts lifted high by heavenly desire. Since battles are also aroused against the more perfect soldiers of Christ not by just any evil spirits but by stronger demons, it is said not that the Philistines in general went up against Israel, but that the satraps of the Philistines did so. Rulers, moreover, preside over many.

From this, therefore, it may reasonably be inferred that, to test the patience of the elect, not one evil spirit is assigned to each of the elect, but countless ones, so that the glory of the faithful may be more abundant because the battles inflicted upon them are more severe.

Nevertheless, in these battles those who have recently been converted are accustomed to be exceedingly afraid. Suddenly they find themselves in the field of labor, beyond the experience of their former way of life. On one side they see desires armed against them, although those desires had previously served them in peace; on the other, heavenly love invites them not to abandon the good they have begun. On one side the spirit raises the mind; on the other, the flesh weighs it down. And because they cannot know the measure of their final outcome, they are terrified by uncertainty about their election. Hence it is appropriately added here:

**(Verse 7.)** “When the children of Israel heard this, they were afraid because of the Philistines.”

16. They are afraid because of the face of the Philistines so that they may not fear what lies behind them. For what is the face of evil spirits except worldly desire? Whoever is fashioned according to this appearance is conformed to their image.

But because Israel is said not to have feared the face of the Philistines, but to have feared because of their face, the text discloses the minds of the elect while also subtly censuring the foolishness of the reprobate. They did not fear the face itself but feared because of the face, because holy men see one thing outwardly and fear another inwardly.

Even if at times they consider the flourishing world according to human judgment, they suddenly turn and raise the eyes of the mind toward the evils that follow the world’s joys. They tremble, as it were, because of the face, since they avoid the present pleasures that are followed by punishments. But the reprobate, who do not fear this face of the Philistines at all, do not escape the subsequent assaults of their ferocity. For while they embrace the empty joys of the world with all their strength, through the power of the demons they seize everlasting afflictions.

The Truth threatens them, saying: “Woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation in your life” (Luke 6:24). Again he declares: “Woe to you who laugh, because you will weep” (ibid., 25). It is as though he said: Because you do not fear the face of the Philistines at all, when their powers rush upon you, you cannot find a refuge of salvation. Then fear is present, but no help is present. Punishment is inflicted for the crime without hope of deliverance; and those who desired the blandishments of their face in the love of the world learn how horrible are the things that follow the Philistines’ face.

Thus it is rightly said of the Israelites, as a figure of the elect: “They were afraid because of the face of the Philistines,” because, while they carefully order the manner of their conduct, they do not arrange to fear eternal evils when they come, but tremble before temporal desire, by whose merit those evils are inflicted.

And because they believe that they can obtain this less by their own merits than through the intercession of their superiors, it follows:

**(Verse 8.)** “And they said to Samuel: Do not cease crying out to the Lord our God for us, that he may save you from the hand of the Philistines.”

17. But good shepherds, when their subjects are tested, provide not only the protection of prayers but also that of sacrifices. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 9.)** “Samuel took one suckling lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the Lord, and Samuel cried out.”

What is Samuel’s cry except the great strength of desire in the supplication of the high priest? Hence, although Moses was silent with his lips while desiring the salvation of his subject people with fervent devotion, the Lord said to him: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. 14:15).

But who is the suckling lamb except the one whom his forerunner pointed out, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29)? He is called suckling because true humanity is proclaimed in his innocence. But one lamb is offered because, apart from him, no one else is found who can take away the sins of the world.

He offered this lamb whole. The wholeness of the lamb pertains to the solidity of Catholic confession. He divides the lamb, as it were, who is separated from the canon of faith by the sword of error. Thus the lamb is so called because of innocence, suckling because of the assumption of human nature, one because of the singularity of his power, and whole because of the firmest solidity of our faith.

18. If anyone wishes to refer these things not to Christ himself but to his imitator, he may do so. We offer a lamb when, through the goodness of chastity and innocence, we are conformed to our Redeemer; and when we are nourished by the teaching of our innocent Fathers, we suck, as it were, the breasts by which we are nourished for eternal life.

We also offer one lamb if, after the beginning of a religious way of life, we are stained by no defilement of wickedness. For he offers one lamb who never slips from his purpose of innocence into the stains of a polluted life, from which he might return through renewed good works.

To offer a whole lamb is also to prepare for eternal life not merely chastity of the flesh but integrity of mind. He certainly does not offer a whole lamb to the Lord who consecrates his flesh to God through continence but does not restrain the hidden places of his mind from the wantonness of unclean thoughts. He steals part of the lamb from the sacrifice, as it were, who does not join purity of heart to continence of body.

Hence, commanding his disciples to offer the lamb whole, he himself says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say to you, whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:27–28).

Hence also the foolish virgins are marked out in the Gospel: they prepared lamps but did not prepare oil (Matt. 25:3). Those have prepared lamps who preserve the good of chastity in the body; they also have oil who maintain the brightness of purity through vigilance over their minds.

Let it therefore be said of Samuel: “He offered a whole lamb to the Lord,” because, for the good of chastity to suffice for divine reconciliation, it must be preserved not only in the whiteness of the body but also in the radiance of inward purity. Thus it is rightly added:

**(Verse 9.)** “And the Lord heard her.”

19. The one who prays for others can be heard by the Lord if, in some respect, he is not hateful to the Lord to whom he makes supplication. For if he is still weighed down by his own weakness, he is not heard in obtaining strength for his neighbors; and he does not raise his desire to the citadel of divine majesty to the degree that he does not strive, through more fervent devotion, to climb from the depths where he lies through his fall.

The manner of being heard is also explained when it is added:

**(Verses 10–11.)** “And it happened, while Samuel was offering the burnt offering, that the Philistines entered into battle against Israel. But the Lord thundered with a great roar on that day against the Philistines, and terrified them, and they were struck down by the children of Israel. And the children of Israel went out from Masphath, pursued the Philistines, and struck them as far as the place below Bethchar.”

20. While Samuel is offering the burnt offering, the Philistines enter into battle against Israel, because evil spirits stir up more serious temptations against faithful subjects when they see pastors standing against them more resolutely.

But the Lord thunders against the Philistines, because when teachers and faithful subjects pray, divine grace supplies strength. Thunder usually arises through clouds. The lofty clouds signify souls raised by heavenly desire. Hence the prophet, admiring the minds of the elect raised in love of heavenly things, said: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60:8).

What are the thunders of the clouds except those fervent and heavenly desires of the elect? When their minds are kindled by divine grace, these desires entirely drive out from them everything that evil spirits suggest through deception.

Thus it is rightly said: “The Lord thundered against the Philistines and terrified them.” For when through his grace he infuses heavenly desires into elect minds, because he also makes them despise all earthly things, he puts to flight the evil spirits who suggest that they desire those earthly things. They flee as though terrified by thunder, when in the elect minds that they had assailed by temptation they dread the great sound of divine power.

But because the Lord is said to have thundered with a great roar, what else does this mean except that the imperfect desires of Christians are not terrifying to demons? The great roar of thunder is the perfect desire of each of the elect.

When, therefore, the Lord thunders against the Philistines with a great roar, they are struck down by the children of Israel, because when perfect devotion raises the minds of the elect to heavenly joys, it cuts away entirely from itself everything that serves the opposing side.

The Philistines are also rightly said first to have been terrified and then to have been struck down by the children of Israel: they are terrified by the devotion of the elect and struck down by their action. And because devotion precedes action, they are rightly said to be terrified first and struck down afterward. For we first receive from the Lord the gift of good will, so that afterward we may refute the counsels of evil spirits.

It is also rightly said that the Lord thunders against the Philistines and terrifies them, while the children of Israel are said to strike them down, because good desires are supplied to us by divine grace, but we advance the gifts of grace toward victories of virtue through the exertion of free will.

The order of the heavenly warfare is therefore that God should first be heard thundering with a great roar, and afterward the soldier should advance to strike the enemy ranks: so that he may first see in himself the gifts of grace, then break forth more powerfully into the field of battle, and confidently hope for victory, since before the time of combat he has been strengthened by the powers with which he is to be crowned.

21. It is rightly said that those who strike down the Philistines went out from Masphath. They remain in Masphath, which means contemplation, who persist in contemplation of divine things. But they go out to strike down the Philistines when, coming instructed from the secret place of inward meditation, they suppress the powers of the hostile dominion. Within, they quietly arrange how they will break into the enemy ranks outwardly through organized action.

They present more severe battles to their enemies as they advance, to the degree that, while they are thinking inwardly, they lie more quietly within themselves. And because evil spirits must always be restrained by God’s elect, the Philistines are said to have been struck down as far as the place below Bethchar.

Bethchar means “house of the lamb.” Isaiah, indicating this lamb to us, says: “He will be led like a lamb to the slaughter, and like a sheep before its shearer, without a voice” (Isa. 53:7).

What, then, was the house of the lamb except that lofty and uniquely fortified way of life of the Redeemer, which, because it was free from sin, remained inaccessible to all evil spirits? No one can reach Bethchar, that is, the house of the lamb, because whoever makes great progress remains inferior to the holiness of the Redeemer.

Hence the outstanding preacher, dwelling upon the praises of that same Redeemer, says: “Such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens, who has no need, like the priests, to offer sacrifices first for his own sins” (Heb. 7:26–27).

What, then, is the place below Bethchar to which we ought to strike and pursue the Philistines? If Bethchar signifies the perfection of the Lord’s way of life, the place below Bethchar expresses the common summit of the saints’ holiness. They humble themselves before the same Redeemer through obedience and draw near to his glory through the pursuit of an innocent life.

The place shown to lie below Bethchar is understood to be both lower than the place beneath which it lies and near to it. For the closer holy men are to God through the height of their life, the more subject they are through humble thought.

Thus, while the triumph of new believers is shown in the deeds of the Israelites, the foreigners are said to have been struck down as far as the place below the house of the lamb, because through unceasing effort in combat we must strive toward the citadel of perfection, where we are already more terrifying to our enemies in proportion as we are nearer to our Redeemer. There is already a certain security there that cannot be disturbed by fear of enemies.

Indicating the gifts of virtue granted to such people, the Lord says: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19). Hence the one who had reached the place near the house of the lamb says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ—tribulation, or distress, or hunger” (Rom. 8:35), or anything else of this kind?

The house of the lamb may also designate the heavenly homeland. Hence John says: “I saw a lamb standing upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads” (Rev. 14:1).

What, then, is the place below the house of the lamb except the end of temporal life, from which the elect are taken up to the joys of the heavenly homeland? For when we are led to the appointed boundary set for us, which we cannot pass beyond while living, we come, as it were, to the place from which we are to be transferred elsewhere.

The end of the life of the elect is shown to lie below the house of the lamb because from the place where they are brought down through the narrowness of mortality, they are raised to the joys of unfailing life. For the lamb himself, who joyfully inhabits his own house among harpists playing and singers singing, was below the house before he was led into the joy of that house. Hence it is that at the time of his passion he says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38; Mark 14:34).

When the end of each of the elect is shown by the place, it is said to be below Bethchar, that is, the house of the lamb, because when holy men abandon temporal things through the punishment of death, they ascend from nearby into the heavenly homeland that rises above them.

For Paul confidently asserts: “We know that if our earthly house, this dwelling, is dissolved, we have a dwelling from God, not made with hands, in heaven” (2 Cor. 5:1).

We therefore strike down the Philistines as far as the place below the house of the lamb if, for as long as we are in this life, we triumph over evil spirits. It follows:

**(Verse 12.)** “Samuel took one stone and placed it between Masphath and Sen; and he called its name the Stone of Help, saying: ‘Thus far the Lord has helped us.’”

22. In sacred Scripture a stone signifies the Lord and our Redeemer. Samuel takes one stone when the preacher of holy Church proclaims the Redeemer’s strength as unique. This stone is placed between Masphath and Sen because at the end of life he protects the elect and crushes the reprobate.

Sen means “shaking.” The reprobate have been shaken, that is, separated from the fellowship of the faithful. Thus, while the Philistines are said to have been struck down as far as the place below Bethchar, the stone is asserted to have been placed between Sen and Masphath, because when God’s elect receive the title of their victory at the end, they are separated from the fellowship of the wicked by the judgment of the Redeemer.

For now we are like grain and chaff together on the threshing floor; but when we are led to the end of life, the elect are divided from the reprobate by the Lord’s power. They have the stone set between them, as it were, while the former bear the weight of the Redeemer for the judgment of their condemnation, and the latter hold the palms of eternal glory in his strength.

The evil spirits may also be designated by Sen. They have been shaken because they were cast out from the heavenly secret place through pride. And because they now fight against us in this life, it is rightly said, when the time of our victory is asserted, that a stone is placed between us and them. For when we receive the rewards of our warfare, their battles against us are never renewed again.

Samuel places this stone in the midst because the teacher of holy Church shows us the goodness of our Redeemer. And because everything prosperous that is accomplished by us throughout our life is ascribed to divine grace, the stone that is set in the middle is appropriately called by him the Stone of Help.

He is himself the Stone of Help: if he is unwilling to help us, we can be defeated but cannot conquer. Of this stone, now placed in the midst, it is said: “Thus far the Lord has helped us,” because his protection accompanies his elect even to the time of eternal reward.

And because, as we have said, once we have been received into eternal rest, no battles are stirred up against us by our defeated enemies, it follows:

**(Verse 13.)** “And the Philistines were humbled, and they did not continue to come any further into the territory of Israel.”

23. These events express the deeds of individual members of the elect in such a way that they also indicate the warfare of the holy Catholic Church and the joys of reward. Blessed Paul reveals this future victory of the universal Church after the glory of our resurrection. As though already present in the future incorruption, he insulted death, saying: “Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15:54–55).

He also saw the Philistines humbled. Recalling the apostate angels, he arouses the elect to love of their future dignity, saying: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3).

The Philistines are humbled when the demons are cast into the fires of eternal fire prepared for them from the foundation of the world. They do not continue to come into the territory of Israel because they do not go out to test the hearts of the elect.

What are the territories of Israel except the heavens? How will evil spirits come into the territories of Israel when they are so condemned in the depths of hell that they will never rise from their immersion in punishments? Because, therefore, they are cast down into eternal oppression, it is aptly added:

**(Verse 13.)** “The hand of the Lord was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.”

24. What are the good days of a good teacher except those springlike rays of shining eternity? They are appropriately said to be Samuel’s because, although they are common to all the elect, they shine with a special grace toward the joys of preachers. Or they belong to preachers because they shine more especially in the minds of those through whose preaching they are now demonstrated to holy Church.

The hand of the Lord is said to have been against the Philistines throughout all Samuel’s days because divine power always oppresses evil spirits, and in the glory of eternal brightness never ceases to gladden the elect. The losses of the angels are then repaired when whatever was taken away from the blessedness of the order of created spirits through their pride is filled up from among elect human beings. Hence it follows:

**(Verse 14.)** “And the cities that the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel.”

25. The cities that were taken away are the lost multitudes of angels. But they are restored when something is taken from elect human nature to replace what was lost among the angels.

This can also appropriately be understood in the conversion of sinful people. The Philistines take cities when, by tempting them, they deceive the unity of the faithful and subject their minds to themselves by immersing them in sins. But the cities taken away are restored to Israel because penitents in this life make satisfaction in such a way that, splendid in eternal glory, they are presented for the joy of the elect.

For the sins of those who have not forgotten to erase them through the affliction of repentance do not come into God’s memory. And because not only those who neglect to do good but also those who commit abundant iniquity are saved through repentance, it is added:

**(Verse 14.)** “From Ekron as far as Gath.”

26. Ekron means “sterile,” and Gath means “winepress.” Those who do not perform good works are sterile. In the winepress the grape is pressed, and wine [Note: Probably read, “may be proclaimed.”] is proclaimed.

What is worldly desire except the grape of a reprobate mind? And what is the ardor of sinning except the liquor of wine, which makes the sinner’s mind forgetful of eternal goods? For when sin is generated from the desire of the heart, wine is produced from the grape in the winepress, as it were.

From Ekron, therefore, as far as Gath, the cities taken away are restored to Israel, because the minds of those who neglect to do good and boldly perpetrate evil—when they return to the Lord through repentance—are then shown resplendent in the common glory of the elect. Their sins do not come into God’s memory, since they themselves have not neglected to erase them through the affliction of repentance. It follows:

**(Verse 14.)** “And there was peace between Israel and the Amorite.”

27. What is this peace except the one proclaimed by the prophet Micah, who says: “And this one will be peace in the land when he comes” (Mic. 5:5)? Hence Paul says: “He himself is our peace, who has made both one” (Eph. 2:14).

What does it mean that peace is shown to exist between Israel and the Amorite? What else is designated by the Amorite except the reprobate portion of humanity? And whom do those represented by Israel signify except the elect?

Because the elect will be at the right hand of God, while the reprobate will be at the left (Matt. 25:33), when peace is asserted to exist between both, the renowned blessedness of the saints is demonstrated: they agree so fully with the justice of their Creator that, when they behold the punishment of the reprobate, they are moved by no compassion.

Thus, when peace is shown to exist between Israel and the Amorite, it is not a good that the reprobate share with the saints that is demonstrated, but the protection by which the elect are secured. Hence, under the figure of Israel, the prophet promises holy Church: “He has made your borders peace, and fills you with the fat of wheat” (Ps. 147:14).

He makes the borders of the Church peace because, while the power of the Redeemer raises it to the height of inward equity, the misery of the lost does not afflict it through the pain of compassion. But he explains through what pastoral diligence good subjects are advanced to such blessedness, saying:

**(Verse 15.)** “Samuel also judged Israel all the days of his life.”

28. What are the days of each teacher’s life except the brightnesses of spiritual virtues? He judges Israel throughout all the days of his life who, for the example of faithful subjects, manifests through the perfection of good conduct the light of justice that he asserts in speech.

But one who does not have the light of spiritual virtues, because he undertakes to teach what is foreign to his own conduct, judges according to the days of another’s life. Of such people the Lord says through the prophet: “Behold, I am against the prophets who steal my words, each one from his neighbor” (Jer. 23:30).

They steal words who do not follow in their deeds the good that they preach in their teaching. For they secretly take from another what they do not make their own by paying the price of their own labor.

After the future blessedness has been proclaimed, the kind of pastor the faithful should have in the meantime is shown, since Samuel is said to have judged Israel throughout all the days of his life. For he presents the way of perfection badly if someone wishes to open the path of light by his voice while darkening it through his actions.

The one who had devoted all the days of his life to judging Israel says: “I do not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me, in the obedience of the Gentiles by word and deed” (Rom. 15:18).

Let the teacher therefore judge—but let him be one who possesses illustrious days of life—so that he may first nourish within himself, by living well, the rays of spiritual virtues that he administers in speech for the guidance of his subjects’ paths. For a lamp is then usefully displayed to those who are in the house if it has first been filled with the light that it is going to spread. It follows:

**(Verse 46.)** “And he went around year by year to Bethel, Galgal, and Masphath, and judged Israel in those places.”

29. Bethel is called “house of God”; Galgal, “wheel”; Masphath, as already explained above, is interpreted as “watchtower.” What, then, does Bethel signify except men appointed to the service of the sacred altar, who, while they devote themselves to spiritual pursuits, are like household members and familiar friends of almighty God? And what does Galgal, which is called “wheel,” signify except the order of married people? For they go around as on a wheel, since they cannot be entirely free from the cares of the world, which continually turns. And what are represented by Masphath, which is interpreted as “watchtower,” except those who, devoting themselves to divine contemplation, burn with desire for heavenly joys alone?

What, then, does it mean that Samuel is said to go around Bethel, Galgal, and Masphath, and to judge Israel in those same places, except that the chosen preacher follows the examples of all the chosen orders, so that he may be a learned judge of the faithful who are subject to him? For he cannot be an impartial examiner if he disdains to take from the examples of preceding chosen men what he himself decrees. But let him also go around these places every year, so that the prudent teacher may examine individually the perfection of each order; so that, the more carefully he observes the goodness of those who preceded him, the more suitably he may arrange what belongs to the present. There, then, let him judge Israel—there, so that he may correct the faithful subject to him, whom he trains for the vision of God, by the uprightness of those whom he unquestionably believes to have pleased God.

Bethel, which is called “house of God,” may also signify the whole Church of the chosen; and Galgal, which is interpreted as “wheel,” may signify sacred Scripture. Whatever the teacher presents for the progress of those subject to him, he receives either from the example of the chosen, from the teaching of sacred eloquence, or from the revelation of inward and secret contemplation.

30. Samuel, therefore, goes around Bethel when the preacher seeks from the examples of the elders the authority by which works are to be arranged. He goes around Galgal—that is, the wheel—when he derives the authority of his teaching from the instruction of holy Scripture. He also goes around Masphath when, through meditation on secret contemplation, he merits receiving a revelation of the truth. There he judges Israel, because whatever he proposes to his subjects as the standard of uprightness, he receives either from the examples of the chosen, from the teaching of sacred eloquence, or from the revelation of inward contemplation.

These words plainly show not only what a perfect teacher does, but also that he is not perfect if he cannot do these things. For if he knows only the examples of good people, or if he is learned in sacred Scripture but lacks the revelation of contemplation, he will not be a perfect man in the order of preaching. Contemplation is the virtue by which not only the Scripture already composed is recognized, but by which what had not yet been composed would be composed, and by which what has been composed may daily be ordered according to God’s will.

Thus it is rightly said: “And he judged Israel in the places mentioned above.” For he judged not only in Bethel and Galgal, but also in Masphath, so that whoever strives [perhaps read *enititur*, “strives”] for the perfection of preaching—while following the examples of the elders through humility and being supported by learning through study of sacred eloquence—must take the utmost care to recognize by contemplation, with a pure mind, the things that are to be arranged.

For the person who wishes to teach human beings after undertaking the office of preaching must be teachable by God. Yet one who is instructed by the learning of secret contemplation should presume only in such a way that he neither despises the Scriptures composed through the Holy Spirit nor disdains to follow the examples of the chosen.

Samuel is described as going around Bethel, Galgal, and Masphath so that one may not be separated from another through discord: that he may receive the examples approved by sacred Scripture; recognize those sacred Scriptures which chosen men had written; and perceive those revelations of contemplation shown to him by God which disagree neither with the works of the chosen nor with the authority of sacred Scripture. He should also bring everything he does into conformity with the uprightness of heavenly intention. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 17.)** “He returned to Ramatha; for there he judged Israel, and there was his house.”

31. As we said above, Ramatha is interpreted as “consummated vision” and signifies that blessed and perfect society of the citizens above, to which Samuel returns so that he may not be crushed beneath the burden of his labor. Samuel returns to Ramatha when the preacher’s mind is lifted up through love of heavenly things. For he would collapse under the immense burdens of his office if he did not return, through the desire of hope, to love of heavenly things.

For preachers to return means to bring the intention of their minds back to the joys of the heavenly homeland. And there they judge Israel, because they strive, through preaching, to make the faithful subject to them conform to the beauty of the heavenly homeland, which they retain in their minds. They judge Israel there because, seeing the form of that already perfected city, they draw from it the pattern which, by their speech, they impress upon the minds of their children; and whatever they see to be unworthy of that beauty, they strive to cut away from their minds.
