And because they rest with complete love in the glory of that blessed homeland, his house is said to be there. For he is recognized as having his house in the place where he dwells in love. Hence that outstanding preacher also boasts, saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

Samuel goes around Bethel, Galgal, and Masphath, and has no house in any of them; but in Ramatha he has a house. For whatever the teachers of the holy Church now receive from the examples of the chosen, whatever they receive from learning in the sacred books, and whatever they transiently investigate from the height of heavenly revelation, they possess as assistance for the journey, not as the object of their love and reward. But what they love in the heavenly city they possess not for the progress of the journey, but for the sufficient—indeed, abundant—fullness of their reward. And because all good things are gathered there, it follows:

**(Verse 17.)** “He also built an altar there to the Lord.”

32. For what is the Lord’s altar except the heart of the righteous? The judgment of truth says: “Where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matthew 6:21). Whoever does good out of love for the heavenly homeland, while ardently desiring to reach what he gathers above, certainly builds an altar upon which he may burn the sacrifices of daily desire.

It is rightly said: “He built an altar there to the Lord,” because as the flame of good desire grows in the heart through increasing devotion to heavenly things, so the altar is built above, as though stones were being added, so that offerings of love may be presented to God.

This may also appropriately be referred to the gaining of souls. The teacher builds an altar to the Lord in Ramatha when he places the merits of those subject to him in heaven; and when, through his daily devotion, chosen souls ascend to the heavenly kingdom, stones are, as it were, carried for the structure of the altar above.

Let it therefore be said of Samuel—let it be said: “He built an altar there to the Lord.” For the teacher’s labor is unquestionably very idle if, through what he does on earth, the heavenly building is not increased.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0217]

## CHAPTER ONE

175 1. The deeds of holy men who preceded them are often consolations for the chosen who follow. By a wondrous dispensation of the divine purpose, they were raised to such heights of sublime conduct that they could perform courageous deeds for themselves and provide what was right for those subject to them; yet they were sometimes left to themselves in such a way that what they arranged with right intention was not right according to God’s providence. Thus their weakness might become the steadfastness of the chosen who followed them. For even if, as human beings, they can err in arranging the affairs of the holy Church, the ecclesiastical arrangements themselves must nevertheless not be abandoned.

For behold, it is said:

**(1 Samuel 8:1–3.)** “Now it came to pass, when Samuel had grown old, that he appointed his sons judges over Israel. The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of the second was Abiah; they were judges in Beersheba. And his sons did not walk in his ways.”

2. Behold: the man who had been full of the spirit of prophecy did not know that those whom he appointed judges over Israel would later turn aside after avarice, accept gifts, and pervert judgment. What wonder, then, if those who do not receive the grace of prophecy can err in arranging offices, when those who possess the spirit of prophecy do not possess that same spirit for arranging everything?

Who could doubt that, if so great a man had foreseen the future perversity of his sons, he certainly would not have preferred them to judicial honors? Those who knowingly advance the reprobate, therefore, cannot flatter themselves by the prophet’s example, since an action is harmless only when, at the time they were promoted, no signs of the iniquity that later followed were apparent in them.

Accordingly, those who were appointed judges over Israel by Samuel are appropriately called his sons when they were appointed, so that they might be believed to have been begotten not only in the flesh, but also adorned with the splendors of his conduct. Their names, too, are carefully given, so that from the title of the name the form of virtue then present in them may be recognized. “The name of the one,” he says, “was Joel, and the name of the other Abiah; they were judges in Beersheba.”

The case of those who are said to have turned aside to avarice after receiving their dignity is also plainly demonstrated: before they attained the summit of that dignity, no signs of their future perversity appeared in them.

But behold: while we consider the consolations provided by pastors, we also observe the considerable dangers of the Lord’s flock. [Note: Gussanville and the Vatican manuscript read, “we behold the evil dangers.”] For the subjects stood firm, while the sons of the prophet, placed at the summit of authority, fell. Thus, if an unceasing devotion to holy living or the security of an eminent way of life pleases us who have been placed under the care of our elders, we should nevertheless not desire to preside over others out of longing, but undertake it with great fear.

Yet carnal people, attending only to visible things, do not merit knowing the spiritual conduct of the saints. They see the summit of the pastors of the holy Church, but do not know how unwillingly those pastors inwardly bear the splendor which they outwardly maintain in the brilliance of their office; how they endure the height of honor as the oppression of a great burden; how they flee with great desire what they pursue through their external ministry.

For, as the outstanding teacher testifies, we have learned that “the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:14). Hence the more foolishly the person who follows carnal things goes astray, the less he penetrates spiritual things through the virtue of discernment.

Some such people advance so far into the evil of foolishness that they do not fear even to disturb the state of ecclesiastical authority. Hence it follows:

**(Verses 4–5.)** “Then all the elders of Israel assembled, came to Ramatha, and said to him: ‘Behold, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Appoint a king over us, to judge us like all the nations.’”

3. For those who were living under spiritual rule, to ask for a king means what else than to desire to transfer that same spiritual authority into secular domination? But when holy men see themselves despised by their subjects, they are troubled not so much that they are despised as that those who despise them do not please God.

In their subjects’ contempt they see an increase of their own inward glory; yet they grieve that their merits are increased by the failings of those subject to them. They would wish those subjects to advance in merit in such a way that, in the eternal recompense of merits, they might have with them those over whom they preside. Therefore it is added:

**(Verse 6.)** “The word displeased Samuel, because they had said: ‘Give us a king to judge us.’”

4. What displeased him was what he believed displeased God, whom they were addressing. But it is not simply said, “The word displeased Samuel,” but “in the eyes of Samuel,” and immediately it is added:

**(Verse 6.)** “And Samuel prayed to the Lord for the people.”

[Col. 0219D] We must consider these matters somewhat more subtly. Holy men, who greatly fear displeasing almighty God, are not quick in their judgments; rather, they first order everything rationally within, so that they may arrange it irreproachably in outward action. They make no choice by judgment unless it has first been tested by the contemplation of reason.

The Lord wished to open precisely these eyes of the prophet when he said: “See with your eyes and hear with your ears” (Ezekiel 40:4). In the Gospel he likewise said to his disciples: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke 10:23).

The eyes of the saints are the understanding of reason, opened by the grace of the Holy Spirit. They are therefore called Samuel’s, because carnal people, even if they seem rational through human wisdom, are all the blinder to this light of reason insofar as they see only with those eyes which the serpent opened. For if they saw the splendor of spiritual virtues, they would certainly desire to possess it as the adornment of their minds. So great is their beauty that their appearance can never fail to arouse the desire of the one who sees it.

When the wise men of this world imagine that they possess the eyes of reason, they can thereby recognize how foolishly they rave: since they are not attracted by the beauty of holy virtues, they evidently not only fail to see their glory, but cannot even dream of it.

Holy men, therefore, who have already been bound by the illumination of the Holy Spirit to love inward things, possess eyes of the mind that are clearer for seeing the glory of inner radiance, in proportion as they have nothing in their desire from the world’s darkness. They can also discern carnal things more correctly in proportion as, having been taken far away from carnal things, they have advanced more deeply in the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Hence the apostle Paul, speaking from the experience of such vision, expressed this judgment: “The spiritual person judges all things” (1 Corinthians 2:15).

It is rightly said: “The word displeased Samuel in his eyes,” because spiritual men despise nothing before judging, through the spiritual insight of the mind, that it ought to be despised. And because the more abundantly they are filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, the less they presume upon the loftiness of their virtue, it follows: “And Samuel prayed to the Lord.” For what did he pray to the Lord except that he might deign to show him whether he ought to consent to the petition of the tumultuous people?

**(Verses 7–8.)** “But the Lord said to Samuel: ‘Hearken to the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For they have not rejected you, but me, that I should not reign over them, according to all their deeds which they have done from the day when I brought them out of Egypt until this day.’”

5. Since the prophet, while praying, is told, “Appoint a king over them,” it is clearly shown that he had asked to have revealed to him whether this ought to be done. And since the Lord adds, “They have not rejected you, but me, that I should not reign over them,” it is appropriately shown how greatly the word displeased him—the word that is said to have displeased Samuel in his eyes.

This harmony of judgment arises in the saints from the virtue of charity. Because they love the Creator with their whole mind and devoutly strive to obey his will, they receive, as the reward of heavenly recompense, the grace not to differ in judgment from the will of almighty God, which they always keep in their good works. For it is written: “He who adheres to God is one spirit with him” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

He adheres to the Lord who always strives to fulfill the commands of his will. Yet he becomes one spirit with him because, through long-standing devotion to pious action, he is admitted into such great knowledge of divine grace that he can no longer, through error inspired by the worldly spirit, dissent from the equity of God’s inward judgment.

But it is very difficult to answer when one asks why almighty God both complains that he has been rejected in the request for a king and nevertheless decrees that what was requested should be done; and again, if royal dignity was to be established, why it was permitted as though in indignation at God’s majesty; and, when a king is provided and ordered to be chosen, why one who is to be rejected is chosen.

What else can we answer to these questions except what the apostle Paul replied to those who dared to investigate the ineffable abyss of God’s judgments: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20).

Although we cannot define this effectively, we can touch upon it by inquiry. Perhaps, then, does he complain that he has been rejected in the request for a king? The king requested by the people, who were asking perversely, is granted as punishment for their perverse will. If this is stated reasonably, then, by presenting both aspects, he displays guilt and vengeance together.

The one who demonstrates by asking that he has rejected the Creator is convicted of having made an unjust request out of a perverse will. The punishment of strict justice therefore followed the guilt of the evil request. For great is the vengeance that proceeds from the strictness of inward judgment, when the perverse mind is cast down in such a way that it is permitted to do what it wrongly deliberates.

Those, therefore, who were convicted of rejecting the Lord in asking for a king, received no heavier punishment than to be permitted to do what would cause them to reject the Lord from themselves.

179 6. At this point it should be noted that the Lord makes the prophet’s rejection his own. He does not simply say, “They have rejected me, that I should not reign over them,” but, “They have not rejected you, but me, that I should not reign over them.” Thus he plainly shows that, in the person of an elected ruler, he himself presides over those subject to him; and when a carnal ruler is raised to the spiritual summit of the chosen, he appears to be rejected whose commands are scattered.

Therefore it is clear how worthy of reverence are the excellent pastors of the holy Church. Behold: while they serve God faithfully, they are joined to him by so strong a bond of love that whatever is inflicted upon them is reckoned an injury against God. Hence in the Gospel he says to the first pastors of the Church: “He who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

Here something even more serious is discerned: when he complains that the pastor has been rejected, all the sins of those rejecting him, and even the evils of their ancestors, are recalled. “According to all their deeds,” he says, “which they have done from the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt.”

The supreme crime is recognized when all past sins are brought back into God’s memory for examination. Thus the Lord both complains that he has been rejected and nevertheless permits the establishment of the one in whom he is rejected, because, when he carries out the force of his strict justice, the desires of carnal people are not prevented from being fulfilled through his mercy.

Yet the dignity that could be granted as punishment ought not to be granted with the calm majesty of divinity, but as though in indignation. We do not assert that God’s majesty itself is indignant, since it is not subject to passion; rather, when it examines sins, it speaks through Scripture in the language of indignation.

Again, because the king is taken as a type of carnal rulers, a king who is to be rejected is chosen, not one who is approved. Or perhaps the reprobate king is chosen so that David, his chosen successor, might learn from him what he ought to avoid.

In the same way we read concerning that assembly of angels: of the apostate first angel it is written, “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40:14). Yet he who was created first of all fell through pride, and in his ruin the holy angels learned by what virtue they could stand.

Whoever is able to contemplate this with the open eyes of right faith also perceives that almighty God even then bestows gifts of great mercy when he inflicts vengeance: for while he punishes the reprobate, he instructs the saints, so that the downfall of the former may aid the progress of the latter.

7. With strict judgment he permits evil to be done, but mercifully provides what good he will bring forth from the evils that he inflicts through judgment. For what greater guilt is there than the one by which we all die? And what greater goodness than that by which we are freed from death?

Indeed, unless Adam had sinned, it would not have been necessary for our Redeemer to assume our flesh. “For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Mark 2:17). If, then, he came for sinners, he would not have needed to come had sins been absent. If the sins which he is believed to have come to destroy are understood to have been permitted by God’s justice, then, since God was to become human for sinners, almighty God had foreseen that from the evil by which they were to die he would bring forth the good that would overcome that evil.

Who among the faithful does not see how wondrously the greatness of that good surpasses all else? The evils we suffer through the merit of the first sin are indeed great, but what chosen person would not rather endure worse things than be without so great a Redeemer?

Let a king therefore be chosen—but one who is to be rejected. Let him be chosen as though in indignation, not by God’s will. Then let a king according to God’s heart follow, so that from the strictness of his judgment the evil of vengeance may proceed against the reprobate, while the good that God was to bring forth from evil may overflow upon the faithful through the abundance of divine grace, as the former are permitted to fall into the evil they desire.

What causes them to plunge headlong is made to ensure that others do not fall at all. But since these words assert the judgment of divine strictness, let us now see with what great dispensation he acts so that they may not do, through evil deliberation, what would bring punishment upon them. For it follows:

**(Verse 9.)** “Now therefore, hearken to their voice; nevertheless, testify against them and proclaim to them the right of the king who will reign over them.”

8. As though openly displaying clemency, he says: “Hearken to their voices, but first let them themselves hear from you the rights of the king whom they seek—those things that will make them afraid. Let them then abandon their evil undertaking when they learn how burdensome the matter is which they were seeking.” It follows:

**(Verses 10–17.)** “And so Samuel spoke all the words of the Lord to the people who had asked a king from him, and he said: ‘This will be the right of the king who will rule over you. He will take your sons and place them in his chariots; he will make them his horsemen and forerunners of his four-horse chariots; he will appoint them tribunes and centurions, plowmen of his fields, reapers of his crops, and craftsmen of his weapons and chariots. He will also make your daughters his perfumers, cooks, and bakers. He will take your fields, vineyards, and finest olive groves and give them to his servants. He will also tithe your crops and the produce of your vineyards, to give to his eunuchs and servants. He will take your male and female slaves, your finest young men, and your asses, and put them to his work. He will also tithe your flocks, and you yourselves will be his servants.’”

[Note: Gilot and the Vatican manuscript read “persecutors”; “forerunners” (*praecursores*) should be read, as is clear from chapter 2, section 4. Nevertheless, this also teaches us that “persecutors” was formerly read in many manuscripts.]

9. When submission is required of carnal people, whatever is commanded to them is burdensome, even if it is not difficult, because, swollen with pride, they are accustomed to follow the judgment of their own will; and whatever conflicts with their deliberation they consider extremely burdensome.

But when harsh and contrary commands are imposed, what a weight of burden and swelling of heart do they experience? They could scarcely bear even gentle and light commands unwillingly, though if they had wished to do so, they would have endured them very easily.

Let us therefore see how appropriately the pious dispensation of the Creator responds to the foolish audacity of human beings. The rights of human rulers are set before those who have disregarded the rights of God; and harsh, unbearable burdens of human servitude are proclaimed to those who had rejected the gentle and salutary counsels of divinity, so that they might reason among themselves how intolerable the commands of a human ruler would be to those who had refused to obey God’s counsels—not merely when he commanded, but when he warned them not to make such a request.

Yet the hearts of carnal people possess temerity through the increase of boldness, and hardness through the logic of pretence. Through temerity they easily deliberate about what must be done; but because they do not understand what they wrongly propose, they cannot be helped by better counsel.

Therefore it is added here as well:

**(Verse 19.)** “The people refused to listen to Samuel’s voice. And they said: ‘By no means; there shall be a king over us. We too shall be like all the nations, and our king shall judge us, and he shall go out before us and fight our battles for us.’”

10. It was certainly great temerity to ask for a king against God’s will; it was great hardness not to be overcome by the prophet’s counsels. It was great temerity to offer arguments to one whom they knew, through the Lord’s revelation, to know beforehand everything he was going to do. It was great hardness not to obey one whom they knew commanded only what he had learned through the Lord’s revelation.

For what does their response mean: “By no means, but there shall be a king over us”? Those who say “By no means” evidently deny what they hear. This word therefore plainly shows that the prophet explained the burdensome rights of the king so that the king might not be requested.

They hear the rights of the king, but detest the very reason for which those rights are explained, so that the progress of reprobate hearts may be expressed: in them there is both the completion of an evil purpose and the unchangeability of the will.

But we criticize ancient times while taking no care to see our own. Those times, as the world grows old, are more ancient; and through the vice of time and negligence they are also more lax in many respects. For we now propose evil with greater boldness, just as the strength of human nature has withered along with the once robust youth of the world; and we recall what has been wrongly proposed with greater difficulty, insofar as, through the weakening of spiritual vigor, our mind becomes carnal.

Such are human falls: what fails in spiritual virtue is strengthened in carnal life. All these things, in the words of the outstanding teacher, “happened to them as a figure; but they were written for us” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

We now clearly recognize the audacity of these Israelites and the judgments of divine indignation that followed it; yet we do not fear proposing actions against God’s will and against the counsel of the rulers of the holy Church. When rebuked for an evil purpose, we resist and try to overcome the salutary counsels of our elders with the unconquerable evil of obstinacy.

We see how great an increase of evil it is to watch people perishing and not fear following their footsteps into destruction; to see them falling into the punitive snares of death and not fear becoming entangled in those same snares.

Those people asked for a king against the Lord’s will; but afterward, through the royal dignity, the people who had rejected God were led to worship idols and adore images. We therefore see how worthy of reverence are the counsels of our elders, if we consider this carefully: those who dared to despise them did not foresee that they were undertaking the very actions by which they could be submerged in so deep a sea of error.

The Lord therefore rightly complains that he was rejected in the request for a king, and rightly grants royal dignity in indignation. The iniquity of those making the request was so great that, when they asked for what would cause them to depart from God, it could be permitted by God’s judgment but could not be forbidden.

Since we have discussed these matters according to the literal sense, let us also see what the things contained in the rights of the king signify spiritually.

# CHAPTER TWO

1. A king is requested after Samuel has been rejected when a reprobate multitude of people despises the spiritual pastor and seeks to have a carnal ruler preside over it. Divine justice often deals with such people by permitting them, precisely because they despise the chosen preacher, to become subject to a reprobate ruler. Through imitation of that ruler they perish all the more disastrously, because with greater pride they had more audaciously despised the one through whom they could have lived forever.

When the rights of the king are proclaimed, therefore, it is clearly shown in the conduct of one carnal ruler what the rest of the carnal people will do through tyranny—not what the chosen ought to imitate. For in the same history of the Kings we read that when King Ahab took Naboth’s vineyard, he incurred the anger of almighty God. Here, however, when the rights of the king are proclaimed, fields, vineyards, and the finest olive groves are said to be taken (1 Kings 21:2ff.). Since what is punished there is proclaimed here, this shows that it is not commanded by divine judgment.

Accordingly, when the chosen king David asked Ornan the Jebusite for his threshing floor in order to build an altar to the Lord, he did not wish to use that royal right of tyrants (1 Chronicles 21:24), since he absolutely refused to accept it unless he had first paid a worthy price for it.

2. Since, then, the things contained in the rights of the king are proclaimed as things to be avoided rather than imitated, they must be considered with all the greater subtlety, since they cannot be avoided if they are unknown.

He says, therefore: “He will take your sons and place them in his chariots.” The sons of the chosen are those who imitate their virtues. The chariots of carnal rulers are the arrogance of worldly pride. For, while they boast that they are higher than others, they walk through lofty places as though carried in chariots.

The sons of the faithful are therefore placed in chariots when they follow reprobate pastors through an appetite for worldly glory; when, abandoning spiritual pursuits, they seek the comforts of carnal life; and when, laying aside that sublime intention directed toward heavenly things, they strive to attain the heights of the world.

It is rightly said that the sons of the Israelites are to be placed not in one chariot but in chariots, because everything that stands out in the eminence of carnal rulers contributes to their pride. They raise themselves to the heights as though in so many lofty chariots as there are heights that they see and by which they consider themselves superior to others.

The king therefore places the sons of the good in chariots when a carnal ruler, through the example of his own depravity, draws imitators of the chosen into the vices of pride, so that they set heavenly things aside, desire earthly things, and rejoice in this alone: that, because something has been made temporally high, they may be preferred to others.

31. And because they are not only raised up against their inferiors but also strong, it follows: “And he will make them his horsemen.” For those who are both elevated in dignity and savage in power rage as though upon horses. They are horsemen also because, when they direct the fierce movements of their hearts against the powerless, they are swift for everything they desire to exercise through tyranny.

They pant with force, foam with rage, and strike down those whom they attack in the course of their tyranny.

But while some among reprobate pastors imitate the arrogance of worldly elevation, and others, following their example, oppress those whom they can, there are also some who, in order to perform evils which they themselves cannot inflict upon the good, introduce others more wicked than themselves. Hence it follows: “And the forerunners of his four-horse chariots.”

4. For what are the king’s four-horse chariots except the perverse minds of evil subjects, in whose counsels the reprobate ruler rests? They are four-horse chariots because the rulers’ actions are assisted by the wicked counsels of the depraved. In them the king is, as it were, carried aloft, since through those who favor them in the pursuit of temporal honors, carnal rulers carry out whatever they desire from the height of worldly power.

They are rightly designated by the name “four-horse chariots.” For a chariot stands upon what makes it roll, because a reprobate mind has the world’s mutability as the goal of its intention. It rests, indeed, upon that from which it never ceases to stir up the affairs of the world through the innumerable cares of a mind that continually turns like a wheel.

They are therefore the king’s four-horse chariots, since through everything lofty that they consider while turning things over, they carry within themselves the commands of carnal rulers.

But those who hold a place of familiarity beside carnal rulers have inferiors over whom they may command. These men, therefore, are like the king’s four-horse chariots, while those others are the forerunners of the chariots, because, in the very manner by which they carry the carnal ruler toward oppressing the humble, they too are led, through the service of others, toward harming whomever they can.

The forerunner of a chariot is, as it were, one who, through the evil cunning of his mind, devises a method by which to bring the ruler in to inflict evils upon the gentle.

If, however, as many manuscripts have it, we read not “forerunners” but “persecutors of the chariots,” they are plainly those who imitate the reprobate as they run toward evil.

A chariot is also customarily used to carry kings as a mark of honor. The king is therefore set, as it were, in a chariot when a carnal ruler glories in the flattery of the great who appear beside him. Whoever precedes or follows these men in praising them is a forerunner or persecutor of the chariots, because such people utter their flatteries either before or after the praises which those men have spread among the people by preceding or following them.

5. It follows: “And he will appoint them tribunes and centurions.” They become tribunes and centurions when they advance so far in evil that they preside over impious henchmen for carrying out the tyrant’s commands, and when they arrange the ranks of worldly forces to lead them into wars against the innocent.

Tribunes are those who, through the many supporters they have secured, lie in wait for those who live uprightly. Centurions are those who omit no kind of harm. They attain perfection in iniquity because they always strive to inflict the many great evils that lie within their power.

The word *centurion* is derived from the number one hundred. And because the number one hundred signifies perfection, it is perfected in the evil sense when the impious reach the fullness of wickedness. Such men are smooth in cunning but violent in terror. They flatter others gently so that, with their help, they may terrify others savagely.

Accordingly, it is rightly added: “And plowmen of his fields, and reapers of his crops.”

### 6.

The fields of the carnal ruler are the minds of his subjects; the ploughmen of these fields, moreover, are those who, by the skill of worldly cleverness, persuade them to perform wicked deeds. For they open up the solidity of the fields, as it were, by their speech, when through reprehensible counsels they corrupt the hearts of the simple. They reap the crops when hearts of the lesser, deceived by the seed of wicked counsel, yield the fruit of evil action. These actions are plainly designated by the name “crops,” because the perversity of a reprobate subject, when it is gladly accepted by carnal rulers, is, as it were, their chosen food of the mind.

And because in this perversity they advance little by little, it follows:

“And the smiths of his weapons and of his chariots.” [Col. 0226D]

What are the weapons and chariots of tyrants except all those instruments of wrongdoing that are prepared for overthrowing the hearts of the lesser? But since one arrives by chariot at the place from which one strikes with weapons, they become the smiths of the king’s weapons and chariots when, through the most wicked contrivance of their hearts, they discover both the evils they are to commit and how to inflict those evils once discovered. To forge weapons, then, is to gather together in a reprobate mind the various ways of doing harm; to forge chariots is to discover the means by which they may approach in order to inflict those same evils.

### 7.

It follows:

“Your daughters also he will make perfumers, cooks, and bakers.” [Col. 0227A]

By the name “daughters” are signified the minds of the weak placed within the holy Church. They become the king’s perfumers because, when they see carnal rulers exalted in the height of passing glory, they attempt to soothe them with flattery. Condemning the use of such perfumes, the Psalmist says:

“Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Psalm 140:5).

The daughters therefore become perfumers because, while the weak fear displeasing carnal rulers, they soften by flattery the ferocity to which they are subject through fear.

It should also be noted that the sons are first said to be taken by the king, and then to be made horsemen, centurions, or smiths of weapons; but the daughters are not said to be taken, only to be made perfumers and bakers. To be taken is an act of violence. The sons are therefore taken because the strong are difficult to overthrow. When, then, the daughters are said not to be taken but to be made perfumers, what else is meant except that those who are weak in goodness are easily scattered through the examples of the wicked?

They also become the king’s cooks and bakers, because those who serve tyrants by flattery, pleasing them through their favor, provide them, as it were, with food. Cooks are those who prepare on the hearth what kings eat. Thus cooks are those who, through services of favor, kindle swelling pride of heart in a carnal ruler, so that they receive favors more boldly, as though by the fire of aroused devotion they were preparing more delicate foods for themselves.

They also become bakers because, when they praise a reprehensible life, they strengthen the tyrant’s carnal mind to practice wickedness.

### 8.

It follows:

“He will also take your fields, vineyards, and olive groves, and give them to his servants.” [Col. 0227C]

What are the fields of the good except the devoted minds of subjects? When these willingly hear the words of the good, they yield an abundant fruit of good works. And what are their vineyards except their minds, so advancing through imitation that they also offer the word of life to others and make those whom they kindle by their speech to love the Creator drunk, as it were, by giving them wine?

And what are the olive groves except the hearts of hearers who, through the example and exhortation of the good, advance toward works of mercy?

But when the king is established, the fields are taken away, because when carnal men reach the summit of rule, some hearers of the good receive examples of wickedness. The fields are therefore taken away when recently devoted hearts are seduced, so that from the seed of wickedness they yield fruit in an evil way of life.

The olive groves and vineyards are taken away when, through the example of a wicked ruler, works of mercy and the words of holy preaching that should be offered and spoken are abandoned. [Col. 0227D]

It is rightly said that the fields, vineyards, and olive groves that have been taken away are given to the king’s servants. Servants are those who are always subject to their masters’ authority and cannot escape the yoke of domination. The king’s servants, therefore, are those who, through abundant iniquity, bind themselves to the wills of tyrants in such a way that they no longer withdraw from them.

The servants receive the fields, vineyards, and olive groves that have been taken away because the wicked supporters of carnal rulers, when they transfer deceived hearts to a purpose of evil action, impose, as it were, upon the fields, vineyards, and olive groves of the chosen the title of tyrannical power.

It follows:

“But he will also tithe your crops and the produce of your vineyards, in order to give it to his eunuchs and servants.” [Col. 0228A]

When the wicked rule, it is very difficult for one subject to them to suffer no loss of religion. The minds of some are utterly ruined; but those whom they cannot completely corrupt, while continually observing both their wicked words and deeds, are stained with some kind of defilement.

It is therefore rightly said:

“He will tithe your crops and the produce of your vineyards.”

As if he said: Under a reprobate shepherd, even the good things of the chosen are not left whole.

But what is taken away from the good is given to the king’s eunuchs and servants. The eunuchs and servants of carnal rulers are their hypocritical hearers. They are eunuchs because they display themselves as having cast off worldly pleasure; but they are the king’s servants because, through everything they pretend to possess of virtue, they carry within themselves the yoke of reprobate rulers.

The tenth of the crops and vineyards is rightly said to belong to the eunuchs, because the poison of hypocrites is not easily recognized. Since even holy men can be deceived by it, what they lose is attributed to those by whose fraud they are captured. [Col. 0228B]

It follows:

“He will also take your male servants and maidservants, your finest young men, and your donkeys, and put them to his work.”

The male servants and maidservants of the saints are those who provide them with the temporal necessities of life. They are male servants and maidservants because, while supplying the necessities of the body, some are stronger than others in this work of mercy.

And they are “finest young men” because those who can do much and those who can do little, when they expend in the work of mercy everything they are capable of, perform divine service vigorously like chosen young men.

The donkeys of the chosen are those upon whom the burdens of obedience are imposed, so that they may assist their weakness by carrying with them what they could in no way carry without them. [Col. 0228C]

What does it mean, then, that they are foretold to be put to the king’s work? Those who are put to the king’s work, on appointed days, pay the required corvée to the authority of the public power.

What, therefore, does it mean that the king’s male servants and maidservants and finest young men are foretold to be put to his work, except that when carnal men become pre-eminent, both the ministers of the chosen and the hearts of those who obey devoutly are often stained?

For, while they incessantly observe their reprobate life, they gradually fall so far that they imitate something of their deeds. Through long practice they serve the chosen; but, while they often see the height of their excellence, they eventually desire others to serve them as well, under the impulse of pride. They mercifully give away what is their own, but often, following the example of tyrants, take what belongs to others. [Col. 0228D]

Yet because they are servants of the saints, they cannot leave their rightful service. They may indeed abandon it for a time, but through divine mercy they are easily lifted from the error into which they have fallen.

Because, then, they fall through the examples of the wicked but quickly recover their senses, they are put, as it were, by corvée into the king’s work, in which they do not remain long through continuous servitude.

### 9.

It follows:

“He will also tithe your flocks, and you will be his servants.” [Col. 0229A]

As if he said: When a carnal shepherd is set over you, the spoils of your virtues are inflicted not only on what is yours, but on you yourselves as well.

The flocks of the chosen are the multitudes of spiritual virtues. When these spiritual virtues too are scattered through the example of the wicked, the king takes a tenth of the flock when the one who rules carnally destroys certain virtues in the hearts of the saints.

He takes a tenth because, while he disrupts the integrity of the mind, he leaves the number of virtues incomplete. The number ten signifies perfection. Thus, when the Lord openly demonstrated the losses of our fallen humanity by comparison, he brought forward the woman who had lost one of ten drachmas (Luke 15:4ff.), so that by showing that the number ten had suffered loss, that heavenly society which remained among the angels in the number nine might be understood to be incomplete without the restoration of our condition.

And because tithes are exacted each year, those who do not cease to offer tithes are aptly said to be the king’s servants. They serve those year after year through whose example they often become worse. [Col. 0229B]

The fact that this servitude is asserted after the tithes have been given can also indicate the progress of evil. Those who gradually fail act each day in such a way that they are led into the depths of iniquity.

He therefore says:

“He will tithe your flocks, and you will be his servants.”

As if he said: Through the example of the wicked you will gradually fall, but in falling you act in such a way that you never withdraw from their imitation.

For it is written:

“By whom anyone is overcome, by him he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

Because through imitation of a reprobate shepherd they fall into the slavery of sin, they cannot, whenever they wish, free themselves from his yoke.

Hence it follows:

> **(Verse 18.)** “And you will cry out on that day because of the presence of your king whom you chose for yourselves, and the Lord will not hear you on that day, because you asked for a king for yourselves.” [Col. 0229C]

### 10.

As if he said: You are gradually sinking into knowledge of his wicked imitation, but you cannot willingly abandon the examples of his depravity to which you voluntarily submit yourselves. For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin (John 8:34). Those, therefore, whom sins dominate cannot free themselves from their yoke by their own power.

They often come to the Lord with prayers and ask to be freed, but they cannot be heard. For by divine judgment it is done with them that those who were unwilling to avoid evils when they could do so cannot avoid them when they wish, and that those who voluntarily rush into foreknown evils cannot flee from them once experienced.

Therefore, indicating the reason why they are prevented from being heard, he says:

“Because you asked for a king for yourselves.”

As if he said plainly: Because you asked to be given that in which, while I foretold it, you learned that all these things would occur.

As I said above, these things are foretold figuratively of the future conduct of carnal rulers, so that they might desist from asking for one in whom they had learned that such great evils would be found. But the hearts of the wicked are such that they quickly propose evil and do not quickly recover from an evil purpose.

Therefore it follows:

> **(Verses 19–20.)** “But the people were unwilling to hear Samuel’s voice, and they said: ‘By no means! A king shall be over us, and we also shall be like all the nations; and our king shall judge us, and he shall go out before us and fight our battles for us.’” [Col. 0229D]

### 11.

These words plainly describe the character of carnal subjects, because, while they desire external things, they pay no attention even to the internal losses that have been explained.

But those who rule carnally, by the very display of temporal power, give their lesser subjects great hope of protection. When, therefore, they say, “A king shall be over us, and he shall fight our battles for us,” what else do they reveal except the character of reprobate subjects who despise humble and spiritual preachers in order to be helped temporally by carnal men? [Col. 0230A]

They would certainly never do this unless they had first lost the light of their hearts. For if they despise outwardly the humility of spiritual men, they do not deserve to see with what exalted power they inwardly excel. In those carnal rulers they see the external tyranny of power, but they do not see by what weakness they are inwardly oppressed.

Because the spiritual men cling to God, they are powerful even in external matters whenever they wish; but those who withdraw from the Lord cannot, by the strength of their actions, provide the hope they promise from worldly power.

To take an example from a nearby case: Saul was chosen as a strong and powerful king to fight the battles of those who demanded a king, so that, as this sacred history testifies, he rose above all the people from the shoulders upward (1 Samuel 9:2). Chosen by God, therefore, to govern the kingdom, although he was good and no one among the children of Israel was better than he, nevertheless, when so great and so distinguished a man was abandoned to carnal strength, he lost the battles that he had undertaken to fight and lost his life as well (1 Samuel 31:1).

Samuel, however, who did not become exalted through worldly power, who humbly served not only God but also human beings, also displayed triumphs powerfully in external wars. For not long before it was said of him:

“Samuel took one suckling lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the Lord. And Samuel cried out to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him. And it came to pass, while Samuel was offering the burnt offering to the Lord, that the Philistines began the battle against Israel. But the Lord thundered with a great roar against the Philistines on that day, and terrified them, and the Philistines were struck down by the children of Israel” (1 Samuel 7:9–10). [Col. 0230C]

Let him therefore say, “The people were unwilling to hear Samuel’s voice,” so that in their disobedience the hearts of the proud may be signified as cast away by the judgment of divine justice, with great evils impending that they are destined to suffer, yet which they cannot see.

It follows:

> **(Verse 21.)** “And Samuel heard all the words of the people.” [Col. 0230D]

### 12.

Samuel certainly heard what the people said, but the people did not hear Samuel. For the reprobate people’s speaking and not hearing consisted in uttering words against God’s will while failing altogether to foresee the punishment of their wicked speech.

Samuel, however, heard the words of the people because spiritual men, when they hear the voices of proud speech, recognize the future desert of divine vengeance in them.

Let him therefore say, “Samuel heard all the words of the people,” because holy and spiritual men weigh inwardly, in the divine judgment, whatever carnal people loudly proclaim outwardly.

But because, when they discover the condemnable life of carnal subjects, they intercede for the wiping out of their crimes, it follows:

> **(Verse 21.)** “And he spoke them in the ears of the Lord.” [Col. 0231A]

We speak in the ears of those with whom we enjoy the grace of great intimacy. Holy men, because they are joined to almighty God by the bond of great love, speak to him in his ears: they seek the hearing of his divine favor with all the greater confidence because they have received a higher place for obtaining their requests before his mercy.

They speak the sins of the people through the humility of confession, but they speak them in the ears of the Lord because with great devotion they knock at the door of the Lord’s mercy through prayer.

Perhaps, however, he is said to speak in the ears of the Lord because, when holy men plead for sinners, they do not reveal to human beings the prayers they offer to God on their behalf. Hence in the Gospel the Lord forbids the disciples, saying:

“When you pray, do not become like the hypocrites, who are sad and love to pray standing in the synagogues and at the corners of the streets, so that they may be seen by people” (Matthew 6:5). [Col. 0231B]

They speak the words or deeds of the people when they lay before the Lord in prayer the sins of speech and action, so that they may be wiped away. They speak them in the ears of the Lord so that, while avoiding human testimony in their prayers, they may be heard more quickly by him who sees what is hidden.

When, therefore, Samuel is said to speak in the ears of the Lord, the manner by which someone may merit the hearing of divine favor is clearly indicated. A prayer can in no way reach God if it is uttered with the intention of being known by human beings.

Therefore, the one who is said to have spoken in the ears of the Lord is also said to have received his answer. For it follows:

> **(Verse 22.)** “But the Lord said to Samuel: ‘Hear the voice of the people and appoint a king over it.’” [Col. 0231C]

### 13.

Here it should be noted that Samuel spoke in the ears of the Lord the words of the people by which they had asked for a king, and the Lord declares himself rejected in the fact that the people asked for a king.

When he responds to the one who is praying and commands the one praying to make a king, what else does he indicate except that the devout prayer of a chosen man is never fruitless? For although it did not obtain the correction of the people, it obtained the good of instruction, since he learned that the people had been cast away because of their wicked request and nevertheless also learned what he himself ought to do for those who had been rejected. [Col. 0231D]

The prophet could therefore be both heard and not heard: by praying, he learned what he ought to be, but he did not remove the hardness of heart from the reprobate people who were making their wicked request.

Yet he could obtain this because he spoke in the ears of the Lord. For holy men, precisely because they devoutly beseech the Lord on behalf of sinners, are fortified by the help of divine mercy, so that they are in no way polluted by the crimes of those whose stains they cannot remove through prayer.

What, then, does the Lord mean when he says, “Hear their voices,” when above it was said, “Samuel heard all the words of the people”? He had heard the words of the people in order to know what was being said, not in order to grant what they were requesting.

When the Lord therefore says to him, “Hear the voice of the people and appoint a king over them,” he commanded the prophet to comply with the people’s will.

And behold, as is plainly evident, the prophet who prayed is not heard, while the people who rejected God and asked for a king are heard.

What are we to say this means except that, by the wondrous and fearful judgment of divine incomprehensibility, holy men praying for the reprobate cannot be heard, whereas the reprobate sinners themselves can be heard in the fulfillment of their wickedness? Thus the free iniquity of the latter may increase their desert of eternal vengeance, while for the former the reward of eternal recompense may increase through the affection of compassion.

And immediately, beginning to show the order by which the appointment of that same king was reached, he says:

> **(Verse 22.)** “And Samuel said to all the children of Israel: ‘Let each one go to his own city.’” [Col. 0232A]

### 14.

When we wish to examine spiritual matters, it is necessary to remove carnal concerns from our attention, because the inner mind does not penetrate what the dust of external actions blinds.

When, therefore, the prophet of the Lord commands the whole people to go away to their own places, he thereby drives away the tumult of carnal concerns from himself, so that he may see more clearly the spiritual matters that must be arranged, in proportion as the attention of earthly actions does not obscure the sharpness of his mind. [Col. 0232B]

But, indicating what sort of man was foreseen by divine judgment, he says:

## CHAPTER III

> **(1 Samuel 9:1–2.)** “There was a man from Benjamin, named Kish, son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Bechorath, son of a Benjaminite (viri Gemini), a mighty man of strength. And he had a son named Saul, chosen and good, and there was no man among the children of Israel better than he; from his shoulders and upward he towered above all the people.”

### 1.

When the person of the king who is to be appointed is described, why are the names of his fathers recorded except to indicate that his kingdom would not be understood as enduring?

Concerning the kingdom that he foresaw would come, Moses said:

“The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49:10).

Because the tribe of Judah had been foreseen for the permanence of the kingdom, the ancestry of Kish is recalled so that the royal dignity established in his son might plainly be known to be provisional rather than enduring.

But the one who begets a carnal king is called Kish, which in our language means “hard,” and he is described as mighty in strength.

Even now there are many carnal people within the holy Church who appear to accomplish great things; but they are carnal because they do not possess the grace of the Holy Spirit. They are therefore strong in bodily power because everything great that they appear to accomplish is bodily.

Kish, the father of Saul, is likewise called mighty in strength so that he may be understood to have possessed great physical power. “Mighty in strength,” therefore, means “hard,” because one who displays great things carnally does not have a heart softened through compassion in brotherly charity. [Col. 0232D]

He vigorously does deeds that people cannot imitate outwardly, but inwardly he does not know how to unite himself to the minds of his brothers through the affection of love. He performs mighty deeds that God rejects and does not care to display the affection of charity that God approves.

He is therefore hard because, while he acts with a proud heart in bodily matters, the grace of the Holy Spirit does not soften his mind.

In contrast, the holy man exults, saying:

“God has softened my heart, and the Almighty has troubled me” (Job 23:16).

Often, too, those who imitate the conduct of such men are made rulers by God’s judgment. Hence it is appropriately recalled that Saul was the son of Kish.

### 2.

But it must be asked why this same Saul is called chosen and good when he is said to be the son of a hard man.

He is called “chosen,” not according to grace but according to judgment. He is also called “good” so that the disposition of divine justice may be commended. The evils that we often suffer because of our sins are also good, since they are inflicted upon us through divine justice. Whatever is just is truly good.

Through God’s justice, reprobate shepherds are permitted to rise to the governance of the holy Church. Those who are evil through their own iniquity are nevertheless good by divine disposition; and those who are now chosen by the hidden ordering of God will ultimately be rejected at the universal judgment.

A reprobate shepherd, therefore, because he is appointed by God’s indignation to occupy his position, is called chosen; and because he is justly permitted to occupy it, he is called good.

Likewise, because he is provided as more useful than others for carrying out divine judgments, no one among the children of Israel is said to be better than he. [Col. 0233B]

He is also remembered as rising above all the people from the shoulders upward because one who follows the conduct of carnal people in his way of life strives greatly to do what another cannot do.

A carnal ruler towers above all the people from the shoulders upward when he is incomparably strong in external matters.

### 3.

All these words of praise may also be understood as intended to confound the intention of those who were asking for a king. They say:

“A king shall be over us, and he shall judge us, and he shall fight our battles for us” (1 Samuel 8).

He is called chosen and good, and it is said that no one among the children of Israel is better than he, so that every good quality might excel in the person of the king they requested. But when he proves unequal to the things the people had proposed, human presumption is confounded and, overcome, wastes away.

As I said above, the king chosen to lead the people and fight their battles, when abandoned by divine help, died crushed in battle; and to the people whom he had led into those same battles, he was then a cause not of salvation but of death.

The people would finally have attributed this to God if the one who had been chosen king by God’s judgment had not proved so suitable for carrying out what the people desired.

“Chosen and good” can also be understood as referring to what he was asserted to be, not to what he was foreseen to be in the future. He is therefore called chosen and good so that he may be understood to have been chosen by the Lord as one who was later rejected through disobedience.

For this reason, the argument itself requires that what is said of the chosen and good man up to the time of his rejection be understood in a favorable sense. [Col. 0233D]

## CHAPTER IV

### 1.

Let us therefore briefly review everything and consider, according to another meaning, what edification it contains.

Since we have said that a new priesthood is signified in Samuel, what does it mean that he grew old except that, while the holy Church is led through the passing ages of time, the beauty of conduct grows old in some priests?

Samuel grew old because the vigor of authority withered.

Samuel was, as it were, young when the priestly order, intent only on heavenly desires and seeking nothing earthly, kindled the minds of its subjects toward those things by words and examples all the more because it was able to preach the things above effectively. It possessed strength and shone with youthful beauty when it displayed the power of the heavenly word in the splendor of holy conduct, because whatever it was able to proclaim forcefully in speech, it also strove to demonstrate sublimely in life.

By the word it gave life even to dead souls; but, shining with the wondrous flower of youth, it also raised dead bodies by command. It restored sight to the blind, walking to the lame, and healing to every illness; and it shone with such beauty of holy conduct that it was a greater virtue to be able to live in this way than, by that other power, to help others. [Col. 0234A]

Samuel therefore flourished in his youth when, in the priestly order, both the wondrous power of his work and the immeasurable beauty of holy conduct shone together.

But it has now been a long time since Samuel grew old. For many ages have passed during which many of those whose virtue ought to have driven worldly joys from the hearts of others have followed the love of the world themselves.

We do not say this, however, because the holy Church has no religious men, but because few are those who, at the height of preaching, know perfectly how to despise the world and cling to the highest desires.

Samuel is therefore appropriately called both old and prophetic. He is old because in many he has lost the rigor of an austere way of life; yet he does not cease to prophesy because, while he retains some spiritual strength, he vigorously displays the power of a discerning spirit.

This can suitably be understood of one and the same preacher. They are old and prophesy who are so relaxed through negligence that they teach well but live badly.

They appoint their sons as judges when they establish in the dignity of the priesthood those who observe the periods of their more lax life.

Yet young men are ordained by the old because those who come for promotion make bold promises. They pledge the most vigorous profession of priestly life, but they do not possess its strength in their future conduct.

Young men are therefore promoted because those who ordain them do not admit them to the height of so great an order before receiving from them a profession of virtue.

First, they explain to them how sublimely they must live and how subtly they must teach: that they must live sublimely so that they may preach usefully; that they must always direct their way of life toward heavenly things; that they must not seek temporal rewards from the labor of preaching; that they must not show partiality in judgment but arrange all things according to the just balance of equity; and that they must hear of the difficulties of God’s ways and say whether they are willing to undertake their labors. [Col. 0234D]

### 2.

Many, while aspiring to sacred orders, profess that they will walk these difficult ways; but when they reach what they seek, they abandon the steadfastness of their promise.

Hence Samuel’s sons are aptly said not to have walked in his ways, but to have accepted gifts and perverted judgment.

Samuel’s ways are those that are set forth in the office of the preacher. His sons therefore do not walk in their father’s ways when those who ambitiously attain sacred orders abandon the arduous paths of religion shown to them by their elders and, with perverse intent, plunge more deeply into the desire for earthly things.

Hence they are plainly reported as turning aside after avarice, accepting gifts, and perverting judgment.

[Note: The Vatican and Gilot editions read “are forbidden.”] [Col. 0235D]

For those who neglect to labor for heavenly things must necessarily become more tightly entangled in the desire for earthly things.

To turn aside after avarice is to fall away with one’s whole attention through ambition for earthly possessions. Some people seek earthly profits through avarice but do not turn aside after avarice, because although they desire temporal things, they avoid incurring guilt in their desire for them.

Those turn aside after avarice who, for the sake of earthly things that they eagerly pursue, do not fear incurring guilt.

They consider their own soul inferior to every possession they are able to desire. Hence comes violent robbery; hence hidden thefts arise: they violently oppress those over whom the avaricious have power, and against those whose possessions they cannot attack by force, they attempt to commit theft. [Col. 0235B]

Often they also plot against those whom they cannot overpower by theft of the hands, using the falsehood of words.

Thus Samuel’s sons are marked, in an ordered progression, by the disordered confusion of avarice when it is said:

> **(1 Samuel 8:3.)** “They turned aside after avarice, accepted gifts, and perverted judgment.”

### 3.

Those who perverted judgment in order to accept gifts did not seek the darkness of night in order to steal the object they desired, but the darkness of reason.

It should be noted that the ardor of avarice is the cause of accepting gifts, and the acceptance of gifts is the cause of perverting judgment. In this way the prophet’s narrative shows the wickedness of this vice, not only how it advances in the hearts of the reprobate, but also how it can be utterly uprooted from the minds of the saints. [Col. 0235C]

For if this perversion of judgment arises from accepting gifts, the one who accepts no gifts does not pervert judgment; and the one who has completely uprooted the root of avarice from his heart easily rejects gifts when they are offered.

We gather the guilt of Samuel’s sons more fully by observing it than by describing it. If we look at abandoned churches, where the father grows old, the sons incur the disgrace of avarice, accepted gifts, and perverted judgment. For where the ruler’s character is corrupted by shameful profits, the hearts of the subject flock are easily scattered, so that they live wickedly themselves and offer examples of wickedness to others.

But it is fitting to marvel greatly at the judgments of almighty God in these matters. Samuel’s sons, when they turned aside after avarice and accepted gifts as the means of perverting judgment, provided examples of wickedness to the people over whom they ruled. Yet the people, when they asked for a king, rejected the prophet’s sons from the height of power. Almighty God both accepted the prayers of those asking for a king and was angry that they asked for one. [Col. 0235D]

We may be disturbed by these events if we do not examine their meaning carefully. For what is more just than that one should fall by the judgment of the people who, through the reprobate judgment of his own mind, so labored that the people following him would perish?

Nevertheless, when priests live badly, they are not to be judged by laypeople. Those who had presumed unjustly to cast out one who was unworthy rightly received one who was even more unworthy. [Col. 0236A]

For it is said of Samuel’s sons:

“They accepted gifts and perverted judgments.”

But concerning the king whom the children of Israel requested, very dreadful threats are pronounced, since it is said:

“He will take your fields and olive groves and give them to his servants” (1 Samuel 8:14).

And what wise person would not recognize that it is more wicked to take fields and vineyards through public violence than to alter judgment under the pretext of truth in order to accept gifts?

The former guilt is concealed by a certain shame and overshadowed by modesty. The latter guilt is seen to be all the more wicked the more openly and atrociously it is committed.

But we have not yet reached the period of the kingdom for examination, in which these evils are also described literally. Since, then, in accordance with our purpose we are speaking of the chosen and good man, it seems useful to examine carefully how the right of the king that is foretold can be understood in a favorable sense. [Col. 0236B]

For if it did not display something good spiritually, it would certainly not be said in this sacred history:

> **(1 Samuel 10:25.)** “Samuel spoke to the people the law of the kingdom, wrote it in a book, and placed it before the Lord.”

4. What does it mean that the sons of the Israelites are said to be placed in the king’s chariots? The chariots of the rulers of holy Church are their devoted desires. For when they ardently seek the joys above, they are carried aloft, as it were in chariots, through the heights. Hence Elijah is said to have been lifted up into heaven in a fiery chariot [Col. 0236C] (IV Kings II, 1): for surely no one can be raised to the joys above who does not seek them through lofty and fervent desires.

When good hearers therefore begin, through the examples of preachers, to despise earthly things and love eternal ones, then indeed the sons of the Israelites are placed in the king’s chariots. It should be noted that they are said both to be taken away and to be placed in chariots: for first they must be withdrawn from carnal desires, so that they may be properly inflamed by the fires of heavenly love. These earthly desires are not easily abandoned; hence the sons are said to be taken away. Great force is required for an elect hearer wholly to abandon earthly desires and raise himself sublimely toward heavenly things. Concerning this force the Lord says: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” [Col. 0236D] (Matthew XI, 12). Paul says: “No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (II Timothy II, 5).

This is also secretly indicated by the fact that the sons who are taken away are said to be placed not in seats but in chariots. The ancients were accustomed to fight from chariots. Moreover, one who is conveyed in a chariot is carried high and fearsome against the enemy. Elect men are all the higher and more fearsome to hidden enemies the further they have advanced in the height of inner love. They are lofty because the suggestion of wicked spirits cannot reach the level of their intention. They are also fearsome because they can reject the counsels of those spirits [Col. 0237A] all the more easily insofar as, through the strength of their inmost affection, they remain in contemplation of heavenly joy.

Whenever this is said to those who are still carnal, the goodness of compassionate threats is offered to them. It is as though he said: “Since you seek the status of virtue, you cannot remain idle in life under its discipline.” Thus they are also said to become the king’s horsemen and pursuers of the royal chariots, tribunes and centurions. All these offices belong to earthly warfare. When they are declared to become horsemen, pursuers of chariots, tribunes, and centurions, they are summoned to every exercise of battle.

They are horsemen when [Col. 0237B] the fleeting pleasures of their flesh are restrained by the power of the spirit and they rule with great authority over every seductive impulse. For one rides high like a horseman when, having been placed over his flesh through the virtue of chastity, he is free and swift, able—when he disdains—to flee the enemy, and—when he chooses—to attack. Because he has learned to preside well, he has received such increases of virtue that the enemy cannot withstand the assault of a charging horseman.

And because they follow the examples of the elect Fathers in the strength of their virtue, they are pursuers of the royal chariots. [193] The chariots of the king are the good examples of an elect preacher. In them he is shown both fighting and triumphing: for when we behold the holy works of a preacher, we see him exalted both in the contest of battle and in the power of triumph.

Those weighed down by carnal desires can see him in his chariots, but they cannot pursue his chariots. Like foot soldiers, they are sluggish for running on level ground and weak for combat. [Col. 0237C] Therefore, if they are to be able to pursue the royal chariots, they must first become horsemen: they must crush earthly desires, preside over their flesh, and shine in the armor of chastity. Then we can run after the elect Fathers in spiritual combat with all the greater propriety, insofar as, through that by which we commendably preside over ourselves, we powerfully strike the ranks of hidden enemies.

[Col. 0237D] If, however, as several manuscripts have it, we read not “pursuers” but “forerunners,” this too is not without a good meaning. The forerunner of the royal chariots is the one who praises the examples of the righteous in words. He ought indeed to be a horseman: for the reprobate is a praiser who proclaims the lofty life and teaching of the saints, which he does not at all care to imitate with an exalted purpose. But one who knows how to set before others the life and teaching of others for imitation has already begun to be a teacher of spiritual warfare. Accordingly, it is rightly added:

> (I Kings VIII, 12.) “And he will appoint for himself tribunes and centurions.”

5. They are tribunes when they are beginning; centurions when they are perfected in spiritual instruction. As we said above, the word *centurion* derives from the number one hundred. Tribunes may also be understood as spiritual men who are simple in knowledge but inflamed with love of God and neighbor. Although they do not know how to speak lofty and spiritual things, they nevertheless try, through [Col. 0238A] the examples of the elect that they know, to kindle those whom they can toward love of the Creator.

A tribe is called a kinship, or a curia. If, therefore, those who bring forward the examples of the saints for the advancement of their neighbors are called tribunes from *tribe*, they are named tribunes. They come, as it were, as a curia to destroy our rusticity when they set before us the things by which holy men pleased almighty God. And when they explain the particular virtues of many saints, they disclose to us, as it were, the nobility of spiritual kinships.

Centurions, then, may be understood as more perfect men who, while making good progress under the teaching of preachers, become their hearers and fellow workers [Note: [Col. 0237D] Gilot., “they become their assistants and associates.”]. Concerning such men the Lord says in the Gospel: “Every learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder [Col. 0238B] who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matthew XIII, 52).

Such men are distinguished not only in action but are also instructed in knowledge of the word of God. Hence they can exhort their neighbors to the struggle of spiritual warfare all the more usefully, insofar as they demonstrate in the work of virtue the lofty things they know how to preach. In their instruction they possess words; for the examples of the simple they possess works, so that the wise may understand the lofty things they say, while those who do not perceive the secrets of words inwardly may imitate the works they see outwardly.

Centurions are appointed, therefore, when through perfection of virtue they attain the summit of dignity, so that they may live sublimely and teach more usefully the higher they live.

6. But those who are centurions, when they organize the times of war [Col. 0238C], ought to make progress so that they may be recognized as capable of bearing the fruits of peace as well. After the tribunes and centurions, therefore, they are said to become cultivators of fields and reapers of crops, so that they may open, with the plow of exhortation, the hearts of those already victorious and reap from them more abundantly the wheat [194] of good works.

They plow, as it were, in a time of peace when they stir those hearts that have conquered spiritual assaults to carry out works of piety. They reap the crops when they rejoice that elect works have sprung forth from the seed of the divine word that they had scattered in the hearts of hearers. They reap wheat from a field with sickles, as it were, when through the embrace of charity they receive from heavenly conduct that with which they may be satisfied in inner devotion.

7. But as long as we live in this life, we possess no peace [Col. 0238D]. Since the ancient enemy always opposes those who act well, we must necessarily always defend the good things we do. Hence, after the cultivators of fields and the reapers of crops, they are rightly said to become makers of weapons and of the king’s chariots. They make weapons and chariots so that they may defend the very fields they cultivate and the crops they reap.

They make a chariot so that they may be swift in meeting their adversaries; weapons, so that they may be powerful. They mount the chariot so that with a great assault they may crush the camps of demons; they carry weapons so that they may destroy those whom they attack.

He stood in the exaltation of this chariot [Col. 0239A] who said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III, 20). And already secure, appearing superior to all his enemies, he declared: “No creature will be able to separate us from the love of Christ” (Romans VIII, 39). But the one who had mounted the chariot held weapons; hence he explains further: “I therefore run not as uncertainly; I fight not as one beating the air, but I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (I Corinthians IX, 26–27).

What, then, is expressed more fittingly by this chariot than the exaltation of right intention? To make a chariot, therefore, is to raise up in the minds of hearers the height of right intention. Those who receive the ministry of preaching through the examples of better men make chariots [Col. 0239B] after the labor of plowing and reaping when they teach their subjects who act well to await, from all the good works they perform, only the eternal rewards of recompense.

To despise earthly things, desire nothing transitory, love eternal things, and hasten toward them with great desires is already to preside over a lofty chariot. Concerning such chariots the Psalmist says: “The chariot of God is multiplied ten thousandfold, thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord ascends in them” (Psalm LXVII, 18).

Their weapons are sharp counsels, with which they strike the enemy [Col. 0239C] all the more powerfully because they detect his deceits more quickly. Hence, as one armed and powerful, he said: “We are not ignorant of his designs” (II Corinthians II, 11). He also made weapons when he said: “And the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one; and take up the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians VI, 16–17).

Placed in these chariots and weapons, the elect are swift and powerful. They are swift because, while they desire spiritual things, they detect spiritual wickedness in an instant. They are powerful because, while they desire the highest things more ardently, they count as nothing whatever is suggested to them from the world below by love of the world. Carried, as it were, in a chariot by its weight, they make a great assault upon the enemy; filled with holy virtues and sharp counsels, they destroy in an instant every temptation brought against them.

Nor is it without meaning that, while a chariot rolls along the earth, it raises its lower part upward and presses its upper part downward. So too the right intention of holy men, while it expects heavenly things from the earthly activities it performs, directs upward the part that it draws along the earth. And because it humbles itself before the Creator both on account of its good work and on account of its expectation of eternal recompense [195], it sinks toward the earth the part that it raises upward.

Our chariot continually rolls upon its wheels when we always direct our attention from good works toward eternal things [Col. 0239D] and take care to remain humble amid every height of our progress. These weapons and chariots are truly the king’s when they are seen not to differ at all from the form and teaching of the preachers of holy Church.

Elect preachers make chariots and weapons, therefore, when they teach their hearers to hasten toward the heavenly homeland through rightness of intention and fortification by virtue.

Nothing prevents us from understanding all these things, which we have shown in the progress of one person, as distributed individually among many [Col. 0240A]. We have shown the elect advancing through the stages of virtue: first placed in chariots; then appointed horsemen and forerunners of the royal chariots; then established as tribunes, centurions, cultivators, and reapers; and finally made makers of weapons. But since holy Church makes use of the different ministries of different elect persons, anyone who wishes may assign the individual gifts of grace to individual orders, so that each gift may properly belong to those who are more closely joined to those orders by their dispositions.

8. What, then, does it mean when it is added that the daughters of the Israelites will become makers of ointments, cooks, and bakers? The designation “daughters” sometimes signifies weakness and sometimes fruitfulness. Who, then, are the daughters of the Israelites except the elect minds prepared for the conception of the divine word?

They become the king’s makers of ointments because, while they advance through the instruction of their preacher, [Col. 0240B] they receive within themselves an abundant grace of the Holy Spirit, through which they can beneficially heal contrite hearts.
