They also become cooks because, while they are full of the fervor of the Holy Spirit, they kindle the hearts of their neighbors to love the Creator by their example. They become bakers when they refresh elect minds with the nourishment of the word of God.

The daughters become makers of ointments when they heal the wounds of sinners; cooks when, after cleansing hearts from the filth of sins, they inflame them by the example of their virtue to pursue good works; bakers when, as those making progress through examples, they no longer set examples before them but bring forth words of lofty knowledge, so that, fed as it were with solid food [Col. 0240C], they may act more vigorously insofar as, now instructed spiritually, they desire eternal things more fervently.

It follows:

> (Verse 14.) “He will also take away your fields, vineyards, and finest olive groves, and give them to his servants.”

9. What are the fields, what the vineyards, and what the olive groves that are lawfully taken away from us by rulers? When holy preachers speak for the correction of sins, they rebuke the pleasures of the flesh, the desires of the mind, and the pretenses of good works.

For if the pleasures of the flesh were not the field of an unrighteous possession, the Apostle would certainly not say: “He who sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh” (Galatians VI, 8). To sow in the flesh is to overwhelm the purpose of the mind with bodily pleasures. Those who reap corruption from the flesh do not receive the renewal of eternal incorruption in the resurrection of the elect.

The desires of the mind are rightly represented by the designation “vineyards,” because they intoxicate the hearts of the reprobate and estrange them from knowledge of the truth. Moses, reproving the fruit of this vineyard, says: “From the vineyard of Sodom is their vine, and from the suburbs of Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster most bitter” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 32). He draws a vine from the vineyard of Sodom and a shoot from Gomorrah who fills his mind [196] with the most unspeakable desires.

For one makes a vineyard, as it were, when he forgets eternal things through that by which he is also intoxicated through desires; and one who refreshes himself, as it were, beneath the shade of a vineyard and in the pleasantness of wicked delight prepares for himself the recompense of eternal fire. Hence, most aptly explaining the fruit of that same vineyard, he spoke of a grape of gall and a cluster of bitterness. A grape is seen, whereas gall is tasted: it delights the sight but makes the taste bitter. For the reprobate mind greatly pleases itself in what it desires, but in eternal punishment what is now sweet to it becomes bitter.

The king takes away our fields when an elect preacher, by his speech, removes the cheerful movements of our flesh in pleasure [Col. 0241A]. He takes away our vineyards when he cuts away entirely from our hearts the desires that intoxicate them. He also takes away our olive groves when he rebukes works of false mercy and rightly suggests through exhortation that no work has merit unless it proceeds from the purpose of a good intention.

[Col. 0241B] 10. But it must be asked very carefully why these things are said to be given to the king’s servants. For if they are lawfully taken away from us, who will be those to whom they may be fittingly assigned? Yet if we investigate this subtly, we find our holy preachers to be great ones in their dominions.

Who, then, are these servants except those of whose head the Lord says to blessed Job: “Will you take him as an everlasting servant?” (Job XL, 23). Wicked spirits are servants of holy men: servants for a time in this life, but everlasting servants in the life to come. Every day they bring about that by which holy men are crowned. For when the victory of eternal glory is granted to us from the battle of this life, those who renew against us the wars through which we are led to eternal rest undoubtedly render us a great service.

They are also servants of the victorious [Col. 0241C], as the Truth testifies: “By whom a person is overcome, of that one he becomes the servant” (II Peter II, 19). For while they stir up battles against those who are destined to conquer, they serve those who are crowned precisely because they powerfully withstand their battles for a time.

But because what advances the glory of holy men increases the condemnation of wicked spirits, the fields, vineyards, and olive groves that have been taken away are given to the servants. The demons will indeed be punished for all their wickedness in eternal punishment. In the encounter of hidden combat, when the elect conquer, they assign to their enemies the evils they repel: for the elect are tested like gold in a furnace (Wisdom III, 6), while the demons are punished for their wicked suggestion.

The servants therefore receive the fields, vineyards, and olive groves because, when sinners return to life through the preaching of teachers, [Col. 0241D] it contributes to the demons’ accumulation of condemnation that those penitents had been held for so long in their former guilt through demonic deception. These things are also given to the servants when sinners converted to the Lord through the office of a preacher recognize that they had been held by the deceit of demons in love of their former crimes.

11. What does it mean that the crops and the produce of the vineyards are said to be tithed and given to the king’s eunuch-servants? The crops of the elect are tithed when we gather their more excellent works in order to bring them forth as examples for the faithful.

There was only one who possessed in himself the fullness of every virtue, into whom the whole fullness of divinity was poured bodily [Col. 0242A] (Colossians I, 19). But because we have all received from his fullness, we possess the gifts of grace divided among us in parts. Hence Paul says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues; to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits” (I Corinthians XII, 8).

Because the number ten [197] is perfect, we tithe virtues according to the number ten when we gather the gifts of individual elect persons for the imitation of those who are less advanced. For it is written of Moses: “He was the meekest of all the men on earth” (Numbers XII, 3). Of Abraham it is also said: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis XV, 6). When, therefore, we wish to imitate meekness together with faith, we must take, as it were, tithes of food from the example of Moses and Abraham [Col. 0242B] for the refreshment of our mind, like crops belonging to the elect.

Thus the preachers bring forward Joseph’s chastity (Genesis XXXIX, 8), Job’s patience (Job I, 21), and Phinehas’s zeal (Numbers XXV, 7) as examples for us. For when they display the virtues of the perfect, they gather, as it were, the tithes of chosen harvests, which they may set before those making good progress.

Hence these same tithes of the crops are rightly said to be given to eunuchs and servants. Eunuchs are those who, by the strength of their spirit, have crushed within themselves every source of lust. Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XIX, 12).

Servants are those who still serve under another’s care in the pursuits of the active life [Col. 0242C] and cannot yet emerge into the height of charity as free men. We also find in Moses that they must serve their masters for six years (Exodus XXI, 2), so that in the seventh they may go out free. For they must first be perfected in work, so that they may proceed in due order into the height of contemplation.

The teacher of the harvests therefore gives tithes to eunuchs and servants [Col. 0242D] when those who obey him in the purity of chastity follow the chosen works of their elders. He also gives them tithes of the vineyards when he shows them with what wondrous charity our Fathers loved God and neighbor, so that they too may strive to be filled with the abundance of that same charity and, as though intoxicated and forgetful of what lies behind, love only what is future and not fail to hasten fervently toward it.

12. After all this, the servants and maidservants of the Israelites, the finest young men, are said to be taken away and placed in the king’s service.

Who are the servants of the carnal except those who, corrupted by the example of evil people and by long habit, seem to have perpetually subjected the necks of their minds beneath the yoke of the most wicked imitation? Their servants are taken away when, through the zeal of elect preachers, even those abandon their sins who seemed to be vehemently subject to the reprobate imitation of carnal people.

They are also called “finest young men.” They are young because they are strong in evil; they are called finest because they are worse than the other sinners. To them the prophet says: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isaiah V, 22).

They drink wine who, by a decision of the mind, recklessly receive the fervor of desire [Col. 0243A] and mix drunkenness, because, while they are inflamed by the fires of desire, they do not know how to return to the paths of righteousness after losing their reason. They are mighty and strong both at drinking and at mixing drunkenness, so that, because of their fervent commitment to evil, they may be shown to be finest servants.

The divine word likewise demonstrates these finest young men when it explains the devil’s appetite, saying: “His food is choice” (Habakkuk I, 16). For the ancient enemy is greatly refreshed by the wickedness of those who are worse than the wickedest.

13. By the name “maidservants” [Col. 0243B] that most wicked condition of sinners is signified: those who are exceedingly evil through iniquity and provide others with examples of depravity. For maidservants give birth to servants, as it were, when they are not merely workers but also mothers of great iniquity.

Because such people too are converted through the preaching [198] of the saints, and afterward render great service to almighty God, it is fittingly described that servants and maidservants are taken away and placed in the king’s service.

Did not the King of kings take away a maidservant when he said of that great sinner: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII, 47)? He placed her in his service when he entered a village and she received him into her house (Luke X, 38). He also placed her in his service when, rising from the dead, he entrusted her with the preaching of his resurrection (Mark XVI, 7).

He likewise took away a servant when he called Matthew from the profit of the tax office to follow him [Col. 0243C]. He also placed him in his service because Matthew prepared a banquet for him in his house and he made him the preacher to Ethiopia and the evangelist of the converted world (Matthew IX, 9; Mark I, 14; Luke V, 27).

Because, through the ministry of preachers, even those return to the Lord whose salvation human judgment might have despaired of, it is rightly described that servants, maidservants, and finest young men are to be placed in the king’s service.

14. By the name of servants and maidservants, movements and affections of the heart may also be understood. When they suggest reprobate things to us, they are servants; when the affections of the mind seek to subject themselves to the suggestions of wicked impulses, they are maidservants. Then it is necessary for us to rule over both by the strictness of our purpose.

Preachers take away our servants and maidservants when they instruct the movements and affections of our hearts [Col. 0243D] in how they are to be directed toward God’s service. They place them in the king’s service when we exercise the service of almighty God that we have learned through their teaching.

What, then, could be represented more aptly by asses than the wanton movements of the soul? They are placed in the king’s service when that mind which was accustomed to be moved toward wantonness by wicked thoughts advances through the preaching of a teacher and places its affections in the pursuit of imitating chastity.

The names of servants, maidservants, and asses may also designate those who strongly render bodily service to secular people. Yet they are placed in the king’s service because, once converted to the service of almighty God, they endure spiritual things all the more devotedly for the sake of eternal recompense, the more clearly they recognize that they had previously endured great things without fruit.

The king is also said to tithe flocks because whoever desires to please almighty God [Col. 0244A] must be pure through innocence and intent upon the pursuit of good works. Through the former one is a good tree; through the latter one also bears fruit. Because we employ many means in order to preserve innocence and display good works, the crowds of innocent thoughts themselves are our flocks.

What, then, does it mean that they are tithed, except that the subtlety of thoughts is not easily seen? Often we think that we are thinking good thoughts, but when they are examined subtly, they are not good. The flocks must therefore be tithed, so that only what is contained in the number ten may belong to the king’s right.

This is rightly accomplished in us when, through the teaching of our preachers, we learn to be perfect [Col. 0244B] not only in the performance of our works but also in the examination of our thoughts.

Finally it is said:

> (Verse 17.) “And you will be his servants.”

15. That is, they should know themselves to be subject to his authority in such a way that they dare not disregard his commands. The Lord wished to establish this royal dominion when he said: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matthew XVI, 19).

He also demanded this power from his subjects when he said: “If anyone preaches to you anything other than what I have preached to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians I, 8). Again, when sending his disciples [199] [Col. 0244C] to preach, the Lord says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke X, 16). Concerning the preachers of Judaea he likewise says to the same disciples: “Whatever they tell you, do” (Matthew XXIII, 3).

We are therefore servants of our kings when we submit ourselves to the command of our rulers in such a way that we presume to do nothing apart from their authority. Because those who strengthen their virtues through the virtue of obedience preside over them, it is said at the end of the king’s right: “And you will be his servants,” so that faithful subjects may recognize that they must remain subject to the command of preachers even when, through progress in virtue, they are led to the summit of perfection.

Teaching his disciples the same truth in the same words, he says [Col. 0244D]: “When you have done all these things, say: We are useless servants” (Luke XVII, 10). Nevertheless, because he was speaking these things to carnal people, he added:

> (Verse 18.) “And on that day you will cry out because of the king whom you have chosen, and the Lord will not hear you on that day, because you asked for a king.”

16. Those who had asked for a king cry out because of the king when those who had vowed to lead a spiritual life under a good ruler try to abandon the labors of that same life. Everyone is recognized by the face. The face of the king, therefore, is the known conduct [Col. 0245A] and instruction of a good preacher. Because such men undertake hard and difficult things for eternal life and command hard things, their carnal subjects try not to imitate but to flee their life and teaching.

Those who had asked for a king then see the face of the king whose appearance they did not know, because in their ruler they contemplate how laborious is the strictness of the heavenly journey that they had sought, before knowing it, as though it were an easy matter.

Those who asked for a king cry out because of the king when, unwilling to abandon the custom of carnal life, they strive to escape the praiseworthy imitation of the excellent shepherd whom they had wished to rule over them [Note: [Col. 0245D] In Vatic. and Guss., “they wish,” which reverses the sense intended by Gregory.].

And because with blind hearts they cannot see the light, they cry out to the Lord—that is, they entreat the Lord so that they may escape the spiritual yoke of God. But the Lord does not hear them on that day. What is that day on which the reprobate subjects entreat the Lord except the inclination toward vain prosperity? They are not heard because, by divine grace, it never happens that those who have once promised submission to good rulers can freely depart into the pleasures of the world.

Hence he added the reason, saying:

> (Verse 18.) “Because you asked for a king.”

[Col. 0245B] 17. It is as though he said: “The submission promised to spiritual shepherds is indissoluble. You readily ask for a king, but because royal authority is burdensome, you cannot easily escape their power.”

Since we are saying this with reference to the historical sense, we consider it necessary to note that almighty God, while foretelling the king’s right, provides religious superiors with a model for their discipline. Why? So that those who command the strictest way of life may not offer easy access to those who newly approach it [Note: [Col. 0245D] These words are taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 58, not only in sense but also in wording: “Let easy entry not be granted to one newly coming for conversion; but, as the Apostle says, test the spirits to see whether they are from God,” etc. We have observed many other passages taken from the same Rule in the Preface.].

Therefore the excellent teacher of that most rigorous life, an instructed disciple of the highest Truth, commands, saying: “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (I John IV, 1). And again: “Let hard and difficult things, by which one goes to God, be announced to him, so that he may know to what he is entering.”

The Lord therefore sets forth the king’s right, so that [the novice] may learn and know in every respect what carnal people will be like in observing it [Col. 0245C]; and so that the weak may not easily approach a life of virtue [200], strong superiors should by no means readily accept the weak.

The speed of conversion usually arises from rashness of decision, not from an increase of devotion. For when the weak promise strong things, this is not tested strength of spirit but confusion of discernment. The wise man admonishes all such people under one designation when he says [Note: [Col. 0246D] Perhaps Ecclesiasticus III, 22, where it reads: “Do not seek what is higher or more difficult than you.” In the Arabic version: “Do not seek what exceeds your strength.” See above, Book I, chapter 2, no. 17.]: “Do not take a burden upon yourself beyond you.”

Those who preside over others in the strong commitment of regular life must therefore receive those converted to the same life with all the greater discernment, insofar as it must be more usefully determined whether the petition of those approaching arises from strength of spirit or from rashness of will. For those who are easygoing in their actions commonly desire the hardship of spiritual life urgently, so that they may appear to desire with great strength of spirit what they seek.

> (Verses 19–20.) “But the people refused to hear Samuel’s voice, and they said: ‘By no means; rather, a king shall be over us, and we too shall be like all the nations. Our king shall judge us, and he shall go out before us and fight our battles for us.’”

[Col. 0245D] Since this has already been explained at length above, it would be pointless to linger over its examination. It follows:

[Col. 0246A] (Verse 21.) “And Samuel heard all the words of the people and spoke them in the ears of the Lord.”

18. To hear the voice of the people is to recognize what those seeking the habit of holy conduct say outwardly. We hear only the voice of those approaching, as it were, when we know what they assert outwardly; but what they will be like amid their professions, we do not see.

We must therefore speak these things in the ears of the Lord, so that he himself may receive the words of their profession. While he hears the words, he examines the hearts and, from the text of their progress, seeks the interest yielded by strong works.

Let this be heard by the minds of our novices, and let them be afraid: for what they say to us, we speak in the ears of the Lord. What they promise before us, we offer to God, so that he may now hold in our hands what he will demand.

This freedom of the ruler is the obligation of the subject, because the subject is bound [Col. 0246B] to a judgment all the stricter insofar as he can know more openly that he must render an account to almighty God for what he answers.

When, therefore, we offer to God what novices promise, we give him the written bond that they make with us. And because this is done secretly, Samuel is said to have spoken in the ears of the Lord what the people had said. We speak in the ears of friends when we conceal from outsiders what we say.

It follows:

> (Verse 21.) “But the Lord said to Samuel: ‘Hear their voice and appoint a king over them.’”

[Col. 0246C] 19. Earlier, looking ahead to the future, the prophet said: “You will cry out to the Lord, and he will not hear you, because you asked for a king.” But now the Lord says: “Hear their voice and appoint a king over them” (I Kings VIII, 18).

What is shown to us by this except that good rulers of holy Church are often divinely inspired to subject to the practices of heavenly life those who afterward will not remain devoted under the discipline of that same profession? These people will later cry out because of the face of the king, and yet by divine command they receive a king, because they are divinely inspired to approach the service of God devotedly; and, for the increase of their eternal reward, the pastoral care of their rulers must restrain them under the bond [201] of that same service, even at the cost of great labor.

They are said to cry out to the Lord because of their king; but the kings themselves should hear what the prophet sent by the Lord answers, so that amid their very cries they may know what they ought to do. “He will not hear you,” he says. Therefore they themselves ought not to hear either.

Those who are lukewarm in holy monasteries should be treated as sick people, to be healed [Col. 0246D]; they should not be expelled as dead. For if they have been sent by the Lord, they will recover amid the applications of spiritual ointments.

Let the Lord therefore say: “Appoint a king over them,” because some come to God’s service devotedly and are permitted to grow cold, yet through the zeal of the shepherds to whose command they had submitted by divine inspiration, they grow warm again in love of the heavenly homeland.

But he now explains what sort of shepherd is suitable for this, saying [Col. 0247A]:

> (I Kings IX, 1–2.) “There was a man from Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel [Note: [Col. 0247D] Omitted in Gilot. and Vatic.], son of Zeror, son of Bechorath, son of Aphiah, son of a Benjaminite, a mighty man. He had a son named Saul, chosen and good, and there was no man among the Israelites better than he; from his shoulders and upward he rose above all the people.”

### 20

What is meant by the fact that, when the king to be appointed is presented, the names of his fathers are proclaimed, except that one is unworthily raised to rule the holy Church who does not possess the nobility of the holy Fathers in his conduct? Six names of fathers are assigned, so that the perfection of their holy way of life in good action may be signified. For the world was created in six days and is brought to completion in six ages. Thus there are six fathers who are named in the genealogical order of the chosen pastors of the holy Church, because those who attain the summit of perfection in the pattern of those who follow are their sons by imitation.

The father of the king, Cis, is said to mean “hard,” because those whom holy preachers imitate are certainly not slack in life or zeal. They are hard because they do not speak soothingly to sinners; they are also hard because, in order to correct others well, they demonstrate in their own conduct the stern things that they prescribe to them.

He appeared hard who reproved the Jews, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Produce worthy fruits of repentance” (Matt. 3:7). But although he was hard toward others, he was not lenient toward himself. For to show that he maintained the austerity of repentance that he preached, the Evangelist says: “He had a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist; his food was locusts and wild honey” (Mark 1:6).

To Ezekiel also it is said: “Behold, I have made your forehead harder than their foreheads; I have made your face like adamant and flint” (Ezek. 3:8). But he who came so hard against those who were hardened in evil that he showed himself about to speak of the harsh things that were to come wept among them for seven days before speaking. For he says: “I sat where they were sitting, and I remained there seven days, mourning in their midst.”

Therefore, since holy preachers are neither gentle nor meek toward obstinate sinners, and practice what they preach with severity, Saul is rightly called the son of the hard man. The chosen preacher must imitate those who preach sharp things and observe what they say.

Hence it is further said of the father of the same king: “Strong in power.” There are some within the holy Church who are strong through pride and arrogance. They do great things; but when people cease praising what they do, they themselves cease doing those great things. He, therefore, is “strong in bodily power” who possesses from the Holy Spirit the virtue that he displays in good works.

Of this power Anna prophesied earlier in her song (1 Sam. 2:4), saying: “The weak have girded themselves with strength.” [Page 202] Of this strength the Lord promises his disciples, saying: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). In this strength he walked courageously of whom it is written: “Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee” (Luke 4:14).

Thus he who is called hard is declared strong in power, because chosen men, while preaching the highest things, demonstrate great deeds; and everything lofty that they command, and everything great that they do, they accomplish in the power of the Holy Spirit.

Of him it is fittingly added: “And he had a son named Saul, chosen and good.” For one who imitates such men is not only useful for the labor of ministry but also suited to the fruit of inheritance. Judas too was chosen for ministry, but because he was not good, he lost the right of succession.

Who, then, are signified in Saul, still chosen and good, except the chosen imitators of the holy Fathers—men useful to others through teaching and to themselves through their manner of life, able to govern others without ever ceasing to care for themselves? They are chosen and good because they seek the profit of others without suffering any loss themselves. They are full in themselves and overflowing toward others; from their own abundance they give to others in such a way that they lose nothing of their fullness. They have what they can provide to others, but, possessing what is sufficient for themselves, they provide it to no one. They strive to provide oil to others without removing from themselves the fuel of light, so that, while illuminating others, they do not extinguish themselves.

He is therefore rightly called chosen and good, because certainly one who assumes the governance of the holy Church ought to be rich, adorned with spiritual gifts, and full of merits.

And because those who excel are to be chosen from the common order, it follows: “And there was no one among the sons of Israel better than he.” His excellence is commended when it is added: “From his shoulders and upward he rose above all the people.”

By this bodily appearance, the deeds of virtue in the person of the bishop to be ordained are foreshadowed. For what is signified by the shoulder except strength? But he who rose above all the people from the shoulders upward was of such lofty stature that the tallest person among the people reached only to the king’s shoulder; the future king, however, surpassed everyone in height by his neck and head.

What are the heads except the minds of the subjected people? When they are stretched upward with great effort, they reach to the shoulder of the king who is to be appointed. For the man sought for governing the summit of the holy Church ought to possess such perfection that whatever the people wish to set before themselves as a good work, he should demonstrate in his own conduct.

The heads of the people touch the king’s shoulder, as it were, when their hearts find in their pastor whatever virtue they seek in him. But the king surpasses them in neck and also in head. For what is signified by the neck except speech, and by the head except contemplation of the mind? He excels all the heads of his subjects in head and neck if he is remarkable for the height of contemplation and the loftiness of doctrine.

He is lofty in head, as it were, when he contemplates from the heavenly mysteries things that others cannot contemplate. He has a neck above others who, remarkable for the loftiness of his speech, cannot be equaled by others.

He had raised his head on high, as it were, who said: “I shall come to visions and revelations of the Lord. I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (2 Cor. 12:1–2).

[Note: Other printed editions corruptly read “to the divisions of graces and revelations.”]

But, like a chosen and good king, to show that he also held his neck above all the heads, he said: “He heard secret words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak” (ibid., 4).

Why, however, should we admire his neck as it rises above others in the things he kept silent about? Let us match him, if we can, in the things he said. The letters of the apostle Paul proceeded from his neck; and from the time when wise men began to expound them, they have still been striving to understand better what he said. Although they make daily progress in his instruction, they can by no means reach the summit of his neck, as though leaning against it.

Let the king therefore excel in neck, excel in head, and be lofty in shoulder, so that he may be perfect in conduct, remarkable in eloquence, and higher than the rest in the citadel of contemplation.

But one who is great in conduct, distinguished in eloquence, and raised above all others in contemplation ought, before reaching the summit of governance, to possess outward signs of fraternal charity: namely, he should be so concerned for his neighbors that he seeks the gain of souls for eternal life.

Thus, in their figure, it is appropriately added:

> **(Verses 3–4.)** “Now the she-asses of Cis, Saul’s father, had gone astray. And Cis said to Saul his son: ‘Take with you one of the servants, rise, go, and seek the she-asses.’ When they had crossed Mount Ephraim and the land of Salisa and had not found them, they also crossed the land of Salim, but they were not there, and the land of Jemini, and they found them nowhere.”

### 21

Cis, who is called “hard,” signifies not only his chosen ones but also the Redeemer himself. For no one was harder toward himself than he. Indicating the harshness of this hardness, the prophet says: “Truly he himself bore our sicknesses, and he himself carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53:4).

For mortals, dying is not suffering, since they belong to a condemned and passible nature. He, therefore, was exceedingly hard toward himself, who had nothing in himself from which he could suffer; but, in order to free us by suffering, he mercifully assumed that by which he could be hard toward himself and could suffer.

The she-asses of Cis are sinful souls (1 Sam. 10). Since they have also been regenerated in the faith of the Redeemer, they are called “she-asses”; but they are lost she-asses because, through uncleanness, they have been separated from his service.

Hence, as he approached his Passion, he sat upon a loosed she-ass and a colt (Matt. 21:7), clearly showing that he had come to suffer in order to assist sinners. He confessed that he was seeking the lost she-asses when he said: “The Son of Man has come to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

He sought these she-asses both personally and still sends preachers to seek them. Cis tells his son to seek the she-asses when the Redeemer, through spiritual inspiration, commands the hearts of the chosen to undertake the ministry of preaching.

Those who proceed to the office of preaching are commanded to take with them one of the servants, because they ought to carry with them only a spiritual sense.

[Note: Gilot and the Vatican edition read: “are commanded.”] He takes one servant who, while proceeding to provide others with a pattern of life, is spiritual in everything he does.

He took one servant of whom it was foretold: “He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). He who said, “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God” (1 Cor. 2:12), had taken one servant with him. Again he says: “We have the mind of Christ” (ibid., 16).

Hence it is said through Ezekiel of the holy living creatures: “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” (Ezek. 1:12).

Thus he takes one servant when, in seeking the profit of souls, the person who is beginning this work anew determines to act spiritually in everything he undertakes. To find the she-asses is to see sinners converted into the light of holiness. They are not found as lost she-asses when reprobate hearts bury themselves in the darkness of sins.

### 22

And because they fall into the same darkness of sins through the five bodily senses, they are sought in five regions so as not to be found: namely, Mount Ephraim, the land of Salisa, Salim, the land of Jemini, and Zuph. For each person is hidden wherever he is cast by sin; and, like one who is lost, his location is unknown when he abandons the light of justice in which God placed him.

Hence, after the sin, he first seeks the human being in paradise, saying: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9). It is as though he said: “Since I do not find you in the light in which I placed you, show me where you have placed yourself.”

Hence he asks about the dead Lazarus, saying: “Where have you laid him?” (John 11:34). But the one whom he sought as though lost, in order to find him, he commanded to come forth, saying: “Lazarus, come out.”

A human being is lost when he sins; he is found when, through repentance, he now pronounces judgment against the sin. For through the sacred writings the sinner is commanded: “Speak first of your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26, according to the Septuagint). When the one who sinned begins to be justified by confessing, he is already seen in the light, where he is found to have been placed.

Saul, however, who sought the she-asses but did not find them, signifies the person of an instructed preacher, but one just beginning. The almighty God does not permit him to produce the fruit of preaching, lest he undervalue the conversion of sinners by thinking that he can convert them easily to the Lord.

Conversion is therefore deferred so that the converted may be loved; and the preacher loves them all the more because he sees more clearly that he cannot quickly win them. But while holy men cannot convert others through their preaching, they begin to fear intensely for themselves: lest they displease almighty God precisely where they had thought they were pleasing him greatly.

Often, therefore, the hearts of new preachers are so terrified that they now propose to abandon the office of preaching and devote themselves to God in silence. Hence it is added:

> **(Verse 5.)** “When he had come to the land of Zuph and had not found them, Saul said to his servant: ‘Come, let us return, lest perhaps my father has abandoned the she-asses and be anxious about us.’”

### 23

He resolves to return to his father who, setting aside his intention of preaching, desires to devote himself to God in the secrecy of silence. He is said to return who is previously said to have been sent.

The sons are, as it were, before their father when chosen men remain in the secret contemplation of the Redeemer. They return, therefore, when they come from the public work of holy preaching to examine the joys of eternal brightness.

But because holy men do nothing without counsel, Saul consulted his servant about returning to his father. We consult the servant when, with attentive mind, we take care that what we are planning should not depart from the spiritual sense.

He had resolved to return to his father who said: “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue.’ I placed a guard over my mouth, while the sinner stood against me” (Ps. 38:1–2).

The sinner stands against preachers when, in response to their preaching, he does not abandon the condition of his iniquity. And because at that point the preacher proposes to be silent before him and devote himself to God, so that he may return to his father, he becomes speechless.

But because through silence he learned God’s will more fully, his heart grew warm; and, as the fire of inward meditation blazed up, he spoke. This is also shown in this passage, because the servant, consulted, gives counsel to the one consulting him, saying:

> **(Verse 6.)** “Behold, there is a man of God in this city, a noble man; everything that he says surely comes to pass. Now therefore let us go there, perhaps he will tell us about our way, on account of which we have come.”

### 24

He calls Samuel a man of God, in whom, as we have already said, the preachers of the holy Church are signified. He is called a man because of the reverence due to his holy way of life, and everything he says is declared to come to pass without ambiguity: whatever he threatens concerning eternal punishments and whatever he promises the righteous concerning eternal joy—just as he announces it, so “the impious will go away to punishment and the chosen to glory.”

He is also said to be in the city because the chosen pastor is always known to keep watch in the common guardianship of the people subject to him. The pastor is in the city because, while guarding others, he is fortified within himself.

Hence through the prophet, in praise of all men of God, one is described in these words: “He dwells on high; the height of rocky fortifications is his stronghold” (Isa. 33:16). For the higher he is suspended in the vision of the eternal citizens, the stronger he is found to be for himself and the more useful for his neighbors.

### 25

He is also called noble because he is conspicuous for a heavenly way of life and possesses nothing of the rusticity of worldly life. He is seen to be noble from the same source from which he is seen to be a citizen.

Worldly people, because they have no ordered moral character, are rustic, as though raised in places outside the city. From their customary shamelessness of spirit they produce shameful bodily movements; and, like those who are greatly degenerate, they do not know the bearing of civilized conduct, since in everything they do they cover the appearance of their life with the earthbound obscurity of their condition.

By contrast, the men of God are noble: while vigorously doing what belongs to God, they shine with heavenly light in all their works. They have nothing degenerate about them, for in the great light of their entire way of life they emit the rays of their heavenly origin.

Saul is therefore led by the servant to be instructed, because those who are to be placed in the citadel of authority are admonished to submit to spiritual understanding under the teaching of perfect preachers.

He who says, “If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law” (Gal. 5:18), admonishes us to be led by this servant.

It must, however, be asked why the words are spoken with hesitation: “Perhaps he will tell us about our way, on account of which we have come.” Since he desires to learn spiritual things and longs to receive great gifts, he cannot know whether he is worthy of those gifts.

He therefore begins to doubt who does not presume, on the basis of his own merits, that he deserves such great things. This doubt arises in the chosen from the virtue of humility.

Hence Saul is told through the voice of the accompanying servant: “Perhaps he will tell us about our way.” For spiritual understanding does not urge us to think lofty thoughts of ourselves or to presume boldly upon almighty God, but to ask for his gifts with the greatest reverence and holy fear.

The boy is rightly called a boy because he is said always to teach humble things. When he says, “Let us go there,” and immediately adds, “Perhaps he will tell us about our way,” he plainly indicates that the Spirit works in the understanding of God’s chosen: he makes them approach spiritual gifts devoutly, while also making them fear, with great reverence, the almighty power of the giver.

Thus the one who is led by the Spirit is shown to regard the poverty of his merits, as follows:

> **(Verse 7.)** “And Saul said to his servant: ‘Behold, if we go, what shall we bring to the man? Bread has failed in our bags, and we have no small basket to give to the man of God, nor anything else.’”

### 26

It is characteristic of humble minds that, although they possess spiritual gifts, they do not consider themselves in what they possess. Because they receive the gifts of virtues from the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit who grants the gifts removes them from their estimation, so that they possess them in the virtue of their conduct but do not possess them in the swelling of pride.

Thus it is rightly said of Saul: “From his shoulder and upward he rose above all the people.” And he said to his servant: “Bread has failed in our bags, and we have no small basket,” because chosen men, fit to arrange the summit of the holy Church, also regard themselves as small through humility in the very thing in which they are great through virtue.

They have bread for the refreshment of faithful souls in the wisdom of the word, and a basket in the memory of inward meditation. When they preserve in memory for the instruction of the faithful what they gather in secret meditation, they place bread in a basket, as it were.

Of these baskets it is said in the Gospel: “They filled seven baskets with the fragments” (Matt. 15:37; Mark 8:8). When breads abound at the Lord’s table, the baskets are commanded to be filled, because when the chosen soul is refreshed in contemplation of the Redeemer above, it is instructed in the contemplation of that same truth, so that the nourishment of the word, which is seen to increase within it, may be stored in its memory for the instruction of the faithful.

They also possess abundantly something besides bread and the basket when, along with the virtue of contemplation and the teaching of the word, they abound in the resources of holy action.

Thus, so that the humility of the saints might resound in the speech of the king to be appointed, he says: “Bread has failed in our bags, and we have no small basket to give to the man of God, nor anything else.” For the Holy Spirit makes those prepared to govern the summit of the Church great in the virtue of their inward gift, but altogether small in their assessment of themselves.

Let the servant therefore say: “Let us go there, perhaps he will tell us about our way.” But let Saul regard himself as empty, because the Holy Spirit, while instructing the understanding of those who live honorably, makes them at one moment bold and at another fearful: bold, so that they may presume; fearful, so that they may not become proud. He urges them to ask for what is necessary and restrains them from falling into the vice of rashness through excessive presumption.

And because he raises those whom he makes fearful, through the strength of confidence, to presume, the passage immediately continues:

> **(Verse 8.)** “Again the servant answered Saul and said: ‘Behold, a fourth part of a silver shekel has been found in my hand. Let us give it to the man of God, and let him tell us about our way.’”

### 27

The understanding of the chosen man speaks good things like a servant when it is impelled to speak by the sign of the Holy Spirit.

What, then, does he mean by saying: “A fourth part of a silver shekel has been found in my hand”? What is this part of a silver shekel?

Since divine utterances are signified by the name “silver,” silver in the servant’s hand is the divine word in the power of understanding. It is one thing to be able to speak a word and another to be able to perceive it. For even the reprobate utter the divine utterances, but only the chosen can perceive them.

[Note: The negation is absent in Gilot and the Vatican edition.]

A thing is perceived when its power is recognized. Sick people too eat fish, but the force of their illness removes from them the experience of taste, so that they are prevented from perceiving what they appear to eat.

In the same way, carnal people speak of heavenly things that they do not love; like the sick, they make use of things that they are forbidden to perceive.

Silver is therefore found in the servant’s hand when holy men, through the merit of humility, receive the heavenly things they speak of with a great affection of charity. It is exceedingly sweet for them to speak of heavenly things, because through love they are nourished by them with a sweetness that grows ever greater.

Hence it is also written: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. 22:27). Since the word of God is food for the soul, the poor eat and are satisfied, while the rich cannot be satisfied. The chosen, who love heavenly things, grow more fervent toward them whenever they hear them; the reprobate speak and hear of heavenly things but receive them with no sweetness for the nourishment of their minds.

The “fourth part of a silver shekel” is spoken of according to the character of the age. To see the other parts of this shekel, one must consider the prophets, apostles, and martyrs. Since the sound of preaching has been distributed among the several orders according to the character of the age, each order possessed, as it were, a fourth part of the shekel.

The prophets offered their fourth part when they promised the Synagogue the coming of the Redeemer. The apostles gave their part when they preached to the Jews that the one who had been promised had already come. The martyrs also contributed their part when they brought unbelievers to faith in the Redeemer.

The fourth part of the shekel is therefore understood to remain, because through the bishops and teachers of the holy Church the word of faith is offered to the chosen faithful until the end of the world.

This part of the shekel is rightly preached by those to whom it is supplied through the servant’s hand, because those ought to preach heavenly things who have deserved to know their sweetness in the sweetness of their own minds.

This part is given so that a person may more fully deserve to recognize the way of right preaching, because the supreme teachers of the holy Church entrust the authority of preaching to no one except those whom they know to love the heavenly things they proclaim.

By these words, simpler readers should be admonished not to dare suspect the man of God of the depravity of avarice because it is said: “Let us give it to the man of God, and let him tell us about our way.” For if the prophet had a saleable word, he would not be a man of God and could by no means possess the spirit of prophecy.

When this is said, the character of the man of God is not being explained, but the devotion of the one approaching him: Saul held him in great reverence and was ashamed to appear in his presence empty-handed.

And because widespread fame invited them to venerate this same man of God, it is added:

> **(Verse 9.)** “For he was called a Seer.”

### 28

To be called is to be designated by public report. A seer is one who also looks upon inward things, which the minds of carnal people do not attend to.

Hence it is said of the holy living creatures: “All around and within they were full of eyes.” They are watchful in outward matters and provident inwardly.

By contrast, reproving the presumption of carnal teachers in the Gospel, the Lord says: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14).

A seer is also one for whom distant and absent things are present. This aptly describes holy preachers, who through knowledge are as present to spiritual things as they disdain to fix their attention on outward matters.

They possess hidden things as open and distant things as present, so to speak, because they continually understand what carnal people cannot know.

Such ought the pastor of the holy Church to be, because he has been established on the way to the heavenly homeland to provide light for his subjects. Let him therefore always scatter rays of light, so that the faithful who are subject to him, from their experience of his illumination, may draw others toward illumination.

The passage continues:

> **(Verse 9.)** “Formerly, thus in Israel everyone who went to consult God used to say: ‘Come, let us go to the Seer.’”

### 29

We go to consult the Lord when we approach learned preachers in order to find counsel for our salvation.

But because such perfect men are now rare, when we consider the flourishing religious life of former times, let us lament its decline in the present age. Struck by the misery and calamity of the present time, let us sigh that the flower of the past has withered together with the beauty of holiness.

When, therefore, we see the pastors of the Churches clinging to earthly things, seeking what passes away, and displaying no distinction of spiritual life; when no light flows into us from our prelates, let us recall what has gone before as an exercise in compunction and say: “Formerly, thus in Israel everyone who went to consult the Lord used to say: ‘Come, let us go to the Seer.’”

Israel is said to mean “seeing God,” or “in whom God is.” This name is suitably applied to the holy Church, whose people are so called. For it is also said in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Because in former times it had pastors flourishing in spiritual conduct and learned in great knowledge—men who despised earthly things with profound contempt and thought about heavenly things—the people could exhort one another toward the light they saw in them, saying: “Let us go to the Seer.”

If, then, we must go to seers, we must likewise turn away from the blind. We ought not to imitate the examples of reprobate prelates but flee them; from those who, by the merit of their conduct, know spiritual things, we should always seek instruction for our edification.

And because only spiritual men do this, it follows:

> **(Verse 10.)** “And Saul said to his servant: ‘Your speech is good; come, let us go.’”

### 30

Good is the speech than which no better can be heard. Whenever the counsels of our salvation are suggested to us spiritually, an inward word is formed in us than which none better can be found.

We praise the servant’s speech whenever we are pleased with the purpose of our spiritual understanding. We promise to go with him when we consent to spiritual thoughts.

But because a good thought is fruitful only when it is completed in action, it follows:

> **(Verses 10–11.)** “And they came into the city in which the man of God was. As they were ascending the slope of the city, they found girls going out to draw water, and they said to them: ‘Is the Seer here?’”

### 31

Those who seek the man of God come into the city, because it often happens that the life and teaching of a prelate are sought in the conduct of his subjects.

So trees too are often sought whose appearance is found not in their leaves but in their fruit. Frequently, however, newly grown shrubs are mixed with great trees and falsely claim their fruits as belonging to the trees with which they have been mixed.

Therefore, whoever wishes to distinguish the fruit should first distinguish the branches, so that he may recognize from which tree the fruit proceeds.

This is precisely how it is in the conduct of the faithful: in a chosen people, while many wicked people are mixed in, thorns arise, as it were, among good trees.

The conduct of the chosen preacher should therefore not be examined in all his subjects but only in the chosen. We distinguish the branches of the good tree with discernment when, among the people, we imitate as chosen fruits those rulers who advance through the example of their teacher, and flee as brambles those who are rejected through the deception of the ancient enemy.

It is rightly said of Saul and his servant that they came into the city and ascended the slope of that city, because when the perfection of holy men is sought among their subjects, imperfect members should not be sought but chosen and perfect ones.

Craftsmen, too, first begin their works and then complete them. A painter, when he wishes to apply beautiful colors or gold over a surface, first lays down a cheaper color.

Therefore, whoever wishes to judge the skill of craftsmen should look not at their unfinished works but at their completed ones. Let him ascend the slope of the city, so that, desiring to find the Seer, he may discover him.

For a slope is a low and excavated place. In this part of the city those are signified who have not yet advanced to a higher way of life. We ascend the slope when we avoid setting before ourselves, as an example, the level ground of weak hearers.

### 32

Then we find girls going out to draw water, because we behold the beauty of holy minds in a more perfect way of life.

The girls are the minds of the chosen: undefiled through innocence and beautiful through the brightness of virtues. Because they preserve their beauty in a more secluded life, they cannot be seen unless they go out to draw water.

The girls draw water when chosen souls pour forth streams of tears from the depths of their grief over their present exile. They are said to draw water because, while remembering with mourning that they have been cast down into this valley of tears, they cast the rope of thought, as it were, into the depths and laboriously draw up waters of tears from it.

They are also then seen to have gone out, because although what they are like inwardly remains hidden, it appears in their eyes. Those who endure life in the present age amid such great sorrow reveal how much they love their Creator.

These, then, should be asked: “Where is the Seer?” For the place of the perfect is properly known when it is shown to us by those who, through the progress of their life, are close to their way of living.

But preachers have different places: one place for themselves and another for their subjects. They remain in themselves in the highest contemplation, but for the sake of their subjects they descend to the mountain of teaching.

Through contemplation they are, as it were, in heaven; and because the things they teach are lofty, they descend when they teach while retaining their position on high as they speak of sublime matters.

More perfect hearers, therefore, are near their ruler not when he is in the height of contemplation but on the lower mountain of teaching. Hence the girls reply:

> **(Verse 12.)** “He is here, behold, before you; for today he has come into the city.”

### 33

It is as though they said: “We can indicate his location because he has gone there, where we used to see him. For if he were sitting in the citadel of his own loftiness, no one could point him out to you.”

The teacher is in the city when, through the ministry of preaching, he remains engaged in instructing the people subject to him. He is in the city when he leaves what belongs to him personally in order to administer what is common.

Because the peoples of a good preacher are fortified and strong through his exhortation, he is understood to be in the city when he remains in their service.

[Note: Gilot and the Vatican edition read: “through them.”]

Likewise, because among the multitude of the subject people some are simple and others wise, the girls add:

> **(Verses 12–13.)** “Hurry now; today he has come into the city, because there is a sacrifice of the people on the high place. As soon as you enter, you will find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat. For the people will not eat until he comes, because he will bless the sacrifice, and afterward those who have been invited will eat.”

### 34

When Samuel comes into the city, he goes up to the high place, because the chosen preacher, in instructing his subjects, speaks sometimes in plain words and sometimes in lofty ones.

When, therefore, he gives plain and intelligible commands, he is in the city; when he speaks sublime things that are scarcely understood, he is on the high place.

He is in the city when he sets examples before the simple; he is on the high place when he speaks lofty spiritual words to the perfect.

He was, as it were, in the city when he said: “I resolved to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). Again, he was in the city when he showed remedies to the weak, saying: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (ibid., 7).

But he ascended to the high place because shortly afterward he added: “Concerning virgins, I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel. I would that all people were as I myself am” (ibid., 8). He also often confesses that he ascends to the heights of speech when he says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (ibid., 6).

### 35

What, then, do the girls mean when they say: “Hurry now; today he has come into the city,” except that he was rarely seen in the city—coming late and departing quickly?

By this teaching the teacher of the holy Church is instructed to be rarely in public and frequently in secret, so that the more slowly he is seen, the more devoutly he may be venerated.

He is then received as though he were heavenly, because the longer he has remained hidden in the secrecy of contemplation, the richer are the treasures of God’s word that he brings to those awaiting him.

He can speak many good things in lowly matters who, through the secret vision of his mind, is granted to see the highest things.

And because the things that are said are seen more sweetly, the girls say: “Hurry.” It is as though they said: “If he completes what he came into the city to do, you cannot see him as he is withdrawn into his secrecy.”

### 36. [Col. 0257D]

This expression, to be sure, is now to be understood not literally as a word but as an example for religious persons. [Note: Perhaps read: “now not literally as a word,” etc.] For the holy man was so strict that he had appointed days and hours at which anyone who wished could see him. Thus they say, “Hurry.” As though they were saying: If the appointed time has passed, during the hours of his rest he does not attend to words or activities.

We who have adopted a secluded way of life must therefore observe this more attentively. We must establish hours for our ministry, so that we may remain briefly at our work and be able to hasten back to the citadel of contemplation. The periods of our secret silence must themselves be guarded with such a strict rule that even those who customarily come to us may know that, contrary to our purpose, they have no access to us.

### 37. [Cols. 0257D–0259A]

Since we have begun to explain these things spiritually, this can suitably be understood as being said against the simple. In the city, someone who appears to be a stranger is thought able to speak with Samuel; but in the high place he is not thought able to do so. For we believe that those who are simple require instruction that is plain, not elevated.

Therefore they ought to listen to holy preachers when they speak plainly to the simple, in terms they understand—not when they utter lofty things that they cannot possibly understand. Thus they say: “Hurry now; today he has come into the city,” because the people’s sacrifice is in the high place. This is as though they were saying: Since there are many who desire to hear sublime things, you must hurry now, when he appears to be instructing people who are simple like you.

The people’s sacrifice is the devotion of the chosen people. Since this devotion is aroused in the hearts of the elect by the word of preaching, it is, as it were, brought to completion by Samuel. The people’s sacrifice is in the high place when the hearts of faithful subjects eagerly desire to hear, with devotion, the lofty words of holy preaching.

Hence it is also appropriately said: “The people will not eat until Samuel has blessed the sacrifice.” [211] For more advanced hearers, while desiring to reach the highest perfection of the virtues, await with great longing the word of knowledge by which they may arrive at what they desire.

Here it must be noted that the sacrifice had not yet been offered, and yet he says: “The people’s sacrifice is in the high place.” For if a sacrifice is not a sacrifice before it begins to be offered, how was that which did not exist a sacrifice? But because we are following spiritual things, the sacrifice both did not yet exist and did exist. When the faithful elect desire to be taught more deeply, they already possess a great devotion to hearing, which after they have heard the preaching becomes much greater.

The sacrifice has not yet been offered, because that greatness of devotion which is born in the heart of the elect from the word of preaching does not exist in the heart before the preacher’s word. Yet the sacrifice is in the high place, because, through the expectation of the word, there is already in the heart of the one who desires to hear a great force of devotion.

Thus it is rightly said: “The people will not eat until he blesses the sacrifice.” Since they ardently love what is highest, they do not rest until they receive that same highest good. If the sacrifice of the mind is its devotion, the sacrifice is blessed when it is sanctified by the voice of preaching, so that, the purer it becomes, the more acceptable it may be in the divine reception.

What is blessed in God’s sacrifice is clean when it is offered, but material; once offered, it is all the cleaner because it is not merely material but spiritual, not merely clean but also cleansing. Who would doubt that sins are cleansed by the offerings of sacrifices?

Such, then, such is the devotion of the mind. When it eagerly desires to hear good things, it is clean; but when it has received holy preaching and has been blessed by its hands, it becomes all the more ardent and sacred, the more clearly it learns whom it may know in order to love more sweetly.

Beforehand it was clean, like a preparation for sacrifice, because it desired to know what is good; yet its preparation was material, because it did not yet know what it desired to learn. But it is very clean and spiritual when, having been sanctified by the words of instruction, it no longer desires to hear what it may know, but delights to experience what it loves after hearing it.

Then the sacrifice is not only clean but cleansing, because the more fervently it is kindled with love of heavenly things, the more powerfully the darkness of carnal negligence is driven away from it. For it is written: “Love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8), because we destroy our carnal tendencies when we are lifted up to heavenly things by ardent devotion.

### 38. [Cols. 0259A–0259C]

And because it follows, “Then those who have been invited will eat,” what else does this signify except that the affection of devotion is food for the mind?

We shall eat when the sacrifice is blessed, because when our devotion is lifted up by the preacher’s voice into love of the Creator, the soul that reaches the sweetness of the Creator already possesses its food. Those who refused to eat before the blessing of the sacrifice then eat.

For those who prepare themselves to receive divine sweetness with the greatest intensity of expectation, while admitting no evil desires through appetite, are filled more avidly, like the hungry, with the nourishment of devotion. Those who flee every illicit desire in order to be satisfied through devotion by the vision of inward glory await, as it were, the blessing of the sacrifice for their refreshment.

For it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Whoever, while desiring heavenly things, admits nothing foolish into his heart is pure in heart; and when he is led through the goodness of preaching to the sweetness of divine contemplation, he possesses [212], as it were, the blessing of the sacrifice in the soul’s satisfaction.

Thus he says: “Then those who have been invited will eat.” They are called hungry to the meal while the preacher speaks outwardly—those who guard their minds from wicked desires and are drawn by the grace of the Holy Spirit to experience inward sweetness.

Those who had come were already invited guests. The invited therefore eat while hungry when those who have prepared themselves to receive spiritual grace with great vigilance of mind are nourished by devotion to it.

What, then, does it mean when they say:

> “Go up, for today you will find him”?

### 39. [Cols. 0259C–0260A]

But while the elect praise the good deeds of preachers, they illuminate the hearts of their hearers with great light. For that heavenly conduct of the good teacher which they praise is day. Thus let them say: “Today you will find him.”

The preacher is found on that day when his life is no less than his reputation—when he is praised by the voice of the elect, and those who hear the praises find and recognize in his praiseworthy conduct everything they have heard.

By contrast, the Lord rebukes the Pharisees, saying:

> “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead” (Matthew 23:27).

Again he compares the vainglorious with unbelievers, saying:

> “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another?” (John 5:44).

People like these are praised in the daytime, but on that day they are not found. Those who hear their praises see, as it were, the whiteness of a tomb from outside; but when they seek the virtues that have been praised, they find within the night of sins, like the grim and rotting bones of the dead.

Thus, to signify the true glory of the just, let them say: “Today you will find him,” because when the just are praised, they possess in the truth of their conduct whatever shines brightly from them through the voice of praise.

And because such great men must be sought with eager devotion, it follows:

> “And they went up into the city. And while they were walking in the middle of the city, Samuel appeared, coming out to meet them, in order to go up to the high place.”

### 40. [Cols. 0259D–0261C]

When we hear the praises of holy men, we go up into the city, because we seek them where they descend, not where they are.

But, as I said above, the preachers’ place for themselves is the secret contemplation of divinity; their place for their subjects is preaching. Sometimes they speak plainly, sometimes loftily. Thus they have a common place for everyone, an exalted and special place for some, and a secret place for themselves.

These three spiritual places are signified here, because Samuel is said to come out, to appear in the middle of the city, and to go up to the high place. For the one who came out in order to appear had been where he had previously remained hidden.

Priests therefore come out when they come from the secrecy of meditation to preach. They appear in the city when they speak more plainly, that is, about what must be done or understood. They go up to the high place when they either command the wise to perform difficult works or reveal lofty mysteries.

Our ordered ascent is therefore shown by the fact that Saul is said to go up in the city. The places of our pastors where they customarily pray or remain in solitude are to be venerated, not entered. We can recognize this not only by example but also through divine exhortation.

In the Song of Songs the bridegroom declares:

> “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not awaken the beloved until she herself wishes” (Song of Songs 3:5).

The minds of the perfect are brides, because when they place themselves in the secrecy of divine love as though [213] in a bridal chamber, there, through vision, they find the one to whom they are joined by ineffable love.

When the bride sleeps in the bridal chamber, she is joined to the bridegroom, because when the elect soul of the preacher is hidden in secret contemplation, it is placed, as it were, in the bridegroom’s chamber.

Whoever awakens her takes her away from the bridegroom, because the rest of the elect soul is not only its own delight but also the bridegroom’s. Hence the prophet says:

> “The bridegroom will rejoice over the bride” (Isaiah 62:5).

The bridegroom therefore rightly adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken the bride as long as she wishes to sleep, lest, when she rises from the rest of the bridal chamber, he himself lose the enjoyment of love.

Samuel’s coming out is therefore to be awaited, because holy men are to be venerated in the secrecy of their silence, not disturbed.

We must therefore go up in the city, because the elect teacher in the common place of instruction appears to be of greater benefit to his people precisely insofar as he is known to come out in order to benefit them.

Here it must be noted that it is not said of Samuel, “Today he went up into the city,” but, “Today he came into the city.” Of Saul and the boy, however, it is not said that they came but that they went up. He came as though along level ground; they ascended as though to a height.

What else is shown to us by this except that the plain things preachers speak are not plain to us? We do not therefore come into the city but ascend when we either perceive the plain things of preaching with difficulty or bear with labor the small things commanded to us.

But because standing in the city means being fortified, we ascend: for when great men teach us to do small good works, they strongly forbid us to yield to the counsels of evil spirits. And because it is very laborious to overcome every temptation, we strive to reach the words of the teachers that command this as though through the labor of ascent.

But because it is written, “Each one will receive his reward according to his labor”—which is understood not only of eternal recompense but also of the present—the almighty God grants his elect increases of virtue in proportion to the merit of their work (1 Corinthians 3:8).

To Abraham, who did not spare his son, it was said:

> “By myself I have sworn: because you have done this thing and have not spared your son for my sake, I will bless you and multiply your offspring” (Genesis 22:16).

Often those who labor faithfully in doing what they know deserve, through divine grace, to learn greater things that they may do.

In their figure Saul is rightly said first to go up in the city and afterward to be led by Samuel into the high place.

To come out to meet someone means to encounter one who is coming along the same road. When we wish to learn the way of salvation from holy preachers, they come out to meet us when they encounter us with the word of salvation that we seek.

They come, as it were, along the same road when they hasten to teach us what we have resolved to learn.

This is plainly a moral interpretation applicable to all. If we investigate what spiritually concerns certain people, he comes out to meet us, because he foreknows that the one to be ordained king is coming to him.

How he knows this is then added:

> “The Lord had revealed Samuel’s ear one day before Saul came, saying: ‘At this very hour tomorrow I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him as leader over my people Israel, and he shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines.’”

### 41. [Cols. 0261C–0262D]

He therefore went out to meet him in order to lead him into the high place, because the one who is sought for the governance of holy Church must both be shown by divine grace and called to an exalted way of life.

Why is Samuel’s ear called by a diminutive, except to signify the humble [214] understanding of a spiritual teacher? Samuel’s ear is revealed by the Lord when the preacher’s humble understanding is instructed by the Holy Spirit, so that he may hear what he is to do and arrange what he has heard.

But we must examine carefully what is said: “One day before.” Day is the life of the just, as Paul testifies:

> “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

When the life of the elect is revealed, the hidden day is revealed. A human being sees the outward appearance of a good work, but God sees the light of the heart.

Because both the elect and the reprobate are hidden in their heart’s intention, the Lord indicates the coming king “one day before” when, by his grace, holy preachers recognize in those who are to be promoted that purity of intention precedes the testimony of good works.

There is no light of action that is not preceded by uprightness of intention. The king to be ordained is therefore rightly recognized one day beforehand.

But they do not see the following day unless it arises from the preceding one, so that they consider day before day, intention before action, and see as sent by God in the light of holy action the one whom divine grace shows to shine through the purpose of his heart.

And because he is presented at the very hour at which he is promised, what else is meant except that the one who is chosen must be perfect not only in body but also in mind?

When God speaks to holy men, it is the full light of day. Day has a beginning and an end. Near the end he reproves sinners, saying:

> “Adam, where are you?” (Genesis 3:2).

Since neither those who are beginning good works nor those who grow sluggish in good works are to be promoted, the preacher is sent at the hour of perfect speech, when one is presented who shines with the full light of good works and gleams with the complete radiance of truth.

He is also described as a man coming from the land of Benjamin. He is called a man because of the strength of his works; he comes from the land of Benjamin because of the orthodox confession of faith.

Benjamin means “son of the right hand.” Who, then, is this son of the right hand except the one of whom it is written:

> “He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father” (Mark 16:19)?

The land of Benjamin is therefore holy Church. Since heretics have been expelled from this land, the king comes from the land of Benjamin when, untainted by any heresy and catholic in faith, he assumes primacy in holy Church.

He enjoys the designation “man” if he is firm in faith and strong in action.

He is commanded to be anointed as leader over the Lord’s people, because outward sacraments benefit those priests who are not unworthy of the gifts of those same sacraments.

Alternatively, priests are anointed when, through the ministry of those who ordain them, they receive increases of spiritual graces.

Hence it follows:

> “He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines.”

As anointed men, they can save others because they have received spiritual graces more abundantly. Those who save the people are anointed over the people, because those whom the Lord appoints to govern others receive the spiritual gifts of charisms by which they can benefit them; and they are superior in merit to those whom they precede in rank.

And because often a good pastor is chosen on account of the merit of a good people, it is rightly added:

> “For I have looked upon my people.”

Again, because a good pastor must be sought from the Lord with great prayers, he adds:

> “Their cry has come to me.”

### 42. [Cols. 0262D–0263C]

But perhaps some are troubled because what is said here appears contrary to what was said above. There he says:

> “They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them, according to all their works which they have done from the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt until this day” [215] (1 Samuel 8:7).

Now, however, he says:

> “You shall anoint him as leader over my people Israel, and he shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines, because I have looked upon my people; for their cry has come to me.”

Earlier, the king appears to be permitted in anger; now he is appointed as if by a merciful and gracious God.

Who does not see how far these words of graciousness differ from that sentence which Samuel later pronounced against him?

> “Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, so that you shall not be king” (1 Samuel 15:26).

We quickly resolve this if we examine carefully the force of the words themselves. All these words of divine graciousness are attributed to the merits of the people: “He shall save my people”; “I have looked upon my people”; and “Their cry has come to me.”

The king is therefore decreed for the sake of those whose cry is heard. Although Saul was to be rejected from the kingdom because of future wickedness, he nevertheless possessed, as long as he reigned, something by which he could benefit the people subject to him.

He was to be vigorous in war but proud in mind. He was to have that by which he could fall, and that by which others could stand.

Foreseeing what could benefit his subjects, the Lord therefore says:

> “He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines”;  
> “Their cry has come to me.”

Yet it still appears very contrary that the cry of a people who are reproved for rejecting him should be heard. The answer is that there were both reprobate and elect among that people.

The reprobate are reproved there for rejecting the Lord; here the desires of the elect reach the ears of almighty God.

What should we conclude from this except that it is often beneficial for the elect when wicked rulers are appointed? It is therefore no wonder if God becomes angry over his rejection and appoints a king, because the dignity of the future king was both bad and good: bad because it was proud, but good because it was vigorous in defending his subjects.
