We see all of this now taking place in holy Church. Often the one who assumes primacy over it is useful to others in speech but proud in mind for himself.

By preaching virtues he destroys vices as though standing upright, but by thinking highly of himself he falls. By preaching he saves God’s people, but through pride he brings himself to ruin.

As a powerful king, he crushes the hidden enemies of God’s people through speech, but through arrogance he falls from the height of the kingdom.

He is therefore constituted king not for himself but only for the people, when in holy Church one is permitted to preside who, through pride or wicked living, tramples upon the good things he preaches.

### 43. [Cols. 0263C–0264C]

Here it must be noted that when a pastor is chosen in holy Church, he is sometimes appointed for himself and for the people; sometimes neither for the people nor for himself; sometimes for himself but not for the people; and sometimes for the people but not for himself.

He is appointed for himself and for the people when an elect preacher is given to elect subjects, because by the means through which the multitude of his subjects is led to the eternal homeland, the good pastor’s rewards of merit are increased.

A pastor is given neither for himself nor for the people when a reprobate people is permitted to have a reprobate pastor, so that he presides and they obey in such a way that neither the teacher nor those taught deserve to reach eternal goods.

Concerning these the Lord says through Hosea:

> “I will give them kings in my wrath” (Hosea 13:11).

A king is given in God’s wrath when it is decreed that one worse than the wicked should rule over them. Such a pastor is given when such a people is accepted for governance that both together are condemned to eternal punishment.

A pastor is given for himself but not for the people when a good man is placed over the wicked, as the Lord says to Ezekiel:

> “I am sending you to the children of Israel, to an apostate nation [216] that has departed from me” (Ezekiel 3:3).

A pastor is then given for himself but not for the people when, even if the elect preacher cannot convert his hearers to God, he nevertheless does not lose the eternal rewards of his own labor.

A pastor is given for the people but not for himself when a pastor is assigned to good subjects who possesses gifts by which he benefits them but does not benefit himself.

Such were those of whom the Lord commands his disciples:

> “Do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23:3).

It is as though he were saying: Take from them as your own what they have received for your benefit; but leave in them as their own what they possess not for your gain but for their destruction.

Saul, therefore, is chosen after rejecting the Lord, and yet he is said to free the Lord’s people from the hand of the Philistines, because almighty God often benefits his good and faithful people through those rulers who do not please him in the office of their rule.

It follows:

> “When Samuel looked upon Saul, the Lord said: ‘Behold the man of whom I spoke to you; he shall rule my people.’”

### 44. [Cols. 0264B–0264D]

This was accomplished on the following day, which the Lord had promised on the preceding day, saying:

> “Tomorrow at this same hour I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him over my people Israel.”

The one who was promised on the first day is therefore seen on the second, because the preachers of holy Church seek the virtues of the elect in the secrecy of their life.

Those who are to be promoted promise something great about themselves while they bring forth good things. Thus on the first day the king is promised, because preachers see the great works of the elect and, as though the Lord were speaking, recognize inwardly those whom they wish to appoint as rulers of holy Church.

Samuel looks upon him on the following day when the preacher sees in the great light of conduct the one who is to be promoted. Then, as though the Lord were indicating it, he recognizes the king who is to be appointed, because he sees that the one who excels in the lofty citadel of holiness is worthy to be preferred to others.

And because those who are great in merit are small through humility, it follows:

> “Saul approached Samuel in the middle of the gate. ‘Tell me, I beg you,’ he said, ‘where is the house of the Seer?’”

### 45. [Cols. 0264D–0265A]

If the preacher is in the city when he speaks plainly and commonly understood things, what is the gate of this city except humility?

Knowledge of the divine word is hidden from the proud and revealed to the humble. Hence in the Gospel he speaks to the Father, saying:

> “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11:25).

By “the wise” he meant the proud, who think highly of themselves; by “little ones,” the humble. Another Scripture speaks of them, saying:

> “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5).

He resists the proud so that they may not understand eternal goods, but gives grace to the little ones so that, with him revealing them, they may know those same eternal goods.

The elect therefore come to spiritual understanding through humility; to hear the preachers they go, as it were, through the gate.

The elect preacher, Samuel, also meets Saul at that same gate because he speaks spiritual things humbly. Both are, as it were, in the gate when what the elect preacher says is heard humbly by another elect person.

### 46. [Cols. 0265A–0265D]

But the newcomer had found the one whom he was seeking and did not know it. Thus Saul says to Samuel:

> “Tell me, I beg you, where is the house of the Seer?”

This is characteristic of great men: they are difficult for the least to recognize. They are despised in the flesh [217] but exalted in mind. They desire to appear contemptible outwardly, yet do not cease to perform venerable deeds.

Because those who greatly desire to advance through their example admire them not only in outward matters but also in their innermost qualities, they see in them outwardly what carnal people may despise, while at the same time observing what spiritual men ought to venerate with great admiration.

When they hear that these men are exalted by reputation, they desire to recognize them in the height of their conduct.

According to the historical account, Saul saw Samuel but did not recognize him, so that what happened to them figuratively might signify spiritual things for us.

When we are little, we seem to see perfect men when we hear their virtues reported, but we do not recognize those whom we see, because we cannot know them through experience; we retain in the eyes of the heart what we have received through hearing.

When we ask them to disclose the secrets of their conduct for imitation, we question them, as it were, about their own house.

Their house is their way of life. John’s disciple wished to know this house when he asked the Lord:

> “Teacher, where are you staying?” (John 1:38).

Since he was to be led, as a member of the household, into the Lord’s intimacy, he heard:

> “Come and see.”

Philip had seen this house but did not recognize it, and the Lord said to him:

> “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

It is also written of the Lord that he spoke with Moses as with his friend. Yet Moses, seeing but not recognizing, asked:

> “If I have found favor in your sight, show me your face” (Exodus 33:13).

Since the spiritual conduct of the saints is disclosed only to the devoted and those who plead for it, Saul likewise begs that Samuel’s house be indicated to him.

Holy preachers, when they hear great things about themselves, humble themselves through humility rather than becoming inflated. They know that they show those who ask great things to imitate; they also know that, amid the great things they show, they must not appear great through boasting.

Thus it follows:

> “Samuel answered Saul and said: ‘I am the Seer. But go up before me to the high place today, so that you may eat with me, and tomorrow I will send you on your way.’”

### 47. [Cols. 0265D–0266D]

What does he mean by saying, “I am the Seer,” except that he shows himself humble, just as he appeared to the eyes?

It is as though he were saying: You consider the one you seek great, but the one you see is small. In the word “Seer” there is no proclamation; rather, it lies in the word “I.” It is as though he were saying: “The Seer is I”—not the one you imagine, but the one you see.

But whoever knows how to humble himself knows how to give gifts not as a humble man but as an exalted one. Thus he commands Saul to go up before him to the high place so that he may eat with him.

He goes up to the high place who raises his mind to know higher things. To go up to the high place is to prepare the heart to understand what is higher.

Hence Peter is taken up onto the mountain so that he may be worthy to see the glory of the transformed Redeemer (Matthew 17:1). In that ascent of the mountain the lofty preparation of the mind is expressed, because the one who does not set his mind on exalted things through intention cannot see what is high.

Since we understand sublime things better when prepared, Saul is commanded to go up to the high place before Samuel. We ascend, as it were, to the high place before the preacher when we first direct our minds toward knowing higher things, and afterward he speaks to us of the things toward which we have directed ourselves.

What, then, does he mean when he says, “So that you may eat with me today”?

When holy preachers [218] speak of heavenly things, they refresh the hearts of their elect hearers. Truth itself testifies that the word of God is food for the soul:

> “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).

Bread is nourishment for the body; the word is nourishment for the mind. Those who refresh the body without the mind are dead in mind though alive in flesh.

Thus Paul says of the luxurious widow:

> “She is alive but dead” (1 Timothy 5:6).

The widow would not die through the delights of food if she satisfied her soul with the food of God’s word, since Paul himself says:

> “Nothing is unclean that is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:4).

But the living widow dies when she nourishes the body with food and kills the soul with hunger (Matthew 4).

A person therefore does not live by bread alone, because a human being consists of soul and body. Just as he lives in one way through the body, so each part must be nourished by different foods.

Therefore we eat when we ascend with the prophet, when we raise our minds to the heights of the divine word so that we may be filled through devotion with its heavenly flavor.

### 48. [Cols. 0266D–0267C]

And because the preachers themselves greatly love the heavenly things they speak, we eat together, as it were, when they bring forth through devout speech what we place in the belly of the soul by devout hearing.

We eat together because we hear the word of God together. Truth says to the preachers:

> “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

Paul also confirms this when he asks his hearers:

> “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3).

Since Christ and his Spirit speak in holy preachers, the preachers themselves hear the one speaking all the more clearly the nearer they are to him whose dwelling they are worthy to be. [Note: [Col. 0265] Vatican and Gilot read quanto eis (“the nearer they are to them”); below, Gilot has meruerunt (“have deserved”) for merentur (“deserve”).]

They can therefore be nourished more fully by the food of the word because they already possess within themselves the chamber of refreshment.

They are friends of the bridegroom, standing and rejoicing with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. When holy preachers speak divine things, they hear; but because they know through certain experience when the Spirit speaks in them, they hear themselves but not from themselves. They themselves speak, but they venerate another who speaks through them.

In what they hear, speak, and refresh, they both refresh and are refreshed. They refresh their hearers when they bring forth the word with their own voice; they themselves are refreshed when the word they bring forth is brought forth to them through divine revelation.

Yet those who have experienced the delights of the mind in the Spirit’s speech are filled more devoutly. Is it not the experience of the Spirit speaking when they see themselves unconsulted and unprepared, and suddenly consulted and ready? When they know what they did not know, possess what they did not possess, lose the mind’s torpor, and suddenly burn with wondrous devotion? When they are immediately and in a moment wonderfully filled with the fullness of knowledge, and express with marvelous eloquence what they have understood?

Elect preachers therefore experience the Spirit speaking within them in the sudden revelation of truth. They possess sudden ardor of love, fullness of knowledge, and most eloquent preaching of the word. They are suddenly instructed, suddenly inflamed, filled in a moment, and enriched with marvelous power of speech.

The Lord speaks of that sudden experience:

> “It will be given to you in that hour what you are to say” (Matthew 10:19).

Cleopas speaks of the sudden ardor of love:

> “Was not our heart burning on the way, while he was speaking and opening the Scriptures to us?”” (Luke 24:32).

Luke also mentions the experience of fullness and eloquence:

> “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a powerful [219] spirit coming, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting” (Acts 2:2).

Filled with the same Spirit, they also spoke, signifying what we assert: namely, that by speaking they nourish others, while by hearing they are nourished by what they say.

Because they recognize the sound of the mighty Spirit as ardor, speech, or fullness, they feast more sweetly on spiritual gifts the more worthily they have been admitted to his banquet.

Thus he says:

> “Go up, so that you may eat with me today,”

because the good teacher, when he devoutly receives into the devotion of his mind the things he says, feeds himself and those who hear him together.

49. By contrast, reprobate teachers, because they do not love what they say, go hungry while they feed others with their words. For since the Lord has declared the word of God to be the nourishment of the soul, and the word of God in a mind to be instruction filled with learning and devotion, those are not nourished by the word of God who do not devoutly listen to what they themselves utter. The Apostle, already filled, as it were, with that sweetness of the word, says: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). There is one kind of fullness belonging to the word, and another belonging to a book. Only the elect can receive from the fullness of the word, whereas even the reprobate can receive from the fullness of Scripture. The book of the blessed apostle John and the book of the blessed apostle Paul are indeed fullnesses—the fullnesses received from them. Paul or John wrote their words, but the one who inspired each of them was the Word speaking through them. Whoever therefore receives the word of Scripture [Col. 0268A] not in love but in knowledge receives it from fullness—not of the word, but of the book. And because he receives a dead thing, he himself does not live in receiving it.

But why do I call Scripture dead? It is not merely dead, but killing. For it is written: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Every divine writing does this. The letter is the body, while the spirit is the life of that body. One receives a body that has been given life and that gives life when one reads the letter and refreshes the mind with the love of understanding.

Reprobates, then, who search through the Scriptures they do not love, who speak boldly outwardly about what they do not inwardly understand, while others receive with devout minds the nourishment of the Scriptures that they expound—these are as though others, rather than they themselves, were being filled by what they give. Let Samuel therefore say [Col. 0268B]: “Come up, so that you may eat with me today,” because elect teachers give their subjects the word, and both hear it and are filled by it together.

This is clearly demonstrated in the very word we are discussing. For who doubts that Samuel wrote this Scripture which we are expounding? Yet he who wrote it says: “Samuel answered,” plainly showing that what he himself was writing was being imparted by another. Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit who speaks through him speaks through him about him, he says: “Samuel answered Saul: Come up before me to the height, so that you may eat with me today.” He says what he hears; he both hears and speaks at once.

Thus, while the elect preacher listens and speaks with great reverence and love, good hearers receive what is said with great devotion; Saul and Samuel are said to eat together on the height. Again, because preachers are more worthy and fervent than their hearers in the nourishment of the same word, it is said not that Samuel will eat with Saul, but that Saul will eat with Samuel.

And because such splendid instruction of the mind exists in the great light of spiritual life, he does not say, “So that you may eat with me tonight,” but “today.” He also sends him away in the morning. “Morning” signifies the beginning of the following day. The day that follows is the clear light of holy conduct. He therefore says:

220 (Verse 19.) “I will send you away in the morning.”

50. He is sent away from the height in the morning who, when he advances toward the light of higher knowledge, resolves to remain in the great light of good works. Or he is sent away in the morning who intends to preach to others the word of great knowledge that he has learned from the preacher’s mouth.

For whenever we make good resolutions, we are, as it were, in the morning, at the beginning of the day, because we have already begun to behold the brightness of goodness which we are to follow. But this morning grows into full day when the person who has resolved either to perform great good works or to preach the lofty joys of eternity displays what he has resolved to do in the great light of virtue.

Saul is therefore sent away from the height in the morning because hearers of good preachers do not delay in loftily practicing what they have heard from them on high. Yet elect men know both how to conceal and how to reveal the good things they possess. They conceal them so that they may not perish through pride, but reveal them so that they may not remain fruitless. While they conceal them, they guard them; but while they reveal them, they bring forth fruit. For it follows:

[Col. 0269A] (Verses 19–20.) “I will tell you everything that is in your heart; and concerning the donkeys that you lost three days ago, do not be anxious, for they have been found.”

51. How preachers strive to conceal themselves is shown above in Samuel’s words, where he says: “I am a Seer.” But now, because he says, “I will tell you everything that is in your heart,” what else do we understand except that holy men often both conceal and reveal the virtues they possess?

But, as I said, they conceal them so that they may not appear great because of their great virtues; they reveal them so that the elect may imitate them. They assert that they possess the word of wisdom or the spirit of prophecy, not so that they may be revered, but so that they may be heard. Thus the Psalmist, indicating that he possesses the grace of the word, says: “I have understood more than all my teachers” (Ps. 118:99).

Confident, then, in his spiritual expertise, he invites us boldly, saying: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33:11). The prophet Micah affirmed that he was a prophet when he said: “Would that I were not a man who had the spirit, and that I spoke falsehood instead” (Mic. 2:11). Hence Elisha says of the Syrian Naaman: “Let him come to me, and let him know that there is a prophet in Israel” (2 Kings 5:8). Hence Paul says: “Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they the offspring of Abraham? So am I. Are they ministers of Christ?—I speak as one less wise—I am more” (2 Cor. 11:22–23).

By contrast, Amos says: “I am not a prophet, but a herdsman, one who nips sycamores” (Amos 7:14). Hence also Paul, when he wishes to conceal himself for the sake of guarding himself, says: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9). When John the Baptist was questioned, he said: “I am not a prophet” (John 1:21). He was not a prophet for the sake of self-exaltation, but he was a prophet, and more than a prophet, for the sake of his ministry.

Samuel therefore says, “I am a Seer,” in order to guard himself; and, in order to make himself useful for winning souls, he says: “I will tell you everything.” Anyone who wishes may understand this in the same way: when he says, “I am a Seer,” if he asserts that he is a seer, he says it in order to share with the elect the good that he possesses. To prove what he has asserted, he adds immediately: “I will tell you everything.”

This is what the teachers of holy Church do. When they discern the virtues and vices of minds, they plainly know both how to heal vices and how to advance virtues. He tells everything that is in the heart when he deigns to explain, through evident instruction, the path of virtue that the good hearer desires to follow.

And if he is a great man who has resolved not only to perform good works but also to preach them, preachers tell everything that is in his heart when they open to his mind whatever he desires to know from their teaching. Since the person to whom he speaks signifies one who devotes himself to the gains of preaching, he adds:

“And concerning the donkeys that you lost three days ago, do not be anxious, for they have been found.”

52. Above, this was explained in the person of Saul as applying to inexperienced preachers. He has lost the donkeys who has in no way led to repentance the sinners to whom he supplied the word of life. He would indeed find them if those who had hidden themselves in the night of wickedness [Col. 0270A] returned to the light of righteousness, in which men could be found.

Why, then, does he say, “They have been found,” except because great men often perceive that the good of salvation can readily be found in those whose salvation the unlearned despair of? Even skilled physicians of the body often undertake to cure those whose recovery the inexperienced cannot hope for.

In the same way, sinners are often drawn to repentance and satisfaction by learned teachers [Note: [Col. 0269] Alternatively, “to satisfaction for repentance,” as Gussanv. observes], though they could not be drawn by inexperienced beginners. Since, therefore, through the preaching and example of the perfect, those return to the Lord in repentance who could not be converted through the ministry of others, Samuel rightly says that the donkeys have been found—those whom Saul was unable to find.

This saying may also be understood as referring to the progress of the person being appointed as ruler. It is as though he said: “As you advance in learning and in life, you will also be able to win for the Lord those whom you have not yet been able to win.” The virtue of progress is so certain that its fruits, though they do not yet exist in reality, exist securely in hope.

And because by these words he is invited to endure the labors of holy preaching, Samuel explains what gains of reward it should expect, saying:

(Verses 20.) “And to whom will belong all the best things of Israel, if not to you and to all the house of your father?”

53. Israel, which is interpreted as “seeing God”—what does it signify more appropriately here than that blessed society of the citizens of eternity who, having come through the labor of this life, have attained the eternal vision of almighty God?

What, then, are the best things of Israel except the gifts of eternal recompense? Paul says: “Each will receive his reward according to his labor” (1 Cor. 3:8). Again he says: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15:41).

The rewards and prizes of all the faithful are therefore the good things of Israel. But because the reward of elect preachers is supreme, the best things of Israel belong to them. Concerning these best things of Israel, the Lord promises his faithful servant, saying: “He will set him over all his goods” (Matt. 24:47). For whoever is appointed not merely over all goods but above all goods is shown to possess not only the good things of Israel but also its best things.

Let Samuel therefore say: “To whom will belong all the best things of Israel, if not to you and to all the house of your father?” It is as though he said: “Even if the labor of preaching is great, it should be borne with that much greater devotion because it has greater gains of reward.”

The teacher of holy Church should therefore weigh this carefully: the best things of Israel belong not only to him but also to his whole house, so that the one who expects such supreme and excellent things may always perform greater and more excellent works. For these supreme rewards are owed not to the highest rank but to the highest labor.

The distinguished teacher did not say, “Each will receive a reward according to his dignity,” but “according to his labor.” When, therefore, the best things of eternal life are promised to preachers, great labor is imposed upon them in this life. For the one who does not strive to be better cannot prevail upon himself to possess what is better than others.

And because this is common to all preachers of holy Church, the best things of Israel are promised not only to Saul but to the whole house of his father. For sons are born, as it were, from a father when, within the order of preachers, others are newly appointed after others, shining with the same nobility of holiness.

The house of the preacher is also his spiritual way of life. The best things of Israel therefore belong to his whole house, because wherever priestly conduct exists, there is that house; and it is so exalted that, by the height of its merit, its rewards in eternal life are the best.

Preachers should therefore examine themselves carefully in this matter: the best things of Israel will belong not only to them but to their whole house, because if they depart from that house, they will not possess the best things. If they hold only the loftiness of preaching, they will not possess the best things, because they do not maintain the elevation of life.

But each elect person, when he hears great things about himself, brings his weaknesses to mind, so that he may guard himself against pride and not lose the good things he possesses. Hence it follows:

(Verses 21.) Saul answered and said: “Am I not a son of Gemini, from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least among all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? Why, then, has he spoken this word to me?”

54. It is as though he said: “Why do you attribute such great things to me, when I am nothing?” He is a son of Gemini who imitates the negligent in caring for himself and in providing an example to his neighbor. He is called “Gemini” because, while neglecting care of himself, he does not offer others examples of good works.

Whoever imitates such people is therefore called a son of Gemini. He is said to be from the smallest tribe of Israel because the lowest order in holy Church is that of sinners who have been converted. It is rightly said, then, that the one who confesses himself a sinner is from the smallest tribe of Israel.

His clan is also said to be the least among the others because, according to the word of Truth: “Whoever relaxes one of the least commandments will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19).

Benjamin is called “son of the right hand.” By this designation the people of holy Church are signified: having been born in faith in the Redeemer, they are prepared through good works for the goods of the heavenly homeland. The right hand of God is that strength of eternal life.

The clans of the tribe of Benjamin are the various ways of life of the elect. Just as various clans come from one beginning of generation, so various ways of life among the faithful arise from one origin in orthodox faith.

When holy men humble themselves, confessing that they are sinners and yet affirming that they rightly believe in God, they assert themselves, as it were, to be both sons of Gemini and of the least clan of Israel. But because, in accordance with the word of Truth, the more they humble themselves, the more they are exalted (Luke 14:10–11), it follows:

(Verses 22.) Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the dining hall, and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited.

55. Samuel takes Saul up when the preacher of holy Church opens the heights of his preaching to an elect hearer. A subject is taken up when, through the teacher’s word, he is raised to knowledge of heavenly things.

And because he desires to know spiritual things not with a carnal intention, Samuel took not Saul alone but also his servant. He had remained below without the servant, as it were, when he said: “My heart has forsaken me” (Ps. 37:11). Our heart forsakes us when we are so overcome by carnal desires that we place the intention of our heart on earthly, carnal, and bodily things rather than on heavenly and spiritual things.

He had found this lost servant who said: “Your servant has found his heart” (2 Sam. 7:27). We find our heart when we seek spiritual things with the intention of the heart, when we tear it away from earthly things in order to direct it toward heavenly things.

An elect preacher does not impose difficult commands or reveal lofty things to those who are still carnal. Paul says to the Corinthians: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3:1).

It is as though he said: “For this reason I did not lead you to the height, because you did not possess spiritual understanding with me, like Saul’s servant.” Explaining the reason, he says: “For you are still carnal.”

Samuel is therefore rightly said to have taken up Saul and his servant, because teachers of holy Church impose difficult commands and reveal lofty things to those whom they perceive to be spiritual.

They are also brought into the dining hall because the breadth of charity is shown to them. One is placed, as it were, in the dining hall when, through what he has learned on high, he dwells in the breadth of charity. Or certainly, our entrance into the dining hall is love, and the dining hall is the beauty of spiritual life.

Thus John says: “Whoever does not love remains in death” (1 John 3:14). If the one who does not love remains in death, then the one who loves remains in life. We are therefore brought into the dining hall when, through the affection of charity, we rise into the affection of heavenly conduct.

In this breadth of dwelling the holy preachers occupy the higher place, because the blessed evangelist John says: “Around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the seats were twenty-four elders” (Rev. 4:4). The elders are holy preachers, mature in understanding and serious in conduct, who surround God’s throne with seats placed nearby. Those who love the Creator more than others rest nearer to him through the loftiest way of life.

Saul therefore rightly obtains a place at the head of those who had been invited, together with his servant, because in him the type of those who are to be chosen as pastors is displayed. A ruler is placed at the head when, through the force of great love for heavenly life, he receives a singular commitment while holding the Catholic faith in common with others but possessing a sublime virtue beyond them.

Hence it follows:

(Verses 22.) For there were about thirty men.

56. Three times ten makes thirty. The number three signifies faith in the holy and undivided Trinity. The number ten, through the ten commandments of the Law, signifies the perfection of good works. The number thirty therefore signifies those who hold the faith that works through love.

Saul is placed at their head when, by divine grace, the one who is to become pastor of the Church is made superior in merit to those over whom he ought to be superior in dignity. Samuel gives him this exalted place because the one who merits such elevation of life advances toward it through the instruction of his elders.

Since great things to be done, and not insignificant ones, are now shown to him, it follows:

(Verses 23–24.) Samuel said to the cook: “Give the portion that I gave you and commanded you to set aside with you.” The cook took the shoulder and placed it before Saul. Samuel said: “Behold what remains; place it before you and eat, because it was deliberately kept for you when I invited the people.” And Saul ate with Samuel on that day.

57. What is signified by the shoulder except the strength of action? Samuel gives it to the cook when great preachers demonstrate it to lesser ones. The priests are cooks, because when they speak to elect believers in the fervor of the spirit, they cook the food of the mind, as though by fire.

The portion that is given is said to have been placed separately because the strength of good works in a preacher ought to be distinctive. Samuel places it before Saul when he commands the man who is to be appointed pastor of holy Church to consider how great his strength must be.

Samuel also says to Saul concerning what the cook has set before him: “Behold what remains; place it before you.” It remains because Christ did not complete everything for us. Through his cross he redeemed all, but something remains: the one who strives to be redeemed and to reign with him must be crucified.

The one who said, “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2:12), had clearly seen this remainder. It is as though he said: “What Christ completed is of no benefit unless the person concerned completes what remains.”

Hence the blessed apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21). Hence Paul says: “I complete in my body what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ” (Col. 1:24).

58. But it should be noted that the cook placed the shoulder before Saul, and yet Samuel commands Saul to place it before himself. What does this mean?

A server customarily places a dish before those reclining at table; when the person reclining draws it toward himself, he places it nearer before himself, whereas previously it had been somewhat farther away before him.

The cook therefore places the shoulder before Saul, while Samuel commands Saul to place it before himself, because what is enjoined upon a new preacher concerning the strength of good works he should draw nearer to himself through diligent reflection.

After drawing it toward himself, he eats it, because he plans to put into practice what he has long considered. To eat the shoulder means to store within the mind, through intention, what is outwardly commanded concerning strong action.

He was urging each elect person, as it were, to place the shoulder before himself and eat it when he said: “If you sit at the table of a powerful man, pay careful attention to what is set before you, for you must prepare similar things” (Prov. 23:1).

At the table of the powerful man he signified the virtue of the shoulder. When he said, “Pay careful attention to what is set before you,” he taught the person addressed to place the shoulder before himself. He indicated that he ought to eat it when he said: “You must prepare similar things.” We eat similar things by preparing them, because when we resolve to do the strong things we hear, we store the food of life in the belly of the heart, as though we were eating.

But the vessel of election gives this command even to the foremost teachers, in the case of the instruction of a single disciple: “Do not be hasty in laying hands on anyone” (1 Tim. 5:22). Since those who are to be raised to the summit must be chosen after much deliberation, it is appropriately added: “Because it was deliberately kept for you when I invited the people.”

It is as though he said: “Place before yourself what I placed before myself before it was set before you; consider what I considered.” The shoulder portion is deliberately kept because the strongest action of a preacher is rightly entrusted to one whom the foremost men, after great consideration, judge worthy of so great a ministry.

This portion was deliberately kept when the people were called, because when faithful subjects come to receive the ministry of preaching, good preachers assign not weak things to the weak but strong things to the strong.

Those who make good progress, however, strive above all to maintain the good of obedience in their elevated way of life. It is therefore rightly added: “And Saul ate with Samuel on that day.”

As I have already said, for a teacher being promoted to eat means to prepare himself to do what is commanded concerning virtue. He is rightly said to have eaten with Samuel because when those who have newly arrived resolve to do great things, the foremost men become more fervent in the virtue of good works.

This eating may also signify the one Samuel promised earlier when he said: “Come up before me, so that you may eat with me today.” Saul therefore eats with Samuel because when the preacher hears inwardly the heavenly sweetness of the word of God, what his subjects hear outwardly while he speaks, they are indeed nourished by divine refreshment [Note: [Col. 0273D] Gilot.: “both are satisfied”].

It follows:

(Verses 25.) They came down from the height into the town, and Samuel spoke with Saul on the roof. Saul spread bedding for himself on the roof and slept.

59. Whoever is raised to the height of pastoral care ought, in the same elevation of his office, to possess both a lofty way of life and compassion for the weakness of others. Let Saul therefore ascend with Samuel and descend into the town.

Let the ruler know what lofty things he should do; let him know what common things he should arrange. Let him say with Paul: “Our way of life is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20); and let him say with us: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? I see another law opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Rom. 7:24).

The ruler is on the height when he speaks wisdom among the perfect. When he arranges carnal matters, he descends into the town, saying: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband; let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Cor. 7:2–3).

He is on the height when he says: “No creature will be able to separate us from the love of Christ” (Rom. 8:39). But he descends into the town when he says: “I became weak to the weak, so that I might win the weak; I became all things to all people, so that I might save all” (1 Cor. 9:22).

Samuel therefore brought Saul up to the height and set him down in the town, because when great men appoint the summit of holy Church, they teach those whom they place upon that summit to live loftily, to preach plainly, to be strict with themselves but moderate toward their subjects, and to attend to their own salvation in such a way that they can become weak with the weak. I mean weak through the affection of the mind, not through the illness of inward weakness. For if the teacher lies sick through weakness of mind, he cannot heal the sick or raise up those who lie fallen.

Saul is therefore rightly reported to have descended with Samuel into the town and to have spoken on the roof. The town is on level ground, whereas the roof is elevated. The roof is level in relation to the height, but in relation to the town it is not level but high.

In the same way, when elect preachers have compassion on lesser members, they abandon the height, as it were; but, descending into the town, they are on the roof, because they come from above yet assume the weakness of their subjects by pitying and advising them, not by acting weakly or becoming weak themselves.

In compassion for the weak, they command people to marry, yet they themselves do not marry by becoming weak. Descending into the town, they are on the roof because, although they issue ordinary commands, they do not retain weakness in themselves.

And since Samuel is said not simply to have been on the roof but to have spoken with Saul there, this plainly signifies that the future doctor must be taught to have compassion on weak subjects while nevertheless maintaining a lofty way of life himself.

60. And because the new preacher needs much reflection in order to do these things, Saul is said to have spread himself out and slept. For a new preacher to sleep on the roof means to determine, in his lofty reflection, how he ought to bear the burdens of his subjects.

If he remains awake to worldly concerns, he is clearly acting in such a way that he does not seek the good of such discretion in his inmost self. He must therefore sleep so that he may think of nothing worldly, because one oppressed by worldly matters can never arrange spiritual things.

But he will not be able to sleep if he does not spread something beneath himself. For if he does not consider the examples or teachings of the good, it is impossible for him to rest from outward concerns. We place soft things beneath us, as it were, when we think about the teaching or life of the elect. We sleep upon those same coverings because we can then rest well through reflection, when we are occupied with spiritual matters.

Let him therefore say that Saul spread himself out and slept, to impress upon the elect mind that, if it busies itself carelessly with outward things, it will not obtain the grace of inward rest. But whoever wishes to arrange spiritual things well through reflection should not wake to outward matters until he has ordered them perfectly within.

It is aptly added:

(Verses 26.) When they had risen in the morning and it was already growing light, Samuel called Saul on the roof, saying: “Rise, and I will send you away.”

61. Morning grows light when the splendor of truth opens itself to a quiet mind. The human mind is dark through ignorance and becomes bright through the illumination of truth. In ignorance, therefore, it is in night; when illuminated, it is in day.

The one who sleeps at night rises in the morning when he lifts himself up to perform what he has arranged through reflection. And because the matter of appointing a king was being dealt with, both are said to have risen.

The foremost preacher rises in order to appoint his hearer to the ministry of that same preaching. The one who is to be appointed rises so that he may not presume to receive so lofty an office with a lowly disposition of heart. They rise together because the lofty office is given in a lofty manner and received in a lofty manner.

Something else should be noted here: both first rose, and then Samuel called Saul, saying: “Rise, and I will send you away.” But if both rose according to the historical account, Saul is commanded to rise because, having risen from sleep, he is admonished to prepare himself for work.

Since both the foremost priests and the one who is to be raised to the order of preaching carefully consider the burden of so great a ministry, they sleep together, as it were, and rise together. But the one who is newly to be ordained is commanded, after rising from sleep, to rise again for work, because although he has diligently considered the height of the office through meditation, he must nevertheless reach it through the merit of his way of life.

He is therefore commanded, after rising, to rise again so that he may resolve to equal through his merits the lofty order that he has decided to undertake. Hence he is called on the roof, because he is commanded to strive toward high things.

He also says: “And I will send you away.” He rises in order to be sent away because the one who has grown in the height of a great way of life will be able to be free in the ministry of preaching.

The one who had risen rose again because the one who had learned through reflection the height of dignity took care to raise himself to that same height of dignity through the loftiness of his life. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0276C] (Verses 26.) And Saul rose.

Then it follows:

(Verses 26.) And they both went out, that is, he and Samuel.

62. The pastor goes out when he comes from the secrecy of meditation to the public work of action. When he determines what he wishes to do, he is within; but when he performs outwardly what he has thought through, he goes out, as it were.

Saul also went out because, in the external dignity of the person being promoted, he receives what he had considered for a long time—whether it ought to be received. They are therefore both said to have gone out because both had been within: the one had carefully foreseen what he should give and to whom; the other had carefully considered what sort of man he should be who was to receive such supreme things.

Since, therefore, the ministry of holy preaching must be given and received with the greatest discretion, when the king of Israel is anointed, both the king and the prophet who is to anoint him are said to have gone out.

Many books, however, read: “When they had risen in the morning, before it grew light.” This can appropriately be understood as follows. It is morning before it grows light when day has begun, in a manner of speaking, to breathe forth, but the full light of day is not yet present.

It is morning for the preachers of holy Church when they consider the good conduct of those whom they intend to appoint. But because they cannot know what those people will be in the future, it is morning, but before it grows light.

This is well said concerning the appointment of one who is later remembered to have displeased almighty God. The prophet saw him, as it were, in the morning before it grew light—he who appeared to him in the light of good conduct. But the full brightness of day was not yet present, because by the present light of knowledge he could not see the darkness that would later be in him.

This takes place so often in holy Church whenever those who are chosen are good in the present but will not persevere in that same goodness. He goes out, as it were, in the morning before the light, who displays the present light of good works but conceals the future darkness of his life.

But what happened next follows:

(Verses 27 and following.) When they were descending at the edge of the city, Samuel said to Saul: “Tell the servant to go ahead of us and pass on; but you remain here for a little while, so that I may declare the word of the Lord to you.” Then Samuel took a flask of oil, poured it over his head, and kissed him.

[Col. 0277B] 63. Why is the king led and anointed at the edge of the city? The edge of the city is the farthest part of the subject people. Those who occupy the lowest place in holy Church are therefore, as it were, at the edge of the city.

Within that Church, converts from sin appear to occupy the farthest place. The righteous are in the higher or first part. Or perhaps virginity occupies the first place, continence the second, married life the third, and the conversion of sinners the last.

The king is therefore anointed at the edge of the city because the ruler of holy Church is appointed for sinners, not for the righteous. For Truth himself says: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9:13). Again he says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (ibid., 13).

64. We have said that Saul’s servant signifies spiritual understanding. What, then, does it mean that Samuel commands him to go ahead and pass on?

The servant goes ahead when what is suggested to us by spiritual understanding is being done, rather than what is commanded by a carnal impulse. But in the case of some he goes ahead and passes on, while in the case of others he goes ahead but does not pass on.

The servant who goes ahead does not pass by the proud, but he passes by the humble. When the proud perform great and spiritual things, they are great in their own eyes. They have, as it were, the servant with them whom they follow, and they boast that they are spiritual in the spiritual things they do.

The prophet reproaches such people, saying: “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight” (Isa. 5:21).

The elect therefore take care to be spiritual in everything they do, but they avoid considering themselves spiritual. They are great in merit but humble in their own estimation, because they always perform great things but never regard themselves as great in those same great things.

They therefore cause the servant whom they send ahead to pass on when they possess spiritual understanding in their actions but keep it far removed from their own self-estimation.

What does it mean that he is commanded to remain for a little while so that the word of the Lord may be declared to him? He remains for a little while, with the servant sent ahead, who for a time withdraws from his own judgment and does another’s will.

He therefore causes the servant to pass on and remains for a little while when, at the command of a superior, he abandons even what he considers spiritual, abandoning it so that he may carry out appropriately what is enjoined upon him.

This certainly applies to the preacher who is being appointed. When he considers the burden of pastoral care and his own weakness, the spirit that goes before him says to him: “Such a weak man is unworthy to undertake so great a burden.”

Let him therefore not merely set the servant aside but make him pass on, so that he may not follow his own judgment but receive what is determined for him through the better provision of another.

Of the one who remains, it is immediately added:

CHAPTER V

(I Samuel 10:1.) Then Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it over his head.

1. What is expressed by this anointing is certainly also now materially displayed in the holy Church: for the one who is placed at the summit receives the sacraments of anointing. Since the anointing itself is a sacrament, the one who is promoted is rightly anointed outwardly if inwardly he is strengthened by the power of the sacrament.

Let us therefore first examine more attentively the properties of oil. Oil surpasses other liquids; oil feeds fire; oil is accustomed to heal wounds. Through it, therefore, the goodness of mercy is signified, since it is written of the Lord: “His mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 144:9). Because it feeds fire, it signifies the grace of preaching, which illumines the minds of the elect. Because wounds are healed by oil, it clearly indicates that the wounds of sinners must be cleansed.

Let the king’s head therefore be anointed, because the mind of the teacher must be filled with spiritual grace. Let him have oil in his anointing—an abundant mercy that is preferred to all his other virtues. Let him have oil, so that while he nourishes within himself the ardor of the Holy Spirit, he may shine brightly upon others through the word. Let him likewise have the oil of medicine, so that he may wisely determine how to cleanse the foulness of sins and restore sick minds to health.

But Saul is anointed with a small flask, not to prefigure doctrine, but to express what would happen in the future. A small flask is indeed a small vessel. What, then, does it mean that Saul is anointed with a small flask of oil, except that he will be rejected in the end? For because he later refused to obey God, he heard from Samuel: “Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, so that you are not king” (1 Samuel 15:26). Like a small flask of oil, he had little of the oil who received spiritual grace only to be rejected.

This is also appropriately understood of the rulers of the holy Church. Often those who are not perfect in love of God and neighbor receive the summit of authority. They possess a certain affection of charity, but they do not possess its fullness. What, then, is that immature and imperfect affection of the mind except a small flask of oil? For while it anoints the head without filling it, it is indeed poured out completely, but it provides little.

By contrast, when the elect king is commanded to be anointed, the Lord says to the same prophet: “Fill your horn with oil, and come; I shall send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided a king for myself among his sons” (1 Samuel 16:1). Hence this same elect king, attributing the fullness of his anointing to the praises of God, says: “You have anointed my head with oil, and my cup, making me drunk, is exceedingly glorious” (Psalm 22:5).

The one who received the grace of anointing without persevering in it is therefore anointed, by God’s dispensation, with the liquid of that vessel by which the failure of the anointed one was to be signified.

It follows:

[Col. 0279A] **(Verse 1.)** “And he kissed him and said: Behold, God has anointed you as prince over his inheritance, and you shall deliver his people from the hand of their enemies who are around them.”

**2.** The ruler is led to the summit of the holy Church so that he may possess this office: to establish peace between God and human beings. For by sinning we incur the enmity of the Creator. When a ruler is therefore appointed for the correction of sinners, he removes what made us enemies of God.

Samuel is rightly said to have kissed Saul’s head. The one bears the prophet’s kiss fixed upon his head who bears the support of our reconciliation in his mind: namely, the one who harbors within himself no fuel for divine discord, while striving in his mind to restore those at odds to peace.

After he has kissed the prince, it is said: “God has anointed you as prince over his inheritance.” It is as though he admonished him in concrete terms, saying: “You know that you have been placed here to dissolve the enmity of sin. What you destroy in others, you must not retain in yourself.”

For some are both anointed and do not receive the kiss; they strive to free the Lord’s people, but they do not fear subjecting themselves to the yoke of their enemies. Whoever preaches to others the good things he does not practice gives, as it were, a kiss that he does not receive. He seeks to make others friends of God, yet does not cease to be God’s enemy himself. He builds within himself the enmity of sin, which he attempts to destroy in others by his word.

Since, therefore, only the one who is a friend of God through the affection of great charity presides usefully, Samuel is said to have kissed the king’s head. Hence Truth himself first kisses those whom he appoints, and afterward sends them to free others. “You are my friends,” he says; then he adds: “I have appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:14).

Again, rising from the dead, he says: “Peace be with you”; then he adds: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:23). Thus he fixed the kiss of peace in the minds of those whom he commanded to dissolve the hatred of sin.

After the king has been kissed, he is established over the Lord’s inheritance, because the elect teacher is chosen so that he may preside in dignity over the faithful who are subject to him, while seeking through his authority not his own gain but the Lord’s. He is declared to have been appointed for this purpose: that those under him may be freed from the hands of their enemies.

The Lord’s inheritance is the multitude of the faithful. Every worldly concern is therefore removed when the king is declared to have been anointed as prince over the Lord’s inheritance. The fruit of anointing is therefore the cultivation of God’s inheritance. The one carries out the office of anointing who seeks only the gain of souls. He remembers that he has been anointed as prince over the Lord’s inheritance who seeks from earthly authority only what Christ sought through his ministry. By this statement, therefore, the intention of negligent rulers is condemned.

**3.** They hear that they have been anointed over the Lord’s inheritance, because the Lord seeks from the earth only the elect. They know that he calls not the breadth of the earth, nor an abundance of gold, nor an overflow of riches, but his faithful ones, his inheritance; and yet they do not cease seeking earthly things and gathering what perishes.

They devote all their concern to what the Lord does not seek, and neglect to seek what alone he does seek. It is said, therefore, so that they may see their own negligence; it is said, so that the good may become better: “God has anointed you as prince in his inheritance.” It is as though he said: “He has made his inheritance yours; see to it that you do not rule over it in another manner.”

“You shall deliver the people from the hand of the enemies who are around them.” Through this, the preacher is commanded to undertake a great labor, since the enemies are said to be all around. The battle would be sufficiently grave if they had to endure the savagery of the evil spirits on only one side.

Hence, speaking through the prophet, he declares: “The wicked walk around” (Psalm 11:9). Hence blessed Peter exhorts us, saying: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Peter 5:8).

Our enemies are therefore around us because unclean spirits are always lying in wait for our thought, word, and action. When they seek to suggest evil things to us, they are on one side; when they drag us toward evil, we are struck by their battle from another side; when they invite us to evil deeds, they raise up war from yet another direction.

We therefore have enemies all around us because in everything we think, say, and do, we suffer the battles of evil spirits. But because the people are said to be delivered not from war but from the hands of their enemies, great marks of virtue are attributed to preachers: they must not only protect the free so that they are not captured, but also free those who have been captured from their servitude.

This is accomplished by our kings when, through their preaching, those recover their senses who have been subjected by the audacity of transgression to the yoke of the devil’s power. Only those preachers can accomplish this who reach the summit of governance by divine appointment. For those whom almighty God appoints he sends to endure the battles of the ancient enemy, but he does not abandon them amid the battles themselves: he protects his soldiers and makes them victorious.

But when holy men are raised to the primacy of the holy Church, they are greatly afraid lest the burden of so great an office has been imposed upon them by human judgment and not by the ordering of the Creator. For the strengthening of the humble, signs are therefore given by which they may know that they have been chosen by God and not by human beings.

Thus Samuel continues:

**(Verse 2.)** “And this shall be a sign for you that God has anointed you as prince. When you depart from me today, you will find two men near Rachel’s tomb, within the borders of Benjamin, leaping over great pits at midday. They will say to you: The she-asses have been found, which you went to seek; and your father, having abandoned the asses, is concerned for you and says: ‘What shall I do about my son?’”

**4.** It is as though he were saying to the humble shepherd, trembling before so great a ministry: “You are trembling because you do not know whether what has been done concerning you is from God. But because you can know this, you ought not to tremble.

“This shall therefore be a sign for you that it was not a human being but God who anointed you as prince: those two men will say to you, ‘The she-asses have been found, which you went to seek.’”

It is as though he said: “If you find those two men and they tell you this, know that it was God, not I, who appointed you prince.”

What, then, do these two men signify for us except the perfect preachers of the holy Church? They are two because they are perfect in both commandments of charity; they are men because they are strong in holy conduct.

They are said to be found near Rachel’s tomb because, through their devotion to the contemplative life, they are separated from worldly concern; and while they seek the gain of souls, they are not buried. It is the unambiguous judgment of venerable fathers that Rachel signifies the beauty of the contemplative life.

The men therefore stand near Rachel’s tomb because perfect teachers devote themselves to heavenly contemplation in such a way that they also bear responsibility for the holy Church. They stand near Rachel’s tomb because they direct the state of good works through the power of contemplation, and because they do nothing in action except what they have arranged through contemplation.

And because, even at the height of heavenly contemplation, they strive to preserve not their own presumption but the order of the holy Church, Rachel’s tomb is described as being within the borders of Benjamin.

As I have already said, Benjamin, who is called “son of the right hand,” signifies the Redeemer of the human race. The borders of Benjamin are therefore the rules of the holy Scriptures. Concerning these borders it is written: “Do not move the ancient boundaries that your fathers have established” (Proverbs 22:28).

Because holy preachers, when they see the highest things through contemplation, do not depart from the rule of faith, the tomb near which they stand is rightly said to be within the borders of Benjamin.

**5.** Blessed Paul sought, as it were, a sign of his anointing when he came to Jerusalem to see Peter and conferred the Gospel with him and the other apostles. For he had received the apostolate not from a human being nor through a human being, but from heaven, when the Lord Jesus called him (Galatians 1); yet he tested the ministry of his anointing through conference with his fellow apostles. For he says of himself: “I conferred with them concerning the Gospel, lest perhaps I should run, or had run, in vain” (Galatians 2:2).

The Forerunner of the Redeemer had also anointed his disciples; but, that they might recognize the signs of his anointing, he sent them, as it were, to one leaping over great pits, saying: “Are you he who is to come, or do we look for another?” (Matthew 11:3). John knew the one whom he had preached and baptized; but he sent the disciples so that, after seeing the signs, they might believe more firmly and hold more securely the indications of his election.

Those, therefore, who are found fit for the office of preaching recognize, as a sign of their election, that the souls of sinners whom they seek have been found. And because almighty God delights not only in the preaching but also in the manner of life of the elect teacher, he adds: “And your father, having left the asses, is concerned for you and says: ‘What shall I do about my son?’”

We have said that Saul’s father Kish—whose name in our language means “hard”—signifies those who teach by word and example that earthly things are to be despised and that one must hasten to the heavenly homeland by a hard and austere manner of life. We have recognized this same hardness of the heavenly life both in the word and in the life of our Redeemer. If, therefore, we look to the summit of our instruction, we are sons of the Redeemer.

Our Father, then, having left the asses, is concerned for us, because our Redeemer wishes us to seek the salvation of others in such a way that we do not neglect our own. He wishes sinners to be called to repentance, but he does not wish those who call those sinners to perish. He wishes the converted sinner to possess the righteousness which he did not possess, but he does not wish the righteous person to lose the crown of righteousness which he possesses.

He is therefore concerned for his son after leaving the asses, because he wishes his preachers to rest for a time from anxious attention to others, so that through repose they may provide better for themselves. And because a good ruler must resume this very concern for the holy Church, our rest is interrupted: for a prior concern precedes it, and a subsequent concern follows it.

Let the elect preacher therefore devote himself to the benefit of those subject to him, and to his own benefit; but let him take such care for himself that he immediately returns to the care of another which he has left. For then our Creator loves us as sons, when we love those subject to us as brothers and love him as a father: through the affection of concern we are joined to these, and through our repose—which he loves—we hasten to him as to a father.

This love for our repose is expressed in the words: “What shall I do about my son?” Certainly the father who loves to keep his son says this. This, then, is not said of a son who is present, but absent. Yet because he seeks his father’s lost asses, he is exceedingly dear to him; for the one who strives by preaching to convert the souls of sinners is already joined to our Redeemer in great charity. Although he is, as it were, far from him through concern for others, he is near through the repose of contemplation and the affection of prayer.

Because, therefore, he desires us to be near to him both by contemplation and by prayer, he says like a loving father: “What shall I do about my son?” It is as though he said: “How shall I make him who is absent present to me?” And because great men of the holy Church praise the concern of our preaching but censure its excess, those who say that the father’s asses have been found declare that the father is concerned for his son.

The elect can therefore know the sign of their anointing: they are indeed brought by God to the summit of the holy Church when they are fit by word and example for the salvation of others, and diligent through repose for their own; and when they seek sinners for heaven, they do not abandon themselves to the world.

It follows:

**(Verses 3–4.)** “When you have departed from there and passed farther on, and have come to the oak of Tabor, three men ascending to God at Bethel will find you there: one carrying three young goats, another three round loaves of bread, and another a flask of wine. And when they have greeted you, they will give you two loaves, and you shall receive them from their hand.”

**6.** When we desire to make good progress in holy conduct, it is necessary for us to gather examples from very many of the elect; for bees cannot make honey unless they collect it from diverse flowers. Saul therefore rightly comes from some men to others, because the more abundantly we behold examples of the saints, the better we are instructed.

The flowers of eternal fruits are the works of the saints; when they are moistened with the dew of heavenly love, we gather from them that by which we may be filled for our own instruction and for the benefit of others. Saul departs from there and passes farther on when the inexperienced preacher advances through the examples of the elect, and from the virtue he has beheld in one goes on to examine another’s way of life.

Often he delights in admiring in some the labor of preaching, and in others the strength of good works; he reveres the former as they speak, and strives to imitate the latter as they act. He looks upon the former to see with what beauty they shine outwardly; he investigates the splendor of the latter not in outward conduct but inwardly.

Thus he is rightly said, as he passes on, to come to the oak of Tabor. An oak is a shady and strong tree. This tree signifies the more hidden way of life of the saints. Since men of this way of life do not go out to the external works of the active life, they are, as it were, in shade, because they cannot feel the fires of temptations. Because they rest in heavenly desire, the farther removed they are from love of the world, the more quietly they remain in the shade of refreshment.

But this shade belongs to a strong tree, because the way of life of the saints despises earthly things more vigorously in proportion as it rises more purely into love for heavenly things. It is also strong because those who love only the heavenly things they see powerfully endure the adversities of the world. And because those who disdain through love to look upon earthly things are in the great light of inward splendor, the oak itself is said to be Tabor.

Spiritual men therefore leap over pits because, while they raise themselves through heavenly desire, they despise earthly things. They leap as though over pits seen before them when, in order to despise earthly things, they elevate themselves to desire eternal goods.

These men leap over great pits at midday because, through the fervor of perfect charity in which they have been taken up, they despise all the heights that appear in the world. Whatever appears high in this world is not true height but a pit, which lowers into hell all whom it receives in its ambition.

The heights of the world must therefore be avoided, not desired, by spiritual men, because they reveal themselves from concealment and carry those whom they swallow down into hell. Spiritual men leap over pits because, while they raise themselves through heavenly desire, they despise earthly things. They leap as though over pits seen before them when, in order to despise earthly things, they elevate themselves to desire eternal goods.

They leap over pits at midday because no one can despise the world except one who possesses the full light and ardor of heavenly charity. Since those who disdain to look upon earthly things through love are in the great light of inward splendor, the oak itself is said to be Tabor. For *Thabor* is interpreted as “coming light.”

Light comes when the inward brightness of the Creator reveals itself to the elect mind. The oak is therefore called Tabor because the secret life acts by despising earthly things, so that it may see more clearly the inward light of the Creator.

We are secret when we guard our senses in the fear of God. Then we see the coming light, because when the members of the body are well governed, the grace of the Creator is poured back into our mind.

It should also be noted that the one who knew from those leaping over pits that the father was concerned for him is said to come to the oak of Tabor. For the preachers of the holy Church often praise virtues to which they themselves cannot devote themselves. They preach the secret of the contemplative life, but because they are concerned with guarding those subject to them, they avoid adhering to the secrecy of that life.

It is as though Samuel said: “Those men praise to you the devotion of contemplation; but because they cannot hold what they praise, it must be sought in others.” We therefore pass on to the oak of Tabor when we recognize from holy preachers that devotion to the contemplative life is praiseworthy, but seek its perfection in those who devote themselves spiritually to it.

The three men who find the anointed king at the oak of Tabor therefore signify those who are perfect in the devotion of the contemplative life. They are rightly said not to be found by the king, but to find the king there. They are not found because they are hidden. They themselves find us because, when they deign to do so, they disclose to us the light of their hidden way of life.

They are not found because they withdraw their life from all human testimony. But they find us because, through the affection of charity, they show us something of their light for imitation. Nor do they reveal their virtues for imitation except to those who desire with great longing to obtain and practice them.

We must therefore first come to the oak of Tabor, so that we may be found by those three men. For we are already, as it were, in the shadow of the coming light when we are inflamed with great desires for the highest contemplation.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] Gussanv. and Vatican: *magni summae*, etc.]

**7.** Then the three men appear to us because those who deign to reveal themselves to us when we desire them are strong in guarding speech, thought, and action. They cannot belong to the hidden life if they have kept the gates of the eyes, heart, and mouth open.

Because they guard the heart from foolish thought, the mouth from idle speech, and the whole body from evil action, they are three; they are men because they observe that same guardianship with the greatest strength.

Three men therefore appear to us because when we see such people, we behold in them the strength of virtue. They are in the shadow of the coming light because they can see the inward light of the Creator more clearly in proportion as they guard a pure heart more diligently from the world’s defilement.

The Lord appeared in this manner to such men when he rose from the dead, and the Holy Spirit filled such men. Concerning that hidden place it is said: “When it was evening on the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were because of fear of the Jews” (John 20:19). And again: “After eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came when the doors were closed, stood in the midst, and said to them: ‘Peace be with you.’”

Concerning another hidden place it is written: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together in the same place. Suddenly there came a sound from heaven, as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one rested upon each of them; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:1).

Those have closed doors who, against the negligence of human frailty, keep the functions of the body confined under strong custody. They are also inside because they rest in the inward love of the heavenly life.

The risen Lord appears to such people because they see his glory more clearly in proportion as, through contempt for the world, they follow more strictly the mystery of his Passion. They can also be filled with the Holy Spirit as though in a house, because those receive the gifts of his graces abundantly who prepare themselves to receive them by despising visible things.

**8.** They are rightly said to ascend to the Lord at Bethel. For Bethel is called “the house of God.” And what is the house of God except that house inhabited by inaccessible light?

The revelation of his divinity is also inaccessible light. It is light because it can in some way be seen by pure hearts. In itself it fills all things completely; yet, while filling everything abundantly, it is not contained. It is contained in order to fill, but while filling it is not contained; after filling all things, it is not itself filled.

The revelation of the Creator is therefore inaccessible light because it is such an immense light that it illumines everything and is confined by nothing: it is seen but not comprehended.

These three men therefore ascend to the Lord because those who guard themselves in the more hidden life are raised up in the contemplation of divine light. But because they cannot yet reach the very vision of almighty God, they are said to ascend to Bethel.

Whatever the human mind can think about almighty God is not God. But while the mind transcends everything in thought, and while whatever it can imagine of inward light, inward sweetness, and spiritual delight is believed to be less than that reality, it nevertheless reaches a certain light which is not God but which God inhabits.

And because the soul of the elect is then wonderfully inflamed, wonderfully refreshed, and enjoys delight ineffably, it is compelled to consider how ineffable the light, sweetness, and delight must be which God himself is, if the light he inhabits is so immense and yet is not himself.

Moses had ascended to the Lord at Bethel when he spoke with him on the mountain. But although he had reached the light which God inhabits, he sought the light which was God himself, saying: “Show me your face” (Exodus 33:13). It is also written of him: “The Lord spoke with Moses face to face” (ibid.).

What does it mean that Moses speaks with the Lord face to face, and yet begs the Lord to show him his face? The face of God is his knowledge. God is known through a mirror, and he is known through himself: through a mirror here, through himself in heaven.

The mirror is that light which God inhabits; God himself is the light which he is (1 Corinthians 13:12). What, then, does Moses signify—he who is said to see God face to face and who asks to see his face (Exodus 33:13)—more fittingly than the perfection of the elect, who already behold the mirror of that highest light, yet ardently desire to reach the truth of the light itself?

This knowledge of the light does not know how to satisfy the desires of the elect, but rather to arouse them; that knowledge both satisfies and arouses them. For it is so delightful that it is desired ineffably, and so full that those who have already always seen it with great desire will always be satisfied by its ineffable fullness.

The men who ascend to the Lord are therefore said to ascend to Bethel because, when we make much progress in this life, we can see the light of the Creator itself through a mirror, but cannot at all reach it in itself.

**9.** And because only the humble are exalted to this sublime vision, it is rightly said of these men: one carried three young goats, and another three round loaves of bread.

The one carries three young goats who, in repentance, considers that he has sinned in mouth, heart, and action. Because sinners are signified by young goats—for those who are to be placed on the left hand of the eternal Judge at the final judgment are expressed by the name of goats—the one carries three young goats to the Lord who does not cease, in repentance, to consider the sins of action, speech, and thought.

He is indeed a man, and yet he carries young goats, because he vigorously guards against sinning but does not cease to make satisfaction as a sinner. For he was a man and carried young goats who said: “We all offend in many things” (James 3:2).

And because they strive through repentance to erase the sins they confess, one carries three young goats, while another carries three round loaves of bread. We have previously referred round loaves of bread to the affliction of repentance: if bread sometimes signifies the delight of the present life, bread is twisted when we are tormented on account of the past delight of the flesh.
