Hence King Hezekiah, when pierced by repentance, promises to torment his royal pleasures, saying: “I shall recall all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isaiah 38:15). For when the carnal mind is dissolved in the pleasures of sin, it is as though it has a day, because it sees with joy what it does. The days of the reprobate mind are therefore evil pleasures.

The sinner recalls all his days because, when he comes to his senses through divine grace, he does not cease to make satisfaction for all his evils.

It is first said that one carries three young goats, and afterward that another carries three round loaves of bread, so that the virtue of each of the elect may appear: he is strong in good works, humble in his self-estimation, and afflicted through the contrition of repentance.

And because those cannot possess such perfection who have not forgotten temporal things through love of eternal goods, the third is said to carry a flask of wine. He carries a flask of wine who has filled his mind with the heat of the Holy Spirit, by which he both eagerly pursues what lies ahead and abandons what is behind as though in the great drunkenness of forgetfulness.

For he carried young goats who said: “Christ came to call sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Timothy 1:15). And because he also carried a round loaf of bread, he says: “I discipline my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Corinthians 9:27). But as though drunk with the wine of an amphora, he says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the appointed prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:13).

The three men therefore ascend to the Lord and carry three young goats, three round loaves of bread, and a flask of wine because, devoted to the practices of the more withdrawn life, they rise toward contemplation of the true light through the merit of humility.

But what they are in themselves and what they are for others he explains, saying: “When they greet you, they will give you three round loaves of bread, and you shall receive them from their hand.”

Holy men greet us when they announce to us the good things of eternal salvation. Those who greet us bodily bow their heads to show reverence to the person greeted. For spiritual men to bow their heads is to lower the mind from the heights of contemplation.

For if they do not bow their heads, they cannot greet us: they do not instruct us with saving teaching if they do not lower their minds from the highest contemplation of heavenly things. They show us great reverence when they do this, because they do not regard as small those for whom they deign to descend from their lofty height.

**10.** But when the future king is greeted, two loaves are given to him. Two loaves are given to the ruler who is being appointed as preacher when he is taught to mourn not only his own sins but also those of others.

He has one round loaf when he is afflicted for his own sins; he has another when he strives to mourn the sins of those subject to him. The Psalmist more clearly indicates this bread when he says: “Rise up after you have sat, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Psalm 126:2). Hence he confesses to the Lord, saying: “You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us drink with tears in measure” (Psalm 79:9).

A round loaf, therefore, is the bread of sorrow and the bread of tears. Perhaps that one man carried three round loaves of bread for this reason: there were three of them traveling together, so that when they divided them among themselves, each might have one loaf. The same may appropriately be understood of the young goats.

What should be noted in this matter except that men of the more withdrawn life, while maintaining a solitary way of life, do not bear responsibility for others? They have one young goat and one loaf who are pierced only for their own sins and are not burdened by others through pastoral office.

And because those who belong to the same perfect way of life imitate the affliction of the flesh in themselves, it is fitting that one carries three loaves, another three young goats, and a third a flask of wine. It is as though one carries what all will offer or eat, and all eat or offer what one carries, when each, inflamed by holy emulation, possesses within himself good examples for others and does not neglect to imitate the good things possessed by others.

And because the round loaves of bread are spoken of in the feminine gender, this clearly signifies that one who is accustomed to contrition produces from tears more tears: as though the affliction of the penitent were fertile in the feminine sex, because the more frequently anyone is pierced with repentance, the more abundant streams of tears are supplied to him.

Saul is therefore given not one loaf but two, because it is not enough for a preacher to weep only for himself. Let him receive two loaves from the hands of the men, so that he may learn from the example of the perfect to weep, and recognize that weeping is necessary both for himself and for those subject to him.

And because power is sometimes understood by the hand, the three men have the loaves in their hands: those who have advanced to the stronghold of contemplation possess weeping through the power of authority. For because they do not wish to be dissolved in empty joy when they can rejoice, they can rightly weep when they wish.

We who are weak and negligent in guarding our minds are unable, even when we wish to be pierced with repentance and to weep for our sins. Since spiritual tears are produced from great fervor of spirit, we who are constricted by the coldness of our negligence are quickly prevented from becoming warm enough for tears.

The men who appear to the future king at the oak of Tabor are therefore rightly said to have loaves in their hands, because those who are perfect in the contemplative life of solitude possess the gain of those subject to them through the observance of virtues.

11. And it should be noted that Samuel commands the anointed king, saying: “And you shall receive from their hand.” What better meaning can be drawn from this statement than the one plainly evident: namely, that we do not willingly imitate affliction in holy men? For countless are those who desire the honor of leadership and dignity; but few desire, along with that leadership, the labor of ministry and the affliction of the flesh. We gladly wish to be exalted above others, but we avoid mourning their sins. Then indeed we see the loaves offered to us, but we do not wish to receive them from the hands of those offering them, because we behold affliction in chosen men but do not imitate it. Let the prophet therefore command, saying: “You shall receive from their hand,” so that whoever desires to be suitable as a ruler of the Church may not in any way avoid taking up what has been said.

It is also appropriate that Saul is first led to the men leaping over great pits, and afterward to those carrying loaves, young goats, and wine: so that the inexperienced preacher may learn from some to despise the lofty things of the world, and from others to offer to almighty God the affliction of the flesh and the sacrifices of tears, both for himself and for his subjects. But, further indicating the culmination of his progress, the prophet adds:

**(Verses 5–6.)** “After this you shall come to the hill of the Lord, where there is a Philistine garrison; and when you have entered the city, you will meet a company of prophets descending from the high place, with a psaltery, a tambourine, a flute, and a harp before them; and they themselves will be prophesying. And the spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them, and you will be changed into another man.”

12. A hill is the height of a mountain. What, then, is more fittingly understood by this hill than the holy intention of the Scriptures? It is indeed the height of a mountain, because it does not lie on the level ground of the letter but rises exceedingly high in the sublimity of spiritual meanings. The inexperienced preacher therefore rests upon the straight path of the virtues if, after seeing public preachers and secluded anchorites, he beholds and recognizes the height of Scripture.

In this matter it should be noted that we said Saul, in that he rises above all the people from the shoulder upward, signifies an educated man and one of great manner of life. Why, then, does he ascend to the hill of the Lord in order to come to the height of the Scriptures, which he knows? A similar question could be raised about his going to see the men leaping over great pits, since he was said to be a man of great manner of life. The answer is that he was shown to signify great men in their manner of life, but men inexperienced in the ministry of preaching. Therefore, whoever can advance through the examples of better men both in purity of contemplation and in the office of preaching ought to return to the height of the Scriptures, because the more he advances in a higher way of life, the more subtly he attends to the sublimity of sacred eloquence.

Let the prophet therefore say: “After this you shall come to the hill of the Lord.” It is as if he said: “When, through perfect imitation, you have grasped the perfection of holy men, you will advance to such an understanding of sacred Scripture that you will now see plainly what you had thought you must behold there in a sublime manner.”

13. There is a Philistine garrison there, because those who fell from heaven through the intoxication of pride mock Jews and heretics through the Scriptures. They therefore stand on the hill, because they deceive in the Scriptures the hearts that they possess by the falsity of their understanding. Whenever, then, Jews presume to ascend to the hill of the Lord, they are captured by the Philistines standing there. For while they imagine that they understand the meaning of Scripture in a sublime manner, demons meet them on their ascent and, deceiving them, destroy them.

It is rightly commanded that Saul go to the hill of the Lord not immediately, but first after seeing those leaping over pits and those carrying loaves and wine, because faithful men are fortified by the great protection both of the teaching and of the examples of their betters. Hence it is also said to that same Saul: “You will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place.” It is as if he said: “You will be able to fear the garrison of the Philistines all the less because you will have prophets coming to meet you for your security.”

And because a company of prophets is mentioned, a great multitude of our defenders is signified. Let the Jew therefore fear, because while he ascends alone, he perishes. What indeed do those same prophets who come to meet us say? “Woe to him who is alone, for if he falls, there is no one to raise him” (Eccles. 4:10). For he is alone who is abandoned by God. No one raises this fallen man, because no one among the saints takes up one who has been abandoned by God.

Every chosen person therefore ascends securely, because he is not alone. He who speaks through us is with us. For he also promises, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). He was not alone who said: “I am not alone, but he who sent me is with me” (John 8:16). He likewise was not alone who asked: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

This can suitably be understood not only of the Lord’s spiritual presence but also of the material teaching of the elect. Holy preachers ascend the hill of the Lord, where there is a Philistine garrison; but because they have a company of prophets coming to meet them, they are not at all afraid of the Philistines. Who are these prophets, then, if not the great preachers of the holy Church? The ministry of a prophet is to reveal hidden things and proclaim the future. But when teachers of the holy Church draw the hidden meanings of Scripture into common knowledge, they disclose secrets that are unknown; and when they proclaim eternal joys, they reveal the future.

The prophets therefore come to meet us, because the teachers of the holy Church show us the truth of sacred Scripture. When they tell us what we wish to know from sacred eloquence, they encounter us as we travel along the way by which one proceeds to the hill of the Lord. We are therefore secure there through the prophets’ encounter, where the Philistines are, because through the authority of holy preachers we recognize the meaning of Scripture, in which Jews and heretics are slain by demons with the sword of their errors.

For behold, if we turn to the Law of Moses, we certainly find the hill of the Lord. There we read about the tabernacle, there about the great high priest, there about the blood of goats and calves together, and about the blood of the paschal Lamb. The Jews understand these things according to their own spirit, literally; and because they have none of the prophets with them, they perish. But if I wish to ascend this mountain, I first see the descending prophets, and I ascend securely. And, leaving aside the newer prophets for the moment, Isaiah first meets the one ascending, saying: “Like a sheep he will be led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he will not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). Hence Paul says:

“Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, entered once for all into the holy places through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands—that is, not of this creation—and not through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9:11–12).

But if we wish to have more prophets on this hill, we find them all when we seek them, because the new preachers demonstrate that what the ancient teachers had promised has been fulfilled in our Redeemer.

14. For this reason the Redeemer of the human race can appropriately be designated by the name “hill.” Hence Isaiah, prophesying, says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2:2). He is called a hill because of the sublimity of holiness; “of the Lord,” because he is the Son of the supreme Begetter.

On this hill, then, a Philistine garrison is said to be present, because he was also born as a sign against which opposition would be directed. The Philistine garrison is the opposition of heretics. Like men standing on a hill, they lie in wait for those ascending the hill; and while they pervert the sacred Scriptures by interpreting them wrongly, they destroy those who ascend carelessly in order to know the Redeemer.

Let the chosen person therefore not tremble: as he ascends, he has a company of prophets coming to meet him, because all the preachers of the Old and New Testaments announce the Redeemer himself to him. They come from the high place, because what they preach on earth they see in heaven. Hence John, as though truly one of the chosen company of prophets, is told from heaven: “Ascend here, and I will show you what must take place after this” (Rev. 4:1).

When he had ascended, he saw and recognized the Lamb whom Moses had prefigured as destined to be slain and whom he had himself seen offered on the cross, now reigning; and he learned how many thanks were being offered to him by those for whom he had been slain. The preachers therefore come from the high place because, through heavenly contemplation, they have learned what they preach to those below.

15. It is also appropriate that the company of prophets is said to meet Saul at the entrance of the city, because we can see the highest preachers of the holy Church where they descend, not where they are exalted. We hear what they say to us little ones, but we do not see how they see or how sweetly they love the things they behold in heaven.

For the apostle Paul was caught up into paradise and taken up to the third heaven; he also heard secret words that it is not permitted a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12:4). Who, then, could find such a great preacher, caught up into paradise or taken up to the third heaven? Yet blessed Paul spoke these things about himself under compulsion. Hence, at the end, humbling himself after explaining such sublimity, he says: “I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Cor. 12:11).

How great, then, were those things he was unwilling to speak of, if he came under compulsion to disclose even these? For he both heard what it is not permitted a human being to speak and saw what it is not permitted a human being to know. Perhaps you will say: “If he had wished, how could he have conveyed in human speech the beauty of that third heaven, the light of its innermost brightness, the ineffable splendor of the angels, and the inaccessible radiance; how sweetly all those eternal citizens, chosen and blessed, receive from his fullness; how eagerly they take it in; how completely they are filled; how delightfully they taste the sweetness of divine goodness; how they are satisfied with delectable fullness; what radiances each receives from that one ineffable light of the Creator; what beauty all possess together from that one glory; by what excellence of dignity some surpass others; and with what ineffable joy of justice the good are subject to those who are better?”

16. We cannot therefore follow Paul to that height, but we enter the city, where he comes down from above, as it were, to meet us. Since we cannot behold the heights that preachers see, we ought reverently to hear the plain things that they teach.

But when they descend, they carry before them a psaltery, a tambourine, a flute, and a harp. They have a psaltery because they announce the kingdom of heaven; they have a tambourine because they preach the mortification of the flesh; they have a flute because they command their subjects to weep for the attainment of eternal joy; and they also have a harp because they teach the devout to rejoice in the certainty of eternal goods.

The psaltery, which resounds from its upper part, also signifies the preaching of eternal joys, because when it encourages us to love heavenly things, it sends forth, as it were, from its upper part a sound of sweetness. The tambourine, since it is stretched over the hide of a dead animal, not inappropriately represents the mortification of our flesh. We have learned from the Gospel that the flute is customarily used at the funerals of the dead: when the Lord wished to raise the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, he expelled the flute players from his house and drove out the noisy crowd (Matt. 9:25). What, then, is expressed by the flute if not the mourning of the saints? For when they see themselves cast away from that eternal life which they desire, they mourn themselves as though they were dead.

The harp, however, is a very joyful musical instrument. By this instrument the word of consolation offered to the elect is aptly represented, because we become cheerful, as though at the sound of a harp, when chosen preachers console us amid the hardships of our present exile.

The psaltery is therefore placed first among the preachers’ instruments, because above all the glory of the heavenly kingdom must be preached, so that when we recognize the good that we should love, we may desire to labor for the attainment of that good. Hence, when Matthew was asserting in the Gospel the beginnings of the Lord’s Incarnation, he said: “John began to preach, saying: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 4:17).

But because, when we know heavenly things, if we wish to reach them we must mortify the sufferings of the flesh, the preachers of the holy Church produce the sound of the tambourine, as it were, after the psaltery. What else is the mortification of the body than preparation for eternal blessedness? We love, therefore, to prepare ourselves for heavenly things, and we are commanded to ask for them with the most ardent tears. We mourn the dead as though with a flute when we grieve intensely because we do not yet live in that eternal life. Our preachers therefore have the flute after the tambourine when they both teach us to mortify our members and to groan out of love for eternal life.

They also carry the harp after the flute, because they command us to mourn the hardships of our present exile in such a way that we rejoice in the promise of the eternal inheritance. For the great prophet sounded the psaltery when he said: “My sheep hear my voice, and I give them eternal life” (John 10:27). Striking the psaltery again, he said: “The Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:14).

He sounded the tambourine who said: “Put to death your members that are on earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, and covetous desire” (Col. 3:5). He sounded the flute who said: “Be wretched, mourn, let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (James 4:9). He sounded the tambourine who said: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 43:22).

He has the flute before him who likewise speaks to God, saying: “You will feed us with the bread of tears, and you will give us drink in measure” (Ps. 79:6). The Lord had the flute before him when he said: “Truly I tell you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful” (John 16:20). Then, adding something like the sound of a harp, he said: “Your sorrow will be turned into joy” (ibid.).

He sounded the harp for us who said: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your moderation be known to all; the Lord is near” (Phil. 4:4). He sounds the harp for us who, announcing the blessings of our city, says: “Joy and gladness will be found in it, thanksgiving and the voice of praise” (Isa. 51:3).

Because the preachers of the holy Church announce the heavenly kingdom and command us, in order to attain that kingdom, to mortify the flesh, mourn our captivity, and exult in hope of future blessedness, the prophets are said to descend from the high place carrying before them a psaltery, a tambourine, a flute, and a harp. They are called a company of prophets because there are many pastors of the holy Church, and they have one shepherd, the Lord Jesus Christ.

17. It should also be noted that the prophets are said to have the psaltery, tambourine, flute, and harp before them so that the model of chosen preachers may be displayed. The reprobate, however, have behind them the things they preach, because they say and do not do; they neglect to perform the good things they know. Hence it is also said to King Saul, who was already despising the Lord’s commands: “Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, so that you shall not be king” (1 Sam. 15:23). Through the prophet the Lord also complains about the Jews, saying: “They have cast me behind their body” (1 Kings 14:9).

Holy teachers, therefore, because they continually preserve by good works the path of heavenly conduct that they preach, are represented by the statement that the prophets, descending, had the psaltery, tambourine, flute, and harp before them.

These instruments can also be referred to the preaching of the Redeemer. And because we said above that the hill of the Lord itself is the Redeemer, let us consider the correspondence of the instruments. Whoever names him king of the eternal kingdom sounds the psaltery for us. Whoever asserts in him the discipline of our mortification strikes, as it were, the tambourine. He sounds the flute who proclaims that the Redeemer died for the salvation of the world. He strikes the harp who says that he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven.

But we rejoice at the delight of such great instruments if we listen to that entire company of prophets sounding together. David says: “His going forth is from the end of heaven, and his course reaches to its end” (Ps. 18:7). He says again: “All the kings of the earth worship him; all nations will serve him” (Ps. 71:11). He held the psaltery, as it were, in praise of the Redeemer, because he attained the higher part of praise and proclaimed the Redeemer’s coming from the highest heaven.

Isaiah touched the tambourine of his mortification, saying: “And we saw him, and there was no appearance in him; and we desired him, despised and last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity. His face was as though hidden and despised; therefore we did not esteem him” (Isa. 53:3). Sounding the flute of his death, he likewise says: “He will be led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb he was silent” (ibid., 7).

David, striking the harp of the resurrection, rebukingly says: “Let all the earth be moved before his face; say among the nations: The Lord has reigned from the wood. For he established the world, which shall not be moved” (Ps. 95:10). Also touching the harp of the ascension, he said: “Sing to God, kingdoms of the earth, who ascends above the heaven of heavens toward the east” (Ps. 67:33–34).

The prophets therefore descend from the high place when holy preachers announce to us those mysteries that they have learned through lofty contemplation. They sound the psaltery, flute, and harp because they assert that our Redeemer is Lord of the eternal kingdom, humbled through the human condition, redeeming the world by his death, and restoring heavenly things by his resurrection. They have these instruments of praise before them because they understand the things they say.

By contrast, Caiaphas is said to prophesy (John 11), while not knowing what he said; when he touched the flute of the Lord’s death, he had it not before him, as an elected prophet would, but behind him.

It is therefore rightly added concerning the chosen prophets: “And themselves prophesying.” For while they see what they are going to say, they have before them, as it were, the instruments they are to play; and while they preach, they bring forth what they have come to know through foreseeing.

Saul therefore comes to the hill of the Lord when the chosen but inexperienced preacher advances in spiritual knowledge and recognizes the Redeemer of the human race not on the level ground of his humanity but in the lofty majesty of his divinity. Then he hears the choirs of prophets singing together, because he perfectly understands all the Scriptures that concern him. He who saw men leaping over great pits and observed men carrying young goats, round loaves, and a jar of wine reaches the hill of the Lord when the one known to have advanced through the examples of the elect is raised to the summit of knowledge; and, knowing the Redeemer in a sublime manner, he loves him ineffably, from whom, as though from a familiar friend, he may [obtain] whatever else he desires to know about him.

18. It is rightly added [Note: Vaticanus and Gilot: “therefore, it is rightly added”]: “And the spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them.” The spirit of the Lord is said to rush upon them because the hearts of the elect are suddenly filled with his gifts. They immediately begin to prophesy, because those who are filled with the divine Spirit cannot keep silent about the mighty works of God.

He is also declared to be about to prophesy to whom Samuel promises the grace of the divine word. It is as if he said: “You who now cannot speak amid the abundance of the spirit coming upon you—when that fullness has poured itself into you, you will abound in the power of speech.” Promising this rushing Spirit to his disciples, the Lord says: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth, and he will announce to you the things that are to come” (John 16:13).

The Spirit rushes upon those whose hearts he suddenly comes upon and illumines (Acts 2:2). And once illumined, they prophesied, because they proclaimed the Redeemer of the human race in every language. We still see this happening in the holy Church: often those who desire to speak divine things are suddenly taught by that same Spirit, and they can speak excellently even of things they had learned through no prior preparation.

For the sake of guarding God’s commandments, they receive the grace of speech through a lofty revelation of the Redeemer. What is surprising if they can suddenly receive the light of knowledge, when through purity of life they are always seats of the Holy Spirit?

But what kind of gift would the Holy Spirit be if he gave knowledge without also giving the affection of great charity? Those who are filled with that Spirit preach heavenly things, but they love what they proclaim. He therefore appropriately adds: “And you will be changed into another man.”

What else is the love of the elect mind than a transformation from its old condition? For our nature was so condemned through the fall of the first man that each day it declines through falling and grows old through declining. But although we fail in ourselves, when that Spirit rushes upon us we are renewed, because immediately we become what we were not.

Someone was lukewarm, but suddenly visited by the Spirit he becomes fervent. He begins to burn with devotion and to exercise himself vigorously in good works. He has therefore been changed into another man, because he began to be what he could not have been before the Spirit rushed upon him.

Someone is already of good conduct, loves heavenly things, and despises earthly things, but cannot prevail to weep for those things he loves above and those he hates below. Often he desires to weep but cannot, recalling that he has committed many things for which he ought to weep. But when that Spirit suddenly rushes upon him, he bursts into fountains of tears.

He is changed into another man when, through the coming Spirit, he receives the grace of compunction that he did not possess before the Spirit’s arrival.

Someone desires to attain purity of heart, to think of heavenly things, and not to be hindered by the intrusions of worldly cares; but through the affection of purity he cannot rise toward what he desires through devotion. Suddenly, however, seized by the power of the Spirit that has come upon him, he ceases to be carnal, casts away the cares of the world with strength, and rises with wondrous purity into contemplation of eternal things.

Then he marvels that he is what he was not; then he marvels that he was not what he is. For when he sees himself to be such in spiritual matters, the one who is such marvels that he could not have been such before. He is changed into another man when he sees himself to be what he was not and sees himself no longer to be what he had been.

It is therefore rightly said of Saul: “You will be changed into another man.” For when the preachers of the holy Church receive the grace of divine preaching, they receive not merely knowledge of the word but the power of love, so that through the word they may benefit others and through love of the word become better themselves.

When they speak, they are changed into another man, because when the Spirit speaks through them, they are joined to that Spirit by wondrous charity and now dissent from his will neither in word nor in action. Of such a man sacred Scripture gives high praise, saying: “Whoever is joined to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). We are joined to God when we abundantly receive the grace of the Holy Spirit; and we become one spirit with him when in mind, mouth, and deed we agree with the divine will.

The prophet Samuel therefore appropriately continued, saying:

**(Verse 7.)** “When all these signs have come upon you, do whatever your hand finds to do, because the Lord is with you.”

19. These are indeed the signs by which the preacher recognizes himself; and then he should dare to do whatever he intends only when he knows through certain experience that, in great abundance of charity, he has received the power of the Holy Spirit.

But the preacher must teach the things he does, as Luke says concerning the Lord: “Jesus began to do and to teach, until the day when, after giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up” (Acts 1:1–2). Hence Paul says: “I do not dare to speak of anything that God has not accomplished through me, in the obedience of the Gentiles by word and deed” (Rom. 15:18).

Samuel therefore commands the anointed king, saying: “Do whatever your hand finds to do.” It is as if he said: “When you see yourself full of divine grace, teach others whatever you do, because from that same divine grace presiding over you, you have both the ability to live very well and to preach profitably.”

Nevertheless, he adds what he must observe before all these things, saying:

**(Verse 8.)** “And you shall go down before me to Gilgal. Indeed, I shall come down to you, so that you may offer an offering and sacrifice peace offerings. You shall wait for me seven days, until I come and show you what you are to do.”

20. What does it mean that he first says, “Do whatever your hand finds to do,” and then adds, “You shall wait for me seven days, until I come and show you what you are to do”? But the one who had received the signs by which he knew himself to be an anointed king from the Lord had to be tested as to whether he recognized those signs. This is more fitting for a spiritual than for a historical explanation.

For we said that coming to the hill of the Lord pertains to perfect knowledge and love of the Redeemer, and being filled with the gift of prophecy to the power of the Holy Spirit. He therefore says: “When all these signs have come upon you, do whatever your hand finds to do,” because anyone who is certain of the Holy Spirit’s inner inspiration may presume both upon the purpose of good works and upon the ordering of preaching.

He also said: “You shall wait for me seven days, until I come and show you what you are to do,” because the supreme shepherds of the holy Church, when they are uncertain about the progress of their subordinates, are extremely solicitous to recognize it in them through definite signs.

What are the signs of the Spirit if not outstanding gifts of humility? For the more brightly the Holy Spirit illumines the hearts of the elect with the light of the virtues, the more abundantly he enriches them with the gift of humility. The higher they are in merit, the more level they are through the virtue of humility.

Therefore, when he is commanded to go down and wait in Gilgal before the prophet, the burden of obedience is imposed upon him so that his humility may be recognized. It is also the proper order of chosen conduct that one should not impose obedience on others when he himself has not taken care to render it to others.

He is therefore commanded to wait so that it may be recognized whether he is truly humble. If, then, the sign of a perfect preacher is fullness of the Holy Spirit, and the virtue of humility is the sign of that fullness, what is said in praise of humility except that its gifts are signs of signs?

21. But because the king who is going to sacrifice is commanded to go ahead through the prophet, we understand the statements better if they are considered in their order. Gilgal is interpreted as “wheel.” What, then, does the wheel signify in this passage if not the life of those who obey?

A wheel advances by rolling, sometimes seeking what is high and sometimes what is lower. So too the life of those who obey: because it performs below what draws it upward, and above it sees what it displays below, it is lifted toward high things, as it were, and lowered toward low things.

For what the obedient perform below, they raise upward, because when they obey the commands of their superiors, the things they do are earthly; but from the earthly things they do, they await heavenly rewards. Likewise, what they possess above they bend toward the earth, because in order to perform earthly things well they contemplate heavenly things, and they perform only what they see to be fitting for that supreme happiness.

The Lord commanded Moses to bend this wheel when he said: “Make everything according to what was shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. 25:40). He who saw in the heights what he made below bent the upper part of the wheel toward the earth.

He also raised the lower part toward higher things who said: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand” (1 Kings 17:1). He stood below through the humility of obedience while rebuking the wicked king; but he raised the level ground of his work into the sublimity of divine contemplation, so that he might roll the wheel excellently as it ran, while in earthly work he looked toward what heavenly reward he might merit.

This is certainly the pattern of chosen obedience: that in everything we do outwardly, we look everywhere to the power of the Creator, who is present. In this way, through the submission of our obedience, we can possess both uprightness in action and growth in devotion.

We are upright in action because we exercise ourselves in the labor of obedience for the sake of the one whom we behold. We are also devout because we believe that we please the one whom we regard as the observer of our labors and the giver of eternal recompense.

And because the commands of superiors must be observed with perfect humility, Saul is rightly told: “You shall wait seven days.” The number seven refers to the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit. We wait seven days for the teachers of the Church when, through the power of the sevenfold Spirit, we receive such brightness of inner devotion that we neglect none of their commands.

Here it should be noted that he did not say, “You shall be in Gilgal for seven days,” but, “You shall wait for me seven days, after you have gone down before me.” We go down before the preacher when we do what is commanded to us by his judgment. We are said to go down because we subject our minds to their authority.

To wait seven days is to fill the good of obedience with the whole light of the heart. We do this when we pass over none of the commands of our superiors, whether hard or easy. The Lord did not wish any day to be empty of this light when he said: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19).

And because the perfect obedience we show to human beings is the Creator’s gift, the one who waits seven days is said to offer an offering and sacrifice peace offerings. The offering is the Lord’s because it is offered to human beings on God’s behalf, but what is offered to human beings is received from God.

The sacrifices are the services of the obedient, because when we submit to human beings for God’s sake, we overcome proud spirits. We attack demons with other virtues, but through obedience we conquer them. Those who obey are therefore conquerors, because while they perfectly subject their own will to others, they themselves rule through obedience over the angels who fell.

22. But it should be noted that Samuel commands Saul to go down before him in Gilgal, yet did not wish him to offer the offering and sacrifices without him. For he said: “I shall indeed come down to you so that you may offer an offering and sacrifice peace offerings. You shall wait seven days, until I come to you and show you what you are to do.”

What does this mean except that we ought wisely at times both to be ignorant of our good works and at times profitably to know them? They must be unknown to us so that, while we are weak, they may not provide us with grounds for elation; but they must be known to those who are more perfect, so that they may grow through devotion.

Hence it is also rightly said in the Gospel concerning the pregnant Elizabeth: “And she kept herself hidden for five months” (Luke 1:24). Those who are not yet able to be spiritual and strong are signified by the number five. The woman who has newly conceived hides herself for five months because she performs good works through the bodily senses; but because she is not yet spiritual and strong in this good work, she wisely conceals the things she does.

That one offers sacrifices to God, that one offers an offering, who, waiting seven days, receives the prophet when he comes. For what he offers is worthy of God when the one offering it is made just by the virtue of obedience and awed by consideration of the divine immensity; when he believes himself to be nothing other than what he is found to be by the testing of his superiors.

We offer, as it were, in the presence of the prophet when we believe that only those of our works are worthy of divine acceptance that have been approved by the judgment of holy preachers. And because he is said to sacrifice before the prophet, this clearly signifies that we ought to trust our works to wise and spiritual men [or: in our works, to wise and spiritual men].

Likewise, because Saul waits seven days, the preacher of the holy Church ought wisely to arrange the virtue of his subordinate, so that he does not praise that person’s good qualities in his presence except when the person is able to despise the favor of his praise. Hence the same offering and sacrifices are said to be offered by Saul to God, not to himself [Note: Gilot: “that Saul be said to offer . . .”]. He offers sacrifices to God who does not vainly exalt himself over the virtue he possesses but attributes everything he accomplishes to the grace of the Creator.

Because we learn this also through the teaching of teachers, Samuel appropriately concludes his speech, saying: “And I will show you what you are to do.” He indicates to the one waiting what he is to do when the one who is recognized as perfectly obedient is taught how he ought to command others.

But this is not yet exhibited to Saul; it is promised. He is not sent to sacrifice but to wait. And because we advance through conversation with the saints, it is aptly added:

**(Verse 9.)** “And so, when he had turned his shoulder to leave Samuel, God changed his heart into another one.”

23. For the heart is changed when it is directed toward seeking better things; the heart is also changed when it is abandoned to evil. In Saul, however, who was first good and later evil, it is not altogether clear how this ought rather to be understood literally. But if it is said with reference to his advancement, he had a changed heart because he who had sought the she-asses was now thinking about the establishment of the kingdom. If, however, it is understood that he then received an evil heart, he was humble in the presence of the prophet; but as soon as he began to depart, he also began to become proud. In his mind he was already thinking that he was no longer a little man but a king. He was not yet exalted in rank, but he was exalted in his own estimation. Yet because, throughout this sacred history, nothing is still openly said about his pride, we too act more rightly if for the time being we remain silent about whatever may appear unfavorable concerning him.

What may still support his innocence is said in what follows: “Saul was one year old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years over Israel” (1 Sam. XIII, 1). For if he was a humble king for two years, his changed heart is asserted on account of the vigor of his purpose, not on account of the novelty of arrogance.

Therefore, in the statement that Saul had a changed heart, he is compared with the new preachers of the holy Church, who, when they receive the office of preaching, become better through divine grace. Samuel anointed Saul as ruler, but God changed his heart into another heart, because we receive the sacraments of the sacred orders outwardly from the teachers of the Church, while inwardly we are strengthened by the power of the sacraments from almighty God. The power of the sacrament, moreover, is the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. Those who certainly receive this grace are changed as though they had received another heart, because the Holy Spirit, by strengthening them with his grace, immediately makes them to be what they were not.

Thus, too, the disciples of the Redeemer were previously afraid; but when, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, another heart had been changed in them, they preached the word of God with confidence (Acts IV, 31). God changed another heart in those to whom he granted knowledge of all languages (Acts II, 6). He changed another heart in those whom he clothed with extraordinary love and illumined with the splendor of every virtue.

And it should be noted that God changed another heart in him when he turned his shoulder in order to depart from the prophet. For he turns his shoulder as though to depart when the one who undertakes the office of preaching resolves to do what is commanded him concerning pastoral service. He resolves to do so, but does not prevail unless God changes his heart into another heart, because the highest office is not well governed unless the mind of its ruler is filled with the supreme grace of the divine gift. But because this is promised to him in the future, it is added:

**(Verse 10.)** “And all these signs came upon him on that day.”

[Col. 0299D] 24. For what else is the teaching of the chosen preacher than the day of the instructed disciple? Whoever walks in daylight sees both the level paths on which he should walk and the precipices that he should avoid. Thus, while we are illumined by the teachings of holy preachers, we clearly perceive what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided.

Therefore, on that day on which the prophet preaches, the good hearer perceives the signs of his election: he sees in himself those gifts of virtue which his preacher had previously shown would come to him. They are called signs because by means of them those who are promoted to the office of preaching understand that they have been chosen by God.

Let no one who has been anointed for leadership in the Church consider himself truly anointed if he does not see the signs of that day present in the power of perfection. Let him first carefully examine the first sign—namely, whether he has already learned, by the example of men, to leap over the great pits. Let him also recognize the following sign: whether he has met three men going toward him at the oak of Tabor, whom he saw carrying young goats and round loaves to Bethel, to the house of the Lord, and whether he received two loaves from their hands. Let him likewise observe the third sign: whether he came to the hill of the Lord, whether he saw companies of prophets, whether the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, and whether he is now able to prophesy in their midst.

He saw men leaping over pits if, by the example of the perfect, he has already learned to reject all worldly things. He came to the oak of Tabor if he has already learned to experience the strength and delight of the contemplative life. There he saw men carrying young goats, round loaves, and wine to the Lord, because from lovers of the contemplative life he has already learned both continually to recognize himself as a sinner, to afflict his flesh for those sins, and gratefully to offer the pain of his affliction to almighty God.

He came to the hill of the Lord if, by advancing, he climbed either to the revealed inner glory of the Redeemer or to the lofty understanding of the Scriptures. He met a flock of prophets if he understood the harmonious knowledge of the preachers of the holy Church. In their midst he felt the Spirit of the Lord rushing upon him [Note: The Vatican and Gilot editions read, “if by that ineffable sweetness,” etc.] when, in the ineffable sweetness of inner experience, he recognized in himself the gift of the divinity that had come upon him and poured out, by speaking, the abundance of the grace he had received.

Whenever holy preachers show all these things to us who are imperfect, through the teaching by which they illumine us they reveal, as it were, the clearest day. And preachers who have already been promoted know all these things when their ordainers explain them.

25. Since, therefore, they have a day of signs, let them profitably consider whether they already see the promised signs. Whoever has not yet learned to despise the glory of the world may have heard the first sign promised, but has not seen it displayed. If he does not know the strength and sweetness of the contemplative life, he has not deserved to see the good of the next sign. If he has not climbed to the heights of the Scriptures through intimate knowledge of learning, he has not yet come to the hill of the Lord. If he does not yet possess the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon him, he cannot prophesy.

For without that Spirit the shepherd is carnal, and what he says cannot be attributed to the dignity of preaching but to the audacity of presumption. By what fear, then, can we wretched men be terrified? Behold, we have undertaken the leadership of others, although we do not possess the virtue required by the rule we have undertaken. We have heard of the signs of spiritual authority, but through the light of experience we do not see them in ourselves. We desire earthly things, we are occupied with outward concerns, and the more we are weighed down by anxiety over earthly actions, the farther we are driven from heavenly contemplation.

Depressed by this burden of earthly life, when shall we reach that splendor of the Redeemer’s inner glory? When shall we be able to attain the loftiest meanings of the holy Scriptures? Yet we cannot speak of the heavenly things we do not know as though they were familiar. And because we do not wish to devote ourselves in quiet to the love of the inner life, we do not feel the Spirit of the Lord rushing upon us.

Let the signs that are known but not possessed therefore terrify us, so that, when we are pierced by the immensity of our negligence, we may seek through tears and lamentations the virtue of the office we have undertaken. Hence the Psalmist, lamenting in the voice of the weak, says: “We have not seen our signs; there is now no prophet” (Ps. LXXIII, 9). For he is a prophet when these signs of prophecy, already mentioned, are foreseen to be present in him.

If, then, he is raised to the summit of authority, let him not consider himself according to the height of his office, but according to the virtue of perfection. Let him say: “We have not seen our signs; there is now no prophet.” As though he were saying: “I would now say that I was a prophet if I saw the gifts of the Spirit with which the person of a prophet ought to shine.”

Therefore, whoever has heard of the perfection of pastoral office that he has undertaken, but has not deserved to possess it in his way of life, is not a suitable teacher of the holy Church. Thus, in the first king, the advancement of all the shepherds of the holy Church is displayed when it is said: “All these signs came upon him on that day.” And because the advancement of chosen preachers is marvelous, it follows:

**(Verse 11.)** “But those who had known him yesterday and the day before, seeing that he was with the prophets and prophesied, said to one another: ‘What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?’”

26. What does their question mean—“What has happened?”—except that they greatly marveled at something they could not comprehend? They knew him as a man, the son of a man; they saw him associated with prophets. They knew him as carnal; they saw him as spiritual. They knew him as simple; they saw him as a prophet.

Thus they say: “What has happened to the son of Kish?” They were able to know what he had been, but they did not understand how he could be what he was. This, finally, is the advancement of a spiritual preacher: that one who was once known in ordinary life should possess, in a higher order, something that remains unknown.

Three stages of perfection are displayed, because he says: “Yesterday and the day before.” In two days the preacher is recognized; on the third he possesses something that even those who knew him do not recognize. The first day belongs to hearers, the second to companions, and the third to preaching.

The shepherd had his first day when he obeyed his superiors as a disciple. [Note: In other editions “disciples” is read; we judged that this should be corrected.] For he is seen, as it were, in great light who is devoted in the virtue of obedience. He had his second day when he began to be a co-worker of those who were better. The brightness of great conduct makes this a great day in the example of the elect.

The Lord, implying this day, says: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

The third day, however, is the day of the Spirit rushing upon him and of prophecy. On the third day the shepherd is seen when he matches the greatness of his dignity with the splendor of his conduct; when, clothed with heavenly virtue, his life and teaching shine before his subjects so that they can see him, but cannot scrutinize or judge him.

Such was Moses when he descended from the mountain with a radiant face. His subjects saw the splendor, but could not fix their gaze upon the radiance of that glory (Exod. XXXIV, 35; 1 Cor. III, 7). Such was the one who gloried, saying: “But we, with unveiled face beholding the glory of God, are transformed into the same image, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (1 Cor. III, 18).

Such indeed were those whom the Holy Spirit had filled. Hence those who had gathered in Jerusalem, marveling, said: “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans?” (Acts II, 7). They asked in order to learn what they were hearing, yet they could not understand it.

Those who knew Saul marvelingly ask what has happened to him because we sometimes see men who were humble and despised in the humbler order of the holy Church, but who, when the Holy Spirit raises them to the office of preaching, clothes them with the splendors of his gifts and makes them marvelous in those same splendors.

We rightly marvel at the virtues of the saints when we ascribe them to the goodness of the Creator. Thus Moses, confessing to the Lord, says: “Who is like you among the gods, O Lord? Who is like you, glorious among the holy, marvelous in majesty, performing wonders?” (Exod. XV, 11). Hence the Psalmist says: “God is marvelous in his saints; he himself will give strength and power to his people” (Ps. LXVII, 36).

It is rightly added:

**(Verse 12.)** “Another answered the other, saying: ‘And who is their father?’”

27. What is the reason that until now it was said only of Saul, “What has happened to the son of Kish?” and now the answer is given, as though concerning many: “And who is their father?” If this is understood historically, it cannot stand in any way. Therefore, the meaning that is removed from the literal sense must be sought in the spiritual sense.

When it is said, “Who is their father?” it is not only Saul prophesying who is being considered, but that entire company of prophets. All those prophets, because they were very spiritual, were reckoned not from carnal descent but from heavenly origin.

The father of the prophets is the one who asks through Malachi, saying: “If I am Lord, where is my fear? And if I am Father, where is my love?” (Mal. I, 6). Because they are joined to almighty God in great love, they are called the sons of him whom they love as a father.

This applies all the more appropriately to the preachers of the new Church, insofar as he has raised them higher into heavenly nobility who revealed to them the glory of so great a lineage in the form of a prayer. “Thus,” he says, “you shall pray: Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. VI, 9).

It is as though he were saying: “The holy preachers would be astonishing if they accomplished the marvelous things they do by their own virtue. But what is seen is not astonishing, because through them he accomplishes it for whom nothing is difficult.”

Let one say to another: “And who is their father?” As though he were saying: “Why is it astonishing if they teach marvelously, when they themselves are not the ones who speak, but the Spirit of their Father who speaks in them?”

It is not therefore said, “Who is his father?” (John VI, 42), lest what applies to many sons be attributed to one alone. For only he who is Son by nature dares to say: “My Father works until now” (John V, 17). And again: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II, 7).

But to demonstrate the difference between the two dignities, he says to Mary Magdalene: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John XX, 17).

Whenever, therefore, one preacher is seen to be distinguished by a marvelous life or preaching, he is seen in the heavenly generation not alone but together with countless others. For almighty God, who is shown to be marvelous in one person, makes himself far more marvelous in the judgment of men when innumerable others are observed to possess what they marvel at in one.

This may, however, suitably be referred to the detraction of carnal people. When they attempt to diminish the reputation of spiritual men, they investigate their carnal circumstances in order to produce something derogatory. Often, in the holy Church, those who have a marvelous reputation for holiness possess no worldly eminence.

When carnal people criticize either their bodily origin or their poverty, although they are already great and rich through divine generation, they ask mockingly about the father of the prophets. And because they regard it as a very strange thing that insignificant men of the world can appear so great, it is added:

**250 (The same passage.)** “Therefore it became a proverb: ‘Is Saul also among the prophets?’”

28. If they were to look rightly [Note: Gilot reads “rightly, with the eyes of the heart.”] with the eyes of the heart, they would not regard this as something new. For the Holy Spirit acts according to his customary manner when he raises the poor, the humble, and the simple to the summit of virtue. It is written of him: “He sets the lowly on high and raises the sorrowful to safety” (Job V, 11).

Hence almighty the Father says through the prophet concerning that same almighty Spirit: “Upon whom does my spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

Hence Paul says: “Not many wise according to the flesh, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong. And God chose the base things of the world, and the things that are not, to destroy the things that are, so that no flesh might glory in his presence” (1 Cor. I, 26 ff.).

This proverb can certainly also be attributed to the elect. For there was no lesser astonishment concerning the blessed apostle Paul when the Church heard that the man who had been accustomed to assault the Church by threats and slaughter was now defending it by preaching.

Then those who heard could say: “Is Saul among the apostles? Is that the man preaching Jesus who used to persecute Jesus?” But this has now become a proverb concerning the elect.

A proverb exists when something else is concealed in what is said. The conversion of the blessed apostle Paul became a proverb concerning the sinner. Let every sinner hear of the conversion of blessed Paul and not despair because of the multitude of his crimes.

For Saul, breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, afflicted the elect everywhere. He guarded the garments of those who stoned the protomartyr Stephen and, as though stoning him with everyone’s hands, made all those who were ready to stone him even more ready to do so (Acts IX, 1 ff.).

But he who had been such a man, persecuting Christ, was converted to Christ and became the head of the nations, because he obtained leadership over the whole Church. When we behold so great a sinner converted and honored by the Lord with so exalted a dignity, let us presume that we too can find forgiveness for our sins.

Our proverb, therefore, is this: that a persecutor is chosen to evangelize. It contains this mystery: that a converted sinner should not merely hope for pardon from the Lord, but should also be able, by fighting courageously, to reach the crown.

There is usually this difference between carnal and spiritual preachers: carnal preachers descend from lofty words of preaching to the depths of wicked conduct, whereas spiritual preachers, after the sublime things they speak, raise themselves to still higher desires for the heavenly homeland.

Hence it is added:

**(Verse 13.)** “But he ceased prophesying and came to the high place.”

29. He came to the high place after the ministry of prophecy who raises his mind to the heavenly joys that he preaches and lifts himself by loving those things that he displays in his speech.

When teachers preach ordinary and accessible things to the lesser, they are, as it were, on level ground with those whom they teach.

And because, after words of preaching, they prepare themselves by good works to obtain what they preach, they are said to come to the high place. [Note: These words are absent from Gussanville.] They are exalted in word and deed, but not in the thought of pride. They always do great things, but never desire to appear great.

It is rightly added:

**(Verses 14, 15, and 16.)** “Saul’s uncle said to him and to his servant: ‘Where did you go?’ They answered: ‘To seek the she-asses; and when we did not find them, we came to Samuel.’ His uncle said to him: ‘Tell me what Samuel said to you.’ Saul answered his uncle: ‘He told us that the she-asses had been found.’ But he did not tell him about the word concerning the kingdom which Samuel had spoken to him.”

251 30. The word concerning the kingdom is the honorable dignity of pastoral office. For by its very appearance it speaks, since one who is raised to so great an order is not an uncle.

The king therefore does not disclose the word of the kingdom, because the shepherd of the Church speaks with great splendor of divinity, but does not speak with arrogance. Whoever does not disclose the word conceals what he speaks. For the word always speaks to the one for whom it is a word; otherwise it is not a word.

The word of the kingdom belongs to the one who shines with a manner of life that, as though by speaking, offers others examples of the heavenly journey. He does not disclose the word because he does not reveal the greatness of his holiness through empty glory. He has something to disclose, but does not wish to disclose what is shown through him.

For whoever radiates great dignity and great holiness displays many things by living that he does not say by speaking. The Lord plainly wished his preacher to possess this word of the kingdom when he commanded that bells be placed on the priestly robe (Exod. XXVIII, 34).

The priestly robe is the display of good conduct. It is, as it were, fitted with many bells when it multiplies good works that cry out as examples to the lesser.

But the king does not dare to disclose the word of the kingdom, because the priests were commanded to wear the beauty of their robe before the Lord. He wears the beauty of the robe before the Lord both who displays good things and who desires to please, by the display of good works, not human beings outwardly through vanity but God inwardly through love.

Then the priest is silent, but as he walks, what he wears cries out. For the chosen preacher does not announce himself by boasting, but never ceases to speak by living well.

Let it therefore be said of Saul that he did not disclose the word concerning the kingdom to his uncle, because chosen men, when they receive the splendor of dignity or an increase of good conduct, make themselves known through examples but conceal themselves in silence.

And because they believe themselves inferior in merit to other chosen men, the one to whom he does not disclose the word is said to be his uncle. An uncle is called the brother of one’s father.

The Redeemer of the human race, however, makes all whom he instructs through the sacraments of his faith and teaching into sons, as many as there are, for the glory of the unfading inheritance of eternity. Those who are instructed in the Church are still like little sons. But the one who already meets him in perfect manhood through great merits is the brother of the Redeemer.

The blessed apostle Paul praises such men together, saying: “Heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ” (Rom. VIII, 17).

Because, therefore, perfect preachers regard other chosen men as perfect and themselves as imperfect, Saul’s uncle is said to have questioned him about the word concerning the kingdom. Samuel had told Saul that same word concerning the kingdom, because chosen men learned the spiritual conduct they possess through the speech of their elders.

But the king who had been initiated through anointing had not yet been chosen by the people. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0305C] **(Verse 17.)** “Samuel called the people together before the Lord at Masphath.”

31. Masphath, as I have said, is interpreted as “watchtower” or “observation.” The people are called together at Masphath for the appointment of the king because those who gather to appoint a shepherd of the holy Church are taught to attend to his spiritual qualities, not his carnal ones.

To observe means to recognize the preacher who is to be appointed through the pattern of sacred Scripture. For sacred Scripture is the mirror of the elect. The shepherd is known, as it were, through a mirror when he is shown to possess the character that is proclaimed in sacred eloquence.

Samuel therefore rightly gathers the people at Masphath, so that the election of a good bishop may not be human but divine: not one is chosen who can be determined by human judgment, but one who is declared in sacred eloquence.

Because this is a divine gift, it is necessary that the people, who are known to expect such great things from God, be cleansed from their guilt through the satisfaction of repentance. The very recognition of sin is preparation for the divine gift, because often, when we consider ourselves unworthy of a divine gift, we merit it through humility.

Hence Samuel first strives to turn those who had gathered to receive the king toward consideration of their sins, because it is added:

**(Verses 18 and 19.)** “Samuel said to the children of Israel: ‘Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I brought Israel up from Egypt, and rescued you from the hand of all the kings who oppressed you. But today you have rejected the Lord your God, who alone saved you from all your evils and tribulations, and you said: “No, but a king shall be over us.”’”

32. He carefully showed them both the good things that the Lord had done for them and the evil things that they themselves had done against the Lord, so that they might recognize that they had sinned all the more gravely because they had dared to offend by sinning the one from whom they had received such great benefits.

What it means to reject the Lord, and how this should be understood both according to the literal and according to the spiritual sense, has been explained at length above (above, in the exposition of verse 7, chapter VIII), where the Lord says to Samuel: “They have not rejected you, but me, according to all their works, which they have done from the day when I brought them up from the land of Egypt.”

But because holy preachers instruct those whom they pierce by their rebukes, he added, saying:

**(Verse 19.)** “Now therefore stand before the Lord by your tribes and by your families.”

33. We are commanded to stand before the Lord when, at the command of our elders, we prepare our hearts to know his commandments. Or the elect stand before the Lord when they are examined in spiritual virtues by the highest men, so that the one found to be better among them may be preferred to the others through pastoral care.

And because there are many orders of the faithful, they are commanded to stand before the Lord by tribes and families. Explaining this more fully, he adds:

**(Verses 20 and 21.)** “Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel forward, and the lot fell upon the tribe of Benjamin. He brought forward the tribe of Benjamin and its families, and the family of Metri was selected, and it came down to the son of Kish.”

34. He made all of them stand by tribes and families, so that he might examine them all and, after examining them all, choose the more useful one.

But because he already knew the king through the Lord’s revelation and, at the Lord’s command, had anointed him as ruler, why is he still sought for selection by tribes and families? [Forte, eligendus: “perhaps, the one to be chosen.”] The king had been found by the prophet alone. He is therefore sought after he has been found, so that he may be found as one not found by the people.

He is also sought by lot, so that the people could not doubt that the one chosen by the prophet had been provided through divine dispensation. [Note: The Vatican and Gilot editions read: “so that the people, once provided for, could not doubt.”]

What, then, is signified by this action except that the rulers of the holy Church must be chosen after much consideration? For the highest preachers, from the inner grace of the Holy Spirit that they possess, are filled with the great light of foresight. And because they are very humble, they do not presume upon the greatness of their inner illumination. Therefore they test before others what they have rightly arranged among themselves.

The prophet alone knows the future king when the highest ruler of the holy Church perceives both the person and the merits of the one to be appointed ruler. He anoints him as ruler when he affirms that he is full of spiritual gifts. Yet he still calls the people together, divides them by tribes and families, casts lots, and finds as though by a procedure the one whom he knows.

The tribes and families stand as though divided when the various orders of the holy Church are considered according to their state of virtue. For when we contemplate the many perfections of the elect—when we see the purity of virgins, the strength of the continent, the honorable ministries of clerics, and the diligence of monks—we attend, as it were, to standing tribes.

And because there is much variety in the service of God, when we observe the various qualities found within each order, we see, as it were, not only tribes standing but also families.

The lot falls upon a tribe because better men are often found in one order than in another. For a tribe seems to receive the lot when those who are more perfect than others appear suited to the ministry of preaching. But the lot does not yet fall upon a person, rather upon a tribe, when there are several in whom a worthy person is concealed. Thus, for the highest men, something still remains to be sought.

It is rightly said that the lot fell upon the tribe of Benjamin, while Samuel brought forward that tribe and its families and proceeded to the son of Kish. For the chosen and highest men of the holy Church do not cease to consider the virtues of individuals until they come to the one who is found worthy, by lot, of the pastoral ministry.

But those who are worthy greatly dread undertaking the burden of so great an office. Hence it follows:

**(Verses 21 and 22.)** “They sought him, therefore, and did not find him. And they consulted the Lord concerning him, whether he would come there. The Lord answered: ‘Behold, he is hidden at home.’”

35. They hide themselves so that they may not be found, because they avoid undertaking a dignity whose burden they judge themselves unequal to bear.

Spiritual authority possesses both the outward glory of dignity and the inward greatness of work. For the ruler is honored by his subjects, and he bears those by whom he is honored. With the beginning of honor, therefore, the cause of burden arises, because from the place where honor is received by the ruler, he takes upon himself the very thing by which he is weighed down.

Although the honor of dignity itself is a great burden upon the mind, because it must be despised and yet accepted. It must be despised lest it raise the mind through pride, and it must be accepted so that subjects may honor the heavenly things that the teacher speaks.

A heavier burden therefore arises from honor, because the chosen shepherd can bear it with great strength of mind: he despises in himself what he receives for God, so that he may be such for God but not such for himself; he denies himself and does not deny himself, so that he may be what he is for God and not be what he is for himself.

The honor offered by a subject is therefore accepted so that preaching may be commended. The preacher also despises the honor offered, because he is not exalted by being honored but rejoices that the ministry of the word of God is commended.

How difficult this is can be understood better by thinking than by speaking. For weak minds cannot strongly bear the burden of others and arrange, by the strength of the mind, the reverence due to offered honor, so as to know how to rejoice in the progress of their subjects amid the services of that same honor and not know how to swell with pride because of their own reverence.

Because chosen men do not wish to displease God, they refuse, when called, to undertake the office of authority. But they possess this same flight from ministry as a virtue of humility, not as a boast of dignity. They flee as far as they can; but if they have been appointed by the Lord, they cannot remain hidden.

Thus Saul is hidden at home but is revealed when the Lord brings him forth, because chosen men withdraw themselves from the external ministries of the holy Church, yet, when the Lord disposes it, they are brought forth to arrange those external ministries.

But because now in the holy Church there are few who withdraw from such honors and many who thrust themselves forward, those who thrust themselves forward ought to take notice of this: the one who is said to have been hidden at home by the prophet was being sought not for spiritual dignity in the Church but for the worldly glory of kingship. They were not seeking him as a bishop but wanted to make him king.

Let the priest therefore consider with what state of mind the summit of the holy Church ought to be fled, if kings flee so cautiously from ascending the summit of the world.

But because holy men, the more earnestly they refuse to undertake the office of authority, are sought more devotedly by devoted peoples, it follows:

**(Verse 23.)** “They ran and brought him out from there.”

After this it is also added:

**(The same passage.)** “And he stood in the midst of the people.”

36. The ruler stands in the midst of the people when his strength is seen by all his subjects. For standing is a mark of virtue. Whoever works good things with perseverance stands firmly. And because good works provide an example to the lesser, he is seen standing in the midst of the people, not in solitude.

This can also suitably be understood as referring to uprightness of intention. Whoever stands upright in body raises his head on high. But whoever does good publicly does not stand firm in his work if he lacks uprightness of intention.

The king is therefore said to stand in the midst of the people so that the form of the rulers of the holy Church may be displayed: they ought to show good works as an example to their subjects, but avoid receiving worldly glory from the same good work.

And he adds how great he ought to appear:

**(The same passage.)** “And he was taller than all the people, from his shoulder and upward.”

37. Above we showed at length (Book IV, chapter 4, no. 20) that outstanding bodily stature in holy preachers signifies an increase of perfection.

He is therefore seen as exalted in the midst of the people who, placed at the summit of virtue, is not unknown to his subjects. The proper order of a chosen preacher is that, before climbing to the summit of ecclesiastical office, he should climb to the summit of virtue; that, for the honor of God, he should attain the summit of glory, and shine with still greater sublimity through the revealed perfection of his virtues. [Note: The Vatican and Gilot editions add *in*.]

Such a shepherd ought to be greatly praised by perfect men and desired and loved by the lesser. It is rightly added:

**(Verse 23.)** “And he said to all the people: ‘Surely you see whom the Lord has chosen, that there is none like him among all the people.’”

[Col. 0309A] **(Verse 23.)** “And all the people shouted: ‘Long live the king!’”

It follows:

**(Verse 24.)** “Samuel spoke to the people the law of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book, and placed it before the Lord.”

38. Concerning the law of kingship, since we have discussed it at length above (Book IV, chapter 4, section 4 and following), we shall recall only this much: it is not prescribed as historical fact, but shows what wicked kings will do and what good kings will avoid. Subjects are to be defended by kings, not stripped of their own possessions. Kings ought to provide assistance to their subjects; they ought not take away their fields, vineyards, and olive groves. But if someone should insist that these things were written not as warnings but as prescriptions, the law of tyrants is written for that king who is requested after the Lord has been rejected. The cruel law of kingship is therefore the punishment of a people that rejects the Lord. For it was not unjust that the people should lose their fields and vineyards, since it was willingly abandoning the Lord who reigned over it. Thus we see that everything contained in this royal law is equitable if we consider whatever the people had done wrong in requesting a king. For what great burden would this law impose according to divine justice if they unwillingly placed in the king’s service sons and daughters whom they had willingly removed from God’s freedom? And what seems inappropriate if those who rejected God reigning over them were finally made servants of human beings? When the law of kingship is written, therefore, the punishment by which the presumptuous are to be punished is entrusted to perpetual memory; and because it had been imposed by the Lord’s justice, it is said to have been deposited before the Lord.

But perhaps that right of kingship was something different from this law that is written. If so, Samuel speaks this law before the king to the people, so that the king may know what he is to demand from the people, and the people may know what they ought to render to their kings. This law is written in a book so that it may be preserved for the memory of future generations. It is placed before the Lord so that it may be held in reverence.

We have said that the saints who preach are kings of the churches, and we have shown clearly that everything contained in the royal law applies to them. Samuel therefore speaks this law to the people when the chosen teacher instructs the faithful of the holy Church with what humility they ought to submit to their superiors. It is also written in a book when he firmly implants these things in their minds. For one who speaks in such a way that his hearers forget what they have heard speaks the law to the people, but does not write it in a book. To write in a book the words spoken by a teacher is to commend them attentively to the minds of his hearers.
