It is as though the Lord wished to write what he had said when he declared: “Remember my word, which I spoke to you: ‘A servant is not greater than his lord’” (John 15:20). Hence Paul, describing the law of kingship spoken and written in a book, says: “Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13:7).

If, however, someone wishes to understand that another law was also prefigured here, let him consider the one blessed Paul sets forth when he says: “Let the one who proclaims the gospel live from the gospel, and the one who serves at the altar live from the altar” (1 Corinthians 9:14). The Lord was speaking this law of kingship to the people when he said: “The one who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and the one who receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matthew 10:41). And, to inscribe this law still more firmly in a book, strengthening his statement by an example from the lesser matter, he says: “Whoever gives one of my least ones even a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple will not lose his reward” (Mark 9:40).

It follows:

**(Verses 25–27.)** Samuel dismissed all the people, each to his own house. But Saul went to his house in Gibeah, and part of the army went with him—those whose hearts God had touched. But the sons of Belial said: “Will this man be able to save us?” And they despised him.

39. If a straightforward historical account is sought, what could ever have been said more plainly? But if we attend to the force of each word, great matters are enclosed within this verbal simplicity. For the people are said to have been dismissed to their houses, whereas the king is not said to have been dismissed to his house but to have gone there. The houses of the people and the house of the king are also mentioned separately: the people are said to have been dismissed, each to his own house, while the king is said to have gone to his own. Yet the people were dismissed before the king went away. With regard to the departing people, the text carefully indicates that they did not go all together but each went to his own house. Of those who followed the king, it does not say, “The part of the army went away, each following the king,” but, “A part of the army went with him.” Finally, those who follow the king are said to have had their hearts touched by God; those who despise the king are called sons of Belial.

This manner of speaking is not simple but exceedingly subtle for anyone who knows how to consider not merely what sounds plainly on the surface, but what it wisely conveys inwardly.

What, then, does it mean that the king is said to go to his house, while the people are said to be dismissed? We have shown that the king signifies the pastor of the Church and the peoples signify his subjects. To go is the act of one who is free; to be dismissed is the act of one who can be detained. The king is therefore said to go away so that, in the person of the preacher, freedom of spirit may be signified. Teachers can go away and return whenever they wish, because they are strong in good works and wise in inward deliberation. They come when they go out to their subjects either by the example of good works or by the word of preaching. They go away when they return to the secrecy of the mind and inwardly arrange what they are to do outwardly. Since they remain daily in this reflection, they are, as it were, hidden within a house. The king is therefore said to go to his own house because the preacher, proven by the practice of eternal life and secure through the teaching of wisdom, can freely go out to works and enter into the counsels of the mind.

40. The people, however, are dismissed to their own houses because the faithful subjects are not free to arrange whatever they wish, but only what they are commanded. They are dismissed as though held in custody: they are commanded to do what is ordered and to avoid presuming upon what is not ordered. And because they are sent to different works, each one is dismissed to his own house. For in order that we may accomplish well what is commanded us, before appearing in action we are first withdrawn within, into inward reflection.

Our kings therefore dismiss us individually to our own houses because they command us to proceed to what they enjoin upon us through the hidden ordering of the mind. They indeed issue good commands; but if we neglect to foresee the manner of our action, we scatter what has been rightly commanded through an unconsidered mind. Each one therefore returns to his own house when each faithful subject anticipates the work of obedience he proposes by arranging it through the counsel of the mind.

But because, after the king was chosen, the people are said to have been dismissed to their houses before the king went away, this may signify something else. Those who receive the king into their house go there when each subject prepares himself through reflection to offer faithful obedience to the one whom he has requested to rule over him. In this passage, therefore, the point is not that they are commanded to reflect, but that they submit themselves in lowly disposition to what is to be commanded. The king’s going to his own house means that he considers what he should command those who have been discreetly prepared.

The king has one house and the subject people another, because the former, with an elevated mind, considers how the paths of his subjects are to be arranged, while the latter prepare themselves, through the strength of their innermost purpose, to carry out the commands of their superiors. Hence the king’s house is said to be situated in Gibeah. *Gibeah* means “lofty.” The king’s house is therefore shown to be in Gibeah because the chosen teacher strives not to dwell by thinking upon low and earthly things, but to meditate upon what is high and heavenly.

It is also fittingly said that part of the army went with him to Gibeah, because those who are strong against the devil follow their chosen pastor toward the heights of virtue. Part of the army is therefore said to go with the king because within the holy Church there are many faithful people who know how to obey their superiors humbly but do not know how to contemplate elevated matters. They know how to carry out commands, but do not know how to foresee what should be commanded to others.

Paul seemed to recall the soldiers of this part when he wrote to the Colossians: “Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, as do Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, and John who is called Justus. These alone are from the circumcision who are my co-workers for the kingdom of God” (Colossians 4:10). Likewise, addressing the Romans, he says: “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my co-workers” (Romans 16:5). A little later: “Timothy, my co-worker, greets you, as do Luke and Jason” (ibid. 21).

He called his disciples co-workers because they were inferior in rank but participants in his labor. They were subject to the Apostle through the humility of obedience; but while they proclaimed with him the glory of the eternal kingdom, defended the truth together with him, resisted unbelievers, and bravely endured the persecutions inflicted upon them, they were, as it were, the king’s soldiers in God’s war. Part of the army is said to go with the king to Gibeah because perfect disciples are their teachers’ co-workers in the lofty ordering of the holy Church: they provide whatever assistance they can through the height of virtue, but serve those whom they assist through humility.

41. And because only those who have been anticipated by the grace of the Holy Spirit can do this, when part of the army is said to go with the king, it is added: “Those whose hearts God had touched.” Since we customarily touch with a finger, God touches the hearts of the saints when he grants them the grace of the Holy Spirit. They feel his touch because, having received the gift of inward virtue, they are moved away from the weakness of their carnality. They immediately become soldiers of the heavenly army, because through the power of the Holy Spirit they abandon weakness and prepare themselves for courageous deeds in Christ’s warfare.

But because within the holy Church certain people do not hesitate to despise their superiors, let them hear that those who despise the king are called sons of Belial. Through the vice of pride they are begotten in the likeness of the one of whom it is written: “He sees every lofty thing; he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25). They aptly reveal the character of the proud when they say: “Will this man be able to save us?” For holy men, since they despise present things and seek eternal ones, display outwardly in their conduct the contempt for the world that they retain inwardly; inwardly they are worthy of reverence, but outwardly they appear contemptible.

The proud, therefore, because they look only at what can be despised outwardly in the saints and are not worthy to see what is greatly deserving of reverence, say: “Will this man be able to save us?” It is as though, in their contempt, they were asking: “Can such great things be expected from someone so insignificant? Should this man, so small, save us, who are so great; this weak man, us who are so strong?” For what else do they mean by saying, “This man—and us,” except that the proud and arrogant, when they look upon others, always consider them small and weak, while they consider themselves great, strong, and wise?

They are therefore rightly called sons of Belial, because in exalting themselves through pride they conform themselves to the one who is said to have fallen from heaven in the same manner. Of these men, who despised the king, it is also said:

**(In the same passage.)** They brought him no gifts.

42. If we examine these words literally, they certainly indicate that both earthly rulers and the spiritual superiors of the holy Church are to be honored by outward services. Hence blessed Paul addresses the proud Romans, saying: “Render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due, taxes to whom taxes are due” (Romans 13:7). From this the chief of the Apostles exhorts us, saying: “Be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human creature, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him” (1 Peter 2:13).

We offer spiritual gifts to our rulers when we show them the reverence of honor that is their due and observe with great devotion what they command. Reverence of honor and humility of submission are great gifts. For when we submit inwardly to our rulers through humility and outwardly show them reverence through acts of honor, we present them with one gift from the body and another from the heart.

Thus, to disclose the figure of the proud, the prophet does not say, “They brought him no gift,” but, “They brought him no gifts,” because when they despise the chosen preachers, they refuse to offer them honor outwardly and humility inwardly.

But when chosen preachers recognize the fault of their subjects, they sometimes immediately desire to correct it by rebuke; at other times they pretend not to know it, so that they may seek an appropriate time to eliminate it. Hence it is immediately added concerning this same despised king:

**(In the same passage.)** But he pretended not to hear.

43. He hears the wickedness of his subjects who knows it; yet he hears and does not answer—indeed, he pretends not to hear. For often, when circumstances require it, the known pride of subjects is left uncorrected, so that it may be struck down at a more opportune time, as something already recognized.

We can properly discern this discretion of ecclesiastical discipline in this very king of Israel if we consider the different periods and actions of his reign. For while he was still inexperienced and newly appointed, he is said to have pretended not to hear the words of those who despised him; but after his kingdom had been established over Israel, he is reported to have fought on the right and on the left and to have conquered wherever he turned.

A fault that cannot be struck with deserved severity should therefore be concealed rather than exposed, because subjects transgress more boldly if the weakness of their superiors becomes known. Let what has been discussed in the fourth book of this work suffice; through the opening of the present book, let us renew our effort to explain what remains.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0313]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0313A]

1. When, in the preface to this work, I wished to assert the profundity of this sacred history, I maintained that it is especially evident from the fact that it was written by prophets. They were accustomed to speak of mysteries not only through words but also through events: they presented what was plain, but signified what was lofty. For the Holy Spirit spoke through them, and what they said as human beings was plain, yet it was profound and mysterious because the supreme and boundless Spirit suggested the speech to human beings.

Since, then, we are explaining the prophet Samuel speaking, we require all the greater diligence, inasmuch as he, sublimely taken up by the grace of the Holy Spirit, spoke of outward things but saw inward realities. He often described carnal matters but signified intimate and spiritual ones.

But since it is impossible to reach divine things by human effort, we must not rely upon our own strength, but upon the gracious favor of the Holy Spirit who, sent by the Redeemer, “has filled the whole world,” and who, “containing all things, has knowledge of the voice” in all things (Wisdom 1:7). Let us therefore hear what this same prophet now proceeds to relate concerning the deeds undertaken by the Israelites.

**(1 Samuel, chapter 11, verses 1–2.)** “And it came to pass,” he says, “about a month later, that Nahash the Ammonite went up and began to fight against Jabesh-gilead. And all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash: ‘Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you.’ And Nahash the Ammonite answered them: ‘On this condition will I make a covenant with you, that I may put out the right eyes of all of you and make you a reproach throughout all Israel.’”

2. If history is sought, nothing could be said more plainly or understood more easily. But if we wish to follow the spiritual meaning, let us first hear Paul speaking. Looking back upon ancient events, he says: “All these things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). He also indicates that there are spiritual battles when he says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12).

When, therefore, Nahash is said to go up and fight against Jabesh-gilead, the inward battles of the vices are signified. The progress of the sacred history is shown by these words, so that new battles might be stirred up against the new king; and by bringing them to a good conclusion, he might demonstrate his valor.

Who, then, is this Nahash the Ammonite? What is Jabesh-gilead? Nahash is interpreted as “serpent,” and Jabesh as “dried up.” Concerning the serpent it is said in Genesis: “Because it was more cunning than all the living creatures” (Genesis 3:1). If the likeness of this serpent is sought among the vices, what do we find more similar than the violent movement of *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony?

The movement of lust, the crime of theft, the desire for shameful profit, the impulse of anger, the bitterness of worldly sorrow, the sluggishness of *acedia*, the desire for empty glory, and the swelling of pride are openly detestable. But the vice of gluttony is all the more deceitful because it is also more hidden: it presents food to the body as though it were necessary, yet, while it abundantly nourishes the flesh, it plunges the sword of lust into the mind. It persuades us of something that is not sin; but from the point at which food is received as though eating were not sinful, the soul is subjected to the sin of lust.

Thus, in paradise, the serpent is shown to have come to the woman in order to deceive her through the vice of gluttony: it suggested one thing but obtained another, so that while it displayed something to be eaten, it administered unforeseen death. This serpent therefore signifies the appetite of gluttony, because it creeps in under the appearance of legitimate necessity and spreads the poison of impious pleasure.

It is also rightly called an Ammonite, which is interpreted as “people of sorrow,” because what it urges appears joyful but will be exceedingly mournful in eternal condemnation. It is called a people because all gluttonous persons are weighed down by the multitude of countless cares on behalf of the belly.

It goes up against Jabesh-gilead because it seeks to drive the bodies of the righteous, established in the lofty virtue of abstinence, headlong into desire for food. Flesh is rightly called “dried up” when it is not burdened by the moisture of fatness. Nahash goes up against those whom it sees to be dried up, because the spirit of gluttony imposes heavier battles upon those whom it recognizes as weakened by fasts.

Nahash is rightly said to have begun to fight, because holy men do not have the suggestion of gluttony as a covenant of friendship but as an adversary in battle. Those who abstain fight with the serpent when, through great strength, they suppress the appetite of gluttony so that they are not infected by the poison of lust. The warfare of gluttony is to provoke the hungry bodies of those who abstain to an excessive filling of the belly.

3. But the appetite of gluttony can tempt perfect men; it cannot overcome them. Nahash is therefore rightly said to have begun to fight against the dried-up city, not to have conquered it, because chosen men feel the assault of carnal desires but know how, through the strength of the mind, to resist those same desires; they know how to provide what is necessary with discretion.

They know how to suppress the violently rising assault of gluttony, and they know how to provide the body with proper nourishment according to its need. Hence the outstanding Teacher says: “I know how to eat and how to hunger” (Philippians 4:12). He knows how to eat and hunger who moderately refreshes the body and does not consent to the vice of gluttony when it urges him toward immoderate consumption of food.

Therefore, in answering Nahash, they say: “Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you.” Those who would like to refresh the flesh according to their desire, if they could feel no incitements to lust in the flesh, seek a covenant from gluttony. It is as though they were saying: “We will give you what is justly due to you, so that you do not inflict upon us what is unjust.” It is just that the body be refreshed, but it is exceedingly unjust that, once refreshed, the flesh should be aroused by the heat of lust to insult the spirit.

We therefore seek a covenant when we wish to favor the flesh in receiving food in such a way that we feel none of the evils of lust from the flesh. But we can wish for this; we cannot obtain it. For we offer proper refreshment to the flesh as though it were a tribute, but the flesh promises us none of the blessings of peace.

When we properly direct the hearing of the mind toward the responses of the vices, we recognize this in the voice of gluttony: if we fatten the flesh through increasing desire, we are struck with blindness of heart. Hence that same Nahash says: “On this condition will I make a covenant with you, that I may put out the right eyes of all of you.”

Our right eye is the contemplation of eternal brightness; the left eye is carnal desire. The right eye is put out when the mind is struck by such blindness that it is no longer opened to see heavenly things. An eye is put out when the light is torn from a corrupt mind in such a way that no root remains from which renewed light might burst forth.

Nahash therefore puts out the right eyes of his covenant partners when gluttony so prevails over those who abstain after conquering them that they desire only carnal things and no longer attend to what they formerly loved beyond them.

And because whoever is cast down in this life is condemned in the future before angels and chosen human beings, it is added: “And I will make you a reproach throughout all Israel.” The wicked are then made a reproach throughout all Israel when, at the final judgment, they blush before all the elect over the iniquities they have committed.

Alternatively, they are made a reproach in this life because, while they perpetrate evil boldly with blinded hearts, holy men blush for their sins. But those who disdain to appear shameful after their right eyes have been torn out should attend to what follows:

**(Verse 3.)** “And the inhabitants of Jabesh said to him: ‘Grant us seven days, so that we may send messengers to all the borders of Israel; and if there is no one who will defend us, we will come out to you.’”

4. Who are the inhabitants of Jabesh, that is, of “the dried-up city,” except those who have long practiced, as a virtue, the chastisement of their emaciated flesh? Many begin to resist gluttony, but when they begin to grow weary from the labor of abstinence, they incline themselves toward their customary gluttony. They desire, as it were, to enter the city of Jabesh and become its citizens; but because they cannot endure the torment of dried-up and hungry flesh, they can in no way become its inhabitants.

They inhabit Jabesh who possess the attenuation of the body as their property through the vigor of the mind. They are surrounded, as it were, by the walls of a dried-up city when, by weakening the body, they are protected from the fiery arrows of lust.

When they are wearied by the strongest attacks of gluttony rising against them, they ask for seven days’ respite, during which, if help is lacking, they will go out to Nahash.

But we explain this war of the Ammonites better if we observe in it the weakness of the flesh when it is exposed and the resourcefulness of the trained mind. We see this more clearly if we examine more subtly the contrary case in foolish and weak people.

For some within the holy Church are devoted in desire but slack because of the accustomed weakness of their vices. They can indeed propose good things, but because they cannot carry out what they propose and are overcome by present desire, they trust that they will be able to recover in the near future the good that they abandon in the present.

Often they decide to fast, but when they are overcome by their customary gluttony, they judge that they should eat that day and fast on a future day. And since the violence of gluttony is always present to them, while the desire for future goodness is also always present, this is brought about by the serpent’s deceit: the good that is proposed is never found. For “tomorrow,” which is always promised, is never encountered.

But because this is done by those whose mind is weak and flesh strong, let us see how those whose mind is strong but flesh weak mock the serpent. Concerning this same serpent the Psalmist says to the Lord: “This dragon whom you formed, to mock him” (Psalm 103:27). He is never defeated more appropriately than when his cunning is overcome by a pious deception.

Hence, reproaching blessed Job for his cunning, the Redeemer says: “You will catch him in his eyes, as with a hook” (Job 40:10). He caught the serpent in his eyes, as with a hook, who presented him with flesh but concealed divinity; and while the serpent seized what it desired, it was held and destroyed by what it did not see.

[Note: Gilot: *temptus*, “tempted.”]

5. Holy men therefore possess, in their present way of life, the rigor with which they mock the enemy; in order to deceive him through the weakness of the flesh, they promise the flesh some comfort in the future. They often undertake great things, but because of the weakness of the flesh they do not presume always to promise themselves harsh and difficult deeds.

They endure those same hardships more easily in proportion as they do not see their burdens as permanently imposed upon them. Yet while they live excellently and strive daily to advance rather than fall back, they always promise the flesh, in their future expectation, that lawful pleasure of the flesh from which they cannot despair; but they by no means cease to inflict upon it the pain of the affliction they have begun.

By leaving hope to the flesh in its desire, the spirit, as it were, promises the flesh the presence of its own coming to that flesh’s future good. But because the spirit does not abandon the customary rigor of abstinence by failing, the flesh has the promised pleasure in the future, while the chosen mind has the strength of virtue in the present.

Here it should be noted that they promise, conditionally, to go out against Nahash, but are fortified unconditionally by the walls of the city. Those who abstain trust that, even in their bodily weakness, they are strengthened by divine mercy.

And because they earnestly desire to outwit the vice of gluttony through deception, they say: “Grant us seven days.” Time is, as it were, granted by gluttony when it is restrained with the understanding that its desires will at some time be served.

During this interval of days, Nahash awaits the coming out of the besieged citizens, while the citizens of Jabesh await assistance, because the appetite of gluttony seeks refreshment from weak flesh, whereas the chosen mind seeks to be strengthened in the virtue of abstinence.

Help is sought during seven days when we are raised against the darkness of temptations by every light of the heart; when, against evil counsels, we find through our own reasoning whatever we can; and when we are fortified by the education of others with rays of light that we do not perceive within ourselves. For when we look to the conduct of perfect people for the strengthening of our virtue, we find, as it were, the help of defense through seven days.

We ask for a respite because, when we fight with Nahash, that is, with the serpent, the more hidden its poisons are, the subtler must be the counsels we seek against it. Hence they promise to send messengers throughout all the borders of Israel, because chosen men are assisted for their own edification by the examples of all who see God.

But when they say, “If there is no one who will defend us, we will come out to you,” the voice of the elect shows not uncertainty concerning assistance but certainty. As though mocking the adversary who urges them through crafty words, they utter words that give him hope while in no way removing their own confidence.

Those who say, “If there is no one who will defend us, we will come out to you,” offer some hope that they will come out. But because they say this while certain of assistance, they deceive their enemies by their promise. Where this assistance is now found, the text explains:

**(Verses 4–5.)** “Then the messengers came to Saul’s Gibeah and spoke these words in the hearing of the people. And all the people lifted up their voice and wept. And behold, Saul was coming in the morning, following the oxen from the field; and he saw the weeping people and said: ‘What is wrong with the people, that they are weeping?’”

6. As we have already said above, Gibeah is interpreted as “lofty.” And because not all the elect possess an equal height of merit, the messengers are said to have come to Saul in Gibeah, so that we may be taught spiritually that, when we are driven by powerful temptations, we should have recourse to the counsels of our preachers.

We are also instructed by the distress of the weeping people to join ourselves to the needs of our brothers through the innermost compassion of the mind. Saul saw the people weeping and asked why they were weeping because the chosen teacher makes the need of his subjects his own by compassion and desires to relieve it.

He came from the field because he came forth from the hidden place of his fruitful heart. He came from the field in the morning because, at the rising of the splendor of true light within him, he investigates the causes of his subjects. He follows oxen because powerful affections of charity go before him.

He has, as it were, two oxen before him who is joined to his neighbors through love and inflamed by divine charity. From this he loves his neighbor in an ordered way, because the love of God powerfully kindles him.

Therefore the Lord says through Moses: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass” (Deuteronomy 22:10). The ass is carnal love, because it bears those whom it loves as though it were a strong animal; and because it loves them inordinately, not for God’s sake, it is wanton.

One cannot plow with an ox and an ass because the soul is not cultivated for the fruit of eternal reward if the purity of the love by which it is joined to God is polluted by disordered love of one’s neighbor.

Saul therefore comes from the field and follows oxen because the chosen teacher preserves both affections of charity whole in his fruitful heart, and from them can prepare abundant fruits of eternal reward. He comes in the morning because, when he goes out to his subjects, he opens the day of his virtue.

But now that the needs of the people have become known, let us hear what he did. For it follows:

**(The same passage and verse 6–7.)** “And they had reported to him the words of the men of Jabesh. And the spirit of the Lord rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled. And taking both oxen, he cut them into pieces and sent them throughout all the borders of Israel by the hands of messengers, saying: ‘Whoever does not come out and follow Saul and Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen.’”

7. What are we to say about these words except that the things in holy men that appear weak and carnal are not weak and carnal, but spiritual and strong? We are accustomed to criticize excessive anger in religious people; but behold, before Saul could become exceedingly angry, the spirit of the Lord first rushed upon him.

We can see how fearsome the anger of the saints is if we consider the spirit of the Lord rushing upon them, and if, while we observe them angry outwardly, we also attend inwardly to the spirit moving them. Whenever we are corrected by the zeal of our superiors, we may tremble greatly beneath their indignation if we believe their impulse to be the movement of the Holy Spirit.

And because Saul cut both oxen into pieces and sent them throughout all the borders of Israel, uttering threats that the same would happen to the oxen of all who refused to follow him and Samuel, what else does this signify except that the more sluggish must not merely be invited but compelled to provide assistance to their neighbors? Hence it is immediately added:

**(Verse 7.)** “Then the fear of the Lord fell upon the people, and they went out as one man.”

8. Since we are commanded to love our neighbors as ourselves, we provide them assistance in proper order when we are moved to offer it not by fear but by love. But when we lose the effect of this necessary love, it belongs to the zeal of our preachers to make us rise in fear for the assistance of our brothers.

It is therefore rightly said: “The fear of the Lord fell upon the people, and they went out as one man,” because we are often lukewarm in our love of our neighbors, but we are raised by the threats of our superiors to a state of devotion and undertake good work out of fear; then, from the beginning of fear, we are led to the bond of great charity.

It is therefore fittingly said that fear fell upon the people, but that all went out as one man. Many cannot go out as one man unless they ascend to an equal unity of love. Hence it is also said of the Redeemer’s perfect disciples: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

It follows:

**(Verse 8.)** “And he numbered them at Bezek; and there were three hundred thousand of the children of Israel, while the men of Judah numbered thirty thousand.”

9. The sons of Israel are said to have gone out first, and afterward to have been counted by Saul, because an elected preacher, when he attempts to mobilize the army of his subjects against hidden enemies, first observes the strength of their resolve and then enrolls them among the warriors. For we are, as it were, still within and cannot be counted so long as the strength of our mind remains hidden from our pastors. But when we go out, we are counted, because when we reveal to them the strength of our minds, they trust that we already have companions in spiritual warfare.

When they desire to raise weak minds to the resolve to perform good works, they try not only to instruct us by the teaching of our elders, but also to kindle us by the examples of their lesser chosen ones. Thus it is rightly said that three hundred thousand sons of Israel, but thirty thousand men of Judah, were counted. The number thirty pertains to the rectitude of faith and the zeal for good works, because the precepts of the Law are of no value unless they lead toward contemplation of the supreme Trinity. Appropriately, therefore, the men of Judah are said to be contained in thirty thousand, because they possess the confession of right faith and the strength of good works.

Our fathers possessed this same faith and practice, but because they advanced far higher than we did in contemplation of the divinity, they also displayed stronger works of faith. This is why three hundred thousand sons of Israel are counted. Thirty is derived from three and ten, and ten enters into thirty; yet in the number thirty both ten and three are simple numbers. But when we count up to three hundred, we multiply ten thirty times and thirty ten times, because, although contemplation is great and the works of the subject people are great, those things that preceded us in our fathers were incomparable. For our number, like ten, is gathered tenfold in their perfection, while our perfection is greatly subordinated to theirs.

Therefore, the thirty thousand men of Judah and the three hundred thousand sons of Israel, counted together with us, lead preachers to battle against Naas when, wishing to help subjects who are being tested, they set before them both the outstanding deeds of the strongest fathers and those of the lesser ones. Israel means “seeing God,” or “in whom God is”; and this name certainly does not suit one who is still weak or inexperienced. Whenever we bring forth perfect men in bodily affliction and contemplation of mind, we strike down the serpent Naas with that many armed men.

But let us now hear by what words the army of the king encourages those who are besieged.

> (Verse 9.) And they said to those who had come: “Thus you shall say to the men who are in Jabesh-gilead: Tomorrow you shall have salvation, when the sun grows hot.”

10. Perhaps this is what that wise man’s counsel means when it says to us:

> “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not quickly abandon your place” (Eccles. 10:4).

The place of each of the elect is the position of a good manner of life. When it is permitted, an attacking spirit can have power, because it could in no way attack the hearts of the elect unless divine providence permitted it. He therefore commands us not to abandon our place, because if we are strong during the brief darkness of temptations, divine light will soon be present; at its coming, the power of darkness vanishes.

Thus it is rightly said: “Tomorrow, when the sun grows hot, you shall have salvation.” The exhortation of holy preachers is day, because when it touches the tested hearts of the lesser, it raises them to the hope of victory. But night follows this day, because, even when divine helps are withdrawn, the darkness of invading carnal desires still does not depart. What, then, is the following day except the coming of divine visitation? It is called the following day because, for the tested elect, the splendor of divine help is very near.

Hence the Lord also says through the prophet:

> “Am I a God nearby, and not a God far off?” (Jer. 23:23).

Here the Psalmist says:

> “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144:18).

Again, the Lord himself promises, saying:

> “Before you call, I will say: ‘Here I am’” (Isa. 58:9).

The first day, therefore, is the light of preaching; the following day is the light of divine grace. But it should be noted that he says, “when the sun grows hot,” so that the brightness of day may illuminate the obscurity of the mind, and the sun’s heat kindle the love of the heart: so that the mind may see by the light the good it should desire, and may desire through the mind’s warmth what it sees.

This twofold remedy of the mind is offered against the devil’s twofold warfare. For the evil spirit, in order to overcome the minds of the elect by temptation, first places before them the darkness of evil thoughts and then kindles the flames of desire. Unless he has first blinded the mind, he cannot drive it toward perverse desire. But when the chosen mind is permitted to be tempted, its condition is disturbed in both respects, because it can feel the troubles of desire only insofar as, with God’s permission, it cannot cast away the darkness of its thoughts.

Yet because it is permitted by God to be tempted, at the coming of his grace it is relieved from both evils: it receives light against darkness, and through the warmth of the arriving spirit casts off the mind’s coldness. It begins to see heavenly things, although previously it could not raise its mind above carnal things, and it ardently desires what it regards with love.

Thus it is rightly said: “Tomorrow you shall have salvation, when the sun grows hot,” because if we endure the powerful attacks of the ancient enemy with manly courage, we are swiftly lifted by divine grace to the light of the heart and the strength of great charity. And because the chosen hearts of subjects gratefully receive this counsel of the holy preachers, it follows:

> (Verse 9.) Then the messengers came and announced this to the men of Jabesh. And they rejoiced.

But let us hear what they reply to the Ammonites after the promised aid has been given them. For it follows:

> (Verse 10.) And they said: “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you shall do with us whatever pleases you.”

11. This is clearly said by those who, already secure in the aid that is near, offer some hope to their enemies while deceiving them by their promise. In their words they pretend weakness, but inwardly they retain the strength of the promised aid. They promise one thing and believe another.

For when they said, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you shall do with us whatever pleases you,” they led their enemies to believe that they would surrender themselves into their hands so completely that the enemies could do with them whatever they wished. But because they knew that the king would come on the following day to their aid, they intended to go out with him not into the hands of their enemies but to their slaughter.

In the spiritual sense, we promise our departure to Naas—that is, to the desire of gluttony—on its own day, but on our day we rout its battle lines. Its day is the pleasure of bodily satiety. Whoever proposes to fill his belly according to his desire, as though dedicating the first day to desire, is nevertheless still within, because he has proposed a certain light of pleasure that he has not yet experienced in action.

He goes out on the following day who has displayed, both by action and by enjoyment, that pleasure which he promised to the flesh. But holy men, as I said above, deceive gluttony. Since they cannot forever despair of its appetite, they promise what they do not take, as though promising it again in a future light of pleasure. Outwardly they are compelled by the excessive weakness of the flesh, but inwardly they are clothed with the strength of great charity.

By the former, those who cannot renounce their appetites promise, as though with an outward voice, what they do not hold in intention. By the latter, because they are secure in divine aid, they intend to do something different from what they say in the voice of weakness.

On its own day, therefore, they go out against Naas, because by the light of heavenly aid they advance to attack the desire of gluttony. Visited by heavenly grace, they are now strong against every assault of the flesh, though, when abandoned for a little while, they had feared its attacks.

Because the splendor of divine grace is sometimes poured through the mouths of preachers into the lesser members of holy Church, it follows:

> (Verse 11.) And it happened that, when the following day came, Saul divided the people into three groups. He entered the middle of the camp during the morning watch and struck down Ammon until the sun grew hot.

12. The people are divided into groups so that we may strike the serpent Naas not with a single battle line. They are divided into three groups to show the fruit and dignity of sacred abstinence, because by fasting we are recalled to the contemplation of the Holy Trinity, which we lost by eating. This is why the fasts of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel are commended.

Moses fasted twice for forty days in order to deserve to receive the Law (Exod. 34:28). Elijah, to escape Jezebel’s hands, reached Horeb, the mountain of God, after forty days in the strength provided by a single meal (III Kings 19:8). Our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, fasting for forty days in the wilderness, took no food at all (Matt. 4:2).

Saul therefore divides the people into three groups, because the fasts of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel are brought forward as examples for those who abstain. When the following day comes, the teacher enters the middle of the camp, because when divine grace—which illuminates the hearts of preachers for teaching—also enlightens the minds of their hearers and powerfully raises them to the hope of victory, the teacher enters the camp of the enemies on the following day to triumph; [the Latin then reads *et aperit*, “and he opens,” with no expressed object], and there he powerfully strikes the battle lines of desires.

Because the minds of those subjects advance through hearing, the king is said to enter the camp of the Ammonites during the morning watch and to remain in their slaughter until the day grows hot. The morning watch is the fervor of divine inspiration; the sun’s heat is its fullness. Light rises for us like morning light when, weighed down by the darkness of temptations, we begin to see from the mouth of preachers the light of virtue that we should follow.

The sun grows hot for us when our mind is inflamed by their words and, as though cooked by the heat of a burning sun, is set ablaze with desires. Then Ammon is struck violently, because the people of vices are driven away from our senses. The ruler, therefore, who enters the camp of the Ammonites during the morning watch should not sheathe the sword of slaughter until the day grows hot, because he ought to persist in instructing his subjects until he sees them inflamed by the great heats of inner light.

Here it should be noted that Naas is said to be the king of the Ammonites, while Ammon itself is interpreted as “the people of sorrow.” Since we have said that the vice of gluttony is signified by this serpent, when Naas is struck down, the people of sorrow are defeated, because from the single vice of gluttony countless armies of vices are brought forth to battle the soul. When that same vice of gluttony is cut down, we subjugate many other vices as well.

Gluttony is one vice, but the stings of lust are countless, and they follow it, as their king, in procession. They suggest pleasant things, but lead to the lamentations of eternal weeping. Thus we fight against Naas, but the people of sorrow are struck down, because when we tame the belly, the incentives to lust are killed.

Hence it is rightly asserted that not Naas himself, but Ammon, subject to him—that is, the people—is killed, because the appetite for eating must be restrained, not extinguished. Yet it is never properly restrained if the people of sorrow that follow—namely, the shameful impulses of lust—are not killed.

Our principal struggle is therefore against Naas, because when he is overcome, Ammon is killed: lust is then rightly struck down when its principal beginning has been subdued. How far the progress of chastity extends is subtly shown by what follows. For he says:

> (Verse 11.) But the rest were scattered, so that not even two of them were left together.

13. The proof of true abstinence is not the wasting away of the body but the perfection of chastity. The serpent is rightly crushed when the belly is so restrained that every violent impulse of bodily lust is diminished. An unlawful movement cannot be removed from the flesh so long as it remains flesh, but the violence of that movement can be removed.

The law of the flesh cannot be prevented from moving the members of the flesh; nevertheless, the violence of movement can be removed from the flesh, so that movement remains, while every obscenity of pleasure is taken away from that movement, and it becomes a simple movement in which there is no remaining shamefulness of lust. [Note: Alternatively, “in which there is no shamefulness of lust at all.”]

Thus the others are rightly said to have been put to flight, because when divine grace perfectly rewards those who abstain, it removes from their bodily movements the stings of every obscenity, but leaves them the movements themselves, so that they can always be tempted but can never be overcome. It leaves behind what displeases them greatly, but weakens what it leaves behind so that it cannot prevail over those who conquer.

He had struck down the Ammonites who said:

> “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be disqualified” (I Cor. 9:27).

But after killing the others, he could not kill the fugitives, because he laments, saying:

> “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:23).

Again, seeing that those who remained had been weakened, he says:

> “No creature will be able to separate us from the love of Christ” (ibid. 8:39).

What, then, does he mean by lamenting that a law exists in his members that wars against the law of his mind, if, after the others had been killed, the rest had been put to flight? Only that perfect men deeply grieve that they must endure, against their will, even the simple movements of the flesh.

They would wish to remain in the flesh in such a way that they suffered no movement arising from the flesh against the will of the mind. But because this is impossible, he first said:

> “To will lies near me, but to accomplish it I do not find. For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I hate, that I do” (ibid. 7:18–19).

As though he were saying: “I would wish to be in the flesh, not with that perfection by which one who is perfect in the flesh is perfect, but as God’s angels are in heaven. Yet I do not find this possible, because until the death of sin has been swallowed up in the future resurrection, the sin dwelling within me moves me against myself.”

But what cannot be extinguished can be driven away. The movement of the flesh is, as it were, put to flight when the flesh itself is properly chastised by fasting. It raises itself against the spirit all the less often and with all the greater difficulty, the more the spirit presiding over it subjects it through deprivation, taming it so that it grows proud slowly and comes to rest quickly.

14. But we must examine carefully what is said: “So that not even two were left together.” Two do remain, but they do not remain together. They are an impure thought and the natural movement of the flesh.

In the struggle of the saints, an impure thought sometimes comes first; at other times they feel the law of the flesh rising against the law of the mind. But those who are already victorious do not fear enemies put to flight even if they return to battle, because they cannot fight together with them.

When a perverse thought confronts them, they cast it away before the flesh is moved by its suggestion. When the law of the flesh moves the members, the law of the mind does not nourish the shameful movement by entertaining shameful thoughts. While it casts away one, it does not feel the battle of the other.

Thus it is rightly said of the perfect victory of the elect:

> “The others were scattered, so that not two of them were left together,”

because through bodily mortification they advance to such a summit of perfection that whatever is introduced by the flesh or by the mind is easily overcome by them, since it is not permitted to join the battle.

The elect perceive this victory in all the senses of the body when, through the virtue of abstinence, they are able to subjugate the Naas besieging them. For well-fed and fattened flesh is easily led into the lapse of the tongue, the eyes, hearing, smell, and touch. When, therefore, unlawful movements of the bodily senses are brought from the vice of gluttony into battle with the mind, the people Ammon accompanies King Naas to besiege the Israelites.

But when Naas is perfectly conquered, Ammon is partly extinguished and partly put to flight, so that not even two of them are found together. For when we wear down the body through abstinence, we weaken countless unlawful movements of our senses; and those that we cannot eradicate altogether we drive away as though they were weak. Two of them do not remain together for battle, because we do not unite the mind’s sense with the pleasure of any bodily sense.

Often we look with our eyes, hear with our ears, or perceive by touch or smell things that can draw the carnal mind toward illicit love. Yet by perfectly mortifying our flesh we are victorious, because we do not see two of the defeated adversaries together. We see things that could be desired, but we avoid joining the soul’s appetite to the movements of the eyes.

Often, too, an illicit thought confronts the heart, but the victor over the serpent finds only the fugitive movement that he notices. For he does not raise any bodily sense by an illicit movement toward those things that he happens to think about in his heart.

Such are those whom the prophet marvels at, saying:

> “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60:8).

They are like doves at their windows because they receive things that could be desired but do not lose the simplicity of a pure heart by desiring them. They see what they might desire, but avoid desiring illicitly what they see.

We advance toward this victory through the exhortation of our preachers. Thus it is rightly remembered that, through Saul, the people of the Ammonites were conquered and struck down. Their battles, however, are not uniform but diverse. Sometimes they crush hidden adversaries with great power; at other times they wisely endure false brothers. The former they subdue within with great strength; the latter they tolerate outwardly with remarkable patience.

Within, through immense struggles, they are distinguished by the glory of great triumphs; outwardly, they are adorned with incomparable honors of such gentleness. Since we have learned the account of their inner victory, let us hear how they also conquer outwardly. For it follows:

> And the people said to Samuel: “Who is the one who said, ‘Will Saul reign over us?’ Give us the men, and we will kill them.” And Saul said: “No one shall be killed on this day, because the Lord has brought salvation to Israel.”

15. Earlier the Lord had said to Samuel:

> “They have not rejected you, but me, so that I should not reign over them” (I Sam. 8:7).

Of Saul, however, it had shortly before been said:

> “They despised him and brought him no gifts” (ibid. 10:27).

But after the enemies had been struck down and victory had been won, the rejected prophet and the despised king heard the shouting people say: “Give us the men, and we will kill them.” Each of them could have taken revenge on the enemies, not by killing them but by consenting to their death. Yet because the prophet had been rejected, he speaks, and because the king had been despised, he supports the one who says: “No one shall be killed.”

For our holy preachers are crowned with a greater victory when they endure the adversities inflicted by those near to them than when they conquer enemies from without.

[Note: That is, adversities inflicted by those near at hand. The word “adversity” is used in the same sense in *Moralium*, Book XI, no. 38; Book XVI, no. 45; and elsewhere.]

Hence true wisdom speaks in Solomon, saying:

> “The patient man is better than the strong man” (Prov. 16:32).

[Note: In the Vatican, Gilot, and Gussanville editions, “the wise man” is erroneous.]

But it should be noted that he says, “on this day.” On the day of his victory, the one who draws those whom he leads to the love of God by the splendor of virtues toward harming others desires to kill them. Or he kills on the day of victory because, by that same light of splendor through which he is led into veneration of the preacher, he is stirred up to hatred against those who disparage that teacher.

> “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John 3:15).

Because the good are to be helped through the teaching of the good shepherd in such a way that the wicked are tolerated, the reason why no one should be killed is rightly added: “Because,” he says, “today the Lord has brought salvation to Israel.”

It follows:

> Then Samuel said to all Israel: “Come, let us go to Gilgal, and let us renew the kingdom there.” And all the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the Lord.

16. If, then, we bring everything that happened earlier in the appointment of the king into conformity with the custom of holy Church, the rulers of the Church are appointed with great subtlety. First the king to be chosen was shown to the prophet; then he was sought as though unknown; afterward he was found by lot, hidden at home, revealed by the Lord, raised up by the people, and received by all into royal dignity.

Why, then, do they still proceed to Gilgal so that the kingdom may be renewed there? The king is sought and found with great discernment because the affairs of the Churches are exceedingly lofty; if the weak and inexperienced undertake them, they are crushed by the very magnitude of those affairs. Therefore, with careful and most subtle investigation, the one who is to be preferred to so great a height is sought.

He is truly worthy of praise not when he is appointed according to the judgment of those seeking him, but when he is found capable in the very administration of the highest ministry. Thus, after the victorious king has been appointed, it is rightly said: “They proceeded to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the Lord,” because when the preacher’s strength is recognized, he is honored in the minds of his hearers.

We go to Gilgal—that is, to “the wheel”—when through sacred eloquence we examine the conduct of our teacher and make him king there before the Lord, because we judge the one whom we see to be approved worthy of so great a height.

Saul is therefore first said to have been chosen by the people and finally established as king in Gilgal before the Lord, because although a pastor may be chosen in holy Church with much deliberation, whether he is worthy in merit as he is in office is not known until it is demonstrated by the strength of his works.

Let it therefore be said not of another but of that other one [Possibly, “that other” is superfluous], who shone with a great victory:

> “All the people proceeded to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the Lord,”

so that the dignity of the supreme pontiff may consist not in ambition for high office but in the highest virtue.

We go to Gilgal so that no one may dare to judge about the highest office if the commands hidden in sacred Scripture are unknown to him. The king is established before the Lord because the teacher is then honored by the devotion of his subjects when they themselves recognize his life as pleasing to the omnipotent Lord.

Regarding this recognition of the life and teaching of their pastor, since people often place trust not in themselves but in those who are better, it is rightly said that the people established the king before the Lord in Gilgal. Yet the same people proceeded to Gilgal at Samuel’s urging.

“Let us go,” he says, “to Gilgal, and let us renew the kingdom there.” The kingdom is renewed because when the elected preacher is seen in great virtue, the hearts of his hearers submit to him with a new and fresh devotion.

Thus the kingdom is renewed as though the king’s victory had been displayed, when, after the teacher’s great conduct has become known, the hearts of his subjects receive the splendor of a new devotion and are stirred by his example to undertake a great purpose of virtue.

But now that we have seen triumphs in one inward battle, let us observe how, in another, times of peace pass with marvelous equity.

## CHAPTER II

> (I Sam. 12:1–3.) Then Samuel said to all Israel: “Behold, I have heard your voice in everything that you said to me, and I have established a king over you. And now, behold, the king walks before you. But I have grown old and gray. Moreover, my sons are with you. Therefore, having lived before you from my youth until this day, behold, here I am. Speak concerning me before the Lord and before his Christ: whether I have taken anyone’s ox or anyone’s donkey; whether I have falsely accused anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have accepted a gift from anyone’s hand. I will reject it today and restore it to you.”

1. When wicked pastors preside, their principal aim is the plunder of their subjects. Because they cannot behold the abundance of eternal goods, the more ardently they desire present things, the more greedily they receive what is offered and violently take what is not offered. They lie in wait for the innocent, oppress the weak, accept gifts, and pervert justice.

Regarding such pastors the Lord reproaches Judah through the prophet, saying:

> “Your pastors are wolves in the evening; they leave nothing for the morning” (Zeph. 3:3).

He likewise strikes at those who falsely accuse the innocent and oppress the weak, saying:

> “If anyone does not put something into their mouths, they declare war against him. Therefore night shall be their vision, and darkness their divination” (Mic. 3:5–6).

For when they recognize the evil they commit, through the audacity of their wicked deed they fall into blindness of heart, so that through love they no longer see the light of truth by which they might recover from their perversity.

Isaiah likewise condemns the acceptance of gifts, saying:

> “All love gifts; they pursue rewards” (Isa. 1:23).

Thus, while the holy man displays the simplicity of his innocence, he appears exalted by the height of his merits. This praise of virtue is shown in him as an individual so that the same conformity of goodness may be displayed in all chosen teachers.

2. We possess innocence of life for our own sake, but we ascend the height of authority for the sake of others, not for ourselves. Through the good of innocence we journey toward our eternal homeland; through the height of authority we keep watch over the guardianship of others.

In the former virtue we are secure, but we possess the latter elevation with great fear, because although we greatly dread rendering an account of our own deeds, we must render an account to God of the fact that we preside over others.

If, then, chosen men, by God’s will, unwillingly ascend even the height of authority, by God’s will they also relinquish that same height in devotion. Thus the holy man says:

> “Behold, I have heard your voice, and I have established a king over you; and now the king walks before you. But I have grown old and gray. Moreover, my sons are with you.”

As though in other words he were saying: “Because I presided not for myself but for you, I have gladly given to another the dignity that I held. In that same dignity I have grown old, yet the long practice of preeminence that I held did not bind me to ambition for it.”

What, then, does he mean by saying, “My sons are with you,” except that in holy men there is great power of spiritual love, by which they take away the right of succession from sons who are being born for the height of authority?

But by so calmly leaving the highest office, he shows what kind of person he remained while occupying that height. Because he did not exercise the violence of plunder, he says:

> “Speak concerning me before the Lord and before his Christ, whether I have taken anyone’s ox or donkey.”

Because he sought no opportunity to harm anyone, he adds:

> “Whether I have falsely accused anyone.”

Because he was not burdensome to the weak, he says:

> “Whether I have oppressed anyone.”

Because he sought heavenly rather than earthly things from his authority, he says:

> “Whether I have accepted a gift from anyone’s hand. I will reject it today and restore it to you.”

Since he was known to everyone for such contempt of material things, it follows:

> (Verses 4–6.) And they said: “You have not falsely accused us, nor oppressed us, nor taken anything from anyone’s hand.” And he said to them: “The Lord is witness against you, and his Christ is witness on this day, that you will find nothing in my hand.” And they said: “He is witness.” Then he continued, saying: “The Lord, who made Moses and Aaron and brought our fathers out of the land of Egypt, is himself witness.”

3. Here it should be noted that the holy man did not state the good things he had done but explained the evils he had not done, so that by remaining silent he might preserve good deeds for eternal rewards, and by speaking he might not lose the good reputation he enjoyed.

Paul says:

> “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (II Cor. 2:15).

Rebuking certain people, he also says:

> “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Rom. 2:24).

Again, he admonishes his disciple:

> “A bishop must also have a good testimony from those who are outside” (I Tim. 3:7).

By asserting so carefully that he had avoided evils, while remaining silent about the immense good deeds he had performed, the blessed man plainly showed the height of virtue at which he stood. By rejecting evils, he preserved the fragrance of a good reputation as an example for the elect; by concealing his virtuous deeds, he guarded their rewards for eternal repayment.

But it should be noted that, when he asserted the Lord as witness to his innocence, he said that the same Lord had made Moses and Aaron. What else does this mean except that he displayed the height of his virtue but did not wish to appear alone at such a height?

As though with hidden meaning he were saying: “I am not to be admired for such strength of spirit, because I am not alone in possessing it. I possess contempt for material things as a virtue, but I do not possess it with the intention of seeking empty praise; in this I see many who are far better and more exalted.”

And because he asserted that the Lord himself had made Moses and Aaron, it is as though he also said: “The fact that I was able to avoid evils so firmly must be attributed to the grace of the one who made Moses and Aaron such men.”

But why the holy man said these things beforehand he shows by adding:

> (Verse 7.) “Now therefore stand, and I will contend in judgment against you before the Lord concerning all the mercies that he showed to you and to your fathers.”

4. The order of supreme reason is that one who does not care to do good should in no way rebuke evil in others. The holy man therefore first carefully asserted that he had avoided evil and then proceeded to rebuke others, so as to indicate the character of the chosen preacher, who cannot successfully bear the fruit of preaching unless he demonstrates by a radiant manner of life what he proclaims clearly about eternity.

He says:

> “Now stand, and I will contend in judgment against you concerning all the mercies of the Lord.”

For the hearers to stand means to raise the attention of the mind toward the preacher’s word. They are rightly commanded to stand, because a teacher accomplishes nothing by exhorting if the hearer does not direct the mind toward what he says.

Enumerating these mercies, he says:

> (Verses 8–11.) “When Jacob entered Egypt, our fathers cried out to the Lord, and the Lord sent Moses and Aaron and brought our fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place. But because they forgot the Lord their God, he delivered them into the hand of Sisera, commander of the army of Assur, and into the hands of the Philistines and the king of Moab; and they fought against you. Afterward they cried out to the Lord and said: ‘We have sinned, because we abandoned the Lord and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth. Now therefore deliver us from the hand of the Philistines, and we will serve you.’ And the Lord sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you from the hand of your enemies all around, and you lived in security.”

5. He recalls these historical mercies so that, in having asked for a king, the people may recognize themselves as guilty before the Lord. For those who had the Lord present to avert every danger had no need of a human being as king over them.

He demonstrates the Lord’s presence through the mercies he expended, asserting that they were delivered from the hand of the Egyptians through Moses and Aaron, from the hand of Sisera and the Philistines, and from the hand of the king of Moab through Jerubbaal, Barak, and Jephthah, and by Samuel.

Here it must be asked very carefully why the request by which a king was sought is so strictly rebuked, while at the same time the divine mercies are shown to have been bestowed upon God’s people through human leaders. What answer can be given except that the authority of kings is very different from the authority of judges?

The latter preside as equals, whereas the former display the arrogance of domination in the power of preeminence. The former commend the testimony of their innocence before the Lord and the whole people, because they neither oppress anyone nor take anything belonging to another for their own use. The latter, however, not only take away the possessions of their subjects but also weigh down the very persons of their subjects with the burden of servitude.

He adds:

> (Verse 12.) “But when you saw that Naas was advancing and fighting against you, you said: ‘No indeed, but a king shall reign over us,’ although the Lord was reigning over you.”

**6.** As if he were saying: “For this purpose you chose a man, whereas you had been accustomed to have God.” If we wish to examine this passage spiritually, the following may be gathered from it: those who desire a carnal ruler over themselves drive divine grace away from themselves. For while they live according to the example of humble teachers, they are delivered, as it were, from Egypt, because they flee the darkness of worldly love with their whole desire. Since by their teaching they also escape the tyranny of every vice, they are delivered, as it were, from the hand of Sisera, the Philistines, and the king of Moab, when leaders are sent to them. In these people God alone now reigns as almighty, because while they imitate humble shepherds outwardly, they gladly welcome among themselves the love of the divinity that reigns.

Let the prophet therefore say: ‘You said to me, “No, but a king shall be over us,” when the Lord was reigning over you,’ so that he may show that those who submit themselves by imitating carnal rulers lose the dignity of divine grace.

It should also be noted that the prophet Samuel everywhere presents himself to the elect, through the virtue of humility, as a model of uprightness. For when he affirmed the deliverance of the Israelite people, he did not say, ‘The Lord sent Jephthah and me,’ but, ‘Jephthah and Samuel, and he delivered you from the hand of your enemies.’ He named himself as though he were another, so that the power of deliverance might not be attributed to the person who was sent, but to the grace of the God who sent him. ‘The Lord sent Samuel,’ he says, ‘and delivered you.’ As if he were saying: ‘He sent whom he wished, and through whom he wished he accomplished it.’ Perhaps he speaks of himself as though of another because it is not he himself who speaks through himself, but the Holy Spirit.

And because, by God’s permission, with a king already established, the man of God was speaking these words, he was certainly speaking in order to direct the king and the people toward the worship of God, not to abolish the royal dignity itself. Hence he adds:

**(Verses 13–15.)** “Now here is your king, whom you chose and asked for. Behold, your God has given you a king. If you fear God, serve him, hear his voice, and do not provoke the mouth of the Lord, then both you and your king who rules over you will follow the Lord your God. But if you do not obey the voice of the Lord, and provoke his words, the hand of the Lord will be against you and against your fathers.”

**7.** These words are plainly historical in every respect, not mystical. For when rulers and subjects lead a wicked life, they undergo together the punishment of divine vengeance. But because good things are stated separately and evil things separately [perhaps it should read: “are said separately”], those things for which the hand of the Lord is foretold as coming upon them must be considered more carefully.

What else does he mean by saying, “If you fear the Lord and serve him,” except that many fear the judgments of divine severity and yet do not cease to act wickedly? With a trembling heart they think about the judgments to come, but, overcome by present pleasure, they by no means avoid committing evil. Thus, after the fear of the Lord, his service is rightly mentioned, because that fear alone is worthy of approval which, while shaking the mind, draws it toward zeal for good works.

Likewise, because there are some who through fear of the Lord reject certain evils and do some good things, yet neither completely abandon evil nor perform good sufficiently, it is added: “And hear his voice.” Whoever hears the voice of the Lord both fully does good and entirely abandons evil.

These same good works, moreover, should be undertaken with the delight of sweetness, not with an estimation of harshness. For those to whom the things commanded by the Lord always seem hard and severe gradually fall away and fail. Hence Truth itself says: “For my yoke is sweet, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). Hence John says: “His commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5:3). They are not burdensome to the elect, because while they eagerly desire the glory of eternal life, they gladly bear the evangelical commandments.

The “mouth of the Lord” may also be understood as the preaching of perfect charity. For he seemed to display the pleasing words of his mouth when he said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 15:12). This commandment of the Lord is the yoke of divine sweetness. For what is lighter, or ever more pleasant, than love? What burden, moreover, does one who loves not bear lightly? Whatever is loved is carried with great devotion.

Therefore, since charity toward God and neighbor is the bond of perfection, the prophet rightly declares at the end: “If you do not provoke the mouth of the Lord, then both you and the king who rules over you will follow the Lord your God.” As if he were saying: “Then you truly fulfill the divine will if, in divine charity, you establish both rejection of wickedness and zeal for good works. Then you run well after the Redeemer toward the highest blessedness of eternal life, if you carry with joy, to the end of life, those commandments of charity that seem harsh to carnal people.”

**8.** But because he was speaking to the weak and carnal, he subsequently declares:

“If you do not hear the voice of the Lord, but provoke his word, the hand of the Lord will be against you and against your fathers” (1 Samuel 12:15).

The hand of the Lord is the divine severity of vengeance. That hand is extended over sons and fathers when, on account of their deserved contempt of God, both wicked rulers and subjects are punished. The same hand is extended in vengeance when the voice of the Lord is not heard and his words are provoked, because those who reject the divine commandments as hard and unbearable are weighed down in the future by the burden of intolerable punishment.

The audacity of man is foolish: he refuses for a short time to undergo what seems harsh to him, and by that very refusal subjects himself eternally to harsher things. For if he possessed true wisdom, he would persuade himself of what displeases him: that through the hardships and severities of this very brief time he might escape the hardships and severities of future damnation.

Carnal people quickly hear these hard words, but they cannot easily be softened by wholesome counsel. Therefore it is rightly added:

**(Verses 16–17.)** “But now stand still and see this great thing that the Lord will do before your eyes. Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call upon the Lord, and he will give thunder and rain; and you shall know and see that you have done a great evil in the sight of the Lord by asking a king for yourselves.”

**9.** Because this request for a king is reproved so insistently and so often, it conveys to the elect that those who advance carnal men to the summit of holy Church are held under the most serious obligation of sin. For other sins incur the deserts of an individual punishment; but whoever appoints a carnal superior incurs as many deserts of punishment as that superior provides examples of wickedness to the faithful subjects.

Yet the grave burden of guilt cannot be laid down except through the austerity of great contrition. The grace of contrition, however, is not poured into the mind unless the greatness of the sin is first shown to it. Therefore the prophet of the Lord, wishing to rouse the sinful people to the fruit of fitting repentance, points out to them the enormity of their transgression through a miraculous disturbance of the air. During wheat harvest, however, rain and thunder do not occur in that region.

It is therefore rightly added:

**(Verses 18–19.)** “Samuel cried to the Lord, and the Lord gave thunder and rain on that day; and all the people greatly feared the Lord and Samuel. And all the people said to Samuel: ‘Pray for your servants to the Lord your God, that we may not die. For we have added to all our sins by asking a king for ourselves.’”

**10.** If we apply this to our own times, when the people come to knowledge of their sins, preachers cry out to God on their behalf, because they earnestly seek the salvation of the faithful. For preachers’ crying out is their asking for the salvation of the elect with great devotion.

In response to their cry, the Lord gives thunder, because he stirs the hearts of sinners so that they may recognize the wickedness of their depravity. He gives rain, because he assists awakened hearts through an infusion of heavenly grace, so that each person may not only abandon the evils he has committed but also vigorously perform the good things he desires.

It is said that this happens on the day of wheat harvest in order to signify the power of the miracle. The transformation of the heart is certainly no less a miracle than the disturbance of the air. It is no less a miracle to make withered hearts live again than, in an unprecedented manner, to pour down rain amid the heat of summer. Indeed, it is a greater miracle to shake an insensible mind with an inward sound than to make thunder resound by striking clouds together through the wind.

But the proper order of conversion is shown in the ordered arrangement of the words. For he says: “The Lord gave thunder and rain, and all the people greatly feared the Lord and Samuel.” In a thoroughly ordered conversion, when evil is abandoned, goodness is propagated in the mind; when the converted mind nourishes good seed as though by rain, it subjects itself to God and to human beings through the virtue of obedience.

Thus it is rightly said: “All the people feared the Lord and Samuel,” because whoever receives the coming of the highest Spirit both abandons evil and grasps goodness, and submits to God in such a way that, for God’s sake, he also humbles himself before human beings.

And because they have no presumption within that very virtue of obedience, they say: “Pray for your servants to the Lord, that we may not die.” When the spirit of life pours itself into the mind, it immediately raises it to fear of death, because the instruction of that same spirit is that the mind should act in fear, lest it encounter what it fears. But holy men praying for such people can be heard, since in humility of confession they reveal the hidden sins of the heart.

Hence it is added: “For we have added to all our sins by asking a king for ourselves.” But since these matters have now been sufficiently examined in explanation, let us consider what follows.

**(Verse 20.)** “Then Samuel said: ‘Do not fear. You have indeed done all this evil. Nevertheless, do not withdraw from following the Lord.’”

**11.** The mind of the penitent is rightly directed when it fears the divine judgments and trusts in the mercy of almighty God. Fear without hope plunges one into despair, but when it is joined to hope, it produces the salvation of the mind.

Therefore the excellent teacher must watch with the greatest care, so as to terrify the sinner and restore the terrified person to hope of pardon, so that through fear he may cease to sin and, through hope of obtaining forgiveness, seek the harbor of divine mercy.

Thus Samuel, raising his terrified subjects to the virtue of hope, says: “You have indeed done all this evil; nevertheless, do not withdraw from following the Lord.” As if he were saying: “If you cease to sin, you can quickly attain forgiveness for what you have committed. Therefore do not withdraw from following the Lord.”

Of the praise of the just it is promised: “You will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke 1:76). Hence Elijah says: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand” (1 Kings 17:1). Hence the Psalmist says: “Let the just rejoice in the sight of God” (Psalm 67:4).

To stand in the sight of the Lord, or before the Lord, is to draw confidence from the love of the Creator through the testimony of a good conscience. They stand in his sight who, because of the merit of great action, are secure in the heavenly grace of their Creator.

But when sinners commit evil, they flee from the face of the Lord. When, however, they decide to return through repentance, they are, as it were, behind the Lord’s back, because they do not wish to go farther away, yet cannot presume upon God as friends.
