Hence the sinful woman is said to have stood behind him so that she might deserve to kiss the Lord’s feet (Luke 7:38). She also stood behind him who touched his fringe and deserved to be healed of her flow of blood (Matthew 9:20). She stands behind him out of shame for sin, but touches him through the virtue of hope.

Therefore, since we ought always to blush for the sins we have committed and avoid the things over which we are ashamed, Samuel commands sinners not to withdraw from behind the Lord. But because conversion is not enough for a sinner unless he also ceases to commit sins [Note: Gilot: “conversion for the sinner”], he adds:

**[Col. 0333B] (Verse 20.)** “And serve the Lord with all your heart.”

**12.** We can then obtain pardon if we cease to sin and cling to good works. For to serve the Lord with one’s whole heart is to retain no intention of sinning in the heart. The whole heart is bent toward the service of the Creator when we do good in such a way that we retain no deliberate attachment to evil.

The prophet of the Lord, Samuel, plainly indicates this when he adds:

**(Verse 21.)** “And do not turn aside after empty things, which will not profit you or deliver you, because they are empty.”

**13.** Literally, he calls “empty things” the images of demons. For us, however, those empty things must here be understood of which the Preacher speaks when he says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.”

In comparison with eternal goods, everything—even temporal goods—is empty. Whatever in this world appears joyful, delightful, exalted, or prosperous is truly empty, because it is difficult to obtain and quickly lost. Suddenly the lofty things of the world collapse, the beautiful pass away, and the joyful and prosperous vanish. For when the flattering world is seen flourishing in its blossoms, sudden fortune disturbs it, or a swift death, overthrowing everything, brings it to an end.

The joys of the world are therefore empty: they flatter their lovers as though they were permanent, but by passing away quickly they deceive those who love them.

Let the prophet Samuel therefore say: “Do not turn aside after empty things, which will not profit you.” As if he were saying: “The goods of the world are foolishly desired, since those who desire them will not be able to possess them for long.”

It should be noted that the statement is made in the future tense: “They will not profit you,” because they are now seen to be useful; but when people begin to be punished for them in the future, they will be of no benefit at all.

Hence it is appropriately added: “Nor will they deliver you, because they are empty.” As if he were saying: “For this reason they will not help you then: when they fail along with the world, they will no longer exist after this age.”

The goods of the world last a long time only if they reach the end of life together with their lover. After this age, therefore, those things do not profit which cannot pass beyond the end of life. In this life they bind their lovers to sins; but then they will not deliver them: they will be present as a merit, but not as a help.

Here it must carefully be noted that temporal goods will not profit those who are said to turn aside after them. For to turn aside after the goods of time is to drift into desire for them and to prefer their love to divine love. These empty things will therefore rightly not profit them, because they were unwilling to possess them in the order in which they were created.

The benefit of despising empty things is indicated when it is added:

**(Verse 22.)** “And the Lord will not forsake his people, for the sake of his great name, because the Lord has sworn to make them his people.”

**14.** These empty things inflict great evil on those who turn aside after them, because while they desire earthly things in a disordered manner, they are abandoned by the highest and almighty God to endure future torments.

To those, therefore, who are forbidden to turn aside after empty things, the prophet rightly makes this promise: “The Lord will not forsake his people, for the sake of his great name.” Those who for love of him despise empty things are delivered from true evils and, through faith in the promise, receive the reward of an eternal inheritance.

The Lord makes that person his people whom he raises to the joys of eternal blessedness. There, with the glory of his majesty revealed, he presides over the one whom in this world he keeps, taken from the love of vanity through hidden grace.

For the Lord to swear is to promise; and he swears to make his people the one who does not turn aside after empty things, because earthly things must be despised if we are to deserve to attain the goods of an eternal inheritance.

Yet no one should think that he can be brought to those goods by these merits, because this is expressly stated here: “For the sake of his great name.” It is not through our goodness but through God that an earthly human being enjoys heavenly goods. It is God’s gift, not something from ourselves.

It follows:

**(Verse 23.)** “But far be it from me, in the Lord, that I should commit this sin by ceasing to pray for you.”

**15.** These words are spoken by the one to whom the Lord had earlier said concerning those to whom he is speaking: “They have not rejected you, but me, so that I should not reign over them.”

Behold, the prophet is rejected, yet he speaks to those who reject him, saying: “Far be it from me, in the Lord, that I should commit this sin by ceasing to pray for you.”

Indeed, if this is examined according to the commandment of the Law, it would not be a sin if he did not pray for those who rejected him. For the Law of Moses commands, saying: “You shall love your neighbor, and you shall hate your enemy” (Leviticus 19:18). Moreover, those who rejected the prophet had become not his friends but his enemies.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “Far be it from me,” except that the holy man, raised to the summit of charity, loved not only his friends but also embraced his enemies? Instructed by the commandment of the old Law but illumined by the radiance of the new grace, he censures the permission of antiquity through evangelical perfection.

By this deed we are compelled to reason with ourselves. For through the Gospel we are commanded: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:44). How greatly, then, must enemies now be loved, when we are commanded to do so [Preface, no. 6], if they could then be loved when people were commanded to hate them?

And because he was attempting not only to pray for them but also to instruct them, he adds:

**(Verse 23.)** “And I will teach you the good and right way.”

**16.** Why does he call the way of divine service good and right, when it is not good if it is not right, nor right if it is not good?

But the way was good because the people went up from Egypt to the promised land, yet, while it wandered around through the desert, it was not straight. The good way, therefore, is the way by which one journeys toward the heavenly homeland; the right way is the way by which one arrives there easily.

The way is good and right when we turn to a religious life and carry out divine service with the constant fervor of great devotion. Samuel therefore rightly explains this same way, saying:

**(Verse 24.)** “Therefore fear the Lord and serve him in truth and with your whole heart.”

[Note: In other editions the order is reversed, and it reads: “Serve the Lord and fear him.” In the Hebrew text and in all the versions, fear comes first. That Gregory also read it in this way is clear, since in explaining these words he first says “through fear” and afterward “by serving him.”]

**17.** This is indeed the good and right way, because it tends toward eternal life and reaches it swiftly. Through fear of the Lord evils are avoided; by serving him, his commandments are fulfilled.

We serve him in truth when we carry out his commandments solely for the sake of heavenly reward. For whoever seeks a temporal reward for a good work does not serve God in truth; with a false intention he does not love him in his activity.

Those who desire to serve God in truth are commanded to place their whole heart in divine service, so that they do what belongs to God without retaining in their mind anything that is opposed to God.

This way is not only good but also right, because it tends toward salvation and swiftly leads the one who conquers along it to perfection. For a good way, as it were, is another way by which one is brought to the promised land; a right way is one that avoids a detour. By this way each person reaches the summit of the virtues more successfully in proportion as he does not turn aside through circuits of negligence.

This right way is expressed in that route by which the Lord is said to have wished to lead the children of Israel to the promised land. He wished to impose upon them the labors of the desert in order to smooth for us, who walk after the footsteps of his Only-Begotten Son, the course of so great a journey.

For they could not yet hear: “If you wish to be perfect, sell what you have, give to the poor, and follow me; and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matthew 19:21). While the old people, permitted to possess temporal things, wandered in various directions, they could not be led quickly to the promised land, as though by a circuit of labor.

Therefore, to indicate to us the way of the new life, the prophet says that the way is good and right, and that one must fear God and serve him in truth and with one’s whole heart. For those who do not cease to seek almighty God through good works and fervent desires quickly reach the sublimity of divine grace.

And because he had made the same people attentive to hearing the words of the preaching through the miracle, he adds:

**(Verse 24.)** “For you have seen the great things that the Lord has done among us.”

**18.** As if he were saying: “From what you have seen, conclude how terribly you ought to fear almighty God and how devotedly you ought always to serve him.”

If we wish to apply these words to ourselves, then the more marvelous the things we have seen in our Redeemer, the more reverently we must fear and the more devotedly serve God.

But because the wicked boldly despise what the good hear, he added, saying: “But if you persevere in wickedness, both you and your king will perish together.”

# CHAPTER III

**(1 Samuel 13:1.)** “Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign, and he reigned two years over Israel.”

**1.** Earlier, when the matter of establishing a king was being discussed, it was said of the one who was to be preferred to the others by divine judgment that he was chosen and good. Likewise, concerning this man, already chosen for kingship and placed among the people, Samuel said: “Surely you see whom the Lord has chosen, for there is no one like him among all the people” (1 Samuel 9:24).

Now it is said of this same king: “Saul was the son of one year,” so that, while he is carefully praised, he may be understood to have been chosen good by the Lord.

Why, then, is he said to have been one year old when he began to reign, unless to proclaim his innocence? For, literally, how could he have been one year old when he towered above the entire people from the shoulders upward?

What cannot be understood according to the literal sense must therefore be understood through the reasoning of inward understanding. He is accordingly described as a one-year-old king, so that the gift of childhood in the person of the king may signify the goodness of innocence.

Hence the sons of the eternal kingdom are commanded: “Do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in wickedness” (1 Corinthians 14:20). Truth itself also threatens the pastors of the churches with this, saying: “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3).

Thus it is said of the king who was first good and afterward became evil that he was one year old when he began to reign and reigned for two years. Although he reigned for many years, he is said to have reigned only during those in which he is reported to have been innocent and humble.

For afterward, when he had become proud and disobedient, he heard: “Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, so that you should not be king” (1 Samuel 15:26). He recognized that he had been rejected from the kingdom, yet, though rejected, he did not fear to continue reigning.

How many things he afterward accomplished with strength! Yet behold, none of those periods was counted toward his reign. Let us therefore rejoice only in having lived during the time when we lived innocently and humbly. For those periods that we consumed in the vanity of the world and the fleeting life of the flesh are scarcely remembered, as though they had been lost.

Even now there are people who thrust themselves forward to seize the summit of holy Church. Concerning them the Lord complains through the prophet, saying: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know it” (Hosea 8:4).

While such people accomplish certain things bravely, they suppose that the seizure of the summit they invaded has been consigned to oblivion by God. They count up their own works and think that what they do apart from God will be rewarded by God.

To count correctly the things they do, let them count, like rejected Saul, all the brave deeds which the divine reckoning by no means records. Let Saul therefore say: “He reigned two years over Israel,” so that all may understand that what we live for ourselves is emptied of reward, and that wickedly ruling is not the reality of preeminence but the rashness of presumption destined for punishment.

But now let us hear what the one-year-old king did.

**(Verse 2.)** “Saul chose three thousand men from Israel. Two thousand were with Saul at Michmash and on Mount Bethel, and one thousand with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin.”

**2.** The number one thousand, completed by gathering ten times one hundred, signifies the sum of perfection. When it is repeated three times, it indicates the various perfections of the elect.

Saul therefore chose three thousand men from Israel, because the preacher of truth leads to the defense of holy Church not weak and feeble but strong and vigorous warriors.

They are said to number three thousand because, in the appearance of the highest perfection, they bring forth virgins; alongside them they place the continent and the defenders of truth. While they kindle others toward the highest incorruption by the example of virgins, while through the life of the continent they draw others away from the corruptions of the world, and while they defend the weakness of the humble through the aid of the powerful, good teachers come against the enemies of holy Church as though with three thousand chosen men.

They are called men on account of their strength; they are said to be from Israel on account of divine contemplation. For no one can be contained in the highest number of perfection who either lacks the virtue of great action or lacks knowledge of inward vision.

What does it mean that some of the chosen men are said to be with Saul and others with Jonathan? The very names of the places in which they are said to be should likewise not be thought empty of mysteries.

Jonathan, who is described as the king’s son and has a portion of the warriors, signifies those who are assistants to teachers in the ministry of preaching. They are their sons because they greatly love those through whose ministry they are begotten for God. Yet they command a portion of the warriors because they care for holy Church, advancing some toward love of the virtues by their example and others through exhortation.

For it was as though a great king had sent his son into the army when Paul said to the Corinthians: “Therefore I sent Timothy to you, who is my dearest and faithful son in the Lord; he will remind you of my ways, which are in Christ Jesus, as I teach everywhere in all the churches of the saints” (1 Corinthians 4:17). He says likewise: “When Timothy comes, see that he is without fear among you; for he performs the work of the Lord, as I do” (1 Corinthians 16:10).

**3.** Jonathan is said to have been with one thousand men at Gibeah of Benjamin, while Saul was with two thousand at Michmash and on Mount Bethel.

As we have often said, Gibeah is interpreted as “lofty”; Michmash as “humility”; Bethel as “house of God”; Saul as “request”; and Jonathan as “gift of a dove.”

We have referred the three thousand chosen men from Israel to virgins, the continent, and the defenders of truth. Therefore, since Jonathan is called the gift of a dove and one thousand men are said to be with him at Gibeah, that is, at the lofty place, whom else does he indicate except those who, through the most radiant example of virginity, offer others a model of that same chastity?

The instructor of virgins is rightly called the gift of a dove, because it is through the incomparable grace of the Holy Spirit that those who remain in the flesh are enabled to know nothing of the corruption of the flesh.

Virgins are also rightly said to be in the lofty place, because what surpasses human nature is situated at the highest summit of the virtues. Hence that beloved virgin of Jesus, indicating the place of virgins, says: “I saw a Lamb standing upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads” (Revelation 14:1). He also indicates them by the light of their own manner of life, saying: “These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (ibid., 4).

They are said to be on the mountain with the Lamb because, by the merit of incorruption through which they separate themselves from earthly and carnal pleasures, they are raised up into the heavenly glory of the Redeemer.

They are said to be with Saul, two thousand at Michmash and on Mount Bethel. What else does Michmash, which is interpreted as “humility,” signify except the shame of the continent? For when they recall the pleasures of the flesh that have passed, they are ashamed.

But because they are strong men, they are reported to be with Saul; and while they despise the allurements of the world that they have experienced, they draw countless others through the example of their virtue to despise that same world.

Yet they inhabit Michmash because, while they recall what they once were in the world, they cannot become proud of seeing themselves great in God.

They are rightly said to be with Saul, whose name means “request.” For the preacher of truth ought to possess such great charity that, through constant desire, he is felt to be not one who requests but request itself. He ought to desire the salvation of the faithful so earnestly that, through the habitual experience of inward savor, he directs every movement of his heart toward supplication.

One thousand men are with him because more perfect hearers agree in charity with chosen teachers and together beseech almighty God for the salvation of the faithful. Thus they are with the king at Michmash, because they dwell in humility for themselves so that they may deserve to be heard on behalf of others.

But while the chosen teacher beneficially rules over all his subjects, he advances the virtues of all toward crowns of victory. He supplicates with the humble, fights with the strong, devotes himself to prayers with those who are withdrawn, and protects the weak and feeble with the Church’s exposed defenders.

They are therefore rightly said to be with Saul not only at Michmash but also on Mount Bethel, among the thousands of warriors, because just as the preacher of the Church is preeminent among the various orders of the elect, so he ought to be their fellow worker.

For they guard Bethel, that is, the house of God, who defend holy Church by the authority of the word. They oppose tyrants with the free voice of authority; they rise up against the powerful of this world; and, in defense of the humble, they resist the powers of this world. As the king’s warriors, they guard Bethel, the house of God. [Note: Gilot and Vatican read *bellatoris* (“of a warrior”) for *regis* (“of a king”).]

They are reported to be with Saul because they are the assistants of great teachers in the defense of the Church.

It is rightly said of the rest:

**(Verse 2.)** “But he sent the rest of the people away, each one to his tent.”

**4.** By “the rest of the people” he means those whom the number one thousand does not include. Each one is sent back to his own tent because the weak and imperfect are not to be brought forth for the highest and strongest works.

For the weak cannot become continent, virgins, or martyrs. The former require the greatest strength so that the pleasures of the flesh that have passed may not return to them; the latter, so that they may despise the allurements of the flesh they have not experienced; and the others, so that they may not fear the adversities of the world.

The rest of the people are therefore sent back to their tents, lest they be condemned for presuming upon a higher way of life and perish in battle, like the weak and feeble, by pledging themselves to the discipline of a lofty life without possessing the strength of lofty virtue.

The blessed apostle Paul was, as it were, sending each one back to his own tent when he said: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (1 Corinthians 7:2).

Like an experienced teacher of the inward warfare, considering both the crowns of victory and the seriousness of the battle, he weighed the strength of the soldiers against the burden of war. He judged it best for the weak to live in the cities, lest they perish in a bitter struggle.

Therefore, separating them from the camp of the strong, he likewise says: “Return to the same place, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (ibid., 5).

But once the weak have been removed, what is being done in the strongest battle line of the virgins is explained when it is added:

**(Verse 3.)** “And Jonathan struck the garrison of the Philistines that was at Gibeah.”

**5.** Just as the battle line of the bridegroom excels in rank, so it was the first to receive the honors of victory.

Jonathan strikes the garrison of the Philistines because chosen virginity, raised up from the flesh upon the stronghold of continence, extinguishes shameful impulses.

It is rightly called the garrison of the Philistines because in a virginal body carnal impulses do not possess the repose of pleasure but the position of combat. They stand because they attack, but they cannot rest because they do not delight the holy mind at all.

The garrison of the Philistines is therefore struck at Gibeah when the desires of the flesh are entirely weakened by chosen virgins, and they obtain the peace of triumph because they no longer experience their customary battles.

Since they often advance toward this victory through the exhortation of their elders, one thousand men are with Jonathan at Gibeah; yet Jonathan is said to strike the camp of the Philistines.

And because, through the example of some, others are often stirred to emulate virtue, it follows:

**(Verses 3–4.)** “And Jonathan struck the garrison of the Philistines that was at Gibeah. When the Philistines heard this, Saul sounded the trumpet throughout all the land, saying: ‘Let the Hebrews hear.’ And all Israel heard this report: ‘Saul has struck the garrison of the Philistines, and Israel has risen up against the Philistines.’ Then the people shouted after Saul at Gilgal.”

6. When the Philistine garrison has been struck, Saul sounds the trumpet, and the people shout after Saul: for when the virtues of the elect have been heard of, holy preachers proclaim them and kindle the hearts of their subjects to imitate good works. To sound the trumpet is both to announce victory and, by the example of the victors, to rouse the minds of others to undertake spiritual warfare. For the people to shout after Saul is to take up the courage of great devotion from the preaching they have heard.

Here it must be noted that Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison, but Saul, sounding the trumpet, is said to have struck that same garrison. For triumphs over hidden adversaries are ascribed to elect preachers when those adversaries are overcome by their subjects. Yet whenever we conquer some enemies, we must prepare ourselves for battles in which other enemies are to be overcome. For almighty God, because he rewards his elect more abundantly, always wishes them to remain in combat, so that they may continually prepare for themselves the blessings of eternal reward. Hence, when it is said that the people shouted after Saul, it is immediately added:

**(Verse 5.)** “And the Philistines gathered together to fight against Israel: thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and the remaining common people as numerous as the sand that is on the seashore.”

7. Above, King Saul is described as having chosen three thousand men for himself. If, then, we wish to compare the forces of the two armies, for each one of Saul’s men there are assigned ten Philistine chariots and two horsemen. Ten times three thousand is thirty thousand. In the number six also, the number three is doubled. By this battle, both the multitude and the fierceness of hidden enemies are signified.

They come against us in chariots and on horses because at one time they endeavor to offer harmful attractions of visible things to the bodily senses of the elect, and at another time they offer evil thoughts to their hearts. Horses are swift for running and strong for attack. Evil thoughts are aptly compared with them, for they come quickly to the heart and prick it forcefully. Horsemen come against us in battle when evil spirits both stir up evil thoughts in us swiftly and through them attack us vigorously.

Two horsemen come against each of the faithful because, if we gather together into a single consideration the hidden snares of the reprobate spirits, their particular aim is this: namely, to strike our chief virtue and utterly extinguish the love of God and neighbor. One horse appears to rage when an evil spirit suggests to us through a reprobate thought that our neighbor should be hated. Yet the horse that appears alone is not alone, because no one loves God who hates his brother (1 John 4:20).

Moreover, since divine charity does not coexist in the mind with any principal vice, whenever a spiritual vice is suggested to us through the deceit of demons, we must beware of the excessive speed and violent ferocity of the raging horsemen. In comparison with the attack of a horseman, the blow of an archer or foot soldier is altogether weak. The horseman’s attack, however, is violent through the horse’s strength: for the evil spirit has no power in the battle against the elect if he is not allowed to dwell in an evil thought.

Since, therefore, our enemies are exceedingly strong in battle when they are permitted to sit upon our inner thoughts, the army of the Philistines is counted by its multitude of horsemen.

Ten chariots, moreover, are assigned to each of the elect for battle. We have five bodily senses, through which we experience pleasure. But when evil spirits desire to deceive the mind through the allurements of the flesh, they display to the bodily senses the forms of things that the flesh desires, and through those same forms they suggest that the mind should crave what is offered.

The adversary raises the chariot, as it were, upon its wheels when he offers the allurements of things from one side and holds thoughts from the other: he presents the former and introduces the latter, and, as though carrying himself upward by rolling, conveys himself aloft to the soul, when the evil spirit rises against the elect both through the allurements of things and through the art of suggestion. There are therefore ten chariots because against each of our bodily senses they have forms of visible allurements, and against an equal number of the senses of the soul they have deceptive arts of persuasion.

8. What else is meant by the statement that the remaining common people were exceedingly numerous, like the sand on the seashore, except that, under the leadership of evil spirits, an innumerable throng of vices rages against us? Like a subject populace, vices follow chariots and horsemen when the snares of demons, by attacking the mind, go before them, so that it may be devastated by the vices that follow, as by the multitude of an irrational crowd.

It is rightly that first the chariots and horsemen, and then the multitude of the people, are described in the spiritual battle of the saints: for there is neither multitude nor strength in vices if the crowd of evil spirits does not first go before them, stirring them up and introducing them.

These words also indicate how watchful and circumspect the life of the saints must always be. For if the remaining people are compared with the exceedingly abundant sand of the sea, the multitude of darts is innumerable and almost unavoidable. Although every vice may be known to experienced believers, they cannot possibly know how many movements assail the heart, or by what means and for what reasons they always come to it.

They powerfully cast away the manifest darkness of temptations, but often they do not escape, in lesser matters, the haze of ignorance, like the tiny grains of sand. They always display strength in good works, yet those who overcome great armies of horsemen with great courage do not entirely restrain their tongue from every form of superfluous speech. By continual practice they direct the body in the service of almighty God, but their mind—which perfectly orders the outward members—sometimes does not avoid superfluous thoughts at all.

What else, then, do those experience but the troublesome multitude of the common people who have overthrown chariots and horsemen with great courage?

9. But the eminent teacher says: “All things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28). God permits his elect to be assailed by great temptations so that they may be crowned most magnificently in the heavenly kingdom; but he permits great battles for them to conquer, and stirs up lesser ones in which they may fall, so that the victory of the strong may be great, their fall harmless, that those who fall may easily rise again, and that the strong deeds in which they had stood as victors may not exalt them.

For if we conquer chariots and horsemen, we must not be lifted up by the victory, since there are innumerable things that we commit by thinking, speaking, living, tasting, hearing, and acting. Even he could not avoid the innumerable weapons of this populace who said: “We all offend in many things” (James 3:2). Again the beloved disciple of Jesus says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

Who, then, would now dare to be lifted up as though victorious, if the sins of so great a man show that he could not wholly escape their darts?

But since these things are described in a spiritual battle, we must not now consider what we suffer, but how we may weaken the attack of our enemies. The populace of the Philistines is compared with the sand that is exceedingly abundant on the seashore because the strength and number of vices are increased by the disturbances of the world.

This sea signifies the present world, because, as it is driven by the great variety of things and times, it is disturbed like raging winds. On the seashore, when the water driven by the sea flows back, innumerable grains of sand are heaped together.

What, then, is the seashore except the heart of each person who is negligent in spiritual conduct? Through the order of religious life such a person appears to stand, as it were, on solid ground; but, because he does not restrain worldly thoughts, he receives within himself the waves of the sea as they break, together with heaps of sand. He can be driven by the waves and buried beneath the sand precisely because he does not fear approaching the sea: for if he restrained worldly thoughts through contemplation of spiritual things, he would not experience the vices that worldly occupation brings upon him like sand and waves.

Why, then, is the multitude of enemies said to resemble sand, except because evil spirits attack the elect athletes of Christ through the very vices by which they overcome the negligent? The crowd of worldly tumult comes against those who have learned with their whole mind to despise the world in its pleasures. They fashion the pageantry of visible things and, by feigning it, revive the love of the world already held in contempt, so that they may draw hearts aflame with heavenly love toward harmful pleasures.

But holy men, because they perceive this innumerable crowd of wicked thoughts emerging from the sea of the world, avoid becoming seashores by fleeing the world with their whole mind, and no longer fear so great a populace of enemies. For while they keep themselves in deep contemplation, the crowd of vices cannot gain access to them.

It follows:

**(Verse 5.)** “And they went up and encamped at Magmas, to the east of Bethaven.”

10. For evil spirits to go up is to strive toward lofty things through heavenly desire, in order to deceive the hearts of the saints. It is rightly said: “They encamped at Magmas,” because they dwell in those hearts that do not see, being raised up by lofty love of heavenly things. Magmas is interpreted as “humility.”

To be humbled is often taken in sacred discourse as a defect of virtue. Hence, in this same history of the kings, Tamar, the daughter of King David, whom her brother Amnon is said to have violated, is described as having been humbled. She was corrupted and therefore humbled, because she had stood as a lofty virgin; and when she lost the high summit of virginal honor, she came, as it were, from a lofty place to a level and humble one (2 Samuel 13).

Of the future humiliation of the proud it is also said: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11), because those who vainly glory in the exaltation of this world fall in the judgment of the heavenly Judge.

The Philistines are therefore rightly said to set up camp at Magmas, because through wicked counsels demons dwell in those who do not care to hold the lofty summits of virtues. For while they seek earthly things, they inhabit level and humble places, where invisible enemies can easily set up camp.

Of these enemies the prophet says: “They say to your soul, ‘Bow down, that we may pass over you’” (Isaiah 51:23). The upright soul is lofty; the bent soul is humble, because through the height of virtues it is raised aloft by heavenly desire. But when it sinks toward vices or love of the world, it falls there, where the attacking enemy easily crushes it.

They therefore say to your soul, “Bow down, that we may pass over you,” because if they do not humble it toward doing or thinking earthly things, they neither penetrate it with evil persuasions nor disturb it by the warfare of vices.

11. From this, then, we can gather how far we ought to be removed from the world in deed, word, and thought. Our words, thoughts, and works are level and humble when they are worldly. Through these things we are found in the place where the camps of hidden enemies are freely established, where we can be captured all the more easily because we are raised up by no stronghold of protection.

What believer does not know that they collect the faults of our words, thoughts, and deeds and preserve them for our accusation at the coming of the Judge who is to come? Therefore, indicating that this humble and contemptible place called Magmas must be fled, the Lord says: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36).

The place of the enemies is therefore called humble, so that it may clearly indicate to us that in word, thought, and deed we must always be lofty. And because, when the reprobate are captured in the humble place of their lax way of life, they display examples of depravity to be proposed for imitation by others, Magmas is said to be east of Bethaven.

We see the light of the sun rising in the east. The life of the reprobate, although it possesses the truth of darkness, is nevertheless sought by those who desire it for the vain pleasure of the world, and they are deceived as though by the splendor of a false light. Hence blessed Job says: “Their light shall be taken away from the wicked” (Job 38:15).

For the present, the world’s pleasing allurements seem to them like something bright; but when they depart from the world, they will undergo the perpetual darkness that they believed to be light. Then they will see that it was not light, when prosperity is changed into adversity, light into darkness, laughter into sorrow, sweetness into worms, beauty into deformity, honor into disgrace, and allurements into punishments and eternal torments.

Because the hearts of the wicked do not now perceive these things, they refuse to imitate the conduct of the good. Following the example of the lost, they do not fear to take for themselves whatever pleases them in the world, because they imitate those who through a reprobate life have become dwelling places of demons.

Hence they are rightly called “useless houses”: for they often receive the preaching of the saints, but they do not allow the word they hear from their mouths to dwell within them through love. They are therefore useless houses because they do not make themselves a suitable dwelling for God.

The Truth himself designates this useless house in the Gospel, saying: “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20). Again it is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline flees deceit, and does not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wisdom 1:5).

Magmas is therefore rightly said to have a useless house in the eastern region, because those who despise the preaching of the saints rejoice, as though at the rising of a great light, in the example of the reprobate who seek low and earthly things.

But while the words of sacred history reveal the conduct of the wicked, the watchfulness that belongs to the life of the saints is subsequently shown. For it follows:

**(Verse 6.)** “When the men of Israel saw that they were in difficulty, the people were distressed, and they hid themselves in caves, in secret places, in rocks, in hollows, and in cisterns.”

12. We are in difficulty when we are tempted inwardly by unclean spirits and observe outwardly the examples of evil people. Against the inward temptation of evil spirits it is rightly said: “The people were distressed”; and against the outward examples of wicked people: “They hid themselves.”

The cunning adversary suggests that we should seek what is pleasing and joyful; he is never overcome more effectively than when those who are tempted hasten to the laments of devoted prayer. We can avoid the examples of the wicked more quickly if we judge that they should not even be looked upon.

For the saints to hide themselves is to disdain seeing what is reprobate. And because they guard the five bodily senses from imitating the reprobate, five kinds of hiding places are also described: caves, secret places, rocks, hollows, and cisterns.

Caves are hidden places in mountains. The hearts of the saints are high through heavenly desire, and they are closed and inaccessible to evil spirits. We enter caves when we withdraw into the secrets of the mind, lest, with our eyes wandering outward, we see things to be desired.

We hide in secret places when, with our mouths closed, we preserve the hidden silence of restraint. We climb rocks when we place the activity of the body in vigorous action.

Hence the prophet speaks of these hidden places under a single description: “Whoever closes his eyes so as not to see evil, and stops his ears so as not to hear of bloodshed, and shakes his hands free from every bribe—in the heights he shall dwell; the loftiness of the rocky strongholds shall be his” (Isaiah 33:15).

We enter hollows and cisterns when we guard both the sense of smell from the foulness of the world and the ears from hearing empty talk. Cisterns are the words of the sacred Scriptures, which contain holy waters. We hide in cisterns when we enter the waters of sacred speech, so that through the function of the ears we may water the meadows of the mind.

It is rightly that the hiding places of Israel are mentioned as a type of the elect, because whoever does not protect the bodily senses from the defilement of carnal pleasures does not escape the sword of hidden enemies.

Let him speak of the victory of that hidden encounter; let him speak of it: “The people were distressed.” Let him openly recount the triumphs of the battle set before them: “They hid themselves.”

The distress of the elect mind is the deadly sword of every diabolical temptation. For while it is deeply pierced with compunction, it is lifted up into the love of heavenly joy; and it rejects the pleasures of the world offered to it all the more forcefully because it loves heavenly things more fervently—things to which it ascends by weeping.

The eminent teacher says: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21). The entrance into the heavenly kingdom is indeed hoped for at the end of time, but it is experienced in the daily life of the saints. Our tribulation, therefore, is the entrance into heavenly joy.

Whenever, accordingly, the elect mind is pierced by the lament of its distress, it obtains through its tribulation this result: that it enters into contemplation of that heavenly kingdom in which it rejoices ineffably.

And when holy men refuse to look upon lovers of the world passing through the flower of fleeting joy, and hide their bodily senses from imitating them, their flight, which is visible, is not flight but glorious victory. They flee earthly actions but attain heavenly ones; they seem to hide from the world but are revealed to heavenly glory.

By fleeing what is harmful, therefore, they pursue their enemies more vigorously and triumph far more nobly, since they hasten toward heavenly things in such a way that the polluted ferocity of their adversaries does not touch them.

[Note: The passage is obscure. Perhaps one should read: “so that the polluted vices do not touch them.” Or, by deleting *eos* (“them”): “so that the adversaries’ polluted vices do not touch themselves.”]

It follows:

**(Verse 7.)** “But the Hebrews crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead.”

13. If we first wish to understand this according to the literal sense, these Hebrews are understood to have fled to their enemies, terrified by fear. For not long afterward, in the account of Jonathan’s open victory, it is written: “The Hebrews who had been with the Philistines yesterday and the day before, and who had gone up with them into the camp, returned to be with Israel, who were with Saul and Jonathan” (1 Samuel 14:21).

What is signified by this event except what we see happening daily in holy Church: that the life of the good is safe and most cautious, while the impatience of the negligent is rash? The weak and presumptuous are inquisitive about the affairs of the world, but weak in enduring the battle of temptation.

If we examine such people among ourselves, many of this sort are found in monasteries. They dwell peacefully within harbors, but give no thought to the storms of the open sea or the whirlwinds of tempests. And when they consider themselves strong because they act boldly outside, they readily go forth into the gravest battles of temptation, impotent before powerful adversaries.

Unwise in judgment and weak in strength, they neither understand the deceits of crafty temptation nor escape the manifest snares of allurements.

They therefore cross the Jordan because they bend toward committing the sins of the flesh. Jordan is interpreted as “their descent.” Those who abandon righteousness fall from the lofty mountain of virtues.

Since all the weak readily desire the worldly allurements they see, the Hebrews are said, in their type, not to be carried across the Jordan but to cross the Jordan. To cross belongs to one who wills. They therefore cross the Jordan who turn toward carnal pleasures by a voluntary and hasty decision.

Those who have recently begun to sin can also be understood as crossing the Jordan, but they surpass the wickedness of other sinful people by sinning. They would reach their descent by ceasing, not by crossing, if they did evils equal to those of others and did not surpass them by daring greater ones.

And because they find equals to themselves even in a more wicked life, they are rightly said to arrive, beyond the Jordan, at the land of Gad and Gilead. They dwell, as it were, beyond the Jordan who become worse than the wicked through the practice of sinning.

To raise sinners from this descent into guilt, he came of whom it is written: “He came into all the region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins” (Luke 3:3). Since he came to preach repentance from all sins, he is said to have come into all the regions of descent.

It follows:

**(Verses 7–9.)** “While Saul was still in Gilgal, all the people who followed him were terrified. He waited seven days according to Samuel’s appointed time, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people dispersed from him. Then Saul said: ‘Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings’; and he offered the burnt offering.”

14. Up to this point, as was said above, divine speech has spoken about Saul as an elect and good man. It therefore seemed reasonable to understand what was said about him in a favorable sense, both historically and morally.

But now, since we have reached the place of his transgression, it is necessary that we also see in him what must be avoided. What should all the elect have regarded as more carefully to be avoided than the evil of pride and disobedience? Pride cast down the exaltation of the first angel; pride struck down the glory of the fallen spirits. Pride took happiness away from the first human being; pride introduced the perpetual hardships of human captivity.

And behold, the first king of the elect people is joined to the first angel and the first human being through disobedience, so that, while great things fall, lesser ones may be raised up. We are rightly lifted up when we both contemplate their falls and avoid them.

We must therefore consider attentively where Saul fell. For above Samuel had said to him: “Go down before me to Gilgal. I will indeed come down to you, so that you may offer a burnt offering, an offering, and peace offerings. You shall wait seven days until I come to you, and I will show you what you are to do” (1 Samuel 10:20).

He therefore fell through disobedience because he did not wait through the full seven days, as he had been commanded. For in the same place it is immediately added:

**(Verse 10.)** “And when he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel was coming.”

15. Here we must consider with a trembling heart how, by neglecting an expectation lasting only the briefest time, he was rejected. “When he had finished,” he says, “the burnt offering—behold, Samuel was coming.”

If, then, he had waited for him only during the very brief interval in which he offered the burnt offering, he could have securely retained the strength of his kingdom. If the penalty is so great when a prophet is despised, what do we think will happen in that sea of divine retribution when the divine commandments themselves are disregarded?

The pleasure of the flesh passes in a moment, as does every sinful act; and although the hour of transgression is brief, the punishment of the crime is not brief. For when we raise up the reign of sin within us for a moment, we lose the kingdoms of all the ages.

Immediately after sin, prophetic speech comes to rebuke—the speech that would have been present to strengthen us in goodness had we not sinned. A polluted conscience already has divine speech against it; if it had avoided pollution, it would have stood firm through its own vigor, aided and lifted up by that speech.

What else, then, is spiritually signified by the words: “When he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel was coming”? Even if he had not offered the burnt offering, Samuel would nevertheless have come.

So, when we are tempted, divine grace is near to help those who endure, and divine justice is near to condemn those who fail. Hence sacred Scripture exhorts us to wait, saying: “If the spirit of one who has authority rises against you, do not leave your place quickly” (Ecclesiastes 10:4).

The prophet likewise testifies: “The Lord is my helper, and therefore I have not been confounded” (Isaiah 50:7). The Psalmist, contemplating the same nearby assistance, says: “I kept the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken” (Psalm 15:8).

But let us now hear what the prophet says to the one who did not wait, and what the one who refused to wait replies:

**(Verse 11.)** “And Samuel said to him: ‘What have you done?’”

16. The prophet knew what he had done, but by questioning him he condemned the act of disobedience. Hence the Lord also says to the sinful Adam in paradise: “Adam, where are you?” (Genesis 3:9).

This question can also indicate the magnitude of his guilt. It is as though he said openly: “Does it seem a small thing to you that you have sinned by disobeying? By your sin you have fallen from the lofty summit of your glory.”

Now many within holy Church bury themselves in crimes and are secure as though they had lost nothing, or only something insignificant. Let it be said to the fallen, let it be said: “What have you done?” Does it seem a small thing to you that you have polluted yourself with the filth of sin, because you do not consider what glory of eternity you have lost and what punishment of Gehenna you have deserved?

The sinner is questioned about what he has done so that he may be brought to his heart through lamentation, so that he may know that he has incurred great things and may not grieve too little.

But because the guilt of disobedience arises from the root of pride, the disobedient often hear the greatness of their guilt from teachers who rebuke them, yet do not make satisfaction by humbly confessing it. When they desire to appear exalted, they disdain to reveal their falls; and therefore they offer excuses and put forward their own justice, because they are ashamed to appear as sinners.

It is therefore rightly added:

**(Verses 11–12.)** “Saul replied: ‘Because I saw that the people were dispersing from me, and you had not come according to the appointed days. Moreover, the Philistines had gathered at Magmas. And I said: “Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not entreated the favor of the Lord.” Compelled by necessity, I offered the burnt offering.’”

17. Behold, the man accused of the rashness of great transgression does not hesitate to assert great grounds of justice. “I saw,” he says, “that the people were dispersing from me.” Here he claims that he had been deserted by the people. “Moreover, you had not come according to the appointed days.” Here he presents himself as defrauded of the prophet’s promise. “Moreover, the Philistines had gathered at Magmas.” Here he likewise alleges the impending danger of battle.

Therefore, drawing a statement from his action, he says: “Compelled by necessity, I offered the burnt offering.” It is as though he said: “You accuse me of great guilt, although the guilt is so much lighter because it was not caused by rashness but by necessity.”

But let us hear how the prophet knew him, since he refused to know himself. He adds:

**(Verse 13.)** “You have acted foolishly, and you have not kept the commandment of the Lord your God.”

18. Since the proud, through their arrogance, imagine that they are above other people, they are appropriately rebuked when the divine will—which they offend—is set before them. Saul is therefore rebuked in the manner of the proud, since he is said to have despised the commandment of the Lord his God.

This is as though he were frightening the proud and contemptuous person by saying: “Even if you despise human beings, now you have disregarded not human counsel but the commandment of the Lord your God.” You rightly assess your guilt if, with a trembling heart, you consider the one whom you despise.

It must also be noted that he does not say, “You have not kept the commandment of your God,” or “the commandment of your Lord,” but, “You have not kept the commandment of the Lord your God.”

It is as though he said openly: “It would be daring enough to commit a great transgression if the one whose commandment you despise were merely your Lord and did not also exist as God. How great, then, is the offense committed when the commandments of God and Lord are neglected?”

Likewise, because he did not say, “of my Lord and God,” or “of our Lord and God,” he rebukes him for having offended the grace of divine intimacy. It is as though he said: “You have despised the commands of the one who, while lifting you from a lowly state, setting you over others, and making you king, became, through the bestowal of such great gifts, specially your own.”

He adds further, showing that the boldness of his transgression was even greater:

**(Verse 13.)** “Which,” he says, “he commanded you.”

19. Some of God’s commands are common to all; others are special to particular people. To convict this bold offender of his presumption by an evident charge, he demonstrates that Saul despised not common commands but his own particular and singular command.

“Which,” he says, “he commanded you.” It is as though he said: “You despised those commands of God and your Lord which you ought to have observed not as common to everyone, but as your own, entrusted uniquely to you.”

But he explains what Saul deserved, saying:

**(Verses 13–14.)** “For if you had not done this, the Lord would already have established your kingdom over Israel forever; but it shall by no means rise again.”

20. Behold how much he lost who thought he had despised nothing. Behold, he waited for the prophet for seven days; but when he ceased waiting for him at the end of the day, he lost the glory of so great a dignity.

Hence the prophet says: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Sirach 2:16). They lose endurance who do not complete the good things they begin. Woe is said to belong to them because they not only lose the reward of the work they began, but are also struck by the punishment of their apostasy.

The punishment of the proud and disobedient king is made clear when it is said: “If you had not done this, the Lord would already have established your kingdom over Israel from now and forever; but it shall not rise.” The kingdom of the elect is established now and forever, because those who order temporal things well prepare for themselves the exaltation of eternal glory.

The kingdom of the elect is now being prepared when, through divine grace, their ministries are rightly administered. It advances from now and forever because, from the exalted action of the present time, they earn in heaven that still more exalted glory of eternity.

In the end, therefore, it is said to the reprobate king: “Your kingdom shall by no means rise again.” It is as though he said: “Since he has fallen away from temporal rectitude, he does not reach the height of eternity.”

Or he is said literally not to rise again because it fell together with him and did not remain after him in his sons.

But so that he may be struck by the punishment of envy, he is compelled to hear not only of his own rejection but also of another’s election. For the prophet adds:

**(Verse 14.)** “The Lord has sought for himself a man according to his heart, and has commanded him to be leader over his people Israel.”

21. The proud man is crushed by every one of these words: “He has sought,” he says, “a man according to his heart.” It is as though he said: “He sought him because you were unwilling to be according to his heart.”

It is as though he said: “He appointed as leader of his people a man who carries out the command of the divine counsel through the strength of devotion.” Because we customarily deliberate in our heart about what we intend to do, when the heart of God is mentioned in sacred speech through the usage of our language, his innermost will is signified by it. This will is recognized outwardly by us when his commands are revealed.

We are according to it when we recognize it both through understanding and through love, and keep it. Samuel the prophet therefore rightly says of the Lord: “He has sought for himself a man according to his heart, and commanded him to be leader over his people.” For the one gives useful commands to others who has already learned perfectly to obey God, and who commands only what proceeds from the counsel of intimate truth.

22. But what does it mean that it is spoken as though of the past—“The Lord has sought for himself a man and commanded him to be leader”—when no one had yet been sought and no command had been given to rule his people?

This question is easily resolved if we consider the foreknowledge and predestination of almighty God. For God’s predestining is his making, and with him the things that he has foreordained to make are already made. Hence it is written of him: “He has made the things that are to be” (Isaiah 45:11, according to the Septuagint).

God is said to have sought a man so that a model for the selection of leaders might be offered to human beings. We ordinarily seek what we do not know to be present or do not see because it is absent. But God, for whom nothing is absent and nothing hidden, is not said to have sought a man as though he were absent or concealed. He is said to have sought him so that everyone who is chosen for the summit of holy Church may be taught that he must be examined by human beings.

He must be sought according to God’s heart, so that he may not only understand the divine will but also demonstrate it through good works.

Likewise, because elect men do not come to the honor of primacy through ambition but are led to it under compulsion, it is rightly said: “And he commanded him to be leader.” It is as though he said: “He did not rise to the honor of governance through ambition, but ascended under compulsion.”

The man may also be understood as signifying strength, and “according to God’s heart” as signifying inward charity. When necessity demands it, therefore, let a man be sought for the care of holy Church who is strong in his way of life; let him be sought according to God’s heart, so that through the effect of great love he may be, as it were, united to the divine will.

Let him be commanded to be leader so that he does not aspire to climb the order of exaltation out of desire, but fears it out of humility; and so that he fears for himself in humility while recognizing more devotedly that he must submit to God’s command.

But because in these words the prophet had rebuked the life of the fallen king, it follows:

**(Verse 15.)** “Samuel rose and went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin.”

[Source pagination and column references: 282; Col. 0340B, 0340C, 0340D, 0341A, 0341B, 0341C, 0341D, 0342A, 0342B, 0342C, 0342D, 0343A; note at Col. 0343D; Col. 0343B, 0343C, 0343D, 0344A, 0344B, 0344C, 0344D, 0345A, 0345B, 0345C; note at Cols. 0345D and 0346D; Col. 0345D, 0346A, 0346B, 0346C, 0346D, 0347A, 0347B, 0347C, 0347D, 0348A, 0348B, 0348C, 0348D, 0349A, 0349B, 0349C, 0349D, 0350A, 0350B, 0350C; 283–290.]

### 23

As though from a high place to the level ground, the teacher of the holy Church comes down when he rebukes the sins of sinners; and he bends the height of his position when, moved by affection of charity, he humbles himself to examine the crimes of the wicked. Thus it is rightly said of him who had rebuked the sinner: “He arose and went up.” The chosen preacher rises when, by the intention of his mind, he raises himself to the height of his spiritual way of life; but he ascends when, through his customary practice, he reaches the arduous height of that same life.

Heavenly desires, spiritual virtues, and good works are on high; earthly inclinations, worldly desires, vices, and sins are in the depths. But the teacher, in order to correct those who have fallen properly, first discovers their faults by examining them, and then strikes the faults he has discovered. Therefore, so that he may see clearly and openly what he must strike, he bends the eyes of his mind toward seeing the lowest wounds of sins. Yet he does not strike what he has discerned if he does not descend into the depths to touch it.

Therefore the prophet is said to rise and ascend, because the chosen preachers often come down to see and amend our lowest faults, yet they never forget immediately to return to the heights of their own way of life. These words also affirm the freedom of the priestly spirit. For many rebuke others while disturbing themselves through a most violent battle with anger. After rebuking the faults, they cannot rise and ascend, because, troubled within themselves, they are in no way permitted to advance to the heights of inward peace. They hear that the shameful conduct of others must be restrained; but when they descend to consider those low things, they are defiled by the harmful pleasure they take in them. Weak and unequal to so great a ministry, while they desire to untie the lower knots of others, they do not free them but bind themselves.

What, then, does it mean that it is said of Samuel, “He arose and went up,” except that we see the same in more perfect men, who examine our impurities without ever being soiled by them, and who become angry with us in such a way that they can quickly ascend to the heights of their inward, secret peace? For they are strong and powerful, and those who bear their own great and difficult burdens lightly are not weighed down by our weaknesses.

And because, in correcting us, they produce testimonies from holy Scripture, they are said to rise and ascend from Galgal. Galgal, as I have often already said, means “wheel.” The testimonies of Scripture, because they revolve through various meanings for our instruction, are like wheels. And because, when holy preachers set aside concern for their subjects, they are raised up into contemplation of eternal life, Samuel is said to ascend into Gabaa of Benjamin.

Gabaa of Benjamin, finally, is interpreted as “the hill of the son of the right hand.” Who, then, is the son of the right hand except the one whom the holy Gospels confess to have ascended into heaven and to sit at the right hand of God the Father? The hill of the son of the right hand is therefore the eternal height of the Redeemer. For whenever holy preachers leave our lowest things, they rise by intention into those divine heights of the Redeemer and ascend them by vision.

### 24

What is said—“He arose and went up”—can also be understood more simply according to the historical sense: namely, that he did not recognize in the king whom he had rebuked the humility of repentance by which the king would have been compelled to remain. Nevertheless, that same king is left in office so that he may be corrected by the prophet’s very separation; for often those whom the preacher’s words do not correct fear being separated from the preacher’s companionship or from the unity of the holy Church. Beside preachers they are obstinate, but when separated they come to their senses; and those who sinned through disobedience now humbly prepare to obey God.

Thus, not long afterward, King Saul is commanded to destroy the Amalekites, so that, if he fulfilled the Lord’s command by slaughtering that nation, he might loosen the bond of his former disobedience (1 Kings 15). Separated from the prophet, he appeared to perform one task so that he might be commanded to perform another. Therefore it follows:

> **(Verse 15.)** “And the rest of the people went up after Saul to meet the people who were attacking them, coming from Galgal into Gabaa of Benjamin.”

### 25

Some fall into sin in such a way that they are held by no good work; others, when they recall that they have committed evil, try more eagerly to do good. By doing good, they cover over the evils they abandon, so that they may not be exposed and judged by the eternal Judge.

If we interpret this action of Saul in a favorable sense, we find precisely this: the man who had earlier feared the prophet and disregarded his command in the matter of the sacrifice afterward hastened to crush the enemies of God’s people, those whom he had feared. Here too it should be noted that the man whom the prophet abandoned went up from Galgal to undertake battles against the enemy. For the righteous severity of preachers casts many sinners aside, whom divine remembrance nevertheless does not abandon. They lose the consolations and exhortations of their leaders because of their sins, but they consult the holy Scriptures and take up their resolve again; and those who had lain fallen, as it were, through the evil of disobedience advance, raised up by the fervor of obedience, to battles against hidden enemies.

They are rightly said to come from Galgal, that is, from the wheels, because from the holy Scriptures they receive what enables them to suppress the army of the opposing side with courage. And because they strive to recover, by conquering, the height of their ruined way of life, they are said to ascend into Gabaa of Benjamin.

Furthermore, because some had shut themselves away in hiding places while others had fled to the enemy, the remaining people are mentioned: they were terrified by no fear but hurried with their king to the place of battle. We see this also now in the Church. Many, like little ones, propose to advance through the discipline of private life; many strong men are bold even in the exposed contests against the malicious enemy, so that they plainly see the allurements of the world which they desire, yet despise what they are seen to desire.

These do not stand in hiding places but in the field of open combat, exposed to battle and strong for triumph: they can fight and cannot be overcome. Hence they are designated by a perfect number, when it follows:

> **(Verse 15.)** “And Saul counted the people who had been found with him, about six hundred men.”

### 26

The week is completed in seven days, but one of these is forbidden for work, while six are granted for the pursuit of good works. The number one hundred, moreover, contains the totality of numbers. Who, then, are signified by the six hundred men except those who are robust in work and in the deliberation of their hearts? For some make strong resolutions, but because they do not do what they resolve, they do not reach the number of the six hundred men.

The six hundred men therefore signify the strong workers of the holy Church, because they make great resolutions and complete the firmness of their resolve through the strength of good action. They are rightly said to have been found with the king, because they agree with the pastors of the holy Church in good will and pious action. They are with those from whom they differ neither in will nor in deed.

They are said to agree in such a way that the excellence of preachers is recognized. For even if subjects do the same good that preachers desire, those are nevertheless foremost in that good whose order is higher and whose virtue of spirit is therefore more ardent and whose effort in action is stronger. Hence the king and his son are mentioned separately:

> **(Verse 16.)** “And Saul and Jonathan.”

Why, then, are the king and his son named separately except because the good action of a worthy ruler is shown to be distinctive? And because there is not a uniform equality among all faithful subjects, it follows:

> **(Verse 16.)** “And the people who had been found in Gabaa of Benjamin.”

### 27

It has been sufficiently repeated that Gabaa is interpreted as “hill.” A hill, however, is not a summit but the height of mountains near the summit. What, then, is understood by this hill except the lofty and perfected life of faithful subjects? Although it is not equal to the height of preachers, it is nevertheless seen to be very exalted in comparison with the merits of others.

Thus it is written of certain outstanding elect in the Apocalypse:

> “No one could sing the song except those hundred and forty-four thousand” (Rev. 14:3).

And, describing them more clearly, he says:

> “These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes.”

Therefore, while spiritual battles are being described, the people found in Gabaa of Benjamin are specifically counted, because the chorus of virgins is all the more forceful against the ferocity of unclean spirits insofar as it is wounded by none of their blows and polluted by none of the filth of their suggestions. Free, whole, and unencumbered, it is ready for encounter and strong for striking.

Are not those on the hill of the son of the right hand whom the beloved Jesus regards because of their integrity, saying:

> “I saw the Lamb standing upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand” (Rev. 14:1)?

And unless they were very strong, they could never have climbed, wearied, to so great a height. Likewise, unless they were free from all thoughts, they could not run everywhere after the Lamb. Because, then, each virgin is wondrous in the triumph of the hidden battle, when the order of the encounter is described, the special dignity of virginity is recalled under the figure of the people of Gabaa.

It follows:

> **(Verses 16–18.)** “Now the Philistines had gone up into Magmas. And three divisions came out from the camp of the Philistines to fight: one division went along the road of Ephraim, toward the land of Saul; another entered by way of Bethoron; and the third turned toward the road of the boundary in the land of Sabaa, overlooking the valley of Seboim, opposite the desert.”

### 28

What does it mean that the Philistines make three divisions except that malicious spirits attempt to insert perversities into our heart, tongue, and action? Because every sin is committed by thinking, speaking, or doing, there are three divisions of the Philistines: malicious spirits strive to drive souls to sin through negligence of the heart, unrestrained speech, and the boldness of perverse action.

Hence the first division is said to proceed along the road of Ephraim, because they begin their assault on innocence from the heart. The road of Ephraim—that is, of the fruitful heart—is good thought. The first division of the Philistines therefore advances against the road of Ephraim, because hidden adversaries cannot reach the point of uprooting the fruits of virtue from the mind unless they first remove from it the practice of good thought.

They come against the road of Ephraim when they lie in wait for good thought; and this road is said to extend toward the land of Saul. For what else is the mind of an elect disciple than a very fruitful land belonging to the teacher? Thus, explaining the parable of the seeds in the Gospel, the Lord says:

> “That which fell on good soil—these are those who receive the word in a good and excellent heart and bear fruit with patience” (Luke 8:15).

It is therefore said of the first division of the Philistines, “They proceeded against the road of Ephraim,” so that, when we grasp the spiritual meaning of the letter, we may close the entrance of thought against malicious spirits.

But when we fortify the heart, we are likewise compelled to restrain the tongue from superfluous speech. Hence the second division is said to enter by way of Bethoron. Bethoron is interpreted as “house of anger.” The house of anger is the mind serving a contentious tongue. The wise man indicates this house when he says:

> “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Eccl. 7:11).

Through this house enemies enter the fool’s heart, because malicious spirits, when they loosen the tongue for unrestrained words, kindle anger and wound the mutual charity of the faithful. Therefore, whoever has learned to beware of harmful thoughts, but does not know how to keep watch over his mouth, has overcome the attack of one division but has not escaped the other.

The third division, however, turns toward the road of the boundary. What is the boundary of thought and speech except the completion of good work? For this is why we think and speak good things: so that we may bring them to the end of good action. But when the ancient enemy cannot prevail against us through words and thoughts, he stretches his snares toward the end and seeks to empty out or hinder the good work of the faithful.

What is the road of the boundary except devotion to good action? Because malicious spirits strive through many ambushes to make the pursuit of good work abandoned, the third division is said to turn toward the road of the boundary. The boundary may also signify the end of our life. The division turns toward the road of the boundary because the enemy strives to interrupt the good work, lest it be carried through to the end of life.

Thus the Psalmist, expressing in himself the weeping of those who have fallen, says:

> “They stretched out ropes as a snare for my feet; beside the road they placed a stumbling block for me” (Ps. 139:6).

A stumbling block is placed beside the road so that the good works of the elect may be abandoned before the completion of this life.

### 29

What does he mean when he says, “In the land of Sabaa, overlooking the valley of Seboim, opposite the desert”? These names of places have been inserted to designate the location of the boundary he had mentioned. Sabaa, in our language, is called “captive”; Seboim means “does” or “female deer.”

What is this captive except human nature, which was placed in paradise and is now bound in this world to endure the hardships of mortality? And what is the land of this captive except the pilgrimage of temporal life?

Thus, rightly, when the division is said to turn, the land of the captive is mentioned: malicious spirits can stir battles against us in this land of our pilgrimage, but they cannot do so in that other life. Yet although the present way of life of the elect has been placed in this exile of captivity, if it carefully guards the road of the boundary, after the narrow confines of this boundary it reaches the height of immortality.

Hence the boundaries of this land are said to overlook the valley of Seboim, that is, of the does. The valley of the does is the precious death of the saints, because from the place where they are lowered through dying, they are lifted up to eternal joys. Who does not know that does are swift animals and make great leaps? The doe rightly designates the dignity of holy souls: in death they leave their bodies, but, as though making great leaps, they ascend to the heavenly kingdoms through their immense merits.

Let him therefore say that the boundary of the captive land overlooks the valley of Seboim, because, although the human condition has been condemned, it has nevertheless been exalted in the Son of God, so that when it is led to the end of temporal life and given over to death, it may be lifted to the height of eternal life.

Let him therefore say that the third division turns toward the road of the boundary in the captive land, which overlooks the valley of the does, so that he may assert that malicious spirits strive to pervert the final good works of the elect for the purpose of preventing them from ascending to heavenly joys.

This valley is also said to be situated opposite the desert. What is understood here by the name “desert” except hell? A desert is rightly understood as a place where none of the elect is found. It is also called a desert because no consolation amid hardships is experienced there. The valley of the does is therefore said to lie opposite the desert, because the death of the saints differs wholly from the deserts of hell and possesses nothing compatible with or worthy of the punishments of hell.

It follows:

> **(Verses 20–21.)** “Now a blacksmith was not found throughout all the land of Israel. For the Philistines had taken precautions lest the Hebrews should make a sword or a spear. Therefore all Israel went down to the Philistines, so that each one might sharpen his plowshare, or his hoe, and his axe, and his mattock.”

### 30

All these things are certainly described so that the manner of the victory that follows may be disclosed. Armed men were defeated by unarmed men, so that everything conquered might be attributed to the praises of almighty God. If, however, following our customary method, we pursue these matters spiritually, we shall not find them empty of mysteries.

What, then, does it mean when it is said, “A blacksmith was not found in Israel,” except that we are equipped for spiritual battles not through secular literature but through divine writings? A blacksmith is not found in Israel because the faithful of the Lord do not fight against malicious spirits by means of the arts of secular knowledge. They would win with the aid of the smith’s craft if they could overcome hidden enemies with the weapons of secular eloquence.

This learning from secular books, although it is of no benefit by itself for the spiritual conflict of the saints, does make knowledge of divine Scripture more precise when joined to that Scripture. Liberal arts should be learned only to the extent that, through their instruction, the divine words may be understood more subtly.

Malicious spirits remove from some hearts the desire to learn so that they may know neither secular matters nor reach the height of spiritual things. Thus it is rightly said: “The Philistines had taken precautions lest the Hebrews should make a sword or a spear.” Demons plainly know that, while we are instructed in secular literature, we are helped in spiritual matters. When, therefore, they dissuade us from learning these things, what else are they taking precautions against than our making a spear or a sword?

Let the historical account speak, and let it indicate and explain the zeal of the elect: “Israel went down to the Philistines so that each one might sharpen his plowshare or his hoe.” We descend to the Philistines when we incline our minds toward learning secular books. It is called a descent because Christian simplicity is on high.

But what does it mean that secular literature is said to be on level ground while the method of teaching is lofty? It means that although secular writings narrate nothing heavenly, they explain what they propose with a marvelous order of speech and are elevated by their narration, while they are brought down by speaking of earthly things.

[Note: Gilot and the Vatican manuscript read *et carnalia docendi deponuntur*—“and earthly things … are laid down for teaching” (reading uncertain).]
