Whoever desires to know this method of speaking or understanding should descend to the Philistines and sharpen his plowshare and hoe, so that he may lower himself to hear even earthly matters, if he earnestly seeks to be instructed by their eloquence.

Almighty God placed this secular knowledge below, so that it might provide us with a step for ascending, by which we ought to be raised to the height of divine Scripture. For this reason he wished it to precede, so that through it he might instruct us to pass over to spiritual things.

Thus Moses, who gave us the beginnings of the divine words, did not first learn divine things; rather, so that he might be able to grasp or express them, he formed his inexperienced mind in all the knowledge of the Egyptians. Isaiah also surpassed the other prophets in eloquence: for he was neither, like Jeremiah, an Anathothite, nor, like Amos, a herdsman, but was nobly educated and cultured. Paul too, the vessel of election, was instructed first at the feet of Gamaliel before he was caught up into paradise or raised to the height of the third heaven (Acts 22). Perhaps he therefore excels the other apostles in learning, because, destined for heavenly things, he first diligently learned earthly matters.

### 31

But now, as I think, the properties of the agricultural implements must be sought spiritually. What, then, is signified by the plowshare, which is drawn by oxen going before it, except the affection of twofold charity? And what is shown by the hoe, with which each person works alone in cultivating the field, except devotion to private life?

Some, both wealthy and strong farmers, plow with oxen because they love the Lord strongly and, through fraternal love, devote themselves diligently to gaining souls. They sharpen their plowshare among the Philistine smiths because they construct the work of holy preaching from secular learning.

Others, like the poor, use a hoe because those who consider themselves unable to suffice for gaining the souls of others do not cease to prepare for themselves whatever they can obtain from eternity. Each of them uses a hoe, as it were, because he does not cease to prepare the field of his own mind for divine worship.

And because secular learning is also very useful to them in this pursuit of private life, he sharpens the hoe while it is being taught: an educated person attends more subtly to the matters involved in the pursuit of his own life.

With an axe we do not dig the earth but cut off the branches of trees. What else, then, does the axe signify except the zeal of good emulation? When we are inflamed to imitate the examples of those who are better, we cut off branches for ourselves, as it were, with which we may kindle a fire to drive away the coldness of our negligence.

The Apostle Paul commands us to hold this axe, saying:

> “Emulate what is good among all that is good” (Gal. 4:18).

This axe is sharpened because, just as educated faithful people recognize the examples of the faithful more clearly, so they desire to imitate them more fervently.

The mattock, or three-pronged hoe, digs the earth more finely, so that it is understood to dig less than to scrape and break up clods. What is expressed by this three-pronged mattock except the virtue of discernment? Through it, when we examine things done or to be done with subtle consideration, we level the clods of our earth, as it were, into fine dust for sowing.

This mattock is rightly said to be three-pronged because the power of discernment orders not only what must be done but also what must be thought and said. From the hand, heart, and tongue it removes every harmful thing, so that the seed we entrust to the soil of our mind may bear abundant fruit.

It is therefore aptly said: “All Israel went down to the Philistines so that each one might sharpen his plowshare, his hoe, his axe, and his mattock,” because in sacred eloquence we read of the affection of twofold charity, devotion to private life, and the examples of the perfection of others; but, ignorant of secular learning, we cannot penetrate the depths of that same sacred eloquence.

Therefore, rationally adding what follows, he says:

> **(Verse 21.)** “The edges of the plowshares, the hoes, the axes, and the three-pronged mattocks were therefore blunted, even as far as the point for setting right the goad.”

### 32

They are not said to have been folded back or worn down, but blunted. For if they had been folded back or worn down, they would cut nothing at all. A blunted edge, although it does not cut everything quickly, cuts through certain obstacles by delaying the labor.

So are the hearts of the simple: although they do not understand spiritual matters subtly, when they nevertheless understand certain things slowly, they possess not a sharp but a blunted keenness of intellect. They often wish to examine obscure matters; but, while they scarcely reach even what is clear after long reflection, they cut through things by lingering, as with a blunted edge.

This is shown not only in the hidden mysteries of Scripture but also in the concealed suggestions of demons. They cannot drive away an enemy whom they cannot quickly recognize. When, therefore, they dispel the snares of an evil suggestion only after a great delay in thought, they cut through it as with a blunted edge, although they could have severed it more quickly through keenness of intellect.

What, then, does it mean when it is said, “Even as far as the point for setting right the goad”? The goad signifies the rebuke of rulers. Hence it is written:

> “The words of the wise are like goads” (Eccl. 12:11).

A rebuke is called a goad because, when it reproves faults, it pricks the mind. But the goad is blunted when the understanding of rulers grows dull, so that they neither discover the faults of their subjects by recognizing them nor rebuke them once they have discovered them.

The rebuke of a ruler is therefore rightly asserted to be a goad, because it cannot prick the swellings of vices if his mind, lacking the instruction of knowledge, does not see what must be pricked.

Hence, as a figure of educated rulers, it is rightly added:

> **(Verse 22.)** “When the day of battle had come, neither sword nor spear was found in the hand of all the people who were with Saul and Jonathan, except Saul and Jonathan his son.”

### 33

What is understood by the spear except the sharp foresight of holy preachers? And what is demonstrated by the sword except the subtlety of their understanding? With a spear we pierce enemies placed far before us; with a sword we slaughter enemies who are near and almost joined to us.

Thus foresight is rightly shown in the spear, by which the elect strike hidden enemies before they suffer their close assault. By taking precautions against future ambushes of demons, they strike them from afar, as with a spear, because they do not wish to receive their blows at close range.

Therefore blessed Paul the Apostle, when he saw from afar the spirits of fornication armed against him, held conjugal chastity like a spear and did not allow them to come nearer, saying:

> “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render what is due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Cor. 7:2).

And again:

> “Return to the same, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (ibid., 5).

For this reason he also says of himself:

> “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27).

The man who had chastised his body so that he would not become disqualified was clearly piercing his enemies, positioned at some distance, with a spear before they reached him. The foresight of abstinence for subduing the lust of the flesh is therefore understood as a spear, by which future enemies are struck.

Understanding is also rightly expressed by the sword, because whoever recognizes and rejects the perverse suggestions of a malicious spirit in the present strikes an enemy who is near and positioned beside him, as with a sword. He cuts as with a two-edged sword because he reproves both false goods and genuine evils.

What, then, does it mean that a sword is said to be in the hand of Saul and Jonathan? These weapons are not in the hand of those who sharply understand what is near and present, foresee what is future, but do not exercise their strength to extinguish these things. They plainly know that the ancient enemy drives a very large part of the human race into fornication through the strength of the flesh, yet they do not take care to chastise the flesh through abstinence. Likewise, some clearly see present evils but make no effort to avoid them. Such men have a sword and spear, but do not have them in their hand.

Thus it is rightly found that the sword and spear are in the hand of Saul and Jonathan on the day of battle, because only chosen men understand both present and future evils and ardently desire to conquer them through the intention of the heart.

This is said here, however, so that the people may be shown to have held nothing in their hands, although they are shown holding plowshares, hoes, axes, and mattocks. These words do not distinguish the elect from the reprobate but the dull from the knowledgeable.

But since we have now shown the armed men, let us explain the manner of the battle. It follows.

## CHAPTER IV

> **(1 Kings 14:1.)** “The garrison of the Philistines went out to ascend toward Magmas, and it happened one day that Jonathan the son of Saul said to his young armor-bearer: ‘Come, and let us cross over to the garrison of the Philistines, which is beyond that place.’”

### 1

The garrison of the Philistines goes out when a crowd of evil spirits is displayed to elect minds through harmful suggestions. It is called a garrison because the battles of the elect are being described. For evil spirits “to stand” means to exercise great strength in the battle against the elect. By standing, each person can strive to accomplish something with greater force than by sitting. The garrison of the Philistines is therefore said to have gone out so that the demons’ efforts in our battle may be clearly understood.

And because they think they will crush the faithful as though they were lower and smaller, those going out prepare to ascend into Magmas. Or they desire to ascend into Magmas when they attempt to deceive the hearts of the little ones.

But elect preachers, when they understand that the hearts of their subjects are being tempted, do not delay in bringing assistance. They place some in a secure position and lead others with them to endure the dangers of battle.

Why is an armor-bearer led into battle except because subjects instructed through knowledge must be advanced toward victory in inner conflicts? Some know the art of medicine but lack experience in healing; similarly, in the holy Church there are some who have learned the art of the inward battle but have not yet been led into the strict demands of combat.

They hear great men fighting, but the battles that great men endure magnificently they know by hearing, not by virtue. Such are those who are invited to imitate the Redeemer’s footsteps. He says:

> “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24).

Jonathan’s weapons are the teacher’s exhortations. An armor-bearer carries weapons with which he himself does not fight, but another does. Such, certainly, are those who are newly instructed in the holy Church. When they hear from teachers about the virtues with which those teachers themselves fight against the cunning of evil spirits, they possess in their mouths what they do not yet possess in the display of virtue.

Jonathan therefore said to his armor-bearer, “Come, let us cross over to the garrison of the Philistines,” because elect teachers teach their subjects not only the art by which they may fight but also draw them into battle, so that they may triumph.

### 2

And because negligent pastors do not take care to undertake the battles they describe, Jonathan does not say, “Go and cross over to the garrison of the Philistines,” but, “Come, let us cross over.” They summon others to battle, but they themselves are the first to attempt those same battles.

What does he mean by saying, “Which is beyond that place”? There is a certain place in the holy Church that is protected from great battles and is not exposed to them. To possess the goods of the world, to marry, to beget children, and to provide the body with the comforts of all lawful things is to remain protected from the enemy in a place where nothing imposed upon those established in that order is burdensome.

But if someone, inflamed by a desire for a better life, tries to cross beyond this place, he must prepare himself for very serious battles. Those who despise riches and embrace Christ’s poverty, who reject marriage and always embrace the love of chastity, immediately encounter very grave battles of the flesh and attacks upon the heart. Poverty is not borne lightly, nor are bodies subjected to chastity without great struggles.

Hence a certain wise man rightly says:

> “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir. 2:1).

As though he were saying: “Because you wished to leave the place of protection, you must now fortify yourself in open battle against the strongest enemy camps.”

When Jonathan the teacher says “beyond that place,” not “this place,” he indicates the virtue of those teachers who, through the singular commitment of religious life, are always in the open field of battle. And because they avoid the vice of boasting and pride in everything they fight for vigorously and in everything over which they triumph nobly, it follows:

> **(Verse 1.)** “But he did not disclose this very thing to his father.”

### 3

The virtues of the elect should indeed be kept silent, lest they be proclaimed boastfully; yet at times it is not blameworthy to reveal them for the glory of God. Since we have represented great preachers by Saul, the fact that Jonathan conceals from his father the beginning of the battle signifies that we sometimes laudably conceal the great things we do out of humility.

Through corruption we have become such that we cannot be seen to be good even by those who rule over us without becoming proud. Therefore, when a hidden evil arises from something publicly displayed, good is wisely concealed lest it be stained by what follows.

It must nevertheless be understood that those who can conceal their virtues from their superiors out of this necessity are those who know how to recognize properly the good they are doing. For if they are excessively simple, what they consider good is often not good; and while they do not disclose a vice because they mistake it for virtue, they carry a hidden enemy within themselves.

Thus Jonathan, who concealed his intention of war from his father, is declared to be so great that part of the army is reported to have been led under his command. “There were,” it says, “two thousand men with Saul in Magmas and on Mount Bethel, and one thousand with Jonathan in Gabaa of Benjamin” (1 Kings 13:2).

Let it therefore be said of Jonathan, “But he did not disclose this very thing to his father,” because educated men, fearing that they may incur the vice of pride through their great works, hide those works from the very people by whom they could have been helped.

We learn these forms of the preacher’s assistance more clearly if we observe them in the place of their perfection. For it follows:

> **(Verse 2.)** “Now Saul was staying at the farthest part of Gabaa, beneath the pomegranate tree that was in Magron.”

[Note: In Gilot and the Vatican manuscript, *modos* (“mattocks”) is found here; this should not be accepted.]

[Note: In Gilot and other printed editions, *malo granata* and *malus granata* are incorrectly read here and below.]

### 4

Gabaa, as we said, is interpreted as “hill”; Magron is said to derive from *guttur*, “throat.” The holy preachers, moreover, are very exalted, not only in their works but also in contemplation. This outermost part, therefore, is the exaltedness of their works, while that innermost part is the exaltedness of contemplation. Through the outermost part of their height they are set before us as examples; through the innermost they are joined with their Creator in great love.

[Col. 0361A] The prophet shows these men to us as objects of wonder through the outermost part of their sublimity when he says: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60:8). They fly like clouds because they are lightened of the burden of guilt and made swift in good works by the grace of the Holy Spirit. They are like doves at the windows because, through their good works, they extend themselves to us as examples, as through openings; yet, despite the purity of life they display, they are by no means captivated by the desire for praise.

The king also sits beneath the pomegranate tree, because the preacher finds rest in the shadow of the Redeemer. He is wearied by great labor, but is refreshed by the consolation of the Lord’s words. Hence that same tree is said to remain in the place whose name is derived from “throat.” What is more appropriately signified here by “throat” than the sweetness of the holy Gospel?

[Col. 0361B] Thus we can now remain in the shadow of the Redeemer, if we draw his words from meditation on the Gospels for our consolation. Preachers, however, can sit more peacefully in this place when, the more deeply and closely they receive that word from the divine throat, the more sweetly they are nourished.

This is also why King Saul is said not to stand or sit, but to remain beneath the pomegranate tree at Magron: the perfect teacher is teachable by God, and while he strives to feed others with nourishment, he himself is satisfied with the sweetness of manifold spiritual delights. For while he beholds the Redeemer’s singular loveliness, he rises into wondrous contemplation of his virtues; and, as though gathering many seeds from a single rind, he gladly leads his delighted mind through all the things that he recalls concerning the Redeemer.

In this loveliness of the Redeemer the bride also boasts that she has rested, saying:

[Col. 0361C] “I sat beneath the shadow of him whom I had desired” (Song 2:3). To sit beneath his shadow is to rest in his contemplation. His contemplation is indeed a shadow, because in beholding him we are protected, lest we be blackened by diabolical temptation as by the heat of the sun.

Those who rest so sublimely can therefore usefully offer assistance to those who seek their counsel. Yet some chosen subjects, while fearing their own weakness and seeking God alone as witness of their struggle, avoid the judgment of such men, so that their good actions may be seen by God alone. Thus Saul is rightly said to remain beneath the pomegranate tree in the outermost part of Gabaa, and Jonathan is said not to have disclosed his plan of war to him: because, when we cannot perfectly guard against pride, the good from which pride might arise ought to be concealed from everyone.

It follows:

[Col. 0361D] **(Verse 2.)** “The people who were with him were about six hundred men.”

### 5

By this number, as we said above, strong men in good works are signified; they are reported to be with the king because, through their zeal for good works, they are united with the life of their teacher. But the preachers of the Church have beneath them not only those who perform great deeds, but also fellow ministers of the word who teach sublime things. They have leaders who strengthen those fervent for battle; they have men who run boldly; they have men who powerfully protect. Thus it is fittingly added:

**(Verse 3.)** “Achiah, son of Achitob, brother of Ichabod, son of Phinees, who had been born from Heli, the priest of the Lord at Shiloh. He was carrying the ephod.”

[Col. 0362A]

### 6

Achiah, in our language, means “a little shade.” What, then, is signified here by this little shade except protection? Those who protect any of the lesser members of the holy Church from hidden adversaries are rightly represented by the little shade. Whoever rests beneath a shade cannot feel the sun’s heat.

Why, moreover, are shades proclaimed in sacred discourse except because they also reveal the sun of reprobation, by which the green vitality of the mind is scorched? Concerning this sun Truth says, in the parable of the seeds: “When the sun had risen, they withered” (Matt. 13:6). The burning heat of desire is a sun: it seems to shine like light, but it scorches the mind upon which it shines.

When, therefore, through the exhortations of our superiors, we reject the blandishments of every desire, beneath what else are we spread out than beneath a pleasant shade, where we may avoid the fires of temptation?

[Col. 0362B] Yet the Church’s minister is called a “little shade” in the diminutive form, so that no one may be compared with the Redeemer. Of his protection the bride boasts in the Song of Songs, saying: “I sat beneath the shadow of him whom I had desired” (Song 2:3). And the Psalmist, praying, says: “Protect me beneath the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16:9).

But the origin of this great Achiah is explained, since he is remembered as the son of Achitob. Achitob means “my good brother.” Who, then, is understood by this good brother except our Redeemer? He is a brother because he shared our nature; but he is good because he freed from eternal death the nature that he assumed. Or he is good because we are all evil, as he himself says: “If you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children” (Matt. 7:11).

Achiah, therefore, is called the son of Achitob so that those who are powerful in the Church may recognize that their power is present in them solely through imitation of the Redeemer. The same Achitob is also said to be the brother of Ichabod, because Ichabod is named from “the transfer of glory.” For our Redeemer was born according to the flesh from the Jewish people. Since all the adornment of the temple, all the rites of sacrifice, and all the mysteries of the Scriptures passed from that people to the Gentile people, the transfer of glory is rightly recalled in Achitob’s brother.

[Col. 0362C] That same Achitob is said to have been the son of Phinees because the Jewish people, in the faithlessness of their error into which they plunged themselves, had teachers of their own nation who were far worse than themselves. Hence Phinees is interpreted as “a mute mouth,” or “one who spares the mouth.” He is called “mouth” because through that people the Lord spoke. But he is now recognized as a mute mouth because, when it rejected the Redeemer, it likewise lost the Spirit who once spoke within it.

He is also rightly called “one who spares the mouth,” because he fell once into the guilt of such great bloodshed that he could never be converted to him through penitence and confession. He is therefore called one who spares the mouth because he disdains to blush piously through confession. In contrast, blessed Job, speaking in the person of the converted, promises, saying: “I will not spare my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit” (Job 7:11).

[Col. 0362D] But because that people also possessed the dignity of religion in the patriarchs and prophets, the same Phinees is said to have been born from Heli, the priest of the Lord. Heli is interpreted as “my God”; Shiloh as “sent.” In sacred Scripture, “gods” sometimes signifies chosen preachers. Thus the Lord says to Moses: “I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1). And in the Law he commands, saying: “You shall not speak evil of the gods” (Exod. 22:28).

[Col. 0363A] The father of Phinees is therefore called “my God” because the Jewish people imitate, according to the letter, those who deserved to behold the word of God with an unveiled mind and not to conceal it in the sheath of the letter. Truth itself displays them when it explains the Psalmist’s words, saying: “He called them gods, to whom the word of God came” (John 10:35).

He is said to have been born at Shiloh because the Jewish people, although still in a carnal manner, are nevertheless instructed in the spiritual Scriptures. Therefore, since every chosen and wise person in the holy Church follows the Lord born from the Jewish people through teaching, Achiah—who is called “a little shade”—is said to be the son of Achitob, brother of Ichabod, son of Phinees, son of Heli.

[Col. 0363B] He is also described as carrying the ephod, so that it might be clearly shown that no one can protect others who does not shine with the beauty and light of a good way of life.

It follows:

302 **(Verse 3.)** “But the people did not know where Jonathan had gone.”

### 7

What does it mean that the people did not know where Jonathan was going, except that the chosen teacher strives to conceal through humility the things he intends to do? Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. 6:3).

If eternal things are represented by the right hand and the present life by the left, we have human beings on the left and angels on the right. When, through good works, we strive toward fellowship with the citizens above, our right hand is said to be at work. Our left hand does not know the works of our right hand if we have the faithful of the holy Church as fellow workers and helpers in the work, but do not wish to have them as praisers, lest we become proud.

[Col. 0363C] It is therefore rightly said: “The people did not know where Jonathan had gone,” because we strive to act greatly and well only when we avoid displaying what we do for the sake of ostentation. But since we present these things as examples for the elect, we must examine more attentively not only where he goes, but also by what way he goes.

It follows:

**(Verse 4.)** “There were crags between the passes by which Jonathan was attempting to cross over to the Philistines’ garrison, rising on either side, like teeth, with cliffs broken off on both sides. The name of one was Bores, and the name of the other Sene.”

[Note: [Col. 0363D] In the Hebrew text and in all the versions this is written *Boses*, with a doubled *tsade*. Gregory nevertheless evidently read *Bores*, as is clear from the meaning he assigns to the word below, in section 9. For *Bores* means “at the beginning,” being derived from *ros* or *resith*, which signify “beginning,” “head,” and similar things.]

[Col. 0363D] [Note: [Col. 0364D] Since this word, as Gregory explains below in section 9, signifies “sun” or “hearing,” it seems preferable to read *Seme* here. In Hebrew, *shemesh* means “sun,” while *Seme* or *Sama* means “hearing.”]

### 8

Since the life of the elect is high in merit, while the condition of evil spirits is low, what does it mean that there are said to be passes from which Jonathan attempts to advance toward the Philistines’ garrison? For, concerning these same Philistines as a type of demons, it was said not long above: “They went up and encamped at Magmas” (1 Sam. 13:5).

[Col. 0364A] They are said to be above us because we appear weaker in strength. They are also understood to be above us because we are unable to penetrate them through understanding. Whenever, therefore, we propose to fight with rejected spirits, we must prepare strength for an ascent, because we human beings are striving to fight with angels.

Hence that vigorous athlete, strongly encouraging his fellow soldiers, says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). Since he knew beforehand that he would fight against the spiritual wickednesses of principalities and powers, he prepared the strength of his mind for an ascent to the heights.

[Col. 0364B] When evil spirits subject the hearts of sinners to themselves, they dominate them through manifold vices. If, therefore, we also strive to defeat them there, we must ascend very high, so that we may be able powerfully to strike their ranks. The slippery must be saved in one way, the slothful in another; the vainglorious in one way, the proud in another. But so that the chosen teacher may be equal to all these things, he lifts his mind through the sharp counsels of continual meditation and, as it were, strengthens himself for an ascent against the Philistines.

### 9

It is rightly said not that there was one ascent, but that there were several, because innumerable enemies must be confronted by many paths. This is done well when remedies suited to each vice and to its particular disease are applied.

[Col. 0364C] To touch briefly on some of them: the spirit of fornication is driven away by the virtue of continence; yet it is overcome more easily if the flesh reduces its impulse through abstinence, lest, once conquered, it surrender itself to worldly desire. Gluttony is broken by abstinence; but one cannot maintain abstinence from bodily food if one does not fill the mind with spiritual food. For one powerfully weakens the body who inflames the heart with love of heavenly things: while he loves spiritual things fervently, he firmly restrains the desires of the flesh.

The vice of avarice is opposed by the good of voluntary poverty; but no one can be poor in spirit who still does not know how to love eternal treasures. Anger is overcome if, through love of heavenly things, all earthly things are despised perfectly, because one who does not fear temporal loss no longer has anything for which to become angry. Likewise, the vice of acedia—that is, weariness of heart—is driven away if heavenly goods are always considered. The mind cannot in any way grow weary when it joyfully beholds such delightful goods.

[Col. 0364D] The distressing evil of sadness is also swallowed up in the field of spiritual joy; yet spiritual joy does not pour itself into a mind that does not know, through contemplation, how to pass beyond the distress of temporal life. Sadness is rightly overcome when the rewards of temporal labors are contemplated, because the chosen mind considers where it is afflicted temporally and therefore hopes to rejoice eternally in the heavenly homeland.

[Note: Vatic. and Gilot., *enim*.]

[Col. 0365A] Since, therefore, the preacher uses counsels of great variety to cure the diverse illnesses of souls, and since the same counsel is grasped through profound consideration of the mind, it is rightly said that there were ascents from which Jonathan desired to cross over to the Philistines’ garrison.

And because many difficulties arise in overcoming evil spirits from the hearts of sinners, rocks are said to stand between the ascents. What, then, is signified by these two rocks, Bores and Sene, except desire and sin? Bores means “at the beginning,” while Sene means “sun,” or “hearing.”

[Col. 0365B] The name “beginning” aptly suits desire, because it occupies the mind first, before the mind subjects itself to sin. The delight of sin is also rightly represented by the name “sun,” because it closes the eyes of the mind to the contemplation of truth and opens them to vanity.

Hence the seducing spirit is said through the serpent to have spoken to the first human beings: “On whatever day you eat from the tree that is in the middle of paradise, your eyes will be opened” (Gen. 3:5). At that eating, the eyes of the transgressors were opened through sin, so that they might experience the rays of a false light in the experience of wrongdoing and become blind to the lofty contemplation of the light above.

The Psalmist, refusing to open his eyes to this light, entreats the Lord, saying: “Turn my eyes away, lest they behold vanity” (Ps. 118:37). Blessed Job, despising this light with profound understanding and desiring to be joined to the merits of the perfect, says: “For now I would be lying down and silent, and I would sleep and have rest; or, like a hidden untimely birth, I would not exist; like those conceived who have not seen the light” (Job 3:13, 16). Who are these except those who have taken great care to avoid sin?

[Col. 0365C] One cliff, therefore, is called Bores and the other Sene, because if desire claims a place for itself in the mind, it raises the eyes of that mind toward the pleasing allure of sin, as though to behold the light of the sun. They are also rightly called rocks, because these two things are characteristic of the minds of the wicked: they no longer readily allow preachers to return to them.

They are also called cliffs, because on either side—that is, both in mind and in body—they maintain a precipitous practice of depravity. Since they are made firm by neither integrity of character nor integrity of works, they are broken off on either side like a cliff.

And since they are said to be “in the form of teeth,” what else does this suggest than what we often see: those who despise the exhortations of preachers try to bite into their lives through detraction?

[Col. 0365D] But concerning these same cliffs it is added:

**(Verse 5.)** “One projected toward the north, opposite Magmas, and the other toward the south, facing Gabaa.”

### 10

The first cliff projects toward the north, and the other toward the south, because through desire the fervor of charity is extinguished, while through sin the ardor of desire is increased. When the corrupt mind submits to desire, it is stripped of charity; and when it does not fear sinning, it kindles within itself ever sharper desires for sin.

[Col. 0366A] Placed, as it were, at the height and heat of midday, it both rejoices immoderately in the flow of sin and is ardently dissolved by it. Therefore one strives poorly to cure the disease of desire who thinks that he will come to rest by satisfying desire through further sinning. After sin, desire will be all the greater in proportion as the delight of sin itself begins to seem more pleasing to it.

The first cliff is said to be situated opposite Magmas, while the other projects against Gabaa. Magmas, as we have sufficiently explained, is interpreted as “humility”; Gabaa as “hill.” Desire therefore has humility opposite it, while the delight of sin has heavenly conduct opposite it.

Everyone who desires what is forbidden becomes proud when he despises the one who commands him. Thus desire has humility opposite it, but does not preserve it in the devotion of obedience. Again, one who is dissolved in the heat of sin as in the brightness of midday projects against Gabaa, that is, against the hill, because while he opposes heavenly things, he prepares himself for Tartarean punishments.

[Col. 0366B] But since such people are also led to eternal life through the preaching of the saints, let us observe the zeal of those preachers in Jonathan’s action. For it follows:

**(Verse 6.)** “Come, let us cross over to the garrison of these uncircumcised men, if perhaps the Lord may act for us; for it is not difficult for the Lord to save, whether by many or by few.”

### 11

What is the Philistines’ garrison except the strength of evil spirits? Holy men, when they prepare themselves for the correction of sinners, know clearly that they are fighting with angels who have fallen from heaven. This battle, therefore, since it is between angels and human beings, is fought by the strong against the weak, by the simple against the cunning.

The strong had indeed attacked the one who said: “The mighty have rushed upon me; neither is there iniquity nor sin in me, Lord” (Ps. 58:4). Paul also observed the cunning of the fallen angels and said: “We are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Cor. 2:11).

[Col. 0366C] Against the cunning, therefore, a path of cautious reasoning must be sought; against the strong, divine assistance must be requested. Thus, to show that preaching must be conducted with great caution, Jonathan is said to have invited his armor-bearer to cross over with him. And so that confidence might be placed in God’s mercy when expelling the enemies, he says: “For it is not difficult for God to save, whether by many or by few.”

And because the conversion of the wicked is not easy, he says: “If perhaps God may act for us.” He says “if perhaps” because he does not yet presume with complete confidence upon the full salvation of criminals.

But he displays the form of the chosen subject in the virtue of humility, for it is added:

[Col. 0366D]

### 12

**(Verse 7.)** “His armor-bearer said to him: Do everything that pleases your mind. Go wherever you desire, and I will be with you wherever you wish.”

Some subjects, while neglecting the measure of their rank, confuse that same measure by sharing in the arrangements of their superiors but refusing to obey their commands. They readily dare to correct the words of their elders, but do not readily attempt to fulfill what those elders command.

What, then, is shown to us in the voice of this armor-bearer except that free authority of disposition must be left to superiors, while the virtue of obedience must be firmly retained by subjects? To assign preachers free authority to make arrangements, he says: “Do everything that pleases your mind.” And to show the subjects’ ready willingness for every service, he adds:

305 [Col. 0367A] “Go wherever you desire, and I will be with you wherever you wish.”

He did not say there: “Do some things that are in your mind, but do not do others, or do them differently.” Nor does he say here: “Go there, and I will be with you, but I will not be with you elsewhere.” “Do everything,” he says, because everything must be arranged according to the disposition of superiors. “I will be with you wherever you wish,” he likewise says, because the best subject must not be absent from any command of obedience.

It follows:

**(Verses 8–10.)** “Jonathan said: Behold, we will cross over to these men; and when we appear to them, if they speak to us in this manner: ‘Stay until we come to you,’ we will remain in our place and will not go up to them. But if they say: ‘Come up to us,’ we will go up, because the Lord has delivered them into our hands.”

### 13

[Col. 0367B] It is a certain and indisputable judgment of the holy Church that chosen preachers must consider not only what, how much, and when they should say, but also to whom they should speak. Hence the Lord, withholding the word from the knowledge of certain people, forbids his disciples, saying: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6). Scripture likewise forbids the word to be poured out uselessly and says: “Where there is no hearing, do not pour out discourse” (Sir. 32:6).

What, then, does Jonathan mean when he says, “If they say, ‘Stay until we come to you,’ we will remain in our place; but if they say, ‘Come up to us,’ we will go up, because the Lord has delivered them into our hands,” except that the chosen preacher must carefully discern to whom he ought to offer the word of life?

[Col. 0367C] Since this now seems to be shown in the literal sense, let us express it more subtly. Preachers cross over to sinners when, for those to whom they offer words, they are pleasing not only in speech but also in life. Who, then, are those who say, “Come up to us,” except those who produce signs of devotion, because they both hear the word of salvation with reverence and eagerly desire to retain it firmly? We must therefore go up to such people, in whom, although the labor of ministerial work is great, the profits of salvation are also great.

Conversely, sinners are eager to cross over to the teachers when they are sunk in such profound blindness that they try to turn even the preachers toward the example of their own depravity. They are inclined toward evil, unrepentant in heart, and do not fear infecting others with the leprosy of sin that they wear. The wise man speaks of them, saying: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14). And the Prophet prophesies concerning them: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom” (Isa. 3:9).

[Col. 0367D] What, then, does Jonathan mean by saying, “Let us remain in our place”? It is as though he said: “If we cannot win them, let us preserve ourselves in a good way of life.” Our place is indeed a good way of life, concerning which it is written elsewhere: “If a spirit having power rises up against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. 10:4).

This place must be guarded not only against a spirit but also against a human being, because the spirit does not oppose us only by itself; it also fights against us through a human being. If our place is the Lord, then when evil people oppose us, let us persist in our place, because when the incorrigible do not receive the admonitions of preachers, the preachers themselves must carefully watch that none of their examples can reach them.

It follows:

306 [Col. 0368A]

### 14

**(Verses 11–12.)** “Thus they appeared to the Philistines’ garrison, and the Philistines said: ‘Look, Hebrews are coming out of the caves in which they had hidden themselves.’ And the men of the Philistines’ garrison spoke to Jonathan and to his armor-bearer: ‘Come up to us, and we will show you something.’”

What does it mean that Jonathan is said to have appeared to the Philistines with his armor-bearer except that the teacher himself must first display the good that he seeks to teach others? He cannot be received with reverence in preaching if he does not first commend the dignity of his ministry in himself through the light of a good way of life.

[Col. 0368B] Hence the outstanding preacher confidently asserts: “As long as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry” (Rom. 11:13). The teacher appears, therefore, not so much when he speaks with words as when he is reverently displayed through life and conduct.

When the Prophet was showing the conduct of preachers through the types of sacred history, he reasonably added: “Thus both appeared to the Philistines’ garrison.” It is as though he said: Since he had decided to teach, he first showed his life to those to whom he had decided to speak.

But what does it mean that the Philistines despise those who appear and nevertheless say to them, “Come up to us,” except that often those who will run to the lamentation of repentance through the preaching of preachers nevertheless despise their excellent life? When they reproach them for abandoning the pursuit of a more withdrawn life, they assert that the preachers have come out of caves. It is as though they said: “Those who seemed to flee from the world with their whole purpose are now coming out into the world under the pretext of preaching.”

[Col. 0368C] Many people also accuse righteous preachers, suspecting that the evils they cast before them are present in the preachers themselves. Yet by condemning evil they thereby give the preachers hope, because they can more easily be drawn to carry out the good that the preachers defend.

When, therefore, they falsely criticize the evils of the righteous with apparently good intention, they rave in their speech; but even in their madness they promise the preachers the fruit of their salvation.

Since an ascent was mentioned above, it remains to inquire what they mean when they say: “We will show you something.” Literally, this signifies threats. It is as though they said: “If you come up here, you will learn by suffering how powerful we are.”

[Col. 0368D] In the conversion of the wicked it is likewise easy to recognize how much harm they usually do when they drive away the righteous. But since, with God as our guide, we have led the corporeal sense of the history toward spiritual understanding, when holy teachers observe the conversion of sinners through certain emerging signs, they also promise to show them “something,” because they promise that they will return to true being.

A thing possesses being; sin, however, possesses no being. Hence Paul says to the Corinthians: “We know that an idol is nothing in the world” (1 Cor. 8:4). But because the sinner, by sinning, tends toward nothingness, when he abandons that nothingness to which he had clung, he returns, as it were, to being. He can therefore show “something” in himself—that is, something that possesses being—because by divine grace he now possesses works of virtue.

[Col. 0369A] They therefore say: “Come up to us, and we will show you something.” It is as though sinners promised by some sign and said: “If you intend to labor among us by your word, your labor will not be without great profit.”

Hence, concerning the certainty of the others, it is added:

**(Verse 12.)** “Jonathan said to his armor-bearer: ‘Let us go up; follow me. The Lord has delivered them into the hands of Israel.’”

### 15

307 Who­ever strives to accomplish great things knows how to weigh this well, if he has always made a practice of attributing them to divine praise. Thus Jonathan, confident of attaining victory, declared that the enemies would be delivered not into his own hands but into the hands of Israel, both displaying the triumph and indicating what the victor ought to be like.

[Col. 0369B] Israel is interpreted as “seeing God.” The one into whose hands the enemies are delivered is therefore called “seeing God,” so that he may be taught not to attend to the things placed in his hand, but, while holding the gift, to lift his heart toward the giver of gifts. He holds one thing in his hands and sees another with his eyes, so that he may hold the palm of triumph firmly, but, as one who sees God, may not be exalted by the victory he holds.

Since he speaks these things in confidence, not as though he already possessed them, let us hear how he comes to possess them. It follows:

### 16

**(Verse 13.)** “Jonathan went up, crawling on his hands, and his armor-bearer behind him.”

What does it mean to crawl on one’s hands except to bend the whole body, leaving nothing exalted in oneself, and to incline one’s higher members toward the performance of lower duties? What else is suggested to us by this action except that the conversion of sinners requires great compassion from preachers?

[Col. 0369C] What else did our Redeemer seem to do than crawl on his hands when he became the friend of tax collectors, received sinners, and ate with them? He crawled on his hands when he said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12). Again he says: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

Sacred discourse also designates this stooping of the crawl by the word “camel.” The Savior humbled himself to the lowest depths of our condition for this purpose: to raise us to the heights of his divinity. Paul indicates that he followed this one who crawled on his hands when he says: “I have become all things to all people, so that I might save all” (1 Cor. 9:22).

[Col. 0369D] And because works are usually signified by hands, the shepherd crawls on his hands when he presents to sinners the way that converts ought to follow not through the wisdom of speech but through the example of his way of life. The Lord taught his preachers to crawl on their hands when he said: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

Jonathan is rightly said to have gone up to the Philistines’ garrison while crawling, because that teacher can reach the destruction of sinners’ vices who wins over the sinners themselves by a great display of humility and a great affection of charity. While he extends the fittingness of grace outwardly, he reaches inward with his hand to cut out the mind’s disease.

Hence it is fittingly added:

### 17

**(Verse 13.)** “When they saw Jonathan’s face, some fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer killed others.”

[Col. 0370A] Jonathan’s face is seen when those who hear the preacher’s word also recognize his love of heart—namely, when they hear him preach heavenly things and at the same time perceive that he loves with wondrous charity those to whom he discloses those heavenly things.

They are rightly said to fall before his face because, when they recognize the good that is in the preacher’s mind, they abandon their former state of depravity. Moreover, when many come to the remedy of repentance, some take refuge in the examples of the great, others in those of the lesser.

It is therefore appropriately said: “His armor-bearer killed others.” To be deprived of a wicked life is to be killed; and the person who abandons evil because of someone’s example or admonitions falls before that person’s feet as though slain.

[Col. 0370B] James explains the victories of individuals in a general statement, saying: “Whoever brings a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:20).

It follows:

### 18

**(Verse 14.)** “The first slaughter, by which Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men, took place in the middle part of an acre, which a yoke of oxen ordinarily plows in a day.”

[Col. 0370C] This is called the first slaughter because the saints are also described as striking down the wicked afterward, at the final judgment. Hence Paul exhorts the Corinthians, saying: “Do you not know that we will judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3). The Psalmist likewise prophesies: “The saints will rejoice in glory; they will exult upon their beds. The praises of God will be in their throats, to execute vengeance upon the nations and rebukes upon the peoples” (Ps. 149:5–6).

This is the first slaughter of conversion; the second is that of condemnation. For now the saints plead with us to be converted to the Lord, but then they will condemn those who have not been converted with greater severity.

[Col. 0370D] Twenty men are reported to have been killed so that the mystery of the number five may be commended. Five repeated four times, or four repeated five times, makes twenty. Since the whole time of sin is completed through the power of the five senses, and since we find the remedies of our salvation in the four books of the Evangelists, the figure of the twenty men expresses all sinners who are to be saved.

They are said to have been killed in the middle part of an acre, which a yoke of oxen ordinarily plows in a day. The oxen are the preachers of the Church: while they preach, they plow; while they open the hearts of their hearers with heavenly words, they scatter seed as though in good soil.

But the oxen plow in the day because the Lord threatens: “The night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9:4). Two oxen likewise plow—namely, Jonathan and his armor-bearer. By these two oxen we may understand either the wise and the simple, or those of lesser and those of higher priestly rank.

[Col. 0371A] More generally, all the preachers of the holy Church can be understood in the two oxen, because they are filled with the grace of the twofold love, and because they do not love themselves with a private love.

The middle part of the acre, therefore, is the present life. This part is softened for cultivation by the rains of winter, while that part is scorched toward the barrenness of the idle by the heats of summer. The oxen can plow this part, but they cannot plow that one, because good works must be sown in this life, whereas in the other life works are not to be sown but the recompense of works is to be reaped.

It is therefore rightly reported that twenty men were killed in the middle part of the acre, because sinners can be profitably converted only here, where the greatness of their crimes is believed to be cleansed through the lamentation of conversion.

Some, however, are astonished at the sudden conversion of sinners, because, through their habitual concern with external matters, the many wonders that God performs each day have become cheap in their eyes. Hence it is added:

### 19

**(Verse 15.)** “A miracle took place in the camp and throughout the fields.”

[Col. 0371B] All the perfect continually marvel at the power and wisdom of almighty God in all things that have been made or are being made. Hence the Psalmist, intent upon divine praises, says: “God is wondrous in his saints; the God of Israel himself will give power and strength to his people; blessed be God” (Ps. 67:36).

Moses likewise confesses this to the same Lord, saying: “Who is like you among the gods, O Lord? Who is like you, glorious among the holy ones, wondrous in majesty, doing marvels?” (Exod. 15:11).

He is called wondrous in the saints because the more deeply they behold divine things, the more wondrously they are astonished. In their highest contemplation they see the things at which they should marvel, not the things that they can comprehend by reason.

Whenever, therefore, something new occurs beyond the ordinary course of daily events, which worldly and simple people admire, a miracle is said to take place throughout the fields. In comparison with the saints, those who do not know how to marvel at so many ancient works of the Creator, so many arrangements of times, and so many orders of creatures are like rustic people.

[Col. 0371C] All are therefore fittingly enclosed within the same dull rusticity when it is added:

**(Verse 15.)** “But the whole population of their garrison, which had gone out to plunder, was astonished.”

## 20.

What station do they call it, if not that of the Philistines? What, then, does it mean that the Philistines are amazed, except that at times sinners behold, in astonishment, the conversion of other sinners, and, when they recognize God’s goodness in his visitation of them, are kindled toward a similar purpose of conversion? The people of the station go out to plunder whenever they do not fear committing perverse acts. For whatever someone dares to do—despite God’s prohibition, the threats of Scripture, and the objections of teachers—he strives, as though by violence, to seize for his own use.

If someone wishes to understand demons by this people, he may do so, since they go out to plunder when they inflict violent temptations and lead sinful souls away captive. This people is said to be amazed because they do not understand by what grace converted sinners receive a contrite heart, which demons cannot possess. Yet when sinners repent, they benefit both themselves and others, because some are corrected by their example. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 15.)** “And the earth was thrown into confusion.”

## 21.

When the people see new and marvelous things, the earth is thrown into confusion, because it often happens that, while some are converted through outward miracles, the hardness of others is stirred by various incentives toward the purpose of good works. The earth is in a bad state of tranquility when the carnal life lies secure amid the world’s pleasures, when the things it ardently desires—though destined to perish—delight it sweetly.

The earth is thrown into confusion when the carnal mind is shaken from its evil firmness and begins, wavering, to reflect between the evils it rejects and the goods it loves. For the mind is thrown into confusion when the serenity of evil pleasure is obscured by the purpose of Christian religion. The carnal inclination is shaken so that spiritual life may be revealed. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 15.)** “And something like a miracle from God occurred.”

## 22.

When the human mind is weighed down by carnal pleasure, its sight is consequently dulled, so that it is unable to recognize spiritual goods. But when it begins to grow weak in regard to its carnal concerns, it gradually grows strong in spiritual matters, so that, advancing, it sees heavenly things and, forgetting, abandons what is infirm. The progress of the converted mind is shown by the fact that first the earth is said to be thrown into confusion, and then a miracle is remembered as having occurred, as it were, from God.

A miracle from God is what God does without a human being. The Lord caused manna to rain upon the children of Israel in the desert (Exod. XVI), and provided birds for those who desired them (Exod. XIV): these were miracles God performed without a human being. But when he wished to divide the sea, he commanded Moses to touch it with his staff, so that he might display a miracle which he would demonstrate to the people through a human being. In the same way, the rock is struck with the staff so that streams of water may flow forth (Num. XX), because the miracle he wished to reveal he performed through a human being, not by himself, so that, by making the human being worthy of honor, he might require the Israelite people to submit humbly and obey devoutly.

What, then, does it mean that a miracle is asserted to have occurred “as it were from God” after the earth is thrown into confusion, except that, when the Holy Spirit stirs the mind toward conversion, he presents to the moved mind the examples of the elect, which it both beholds with reverence and devoutly desires to imitate? Historically, this miracle is understood in this way, because many were being killed. But now, in the holy Church, sinners are converted to a religious life, and others follow them as examples of virtue.

The Holy Spirit draws the former; and because they are drawn, he displays them to others, so that he may draw those who see them and, by joining those who see to those already drawn, bring both groups within the reach of his abundant grace. For when he accomplishes this by himself, without a human being, in the hearts of the faithful, a miracle does not occur “as it were from God,” but from God. When he accomplishes it through preachers, the teachers of eternal life, the miracle is “as it were from God,” because he reveals his ministers as marvelous, so that those who behold them may be able devoutly to imitate them.

But since we said above that Saul signifies the high priests, while his son Jonathan signifies the subordinate persons of preachers, if we attend to what follows, we find in the supreme pontiffs the apostolic concern which they retain. Blessed Paul speaks of it, saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning? Besides those things that are external, my daily pressing concern is the care of all the churches” (II Cor. XI, 29).

He who bore concern for all the churches watched not only over the little ones, but also to examine the deeds of the great. Hence it is added here:

**(Verses 16–17.)** “And Saul’s watchmen, who were in Gibeah of Benjamin, looked, and behold, the multitude lay scattered, fleeing here and there. And Saul said to the people who were with him: ‘Search and see who has gone away from us.’ And it was discovered that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were absent.”

## 23.

Saul’s watchmen observe Jonathan’s battle because supreme pontiffs examine not only the deeds of their subjects but also the teaching of those placed over them. They investigate the former to see whether they act well, and the latter to see whether they teach correctly. They often hear of the conduct of others, but they fear that those others may not be properly instructed.

What else does the inquiry about who has gone away signify except that the person sent to preach must be such that the burden of ministry can safely be laid upon him? The mind of the one who sends must not waver with any doubt that he teaches correctly and demonstrates the words of his teaching by his works.

And because there are innumerable rulers of the churches, Jonathan is observed by the watchmen: the supreme summit of the universal Church organizes preachers throughout the world in such a way that it has ministers around itself through whom it may examine their teaching and diligently investigate their works.

But those who perform the ministry and embassy of the highest summit are raised to the lofty seat of life and knowledge. Hence these watchmen are rightly said to be in Gibeah of Benjamin. Gibeah of Benjamin is called “the hill of the son of the right hand.” On the hill of the son of the right hand are those who, through exalted life and profound knowledge, appear already to have attained conformity to the Redeemer.

They behold the deeds of the victorious from on high, because from the height of life and the perfect instruction of supreme knowledge they are worthy to approve the lives of the good and examine the wicked. They discover that Jonathan is absent because they judge the gains of preaching to be best when they approve the preacher’s commendable character. It follows:

**(Verse 18.)** “And Saul said to Ahijah: ‘Bring the ark of God here.’”

## 24.

Why does Saul command the priest Ahijah to bring the ark, except because they hear from the watchmen the manner of the battle? This is spiritually well done by supreme priests when they do not judge beforehand what they hear from informants, but first seek its rationale in the counsel of inner meditation.

And because they often follow the counsels even of another mind, Ahijah is ordered to bring the ark. The priest possesses the ark who is not empty of spiritual knowledge. Saul therefore orders Ahijah to bring the ark when the supreme teacher seeks counsel from his lesser and learned ministers. Counsel must be sought where the grace of spiritual knowledge shines forth. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 18.)** “For the ark of God was there on that day with the children of Israel.”

## 25.

It is as though he said: He commanded him to bring what he knew to be there. To seek counsel about religion from the irreligious, or wisdom from fools, is not to receive counsel but to rush headlong into ruin. It is rightly said, therefore: “For the ark of God was there,” because in doubtful matters we ought to consult those whom we clearly know are not lacking in spiritual gifts.

Yet some things are improved by counsel, while others are improved by assistance. Where the need is open and certain, delay for counsel is not appropriate; the speed of intervention is. We deal with ambiguous and obscure matters better by taking counsel, but we relieve what is clear and known by helping and hastening. Hence it is added:

**(Verses 19–20.)** “And while Saul was speaking to the priest, a great tumult arose in the camp of the Philistines; it increased little by little and sounded more loudly. And Saul said to the priest: ‘Withdraw your hand.’ Saul and all the people who were with him shouted, and they came as far as the place of battle.”

## 26.

What else is signified by the fact that Saul first asked that the ark be brought and then ordered the priest to withdraw his hand, except that we ought to arrange obscure matters through counsel and complete with haste what becomes clearer?

For a preacher to hear a tumult gradually increasing is to perceive the devotion of converted sinners. It is said to increase gradually because, when the Spirit directs our mind toward good works, he gently leads it to better things through daily progress.

What else does it mean that Saul and all the people with him shout, except that they join themselves to the fighters? They also come as far as the place of battle. The place of battle is the heart of one who hears the word of God. It is called the place of battle because the word that is received fights against the former way of life.

He already delights in the heavenly things he hears, but the old habit rises up and urges him to despise what he has heard. The battle becomes more severe because what the preacher praises, evil spirits disparage by dissuasion; they raise themselves up as if in battle against the saints when, by fighting, they destroy what is preached by the saints’ voice.

What, then, does it mean to come as far as the place of battle except to reach, by the way of inquiry, the secrets of the hearer’s heart, where one may quickly find the enemies and strike them powerfully? For those who do not know how to examine inner things cannot reach the place of battle.

Alternatively, the place of battle is where the report of great religion is widespread. Innumerable people run there, desiring both to lay aside their former life and to put on a new one; it is rightly called the place of battle because there the army of spiritual virtues daily fights against the multitude of vices.

There the heavier the battles, the more glorious the victories. There, the more frequent the approach of the enemies, the more praiseworthy the number of triumphs: not only is the lofty virtue of the great exalted, but the vigor of all alike is displayed with a marvelous demonstration of courage. Hence it follows:

**(Verse 20.)** “And behold, each man’s sword was turned against his neighbor, and there was a very great slaughter.”

## 27.

What is this sword except the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God? Since those who have been converted to the service of almighty God in innumerable places cling inseparably to the word of God, each one seems to hold a sword beside him.

Each man’s sword is therefore turned against his neighbor when those who have been converted in monasteries pierce one another with the word of God and completely kill the carnal element within themselves. They are slain, as it were, by mutual wounds when one strikes the other with the word of God and extinguishes whatever lives carnally within him.

Because they had recently been converted and had fallen away from secular life, they are marked by the figure of the Philistines.

Alternatively, one man’s sword is turned against his neighbor when, through the exhortation of the converted, sinners who have not yet been converted are turned to the Lord; when not only those who preside over the word of preaching win others, but also the multitude of subjects strive, by as many words and examples as they can, to instruct others, withdraw them as though slain from the desires of the present life, and present them alive to eternal life.

We see these gains of the slain already spread throughout the whole Church and across the entire world, because all who now live to God through divine grace appear dead to this world by the sword-point of mutual love. Each man’s sword is turned against his neighbor because all the elect in the holy Church strengthen one another and kindle one another toward the heavenly homeland through the zeal of mutual preaching.

And because an innumerable people is acquired daily for God, it is rightly added there: “And the slaughter was very great.” What is “very great,” indeed, is something whose magnitude can in some way be recognized, but whose excellence cannot be comprehended.

He had raised his eyes toward this very great slaughter who said: “But to me your friends have been exceedingly honored, O God; their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened. I will number them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 17).

The very great slaughter may also be understood to mean not only that many appeared to have been killed, but that they had been killed well. This is seen in the conversion of sinners, when they abandon their former pleasures in such a way that they never return to life in those same delights.

For sinners, to be killed means to be separated for a time from a shameful life. To be killed vehemently, or exceedingly, therefore, means to abandon perfectly the enticements of temporal life and to yearn for the joys of the future.

But because there is great diversity among those who are converted, it follows:

**(Verse 21.)** “Moreover, the Hebrews who had previously been with the Philistines, yesterday and the day before, and had gone up with them into the camp, returned to be with Israel and with those who were with Saul and Jonathan.”

## 28.

Who are the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines except sinners who have fallen away from religious conduct? Of these it was said somewhat earlier: “The Hebrews crossed the Jordan.” They are Hebrews according to the order of religion, but they are with the Philistines and go up with them as long as they are deceived by harmful suggestions and advance in evil action.

They are with the evil spirits in the purpose and will of sin; but they go up with them because, under their impulse, they exalt themselves in the boldness of wicked action. Or they are with them when they complete their sins by carrying them out; they go up with them when they do not fear presenting the examples of their wickedness for others to imitate.

What, then, does it mean that they are said to return and be with Israel except that such people also often repent? To return is to take up again the love of religious life. To be with Israel is to remain within the holy Church in the unity of charity.

They must return for the purpose of being with Israel, because there is no conversion of a sinner if, after conversion, he lacks perseverance in good works and the unity of charity. It follows:

**(Verse 22.)** “All the Israelites who had hidden themselves in Mount Ephraim, hearing that the Philistines had fled, joined their own people in the battle.”

## 29.

This happens whenever those devoted to a more withdrawn life deign to turn their efforts toward seeking the gains of souls. They join their own people in battle when they preach, together with the teachers of the holy Church, the true joys of eternal life and together drive evil spirits from the hearts of sinners.

Yet it must be asked carefully how it can say: “Hearing that the Philistines had fled.” A splendid victory does not consist in pursuing fugitives, but in driving away those who resist. What, then, does it mean that, “hearing that the Philistines had fled, they joined their own people in battle,” except that these words signify gains appropriate to the more withdrawn life?

It is customary for those men to speak the word rather to those who consult them than to those who resist them, because, unless they recognize a devoted heart in the hearer, they disdain to cast their preaching forth as though it would perish in emptiness.

Before they join their own people in battle, therefore, they hear that the Philistines have fled, because they do not so much devote themselves to converting the wicked as to raising the converted to the heights of a more perfect life.

The sublimity of the more perfect life is usually commended through the labors of great exhortation. Those who hear that the Philistines have fled are therefore rightly said to fight. The enemies flee, but those who had recently been hidden fight, because men of the withdrawn life do not deign to speak except to devoted hearers; yet, when they speak, they can scarcely persuade them of the height of the life they themselves lead except through a great battle of words and examples.

And because the weak and imperfect cannot gather great gains from preaching, it follows:

**[Col. 0376D] (Verse 22.)** “There were with Saul about ten thousand men.”

It does not say “ten thousand,” but “about ten thousand.” The complete perfection of this number is not found on earth, but in heaven. Since there are nine orders of angels, and that multitude of human beings—the elect—is raised into their company, the ten thousand men are those who rejoice among the holy angels and elect human beings in that seat of eternal glory.

“About ten thousand men,” therefore, are those who, still placed in the exile of this present age, have taken on in their conduct the form of that blessed fellowship.

And because the darkness of sins is abandoned through love of that heavenly life, it follows:

**(Verse 23.)** “And the Lord saved Israel on that day.”

The contemplation of inner light is a very splendid and radiant day, on which the Lord saves Israel, because he raises to the height of perpetual salvation those whose hearts he illuminates with the light of inward splendor.

The Lord is said to save “on that day” because no one is kindled with love of eternal life when the splendor of inner light remains hidden from him.

Not only the elect but also those who appear despised by the world attain this grace of salvation. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 23.)** “And the battle reached as far as Beth-aven.”

## 30.

Beth-aven means “useless house.” To display this useless house in parables, the Lord introduces a king ordering his servant at the wedding feast, saying: “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and the weak, the blind and the lame” (Luke XIV, 21).

[Note: [Col. 0377D] Gussanv. with the Vatican manuscript: “he introduces him as giving the command.”]

The poor are those who do not at all store the treasures of God’s word in their hearts. The weak are those who cannot labor sufficiently for eternal life. The blind designate the uneducated and simple, because, since they do not see heavenly things, they lack the light of the mind. The lame are those who have lost the step of good works.

But “the battle reached as far as Beth-aven” because useless persons are often captured by the battle of God’s word and, reduced to its service, become useful. The battle is waged with the blind so that they may see, with the lame so that they may stand, with the poor so that they may receive the treasures of conduct, and with the weak so that they may grow strong for good works.

The battle is carried as far as Beth-aven, therefore, when those who appeared to have no usefulness necessary to anyone are captured by the preaching of the saints. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 24.)** “And every Israelite joined himself to him on that day.”

## 31.

Every man joins himself to the preacher when no human condition is left from which people cannot be led to a good way of life after conversion.

They are called men who join themselves to Saul because, whatever we may be in the world, we are admonished to be strong in the service of almighty God. For men would never join themselves to preachers unless they themselves performed the strong deeds which the preachers praise in their teaching.

But now that the enemies have been conquered and the strong have been joined to him, we must carefully consider what the king does. It follows:

**(Verse 24.)** “And Saul adjured the people, saying: ‘Cursed is the man who eats before evening, until I have taken vengeance on my enemies.’”

## 32.

The enemies of preachers are those concerning whom the Psalmist pleads, saying: “Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise up against me” (Ps. LVIII, 1).

Unclean spirits are rightly called the enemies of the saints, because the saints reject with great zeal the attractions of the world which those spirits suggest. For one to whom something from the counsels of an evil spirit is still pleasing is not truly that spirit’s enemy, since he has not yet learned to hate the one whose blandishments he does not reject.

They are also called the saints’ enemies so that sacred utterance may expose them. Through everything they suggest and everything with which they flatter, they try to destroy the souls toward which they show their pleasing favor.

What, then, does it mean that he adjures the people not to eat before evening, until he has taken vengeance on his enemies? It must be noted that he said this after the enemies had already been defeated.

What does eating mean for victors except to receive with delight the food of empty praise from a work of virtue already accomplished? “Cursed,” he says, “is everyone who eats before evening,” because whoever now gladly accepts empty praises then loses the eternal praises of the Creator.

The people are adjured not to eat because, by the command of teachers, they are restrained from boasting vainly about a good work. Let them perform strong deeds by living well, but, as long as they live, let them beware of seeking praise for their strength, so that they may not lose eternal praise after death.

He who prohibited the people from eating before evening clearly allowed them to eat in the evening. Since evening is the end of the day, those who can abstain before evening eat toward evening: whoever now disdains being praised for a great deed is found worthy of eternal praises when he is led to the end of life.

This is what the Lord promises in the Gospel that he will give to the elect, saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. XXV, 23). Again, when he comes to judgment, he says: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 34).

Then we take vengeance on our enemies, because all demonic temptations vanish. Since the snares of demons can no longer harm us by tempting us when we die in the flesh, we take vengeance on our enemies, whom, as though already slain, we no longer fear at all.

We therefore defer eating until evening if we reserve the proclamations of our praise for the coming judge at the end. Then we must eat, because the judge who comes then now promises his fellow soldiers, as the leader of our army: “He will have them recline, and he will pass by and serve them” (Luke XII, 37).

Then the victors recline, because, received into the lofty seat of inner rest, they delight in the praises of everlasting life. While they themselves are silent, the proclamations of all their good works resound, and for glory there are brought forth together the things that here were carried into battle with great courage. It follows:

**(Verses 25–26.)** “And all the common people of the land came into the forest, where there was honey on the surface of the field. So the people entered the forest, and behold, honey was flowing; yet no one brought his hand to his mouth.”

## 33.

A forest is a wooded and sloping place. By this name the hearts of secular people are appropriately designated, because, while they serve outward concerns with their whole attention, they are like wooded places, not cultivated for the fruit of good works by the plow of preaching.

But who are designated here by the name “common people” [perhaps read: “of the common people”] except religious and simple men? They are called the common people of the land because they are great in good works, though they are not great in the loftiest contemplation. They are noble in action, but common people in comparison with the highest men.

What, then, does it mean that the common people of the land came into the forest except that religious and simple men are often brought, through examples of good works, to the knowledge of secular people?

Honey appears in the field because, through the example of good work, secular people find there both breadth of devotion and the fruit of reverence. For what is the field in the forest except devotion in the uncultivated and unpurified heart of secular people? And what is honey upon the surface of the field except the sweetness of approval?

It is rightly said to appear after the entrance of the common people, because the harsh hearts of secular people, unless they first see the examples of religious persons, can neither stretch themselves out in the breadth of devotion nor proclaim the glory of another’s holiness.

Before the entrance there is only a forest; it has neither a field nor flowing honey.
