After the entrance, however, it has both the breadth of a field and the sweetness of honey, because those who love the world often receive the examples of the saints with ardent love, so that the good they see not only pleases them but also makes them desire more earnestly to proclaim it.

Nevertheless, the life of the saints ought to be praised, and that praise must in no way be appropriated through vainglory by those to whom it belongs. It ought merely to be seen, not consumed, so that each person may rejoice in God’s glorification through his work but disdain to be exalted by God’s grace.

Hence it is carefully expressed that flowing honey appeared on the surface of the field, and yet no one brought his hand with the honey to his mouth. Honey flows because the sweet fame of the saints runs sweetly and swiftly. But no one brings his hand to his mouth because he does not take the sweetness of praise from a good work.

To bring the hand with honey to the mouth is to receive the praise of one’s work gladly. Let the honey therefore flow, and let no one bring his hand to his mouth, so that the fame of the saints may flow sweetly without exalting those from whom it flows. Let it flow to satisfy others, but let it not be consumed, lest it offer death. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 26.)** “For the people feared the oath.”

The king’s oath is: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XVIII, 14). Again, the king’s oath is what he pronounces against hypocrites, saying: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 16).

The people therefore fear the oath because, lest they lose eternal praise, they avoid receiving temporal praise. It follows:

**(Verse 27.)** “But Jonathan had not heard when his father adjured the people; so he extended the end of the staff that he held in his hand, dipped it into a honeycomb, and brought his hand to his mouth, and his eyes were enlightened.”

## 34.

Whom does Jonathan signify here except those who are great in word and deed but are not great in the practice of watchful self-restraint? They preach lofty things and perform strong deeds, but they do not hold themselves manfully in the watchfulness of humility.

What does it mean that he holds a staff in his hand except that he does not restrain himself by the discipline with which he prohibits others from sinning? The staff with which children are accustomed to be corrected can aptly signify a word of correction. Preaching and good work are therefore the staff and the hand.

What, then, does it mean to extend the staff and bring the hand with honey back to the mouth except to receive a taste of vain approval both from the word of preaching and from the practice of good work?

But because he sins in the manner of the elect, he is said to lift honey not from the staff itself but from the end of the staff. Those who turn the staff and hand, full of honey, toward their mouth are those who, according to the voice of truth, “do all their works so that they may be seen by people” (Matt. XXIII, 5).

While they are filled with their own praises, they do not have honey merely for a slight taste at the end of the staff, but either in the whole staff or in the hand, for complete refreshment. Such were those whom the Lord reproaches in the Gospel, saying: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another?” (John V, 44).

What, then, is this end of the staff except that they often wish to glorify the Lord in their work, yet do not refuse to appear praiseworthy themselves? Jonathan is rightly said not to have heard the voice of the father by which he adjured the people, because one who neglects to fulfill the words of God or of his preacher does not hear them.

What, then, does it mean that Jonathan’s eyes were enlightened by tasting the honey, except that those who receive the breath of vain approval are thereby strengthened to perform strong deeds?

Here his eyes are not said to have been opened, as though they had been understood to be closed, but to have been restored in bodily vigor, so that he might be understood to have been restored for seeing and for destroying the enemies. This entirely suits the proud, who perform greater and stronger deeds insofar as they see their praiseworthy works being exalted.

But often a lesser person is kindled by the zeal of charity when he tries to bring great men who are delinquent back to the remembrance of Scripture. Hence it follows:

**(Verse 28.)** “Then one of the people answered and said: ‘Your father bound the people by an oath, saying: “Cursed is the man who eats bread today.”’”

## 35.

He reported that the father had adjured the people and pronounced a curse because, when a lesser person wishes to correct a prelate who is in error, he ought not to rebuke him harshly, but gently and humbly to lead him back to remembering the statutes of his predecessors.

Hence he says: “Your father bound the people by an oath.” To admonish gently the one who bound the people by an oath, he asserted that he was his father. It is as though he said in other words: You ought to preserve the institutions of your predecessors all the more lovingly, the more fully you appear to retain their place through the dignity of succession.

The people are also said to have been bound by the father’s oath so that attention might be paid not to the humility of the person speaking but to the authority displayed; so that, if the rank of the one making the suggestion is despised, the dignity of the one pointed out may be feared.

He calls him father so that the commands of the predecessors may be objects both of fear and of love. Let him therefore say: “Your father bound the people by an oath, saying: ‘Cursed is the one who eats bread today.’”

This is as though he said: I want you to remember what belongs to you, not to me, because, while you occupy the summit of your predecessors, you ought to preserve their laws as though by hereditary right.

The name “bread” rightly expresses the favor of flatterers, because it both satisfies a mind intent on vanity and strengthens it, making it more vigorous for performing deeds that ought to be praised. This is seen to suit the proud very well, who are stirred to speak by praises brought forth for them.

And because an arrogant preacher has subjects like himself, desirous of praise, it follows:

**(Verse 28.)** “But the people had grown faint.”

## 36.

What does it mean literally to grow faint except to become weary? Those who seek passing praise from preaching the word grow faint when they are praised, because they utter no words with vigor when they do not see that they are being praised. They grow faint like people becoming weary when, having been despised, they fall silent.

They also appear to grow faint while they do not eat, because, if they were permitted the food of approval, they would attack vices by the preaching of the word as though refreshed and strong. Hence the form of the arrogant preacher is displayed by what follows:

**(Verses 29–30.)** “And Jonathan said: ‘My father has troubled the land. You yourselves have seen that my eyes were enlightened because I tasted a little of this honey. How much greater would the slaughter among the Philistines have been if the people had eaten the spoil of their enemies which they found?’”

## 37.

What does it mean that he reproves his father for having troubled the land except that he accuses the great of having confused their statutes through inexperience? The humility of subjects is designated by the name “land”; it is seen to be thrown into confusion when, because of the shepherds’ erroneous judgment, it appears to abandon the order of tranquil truth.

And because, while the proud eagerly seek human approval and try to assert that this is permissible, they bring their progress forward as testimony, he says: “You have seen that my eyes were enlightened because I tasted a little of this honey.”

It is as though he said: “I grew through the praise of my subjects, since I took care not to be lesser in the midst of praises.” It is also customary among elect preachers that, when they see themselves being praised, they strive to make themselves equal in strength to what they hear said about them publicly.

For this reason Jonathan reported that he had eaten a little honey: the arrogant person thinks that he may freely receive the approval of tongues for the advancement of his life, not for the intention of vanity.

But it is altogether one thing to strive to match proclamations of praise by one’s conduct, and another to desire praise so that one may find advancement of life in those same praises.

Those who strive to make their conduct equal to their praises are the ones who despise those praises and never wish to be praised by people. As far as lies within them, they strongly avoid being praised; but because they cannot entirely escape praise, they strive to be what they hear.

Some, however, having displayed good works, wish to be praised for this reason: so that, once praised, they may rise to a greater work of virtue. Yet they are deceived by this estimation of their presumption, because one who seeks praise in small matters, when he has performed greater works, seeks praise still more ardently and eagerly.

Perhaps this is why Jonathan could not reign after his father: he signified those who, while vainly exalting themselves, truly grow faint.

He also added by way of reasoning, saying: “How much greater would the slaughter among the Philistines have been if the people had eaten the spoil of their enemies?”

To taste a little honey from the end of the staff is to glory, in some fashion, in eloquence of doctrine. To eat the spoil of the enemies is to recall works of virtue to mind and rejoice in remembering them.

A person makes the spoil of his enemies, as it were, when he recalls the things in which he has prevailed over hidden enemies. He eats these things to satiety when, as though he had accomplished them by his own virtue, he exalts himself vainly and excessively.

He therefore says: “How much greater would the slaughter among the Philistines have been if the people had eaten the spoil of their enemies?” It is as though he said: “Since such progress results from a brief taste of approval, what would the elect fighters do if they had full, lawful, and just praise for their works?”

It follows:

**(Verse 31.)** “So they struck the Philistines on that day, from Magmas to Aion.”

38. The day of the mind is the splendor of learning. But those whom the arrogant instruct, because they are inflamed by ambition for temporal glory, receive the appearance of light, not the truth. When, therefore, that day is mentioned, what else is signified except that they often appear to perform courageous deeds for the sake of temporal glory? On that day, that is, through the teaching or example of the proud, they strike down the Philistines, because they devote themselves to the ministry of preaching for the purpose of acquiring the splendor of worldly glory. And because they desire to become known to everyone, he says: “From Magmas as far as Aion.”

Magmas, as has already been sufficiently stated, is interpreted as “humility”; Aion, however, is interpreted as “my mourning brother.” The humble in this passage signify the small and simple within holy Church. But whom does the mourning brother indicate except those whom the Lord praises in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5)? For whoever already knows how to despise all temporal things and yearns for eternal things with great desires, while dreading confinement in the body and grieving that he is not yet in the joy of eternal life, is rightly called “my mourning brother.” He is called a brother because he has already begun to be a fellow-heir of Christ, for whose most blessed and joyful inheritance he sighs with all his desires. He is called mourning so that the inexpressible character of the perfected person’s grief may be indicated.

To mourn does not mean to weep casually, but to weep most deeply. Since they have been filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, they have reached that abundance of tears of which the distinguished Teacher declares: “The Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. VIII, 26). He is also called the mourning brother because all the perfect are joined to the Redeemer in great intimacy. When one whom the Redeemer loves in a singular way, whom he nurtures with singular dignity for possession of the perpetual inheritance, is called his brother, he is designated by the singular number. Hence he says to Moses, as to a singular friend: “I know you by name” (Exod. XXXIII, 12). This is why it is said of John in the Gospel: “This is the disciple whom Jesus loved” (John XXI, 20). Although he loved all the disciples very greatly, when this one is said to be loved, the brother is indicated in the singular number.

On that day, from Magmas as far as Aion, the arrogant strike down the Philistines, because, in order to receive the light of worldly glory, they preach not only small things to the little ones, but also lofty things that the more perfect can recognize. And because, while harming some little ones in Christ through the perversity of their intention, they also benefit many more perfect people by their speech, they are said not to fight but to strike—from Magmas as far as Aion.

To strike the Philistines means to destroy the ambushes of demons or the tyranny of vices in the hearts of the elect. But proud teachers often benefit others through the word, while receiving none of the praises of that same word which they desire. Hence it frequently happens that, when they fail to notice themselves being praised and exalted, they fall silent as though exhausted by great labors. Therefore it is added:

**(Verse 31.)** “But the people were exceedingly weary.”

It is also customary among the exalted that, when another person’s tongue is silent about their praises, their own self-estimation does not remain silent. While others are silent, they themselves cry out, because they carry within their hearts the proclamations of their own self-estimation. Thus it is rightly added concerning the same people:

**(Verse 32.)** “And the people turned to the spoils, and took sheep, and oxen, and calves, and slaughtered them on the ground; and the people ate with the blood.”

39. He takes sheep who recalls the many grounds for his innocence in order to become exalted. He takes oxen as spoils when he considers the labors of his preaching and, by recollection, heaps up whatever he accomplished by speaking to others, as though cultivating the earth. He takes calves when he is exalted by bringing back to mind the suppressed impulses of lust.

Because two things are commanded in the great praise of the righteous—namely, the splendor of charity together with the light of good works—when an arrogant person is exalted in his own estimation, he is said to take sheep and calves. He takes sheep in relation to the innocence of good works, and calves in relation to the mortification of bodily passions. He also included oxen among them, because no one is completely exalted who contemplates himself as weak and powerless in some respect. He is already great in his own estimation because of chastity and good works, but he raises himself in the pride of greater exaltation when he remembers himself as perfect in the labor of preaching.

But the end to which all these things are brought is explained subsequently: “And they slaughtered them on the ground.” To slaughter sheep, oxen, and calves on the ground means to exult in a low and carnal joy over the consciousness of one’s virtues. Hence Hosea says of the exalted and arrogant: “They were plunging sacrifices into the deep” (Hos. V, 2). They plunge heavenly sacrifices of virtue into the deep when they do not lift them toward heaven through thanksgiving, but incline them toward the earth through the desire for empty praise.

Hence it is also aptly added: “And the people ate with the blood.” The food of the mind is its inward joy. What, then, does it mean to eat with the blood except not to remove the intention of vain favor from the mind’s inward appetite? Blood is cast away, as it were, when the mind removes the intention of vanity from the joy of a good work. Such a mind knows how to rejoice in a good work because it rejoices to draw near to heavenly things through good works, yet for a time shuns being seen in those same works.

To eat with the blood, therefore, means to take up the joy of a good work mixed with an intention of vanity. When this is offered by others, it is simple food for the exalted; but when, with no one praising them, the conscience of the proud swells up, they seize as spoils by force what no one has freely given.

It follows:

**(Verses 33–34.)** “They reported to Saul, saying that the people had sinned against the Lord by eating with the blood. He said: ‘You have acted treacherously. Roll before me now a great stone.’ And Saul said: ‘Disperse yourselves among the people and tell them that each one should bring his ox and his ram, and slaughter them upon this stone, and eat; then you will not sin against the Lord by eating with the blood.’”

40. It is proper to the preachers of holy Church both to rebuke sins that have been committed and to show how the sins rebuked ought to be avoided. Sins are indeed made known, but if people do not learn how to avoid them, those sins are repeated. What is shown by this eating of blood except the hidden poison of pride? Hidden vices are not cured unless they are exposed.

Therefore, to indicate the conduct of preachers, Saul first declares that the people have acted treacherously; then he commands that the animals they are to eat be slaughtered on a stone. But we know what the rock or stone signifies, because Paul identifies it, saying: “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4). The stone is rolled before the preacher when the examples of the Redeemer are recalled in his presence. It is also said to be rolled so that it may be seen from every side.

It is called great because Daniel says that it grows and fills the entire face of the world (Dan. II). It is therefore not viewed casually, but rolled from both sides, so that God may be seen by the arrogant and their arrogance may be brought low. Let the arrogant person see how powerful in virtue, how exalted in majesty, and how humble in virtue our Redeemer appeared.

For while illuminating the blind and healing the sick (Matt. IX), he commanded that what he had accomplished powerfully should be told to no one. On the mountain he shone with splendor and produced the Father’s testimony to his divinity, yet he said to the disciples: “Tell no one this vision until the Son of Man has risen from the dead” (Matt. XVII, 9).

And perhaps for this reason, after the Lord had risen, an angel appeared at the tomb and rolled away the stone from its entrance. The stone was then to be rolled away because Christ, true man and powerful God, was to be recognized after the glory of the resurrection. If the exalted person has looked at one side of the stone, let him roll it and see the other. Let him not look at the stone in an arbitrary way: Christ is not dead, but the stone has been rolled away by the angel because he rose from the dead.

Let him therefore observe the power of preaching on one side, roll the stone, and marvel at the splendor of humility on the other. Let him see the power of signs on one side, and on the other see that he who shone through the power of virtue concealed that same virtue by the command of silence.

But while he sees the humble side, let him also see the exalted side. Behold, the humble side of the stone is visible, because it says: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. II, 8). But when this side is turned, the other is revealed, because it continues: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.”

We roll the stone before the preacher when we recall before him the power and humility of our Redeemer, when we observe him humble in his works and exalted in heaven because of his humility.

An ox and a ram are to be slaughtered upon this stone so that, in every kind of human being, the vice of pride may be put to death through contemplation of Christ. There all the blood is poured out, because the person instructed by Christ’s example accomplishes great things but does not exalt himself because of those great deeds. He is nourished by the joy of a good work, but his food is not stained with the blood of empty praise.

For if that stone is turned in words, it says: “If I had not done among them the works that no one else has done, they would not have sin” (John XV, 24). But because he did not swell with pride over his words, turning himself, he says: “I do not seek my own glory” (John VIII, 50).

An ox and a ram are therefore slaughtered upon the stone when every horned form of pride is condemned by the Redeemer’s example; when any member of the elect both acts well and teaches excellently, but is raised up neither by his own life nor by another’s learning.

In the ram the strength of one’s own innocence is expressed; in the ox, the labor and strength of preaching. They are killed upon the rock so that they may refresh the chosen mind with joy, but not offer it flesh mixed with their own blood.

The chosen preacher not only speaks this, but also persuades others of it. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 34.)** “And the people each brought his ox by the hand until night, and slaughtered them there.”

41. To bring an ox by the hand means to erase the sin of pride through the affliction of repentance. While he erases by doing what he committed through pride, he leads the ox to be slaughtered upon the stone by the hand.

What does it mean that he says, “Until night,” except that although it is not permissible to sin, it is permissible to erase sins until death? Oxen must therefore be slaughtered until night, not during the night, because while we live we can erase sins through repentance, but after death we cannot perform fruitful repentance.

It is aptly added in the same place:

**(Verse 35.)** “And Saul built an altar to the Lord.”

41. This is because, when sinners are converted, a heavenly building is fashioned, as it were, from stones. And since many manuscripts read, “Then Saul first began to build,” the name of the altar may be understood as signifying compunction of heart. When compunction of heart is raised up through the preacher’s word, an altar is truly built for the Lord.

It is said to have been built first because it is the compunction of love. Hence in the tabernacle of the covenant the Lord commanded that two altars be made: one for burning incense, and the other for burning flesh (Exod. XXVII, XXXVII). The first altar was outside; the second was within the Holy of Holies.

The first altar, therefore, is compunction of fear; the second is compunction of love. The former belongs to those who mourn their sins; the latter to those who long with all their desires for eternal joys. The stones of the former are reflections upon sins; the stones of the latter are meditations upon everlasting joys.

The teacher builds the first altar when he exposes faults, which the sinner beholds in himself and therefore groans over. Compunction is also rightly called an altar because it burns incense. But when each person has long been pierced with compunction for his sins, he advances through repentance toward the practice of security.

After the periods of affliction, he begins to burn for eternal life; and the one who previously mourned through fear of punishment now begins to weep more abundantly because the reward is delayed. Since the first compunction of the elect arises from fear, and since, through the type of the king and the people, preachers and newly converted subjects are signified, Saul is said at that time to have built the altar first.

But a teacher is often kindled by the progress of others to seek the gain of others. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 36.)** “And Saul said: ‘Let us fall upon the Philistines by night, and devastate them until morning dawns, and leave none of them alive.’”

42. This has been sufficiently explained above. But since he desires to strike the Philistines during the night until day dawns, he plainly indicates that demons must now be expelled and destroyed from the hearts of sinners, lest they be able to harm them in the future.

This life is called night when it is compared with eternity. For whoever is able to contemplate that life worthily judges, by comparison with it, that whatever appears bright here is the darkness of night. That day dawns when, at the end of this life, it opens itself to the chosen souls. At its departure from the body, the chosen soul sees eternity dawning upon it, because it did not regard the light of the present age except as darkness.

43. But what does it mean when he says, “And let us not leave a man among them”? Every Philistine who is a man must be devastated, but not every little one can be devastated. No one is without sin except God alone. The men, therefore, signify capital crimes and principal vices. They are designated by the name “men,” that is, “strong ones,” when they bring the hearts of sinners under their power.

It is therefore rightly said: “Let us not leave a man among them,” because converted sinners, by the counsel of holy preachers, abandon their stronger sins and vices, but cannot exist without any sin or vice. They can avoid crimes, but cannot avoid all sins. They can extinguish vices, but cannot prevent themselves from being struck in some way by one of them.

He therefore says: “Let us not leave a man among them,” because the preachers of holy Church command us to root out vices; yet, while they kill the strong and principal ones within us, they cannot ensure that none of them continues to live through some slight movement.

Speaking next of the people’s obedience, he says:

**(Verse 36.)** “The people said: ‘Do whatever is good in your eyes.’”

44. The eyes of preachers are the vision of reason. Therefore the person who is entrusted to a teacher’s judgment is rightly said to tell him: “Do whatever is good in your eyes.” It is as though he said: “We, who distrust the illumination of our own reason, entrust to the light of your reason what we judge to be lacking in us.”

But what Saul said—“Let us fall upon the Philistines”—can be understood to mean that he did not state a settled decision, but, by saying this, consulted whether they ought to attack the Philistines. The fact that the people immediately gave their assent indicates what we see: some within holy Church approve the words of their superiors before they understand them. For it immediately follows:

**(Verses 36–37.)** “And the priest said: ‘Let us approach the Lord here.’ And Saul consulted the Lord, saying: ‘Shall I pursue the Philistines?’ And the Lord did not answer him on that day.”

45. What does it mean that the priest declares that the words of the consulting king, which the people praise, must be brought before the Lord, except that obscure and important matters, hidden from the simple, are never rightly ordered if we do not seek their outcome in the sanctuary of the mind through subtle meditation?

To approach the Lord means to learn his will through secret contemplation. It is rightly called an approach because we move from external things toward the interior when we attempt to learn the outcome of our work in the divine will. For whoever seeks what is hidden and inward but does not abandon external things does not find what he is unable to approach.

Therefore, whenever counsel is sought from us concerning hidden matters, let us approach the Lord, so that only then may what must be done be proposed when it is known in the divine will. Many things appear good but are not. Many things also ought to be done, but they are done more usefully if reserved for the appropriate time. Some things ought to be done by certain people, while others ought not to do them.

If any member of the elect neglects to see these matters in the secrecy of meditation, he certainly does not arrange them in proper order. But the person accustomed to examine or undertake them through meditation learns not only what must be done, but also what must be avoided. Hence it is rightly said:

**(Verse 37.)** “Saul consulted the Lord, and the Lord did not answer him on that day.”

46. The day is the thought of the mind, which is considered good but is not recognized as such. While it pretends to be good, it carries light, as it were. On that day, therefore, the Lord did not answer the one consulting him, because the word of God cannot accord with an evil deliberation.

Through an answer of the word we customarily disclose the meaning of our innermost will. On that day, then, the Lord does not answer because almighty God is not seen in the feigned light of thought, though he is always found in the brightness of truth.

It should also be noted that the one who gave the counsel to approach the Lord was a priest. For what is holier than the counsel to approach God? We are priests as often as we provide good counsel to our brothers. Nothing more sacred can be given than that by which each person ought to go to his Creator.

But because we are describing the order of spiritual battle, we must connect what follows with what came before.

47. Saul’s word was that he should devastate the Philistines in such a way that he left none of them alive. This can also be understood to mean that he wished to destroy the Philistines so completely that none of them could ever again wage war.

This is a great day of the mind: one in which eternal things are sought in such a way that no temporal enemy is left alive after the slaughter. But since no one is granted such a temporal victory that he no longer needs to fight at all times, it is rightly said: “The Lord did not answer him on that day.”

God’s answer is not only the word of his inmost counsel; it is also grace and gift. When he graciously grants what is devoutly requested, he is said to answer. The Lord therefore does not answer on that day because he permits the elect to conquer, but abandons their enemies as though they were still alive, so that they may find enemies with whom they must always fight.

Yet if this is said because Jonathan’s guilt is concealed, it strikes those in authority with great fear. A son sins, and his father is denied an answer. One person is known to have transgressed, yet because of the guilt of one person all fear to pursue their enemies.

What is signified by this deed except that the sins of subjects harm not only the subjects themselves, but also their superiors and those who live together with them? But because this hidden guilt is investigated by the king, let us now see with what exalted care hidden matters are sought. For it follows:

**(Verses 38–39.)** “Bring here all the corners of the people, and know and see through whom this sin has occurred today. As the Lord lives, the Savior of Israel, if it has been done through Jonathan, he shall die without reconsideration [perhaps ‘without retractation’ should be read here and below].”

48. In these words he demonstrated a very orderly procedure of judgment: first the guilt must be discovered, and afterward the penalty imposed. The order of judgment is confused if the sentence is pronounced before the discovered guilt has been examined.

Therefore, lest he strike before the investigation, he says: “Bring here all the corners of the people, and see and know through whom this sin has occurred today.” And because known guilt must be struck more severely, he swears, saying: “As the Lord lives, if it has been done through Jonathan my son, he shall die without reconsideration.”

The matter should indeed be treated at length so that the guilt may be found; but after it has been found, no one who is guilty should be left alive in it. He is killed “without reconsideration” when he is forbidden to remain in sin as soon as it has become known.

But this “without reconsideration”—that is, to kill without reconsideration—is not itself done without reconsideration, because the shepherd employs much discernment so that the guilt he discovers through investigation may be struck without hesitation and swiftly extinguished.

49. If, according to the historical account, we consider the weight of this paternal oath and look together upon the fervor of that age and the tepidity of our own, we see that the ancient fathers, in order to please God, did not even spare their sons from death. We, however, do not dare to pursue those whom we love according to the flesh even with the slightest harshness of words.

Behold, the man who was raising his son toward kingship says: “If the sin was committed through him, he shall die without reconsideration.” We see people sinning, yet either do not wish or are afraid to rebuke them.

Why do we do this except because we do not love God as they did? For Moses, in order properly to avenge the sin of idolatry, ordered the Levites to kill twenty-three thousand men. In carrying out this slaughter he said: “If anyone belongs to the Lord, let him join me. Let each man put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate, and let each one kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor” (Exod. XXXII, 26–27).

It is as though he said: “Each person will show in this way that he belongs to the Lord, if for love of him he spares neither brother, neighbor, nor friend.”

Saul therefore says of his son: “He shall die without reconsideration,” because for us, who now live under the grace of the Redeemer, even if bodily death is not decreed, the life of sin must not be prolonged. A ruler kills without reconsideration when he does not regard the affection of the flesh, but, upon finding the crime, strikes it swiftly.

He deliberates again who, in order not to wound the wicked person sharply, considers either the services rendered to him or the affection of kinship.

Here it should be noted that not every fault must be struck sharply. Light stains of dust are better removed by shaking them out than by washing them or applying fire. Nor should grave faults always be pursued with equal harshness, because bodily wounds require a strength of medicine proportionate to the nature and strength of the bodies themselves.

Yet ecclesiastical superiors often become more inflamed than is right when they hear of faults; and while measuring out punishment, they regard neither the quality of the wounds nor the strength of the offending persons. They should be tolerated when they threaten, but brought to calm by the good counsel of the devout.

Hence it is added:

**(Verse 39.)** “No one from all the people contradicted him.”

Because the threats of superiors must be endured humbly, it is said: “No one contradicted him.” And because their excess must be restrained by the salutary counsel of the devout, not much later, when the king attempts to inflict the same death upon his son, all the people cry out: “Shall Jonathan die, who brought about this great salvation in Israel?”

Thus the people delivered Jonathan so that he would not die. But because Saul is intent not on striking an undiscovered guilt but on discovering the hidden one, it follows:

**(Verse 40.)** “And he said to all Israel: ‘Separate yourselves into one part, and I and my son Jonathan will be in the other part.’”

50. What does it mean that, at the king’s command, the people are separated from the king and his son, except that, while hidden and suspected guilt is being sought, both superior and inferior persons must be examined?

Often the people sin; often their ruler sins. Sometimes the fault of the subjects themselves is attributed to the superior, because it is said to be fulfilled through his negligence. When, therefore, the indications mentioned above show that guilt is hidden among the people, but it is not known in whom it lies, let the king mingle himself with them, so that the shepherd may discover whether the guilt is his own or the people’s.

King Saul was certainly not conscious of the guilt that he himself had committed neither by consent nor by deed; nevertheless, he joins the investigation so that, if anything is hidden in him as well, it may be found.

He was searching himself, as it were, when he said: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified; it is the Lord who judges me” (I Cor. IV, 4). It is as though he said: “I do not cease to seek and examine myself, because if I am hidden from myself, I will not be hidden from the one to whom all things are naked.”

Let the king, therefore, who was not conscious of the guilt being investigated say: “I and my son Jonathan will be in the other part,” because chosen teachers, when they rage against others through zeal for uprightness, do not spare themselves or their intimates.

They separate the people into one part, as it were, but do not separate themselves, when they investigate the faults of their subjects but do not take care to investigate themselves in order to discover themselves. The sea of human ignorance is indeed vast.

For if we can scarcely, or perhaps never, seek ourselves and discover what we are like, when can we seek others? What does the Prophet lament when he says: “My heart has abandoned me” (Ps. XXXIX, 13)? What does sacred Scripture declare: “A person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Eccl. IX, 2)? Again, the Prophet announces the fruit of his inquiry when he says: “Your servant has found his heart” (II Sam. VII, 27).

If the saints can scarcely find their own hearts, with what audacity do we cease to examine ourselves? But perhaps even the Prophet could not fully do so, because he added: “So that he may fear you.” He would certainly have found his heart if he had completely known whether he was worthy of hatred or love.

The one who did not find it in order to be secure before God did find it in order to fear. But we cannot easily do even this, because, while we neglect to find our sins and weigh them once found, we remain secure as though our heart had been lost.

They are therefore placed in one part and the others in the other, so that the hidden things of each may be considered and the guilt, once found, may be struck with its deserved punishment. Since this is greatly to be praised and not discouraged, it follows:

**(Verse 40.)** “The people answered Saul: ‘Do what is good in your eyes.’”

51. What does it mean that Saul commands the people to separate themselves into one part, while the people ask the king to do what he commands, except that simple people do not know how to investigate themselves, even when ordered to do so?

He says: “Do what is good in your eyes.” It is as though he said: “You can act on our behalf better than we can, for you have received the light of the heart not only for yourself but also for foreseeing our paths.”

But a ruler is praised for inward illumination, which he possesses through grace but not through self-estimation. He is praised because he can recognize the secrets of others, yet he distrusts his ability to know himself.

Because he does not attribute the light of such grace to himself, he does not cease to ask God for it in prayer. Hence it follows:

**(Verse 41.)** “And he said to the Lord God of Israel: ‘Give a sign. Why have you not answered your servant today? If this iniquity is in me or in Jonathan my son, give a manifestation; but if this iniquity is in your people, give holiness.’”

52. We ask that a sign be given when we demand that what is hidden from us be revealed. But we must ask what is meant by such diversity of wording. For himself and his son he asks for a manifestation; if the iniquity is in the people, he asks for holiness.

This can be stated briefly: chosen teachers know their own strength and know the weakness of the people subject to them. For themselves, therefore, they ask only for the manifestation of guilt, because they know that they customarily pursue it with the severity of repentance. For the people, however, they seek holiness, because they desire only to know the faults of their subjects; but those whom they find doing wrong, they ask to reach forgiveness through lamentation.

What does “Give holiness” mean except “Sanctify those whom you reveal”? You disclose their hidden matters to me, but disclosure accomplishes nothing if, by pouring back grace, you do not bring about a change of conduct in those whom you reveal.

But because subjects often stand while superiors fall, it follows:

**(Verse 41.)** “And Jonathan and Saul were taken.”

And because even then it is not easily known by whom the guilt was committed, it follows:

**(Verse 42.)** “And Saul said: ‘Cast lots between me and my son.’ And Jonathan was taken.”

53. Those who cast lots often discover hidden things through indications drawn from visible matters. Thus Jonah is recognized while fleeing (Jon. I); thus Matthias is found worthy of the apostolic dignity (Acts I).

We cast spiritual lots when, through external signs of deeds, we arrive at knowledge of hidden things. The lot of each person is his manner of life. Hence the wicked say in Wisdom: “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let there be no meadow that our wantonness does not pass through; everywhere let us leave signs of joy, for this is our portion, and this is our lot” (Wis. II, 8).

By contrast, the Psalmist prays, saying: “May my portion, O Lord, be in the land of the living” (Ps. CXLI, 6). Paul also declares: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20).

The teacher therefore holds, as it were, the lots of individuals when he observes each person’s manner of life. When the guilt is known but the guilty person is not known, he casts lots, as it were, when he compares the nature of the crime with the character of the negligent person.

Perhaps he also discovers the guilt when, through a certain conjectural sign, he reaches evident knowledge of the crime. A superior is negligent if he does not know both the strength and the weakness of the faithful entrusted to him. He ought to know which virtues suit the strong among his subjects and which vices, through negligence toward their neighbor, afflict the weak.

He ought to know what devotion to virtue stirs these people and what quality of vice disturbs those others. He holds the lots of each in external matters, as it were, when he foresees by which vices some may be overwhelmed and by which virtues others may be exalted.

Once the cause is known, he impresses signs upon them as though by lots when he ascribes the mark of an evident fault to the conduct of the person who previously appeared, through negligence, inclined and close to committing that crime.

But this conjecture should be used to investigate the truth, not as certainty regarding the person discovered, because the text immediately adds:

**(Verse 43.)** “Saul said to Jonathan: ‘Tell me what you have done.’”

54. Why is the one who has been taken questioned except because faults that seem to have been discovered through signs or conjectures must not yet be punished? The wound is already held, as it were, but is still covered. Let it therefore be uncovered so that it can be treated and healed.

He must be compelled or admonished to confess the fault that is already seen, as it were, openly. He says: “Tell me what you have done,” because a crime known through certain evident indications must not be judged before it has been demonstrated with complete clarity.

And because it belongs to the elect both to sin and to repent—to commit faults and to uncover those committed by confessing them—it follows:

**(Verse 43.)** “Jonathan told him and said: ‘While tasting, I tasted a little honey at the tip of the rod that was in my hand; and behold, I am dying.’”

55. What does he mean by saying, “While tasting, I tasted”? Why did he not earlier say, “While tasting, I tasted a little of this honey,” when he said: “You have seen that my eyes were enlightened because I tasted a little of this honey”?

Some people, when they confess their sins, diminish them by certain expressions, showing that they did not commit them with their whole heart. By contrast, when chosen men accuse themselves of small matters, they pronounce them not as small but as great.

What does “While tasting, I tasted” mean except that I outwardly committed the sin and completed it with the great ardor of desire? And what does it mean, after confessing the sin, to say, “I am dying,” except to drive death away from oneself through repentance and confession, and then to fear the death that has been driven away?

This properly belongs to the elect, who abandon their sins and nevertheless fear them as though they had not abandoned them. They erase them through pure confessions and severe torments of repentance, yet fear them intensely as though they had not been erased.

But what does “at the tip of the rod” mean except that, when we pursue ourselves through confession, we must not bring a lie against ourselves? A sin must be disclosed in confession, but it must not be increased by a lie. Confession should correspond to the deed.

Therefore, in order properly to disclose the ardor of desire, he says: “While tasting, I tasted.” And so that its quality may appear, he adds: “At the tip of the rod,” as though he said: “I acted boldly, inflamed with desire—but I did act.”

And because the king’s son is confessing, he says: “Which was in my hand.” Jonathan’s rod signifies the preacher’s teaching and discipline. It is held in the hand when he not only teaches but also practices through his deeds what he teaches.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “Which was,” rather than “Which is in my hand,” except that he conveys the self-estimation of the elect, who, even when they commit wrong, regard themselves as unworthy of the ministry of preaching?

He says: “At the tip of the rod which was in my hand.” It is as though he said: “I sinned by becoming proud of that by which, through sinning, I made myself unworthy.” It was therefore in my hand, and it is not: although at some time I did what I taught, through pride I lost what I held by my conduct.

Now terrified by fear, he says: “Behold, I am dying.” And because this same fear is sometimes placed in the mind by divine inspiration and sometimes by the threat of teachers, it is added:

**(Verse 44.)** “And Saul said: ‘May God do this to me, and add this also: you shall surely die, Jonathan.’”

It follows:

**(Verse 45.)** “And the people said to Saul: ‘Shall Jonathan die, who brought about this great salvation in Israel? This must not be! As the Lord lives, not a hair from his head shall fall to the ground, because he has acted with God today.’ Thus the people delivered Jonathan so that he would not die.”

56. What, then, does he mean by saying, “Will Jonathan indeed die?” except that someone else would die for the same fault? [Note: In other printed copies one reads *quia aliud* (“because it was something else”), which we were unable to retain.] By these words the people clearly show us the great virtue of discernment: in judging the elect, not only the causes of their faults but also the merits of the persons must be weighed. This is plainly demonstrated by the words that follow, since Jonathan is not declared exempt from death because he was the king’s son, but because he had brought about this great deliverance in Israel. Therefore, when great men fall, they should not be handed over to a common judgment, because their earlier deeds deserve that the severity of their later deeds be mitigated.

Yet this mitigation of guilt must not be determined by favoritism toward a person, but with regard to his former life. For the gains of holy Church must be weighed toward his absolution; carnal affection must not be admitted. But why should it seem strange if a sinner’s own merits assist toward his absolution, when we learn from the authority of sacred Scripture [Col. 0393B] that some have been delivered on account of others? Some are helped by the good work of others, just as the Lord says to the sinful king Solomon: “Because you have not kept my commandments, I will tear your kingdom apart and give it to your servant. Nevertheless, I will not do this in your days, for the sake of David your father; rather, I will tear it from the hand of your son” (3 Kings 11:11).

Hence we recognize that not only the deeds of fathers benefit their sons, but also that citizens may be delivered for the sake of their fellow citizens. The Lord promised that he would spare Sodom from destruction if he found only ten righteous people in it (Genesis 18). Jerusalem, too, is said to have been regarded mercifully because some good works were found in it. Hence Eli, righteous in his personal life but negligent [Col. 0393C] in pastoral authority, heard from the man of God: “A great part of your house shall die when it reaches manhood; nevertheless, I will not wholly remove from you a man from my altar” (1 Samuel 2:33). Thus sacred Scripture openly showed both that he was struck for his negligence and that consideration was nevertheless given to his former conduct.

Yet perhaps he could be struck only in part because he had some kind of impurity in his life. Of Jonathan, therefore, it is rightly said: “Will Jonathan indeed die, who brought about this great deliverance in Israel? This is wrong. As the Lord lives, not a hair of his head shall fall to the ground, because today he has worked with God.” As if he were saying: “He who performed great works has fully deserved to be absolved.” Since, therefore, in ecclesiastical judgment there is no favoritism toward persons, but there is discernment concerning merits, the sentence was fittingly concluded with the words: “So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.”

57. At this point it should be noted that earlier the king twice pronounced an oath concerning Jonathan’s death, yet he did not kill him, overcome by the people’s insistence. What does it mean that he swore an oath but in no way kept the assertion of his oath? From this matter two lessons arise for us, namely, that we must be cautious and discerning. We must be cautious lest we swear, and discerning if we have sworn to do something perverse. For whoever avoids swearing altogether cannot possibly perjure himself. But when an evil oath has been sworn, it is more just to abandon the oath than to carry out the crimes to which one has sworn.

Let each person, therefore, be cautious before swearing, so that he either does not swear at all or does not swear that he will do evil. The Lord indicates that we should be cautious when he says: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; no, no. Do not swear by heaven or by earth” (Matthew 5:37). The reprobate, on the other hand, are both incautious and undiscerning. They often promise that they will do evil, yet do not trouble themselves to withdraw their promises, as though they would thereby incur perjury. Hence Herod swore incautiously and fulfilled the wicked oath he had uttered by putting the Lord’s forerunner to death (Mark 6).

We must therefore be cautious in our decisions. But if we neglect to be cautious, our plans must be abandoned, not carried out. For to desist from a plan in this way is not the fault of fickleness but the virtue of discernment. Nevertheless, one must altogether avoid, and greatly dread, swearing to things that ought to be withdrawn and detested, because when such an oath is not fulfilled, guilt is not entirely avoided; rather, the lesser guilt is chosen.

It follows:

**(Verse 46.)** “And Saul withdrew, and did not pursue the Philistines.”

58. When Jonathan’s guilt is discovered, and it is recognized that the king did not fulfill his oath, he is said to cease pursuing the Philistines, because when pastors are cast down by their own weakness, they cannot vigorously seek the gains of others. To cease pursuing the Philistines is to desist for a time from attacking the vices of others through preaching. They judge that they must first attend to their own purification, and then, once purified, keep watch for the salvation of others, because while they are silent they are preparing themselves, so that through their own repentance they may rise again with strength for the gain of others.

And because often, while a teacher conscious of guilt remains silent, evil spirits do not remain silent among certain of his subjects, suggesting impious things to them, it follows:

**(Verse 46.)** “Moreover, the Philistines departed to their own places.”

59. When teachers are silent, demons depart to their own places, because through the silence of pastors they do not perish, except because they were not predestined to eternal life. The places of demons are so called because by divine foreknowledge they were not ordained to be a dwelling place of God. Hence, while the first teachers were preaching, it is said: “All who were predestined to eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48). Hence Paul says: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called” (Romans 8:30). Hence, when the apostles wished to cross into Asia, they were prevented by the Holy Spirit (Acts 16).

Those, therefore, who are not predestined cannot be called into God’s dwelling, whether they hear the teachers’ words or do not hear them. For through the wickedness in which they were foreknown before the foundation of the world, they have prepared a place within themselves for evil spirits.

Thus, when it is said that he ceased [perhaps *cessari*, “to cease”] pursuing the Philistines, it is rightly reported that the demons went to their own places, because sometimes, by God’s dispensation, teachers remain silent so that, while they are silent, those who do not belong to the Lord may be taken back by evil spirits. But, as I have said, when pastors remain silent after their fault, they humble themselves so that, once purified, they may rise powerfully for the ministry of preaching. While they are silent, they weigh their weakness; but by considering themselves, they strengthen themselves more firmly against hidden enemies.

Therefore it is fittingly added:

**(Verse 47.)** “But Saul, having established his kingdom over Israel, fought on every side against his enemies.”

60. The kingdom is indeed weakened when pastors fall into certain faults. But what is weak is strengthened when, through the satisfaction of repentance, they are raised up again for the work of great virtue. He is said to be strengthened over Israel because, while he advances toward the height of life, he surpasses in conduct those over whom he presides by rank. He is set above those who see God, but he is exalted above those who see God when he is taken up above the others into divine contemplation.

Therefore it is rightly said: “He fought against all his enemies” [Note: *superabat* (“he overcame”) is absent in Gilot and the Vatican manuscript], “and wherever he turned, he overcame.” For one who perceives eternal things from a higher position easily crushes whatever comes against him from the depths below. Since nothing earthly now pleases him, he who reigns over Israel—that is, in heavenly things—through great love overcomes wherever he turns. What could the evil spirit suggest to one who considers nothing earthly and no longer loves any worldly delight?

The teacher fights when he preaches, but he overcomes because what he forbids by preaching to be sought from the world’s pleasures, he persuades others to reject through the virtue of his conduct. And because he is said to fight against enemies on every side, his victory is shown to be greatly praiseworthy. He teaches that the teacher is perfect on every side when he has the strongest enemies on every side.

What, then, does it mean that he is said to have enemies all around him, except that evil spirits lie in ambush against all our senses? They deceive some through speech and others through sight. They mislead some through hearing, others through taste or smell. They also strive to draw some through the snares of enticing pleasure or thought into impurity. To others they offer obscene things outwardly, so that they may pursue them by deliberate choice.

To show this surrounding more clearly: when they draw one toward pleasant things, they place their snares, as it were, on his right; when they cast another down through adversity, they bind him, as it were, from the left. When they invite us to past pleasures, they seem to hurl us down from behind. They confront others, as it were, from the front, because they often display to the minds of the weak, seemingly as advice, the strictness and length of the disciplined life. They come from before because they do not allow souls to advance toward heaven.

We therefore have enemies all around us, because we suffer the combat of evil spirits before us, behind us, on our right, and on our left. Hence blessed Peter the apostle exhorts us, saying: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Peter 5:8).

61. We now understand the surrounding of the battle; let us see how kings conquer on every side. They conquer on every side who guard their tongue, mouth, eyes, and all the members of their body from unlawful action. When they fortify their tongue perfectly through silence, they are victorious on one side, as it were; and when they see with their eyes what they disdain to desire, they become victorious on another side.

Often they also hear evil things and reject them; and because they condemn what is harmful, they triumph by condemning it. They are victorious through all their senses because they refuse to be subjected to evil spirits through any one of them. When an inept thought is presented to the heart, the rejected enemy is struck down. For whoever casts away whatever is harmful presses the enemy down with strength.

And because such a person also despises what is pleasant, does not fear adversity, does not return to the perverse things he once abandoned, and runs fervently toward heavenly things, he is shown to overcome the enemies whom he suffers around him. Since the snares set against the five bodily senses are signified by these adversaries, they are appropriately expressed by the number five.

**(Verse 47.)** “Against Moab,” he says, “and the sons of Ammon, and Edom, and the king of Zobah, and the Philistines.”

62. By setting down the names of five nations, he signified the demonic deceptions directed against the five bodily senses. But because a teacher fights not only by living rightly but also by teaching—when he argues against all vices and kills them in the minds of his hearers with the sword of the word—he is plainly seen to fight on every side and to overcome wherever he turns.

Certain enemies are specifically named because they principally oppose him: “Against Moab,” he says, “and the sons of Ammon, Edom, the king of Zobah, and the Philistines.” *Moab* is interpreted as “from the father”; *Ammon*, “a people of sorrow”; *Edom*, “red”; *Zobah*, “burned” or “turning”; *Philistine*, “falling by a cup.” What is signified by these names except the stages of an utterly wicked life? [Note: Gilot and the Vatican text read: “the stages of a most wicked life are expressed.”] In Moab, which is called “from the father,” desire is signified. In a reprobate mind, because it is implanted by the devil, it is generated, as it were, by a father.

What, then, is shown by Ammon, which is interpreted as “a people of sorrow,” except the frequency of evil deeds? Because they are many, it is called a people; and because they lead each reprobate person to the bitterness of eternal mourning, it is rightly called a people of sorrow.

But Edom, which is called “red,” signifies nothing other than an excessive ardor for sin. At first each person becomes accustomed to sinning; then, through the practice of sinning, he advances into an increase of ardor, so that he dares to sin more often and, through daring to repeat it, desires ever more ardently to repeat it. Through this heat of sinning, whatever virtue or good work once flourished in the reprobate mind is burned up.

Thus “burned” is described after Edom in the spiritual battle, because the fall of the lost mind is such that, when it strives fervently to accumulate evil, it is stripped of all good things, as though they had been consumed and reduced to nothing.

Zobah is also called “turning,” because fervent sin both removes the form of God from the reprobate mind and reduces it to the form of the apostate angel. Of this it is now said by divine judgment: “When the wicked comes into the depths of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3). The proud mind despises the divine commandments and subjects itself to carnal desires.

Who, then, is the king of Zobah except the one of whom the Lord says to blessed Job: “He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:2)?

But who are the Philistines, who “fall by a cup,” except those who are drunk with all the evils mentioned above? They forget heavenly things so completely that they seem scarcely, or never, to awaken to them.

Through Moab, therefore, the desire of the flesh is expressed; through Ammon, the frequent practice of evil deeds; through Edom, the burning desire to sin; through Zobah, the devastation and burning up of virtues; through the Philistines, forgetfulness of heavenly things.

When an elect teacher seeks to lead someone out from the midst of so many snares, what a contest of virtue he undertakes! And because, through the labor of teachers, people return from every stage of this destruction to repentance, he is said to overcome wherever he turns. By preaching, he sometimes kills desire in someone’s heart, and sometimes the practice of wicked action. Now he draws away those who had passed into the habit of sinning; now those who, with their virtues burned up and reduced to nothing, served their king, the devil, as though they had been consumed.

And because by preaching he recalls heavenly things, he arouses those who are falling by the cup and have forgotten heavenly things to pursue the spiritual life, and inflames them ardently through love. Therefore it is rightly said:

**(Verse 47.)** “Wherever he turned, he overcame.”

63. Because he draws sinners from every kind of evil into life, he is recognized as triumphing everywhere. The Lord commanded his soldiers and princes to win such triumphs when he said: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). He commands the Gospel to be preached to every creature because he wished every kind of human being to be led to faith, so that, while he displayed the noble triumphs of their kings, he might show them overcoming everywhere.

Hence it is written: “He desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). He desires all people to be saved because from every kind of human being he chooses those whom he draws to the joy of eternal salvation.

But he explains what he does with particular strength, for he says:

**(Verse 48.)** “Having gathered an army, he struck Amalek and rescued Israel from the hand of its devastators.”

64. *Amalek* is interpreted as “a people licking.” What, then, is signified by Amalek except the spirits of fornication? Their licking consists in soothing the mind into sin through the blandishments of the flesh. They seek to lick, as it were, with the touch of the tongue when they touch the mind with subtle suggestions.

Why is it said that he fought against Moab and Ammon, against Edom and the king of Zobah, and conquered them, but is not said to have gathered an army, whereas he gathered an army in order to conquer Amalek? What does gathering an army mean except that, for extinguishing the spirit of fornication, one virtue is not sufficient?

Abstinence from food is indeed exceedingly powerful against this vice, but it does not prevail by itself. It is like a soldier: it can fight, but it cannot conquer, because Amalek is not conquered unless an army is gathered.

Whoever, then, desires to strike down fornication should add to bodily abstinence the virtue of humility. For if the mind disdainfully refuses to submit humbly to God, it does not suppress the desires of the flesh by ruling over them and exercising authority. But it is still necessary to gather more, because the army is small. To the virtue of humility and bodily abstinence, therefore, let a frequent succession of prayers be added.

The affections of a heart intent upon heavenly things are strong soldiers against the battle of the flesh. Now, through the frequent persistence of prayers, it has a battle line; but an army has not merely one battle line, but several. Thus it still does not have a complete army and cannot overcome Amalek.

Does it help such a person that he wears himself down by fasting and is pricked with compunction for a time in prayer, if his mind thinks slippery thoughts and carries within itself fantasies of lust? He cannot prevail in avoiding shameful thoughts if he does not possess honorable thoughts. Since we are always thinking, we must seek good things so that we may not think evil things.

What, then, are all the hosts of good thoughts except countless battle lines of the mind? For while they surround and fortify the mind, they do not permit the most shameful enemies to approach it. And because by thinking we are kindled with desire for great purity, our soldiers are clothed in powerful arms. With these they both drive back the attack of fornication and kill it by reducing it to nothing.

For thoughts cannot find a way to enter the soul that is adorned on every side, like a very strong soldier, with the propriety of good thoughts. Let the soul, then, gather an army if it wishes to destroy Amalek and free from the hand of its devastators the spirit that it sees. Let it take its position amid these forces, so that, surrounded on every side by the examples of the strong elect and by the teachings of Scripture, it leaves no part of itself empty through which the enemy might break in.

Since there are countless examples of the faithful and many teachings of Scripture, the army is great and strong, though it is not difficult to gather. Thus it is rightly said of the king of Israel: “Having gathered an army, he struck Amalek.” For the spirit of fornication is not conquered until the body has been subdued by abstinence, and every shameful impurity of thought has been driven away by filling the mind with good thoughts.

Then the “people licking,” that is, the spirit that soothes by delighting, cannot lick it, because, with the flesh subdued by fasts, the mind fortified by the stronghold of humility, armed with the weapons of prayer, intent upon heavenly teachings, and fortified by examples, it cannot, by consenting, give access to wicked suggestion.

This gathering of an army fittingly belongs to kings, that is, to teachers of the Church, because whoever strives to instruct elect subjects in extinguishing the fury of fornication must gather these many ranks of auxiliaries for them through his word.

65. Israel is also rightly said to have been rescued from the hand of its devastators. “To rescue” means to tear away; and what is torn away is understood to have sent deep roots into the depths. The hand of the devastators is the power of evil spirits. Hence it is also written: “By whatever a person is conquered, by that he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19).

What, then, is inferred except that, when fornicators consent to the desires of the flesh, they are subjected to the power of evil spirits? Since the allure of fornication is deep, when the soul is immersed in it through desire, it is held as though by roots in the depths.

To be rescued from the hand of the devastators, therefore, is for one who lies under the power of demons to be freed from the abyss of fornication. The impulses of fornication are also rightly called “devastators,” because concerning the vice of lust it is said through blessed Job: “It is a fire that consumes unto destruction and eradicates all growth” (Job 31:12).

The spirit of fornication is called a devastator because it leaves no gifts of virtue in the person whom it has invaded. Such a person may possess some good qualities for the labor of ministry, but he cannot possess them for the merit of salvation. The one whose chastity has been lost is therefore said to be devastated, because no other good deeds benefit him for life.

Tender gardens are also said to be devastated. What are the gardens of the heavenly Bridegroom except the hearts of the saints, fortified by watchfulness and flowering with the fragrance of chastity? Since they admit no shameful impulses, they are adorned with the white flower of modesty.

Hence it is said to the bride in the Song of Songs, in praise of the Bridegroom: “You who dwell in the gardens, let me hear your voice” (Song of Songs 8:13). And again: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride” (Song of Songs 4:12). A garden, because it flowers with the virtue of exceptional chastity; enclosed, because it is fortified by continence.

The bride explains what delights the Bridegroom when she says: “My bridegroom is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline” (Song of Songs 2:16). Unclean spirits are therefore devastators because, if they deceive chaste hearts, those deceived hearts lose the tender flowers of so great a virtue.

Those who return from impurity to chastity, therefore, because they escape the dread powers of demons and rise from the depths of perdition, are rightly said to have been rescued from the hand of the devastators.

But let us see what kind of helpers the king who is said to rescue the people has. For it follows:

**(Verse 49.)** “Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Jesui, and Melchisua; the names of his two daughters were Merab, the name of the firstborn, and Michal, the name of the younger.”

66. The sons of Saul, who are born not for an ordinary inheritance but for a kingdom, signify those of whom the Psalmist says to the holy Church: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44:17). We recognize that they are three because by preaching they defend faith in the holy Trinity.

But because the king’s sons are named after Amalek has been struck down, let us refer their number to the merits of virtues. Bodily mortification, vigilance of mind, and purity of intention are three things. Since, therefore, the teachers of the holy Church are strong in restraining the lust of the flesh, wise in guarding the heart, and exalted in lifting the heart’s intention toward heaven, they are said to be the three sons of Saul.

There are also three other things: strength in action, the virtue of charity, and the most abundant grace of preaching. Since the teachers of the holy Church are exalted through great conduct, fervent through great charity, and eloquent through great wisdom of the word, they are appropriately signified by the number three.

Their names certainly correspond to their virtues. Jonathan is said to mean “the gift of the dove”; Jesui, “plain” or “my desire”; Melchisua, “my king is salvation.” Since teachers possess the outstanding gifts of the Holy Spirit, they are rightly called “the gift of the dove.” Since, moreover, they are humble amid sublime gifts, they are called “plain.” Since they ardently request eternal things for the faithful entrusted to them, they are said to be “my desire.”

This expression is understood to belong to their little subjects, while the virtue of so great a name belongs to their prelates. We who still lie small and cold in our negligences do not burn with ardent desires for our heavenly homeland. But what we cannot ardently demand for ourselves, he requests for us [Note: Gilot and the Vatican text read *quia ad illam*, “because toward that [homeland]”] who yearn with great desires for that homeland which he desires us to attain. Therefore, because of the excellence of charity, the king’s son is called not “those who desire” but “desire,” so that the fire of love may be shown to burn especially in the teacher’s mind.

Hence the Psalmist also says of the Lord: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Psalm 103:4). Likewise Daniel is called “a man of desires” (Daniel 9), because he is said to have sought the prosperity of his people with great prayers.

Melchisua is said to mean “my king is salvation.” The preacher is called a king because he possesses the height of rank and the dignity of an eminent way of life. He is likewise called a king because he holds the summit of exaltedness and the force of authority. He is also called salvation, so that it may be understood that the sickness of the people can be driven away through his integrity. The teacher ought rightly to act each day through his life and devout prayer, so that each person subject to him may be able to reach salvation.

The teacher should note again that when he is named by his subjects, he is called not “our king” but “my king.” What, then, does “my king” mean except that he should be so familiar to everyone that each person feels him to belong to him through love? Yet he is called “my king” because a humble and approachable preacher does not regard what makes him eminent as belonging to himself alone, but as something special to each individual, striving to be so graciously common to all that his dignity appears to belong personally to each one.

Moreover, the transmitted reading is *onus verbi* (“burden of the word”), evidently in connection with “my salvation,” by which the diligent care and concern of the preacher are commended. He must attend to everyone together in such a way that he seeks and accomplishes what is proper to each individual. He is called “my salvation” by each person if he takes up the care of each individual who is weak and leads that person to the blessings of eternal salvation.

67. What, then, are Saul’s daughters except the qualities of the elect subject to the preacher? Some serve the pursuits of the active life; others are hidden away in the withdrawal of contemplation. They are called daughters because of their fruitfulness. The former gives birth to an abundance of good works; the latter to a fullness of inward joys.

They are rightly called the king’s daughters because, conceiving from the word of God, they bring forth heavenly fruits. Hence Merab is rightly said to derive from “multitude.” Since the active life is perfected through many good works, it is rightly named from multitude. Or it is called “from multitude” because those who please God through the active life are many. Since fewer in number are those who yearn for heavenly joys through contemplation, he calls those who devote themselves to the active life “many” in comparison with them.

These many are divided according to their ministries. Although they seek one heavenly homeland through good works, they serve through various works of mercy. Some of them advance so far in love of the Creator that they even abandon good works themselves and desire to pass over to the sweetness of the contemplative life and devote themselves to God in it.

Hence Michal is rightly said in our language to mean “from all.” It is “from all” because no one is perfect in contemplation who has not reached the summit of that contemplation from the labor of good work. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

The laborer is called when desire for eternity, expressed in good action, is infused. They approach the one calling them when they come to the rest of the contemplative life. In this way those who labor are refreshed, because they abundantly receive the joys of love from divine contemplation. He himself refreshes those who approach, because he reveals himself to pure minds. Since in his revelation they find many joys of contemplation, they are filled not by another but by him himself, as though with every sweetness of delight.

Michal, therefore, is said to mean “from all,” because no one seeks the secret of the contemplative life who was not previously engaged in some good work. She is called the younger sister not because she is lower in dignity, but because she comes later in time.

If someone wishes, however, to understand the contemplative life through the firstborn daughter and the active life through the younger, then Merab is said to derive from “multitude” because the contemplative life leaves the crowds of the multitude and comes to the rarer number of the perfect in contemplation. It is therefore said to be not “the multitude” but “from the multitude,” so that one may recognize not those with whom it is, but from where it came.

Michal is said to be “from all,” so that the universal life of the holy Church may be signified in the active life. In the active life are also those who later pass into the secrecy of contemplation; but in the withdrawal of contemplation they are not burdened by the concerns of exterior life.

The one, therefore, may be called “from the multitude,” and the other “from all,” because the active life contains everyone, while the contemplative life withdraws from the sight of everyone in order to join itself to heavenly things through the sight of the mind.

Why, then, are they called the daughters of Saul except because [Note: Gilot and the Vatican text read *quia utraque ista*, “because both these”] both ways of life are displayed through the zeal of a good ruler? Those who teach us to do good and devote ourselves to the pursuits of eternal life are generated for us by the one whose instruction is learned in our hearts.

This is plainly established from the works of the active life; but it seems surprising concerning the contemplative life, which is represented by Mary, the sister of Martha, who is described as sitting at the Lord’s feet and listening to his word (Luke 10). The answer is easy: while Mary sits, she signifies the perfect in contemplation. Yet she is rightly called Saul’s daughter Merab, because although she sits at the Lord’s feet and hears and learns from him what she desires, she must first learn how she may sit. Since this is learned through the instruction of a wise and educated teacher, Merab is rightly remembered as Saul’s daughter [OCR: *finam*; evidently *filiam*, “daughter”] (1 Samuel 18).

He promised to give her in marriage to David, but gave him the younger instead, because some love the beauty of the contemplative life but are not permitted to approach its embrace. Since they are needed outwardly for governing faithful flocks, the supreme King orders matters in such a way that they receive the younger Michal and never grasp the elder Merab.

Many, however, receive the elder after the younger, because after devoted works of charity they are admitted to the love of the innermost secret. Jacob illustrates this well: he loved Rachel, but first received Leah, and afterward took Rachel in marriage (Genesis 29).

What does it mean that Jacob was permitted to have both sisters, while David did not reach the chamber of the elder, except that David was a king whereas Jacob was not a king? Whoever undertakes the governance of souls is not permitted by ecclesiastical discipline to abandon the flock he has received and devote himself to the leisure of a withdrawn life.
