Merab is promised to David but never given; only Michal is given, because some, when they undertake the care of souls, think that they can attend to the concerns of others in such a way as to have leisure for themselves through that very concern. Yet they never find the rest they seek in authority. And when they cannot obtain from the Lord the grace of such purity, it happens that they fear as though they had incurred the Lord’s anger.

Thus, as though from an angry king, they lose the firstborn daughter promised to them, because they cannot embrace the love of inward rest which they thought they would possess in their position of authority.

We have said these things briefly by way of digression; now let us return to what we had left aside.

68. Both, therefore, are called Saul’s daughters, but they receive different names because they both differ and agree. They agree because, through love, they strive toward the eternal life they cherish. They also agree because the one performs in some manner the good works through which the other is continually extended.

Since both love the eternal things they see and both desire to reach them through good action, they agree in some way. Yet they differ because one does more, while the other sees more. For Leah is not said to have been blind, but weak-eyed. And although Rachel did not bear as many children, she did not remain altogether barren. Thus, although one life surpasses the other in contemplation or action, the clarity of vision is taken away from neither, nor is the glory of fruitfulness denied to either.

They differ, nevertheless, in seeing and acting: the active life has vision in passing, but action as its aim; the contemplative life has action along the way, but its aim in rest. Hence the evangelist Mark, when he showed the love of the contemplative life under the figure of those three women, rightly said: “They bought spices so that, when they came, they might anoint Jesus” (Mark 16:1).

As if he were saying: “They stood firm in action so that they might be able to run toward contemplation.” To buy spices is, through the labor of good work, to spread everywhere the fragrance of a good reputation. To anoint Jesus in the tomb is, through the mortification of the flesh, to reach the inward richness of devotion. He is anointed in the tomb, as it were, when those who have been buried with him attain most devoutly to the joy of his inward brightness.

Those devoted to the contemplative life, therefore, have work along the way, because although they sometimes act, they leave it behind as though running, driven by a great impulse of the spirit toward the place of their beloved solitude. Since they rest with all their desires in the love of eternal things, they desire to see more than to minister. Thus they are rare in public action but constant in the secrecy of contemplation; outwardly they linger little, inwardly very much. They even tend to judge it fornication to depart, even for a moment, from contemplation of Christ.

69. On the other hand, the active life, which busily devotes itself to frequent service, is rare in the secrecy of contemplation. For since it has resolved to prepare eternal things for itself not by sitting and listening, but by laboring and serving, it considers it not a loss but a deprivation if, attending to itself and seeking its own concerns rather than those of others, it should rest from its accustomed offering of service. It therefore labors more by working and entreats less. Hence Martha, who was busily occupied with frequent service, stood and spoke [Col. 0403B] (Luke 10:40). For she who stood was plainly not permitted to sit, because if she had sat down to listen, she might perhaps have provided an unprepared and inadequate service. It should also be noted that Martha saw the Lord while passing by, but did not speak while passing by; she spoke while standing. For the Evangelist carefully expressed this, saying: “She stood and said” (ibid.).

By this example we are instructed that those who provide services for their brothers, if they cannot sit for a while at the feet of the Redeemer, should nevertheless stand before the Redeemer for a little while. But we stand before him well if, while passing by and serving, we see him. What is it to behold the Lord while passing by, except to direct the intention of our heart toward him in every good work of ours? We pass by when, running here and there, we minister to the Lord in his members. [Col. 0403C] But we behold the Lord while passing by if, in everything we do, we contemplate him as present to us, the one whom we desire to please.

At this point it should be noted that Martha speaks confidently, saying: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me alone to serve?” (Luke 10:40). This certainly suits certain perfect workers in the holy Church, who offer prayers to almighty God with the greater confidence because they remember that they have served him laboriously in his members. Yet because excessive anxiety must be restrained even in those who devote themselves to the active life, Martha is reproved: she is said to be so anxious that she is troubled about many things. The fervor of activity is properly ordered when we devote ourselves to the work in such a way that, with a tranquil heart, we see the one to whom we strive to consecrate our works.

What, then, is excessive anxiety except confusion of heavenly intention? For while the mind divides itself among many things, once divided it no longer rises to contemplate heavenly things. Since the soul scarcely comprehends that eternal and simple good of eternal vision unless it is united, it plainly does not raise itself to it when divided. Therefore the disposer and receiver of our works says: “One thing is necessary”: the mind must not divide itself among many things, so that, united through tranquillity, it may rise powerfully to contemplate the supreme good.

337 Thus the two daughters of Saul, although both are equally the king’s daughters, differ in name, because the active and contemplative lives are both noble through the nobility of religious devotion; yet they are not equal because their functions differ. But since we have shown their father, let us likewise show their mother. It follows:

**(Verse 50.)** “And the name of Saul’s wife was Achinoam, daughter of Achimaas.”

70. For who is the preacher’s wife except good will? Whoever is joined to good will through love, from her—as from a noble wife—sons are born to him. For when we wish to bring forth the fruits of good works, we must first sow them in good will. Hence Achinoam is properly interpreted as “the repose of a brother.” For our brother is the one who, rising from the dead, spoke to Mary Magdalene, saying: “Go and tell my brothers: I am ascending to my Father and your Father” (John 20:17). Therefore Paul, asserting the nobility of the elect, says: “Heirs indeed of God, and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17).

What does “the repose of a brother” mean except that the Redeemer of the human race rests in the good will of his fellow heirs? And because good will is bestowed upon us by the one by whom we are inhabited, she is said to be the daughter of Achimaas. Achimaas is interpreted as “the beauty of a brother” or “a beautiful brother.” Our Redeemer is called both brother and beauty, because human nature lost the strength of its dignity through the sin of the first man, but in the person of the Redeemer it shone with a splendor increased for it.

He is our beauty because all who shine in the holy Church with the radiance of virtues receive everything from the fullness of his light. Hence Paul says: “All the fullness of divinity dwelt in him bodily” (Colossians 2:9). When, therefore, the prophet Samuel beholds the good will of our preachers, he expresses what he sees figuratively, saying: “Achinoam, daughter of Achimaas,” because good will is indeed of great beauty, but is born from the Redeemer’s infusion. It ought to be loved as a wife; but if the father is considered, it is loved still more because of its nobility.

**(Verse 50.)** “And the name of his prince [Note: [Col. 0403D] It seems that *princeps militiae* should be read, as it stands in the sacred text. Nevertheless, it is clear from the exposition of those words in the following number that Gregory read *princeps ejus*: ‘The son of a lamp is called the king’s prince.’] was Abner, son of Ner, his cousin.”

71. Abner means “my father is a lamp”; Ner also means “lamp.” What, then, is Ner understood to be except the word of the Scriptures? The letter of holy Scripture is, as it were, the shell of this lamp; spiritual understanding is the brightness of its light; and its oil is the devotion of love. He therefore is the son of the lamp who willingly hears the words of Scripture, understands them wisely, and embraces through affection of charity what he gathers through understanding.

Why, then, is he called the son of the lamp except because what is born from light is itself light? For what is sin except darkness? And what, likewise, is a good work except light? When holy men direct the steps of their works under the guidance of Scripture, they receive, as it were, light from light through spiritual instruction. Expressing this light from light, John says: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin, because heavenly generation preserves him” (John 5:18). What is it to be born of God except to love his will, once known in the holy Scriptures? And what is it not to sin except always to remain in the light of righteousness?

The blessed apostle Peter wished, as it were, to make us light from light when he said: “You possess the prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Peter 1:19). Rightly, therefore, Abner is called “my father is a lamp,” and his father too is called a lamp, 338 because those can shine through examples for others in the holy Church who have received both the brightness of light through instruction in the Scriptures and the oil of perfect charity.

But through John “not sinning” is mentioned in order to indicate the strength of preachers: they extend a hand to sinners in such a way that they themselves are not stained by the darkness of sins. But why is he called Saul’s cousin? A cousin is one who is born from one’s father’s brother. Hence the text continues:

**(Verse 51.)** “Kish was Saul’s father, and Ner, Abner’s father, was the son of Abiel.”

72. When a king was being sought for election, it was said: “There was a man named Kish, son of Abiel” (1 Samuel 9:1). Since we have explained more fully what these names of the royal lineage signify, let us express here only how Abner is said to be Saul’s cousin. Saul is known as the son of Kish—that is, of “the hard one”; Abner, too, is called the son of the lamp.

What does it mean, then, that “the lamp” and “the hard one” are said to be sons of the same father, except that both what holy Scripture commands austerely and the external virtue of a hard way of life come from God? The brother of the lamp is hard because he receives the grace of fulfilling the law from the one from whom the law itself has its origin. Hence the Psalmist confidently promises, saying: “Indeed, he will give blessing, the one who gave the law” (Psalm 83:7). To give the law is to set forth the precepts of life for the elect; to give blessing is also to bestow the grace of fulfilling the law.

Therefore, because both the light of Scripture and the harshness of our way of life come from one source, Kish and Ner are said to be sons of the same father. Abner, then, son of Ner, is rightly called a cousin of King Saul, because one chosen for the care of souls is judged to be obliged to have a hard and austere life.

But those who desire to be helpers of preachers never accomplish what they desire unless they perfect, as though by being born, in good works and holy preaching, the light of holy Scripture in which they were conceived through knowledge. Yet when knowledge of the holy Scriptures is attributed more to the chief teachers than to their subordinate helpers, and when following examples of conduct appears more suitable to inferiors than to superiors, what is meant by saying that the son of the hard one is king, while the son of the lamp is the king’s prince?

By these words he does not signify what the chief teachers and their helpers possess; rather, suppressing what they possess, he explains what each ought to do. The king—that is, the supreme and chosen preacher—already possesses the light of Scripture through the knowledge of the highest instruction. He must not therefore rely on knowledge in such a way that he fails entirely to follow the examples of others. The prince, that is, the helper of the great teacher, because he is subject to the examples of his superior, must lean upon the light, so that he who follows examples may be born into the higher instruction of doctrine, as it were into the great light of a lamp.

Thus, when one who has been instructed is led back through humility to the examples of his superiors, and one instructed by examples is raised through learning to the splendor of the Scriptures, he is rightly said to be a king, son of the hard one, and a prince, son of the lamp. Since such men usefully preside over the elect faithful and strongly advance their subjects toward victories in virtue, the text continues:

**(Verse 52.)** “There was a powerful war against the Philistines throughout all the days of Saul.”

73. The war of those teachers who possess neither the light of divine knowledge 339 nor the strength of good works is weak and altogether ineffectual. A war is therefore called powerful when the sons of the hard one rule over elect peoples, because the one who is accustomed to precede his words by great works can speak good things usefully to others.

But we must also examine carefully why it is said in a more involved way: “Throughout all the days of Saul.” What are Saul’s days except works of light? What else is the teacher’s warfare than something accomplished by the tongue? He fights throughout all the days who teaches many things to others but brings forth nothing by teaching except what first shines forth in his own work. He fights in his own day who draws the words of preaching from the light of his own virtue. He wishes to fight in another’s day who strives to oppose wicked spirits, not speaking what he does but preaching what he knows.

Yet he fights throughout all the days because he displays all God’s commandments in the light of his works, which, by following them, he wishes to disclose through the ministry of preaching. Rightly, therefore, the war is called powerful when it is fought with the complete light of virtues and works.

It is also possible that the statement that he fights throughout all the days signifies the persistence of spiritual struggle. For one who leads a life full of virtues lives in the days. Thus the powerful war of the elect teacher is recognized throughout all the days, because he is always seen to overcome wicked spirits who is never separated from the light of virtues.

But elect men possess the virtue of fighting, and they also possess the humility of fear. By virtue they triumph, but through fear they do not cease to gather auxiliaries. Thus they fight more strongly insofar as they do not cease to gather forces for combat. Accordingly, the cause of the powerful war is properly added:

**(Verse 52.)** “For whenever Saul saw a strong man and one fit for battle, he joined him to himself.”

74. It is as though he said: He was able to wage war powerfully for this reason: he never ceased to assemble an army. But because he is said to have joined to himself not only strong men but also those fit for battle, the careful teacher is shown in his choice of Christ’s soldiers.

Some are strong for bearing burdens but not for engaging in battles, because, not knowing how to fight from their strength, they are altogether unable to do so. Strong men and fit for battle, therefore, are those who know how to fight and are willing to do so. They are strong through their will and fit for battle through their knowledge. 340

The rashness of some is therefore excluded from Christ’s warfare when the elect are described as both fit and strong. For some know how to fight against the devil but are unwilling. They are “wise to do evil, but do not know how to do good” (Jeremiah 4:22). They wish to serve the ancient enemy and do not wish to resist him.

What would a teacher accomplish if he joined such men to himself as fit for battle? Such men can destroy others more through their examples than he himself can build them up through his word. Often such men even dare to teach, but they do not retain the virtue of teaching through their actions. When they speak with us, they rush against the enemy, but through their works they suddenly turn their weapons against our very vitals.

Like certain traitors within an army, they put on the armor of Christian doctrine and suddenly wound Christ’s little ones by their examples—those whom, by speaking, we had thought they wished to protect. Strong men who are not fit for battle must therefore be rejected, not joined to us, because through wise reprobates our strength is destroyed, not increased.

Who, then, are the strong but unfit, except those whom we see bearing the burdens of the world bravely, yet unable to transfer their strength into the service of the Creator? They bear the yoke of men and the great labors of the world bravely, but they fear to approach the service of God as though they were weak.

What are such men, then, except strong but unfit—men who accomplish great things in the world but cannot do the light and gentle works of Christ? They are often converted in monasteries, and those who had bravely borne the burdens of the world sweat, as though amid great labors, over the small things they undertake.

What, then, is shown by these words except that we should join men to Christ’s army with great discernment, and not grant entry to those who approach before we know them to be fit through knowledge and strong through good will?

Strong men and fit for battle may also be understood as those who pursue the battles against Amalek—that is, against lust. For they are not strong who cannot extinguish carnal desires, nor do those appear fit for battle who are not fit to fight for chastity.

Let the teacher, then, choose Christ’s soldiers; let him choose the strong, so that, while they bravely subdue the flesh, they may powerfully conquer unclean spirits. Let him choose those fit for battle, so that, while they do not grow proud amid the gifts of strength, they may be exalted by the glory of triumph in heaven.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0407]

## 339 CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0407B]

**(1 Samuel 15:1–3.)** “And Samuel said to Saul: ‘The Lord sent me to anoint you king over his people Israel. Now, therefore, hear the voice of the Lord. Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have reviewed all that Amalek did to Israel, how he opposed him on the way when he came up from Egypt. Now, therefore, go and strike Amalek, and destroy all that belongs to him.’”

1. Above we said that Amalek signifies the vice of lust, which “licks,” as it were, when it suggests pleasure by flattering enticement. Progress in one’s way of life is therefore shown by the fact that above Amalek is said to have been struck by Saul, while now he is commanded to be struck not simply, but to be utterly destroyed.

At first the teacher strikes this vice when, through his word, he brings it about that chastity is maintained in the hearts and bodies of converts. Lust is struck, as it were, when the flesh has been subdued to some extent by the weapons of chastity, though it has not been perfectly subdued. For one who has already abandoned the defilements of lust but still feels shameful movements rising up against him from within no longer performs the wicked deed, yet cannot drive it away from his thoughts.

Often, unwilling and unwary, he is drawn toward unclean thoughts; but what he thoughtlessly entertains within arouses the flesh without, so that it rises toward shameful movements of pleasure. What, then, does it mean that Amalek, after being struck, is commanded to be struck again and destroyed, except that the preacher ought to advance those whom he teaches a chaste life toward the perfection of virtue?

Amalek is therefore commanded to be struck again because, not yet properly killed, he remains alive. Amalek is struck again when, through the teacher’s words, even those movements that assault the flesh are beaten down, when the teacher teaches his subjects to be crowned for this purpose: that they should so master the body that it may never rise toward seductive movements.

But because the flesh is never so restrained if the mind slips into unclean thoughts, after striking Amalek it is commanded to destroy him. He is struck in the body and destroyed in the heart, when the flesh is worn down suitably through abstinence and the mind is restrained from all unclean thoughts.

At this point we must also consider the earlier words that Samuel speaks in the person of the Lord, saying: “I have reviewed all that Amalek did to Israel, how he opposed him on the way when he came up from Egypt.”

2. What does it mean that the deeds of the Amalekites are reviewed except that the defilements of lust are exceedingly hateful to God? Hence the blessed apostle Paul says: “Every sin is outside the body, but he who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians 6:17). He also says: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Hebrews 13:4). Rebuking them even more sharply and excluding them from the kingdom of God, he says: “Nor will the unclean possess the kingdom of God” (Ephesians 5:5).

Why is lust reviewed except because the sinner is cast away by God’s justice when he is bent toward committing its defilements? Thus one who is reviewed in order to fall is sometimes reviewed in order to perish, and sometimes reviewed in order to rise. And because, after so many stretches of time, the deeds of Amalek are said to be reviewed, this is suggested to us to some extent: such people sometimes come to their senses after a long time.

His deeds themselves are expressed when it is said: “How he opposed him on the way when he came up from Egypt.” Israel is said to mean “seeing God.” Since Israel is said to come up from Egypt, this signifies recent converts, who abandon the darkness and depths of sins, approach the light of truth, and climb the mountain of good works.

3. Amalek opposed Israel on the way because lust throws up weapons of pleasure against those striving toward the summit of perfection and strikes with the sword of unclean suggestion the hearts it can reach. And because the battle of fornication is exceedingly strong and violent, Amalek is said not merely to have encountered Israel but to have opposed him.

That Israelite, ascending, saw these resisting Amalekites when he said: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind” (Romans 7:23). Hence, looking to his helper, he says: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 7:24).

Amalek is therefore said to resist because, while we are in the flesh, we endure the powerful battles of lust. But why is he said to resist those ascending from Egypt? Behold, the one who had lifted himself to the secrets of the third heaven possessed movements of the flesh that resisted him. Thus Israel ascending from Egypt signifies not only novices but also those endowed with great virtue.

The name Egypt signifies the darkness of this world. Israel ascends from Egypt because all the elect, while progressing through holy living, strive to reach their heavenly homeland. And because, as long as they are in the flesh, they possess the law of the flesh contrary to the law of the mind, they see Amalek resisting them with powerful movements.

The violence of this passion is shown when the battles of Amalek that are reviewed are described. For when Israel fought, Amalek was defeated whenever Moses raised his hands; but Amalek prevailed when Moses lowered them (Exodus 17).

What does it mean that Moses fought against others with weapons alone, but against Amalek not with weapons alone but also with the power of prayer? What strength and persistence of supplication was then necessary, when, if he lowered his hands, he would grant Amalek the honor of victory? Clearly, the great struggle of fornication is shown: it is overcome with such strength and such difficulty.

Prayer of the utmost intensity is therefore necessary as the army’s weapon. Weapons are necessary because those who wish to fight against fornication cannot conquer unless they are fortified by the other virtues. The army, as we showed above, consists of the examples of the Fathers and the precepts of the Scriptures. Everyone ought to consider these and occupy his mind with them in such a way that he does not look upon the defilements of wantonness.

Yet, instructed by examples and teachings, he can in no way trust in himself. Let him therefore raise his hands—let him raise his mind—so that he may shine through good works and devotion, while attempting to cut the battle of lust completely away from himself.

4. What else does it mean that Amalek is defeated when the hands have been lowered except that often, through the audacity of a wicked deed, even the beauty of chastity itself is removed? Often it is not removed altogether [Note: [Col. 0409D] Gilot: “it is lifted up.”], but is weakened when one’s works grow weak.

In the midst of spiritual works and labors we are strong against the goads of the flesh; but if, as though weary, we grow numb or soften from our accustomed strict way of life, the barbs of the flesh rise up as we gradually become negligent, and they defeat Israel as though Moses had lowered his hands (Exodus 17).

Therefore, lest the hands grow weary, let Aaron and Hur place a stone beneath him, sustain Moses’ heavy hands, and never allow them to be lowered. Aaron is called “mountain of strength,” and Hur is called “fire.” For whenever we grow weary, we are strengthened by contemplating heavenly things.

What, then, is the mountain of strength except the height of heavenly contemplation? Since this is certainly not present in an elect heart without great charity, the mountain of strength is rightly said to stand beside Moses. They support the stone and sustain his hands because one who ardently looks upon the highest rewards of heaven receives great strength and does not cease both to do good and to entreat the Creator.

Since, therefore, the battles of the flesh are strong and altogether violent, Amalek is aptly said to have opposed Israel as he ascended. The Prophet therefore commands the king, saying: “Hear the voice of the Lord. I have reviewed all that Amalek did to Israel.”

5. What does he mean by saying, “Hear the voice of the Lord,” except that those who wish to live chastely must watch subtly against the deceits of the spirit of fornication? It is as though he said: Do not cease to consider with how many ambushes it prepares to subjugate the elect.

For this reason he did not say: “I have reviewed how he resisted Israel,” but: “Hear the voice of the Lord. I have reviewed how he resisted Israel.” It is as though he said: If you know the manner of his ambushes, you will be able to overcome the enemy more easily.

He therefore properly adds: “Now, therefore, go and strike Amalek, and destroy all that belongs to him.” It is as though he said: Because you know how you ought to go, “go and destroy all that belongs to him,” and so erase him that nothing further of him may remain alive.

But who has ever been able so to subjugate the flesh, or so to restrain the mind, or so to remain in the flesh that he experienced no shameful movements arising from the flesh? Who has been able so to bridle thought that no darkness of impurity ever reached it through thought?

Yet if the shamefulness of movement cannot be removed from the flesh, the strength of the shamefulness is nevertheless weakened when a simple movement exists in the flesh but no itch of lust exists within the movement. This movement is not Amalekite, because it does not “lick” the mind, which it cannot delight.

What the mind does not see as unclean in some manner cannot be removed from it; but what it sees as unclean is led into the astonishing practice of purity, so that, seeing unclean things, it is not stained by any blemish of delight.

Whoever, then, governs the flesh in this way, whoever rules the mind in this way, governs and rules it because he has been able to destroy all that belongs to Amalek with strength. But he now explains one by one what “all that belongs to him” means:

**(Verse 3.)** 343 “Do not spare him, and do not covet anything that belongs to him; but kill man and woman, child and infant, ox and ass, sheep and camel.”

6. Who is it who spares Amalek except one who retains something of wantonness either in thought, speech, or the flesh? For many do not perform shameful deeds but do not restrain their tongue from shameful speech. Many avoid lust in their actions but do not avoid it in thought. Some do nothing shameful, but in their hearts they covet what they avoid in action.

He therefore spares Amalek who retains the allurements of wantonness either in speech, intention, or thought. Thus it says: “Do not spare him,” because nothing from so wicked a vice ought to be kindled in the mind, and nothing ought to be permitted to burn in one’s actions.

Let it say, then, “Do not spare him,” so that all lustful movements and all obscene speech may be utterly killed in the body. It says: “Do not covet anything that belongs to him,” so that it may be completely uprooted from thought.

For what is lust except fire? And what are the virtues arising from flesh and mind except flowers? What, likewise, are shameful thoughts except straw? Who does not know that if fire in straw is extinguished carelessly, all the straw is kindled from the small spark that remains?

Therefore, one who does not wish to burn up the flowers of virtue in the mind must extinguish the fire of lust in such a way that it can never burn again through a tiny spark. Let him also remove the straws of carnal thoughts, lest, when natural heat—which cannot be extinguished—is kindled, the green growths of virtue—which cannot be kindled by themselves—be burned as though by straw mixed with them.

7. What, then, does “Do not spare him, and do not covet anything that belongs to him” mean except that all lust must be perfectly subdued in the flesh and uprooted from the mind? It can also be understood as follows: “Do not spare him, and do not covet anything from him,” because men and women, children and infants, are commanded to be killed. Women could be objects of desire, while children and infants could arouse pity.

Who, then, are the men to be killed, and who the women, the children, the oxen, the sheep, the camels, and the asses? This must be considered carefully.

For who are the male Amalekites except movements suggesting shameful things? They are men because they make violent suggestions and pour seeds of depravity into corrupted minds. Women are the desires of the mind, which are laid beneath the aforementioned movements for the production of wicked offspring.

But who are the children and infants except those generated by the mingling of the male and female Amalekites? For if a movement of evil suggestion is received into the mind like an adulterer, desire is impregnated like a prostitute.

Thus, if desire is allowed to bring forth a wicked offspring, movements of lust are generated not only in the mind but also in the flesh. When they are born, they are children because they do not yet inflict violence upon the flesh by moving it. They are infants when they are nourished by a slight and negligent thought.

For one who already refreshes shameful movements in the flesh by free and deliberate thought supplies not milk to infants but food to adults. The milk of the infant Amalekites is therefore a slight thought of impurity: if a shameful movement is not fed through thought, the infants are killed as though milk had been denied them.

The prostitute mother supplies this milk, because when the heat of desire anticipates the mind, it is stirred up, as it were, from the worst abundance of the heart, so that worse offspring of movements may be nourished in the flesh.

What, then, is understood by the ox except a fraudulent counsel that suggests carnal pleasure by the example of the ancients, who pleased almighty God amid the works of the flesh? For it appears, as it were, to cleave the earth with the plowshare of discernment; but if it is accepted after deliberation, it entangles the neck of the wretched mind in the yoke of shamefulness, which it carries under the guise of pretense.

8. By the name “sheep,” however, the life of the innocent is signified. Hence all the elect are called sheep by the voice of our Redeemer when he says: “My sheep hear my voice” (John 10:27).

What, then, is the sheep of Amalek except a pretense of innocence? For some, while considering the very form of the human body and the distinct characteristics of each sex, and while contemplating the innate lust in the members, think that they may licitly use it as a natural good.

Thus it is like an Amalekite sheep when something is suggested to the continent as good that is clearly proved not truly to be good.

What, moreover, is signified by the camel? A camel chews the cud but does not at all divide its hoof. What, then, is signified by the camel except a certain thought of lust that seems to begin from reason but is not brought to completion through discernment?

For while it thinks, the camel, as it were, chews the cud inwardly; but while what it thinks is not ordered according to truth, its hoof is not seen to be divided.

Some who profess continence, when they are overcome by carnal desire, trust that they can be saved in married life. Others, when they hear the apostle’s permission—“Let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband” (1 Corinthians 7:2)—admit without distinction of persons that all are included in this precept and that men in sacred orders may use marital intercourse.

This kind of understanding is the Amalekite camel: it seems to begin from reason but leads to an irrational life.

What, then, is the ass except open wickedness in fornication? The devil drives some into the open chaos of fornication, while he deceives others through fraud. The ass is also accustomed to carry another’s burdens.

When the teacher of the nations taught that a man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman does, and likewise: “Nor does the woman have authority over her own body, but the man” (ibid., 4), what else did he command them than to carry one another’s burdens?

By the name “ass,” therefore, the strength of marital union is signified, because elect spouses bravely bear one another’s burdens [Note: [Col. 0411D] Gilot. and Vaticanus: “so that”], lest through the weakness of the flesh they fall too readily into the pit of fornication.

The Amalekite ass must therefore be killed, because marital union is to be strengthened in the honor of the marriage chamber, but killed with respect to shamefulness. Spouses ought indeed to render the marital debt to one another, but they ought not to come together shamefully.

The Amalekite ass is killed when, in good spouses, charity maintains honorable union while every obscenity is avoided in an improper joining.

Everything belonging to Amalek is therefore commanded to be destroyed, because those who propose to live chastely ought not to retain anything of the flesh’s allure within themselves. They ought to be in the flesh so that they may do good through the flesh, but they ought to depart from the flesh’s pleasure through the elevation of the mind in such a way that they do not suffer insults from the flesh.

He wished them to be such when the Apostle spoke to them, saying: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Romans 8:9).

But since Amalek is commanded to be destroyed, let us consider with whose assistance this can be accomplished. For the text continues:

**(Verse 4.)** “Saul commanded the people and counted them as lambs.”

9. Men of great prudence are commonly signified by the name “lambs.” Hence John says: “I saw a Lamb standing upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred forty-four thousand who had his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads” (Revelation 14:1).

Those who had assumed the name of the Lamb were called lambs. Explaining them further, he says: “These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins.”

What, then, does it mean that, when Amalek is commanded to be destroyed, the king’s soldiers are counted as lambs, except that when we wish through preaching to destroy the spirit of fornication, we must bring forward the examples of the perfect?

All those whom we display to worldly converts as distinguished by the glory of chastity, like so many soldiers counted as lambs, we bring into the battle against Amalek.

The ministers of divine preaching themselves may also be understood by the name of those who were counted. They are like lambs because, through the glory of perfect chastity, they are already made like those virgins who rejoice with Christ in the kingdom.

These words clearly show that those who undertake the ministry of preaching must first be adorned with the exceptional splendor of chastity. For if they fall through lack of self-restraint, they can never make others continent, nor can they summon others to the good of such great light if they do not possess its rays in the splendor of their own conduct.

The statement is therefore fitting: “He counted them as lambs,” because those who, by the authority of the office they have received, must drive away the spirit of fornication ought to be exceedingly chaste.

Hence in the Gospel the Lord says to them: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35), so that their subjects may hear the word of preaching, but the brightest examples of their way of life may draw them toward the good of chastity that they hear.

Accordingly, they are properly designated by a perfect number, when it is added:

**(Verse 3.)** “Two hundred thousand foot soldiers, and ten thousand men of Judah.”

10. By the name “foot soldiers” the elect are represented—not when they preach lofty things, but when by good examples they show others the straightness of the heavenly journey. Foot soldiers run with their feet to the place where they wish to bring their weapons. What, then, are examples of chastity except the footprints of heavenly soldiers impressed upon the earth? For, in order to strike the vices of lust in their slippery places, they hasten toward the darkness of hearts with the light of good examples; and, arriving as if by their stride, they slay the enemies who, once recognized through their deeds, draw the hearts of sinners toward the good of chastity. Therefore, when by examples of chastity they destroy the darkness of impurity in sinners’ hearts, they are rightly called foot soldiers.

And because they shine not only by the outward appearance of bodily purity but also by the light of the heart, they are said to number two hundred thousand. For in the number one hundred and in the number one thousand the whole sum of the Decalogue is contained. Perfect men, therefore, are included in the two hundred thousand, because by divine grace they have reached the summit of chastity through both bodily continence and integrity of mind. For they possess perfection of purpose both in body and in mind. Or, because they serve God through chastity neither sluggishly nor negligently, they possess the hundredfold of work; and because they do not cease to serve him, they possess the thousandfold of multiplication. They are strong and constant in bodily continence, and perfect and diligent in guarding the heart through the perfection of virtue.

The Apostle likewise commands that a widow be such, saying: “That she may be holy both in flesh and in spirit” (1 Cor. 7:34). She is holy in flesh and spirit if, by the perfection of chastity with which she shines in body, she also shines in mind. But if widows are such, what must virgins be, since they are commanded to be such? Concerning the many, indeed, it is said under the description of one: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold” (Ps. 44:10).

346 In the same psalm (v. 14) this queen is likewise praised when it says: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; she is clothed round about with golden fringes and varied adornments.” For what is the golden garment except the beauty and honor of the virginal body? It is called a garment because it shines outwardly in the body, but golden because it surpasses in dignity. Every kind of metal is inferior to gold. In the same way, no other chastity can be compared with the beauty of virginity.

What, then, does it mean when it says, “All the glory of the kings’ daughter is within,” if the glory of the golden garment is proclaimed to be outward? If some great glory of the golden garment is outward, all glory cannot be seen to be within. What, then, does it mean that all glory is said to be within, except that the glory which is outward is also recognized, together with countless others, as being within? For virginity is not golden if it is outward but not inward. Since it is both inward and outward—since the same quality shines in the body and gleams in the mind—it can appropriately be understood that all the glory of the kings’ daughter is within. All glory is within because it is not outward alone, nor inward alone. Since there are many splendors of virtues in the virgin’s mind, the radiance of virginity is asserted in such a way that all glory is proclaimed to be within.

This is precisely what follows: “She is clothed round about with golden fringes and varied adornments.” For the golden fringes are splendors that never depart from the mind. Fringes are the final parts of a garment. They are praised in the beauty of Christ’s bride for this reason: there is no glory of virtue if it ceases to shine before the completion of life. Thus the queen is called “beloved” [Note: [Col. 0413D] Gussanv. and Vatic. read *amor*, “love”]; in the golden garment, virginity is praised. But all glory is asserted to be within, in golden fringes, and clothed round about with variety, so that integrity joined to countless virtues may be understood to be carried through to the end.

Therefore, two hundred thousand foot soldiers are rightly counted against Amalek, because those are fit to defeat unclean spirits by examples of chastity who have learned to preserve chastity both in the light of their conduct and in the splendor of their vigilance.

11. Likewise, because they are learned and perfect in the word of God, they are represented by the number ten thousand men of Judah. They are “men” because of their strength, but “Judah” because of their preaching. For *Judah* is interpreted as “confessing.” They are designated by the number ten because through the grace of the Holy Spirit they have attained the perfection of doctrine. Hence Moses too was given the ten precepts of the Law, which were written by the finger of God (Exod. 31). For what is the finger of God except the Holy Spirit? When he wrote the Law, he issued it in ten precepts, because although he brought forth something carnal in it outwardly, inwardly he signified the perfection of spiritual understanding.

Therefore ten thousand men of Judah are to be led out against Amalek, so that the spirit of fornication may be overcome by suitable strength. It licks by suggestion, because it gives smooth and flattering advice; but the things which it recommends by licking it displays through the phantasms of thoughts. Therefore, so that the mind may not see the obscene things shown to it by demons, the examples of the elect must be revealed. And so that the unclean spirit may not be able to charm it with shameful suggestions, the tongue of preachers must touch it through praise of chastity. Let the preacher lick it, so that the evil spirit may in no way be able to lick it. Let him delight it with words, so that where heavenly things are lacking the devil may not tear it apart through the pleasures of his suggestions.

Against this double warfare of the heart, therefore, because a double good of assistance is necessary, both foot soldiers and men of Judah are rightly said to be prepared against Amalek. If, however, some wish the foot soldiers to signify one group and the men of Judah another, the meaning of the truth is plainly evident: the highest teachers have people who cannot teach by preaching but can nevertheless be of benefit by their conduct.

But let us now hear by what art those who have been counted for such great battles subsequently fight. It follows:

> (Verse 5.) And when Saul had come as far as the city of Amalek, he laid an ambush at the torrent.

[Col. 0415C]

12. What torrent is this except the one of which the Psalmist says: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way” (Ps. 109:7)? The torrent signifies the course of our mortality. Saul, therefore, lays an ambush at the torrent when a preacher of the Church inserts consideration of our mortality into the subject of eternal rewards. For, in order to catch slippery souls as if by deception, he begins by speaking of heavenly things, but suddenly turns to expound the bitterness of eternal punishments, so that minds secure in the delight of the flesh may be frightened. He draws them out, as it were, by deception, and strikes them by ambush: while speaking of joys he invites them to listen, and introduces the sorrows of death [Note: [Col. 0415D] Gilot. and Vatic. read “the sorrow of death”], so that the pleasure-seekers may hear what they will fear.

Saul, then, comes to the city of Amalek when the teacher attracts hearts fortified by illicit love with the sweetness of eternal joy. But he conceals an ambush for it at the torrent, because he introduces consideration of death, so that the sinner may see a soldier bursting forth against him as if from an ambush; and, while he considers that he will soon die, may fear to prolong his sin any further.

It follows:

> (Verse 6.) Saul said to the Kenite: “Depart from Amalek, lest I perhaps involve you with him. For you showed mercy to all the children of Israel when they came up from Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0416D] Gilot. reads “when he came up from Egypt.”]

13. Who is the Kenite, who is known to dwell with Amalek and is compelled to depart lest he be involved with him as well? Perhaps he is the one of whom the Apostle says: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Cor. 7:3). His name too is appropriate, since *Kenite* is said to mean “possessing.” Married people, because they are bound by marriage, are not compelled to leave everything.

What, then, does it mean that the Kenite is told, “Depart from Amalek,” except that by these words every disgrace of impurity is condemned in married people? They are joined to Amalek who unite in the manner of prostitutes. The teacher commands them to depart from Amalek when he strives to recall them to honorable marriage. It is as though he said: “If you cannot abstain from one another, let your marriage be honorable and your marriage bed undefiled.” To depart from Amalek, therefore, is for married people to use one another not for the disgrace of prostitution’s obscenity, but for the moderation of honor and for the fruit of offspring.

Hence the same excellent teacher says of a widow who cannot remain as she is according to his advice: “But if she does not contain herself, let her marry, only in the Lord” (ibid., 9)—not in Amalek, but in the Lord—so that she who cannot abstain from marriage may avoid obscene behavior within the marital covenant.

He also threatens her, saying: “Lest I involve you with him.” To be involved with sinners is to be condemned to eternal punishment. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says of the wicked servant: “Bind his feet and hands, and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 22:13). At present, therefore, preachers do not involve reprobate hearers, because although they despise the word, they can still, while they live, return to repentance whenever they wish.

Marital honor must therefore be insistently enjoined upon married people, since it is said with a severe penalty: “Go away; depart without injury. Depart from Amalek, lest I involve you with him.” One departs without injury now, but not then, because those who resemble the immoral in every respect will not escape their injury.

The Kenite is also said to have shown mercy to the children of Israel when they came up from Egypt, because the weak children of the holy Church, when they cannot preserve the good of perpetual continence, are received through the mercy of marriage. They come up from Egypt because they abandon the darkness of luxury and fornication. They receive mercy from the Kenite because they obtain the indulgence of marriage. Hence the teacher of the nations says: “I say this according to indulgence, not according to command” (1 Cor. 7:6).

And because the holy Church persuades its elect subjects of the good things which it presents by speaking, it follows:

> (Verse 6.) And the Kenite departed from the midst of Amalek.

14. The husband departs from the midst of Amalek, but he cannot depart from its portion, because although he avoids immoral behavior, he cannot avoid the affection of pleasure. Married people can moderate the fire through honor. They therefore come out from the midst of Amalek because, although they cannot be entirely free from carnal desires, they nevertheless restrain the dominion of the flesh itself under the bond of the commandment of honor.

It follows:

> (Verse 7.) And Saul struck Amalek from Havilah until he came to Shur, which is opposite Egypt.

15. Havilah is interpreted as “giving birth,” Shur as “distress,” and Egypt as “darkness.” Desire gives birth to sin. Therefore desire is appropriately represented by the name of one giving birth. The prophet too, fearing to fall into the distress of an impenitent heart, pleads, saying: “Let not the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. 68:16).

The teacher therefore strikes Amalek from Havilah to Shur when he suppresses in the hearts of his hearers the vices of conceived pleasure and the firmness of their resolve. He also strikes Shur when he appears to draw those minds toward the love of chastity which had resolved to end their lives in the stench of luxury. Those who have already been caught and confined by the snare of evil habit are in distress.

It should also be noted that Shur is shown to be opposite Egypt, because the person who has resolved to end life in luxury is now shut within inner darkness, from which he will be led into outer darkness.

But let this book also be brought to a close, so that in silence we may proceed to the consideration that follows [Note: [Col. 0417D] Perhaps this fifth book ends here and the sixth begins; accordingly, the preceding chapter would belong to the fifth book. Nevertheless, we cannot depart from the common division of all editors, since no manuscripts are available to guide us.]

## CHAPTER II

1. King Saul, who had good beginnings but did not at all persevere in the good things he had begun, is displayed through the text of Sacred History so that in him we may see what is to be imitated and what avoided. In the same way we harvest poorly cultivated crops, which rise up for the harvest with thorns mixed among them. He knows how to gather them well who takes care to pluck the ears while striving to avoid the thorns. Likewise, when the care of a garden is neglected, the vetch that wounds grows together with the nourishing herb.

The Lord was, as it were, warning his disciples to enter cultivated fields cautiously when he said: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses. Whatever they tell you, do; but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:2–3). It is as though he said: “Because the deeds and words of the reprobate are mixed together, they must be used in such a way that what gives life is taken from them, while what kills is avoided.”

Again, foretelling this, he says: “They will come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7:15). Thus far we have willingly observed King Saul diligently administering the affairs of the kingdom; now let us carefully examine the contempt for the Lord’s command in him, so that we may see what must be avoided and rejected. For it follows:

> (Verses 8–9.) He seized Agag, king of Amalek, alive, but he killed all the common people with the edge of the sword. And Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best flocks of sheep and herds of cattle, and garments, and rams, and everything that was beautiful; nor did they wish to destroy them. But whatever was vile and rejected, that they destroyed.

2. The word of the Lord had been: “Now go and strike Amalek, and destroy all that belongs to him. Do not spare him” [Note: [Col. 0418D] Gilot. and Vatic. read “do not spare them”], “and do not desire anything of his possessions.” Clearly, then, he proved himself a transgressor through disobedience, because in his pride he refused to fulfill the Lord’s command. The Lord had commanded the prophet, saying: “Do not spare him, and do not desire anything of his possessions.” But Saul is shown both to have spared him and to have desired all his choicest things. Thus, while the extent of the transgression is revealed, the detestable character of the sin of disobedience is demonstrated.

3. But if we describe the battles of the flesh, we find that royal falls are great. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “If the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted?” (Matt. 5:13). The kings of the Church are its preachers, as has already been shown above. Who, then, is Agag, king of Amalek, except the carnal sense? For since we possess rationality and sensuality from the soul, rationality is attributed to the mind and sensuality to the flesh; through the former we are like the angels, through the latter like brute animals. Through the former, the higher we rise, the nearer we approach the citizens above. Through the latter, the further we slide toward the blandishments of the flesh, the more carnal, so to speak, we are found to be.

Hence, after the daughters of men had been seen and desired, and after the pleasures of luxury had been fulfilled, the Lord threatens those who had been called sons of God because of the merit of their purity, saying in Genesis: “My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh” (Gen. 6:3). A human being becomes flesh when reason is subjected to the sense of the flesh.

The king of Amalek, therefore, is the power of the carnal sense, which commands shameful impulses so as to draw captive reason toward the allurements of obscenity. The name of the Amalekite king suits the carnal sense well. For Agag is interpreted as “meditating” or “speaking.” To meditate, for it, is to gather images of lust through inward meditation. To speak, for it, is to arouse the flesh to lust through shameful impulses. It has, as it were, a great cry of speech because, by striking the flesh, it stirs it more ardently.

It gathers by meditation what it may disclose by speaking, because the more freely one subject to the carnal sense sees images of lust within, the stronger the movements of shame he feels outwardly. It therefore meditates through an inward vision of obscenity, but speaks through an outward movement of pleasure.

The king of Amalek is thus called “speaking and meditating,” because he is able to arouse the fleeting blandishments of the flesh in those whom he deceives through shameful thoughts and whom he instructs through the experience of alluring movement. But it should be noted that the more freely he meditates, the more freely he speaks, because he stirs the flesh more powerfully the more firmly he holds inwardly, through thought, the causes of its agitation. For, as with fire, the more intensely it is blown upon, the more it is kindled: if the breath of impure thought is absent, the heat of lustful movement cannot be present.

The king of Israel fights against the king of Amalek when the teacher of the Church argues against fornication. He captures him when he receives converted sinners into pardon—not only as penitents but also as confessors. Thus he holds the king of Amalek already bound when he sees the carnal sense, in converted sinners, already subjected to reason through the love of chastity.

But what does it mean that he lives while bound, except that there are some who are not moved by their own passions but are moved when they hear the obscenities of others? They are strong while fighting, but fall after victory. For whoever preserved the conquered king alive plainly shows that, in the triumph of the same battle, the person of the captured king pleased him.

4. What else do those do who receive the confession of sins from others? While they consider what the confessors have done, they burn with desire for the crimes they hear about. Often, while they hear the allurements with which others had overwhelmed themselves, they themselves begin to love what those others confess while dying to it at their exhortation.

Agag, therefore, has been conquered and captured in their own city, but is preserved by the victor, when what is detested by subjects is loved by their leaders: for the carnal sense begins to flourish in those who have lost its power of wicked domination in the others.

And because when shepherds run toward the precipice, their subjects accompany them, the king is said to have captured Agag alive, but the same king, the people, and all the best things of Amalek are remembered to have been spared by that king. To spare is an affection of the mind, expressing love for the one whom it spares. This certainly suits the vice of lust, because as it begins to please, it draws the mind into love of itself. Since its power is also vehement, it does not know how to remain stable; indeed, it quickly accomplishes its purpose if the waking mind does not quickly drive it away.

For when lust invades the mind, it spreads itself through innumerable thoughts of obscenity. Hence Saul and the people are rightly remembered to have spared the best flocks and herds. Thoughts of lust are called flocks and herds because they are innumerable and feed upon contemplation of impurity in the reprobate heart.

They are called “best” not because goodness has tested them, but because the one who chooses them desires them. In the reprobate heart, since nothing is loved more dearly, they are called the best flocks, because nothing else is compared with them. They are called “best” because of the blindness of the heart, but “herds” because of the guilt of transgression.

For reprobate minds do not consider it a great matter to think impure thoughts; but before God it is not a small thing to store impurity in the temple of God, that is, in the regenerated spirit. He therefore spares not only sheep but also herds: whoever, through love of lust, regards impurities as though they were small faults, spares what seem to be small things for the moment, but finds that the deserved punishments are not small.

The name “sheep” may be understood as signifying lighter thoughts of luxury, and “herds” as stronger and more troublesome ones. The king and the people spare these when the reprobate teacher and his subjects are subjected to the vexations of impure thought, whether light or strong.

What, moreover, does it mean to spare garments except to deliberate impurity in a mind already condemned? If the golden garment is the glory of the virginal bride, what are the garments of Amalek except the foul pollutions of luxury? They are called garments because through their covering both soul and body are defiled. Since the perpetration of luxury defiles both soul and body, they are called not one garment but garments.

But, as I said, to spare them is to deliberate—to love impurity through the mind’s affection. The unhappy soul, captured and ensnared in this way, because it is driven by strange impulses to perpetrate the evil it has resolved upon, is rightly remembered to have spared the rams after the sheep, herds, and garments. 351 For the horns of rams seem pleasing to it for the gentle blows of lust, when it strives to retain in itself that one thing by which it may be pierced to the death of impurity. Therefore, he spares the rams who gladly receives the blows of his own precipitousness. He is pricked so that he may serve the desires of his flesh, but what pricks him strongly delights him gently.

Likewise, because lust entices the mind toward obscenity in countless ways, they are remembered to have spared not only the things named but everything that was beautiful [Note: [Col. 0419D] Vatic. and Guss. read *illicite*, “illicitly,” in error]. Everything that the impure soul is seen gladly to imagine from the pleasure of luxury is called beautiful by Amalek. It could not desire these things at all if their appearance did not please it exceedingly [Note: [Col. 0420D] Guss. and Vatic. corruptly read *gratantem*, “one who rejoices”].

5. But because the fall of the victors is asserted, it is said: “Nor did they wish to destroy them.” It is as though he said: “They could have destroyed them if they had wished.” For nothing is easier than to overcome lust, if every impure thought is avoided. It can therefore be destroyed more easily in proportion as each person is able to think of something other than the pleasures of the flesh. Because we cannot imagine two things simultaneously, while we think of whatever else it may be, we cannot think impure thoughts.

The swift and easy victory over lust is therefore vigilance in thought: whenever carnal things appear, let us turn to something entirely unrelated to the blandishment of lust. This I would call easy for those who are standing, but not easy for those who have fallen. For one who becomes the slave of the unclean spirit through the perpetration of sin can neither freely avoid thoughts of the flesh nor quickly turn to other thoughts.

Thus it is said of the victors, “They did not wish to destroy them,” although they could have done so, because before the fall sins are easily avoided by those who are free; but if they do not wish to avoid them when they can, afterward they cannot avoid them even when they wish, because they cannot wish perfectly.

To such people the Truth himself says: “If the Son makes you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36). It is as though he said: “Because you voluntarily ceased to be free, you no longer possess within yourselves the power to obtain freedom.”

What, moreover, does it mean when it says, “Whatever was vile and rejected, that they destroyed,” except that some, through their use of greater pleasures, disdain lesser ones? What is rejected and vile to them is what they despise because they have chosen what pleases them more. Since they seek more refined sins, they reject certain others; and because they approve more valuable sins, they consider lesser ones cheap.

It is therefore rightly said: “Whatever was vile and rejected, that they destroyed,” because they choose more refined sins and reject as useless, despising as vile, those which please them less.

6. All these things, understood morally, signify the battles and victories of lust; but in their historical sense they signify the swelling pride of the arrogant and disobedient. Saul had been commanded by the Lord to destroy Amalek in such a way that he spared none of them and desired nothing. Since he is said both to have spared the king of Amalek and to have spared all the best things, he is plainly shown to have been proud and disobedient.

Perhaps he despised the command because he heard it from the prophet, not from the Lord. Yet he ought to have listened to the prophet in such a way as to heed the authority that the prophet had announced beforehand. Before commanding him to strike the king of Amalek, the prophet began by saying: “Thus says the Lord,” so that the king would not dare to despise as merely human the command he heard through a human being.

And lest the elevated king again disparage his ministry, he likewise prefaced his words by saying: “The Lord sent me to anoint you king.” It is as though he said: “The Lord commands you to exercise royal authority through the one through whom he raised you to royal dignity.” Saul ought therefore to have obeyed with all the greater humility the more clearly he recognized that this man had been sent by God. But when he despised the prophet who had been sent, he likewise despised the Lord who had sent him.

Hence it follows:

> (Verses 10–11.) The word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying: “It repents me that I made Saul king, because he has abandoned me and has not fulfilled my words in deed.”

7. Saul thought that he was not listening to the prophet’s words, but the Lord complains that he has been abandoned, showing that his words were not fulfilled in deed. Now the Lord speaks to the Church, saying: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

Those who through disobedience depart from the word of preachers therefore abandon the Lord, because they withdraw from those through whose ministry they are brought into the presence of the divine will. They do not fulfill the Lord’s words in deed because human beings speak outwardly, while inwardly God speaks in human beings. “For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 10:20).

The outward lowliness of the flesh of preachers must not therefore be despised, since the sublimity of divinity dwells so graciously in their minds.

What, then, does it mean that the Lord is said to repent, when he is not believed to change in his affections? Since supreme unchangeableness speaks with changeable beings, he is said to repent in the manner of those with whom he speaks; and by this the displeasure of the arrogant is signified. We customarily repent when those to whom we remember having given honors or gifts repay us with evils.

Because, therefore, almighty God complains of the ungratefulness of the proud king in our manner of speaking, he is said to repent that he had conferred royal dignity upon him. This is said of the proud as the culmination of great condemnation: their very being is now not for merit but for punishment, because they are not in the will of God.

The repentance of God, therefore, is his not having the reprobate in his will, although he remembers that he bestowed honors upon them; it is his recognition that those to whom he granted good things misuse the good things he granted. Through the prophet Malachi, God intimates this repentance of his in other words to the Jews, saying: “I have no pleasure in you, and I will not accept an offering from your hand” (Mal. 1:10).

We therefore see how carefully the fault of disobedience must be avoided if we attend to how sternly it is struck by these words of the Lord.

8. We have described the battle of fornication in the war against Amalek, which we are commanded to destroy completely through the sacred Scriptures. Therefore, this statement of the Lord’s complaint can rightly be understood of teachers who have fallen in the battle of the flesh: “It repents me that I made Saul king, because he has abandoned me and has not fulfilled my words in deed.”

His word is the command to preachers: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35). Whoever therefore possesses the word in preaching but does not possess it in the girding of chastity is seen to belong to God in speech, but is proved to abandon God in conduct. Outwardly he carries out divine things, but secretly, while he dissolves in the pleasure of the flesh, he is shown not to fulfill the Lord’s words in deed. He has abandoned the Lord by proposing evil; he does not fulfill his words by presuming upon what was forbidden.

It is therefore rightly said: “It repents me that I made Saul king.” It is as though he said: “I then wished him to rule over others, but now I do not, because the one whom I preferred when humble I now see transgressing in pride and arrogance.”

This is not said of just anyone who has fallen, but of those whose fall is revealed and whose repentance is in no way foreseen. For it is written of the fall of the righteous: “The righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. 24:16). Their falls are, in a certain sense, their stability, because they are sometimes permitted to fall so that they may always be able to stand more firmly. They are permitted to collapse into evils lest they lose the highest gifts of virtue through elation.

Such people, even if at some time they do not fulfill the Lord’s words, do not depart from the Lord, because they are abandoned for a time so that they may be held forever; they lose their senses for a little while, but shortly afterward recover them.

Since Saul is reproved not only for failing to fulfill the Lord’s words in deed but also for abandoning the Lord himself, whom does he signify better than those who have fallen and remain impenitent? Of them the prophet says: “They have made a covenant with death and with hell” (Isa. 28:15).

To make a covenant with death is to perpetrate evils boldly and promise that they will always be done. They continually do evil, but because they love what they do, they promise, as it were, never to withdraw from friendship with death. The more insensitive they become in the covenant of death, the more violently the bowels of Mother Church are shaken with pity.

Hence it is rightly added:

> (Verse 11.) And Samuel was grieved, and he cried to the Lord all night.

9. Samuel is grieved because the highest preacher is afflicted over the destruction of his subject. He cries to the Lord all night because with devout prayers he implores divine mercy for the restoration of the fallen. To cry, for a teacher, is to ask the mercy of almighty God with great desires for the sins of his subjects.

He cries all night when, through affection, he takes upon himself the whole darkness of that sin and, as though for his own crime, makes penitential satisfaction to God on its behalf. For a preacher to cry all night is to take up the entire case of his subject and to strive to destroy all the darkness of that person’s sin through the affection of devoted compunction.

But what does it mean that he is said to have cried and that the Lord did not answer, except that the darkness of the impenitent heart which I have described is signified in Saul, for whom he cries? The Lord would indeed answer if he heard the voice of the one crying.

It follows:

> (Verse 12.) When Samuel rose at night to go to Saul in the morning, it was reported to Samuel that Saul had come to Carmel and had erected for himself a triumphal arch.

10. What is the sinner’s life except night? And what else is the light of the righteous except day? Hence Paul says to converted sinners: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

For the preacher to rise at night is to raise the affection of his mind from taking upon himself another’s fault. The teacher lies, as it were, in the night when he mourns the darkness of another’s sin, because he is brought down from the high security of his own innocence so that the darkness of another’s sins may be destroyed in the depths of his consideration.

He rises at night when he lifts himself from affliction and prepares to come to the guilty person in the morning, because inwardly he weeps through compassion but openly strikes through zeal by rebuke. The teacher also mourns at night but comes in the morning to rebuke: inwardly he loves the sinful subject, but he is in no way ashamed to rebuke the one who errs publicly.

It is as though morning dawns when the teacher begins to disclose the crime that lies hidden.

What, then, does it mean that the one to whom he comes is said to have come to Carmel and erected a triumphal arch for himself, except that the progress of evil is clearly proclaimed? After the sin of disobedience, to erect a triumphal arch or structure is to do evil and to take pride in the perpetration of those same evils.

They raise triumphal monuments, as it were, when they display with a certain ostentation those things by which they think they excel others. This certainly applies both to arrogant and to lustful teachers. The former, while saying great things, raise themselves to the heights of esteem; and what they see themselves to be inwardly, they make known outwardly through boasting and ostentation.

When they also turn to the praise of their own reputation what others accomplish through them, what else do they seem to be doing except displaying a lofty sign of victory with an imposing title?

Others live shamefully but speak most honorably. They consider the respectability of their words but do not take into account the shamefulness of their own lives. When they desire to appear not through the reality of their deeds but through the splendor of their words, they plainly construct a triumphal arch in which they may exalt themselves as though victorious.

And because many others recover from shameful conduct through the words of the shameful, for them, after Amalek has been conquered, to come to Carmel and erect a triumphal arch is to boast vainly before the simple of the lust extinguished in their subjects.

Carmel is interpreted as “soft” or “tender.” Who are understood by the name “tender” except those who are still inexperienced in holy conduct? And who are called “soft” except those who have not yet been solidified through the practice of virtue in the goodness they have begun?

In Carmel, therefore, they erect a sign of victory, because they display themselves to the inexperienced and weak, lest they be found by the knowledgeable and strong to be what they truly are.

Source preparation: Supplied textual variants, notes, and column transitions retained.

### 11.

For these men seek the splendor of victory not in words but in deeds, because they do not judge trees by the beauty of their leaves but test them by the taste of their fruits. Hence the Lord, teaching this, says: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:20). Since, therefore, they desire empty praise, avoid the judgments of men of proven worth, and pretend to the inexperienced and weak that they are other than they are, Saul is said to have come to Carmel and erected a triumphal arch for himself. [Col. 0424A]

But what does it mean that he passes on to Gilgal, unless that, in the same manner by which he displays himself to the simple and devout, he desires to become known among the devout and learned? For, as I have already said many times, Gilgal is called a wheel. Yet within holy Church there are some who are learned in sacred Scripture but are not devout, because they do not possess the virtue of Scripture, namely charity. When they hear eloquent and worldly men speaking, they admire the words they recognize. But they cannot examine their hidden realities, which they do not know. [Col. 0424B]

Saul is therefore rightly said to pass on to Gilgal, because those who seek favor through eloquent speech find what they desire not among the learned and devout, but among the simple and inexperienced, or among worldly wise men who are irreligious.

But when eminent men see the wicked teaching good things, they fear more for their chosen subjects, lest those whom the tongue builds up, the hand—that is, conduct—should pervert. Since, therefore, slippery teachers must not be left long in the ministry of preaching, the following is appropriately added:

> **(Verse 12.)** Samuel therefore came to Saul, and Saul was offering a burnt offering to the Lord, the first portions of the spoils that he had brought from Amalek.

### 12.

He came to Saul in order to bring down the proud man whom he had raised up, humble, to the summit of the kingdom. He found him as he was, not as he had displayed himself through the signs of pride. [Col. 0424C]

What, then, does it mean that he offers the first portions of Amalek to the Lord as a burnt offering, unless that some live wickedly yet suppose that they please God through the progress of others? And because they believe that what they offer pleases God greatly, they are said to offer not a sacrifice or victim but a burnt offering.

They are called “the first portions of the spoils” so that Samuel’s vigilant zeal as an eminent and chosen bishop may be signified, for by him the beginnings of evils are swiftly restrained. It is as though he said: “He came with great haste, since, while he was absent, he could not freely possess even the beginning of burnt offerings.” [Col. 0424D]

“The first portions of the spoils” may also be understood as the choicest things taken from the spoils. Slippery men, openly speaking but struck by hidden blindness, offer these when they believe that they please God by destroying in their hearers the things they allow to live in themselves. It is as though he were more openly reproving one who offers indiscriminately, saying: “He was offering alive what he would more rightly offer dead.” For if, in accordance with the Lord’s words, he had destroyed all the spoil in Amalek, he would have offered an entirely acceptable burnt offering to almighty God.

So also, if the slippery teacher rejected by his will all the enticements of the flesh that he condemns in speech, he would burn a burnt offering that could not be rejected. What, then, does it mean that he is said to have offered the first portions of the spoils that he had brought from Amalek, unless that the darkness of a blind heart is condemned—one that so considers what benefits others that it neglects to see what harms itself? [Col. 0425A]

It is as though he said: “As a victor, he rejoiced in what he had conquered in others, while carrying within himself alive and unconquered that which he had not conquered.” And because they often rave so insanely that they even attempt to offer to chosen and eminent preachers a pretext of virtue, the text continues:

> **(Verse 13.)** When Samuel had come to Saul, Saul said: “Blessed are you by the Lord; I have fulfilled the word of the Lord.”

### 13.

The word of the Lord was that he should destroy Amalek. What, then, does he mean by saying, “I have fulfilled the word of the Lord,” unless that the more loathsome the guilt of sexual immorality appears, the more diligently it is concealed by the reprobate? Since, therefore, those subject to this same vice of sexual immorality always desire to remain hidden, Saul, representing them, disdained to destroy Amalek and said to Samuel: “I have fulfilled the word of the Lord.” [Col. 0425B]
