It is as though he said: “In others I subdued lust, and in myself I destroyed its enticements.” And because he attempts to bend the mind of the eminent man by flattering praise, he began by saying: “Blessed are you by the Lord.” It is as though he said: “I did this, certainly, but I was able to do it not by my own strength, but by your merits and intercessions.”

But perfect men can hear their praises without being bent from the strictness of justice. Therefore it is added:

> **(Verse 14.)** And Samuel said: “What, then, is this sound of flocks that resounds in my ears, and of herds that I hear?”

### 14.

The sound of Amalek’s flocks and herds is the report of shameful deeds. When someone is defamed for lesser sins of lust, the sound of flocks is said to resound. When, likewise, he is accused of more criminal and obscene acts, it is the sound of herds. Samuel strips bare what is concealed beneath the pretense of his false virtue, saying, as it were: “You justify yourself with your own mouth, but the crowds of your impurities cry out through everyone’s mouth.” [Col. 0425C]

But let us now see how he, who has begun to put forward excuses, tries by what defenses to escape the charge of the infamy alleged against him. The text continues:

> **(Verse 15.)** They brought them from Amalek. The people spared the better sheep and cattle in order to sacrifice them to the Lord your God; we killed the rest.

### 15.

What does he mean by saying, “They brought them from Amalek,” and not “We brought them”? When the reprobate are accused, they sometimes conceal their faults by denying them, and sometimes transfer them to others. [Col. 0425D] They conceal them by denial when they are able to remain hidden; but when they are held as though caught in the open, they ascribe to others what they cannot deny.

Indicating their character through Saul, he says: “They brought them from Amalek. The people spared the better sheep and cattle.” It is as though he said: “The evil that is heard of should be weighed as arising from the weakness of the people, not from the virtue of the shepherd.” The sins of subjects should indeed be disregarded in comparison with their rulers. He says, therefore: “They brought them from Amalek.” It is as though he said: “What is heard concerning a shameful life is true, but that same shamefulness flourished among the little ones, not among the great.”

Still further diminishing the same fault, he says: “The people spared the better sheep and cattle in order to sacrifice them to the Lord your God.” [Col. 0426A] It is as though he said: “The people truly sinned, but not unto death, because, at my exhortation, they are already striving to erase the sins of their conduct through the humility of confession.”

Amalek’s flocks and herds are sacrificed to the Lord when the slippery and incontinent come to confession and strive through repentance to erase what they have wickedly done. He says, therefore: “The people spared”—that is, they indulged the sin. “But they brought them in order to sacrifice them,” because in those things in which the people remember that they fell, they now, by confessing and repenting, are pierced with compunction.

The better flocks and herds, as above, signify the choicer sins of lust. It is as though he said: “Even if the people sinned gravely, we should not be accused, because, in proportion to the greatness of the crime, they have the lamentation of compunction.”

What does he mean by saying, “In order to sacrifice them to the Lord your God”? Through this the practice of deceivers is revealed: while they desire to remain hidden from eminent men, they flatter them. Why does he assert that this is singularly “your God,” unless because he presents him as God’s familiar friend? “To the Lord,” he says, “your God”—not mine, but yours, because I am a sinner while you alone are holy.

But through a marvelous use of deceit, the false conceal themselves in such a way that they bring themselves forward, and justify themselves in order to accuse. They so regulate the manner of their accusation that, by accusing, they appear righteous, lest by excusing themselves they become known. When he calls him “his God,” he exalts him and diminishes himself. But when he asserts that those brought from Amalek are to be sacrificed to the Lord, he silently brings forward not what should cause him to be reproved but what should cause him to be praised.

Adding still further, he says: “But we killed the rest.” [Col. 0426B] Sins are killed when they are forgiven. Sins are alive when they still reign in the mind through desire, or when, though despised through conversion, they have not yet been erased through repentance. The former still live for pleasure; the latter live for punishment. For even if we have ceased to sin, unless we mourn what we have committed, we remain held by the obligation of our offenses.

But he attributes greater things to lesser ones and lesser things to greater ones. For what does he mean by saying, “We killed the rest,” unless that there are very small sins in comparison with greater ones, which are washed away by confession alone? Teachers kill these when, by apostolic authority, they forgive those who confess humbly.

Because in all these words they try to conceal themselves as deceivers, not to reveal themselves, the authority of chosen preachers by which they are reproved is added. [Col. 0426C]

[Col. 0426D]

> **(Verse 16.)** Samuel said to Saul: “Stop, and I will tell you what the Lord said to me during the night.”

### 16.

What does he mean by saying, “Stop, and I will tell you,” unless that, while deceivers persist in wordiness, they do not allow examining superiors an opportunity to speak? It is as though he said: “While you do not cease from your verbosity, you do not permit me to say what you ought to hear.”

This expression may also mock the flatterer’s intention: while he believes that he makes himself pleasing by flattering praise, he thinks that he himself, as it were, holds those whom he praises by those same praises. It is therefore as though the chosen prelate were mocking his flatterer with dignified seriousness, saying: “You who praise me, I cannot speak harsh things to you. Allow me, then”—that is, permit me to speak—and understand what I am about to say. [Col. 0427A]

And because, as I have said, flatterers believe that they make themselves pleasing by praising, they do not at all expect to hear harsh words from those whom they praise. Saul therefore follows as though about to hear pleasant and prosperous things, saying: “Speak.”

But chosen men, when they hear their praises, do not grow soft amid the comforts of praise and abandon the strictness of justice. Those who despise the deeds of the reprobate cannot at all accept their words. Since, therefore, they cannot be bent by praise, they examine wicked flatterers with subtle reasoning and pursue them with stern judgments. Hence it follows:

> **(Verses 17–19.)** Samuel said: “Were you not little in your own eyes, and were you not made head of the tribes of Israel? The Lord anointed you king over Israel; the Lord sent you on your way and said: ‘Go, strike down the sinners, Amalek, and fight against them until you have exterminated them.’ Why, then, did you not listen to the voice of the Lord, but turned to the spoil and did evil in the eyes of the Lord?” [Col. 0427B]

### 17.

[Col. 0427C]

In these words the disobedience of the proud king is subtly examined: first, the gifts bestowed on him are brought forward; then the audacity of his transgression is struck by an investigation of the same fault.

The examination is subtle when a cunning sinner is examined in such a way that no excuse for his fault is left to him, so that the sentence of God holds him bound, as it were, for death, with no refuge from sin remaining. To block every path of escape for deceitful and proud men, both the exalted dignity and the manner of his ministry are recalled when he says: “Were you not little in your own eyes, and were you not made head of the tribes of Israel?” And the Lord said to you: “Strike down the sinners, Amalek.”

And, in order to seize him now surrounded and besieged by arguments, he lays a hand on his fault, saying: “Why, then, did you not listen to the voice of the Lord, but turned to the spoil and did evil before the eyes of the Lord?” It is as though he said: “See what you were, and what you became; see what you ought to have done, and see what you did; see how far you have departed from what you ought to have undertaken.” When, therefore, he added, “Why did you do evil in the eyes of the Lord?” he enclosed and seized the deceitful defendant.

### 18.

But in this passage it should be noted that, while the proud king is accused, the time of his election is recalled, so that it may be perceived that the swelling of his heart did not accompany him when he was chosen but grew after he had been raised to the summit of authority. He was chosen good by the Lord, but as he grew in elevation, he diminished through pride. [Col. 0427D]

He therefore says: “When you were little in your own eyes, you were made head of the tribes of Israel; now, having turned to the spoil, you have done evil in the eyes of the Lord.” It is as though he said: “Through the truth of humility you merited the kingdom, but now, under the pretext of humility and swollen in truth, you lose the kingdom.”

For what are the eyes of the heart except the sight of reason? Whoever possesses sound vision of reason is perfectly enlightened. He is humble in his own eyes who regards himself perfectly and, with perfect vision, recognizes himself as humble.

In these words, therefore, not only the fallen king’s former humility but also his acuity of reason is praised: he was so great in reason that he knew himself perfectly, and so great in virtue that, looking upon himself with subtle attention, he truly saw himself as humble.

Since, when he is accused, his former state is recalled, what else is described than that he has been deprived of what he once possessed? For men cannot become proud unless they first lose the eyes of the heart. [Col. 0428A] In the case of the lustful this is especially clear: they would never plunge themselves into the abyss of fornication if they had not first grown dark, losing the light of inward glory.

Because they despise the lofty precepts of chastity, they are also accused of swelling pride. Thus the one who had come to depose the ruling king says: “When you were little in your own eyes, you were made head of the tribes of Israel; now you have done evil in the eyes of the Lord.” It is as though he said: “Now, proud and blind, you are justly deposed, though formerly, seeing and humble, you deserved to receive the kingdom.”

The proud Pharisees are likewise called blind by the Truth itself, which says to the disciples: “Let them alone; they are blind guides of the blind” (Matt. 15:14). [Col. 0428B] This blindness is especially attributed to the lustful, because no vices bring thicker darkness upon the mind than lust.

But now one may see many clerics standing while priests have fallen. To them, certainly, through Samuel’s command it is said: “When you were little in your own eyes, you were made head of the tribes of Israel.” It is as though he said: “When, in the lesser order, with an enlightened heart, you kept the precepts of chastity, now, having lost your eyes, you have fallen into the abyss of fornication.”

“You turned to the spoil,” because by violent presumption you broke the divine precepts. For when, despite God’s prohibition—as though he were armed with threats and standing in the way—they burst in to violate the sanctuary of chastity, they lead Amalek’s chosen things away as plunder into the Lord’s land.

And because, as far as they can, the slippery hide from preachers, Saul is reproved for having done evil in the sight of the Lord. It is as though the preacher, threatening and frightening one who has fallen into carnal pleasure, were saying: “The crime of impurity is indeed hidden from human beings, but it is not concealed from the One who sees all things.” [Col. 0428C]

When the impenitent hear these and similar words, they cannot be frightened. Therefore, even when they have already been caught by reasoning, they strive to slip away like snakes through slippery ground from the hands that hold them. They bring forth the tail and hide the head: the outward end of their actions is already visible, but the quality of those same deeds is concealed. Hence it follows:

> **(Verse 20.)** Saul said to Samuel: “Indeed, I heard the voice of the Lord, and I walked by the way along which the Lord sent me, and I brought Agag, king of Amalek, and I struck down Amalek.”

### 19.

[Col. 0428D]

As though concealing what is hidden and bringing forward what has been exposed in others, the slippery teacher commends himself for the success of his preaching, saying: “I should not be reproved for the fault of my subjects but praised, because through preaching I have destroyed it in those who offend.”

“I struck Amalek,” because the spirit of fornication has fallen in the hearts of my hearers by the sword of my tongue. Though the king lives, he has been brought in: although the sense of the flesh cannot be entirely destroyed while we are in the flesh, it has been captured as far as it could be captured, because it cannot prevail over reason.

Desiring to display the subjects whom he had corrected and who had confessed their sins, he added:

> **(Verse 21.)** But the people took sheep and cattle from the spoil, the first portions of what had been killed, in order to sacrifice them to the Lord their God at Gilgal. [Col. 0429A]

### 20.

When something belonging to someone is violently taken by armed men, it is called spoil. The vices of the flesh and of the soul, because they are propagated at the devil’s suggestion, are as though his property. Therefore whoever, having recently been lax in himself, now violently destroys vices, takes spoil, because he forcefully seizes what belongs to another.

It should be noted that the text speaks both of killing and of spoil, so that it may teach that some things were left dead and others carried away alive. The pleasures of lust are killed when they are driven from the heart by the power of heavenly purpose and cut away from the body by contrition of spirit.

But living things are led away for sacrifice, because even when the pleasure of the flesh or mind is abandoned through conversion, the punishment of past pleasure is not completely removed. [Col. 0429B]

Let vices therefore be killed; let no living first portions be kept for sacrifice, so that the one who forcefully destroys the power of sin by despising its pleasures may fear to allow the punishment of pleasure to remain alive in him for sacrifice.

What, then, are the first portions of those that have been killed, unless the pleasures of sins? He is said to offer these who confesses them before God’s priests. The things offered are sacrificed when their punishment is destroyed through repentance.

They are offered as though killed in their first portions but live on afterward when someone confesses sins yet does not strive to sacrifice them—that is, to slaughter them before God—through repentance. Thus, when the first portions of what has been killed are said to be reserved for sacrifice, the error of those who abandon their sins but nevertheless do not mourn them is exposed.

Since sins must therefore not only be confessed but also destroyed through the austerity of repentance, Saul, while pretending to represent a good teacher, asserts that his subjects brought the first portions of what had been killed to be sacrificed.

And because the measure of repentance must be determined according to the principles of Scripture, the first portions to be sacrificed are brought to Gilgal. Cattle are kept for sacrifice, and sheep as well, so that those concerned for their salvation may strive to erase great sins through repentance in such a way that they do not omit mourning lesser ones.

The case of the proud is clear: since they always desire to appear great, they are ashamed to be marked as sinners. Even when caught, they resist and desire to appear righteous in the very things they do.

[Col. 0429C]

What, then, does he mean by saying, “Indeed, I heard the voice of the Lord,” while Samuel says, “Stop, and I will tell you what the Lord said to me during the night,” and shortly afterward, “Why did you turn to the spoil and do evil before the eyes of the Lord?” It is evident how astonishingly swollen with pride is the man who seeks to justify himself precisely when he recognizes that the Lord is reproving him for sin. [Col. 0429D]

### 21.

If, however, he is thought to have answered in this way because he believed the prophet’s words were not the Lord’s but the prophet’s, we still see imitators of Saul who, while trusting in their own learning, both despise the commands of their elders when they hear them, because of their pride, and believe that they improve them by altering them.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “Indeed, I heard the voice of the Lord, and I brought Agag, king of Amalek”? It is as though he said: “I endeavored to fulfill what was commanded, and I supplied what was lacking. It was commanded that Amalek be struck down; but because he was conquered with God’s help, it remained to be supplied that those things which were to be sacrificed to God should be preserved.” [Col. 0430A]

This is plainly apparent in the proud: when they cannot conceal an evident fault, they attempt to alter or diminish it. It is as though they said: “Even if you judge the manifest faults of my conduct, you must consider the hidden simplicity of my intention. It would indeed have been a fault to bring anything from Amalek, unless what was brought was meant to be sacrificed to God.”

This often occurs in monasteries when a subject, excessively zealous in religion, presumes to add something to the commands of spiritual superiors; when he despises the common regular life and follows the choice of his own will. For when he tries to improve his life by choosing rather than by obeying, what else is shown than that he is coloring manifest disobedience with the intention of virtue? [Col. 0430B]

Superiors as well as subjects ought to examine this passage carefully. Subjects should observe it carefully because Saul displeased God by attempting to sacrifice to God something beyond the prophet’s command. Superiors should observe carefully that the prophet commanded the king to demolish Amalek.

Thus a teacher ought to commend what is common in such a way that he does not despise what belongs to individuals. The common life is commendable when it is joined by charity and not darkened by vices.

The Apostle says: “Each one has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that way” (1 Cor. 7:7). Those whose food and table are shared should consider not only the common good of nourishment but also the particularity of their struggle, so that they may eat together but not all strive equally, through abstinence, against the impulses of fornication. The flesh of the one who is more severely harassed by the impulse of the flesh must be disciplined more intensely. [Col. 0430C]

Thus common life does not operate on an equal basis merely because the sharing of food is considered; rather, each person is said to fight his individual battle individually. Nor does a teacher give good commands if he does not command what strikes Amalek, but only what allows it to live.

Let the teacher command, then, so that the spirit of fornication may be overcome. Let subjects shun refusing obedience where the crime of pride is incurred, not where the abyss of death is avoided.

When the disobedient, with swelling hearts, fail to carry out the commands of their elders and attempt to improve what has been enjoined upon them, while wishing to offer their own works to God, they take themselves away from him. For through other virtues we offer something of ours to him; through obedience we present ourselves. [Col. 0430D]

Samuel therefore continues, saying:

> **(Verse 22.)** Does God desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, and not rather that one obey the voice of the Lord?

### 22.

For what are the good works of chosen men, unless sacrifices and burnt offerings? Since the Lord had commanded burnt offerings and sacrifices to be offered through the Law, what does it mean that the Lord is said not to desire burnt offerings and sacrifices but to promise that he desires obedience to him, unless that things done apart from obedience are neither burnt offerings nor sacrifices?

It is as though he said: “Good works are good when they do not conflict with the conscience of superiors.” If this is said in order to commend the virtue of obedience, it is clear how sublime a good it is—one that surpasses victims and sacrifices. [Col. 0431A]

What, then, does it mean that he is said to desire obedience to the voice of the Lord, unless that all good works must be placed after those things that are commanded? For when superiors give good commands, the good things subjects choose according to their own judgment are placed after the commands of their superiors.

Those works, placed after obedience, are called burnt offerings and sacrifices. Thus it is made clear not only that small things ought not to be compared with the commands of elders, but also that the greatest works may be burnt offerings.

Burnt offerings belong to those who wish to withdraw entirely from public activity in order to offer themselves wholly consumed by love of God in the secrecy of contemplation. Sacrifices belong to those who do not at all separate themselves from the common public life but act with singular virtue, so that by living more strictly they may surpass the virtues of others. [Col. 0431B]

These and similar practices, when undertaken with the permission of good superiors, are sacrifices and burnt offerings approved by God. But when they are performed in such a way that the commands of elders are neglected through them, let those who offer them hear what the prophet, sent by the Lord to the disobedient king, says:

> “Does God desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, and not rather that one obey the voice of the Lord?”

He terrifies those who despise their fathers’ commands as though they were lesser things and present their own as though they were greater, saying: “You think this is great, and therefore despise what is small and worthless; but if you look at it plainly, through this you do not please the Lord.”

When the work of the proud is examined, the prophet rightly and sharply asks:

> “Does God desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, and not rather that one obey the voice of the Lord?” [Col. 0431C]

He asks this so that the swelling of pride may be struck down by pastoral authority. He says: “Does God desire burnt offerings and sacrifices?” Those who choose to follow their own will think that they please God; but God does not approve their works, even when they are great and enormous.

But he then adds with what praises obedience should be proclaimed, saying:

> **(Verse 22.)** For obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams.

### 23.

Since he previously said, “Does God desire burnt offerings and sacrifices?” and then places sacrifices and the fat of rams beneath the praises of obedience, did he understand a burnt offering in the fat? Whatever is better is better than something good. But those burnt offerings and sacrifices that God does not desire are not good at all. [Col. 0431D]

What, then, does it mean, in praising obedience, to say, “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams,” unless that obedience is better when the burnt offering and sacrifice are not evil? It is as though he were bringing the proud and disobedient back to consideration of so great a good, saying: “Even if you did nothing presumptuously, the virtue of obedience would still be better than the works you choose.”

It is therefore clear to what height he saw obedience raised—higher than divine offerings. If, as above, we follow the spiritual sense, sacrifices should be referred to the austerity of a great way of life, and burnt offerings to the compunction of a more hidden life:

> “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams.”

For it is a far higher merit always to subject one’s own will to another’s will than to wear down the body through great fasts or to slaughter oneself through compunction in a more secluded sacrifice.

What is the fat of rams unless the rich and inward devotion of the one who chooses [the hidden life]? He offers the fat of rams who, in the practice of a hidden life, possesses the devoted affection of prayer. [Col. 0432A]

Yet obedience is better than sacrifices and than offering the fat of rams, because one who has perfectly learned to fulfill the will of his preceptor surpasses in the heavenly kingdom both those who abstain and those who weep.

Because he says this against one who is proud and openly despises the Lord’s commands, he does not compare the good that Saul did with the good that he despised. Rather, he destroys the pretense of goodness by displaying the truth of a better good. It is as though he said: “If you were seeking an excellent good for the glory of surpassing virtues, you ought rather to have chosen the good of obedience, which surpasses even excellent things.”

Thus, by reasoning, he destroys the pretense of goodness; but, by what follows, he openly exposes [Col. 0432B] the evil of disobedience, saying:

> **(Verse 23.)** For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to comply is like the crime of idolatry.

### 24.

[Note: At Col. 0431D, other editions corruptly read “simulantur.”]

[Col. 0432C]

Why, then, does the prophet compare those who rebel and refuse to comply with diviners and idolaters, unless because diviners attempted to know divine things and foretell hidden matters, while idolaters submitted themselves to images by venerating them?

Those who rebel against the commands of their superiors rebel for this reason: they believe that they know the divine will better. Thus rebellion is like the sin of divination, because, as though they had despised the divine altar and gone to the altars of demons to receive answers, they trust the deceptive and proud inventions of their hearts and oppose the salutary counsels of their superiors by thinking contrary thoughts.

Refusal to comply is said to be like the crime of idolatry because no one would persist in the obstinacy of disobedience if he did not carry in his heart, as an idol, the fabrication of his chosen purpose. When he conceives in his heart what is to be done, he makes an idol, as it were; and when he decides to carry out the purpose conceived in his mind, he bows down, as it were, to worship an image.

Thus refusal to comply is like the crime of idolatry, because whoever is obstinate in his own decision is raised outwardly in contempt of his elders for this reason: inwardly he bows before the images of his purpose, the things he has fashioned by invention. [Col. 0432D]

But it must be asked very carefully why rebellion is compared to the sin of divination and refusal to comply to the crime of idolatry. A crime is called only a great sin, whereas even something slight is called a sin. But if diviners were said to come from the altar because they were accustomed to consult it in order to receive answers, then the sin of idolatry was a crime by comparison, because it was more insane to worship stones than, under the guise of divine matters, to receive false answers about living well.

Why, then, is rebellion said by comparison to be a sin, while refusal to comply is called a crime? To rebel is to disagree with the will of one who commands. Many appear to rebel for a time when they do not immediately accept the commands of their superiors, yet after a short while they comply with those same commands.

But what is refusal to comply except both to rebel against the obedience enjoined and to persist obstinately in that rebellion? Those do not comply who are unconquerable in the purpose of their hearts and do not omit, on anyone’s authority, what they have decided to do. [Col. 0433A]

It is therefore rightly said, in comparison with rebellion, that refusal to comply is a crime, since it appears to the sinner to be a much greater and more horrifying fault. Since those who are of this kind cannot be overcome by arguments, the prophet indicates what punishment should restrain them, saying:

> **(Verse 23.)** Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, so that you may not be king.

### 25.

What does it mean that Saul is rejected, unless that he is judged incorrigible? It is as though he said: “Because you reject all the counsels of salvation, you should no longer be corrected by words for the fault of your obstinacy, but condemned by the punishment of rejection.” [Col. 0433B]

The extent to which the fault of disobedience must be feared is shown if this is carefully considered: because of it even kings are deposed.

What does he mean by saying, “Because you rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you”? The word is rejected when it is not reverently preserved in its sublimity. To reject is to let something slip from the hand onto the ground, either through negligence or by throwing it down forcefully.

The word of the Lord, because it speaks heavenly and sublime things that bring salvation, is thrown negligently onto the ground when it is not fulfilled through laziness. It is rejected through contempt when the proud and disobedient repel it with swelling hearts and disdain to observe it through the work of their hands. [Col. 0433C]

But because the text does not say merely that the word should not be thrown down, but that it is rejected, this signifies that, while the proud follow their own judgment, they become far from the Lord. To reject is to drive something far away.

Those who worthily accept the leadership of others are not only near to God through obedience but also make near to him those who, through vices and crimes, are far from him. The meaning is therefore as though he said: “You are driven far from the rank of dignity because you did not wish to be present in the merit of that same dignity.” For the merit of dignity is observance of the divine word. When it is rejected, the merit of dignity is lost, and the dignity itself is removed.

It is therefore worthwhile to consider how much the proud lose through disobedience, and how much the humble gain. While the former rejoice in fulfilling the judgment of their own will, they offer God great labors of works but receive no rewards for those labors. The latter, while abandoning themselves and following the judgment of another’s will, merit the glory of eternal exaltation. Hence it is said through the blessed Mary, mother of our Lord and Redeemer:

> “He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted the humble” (Luke 1:52). [Col. 0433D]

The Lord brings the mighty down from their thrones when he rejects disobedient and proud men and exalts the humble: he glorifies the obedient with eternal glory. But the proud do not correct themselves through words; instead, while fearing to lose their honors, they merely pretend to possess a humility they do not have, lest they lose the summit of glory. Hence it is added:

> **(Verse 24.)** Saul said to Samuel: “I have sinned, because I have transgressed the words of the Lord and your words.” [Col. 0434A]

### 26.

What does it mean that Saul is reproved by the prophet for not having heard the voice of the Lord and for having done evil in his sight, yet does not admit that he has sinned; but, when he sees himself being rejected from the kingdom, then confesses that he has sinned and transgressed the word of the Lord and the prophet’s words?

It means that the proud are bold in despising the words of the humble, but cannot despise, after the manner of the chosen, the honors that they pursue. They are bold enough to despise the commands of their superiors, but are not prepared to abandon high positions.

The humble, by contrast, are ready to obey the commands of their superiors and secure in losing high positions. Because they seek not earthly but heavenly things, [Col. 0434B] they despise the heights of earthly eminence and strive for heavenly realities; they willingly wish to be subordinate and refuse precedence.

Saul, therefore, refusing to obey God and fearing to lose the kingdom, reveals to us the character of the proud: when they prevail, they avoid appearing insignificant or sinful; when compelled, they pretend to the virtue of humility.

But when compelled to confess, they lessen the sin they accuse themselves of in their words. For although he says that he sinned by transgressing the word of the Lord, he recalls that he incurred the same transgression through necessity rather than will, saying: “Fearing the people and obeying their voice.”

It is as though he said: “The sin for which I am reproved ought to be punished all the more lightly, since it is clear that it was committed not through malice but through [Col. 0434C] weakness.” To sin deliberately and willingly is a great transgression; to sin through weakness is more tolerable in proportion to the inability of the one subject to that sin to resist its power.

And because such men think that, by this same cunning of heart, they can prevail over the humility of simple teachers, he added, as though he had already persuaded them:

> **(Verse 25.)** “But now, please forgive my sin, and return with me, so that I may worship the Lord.”

27. Correctable sins are indeed “carried,” because once they have departed from the sinner’s will, they can salutarily be cleansed through satisfaction. But the sins of those in whose minds they have become deeply rooted through impenitence are not carried. Hence John also says: “There is a sin unto death, that one should not pray for it” (1 John 5:16). A sin unto death is committed by one who can never come to repentance. Such a sin is not carried by superiors, because it is not erased by the prayers or offerings of priests.

Saul, signifying in every respect the proud and obstinate, does not cease swelling with pride, yet begs that his sin be carried. He piles up an unbearable burden, but asks that it be carried as though it were light. This happens continually in the Church whenever those who willingly commit great crimes fail to consider their magnitude. They gather unbearable burdens, yet reckon them light and of no weight. They hide their sins from their superiors and, so far as they can, make those sins appear insignificant, so that those set over them may not notice their enormity, and so that the sins may scarcely be discovered or reproved.

They are strong for committing sin, but weak for weeping over their sins. They willingly dissolve into the pleasures of sin, but refuse to be cleansed by the bitterness of repentance. What, then, does he mean by saying, “Carry my sin,” except that they welcome within themselves the sweetness of their sins, while wishing their superiors to bear the burden of those same sins? Some even come voluntarily to confess, but they themselves do not mourn for the sins of which they accuse themselves; instead, they beg others to repent for them. They think they can be saved by faith alone and do not take care, through repentance, to return from their fallen state.

Hence Saul continues:

> “And return with me, that I may worship the Lord.”

The preacher is, as it were, departing when he rejects the shameless. Saul therefore says: “Return with me, that I may worship the Lord.” He thinks that he is not separated from the fellowship of the elect insofar as he preserves the common faith. Or, certainly, to worship the Lord is to submit to the religion of faith and to the custody of good works.

Since Saul thus represents hypocrites, it follows:

> **(Verse 26.)** Samuel said to Saul: “I will not return with you, because you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord has rejected you, so that you will not be king.”

28. Why, then, did the prophet refuse to carry the sin of the penitent king, except because he saw that this man was not truly penitent? He had already answered him with the words of rejection, since he knew that Saul would by no means be changed.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript and Gussanville read *nomine cognovit* (“he recognized by name”). This is an error, which we have corrected from Gilot.]

By this firmness of the prophet, certain priests of the present time who are excessively lenient are reproved: they are weak in their manner of life but bold in their rashness. They scarcely sustain themselves, yet dare to take up burdens that others must bear. They do not carry their own light burdens, yet subject themselves to unbearable ones.

Behold, the strong prophet refuses to take upon himself the burden of the king’s sin, so that a priest of the Church may fear and dread undertaking the weight of unbearable sins. Often, however, one may take on another’s sins in such a way that he nevertheless permits the person who committed them to weep over those sins he has undertaken to expiate. Thus Samuel did not at all promise to carry the king’s sin, yet he mourned for the one with whom he had returned, though rejected. For shortly afterward it is written: “Samuel mourned for Saul, because it repented the Lord that he had made Saul king over Israel.”

He did not promise to carry the king’s sin so that the king might mourn over it; nevertheless, he mourned for the one with whom he had returned, though rejected, in order to make the Lord propitious toward him.

In the literal sense, when the prophet repeats the sentence, he shows the irrevocable judgment of divine justice, by which the sinner is so rejected that he is never permitted to return to the hand of divine mercy.

It can also be understood in another way: Saul asks the prophet to return with him so that he may worship the Lord. Holy men who do not abandon the Lord by sinning do not need to return to him through repentance. To return belongs to one who has departed. This properly applies to sinners who depart from the Lord through sin; it does not apply to the righteous who remain steadfast.

What, then, does it mean that the righteous Samuel is asked to return with the sinful Saul, except that elect preachers are afflicted on behalf of fallen subjects as though they were themselves penitent, and come as though they had departed, when they accompany fallen subjects in paternal affliction? They return with them when both the sins of their subjects and the subjects who have sinned, together with the superiors who have remained steadfast, mourn in common.

It is therefore as though Samuel were saying: “Through the rebuke of my preaching, I have learned that you cling to me with paternal affection, since you have not allowed me to leave you any longer in sin. Because I have come to my senses when you rebuked me, I ask you to return with me, since by my own strength I am utterly insufficient to erase the magnitude of such great depravity.”

Yet such expressions of affection ought to be received only if they proceeded from the truth of the heart. Accordingly, the hypocrite receives the fitting answer:

> “I will not return with you.”

It is as though Samuel were saying: “I do not know how to offer sacrifice to God on your behalf, since I do not see you submitted to God in the truth of humility.” Repeating what he had said earlier, he adds:

> “Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, so that you will not be king.”

And because the crafty are to be rejected and abandoned, it follows:

> **(Verse 27.)** “And Samuel turned to go away.”

In this departure of his superior, the hypocrite fears the loss of temporal honor more than the loss of eternal inheritance. Therefore, even when abandoned, he cannot rest; rather, he strives, through the intervention of others, to obtain what he does not dare to accomplish by himself. Accordingly, it is rightly added:

> **(Verse 27.)** “But he grasped the hem of his cloak, and it was torn.”

29. What are the garments of a teacher except the qualities of the subjects who cling to him? Concerning these garments, the great shepherd is promised through the prophet: “As I live, you shall clothe yourself with all these as with a garment” (Isaiah 49:18). And the Psalmist sings: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength” (Psalm 92:1).

He has clothed himself with beauty because he has joined to himself the radiant minds of the faithful as garments. Saul therefore grasps Samuel’s cloak when any proud and rejected person seeks, through beloved and familiar associates attached to him, to have the honor of high office conveyed to him by eminent men. And because no one among perfected hearers pleads on behalf of the rejected man, he is said to have grasped not the cloak but the hem of the cloak—that is, its edge. But that edge is torn because the person who offers useless advice is rejected.

When an inferior person is repelled while making an indiscreet request, the hem of the garment is, as it were, torn. Thus a portion of the cloak of the supreme prophet was torn when he answered Peter, who was giving bad advice: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not understand the things that are of God, but those that are of men” (Matthew 16:23).

For this reason he also commands: “If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you; and if your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you” (Matthew 5:30). By these words not only the hem of the cloak but also its middle portion is shown to be cut off, because even perfected hearers must be disregarded when they offer bad advice.

This is why the sons of Zebedee, together with their mother, ask that one sit at the right hand and the other at the left of the Redeemer; but, as though ignorant of a good request, they are rejected (Matthew 20). The Lord, as it were, tore a portion of his cloak when by rebuking he refuted those members who were causing scandal.

It should be noted that not the whole cloak but only a part of it is torn. When a good person offers bad advice, he should be rejected in what he wrongly suggests, but retained in affection for whatever else makes him good.

30. The manner of life of a ruler is also signified by a garment, as the Psalmist attests: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 132:9). The hem of the cloak is grasped when a teacher is praised for great holiness, when something that appears outwardly seemly is said in his praise.

But since the good qualities of the righteous are more numerous in what remains hidden, only the hem of the cloak can be grasped: little of the righteousness of an elect teacher is visible, while much is concealed. Even that little which is known is torn when it is grasped, because the righteous are not held by their praises. Since they despise them in an instant, they cannot be held, as it were, by a tear in the cloak.

The torn portion of the garment is held, but the prophet himself is not held. What is said in praise of the righteous is true; yet, when the righteous despise what they hear, they leave something like a torn fragment in the hands of the one who grasps it.

Since some things about the great may be known, a portion is, as it were, grasped. But when everything that is done is known by the little ones, it must nevertheless be rejected if it is praised, because no part of good works should be retained for the sake of vanity.

This is why, when John, still a young man, follows the Lord who has already been seized, he is first held by his cloak, but is then described as fleeing naked after leaving the cloak behind (Mark 14). The young man is captured by the garment when he is praised for the beginning of a good way of life; but he flees naked after leaving the linen garment behind when he despises the praises he hears.

To flee naked is to possess a praiseworthy life while scorning the praise of an elect life. He flees as though naked who attributes nothing to himself through empty glory from the adornment of virtues.

It may also be understood that he fled naked for this reason: although he is said to have been seized by part of the linen garment, he is also said to have left the linen garment behind. For it often happens in the consciences of the elect that, because they are praised in part, they suspect that they have lost not merely part of their merits but the whole merit of a good life.

Samuel’s cloak is therefore torn because elect teachers despise their praises. And because they are not swayed by praise, he repeats the severity of the earlier sentence, saying:

> **(Verse 28.)** “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today.”

31. Perfect men, because no praise makes them soft toward the rigor of justice, are the same after the testimony of their praise as they were before it; and by repeating afterward what they had said earlier, they confirm it.

But we must ask what is signified by the word “today.” If the life of the rejected is night, why is Saul’s kingdom torn in the daytime? Yet if the life of a rejected shepherd is night, then when his kingdom is torn away, he makes day. Day does not come unless night departs.

He says “today,” because the darkness of the disobedient is declared condemned. Hence, when Judas went out, the Lord said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified” (John 13:31), because he saw the night of Judas’s life departing and the pure light of righteousness remaining in the other disciples.

“Today” is also said because, once the proud man was removed, the kingdom was being handed over to a humble king. Hence it follows:

> **(Verse 28.)** “And he has given it to your neighbor, who is better than you.”

When “day” is mentioned, therefore, nothing luminous is perceived in the rejected king; rather, the glory of his successor is proclaimed, for the successor was destined to radiate from the height of the kingdom with the splendor of great virtue.

Asserting the unchangeability of the divine sentence, he adds:

> **(Verse 29.)** “Moreover, the triumphant one in Israel will not spare, and he will not be moved to repentance.”

32. Who is to be understood by the name “the triumphant one” except the Creator of the human race? Whoever overcomes hidden adversaries conquers by his power, since he supplies the grace by which temptation is overcome.

Why is the triumphant one said not to spare when Samuel is being entreated? Because when preachers grow angry with sinful subjects, when divine judgment strikes the proud or the lustful, they are carrying out not the judgment of their own fury but the judgment of the divine will.

It is as though he were saying: “I have pronounced not my own sentence but that of the one whose decision, once issued, cannot be revoked.” He therefore does not spare and is not moved to repentance—but he does not spare those who can neither cease from their sins nor repent of the sins they love. Giving the reason, he adds:

> **(Verse 29.)** “For he is not a man, that he should repent.”

It is as though he were saying: “He is, and remains, one for whom there is no mutability.”

The perfection of the substituted king can also be signified by the name “the triumphant one”: he was to possess the glory of many triumphs and would not dare to spare anyone against the will of the Creator. Thus, in this same book, it is written of him: “David struck all the land, and did not leave alive either man or woman” (1 Samuel 27:9).

It is also said of him: “For he is not a man, that he should repent.” What, in this passage, is signified by “man” except one subject to carnal passions? It is as though he were still biting the proud man, saying: “You repent of your sins now that you are receiving the sentence for your audacity; but he will not repent, for, unlike a man, he is not subject either to disobedience or to swelling pride.”

Still he confesses with his own mouth, saying:

> **(Verse 30.)** “I have sinned.”

He shows the quality of this confession by adding:

> **(Verse 30.)** “But now honor me before the elders of my people and before Israel.”

33. It is clear what sort of repentance he practices when he still desires to be honored. If he truly regretted his sin, he would have desired to be dishonored rather than honored.

It is astonishing to contemplate the hardness of this rejected heart. The man of God, carrying out the command of the Creator, says: “The Lord has rejected you, so that you will not be king.” Yet the man who receives the sentence of rejection seeks honors through his desire for exaltation.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “I have sinned”? Confession of sin ought to be followed not by honor or glory but by usefulness and contempt. For what does it profit to confess crimes if the voice of confession is not followed by the affliction of repentance?

Three things must truly be considered in anyone who is penitent: the conversion of the mind, confession of the mouth, and punishment of the sin. For what does it profit one who is not converted in heart to confess his sins? The sin that is loved is not erased at all by confession.

There are some who disclose their sins by confessing them, but do not detest them because they do not convert. Their confession accomplishes nothing, because what they cast out by speaking they bring back in by loving.

Therefore Scripture gives salutary instruction to those who wish to confess properly: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

What is it to believe with the heart unto righteousness except to direct one’s will toward faith that works through love? When someone directs the intention of the heart toward righteousness through love, he receives, through the beginning of a good will, the fruit of a good conversion.

Such a person already confesses unto salvation, because by speaking he casts more out from the wound than he has pierced through conversion and contrition.

The third element, therefore—that is, punishment—is necessary like medicine, so that the abscess of guilt, pierced by conversion and confession, may be cleansed and healed by the medicine of affliction.

Therefore, one who does not believe with the heart unto righteousness does not confess unto salvation at all. He displays, as it were, the leaves of a bad tree whose deep roots he fixes in his heart.

The sign of true confession is therefore found not in confession of the lips but in the affliction of repentance. We recognize that a sinner has truly converted when he strives, with the fitting severity of affliction, to erase what he confesses in words.

Thus John the Baptist rebuked the badly converted Jews who flocked to him, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3:7).

Repentance must therefore be recognized in its fruit, not in its leaves or branches. A good will is like a tree. What else, then, are the words of confession except leaves? We should not seek leaves for their own sake but for the sake of fruit, because every confession of sins is received for this purpose: that the fruit of repentance may follow.

Hence the Lord cursed a tree adorned with leaves but barren of fruit (Mark 11), because he does not accept the ornament of confession without the fruit of affliction.

Saul, then, who confesses but wishes to be honored rather than afflicted and humbled, signifies those who have a barren confession and no fruit; those who put forward the beauty of confession in humble words but do not follow the force of those words with the humility of repentance.

34. But why should we attend to the ancients when now we see such a multitude of fallen kings? They fall in crowds into crimes—not only weak subjects but also negligent superiors and priests. Those appointed by the order of their ministry to the heavenly sacraments live dissolutely through sinning.

Many of them, however, when they in some way return to their senses, confess that they have gone astray. Yet they wish to bring their sins against themselves into the open in such a way that they may still be honored in the office of the sacred order. They present themselves as disgraceful in secret, but blush to appear humble in public beneath the dignity of their rank.

What, then, do such men signify except those who see themselves rejected and yet dare to wish to be honored? Often they do not come of their own accord but are seized unwillingly. They receive the command of their rejection, yet still ask to be honored.

They wish to perform unclean acts, but dare to cling to the sacred altars. Behold how many Sauls we observe, how many fallen kings we contemplate cast down from the summit of the holy Church. To each of them it must be said: “Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, so that you will not be king”—so that those whom earthly crimes do not cease to defile may no longer perform a heavenly ministry.

But although we can say this, we cannot persuade lustful ministers to act accordingly. Saul both heard that he had been rejected and continued to reign. In the same way, unclean priests recognize that they have been cast down from the priestly height through the defilements of lust, yet do not cease to handle the sacred mysteries against the will of God.

But a king who reigns against the Lord’s will is not a king but a tyrant; likewise, an unworthy priest who is rejected because of his deserved defilement, yet presumes to minister, ascends toward the height of such great glory only to be condemned.

[Note: Gilot reads *damnatus ascendit* (“he ascends condemned”).]

Therefore, wishing to terrify tyrants, that great senator of heaven says: “Whoever eats the bread and drinks the blood of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11:27).

Often, persistent confession is used to make people believe that those who confess have also undergone conversion of heart. Sometimes elect preachers accept the false humility of the rejected so that others may be led to salvation by their example.

They recognize two things in hypocrites: one within and the other outwardly. Within there is pure evil; outwardly, simulated good. They detest both, but often pretend goodness in them as a pretext, so that those who see the outward good, but do not know the inward evil, may follow the examples of the good they observe.

Accordingly, it is rightly added:

> **(Verse 31.)** “So Samuel returned and followed Saul, and Saul worshiped the Lord.”

35. Because of the evil that lay hidden within him, Saul deserved to hear: “The Lord has rejected you, so that you will not be king.” But so that, under the pretext of goodness, he might draw others toward the truth of that same goodness, Samuel wished to follow Saul and saw him worshiping the Lord.

At times, too, the evils of kings and of the great of the earth must be tolerated, lest, being provoked, they slide into worse things. The children of Israel often worshiped the gods of the nations. Hence it was said above concerning those converted by Samuel: “The children of Israel removed the Baals and the Ashtaroth from their midst” (1 Samuel 7:4).

Perhaps, if the rejected king had not seen the prophet returning with him to worship, he would have worshiped images of demons. The prophet therefore rejects him yet returns with him, because among the powerful of this age iniquity must be condemned in such a way that, once provoked, they do not lose whatever good they possess.

The wicked are often evil in secret, while others imitate the good that is visible in them with greater devotion. The evils of the powerful of this world are certainly great evils for them; but the good they display benefits the faithful as an example more than the good displayed by others.

Samuel therefore rightly returns with the rejected king, because elect preachers both strike the powerful of the world for their iniquity and permit them to perform certain good acts for the sake of example.

Hence it follows:

> **(Verse 32.)** “And Samuel said: ‘Bring Agag, king of Amalek, to me.’ And Agag was brought to him, trembling and exceedingly fat.”

36. Kings worship the Lord when the proud and contemptuous humble themselves to carry out the Lord’s commands. The lustful worship him when they submit themselves to God through obedience to chastity.

Sometimes, however, they merely pretend to worship, because some possess a pretext of humility or chastity; and while they are believed to possess goodness in truth, others, through the goodness they believe them to possess, abandon the practice of evil.

They therefore hand over King Agag to Samuel when, by confessing, they bring forth the power of their sensuality. When they confess sins of lust committed through the strength of the flesh, what else do they offer to the prophets than King Amalek, who must be killed?

But why is Agag called exceedingly fat, when the power of sensuality is fat in some and lean in others? What, then, does it mean that he is offered fat, except that he was being led forth by the subjects of the rejected king? Subjects are often negligent; yet, when they see the example of their elect shepherd, they groan amid the evils they commit.

They fall into impurity through the weakness of the flesh; but, struck by the examples of their superiors, they cannot rejoice completely amid the pleasures of impurity. In whom, then, is Agag exceedingly fat except in those of whom it is said: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs 2:14)?

Subjects under a wanton teacher sin with so much greater boldness because they have no examples of their superiors placed before them to see. But they plunge themselves into ruin far more foolishly when they do not see in their shepherds any good example to follow, while they do see the evil by whose example they perish.

In these people Agag grows fat, because the power of the flesh is stretched out joyfully, securely, and freely in the pleasure of lust, when the practice of enticement is not checked by anything.

The exceedingly fat Agag is therefore offered for slaughter when those who have taken great delight in the pleasure of lust are converted. The king is handed over, as it were, when the carnal sense—which ruled the mind—is revealed through confession to the priests of Christ.

Fat also commonly serves to feed a fire. Agag the Amalekite king is therefore aptly described in these terms: when the spirit of fornication possesses the mind, the more sweetly and frequently it feeds there through shameful thoughts, the richer fuel is supplied to increase the fire of desire.

[Note: The Vatican and Gussanville manuscripts read *ad agendum* (“for doing”).]

He is called “trembling” because, when the carnal sense is handed over through confession to spiritual men, it is weakened. It shows itself trembling because it no longer possesses the strength of its members.

When the power of sensuality therefore begins to weaken, what else happens than that the king of the Amalekites trembles? Or he is said to tremble because, when they begin to convert, many are terrified by the rigor of repentance.

And because carnal people cannot abandon their customary bodily pleasures without sorrow, it follows:

> **(Verse 32.)** “And he said: ‘Does bitter death separate in this way?’”

37. For the carnal sense to say this is for it to strike the mind with a change into sadness over the loss of its accustomed pleasure. Since the newly converted suffer great darts of bitterness, the king whom they had served complains about death, because carnality is not killed in them without great tribulation.

To inquire of the carnal sense about the manner of death’s separation is to strike the still-sad mind of the convert over the loss of its former delight. The manner of separation is also questioned when he says, “in this way?” For, seeing the austerities to which it must be subjected, sensuality seems to say to the mind: “Do you reject pleasure for the sake of such sadness?”

Samuel hears this voice because an elect preacher recognizes, by certain signs, the heart of a subject who is being tempted. But what does recognition profit if he says nothing against what inwardly rages in the subject’s heart? It follows:

> **(Verse 33.)** “And Samuel said: ‘As your sword made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women.’”

38. What is the mother of the carnal sense except original sin? Before the first human being’s sin, no lust existed in the members; therefore there was no Amalekite king. The sense of the flesh existed, but it was neither shameful nor lustful. As soon as the human being fell into sin, however, he felt the itching of his members, because he could no longer have a carnal movement obedient to him when he himself had been disobedient to God.

Original sin is therefore rightly understood as the mother of the contemptuous carnal sense, because the one who began to exist through it emerges from it by birth.

Hence the Apostle, as though dreading the law of the most savage tyrant, the carnal sense, points out not only the king himself but also his mother, saying: “Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Romans 7:29).

By the sin which he said he did not perform, he understood the movement of the flesh; by the sin dwelling in him, original sin. Since the sin of the flesh’s movement arises from original sin, when we attend to the carnal king, we rightly call the first sin his mother.

The children of this mother are all desires, sins, and vices. The mother is made childless when every fault appears to have been removed from both flesh and mind.

She is then childless because, even if no shamefulness now remains in the flesh and no desire now reigns in the mind, the sin that remains in us cannot at present be destroyed by the strength of the teacher.

For what does the Apostle mean when he says: “Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me”? From that sin, which we contract from the corrupt root of our nature, we derive the capacity to be corrupted by the passions of vices.

Therefore, when the disordered law of the members moves them against our will, it is not we who perform this action but the sin dwelling in us. At that time we do have the will, but we do not yet find the ability; indeed, we would wish that nothing in us could move against our will.

Perhaps these conceptions of the worst mother, by which that sin is impregnated, are said to be nourished if they are allowed to pour themselves out into shameful and obscene acts. Her children are therefore the movements that are not merely naturally present within but are manifested in shameful and obscene deeds.

Agag’s mother is made childless when original sin is so restrained that it is permitted to produce no acts or movements. Or perhaps she is made childless because she had children: when converted sinners cease to be shameful both in action and in behavior, the sin dwelling in them is deprived of its children.

39. It should be noted that the mother is said to be made childless by comparison: “As your sword made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women.”

The virtues of the mind, from which good works proceed, are mothers. Agag’s sword, however, is called the weapon of lust, which makes women childless because lust kills every good work.

Or certainly, the minds of the faithful are understood as women, while the children of holy minds are good thoughts, virtues, and good works. Agag’s sword made mothers childless because, if the pleasure of lust is allowed to be unsheathed like a sword, it kills in them all good thoughts, all virtues, and all good works.

The sharp plague of this pleasure, once received by the mind, makes it impossible to think of anything pure and holy while one delights in looking more intently upon what is impure; and while it vigorously drags one toward the completion of a wicked deed, it permits no virtuous action.

Because everything perishes through its burning, not only Agag’s children but all the children of the women are slaughtered. It makes mothers childless because, when the pleasure of lust strikes the fruits of the mind like a sword, it allows neither thoughts of virtue nor the good of action to live.

Just as it made mothers childless, so its mother is also made childless when the sinner is converted in such a way that, apart from the natural fault implanted in us, nothing of obscene actions or movements appears to remain in the converted person.

Accordingly, it is aptly added:

> **(Verse 33.)** “And Samuel cut Agag into pieces before the Lord at Gilgal.”

40. What is cut into pieces is a dead body divided into small parts. Agag is killed when the power of the flesh is so crushed by abstinence, vigils, and spiritual meditations that no wanton or lustful movement is perceived.

To kill him is to render the flesh incapable of moving shamefully. But the corpse of the slain remains whole when its movement remains. Lust does not remain when it burdens the mind only by its weight—that is, when a simple and natural movement of the flesh resides in the members but has none of the heat of lust.

The elect nevertheless endure even this heavily, and therefore carry, as it were, the whole corpse of the dead king. What, then, does it mean that he is cut into pieces except that they do not wish even the natural movement to retain its strength?

He is therefore cut into pieces because, whenever it strikes, it is killed. When the several movements are not permitted to come together, Agag’s corpse is, as it were, cut into pieces.

Or perhaps this Agag is such that he cannot die unless he is cut into pieces. As I said above, lust is kindled like fire; and if it is extinguished carelessly, the nearby straw is quickly set alight. A great fire that has been scattered can often be extinguished more easily.

When many coals come together in one place, they form a huge mass of embers. Therefore, lest the person extinguishing it be burned, the mass of embers is first wisely scattered, so that it may be quickly extinguished in separate pieces, one coal at a time.

What are lustful thoughts and the lustful movements of the body except fiery coals? If they come together in the heart or in the flesh, they can quickly burn, but they can never easily be extinguished.

Let the fire therefore be scattered; let Agag be cut into pieces; and let the mind be guarded, so that it scatters impure thoughts and does not permit one to cling to another.

Since it cannot ensure that it never entertains harmful thoughts, let it do what it can: let it immediately cast out the thought that enters the mind through negligence.

In this way, if it separates all the flames of its thoughts so that it does not permit them to come together in the mind, whether through negligence or desire, it divides and extinguishes the greatest fire quickly, as though into separate coals.

In the same way, the strength of the mind represses the body’s movement when it does not permit the movements to come together. The alluring movement of the flesh, if it is not nourished by thought, does not appear to join with another.

Impure thought is the glue of alluring movements. One who willingly looks upon what is impure immediately moves the flesh violently toward what he desires through lust; and the more willingly and persistently he thinks, the more he binds shameful movements to still more shameful movements, like coals to coals.

Let the person who wishes powerfully to scatter the movements of the flesh maintain a strong guard over the mind. Agag is first divided within, so that he may likewise be divided into pieces outwardly; for one who does not allow evil thoughts to come together also divides shameful movements of the flesh, as it were, into pieces.

Thus exceedingly fat Agag is killed if he is divided into pieces: we extinguish the carnal sense and its impure movements powerfully, both in body and soul, if we watch over each of its snares with individual attentiveness.

Therefore that wise man diligently admonishes us: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds, and from a neglected heart death comes forth” (Proverbs 4:23).

Life proceeds when the heart is guarded, because, when every impurity is driven away, the spirit of the converted is stirred toward the virtues.

Agag is cut into pieces by the prophet when, through the counsel of teachers, the individual particles of impurity are destroyed both in the body and in the mind of the hearers.

He is rightly said to be cut into pieces before the Lord and at Gilgal, because those can powerfully divide the small pieces of alluring thoughts and shameful movements who know wisely how to think both about almighty God and about the holy Scriptures.

But, as I said, teachers often tolerate the simulated good deeds of the wicked not for the sake of the wicked themselves but for the sake of others. What the wicked do hypocritically benefits not the hypocrites but those who observe them.

Elect people often see the simulated good deeds of the wicked; but because they do not know their hearts, they imitate the goodness that appears to shine outwardly.

Saul asked Samuel to return with him to worship the Lord; but Samuel returned and cut Agag into pieces, because elect teachers use the works performed by the rejected to convert the elect to the pursuit of right living.

But because they do this providentially—that is, for another purpose—when the need for such an arrangement has passed, they abandon the rejected themselves, whom they had followed, as it were, toward good works, once they have fallen into the impenitence of their rejected hearts.

Accordingly, it is rightly added:

> **(Verses 34–35.)** “Samuel went to Ramah, but Saul went up to his house in Gibeah; and Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death.”

41. What is the transgressor’s house except the habit of sinful action? For whoever is enclosed in a perverse habit dwells, as it were, in a house. Saul therefore ascended into his own house when each reprobate, after the teachers’ rebuke, returns to the practice of sinful action. For he descends, as it were, to level ground when he feigns humility in order to learn the commands of his superiors. But why is Samuel said to depart before Saul is said to ascend into his house? As I said, when there is no need to attend to others, an elect preacher cannot remain with a deceitful man; and because the pretender makes progress in the teacher’s absence, Saul did not go into the house but ascended. For “ascending” in the case of the reprobate means progressing from evil to worse [Col. 0445C]. When a proud man is said to descend, he is nevertheless said to ascend. For the proud man’s ascending into his own house means exalting himself through pride up to the measure [Note: [Col. 0445D] Gilot., “by which he was condemned”] at which he is to be condemned. The house of the proud is, in fact, the measure of his wickedness. While they are permitted, through the prosperity of the world, to exercise tyranny, disturb the earth, oppress the good, and afflict the innocent, what else do they appear to do but ascend? But because God has predetermined how much they may harm, how fiercely they may rage, and how far they may exalt themselves through tyranny, they are permitted to ascend as far as their own house. Their house is the measure of their wickedness, in which they will always remain, because when they have reached the fullness of their crimes, they are seized by death and punished through eternal torments. The one who can never leave the punishments of his way of life remains, as it were, in a house. This can properly be understood not only of the proud but also of the lustful and of all the reprobate. Those of whom it is said, “The sins of the Amorites have not yet reached their full measure” (Genesis 15:16), were still in the ascent and not yet in the house. Likewise, the blessed apostle Paul says: “So as to fill up their sins” (1 Thessalonians 2:16). They therefore ascend to the house when, by progressing in evil, they advance to more wicked deeds, for which they will endure eternal torments.

42. Samuel, however, is said to depart to Ramah. Teachers separated from the reprobate do not merely go; they depart. They go when they abandon those who are to be corrected, because those whom they dismiss as if in anger they later return to when invited by their good amendment. The teacher’s departure, therefore, is the abandonment of the unrepentant wicked through perpetual judgment. Thus they abandon those who work sins leading to death through impenitence, so that they are no longer compelled to return to them. Therefore he rightly said: “Saul did not see Samuel again until the day of his death.” And because they perceive that this must be done in the contemplation of supreme truth, Samuel is said to depart to Ramah. For completed vision is the perfect understanding of intimate truth. So that the strictness of preachers may not seem excessive to worldly people when they separate the reprobate permanently from communion with the Church, let them listen: after Samuel came to Ramah, Saul did not see him again, because that teacher eternally separates the one whom he recognizes as not belonging to the number of the elect. But this is believed confidently if, in the figure of Samuel, the stricter expression of the holy Church’s charitable affection is observed in preachers [Col. 0446B]. For the zeal of severity is shown by the statement that Saul did not see him until the day of his death. Concerning the affection of charity, however, it is added:

**(Verse 35.) Nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul, because the Lord regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.**

43. For what does it mean that he mourns one whom he disdains to see, except that holy teachers, even when they outwardly display the zeal of righteousness, also possess an affection of great charity? The greatness of that charity is shown precisely because he is said to mourn the rejected king [Col. 0446C]. With what affection, then, do they mourn the sins of their elect subjects, when they have learned to mourn so tenderly for rejected reprobates? The intensity of the mourning is shown by what follows:

## CHAPTER III

**(1 Samuel 16:1.)** The Lord said to Samuel: “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from reigning over Israel?”

1. When someone is asked, “How long will you mourn?”, he is shown to be mourning continually. Great, therefore, is the affection of the saints, even when they outwardly express the severity of vengeance. For outwardly they rage, but inwardly they melt with love. Like mothers, they beat their little children, yet in affection they grieve with the children whom they discipline. But what does the Lord’s saying, “How long will you mourn for Saul?” mean? Can a mother see her dying child and not weep at all through the rending of her innards [Col. 0446D]? She who endures her child dead without mourning is herself dying, though she is merely sick. What, then, does he mean by saying, “How long will you mourn for Saul?” Is it not that the lost are not to be mourned excessively? For a teacher is often deeply distressed over the destruction of a subject, but is consoled by consideration of supreme justice. What, then, does God’s saying this to the prophet mean except that, through inward consolation, he relieves the preacher’s mind from grief? And because, when rulers fall, the elect are appointed in their place through divine mercy, the Lord adds:

**(Verse 1.)** “Fill your horn with oil and come; I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite. For I have provided a king for myself from among his sons.”

2. As if consoling him in his mourning, he says: “Why is the rejected man mourned when a better one is appointed in his place?” Thus Saul is shown not to have been provided for, whereas David was provided for. Let us consider briefly how great and what kind of man he was, since he was appointed by the judgment and choice of almighty God. What does it mean that God makes provision and the prophet is sent to anoint, except that the spiritual customs of the holy Church are being described? The Church is seen to establish no one unless it first contemplates God choosing and predestining him. “Come,” he says; “I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite. For I have provided a king for myself from among his sons.” It is as though he said: “Presume nothing on your own, but follow in the ordering of the one whom I have foreseen.” Hence shortly afterward he adds: “You shall anoint the one whom I show you.” What does this mean except that those who wish to appoint others to the summit of the Church ought to be prophets? They can recognize one foreseen by God if, in order to find the person to be chosen as bishop, they consult the sacred Scriptures. It is as though God were speaking when such a shepherd is chosen as is commended by sacred eloquence.

Literally, Samuel is told by the Lord to come so that he may be recalled from compassion for the reprobate and rejected king. If he was persistently seeking the restoration of the fallen man through mourning, his coming meant ceasing from such an intention. And he filled his horn with oil because, in anointing the king, he tempered pastoral exaltation with the radiance of praise. With the harsh horn he attacked Saul, because he struck down the sinner as if with a great assault, saying: “Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you, so that you shall not be king” (1 Samuel 15:23). What, then, does the command that the horn be filled with oil mean except that the justice of the king to be anointed is being commended? It is as though he said: “The king who is now being anointed is not to be struck with rebuke but praised with remarkable favor. He does not need to be attacked but supported.”

He is sent to Jesse the Bethlehemite so that the king who is chosen may be taught to be one who will remain. Through the patriarch Jacob, the condition of a kingdom destined to endure was shown long beforehand, for he said: “The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor a ruler from his thighs, until the one who is to be sent comes” (Genesis 49:10). The king is therefore declared to have been foreseen among Jesse’s sons, so that the king commanded to be anointed may be shown to be enduring, not like Saul, who would depart. It is as though he rouses the prophet, wasting away in distress over the rejected man, saying: “Why is one rejected for his fault mourned, when one worthy of praise is appointed in his place?”

3. We have touched on these matters literally; now, beneath the literal narrative, let us examine the election of our own rulers [Col. 0447D]. What does the command to fill the horn with oil mean except that in the holy Church such a pastor is to be chosen as should not be reproved as a transgressor but commended to others’ example with extraordinary praise?
