The horn is an animal’s weapon. What else are the authority and rebuke of the supreme bishop but weapons? They strike with the horn when the sharp points of rebuke are applied to sinners. To strike with the horn is to reprove sinners sharply. The horn is filled with oil when the preacher’s exaltation has not the harshness of threats but the soothing appeal of favor. Or the horn is filled with oil when the chosen pastor receives both the exalted dignity of office and the power of anointing—when he ascends to a high rank and, being raised to lofty things, is filled with an abundance of merits. Priests are therefore anointed with a full horn when they reach the highest rank with a fullness of graces.

Since fire is kindled with oil, the doctor’s oil is the love of the heart. Fire is kindled in it because, in the richness of speech, the power and grace of the Holy Spirit burn. Since a teacher ought to possess the richness of great charity, the king who is commanded to be anointed is said to be anointed with a full horn. The fullness of the horn may also signify perseverance in grace, for those who fail before the end do not deserve to be anointed with the fullness of the horn.

Something further must be said about the fullness of this horn: it is commanded because one who must fill others from his own fullness needs a great anointing. Hence Moses is also said to have been so full that the Lord is taught to have taken from his spirit and given to others (Numbers 11). Or the prophet’s horn is filled when the episcopal dignity is prepared to teach more perfect things. When leaders of the Church are appointed, what they ought to do must not be preached to them in half-measures. Bishops therefore fill the horn when they display full and perfect virtues for the chosen leaders of the Church to imitate.

Since those who anoint ought themselves to be spiritual, they are commanded to fill the horn. The horn is indeed made of flesh, but it is not enclosed within flesh. The horn, therefore, is the teacher’s spiritual manner of life. The horn pours out oil when the one who proclaims lofty things demonstrates them through a lofty way of life. To fill the horn with oil is to undertake the proclamation of great virtues through an elevated manner of life. It pours upon the head when it impresses these things upon the mind of one who newly comes to the highest order [Col. 0448C]. When the elect are promoted, they are anointed with a full horn because they advance to the height of office through the virtue of perfection.

4. But the prophet is sent to Jesse the Bethlehemite, and a king is provided from among his sons, because that pastor is chosen who has been instructed in ecclesiastical religion. Bethlehem, therefore, which is called “house of bread,” signifies nothing other than each religious household. By the name of bread, the teaching of perfection is indicated, as Paul testifies. Raising the weak toward conversion, he says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food. For you were not yet able—and even now you are not able” (1 Corinthians 3:2). If milk belongs to little children, bread belongs only to the perfect. Hence it was said of the strength of the perfect man: “He shall dwell in the heights; the fortress of rocks shall be his exaltation; bread shall be given to him” (Isaiah 25:12).

The king is therefore sought for anointing in the house of bread, because those who are nourished in the order of a perfect way of life are rightly promoted. For the one who has not been nourished by a lax and negligent manner of life can make others strong. Bread is sought in the house, because when promoting a bishop, the strength of his manner of life must be sought. A person of virtue is almost never taken from a weak congregation. Thus he is rightly sought among Jesse’s sons, for Jesse is called either “the salvation of the Lord” or simply “salvation.” A ruler is rightly called salvation. For what are sins and vices except illnesses of souls? The chosen preacher is rightly called “the salvation of the Lord” through the integrity of sound doctrine, the solidity of innocence, and the radiance of a chosen life.

There are other teachers whose speech spreads like cancer. A king is not taken from their household, because such a teacher does not lead sick minds to salvation but destroys them. It should also be noted that Isai is called by another name, namely, Jesse. He has a double name because a good teacher is not always at peace. In a time of peace he is called “the salvation of the Lord,” so that he may be taught to heal the spoils of wars as though within the secure vestibules of a house. In war, however, he bears the name Jesse, because he strongly fortifies himself and valiantly protects others.

Jesse is said to mean “relief of the islands.” What are understood by the name “islands” except minds surrounded by the waves of temptations? They are islands because, although they endure great conflicts, they are not moved. Hence the Psalmist, proclaiming the victory of the elect, says: “The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands be glad” (Psalm 96:1). The Lord reigns when no storm of enemies disturbs his seat—that is, the elect minds. The earth rejoices because the solid hearts of teachers give thanks. The islands rejoice because, when they overcome temptations through his grace, the hearers of their elders are gladdened.

The earth is the strong mind and steadfast tongue of the teacher. The island is the strong heart of a subject, which is still assailed by temptations but is nevertheless not moved. What, then, does it mean that Jesse is called “relief of the islands,” except that through the strength of teachers the hearts of the lesser are raised? They would fall amid so many waves of temptations if the strength of their elders did not lift their hearts toward the desire for an exalted life [Col. 0449C].

The king is therefore described as hidden among the sons of Isai and Jesse, because those usefully come to the summit of the Church who have learned through the teaching of the elect both to preserve and order peace and to wage spiritual wars. Thus it is rightly said: “For I have provided a king for myself among his sons.” A king is provided among these and not among others because, through divine grace, no one reaches the summit of the Church who does not follow the teaching of the elect through every stage of time.

The text continues:

**(Verses 2–3.)** Samuel said: “How shall I go? Saul will hear of it and kill me.” And the Lord said: “You shall take a calf from the herd in your hand, and say: ‘I have come to sacrifice to the Lord.’ You shall invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you are to do.”

5. What is shown by these words except that the cunning and cruelty of tyrants must sometimes be outwitted by a pious deception? At the Lord’s command, a calf is taken from the herd, a sacrifice is feigned, and the royal anointing is attained, because when tyrants desire to cause harm, certain things must be placed before them for them to believe, so that they may find no opportunity to do harm. Tyrants must be outwitted in such a way that the guilt of lying is avoided. This is properly accomplished when what is asserted is in fact done, but what is done is expressed in such a way that it remains concealed—because it is partly stated and partly withheld.

The prophet Samuel is commanded to go to anoint the king and to declare that he is going to sacrifice to the Lord, not that he is going to anoint a king. Thus, by sacrificing, he speaks truth; and by concealing the anointing, he outwits the tyrant’s cruelty while speaking truth. That he went intending to sacrifice he makes clear shortly afterward, where he says: “So Samuel sanctified Jesse and his sons, and called them to the sacrifice.”

6. But let us now proceed more fruitfully by examining what these things signify spiritually. What does it mean that the prophet takes the calf in his hand and thus reaches the point of anointing the king? What is the calf except the splendor of the Redeemer’s image? Because the one whom he chooses he strives to make conformable to the Redeemer, whenever he preaches the Redeemer’s very form he carries, as it were, a calf in his hand. And because he shows in the power of his deeds the splendor of the Lord’s manner of life that he proclaims, he leads by his hand the calf that he takes from the herd. To take the calf in one’s hand is to preserve the preaching of the Lord’s manner of life in the power of one’s deeds.

Going in this way, he is not killed; otherwise he would be killed, because one who speaks and does not act is condemned by the sword of his own mouth. What does the command to say, “I have come to sacrifice to the Lord,” mean? And what does it mean that he does what he says, coming and sacrificing, except that the one who promotes others must be so effective that he not only speaks good things but persuades others of them?

The sacrificial victim that appears in the prophet’s hand is recognized on the altar. For what is the heart of an elect hearer except God’s altar? When a good teacher speaks with his mouth and demonstrates through his works, the calf is in his hand. But when he persuades his hearers of what he both says and does, the victim is on the altar. He sacrifices, then, when elect hearts receive through love what shines forth in the teacher’s word and example, for imitation of the Redeemer.

The text continues: “And you shall invite Jesse to the sacrifice.” Perhaps this passage suggests that subjects who are to be promoted should not be advanced without the knowledge of their superiors. Jesse is first invited to the sacrifice so that the good deed which the subject is seen to undertake may be established in the mind of his teacher. It is rightly added: “And I will show you what you are to do.” Expressing the same point, he says:

**(Verse 3.)** “And you shall anoint the one whom I show you.”

7. Unless Jesse is first invited, the things that must be done will not be disclosed to him, because nothing concerning a subject is to be done without the teacher’s consent. Once he has been invited, what must be done is shown, because the humility of a subject is raised to the height of leadership with the consent of a religious teacher.

What does the statement, “You shall anoint the one whom I show you,” mean except that not all disciples of an elect pastor are equal? Some are useful for obeying; others both obey humbly and have learned to command with discretion. He therefore says: “You shall anoint the one whom I show you,” so that when a person is sought for the summit of priesthood, he may be sought with great discernment.

By these words, nothing of their own is left to those who order the Churches in the election of others. “The one,” he says, “whom I show you—you shall anoint.” Who are those who anoint people whom God does not show, except those who bring forward for the summit of the Churches persons chosen through carnal affection? They do not distinguish merits but accept persons. They anoint kings, but not those shown by God. They do what is their own and take away what belongs to God.

To show God’s person is to provide the anointing of the one who orders. When they themselves point out whom they will anoint, they refuse to have God as their collaborator. Hence through the prophet Hosea the Lord complains of such chosen men, saying: “They reigned, not through me; they became princes, and I did not know” (Hosea 8:5).

The elect are therefore told what the reprobate cannot hear: “You shall anoint the one whom I show you,” so that no one may be promoted unless he is judged worthy of so great an office by the praise of the holy Scriptures. In those Scriptures the Lord speaks; there it is recorded what kind and how great the teacher of the Church ought to be. The one shown by the Lord is therefore chosen who is commended through sacred eloquence.

The wicked rulers despise these things; the good do them. Concerning the obedience of the good, it is rightly added:

**(Verse 4.)** Samuel did what the Lord had spoken to him. He came to Bethlehem, and the elders of the city were astonished and came out to meet him.

8. Historically, the elders are astonished because the prophet was not accustomed to come there. This perhaps signifies that elect teachers should rarely be seen in public; they should be frequent in seclusion, free from civic affairs, and filled with spiritual things. The appearance of the shepherd in public therefore becomes a wonder to the people. They marvel that he has come out, since they knew him as a lover of seclusion. Because he is raised in great veneration by the people, the elders of the city are reported both to have been astonished and to have come out to meet him.

Since it is not the people but the elders who are astonished, the perfect virtue of teachers is indicated, for they are praised not by little ones and the simple but by the great and learned. They also inquire about the prophet’s peaceful arrival. The one who said, “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Corinthians 4:21) was threatening, as it were, a non-peaceful arrival. What, then, does the statement mean:

**(Verse 4.)** “Is your arrival peaceful?”

9. It means that the faithful elect, when they rightly consider the actions of spiritual teachers, discern God’s will in them. Since they knew Samuel to be a prophet, they also knew that he had learned the secrets of divine dispensation. When, therefore, they ask about a peaceful arrival, what else do they do by asking than show their desire to know the secret of the divine plan?

Would that whenever we see holy men, we too might strive to inquire about the security of our peace and diligently learn from them how God sees us, since we do not possess the eyes of self-knowledge. The arrival of teachers is peaceful when they come to those who are not to be struck for their fault but praised for their righteousness.

The one who had come to promote a just man therefore answered:

**(Verse 5.)** “Peaceful. I have come to sacrifice to the Lord. Sanctify yourselves and come with me, so that we may sacrifice.”

10. Those who direct their intention toward heavenly things go with teachers so that they may sacrifice. The prophet sacrifices in the presence of those who go with him when the teacher binds to the hearts of those standing by through love what he proclaims in words.

But let us attend briefly to the historical sense and examine carefully the statement: “Sanctify yourselves and come with me.” If no one dares to take part with those sacrificing unless sanctified, what must be thought about those who sacrifice? To sanctify is to cleanse. How pure, then, ought bishops to be, when the peoples invited to the sacrifice are admitted only if sanctified?

The sanctification of the body is chastity; the sanctification of the mind is charity and humility. Let the one invited to the sacrifice therefore be sanctified—but let the one who invites him be compelled to this even more. Let priests observe what they say to those whom they invite: “Come with me.” They come with them sanctified if clean priests approach God’s service together with clean peoples. To go with them is to approach together with the clean.

For if the peoples are clean but the priests are not, they do not come with them, because they do not approach according to an equal order of purity. Let such priests hear what another prophet admonishes: “Cleanse yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52:11). Let them also hear what he says: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah 1:16).

Because the peoples must be cleansed, he says: “Sanctify yourselves.” Because, moreover, the highest men must always remain in a continuous state of purity and draw others toward the pattern of their own purity, he adds: “And come with me.”

But because the elders are invited to the sacrifice, what do they demonstrate typologically except that many wise and religious men must be summoned to choose a bishop, or to anoint and consecrate him? They are sanctified and come if they resolve to follow nothing carnal in that election. For them, to be sanctified is to bring a spiritual and holy intention to bestow the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

In the type of the elect, it is rightly said both of Jesse and of his sons:

**(Verse 5.)** So Samuel sanctified Jesse and his sons, and called them to the sacrifice.

11. Since we have shown through the sacred words that the Lord indicates those who are to be chosen as bishops, let us now see what kind of persons he indicates and what kind he rejects, as the mysteries of this sacred history unfold through the words that follow:

**(Verses 6–7.)** When they had entered, he saw Eliab and said: “Is the Lord’s anointed before the Lord?” And the Lord said to Samuel: “Do not look at his face, nor at the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I do not judge according to human appearance” [Note: [Col. 0451D] Gilot. and Vatican manuscripts: “for he does not see”]. “For man sees what appears, but the Lord looks upon the heart.”

What does it mean for the wise to enter except to enter the sanctuary of subtle discernment? But he saw Eliab enter because the pastor recognizes as worthy of leadership in the holy Church one who possesses both strength in good works and knowledge of the truth.

What does the Lord’s command that he look neither at Eliab’s stature nor at his face mean except that in the holy Church neither work nor knowledge is praised without humility? For what is someone’s face except his outward manner of life, by which he is known? And what is his stature except the height of knowledge, by which he is raised toward higher things? Whom, then, does Eliab more fittingly signify than those who do good and are learned, but arrogant?

Hence Eliab is interpreted as “My God is father.” This is precisely what his name dares to presume. What does it mean that he is called “My God is father” except that, while doing good works bravely and understanding spiritual things wisely, they boast that through their singular merit they have passed into the number of God’s children? They would call the almighty Lord not “my Father” but “our Father” if, through humility, they recognized themselves as sharing with the other elect in the order of heavenly generation.

He is therefore rightly rejected, because only the humble are placed in spiritual high office. The prophet therefore subtly inquires about the person to be anointed, saying: “Is the Lord’s anointed before the Lord?” This is what happens when the supreme teacher recognizes both the life and understanding of the one to be chosen but still investigates the virtue of humility.

He sees that Eliab’s face and stature have been rejected when he recognizes whatever beauty he possesses in his conduct and whatever height he possesses in his learning, yet sees that he lacks the virtue of humility. The Lord therefore rightly says: “I have rejected him; I do not judge according to human appearance, because man looks at the face, but God looks upon the heart.” It is as though he said: “Human beings customarily praise great works and words of knowledge; but I do not praise words or works that I do not see to be founded upon true humility.”

Those who are such would tremble at the rejection of their unworthiness if they wished to hear attentively what the Lord says to the prophet: “Do not look at his face, nor at the height of his stature, because I have rejected him.” They consider what the arrogant do to be something great; but behold, the Lord says that it is so worthless that he judges it unworthy even to be regarded.

With Eliab removed, what follows is shown:

**(Verse 8.)** Jesse called Aminadab and brought him before Samuel. He said: “The Lord has not chosen this one either.”

12. Aminadab is interpreted as “urbane.” He is therefore rightly rejected after the Lord has been consulted, because the holy Church does not choose for the governance of souls someone energetic in worldly affairs but someone adorned with a spiritual way of life. Those are “urbane” who, setting aside their intention toward heavenly things, strive to display their energy in outward pursuits. The Lord therefore did not choose this one either, because the flocks of the faithful ought to be cared for through a pious pastor’s concern for heavenly things, not earthly ones—not through what is weak and passing, but through what is exalted and eternal.

**(Verse 9.)** Then he brought Shammah, of whom he also said: “The Lord has not chosen this one either.”

13. Shammah is interpreted as “hearing.” What, then, does Shammah signify except the obedient and simple? For them, hearing means fulfilling through obedience what they are commanded by their elders. Hence the Psalmist says concerning the obedience of the Gentile people: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Psalm 18:45).

What does it mean that they are said not to be chosen by the Lord except that the unlearned humble are not placed at the summit of the Church, but humble and wise men, who know both how to do what is commanded and how to command wisely? He ought both to act and to teach. Let him act humbly, therefore, and teach wisely.

Because those who know how to act through humility but do not know how to command through learning are not to be assumed into royal dignity, Shammah is said not to be chosen by the Lord for kingship. From this, let the simple and disobedient learn how perilously they thrust themselves forward to preside, if almighty God does not even accept for governance one who is called “hearing” because of the humility of obedience.

And because the holy Church has many of this kind—both simple and well-living people and humble wise men—the text continues:

**(Verse 10.)** So Jesse brought all his sons before Samuel. And Samuel said: “The Lord has not chosen any of these.”

14. That perfection is customarily signified by the number seven is attested by the prophet Isaiah. Affirming that the gifts of the Holy Spirit would remain upon our Redeemer, he says: “The spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11:2).

What, then, does it mean that these men, because they are rejected from the ministry of preaching, are represented by the number seven, since that same number signifies perfection, which no one possesses except through the infusion of the Holy Spirit? This is rightly asserted because grace of the Holy Spirit is given to many for living well but not given for teaching. Since they are numerous and perfect in good works, they are aptly contained under the number seven.

Moreover, because they do strong things but do not understand subtle ones, they are rejected from governing the kingdom. Thus there are seven sons, and none of them is assumed to govern souls, because although they know how to govern themselves strongly by living well, they cannot by teaching protect others with strength.

Let the Church’s ordinator never rush so precipitously in appointing someone. Even if he has many who are not suitable to undertake the care of souls, there cannot be none who can preside. Let the teacher therefore seek insistently; let him not cease seeking until he can discover those who are hidden.

The great virtues of the elect are almost always hidden, like treasures of almighty God. Almighty God acts like wealthy men who are careful with their riches: lest he lose the treasures of virtues, he places them in elect minds and conceals those minds in secrecy. Let the one who desires to order—or rather, adorn—the head of the Church seek hidden treasures. He desires to adorn Christ’s bride, but he cannot do so unless he brings forth the Bridegroom’s hidden treasures for her adornment, and does not cease until he finds what lies hidden.

But why do I urge pastors to seek, when they cannot find them unless God brings forth the hidden [ones—perhaps to be read for the corrupt “eyes”]?  What else does “You shall anoint the one whom I show you” mean? Nevertheless, they must be sought, because they are scarcely shown unless they have been sought for a long time. The Lord promises to show them, yet the prophet strives to seek so that he may deserve to find. Hence the Lord commands persistence in seeking, saying: “Seek and you will find; ask and you will receive; knock and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7).

What, then, does the prophet seeking, and persevering in seeking after so many have already been rejected, signify to us except that we must not allow [perhaps: that they may not be allowed] the unworthy to come to the summit of religion under any pretext? For although prudent discretion is beneficial in many matters of the holy Church, it is plainly deadly and destructive when either the blind through ignorance, or irreligious men who are wise, or those devoted to worldly affairs, are permitted to rise to primacy over others.

The former destroy the souls of their subjects through ignorance; the latter through knowledge without action; and still others by neglecting spiritual things and pursuing carnal and earthly ones. The former labor with all their strength so that what they say may be praised; the latter do not know what to say. The former strive with all their intention to be honored more abundantly among the great of this world. These are certainly worse than the former, to the extent that the former wish to appear exalted in spiritual matters, while these wish to appear exalted in carnal and worldly matters.

The end desired by such men is to be supported by riches, raised up by honors, and exalted through the companionship of the powerful of this world. From all these inclinations of the reprobate mind can arise negligence toward the souls of subjects, contempt for Christ, and the squandering of the Church’s resources.

Let the teacher therefore seek, so that he may not promote anyone unworthy under any pretext, because what is deadly must never be permitted. Hence it is added:

**Samuel said to Jesse: “Are these all your sons?”**

Why does he seek another except because the one who is seeking must not rest before he deserves to find? And because things rejected and worthless outwardly are often exalted inwardly, the text continues:

**(Verse 11.)** He answered: “There still remains one, and he is tending the sheep.”

15. What does “remaining” mean except “rejected”? I call him rejected from himself, not from God, because someone is rejected by God through pride, while he is rejected from himself when he is regarded as worthless and humble. Or he is called “remaining” because, in comparison with the others, he does not appear to be anything.

He is therefore called a rejected humble man because he sees that he is despised and endures it; he makes no effort to display himself, but tends the sheep, because he nourishes simple thoughts in contemplation of the eternal inheritance. Concerning these pastures of the elect, the Lord says: “They will enter and go out and find pastures” (John 10:9). Within, they have the pastures of contemplation; outwardly, the pastures of good works. Within, they enrich their minds with devotions; outwardly, they satisfy themselves with pious works.

This little one is rightly said to tend sheep, because every elect person who is humble is not barren: he does great things daily but does not think great things of himself. He is rightly described not only as little but also as a shepherd, because those who are truly humble abase themselves outwardly, but through inward fellowship remain among the highest and in eternal pastures.

For it is written: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5). What grace? The grace to see and know sublime things, to know and love them, and to run toward those beloved things like well-nourished and strong people.

Since this man is therefore very suitable, he is commanded to be brought without delay. For the text continues:

**(Verse 11.)** Samuel said to Jesse: “Send and bring him, for we will not sit down until he comes.”

## 16

What, then, does “We shall not recline until he comes” mean? Whom does he seek, unless it is because the sacraments of anointing are to be celebrated in the observance of fasting? For us, however, attention must be paid not only to the sacraments themselves but also to the force of the sacraments. There are indeed certain foods which, if they are not avoided, by no means permit one to anoint kings properly.

The external affairs of the Church are, in a certain sense, foods of the soul, and the elect administer them devoutly. But if the soul is filled to satiety by the multitude of these affairs, it is not permitted to enter fully into the reception of spiritual things. Therefore, when spiritual matters press upon us, let external matters be postponed, because the former must be arranged with great tranquillity of mind. It follows:

> **(Verse 12.)** “Therefore he sent and brought him.”

The future king is brought forth when the humble are led out from the hiding places of their concealment. They are hidden, indeed, but in the pastures; for although they conceal themselves from human beings within the lowliness and weakness of the flesh, there is a great expanse of heavenly contemplation in which they dwell. But let us see what kind of ruler he already appears to be. For it follows and says:

> **(Verse 12.)** “Now he was ruddy, handsome in appearance, and comely in face.”

## 17

What does it mean that the king is asserted to possess such great beauty, unless it is because the person of the teacher ought to be adorned with the great radiance of virtues? For it is said of the Redeemer:

> [Note: [Col. 0455D] Corruptly printed in other editions: “By his spirit he adorned the heavens.”]

> “His spirit adorned the heavens” (Job 26:13).

The heavens are the sublime preachers. These heavens have indeed been adorned by the Spirit, because they receive from the Holy Spirit the virtues by which they shine.

What does it mean, then, that he is said to be ruddy, unless it is because the fervor of charity is often signified by the color red? Hence scarlet, twice dyed, is placed in the priest’s vestment, so that he may be clothed with a twofold charity. He is therefore called ruddy because of the ardor of charity: while he displays charity’s burning commandments, he becomes red, as it were, through the heat.

What, again, does “handsome in appearance” mean, unless it is being conspicuous through inward contemplation? For he seems to have a handsome appearance who shines with the beauty of vision in inward contemplation.

What, then, does the face signify unless the outward glory of moral integrity? Since each person is recognized by the face, the beauty of the face is the splendid integrity of one’s manner of life. For he seems to be discerned by the beauty of his face who is found to be radiant in every bodily gesture.

Thus he is ruddy in love, handsome in appearance because of knowledge, comely in face, and splendid in integrity. Since, however, the fervor of charity is demonstrated through holy works, the labor of action itself may be signified by redness. One who labors intensely displays redness in his face: as he grows hot within, he draws redness outward into his countenance.

Such is all spiritual labor. The more each person strives to labor for eternal life, the more fervently he is kindled to labor by the ardor of the Holy Spirit; and, as he grows hot, he arouses a redness which he carries outwardly. The teacher, therefore, is ruddy through the labor of pious action and handsome in appearance through the radiance of contemplation.

The beauty of the face, however, is the very beauty of charity. Through the other virtues we receive the form of holiness; through charity itself we clothe that form in ourselves, as it were, with marvelous beauty. Those other virtues are the body of righteousness, while charity is rightly understood as the face of that body. For each person is recognized by the face, not by the body. If you see the body but do not see the face, you do not recognize the person whose body alone you observe.

What else, then, is meant by the bridegroom’s reply to the foolish virgins, “I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12)? Behold, virginity is preserved through great labors, and virginity itself is recognized as a great and incomparable virtue. Why, then, are the foolish virgins not recognized by the bridegroom, unless because they have a body by which they endure but do not have the beauty of face which the bridegroom recognizes? They possess labor in preserving the body, but they do not possess the beauty of countenance found in perfect charity.

These three qualities advance in the life of the elect in the order in which they are set forth. No one can attain beautiful contemplative visions unless he has first exercised himself vigorously in the labor of pious action. The joys of eternal light—the immensity of that supreme radiance, that eternal vigor of ineffable splendor—open themselves more generously to those who seek them, the more laboriously they are sought.

One who is already such a person is seen to be suitable for teaching. But unless he shines with a comely face, unless he bears a mind illumined by the rays of perfect charity, he is not judged worthy of such great eminence. Let the shepherd, then, be ruddy and not slack in his work; let him be handsome in appearance, that is, let contemplation within him be sublime; let him be comely in face, so that the whole strength of his work and the height of his contemplation, known to the eyes of heavenly majesty, may be displayed through the ineffable beauty of charity.

Since these three are the insignia of immense beauty which the teacher of the holy Church ought to possess, Peter is chosen on behalf of them all, and is asked three times whether he loves the Redeemer. First he is asked, “Peter, do you love me?” (John 21:16), so that through love he may strive to accomplish courageous deeds; second, so that through contemplation he may know lofty things; third, so that through the affection of perfect charity he may burn both toward his neighbor and, with greater fervor, toward the vision of the Creator.

Let us therefore hear by what testimony such a great and beautiful, such a comely boy, is presented. For it follows:

> **(Verse 12.)** “Arise and anoint him, for this is he.”

## 18

What does “Arise and anoint him” mean? Was the boy so tall that he could not be anointed while sitting? While sitting, we cannot touch lofty things. Great, therefore, is the virtue, great the exaltation of the humble, if even prophets do not reach their heights.

The prophet therefore rises when the bishop raises himself to a wondrous reverence for the chosen preacher. Outwardly, he sees him as humble, as though before his eyes; but inwardly he does not recognize his merit unless he raises himself in inward contemplation.

The teacher is therefore commanded to rise, because before he can bestow such great sacraments upon the one to whom he wishes to give them, he must first recognize the sublimity of that person’s merits.

What, then, does “Arise and anoint him, for this is he” mean, unless: “Provide sublime sacraments sublimely to one who is sublime”? For often undiscerning shepherds know that the life of those who approach is negligent and reprobate, yet they do not hesitate to promote them. These men anoint but do not rise, because they do not perceive those to whom they give the sacraments of anointing as occupying a lofty position of merit.

Therefore, when a teacher is shown to be sublime, his ordainer is admonished to rise; for the sacraments of anointing are then worthily bestowed through the ministry when the one to be anointed is seen to possess the lofty eminence of virtue.

Of him, when it is said, “For this is he,” the meaning is: if this is he, there is no other; for unless he shines with these virtues, he cannot attain the rank of such eminence. The one whom the Lord promised to show, ruddy, handsome in appearance, and comely in face, he presents by saying, “For this is he.” No one ought to ascend the summit of rule who does not possess the strength of great action—namely, knowledge of contemplation and fervor of charity.

Accordingly, it is rightly added:

> **(Verse 13.)** “Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers.”

## 19

The horn of oil is taken up, so that the whole life of the bishop may be taught to be spiritual. The horn of oil is taken up, so that, in the excellence of this liquid, the teacher of the Church may strive to be a man of great mercy.

The king’s head is anointed with oil because he ought to shine upon the lampstand through the flame of the word. The horn receives oil so that it may cleanse by reproving and draw by gentle compassion through mercy. It also receives the oil, in the sublimity of its office, for the fostering of virtue.

He is anointed with a full horn so that the bishop’s virtue may be shown to be complete. The horn is full in its anointing when he is perfect both in the virtue of mercy and in charity and the word. He is also known to possess a full horn in his anointing when all his authority is administered through mercy.

The authority of the holy Church itself is nothing when it is without mercy, because the rigor of spiritual discipline is truly spiritual only when it is not deprived of the soothing application of mercy. The horn and the oil are therefore displayed together, so that discipline may always be maintained with mercy.

The horn is said to be full of oil so that wherever the horn displays its sharpness, it may also display the anointing of poured-out grace. But while the anointing is carried in order to anoint the king, the horn is visible outwardly, while the fullness of the oil is hidden within.

Let the prophet therefore carry the horn outwardly and fill it with oil inwardly; let him convey the text outwardly and explain the sacraments inwardly. Let the prophet know what he is giving; let the anointed king, by receiving what has been given, know what he is to do.

What, then, does it mean that there is a horn outwardly and oil inwardly, unless that the hardness of subjects often deserves to feel the shepherd’s reproof but does not attend to something of his mercy? The ruler therefore displays the horn in which the oil lies hidden: when someone is sharply corrected out of charity, punishment is felt but charity is not seen.

A savage ruler is perceived, one who reproves as though he did not love and rebukes as though he vehemently hated. What is then visible to the contrite person except the sharpness of the horn, by which he is struck more harshly? But because the shepherd first loves inwardly the one whom he strikes outwardly by reproving him, what does he show other than the horn in reproving and conceal the oil in loving?

The horn is therefore asserted to be full in the king’s anointing, so that both qualities may be taught to be perfect in the chosen preacher. He ought to be sharp in reproving and gentle in showing mercy. Let him strike perfectly, so that he may completely pierce the disease’s entire force; let him anoint perfectly through mercy, so that he may restore to health the wounds which he pricks.

If he strikes less violently than he ought, he does not expel what is hidden to a sufficient degree. And if he strikes violently but does not anoint abundantly, he kills the wounded person through severity and does not restore him to health. Let the horn therefore be whole, and the fullness of the oil whole, so that wounds may be struck austerely by the horn and soothed by the oil.

## 20

But what does it mean that he is anointed in the midst of his brothers, unless that he is commanded to scatter examples of virtue all around? He is anointed in the midst of his brothers so that all may be able to share in such an anointing.

For one who is placed in the middle is seen from every side. He is anointed with oil in the midst of others because one who has been placed as an example to others ought not to have any part of himself obscure, so that all may look upon him and receive from him an example of light.

Hence the holy living creatures are described as having eyes all around them (Ezekiel 1), because the chosen teacher, when he receives from the gift of the Holy Spirit the ardor of charity, the virtue of mercy, and zeal for uprightness, dwells, as it were, within a sphere of light which makes him shine on every side for those who surround him.

Alternatively, he is anointed in the midst of his brothers so that he may always regard himself as both anointed and in the middle. Let him recognize his dignity and exercise the power of his dignity, because he has been anointed. Let him see himself as in the middle and as a man of the common condition, so that he may recognize those over whom he is elevated as his equals.

He is therefore anointed in the midst of his brothers so that he may be humble and exalted: exalted in rank, humble in estimation. Again, he is anointed in the midst so that he may not love himself with private affection but may seek the gain of others from everything in which he excels.

Hence Saul is also said to have been anointed alone in the remotest part of the city (1 Samuel 9). What does it mean that he is anointed alone by one person, unless that he was destined to swell with private love because of the power of his eminence? When he wished to love himself uniquely because of the dignity he had received, he carried the nourishment of light alone, as it were.

Hence the boy who accompanied him is sent ahead, because none of the elect follows the example of one who is rejected by divine authority. David, therefore, is anointed in the midst of his brothers because the chosen teacher does not at all glory in private love because of the unique eminence to which he has been raised.

And because spiritual gifts in chosen rulers are increased through the ministry of human beings, it is added:

> **(Verse 13.)** “And the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day and thereafter.”

## 21

The Spirit of the Lord is directed after the anointing because outwardly we receive the sacraments so that inwardly we may be filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Outwardly, a human being acts; inwardly, God acts, and not a human being. Outwardly, a human being rises; inwardly, the Spirit directs him, because a human being confers the order of religion upon another human being, but the Spirit is directed into the one upon whom the order is bestowed, so that outwardly he may receive the dignity of the order and inwardly the strength of the Holy Spirit.

Outwardly, the order is entrusted to him so that he may do the things of God; inwardly, the Spirit is directed so that he may carry out powerfully what is commanded. The burden of the order is great, and the weakness of the flesh is great. Since so great a burden is entrusted to one who is weak, the Spirit is directed so that the weak person may be strengthened and bear the great burden with greater joy, insofar as the omnipotent Spirit more powerfully helps him to bear it.

> [Note: [Col. 0459D] Gussanville: “bear it all the more heavily.”]

But the Spirit is said to be directed so that he may be understood to have turned away from the proud king. The Spirit directs himself toward another when the grace of that same Spirit flees the proud and hypocritical. Hence it is written:

> “The Spirit of the Lord’s discipline will flee from the deceitful” (Wisdom 1:7).

Likewise, in the Gospel he says of himself:

> “The Spirit blows where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he is going” (John 3:8).

The Spirit comes and goes because he abandons the reprobate and takes up the elect. And because the judgment of almighty God is inscrutable, a person does not know where he comes from and where he goes, because it cannot be known whether someone will have to persevere forever in the grace he receives.

The Spirit is therefore said to come from one who has fallen away and to go to one who will persevere, because he abandons some in time and takes up others, yet does not abandon the latter. Hence, in the figure of the elect, it is said of David:

> “The Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day and thereafter.”

On the day of the anointing the Spirit is directed, when we receive the sacraments of Christ outwardly in such a way that inwardly we are filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. And the Spirit is directed thereafter when he never departs from the grace he has received.

We ascribe this grace of the directed Spirit to preachers in such a way that we attribute it to all the orders of the holy Church. Whoever receives the faith of our Redeemer is reborn through the baptism of our redemption and is freed from every sin by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Accordingly, the apostle Paul, indicating the gift of that same Holy Spirit to the redeemed elect, says:

> “In whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30).

If we consider the people who formerly boasted in circumcision losing the Holy Spirit, we see at the same time the direction of that same Spirit in those who have been baptized. We are directed in him because they lost the grace of the Holy Spirit through pride.

What, then, does “from that day and thereafter” mean, unless that the grace of the Holy Spirit is received in such a way that the elect are taught to persevere in it to the end? Many commit sins deserving death after the remission of sins; in them, certainly, the Spirit does not appear to be directed thereafter.

The Spirit is therefore directed thereafter in the elect alone from that day, because sins are forgiven the reprobate at the beginning of faith through the Holy Spirit, but afterward they lose the grace of the Holy Spirit through iniquity. The Spirit is directed thereafter, but in David, because *David* is interpreted as “strong of hand.”

Strong of hand is the one who prevails over the devil and holds fast through perseverance to the good he has received, even to the end. Of such people the Lord says:

> “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

But if the condition of the universal Church is considered, we see that the Spirit of the Lord was directed thereafter in David, because from the beginnings of that Church he began to fill the elect of the holy Church with the grace of the Holy Spirit, and he does not cease to preserve them until the end of the world.

## 22

Now, according to our plan, the book ought to be brought to its conclusion; but the recollection returns to us that at the beginning of the volume we referred the matter to the conduct of the Redeemer. And because through John the same Redeemer is asserted to be both beginning and end, the book is most fittingly brought to completion if it is concluded in the account of our Redeemer (Revelation 1:8).

David, therefore, “strong of hand,” signifies the Redeemer himself of the human race, who overcame the ancient enemy and took the elect away from his power. He is called the son of Jesse the Bethlehemite because he wished to be born from that people which the knowledge of the holy Scriptures had, as it were, filled with bread.

Judaea was indeed the house of bread, since in spiritual understanding it possessed, as it were from bread, the solid nourishment of the Scriptures. What, then, is Samuel except, as we have often said, a figure of the order of the new preachers? What, then, is David except an indication of the Redeemer?

Samuel is therefore sent to anoint him. To anoint him is to preach his incomparable sanctification to those who are ignorant of it. For he is anointed, as it were, when the fragrance of his renown is disclosed to those who do not know. The one who said this was anointing him:

> “For in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

But why do we accept so many new preachers for his anointing, when we also see that the ancient ones anointed him with such reverence? What smells better and more sweetly than what the prophet Isaiah poured out upon him, saying:

> “The Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him” (Isaiah 11:2).

> [Note: [Col. 0461D] Gilot and Vaticanus: “here likewise.”]

Here too David—[the text is uncertain: *qui tenetur in manibus*, “who is held in [the] hands”]—speaking to him, says:

> “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips” (Psalm 44:3).

And shortly afterward:

> “Your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”

Daniel also anointed him and provided the Jews with the sacrament of every anointing, saying:

> “When the Holy of Holies comes, your anointing will cease” (Daniel 9).

The prophet is therefore sent to anoint him, because his fragrance is never apprehended by the little ones unless it is disclosed through the mouths of preachers. Hence those three women prepare spices and anoint the Redeemer in the tomb (Mark 16).

Jesus is anointed in the tomb when the glory of his resurrection is preached. Hence, when they come, Jesus is not found: when they rightly discuss the Lord’s death, they show that the one who died has already risen. They do not find him as they come, as it were, because when they understand well the cause of his death, they discover that life has been restored through his death.

## 23

But what does it mean that he is commanded to fill the horn with oil? For what was the austerity of the Law except the sharpness of the horn? It struck like a horn because it did not forgive sins through mercy but exacted punishment by inflicting penalties.

The horn is therefore filled with oil because such a King is anointed as will mercifully forgive human sins and will not punish them through the austerity of the Law. Those who brought forward the horn of Moses said to the Lord concerning the woman who had been caught in adultery:

> “Moses commanded that such women be stoned. What do you say about her?” (John 8:15).

But the one who had been anointed with a full horn said:

> “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.”

The horn of striking had been taken up, as it were, by the one who said:

> “If this man were a prophet, he would know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner” (Luke 7:39).

But Jesus, who had been anointed from the fullness of the horn, forgave everything, saying:

> “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.”

To those who murmured about his receiving sinners he says:

> “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners” (Matthew 9:13).

The prophet is therefore sent with a full horn to anoint David, because teachers now preach the one who loosens the harshness of the Law and restores through the soothing applications of his grace everything that it had presented rigidly.

Was that man not anointing him, sent to anoint him, of whom it is said:

> “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came for testimony, to bear witness to the light” (John 1:6)?

But we have heard how he had been sent; let us hear how he anoints:

> “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold, the one who takes away the sins of the world” (ibid., 1:29).

## 24

The horn may signify the exaltation of his kingdom, namely, of the holy Church, which is great but neither austere nor proud. Concerning this horn, Anna, the mother of Samuel, says above:

> “He will exalt the horn of his Christ” (1 Samuel 2:10).

Hence Zechariah says:

> “He has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant” (Luke 1:69).

What, indeed, is the horn of salvation except the exaltation of ecclesiastical power? For what is nowhere said to the ancients is now said to the universal Church:

> “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

This raised horn is said to be full of oil because the holy Church, together with the exaltation of power, extends the inner organs of compassion.

And because, through the defect of condemned humanity, we can more easily be elevated into authority and power than bent toward gentleness and piety, he is rightly commanded to prepare not the horn but the oil. For the one who says, “Fill your horn with oil” indicates that the horn is without oil.

What does this mean except that we can even rashly become angry and reprove, but cannot bend toward mercy unless through great reflection? It is as though he says: “Fill with oil the zeal which you naturally possess; if you do not have the oil from yourself, you can have it through virtue.”

This is certainly said to the one who is sent to anoint the Redeemer, so that the one who is placed in the ministry of preaching may always strive to be rich in mercy.

## 25

> [Note: [Col. 0462D] Vaticanus and Gussanville, after “this horn,” where the sense entirely fails.]

This horn may signify the mind’s affection. It is commanded to be filled because the anointing of our Redeemer—that is, his sanctification—must first be perfectly known before it can be adequately preached. The horn is filled when the Redeemer’s holiness is rightly recognized; he is anointed with the full horn when he is preached most perfectly.

John, because he had come to anoint him by preaching, filled the horn, as it were, by knowing, so that he might be able to anoint him properly by speaking. If we wish to understand what it means to fill it by knowing well, let us hear what is said in the Gospel:

> “The word came upon John, son of Zechariah, in the wilderness” (Luke 3:2).

He therefore anointed him with the full horn: he was first perfectly instructed by the Word before he could speak of the divinity of the Word and the human nature he had assumed.

But when he came, he held a calf in his hand, because, in order to become a worthy herald of the Redeemer, he sacrificed his own flesh to God through abstinence.

The Lord himself may also be signified by the designation “calf.” What, then, does it mean that the prophet carried a calf in his hand, unless that one who wishes to reveal Jesus by preaching ought, through the mortification of the flesh, to imitate the sufferings of the one whom he preaches?

To hold a calf in one’s hand is to display the likeness of Christ’s passion in the strength of one’s actions. Otherwise, the one who comes to anoint the king is himself killed, because the preacher of truth places his own salvation in danger when he tramples underfoot by wicked conduct the word he preaches with his mouth.

Samuel, then, came to anoint the king carrying a calf in his hand, because the Lord’s precursor first presented himself as remarkable through the radiance of a heavenly way of life, and thus made known to the ignorant the goodness of such great grace.

## 26

But what does it mean that he is commanded to seek among the sons of Jesse, unless that he was to be born from the ancient people and would have no equal? He is therefore commanded to be sought so that we may believe in him rationally.

And because he says of himself:

> “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44),

Samuel is rightly told by the Father:

> “You shall anoint the one whom I show you.”

The one who heard from the person he had anointed:

> “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17),

had first anointed him, as it were, after he had been shown to him.

He is sent to Bethlehem because, when Christ is sought according to the flesh, he is found to have been born from the Jewish people. He also comes to Bethlehem because the order of preachers first strove to convert Judaea and afterward preached to the Gentiles the Redeemer’s [reading apparently should be *fidem*, “faith,” rather than *finem*, “end”].

What does it mean that the elders of the city marvel, unless that those who had attained mature understanding were astonished at the preaching of such great novelty? Yet they meet him in wonder because they gladly hear the preaching of truth.

To meet preachers is to hear eagerly the word of faith which they preach. What do they ask about his peaceful arrival? What is a peaceful arrival except one in which he has come with the presence of peace? He displays this peace when he says:

> “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14).

What, then, does it mean that they inquire about his peaceful arrival, unless that the hearts of the elect among the Jews were eagerly awaiting the promise of the fathers? As though those who were waiting, wavering, were saying: “Has the peace now come which, after so long a succession of ages, was foretold as destined to come?”

And because the new teachers declare that what the ancient fathers had promised has been brought forth, they say:

> “Peaceful.”

It is as though he says: “We do not promise future gifts; we display the gifts of peace that are present. It is present in our arrival; in our word it is not future.”

The righteous Simeon has already seen it, held it, and worshiped it, saying:

> “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace” (Luke 2:29).

It has already appeared to the shepherds, and, when the long-awaited peace had been sent from heaven, the multitude of angels sang:

> “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

And because he had come not only to preach peace but also to persuade people to accept it, he adds:

> “I have come to sacrifice.”

## 27

What is it for a priest to sacrifice except to unite the hearts of the elect to our Redeemer through love? It is as though he says: “You want to know whether he has come, but knowing is of no benefit unless it benefits you to love.”

> “I have therefore come to sacrifice to the Lord.”

Hence Paul drives away those in whom he could not sacrifice, saying:

> “Let the one who does not love the Lord Jesus be accursed” (1 Corinthians 16:22).

But those invited to the sacrifice are told:

> “Sanctify yourselves and come.”

The Jews are unable to come with us to the sacrifice of faith for this reason: they do not wish to judge the Lord Jesus from the Scriptures, but, moved by hatred alone, they avoid hearing his preaching. Hence the Lord himself complains, saying:

> “If I had not done among them works which no one else has done, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse, because they have seen and hated both me and my Father” (John 15:24).

What, then, does “Sanctify yourselves and come” mean? To be sanctified for hearers is to prepare the secret place of a pure mind for what is to be heard. To be sanctified for them is to cast hatred out of the heart and prepare purity of intention for hearing the word of preaching.

They are therefore commanded to come sanctified, because coming is of no benefit to those who do not possess purity of intention in listening. And because the Holy Spirit speaks through holy teachers, he says:

> “Come with me.”

It is as though he says: “Attend to the one who speaks in such a way that you believe him as one who hears with you, because I speak in such a way that I hear, while I myself am both the one who speaks and the one who administers speech.”

And because at the beginning of the newborn Church many Jews both listened devoutly and believed faithfully, it is rightly said that Jesse and his sons were sanctified by Samuel and invited to the sacrifice.

## 28

But the king is not found among Jesse’s seven sons. What, then, are Jesse’s seven sons except all the perfect members of the Synagogue? They come to the prophet, but none of them is chosen, because the chosen preacher looks upon the perfect sons of the Synagogue and believes that none of them is the Redeemer of the human race.

He therefore brings forward all the elder sons, so that, when we look upon all the perfect ones, we may consider the Redeemer’s excellence. Among them, unless the little one is brought forward, no one is shown by the Lord to be king, because when we compare great men with our Redeemer, the extent of his dignity becomes visible.

He is therefore not found in the others because they are merely human beings. The boy who feeds the sheep is therefore sought in the pastures, because by obeying the Father he submits himself even unto death. Yet “who shall recount his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8).

He is called little because the grace of his humility is commended. He is called little because the Psalmist declares that he was made lower than the angels (Psalm 5).

But the little one feeds the sheep because through humility he is humble and through majesty exalted. Here he labors and hungers, but there, from the glory of his majesty, he feeds the angels. Since all receive from the fullness of his glory, they are filled, as it were, in those most blessed pastures through the boy.

He is also asserted to be a little shepherd because the citizens above rejoice ineffably in the assumption of his flesh. That ineffable joy of the blessed citizens is, as it were, the food of the sheep.

This one, therefore, is urgently commanded to be brought; until he comes, the meal must necessarily be postponed. The meal would have been set out before he came if the people had believed in another. He therefore had to be awaited who was the singular and only food of blessed souls.

Hence he says of himself:

> “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51).

But because the one who ascended is himself the one who descended (Ephesians 4:10), he is sent there so that he may be brought here.

To send to the pastures is to extend the mind above the angels even to equality with the eternal Father. To find him is to believe him equal in all things to the supreme Father.

He brings him, moreover, who already asserts that he came for the redemption of the human race through the humanity he assumed. The one to whom Samuel is sent in David’s figure had sent and brought him forth when he said:

> “The one who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3:31).

Isaiah was bringing forward the little one who feeds the sheep when he said:

> “A little one has been born for us, and a son has been given to us; and his name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty One, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6).

But because the teacher’s faith benefits only himself for salvation and not his hearers, he is commanded to be sent and brought forward, so that each person may possess the faith by which he may deserve to be saved.

Each person ought to go and bring him, for each must firmly believe him to be equal to the eternal Father in divinity and, through the [apparent OCR reading: *manitatem*; likely *humanitatem*, “humanity”] of our nature, a participant in it.

29. Concerning his appearance it is also said: “He was red, handsome in appearance, and fair of face.” Red, indeed, because he was wounded by a spear; red because he was reddened by his Passion. Hence the prophet says to him: “Why is your garment red?” (Isa. 63:2). He was red, whose whiteness of such great innocence was tinged with the redness of precious blood.

He was also handsome in appearance, because by rising again he put on the beauty of immortality, and because in great love he looked upon us mortals. As though promising his disciples the beauty of his appearance, he said: “I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice” (John 16:22). Again, promising this, he said: “I go to prepare a place for you, and I shall come and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be” (John 14:2–3).

What is the fairness of his face except the glory of his majesty? For his face is perfect knowledge. Paul, recalling this, says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I also am known” (1 Cor. 13:12). What, then, is the fairness of his face except the splendor of eternal divinity? This fairness is now believed, but is not seen; then it will not be believed, but seen, because the Apostle says: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Hence, when Moses asked for that same fairness of face, he was told: “You shall see my back” (Exod. 33:23). Whatever of his divinity we are now able to contemplate is not the fairness itself, but only the veil of that fairness. We see his back so that we may follow; but when, by following, we reach him, we shall see what is before him—that is, the fairness of his face.

391 Thus he was red in the world, handsome in paradise, and everlasting in heaven, with a fair face. This threefold beauty can also be understood in the conduct of his present life. He was red, because he fervently loved those for whom he laid down his life. He was handsome in appearance, because he knew all things. He was fair of face, because he did all things good.

But what was the beauty of his appearance? “No one knows the Father except the Son” (Matt. 11:27). Peter, admiring this, likewise said: “Now we know that you know all things, and there is no need for anyone to question you” (John 16:30). The fairness of his face is proclaimed by the crowds who looked upon him and said: “He has done all things well; he has made the deaf hear and the mute speak” (Mark 7:37). Others, likewise admiring him, said: “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” (Matt. 8:27).

What, then, is the fairness of his face except the beauty of holiness? What else is the fairness of his face except the splendor of his incomparable conduct? For in everything he did, he shone with the incomparable light of grace. Admiring this fairness of face, the Psalmist says: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips” (Ps. 44:3). Proclaiming this, Paul says:

“He is the splendor of his glory and the likeness of his substance, sustaining all things by the word of his power, making purification for sins, and sitting at the right hand of the majesty on high, having become so much better than the angels as he has inherited a name more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?” (Heb. 1:3–5).

Concerning him, therefore, the prophet is rightly commanded: “Rise and anoint him; for he is the one.”

30. The Apostle Peter, not merely a prophet but also the foremost patriarch, saw an indescribable light poured down from above, with a cloud overshadowing him and the Father crying out: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5; Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22; 2 Pet. 1:17).

There it is said: “For he is the one.” Here it is said: “This is my beloved Son.” There, because he was being shown in types, he is seen as though more distant, when it is said, “He is the one.” Here, because his glory had already been revealed, he is seen as more present, since it says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

He, then, is to be anointed, he is to be praised, and he is to be caressed with perpetual favor. But who could praise him worthily, when no one is sufficient even to see the glory that he praises? What does it mean that Peter falls when he hears the voice proclaiming such great words of praise? He was still a little one; he was still seeing what he was not sufficient to see. He saw, and because he fell in seeing, he signified that he could not attain to what he was worthy to see.

“No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3). Since Peter had not yet received that fullness of the Spirit, he could not, like a little one, proclaim Jesus. He is therefore first commanded to rise and to tell no one of the vision until he had risen from the dead. After the Resurrection he was to receive the Holy Spirit. Hence it is written: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39).

Peter therefore was not yet to speak of the vision before the Resurrection, because although he saw well, before he had the Spirit he did not understand.

31. What, then, does it mean that the Lord says to Samuel: “Rise and anoint him”? What does it mean that he is commanded to rise in order to anoint, except that the one who desires to proclaim the Lord’s sublimity must be raised up greatly toward heavenly things?

But how greatly was Peter raised up, when he was lifted to see such things? If he still awaited a higher state of perfection, who would not fear undertaking the office of such preaching? If the Lord admonishes the prophet to rise, does one who lies prostrate through the fall of wickedness dare to preach the Lord?

Hence each preacher is commanded through Isaiah: “Ascend upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isa. 40:9). The high mountain is the perfection of doctrine and of works.

Let him rise, then, who is commanded to anoint the king; let him extend himself toward lofty things. Let him rise in lofty work, rise in lofty contemplation, rise in wisdom of speech, rise in the strength of charity. He whom he anoints by preaching is so great that even those who are lofty can scarcely reach him.

Perhaps Paul was therefore able to anoint him because he says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). He was able to anoint him because he had raised himself to the secrets of the third heaven and heard hidden words in paradise.

Since, therefore, the Lord Jesus must be proclaimed sublimely by those who are sublime, the prophet is commanded to rise, because he is commanded to anoint the one whom he himself signifies. This is a high—indeed, an exceedingly high—virtue of perfect conduct, but it is perfectly fulfilled by many. Great indeed is this sublimity, yet the holy Church has many who are sublime. For after it rejected the Synagogue, God exalted the holy Church to an immeasurable height of virtue.

Rightly, therefore, it is said: “And the Spirit of the Lord was directed toward David from that day and thereafter.” The day is the faith of the Redeemer, in which the holy Church is illumined and the rejected Synagogue is brought low in marvelous blindness. On that day, therefore, the Holy Spirit is directed toward David, because by his grace it is taken away from the Synagogue and given to the elect of the holy Church. He is directed because he abandons some and takes up others. He is directed on that day because whoever has not been illumined by faith in the Redeemer cannot have within himself the Spirit who directs him. The Spirit, therefore, is directed on that day because he is given to those who possess the light of faith.

He is directed toward David because the holy Church alone receives him, and the holy Church is the body of the Redeemer. But since, by God’s authority, we have completed what we proposed to treat from the Book of Kings, we must pray to the supreme and almighty Spirit that he who uttered these words through whomever he wished may grant both writer and reader the affection for virtue. Amen.

# EXPOSITION ON THE SONG OF SONGS

[Col. 0467]

## ADMONITION CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING EXPOSITION OF THE SONG OF SONGS

393 I. Of all the songs of Sacred Scripture, that one is pre-eminent which is therefore called the Song of Songs by Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins alike. It should not seem surprising, then, that in interpreting and explaining it the minds of so many learned men—both Christian and Jewish—have labored.

Among the teachers of the Hebrews, the most famous are Rabbi Solomon, Ibn Ezra, and David Kimhi. Among Christians, beginning with the Greeks, the more distinguished Fathers and teachers of the Greek Church devoted their industry to investigating and searching out the mysteries of this divine Song, especially Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, and Theodoret.

Among the Latins, even leaving aside more recent interpreters such as Nicholas of Lyra, Hugh the Cardinal, Dionysius the Carthusian, and six hundred others, nearly all who flourished in earlier centuries with a reputation for piety and learning diligently searched out the hidden meanings of this sacred Song, by which they might inflame themselves and others with divine love.

Among them were Thomas Aquinas, Honorius of Autun, Richard of Saint Victor, Bernard of Clairvaux, Rupert, abbot of Tuitius, Robert of Tumbalenia—whose Commentary is mentioned by Orderic Vitalis in Book VIII, under the year 1087—Angelomus of Luxeuil, Alcuin, the Venerable Bede, Aponius, Cassiodorus—or whoever else was the author of the Commentary attributed to Cassiodorus—and Justus of Urgel.

We pass over Julian of Celano—or rather of Eclanum—bishop in Campania, whom the Venerable Bede testifies to have written on the Song (Book I on the Song), since he was an enemy of grace, which is poured out most abundantly in this sacred book.

II. Nevertheless, before our Gregory, among the four holy teachers whom the Latin Church especially honors and observes, no one had deliberately undertaken to explain the book of the Song of Songs.

It was therefore not enough for the most holy Father to insert, scattered through his writings, flowers gathered from the Song of Songs and to intertwine them, together with various interpretations corresponding to the manifold senses of Sacred Scripture, like so many scarlet and golden ribbons. From these little flowers, however, the Venerable Bede, delighted by their fragrance, wove an entire seventh book on the Song; and he readily acknowledges that the Father had served as his prelude in this kind of writing.

Rather, intoxicated by the most gentle contemplation of the divine mysteries hidden in that sacred book, Gregory poured forth in the Commentary which we are undertaking to publish what he had drunk in through constant meditation.

III. Peter Gussanvillaeus, who labored last in publishing Gregory’s works, attempted to deny this outstanding exposition to our Gregory. We once followed him in error in a French life of Saint Gregory, when we had not yet come upon so many handwritten books—both of this exposition, in which it had until now lain hidden for the most part, and of the genuine Paterian collection, from which an invincible argument emerges for attributing this work to Gregory.

It is not difficult, however, to blow away all the arguments with which he supports his opinion, on the basis of so many ancient monuments brought to light by us.

IV. No one can deny that Gregory discussed the Song of Songs and delivered Homilies which were later written down by his disciple Claudius, subsequently abbot. This is taught by Gregory himself in Letter 24 of Book XII, Indiction V, addressed to John the subdeacon, a letter already cited in the Preface to the Commentary on the First Book of Kings.

Moreover, Gussanvillaeus himself does not deny that Ildefonsus, bishop of Toledo, attributes a moral work on the Song of Songs to our Gregory. Nor is it easy to diminish the authority of so great a man, as Gussanvillaeus supposes. Ildefonsus was only sixty years younger than Gregory, and he flourished in the Spanish Church, which was almost the first to obtain the books of this distinguished pontiff, namely through their being sent to Saint Leander, bishop of Seville and his closest friend.

We willingly agree, however, with Gussanvillaeus when he responds that the authority of a single Paterius outweighs many others in this matter. But Paterius himself supports us—not the spurious Paterius published by Gussanvillaeus, who followed others previously in error, but the genuine and authentic Paterius whom we shall shortly bring to light from numerous manuscripts of unquestionable reliability.

In the Explanation of the Gospel according to Luke, chapter 17, on the words “And he was spending the night in the prayer of God,” our Paterius reads as follows:

“Likewise concerning the same matter, in Book I of the Exposition of the Song of Songs: ‘The compunction that comes through charity, which is kindled by desire, is like a certain kiss. For the soul kisses God as often as it is pierced with compunction in his love,’ and so forth,” as you will read in almost the whole of Book I, namely down to the words: “There is no necessity”—or, “it is by no means necessary”—“for us to make a solemn day for the Lord out of our lamentation.”

These words occur in all the genuine Paterian manuscripts that we have been able to consult: namely, in the Vatican manuscript, that of Saint Peter of Beauvais, the Bec manuscript, the Vallicellian manuscript, and the Michaeline manuscript. For a long time, with fruitless labor, we sought them in the published editions under Gregory’s name in the exposition of the Song of Songs. But in all the manuscripts that we shall soon enumerate, they are found in the place already indicated, in exactly the same words.

Therefore Paterius, Gregory’s disciple and notary, regarded the exposition on the Song of Songs for which we are contending as the legitimate offspring of the holy Father Gregory.

If anyone should still have doubts about the authenticity of our Paterius, let him read what we prefaced concerning him. There we not only restore to Paterius, on the basis of incontrovertible testimonies, his own Collectanea, brought forth from darkness, but also vindicate for Alulf, a monk of a much later age, the excerpts that until now have been circulated as Paterian.

We must now establish the reliability and authenticity of the manuscript copies of the Exposition on the Song of Songs, upon which the resolution of this controversy partly depends.

V. First of all, the codex of Saint Benignus at Dijon bears the mark of great antiquity. In it one reads:

“In the name of the Lord, etc. Here begins the Exposition on the Song of Songs of blessed Gregory, pope of the city of Rome. After being expelled from the joys of Paradise, etc.”

The first homily contains a notable passage cited by Paterius. In this manuscript the earlier homily ends with these words: “For then we run after him, when, both by loving and by fearing, we do not anticipate the divine judgments.” After these words, which you will read in Book I, no. 11, at the end, follows: “The first homily ends. The second begins: ‘The king brought me into his chambers,’ etc. The Church of God is like a certain house of the king. And this house, etc.”

It will not seem surprising that this work of Gregory is here divided into Homilies, since in the same letter cited above as testimony it is evident that the Expositions on the Books of Kings, on the Song, and so forth, were extracted and collected from Homilies:

“For,” he says, “my once most dear son Claudius, while I was speaking on Proverbs, on the Song of Songs . . . and also on the Books of Kings . . .—things which, because of weakness, I could not commit to writing—dictated them according to his own understanding and style,” and so forth.

With regard, therefore, to the first and more rudimentary design of this work, it could have been divided into Homilies. Yet it is clear that by Paterius’s time the division into books had already been accepted, since he praises the notable passage on compunction as taken from the first book of Saint Gregory’s Exposition on the Song.
