This division into various books also seems to have been preserved in a codex of excellent quality belonging to Saint Martin of Tours and more than five hundred years old. At the beginning it reads:

“Here begins Book I of blessed Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, on the Song: ‘After being expelled from Paradise.’”

It continues up to verse 3 of chapter I of the Song, “The king brought me into his chambers.” Here, as though it were the beginning of another book, the line begins with a very large initial letter. Here too the first homily ends in the Dijon manuscript, and in the Vallicellian manuscript there are signs of a similar division.

This second book extends to part of verse 9 of chapter II, “Behold, he stands behind our wall,” etc. These words begin a line with a large square initial letter, as though they introduced a new book, namely the third. This third book ends in the exposition of verse 5 of chapter IV. After it follows, with a very large initial letter at the beginning of the line: “I shall go to the mountain of myrrh,” which is verse 6 of the same chapter.

The fourth book, beginning here, extends to verse 3 of chapter VI, “You are beautiful, my beloved.” These words are written in the same manner as the beginnings of the other books. From this we infer that here begins Book V. The end of Book V and at the same time the beginning of Book VI, the final book, appear to be marked at these words of verse 9 of chapter VI: “Who is she who comes forth,” etc., as we observe from the large initial letter at the beginning.

In Book I there occurs the passage on compunction cited by Paterius, as in the other manuscripts listed below.

The most outstanding of these manuscripts is preserved in the monastery of Clairvaux. Indeed, because of its antiquity and elegance, it seems preferable to the others we have used, and therefore it deserves to be described here more carefully.

This codex first contains the Book of the Pastoral Rule, at the end of which one reads in red letters:

“The Book of the Pastoral Rule of blessed Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, ends.”

Then, in the same hand and in the same characters shining with vermilion:

“The Prologue of blessed Gregory, pope, on the Song begins: ‘After being expelled from Paradise,’ etc.”

When the prologue has ended, one reads, written in vermilion:

“The Prologue ends. The Explanation of the Song of Songs begins: ‘Let him kiss me.’”

In this codex there is no division into books or chapters. The final words are the same as in the printed editions and in our manuscripts:

“To him who was handed over to death for us and rose to immortality, we owe ourselves, both spirit and body. He lives and reigns, etc.”

Immediately afterward it adds:

“The Exposition of blessed Gregory, pope, on the Song of Songs ends.”

This codex appears to have been written by the same hand as the earlier documents concerning the foundation and endowment of the monastery. The beginning of that monastery is assigned to the year 1134.

That this codex was formerly read in the friars’ convent before Compline—as is customary among Cistercians and others living under the Rule of Saint Benedict—is made clear by the punctuation and by the marks indicating that the voice was sometimes to be raised and sometimes lowered.

This provides a substantial argument that it was written and used for daily public readings before Saint Bernard’s distinguished work on the Song had been composed, or at least before it had been published. For it is not reasonable to believe that the Cistercians, after this exposition of the Song—far superior to all others—had been issued by so great a member, indeed the father, of the Cistercian family, would have wished to use another reading at the conference before Compline.

From the antiquity of this codex it can easily be established that the prologue contained in it, “After being expelled from the joys of Paradise,” was wrongly attributed to Richard of Saint Victor. When the cited codex was written, Richard perhaps had not yet even thought of writing on the Song. What, then, would the editors of Richard’s works say if codices much older than Richard were presented to them, such as the Dijon codex already mentioned, written in the tenth or at least the eleventh century?

A codex from Utica, or from the monastery of Saint-Evroult, approaches this age. Here—so that we may not appear to conceal anything adverse to our case—the name of Saint Gregory or of any other author is absent both at the beginning and at the end. Instead one simply reads: “The Prologue begins,” etc.

Yet since in this codex, as in the others, there is the notable sentence on Compunction which Paterius judged worthy of inserting into his Collection, there can be no doubt that the prologue attached to the Gregorian Exposition, written continuously and consecutively in these words—“The Prologue ends. The Exposition on the Song of Songs begins”—was then regarded as Gregorian.

Those who copied this codex, however, and gathered into it various little works from different Fathers, do not ordinarily place the names of the authors before them. The book has been copied with the greatest accuracy, so that we have scarcely noticed a single error in it.

It is not divided into books, Homilies, or even chapters. Rather, the writing proceeds in the same continuous sequence without any interruption of the lines, even where the explanation of one verse has ended and another is introduced for explanation. There are only seven exceptions, which begin a line:

“The sons of my mother fought against me.”

“Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.”

“Go forth, daughters of Zion.”

“Your two breasts are like two young roes.”

“Return, return, O Shulammite.”

“Who is she who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights?”

“There was a vineyard belonging to the Peaceful One.”

Many other verses, however, begin with a larger red letter, but the continuous sequence of the writing is not thereby interrupted.

Finally, two other codices must be mentioned: one from the Remigian Library at Reims, the other from the monastery of Theoderic, not far from that city. Neither codex is more than four hundred years old, but the Theoderic codex was copied from a much older manuscript of the same monastery, which is now lost.

VI. Confirmed by inspection of so many manuscripts, and especially by the testimony of Paterius, we did not hesitate to conclude that this labor of Gregory—so worthy, indeed, of so great a teacher—ought to be restored to him.

The authority of the Master of the Sentences also supports us. In Book I, distinction 37, no. 1, one reads:

“Blessed Gregory says concerning the Song of Songs: ‘Although God is present to all things in the common manner—by presence, power, and substance,’” etc.

Saint Thomas also cites this passage. Although both of them appear to have erred in praising this statement—for it is absent from the Exposition on the Song—it nevertheless proves that in the time of Peter Lombard, who flourished in the twelfth century and was Richard of Saint Victor’s contemporary, and afterward, there was no doubt that Saint Gregory had explained the Song. His work was then in everyone’s hands.

VII. Nor should anyone suppose that the work already printed is rather to be regarded as Gregory’s, whose Prologue begins: “For if to a blind man, if to one placed far from God.” There are indeed some manuscript codices in which this Prologue is found, followed by an Exposition beginning with these words: “The kiss of the bridegroom is the inspiration of Christ,” etc., as in the printed editions.

We found three such manuscripts in Paris, in the Victorine Library. In them the author’s name is omitted, except that in one a later hand has written “Saint Gregory,” while traces remain of another name that has been erased.

Those who prepared the first edition of Gregory’s exposition on the Song, printed in Paris by Rembold in 1498—a book which we were unable to see—used these or similar codices. We used another Paris edition of 1518, the Gilot edition of 1571, the Vatican edition, and others. We easily determined that this Prologue is nothing other than an abridgment of ours, as will immediately be clear to anyone who reads and compares them.

As for the Exposition now in circulation, which differs from ours up to the words “Your cheeks are beautiful,” verse 9 of chapter I, who could deny, after the incontrovertible testimony of Paterius produced in favor of ours, that ours ought to be preferred to the other?

John Trithemius knew this work. In the catalogue of volumes written by Saint Gregory, pope, which Gussanvillaeus himself presents, Trithemius identifies the works by their opening words and records this one:

“He wrote several necessary volumes, among which the following are said to be included: On the Book of Job: ‘Among many, it is often asked . . .’; on the Song of Songs: ‘After being expelled from the joys of Paradise,’ etc.”

VIII. We therefore judged that this distinguished work, lying hidden in so many manuscripts, ought to be brought out of darkness and given to the public light.

But concerning its division and partition, on which the codices do not agree, we deliberated for a long time in uncertainty. At last, the division seemed preferable which the sacred book itself, here expounded, appears to offer. For just as it is divided into eight chapters, so we thought its explanation should be divided into the same number.

We distributed the chapters into various numbered sections, according to our customary practice. In the remaining matters also, we followed the same method as in the other works of Saint Gregory that we have edited, with regard to brief annotations, some to be written in the margins and others beneath the columns; we know that learned men approve this method.

IX. It remains for us to address the objection that may be raised from the difference of style, for we do not deny that some difference can be detected here.

The unusual character of the subject proposed and treated may perhaps have compelled a temporary change of style—namely, the explanation of the Song of Songs, in which an entirely different kind of writing is observed from that found in the other books of Sacred Scripture.

Moreover, since we read that this exposition was taken down by Claudius, as was said above concerning the Commentaries on the Book of Kings, and since we hear Gregory complaining in the letter already cited above about the alteration of his style, this difference of style—especially noticeable in the prologue—more and more confirms our position.

We therefore vindicate this work for Gregory in such a way that a small share of it is also attributed to Claudius, who took it down and arranged it, and who was compelled, because of lapses of memory, to supply certain things.

On the other hand, many traces of the Gregorian style remain, as a diligent reader will easily observe, especially up to verse 9 of the first chapter, where the same verses are bent and turned toward various senses—typical, allegorical, and moral—by a method familiar to the holy Doctor and especially well known from the Books of Moralia. These features will not escape the diligence of the learned reader.

Yet the reader’s chief concern, as he unfolds this book, should be to be consumed together with Gregory by the sacred flames of divine love; for as many words as it contains, so many sparks of divine love are found in it. Through Gregory, God sent fire upon the earth—and what does he desire except that it be kindled?

[Col. 0471]

# EXPOSITION OF THE SONG OF SONGS BY SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT, ROMAN PONTIFF (C, G, S)*

[Note: [Col. 0471A] In the Rouen codex, the Prologue is as in the edition of Richard of Saint Victor.]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0471A]

397 1. After the human race was expelled from the joys of Paradise and came into this pilgrimage of the present life, it possesses a blind heart deprived of spiritual understanding. If one were to say to this blind heart in a human voice, “Follow God,” or “Love God,” as it was told in the Law, once it had been sent outside and had grown cold through the sluggishness of unbelief, it would not grasp what it heard.

Therefore the divine word speaks to the sluggish and cold soul through certain riddles, and by means of things it knows secretly insinuates into it a love that it does not know.

2. Allegory constructs, as it were, a kind of mechanism for the soul placed far from God, so that through it the soul may be lifted to God. For when riddles are interposed, the soul recognizes in the words something that belongs to it, yet in the meaning of the words it understands something that does not belong to it; and through earthly words it is separated from the earth.

Through the fact that it does not recoil from what is familiar, it understands something unfamiliar. Divine meanings are clothed in things known to us, by which allegories are formed; and while through the thing itself we recognize the outward words, we arrive at the inward understanding.

3. Hence it is that in this book, which is written in the Song of Songs, words of almost bodily love are set forth, so that the soul, rubbed and warmed from its sluggishness by the language of its accustomed experience, may grow hot again; and through the words of the love that is below, it may be stirred to the love that is above.

In this book kisses are named, breasts are named, cheeks are named, thighs are named. In these words the sacred description is not to be mocked; rather, the greater mercy of God is to be considered. For when he names the members of the body and thus calls us to love, we must observe how wonderfully and mercifully he works with us.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] Richard, Sacred Scripture.]

In order to kindle our heart through the prompting of sacred love,

[Col. 0473C]

he extended his words even to the words of our shameful love.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] The word “se” is absent from the Theoderic and Reims manuscripts. In the Rouen and Richard manuscripts one reads: “he descended to the words of our shameful love.”]

But by the very fact that he humbles himself in speaking, he raises us up in understanding, because from the language of this love we learn by what power we should burn with love of the divinity.

4. We must carefully beware of this: when we hear the words of outward love, we must not remain fixed on outward meanings, lest the mechanism that was placed there to lift us should itself press us down so that we are not lifted.

Therefore, in these bodily and outward words we must seek whatever is inward; and when speaking of the body, we must become, as it were, outside the body.

[Note: [Col. 0474D] In the Vallicellian and Richard manuscripts, this word begins the following sentence; in that sentence the word “necessary” is entirely absent.]

We must come to this wedding of the bridegroom and the bride with an understanding of intimate charity—that is, wearing the wedding garment—lest, if we are not clothed in the wedding garment, namely a worthy understanding of charity, we be driven away from this wedding feast into the outer darkness, that is, into the blindness of ignorance.

[Col. 0473D]

Through these words of passion we must pass to the virtue of freedom from passion. Sacred Scripture is in its words and meanings as a painting is in its colors and objects; and he is exceedingly foolish who clings so closely to the colors of a painting that he ignores the things painted.

If we embrace the words spoken outwardly and ignore their meanings, then, like those who do not recognize the objects depicted, we hold on to colors alone.

“The letter kills, but the spirit gives life,” as it is written (2 Cor. 3:6). The letter covers the spirit just as straw covers grain; but it belongs to beasts of burden to feed on straw, and to human beings to eat grain.

Whoever, therefore, uses human reason should cast away the straw of beasts and hasten to eat the grain of the spirit. For this purpose it is useful: so that the mysteries enclosed in the letter may be concealed.

Hence it is written: “The wise hide understanding” (Prov. 10:14). For spiritual understanding is covered beneath the covering of the letter.

Again, in the same book it is written: “It is the glory of God to conceal a word” (Prov. 25:2). To the mind seeking God, God appears more gloriously the more subtly and inwardly he is investigated so that he may appear.

But should we not seek what God conceals in mysteries? Indeed we should, for it follows: “And it is the glory of kings to investigate a word” (ibid.).

Those who have learned to govern and investigate their bodies and the movements of the flesh are kings. It is therefore the glory of kings to investigate a word, because it is the praise of those who live well to search out the secrets of God’s commandments.

When we hear words concerning human conduct, we must be, as it were, outside human beings, lest, if we hear what is said in a merely human way, we should be unable to perceive anything divine in what we ought to hear.

Paul seemed to desire that his disciples should no longer be human beings when he said to them: “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not human beings?” (1 Cor. 3:3).

The Lord likewise seemed no longer to regard his disciples as human beings when he said: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16:13). When they had answered with the words of human beings, he immediately added: “But who do you say that I am?”

When above he says “people,” and then adds “but you,” he establishes a certain distinction between people and the disciples, because by revealing divine things to them he made them superior to human beings. As the Apostle says: “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away” (2 Cor. 5:17).

And we know that in our resurrection the body will be joined to the spirit in such a way that everything that had belonged to suffering will be taken up into the power of the spirit.

Therefore whoever follows God must imitate his own resurrection every day, so that just as then he will have nothing subject to suffering in his body, so now he may have nothing subject to suffering in his heart; so that according to the inner person he may already be a new creation, may already trample underfoot whatever is old, and may seek in old words only the force of newness.

5. Sacred Scripture is indeed a mountain, from which the Lord comes into our hearts so that we may understand. Concerning this mountain the prophet says: “God will come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from the shadowed and dense mountain” (Hab. 3:3).

This mountain is dense with meanings and shadowed by allegories. But we must know that when the voice of the Lord sounds on the mountain, we are commanded to wash our garments and to cleanse ourselves from every defilement of the flesh, if we hasten to approach the mountain.

For it is written that if a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned (Heb. 12:20).

The beast touches the mountain when those devoted to irrational impulses draw near to the height of Sacred Scripture and do not understand it as they ought, but irrationally bend it toward an interpretation dictated by their pleasure [perhaps: their will].

Every absurd or sluggish mind, if it is seen near this mountain, is killed by the most terrible judgments, as though by stones.

This mountain burns, because Sacred Scripture kindles with the fire of love those whom it fills spiritually. Hence it is written: “Your word is fiery” (Ps. 118:140).

When certain people walking along the road heard the words of God, they said: “Was not our heart burning within us when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

Hence Moses says: “In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deut. 33:2).

The wicked are understood as God’s left hand, those who do not pass over to the right-hand side. God’s right hand consists of the elect, who are separated from the left.

The law is therefore fiery in the right hand of God, because in the hearts of the elect, who are to be placed at the right hand, the divine commandments blaze, and they are kindled with the ardor of charity.

May this fire consume whatever outward rust and oldness there is in us, so that it may offer our mind to the contemplation of God like a whole burnt offering.

6. Nor should it be overlooked that this book is called not merely the Song but the Song of Songs. For just as in the Old Testament some things are holy and others are the Holy of Holies, some are Sabbaths and others Sabbaths of Sabbaths, so in sacred Scripture some are Songs and others Songs of Songs. The things in the Tabernacle and those performed outwardly were holy; Sabbaths were those celebrated every week. But the Holy of Holies was received with a more secret kind of veneration, and the Sabbaths of Sabbaths were observed only on their own festivals. In the same way, the Song of Songs is a certain secret and solemn interior reality, a secret penetrated through hidden meanings. For if attention is given only to the outward words, it is not secret.

7. It must also be understood that in sacred Scripture there are Songs of victory, Songs of exhortation and testimony, Songs of rejoicing, Songs of assistance, and Songs of union with God.

The Song of victory is the one that Mary sang after crossing the Red Sea, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exodus 15:1).

The Song of exhortation and testimony is the one Moses spoke to the Israelites as they approached the promised land: “Attend, O heaven, to what I shall say; let the earth hear the words from my mouth” (Deuteronomy 32:1).

The Song of rejoicing is the one Hannah sang when she perceived in herself the fruitfulness of the Church, saying: “My heart has exulted in the Lord” (1 Kings 2:1). There she expressed, through the figure of herself, the fruitfulness of ecclesial offspring when she says: “The barren woman has borne many, and she who had many children has grown weak” (ibid., 2:5).

The Song of assistance is David’s, which he sang after battle, saying: “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Psalm 17:1).

The Song of union with God is what is sung at the wedding of bridegroom and bride, namely, the Song of Songs. It is as much higher than all the other Songs as the solemnity offered at its wedding is higher. Through those Songs, vices are avoided; through this one, each person is enriched with virtues. Through those, the enemy is guarded against; through this, the Lord embraces the soul with familiar love.

8. It should also be noted that in sacred Scripture the Lord sometimes calls himself Lord, sometimes Father, and sometimes Bridegroom. When he wishes to be feared, he names himself Lord; when he wishes to be honored, Father; when he wishes to be loved, Bridegroom. Through the prophet he says: “If I am Lord, where is my fear? If I am Father, where is my honor?” (Malachi 1:6). And again he says: “I betrothed you to myself in righteousness and faith” (Hosea 2:20). Or certainly: “I remembered the day of your betrothal in the wilderness” (Jeremiah 2:2).

Indeed, with God there is no “when” and “when not”; but because he first wishes to be feared so that he may be honored, and first honored so that one may come to him, he names himself Lord on account of fear, Father on account of honor, and Bridegroom on account of love. Through fear one comes to honor, and through his honor one comes to love. Therefore, the more honor is worthier than fear, the more God rejoices in being called Father than Lord; and the dearer love is than honor, the more God rejoices in being called Bridegroom than Father.

In this book, therefore, it is the Lord and the Church—not Lord and handmaid—but Bridegroom and bride, so that service may be rendered not to fear alone, nor to reverence alone, but also to love, and so that inward affection may be stirred by these outward words. When he calls himself Lord, he indicates that we have been created; when he calls himself Father, he indicates that we have been adopted; when he calls himself Bridegroom, he indicates that we have been united. To be united with God is more than to be created and adopted. Thus, in this book, where he is called Bridegroom, something more sublime is suggested, since the covenant of union is displayed in it.

These names are frequently repeated in the New Testament, because the union of the Word with Christ’s flesh, and of Christ with the Church, has already been accomplished and celebrated. Hence John says, when the Lord comes: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29). Hence the same Lord says: “The children of the bridegroom will not fast as long as the bridegroom is with them” (Matthew 9:15). Hence it is said to the Church: “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). Again: “That he might present the Church to himself in glory, without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27). And again in the Apocalypse of John: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). And again there: “I saw the bride descending from heaven, as though newly married” (Revelation 21:2).

9. Nor is it contrary to a great mystery that this book is placed third among Solomon’s works. For the ancients said that there are three orders of life: moral, natural, and contemplative, which the Greeks called the ethical life (*ethikē*), the physical life (*physikē*), and the theoretical or contemplative life (*theōrētikē*).

In Proverbs, moral life is expressed, where it says: “Hear, my son, my wisdom, and incline your ear to my prudence” (Proverbs 1:8). In Ecclesiastes, natural life is expressed; there, indeed, the fact that everything tends toward an end is considered, when it says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). In the Song of Songs, contemplative life is expressed, since in it the Lord’s coming and appearance are desired, when the bridegroom’s voice says: “Come from Lebanon, come” (Song of Songs 4:8).

Or perhaps he also signified the orders and lives of the three patriarchs, namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Abraham maintained the moral life through obedience; Isaac represented natural life by digging wells. For to dig wells below is, through natural contemplation, to search out and investigate everything that lies beneath. Jacob maintained the contemplative life, for he saw angels ascending and descending.

But because natural contemplation does not lead to perfection unless morality is first maintained, Ecclesiastes is rightly placed after Proverbs. And because heavenly contemplation is not seen unless what lies below and passes away has first been despised, the Song of Songs is rightly placed after Ecclesiastes.

First, then, one must order one’s conduct; afterward, one must consider all present things as though they were not present; and in the third place, with a pure vision of the heart, one must behold heavenly and interior realities. By these steps of the books he thus made a kind of ladder to contemplation: first, things are rightly done in the world; afterward, even the honorable things of the world are despised; finally, the inmost things of God are perceived.

In this way, the coming of the Lord is generally awaited in this work through the voice of the Church, so that each soul in particular may also behold God’s entrance into its own heart as the bridegroom’s entrance into the bridal chamber.

10. It must be understood that in this book four speaking persons are introduced: the bridegroom and the bride, the young women together with the bride, and the companies of the bridegroom’s companions with the bridegroom.

The bride herself is the perfected Church; the bridegroom is the Lord; the young women with the bride are souls who are beginning and, through new zeal, reaching maturity; the bridegroom’s companions are either angels, who often appeared to human beings when sent by him, or certainly all the perfected men in the Church who know how to proclaim the truth to human beings.

Yet those who individually are young women or companions are, taken together, the bride, because together they are the Church. Nevertheless, with respect to each individual, all three names may be understood. For whoever loves God perfectly is the bride; whoever proclaims the bridegroom is a companion; whoever, still new, follows the way of good things is a young woman.

[Note: Thus all the manuscript copies read. In Richard’s edition it says *let us lean upon* (*innitamur*).]

We are therefore invited to be the bride. If we are not yet strong enough for this, let us be companions; if we have not attained even this, let us at least come together as young women to this bridal chamber. Since, then, we have said that the bridegroom and bride are the Lord and the Church, let us, as young women or companions, hear the words of the bridegroom; let us hear the words of the bride, and learn the fervor of love from their speeches.

Thus the holy Church, long awaiting the Lord’s coming and long thirsting for the fountain of life, declares how she longs to see the presence of her bridegroom and how she desires it.

# CHAPTER ONE

## (Chapter 1:1) “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

1. The Lord had sent angels to her, patriarchs to her, and prophets bearing spiritual gifts; but she sought to receive the gifts not through the bridegroom’s servants, but from the bridegroom himself.

Let us place before our eyes the whole human race, from the beginning of the world to its end—namely, the whole Church—as one bride who had received spiritual pledges through the Law, yet sought the presence of her bridegroom, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

For the holy Church, sighing for the coming of the Mediator between God and human beings, for the coming of her Redeemer, addresses a prayer to the Father, asking him to send the Son and enlighten her with his own presence, so that he might now address that same Church not through the mouths of the prophets, but with his own mouth.

Hence it is written of the same bridegroom in the Gospel, when he sat on the mountain and spoke words of sublime instruction: “And opening his mouth, he said” (Matthew 5:2), as though it were plainly said: He then opened his own mouth who had previously opened the mouths of the prophets for the exhortation of the Church.

But behold: as she sighs, as she seeks him as though he were absent, suddenly she perceives him present. This is the grace of our Creator: when, seeking him, we speak of him, we enjoy his presence. Hence it is written in the Gospel that while Cleopas and another were speaking about him on the road, they were found worthy to see him present.

While, therefore, the holy Church still desires the bridegroom who is to be incarnate as though absent, suddenly she perceives him present and continues:

## (Verse 1) “For your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.”

2. Wine was the knowledge of the Law and the knowledge of the prophets. But when the Lord came, because he wished [Note: In Codex Theodulf it reads “did not wish,” with the other manuscripts dissenting.] to preach wisdom through the flesh, he made it, as it were, lie hidden in the breasts of the flesh. For [Note: Something appears to be lacking here. The sense would be clear if [Col. 0478D] one read: “so that what in his divinity, etc.” But because all the manuscripts agree in this reading, we do not dare depart from it.] what we could not at all contain in his divinity, we might recognize in his incarnation.

Therefore his breasts are not without reason praised, because the condescension of his preaching accomplished in our hearts what the teaching of the Law was entirely unable to accomplish: [Note: Vallicelliana, the Cluniac manuscript, and Rothomagensis read “for more.”] the preaching of the incarnation nourished us before the teaching of the Law did.

Let him therefore say: “Your breasts are better than wine.” Confirming this further, he adds: “And the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.”

The Lord’s ointments are his virtues; the Lord’s ointment was the Holy Spirit, of whom the prophet says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8).

He was anointed with this oil when he was incarnate. He did not first exist as a human being and afterward receive the Holy Spirit; rather, because he was incarnate through the mediation of the Holy Spirit, he was anointed with this same oil when he was created as a human being.

The fragrance of his ointment, therefore, is the burning presence of the Holy Spirit, who proceeded from him and remained in him; the fragrance of his ointments is the burning presence of the virtues that he performed.

[Note: Thus Vallicelliana, with the others reading differently, “but let him draw.”]

The Church had spices because she had many gifts of the Holy Spirit, which in the house of God—that is, in the assembly of the saints—gave forth the fragrance of a good reputation and announced the sweetness of the coming Mediator.

But “the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices,” because the burning fragrance of the bridegroom’s virtues, accomplished through his incarnation, surpassed the proclamations of the Law, which had been granted by the bridegroom as pledges. For the Church grew in understanding in proportion as she was found worthy to be enlightened by the grace of a greater vision.

Those spices of the Law were administered through angels; this ointment was given through presence. But because the goods of the Law, which were believed to be sublime, were surpassed by the brightness of his presence, it is rightly said: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.”

3. What we have said generally about the entire Church, let us now understand particularly of each soul. Let us place before our eyes a soul devoted to the study of gifts, receiving understanding from another’s preaching, yet desiring also to be enlightened by divine grace, so that at some time it may understand by itself what it considers itself unable to understand except through the words of preachers. Let it say: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Let him touch me inwardly, so that I may know through understanding; and let me no longer enjoy the voice of preachers, but the touch of inward grace.

[Note: This is how Rothomagensis reads. In three others it says “from the act.” The former reading was judged preferable by what is read a little later: “For to speak mouth to mouth is, as it were, to kiss, and to touch the inward understanding with the mind.”]

He kissed Moses, as it were, with the kiss of his mouth when he granted him understanding through the confidence of familiar grace. Hence it is written: “If there is a prophet among you, I will speak to him in a dream; but not so with my servant Moses: mouth to mouth I speak with him” (Numbers 12:6–8). For to speak mouth to mouth is, as it were, to kiss, and to touch the inward understanding with the mind.

It follows:

## (Verse 1) “For your breasts are better than wine.”

4. The breasts of God are, as we said earlier, the condescension of his most humble incarnation. The wisdom of the world, however, is like a kind of wine: it intoxicates the mind, for it makes it alien to the understanding of humility.

Philosophers are intoxicated with a kind of wine when they pass through the worldly love of the crowd. Let the Church despise this wisdom and desire the most humble preaching of the Lord’s incarnation. Let it taste more deeply what is nourished through the weakness of his flesh than what this world exalts through the pride of false prudence. Let it say: “For your breasts are better than wine”—that is, the most humble preaching of your incarnation surpasses the wisdom of the world, which is veiled.

Hence it is written: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings, and what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25).

But because the wise of this age sometimes appear to devote themselves to certain virtues—you may see many of them possessing charity, preserving gentleness, and practicing outward respectability in everything—and because they display these virtues not in order to please God but in order to please human beings, these virtues are not virtues, since they do not seek to please God. Yet they smell pleasant to human nostrils, because they produce a good reputation according to human judgment.

Let these things, however, be compared with the fragrance of our Redeemer; let them be compared with true virtues, and let it be said: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.” That is: the burning fragrance of your virtues surpasses every appearance of virtue among the wise of the world, because it transcends their fabricated images through truth.

Since we said that this should be understood a second time of each soul, let us, with the Lord’s help, pursue the same meaning more subtly.

5. Every soul that fears God is already under his yoke, but still far away, because it fears. For each person progresses toward God in proportion as he loses the punishment of fear and receives from him the grace of charity.

Let us place before our eyes the soul of any one of the elect, kindled by a continual desire for love of the bridegroom’s vision, because it cannot fully possess in this life what it contemplates: his sublimity. It is pierced by that very love.

[Note: This passage is cited in the genuine collection of Paterius, which we shall publish, as spoken by Gregory in his exposition of the Song of Songs; this is worthy of notice. Lest any suspicion of fraud arise, I point out that this sentence is found entire in all our manuscripts: namely, those of Tours, St Martin; Dijon, St Benignus; Vallicelliana; Theodulf; Remigius; and Rothomagensis.]

For the piercing that occurs through charity and is kindled by desire is, as it were, a kind of kiss. The soul kisses God as often as it is pierced by love for him.

There are many who already fear the Lord and already undertake good works, but do not yet kiss him, because they are not at all pierced by love for him. This was well signified in the banquet of the Pharisee. Although he had received the Lord, he disparaged in his heart the woman who kissed his feet. He heard: “When I entered your house, you did not give me a kiss; but she, from the moment she entered, has not ceased kissing my feet” (Luke 7:44–45).

Everyone who already gives alms and devotes himself to good works receives Christ at a banquet, feeds Christ, and does not cease sustaining Christ in his members. But if he is not yet pierced by love, he still does not kiss his footprints.

The woman who kisses is therefore preferred to the man who gives, because the one who is pierced inwardly in the desire for the Lord through the ardor of the mind is preferred to the one who gives his outward possessions.

[Note: In Theodulf and Remigius alone it says: “he is preferred to the one who gives.”]

It was rightly said: “She has not ceased kissing my feet.” For it is not enough to be pierced by love of God once and then rest; the piercing must continue and increase. Hence the woman is praised because she did not cease kissing—that is, she did not cease being pierced.

Hence the prophet says: “Establish a solemn day with frequent observance, even to the horn of the altar” (Psalm 117:27). A solemn day for the Lord is the piercing of our heart. But the solemn day is established through frequent observance when we are continually moved to tears by love for him.

If we were to say to her, “How long will we do these things? How long will we be afflicted by tribulations?” he immediately adds the limit until which they must be done, saying: “Even to the horn of the altar.”

For the horn of the altar is the exaltation of the inward sacrifice. When we have reached it, there is no longer any need for us to make a solemn day for the Lord through our lamentation.

Let the soul, therefore, that already desires to be pierced by love and longs already to contemplate the vision of its bridegroom say: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

[Col. 0481B] 6. Or certainly, the kiss of his mouth is the perfection of inward peace itself. When we have reached it, nothing further will remain for us to seek. Hence what follows is fitting: “For his breasts are better than wine.”

Wine is the knowledge of God that we have received while placed in this life; but we embrace the bridegroom’s breasts when, in the eternal homeland, we contemplate him through the embrace of his presence.

Let him therefore say: “Your breasts are better than wine.” As though he were saying: Great indeed is the knowledge of you that you have bestowed on me in this life; great is the wine of your knowledge with which you intoxicate me. But your breasts are better than wine, because then, through the beauty and sublimity of contemplation, whatever is now known of you through faith will be surpassed.

“And the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices,” since he excels in the virtue of knowledge, the virtue of chastity, the virtue of mercy, the virtue of humility, and the virtue of charity.

If the life of the saints did not possess the fragrance of spices through virtues, Paul would not say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Corinthians 2:15).

But far more excellent is that anointing of God to which we shall one day be led. Far more excellent is the fragrance of God’s ointments than the spices of our virtues. Even if the things we have received are already great, those we shall receive from contemplation of our Creator are nevertheless much greater.

Let the soul therefore pant and say: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices”—that is, those good things that you prepare through contemplation surpass all these gifts of virtue that you have granted in this life.

Let us ask this Church, let us ask this soul that loves in this way and burns in love for its bridegroom: From where did it receive such great desire? From where did it grasp knowledge of his divinity? But behold, it says from where it might express this:

## (Verse 2) “Your name is poured-out ointment.”

7. “Poured-out ointment” is divinity incarnate. If ointment remains in a vessel, it gives off less fragrance; but if it is poured out, the fragrance of the poured ointment spreads more widely.

The name of God, therefore, is poured-out ointment, because from the immensity of his divinity he poured himself outward into our nature and made himself visible from being invisible. If he had not poured himself out, he would in no way have become known to us.

The ointment poured itself out when he preserved himself as God and displayed himself as human. Paul speaks of this outpouring: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7).

What Paul called “emptied himself,” Solomon called “poured out.” Because, then, the Lord became known to the human race through the humility of his incarnation, let it be said to him: “Your name is poured-out ointment.”

It follows:

## (Verse 2) “Therefore the young women loved you.”

8. Whom do we understand by the young women in this passage except the souls of the elect, renewed through baptism? The life of sin belongs to the old person; the life of righteousness belongs to the new.

Because, then, he poured out the ointment outwardly, he made the young women burn with love for him; because he displayed renewed souls fragrant with desire for him.

Childhood is not yet suited to love; old age ceases from love. A child is one who has not yet begun the pursuit of an ardent life; an old person is one who had begun but has ceased.

Because, then, neither those who have not yet begun to burn for the Lord nor those who had begun but have grown cold are aflame, the childish and aged stages being set aside, the young women are said to run—that is, those souls who are in the very love of fervor.

9. Yet we can understand this in another way. Youth may refer to weakness. For the youthful ages are the order of angels, who have been overcome by no weakness and defeated by no infirmity.

Let it therefore be said: “Your name is poured-out ointment; therefore the young women loved you.” That is: because through your incarnation you poured forth knowledge of yourself outwardly, weak souls are able to love human nature.

Those highest Powers, like the age of youth, love you even where you have not been poured out, because they see you there also, where you remain in the state of divinity. Since, therefore, you are seen by those highest orders, as by youthful ages, even without being poured out, you pour yourself out outwardly for the sake of human beings, so that you may also be loved by the young women—that is, by weak minds.

It follows:

## (Verse 3) “Draw me.”

10. Everyone who is drawn is drawn unwillingly, either because he is unable or because he does not wish to be drawn. But the one who says, “Draw me,” has something that he wills and something that he does not will [perhaps it should read: “is unable”].

Human nature wishes to follow God, but, overcome by the habit of weakness, it is unable to follow as it ought. It sees that there is one thing in it toward which it tends and another thing in it that it is unable to do, and rightly says: “Draw me.”

Paul saw himself as willing but unable when he said: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7:25); and: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind” (ibid., 7:23).

Because, then, there is in us one thing that urges us forward and another that weighs us down, let us say: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.” We run in the fragrance of God’s ointments when, breathed upon by his spiritual gifts, we gasp with longing for the love of his vision.

11. It must be understood that when human beings follow God, they sometimes walk, sometimes run, and sometimes run strongly. One who follows sluggishly walks, one who follows frequently runs, and one who follows perseveringly runs perfectly.

The heart was immobile in following God and unwilling to walk after him when the Lord’s coming appeared in the world and moved human minds from their insensible standing still. Hence it is written: “His feet stood, and the earth was shaken” (Habakkuk 3:5, according to the Greek translators).

Here, however, it is not movement but running that is mentioned, because it is not enough to follow unless we also run through desire. And because even running is not enough unless one runs perfectly, Paul says: “Run in such a way that you may obtain” (1 Corinthians 9:24).

Some, while running too much, fall into indiscretion. They are wiser than necessary and already set themselves above the one they were following, choosing their own virtues and putting aside the judgments of the one they followed.

Thus, when it was said, “We shall run,” it was rightly prefaced by “after you.” For those run after God who consider his judgments, prefer his will to themselves, and strive to reach him through worthy action and discernment.

Hence the prophet, considering God’s will, says: “My soul has clung after you” (Psalm 62:9). Hence Peter, when offering counsel, is told: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not think the things of God, but those of human beings” (Matthew 16:23; Mark 8:33).

Because, then, perfected souls observe God’s judgments with the greatest caution and presume neither to go ahead through sluggishness nor to anticipate him through indiscriminate fervor, it is rightly said: “After you we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments.”

We run after you when we follow you in love and, through fear, do not anticipate the divine judgments.

[Note: In Divionensis, the first homily ends here. In Vallicelliana as well, as though the first book were finished, it says “He introduced,” written in larger letters adorned and painted in various colors.]

## (Verse 3) “The king has brought me into his chamber; we shall exult and rejoice in you.”

12. The Church of God is like a certain house of the king, and this house has a door, an ascent, a dining room, and chambers.

Everyone who has faith within the Church has already entered through the door of this house. [Note: Thus read Divionensis and Vallicelliana. Rothomagensis, with Rhemensis and Theodulf agreeing, reads: “who enters the Church.”] For just as a door opens the rest of the house, so faith opens the entrance to the other virtues. [Note: Here we still follow Divionensis and Vallicelliana, whereas the other manuscripts read: “everyone who enters the Church.”]

Everyone who has hope within the Church has already come to the ascent of the house. For hope lifts the heart, so that it desires sublime things and abandons what is low.

Everyone who, placed in this house, has charity walks, as it were, in the dining room. For charity is broad and extends even to the love of enemies.

Everyone who, placed in the Church, already searches out sublime things and considers hidden judgments has entered, as it were, into the chamber.

A certain person spoke of the door of this house: “Open to me the gates of righteousness, and entering through them I shall confess to the Lord” (Psalm 117:19). He spoke of the ascent of hope: “He has arranged ascents in his heart” (Psalm 83:6). Of the broad dining rooms of this house it is said: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Psalm 118:96). Charity is specially signified in the broad commandment.

He spoke of the king’s chamber who said: “My secret is for me” (Isaiah 24:16). And elsewhere: “I heard secret words that it is not lawful for human beings to speak” (2 Corinthians 12:4).

The first entrance of this house, then, is the door of faith; the second advance is the ascent of hope; the third is the breadth of charity; the fourth is the perfection of charity that leads to knowledge of God’s secrets.

Because the holy Church, in its perfected members—that is, in its holy teachers, in those who are already full-grown and rooted in the mysteries of God—reaches sublime secrets and, while still placed in this voice, already penetrates them, it says: “The king has brought me into his chamber.”

Through the prophets, apostles, and teachers who, while placed in this life, already penetrated the sublime secrets of that life, the Church had entered the chamber of that king.

13. It must be carefully observed that he does not say “into the chamber of the bridegroom,” but “into the chamber of the king.” By naming him king, he wishes to display the reverence due to secrets, because the more powerful the chamber, the greater the reverence that must be shown toward the things into which one enters.

Therefore, lest anyone, while learning God’s secrets, searching out hidden judgments, and being lifted to the heights of contemplation, become exalted and fall into pride, he is said to enter the king’s chamber—that is, the chamber to which greater reverence must be shown the more the soul is led toward knowledge of his secrets.

For anyone who progresses, having already been exalted by grace to sublime secrets, let him consider himself and humble himself more deeply because of that very progress.

Hence Ezekiel, whenever he is led to contemplate sublime things, is called “son of man,” as though he were being told: Consider what you are, and do not become exalted by the things to which you are exalted.

But few in the Church are able to search out and comprehend these sublime and hidden judgments of God. Nevertheless, when we see strong men able to attain such great wisdom that they contemplate God’s secrets in their hearts, we little ones also gain confidence that at some time we may come to forgiveness and at some time to his grace.

Hence the words of the young women are added:

## (Verse 3) “We shall exult and rejoice in you.”

408 14. While the Church, in those who are perfected, enters the king’s chamber, the young women promise themselves hope of exultation, because when the strong reach the heights of contemplation, the weak gain hope of forgiveness for their sins.

## (Verse 3) “The king has brought me into his chamber; we shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts as better than wine. The upright love you.”

15. This bridegroom has breasts, although he is also called king on account of reverence. He has breasts: holy men who cling to him in their hearts. The breasts are fixed in the secret chamber of the heart [Note: Vallicelliana reads: “are fixed in the hidden recess of the breast.”] and, through inward nourishment, draw toward themselves those whom they nourish as strong persons.

Holy men, therefore, are the bridegroom’s breasts, because they draw from inward things and nourish outwardly. His breasts are the apostles; his breasts are all the preachers of the Church.

Wine, as we said above, was in the prophets; wine was in the Law. But because greater commandments were given through the apostles than had been given through the prophets, it is rightly said now: “Remembering your breasts as better than wine,” because those who can fulfill what has been commanded in the New Testament undoubtedly surpass the knowledge of the Law.

16. Yet we can understand this in another way: “Remembering your breasts as better than wine.” There are many who possess the wine of wisdom but do not possess knowledge of humility. Knowledge puffs them up, because charity does not build up.

There are others who possess the wine of knowledge in such a way that they know how to consider the gifts of teaching and the gifts of spiritual grace. The gifts of spiritual grace are like breasts in the heart, which subtly provide and nourish through hidden spiritual channels.

“Remembering your breasts as better than wine”: those who know how to follow the gifts of your grace, so that they do not attribute to themselves what they understand and are not exalted by the wisdom they have received, are raised above those who are exalted by their own wisdom.

For it is more excellent to know humbly than merely to know; indeed, it is not true knowledge if one does not know humbly.

“Remembering your breasts as better than wine”: those who know how to consider the gifts of spiritual grace surpass those who possess knowledge but do not retain knowledge of the gifts in their memory.

It therefore means plainly: “Remembering your breasts as better than wine,” because humility is stronger than knowledge. Wine is knowledge that intoxicates; the memory of the breasts is what sobers, recalling one to knowledge of the gifts.

“Remembering your breasts as better than wine,” because humility conquers an abundance of knowledge.

17. “The upright love you.” As though he were saying: Those who are not upright still fear. “The upright love you.” For anyone who performs good works out of fear, although he is upright in his action, is not upright in his desire. He would wish that there were nothing to fear and would not perform good works.

But whoever performs good works out of love is upright both in action and in desire. The sweetness of love, however, is hidden from those who fear. Hence it is written: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you and perfected for those who hope in you” (Psalm 30:20).

The sweetness of God is unknown to those who fear God; it becomes known to those who love him.

Whoever, therefore, strives to be upright through love possesses perfect love, so that he does not fear the Judge when he comes and does not dread whatever he may hear about eternal punishments.

Hence Paul, while awaiting the Judge’s coming and seeking the rewards of eternal life, says: “Which God has prepared not only for me but also for all who love his coming” (2 Timothy 4:8).

Eternal rewards are prepared for those who love, because everyone who knows that he performs evil deeds fears the coming Judge; but whoever is confident about his deeds seeks the Judge’s coming.

Rewards, then, are prepared for those awaiting God’s coming and loving his coming, because no one loves the Judge’s coming unless he is confident about his own case.

All certainty—the uprightness of certainty—lies in love.

[Note: Thus Rothomagensis, Theodulf, and others. In Vallicelliana it reads: “All certainty of uprightness lies in love.”]

And therefore it is rightly said: “The upright love you.”

(Verses 4–5.) “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, [Note: [Col. 0486D] Rothom., ‘like skins’; but below, together with the others, it has ‘like a skin.’] like Solomon’s skin. Do not look at me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me.”

18. We know that, in the beginnings of the Church, when the grace of our Redeemer had been preached, some believed and others did not believe. But those who believed were despised by the unbelievers and, as though they had suffered persecution, were judged to have departed into the way of the Gentiles. Therefore the Church cries out in these same believers against those who were not converted: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” I am indeed black in your judgment, but beautiful through the illumination of grace.

How am I black? “Like the tents of Kedar.” Kedar is interpreted as “darkness.” Kedar was the second in the line of Ishmael, and the tents of Esau were Kedar’s. How, then, am I black like the tents of Kedar? Because in your sight I have been judged similar to the Gentiles, that is, similar to sinners.

How am I beautiful like Solomon’s skin? It is said that, when Solomon built the Temple, he covered all the Temple vessels with skins that had been made. Surely Solomon’s skins could have been beautiful in the service of the king. But because Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful,” let us understand him as the true Solomon: all souls clinging to God are Solomon’s skins, mortifying themselves and returning to the service of the King of peace. In judgment I am like the tents of Kedar, since I am judged to have departed into the way of the Gentiles; but according to the truth I am like Solomon’s skin, because I cling to the service of the King.

(Verses 5.) “Do not look at me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me.”

19. He was looking upon the sinful woman, that part which had believed in Christ. But let her say: “Do not look at me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me.” The sun itself is the Lord; he himself, coming, discolored me. By his commandments he showed that I was not beautiful under the commandments of the Law. The sun discolors the one whom it touches more closely; so also the Lord, coming, discolored the one whom he touched more strictly through his grace. For the closer we approach grace, the more we recognize ourselves to be sinners.

[Col. 0486D] Let us see Paul, coming from Judaism, discolored: “But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves were found to be sinners” (Gal. 2:17). Whoever finds himself a sinner in Christ finds himself discolored in the sun.

But behold, this part that believed from Judaism suffered persecution from the unbelieving Jews, afflicted by many tribulations. Hence it follows:

(Verses 5.) “The sons of my mother fought against me.”

[Col. 0487A] 20. Because the sons of the Synagogue who remained in unbelief waged the warfare of persecution against the faithful of the Synagogue. But while that part which came from the Jews to faith suffered persecution, it departed to [410] preach to the Gentiles. Hence it also follows:

(Verses 5.) “They appointed me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.”

21. Because while those who are in Judea persecute me, [Note: [Col. 0487D] Val. Cl., ‘in the Church.’] they made me keeper in the Churches. “My own vineyard I did not keep,” because I abandoned Judea. Hence Paul also says, and so do the apostles: “The word of God had to be spoken to you; but since you judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). It is as though he said: “We wished to keep our own vineyard, but because you yourselves rejected us, you send us to keep other people’s vineyards.”

So let us now say of the Church called to faith what we have said of the Synagogue converted to faith: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” The Church coming from the Gentiles looks upon the souls of the faithful whom she has found and calls them daughters of Jerusalem. Jerusalem is called “vision of peace.” She considers what she did and what she has become, and confesses her former sins, lest she become proud; she confesses her present life, lest she become ungrateful, and says: “I am black, but beautiful.” Black in merit, beautiful through grace; black through my former life, beautiful through the conduct that follows.

How am I black like the tents of Kedar? Kedar’s were the tents of the Gentiles; they were tents of darkness. And it was said to the Gentiles: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

How am I beautiful like Solomon’s skin? We have been made lean through repentance. The flesh mortified through repentance is brought, like a skin, into the service of the King. All who afflict themselves through repentance make themselves members of Christ. The members of Christ, therefore, afflicted through repentance, are Solomon’s skins, because they become mortified flesh.

22. But behold, there were faithful people in Judea who disdained the Gentiles’ coming to faith; hence they reproved Peter because he had received Cornelius. Therefore in the Church of the Gentiles it is added: “Do not look at me because I am dark.” Do not despise the Gentile condition of my unbelief; do not despise my former sins; [Col. 0487D] do not consider what I was.

Why? “Because the sun has discolored me.” The sun discolors where it presses itself more closely and strictly. When God holds a strict judgment, he displays his severity more fully; and he discolors by shining more brightly, because, while he exercises his severity more exactly, he judges more strictly. For the sun seems to suspend its rays when it considers our works mercifully; it seems to display its power strictly when it weighs our works strictly.

Let the Church therefore say: I am dark from the same source from which I am sinful, because the sun has discolored me; because, when my Creator abandons me, I have fallen into error.

[Col. 0488A] 23. But you who are so afflicted, so abandoned—what have you deserved? What have you received as a gift? “The sons of my mother fought against me.” The sons of my mother are the apostles, for the mother of all is the heavenly Jerusalem. They fought against the Church when, through their preaching, as with certain spears, they pierced her from unbelief to faith.

Hence Paul, like a warrior, says: “Destroying arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Cor. 10:5). Whoever destroys a height is certainly a warrior. These warriors, then, these sons of the mother Jerusalem, conquered the Church in her error in order to establish her in righteousness.

“The sons of my mother fought against me.” And what did they do while fighting? “They appointed me keeper of the vineyards.” The vineyards of the Church are the virtues that bear fruit. For while they fight down the vices in me, as though they were overcoming me because of my evil, they gave me the pursuit of virtues; [411] they made me keeper in the vineyards so that they might produce fruit.

After the specific conquest, she says: “My own vineyard I did not keep.” The vineyard of the Church is the ancient habit of error. When she is appointed keeper of the virtues, she abandons the ancient habit of her error.

24. We have spoken of the Synagogue coming to faith; we have spoken of the Gentile world converted. Let us therefore speak generally of the whole Church together and specifically of what is to be understood concerning each soul.

Wicked hearers are accustomed to consider their teachers not for what they are, but for what they were. Sound teachers therefore confess to her what they were [Col. 0488C] and declare what they are, so that they neither conceal themselves as sinners nor, again, deny their gifts as though they were ungrateful.

Let the Church say concerning these people: “I am black, but beautiful.” Black through myself, beautiful through the gift; black in what is past, beautiful because of what I have become in the future. How black, how beautiful? Black like the tents of Kedar, beautiful like Solomon’s skin.

And it is not right for anyone to be assessed according to his former life, [Note: [Col. 0487D] Here “not more” seems to signify the same as “least of all.”] and that attention be paid not so much to what he was as to what he is. Hence it adds: “Do not look at me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me.”

At times in Sacred Scripture the sun signifies the excessive heat of earthly desires. Why, then, am I dark? “Because the sun has discolored me,” and through the ardor of earthly love I have been discolored before the Bridegroom, that is, I have been made unbeautiful before the King.

(Verses 5.) “The sons of my mother fought against me.”

25. In all creation two rational creatures were made: human and angelic. The angel fell; he persuaded the human being [Note: [Col. 0488D] Supply: “to fall,” the fallen angels following pride.] to fall. The mother of every creature is the benevolence and power of God.

Therefore we and the angels, insofar as we were created rational, have a kind of fraternal fellowship. But because the angels were created by the same power by which we were created, and yet the fallen angels wage war against us every day, let her say: “The sons of the mother Church fought against me.”

Behold, while these rational spirits, these spirits who are sons of the mother, fight against the soul, they make it devote itself to earthly things, occupy itself with worldly actions, and seek transitory possessions. Hence it adds: “They appointed me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.”

The vineyards are earthly activities. It is as though she said: “They appointed me keeper in earthly affairs, [Note: [Col. 0489D] Perhaps it should read ‘and.’] and I did not keep my vineyard,” that is, my soul. I neglected to guard my life and my mind, because, while I was entangled externally in the activity of earthly things, I slipped away from the inner watch.

Many people consider themselves according to what is near them, not according to what they are. Near them are dignities; near them are external offices. While they guard what they have near them, they neglect to guard themselves.

Let her therefore say: “They appointed me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep,” that is, while I serve external guardianship in worldly activities, I have lost the concern for inner guardianship.

But behold, the soul has been brought back to the grace of its Creator. Let it now love; let it now seek where it may find its Redeemer.

(Verses 6.) “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.”

26. At noon the sun is hotter. Everyone who burns with faith burns with the love of desire. This Bridegroom, who below is called a young stag, pastures the greenness of virtues in their hearts; he lies down in their hearts at noon, in the fervor of charity.

“Tell me, [412] you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.” Why she asks where he pastures and where he lies down, she explains by giving the reason for her inquiry.

(Verses 6.) “Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

27. God’s companions are his familiar friends, such as all who live well. But many appear to be companions and are not companions. For many teachers, while persuading people to a perverse doctrine, seemed to be companions but proved to be enemies.

While Arius, Sabellius, and Montanus were still teachers, they seemed like companions; but when they were strictly exposed, they appeared as enemies. Frequently faithful souls, while clinging to the word of God and loving in teachers whatever might make them advance, do not know how to beware of the words of perverse teachers and fall away through their mouths.

How many peoples are there who believed in such companions and, while they persecuted them, wandered after the flocks of companions! Let her therefore say: “Tell me where you pasture, where you lie down at noon, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.”

Tell me in whose hearts you truly rest, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of those who seem to be your companions, that is, who are believed to be your familiars but are not.

All priests and all teachers are God’s companions in appearance; but with respect to life, many are not companions but adversaries. What we have said about heretical teachers can also be said about Catholics who do not act well.

Many faithful little ones within the Church desire to live well and wish to maintain a life of uprightness. They look to the life of the priests who have been placed over them; and when the priests themselves do not live well, when those who preside do not live rightly, those who follow fall into error.

Therefore the Church, as though speaking in the person of these little ones and faithful people, says: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at noon.”

Show me the life of those who truly serve you, so that I may know where you pasture; show me the greenness of virtues, so that I may know where you lie down at noon, that is, where you rest in the fervor of charity. Otherwise, while I look upon the flocks of your companions, I myself may begin to wander, not knowing to whose words and teachings I should entrust myself.

Every hearer, every weak person, must carefully consider whose words he ought to believe, whose teaching he ought to use, and whose examples he ought to follow.

And behold, the Bridegroom’s words are returned to the bride.

(Verses 7.) “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out and depart after the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds’ tents.”

28. Every soul ought to care for nothing more than knowing itself. For whoever knows himself recognizes that he was made in the image of God. He ought not to follow the likeness of beasts, whether by dissolving himself in luxury or by surrendering to present desire.

Of this ignorance it is said elsewhere: “When a man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13).

The tracks of the flocks are the actions of peoples, which, the more numerous they are, are the more confused and the more perverse. Let it therefore be said to the Church: “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out and depart after the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds’ tents.”

O you who were made ugly through ignorance but beautiful among other souls through faith: these words are clearly spoken to the Church of the elect. “If you do not know yourself,” that is, if you do not know this very thing—that you were made in my image—“go out,” that is, outside.

But if you do not recognize from whom you were made, go out and depart; go after the tracks of the flocks. Follow not my examples, [Col. 0490D] but the examples of peoples, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds’ tents.

[413] Our young goats are carnal impulses; our young goats are unlawful temptations. “Depart after the tracks of the flocks,” that is, descend after the tracks of the peoples, and pasture your young goats, that is, nourish carnal impulses, no longer spiritual perceptions but carnal impulses.

“Go beside the shepherds’ tents.” If you pasture lambs in the shepherds’ tent, you are pastured there, that is, in the teachings of teachers, in the teachings of the apostles, in the teachings of the prophets. But if you pasture young goats, pasture them beside the shepherds’ tents, so that you may be called Christian by faith and not by works; for you appear to be inside through faith, but not inside through works.

For behold, you have rebuked; behold, you have reproved—what do you not say? But what have you kindly done already? Say it clearly, for what follows is:

[Col. 0491A] (Verses 8.) “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.”

29. All who serve luxury, pride, avarice, envy, or deceit are still beneath Pharaoh’s chariot, that is, under the rule of the devil. But everyone who burns with humility, chastity, teaching, and charity has already become a horse of our Creator; he has already been placed in God’s chariot and already has God as his rider.

Hence it is said to one over whom the Lord presided: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:5). It is as though he said: “You are my horse; you can no longer kick against me; I already preside over you.”

Elsewhere it is said of these horses: “You sent your horses into the sea, stirring up many waters” (Hab. 3:15). God therefore has a chariot, because he presides over holy souls [Col. 0491B] and runs everywhere through holy souls.

Hence it is written: “The chariots of God are ten thousand, countless thousands; the Lord is among them in joy” (Ps. 67:18).

Pharaoh has a chariot as well, but those chariots were submerged in the Red Sea, because many perverse people were changed in baptism.

Let the Bridegroom therefore say: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my horse in Pharaoh’s chariots.” That is: while you were still in Pharaoh’s chariots, while you were still serving demonic works, I compared you to my cavalry, because I considered what I had done in you by predestination and compared you with my horses.

For God sees many still serving luxury and many still serving avarice, yet he considers, in his secret judgment, what he has already worked in them, because God has horses. But he sees many who are still Pharaoh’s horses.

[Col. 0491C] And because he considers, by a hidden judgment and hidden predestination, that they will be changed for the good, he already regards them as like his horses, because he sees that he will lead them to his chariot, although previously they served in Pharaoh’s chariot. Here the hidden judgments must be considered.

Many appear, through preaching, wisdom, chastity, generosity, and patience, to be God’s horses; yet by God’s hidden judgment they are compared with Pharaoh’s horses. And many appear, through avarice, pride, envy, and luxury, to be Pharaoh’s horses; yet by God’s hidden judgment they are compared with God’s horses.

For he sees the former turned from good to evil, and the latter brought back from evil to good. Thus, just as through discernment many who appear to be God’s horses are Pharaoh’s horses because of the reprobate life that follows them, [Note: [Col. 0491D] Val. Cl., “through indiscretion”; Rothomag., “through predestination.”] so through mercy many who appear to be Pharaoh’s horses are compared with God’s horses as his elect because of the holy life they will preserve at the end.

[414] Hence the Bridegroom speaks tenderly and says: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots.” That is: you were still subject to Pharaoh’s chariots and serving beneath them; you ran beneath vices. But I considered what I had done with you through predestination. [Col. 0492A] “I have compared you to my cavalry,” that is, I regarded you as like my elect. [Note: [Col. 0491D] Here the second homily ends in the Divion manuscript.]

(Verses 9.) “Your cheeks are beautiful like a turtledove’s; your neck like necklaces.”

30. After a turtledove has once lost its mate, it never joins itself to another but always lives alone and perseveres in mourning, because, not finding the one it loved, it seeks him.

So every holy soul, while it is absent from its Bridegroom, does not depart from his love but always breathes and groans with longing for him. While it does not find the one whom it loves intensely, because it withdraws from every foreign love, it displays the chastity of its heart by the modesty of its cheeks, through its very outward appearance and conduct.

It follows: “Your neck like necklaces.” By the bride’s neck the preachers of the holy Church are signified. [Note: [Col. 0491D] In the common editions the following is added: “The preachers are compared with necklaces, either because they are the Church’s ornament, or because they fortify the Church, like a necklace the breast, or because of their roundness, that is, perfection. In the manuscripts, these words are found in none of our manuscript codices. [Col. 0492D]”]

In necklaces, gems are set in gold. By gold, therefore, wisdom is expressed; by stones, works. The bride’s neck is therefore like necklaces, because every upright preacher of the Church clothes himself inwardly with wisdom and outwardly performs the works that he sees in wisdom.

To her it is further said:

(Verses 10.) “We will make you little golden chains, inlaid with silver.”

31. [Note: [Col. 0492D] In none of the manuscripts have we found what precedes this in the printed editions, namely: “The moray is a fish which, when caught, curls itself into a circle; after its likeness an earring is made which is called a *murenula*, by which preaching is signified, since it clings to and penetrates the ears. By *murenulae* . . . .”] Necklaces are fastened around the neck with little chains; likewise, wisdom and religion are joined to preachers from the Holy Scriptures. For by the chains the Holy Scripture is understood.

These are rightly called golden and worked with silver, because Holy Scripture shines with wisdom and is heard throughout the world through resounding preaching. For just as wisdom is shown by gold, so holy preaching is shown by silver.

The bride responds to the Bridegroom in these words, and through bodily images conveys the love with which she burns inwardly in a spiritual way, saying:

(Verses 11.) “While the king was at his banqueting couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance.”

32. [Note: [Col. 0492D] The printed editions preface this: “Nard is a lowly herb which, when tasted, drives out cold and warms the limbs”; the manuscripts do not contain it.] The king entered his banqueting couch when our Lord Jesus Christ bodily penetrated the inner regions of heaven. While he rested there, the bride’s nard gave forth its fragrance, because the virtue of the holy Church spread the sweet reputation of its goodness far and wide.

For the Lord ascended into heaven and sent his Holy Spirit upon the disciples (Acts 2). Filled with him, they preached words of salvation to the world and spread everywhere the reputation of the good odor of holy works.

Every faithful soul receives this Spirit in baptism, so that through him it may prepare for itself ointments from the combination of virtues and refresh its neighbors by the display of its example, as though by the fragrance of ointment.

It follows:

[Col. 0493A] (Verses 12.) “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will lodge between my breasts.”

33. The bodies of the dead are customarily embalmed with myrrh so that they may not decay.
