We apply myrrh to bodies so that they may not decay when, by mortifying our members in imitation of Christ, we restrain them from the corruption of luxury. Otherwise, if we leave them without seasoning, we make our bodies, dissolved by corruption, food for [415] eternal worms.

But why does the bride call her beloved not myrrh but a bundle of myrrh? Because, when the holy mind considers the life of Christ in every respect, it gathers, in imitation of him, virtues that resist all vices and makes a bundle of them for itself, with which to wipe away the everlasting corruption of its flesh.

[Col. 0493B] He is rightly said to dwell between her breasts, because Christ’s holy dwelling is built in the love of God and neighbor. For when a holy soul loves God in such a way that it does not despise its neighbor, and fulfills love of neighbor in such a way that it does not diminish divine love, it undoubtedly places breasts in its bosom, with which it embraces Christ and nourishes him.

Christ is strengthened as though nourished by breasts when he delights in this twofold love, so that he may cling more firmly.

Of him it is further said:

(Verses 13.) “My beloved is a cluster of henna in the vineyards of Engaddi.”

34. Cyprus is an island in which more abundant vineyards grow than elsewhere. Cyprus therefore signifies the universal Church, which nourishes many vineyards. Divided into many Churches, it produces the wine that gladdens the human heart.

[Note: [Col. 0493D] In other printed editions the following is inserted here: “In Engaddi balsam is produced; when mixed with oil and blessed by a bishop, it becomes chrism, by which the gifts of the Holy Spirit are signified. Engaddi, etc.” Since this was unknown to the manuscripts, we have removed it. It seems to have been taken from Bede, Book II on the Song of Songs, at this same verse, “A cluster.”]

Engaddi is interpreted as “spring of the young goat.” In ancient times the young goat was sacrificed for sins. What, then, is signified by the spring of the young goat except the baptism of Christ? In it, while the body is immersed, the soul is washed; and through faith in him who endured death for sinners, the human soul believes that it is cleansed from all sins.

Immediately the beloved responds to her:

(Verses 14.) “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are like those of doves.”

35. The Bridegroom calls his bride beautiful twice, because to the one to whom he gives love of God and neighbor he inserts a twofold beauty, in which he delights and which he praises.

Her eyes are rightly said to be like those of doves, because, while she mourns over temporal things and is snatched away by desire toward eternal things, [Note: [Col. 0494D] Printed editions: “toward eternal desires.”] she guards her senses in simplicity and detests carnal desires. The dove groans in love instead of singing.

The holy soul is rightly compared with a dove, because while the reprobate chatter and rejoice in their love of the world, the elect mind is worn down by heavenly desire. It fears losing what it loves while it is delayed.

The eyes of doves may also signify the preachers of the Churches [Col. 0494A], who preserve the simplicity that they preach and, despising visible things, long for eternal things with great groaning.

The bride’s voice follows, saying:

(Verses 15–16.) “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely; our couch is flower-covered, the beams of our houses are cedars, our ceilings are cypresses.”

36. The beloved is called beautiful and comely because, in his divinity and humanity, he is seen without any blemish worthy of reproach by every mind that loves him. While the bride follows him with complete desire, she forgets all the disturbances of the world; and while she rests in his peace, she is adorned more and more.

Hence it follows: “Our couch is flower-covered.” What are we to understand by the bride’s couch except the repose of leisure? The mind that loves Christ its Bridegroom uniquely is, insofar as it can be, free from all the world’s anxieties and inwardly accumulates [416] virtues with which to please its Bridegroom.

While it despises everything temporal, it makes a couch for itself with its Bridegroom in the peace of victory. There, the more peacefully it rests, the more flowers it finds with which to show itself beautiful to its Bridegroom.

It follows: “The beams of our houses are cedars, our ceilings are cypresses.” [Note: [Col. 0494D] At this point we have excised an addition of eight lines, rejected by the unanimous agreement of all the manuscripts.] By houses we understand the many Churches; [Note: [Col. 0494D] We have restored this material, which had been omitted, from the manuscripts.] by cedar beams we signify preachers; by cypress ceilings we signify the peoples themselves.

Beams support the roof, while ceilings fill and adorn the house. Thus, in the holy Church, good preachers carry divine Scripture in their hearts and mouths and proclaim it by spreading it before the faithful, so that, while the Church is instructed by heavenly preaching, it may receive protection by which it is shielded from the rains of temptation.

Cedar and cypress are said to be incorruptible woods. By them all the elect are rightly signified, because, while they pursue temporal things with no desire, they become eternal, since their minds are fixed on eternal things.

The Bridegroom responds and says:

CHAPTER II

(Chapter II—verse 1.) “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.”

1. Christ rightly calls himself a flower. While he exterminates the thorns of sins, he adorns the bride’s mind with the beauty of his righteousness; and when he brings heavenly desire to the nostrils of the heart, he refreshes the soul’s interior as though with fragrance.

He continues and says:

(Verses 2.) “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters.”

2. The bride is rightly said to be like a lily among thorns, because, although there are many in the Church who confess Christ with words alone but in their works pursue nothing except human concerns, only that soul is counted worthy of the dignity of the lily which rises from the root of mortality to heavenly beauty, guards the radiance of purity for itself in heart and body, and refreshes all its neighbors with the fragrance of a good reputation.

But because the Bridegroom judged his bride worthy of such great praise, she now praises the one by whom she sees herself praised, as she is bound to do, and says:

(Verses 3.) “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.”

3. Forest trees do not produce fruits suitable for human consumption, but people fittingly and wholesomely eat what the apple tree produces. Therefore Christ is rightly signified by the apple tree, and other human beings by the forest trees, because whenever we seek the food of salvation, we find it in Christ alone. In his words and examples we refresh our souls with sweet and wholesome fruit.

For he is the tree of life, [Note: [Col. 0495D] The printed editions read, “which he grants to us.”] which [Col. 0495B] bestows life upon us. He is the one who, when he breathes himself into us, nourishes the soul. If we find any refreshment in others, we take from them not what belongs to them but what belongs to Christ, because whatever is in them apart from God we undoubtedly find deadly for us.

(Verses 3.) “I sat down beneath the shade of the one whom I desired, and his fruit was sweet to my throat.”

4. Christ’s shade is the protection of the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit overshadows the mind that he fills, because he moderates all the heat of temptations. When the breeze of his inspiration gently touches the mind, he drives out whatever harmful heat it had endured. And when the excessive heat of vices had perhaps already [417] withered the mind, the shade of the Holy Spirit protects and revives it, so that, resting while it sits beneath his inspiration, it gathers strength with which to run more powerfully toward eternal life.

It follows: “And his fruit was sweet to my throat.” Christ himself is the fruitful tree planted in the heart. If our mind loves and diligently cultivates him as it ought, it undoubtedly produces beautiful and useful fruits within. When the mind receives and eagerly eats them, it sets aside all the pleasures of the world because of their sweetness.

It is exceedingly sweet for the mind to think of heavenly things, to fix its inner eye upon eternity, so that at times the inflamed mind may be pierced even amid tears; and, lifted up among its tears, it may be nourished by the food of angels—that is, by wisdom—with a sweetness proportionate to its eagerness.

Hence it is added:

(Verses 4.) “The King brought me into the wine cellar; he ordered charity within me.”

[Col. 0495D] 5. What should we understand more fittingly by the wine cellar than the secret contemplation of eternity itself? In this eternity the holy angels are intoxicated with the wine of wisdom. Seeing God himself face to face, they are filled with every spiritual delight.

If the holy mind, setting aside all temporal things, is brought into this place by the Bridegroom, it enters and tastes there, insofar as it is granted, of those angelic delights. And because it is still held in corruptible flesh, it is not perfectly satisfied; nevertheless, from that little which it takes in passing, it considers how greatly it ought to love what it loves.

The wine cellar can also signify divine Scripture. Through it charity is ordered in the bride, because its teaching clearly shows how God and neighbor are to be loved in the proper order.

Struck by this charity, she continues and says:

(Verses 5.) “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I am sick with love.”

6. The tender and inexperienced are signified by flowers, while the mature faithful are signified by apples. Because the bride is sick with love, she desires to be strengthened with flowers and surrounded with apples. While she afflicts herself with longing for eternity and searches with complete anxiety for how she may reach it, [Note: [Col. 0495D] Thus it is read in all the manuscripts. Although more obscure, we judged this reading preferable to the Editors’ alternative: “she searches, because, while she lives in the flesh, she rests in perfection . . . .”] she does not find complete arrival while she lives in the flesh. Weary in her desire, she rests; and she rejoices in this alone if she sees around her either those whom she may help or in whose perfection she may perceive consolation for her weariness.

Concerning her Bridegroom she then says:

(Verses 6.) “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.”

7. By the Bridegroom’s left hand the present life is signified; by his right hand, eternal life. By the bride’s head is understood the mind that rules the soul.

The Bridegroom’s left hand is said to be beneath the bride’s head, and his right hand embraces her, because she always places temporal life beneath her mind, while she longs to embrace eternal life in every way. She tramples magnanimously under the feet of her lofty mind the things she sees and occupies herself with heavenly duties.

She bears these things out of necessity; toward those things she sighs with the highest desire, as though bound by the Bridegroom’s right arm. When she enters them even a little, she rests in delight; and because she loves this rest, she utterly detests worldly tumult.

The Bridegroom loves her all the more as she rests in this way and drives away from her every wicked person who would awaken her, saying:

(Verses 7.) “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the does and the [418] stags of the fields, do not awaken or rouse my beloved, [Note: [Col. 0496D] In Rothomag. and Val. Cl., ‘until she herself wishes it.’] until she herself wishes it.”

8. Deer and does are declared clean animals in the Law. What, then, do we understand by deer and does except faith, hope, and charity? While we keep these pure for ourselves, by them we ascend the lofty mountains of contemplation. The holy soul, the bride of Christ, desires to rest from all the disturbances of the world; it longs to sleep in holy leisure in the bosom of the bridegroom, with earthly desires lulled to sleep, so that it sometimes grows weary even of necessary conversations and rejoices in the conversation of the bridegroom alone—more serenely the quieter it is. But carnal people in the Church sometimes rouse this sleeping soul at inopportune times, wishing to involve it in worldly affairs, because they consider its life useless when they see it abstaining from their concerns. Such people are appropriately called not sons but daughters, because, while they foster effeminate ways and lose their manly dignity, their inward character is outwardly indicated by a feminine name. These are forbidden, under the weight of an oath, to rouse the beloved, lest they disturb with untimely solicitations the mind that girds itself for devotion to God and desires to cling solely to spiritual pursuits, and lest they darken the eye of its heart with the shadows of earthly cares. Yet not every concern for one’s neighbor is forbidden to it; rather, when it should be roused is left to its own will, since every perfect soul must certainly discern both when to devote itself to heavenly contemplation and when to serve the needs of its neighbors. The bride gladly receives this permission to devote herself to God, and immediately embraces the bridegroom’s word and says:

[Col. 0497B] **(Verse 8.)** The voice of my beloved: behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.

9. It is as though she said: “I recognize this as the voice of my beloved bridegroom; I always desire to hear it from his mouth, because in this I see how much he loves me, since he forbids me to be hindered from his desirable embraces.” How he reached these embraces she immediately relates, saying: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.” As Christ prepared to come to the embraces of his bride, he graciously assumed our humanity. To accomplish this mystery, he came as one leaping upon the mountains, because he displayed among human beings certain works so lofty and above humanity that the human race could marvel at them but could not attain them. For he was born of a virgin; an angel instructed shepherds to go and adore him as he lay crying; a star led the Magi; while hanging on the cross, he gave up his spirit at the hour he chose; after dying, he raised himself on the third day; having entered heaven, he gave the Holy Spirit to those whom he wished; and through fishermen and uneducated men he subjected the world to his faith. In doing these things he walked, as it were, upon the mountains, where no creature could reach him. In these works he certainly bounded over the hills, because by the power of his action he surpassed all the saints, however greatly they may have grown. Concerning him it also follows:

**(Verse 9.)** My beloved is like a doe and a fawn of the deer.

He is rightly said to be like a doe, because he drew his flesh from the Synagogue, which is represented by the doe. And because he was born from the stock of the ancient saints, he is rightly described as a fawn of the deer. It follows:

**(Verse 9.)** Behold, he himself stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, peering through the latticework.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Val. Cl.: “through the windows and through the latticework.” Rothom.: “through the windows and the latticework.”]

10. Christ stood, as it were, behind our wall when he was made flesh, because divinity lay hidden in the humanity he assumed. And because, if he had revealed his immensity, human weakness could not have borne it, he placed before it the obstacle of flesh and performed whatever great things he did among human beings as one hiding behind a wall. Through windows and latticework, one who looks is partly seen and partly conceals himself. So also the Lord Jesus Christ, while performing miracles through the power of his divinity and enduring lowly things through the weakness of his flesh, looked out as if through a window and latticework: hidden in one respect, he appeared in another as to who he was. Thus, having become incarnate, he speaks to his Church, or to every perfect soul, and exhorts it toward the eternal homeland, saying:

**(Verse 10.)** Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.

11. Christ calls his bride “friend” on account of faith, “dove” on account of simplicity, and “beautiful” on account of her works. Since we cannot please God without faith, we are rightly called friends through faith, because, while seeking heavenly things by faith, we cling to God after rejecting earthly things. The soul is rightly called a dove on account of simplicity, because, while searching for the simple God with a simple heart, it does not recklessly pursue the foolish joy of the world in dissipation; rather, always hastening toward eternal things, it lovingly imitates the dove’s lament. The soul is rightly called beautiful on account of its works, because, while redeeming the sins of its former life through good works, it conceals its former ugliness from the bridegroom’s eyes as though it had assumed a better form. The bridegroom therefore urges her to arise and come, because it is fitting that whoever hastens toward the love of Christ should cast off the sluggishness of the flesh as far as possible and prepare himself swiftly to obtain eternal things. But because we have received from God, through the manifestation of the New Testament, the means by which we hasten toward heavenly things, it rightly follows:

[Col. 0498C] **(Verse 11.)** For now winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed.

12. What should be understood by winter except the austerity of the Law? While it held the ancient people to carnal sacrifices, it did not help those who observed it to desire spiritual and heavenly things. We may also understand the present life by winter: while it assails us with continual temptations, it compels us, as though by unwelcome rains, to grow sluggish in following Christ. But now let the bride arise, because winter has passed: the nearer the last day approaches, the more the present life recedes, and the farther time is carried toward its end, the more swiftly we must run, lest the chosen soul be deprived of the eternal gifts offered to it. It is said to have passed because there is no doubt that it is soon to pass. It follows:

**(Verse 12.)** The flowers have appeared on the earth; the time of pruning has come.

13. The flowers are said to have appeared on the earth because, when holy souls depart from their bodies, they are received into heaven. And because, although there was winter in this life, they did not grow sluggish in good works, as soon as they departed they flourished gloriously in the land of the living. Thus it rightly follows that he says: “The time of pruning has come,” because the more the number of the elect is gathered in heaven, the more swiftly the wicked are cut off from the Church like useless branches, so that the world may come to an end more quickly. It follows:

**(Verses 12–13.)** The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land; the fig tree has put forth its unripe figs, and the flowering vines have given their fragrance.

14. What is signified by the turtledove except the Church, and by the bridegroom’s land except that blessed life? Yet the voice of the turtledove is said to have been heard in the bridegroom’s land because, while the holy Church prays out of desire for it, she is most mercifully heard by Christ in heaven. Concerning her it is rightly added: “The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs, and the flowering vines have given their fragrance.” The fig tree put forth its unripe figs because the holy Church sent her martyrs ahead to the eternal homeland. After them, the flowering vines gave their fragrance because examples of good works grew throughout the world. The vines produce flowers when individual churches bring souls previously unbelieving into the newness of faith through baptism. But the flowers themselves produce fragrance when believing souls scatter good examples among one another and among others through their sweet reputation. Because Christ draws us by both kinds of exhortation—admonishing us by commands and raising us up by the examples of the saints—the bridegroom first instructed his bride to arise by admonition, then brought the examples of the saints to her knowledge, and after displaying those examples again turned to reminding her of the command, saying:

**(Verses 13–14.)** Arise, my friend, my sister, and come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall.

[Col. 0499C] 15. The soul arises when it lifts itself up from the perpetration of sin; it comes when, by good works and the steps of holy desire, it advances toward heavenly things. Indeed, when the holy mind sees the ugliness of its former life and counts the sins it has committed, it immediately feels shame within its conscience. Turning whatever it had loved in the world into an object of hatred, it punishes itself with tears; strengthened by this very repentance, it leaps away from every defilement [Note: [Col. 0499D] In the printed editions: “even from the defilement of thought.”] and shakes off all sluggish negligence, so that it no longer lies in lowly thoughts but stretches itself through holy desires toward invisible things. This mind therefore arises and comes, because through compunction it raises itself from the weakness of sluggishness and, exercising itself in holy pursuits, runs toward eternal things on the feet of love.

By the clefts of the rock I would gladly understand the wounds of Christ’s hands and feet as he hung upon the cross. By the hollow of the wall, in the same sense, I would understand the wound in his side made by the lance. And the dove is rightly said to be in the clefts of the rock and in the hollow of the wall, because, while imitating Christ’s endurance in remembering the cross and recalling those wounds for the sake of example, the simple soul finds in the wounds, as a dove in the clefts, nourishment by which it may recover.

The clefts of the rock may nevertheless signify the mysteries of Christ’s incarnation, and the hollow of the wall the very protection of angelic guardianship. When the soul is placed within this protection, the bridegroom rightly says to it:

**(Verse 14.)** Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet and your face is lovely.

16. What do we understand by the face except faith, by which we are known by God? And what by the voice except preaching? The bridegroom commands the bride to show him her face because whoever says that he has faith must exercise himself in good works, so that interior faith may become known through exterior works. But works must also be followed by the voice of preaching, because whoever expands himself in holy works must consequently exhort his neighbors to do the same. Therefore it follows: “For your voice is sweet and your face is lovely.” The voice is pleasing and the face is made beautiful when preaching follows works and, in turn, good works accompany preaching. To preachers of this kind it is appropriately said:

**(Verse 15.)** Catch for us [Note: [Col. 0499D] Thus we read in all the manuscripts, where the printed editions have “the little foxes,” perhaps because “little” is read later.] the little foxes that ravage the vineyards, for our vineyard has blossomed.

17. By the foxes heretics are signified, and by the vineyards the individual churches. The foxes ravage the vineyards because through heretics the churches are dried up, losing the verdure of right faith. They are rightly called little, because although they are inwardly proud against the truth, outwardly they pursue humility in their words by pretense. They are caught by holy preachers when, in the course of controversy, they are refuted by judgments of truth.

Holy preachers are sometimes called dogs by analogy, because through continual preaching, like persistent barking, they strive to keep all adversaries away from the flock of sheep. These dogs catch foxes for Christ: while faithfully loving their leader and laboring for his sake, they lead deceitful heretics out of the entanglements of questions, as though from dark caves into the light of truth.

Why the destruction caused by the foxes should be feared is made clear when it is said: “For our vineyard has blossomed.” The vineyard has blossomed because the holy Church has brought forth children through baptism into a new way of life in faith. It must be feared that these children may be corrupted by heretics, because, while believers are regenerated into the newness of Christ, the more tender each one is, the more quickly he is led astray into wickedness. The flowers must especially be feared lest they perish, because while a person has not yet grown strong toward perfection through long exercise, he easily withers from what he had attained if he is bitten by a poisonous tooth. Every perfect soul does not easily lose what it has long practiced, because the more frequently it has tasted inwardly how sweet the Lord is, the more firmly it holds to the bridegroom’s rectitude and rejects what is crooked. It appropriately continues and says:

**(Verses 16–17.)** My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline.

[Col. 0501A] 18. It is as though she said: “I hold firmly to the friendship of my beloved because I perceive his steadfast goodwill toward me. Since I enjoy his kindly intimacy, whatever I hear opposed to him from enemies who bark seems harsh to me. And as I see what he is in his continual presence, if his adversaries utter any error, I do not depart from the truth that I have recognized in beholding him.”

Concerning him it rightly follows: “Who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” What is signified by the lilies except souls? [Note: [Col. 0501D] The printed editions add “except pure souls”; the manuscripts are silent.] While they retain the whiteness of chastity, they spread a sweet fragrance to their neighbors through the reputation of a good life. The bridegroom therefore feeds among the lilies because, without doubt, he delights in the chastity of souls, which preserve purity of flesh within themselves, please him through radiant thoughts, and give their neighbors examples like the sweetness of fragrance.

The day will breathe and the shadows will incline when eternal life appears and the present life comes to an end. It will be day, but this is night, because here our vision is dim; there the day itself—that is, the whole truth—will shine upon our minds. [Note: [Col. 0501D] Thus it is read in all the manuscripts. But the printed editions have: “Here, then, is night; there it will be day, because here we grow dim in the vision of truth, whereas there God himself, the whole truth, will shine upon our minds.”]

Souls strive with all their strength to reach this day; for its sake they preserve unblemished justice as far as they can. And because they can do nothing without Christ, they invoke his help and desire his intimacy. While he considers their minds, the merciful one is near and helps them; and the more they progress, the more familiarly he always loves them, until, when the darknesses of the world have ended, he leads the perfect into the light of eternal life. Because they greatly desire this light and believe that they will see it when the Lord comes for judgment, they say with the greatest longing:

[Col. 0501C] **(Verse 17.)** Return; be like a doe, my beloved, and like a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of Bethel.

19. Our beloved departed from us bodily when, after the resurrection, he ascended into heaven. He will return when, at the end of the world, the bodies of human beings have been raised and he is revealed to all in judgment. He will truly appear like a doe and a fawn of the deer, because, coming to judgment in our flesh, he will show himself to all.

By the doe, which is a clean animal, the Church is signified, since, while she dwells in heavenly things in her mind, she feeds, as it were, upon the mountains. By the deer, what else is signified except the ancient fathers, from whose flesh Christ was born and presented to the world as a fawn of the deer? [Col. 0501D] Bethel, moreover, is interpreted as “house of God.” It is rightly called the Church of God because the Lord dwells in it while our hearts are cleansed through faith.

He will therefore appear like a doe and a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of Bethel, because he will come to judgment in the form of the humanity that he took from the Church, when in this world he was humbly born from the lineage of the fathers like a fawn from deer. He will truly appear both like a doe and upon the mountains of Bethel, because in the form of his humanity he will be like the Church, yet he will stand exalted above those very highest ones who tower like mountains within the Church. While he delays his coming, because the holy soul always strives to seek him, it therefore follows:

# CHAPTER III

**(Chapter III—Verse 1.)** By nights, on my bed, I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him.

1. The holy soul makes a bed for itself by night when, fleeing all the disturbances of the world, it prepares a place of retreat in which it may rest. On this bed it seeks the one whom it loves, because, while free from all the world’s anxieties, it does not rest in its search for how it may reach him. It should be noted that it seeks by night: living now in this world, it completely casts the darkness of temporality from itself. [Note: [Col. 0501D] The printed editions, against all the manuscripts, have “does not cast it from itself.” Although our reading may at first appear to lack truth, it is nevertheless more accurate according to Saint Gregory’s meaning: the soul, fleeing all the disturbances of the world and making a bed for itself, casts the darkness of temporality from itself completely, insofar as it is able.]

The heavier the darkness it endures, the more fervently it seeks the one whose discovery will cause it to suffer darkness no longer. But because it never finds the one it seeks perfectly in this world, it adds: “I sought him and did not find him.” Since it burns with the greatest desire, and nothing it possesses is sufficient until it finds its beloved, it adds the persistence of its search, saying:

**(Verse 2.)** I will rise; I will go around the city. Through the streets and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him.

2. What is signified here by the city except the Church, and by the streets of the city except the spiritual people? [Note: [Col. 0502D] The printed editions read: “who, while [they walk] toward heavenly things.”] While they walk toward the Church with their whole heart, they keep the narrow way by which they may be led to life. By the squares, however, secular people are signified, who, while pursuing their many pleasures, walk along broad ways. The bride therefore rises and goes around the city, because the perfect soul, which despises visible things, considers in her mind all the saints who are or have been in the Church, to see whether she might perhaps find in their deeds something that, by imitating it, could eventually enable her to find the bridegroom.

She seeks through the streets and squares because, while striving through the imitation of the good to reach the beloved’s intimate embraces, she sometimes finds something worthy of imitation not only in spiritual people but also in carnal people. But after indicating the doubled labor, she again adds the difficulty of finding him, saying: “I sought him and did not find him.” Yet while she seeks and does not find, she herself is also sought and found; therefore it is added:

**(Verse 3.)** The watchmen who guard the city found me. “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?”

3. What is signified by the watchmen except the teachers of the Church? While they keep watch over the gaining of souls by their writings and words, wherever they perceive even a little desire, they never cease to increase it toward what is better. They find the bride seeking because they receive the devout soul striving to find Christ; and, so that it may find him more quickly, they instruct it by commands and kindle it by examples.

Questioning them, she says: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” The bride is rightly said to question them because, while she examines their writings or words with an attentive mind, she asks what they have understood about Christ, speaking in the intention of her mind as though to persons present even when they are absent. Because, while she fixes her attention on them, she never finds the bridegroom, she consequently adds:

**(Verse 4.)** Shortly after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.

4. She passes the watchmen shortly and finds the beloved because, while she thinks of them as pure human beings, she raises her mind to divinity and there recognizes her bridegroom as equal to the Father and above human beings. She says that she has found him when, aided by holy labors, she fixes the eye of faith for a little while in contemplation, as in a mirror, upon the radiance of his divinity. How eagerly her mind receives this small glimpse she shows by saying:

**(Verse 4.)** I held him and will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.

5. The mother of the Church was the Synagogue, because from it she received holy preachers, from whom she received the word of truth by which she was regenerated in faith. The Church therefore holds the bridegroom until she brings him into her mother’s house, because she does not depart from his faith and love until the end of the world, when she brings the Jews to faith. This does not mean that she will depart from him afterward; rather, the one whom she loves in exile she will love even more when she sees him in the homeland. But the statement had to concern the time about which anyone might doubt because of the temptations that resist it.

She will bring the beloved into her mother’s house when, at the end of the world, the Church introduces Christian mysteries among the Jewish people through preaching. She will bring him into the chamber, as into a more private part of the house, because she will convert many from that people in such a way that they cast away all the burdens of the world and desire to please God alone in their inmost thoughts. Such people will make a chamber for the bridegroom because, while casting away all the filth of desire from themselves, they will fashion within their minds a secluded place in which he may delight.

While the bridegroom rests delightfully in them, he forbids those who would disturb them, saying:

[Col. 0503D] **(Verse 5.)** I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the does and the deer of the fields: do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she wishes.

6. Here he shows that after the conversion he will find some among the Synagogue possessing the same perfection as very many in the Church, and, delighting similarly in their rest, he forbids anyone to disturb them, just as he forbade such disturbance in the Church. [Note: [Col. 0503D] Rothomag. reads “disturbance” (*inquietationem*); the reading of the earlier editors differs slightly.] Thus, once the Synagogue has been brought to faith, she observes the mind of the Church through the works she sees, and, greatly admiring its sublimity, says:

**(Verse 6.)** Who is this who ascends through the desert like a column of smoke from perfumes of myrrh and frankincense and every powdered spice?

7. The Church, or every holy soul, lives in the desert—that is, in this world—while dwelling in exile from the kingdom among beasts, namely demons. Here, although she is not wholly abandoned by the bridegroom, while she is still in the flesh she is not yet admitted to the certain vision of him. She wanders from him through exiles and temptations; because she does not yet reign with him, she seems to herself to have been abandoned by him.

For this reason she always labors to ascend, so that she may feel more and more deeply the one whom she loves greatly; since she does not possess him perfectly in the desert, she at least refreshes herself in the desire for him, so that, strengthened on the way, she may eventually reach what she has long desired. There are indeed some who, while they grow weary of all visible things, raise their minds to heavenly things; and because they see nothing in lowly things that gives them pleasure, they turn their whole heart toward what is above. They strip themselves of all evil habits, despise the world’s wealth together with its desires, stretch toward invisible things in hope, and the more ardently they cling to them, the more grievously they bear the corruption they possess.

Such people ascend through the desert because, while living amid temptations in this world, the more they fear being abandoned while they remain here, the more firmly they abandon these things and the more fervently walk toward those things in which, once they have arrived, they will fear nothing further that can remove them.

8. They are rightly said to ascend like a column of smoke, because they are said to possess both the fragrance of a good reputation and subtlety of mind. Yet this smoke is not said to arise from just any substances; it is declared to come from perfumes of myrrh, frankincense, and every powdered spice. The bodies of the dead are embalmed with myrrh so that they do not decay; frankincense is burned so that it may give off fragrance.

By myrrh, therefore, the mortification of the flesh is signified; by frankincense, the purity of prayers is understood. Thus, when the holy soul mortifies its flesh so that it does not decay through vices, and renounces all the pleasures of the world through continence, it applies myrrh to its body as to one destined to die, so that after judgment it may remain sound from eternal corruption.

But when it kindles itself toward heavenly things with greater desire and fervently casts every superfluous thought from the chamber of its heart, it makes its heart, as it were, a censer before God. While it gathers virtues in it through love, it fits them together like coals in a censer, so that the mind may kindle itself before God with the fire of charity. And while it sends fervent and pure prayers to God, it brings smoke of perfumes out of the censer, so that it may give off a sweet fragrance before the beloved and never cease to stir its neighbors toward his love through good examples.

It should be noted, however, that he does not say “of every spice,” but “of every powdered spice.” We make spices when we gather virtues in the heart. But when we examine our virtues more carefully through each individual work, lest anything uncultivated remain in our deeds or a vice lie hidden among the virtues, then without doubt we pound the ointments of virtues into powder, so that our works may be purer the more subtly we distinguish them from every stealthy intrusion of vice.

Minds of this kind make themselves pleasing to their beloved through his grace; and, while separating themselves from all worldly noise, they prepare within themselves a place in which the bridegroom may rest. Concerning this rest it is added:

**(Verses 7–8.)** Behold, King Solomon’s bed; sixty mighty men, among the mightiest of Israel, surround it, all holding swords and most skilled in war, each one’s sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night.

9. Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful.” What, then, is understood by Solomon except Christ, of whom it is written: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14)? We make a bed for Solomon when we cease entirely from worldly anxieties, willingly rest in the sole desire for Christ, and cleanse our heart of every earthly desire so that he may rest with us.

When the number ten is multiplied by six, sixty is completed. By ten, therefore, we understand the Decalogue of the Law; by six, we understand all this time that we see unfolding through the six working days. By sixty, then, we understand all the perfect people who lived before us in the Church: by fulfilling the ten commandments of the Law in the six days more spiritually and therefore more powerfully, they completed, as it were, the number sixty.

These surround Solomon’s bed because they fortify the holy mind in which Christ rests by their words and examples, repelling from the entrance of the mind the enemies who come, supporting that mind by their examples and teaching it through their writings. They hold swords and are most skilled in war because, while fulfilling in deed the word of God that they know in their hearts, they become ever more skilled and overcome their enemy—namely, the demon—with wisdom and strength.

By the sword the word of God is signified; by the hands holding the swords, the works themselves are represented. Concerning these it is rightly added: “Each one’s sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night.” What do we understand by the sword except the rigor of conduct, and by the thigh except the appetite of the flesh? Thus all the elect who have already advanced to the perfection of life always carry a sword upon their thigh, because by the rigor of their conduct they continually break the appetite of the flesh, lest the enemy whom they fear in the night of this world come suddenly, find an easy entrance, and lead them more readily into graver sins through the softness of pleasure, the more pleasure-loving he finds them.

Concerning Solomon’s praise it is further added:

**(Verses 9–10.)** King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon: silver columns, a golden backrest, a purple ascent; its middle he paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem.

10. The woods of Lebanon are said to be imperishable. Therefore King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon because, by the grace of his foreknowledge, Christ constructed the holy Church from saints destined to endure forever. [Note: [Col. 0505D] Val. Cl.: “by the grace of his presence,” which we do not at all approve. Other manuscripts also disagree.]

He made its columns of silver because he gave that Church preachers who, both to support it by their examples, strengthened it with great uprightness of justice, and to instruct it by their preaching, adorned it with the splendor of eloquence like the brightness of silver. He made a golden backrest because, while shining in the hearts of the perfect, he showed them the power of his divinity through contemplation. In this contemplation, while he showed them the beauty of heavenly joys, he constructed, as it were, a backrest of gold, because he supplied a place where they might rest and refresh themselves.

This backrest is rightly said to be golden, because “wisdom is better than all riches, and all that is desired cannot be compared with it” (Proverbs 8:11). To this backrest one comes through many labors and ascends through many tribulations, so that, if necessary, even blood is permitted to be shed. Therefore the ascent is rightly said to be purple. When the holy martyrs handed their bodies over to punishment for the sake of eternal life, when they patiently endured scourges, wooden horses, fires, swords, and countless other torments, did they not ascend by this purple ascent to this backrest—that is, to the blessed life? [Note: [Col. 0506D] Thus all the manuscripts and the Paris printed edition of 1518. Other editions have “spikes.” The error arose from the way ancient scribes wrote *eculeos*.]

But what do we wretches do? We are not silver columns in this litter because we neither support the holy Church by our examples nor teach it by preaching. We do not possess a golden backrest in it because, entangled in earthly thoughts, we do not rise through contemplation to the splendor of wisdom. We do not even recognize the purple ascent because, devoted to pleasures, we refuse to endure labors and persecutions for the sake of eternal blessedness.

What is said concerning this litter gives us some consolation: “Its middle he paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem.” What do we understand by the daughters of Jerusalem, since he said not sons but daughters, except ourselves, the weak ones who in the Church are not men but women, because we do not fight courageously against vices or resist manfully, but submit in a womanly manner? Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” by which the Church, our mother, is signified, because she continually contemplates perpetual peace.

If, then, we are not silver columns in the King’s litter, do not possess a golden backrest, and cannot ascend by the purple ascent, let us at least hold the love that is placed in the middle, as common to all the elect. Through this love King Solomon recognizes that we are in his litter, because in it, together with the silver columns, the golden backrest, and the purple ascent, he paved the middle with love for the daughters of Jerusalem: we reach the same blessedness of the bridegroom with the members of the Church if we preserve tireless love. It follows:

**(Verse 11.)** Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon with the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of the joy of his heart.

11. The blessed Mary is believed to be Christ’s mother. She crowned him with a diadem because he himself assumed our humanity from her, as is related in the Gospel (Matthew 1). This is said to have happened on the day of his betrothal and on the day of the joy of his heart because, when the only-begotten Son of God wished to join his divinity to our humanity, when by his good will he chose at the appointed time to take his Church to himself, [Note: [Col. 0507D] For explanatory purposes, more recent printed editions insert “his bride”; our reading is that of the manuscripts and the old Paris edition.] then with the exultation of love he wished to receive our flesh from the Virgin Mother. While living in that flesh for a time amid sufferings, he rejoiced exceedingly in our redemption.

But since a diadem is assumed for glory, while in the assumption of humanity not the glory of the Word of God but humility is recognized, how is he said to have been crowned with our humanity as with a diadem? Yet since his incarnation itself was truly our glory, because we are his members through communion in his body, Scripture appropriately called the diadem of the members the crown of the head.

Because he is praised here by the bride, and he in turn graciously deigns to praise the bride, he says:

# CHAPTER IV

**(Chapter IV—Verse 1.)** How beautiful you are, my friend; how beautiful and lovely you are! Your eyes are like those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within.

Because we explained these matters above (Chapter 2, no. 35), as best we could, we now avoid repeating them in order to preserve brevity [Col. 0507C]. But since the phrase “apart from what lies hidden within” has been added, we must briefly consider how it is to be joined with what precedes. The bride is therefore beautiful, and her eyes are like those of doves, “apart from what lies hidden within,” because whatever she does outwardly is exceedingly honorable: she conducts herself simply among human beings; she disdains desiring temporal things that she sees; and, if anything in this world pleases her, she detests following after her desires. Yet far more beautiful and honorable is her effort to preserve the desire of her heart undefiled; to retain in her mind the splendor of eternal blessedness and contemplate it with uplifted gaze; and to rest sweetly and be cleansed in those things that she sees inwardly. It follows:

**(Verse 1.)** Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead [Col. 0507D].

**2.** If the eyes signify the preachers of the Church, because the Church shows the way to others, the hair is rightly understood as signifying the peoples, because they provide the same Church with adornment. The bride’s hair is therefore said to be like a flock of goats, because the peoples of the Church, while ruminating on the precepts of the Law and contemplating heavenly things by faith, are clean animals and feed in high places. Gilead, moreover, is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” What else, then, do we understand by the heap of testimony except the multitude of martyrs? Since they held the faith of Christ unconquerably, we know that they bore witness to the truth even through their death [Col. 0508A]. This flock of goats therefore comes up from Mount Gilead, because the people of the Church lift themselves by faith toward eternal things all the more as they know that the holy martyrs bore testimony to that same faith with greater strength. It follows:

**(Verse 2.)** Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep [Note: The manuscripts of Rouen and Reims read, “a flock of shorn sheep.”], which come up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, and none among them is barren [Col. 0508D].

**3.** Just as the eyes are understood as the preachers, because through them the Church is illumined, so the teeth of the same bride may likewise be understood, because through them unbelievers are consumed and little ones are nourished. The holy preachers are rightly called teeth, because, by expounding Holy Scripture and making it clear to their younger brethren, they chew it like bread for little children, as mothers chew food for their sons, so that the weak may grow strong enough for greater things [Col. 0508B].

These preachers are rightly said to be like a flock of shorn sheep that comes up from the washing, because, while remembering that they have been cleansed from all sins in baptism, they willingly lay aside the burdens of the world, so that they may proceed more freely—and therefore more easily—to attain and proclaim heavenly things. Of them it is added: “All of them bearing twins, and none among them is barren.” All holy preachers bear twin offspring, because, while they surpass other human beings in the two commandments of charity, they proclaim a twofold love and do not cease to beget in it two peoples, the Jewish and the Gentile. None among them is barren, because one certainly ought not to be called a preacher if he scorns begetting spiritual children. Of these it is further said [Col. 0508C]:

**(Verse 3.)** Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet.

**4.** These same preachers are called the lips of the Church, because through them she speaks the precepts of life to the peoples. They are rightly compared to a ribbon, because, by their preaching, they restrain the wandering thoughts in human hearts, just as one holds back scattered hair so that it does not flow excessively. But why are they compared not merely to a ribbon, but to a scarlet one? Is it not because scarlet signifies the flame of charity, with which they burn and by which they kindle others? Through them the speech of the holy Church is sweetened, because, while doing what they say, they set their preaching before people like tasty food. It follows:

**(Verse 3.)** Your cheeks are like a slice of a pomegranate, apart from what lies hidden within [Col. 0508D].

**5.** What do we understand by the cheeks of the Church except these same preachers, who, while standing out among the peoples for their benefit, appear as though manifest upon the face of the Church? The pomegranate signifies the Church herself, because, while nourishing many peoples in the unity of faith, she gathers many seeds beneath a single rind. The holy preachers are therefore a slice of the pomegranate, because, while they afflict themselves more vigorously than others in divine service like seeds; while they despise all worldly things; while they renounce their pleasures; while they completely mortify their vices [Note: The printed editions read, “they deny their own wills.”]; and while they exalt others [Col. 0509A], they offer themselves as food, as though broken open and exposed, while nourishing others through their examples. [Note: In the same place, after “they completely mortify,” the printed editions add, “while they humble themselves.” These words are absent from the manuscripts.] Yet although the things that appear outwardly are great, they retain still greater things hidden within, which the divine eyes alone see. Therefore it is added: “Apart from what lies hidden within.” It follows [Col. 0509D]:

**(Verse 4.)** Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements; a thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of the mighty.

**6.** We extend the neck when we wish to see farther. For one reason, then, the holy preachers are fittingly called eyes; for another, teeth; for another, cheeks; and for another, the neck. The neck of the holy Church is therefore rightly said to be like the tower of David, because the holy preachers watch for enemies approaching from afar against the holy Church and resist them courageously if they attempt to harm anything in the Church; and, freely despising earthly things, they contemplate heavenly things [Col. 0509B]. They are called the neck because they watch for enemies, the tower because of their strength, and because of their lofty contemplation of heavenly joys. This tower is rightly said to be David’s, because David is interpreted as “strong of hand”; by this Christ is signified, for whatever is strong and lofty is his work.

Of it follows: “Built with battlements; a thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of the mighty.” The tower of David is said to be built with battlements because the holy preachers, when necessary, are armed with miracles against human adversaries. Against vices, however, they fortify themselves with shields, because they defend themselves with virtues so that they may not succumb to spiritual enemies. All the armor of the mighty hangs upon them, because whoever wishes to resist the enemy ranks courageously sees in them examples by which he is able vigorously to overcome armed enemies [Col. 0509C]. [Note: The printed editions read, “by which he can overcome armed enemies.”] “A thousand” is used here to signify perfection, because in the number one thousand all perfect numbers are completed. It follows:

**(Verses 5–6.)** Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, which feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline [Col. 0509D].

**7.** By the two breasts, two orders of preachers are signified: one among the circumcised and the other among the uncircumcised. They are rightly compared to two fawns of a gazelle, because they are both sons of the Synagogue and feed upon the mountains of contemplation. They are called twins because they preach in harmony and understand in harmony. They feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline, because they pursue purity without weariness until they receive their rewards on the day of judgment—those rewards which they continually contemplate amid the labors of the night. The bridegroom continues, saying:

**(Verse 6.)** I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.

[Note: Rouen, Tours, Reims, and Theodulf read, “I will go for myself to the mountain of myrrh.” Concerning this manner of expression, see already Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 4, column 173.]

**8.** What do we understand by the mountain of myrrh except the strong height of mortification in action? And what by the hill of frankincense except the lofty humility of prayer? The bridegroom therefore goes to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense because he visits familiarly those whom he sees advancing to lofty things through the mortification of vices and giving forth a sweet fragrance through pure and humble prayers [Col. 0510A].

Through these virtues the holy Church, or any pure soul, is made clean. While resisting vices through the mortification of pleasures and frequently washing herself with tears through holy prayers, she washes away her filth in order to please the bridegroom, before whom she strives to appear beautiful. The bridegroom brings her effort to fulfillment by his grace, and kindly praises his work in the bride, saying:

**(Verse 7.)** You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you [Col. 0510B].

**9.** Since it is written, “No one lives without sin, not even an infant whose life is but one day upon the earth” (Job 24:4, according to the Septuagint), what does it mean that the bride is said to be wholly beautiful, with no blemish in her? Elsewhere it is written: “The stars are not pure in his sight” (Job 25:5). And elsewhere: “We all offend in many ways” (James 3:2). The apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). And again: “If we say that we do not sin, we lie and do not speak the truth” (ibid., verse 6).

But when a holy soul cleanses herself from daily sins through repentance; when she washes away minor sins daily with tears; and when she guards herself from greater sins, then, although she sins frequently, she nevertheless preserves her purity continually through constant repentance [Col. 0510C]. Hence it is commanded elsewhere: “Let your garments always be white” (Ecclesiasticus 9:8). And: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17). For although he immediately departs from righteousness when he sins, nevertheless, while he always believes in the one who justifies the ungodly and continually bewails his sins under his faith, he retains his righteousness through continual washings.

To the bride who thus cleanses herself it is consequently said:

**(Verse 8.)** Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come! You shall be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Senir and Hermon, from the lions’ dens, from the mountains of leopards [Col. 0510D].

**10.** Lebanon is interpreted as “whitening.” What, then, is signified by Lebanon except baptism, in which the holy Church is washed with water and whitened from the blackness of sins by the Holy Spirit whom she receives and by faith in Christ? Hence it is written: “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Psalm 50:9).

The holy Church therefore comes from Lebanon to the crown, because in Christ’s baptism she receives the faith under which, through Christ’s grace, she is deemed worthy to receive the reward. But what does it mean that “come” is said three times, except that whatever she does subsists in faith, hope, and charity, so that, fortified by these three virtues, she may possess the strength by which she does not grow weary on the way [Col. 0511A]?

Of faith it is said: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). And again: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6). Of hope it is said: “None who hope in you, Lord, shall be put to shame. For who has hoped in you and been forsaken?” (Ecclesiasticus 2:11–12). Of charity it is said: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). And again: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3). The apostle John says: “God is charity” (John 4:16).

Nevertheless, the threefold “come” can also be understood in another way. The holy bride comes to Christ while living in this world and doing the good she can. She comes when, at the hour of death, the soul—that is, the bride herself—is stripped from the flesh. She comes a third time when, on the day of the final judgment, she takes up the flesh again and enters the heavenly bridal chamber with Christ [Col. 0511B]. There she receives the rewards of all her labors; there, when her enemies have been utterly cast down and excluded, she is gloriously crowned.

Therefore she is here also promised: “You shall be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Senir and Hermon, from the lions’ dens, from the mountains of leopards.”

**11.** What are Amana, Senir, and Hermon—the names of mountains—understood to signify except the powerful of this age? The richer they are, the loftier and stronger they appear to the weak. Yet the holy Church is crowned from these mountains, because, while she proclaims the eternal kingdom and demonstrates by her example that all worldly things are worthless, she bends even the powerful toward repentance and prepares for herself in heaven a crown through seeking them [Col. 0511C]. [Note: The editors changed this word to “acquisition,” which certainly seems more suitable. Nevertheless, the former reading occurs in all our manuscripts.]

Thus it happens that the humble overthrow the proud, and the weak bend the lofty. [Note: The manuscripts and the old Paris edition have this reading; in other printed editions it is “the lowliest.”] Therefore it is written: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low” (Isaiah 40:4).

But why is she said to be crowned not only from the mountains but also from the heads of the mountains? Is it not because we see this fulfilled, since the loftiest persons themselves now believe in Christ and obey his commandments through the preaching of the Church? Kings and emperors serve Christ, lay down their crowns, and seek forgiveness in the Church through repentance [Col. 0512D].

If, then, by the heads of the mountains we understand the highest persons, the princes and ministers who serve cruelty and, through their deceits, trick those whom they cannot harm by force are rightly signified by the lions’ dens and the mountains of leopards. Leopards always bear spots upon their skin; and whom do these signify except hypocrites or those who are divided? [Col. 0511D]

Among those who pursue belief, demons lie in wait like lions. Among others they build mountains, as it were, of leopards: while they consent to mingle certain virtues with their vices, they compel them to seek the glory of praise for all their good deeds. They truly imitate the variety of leopards, because, while pursuing vices together with virtues, they are divided, as though by the dissimilarity of colors in a variegated hide.

Yet the Church is crowned from the lions’ dens and the mountains of leopards, because, through her preaching, the cruel are converted to mercy and hypocrites to the unity of a humble life; for all these she will receive the reward she deserves [Col. 0512A]. To her it is said again:

**(Verse 9.)** You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of the hair of your neck.

**12.** As has been said, the eyes of the bride signify the preachers of the holy Church; the hair signifies the multitude of the peoples; and the neck demonstrates the union of the holy head and body, which is understood as the faith of the Church. Through this the head and body are joined, since each person clings to Christ more firmly in proportion as he is found more faithful in good conduct [Col. 0512B].

The bridegroom is therefore wounded by one of the bride’s eyes and by one lock of the hair of her neck, because he is afflicted even to the death of the cross, so that the unity of the preachers and the people may be confirmed in the Church. Concerning his love for the bride, the bridegroom adds:

**(Verse 10.)** How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride!

**13.** What is more appropriately understood here by the breasts than the love of God and neighbor, about which we spoke above? Through these the holy mind nourishes all its senses in love, while it is joined to its God by the bond of charity and willingly gives whatever benefit it has to its neighbors whenever permitted.

How greatly the bridegroom loves these breasts of the bride he clearly reveals by repeating his praise, saying:

**(Verse 10.)** Your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices [Col. 0512C].

**14.** What we said above concerning the bridegroom’s breasts, we believe may also be understood here when he speaks of the bride. “And the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.” By the ointments are understood the virtues that arise from charity. Even the reprobate sometimes possess spices by which they give off a fragrance, because they possess certain virtues and perform good works. But because they live without charity, none of what they do pleases God.

Hence, when they say at the judgment, “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name perform many mighty works?” (Matthew 7:22), they will be answered: “I never knew you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.” The ointments of the Church are therefore rightly said to give off a fragrance surpassing all spices, because although the works of the reprobate sometimes please human beings, those which the holy Church produces from charity continually give off their fragrance in the divine nostrils [Col. 0512D]. It follows:

**(Verse 11.)** Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.

**15.** The preachers of the Church are rightly said to be the lips of the bride, because through them she speaks to the peoples, and through them all the little ones are instructed in the faith, since through them the hidden things of divine Scripture, as though concealed within the heart, are made manifest [Col. 0513A].

Honey is hidden in the honeycomb, while wax is visible. The lips of the bride are therefore rightly called a honeycomb, because, while great wisdom is held within the frailty of the flesh, honey is concealed, as it were, in wax. When an elect person preaches, when he reveals heavenly joys to those who do not know them, then the honeycomb drips, because he manifests to his hearers, through the frailty of his mouth, how great is the sweetness of wisdom hidden in his heart. Hence it is written: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Therefore it is added: “Honey and milk are under your tongue.” False preachers carry honey on their tongue but do not have it under their tongue, because they sometimes proclaim heavenly joys as though they were true preachers, while they desire earthly goods with all their longing. The holy mind, however, displays honey on its tongue, because by speaking it shows the sweetness of wisdom, which, when it preaches truthfully, refreshes its hearers like the sweetness of honey. It carries milk because, with doctrine suited to them, it nourishes the little ones in the Church. All these things are under its tongue because it reserves them for itself inwardly and continually carries its inner sweetness with it [Col. 0513B]. While it rejects earthly things and refuses the bitterness of vices, it feeds within its inner senses upon the sweetness of wisdom, by which it gathers strength, so that, advancing toward eternal things, it cannot grow weary in the labor of the journey.

**16.** To her it is rightly said: “And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.” What is signified by these garments except holy works, by which the shamefulness of former evils is covered so that it may not be seen? Hence it is written: “Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments, lest he walk naked and his shame be seen” (Revelation 16:15).

Frankincense is figuratively used for prayer, as it is written: “Let my prayer rise like incense in your sight” (Psalm 140:2). The holy soul therefore performs as many good works in this world as it can; and by acting well, with holy desire and intention, it extends itself toward eternal things. It does nothing good except with the intention that it may one day reach the heavenly things it loves [Col. 0513C].

The fragrance of its garments is therefore rightly said to be like the fragrance of frankincense, because it prays in all its works: with the intention of reaching heaven, it does whatever good it can. It follows:

**(Verse 12.)** A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.

**17.** The holy Church is a garden, because, while she begets many peoples in faith, she sends forth beautiful flowers from good soil [Col. 0513D]. This garden is rightly said to be enclosed, because it is fortified on every side by the rampart of charity, so that no reprobate person may enter among the number of the elect.

Each holy soul is likewise understood to be an enclosed garden, because, while it hides its good deeds through the intention of eternal life and completely despises human praise, it surrounds itself with this good intention, so that the ancient enemy cannot burst in to seize its inner things. [Note: In recent editions the following is inserted: “Because, while it nourishes virtues, it produces flowers; and while it refreshes itself with the joy of virtues, it likewise guards the fruits it has produced. It is called an enclosed garden because, while it does good …” No trace of this addition exists in the manuscripts or in the old Paris edition.]

The soul is also called a fountain, because, while it continually thinks about heavenly things and always gathers knowledge of the Scriptures into the storehouse of memory, the holy mind never ceases to generate within itself living waters, which it can offer to thirsty neighbors so that they may be refreshed [Col. 0514A]. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst; but the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water leaping up into eternal life” (John 4:13). And elsewhere: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

But why is that fountain called sealed, except because the spiritual meaning is hidden from unworthy minds? To the unbelieving person the Lord says: “The Spirit blows where it wills; you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John 3:8). And again it is written: “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm 4:7). What is there called a marked light is undoubtedly here described as a sealed fountain [Col. 0514B].

The Holy Spirit both moistens and illumines the mind that he fills, and illumines it by moistening it, so that through his light it may see what it ought to desire and through his dew be refreshed, lest it grow weary. It follows:

**(Verse 13.)** Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruits of orchards [Col. 0514C].

**18.** What does the holy Church send forth except holy words together with holy works, by which she begets and nourishes children? While she leads some of them even to martyrdom and instructs others in holy conduct; while she sends those reddened by the blood of martyrdom to their eternal homeland and offers those living in holy works to their neighbors as examples of holiness, what else does she send forth than pomegranates and the fruits of orchards?

Pomegranates contain a multitude of seeds beneath a red rind; the fruits of orchards, however, contain within themselves the sweetness of refreshment. Thus the martyrs, while laboring under the fire of tribulation and not hesitating to pour out their blood outwardly for Christ, gather within their minds a multitude of virtues. The other holy people who live in the peace of the Church also bear the fruits of orchards, because, while performing holy works, they offer examples to their neighbors, by the display of which those who wish may refresh themselves.

All the holy people in the Church—whether they burn in the fire of suffering or grow while resting in the peace of the Church—do not cease, while they live, to build within themselves a paradise of sweetness and delight through the fragrance of holy virtues. Scripture demonstrates the abundance of this paradise when, under the bridegroom’s voice, it signifies the various virtues by naming trees and plants, saying [Col. 0514D]:

**(Verse 14.)** Cyperus (*cypri*) with nard, nard and saffron, reed and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon; myrrh and aloe, with all the finest ointments.

**19.** What is signified by these various kinds of spices except the fragrance and growth of the holy virtues found in the saints? For royal ointments are prepared from these species, and bodily health is found through them. They therefore rightly signify the virtues of souls: when gathered and compounded, they produce both a good reputation and the appropriate healing of sick souls. [Note: The manuscripts of Val-Clos and Rouen read “honor.”]

But the bridegroom continues to repeat the praise of the Church, adding:

**(Verse 15.)** A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters that flow forcefully from Lebanon [Col. 0515A].

**20.** The fountain of gardens and the well of living waters are rightly described among the shoots. What else are the fountain and the well understood to signify except Holy Scripture? It generates the water of wisdom in such a way that it continually refreshes those who drink, yet does not cease to flow.

It is rightly said to belong to gardens, because Holy Scripture especially belongs to those whose mountains produce seeds of virtue. But we must ask why Scripture is called both a fountain and a well, since a fountain appears on the surface, whereas a well lies hidden in the depths and exercises all who seek it through greater labor [Col. 0515B].

We must understand that divine Scripture is manifest in some places but presents itself as obscure in others. Sometimes it is drunk lightly, as it is found, like a fountain; sometimes it requires extensive investigation before it can be taken once discovered. [Note: In the printed editions, except the old Paris edition, the words “like a well” are added after “it requires.” This is a gloss absent from the manuscripts.]

That the understanding of Holy Scripture is signified by water is shown elsewhere, when the divine voice says of the reprobate: “I will send them a thirst for water and a famine for bread” (Amos 8:11). Through Isaiah it is said: “The Lord will take away from Jerusalem and Judah every support of bread and every support of water” (Isaiah 3:1). Here it should be noted that the support of bread is taken away first, and afterward the support of water. For when the difficult sayings of Scripture are not investigated as they are commanded, the mind gradually falls away from knowledge, so that eventually it cannot grasp even the easier meanings [Col. 0515C].

These waters are rightly said to flow forcefully from Lebanon. For Lebanon, as has been said, is interpreted as “whitening.” We are whitened in baptism, when, having lost the blackness of sins, we are restored to the purity of a new life. The waters of the well therefore flow forcefully from Lebanon, because in baptism each of the elect receives the gift of the Holy Spirit, by which he is illumined to understand the meaning of Sacred Scripture. [Note: The words “with force” are omitted in the common printed editions.]

The knowledge of Holy Scripture flows with such force that, when it touches the elect, it removes them from the love of this life and, by the force of its current, carries those who cling to it toward eternal joys. Hence it is written in the psalm: “The force of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45:5). The force of the river makes the city of God glad when the wisdom of Scripture, pouring forth powerfully through the gift of the Holy Spirit, refreshes the holy Church—or the mind of any person capable of receiving it—by its infusion [Col. 0515D].

At the coming of this Spirit the evil spirit is rebuked, as is said later:

**(Verse 16.)** Arise, North Wind, and come, South Wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow.

[Note: The manuscripts of Rouen and Val-Clos read, “and let its spices flow.” This reading is also found in the Vulgate and occurs again shortly below: “Let the North Wind arise … and let them flow,” and so forth.]

**21.** What is signified by the North Wind, which constricts with cold and makes things sluggish, except the unclean spirit, who, while possessing all the reprobate, makes them sluggish toward good works [Col. 0516A]? By the South Wind—the warm wind—the Holy Spirit is signified, who, when he touches the minds of the elect, loosens them from every sluggishness and makes them fervent, so that they eagerly perform every good work. [Note: The manuscripts preserve this reading. The printed editions have, “so that they may perform whatever good things they desire.”]

Hence it is said: “Restore our captivity, Lord, like a torrent in the South Wind” (Psalm 125:4). Let the North Wind therefore arise, and let the South Wind come; let it blow through the bridegroom’s garden, and let its spices flow, so that the evil spirit may depart from the Church or from any soul and the Holy Spirit may come.

When he comes, let him pour the fire of charity into their thoughts and, when he has infused himself, loosen them from the sluggishness of negligence. When he does this, the spices flow, because, when the Holy Spirit comes, the heart that had previously been sluggish is immediately stirred to works; and then the reputation of holy action gently spreads among all its neighbors, so that everyone who hears may be kindled to the same works.

As the South Wind blows—that is, as the Holy Spirit infuses himself—they emit the fragrances of virtues, so that the holy garden may flower everywhere and, after the flower, produce fragrant and refreshing fruits [Col. 0516B]. The bride invites the beloved into this garden when she adds:

## CHAPTER V

**(Chapter 5—Verse 1.)** Let my beloved come into his garden, to eat the fruit of his trees.

**1.** The beloved comes into the garden and eats the fruit when Christ visits minds and satisfies himself with the delight of good works. Hence, continuing, he says:

**(Verse 1.)** I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk [Col. 0516C].

[Note: The printed editions add, “and let him eat.”]

**2.** The beloved gathers myrrh with spices when Christ, bringing the mortification of life to perfection, cuts down his elect person from this life and brings him, with a holy reputation, into the heavenly granary. He eats the honeycomb with honey when he brings to fulfillment the holy desire hidden in holy works and leads the holy soul to the banquet of the saints, there to be fattened by his delight. He drinks his wine with milk when he refreshes himself both with the perfection of some and, lovingly cherishing the innocence of others, brings both groups to the eternal banquet [Col. 0516D].

To the example of these he invites those who remain when he adds:

**(Verse 1.)** Eat, my friends; drink and be drunk, my dearest ones.

**3.** It must first be noted that those who eat are called “friends,” whereas those who drink and become drunk are called “dearest ones.” These words indicate that, in this passage, eating is good, but drinking and becoming drunk are a greater good.
