There are certainly some in the holy Church who hear the divine commandments in such a way that they learn to love heavenly things more than earthly ones; who give much to the poor for the sake of their desire for those things; who guard themselves from evil deeds; who violently seize nothing from anyone; who willingly hear the preaching of the Church; who instruct themselves in the faith and practice it through holy works; and yet who have wives, raise children, and love their possessions, although they place Christ above all these things [Col. 0517A].

These people eat and are friends, because, hearing Holy Scripture, they take such refreshment from it that, although they do not yet rise to the highest perfection, they are nevertheless perfect according to their measure and live without blame in the divine commandments.

Because the blessed John’s parents—namely, Zechariah and Elizabeth (Luke 1)—strove to preserve this way of life, they merited, through an angelic revelation, to receive a son in their old age. No one greater among those born of women arose than he, and he merited to point out the Savior of the world with his finger and to baptize him (Matthew 11). Of his parents it is said: “They were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame” (Luke 1:6) [Col. 0517B].

There are others who hear or read divine Scripture with such eagerness that, immediately renouncing all earthly works, they seek only heavenly things; they cast aside parents, wives, homes, children, and everything transitory; and they desire to follow and embrace Christ alone. For the sake of this desire they afflict themselves with fasts, devote themselves to tears, exercise themselves in divine meditations, think only about eternal things, and occupy themselves with contemplation. They labor for this purpose: that, forgetting what lies behind, they may extend themselves more and more toward what lies ahead (Philippians 3).

What else do these people do except drink and become drunk? Since they forget all earthly things through desire, they rightly merit to be called by the heavenly bridegroom not only “friends” but also “dearest ones.” Concerning them the bridegroom continues:

**(Verse 2.)** I sleep, but my heart is awake.

**4.** Such elect people may rightly be called the heart of the bridegroom, because the more completely they flee the outward things that belong to the world, the more secretly they come to know the bridegroom’s inward things. Concerning them the same bridegroom says elsewhere: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14:21) [Col. 0517D].

The bridegroom therefore sleeps and his heart is awake, because, while Christ, already glorified, rests in blessedness, whoever loves him perfectly labors to reach him. Concerning this wakefulness the bride said above: “While the king was at his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1:11).

That this resting is called sleeping is shown by what is read elsewhere: “In peace, in the same place, I shall sleep and rest” (Psalm 4:9). Yet the bride herself can also say this about herself. Let her therefore say: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.” As though the holy mind were speaking openly, she says: “While outwardly I sleep from worldly disturbances, inwardly I remain awake, pondering what heavenly things are” [Col. 0518A].

For holy people, while despising all earthly things, while completely fleeing the world’s disturbances, and while taking up quiet in the way of God, do not abandon these things in order to give themselves to sluggishness. Rather, laboring inwardly, they strive to contemplate in their hearts what those things are for which they were made. They do not sleep in order to grow sluggish, but rest from transitory things so that they may contemplate eternal things more freely.

Yet at times the bridegroom awakens them for the benefit of their neighbors and, so that they may benefit those with whom they live, calls them back from the quiet they love. Hearing his voice, the bride says even while sleeping:

**(Verse 2.)** The voice of my beloved, who knocks.

What he says while knocking she adds:

**(Verse 2.)** Open to me [Col. 0517D], my sister, my friend, my dove, my undefiled one [Col. 0518B].

[Note: The printed editions add “my bride,” which is contrary to the manuscripts and to the sacred text.]

She also gives the reason for his cry, saying:

**(Verse 2.)** For my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights.

5. While the bride sleeps, the beloved knocks so that she may open to him; for while the holy mind devotes itself to itself in contemplative leisure, Christ endures many sinful deeds in this world—deeds which carnal people neither recognize nor take care to correct on their own unless spiritual men gird themselves for instruction. The bridegroom therefore wishes leisure to be abandoned at times, and all spiritual people to be stirred to the edification of their neighbors; for while perfect men attend only to themselves in interior repose, the bridegroom grieves that worldly people are falling more and more into worse things, since, because of the silence of spiritual men, they know him less and less. He reveals this himself when he says:

> Because my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights.

What else is meant by the bridegroom’s head than God, and what else by dew in this passage—where the words are spoken in lament—than the coldness of minds? For it is written:

> The head of Christ is God (1 Corinthians 11:3).

And of the coldness of any carnal mind it is likewise written:

> As a cistern makes water cold, so he has made his wickedness cold (Jeremiah 6:7).

The head of Christ, therefore, is full of dew, because many placed in the Church believe that he is God, and yet, remaining cold, are not kindled to the ardor of charity.

[Note: The Old Paris Edition, supported by all our manuscripts, reads “through the locks, however, those same peoples.” Yet the other reading seems preferable.]

By his locks, however, we understand those same peoples, whom we know to hang from and weigh upon Christ’s head, as it were, in their faith in his divinity.

But the locks are said to be full of the drops of the nights because, while they hang suspended in the time of this dark temporality, they flow more and more with the tricklings of iniquities.

[Note: The same Old Paris Edition, together with all the manuscripts, reads *in tempore* (“in time”), whereas other printed editions have *in torpore* (“in torpor”). A little later, the Rouen edition has *titillationibus* (“titillations”) instead of *stillationibus* (“tricklings”).]

To kindle these people, the bride is roused, whenever any spiritual person, for the edification of the many, is called from leisure to the governance of the Church. But because she fears that, if she comes to a position of governance, she will necessarily be occupied with worldly cares—and that, while bending herself toward temporal matters on the pretext of edifying the many, she may lose her repose and even be infected by the filth of sins—she answers the bridegroom as he calls, saying:

> (Verse 3.) I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them again?

6. The bride has stripped off her tunic because she has cast away all the external things with which she was burdened.

[Note: All the printed editions have “with which she was honored and burdened.”]

Of this tunic it is said:

> But now, whoever has a tunic, let him sell it and buy a sword (Luke 22:36).

He buys a sword by selling his tunic who renounces temporal things for the sake of eternal ones; and, living in a holy way of life, acquires the word of preaching. Of this it is said:

> And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6:17).

The bride has also washed her feet, because while the holy soul lives in holy leisure, she carefully recalls her deeds to memory; and whatever she discovers to be soiled in them through examination, she mourns with daily tears and sighs. She has therefore washed her feet because she has lamented the past deeds with which she had walked dissolutely through this world. She has washed her feet because, cleansing her sins with tears, she has desired to appear clean in the sight of her beloved.

She fears soiling these feet again because she is very anxious that, if she is placed in a position of governance, she may once more walk through earthly things and take up again what she abandoned. Thus she withdraws unwillingly from leisure, because while she is apart from the waves of the sea, living as though placed on the shore, she lives more securely.

But the beloved does not lightly endure the death of those near him. Therefore, drawing closer, he does not hesitate to rouse her himself, as it is said:

> (Verse 4.) My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch.

7. The beloved puts his hand through the opening toward the bride so that she may rise when, by inspiring her, he reveals to her through subtle understanding how great is the power of divine action: namely, that he can save even amid dangers; that no one is safe even in peace except through him; and that amid the turmoil of conflict he does not abandon those who hope in him.

At his touch the bride’s belly trembles, because the more fully the holy soul presently feels divine power through an interior visitation, the more strictly she judges whatever carnal thing she discovers in herself. For the more ardently she burns with charity toward him whom she desires in mind, the more timidly she submits herself to him, and the more greatly she fears that the bridegroom may find something in her on account of which he might wish to dismiss her from himself.

Therefore, obeying the bridegroom, she prepares herself for labor, so that she may appear as devotedly serving him in labor as she is familiar with him in repose. Thus she continues, saying:

> (Verse 5.) I rose to open to my beloved.

8. She rises when touched so that she may open to him, because, when she receives the spirit of love more abundantly than usual, she immediately thinks of the edification of her neighbor; and by preaching she acts so that, coming to dwell in her neighbors’ open hearts, the Bridegroom may find an entrance.

She also demonstrates to her hearers examples of good works along with her preaching, saying:

> (Verse 5.) My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the finest myrrh.

9. What is meant by the hands if not works, and what by myrrh if not the mortification of the flesh?

[Note: In agreement with all the manuscripts and the Old Paris Edition, the reading is *praedicantis* (“of the preacher”), whereas the more recent editions have altered it to *praedicationis* (“of preaching”).]

The hands of the preaching bride therefore drip with myrrh, because whoever preaches to others must strive in every work to mortify carnal life if he wishes to benefit many. But that this should be done with great discernment, he makes clear when he adds:

> My fingers are full of the finest myrrh.

For just as several fingers branch out from one hand, so within one holy way of life various virtues are found through discernment. One virtue is generosity, another frugality; one work is humility, another free reproof. We do one thing when we restrain ourselves in silence for our own edification, and another when we speak to our neighbors for their benefit.

But the fingers are said to be full of the finest myrrh because in everything that is done it is always necessary to maintain the mortification of carnality. It is rightly called finest when, in every suggestion introduced by the enemy, carnal pleasure is continually guarded against lest it be accepted. When this occurs, every hardness of mind is dissolved, and an entrance is prepared for the Bridegroom to enter the heart. Hence what follows:

> (Verse 6.) I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved; but he had turned aside and passed by.

10. We make a bolt for the door when, through carnal pleasures, we bar the entrance of the heart against the bridegroom. We open the bolt when, once fleeting pleasures have been removed, we dissolve our previously hardened heart into love of Christ and give free entry to the Bridegroom knocking at the door.

Since, while we live in this flesh, this cannot happen suddenly, it remains for us to do it more and more each day. For no one, as it is written, becomes perfect suddenly. Sometimes, while placed in this corruption and seeking our Lord, he seems to draw farther away from us rather than come nearer. Therefore it follows:

> But he had turned aside and passed by.

At one moment the Bridegroom touches the beloved; at another he turns aside. When he sees us sluggish, he incites us to love; but when he seems able to be grasped by us in our labor, then, lest he be grasped, he passes by and turns aside.

This is accomplished in us by his greatest grace: that we neither lose him altogether while lying in our sluggishness, nor grow proud because we seem to have grasped him fully. Yet as soon as he has withdrawn, he returns; and lest the holy soul remain separated from her beloved for too long, he pours himself into the desiring soul through the word of his inspiration and melts her. Hence the bride rejoices, saying:

> (Verse 6.) My soul melted when my beloved spoke.

11. She says that she was melted at the Bridegroom’s word because, when Christ pours himself through his Spirit into the desiring soul, he immediately dissolves every hardness of heart. At times he melts the mind into such abundant tears that it can scarcely contain what it rejoices to contain within itself; and inwardly she marvels at what she had been and sees herself suddenly transformed into something else.

When she feels this liquid state, she desires to grasp it more perfectly; yet sometimes, while thinking about this very thing, she no longer feels what she had just been feeling. Thus she is troubled and compelled to seek, in order to find the same experience again; but sometimes, even after being wearied for a long time, she does not find what she had just held so present. Therefore it follows:

> (Verse 6.) I sought him, but I did not find him; I called him, but he did not answer me.

12. The bride seeks the beloved but does not find him, because the mind inspired by God continually desires to enjoy that inward sweetness, but the corruption it bears in this life prevents it. She calls, therefore, and receives no answer, because by her prayers and works she desires to be satisfied with the sweetness of his presence, but what she invokes does not come to her according to her wish.

It remains, then, that returning to herself she should come to know herself, and, aided by that taste, seek her beloved more deeply through the Holy Scriptures. This is what follows:

> (Verse 7.) The watchmen who guard the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak.

13. While the bride is troubled by her search for the beloved, she encounters the watchmen of the city. When the holy mind afflicts itself with desire for Christ her Bridegroom, she receives the words of preachers in the divine Scriptures and, as long as she is exiled from Christ, directs herself toward the love of the one she was seeking.

What exercise she finds in them, he adds:

> They struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak.

The watchmen strike and wound the bride because, while the holy preachers speak of heavenly things, they affect the loving soul and shoot her with a greater love. They take away her cloak because, if any remnant of worldly pomp remained in her heart, they remove it from her soul through their exhortations. They take away her cloak because sometimes, before hearing the preachers’ words, we did not know ourselves; but while they speak, they uncover everything that lay hidden within.

When this occurs, they should be loved more greatly, and we should pray to them more devoutly that they speak to the beloved on our behalf. The bride does this when she continues:

> (Verse 8.) I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love.

14. When we open our thoughts to holy men, when we disclose our desire to them—whether they are living with us or have already entered eternal life—and pray through God that, by praying to the Lord Christ on our behalf, they may present to him the desire by which we are moved, what else are we doing than adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem to tell the beloved, to whom they are closer than we are, that we languish with love?

But the saints themselves, if they are still with us, both pray for those who ask their prayers and, when asked to announce our desire, question us in humility as though they were unaware, saying:

> (Verse 9.) What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest among women?

But because the more ardently they love him, the more sweetly they repeat words about him, they say the same thing again:

> (Verse 9.) What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have so adjured us?

The Bridegroom is called “beloved above the beloved” so that, through the repetition of love, the speaker’s greatest love may be shown. Or Christ is rightly called “beloved above the beloved” because, if we love the Son, we consequently love the Father from whom he is.

The bride responds, continuing:

> (Verse 10.) My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from thousands.

15. Christ is said to be white and ruddy because, committing no sin at all, he wholly maintained the beauty of righteousness, and yet approached the suffering of death as though he were a sinner. To him the prophet says:

> Why, then, is your garment red? (Isaiah 63:2.)

He is chosen from thousands because, from the mass of the entire human race, no one is found without sin; but he alone was not merely without sin—he also redeemed sinners by his righteousness and blood.

It follows:

> (Verse 11.) His head is finest gold; his locks are like raised palms, black as a raven.

16. The head of Christ is God. This head is rightly called gold because, by comparison with the Creator, every creature is judged to be of exceedingly little worth (1 Corinthians 11).

“His locks are like raised palms, black as a raven.” What else do we understand by Christ’s locks than each of the faithful? While they preserve faith in the Trinity in their minds, adhere to God, and do what they believe, they hang, as it were, from the head and confer honor upon him who bears them.

The palm rises high as it ascends and signifies victory. The locks, therefore, are like raised palms because the elect, continually lifting themselves toward the heights of virtue, are eventually brought by God’s grace to victory. Yet they are black as a raven because, although they raise themselves through virtues, they always recognize that they are sinners.

It follows:

> (Verse 12.) His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk, sitting beside overflowing channels.

17. [Note: In some manuscripts and all the printed editions, “the eyes of the bride”; this is clearly an error.]

The bridegroom’s eyes are like doves because Christ’s preachers, who show us the way, live in simplicity. They are said to be beside streams of water because they continually dwell in the refreshment of the divine Scriptures. They are washed with milk because, by the grace of creative wisdom, as though by a mother’s milk, they have been cleansed from sins through baptism.

What else do we understand by the overflowing channels beside which they sit than the profound and hidden sayings of Sacred Scripture, which we investigate and by which we refresh ourselves as we draw them in by reading or hearing?

Doves also customarily sit beside channels so that they may see in the water the shadow of flying birds and, throwing themselves upon it, escape the talons of birds of prey. So holy men perceive the deceits of demons in Sacred Scripture; and from the image they see, they recognize the enemy as though from a shadow. While they devote themselves wholly to the counsels of Scripture—so that they do nothing except what they hear in response from the Scriptures—they throw themselves, as it were, into the water and mock the enemy.

These channels are called overflowing because, whenever counsel is sought in the Scriptures concerning any scruple, an answer concerning everything is found there fully, without diminution.

> (Verse 13.) His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by perfumers.

18. If the eyes signify the preachers, the cheeks are rightly represented by those in the Church who are said to have ended their lives in martyrdom. For, since they do not hesitate to pour out their blood for the faith of Christ, they blush like cheeks on the Bridegroom’s face. Through them the beauty of the Christian faith is proclaimed, because when they die for it, they show toward what great reward of faith they are striving.

[Note: In the Vallicellian, Clairvaux, Rheims, and Theodore manuscripts, *qui* (“which,” namely the martyrs) is rightly followed by *sicut* (“like”).]

They are rightly said to be like beds of spices because, while the chosen are exercised in martyrdom through steadfastness of faith, the fame of their holy reputation spreads like the fragrance of spices through the cultivation of virtues.

But beds of spices are planted by perfumers because holy martyrs are both strengthened for confession by the preachers who preceded them and presented by those who follow as examples for the people to imitate. From those who preceded them, the spices of virtues are cultivated; from those who follow, the spices of examples are taken.

Hence it also follows:

> (Verse 13.) His lips are lilies, dripping first-rate myrrh.

19. What else do we understand by the Bridegroom’s lips than those very preachers of Christ whom we have mentioned? When they preach the deaths of the martyrs to the people, they drip myrrh, as it were, for the seasoning of flesh that must be mortified.

This myrrh is rightly called “first-rate” because no one is mortified in the way that one is who dies as a martyr for Christ. He said “first” not with reference to time, but to dignity.

Why are the Bridegroom’s lips said to be lilies, unless because those through whom Christ speaks must be pure, and through them a good fragrance must be spread? The Apostle Paul was such a one, saying:

> We are a good fragrance to God in every place, both among those who are perishing and among those who are being saved (2 Corinthians 2:15).

But it should be noted that whatever righteousness and strength there is in the Church is drawn from Christ himself through the examples of his works. Therefore it follows:

> (Verse 14.) His hands are turned, golden, full of hyacinths.

20. What else is signified by Christ’s hands than the holy works he performed in the world and set before us for imitation? He himself says:

> Whoever loves me, let him follow me (perhaps John 12:26).

And the Apostle says:

> Whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked (1 John 2:6).

His hands are said to be turned because his holy works proceeded in righteousness on every side, without any imposition of iniquity. What is turned on a lathe rolls around in its circular form without obstruction. So Christ’s works moved in the circular perfection of uprightness because no fault adhered to him; for his righteousness would be less than perfectly rounded if any fault were attached to it.

His hands are also said to be golden because whatever he performed outwardly among human beings was inwardly ordered in the beauty of divinity.

[Note: In the other editions, except the Old Paris Edition, the following is added after *disponebatur* (“was ordered”): “But what else is signified by the hyacinth, which is a very precious stone, than the gift of eternal recompense? Therefore the hands of the bridegroom…” These words occur in none of the manuscripts.]

The Bridegroom’s hands are also said to be full of hyacinths because whoever imitates his works with a devout heart is enriched in recompense with the gifts of eternal happiness. Hence the same Redeemer says:

> Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my minister be (John 12:26).

It follows:

> (Verse 14.) His belly is ivory, variegated with sapphires.

21. What is meant by the belly if not mortality, and what by ivory if not incorruption? Ivory is considered a very durable bone and is used for the adornment of kings. Christ’s belly, therefore, is rightly said to be ivory because Christ’s mortality is brought to immortality when, through the resurrection, he is placed in eternal life in the glory of his Father, namely the eternal King. Of him it is said:

> Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Romans 6:9).

He is truly taken up into the adornment of kings because whoever proves to be king and lord of his own flesh is adorned by the mortality and resurrection of Christ with the love of knowledge and the hope of immortality.

Hence it is said elsewhere:

> Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31).

But the belly is said to be variegated with sapphires because, in the corruption he bore for us, he inserted heavenly works—through the miracles he performed—into our sufferings. Since sapphire bears an airy color, it aptly signifies the heavenly deeds displayed in miracles. Christ’s belly is variegated with sapphires because, while he worked divine miracles amid the sufferings of the flesh, corruption was varied, as it were, with incorruption. Through this dispensation the apostles were instructed in faith and became strong for enduring sufferings.

Therefore it follows:

> (Verse 15.) His legs are marble columns, founded upon golden bases.

22. By the legs we understand the apostles, through whom he traversed the whole world and spread the faith as they preached and the peoples listened. In the Gospel he himself says to them:

> Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature (Mark 16:15).

But the legs are said to be marble columns because they support the Church inflexibly, while she is strengthened against all adversaries by their preaching and examples.

The columns are founded upon golden bases because they received complete faith from the sayings of the prophets, so that they might be strong. Hence the first of the apostles himself says:

> We have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place (2 Peter 1:19).

They are called golden because they are known to shine with the light of wisdom.

It follows:

> (Verse 15.) His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen like the cedars.

23. Lebanon is a mountain on which very tall and fragrant trees are found. Lebanon is interpreted as “whiteness” or “whitening.” Concerning Christ the Apostle Paul says:

> He was made for us by God wisdom and sanctification and righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30).

His appearance, therefore, is rightly like Lebanon because through him we believers are whitened; and if we cling to him by our roots, we become exalted. From his grace, too, we receive whatever fragrance of a good reputation we possess.

He is also said to be chosen like the cedar because the Father speaks of him:

> Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased (Isaiah 42:1).

The cedar is a very lofty, fragrant, and incorruptible tree. Christ, however, is loftier than the cedars because, although he is human, he does not cease to be God. Of him Isaiah says:

> And he shall be exalted exceedingly (Isaiah 52:14).

Christ is also more fragrant than all others, for he says of himself:

> I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys (Song of Songs 2:1).

And the bride says to him:

> We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments (Song of Songs 1:3).

Of him what follows here is also fitting:

> (Verse 16.) His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable.

24. Through the throat, voices are conveyed, and flavors are drawn into the belly. What, then, is meant by the Bridegroom’s throat if not the Testament of Christ, through which Christ speaks to us and in which the faithful taste how sweet the Lord is?

He is therefore said to be altogether desirable because, through everything good that the holy soul hears about him, she desires more and more always to see him. Having recounted so many of his goods, she consequently concludes and says:

> (Verse 15.) Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.

25. But when so many praises have been enumerated and so many gifts displayed, who, hearing them, does not long for him? Who, attending to them, is not set aflame? For the more sweet and abundant the things a faithful soul hears about her Redeemer, the more ardently she thirsts for him and desires to know more clearly what he is. Thus she says:

> (Verse 17.) Where has your beloved gone, O fairest among women? Where has your beloved turned aside, and we shall seek him with you?

When one neighbor speaks to another about Christ, when one asks another how he may be found, what else does he investigate than how he ought to be sought? This may also be understood of the Synagogue, as though at some point, after being converted, it should question the Church, to which the Church immediately responds.

## CHAPTER VI

> (Chapter 6—Verse 1.) My beloved has descended into his garden, to the bed of spices, to pasture in the gardens and gather lilies.

1. The beloved has descended into his garden, to the bed of spices, because, visiting the Church, he comes with greater grace to those whom he recognizes as sending forth from themselves to their neighbors the fragrance of a good reputation through holy works and examples of virtues. He pastures in the gardens when he delights in the virtues of many souls. He gathers lilies when he cuts down the perfect from this life.

But because the holy Church is so joined to Christ in her children by faith, suspended in hope, and bound together by charity that she loves nothing outside Christ and holds him familiarly inseparable from herself through faith and love, she therefore adds:

> (Verse 2.) I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine, who pastures among the lilies.

2. It should be noted that the Synagogue will at some time be converted to the faith through the preaching of the Church, so that, denying itself, it will follow Christ alone and love Christ with the same desire with which the Church loves him, loving him alone after setting all others aside.

The Bridegroom, now made a friend and joined to himself as a bride, addresses her with congratulations, saying:

> (Verse 3.) You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely like Jerusalem, terrible as an army set in ordered battle.

3. The Synagogue is said to be beautiful and a friend, sweet and lovely like Jerusalem, because, once converted, it will follow the holy four Gospels as the Church does. Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” The holy Church is aptly represented by it because, while she continually suffers oppression in the world, she despises the way and, running onward, contemplates what the peace of the heavenly homeland will be, trusting in him who said to his disciples:

> In the world you will have tribulation; but be confident, I have overcome the world (John 16:33).

The converted Synagogue is rightly called beautiful, a friend, sweet, and lovely like Jerusalem because, while imitating the holy Church, it practices the commands of the four Gospels. From them it receives beauty of conduct, so as to please; gathers the exercise of holy action, so as to remain in friendship; learns the sweetness of gentleness, so as to persevere; and displays the appearance of an attractive way of life, so as to draw others by example.

Of her it is consequently said:

> Terrible as an army set in ordered battle.

Those experienced in such matters know that when soldiers march into battle against enemies, if they advance in close and harmonious order, they are feared by the opposing forces. Since the enemy sees no opening through a breach in their ranks, he cannot discover how to penetrate them. Their impenetrable defense is formed by their harmonious arrangement, by which they protect one another. For while they make a rampart of themselves for themselves, they leave their enemies no entrance by which to reach them; and, though sought out for slaughter, they themselves kill more easily.

The same occurs among the multitude of the faithful. Since it does not cease to fight against wicked spirits, it must be bound together by the peace of charity, so that it may remain safe.

[Note: The Vallicellian and Rheims manuscripts read “by which it may remain safe.”]

If it preserves peace, it appears terrible to its enemies; if it is split by discord, it is easily penetrated by the enemies from every side. Let it therefore fortify itself with peace, bind itself with unity, and unite itself in charity, so that, suffering no harm within itself through division, it may always follow its leader exultantly and without shame.

In peace the eye of the mind is cleansed, so that it may gaze upon the vision of blessedness itself. No one sees that homeland as it is in this life because it is impossible to possess the homeland while each of us groans in exile.

Therefore the Bridegroom responds to the holy soul as she burns, thirsts, and draws near:

> (Verse 4.) Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away.

4. We direct our eyes toward the Bridegroom when we open the gaze of the mind somewhat to see Christ’s blessedness. But we are commanded to turn our eyes away, lest we imagine that, however much we may see, we behold it as it truly is.

Those eyes have made him fly away because the more he is seen, the more he is recognized as invisible. He flies away from us because, however little he may be grasped by a stroke of the mind, he reveals himself to be incomprehensibly exalted above all our striving.

The eyes of the mind seem to cause him to fly away because, through the tiny portion that is seen, he appears, as has been said, exceedingly distant and flying away from us.

It follows:

> (Verses 4–6.) Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing; all bearing twins, and none among them is barren.

> Your cheeks are like a pomegranate’s rind, without hidden things.

5. We have explained all these things said above about the Church as best we could; therefore we now avoid repeating the same explanations concerning the Synagogue. There is, however, one feature that is not repeated in the same way: there it says “like fragments of a pomegranate,” whereas here it says “like a pomegranate’s rind.” I think this signifies nothing other than the blood of the martyrs who will die under the Antichrist, and the unity of faith under which many Jews will be bound. While they endure the shedding of blood in that steadfastness, they will be adorned by the tribulation of faith as by the redness of a rind.

It follows:

> (Verse 7.) There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and there is no number of maidens.

6. What else is signified by queens than the souls of the saints, who, while wisely ruling their bodies and presiding over others, acquire an eternal kingdom for themselves?

There are some in the holy Church who discipline their flesh and afflict it for God’s sake, conquer vices, subject demons to themselves like tyrants, wisely govern all their impulses so that they proceed in due order, preach to others what they themselves do, and, fighting with the sword of the word, snatch many from the jaws of demons. What are souls of this kind except queens? While they love Christ the King, their bridegroom, exceedingly, through the union of love and the abhorrence of lust they beget royal sons, that is, faithful peoples.

To all such people the blessed Apostle Peter said:

> You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession (1 Peter 2:9).

But the queens are said to number sixty. The number ten, multiplied by six, is completed in sixty. What else is signified by ten than the ten commandments of the Law, and what by six than the labor of this life? For six days we perform what is necessary, and on the seventh the Law commands us to rest (Exodus 23 and 31).

The queens are therefore rightly said to number sixty because, while they practice the ten commandments in this world, and this world unfolds through six working days, the ten is repeated in them, as it were, through the number six. They preach the ten commandments of the Law, in whose practice they exercise themselves during the temporality of this corruption.

Thus they multiply six ten times, or ten six times, because by their works they make manifest and by their word they preach that this entire period must spiritually be spent in fulfilling the ten commandments of the Law.

The wicked sometimes observe their praise in this world, and, in order to be praised in the same way or to obtain some advantage in this life by whatever means, they too become preachers on their own.

Concerning these it is aptly added:

> And eighty concubines.

7. Concubines do not truly but falsely love their lords. They seek from them not offspring, but their presence, and they do not exercise themselves in continence; rather, they desire to satisfy their lust.

[Note: Recent editors inserted *commodorum* (“of advantages”) for explanatory purposes. Thus they present the reading: “but seek the presence of advantages,” evidently not understanding what *praesentiam* (“presence”) should refer to. It refers most appropriately to the lords, whose presence they desire in order to satisfy lust.]

So false preachers exist in the Church because, loving not Christ but profit or praise, they join themselves to Christ not spiritually and chastely, but carnally and lustfully. They are therefore rightly called concubines because they follow the Christ whom they preach not in spirit but in the flesh.

Concerning them the Apostle Paul said:

> Many walk according to the flesh, but not according to Christ (Philippians 3:38 [citation as printed]).

Of them he also says:

> Those of whom I often told you, and now tell you even weeping, are enemies of the cross of Christ; their end is destruction, their god is their belly.

Of them he says again:

> Such people do not serve the Lord Jesus, but their own belly (Romans 16:18).

Yet these concubines are rightly said to number eighty because, although they love earthly things with their whole heart, they nevertheless speak of heavenly things. We multiply the number eight by ten and arrive at eighty. By ten, as has been said, the Decalogue is signified; by eight, the resurrection, because our Redeemer is shown to have risen on the eighth day.

Although the preachers are false, they nevertheless make known through their desire, the divine Scripture, and the resurrection in which we believe—through their word. For if preachers preached something else, they would not be among Christians. Concerning them the Truth says in the Gospel:

> The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat: therefore whatever they tell you, do and observe; but do not do according to their works (Matthew 23:2).

8. But because very many come to faith through the preaching both of false and of true preachers, and many enter together with the elect who do not attain to the lot of the elect, therefore it is added: “And of the maidens there is no number.” For since it is written, “Adolescence and youth are vanity” (Eccles. II, 10, according to the Hebrew), what are we to understand by these maidens except souls who, while pursuing the vain things of this world that they love, exceed the number of the elect?

[Note: The edition adds *vagas* (“wandering”) to “souls”; this addition is unwarranted once the punctuation is restored.] Of them the Psalmist says: “I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX, 6). That the number of the elect is fixed with God is made clear by the apostle Paul, who says: “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 19). And the Lord himself says: “I know whom I have chosen” (John XIII, 18). Since he knows them not imperfectly but perfectly, there is no doubt that he also knows the number in which they are chosen. Of them Paul says: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. VIII, 29).

“Of the maidens there is no number” is therefore aptly said, because, while through the vanity that they love they do not hasten into the number of the elect, they remain outside, as though they do not come within the sphere of divine knowledge. To them Truth himself will say at the future judgment: “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 12); and: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Ps. VI, 9).

But while the reprobate seek worldly things and divide their minds among numerous desires, every holy soul binds itself to the number of the elect. Disdaining many things that it sees, it ardently desires the one thing that it does not see; and as long as it does not possess that one thing, it nourishes itself in faith and unites itself in charity. And while it follows what is one and the same, one Church is formed from many such persons. Of this the Bridegroom says:

**(Verse 8.) “My dove is one, my perfect one; she is one to her mother, chosen to her who bore her.”**

9. Our mother is regenerating grace, with whom one dove is chosen, because she chooses only those who remain in simplicity and are not torn away from unity. For many believers, while they direct their attention to the same thing, while they nourish one another in Christ with a single desire, while having one heart and one soul they bind themselves together in charity, become one body from many members. And all who live in the simplicity of unity exist as one dove.

She alone is called perfect and chosen by her mother, because outside this Church that we speak of no one is brought to perfection, and no one is nourished unto life except through her alone, with grace fostering him. Of her it is aptly added:

**(Verse 9.) “The daughters of Zion saw her and proclaimed her most blessed; queens and concubines praised her.”**

10. The daughters of Zion are the daughters of the Church. While they contemplate eternal life in this flesh, they are raised from the pilgrim Church to the reigning Church. The daughters of Zion see the dove and proclaim her most blessed, because holy souls, while they behold the virtues of the Church, burst forth into praise and long for her blessedness.

The holy Church is nourished by grace her mother: she is instructed by faith, fed with the flesh of her Bridegroom, washed with his blood, and fattened on divine Scripture. Strengthened by such nourishment, she conquers demons, suffocates vices, subdues the flesh, strengthens the spirit, and awaits life. Whoever beholds all these things rightly rises at once in admiration and declares her most blessed, because he sees to what glory she rises through so many virtues.

The concubines also praise her along with the queens, because although false preachers contradict her by their deeds, by their words they nevertheless show the peoples the same things as the true preachers. Truth himself says of such men: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. XV, from Isa. XXVII). He makes this clear when he says again: “For they say, and do not do” (Matt. XXIII, 3). Of them it is also said through the apostle Paul: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. I, 16).

Holy men, however, confess God both in words and in deeds, because they do what they believe, and by words and examples draw others to the good things they do. Their adversaries are stirred to faith by their virtues, when they admire in them both the devotion of faith and the steadfastness of their works. Hence the Synagogue too is raised to faith when, contemplating with admiration what merits faith has in the Church, she says:

**(Verse 9.) “Who is this who comes forth like the dawn, rising beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army set in battle array?”**

11. The holy Church comes forth like the rising dawn at the final judgment, because, having left behind the darkness of corruption, she is renewed in the brightness of incorruption. She is aptly called “chosen as the sun,” because she is brought to the same glory as her head, Christ, who is said to be the sun of justice. Hence the same Sun says: “Father, I will that where I am, there my servant also may be” (John XIX, 26; XVII, 24).

This may also be understood of the members of that same Church who are still living in this flesh. For there are some who, with great attention, contemplate the torments of the reprobate and strive to examine their own deeds without flattery. When they recognize that they have sinned and therefore fear that they are going to the torments of the reprobate, they suddenly abandon the darkness of iniquity and desire to be kindled by the light of justice. At once they rise to holy action, and through the good works they perform they begin to shine before their neighbors.

Without doubt these go forth like the rising dawn, because, suddenly dispelling the night of sin, they expand more and more toward the light. Thus the soul that was previously in darkness now appears radiant; and what had been darkened even within itself now shines upon others through the light of holy action. Of it it is aptly added: “Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun.”

The moon, while illuminating the night, shows to dim eyes the road on which a person should walk. So every soul that abandons darkness and extends itself into holy action, while offering its neighbors an example of good conduct, scatters light, as it were, upon eyes growing dark. For when sinners behold a good work and turn to do the same, they return to the way like travelers who have gone astray in the night and are guided by the moon’s light.

Thus this holy soul, while offering examples to sinners, shines like the moon in the night. But when it grows more and more and, through habitual practice of good works, receives the light of justice so perfectly from day to day that it also offers examples for imitation to the good—whereas previously it had appeared worthy of imitation only to sinners—it truly becomes the sun. For what formerly shone upon those wandering in the night now manifests the light of truth to those walking in the day. Hence what follows: “Chosen as the sun.”

Of her it is aptly added: “Terrible as an army set in battle array.” Since this has already been said, it is not necessary to explain it again, lest weariness be produced. The Bridegroom therefore continues and states the reason from which such great virtue can grow in the Church. She is renewed by his visitation, and whatever is dark in her is illuminated by his regard. Hence he goes on to say:

**(Verse 10.) “I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys; and to look whether the vines had blossomed and the pomegranates had budded.”**

12. What are we to understand by nuts except all the perfect, who, while retaining divine wisdom within their bodies, carry the kernel in a fragile shell? There are very many in the Church who continually devote themselves to divine Scripture. Tasting how sweet the Lord is, they desire to taste him more; they ruminate on holy joys in their hearts and grow stronger by ruminating. Yet outwardly, unknown to those who do not understand them, they appear insignificant, because people do not know how sweet a food they carry within themselves.

What are such people except nuts, who bear the sweetness of the kernel within, while outwardly displaying the lowliness of the flesh? Such was the Apostle, who said: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV, 7). The garden of nuts, then, is the hearts of the saints, who, because they love, carry heavenly sweetness in their inmost being. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. XXX, 20).

But what does it mean that the Bridegroom descends into the garden of nuts to see the fruits, when he ought rather to see the nuts? We must nevertheless understand that he often visits the hearts of the perfect and manifests to them the sweetness of his kindness, so that afterward through them he may come to the weaker, and through them may recognize how far they have advanced in the increase of justice. Hence it is written: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God” (Ps. XIII, 2).

For when divine goodness illumines the hearts of the perfect and urges them, through the solicitude of charity, to care for their neighbors, what else does this mean than that, coming to the garden, he looks through those over whom he presides upon the fruits of the valley? The Lord is then said to see or know when he exhorts the saints whom he illumines to see.

But what does it mean that he descends to see, not the fruits of the mountain but the fruits of the valley, except that he grants the regard of his mercy to those whom he knows to persist in humility? Of this the Psalmist says: “For the Lord is exalted, and he regards the lowly, but the proud he knows from afar” (Ps. CXXXVII, 6). And the Lord himself says through the voice of the prophet: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one, and him who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

The Bridegroom continues and says: “And to look whether the vines had blossomed and the pomegranates had budded.” The vines blossom when new children are born in the Church through faith and are prepared, as it were, for the solidity of fruit through holy conduct. The pomegranates bud when all the perfect edify their neighbors by their examples and, through preaching and the display of good works, change them into the newness of holy conduct.

[Note: The editions wrongly read *invitant* (“invite”) for *immutant* (“change”), the reading of all the manuscripts.]

That pomegranate was the apostle Paul, who had budded when he said: “My little children, of whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. IV, 19). For this is how it is carried out in the holy Church: through the good, the evil are converted; through the perfect, the imperfect are nourished, until they too come to perfection and lead the weak to better things, just as they themselves were led.

Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, looks upon this through his visitation and unites the holy body by his regard.

[Note: The printed editions read “brings to perfection by visiting.”] He is known to have assumed the body of weakness for this reason: so that the whole Church together might be transformed into the body of his glory. Hence blessed Paul says: “Who will reform the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. III, 21).

At the end of the world the Synagogue, finally aroused, will perceive all these things and reproach herself for having remained ignorant of them for so long, saying:

**(Verse 11.) “I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.”**

13. It is as though she were saying: “Seeing so many virtues being performed in the holy Church, why did I not perceive them for so long? Why did I persist in unbelief? Why did I remain so long in the darkness of ignorance through my unbelief?”

But she is troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab, because at last she is stirred through Christ’s preaching to receive the faith. Aminadab is interpreted as “spontaneous of my people.” Without doubt Christ Jesus is rightly called by the Father “spontaneous of my people,” because he descended to save the people with truly spontaneous charity and, in pious willingness and gracious kindness, accepted death on the cross in order to raise us from death. Hence he says to the Father: “I will sacrifice to you freely” (Ps. LIII, 8). And one of the redeemed, speaking to Christ, said: “Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is kind” (Ps. LXVIII, 17).

The Synagogue, therefore, is troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab, because, when at last she beholds the four Gospels of Christ running throughout the world and burning in human hearts through faith, she is immediately confounded by the darkness of her unbelief; and, when a salutary confusion has arisen, she is moved to repentance. To her the Church speaks kindly, saying:

**(Verse 12.) “Return, return, O Sunamite; return, return, that we may look upon you.”**

14. Sunamite is interpreted as “captive.” The Sunamite is therefore called to return, because at the end of the world the faith of the Synagogue will be offered by the Church, so that she may recover her former dignity, having been held captive by demons under the yoke of unbelief.

She is rightly admonished four times to return, because the Jews are now dispersed throughout the four parts of the world. Wherever they may be, they will be converted at the end of the world, as was foretold through the prophet: “If the number of the children of Israel should be as the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. X, 22).

Let the Sunamite therefore return, that we may look upon her—that is, let the Synagogue be converted to the faith and, in her repentance, show everyone how great an evil she committed when she crucified her God.

But immediately, when the Church desires to behold the Synagogue’s faith, the Bridegroom responds as though congratulating her and asking a question, and says:

## CHAPTER VII

**(Chapter VII—Verse 1.) “What will you see in the Sunamite, except the choirs of armies?”**

1. Camps belong to those who wage war. Camps will therefore be seen in the Shulamite, because for the faith that she now attacks she will then fight vigorously against the faithless.

But because this will happen through the holy Church, so that the Synagogue may be converted, since she will be converted to the faith through the words and examples of the preachers, the Bridegroom rightly turns to the praise of the bride, saying:

**(Verse 1.) “How beautiful are your steps in your sandals, daughter of the prince?”**

2. The holy Church is called the daughter of the prince because she is regenerated into a new life through the preaching of Christ, who, through the power of his divinity, rules over every creature that he created.

But what are the sandals of the Church except the examples of the fathers who went before her? By these she is fortified on the road of this world, so that she may walk confidently shod through all the tribulations that arise. Hence Paul says elsewhere to preachers: “With your feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace” (Eph. VI, 15).

Sandals are made from dead animals. Spiritually, we too put sandals on our feet when we take examples from the holy fathers who are dead in the flesh, so that in their likeness we may conquer the temptations of this world.

It may also be understood that the Church is shod when, in her preaching, she is fortified by the death of Christ to endure the evils that arise. Beautiful, therefore, are the steps of the shod bride, who is the daughter of the prince, because in the sight of divine eyes the ministry of every elect person who preaches according to the examples of the fathers is pleasing. It follows:

**[Col. 0534A] (Verse 1.) “The joining of your thighs is like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artisan.”**

[Note: The manuscripts read *feminum* (“of the thighs”) instead of *femora* or *femorum*, which is found in the printed editions.]

3. By the bride’s two thighs, the Church’s two peoples are signified; by the joining of the thighs, the harmony of the preachers is signified. Through them the peoples are united, while through their instruction circumcision and uncircumcision are brought to the Catholic faith.

They are like necklaces because, while doing holy works in the wisdom with which they shine, they carry stones, as it were, set in gold. Of them it follows: “Which are fashioned by the hand of an artisan.” Necklaces are fashioned by the hand of an artisan because through Christ’s work preachers are made beautiful and useful. It follows:

**(Verse 2.) “Your navel is a turned bowl, never lacking cups.”**

4. The navel also signifies the order of the holy preachers. It is aptly called a bowl because, while through them the people are instructed, the people are made drunk with spiritual wine through their ministry.

It is aptly called “turned” because, in accordance with the ways of all human beings, the preacher’s tongue must turn and adapt itself. It never lacks cups because what it pours out for others it must drink more abundantly than the rest, and it must contain more fully what it gives.

It follows:

**(Verse 2.) “Your belly is like a heap of wheat, enclosed with lilies.”**

5. By the belly, the breadth of the peoples is signified. It is aptly enclosed with lilies like a heap of wheat, because, while intent upon holy works and being prepared for the heavenly granary, it is fortified on every side by the examples of the saints, so that it may persevere. Of these it is said again:

**(Verse 3.) “Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.”**

6. The two breasts are the two peoples, because, while they always live in fraternal love, they nourish one another with the milk of compassion in charity.

They are aptly called two fawns, twins of a gazelle, because, born through the Synagogue’s preaching in the faith and nourished in her Scriptures, they direct their attention toward the hope of eternity and feed together, as it were, upon the mountains.

Of these preachers it follows:

**(Verse 4.) “Your neck is like a tower of ivory.”**

7. The bride’s neck is called like a tower of ivory because the preachers of the Church are regarded as lofty through contemplation, strong through the practice of holy works, and precious through divine wisdom. Of them it is said again:

**[Col. 0534D] (Verse 4.) “Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, which are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude.”**

8. Heshbon is interpreted as “a girdle of sorrow.” The bride’s eyes are therefore said to be like the pools in Heshbon because, while they grieve over their pilgrimage and, strengthened by sorrow, gird themselves against spiritual enemies, they wash themselves with tears, so that through them the peoples may be suitably cleansed before God.

They are at the gate of the daughter of the multitude because they stand in the faith, through which they introduce the multitude of the Church into heavenly things. It follows:

**(Verse 4.) “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.”**

9. The discernment of odors is found in the nose. The order of the preachers is therefore signified by the nose, because through them the fragrances of virtues and the stench of vices are shown to us.

[Note: The printed editions read “the discernment of preachers.”]

But the nose exists like the tower of Lebanon because, when the preachers have once been washed by the water of Baptism and are whitened daily by tears for the sins they have committed against God, they become worthy to be raised ever higher through strength.

But the tower looks toward Damascus because every holy preacher continually speaks against sinners. Damascus is interpreted as “bloody,” and it is said to the sinful nation: “Your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I, 16).

But because he has spoken of the members, it is fitting that he speak of the head. Therefore he adds:

**(Verse 5.) “Your head is like Carmel, and the locks of your head like the purple of the king joined to the channels.”**

10. The head of the Church is Christ. He is aptly called like Carmel because through the passion he endured he was exalted to the glory of the Father. Of him it is written: “And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains” (Isa. II, 2).

On Carmel Elijah obtained rain by praying (III Kings XVIII); and we obtain rain by praying on Carmel when, believing in Christ, we desire Christ and receive from the Father the shower of grace for which we ask.

Morally, however, the bride’s head is called the mind, because just as the members are governed from the head, so all our thoughts are ordered from the mind. Carmel is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision.” The bride’s head is therefore said to be like Carmel because every holy mind knows how it may be worthily circumcised. It knows that whatever is done in the body is nothing if the mind is unclean; but if the mind becomes Christ’s temple, it is inhabited by him.

Because the Pharisees did not do this, blessed Stephen said to those who were killing him: “You stiff-necked men, uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts VII, 51).

The locks of her head are also said to be like the purple of the king joined to the channels. Purple is bound in bundles upon channels; when water is poured over these, it runs through the channels to the garment placed beneath, so that the garment is dyed. From this it receives its name: once dyed with purple color, it is called *purpura*. All these things aptly correspond to the holy mind if they are understood.

[Note: Several details here have been altered with the aid of the manuscripts, although the printed reading does not greatly depart from the sense.]

The locks of the head are the thoughts of the mind. They are bound in channels because they are restrained in the divine Scriptures, lest they flow uselessly. Water is poured over them, and it dyes the royal garment, because heavenly grace is received in the thoughts of the holy mind and shapes the whole soul into heavenly adornment, so that the whole soul may now burn for eternal life and desire to go even through the blood of martyrdom to the eternal Bridegroom.

Of the whole Church Paul says: “He presented the Church to himself, a garment without stain or wrinkle” (Eph. V, 27). And of each of the faithful of the Church it is said: “With all these things you shall be clothed as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX, 18).

To the bride, thus dyed, thus beautiful, thus made purple, the rejoicing Bridegroom speaks, saying:

**[Col. 0536A] (Verse 6.) “How beautiful you are and how lovely, most dear one, in delights.”**

11. It should be noted that she is called “most dear in delights,” because no one reaches the charity and intimacy of Christ who does not strive to abound in the delights of holy Scripture.

[Note: Val. Cl. reads *abundare contemnit*: “who scorns abounding.”]

Hence it is said: “To everyone who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who does not have, even what he seems to have shall be taken away” (Matt. XIII, 12).

The one who abounds in these delights is refreshed by them; and once refreshed, he is continually prepared to receive greater things. Hence it is said to this most dear bride:

**(Verse 7.) “Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts like clusters of grapes.”**

12. As the palm grows, it is constricted below and spreads out above. So the holy soul begins with the lowest and smallest things and, gradually growing toward greater things, reaches the breadth of perfect charity. For no one, as it is written, suddenly becomes supreme.

In the Psalm it is said of the just man: “The just shall flourish like the palm tree” (Ps. XCI, 13).

The bride’s breasts are the two commandments of charity. When they possess the soul, they intoxicate and nourish it with heavenly wine.

The palm may nevertheless be understood as the cross of Christ. The palm, growing very high toward the heavens, produces exceedingly sweet fruits; and the cross of Christ prepared heavenly food for us. The bride’s stature is likened to it because whoever loves Christ greatly and worthily imitates him does not hesitate to die for Christ.

Concerning the palm the Bridegroom continues, saying:

**(Verse 8.) “I said, I will climb the palm tree and take hold of its fruits; and your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, and the fragrance of your mouth like apples.”**

13. He truly said this, and he climbed it, because just as before the ages he determined to die for our death, so at the end of the world he fulfilled this mercifully and truly.

He climbed the palm and took hold of its fruits because, suspended on the cross, he found the fruit, seized it, and bestowed it upon us. Hence what follows was fulfilled: “And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine.”

Truly through the cross the bride’s breasts are like clusters of the vine, because in Christ’s death the senses of the soul received the two commandments of charity. Nourished by them, the soul becomes drunk, and once drunk forgets what lies behind and stretches forward to what lies ahead. With these breasts it also nourishes its neighbors and, having strengthened them, leads them with itself to the things it desires. Hence it is written: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come.’”

It follows: “And the fragrance of your mouth like apples” (Rev. XXII, 17). The pomegranates, of which so much has been said above, are recalled here, and the fragrance of the bride’s mouth is aptly likened to their fragrance.

Above we said that the pomegranates signify the martyrs (chapter 4). Here, by the bride’s mouth, we think her preaching must be understood. While she proclaims the virtues of the martyrs, while she urges the minds of her hearers to imitate them, and while she shows that many virtues exist within the one preaching of the faith, what else does she carry in her mouth than the fragrance of apples?

For she displays in martyrdom the redness of the rind that she proclaims, and under the same faith, as under the same rind, she shows the multitude of grains in the virtues. Of this it is also added:

**(Verse 9.) “Your throat is like the finest wine, worthy of my beloved to drink, and of his lips and teeth to ruminate.”**

14. The voice is in the throat. The preaching itself is therefore again signified by the throat. It is said to be like the finest wine because it intoxicates human minds, so that they forget what lies behind, as has been said, and, running toward what lies ahead, do not grow weary.

The bride, receiving a word from the Bridegroom’s mouth, adds: “Worthy of my beloved to drink, and of his lips and teeth to ruminate.”

The bride’s wine is such that it is worthy for the beloved to drink, because while the holy Church proclaims the true faith, while she urges her hearers to holy works, and while she shows by words and deeds that it is good to love, imitate, and embrace Christ alone, what else does she do than make her wine worthy to be tasted in the Bridegroom’s mouth?

Christ is aptly said to drink it, because he lovingly drinks it from his own body, that is, from the faithful peoples.

It should be noted that all drink, but only the lips and teeth ruminate. For while the Church preaches through her saints, everyone indeed hears, but not everyone discerns how great is the power of the sayings that are spoken.

The lips and teeth ruminate because, when the more perfect recall the words after hearing them, and when they ponder what they have heard through constant practice, they sense how great is the power of the food they eat, as though bringing back to the mouth what they have taken in.

For this reason it is written in the Law that an animal that does not ruminate is considered unclean (Lev. XI), because whoever does not reconsider the good things he hears or reads, remaining empty of holy thoughts, necessarily thinks unclean thoughts.

[Note: The printed editions read “necessarily gathers unclean thoughts.”]

The bride continues and says:

**(Verse 10.) “I am my beloved’s, and his turning is toward me.”**

15. It is as though she were saying: “Because in faith and love I cling to Christ alone, follow him alone, and desire to see with the Father and the Holy Spirit the one God alone, I joyfully experience the sweetness of his regard, the kindness of his visitation, and the sweetness of his turning toward me.”

[Note: The same editions read *conversationis* (“of his intercourse/conversation”) for *conversionis* (“of his turning”).]

Experiencing this, she proclaims:

**(Verses 11–12.) “Come, my beloved; let us go forth into the field; let us lodge in the villages. Let us rise early to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, whether the flowers have brought forth fruit, whether the pomegranates have blossomed. There I will give you my breasts.”**

16. When the bride, having experienced the sweetness of the Bridegroom, refreshes herself, she also thinks of her neighbor, whom she loves as herself according to the Bridegroom’s command. Because she understands the Bridegroom’s commands, she desires others to understand them as well, saying:

[Note: The recent printed editions add “commands or secrets,” a phrase absent from the manuscripts.] “Come, my beloved; let us go forth into the field.”

The field, according to Truth, is this world (Matt. XIII). The Bridegroom goes forth into the field with the bride when the Word of God, having assumed flesh, is displayed to the world in the chamber of the Virgin.

[Note: Here the manuscripts disagree. Val. Cl. reads: “when the Word of God, received in the chamber of the Virgin, is displayed in the world.” The Theod., Rhem., and Rothom. manuscripts read: “when the Word of God, having assumed . . . flesh, is displayed in the world.”]

He dwells in the villages when he visits the Gentiles through the faith that he grants to those who receive it.

He rises early to the vineyards because, after his resurrection, sitting in the glory of the Father, he also protects the churches that he builds.

He observes whether the vine has blossomed because he weighs every progress of the Church with strict examination. He sees whether the flowers bring forth fruit because he perceives toward what progress the tender and imperfect grow. He also sees whether the pomegranates have blossomed because he regards the perfect and, as though in flowers, recognizes what usefulness they have for their neighbors in the fruit.

Of these it is aptly added: “There I will give you my breasts.”

In the pomegranates the bride gives her breasts to the Bridegroom, because in the perfect there lives a twofold charity. Through it they nourish the weaker members in the Church, as though they were nursing Christ, whom they recognize as present in his least ones.

Of these it is aptly added:

**(Verse 13.) “The mandrakes have given their fragrance at our gates.”**

17. What are we to understand by the mandrake, that is, a medicinal and fragrant plant, except the virtue of the perfect?

Through it the perfect, while healing the infirmities of the imperfect, are shown to be true physicians in the faith they preach, that is, at the gates of the Church. While they spread everywhere examples of good works through holy renown, they scatter, as it were, a fragrance by which the sick may be healed.

It follows:

**(Verse 13.) “All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you.”**

18. Here the fruits signify the meanings of the holy Scriptures. Since they come down to us from the holy fathers and are believed, they rise, as it were, from trees as fruits by which souls delight.

The bride therefore keeps all fruits, new and old, for her beloved, because the Catholic Church receives the New Testament without rejecting the Old. She reverences the Old in such a way that she always understands the New spiritually within the very carnal sacrifices; rejoicing that Christ has come in the New, while in the Old always awaiting him who is to come, and saying:

## CHAPTER VIII

**(Chapter VIII—Verse 1.) “Who will give you to me as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, so that I may find you alone outside and kiss you, and no one may now despise me?”**

[Note: Val. Cl., Theod., and Rhem. read: “and even when no one despises me.”]

1. Placed under the Old Law, she awaited Christ and greatly desired that he, remaining in the Father’s secret place, should come forth through the flesh to human eyes.

[Note: Recent editions read “she desired and awaited Christ”; the old Paris edition has only “she desired Christ.” The word “desired” is superfluous, since “she longed” follows shortly; otherwise it is absent from all the manuscripts.]

Hence David, longing for him, said: “Arise, and do not reject us forever” (Ps. XLIII, 23). And elsewhere: “Bow your heavens and descend” (Ps. CXLIII, 5). Isaiah too, ardently desiring to see him, said: “Would that you would rend the heavens and descend” (Isa. LXIV, 1).

The bride therefore wishes to find the Bridegroom outside and kiss him, because, while placed under the Law, she longs for him to appear in the flesh, so that she may serve him through love, whereas previously, when grace had not yet been granted, she served him more through fear than love.

After his kiss she is despised by no one, because after Christ came and poured the spirit of freedom into his faithful, the Church is honored even by the angels.

Hence Joshua worshiped the angel (Josh. V); but when John wished to worship him, he said: “See that you do not do it, for I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers who have the testimony of Jesus” (Rev. XXII, 9).

[Note: The printed editions read “and one of the brothers.”]

But because the Church received the one who came, whereas the Synagogue rejected him—and will again receive and love him at the end of the world—the Church therefore continues and says:

**(Verse 2.) “I will take hold of you and lead you into the house of my mother and into the chamber of her who bore me. There you will teach me, and there I will give you a cup of spiced wine and new wine from my pomegranates.”**

2. She leads him, once seized, into her mother’s house because at the end of the world she will preach Christ to the Synagogue, in whom she believes. And once he has been received through the preaching of the Church, he will teach the Church there, because she will rejoice to be taught when she sees the Synagogue, now made the same body, being instructed together with her.

The Church will give a cup of spiced wine because she will preach the New Testament together with the Old to the Synagogue. She will season the cup as with wine because, so that the sweetness of the Gospel may be held more firmly, she will gird it with the testimonies of the Law, which is harsh.

She will give the new wine of her pomegranates because she will set forth the examples of strong men who maintained the unity of the Church even in martyrdom, so that the Synagogue may burn to imitate them and, strengthened by the examples of earlier martyrs, may not succumb to the persecutions of Antichrist.

When she hears of the victories of strong warriors, she will not hesitate to undertake the struggle in imitation of them. This is made clear when she adds:

**(Verse 3.) “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.”**
3. The left hand of Christ is understood as the present life, while the right hand is the blessed life.[^c0052-1] Our head, spiritually speaking, is held to be the mind. Thus the Synagogue, already converted through the preaching of the Church, strengthened by examples and supported by imitation, says: “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” As if she were saying: “Since at last I hold to faith in Christ, I experience his ineffable and desirable grace, and I feel a sweetness whose desirability I did not know; now I set aside all earthly things, even despising this bodily life itself for love of him, and with all my desires I yearn to behold his blessedness.” For when something embraces another thing, it is understood to contain the thing embraced within itself on every side. The left hand, therefore, is beneath the head and the right embraces when the holy soul places beneath the mind the things it sees, and pursues with every effort and all its thoughts the things it does not see.

There are indeed some who pursue heavenly things with such great desire that they regard all visible things as worthless; they occupy their minds continually with heavenly studies, so that they take pleasure in doing nothing else; their spirit finds distasteful whatever lies outside spiritual activity, loves this alone, and despises everything else—unless, perhaps, it recognizes those other things to be necessary. Such people have the left hand beneath their head,[^c0052-2] because, with their minds raised toward the blessedness of Christ, they see the present life beneath them. Christ’s right hand also embraces them, because heavenly love, retaining them within itself on every side, protects them. Such men delight in holy leisure, in which, through contemplation, they enjoy with desire the love of the blessed life. In this contemplation they cleanse the eye of the heart, so that, while they are still placed in this flesh, they may see God as far as human weakness permits; by seeing him they are illumined and by his sweetness refreshed.

These already experience to some degree that blessedness of which the Gospel speaks in the voice of Truth: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). What will be is already beginning to be fulfilled in them; for although they still live in the flesh in this world, yet, through that which is greater in them, they are already outside the flesh. In them is fulfilled what is commanded by the divine voice through the Psalmist: “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 45:11). For the less they live amid the world’s commotion, the more they fix their minds, through desire and contemplation, upon the vision of God.

And since, as we believe, many such people will come from the Synagogue at the end of the world through conversion, the saying is rightly understood of them: “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” Concerning and on behalf of them the Bridegroom next speaks:

**(Verse 4.)** “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes it.”

But since we explained this above (at verse 7 of chapter 2 and elsewhere), we decline to explain it again. The daughters of Jerusalem, however, marveling at that same Synagogue now made the Church, ask and say:

**(Verse 5.)** “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?”

4. The holy Church, or any holy soul, comes up from the wilderness because, placed in the exile of this pilgrimage, it directs its mind and thoughts toward heavenly joys. Hence Paul also said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). She overflows with delights because, devoting herself to meditation on Holy Scripture, she continually feeds her mind with heavenly nourishment. She leans upon her beloved because, trusting in Christ’s help alone, she is transferred from exile to her homeland by his generosity. For Truth himself says to all the faithful: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).
