But how she has received the ability to ascend from lower things to higher, from the wilderness to the kingdom, the beloved reveals when he adds:

**(Verse 5.)** “Under the apple tree I awakened you; there your mother was corrupted, there she who bore you was violated.”

5. What is signified by the apple tree except the holy cross? It bore that “apple” of which the same Bride says above: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons” (Song of Songs 2:3). But Christ awakened his bride under the apple tree because, hanging upon the cross, he called the Church subject to him to life, so that she might rise from the sleep of death and, crucifying herself with him, hasten toward a new resurrection. Hence the Apostle also says to every dead soul: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14). Elsewhere he says to certain people who had already risen: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Colossians 3:1).

But because the Synagogue’s unbelief crucified Christ, it follows: “There your mother was corrupted.” The mother of the Church is said to have been corrupted under the apple tree because, when she fastened her Savior to the wood, she corrupted herself by an unspeakable crime. He emphasizes the magnitude of this crime by repeating it, saying: “There your mother was violated.” But because blindness happened to Israel so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter (Romans 11), the Church entering is told:

**(Verse 6.)** “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.”

6. Thoughts are in the heart, and actions in the arm. The beloved is therefore placed as a seal upon the Bride’s heart and arm, because in a holy soul the extent of her love for him is marked both by will and by action. The holy mind bears Christ as a sign, inwardly and outwardly; for while it labors continually in meditation on him, it does not cease to imitate him in outward action, so that there can be no doubt that she is his beloved. Concerning this sign the Bridegroom himself said to his disciples: “By this everyone will know that you are truly my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). Of this love it is immediately added:

**(Verse 6.)** “For love is strong as death; jealousy is harsh as hell; its lamps are lamps of fire and flames.”

7. Without doubt love is rightly said to be strong as death, because when we are put to death to our vices through love, what death does to the bodily senses, love does to the desires of the mind. There are some who love God so greatly that they disregard all visible things; and while their minds strive toward eternal things, they become almost insensible to everything temporal. In such men love exists as strongly as death, because just as death kills the body’s outward senses, together with every proper and natural appetite, so love compels the mind, intent upon other things, to despise all earthly desires.

To such people, dead and alive, the Apostle said: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). Without doubt they hide their life with Christ; for while they set aside everything we see, they truly and secretly live in what we do not see—in the blessedness of Christ. Because they despise the false life that appears visibly, they hide themselves in the true life, which reveals itself only to invisible eyes.

It can nevertheless be understood that Christ says this of himself, declaring: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death.” As if he were saying: “It is right that you carry with you, in mind and action, the sign of my love—myself—for in the strength of your love I underwent death, so that you, who were dead in unbelief, might rise with me and live spiritually in the newness of faith.”

8. But because he would never have been suspended upon the cross unless the heart of the Synagogue had blazed with great envy, it is therefore added: “Jealousy is harsh as hell.” Jealousy can be understood both positively and negatively. It is understood positively, as the Apostle says: “Be zealous for the greater gifts” (1 Corinthians 12:31). It is taken negatively where Samuel says to Saul: “The kingdom will be taken from you and given to your rival” (1 Samuel 15:28). David is called his rival, and Saul is known to have envied him.

Jealousy, then, is harsh as hell, because, thinking that it could send Christ down to the underworld, the Synagogue envied him with a merciless heart even unto death. Jealousy proved harsh as hell because, just as hell tortures without mercy those whom it holds, so the Jewish people, having seized Christ, dragged him to death without any regard for compassion.

Of this it is rightly added: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames.” For just as fire consumes what it sets ablaze, so the Jews’ envy destroyed them of every power of faith. Concerning them it is rightly said elsewhere: “Even now fire consumes the adversaries.”[^c0052-3] As if it were said: “Before they come to the eternal fire, they are consumed in the present, because they carry within themselves the fire of envy, and that fire cannot be carried without burning its bearer.”

This fire of envy produced flames when, through the examples in which it had been kindled, it grew even among the Gentiles throughout the whole world, reaching the martyrdoms of Christians. But because on the one side the fire of envy and on the other the fire of charity arose, it is therefore added:

**(Verse 7.)** “Many waters cannot extinguish charity, nor will rivers overwhelm it.”

9. The holy martyrs burned vigorously with charity, because they blazed wondrously with love of God and neighbor. Many waters could not extinguish this charity, because no matter how great the tribulations inflicted upon them, they could not transform them into hatred. Charity would have been extinguished if, amid the tribulations they inflicted, they had been able to reduce them to hatred of God or neighbor.

But since waters have been mentioned, what else is meant by rivers than the increase and force of those waters? We know that flowing waters are commonly called rivers. By rivers, therefore, we understand the greatest tribulations, which, when they boiled over the martyrs throughout the whole world, converged with great force to extinguish the fire of charity.

But because charity lives among the rivers so powerfully that it rather consumed the rivers than allowed itself to be extinguished by them, many even of the persecutors converted to that same charity, so that they abandoned whatever they possessed in the world and gave themselves over to the death which they had previously inflicted cruelly upon those who endured it. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 7.)** “If a man gives all the substance of his house for love, he will despise it as nothing.”

10. God is not loved while one is possessed by desire for earthly substance, because earthly love soils the eye of the heart, preventing the divine brightness from being seen. Against this it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). The apostle John also says: “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15). Nor is it surprising—for how can he love one whom he does not know? Or how can he know one toward knowing whom he closes the eye of his heart?

But a man gives all the substance of his house for love when he distributes for Christ whatever he possesses in the world, so that, casting aside what hinders him, he may love God and, clearing away the dust of worldly concerns, open his eyes to see. And when he has given all his substance, he despises it as nothing, because once he has cleansed his eye and looked upon God, he considers as nothing whatever he had possessed in comparison with that vision.

The apostles did this. They abandoned not only what they possessed but even what they desired, in order to follow Christ. Christ himself, for whom they had abandoned everything, said to them: “When you have done everything commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done’” (Luke 17:10).

But since, after earthly substance has been cast aside, one does not immediately rise to perfection—for once possessions have been renounced, there remains the labor by which the same person must also renounce himself, so that he may advance step by step and eventually, having been perfected, draw not only himself but others with him to life—therefore the new and still tender Church, or any soul, is next described:

**(Verse 8.)** “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts.”

11. Christ calls the Church his sister, for he said of the apostles themselves: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matthew 28:10). She was a little sister without breasts when the Church existed only in the apostles, in whom she was unable to nourish herself or others with the milk of preaching (Matthew 26). For what could Peter preach to others when, cursing and swearing at the voice of a single servant girl, he denied that he was Christ’s disciple (John 18)?

The Church was little and had no breasts because, after the resurrection, enclosed in one house (Acts 1), she feared among her persecutors not only to preach but even to be seen. Accordingly it is said:

**(Verse 7.)** “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?”

Christ addressed his sister when he sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles (Acts 2); speaking to them inwardly, he taught them all the languages of the world through a manifold distribution. But who should be understood as asking this question—he who knows all things—if not the holy fathers, whom he stirred up through the Holy Spirit to ask? By that same Spirit with which he led them into the question, he immediately and fittingly answers them, saying:

**(Verse 9.)** “If she is a wall, let us build upon her silver battlements.”

12. Once the Holy Spirit has been given, the holy Church becomes a wall, because she who was previously timid is strengthened by that same almighty Spirit to resist her adversaries with impregnable firmness. Peter demonstrates this: formerly timid before a servant girl, he soon became unyielding before the rulers, saying to them: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). And again: “Whether it is right to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves; for we cannot refrain from speaking of what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:19).

And of the other disciples it is written: “The disciples went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41). Behold what kind of wall the Church became: formerly so very tender that she could not endure the foot of any passerby without injury to herself, but now, having received the Holy Spirit as a wondrous craftsman, she endures unharmed the insults of every attacking army.[^c0052-4]

Battlements are built upon her because she is granted the power to perform miracles, not merely to defend herself but also, by resisting, to overthrow her attackers; when her enemies see these miracles, they are terrified and fear to hurl their darts against her. These battlements are rightly said to be silver, because the miracles are bestowed together with the preaching of the word. And because silver is a highly resonant metal, the battlements are silver because through the miracles it happened that their words grew strong throughout the world and spread the preaching of the faith everywhere with unbending force. The Psalmist makes this clear, saying: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5).

It follows:

**(Verse 9.)** “If she is a door, let us fasten it with cedar boards.”

13. We also rightly say that the Church is a door, for we know that she received from Christ himself the power of opening and closing. The door certainly exists in her preachers, because through them access to life is opened to us. Hence it is said to the first shepherd of the Church: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

Or the door exists in her head himself, because he truly says of himself: “I am the door” (John 10:7). The door is fastened with cedar boards because the holy Church, preaching the faith, is adorned with multitudes of peoples. As the peoples are sprinkled with various virtues—one gives the needy what is necessary from the possessions he owns; another, abandoning everything, abstains even from lawful marriage; another advances so far as to become a preacher to others—the Church is embellished, like a painting with many colors, with many domains (*ditionibus*).[^c0052-5] Growing strong through the Holy Spirit, she responds joyfully, saying:

**(Verse 10.)** “I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower, from the time I became in his presence as one finding peace.”

14. She had breasts like a tower from the time she found peace in the presence of the Bridegroom, because after receiving the spirit of peace under him, she nourished preachers lofty in contemplation and unyielding in strength.

But why does she not say “finding peace,” but “as one finding peace,” unless because, while we are in this world, we do not cease entirely from sin, and as long as we live with sin, we do not possess perfect peace with him who lived in the flesh without sin? But because the little peace we possess we hold through the Mediator himself between God and humanity, it is therefore added:

[Col. 0545B] **(Verse 11.)** “There was a vineyard belonging to the peacemaker, in the one that has peoples; he entrusted it to keepers; a man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.”

15. He is called our peacemaker because through him the whole human race is reconciled to God. The vineyard belonged to this peacemaker because he planted the Synagogue amid the labor of carnal commandments. Of it is said: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7). This vineyard existed “in the one that has peoples,” because it was established in the Law, which gathered many peoples under it. Of these peoples it is said: “The peoples meditated on empty things” (Psalm 2:1).

He entrusted this vineyard to keepers because he subjected the Synagogue to Moses and the other fathers for safekeeping. Of it he rightly adds: “A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.” This vineyard produced fruit because from the Synagogue there came forth that great cluster brought from the promised land—namely, Christ Jesus according to his humanity. Concerning this fruit the Father says to David: “I will set the fruit of your womb upon your throne” (Psalm 131:11). Hence the Apostle writes: “Whose fathers are, and from whom is Christ” (Romans 9:5).

By the silver pieces in this passage we understand all earthly substance, concerning which Peter said to the lame man asking for alms: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts 3:6). A man therefore brings a thousand silver pieces for the fruit of the vineyard because whoever conducts himself manfully in the faith he has received gladly and perfectly abandons all earthly things in order truly to possess Christ. For a thousand is a perfect number; therefore perfection in any matter is represented by it.

In the primitive Church these silver pieces were offered by those of whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “As many as were owners of fields or houses sold them and, bringing the proceeds of what they sold, laid them at the apostles’ feet” (Acts 4:34). Having been gathered together, these people built another vineyard—the holy Church—from themselves; and, like good farmers, they propagated it by their own blood and spread it through their preaching to the ends of the earth, so that it might now fill almost the whole world and, planted among its farmers, return acceptable fruit in its proper seasons. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “He will destroy those evil men evilly, and will lease his vineyard to other farmers who will render him the fruit in its seasons” (Matthew 21:41). Of this vineyard, now leased to good farmers, the Peacemaker himself says:

**(Verse 12.)** “My vineyard is before me.”

His vineyard exists before him because, after the evil farmers have been destroyed, he teaches the holy Church with benevolent regard through good teachers. To her he says:

**(Verse 12.)** “A thousand are yours, O Peacemaker, and two hundred for those who guard its fruits.”

16. What are these thousand belonging to the Peacemaker, and the two hundred, except the silver pieces mentioned above—those which, when we abandon them perfectly, enable us through their distribution to acquire peace for ourselves with the saints? Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

But what do we understand by the two hundred except the double recompense that we acquire when we despise earthly things perfectly for Christ in this world?[^c0052-6] Thus the Church’s silver consists of a thousand and two hundred, because when the faithful each abandon completely everything they possess, they both make peace for themselves with the saints and receive a more richly rewarded present life together with the heavenly one.

This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you, there is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or fields, for my sake and for the sake of the Gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this present time—houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children, and fields, with persecutions—and in the age to come eternal life” (Mark 10:29–30).

But to whom is this recompense doubled in this way except to those who guard its fruits? And who are those who guard the fruits of the vineyard except those who persevere in the holy work they have begun? For a work begun with holy desire, if it is not held through the constancy of the mind to the end, is considered fruitless, because it is emptied prematurely of that from which it had proceeded. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

The Bridegroom follows and says:

**(Verse 13.)** “You who dwell in the gardens, friends are listening; let me hear your voice.”

17. The Bride dwells in the gardens because the holy Church, or any holy soul, turns the mind toward the fruitfulness of virtues. The Bridegroom desires to hear her voice because this is supremely pleasing to Christ: that every perfect man should admonish the weak with the word of holy preaching. Friends are listening because the faithful in the Church await with devout desire the speech of the Bridegroom’s friend.

It should be noted that the one listening is called a friend, because whoever loves God with an undivided mind willingly hears the one preaching what he loves. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God” (John 8:47).

But because, while the Church preaches the truth, many do not understand it, and many overturn what they grasp through a perverse interpretation, the Bride responds to the one urging her to preach and says:

[Col. 0547A] **(Verse 14.)** “Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices.”

18. The beloved flees because he hides himself from reprobate hearts so that he may not be understood by them. For when reprobate minds approach the hearing or reading of God’s words with perverse intention, by a fitting judgment they do not find the truth, which they do not seek with a worthy desire. Hence the Wisdom of God herself says: “The wicked will seek me, and they will not find me” (John 7:34).

But while the beloved flees from the reprobate, he seeks the mountains of spices because, leaving the perverse, he does not cease to visit holy souls, who become lofty through contemplation and produce fragrant perfumes through the compounding of virtues. Upon these mountains the beloved is likened to a gazelle and a young stag,[^c0052-7] because he is manifested in the hearts of holy men, having assumed humanity for us in loving compassion.

Since he was born from the ancient fathers, he came like a young stag from among stags, as was said above. Though he was rich, he made himself poor so that we might be enriched; and though he was exalted above all things, he received our lowliness with ineffable condescension. To him let us give immense thanks for as long as we live. To him, who was delivered to death for us and rose to immortality, we owe ourselves, spirit, and body (2 Corinthians 8). He lives and reigns with God the Father, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

---

# EXPOSITION OF THE PENITENTIAL PSALMS

[Col. 0547]

## CRITIQUE OF THE WORK THAT FOLLOWS

463. Whether this commentary on the seven Penitential Psalms is by Saint Gregory, the first pope, or by another author is no slight or easy question. Berthold Rembold, who first brought it out of darkness and gave it the light of publication in 1512 and again in 1518, attributed it to the holy Doctor. All who subsequently published Gregorian works followed his judgment, with the sole exception of Peter Gussanvillaeus. Let that most learned man himself explain the principal reason that led him to abandon the path well trodden by the others.

“I now wish to add another argument,” he says, “and one which, unless I am mistaken, ought to be decisive in this matter. It is drawn from three passages of the same Commentary, in which there are many things that conflict both with history and with the teaching and piety of Saint Gregory.

“The first is Psalm 5, verse 9, where the author, inveighing against the vice of simony, speaks as follows:

> ‘Although the madness of this error was condemned from that time onward, it nevertheless afterward sprouted in the Church as a pestilential growth. In our own times especially it exercised the poison of its wickedness and disturbed the peace of the whole Church by schismatic harassment. For it stirred up against the Church of God not only an innumerable multitude of the people but also, if it is lawful to say so, royal power. No reason permits him to be counted among kings who destroys rather than governs the empire and makes all whom he can have as accomplices in his perversity strangers to fellowship with Christ. Enticed by the desire for the most shameful gain, he wishes to lead away the bride of Christ as a captive and rashly presumes to empty the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion of its force. Our Savior wished the Church, redeemed at the price of his blood, to be free; but this man, overstepping the rights of power, attempts to make her a servant. How much better it would be for him to acknowledge her as his mistress and, following the example of religious rulers, offer her the service of devotion, rather than stretch out against God the arrogance of a domination received from him, from whom he received the authority of his power. For he himself says: “Through me kings reign.” But blinded by the darkness of immense greed, evidently ungrateful for the divine favor and arrogant against God, he crosses the boundaries established by our fathers, abandoning reverence for God, and rages against Catholic truth in the fury of his tyranny. He has extended the rashness of his madness so far that he claims the Roman Church, the head of all the Churches, for himself and usurps in the mistress of the nations the right of earthly power, etc.’

“The second is in the same psalm, verse 26, where he magnifies the emperor’s impiety as follows:

> ‘There are also certain powers of this world that are the gates of hell. For what was Nero, what was Diocletian, and finally what is this man who at the present time persecutes the Church? etc.’

“The third is in the prologue to Psalm 7, where he attacks the emperor then reigning in these words:

> ‘Even at this time the schismatic persecutes the body of Christ; the heretic attacks the Church; the unbeliever disturbs unity.’

“Which emperor, then, was persecuting the Church in the time of Gregory the Great? Who was raging against Catholic truth? Who was disturbing the unity of the Church? Certainly, in the time of Saint Gregory only two rulers administered the Roman Empire: Maurice and Phocas.

“These things cannot be said of Maurice, whom all historians call a Catholic emperor, most religious, most generous, and exceedingly lavish toward the poor. Gregory himself repeatedly calls him most devout and most merciful, and sends letters to various persons so that he may long administer the empire for the glory of God and the benefit of the Church. Let the letters be read: Book 2, Letter 62, indiction 10; Book 2, Letter 48, indiction 11; Book 9, Letter 40; and many others, in which he gathers together much concerning Maurice’s piety and goodness.

“Nor do the three passages we have cited seem to pertain to Phocas, who ruled for only one year during Gregory’s time. How could he have attacked Phocas, whom he congratulated on acquiring the empire in these words: ‘Glory to God in the highest, etc. Strengthened by this abundance of rejoicing, should we not quickly believe that we are to rejoice that your piety’s kindness has reached the imperial height?’ The entire letter similarly runs on in praise of Phocas’s piety and kindness, as does Letter 45 of the same book, which he concludes as follows: ‘We trust in the omnipotent Lord, who will complete for us the good things of his consolation that he has begun; and he who has raised up pious lords in the commonwealth will also extinguish its cruel enemies.’

“From this it clearly appears that the passages cited from the Commentary concern neither Maurice nor Phocas. If, however, they concern one of the emperors, it is truly Henry IV, a contemporary of Gregory VII and indeed violently hostile to him, since he carried on serious hostilities against him, as can be seen in the writers of that period. Hence some not unreasonably assign this Commentary to Gregory VII.

“In these three passages only one consideration causes difficulty: that the subject is an emperor who was most hostile to the Church and supported simony, which was rampant everywhere. It cannot be supposed that our Gregory said this either of the most pious emperor Maurice or of Phocas, whom he praised beyond measure. One may answer first that those harsh attacks upon some ruler were stitched into the Gregorian Commentary, just as there are very many additions of this sort which, with the help of manuscript codices, we have torn out of almost all the works of Saint Gregory. But here we lack ancient written codices.

“Second, what prevents us from understanding these statements of the Arian kings of the Lombards, the most savage enemies of the Roman Church, the despoilers of all the Churches, and patrons of simony? Such was the utterly wicked Authari; for this is how Gregory himself calls him in Book 1, Letter 17. It is certainly permissible to interpret the passage of a king no less than of an emperor: ‘He stirred up against the Church of God not only an innumerable multitude of the people but also, if it is lawful to say so, royal power. No reason permits him to be counted among kings who destroys rather than governs the empire.’ Yet in these words lies the sole knot of the difficulty.

“Third, it does not seem altogether absurd to us to understand these things of the emperor Maurice, during whose reign simony had become widespread in the Churches subject to him, as is clear from many of Gregory’s letters. See Book 5, Letter 57, to John, bishop of the Corinthians, and Letter 58, to all the bishops established throughout the province of Hellas. In both letters these words are found: ‘It has come to our attention that in those regions no one reaches the sacred order without payment of a fee.’ Consult also Book 4, Letter 27; Book 11, Letter 46; Book 12, Letter 28; and Book 13, Letter 41.

“Moreover, John the Deacon, who wrote Gregory’s life, calls Maurice most avaricious and rapacious in Book 3, chapter 50, where he speaks of the disastrous law enacted by him. John goes on to discuss his tyranny toward Gregory in Book 4, chapters 16 and 17.

“Of this same emperor Gregory himself, although more cautiously, writes as follows in Book 13, Letter 31: ‘When the sins of many unjust men must be punished, one unskilled man is raised up, through whose harshness the necks of subjects are bowed beneath the yoke of tribulation. We have experienced this for a long time in our own affliction.’ And, explaining how under Maurice the commonwealth had been exposed to plunder, he adds: ‘Let the stratagems concerning wills cease, and the favors of donations violently exacted. Let secure possession of their own property return to all.’ In Letter 38 he continues to complain of the yoke of sorrow and the harsh times that he had endured while Maurice reigned. Finally, in Letter 39 he repeats the same complaints and rejoices that such harsh burdens of a long period have at last been removed from people’s necks.

“Who, then, would be so astonished that Gregory, so often attacked by Maurice, indeed grievously harassed, should have written or said about him what Gussanvillaeus excerpted from the Commentary on the Seven Psalms—not, however, with the intention that this Commentary should be published while the emperor was alive?

“But how, you will ask, could Maurice, so devoted to the Catholic faith and praised by the holy Pontiff for this reason, have been denounced by him as a heretic, schismatic, and unbeliever? I answer that what is read in the prologue to the seventh and final psalm—‘Even at this time the schismatic persecutes,’ and so forth—can be referred to any schismatics, heretics, and unbelievers. Who does not know that in Gregory’s time the Church suffered from many schisms and endured much from heretics and enemies of the faith?”

Nevertheless, we readily concede that the statements brought forward by Gussanvilla fit Henry IV better than Maurice. This consideration persuaded that most learned man that this Commentary was the work of Pope Gregory VII. Yet the entirely different style of this treatise decisively excludes its attribution to that Pontiff. We possess ten books of letters written by Gregory VII; if these are compared with the Commentary on the Seven Psalms, it will plainly become evident that they do not have the same author. In this Commentary, on the contrary, the whole phrasing is Gregorian; hence it seems that it should be attributed to the holy Doctor rather than to anyone else. Let the prudent reader, however, judge this controversy. We assert only this: the work is worthy of being claimed for the most holy Father. In support of our conjecture, we have not used what Gregory himself writes to John the subdeacon in Book XII, Letter 24: “Tell him”—that is, Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna—“to have the commentaries on the Psalms read at the vigils”; although some use this testimony to prove that Gregory revealed himself to be the author of the Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms. For what follows—“For I do not wish, while I am in this flesh, that whatever I may have happened to say should easily become known to people”—shows sufficiently that the holy Doctor was not speaking of his own Commentary on the Psalms, but of someone else’s, whether Jerome’s, Augustine’s, Ambrose’s, or another’s.

It must not, however, be passed over that certain passages appear to have been excerpted from this Commentary by Paterius, Saint Gregory’s disciple. For the material he uses to explain the first verse of Psalm 31 is partly taken from the exposition of the first verse of this psalm. Gussanvilla himself also acknowledges this: in publishing Paterius, he indicates in the margin at this passage the Commentary on the Psalms as the source from which Paterius’s statement was drawn.

The same may be observed in chapter 68 of Paterius’s work on the Psalms, where Gussanvilla notes that the passage is found in the explanation of the fourth Penitential Psalm. This certainly seems to show that the learned man was not consistent in his own judgment and finally recognized that the Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms should be attributed to Gregory. He should likewise be thought to have later formed a better opinion concerning the Commentary on the Book of Kings, which he had denied to Gregory. For in chapter 39 of Paterius’s work on the Psalms, he notes in the marginal annotation that the passage is found in Book I, chapter 1 of the Book of Kings.

In this edition we have prefixed to the proems the titles of the psalms, which were omitted in all the other editions, because we observed that these proems had been placed before them for the purpose of explaining their titles. Thus, unless the titles are read first, the intention of the author who introduces them can scarcely be understood. We have also carried out the other practices observed in publishing Gregory’s works.

[Col. 0549]

EXPOSITION OF SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT, ROMAN PONTIFF, ON THE SEVEN PENITENTIAL PSALMS. (C, G, S)*

466 PROEM ON THE FIRST PENITENTIAL PSALM.

[Col. 0549]

For the end, in hymns; a Psalm of David, for the eighth.

[Col. 0550] If that king and prophet was appropriately called David—“strong of hand”—because he killed a bear, strangled a lion, struck down the exceedingly strong Goliath with a single blow of a stone, and subjected countless nations to the rule of his empire (I Kings 17), then not incongruously we understand by the same name the holy soul, which killed within itself him who, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking someone to devour (I Peter 5). And whenever he attacks it openly in direct combat, like a strong armed man, it strikes him down with the stone “which the builders rejected”; it also subdues the passions of the body and turns them toward the service of the virtues (Luke 11; I Peter 2).

We likewise appropriately call that same soul, accustomed to spiritual exercises, a psalter. For just as that musical instrument, a triangle with ten strings, is struck below but seems to sound above, so the soul formed by faith in the Holy Trinity and instructed in the ten commandments of the Law is struck below [Col. 0551B] and heard above; for when someone has perfectly afflicted the flesh, then he offers God an exceedingly sweet melody in delight.

By “psalm,” therefore, we understand the meditations, praises, and joys conceived in the mind concerning God, just as we call the song of that musical instrument a psalm. This psalm—that is, this meditation—is therefore attributed to David, that is, to the faithful soul exercised in the virtues [Note: [Col. 0551D] He alludes to the title of the psalm, which reads: “For the end, in hymns; a Psalm of David, for the eighth.”]—namely, to the soul striving toward the end, that is, toward Christ, who is both beginning and end (Revelation 21).

Christ is called the end either because he is the completion of the Law and the Prophets, as he himself testified while hanging on the cross when, after being given vinegar and gall, he said: “It is finished” (John 19:30); or because he is the perfection of all good things, since no good is perfected unless it is made firm in the highest Good. For just as it is not enough for us to seek other good things unless we strive to attain knowledge of him, so, once he has been found, no one seeks anything better, because every creature is found inferior to him, beneath whose feet the Father has subjected all things.

This psalm is said to have been made “for the eighth” [Note: [Col. 0552D] See the preceding note.] because it is sung to the Lord with consideration of the future resurrection. The whole period of the present life unfolds through seven days; therefore the eternal day that will come after the cycle of these days has been completed is called the eighth. And because this psalm is sung in consideration of the final judgment, it is rightly entitled “for the eighth.” Or it is called the eighth because it follows the end of carnal and spiritual generation, and is therefore called the eighth of the resurrection.

The flesh consists of four elements; the soul is enlivened by three faculties. It is rational for discerning, concupiscible for desiring the virtues, and irascible for rejecting vices. Of this anger the same prophet says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5). For whoever rises up against himself and, inflamed with zeal for righteousness, vigorously sets himself against the assaults of vice, has in no way sinned in the sight of the interior Judge.

Or, according to some, it is called the eighth because it follows the six ages of those living in this world and the seventh age of the righteous who sleep. The title affirms that this psalm is to be counted among hymns, because one who is inwardly touched by grief, confesses his sins, and crushes his heart in penitence offers a sweet voice of rejoicing to the ears of merciful God. There is greater joy among God’s angels over one repentant sinner than over the perseverance of ninety-nine righteous persons (Luke 15). And whoever proclaims his iniquities out of a desire for forgiveness sings sweetly among the tents of the righteous.

468 In this psalm, therefore, the faithful soul speaks while considering that eighth—that is, the fearsome day of judgment—and contemplating with prudent insight the terror of divine severity and the eternal condemnation of the reprobate. Since, distrusting its own merits, it finds no way to escape the wrath of divine vengeance in that terrifying examination, it approaches boldly yet confidently the fountain of mercy, anticipating his face, preferring to be crushed in this life through repentance and scourging [Col. 0552B] rather than to be afflicted in the future by the dreadful torments of punishment. Let us hear what it says, then, and following its example let us approach the throne of God’s glory with confidence.

EXPLANATION OF THE FIRST PENITENTIAL PSALM.

(Psalm 6.—Verse 1.) Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.

1. You see how good a beginning this is, how full of feeling, how full of grace. In calling him “Lord,” the speaker shows that by right he ought to have mercy on him. For it belongs to lords to nourish servants, not neglect them; to correct those who offend, not kill them; to seek those who flee, not disown them.

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury.” It commonly happens that those who incur the anger of their lords, if they desire to be reconciled to them, seek patrons, employ intercessors [Col. 0552C], and enlist advocates. But this soul, struck by terror of that dreadful judgment and kindled by desire for God’s love, tolerates no delay and rejects postponement. If it should defer meeting God even for an hour, it believes that it cannot escape condemnation. Desire does not endure delay, nor does it observe any measure in patience.

It therefore gathers its strength, trusts in the Creator’s mercy, and, as though it saw him present, dares to speak. It says, as it were: “I know indeed that my merits exclude me from your sight; nevertheless, I am less than all your mercies. Therefore, Lord, whose servant I do not deny myself to be, whose commands I desire to obey, and whose gentle yoke I by no means refuse to bear, do not rebuke me in your fury. Rebuke me here instead, while it is the time of mercy; correct me here, while it is the day of salvation; discipline me. Whoever in this life is worn down by scourges is corrected in gentleness, because he is amended through corrections. But in that terrifying examination every wicked person is rebuked in fury, because no pardon accompanies the endless punishment.”

Far be it from us to believe that there is fury in God. He would not be immutable if the necessity of some passion could move him. But since we cannot speak of God otherwise than according to human usage, we call the sentence of infinite condemnation “fury.” This does not mean that God is moved by any disturbance in that severity of justice, but that those who are to be crushed by a double contrition are punished without remedy.

“Do not rebuke me in your fury”—not human or transitory fury. Human fury passes as quickly as it arises and extends the force of its power only over bodies; the judgment of divine vengeance, however, not only multiplies punishments in body and soul but also remains immovably upon the condemned.

“Nor correct me in your anger.” Just as fury is greater than anger, so to rebuke is greater than to correct. We correct those whom we amend as people who love them. And because after the death of the flesh some are assigned to eternal punishments while others pass through fire toward life by purification, 469 the faithful soul fears not only fury but also abhors anger, as blessed Augustine testifies:

“All those who did not lay Christ as their foundation are rebuked in fury, because they are tormented by eternal fire. But those who placed wood, hay, and straw upon that foundation are corrected in anger, because, purified by fire, they are led to the repose of blessedness” [Note: [Col. 0553D] Gilot. and Vatican: “they will be led back.”] (I Corinthians 3).

Let the faithful soul, therefore, consider what it has done and contemplate what it is to receive, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.” It says openly, as it were: “This alone I ask with the whole intention of my heart; this alone I desire unceasingly with all my prayers: that in that terrifying examination you neither strike me together with the reprobate nor afflict me with avenging flames together with those who must be purified.” And that this may happen:

(Verse 2.) Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled.

[Col. 0553C] 2. By repeating the venerable name, he shows that he possesses the devotion proper to prayer. He says, as it were: “You, Lord, whom I find it pleasant to invoke more often [Note: [Col. 0553D] Rembold, Gilot., and Vatican manuscripts: “to invoke,”]—have mercy on me while it is the time of mercy. Correct me mercifully here; crush me here through scourges; burn me here in the fire of tribulation. And so that you may find nothing in me requiring punishment after the end of this life, I pray you to consume in me every rust of vice through the fire of your love.”

You must do this because I am weak. From the sin of my first parent I have contracted the punishment of great weakness (Romans 7): I do not do what I want, but I do the evil that I hate. I am weak because I am inclined toward evil. But you, Lord, swift physician of weak souls, heal me; that is, cleanse me inwardly from every stain of vice, because all my bones are troubled—that is, the virtues of the soul have been obscured [Col. 0553D] and weakened, and the virtues, all together, have been thrown into confusion.

Charity is confounded, humility is tripped up, fortitude is cast down, chastity is assailed. By “bones” we understand the virtues, through which we sustain the soul. For just as the strength of bodies resides in bones, so strength is found in the virtues of souls. Clearly, every soul is weak unless it has been supported by the strength of the virtues.

After the first parent of the human race incurred guilt through transgression, he fell from the lofty state of mind in which he had been placed; he lost the brightness of divine vision; he lost the exceedingly sweet feasts of God’s words by which he was inwardly refreshed; he opened the eyes of the flesh to see indecent and shameful things, and thereby obscured the mind’s vision with which he had previously contemplated the radiance of the highest light.

(Verse 3.) And my soul is greatly troubled; but you, Lord—how long?

3. Because I feel myself to be weak, because I acknowledge that my bones are troubled, my soul—because it is mine, because it has been corrupted through me, because through me it has become weak and sick—is troubled toward groaning, stirred toward compunction and lamentation, troubled with a very great and manifold disturbance.

It is troubled because it has sinned, because it has offended the good Lord, [Note: [Col. 0554D] Omitted in Gussanvilla: “because it has lost life.”] because it has lost life and incurred death. But you, Lord, how long will you be troubled against me because I have sinned, because by transgressing I have provoked you to anger? Or:

“You, Lord.” Demons, indeed, who are invaders, not lords, naturally prefer my destruction to my salvation. But you, Lord, who do not desire the death of the sinner (Ezekiel 33)—Lord in the singular, not improperly but properly—how long, that is, how long will you delay healing me? Behold, I stand in the presence of the good physician who is able to heal; I uncover my wounds, I send forth prayers, I increase my pains, I pour out tears. Why, then, do you dissemble, when your power is no less than your will? Although you conceal this in your heart, I know that you remember all things. The more difficult any healing is to obtain, the more carefully it is guarded once obtained.

(Verse 4.) Turn, Lord, and rescue my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy.

[Col. 0554C] 4. “I beg you not to be troubled any longer; I ask you not to delay mercy any further. Rather, turn, Lord.” Just as my soul has been turned toward you through the disturbance of repentance, so turn toward it through the serenity of mercy. And when you have turned, rescue my soul.

The briars of carnal pleasures hinder it; the allurements of worldly desires hold it fast. But you, who are powerful to do far more abundantly than we ask or understand (Ephesians 3), rescue it. Burn away with the fire of your love the thickets of earthly pleasures in which it is entangled; draw it out from every desire for sin by the hand of your strength.

“Save me for the sake of your mercy.” It is little to free my soul from the pleasures of the world unless you also preserve me from the temptations of the enemies through the protection of your power. It is the duty of a good physician not only to restore health but also to preserve restored health through diligent care. Thus, when you have rescued my soul from carnal desires, grant me perseverance in goodness, so that I may not again fall into the snares of temptation laid out for me. And do this for the sake of your mercy: I do not confidently ask you to save me on the basis of my merits, but, relying on your mercy alone, I seek to obtain what I do not hope for from my merits.

(Verse 5.) For in death there is no one who remembers you; and in the underworld, who will confess you?

5. Completed sins produce death (James 1) [Col. 0555A]. For unless you turn toward me, unless you rescue my soul, unless you save me, you will leave me in the darkness of my sins—that is, in death. If I am in death, I will undoubtedly lose the memory of you. I know this from the fact that in death I shall be utterly unable to remember you: “For in death there is no one who remembers you.” How could I be granted what is denied to everyone else?

“And in the underworld, who will confess you?” Just as the sinner passes from death to the underworld, so from the multitude of sins he falls into the pit of despair. Hence it is also written: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3). The faithful soul, fearing that it will not be heard, lists the miseries it will have to endure if it is not heard, so that it may be shaken by the greatest fear and move God more quickly to mercy.

It says, therefore: “In the underworld, who will confess you?” As though it said: “I foresee that, unless you rescue me, [Note: [Col. 0555] Here we have restored much material from other printed editions that was omitted in Gussanvilla’s edition; hence the sense had been weakened.] I shall be in death. And I foresee not only that I shall be in death, but also that I shall be buried in the underworld, that is, in despair. If I am in the underworld, I understand that I shall not be able to confess you. No one in the underworld will confess you.” This is what he says in the form of a question: “In the underworld, who will confess you?” Namely, no one. “For praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 15:9).

Alternatively: “For in death there is no one who remembers you”—I ask you to free my soul from carnal desires, which wage war against it (I Peter 2). If you do not do this, they will kill me, because they will separate me from you, who are my life. Since you are to the soul what the soul is to the body, if I do not cling inseparably to you, I necessarily incur death. And if I am in death, I will not remember you: “For in death there is no one who remembers you.” Just as dead flesh remembers nothing, so a soul separated from you, God, cannot perceive you. There is no fellowship between light and darkness. Wherever the memory of you enters, there is the immeasurable light of truth.

Yet this may also be understood in another way, as though he said: “An incurable body must be cut off with the sword, and the amputation of a dead member from the body is more necessary than medicine. But I am not like a dead member, for whom medicine is useless and diligence accomplishes nothing. For I remember you—that is, your mercy. I know you to be a physician, I do not doubt that you are merciful, and I recognize your patience; I would not do this if I were in death.” This is evident from the whole statement: “For in death there is no one…”

[Col. 0555D] (Verse 6.) I have labored in my groaning; every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch.

6. Above he had said, “Save me,” and the time has come for you to do so; for “I have labored in my groaning.” Let the afflicted one be present, and let mercy also be present. I recognize my misery; I do not conceal my wound; I do not hide my sin. For unless I recognized myself as miserable, I would not labor in groaning.

“But I have labored”—that is, I have earnestly undertaken—to remain in groaning, namely, to consider that I must groan for as long as I live. And I have labored in groaning in a manner proper to me. For I think that no one should groan as I must, because I consider that I have sinned more than all others.

And because it is not enough to begin well unless one strives to persevere in good works, he adds: “I washed every night”—that is, through every dark thought—“my bed.” By “bed” we understand the conscience, because just as we rest while lying in bed, so in the conscience we consent either to the law of God or to the law of sin. And just as, pressed by labors, we are refreshed when resting in bed, so, while weighed down by the adversities of this world, we take inward delight in a good conscience, as Paul testifies when he says: “For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (II Corinthians 1:12).

He therefore washes his bed through every night who cleanses his conscience from dark thoughts with tears of compunction. And not only will I purify my conscience, but “with my tears I shall water my couch.” Since a couch is a meaner bed, by it we understand the flesh. And since, just as a couch is easily shaken, so the flesh is variously agitated by a weakened soul, the same prophet says: “You have turned his entire bed in his infirmity” (Psalm 42:2).

He therefore waters his couch with tears because through continual grief and sorrow he washes away the stains of the flesh and softens the hardness of the heart with the rain of compunction. Thus, just as a garden visibly germinates after receiving gentle rain, so the flesh, watered by streams of tears, produces the germ of good works and righteousness.

He then gives the reason why he has labored, saying, as it were: “For this reason I have labored, for this reason I have groaned, because—

(Verse 7.) My eye is troubled because of fury; I have grown old among all my enemies.”

[Col. 0556C] 7. Human nature, originally created in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1), was expelled from the brightness of divine contemplation through the guilt of transgression. Just as it lost the blessedness of eternal immortality, so it darkened the soul’s inner eye, namely, its rational faculty. And because afterward it did not wish to distinguish good from evil, it was subsequently unable to know what it ought to pursue and what it ought to avoid (I John 3).

And because it did not retain him who is light and in whom there is no darkness at all, it later groped at midday just as in the night.

Let the faithful soul say, therefore: “My eye is troubled because of fury.” Because I did not possess a will capable of rightly discerning, through fury—that is, the sentence of condemnation—I lost the very power of choosing. Or again, his eye is troubled because of fury when, fearing condemnation, he looks toward the terrifying day of judgment. For when each person considers what he has done and what reception awaits him there, the terror of judgment itself disturbs the mind that foresees this, conscious of its evils.

And because no one trembles at coming to that judgment unless conscience accuses him of sins, he therefore adds: “I have grown old among all my enemies.” He says, as it were: “I fear being led to that dreadful examination because, through the habit and persistence of wicked deeds, I recognize that I am not a new but an old sinner.”

Since I am among my enemies, namely, the evil spirits—because I did not repel their suggestions, but consented to them and grew old in the works of darkness [Col. 0557A]—I have returned to the disobedience of the old man. I have become comparable to an old garment. For just as an old garment neither adds adornment nor keeps out the cold, so I am able neither to drive away the cold of temptation nor to adorn the souls of my neighbors through the word of instruction.

Or: “I have grown old while dwelling among my enemies,” namely, the enemies of the Catholic faith and the Christian religion.

(Verse 8.) Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.

8. What fellowship is there between light and darkness? What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Or what share does the faithful have with the unbeliever? (II Corinthians 6:15). For just as one who follows the devil rejects the fellowship of the saints in affection and action, so one who has perfectly adhered to God by no means admits the company of the ungodly.

Because, then, I grew old while associating with my enemies, so that no further trace of oldness might appear in me and the company of my enemies might not imprint upon me the mark of transgression: you who work iniquity, who neglect to confess your faults, and who persist impenitently in evil works, depart from me here in affection; here separate yourselves from me through the dissimilarity of our works. Thus, because here you withdraw in spirit from God, in the future you may also withdraw from me in body.

“Depart, so that I may no longer share in your wicked works, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.” “I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (Song of Songs 5). The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping because he has cleansed me from every pollution of flesh and spirit.

He shows how he was heard:

[Col. 0557C] (Verse 9.) The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer.

9. “The Lord has heard my supplication,” by forgiving my sins. “The Lord has received my prayer,” by granting perseverance. He says, as it were: “He has not only bestowed forgiveness of sins upon me as I wept for my transgressions, but has also granted me an abundance of his grace, so that I would not commit the same sins again.”

Above he had said: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity.” But because charity does not seek what is its own (I Corinthians 13), and because it proves itself genuine when the one who opposes it is loved, he therefore adds:

(Verse 10.) Let all my enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled; let them turn back and be exceedingly and very quickly ashamed.

[Col. 0557D] 10. He truly possesses charity who loves his friend in God and loves his enemy for God’s sake. Hence Truth itself says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6:27).

So that the soul, having been heard, might not pass over the Lord’s commands with deaf ears, it prays for its enemies: “Let them be ashamed and troubled.” Because I was ashamed on account of the sins I had committed, and in my shame labored in groaning in order to cleanse them, I obtained forgiveness after being heard.

Would that anyone who understands that he was made in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1), and recognizes how he disfigured that image by sinning, might be ashamed by my example. If, looking around himself, he considers both the beauty he has lost and the obscenity with which he has covered himself like some most hideous color, he will be ashamed of the character of his deeds, unless he is a stone.

If a noble soul has at some time admitted stains of sin, it nevertheless does not entirely cast modesty away from itself. Indeed, it is a true sign of open despair if shame does not follow sin. Hence, under the figure of contemptuous Judah, the soul is told: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you did not wish to be ashamed” (Jeremiah 3:3). For whoever, neglecting fear of God, piles sin upon sin plainly hardens his forehead like a prostitute.

11. But because it is not enough to be ashamed of one’s former life unless one also strives to correct through repentance what one has committed, he adds: “And let them be greatly troubled.” Whoever, considering the extent of his sin, becomes angry with himself and severely attacks himself by punishing what he has done is greatly troubled through the tears of compunction.

But because one reaches the conversion of life through the pain of repentance, he immediately adds: “Let them turn back.” The person turns to God who strives always to direct both his thoughts and his actions toward God.

And because time is short and the end of sins is death, lest anyone think that it lies within human power to correct his ways whenever he wishes, he repeats: “Let them be ashamed”—that they have sinned; let them be ashamed that they have delayed conversion. And let them do this very quickly. “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (II Peter 3:10). Hence Solomon says: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not defer it from day to day” (Ecclesiasticus 5:8).

PROEM ON THE SECOND PENITENTIAL PSALM.

[Col. 0558C]

To David himself, understanding.

As we have already said above, “David” signifies the faithful soul, to which both the interpretation of the name and the magnificence of its deeds are suitably applied. Therefore let the faithful soul understand the things said in this psalm, and never depart from this understanding. [Note: [Col. 0557] These words refer to the title of the Psalm: “To David himself, understanding.”]

The understanding of David in this psalm is that no one should exalt himself before faith on account of his merits, which are nonexistent; no one, having received faith through grace, should presume upon exemption from punishment for sin; no one should attribute the good he does to himself, but to the grace of God; and no one should grow sluggish in good works through the torpor of indolence. Let us now see what he says.

EXPOSITION OF THE SECOND PENITENTIAL PSALM.

[Col. 0558D]

(Psalm 31.—Verse 1.) Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered.

1. He says, as it were: “Since everyone wishes to be blessed, different people hold different opinions about blessedness. Following the error of their desires, they propose to reach the harbor of blessedness by devious paths. But whatever they may think, this is certain, this is Catholic: only those are blessed whose original iniquities have been forgiven through baptism, and whose actual sins committed after baptism have been covered.”

If a sick person covers his wounds, how can medicine be applied to him by the physician? If he begins to hide the wound, will it not spread more widely and putrefy within? So sin, unless exposed through confession, expands lethally in the depths. And just as an unshown wound infects even healthy flesh with putrefaction, so sin, unless revealed through confession, corrupts whatever good may be present there. For those good things are not acceptable to God that are stained by the admixture of evil.

But one thing is what a sinful person covers through obstinacy, and another is what God, in his mercy, covers through forgiveness. A physician covers a wound with a healing remedy; God covers sin with the charity that covers a multitude of sins (I Peter 4:8). Therefore, if anyone desires his sins to be covered, let him show them to God through the voice of confession.

There are, however, certain sins from which, as long as one lives in this life, even perfect men can scarcely or not at all refrain. Holy men have something that they ought to cover in this life, because it is entirely impossible for them never to sin in speech or even in thought. Therefore the men of God strive to cover the faults of their eyes and tongue with the merits of their life; they strive to suppress immoderate speech beneath the weight of good works.

But how can it be possible for the transgressions of the elect to be covered, since they cannot be hidden from him whose eyes see all things naked and open? (Hebrews 4:13). Because what is covered is placed below and something else is brought over it, so that what has been put underneath may be covered, we say that we cover sins when, placing them beneath us, we renounce them. We lay over them, as it were, a covering when we clothe ourselves in the garment of good works. We therefore cover sins if we place good deeds over evil actions.

(Vers. 2.) Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.

2. If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged. If we impute our sins to ourselves, God does not impute them to us (I Corinthians 11:31). If we punished them by making satisfaction, we would find no one to punish us in the future.

Adam did not wish to impute his sin to himself when he shifted his guilt back onto the Creator, saying: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me of the tree, and I ate” (Genesis 3:12). Since he refused to confess himself guilty, he transmitted the sentence of deadly condemnation to his descendants.

No one can judge himself unless he takes up a manly spirit for pursuing vices, as the same prophet says: “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they fail” (Psalm 17:38). For whoever is soft and negligent in his work is a brother to one who dissipates his own work (Proverbs 13:9).

That is why he says: “Blessed is the man.” He says, as it were: “No one can rise to this task unless he possesses the strength of holy fortitude.” For what is stronger than to subject all the movements of one’s soul to reason, to restrain every desire of the flesh through the power of the spirit, to cast aside one’s own wills, and, having despised visible things, to love things unseen? Hence Solomon says: “The patient man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit is better than one who captures cities” (Proverbs 16:32).

“Nor is there deceit in his spirit.” Sin will not be imputed to the one in whose spirit the deceit of falsehood is not found: to the one who does not pretend to be righteous, who does not conceal even those things he has secretly done wrong.

There was no deceit in the spirit of the tax collector ascending to the temple, because, wishing to appease the Judge whom hidden things do not escape, he was not ashamed to confess himself a sinner. For he said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). He therefore descended more justified than the man who boasted of an enumeration of his merits.

Finally, “the righteous man is an accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” (Proverbs 18:17). But there was deceit in the spirit of the Pharisee, who desired rather to appear righteous than to be righteous. While he kept silent about the things he ought to have proclaimed, wretched man that he was, he proclaimed what he ought to have kept silent. And through pride, he diminished whatever merits there may have been in him; by refusing to humble himself, he increased his sins.

Let us therefore, following the example of this tax collector, anticipate the face of this Judge through confession and pour out our hearts before him, lifting up holy hands without anger and [Note: [Col. 0559] Rembold, together with Gilot. and the Vatican manuscripts, has “deception”; this should be regarded as an error carelessly transferred from one edition into others.] disputation, in orderly conduct, with modesty and sobriety, so that although we are open to every temptation and cannot escape the hand of the Judge, having been cleansed through confession, we may experience the mercy of the merciful one (I Timothy 2:8–9).

(Vers. 3.) For when I was silent, my bones grew old, while I cried out all day long.

3. Blessed is the one in whose spirit there is no deceit; conversely, wretched is the one in whose spirit there is deceit. This must be believed by one who has experienced it: “My bones grew old,” because I kept silent while I cried out. By “bones,” surely, we understand the virtues, because through them we support the soul just as the body is supported by bones. These indeed grow old when they are weakened from their state of strength. For just as bodily bones are weakened by the assaults of diseases, so the virtues of the soul are weakened by the persistent disturbances of vices.

He therefore says: “My bones grew old.” As though he were saying: “My virtues and righteousness, or reason and understanding, have been so weakened in me that I am unable by my own power either to resist vices or to sustain with the strength of the virtues my sick soul as it rushes downward.” And because I did not wish to reach the new person through the humility of confession, through the boastfulness of arrogance I remained in the weakness of the old person.

But he discloses the reason why they grew old when he says:

“Because I kept silent while I cried out all day long.”

Since crying out and keeping silent contradict one another, how can it happen that someone both keeps silent and cries out? But that person certainly keeps silent and cries out who conceals his sins in silence, yet exalts his merits through the voice of self-praise. Or that person keeps silent and cries out who does not announce his past sins through confession, and, through an impenitent heart, does not cease committing others, having received the freedom to sin.

That sin is a cry is attested by Scripture, which says: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has risen up to me” (Gen. XVIII, 20). And again: “I will go down to see whether they have completed in deed the cry that has come to me” (ibid., 21). Sin accompanied by a voice is guilt in action; sin accompanied by a cry is guilt joined to freedom.

“All day long.” The one cries out all day who desires to be praised for every good work he does; or the one cries out all day who does not fear to sin publicly.

*(Verse 4.)* “For day and night your hand has grown heavy upon me; I was turned in my misery while the thorn was being fixed.”

4. Just as by “night” we understand the works of darkness, so by “day” we understand the light of good actions. Therefore, whoever does not cease sinning and, preferring himself to others, grows proud through good works, incurs the anger of divine power day and night. Or “day and night” means in prosperity and adversity.

“Your hand has grown heavy upon me.” [Col. 0561B] Because I succumbed in adversity and raised myself excessively in prosperity, I provoked the anger of your power against me.

“I was turned in my misery while the thorn was being fixed”: because your hand, which humbles the proud and exalts the humble, has grown heavy upon me. It pressed me down in my pride, because it not only allowed sin to rule over me, but also made righteousness—which I had boasted of excessively—difficult for me.

“Therefore I was turned in my misery.” For the one who had previously presumed upon himself and believed himself rich and in need of nothing, afterward returned to himself and recognized how wretched and unhappy he was.

“And I did this while the thorn was being fixed.” By “thorn,” every sin is understood, because while it offers delight, it tears the mind as though by pricking it. The soul of the penitent is led to lament when the wickedness it has committed is held fixed in its memory. [Col. 0561C] In another translation it is said not “the thorn was fixed,” but “the thorn was broken,” because the mind is turned toward mourning, so that the compunction of sin may be broken through repentance.

He shows how he was turned when he adds:

*(Verse 5.)* “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my injustice.”

5. Although all things are naked and open to your eyes (Hebr. IV, 13), nevertheless, because confession is made with the mouth for salvation (Rom. X, 10), I made the sin known to you by saying that it was mine. I attribute it to myself, because I sinned; I proclaim that I alone am culpable in the wickedness of my actions.

To make a sin known is more than to disclose a sin. For the one makes a sin known who not only announces what he has done, but also recounts the whole cause and origin of the sin. He does not speak of sin superficially, but confesses when, where, and how he sinned, and whether he transgressed through ignorance, by chance, or deliberately.

“And I did not conceal my injustice.” I retained in my heart no scruple of deceit; I declared that whatever I possess from myself is unjust. For “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (Jas. I, 17). “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my injustice.” Not only did I disclose what I had done wrong, passing over the good things that ought to have been done for me, but I also recounted whatever I had committed, doing the evil things that ought to have been passed over.

*(Verse 6.)* “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the wickedness of my sin.”

6. That I made my sin known to you and did not conceal my injustices did not arise from necessity or from some occasion of levity, but from deliberate preparation for repentance and confession. For “I said” means: I determined in my heart, “I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord.”

The one confesses against himself who confesses everything that he discloses. In confessing sin, he spares himself nothing: whatever he has sinned, he does not attribute to God, charge to God, ascribe to fortune, blame on the devil, or assign to the constellation. He believes that he will escape by accusing himself without restraint in anger against himself.

“And you forgave the wickedness of my sin.” Consider how great is the swift indulgence of life, how great the commendation of God’s mercy: pardon accompanies the penitent’s desire before repentance reaches punishment; remission reaches the heart before confession bursts into speech.

“You forgave the wickedness of my sin.” You, who alone spare and alone forgive sins—for who can forgive sins except God alone? (Luke IV, 21.) “You forgave the wickedness of my sin; you cast all my sins behind your back” (Isa. XXXVIII, 17). You did not merely forgive the sin, but also the wickedness itself—that is, the intention of evil action—so that no root of malice might now remain in my heart from which the shoot of destructive action could afterward grow.

*(Verse 7.)* “For this every holy person will pray to you at an opportune time.”

7. It is written that no one is without sin, not even an infant whose life upon earth is but a single day (Job XIV, 41, according to the Septuagint). Job again bears witness that the heavens are not clean in his sight and that he finds perversity in his angels (Job XV, 15; IV, 18).

Therefore, the greater the holiness with which each of the elect excels, the more he grieves over those venial sins without which this life is not lived. Yet who was holier than Paul? When he delighted in the Law of God according to the inner person and saw another law in his members resisting the law of his mind, he cries out that he is wretched and, distrusting himself, awaits liberation by the grace of God from that body of death (Rom. VII). The same man was conscious of nothing against himself, yet by no means believed himself justified on that account (I Cor. IV, 4).

For holy men, although they already possess great strength in virtues, still have something arising from the obscurity of guilt with which to strike themselves. Although they already shine with the great brightness of their life, they nevertheless unwillingly drag along certain clouds of sin, like remnants of night.

This is certainly brought about by the dispensation of divine goodness: the one who has established ascents in his heart is more effectively raised to the height of humility through his own weakness (Ps. LXXXIII, 6). Thus, from the very things through which he humbly suffers small faults, he may be strengthened more truly in the power of righteousness; and, raised to the summit of virtue, he may feel himself least secure precisely because by his own strength he cannot conquer even the small things that impede him.

Therefore every holy person prays for the remission of sin, because the man Jesus Christ alone is found without the stain of sin. Accordingly, of him alone we read that he did not have the necessity, like the priests, of offering a sacrifice daily, first for his own sins and then [Note: In Rembol., Vatican, and Gilot, “for the people.”] for those of the people (Hebr. VII, 27).

8. But lest you understand the prayer of the holy ones to seek something transitory, “to you” is added. For the elect of God, when they pray to reach God, continually lament the excesses of their weakness. From the very place through which they pour forth the force of their sweetest love in tears, they also feel the sweetness of their innermost refreshment.

“At an opportune time.” “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation,” says the Apostle (II Cor. VI, 2). The opportune time is the time of grace, the day of remission, the fullness of time (Eph. II, 4): the time in which, because of the exceedingly great love with which God loved us, he sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law and so that we might receive adoption as sons (Gal. IV, 5).

But what does he mean by saying, “At an opportune time”? Did there not exist, even before Christ’s coming, holy people who prayed for their own ignorance and that of the people? Certainly there were. But because they awaited his coming in the flesh and knew that he alone was their Savior, they were saved through faith in him. They had already received that opportune time in their hearts, because without hesitation they sighed for him with the whole desire of their hearts.

*(Verse 8.)* “Yet in the flood of many waters they shall not draw near to him.”

9. “Deep water is the word from the mouth of a man” (Prov. XVIII, 4). And concerning the inventions of heretics it is written: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. IX, 17). Therefore, by the flood of waters we understand the multiplicity of doctrines. [Col. 0563C] Paul certainly forbids these when he says: “Do not be carried away by varied and strange doctrines” (Hebr. XIII, 9).

For whoever accepts heretical and profane novelties is carried far from the truth. He does not draw near to the shore of God’s mercy to the degree that, swept along by the waves of empty chatter, he hurls himself into the stormy darkness of disputation, admitting every absurdity.

Therefore, there is no opportune time for those who, puffed up by their foolish wisdom, provoke God all the more through the blasphemy of empty assertions, instead of using what should have appeased him to appease him. By making excuses for excuses in sins, they find no remedy by which to come to God, though through the shortcut of confession they could have him reconciled.

[Col. 0563D] *(Verse 9.)* “You are my refuge from the tribulation that has surrounded me; my exultation, deliver me from those surrounding me.”

10. As though he were saying: “Those persons, in the flood of waters—that is, in the multiplicity of doctrines and excuses—shall not draw near to you; but I, who have made my sin known to you, who have not concealed my injustices, who have not departed from the unity of faith, who distrust myself and place confidence in the multitude of your mercies, draw near to you through the humility of confession. For you are my refuge.” “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jer. XVII, 5), and blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord. The enticements of the flesh assail me, shameful passions surround me, and disordered tumults of desires disturb me; but I despise all these the more safely because, thinking little of myself, I trust in the protection of your strength alone.

“My exultation, deliver me.” The more grievous the tumults of temporal things that the minds of the elect endure in the brightness of divine contemplation, the more sweetly do they exult in meditation upon the happiness that is to come and endure forever. When the inequalities of worldly perversity begin to grow bitter to them, then for the first time they are able to feel the sweetness of inner peace. And because they gather from the world nothing but the fruits of sorrow, they regard God alone as their joy. Moreover, because, according to the Apostle, “All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (II Tim. III, 12), it is therefore added: “Deliver me from those surrounding me.” For when the holy soul, wounded by the arrows of divine love, begins to pant for God and stretches itself toward its heavenly homeland by desire, everything in this world that had formerly seemed friendly and pleasant becomes a temptation to it, because those accustomed to love it while it sinned cruelly assail it when it lives uprightly. Its former pleasures likewise return to memory and afflict it, as it resists, by the grievous disturbance of open conflict. It therefore prays that in all these things it may have from God the aid of deliverance, fearing lest, overcome by the very weariness of its struggle, it succumb.

*(Verse 10.)* “I will give you understanding and instruct you; in this way in which you shall walk, I will fix my eyes upon you.”

11. The lower matters depend upon the higher. For the prophet had said above: “You forgave the wickedness of my sin”; but now he inserts the words of that same divine propitiation, in which he indicates that he has not only obtained pardon for past sins, but that provision has also been divinely made for him against future sins, saying: “I will give you understanding and instruct you.” “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII, 21).
