We who, by pridefully opposing the commands of our Creator, lost the dignity of rational nature, recover through the humility of confession the light of understanding, obscured in us by sin, through the grace of the Holy Spirit poured into our hearts. For when we enter the inner chamber of the heart and consider how strict will be the Judge who is now patient and long-suffering; when we raise the eyes of the mind to behold the rewards of the saints and the condemnation of the wicked; when, uncertain concerning the future, we fear lest we fall, and punish by weeping the evils we have done—then indeed, receiving saving understanding from God, we drive the darkness of ignorance from the dwelling-place of our heart.

But because it is insufficient to understand rightly unless one endeavors to fulfill what has been rightly understood through moral uprightness, it is added: “And I will instruct you.” I shall not permit you merely to know superficially the mysteries of my will; I shall also grant you this: that you may perform the good which you have understood, and may discern by careful consideration how it is to be done. For there are some who indeed offer rightly but do not know how to divide rightly: they begin some good work with a right intention, but neglect to possess, in that good work, the virtue of discernment. Such persons frequently bring to an evil end what they have begun well, because they incur the guilt of sin from that from which they could have had the fruit of virtue.

12. But because nothing which we begin is good unless we complete it with a persevering end, it is rightly added: “In this way in which you shall walk, I will fix my eyes upon you.” So long as we live here, we are on the way by which we journey toward our homeland. Malignant spirits, however, like a kind of bandits, watch our road and, lying in wait for our work, everywhere set the snares of their deception. We therefore easily stumble while walking among snares unless we are guided by the leadership of God’s wisdom. But that person does not walk in this way who, either desiring an abundance of temporal things or fearing their lack, is drawn back from the pursuit of upright action. Yet because one who works by the Spirit of God is neither corrupted by idleness, driven back by fear, nor wearied by labor, it is fittingly added: “In which you shall walk”; for he continually advances from virtue to virtue who is overcome by no cunning of the ancient enemy in his pursuit of holy action. Therefore God fixes his eyes upon one who walks in this way, because the regard of divine mercy never departs from whoever does not fall away from the intention of a good resolve, so that he may always have as his helper the One for whom he continually pants with the desire of unfailing love. Hence elsewhere it is written through the same prophet: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII, 16).

*(Verse 11.)* “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding.”

13. When holy men overcome their evils and soar to behold things above through the perfections of good works, they reckon as nothing what they do unless they also restrain others from error. For it is written: “Charity does not seek its own things” (I Cor. XIII, 5). Thus, by the examination of careful discernment, they seek in the secrets of hearts charity itself, the mother of virtues; and they certainly discover that they do not possess it unless they wish even for all their enemies the same things that they desire to be bestowed upon themselves. Hence the holy soul, which does not doubt that its sins have been forgiven through the voice of confession and, strengthened by the oracle of that divine promise, does not fear to encounter the snares of enemies in the remaining course of its way, turns to address its neighbors and, lest they too be found excluded from this immensity of God’s mercy, exhorts them, saying: “Do not become like horse and mule.” As though it were saying: “Since divine mercy calls you back to the state proper to your nature, and the kindness of our Savior reforms in you the image of his likeness which disobedience had destroyed, do not despise the riches of God’s goodness; do not, like a horse, indiscriminately carry an alien rider.” For just as a horse receives its master to carry, so also, without discernment, it admits as riders others who wish to mount. Therefore whoever, setting aside the fear of God, who is Lord of all, subjects himself to the power of the devil and enslaves the soul—which ought to have been the seat of wisdom—to the dominion of a deceitful master, is undoubtedly like a horse without understanding. A mule, moreover, just as it bears its master’s burden, so offers itself as burden-bearing to any stranger whatsoever. Therefore whoever, rejecting the commands of that Lord whose yoke is sweet and whose burden is light (Matt. XI, 30), does not refuse to bear the most grievous loads of sins, certainly shows himself irrational like a mule.

[Col. 0566B] *(Verse 12.)* “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not draw near to you.”

14. Often those who refuse to hear the commands of God with the ear of the heart are admonished by the blows of persecutions, so that the pains of punishments may draw to the love of virtue those whom the rewards of eternal life do not invite. Of these it is written: “Affliction alone will give understanding to the hearing” (Isa. XXVIII, 19). Often indeed the lover of the present world is so despised and assailed by that very world which he loves that he can no longer run with it but, broken by adversity, becomes numb. This is certainly done by the dispensation of divine mercy: [Note: [Col. 0565D] Gilot. and Vatican: “because in this.”] because, when despised in this world, he is drawn to God all the more swiftly in proportion as he has nothing in the world in which to delight. The faithful soul therefore prays that divine power may check the slippery courses of sinners by worldly adversity, so that they may be unable to pursue the desires of their error and, thus returning to themselves, may at least come to their senses through the difficulty and inability to sin.

We may also understand by bit and bridle the words of the divine Law. Since these sometimes gravely threaten sinners with punishment and sometimes sweetly allure them with pardon, when they enter the mouths of the faithful they turn back their wandering steps in the manner of bridle and bit. They constrain their jaws because they suppress the voice of boasting: those who used through the vice of pride to boast of their merits learn, through the virtue of humility, to confess their sins. He then shows why he so greatly desires even the unwilling conversion of insignificant people, when he adds:

*(Verse 13.)* “Many are the scourges of the sinner; but mercy shall surround the one who hopes in the Lord.”

15. For one who, lifted up by pride against the Creator, does not cease to increase his sins is afflicted here by the scourges of opposing cares, and in the future will likewise be crushed by a twofold destruction (Jer. XVII). If, to fill up the measure of his iniquity, it should happen to a sinner to prosper outwardly, this very thing is for him to endure the scourges of divine judgment, because he is thereby cast down inwardly before God in proportion as false glory raises him outwardly in the sight of men. And his fault is turned into punishment for him, because it was truly to fall inwardly that he is shown to have prospered outwardly. These things indeed befall those who do not trust; but “mercy shall surround the one who hopes in the Lord” (Rom. VIII, 28). For “all things work together for good to those who love God.” One fixed in love for heavenly things and who has perfectly despised the world yields to no vanity at all: no adversity casts him down, no prosperity corrupts him; he profits by scourges, since he either effaces the sins he has committed or avoids those future sins which he might have committed. And he considers all things prosperous for himself which lovers of the world deem adverse.

*(Verse 14.)* “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; and glory, all you upright of heart.”

16. As though he were saying: “Since those who hope in the Lord are fortified by the shield of divine mercy, rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous” (Isa. XLVIII, 2). “There is no rejoicing for the wicked,” says the Lord, because one conquered by love of earthly things takes no delight whatever in God. And the more keenly anyone burns with concern for temporal things, the more he grows cold toward eternal things in condemnable sluggishness. Therefore only the righteous are told to rejoice in the Lord, because those who do not love God with their whole heart cannot rejoice in him so long as they take delight in worldly things. For it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (Jas. IV, 4). We cannot rejoice here with the world and reign there with Christ. But only the righteous exult in the Lord, because they have become so detached from the world that they neither desire prosperity in the world nor, touched by no love of present things, fear to suffer adversity. Notice that he said not only “rejoice,” but also added “and exult,” so that you may understand that those in whose minds the brightness of divine mercy shines cannot be made sorrowful in body. “And glory, all you upright of heart.” Those whose hearts are bent toward earthly things do not glory in the Lord, because they have placed their hope in the world. But you who direct your hearts according to God’s will ought to glory in the hope of eternal blessedness, so that “the one who glories may glory in the Lord” (II Cor. X, 18). For that without doubt is true glory which no punishment of sorrow darkens.

## PROEM. ON THE THIRD PENITENTIAL PSALM

A psalm of David, for remembrance, concerning the Sabbath.

Sabbath is interpreted as “rest.” The human race had its Sabbath in the first parent, who, so long as he remained in obedience to his Creator, rested upon the most delightful bed of divine contemplation. For the first man, enjoying delights in paradise, was as unable to feel any hunger in his soul as he was ignorant of every passion arising from the flesh. But after he lost by sinning the familiarity of divine converse, yielding to the laws of death, he lost the rest of eternal happiness and fell into the stormy waves of worldly instability because he scorned to preserve the state of uprightness. Therefore the faithful soul, recalling the rest lost in the first man and likewise contemplating, through the swiftness of the spirit, the future Sabbath of eternal life, desires to be delivered from every corruption of spirit and flesh and prays, when the course of this life has been completed, to be led without delay to the future rest of unfailing blessedness. It therefore says:

## EXPLANATION OF THE THIRD PENITENTIAL PSALM

*(Ps. XXXVII—Verse 1.)* “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger.”

1. As though it were saying: “I know that after the departure from this life some will be purified by purgatorial flames, while others will undergo the sentence of eternal condemnation. But because I judge that transient fire to be more unbearable than every present tribulation, I desire not only not to be rebuked in the fury of eternal condemnation, but also fear to be purified by correction in the anger that passes away. Therefore, Lord, whom I serve in my spirit and know to be the Savior of all, do not rebuke me in the fury of perpetual condemnation, nor correct me in the anger of purging punishment.” Since we have sufficiently explained fury and anger above (on Psalm VIII), we think it superfluous to discuss them again, lest by repeating the same things we create weariness for readers. He then adds why he ought not to be corrected in anger and condemned in fury:

*(Verse 2.)* “For your arrows have been fixed in me, and you have made your hand firm upon me.”

2. The more anyone begins to understand what he has lost, the more he begins to mourn the sentence of his corruption which he has undergone. Thus the faithful soul, weighing what it has lost, considering what it has found, and seeing that it has come from the joys of paradise to the miseries of the present life, from the society of angels to the cares of necessities, reflects that it is subject to dangers and that by sinning it has lost the glory of eternal incorruption. It also knows that it can in no way escape death, though it could have lived forever had it not sinned. It laments that these arrows have been fixed in it, because what was inflicted upon the first man as punishment for guilt has now been naturally implanted in us. Mortality and capacity for suffering are the arrows fixed in us, because so long as we live in this present world, we can by no means be freed from them. Therefore let the faithful soul say: “Since, made mortal by the original transgression, I endure the great misery of this world and yet do penance for myself, you who visit iniquities with a rod, do not fill everything with bitterness; but while I mourn the penalty of sin in this world, may I at least escape in the future the terror of strict judgment.”

You ought to do this because “you have made your hand firm upon me.” Just as a diligent teacher frequently corrects a child with the rod, so the hand of your vengeance never departs from me. By the hand of the Lord, which he declares has been made firm upon him, understand the frequency and constancy of miseries. He mentions it so that pardon may be obtained more readily in the future in proportion as greater punishment has been inflicted here. We may also understand by arrows the words of God, which pierce our hearts when, fixed more deeply within us, they wound us with the love of God. He shows how continuous is this punishment that he suffers when he says:

*(Verse 3.)* “There is no health in my flesh because of your anger; there is no peace in my bones because of my sins.”

3. Since it incurred the sentence of the curse, human flesh has not ceased to bear the continual punishment of sin. And because its weakness unceasingly debilitates us, it continually sets before us the face of God’s anger. For we bear a mortal body, subject to pains and hampered by needs: it is beset by temptations, pressed by cares, worn down by distresses, afflicted by crushing troubles; and even if it sometimes seems strong, it is found to be weaker precisely in its health. For what is weaker than continually wasting away with hunger, languishing through the difficulty of sleep, being dissolved by cold, and scorched by heat? What health can there be where so great a multitude of evils meets together? Therefore let the faithful soul say: “There is no health in my flesh,” so that it may perceive as weak a body so easily altered by the inequality of sufferings. But lest you understand that the mind is not weakened by the punishment of sin because he said that there was no health in his flesh, he adds: “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins” (Ps. I and Ps. II). As has already been said, by bones we understand the virtues, because without them we have no strength in the soul. All virtues, moreover, uphold one another in the sight of God by mutual aid, and virtues are not genuine if they disagree with one another through any difference. For one virtue without another is either altogether nothing or very little. If humility abandons chastity, for example, or chastity deserts humility, then, since God detests both pride and impurity, how can proud chastity or impure humility be acceptable in his eyes? Things good are not acceptable to God when they are stained by an admixture of evils, because “a little leaven corrupts the whole mass” (I Cor. V, 6); and one who stumbles in one point loses many good things; one who gathers virtues without humility carries dust, as it were, into the wind. Therefore, because the virtues of the soul are either assailed by vices or often cast down by pride, it is rightly now said: “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins”; and daily I suffer the punishment of sins, which I behold in the very face of sins. Or: “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins,” because my soul can have no rest so long as it has any remembrance of sin within itself.

*(Verse 4.)* “For my iniquities have passed over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me.”

4. As though he were saying: “It is no wonder that there is no peace in my bones, for my iniquities have weighed upon me like a heavy burden.” “Iniquity sits in a talent of lead” (Zech. V, 7). Often a soul is inflamed by desire for the love of God, so that it even seems to be raised up to seek the heights; but because it is weighed down by the heavy burden of sins, it slips more swiftly to the depths in proportion as it is inwardly burdened by the consciousness of its offences. It indeed strives with all the strength it can to ascend to God, but wearied by its very effort, it is compelled to fall back. He had already given the cause of such great weight when he said: “For my iniquities have passed over my head.” Unless iniquities rose above the governing faculty of my heart, they would not weigh me down by so great a depression of wicked deeds. For whenever holy men endure temptations in the mind, they restrain the unlawful desire of the heart by the great mastery of virtue, lest, if they consent to the tempter in any lapse, they should no longer be masters of their thoughts but servants of cruel lords. For once the soul begins to be subject to diabolical persuasions, the more frequently it subjects itself to the cunning enemy, the more unbearable it makes him for itself, so that it is unable thereafter to resist him in anything when, forgetful of itself in one matter, it gives assent. We must therefore watch carefully, so that when sin begins to knock upon the mind, one may consider what end follows sin when it has been committed, lest, if one does not perceive the allurements of evil persuasion, one unknowingly fall into the darkness of most wicked perpetration.

*(Verse 5.)* “My scars have putrefied and decayed because of my foolishness.”

5. The faithful soul, reproaching itself and sparing itself nothing, confesses still worse things about itself than it had previously said: “My scars have putrefied and decayed.” A scar is drawn over a healed wound when the mark of a past injury appears in repaired skin. This scar necessarily decays if the healed flesh is wounded again. The more widely the bodily lesion extends there, the more difficult it is for the efficacy of healing to appear. But what is signified by a wound except sin? And what by a scar except the work of repentance? For one who corrects sin by the laments of repentance draws a scar, as it were, over the wound. But if abandoned wickednesses draw the mind again to delight, the scars drawn over the wound rot. For scars to rot is for wounds of sins already healed to creep again toward temptation and to take pleasure in repeating them. For scars to decay utterly is, after the skin of repentance has been drawn over, again to suffer secretly in the heart the pain of guilt through rotten thoughts arising from the suggestions of sins, and finally to be corrupted through a wretched deed, as though a foul odor had been emitted. He shows why this happened to him when he says: “Because of my foolishness.” Just as the highest prudence is for someone, after receiving repentance, to provide for himself in the future through the diligent effort of watchful self-examination, so it is miserable foolishness to sleep in the uncertainty of this life as though one had received security. Therefore, through the foolishness of negligence, the wound already healed decayed utterly, because, when the mind refused through the effort of vigilance to provide for its ungrateful self in the future, it committed more miserably the evils it had formerly rejected.

*(Verse 6.)* “I was made miserable and bent down unto the end; all day long I went about sorrowful.”

[Col. 0571A] 6. Each soul becomes more precious in the sight of God the more contemptible it has become in its own sight. What, however, is more wretched than not recognizing one’s own wretchedness and, amid the very dangers of life, feeling no pain from one’s weakness? For just as those suffering from madness endure an alienation of mind while thinking themselves not only to be suffering nothing but even to be unharmed, so anyone clothed in mortal flesh who does not feel the hardships of the present life is alienated from the virtue of wisdom. For innumerable are the miseries of human degradation: just as they wound the hearts of the righteous with the grievous pain of sorrow, so they delight the minds of the wicked by their very offensiveness. For when they are open to every vanity [Note: [Col. 0571D] Rembol., “parents.”], think only of the things that belong to the flesh, and joyfully pursue the causes of tears, they laughingly carry out the business of their own death. Of such people it is certainly written: “For they rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14).

But whoever desires to reach the Sabbath of eternal rest, considering with vigilance the multitude of miseries he suffers, should humble himself and say: “I have become wretched, and I have been bowed down to the end.” He is bowed down to the end who prolongs the pursuit of an evil will all the way to the accomplishment of a wicked deed, while yearning for earthly things; and who, in striving to embrace heavenly things, rises not only not by the step of action, but not even by the flight of intention.

7. But because guilt is often followed by repentance, and frequently the one who falls adds an effort to rise again, it follows: “All day long I went about sorrowful.” When the human mind looks about itself with anxious fear, at one moment it counts the evils it has committed; at another it recalls to memory the good deeds it neglected to perform; at another it sees that the things in which it is engaged are blameworthy; at another it recognizes that it still lacks righteous works. Since it finds no remedy within itself for so many evils, weighed down by an unbearable burden of sorrow it wastes away; and it tears itself apart in thought all the more harshly as it weighs more terribly the judgment that threatens.

He goes about sorrowful all day who considers it a misery whenever worldly prosperity deceptively and ruinously flatters him, just as the Bridegroom speaks to the bride in the Song of Songs, saying: “Your eyes are like those of doves” (Song 4:1). [485] For the dove has a moan instead of a song. Therefore, because holy men, fearing the blandishments of the world, endure with mourning and groaning those things in which lovers of the world exult, secure and joyful, holy Church is likened to doves: every holy person groans with sorrow over what makes every wicked person laugh with joy. Hence Solomon says: “I reckoned laughter an error, and of joy I said, ‘Why are you deceived in vain?’” (Eccl. 2:2).

Why, then, he enters upon the road of the present life sorrowfully, he shows by saying:

**(Verse 7.) “For my loins are filled with delusions, and there is no health in my flesh.”**

8. Carnal pleasure is contained in the loins, and from them, naturally, the human race is propagated. I may therefore understand the soul by the loins: just as carnal pleasures proceed from the loins, so all thoughts proceed from the soul. Then, when temptation to an unlawful deed creeps in, the evil spirit mocks us through the phantasms of vain thoughts. Often, indeed, unlawful thoughts defile even the minds of holy men; and, as these minds already strive toward the heights, such thoughts touch them with the pleasures of earthly things. Often, too, they intrude upon them importunately during the very time of prayer, so that they may somehow pollute the very sacrifice which, offered in the fragrance of sweetness, is acceptable to God and slain with a contrite heart and humbled spirit.

This is clearly suggested to us by what is written about Abraham (Gen. 15:11): as he offered sacrifice around sunset, he endured the birds swooping upon it and diligently drove them away so that they would not snatch away the sacrifice he had offered. Therefore, whenever we offer sacrifice to God upon the altar of our heart, let us guard it carefully from evil spirits, lest the importunities of dark thoughts ever succeed in snatching away what we hope usefully to offer to God.

What follows—“There is no health in my flesh”—is the same as what the Apostle says: “I do not find in myself, that is, in my flesh, what is good” (Rom. 7:18). For all the members of the body that we have received for the use of life, we bend toward the material of error. We turn our eyes toward seeing obscene and shameful things; we willingly lend our ears to hear slander; we desire to draw seductive scents through our nostrils; we speak iniquity on high and sow discord among our brothers; we even reduce the well-being of the body to the service of vices; finally, everything that we could use profitably for the service of God, we turn into an instrument of wicked action.

There is no health in our flesh, because no part of our body remains untouched by the desire of sin, through which it does not sting us. It follows:

**(Verse 8.) “I am afflicted and humbled exceedingly; I roared because of the groaning of my heart.”**

9. Since he had said, “There is no health in my flesh,” lest anyone think that he suffered nothing in his soul, he added: “I am afflicted and humbled exceedingly.” Thus you may understand that he is overwhelmed in his soul by the most grievous weight of iniquity whom you see afflicted in his flesh by so many miseries and sufferings. For just as sin entangles the mind of the sinner in nets of pleasure, so it also weighs down the entangled mind, as though a mass had been placed upon it, so that it can no longer be lifted toward sublime things, because the heaviness of iniquity constrains it, as the Psalmist says: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. 4:3).

Often we see the good things that ought to be done, yet cannot rise toward them in the desire of our heart. And if at some point the mind begins to yearn for the good, the weight it bears forces it to fall, because it is a punishment of sin that the weak soul is driven away by the conduct of life from the good that it clearly perceives through the judgment of reason. Hence, since it cannot ascend to behold the light above, it is compelled by its sins to delight in lying in darkness; and unlawful pleasure keeps in low things the soul which necessity cast down from heavenly things.

He is therefore humbled exceedingly who, as a punishment for sin, not only does not desire heavenly things but also attends to carnal and earthly things with love and delight. But because the soul is often converted to God all the more quickly the farther it sees itself separated from him, it is added: “I roared because of the groaning of my heart.” A roar is the groaning of the heart in great pain, because the more intensely it shakes the soul of the penitent, the more swiftly it rises to the ears of divine mercy. It should be noted that he said, “Because of the groaning of my heart,” since just as the loss of money and loved ones produces bodily pain, so the destruction of virtues brings pain to the heart.

**(Verse 9.) “Lord, all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you.”**

10. My desire is such that it is worthy to stand in your sight. Since I desire the rest for which one must always pray, I trust that my desire is before you. Because holy men despise the glory of the world and desire only to be illumined by the light of heavenly splendor, they always stand before the sight of the divine majesty. When they desire heavenly things alone, they ascend through the desire of their mind even to the contemplation of God. And because they inwardly perceive how sweet the Lord is, they never withdraw from him through the pursuit of a wicked will.

For if the prophet Elijah had in any way departed from God, he would never have said: “The Lord lives, before whose presence I stand” (3 Kings 17:1). In contrast, it is said of the reprobate: “No hypocrite will appear in the sight of God” (Job 13:16). The hypocrite does not penetrate heaven, because through good works he seeks not God but human praise or passing gains. And because he does not direct his desire toward God, he hides himself from God’s eyes beneath the concealments of wickedness.

Whoever, however, desires heavenly things through love of the spirit displays his intention to the eyes of God. Let us therefore despise earthly things and love heavenly things, so that we too may say with the Prophet: “Lord, all my desire is before you.” Whoever loves God desires him alone. Whoever desires him does not cease to cry out to him in the voice of the heart. For unless a great cry proceeded from the heart of the one who desires, to the ears of merciful God, it would never have been said to Moses: “Why are you crying out to me?” (Exod. 14:15).

Therefore, just as the heart is silent concerning good things when charity grows cold, so it emits a cry when charity burns fervently. It should also be noted that, intending to speak of desire, he prefaced it with “all,” so that you may understand that a desire which is stained by the addition of a wicked will cannot please God.

“And my groaning is not hidden from you.” Every desire is turned into punishment if what is desired does not quickly come to pass. Desire does not endure delay, for, as it is written: “For longing itself, swiftness is slow, and for the eager heart nothing is hastened enough.” Whoever therefore conceives a desire for God in his heart, because he does not immediately obtain what he desires, groans. Thus, after prefacing the desire, he immediately added the groaning, saying: “And my groaning is not hidden from you.” [Note: [Col. 0573D] Rembol., “this soul.”]

As though he were saying: Because you approve through judgment the desire that I conceive for you, you therefore do not fail to know the pain that I endure on its account. For God’s knowing is his approving; his not knowing is his rejecting. To Moses he says: “I know you by name” (Exod. 33:12). And at the end he will say to the reprobate: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). The groaning, therefore, that is acceptable to that Spirit who is the discerner of thoughts is not hidden from God.

**(Verse 10.) “My heart was troubled within me; my strength has abandoned me, and even the light of my eyes is not with me.”**

11. It is as though he were saying: It is no wonder that I grieve and groan, for my heart is troubled within me. I fear robbers, I dread temporal losses, I shudder at the movements of heaven and earth; everywhere I am hemmed in by anxieties, everywhere pressed by afflictions, everywhere cast down by hardships. Adversity depresses me, success exalts me, insults disturb me, flatteries soothe me. I suffer all these things because “my strength has abandoned me.”

The human heart is easily shaken by every impulse of temptation unless it is inwardly strengthened by the virtue of steadfastness. By this virtue we may also understand rationality, which has been so dulled in us through the sin of our first parent that, obscuring the image of God within us and following creatures, we abandon the Creator.

It follows: “Even the light of my eyes is not with me.” It often happens to the sinful soul that, as soon as it slips into guilt, it is separated farther from knowledge of itself. The very sin it commits sets itself before the eyes of the mind like a wall, so that it can neither see from where it has fallen nor recognize the good it ought to seek. Wrapped in voluntary darkness, the more tenaciously it clings to evils, the more difficultly it understands the eternal goods it has lost.

The light of truth, subtly examining the sins of the wicked, does not dwell in the heart if it is driven away from action. For by a strict and hidden judgment it comes about that the one who neglects the light when it is found does not afterward even seek it when it has been lost; and the one who does not preserve its knowledge in action does not possess that knowledge in the heart.

A person then begins, in a certain sense, to possess the light of understanding when he recognizes the darkness of his own blindness. Whoever, therefore, desires to be illumined by the brightness of the divine light, first acknowledging the darkness of his ignorance, should say: “The light of my eyes, even it, is not with me.” Nor is it without significance that he says, “even it.” “Even it” without which the human heart is in darkness, without which I cannot live, without which I cannot distinguish good from evil. It follows:

**(Verse 11.) “My friends and my neighbors approached against me and stood.”**

12. We must know that those who are filled with the spirit of prophecy sometimes speak words concerning themselves as though concerning others, and at other times speak concerning God as though concerning themselves, thereby indicating that they are one with God when they recount God’s works as though they were their own. In the same way, all the faithful, because they are placed in the body of Christ, which is the Church, and are members of Christ (Col. 1), sometimes speak of him as though of themselves. By proclaiming the words of their head, clothed with Christ, as though they were their own, they show that it is another who speaks through them.

For the Holy Spirit speaks through them, as the Truth itself testifies when speaking to the apostles. He says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20). Hence Paul also says: “Or do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). For he is the one who said: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11). He also says: “I myself, who spoke, behold, I am here” (Isa. 52:6). When, therefore, he declares that it was not the prophets but he himself who spoke, he plainly affirms that he himself spoke in them. Nor is it surprising that the one who presides within sometimes speaks of himself, since he is the one who fills the mouth and soul through the service of the one who obeys.

Thus also in this passage, after enumerating certain miseries of human weakness, he recalls his own passion, showing that what is appropriate to the members also pertains to the head. It becomes for us a great remedy of consolation if we recognize that the one whom we hope will one day reward the labors we endure also became a sharer in our passion, just as he says elsewhere: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20).

He therefore says: “My friends and my neighbors approached against me and stood.” As though he were saying: Not only are my members troubled in the ways previously mentioned, but I too, in order to restore to them the virtue lost in the first parent, remove their trouble and likewise return the light they lost; I, alone among the dead, am free (Ps. 87:6), having become obedient to the Father unto death. In that death, “my friends and my neighbors approached against me and stood” (Phil. 2:8).

Many among the Jews claimed to be Christ’s friends; many followed him as he performed miracles; many called him Lord, many called him teacher. Thus the teacher of the law, wishing to trap him in his speech, said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. 22:16). He also calls the Jews his neighbors, since they were related to him according to the kinship of the flesh. For even his brothers did not believe in him (John 7:5).

All these approached Christ not in mind but in body; not by the footsteps of faith but by the advance of wickedness; not with the will to follow but with the intention to harm. This happened when, gathered in the courtyard of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas, they took counsel to seize and kill him by deceit (Matt. 26). They stood against him when they persistently accused him and when, crying out, they said: “Crucify him, crucify him” (Mark 15:13).

**(Verse 12.) “And those who were near me stood far away, and those who sought my life used force.”**

13. For it is written: “Then all the disciples abandoned him and fled” (Matt. 26:56). And again: “His acquaintances stood at a distance” (Luke 23:49). “And those who sought my life used force.” When Pilate wished to release Christ, the Jews cried out: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar” (John 19:12). Those who sought his life therefore used force, pressing the judge through threats and shouting to judge unjustly. The Jews sought Christ’s life not in order to believe in him but to destroy him.

Or otherwise: They used force because they thought that by their own force and power they could inflict death upon Christ. But he said to them: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down, and I take it up again” (John 18:18). And again: “I have power to lay down my life” (ibid.).

**(Verse 13.) “And those who sought evils against me spoke vanities, and all day long they meditated deceit.”**

14. The chief priests sought evils against Christ when, as the Gospel reading testifies, they sought false testimony against him. And after all their inquiries, they spoke vanities. For the Evangelist says: “Their testimony was not consistent” (Mark 14:59), as in the case of those who said: “This man said, ‘I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days’” (Matt. 26:61).

“And all day long they meditated deceit.” They did not sin by chance or ignorance, [Note: [Col. 0575D] Rembol., “consciously.”] for they knowingly fabricated lies. They are therefore punished with a heavier penalty, because the sins of those who fall through rashness are surpassed by the sins deliberately devised through planning, as the Truth says in the same passion: “Therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin” (John 19:11). And elsewhere: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (ibid. 15:22). And again: “If I had not done among them the works that no one else has done, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” (ibid. 15:24).

Sin is committed in three ways: it is incurred through ignorance, committed through weakness, or perpetrated deliberately. But just as it is more serious to sin through weakness than through ignorance, so it is worse to sin deliberately than through weakness.

Paul had sinned through ignorance when he said: “I was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor, but I received mercy because I acted ignorantly” (1 Tim. 1:13). Peter fell through weakness when he shook the structure of his mind because the foundation of faith tottered. And because he feared to undergo death, he denied life at the voice of the maidservant at the door (Luke 22:61). Hence, after his bitter tears, the Lord looked upon him, because all the elect find the riches of divine mercy more quickly to the extent that, whenever they have sinned through the weakness of the flesh, they afflict themselves more harshly and bitterly.

The Jews, however, sinned deliberately: they saw him performing unheard-of miracles, yet, inflamed by the fires of execrable envy, they sought counsel in order to hand him over to death. Hence they have no excuse for their sin; for although it is evil not to do good, it is worse still to hate good deeds.

**(Verse 14.) “But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a mute who does not open his mouth.”**

15. Learn, you who suffer curses and mockery, to preserve patience in all things and to hear the tongues of your detractors. Disregard them, lest, if you return insults for their abuse, you be found excluded from the teaching of Christ. For Christ Jesus, the man who is the Mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2:5), who came for this purpose, to provide an example of humility and patience, not only endured insults but did not answer those who reviled him. In this he instructs us that, when we are attacked by the insults of the faithless, even if we can speak the truth, we should not break out into returning abuse, lest we turn the ministry of correction into weapons of rage.

**(Verse 15.) “And I became like a man who does not hear and who has no reproofs in his mouth.”**

16. He was like a man who does not hear, to whom Pilate, when he answered nothing to the charges brought against him, said: “Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?” (Matt. 27:13). He knew the thoughts of the wicked and did not hear the voices of blasphemers. No blasphemy could move him who is entirely untouched by change and who could have answered them with truths in place of falsehoods, so that what was written of him through the prophet might be fulfilled: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7).

Christ had no reproofs in his mouth because he saw nothing praiseworthy in their hearts or actions from which he might reprove them. He had no reproofs in his mouth, although he had at hand grounds for reproving them and possessed in his mouth what he could use to reprove them, since no one was ever able to hear falsehood from him.

**(Verse 16.) “For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, Lord my God.”**

[Col. 0577C] 17. It is as though he were saying: I endured all things patiently for this reason; I did not answer their insults for this reason: because I hoped in you, Lord. “To you, Lord, I have revealed my cause” (Jer. 20:12); in you, Lord, I have hoped—not in the wisdom of the world, not in the riches of the world, not in bodily strength, not in nobility of flesh, not in the protection of rulers, not in the defenses of friends.

These are Christ’s words according to his human nature. Thus also the member of Christ, whenever it is afflicted by persecutions, worn down by scourges, or provoked by insults, should imitate in all things the one set before us as the form of righteousness. Let it not fail if its case is not heard before an earthly judge, knowing that it has in heaven a heavenly king who is aware of it (Job 16). Let it hope, because if in this world it unjustly receives a sentence of condemnation, from God it will receive a crown in heaven.

Let it know that the joy of eternal recompense is never gathered in heaven unless it is first sown on earth with tears, groaning, and bitterness, as it is written: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seed; but coming, they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:6). For just as the spirit grows weak when the flesh rests, so it becomes strong when the flesh labors. And just as soft things nourish the flesh, so hard things lift the soul on high. The flesh is fed by pleasures, while the soul is strengthened by bitterness. Finally, gentle things soothe the flesh, whereas harsh things exercise the soul. And again, just as hard things wound the flesh, so soft things kill the spirit. And just as laborious things make the flesh thin, so pleasurable things constrict the spirit.

Therefore, the more grievous the temptations we endure in this world, the more firmly we fix the anchor of our hope in God, so that we may truthfully say with our head: “For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, Lord my God.”

**(Verse 17.) “For I said: Lest my enemies ever rejoice over me, and when my feet are shaken, they have spoken great things against me.”**

18. The Jews rejoiced at Christ’s death, but they did not triumph over him, because in the cause of his death they themselves were found inferior. For he who subjected himself to the laws of death in order to redeem humanity from death rose again most victoriously from the dead on the third day. This was what the wisdom of God had established before all ages, through the governance of a most merciful dispensation. This was what the flesh assumed without the contagion of sin clearly asked when it said: “Father, glorify your Son” (John 17:1). This too he had revealed long before through the Prophet, saying: “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10). For he spoke, and they were made (Ps. 32:9).

It follows: “And when my feet are shaken, they have spoken great things against me.” The Apostles are called feet because, just as feet carry the body, so the Apostles carried Christ into the knowledge of all nations, according to what is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18:5). They were shaken when they doubted that the one whom they saw suffering was the Son of God, as did the one who said: “We were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). Therefore, when the feet were shaken, Christ’s enemies spoke great things against him, because, while the Apostles were troubled and fleeing, the Jews judged him guilty of death.

16. These words can also apply to the faithful soul. The faithful soul has enemies in this life: it has those who fight against it inwardly, and also those who attack it outwardly. But its enemies cannot triumph over it, because, filled with the spirit of counsel and fortitude, it rejects diabolical suggestions and tramples the fury of its persecutors.

If those who persecute it perceive, through some fear, that the stronghold of its resolve is advancing in purpose, or if invisible foes discover that it delights in their wicked suggestions, they introduce more grievous temptations, the more confidently expecting victory because they seem to have found an entrance. For it is difficult to resist an enemy if the soul delights in his persuasions. Therefore, I trust that my enemies will not triumph over me.

**(Verse 18.) “For I am ready for scourges, and my pain is always before me.”**

20. For I prefer to be killed rather than conquered. I gladly endure scourges, I embrace persecutions, I desire visitations, I long for corrections. Holy men desire to be scourged in this life, so that, corrected by scourges, they may see the sins that threaten and place their past offenses before their eyes. Often scourges open the eyes of those who sin, eyes that the darkness of insolence and security has closed amid vices. Often the mind that is sluggish is touched by persecutions so that it may be awakened, so that one who has lost the state of his uprightness through security may consider in affliction how far he has come.

It follows: “And my pain is always before me.” Just as he gave the reason why he does not fear visible enemies, as though he regarded as a benefit the torment they inflict, so he also reveals why he does not fear the devil’s deceptions by adding: “And my pain is always before me.” For it is written: “A heart that knows the bitterness of its soul will not allow a stranger to share in its joy” (Prov. 14:10). Whoever frequently considers all the hardships of the present life weighs how tranquil were the things he lost and how troubled are the things into which he fell. For whoever, inflamed by desire for the heavenly homeland, dies to the wicked world and its desires is occupied by no pleasures of worldly vanity.

**(Verse 19.) “For I will announce my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin.”**

21. Whoever announces his sin by confessing it and does not cease to reflect in satisfaction for that same sin always has pain before him, because he finds no rest in the world. Hence, after saying, “My pain is always before me,” as though we were asking how this could happen, he added: “For I will announce my iniquity.”

These are the marks of true humility: for each person to recognize his own iniquity, announce what he has recognized through confession, and erase what he has announced through penitential satisfaction. By contrast, it is the universal vice of wicked people both to commit sin by falling [Possibly read: “by concealing”] and to hide what they have committed by denying it, and then to multiply what has become known by defending it.

It must nevertheless be understood that even the reprobate often disclose their sins by confession; but because they disdain to change the manner of their lives, they obstinately refuse to mourn the very things they confess. The elect, however, not only proclaim their faults by the voice of confession but also strive to abolish them through the tears of strict correction. Inciting themselves to the lamentations of repentance, they tear themselves apart through hidden reproach; and, struck by fear of the future judgment, they carefully investigate whether any evil deeds still lie hidden within them. Often what escaped notice in those who were sluggish becomes known through tears. Those who, in security, do not know their guilt detect it within themselves when they rise up against themselves.

Let us therefore also reflect upon our sin and pursue it with the bitter reproach of repentance, lest, while we neglect to weigh our faults, we increase the weight of sin through negligence. It follows:

**(Verse 20.) “But my enemies live and have been strengthened against me, and those who hate me unjustly have multiplied.”**

[492] 22. Through the hidden dispensation of his counsel, our Creator both observes the faults of mortals and determines the spans of their lives, so that the periods of a long life which the righteous use as an aid to good works, the wicked may receive as an increase of condemnation. For if someone turns the time granted for repentance toward guilt, when the strict Judge comes, he turns the periods of mercy granted to him toward punishment.

“And they have been strengthened against me.” At times almighty God allows the wicked to live longer for this purpose: so that they may increase their evil deeds each day through their wicked lives, and so that those who despise the world may nevertheless shine forth through the persecution inflicted by them. Swollen with the arrogance of pride, the wicked rise against the elect all the more grievously as everything in the world turns out according to their wishes.

Nor do they understand that the wicked often receive good things during their life, and therefore adversity rarely or never disturbs them. Such people also find supporters of their iniquities among the lost all the more quickly because they seek the glory of the world through profit and gifts.

Hence it is added: “And those who hate me unjustly have multiplied.” Nothing is more unjust than to return hatred for love, repay good with evil, or answer correction with insults. The wicked commonly do this when they afflict the righteous, who seek their salvation, with the blows of execrable wickedness. And therefore he adds:

**(Verse 21.) “Those who repay evil for good slandered me, because I pursued goodness.”**

23. Whoever returns evil for evil is not good. Whoever does not return good for good is ungrateful. But whoever returns evil for good is unjust. For lost people commonly slander those who live well out of envy, or attach to them the stigma of an invented crime, or call the innocence of a pure life hypocrisy.

Why they do this he shows when he says: “Because I pursued goodness.” Whoever imitates Christ pursues goodness. His imitators endure more grievous temptations in this life the farther they withdraw from the world in heart. For the Apostle says: “All who desire to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12). And elsewhere it is written: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. 33:20).

The righteous, who desire with complete concentration the things that belong to God and, having been raised above the world, trample all worldly things by a certain power of dominion, endure not only the devil’s assaults in the secrecy of the heart but also inflame the malice of the wicked by the beauty of their way of life.

But because no one is found capable of overcoming unless he has been strengthened by the power of divine virtue, the one who is worn down by the scourges of persecutors and bitten by the teeth of slanderers implores the presence and help of the divine majesty, so that, supported by its protection, he may grow strong against all adversities that he suffers. He therefore says:

**(Verse 22.) “Do not abandon me, Lord my God; do not depart from me.”**

24. Without doubt the Lord abandons those to whom he does not grant steadfastness in tribulation. For it necessarily follows that whoever has been abandoned by God is subject to every temptation. Whoever therefore fears the devil’s temptations and dreads suffering adversity in this world should turn to God with all his strength, cry out to God from the depths of his heart, and say: “Do not abandon me, Lord my God.” If he often strives to repeat this word with devotion and desire, I think he will feel in it a certain sweetness that our speech cannot express.

It follows: “Do not depart from me.” The holy soul that desires God alone perfectly prays that God may not depart from it even for an hour. For it knows that it walks among enemies; it knows that the devil opposes it at every moment. Because it understands that dangers threaten it at all times, it cannot be secure even for a moment.

**(Verse 23.) “Attend to my help, Lord, God of my salvation.”**

25. It is as though he were saying: You who are a helper in times of need and tribulation, do not neglect me as though I were a stranger; do not reject me as though I were an outsider. Rather, attend to my help; protect me amid the deadly darts of temptations; defend me from every attack of my enemies; illumine the light of understanding in my heart; [Note: [Col. 0581] Gilot and Vatican manuscripts: “you, with your help, [deliver] me from every evil,” etc.] surround me with the aid of your power.

You ought rightly to do this, because you are my Lord. You alone do I have as Lord; you alone do I confess as God. It is therefore fitting that you who are the restorer of the salvation lost in the first parent should also be its preserver in me, restored by grace.

## PROEMIUM TO THE FOURTH PENITENTIAL PSALM

“When the prophet Nathan came to David, when he went in to Bathsheba.”

[Col. 0581C] The history from which this title is taken is well known (2 Kings 11). David, captivated by the beauty of Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, not only had intercourse with her but also, after killing her husband, took her in marriage. Later, when the prophet Nathan came to him and condemned him by his own judgment, after introducing a comparison involving sheep, David not only refused to conceal or defend his sin but also confessed what he had done and turned to the bitter lamentations of repentance (2 Kings 12). In the psalm, however, no mention is made of the historical account, but the profound feeling of a sorrowful spirit is clearly recognized. In this psalm we are also admonished to fear prosperity and to keep more vigilant guard against every happiness of the world. For present joys are often followed by everlasting lamentation. Just as we are led to joy through tears, so through joy we arrive at weeping. For the one who said, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5), himself also said, “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6:25). Who was holier than David? When he was hard-pressed by Saul’s persecutions, he not only refused to kill his persecutor but also spared him when he had the power to kill him (1 Sam. 24). He had fixed his hope in God’s mercy to the degree that he felt more miserably the weakness of his tribulation. But when he had overcome his enemies and was free from oppression, he carelessly and overconfidently added murder to adultery. We are also admonished in this psalm to restrain carnal desires and never to despair of God’s mercy. Therefore, whoever despairs of pardon and hesitates to undertake repentance should call David’s repentance back to mind (2 Kings 11). Let us also hear David crying out, and let us cry out with him; let us hear him groaning, and groan with him; let us hear him weeping, and weep with him; let us hear that he was corrected, and rejoice with him.

EXPOSITION OF THE FOURTH PENITENTIAL PSALM

(Ps. 50—Verse 1.) Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.

494 1. Let us place before the eyes of our mind someone grievously wounded, scarcely drawing the final breaths of this vital air, lying naked on a dung heap and displaying an unbound wound, wasting away in longing for the physician who is coming, and, once he has recognized him, begging him to take pity on him. For the wound of the soul is sin, of which it is said: “The wound, the bruise, and the swelling sore is not bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil” (Isa. 1:6). Acknowledge within yourself, wounded one, your physician, and uncover to him the wounds of your sins. Let him hear the groaning of your heart, to whom every secret thought is open. Let your tears move him, and by a certain persistence in seeking him continually draw up to him deep sighs from the depths of your heart. Let your sorrow reach him, so that it may also be said to you: “The Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Sam. 12:13). Cry out with David; see what he himself said: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” As though he were saying: “I am in danger from a huge wound, which none of the physicians can heal unless that physician who is almighty comes to my aid.” For nothing is incurable to the almighty physician; just as he heals without payment, so he restores salvation by his word. I would therefore despair of the wound if I did not place my confidence in the Almighty. “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” Let those who incur guilt through ignorance seek a small mercy. But I, just as I have fallen grievously, have also sinned knowingly. Yet you, almighty physician, both correct those who despise you, instruct those who are ignorant, and forgive those who confess. Would that you, Lord Jesus, moved by mercy, would deign to come to me (Luke 10)—I who, descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, that is, rushing down from the heights to the depths, from life-giving things to infirm ones, fell among the angels of darkness, who not only stripped me of the garment of spiritual grace but also, after inflicting wounds, left me half-dead. Would that you would bind the wounds of my sins, granting me the hope of recovering salvation, lest they rage more fiercely if they despair of being healed. Would that you would apply to me the oil of remission and pour in the wine of compunction. And if you place me upon your beast, you will raise the needy from the earth and lift the poor from the dung heap (Ps. 112). For you are the one who bore our sins, who paid on our behalf what you had not seized (1 Pet. 2). If you lead me into the inn of your Church, you will feed me with the nourishment of your body and blood. If you care for me, I will neither pass over your commandments nor fall into the fury of roaring beasts. [Col. 0583A] For I need your protection as long as I bear this corruptible flesh. Hear me, therefore, O Samaritan, stripped and wounded, weeping and groaning, calling upon you and crying out with David: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.”

(Vers. 2.) And according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity.

2. My sins are great and many, and therefore I not only ask for great mercy but also seek the multitude of your mercies, lest I undergo, for other sins, the punishment I fear if even one sin were left unerased. By “mercy” we understand the compassionate disposition of the one who shows mercy; by “mercies,” however, we designate the actual bestowal of mercy, according to what is written: “The Lord is merciful and compassionate” (Ps. 110:4). It would be superfluous to use both expressions unless there were a difference in their meaning. We must know that no one is more incurable than the person who thinks himself healthy. For this is a clear sign of approaching salvation: that a person begins to know himself. David knew himself when he sought the multitude of mercies. Let the sinner also say with him: “According to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity.” You have bestowed upon the world immeasurable and innumerable mercies when you rescued the human race from the bondage of the devil’s tyranny and washed your chosen ones from their sins in your blood. May this blood wash away the stains of my sins—the blood that was able to blot out the offenses of the whole world (Rev. 5). I do not ask you for gold, precious stones, or merchandise obtained through labors and shipwrecks; nor for foreign goods brought to us from distant earthly regions at great risk, which often weaken even the minds of strong men and, seduced by the image of false beauty, hold them captive. Rather, I ask for what is superior and more precious than all these: the remission of sins. This will then be shown to be genuine if, with the fruit of repentance added, it is increased by the gifts of your grace. For what benefit is the impunity of the evils I have committed unless the capacity to do good follows as well?

(Vers. 3.) Wash me yet more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.

3. What is more unjust than to violate another man’s wife? To kill her husband without his knowledge or lament? This indeed had been done by the Prophet, who had been raised from the flocks of sheep, taken from following the ewes to govern the kingdom, endowed with bodily strength, and illumined by the gifts of spiritual grace. He had fallen more grievously in proportion as he had excelled the others more loftily in the glory of the kingdom and in the excellence of his virtues. The praise of his preceding glory increased the guilt of his subsequent fault. For everyone falls more grievously the higher he had previously ascended in God’s sight. Let him therefore say: “Wash me yet more from my iniquity.” Let the fact that I have fallen benefit me, Lord: let the marks of sins, which until now I have neglected, be washed away together with this stain. For often, while we lament certain evil deeds, the very force of our bitterness arouses us to examine ourselves, and we discover other things in ourselves that ought to be lamented. We more easily consign these deeds to oblivion insofar as we regard them as either insignificant or trivial. But the increasing bitterness of repentance not only piles the greater sins upon our heart; it also recalls even the smallest to memory. We pursue all of them with greater determination insofar as we strive more vigilantly to uproot every seed of wickedness from our heart. Therefore, the one who is washed more thoroughly is not only forgiven the sin he punishes in himself, but other sins that oblivion had covered over are also erased. The waters by which iniquity is washed away are the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Coming, as it were, like a torrent from above, they irrigate the hearts of the elect so that they may bear fruit, and likewise cleanse them from every pollution of flesh and spirit. Of this torrent it is written: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5). And “cleanse me from my sin.” The filth of my crimes has defiled me; the contagion of sin has polluted me; but I flee to the fountain of mercies. You are able both to wash me from iniquity and to cleanse me from sin. I have acted wickedly by oppressing the innocent; I have sinned by sparing not even myself. For the Prophet knew that whoever plots to injure another first strikes himself with his own dart. What is more cruel than to kill oneself? If the mouth of a liar kills the soul, how much more does the sword of one who strikes extinguish life? Hence it is written: “Have pity on your soul, pleasing God” (Sir. 30:24). And again: “To whom will one who is evil to himself be good?” (Sir. 14:5.)

[Col. 0584C] (Verse 4.) For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.

496 4. As though he were saying: “I know whom I invoke. I invoke the Just One, who both hates sins and does not leave them unpunished. Just as I seek his mercy, so also I look toward his justice. I do not ask to receive mercy in such a way that I wish him to remove his justice. I do not want my sin to remain unpunished. It is mercy when he forgives the sinner; it is justice when he does not allow the sin to pass unpunished. But because I myself dread my sin, I beseech you not to punish me so severely. For this reason I acknowledge it, so that you may forgive. Therefore, have mercy on me, wash me, cleanse me: ‘For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.’” I have not placed what I did upon another’s back; I do not look at others while forgetting myself. I do not seek to remove the speck from my brother’s eye while failing to consider the beam in my own eye. “My sin is always before me.” Whoever desires to find God’s mercy must already acknowledge his sins as grave, punish his faults with tears, anticipate the Lord’s face through confession, place before the eyes of his heart both the faults of his conduct and the terror of the final judgment, and consider [Note: I suspect that the reading should be *quam districtus* (“how severe”), a phrase that occurs a hundred times in Gregory and is especially appropriate here, where the severity of the supreme Judge is under discussion.] how discerning the Judge will be when he comes—he who sustains sinners for this reason: that, once they have been converted, he may find less to condemn in them. Let him ascend the tribunal of his own mind, set himself before himself, and see his own foulness so that he may correct it, lest he finally see it unwillingly and be ashamed. Let him be an incorruptible judge to himself; let fear torment him, confession break forth, so that with the Prophet he may say to God: “I know my iniquity.”

(Vers. 5.) Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.

5. One human being does not sin against another, because either equal or greater guilt defiles the other. God alone justly avenges sins, because he alone is one in whom nothing deserving punishment can be found. Since God alone spares, he alone judges justly; the sinner points to him alone. For insofar as each person makes himself unlike God by sinning, he offends the dread majesty of the heavenly Judge. Let the sinner therefore cry out to God; let him cry out, conscious of his iniquities; let him cry out from the depths of his heart and say: “Against you alone have I sinned,” because you alone are without sin; “and I have done evil before you.” My sin could perhaps remain unknown to others, but it could not be hidden from you. For you penetrate more sharply than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and you discern the thoughts of the heart. No creature is invisible in your sight, for all things are naked and open to your eyes (Heb. 4:13). You are so entirely without sin that you are even justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. The Apostle writes: “But God is truthful, and every human being is a liar,” as it is written, “so that you may be justified in your words” (Rom. 3:4). If God is truthful, he is necessarily just in his words. For if he inserted falsehoods among truths in his words, he would certainly not be just. But far be it from the hearts of the faithful to think that there is falsehood in God. For he is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works (Ps. 144:13), as he himself also says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). Truth therefore justifies God, while falsehood condemns the human being. It follows: “And prevail when you are judged.”

6. The Prophet foresaw God coming in the flesh, destined to be condemned by human judgment so that the human being might escape the torment of eternal death; therefore he said: “And prevail when you are judged.” As though he were saying: “All who have been judged, even if they had advanced greatly in virtue, did not undergo judgment wholly unjustly, because before they were judged they had in some way committed sin. But you, when you have received the sentence of an unjust death, because you alone among human beings are free from every sin, prevail over all who have been judged when you are judged—whether you are God the Father in the Son or God the Word in the assumed humanity.”

This may nevertheless be understood in another way, as though he were saying: “For this reason I ask you to have mercy, to wash, and to cleanse: so that you may be justified in your words,” that is, may appear truthful in your promises. For you promised the just an eternal kingdom and prepared the prize of eternal life for those who love virtue. But unless you justify me and others, you will be unable to find anyone whom you do not condemn. Justify me, therefore, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. They judge you who deny that restoration takes place after a fall and assert that forgiveness of sins is granted to no one. If you forgive my sin, you will overcome them as fabricators of falsehood and adherents of perverse doctrines.

Or: “Justify me, so that you may be justified in your words.” For you promised that you would assume flesh from my stock; but if you do not cleanse me from so great a crime, I seem unworthy of being the one from whose seed you would assume flesh. For you are the one who said: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11). Wash me from my iniquity, lest I be deprived of the promise.

“And prevail when you are judged.” The Lord prevailed when judged, because by the very means through which he succumbed in his Passion, he displayed the greater glory of himself in rising again. He prevailed when judged because those whose judgment he underwent for a time by dying he punished with eternal death, condemned by a just judgment.

(Vers. 6.) For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins.

7. It is necessary, Lord, that you have mercy, because from the beginning of life I fell into the pit of sin and contracted the beginnings of my birth with the filth of carnal desire. It is not only the iniquity I recently committed that lives in me; I also have within me something ancient for which you must forgive: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities.” Human beings are not conceived in sins because intercourse between married persons is itself sinful. That act has no guilt in a spouse, since the marriage covenant does not depart from fidelity. For God instituted marital union when, in the beginning, he created male and female. They would indeed have produced children without sin if, placed in paradise, they had remained obedient to the Creator (Gen. 1:28). But because the first human being fell from the state of uprightness through sin, he transmitted the punishment of sin to his children. Carnal pleasure is the punishment of sin; it is contracted from the root of sin in such a way that no one is born into the world without it. But just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ (1 Cor. 15:22). Let the penitent therefore confess the guilt he deserved, so that he may obtain the pardon he desires. [Note: Remigius: “what he feared.”]

(Vers. 7.) For behold, you have loved truth; you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.

8. For this reason I rebuke my ways from the beginning and condemn my sins myself: because you have loved truth. God loves truth because he does not leave sin without punishment. Either a person pursues and punishes it in himself, or afterward God avenges it through a strict examination. Therefore, whether the iniquity is great or small, unless it is punished by the repentant person, it will be punished by God the Judge, as a certain wise man says: “Knowing that you would not spare the sinner” (Job 9:28). The sinner is not spared, because sin is not released without vengeance. God therefore loves truth because he does not omit just judgment.

“You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” Whoever is not secure concerning the gift of pardon is not vehement in carrying out vengeance. Before Christ’s coming it was indeed uncertain whether those who had fallen grievously could receive pardon, and the remission of sins was hidden from many. But David, who had foreseen that the Redeemer of the world would come to take away sins, did not doubt the forgiveness of sins. He was not ignorant of the work of God’s wisdom, hidden from the ages, ordained before all times, and manifested at the end of the ages. For God’s Wisdom is the Son of God, of whom it is written: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). He is the one through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1:3). He is the one of whom the Prophet says: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24). It was fitting that remission should be accomplished through the one through whom creation had been accomplished, and that he should be the giver of grace who had been the author of nature for all. Just as he grants this remission to those who confess in the time of grace, so before his coming he granted it beforehand to those who awaited him. These are the uncertain and hidden counsels of the divine plan, revealed in the final times to all nations through God’s wisdom. Because David knew them through the Spirit, he confidently relied upon God’s mercy. Were they not uncertain to the Ninevites, who, doing penance at Jonah’s preaching, said hesitantly: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive?” (Jonah 3:9.)

(Vers. 8.) You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.

9. Hyssop is a lowly herb, clinging to a rock and, in its outward appearance, seeming to display little usefulness in itself; nevertheless, it suppresses inflation of the lungs and, when crushed, reveals the sharpness of its power. What, then, is signified by hyssop if not Christ’s humility? It is this humility that restrains all obstinacy in us, just as that herb provides medicine for an inflated lung. Who would now disdain to humble himself in the world for God when he hears that the Son of God endured insults and mockery? Who would consider suffering punishment for God a disgrace when the King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 19) was condemned for our sake to the most shameful death (Wis. 2)? Especially since he has been set before us as the model of righteousness, whose commands we ought to hear and whose examples we ought to follow, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29).

According to the testimony of the Law (Num. 19), a bunch of this same herb, dipped in the blood of a red heifer, cleansed the unclean. What, then, is signified by the heifer if not the weakness of the Lord’s assumed incarnation, taken for sacrifice? For just as strength is customarily understood through the male sex, so weakness can be signified through the female; and of him it is written: “For although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4). He is our high Priest, who offered the sacrifice of his body on the altar of the cross for the salvation of the whole world (Heb. 9). He is the High Priest of the good things to come, who entered once for all into the holy place through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption. This heifer is called red so that the redness of Christ’s blood might be clearly displayed in it. Of this the bride speaks in the Song of Songs, saying: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5:16)—white, evidently, in the appearance of his divinity; ruddy, in the blood of his Passion.

With this hyssop, therefore, only the one who imitates the ways of the Lord’s Passion is sprinkled. The one sprinkled is sanctified, as Paul says: “For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled, sanctify the unclean for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Heb. 9:13).

It follows: “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.” Just as water washes the body from the filth of dirt, so the grace of the Holy Spirit purifies the soul from the stains of sins. By saying, “And I shall be made whiter than snow,” he shows that no beauty present in the body can be compared with the loveliness of a holy soul. For what is whiter among bodies than snow? And yet the one who follows the ways of Christ’s Passion is made whiter than snow. For it is written of the saints: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43). Who does not know that the sun is whiter than snow? Moreover, the whiteness of snow soon passes away, while the beauty of the saints will remain forever.

(Vers. 9.) You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will exult.

10. The saints will then possess true and immeasurable joy, when the wicked have been punished with eternal death and, by the sentence of final condemnation, sent into the dreadful abyss of perpetual torment, and they hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). In the words “joy and gladness,” understand a twofold honor for the saints: on that day, illumined by the vision of glory beyond what we can conceive, they will enjoy the blessedness of their souls and likewise be clothed with the incorruption of their bodies. For it is written of them: “In their land they shall possess double” (Isa. 61:7).

The holy men, trampling upon the glory of the world through contempt of mind, mortify every carnal pleasure in themselves so that afterward they may live eternally in God. Because they do not at all refuse to suffer the world’s miseries for God, they acquire the recompense of eternal blessedness. This blessedness is granted to their souls before the resurrection and likewise bestowed upon their bodies after judgment, as the Apostle John writes in the Apocalypse: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and because of the testimony they held, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’ And individual white robes were given to them, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers who were to be killed as they had been was fulfilled” (Rev. 6:9–11).

For what does it mean to give each of them a white robe if not to confer upon their souls the immortality of eternal blessedness? And what does it mean to rest until the number of the elect is fulfilled if not to await the glory of the future resurrection? In that resurrection they will again receive individual white robes, because they will resume the immortal and incorruptible garments of their bodies.
