Since, therefore, holy men pass after judgment into the rewards of eternal happiness not only in soul but also in body, it is rightly said of them that “in their land they shall possess double.”

Observing the increase of this happiness, the Prophet says: “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will exult.” The bones of our souls are virtues, which are humbled in this life because they are continually disturbed by the persistent assaults of temptations. “The life of a human being upon the earth is temptation” (Job 7:1). In eternal life, however, they will receive not only the strength of unconquered power but also feel no assault from opposing vices.

(Vers. 10.) Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.

[Col. 0589B] 11. Because he always has his sins before his eyes, the Prophet rightly asks that God turn his face away from them. Earlier the Prophet had said: “My sin is always before me.” Since, therefore, he always saw his sin, he carried continual sorrow for it in his heart. God turns his eyes away from his sin because the sinner himself observes it without ceasing. For God does not avenge the sins of those who are afflicted in the secret recesses of their hearts by the memory of evil deeds. They judge themselves for this purpose: that they may escape the terrible judgment of the Almighty, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31).

But the reprobate, because they do not at all look upon what they have committed, do not hide their deeds from the sight of the Judge. The more they refuse to consider their errors themselves, the more they set them before the sight of the divine majesty. God sees the evil deeds of sinners not to approve them but to condemn them; not to foster them but to punish them; not to endure them forever but to avenge them in judgment. Thus it is written: “The eyes of the Lord are upon those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33:17). Severe vengeance: not only to expel those who do evil from the earth, but also entirely to abolish their memory.

Let us therefore consider the evils we have committed and place them continually before the eyes of our mind, lest, when we come before the sight of that Judge, we then unwillingly see for the first time whatever we have done. For God threatens the unrepentant person terribly, saying: “You thought wickedly that I would be like you; I will accuse you and set you before your face” (Ps. 49:21). I would be like you if I left your sin unpunished. You not only refuse to punish it but also cast it behind your back so that you cannot see it. But I, who see it, what shall I do? Shall I leave it unpunished? I am Judge, and just; I am Judge, and avenger of iniquities. How, then, shall I judge unjustly? How shall I exchange truth for falsehood? “I was silent”—shall I always be silent? I was silent because I granted mercy. I overlooked your iniquity and allowed time for repentance. But shall I always be silent? No: “I will accuse you and set you before your face” (ibid., 21). I will indeed accuse you of falsehood when I reveal the counsels of hearts.

You turn your eyes away from your sins and promise yourself a certain security of vain hope. Because you do not see yourself, you suspect that I do not see you either. Do you think that I do not see you committing fornication, when I see you contemplating adultery? For this I will accuse you and set you before your face. If you do not wish to turn your face toward yourself here, I will make you recognize your misery.

“And blot out all my iniquities.” The Lord says through the Prophet: “I am the one who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them; but you remember, and let us enter into judgment” (Isa. 43:25). Hear on what condition he says that he will forget your iniquities: namely, if you remember them. Take care, therefore, never to let what you have done fall from your memory or to erase your sins through any forgetfulness, lest, if you fail to remember your iniquities because you have been captured by the enticements of carnal pleasures, it be said to you in the time of necessity: “You have cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49:17).

(Vers. 11.) Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.

501 12. It is written in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matt. 5:8). If we wish to have the one who is free from every sin as a guest in the dwelling of our heart, we must first cleanse it from every stain of vice. Let us therefore purify the interior of our mind and carefully examine the hidden recesses of our sins, lest the delight of sin spring up from our inclination; lest an ugly desire secretly tickle the heart; lest conflicts of the passions emerge from it; lest arrangements of perverse thoughts at some time break forth. For the temple of God cannot be polluted, because it is written: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17).

Yet who will boast that he has a clean heart or that he is free from sin (Prov. 20:9, according to the Septuagint)? If the Prophet asserts that he is unclean of lips, although a Seraph cleansed his mouth with the coal he had taken from the altar (Isa. 6), what shall we say of ourselves, whom lust pollutes, envy constricts, ambition overthrows, and pride exalts? It is not within human power to cleanse the mind so completely from unlawful impulses that it does not hear the uproar of clamoring thoughts. But because nothing is impossible for God, let us cry out to God with all our strength: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.”

13. Observe the order: first the Prophet asks God for a clean heart, and then for a right spirit. First, every sin must be renounced by you, and all the foulness of vices must be removed from your heart, so that everything done or said may appear pure and bright in God’s sight in proportion as it flows from the origin of a good intention, as from a kind of pure spring. For how can that which was corrupted at its very origin be clear? It is written: “The good person brings good things out of a good treasure, and the evil person brings evil things out of an evil treasure” (Matt. 12:35).

With all carnal desires therefore excluded from your heart, ask God to renew a right spirit, lest that unclean spirit, finding the house from which it departed empty, take with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself and, entering, dwell there; and the last state become worse than the first. This is the renewal of a right spirit: to despise in your mind all the glory of the world; to fix your mind to the depths in love of your Creator; to preserve patience when insults are inflicted and, with patience preserved, to drive sorrow from your heart; to consider yourself inferior to everyone through humility; never to rejoice at the death of an enemy; not to covet what belongs to others; to distribute your own possessions to the needy; to love a friend in God and an enemy for God’s sake; and, through compassion, to afflict yourself in the affliction of your neighbor.

This indeed is the renewal of the spirit that the Apostle urges, saying: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who has been created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4:23–24). And again: “Therefore, if there is any new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5:17).

It belongs to the old human being to desire the glory of this world, turn the mind away from God, fail to preserve patience, seek an opportunity for vengeance, grow proud while despising those who are better, seize what belongs to others, retain one’s own possessions, love no one for God’s sake, and rejoice at an enemy’s death. But the person who puts on God and strives to walk in newness of life rejects all these things.

(Vers. 12.) Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.

14. The person from whom the hope of pardon after sin is denied is cast away from the face of God. For whoever sins against the Holy Spirit “will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32). Who is the one who sins against the Holy Spirit if not the person who does not believe in the remission of sins? For the remission of sins is the work of the Holy Spirit. Concerning Christ’s baptism, in which the remission of sins was to be granted, John said: “He himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3:11). Hence the Holy Spirit also descended upon the baptized Lord in the form of a dove, so that he might plainly show by this that spiritual grace would cleanse the hearts of believers through the washing of baptism.

Did Cain not sin against the Holy Spirit when he said: “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon” (Gen. 4:13)? And because he despaired of pardon, he said: “Behold, you cast me away from your face.” Of him it is subsequently added that he went out from the face of the Lord. Do you see how the person who falls into the pit of despair is cast away from the face of God?

“And do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” Notice how he asks that he not lose the hope of pardon after sin. Where the presence of the Holy Spirit is, despair cannot exist. Faith is given in the Spirit, as the Apostle says: “Indeed, the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8:26). And no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Anathema to Jesus” (1 Cor. 12:3). For in him we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15), because it is written: “True worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth” (John 4:23).

(Vers. 13.) Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a principal spirit.

15. The prophet rejoiced at the coming of the Son of God before he sinned, and, confident that he was to be born from his own seed, he rejoiced before he fell. But after he was deceived by love for Uriah’s wife (II Kings 12) and observed no restraint in sinning, he became afraid that God, offended by this, might withdraw from him what He had previously promised when He was pleased with him. Therefore he said: “Restore to me the joy of your Savior.” Who is the Savior, except the mediator of God and human beings (I Tim. II)? Concerning him this same prophet, speaking in the person of God the Father, had said: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord. I will place him in salvation; I will act confidently in him” (Psalm XI, 6).

God the Father is said to arise when he sends the Son, who seemed, as it were, to lie down when he sent servants. For they could save no one; but the Son of Man came to seek and save what had been lost (Luke XIX, 10). Therefore He asserts that He will place perfect and enduring salvation in him, and says that He will act confidently in him, since he plainly had no sin at all. Whoever is conscious of serious offenses in himself cannot act confidently, because either the person whom he reproves may rebuke him, or his own conscience may sting him. Our Redeemer, however, could speak freely because from his birth, and even in his deeds, he never incurred the stain of sin. Hence, while the Jewish crowds and the envious chief priests were attacking and slandering him, he himself said: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John VIII, 46). He therefore acted confidently, since his conscience accused him of nothing. For it is also written of him that he was teaching as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees (Matthew VII, 29). David therefore asks that the joy of this Savior be restored to him, in whom every chosen person hoped before his coming.

16. “And strengthen me with a principal spirit.”

It often happens to some people that, while they consider themselves cleansed through satisfaction, they relax their mind’s inner vigilance. Indeed, weighed down by their very exaltation, they fall more disastrously insofar as, flattering themselves about pardon, they promise themselves the security of empty hope. Hence the Prophet prays, saying: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Psalm LXXXV, 11). He does not say “let it rejoice so that it may be secure,” but “let it rejoice so that it may fear.” It is as though he said openly: “Make me rejoice over pardon once I have been corrected, yet in such a way that I never cease to remain wary of guilt.”

So also here, after he had asked that the joy of God’s salvation be restored to him, lest, being released from restraint, he should rush into worse things, he immediately added: “And strengthen me with a principal spirit.” For he knew that every soul is weak unless it has been strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit. Thus it is said of the apostles: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm XXXII, 6). For whom else are the heavens designated except the holy apostles? Indeed, they water the soil of our hearts with showers of words (Psalm XVIII), thunder with threats and terrors of the coming judgment, and flash with signs of miracles and the holiness of their works.

Finally, they are the ones who proclaim the glory of God. The Spirit then granted them power when, appearing in tongues of fire (Acts II), he kindled in their hearts the flames of divine love. We can clearly recognize this if we consider what they were like before and what they were like after the coming of the Holy Spirit. They had abandoned their teacher as he went toward his passion by fleeing (Matthew XXVI); but afterward, strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they boldly and publicly proclaimed the name of Christ.

To pass over the others, the very chief of the apostles, who had denied Life itself because he feared dying (ibid.), later said, when an assembly had been convened and the priests and scribes, after having beaten the apostles, forbade them to speak in Christ’s name: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts V, 29). The power of the heavens, therefore, comes from the Holy Spirit, because through the grace poured into them by the Holy Spirit the apostles became strong in confessing Christ, though previously they had been weak through the frailty of the flesh. For unless those shepherds of the Lord’s flock had received the promised gifts of spiritual powers, their hearts would not have shone with any adornment of strength.

This power of the Spirit makes those whom it fills free from every fear of punishment and death, and likewise makes them secure against every assault of the devil’s temptation. Rightly, therefore, the person to whom the joy of God’s salvation is restored for the remission of sins asks to be strengthened in true innocence by the power of the principal spirit.

(Vers. 14.) “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will be converted to you.”

17. Divine clemency frees from sins through remission those whom it foresees will, after their conversion, be useful to the Church. Thus he said to Ananias concerning Saul: “Go, for this man is an instrument chosen for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel” (Acts IX, 15). His sins, therefore, were forgiven by God with great benefit. For the man who had previously been a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent (I Tim. I) later labored more than all the others.

The Prophet, then, who asks the Lord that his iniquities be erased and that he be strengthened by the Holy Spirit, affirms that this will not happen without fruit, saying: “I will teach the wicked your ways.” “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm XXIV, 10). Mercy is that by which He grants pardon to penitents without any preceding merits; truth is that by which, after the grace of calling and pardon, He punishes the sins of the impenitent.

The person whose sins are forgiven therefore teaches God’s ways to the wicked when, if sinners repent, he gives them hope of pardon by his own example, and when, unless the unconverted return to forgiveness, he brings upon them fear of Gehenna.

“And the ungodly will be converted to you.” O how useful is the remission of sins, which not only frees the converted from sins but also draws others back from the path of ungodliness and injustice and kindles them with the flame of charity! This is the evident proof of charity: that whoever, through God’s grace, has been rescued from the bonds of sins should himself, out of zeal for righteousness, strive to encourage those who are sinning to hope for pardon.

No sacrifice is as pleasing to God as zeal for souls. Therefore let the person to whom God has forgiven sins exercise himself in God’s way and, by his example, admonish every sinner to flee to the remedy of repentance. Let him not be a fruitless tree or an idle laborer (Matthew XX), knowing that the denarius of eternal life is promised not only to those who come to the vineyard in the morning, but is also given to those called at the eleventh hour.

[Col. 0594A] (Vers. 15.) “Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God of my salvation, and my tongue will exult in your righteousness.”

18. Unless you first free me from sins, I cannot be an example of upright conduct to others. Deliver me, therefore, from bloodguilt—that is, from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul. For “flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.”

“God, God of my salvation.” Notice in the repetition of the name the great affection of his heart, as though he said: “I rightly call upon you to save me, because you alone are the author of my salvation.” For “salvation belongs to the Lord” (Psalm III, 9). Salvation comes from you alone, because from all others there is weakness, “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes I, 2). “A king is not saved by great strength, nor will a giant be saved by the abundance of his strength” (Psalm XXXII, 16). Finally, “the horse is deceitful for salvation.” From these words it follows that salvation is acquired neither from temporal riches nor from bodily strength.

“And my tongue will exult in your righteousness.” The righteousness of God is faith, as it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis XV, 6), because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Romans I, 18). If, then, faith is the life of the righteous, it follows that this same faith is righteousness, without which no one can be righteous.

He proclaims this righteousness of God with exultation who, desiring neither the abundance of this world nor fearing its poverty, attacks every heretical perversity. Or the righteousness of God is that He does not desire the death of a sinner. To a human being it seems just to avenge a personal injury; but God’s righteousness is to release the offense of the person who confesses it.

[Col. 0594C] (Vers. 16.) “Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise.”

19. I will not otherwise be able to proclaim your righteousness unless you open my lips. For you are the one who closes the mouths of the proud and makes the tongues of infants eloquent (Wisdom X, 21). Until now I myself opened my mouth, and therefore incurred sin through empty talk. But now I desire you to open it, because I long to speak nothing except what you suggest.

God opens the lips of the person who considers not only what he says, but also when, where, and to whom he should speak. For the Wisdom of God says: “The Lord has given me a learned tongue” (Isaiah L, 4)—that is, one able to speak a word when it is appropriate. The wise person is rightly wise, then, because he has received from the Lord the proper time for speaking. Hence Scripture appropriately says: “A wise person will be silent until the proper time” (Ecclesiasticus XX, 7).

Again it is written: “Make a door and a bar for your mouth, and a yoke and a balance for your words” (Ecclesiasticus XXVIII, 28). Perhaps the Prophet was asking the Lord for this door when he said: “Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of protection around my lips” (Psalm CXL, 3).

We must close our mouth and watch more carefully, lest anyone provoke our voice to anger and we repay insult with insult. We are also commanded to have a yoke and a balance in our words, so that everything we say may be seasoned with humility and weighed with measure. Let us therefore bring forth words tested on the scales of righteousness, so that there may be seriousness in meaning, restraint in words, and weight in speech. Nor should we open our mouths to speak before it is appropriate; rather, let us examine our words: whether this should be kept silent, whether it should be said against this person, whether it is the right time for this speech, and finally whether it is consistent with the virtue of moderation. Let nothing indecent, dishonorable, or sounding envious burst forth.

But because we cannot be competent in all these matters unless we receive them from the giver of every grace, we must cry out with the Prophet: “Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise.” “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus XV, 9). Therefore the Prophet first seeks from the Lord the forgiveness of sins, and afterward promises that he will proclaim God’s praise, plainly indicating to us that only those can experience the sweetness of God’s praise who have deserved to receive remission of their sins.

Hence it is written: “Praise is fitting for the upright” (Psalm XXXII, 1). But what is more worthy of praise in God than mercy? For it is written: “Let them confess to the Lord his mercies” (Psalm CXLIV, 10). Finally, “his mercies are above all his works.” Although it is worthy of praise that He formed the human being from the clay of the earth, it is more worthy of praise that He redeemed the lost through the death of his own Son. The former belongs to power; the latter to grace.

“And my mouth will proclaim your praise.” There are many who do not praise God with their own mouth. The greedy person never praises God with his own mouth; neither does the lustful person ever praise him with his own mouth. Does he not seem to assume a mouth belonging to someone else when he tries to utter what his heart does not feel? Of such people it is written: “Their heart is far from discipline; therefore they will not exult” (Job XVII, 4). Their praise, naturally, is not raised to the ears of almighty God, because their heart has been led away from the path of righteousness by devotion to a wicked intention.

Such were those of whom the Lord said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew XV, 8).

(Vers. 17.) “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings.”

20. The Prophet knew through the Spirit that the ordinances of the legal sacrifices were to be transferred to the understanding of an invisible offering, because the true and acceptable sacrifice is that by which someone praises God with a pure heart. Hence elsewhere he says: “In me are your vows, O God, which I will repay—praises to you” (Psalm LV, 12). And again: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Psalm XLIX, 14). And once more: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me.”

Therefore, after he had said, “My mouth will proclaim your praise,” he immediately added: “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it.” It is as though he said: “I will offer you a sacrifice of praise, knowing that you do not desire the observance of carnal ceremonies.”

“For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings.” I therefore do not wish to trust in the rite of a carnal sacrifice, because I know that you are not pleased by the slaughter of goats and rams. For you are the one who said: “I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks” (ibid., XLIX, 9).

(Vers. 18.) “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.”

21. No one truly practices repentance who does not feel a certain distress of spirit when recalling his sins. This is characteristic of the reprobate: even if they sometimes confess their sins, they do not pursue them with the tears of strict correction.

The elect, however, even when they find only the smallest matters in themselves deserving punishment, kindle themselves eagerly to the lamentation of repentance, rising against themselves in zeal for uprightness. As they raise themselves on the wings of holy contemplation to gaze upon heavenly things, they discover whatever defect was hidden within them all the more subtly as they draw nearer to the brightness of divine light. And the more they delight in what they taste from the sweetness of incorruptible life, the more displeasing to them is the weakness of the flesh that they endure.

Thus they rage fiercely against themselves either for idle words or for vain thoughts, and what they had previously considered trivial they soon dread as grave and deadly. They perceive the benefits divinely bestowed upon them, yet bring their former faults back to memory. They enumerate the grievous necessities of this corruptible life and reflect upon how great is the happiness of heavenly glory. Since they feel themselves held back from it by the weakness of the flesh, they pierce themselves inwardly with the deepest wound of sorrow.

As they gather all these matters before the eyes of their mind with intense reflection, they burn inwardly with the fire of the most vehement distress. This is that spiritual distress of the saints which the bitterness of repentance and delayed desire generates in their hearts. Job certainly felt it when he said: “I will speak in the distress of my spirit” (Job VII, 11). For distress of spirit moves the tongues of the elect, so that the voice of confession may oppose the guilt of wicked conduct.

“O God, you will not despise a contrite and humbled heart.”

22. Many have a contrite heart who do not have a humbled heart. There are many who, although they punish their sins with tears, nevertheless do not cease to oppress the poor through the exercise of their power. Such people certainly do not offer God a pure sacrifice, because they corrupt it by mixing in detestable pride.

Or, as blessed Jerome explains this passage [In this Psalm], they contrite the heart but do not humble it who mourn the sins they have committed but nevertheless do not fear committing the same sins again even after their tears. Recalled from error by consideration of their faults, they return to what they had abandoned and, through wicked deeds, exalt themselves against their Creator.

It is a vice of pride to disregard the fear of God, trample upon the Creator’s commands by transgressing them through wicked action, neglect the enduring joys of heavenly life, and not fear the infinite punishments of perpetual condemnation. God therefore does not accept the sacrifice of those who wash themselves with the tears of remorse but, returning to the very sins from which they had seemed to be cleansed, soil themselves with the stains of their offenses all over again.

Of such people it is written: “Whoever is baptized by a dead person and then touches him again, what benefit is his washing?” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV, 30). The person baptized by a dead person is the one cleansed from sin through repentance. If he happens to commit again the sins he had punished, the washing of satisfaction appears to have accomplished nothing, since the shame of a repeated crime has stained him more disgracefully.

Because it is written, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (I Peter V, 5), divine justice rejects those who return to sins through pride. But God’s clemency does not despise those who, through self-restraint and humility, do not look back behind them, because it is written: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit” (Psalm XXXIII, 19).

(Vers. 19.) “Deal kindly, Lord, with Zion in your good will, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.”

23. “Zion” is interpreted as “watchtower,” and through it the holy Church is signified. For, established on the higher heights of virtue and knowledge, it looks from afar upon the heavenly homeland and detects with inward vision the advancing ranks of spiritual enemies.

God dealt kindly with it when he sent his Son into the world. When the Son of God came, he rescued the holy Church for himself from the power of the devil and united it in the unity of the Spirit. Concerning him John says: “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III, 19).

What is kinder than that the Son of God should assume the form of a servant (Philippians II), submit to the laws of death, redeem us with his own blood, open the entrance to eternal life that guilt had closed, nourish us with his body, and, having rescued us from the power of darkness, transfer us to heavenly glory and the kingdom of light? Finally, what is kinder than that God should hand over his Son in order to redeem the servant?

The Church likewise experiences God’s kindness every day, when God illumines it with the brightness of his knowledge, strengthens it by the power of his Spirit as it tosses amid the storms of the world, refreshes it with the delights of inward sweetness, and through it forgives sins to sinners.

It should also be noted that he says, “in your good will,” so that you may understand that nothing can be regarded as perfect on the basis of merits, but is bestowed only as a free gift of divine mercy.

“So that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.” By Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace,” the holy soul is understood. It sees the future peace of the saints with the mind’s inner vision, and, with all its enemies put to death within it, feels no assault from unlawful impulses. Its walls are the virtues, and the person who does not cease to construct a spiritual building from works of righteousness and piety builds them.

Every person, however, is either a citizen of Jerusalem or of Babylon. Just as each holy person becomes a citizen of Jerusalem through love of God, so every wicked person works upon the structure of Babylon through love of the world.

24. In constructing the building of this spiritual Babylon, all the wicked imitate the example of that ancient Babel (Genesis XI). According to the testimony of Holy Scripture, the founders of that city used bricks instead of stones and bitumen instead of mortar. This signifies that lovers of the world construct a civic community out of carnal life, one that can quickly be overthrown by the force of the winds and the assaults of the river.

It should be noted that those under discussion are said to have come from the East and to have dwelt in the plain of Shinar (ibid.). Since Christ is truly the East, as the Prophet testifies when he says, “Behold, the man whose name is East” (Zechariah VI, 12), those come from the East who wickedly depart from fellowship with Christ.

“Shinar,” however, is interpreted as “shaking off of teeth,” or “their stench.” They dwell in the plain of Shinar who, situated not on the heights of virtues but on the level ground of vices, lacerate their neighbors with the bites of detraction and, lying in the mire of an idle life, exhale everywhere the stench of their disgrace. The Almighty shakes out their teeth when he confounds both their deeds and their words. Hence it is written through the Prophet: “You have crushed the teeth of sinners” (Psalm III, 8). And again: “The Lord will crush their teeth in their mouth; the Lord will break the molars of lions” (Psalm VII, 57).

Concerning their stench it is written through another prophet: “The animals have rotted in their dung” (Joel I, 17). For animals to rot means for carnal people to end their lives in the stench of lust. Isaiah says: “And there will be stench instead of fragrant perfume, and a rope instead of a sash” (Isaiah III, 24). These wicked people emit the stench of evil conduct who, casting aside the belt of chastity, weave a rope of wantonness. Of them the Prophet says: “Woe to those who drag sins along like a long rope” (Isaiah V, 18).

Rightly, therefore, those who dwell in Shinar build a city out of bricks, because those devoted to earthly things serve the pleasures of the flesh and raise up the shifting structure of the mind from fragile material.

25. But those who, despising the desire for earthly wealth and renouncing the enticements of carnal life, accumulate sanctification within themselves through works of holiness and virtue, certainly transform bricks into stones. They do not raise a spiritual structure upon the sand of worldly confidence (I Corinthians X), but upon the rock of faith, which is Christ (Matthew VII), establishing courts subject to no destruction, in accordance with that Gospel parable.

Such people can rightly say with Isaiah: “The bricks have fallen, but we will build with squared stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we will replace them with cedars” (Isaiah IX, 10).

When the bricks have fallen, whoever chastises the wantonness of the flesh with the rigor of stricter discipline builds with squared stones; whoever overcomes the law of the members by the law of the mind; whoever changes bodily strength into the power of the spirit. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “Those who trust in the Lord will change their strength” (Isaiah XL, 31). By saying not “they will receive” but “they will change,” he clearly shows that one strength is laid aside and another is newly begun.

Holy men have their own strength while placed in this flesh: either when, contending for the faith, they disdain every torture through the power of perseverance, or when, protected by spiritual arms, they repel diabolical temptations. Concerning them it is written through Solomon: “Sixty strong men surround Solomon’s bed, the strongest of Israel” (Song of Songs III, 7). The strong surround Solomon’s bed because all the saints contemplate the intimate rest of our Redeemer with tireless diligence of desire.

Concerning the holy Church of the elect it is said: “Strength and beauty are her clothing” (Proverbs XXXI, 25). Whoever displays himself as beautiful in virtues but does not resist the attacks of temptations is clothed in beauty for a time, but is not clothed in strength. Since the saints of God appear both radiant from works of righteousness and clothed with the assaults of their adversaries, it is rightly said of them under the figure of the Church: “Strength and beauty are her clothing.”

Whoever, therefore, despising the weak strength of the flesh, rouses his soul to the manly vigor of the spirit, changes bricks into stones with which the walls of Jerusalem may be built.

We may also understand Jerusalem as that holy city which is constructed in heaven from living stones (Revelation XXI) and prepared by God like a bride adorned for her husband. Concerning it the Apostle says: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians IV, 26). It is rightly called free because it is found to be removed from every affliction of corruption. Nor is it inappropriate that it is called Jerusalem, since it experiences true peace within itself without defect.

For it is the city of peace, into which no enemy enters and from which no citizen departs. It is a city, I say, whose streets are paved with pure gold (Revelation XXI), and in which the song of joy is sung without ceasing. As it is written, it does not need the sun or the moon, because when God illumines it with the presence of his brightness, it is impossible for any shadow of darkness to obscure it.

For God is light, as the Apostle John says in his Epistle, “and there is no darkness in him at all” (John I, 6). If the brightness of the sun is so great that at its rising it illumines the whole earth, how great must we judge the brightness of God to be, who created the sun itself and infused into it, for our benefit, the beauty of light that we behold?

The walls of this Jerusalem are built when the faithful who have been predestined to life are led to the perfection of righteousness. The temple of Solomon represented the figure of this city (III Kings VI); in its construction, although it was built of stones, no sound of a hammer was heard. We who are to remain in the sacred building are still beaten outside by scourges, so that afterward we may be arranged in the temple of the Lord without any blow of discipline. Thus whatever is superfluous or misshapen in us may now be cut away by blows, while then only the harmony of truth will bind us in the heavenly building.

Nor is it surprising that the same city is called both a temple and a tabernacle, as it is written: “Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings” (Revelation XXI, 3).

(Vers. 20.) “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings, and burnt offerings; then they will place calves upon your altar.”

26. Once the heavenly Jerusalem has been built, only the sacrifice of righteousness will be acceptable to the Lord, because there it will not be necessary to offer a sacrifice for sin. In this life, since we offend daily in many ways, we must offer God the sacrifice of a contrite heart and troubled spirit.

But in the resurrection, when “this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality” (I Corinthians XV), no saint will afterward be able to sin, and no one will pray to God for sin. Sin will be so completely erased that even the punishment of sin will be utterly destroyed, as it is written: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? For the sting of death is sin” (ibid. XV, 55). Sin must necessarily be absent where the sting of death is not found.

It is therefore not appropriate for a sacrifice for sin to be offered there, where transgression is not admitted even in thought. The saints will offer God the sacrifice of righteousness in eternal life, because, intent solely upon love of their Creator, they will utter unceasing praises to their Rewarder in the joy of their hearts. Hence it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm LXXXIII, 5). And again: “The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous” (Psalm CXVII, 15).

God will accept the offerings of his elect, because no mixture of wickedness will stain their holy meditations. He will likewise accept their burnt offerings, because everything within them will be kindled by the flame of divine charity.

“And then they will place calves upon your altar.” The altar is the Son of God, concerning whom the Lord himself says: “You will make an altar of earth for me” (Exodus XXIV, 20). For what else is it to make an altar of earth except not to doubt the incarnation of the Son of God?

He is the one upon whom in this life we place the sacrifices of our hearts, and in whom we slaughter unlawful thoughts lest they grow strong. Hence it is written: “Blessed is the one who will seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Psalm CXXXVI, 9). We dash our little ones against the rock when, with the intention of imitating Christ, we put to death unlawful impulses as they arise. For it is written: “The rock was Christ” (I Corinthians X, 1).

He, therefore, is the rock against which we hold our thoughts; he is the altar upon whose mercy we presume to place the victims of our sins. Finally, he himself bore our sins (I Peter II, 24).

The saints, therefore, will place calves upon him in eternal life, because, freed by God’s grace from the law of sin and death, they will no longer be subject to any yoke of the law and will attribute everything to the grace of the Son of God. For no human being would ascend into heaven unless the Son of God had assumed flesh for our salvation.

Or certainly they will place calves upon the altar when, having laid aside the oldness of the first human being and having stripped off mortal garments, they become calves—that is, renewed and pure—and live forever.

27. If, as stated above, we wish to understand the building of Jerusalem according to the moral interpretation, we may also suitably adapt this verse to the same meaning.

The Lord said to King David: “You will not build a house for me, because you are a man of blood” (I Chronicles XVII, 1). But afterward his son, peaceful in reality and in name, obtained from the Lord a gift of wisdom surpassing mortals and, as the book of histories testifies, built for the God of Israel a temple of wondrous workmanship (III Kings VI).

This signifies that while we struggle against the hostile ranks of vices by opposing virtues, we are in no way able to build the house of wisdom. But when we have overcome the armies of our adversaries, driven away the barbarism of the passions, and perceived that peace has been established within us, with the flesh already obeying all the commands of the mind, then we construct our body as an inviolable temple for the Lord.

In it God accepts both the sacrifice that we offer by proclaiming the truth out of zeal for righteousness, and the offerings of holy meditations and the burnt offerings of prayers burning with the fire of fervent desire.

Upon the altar of our hearts we also place calves (Psalm LXVIII), producing horns and hooves if we know how to shatter the opinions of heretics by the authority of both Testaments and to separate virtues from vices through disciplined discernment. By the split hooves of calves we understand discernment; by the horns we designate the precepts of both Testaments.

Or certainly we produce horns if we strive to please God even in matters pertaining to the flesh. For although a horn comes from flesh, it hardens by surpassing the flesh. Whoever, therefore, having laid aside the weakness of the flesh, performs works of virtue even through the service of the flesh, produces, as it were, horns from flesh.

## PROEMIUM TO THE FIFTH PENITENTIAL PSALM

“The prayer of the poor person when he is troubled and pours out his prayer before the Lord.”

Who is this poor person whose prayer is indicated in this psalm, except the one concerning whom the Apostle says: “Although he was rich, he became poor for us” (I Corinthians VIII, 9)? In order to make us participants in his riches, he assumed the necessities of our poverty. For “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians II, 7).

Just as he became poor for us, so also he was troubled for us. Finally, he was handed over to death for us and suspended upon the wood for us. He died, as the Apostle says, “for our sins” (I Corinthians XV, 3), and rose again “for our justification” (Romans IV, 25). He had from human nature the capacity to be troubled, just as from it he also had the capacity to die.

Our head therefore prays in this psalm that we may be brought back by grace to the place from which we fell through the guilt of our first parent. This prayer may also apply to anyone who understands himself to be poor and recognizes the misery of his needs; who considers the riches of this age deceptive and weighs how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God; who, looking back, reflects on where he fell, and, surveying everything that threatens him, considers what calamities he has encountered.

Let every poor person therefore gather all these matters before the eyes of his mind. Considering Christ, who was troubled for us in his poverty, let him attend to the multitude of his own miseries; let him recall how great was the glory in which Adam was created; and, troubled by all these things, let him pour out his prayer not before human eyes but before the Lord, saying:

## EXPLANATION OF THE FIFTH PENITENTIAL PSALM

(Psalm 101.—Vers. 1.) “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.”

In this prayer, which we are about to expound, some things are attributed to the Head himself, while others apply to our weakness. Nor is it surprising if Christ declares as his own those things that pertain solely to us. For the entire holy universal Church is one body, constituted under Christ Jesus, its Head. Hence the Apostle says: “He is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead” (Col. 1:18). For it is she who rejoices through the Prophet and says: “Now he has exalted my head above my enemies” (Ps. 26:6). For the Father exalted the Son, who is the Head of the Church, above his enemies when, having destroyed the dominion of death, he established him in equality with the Father’s majesty; and to him he also said: “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 108:1).

Thus Christ together with his entire Church—both that which still lives on earth and that which already reigns with him in heaven—is one person. And just as there is one soul that gives life to the various members of the body, so the one Holy Spirit simultaneously gives strength and illumination to the whole Church. For just as Christ, who is the Head of the Church, was conceived by the Holy Spirit, so the holy Church, which is his body, is filled with that same Holy Spirit in order to live; by his power it is strengthened, so that it may endure within the bond of one faith and charity. Hence the Apostle says: “From him the whole body, supplied and joined together through its connections and bonds, grows for the increase of God” (Col. 2:2).

This is the body outside of which the Spirit does not give life. Hence blessed Augustine says: “If you wish to live by the Spirit of Christ, be in the body of Christ” [*Tractate 26 on John*]. The heretic does not live by this Spirit, nor does the schismatic, nor the excommunicated person; for they are not of the body. The Church, however, possesses the life-giving Spirit because it clings inseparably to its Head, Christ. For it is written: “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6:17).

Therefore, in this psalm the Head prays for his members, that God the Father may hear the prayer of his body and that its cry may ascend to the ears of the divine majesty. For Christ prays daily for the Church, as the apostle Paul testifies: “He sits at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34). Indeed, “he himself is the expiation for our sins” (1 John 2).

This prayer can also apply to each individual believer who asks God for perseverance in goodness and sends forth a cry both of holy desire and of unremitting action. A “cry,” however, is sometimes understood in a good sense and sometimes in a bad one. The righteous cries out when he performs righteousness out of desire; the wicked also cries out when he adds sin to sin. Moses cried out when he led the people, liberated from Egyptian slavery, through the wilderness toward the promised land. The people of Gomorrah also cried out when, through the most frequent perpetration of sin, they provoked God to anger.

Finally, even to Moses, though he was silent, the Lord said: “Why are you crying out to me?” (Exod. 14:15). And concerning those people the Lord says: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has risen to me” (Gen. 18:20). Hence someone admonishes us, saying: “Let the cry be removed from your midst” [Note: [Col. 0603] Perhaps Eph. 4:31, where we read: “Let all bitterness and crying . . . be removed from you.”].

Here, however, “cry” is understood as unremitting action, when it says: “Let my cry come to you.” It should be noted that after first saying, “Hear my prayer,” he immediately added, “And let my cry come to you.” Those deserve to be heard by the Lord who, inflamed by the zeal of divine love, do all the good that they can. For one who is accustomed to wicked actions and diligently practices works of iniquity is in no way worthy of being heard when he prays. Hence Truth himself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21).

If, therefore, we want our prayer to reach the ears of God, we must take care that our action be cleansed of every admixture of wickedness, so that we may say to God with the Prophet: “Let my cry come to you.”

[Col. 0603B] **(Verse 2.) Do not turn your face from me; on whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me.**

**2.** This is said by comparison with earthly lords, who, when they are seriously offended by the fault of one of their people, customarily drive him from their sight, separate him from the company of their attendants, turn their face away from the one who begs, and deny pardon to the one who asks. Although God, when we turn away from him in pride, justly turns away from us, nevertheless, when in humility we turn back to him, he does not disdain to turn toward us in mercy. For he is the one who says: “Turn back to me, and I will turn back to you” (Zech. 1:3). And again: “If the wicked person repents of all his sins that he has committed and practices judgment and righteousness, he will surely live and will not die. I will not remember any of his iniquities that he has committed; in the righteousness that he has practiced, he will live” (Ezek. 18:21).

Behold, the bosom of God’s mercy is open to us. Why do we shut God’s mercy out from ourselves? Why do we pretend not to hear his call? For he not only does not turn away from those who have turned back, but he also urges those who have turned away to return. Hence through the Prophet he says: “If a man divorces his wife, and she, departing from him, marries another man, will she return to him again? Will not that woman be polluted and defiled? But you have fornicated with your many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (Jer. 3:1).

He introduces the likeness of a forsaken and adulterous woman so that we may recognize his mercy and understand that we offend him more gravely because he does not cease calling us even after our sin. This clemency of God’s call is expressed in part when, through another prophet, he says to a person who has turned away: “Your eyes will see your teacher, and your ears will hear the voice of one admonishing you from behind” (Isa. 30:20). The person who stands before him receives God’s words: he recognizes the commands of his will before he completes his sin. For it is as though one still stands before his face when one has not yet despised him by sinning. But if, having cast aside the fear of God, he begins to practice iniquity, he is as though he turns his back toward God’s face. Yet God, following behind the one who departs, admonishes him, because even after wickedness has been committed he persuades him to return to himself.

Let us therefore hear the voice of the one who admonishes us from behind, and let us return to the God who invites us, at least after our sins—so that if we neglect to fear the justice of the one who punishes, we may at least feel shame before the mercy of the one who calls and shows mercy.

**3. “On whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me.”** Behold, our Head now sits at the right hand of God, and yet he says that he is troubled. Where, then, is he troubled, unless in the body? That he is troubled in the body he clearly shows when he said to his persecutor Saul: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). And he said to Peter: “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again” [Hegesippus, book 3, chapter 2]. He who had long ago been crucified in himself said that he was to be crucified again in Peter.

There is also another kind of trouble in the hearts of the elect, which the continual bitterness of repentance produces in them. For when someone gathers before the eyes of his mind the evils he has committed and is pierced by compunction for each one, he is troubled in the secret recess of his heart by great and bitter anxiety of grief and fear. Elect men customarily turn the gaze of their minds back toward the sins of which they are conscious, and, carefully examining each of their features, mourn each one individually. In this way they prepare the dwelling of their heart, as they lament each excess of their error.

Hence Jeremiah says: “My eye has poured forth divisions of waters” (Lam. 3:48). To pour divided waters from one’s eyes is to allot distinct tears to each sin and to compensate the joys of iniquity with the pains of satisfaction, so that, while the mind is now more sharply touched by the memory of this offense and now of that one, it may be cleansed as it is moved concerning all of them individually.

When he says, “Incline your ear to me,” it is as though he were saying: “I am sick; I cannot raise myself up to you, because it is not within human power to direct one’s own way. But you, like a faithful physician, incline your ear to me. Incline your ear, because I do not raise my neck. I know that if I raise myself up, you withdraw farther away; if I humble myself, you draw nearer. For just as you approach the humble, so you distance yourself from the proud.” Therefore I am troubled, so that you may incline your ear to me.

**(Verse 3.) On whatever day I call upon you, hear me quickly.**

**4.** I no longer desire earthly things as an earthly person; liberated from my first captivity, I long for heavenly things. Hear me, then, as I pray—not for the riches of this world, not for temporal glory, not for the fruitfulness of children, not for the death of enemies. Hear me quickly, so that you may fulfill in me what you said: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Behold, here I am’” (Isa. 58:9).

Many call upon God but do not invoke him, because they take care to pray only with their lips and not with the affection of the heart. But whoever desires God with his whole heart cries out confidently: “On whatever day I call upon you, hear me quickly.” He invokes God “in the day” who entreats him in purity of mind. When such a person has revealed his ways to the Lord, his righteousness is brought forth like light, and his judgment, as the Prophet says, is illuminated like midday (Ps. 36:6).

Hence it is also written: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1:1). Simplicity of heart is a day that deceit does not cloud, falsehood does not darken, envy does not obscure, and trickery does not dim; the light of truth illuminates it, and the brightness of the divine presence enlightens it. For it is written: “His conversation is with the simple” (Prov. 3:32). God’s conversation consists in revealing the secrets of his will to human minds through the illumination of his presence.

Thus God is said to converse with the simple because he illuminates their minds concerning heavenly mysteries by the brightness of his inspiration—those minds that no darkness of duplicity overshadows. By contrast, concerning the non-simple it is said: “The Lord will abominate the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. 5:8). And Solomon says: “The holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful, and will withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding” (Wis. 1:5). It is therefore clear that God enlightens some by dwelling in them, while he blinds others by withdrawing from them.

**(Verse 4.) For my days have passed away like smoke, and my bones have dried up like kindling.**

**5.** This pertains to what he said: “Hear me quickly.” It is as though he were saying: “You must hear me quickly, because my days have passed away; that is, they have reached decay like smoke.” By “his days” he wishes to be understood as referring to the entire time in which he set aside God’s commands and, inflamed by the destructive desires of perishable things, lived carnally, serving himself rather than God.

For the perverse soul has its own day in this life: it rejoices in transitory time and luxuriates in the pleasure of deadly carnal delight. Hence our Savior, threatening faithless Jerusalem with the just destruction of its ruin, says: “If only you had known, even on this your day, the things that are for your peace” (Luke 19:42). That people then had its own day because, trusting in the abundance of passing things, it rejoiced in tranquility and success. Prosperity had closed their eyes, so that they neither recognized the time of their visitation nor saw the crushing evils that threatened them.

For just as punishments open the eyes of the heart, so prosperous successes sometimes blunt the sharpness of the mind, to such an extent that the mind cannot know itself—the mind that worldly prosperity’s delight holds captive. Hence Solomon says: “The turning away of the simple will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Prov. 1:32). Prosperity therefore destroyed the Israelite people, whose eyes on their day it closed, lest they recognize the devastation of the future destruction.

This is the day of which Jeremiah says: “I did not desire the day of man” (Jer. 17:16). Let the faithful soul also say: “My days have passed away like smoke.” As everyone knows, smoke initially rises upward, but soon fades away and vanishes as though it had never existed. So too, when human pride swells with worldly abundance and lifts itself up on high, it falls from the position of its loftiness and rushes down to the depths.

Hence Truth himself says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). Through the Prophet it is written: “I saw the wicked person exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was not there; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 36:35). In this we must consider how the power of the wicked is destroyed, since shortly afterward not even their place is found.

It follows: “And my bones have dried up like kindling.”

**6.** By “bones” we may understand reason and understanding, which remain as though dry when they do not possess the richness of deeds and virtues. Concerning this richness the Prophet says: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62:6). Alternatively, by “bones” we understand those who are stronger in the Church, because just as our body is given strength through its bones, so the body of Christ, which is the Church, is governed and supported through them.

For the body of Christ also has its flesh—namely, the weak, who lack strength in virtue and need the support of the perfect. Concerning this flesh, in the person of Christ Job rightly says: “My bone has clung to my skin and flesh” (Job 19:20). This was fulfilled in Christ’s Passion, when, while the disciples were fleeing, the women stood and followed him as far as the cross (Luke 23). For we know that in the human body the skin projects outward, while the flesh adheres inwardly to the bones.

Thus Christ’s bone clings to his skin, his flesh having been consumed, because, while the apostles who had stood closest to him were fleeing and wavering, the women, who seemed to be more distant, did not depart either from the one hanging on the cross or from the tomb of the buried one.

Since holy men feel compassion for imperfect sinners who fall and sympathize with their weakness, it is rightly said here: “My bones have dried up like kindling.” We shall demonstrate this clearly if we bring forward one example. Let us see how one of Christ’s bones becomes weak with the weak, suffers with those who suffer, and dries up with those who dry up. For he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (2 Cor. 11:19). You see how he transferred all their weaknesses to himself and mourned all their falls as though they were his own. Hence he says: “That I may mourn for all those who have sinned and have not repented” (1 Cor. 12:21). Finally, he became all things to all people, so that he might gain all (1 Cor. 9).

Therefore the bones dry up like kindling when their fat has been consumed, whenever the perfect feel compassion for the weaknesses of carnal people and consider themselves deprived, as it were, of spiritual richness while they see those people lacking the assistance of virtue. He plainly reveals the cause of this misery when he adds:

**(Verse 5.) I have been struck like grass, and my heart has dried up, because I have forgotten to eat my bread.**

**7.** It is written in Isaiah: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field” (Isa. 40:6). And again: “Truly, the people are grass” (ibid., 7). For a human being is comparable to grass: through birth he grows green in the flesh, through youth he whitens in blossom, and through death he dries up into dust. He is the one who, as Job testifies, “comes forth like a flower and is crushed” (Job 14:2).

This death and crushing, which by the sentence of just condemnation has come upon all human beings, descended from the sin of the first man. Hence the Apostle says: “Through the first man sin entered, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings” (Rom. 5:12). Thus the human being who, had he persevered in obedience to the Creator, could have lived forever, was struck with mortality because of the guilt of disobedience.

Concerning this striking the psalm says here: “I have been struck like grass, and my heart has dried up.” Since the first man fell into death by sinning, the succession of the human race, propagated from him, consequently dried up from the innermost greenness of reason. Why the human heart dried up from the greenness in which it was created, he makes clear by adding: “Because I have forgotten to eat my bread.”

The first man, created in paradise, possessed his bread as long as he preserved the commands of his Creator with an undisturbed disposition of mind [Note: [Col. 0607] Remb., “with the trace of an unshaken mind.”]. His bread was the delight of the divine vision, the satiety of God’s word, the joy of inner peace, the splendor of inaccessible light, the nourishment of wisdom, the fellowship of angels, the love of God, the rejoicing of the spirit, the sweetness of contemplation, the desire for conversation, security of mind, and the presence of the Creator.

He plainly lost this bread when he consented to the serpent’s suggestion (Gen. 3). For when he touched what was forbidden, he forgot the command. Thus it came about that the one who possessed the citadel of blessedness fell into the pit of misery; and the one who had been nourished by the innermost sweetness afterward ate the bread of sorrow.

Whoever, therefore, bears the image of that man—having been made earthly from earth—forgets to eat his bread, because, captivated by the allurements of earthly pleasure, he does not delight in the word of God [Note: [Col. 0608] Remb., “does not take delight.”]. For our bread is the word of God. Hence Truth himself says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4).

Let remembrance therefore follow forgetfulness, and let nourishment accompany hunger, so that, eating that bread which came down from heaven (John 6), we may both escape the punishment of everlasting death and share in eternal life, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone eats from this bread, he will live forever” (ibid., 52).

**(Verse 6.) Because of the voice of my groaning, my bone has clung to my flesh.**

**8.** When the heart dries up because of the lack and forgetfulness of bread and wine, the voice of groaning is emitted. For when the mind’s attention has failed in its desire for eternal life, an outcry of evil thoughts consequently proceeds from the heart. In this situation the bone clings to the flesh if reason is subjected to pleasure. This voice is called a voice of groaning because through it one reaches sorrow. It either produces the pain of repentance in this life or gives rise to the torment of punishment in the future.

We may also understand by “the voice of groaning” the voice of the serpent, because it persuaded the first human beings to taste what had been forbidden and, through the deceitfulness of its fraud, promised them that they would become gods (Gen. 3). This is the voice of groaning through which we all sinned, through which we became mortal and subject to suffering; the voice through which we fell from heavenly joys and live in exile amid the gall of tears.

Through this voice the bone clung to the flesh, because Adam consented to Eve. Each one of us contains an Adam and an Eve. For just as in that first transgression of the human race the serpent suggested, Eve took pleasure, and Adam consented, so we see it happening daily: the devil suggests, the flesh takes pleasure, and the spirit consents.

When we are tempted, we often slide into pleasure or even into consent. But just as death followed that sin, so the soul that consents to sin dies, because it is separated from its life, which is God. We are dead when we are filled with the bones of the dead. The evil word that proceeds from our mouth is dead. For it is written: “Their throat is an open tomb” (Ps. 5:11).

We have gates through which we, as dead persons, are carried out—namely, the senses of the body—concerning which the Prophet says: “You lift me up from the gates of death” (Ps. 9:15). These are the gates through which death enters and through which the dead person is carried out. That death enters through them is testified by another prophet, who says: “Death entered through our windows” (Jer. 9:21). Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her admits death through the windows of his eyes (Matt. 5). Whoever sows discord among brothers and speaks iniquity on high is carried out dead through the gate of the mouth.

It seems to me that this is also signified by the young man who was carried outside the gate of the city and whom Jesus raised up (Luke 7). He signifies the person who has died through pleasure and has already been carried outside the gates by the judgments of wicked action.

I beg you, Lord Jesus, make all the gates of my city gates of righteousness, so that when I enter them I may confess your name and your majesty with the righteous who enter through them; so that death may have no access or entry there, suffering may not rule, but salvation may occupy its walls and praise its gates.

**(Verse 7.) I have become like a pelican of the wilderness, and I have become like a night-owl in a dwelling.**

**9.** The pelican (*pelicanus*) is a bird that loves solitude and feeds there on poisonous creatures; therefore it signifies the sinner who, dwelling in the wilderness of this world in his heart, captivated by the troubled allurements of this life, delights in the poison of the devil’s persuasion.

The night-owl (*nycticorax*), which is also called the owl (*bubo*), lives in the rooms of ruined houses. It customarily sings at night, and by this are signified those who dance in a work of darkness and exult in the destruction of their minds.

But because the net of the Church, cast into the sea of the present age, gathers not only bad fish but also draws in good ones, it is rightly said here:

[Col. 0608D] **(Verse 8.) I kept watch, and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof.**

**10.** The person who keeps watch holds the eyes of his mind open for the sight of the true light. The person who keeps watch preserves by his actions what he believes, as it is written: “Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments” (Rev. 16:15). Your garment is your faith; your garment is your action. Guard it, therefore, lest strangers tear away your labor; lest you be stripped and your shame appear.

Be like a solitary sparrow on the roof. Through the sparrow, which is a cautious and plaintive bird that builds its nest in houses, the human being is rightly understood—one who lives in high places, inhabits solitude, and does not cease crying out over his sins. For it belongs to a prudent and watchful man to build his nest on high, to weep over his sins, and to inhabit solitude, so that in his action he may not desire earthly things, in his lamentation may obtain pardon, and in his dwelling may escape the empty clamor of thoughts, so that he may say with the Prophet: “I fled far away, and I remained in solitude” (Ps. 54:8).

Alternatively, our Head was a pelican of the wilderness when he was born in Judea, which was a solitary city filled with people—deprived, that is, of prophets and righteous persons (Lam. 1) and lacking the power of the Holy Spirit. He became a night-owl when he proclaimed the kingdom of God to those who were in darkness. For it is written concerning him: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5). “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

By “dwelling” we understand the Jews, who were partly ruined and partly seemed to stand, because, while retaining circumcision, they possessed the Law and the Prophets, but in no way believed in the one whom the prophets had foretold would come in the flesh. The walls of carnal observance still stood among them, but the roof of faith and discipline had collapsed. Thus the dead killed life, and darkness extinguished the light.

But let us hear what he did next: “I kept watch, and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof.” He kept watch because he rose from the dead. For the one who slept in death kept watch in the resurrection. Hence he says: “I slept and took sleep, and I rose again” (Ps. 3:6).

Hence Jacob says in his blessing: “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son. Reclining, you lay down like a lion and like a lioness; who will raise him up?” (Gen. 49:9). Who is this lion’s cub except the one of whom it is said in the Apocalypse to John: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. 5:5)?

He went up to the prey because, coming upon the strong man armed, the stronger one conquered him (Luke 11). He took away his weapons because he deprived him of the right that he seemed to possess over human beings. For while he pursued what was illicit, he lost what he had acquired. He also distributed his spoils because he made vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy.

Therefore the lion lay down in repose because he willingly underwent death. No one raised him up, because by the power of his divinity he himself rose from the dead. And because after his resurrection he ascended into heaven, after saying, “I kept watch,” he rightly added: “And I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof.” For, alone among the dead and free, he reigns with the Father in heaven. Hence he also says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.”

**11.** Philosophers report that the pelican kills its young as soon as they are born; afterward it afflicts itself with great grief for three days and in some manner displays its natural affection toward them. Then the mother wounds herself and revives them with her own blood.

But who is our father and mother except the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2)? He killed all iniquity in us so that we might find a better resurrection, as he himself says: “I kill, and I make alive” (Deut. 32:39). And concerning him it is written through the Prophet: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. 6:3).

Our Head, or his member, still cries out in the wilderness when he calls those who have not yet recognized the truth. He cries out in the dwelling when he invites those who have fallen to repentance. He cries out on the roof when he admonishes us to cast fear outside. Hence in the Gospel he says to his disciples: “What you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the roofs” (Mark 10:27).

**(Verse 9.) All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me.**

**12.** What could be more unjust? The Son of Man had come to seek and save what was lost. He had come, I say, to take away the groaning of those who suffer and to reconcile us to God (Luke 19). But the Jews, whom the darkness of their iniquity had blinded, repaid good with evil: they hated him as an enemy and attacked him with reproaches and curses, saying, “You have a demon” (John 8:48), along with the other ravings of madness contained in the book of the Gospels.

Even when they sometimes flattered him outwardly, they raged inwardly, like those who, wishing to seize him through his words, said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and you do not care about anyone” (Matt. 22:16). They called him “Teacher,” though they had come not with the intention of learning but with the desire to harm. That this was indeed the case Truth makes clear when he calls them tempters and hypocrites.

Thus they had sworn against him because, following a plan, they fabricated lies against him. Throughout the entire time of this life, the enemies of truth reproach the Church of God when they attack it either with heretical depravity or with dissimilarity of conduct.

**13.** Many who slyly and deceitfully devote themselves to God’s cause both pretend to be in the body of Christ and disturb the peace of the Church of God by secret plotting. Concerning them it is certainly said here: “Those who praised me swore against me.” They are the ones who “come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7:15). In their words they seem to possess the gentleness of fellowship, but in their hearts they carry hostile fury.

Such was Simon Magus, baptized by the Apostles but later rejected by the chief of the Apostles because of his ambition for wicked profit. Hence it was said to him: “You have no share in this matter” (Acts 8:21). For when he wished to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit for money, the wretched man alienated himself from the teaching of Christ. Christ himself had commanded: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matt. 10:8).

This, I say, is the heresy that assailed the very beginnings of the nascent Church and appeared first, before the other heresies. Although the madness of its error was condemned from that time onward, it nevertheless later sprouted within the Church as a poisonous growth. In our own times especially it has exercised the venom of its malice and disturbed the peace of the entire Church through schismatic hostility.

For it stirred up against the Church of God not only an innumerable multitude of the people but also, if it is permissible to say so, royal power. No reason permits one to be counted among kings who destroys an empire rather than governs it; and however many associates in his perversity he can obtain, he makes them alien to fellowship with Christ.

Enticed by the desire for the vilest profit, he wishes to lead away the bride of Christ as a captive and rashly strives to empty the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion of its force. Our Savior wished the Church, redeemed at the price of his blood, to be free; but this man, transgressing the rights of royal power, attempts to make her a slave. How much better it would be for him to acknowledge her as his mistress and, following the example of religious rulers, offer her the service of devotion, rather than direct the arrogance of his rule against God, from whom he received dominion over his power.

For he is the one who says: “Through me kings reign” (Prov. 8:15). But blinded by the darkness of boundless greed, plainly ungrateful for the divine benefaction, and arrogant against God, he transgresses, in contempt of divine fear, the boundaries established by our fathers and, in the fury of his tyranny, rages against catholic truth.

He has extended the rashness of his madness so far that he claims the Roman Church, the head of all the Churches, for himself and usurps earthly authority over the mistress of the nations. The one who specially entrusted this Church to the blessed Apostle Peter wholly prohibited such a thing, saying: “I will give you my Church” (Matt. 16:18).

Therefore let the mouth of those who speak wickedness be closed, and let every force of heretics fall silent, because falsehood has no strength when it is found destroyed by the very voice of truth. It follows:

[Col. 0611C] **(Verse 10.) For I ate ashes like bread, and I mixed my drink with weeping.**

**14.** The scribes and Pharisees especially accused our Redeemer on this account: he not only did not reject tax collectors and sinners, but also shared food and drink with them. Hence some of them, indignantly objecting, said: “Why does your teacher eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” (Matt. 9:11). But what did the one who had come to call not the righteous but sinners say? “Those who are healthy do not need a physician, but those who are ill” (ibid., 12).

O immense clemency of God! O immeasurable love of grace! He wished to heal those who did not want to have salvation—those who, armed against their own salvation and, like madmen, accusing the physician, preferred to meet death through sickness rather than find life through healing.

Our Redeemer ate ashes when he transferred them into his own body. They were ashes because, while they followed the prince of darkness rather than the author of light, the divine fire of love had been entirely extinguished in their hearts, as it were. They were ashes, I say: fit for no use and utterly dissolved because they lacked the bond of charity.

Who would not marvel at these riches of God’s mercy? Who would now despair of the forgiveness of sins? Who would not believe that, if he turns back, he can obtain pardon, when he hears that even unbelievers are admitted with such kindness? Hence the Apostle says: “If, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved from wrath through him” (Rom. 5:10).

Since, therefore, our Redeemer came into the world, made vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy, and opened the bosom of his compassion to all who come to him, he rightly says here: “For I ate ashes like bread, and I mixed my drink with weeping.”

**15.** What his hunger or thirst was, he himself clearly shows when he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father who sent me” (John 4:34). And again: “I must do the works of my Father who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9:4).

What are these works of the Father, which he says are to be done in the day and not at night, except the fruitful cultivation of the intellectual field? For he is the man who sowed good seed in his field (Matt. 13), and afterward sent workers to cultivate it (Matt. 9), when he said: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the workers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest” (Luke 8:2).

He himself shows what this field is when he says that the field is the world and the seed is the word of God. He sowed in order to reap; he harvested in order to eat. Every day he gathers the fruit of this field and is nourished by it, as it were, when he delights in the progress of the elect. Hence the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “I have eaten the honeycomb with my honey” (Song 5:15).

16. This man also has a vineyard, namely the holy Church, to cultivate which he sent laborers early in the morning (Matt. XX), and afterward he did not cease sending them at each successive time. It is therefore clear that, just as he cultivated the field in order to eat, so he planted the vineyard in order to drink.
