A good vineyard, adorned with the colors of grapes and propagated through the branches of love and perseverance, offers the King of all a sweet draught from its fruits. A good vineyard, I say, which can say: “I was a vineyard belonging to the peaceful one, in that which has peoples” (Cant. VIII, 11). What is that which has peoples, except the holy Church spread throughout the whole world? For it has peoples because it contains true believers from every part of the earth. In this vineyard alone, therefore, each of the elect becomes a vine, because no one who departs from the unity of the Church will ever be able to bear fruit. For he withholds a drink from God to the extent that he consents to the senseless chatter of heretics.

What does God thirst for, except our faith (John IV)? Hence he also asked the Samaritan woman for a drink; we do not read that he drank from her water, but the woman offered him a spiritual drink when she acknowledged him as the Savior of the world (John XIX). Even while hanging on the cross he thirsted, desiring both the repentance of sinners and the faith of the unbelieving. But the Lord’s vineyard of hosts, planted by God in the patriarchs and cultivated by the plow of teaching and the hoes of the word through the hands of the prophets, finally turned to bitterness: although it ought to have brought him wine of joy, it offered him the vinegar of deadly envy. For good wine is often spoiled and changed into vinegar. Because that people was holy in its fathers but wicked in its sons, it was like wine at first and afterward vinegar.

Yet there were some among them who believed in this Savior of all, and there were also those who raised themselves from the depths of sins to the Father of mercies. For who was ever bound by more numerous or greater crimes than that sinful woman from whom, as the Evangelist says, he cast out seven demons (Mark XVI)? Zacchaeus too, himself a tax collector and a robber, presided over tax collectors and robbers, and yet the Son of God turned aside to his house (Luke XIX, 6). Simon, moreover, took offense at the woman’s admission, and the crowd murmured at the lodging of the sinner (Luke XIX). For she had mixed her drink with tears, and therefore the insolence of her enemies reproached her for it.

We see this happening daily in the Church, when we see sinners mourning over their sins, putting on Christ, and entering into his unity. Or certainly, to mix a drink for God with tears means to draw some from outside inward, and to cast others from within outward. For we know that drink is drawn from outside to the interior, while tears flow outward from within. Since our Creator examines what is hidden in us and weighs at the root not only our deeds but also our intentions, by his hidden judgment it comes about that he rejects some who seem righteous in the eyes of men, while he saves others who are guilty of crimes but corrected through repentance. And since, according to the Apostle’s statement, it depends “not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16), he mercifully raises some who had fallen, while he justly permits others who seemed to stand to fall. For from the sin of our first parent we received this condition: we cannot remain stable even in righteousness, but either we rise up against God by attributing to ourselves the good we do, or we are lifted up in pride against our neighbors. Hence it is added:

**(Verse 11.)** “From the face of your anger and indignation, because, having lifted me up, you dashed me to pieces.”

17. Because the first man, by sinning, suffered the sentence of just condemnation, which the succession of his descendants subsequently incurred in turn, therefore Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners and to free them from the condemnation in which they were held. The Church, which is his body, to which he granted the keys of the kingdom of heaven and gave the power of binding and loosing, receives sinners daily for this reason: it recognizes that sentence of God’s anger. Since by the face we recognize a person, we rightly understand by “the face of anger” the recognition of condemnation.

That the anger is one of indignation he plainly shows when he adds: “Because, lifting me up, you have dashed me to pieces.” When the other animals had been created, man was raised above all the rest, because he was endowed with freedom of choice and illumined by the light of reason. He was also given this distinction: unlike the other living creatures, he was not always to look upon the earth, but, upright in the posture of his body, was to look toward the heavens; so that from this too he might clearly understand that he ought both to direct his intention toward higher things and to lift his mind to God.

Indeed, terror and trembling fell upon all the animals because he had been set over them by the divine voice. Nor would he ever have incurred death if he had never sinned while obeying the divine commands. But by transgressing the orders of his Creator, he fell all the more grievously because, before he fell, he had stood at a greater height. Falling, therefore, he was dashed to pieces, because, not fearing to sin, he endured weakness for the sake of salvation and accepted death for the sake of life.

**(Verse 12.)** “My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass.”

18. It was a grievous shattering by which light was turned into darkness and greenness was changed into dryness. The first man had his day become like a shadow when he hid himself from the face of his Creator (Gen. III). For he wished to conceal himself among the shadowy trees, thereby also plainly showing what shadows of blindness he suffered inwardly. If he had not been in shadow, he would not have believed that God was confined to a place, nor would he have thought that he could hide from his eyes, since he would have known that even the secrets of the heart are seen by him. He therefore sought the shadow of the body who had first incurred the shadow of the mind.

His day had indeed declined, and therefore the light of wisdom did not shine within him. For when the sun declines, it produces greater shadows and gradually withdraws the strength of its heat. Hence Adam is described as being called by God after midday (ibid.), so that from outward things we might recognize what was taking place within. At midday the light is purer, the air clearer, and the heat more intense. Thus midday, as it were, was present in Adam’s breast while, illumined by the light of divine contemplation, he burned with the flames of supreme love. But wretchedly he lost this midday when he sinned. There the fire of love grew cold, brightness became dark, and vision failed.

When the true light, the Son of God, came into the world, he restored this brightness to us by driving away the darkness of our hearts through the illumination of his presence. Hence it is written: “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isa. IX, 2). The great light is the remission of sins, the gift of grace, the brightness of understanding, the joy of contemplation, and the bestowal of virtues. For, as the Apostle says, he gave us “the pledge of the Spirit” (II Cor. V, 5); “we have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come” (Heb. VI). These are the days of grace that the excellence of God’s goodness has bestowed upon us. If in them we despise the night of wickedness, we walk along an unobstructed path toward the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom.

For this reason the Savior says: “If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world” (John XI, 9). But these days decline in us like a shadow when, placing the clouds of our sins before divine reconciliation, we suffer the darkness of the mind and extinguish the ardor of divine charity. We know, moreover, that as the sun turns toward setting, the shadows grow until night comes and the light of day fails entirely. So, plainly, when the sun of righteousness begins to set in the hearts of the reprobate, the shadow of blindness grows exceedingly, so that they are not illumined by divine light but are enveloped in the deadly darkness of night. It follows:

19. “And I have withered like grass.” No one is unaware that however tender or pleasing a blade of grass may be, if it is cut down by an applied sickle, it is immediately stripped of the beauty of its color and dried up when separated from the moisture of its root.

[Note: [Col. 0615D] Remb., Vatican, Gilot: *ex coloris* (“from [the] color”).]

So certainly whoever has departed from God through works of wickedness necessarily dries up, deprived of the innermost moisture of virtue. Hence the Savior says to his disciples: “As a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me” (John XV, 4). For although sinners often seem to flourish in this life, they recognize their dryness at the end, when they lose at once both the sweetness of their laughing life and the dignity of temporal glory.

Trusting in the vanity of their wisdom, while hoping that everything will easily be supplied to them, they suppose that they have no need of the virtue of religion. And while they boast of their empty wisdom, they do not fear living foolishly. Those who are of the root of true wisdom have withered in their foolish wisdom. If they wish to revive in that very root of living wisdom, they should strive with the greatest zeal to hasten, through the movement of the mind, toward the fountain of life.

**(Verse 13.)** “But you, Lord, remain forever, and your memorial from generation to generation.”

20. This relates to what he said: “I have withered like grass.” It is as though he said: “I who, loving vanity and following falsehood, did not wish to persist in eternity and stability, have become temporal and unstable and have incurred the dryness of death. But you, Lord, remain forever.” This, therefore, is the one hope of my salvation: that I may cling to you; that just as through myself I became dry, so through you I may become eternal; and that, living in you, I may escape death, from whom by departing I lost life.

We too, knowing that “the first man was made from the earth, earthly, and the second from heaven, heavenly” (I Cor. XV), should, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, bear the image of the heavenly, and become one with him who, rising from the dead, dies no more and over whom death shall no longer rule (Rom. VI). For he is the one who was made a life-giving spirit; if we are his members, we shall ascend together to where our Head has gone before us.

He himself has given us the hope of this ascent, saying: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24). But if we are separated from his body, we shall be deprived of participation in life like severed members, nor shall we ascend to heaven with him. Let us therefore be one with him, because, as he himself says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13).

It should be noted that he did not say “you live,” but “you remain forever.” Even if a man lives for a long time, he does not remain for a single day unchanged, because by the condition of death he is destined always to be changed. Concerning this a certain wise man bears witness, saying: “He comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state” (Job XIV, 2). But God, who alone is truly eternal and truly immortal, remains forever, because in him there is nothing transitory, nothing changeable, nothing alien to his everlasting divinity.

“Your memorial from generation to generation.” What is more truly a memorial in God than mercy? Of it, indeed, it is written: “His mercies are over all his works” (Ps. CXLIV, 9); and, “The mercy of the Lord is from eternity and to eternity upon those who fear him” (Ps. CII, 17). Although he created man wondrously, he redeemed him, once lost, still more wondrously through the death of his Son. This memorial mercy of God remains from generation to generation, open to all who live through the course of time until the end of the world.

**(Verse 14.)** “You will arise and have mercy on Zion, because it is the time to have mercy on her, because the time has come.”

21. If we take Zion literally, we can understand this passage as referring to the calling of the Jews and of the Gentiles. It will appear in this way to be an exposition of the preceding statement, showing, when he names two generations, how the mercy of God will remain from generation to generation.

He therefore says: “You will arise and have mercy on Zion.” God the Father arose through the Son, because the one who previously was not known came through him into human knowledge. Hence he is also called the Word and Splendor of the Father (Heb. I), because through him God’s will is known and the very essence of divinity is revealed.

He had mercy on Zion, that is, on the Jewish people, when he wished to be born from their lineage and first called them to faith. Understand “the time to have mercy” as the time of fulfillment, because, according to the Apostle’s statement: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. IV, 4).

When he says, “because the time has come,” he plainly wishes the time of grace to be understood, concerning which the Lord says through the prophet: “At an acceptable time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you” (Isa. XLIX, 8). Explaining this, the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 2).

**(Verse 15.)** “Because her stones have pleased your servants, and they will have mercy on her earth.”

22. By the stones of Zion we can understand the apostles, who, born from the Jewish people, finally built the Church from themselves. These stones certainly pleased the servants of God when the prophets saw through the Spirit what they would become. If the apostles had not pleased the prophets, Isaiah would never have said of them: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. LX, 8). And again: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (Rom. X, 15, from Isa. LII).

Who are those announcing peace except the apostles preaching Christ? For he is our peace, as the Apostle says, “who made both one” (Eph. II, 14). Hence, when he was born, the angels announced to the shepherds that peace had been restored to humanity (Luke II); afterward the apostles publicly preached that peace to all the nations.

By the feet of those who announce the good things, we understand the affections of the apostles. Their feet were beautiful when they sought not their own advantages but the benefit of their hearers. Beautiful, I say, were those who did not contract the stains of earthly profit through the very course of their work. We say that bodily feet are beautiful when they are not defiled by any filth of a muddy road. Since, therefore, the apostles did not seek earthly riches through the office of preaching, it is rightly said of them that their feet were beautiful.

For this reason Hannah prophesied about God, saying: “He will guard the feet of his holy ones” (I Reg. II, 9). Since the prophets saw through the Holy Spirit what the apostles would become, it is rightly said here that the stones of Zion pleased the servants of God.

And the stones had mercy on the earth, because by doing penance they absolved sinners from their sins. By “earth” we understand sinners. Hence the Lord said to the serpent: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. III, 14). For the ancient enemy eats earth because he hides sinners in the belly of his wickedness; and, desiring the destruction of human beings, he is in a sense refreshed when he delights in their evil deeds.

The stones of Zion therefore had mercy on the earth when the apostles absolved Jews who had been converted from error from their sins. Behold, one wall of the house of God, which is the Church, has been built—the wall, I say, from the circumcision. A wall from the uncircumcision will come, so that the two walls, joined to the cornerstone, may construct one city (Eph. II). Let us therefore see what follows:

**(Verse 16.)** “And the nations will fear your name, Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory.”

23. It is as though he said: “You will have mercy not only on Zion, by calling the Jews, but also on the Gentiles, by converting them to faith.” They will not resist the Gospel; rather, having recognized the truth, they will fear your name, Lord. They will fear, I say, not with slavish fear but with chaste and filial fear.

The nations feared God when, having rejected the worship of idols and cast aside the errors of ancient superstition, they were cleansed through the baptism of repentance and received the ordinances of Christian teaching. In these words it should be noted that he does not say, “Zion will fear your name, Lord,” but, “The nations will fear your name,” because although Christ was sent to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel, when they rejected the word of God and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, the apostles turned to the Gentiles, who received the name of Christ with joy (Matt. XV; Acts XIII).

Hence the Apostle says: “I say that Christ Jesus was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers. But the Gentiles are to glorify God for his mercy, as it is written: Therefore I will confess to you among the Gentiles and sing to your name” (Rom. XV, 8).

Again he says: “What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the elect obtained it” (Rom. XI, 7).

“And all the kings of the earth your glory.” God chose the weak things of the world to put the strong to shame (I Cor. I). He called the lowly to conquer the noble; he chose fishermen to subdue kings. Behold, what had been foretold concerning Christ has been fulfilled: “All the kings of the earth will fear your glory.” For every pinnacle of the world bends in reverence to Christ, and every human dignity bows to Christ’s service, as the Apostle says: “Christ became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. II, 8).

The glory of Christ is the resurrection, through which he took the kingdom away from the devil and destroyed the dominion of death. For he who appeared weak in death appeared glorious in the resurrection. Hence the Apostle says: “And if he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (II Cor. XIII, 4).

**(Verse 17.)** “Because the Lord has built Zion, and he will be seen in his glory.”

24. This is the reason why the Gentiles and the Jews are called to faith. For spiritual Zion was built from both peoples. Set upon the height of virtues, it leaves earthly things, fixes its attention on heavenly things, foresees the future, and does not fear the attacks of enemies.

Its foundations are in the holy mountains (Ps. LXXXVI), because, as the Apostle says: “You are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. II, 19).

In this city God is joined to man, as it is written: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with men, and he will dwell with them” (Rev. XXI, 3). For he rejected the synagogue and chose the Church. Therefore it is written: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXVI, 2). God abandoned those tents, but illumined Zion, that is, the Church, with the presence of his dwelling.

Hence he is by no means seen there, but here he is seen by those who are pure in heart, through the vision of the mind. For it follows: “And he will be seen in his glory.” Christ is seen in his glory in the Church, who was seen in weakness in the synagogue. In that weakness he will by no means be seen in death, since, made immortal and impassible, he now rejoices in that heavenly seat as God with the Father. Hence the Apostle says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (II Cor. V, 16).

We can also understand by what was said above—“You will arise and have mercy on Zion”—the remission of sins given in the Church, and the manifold gifts of grace that it receives through daily divine increase. God multiplies these gifts in those to whom the stones of Zion are pleasing, that is, in those who receive the apostles’ teaching and imitate their examples as far as they are able. But now let us return to what follows.

**(Verse 18.)** “He has regarded the prayer of the humble and has not despised their prayers.”

[Col. 0618D]

25. God regarded the prayer of the humble when he sent the Son into the world to restore human nature. This is what the prayer of the righteous sought; this is what the desire of the prophets awaited: that he should come into the world who would both redeem man from demonic slavery and, by the gratuitous gift of his goodness, reopen the entrance to life that sin had obstructed.

Hence Isaiah says: “They will cry to the Lord because of the oppressor, and he will send them a Savior and a champion who will deliver them” (Isa. XV, 20). From these words it is clearly gathered that he regarded the prayer of those who cried out in tribulation, to whom he granted not only a Savior but also sent a champion. The one who was Savior was also Champion.

The Savior is the Son of God, concerning whom it is written through the prophet: “God himself will come and save us” (Isa. XXXV, 4). Hence Jesus was called by the angel even before he was conceived in the womb (Luke I and II). That he is a champion he himself shows when he says through the prophet: “I who speak righteousness and am a champion for saving” (Isa. LXIII, 1).

For this reason he did not despise their prayers: he granted them what they requested. If he had despised their prayers, he would never have sent the Son to free them. Hence Moses says to the Lord: “I beg you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exod. IV, 13). Another prophet cried out, saying: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and descend” (Isa. LXIV, 1). David also said: “Give the king your judgment” (Ps. LXXI, 1).

God the Father gave his judgment to the King when the Son of God assumed the substance of human flesh. Hence the Father himself says to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth; you will rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you will shatter them” (Ps. II, 8).

It is therefore clear that he gave his judgment to the one to whom he entrusted both the kingdom of the good and the shattering of those who cannot be converted. For once a potter’s vessel has been shattered, it cannot afterward be repaired in any way. What, then, is signified by the shattering of the potter’s vessels except final condemnation? Whoever is shattered there by the severity of judgment will never afterward be restored through the remedy of repentance.

This judgment will certainly be carried out by the mediator of God and human beings, because it is written: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22). God likewise regards the prayer of the humble when he hears the faithful praying for themselves or for others.

**(Verse 19.)** “Let these things be written for another generation, and the people that will be created will praise the Lord.”

26. Just as the primitive Church was built from two peoples, so there is a twofold generation gathered into the unity of faith, namely, a carnal and a spiritual generation. Whether, therefore, we understand Zion and the things mentioned above literally, or refer everything mystically to the Church, what follows agrees with what precedes and corresponds to the matters already introduced.

For it was said: “You will arise, Lord, and have mercy on Zion.” And again: “Because the Lord has built Zion.” But now he says: “Let these things be written for another generation.” What was promised to the Jews appears to have been fulfilled among the Gentiles.

If, however, according to the spiritual understanding, we take the Church as Zion, then by “another generation” we understand the spiritual generation in which the divine promises have been written. For whatever Sacred Scripture asserts concerning the remission of sins and whatever it asserts concerning the eternity of blessedness, the spiritual generation inscribes all this in its heart through the love of the Spirit. To it also it is said: “Hear, Israel, the commandments of the Lord, and write them in your heart as in a book” (Deut. VI, 3, 7).

Concerning this inscription of God’s commandments, the Lord says through the prophet: “This is the covenant that I will make with them: I will give my laws in their hearts, and I will write them in their minds” (Jer. XXXI, 33).

A good father, who does not prescribe to his children the rights of an earthly inheritance, houses built of mud or bricks, or heaps of gold and silver—things that are often the seedbed of resentment and envy and the fuel of pride and luxury—but sets before them the grace of charity and love and the commands of justice and piety, writing the law of truth not on stone, parchment, wood, or wax, but upon the tablets of the heart.

Thus the children of the eternal promise are never occupied with empty thoughts. Always holding the testament of the almighty Father, as it were, before their eyes, they consider what they ought to fear and what they ought to hope for, and they strive with all their desires to carry out the heavenly commands.

Of these the Prophet says in the psalm: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob” (Ps. XXIII, 6). What is nobler than a divine generation? What is more sublime than a heavenly generation? What is purer than a spiritual conception?

The immaculate Lord wished man to be born without the stain of sin and the succession of human offspring to be propagated without the defect of carnal pleasure. For this reason he made Adam in such a way that he could have begotten children without sin if he had remained obedient to his Creator. It could have happened that, just as the earth brings forth its fruits without pleasure, so a woman might bear a son without sin; and just as Adam himself had been created purely by God, so a human being might purely beget another human being.

Why should this seem incredible to man, when the same gift is even granted to bees? But because the human soul refused to obey its Lord, the flesh scorned obedience to the command of the soul. Thereafter it was always rebellious toward it and rose up in pride against the one whose servant it had been. Often it rises to such a degree that, in reverse, it itself becomes mistress of its mistress. Hence it happens that in the procreation of children it falls into sin through pleasure and, by doing a good work badly, commits an offense.

27. But the Mediator of God and human beings, just as he bestowed on us the life we had lost, so also restored this generation in us. Hence he wished to be born of a virgin and without sin, so that he might plainly show by this that he would also grant this to us among the countless gifts of his benefits.

Therefore he says: “For this reason the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII, 14). He would never have called the virgin’s conception a sign unless by his birth itself he signified something that we ought to believe. Hence again it is written: “O root of Jesse, who stand as a sign for the peoples” (Isa. XI, 10).

That birth of Christ without sexual union was a sign for the peoples: to those who believe in his name he was to give the power to become children of God—those, namely, “who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John I, 12).

Just as blessed Mary bore Christ as a virgin and remained undefiled after giving birth, so Mother Church gives birth to children for God without pain and remains forever an inviolate virgin. By this too those who love God with their whole heart clearly show that they have God as their Father. For it belongs to children to love, not to fear.

Moreover, in this love they do not grow sluggish through idleness or become insolent through their works. They keep God’s will in the heavenly commandments and seek no praise from human beings for the practice of virtues. Hence it follows: “And the people that will be created will praise the Lord.”

They praise God in their works when they attribute the good they do not to themselves but to God’s grace. Hence Paul, after saying that he had labored more than all, added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (II Cor. XV, 10).

But the works of holiness that are within us must be brought outward for the edification of our neighbors in such a way that human favor or approval is not sought in them; rather, God himself, from whom these things have been granted to human beings, must be praised. Hence Truth itself says to the apostles: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

**(Verse 20.)** “Because he has looked down from his holy height; the Lord has looked from heaven upon the earth.”

28. Neither would a new people be born after creation, nor would the life of the saints perfectly praise God, unless divine mercy had regarded us through him who, in Nicodemus, taught us to be born again, showing that no one could otherwise enter the kingdom except by being reborn of water and the Spirit (John III).

Therefore, when the prophet had said that the Lord would bless the people who were to be created, he immediately added the reason for our redemption, as one who knew beyond doubt that a new people could not otherwise be created unless our Lord and Redeemer, the new man, came into the world. Nor could anyone any longer doubt true salvation, knowing that the almighty physician had descended to the sick.

Let it therefore be said: “Because he has looked forth from his holy height.” We are said to look forth when we gaze from far away. Since, therefore, through the incarnation of the Word of God not only Judea, which seemed to be near, but also the Gentile world was to be freed through mercy, it is rightly said here: “Because he has looked down from his holy height,” in accordance with what is written: “Peace to those who were far off and peace to those who were near” (Eph. II, 17).

Our Redeemer is rightly called exalted, because no mortal can behold the power of his divinity. In the end, he was also holy and was wholly of God. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “The one whom God sanctified and sent into the world” (John XVI, 36). That he was wholly of God he himself testifies when he says: “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing” (John V, 19).

The same one who was exalted was also heaven; he was exalted because of his sublimity, but heaven because of the divine indwelling. For in him, as the Apostle testifies, “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II, 9). The Lord also says through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. LXVI, 1). What throne of God is greater than Christ?

Christ, therefore, is God’s heaven, from which the Lord looked upon the earth: when he granted sinners the hope of forgiveness through him, he looked from heaven upon the earth so that the one who had been earth might become heaven. This is plainly shown when it immediately follows:

[Col. 0622A]

**(Verse 21.)** “To hear the groans of the prisoners, to release the children of those who were slain.”

29. Holy men are not inappropriately called prisoners, because, bound by the chains of God’s discipline, they do not wander toward outward things. They fix the step of their conduct immovably, as it were, while never departing from desire for their Creator. Concerning these fetters it is written: “Put your feet into his fetters and your neck into his collar” (Eccl. VI, 25).

For the one whose step is restrained from wickedness is adorned in faith with the variety of holy virtues. The neck is faith, through which each faithful person is joined to God; and, as through the neck to its head, the Church, which is Christ’s body, is united to Christ its Head. Hence, in praise of the bride, it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like necklaces” (Cant. I, 10).

Because, as James says, “faith without works is dead” (James II, 26), the neck of the bride is surrounded with necklaces when the faith of the holy soul is adorned with works.

Those in fetters groan continually because, as the elect contemplate the darkness of their exile, they sigh without ceasing for the brightness of the vision of God. But God would never hear their groans unless he had given us his Son as mediator. Hence the Apostle says: “Through whom we have access to the Father, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins” (Eph. II, 18). It is therefore established that God would hear no one’s groan unless he had come through whom we have access to the Father.

“To release the children of those who were slain.” The children of those who were slain are the imitators of the martyrs—those, namely, who either handed over their bodies for the covenant of God and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb (Gal. V), or who, by putting their members to death on earth, crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.

We can also understand by “those in fetters” those who recognize that they are bound by the chains of mortality and vulnerability and who, afflicted by the miseries of human necessity, groan without ceasing.

**(Verse 22.)** “To announce in Zion the name of the Lord, and his praise in Jerusalem.”

30. Freed from the bonds of sins, they announce the name of God in the Church all the more as they have been forgiven the offenses arising from sins that they feared. But what else is it to announce the name of the Lord than to proclaim God’s mercy in the Church? For it belongs to lords to show mercy. Hence it is said of Christ: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. XXI, from Ps. CXVII, 26). For we know that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is the judge of the human race, in accordance with what is written: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22). If he had come at his first advent in the name of a judge, surely no one would have escaped the punishment of eternal damnation. For, as the Apostle says, “All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III, 13). He therefore came in the name of the Lord, because he came to forgive sins, not to condemn sinners. I say, he came first in the name of the Lord; at his second advent he will come in the name of the judge. [529] Those, therefore, announce the name of the Lord in Zion who proclaim God’s mercy to the peoples. [Col. 0623A] It follows: “And his praise in Jerusalem.” He calls one Church by different names for different reasons: calling it Zion because it is raised up to the heights; Jerusalem, however, because, as though its enemies had already been put to death, it beholds true peace within itself. It should be noted, moreover, that the name of the Lord must first be announced, and afterward it can be praised. For praise follows the confession of recognition. “How are they to believe in him of whom they have not heard?” (Rom. X). And what greater praise of God is there than that the world, gathered into the unity of faith, not only announces his works but also praises him by its life and deeds? Hence it is added:

**(Verse 23.) “When the peoples are gathered together as one, and kings, to serve the Lord.”**

[Col. 0623B] **(Verse 24.) “He answered him in the way of his strength: declare to me the fewness of my days.”**

31. The peoples have been gathered as one in the Church spread throughout the whole world, which believes that Christ is the Son of God. Of this unity the Apostle says: “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV, 5). Outside this unity no one praises God, no one announces him. This unity was represented by the one man who, after the water had been stirred, descended into the pool and was healed (John V). For no one can find the remedy of true salvation unless he comes to the unity of faith and, putting on Christ through the sanctification of life, becomes one with him. Hence Truth himself says: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3).

By “kings,” understand those who direct the movements of their souls according to God’s will and rule over them in the manner of kings. They preside as though upon a royal throne, in the eminence of reason, subjecting everything rebellious to servitude and ordering within themselves the laws of equity and the rights of innocence, once all things have been pacified. Or understand also those who are set over peoples and seem to stand at the summit of affairs: they abound in riches, are heaped with honors, possess the preeminence of earthly imperial rule, and are exalted by the glory of worldly power. It will not seem absurd to include them, since the former serve the Lord in the very direction of their hearts, while the latter, holding to the teachings of the Christian religion, submit the necks of their minds to the yoke of orthodox faith.

32. In this assembly of peoples and kings, therefore, every believer answered God, placed in the way of truth—namely, in Christ, who set himself before us as the way, saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). [Note: Gussanville holds that “strength” (*virtutis*) should be read. All the printed editions read otherwise, and rightly so, since what follows is consequently: “I am the way, the truth,” etc. In the psalm, indeed, one reads “in the way of strength”; but that passage has not yet been explained here.] This response, however, is measured not by the voice but by conduct. Those who have been called but live perversely do not answer the Lord: after receiving the divine seed in rational soil, they produce the thorns of perversity or the briars of wickedness (Matt. XIII). Rather, those answer him who make themselves suitable for every good thing, give thanks to God for their calling, and bear within the innocence of their hearts a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or even thirtyfold fruit for God.

It should be noted that he says: “In the way of strength” [Col. 0624A] (John XV). For Christ’s strength is the glory of his resurrection. Although he performed works that no one else performed, and the signs of his miracles establish faith in his divinity, no more powerful or fitting way of believing in him has existed than this: that, having died and been buried, he rose again on the third day.

The Church therefore answers God in the way of God’s strength when, asserting nothing doubtful and perceiving nothing obscure concerning the glory of Christ’s resurrection, it strives in its members to die with Christ through baptism and penitence, and, putting on Christ through newness of life, to be brought to life together with him. For when it sees nothing luminous and nothing living within itself, it believes that from God alone it can acquire both the fullness of shining virtues and the desired eternity of unfailing life. Through God’s grace alone, moreover, it can recognize how many defects it is subject to, how many weaknesses enslave it, and how many miseries surround it. Therefore it says: “Declare to me the fewness of my days.” It is as though it were saying: “Since by my own strength I cannot attain to understanding how few my days are, grant that through the grace of your inspiration I may recognize both the deficiency of virtue and the brevity of this life, so that, considering the swift passage of this life, I may feel in my heart no affection arising from love of it.”

**(Verse 25.) “Do not recall me in the midst of my days, from generation to generation are your years.”**

33. By “the midst of my days,” we understand the imperfection of life, in which every believer begs not to be recalled from the exile of this world. Otherwise, if at the day of his departure he is still occupied by love of transitory life, he may be less able to pass into that life of eternity. In this life we receive only half our days, because, even though the radiance of this material sun continually illuminates us, night nevertheless follows and continually darkens those who have been illuminated.

Let each person therefore ask that, while his mind is fixed by love upon the course of this life, God may not recall him before he has begun to concern himself with attaining eternal things. Although holy men are surrounded by mortal flesh, they are not in the midst of their days, because, suspended from earthly things by the love of perfect desire, they already enjoy in hope the eternity of blessed life. Hence Paul says: “In hope we were saved” (Rom. VIII, 24). Again he says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20). Thus they reach the state of eternity by an unhindered course; thus, before the end of this life, they have fixed their minds upon the desire for eternity.

This is clearly shown when he immediately adds: “From generation to generation are your years.” Observe that he designates his own life by the term “a few days,” but eternal life by “years” that remain from generation to generation, so that the prudent reader may also understand from this both the infinite length of that future happiness and the fleeting brevity of temporal glory. For who does not know that years are much longer than days? But because an end can also be understood in years, he says that they will remain from generation to generation.

Wisdom says: “One generation goes, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Eccl. I, 4). This is the unstable change of the present life: as some depart, others succeed them; and when those in turn fail in a similar manner, others arise under a different condition. Yet from all the generations that have existed or will exist in the world, that living and divine generation is brought to completion which will enjoy forever participation in God’s glory.

In this generation, therefore—that is, in God’s eternity, which will remain—the prophet says that we are; namely, when the generation that precedes and the one that follows have become one, since at last death has been destroyed. Before it is swallowed up in victory, death leaves nothing stable, nothing firm, nothing unharmed (I Cor. XV).

34. These words can nevertheless be understood in another way, by referring them as follows to what precedes. It was said above: “The people that shall be created will praise the Lord.” He shows how it will praise him when he says: “He answered him in the way of his strength, and they will announce his praise in Jerusalem.” Jerusalem here is not the one that is enslaved with her children—for that Jerusalem, once called, does not answer in praise—but the one to whom it was said: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor” (Isa. LIV, 1). Once called, she answers the Lord, placed in the way of his strength.

The way of Christ’s strength is imitation of his steadfastness. In this way the created people, or the intelligible Jerusalem, answers the Lord: just as Christ laid down his life for us, so, following Christ’s steadfastness, it did not refuse to lay down its life for its brothers in its children.

He shows what its answer was when he says: “Declare to me the fewness of my days.” The renewed people, or the mother fruitful in spiritual children, asks that the time of its tribulation seem brief in comparison with eternal happiness. Otherwise, if it considers the persecutions it suffers to be prolonged excessively, it may, wearied as though by the delay of rewards, lose the steadfastness of Christ whom it has proposed to imitate.

God announces to us what we ought to follow when he inspires within us the secrets of his will. Had not that God announced the fewness of his days who said: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18)? For he knew that the pressure of temporal sufferings is concluded by a swift end, whereas the happiness of heavenly glory is confined by no limit.

[Col. 0625D] 35. We can also understand “the fewness of days” in another sense. There were heretics who said that the Church was not universal, but existed only in the time of Donatus and would be completed before the end of the world. They did not heed the Lord’s promise to it in the apostles: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

Against them it is now said: “Declare to me the fewness of my days.” It is established that by the multitude of days eternal life is understood, while by the fewness of days the course of this age is signified. For it is written: “Length of days is in her right hand” (Prov. III, 16). What is signified by the right hand except perpetual life? Since the rest of the saints is enclosed by no limit, it is rightly said that length of days is in God’s right hand.

What is said here—“Declare to me the fewness of my days”—is as though the Church were saying: “There are people who, clothed in the darkness of their folly and the errors of detestable unbelief, assert that I will soon come to an end and will have no inhabitant remaining until the end of the age. But you, in whose promises I do not cease to trust, declare to me the fewness of my days.”

The future fewness of days, I say, has been given to the Church, because throughout the whole time of this life the Christian faith must flourish in the world.

“Do not recall me in the midst of my days.” By “the midst of days,” understand the imperfection of passing times, from which God would seem to permit himself to recall her if he favored the opinion of the heretics. She asks this so that the perversity of any error may not lead her away from those years that are from generation to generation.

**(Verse 26.) “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands.”**

36. The Beginning is the Son of God, of whom it is written: “He is the beginning of all creation” (Rev. III). He himself also clearly demonstrates this when he calls himself the Beginning. Finally, in the Apocalypse, the same one says to John: “I am the alpha and the omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end” (John VIII; Rev. I, 8; XXI, 13).

In this Beginning the earth was founded, because in him the Church was founded. Hence the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III, 11). Hence the Mediator of God and human beings himself says to the chief of the apostles: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18). For he himself is the rock from which Peter received his name, and upon which he said that he would build the Church.

The earth is called the Church both because it overflows with the spiritual fruitfulness of the harvest of faithful peoples and because it remains immovably firm in the perpetual stability of faith. Hence it is said through Solomon: “The earth stands forever” (Eccl. I, 4). The earth is said to stand forever because the holy Church will never fail from the Catholic faith in this age and, in the age to come, will remain with God in eternal stability.

That it is not to be broken in this life by any adversities or overcome by any persecutions, the one upon whom it has been built clearly demonstrates when he says: “The gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI, 18). The gates of hell are heresies, which, while deceiving many who are weak in faith by the counterfeit cleverness of their words, open for them, as it were, an entrance to the infernal regions.

There are also certain powers of this world that are gates of hell. For what were Nero and Diocletian—and, finally, the one who is persecuting the Church at this time—if not gates of hell? Who could reckon how many were devoured by their promises? How many were terrified by fear of them? How many were overcome by their afflictions? The depths of perpetual death swallowed all of them, and hell admitted them to the torment of eternal damnation.

But the Church, founded upon the solidity of that rock of which it was said, is shaken by the winds of threats, yet is not moved by the rivers of persecutions; it does not totter under the hardships of bodily punishments, nor does it waver through fear of death itself. Those, however, who open the entrance to hell to their followers, as though they were its gates, do not cease in every way to attack and persecute it. In doing so, what else are they doing than striving to empty the words of truth of their force?

“The gates of hell will not prevail against it,” says the Lord, and yet they attempt to prevail against it. But the Lord is faithful in all his ways and holy in his works.

“For in the beginning he founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of his hands” (Ps. CI, 26). What are we to understand by the heavens except the holy preachers? They water this earth, of which it was said, by preaching with the showers of their words; they thunder, threatening the faithful peoples subject to them with the destruction of eternal damnation; and, to establish the credibility of their words, they flash forth by performing miracles.

That the words of preachers are rain, the Lord testifies when he says through the prophet: “As the rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there, but drench the earth, water it, make it germinate, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall be the word that goes forth from my mouth” (Isa. LV, 10). What could be clearer? Behold: just as rains descend from heaven, so words of teaching flow forth from preachers.

These are surely those who declare the glory of God. Of them it is also said here that they are the work of his hands. Earlier the Prophet says: “I shall behold your heavens, the work of your fingers” (Ps. VIII, 4); here, however, he says: “The heavens are the work of your hands.” What does it mean that there they are called the work of the fingers, but here of the hands, except that in the former passage the diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit, to be infused into the hearts of teachers, are understood, while here the very works of virtue proceeding from those same gifts into human awareness are called the work of his hands?

Because every work is performed by the hands, the operations of virtue themselves are signified by the work of the hands. First, spiritual grace is infused into human minds; afterward, what the Spirit has done in the mind is demonstrated in works.

The teachers of the Church are also called heavens because the Lord presides in them, exercising his judgments through them (Matt. XVIII). For to those to whom he gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven, he also gave the power of binding and loosing (John XX). Through them, therefore, he judges, because whatever is bound by them, he binds.

We know that sitting belongs to one who judges, and the Lord himself says through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. LXVI). If, therefore, heaven is God’s throne, and the Lord judges in the rulers of the Church, and sitting belongs to one who judges, it necessarily follows that the rulers of the Church are called heavens. These heavens are indeed the work of God’s hands, because they received from the grace of his virtue the very fact that they are heavens, as it is written: “By the word of God the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their strength” (Ps. XXXII, 6).

**(Verse 27.) “They will perish, but you remain, and they will all grow old like a garment.”**

37. Let no one now place his hope in a human being. For even these heavens, although they are the work of God’s hands, will nevertheless perish. But how will they perish except according to the body? And if they are to perish according to the body, where is the resurrection? To deny it is not only a crime; even to doubt it is the highest sacrilege.

It is therefore clear that they will not perish in such a way as not to rise again, but so that they may escape the bodily necessities they suffer in this life. In the restoration of their bodies they will seem in a certain sense to have perished, when corruption perishes in them and what is animal is destroyed, so that what is spiritual may live. They will then be, as it were, no longer what they had been, having been changed into another nature and rejoicing perpetually in the light of God’s glory.

God alone is truly immortal, because he alone is eternal and unchangeable. Hence blessed Augustine says: “True eternity and true immortality exist only in the Deity of the Trinity, for in it being is perfect; because its nature, lacking a beginning and needing no increase, admits no end and likewise no mutability.” Created things, however, even those to which God has given or will give eternity, are not wholly free from every end, because they are not outside change.

In this connection it should be understood that these heavens of whom we are speaking will both perish and not perish: the corruption they contracted from carnal generation will die in them. Yet the divine indwelling they will possess in them will be fuller than what they received in this life “through a mirror and in an enigma” (I Cor. XIII). They will not cease to be heavens in this way, as they open more widely the bosom of their hearts to receive God within themselves.

Therefore, when the prophet had said that they would perish, he added: “But you remain.” It is as though he plainly said: “Whatever corruption derived from human beings is in them will perish, but what they received from your power will remain in them. For you remain.” It is therefore evident that whatever they possess from participation in divinity does not die in them.

The flesh, however, will be reduced to dust, so that afterward it may be reformed for the better through the resurrection. Hence he adds:

**(Verse 28.) “And as a covering you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail.”**

38. We must not pass over the fact that, after saying that they would be changed like a covering, he added: “And they will be changed.” By these words he indicated that twofold change of the saints in the future life: not only will their bodies, subject in this age to corruption and death, receive perpetual incorruption, but their souls and hearts as well will pass into eternal stability, so that, just as they will no longer be able to die, they will also be unable to sin. The benefit of God’s manifold goodness will then appear in them, when mortality has put on immortality and their affections no longer experience temptation.

It should be noted that the saints are called God’s covering. For just as nothing is closer to a human being than clothing, so nothing is closer to God than the saints. Just as a person is surrounded by clothing, so God is clothed with his saints. Hence it is written through the prophet: “As I live, says the Lord, you will clothe yourself with all these as with a garment in your exaltation” (Isa. XLIX, 18, according to the Septuagint). Again, another prophet says to God: “Myrrh, and drops, and cassia are from your garments” (Ps. XLIV, 9). Since the fragrances of all virtues proceed from the saints, it is rightly said that myrrh, drops, and cassia proceed from God’s garments.

Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. II, 15). God’s garments are therefore changed because, after the death of the body, the saints pass into the happiness of heavenly life. It follows:

39. “But you are the same.” This is the true eternity and true immortality of God: not only are his power and divinity everlasting and circumscribed by no limit of an end, but his power and will are in no way changed by any variation of imperfection or inconsistency. Hence he says of himself to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14). And again: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (ibid.). Therefore it is said here: “But you are the same.”

A human being, although he may be the same person, is nevertheless not the same, because through the corruption of mortality he has received the condition of being unable to remain long in the same state. To think this of God would be utterly absurd. For just as he is eternal, so he is unchangeable: he experiences neither diminution nor increase; he does not change his purpose, nor does he reject what he has once approved.

Hence it is added: “And your years will not fail.” If by God’s years we understand eternity, we see plainly how his years will not fail. But if we wish to understand by years the multitude of the saints themselves, their years will not fail because they will become one with him who will never fail.

We call a certain revolution of days a year. What, then, are the saints except days, and what are sinners except night? Hence it is written: “Day pours forth the word to day, and night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. XVIII, 3). The years will therefore not fail because, after the choirs of the saints have once received within themselves that incomprehensible light, they will no longer experience any darkness of ignorance or temptation.

A day appears to fail when, obscured by the darkness of clouds or night, it begins not to shine. This will be alien to that life, because the true light, which cannot be obscured, will shine in the saints.

**(Verse 29.) “The children of your servants will dwell, and their offspring will be directed forever.”**

40. Who are the children who will dwell in the years—that is, in God’s eternity—except the imitators of the apostles, who will remain perpetually with God in the heavenly kingdom? For all the faithful are called children of the apostles because they were begotten by them in faith. Hence the Apostle says to the Galatians: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor” (Gal. IV, 19).

By saying that children, and not servants, will dwell there, he shows that no one can reach the heavenly kingdom unless, having cast off the old condition, he becomes a son through newness of life. Even those whom he calls servants were children of the apostles: they renounced their former way of life and walked through Christ in newness of life. They were therefore servants, and they were children: servants because of the labor of their works, children because of the transformation of newness.

Hence it is that, of the children of Israel who were freed from Egyptian slavery and crossed the Red Sea under Moses as their guide, no one entered the promised land except two (Exod. XIV). Their children entered afterward and received the benefits of divine generosity promised to their fathers. This signified that no one can ascend to the land of the eternal inheritance promised to us unless he has first learned to walk in newness of life through love of the Spirit. The two—namely Caleb and Joshua (Josh. XIV)—represent the head and the body, that is, Christ and the Church, who alone enter that land of the living.

41. When he says, “Their offspring will be directed forever,” he intended the works of the elect to be understood. Those works are directed toward eternity when everything is referred to God. No one directs his seed toward it who seeks something transitory from his works. Our works are called offspring because, just as we gather fruit from seed, so we await recompense from our works. Hence the Apostle says: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” [Col. 0630C] (Gal. VI, 8). Whoever sows the seed of a good work in this life will obtain the fruit of eternal reward in the life to come.

By “forever,” the eternity of that blessed life is understood. Since it is in no way divided by the various changes of times, it is appropriately designated by the term “one age.” Let us therefore direct our seed toward that age, and let us work for food that perishes not, but remains unto eternal life. While we have time, let us do good, so that, when we reach the unfailing blessedness of that life, we may gather perpetual fruits in heaven.

For that fruit is truly perpetual by which we live perpetually and rejoice in the never-ending abundance of bread and wine: perpetual, I say, because it is neither diminished by eating nor deteriorated by age.

**PROLOGUE TO THE SIXTH PENITENTIAL PSALM. A Song of Ascents.**

[Col. 0630D]

Among the countless varieties of radiant works and magnificent structures with which Solomon’s Temple was adorned, this too is described as having been the case: it was approached by ascending fifteen steps (III Kings VI). This should not be believed to have been done by chance or without reason. Solomon, the investigator of heavenly secrets and receptacle of divine wisdom, fashioned that temple in such a way that it would thereby signify another temple not made by human hands, so that from the corruptible building of an earthly house the beauty of the incorruptible heavenly temple might somehow be represented.

For one reaches the temple that is built in heaven from living stones neither by a flat or spacious road nor by bodily steps, but by progress in faith and ascent in charity. [Col. 0631A] Hence the Prophet says: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has disposed ascents in his heart” (Ps. LXXXIII, 6). He said that ascents had been arranged in the heart of the blessed man, and he showed from where we must ascend when he added: “In the valley of tears.”

In this valley we lament the condemnation of our exile and mourn the countless troubles of human corruption. For who is free from troubles? Hence Job says: “If I am wicked, woe to me; but if I am just, I shall not lift up my head, filled with affliction and misery” (Job X, 15). And again: “Human life upon earth is a temptation” (ibid., VII, 1). Because he saw that in this life everything was full of snares and temptations, he did not say that temptations exist in it, but declared that life itself is temptation.

Temporal life is laborious: lighter than tales, swifter than a runner, wavering in instability and tottering in weakness. Its dwelling is in houses of clay—or rather, it itself subsists in clay. It has no strength, no constancy of purpose, no rest from disturbances, and no respite from labors. Who, finally, is there whom pain does not torment, anxiety does not press, or fear does not overthrow? Laughter follows weeping, joy is accompanied by sadness; satiety succeeds hunger, and hunger again drives out satiety; at night one longs for day, and by day one seeks night; in cold, warmth, and in heat, refreshment; before food, sighs, and after food, distress. Anger and indignation harass people, and countless disturbances agitate wretched human beings.

This is the valley from which holy men continually resolve to depart through the affections of their minds and to ascend to that ineffable good, that inestimable joy, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (I Cor. II). Although they may appear bodily to be among human beings, they raise their souls to heavenly things. Clinging to that pure, highest, immortal, and perpetual good, they abandon temporal and corruptible things, and, having become superior to the world, they rest in the bosom of divine contemplation.

There, in that heavenly temple, they behold God with the eyes of the heart; indeed, in the structure of that same temple they themselves also become stones. Through the fifteen steps of that temple the spiritual ascent of the saints is signified. For this number is divided into seven and eight, [Col. 0631D] and therefore it signifies the twofold life of the righteous, namely the active and the contemplative. The active life is engaged in the world, whereas the contemplative life is raised toward heavenly things.

Since temporal life is signified by the number seven and perpetual life by the number eight, the contemplative and active lives are rightly expressed through these same numbers. Hence Solomon, the builder of the aforementioned temple, praying to the Lord, says: “Give me seven portions, and also eight” (Eccl. XI, 2). Endowed with the power of royal dignity, he desired to govern the peoples subject to him in such a way that he would nevertheless not be deprived of the perfection of divine contemplation. Bound by the administrative necessities of his office, he was compelled to devote himself to temporal action, but the sweetness of divine contemplation refreshed him inwardly.

It may also be understood that the person who ascends those fifteen steps to the temple of divine illumination is one seized by love of God’s eternal virtue. Having gradually despised temporal things, which are signified by the number seven, he is lifted to the heights by the staircase of the eight beatitudes, until the God of gods is seen by the eyes of his mind in Zion.

But now, as the Apostle says, “we see through a mirror in an enigma” (I Cor. XIII, 12). For it is impossible for anyone enclosed in the prison of this body of clay, or surrounded by the mire of mortal flesh, to behold God ascending above the cherubim and flying upon the wings of the winds (Ps. XVII), or to recognize how great is the power of his divinity. [Col. 0632B] Hence it is said through John: “No one has ever seen God” (I John IV, 18). And when Moses sought to see God, the Lord answered him: “A human being shall not see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 20).

If the radiance of the sun is so great that we are unable to look directly upon it with bodily eyes, how great is the radiance of the one who made the sun, if we are to be able to see him in the corruption in which we now exist?

But the Church’s beholding him “through a mirror in an enigma,” received in the humble coming of the Bridegroom, is a sign of that eternal vision and an image of future perfection. In that perfection we shall no longer walk by faith but by sight, and, with unveiled face, we shall behold the glory of the divine majesty with eyes unable to be dazzled.

Since these fifteen psalms contain a certain form of spiritual ascent, they are rightly all marked beforehand under the same title. Just as one ascended to that material temple by stone steps, so these songs present to us that heavenly temple, by means of which the soul, rejoicing in God, may ascend as though by certain steps.

As we are about to ascend not in body but in spirit, not by steps but by affections, let us sing this psalm and strive in it to draw near through meditation upon God, saying with the Prophet:

**EXPOSITION OF THE SIXTH PENITENTIAL PSALM**

**(Ps. CIX—verse 1.) “From the depths I cried to you, Lord; Lord, hear my voice.”**
1. Let each person consider in what depth he lies and how far he has been driven from God by acting perversely. [Col. 0632D] Let him cry out with all his strength to him who beholds the abysses and sits above the cherubim, until, rescued from the darkness of the depths, he is illumined by heavenly light and enjoys the radiance of divine knowledge. Jonah cried out to God from the belly of the whale, from the depths of the sea, from the depth of disobedience; and his prayer reached the ears of God, who drew him out from the waves, rescued him from the beast, and absolved him from guilt. Let the sinner also cry out—the sinner whom the storm of desires, as he withdrew from God, has crushed; whom the hostile enemy has swallowed; whom the wave of the present age has engulfed. Let him recognize that he is in the depths, so that his prayer may reach God.

Since this psalm [Note: [Col. 0631D] It belongs to the number of the Gradual Psalms.] concerns those who are ascending, let us see how the righteous cries out to God from the depths. For how is he not in the depths who has arranged his ascents in his heart, who directs the intention of his heart toward God, who raises the effort of his labor to the heavens? But it must be understood that holy men consider themselves all the more weak and abject the more, being raised up by the desire of their minds, they draw nearer to God. For then they first begin perfectly to recognize their misery, when they begin to feel God’s presence in their hearts.

Hence Abraham, who merited the grace of divine conversation, remembers that he is dust and ashes, saying: “I shall speak to the Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII, 27). Hence Jacob, after he had seen the Lord, limped on one foot, with the sinew of his thigh withered (Gen. XXXII); for those who lift themselves up to see God through the practice of holy contemplation consider themselves truly weak and infirm. When they cease to place their hope in the flesh, they seem to lose the strength of one leg. They become accustomed to relying solely upon heavenly desire in proportion as they feel themselves weakened with respect to hope in temporal things. And, as though they had no sinew in their thigh, they do not trust in carnal generation. They regard everything beneath heaven as vanity; and when they see themselves everywhere full of and weighed down by the miseries of the present life, they cry out to God as if from the depths.

Great is the depth of mortal life, in which nothing is certain, nothing vital, nothing safe, nothing tranquil. Great, I say, is the depth in which the sinner is overwhelmed, the wicked man submerged, and the righteous man troubled. Therefore he cries out and says: “From the depths I have cried to you, O Lord.”

[Col. 0633C] 2. Here it must be noted that he does not say, “I cry,” but “I have cried.” In this you have a lesson in perseverance: if you are not heard at first, do not withdraw from prayer; rather, persist in your petitions and cries. God wishes to be entreated; he wishes to be compelled; he wishes to be overcome by a certain persistence. Therefore he says to you: “The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI, 12).

Be persistent, then, in prayer; be importunate in your petitions; take care not to withdraw from prayer. If the one whom you entreat pretends not to hear, be a raider, so that you may receive the kingdom of heaven; be violent, so that you may even do violence to heaven itself. What is richer than this plunder? What is more glorious than this violence? It is good violence, by which God is not offended but appeased; one’s neighbor is not harmed but helped; sin is diminished, not multiplied. It is good, I say, violence, by which one does not seek profit that will quickly perish, but acquires a kingdom that will endure without end.

Let those who, setting aside divine fear, seize what belongs to others, and who do not cease by robbing the poor to accumulate sins rather than increase their profits, learn to seize something by which they may claim for themselves true riches and acquire the glory of perpetual praise. Let them not be judged foolish in this also: if they are able to seize precious and eternal things, why should they appear to take away only what is worthless and transitory? Let them do violence even to heaven itself and seize the kingdom of heaven by the force of prayer. Let them be importunate in their petitions, so that after long practice in crying out they may say: “From the depths I have cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my voice.”

The repetition of the venerable name increases the fervor of prayer. [Col. 0634A] Desire is stirred when the name that is loved is repeated. The speaker here seems to put forward a certain reason for being heard, since he declares that he has cried out, so that, as though by right, he ought to be heard who has persisted in crying out for some time. The apostles are likewise said to have presented this reason to the Lord when the Canaanite woman was pleading: “Send her away, because she is crying out after us” (Matt. XV, 23). She deserved to be heard by the Lord for this reason: after being rejected by the Lord’s first answer, she did not cease crying out. Set aflame by faith and love, she did not stop crying out before she obtained the desired healing of her daughter.

**(Verse 2.) Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication.**

3. This man, as he ascends, undertakes to ask something greater, [Col. 0634B] and in his very prayer he ascends, when he asks God to attend to his prayer by, as it were, inclining his ears; lest there perhaps be delay in being heard if his ears are far from the prayer. He seems to be seeking a special expression of divine mercy, when he asks God, in a certain sense, to be inclined to hear, so that, since he wishes to hear the voice of the suppliant, he may not delay carrying out the work of mercy. In this he follows the manner of human speech, as though God needed such affection—God from whom thought does not escape and whose will is not hidden, since neither intention is silent before him nor desire mute.

For when some powerful person neglects to hear a suppliant, the one who pleads, as though rejected at the first approach, loses confidence that he will be heard. But if the person being petitioned begins willingly to listen at once, and, setting other business aside, attends solely to the petitioner’s words, the one who has come to plead immediately conceives some confidence of obtaining his request. Animated, as it were, by this hope, he states his case more freely. The Lord gave him a great sign of his good will when he showed himself readily attentive to the one who was speaking.

So too, when we seek forgiveness from God and ask that the life-giving gifts of heavenly grace be bestowed, if we perceive God to be present to us through certain signs of his kindness and sweetness, we are more eagerly stirred toward desiring him himself. We become somewhat more confident of attaining what we long for, when the one whom our soul desires draws near in mercy to those who desire him.

This man, therefore, as he ascends and has resolved to raise his mind to that incorruptible [Col. 0634D] height, asks that God’s ears be attentive to his supplication, so that, since his prayer is directed toward God through the practice of upright intention, he may be heard quickly by the one whom he entreats. To the man who ascends and progresses, the Lord says through the Prophet: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isa. LVIII, 9).

There is this difference between prayer and supplication: prayer is offered through the virtue of perseverance, whereas supplication is made for immunity from punishment for sins. Therefore the one who strives to ascend to the citadel of the heights says: “Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication.” For he supplicates God to forget his sins and to be willing to be a father, not a judge. Therefore he adds:

[Col. 0635A] **(Verse 3.) If you observe iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who will endure?**

4. He repeats the name in order to stir affection. God would observe iniquity if he denied sinners forgiveness; he would display severity alone and not also apply compassion. If he did this, no one would expect the glory of eternal blessedness, and no one would be strong enough to endure the punishment of the righteous judgment. For, as the Apostle says, “All have sinned and lack the grace of God” (Rom. III, 23).

But because he forgives those who repent from the heart, and when the sinner is converted forgets all his iniquities (Ezek. XVIII), who could now doubt his mercy? Who could now despair of forgiveness? For the Lord promises this through the Prophet, saying: “I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities like a cloud, so that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII, 25).

Observe how confession of sin obliterates sins: it justifies the unrighteous and removes from God the memory of sins. Let us confess so that our sins may be blotted out, and after confession let us not return to them. Rather, according to the Apostle, “stretching ourselves toward what lies ahead,” let us forget what is behind (Phil. III). Let us not desire to return to Egypt or sit beside the pots of meat (Exod. XVI); let us not be desirous of evil things (I Cor. X); let us not worship the idols of the mind; let us not put God to the test; let us not murmur in the desert of this world.

Let us confess by accusing ourselves of past sins; let us confess by praising God for the forgiveness of sins. For there is confession of sin and confession of praise. If there were no confession of praise, our Savior would never have said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI, 25). For how could he confess sin, who committed no sin (I Pet. II)? Let confession therefore precede, so that praise may follow, as it is written: “Praise is fitting for the upright” (Ps. XXXII, 1).

For we have a High Priest who is able to sympathize with our weaknesses (Heb. IV), concerning whom it follows plainly:

**(Verse 4.) For with you there is propitiation, and because of your law I have waited for you, O Lord.**

5. Who is propitiation except Jesus Christ (Heb. IX), who offered himself as a sacrifice to God in order to redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself a people of his own, eager for good works (Tit. II)? Finally, John says: “He is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John II, 2).

He is with God because he sits at the right hand of God, as the Prophet says: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’” (Ps. CIX, 1). The Apostle likewise testifies that, seated at the right hand of the Father, he intercedes for us (Rom. VIII).

6. “And because of your law I have waited for you, O Lord.” The law of God is mercy, by which he has granted forgiveness to sinners and opened the way to eternal life for those who return. Christ fulfilled this law when, while pleading with the Father for his crucifiers (Luke XXIII), he asked mercy for them; and the true teacher enjoined us to keep it. For he says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Luke VI, 27).

In this he plainly showed that we cannot be sons of God in any other way than by keeping the law of mercy and loving our enemies. Paul also indicates that we must keep this law when he says: “Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI, 1).

Who bears another’s burdens except the one who has charity? For whoever truly loves does not injure the one who has injured him, does not repay insults with insults, does not slander those who slander him, and does not hate those who hate him.
