For it is written: “Charity is patient; it is kind” (1 Cor. XIII, 4). Patient, so that it may endure the evils of others; kind, so that it may love even those whom it carries.

Therefore whoever patiently endures the evils inflicted upon him bears, as it were, the burdens of a weak brother. This is the law of mercy, through which we trust that we shall escape everlasting condemnation and through which we also await our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ (Phil. III). If, as was said above, he observed iniquities, no one would be able to endure. Yet we wait for him because of his law: we forgive those who sin against us for this reason, so that we may receive forgiveness for our sins from him. For Truth itself says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI, 37).

**(Verse 5.) My soul has waited in his word; my soul has hoped in the Lord.**

7. Behold the order of perfect charity. This man ascends and advances in divine love; inwardly kindled by faith and love, he is raised by desire toward eternal things and lifted by hope toward the heights. Yet he does not neglect the care of his neighbors or postpone their salvation. Amid the joys of divine contemplation he turns toward them and exhorts them to approach God by the same steps. He sets himself before them as an example, so that if some weakness prevents them from advancing in desire, they may nevertheless be helped forward by the example of one who has already attained.

Therefore he says: “My soul has waited in his word.” Do not lose confidence; do not doubt; “place your hearts in his strength” (Ps. XLVII), because “my soul has waited in his word.” Whoever remains in the Word is not deprived of the kingdom. For we cannot bear fruit in any other way than by remaining in him. Therefore he says: “Remain in me, and I in you” (John XV, 4).

Where should one remain, if not in him? Lords will fail, palaces will collapse, cities will be destroyed, towers will be torn from their foundations; finally, heaven and earth will pass away, but the word of the Lord remains forever (Matt. XXIV). Let us therefore remain in him who remains forever (Isa. XL). Let us not follow vanity and abandon truth; let us not be grieved like the rest, who have no hope (1 Thess. IV), but let us wait for him.

And if he delays, let us wait, lest what is said through the Prophet befall us: “Woe to those who have lost perseverance” (Ecclus. II, 16). Hence it is added: “My soul has hoped in the Lord.” Whoever, broken by the troubles of worldly adversity and cast down by the assault of diabolical temptation, falls away from hope in the heavenly promises loses the reward of the perseverance he previously possessed. But whoever perseveres will receive a great recompense. For the Lord is faithful in all his ways (Ps. CXLIV, 13).

He promised forgiveness in this life to those who repent. It is therefore clear that, just as he grants remission of sins to those who confess, so he will give the kingdom of heaven to those who do not fall away from hope. Therefore the one who has waited in his word says that he hopes in the Lord. For just as the man who trusts in man is accursed (Jer. XVII), so blessed is the one whose hope is the name of the Lord and who has not looked toward vanities and false insanities (Ps. XXXIX).

**(Verse 6.) From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord.**

[Col. 0637B] 8. If we take this literally, it seems to discourage us rather than admonish us. For who would be so fainthearted as to hope in the Lord for only one day? Where then would be Paul’s saying: “If we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience” (Rom. VIII, 25)? How small the patience of a single day, and how brief the waiting!

But to understand this passage better, let us turn to the title of the twenty-first Psalm. It is entitled, “For the morning assumption” (Ps. XXII, 1). What is the morning assumption except the resurrection accomplished by God in the morning? There indeed a watch was kept, as the blindness of Jewish perfidy advanced to such a point that they believed the one whom they had seen dead would not rise again; and, lest his disciples should steal him away at night, they fortified the tomb with guards.

Another translation has, “From the morning watch” (Matt. XXVII); by this the Lord’s resurrection itself is more aptly expressed. For he who slept in death kept watch in the resurrection. Therefore he says: “I slept, and I was drowsing, and I rose again” (Ps. III, 6). And again: “I kept watch, and I became like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Ps. CI, 8).

This resurrection, then, is the foundation of our hope, because we hope that we shall reach the place where we know that our Head has gone before us. We read that many were raised before this resurrection, yet the Apostle says: “Christ the firstfruits of those who sleep” (1 Cor. XV, 20). John likewise calls him the firstborn of the dead (Apoc. I). For all who rose before him died again; but Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more (Rom. VI, 9).

Christ’s resurrection, therefore, is the foundation of our hope, because we believe that we shall rise in that life in which we hope to live with him forever. No one ought now to doubt the truth of the resurrection, since he knows that the true man Christ rose from the dead. For he died so that we might live; he received from us what he was to offer for us. By dying, therefore, he destroyed death; by rising, he opened for us the way to life.

Hence the Church says to him: “You have made known to me the paths of life” (Ps. XV, 10). Before his coming, the way of life had been unknown to all, since everyone was making for death, and even the elect were descending to the underworld, until he came who would call both the impious to justification and the dead to life. He established the true faith by the signs of his death and resurrection and formed us through the principles of his new teaching, by which we might escape death and walk in newness of life through the added grace of the Holy Spirit.

542 9. By the morning watch we may also understand the very beginnings of our faith, so that from the time each person receives baptism, after the illumination of saving grace, he may direct his intention toward God and place his hope in him alone. For the soul receives, as it were, the morning light when, after the darkness of unbelief has been driven away, the gloom of vices wiped out, and the stains of sins cleansed through the bath of regeneration, it gradually begins to recognize God and rejoice in the light of divine knowledge.

For the light is the knowledge of God, concerning which it is written: “Illumine for yourselves the light of knowledge” (Hos. X, 12, according to the Septuagint). It is a great light that dispels the darkness of the heart, purifies the eyes of the mind, raises the spirit, sets hearts aflame, teaches the paths of righteousness, and increases the desire for virtue. It is a great light by which we avoid stumbling blocks, guard against precipices, escape dangers, pass through snares, do not fear prosperity, endure adversity, reject error, and follow truth.

Who would not desire to be illumined by this light? Who would not long to be enlightened by this radiance? Hence the Prophet admonishes us, saying: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII, 6). Whoever draws near through faith is enlightened through knowledge.

Immediately after illumination, hope in grace ought to follow. For this is what he teaches who says: [Col. 0638C] “From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord.” What is this watch? Is it a watch over gold or silver? Over necklaces or precious stones? Over clothing or money? Are these not the things that plunge a person into destruction?

But there is something far more precious than these, something that must be guarded after it has been illumined. For the Prophet says: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves; more desirable than gold and much precious stone” (Ps. XVIII, 10). Finally, it is said of Wisdom that she is more precious than all riches, and that nothing desired can be compared with her (Prov. III).

These, then, are the riches that the one who has come from night to morning must guard: far more precious than earthly things and more enduring than temporal things. Neither fire can consume them, nor moth eat them, nor a robber carry them away (Matt. VI).

The Prophet also seems to me to have understood this when earlier he asked: “How does a young man correct his way?” (Ps. CXVIII, 9). If he asserted this without examination, it might seem that what follows had been uttered more hastily than established by judgment. And so that the counsel might be believed more salutary because it appeared to have been examined with more careful meditation, he went on to add: “By keeping your words.”

Then, turning to God, he responds to the question, so that the remedy of divine mercy might be understood to have been discovered not through human presumption but through divine inspiration. Hence Jeremiah says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He will sit alone and will be silent” (Lam. III, 27–28).

The yoke is the word of God placed upon the neck of our mind, so that we may proceed neither with a stiff neck nor with the gestures of the eyes (Isa. III), nor become puffed up over any grace we have received, nor raise our horn on high, nor speak iniquity against God (Ps. LXXIV); but, presenting ourselves in all things as God’s ministers (2 Cor. VI), may humble our souls and, according to the Apostle, be imitators of God as beloved children (Eph. V).

10. This yoke must be borne from youth, so that each person may anticipate the years of youth with suitable correction through discipline. Otherwise, if he takes up the yoke only after the years of youth have passed, he will be pricked by the memory of his sins, harassed by the habit of error and the practice of sinning, and, as new battles continually arise, will feel within himself the tumult of these struggles, through which each day he is either victorious or defeated.

For if from the very beginnings of youth he subjects his neck to the yoke of the word, with everything properly ordered within him, he will sit in peace. He will sit, indeed, subjecting the flesh to the soul, and from the tribunal of reason, as from a judicial seat, issuing commands to all inward movements as though to citizens.

He will sit, I say, fearing no enemy and experiencing no attack. To stand belongs to one who is fighting, but to sit belongs to one who is at rest. He will also sit alone—that is, removed from all the tumult of carnal desires. Of this solitude David says: “I withdrew, fleeing, and remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV, 8).

For the most powerful king, who ruled over so many thousands of peoples, did not live in physical solitude. Rather, he lived in the solitude of his heart, in which he endured no assaults from spiritual enemies, no tumult of perverse thoughts, and no uproar of wicked clamor.

Whoever sits alone is silent, understanding that it is better to be silent than to speak carelessly. Hence it is written: “A wise person will be silent until the proper time” (Prov. XI, 12). One ought first to learn before teaching. Therefore it is said: “Hear, Israel” (Deut. VI). For he did not first say, “Speak,” but “Hear.”

The Lord said to the Prophet: “Son of man, stand upon your feet and hear whatever I shall speak to you” (Ezek. II, 1). Whoever listens is silent. Therefore the one who meditates on the law of God day and night is silent and hears what the Lord God speaks within him—he who speaks peace to those who turn their hearts toward him (Ps. LXXXIV).

It remains, then, to say what it means that he says one should hope in the Lord until night. Who doubts that night is the end of the day? So also, for each person the end of this life is death. Night may also be understood as the day of the final judgment, which the Prophet calls a day of darkness and gloom, on which the elect are called to the heavenly kingdom (Joel II). There their hope will already come to an end, once they have received everything for which they hoped in this life, and the saints sing to the praise of God: “As we have heard, so we have seen in the city of the Lord of hosts” (Ps. XLVII, 9).

For what a person sees, how can he hope for it? (Rom. VIII.) We have therefore hoped in this life, so that what we conceive here in hope we may possess there in you.

[Col. 0640A] **(Verse 7.) For with the Lord there is mercy, and abundant redemption with him.**

11. He commends God’s charity to us in order to encourage us to hope. For we hope until night because we believe him merciful and know him to be long-suffering. Hence it was not inappropriately said by a certain wise man: [Note: [Col. 0639] This is the beginning of Responsory 8 in the nocturnal office of the First Sunday of Lent.] “I would be afflicted if I did not know your mercies, O Lord” (Ezek. XXXIII).

The remedy of divine compassion comes to meet the tribulation of our hearts; against the evil of distrust it supplies the consolation of the firmest hope, setting before us certain examples of the divine promises, by which God declares that he prefers the salvation of sinners to their destruction. He also recalls to mind the correction of certain people whom error had overthrown from their upright state, but whom the grace of the Creator reformed for the better.

Behold Zacchaeus, weighed down by the mass of grave offenses and distrustful of the quality of his merits (Luke XIX); I look upon Mary (Luke VII), I consider Peter (Matt. XXV), I weigh the thief (Luke XXIII). In them the splendor of divine compassion appeared, and through them God gave sinners hope of forgiveness.

These are the immeasurable riches of God’s compassion, hidden from the human race throughout the ages but revealed in the last times through the mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. II). Because of their immensity they are so incomprehensible that the hand grows numb in explaining them, minds grow weary, and eloquence falls silent. 544 For they surpass sense, transcend speech, and exceed understanding.

Who could adequately relate how great was the mercy by which the only-begotten Son of God descended from the bosom of the Father into our public life, assumed mortal flesh, and endured for us mockeries, bonds, scourges, the cross, and death? Who could conceive how great was the grace by which he sought the lost sheep, found the one he sought, and carried the one he had found upon his shoulders?

Who could explain how great was the compassion by which, through the most sacred outpouring of precious blood, he redeemed the human race and bestowed upon his members the holy mystery of his life-giving body and blood? By receiving it, his body, which is the Church, is fed and given drink, washed and sanctified.

Therefore the fullness of time is also called the time of grace, in which, according to Paul’s words, “the grace of our Savior God appeared to all people, teaching us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires and to live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this age” (Tit. II, 11). And again: “The kindness and humanity of our Savior appeared, not on account of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Zac. XIII, 1).

Hence it is said through the Prophet Zechariah: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the cleansing of sin and of the menstruous woman.” What is this fountain except the only-begotten Son of God? Of him the Prophet says: “With you is the fountain of life” (Ps. XXXV, 10).

It became open at that time when, appearing visibly in the world, he assumed flesh for our liberation (Rom. I). He is also called the house of David because he was born from the seed of David according to the flesh. Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” Those, therefore, inhabit Jerusalem who raise their minds to the love of heavenly things.

The sinner, however, is like a menstruous woman: either one who sins in action or a mind that slips into evil thought. A menstruous woman is polluted within herself without being touched at all by another’s flesh. Thus the soul is like a menstruous woman when, although it does not carry evil thought into the effect of an evil deed, it nevertheless dwells in the delight of unclean thoughts.

Since, therefore, the fountain of mercy—our Redeemer—is now open to us, let us draw from it with our whole heart, so that we may be able to extinguish the thirst of carnal desires. Let us wash away in it the stains of crimes and cleanse the marks of carnal thoughts. We ought to have sought the fountain of mercy even if it were closed; now that it is open and flowing, let us at least not neglect it.

For we ought to hope that there will be a place for our repentance wherever the contrition of countless people has found a place. It is open in order to wash; it flows in order to gladden; it overflows in order to cleanse. For it follows:

**(Verse 8.) And he himself will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.**

12. It remains, therefore, that we become Israel and, rising above every creature, direct the sight of our mind toward him who created all things. Let us arrange ascents in our hearts and ascend through them to the Creator of the angels with pure and simple understanding.

For what is so pleasant and joyful as to contemplate God with the eyes of the mind and the desire of the heart, and to taste his most sweet goodness and feel his sweetest delight? The glory of our Redeemer is present to us: may it raise us from earthly things to heavenly ones, open the eyes of our hearts to see the sun of righteousness, and thereby redeem us from all our iniquities.

He is God, living and reigning throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

545 **PROEMIUM ON THE SEVENTH PENITENTIAL PSALM**

*A Psalm of David, when his son Absalom persecuted him.*

I am about to speak, insofar as divine mercy grants, concerning the title of the one-hundred-forty-second Psalm. First I wish to disclose the modes of prophecy, so that, when its variety has been shown, its meaning may more easily be grasped.

For it must be understood that prophecy occurs in three ways: namely, through words, deeds, and dreams. Whoever made known future events as a prophet prophesied either through words, deeds, or dreams.

Isaiah foretold future events through words when he said: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14). Through dreams Nebuchadnezzar foresaw future events, which Daniel, filled with the Holy Spirit, explained (Dan. II). Abraham announced future events through deeds when he offered his only son as a sacrifice (Gen. XXII).

Whom, then, does he designate in this deed, except the one who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all? The deeds of the ancient fathers are themselves prophecies for us: while they do one thing and signify another, they reveal hidden matters to us as if through the language of deeds (Rom. VIII).

This is clearly shown in the present passage, when the deeds of Absalom are recalled. For Absalom, persecuting his father (2 Sam. XVIII), advanced in the savage envy of his hatred to such a point that he destroyed the laws of nature in himself. The man whom he ought naturally to have loved as a father, he inhumanly persecuted as an enemy.

Absalom is interpreted as “peace of the father”—not because he had any peace with his father, but because, in his perversity, the father displayed how great was his own peace and patience.

Who is signified by Absalom except the Jewish people? And who by David except our Redeemer? Hence Truth says through the Prophet: “The sons of strangers have lied to me; the sons of strangers have grown old” (Ps. XVII, 46).

Finally, he is the elder son who, envying the younger son’s discovery and salvation, refused to enter the house of the Church (Luke XV). He does not sing a song of joy, nor join the choirs of those who sing; lacking the ring of faith, he is not clothed in the robe of immortality, nor is he satisfied with the food of the fattened calf. He also seeks a kid, because he does not follow the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world; and therefore he is placed among the goats at the judgment and is not invited to his wedding feast.

Absalom persecuted his father because the Jewish people, rejecting the admonitions of salvation, refused to receive the Son of God who came among his own (John III). He extended the madness of his rage so far that he dared to kill his own Creator.

In this deed the patience of Christ was declared: he not only failed to repay evil with evil, but, led to death, even prayed for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34). Hence the Apostle also admonishes us, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we should follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth; when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. II, 21).

In this psalm the Head prays for the members, Christ for the Church, strength for weakness. He prays that they may not be judged severely but heard mercifully. Even at the present time the schismatic persecutes the body of Christ, the heretic attacks the Church, and the unbeliever disturbs unity. 546 But the Church cries out to God, joined to her Head, Christ, in unity of spirit.

Although she cries out to God at all times, she especially stirs herself to prayer in tribulation. Hence she says: “On the day of my tribulation I cried out to you” (Ps. LXXXV, 7). But let us see what she says:

**EXPOSITION OF THE SEVENTH PENITENTIAL PSALM**

**(Ps. CXLII—Verse 1.) O Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication in your truth; hear me in your righteousness.**
## 1

The holy universal Church, strengthened according to its more excellent part by hope of heavenly rewards, just as it possesses in the elect what it desires to preserve, so in the weak it finds what it must pray to have forgiven. For it knows that all whom the condition of this unhappy life constrains are in need of divine help: the righteous cannot remain secure amid dangers, and the sinner is absolved only by the grace of divine mercy. Thus, fearful on both sides and suspicious on both sides, it prays for those who are running, that they may reach the goal, and pleads for those who have turned back, that they may run.

The difference between prayer (*oratio*) and supplication (*obsecratio*) is that prayer is made for perseverance in virtues, while supplication is made for the forgiveness of sins. Therefore the Head, or the Church, prays that those who are doing good may also be strengthened in righteousness. But when it says, “Give heed with your ears to my supplication,” it indicates the weakness of sinners, who, like sick persons, need a certain condescension from the almighty Physician, since the sinner is unable to raise himself to Him. Or, “give heed with your ears” means: attend to supplications. For through the prophet He promises this, saying: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. I, 3).

Hence it adds: “In your truth.” In this the promise is shown to be true, because forgiveness of sins is granted to the one who turns back, according to what is written: “That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. L, 6).

“Answer me in your righteousness.” Whoever glories in himself is not heard. Those who, ignorant of the righteousness of God and wishing to establish their own, are not subject to the righteousness of God are not heard. Thus the Pharisee wished to establish his own righteousness in the temple (Luke XVIII), and for this reason was rejected by the Lord.

Let us therefore glory in the righteousness of God if we seek to be heard, so that we may be able to say with the Prophet: “Answer me in your righteousness.” But who glories in the righteousness of God except the one who attributes nothing good to his own merits and recognizes that whatever adversity he endures is just? Paul gloried in his weaknesses (II Cor. XII); he testified that he possessed no good thing that he had not received, setting before us examples of humility, so that “whoever glories may glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31).

### (Verse 2.) “And do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight.”

## 2

Whoever murmurs against the blows of his Creator enters, as it were, into judgment with Him. For the one who considers himself struck unjustly accuses God’s judgment. And the one who displays himself as innocent amid the blows contends, as it were, with God in judgment. Therefore the Lord says to blessed Job: “Will the one who contends with God so easily be silent?” (Job XXXIX, 32). Certainly, whoever arraigns God ought also to answer Him.

Blessed Job, as it were, arraigned God when he doubted whether his affliction had been just. Conscious of no sin, he believed that he had been struck unjustly, because he did not know that his merits were being increased through the affliction. But after speaking at length about his own conduct and remaining silent about the lives of the saints, he, as one contending with God, quickly became silent.

Or certainly, the one enters into judgment with God who, after praying, murmurs if he is not heard. To such people it is said: “Do you wish to contend with me in judgment?” (Jer. II, 29). Those who said, “Why have we fasted, and you have not looked upon us? We humbled our souls, and you did not know it” (Isa. LVIII, 53), were contending, as it were, in judgment.

For it is foolish to abandon prayer if God delays granting what is requested, and unjust to accuse the Creator if the result does not follow the prayer—especially since we do not know what we ought to pray for. Indeed, in anger the Lord has often granted to some impatient people what they asked, while conversely He mercifully refused the Apostle’s request (I Cor. IX, 2). He gave a king to those who asked, according to the desires of their hearts (I Reg. VIII); He also granted the devil’s request, allowing him to test Job, a simple and upright man who feared God (Job I, 2). He heard evil spirits and permitted a legion of demons to enter a herd of swine (Matt. 8).

Therefore no one should consider it a great thing to have been heard when he asks for something which it is more beneficial not to obtain. But if he does not receive what he requested, he should not cast himself down or despair of God’s mercy toward him, since perhaps he was asking for things which, once received, would either afflict him more grievously or bring him prosperity to no good purpose. For it is written: “The turning away of the little ones will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Prov. I, 32).

“For no living person will be justified in your sight.” I know that many appear righteous in the sight of human beings and, raised to the hope of heavenly promises, live innocently in the world. Yet even if they do not sin in deed, they sometimes slip through vain or perverse thought. Whose mind is not torn by vain thoughts? Whose heart is not troubled by temptations? Whose spirit is not disturbed by desires of the flesh? Therefore the one who sins in the heart—which God observes—is not justified in God’s sight.

### (Verse 3.) “For the enemy has pursued my soul; he has humbled my life to the ground.”

## 3

He shows who the enemy of the human race is when, explaining the parable of the weeds (Matt. XIII, 39), he says: “The enemy is the devil” (Luke VIII). The apostle Peter likewise says: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V, 8).

He is the one who pursues souls and strives to inflict everlasting death. He is, I say, the one who deceives the unwary and spreads snares for those walking along the road of this life. Therefore the prophet says: “On this road by which I walked, they hid a snare for me” (Ps. CXLI, 4). Again it is written of him: “His trap is hidden in the ground, and his snare is over the paths” (Job XVIII, 10).

For, desiring the destruction of the innocent out of envy for human salvation, he first shows him something pleasing. While the unwary person strives to grasp at it, he is pierced by the hidden sword of sin. Thus sin is hidden in earthly advantages, as a trap is hidden in the ground. The ancient enemy also places a snare over the path when, in the activity of this world desired by the mind, he prepares a trap of sin. The trap is placed on the ground in such a way that the bait displayed itself is not seen.

In this way the ancient enemy, when he desires to overthrow someone, places gain in guilt, as bait in a mousetrap. While the traveler longs for it out of love of greed, the snare of sin suddenly chokes him. Who would not fear the cunning of this enemy, who is so much more destructive the more hidden he is? He does not strive to take away external things from us for his own possession; rather, he attempts to plunder our inner treasures. He seeks no desire for temporal goods, no ambition for wealth, no longing for status: he desires only what is within, plunders only virtues, kills only the soul.

If he sometimes attacks external things, he does not take them away in order to possess them, but in order to overthrow the soul by taking them away. We know how he daily ensnares many through his deceits: how he strips the deceived of the garments of grace, deprives them of the adornment of virtues, defrauds them of the wealth of their resources, darkens them with the envy of temptations, and pierces them with the wounds of sins.

For this is the purpose of his perversity: to harm everyone and cast everyone down. Accordingly, when he sees people walking in God’s ways and recognizes that they are stronger in their resolve to live righteously, he persecutes them more severely and attempts to overthrow them from their steadfastness.

Therefore he says: “The enemy has pursued my soul; he has humbled my life to the ground.” A grievous persecution! I had begun, out of love for heavenly things, to abandon earthly things and, having despised worldly riches, to live in heaven; now, under the devil’s impulse, I am forced to despise the highest and eternal things and to think about the uncertain provisions of this world. I am weighed down by cares for earthly matters; captured by the allurements of bodily pleasures, I am dragged down to the depths.

“For the earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX, 15). “He has humbled my life to the ground.” When a person, having despised heavenly things, is led downward to desire only what is below, his life is humbled to the ground. Thus he becomes nearer to death precisely insofar as he has been made distant from God through dissimilarity.

Hence the Apostle says: “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and into the devil’s snare, and into many useless desires that plunge people into destruction” (I Tim. VI, 9). Accordingly, it is fittingly added:

### (Verse 4.) “He has placed me in dark places like those who have been dead for ages; my spirit is distressed within me, my heart is troubled within me.”

## 4

What could be more wretched? Formerly I lived for God, dead to the world; now, conversely, I am dead to God and live for the world. For what is sin except death? Hence it is written: “There is no one in death who remembers you” (Ps. VI, 6). And again: “Death has entered through our windows” (Jer. IX, 21).

Death is what separates the soul from God, closes the faculties of the inner senses, disfigures the divine image, and removes the brightness of light. Thus whoever dies to Christ is buried in the tomb of conscience, bound by the cords of desires, cast out from the sight of God, covered over by hardness, and shut within by the stone of iniquity. Of such people it is written: “Their iniquity has come forth as from fatness” (Ps. LXXII, 7).

Yet Jesus sometimes raises these people again and, after removing the stone of impenitence, calls them back from darkness to light. When the Church has interceded for them, He absolves them through the ministry of priests. He comes to the tomb and is moved by the Church’s tears; He commands the one who had previously lain in iniquity to rise again to righteousness.

Only this is required: that he come forth through confession, feel sorrow of heart, fear God’s judgment, and turn away from iniquity.

The prophet also gives instruction concerning this, for it is added: “My spirit is distressed within me; my heart is troubled within me.” The spirit of the penitent is distressed when, desiring heavenly things, it is weighed down by the corruption of the flesh. When burdened by the weight of earthly stain he strives to be lifted to higher things, he grows weary, exhausted by the very effort. Yet he desires what is above more ardently in proportion as he more truly recognizes the burden he carries.

The sinner’s heart is troubled when, in recalling his sin, he first begins to know himself and to consider how far he has withdrawn from God. Nor is it without significance that he added, “within me.” For the one who, having rejected wholesome and eternal things, was thinking about harmful and temporal matters was, as it were, outside himself; he did not feel the distress of his sickness and, although blind, thought that he could see. But he returned to himself when he recognized what he had been.

For it is written: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isa. XLVI, 8). The Lord also narrated concerning the prodigal son that, after he had squandered and dissipated his father’s goods and was in need of the nourishment of heavenly life, he returned to himself (Luke XV). He would not have returned to himself unless he had first gone out from himself.

Therefore his father also says: “This son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke XV, 24). If, then, you desire to be found by the Father from whom you departed through disobedience, and to feast joyfully in His house, return immediately to yourself. Examine your deeds and remember from where you fell, so that you may be moved to repentance all the more deeply as you begin to recognize what you have lost and to lose what you have found.

It follows:

### (Verse 5.) “I remembered the days of old; I meditated on all your works, and I pondered the deeds of your hands.”

## 5

Happy are the days of old, bearing nothing of darkness or gloom. The presence of divinity illumined them, the serenity of security purified them, and an immensity of joy adorned them. They were days of gladness and light, days of virtues and peace, days of delights and sweetness. Sorrow did not disturb them, anguish did not assail them, and weakness did not overshadow them.

The soul possessed these days in paradise before it fell from its state of uprightness through the guilt of transgression. But it then lost those same days unhappily when it scorned to observe the commands of its Creator.

The “days of old” may also be understood as the transgression of our first parents, through which Scripture testifies that their eyes were opened (Gen. III). Or they may signify the seductive prosperity of this world, which smiles upon fools with a kind of deceptive pleasantness, and which the righteous man curses, saying: “Let the day perish on which I was born” (Job III, 3).

For holy men, fearing the prosperity of this world more than its adversity, examine themselves amid their very successes and consider how quickly the smoke of worldly happiness passes away, recalling what is written: “In the day of misfortune do not forget good things” (Ecclus. XXVII, 11).

If they see someone prospering in the world and exulting in the glory of his riches, they do not consider the summit of his dignity but reflect in their minds upon his end. Thus they contemplate true goods with greater earnestness, seeing more clearly that transient things are not good.

Hence Job says: “I saw a fool firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty” (Job V, 3). Whoever trusts in the abundance of his riches has, as it were, planted a firm root in the ground. But the holy man curses his beauty when he disparages his prosperity.

“I meditated on all your works.” Whoever recognizes the riches of this world as deceptive and, out of love for heavenly things, despises earthly things meditates upon good works that remain after this life has passed and that bring the rewards of eternal life. For one does not live profitably in time unless one acquires the merit by which one may live in eternity.

It follows: “And I pondered the deeds of your hands” (Ps. CI, 26). The prophet speaks to God: “The heavens are the works of your hands.” And elsewhere: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII, 1).

They are the heavens that declare the glory of God, who are called the work of God’s hands because they do not disfigure the divine image within themselves, do not exclude the gifts of spiritual graces, and do not destroy the beauty of the soul. They attribute no good to themselves, but everything to God’s grace, knowing that they possess nothing they have not received (I Cor. IV).

For He has accomplished this in them, making them vessels of mercy (Rom. IX); He chose them in Himself before the foundation of the world, so that they would not glory in themselves or think highly of themselves, but would fear (Eph. I), and would not say in their abundance, “I shall not be moved forever” (Ps. XXIX).

He will meditate upon these people who, having returned from Babylon, set their examples before himself for imitation, lest, deceived by the conduct of those who think about earthly things, he fall back into the same things he had abandoned and his error become worse (Luke IX), if, after taking hold of the plough, he begins to look back, or returns home to retrieve his tunic (Matt. XXIV).

By their example, therefore, he arouses himself to good action and, though absent from them in body, dwells with them in mind. He considers the glory of eternal blessedness which they have received or are going to receive, so that he may be encouraged to good work all the more as he begins to recognize what they have done and hope for what they have received.

### (Verse 6.) “I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is like land without water before you.”

## 6

It is not enough to desire what is good unless action also follows. Therefore, after saying that he had meditated upon good works and remained absorbed in contemplating the praise of the saints, he added: “I stretched out my hands to you.”

The prophet accordingly admonishes us, saying: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God” (Lam. III, 41). What does it mean to stretch out one’s hands to God except to raise one’s activity to the Almighty?

Thus the person who gives nothing to the needy and does not heed the voice of the poor draws in his hands. A certain wise man therefore admonishes us, saying: “Let your hand not be contracted for giving and extended for receiving” (Ecclus. IV, 36).

He taught us to stretch out our hands who said: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XI, 41). The prophet also testifies, saying: “In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands” (Ps. LXXV, 3). For what does it mean to seek God with one’s hands except to invoke the Savior through holy works?

Nor was “to you” added without purpose, because there are many who, in doing good, desire to be praised by human beings. These do not stretch out their hands to God, because through works of holiness they seek not God but the glory of the world. Of such people the Lord says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2).

Let us therefore stretch out our hands to God, so that we do not perform our righteousness before human beings (ibid.), and so that we do not take empty lamps with the foolish virgins, but, taking oil in our vessels, may go out to meet the Bridegroom. Then we shall be able to say with the Apostle: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I, 12).

## 7

“My soul is like land without water before you.” This is why every God-fearing person more vigorously arouses himself to good action: if he does not exalt himself because of his merits, if he extinguishes within himself the pride of human presumption, if he considers himself to be nothing, and if he awaits from the Creator an increase of virtue.

Therefore he says: “My soul is like land without water before you.” For a soul without grace is like land without water. Just as land that is not drenched by rain is not clothed with grass, is not adorned with flowers, and does not abound in harvest, so the soul lacking grace is not covered with virtues, does not think about heavenly things, and does not devote itself to what is useful.

For since free will was corrupted in our first parent, we cannot even will what is good unless we are helped by Him by whom human steps are directed. For it is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. VIII, 35, according to the Septuagint). And the Lord says to His disciples: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16). The Apostle says: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to His good will” (Phil. II, 13). And again: “You have been saved by the grace of God, through faith” (Eph. II, 8; the printed reference reads “Ephes. VII, 8”).

If no one possesses faith without the grace of God, who can suppose that he produces fruit without the help of Him who says: “I appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John XV, 16)? For whoever plants or waters labors in vain; the voice of correction resounds externally to no purpose unless He gives the increase, without whom we can do nothing (I Cor. III).

### (Verse 7.) “Answer me quickly, O Lord; my spirit has failed.”

## 8

A certain wise man appropriately said: “For desire, even speed itself is slow.” For one who desires God’s ordinances, it is not enough to be heard unless he is also heard quickly.

He adds the reason why he ought to be heard, as though the one who places all his hope in God already had no spirit left. By saying, “My spirit has failed,” he testifies that he is poor in spirit, that he does not presume upon himself, and that he offers God a broken spirit as a sacrifice.

He also recognizes that he possesses this very humility by God’s grace, trusting that he will be raised by the help of Him whose grace he feels has cast him down. Hence the prophet, entreating the Lord, says: “You take away their spirit, and they fail, and return to their dust; you send forth your spirit, and they are created” (Ps. CIII, 29).

No one becomes a receptacle of God’s Spirit unless he is first emptied of his own spirit. For God’s Spirit rests only upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at God’s words (Isa. LXVI). Thus the one who trembles fails.

Hence the prophet says: “My soul has failed for your salvation” (Ps. CXVIII, 81). Unless a person first fails in himself, he does not draw near to the One who is above him.

Concerning the queen of Sheba it is written that, when she heard Solomon’s wisdom and saw the ministers of his household, she had no spirit left in her (III Kings 10). This is because the Church of the elect, gathered from the nations, having come to know Christ’s grace and the teachers discovered through evangelical doctrine, cast aside the spirit of pride and laid down every display of arrogance. It learned to distrust itself and to hope greatly in the mercy of its King.

### (Verse 8.) “Do not turn your face away from me, and I shall become like those who descend into the pit.”

## 9

Angry masters commonly turn their eyes away from servants by whom they have been offended; and if those servants ever plead for favor, the masters turn their faces in another direction. Since they cannot look upon them with a direct gaze, they display the movements of their minds in the posture of their bodies.

God likewise turns away from sinners, because He disdains to look upon their shame with a serene countenance. Yet He who casts away the sinner turns toward the penitent: He calls those who have turned away, grants forgiveness to those who turn back, encourages the sluggish, consoles the afflicted, teaches the diligent, helps those who struggle, strengthens those who labor, and hears those who cry out from the heart.

For through the prophet He says: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. I, 3). But because we cannot turn to Him without Him, let us cry out daily with the prophet: “Do not turn your face away from me, and I shall become like those who descend into the pit.”

When the Lord turns His face away, the sinner descends into the pit, because, unless God mercifully looks upon him, after committing many crimes he falls into the pit of despair. Peter, too, would not have wept bitterly unless the Lord had looked upon him.

Repentance is one of the perfect gifts descending from the Father of lights. Unless God’s benevolent mercy illumines the human mind, it is impossible for a person to be changed into a new nature (Jas. I), since it is written: “He cannot do anything by himself unless it has been given from above” (John XIX, 11). The Apostle likewise says: “Through Christ we have such confidence toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (II Cor. III, 4).

If, then, we are not sufficient of ourselves even to think anything, how shall we repent without God’s merciful regard? There is darkness where Christ does not look, where that true light does not enter—though it shines in the darkness, the darkness does not comprehend it (John I).

Therefore the prophet, entreating the Lord, said: “Make your face shine upon your servant” (Ps. CXVIII, 135). What is the face of God except a certain brightness of knowledge of Him? Those who are ignorant of His mercy and despair of the forgiveness of their sins do not see this brightness of His knowledge.

They descend, then, into the pit, where they do not see the light of mercy, do not direct the intention of their hearts toward heaven, satisfy the desires of the flesh, and despise God, as it is written: “When the sinner comes into the depths, he despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3).

Concerning such people the Lord thunders through the prophet Amos, saying: “If they hide themselves from my eyes in the depth of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it shall bite them” (Amos IX, 3). For what does it mean to be hidden in the depth of the sea except to lie concealed in the height of despair?

A person hides himself when he does not confess his sins. He does not confess because he despairs of God’s mercy. Or certainly, the one hides himself from God’s eyes who turns away from His commands. For the eyes of the Lord are the Spirit of God, who gave the law—that is, the commandments.

For those who hide themselves from God’s eyes in the depth of despair, the devil receives power to bite them and to bring them into the belly of his wickedness. For he is the serpent to whom it was said: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. III, 14).

### (Verse 9.) “Make me hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you.”

## 10

What is “morning” except the beginning of the coming day? And what day is meant except that of which the prophet says: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. LXXXIII, 11)? The Apostle likewise says: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near; therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day” (Rom. XIII, 12).

That is the day illuminated by the true sun, which knows no setting: clouds do not darken it, mist does not obscure it, and storm does not overshadow it. It is rightly called “one,” because it is not confined by the limit of any ending.

In this life we do not possess that day, for here we walk by faith and not by sight. Here we endure the darkness of our blindness and mourn the gloom of human error. Here we are pressed by continual clouds of sorrow and anguish and dragged along crooked paths, as captives without the light of wisdom, fading away in our thoughts.

But when Christ, our life, appears (Col. III), and we begin to see God with unveiled face, then all the gloom of darkness will flee, all the smoke of ignorance will vanish, and every cloud of temptation will be scattered, because “this corruptible will put on incorruption, and this mortal will put on immortality” (I Cor. XV).

That will be the day of brightness and light which He has prepared for all the elect—He who rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of His love. The morning of this day is the future resurrection, according to what is written: “In the morning I will stand before you and see, for you are not a God who wills iniquity, nor shall the wicked dwell beside you” (Ps. LV). And again: “It is good to confess to the Lord and sing psalms to your name, O Most High, to proclaim your mercy in the morning” (Ps. XCI, 1).

In that day the happiness of the righteous will shine forth, glory will appear, and exultation will be seen: there God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints (Rev. XXI), death will finally be destroyed, and the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. XIII).

## 11

In that morning the Lord will make His mercy heard when, having separated the righteous from the wicked, the sheep from the goats, He will say to those who are at His right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34).

There God’s mercy will become known—a mercy which the human mind cannot grasp in the present life. For the Lord has prepared for those who love Him what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart (I Cor. II).

Therefore the one who, through a good manner of life and the grace proceeding from God, is raised toward the desire for eternal life says: “Make me hear in the morning your mercy”—that is, your eternal mercy. “For the mercy of the Lord is from eternity to eternity upon those who fear him” (Ps. CII, 17).

But if that happiness of the saints is mercy and is not acquired by merits, what becomes of what is written: “And you will repay each person according to his works” (Ps. LXI, 13)? If repayment is according to works, how can it be called mercy?

But “to repay according to works” is one thing, and “to repay on account of the works themselves” is another. In the expression “according to works,” the quality of the works themselves is understood, so that the one whose good works appear will also receive a glorious reward.

No labor can be equal to that blessed life in which one lives with God and from God; no works can compare with it, especially since the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

Nevertheless, it may rightly be called mercy for this reason also: it is given for those works which no one can attain without the prior action of God’s mercy. Hence the Psalms say: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Ps. LVIII, 11).

For unless He had made vessels of mercy out of vessels of wrath, no one would be separated from that mass of perdition by holy conduct, and no one would be freed from the punishment of everlasting death by his own righteousness.

It is therefore clear that to those whom He mercifully grants the ability to do good in this life, He grants even more mercifully, in eternal blessedness, the reward of a hundredfold fruit.

This is the grace which the holy apostle of God declares is to be given for grace: those to whom the grace of sanctification is divinely given in this life receive from it also, in the future, the grace of eternal happiness.

But when he says, “For I have hoped in you,” this is, as it were, the reason for his just petition, because once someone has placed his hope in God, he approaches God in prayer with greater confidence.

Earlier he had said: “My spirit has failed,” but now he says that he hopes in God. By employing greater remedies of confidence, he supplies a most wholesome lesson for our hope, so that we may learn that it is not enough for us to fail in ourselves unless, by transcending ourselves, we advance in God.

### (Verse 10.) “Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for I have lifted up my soul to you.”

## 12

Who can reach the point of hearing the voice of mercy in the morning unless he has walked in the way of righteousness? Hence the prophet, entreating the Lord, says: “Teach me the way of your ordinances” (Ps. CXVIII, 27). And: “Guide me on the straight path because of my enemies” (Ps. XXVI, 11). And: “Direct my way in your sight” (Ps. V, 9).

For he knew that there is a way which appears straight to human beings, but whose end leads to death (Prov. XIV). Therefore he says: “Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for I have lifted up my soul to you.”

Observe the order. First, you must fail in yourself; you must not be carried above yourself by any cause for boasting, but must regard yourself as lower than everyone else, and thus extinguish within yourself the spirit of pride. Let nobility of birth not exalt you; let honor not raise you up; let prudence not inflate you. For “whoever trusts in a human being is subject to a curse” (Jer. XVII).

Next follows hope in God, so that, abandoned—according to the prophet—by father and mother (Ps. XXVI), you may be taken up by the Lord and guided by His protection amid the waves of worldly temptation.

Finally, lift your soul itself to God and, driving out every vanity, dwell in heavenly things, where you may be refreshed by the sweetness of God’s delights and enjoy the brightness of His vision.

Let the pleasure of earthly desires not steal upon you; let no fantasies of vanities occupy your mind. When these have drawn the spirit in different directions, they introduce such a cloud of negligence and set before it such darkness of blindness that, once it begins to desire what is below, it can in no way be raised to what is above.

If you are inflamed with love of heavenly things and have climbed these steps of humility, you too will be able to say with the prophet: “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul” (Ps. XXIV, 1).

Blessed is the person who can say this. Truly blessed is the one whom iniquity does not burden, pleasure does not turn back, delight does not bend, desire does not weigh down, wealth does not depress, and ambition does not drag away, as it is written: “Blessed is the person whose help is from you, who has set ascents in his heart” (Ps. LXXXIII, 6).

### (Verse 11.) “Rescue me from my enemies, O Lord; I have fled to you. Teach me to do your will, for you are my God.”

## 13

Whoever walks along a road fears ambushes, dreads the attack of enemies, and shudders at the assault of robbers. Therefore the one who desires to know the way of salvation also prays to be rescued from enemies.

He knows that he walks among enemies, in the midst of snares; dangers threaten on every side, ambushes are laid everywhere, and the unwary are thrown headlong everywhere. For our adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (I Pet. V, 8).

He seizes the unwary, wounds the unarmed, and strips the careless. He kills some, takes others captive, and suffocates others. Sometimes he transforms himself into an angel of light and proposes certain good things to the unsuspecting mind (II Cor. XI), so that, when the person falls from his purpose after being tempted and begins to be shaken by the winds of temptation like a reed, he may more easily be led to consent to sin.

He implants useless thoughts, introduces vain desires, and depicts counterfeit semblances of virtues. If he finds someone stronger, persevering in a good resolve, he persecutes him more fiercely and, applying more grievous goads of temptation, attempts to extinguish him.

He also has with him ministers of wickedness—his leaders and satellites—with whom he fights against human weakness, so that it may be overcome all the more easily because it is attacked not by one but by many.

Paul was preparing us against this powerful adversary and his many forces when he said: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI, 12).

Who can escape the hordes of so many enemies or discover their ambushes? They are not weighed down by flesh, nor occupied by any cares; they are always prepared to do harm. Who among human beings can fight against them and depart unharmed unless he has been fortified by the help of divine grace and crowned with the shield of God’s good will?

Even if he flourishes through zeal for good works and is strong in the light of virtues, he cannot overcome the wickedness of the roaring enemy or restrain the powers of the evil one unless he relies upon the protection of Him who remains in us in such a way that He also fights on our behalf.

14. It remains, therefore, that in all things we should seek the help of divine grace and should always hasten to that unconquerable refuge in which we need fear no assault from any enemy. To that refuge, indeed, had he fled who said: “Deliver me from my enemies, O Lord; I have taken refuge in you.” And elsewhere: “O Lord, you have become our refuge” (Psalm 89:1). It should be noted that he does not say “protect me,” but “deliver me,” as though he were saying: “Already they are entangling me in the snares of their deceits; already they are binding me with the knots of their deceptions; already they are wrapping me in the nets of their iniquities.” But who is capable of delivering us except the one with whom we sing through the prophet: “Our soul has been delivered like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been set free” (Psalm 123:7)? And lest anyone, pleased with himself, glory in his deliverance, there is added: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (ibid., 8).

As we walk, therefore, along this road on which they have hidden snares for us, let us cry out to God with all the depths of our heart: “Deliver me from my enemies, O Lord; I have taken refuge in you. Teach me to do your will, because you are my God.” It is right that every human being should serve his God, that the creature should obey the Creator, and that a servant should not transgress the commands of his Lord. Let the Christian soul strive to do the will of its God; let it acknowledge its Creator, hear his voice, direct its path, and obey his commands. Let it pray to be taught, ask to be guided, and plead to be strengthened. No one can attain this without the help of divine inspiration; rather, in all things we must entreat divine mercy, so that, when the Spirit whose anointing teaches us about everything (1 John 2) has been poured into our hearts, we may learn what the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God is (Romans 12).

> (Verse 12.) “Your good Spirit will lead me into a straight land; for your name’s sake, O Lord, you will give me life in your righteousness.”

15. Whoever has failed in his own spirit is led by the Spirit of God. Earlier he had said that his own spirit had failed. It is therefore clear that his own spirit had led him toward evil. Perhaps it had led him into a distant region, where he had squandered his substance (Luke 15), where there was a famine of the word of God, and where, clinging to one of the citizens—namely, the devil, who is called the ruler of this world (John 14)—he was sent out to feed swine. There he desired to fill his belly with the food of swine, that is, to satisfy his flesh with the suggestions of wicked spirits.

But when the evil spirit has failed, and the person has been taken up by the good Spirit of God, let him hope to be brought into a straight land—a land that produces neither thistles nor thorns, that is neither deserted, trackless, nor without water, but that overflows with a hundredfold harvest and abounds in eternal delights. For those who are led by the Spirit of God are, in the Apostle’s words, sons of God (Romans 8:15). If sons, then heirs; and if heirs, then possessors of an inheritance. What, then, is that inheritance except the land of the living? Hence the prophet says: “The meek shall inherit the land and shall delight in the abundance of peace” (Psalm 36:11). Again he says: “Those who bless him shall inherit the land” (ibid., 22). And lest anyone should believe that the land which is destined to pass away was being promised as an inheritance to those who bless and to the meek, he added: “But the righteous shall inherit the land and shall dwell upon it forever and ever” (ibid., 29). And: “The Lord knows the days of the blameless, and their inheritance shall be forever” (ibid., 18).

If, then, the inheritance belongs to sons, and those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God, and the inheritance is the land of the living, those who are enlightened by the Spirit of God will be led into a straight land. Whoever is led there delights in the abundance of peace. The Lord promises this abundance of peace through the prophet, saying: “I will give them true consolation, peace upon peace” (Isaiah 57:18–19, according to the Septuagint). In addition to the peace he grants his beloved in this life, divine mercy will give another peace in eternal blessedness, so that the flesh will no longer resist the spirit, nor will any occasion of temptation creep in, all things having been set in order; human nature, restored to what is better, will no longer be able to fall or sin.

This is the peace of Christ which he himself promised to the apostles, saying: “I leave you peace; my peace I give you” (John 14:17). Here it should be observed that, since he promised them his peace twice, we should understand that God’s saints possess a certain peace in this life, but will find true and perfect peace only there where no empty thought will move them, no illusion disturb them, when God has delivered their souls from death, their eyes from tears, and their feet from falling. Christ alone possessed this peace, because alone among the dead he was free and did not feel the sting of sin in his heart.

But as long as we are weighed down by corruptible flesh and entangled in the bonds of the body, ignorant of that complete and perfect peace, we are vainly troubled when the allurements of earthly desires and empty thoughts creep into us. These thoughts frequently burst forth unexpectedly, as though in a marching column, confuse the mind, and draw the soul elsewhere than we had resolved. Our heart is not in our own power; it is not raised to God according to our will. It is led downward and dragged into crooked paths. If, then, we desire to enter the straight land, let us wish to be led by the good Spirit of God.

16. “For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will give me life in your righteousness.” No one lives for righteousness unless he dies to iniquity. Just as what we have sown is not brought to life unless it first dies, so one who does not die to the world and its desires does not multiply in the fruit of good works (Colossians 3). It remains, therefore, that we mortify our members which are upon the earth, so that the author of life may give us life. For this reason he himself died and rose again: so that we, having died to sins, might live for righteousness (1 Peter 2).

Hence the prophet says: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hosea 6:3). That resurrection was our life, through which we were freed from the death of the soul and restored to perpetual life. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13). You see that whoever dies with Christ is brought to life with him, as the Apostle testifies, saying: “For if we have been grafted into the likeness of his death, we shall also be so of his resurrection” (Romans 6:5).

To be given life in righteousness is more than to be given life for righteousness. For whoever is given life in righteousness is introduced into righteousness itself, so that he thinks nothing wicked and does nothing impious. Christ himself may also be understood by “righteousness”: the one who dies to the world is given life in him. Indeed, we are nourished and given life by his body and blood; we are fed and filled by them.

Nor is it without purpose that he adds: “For your name’s sake.” In everything good that we do, we seek not our own glory but the glory of the Lord. A good work becomes acceptable to God when, through the power of the work, the name glorified is not that of the servant but of the Lord.

> (Verse 13.) “You will lead my soul out of tribulation, and in your mercy you will scatter my enemies.”

17. Among the manifold tribulations of the human soul and the innumerable troubles of affliction, no affliction is greater than the consciousness of sins. When a person suffers outwardly, he flees to God and turns again to the man of strength. For one suffering external tribulations, this is a unique and most salutary remedy of consolation: if bereavement grieves him, if poverty oppresses him, if illness comes upon him, let him withdraw from the outward tumult, enter the inner chambers of the mind, and invoke God there, where no one sees.

Let him also close the door of his heart against the troubles inflicted upon him, so that he does not feel the attacks raging outwardly, but, rejoicing in the hope of heavenly promises, postpones his losses, disregards his troubles, despises the blandishments of the world, humbles himself in confession of sin, and magnifies and praises God, who both reproves and consoles.

But if, while enduring the tribulation of an evil conscience, he does not find God in the secret place of his heart—because perhaps God has withdrawn from the heart’s dwelling on account of the abundance of iniquity—what is a person to do? Where will he find consolation? Where will he seek rest? Great is the tribulation when there is no way of escape, no hope of freedom, and no confidence of deliverance.

If he turns to outward things, if he seeks consolation in what is transitory, there the affliction of his soul will press upon him; the calamity of anxieties will spur him; a crowd of miseries will surround him. For what consolation is there in temporal things? What joy is there in riches? Will they remain with us? Are they not thorns that choke the seed of the word (Luke 8)? Just as they bring joy when acquired, so they bring grief when lost.

It remains, therefore, that the sinner, placed in tribulation, should turn back to him in whom alone true consolation exists, and through the nights of this life should seek God on the bed of his heart. If at first he does not find him, let him be encouraged to seek more earnestly; let him rise toward love of heavenly things, go around the city founded as the joy of the whole earth, question the watchmen who guard the Church, strip himself of the cloak of worldly adornment, and be wounded inwardly by the arrow of charity (Song of Songs 3). Let him not cease seeking until he finds the consoler of the sorrowful.

Once he has found him, let him hold him with all his strength until, redeemed by the aid of assisting grace, he is delivered from the tribulation of conscience. For if a shipwrecked man, desiring to preserve his life amid the waves, does not release the plank he has once obtained until, broken by the labor of the raging storms, he collapses, or, aided by the protection of a vessel, reaches the desired shore, who would not embrace the wisdom of God amid the shipwreck of this great and spacious sea, allowing himself to be governed by its protection and led by its direction?

For of this wisdom it is written: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and blessed is the one who holds her” (Proverbs 3:18). And what is the wisdom of God except Christ? As the Apostle says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).

Let us therefore hold the tree of salvation amid the sea of stormy weather. Through it we can both be delivered from the danger of dreadful death and be led out of the tribulation of diabolical temptations. We are given great confidence in our deliverance by what follows: “And in your mercy you will scatter my enemies.”

Who the enemies of the human race and the attackers of the Christian soul are has been sufficiently explained in the preceding exposition. Divine clemency scatters them when it takes away their power to do harm and sets against the darts of diabolical temptation the shield of its protection. They withdraw as though confounded when they recognize that they are powerless to prevail.

> (Verse 14.) “And you will destroy all those who afflict my soul, because I am your servant.”

18. It is right that a good servant should be helped by a good master, fortified against hostile assaults, and delivered from danger. But what does it mean that he calls himself a servant, since a servant does not remain in the house forever? Hence the Truth himself says to the disciples: “I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing” (John 15:15). And the Apostle says: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).

But it must be understood that, just as there are two kinds of fear, so there are also two kinds of servitude. There is a fear that has punishment, which perfect charity casts out (1 John 4). And there is the holy fear of the Lord, enduring forever and ever (Psalm 18:10), of which it is also written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110:10). And again: “Those who fear God lack nothing” (Psalm 33:10).

That fear, therefore, which is excluded by charity seems to belong to the servant who does not remain in the house. But holy fear is recognized as fitting that servant to whom the Lord’s voice says: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25:21).

19. What he says—“You will destroy all those who afflict my soul”—refers to the blessedness of that life in which we shall have no adversary and fear no enemy: when death is swallowed up in victory, when that last enemy, death, is destroyed, when we have been changed and made equal to the angels (1 Corinthians 15).

For now we can find no rest or security, while we still groan within ourselves, weighed down and awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body (2 Corinthians 5). But when this mortal has put on immortality, then there will be no assault of diabolical deceit, no dogma of heretical depravity, no impiety of an unbelieving people. Everything will be so peaceful and ordered that in the tents of the righteous only the voice of rejoicing and salvation will be heard.

There the saints will praise God without end and rejoice in the light of his glory (Psalm 117), having become citizens of that city which is free and eternal in heaven (Galatians 4). Darkness does not obscure it, night does not overshadow it, and age does not consume it. The light of the sun does not shine there, nor the radiance of the moon, nor the brilliance of the stars; no lamp is sought there, no lantern is kindled, and no light is fitted for use. Divine brightness illuminates it; the Sun of righteousness makes it radiant; the true Light enlightens it—the Light, I say, that is inaccessible, not confined by place, not bounded by time, not overshadowed by darkness, and not altered by night.

Illuminated by this immense, unfailing, and most brilliant light, holy Jerusalem, which is our mother, casts out the children of darkness and receives peaceful citizens—namely, children of light and of day, children of adoption, and sharers in the heavenly inheritance. No impious person enters it, no wicked person dwells there, and no unclean person enters it. Its walls are built of living stones; its gates are adorned with the finest pearls; its streets are paved with purest gold; and a song of joy is sung in it without end (Revelation 21).

There is light without failure, joy without groaning, desire without pain, love without sadness, fullness without disgust, health without defect, life without death, and salvation without weakness. There are the saints and the humble in heart (Daniel 3); there are the spirits and souls of the righteous; there are all the citizens of the heavenly homeland and the ranks of the blessed spirits, seeing the King in his beauty and rejoicing in the glory of his power. Perfect charity flourishes in all; there is one joy for all and one gladness.

Good Jesus, Word of the Father, splendor of the Father’s glory, upon whom the angels long to gaze, teach me to do your will, so that, led by your good Spirit, I may reach that blessed city where there is eternal day and one spirit among all; where there is certain security and secure eternity; eternal tranquility and tranquil blessedness; blessed sweetness and sweet joy; where you, God, live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

# Harmony of the Testimonies of Holy Scripture

## Notice concerning the following short work

560. The short work that we present here is not to be despised. In manuscript codices it bears the name of Saint Gregory the Pope, although it survives in very few copies. Indeed, it came to our attention in only one, which belongs to the monastery of Major Monastery near Tours. In the Vatican Library also only a single handwritten copy of this Harmony was found, as D. Claudius Estiennot informed us in a letter written at Rome on 17 March 1699. At the same time he warned us that the distinguished and most learned D. L. de Zacagnis, keeper of the Vatican Library, had told him that scarcely any other copy could be found in the libraries of all Italy.

The fact that this codex was brought to Rome from the Palatine Library persuades us of this: in the Roman edition prepared long before at the Vatican press by order of Sixtus V, before such a great addition of handwritten books had been made to the papal libraries from the Palatine, no mention at all is made of this Harmony. If the most painstaking editors had come upon this work, strengthened and marked by the name of Saint Gregory, and found it not unworthy of being attributed to him, they would certainly not have refrained from either publishing it or at least mentioning it.

Among the short works of the distinguished man Jacques Sirmond there is a letter from Alexander Wilthemius of the Society of Jesus, in which he reports to this most diligent investigator of manuscripts and most skilled explorer that he had found in the library of the college of that same Society at Luxembourg the Harmony of which we are speaking. He writes:

> I came upon a short work of D. Gregory, *On the Harmony of Testimonies*, which Pamelius does not present at the end of that Father’s works, although he had promised it. The title written in our codex, as I think, dating from the time of the emperors Otto, is this: “Here begins the Harmony of the Testimonies of Saint Gregory, Pope of the city of Rome.” Since this short work touches upon certain chapters concerning predestination, or matters closely related to that discussion, I judged that I should report it to your Reverence, in case you should wish it sent.

From the letter that Sirmond replied to it is clear that he very much wished the codex to be sent to him. Whether he obtained it, or what judgment the learned man reached concerning this short work, is unknown to us.

What Johannes Gilotius, a man of extensive learning, thought of it, when he published it in Paris in 1571 together with the other works of Saint Gregory, both genuine and spurious, he made clear in the public testimony which we think should be presented here. While we were examining ancient codices in order to restore the writings of this doctor that survive by comparing them with those books, we found this work in a very ancient copy belonging to the library of Saint-Denis. We have no doubt that it is by D. Gregory, not only because it bore his name, but also because its style is his—easy, popular, and simple—and, what moves us more, its very thought and doctrine are entirely Gregory’s.

In the response to the first question he discusses the two kinds of fear in almost the same words, and certainly the same ideas, as in Book 34 of the *Moralia*, chapter 14—rather, chapter 17, now number 40. In the fourth question he speaks of predestination in the same way as in Book 1 of the *Books of Kings*, chapter 14. He explains the difference between crime and sin in the same words in question 10 and in Book 21 of the *Moralia*, chapter 9—now number 19. Even if we doubted its author, we would nevertheless judge it worthy of publication, since so small a volume contains so much doctrine.

Certainly we cannot deny that the style, whoever its author may be, has the flavor of Gregory’s doctrine. In the fourth question, in a manner familiar and almost peculiar to the holy doctor, he praises the author of the Book of Wisdom: “Because a certain wise man said, ‘He was taken away,’” and so forth (Book 19 of the *Moralia*, number 26; Book 27, numbers 47 and 53). Yet neither from this observation of ours nor immediately from Gilotius’s testimony does it follow that this Harmony must be claimed for Gregory. Why could someone who had diligently studied his works not have woven and pieced together this short work from both his ideas and his words?

In the *Old Library of Spain* (vol. 2, book 7, chapter 6, number 109), a book attributed to a certain Martin, a priest of the Church of León, toward the end of the twelfth century, is called *Harmony of the Old and New Testament*. It is permissible to doubt whether our Harmony is meant by that title. For in this work not only are testimonies from the Old Testament reconciled with others from the New Testament that appear superficially to conflict, but also passages of the New Testament itself that seem opposed are generally brought into agreement and freed from every contradiction.

We have again collated this work, edited under the care of Johannes Gilotius, with a manuscript codex of Major Monastery approximately eight hundred years old. With its help we have corrected many corruptions in the Gilotian edition, though not all: this codex is not free from errors, and we were unable to obtain another manuscript. We have been afraid to indulge our own conjectures excessively, since it is almost certain to us that the greatest corruption of edited books has flowed from that practice.

# Harmony of Certain Testimonies of Holy Scripture by Saint Gregory the Great, Roman Pontiff *(C, G, S)*

*[In the manuscript: “Here begins the Harmony of the Testimonies of Saint Gregory, Pope of the city of Rome.”]*

## I

**Romans 1:1:** “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ.”

**And according to John 15:15:** “I will not call you servants, but friends.”
