*[Manuscript: “I do not say . . . but my friends.”]*

### Question

What is the meaning of this? In one place Christ the Master called the apostles not servants but friends; yet the disciple of that same Master—indeed, the apostle in whom Christ was speaking—called himself a servant. And since both statements were spoken by Christ, how they should be understood must be carefully considered, especially since the same Lord and our Savior said to those same apostles, according to Luke: “Say, ‘We are useless servants, because we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke 17:10).

*[Manuscript: “We have not done.”]*

And again: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:22–23; Luke 19:17). And again: “Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he finds doing so” (Matthew 24:46; Luke 12:37).

*[Manuscript: “I do not say . . . but my friends.”]*

### Response

Without prejudice to another and better opinion, it should be known that there are two kinds of good servitude: one of fear and the other of love; one belonging to fearful maidservants and servants, the other to loving sons who please their father. A maidservant fears being beaten; a married woman fears offending her husband.

But the fear of servitude, which has punishment, casts out perfect charity.

*[Manuscript: “Perfect charity casts out.”]*

Perfect fear in servitude, however, not only has no punishment but arrives at joy itself, as the psalmist testifies when he says: “Let my heart rejoice, so that it may fear your name” (Psalm 85:11). And again: “The holy fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” (Psalm 18:11).

The holy angels also possess this fear; certainly the holy apostles possessed it as well through the coming of the Holy Spirit, through whom charity is poured into our hearts.

*[Manuscript: “descends.”]*

Therefore the Lord did not call them servants but friends, although they were called servants both by themselves and by the Lord—not, to be sure, out of fear, but out of love for pleasing God.

## II

**Romans 1:1:** “Set apart for the Gospel of God.”

**And according to John 17:11:** “Holy Father, preserve those whom you have given me in your name, so that they may be one.”

*[Manuscript: “Holy Father, preserve them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one.”]*

### Question

If Saint Paul believed himself to have become one with those who were preserved, why does he confess that he was set apart? For someone is said to be set apart who has been separated from the flock.

*[Manuscript: “is, as it were, separated from the flock.”]*

This is especially so since the Lord said: “There will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16). And the Holy Spirit spoke by command in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2).

*[Manuscript: “for the work which I have called.”]*

### Response

It must first of all be understood that these testimonies not only do not conflict with one another, but also agree with one another in unity. Paul and Barnabas were not separated from the flock but gathered into it; that is, they had been chosen for the work of the apostolate. Since they had one heart and one soul with the flock, there could be no separation at all. Nevertheless, those who had been chosen for the apostolate had been set apart from the flock. Hands, too, are extended for work, yet they are not separated from the unity of the body.

## III

**Romans 9:1:** “My conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart.”

*[Manuscript: “in my heart.”]*

**In Solomon’s Proverbs 12:21:** “Whatever happens to the righteous will not grieve him.”

### Question

What, then? Was the Apostle Paul not righteous, since he knew that whatever happened to the righteous would not grieve him? Yet if he was righteous, he ought to have grieved; why, then, did he repeatedly commend joy to the Philippians, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Philippians 4:4)? Saint James also commands us to rejoice in various temptations (James 1:2). Paul himself also glories in his tribulations (2 Corinthians 12:9), and Saint Matthew the Evangelist testifies concerning our Lord and Redeemer, saying: “Then he began to be sorrowful and troubled. My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:37; Mark 14:33).

*[Manuscript: “He glories in his weaknesses.”]*

### Response

It must certainly be understood that there is one kind of sorrow according to God and another according to the world, as the same Paul says: “Godly sorrow produces steadfast salvation, but worldly sorrow produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). The latter is despairing; the former is praiseworthy. Filled with the latter, Judas [Iscariot] Scarioth hanged himself with a noose. Saint Paul wrote to the Corinthians that he had possessed the latter, saying: “If anyone has caused sorrow, he has caused sorrow not to me, but in part” (2 Corinthians 2:5).

*[Manuscript lacks “me.”]*

It is as though he were saying more plainly: “I alone do not possess zeal for God; rather, I perceive that my sorrow is joined, in some measure, with your sorrow.” And unless this sorrow were not a vice but a virtue, the Lord would never have blessed it in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:5). He also said that he himself was sorrowful according to his humanity, certainly not according to his impassible divinity.

## IV

**Romans 9:11:** “Concerning Jacob and Esau: when they had not yet been born or done anything good or evil, so that the purpose established through God’s election might remain—not from works but from the one who calls—it was said: ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’”

**In Psalm 61:11:** “For you will repay each person according to his works.”

### Question

When it was said, “Not from works but from the one who calls: ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’” how will God repay each person according to his works? Why, then, did Paul say, “Not from works”? We undoubtedly believe that he did not mean “from future works,” nor does anyone suppose that he meant only past works, since those works did not yet exist when the persons mentioned above were distinguished.

For if future good works still justify a person who is present, and future evils still condemn another, let that belief be far from us. A certain wise man said: “The righteous person was taken away, lest wickedness change his understanding” (Wisdom 4:11). Indeed, he would not be called righteous if he were condemned for wickedness still in the future.

### Response

Before we say anything about this question, let us believe that the prophet and the apostle spoke by the same Spirit. The same Spirit who filled both could not be contrary to himself. This same Spirit, who is God, spoke through the prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Malachi 1:2).

God’s election, therefore, had never been absent; it distinguished those things that took place in time.

*[Manuscript: “and those things which.”]*

For future times were not the cause of divine election, but divine election itself was the cause of all future natural things. Hence our Redeemer said to Ananias concerning Saul—not yet concerning Paul: “Do not be afraid of him, because he is a chosen vessel for me” (Acts 9:15). Observe what he said: “He is,” not “he will be.” For he was not chosen because he would be an apostle; rather, he was an apostle because he had been chosen.

Our God, therefore, is the creator of all good things and the most just disposer of evil things (Romans 9). He is so good to all that he even brings benefit out of evil.

*[Besides this reading, the manuscript offers another: “so that he may make them good.”]*

For if evils did not exist, no good things would be of benefit. God will therefore repay each person according to his works, because to vessels prepared for honor he will give eternal life, and to those fitted for dishonor, the condemnation they deserve.

For even the wicked, if they had wished, could have been good. But the good who are born from Adam see the opposing law in their members, so that these, by not consenting, may reach rewards through mercy, while those others, by consenting, may be dragged to punishment by just judgment.

## V

**Romans 10:13:** “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.”

**And according to Matthew 7:21:** “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

### Question

These statements appear discordant, but we wish to know how they are to be understood. There he said “everyone”; here he said “not everyone.” If, then, everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved, how will not everyone who repeats the name of the Lord be saved?

*[Manuscript: “They conflict.”]*

### Response

To call upon the name of the Lord is one thing; to repeat it is another. The good always call upon it, whereas the wicked repeat it, because they destroy by their conduct the same word of faith that they utter with their speech.

*[Manuscript: “they draw away.” Perhaps because they utter it not willingly, but under compulsion of fear.]*

Hence Paul says of certain people: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16).

*[Manuscript: “professing themselves.”]*

For the good, to call upon the name of the Lord means to please him in all things. Therefore everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.

## VI

**Romans 4:2:** “If Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God.”

**In the Epistle of James 2:21:** “Was not Abraham our father justified by works?”

### Question

Even if Abraham was justified by works, before whom does he have glory, if not before God, whose friend he was called by James? And if there is no true glory except before God, and no true justification except from him, who among the justified has glory without God?

### Response

The Apostle Paul wrote against the Sadducees, whereas Saint James spoke of the righteousness of faith. Those people justified themselves by works of the law, for in Latin the Sadducees are called “the justified.” But those who are justified by the righteousness of faith are shown to be justified by faith through charity’s works.

For, as James himself says: “Faith without works of charity, not of the law, is dead” (James 2:26).

*[Gilotian edition: “Therefore those who are justified by the righteousness of faith, justified by faith, are demonstrated by works of charity.” Nothing could be more obscure.]*

Saint Paul directs his discourse against the person who has glory but not before God, and against the Sadducee who justifies himself, saying: “Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that a person is justified without works of the law” (Romans 3:27).

It is as though he were saying plainly: “Abraham our father existed before the times of the law, yet he was justified before the Lord, because he demonstrated by works the faith that he held in his heart.”

## VII

**Romans 11:29:** “For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable.”

**In Genesis 6:7:** “I regret that I made humankind”; and in Samuel, 1 Kings 15:11: “I regret that I made Saul king.”

### Question

Since one and the same Lord spoke in the patriarchs and in the Apostle, how is he said by them both to have regretted and not to have regretted?

### Response

We must carefully observe that the patriarchs spoke about God acting immutably, while the Apostle uttered his statement about immutable predestination. Hence Saint James says of the same Lord: “With whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (James 1:17).

But apart from predestination God does mutable things. In accordance with the customary use of language, the Lord is called angry, repentant, jealous, and foreknowing; yet he is understood to be angry without anger, repentant without repentance, jealous without jealousy, and foreknowing without acts of foresight.

*[Manuscript: “Apart from determination.”]*

## VIII

**Romans 13:1:** “There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been established by God.”

**In the Prophet concerning certain kings, Hosea 8:2:** “They themselves reigned, and not from me.”

### Question

If there is no authority except from God, how could it truthfully be said by him: “They themselves reigned, and not from me”? Furthermore, if those kings were not from God, how had he said that kings reigned by themselves: “Through me kings reign,” he says (Proverbs 8:15)?

### Response

Kings reign both from him and not from him: they possess authority given by God, yet foolishly deny that they have received it from him. Hence it is written through the prophet: “He makes a hypocrite rule because of the sins of the people” (Job 34:30).

Therefore these kings are not from God because they were permitted to reign not for the sake of good but because of the sins of the people.

Again, all authority is from God alone, because authority is not evil in itself but is certainly good. Evil things, however, cannot exist without good things, nor anywhere except in good things; and therefore they arise only in rational creatures.

*[Printed edition: “And they can exist only in good things”; the manuscript reading, which we follow, removes the obscurity of this passage and is supported by Augustine.]*

The Holy Spirit therefore deigns to speak by way of admonition to good kings when, in the voice of the psalmist, it says to them: “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Psalm 2:10).

## IX

**Romans 14:14:** “We know that nothing is common through him.”

In Acts of the Apostles XV (verse 29): “That you abstain from things sacrificed to idols.”

## QUESTION

[Col. 0664B]

If nothing among material things is common in itself, what are we to think about carrion, blood, what has been strangled, and what has been sacrificed to idols? [Note: [Col. 0664D] Gilot reads: “of the dead.” One must read “carrion,” and thus the response has it: “not because of carrion.”] For these things are read to be unclean not only in the Old Testament, but in the New Testament also the believing Gentiles are commanded by the apostles to abstain from them. Therefore, considerable insight is needed to determine how this apparent discord can be resolved.

## ANSWER

Our Lord and Redeemer, according to Mark, said the following when he wished to speak about these matters: “There is nothing outside a person that can defile him” (Mark VII, 15). And when the disciples did not understand this, he added by way of rebuke: “Are even you without understanding? Do you not understand that everything which [Col. 0664C] enters into the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the privy?” (ibid., 18).

Thus the apostles, still inexperienced and not yet illumined by the Holy Spirit, believed in the Jewish manner that it was not prohibitions but material things that defiled a person. Yet material things do not defile a person: they enter the stomach and pass out; rather, it is the transgression of a prohibition, and what proceeds from that transgression, that defiles. For the first man, too, did not become unclean because of carrion, blood, or something strangled, but because of the fruit, when he transgressed the Lord’s command at the persuasion of his wife.

But let us hear what was said to holy Peter, so that we may understand what we ought to think about these matters. “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts X, 13). Peter, looking to the letter of the command, replied: “Far be it from me, Lord, for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth” (ibid., 14). Immediately, with the prohibition itself being testified to, he receives this answer: “What God has purified, you must not call common or unclean” (ibid., 15).

From this Christians were given permission—apart from the things prohibited in the New Testament—to eat whatever they wished, with moderation and thanksgiving. Carrion and blood, therefore, are not unclean in themselves by nature; rather, when eaten contrary to a prohibition, they defile a person. The fruit, too, possessed no natural uncleanness, [Col. 0665A] but the prohibition against eating it defiled the human being.

[Note: In the manuscript: “The epistle to the Romans ends; the epistle to the Corinthians begins.”]

## X.

I Corinthians I (verse 8): “Who also will confirm you to the end, without accusation [Note: The manuscript reads: ‘at his coming.’] at the coming of the Lord.”

In the First Epistle of John I (verse 8): “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

## QUESTION

Since it is deception to consider oneself without sin, how are we confirmed by the Lord without accusation at his coming, especially since even an infant one day old cannot be without sin? Is accusation, then, also sin, without which a person can be confirmed by the Lord?

## ANSWER

We must certainly understand that not every sin is an accusation, although every accusation is a sin; just as every ungodly person is a sinner, but not every sinner is ungodly. Minor and light faults, therefore, are called sins; accusations, however, are never so called unless they are serious.

[Note: The manuscript adds: “For human life, with God confirming it, can be without accusation; but it cannot in any way be without sin, not even for one day.”]

## XI.

I Corinthians III (verse 9): “For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s cultivated field.”

And in Job XXVI (verse 2): “Whose helper are you? Is it perhaps the helper of the weak?”

## QUESTION

Does holy Paul, by approving this, justify what blessed Job condemns in Elihu: “Whose helper are you? Is it perhaps the helper of the weak?” Yet the Apostle said: “We are God’s fellow workers.” If, then, it is good to be God’s helpers, why is Elihu criticized for helping God?

## ANSWER

We should certainly know that some people offend God while defending him, whereas others, insofar as they are able, defend God’s cause. The latter, by preaching truthfully, are truly God’s helpers; the former, by rebuking, falsely strive on God’s behalf, but in their striving they offend him.

The latter speak about God as people who are not unknown but known to him; the former, even when speaking truthfully, are not known by God at all. The Lord says of Elihu: “Who is this who wraps up judgments in ignorant words?” (Job XXXVIII, 2).

What does it mean that the Lord asks about him, saying, “Who is this who wraps up judgments,” and yet, by asking, rejects him, adding, “in ignorant words”? Elihu was therefore stating true judgments, but he was wrapping them in ignorant words, because he applied the sayings of the Holy Spirit concerning the reprobate to Job, although the Lord had borne witness that Job was blameless.

We do not mean “God is our helper forever” (Psalm LXI, 9) in the same way as we say, “We are God’s helpers.”

[Note: The manuscript reads: “which we say.”]

For he does not need our help; we, however, can do nothing without him.

## XII.

[Col. 0666A]

I Corinthians III (verse 15): “The fire will test what sort each person’s work is.”

According to Matthew XIX (verse 28): “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

## QUESTION

Since the fire will test what sort each person’s work is, will the apostles themselves also be tested by fire, although they are said not merely to be judged but to judge the twelve tribes of Israel? Or will it also test those whom holy Paul included with himself when he said: “But we who remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thessalonians IV, 16)?

## ANSWER

If we weigh the force of Christ’s words, we bring this obscurity into the light, with Christ himself illuminating it. For he said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII, 49).

The Holy Spirit, too, descending upon the apostles, appeared in the form of fire (Acts I); appearing as a sign [Note: The manuscript reads: “appearing to unbelievers.”] among the faithful, he tested the faithful inwardly like fire. Therefore, the fire will test what sort each person’s work is, because those whom spiritual fire does not examine in the present age it tests by fire in the future judgment.

“For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” (Romans VIII, 14); although tested by fire, they have been examined. For after receiving it through the laying on of the bishop’s hands, they did not depart from it in any way; and even if they commit some offense, they are corrected by recognizing and confessing it.

[Note: Where is this written? Perhaps Ecclesiasticus XXXVI, 11: “In the flame of wrath let him who is saved be devoured.” In the Tours manuscript I read: “He will be leaped through fire,” which may refer to Mark IX, 48: “For everyone will be salted with fire.”]

“For everyone,” the Lord says, “will be saved through fire”: either here through spiritual fire or there through bodily fire.

It follows, certainly, that just as not everyone will be tested by fire on the day of judgment, so on that same day not everyone at all will be judged. The Lord testifies to this when he says: “Whoever believes in the Son will not be judged; but whoever is unbelieving has already been judged” (John III, 18).

Whom, then, will the future fire test, if God will judge neither believers nor unbelievers? But as though we were asking him, “What, then, will the judgment be?” he immediately added: “This is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than the light” (ibid.).

Only those, then, will be judged on the day of judgment who, although they knew that the light had come, are nevertheless said to love darkness more. For those who remain in darkness have already been judged, whereas those who have nothing of darkness belong to the light without any judgment.

Those, however, who have been baptized but will be judged in the future—judgment will concern them alone, so that it may be shown whether they ought to belong more to the light or to the darkness. Therefore these will rise to be judged; the righteous, to judge; and the ungodly, to be condemned. For the ungodly also will rise, but not for judgment, as the psalmist testifies: “The ungodly do not rise in the judgment” (Psalm I, 5).

[Note: Here we abandoned Gilot’s text in order to follow the manuscript; although the manuscript still contains some obscurity, it is nevertheless preferable to Gilot’s edition, from which no meaning can be extracted.]

## XIII.

I Corinthians IV (verse 5): “Do not judge before the time.”

Philippians III (verse 18): “Many walk, of whom I often told you, and now I say even with tears, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ; their end is destruction.”

## QUESTION

When the Apostle Paul, speaking to the Corinthians, forbade judging before the time, why does he himself appear to judge before the time when he says of certain people: “Their end is destruction”?

## ANSWER

Christ, speaking in Paul, recognizes future things as though they were already past; therefore, even when Paul spoke, he judged nothing before the time. The Holy Spirit likewise says through the Apostle Peter to Simon Magus: “You have neither part nor share in this matter” (Acts VIII, 21), because the future fate of Simon Magus had been revealed to Peter by the Holy Spirit as though it were already past.

Those to whom future things do not appear as past are forbidden by the Lord to judge before the time. Concerning such people it is also said by way of rebuke through the prophet: “Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart” (Ezekiel XIII, 17). To prophesy from one’s own heart means to say something out of mere presumption and not through the Holy Spirit.

## XIV.

I Corinthians VII (verse 7): “I want all people to be as I myself am.”

And I Timothy V (verse 14): “I desire younger women to marry, bear children, and manage households.”

## QUESTION

Did holy Paul have two wills opposed to each other, since he said that he wished one thing to the Corinthians and another to Timothy? To the Corinthians he seems to have spoken about not marrying; to Timothy he wrote about marrying. There he wished all people to be as he was; here he writes that he wished younger women to marry.

## ANSWER

We must carefully observe that holy Paul was a preacher of the Church and that he had already delivered different speeches from the standpoint of different persons. There, speaking from the standpoint of virgins, he said: “I want all people to be as I myself am.” Here, speaking from the standpoint of those wishing to marry, he wrote: “I desire younger women to marry, bear children, and manage households.”

Solomon likewise speaks from the standpoint of many different persons in Ecclesiastes, where he is expressed in Latin as “the preacher.” There, speaking from the standpoint of certain people, he wrote: “Is it not better to eat and drink?” (Ecclesiastes II, 4). But from the standpoint of the perfect he added: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, for in it the end of all people is brought to mind” (ibid. VII, 3). In this way, too, the virtue of the strong was being expounded.

By the wonderful dispensation of the giver, it comes about that even among married people the elect receive the reward of virginity, although not everyone can be a virgin. For the perfect will to do something is reckoned in place of the deed itself. Hence, when the Lord was born, the holy angels said: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14).

Whatever each of us voluntarily does within himself, he will receive from the Lord as though it had been done on behalf of all people. But conversely, let the malevolent person beware lest he be condemned as though for the evil of all the wicked, because God is merciful as well as just.

Paul therefore praised both marriage and virginity, but preferred virginity to marriage, saying: “He who joins his virgin to marriage does well; but he who does not join her does better” (I Corinthians VII, 38). Since he saw in the Spirit that both were good, he certainly wished both to be practiced.

## XV.

I Corinthians VII (verses 10–11): “To the rest I say—not the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she has departed, she should remain unmarried.”

And II Corinthians XIII (verse 3): “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?”

## QUESTION

If Christ was speaking continually in the Apostle Paul, why does he admit that he says something, and not the Lord?

## ANSWER

If we bring forward two prophets, we shall quickly resolve this apparent discord. David, because he did not possess the prophetic spirit continually, demonstrated this by consulting another prophet. Nathan likewise declared that he did not have the prophetic spirit at that moment regarding the construction of the temple, saying: “Do everything that is in your heart, for the Lord is with you in everything” (II Samuel VII, 3).

But when the Holy Spirit came, he forbade the temple’s construction by a man of blood and devoted to warfare, and through that same Nathan contradicted David’s carrying it out (ibid.). The counsels of those who do not continually possess the prophetic spirit must therefore sometimes be set aside, [Note: We added from the Tours manuscript: “sometimes they must not be.”] and sometimes they must not be.

Nathan’s counsel, then, had to be set aside by David; but the counsel of the Apostle Paul had always to be observed by Christians. For whoever fulfills certain counsels that lie below the commandments is merely just; whoever goes beyond them is already perfect.

The Lord gives such counsel when he says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess, give it to the poor, and come, follow me; and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matthew XIX, 21). Paul, possessing that same Spirit, likewise gave counsel: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel” (I Corinthians VII, 25).

[Note: Gilot: “He gave counsel, not the Lord.” Concerning virginity.]

These counsels are not commandments, [Note: The manuscript adds before this: “But they acquire greater things above the commandments.”] but lie above the commandments, and therefore they acquire greater rewards.

## XVI.

I Corinthians X (verse 13): “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tested beyond what you can bear.”

[Col. 0669A]

And II Corinthians I (verse 8): “We do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of our affliction that occurred in Asia, for we were burdened beyond measure and beyond our strength.”

## QUESTION

Although we are burdened beyond our strength, how does God not allow us to be burdened? Again, if we are not burdened beyond our strength, how are we said to be burdened beyond our strength?

## ANSWER

To resolve this discord more quickly, let us turn to another prophetic testimony, where it says: “Since human salvation is vain, in God we shall act with strength” (Psalm LIX, 13–14).

We are therefore often said to be burdened beyond human frailty, because human salvation is vain; but we are never burdened beyond God’s strength, because he is the physician. A sick person under the physician’s hands sometimes weeps because he does not know how he will reach health; but the wise physician often cuts in order to bring the sick person to health as well.

Paul, looking to his own frailty, therefore said that he was burdened beyond his strength, [Note: The manuscript reads: “Nevertheless he says: ‘I can do all things.’”] but later added: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians IV, 13).

## XVII.

II Corinthians V (verse 16): [Note: Here we restored much from the manuscript that was absent from Gilot’s edition.] “And although we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him according to the flesh.”

According to Luke XXIV (verse 39): “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.”

## QUESTION

How do the disciple’s words agree with those of Christ, his teacher? We read that Christ said this after the resurrection, while at that same time Paul says: “Yet now we no longer know him.” What does this mean? Does the Apostle deny that he knows what Christ confesses?

## ANSWER

We knew our God and Redeemer to have lived according to the flesh—that is, to have shown himself in every respect a true human being, without any sin. But after the resurrection we no longer know him in this way, because we believe that his flesh will live eternally without the support of food.

Before the Passion, we read that he hungered and thirsted, grew weary from travel, and in the Passion was made lower than the angels. But now, with angels, authorities, and powers subjected to him, we no longer know him performing these things.

The Lord therefore confesses that he possesses true flesh after the resurrection, but Paul now no longer knows him as he was before the Passion. Paul brought forward this testimony after putting off the old human being, in order to suggest to us the pattern of renewal, saying: “So that just as Christ rose from the dead, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans VI, 4).

## XVIII.

[Col. 0670A]

II Corinthians XI (verse 5): “For I consider that I have done nothing less than the great apostles.”

I Corinthians XV (verse 9): “I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle.”

## QUESTION

Since Paul confesses that he is the least of the apostles, why does he testify that he has done nothing less than the great apostles?

## ANSWER

It must be understood that Paul had no present crimes; therefore, for the sake of humility, he recalled to memory sins that had already been forgiven: “I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (I Corinthians XV, 9).

When speaking about heretics and false apostles, however, he professes that he had done nothing less than the great apostles. Thus, among the apostles who acted well, he was the least through humility; but against the vices of the delinquent false apostles he stood upright through zeal for justice.

## XIX.

Galatians I (verse 1): “Paul, an apostle not from men, nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.”

I Timothy II (verse 5): “The mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus.”

## QUESTION

Was Paul not called to the apostolate through the human being Jesus Christ, since he calls himself an apostle “not from men nor through a man”?

[Note: Gilot: “Was he not called through”—and in the response, “that is, through the present [humanity],” where the negation had been omitted in both places, leaving the sense mutilated.]

## ANSWER

He was not chosen as an apostle through Christ’s human presence before the Passion, but by the one who called him after the resurrection. The Lord said to Ananias: “Do not be afraid of him, for he is a vessel chosen for me” (Acts IX, 15).

## XX.

Galatians I (verse 10): “If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

I Corinthians X (verse 33): “Just as I please everyone in all things.”

## QUESTION

If Paul pleases everyone in all things, how would he not be Christ’s servant by pleasing people?

[Note: The negative particle appears to be removable, although it is read both in the manuscript and in the edition.]

## ANSWER

Paul both pleases and does not please. He pleases in matters that are not prohibited, but in prohibited matters he did not please. For “he became all things to all people, so that he might win all” (I Corinthians IX, 19).

## XXI.

Ephesians II (verse 3): “And we were by nature children of wrath, as were the others.”

[Col. 0671A]

Genesis I (verse 31): “And God saw everything that he had made, and they were very good.”

## QUESTION

Since everything that God created is blessed and very good, how did Paul write that human beings are by nature children of wrath?

## ANSWER

Almighty God is the creator of all natures, and every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good. A habit confirmed over a long period of time, however, acquires in a certain way the force of nature. Hence Paul says: “We were by nature children of wrath,” as though he were openly saying: “When we were healthy, we became sick, and through that very worst habit we were, as it were by nature, children of wrath.”

## XXII.

Ephesians III (verse 8): “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given among the Gentiles: to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ.”

Psalm IX (verse 1): “I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart; I will recount all your wonders.”

## QUESTION

What does this mean? Could all God’s wonders even be recounted by the prophet himself, when the Apostle Paul wrote that Christ’s riches are unsearchable? Further, how is Paul himself not contradictory when he says that he preaches the unsearchable riches of Christ?

## ANSWER

All the Lord’s wonders are indeed recounted, and Christ’s riches are unsearchable, because by recounting everything they embrace all things together in a brief statement, yet those who see in an enigma know them only in part.

When something is recounted about God, the present age, or the future, everything is embraced together in a brief statement, and listeners hear that these things exist. But how they exist, or what they are like, is not understood even by preachers.

Hence the excellent preacher says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways!” (Romans XI, 33).

The psalmist, however, in order to recount everything together, says of the Lord: “He has done everything whatsoever he willed.” He recounted not only the Creator, but also what the creatures themselves are like.

## XXIII.

Philippians III (verse 13): “But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind, [Note: In the Vulgate: ‘stretching myself toward what lies ahead.’ In Greek, τοῖς δὲ ἔμπροσθεν ἐπεκτεινόμενος, ‘straining toward what is in front,’ corresponding to the reading found here; for he calls future things those that are in front, setting them against past things already placed behind. In place of ‘straining,’ the text here has a word equivalent to ‘grow strong.’] and growing strong toward the future.”

II Timothy IV (verse 7): “I have fought the good fight, I have completed the race, I have kept the faith.”

## QUESTION

Since the Apostle recalled these things from the past, how did he say that he was forgetting what lies behind?

## ANSWER

The more closely what is said corresponds to the times and the circumstances, the more quickly it is understood by the hearers. [Col. 0672A]

The Apostle Paul enumerated these things to confirm his own position, because the time of his release [Note: The manuscript reads: “of his own release.”] was drawing nearer. For it is written: “On the day of good things, do not be forgetful of evil things, and on the day of evil things, do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclesiasticus XI, 27).

Paul, therefore, was not forgetful of evil when, forgetting what lay behind, he said: “I am unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (I Corinthians XV, 9). Again, as the day of his release drew near, he was not forgetful of good things, saying: “I have fought the good fight, I have completed the race, I have kept the faith” (II Timothy IV, 7).

Holy men commonly have this particular trait: in adversity they recall prosperity, and in prosperity adversity.

Hence blessed Job, when he was in prosperity, said that he feared in this way: “For I always feared God, as though waves swelling up against me” (Job XXXI, 23). Again, when he was in adversity, he recalled the good things he had done, saying: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor, and I investigated most diligently the case I did not know” (Job XXIX, 15–16).

Holy men therefore speak of both in turn, so that they may neither be elated in prosperity nor broken by despair in adversity.

## XXIV.

Philippians IV (verses 8–9): “If there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline, think about these things, which you have both learned and received, and heard and seen in me.”

Proverbs of Solomon XXVII (verse 2): “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.”

## QUESTION

If no one is permitted to praise himself with his own mouth, why did Paul, enumerating his good qualities, say of himself: “Things which you have seen in me”?

[Col. 0672C]

## ANSWER

It is one thing to speak from one’s own heart, and another to speak in the Holy Spirit. Paul remembered in the Spirit that he had done good things amid the adversities of imprisonment; therefore he did not speak with his own mouth, because prosperity ought to be recalled amid adversity.

But concerning speaking about oneself when praising oneself and seeking one’s own glory, the Truth says: “Whoever speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but whoever seeks the glory of the one who sent him is truthful” (John VII, 18).

The same Paul says: “It is not the one who commends himself who is approved” (II Corinthians X, 18).

The person who neither in the Holy Spirit nor amid adversity recounts prosperity concerning himself is therefore the one who is truly commended.

## XXV.

Philippians IV (verse 12): “Everywhere and in all things I have been instructed; I know both how to be filled and how to hunger.”

[Col. 0672D]

In the Holy Gospel according to Luke VI (verse 25):

“Woe to you who are filled, for you will hunger.”

## QUESTION

Since the Evangelist reports that the Lord said, “Woe to those who are filled,” why did the Apostle Paul say that he knew how to be filled? Or what is so great about knowing how to be filled and how to hunger, since this appears to be common to all living creatures?

## ANSWER

Almighty and truthful [Note: The manuscript reads: “Judge.”] God said “Woe to those who are filled” because he saw that those who did not know how to be filled, and did not give thanks, were intemperate.

It is a matter of great discernment to know how to be filled—that is, to receive food with moderation and thanksgiving. For Paul says: “Whoever eats, eats for the Lord, since he gives thanks to God” (Romans XIV, 6).

Those, then, do not know how to be filled who stop eating only when, under the command of the flesh, they no longer wish to eat. Conversely, those eat for the Lord who, always temperate, give thanks to the giver.

## XXVI.

[Col. 0673B]

I Thessalonians II (verse 18): “I, Paul, wished to come to you both once and again, but Satan hindered us.”

According to Luke XXII (verses 31–32): “Simon, behold, Satan demanded you, to sift you like wheat; but I prayed for you that your faith might not fail.”

## QUESTION

How is the same Satan not permitted to sift holy Peter as he wished, while Paul is said to have been hindered as though Satan had been able to do so by his own power? And if the Apostle Paul agrees with God’s will in this matter, why did Satan hinder him again?

[Note: The manuscript reads: “why his journey.”]

## ANSWER

We must know without doubt that the devil always has the will to tempt; but he lacks the power to determine how, how much, and when he will do so.

[Col. 0673C]

For the Creator permits him to act in the world only to the extent that he had, before the ages and without limit, in his predestination. And because the Lord often tests his saints through Satan, Paul indicates that Satan himself, as it were, hindered him.

Meanwhile, we must understand that almighty God often accomplishes the purpose of his counsel even through the evil will of his servant. [Note: The manuscript reads: “of the evil servant.”]

Sometimes, however, good servants are permitted to desire things that the Lord does not allow to happen in the way they desire. Abraham wished to obey God’s command, but the same Lord did not permit Isaac to be beheaded; nevertheless, he rewarded this will as entirely perfect, saying: “Because you did not spare your only-begotten son, I will bless you and multiply your offspring” (Genesis XXII, 16).

David, too, was praised for his desire to build the temple, although he did not attain the building of it (II Samuel VII).

Since we have spoken of these matters in particular, let us see how they occur generally. The afflictions of the human race have been dispensed by a just judge, but God’s elect, already filled with love, do not wish them to occur. They therefore oppose God in their will, yet do not depart from him, because they give thanks for all afflictions.

But to make what we are saying clearer, let us proceed by demonstrating it through examples. For example, a son serves his father and, because he is dutiful, does not wish him to die. Likewise, when we visit the sick whom the Lord chastises, we strongly desire that they become healthy.

When we desire these things, therefore, we seem to disagree with God’s will by disagreeing with it. Again, when the Lord commands good things to be done for the human race, our will ought not to be contrary but consenting, so that it may be perfect; and for this reason the piety of the Lord and the justice of the judge are to be praised.

## XXVII.

I Thessalonians IV (verse 15): “And he will descend from heaven with the trumpet of God.”

Revelation VIII (verse 6): “And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound the trumpets.”

[Col. 0674B]

## QUESTION

Since Christ will descend from heaven with the trumpet of God, with which of these seven trumpets is he believed to descend? If with the seventh, how did the others precede it? If with the first, how will the others follow?

## ANSWER

The sevenfold Spirit descended upon the apostles so that, having received what were figuratively seven trumpets, they might thunder among the peoples. And Christ promised, in the person of their successors, that he would remain with them until the consummation of the age, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII, 20).

The seventh preaching, therefore, like the seventh trumpet, belongs to the consummation of the age, because after the sixfold preaching has ended, the final trumpet will sound.

“For the trumpet,” Paul says, “will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible” (I Corinthians XV, 52).

Although it is possible to believe that the final trumpet signifies the seventh preaching, we nevertheless attend to the Gospel reading, where it says of the Son of Man: “And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest heavens to their boundaries” (Matthew XXIV, 31).

It must be understood that a voice like a trumpet was also heard on Mount Sinai when the people of Israel received the Decalogue of God’s words. Those who heard it [Note: The manuscript offers two readings, excausaverunt and excusaverunt. It seems to have intended to provide the etymology of excusare, which, according to the grammarians, means the same as “to remove from a cause” and “to absolve.”] excused themselves so that it would not happen to them again.

But on that occasion he spoke entirely through a created medium, certainly not through his own nature. So too he spoke to his Son after that Son had been baptized by John, when the Father said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew III, 17).

What was signified by the voice belonged entirely to the Father’s divinity; but the syllables and the sound of the syllables certainly belonged to created things.

Since the holy angels are accustomed to being clothed with aerial bodies, as some fathers were able to see them, nothing prevents us from understanding [Col. 0675A] that they will sound such a trumpet at the time when, on the final day, they will thunder for the last time, when the bodies of the dead who sleep will be raised.

[Note: The manuscript reads: “because they are then going to sound such trumpets, since they will thunder with the final trumpet on the last day.”]

## XXVIII.

I Timothy I (verse 13): “But I received mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief.”

The same epistle, in the same place (verse 15): “The saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first.”

## QUESTION

Why do you excuse yourself in one passage, holy Paul, and accuse yourself in the other, when whatever you committed was done in ignorance, since you were the first of all sinners to receive forgiveness for your sins—especially when neither the timing nor the magnitude of your sins shows that you were such?

[Note: Gilot’s text incorrectly reads “and accuse Christians.” Below it has “you accuse Christians through humble confession.” For what has this to do with Christians here, when only Paul is under discussion?]

[Col. 0675B]

## ANSWER

It must be understood that sin is committed in three ways: either through ignorance, through weakness, or deliberately. Sin committed through weakness is more serious than sin committed through ignorance; likewise, sin committed deliberately is more serious than sin committed through weakness.

You therefore excuse yourself, holy Paul, by true reasoning, and nevertheless accuse yourself through humble confession. As one who was truly just, you were your own accuser in the one passage; and, giving thanks for the Lord’s mercy, you praised the Lord in the other.

## XXIX.

I Timothy II (verse 4): “Who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

[Col. 0675C]

Psalm CXIII (verse 3): “But our God is in heaven; he has done everything whatsoever he willed.”

[Col. 0675D]

## QUESTION

Since God has done everything whatsoever he willed, has he brought the entire human race to salvation? Or, if he did not wish to do this, how did holy Paul write that he did wish it, saying: “Who desires all people to be saved”?

It must unquestionably be believed that God did nothing in time other than what he foresaw and predestined before time. This must, of course, be understood in the sense that almighty God says in Holy Scripture that he does something not through his own nature but, plainly, through a creature. Thus he had said to Abraham the father, when he by no means wanted Isaac to be killed: “Now I know that you fear God” (Genesis 22:12)—that is, “Now I have caused it to be known that I knew without any limit.” And similarly, concerning the wicked man, he says through Ezekiel: “I do not desire the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11)—that is, “I have made him unwilling to die,” although he himself does what brings him to death; nevertheless, I have placed in his nature the disposition by which he in no way wishes to die.

The Lord therefore wishes all human beings to be saved, since they have all been created with this disposition: that they wish, although unworthy, always to remain saved. Or God wishes all human beings to be saved because he has saved people from every order of the human race—namely, kings from kings, rulers from rulers, men and women, and people from every category altogether. Paul could therefore speak in this manner when he said: “Who wishes all human beings to be saved.” For the Lord himself also spoke according to the evangelist [Luke], saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who tithe mint and every vegetable”—that is, every kind of vegetable. For how could they tithe everything, when they were altogether unable to gather everything together at once?

[Note: In Gilot’s edition and in our manuscript this is read in this way, although the name of Mark has mistakenly crept in place of Luke.]

XXX.

I Timothy 2:12: “But I do not permit a woman to teach.”

Titus 2:3: Concerning women: “Teaching what is good, so that they may teach prudence.”

QUESTION.

Since the Apostle Paul altogether does not permit a woman to teach, why, when writing about women, did he say “teaching what is good, so that they may teach prudence”?

ANSWER.

We ought not to be detained too long over matters that are clearer, so that we may take somewhat greater pleasure in lingering over obscure matters. Women, therefore, are said to be teaching what is good—not men, but their younger women. “So that they may teach prudence,” he says, so that through their instruction they may act with their daughters in such a way that they may reach eternal life.

XXXI.

I Timothy 5:20: “Reprove those who sin in the presence of everyone, so that the others also, seeing this, may have fear.”

According to Matthew 18:15: “If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone.”

QUESTION.

Since the disciple, dictating that one who sins must be reproved in the presence of everyone, says this, what does the teacher of truth himself mean when he says, “between you and him alone”?

ANSWER.

We shall settle this question more quickly if we consider the force of the words more carefully. There he said “those who sin,” but did not add “against whom”; here he said, “if he has sinned against you.” Therefore, if your brother has sinned secretly against you and you wish to reprove him in the presence of everyone, you are not a corrector but a betrayer. Reprove those who sin against God in the presence of everyone, joining the word “reprove” to the following expression. Hence Paul says: “When Peter came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel” (Galatians 2:11). And shortly afterward: “I said to Peter in the presence of everyone”—as though he had said, because he had practiced dissimulation in the presence of everyone: “If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?” (ibid., 14).

Secret sins, therefore, may be corrected secretly, and public sins ought to be reproved in the presence of everyone, so that the others also may have fear. Whatever moves the minds of others must by no means be kept silent, but must be brought forward with great humility.

XXXII.

I Timothy 6:16: “Whom no human being has seen, nor can see.”

And 1 John 3:2: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

QUESTION.

Since the Apostle Paul said that no human being has seen God, nor can see him, how did Saint John write: “Because we shall see him as he is”?

ANSWER.

In these two testimonies the two holy Apostles seem altogether to disagree, but by disagreeing they truly agree. Yet it must be understood that almighty God was not shown to the ancient fathers in his own nature; nevertheless, he spoke with Moses through a creature, as a friend with a friend. “No one,” he says, “will see me and live” (Exodus 33:20). This fittingly corresponds to what the Apostle Paul says: “Whom no human being sees.” But what he says, “Nor can see,” corresponds to what Saint John said: “Because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

In this present life, therefore, the Lord showed his back through creatures, because he still conceals the truth of his own nature from his children while they are pilgrims. The same John bears witness when he says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (ibid.).

From this testimony it must be understood what Paul says: “Nor can see”—as though he were plainly saying: No child can see the heavenly Father so long as, being a pilgrim in this life, he is unlike the Father. But every elect person will be able to see God, not through creatures but as he is, when what he will be has appeared and he has become like him.

Or certainly, as the Evangelist John says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18)—as though he were saying more explicitly: He sees him as he is in himself. For no creature understands God firmly in the way God understands himself.

XXXIII.

2 Timothy 1:11: “For which I was appointed a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher of the Gentiles.”

According to Matthew 23:10: “But you must not be called Rabbi, for one is your teacher, who is in heaven.”

QUESTION.

Since the Lord said to his apostles, “Do not be called by the name of teachers,” why does the Apostle Paul of Christ confess that he was a teacher of the Gentiles?

ANSWER.

Was the Lord’s command forbidding this being disregarded by the Apostle Paul? Rather, it was being conveyed by him to all believers so that they would not be led astray under the name of the apostles by false apostles, but would follow him as teacher in whom Christ was speaking.

[Note: In Gilot’s edition this is given most corruptly: “The Lord’s speech was never despised . . . but by all.” Our manuscript has supplied the correction.]

XXXIV.

2 Timothy 4:14: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; may the Lord repay him according to his works.”

[Note: The manuscript reads, “according to his works.”]

And shortly afterward (verse 16): “At my first defense,” he says, “no one stood by me, but everyone abandoned me; may it not be counted against them.”

QUESTION.

Why, when writing about Alexander, did Paul say by way of a wish, “May the Lord repay him according to his works,” while, taking pity on the others, he spoke by way of a wish, “May it not be counted against them”?

ANSWER.

In one and the same Spirit Paul foresaw, when he wrote both of these different statements to Timothy, that Alexander, hard-hearted toward God, would never be converted, whereas the acts previously committed would not be imputed to the other peoples through true presence.

[APPENDIX TO THE COMPLETE WORKS OF SAINT GREGORY.]

[EXPOSITION OF BOTH TESTAMENTS.]

PREFACE TO THE BOOK OF SAINT PATERIUS ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, WHERE THE SIMILAR WORK OF ALULF IS DISCUSSED.

I. Here, devoted reader, we present to you Saint Paterius, a disciple of Gregory the Great—indeed, another Gregory, as it were—not mutilated, as he has appeared until now, but enlarged through the greater part of himself and entirely complete.

II. Saint Gregory mentions Paterius in Book V, Letter 29: “We dictated this letter to Paterius, the notary of our Church, for subscription.” In the permission granted to Abbot Probus to make a will—formerly read in the sequence of the letters as Book IX, number 22, but now relegated to the end—Paterius is likewise called a *secundicerius*. John the Deacon mentions him third among the clerics who were familiar with the most holy pontiff and participants in his counsels or assistants in the study of sacred letters (Book II, chapter 11). He bestows on him the twofold title of notary and *secundicerius*, and further praises his collections and excerpts from the works of Saint Gregory.

Concerning him and his work, Sigebert of Gembloux writes in his book *On Illustrious Men* as follows:

“Paterius, notary and *secundicerius* of the Roman Church, collecting all the testimonies of Holy Scripture through which Gregory clarified the obscurities of his exposition, published three books: two on testimonies of the Old Testament and one on testimonies of the New Testament. He called the volume itself the Book of Testimonies.”

John Trithemius says nearly the same in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, adding that Paterius’s work begins with the words, “When the most blessed and apostolic . . .,” which are read at the beginning of Paterius’s preface.

From these ancient testimonies concerning Paterius, in which nothing is said of his episcopal rank, the reliability of Arnold Wion, who asserts that he was bishop of Brescia, appears uncertain and highly doubtful—especially since the inscriptions of the manuscript codices that contain his work do not call him a bishop. Yet in these ancient manuscripts, as well as in the Roman Martyrology, he has acquired the much more distinguished title of saint.

III. Paterius’s work should moreover be valued all the more because it was begun and completed under the authority and encouragement of Saint Gregory, and also had Gregory as its approver, as we understand from its preface. For the method followed in this work and the other matters relating to it, one should read the preface, from which it is especially clear that the work was arranged in three volumes, so that two would contain the books of the Old Testament and the third those of the New Testament.

Of the three parts of which it consists, however, only one began to see the public light in the year 1553. Thereafter the first part, on the Old Testament, was reprinted very often, while the second, likewise on the Old Testament, and the third, which embraces the exposition of the New Testament, still lie hidden and neglected in the dust of libraries.

IV. Nevertheless, in the Vatican edition prepared at the command of Sixtus V, and in subsequent editions, especially the latest Paris edition made public in 1675 through the care and scholarship of Peter Gussanville, there is read under the name of Saint Paterius a book on the exposition of the New Testament. But after comparing this work with the ancient manuscripts of Paterius, we have proved that it is entirely different.

The codices we used for this collation are the Vatican manuscript, of excellent quality; the Beauvais manuscript, from the library of the major church of Saint Peter; the Clairvaux manuscript, that is, of the monastery of Clairvaux of the Cistercian order; the Bec manuscript; and the Michaelinus manuscript, that is, of the celebrated monastery of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea.

All these codices, each of which bears an age of either six hundred or five hundred years, transmit a different work on the New Testament by Saint Paterius from the one we read in the printed editions. Accordingly, having rejected the latter, we judged it preferable to publish that exposition of the New Testament which, through the agreement of so many handwritten codices, is affirmed and vindicated as Paterius’s.

“Whose offspring, then,” you will ask, “are those excerpts of Gregorian testimonies for explaining the New Testament that the printed books attribute to Paterius?”

V. Since we had established from the words and opinions of many of the ancients—men who took particular pleasure in reading Gregory’s works—that they had woven together various bundles of excerpts from them, and since we had seen so many manuscript codices in which these collections are read, but with the name of the excerptor usually concealed, it was not immediately easy to determine to whom this notable work ought to be attributed.

Nevertheless, there was no slight conjecture that the parent of this noble offspring was Alulf, a monk of Saint Martin of Tournai, exceedingly famous in his own age. Nor was the conjecture mistaken. We subsequently encountered manuscripts of excellent reliability, such as those of Longpont and Königsberg, in which this same Exposition of the New Testament is contained with Alulf’s name prefixed.

Even this was not sufficient for us. Returning to the source itself, we took care to consult the codices of the aforementioned monastery of Tournai, with the gracious permission of its most religious and illustrious abbot.

VI. Four codices survive that are believed to be autographs—that is, written by Alulf’s own hand.

In the first codex, concerning the Old Testament, which bears Alulf’s name at its beginning, the following is read:

“The prologue to the following work begins. After the restoration of Saint Martin of Tournai in the year 1092 of the Lord’s Incarnation, when I, Brother Alulf, a monk of that place, repeatedly ran through the sayings of the most blessed and apostolic Gregory by reading them, and was somewhat intent and eager in reading his books because of the exceptionally lucid satisfaction afforded by his words, I discovered in them something beyond comparison, above all something that wonderfully stirred and kindled my mind.

“For while I was endeavoring to examine the most abstruse history of the holy man Job, covered by the shadows of mysteries, under a threefold heading—typical, moral, and historical exposition—and, having driven away the cloud of ignorance, to display it openly to all with a serene revelation clearer than daylight, I was compelled, by the necessity of explaining the matters involved, to expound nearly the whole sequence of the Old and New Testaments, and so forth.”

In the second codex is prefixed:

[Note: This is the title that Alulf affixed to the complete work and to each of its parts, as can be seen both in the manuscripts mentioned above and in those of Königsberg and Longpont.]

“Gregorialis on the Psalms and Prophets.”

VII. The third codex, containing the Exposition of the New Testament, begins with this preface:

“Through the four holy living creatures shown to the prophet Ezekiel,” and so forth, as in the Vatican and Gussanville editions.

The title of this third part is: “On the Four Gospels.” Later:

“Here begins the exposition of Matthew.

“1. The generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Our Lord Jesus Christ, coming for the redemption of the human race, as though some kind of . . .”

“2. And after the Babylonian captivity, the Psalmist says concerning the Lord: ‘The stone . . .’”

“3. Joseph took Mary; he did not know her until she gave birth to her firstborn Son. This must be understood to have been said in this way . . .”

The remainder is entirely similar to what has been printed under Paterius’s name, except that the codex contains ninety-seven chapters of exposition on Matthew, while the printed editions contain 104.

The fourth codex is entitled “Gregorialis on Sentences,” and concludes with these verses by the author:

“May Alulf, who drew these little works from Gregory’s book,

“Rest in peace through Gregory’s prayers.”

What we observed in the codices mentioned above is wonderfully confirmed by the testimony of Herimann, which we shall soon publish.

After seeing these things, there was no longer any room for doubt that this work on the New Testament, carelessly attributed to Paterius by the editors, ought to be restored to Alulf in our edition. We inserted it after Paterius’s work both because it is worthy of the light of publication and because we resolved to omit nothing that has already been published and circulated in print by others.

VIII. We have now identified two parts of Paterius’s three-part work, the first and the third. We must now discuss the second, which has until now remained unpublished.

We had heard and read that it was contained in the codex of the Reverend Fathers of the Celestines of Paris, and therefore we took care to examine the codex with our own attentive eyes. But in the very prologue, which we shall append, it immediately became clear that the work was not Paterius’s, but that of some learned man who, in order to repair the loss of the second part of Paterius’s work, had compiled something similar with great fidelity and diligence from the sayings of Saint Gregory, as he himself admits.

At last, while we were persistently examining every compartment of the libraries, especially to discover whether this other part of Paterius’s collection on the Old Testament might be hidden somewhere—a part whose absence we knew learned men regretted—it was found in the Michaelinus codex already mentioned by us. There, after the first volume, which concludes with the exposition of the Song of Songs, had been completed, the following immediately follows:

“Excerpts from the minor works of blessed Pope Gregory on the chapters of the Book of Wisdom that follow.”

This second part ends with the explanation of the prophet Zechariah. At the end, however, a few Gregorian sentences are added, explaining certain verses of the Psalms.

The third part of Paterius’s work on the New Testament is then attached to it, preceded by the following:

“Chapters taken from the Gospel according to Matthew.”

This is as in the other manuscripts already praised—the Vatican, Beauvais, Bec, and Clairvaux manuscripts—from which we have taken the third part of Paterius’s collection.

Enjoy, therefore, Christian and devout reader, this twofold portion of Paterius’s labors, which, with the help of ancient codices previously not examined with sufficient care, we have restored to you.

IX. We shall now say a few words about the first part, from which we begin the publication of Paterius. Although it has already been printed many times, either separately or together with all the Gregorian works, when we noticed that it was teeming with countless errors, we employed many manuscript codices to revise and purge it: the Michaelinus already mentioned; the Vatican manuscript also mentioned above; the Uticense manuscript of Saint-Evroult; and the Gemeticensis. Finally, we used the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Martin at Sées only to restore the Expositions on the Books of Kings and Proverbs.

Following these codices, we changed the beginnings of nearly all the chapters. Here is a sample of the other errors that we deleted and corrected.

In chapter 5 on the Book of Numbers, both the Vatican and Gussanville editions read: “so that they may serve external vices without offense.” What a monstrosity! It should read: “external duties.”

Chapter 2 of the same Book of Numbers begins, according to both editions, with these words: “Among which Aaron’s staff blossomed.” Where is the sense? It should instead be read as in the ancient codices: “Concerning the twelve staffs placed in the tabernacle, among which . . .”

In the following chapter the same printed editions read: “and sprinkles against the doors of the tabernacle, unless the whole congregation is understood at once.” Do you understand it? Many words have been omitted. After “tabernacle” the following must be added: “What is meant in this passage by ‘tabernacle’ except the whole congregation taken together?”

In the same chapter: “Yet it [hyssop] brings inflation to the lung.” A splendid reason, certainly, for commending this plant! We have restored the reading: “Yet it removes inflammation from the lung.”

A little later one reads: “Let him imitate the one from whom he is, unless we do something outside the imitation of the Passion, not so much . . .” You seek the sense, but how could you extract it? By changing *nisi* (“unless”) to *ne si* (“lest if”), as follows: “Let him imitate him . . . lest, if we do something outside his imitation, we practice not virtue but vice,” as the manuscripts have it.

Not far from these words, we restored in both editions an entire sentence extending over several lines that had been omitted.

We removed six hundred errors of this kind. We have not always thought it necessary to warn the reader about them, for it is tiresome to mark so often with the censor’s rod the faults committed by others, and indeed by learned men.

Nor do we wonder that such blemishes entered the earlier editions produced by Roman printers through the carelessness of the workers. But that Gussanville retained the same errors—even though the clinging and utterly dislocated sense would plainly have been certain evidence of corruption, which it would have been very easy to remedy from Paterius’s manuscripts or even from the reading of Saint Gregory himself—this, certainly, causes us no small astonishment.

Yet this ancient writer ought not to have been published so negligently. Through his excerpts our Gregory can be illuminated more and more; genuine works can be recognized; excellent readings can be confirmed; and many variants, not to be despised, can be supplied.

X. Nevertheless, it must be observed that not everything read differently in Paterius from the passages of Saint Gregory’s works that are cited should be regarded as a different or variant reading. For the disciple sometimes chose to alter his teacher’s sayings slightly.

Thus, in chapter 37 on Genesis, Paterius has: “When the Apostle says, ‘Neither is he who plants anything,’ and so forth.” But in chapter 28 on Job, number 43, from which Paterius drew the saying, you have: “When the Truth says, ‘Who shut in the sea with doors?’ and so forth.” The passages are similar.

He also often presents Gregorian sayings in reversed order and joins passages that are far apart. Consequently, we labored and sweated greatly to find them in Saint Gregory’s works, especially since manuscript codices and, very often, printed editions are misleading in identifying the places from which they were excerpted. Nevertheless, there are very few whose true source we have not indicated.

We encountered many chapters in the printed editions that are not found in the manuscripts. We did not, however, think they should be rejected; it was sufficient for us to point out the manuscripts’ silence, especially since we discovered that the contexts cited occur in Gregory.

XI. Since, after restoring Paterius in this way, we judged that Alulf’s third part of the work on the New Testament—often circulated under Paterius’s name—should be appended, it is worthwhile to warn the reader that in this collection Gregory’s sayings have been altered and interpolated even more freely than in Paterius’s collection, to such an extent that the excerptor often retained only the sense and showed no concern for the wording.

Alulf flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century. Herimann says the following about him in the *History of the Restoration of the Monastery of Saint Martin of Tournai*, volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, number 38, pages 395 and following:

“He was first a cleric and then a monk. In the aforementioned monastery he held the office of librarian or cantor for forty-seven years. Repeatedly rereading all the books of blessed Gregory, he imitated Paterius, excerpting from Gregory all the sayings he had expounded, both from the Old and the New Testament. He then composed three codices and added a fourth on very useful sayings, giving them the name ‘Gregorialis.’”

PROLOGUE OF PATERIUS TO THE SECOND PART OF THE EXCERPTS FROM THE MINOR WORKS OF BLESSED POPE GREGORY. (C)*

To Lord Werner, joined in sacred marriage to the Virgin who is to remain a bride, Bruno offers, from the seed of his own virginity—that is, the word—many spiritual sons spiritually begotten, through and with whom may you deserve to receive eternal rewards.

When a pious and prudent authority commands and arranges that a matter at once conspicuous for the splendor of its honesty and full of the fruits of usefulness should be undertaken, and humble obedience, without offering any evasive resistance to what has been commanded, does not shrink from attacking it with all the effort of its mind and according to its powers, there is no doubt that divine mercy both forewarns the one who commands and assists the one who has humbly undertaken the task so that he may complete it effectively.

The venerable Father Lord Bernard, who, whenever he is granted any leisure, is accustomed to apply himself to Holy Scripture so that through frequent conversation with it he may more fully learn the divine will and follow it in his conduct, happened to find Paterius’s collection, in which he had gathered in order testimonies excerpted from the works of Saint Gregory. When he recognized that it breathed the honey of Gregory’s eloquence, he set other matters aside for a while and devoted to it all the leisure he could command.

But the codex that had come into his hands had been so falsified through the carelessness of scribes that scarcely anyone, even one free from other burdens of care, could find complete sentences in it. He therefore wished to assign me the task of carefully correcting it for him, so that, when time for reading was granted, the corrupted book would not repel him.

After receiving the book and hastening to examine its entire prologue and the work that followed, I discovered that it contained only a third part. For its prologue makes clear that he had collected explanations of testimonies from the Gregorian works from all the books of both Testaments and had divided the entire work into three volumes. Yet in it I found only a few passages concerning the Parables of Solomon and the Song of Songs; concerning the other books called Solomon’s, none; concerning the Prophets, none; and concerning the books of the New Testament, none.

Accordingly, I obtained through friends whatever other copies of a book with the same name I could find, so that the corruption of our codex might be corrected by their form. They appeared so similar to ours in false readings and omissions that one might have conjectured either that they had been written as an example from ours, or that ours and they had been copied from some wholly false exemplar—except that, the newer they were than ours, the fuller they were of false readings.

I therefore set those copies aside and consulted the titles prefixed to the chapters of the testimonies, so that with their assistance both the book and the place in the book from which the excerpted sentence had been taken might be found; thus, if the scribes had corrupted anything, it could be emended by the testimony of the book from which it had been written. But I found the titles so altered that, with very few exceptions, one could never find in that book any chapter that the prefixed title indicated was there.

I then girded myself for the work and began to run through all the books of Saint Gregory that we possess. I did not cease from my labor until I had investigated in which book the chapters contained in that book of Paterius had been placed. I then took care to correct them from the very passages from which they had been taken. To make it easier to correct anything that might later have been corrupted through the fault of scribes in the same way, I wrote above each sentence not only the book in which it was found but also the chapter of the book.

Although, while searching, many testimonies from books that the codex did not contain spontaneously presented themselves to me, I decided to investigate more scrupulously, with greater diligence, whatever could be found and to collect it in the same order in which I had seen those passages arranged.

Thus it happened that, although at the command of that father I had undertaken to correct only a third part, I not only corrected it but also added the two parts that I could not find in these regions.

Lest anyone think that I did this for the sake of boasting, let him know that if anyone can and wishes to show me Paterius’s complete collection, I shall present myself with every eagerness, willingly setting my own work aside, and shall hold his work in the great veneration that is fitting. So long as I cannot obtain it, however, I wish to preserve this work for reading by myself and my friends alone.

I therefore took care to insert this preface at the beginning of the book so that, if it should happen to come into the hands of someone who possesses that complete work, he might recognize the difference between the two and understand which he ought to place first. But since your Magnificence deigned to order that the same work be transcribed for you, I have been pleased to strengthen this undertaking with the authority of your name, so that, when anyone sees your name on the first page, every detractor may place a finger on his lips, and no ill-willed person dare criticize what he sees a man of such probity and prudence not to have disdained.

[Note: The manuscripts have different titles. The Vatican codex has: “In the name of the Holy Trinity: the prologue of Paterius begins.” The Gemeticensis agrees, except that after “Paterius” it adds “disciple of Saint Gregory, pope.” It also reads “Saint Paterius.” The Uticense has: “In the name, etc., begins the book of Saint Paterius, disciple of blessed Gregory, pope.” The Michaelinus has: “The prologue of Paterius begins, on the Testimonies of the New and Old Testaments expounded by blessed Pope Gregory.”]

SAINT PATERIUS’S BOOK ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, COMPOSED FROM VARIOUS BOOKS OF SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT. (C,S)*

Prologue.

When I repeatedly ran through the sayings of our most blessed and apostolic pontiff Gregory—your pontiff as well, and, I shall add, your nourisher—and the exceptionally lucid satisfaction afforded by his words urged me to devote myself to them more eagerly and continually, I discovered in them something beyond comparison, something of the highest importance.

While, therefore, he was endeavoring to examine the history of one holy man, namely blessed Job, covered by the obscure shadows of mysteries, through a threefold exposition—that is, typical, moral, and historical—and, having driven away the cloud of ignorance, to display it openly to all with a serene revelation clearer than daylight, he was compelled by the necessity of explaining the matters involved to expound nearly the entire sequence of the Old and New Testaments.

[Note: The Uticense and Gemeticensis read “into inner light.” The Vatican reads: “or he himself might appear to know the inner matter without the clearest explanation.”]
