Whenever the necessity of clarifying some exceedingly obscure matter arose, so that either something obscure might not remain in the minds of his hearers or he himself might not appear to cast the obscurity into inner light without the clearest explanation, he not only opened what had been closed through the most eloquent assertions of his words, [Note: We have restored this corrupt passage in the printed editions and in most manuscripts with the help of the Vatican edition. In nearly all the others, “he confirmed by assertion, lest” is absent. In the edition, “by himself” is read instead of “to be so.”]

but also confirmed it through the assertion of the testimony that had been brought forward, lest any obscurity that might remain in the matter being explained, because it was not understood, should increase rather than remove the darkness.

He took care to discuss that testimony by adding an explanation of the exposition. For in certain passages, even in the exposition of the testimony, he judged that the satisfaction provided by the words alone was insufficient unless he explained the matter more fully through the evident interpretation of another testimony brought forward in turn.

Thus it came about that, on this occasion, as I said above, nearly the entire hidden sequence of the Old Testament was disclosed. Once opened by the inspiration of the divine will, it satisfied the hunger of our famine with an abundance of heavenly nourishment.

Moved by an exceedingly ardent desire for this, I had begun to excerpt some of these same testimonies with a certain brevity, while passing over others through neglect. As my conscience itself bears witness, while this was happening, and while I wished and carefully took precautions that no one should learn of it in any way, the matter nevertheless reached our apostolic pontiff through certain people.

He immediately began to kindle me with exhortations in words that Your Beatitude knows—words persuasive and drawing one toward heavenly things—so that I should complete with greater diligence what I had begun carelessly, and should indicate in the heading of each testimony both the work and the book in which the testimony was read, or from which it had arisen.

Considering the weight of this task and the impossibility of my own strength, I found myself in doubt. Like a sailor shaken by a violent storm of waves, I fled, I confess, fearfully yet confidently to the harbor of his prayers, knowing that what such a great prelate ordered could not be impossible, since he ordered it so that the work might benefit many people.

Immediately, encouraged by the support of the one giving the command, I undertook the task and, with whatever diligence I could muster, collected into one body the testimonies of the Old and New Testaments. From that point on, I no longer took carelessly to leave anything from his other works unexamined, as I had first begun to do with his exposition of blessed Job.

As I passed through the passages recorded on their separate sheets, scattered just as they had been found, it seemed to me—although the labor would be immense—that I should arrange and compose the testimonies concerning each subject according to the order in which they are situated in their own books, organizing them by book.

In this way, the desire of the diligent reader, seeking to clarify whatever obscurity he wished, would not be delayed even briefly by finding the title of the book he was looking for.

[Note: In the printed editions, many omissions and additions here produce inextricable obscurity. We follow the manuscripts.]

I must above all warn the reader of this work to know the following: because I found certain testimonies situated in different places, and because in some passages they had been developed typologically in the exposition and in others historically, I arranged separately and in sequence the material that I found expounded in the aforementioned ways, transferring the corresponding passages to one another.

In certain places, however, because the standard of explanation required it, I rewove the same material from the same testimony that is read as having been explained earlier. [Note: The printed editions read: “I supplied also the repeated passages”; and a little later: “the same testimony.”]

Elsewhere, I supplied, among repeated passages, certain things that he had said about it not long before.

I excerpted these things from what had already been said and adapted them for insertion into the same testimony wherever the place required it, because they were not matters that could usefully be set down separately, since they depended on what had been said in the preceding and following passages.

For if, because of the novelty of a small matter, what had already been said were stated again, the repetitions would undoubtedly produce tedium. [Note: The printed editions and the Gemeticensis and Vatican manuscripts read “lest” instead of “so that.”]

Thus, if, on returning to the order of the exposition from which these excerpts were taken, you find in certain places of this work something more or less than has been placed in the text of the book, the reason is the one I have explained above.

Considering that, if I wished to collect the testimonies of both Testaments into one work, it would exceed the proper size of a volume and impede the reader’s desire, I arranged it, with the Lord’s cooperation, in three volumes, so that two would contain the sayings of the Old Testament and the third those of the New.

I have taken pains to send these to Your Beatitude, not rashly or presumptuously, but moved by my love for your zeal—the zeal that once burned in the investigation of divine eloquence—and knowing how great your mind’s eagerness for knowledge is, especially concerning the sayings of our aforementioned pontiff. I have composed a small work from many volumes.

With the humble prayer I am able to offer, I beg that, when you or anyone who reads it has found the care of my labor pleasing in this work, you may deign to be intercessors for me before the Lord, so that, once freed from this burden of corruption, I may deserve to be found released from the bonds of my sins.

First Part, in Which These Books of the Old Testament Are Explained: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, Kings, Psalms, Proverbs, and the Song of Songs.

[Note: [Col. 0685D] In the editions it reads: “Here begins the exposition of the books of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges and Kings, and of the Psalms.” Why are Proverbs and the Song of Songs not added to the Psalms? In fact, this title is found in no manuscripts. The title we have prefixed was supplied chiefly by the Michaelian Codex [Col. 0686D].]

## BOOK ONE

### On Testimonies concerning the Book of Genesis

[Col. 0685]

### CHAPTER I  
On the created heaven, which afterward he called the firmament (Gen. 1:8)

[Col. 0685C]

Blessed Pope Gregory, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book twenty-seven (no. 65), speaking of the angels, says among other things:

“The angelic powers, which remained fixed in divine love, received this gift in recompense when the proud angels fell: that they should now be bitten by no rust of encroaching sin, that they should remain in contemplation of the Creator without end to their happiness, and that they should persist with eternal stability in the state for which they were created. Moses’ very words in the account of the world’s origin aptly attest this, when heaven is first said to have been made, and afterward that same heaven is called the firmament. For the angelic nature was first created subtle in the higher regions, and afterward, lest it should ever be able to fall, was more wondrously confirmed.”

### CHAPTER II  
Likewise, from the passage above

[Col. 0685D]

In the *Commentaries on Ezekiel*, homily 7 (no. 18):

“Angels were created in such a way that, if they wished, they could persist in the light of blessedness, but if they did not wish to, they could also have fallen. Hence Satan fell with his legions of followers [Col. 0686C]. But after his fall, the angels who remained were so strengthened that they could not fall at all. This is aptly signified at the very beginning of the Book of Genesis by its historical account: ‘God created heaven and earth,’ which afterward he called the firmament. Therefore, those who were first created well were called heaven, but afterward were called the firmament, because they received the power of unchangeability so that they would no longer fall at all.”

### CHAPTER III  
“Light was made.” And shortly afterward: “Evening was made” (Gen. 1:3)

While the temptations of the elect were being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 8 (no. 21), the following was added:

“‘Light was made.’ And shortly afterward: ‘Evening was made.’—By no means is sin in this life abandoned through the practice of righteousness in such a way that one remains unshakably in that same righteousness. For although uprightness already drives guilt from the dwelling place of the heart, the guilt that is repelled nevertheless sits at the doors of our thoughts and knocks to have them opened. Moses spiritually intimates this when he narrated temporal events accomplished in the material world, saying: [Col. 0687A] ‘Light was made’; and shortly afterward adding: ‘Evening was made.’ The Creator of all things, foreknowing human guilt, then expressed in time what is now enacted in the mind. Light is led toward evening, because the shadow of temptation follows the illumination of uprightness. But because the light of the elect is not extinguished by temptation, it is said that not night but evening was made: temptation often hides the light of righteousness in the hearts of the upright, but does not destroy it; it draws it, as it were, toward the pallor of fear, but does not utterly extinguish it.”

### CHAPTER IV  
“The earth brought forth green vegetation, producing seed according to its kind, and a tree making fruit, each having its seed according to its species” (Gen. 1:12)

While the virtues of the Church were being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 19 (no. 29), the following was added:

“‘The earth brought forth green vegetation,’ and so forth.—What the historical account testifies was truly done in such a way as to signify something that was truly to be done. For by the earth the Church is figured [Col. 0687B], which both refreshes us with the nourishment of the word and guards us with the shelter of her protection; she feeds by speaking and protects by helping, so that she brings forth not only the grass of refreshment but also supplies, with the fruit of good works, the tree of protection.”

### CHAPTER V  
Likewise, from the passage above: “A tree making fruit” (Gen. 1:12)

While love of neighbor was being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 6 (no. 54), the following was added:

“‘A tree making fruit,’ and so forth.—A tree produces seed according to its kind when our mind, by considering itself, gathers itself together in relation to another person so as to bring forth the seed of a righteous deed. Hence a certain wise man said: ‘What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another’ (Tob. 4:16). Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them’ (Matt. 7:12). It is as though he plainly said: Look upon your own kind in one another, and from yourselves recognize what you ought to offer to others.”

### CHAPTER VI  
Likewise, from the passage above: “The earth brought forth green vegetation” (Gen. 1:12)

[Col. 0687C]

While the works of the Church were being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 29 (no. 52), the following was added:

“‘The earth brought forth,’ and so forth.—What is represented here by the grass except good action? Although we accept that this took place historically in the creation of the world, we nevertheless rightly understand the earth to have prefigured the Church, which brought forth green vegetation in that she produced, in response to the word of God, fruitful works of mercy.”

### CHAPTER VII  
“Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26)

While the creation of the first man was being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 9 (no. 75), the following was added:

“‘Let us make,’ and so forth.—Although all things were created through the coeternal Word of the Father, the very account of creation nevertheless shows how greatly man is preferred to all animals and to created things, even heavenly things, though insensible. For when he was making all things, ‘He spoke, and they were made’ (Ps. 32:9). But when he decreed to make man, consider with what reverence he prefaced it, saying: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ For it is not written of him, as of the other things, ‘Let it be made, and it was made’; nor did he produce man as he produced the creatures of the waters or the birds. Rather, before he was made, ‘Let us make’ is said, so that, since a rational creature was being created, he might appear to have been made, as it were, with deliberation. He was formed from the earth, as though with special care, and raised up by the Creator’s inspiration through the power of the life-giving spirit, so that the one made in the Creator’s image might come into existence not through the voice of command but through the dignity of the work.”

### CHAPTER VIII  
“God rested on the seventh day from all the work that he had done” (Gen. 2:2)

[Col. 0688A]

While the perfection of the number seven was being discussed, in the *Exposition of Job*, book 1 (no. 18), the following was added:

“What is understood in the number seven except the fullness of perfection? To leave aside the considerations of human reasoning concerning the number seven—which assert that it is perfect because it consists of the first even number that can be divided and the first odd number that cannot be divided—we know with complete certainty that Holy Scripture customarily uses the number seven to signify perfection. Hence it says that on the seventh day the Lord rested from his works. For this reason the seventh day was given to human beings for rest, that is, as the Sabbath. For this reason the jubilee year, in which complete rest is expressed, is completed after seven weeks; with the addition of one unit, the fullness of our activity is brought to completion. For this reason, too, twelve apostles were chosen to be filled with the perfection of the sevenfold grace. Thus one rises from the number seven to the number twelve; [Col. 0688B] for seven, multiplied by its own parts, extends toward twelve. Whether four is multiplied by three or three by four, seven is transformed into twelve. Hence the holy apostles, because they were sent to preach the Trinity in the four regions of the world, were chosen as twelve, so that by their number also they might display the perfection that they preached by life and word.”

### CHAPTER IX  
From the passage above

In the *Exposition of Blessed Job* (same passage):

[Note: [Col. 0687D] In the Gemetian manuscript it is assigned to book 25; in the Michaelian, to book 35; in the editions, to book 6, where at no. 43 certain similar material is found. But it is much more similar to book 1, no. 18.]

“The perfection of eternity is intimated by the number seven, when the seventh day is called sanctified for the Lord’s rest. It is no longer called evening, because the rest of eternal blessedness is confined by no limit.”

[Note: [Col. 0687D] In the manuscripts this chapter is joined to the preceding one and forms a single chapter [Col. 0688D].]

### CHAPTER X  
“These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created” (Gen. 2:4)

In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 32 (no. 16):

“We must ask how God created all things simultaneously, since Moses himself describes them as created distinctly through the varying succession of six days. We recognize this more readily [Note: [Col. 0688D] Gemetian and Utican manuscripts: ‘if we investigate the origin of the cause itself.’] if we examine carefully the very causes of their origins. The substance of things was created simultaneously, but it was not simultaneously formed according to its species; and what existed simultaneously in the substance of matter did not appear simultaneously in the form of its species.

“When heaven and earth are described as having been made simultaneously, this indicates that spiritual and bodily things were made simultaneously, as was everything that arises from heaven and everything that is produced from earth. The sun, moon, and stars are said to have been made in heaven on the fourth day; but what came forth into visible form on the fourth day already existed on the first day in the substance of heaven through creation.

“On the first day the earth is said to have been created; on the third day the shrubs were established and all the green things of the earth are described. But what brought itself forth into visible form on the third day had undoubtedly already been created on the first day in the substance of the earth from which it arose.

“Thus Moses both reported that everything was created distinctly on each successive day and nevertheless added that everything was created simultaneously, saying: ‘These are the generations of heaven and earth, when [Note: [Col. 0688D] Against the manuscripts, the printed editions read ‘they were created.’] they were created, on the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth and every plant of the field before it sprang up in the earth, and every herb of the region.’ Although he had narrated that heaven, earth, plants, and herbs were created on different days, he now declares that they were made on a single day, clearly showing that every creature came into existence simultaneously in substance, although it did not emerge simultaneously in form.

“Likewise it is written: ‘God created man in his own image and likeness; in the image of God he created him; male and female he made them’ (Gen. 1:27). Eve is not yet described as having been made, and already the human being is said to be male and female. But because the woman was certainly to proceed from Adam’s side, she is already counted in him in substance, from whom she was to be produced in form.

“We can also consider these matters in the smallest things, so that from the smallest we may contemplate the greater. When grass is created, neither the fruit nor the seed of its fruit is yet visible in it. Yet fruit and seed are present in it even when they do not appear, because they are simultaneously present in the substance of the root, although they do not emerge simultaneously through the progress of time.”

### CHAPTER XI  
That the earth is watered by four rivers flowing out of Paradise (Gen. 2:10)

While the four virtues were being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 2 (no. 76), the following was added:

“Prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice contain the solid structure of our mind, because the entire edifice of good works rises upon these four virtues. Thus the four rivers of Paradise water the earth, because when the heart is infused with these four virtues, it is tempered against the entire heat of carnal desires.”

### CHAPTER XII  
“The Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and guard it” (Gen. 2:15)

[Col. 0689B]

While the preservation of the guardianship of good works was being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 19 (no. 34), the following was added:

“We must consider with the greatest care that good works cannot benefit us if the evils that creep in are not avoided. Everything that is done perishes if it is not carefully guarded in humility. Hence it is also well said of that first parent: ‘The Lord placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and guard it’ (Gen. 2:15). One works when one does the good that is commanded; but one does not guard what one has done when what is forbidden creeps in [Above, at the end of no. 33]. Therefore we must always do good works, and cautiously guard ourselves in thought even from those very good works. For if they elevate the mind, they are not good, because they serve not the Author but pride.

[Note: [Col. 0689D] Vatican manuscript: ‘Why do we not act disorderly?’] “We do not act disorderly in this matter if we produce testimony from books that, although not canonical, were nevertheless added for the edification of the Church. Eleazar struck down an elephant in battle, but he fell beneath the very creature he had destroyed (1 Macc. 6). Whom, then, does this man signify—the man whom his own victory crushed—except those who overcome vices but, by becoming proud beneath the very vices they subdue, succumb? For one dies, as it were, beneath the enemy he has overthrown when he is lifted up by the fault he has overcome.”

### CHAPTER XIII  
“Eve proceeded from the side of the sleeping Adam” (Gen. 2:21–22)

While withdrawal of the mind to the Lord was being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 30 (no. 54), the following was added:

“‘From the side of Adam,’ and so forth.—We must know that we never attain the summit of contemplation unless we cease from the burden of external cares. We can never look upon ourselves and know that there is in us one element that is rational and rules, and another that is animal and is ruled, unless, returning to secret silence, we are lulled to sleep away from every external disturbance. Our silence was well represented by the sleeping Adam, from whose side a woman immediately proceeded. For whoever is snatched away to understand inner realities closes his eyes to visible things, and then distinguishes within himself what ought to preside manfully and what is weak and ought to be subordinate, so that within him there is one element capable of ruling like a man and another, like a woman, that is ruled.”

### CHAPTER XIV  
“Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of Paradise?” (Gen. 3:1)

In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 24 (no. 14), [Note: [Col. 0689D] In the editions it is assigned to book 34, chapter 5, toward the end, where, however, we find nothing. In the Utican manuscript no work of Gregory is cited. The Gemetian manuscript indicates book 34 of *Job*. It exists at the place assigned by us.] while the avoidance of the enemy’s temptations was being discussed, the following was added:

“‘Why did God command you not to eat,’ and so forth.—The crafty enemy of the human race does not cease daily doing what he did in Paradise. He strives to tear God’s words from human hearts and to implant in them the seductive blandishments of his false promise. Daily he makes light of what God threatens and alters it in order to deliver what he falsely promises.

“For he falsely promises temporal things so that he may make light in human minds of those punishments that God threatens as eternal. When he promises the glory of the present life, what else does he say than, ‘Taste, and you will be like gods’? As though he plainly said: ‘Touch temporal desire, and appear exalted in this world.’ And when he attempts to remove fear of the divine judgment, what else does he say than what he said to the first human beings: ‘Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of Paradise?’

“But because redeemed humanity has received, by divine grace, the righteousness that it lost after having been created, it now exercises itself more strongly against the blandishments of crafty persuasion, having learned by experience how obedient it ought to be to the commandment. The one whom guilt then led to punishment is now restrained from guilt by his punishment, so that he fears transgressing all the more because, compelled by punishment, he now himself condemns what he has committed.”

[Note: [Col. 0690D] This chapter is omitted in our manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER XV  
“On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5)

While the day of perdition was being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 4 (no. 6), the following was added:

“‘On whatever day,’ and so forth.—The day, therefore, is the promise of better things that was offered; but night is the experience of calamities that was brought forth. The ancient enemy is day by nature, having been created good, but is night by merit, having fallen into darkness. He is day when, by promising good things, he pretends before human eyes to be an angel of light, as Paul bears witness, saying: ‘For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light’ (2 Cor. 11:14). But he is night when he darkens the minds of those who consent to him with the darkness of error.”

### CHAPTER XVI  
Likewise, from the passage above

[Col. 0690C]

In the first part of the *Book of Gospel Homilies*, homily 16 (nos. 2–3):

“The ancient enemy rose up against our first parent, the first man, in three temptations, because he tempted him through gluttony, vainglory, and avarice; but by tempting him he overcame him, since he subjected him to himself through consent.

“He tempted him through gluttony when he displayed the food of the forbidden tree and persuaded him to eat. He tempted him through vainglory when he said: ‘You will be like gods.’ He tempted him through the advancement of avarice when he said: ‘Knowing good and evil.’ For avarice concerns not only money but also elevation; ambition for exaltation beyond measure is rightly called avarice. If the ambition for honor did not belong to avarice, Paul would never have said of the only-begotten Son: ‘He did not regard equality with God as plunder’ (Phil. 2:6).

“In this way, therefore, the devil drew our parent into pride when he stirred him to the avarice of exaltation. But by the very means through which he laid low the first man, he himself succumbed when tempting the second man. He tempted him through gluttony when he said: ‘Command that these stones become loaves of bread’ (Matt. 4:3). He tempted him through vainglory when he said: ‘If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.’ He tempted him through the avarice of exaltation when he showed him all the kingdoms of the world, saying: ‘All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me’ (ibid., 9).

“But he was defeated by the second man by the very means by which he boasted that he had conquered the first, so that, having been captured at the very entrance by which he held us when he entered, he might depart from our hearts.”

### CHAPTER XVII  
“The woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful to behold” (Gen. 3:6)

While the restraint of the lust of sight was being discussed, [Col. 0691A] in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 21 (no. 4), the following was added:

“We must take care not to turn slippery things over in our thoughts, because one ought not to look upon what one is not permitted to desire. To preserve a pure mind in thought from the wantonness of its pleasure, the eyes must be lowered, as though they were plunderers leading us to guilt. For Eve would never have touched the forbidden tree unless she had first looked upon it heedlessly.

“From this we must consider how carefully we ought to restrain our sight from illicit things, we who live under the condition of mortality, if even the mother of the living came to death through her eyes. Hence also, in the voice of Judea—which, desiring what she saw externally, had lost the good things within—the prophet says: ‘My eye has plundered my soul’ (Lam. 3:51). For in desiring visible things, she lost invisible virtues. She who lost her inner fruit through outward sight suffered the plundering of her heart through the bodily eye.

“Therefore, to guard the purity of the heart, we must also maintain discipline over the external senses. For however strong the mind may be in virtue, however firm it may be in gravity, the carnal senses nevertheless make a childish noise outside; and unless they are restrained by the weight of inner gravity and by a certain youthful vigor, they draw the enfeebled mind toward every fleeting and trivial thing.”

### CHAPTER XVIII  
On Adam’s consent in accepting the fruit from the woman (Gen. 3)

While the incentives to vices were being discussed in book 3, chapter 29 (Admonition 30) of the *Pastoral Rule*, the following was added:

“In our first parent we learned that we perpetrate every kind of wickedness in sin in three ways: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. The first is perpetrated through the enemy, the second through the flesh, and the third through the spirit. The deceiver suggests what is evil; the flesh submits itself to pleasure; and finally the spirit, overcome by pleasure, consents.

“Thus the serpent suggested evil (Gen. 3); Eve, like the flesh, submitted herself to pleasure; and Adam, like the spirit, overcome by suggestion and pleasure, gave his assent [These words are absent from the indicated passage]. We recognize sin through suggestion, are overcome through pleasure, and are also bound through consent.

“Therefore we must cry out with the Apostle: ‘Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?’ (Rom. 7:24). And let us hear the consolation that follows: ‘The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (ibid., 25).”

### CHAPTER XIX  
“Adam immediately covered his genitals after the sin of disobedience” (Gen. 3:7)

While the guarding of the mind was being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 26 (no. 28), the following was added:

“Through the guardianship of humility, the purity of chastity must always be preserved. For if the spirit is devoutly kept beneath the Lord, the flesh is not unlawfully raised against the spirit. The spirit has dominion over the flesh entrusted to it, provided that it acknowledges in its own Lord the rights of legitimate servitude.

“But if it proudly despises its Creator, it rightly receives battle in the flesh subject to it. Hence that first disobedient man, as soon as he sinned through pride, immediately covered his genitals. Because he had inflicted an insult upon the Lord through his spirit, he immediately encountered an insult in his flesh. And because he did not wish to be subject to his Creator, he lost authority over the subject flesh that he ruled, so that the shame of his disobedience might rebound upon himself and, having been overcome, he might learn what he had lost through being lifted up.”

### CHAPTER XX  
“When Adam heard the voice of the Lord God walking in Paradise at the afternoon breeze, he hid himself among the trees of Paradise” (Gen. 3:8)

While the manner of divine speech was being discussed, [Note: [Col. 0691D] In the Michaelian manuscript: “concerning the gift.”] in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 28 (no. 7), the following was added:

“Sometimes God speaks through angels by words and by actions together, indicating through certain movements what he conveys in speech. For Adam could not see the Lord in the substance of his divinity after his sin; rather, he heard words of reproof through an angel, concerning whom it is written: ‘When Adam heard the voice of the Lord God walking in Paradise at the afternoon breeze, he hid himself among the trees of Paradise.’

“For what does it mean that after human sin the Lord no longer stands in Paradise but walks, except that, when guilt intervened, he showed that he had moved himself away from the human heart? What does ‘at the afternoon breeze’ mean except that the more fervent light of truth had departed and the chills of its sin were constricting the sinful soul?

“Adam is found hidden after his sin at the afternoon breeze. Because he had believed in the noonday warmth of charity, he was now languishing beneath the shadow of sin, as though in the chill of the breeze. As it is written of the same sinful man: ‘Because he followed a shadow.’ Fleeing the warmth of charity, man abandoned the sun of truth and hid himself beneath the shadow of inner cold. Hence the same Truth says: ‘Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold’ (Matt. 24:12).

“Therefore he reproved Adam while walking, so that he might reveal his wickedness to blind minds not only through words but also through actions. Thus the sinful man heard through words what he had done; through the walking he perceived, after losing the state of eternity, the instability of his mutability; through the breeze, with the warmth of charity driven out, he recognized his own torpor; and through the decline of the sun he understood that he was drawing near to darkness.”

### CHAPTER XXI  
“The Lord God called Adam and said to him: Where are you?” (Gen. 3:9)

While the rejection of those who sin was being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 2 (no. 5), the following was added:

“What does it mean that the Lord seeks Adam after his fall, asking, ‘Where are you?’ Did divine power not know to what hiding places the servant had fled after his sin? But because he saw him fallen into guilt and, under sin, hidden as it were from the eyes of truth, and because he does not approve the darkness of his error, he acts as though he does not know where the sinner is. He both calls and seeks him, saying: ‘Adam, where are you?’

“By calling him, he gives a sign that he is summoning him back to repentance. By seeking him, he plainly indicates that he does not acknowledge sinners as rightly condemned.”

### CHAPTER XXII  
“The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12)

While the avoidance of excuses for sin was being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 4 (nos. 39, 49), the following was added:

“Thus he secretly turned the fault of his transgression back upon its author, as though he were saying: ‘You provided the occasion for my sin, since you gave me the woman.’

“Sin is perpetrated in the heart in four ways, and is completed in action in four ways. In the heart it is perpetrated through suggestion, pleasure, consent, and the audacity of self-defense. Suggestion comes through the adversary, pleasure through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and the audacity of self-defense through pride. Guilt, which ought to have terrified the mind, lifts it up; and while casting it down it raises it, but by raising it it trips it more grievously.

“Thus the ancient enemy broke the uprightness of the first man with these four blows. The serpent persuaded, Eve took pleasure, Adam consented, and when questioned he refused through audacity to confess his guilt.

“This is enacted daily in the human race, just as it was enacted in the first parent of our race. The serpent persuaded, because the hidden enemy secretly suggests evil to human hearts. Eve took pleasure, because the carnal sense immediately submits itself to pleasure at the serpent’s words. Adam, placed over the woman, gave his assent, because when the flesh is swept away into pleasure, the spirit too, weakened, is bent from its uprightness. Adam refused to confess his guilt when questioned, because the spirit, separated from truth through sin, becomes all the more wickedly hardened in the audacity of its ruin.

“Adam had fled intending to hide himself through fear, but when questioned he nevertheless revealed how much he still swelled with pride even while afraid. For when present punishment is feared because of sin, while the lost face of God is not loved, fear arises from swelling pride, not from humility. The person who would not abandon sin if he could escape punishment is proud.

“Sin is likewise completed in action in four ways. First, guilt is committed while hidden; afterward the offense is openly revealed before human eyes without shame; then it is brought into habitual practice; and finally it is nourished either by the seductions of false hope or by the wretched obstinacy of despair.”

### CHAPTER XXIII  
Likewise, from the passage above

In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 22 (nos. 30–31):

“True humility is demonstrated both by each person recognizing his own iniquity and by openly disclosing what he has recognized through confession. By contrast, it is a habitual vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling and to defend the sin committed by denying it, and, by defending what has been exposed, to multiply it.

“For from that fall of the first man we derive these increases of wickedness, since from it we drew the very root of guilt. Thus, when he had touched the forbidden tree, he hid himself from the face of the Lord among the trees of Paradise. In this hiding, since he could not actually remain concealed from God, the effect of concealment is not described; rather, his disposition is indicated. When he was accused by the Lord of having touched the forbidden tree, he immediately replied: ‘The woman whom you gave me as a companion, she gave me from the tree, and I ate’ (Gen. 3:12). The woman too, when questioned, replied: ‘The serpent deceived me, and I ate.’

“They had been questioned for this purpose: so that by confessing they might erase the sin they had committed through transgression. Hence that serpent, the persuader who was not to be recalled to pardon, was not questioned about his guilt. The man, then, was asked where he was so that he might look upon the guilt he had committed and, by confessing, recognize how far he was from the face of his Creator [Note: [Col. 0693D] Gemetian and Utican manuscripts: ‘had gone away.’]

“But both chose the consolations of self-defense rather than confession. When the man wished to excuse his sin through the woman and the woman through the serpent, they increased the guilt that they had attempted to protect. Adam obliquely implicated the Lord, since he himself had been the author of their sin by making the woman; Eve referred the guilt back to the Lord, who had placed the serpent in Paradise.

“For they had heard from the mouth of the deceiving devil, ‘You will be like gods’ (ibid., 5). Since they could not become like him in divinity, they attempted, to complete their error, to make the Lord like themselves in guilt. Thus, while trying to defend their offense, they added to it, so that their guilt became more atrocious when examined than it had been when committed.

“Hence the branches of the human race still draw bitterness from this root. When someone is accused of his fault, he hides himself beneath words of defense as beneath the leaves of certain trees and, as if into the dark recesses of his excuse, conceals his face and flees from his Creator, unwilling that what he has done should be known. In this concealment he hides not himself from the Lord but the Lord from himself. He acts so that he may not see the One who sees everything, not so that he himself may not be seen.

“By contrast, for every sinner the beginning of illumination is the humility of confession. The person who is not ashamed to confess the evil he has done now refuses to spare himself. The one who, by defending himself, could accuse himself most swiftly defends himself by accusing himself.

“Hence, when Lazarus was dead and weighed down by a great mass, the Lord did not say, ‘Come back to life,’ but, ‘Come out’ (John 11:43). In this resurrection, which took place in his body, the manner in which we are raised in the heart is signified: the dead man is told, ‘Come out,’ so that a person dead in sin and already buried beneath the weight of evil habit, lying hidden within his own conscience through wickedness, may come out from himself through confession.

“The dead man is told, ‘Come out,’ [Col. 0694A] so that he may be summoned to leave the excuse and concealment of sin and emerge by his own mouth into self-accusation [Note: [Col. 0693D] Corruptly in the editions: ‘to his own excuse,’ and so forth]. Hence the prophet David, reviving from the death of so great a crime, went forth, as it were, at the Lord’s voice, when, reproved by Nathan, he accused himself of what he had done.”

### CHAPTER XXIV  
“You will crawl on your breast and belly” (Gen. 3:14)

While the poisonous operations of the crafty persuader were being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 21 (no. 5), the following was added:

“‘You will crawl on your breast and belly.’—The evil of lust is perpetrated either in thought or in action. For our crafty adversary, when he is driven away from the effect of the deed, strives to pollute secret places through thoughts. Hence the Lord says to the serpent: ‘You will crawl on your breast and belly.’

“The serpent crawls on its belly when the slippery enemy exercises lust through human members subjected to him, all the way to the completion of the act. The serpent crawls on its breast when it pollutes in thought those whom it cannot draw into the act of lust.

“One person already commits lust in action; for him the serpent crawls from its belly. Another turns over in his mind the lust he is to commit; for him the serpent crawls from its breast. But because through thought one proceeds to the completion of acts, the serpent is rightly described as crawling first on its breast and afterward on its belly.”

### CHAPTER XXV  
“I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. [Note: [Col. 0693D] Thus all the manuscripts read *ipsa conteret* (“she will crush”), not *ipsum conteret* (“it—the seed—will crush”). Therefore *ipsa conteret*, referring to the woman, did not creep in through the fraud of modern writers favoring the immaculate conception of the Mother of God, as some critics loudly assert.] She will crush your head, and you will lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3:15)

While the anticipation of the enemy’s suggestions was being discussed, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book 1 (no. 53), the following was added:

“‘I will put enmity between you,’ and so forth.—To crush the serpent’s head is to observe the beginning of his suggestion and, by the careful hand of reflection, uproot it completely from the entrance of the heart. Yet when he is detected at the beginning, he attempts to strike the heel, because, even if he does not strike the intention through his initial suggestion, he aims to deceive in the end.

“But if the heart is once corrupted in its intention, the middle and the end of the ensuing action are securely possessed by the crafty enemy, since he sees that the entire tree will bear fruit for him after he has wounded it at the root with his poisonous tooth.”

### CHAPTER XXVI  
“Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3:17)

While the distinction between curses was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV (number 1, 2):

> “Cursed is the earth in your work.”

When the divine voice arms the dart of a curse to strike with grave retribution, so that it even closes the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, what does it mean that now, through a curse upon the earth, the divine voice inflicts upon sinful man what man is forbidden to do? It must be understood that Holy Scripture speaks of a curse in two ways: one which it approves, and another which it condemns. A curse is uttered in one way according to the judgment of justice, and in another according to the resentment of vengeance.

The curse according to the judgment of justice was pronounced when the first man sinned, when he heard: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. III, 17). A curse is pronounced according to the judgment of justice when Abraham is told: “I will curse those who curse you” (Gen. XII, 3). Again, because a curse is promised not according to the judgment of justice but according to the resentment of vengeance, we are warned by the voice of Paul preaching, who says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII, 14). And again the Truth says: “Nor will those who curse possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 10).

God, therefore, is said to curse, and yet man is forbidden to curse, because what man does out of the malice of vengeance, God does only with the scrutiny and power of justice. For even holy men, when they pronounce a sentence of cursing, do not burst forth into it from a desire for vengeance, but from the judgment of justice. Within themselves they behold God’s subtle judgment, and they recognize that the evils rising outwardly ought to be struck by a curse. They therefore do not sin in cursing, since in the curse they do not disagree with the inward judgment.

Hence Peter hurled a sentence of cursing against Simon, who offered him money, saying: “Your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts VIII, 20). For by not saying “is,” but “be,” and thus speaking not in the indicative but in the optative mood, he showed that he had uttered these words in that sense.

Hence Elijah said to the two captains of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you” (II Kings I, 10). The outcome of the matter showed with what truth both these sentences prevailed.

[Note: The printed editions, against all the manuscripts, read “with what severity.”]

For Simon perished in eternal destruction, and a flame descending from above consumed the two captains of fifty. The subsequent effect, therefore, testifies with what intention a sentence of cursing is pronounced. When the innocence of the one who curses remains intact, and yet the curse consumes the one who is cursed even unto destruction, the outcome of both parties shows that the sentence was hurled against the guilty by one and the same inward Judge.

[Note: In the Uticensis manuscript: “his innocence remains.”]

[Note: The printed editions, corruptly: “he hurls a sentence taken from the judgment.”]

## CHAPTER XXVII — “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 19)

[Col. 0695B]

While the immortality of the first man and his fall were being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXV (number 4):

> “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.”

The first man was so created that, while he remained, time would pass away, but he himself would not pass away with time. He stood while moments ran on, for he did not tend toward the end of life through the increase of days. He stood all the more firmly the more closely he clung to the One who eternally stands.

But when he touched what was forbidden, he immediately began to go along with time, having offended the Creator. Thus it was said to him: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.” Having lost the state of immortality, he was swallowed up by the course of mortality; and as he was drawn from youth to old age, and from old age to death, by passing away he learned what he had been by standing.

Because we are born from his stock, we retain the bitterness of the root, as though in a young shoot. Since we derive our origin from him, we inherit his course by being born, so that in the very daily moment in which we live we constantly pass away from life, and the span of life—which seems to increase for us—decreases from that same source.

[Note: The Uticensis manuscript reads: “from there we diminish.”]

For while infancy passes into childhood, childhood into adolescence, adolescence into youth, youth into old age, and old age into death, in the course of the present life it is driven toward decline by its very growth, and continually diminishes from the point at which it believes itself to be progressing in the extension of life.

[Note: The Uticensis manuscript reads: “old age, by its own increases.”]

Here we cannot possess a fixed condition, since we have come in order to pass away; and this very living of ours is, each day, a passing away from life. Before his sin the first man could not have possessed this fall, because time passed while he stood. But after he sinned, he placed himself, as it were, upon a slippery path of temporality; and because he ate the forbidden food, he immediately discovered the failing of his standing.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — “He placed before the paradise of pleasure the cherubim and a flaming, turning sword” (Gen. III, 24)

[Col. 0695D]

While the restoration of paradise through the coming of the Mediator was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XII (number 13):

> “He placed before the paradise…”

Before the coming of the Mediator of God and man, every human being, however pure and tested his life might have been, descended to the prison of hell. There is no doubt about this, since the man who fell by himself could not return by himself to the rest of paradise, unless he came who, through the mystery of his incarnation, would open for us the way back to that same paradise.

Hence, after man’s sin, a flaming sword is said to have been placed at the entrance to paradise. It is also called “turning,” because the time would eventually come when it could be removed.

## CHAPTER XXIX — “The Lord looked upon Abel and upon his offering; but upon Cain and upon his offering he did not look” (Gen. IV, 4)

[Col. 0695D–0696A]

While the purity of the heart was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXII (at the end of number 27 and number 28):

> “The Lord looked upon Abel…”

The almighty God does not accept from the hand a gift that is offered with a heart bound by wickedness. The mind of the one who wishes to offer a gift to God must first be cleansed, because everything given to God is assessed according to the mind of the giver.

Therefore every stain of wickedness must be wiped away from our inner person by a change of thought, because an offering cannot appease the anger of the Judge unless it pleases him through the purity of the one who offers it. Hence it is written: “God looked upon Abel and upon his offerings; but upon Cain and upon his offering he did not look.”

For Sacred Scripture does not say, “He looked upon Abel’s offerings, but did not look upon Cain’s offerings.” Rather, it first says: “Because he looked upon Abel,” and then adds, “and upon his offerings.” Again it says that he did not look upon Cain, and then adds, “nor upon his offerings.”

What is given is accepted from the heart of the giver. Therefore it was not Abel who pleased God because of the offerings, but the offerings pleased God because of Abel. For the Lord is read to have first looked upon the one who gave, and only afterward upon what was given. By the order of this narrative we learn that outward gifts are seasoned by the inward purity of the heart, and the power of discernment teaches the reader what sort of person he ought to be when he supplies outward goods not only to God but also to his neighbors.

## CHAPTER XXX — “At the door your sin will be present, but its desire will be beneath you, and you will rule over it” (Gen. IV, 7, 8)

While the restraint of unlawful desire in the heart was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV (number 36):

> “At the door…”

Sin is present at the door when it knocks in our thoughts. Its desire is beneath us, and man rules over it if, once the wickedness of the heart has been perceived, it is quickly suppressed and subdued to the resisting mind before it grows into hardness.

## CHAPTER XXXI — “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. IV, 7, according to the Septuagint)

While the discernment required in good works was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book III (numbers 23, 24):

> “If you offer rightly…”

An offering is made rightly when something is done with a right intention. But it is not divided rightly if what is piously done is not also carefully discerned.

To divide rightly what has been offered means to assess all our good efforts by carefully distinguishing them. Whoever neglects to do this sins even while offering rightly. Often, while we carry out something with good zeal, we fail to discern it carefully and therefore do not know what judgment its outcome will receive. Sometimes what is thought to be a cause of virtue becomes an accusation of crime.

We therefore offer rightly when we perform a good work with good zeal; but we do not divide rightly if we postpone exercising discernment in a good work.

## CHAPTER XXXII — “Cain called his first son Enoch, and after his name he called the city that he founded” (Gen. IV, 17)

[Col. 0696D]

While the glory of the present life was being discussed as something to be avoided, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII (number 92):

Just men desire all the more to cling to heavenly things through the ray of contemplation, and therefore they refuse all the more to build upon earth, where they know themselves to be strangers and sojourners, as Paul bears witness when he says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20). And again: “But you are being built into a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. V, 1).

Because holy men desire to rejoice in what is their own, they refuse to be happy in what belongs to another. But the more the wicked are separated from the inheritance of their eternal homeland, the more deeply they fix the foundations of their thoughts upon earth.

Hence, from the very beginning of the human condition, Enoch is born seventh among the chosen offspring. Hence Cain calls his first son Enoch and names the city he founded after him. Enoch means “dedication.” The wicked therefore dedicate themselves at the beginning, because in this life they plant the root of their heart in what comes first, so that they may flourish here according to their desire and wither away from the homeland that follows.

Conversely, Enoch is born seventh among the elect, because the festive dedication of their life is reserved for the end. Hence, as Paul bears witness, Abraham dwells in tents (Hebr. XI, 9), because he awaits the city having foundations, whose builder is the heavenly artificer.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — Likewise, concerning the preceding matter

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVI (number 15):

While the wicked neglect to pass over in their hearts to eternal things and do not perceive that all present things are fleeting, they fasten their minds upon the love of the present life and build for themselves in it, as though it were a long dwelling, a foundation; for through desire they make themselves solid in earthly things.

Hence the first Cain is described as having built a city, so that it might be plainly shown that he who was alienated from the solidity of the eternal homeland placed his foundation upon earth. A stranger to what is above, he placed his foundation in what is below—he who established the station of his heart in earthly pleasure.

Thus in his line Enoch, whose name is interpreted as “dedication,” is born first, whereas in the lineage of the elect Enoch is said to have been seventh. The reprobate dedicate themselves by building themselves up in this life, which comes first. The elect, however, await the dedication of their building at the end of time, that is, in the seventh age.

You see very many people thinking only about temporal things, seeking honors, yearning to obtain possessions, and desiring nothing after this life. What do such people do except dedicate themselves in the first generation? You see the elect seeking none of the present glory, willingly enduring poverty, and patiently suffering the world’s evils so that they may be crowned at the end.

[Note: Gemeticum and Uticensis read “Electus ergo” (“the elect [man], therefore”); the printed editions corruptly have “electio” (“election”). We follow Michael, who agrees with the manuscripts of the Moralia.]

Enoch is therefore born to the elect in the seventh generation, because they seek the dedication of their joy in the glory of the final recompense.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — “God saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth, and that every thought of his heart was directed toward evil continually; and it repented him that he had made man upon the earth” (Gen. VI, 6)

While the manner of divine speech through expressions customary among human beings was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX (number 12):

> “God saw that the wickedness of man was great upon the earth…”

What does it mean that the almighty God, who is not bound by any mutability belonging to human condition, and to whom nothing is lacking in time—for he is Being itself—is described as repenting of his creation? It means that, just as in Sacred Scripture the wise often draw their speech from the language of worldly men, so now, for the benefit of man, the Creator of men himself assumes within himself the language of human passion, so that it may be said: “It repented him that he had made man upon the earth.”

Yet it is certain that he who sees all things before they come to be does not, after doing something, recover his senses through repentance. Therefore, just as it is not surprising when spiritual beings often use the words of bodily beings, so it is not surprising that the ineffable Spirit, the Creator of all things, forms within himself the speech of the flesh in order to draw the flesh toward understanding.

## CHAPTER XXXV — Concerning the ark of the Flood, which was broad below and narrow above (Gen. VI, 15)

While the multitude of the reprobate, placed within the Church in outward appearance, and the small number of the elect were being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of the Gospels, homily 38 (number 8):

The ark amid the waters of the Flood, which bore the type of this Church, was broad below and narrow above. At its summit it narrowed to the measure of a single cubit.

Below, it is to be believed, it contained quadrupeds and reptiles; above, birds and human beings. It was broad where it held the beasts, and narrow where it preserved human beings, because the holy Church is broad among the carnal and narrow among the spiritual.

Where it tolerates the beastly behavior of men, there it spreads its bosom more widely. But where it contains those who are supported by spiritual understanding, there it is indeed led upward; yet, because they are few, it becomes narrow.

“Broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who go by it. Narrow is the gate that leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Matt. VII, 13).

The ark is narrowed at the top until it is brought to the measure of one cubit, because in the holy Church the holier each person is, the fewer such people there are. At the summit it is brought to the one who alone is man among men and, without comparison, was born holy. In the words of the psalmist: “He became like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Ps. CI, 8).

The wicked must therefore be tolerated all the more because they are also more numerous. In the threshing-floor, too, there are few grains that are preserved in the granaries, while there are great heaps of chaff to be burned by fire.

## CHAPTER XXXVI — Likewise, concerning the preceding matter

In the Commentary on Ezekiel, homily 4 (at the end of number 16):

The ark was commanded to be made three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high; it was brought to completion in one cubit.

[Note: The printed editions read most corruptly, “sixty,” which plainly conflicts with the testimony of Sacred Scripture.]

What is represented by the ark except the holy Church? It is broad below and narrow above. Its three hundred, thirty, and fifty cubits are gathered into one cubit, because, becoming gradually narrower from the breadth that the holy Church still possesses in its weaker members, it advances upward and tends toward one.

Reason itself requires us to believe that in the breadth of that ark all the beasts, quadrupeds, and reptiles were below, while human beings and birds were above. For there was a window in the side toward the upper part, through which the man sent out the raven and the dove in order to learn whether the waters of the Flood had already receded.

Since the ark was completed in one cubit, human beings and birds were situated near the cubit. Thus the whole Church is rightly signified by the ark: it is still broad in its many carnal members and narrow in its few spiritual ones. Because it is gathered toward the one man who is without sin, it is completed, as it were, in one cubit.

We see many people within the bosom of this same holy Church rising up in pride, dissolving themselves in carnal pleasures, yearning to acquire earthly possessions, crossing seas at the command of avarice, serving anger, devoting themselves to quarrels, and injuring their neighbors whenever they can. But because the holy Church still tolerates them so that they may be converted, the beasts dwell below, as it were, in the breadth of the ark.

We see others no longer seeking what belongs to others, bearing injuries inflicted upon them with equanimity, content with their own possessions, and living humbly. But because these are already few, the ark becomes narrow.

We see still others abandoning even what they possess, giving no attention to earthly things, loving their enemies, subduing the flesh from every pleasure, restraining all movements beneath the judgment of reason, and being lifted by the wing of contemplation through heavenly desire.

[Note: The printed editions read, “lifting up wings,” but the manuscripts read otherwise.]

But because such people are extremely rare, the ark is already brought near the cubit, where human beings and birds are contained.

Yet let it be asked whether any of them can be without sin—and none is found. Who, then, is a man without sin except he who was not conceived in sins? The ark is therefore completed in one cubit, because there is one author and Redeemer of the holy Church without sin, toward whom and through whom all who know themselves to be sinners advance.

## CHAPTER XXXVII — “The senses and thoughts of the human heart are inclined toward evil from its youth” (Gen. VIII, 21)

[Col. 0699A]

While the suppression of glory arising from good works was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII (number 43):

The evil of corruption, which each of us has taken from the beginning of our carnal desires, is exercised as our age advances. Unless the hand of divine fear quickly restrains it, guilt suddenly swallows every good of the created nature into the abyss.

Let no one, therefore, claim victory over his thoughts for himself, since the Apostle says: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (I Cor. III, 8).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and let your fear and dread be upon all the animals of the earth” (Gen. IX, 1)

While the distinct manner in which teachers should conduct themselves toward their subjects was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXI (numbers 22, 23, and Pastoral Rule, part II, chapter 6):

> “Increase…”

For powerful men, the consideration of the equality of human condition is a great exercise of humility. By nature we are all equal, but an arrangement established for the administration of things has caused some to appear superior to others.

If we cast down from the mind what has been added temporally, we quickly discover what we are naturally. Often the power received places itself before the mind and deceives it with proud thoughts. The swelling of arrogance must therefore be pressed down by the hand of the humblest consideration.

If the mind descends within itself from the summit of its height, it quickly finds the level ground of natural equality. As we have said, nature brought forth all human beings equal, but the hidden ordering of differing merits has placed some beneath others.

The very inequality that arose from vice has rightly been ordered by divine judgments: because every human being does not walk the path of life equally, one is ruled by another.

When holy men preside, they attend not to the power of their office but to the equality of their condition. They do not rejoice in ruling human beings, but in benefiting them. For they know that our ancient fathers are remembered as shepherds of flocks rather than kings of men.

Hence, when after the Flood the Lord said to Noah and his sons, “Increase and multiply,” he added: “And let your fear and dread be upon all the animals of the earth.” Man is superior to irrational animals, but not by nature to all other human beings. Therefore he is told to be feared by animals, not by man, because it is contrary to nature to be proud and to wish to be feared by one’s equal.

All who preside should therefore weigh not the power of their office but the equality of their condition. For, as we have said, our ancient fathers are remembered as shepherds of flocks, not as kings of men.

Yet rulers must necessarily be feared by their subjects when they discover that their subjects scarcely fear God, so that at least through human fear they may dread sin—those who do not fear divine judgments. Superiors do not become proud because of this fear they have sought, since in it they seek not their own glory but the justice of their subjects.

When fear is demanded from those who live perversely, they rule as though not over human beings but over animals, because in whatever respect their subjects are beastlike, in that respect they ought also to lie subjected to fear.

## CHAPTER XXXIX — “I will place my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth” (Gen. IX, 13)

While the meaning of the divine promise after the Flood was being discussed, the following was added in the Commentaries on Ezekiel, book I, homily 8 (number 29):

> “I will place my bow in the clouds…”

The almighty God placed the bow as a sign between himself and human beings, so that he would not again destroy the world by a flood.

Hence, in that same bow, the color of water and of fire is displayed together. It is partly blue and partly red, so that it may be a witness to both judgments: one already carried out and the other yet to be carried out. That is, the world will be burned by the judgment of fire; it will not be destroyed by the water of the Flood.

[Note: These words are not found at all in the assigned place in another edition, but they do occur in the indicated homily.]

## CHAPTER XL — Concerning Noah’s drunkenness, when his good sons, turning away as they approached, covered his nakedness (Gen. IX, 21, 22)

While the reverence that subjects ought to preserve toward their superiors was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXV (number 37):

To turn away means to reject. What, then, does it mean that the sons cover their father’s nakedness by carrying a cloak upon their backs and approaching with their faces turned away, except that good subjects are displeased by the faults of their superiors, yet nevertheless conceal those faults from others?

They carry the covering while turned away because, judging the deed but reverencing the office of authority, they do not wish to see what they cover.

## CHAPTER XLI — “Cursed is Canaan the boy; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Gen. IX, 25)

[Col. 0700B]

While the distinctions between curses were being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVI (number 37):

> “Cursed is Canaan the boy…”

Severity does not permit sins to remain unpunished, but the anger of judgment begins here with our correction, so that it may come to rest in the condemnation of the reprobate, as it is written: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God. And if first from us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God?” (I Pet. IV, 17).

Let the reprobate go, then, and consume the desires of their pleasures in unpunished wickedness. Let them fail to feel temporal scourges precisely because eternal punishments await them.

Their unpunished wickedness was aptly signified in the sin of Ham, to whom his father said: “Cursed is Canaan the boy; he shall be a servant to his brothers.” Canaan, of course, was the son of Ham.

What does it mean that, when Ham sinned, his son Canaan received the sentence of vengeance? What does it mean that he was struck not in himself but in his offspring, except that the wickedness of the reprobate here indeed advances unpunished, but is struck in the future?

## CHAPTER XLII — “Come, let us descend and confuse their language there” (Gen. XI, 7)

While the manner of divine speech was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book II (number 9):

It is said to those who adhere to God, “Come,” because never to diminish from divine contemplation but always to increase in it, and never to withdraw from the heart, is like a stable motion of continually coming.

To these he also says: “Let us descend and confuse their language there.” Angels ascend insofar as they behold the Creator; angels descend insofar as, through the scrutiny of strict judgment, they press down the creature rising up in wickedness.

It is therefore God who says, “Let us descend and confuse their language there”: he shows them within himself what ought rightly to be done, and through the power of inward vision inspires judgments to be displayed to their minds by hidden movements.

[Note: Our manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “those who were present.” Our reading is found in the assigned passage of the Moralia.]

[Note: The printed editions corruptly read “in hidden minds.”]

## CHAPTER XLIII — Abraham, while offering sacrifice at sunset, drove away the birds that descended upon it (Gen. XV, 11)

While the avoidance of superfluous thoughts was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVI (number 53):

> “Abraham, while offering sacrifice at sunset…”

Often thoughts that arise pollute the hearts of the righteous and touch them with the pleasures of earthly things. But when they are quickly driven away by the hand of holy discernment, action is promptly taken lest the darkness of temptation cover the face of the heart—a darkness that had already begun to touch it through unlawful pleasure.

For often, during the very sacrifice of our reason, thoughts intrude themselves at an unsuitable time, thoughts capable of stealing or defiling what we offer to God with tears.

Hence Abraham, while offering sacrifice at sunset, drove away the birds that descended upon it. He diligently drove them off lest they steal the sacrifice that had been offered.

So, while we offer God a burnt offering upon the altar of the heart, we guard it from these unclean birds, lest evil spirits and perverse thoughts steal what our mind hopes profitably to offer to God.

## CHAPTER XLIV — Abraham is said to have encountered three angelic men: he met them as they came outside the doorway, while Sarah stood behind the doorway (Gen. XVIII, 2)

While the discipline of the spirit and the manner in which care of the flesh should be subordinated were being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX (number 106):

Care of the flesh must be restrained with the great moderation of discernment, so that it may serve and not rule. It must not conquer the mind like a mistress; rather, once subjected to authority, it must serve like a maidservant. It should be present when commanded and, when rejected at the will of the heart, leap away, so that it may scarcely appear behind holy thought and never stand opposed to the face of one thinking rightly.

The history of Sacred Scripture conveys this well when Abraham is said to have encountered three angels. He himself went out to meet those who were coming, outside the doorway, while Sarah remained behind the doorway.

What, then, is suggested to us by Abraham’s going out to meet them except that, as the man and master of the spiritual household—that is, our understanding—he ought in contemplating the Trinity to pass beyond the barriers of the flesh and go out, as it were, through the door of the lower dwelling?

Care of the flesh, like a woman, must not appear openly; it should be ashamed to display itself boastfully. Remaining, as it were, behind the man, under the discernment of the spirit and intent only upon what is necessary, it should not know how to expose itself shamelessly but should be governed modestly.

Yet when it is often told not to presume upon itself and to transfer its whole confidence into hope in God, it scorns this and, when its effort ceases, distrusts that the supports of life can be present to it.

Hence this same Sarah laughs when she hears the promises of God, but she is rebuked for laughing; and once rebuked, she immediately becomes fruitful. She who in the vigor of youth could not conceive conceived when broken by the years of old age, with her womb withered. For when care of the flesh ceases to possess confidence in itself, it receives from the divine promise, contrary to hope, what it had doubted it could possess by human reasoning.

Hence Isaac is aptly called “laughter,” because he is generated when the confidence of heavenly hope is conceived. What else does our mind give birth to then except joy?

[Note: The printed editions, contrary to the manuscripts, read: “when she had become aged in years,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER XLV — Concerning the three men journeying to Sodom who were received by Abraham (Gen. XVIII, 16)

While the manner in which divine conversation is administered through the ministry of angels was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII (number 7):

Sometimes God speaks through images assumed by angels from the air for a time and placed before bodily eyes, as Abraham was able not only to see three men but also to receive them into his earthly dwelling—and not only to receive them, but also to provide food for their use.

Unless angels, announcing certain things to us on earth, assumed bodies from the air for a time, they would certainly not appear to our outward eyes; nor would they eat food with Abraham unless, for our sake, they carried something solid from the heavenly element.

It is not surprising that those very beings who were received are called sometimes angels and sometimes the Lord. They are expressed by the name “angels” because they were ministering outwardly, while the designation “Lord” shows the one who inwardly presided over them. Thus, through the one title, the authority of the presiding one is made clear, and through the other, the ministry of those serving.

## CHAPTER XLVI — “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave; I will descend and see whether they have completed in action the cry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. XVIII, 20, 21)

[Col. 0701D–0702A]

While the need to avoid credulity concerning unapproved reports was being discussed, the following was added in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX (number 46):

> “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied…”

Sin accompanied by a voice is guilt in action; but sin accompanied also by a cry is guilt committed openly. What else are we admonished by this example than never to be too hasty in delivering a sentence, lest we rashly judge matters that have not been investigated?

Let no evils merely heard move us, and let us not believe indiscriminately what is said without proof. We shall certainly fear committing such a fault if we consider more carefully the deeds of our Creator.

Although all things are naked and open to his eyes, he wished to restrain us from passing a hasty judgment. Therefore, when he heard of the evils of Sodom, he did not wish to judge them merely on hearsay, but said: “I will descend and see whether they have completed in action the cry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

Why, then, does the almighty Lord, who knows all things, seem to doubt before investigation, unless he is setting before us an example of gravity, so that we do not presume to believe human evils before we have proved them?

And behold, he descends through angels to learn about the evils, and immediately strikes the guilty. He who is patient, he who is gentle, he of whom it is written, “But you, Lord, judge with tranquility” (Wis. XII, 18), he of whom it is also written, “The Lord is patient, but he repays” (Ecclus. V, 4)—when he finds them involved in so great a crime, he seems to set aside patience and does not wish to await the day of final judgment for vengeance, but anticipates the day of judgment with the fire of judgment.

Behold: when he heard of the evil, he believed it, as it were, with difficulty; yet when he discovered its truth, he struck without delay. He thus gave us an example: greater crimes should be believed slowly when they are heard, but punished more quickly when they are known to be true.

> “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII, 27).

[Note: These words undoubtedly ought to begin another chapter. Nevertheless, they are found in the same sequence in the printed editions and in our manuscripts.]

[Col. 0702C]

All the saints, when they advance in the vision of God, recognize themselves to be nothing the more they behold the inner things of divinity. Nowhere is it read that Abraham professed himself to be dust and ashes except when he was granted conversation with God, saying: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII, 27).

He might perhaps have believed himself to be something if he had not perceived the true essence that exists above him. But when he was carried away beyond himself to contemplate the unchangeable, filled with the power of such contemplation, he saw that he was nothing but dust.

Hence the prophet, filled with the same wisdom, exclaimed: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Ps. CIV, 14).

[Note: The printed editions corruptly read: “having been seized above himself.”]

## CHAPTER XLVII — “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII, 27)

In the exposition of Job, book X (number 49):

There are some whom understanding does not exalt through pride, but whom works of mercy raise up. And there are some who, while they see themselves abounding in earthly riches, do not seek the true riches of God and do not love the eternal homeland, because they think that what supports them with temporal possessions is sufficient for them.

Wealth, therefore, is not itself a crime, but attachment is. Everything that God created is good, but whoever uses good things badly acts as though, through the gluttony of indulgence, he were dying by the very bread by which he ought to live.

The poor Lazarus came to rest, while the proud rich man was tormented; yet Abraham was rich, and he held Lazarus in his bosom. Nevertheless, when speaking with his Creator, he says: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes.”

How, then, did this man know how to esteem his riches, when he weighed himself as dust and ashes? Or when could possessed things exalt him, since he thought so humbly even of himself, their possessor?

We clearly see what place he had assigned himself when he judged himself to be dust and ashes even while speaking with God. If, then, the one who rose to the honor of divine conversation so despises himself, we must carefully consider by what punishment those will be struck who do not advance toward the highest things and yet are exalted by the smallest.
