## CHAPTER XLVIII — “They pressed Lot with great violence, and it was already near that they would break the doors; then the men stretched out their hands, drew Lot in to themselves, shut the door, and struck those who were outside with blindness, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door” (Gen. XIX, 9)

When the innocence of the elect, fortified against the snares of the wicked, was being discussed, the following was added in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book VI (No. 38):

> “They pressed Loth very violently,” and so forth. What is signified by Loth’s being brought back inside the house and protected when wicked men oppose him, except that every righteous person, while enduring the snares of the wicked, returns to his mind and remains undaunted? The Sodomite men cannot find the door in Loth’s house, because those who corrupt minds discover no opening for accusation against the life of the righteous. Struck with blindness, they go around the house, as it were, scrutinizing the deeds and words of those whom they envy. But because a strong and praiseworthy action confronts them from every side in the life of the righteous, they wander about touching nothing but a wall.

**CHAPTER XLIX.—And Loth, fleeing from burning Sodom but finding Segor, did not at once climb into the mountainous country (Gen. XIX, 20, 30).**

While the loftiness of those who practice continence and the pardon granted to married people were being discussed, the following was added in the *Book of the Pastoral Rule*, Part III (Admonition 28, ch. 27):

> “And Loth, fleeing from burning Sodom,” and so forth. To flee from burning Sodom is to avoid the fires of illicit sexuality; the height of the mountains, however, is the purity of those who practice continence. Or, in a certain sense, those are like men on a mountain who remain joined in carnal intercourse but, outside the proper purpose of begetting children, do not release themselves into any carnal pleasure.

[Note: In the Utica and Gemet manuscripts this is omitted. It is read in the same words in the Michael manuscript. Nevertheless, the negative particle seems to us to require removal. In the *Pastoral Rule* it reads: “To stand on the mountain is not to seek the fruit of offspring in the flesh.”]

To stand on the mountain is not to seek the fruit of offspring in the flesh; to stand on the mountain is not to cling carnally to the flesh. But because there are many who indeed abandon crimes of the flesh and yet, while situated in marriage, preserve only the rights of what is strictly required, Loth did leave Sodom but did not immediately reach the mountains: for a life already deserving condemnation is abandoned, but the height of conjugal continence is not yet carefully maintained.

There is, however, in between, the city of Segor, which saves the fugitive and the weak. For when married people come together through incontinence, they flee the falls of crime and yet are saved by pardon. They find, as it were, a small city in which they may be defended from the fires, because this married life is not remarkable for virtues, but is nevertheless safe from punishments. Hence Loth says to the angel:

> “There is a city here nearby, to which I can flee; it is small, and I shall be saved in it. Is it not little, and my soul shall live in it?” (ibid.)

It is therefore called nearby, and yet is declared safe for salvation, because married life is neither far removed from the world nor alien to the joy of salvation. But married people preserve their life in this conduct, as though in a small city, when they intercede for one another with constant prayers. Hence the angel rightly says to that same Loth:

> “Behold, I have also accepted your prayers in this matter, so that I will not overthrow the city for which you have spoken” (Gen. XIX, 24);

for when supplication is poured out before God, such a married life is by no means condemned. Concerning this supplication Paul also admonishes us, saying:

> “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. VII, 5).

**CHAPTER L.—Therefore the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah brimstone and fire (Gen. XIX, 24).**

When the perseverance of the wicked in evil was being discussed, the following was added in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XIV (No. 23):

> “Therefore the Lord,” and so forth. What is expressed by brimstone except the stench of the flesh, and what by fire except the ardor of carnal desire? When, therefore, the Lord determined to punish the crimes of the flesh committed by the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah, he marked the stain of their crime in the very character of the punishment. Brimstone has a stench, and fire has heat. Thus, those who had burned with perverse desires through the stench of the flesh deserved to perish by fire and brimstone together, so that through a just punishment they might learn what they had done through unjust desire.

**CHAPTER LI.—Concerning Abraham’s wife, buried in a double tomb (Gen. XXIII, 19).**

[Col. 0704B] When the active and contemplative life were being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book VI (No. 56), the following was added concerning Abraham’s wife:

> What is suggested to us by Abraham’s double tomb except that every perfect preacher hides his soul, dead to the desires of the present life, beneath the protection of good works and contemplation? Thus, under the active and contemplative life, she lies hidden from carnal desire as though insensible—she who previously lived mortally, sensing the desires of the world. Hence the distinguished preacher also says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III, 3).
>
> The active life is a tomb, because it covers us after we have died to wicked works. But the contemplative life buries us more perfectly, because it completely separates us from all the actions of the world. Therefore, whoever has already subdued the insults of the flesh within himself must still exercise his mind through the disciplines of holy action. And whoever has already enlarged his mind through holy works must still extend it to the innermost reaches of contemplation. For a preacher is not perfect if, because of his devotion to contemplation, he neglects what must be done, or if, because of his insistence upon action, he postpones what must be contemplated.

**CHAPTER LII.—[Note: This chapter is omitted in the Gemet, Utica, and Michael manuscripts, and in the manuscripts seen by us.] A servant is sent to bring Rebekah to Isaac as his wife (Gen. XXIV, 9).**

In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book II (No. 50):

> A servant is sent to bring Rebekah to Isaac as his wife, because prophecy serves as an intermediary in betrothing the Church to the Lord.

**CHAPTER LIII.—“Put your hand under my thigh, so that I may bind you by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell; but that you will go to my land and to my kindred, and from there take a wife for my son Isaac” (Gen. XXIV, 3).**

When the mysteries of the sacrament involving Abraham’s servant and the seeking of a wife for his son Isaac were being discussed, the following was added:

> “Put your hand under my thigh,” and so forth.

[Note: What follows is found nowhere in Gregory. Consequently, in the Michael, Gemet, and Utica manuscripts, no indication is given of the source from which this material was taken; nevertheless, it bears the character of Gregory’s style.]

It is worthwhile to bring forward briefly certain details from the history of Abraham and Isaac, so that we may demonstrate more clearly in these events what is to be understood allegorically. Abraham calls the servant and orders him to place his hand under his thigh, so that, as the ancient translation has it, he may swear by the Lord God of heaven. Immediately he commands him not to take a wife for his son Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites, but to go to Abraham’s kindred and bring back a wife from there.

Accordingly, the servant placed his hand under Abraham’s thigh as he had been commanded and swore. He took with him all kinds of his master’s goods and went to Mesopotamia. There, standing beside the spring, he proposed in prayer that the girl to whom he would say, “Incline your jar so that I may drink,” and who would answer, “Drink, and I will also give water to your camels” (ibid., 4), should be the wife of his master Isaac.

At once Rebekah came out. When the servant asked her for water, she replied, “Drink, my lord.” She quickly lowered the jar from her shoulder, gave him drink, and also drew water for the camels and supplied it. Immediately the servant gave her two gold earrings weighing two shekels and bracelets weighing ten shekels. When questioned, she disclosed her family and explained that there was ample room in her father’s house for lodging and that it had abundant straw and hay.

Rebekah had a brother named Laban. He hurried out, and, seeing the earrings, shekels, and bracelets on his sister, invited the servant inside and gave him straw and hay. He supplied water for washing the feet of the camels and of the men who had come with him. He set bread before him, but the servant refused to eat until he had first obtained the matter concerning his master’s son’s marriage.

As soon as he had obtained the desired consent in the matter, he brought out gold and silver vessels and clothing and increased Rebekah’s gifts; he also offered gifts to her brothers and mother. Rebekah and her attendants mounted the camels and followed the man, who hurried back to his master.

At that time Isaac was walking along the road that leads to the well whose name is “of the living one who sees.” He lived in the southern land. He had gone out into the field to meditate, as the day was already declining. But as soon as Rebekah saw Isaac, she dismounted from the camel and asked the servant, saying, “Who is that man coming across the field?” He answered her, “He is my master.” Then she took her veil and covered herself. Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah, took her as his wife, and loved her so greatly that he softened the grief that had come from his mother’s death.

What is meant by Abraham’s ordering the servant to place his hand under his thigh and swear by the Lord of heaven, except that the flesh of the one who would descend through that limb would be both Abraham’s son according to humanity and Lord according to divinity? Thus the servant is told: “Put your hand under my thigh and swear by the God of heaven.” It is as though he were plainly saying: “Touch my son and swear by my Lord.”

He is therefore ordered to put his hand not upon the thigh but beneath the thigh, because the one who would descend from that thigh would come as a human being, yet above all human beings. It was therefore not fitting for him to place his hand upon the thigh, because no flesh is above that flesh which the Only-Begotten of the Father united to himself for our redemption.

What is meant by Isaac’s being forbidden to have a wife brought to him from the daughters of the Canaanites, except that the one of whom it is written, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17), is joined to no rejected soul? The servant is commanded to bring a wife for the son from Abraham’s kindred, because only the holy Church of the elect was to be joined to the Only-Begotten Son; and by his predestination the Only-Begotten himself did not regard her as a stranger, even before her presence.

But who is the servant sent to bring the wife except the order of the prophets, the apostles, and all teachers? By bringing the word of preaching to good minds, they become, as it were, stewards charged with joining each soul to the Only-Begotten Son. He carried with him all his master’s goods, because, in the things they proclaim about the Lord, they display within themselves the riches of virtue; and they draw their hearers more quickly to follow God insofar as they show in themselves what they proclaim.

The same servant stood beside the spring and, according to the predetermined sign, proposed which girl should be chosen, because holy preachers consider the streams of sacred eloquence and from them discern to whom they should entrust the words of their preaching and from which hearers they may derive confident assurance.

He asked for a drink because every preacher thirsts for the soul of his hearer. But Rebekah supplied the drink because the holy Church of the elect satisfied the desire of her preachers through the strength of her faith. For, confessing the God whom she had heard, she offered her preacher water for refreshment and restored his spirit.

It should be noted that she placed the jar from her shoulder upon her arm, because the confession that pleases God proceeds from good works. Or certainly she supplied water because she did not remain empty in what she believed. For she immediately endeavored to preach what she had heard and, by teaching, produced many preachers from herself.

The water in the jar is knowledge of preaching in due measure, because the holy Church strives not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sober judgment (Rom. XII, 3). The jar of water upon the arm is the teaching of preaching expressed in action. She supplies drink not only to the servant’s companions but also to the camels, because she preaches the word of life not only to the wise but also to the foolish, in accordance with Paul’s words: “I am under obligation both to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. I, 14).

Or water is also given to beasts when provision is made for how care of the flesh should be exercised: it must not be indulged for pleasure, yet it must not be denied in necessities, as it is written: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII, 14). For whoever forbids this provision in desires plainly permits it in necessity, in accordance with the further statement: “No one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph. V, 29).

The servant gave Rebekah earrings and bracelets because every preacher adorns the hearing of the holy Church through obedience and her hands through the merit of good works. The earrings weigh two shekels, whereas the bracelets weigh ten, because the first virtue of obedience is love, and this love is distinguished in two commandments, namely, that God and one’s neighbor be loved. Right action is brought to completion through the fulfillment of the Decalogue, so that once good deeds have begun, no evil deeds are perpetrated thereafter.

While Rebekah was in her father’s house, she declared that there was ample room for lodging, because the holy Church showed that she knew the law of nature already given to the former people, and she received the words of preaching in the broad bosom of charity. For the heart of a hearer, broadened by goodness, is an ample place for a teacher to dwell. Hence Paul says to certain people: “Make room for us; we have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one” (2 Cor. VII, 2); and again: “You are not restricted in us, but you are restricted in your own affections” (ibid. VI, 12). It is as though he were plainly saying: “Make a spacious place in your mind to receive teaching, but remain confined when entertaining carnal thoughts.”

She indicated that she had abundant straw and hay because the holy Church, hearing the words of life, repaid earthly stipends to preachers. Although Paul accepted these as though they were nothing, he said: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. IX, 11).

Rebekah’s brother was Laban, who hastily came out and, seeing the earrings and bracelets on his sister, invited the servant inside. For there are carnal people associated with the faithful who, when they see the gifts of spiritual persons, are held in amazement and admit the word of preaching into their souls so as to receive faith, even if not to the point of works.

For when they observe good people shining through miracles, they do not reject what they hear about eternity, although they do not follow the holy Church of the elect in their conduct and remain in carnal action.

[Note: The printed editions have, very corruptly, “in admiration, a guest.” We have corrected many similar errors here with the help of the manuscripts.]

Laban offered the servant straw, hay, water, and bread, but the servant refused to accept anything unless he first obtained the matter concerning the marriage. For many are prepared to support their teachers with temporal stipends.

[Note: The printed editions read “to despise.” In the letters, “continence” often signifies the supplying of necessities. See Book I, Letter 5.]

But holy preachers do not wish to receive temporal things unless they first obtain eternal things. If they do not find fruit in souls, they disdain to accept bodily stipends.

[Note: The printed editions read, “These wash their feet with water,” contrary to the sense and to the manuscripts.]

Nor do they wash their feet with water, because they provide no consolation to relieve the labor of their desire.

But as soon as the servant had obtained the matter concerning the marriage from his master, he brought out gold and silver vessels and clothing and gave them to Rebekah, because the teachers of the holy Church provide as many ornaments as they have taught good virtues.

She had first received earrings and bracelets, but now she received gold and silver vessels and clothing, because the holy Church, having previously received faith, obedience, and action, later grows stronger also in spiritual gifts, so that, filled with the spirit of prophecy and the grace of virtues, she may grow rich through enlarged gifts.

The servant offered gifts to her mother and brothers because the Gentile world, from the time when the Church came to faith, grew strong in temporal glory after her conversion. We see this even now: Christians often experience affliction, while various Gentiles glory in earthly power.

Her brothers also receive gifts because those who hold this faith in words alone, yet do not follow its progress in their conduct and live carnally, are often kindly honored by the faithful because they appear to be faithful.

Her mother and brothers therefore receive gifts, though they remain excluded from the lot of the inheritance, because whether unbelievers or carnal people held within the profession of faith, they do not attain the lot of the eternal inheritance, yet they temporarily enjoy the glory of heavenly generosity.

[Note: The printed editions have “do not follow temporally.”]

Rebekah followed the man with her attendants because the holy Church has with her souls of lesser merit as companions.

[Note: We have restored many corrupt passages here with the help of the Michael manuscript.]

For some, through an ascent of the mind, do not possess contemplation in the marriage bed; such souls are like Rebekah’s attendants, because they follow in conduct but do not ascend to the bed of contemplation.

The servant also had certain people in his company, because among the holy prophets there were some who lived well but did not possess the spirit of prophecy; and among the holy apostles and teachers there were many who maintained a good life but did not bring forth the words of preaching.

The servant hastened back to his master because, when holy preachers obtain the lives of their hearers through preaching, they immediately return thanks to the one from whose gift they received this accomplishment, attributing nothing of it to themselves but everything to the Author.

At that time Isaac was walking along the road that leads to the well whose name is “of the living one who sees.” Who is the living one who sees except almighty God, of whom it is written: “I live forever, says the Lord” (Deut. XXXII, 40)? Of him it is also said: “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV, 13).

The well of the living one who sees is the depth of sacred Scripture, which almighty God has given us for the watering of the mind. But what is the road that leads to the well of the one who sees and lives except the humility of the Only-Begotten’s passion, through which what the streams of Scripture had previously spoken in secret was opened to us?

For unless the Only-Begotten Son of God had become incarnate, been tempted, seized, struck with blows, smeared with spittle, crucified, and killed, the depth of this well—that is, of sacred Scripture—would not have been revealed to us.

What, then, has the humility of his passion become for the faithful except the key to action, through which we find the well of God’s mysteries and drink the water of knowledge from its depths? The pages of sacred eloquence speak of his incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension. Because we know that these things have happened, let us now understand what we have heard. These matters could previously be read, but because they had not yet occurred, they could not be understood.

Hence John also says: “The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, to open the book and to release its seals” (Rev. V, 5). He opened the book and released its seals who, by being born, dying, rising again, and ascending into heaven, disclosed to us the secrets of sacred Scripture.

It should be noted that it does not say that he was walking along the road leading to the well, but that he was walking up and down. For one walks up and down when, going and returning, one treads the road upon which one walks.

The Lord walked up and down in the humility of his passion because he endured at one time verbal insults from the Jews, at another false testimony against himself, at another blows, at another spittle, at another a crown of thorns, and at another the cross. To have walked up and down in the humility of his passion is to have borne so many adversities and insults by repeating them in different forms.

Isaac dwells in the southern land when Rebekah comes because, when the Church comes to him, the Only-Begotten Lord and our Redeemer dwells in the minds of those born from Judea whom not the coldness of apathy but the warmth of charity possessed. From that people came the prophetess Anna; from it came Simeon, who received the Lord into his arms.

He had gone out to meditate in the field because the field signifies the world, as the Lord himself explains when he says: “The field is the world” (Matt. XIII, 38). He went out into it because he deigned to appear visibly, as it is written: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones” (Hab. III, 13).

Young men trained in arms commonly practice the use of weapons. Isaac therefore went out to meditate in the field because our Redeemer, offering those who follow him a pattern of humility, displayed in himself, through the exercise of his long-suffering passion, examples of endurance and patience.

Meditation upon weapons is the repeated experience of sufferings. For the one who endured words, hands, a spear, and the cross permitted his passion to be repeatedly enacted in himself even unto death. We call sufferings weapons because through them we are freed from the hidden adversary, as the Lord himself says: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI, 19).

He went out to meditate in the field when the day was already declining because he undertook the exercises of suffering near the end of the world, as he speaks through the Psalmist of the expression of his crucifixion, saying: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL, 2).

What is meant by Rebekah’s being brought to Isaac on the back of a camel except that, as we have said above, Rebekah signifies the Church, while the camel beneath her signifies the Gentile people, crooked in conduct and burdened with the worship of idols? For, having invented gods for themselves to worship, they had, as it were, a burden grown upon their own backs which they carried.

Rebekah, therefore, comes to Isaac carried on the back of a camel because the Church, hastening from the Gentiles to Christ, is found in the crooked and vicious conduct of her former life.

When she saw Isaac, she descended from the camel because, the more subtly the holy Church recognizes her Redeemer, the more humbly she abandons the practices of carnal life and rejects vicious crookedness within herself. The Gentiles, therefore, descended when they saw the Lord: having recognized him, they abandoned their vices and sought the depths of humility instead of the height of pride.

What is meant by Rebekah’s seeing Isaac while seated upon a camel except that the Church coming from the Gentiles, while still supported by vices and still clinging not to spiritual but to animal ways of life, sees her Redeemer?

We should not be troubled by the fact that the servant also came with camels on which he carried his master’s riches, because holy preachers too, although they already shine in understanding and proclaiming higher things through their intellect and life, nevertheless still feel within themselves the opposition of the flesh.

For they see another law in their members resisting the law of their mind and taking them captive under the law of sin (Rom. VII); and they carry riches upon camels because, lest the greatness of revelations should exalt them, a thorn in their flesh was given to them (1 Cor. XII).

They have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may belong to God and not to them. Those who therefore speak heavenly things through the flesh, yet still feel within the flesh the contradiction arising from vice—what else are they doing but carrying riches upon the crooked backs of camels?

When Rebekah saw Isaac, she asked the servant who that man was and came to know him, because every day the holy Church understands, through the words of the prophets and apostles, what she ought to believe concerning her Redeemer.

She immediately covered herself with her veil because, the more subtly she penetrates the mysteries of her Savior, the more deeply she is ashamed of her former life. Because she had acted perversely, she was ashamed and took care to cover herself with a veil; seeing the Lord, she blushed at the weakness of her conduct. She who had previously been carried openly upon the camel later descended and was covered by shame.

Hence the apostolic voice says to that Church, converted from her former pride, as to Rebekah descending from the camel and covering herself with her veil: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI, 21).

Isaac brings her into the tent of his mother and takes her as his wife because the Lord, in place of the Synagogue from which he was born according to the flesh, loves the holy Church and joins her to himself in love and contemplation. She who had previously been near to him through kinship and known to him by predestination later becomes, once joined to him, his wife in enduring love.

He loved her so greatly that he softened the grief arising from his mother’s death because, through the gain of the holy Church, our Redeemer removed the sadness that could have arisen from the ruin of the Synagogue. When he is joined to Rebekah, the grief over his mother is cut away, because, when the holy Church coming from the Gentiles is brought to the bed of contemplation, Judea is counted as nothing.

If we consider the interpretation of their names, Isaac is said to mean “laughter,” while Rebekah means “patience.” Laughter arises from joy, whereas patience arises from tribulation. Although the holy Church is already suspended in contemplation of heavenly joy, she still has to endure something sad from the burden of mortal flesh.

Isaac and Rebekah are joined—that is, laughter and patience are mingled—because in the holy Church what is written comes to pass: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. XII, 12). Thus prosperity from contemplation makes her glad, while adversity from tribulation still disturbs her.

**CHAPTER LIV.—Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife because she was barren; and he heard him and granted Rebekah conception (Gen. XXV, 2).**

When the effect of predestination was being discussed, the following was added in the *Book of the Dialogues*, Book I (ch. 8):

> “Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife,” and so forth. Those things which holy men bring about through prayer have been so predestined that they are obtained through prayers. For even the predestination of the eternal kingdom has been arranged by almighty God in such a way that the elect reach it through labor, so that by asking they may deserve to receive what almighty God determined before the ages to give them.
>
> Whether this is so can readily be proved. Certainly we know that God said to Abraham: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI, 13). He had also said to him: “I have established you as the father of many nations” (ibid. XVII, 4); and again he promised him, saying: “I will bless you and multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the seashore” (Gen. XXII, 17).
>
> From this it is plainly evident that almighty God had predestined Abraham’s offspring to be multiplied through Isaac. Yet it is written: “Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife because she was barren; and he heard him and granted Rebekah conception.”
>
> If, therefore, the multiplication of Abraham’s descendants through Isaac was predestined, why did he receive a barren wife? Clearly, predestination is fulfilled through prayers, since Isaac—in whom God had predestined Abraham’s offspring to be multiplied—obtained through prayer the ability to have children.

**CHAPTER LV.—Esau became a man skilled in hunting and a farmer; but Jacob was a simple man and dwelt in tents (Gen. XXV, 27), or, as another translation says, “he dwelt at home” [according to the Septuagint].**

When the vices of the reprobate and the progress of the elect were being discussed, the following was added in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book V (No. 20):

> What is signified by Esau’s hunting except the life of those who, spread out among external pleasures, follow the flesh? He is also described as a farmer because lovers of this age cultivate external things all the more as they leave their inner selves uncultivated.
>
> Jacob, however, is said to be simple and to dwell in tents or at home because all who refuse to be scattered among external concerns remain simple in thought and in the dwelling place of their conscience. To dwell in tents, or at home, is to confine oneself within the secrets of the mind and not disperse oneself outwardly through desires, lest, while they gape after many things outside, they become alienated from themselves and depart in their thoughts.

**CHAPTER LVI.—Concerning Esau, who sold his birthright to his brother for a dish of lentils (Gen. XXV, 30).**

When the desire of the appetite was being discussed, the following was added in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXX (Nos. 60–61):

> It must be understood that the vice of the appetite tempts us in five ways. Sometimes it anticipates the time of need; sometimes it does not anticipate the time, but seeks more sumptuous foods; sometimes, whatever is to be eaten, it demands that it be prepared with excessive care; sometimes it conforms both to the quality and the timing of the food, but exceeds the measure of moderate refreshment in the very quantity consumed. At other times, what it desires is more lowly, yet it sins more grievously through the very heat of its boundless desire.
>
> We can display these forms of vice more clearly if we establish them through more evident examples. Jonathan incurred the sentence of death from his father’s mouth because he anticipated the appointed time for eating by tasting honey (1 Sam. XIV, 27). The people led out of Egypt fell in the wilderness because, despising manna, they sought meat, which they considered more sumptuous (Num. XXI, 5). The first fault of the sons of Eli arose when, at their request, the priest’s servant did not wish to receive sacrificial meat cooked according to the ancient custom, but sought it raw, so that it might be presented with greater care (1 Sam. II, 12).
>
> And when it is said to Jerusalem, “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, satiety of bread, and abundance” (Ezek. XVI, 49), it is plainly shown that she lost salvation for this reason: together with the vice of pride, she exceeded the measure of moderate refreshment.
>
> Hence Esau lost the glory of the firstborn because, in the great heat of desire, he coveted a worthless food, namely lentils.

[Note: The printed editions corruptly read “a desirable food.”]

Although he preferred this food even to his birthright when he sold the latter, he showed by the appetite with which he panted for it how intensely he desired it. For it is not the food but the appetite that is at fault.

Thus we often consume more sumptuous foods without guilt, while we taste more lowly foods not without a guilty conscience. This Esau, whom we have mentioned, sold his primacy for lentils, whereas Elijah preserved his virtue in the wilderness by eating meat.

The ancient enemy understands that the cause of condemnation is not food but desire for food. Thus he subjected the first man to himself not through meat but through a fruit, and tempted the second not through meat but through bread.

Hence Adam’s sin is often committed even when lowly and cheap things are consumed. For Adam alone did not receive the command of prohibition so that he might restrain himself from the forbidden fruit. Whenever God identifies certain foods as contrary to our health, he forbids them to us, as it were, by sentence; and when we touch harmful things in our desire, what else do we do but taste forbidden things?

Therefore, we should consume what the necessity of nature requires, not what appetite suggests,

[Note: The printed editions read: “unless, through this . . . someone turns himself into a chasm of illicit desire,” with the sense corrupted. The Utica manuscript reads: “unless someone plunges himself into the chasm of illicit desire.”]

lest, if prudent moderation has attended to this too carelessly, someone plunge himself into the chasm of illicit desire.

**CHAPTER LVII.—Concerning Isaac, who dug wells among a foreign people, and the Allophyli, lying in wait, filled the wells dug by him with earth (Gen. XXVI).**

When perseverance in good works and the enemy’s attacks arising from them were being discussed, the following was added in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXXI (No. 53):

> What is suggested to us by the wells dug by Isaac and filled by the Allophyli except that, placed in the hardship of this pilgrimage, we should penetrate the depths of our thoughts, and that, until the water of true understanding responds to us, the hands of our inquiry should never grow sluggish in emptying out the earth of the heart?
>
> The Allophyli lying in wait nevertheless fill these wells, because unclean spirits, when they see us diligently digging into the heart, pour upon us heaps of tempting thoughts.
>
> Therefore the mind must always be emptied and ceaselessly dug out, lest, if it is left unexplored, the earth of thoughts pile up over us until it produces the swelling of perverse works. Hence it is also said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, dig through the wall” (Ezek. VIII, 8)—that is, break through the hardness of the heart with repeated blows of scrutiny.

**CHAPTER LVIII.—Again, concerning the foregoing.**

In the *Exposition of Job*, Book XVI (No. 23):

> Often, while we devote ourselves to sacred writings, we endure the snares of evil spirits more severely, because they sprinkle the dust of earthly thoughts upon our minds, so that they obscure the eyes of our attention from the light of inward vision.
>
> We recognize this also as signified in Isaac’s work by the wickedness of the Allophyli, who filled with heaps of earth the wells Isaac had dug. We dig these wells whenever, in the hidden meanings of sacred Scripture, we penetrate into the depths; but the Allophyli secretly fill them when unclean spirits, as we reach toward higher things, inject earthly thoughts into us and take away the water of divine knowledge, as though it had been found.
>
> The Psalmist had endured this when he said: “Depart from me, you evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God” (Ps. CXVIII, 115), plainly indicating that he could not scrutinize God’s commandments while enduring in his mind the snares of evil spirits.

## Chapter 59 — Concerning the Blessings of Jacob and Esau (Genesis 27:27–28)

When the mysteries of the blessings of Jacob and Esau were being discussed, the following was added in the *Commentary on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 6 (no. 2 and following):

Who among the little ones, on hearing the account of Esau and Jacob—one sent out to hunt in order to be blessed, while the other was blessed by his father through his mother’s substitution—does not receive nourishment according to the history of sacred Scripture? If, in this history, the matter is examined with somewhat greater subtlety and applied to the understanding, it appears that Jacob did not steal the blessing [Col. 0711D] of the firstborn by fraud, but received it as something owed to him, having purchased it from his brother in exchange for the lentils.

But if someone with a deeper understanding wishes to examine the actions of both brothers through the hidden meanings of allegory, he immediately rises from history into mystery. For what does Isaac’s desire to eat from the hunt of his elder son signify, unless that almighty God desired to be nourished by the good works of the Jewish people? But while that son delayed, Rebekah substituted the younger one, because, while the Jewish people seek good works outwardly, maternal grace instructed the Gentile people to offer the omnipotent Father the nourishment of good works and to receive the blessing of the elder brother. He supplied those same foods from domestic animals, because the Gentile people, not seeking to please God through outward sacrifices, say through the voice of the Prophet [Col. 0712A]: “My vows are upon me, O God; I will repay them with praises to you” (Psalm 55:12).

What does it mean that this same Jacob covered his hands, arms, and neck with the skins of young goats, unless that a young goat was customarily offered for sin? And while the Gentile people do not blush to confess themselves sinners, they put to death within themselves the sins of the flesh.

What does it mean that he was clothed in his elder brother’s garments, unless that he was clothed in good works with the precepts of sacred Scripture, which had been given to the elder people? The younger uses them in the house, while the elder, going outside, left them within, because the Gentile people hold in their minds the precepts that the Jewish people could not possess while attending only to their letter.

And what does it mean that Isaac did not recognize the son whom he blessed, unless it signifies what the Lord says through the Psalmist concerning the Gentile people: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Psalm 18:43).

What does it mean that he does not see the one who is present, yet sees what will come in the future, unless that almighty God [Col. 0712B], when he foretold through his prophets that grace would be granted in preference to the Gentiles, did not see it in the present through grace, because at that time he left them in error, and yet foresaw it because he was eventually going to gather them into the grace of blessing?

Hence this same Jacob represents the figure of the Gentile people, and in the blessing it is said to him: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field, which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27). For, as the Truth says in the Gospel, “The field is this world” (Matthew 13:38); and because the Gentile people, brought to the faith, spread fragrance through their chosen ones throughout the whole world by their virtues, “the fragrance of the son” is “the fragrance of a full field.”

The flower of the vine has one kind of fragrance, because great is the virtue and reputation of preachers who intoxicate the minds of their hearers. The flower of the olive has another, because the work of mercy is sweet, refreshing and shining like oil. The flower of the rose has another, because marvelous is the fragrance that gleams and smells forth from the blood of martyrs. The flower of the lily has another, because the life of the flesh is made white by the incorruption of virginity. The flower of the violet has another, because great is the virtue of the humble, who, holding the lowest places out of desire [Col. 0712C] for them, do not raise themselves from the earth to the heights through pride, and preserve in their minds the purple of the heavenly kingdom. The ear of grain gives forth another fragrance when it is brought to maturity, because the perfection of good works is prepared to satisfy those who hunger for righteousness.

Since, therefore, the Gentile people are scattered throughout the world in their chosen ones, and through the virtues they practice fill all who understand with the fragrance of a good reputation, it is rightly said: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field.” But because it does not possess these virtues from itself, the passage adds: “Which the Lord God has blessed.”

And since the people of the elect rise through some of their members to contemplation, while through others they grow rich solely in the work of the active life, it is rightly added there: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth” (Genesis 27:28). Dew falls subtly from above, and we receive something of the dew of heaven whenever, through the infusion of inward contemplation, we perceive something of the things above in a delicate manner. But when we perform good works through the body as well, we are enriched by the richness of the earth.

[Col. 0712D] What does it mean, however, that Esau returns late to his father, unless that the Jewish people return late to appease the Lord? To him also it is said in the blessing: “The time will come when the yoke will be removed from your neck” (Genesis 27:40), because at the end the Jewish people will be freed from slavery to sin, as it is written: “Until the full number of the Gentiles has entered, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25).

## Chapter 60 — Concerning Isaac, who, while his eyes were dim [Col. 0713A], blessed his son Jacob without recognizing him, foresaw what was to come in the future, and did not recognize the one who stood present before him (Genesis 27:29–31)

When the ignorance of the Jews and the presence of our Redeemer were being discussed, the following was added in the *Exposition of the Blessed Job*, book XXXV (no. 26):

Concerning Isaac, whose eyes were dim, and so forth.

It is plainly evident that no Jew who had fully learned the Law was ignorant of the coming of our Redeemer. Hence King Herod, terrified by the arrival of the Magi, diligently sought to inquire of the priests and leaders where they knew Christ was to be born. They immediately answered him: “In Bethlehem of Judea.” They therefore knew beforehand the one whom, when they despised him at the time of his Passion, they afterward failed to recognize.

Their earlier knowledge and later ignorance are well and briefly signified by Isaac’s dim eyes: while blessing Jacob, he foresaw what would happen in the future, yet did not know who stood present before him. Such was the people of the Israelites, who received the mysteries of prophecy but retained blind eyes in contemplation. They did not see him present concerning whom they had foreseen many things in the future. They were entirely unable to perceive the one placed before them, whose coming they had announced long beforehand.

## Chapter 61 — Then Jacob went out from Beersheba and journeyed toward Haran; when he came to a certain place and wished to rest there after sunset, he took one of the stones lying there, placed it under his head, and slept in that place. In a dream he saw a ladder standing upon the earth, whose top touched the heavens; and he also saw angels ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder (Genesis 28:11).

When the condescension of teachers toward their hearers was being discussed, the following was added in the *Exposition of the Blessed Job*, book V (no. 54):

[Col. 0713B]

Then Jacob went out from Beersheba and journeyed toward Haran, and so forth.

To sleep on a journey is, in this passage through the present life, to rest from love of temporal things. To sleep on a journey is, in the course of passing days, to close the eyes of the mind to the desire for visible things—the eyes that the deceiver opened for the first human beings when he said: “For God knows that on the day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened” (Genesis 3:5). Hence a little later it is added: “She took of its fruit and ate, and gave it to her husband, who ate; and the eyes of both of them were opened” (ibid., 9). Guilt opened the eyes [Col. 0713C] of desire, which innocence had kept closed.

To see angels ascending and descending is to contemplate the citizens of the heavenly homeland: either how, by rising above themselves, they cling to their Creator with what love, or with what compassion of charity they descend to our weaknesses.

It must also be carefully noted that the sleeper sees angels who places his head upon a stone. For it is the person who ceases from outward works and penetrates eternal things, while attentively observing the imitation of his Redeemer with the mind, which is the principal part of the human being. To place one’s head upon a stone is to cling to Christ in the mind.

Those who withdraw from the activity of the present life but are drawn by no love toward heavenly things may sleep, but they cannot see angels, because they disdain to keep their head upon the stone. There are indeed some who flee the activities of the world but exercise themselves in no virtues. These sleep through torpor, not through devotion; and therefore they do not see inward things, because they have placed their head not upon a stone but [Col. 0713D] upon the earth.

It often happens to such people that the more securely they cease from external activities, the more widely, through idleness, they accumulate within themselves the tumult of filthy thoughts. Hence, under the figure of Judea, the soul lying torpid in idleness is lamented by the Prophet when it is said: “Her enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lamentations 1:7). For by the commandment of the Law one ceases from outward work on the Sabbath. The enemies therefore mock when they see the Sabbaths, because evil spirits drag the very leisure of rest toward unlawful thoughts, so that each soul, the more it believes it is serving God because it has withdrawn from external activities, serves their tyranny all the more by thinking unlawful thoughts.

Holy men, however, who are lulled to sleep from the works of the world not by torpor but by virtue, sleep more laboriously than they could have kept vigil. For in abandoning the activities of this age and rising above them, they daily struggle vigorously [Col. 0714A] against themselves: lest the mind grow torpid through negligence; lest, subdued by idleness, it cool through filthy desires; lest it burn more intensely than is right even with good desires; and lest, under the guise of discretion, it grow weak in perfection by sparing itself.

They do all this, withdrawing themselves completely from the restless desire of this world, abandoning the tumult of earthly activities, and, through the discipline of repose, sleeping wakefully while intent upon the virtues. For one is not led to contemplate inward things unless one diligently withdraws from those activities that occupy one outwardly.

Hence the Truth itself says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24). Hence Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Timothy 2:4). Hence the Lord admonishes through the Prophet, saying: “Be still and know that I am the Lord” (Psalm 46:10).

## Chapter 62 — Likewise, from the foregoing

In a letter from the *Register*, book I [formerly Epistle 24, now 25]:

[Note: [Col. 0713D] In the Uticensis manuscript, the source from which this was copied is not indicated. In the Michaelian manuscript, however, book V of the *Exposition of Job* is assigned.]

What is signified by Jacob, if not the person of preachers? [Col. 0714B] Perfect preachers desire only what is above, contemplating the Head of the Church, namely the Lord; yet they also descend below in compassion toward his members. This is demonstrated by the angels ascending and descending.

Hence Moses frequently enters and leaves the tabernacle. Within, he is carried away into contemplation; outside, he is pressed by the affairs of the weak. Within, he considers the mysteries of God; outside, he bears the burdens of those subject to the flesh. Whenever there are doubtful matters, he always returns to the tabernacle and consults the Lord before the ark of the covenant. Without doubt he thereby provides an example for rulers, so that whenever they are uncertain outside about what they should arrange, they may always return to the mind as though to a tabernacle and consult the Lord, as before the ark of the covenant, if, concerning the matters about which they are uncertain among themselves, they seek within the page of sacred eloquence.

## Chapter 63 — Concerning Leah and Rachel, and how Jacob, serving for Rachel, first received Leah (Genesis 29:24–25)

[Col. 0714C] When the contemplative and active life were being discussed in *Ezekiel*, book II, homily 2 (no. 10), the following was added:

Concerning Leah and Rachel, and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0714D] If we trust the Michaelian manuscript, these excerpts are from book VI of the *Commentary on Job*.]

What else are these two wives of Jacob—namely Leah and Rachel—but figures of the active and contemplative life? Leah is interpreted as “laborious,” while Rachel means “sheep,” or “the beginning that is seen.” The active life is laborious because it sweats in work; the contemplative life, being simple, yearns only to see the beginning—namely, him who says: “I am the beginning, for which reason I speak to you” (John 8:25).

Blessed Jacob desired Rachel, but received Leah during the night, because everyone who turns to the Lord desires the contemplative life and longs for the rest of the eternal homeland. Yet it is first necessary for him to do whatever good he can during the night of the present life, to sweat in labor—in other words, to receive Leah—so that afterward he may rest in Rachel’s embrace, beholding the Beginning.

Rachel was seeing but barren, whereas Leah was bleary-eyed but fertile. For when the mind, in contemplating [Col. 0714D], seeks repose, it sees more but produces fewer children for God; when it turns toward the labor of preaching, it sees less but gives birth to more. The contemplative life is beautiful in the mind, but while it seeks to rest in silence, it does not generate children through preaching. It sees but does not give birth, because in its pursuit of repose it devotes itself less to gathering others, and the more it looks inward, the less able it is to disclose what it sees to others through preaching.

Leah, however, is bleary-eyed and fertile, because the active life, while occupied with work, sees less; but while it kindles those near it to imitation, now by word and now by example, it generates many children in good works. And if it cannot hold the mind in contemplation, nevertheless, through what it does outwardly, it can beget followers.

After embracing Leah, therefore, Jacob came to Rachel, because every perfected person is first [Col. 0715A] joined to the active life for fruitfulness and afterward united to the contemplative life for rest.

## Chapter 64 — Jacob took green rods of poplar, almond, and plane tree; he partly stripped them of their bark, and when the bark had been removed, whiteness appeared in the places that had been exposed. But the parts that remained intact stayed green, and in this way the color became varied. He placed them in the channels into which the water flowed, so that when the flocks came to drink, they would have the rods before their eyes and conceive while looking at them. Thus it happened that, in the heat of mating, the sheep gazed upon the rods and gave birth to spotted and variegated young, marked with different colors (Genesis 30:37 and following).

When the allegories hidden in history were being examined in the *Exposition of the Blessed Job*, book XXI (no. 1), the following was added:

Jacob took green rods of poplar, and so forth.

The meaning of sacred eloquence must be weighed between text and mystery with such balance that, with the scales of both sides held in moderation, neither is it depressed by the weight of excessive examination [Col. 0715B] nor left empty through the torpor of negligence.

Many of its meanings are so pregnant with allegorical conceptions that anyone who attempts to hold them strictly to history alone is deprived of their knowledge through his own negligence. Others, however, serve external precepts so completely that if someone wishes to penetrate them more subtly, he finds nothing within and even conceals from himself what they say outwardly. Hence, through its significance, the historical narrative rightly says: “Jacob took green rods of poplar, almond, and plane tree; he partly stripped them,” and so forth.

What does it mean to place green rods of poplar, almond, and plane tree before the eyes of the flocks, unless it means to offer the lives and teachings of the ancient Fathers, through the sequence of sacred Scripture, as an example to the people? Since these are straight according to the test of reason, they are called rods.

He partly removes their bark so that an inward whiteness may appear [Col. 0715C] in what has been stripped, and partly preserves the bark so that they may remain green outwardly, as they had been. The color of the rods becomes varied because the bark is partly removed and partly retained.

The teachings of the Fathers who preceded us are set before the eyes of our consideration like various rods. When we generally avoid the meaning of the letter, we remove the bark, as it were; when we generally follow the meaning of the letter, we preserve the bark, as it were. When the bark of the letter is removed from them, the inner whiteness of allegory is revealed; when the bark is left, the outward, flourishing examples of understanding are displayed.

Jacob rightly placed them in channels of water, because our Redeemer fixed them in books of sacred knowledge, through which we are inwardly watered. When rams mate with the ewes while looking upon these rods, our rational spirits, fixed in their contemplation, mingle with their various actions, so that they produce offspring of works corresponding to the examples of those who preceded them, which they see in the words of instruction. The offspring of good work [Col. 0715D] has a varied color because sometimes, when the bark of the letter has been removed, it considers inward things more keenly, and sometimes, when the covering of history has been retained, it forms good things in outward conduct.

## Chapter 65 — Concerning Laban, who, pursuing Jacob in fury, searched for his idols among Jacob’s possessions (Genesis 31:33–34)

When the temptations of the devil and the virtues of the Church were being discussed in the *Exposition of the Blessed Job*, book XXX (no. 72), the following was added:

Concerning Laban, who, pursuing Jacob in fury, and so forth.

Laban is interpreted as “whitening.” This whitening is not improperly understood as the devil, who, although dark by merit, transforms himself into an angel of light.

Jacob served him—that is, the Jewish people, in part belonging to the reprobate, served him; and from the flesh of that people the Lord came incarnate.

Laban may also represent this world, which pursues Jacob in fury, because it tries to oppress through persecution all the elect, who are members of our Redeemer [Col. 0716A].

Jacob took away Laban’s daughter—that is, whether the daughter of the world or of the devil—when Christ joined the Church from among the Gentiles to himself. He also took her away from her father’s house, for through the Prophet he says to her: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 45:10).

What is signified by idols, if not greed? Hence Paul says: “And greed, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3:5).

Laban therefore came to Jacob but did not find the idols, because, though the devil displayed the treasures of the world, he found no trace of earthly desire in our Redeemer.

But what Jacob did not have, Rachel covered while sitting. Through Rachel, who is also called a sheep, the Church is represented. To sit is to seek the humility of repentance, as it is written: “Rise after you have sat” (Psalm 127:2).

Rachel therefore covered the idols by sitting, because the holy Church, following Christ, covered the vices of earthly desire through repentance. Concerning this covering of vices the Prophet says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven [Col. 0716B] and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 32:1).

That Rachel therefore signified us: we press down the idols by sitting when we condemn the faults of greed through repentance.

Greed, to be sure, does not usually befall those who run manfully along the way of the Lord, to whom it is said: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Psalm 31:24). Rather, it chiefly befalls those who, walking with an effeminate step, are weakened by the world’s flatteries. Hence Rachel’s words there are also: “It has befallen me according to the custom of women.”

Laban therefore did not find the idols with Jacob, because the crafty exactor found nothing in our Redeemer that he could criticize.

## Chapter 66 — Concerning Jacob’s Wrestling with the Angel (Genesis 32:24)

When the power and usefulness of contemplation were being discussed in *Ezekiel*, book II, homily 2 (no. 12), the following was added:

Concerning Jacob’s wrestling with the angel.

Great is the mind’s struggle in the contemplative life [Col. 0716C]: when it raises itself toward heavenly things, when it stretches its spirit toward spiritual realities, when it strives to transcend everything that is perceived bodily, and when it constricts itself in order to expand.

At times it wins and overcomes the darkness resisting it in its blindness, so that it may secretly and delicately touch something of the unbounded light. Yet, immediately thrown back upon itself, it returns, and from the light toward which it passes in aspiration, it returns with sighs and lamentation to the darkness of its own blindness.

The sacred history aptly represents this when it narrates that blessed Jacob wrestled with an angel. As he was returning to his own relatives, he met an angel on the way, with whom he engaged in a great contest of wrestling. One who struggles in wrestling sometimes finds himself superior and sometimes inferior to the one with whom he contends.

The angel therefore represents God, while Jacob, who contends with the angel, expresses the soul of every perfected man engaged in contemplation. When the soul strives to contemplate God, it is placed, as it were, in a contest [Col. 0716D]: at one moment it seems to overcome, because through understanding and perception it tastes something of the unbounded light; at another it succumbs, because even while tasting it, it again fails.

The angel is therefore as though defeated when God is grasped by inward understanding. But it must be noted that the same angel, after being defeated, touched Jacob’s thigh sinew and immediately caused it to wither; from that time Jacob limped on one foot. This signifies that when almighty God has already become known to us through desire and understanding, he dries up in us every pleasure of the flesh.

Previously we seemed to seek God while also holding on to the world, as though relying upon two feet. After recognizing the sweetness of God, one foot remains sound in us while the other limps, because it is necessary that, as love of the world is weakened, the love of God alone should grow strong.

If, therefore, we hold the angel, we limp on one foot, because as the strength of inward love increases in us, the strength of the flesh is [Col. 0717A] undoubtedly weakened. Everyone who limps on one foot relies upon the foot that remains sound. Likewise, if earthly desire has already withered in anyone, he supports himself with all his strength upon the single foot of love for God and stands upon it, because he now carries suspended from the earth the foot of worldly love that he was accustomed to place upon the earth.

If, then, we return to our own relatives—that is, to spiritual fathers—let us hold the angel on the way, so that we may grasp God in inward sweetness.

The sweetness of the contemplative life is exceedingly lovely. It carries the mind above itself, longs for heavenly things, shows that earthly things ought to be despised, and reveals spiritual realities to the eyes of the mind while concealing bodily things.

Hence the Church rightly says in the *Song of Songs*: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2). One sleeps with a wakeful heart when, by progressing inwardly through contemplation, one rests from wicked outward activity.

## Chapter 67 — Likewise, from the foregoing

In the *Exposition of the Blessed Job*, book IV (no. 67):

[Note: [Col. 0717D] In the manuscripts, the chapter begins with these words.]

[Col. 0717B] Jacob, who held the angel, immediately limped on one foot, because whoever looks upon exalted things with love no longer wishes to walk in this world with divided desires. He relies upon one foot who is strengthened by the love of God alone. It is necessary that the other wither, because as the strength of the mind increases, the strength of the flesh must undoubtedly grow numb.

Hence the Prophet, after saying that he had seen a vision of God, adds: “I languished and was sick for many days” (Daniel 8:27), because when the mind is drawn tightly toward the power of God, the flesh is wearied of its own strength.

## Chapter 68 — “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was preserved” (Genesis 32:30)

When the manner in which the vision of God should be understood was being discussed in the *Exposition of the Blessed Job*, book XXIV (nos. 11–12), the following was added:

“I saw the Lord face to face,” and so forth.

Since the Truth itself says: “No one has ever seen my face” (Exodus 33:23), how does Jacob [Col. 0717C] testify, saying: “I saw the Lord face to face”?

When the inner eye of the human mind has been purified, and the rust of all vices has been burned away in the fire of tribulation, then, with the eyes of the heart cleansed, the joy of the heavenly homeland is opened to us. First we must purify ourselves by mourning what we have done; afterward, through joy, we contemplate more clearly what we seek.

First, the darkness of evils interposed before the mind’s vision is wiped away by grief as it burns; then the heart is suddenly illumined by the flashing radiance of the unbounded light. Having perceived it in some fashion, the mind is absorbed into the joy of a certain security and, as though snatched beyond the present life after its exhaustion, is somehow renewed in a kind of newness of life.

There the mind is sprinkled from an immense fountain by the infusion of heavenly dew. There it sees that it is not sufficient for the contemplation to which it has been carried away; and, while perceiving the truth, it sees that it does not see how great the truth itself is.

The more it approaches that truth, the farther away it believes itself to be, because unless it perceived it [Col. 0717D] in some way, it would not at all feel that it was unable to perceive it. When the mind’s striving is directed toward it, it is thrown back by the flashing radiance of its immensity surrounding it.

For the truth itself, filling all things, surrounds all things. Therefore our mind cannot expand itself sufficiently to grasp an unbounded substance, because the inadequacy of its own limitation constricts it. Hence it quickly slips back to itself and, having glimpsed what are as it were certain traces of truth, is recalled to its lower condition.

This experience produced through contemplation is nevertheless called not a solid and enduring vision but, so to speak, a kind of imitation of vision—the face of God. Since we know someone through his face, it is not inappropriate to call the knowledge of God his face.

Thus, after Jacob had wrestled with the angel, he said: “I saw the Lord face to face,” as though he were saying: “I came to know the Lord, who himself graciously allowed me to know [Col. 0718A] him.”

Paul testifies that this knowledge will be made complete at the end, saying: “Then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

## Chapter 69 — Dinah went out to see the women of that region; when Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite and prince of that land, saw her, he fell in love with her, seized her, and slept with her, violating the virgin by force; and his soul was joined to her, and he soothed her sorrow with flattering words.

When the need to guard against the mind’s wandering was being discussed in the *Pastoral Rule* (part III, chapter 29, admonition 30), the following was added:

“Dinah went out,” and so forth.

Dinah goes out to see the women of a foreign region whenever any mind neglects its own concerns, takes care of the activities of others, and wanders outside its own character and proper order.

Shechem, the prince of the land, violates her because the devil corrupts the mind when he finds it occupied with external cares. “And his soul was joined to her,” because he regards her as united to him through iniquity [Col. 0718B].

And because, when the mind attempts to recover from guilt and mourn what it has committed, the corrupter recalls empty hopes and false assurances before its eyes in order to remove the benefit of sorrow, the passage rightly adds: “And he soothed her sorrow with flattering words.”

At one moment he speaks of the more serious deeds of others; at another, that what has been committed is nothing; at another, of the Lord’s mercy; and at another, promises that there will still be time afterward for repentance. Thus, while the deceived mind is led along by these things, it is suspended from its resolve to repent, so that it perceives no good then because no evil now causes it sorrow, and is afterward overwhelmed more completely by punishments because it now even rejoices in its offenses.

## Chapter 70 — Concerning Joseph’s ankle-length tunic (Genesis 37:24)

When perseverance in good works was being discussed in the *Exposition of the Blessed Job*, book I (no. 55), the following was added:

Concerning Joseph’s ankle-length tunic.

Joseph is described as having persevered in righteousness to the end among his eleven brothers [Col. 0718C], and he alone is said to have possessed an ankle-length tunic.

What, then, is the ankle-length tunic except a completed action? For a tunic extended downward covers the body to the ankle; likewise, a good action covers us before the eyes of God all the way to the end of life.

Hence Moses also commands that the tail of the animal be offered upon the altar (Exodus 29; Leviticus 3), so that whenever we begin any good, we may complete it with a persevering conclusion.

## Chapter 71 — “Behold, our dreamer is coming; come, let us kill him and see what his dreams will profit him” (Genesis 37:7).

While the subject under discussion was the perverse thoughts of depraved minds, in opposition to the foreknowledge of the inner disposition, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book VI (Nos. 28–29), the following passage was added: “Behold, our dreamer is coming,” etc.—Often, certain people, puffed up with human wisdom, observe that divine judgments run counter to their desires and try to resist them by crafty schemes. In order to bend the force of the heavenly disposition toward their own wish, they persist in cunning plans and seek out more subtle strategies. Yet they accomplish God’s will precisely by attempting to change it, and while striving to resist the counsel of almighty God, they obey it. For it often serves his disposition appropriately that which, through human endeavor, foolishly rebounds against him, as it is written: “He catches the wise in their craftiness” (Job 5:13).

He catches the wise in their own craftiness when human actions serve his plans fittingly even while they resist them. Hence the Psalmist also says: “The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain” (Psalm 93:11). We shall show this more clearly if we bring forward a few examples from the events that took place.

Joseph had dreamed that his sheaf stood while the sheaves of his brothers prostrated themselves before it; he had dreamed that the sun and moon, together with the remaining stars, worshiped him. Because he reported these dreams plainly to his brothers, their hearts were immediately struck by envy and fear of the condemnation that was to come. When they saw him approaching, they said in their wicked fury: “Behold, that dreamer is coming; come, let us kill him and see what his dreams will profit him.” Fearing that they would be subjected to his rule, they lowered the dreamer into a pit and sold him to passing Ishmaelites.

Brought into Egypt and subjected to slavery, condemned on an accusation of sexual misconduct, aided by the merit of his chastity, rescued through the judgment of prophecy, he was placed over all Egypt. Through heavenly wisdom he prudently gathered grain and forestalled the danger of future want. When famine raged throughout the world, Jacob, concerned about the preparation of food, sent his sons to Egypt. Not knowing Joseph, who had been placed in charge of the distribution of grain, they found him there and, compelled in order to receive food, worshiped its steward with their necks bent to the ground.

Let us therefore consider how divine power apprehends human thoughts in the very act of their planning. Joseph had been sold by them so that he would not be worshiped; yet he was worshiped precisely because he had been sold. They had cunningly dared to do something in order to alter God’s plan, but by resisting they served, through divine judgment, the very plan they had tried to avoid. They were compelled to accomplish God’s will by the very means through which they had craftily sought to change it.

Thus, thus, the divine plan is fulfilled while it is being evaded; thus human wisdom, while resisting, is caught. The brothers feared that Joseph would rise above them, but by taking precautions they brought about what had been divinely ordained. Human wisdom was therefore caught in itself: by the very intention through which it resisted God’s will, it served its fulfillment.

So too, when Saul saw that David, though subject to him, was increasing daily through the success of his virtues, he promised him his daughter in marriage and demanded that David give a hundred Philistine foreskins as her dowry. He intended that, when the soldier was provoked to seek still greater achievements, he would be handed over to the swords of his enemies and meet his death, as it is written: “The king requires no bridal gift except a hundred Philistine foreskins, so that vengeance may be taken on the king’s enemies” (1 Samuel 18:25).

Saul was thinking of handing David over to the Philistines, but David, strengthened by the favor of the hidden disposition, declared that he would give a hundred and returned with two hundred foreskins. Saul was plainly defeated by the evidence of this deed and was caught by heavenly providence in the plan of his own wisdom, because the very means by which he thought he would extinguish the life of the rising soldier instead increased the glory of his valor.

But since even the elect sometimes contrive, in their cleverness, to display some wisdom, let us bring another wise man into the discussion and demonstrate within what recess of the inner counsel the craftiness of mortals is caught.

Jonah wished to act wisely when, sent to preach repentance to Nineveh, he refused to fulfill his prophetic ministry. He feared that Judea would be abandoned when the Gentiles were chosen, so he sought a ship and decided to flee to Tarshish. But immediately a storm arose, and lots were cast so that it might be discovered whose fault had stirred up the sea. Jonah was found guilty, plunged into the depths, swallowed by a sea creature, and carried by the beast to the place where he had refused to go voluntarily (Jonah 1–3).

Behold: the storm finds God’s fugitive, the lot binds him, the sea receives him, and the beast encloses him. Because he resists obeying the voice of his creator, he is carried as a guilty man in his own prison to the place to which he had been sent. At God’s command, the man refused to minister prophecy; under God’s direction, the beast vomited out the prophet.

God therefore bends human prudence to his service when he turns even that by which the human will contradicts him to the use of his own will. Let us examine further the wisdom of the Hebrews and see what it provoked by planning and what by attempting to prevent.

Certainly, when a crowd of believers flocked to the miracles of our Redeemer, and when the priests of the people, inflamed by the torches of envy, saw the world going after him and cried out, saying, “Do you see that we are accomplishing nothing? Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19), they tried to put an end to his power by killing him. They said: “It is better that one man should die than that the whole nation should perish” (John 11:56). But the death of the Redeemer served the joining of his body—that is, the Church—not its separation.

Thus he turned to the service of his mercy even that which human cruelty had kindled against him. The just and merciful one, arranging the deeds of mortals, graciously grants some things and permits others in anger; and what he permits, he tolerates in such a way that he turns it to the use of his plan. In this marvelous way, what is done without God’s will is nevertheless not contrary to God’s will, because when evil deeds are turned to a good use, even those that resist his plan serve it.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Psalm 111:2). His works are indeed so great that through everything human beings do, his will is sought out; for it is often accomplished through the very means by which it was thought to be opposed. Again it is said: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 135:6). Solomon also says: “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21:30).

It remains, therefore, that in everything we do we should seek the force of the heavenly will. Once it is known, our action ought devotedly to serve it and to follow it as the guide of its journey, lest, if it proudly turns away from it, it serve it even against its will. The force of the heavenly counsel cannot be avoided at all; but the person who restrains himself beneath its commands tempers it for himself with great virtue, and lightens its burdens for himself by willingly carrying them on the shoulder of a submissive heart.

## CHAPTER LXXII.—“Behold, my lord, having entrusted everything to me, does not know what he has in his house, and there is nothing that is not in my power” (Genesis 39:8).

[Column 0720C]

**Note:** In our manuscripts this chapter has no other title, nor is anything else prefixed to Gregory’s statement.

In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXX (No. 38):—Whoever, lifted up by the successes of this world, feels himself, through the seductive joy of his heart, being tempted by the goads of lust, should recall Joseph’s deed to mind and preserve himself in the citadel of chastity. When he saw his mistress urging him toward the loss of his purity, he said: “Behold, my lord, having entrusted everything to me, does not know what he has in his house, and there is nothing that is not in my power, nor has he withheld anything from me except you, who are his wife. How, then, can I do this great evil and sin against my lord?” By these words he showed that he suddenly brought to mind the good things he had obtained and overcame the evil that was assaulting him. Because he remembered the grace he had received, he broke the force of the impending sin.

For when slippery pleasure tempts us amid prosperity, that very prosperity must be set against the goad of temptation, so that we may be ashamed to commit wrongdoing precisely because we remember that we have freely received good things from God. We must turn the grace bestowed through outward gifts into weapons of virtue, so that what we have received may stand before our eyes and we may subdue whatever entices us. Since pleasure itself arises from prosperity, prosperity must be struck by reflection, so that our enemy may die at the point from which he arises.

We must take care not to turn a gift received into vice, lest the abyss of wickedness swallow us through the favor of this life. For we kindle the anger of the heavenly Judge against ourselves unquenchably if we fight against his kindness—and even against his own generosity—with that very generosity.

**Note:** In the printed editions, the text is extremely corrupt: “when slippery *will* tempts in prosperity, [prosperity is] to be set against the goad of temptation”; and below, “so much the more,” instead of “by God.” Gussanville retained these defects of the Vatican edition and compounded them.

## CHAPTER LXXIII.—“But he left his cloak in her hands, fled, and went outside” (Genesis 39:12).

[Column 0720D]

[Column 0721A]

While the veil that remains upon the hearts of the Jews was under discussion in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book II (No. 59), the following passage was added: “But he left his cloak in her hands and fled,” etc.—When the adulterous woman wished to misuse Joseph, he left his cloak and fled outside. In the same way, when the Synagogue, believing the Lord to be merely a man, wished to bind him in an adulterous embrace, he left the covering of its letter to its eyes and presented himself openly to the Gentiles so that they might recognize the power of his divinity. Hence Paul also says: “To this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart” (1 Corinthians 3:12). The adulterous woman retained the cloak with herself and lost naked the one whom she had held wrongly.

## CHAPTER LXXIV.—“Jacob entered Egypt with seventy souls” (Genesis 46:27).

**Note:** This chapter is absent from our manuscripts.
