In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book III (No. 22):—Sacred Scripture often customarily places a part for the whole, as in: “Jacob entered Egypt with seventy souls.” When it speaks of “souls,” it is plainly including the bodies of those who entered.

## CHAPTER LXXV.—That, while Joseph governed, the Egyptians received grain for food before they were subjected to Pharaoh by the law of servitude because of the famine; but after they sold themselves into slavery under the pressure of hunger, they then received grain for seed (Genesis 47).

While the reward of those who serve steadfastly was under discussion, in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book VI (No. 55), the following passage was added: “That, while Joseph governed, the Egyptians,” etc.—The Egyptians, subjected to public service under Joseph’s administration, humble themselves by surrendering themselves to the king’s authority and also carry away grain for seed.

We receive the produce for food even while we are free, when we are nourished by sacred Scripture and yet remain at leisure for certain things we desire in this world, indulging our pleasures. But once made servants, we also receive grain for seed, because when we submit ourselves wholly to God, we are likewise filled with the word of preaching.

## CHAPTER LXXVI.—“Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries; he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he put his shoulder to bear the burden” (Genesis 49:14).

[Column 0721C]

While the works of the Gentiles were under discussion in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book I (No. 24), the following passage was added: “Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries,” etc.—To lie down between the boundaries means to rest while awaiting the end of the world, seeking nothing of the things now present in between, but desiring the final things. The strong ass sees rest and an excellent land when the simple Gentile raises himself to the strength of good works for this reason: because he is journeying toward the homeland of eternal life.

He puts his shoulder to bear because, having seen the heavenly rest, he submits himself to God in action even under difficult commands; and whatever weakness declares intolerable, the hope of reward shows to be light and easy for him.

## CHAPTER LXXVII.—“Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hooves, so that its rider may fall backward” (Genesis 49:17).

[Column 0721D]

While the coming and works of Antichrist were under discussion in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXXI (No. 43), the following passage was added: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent on the path,” etc.—What is signified here by the name “horse” except the present world? We have explained more fully elsewhere what the horse signifies in this passage, and whose hooves the serpent bites, if we examine the surrounding material somewhat more subtly.

Some say that Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan, because Dan is here described both as a serpent and as one who bites. Thus, not without reason, when the Israelite people were receiving lands in the division of the camps, Dan first encamped toward the north (Numbers 2:25), signifying the one who had said in his heart: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13). Of him the prophet also says: “From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard” (Jeremiah 8:16).

He is called not only a serpent but also a *cerastes*, for *cerata* in Greek means “horns.” This serpent is said to be horned, by which the coming of Antichrist is fittingly signified, because against the life of the faithful he is armed not only with the poisonous bite of his preaching but also with the horns of power.

Who does not know that a path is narrower than a way? Dan therefore becomes a serpent in the way because he invites those whom he flatters as though sparing them to walk in the breadth of the present life. But he bites in the way because he destroys with the poison of his error those to whom he grants liberty. He becomes a horned serpent on the path because he attacks those whom he finds faithful and who constrain themselves to the narrow roads of the heavenly commandment—not only with the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also with the terror of power. In the anguish of persecution, after the benefits of feigned sweetness, he exercises the horns of his power.

In this passage the horse signifies this world, which, through its pride, foams as it runs along the course of passing times. Because Antichrist attempts to seize the world’s final period, this horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s hooves. To bite the horse’s hooves means to reach the world’s final things by striking them, so that its rider may fall backward.

The rider of the horse is anyone who is exalted by the dignities of the world. He is said to fall backward, and not on his face, as Saul is remembered to have fallen. To fall on one’s face is, in this life, for each person to recognize his own sins and mourn them through repentance. To fall backward, where one cannot see, is to depart suddenly from this life and not know to what punishments one is being led.

And because Judea, caught in the snares of its error, awaits Antichrist in place of Christ, Jacob, in the same passage, fittingly turned suddenly into the voice of the elect and said: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (Genesis 49:18)—that is, I do not faithfully believe in Antichrist as the unbelievers do, but in the true Christ, who is to come for our redemption.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII.—Likewise, from the passage above.

While the destruction of the reprobate and the humility of the elect were under discussion in the *Commentary on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 9 (Nos. 4–5), the following passage was added:—

**Note:** The editions contain the very serious error *verendum* (“to be feared”), whereas the manuscripts—both those of Paterius and those of the homily on Ezekiel—read *quaerendum* (“to be sought”). The other reading makes no sense.

“We must ask why Paul, traveling to Damascus and illuminated by heavenly light, falls on his face, while it is said of the rider of the horse—that is, of the one exalted by the glory of this world—‘so that its rider may fall backward.’ For it is written of the persecutors of the Lord: ‘They went backward and fell to the ground’” (John 18:6).

What does it mean that the elect fall on their faces and the reprobate fall backward, except that everyone who falls backward undoubtedly falls where he cannot see? The wicked are said to fall backward because they fall into invisible things, collapsing where they cannot now see what follows them. The righteous, however, because they willingly cast themselves down in these visible things so that they may be raised up in the invisible things, fall as though on their faces: seeing, they humble themselves, pierced by fear.

## CHAPTER LXXIX.—“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he eats the prey, and in the evening he divides the spoils” (Genesis 49:27).

While the persecution and teaching of the apostle Paul were under discussion in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XVIII (No. 25), the following passage was added: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he eats the prey,” etc.—Who is signified here by the name Benjamin except the apostle Paul? Born from the tribe of Benjamin, he eats the prey in the morning because, at the beginning of his career, he seized as many of the faithful as he could and satisfied his own cruelty. In the evening he divides the spoils because, afterward becoming faithful, he distributed the sacred writings by explaining them.

# BOOK TWO  
## On the Testimonies of the Book of Exodus

[Column 0723]

## CHAPTER ONE.—“Because the midwives feared God, he built houses for them” (Exodus 1:21).

[Column 0723A]

While the avoidance of lying was under discussion in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XVIII (Nos. 5–6), the following passage was added: “Because the midwives feared God,” etc.—Every lie must be avoided with the greatest care, although sometimes a certain kind of lie is a lighter fault, as when someone lies in order to preserve another’s life. But because it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11), and: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm 5:7), perfect men also avoid this kind of lie with the greatest care. They do not defend anyone’s life through their deception, lest they harm their own souls while striving to preserve another’s flesh. Nevertheless, we readily believe that this very kind of sin is easily forgiven. For if any fault is usually cleansed by a subsequent pious deed, how much more easily is this fault wiped away when piety itself, the mother of good works, accompanies it? (22, Question 2, chapters 29 and 51, *Quaelibet*).

Some, however, try to assert from the deception of the midwives that this kind of lie is not a sin, especially because, when they lied, it was written of them: “The Lord built houses for them” (Exodus 1). Yet in this very recompense it becomes clearer what reward the fault of lying deserves. The reward for their kindness—which could have been repaid to them in eternal life—was, because of the fault of the admitted lie, diverted into an earthly recompense. Thus, in the life which they had sought to preserve by lying, they received the good things they had done, but they had no further reward of their merit to await.

For, if the matter is carefully considered, they lied out of love for the present life, not with the intention of gaining a reward. They tried to protect the infants’ life by sparing them, while protecting their own through lying.

## CHAPTER TWO.—Concerning Moses: after he had withdrawn into the desert because he had killed an Egyptian, he saw a vision of flame in a bush (Exodus 2).

While the pursuit of mental quiet and the avoidance of the tumult of worldly cares were under discussion in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXIII (No. 37), the following passage was added: “Concerning Moses: after he had killed an Egyptian and withdrawn into the desert,” etc.—Moses, mixed in with the Egyptians, was, as it were, awake, and therefore, while he remained in Egypt, he did not hear the voice of the Lord. But after the Egyptian had been killed, when he fled into the desert and spent forty years there, he, as it were, fell asleep away from the tumult of restless earthly desires. For this reason he deserved to receive the divine voice: through heavenly grace, the more he grew sluggish toward external pursuits, the more truly he became watchful for the knowledge of inward things (No. 40).

When the mind is lulled by external activities, then it recognizes more fully the weight of God’s commandments. The mind penetrates God’s words more keenly when it refuses to admit into itself the tumult of worldly cares. A person is badly awake when the heat of worldly affairs disturbs him arrogantly. The crowd of earthly thoughts, by its uproar, closes the ear of the heart; and the less the noise of turbulent cares is restrained in the mind’s inner chamber, the less the voice of the presiding Judge is heard. For a person divided between both is not fully sufficient for either. While he wishes to be instructed inwardly in such a way that he is nevertheless entangled outwardly, the very thing by which he opens his hearing outwardly makes him deaf inwardly.

## CHAPTER THREE.—[Note: This chapter is entirely absent from our manuscripts.] Likewise, from the passage above.

From homily 7 on Ezekiel (No. 10):—For when Moses had been called from the burning bush, he came nearer to see the vision; and behold, the bush was burning but was not consumed. This is a great miracle. If you seek only the historical meaning, there is something here to nourish the mind of the reader: you see fire burning in wood without consuming it.

But if you seek a typological interpretation, what is the flame except the Law, of which it is written: “A fiery law was in his right hand” (Deuteronomy 33:2)? And what did that bush signify except the Jewish people, covered with the thorns of their sins? Yet the burning bush could not be consumed, because the Jewish people received the fire of the Law but did not abandon the thorns of their sins, nor did the flame of the divine word burn away their vices.

Perhaps someone wishes to contemplate greater things typologically in this event. As its meaning grows, the wheels too are raised together. Among human beings, the one Son of God was made fully human: he had no sins of his own, but took upon himself the thorns of our wickedness. He deigned to humble himself for us even unto the Passion and to receive into himself the fire of our tribulation. Yet he burned and did not burn, because although he died according to his humanity, he remained immortal according to his divinity. He received from us that from which a sacrifice could be made for us, yet in himself he remained impassible and unchangeable, so that he might change us from our own condition.

## CHAPTER FOUR.—Concerning the flame in the bush.

While the divine mysteries enacted through symbolic signs were under discussion in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXVIII (No. 8), the following passage was added: “Concerning the flame in the bush.”—God often speaks through angels by joining earthly and heavenly substances, as he did to Moses on the mountain when, uttering the words of his command, he joined fire and bush together, connecting one above with the other below. This occurs, however, only when something is signified by the conjunction itself.

When he addressed Moses through the burning bush, what else did he show except that Moses would become the leader of that people which would receive the flame of the Law and yet would by no means avoid the thorn of sin? Or did he show that from that people would come the one who, in the fire of divinity, would receive the pains of our flesh like the thorns of a bush and preserve the substance of our humanity unconsumed even within the flame of divinity?

## CHAPTER FIVE.—That the land of Canaan is promised to the Israelite people (Exodus 3:8).

While the providential invitation of those newly coming to the faith was under discussion in book III, part 3, of the *Book of Pastoral Rule* (chapter 26, admonition 27), the following passage was added: “That the land of Canaan is promised to the Israelite people.”—It must be considered that the prosperity of the present life is sometimes given to summon a person to a better life, but sometimes to condemn him more fully for eternity. Hence the land of Canaan is promised to the Israelite people, so that they might eventually be summoned to hope for eternal things.

That inexperienced people would not have believed God’s promises concerning things far away if they had not also received something nearby from their Promiser. Thus, to strengthen them more certainly in faith in eternal things, they are drawn not only by hope toward realities, but also by realities toward hope. The Psalmist clearly testifies to this, saying: “He gave them the region of the nations, and they possessed the labor of the peoples, so that they might keep his justifications and seek his law” (Psalm 105:44–45).

## CHAPTER SIX.—Likewise, from the passage above.

In the *Exposition of the Gospel*, homily 32 (No. 6):—When the Israelite people were being liberated from the land of Egypt, the land of promise was promised to them; and when they were to be called, they were persuaded toward heavenly gifts by earthly promises. Why was this done? Was it not so that, since they received something nearby, they would now believe more faithfully what they could hear about something far away?

If we attend to this carefully, we recognize how great a dispensation of mercy was involved. Something concerning the present life had to be promised even to an inexperienced people, so that they might be made more firmly established in the future. For a carnal people would not have believed great things if they had not received small ones. Almighty God, therefore, by bestowing earthly things, persuades them toward heavenly things, so that, receiving what they could see, they might learn to hope for what they could not see. They would become more firmly established concerning invisible things in proportion as visible promises supported them toward certainty of hope.

## CHAPTER SEVEN.—That the angel who is described as having appeared to Moses is sometimes called an angel and sometimes the Lord (Exodus 3).

**Note:** In the Michel manuscript: “concerning the divine ministries administered through an angel.”

While the ministry administered through an angel was under discussion in the *Exposition of Blessed Job* (No. 3, preface), the following passage was added: “That the angel who is described as having appeared to Moses,” etc.—What does it mean that the vision described as having appeared to Moses in the wilderness is sometimes called an angel and sometimes the Lord, except that he is called an angel because he served by speaking outwardly, but the Lord because, presiding inwardly, he supplied the efficacy of speech?

**Note:** In the same source: “except that he is an angel.”

Thus, when the speaker is governed from within, he is remembered both as an angel through his service and as the Lord through his inspiration.

## CHAPTER EIGHT.—That Moses was sent to free the people only when Pharaoh had already been stirred up to oppress them with harsh labor (Exodus 3:7–8).

While the avoidance of prosperity and the pursuit of the exercise of temptations were under discussion in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXVI (Nos. 20–21), the following passage was added: “That Moses was sent to free the people,” etc.—For minds scattered outwardly, it is difficult to return to themselves. Once they have taken up wicked paths, those paths hold them all the more delightfully because everything they desire is permitted in them. No wall of discipline stands in the way to restrain them, and no punishment of retribution is seen to frighten them. With the eyes of the heart closed, the soul is hurled into the lowest depths precisely as it is darkened with respect to the highest things; and it perpetrates temporal evils with greater security the more harshly it despairs of eternal goods.

But this wickedness of the reprobate, like threshing, presses the life of the elect, separating the grain from the chaff, so that it may purify them. The wicked free the good more effectively from the desires of this world by afflicting them. For while they inflict many forms of violence upon them here, they compel them to hasten toward heavenly things.

This was well signified by Moses calling the Israelite people while King Pharaoh raged. Moses was sent to call them precisely when Pharaoh had already been stirred up to oppress them with harsh labor, so that, while one called and another, by raging, drove them onward, the minds of the Israelites, shamefully attached to Egypt, might be drawn away—one as though pulling them, the other as though pushing them—and the people, fixed disgracefully in slavery, might be moved either by the invitation of good things or by the pressure of evils.

This happens daily when the reprobate are permitted to rage against the elect while heavenly rewards are being preached, so that, if we neglect to leave when called to the land of promise, we may at least be driven out by the pressures of persecution. Thus Egypt—that is, the present life, which has oppressed us by flattering us—may help us by pressing us; and what, while cherishing us, crushes us beneath the yoke of slavery may, while tormenting us, show us the way to liberty.

This, then, is why the just are allowed to be afflicted by the unjust: so that, while they hear of future goods that they may desire, they may also experience present evils that they dread; and while love summons them toward an easier departure, suffering may drive them onward.

## CHAPTER NINE.—“What is that which you hold in your hand?” He answered: “A staff.” He said: “Throw it on the ground.” He threw it down, and it became a serpent, so that Moses fled from it. And the Lord said: “Stretch out your hand and seize its tail.” He stretched it out, held it, and it became a staff again (Exodus 4:2–3).

[Column 0726A]

**Note:** In the Michael manuscript no homily number is assigned. The passage indicated in the printed editions does not occur in homily 10, nor in homily 4, which the Gemet manuscript cites.

While the mysteries of the miracles performed by Moses in the wilderness through the staff were under discussion in the *Commentary on Ezekiel*, the following passage was added: “What is that which you hold in your hand?” etc.—What is signified by Moses except the Jewish people? And what by the staff except the power of divinity? What is expressed by the serpent except the mortality of our Redeemer? Since death is rightly signified through the serpent, mortality is rightly represented in the serpent.

Or certainly, since it is written, “Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10:16), and since supreme Wisdom itself—that is, the Wisdom of God—deigned to become incarnate, is not its mortality rightly figured in the serpent? Hence, speaking in the Gospel about his Passion, he says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14).

Moses therefore held the staff because, before the coming of the Redeemer, the Jewish people trusted in divine power. But he threw the staff onto the ground because that same people, through the patriarchs and prophets, announced that God would become incarnate. The staff is turned into a serpent because our Redeemer, remaining God in himself, became mortal among human beings.

But Moses was terrified when he saw the serpent and fled because, when the Jewish people saw the Redeemer of the human race as a mortal, they were afraid to believe that he was God. Why is he commanded to seize the serpent by its tail? Because that faithless people, which now refuses to believe, gathers itself back to the faith in the final part of the Lord’s body—that is, in the later age of the holy Church, at the end of the world—and seizes the serpent by its tail. It confesses in the final period of the Church that the one whom it had previously despised as mortal is its Redeemer.

But immediately the serpent returns to a staff, because as soon as the Jewish people believes in our Redeemer, that same Redeemer will appear to the Jewish people in the power of his divinity, so that the serpent may now be a staff for it; for the one who was despised as a man on earth will, coming from heaven, be seen as God above the angels.

## CHAPTER TEN.—“Let the Lord see and judge, for you have made our odor offensive before Pharaoh and his servants” (Exodus 5:21).

[Column 0726C]

While the increase of temptations was under discussion in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXIX (No. 44), the following passage was added: “Let the Lord see and judge,” etc.—When the light sent by God deigns to illuminate the human heart, temptations immediately increase from the hidden adversary against the mind that has begun to shine.

For the crafty enemy strives to inflame with unlawful desires the minds of those whom he sees shining with the light of righteousness, so that they often feel themselves more intensely harassed by temptations than when they did not see the rays of inner light. Hence, after they had been called, the Israelites complained against Moses and Aaron about their increased labor, saying: “Let the Lord see and judge, for you have made our odor offensive before Pharaoh and his servants, and you have given him a sword with which to kill us.”

When they wished to depart from Egypt, Pharaoh had taken away their straw and nevertheless demanded work in the same measure. Thus the mind murmurs, as it were, against the Law after gaining knowledge of it, because it bears sharper goads of temptation. When it sees its labors increasing, it grieves that it has become, as it were, offensive in Pharaoh’s eyes precisely because of what displeases the adversary.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN.—Likewise, from the passage above.

**Note:** This chapter is omitted from our manuscripts.

In the *Exposition of Ezekiel*, book I, homily 12 (No. 24):—In Moses and Aaron, the Law and the prophets were prefigured. The weak soul often murmurs against the sacred writings, as it were, because after it has begun to hear and follow heavenly words, the adversity of the king of Egypt—that is, the temptation of the evil spirit—increases.

Therefore, the teacher must attentively make known to the progressing soul what temptations will follow it, so that it may be able to prepare itself cautiously against the snares of the evil spirit.

## CHAPTER TWELVE.—“Behold, I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh” (Exodus 7:1).

While the designation “God” was under discussion in book I, homily 8 (No. 3), on Ezekiel, the following passage was added: “Behold, I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh.”—In sacred Scripture, God is sometimes spoken of by designation and sometimes essentially.

He is spoken of by designation, as in what was now said to Moses: “Behold, I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh.” And again Moses says: “If someone does this or that, bring him to the gods” (Exodus 22:8), that is, to the priests. He also says: “You shall not speak evil of the gods” (the same passage), that is, the priests.

So too the Psalmist says: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges among the gods” (Psalm 82:1).

God is spoken of essentially, however, as when he himself says to Moses: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Therefore the apostle Paul, wishing to distinguish the designated name of God from the essential one, says: “Their fathers are theirs, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5).

The one who is called God by designation is God among all things; the one who is God essentially is God above all things. Thus, to show that Christ is God by nature, Paul mentioned that he is not merely God, but God above all. Any righteous person, too, is called “god,” but only among all things, because he is god by designation; Christ, however, is God above all because he is God by nature.

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN.—“We shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to our God” (Exodus 8:26).

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the innocence of mind that the reprobate reject as hostile to themselves—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book X (no. 48), the following was added: “We shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to our God.” The Egyptians disdain eating sheep; but what the Egyptians abominate, the Israelites offer to God, because the upright turn into a sacrifice of virtue the simplicity of conscience that all unjust people despise as lowly and contemptible, and, cultivating rectitude’s purity and gentleness, sacrifice to God what the reprobate abominate and consider foolishness.

## CHAPTER XIV—Likewise, concerning the foregoing

[Col. 0727C] In the commentary on Ezekiel, homily 10.—For perverse people, certain good works are abominations. Hence Moses, since he was going to slaughter sheep for the Lord, says to the Egyptians: “Shall we sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God?” Holy men offer sheep to the Lord, for they show that their simplicity is a sacrifice to almighty God. But the Egyptians abominate sheep, because the citizens of this world disdain and despise the simplicity of the good.

Therefore, just as there are abominations of evil works that the good detest, so the causes of good works are abominations to the reprobate. Hence it is written: “The righteous abhor an ungodly man; the ungodly abhor those who are on the right path” (Prov. XXIX, 27).

## CHAPTER XV—That Egypt was struck by the plague of flies (Exod. VIII, 21)

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the pursuit of mental repose and the avoidance of the tumult of worldly cares—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XVIII (no. 68), the following was added: “That Egypt was struck by the plague of flies.”

What is more laborious in this life than to burn with earthly desires? Or what is more peaceful here than to desire nothing of this world? Hence the Israelite people received the observance of the Sabbath as a gift; conversely, Egypt was struck by a multitude of flies. The people who follow God received the Sabbath—that is, repose of mind—so that they would not be wearied in this life by any desire for carnal longings.

But Egypt, which represents the appearance of this world, is struck by flies. For the fly is an exceedingly insolent and restless creature. What else is signified by it than the insolent cares of carnal desires? Hence it is said elsewhere: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment” (Eccl. X, 1). For superfluous thoughts, which continually arise and perish in the mind of one who thinks about carnal things, destroy that sweetness with which each person has been inwardly anointed through the Spirit, since they do not permit him to enjoy its fullness.

Egypt, therefore, is struck by flies, because the hearts of those who love earthly life, while they are struck by the restlessness of their desires, are driven down to the depths by the turmoil of carnal thoughts, so that they are not lifted toward the desire for inward repose.

Hence, when Truth comes to the heart with wondrous works of mercy, it first drives out from it the fever of carnal thoughts, and afterward arranges within it the gifts of the virtues. The sacred history of the Gospel aptly suggests this to us. When the Lord was being led after being invited to raise the ruler’s daughter, it immediately adds: “And when the crowd had been put outside, he entered, took her by the hand, and the girl arose” (Matt. IX, 25).

The crowd is therefore driven outside so that the girl may be raised, because, unless the intrusive multitude of worldly cares is first expelled from the heart’s inner chambers, the soul lying dead within does not rise again. For while it scatters itself among countless thoughts of earthly desires, it does not gather itself at all for self-examination.

No one fully receives wisdom, which is God, except one who strives to withdraw himself from every agitation of carnal activity. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Write wisdom in a time of leisure, and the one who is less occupied with activity will receive it” (Eccli. XXXVIII, 25). And again: “Be still and see that I am the Lord” (Ps. XLV, 11).

## CHAPTER XVI—A burning wind raised the locusts, which came up over the whole land of Egypt and covered the entire surface of the earth, destroying everything. Thus the grass of the land was devoured, and whatever fruit there was on the trees (Exod. X, 13–14)

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the need to avoid the harmful praises of flatterers—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXXI (no. 47), the following was added: “A burning wind raised the locusts,” and so forth.

The plagues of Egypt, brought down from heaven and inflicted bodily once, in accordance with the demands of their merits, spiritually signified the evils that strike perverse minds every day. Egypt was afflicted by those plagues so that, shaken and suffering from an external blow, it might perceive what losses of devastation it was inwardly enduring through negligence; so that, while it saw small but more dearly loved things perishing outside, it might feel, through their likeness, the more serious things it had suffered within.

What, then, do locusts signify by their symbolism? They harm human crops more than all other small creatures. What else do they signify but the tongues of flatterers, who, whenever they see the minds of earthly people producing some good, corrupt them by praising it excessively?

The fruit of the Egyptians is the activity of those who seek empty glory; the locusts destroy it when flattering tongues incline the worker’s heart to seek passing praise. The locusts eat the grass when flatterers exalt the words of speakers with applause. They also devour the fruit of the trees when, with empty praises, they weaken the works of those who have already become, as it were, strong.

## CHAPTER XVII—The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart (Exod. X)

[Col. 0728D] In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXXI (no. 26): Not that he himself imparted hardness, but that, in accordance with the demands of Pharaoh’s merits, he did not soften it by any awareness of fear infused from above.

## CHAPTER XVIII—Concerning the golden and silver vessels taken from Egypt (Exod. XII, 35)

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the condescension to the uneducated who are to be called to the heights of virtue—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXVIII (no. 41), the following was added: “Concerning the golden and silver vessels taken from Egypt.”

Minds clinging to the use of carnal life cannot be torn away from lowly things unless they advance through preaching gradually adapted to them. Hence, while they were in Egypt, their hidden desire was approached with pious and righteous moderation, and they were ordered to depart after taking the golden and silver vessels of their neighbors.

When they had been led to Mount Sinai, they soon heard, after receiving the law: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property” (Exod. XX, 17). Hence, in that same law, they were commanded to demand an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth (Exod. XXI, 24); yet later, when grace had been revealed, they were commanded to offer the other cheek when one had been struck (Matt. V, 39). For anger always demands more in revenge than the injury it received. Thus, by learning not to repay evils with greater evils, they might eventually learn willingly to endure even multiplied injuries.

Hence he prohibited that inexperienced people from certain practices, while preserving certain others for their former use. Yet he also shaped these very things as figures of a better life. In Egypt they slaughtered brute animals for idols, and he retained the slaughter of animals for their later use, but forbade the worship of idols, so that, while they lost something from their customary use, their weakness might be consoled by having something from that use.

By a wondrous dispensation of providence, what the Lord retained for them from their carnal custom he turned more powerfully into a figure of the spirit. For what do the sacrifices of those animals signify if not the death of the Only-Begotten? What do the sacrifices of those animals signify if not the extinguishing of our carnal life? Thus, from the point at which condescension is shown to the weakness of an inexperienced people, greater strength of spirit is proclaimed through the shadowed forms of allegory.

[Note: [Col. 0727D] This chapter is entirely absent from our manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XIX—They shall take some of the lamb’s blood and put it on both doorposts and on the lintels of the houses in which they will eat it; and they shall eat the meat roasted by fire during that night, with unleavened bread and wild lettuce. You shall not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted by fire. You shall consume its head with its feet and its entrails; nothing of it shall remain until morning. If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire. You shall eat it in this manner: you shall gird your kidneys, have shoes on your feet, hold staffs in your hands, and eat it hastily (Exod. XII, 7 ff.).

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the paschal mystery, which was set forth in advance as a figure of this future solemnity now present—in homily 22 (from no. 7 to the end) on the Gospel, the following was added: “They shall take some of the lamb’s blood and put it on both doorposts,” and so forth.

All these things plainly bring us great edification if they are examined through mystical interpretation. For we have learned what the lamb’s blood is, not merely by hearing but by drinking. That blood is placed on both doorposts when it is taken in not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart.

For one who receives the blood of his Redeemer in such a way that he is not yet willing to imitate his passion has placed the blood on one doorpost, although it must also be placed on the lintels of the houses. For what do we understand spiritually by houses except our minds, in which we dwell through thought? The lintel of the house is the intention itself, which rises above the action.

Therefore, whoever directs the intention of his thought toward imitation of the Lord’s passion places the lamb’s blood on the lintel of the house. Or certainly our houses are our bodies themselves, in which we dwell as long as we live. We place the lamb’s blood on the lintel of the house because we bear the cross of his passion on our forehead.

The text further says concerning this lamb: “And they shall eat the meat roasted by fire during that night.” We eat the lamb at night because, in the sacrament, we now receive the Lord’s body while we do not yet see one another’s consciences. This meat, however, must be roasted by fire, because fire dissolves meat that has been cooked in water, whereas meat that fire cooks without water it strengthens. The meat of our lamb was therefore cooked by fire, because the very power of his passion made him stronger for resurrection and strengthened him for incorruption. For he who recovered strength from death had, so to speak, his flesh hardened by fire.

Hence he also says through the Psalmist: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. XXI, 16). For what is a potsherd before fire except soft clay? Yet fire causes it to become solid. The strength of his humanity therefore dried up like a potsherd, because through the fire of his passion it grew toward the strength of incorruption.

But merely receiving the sacraments of our Redeemer is not sufficient for true solemnity of mind unless good works are also joined to them. For what does it profit to receive his body and blood with the mouth and oppose him by perverse works?

Hence the text fittingly continues: “And unleavened bread with wild lettuce.” One eats bread without leaven who performs righteous works without the corruption of vainglory, who carries out the commandments of mercy without an admixture of sin, lest he perversely seize what is administered as though rightly.

Those to whom the Lord spoke through the prophet in rebuke mixed this leaven of sin into their good action: “Come to Bethel and act impiously” (Amos IV, 4). And shortly afterward: “And sacrifice praise from what is leavened” (ibid., 5). He sacrifices praise from what is leavened who prepares a sacrifice for God from plunder.

Wild lettuce, however, is exceedingly bitter. The meat of the lamb must be eaten with wild lettuce, so that, while we receive the Redeemer’s body, we may afflict ourselves in tears for our sins, in order that the very bitterness of repentance may wipe from the stomach of the mind the foul moisture of life.

The text continues: “You shall not eat any of it raw or boiled in water.” Here the very words of the historical account already drive us away from a historical understanding. Did that Israelite people living in Egypt habitually eat the lamb raw, so that the law would say to them, “You shall not eat any of it raw”? It also adds: “Nor boiled in water.”

But what does water signify except human knowledge? In accordance with what is said through Solomon in the voice of heretics: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. IX, 17). What does meat raw to the fire signify except his humanity left unconsidered and without reverence in thought? For everything we consider carefully we, as it were, cook in the mind.

The lamb’s meat, then, must be eaten neither raw nor cooked in water, because our Redeemer must be regarded neither as merely human nor considered through human wisdom as though one could understand how God was able to become incarnate.

Everyone who believes our Redeemer to be merely human—what else does he do than eat the lamb’s meat raw? He has refused to cook it through understanding of the Redeemer’s divinity. But everyone who attempts to examine the mysteries of his incarnation according to human wisdom wishes to cook the lamb’s meat in water; that is, he wishes to penetrate the mystery of his dispensation through an uncontrolled knowledge.

Therefore, whoever desires to celebrate the solemnity of paschal joy must neither cook the lamb in water nor eat it raw. He must neither seek to penetrate the depth of the incarnation through human wisdom nor believe in him as a merely human being, but must eat the meat roasted by fire, so that he may know that all things are administered through the power of the Holy Spirit.

The text rightly continues concerning this: “You shall consume its head with its feet and its entrails.” As we have already said above, and have learned with Paul as witness, “the head of Christ is God” (I Cor. II, 3). To consume the head of the lamb, therefore, is to receive his divinity by faith. To consume the lamb’s feet is to seek out the traces of his humanity with love and imitation.

What, then, are the entrails except his hidden and mystical commandments? We consume them when we take in the words of life eagerly. In this expression, “consume,” what else is reproved than the sluggishness of our laziness? We neither seek his words and mysteries for ourselves nor willingly hear them when spoken by others.

“Nothing of it shall remain until morning,” because his sayings must be examined with great diligence, so that, before the day of resurrection appears, all his commandments may be penetrated through understanding and practice during the night of this present life.

But because it is very difficult for all sacred Scripture to be understood and all its mystery to be penetrated, the text rightly continues: “If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire.” We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly entrust to the power of the Holy Spirit what we cannot understand or penetrate concerning the mystery of his incarnation. Thus no one should presumptuously dare either to despise or to denounce what he does not understand; rather, he hands it over to fire when he entrusts it to the Holy Spirit.

Since we have learned how the Passover is to be eaten, let us now recognize what sort of people ought to eat it. The text continues: “You shall eat it in this manner: you shall gird your loins.”

What is understood by the kidneys except the pleasure of the flesh? Hence the Psalmist also asks, saying: “Burn my kidneys” (Ps. XXV, 2). If he had not known that the pleasure of lust resides in the loins, he would not have asked that they be burned.

Because the devil’s power has prevailed especially through lust over the human race, it is said of him in the Lord’s voice: “His power is in his loins” (Job XL, 11). Whoever eats the Passover ought therefore to have his loins girded, so that one who celebrates the solemnity of resurrection and incorruption may no longer be subject to corruption through vices, but may subdue pleasures and restrain the flesh from lust.

For one who is still subject to corruption through lack of self-control does not know what the solemnity of incorruption is. These things are hard for some people, but narrow is the gate that leads to life (Matt. VII, 13–14). We already have many examples of those who have practiced continence.

Hence the text fittingly continues: “You shall have shoes on your feet.” What are our feet except our works? And what are shoes except the skins of dead animals? Shoes protect the feet. What are the dead animals from whose skins our feet are protected except the ancient fathers who went before us to the eternal homeland? When we observe their examples, we protect the feet of our works.

Therefore, to have shoes on one’s feet is to observe the lives of the dead and guard our steps from the wound of sin.

“Hold staffs in your hands.” What does the law signify by a staff except pastoral care? It should be noted that we are first commanded to gird our loins and afterward to hold staffs, because those should undertake pastoral care who already know how to subdue the flows of lust in their own bodies, so that, when they preach strength to others, they themselves may not weakly succumb to tender desires.

The text fittingly continues: “And you shall eat it hastily.” Learn with haste the commandments of God, the mysteries of the Redeemer, and the joys of the heavenly homeland, and take care to fulfill the precepts of life with haste. For we know that today we are still permitted to act well, but we do not know whether it will be permitted tomorrow.

Eat the Passover hastily, then—that is, hasten toward the solemnity of the heavenly homeland. Let no one grow sluggish on the journey of this life, lest he lose his place in the homeland. Let no one delay in pursuing good endeavors, but let him complete what he has begun, lest he be unable to fulfill what he has commenced. If we are not sluggish in the love of God, he himself assists us—the one whom we love.

## CHAPTER XX—You shall exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep (Exod. XIII, 13)

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the rejection of past filth and the renewal of innocence of heart—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXVII (no. 38), and in homily 8 on Ezekiel, the following was added: “You shall exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep.”

[Note: [Col. 0731D] The printed editions read: “Concerning the restoration of innocence of heart through the rejection of past impurities.” We follow the unanimous reading of the manuscripts.]

What is signified by the donkey except uncleanness? And what by the sheep except innocence? To exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep is to convert the beginnings of an unclean life into the innocence of simplicity, so that, after the sinner has committed those things that the Lord rejects as unclean, he may now produce by his actions what he may offer in sacrifice to God.

[At the end.]

For all human beings are born in sins, and conceived through the pleasure of the flesh; we have drawn the origin of guilt along with us. Consequently, we become entangled in sins also through our own will. But whoever turns from the wickedness of the flesh to innocence of heart exchanges the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep, because he converts the uncleanness of his former life into innocence.

Whoever ceases to be what he previously was and, having attained purity of flesh, guards innocence has exchanged the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep as an offering to God.

## CHAPTER XXI—When Pharaoh had sent the people out, God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, which was nearby, thinking that they might perhaps later repent if they saw wars rising against them and return to Egypt (Exod. XIII, 17)

[Col. 0731D–0732A]

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the providential alteration by which those newly coming to conversion are led from within according to a measured discipline—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXIV (no. 29), the following was added: “When Pharaoh had sent the people out,” and so forth.

Often converts, even at the very entrance and beginning of their conversion, receive either the most peaceful tranquility of the flesh, or gifts of prophecy, or teachings of doctrine, or miracles of signs, or the grace of healing. After this, however, they are wearied by harsh trials of temptation, although when they first began they believed themselves entirely free from such temptations.

This happens through the dispensation of divine grace, lest they be broken by the harshness of temptations at the beginning of their conversion. For if the bitterness of temptation met them at their outset, they would return to what they had abandoned as easily as they had scarcely departed from it. Having first despised their vices as though they were close at hand, they would become entangled in them again.

[Note: [Col. 0732D] That is, they would become entangled again, or entangled a second time.]

Hence it is written: “When Pharaoh had sent the people out, the Lord did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, which was nearby, thinking that he might perhaps repent if he saw wars rising against him and return to Egypt.”

Therefore, for those departing from Egypt, nearby wars are held back, because a certain tranquility is first shown to those abandoning the world, lest, disturbed in their very tenderness and beginnings and terrified, they return to what they escaped.

At first, then, they experience the sweetness of security and are nourished by the quiet of peace. But after they have come to know this sweetness, they endure the contests of temptation more tolerably, since they have come to know more deeply in God what they love.

## CHAPTER XXII—The Lord went before them to show the way, by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire (Exod. XIII, 21)

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the nature of the future judgment—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book II (no. 57), and in homily 21 (no. 3) on the Gospel, the following was added: “The Lord went before them,” and so forth.

What is signified by fire except terror? And by the cloud, the gentle charm of vision? Day is understood as the life of the righteous, and night as the life of the sinner. Hence Paul also says to converted sinners: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8).

The pillar was therefore shown by a cloud during the day and by fire during the night, because almighty God will appear gentle to the righteous and terrible to the unjust. When he comes in judgment, he will soothe the righteous through the mildness of gentleness, but terrify the unjust through the severity of justice.

Again, this pillar of fire and cloud can be understood in another way through careful investigation. What does it mean that the pillar of cloud, which went before the people in the wilderness, shone with the brightness of fire not during the day but at night, except that our Redeemer, offering leadership to those who follow him through the example of his conduct, did not shine with any light for those confident in their own righteousness, but kindled the fire of his love in those who acknowledged the darkness of their sins?

## CHAPTER XXIII—Why do you cry out to me? (Exod. XIV, 15)

[Col. 0732D] While the subject was being discussed—namely, the kindling of the heart’s desire for God—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXII (no. 43), the following was added: “Why do you cry out to me?”

It is not our words but our desires that make voices before the most secret ears of God. For if we ask for eternal life with the mouth but do not desire it with the heart, we remain silent while crying out. But if we desire it from the heart, then even when we are silent with the mouth, we cry out while keeping silent.

Hence, in the wilderness the people make a din with their voices, while Moses is silent amid the clamor of words; yet, though silent, he is heard by the ear of divine mercy when it is said: “Why do you cry out to me?”

There is therefore an inward, secret cry in desire, because it does not reach human ears, yet it fills the hearing of the Creator.

## CHAPTER XXIV—Concerning the manna given from above to the children of Israel (Exod. XVI, 15)

[Col. 0733A]

While the subject was being discussed—namely, preparing the mind to receive the sweetness of heavenly compunction—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXVII (no. 42), the following was added: “Concerning the manna given from above to the children of Israel.”

What is signified by the manna given from above to the people except wonder at heavenly sweetness? The sweet food received from above is called *manhu*. *Manhu* means, “What is this?” We say, “What is this?” when, not knowing what we see, we marvel at it.

The soul therefore receives heavenly manna when, lifted up by the voice of compunction, it is astonished at the new form of inward refreshment, so that, filled with divine sweetness, it rightly responds, “What is this?” For, while it is suspended above lowly thought, it marvels at what it sees from above.

When the deafness of our sluggishness is broken by this utterance, the practice of the old life is immediately changed, so that the soul, breathed upon by the heavenly Spirit, desires in the heights what it had despised and despises in lowly things what it had desired.

## CHAPTER XXV—Moses’ hands were heavy. So they took a stone and placed it beneath him, and he sat upon it. Aaron and Hur supported his hands (Exod. XVII, 2)

[Col. 0733B]

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the coming of the Mediator and the easing, through spiritual understanding, of the law’s hardness—in homily 33 (no. 8) on the Gospel, the following was added: “Moses’ hands were heavy,” and so forth.

Moses sat upon the stone when the law came to rest in the Church. Yet this same law had heavy hands because it did not bear sinners with mercy but struck them with severe strictness.

Aaron, however, means “mountain of strength.” Hur means “fire.” Whom, then, does this mountain of strength signify except our Redeemer, concerning whom the prophet says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared at the top of the mountains” (Isa. II, 2)?

Or who is signified by fire except the Holy Spirit, concerning whom the same Redeemer says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII, 49)?

Aaron and Hur therefore support the heavy hands of Moses and make them lighter by supporting them, because the Mediator of God and human beings, coming with the fire of the Holy Spirit, showed us through spiritual understanding that the commandments of the law—which could not be carried while they were held carnally—are bearable.

He makes the hands of Moses lighter, so to speak, because he turned the burden of the law’s commandments toward the strength of confession. He suggests this promise of frequent mercy to us when he says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

Again, under the figure of Judea, he says to every sinful soul: “If a man divorces his wife, and she, departing from him, takes another husband, will she return to him again? Will that woman not be polluted and defiled? But you have prostituted yourself with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (Jer. III, 1).

He presents the example of a shameful woman. He shows that after disgrace she cannot be received. Yet he overcomes this very example through mercy, saying that a woman who has prostituted herself cannot be received, while he himself waits to receive the prostituting soul.

Let us consider the weight of such great mercy. He says that something cannot be done, and demonstrates that he himself can do it even contrary to custom. Behold, he calls, and those whom he declares polluted he also seeks to embrace, though he complains that he has been abandoned by them.

He therefore bent the hardness of the law toward mercy, because those whom the law justly condemns he himself mercifully liberates.

## CHAPTER XXVI—That the Lord descended in fire and smoke when he was about to give the law (Exod. XIX, 8)

While the subject was being discussed—namely, first uprooting the desire for carnal longings and then directing the mind’s gaze toward the contemplation of higher things—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book VI (nos. 58–59), the following was added: “That the Lord, when about to give the law, descended in fire,” and so forth.

What does it mean that the Lord descended in fire and smoke when he was about to give the law, except that he illuminates the humble through the brightness of his manifestation and darkens the eyes of the proud through the mist of error?

The mind must therefore first be cleansed of the desire for temporal glory and of every pleasure of carnal concupiscence, and then raised to the sharpness of contemplation.

Hence, when the law is received, the people are forbidden to approach the mountain, so that those who, with minds still weak, desire earthly things may not presume to contemplate the heights.

The text rightly says: “If an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Exod. XIX, 12–13). An animal touches the mountain when a mind subjected to irrational desires raises itself toward the heights of contemplation. But it is struck by stones because, unable to bear the heights, it is killed by the very blows of the heavenly weight.

Those who strive to grasp the summit of perfection, then, and desire to hold the citadel of contemplation, should first test themselves in the field of action through practice. Let them carefully consider whether they no longer inflict any evil upon their neighbors; whether they bear with equanimity evils inflicted by their neighbors; whether their minds are not dissolved in joy by temporal goods set before them; whether, when such goods are taken away, they are not wounded by excessive grief.

Then let them consider whether, when they return inwardly to themselves, they draw along with them no shadows of bodily things while they search into spiritual matters—or, if they do draw them along, whether they drive them away by the hand of discernment; whether, desiring to see the unbounded light, they suppress all images of their own bounded nature; and whether, in seeking to reach what is above them, they overcome what they themselves are.

## CHAPTER XXVII—Israel, unable to hear God’s words on the mountain, received the commandments in the plains (Exod. XIX, 19)

While the subject was being discussed—namely, understanding the mysteries of Scripture, arranged according to the nature of things and the time of their expression—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book II (no. 2), the following was added: “That Israel,” and so forth.

It is worthwhile to observe how, at the beginnings of its narratives, sacred Scripture expresses qualities and defines the limits of matters. At times it indicates what it is about to say concerning a future action by the position of a place, at times by the position of a body, at times by the quality of the air, and at times by the quality of the time.

By the position of places, divine Scripture expresses the merits of what follows and the limits of matters. Thus it says of Israel that it could not hear the words of God on the mountain but received the commandments in the plains. It thereby indicates the people’s subsequent weakness: they were unable to ascend to the heights but, by living negligently, loosened themselves in lowly things.

By the position of the body it announces what is to come, as in the Acts of the Apostles, where Stephen declares that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of the power of God (Acts VII). To stand is the posture of one who assists. And rightly he is seen standing who gives help in the battle of the contest.

The subsequent event is shown by the quality of the air. Thus, when the Evangelist said that none of the Jews would believe at that time while the Lord was preaching, he prefaced it by saying: “It was winter” (John X, 22). For it is written: “Iniquity will abound, and the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV, 12). He therefore took care to specify the season of winter in order to indicate the coldness of wickedness present in the hearts of the hearers.

Hence it is said beforehand concerning Peter, who was going to deny the Lord: “Because it was cold, and he stood warming himself at the coals” (John XVIII, 18). For he had already grown cold inwardly from the warmth of charity, and, with weakness burning in him, he was warming himself toward the love of the present life as though toward the coals of his persecutors.

The end of an action is also expressed by the quality of time. Thus Judas, who would not return to forgiveness, is said to have gone out at night toward the treachery of betrayal. As he went out, the Evangelist says: “And it was night” (ibid. XIII, 30). Hence it is also said to the wicked rich man: “This night they will demand your soul from you” (Luke XII, 20). For the soul that is led to darkness is said to be demanded not in the day but in the night.

Hence Solomon, who received wisdom but did not persevere, is described as receiving it in a dream during the night (III Kings III). Hence the angels come to Abraham at midday (Gen. XVIII), but when they are going to punish Sodom, they are said to have come to it in the evening (Gen. XIX).

## CHAPTER XXVIII—Moses ascended, and the Lord descended upon the mountain (Exod. XIX, 3, 23)

[Col. 0735A]

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the reception of heavenly grace through the merit of contemplation—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book V (no. 66), the following was added: “Moses ascended,” and so forth.

What is signified by the mountain except our very contemplation, into which we ascend so that we may be lifted up to see those things that are beyond our weakness?

But the Lord descends into it, because, when we have made much progress, he opens a little of himself to our senses—if one may say that anything in him is little or partial. He always remains one and the same and cannot be understood in parts, yet he is said to be shared by his faithful, although no division is admitted in his substance.

But because we cannot express him in perfect speech, hindered by the weakness of infancy, as it were, within the measure of our humanity, we stammeringly echo him to some extent.

## CHAPTER XXIX—The people stood far away, but Moses approached the darkness in which God was (Exod. XX, 21)

[Col. 0735B]

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the discernment required in maintaining allegory and history—in homily 9 on Ezekiel, the following was added: “The people stood far away,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] These words are by no means found in the place indicated.]

In sacred Scripture there is a great need for discernment in understanding. Often, in some passages, both the history and the allegory must be preserved; often, in others, only the allegory must be sought; and sometimes only the history must necessarily be retained.

In certain passages, as we have said, history and allegory must be held together, so that the slower may be nourished through the history and the more intellectually agile through the allegory.

Thus, when the Lord spoke and the people saw the lamps, the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain, they were terrified and asked that the Lord speak to them through Moses. It is written: “The people stood far away, but Moses approached the darkness in which God was” (Exod. XX, 21).

The crowd of the people cannot penetrate the darkness of allegory, because it belongs to very few to investigate spiritual understanding. Since carnal minds are often nourished by history alone, the people stood far away while God spoke.

But because spiritual people penetrate the cloud of allegories in order to understand God’s words spiritually, Moses approached the darkness in which God was.

## CHAPTER XXX—You shall make an altar of earth for me (Exod. XX, 24)

While the subject was being discussed—namely, the Lord’s incarnation—in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, book III (no. 51), the following was added: “You shall make an altar of earth for me.”

To make an altar of earth for God is to hope in the incarnation of the Mediator. We receive a gift from our God when our humility places upon this altar—that is, upon faith in the Lord’s incarnation—whatever it does.

We therefore place an offering upon an altar of earth when we establish our actions firmly upon faith in the Lord’s incarnation.

### CHAPTER XXXI

“If you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve you for six years; in the seventh he shall go out free, without payment. With whatever garment he entered, with such shall he go out. If he has a wife, his wife shall also go out with him. But if his master gives him a wife, and she bears sons and daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, while he himself shall go out with his garment. But if the slave says, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,’ his master shall present him to the gods; he shall be brought to the door and the doorposts, and his master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall be his slave forever” (Exod. XXI, 2 ff.).

When the active and contemplative life were being discussed, Homily 3 (Nos. 10–13) on Ezekiel adds: “If you buy a Hebrew slave,” etc.

It must be understood that although the active and contemplative life are both gifts of grace, nevertheless, as long as we live among our neighbors, one is necessary for us and the other voluntary. For who, knowing God, enters his kingdom unless he acts well? Those who do not neglect the good they are able to do can enter the heavenly homeland without the contemplative life. But they cannot enter without the active life if they neglect to do the good they are able to do. The active life, therefore, is necessary; the contemplative life is voluntary. The former is servitude; the latter is freedom.

Hence Moses is told: “If you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve you for six years; in the seventh he shall go out free, without payment” (Exod. XXI, 2), and the rest that follows. “Hebrew” means “one who passes over.” A Hebrew slave is bought when anyone who has already passed over from this world in mind is subjected to the service of the almighty Lord. For the person who has learned to pass over from this world in mind truly desires to serve God.

Thus Moses passed over into the desert to see the vision (Exod. III). Thus David, when he saw the wicked exalted and lifted up above the cedars of Lebanon, “passed over, and behold, he was no more,” because we perhaps believe the power of the wicked to be something great unless we pass over in mind to the everlasting age.

The Hebrew slave who has been bought is commanded to serve for six years, so that in the seventh he may go out free, without payment. For what is signified by the number six except the perfection of the active life? And what is signified by the number seven except the contemplative life? He serves for six years and goes out free in the seventh who, through the active life that he has perfectly practiced, passes into the freedom of the contemplative life.

It should be noted that he goes out free without payment because those who, after doing everything, call themselves unprofitable servants (Luke XVII) will undoubtedly receive the contemplative life by grace, just as the active life itself came to them as a gift.

“With whatever garment he entered, with such shall he go out,” because it is altogether necessary that each of us persevere in what he begins and continue to the end of his work in the intention with which he began. For the person passes well to the contemplative life who has not changed the garment of his intention for something worse while living the active life.

There are some who, before they are joined to the service of almighty God, already love to perform good works. There are others who learn good works only after they have come into the service of almighty God. Therefore, the person who strove to possess good works before coming into God’s service is a Hebrew slave bought together with a wife. Often such a person can pass to the contemplative life and nevertheless not abandon the active life. Hence it is added there: “If he has a wife, his wife shall also go out with him.”

For the wife goes out with him into freedom when the person who reaches contemplation does not abandon, in the external sphere, the action of good works by which he can benefit others.

“But if the Lord gives him a wife, and she bears sons and daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, while he himself shall go out with his garment.” The Lord gives a wife to the purchased slave when a preacher joins to good action the person whom he has subjected to the authority of almighty God. For preachers are also called “masters,” as it is said to the prophet Elisha concerning his preacher: “Do you know that the Lord is taking your master away from you?” (IV Kings II, 3).

The wife of the purchased slave bears sons and daughters when good action produces for him strong or weaker fruits. But the woman given by the Lord remains with that same Lord together with her children, while the slave himself goes out with his garment, because good action, or the fruits of that good action, are reckoned to the preacher as his reward. He himself, however, persevering in the intention of his desire, goes out free into contemplation through heavenly grace.

“But if the slave says, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free.’” The slave loves his master when he carefully preserves the words of his preacher. He refuses to go out free, loving his wife and children, when he loves the active life and its fruit and does not wish to pass into contemplation, because, seeing that he possesses good works in the service entrusted to him, he refuses to pass into the repose of freedom.

“But let the Lord present him to the gods, and let him be brought to the door and the doorposts, and let him pierce his ear with an awl, so that he may be his slave forever.” The person who has decided to remain in the active life is presented by the Lord to the gods when he is instructed by his preacher in the sayings of the ancient fathers, who were priests for us on the way of almighty God.

He is led to the door and the doorposts of the tabernacle so that he may hear something more profound concerning entry into the eternal tabernacle and may carefully recognize the day of the dread judgment, lest he seek to please human beings through the good works he performs. His ear is pierced with an awl when his mind is struck by the subtlety of the fear of God, so that, pierced by the point of the word, he may recognize in everything he does that he must always attend to the entrance of the kingdom, and may carry an ear pierced as it were at the door and doorpost of the tabernacle.

He will be a slave forever, so that after this age he may be able to be free. For he is a slave in this age who has decided to serve human beings through the active life, so that after the present age he may be able to attain true freedom. Concerning this Paul says: “For creation itself will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII, 21).

Then there will be true freedom in us, when our adoption reaches the glory of the children of God. But now not only the active life is in servitude; contemplation itself, by which we are lifted above ourselves, does not yet possess the freedom of mind perfectly, but imitates it, because that innermost repose is seen only in a mystery.

### CHAPTER XXXII

“If anyone opens a cistern and digs it, and does not cover it, and an ox or an ass falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall repay the price of the animals” (Exod. XX, 33).

When the proper measure in retaining the sacred word according to the capacity of the hearers was being discussed, the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVII (No. 38), adds: “If anyone opens a cistern and digs it,” etc.

What does “to open a cistern” mean except to penetrate the mysteries of Holy Scripture with vigorous understanding? And what is meant by the ox and the ass—that is, by a clean and an unclean animal—except a believer or an unbeliever?

Therefore, let the person who digs a cistern cover it, lest an ox or an ass fall into it; that is, let the person who already understands lofty things in sacred speech conceal profound meanings in silence before those who cannot grasp them, lest through mental scandal he destroy either a little believer or an unbeliever who might have been able to believe.

For the death of the animals he must pay the price, because he is shown to have lost that for which he is held guilty and bound to perform penance. For whoever, having reached the lofty streams of knowledge, fails to cover these things before the dull hearts of his hearers is condemned as liable to punishment if, through his words, either a pure or an impure mind is caught in scandal.

The cistern must therefore be covered, because lofty knowledge must be concealed before immature minds, lest from the very place by which the heart of the teacher is lifted to the heights, the weakness of the hearers fall to the depths.

### CHAPTER XXXIII

“When your brother owes you anything, and you take his pledge from him, return the pledge to him before sunset” (Exod. XXII, 26).

When the usefulness of confession was being discussed in the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVI (No. 32), it adds: “When your brother owes you anything,” etc.

What is understood in this passage by the name of a pledge except the confession of sin? Our brother becomes our debtor when some neighbor is shown to have sinned against us. We call sins debts. Hence it is said to the sinful servant: “I forgave you all the debt” (Matt. XVIII, 32). And every day in the Lord’s Prayer we pray: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12).

We receive a pledge from our debtor when, from someone whom we know has also sinned against us, we already possess his confession of sin, through which we are asked to release the sin committed against us. For the person who confesses the sin he committed and asks for pardon has already given a pledge, as it were, for the debt.

We are commanded to return this pledge before sunset because, before the sun of righteousness sets in us through the sorrow of the heart, we ought to return to him the confession of pardon from whom we receive the confession of guilt, so that the person who remembers having sinned against us may immediately feel from us that what he did has been forgiven.

### CHAPTER XXXIV

“Moses ascended the mountain in order to receive the law” (Exod. XXIV, 4).

When the desire for inner repose and purity of heart was being discussed in the exposition of Blessed Job, it adds: “Moses ascended the mountain in order to receive the law.”

[Note: In the manuscripts it is not indicated from which passage this was taken. Certainly it is not found in Book XXIV of Job, chapter XII, as it appears in the printed editions.]

What does it mean that Moses ascended to the heights in order to receive God’s sublime commandments, and that, in order to penetrate inward things, he is hidden from external disturbances, except that holy men who are compelled by the necessity of their office to serve in external ministries always diligently withdraw to the secrets of the heart? There they ascend to the summit of innermost thought and receive the law, as it were, on the mountain, when, setting aside the disturbances of temporal activities, they search out the judgment of the heavenly will at the summit of their contemplation.

### CHAPTER XXXV

“You shall make four golden rings and place them at the four corners of the ark. Two rings shall be on one side and two on the other. You shall also make poles of acacia wood, cover them with gold, and insert the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark, so that it may be carried on them. They shall always remain in the rings and shall never be removed from them” (Exod. XXV, 12 ff.).

When the preaching of the teachers of the Church was being discussed in the *Book of the Pastoral Rule* (Part II, chapter 11), it adds: “You shall make four golden rings,” etc.

What is represented by the ark except the holy Church? Four golden rings are commanded to be attached to its four corners because, as it is extended and spread through the four regions of the world, it is undoubtedly girded by the four books of the holy Gospel.

Poles of acacia wood are made and inserted into those same rings for carrying it, because strong and persevering teachers are to be sought as incorruptible wood. Always adhering to the instruction of the sacred books, they should proclaim the unity of the holy Church and carry the ark as though the poles had been inserted into the rings.

To carry the ark on poles is for good teachers, by preaching, to bring the holy Church to the untutored minds of unbelievers. They are also commanded to be covered with gold, so that while they resound to others in speech, they may themselves also shine with the splendor of their lives.

The passage appropriately adds: “They shall always remain in the rings and shall never be removed from them,” because it is certainly necessary that those who keep watch over the office of preaching should not withdraw from the study of sacred reading.

The poles are commanded always to remain in the rings so that, whenever the need to carry the ark arises, no delay in inserting the poles may arise in carrying it. For when something spiritual is being sought from those under his care, it is exceedingly disgraceful if the pastor then seeks to learn when he ought to be resolving the question.

Let the poles adhere to the rings so that teachers, always meditating on sacred words in their hearts, may raise the ark of the covenant without delay and immediately teach whatever is necessary. Hence the first pastor of the Church aptly admonishes the other pastors, saying: “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you” (I Pet. III, 15). It is as though he were saying plainly: Let no delay hinder the carrying of the ark; let the poles never leave the rings.

### CHAPTER XXXVI

“You shall also make two golden cherubim, fashioned by hammering, on the two sides of the inner sanctuary. Let one cherub be on one side and the other on the other; they shall cover the two sides of the mercy seat, spreading out their wings and covering the inner sanctuary, and they shall look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy seat” (Exod. XXV, 18).

When the harmony of the New and Old Testament and the coming of the Mediator were being discussed, Homily 6 (No. 15) on Ezekiel adds: “You shall also make two golden cherubim, fashioned by hammering,” etc.

What is represented by the mercy seat except the Mediator of God and human beings? Concerning him Paul says: “God put him forward as an atoning sacrifice through faith in his blood” (Rom. III, 25).

What, moreover, is signified by the two cherubim, which are said to represent the fullness of knowledge, except the two Testaments? One stands at one end of the mercy seat and the other at the other end, because what the Old Testament began to promise prophetically concerning the incarnation of our Redeemer, the New Testament narrates as perfectly accomplished.

The two cherubim were made of the purest gold because the two Testaments are written in pure and simple truth. They spread their wings and cover the inner sanctuary because we, who are the oracle of almighty God, are protected from impending faults by the edification of Holy Scripture. As we carefully contemplate its judgments, we are veiled by its wings from the error of ignorance.

The two cherubim look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy seat, because the two Testaments do not differ from each other in any variation.
