They hold their faces, as it were, toward each other because, while one fulfills what the other promises, they behold the Mediator of God and human beings placed between them.

The cherubim would turn their faces away from each other if one Testament promised what the other denied. But since they speak harmoniously about the Mediator of God and human beings, they direct themselves toward the mercy seat so as to look at one another. What the Old Testament prefigured, the New Testament fulfilled.

To speak briefly of many examples: What is signified by Eve being brought forth while Adam slept except that the Church of the faithful was born when Christ died? What is signified by Isaac being led to sacrifice, carrying the wood, being placed upon the altar, and yet living, except that our Redeemer was led to his passion, carried the wood of the cross himself, and died in his humanity while remaining immortal in his divinity?

The Testaments, therefore, truly correspond to each other in the Mediator of God and human beings, so that what one signifies the other fulfills.

### CHAPTER XXXVII

The same as above.

In the exposition of the Gospel, Homily 25 (No. 3):

“Cherubim” means “the fullness of knowledge.” And what is signified by the two cherubim except the two Testaments? What, moreover, is represented by the mercy seat except the incarnate Lord? Concerning him John says: “For he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (I John II, 2).

While the Old Testament announces that this is to be done, and the New Testament proclaims that it has been done by the Lord, the two Testaments look toward each other like cherubim, turning their faces toward the mercy seat. For when they see the incarnate Lord placed between them, they do not differ in their vision, since they recount the mystery of his dispensation in harmony.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII

“You shall prepare bowls and dishes, censers and cups, in which libations are to be offered” (Exod. XXV, 25).

When the measure of preaching to be observed discreetly by teachers was being discussed in the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XX (No. 4), it adds: “You shall prepare bowls,” etc.

What is understood by bowls and cups except the measure of preaching, by which the grace of exhortation ought to be communicated to each person according to the capacity of his understanding?

The teacher must carefully discern that he does not strive to preach more than the hearer can grasp. He must also descend by contracting himself to the weakness of his hearers, lest, while speaking lofty things to the simple—things that therefore will not benefit them—he care more to display himself than to benefit his listeners.

At the Lord’s command, not only bowls but also cups are prepared for the table of the tabernacle. For what is signified by bowls except abundant preaching? And what by a cup except a small and modest discourse about God?

Thus, on the Lord’s table both bowls and cups are prepared, because in the teaching of sacred speech one must provide not only great and hidden matters that intoxicate, but also small and subtle things that provide knowledge as though by tasting.

### CHAPTER XXXIX

The same as above.

In the exposition of the Gospel, Homily 6 (No. 6):

What is signified by bowls except overflowing doctrine? And what by cups except small and narrow knowledge?

One person, full of the doctrine of truth, intoxicates the minds of his hearers; by what he says, he plainly offers a bowl. Another cannot express fully what he understands, but because he announces it in some fashion, he plainly provides a taste through a cup.

Therefore, placed in God’s tabernacle—that is, in the holy Church—if we cannot serve bowls through the doctrine of wisdom, we ought, insofar as divine generosity enables us, to give cups of good speech to our neighbors.

### CHAPTER XL

“You shall also make a lampstand of beaten work, of purest gold, together with its shaft, its branches, its cups, its spherical ornaments, and its lilies proceeding from it” (Exod. XXV, 31).

When the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and of the members joined to him by faith was being discussed, Book I, Homily 6 (No. 8) on Ezekiel adds: “You shall also make a lampstand of beaten work, of purest gold,” etc.

Who is represented by the lampstand except the Redeemer of the human race? In the nature of his humanity he caused the light of divinity to shine, so that he might become the lampstand of the world, in whose light every sinner might see the darkness in which he lay.

Because he assumed our nature without sin, the lampstand of the tabernacle is commanded to be made of purest gold. It is produced by beating, because our Redeemer, who from his conception and birth existed as perfect God and human being, endured the blows of sufferings and thus reached the glory of the resurrection.

The lampstand was therefore made of purest gold by beating, because he had no sin, and yet his body advanced through the insults of the passion toward immortality. As regards the merit of his soul, by which he might have advanced through blows, he had no such need at all.

But in his members, which are us, he advances daily through blows, because while we are struck and afflicted so that we may deserve to be his body, he himself advances—he of whose body it is written: “From whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its ligaments and connections, grows with the growth of God” (Col. II, 19).

[Note: The words that follow, up to “its shaft,” were omitted in the printed editions; we have restored them from all our manuscripts.]

We are all his body. The body is bound together through ligaments and connections: the breast is joined to the head, the arms to the breast, the hands to the arms, the fingers to the hands, and the other members adhere to the other members; thus the whole body is completed.

In this way the holy apostles, who stood close to our Redeemer, adhered to him like the breast to the head. Because martyrs followed them, they were like arms joined to the breast. When pastors and teachers were joined to them through good works, the hands adhered to the arms.

This whole body of our Redeemer is supplied and constructed daily in heaven through ligaments and connections, because when the elect souls are led there to him, his members are joined to him. Of him it is rightly said: “Supplied and constructed, it grows with the growth of God,” because almighty God, our Redeemer, who has no way to advance in himself, still receives daily increase through his members.

Hence it is written again: “Until we all attain to the measure of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV, 13).

His shaft should be understood as the Church itself, which is his body, because it stands free amid so many adversities. The branches that proceed from the shaft are the preachers, who have given forth a sweet sound in the world, namely, a new song.

Cups are usually filled with wine. What, then, are the minds of the hearers except cups filled with the wine of knowledge by holy preachers?

[Note: I do not know why this sentence has been inserted here in the printed editions: “In some copies of Gregory it is read thus.”]

What, then, are the mouths of teachers except cups that intoxicate us with the wine of knowledge, so that we may forget the pleasures of the world that we loved?

What else is a spherical ornament except the mobility of preaching? A spherical ornament rolls in every direction, and preaching—which cannot be held back by adversity or lifted up by prosperity—is a sphere, because it is strong amid adversity and humble amid prosperity, possessing neither an angle of fear nor one of pride.

It cannot be fixed in its course, because it moves freely through everything. To complete the example we have introduced, lilies are rightly described on the lampstand after the branches, cups, and spherical ornaments, because after the intoxication and mobility of preaching that we have mentioned comes that green homeland, which blooms for holy souls as eternal flowers.

The cups and spherical ornaments therefore pertain to labor; the lilies to reward.

### CHAPTER XLI

“The tabernacle shall be made in this way: you shall make ten curtains of twisted linen and blue, variegated with embroidered work.” A little later: “You shall also make eleven curtains of goats’ hair, to cover the roof of the tabernacle.” And again: “You shall also make another covering of rams’ skins” (Exod. XXVI, 1).

When the spiritual subjects of their rulers were being instructed in the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXV (No. 39), concerning the need to avoid murmuring against their superiors, it adds: “The tabernacle shall be made in this way,” etc.

What are signified by the skins and goat-hair cloth with which the tabernacle is covered except the coarse minds of human beings, who are sometimes, by the hidden judgment of God, given precedence in the Church, although they are harsh?

Because they are not afraid to serve temporal concerns, they must bear the winds of temptation and the rains arising from the adversities of this world.

What, moreover, is signified by the blue, scarlet, and linen except the tender yet radiant life of the saints? When this life is carefully hidden in the tabernacle beneath the goat-hair cloth and skins, its unblemished beauty is preserved.

For the linen to shine within the tabernacle, the scarlet to gleam, and the blue to radiate with its azure color, the skins and goat-hair cloth above bear the rains, winds, and dust.

Those who advance in great virtues within the bosom of the holy Church ought not to despise the life of their superiors when they see them occupied with external matters. Their ability to penetrate inner things securely is due to the help of those who labor externally against the storms of this age.

What grace of its whiteness would linen retain if rain touched it? Or what brightness and splendor would scarlet or blue display if dust settling upon them defiled them?

Let the texture of goat-hair cloth above be strong against dust; let the blue color below be suited to beauty. Let those who devote themselves solely to spiritual matters adorn the Church; let those whom the labor of bodily affairs does not burden cover the Church.

Therefore, the person who already shines spiritually within the holy Church should by no means murmur against the ruler who is engaged in external affairs. If you shine securely within like scarlet, why do you accuse the goat-hair cloth that protects you?

### CHAPTER XLII

The same as above.

[Note: None of our manuscripts contains this passage.]

In the exposition of the Gospel, Homily 38 (No. 10):

“The tabernacle curtains are commanded to contain twice-dyed scarlet. You are the curtains, brothers—you are the curtains of the tabernacle, who by faith veil the heavenly mysteries in your hearts.

But the curtains of the tabernacle must contain twice-dyed scarlet. Scarlet has the appearance of fire. And what is love except fire? Yet this love must be twice dyed: it must be dyed through love of God and dyed through love of neighbor.

The person who loves God in such a way that, through contemplation of him, he neglects his neighbor is indeed scarlet, but not twice dyed. Again, the person who loves his neighbor in such a way that through this love he abandons contemplation of God is scarlet, but not twice dyed.

Therefore, in order that your love may be twice-dyed scarlet, let it kindle itself both to the love of God and to the love of neighbor, so that neither, through compassion for a neighbor, does it abandon contemplation of God, nor, by clinging more than it should to contemplation of God, does it cast aside compassion for a neighbor.

Thus every person living among human beings should yearn for the one whom he desires without abandoning the one with whom he was running, and should offer help to the latter without growing sluggish with regard to the one toward whom he was hastening.”

### CHAPTER XLIII

“When the Lord commands the boards of the tabernacle to be erected, he commands that their bases be cast in silver” (Exod. XXVI, 16, 19).

When the mystery of the height foretold by the prophets and apostles was being discussed in the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVIII (No. 18), it adds: “When the Lord commanded the boards of the tabernacle to be erected,” etc.

What else can be signified by the silver bases of the boards except the order of the prophets? Since they were the first to speak openly about the Lord’s incarnation, we see them rising from the foundations like certain bases and supporting the weight of the structure placed upon them.

Therefore, when the Lord commanded Moses to erect the boards of the tabernacle, he commanded that their bases be cast in silver.

For what is signified by the boards except the apostles, extended and spread throughout the world by their preaching? And what by the silver bases except the prophets? They themselves, firm and cast, support the boards placed upon them, because the life of the apostles, while instructed by the prophets’ preaching, is also made firm by their authority.

Hence two joined bases are placed beneath each board, because when the holy prophets agree in their words concerning the incarnation of the Mediator, the subsequent preachers of the Church are built up without doubt. Since the prophets do not differ from one another, they establish the apostles more firmly.

Nor is it without reason that the bases by which the prophets are signified are commanded to be cast from silver. The brightness of silver is preserved through use, but without use it turns black.

Before the Mediator’s coming, the sayings of the prophets, because they were not yet applied to spiritual understanding and could not be seen on account of their obscurity, remained, as it were, black. But after the Mediator came and polished them before our eyes with the hand of his incarnation, whatever light was hidden in them shone forth. He put the meaning of the preceding fathers to use, because he explained their words through realities.

### CHAPTER XLIV

“The Lord commands that the four columns before which the veil is to hang have silver bases” (Exod. XXVI, 26).

When the mystery of the preaching of the teachers of the Church was being discussed in the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVIII (No. 17), it adds: “The four columns,” etc.

When the tabernacle was being erected as a figure of the Church, Moses was told that the bases of the four columns placed within should be silver.

For what else is understood by silver except the brightness of the divine word, as it is written: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, refined in the earth” (Ps. XI, 7)?

The bases clothed in silver therefore support the four columns of the tabernacle, because the preachers of the Church, adorned with the divine word so that they may offer themselves as examples in all things, carry the words of the four Evangelists both in speech and in deeds.

[Note: The printed editions read “as a figure”; the manuscripts resist this reading.]

### CHAPTER XLV

“In the construction of the tabernacle, while the silver columns stood within, bronze pegs were ordered to be placed all around outside, by which the tabernacle, tied with ropes, would be held” (Exod. XXXVI, 36).

When the unity of the Old and New Testaments through the Spirit was being discussed in Homily 15 (Nos. 16–17) on Ezekiel, it adds:

[Note: We have corrected this chapter, which is corrupt in many places, with the aid of the manuscripts.]

 “In the construction of the tabernacle, while the silver columns stood within,” etc.

A little later it is also written: “You shall make pegs for the tabernacle and for the court, with their ropes.”

The fathers of the Old Testament, because they stood at a greater distance from the incarnation of our Redeemer through the intervals of time, were commanded to be outside. Indeed, the passion of the Church began already with Abel’s blood, and there is one Church of the elect who preceded and those who followed.

Nevertheless, because it is said to the disciples, “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke X, 24), for the ancient fathers to have stood outside means that they did not see the bodily presence of our Redeemer.

They were therefore external, but not separated from the holy Church, because in mind, deed, and preaching they already possessed these sacraments of faith and beheld the height of the holy Church, which we behold not while awaiting it but already while possessing it.

For just as we were saved through faith in the past passion of our Redeemer, so they were saved through faith in the passion that was still to come. They were therefore outside not the mystery but the time.

Hence, in the construction of the tabernacle, while the silver columns stood within, bronze pegs were ordered to be fixed all around outside, and the tabernacle was to be held by ropes tied to them.

The silver columns are therefore fixed within, while bronze pegs are fixed all around, and ropes are tied to them, so that the tabernacle may remain firm. In this way, so that the holy apostles might stand firm in the light of their preaching and the entire tabernacle—that is, the holy Church—might stand in the integrity of faith, the fathers and prophets of the Old Testament were fixed outside like bronze pegs, so that by the ropes of their words they might bind the minds of the preachers in firmness and secure this tabernacle of God in the stability of faith.

The pegs are outside because those who existed before the time of this holy Church were outside. Yet they bind those who are within it, because by preaching the heavenly mysteries that were to come, they made them credible to all once they had been revealed.

Thus, in order that the columns within might stand immovable, the ropes outside are held by the pegs. For the preaching of those who were able to see and preach the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation before it occurred obtained this result: that the holy apostles might perfectly believe it.

Nor is it without reason that the columns were made of silver but the pegs of bronze, because what the apostles now preach clearly, the prophets spoke obscurely under mystical understanding. They were rightly signified by bronze, since their preaching was not clear.

The holy apostles, however, because they possessed the light of preaching concerning the mystery of our Redeemer, were represented by silver columns.

It should also be noted that silver gives both sound and light, whereas bronze gives sound but does not shine. The preachers of the New Testament spoke openly of things that they were also able to show. The preachers of the Old Testament, however, because they uttered obscure sayings about the heavenly mystery through the shadows of allegories, gave forth, as it were, sound without light.

### CHAPTER XLVI

“They shall make the ephod [shoulder-piece] of gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen” (Exod. XXVIII, 4).

When, in the treatment of the good character of priests and the clarity with which their work should be displayed (Book I, Letter 25, formerly 24), the following was added:

> “They shall make the superhumeral [*superhumerale*] of gold and violet-blue, etc.”

[Note: In the Gemet and Michaelino manuscripts, this is assigned the title “Book Fourteen of the Pastoral Rule.” These passages, however, are found at the place indicated by us.]

By the command of the heavenly voice, the priest is fastened with the covering of the superhumeral upon both shoulders, so that he may always be fortified against adversity and prosperity by the adornment of virtues. Thus, in accordance with Paul’s words, “walking with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left” (II Cor. VI, 7), when he strives only toward the things that are before him [Note: The printed editions read: “the inward things”], he must not be bent in any direction by the allurements of worldly pleasure. Let not prosperity exalt him, nor adversity disturb him; let flattering words not caress him into pleasure, nor harsh ones crush him into despair. Thus, while he humbles the purpose of his mind under no passions, he may show by how great a beauty of the superhumeral he is covered upon both shoulders.

Rightly, too, the superhumeral is commanded to be made of gold, violet-blue, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and twisted linen, so that it may demonstrate how greatly the priest ought to shine with the diversity of virtues. In the priest’s clothing, gold shines before all else, so that the understanding of wisdom may principally gleam in him. Violet-blue, shining with a bronze-blue color, is added to it, so that through everything he penetrates by understanding he may rise not toward lowly human approval but toward love of heavenly things. He must not, while heedlessly becoming engrossed in his own praises, be emptied even of his understanding of truth.

Purple is mingled with the gold and violet-blue [Note: The Uticensis manuscript reads: “and purple is mingled with linen”], so that the priestly heart, while hoping for the highest things that it preaches, may also restrain within itself the promptings of vice and oppose them as though by royal authority. In this way it may continually regard the nobility of inward regeneration and defend for itself, by its conduct, the character of the heavenly kingdom. Concerning this nobility of the spirit, Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II, 9). Concerning this power, by which we subdue vices, we are strengthened by John’s words: “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John I, 12).

The Psalmist considers this dignity of strength when he says: “But to me your friends, O God, are exceedingly honorable; their principality has been exceedingly strengthened” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 17). For assuredly the minds of the saints are principally raised toward the highest things when they are seen outwardly enduring what is lowly.

Scarlet twice dyed is added to the gold, violet-blue, and purple, so that in the sight of the inward Judge all the good qualities of the virtues may be adorned by love, and so that everything that gleams before human beings may be kindled in the sight of the hidden Arbiter by the flame of inward love. This love, because it loves God and neighbor together, shines like scarlet from a double dyeing. Therefore, whoever longs for the appearance of the Creator in such a way that he neglects the care of his neighbors, or carries out the care of his neighbors in such a way that he grows sluggish in divine love—for he neglects either one of these—does not know how to possess twice-dyed scarlet in the adornment of the superhumeral.

But when the mind is directed toward the commandments of love, it unquestionably remains that the flesh must be disciplined through abstinence. Hence twisted linen is added to the twice-dyed scarlet. Linen arises from the earth with a shining appearance. What, then, is expressed by linen except the glowing beauty of bodily purity? This twisted linen is attached to the beauty of the superhumeral because chastity is led to the perfect beauty of purity when the flesh is wearied through abstinence. And when, along with the other virtues, the merit of afflicted flesh also advances, twisted linen shines white amid the superhumeral’s varied appearance.

## Chapter XLVII

“Moreover, you shall make the breastpiece of judgment [*rationale judicii*] in variegated work” (Exod. XXVIII, 15).

When, through the mystery of the promised priestly garment, the treatment concerned the beauty of doctrine that was to be displayed by succeeding teachers, the following was added in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part II, chap. 2):

> “Moreover, you shall make the breastpiece of judgment in variegated work.”

By the divine voice it is commanded that the breastpiece of judgment be impressed upon Aaron’s chest with fastening bands, so that unstable thoughts may in no way possess the priestly heart, but that reason alone may restrain it, lest it think anything indiscriminate or useless. He who has been appointed as an example to others ought always, by the gravity of his life, to show how much reason he carries in his breast.

In this breastpiece it is also carefully prescribed that the names of the twelve patriarchs be inscribed. To carry the inscribed fathers always upon one’s breast is to think without interruption about the life of the ancients. For the priest walks irreproachably when he continually regards the examples of the fathers who came before, when he unceasingly considers the footsteps of the saints, and suppresses unlawful thoughts, lest he extend the foot of his conduct beyond the boundary of his order.

It is rightly also called the breastpiece of judgment, because a ruler ought by subtle examination to distinguish good from evil, and diligently to consider what things are suitable, for whom, when, and in what manner. He must seek nothing for himself, but regard the advantages of those near him as his own good.

Hence it is written there:

> “You shall place in the breastpiece of judgment the doctrine and the truth, which shall be upon Aaron’s breast when he enters before the Lord; and he shall bear the judgment of the children of Israel upon his breast before the Lord always” (Exod. XXVIII, 30).

For the priest to bear the judgment of the children of Israel upon his breast before the Lord’s presence is to examine the cases of his subjects solely with a view to the inward Judge, so that no human consideration may mingle with what he administers while placed in God’s stead, and so that private grief may not embitter his efforts at correction. When he shows himself zealous against the vices of others, he should deal with his own, lest the calmness of judgment be stained by hidden envy or disturbed by rash anger. But while he considers the terror of him who presides over all, namely, the inward Judge, let his subjects be governed with no small measure of fear.

## Chapter XLVIII

“That when the priest enters the tabernacle, he is commanded to carry twelve stones upon his breast, engraved with the names of the children of Israel” (Exod. XXVIII, 17).

[Col. 0745B]

When the significance of the first preachers was being treated in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXVIII, no. 14, the following was added:

> “That when the priest enters the tabernacle, etc.”

Who is represented by this high priest except the person of our Redeemer? For our High Priest, offering himself as a sacrifice for us, carried twelve stones beneath his head, in the first part of his body, when at the very beginning he displayed strong preachers. Thus the holy apostles are stones upon the breast as the first display of adornment, and, as the foundations of a building laid upon the ground, they are foundations.

## Chapter XLIX

“Below, around the hem of the robe, you shall make something like pomegranates” (Exod. XXVIII).

When the treatment concerned the preservation by teachers of concord in unity, through the discerning mystery of preaching, the following was added in Book I, Letter 25 of the *Register* (formerly Letter 24) [Note: This is indicated in the Michaelino manuscript as Book Fifteen of the *Pastoral Rule*, and in the Gemet manuscript as Book Three. See Book II, chapter 4, where these passages are found]:

> “Below, around the hem of the robe, you shall make something like pomegranates.”

When a ruler prepares to speak, he should consider with what careful attention he must speak, lest, if he is carried headlong into speech without order, the hearts of his hearers be struck by the wound of error, and, while perhaps desiring to appear wise, he foolishly sever the bond of unity. Hence the Truth says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX, 49). For by salt the wisdom of the word is signified. Whoever strives to speak wisely must greatly fear that the unity of his hearers may be thrown into confusion by his eloquence.

Hence Paul says: “Do not think more highly than it is necessary to think, but think with sobriety” (Rom. XII, 3). Hence, in the priest’s clothing, according to the divine voice, bells are joined to pomegranates. For what is signified by pomegranates except the unity of faith? Just as within a single pomegranate many seeds are protected by its outer rind, so the unity of faith covers the countless peoples of the holy Church, who are held within by a diversity of merits.

Therefore, lest a ruler rush heedlessly into speaking, the Truth itself cries out to the disciples in the words already mentioned: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX, 49). It is as though he were figuratively saying through the priestly garment: “Join pomegranates to bells, so that in everything you say you may, with watchful care, preserve within yourselves the unity of faith and the love of peace.”

## Chapter L

“That, by the divine voice, bells are commanded to be mixed with pomegranates at the edge of the priest’s robe” (Exod. XXVIII, 33).

When the treatment concerned the continual urgency of preaching that teachers should display, the following was added in chapter 15 of the *Pastoral Rule* (Part II, chap. 4) [Note: This also appears in Book I, Letter 25, formerly 24]:

> “That, by the divine voice, bells are commanded to be mixed with pomegranates at the edge of the priest’s robe, etc.”

Moses is commanded that, when the priest enters the tabernacle, he be surrounded by bells, so that he may have the voices of preaching and not offend the judgment of the heavenly Inspector through silence. For it is written:

> “Let the sound be heard when he enters or leaves the sanctuary before the Lord, and let him not die” (Exod. XXVIII, 35).

The priest entering or leaving dies if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes the anger of the hidden Judge against himself if he walks without the sound of preaching. The bells are appropriately described as inserted into his garments. For what else should we understand the priest’s garments to be than good works? The prophet bears witness, saying: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI, 9). Thus bells cling to his garments, so that the priest’s works themselves may proclaim the way of life together with the sound of his tongue.

## Chapter LI

“Take for yourself spices: stacte, onycha, fragrant galbanum, and the clearest frankincense; all shall be of equal weight. You shall make a compounded incense, carefully blended and pure, by the work of a perfumer” (Exod. XXX, 34).

[Col. 0746B]

When the treatment concerned the display of good works through strict guardianship of the mind, the following was added in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book I, no. 54:

> “Take for yourself spices: stacte, onycha, etc.”

We make incense compounded from spices when we give off the fragrance of a multiplicity of virtues upon the altar of good works. It is blended and pure because the more one virtue is joined to another, the more sincerely the incense of good work is offered.

There it is also aptly added:

> “When you have crushed all the spices into the finest powder, you shall place some of it before the tabernacle of the testimony.”

We crush everything into the finest powder when, as though in the mortar of the heart, we beat our good deeds through hidden examination and reconsider whether they are truly good. To reduce spices to powder is to wear down virtues by reflection and recall them for scrutiny down to the subtlety of hidden examination.

It should also be noted that the same powder is mentioned:

> “You shall place some of it before the tabernacle of the testimony” (Exod. XXX, 36).

For our good deeds truly please the Judge’s sight when the mind crushes them through more subtle reflection and, as it were, produces powder from spices. This prevents the good being done from being coarse and hard, and prevents it, if the strict hand of reconsideration does not break it down, from scattering its fragrance with greater subtlety.

## Chapter LII

“The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII, 6).

When the treatment concerned restraining the vice of gluttony, the following was added in the *Moralia*, Book X, no. 21:

> “The people sat down to eat, etc.”

Eating and drinking drove them to play, and play dragged them into idolatry. For if the fault of greediness is not carefully restrained, the heedless mind is immediately devoured by iniquity, as Solomon testifies when he says: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Eccl. XIX, 1). For if we neglect to take care of small matters, we are imperceptibly led astray and even commit greater offenses boldly.

## Chapter LIII

“Go down, for your people have sinned” (Exod. XXXII, 7).

[Col. 0746D]

When the treatment concerned the proper balance of discernment and severity that rulers should maintain toward their subjects, the following was added in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XX, no. 14:

> “Go down, for your people have sinned.”

It can greatly edify a reader, even according to the historical sense, if he considers how authority in governing and kindness in consoling are mingled in good rulers. Discipline or mercy is greatly weakened if either is held without the other. A ruler should therefore possess toward his subjects both mercy that offers just counsel and discipline that acts with pious severity.

It is pleasing to observe mercy joined with severity in Moses’ heart. Let us see him loving with tenderness and acting with strictness. Certainly, when the Israelite people had incurred an offense almost impossible to expiate before God’s eyes, so that their ruler heard, “Go down, for your people have sinned” (Exod. XXXII, 7), the divine voice seemed to say to him: “He who has fallen into such a sin is no longer mine.” It then added:

> “Let me alone, so that my anger may burn against them, and I may destroy them; but I will make you into a great nation” (Exod. XXXII, 10).

That man, placing himself once and again in the way of the angry God’s attack on behalf of the people over whom he presided, said:

> “Either forgive them this offense, or, if you will not, erase me from your book that you have written.”

Let us consider with what inward affection he loved that same people, for whose life he asked to be erased from the book of life. Yet this man, bound to the people by such great love, should also be considered in regard to how fiercely he burned with zeal for righteousness against their offenses.

As soon as, by his first petition, he had obtained pardon for the offense, so that they would not be destroyed, he came to that same people and said:

> “Let each man put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the middle of the camp; and let each man kill his brother, his neighbor, and his friend.” And on that day about twenty-three thousand men fell (ibid., 27).

Behold: he who had sought the life of all, even at the cost of his own, extinguished the lives of a few by the sword. Within, he burned with the fires of love; outwardly, he was kindled by the zeal of severity. His compassion was so great that he did not hesitate to offer himself to death before the Lord for them. His severity was so great that those whom he had feared God would strike, he himself struck with the sword of judgment.

He loved those over whom he presided so much that he did not spare himself for their sake; yet he pursued those offenders whom he loved so sternly that, even when the Lord spared them, he laid them low. In both respects he was a strong envoy; in both, a remarkable mediator. By prayers he pleaded the people’s cause before God, and by swords he pleaded God’s cause before the people. Within, by supplication, he opposed the divine anger; outwardly, by striking the guilt, he brought it to an end. He hastened to rescue all by displaying the death of a few.

For this reason almighty God more quickly heard his faithful servant acting on behalf of the people, because he saw what he himself, acting for God, would do to the people. In governing the people, therefore, Moses blended both qualities, so that neither discipline would be lacking in mercy nor mercy in discipline.

## Chapter LIV

“Let me alone, so that my anger may burn against them” (Exod. XXXVIII, 16).

[Col. 0747C]

When the treatment concerned extinguishing divine anger, the following was added in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book IX, no. 23, with the order somewhat reversed:

> “Let me alone, etc.”

All the saints who confront God’s anger receive from God himself the ability to oppose the assault of his striking hand. So, if I may put it this way, they are raised up with him against him, and the divine power sets them against itself. For in the fact that outwardly they prevail over the wrath raging against them, inwardly the grace of the one who is angry cherishes them; and it raises up those who serve it inwardly, while outwardly it tolerates them as though they were opponents.

He therefore carries the contradiction of those who implore, although he inspires it, and what he commands to be done by himself is, as it were, imposed upon him unwillingly. Thus he says to Moses:

> “Let me alone, so that my anger may burn against them, and I may make you into a great nation.”

What is it for him to say to his servant, “Let me alone,” except to grant him the courage to intercede? It is as though he were openly saying: “Consider how much you are worth before me, and recognize that you will be able to obtain whatever you ask for the people.”

Yet, although this is so, the reader’s mind is greatly troubled by the contrary statement made by the same holy man in the history of Blessed Job:

> “God, against whose anger no one can resist” (Job XIX, 13).

It is very strange that no one is said to be able to resist God’s anger, when the divine writings testify that many have opposed the indignation of heavenly judgment. Did not Moses resist God’s anger when, standing upright on behalf of the falling people, he restrained the very assault of heavenly destruction by offering his own life, saying:

> “Forgive them this offense, or else erase me from the book that you have written” (Exod. XXXII, 31–32)?

Did not Aaron resist God’s anger when he took the censer and stood between the living and the dead (Num. XVI, 47), tempering the fire of judgment with the smoke of incense? Did not Phinehas resist God’s anger when he slew those committing fornication with foreigners in the very act, offered his zeal to the divine indignation, and appeased the fury with the sword (Num. XXV, 11)? Did not David resist God’s anger when, offering himself to the striking angel, he obtained the grace of appeasement even before the appointed time (II Sam. XXIV, 25)? Did not Elijah resist God’s anger when, after a long period in which rain had been withheld from the dry earth, he recalled the rains from heaven by his word (I Kings XVIII, 44)?

How, then, is it said that no one can resist divine anger, when examples demonstrate that many have often resisted it?

But if we carefully weigh both the words of Blessed Job and the deeds of those men, we shall recognize both that divine anger cannot be resisted and that many have often resisted it. Many saints, as the order of each account given above has shown, resisted the Lord’s anger. No one can resist the anger of God when his indignation moves, so to speak, from the very marrow. When it has begun to move, human opposition cannot hold it back, nor can anyone’s supplication usefully place itself in its way, when God, once angry, determines something from his inmost will.

This is why Moses, who wiped away the guilt of the entire people before God by his prayers and, by offering himself as a barrier, appeased the force of divine anger (Num. XX, 12), could not enter the promised land when, coming to the rock of Horeb and distrusting God concerning the provision of water, he provoked the Lord’s anger. He was often distressed on this account, often troubled as desire stirred him, and was unable to turn away the anger of the vengeance that had been decreed from himself, although, when the Lord willed it, he had removed that anger from the people (II Reg. XXIV, 10).

[Note: These words are absent from the printed edition; we have restored them from the Vatican, Michaelino, Gemet, Uticensis, and other manuscripts.]

This is why David, who later restrained the angel’s sword by prayer after the people had been struck down, first wept and fasted, fled barefoot from his son, and was in no way able to temper God’s anger on his own behalf until he had fully received the vengeance for the crime he had committed (XXX Kings XVII).

This is why Elijah, so that he might experience something, as a human being, of divine judgment—for he had opened the heavens by his word—fled through the wilderness in terror before a woman’s anger and was weakened by fear on his own behalf, although by his intervention he appeased God’s fury for others.

God’s anger can therefore be resisted when he himself who is angry gives assistance; but it cannot be resisted at all when he rouses himself to vengeance and does not inspire the prayer that is poured out to him.

## Chapter LV

“Let each man put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the middle of the camp; and let each man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor” (Exod. XXXII, 27).

When the treatment concerned the life and doctrine of preachers, the following was added in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part III, chap. 25, Admonition 26):

> “Let each man put his sword upon his thigh, etc.”

To put the sword upon one’s thigh is to place the zeal for preaching before the pleasures of the flesh, so that whoever strives to speak holy things must necessarily take care to subdue unlawful promptings. To go from gate to gate is to move by rebuke from vice to vice, through which death enters the mind. To pass through the middle of the camp is to live within the Church with such equality that he who rebukes the faults of delinquents must not incline toward anyone’s favor.

Hence it is rightly added:

> “Let the man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.”

He kills his brother, friend, and neighbor who, when he finds things that must be punished, does not spare them with the sword of rebuke, not even those whom he loves by kinship. If, then, the one who is stirred to strike down vices by zeal for divine love is called God’s man, surely the one who refuses, insofar as he is able, to rebuke the lives of carnal people denies that he is God’s man.

## Chapter LVI

[Note: We have corrected many errors in the printed editions, some of them very serious, with the help of manuscripts that agree with one another.]

“When Moses went out to the tabernacle, all the people rose, and each man stood at the entrance of his tent; and they looked at Moses’ back until he entered the tent. When he had entered the tabernacle of the covenant, the pillar of cloud descended and stood at the entrance, and it spoke with Moses. All saw that the pillar of cloud stood at the entrance of the tabernacle; and they stood and worshiped at the doors of their tents” (Exod. XXXIII, 8).

[Col. 0749A]

When the treatment concerned the gift of the Spirit bestowed upon those who desire it through the illumination of heavenly grace, the following was added in the *Commentary on Ezekiel*, Homily I, second part, no. 17:

> “When Moses went out to the tabernacle, etc.”

The Hebrew people, liberated from Egyptian slavery, when the Lord spoke and they beheld the pillar of cloud, each stood at the door of his tabernacle and worshiped. Of them it is also said:

> “When Moses went out to the tabernacle, all the people rose, and each man stood at the entrance of his tent.”

What does it mean for the people to look upon the pillar of cloud, stand at the doors of their tabernacles, and worship, except that when the human mind perceives, however obscurely, those higher and heavenly things, it already leaves the enclosure of its bodily dwelling through elevated thought and humbly worships him? Although it cannot see his substance, it already marvels at his power through the Spirit’s illumination.

When Moses enters the tabernacle, the people look upon his back and stand at the doors of their tents, because when a holy preacher speaks lofty things about the Lord, he already enters, in some fashion, the tabernacle of the heavenly dwelling. The lowliest hearers cannot fully weigh the truth of his preaching, but they look, as it were, upon his back, because they follow by understanding those final things that they are able to grasp. Even in the smallest matters that they can comprehend, they already go out, as it were, from their tents and stand at the entrances, because they strive both to leave the dwellings of the flesh and to advance toward the joys of eternal life that they hear proclaimed.

## Chapter LVII

“You cannot see my face. For no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 20).

[Col. 0749D]

When the treatment concerned the vision of knowledge, the following was added in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XVIII, nos. 88–91 [Note: The printed editions read: “concerning the division of knowledge”]:

> “You cannot see my face, etc.”

To this saying of the Lord, in which he says to Moses, “For no human being shall see me and live,” John is heard to agree when he says: “No one has ever seen God” (I John IV, 12).

Yet when I look upon the fathers of the Old Testament, I recognize that many saw God, as the history of sacred Scripture itself bears witness. Jacob saw God, for he said: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my life has been preserved” (Gen. XXXII, 30). Moses saw the Lord, of whom it is written: “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend” (Exod. XXXIII, 11). Job saw God, for he says: “I heard you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (Job XLII, 5). Isaiah saw the Lord, for he says: “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty and elevated throne” (Isa. VI, 1). Micaiah saw the Lord, for he says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and all the army of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left” (I Kings XXII, 19).

What, then, is meant by the fact that so many fathers of the Old Testament testified that they had seen the Lord, while he himself says, “No human being shall see me and live,” and John says, “No one has ever seen God” (I John IV, 12)? It is plainly understood that while one lives here in mortal condition, God can be seen through certain images, but cannot be seen through the appearance of his very nature. Thus the soul, breathed upon by the grace of the Spirit, sees God through certain figures but does not reach the very power of his essence.

This is why Jacob, who testifies that he saw God, saw him only in an angel. This is why Moses, who speaks with God face to face, as a man speaks with his friend, says to him amid the very words of their conversation: “If I have found grace in your sight, show yourself to me plainly, so that I may see you” (Exod. XXXIII, 13). Certainly, if the one with whom he was speaking was not God, he would have said, “Show God to me,” rather than, “Show yourself to me.” But if he was God with whom he spoke face to face, why did he ask to see the one whom he was seeing?

His request makes clear that he thirsted to behold, through the unbounded radiance of God’s nature, the one whom he had already begun to see through certain images. He desired that the heavenly essence should be present to the eyes of his mind in such a way that no created, temporal image would intervene between him and the vision of eternity.

Thus the fathers of the Old Testament did see the Lord, and yet, in John’s words, “No one has ever seen God”; and, in the Lord’s own words, “No one has seen God and lived.” For those who remain in this mortal flesh, God could be seen through certain circumscribed images, but cannot be seen through the uncircumscribed light of eternity.

But if some people, while still living in this corruptible flesh and yet growing through immeasurable virtue, can see the eternal radiance of God through a certain intensity of contemplation, this too does not conflict with the same saying of the Truth: “No human being shall see me and live.” For whoever sees the wisdom that belongs to God dies completely to this life, so that he may no longer be held by love of it. No one has seen it who still lives carnally, because no one can embrace God and the world at the same time. Whoever sees God dies by that very act, in that he is separated with his whole mind from the pleasures of this life, whether in the purpose of his heart or in the affection expressed through his works.

No one, therefore, has seen God and lived; as though it were openly said: No one has ever seen God spiritually and continued to live carnally in the world.

It must be known, however, that there were some who said that God is indeed seen in that blessed region in his radiance, but is not seen in his nature. A lesser subtlety of inquiry deceived them. For in that simple and immutable essence, radiance is not one thing and nature another; rather, its nature itself is its radiance, and its radiance itself is its nature.

Since this wisdom of God would one day show itself to those who love it, he himself promises this, saying:

> “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV, 21).

It is as though he plainly said: “You who now see me in your nature must finally see me in my nature.”

Again he says:

> “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8).

Paul says:

> “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know even as I am known” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

But because the first preacher of the Church says of God, “Into whom angels desire to look” (I Pet. I, 12), there are some who suppose that not even the angels see God. Yet we know that the Truth said:

> “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 10).

Does the Truth, then, utter one thing and the preacher of the Truth another? But when the two statements are compared, it is recognized that they are in no way different. The angels both see God and desire to see him; they long to contemplate him and contemplate him.

For if they desired to see him in such a way that they did not enjoy the fulfillment of their desire, desire without fruit would contain anxiety, and anxiety would contain punishment. But the blessed angels are far from every punishment of anxiety, because punishment and blessedness never coexist.

Again, when we say that they are satisfied by the vision of God, as the Psalmist says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. XVI, 15), we must consider that satiety is usually followed by disgust. Therefore, so that both statements may rightly agree, let the Truth say that they always see, and let the excellent preacher say that they always desire to see. To prevent anxiety from existing in desire, they are satisfied while desiring; and to prevent disgust from existing in satisfaction, they desire while satisfied. They desire, therefore, without weariness, because satisfaction accompanies their desire; and they are satisfied without disgust, because that very satisfaction is always kindled by desire.

So shall we also be when we come to the very fountain of life. Thirst and satisfaction will be delightfully impressed upon us together. Necessity will be far from thirst, and disgust far from satisfaction, because while thirsting we shall be satisfied, and while satisfied we shall thirst. We shall therefore see God himself, which will be the reward of our labor, so that after the darkness of this mortality we may rejoice, kindled by his light.

## Chapter LVIII

“There is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock. When my glory passes by, I shall place you in a cleft of the rock.” And shortly afterward: “I shall remove my hand, and you shall see my back” (Exod. XXXIII, 21).

When the treatment concerned the belief of the Jewish people, the following was added in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXV, no. 25:

> “There is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock, etc.”

By the place the Church is signified; by the rock, the Lord; and by Moses, the multitude of the Israelite people, who did not believe when the Lord preached on earth. That people therefore stood upon the rock, looking upon the back of the passing Lord, because, after the Lord’s Passion and Ascension, it was brought within the Church and deserved to receive faith in Christ; and although it did not see his presence, it recognized what came afterward.

## Chapter LIX

“Likewise, concerning the foregoing.”

When the exalted state of the holy Church was being treated in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXV, no. 13, the following was added:

> “There is a place with me, etc.”

Because truth is seen solely from within the catholic Church, the Lord declares that there is a place with him from which he may be seen. Moses is placed upon the rock so that he may contemplate God’s face, because unless a person holds the solidity of faith, he does not recognize the divine presence. Concerning this solidity the Lord says:

> “Upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18).

For it alone is the place in which the Lord willingly accepts sacrifice; it alone confidently intercedes for those who have gone astray. Hence, concerning the sacrifice of the lamb, the Lord also commanded, saying:

> “It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not carry any of its flesh outside” (Exod. XII, 46).

The lamb is eaten in one house because in the one catholic Church the true sacrifice of the Redeemer is offered. Divine law forbids its flesh to be carried outside because it forbids holy things to be given to the flesh.

It alone is the place in which good work is fruitfully performed. Hence those who had labored within the vineyard alone received the wage of the denarius. It alone preserves within itself those who have been placed in it by the strong bond of love. Hence the water of the Flood raised the ark to higher places, but destroyed all whom it found outside the ark.

## Chapter LX

“You repay the iniquity of the fathers to their children and grandchildren, to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. XXXIV, 7).

While the question was being discussed—namely, that the guilt of parents, transmitted through their offspring, derives from original sin, whereas the imitation of depravity is what ought to be punished—in the exposition of blessed Job, book XV (no. 57), the following was added:

> “You repay the iniquity of the fathers upon their sons and grandsons,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] The printed editions read: “How the iniquity of parents is punished in their descendants.” We follow the manuscripts, which remarkably agree.]

Since it is written: “What is this proverb that you turn into a saying in the land of Israel, saying, ‘The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the children have been set on edge’? As I live, says the Lord God, this proverb shall no longer be a saying for you in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII, 2 ff.; Jer. XXXI, 29), what does it mean that Moses now says to the Lord: “You repay the iniquity of the fathers upon sons and grandsons”? Yet in both these statements, since a different meaning is found, the mind of the hearer is instructed to seek carefully the path of distinction.

We draw original sin from our parents; and unless we are released through the grace of baptism, we also bear the sins of our parents, because we are still, so to speak, one with them. He therefore repays the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons when, because of the parent’s guilt, the soul of the offspring is polluted by original sin. Yet again he does not repay the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons, because when we are freed from original guilt through baptism, we no longer possess the sins of our parents, but only those which we ourselves commit.

This may also be understood in another way: whoever imitates the iniquity of a wicked parent is also held guilty because of that parent’s offense. Whoever, however, does not imitate the iniquity of the parent is in no way burdened by the parent’s offense. Thus it happens that an unrighteous son of an unrighteous father pays not only for his own sins, which he has brought upon himself, but also for his father’s sins, when he does not fear to add his own wickedness to the father’s vices, by which he knows that the Lord was angered.

And it is just that one who, under a strict judge, does not fear to imitate the ways of an unrighteous parent should be compelled in the present life also to pay the penalties of that unrighteous parent. Hence it is also said there: “The soul of the father is mine,” etc., “the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. IV), because in the flesh children are sometimes put to death even because of their father’s sin. But once original sin has been blotted out, the sins arising from the wickedness of parents are not retained in the soul.

For what else does it mean that little children are often seized by demons, except that the child’s flesh is punished for the father’s offense? The unrighteous father is struck in himself, but disregards feeling the force of the blow. Often he is struck in his children, so that he may be burned more severely; and the father’s pain is inflicted upon the flesh of the children, so that the father’s wicked mind may be punished by the children’s suffering.

When not little children but already more mature sons are struck because of their parents’ guilt, what else is plainly indicated except that they also pay the penalties of those whose deeds they have followed? Hence it is rightly said: “To the third and fourth generation.” Since sons can see the life of their parents whom they imitate only as far as the third and fourth generation, vengeance extends to those who saw what they would wrongly follow.

## CHAPTER LXI

Whatever was necessary for the worship of the tabernacle and for the holy vestments, men and women contributed: bracelets, earrings, rings, and armlets. Every golden vessel was set apart as an offering to the Lord; whoever possessed blue-purple cloth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, or goats’ hair brought it (Exod. LV, 22).

[Col. 0752A]

When the works of the elect within the holy Church were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXX (no. 24), the following was added:

> “Whatever was necessary for the worship of the tabernacle,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] In this chapter we corrected many corruptions, following earlier editions, from the Vatican, Gembloux, and other manuscripts.]

Men offer gifts with women for the adornment of the tabernacle, because in fulfilling the worship of the holy Church both the exalted deeds of the strong and the lowliest works of the weak are counted.

What else is signified by bracelets, which bind the arms, except the works of those set over others who labor vigorously? What else by earrings except the obedience of subjects? What else by rings except the seal of God’s secrets? For teachers often seal what they perceive cannot be grasped by their hearers.

And what else is signified by armlets except the adornments of first works? What else by the golden vessel set apart as an offering to the Lord except understanding of the divinity? This is separated from love of lower things in proportion as it is lifted toward the love of things eternal alone.

What else by the blue-purple cloth except hope of heavenly things? What else by purple except blood and endurance of sufferings offered through love of the everlasting kingdom? And what else by twice-dyed scarlet except charity, which is dyed twice for the sake of perfection, because it is adorned by love of God and neighbor?

What else by fine linen except the incorruptibility of an unstained body? And what else by goats’ hair, from which the roughness of sackcloth is woven, except the pure affliction of repentance?

Thus, while some exercise a strong teaching office through bracelets and rings, others display devoted obedience and upright action through earrings and armlets, others possess a splendid and more subtle understanding of God through the golden vessel set apart, and others, through the blue-purple cloth, purple, and scarlet, do not cease to hope for, believe in, and love the heavenly things they have heard, even though they do not yet know them through a more subtle understanding; while others offer bodily incorruption through fine linen, and others, through goats’ hair, harshly lament what they willingly committed—as though the ministries of these gifts, gathered together from one work of the craftsman, are offered, according as he himself grants it, into the tabernacle of the Lord, that is, within the holy Church.

## CHAPTER LXII

He also made a bronze basin with its base, from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle (Exod. XXXVIII, 8).

When the cleansing of the filth of sins through observance of the divine commandments was being discussed, the following was added in Homily 17 on the Gospels (no. 10):

> “He also made a bronze basin with its base,” etc.

Moses places a bronze basin in which the priests are to wash before entering the Holy of Holies, because the law of God first commands us to be washed through compunction, so that our impurity may not be unworthy of penetrating the purity of God’s secrets.

The statement that the basin was rightly made from the mirrors of the women who continually keep watch at the tabernacle’s door is significant. The mirrors of the women are the commandments of God, in which holy souls always behold themselves and discover the stains of deformity that are in them. They correct the faults of their thoughts and, like faces resisting correction, compose them as though from an image reflected back, because when they attend carefully to the Lord’s commandments, they undoubtedly recognize in them what pleases or displeases the heavenly man within themselves.

As long as they are in this life, they cannot enter the eternal tabernacle. Yet the women keep watch at the tabernacle’s door, because holy souls, even while still weighed down by the weakness of the flesh, continually watch in love for entry into the eternal dwelling.

Moses therefore made a basin for the priests from the women’s mirrors, because the law of God provides the washing of compunction for the stains of our sins, while the heavenly commandments set before us those things through which holy souls pleased the heavenly Bridegroom. If we attend to these diligently, we see the stains of our inner image. When we see the stains, we are pierced with the grief of repentance. Once pierced, we are washed, as it were, in a basin made from the women’s mirrors.

We are truly pierced with compunction when we diligently consider the deeds of our preceding fathers, so that, from the glory we behold in them, our own life may become sordid in our own eyes. We are truly pierced with compunction when we diligently examine God’s commandments and strive to advance through those things by which we know that those whom we venerate have already advanced.

## BOOK THREE

### On Testimonies from the Book of Leviticus

[Col. 0753]

## CHAPTER I

After removing the skin of the victim, let them cut its limbs into pieces. They shall place fire upon the altar, having first arranged a pile of wood; and, arranging the pieces that have been cut above it—namely, the head and everything attached to the liver—after washing the intestines and feet with water (Lev. I, 7 ff.).

[Col. 0753B]

When the need to avoid the desire for earthly appetite was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book I (no. 54), the following was added:

> “After removing the skin of the victim, let them cut its limbs into pieces,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] In the Vatican manuscript: “the avoidance of earthly things by spiritual means,” etc.]

We remove the skin of the victim when we take away from the eyes of our mind the outward surface of virtue. We cut its limbs into pieces when, distinguishing its inner parts subtly, we consider them member by member.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] The following passage, up to “but amid these things,” is absent from the manuscripts.]

We must therefore take care that, when we conquer evil, we are not overthrown by luxuriant good works; lest something unstable emerge, lest something unguarded be seized, lest we depart by the path of error, or lest, broken by weariness, we lose the merit of our previous labor. In everything the mind must watchfully look around itself and persevere in the very prudence of its vigilance (Moral Commentary, book IX, no. 84).

But amid these things we must know that we are sometimes afflicted by the impulse of an unlawful thought because we willingly occupy ourselves in certain acts of earthly life, although they are lawful. And whenever earthly action is touched, even in the smallest things, by desire, our mind is stained by no small importunity of temptation, as the strength of the ancient enemy increases against us.

Hence the priest of the law is commanded to burn the limbs of the victim, cut into pieces, together with the head and those parts that are around the liver, while first washing the feet and intestines of the victim with water.

We offer ourselves as a sacrifice to God when we dedicate our life to divine worship. We place the limbs of the victim, cut into pieces, upon the fire when we sacrifice the works of our life, distinguishing them according to the virtues. We burn the head and the parts contained near the liver when we burn with the flame of divine love in our understanding, by which the whole body is governed, and in our hidden desires.

Yet it is commanded that the feet and intestines of the victim be washed. The feet touch the earth, while the intestines carry dung, because often we are already kindled by desire for eternity and already yearn with the whole devotion of our understanding for the longing of our mortification. But because, through weakness, we still do something earthly, we tolerate in our hearts certain unlawful things that we have already subdued.

When an unclean temptation stains our thoughts, what else do the intestines of the victim carry except dung? But they are washed so that they may be burned, because clearly it is necessary that the tears of fear wash away the unclean thoughts which heavenly love kindles when the sacrifice is accepted.

And whatever the mind suffers either from an inexperienced struggle or from memory of its former way of life must be washed, so that it may burn more sweetly in the presence of its observer, in proportion as, when it begins to stand before him, it places nothing earthly and nothing slippery upon the altar of its prayer.

## CHAPTER II

Concerning an oath that has been uttered and then omitted through forgetfulness, Moses says: “Let him offer a ewe lamb from the flocks, or a she-goat, and the priest shall pray for him and for his sin. But if he cannot offer an animal, let him offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for sin and the other as a burnt offering” (Lev. V, 6–8).

When the means of recovering life was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXII (no. 4), the following was added:

> “Concerning an oath that has been uttered,” etc.

To utter an oath is to bind ourselves by a vow to divine service. When we promise good works, we pledge ourselves to do well. But when we vow abstinence and the mortification of our flesh, we swear that, for the present, we shall do evil to ourselves.

Yet since no one in this life is so perfect that, however devoted to God he may be, he does not sin amid even his most pious vows, a ewe lamb or she-goat is commanded to be offered for sin.

What else is signified by the ewe lamb except the innocence of the active life? What else by the she-goat, which often feeds while hanging upon the highest and most remote crags, except the contemplative life?

Whoever therefore sees that he has not fulfilled what he promised and resolved must prepare himself more diligently for God’s sacrifice, either through the innocence of good works or through the lofty nourishment of contemplation.

And it is rightly commanded that the ewe lamb be offered from the flocks, whereas the she-goat is not commanded to be offered from the flocks, because the active life belongs to many, whereas the contemplative life belongs to few. When we do those things that we see many doing and having done, we give, as it were, a ewe lamb from the flocks.

But when the virtue of the one offering is not sufficient for a ewe lamb or a she-goat, two young pigeons or two turtledoves are added as a remedy for the penitent.

We know that young pigeons and turtledoves have a song of lamentation. What therefore is signified by two young pigeons or two turtledoves except the double lamentation of our repentance? When we do not rise to offer good works, we should mourn ourselves doubly, because we have neither done what is right nor ceased from doing what is wrong.

Hence one turtledove is commanded to be offered for sin and the other as a burnt offering. A burnt offering is so called because it is wholly burned. We therefore offer one turtledove for sin when we utter a groan for our guilt; and from the other we make a burnt offering when, because we have neglected good things, we set ourselves wholly aflame and burn with the fire of grief.

## CHAPTER III

Concerning the turtledove or pigeon offered for sin, it is commanded that its head be twisted back toward its feathers, so that the head remains attached to the neck and is not completely severed (Lev. V, 7).

When, through the mystery of the promised sacrifice, the unity of the holy Church, confirmed in its head—that is, in our Redeemer—and the glory of his passion were being discussed in Homily 7 on Ezekiel (no. 10), the following was added:

> “Concerning the turtledove or pigeon,” etc.

What else is signified in this offering of the turtledove or pigeon, which is commanded to be offered for sin, and in the command that after the victim’s death its head remain attached to its body, except the person of our Mediator?

The death of our Redeemer served to unite him with his body, that is, the Church, not to separate him from it. The Mediator of God and human beings, that is, the head of us all and the true sacrifice of purification, through the very thing by which he endured death for us became more truly joined to us.

Thus, after the turtledove’s head has been cut, it remains attached to its body, because even intervening death does not divide Christ from the Church.

The persecutors therefore accomplished what they had wickedly attempted. They inflicted death in order to cut off the devotion of the faithful from him. But faith grew from the very thing by which the cruelty of the unbelievers believed it would extinguish it. And when they thought that by persecuting his miracles they would cut them off, they were compelled, without knowing it, to spread them further.

For who is our head except the Redeemer of the human race? Of him it is written: “He gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body” (Eph. I, 22). When the Jews persecuted him, they tried to erase his name from the earth. When they saw him crucified and buried, they believed that they had separated him from the love of all.

But the head of the turtledove was cut, yet was not severed from its body, because by enduring death for us our Redeemer joined us to himself more truly in that very death. And by visibly withdrawing himself from our eyes, he rooted himself invisibly in our minds.

The turtledove’s head therefore remained attached to the body after being cut, because our Redeemer suffered for us but was not separated from us.

## CHAPTER IV

The same subject as above.

When the manner of maintaining the active life was being discussed in Homily 7 on Ezekiel, the following was added:

Those who wished to understand this according to the historical sense, until the true sacrifice should come, held to the fulfillment of the letter. In this sacrifice, if we seek a moral meaning, we find something applicable to us.

We ourselves must be the turtledove in the sacrifice of almighty God, so that our head may be twisted back toward its feathers, that is, our understanding toward the virtues. We rightly understand the mind by the head, because as the head governs the body, so the mind governs actions.

But the head must remain attached to the neck and not be completely severed, because our mind must be cut away from the pleasure of the flesh, but must not be cut off from the necessary care of the flesh. Hence it is written: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII, 14). What is therefore forbidden in desires is plainly permitted in necessity.

The turtledove’s head should thus be severed in part and remain attached to the neck in part, so that, as has been said, our mind may be cut away from the will of the flesh but not severed from necessity.

[Note: [Col. 0755] Gembloux and Utica read “from pleasure.” We retain the received reading, which is “Michael.”]

## CHAPTER V

Fire shall always burn upon the altar; the priest shall tend it, placing wood upon it every morning. And, having placed the burnt offering upon it, he shall burn the fat of the peace offerings above it (Lev. VI, 12).

When the nourishment of divine love and the preservation of purity of heart were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXV (nos. 15–16), the following was added:

> “Fire shall always burn upon the altar,” etc.

This is the perpetual fire that will never fail from the altar. The altar of God is our heart, in which fire is commanded always to burn, because it is necessary continually to kindle from it the flame of charity toward God.

The priest should place wood upon it each day, lest it be extinguished. Everyone endowed with faith in Christ has become a member of the High Priest, as the apostle Peter says to all the faithful: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. II, 9). And as the apostle John says: “You made us a kingdom and priesthood for our God” (Rev. I, 6).

The priest therefore, tending the fire on the altar, should place wood upon it daily. That is, each faithful person, lest the flame of charity fail within him, should not cease to gather in his heart both the examples of those who preceded him and the testimonies of sacred Scripture.

For to provide the fire with fuel, so to speak, is to supply either the examples of the fathers or the Lord’s commandments for the exercise of charity. Because our inner newness grows old each day through the conduct of this life, this fire must be nourished with wood, so that, while the use of our old age wears it down, it may revive through the testimonies and examples of the fathers.

And it is rightly commanded there that wood be gathered each morning, every day. These things are done only when the night of blindness is extinguished. Or certainly, because morning is the first part of the day, each of the faithful should, putting aside thoughts of the present life, consider first of all how to kindle the zeal of charity by whatever efforts he can, since it is already failing within him, so to speak.

For this fire on the Lord’s altar—that is, in our heart—is quickly extinguished unless it is diligently restored through the examples of the fathers and the Lord’s testimonies.

It is rightly added there: “And having placed the burnt offering upon it, he shall burn the fat of the peace offerings above it.” Whoever kindles this fire of charity within himself places himself upon it as a burnt offering, because he burns up every vice that was living wickedly within him.

When he considers the inner movements of his thoughts and puts his reprobate life to death with the sword of transformation, he has placed himself upon the altar of his heart and kindled himself with the fire of charity.

From this sacrifice of peace offerings comes the fragrant fat: the inward richness of a new life, making peace between us and the Lord, gives forth from us a most pleasant fragrance.

Because this same charity remains inextinguishable in the hearts of the elect, it is aptly added there: “This is the perpetual fire, which shall never fail from the altar.” This fire never fails from the altar because, even after this life, the fervor of charity increases in their minds. For through eternal contemplation it comes about that the more clearly almighty God is seen, the more greatly he is loved.

## CHAPTER VI

The same subject as above.

In the Commentary on Ezekiel, Homily 12 (no. 30):

The fine flour that the law commands to be offered as a sacrifice: no sacrifice is such for almighty God as zeal for souls. Hence the Psalmist says: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Ps. LXVIII, 10).

(no. 3.) How greatly the frying of the heart, which is carried out through spiritual zeal, pleases almighty God is clearly shown when the law commands fine flour to be offered as a sacrifice. Of it is written: “It shall be fried in a pan sprinkled with oil, and the priest who lawfully succeeds his father shall offer it hot as a most sweet odor to the Lord, and it shall be entirely burned upon the altar” (Lev. VI, 21).

The fine flour is fried in a pan when the pure mind of the righteous is burned through the ardor of holy zeal. It is commanded to be sprinkled with oil because mercy is called ἔλεος in Greek; and not without reason is mercy signified by oil, since it burns and shines in the sight of almighty God.

Let the mind that is fried in the pan therefore be sprinkled with oil, because in the strictness of holy zeal it is necessary that, through the virtue of mercy, it both burn and shine.

For the zealous person loves the very one whom he appears to pursue. Hence it is commanded to be offered hot to the Lord as a most sweet odor, because if zeal does not possess love, the fine flour offered in the pan has lost its warmth.

And we should note who is commanded to offer it: the priest who lawfully succeeds his father. He succeeds his father lawfully who demonstrates by his conduct that he is a son of almighty God and does not depart from his inner nobility through the ignobility of his works.

It is commanded to be entirely burned upon the altar, so that it may become a burnt offering. We call a burnt offering something wholly burned. Hence in another translation this same fine flour fried in the pan is commanded to become a burnt offering.

The difference between a burnt offering and a sacrifice is that every burnt offering is indeed a sacrifice, but not every sacrifice is a burnt offering. Many good things are performed as sacrifices but are not burnt offerings, because they do not set the entire mind aflame with spiritual love.

Those who perform the things of God in such a way that they nevertheless do not abandon the things of the world offer a sacrifice, but not a burnt offering.
