Those, however, who abandon everything belonging to the world and kindle their whole mind with the fire of divine love offer both a sacrifice and a burnt offering to almighty God.

The fine flour in the pan is therefore the pure mind of the righteous in the affliction of spiritual zeal, fried through concern for souls; and it is reckoned to be not only a sacrifice but also a burnt offering to the Lord.

## CHAPTER VII

That the tail of the victim is commanded to be offered in the sacrifice (Lev. VII, 3).

When perseverance in good works was being discussed in Homily 25 on the Gospels (no. 2), the following was added:

> “That the tail of the victim is commanded to be offered in the sacrifice.”

What is signified by the tail except the end of the body? And he sacrifices well who carries the sacrifice of good work through to the end of the required action.

The tail of the animal is therefore commanded to be offered upon the altar, so that, whenever we begin any good work, we may also complete it with a persevering ending.

## CHAPTER VIII

That the priest is commanded to receive from the sacrifice the right shoulder, set apart (Lev. VII, 33).

When the guardianship of the priestly office was being discussed, the following was added in the Pastoral Rule, title 14:

> “That the priest is commanded to receive from the sacrifice,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0757D] That is, Part II, chapter 3. The same words are found in Letter 25 of Book I, formerly Letter 24.]

What does it mean that, by the command of the law, the priest is ordered to receive not only the right shoulder but also the portion set apart, except that his work must be not only useful but also distinctive?

He must not merely do what is right among the wicked; he must also surpass his well-doing subjects in moral virtue just as he surpasses them in the dignity of his office.

He is also given the breast together with the shoulder in eating, so that he may learn to sacrifice to the Creator from himself what he is commanded to take from the sacrifice. He should think in his breast about what is right, but also invite those who observe him to higher things by the shoulder of his works.

Let him desire nothing belonging to the present life and fear nothing. Let him despise the flatteries of the world by considering the inward terror, and let him scorn its terrors by considering the sweetness within.

## CHAPTER IX

That fish without fins are forbidden to the eating of the faithful people; and that fish possessing fins and scales are accustomed to leap even above the waters (Lev. II, 9).

When the desires of the elect living spiritually were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book V (no. 19), the following was added:

> “That fish without fins,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0757D] In Michael, Homily 26 on the Gospels is cited.]

What therefore are represented by fish with fins except the elect souls? They alone certainly pass into the body of the heavenly Church. Now, supported by the fins of the virtues, they know how to leap through heavenly desire, so that they seek what is above through contemplation of heavenly things, although they again slip within themselves because of mortal flesh.

## CHAPTER X

The same subject as above.

(no. 19.) Fish that have fins are accustomed to leap above the waters. Therefore only those pass over as fish into the body of the elect who, while serving things below, sometimes know how to climb to things above through leaps of the mind, lest they always lie hidden in the depths of cares and no breath of the highest love, like the air of freedom, touch them.

Those who are occupied with temporal affairs therefore arrange outward things well when they flee attentively to inward things, when they do not at all love the noise of disturbances outside, but rest within themselves in the bosom of tranquility.

## CHAPTER XI

If afterward a flying and spreading leprosy appears in those places that were previously clean, it must be burned with fire (Lev. XIII, 57).

[Col. 0758B]

When the vices alternating within a reprobate mind were being discussed in Homily 10 on Ezekiel, the following was added:

> “If afterward it appears in those places,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0757D] In Michael it is assigned to Homily 11. We find what is written here in neither source.]

Sometimes we recognize that we have acted wrongly and avoid these faults in our conduct; but the very fault steals upon us through other actions, although previously it held us in other ways.

There are some who, subject to carnal impurity, return to themselves upon reflection and recognize the guilt of their wickedness. When they have corrected themselves from the unclean action, they immediately boast foolishly, with arrogant elation, of the good of chastity; and those whom the impurity of action previously held in the body are afterward held by the impurity of elation in thought.

What else therefore possesses such people except a flying leprosy, which has not entirely abandoned the garment but has changed its place within it?

The garment of the holy Church is each individual believer. Hence the prophet says to it: “As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these things as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX, 8).

Flying and spreading leprosy holds the garment when a fault possesses a soul that is seen to be faithful through a changed form of vice.

[Note: [Col. 0758D] This passage is corrupt in the printed editions and in many manuscripts. The true reading is supplied by the manuscript of Michael.]

If someone perhaps becomes proud of the riches he possesses in this world, but, hearing from the mouth of a preacher that all these things are perishable, distributes what he possesses among the poor, yet harbors pride in his heart because of that distribution, then, as we have said, the leprosy has changed its place in the garment: first pride held him through hoarding, afterward through generosity.

Another person is devoted to immoderate and undisciplined words of foolish merriment. When he is perhaps rebuked by a preacher, he strives to restrain himself by the discipline of seriousness, lest he rejoice with uncontrolled gaiety. But often, when he is restrained from joy more than he should be, his mind turns to anger; his sadness arouses the goads of wrath in him, and constrains his mind with the thorn of fury.

Thus, because the vice of foolish joy passes through excessive restraint into the vice of anger, the wandering and flying leprosy abandons the place it occupied and takes possession of one it did not occupy.

## CHAPTER XII

Whoever suffers an emission of semen shall be unclean (Lev. XV, 10).

[Col. 0758D]

When the proper measure of speech was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXIII (no. 28), the following was added:

> “Whoever suffers an emission of semen,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0758D] In Gembloux: “What is signified by an emission of semen except the seed of speech? When it is emitted in due order …”]

What is speech except seed? When it is emitted in due order, the mind of the hearer, like a womb conceiving, becomes pregnant with the offspring of good work. But if it flows out inappropriately, it pollutes the one who emits it and loses the power of generation.

In the minds of hearers, the seed of a subsequent thought is the quality of the speech heard, because when speech is conceived through the ear, thought is generated in the mind.

For if speech were not seed, the Athenians would never have said of the preaching Paul: “What does this seed-scatterer of words mean to say?” (Acts XVII, 18). Luke also says of him: “For he was the leader of speech” (Acts XIV, 11).

Seed devoted to the use of procreation, when it flows out improperly, pollutes the other members; so speech, through which knowledge ought to be born in the minds of hearers, if it proceeds disorderly, defiles even what it has rightly understood.

Whoever therefore suffers an emission of semen is declared unclean, because one subject to excessive speaking pollutes himself through it (Pastoral Rule, Part II, chapter 4, at the end). If he were to bring it forth in due order, he could produce offspring of right thought in the heart of his hearers.

But when, heedless, he pours himself out through loquacity, he sheds seed not for the use of generation but for uncleanness.

Hence Paul, when admonishing his disciple about perseverance in preaching, says: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, by his coming and his kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season” (2 Tim. IV, 1).

When he was about to say “out of season,” he first added “in season,” because, clearly, speech destroys itself in the mind of the hearer by its very usefulness if its being out of season does not know how to have an appropriate occasion.

## CHAPTER XIII

You shall not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling block before the blind (Lev. XIX, 14).

[Col. 0759B]

When the vice of detraction and scandal was being discussed in the Pastoral Rule, Part III (chapters 35 and 36), the following was added:

> “You shall not curse the deaf,” etc.

To curse the deaf is to disparage someone who is absent and unable to hear. To place a stumbling block before the blind is to do something that is in itself discerning, yet to provide an occasion of scandal for one who does not possess the light of discernment.

## CHAPTER XIV

When you enter the land that I shall give you, and plant in it fruit-bearing trees, you shall remove their foreskins. The fruit that they produce shall be unclean for you, and you shall not eat it (Lev. XIX, 23).

When the avoidance of the desire for transitory praise was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book VIII (nos. 79–80), the following was added:

> “When you enter the land,” etc.

Fruit-bearing trees are works fruitful in virtues. We therefore remove the foreskins of the trees when, suspicious of the weakness of our very beginning, we do not approve the beginnings of our works.

We call the fruit that they produce unclean and do not adapt it to our eating, because when the beginnings of a good work are praised, it is right that this should not nourish the soul of the one performing it, lest, while the praise received is pleasantly plucked, the fruit of the work be eaten before its time.

Whoever therefore receives praise from human lips for a virtue he has begun has eaten, as it were, the fruit of a planted tree before the proper time.

Hence Truth says through the Psalmist: “It is vain for you to rise before the light; rise after you have sat down” (Ps. CXXVI, 2).

To rise before the light is to rejoice in the night of the present life before the brightness of eternal recompense appears.

One must therefore sit down first, so that afterward one may rise correctly, because whoever does not willingly humble himself now will not be exalted by the glory that follows.

[Note: [Col. 0759D] “Sciendum” entered the printed edition in place of “sedendum.”]

## CHAPTER XV

Speak to Aaron: Anyone among your descendants, throughout their families, who has a blemish shall not offer the breads to his God, nor approach his ministry. And immediately thereafter it is added: If he is blind, if lame, if he has a small or large or crooked nose, if he has a broken foot or hand, if he is hunchbacked, if bleary-eyed, if he has a white spot in his eye, if a persistent itch, if an ulcerous eruption on his body, or if he is heavy-set (Lev. XXI, 17 ff.).

[Col. 0759D]

When the vices of character, distinguished through bodily infirmities, were being discussed in the *Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chapter 9, the following was added: “Speak to Aaron, etc.” It must be carefully considered that, when an elected bishop undertakes responsibility for the people, he approaches as a physician approaches a sick person. If the passions are still alive in his conduct, with what presumption can one heal another who bears a wound upon his own face? (Chapter 10.) Therefore, the person who must be drawn in every way toward the example of right living is one who, dying to all the passions of the flesh, already lives spiritually; who has set aside worldly prosperity; who fears no adversity; [Col. 0760A] who desires only inward things; whose purpose is well matched by a body that neither resists entirely through weakness nor excessively through stubbornness; who is not led to covet what belongs to others, but gives away what is his own; who, through the compassion of mercy, is quickly moved to forgive, but, in forgiving, never inclines away from the stronghold of righteousness more than is fitting; who commits no unlawful acts, but grieves over the unlawful acts committed by others as though they were his own; who, from the affection of his heart, sympathizes with another’s weakness and thus rejoices in his neighbor’s good things as in his own advances; who presents himself as worthy of imitation by others in everything he does, so that among them his mind has nothing, even among past actions, for which to blush; who strives to live in such a way that he can irrigate even the parched hearts of his neighbors with the streams of his teaching; who, through the practice and experience of prayer, has already learned that he can obtain from the Lord whatever he asks. (Chapter 11.)

Hence it is that, by a voice from above, the vices of character are signified through bodily infirmities, when the Lord says to Moses: “Speak to Aaron: No man of your offspring, throughout your families, who has a blemish shall offer bread to the Lord his God, [Col. 0760B] nor shall he approach his ministry” (Leviticus 21:17). Immediately afterward it is added: “If he is blind, if lame, if he has a small or large or crooked nose, if he has a broken foot or hand, if he is humpbacked, if he is bleary-eyed, if he has a white spot in his eye, if he has a persistent scab, if he has an impetigo on his body, or if he is ponderous.”

For he is blind who does not know the light of heavenly contemplation. Pressed by the darkness of the present life, he does not perceive the light that is to come, because he does not love it, and so he does not know where to direct the course of his action. Thus Anna says in prophecy: “He will guard the feet of his saints, and the wicked will be silenced in darkness” (1 Samuel 2:9).

He is lame who sees where he ought to go, but, through weakness of mind, is unable perfectly to keep to the way of life that he sees. Since he is not raised to the state of virtue by a firm habit, his deeds do not effectively follow where his desire leans. Hence Paul says: “Raise your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that no one who is limping [Col. 0760C] may stray, but rather be healed” (Hebrews 12:12–13).

He has a small nose who is not capable of maintaining the measure of discernment. We distinguish odors and stench through the nose. Thus discernment is rightly expressed through the nose, for by discernment we choose virtues and reject sins. Hence it is said in praise of the bride: “Your nose is like the tower that is in Lebanon” (Song of Songs 7:4). For holy Church perceives through discernment what kinds of temptations arise from each individual circumstance, and from a height detects the battles with vices that are to come.

But there are some who, because they do not wish to be considered dull, often exercise themselves in certain inquiries more than is necessary and are deceived by excessive subtlety. [Note: The printed editions read *ex minima*, “from the least,” contrary to Gregory’s meaning.] Hence it is also added here: “or one with a large and crooked nose.” A large and crooked nose is an excessive subtlety of discernment which, when it grows beyond what is proper, itself confounds the rightness of its action.

He has a broken foot or hand who is altogether unable [Col. 0760D] to proceed along God’s way and remains completely deprived of good works, so that he does not retain these even as a lame man does, with infirmity, but is entirely alien to them.

He is humpbacked whom the weight of earthly concern presses down, so that he never looks toward heavenly things but attends only to what is trodden underfoot in the lowest places. Even if he sometimes hears something concerning the good of the heavenly homeland, he does not raise the face of his heart toward it, weighed down as he is by the burden of perverse habit. He cannot raise the posture of his thoughts, because the practice of earthly concern holds him bent. Of such people the Psalmist says: “I am bent and humbled exceedingly” (Psalm 38:8).

Truth itself also condemns their fault, saying: “The seed that fell among thorns: these are those who have heard, but as they go on their way are choked by the cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and do not bring forth fruit” (Luke 8:14).

He is bleary-eyed whose natural intelligence shines toward knowledge of the truth, [Col. 0761A] but whose carnal works nevertheless obscure it. In bleary eyes the pupils are healthy, but the eyelids, weakened by the discharge of moisture, become thickened. Because they are repeatedly irritated by the flow, the sharpness of the pupil is also impaired. There are likewise some whose understanding is wounded by the activity of carnal life: they could see what is right with subtle intelligence, but they grow dim through the practice of evil deeds. He is therefore bleary-eyed whose nature sharpens his understanding, but whose corrupt manner of life confounds it.

To such a person the angel rightly says: “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, so that you may see” (Revelation 3:18). We anoint the eye with eye-salve so that we may see when, in order to recognize the brightness of the true light, we assist the sharpness of our understanding with the remedy of good works.

He has a white spot in his eye who is prevented from seeing the light of truth because he is blinded by arrogance concerning wisdom or righteousness. The black pupil of the eye sees, whereas one suffering from a white spot sees nothing. Thus, when the understanding of human thought recognizes itself as foolish and sinful, it grasps the thought of inward brightness. But when it attributes to itself the whiteness of righteousness or wisdom, it excludes itself from the light of heavenly knowledge. It penetrates the brightness of the true light no further precisely because it exalts itself before itself through arrogance. As it is said of certain people: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1:22).

He has a persistent scab whom the wantonness of the flesh continually dominates. In a scab, the heat of the inward organs is drawn toward the skin; this rightly signifies lust. For if temptation of the heart leaps forward into action, the inward heat bursts out as far as the scab of the skin and now wounds the body externally. When pleasure is not restrained in thought, it also dominates in action.

Paul was, as it were, trying to wipe away the itch of the skin when he said: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human” (1 Corinthians 10:13). It is as though he openly said: “It is human to suffer temptation in the heart; but it is demonic to be overcome in the struggle with temptation and in action.”

Anyone whose mind is ravaged by greed also has an impetigo on his body. If greed is not restrained in small matters, it expands immeasurably. An impetigo takes possession of the body without pain and, growing without distress to the person afflicted, disfigures the beauty of the limbs. So too greed, while seeming to delight the mind of its captive, wounds it; by presenting to thought whatever is to be acquired, it inflames hostility, yet causes no pain in the wound, because it promises abundance to the mind in its fever.

The beauty of the limbs is lost because through greed the beauty of the other virtues is also corrupted. It is as though it irritates the whole body, because through every vice it undermines the mind. Paul bears witness to this when he says: “The love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6:10).

He is ponderous who does not practice disgraceful behavior in action, but is nevertheless continuously and immoderately burdened by such thoughts in his mind. He is not actually dragged all the way to the wicked deed, but his mind delights in the pleasure of lust without any obstacle of resistance. The condition of being ponderous is symbolized when the moisture of the inward organs descends toward the genitals, which swell with the discomfort of disgrace. He therefore is ponderous who, flowing wholly in his thoughts toward wantonness, carries the weight of disgrace in his heart. Although he does not practice evil in action, he is not torn away from it in mind and cannot rise openly to the practice of good, because a shameful weight burdens him in secret.

Whoever is subject to any one of these vices is forbidden to offer bread to the Lord. [Note: The printed editions, against the manuscripts, read: “for surely he cannot wash away the sins of others if he is still ravaged by his own.”] Certainly, one cannot wash away the sins of others when one is still ravaged by one’s own.

## BOOK FOUR. On Testimonies from the Book of Numbers

[Col. 0761]

### CHAPTER ONE. That the Nazirites grow their hair, which after their vow they place in the sacrificial fire (Numbers 6:18)

[Col. 0761C]

When, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book II, number 34, there was discussion of avoiding superfluous thoughts, the following was added: “That the Nazirites grow their hair, etc.”

[Note: The printed editions read: “concerning the cutting away of the excess of thoughts.” We adhere to the manuscripts Vaticanus, Michael, Uticensis, and others.]

What does it mean that the Nazirites grow their hair, except that, through a life of great self-restraint, presumptuous thoughts grow? But what does it mean that, when his devotion has been completed, the Nazirite is commanded to shave his head and place his hair in the sacrificial fire, except that we reach the summit of perfection when we conquer external vices in such a way that we also cut away superfluous thoughts from the mind? To burn these in the fire of sacrifice means to set them aflame with the fire of divine love, so that the whole heart burns with love of God and, consuming its superfluous thoughts, consumes them like the hair of the Nazirite through the perfection of devotion.

### CHAPTER II. That Moses frequently enters and leaves the tabernacle (Numbers 7)

[Col. 0761D]

When, in Part II, chapter 5 of the *Pastoral Rule*, there was discussion of establishing a rule of governance for superiors, the following was added: “That Moses frequently enters, etc.”

What does it mean that Moses frequently enters and leaves the tabernacle, except that the person who is carried away in mind into contemplation is pressed outside by the affairs of the weak? Within, he considers God’s mysteries; outside, he bears the burdens of carnal people. He also always returns to the tabernacle concerning doubtful matters and consults the Lord before the ark of the covenant, undoubtedly offering rulers an example: whenever they are uncertain outside about what they should arrange, they should always return in mind, as though to the tabernacle, and, as though before the ark of the covenant, consult the Lord, if, concerning matters about which they are uncertain, they search inwardly within themselves through the pages of sacred discourse.

Hence Truth itself, revealed to us through the assumption of our humanity, remains devoted to prayer on the mountain (Luke 6:12) and performs miracles in the cities, thereby laying out a path of imitation for good rulers. Even if they already seek the heights through contemplation, they must nevertheless mingle with the needs of the weak through compassion, because love rises wonderfully to lofty things when it mercifully draws itself down toward the lowly; and when it kindly descends to the lowest places, it returns powerfully to the highest.

### CHAPTER III. The Levites shave all the hair of their flesh (Numbers 8:7)

When, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book V, number 59, there was discussion of avoiding carnal desires in the hearts of the elect, the following was added: “The Levites shall shave all the hair of their flesh.”

The hairs of the flesh are every kind of superfluity belonging to human corruption. The hairs of the flesh are the thoughts of the former life, which we cut away from the mind in such a way that we are not wearied by any grief over their loss.

A Levite is so called because he is one who has been taken up for service. Therefore all Levites ought to shave the hairs of their flesh, because the person taken up for divine service ought to appear pure before God’s eyes from all thoughts of the flesh, lest the mind bring forth unlawful thoughts and, like hairs bearing fruit, disfigure the beautiful appearance of the soul.

But however greatly, as we have said, the virtue of holy conduct may raise someone up, something nevertheless continues to arise from the old life that must be endured. Hence the hairs of the Levites were commanded to be shaved, not plucked out. For when the hair is shaved, its roots remain in the flesh and grow again, so that it may again be shaved. In the same way, superfluous thoughts must indeed be cut away with great diligence, but they can never be entirely eradicated. The flesh always generates what is superfluous, and the spirit must always cut it away with the sword of vigilance. We perceive these things more subtly within ourselves when we penetrate the heights of contemplation.

### CHAPTER IV. That the Levites must minister from their twenty-fifth year, but from their fiftieth year become keepers of the vessels (Numbers 8:24–25)

When, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIII, number 21, there was discussion of the works of the perfect and imperfect within holy Church, the following was added: “That the Levites must minister from their twenty-fifth year, etc.”

What is signified by the twenty-fifth year, in which the flower of youth appears, except the battles themselves against each individual vice? And what is signified by the fiftieth year, in which the rest of the jubilee is contained, except the inward rest expressed after the battle of the mind has been subdued? What, moreover, are signified by the vessels of the tabernacle except the souls of the faithful?

Let the Levites therefore serve the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year, and from their fiftieth year become keepers of the vessels, so that those who still endure the struggles of attacking vices through consent to pleasure do not presume to take charge of others. [Note: The phrase “through consent to pleasure” is absent from the manuscripts Uticensis and Gemetensis; it is found in Michael.]

For the elect, while they are still in temptation, must necessarily be subject, serve, and be wearied by duties and labors. But when they have conquered the battles of temptation, so that they are now secure in themselves concerning inward tranquility, let them receive the guardianship of souls. When the mind has reached tranquil maturity and the heat of temptation has withdrawn, they are keepers of the vessels, because they become teachers of souls.

### CHAPTER V. That Moses frequently returns to the tabernacle in doubtful matters (Numbers 9:7–9)

When, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIII, number 38, there was discussion of the good of inward rest and the avoidance of the tumult of secular life, the following was added: “That Moses frequently returns to the tabernacle in doubtful matters.”

To leave the crowds and return to the tabernacle is, after setting aside external disturbances, to enter the secrecy of the mind. There the Lord is consulted, and what must be done publicly outside is heard silently within.

Good rulers do this daily. When they recognize that they cannot discern doubtful matters, they return to the secrecy of the mind as though to a certain tabernacle. Having examined the divine law, they consult the Lord as though before the ark placed there; and what they first hear inwardly in silence, they later make known outside through their actions.

So that they may serve external duties without stumbling, they take constant care to return to the secrets of the heart. Thus they hear the voice of God, as though through hidden inspiration, when in the meditation of the mind they are withdrawn from bodily senses.

### CHAPTER VI. “Make for yourself two silver trumpets of beaten work.” And shortly afterward: “When the signal is sounded in a broken blast, they shall move the camps” (Numbers 10:2, 5)

When, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXX, number 14, there was discussion of the operation of the two commandments—namely, love of God and love of neighbor—administered in the hearts of hearers through the supreme institution of the good teacher, the following was added: “Make for yourself two silver trumpets of beaten work, etc.”

An army is led by two trumpets because, through the two commandments of charity, the people are summoned to the battle line of faith. They are commanded to be made of silver so that the words of preachers may shine with the brightness of light and not confuse the minds of their hearers through any obscurity of their own.

They are commanded to be of beaten work because those who preach the life to come must grow through the blows of present tribulations. It is rightly said: “When the signal is sounded in a broken blast, they shall move the camps,” because when the word of preaching is delivered with greater subtlety and precision, the hearts of hearers are aroused more fervently for the battles of temptation.

### CHAPTER VII. “We are setting out for the place that the Lord is to give us; come with us, so that we may do good to you” (Numbers 10:29)

In Book III of the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 17, near the end of the chapter, the following was added: “We are setting out for the place, etc.”

We can often persuade the proud more effectively to do what is useful if we say that their progress will benefit us rather than themselves, if we say that their improvement will benefit us more than themselves, and if we ask that this improvement be bestowed upon us more than upon them. Pride is easily bent toward the good if it believes that its bending will benefit others as well.

Thus Moses, who, with God guiding him, was traveling through the wilderness under the leadership of an aerial pillar, wished to draw his kinsman Hobab away from the conduct of the Gentiles and subject him to the rule of almighty God. He said: “We are setting out for the place that the Lord is to give us; come with us, so that we may do good to you, because the Lord has promised good things to Israel” (Numbers 10:29 and following).

When Hobab replied, “I will not go with you, but I will return to my land, in which I was born,” Moses immediately added: “Do not leave us, for you know in what places in the wilderness we ought to pitch camp, and you will be our guide.”

For ignorance of the route did not trouble Moses’ mind. Knowledge of divinity had enlarged him even to prophetic understanding; the pillar went before him externally; and familiar speech, cultivated through constant fellowship with God, instructed him inwardly concerning everything. Rather, the prudent man, speaking to a proud hearer, asked him to provide assistance. He sought him as a guide on the journey so that he might become his guide to life.

He therefore acted so that the proud hearer would become all the more devoted to the voice persuading him toward better things because he was thought necessary; and from the very point at which he believed himself to precede his exhorter, he would be humbled beneath the words of the one exhorting him.

### CHAPTER VIII. That, while the people were receiving manna, they craved from Egypt pots of meat, melons, leeks, and onions (Numbers 11:5–7)

When, in the exposition of blessed Job, Books XX, numbers 39–40, there was discussion of the vices of reprobate minds through their contempt for the sweetness of heavenly inspiration, the following was added: “That, while the people were receiving manna, etc.”

Carnal minds, because of their love of the world, are prepared to endure harsh things as though they were soft and delightful, while they strive in this life to seize the heights of worldly affairs. The Lord commands them to cease from the labors of the world and commends the sweetness of holy rest. Yet the deranged mind of the wicked rejoices more in attaining harsh things carnally than in possessing gentle things spiritually. It feeds more on the bitterness of weariness than on the sweetness of rest.

The Israelite people openly demonstrated this in themselves. While they were receiving nourishment from the manna sent down from above, they craved from Egypt pots of meat, melons, leeks, and onions.

What is signified by manna except the food of grace that tastes sweet, given from above to those who devote themselves well to the restoration of the inner life? And what is signified by pots of meat except carnal works in the labors of tribulations, to be cooked as though by fires? What by melons except earthly sweetnesses? What is expressed by leeks and onions, which usually make those who eat them shed tears, except the difficulty of the present life, which is endured by its lovers not without lamentation and yet is loved amid tears?

Therefore, abandoning manna, they sought melons, meat, leeks, and onions, because perverse minds despise the sweet gifts of rest bestowed through grace. In place of carnal pleasures, they desire the laborious paths of this life, paths full of tears. They scorn having a place where they may rejoice spiritually, and in their desire they seek a place where they may also groan carnally.

### CHAPTER IX. “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people” (Numbers 11:16)

When, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XIX, number 26, there was discussion of considering the gravity of character rather than age in appointing superiors, the following was added: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, etc.”

Just as those who are supported by no gravity of counsel are often called young men, so sacred Scripture is not accustomed to call people old merely because of the length of time they have lived, but because they are mature through the greatness of their character. Hence a certain wise man says: “Old age is honorable, not that which lasts long, nor that which is measured by the number of years. The gray hair of human beings is understanding, and an undefiled life is the age of old age” (Wisdom 4:8).

Hence the Lord says to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people.” What else is sought in them except old age of heart, when those are commanded to be chosen who are known to be old? If bodily old age were being sought in them, they could be recognized by many and seen by many. But when it is said, “whom you know to be elders of the people,” it is plainly announced that old age of mind, not of body, is to be chosen.

### CHAPTER X. “Why are you jealous on my behalf? Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord would give them his spirit” (Numbers 11:29)

When, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXII, number 54, there was discussion of the shepherds’ devout desire of heart in winning their subjects, the following was added: “Why are you jealous on my behalf? etc.”

The devout mind of shepherds, because it seeks not its own glory but that of the Creator, wishes what it does to be assisted by all. A faithful preacher desires, if it could be brought about, that the mouths of everyone should sound forth the truth that he alone is not sufficient to speak.

Thus, when Joshua wished to oppose two men who had remained in the camp and were prophesying, Moses rightly said: “Why are you jealous on my behalf? Would that all the people might prophesy and that the Lord would give them his spirit!” He wished everyone to prophesy because he did not begrudge others the good that he possessed.

### CHAPTER XI. That Aaron stood between the living and the dead after taking the censer (Numbers 16:47–48)

When there was discussion of the diligence of the good shepherd, the following was added: “That Aaron stood between the living and the dead after taking the censer.”

[Note: In the manuscripts Gemetensis and Michaelinus this is identified as the eleventh homily on Ezekiel, although it is not found there.]

What does it mean that Aaron, in order to appease the Lord’s anger, took a censer and stood between the living and the dead, except that it is the priest’s task to pour out prayer to almighty God both for the righteous, so that they may not fall, and for sinners, so that they may rise again? Hence the Psalmist says: “Let my prayer enter as incense in your sight” (Psalm 140:2).

### CHAPTER XII. On the twelve rods placed in the tabernacle, from which Aaron’s rod blossomed (Numbers 17:2)

When, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XIV, number 68, there was discussion of the mystery of the resurrection, the following was added: “On the twelve rods placed in the tabernacle, etc.”

When Aaron’s priesthood, since he was from the tribe of Levi, was despised and the tribe was not considered worthy to offer holocausts, twelve rods corresponding to the twelve tribes were commanded to be placed in the tabernacle. And behold, the rod of Levi blossomed and showed what power Aaron possessed in his office.

What is signified by this sign except that all of us who lie in death until the end of the world remain, as it were, like the other rods in dryness? But while all the other rods remain dry, the rod of Levi returned to blossom, because the body of the Lord, that is, of our true priest, placed in the dryness of death, burst forth into the flower of resurrection.

By this flower Aaron is rightly recognized as a priest, because through this glory of resurrection our Redeemer, who arose from the tribe of Judah and Levi, is shown to be an intercessor for us. Behold, then, Aaron’s rod now blossoms after its dryness, but the rods of the twelve tribes remain dry, because the Lord’s body already lives after death, whereas our bodies are still deferred from the glory of resurrection until the end of the world.

### CHAPTER XIII. “Command the children of Israel to bring you a red heifer, of full age, in which there is no blemish and which has not borne a yoke. You shall hand it over to Eleazar the priest, who, after leading it outside the camp, shall sacrifice it in the sight of the Lord. He shall dip his finger in its blood and sprinkle it seven times toward the entrance of the tabernacle. He shall burn it while all look on, committing both its hide and flesh, its blood and dung, to the flames. The priest shall also throw cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet twice-dyed into the flame that consumes the heifer. Then, having washed his clothes and his body, he shall enter the camp, and he shall be unclean until evening. The man who burned it shall also wash his clothes and his body, and he shall be unclean until evening. A clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer and pour them outside the camp in a very clean place, so that they may be kept for the multitude of the children of Israel and used for the water of sprinkling, because the heifer was burned for sin” (Numbers 19:3 and following).

[Col. 0766B]

While the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, the following was added: “Command the children of Israel to bring you a red heifer,” etc.—

[Note: [Col. 0765D] In Gemet., this is noted as having been taken from Book XIV on Job. In Michael., no work of Saint Gregory is identified. We have found it nowhere.]

The masculine sex commonly signifies strength, whereas the feminine signifies weakness. What, then, is signified by the heifer except the weakness of the Lord’s assumed incarnation, which is brought to sacrifice, concerning which it is written: “For although he died through weakness, yet he lives through power” (II Cor. XIII, 4)?

This heifer is rightly also called red, because its humanity was reddened by the blood of the Passion. Hence, too, in the Song of Songs she is described by the bride, who says: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Cant. V, 10): white, evidently, in his divinity; ruddy, in his blood; white through the righteousness of his life; ruddy through the blood of his Passion.

The age of the Lord’s humanity is complete: all his activity was perfect. In that humanity there was no blemish, for it is truly written of him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. II, 22). It is rightly said also that she “has not borne a yoke.” For it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII, 34). Since, therefore, the Lord yielded to no sin, he bore no yoke.

It follows: “You shall hand her over to Eleazar the priest, who, having led her outside the camp, shall sacrifice her in the sight of the Lord.” Why is this heifer handed over to the priest for sacrifice, except that the incarnate Lord, for our redemption, is given as a sacrifice into the hands of the Jewish people? He was also sacrificed outside the camp in the sight of the Lord, because he suffered outside the gate. Hence Paul says: “Jesus, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we have no lasting city here, but we seek the one that is to come” (Heb. XIII, 12).

He suffered outside the gate in order to lead us away from the manner of life of the present world, as though from a city, and to persuade us to tear our hearts away from an earthly dwelling.

It is rightly said that he “shall sacrifice her in the sight of the Lord.” Our Redeemer appeared to be put to death in the sight of human beings, but he is sacrificed in the sight of the Father, because what was punishment before human eyes was sacrifice before the Father’s eyes.

“And he shall dip his finger in her blood.” What is signified by the finger except the discernment of our action? To dip the finger in the heifer’s blood, therefore, is to consecrate our works in the Passion of the Lord’s incarnation, so that we may imitate the Passion which we acknowledge. As it is written: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you should follow in his footsteps” (I Pet. II, 21).

Eleazar the priest thus both sacrifices and dips his finger in her blood, because the Jewish people, from the company of the reprobate, persecuted the Lord’s humility even to the Passion, while, from the company of the elect, it imitated the action of his humility.

“And he shall sprinkle it toward the entrance of the tabernacle.” What is understood here by the tabernacle except the Synagogue as a whole? Whoever, therefore, has dipped his finger in his blood should sprinkle that same blood toward the entrance of the tabernacle. That is, whoever imitates the ways of his Passion should offer to the unbelieving and resisting Synagogue, through good examples and upright preaching, a sign of how to live well.

To sprinkle the heifer’s blood toward the entrance of the tabernacle is to display, through upright preaching and holy works, examples of his Passion to the resisting Jewish people.

It is rightly said that the finger is to be dipped in his blood and the blood sprinkled seven times; for perfection is understood in the number seven. Thus the whole of time is completed in seven days, and the Holy Spirit is called sevenfold (Isa. XI). To dip the finger in his blood seven times, therefore, is to imitate the mystery of his Passion through perfect action. To sprinkle seven times against the Synagogue is to proclaim, through perfect preaching, the sacraments of his incarnation and Passion to unbelievers.

“And he shall burn her in the sight of all, near the camp, giving her hide, flesh, blood, and dung to the flames.” What is signified by the flesh and hide, the blood and dung of the heifer, except the carnal sacrifices found in the Old Testament, which proclaimed the Lord’s weakness? Once understood spiritually by the Fathers, all these things were marked as dung in relation to the external ministry. Hence Paul, speaking of carnal sacrifices, says: “For his sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and regard them as dung” (Phil. III, 8).

They are handed over to the flames because, although they were first offered in a carnal manner, they were afterward consumed by the fire of spiritual understanding through the Holy Spirit.

We may nevertheless understand in this same heifer—that is, in the very weakness of the Lord’s incarnation—the several things represented by its flesh, hide, blood, and dung. What is signified by the flesh and hide except his outward activity? What by the blood except the subtle and inward power that gives life to outward deeds? What by the dung except weariness, thirst, hunger, fear of death, and all the things he willingly assumed from humanity? Whatever he possessed from the deficiency of our mortality had to be cast away from him like dung.

Yet all the things he assumed from our weakness, because he offered them for our redemption, must be consumed by fire—that is, understood according to the power of the Holy Spirit—so that whatever he did bodily may be recognized as arranged through the incorporeal spirit of his divinity.

Here it is rightly added: “The priest shall also throw cedar wood, hyssop, and twice-dyed scarlet into the fire that consumes the heifer.”

Cedar is both a tall and incorruptible wood; hyssop, however, is a very lowly herb, though it removes inflammation from the lungs. What, then, is signified by cedar except lofty and persevering contemplation? And what by hyssop except the humility of a gentle heart? For whoever is already raised above through lofty contemplation must descend to those below through the compassion of humility. He must not exalt himself because of what he possesses, but must willingly distribute through preaching whatever he has even to those who do not possess it.

What, moreover, is expressed by twice-dyed scarlet except the virtue of charity? It is called twice-dyed scarlet because charity, kindled by the fire of holy love, is commanded to be displayed in two precepts: love of God and love of neighbor. Twice-dyed scarlet, then, is charity formed by a double commandment: God is to be loved in such a way that one does not abandon one’s neighbor, and one’s neighbor is to be loved in such a way that God is not despised.

Into this fire that consumes the heifer, therefore, let the priest cast cedar, hyssop, and twice-dyed scarlet. For all who believe in Christ are priests. Hence it is written: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II, 9).

Whatever we deeply perceive through the fire of contemplation, whatever we do through the gentleness of humility, whatever we possess through the fire of charity—we must dip all this into the spirit of the Lord’s Passion, so that everything within us may imitate the one from whom it comes. Otherwise, if we do anything apart from imitating his Passion, we practice not virtue but vice.

Let cedar, then, be cast into the fire that consumes the heifer: that is, let the perseverance and height of our contemplation be consumed in the fire of the Lord’s Passion. Let hyssop be cast into the fire that consumes the heifer: that is, let the humility of our hearts draw truth, gentleness, and examination of the Lord’s Passion.

[Note: [Col. 0767D] In addition to the many corruptions that we have corrected in this chapter, here we restore a complete sentence that had been omitted, from the manuscripts.]

Let twice-dyed scarlet be cast into the fire that consumes the heifer: that is, let charity, which continually arouses us to love the Lord and our neighbor, compel us to contemplate the Lord’s Passion, so that in it we may learn what right actions to perform.

This may nevertheless be understood in another way: cedar may signify hope, which seeks lofty things;

[Note: [Col. 0767D] So Michael. In Gemet., “but by hyssop that which …” [Col. 0768D] Strictly speaking, *hyssopum* is neuter in gender, but in Gregory it is not so used above: “hyssop is a very lowly herb,” and in the following chapter: “hyssop, surely, is our inward …”]

hyssop, which by its heat also cleanses the impurity of the stomach, may signify faith, which patiently endures adversity in lowly circumstances and cleanses whatever had been contracted from former sins. Scarlet, as has been said, expresses charity.

Let each one of us, therefore, cast cedar, hyssop, and twice-dyed scarlet into the fire that consumes the heifer—that is, let us offer hope, faith, and charity in the sacrifice of the Lord’s Passion. Otherwise one hears the Passion of one’s Redeemer without profit if one does not necessarily add these works as well.

The Apostle Paul speaks of these three things: “But now faith, hope, and charity remain; and the greatest of these is charity” (I Cor. XIII, 13). Hence scarlet is placed last here, because when faith and hope have been completed, and we have come to our eternal homeland, only charity is finally increased within us.

This priest, or the one who burns the heifer’s flesh, hide, blood, and dung, may signify the order of the Jewish priesthood together with the people subject to it, consenting in the Lord’s death.

Hence it is aptly added: “Then, after washing his clothes and his body, he shall enter the camp, and he shall be unclean until evening.”

What is understood by evening except the end of the world? This priest, or the one who handed the heifer over to the fire—that is, the Jewish people—remains unclean until evening because it remains unbelieving until the end of the world.

But after washing its clothes and body, it enters the camp at evening, because when the end of the world comes, after the works of its unbelief have been cleansed, the Jewish people too will return to knowledge of its Creator. As it is written: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. X, 22; Rom. IX, 27). And again it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. II, 25).

At evening, therefore, the priest whose clothes have been washed returns inside the camp, though before evening he was unclean, because the unbelieving people remains outside the commandments of life, as though outside the camp, until the end of the world. But when it is washed with baptismal water and repentance, then, at evening—that is, at the end of the world—it returns to knowledge of the faith as though to the camp.

It may be understood that this priest has washed his clothes and yet remains unclean until evening, because the same Jewish people, from the company of those who have believed, has already washed its clothes, as it were, but from the company of those who have not yet believed, it remains unclean until evening.

It therefore washes its clothes and body because, by believing, it cleanses its outward works and inward mind from evil deeds. It then fully returns to the camp when it is completely recalled to the faith.

But because, while Judaism persists in unbelief among the reprobate, the Gentiles enter the faith and understand the mysteries of the divine incarnation, it is rightly added there: “A clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer”—that is, the Gentile people, already cleansed by faith. Hence it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV, 8).

He gathers the ashes of the heifer who recognizes the most subtle mysteries of the divine incarnation. The clean man gathers the ashes of the heifer that the priest burned, because the Gentile people understands the most subtle mysteries of the Lord’s weakness, which the Jewish people slaughtered in his death.

It is rightly added: “And he shall pour them out in a very clean place outside the camp.” The same Gentile people, which recognizes the hidden and mystical realities of the divine incarnation, does not cease to preach the good things it receives, so that what it has learned may also become known to those who do not know it.

But because the hidden and mystical realities of the Lord’s incarnation must not be handed over to depraved and polluted minds, it is rightly said: “He shall pour them out in a very clean place outside the camp.”

All the Gentiles had been outside the camp, because they were outside the law, outside the sacrifice, and outside the Synagogue; nevertheless, on coming to the faith, they cleansed their hearts. The ashes of the heifer are poured into them because, with a clean heart, the Gentiles believe the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

Many converts from the Gentiles became preachers and handed over the mysteries of our Redeemer to the same Gentiles for their conversion to the faith. Thus the clean man pours out the ashes of the heifer in a very clean place when any teacher taken from the Gentiles seeks hearts of the Gentiles made clean through humility and does not cease to hand over to them the mysteries of our Redeemer.

When this is done, the faith of the Gentiles increases, divine power is recognized, and the discipline of the commandments is maintained. Hence it is rightly added: “So that they may be kept for the multitude of the children of Israel.”

For Israel is interpreted as “seeing God,” and the converted Gentiles are rightly called Israel because they already contemplate God by faith.

These ashes, therefore, become a safeguard for the multitude of the children of Israel because the subtle sacraments, handed over to the clean hearts of the Gentiles, are turned into a fortification of the mind.

It is rightly added: “And for the water of sprinkling.” Because of their operation, the ashes serve as a safeguard for us; because of baptism, we use the ashes in the water of sprinkling. While we bring our actions under discipline by considering his works, we preserve the ashes of the heifer as a safeguard for ourselves, because, by attentively imitating the hidden and subtle character of his activity, we provide ourselves through it with both purity and perseverance.

It is aptly added: “Because the heifer was burned for sin.” For concerning these same ashes he says that they are to be “for the multitude of the children of Israel as a safeguard and as water of sprinkling,” because the heifer was burned for sin.

We then carefully guard ourselves under a safeguard when we attentively contemplate our Redeemer suffering for our iniquities. We consider what he gives in return to the good, since he willed to die for the wicked. We consider what we owe to his grace, having been brought to the justice of faith, since even while placed in iniquities we received the intercession of his death.

The ashes therefore become a safeguard for us because the heifer was burned for sin: while we carefully contemplate the mysteries of his Passion, we recognize what we ought to do, since we know that our Redeemer died even for us, the unrighteous.

## CHAPTER XIV

Again, the subject treated above.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book VI (No. 56):

“We slaughter the heifer when we put to death the flesh with its own wanton pleasure. When we offer it with hyssop, cedar wood, and scarlet, we burn the sacrifice of faith, hope, and charity together with the mortification of the flesh.

Hyssop is accustomed to cleanse our inward parts. And through Peter it is said: ‘Cleansing their hearts by faith’ (Acts XV, 9). Cedar wood does not decay through any rot, because the end does not consume hope of heavenly things. Hence the chief shepherd immediately says: ‘He regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, into an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading.’

Scarlet glows with the red heat of the flame, because it sets ablaze the one whom charity fills. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: ‘I have come to cast fire upon the earth’ (Luke XII, 49).

But the scarlet is commanded to be twice-dyed so that, before the eyes of the inward Judge, our charity may be colored by love of God and neighbor. Thus the converted mind must neither love quiet for the sake of God in such a way that it neglects the care and benefit of its neighbor, nor serve activity for the sake of its neighbor in such a way that, completely abandoning quiet, it extinguishes within itself the fire of heavenly love.

Whoever, therefore, has already offered himself as a sacrifice to God, if he desires perfection, must take care to extend himself not only to the breadth of action but also to the heights of contemplation.

Among these matters, however, it must be understood with the greatest care that the dispositions of souls differ greatly among themselves. Some people are so disposed toward inactivity of mind that, if the labor of activity overtakes them, they collapse at the very beginning of their work. Others are so restless that, if they have freedom from labor, they labor more heavily, because the more freely they have time for thoughts, the worse are the disturbances of their hearts that they endure.

It is therefore necessary that the peaceful mind neither stretch itself toward immoderate activity nor the restless mind restrict itself to the pursuit of contemplation. Often those who could contemplate God in quiet have fallen under the pressure of activity. And often those who, while active, could have lived well for human purposes have been destroyed by the sword of their own quiet.

This is why some restless spirits, while seeking through contemplation more than they can grasp, break out into perverse doctrines. By humbly neglecting to be disciples of the truth, they become teachers of error.”

## CHAPTER XV

“A vessel that has no covering or cord fastened over it shall be unclean” (Num. XIX, 15).

[Note: [Col. 0769] In Michael. and Gemet.: “On maintaining the discipline of prudent silence.”]

When the discipline of preserving silence was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIII (No. 17), the following was added: “A vessel that has no covering,” etc.—

The covering of the lid or the fastening is the restraint imposed by the discipline of silence. Whoever is not held in check by it is rejected as a vessel that is unclean and polluted. For a vessel without a covering or fastening is polluted; likewise, the person who stands open through a desire for display, covered by no veil of silence, is polluted.

## CHAPTER XVI

“How Balaam is hindered from the journey he had begun by the vision of the angel and the slowness of the donkey” (Num. XXII, 31, 32, 33).

[Col. 0770D]

When the mind’s initial impulse, restrained so that it might come to knowledge of itself through the mortification of bodily weakness, was being discussed in the *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, Chapter 12, Admonition 13, the following was added: “How Balaam is hindered by the vision of the angel and the slowness of the donkey,” etc.—

Balaam strives to reach his intended goal, but the animal he rides obstructs his desire. For while the donkey remains delayed by the prohibition, it sees the angel whom the human mind does not see. Often the flesh, slowed by hardships, reveals God to the mind through its chastisement, whom the mind itself, ruling the flesh, had not seen. Thus it obstructs the anxiety of the spirit that longs to advance in this world, as though traveling on a road, until the invisible one who stands in its way is made known to it.

Hence Peter rightly says: “The dumb animal, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s madness” (II Pet. II, 15). A madman is corrected by a mute beast of burden when the afflicted flesh reminds an exalted mind of the good of humility, which it ought to maintain.

Balaam did not obtain the gift of this correction, however, because, while proceeding to curse, he changed his voice but not his mind.

## CHAPTER XVII

“Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like theirs” (Num. XXIII, 10).

When perseverance in good works was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXXIII (No. 43), the following was added: “Let my soul die the death of the righteous,” etc.—

There are some within the holy Church who offer lengthy prayers to the Lord but do not possess the life of those who pray. They pursue heavenly promises in their petitions but flee from them in their works.

Sometimes they even experience tears in prayer, but when, after the time of prayer, pride strikes their minds, they immediately swell with the arrogance of self-exaltation. When avarice urges them, the flames of greedy thoughts at once boil over. When lust tempts them, they immediately pant after illicit desires. When anger advises them, the flame of madness quickly burns up the gentleness of their minds.

Thus, as we have said, they receive tears in prayer, but when their prayers are completed and they are struck by the suggestion of vices, they do not at all remember that they wept from desire for the eternal kingdom.

Balaam openly revealed this about himself. Seeing the tents of the righteous, he said: “Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like theirs” (Num. XXIII, 10). But when the time of compunction had passed, he offered counsel against the life of those to whom he had asked to be made like even in death. When he found an opportunity through avarice, he immediately forgot whatever he had wished for himself concerning innocence.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Again, the subject treated above.

In the *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, Chapter 30, Admonition 31:

“It must be carefully considered that, just as the wicked are often uselessly moved to compunction toward righteousness, so the good are often harmlessly tempted toward guilt. By a marvelous measure of inward disposition, according to the demands of their merits, it happens that some, while doing something good that they nevertheless do not complete, become proud amid the very evils they commit most fully.

Others, while being tempted by evil to which they in no way consent, are more truly established in righteousness through patience and humility precisely where they totter through weakness and frailty.

Balaam, looking upon the tents of the righteous, said: ‘Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like theirs’ (Num. XXIII, 10). But when the time of compunction withdrew, he gave counsel for the destruction of those to whom he had desired to be made like even in death. When he found the occasion of avarice, he immediately forgot the good of innocence that he had wished for himself.

Hence Paul says: ‘I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin that is in my members’ (Rom. VII, 23). He is certainly tempted so that, through knowledge of his own weakness, he may be strengthened more firmly in the good.

What, then, is the reason that one person is moved to compunction and yet does not draw near to righteousness, while another is tempted and yet is not defiled by guilt, except what is clearly demonstrated here: imperfect good does not help the wicked, and unfinished evil does not condemn the good” (*In the exposition of blessed Job*, Book XXXIII, No. 43).

Prayer has no weight of virtue when perseverance in continuous love does not hold it. In contrast, it is rightly said of Hannah while she wept: “And her face was no longer changed in different directions” (I Sam. I, 18), because after her prayers her mind did not lose through foolish merriment what it had sought during the time of prayer through the firmness of its groaning.

## CHAPTER XIX

Again, the subject treated above.

In the exposition of the Gospel, Homily 15 (No. 2):

“Many, when they hear a word against avarice, detest that same avarice and praise contempt for all things, but as soon as the mind sees something it desires, it forgets what it was praising.

Many, when they hear a word against lust, not only do not desire to commit bodily pollution but are even ashamed of what they have committed. Yet as soon as the appearance of the flesh comes before their eyes, the mind is carried away to desire as though it had never made any decision against those very desires, and it does what it condemned after remembering that it had done it.

Often we are also moved to compunction against our sins, yet after weeping we return to those same sins. Thus Balaam contemplated the tents of the Israelite people, wept, and asked to be made like them in death, saying: ‘Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like theirs’ (Num. XXIII, 10). But as soon as the hour of compunction had passed, he burned with the wickedness of avarice.

For the sake of promised gifts he gave counsel for the death of the people whose death he had desired to resemble, and he forgot what he had lamented because he refused to extinguish what burned within him through avarice.”

## CHAPTER XX

“Thus spoke the man whose eye was closed; thus spoke the hearer of the words of God, who saw the vision of the Almighty, who falls, and thus his eyes are opened” (Num. XXIV, 34).

When the praiseworthy foresight of the elect and the blindness to be avoided by the reprobate were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XV (No. 58), the following was added: “Thus spoke the man whose eye was closed,” etc.—

The wicked person does not know the evils he commits until he has already begun to be punished for those same evils. Balaam, for example, gave counsel against the Israelites, but afterward, in his punishment, he saw what he had previously committed through guilt.

The elect, however, foresee that they must not sin; their eyes are open before their fall. The unrighteous person opens his eyes after his fall, because after the guilt, in his punishment, he sees that he ought to have avoided the evil he committed.

## CHAPTER XXI

Again, the subject treated above.

[Col. 0772C]

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXVII (No. 59):

“Often certain people marvel at the eternal judgments, love the proclamations of the heavenly homeland when they hear them, and are astonished at the marvelous works of inward providence, yet by loving and living they neglect to rise toward those same works.

Thus they lie on the ground while contemplating God’s miracles: they weigh his power by knowing it but do not love it by living accordingly. Through contemplation they stretch their eyes toward consideration, yet through their intention they do not raise themselves from the earth.

Hence Balaam is reproached in these words: ‘Who, falling, has his eyes open.’ He had said many things about the coming of the Redeemer and foresaw what was to come in the last times, yet he refused by his life to rise toward the one whom he proclaimed in his foresight.

He had his eyes open while lying on the ground because prophecy lifted his mind toward heavenly things, while avarice held him on earth. He had his eyes open while lying down: he was able to see from above the one whom, prostrate in the depths, he did not love.”

## CHAPTER XXII

“Your dwelling is indeed strong, but if you place your nest in the rock,” etc. (Num. XXIV, 21).

[Col. 0772D]

When the fixed certainty of hope by which the elect adhere to God was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXXI (No. XCIV), the following was added: “Your dwelling is indeed strong,” etc.—

Cinaeus is interpreted as “possessor.” And who are those who possess present things except those skilled in the ingenuity of secular wisdom?

They truly build a strong dwelling for themselves in this world if, having become little in their own eyes through humility, they are nourished in the sublimity of Christ; if they regard themselves as weak and, recognized in lofty humility, place the confidence of their minds in the Redeemer; if they do not seek lowly things; if, with the flight of their hearts, they transcend everything that passes away.

Let us see how the holy man places his nest in the rock. For he says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. II, 6). And again: “He raised us up with him and made us sit with him in the heavenly places” (Eph. III, 21).

He places his nest in the rock because he fixes his purpose in heavenly things. He does not wish to cast his mind down into what is fleeting; he does not wish to dwell in lowly places through the degradation of human conduct.

Paul may perhaps have been held in prison when he testified that he was seated with Christ in the heavenly places. Yet he was where he had already fixed his ardent mind, not where the sluggish flesh that still necessarily held him remained.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“The land that the Lord struck before the children of Israel is a very fertile region for feeding animals; and we, your servants, possess very many beasts. We ask, if we have found favor in your sight, that you give it to us, your servants, as a possession, and do not make us cross the Jordan” (Num. XXXII, 4 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0773] Instead of “concerning reprobation,” as is read in Gemet. and Utic., Michael. has “concerning reproach.”]

When the reprobation of certain people placed within the Church, who held the faith not inwardly but only outwardly, was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXVII (Nos. 24–25), the following was added: “The land that the Lord struck before the children of Israel,” etc.—

There are some in the Church who disdain to be little and do not cease to be inwardly monstrous even in a position of humility. You will often see them exalted by honors, enjoying pleasures, and expanding through an abundance of possessions.

They often desire nothing so much as to rule over others; they rejoice to be feared by many; they neglect to live rightly but desire to possess the reputation of right living. They seek flatterers and swell with favor.

Because they are ready for present affairs, they do not seek future joys. When a multitude of activities occupies them, it shows that they are alien even to themselves.

Yet if some temptation against the faith arises, because they at least retain it outwardly, they defend it with words and labors, claim the heavenly homeland, and nevertheless do not love it.

The sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh aptly represent such people before Moses. Possessing many flocks and beasts, they desired outside the Jordan the plains they had seen and refused to have an inheritance in the land of promise, saying:

“The land that the Lord struck before the children of Israel is a very fertile region for feeding animals; and we, your servants, possess very many beasts. We ask, if we have found favor in your sight, that you give it to us, your servants, as a possession, and do not make us cross the Jordan.”

Those who possess very many beasts therefore refuse to cross the Jordan, because those whom many entanglements of the world occupy do not seek a dwelling in the heavenly homeland. Yet the faith that they hold only outwardly rebukes them, lest they grow sluggish through the pleasure of leisure and, by their example, weaken others in endurance of labor and perseverance.

Hence Moses says to them: “Will your brothers go to war while you sit here? Why do you overturn the minds of the children of Israel?” (Num. XXXII, 7).

But because they are ashamed not to defend what they confess, they hasten into battle for the very faith they profess, claiming it not for themselves but for their neighbors. Hence they say to Moses:

“We will build sheepfolds for the sheep and stalls for the beasts, and fortified cities for our little ones; but we ourselves, armed and equipped, will go forth to battle before the children of Israel” (ibid., 16).

They soon come forth as strong men on behalf of others, liberate the land of promise from its enemies, leave it, and return beyond the Jordan to feed their herds.

Many, although faithful, are occupied by present concerns and thus feed herds beyond the Jordan, because with their whole mind and every desire they serve perishable things against the faith of baptism.

Yet, as we have said, when a temptation against the faith arises, they gird themselves with the weapons of defense, overcome the enemies of the faith by slaughtering them, and do not love the inheritance of the land of promise—that is, the fruit of faith. Thus they fight for it while nevertheless placing their own children outside it.

Because they have little ones outside, they have no affection for dwelling in that land. Hence they return to the plains: they slide down from the lofty peaks of the mountains, as from hope in heavenly things, in order to nourish brute animals outside the land of promise.

They labor to feed irrational movements of the mind with empty desires. They do not know how great is the splendor of eternal light, because they are occupied with passing concerns; and while they grow proud over earthly matters, they close the entrance of heavenly light to themselves.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“That after the death of the high priest the killer is commanded to return to his own land” (Num. XXXV, 27–28).

[Col. 0774C]

When the absolution of the human race through the intervening sacrifice of Christ’s death was being discussed in Homily 6 on Ezekiel (No. 15), the following was added: “That after the death of the high priest,” etc.—

What does it mean that the killer returns to absolution after the death of the high priest, except that the human race, which by sinning inflicted death upon itself, received absolution from its guilt after the death of the true priest, namely, our Redeemer?

# BOOK FIVE

## On Testimonies in Deuteronomy

[Col. 0773]

## CHAPTER ONE

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deut. VI, 5).

Since the manner of loving God and one’s neighbor, and the exercise of that love, were being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book VII (No. 28), the following was added: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” etc.—There are two commandments of charity: love of God, namely, and love of one’s neighbor. Through love of God, love of one’s neighbor is begotten; and through love of one’s neighbor, love of God is nourished. For whoever neglects to love God certainly does not know how to love his neighbor. We therefore make fuller progress in the love of God if, within the embrace of that same love, we are first nourished by charity toward our neighbor.

[Note: [Col. 0773] Thus the Gemet and Utica manuscripts. We followed this reading in the *Book of Morals*. Michael’s manuscript has “we rejoice” (*laetamur*). The printed editions read “we are bound” (*ligamur*).]

Because love of God generates love of one’s neighbor, the Lord, when about to say through the Law, “You shall love your neighbor,” first said, “You shall love the Lord your God,” so that he might first fix the root of his love in the soil of our hearts, in order that brotherly love might afterward sprout through its branches. And again, because the love of God grows warm through love of one’s neighbor, John bears witness when he rebukes us, saying: “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God, whom he does not see?” Yet this divine love is born through fear, and as it grows in affection it is transformed.

Often, moreover, almighty God, so that it may become known how far each person is from his charity, or how much he has advanced in it, disposes everything in a wondrous order: he brings some low through scourges and supports others through success. And when he temporarily abandons certain people, he reveals what evil lies hidden in the hearts of others. For very often those who have honored us as happy beyond comparison persecute us when we ourselves are wretched. When someone is loved while established in prosperity, it is very uncertain whether prosperity or the person is being loved. The loss of happiness, however, tests the strength of love. Thus a certain Wise Man rightly says: “A friend is not recognized in prosperity, and an enemy is not hidden in adversity” (Ecclus. XII, 8). Prosperity does not, in fact, prove a friend, nor does adversity conceal an enemy, because the former is often concealed by respect for our prosperity, while the latter is exposed by the confidence adversity inspires.

## CHAPTER II.—“I will give rain to your land, early rain and late rain” (Deut. XI, 14).

When the preaching of the Old and New Testaments was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XX (No. 5), the following was added: “I will give rain to your land, early rain and late rain.”—What are we to understand here by rain, except the words of sacred preaching? We understand this in the case of the holy teachers, who were suspended from the preaching of Judea. Concerning them it is also written: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon her.” We are watered by the word of their holy preaching when, with true humility, we acknowledge the dryness of our heart. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “My soul is before you like land without water” (Ps. CXLII, 6). The prophet urges us to be filled with these streams of teaching, saying: “You who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. LV, 1).

Since we receive the words of sacred preaching at the world’s final age, we are watered, as it were, by late rain. This preaching of the late rain plainly proceeded to us from the sacrifice of him who says through the Psalmist: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL, 2). Because our Redeemer endured the force of his persecutors near the end of the world, he offered himself for us as an evening sacrifice.

Therefore, as the people of promise were about to enter the land, early and late rain was promised as a gift—a thing which we now see fulfilled spiritually. For he gave early rain because, in the former time, he bestowed understanding of the Law upon his elect; and he also granted late rain because he caused the mystery of his incarnation to be preached in the last days.

## CHAPTER III.—“Circumcise the foreskin of your heart” (Deut. X, 16).

[Col. 0775C]

When the cutting away of superfluous thoughts was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXVIII (No. 12), the following was added: “Circumcise the foreskin of your heart.”—What is signified by this circumcision of the foreskin except that, after extinguishing lust from the flesh, you must also cut away what is superfluous from your thought?

## CHAPTER IV.—“You shall not plow with the firstborn of your ox, and you shall not shear the firstborn of your sheep” (Deut. XV, 19).

When the avoidance of ostentation at the beginning of a good work was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book VII (Nos. 78, 79), the following was added: “You shall not plow with the firstborn of your ox,” etc.—What did Moses prohibit by this example of prohibition except that he forbade those beginning a virtuous life to exercise it in worldly occupations? To plow with the firstborn of an ox is to display the beginnings of a good way of life in public activity. To shear the firstborn of sheep is to strip our beginning good works of the covering of their concealment and expose them to human eyes.
