We are therefore forbidden to work with the firstborn of an ox and restrained from shearing the firstborn of sheep, because, even if we begin something vigorous, we ought not immediately to exercise it openly; and when our life begins something simple and innocent, it is fitting that it not abandon the veils of its secrecy, lest it display itself naked to human eyes, as though its fleece had been removed.

Let the firstborn of oxen and sheep therefore be used only for divine sacrifices, so that whatever strong, simple, and innocent thing we begin, we may sacrifice it in honor of the inward Judge upon the altar of our heart. Without doubt, he accepts it all the more willingly when, hidden from human beings and stained by no desire for praise, it remains undefiled.

Often, however, the beginnings of a new way of life are still mixed with the carnal life; and for that reason they ought not be made known too quickly, lest, when the good things that please are praised, the mind, deceived by its own praise, be unable to detect in them the evils that lie hidden.

## CHAPTER V.—Also, concerning the foregoing.

In the *Exposition of Ezekiel*, Homily 2:—We understand the firstborn of an ox as the good work of the weakness belonging to the earliest period of our life. Yet one must not plow with it, because, when we are in the first years of adolescence or youth, we must still refrain from preaching, so that the plowshare of our tongue may not dare to furrow the soil of another’s heart.

For as long as we are weak, we must restrain ourselves among ourselves, lest, by displaying tender virtues too quickly, we lose them. Trees planted in the ground, if they have not first taken root, quickly wither when touched by a hand; but if they have once fixed their roots, a hand touches them without causing harm. Winds push them, yet the pushing does not injure them. Walls that have been built are pulled down if pushed, unless they have first been dried by their own moisture.

Thus, until the mind has been completely dried of the moisture of its perversity, it ought not to be touched by the hand of another’s tongue, lest, before it has fully taken hold, it lose its firmness; lest, struck, it fall; lest, like a tree without roots, it wither while being shaken by gusts stronger than it can endure. Therefore only what is firm should be displayed as an example. The mind must first grow strong and then be shown for the benefit of its neighbors, once it can neither fall when elevated by praise nor wither when struck by reproach.

For although it is said to Timothy, “Command and teach these things; let no one despise your youth” (1 Tim. IV, 12), it must be understood that his youth lay in years, not in conduct. Although in sacred language youth is sometimes called adolescence. Hence it is written: “Rejoice, young man, in your adolescence” (Eccl. XI, 9).

## CHAPTER VI.—“You shall not appear before the Lord empty-handed” (Deut. XVI, 16).

When, through the cessation of passing things, the enduring practice of good works was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book VII (No. 38), the following was added: “You shall not appear before the Lord empty-handed.”—He appears empty before the Lord who carries with him nothing from the fruit of his labor. One person burns with the multiplication of his possessions; another pants after winning praise. But because everyone abandons all these things when he dies, he appears empty before the Lord, since he has brought nothing with him before the Judge.

We are therefore salutarily admonished by the Law, which says: “You shall not appear before the Lord empty-handed.” Whoever does not provide, by doing good, for the reward of life that is to be won appears empty before the Lord. Hence the Psalmist says of the righteous: “They shall come, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV, 6). They come carrying sheaves to the examination of judgment who display in themselves the right works by which they may merit life.

## CHAPTER VII.—“You shall justly execute what is just” (Deut. XVI, 20).

When the preservation of uprightness of mind in the performance of a work was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book IX (No. 38), the following was added: “You shall justly execute what is just.”—He unjustly executes what is just who is aroused to defend justice not by zeal for virtue but by love of temporal reward. He unjustly executes what is just who is not at all afraid to sell the very justice he pretends to uphold. To execute what is just justly, therefore, is, in asserting justice, to seek that same justice.

## CHAPTER VIII.—“If someone goes with his friend into the forest simply to cut wood, and the wood escapes from the hand of the ax, and the iron slips from the handle, strikes his friend, and kills him, he shall flee to one of the cities mentioned above and live there, lest perhaps the nearest relative of the one whose blood was shed, urged on by grief, pursue him, seize him, and strike his life” (Deut. XIX, 5).

When the measure to be observed in rebuking one’s neighbor was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book X, the following was added: “If someone goes with his friend into the forest simply to cut wood,” etc.—We go into the forest with a friend whenever we turn with some neighbor to examine our faults. We cut wood simply when we remove the vices of delinquents with a devout intention.

But the ax escapes from the hand when rebuke drives itself into harshness beyond what is necessary; and the iron leaps from the handle when a word in correction exceeds the proper measure in severity. It strikes and kills the friend when an insult that has been uttered kills its hearer by driving him away from the spirit of love. For the mind of one who is rebuked suddenly falls into hatred if immoderate rebuke subjects it to more than it ought to bear.

But the one who carelessly strikes the wood and extinguishes his neighbor must flee to three cities so that he may live, protected, in one of them. For if, turning to the lamentation of repentance, he hides within the unity of the sacrament under hope, faith, and charity, he is not held guilty of the homicide he committed; and the relative of the slain man, even when he finds him, does not kill him.

For when the strict Judge comes—he who joined himself to us through sharing our nature—he will unquestionably not demand vengeance for the guilt from one whom hope, faith, and charity have hidden beneath his pardon. A fault is therefore forgiven more quickly when it is committed without the purpose of malice.

[Note: [Col. 0777D] In the Utica manuscript three chapters are added here which are absent from the Gemet and Michael manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER IX.—“If, while walking along the road, you find a bird’s nest in a tree or on the ground, with the mother sitting above the young or the eggs, you shall not take her with her offspring; you shall let her go, keeping the young for yourself, so that it may be well with you and you may live for a long time” (Deut. XXII, 6).

[Note: [Col. 0778D] Michael indicates Homily 9 on Ezekiel. These passages are not found in Gregory.]

When the distinction to be observed between allegory and history was being discussed, the following was added: “If, while walking along the road, you find a bird’s nest in a tree or on the ground,” etc.—We walk along the road because we journey through the present life. A bird’s nest in a tree or on the ground exists when the words of the history concern either the contemplative life or the active life. The precepts of the active life are a bird’s nest on the ground; the precepts of the contemplative life are a nest in a tree.

The mother sits over the young or the eggs when the history itself produces spiritual understanding: in some matters it speaks fully, as though bringing forth young; in others it conveys its meaning in such a way that it still leads the reader’s mind toward higher things, as though it still held eggs beneath itself from which it will produce young. Eggs are laid for this very reason: so that young may be produced from them.

There are also matters of the contemplative life that appear for now through certain images, so that afterward they may be seen as they are, through their own power and nature. Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. XIII, 12). When the blind man, through the laying on of the Redeemer’s hands, had already begun to receive light, he was asked what he saw and replied: “I see people like trees walking” (Mark VIII, 24). A human being is rational by nature, whereas a tree is neither sentient nor living. What does this blind man, once enlightened, signify except the human race? When the Lord opened the eyes of its contemplation, it first saw certain things in an enigma, so that afterward it might be able to behold the true and rational heavenly hosts as they are.

Hence it is added there: “Then he again laid his hands upon his eyes, and he began to see, and was restored so that he saw everything clearly.” First, therefore, he saw through a mirror by resemblance, so that afterward he might see clearly in perfection.

In these words, then, the mother bird sits upon eggs with respect to the contemplative life, because sacred history, beginning with an enigmatic indication, conveys something through which it afterward produces living young by revealing it more certainly.

The apostle Paul, moreover, when he learned that some people were living continently, admonished them, saying: “But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (1 Cor. VII, 2). Since a wife ought to be taken only for the sake of producing children, he granted married couples something from which they could still rise to better things, lest anyone fall into the guilt of fornication. He who granted this—something by which the minds of married couples could be led even to lawful fault—placed eggs, as it were, as a mother bird on the ground, that is, history in the active life.

The holy preachers themselves also desire God to be loved more than feared; but if they do not instill fear, they do not lead people to love. Hence they customarily speak first of terrifying things and afterward of sweet ones, as the Psalmist says: “They shall speak of the power of your terrors, and they shall tell of your greatness” (Ps. CXLIV, 6). Then it follows: “They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness.” When they terrify in order to provoke love, they lay eggs. Perfect love casts out fear, because the young begin to live when they no longer succumb to fear (1 John IV, 18).

The Law itself also laid eggs when it said: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exod. XXI, 24). But afterward it produced young when it said: “You shall not seek revenge, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens” (Lev. XIX, 18).

It must be noted, however, what is said about this mother of the young: “You shall not take her with her offspring; you shall let her go, keeping the young for yourself.” In certain passages, history must indeed be passed over, so that only the young of the mother—that is, the meaning of spiritual understanding—may come to us as food; and it is not the mother but the young that must refresh us. We ought not to be satisfied by the example of history but by the spiritual meanings of its understanding.

When we read that the Israelite people deceitfully obtained the gold and silver of the Egyptians, and when again we read that carnal sacrifices were offered to almighty God, what is present in this nest of words except that the mother must be released and the young kept? When we draw intellectual vigilance from secular people in defense of the truth and turn their eloquence to the use of righteousness, what else are we doing than taking gold and silver from the Egyptians? Thus we become rich, while they may be shown to be poor. As it is written: “Bringing every understanding into captivity in obedience to Christ” (2 Cor. X, 6).

And when we subdue our bodies through abstinence, what else are we doing than offering carnal sacrifices to almighty God? As Paul says again: “That you may present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Rom. XII, 1).

We therefore eat the young while releasing the mother when we leave aside the examples of history but retain in our mind the meanings of its allegories. The verse rightly adds: “So that it may be well with you and you may live for a long time,” because the one who grasps the years of eternity through spiritual understanding lives for a long time.

## CHAPTER X.—“You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together” (Deut. XXII, 10).

When the avoidance of association with unskilled teachers was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book I (No. 23), the following was added: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together.”—A person is forbidden to plow with an ox and an ass together, as though it were plainly said: Do not join fools with the wise in preaching, lest the one who is unable to fulfill the task obstruct the one who is capable.

## CHAPTER XI.—“You shall not wear a garment woven from wool and linen together” (Deut. XXII, 11).

[Col. 0778D]

When the avoidance of the vice of duplicity was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book VIII (No. 87), the following was added: “You shall not wear a garment woven from wool and linen together.”—What is signified by this garment except the person of hypocrites, who display kindness toward their neighbors while concealing their own iniquity beneath it? In everything they do or say, they outwardly exhibit simplicity, but inwardly they possess the cunning of duplicity. They feign purity on the surface, but always hide malice beneath the appearance of purity.

Wool signifies simplicity; linen signifies subtlety. A garment made of wool and linen plainly hides the linen inside while displaying the wool on the surface. Therefore, he wears a garment woven from wool and linen who, in his speech or action, covers inwardly the subtlety of malice and displays outwardly the simplicity of innocence. Since cunning cannot be detected beneath the appearance of purity, the linen lies hidden, as it were, beneath the coarseness of wool.

## CHAPTER XII.—Also, concerning the foregoing.

In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book VIII (No. 87):—We know that wool is thick and greasy, whereas linen is fine. A garment made of wool and linen always displays the wool on the surface and conceals the linen underneath. What, then, is signified by wool except simplicity, and what by linen except subtlety? Often a subtle and clever person outwardly displays the simplicity of gentleness while inwardly concealing the subtlety of malice. Such a person clothes himself in an action made, as it were, of wool and linen when simplicity is shown by him on the surface while the subtlety of malice is preserved in his mind.

## CHAPTER XIII.—“If there is among you a man who has been polluted by a nocturnal emission, he shall go outside the camp and shall not return before washing himself with water in the evening; after sunset he shall return to the camp” (Deut. XXIII, 10).

[Col. 0779B]

When the cleansing of illicit thought was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book IX (No. 84), the following was added: “If there is among you a man,” etc.—What is signified here by a nocturnal dream except a hidden temptation, through which something shameful is conceived in the heart by a dark thought but is not completed in bodily action?

A person polluted by a nocturnal dream is therefore commanded to go outside the camp, because it is fitting that one polluted by an unclean thought consider himself unworthy of the fellowship of all the faithful. Let him place the merit of his fault before his eyes and despise himself in comparison with the good. To go outside the camp while polluted is for one struggling with a shameful assault to regard himself with contempt in comparison with the continent.

He washes with water in the evening when, seeing his own failure, he turns to the lamentation of repentance, so that through tears he may wash away everything that hidden pollution accuses in his soul. But after sunset he must return to the camp, because, when the heat of temptation has cooled, he must again take confidence in fellowship with the good.

After water, when the sun has set, he returns to the camp who, after the lamentation of repentance, when the flame of illicit thought has grown cold, is restored to confidence in the merits of the faithful, so that he no longer considers himself far from the others, rejoicing that he has been cleansed through the death of his inward ardor.

## CHAPTER XIV.—“When someone goes out to relieve himself, he shall carry a peg on his belt and dig a hole in the ground, concealing what has been expelled” (Deut. XXIII, 12).

When the stains of hidden temptation were being washed away through the grace of compunction, the following was added in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXXI (No. 54): “When someone goes out to relieve himself,” etc.—Burdened by the weight of corruptible nature, certain superfluities of thought burst forth from the womb of our mind, like the burdens of the belly. But we must carry a peg beneath our belt, so that, always girded to rebuke ourselves, we may have near us a sharp goad of compunction. It must continually pierce the soil of our mind with the pain of repentance and conceal what bursts forth from us with foulness.

The discharge of the belly is covered with earth in a hole dug by the peg when the superfluity of our mind, examined by subtle reproof, is hidden from God’s eyes through the goad of its own compunction.

## CHAPTER XV.—“If a man takes a wife and has her, but she does not find favor in his eyes because of some disgrace, he shall write a bill of divorce, put it in her hand, and send her away from his house” (Deut. XXIV, 1).

When the postponement of concern for transitory matters for the sake of spiritual benefit was being discussed, the following was added: “If a man takes a wife,” etc.—

[Note: [Col. 0779D] Michael indicates Book V of the *Exposition of Job*; other manuscripts indicate Book XIII. We have found it in neither.]

It is exceedingly necessary that concern for the present life be firmly subdued, lest it perhaps gain mastery. And once earthly activity has been rejected, it must not be taken up again, lest the one who seemed to have put his hand to the plow look back.

Hence Moses says: “If a man takes a wife and has her, but she does not find favor in his eyes because of some disgrace, he shall write a bill of divorce, put it in her hand, and send her away from his house. And when she has gone out and married another husband, and he too hates her and gives her a bill of divorce and sends her away from his house, or certainly when he has died, the first husband may not take her again as his wife, because she has been defiled.”

Here it is plainly evident that the force of the command, according to the letter, lacks rational coherence. Since the Truth says that a wife may not be sent away except on account of fornication (Matt. V), it is not without guilt that she is dismissed because of disgrace.

But a man takes a wife when he undertakes responsibility for earthly activity. If he recognizes its disgrace, he gives it a bill of divorce and sends it away from his house, because earthly activity was often loved intensely before it was possessed; but once possessed, its disgrace is recognized, when it appears to have been defiled by sins.

Let the husband therefore send it away from his house, so that he may cast its love from his mind. Once it has gone out, it takes another husband, because another desires the earthly activity that you have abandoned. But perhaps it will eventually become hateful even to him, so that he may usefully dismiss it.

The words “he has sent her away, or certainly he has died” are rightly added, because each person either dismisses earthly concern or dies: either he does not inwardly succumb to it, or he utterly succumbs to it at the cost of the soul’s life.

Whether, then, the husband who follows it dismisses it or dies, the first husband may not take it again as his wife, because it has been defiled. In other words, once someone has abandoned concern for earthly things and the interests of the present life, he must in no way return to them, since he has already defiled himself by his own judgment if he first abandoned them because he recognized them to be defiled.

## CHAPTER XVI.—“You shall not take as a pledge the upper or lower millstone” (Deut. XXIV, 6).

[Col. 0780C]

When the measure teachers should observe in preaching concerning the confession of erring neighbors was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXXIII (No. 24), the following was added: “You shall not take as a pledge the upper millstone,” etc.—Sometimes we use “take” to mean “take away.” Hence those birds that are greedy for seizing other birds are called *accipitres*, “hawks.” Paul likewise says: “For you endure it if someone devours you, if someone takes” (2 Cor. II, 20)—as though he said, “if someone robs.”

A pledge is the confession of a sinner who is in debt. A pledge is taken from a debtor when a confession of sin is already received from a sinner. The upper and lower millstones are hope and fear. Hope lifts the heart upward, while fear presses it downward. But the upper and lower millstones are necessarily joined together, so that one is useless without the other.

Hope and fear must therefore continually be joined in the sinner’s breast, because he hopes for mercy in vain if he does not also fear justice; and he fears justice in vain if he does not also have confidence in mercy.

The upper or lower millstone is therefore forbidden to be taken as a pledge, because the person who preaches to a sinner must arrange his preaching with such discretion that, without abandoning hope, he does not remove fear, and, without removing hope, he does not leave the sinner in fear alone. The upper or lower millstone is taken away when, through the preacher’s tongue, either fear is separated from hope or hope from fear in the sinner’s heart.

[Note: [Col. 0779D] This chapter and the three immediately following it are absent from the Utica and Gemet manuscripts. In Michael’s manuscript it appears as Chapter 18, with the others omitted.]

## CHAPTER XVII.—“When your brother owes you something, and you have taken a pledge from him, return the pledge to him before sunset” (Deut. XXIV, 10 ff.).

When the forgiveness of an injury committed by one’s neighbors, especially those who ask pardon, was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XVI (No. 6), the following was added: “When your brother owes you something,” etc.—Our brother becomes our debtor whenever some neighbor is shown to have offended against us. We call sins “debts.” Hence it is said of the sinful servant: “I forgave you all that debt” (Matt. XVIII, 32). And every day in the Lord’s Prayer we ask: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12).

We take a pledge from our debtor when, from one who is known to have sinned against us, we receive his confession of sin, through which we are asked to release the sin committed against us. Whoever admits the sin he has committed and asks forgiveness has already given, as it were, a pledge for the debt.

We are commanded to return this pledge before sunset because, before the sun of justice sets in us through the pain of the heart, we ought to return to him the confession of forgiveness from whom we receive the confession of guilt. Thus the person who remembers that he has offended against us may immediately feel from us that his offense has been forgiven.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—“The surviving brother shall take the wife of his brother who died without children and raise up a son in the name of his brother. But if he refuses to take her, the woman shall spit in his face; then his kinsman shall remove one of his shoes from his foot, and his house shall be called the house of the barefooted man” (Deut. XXV, 5).

[Col. 0781B]

When the gift of governance was being discussed as something that must not be withheld, the following was added in the *Pastoral Rule*, Part I (Chapter 5): “The surviving brother shall take the wife of his brother who died without children,” etc.—The dead brother is the one who, appearing after the glory of the resurrection, said: “Go, announce it to my brothers” (Matt. XXVIII, 10). He died, as it were, without children because he has not yet completed the number of his elect.

The surviving brother is therefore commanded to take this man’s wife, because it is plainly fitting that responsibility for the holy Church be imposed upon one who is capable of governing her well.

When he refuses, the woman spits in his face, because whoever does not take care to benefit others from the gifts he has received is reproached by the holy Church even with the gifts he possesses, and she casts saliva, as it were, into his face. His shoe is removed from one foot, so that his house may be called the house of the barefooted man.

For it is written: “With your feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace” (Eph. VI, 16). If, therefore, we care for our neighbor as we care for ourselves, we protect both feet with shoes. But whoever considers his own advantage and neglects that of his neighbors loses, with disgrace, the shoe from one foot, as it were.

## CHAPTER XIX.—“Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words from my mouth” (Deut. XXXII, 1).

In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book II (No. 51), the following was added: “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak,” etc.—By “heaven” he signifies the order of those set over others, and by “earth” the people subject to them. “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak”; for he was not speaking to an insensible but to a rational creature.

## CHAPTER XX.—“He spread out his wings and took him up” (Deut. XXXII, 11).

In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXXII (No. 7), the following was added: “He spread out his wings and took him up.”—When the Lord protects us little ones, he nourishes us; and he refreshes us with a protection that is light and gentle, not heavy and burdensome. When he extends his mercies over us, he stretches his wings over us, as birds do.

## CHAPTER XXI.—“They sucked honey from the rock and oil from the hard rock” (Deut. XXXII, 13).

When the opening of mysteries through Christ’s coming, and the merits of his faithful, was being discussed in Homily 2 on the Gospels (Nos. III, 4), the following was added: “They sucked honey from the rock and oil from the hard rock.”—Nothing of this kind is ever read according to the historical sense if the entire sequence of the Old Testament is reviewed. That people never sucked honey from a rock, nor oil. But because, in Paul’s words, “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X, 1), they sucked honey from the rock who saw the deeds and miracles of that same Redeemer of ours.

They sucked oil from the hard rock because, after his resurrection, they deserved to be anointed through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. He gave honey, as it were, in the hard rock when the Lord, still mortal, showed his disciples the sweetness of his miracles.

[Note: [Col. 0781D] Gussanville: “Into the sweetness of their eyes”—a very serious error.]

But the hard rock poured forth oil because, after his resurrection, having become impassible, he caused the gift of holy anointing to flow forth through the affliction of the Spirit.

Concerning this oil the prophet says: “The yoke shall rot before the face of the oil” (Isa. X, 27). We were held beneath the yoke of demonic domination, but we were anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit; and because the grace of freedom anointed us, the yoke of demonic domination rotted away.

## CHAPTER XXII.—“A fire has been kindled by my anger, and it shall burn down to the depths of hell; it shall consume the earth and its produce” (Deut. XXXII, 22).

When the perpetual punishment of those who offend without correction was being discussed in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XVIII (No. 35), the following was added: “A fire has been kindled by my anger,” etc.—Concerning those whom scourges condemn but do not free, it is written: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept correction” (Jer. V, 3). For such people the scourges begin in this life and continue in eternal punishment.

Hence the Lord says through Moses: “A fire has been kindled by my anger, and it shall burn down to the depths of hell.” With regard to present punishment, it is rightly said: “A fire has been kindled by my anger.” With regard to eternal damnation, it is appropriately added immediately: “And it shall burn down to the depths of hell.”

Some customarily say what is written: “God does not judge twice for the same thing” (Nahum I, 9). Yet they do not consider what is said elsewhere by the prophet concerning the wicked: “Crush them with a double crushing” (Jer. XVII, 18). Nor do they consider what is written elsewhere: “Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, destroyed a second time those who did not believe” (Jude 5).

If we grant assent to these passages insofar as they mean that no fault can be struck twice, this must be understood of those who are struck because of sin and die in their sin: their striking begins here and is completed there. Thus, for those who are not corrected, there is one scourge—one that begins in time but is completed in eternal punishments—so that, for those who entirely refuse correction, the striking of present scourges is already the beginning of the torments to come.

It follows: “It shall consume the earth and its produce” (in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXI, No. 19). Fire consumes the earth and its produce when lust consumes the flesh and, through the flesh, all good works. For whatever emerges from the harvest of righteousness, the flame of corruption inevitably burns up.

[Note: [Col. 0782D] We have not found this chapter in the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XXIII.—“Are not these things stored up with me and sealed in my treasuries? On the day of vengeance I will repay them” (Deut. XXXII, 34–35).

(*Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XII, No. 21, near the beginning.)—Our sins are marked, as it were, in a purse, because what we do outwardly, unless we wash it away through repentance, is kept hidden within the secrecy of God’s judgments under a certain concealment, so that one day it may emerge from the seal of secrecy into the public judgment.

Hence Moses also says: “Are not these things stored up with me and sealed in my treasuries? On the day of vengeance I will repay them.” But when, for the evils we have committed, we are worn down by the scourge of discipline and lament them through repentance, he both marks and heals our iniquity, because he neither leaves it here unpunished nor reserves it for punishment at the judgment.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—“I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I myself heal” (Deut. XXXII, 39).

When the purification of the elect and the regard owed to divine grace were being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 6 (no. 42), the following was added: “I kill, etc.” — The almighty God wounds those whom he takes care to restore to salvation in two ways. Sometimes he strikes the flesh and dissolves the hardness of the mind through fear of him. By wounding, he recalls them to salvation when he afflicts his elect outwardly so that they may live inwardly. Rightly, therefore, he speaks through Moses, saying: “I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal.” He kills in order to give life; he strikes in order to heal. For this reason he inflicts blows outwardly, so that inwardly he may cure the wounds of sins.

Sometimes, however, even when outward chastisements seem to cease, he inflicts wounds inwardly, because he strikes the hardness of our mind with desire for him; yet by striking he heals, because, pierced by the dart of his fear, he recalls us to an awareness of righteousness. Our hearts are unhealthy when they are wounded by no love of God, when they do not feel the distress of their exile, and when they do not languish with even the slightest feeling for the weakness of their neighbor. But they are wounded in order to be healed, because God strikes insensible minds with the arrows of his love and immediately makes them sensitive through the ardor of charity.

## CHAPTER XXV

“And my sword shall devour flesh” (no. 42).

[Col. 0783B]

When the final striking down of those living according to the flesh was being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 18 (no. 20), the following was added: “And my sword shall devour flesh.” — The sword of God consumes flesh because, at the final judgment, his sentence kills those who think according to the flesh.

## CHAPTER XXVI

“In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deut. 33:2).

When the grace of love for the divine commandments impressed upon the hearts of the elect was being discussed, in Homily 30 on the Gospel (no. 5), the following was added: “In his right hand was a fiery law.” — What is meant by the left except the reprobate, who are also to be placed on the left? The elect, however, are called God’s right hand. Therefore, in God’s right hand there is a fiery law, because the elect do not hear the heavenly commandments with a cold heart; rather, they burn toward them with the torches of their deepest love. The word is brought to the ear, and their mind, angered against itself, is consumed by the flame of inward sweetness.

## CHAPTER XXVII

“He who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize them,’ and who did not know his own sons: these have guarded your word and kept your covenant” (Deut. 33:9).

[Col. 0783C]

When the love of God, which must be preferred to love of one’s neighbors, and the manner in which they should be loved with carefully measured compassion, were being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 7 (nos. 41–42), the following was added: “He who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ etc.” — The person who desires to know God more intimately desires, out of love for piety, not to know those whom he knew according to the flesh. For divine knowledge is seriously diminished if it is shared with knowledge of the flesh. Therefore everyone must become detached from relatives and close associates if he wishes to be joined more truly to the parent of all, so that he may love with greater firmness those whom he vigorously neglects for God’s sake, since in them he no longer recognizes the unstable affection of a carnal bond.

Certainly, in temporal matters we ought to benefit more than others those to whom we are more closely joined, because a flame also carries fire to things brought near it; yet it first burns the very place where it arises. We ought to acknowledge the bond of earthly kinship, but nonetheless, when it obstructs the course of the mind, to disregard it, so that the faithful soul, kindled by devotion to God, neither despises those joined to it in the lowest things nor, while rightly ordering these within itself, fails to transcend them through love of higher things.

Therefore we must take vigilant care lest affection of the flesh steal upon us and turn the step of the heart away from the right path, lest it impede the force of heavenly love and press the rising mind downward beneath a weight laid upon it. Thus each person ought to sympathize with the needs of relatives in such a way that compassion does not allow the force of his intention to be impeded: the feeling should fill the inward parts of the mind, but should not turn it away from its spiritual purpose.

For holy men do not fail to love their bodily relatives when they provide what is necessary for them; rather, through love of spiritual things they overcome that very affection within themselves. Thus they moderate it by the rule of discernment, so that through it they do not deviate even slightly from the right path. The cows aptly signify this for us: they went toward the hills beneath the ark of the Lord, advancing at once with affection and with firm resolve. When they had shut their calves inside, it is written: “They went and lowed,” uttering lowings from their inmost parts, yet not turning their steps away from the journey they had begun (1 Sam. 6:10).

## CHAPTER XXVIII

“Iron and bronze are his footwear” (Deut. 33:25).

When the preaching of the holy Church was being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 34 (no. 19), the following was added: “Iron and bronze are his footwear.” — This is said by Moses figuratively of the holy Church. In Sacred Scripture, footwear signifies the protection of preaching, as it is written: “With your feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace” (Eph. 6:15). Therefore, because strength is expressed by iron and perseverance by bronze, it is said that iron and bronze are his footwear: his preaching is fortified both by sharpness and by steadfastness. Through iron it penetrates hostile evils; through bronze it patiently preserves the good that it has undertaken.

# INTO THE BOOK OF JOSHUA

[Col. 0783]

## CHAPTER ONE

“Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, sitting upon a donkey, sighed; and her father said to her, ‘What do you have?’ She answered him, ‘Give me a blessing. You have given me a southern land, dry land; join to it also a watered land.’ And her father gave her an upper water-source and a lower water-source” (Josh. 15:19).

[Col. 0783D]

When the distinct kinds of compunction were being discussed, in the Dialogues, book 3 (chapter 34), the following was added: “Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, sitting upon a donkey, sighed, etc.” — [Note: The same passage should be read in book 7, indiction 15, letter 26, formerly book 6, letter 23.] Achsah sits upon a donkey when the soul presides over the irrational movements of its flesh. Sighing, she asks her father for watered land, because the grace of tears must be sought from our Creator with profound groaning.

There are indeed some who have already received the gift of speaking freely on behalf of justice, protecting the oppressed, distributing what they possess to the needy, and possessing the ardor of faith, but who still do not have the grace of tears. Such people have southern and arid land, but still need watered land, because, established in good works—in which they are great and fervent—they ought also to lament, either from fear of punishment or from love of the heavenly kingdom, the evils they previously committed.

Although compunction is divided into many forms, since each separate sin is mourned by penitents—for which reason Jeremiah also says in the voice of penitents, “My eye has brought down divisions of waters” (Lam. 3:48)—there are nevertheless principally two kinds of compunction, because the soul thirsting for God is first pierced by fear and afterward by love.

At first it afflicts itself with tears because, when it remembers its evils, it fears suffering eternal punishments for them. But when the fear has been consumed by a long anxiety of sorrow, a certain confidence in the presumption of pardon arises, and the spirit is inflamed with love of heavenly joys. The one who previously wept lest he be led to punishment afterward begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom.

The mind beholds what the choirs of angels are, what the fellowship of blessed spirits is, and what the majesty of the eternal vision of God is; and it weeps more because it is absent from everlasting goods than it wept earlier when it feared eternal evils. Thus perfect compunction of fear hands the soul over to compunction of love.

This is well portrayed in the figurative narrative of this sacred and truthful history. Since, as I have said, there are two kinds of compunction, her father gave her an upper water-source and a lower water-source. The soul receives the upper water-source when it afflicts itself with tears out of desire for the heavenly kingdom. It receives the lower water-source when it fears the punishments of hell and weeps over them.

The lower water-source is indeed given first, and afterward the upper. But because compunction arising from love surpasses the other in dignity, it was necessary to mention the upper water-source first and the lower afterward.

## CHAPTER TWO

“The Canaanite dwelt in the midst of Ephraim as a tributary” (Josh. 16:10).

When the training of the elect through certain reprehensible actions, retained within them for the benefit of nourishing humility, though not yet subdued, was being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 4 (no. 44), the following was added: “The Canaanite dwelt in the midst of Ephraim as a tributary.” — Often those who already shine with great virtues, while still retaining something from the darkness of sin, are made to shine with the great brightness of their life and yet unwillingly drag along the remnants of night. This is done, as has been said, so that the mind progressing toward the virtue of justice may be strengthened more effectively by its own weakness, and may shine more truly in good works precisely where small reprehensible faults, even against its will, humbly obscure it.

Hence, when the promised land was divided among the Israelite people, it is rightly said that the Canaanite, a gentile people, was not killed but made tributary to the tribe of Ephraim. For it is written: “The Canaanite dwelt in the midst of Ephraim as a tributary.”

What does the Canaanite, that is, the gentile people, signify except vice? Often we enter the promised land through great virtues, because we are strengthened by an inward hope of eternity. But when, amid sublime deeds, we retain certain small vices, we allow the Canaanite to live in our land, as it were. Yet he is made tributary to us, because we humbly turn to our own advantage the very vice that we cannot subject completely.

Thus the mind feels what is base in itself even in the highest matters, since by its own strength it cannot conquer even the small things it desires to conquer. Hence it is also written: “These are the nations whom the Lord left, so that through them he might instruct Israel” (Judg. 3:1). Certain small vices are retained in us for this purpose: that our vigilant intention may continually exercise itself in combat and not grow proud of victory, since it sees enemies still living within it, whom it fears it may yet fail to overcome.

Israel is therefore instructed while the nations are kept in reserve, when the elation of our virtue is restrained by certain small vices and, through the little things that resist it, learns that it cannot subdue greater things by its own power.

# BOOK SIX  
## On Testimonies for the Book of Judges

[Col. 0785]

## CHAPTER ONE

“When Gideon was threshing wheat from the chaff, he saw an angel; at his command he immediately cooked a kid, placed it upon a rock, and poured broth over it. The angel touched it with his staff, and fire coming out of the rock consumed it” (Judg. 6:11 ff.).

[Col. 0785B]

[Col. 0785C] When the firm intention of mind with which the perfect adhere to their pursuits was being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 3 (no. 59), the following was added: “When Gideon was threshing wheat from the chaff, etc.” — What does it mean to strike wheat with a staff except to separate, by the uprightness of judgment, the grains of virtue from the chaff of vices?

But an angel appears to those doing this, because the more diligently people cleanse themselves from outward things, the more clearly the Lord announces inward things to them. He commands the kid to be killed—that is, every appetite of our flesh to be sacrificed—and the flesh to be placed upon the rock and its broth to be poured over it.

What else does the rock signify except the one of whom Paul says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4)? We place flesh upon the rock when we mortify our body in imitation of Christ. The person who pours the broth of the flesh over it is one who, in the way of life of Christ, has emptied himself even of carnal thoughts. For the liquid broth from flesh is poured upon the rock, as it were, when the mind is emptied of the flow of carnal thoughts.

Then the angel touches these things with his staff, because the power of divine assistance never abandons our intention. Fire comes out of the rock and consumes the broth and the flesh, because the Spirit breathed forth by the Redeemer burns our heart with such a flame of compunction that it consumes everything unlawful in it, whether in deed or thought.

The perfect mind watches carefully so that it may not only refuse to do perverse things, but also wipe away everything that melts shamefully within it through its thoughts.

## CHAPTER II

“On Gideon’s battle against the Midianites” (Judg. 7:5, 6, 16, 17).

When the prefigured incarnation of the Redeemer and the miracles of his elect were being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 30 (no. 73), the following was added: “On Gideon’s battle against the Midianites.” — When Gideon was leading a large army into battle, he was commanded by divine instruction to come to the river and remove from the battle all whom he saw drinking water on bent knees. It happened that only three hundred men remained, those who had drunk the water standing and using their hands.

With these he went to battle, arming them not with weapons but with trumpets, lamps, and jars. For, as it is written there: “They placed the lighted lamps inside the little jars, held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left, and, coming close to their enemies, they sounded the trumpets and broke the little jars; the lamps appeared, and the enemies, terrified on one side by the sound of the trumpets and on the other by the flashing of the lamps, were put to flight” (no. 72).

Of this battle the prophet says: “You have broken the yoke of his burden, and the rod of his shoulder, and the scepter of his oppressor, as on the day of Midian” (Isa. 9:4). In rescuing the gentiles, the Lord overcame their yoke of burden when, by his coming, he freed them from the slavery of demonic tyranny. He overcame the rod of their shoulder when the Redeemer restrained from the human race the blows of that tyranny, which had weighed heavily upon it because of evil works. He overcame the scepter of its oppressor when he destroyed in the hearts of the faithful the kingdom of that devil who, because of the pestilence of sins committed, had been accustomed to exact the due tribute of punishments (no. 73).

[Col. 0786D] Why does the prophet bring such a battle into the midst of his prophecy and compare the victory of this battle with the coming of our Redeemer? Did the prophet perhaps wish to show us that the victory of the battle fought under Gideon’s leadership signified the coming of our Redeemer against the devil?

Events were indeed performed there which, the more they surpass ordinary warfare, the more they do not depart from the mystery of prophecy. For who ever went into battle with jars and lamps? Who, coming against weapons, abandoned weapons? These things would certainly have seemed ridiculous to us if they had not been terrifying to the enemy. But the victory itself bears witness that we must not regard as insignificant the small things that were done.

Gideon, therefore, coming into battle signifies the coming of our Redeemer. Of him it is written: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the king of glory shall enter. Who is this king of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:7).

Here he prophesied our Redeemer not only through his deed but also through his name. For Gideon is interpreted as “going around in the womb.” Our Lord embraces all things through the power of his majesty, yet, through the dispensation of grace, he came by taking humanity within the Virgin’s womb.

Who, then, is “going around in the womb” except almighty God, redeeming us through his dispensation, embracing all things in his divinity, and taking humanity within the womb? In that womb he was both incarnate and not confined. He was within the womb according to the substance of weakness, and outside the world according to the power of his majesty.

Madian, however, is interpreted as “from judgment.” Their being repelled and destroyed was not due to a defect in the one repelling them, but to the judgment of the one judging justly; and for this reason they are called “from judgment”: because, alienated from the Redeemer’s grace, they draw the merit of just condemnation even into the designation of their name (no. 74).

Against these Gideon proceeds to battle with three hundred men. The number one hundred is customarily understood to signify the fullness of perfection. What, then, is signified by the number one hundred multiplied three times except perfect knowledge of the Trinity? With these our Lord destroyed the adversaries of the faith; with these he went forth to the battles of preaching—those who can know divine things and who know how to hold perfect convictions concerning the Trinity, which is God.

It must be noted that this number, three hundred, is contained in the letter tau, which has the appearance of a cross. If the part that projects above the crossbar in a cross were added to it above the transverse line, it would no longer be the appearance of a cross but the cross itself. Since, therefore, the number three hundred is contained in the letter tau, and through the letter tau, as we said, the form of the cross is displayed, it is not without reason that in these three hundred who followed Gideon those were signified to whom it was said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23).

Those who follow the Lord take up the cross more truly the more vigorously they subdue themselves and are afflicted for their neighbors through the compassion of charity. Hence it is also said through the prophet Ezekiel: “Mark a tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve” (Ezek. 9:4).

Or certainly, in these three hundred, who are contained in the letter tau, this is expressed: that the iron of the enemies is overcome by the wood of the cross.

They were led to the river to drink water, and those who drank the water on bent knees were removed from the intention of warfare. Water signifies the teaching of wisdom, while the standing knee signifies upright action. Therefore those who are said to have bent their knees while drinking water withdrew, barred from the battle, because Christ goes into battle against the enemies of the faith with those who, while drinking the streams of teaching, do not bend the uprightness of their works.

All are said to have drunk water at that time, but not all are said to have stood with an upright knee. Those who bent their knees while drinking water were rejected, because, as the Apostle attests: “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Rom. 2:13).

Because, as we have said, looseness of conduct is signified by the bending of the knees, Paul rightly says again: “Raise up the drooping hands and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Heb. 12:12).

Those, therefore, go forth to war under Christ’s leadership who show in their deeds what they proclaim with their mouths; they spiritually drink the streams of teaching, yet do not bend carnally into wicked works. For, as it is written: “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15:9).

(No. 75.) They went, then, into battle with trumpets, lamps, and jars. [Note: Codex Michael disagrees slightly here.] This was, as we have said, an unusual order of warfare. They sounded the trumpets, and jars were held in their left hands; the lamps were placed inside the jars. When the jars were broken, the lamps were revealed, and, terrified by their flashing light, the enemies were put to flight.

Thus the cry of preachers is signified by the trumpets, the brightness of miracles by the lamps, and the fragility of bodies by the jars. Such men our leader took with him into the battle of preaching: men who, scorning the preservation of their bodies, would overthrow their enemies by dying and overcome their swords not with weapons and swords but with patience.

Our martyrs came armed into battle under their leader, but with trumpets, jars, and lamps. They sounded the trumpets when they preached; they broke the jars when they exposed their bodies, destined to be dissolved in passion, to the swords of their enemies. They shone as lamps when, after the dissolution of their bodies, they flashed forth through miracles. Then the enemies were put to flight, because, seeing the bodies of the dead martyrs shining with miracles, they were broken by the light of truth and believed what they had attacked.

They sounded the trumpets so that the jars might be broken; the jars were broken so that the lamps might appear; the lamps appeared so that the enemies might be put to flight. That is, the martyrs preached until their bodies were dissolved in death; their bodies were dissolved in death so that they might flash forth through miracles; they flashed forth through miracles so that they might overthrow their enemies by divine light, so that those who had stood erect against God would no longer resist him but, subjected, would fear him.

(No. 76.) It should also be noted that the enemies stood before the jars but fled before the lamps. For the persecutors of the holy Church resisted the preachers of the faith while they were still in the body; but when miracles appeared after the dissolution of their bodies, they were put to flight, because, terrified by fear, they ceased persecuting the faithful. The jars of their bodies were broken by the preaching of the trumpets, and, seeing the lamps of miracles, they were afraid.

(No. 77.) It must also be considered that “they held the trumpets in their right hands, but the jars in their left.” We are said to regard as right whatever we value greatly, and as left whatever we consider worthless. It is therefore rightly written there that they held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left, because the martyrs of Christ value the grace of preaching greatly, but regard the usefulness of their bodies as of little importance.

Whoever values the usefulness of the body more than the grace of preaching holds the trumpet in his left hand and the jar in his right. If the grace of preaching is considered first and the usefulness of the body afterward, it is certain that the trumpets are held on the right and the jars on the left.

## CHAPTER III

“When Manoah saw the angel, he was afraid and said, ‘We shall surely die, because we have seen the Lord.’ His wife immediately consoled him, saying, ‘If the Lord had wished to kill us, he would not have received a burnt offering and libations from our hands’” (Judg. 13:21 ff.).

When the confidence of hope that the faithful must hold was being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 5 (no. 56), the following was added: “When Manoah saw the angel, he was afraid, etc.” — What does it mean that the man becomes fearful at the sight of the angel while the woman is bold, except that whenever heavenly things are shown to us, the spirit is shaken by fear but hope nonetheless presumes?

Hope rises from this disturbance of the spirit to dare greater things, because it first sees the things that are above. When the uplifted mind beholds the higher secrets of heavenly things, every firmness of human strength trembles.

## CHAPTER IV

“When Samson had entered the city of Gaza of the Philistines, they immediately set guards; but he went out, took away the gates of the city, and climbed to the summit of the mountain” (Judg. 16:3).

When the prefiguration of the Lord’s resurrection was being discussed, in Homily 21 on the Gospel (no. 7), the following was added: “When Samson had entered the city of Gaza of the Philistines, etc.” — Whom does that Samson signify in this deed except our Redeemer?

What does the city of Gaza signify except hell? What is demonstrated by the Philistines except the faithlessness of the Jews? When they saw the Lord dead and his body already placed in the tomb, they immediately set guards and rejoiced as though they had caught Samson in Gaza—the one who had been renowned as the author of life, now held within the prison of hell.

But Samson not only went out in the middle of the night; he also carried away the gates, because our Redeemer, rising before daylight, not only came forth free from hell but also destroyed the very prison of hell and carried away its gates. And he climbed to the summit of the mountain, because, by rising, he removed the barriers of hell and, by ascending, entered the kingdoms of heaven.

## CHAPTER V

“Concerning Samson: after he had killed many with the jawbone of a donkey, he threw it upon the ground and water flowed from it” (Judg. 15:15, 19).

When the instruction provided by divine action and the miracles of the Church’s preachers were being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 13 (no. 15), the following was added: “Concerning Samson: after he had killed many with the jawbone of a donkey, etc.” — Whom are the persons of the Church’s preachers represented by here except through the jawbone of the donkey?

For our Redeemer, holding in his own hand, through the power of his virtue, the simplicity and patience of preachers, killed carnal people with respect to their vices. Afterward the jawbone, thrown upon the ground, poured forth water, because the bodies of preachers, given over to death, displayed great miracles to the peoples.

## CHAPTER VI

“Concerning Samson, who, after losing his eyes, was assigned by the Philistines to the mill” (Judg. 16).

When the torpor of human hardness in need of correction was being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 7 (no. 37), the following was added: “Concerning Samson, who, after losing his eyes, was assigned by the Philistines to the mill.” — It must be understood that sometimes the eyes of understanding are first dulled, and afterward the captive mind wanders through outward desires, so that the blind mind does not know by whom it is led and willingly submits to the enticements of its flesh.

Sometimes, however, the desires of the flesh first boil up, and after long practice of unlawful action they close the eye of the heart. Often the mind sees correctly but does not boldly rise against what is perverse; and while resisting, it is defeated, because, although it judges what it is doing, it is overcome by the pleasure of its flesh.

Since the eye of contemplation is often lost first, and afterward the mind is subjugated through the desires of the flesh to the labors of this world, Samson bears witness to this: he was captured by the Philistines and, after losing his eyes, was assigned to the mill. For the evil spirits, after digging out the inner vision of contemplation with the goads of temptation, send the mind outward into the circuit of labors.

## CHAPTER VII

“Concerning Samson: while he was alive he killed a few, but when the temple had been overthrown, he killed many when he died” (Judg. 16:30).

When the great multitude of believers through the death and resurrection of our Redeemer was being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 29 (no. 26), the following was added: “Concerning Samson: while he was alive he killed a few, etc.” — Whose person is signified here by Samson except that of our Redeemer?

While he lived, Samson killed a few; but when he overthrew the temple, he himself, even in dying, struck down a very great multitude of his adversaries. Likewise, while our Lord preached, few from the people of Israel believed, but innumerable peoples of the nations followed the way of life when he died.

While he still lived a passible life, he endured the proud; but when he died, passing from that life subject to suffering, he struck down many. Samson once represented this figuratively in himself: while alive he killed a few, but when the temple had been destroyed, he killed countless enemies as he died. In the same way, the Lord extinguished a few through the arrogance of pride while he lived, but many more when the temple of his body was dissolved; and, by dying, he struck all together down—the elect from the nations whom he had endured while living.

## CHAPTER VIII

“When the whole of Israel had gathered and wished to avenge the tribe of Benjamin, which had been discovered in a sexual crime, Israel itself was first struck down, and then it utterly destroyed the sinful tribe” (Judg. 20:3).

[Col. 0790B]

When the necessity of avenging our own sins before rushing to punish those of others was being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 14 (no. 34; the order is reversed more than once), the following was added: “When the tribe of Benjamin, discovered in a sexual crime, etc.” — Whoever does not first judge himself does not know what is right to judge in another. And even if he perhaps knows by hearing what he ought to judge rightly, he is nevertheless unable to judge another’s merits correctly, because his own conscience provides him with no rule of judgment grounded in innocence.

Hence, when the tribe of Benjamin had been overwhelmed by sexual crime, all Israel gathered and wished to avenge the iniquity; yet Israel itself was struck down once and again in battle. After consulting the Lord about whether they should go to avenge it, they were commanded to do so. They proceeded according to the divine command, suffered defeat the first and second time, and only then, striking the sinful tribe very severely, almost utterly destroyed it.

What does it mean that Israel is inflamed to avenge a crime and yet is first struck down itself, except that those through whom the faults of others are punished must first be cleansed themselves? Thus those who hasten to correct the vices of others should already come purified to the punishment.

Hence, when certain people were lying in wait and bringing an adulterous woman forward for punishment, it was said to them: “Let the one among you who is without sin cast the first stone at her” (John 8:7). They were going to punish the sins of others while leaving their own behind. They are therefore recalled inwardly to their conscience, so that they may first correct their own sins and then rebuke those of others.

Therefore, when the vengeance of divine judgment against us is delayed, it is necessary that our conscience itself rebuke us and raise itself against itself to the lamentation of repentance. It should not be arrogant against the good and humble toward itself, but rigid against itself and submissive toward every good person.

# BOOK SEVEN  
## On Testimonies for the First Book of Kings

[Col. 0789]

## CHAPTER ONE

“Her face was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Sam. 1:18).

[Col. 0789D]

In the exposition of Job, book 33 (no. 43), the following was added: “Her face was no longer changed in different directions.” — [Note: This chapter is absent from our manuscripts.] For, clearly, after prayer she did not squander through frivolous joy what she had sought during the time of her prayer with the severity of her groans.

## CHAPTER II

“The Lord will judge the ends of the earth” (1 Sam. 2:10).

When the dispensation of divine mercy toward the human race was being discussed, in the exposition of Blessed Job, book 29 (no. 20), the following was added: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth.” — At first our Creator, not abandoning his creation, both tolerates human evils through his wisdom and at times removes them through their conversion.

When he regards hard and insensible minds, he terrifies them now with threats, now with blows, now with revelations, so that those who had grown hard in the worst security may become softened by salutary fear. Thus they may return even late and at least be ashamed that this very thing was long awaited from them.

For the Lord knows that he judges the end of our life more strictly, and therefore he carefully purifies his elect at the end. Hence it is written: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth,” because he watches over our final moments with the greater care, the more he considers that the beginnings of the life to come will depend upon them.

## CHAPTER III

“They took two cows that were nursing calves and yoked them to a cart” (1 Sam. 6:10). And shortly afterward: “The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh, going and lowing” (ibid., 12).

When the good of measured compassion to be shown toward one’s neighbors was being discussed, in Homily 31 on the Gospel (no. 4), the following was added: “They took two cows that were nursing calves and yoked them to a cart.”

When the ark of the Lord returned from the land of the Philistines to the land of the Israelites, it was placed upon a cart, and cows were yoked to the cart; they are remembered to have been nursing. Their calves were shut up at home. And it is written: “The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh; they proceeded along one road, going and lowing, and they did not turn either to the right or to the left.”

What, then, do the cows signify except the faithful in the Church? When they attend to the commands of Sacred Scripture, they carry the ark of the Lord placed upon them, as it were. It should also be noted about them that they are said to have been nursing, because there are many who, inwardly established on the way of God, are outwardly bound by carnal affections, yet do not turn from the straight path: they carry the ark of God in their minds.

Behold, the cows proceed to Beth-shemesh. Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun.” And the prophet says: “But for you who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. 4:2). If, therefore, we are journeying toward the dwelling of the eternal sun, it is surely fitting that we should not turn from God’s way on account of carnal affections.

We must consider with all our strength that the cows placed beneath God’s cart proceed and groan. They utter lowings from their inmost parts and yet do not turn their steps back from the road. They feel love through compassion, but do not turn their necks backward.

Thus God’s preachers, and likewise all the faithful within the holy Church, ought to be such that they sympathize with their neighbors through charity and yet do not deviate from God’s way through compassion.

[Col. 0791C] (In the exposition of Blessed Job, book 7, no. 42; the order is often reversed.) For the ark proceeding to Beth-shemesh means drawing near to the dwelling of eternal light with heavenly knowledge. But we truly journey toward Beth-shemesh when, walking along the path of righteousness, we do not turn toward the neighboring paths of error, even because of affection for our children.

Thus, indeed, those who have been placed beneath the yoke of Sacred Law and now carry the ark of God through inward knowledge must proceed, so that, while they grieve over the needs of their relatives, they do not turn away from the path of righteousness they have begun.

Their affection should hold our minds, but should not turn them back, lest the mind be either hard because it is untouched by affection or, if touched too much and bent, become lax.

## CHAPTER IV

“Were you not little in your own eyes when I made you head over the tribes of Israel?” (1 Sam. 15:17)

While there was discussion of avoiding arrogance and pursuing humility of heart, the following passage was added in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXIV (nos. 42–43):

> “Was it not when you were little in [Col. 0791D] your own eyes, etc.?”

A person is little in his own eyes when, in considering himself, he judges himself unequal to the merits of others. For anyone who stretches himself above the merits of others through the arrogance of his thoughts sees himself, as it were, as great. But Saul, rejected by God, did not persevere in the good that he had begun, because he swelled with pride at the power he had assumed.

David, on the contrary, always thinking humbly of himself and placing himself below that same Saul in comparison, found an opportunity to strike him but spared him; then he prostrated himself before his raging adversary in a humble declaration, saying: “Whom are you pursuing, king of Israel? Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog and a single flea” (1 Samuel 24:15).

Certainly, he had already been anointed king; already, when Samuel interceded for him and poured oil from the horn over him, he had learned that, after rejecting Saul, divine grace was preserving him to possess the government of the kingdom. Yet before the persecuting adversary he humbly bowed his mind, although he knew by divine judgment that he had been preferred to him. He therefore humbly placed himself below the one whom, through the grace of election, he knew himself to be incomparably better than.

Let those who still do not know what standing they have before God learn how they ought to humble themselves before their neighbors, if even the elect humble themselves before those whom they recognize, through inward judgments, to have already been placed beneath them. This is usually the distinctive mark of the elect: they always think less of themselves than they are. Hence David says: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul” (Psalm 130:2).

Hence Solomon calls the little ones to wisdom, saying: “If anyone is little, let him come to her” (Proverbs 9:4). For whoever does not yet despise himself does not grasp the humble wisdom of God. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11:25). Again the Psalmist says: “The Lord preserves the little ones” (Psalm 114:6). Hence the Teacher of the nations says: “We became little ones in the midst of you” (1 Thessalonians 2:7). And, admonishing the disciples, he says: “Considering one another superior to yourselves” (Philippians 2:3).

For because every wicked person considers everyone he knows to be beneath him, the righteous, conversely, strive to regard every neighbor as superior. And lest, while one humbles himself before another, the person humbled should rise into arrogance, he rightly admonished both parties, saying: “Considering one another superior to yourselves”—so that in the thoughts of the heart I may prefer him to myself, and he in turn may prefer me to himself; thus, while the heart is pressed down from both sides, no one is lifted up by the honor bestowed.

## Chapter V — Also on the preceding subject

In the exposition of the Gospel, homily 7 (at the end):

What is driven away by the rebuke of Saul except the arrogance of an exalted king? Anyone placed in authority can profitably apply this to his own correction. When Saul therefore considered himself little in his own eyes, he was made head over the tribes of Israel. It was as though he were being told openly:

> “When you saw yourself as little, I made you great above the others; but because you see yourself as great, you are judged little by me.” [Col. 0792C]

By contrast, when David despised the power of his kingdom by dancing before the ark of the Lord, he said: “I shall play, and I shall become even more contemptible than I have become; and I shall be humble in my own eyes” (2 Samuel 6:22).

If, then, holy men think little of themselves even when they perform great deeds, what will those say in their defense who swell with pride without any work of virtue? But even when works are present, they are worthless unless seasoned with humility. A remarkable deed accompanied by arrogance does not elevate but burdens. For whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust in the wind: from the very point at which he is seen to carry something, he is more grievously blinded.

Therefore, in everything we do, let us hold humility as the root of a good work. Let us consider not those over whom we are already superior, but those beneath whom we still are, so that, while we set before ourselves the examples of better people, we may always ascend to greater things through humility.

## Chapter VI — Also on the preceding subject

[Col. 0792D]

*Pastoral Rule*, part II, chapter 6, before the middle.

[Note: The manuscripts of Utica and Gemet assign this passage to book VI of the *Moralia on Job*; they also add: “Also book XXVI.” It is read in the place indicated by us.]

Saul had first seen himself as little in his own eyes, but, supported by temporal power, he no longer saw himself as little. Preferring himself to others because he had more power than all of them, he considered himself greater than everyone.

In a remarkable way, while he was little in his own estimation, he was great before God; but when he appeared great in his own estimation, he was little before God. Frequently, therefore, when the mind is inflated by the abundance of subjects, it is corrupted into the luxury of pride, with the summit of power itself enticing it.

That power is well governed by the person who knows both how to retain it and how to oppose it. He governs it well who knows through it to rise above faults and, while possessing it, to place himself on an equal footing with others. For the human mind is often exalted even when it is supported by no power. How much more does it raise itself on high when power is also joined to it?

Yet that person rightly administers power who carefully knows both how to take from it what helps and to defeat what tempts; who knows how to see himself as equal to others while possessing it, and nevertheless to prefer himself to sinners through zeal for correction (same work, much later). For it is written: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Sirach 32:1).

## Chapter VII — Also on the preceding subject

When there was discussion of the virtue of obedience, the following passage was added in the exposition of blessed Job, book XVIII (no. 59):

Every soul is more precious in God’s sight in proportion as, out of love for the truth, it is more contemptible in its own sight. Hence it is said to Saul: “Was it not when you were little in your own eyes that I made you head over the tribes of Israel?”

It was as though he were saying openly: “You were great to me because you were contemptible to yourself; but now, because you are great to yourself, you have become contemptible to me.” [Col. 0793B]

Hence the prophet says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isaiah 5:21). Therefore, the more precious someone is to himself, the more contemptible he becomes to God; and the more contemptible he is to himself for God’s sake, the more precious he is to God, “because he regards the lowly, but recognizes the proud from afar” (Psalm 137:6).

## Chapter VIII — Obedience is better than sacrifices, and listening than offering the fat of rams (1 Samuel 15:22)

Also, when there was discussion of the virtue of obedience, the following passage was added in the exposition of blessed Job, book 35 (nos. 28–31):

“Obedience is better than sacrifices,” and so forth. Obedience is rightly placed before sacrifices, because in sacrifices another person’s flesh is slaughtered, whereas through obedience one’s own will is slaughtered. Therefore, a person placates God more quickly when, suppressing the arrogance of his own will before God’s eyes, he sacrifices himself with the sword of the commandment.

Conversely, disobedience is called the sin of divination, so that the greatness of obedience may be demonstrated. Its praise is therefore shown more clearly by contrast. If resisting is like the sin of divination, and refusing to comply like the crime of idolatry, obedience alone possesses the merit of faith, without which anyone is proved unbelieving, even if he appears faithful.

Hence Solomon says in praise of obedience: “An obedient man speaks of victories” (Proverbs 21:28). An obedient man speaks of victories because, when we humbly submit to another’s voice, we overcome ourselves in our hearts.

Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “I will not cast out the one who comes to me, because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:37). For if he did his own will, would he have cast out those who came to him? Yet who does not know that the Son’s will does not differ from the Father’s will?

But because the first human being wished to do his own will and therefore departed from the joys of paradise, the second, coming for the redemption of humanity, showed that he was doing the Father’s will rather than his own, and taught us to remain within. Thus, when he does not do his own will but the Father’s, he does not cast out those who come to him, because by subjecting us to obedience through his example, he closes the way by which we might depart.

Again he says: “I cannot do anything of myself, but as I hear, I judge” (John 5:30). We are commanded to preserve obedience even unto death. But he too, if he judges as he hears, obeys even when he comes as judge. Therefore, lest obedience seem burdensome to us until the end of our present life, our Redeemer shows that he preserves it even when he comes as judge.

What wonder, then, if sinful human beings submit themselves to obedience during the brief span of the present life, when the Mediator of God and humanity does not abandon obedience even while rewarding the obedient?

It must, however, be understood that evil must never be done through obedience, while at times the good being done ought to be interrupted through obedience. For the tree in paradise was not evil, the tree which God forbade human beings to touch. Rather, so that the human being, well created, might grow through the superior merit of obedience, it was fitting that he should even be prohibited from doing something good. Thus the virtue would be more genuine in what he did, the more humbly he showed himself subject to his Creator by refraining even from something good.

But we should note what is said there: “Eat from every tree of paradise, but do not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Genesis 2:16). When someone forbids his subjects one particular good, he must grant many others, lest the obedient mind perish completely if it is entirely deprived of good things. The Lord therefore permitted the eating of all the trees of paradise while prohibiting one, so that he might more easily restrain his creature from one thing—the creature he did not wish to destroy but to advance—the more broadly he released it to all the others.

Since we are sometimes commanded to accept the prosperity of this world and sometimes its adversities, we must understand above all that obedience is sometimes nothing if it contains something of one’s own will, and sometimes very slight if it contains nothing of one’s own will.

When success in this world is commanded, when a position of superiority is ordered, the person who obeys in order to obtain these things nullifies the virtue of his obedience if he also longs for them from his own desire.
