For he does not place himself under obedience who serves the appetite of his own ambition in order to obtain the prosperity of this life.

Conversely, when contempt for the world is commanded, when disgrace and dishonor are ordered, the person who descends unwillingly and reluctantly to what is despised in this life diminishes the merit of his obedience unless his mind desires these things of itself. Obedience is brought to harm when the mind’s own wishes do not in any way accompany it in accepting the insults of this age.

Obedience must therefore contain something of its own will in adversity, but must contain absolutely nothing of its own will in prosperity, so that in adversity it may be more glorious insofar as it joins itself to the divine order even through desire, and in prosperity it may be more genuine insofar as the glory received in the present is wholly separated from the mind.

[Note: Utica reads: “the more contemptible it is.” We have preferred the reading of Gemet and Michael. Otherwise, the *Moralia* reads in this place: “the more contemptible it is.”]

We can show the weight of this virtue more clearly by recalling the deeds of two men destined for the heavenly homeland.

When Moses was tending sheep in the desert, the Lord spoke through an angel in fire and called him to lead the entire multitude of Israelites out. But because he was humble in his mind before himself, he immediately feared the glory of so great a government when it was offered to him. He promptly sought refuge in pleading his weakness, saying: “I beg you, Lord, I am not eloquent from yesterday or the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant; I have become slower and more impeded in tongue” (Exodus 4:10). And, putting himself aside, he asked for another, saying: “Send the one whom you will send.”

Behold: he speaks with the author of speech, yet, lest he assume the power of so great a government, he claims to be without speech.

Paul likewise had been divinely instructed that he ought to go up to Jerusalem, as he himself says to the Galatians: “Then after fourteen years I again went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus. I went up according to a revelation” (Galatians 2:1). [Col. 0794D]

On the journey, when he encountered the prophet Agabus, he heard how much adversity awaited him at Jerusalem. For it is written that Agabus took Paul’s belt and bound his own feet with it, saying: “The man whose belt this is will be bound in this way at Jerusalem” (Acts 21:11). Paul immediately replied: “I am ready not only to be bound but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of Jesus. For I do not consider my life more precious than myself” (ibid., 13).

Thus, going to Jerusalem at the command of revelation, he learns of adversity and nevertheless eagerly desires it. He hears what he should fear, but toward it he hastens with even greater ardor.

Moses, then, has nothing of his own will in prosperity, because he resists with his pleas lest he be placed over the Israelite people. Paul, however, is led toward adversity even by his own desire, because he perceives the knowledge of the evils threatening him, yet through devotion of spirit he grows fervent even for harsher things.

The former wished, at God’s command, to decline the glory of present power; the latter, with God arranging harsh and difficult things, prepared himself for still heavier ones.

Instructed, therefore, by the unbroken virtue of these two leaders, let us strive to grasp the palm of obedience truly: let us serve in the prosperity of this age solely from command, but in adversity also from devotion.

## Chapter IX — Behold, an evil spirit from God is troubling you (1 Samuel 18:10)

When there was discussion of the hidden dispensation of divine judgment, the following passage was added in the exposition of blessed Job, book 18 (no. 4; book II, nos. 16–17):

“Behold, an evil spirit from God is troubling you.”

[Note: Printed editions read: “For Job knows that the devil, although he always desires the affliction of the righteous …”; all our manuscripts resist this reading.]

The ancient enemy of the human race knows how always to seek the affliction of the righteous; nevertheless, if he does not receive power from our Creator, he is wholly unable to prevail at the point of temptation.

Thus every desire of the devil is unjust, yet, when God permits it, all his power is just. Of himself he unjustly desires to tempt anyone he can; but God justly permits those who are to be tempted to be tempted, and to be tempted in the manner in which they are to be tempted.

Therefore it is rightly said: “An evil spirit of the Lord is troubling you.” Behold, one and the same spirit is called both the Lord’s and evil: the Lord’s by permission of just power, but evil by the desire of an unjust will.

Hence a question is often raised in this passage: if it is the Lord’s, why is it evil? If it is evil, why is it called the Lord’s? In two words, both the just power possessed by the devil and his unjust will have been included. He is called an evil spirit because of his most wicked will, and the Lord’s spirit because of the supremely just power he has received.

For although the enemy rages because he desires to strike, the Creator is nevertheless the one who permits him to prevail for some purpose. Therefore, the one who can do nothing except by permission should not be feared. In the Gospel, the legion of demons being expelled from a man said to the Lord: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of pigs” (Matthew 8:31).

Only that command should therefore be feared which, while permitting the enemy to rage, makes even his unjust will serve the use of just judgment.

## Chapter X — When an unclean spirit invaded Saul, David took up the lyre and calmed his madness (1 Samuel 16:14, 23)

When there was discussion of the management of teaching by those who govern, the following passage was added in the *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 2, admonition 3:

“When an unclean spirit invaded Saul, David took up the lyre and calmed his madness,” and so forth.

Often an arrogant rich man must be soothed by the charm of exhortation, because hard wounds frequently soften through gentle applications, and the fury of the insane is often restored to health when the physician uses soothing words. When they are accommodated through sweetness, the sickness of madness is eased.

We must not overlook the fact that, when an adverse spirit invaded Saul, David took up the lyre, calmed his madness, and quieted it. What is signified by Saul except the arrogance of the powerful, and what by David except the humble life of the saints?

When Saul is therefore seized by an unclean spirit, his madness is moderated while David sings, because when the understanding of the powerful is turned through arrogance into fury, it is fitting that it should be recalled to the health of the mind, as though to the sweetness of a lyre, by the tranquility of our speech.

## Chapter XI — David and Goliath (1 Samuel 17:32–34)

When there was discussion of refuting teachers of error, the following passage was added in the exposition of blessed Job, book XVIII (no. 24):

“David and Goliath.”

A man full of right faith—which is ordinarily credited to the saints as righteousness—collects the very testimonies of Holy Scripture that a heretic brings forward and uses them to refute the stubbornness of his error. For when they bring against us the testimonies of sacred law, they bring with them the means by which they may be defeated.

Thus David, a type of the Lord, whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand,” and Goliath, signifying the pride of heretics, spoke through events what we express in words.

Goliath came to battle with a sword, but David with a shepherd’s bag. David nevertheless overcame Goliath and killed him with his own sword. We too do this, since by his graciousness we have been deemed worthy to become members of David. When we defeat proud heretics who bring forward sentences from Holy Scripture with the very words and sentences they themselves produce, we cut down the arrogant Goliath with his own sword.

## Chapter XII — Saul the persecutor entered a cave to relieve himself; David was there with his men, enduring the evils of his persecution for so long. When his men incited him to strike Saul, he restrained them with his reply, saying that he ought not to lay a hand upon the Lord’s anointed; nevertheless, he secretly rose and cut off the edge of his cloak (1 Samuel 24:4–5)

[Col. 0796B]

When there was discussion of avoiding detraction and showing humility even toward wicked rulers, the following passage was added in the *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 4, admonition 5, near the end:

“Saul the persecutor entered a cave to relieve himself,” and so forth.

What is signified by Saul except wicked rulers? What by David except good subjects?

Saul’s relieving his bowels therefore signifies wicked superiors extending the malice conceived in their hearts into deeds of miserable odor and displaying, through the execution of harmful thoughts, what they have devised within themselves.

David nevertheless feared to strike him, because the devout minds of subjects, abstaining from every plague of detraction, do not strike the life of their superiors with the sword of the tongue, even when they rebuke them for their imperfections.

If at times, because of weakness, they can scarcely refrain from speaking of certain extreme and outward faults of their superiors, they nevertheless speak humbly. They cut off the edge of the cloak silently, as it were, because, when they detract at least harmlessly and secretly from the dignity placed over them, they cut the garment of the king set above them.

Yet they return to themselves and severely reproach themselves even for the slightest tearing of a word. Hence it is rightly written there: “After this David struck his heart, because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak.”

The deeds of superiors are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they are judged rightly subject to correction. If the tongue at any time slips against them, even in the smallest matter, the heart must be pressed through the affliction of repentance, so that it may return to itself; and, when it has sinned against the power placed over it, it may dread that power’s judgment, since it was placed over us by God.

For when we sin against superiors, we oppose the ordering of the one who placed them over us. Hence Moses, when he learned that the people were complaining against him and Aaron, said: “For what are we? Your murmuring is not against us but against God” (Exodus 16:8).

## Chapter XIII — Abigail’s renunciation to Nabal (1 Samuel 25:14, 18, 23)

[Col. 0796D]

[Note: In the manuscripts of Michael, Gemet, and Utica: “When there was discussion of the proper times for correction.”]

When there was discussion of the appropriate time for correction, the following passage was added in the *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 16, admonition 17:

“Abigail’s renunciation to Nabal.”

What does Abigail signify for us through the prudence of her intervention except that we correct angry people more effectively if we withdraw during the very disturbance of their anger?

People who are agitated do not know what they are hearing; but once restored to themselves, they receive words of exhortation all the more willingly because they are ashamed that they have been endured so calmly.

To a mind drunk with fury, everything right that is said appears wrong. Hence Abigail commendably kept silent about Nabal’s fault while he was drunk, and commendably spoke of it once the wine had been digested. For this reason he was able to recognize the evil he had done: he had not heard of it while drunk.

## Chapter XIV — The Amalekites abandon an Egyptian boy who has fallen ill on the journey; David restores him with food and makes him the guide of his journey. He pursues the Amalekite, finds him feasting, and utterly destroys him (1 Samuel 30:11–13)

[Col. 0797A]

When there was discussion of the conversion of sinners through the gift of heavenly grace, the following passage was added in the exposition of blessed Job, book V (no. 73):

“The Amalekites abandon an Egyptian boy who has fallen ill on the journey,” and so forth.

What does it mean that the Egyptian boy of the Amalekite grows weary on the journey except that the lover of the present age, covered by the blackness of his sin, is often left weak and despised by that same age, so that he is completely unable to run with it but, broken by adversity, grows numb?

David finds him, because our Redeemer, truly strong of hand, sometimes converts to his love those whom he finds despised by worldly glory. He feeds him, because he refreshes him with the word of knowledge. He chooses him as a guide for the journey, because he also makes him his preacher.

And because he was unable to follow the Amalekite, he becomes David’s guide. The one whom the world abandoned as unworthy not only receives the Lord into his mind after conversion but, by preaching, also brings him into the hearts of others.

With this guide David finds the Amalekite feasting and destroys him, because Christ, through those very preachers whom the world disdained to have as companions, destroys the world’s joy.

## Chapter XV — Also on the preceding subject

In the exposition of the Gospel, homily 36 (no. 7):

God chooses those whom the world has despised, because often that very experience of being despised recalls a person to himself. The one who left his father and squandered prodigally the portion of his property that he had received, after he began to hunger, came to himself and said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have bread in abundance!” (Luke 15:17).

He had indeed departed far from himself when he was sinning; and if he had not hungered, he would never have returned to himself. After he came to lack earthly things, he began to consider what he had lost of spiritual things.

Thus the weak and despised in this world often hear the Lord’s voice more quickly, precisely because in this world they have nothing in which to take delight. This is well represented by that Egyptian boy of the Amalekites, who, while the Amalekites were plundering and running, remained sick on the road and wasted away from hunger and thirst.

When David found him, he gave him food and drink. Immediately recovering, he became David’s guide; he found the Amalekites feasting and, with great strength, struck down those who had abandoned him as weak.

“Amalekite” is interpreted as “a people who lick.” What is signified by a people who lick except the minds of carnal people? They lick, as it were, all earthly things by coveting them, since they delight only in temporal matters.

A people who lick, as it were, makes plunder when those who love earthly things amass profits from the losses of others. But the sick Egyptian boy is left on the road, because, when each sinner begins to grow weak with regard to the condition of this world, he immediately becomes despised by worldly minds.

David nevertheless finds him and gives him food and drink, because the Lord, strong of hand, does not despise the outcasts of the world. Often he converts to the grace of his love those who, unable to follow the world, remain as though on the road; he extends to them the food and drink of his word and, as it were, chooses them as guides for himself on the journey by making them his preachers.

When they bring Christ into the hearts of sinners, they lead David, as it were, against his enemies. They strike the feasting Amalekites with David’s sword, because by the Lord’s power they overthrow the proud who had despised them in the world.

Thus the Egyptian boy who had remained on the road killed the Amalekites, because often those who first could not run in this world with worldly people overcome the minds of worldly people by preaching.

# BOOK EIGHT  
## Testimonies for the Second Book of Samuel

[Col. 0797]

## Chapter I — Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain fall upon you, nor let there be fields of firstfruits; for there the shield of the mighty was cast away, the shield of Saul, as though he had not been anointed with oil (2 Samuel 1:21–22)

[Col. 0797C]

When there was discussion of the distinction between curses in the preface to book IV of the *Moralia on Job*, chapter 4, the following passage was added:

“Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain fall upon you,” and so forth.

What had the mountains of Gilboa done wrong, when Saul died, so that neither dew nor rain should fall upon them and the word of the sentence should dry them of every growth of green?

But since “Gilboa” is interpreted as “a descent,” and Saul, the anointed one who died, represents the death of our Mediator, the mountains of Gilboa not improperly signify the proud hearts of the Jews. While they flow downward into the desires of this world, they became involved in the death of Christ, that is, of the Anointed One. And because the anointed king died bodily among them, they themselves were dried of every dew of grace.

Of them it is also rightly said: “So that they cannot be fields of firstfruits.” The proud minds of the Hebrews do not produce first fruits, because, remaining for the most part in unbelief at the Redeemer’s coming, they refused to follow the beginnings of faith.

In her first fruits, holy Church was made fertile by the multitude of the nations; only at the end of the world will she scarcely receive the Jews whom she finds, gathering the last and placing them like remnants of the harvest. Of these remnants Isaiah says: “If the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isaiah 10:22).

The mountains of Gilboa may nevertheless have been cursed by the prophet’s mouth for this reason: so that, while no fruit grows from the withered earth, the owners of the land might be struck by the loss of its barrenness; thus they might themselves receive the sentence of the curse, since by their wickedness they had deserved to accept the death of the king among them.

## Chapter II — Abner spoke to Asahel, saying: Withdraw from me; do not follow me, lest I be forced to pierce you through to the ground. But he refused to listen and would not turn aside. Abner therefore struck him with the butt of his spear in the groin, pierced him through, and he died (2 Samuel 2:22 and following)

When there was discussion of discreet correction toward offenders in the *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 16, admonition 17, near the end, the following passage was added:

“Abner spoke to Asahel, saying,” and so forth.

Whom did Asahel represent except those whom violent anger seizes and drives headlong? Such people must be avoided with as much care as they are violently carried away in their madness.

Thus Abner—whose name, in our language, means “lamp of the father”—fled, because the speech of teachers, which indicates the supernal light of God, sees someone’s mind being carried over the precipices of fury. When it refrains from returning verbal darts against the angry person, it does not wish to strike the pursuer.

But when angry people are not softened by any consideration and, like Asahel, do not cease pursuing and raging, those who try to restrain them must not raise themselves in anger but must display whatever tranquility they possess. They should bring forward certain things subtly, by which they may prick the furious person’s mind indirectly.

Hence, when Abner stood against his pursuer, he pierced him not with the point of his spear but with its butt. To strike with the point of the spear is to meet someone with the force of open rebuke. To strike the pursuer with the butt of the spear is to touch the furious person calmly in certain matters and, as though sparing him, to overcome him.

Asahel immediately fell dead, because agitated minds, while sensing that they are being spared and yet being inwardly touched under the guise of tranquility by the reasoning of the replies, immediately fall from the position into which they had raised themselves. Those who recoil from the violence of their own fury under a blow of gentleness die, as it were, without iron.

## Chapter III — The sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, came and entered Ish-bosheth’s house during the heat of the day, while he was sleeping on his bed at noon. They entered the house while the female doorkeeper of the house was cleaning wheat and fell asleep; taking ears of wheat, they entered secretly and struck him in the groin (2 Samuel 4:5)

When there was discussion, in the exposition of blessed Job, book I (no. 49), of maintaining a strong guard over the mind through vigilant watchfulness, the following passage was added:

“The sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, came and entered Ish-bosheth’s house during the heat of the day,” and so forth.

The doorkeeper cleans wheat when the guardian of the mind separates virtues from vices through discernment. If she falls asleep, she admits assassins against her own lord, because when vigilance in discernment ceases, it opens a path for evil spirits to kill the soul.

They enter and carry away the ears of wheat because they immediately remove the shoots of good thoughts; and they strike him in the groin because they kill the strength of the heart through the pleasure of the flesh. To strike in the groin is to pierce the life of the mind with carnal pleasure.

Ish-bosheth would certainly not have succumbed to this death if he had not appointed a woman—that is, a soft guard—to the entrance of the house, the entrance of the mind. A strong and manly understanding must be set over the doors of the heart, one that is overcome neither by the sleep of negligence nor deceived by the error of ignorance.

[Note: In the Sagien manuscript: “watchful.”]

Hence Ish-bosheth was rightly named thus, since he was stripped by hostile swords while guarded by a woman. Ish-bosheth means “man of confusion.” A man of confusion is one who is not fortified by a strong guard of the mind. For while he thinks he is practicing virtues, vices entering secretly kill him without his knowledge.

The entrance of the mind must therefore be fortified with every virtue, lest at any time the enemies lying in wait penetrate it through a breach made by neglected thought.

## Chapter IV — The ark was tilted by kicking cows; when Uzzah the Levite wished to raise it, he was struck down (2 Samuel 6:6–7)

When there was discussion, in the exposition of blessed Job, book V (no. 24), of restraining the audacity of subjects in criticizing their rulers, the following passage was added:

“The ark, tilted by kicking cows,” and so forth.

Often, because they cannot understand, worse people take offense at either the deeds or the words of their betters. Yet they should not rashly criticize them precisely because they cannot truly grasp them.

Often something is done or ordered by great people as an act of stewardship, but is considered an error by lesser people. Often strong people say many things which the weak judge precisely because they do not understand them.

This was well signified by that ark of the covenant, tilted by kicking oxen. Because the Levite thought it was about to fall and wished to raise it, he immediately received the sentence of death.

For what is the mind of the righteous except an ark of the covenant? Carried by kicking oxen, it is tilted because sometimes even one who governs well, shaken by the disorder of subject peoples, is moved, solely by love, to accommodate himself to their condition in the exercise of stewardship.

But in what is done as an act of stewardship, the ignorant consider the very inclination to be a fall from strength. Hence some subjects stretch out the hand of criticism against it, but immediately perish through their own rashness.

The Levite therefore extended his hand as though to help, but by his offense lost his life, because whenever weak people criticize the deeds of the strong, they themselves are rejected from the lot of the living.

Sometimes holy men, accommodating themselves to the weak, say certain lesser things; at other times, contemplating certain lofty realities, they speak of greater things. While foolish people do not understand either the force of accommodation or the height of what is said, they boldly criticize it.

What is it to wish to correct the righteous in his accommodation except to raise the tilted ark with the proud hand of criticism? What is it to criticize an unfamiliar statement except to regard the movement of his strength as a fall into error?

But the person who presumptuously raises God’s ark loses his life, because no one would presume to correct the saints’ right actions unless he had first thought better of himself.

Hence the same Levite was rightly called Uzzah, which is interpreted as “strong” or “mighty of the Lord,” because presumptuous people would never judge the deeds or words of their superiors to be weak unless, in their bold minds, they believed themselves strong in the Lord.

## Chapter V — When David brought back the ark of the Lord to Jerusalem by dancing, he was mocked by Michal, daughter of Saul and his wife (2 Samuel 6:16–17, 21–22)

When the goodness of humility among rulers was being discussed through the grace of the heavenly gift [Col. 0800B] in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXVII (No. 77, 78), the following was added:

[Note: Col. 0800D: The printed editions are most corruptly: “Concerning the homeland of the heavenly gift.”]

> That when David was bringing the ark of the Lord back to Jerusalem by dancing, etc.

It is worthwhile to contemplate how many gifts of virtue David had received, and how firmly he preserved humility amid them all. Who would not have been elated at having torn apart the jaws of lions, scattered the limbs of bears, been chosen over his older brothers, been anointed to govern the kingdom after the rejected king, struck down the terrifying Goliath with a single stone, brought back from the slain Philistines the numerous foreskins demanded by the king, finally received the promised kingdom, and possessed the whole Israelite people without opposition?

And yet, when he brings the ark of God back to Jerusalem, as though he had forgotten that he was set above everyone else, he dances before the ark among the people. Since, as is believed, it was the custom of the common people to dance before the ark, the king whirls himself about in a dance of divine service. [Col. 0800C] Behold how the man whom the Lord had uniquely set above all others despises himself beneath the Lord, both making himself equal to the least and displaying himself as despised. He does not recall the power of the kingdom; he does not fear becoming contemptible in the eyes of his subjects by dancing; he does not recognize himself as exalted above the others in honor before the ark of the one who had bestowed that honor.

Before God he performed what was weak and lowly, so that through these acts of humility he might strengthen what he had done bravely before men. I do not know what others may think of his deeds; I am more astonished at David dancing than fighting. By fighting he subjected his enemies, but by dancing before the Lord he conquered himself.

When Michal, daughter of Saul, still insane with the pride of royal descent, looked down upon him in his humiliation and said, “How glorious the king of Israel was today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants, and exposing himself as one of the buffoons exposes himself” (2 Samuel 6:20), she immediately heard his reply: “As the Lord lives, I will dance before the Lord, who chose me rather than your father” (ibid. 6:21–22). A little later he said: “I will dance, and I will become even more contemptible than I have become, and I will be humble in my own eyes.” It is as though he openly said: “I seek to become contemptible before men, because through humility I seek to preserve myself as free before the Lord.”

[Col. 0800D] There are, however, some who think humbly of themselves because, placed in positions of honor, they understand that they are nothing but dust and ashes; nevertheless, they refuse to appear contemptible before men. Contrary to what they think inwardly about themselves, they cloak themselves outwardly with a kind of rigid dignity. There are also some who desire to appear contemptible to men and, by displaying themselves as abject, despise everything they are; yet inwardly they swell with pride in the very merit of their apparent lowliness. The more they suppress pride in their outward appearance, the more they are exalted in their hearts.

David detected and overcame both these struggles with pride through great vigilance and marvelous strength.

[Note: The manuscript of Utica reads “rebuked”; Gemmeticense, Michaelian, and Sagiensis are followed.]

[Col. 0801A] For, since he thought humbly of himself inwardly, he shows that he does not seek outward honor when he says: “I will dance, and I will become more contemptible.” And since, by displaying himself as contemptible outwardly, he does not swell inwardly, he adds: “And I will be humble in my own eyes.” It is as though he said: “I regard myself inwardly as the one whom I display outwardly, despising myself.”

What, then, will those whom doctrine elevates do, if David knew the Redeemer who was to come from his own flesh and announced his joys prophetically, yet nevertheless pressed down the neck of his heart with the strong heel of discernment, saying: “And I will be humble in my own eyes”?

## CHAPTER VI — “You shall not build a temple for me, because you are a man of blood” (1 Samuel 7; or rather 1 Chronicles 22:3).

When the purity of heart and conduct that teachers must preserve was being discussed in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VII (No. 56), the following was added:

> “You shall not build a temple for me,” etc.

[Col. 0801B] He who cares to correct the faults of others must be pure from vices in himself: he must not think about earthly things, nor succumb to low desires, so that he may see more clearly what others must avoid, the more truly he himself shuns these things through knowledge and life. For an eye burdened by dust cannot examine a blemish purely in a limb, and hands holding mud cannot wipe away filth that has been spread over them.

In accordance with the wording of the ancient translation, the divine voice aptly conveys this symbolically concerning David, who was laboring against external wars, when it says: “You shall not build a temple for me, because you are a man of blood.” He builds the temple of God who devotes himself to correcting and instructing the minds of his neighbors. We are the temple of God, for we are built for true life by his indwelling, as Paul testifies when he says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17). But a man of blood is forbidden to build the temple of God, because one who is still occupied with carnal deeds must be ashamed to instruct the minds of his neighbors spiritually.

## CHAPTER VII — “David struck the Valley of Salt” (1 Kings 8:13).

[Col. 0801C] When vengeance against those who think perversely about God was being discussed in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book III (No. 45), the following was added:

> “David struck the Valley of Salt.”

What is signified by the multitude struck down by David in the Valley of Salt, except that our Redeemer, by the strict examination of his judgment, extinguishes the folly of an immoderate taste in those who think perversely about him?

## CHAPTER VIII — That David, walking on the roof, desired Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah (2 Samuel 11:2–3).

When the discernment to be applied in investigating the mysteries of Scripture was being discussed in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book III (No. 55), the following was added:

> “That David, walking on the roof,” etc.

[Note: Alternatively, as is read in most manuscripts: “When, through the study of most subtle discernment, the interpretation of the meaning of sacred discourse was being discussed …”]

[Col. 0801D] Thus, very often, a thing is virtue according to its historical sense but guilt according to its symbolic meaning. Likewise, something that happened may be a cause of condemnation in the deed, yet a prophecy of virtue in the written account. We can show this more quickly to be true if we produce one testimony of sacred Scripture to prove both points.

Who, on hearing it, would not detest—not only among the faithful but even among unbelievers—the fact that David, walking on the roof, desired Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah? Yet when Uriah returned from battle, David urged him to go to his house and wash his feet. He immediately replied: “The ark of God dwells under tents, and shall I go into my house to rest?” (2 Samuel 11:11). David received him at his own table and gave him the letter by which he was to die.

But whose figure does David represent as he walks on the roof, except the one of whom it is written: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun” (Psalm 18:6)? And what does bringing Bathsheba to himself signify except joining the law of the letter, associated with the carnal people, to himself through spiritual understanding?

[Col. 0802A] Bathsheba is said to mean “the seventh well,” because through knowledge of the law, by the infusion of spiritual grace, perfect wisdom is supplied to us. Whom, then, does Uriah designate except the Jewish people? His name is interpreted as “my light is God.” The Jewish people, because they are lifted up by the knowledge of the law they have received, glory, as it were, in the light of God.

But David took Uriah’s wife from him and joined her to himself, because the strong-handed one—David’s meaning—appearing in the flesh as the Redeemer, made known that the law spoke spiritually about him. By what had been held according to the letter, he showed that the law had become foreign to the Jewish people, and he joined it to himself because he declared that he was preached through it.

David nevertheless urges Uriah to go home and wash his feet, because the incarnate Lord, coming into the world, commanded the Jewish people to return to conscience and cleanse the filth of their deeds with tears, so that they might understand the commandments of the law spiritually and, after such hardness regarding its precepts, finding the fountain of baptism, return to the water after their labor.

[Col. 0802B] But Uriah, remembering that the ark of the Lord was under tents, replied that he could not enter his house. It is as though the Jewish people said: “I see the commandments of God in carnal sacrifices, and I do not seek to return to conscience through spiritual understanding.” For he says, as it were, that the ark is under tents who understands the commandments of God only as providing the service of carnal sacrifice.

Although Uriah refuses to return home, David calls him to his table, because, although the Jewish people disdain returning to conscience, the coming Redeemer nevertheless preaches spiritual commandments to them, saying: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). The Jewish people therefore hold the law, which speaks of his divinity, while that same people disdain believing in him.

[Col. 0802C] For this reason Uriah is sent to Joab with the letter by which he is to be killed, because that same Jewish people carries the law by which it is convicted and must die. While retaining the commandments of the law, yet refusing to fulfill them, it itself bears the judgment by which it is condemned.

What, then, could be called more wicked than David in this deed? What could be called purer than Uriah? Yet again, in the mystery, what is found more holy than David, or more faithless than Uriah, when the one signifies the innocence of prophecy through the guilt of his life, while the other expresses guilt in prophecy through the innocence of his life?

The power of sacred eloquence narrates past events in such a way as to express things to come; it approves a matter in the deed without contradicting it in the mystery; it condemns events as they happened while persuading us that they are to be accomplished mystically.

## CHAPTER IX — Concerning David’s desire for Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:4).

When the restraint of the sight that gives rise to illicit desire was being discussed in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXI (Nos. 12–13), the following was added:

> “Concerning David’s desire for Bathsheba.”

[Col. 0802D] Still weighed down by the burden of corruptible flesh, we cannot live in such a way that no pleasure of sin can assail us. But it is one thing to be touched unwillingly, and another for the consenting mind to be destroyed.

Holy men guard themselves with vigilance all the more carefully because they disdain allowing themselves to be assailed by sinister impulses or passing pleasure. Thus, if the heart should perhaps desire something illicit, the eye, pressed by the discipline of instruction, refuses to look at it.

For just as temptation is often drawn in through the eyes, so sometimes desire conceived inwardly compels the eyes to serve it outwardly. Frequently some object is looked upon by an innocent mind, but by that very sight the soul is pierced by the sword of desire. David did not deliberately look upon Uriah’s wife because he had desired her; rather, he desired her because he had looked upon her carelessly.

[Col. 0803A] By the examination of righteous retribution, it comes about that the one who uses the exterior carelessly is justly blinded in the interior eye. Often, however, desire rules inwardly, and the enticed mind tyrannically requires the bodily senses to serve its purposes. It compels the eyes to serve its pleasures and, so to speak, opens the windows of light onto the darkness of blindness.

Therefore, when holy men feel themselves assailed by sinister pleasure, they restrain the very lights through which the appearance of beauty enters the mind, under the discipline of instruction, lest the vision of an evil thought, having enticed them, become its servant. If this is ever neglected and not carefully guarded, the uncleanness of thought immediately passes into action.

## CHAPTER X — Concerning David’s repentance for Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:13).

When the humility of mind that must be preserved was being discussed in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXIII (No. 23), the following was added:

> “Concerning David’s repentance for Bathsheba.”

[Col. 0803B] The sins of such men—David and Peter—were inserted into sacred Scripture so that the downfall of the great might be a warning to the lesser. Their repentance and forgiveness are also shown there so that the recovery of those who have been lost may be the hope of those who are perishing.

Therefore, let no one be proud because of David’s fall from his position. Let no one despair because David rose after his fall. Behold how wonderfully sacred Scripture presses down the proud with the very word by which it raises the humble. It related one event, yet in different ways it recalled the proud to the fear of humility and the humble to the confidence of hope.

O immeasurable medicine of a new kind, which, set forth in one and the same pattern, dries up what is swollen by pressing it down and pours moisture into what is parched by lifting it up! It terrified us by the fall of the great, but strengthened us by their restoration.

Thus always, and thus by the mercy of divine providence, God both restrains those who are proud and supports us lest we fall into despair.

[No. 25] But since the occasion required David to be brought forward and we have recalled so great a crime, the reader’s mind may perhaps wonder why almighty God does not preserve from bodily vices those whom he has chosen forever and whom he has raised even to the summit of spiritual gifts. Since we believe that an answer should be given quickly, we respond briefly.

Some fall into the vice of pride through the virtues they have received and through the grace devoted to good works, yet they do not recognize what they have fallen into. Therefore, because the ancient enemy already rules inwardly over us, he is permitted to rage outwardly as well, so that those who are exalted in thought may be cast down through the pleasures of the flesh.

We know that sometimes falling into bodily corruption is a lesser evil than sinning through deliberate pride in silent thought. But because pride is considered less disgraceful, it is less carefully avoided. People are more ashamed of lust because everyone recognizes its disgrace. Thus it often happens that some who fall from pride into lust become ashamed of the hidden evil of their fault through their open fall, and then correct even greater matters when, being prostrate in lesser ones, they are more gravely confounded.

[Col. 0803D] They see themselves guilty in lesser matters who had believed themselves free in more serious ones. Therefore, by the merciful dispensation of the Lord, the evil spirit is sometimes released and draws a person from one fault to another; and while he strikes more forcefully, he loses the one whom he had seized. By the very means through which he appears to have conquered, he is overcome.

It is worthwhile to consider how greatly God holds us within the secure embrace of grace through the favor of his mercy. Behold: the one who exalts himself through virtue returns to humility through vice. The one who is exalted by the virtues he has received is wounded not by a sword but, so to speak, by a medicine. For what is virtue except medicine, and what is vice except a wound?

Because we make a wound out of medicine, he makes medicine out of a wound, so that we who are struck by virtue may be healed by vice. We turn the gifts of virtues to the [lacuna]use of vices; he takes the allurements of vices [Col. 0804A] into the fortress of virtues. He strikes the state of our salvation in order to preserve it, so that, having fled from humility while running, we may at least cling to it when fallen.

Amid these things, however, it must be understood that many people, the more they fall in numerous ways, are bound more tightly. When the ancient enemy strikes them with one vice so that they fall, he also binds them with another so that they cannot rise again.

[No. 28] Let a person therefore consider what adversary he is fighting. If he already recognizes that he has sinned in some matter, let him at least fear being drawn from one fault into another, so that he may diligently avoid the wounds by which the enemy frequently kills. For it is exceedingly rare that our enemy serves the salvation of the elect even through wounds.

The Lord often subjects his elect to the tempter for their instruction. Thus, after the barriers of paradise, and after the secrets of the third heaven, so that Paul might not be exalted by the greatness of his revelations, an angel of Satan was given to him (2 Corinthians 12:7). Through this very temptation it was arranged that those who might have perished through pride would be saved from destruction through humility.

[Col. 0804B] Thus, by the hidden order of divine providence, from the place where the devil’s wickedness is permitted to rage, the goodness of God is mercifully perfected. Our adversary obeys the commands of heavenly grace precisely where he exercises the wrath of his most wicked will.

## CHAPTER XI — “The Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13).

When the remission of the sins of offenders, together with the fitting vengeance of punishment, was being discussed in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book IX (No. 54), the following was added:

> “The Lord has taken away your sin.”

[Col. 0804C] If the Lord took away David’s sin, so detestable as it was, why did he afterward allow all the things that the Lord had spoken to him through the prophet concerning that same sin?

Without doubt, the Lord does not leave a crime without punishment. Either the person himself punishes it in himself through repentance, or God strikes him while taking vengeance together with him. Sin is therefore not spared, because it is never released without punishment.

Thus David deserved to hear after his confession: “The Lord has taken away your sin”; yet afterward, afflicted by many sufferings and fleeing, he paid the debt of the guilt he had committed. In the same way, we are absolved from the guilt of our first parent through the wave of salvation, yet, cleansing away the debt of that same guilt, we who have been absolved still die bodily, because our sins are cut away either by us or by God himself, even when he releases them.

From his elect he strives to wipe away through temporal affliction the stains of iniquity that he does not wish to punish in them forever.

## CHAPTER XII — “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, for the Lord has commanded him to curse David” (2 Samuel 16:10).

When patience amid adversity, in the face of temptation, was being discussed through the recollection of past sins in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXX (No. 37), the following was added:

> “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?”

[Col. 0804D] Whoever is rightly ordered by the illumination of divine grace should hasten by the wing of holy desire from the lowest things to the highest, toward contemplation above. Let him place before the eyes of his mind the deeds of the holy fathers who preceded him, make progress by exercising himself in their imitation, and restrain what presently provokes him through vice either by recalling past evils, by the consolation of former gifts, or, as has been said, by imitation of the fathers who preceded him, so that he may be moved toward what is better.

As we have proposed, this must be demonstrated by clearer examples, so that, to speak of one among many, the diligent reader may understand many things from a few. Whoever, oppressed by verbal insults, is unable to preserve the virtue of patience should recall David’s conduct. When Shimei pressed him with so many reproaches [Note: Utica reads: “reproached him”] and armed nobles sought to avenge him, David said: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, for the Lord has commanded him to curse David.”

[Col. 0805A] Who would dare to ask why he acted in this way? A little later he said: “Let him curse, according to the Lord’s command, if perhaps the Lord looks upon my affliction and repays me good for this day’s cursing.”

By these words he clearly indicates that, while fleeing from his son who had risen against him because of his crime with Bathsheba, he recalled to mind the evil he had committed, endured calmly what he heard, and regarded the insulting words not so much as reproaches as aids, by which he judged that he might be cleansed and receive mercy.

We tolerate insults well when, in the secret of our mind, we return to the evils we have committed. What seems light is the injury with which we are struck when we see in our conduct that what we deserve is worse. Thus it comes about that gratitude rather than anger is owed for insults, since, through their intervention, we trust that a heavier punishment may be avoided before God the judge.

## CHAPTER XIII — Concerning Joab, who held Amasa’s chin with his right hand and struck him with his left (2 Samuel 20:9).

When the malice of hypocrites was being discussed in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XV (No. 13), the following was added:

> “Concerning Joab, who held Amasa’s chin with his right hand,” etc.

[Col. 0805B] What does it mean that Joab held Amasa’s chin with his right hand but secretly brought his left hand to the sword and spilled out his entrails, except what is plainly understood? To hold the chin with the right hand is to flatter as though out of kindness; but he brings his left hand to the sword because he strikes secretly out of malice.

## CHAPTER XIV — That David, who earlier did not fear desiring another man’s wife, afterward recoiled when he desired water from the cistern (2 Samuel 23:16–17).

When the purification of the elect’s life through the recollection of their own excesses was being discussed in Homily 34 on the Gospels (No. 16), the following was added:

> “That David, who earlier did not fear desiring another man’s wife,” etc.

[Col. 0805C] It must be considered with the greatest care that one who remembers having committed illicit acts should strive to abstain even from certain licit things. In this way he may make satisfaction to his Creator: the one who committed what was forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what was permitted, and the one who remembers that he sinned in great matters should rebuke himself in small ones.

What I say is excessive if I do not establish it from the testimonies of sacred eloquence. Certainly, the law of the Old Testament forbids desiring another man’s wife (Exodus 20:17); but it does not prohibit the king from ordering brave deeds from his soldiers, or from desiring water, under penalty. We all know that David, pierced by the sword of desire, both desired and took another man’s wife; fitting blows followed his guilt, and through the lamentations of repentance he corrected the evil he had committed.

[Col. 0805D] Much later, while he was sitting opposite the ranks of the enemy, he desired to drink water from their cistern. His chosen soldiers broke through the midst of the enemy forces and brought back unharmed the water the king had desired. But the man trained by scourges immediately rebuked himself for desiring water at the risk of his soldiers, and poured it out to the Lord as a libation. As it is written: “He poured it out to the Lord” (2 Samuel 23:17).

The water poured out was transformed into a sacrifice to the Lord, because through the repentance of his self-reproach he sacrificed the guilt of desire. Thus the man who once did not fear desiring another’s wife afterward recoiled when he desired water. Because he remembered that he had committed illicit acts, he was now strict with himself and abstained even from what was permitted.

## CHAPTER XV — That David sinned by numbering the people (2 Samuel 24:2).

When it was being discussed that subjects should not judge the life and conduct of their rulers, in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXV (No. 3), the following was added:

> “That David sinned by numbering the people.”

[Col. 0806A] The actions of rulers are arranged according to the qualities of their subjects, so that often, because of the wickedness of the flock, even the truly good life of the shepherd falls into sin. David—the man praised by God, the prophet conscious of heavenly mysteries—was inflated by the sudden swelling of pride, sinned by numbering the people, and yet, while David sinned, the people received punishment.

Why was this? Because the hearts of rulers are arranged according to the merits of the peoples. The just Judge corrected the ruler’s vice through the very people whose cause had occasioned his sin. But because David himself, who had become proud by his own will, was not free from guilt, he too received punishment for his sin. The wrath that raged and struck the people bodily also prostrated their ruler through inward grief of heart.

It is certain that the merits of rulers and peoples are so mutually connected that often the life of the people becomes worse through the fault of their shepherds, and often the life of shepherds is changed through the merit of their people.

[No. 36; Col. 0806B] But because rulers have their own judge, it is a matter of great caution for subjects not rashly to judge the lives of their rulers. For the Lord did not without reason himself drive out the money changers and overturn the seats of those selling doves (Matthew 21), clearly signifying that through teachers he judges the life of the people, but by himself examines the deeds of teachers. The faults of subjects, moreover, which teachers either neglect to judge or are unable to judge at present, are undoubtedly reserved for his judgment.

Therefore, when the matter is conducted in sound faith, it is a mark of virtue to tolerate whatever belongs to the one who precedes us. Yet one should humbly suggest what displeases, if perhaps it can be corrected. The greatest care must be taken, however, lest the disordered defense of justice turn into pride; lest, while righteousness is loved carelessly, humility—the teacher of righteousness itself—be lost; and lest anyone despise having as his superior one whom he may happen to criticize in some action.

Against this swelling of pride, the mind of subjects is subdued for the preservation of humility if they continually attend to their own weakness. For we neglect to examine our strength truthfully, and because we believe ourselves stronger than we are, we judge strictly those who have been placed over us. The less we know ourselves, the more we see those whom we strive to rebuke.

[Col. 0806C] All these are evils that are often committed by subjects against superiors and by superiors against subjects. Those who govern consider all their subjects less wise than themselves; and those who are subject judge the actions of their rulers. If they happened to hold authority themselves, they think they could act better.

Thus it often happens that rulers see less prudently what ought to be done because the fog of pride itself obscures their eyes. Sometimes the one who is subject does, once he has become a superior, what he previously criticized as a subject; and because he commits what he had judged, he ought at least to be ashamed that he judged it.

Therefore, just as superiors must take care that their hearts are not exalted by the position above them through an estimation of their unique wisdom, so subjects must take care that the actions of their rulers do not displease them.

[No. 37; Col. 0806D] But if the life of teachers is rightly reproved, subjects must nevertheless respect them even when they displease them. This must be observed carefully: do not desire to imitate one whom it is necessary to respect, nor, because you disdain imitating someone, refuse to respect him.

A subtle path of righteousness and humility must be maintained, so that the reprehensible deeds of teachers may displease the mind of subjects without causing that mind to depart from preserving reverence for the teaching office.

# BOOK NINE [Col. 0805]
## Concerning Testimonies from the Third Book of Kings

## CHAPTER I — Solomon, after receiving wisdom from God, is tested in judgment by women of ill repute (1 Kings 3:16).

[Col. 0805D–0807A] When the temptations of the elect, for the benefit of those making progress, were being discussed in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VIII (No. 48), the following was added:

> “Solomon, after receiving wisdom from God,” etc.

It should be noted that, after the Lord illuminates the darkness of our error with the light of his knowledge, he immediately tests us by visiting us with the goad of temptation. He advances us toward virtues by kindling our hearts, yet by withdrawing he permits us to be shaken by temptation.

For if the mind is shaken by no temptation after receiving gifts of virtue, it boasts that it possesses these things from itself. Therefore, so that it may both possess the gifts of firmness and humbly recognize its own weakness, it is lifted to high things by the approach of grace, and by grace’s withdrawal it is shown what it is of itself.

This is aptly indicated to us by the historical account of sacred reading, for Solomon is recorded both to have received wisdom from God and, immediately after receiving that same wisdom, to have been tested by the case of the prostitutes. As soon as he received the grace of so great a revelation, he endured the contest involving wicked women. For often, when an awareness of inward generosity illuminates our mind through the virtues granted to us, slippery thoughts immediately disturb it, so that the mind which rejoices at having been raised up by an immense gift may discover what it is when struck by temptation as well.

[Col. 0807B] Thus Elijah, visited by a word from above, opened the heavens (3 Kings 19:3), yet, suddenly tested, fled weakly through the wilderness and was afraid of one woman. Thus Paul, caught up to the third heaven, contemplated the secrets of paradise, yet, returning to himself, struggled against the battles of the flesh. He bore another law in his members, and his spirit grieved to be wearied by the rebellion of that law within him (Romans 7:23).

[Note: Utica reads: “against the vices of the flesh.”]

After granting a gift, therefore, God tests a person because, by bestowing the gift, he raises him up, while by withdrawing it for a little while he shows the person to himself. We suffer this, without doubt, until, with the stain of sin completely wiped away, we are restored to the substance of the incorruption that has been promised.

## CHAPTER II — Concerning Solomon’s judgment between the women, one of whom killed her son, whom she had been accustomed to nurse while awake, while she was asleep (1 Kings 3:17).

[Col. 0807C] When preachers who speak correctly but offer their hearers wicked examples through their own conduct were being discussed in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXI (Nos. 16–17), the following was added:

> “Concerning Solomon’s judgment between the women,” etc.

What is signified by the names of the nursing mothers except the order of teachers, and what by their sons except the persons of disciples?

Teachers are awake in knowledge but asleep in life. They nourish their hearers through the vigils of preaching, but, while neglecting to do what they say, they kill them through the sleep of sluggishness and crush those whom they seemed to be feeding with the milk of words.

Hence, while they themselves live reprehensibly and cannot have disciples of praiseworthy life, they often try to draw others to themselves, so that, by showing that they possess good followers, they may excuse before human judgments the evils they commit and, as it were, conceal their deadly negligence through the life of their subjects.

Thus there the woman who had killed her own son sought another’s; yet Solomon’s sword discovered the true mother, because at the final judgment the anger of the strict Judge will reveal whose fruit lives and whose perishes.

[Col. 0807D] There is also something here that must be carefully observed: the living son is first ordered to be divided, so that afterward he may be given to the one mother alone. For in this life the disciple’s life is permitted, as it were, to be divided, when one person is sometimes allowed to have merit before God and another praise before men.

But the false mother does not fear having the child she did not bear killed, because arrogant teachers, ignorant of charity, if they cannot obtain the fullest name of praise from other people’s disciples, cruelly pursue their lives. Kindled by the torch of envy, they do not want those to live for others whom they see themselves unable to possess.

[Col. 0808A] Thus the perverse woman cries: “Let it be neither mine nor hers” (1 Kings 3:26). As we have said, they begrudge others the life in truth, for temporal glory, of those whom they do not see obeying them.

But the true mother strives that her son may at least belong to another and live. For truthful teachers allow other people to receive the praise of teaching from their disciples, provided that those disciples do not lose the integrity of their life.

By these compassionate entrails the true mother is recognized: all teaching is approved in the examination of charity, and she alone deserved to receive the whole child who, as it were, granted the whole child away. Faithful superiors, because they not only do not begrudge others the praise arising from their good disciples but also pray that others may benefit from their progress, receive their children whole and living when, at the supreme examination, they obtain the joys of perfect recompense from their disciples’ life.

## CHAPTER III — “When the house was being built, it was built of stones hewn and finished; and neither hammer nor axe nor any iron tool was heard in the house when it was being built” (1 Kings 6:7).

[Col. 0808B] When the purification of the present life and the reward of perpetual rest were being discussed in the *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIV (No. 23), the following was added:

> “When the house was being built,” etc.

What did that house figure except the holy Church, which the Lord inhabits in the heavens? For its construction the souls of the elect are brought like polished stones.

When they are built in heaven, no hammer of discipline resounds there, because we are brought there as hewn and finished stones, to be arranged in places corresponding to our merits. Here we are beaten outside, so that there we may be found without reproach.

Here the hammer, here the axe, here all the iron tools of blows resound; but in the house of God no blows are heard, because in the eternal homeland every noise of striking falls silent. No hammer strikes there, because no punishment afflicts; no axe cuts there, because no sentence of severity casts those received inside back outside. No tools resound, because no lashes, however slight, are felt any longer.

[Col. 0808C] The stones were therefore struck outside so that they might be placed in the construction of the Lord’s temple without the sound of the hammer. For now we are struck outside by scourges so that afterward we may be arranged within the temple of God without the blows of discipline, so that whatever is excessive in us may be cut away now by blows, and then only the harmony of charity may bind us together in the building.

## CHAPTER IV — That before the doors of the temple the bronze sea, that is, the basin for washing the hands of those entering, is carried by twelve oxen, whose faces project outward but whose hindquarters are hidden (1 Kings 7:23).

When, in considering the cleansing of the stains of subjects through the merit of the lives of rulers, the discussion turned to *Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapter 5, near the end, the following was added: “That before the entrance of the temple the bronze sea—that is, the basin for washing the hands of those entering—is carried by twelve oxen,” etc. —What is signified by the twelve oxen except the entire order of pastors? Concerning them, as Paul explains, the Law says: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing” (1 Cor. IX, 9; from Deut. XXV, 4). We see their works openly, but we do not know what will later await them from the strict Judge in hidden retribution. Yet when, with the patience of their condescension, they prepare themselves for washing away the confessions of their neighbors, they carry the basin as it were before the entrance of the temple, so that whoever strives to enter the gate of eternity may disclose his temptations to the pastor’s mind and, as in the basin of the oxen, wash the hands of his thought or deed.

### CHAPTER V.—That in the temple service, on the bases of the temple, lions, oxen, and cherubim were represented in sculptured work (1 Kings VII, 29).

When the perfection of the priestly office was being discussed, in *Homily 17 on the Gospels* (No. 12), the following was added: “That in the temple service,” etc. —The cherubim are called the fullness of knowledge. But what is the meaning of the fact that on the bases neither lions are made without oxen, nor oxen without lions? For what else do the bases in the temple signify except priests in the Church? While they endure the responsibility of governance, they bear a burden placed upon them, as bases do. Thus cherubim are represented on the bases, since it is fitting that the hearts of priests should be filled with the fullness of knowledge.

By the lions, the terror of severity is signified; by the oxen, the patience of gentleness. Therefore neither lions without oxen nor oxen without lions are represented on the bases, because in the priestly heart the virtue of gentleness must always be guarded together with the terror of severity, so that gentleness may temper anger, and zeal for strictness may kindle that same gentleness lest it become lax.

### CHAPTER VI.—A cloud filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not minister because of the cloud (1 Kings VIII, 10).

When the discussion concerned the blind minds of the Jews, through a depraved understanding, searching into the mysteries of the sacred word, in *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXX (No. 2), the following was added: “A cloud filled the house of the Lord,” etc. —Because of their deserts, while the proud Jewish priests heard the divine mysteries through parables, the priests could not minister in the house of the Lord, as though because of a cloud. Likewise, in the Old Testament, when they disdained to investigate the mystical meanings concealed beneath the veil of the letter amid the dark obscurities of allegories, they lost the ministry owed by their faith because of the cloud.

At that time, too, the Lord uttered the voice of his teaching within the cloud, when he also spoke openly about himself. For what is clearer than: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30)? What is clearer than: “Before Abraham was, I am” (John VIII, 58)? But because the minds of the hearers had been filled with the darkness of unbelief, the intervening cloud concealed the ray of sunlight, so to speak.

What is signified by the cloud except the darkness of understanding? And because, when the Lord appeared in the flesh, the minds of the priests suffered darkness concerning the understanding of him, the cloud—that is, the Synagogue, the house of the Lord—filled it. The priests could not minister because of the cloud, because, having been darkened by the plague of their faithlessness concerning the understanding of the incarnate God, they lost the ministry of the true priesthood.

### CHAPTER VII.—Concerning the prophet whom a lion killed as he was returning on the road (1 Kings XIII, 16–18).

When the discussion concerned restraining the heart’s self-assurance amid prosperity through recognition of human weakness, in *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXIII (Nos. 53, 54), the following was added: “Concerning the prophet whom a lion killed as he was returning on the road.” —What is a human being, whatever his merit may be, if he is abandoned by the protection of his Creator? That protection seems less necessary if it is always possessed. Yet it is often usefully withdrawn, so that a person may be shown what he is without it.

The hand of the Lord therefore sometimes reveals us to ourselves through adversity—the same hand that, even without our knowing it, carries us in prosperity. For when we are abandoned, we begin to fall, yet when we are assisted, we are held back; thus our trembling in the fall becomes instruction, and our remaining upright becomes guardianship.

Let no one, therefore, consider himself possessed of any virtue, even when he can do something bravely, because if divine protection abandons him, he is suddenly overwhelmed weakly precisely where he had boasted that he stood firmly. For what does it mean that the man of God, sent to prophesy against the altar of Samaria, exercised the authority of a free voice in the presence of the king and miraculously stiffened the king’s outstretched arm into rigidity, yet soon mercifully restored it to health? He refused to eat in the king’s house when invited, because he kept the Lord’s command forbidding him to eat on the way; yet on that same road he was both deceived into eating and, after being fed, perished.

What do we gather from this on careful consideration—or, so to speak, what do we suspect should be feared—except that perhaps, while he silently gloried before himself in having despised the king for the sake of the Lord’s commands, he was soon shaken from his inward firmness, and from the place where glory arose in his heart, guilt slipped into his action, so that, deceived by the words of the false prophet, he might learn that it had not been through his own strength that he had resisted the king’s words?

He rightly received the sentence of death from the mouth of the one whose deception had caused him to deviate from the command of life, so that he might truly receive punishment from the place where he had negligently incurred guilt.

### CHAPTER VIII.—The Lord God of Israel lives, in whose sight I stand (1 Kings XVII, 1).

When the discussion concerned the interpretation of sacred speech, in *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XI (No. 49), the following was added: “The Lord God of Israel lives,” etc. —It should be known that we come into the sight of the Lord in two ways. In one way, we place ourselves in his sight here by carefully weighing our sins and judging them with tears.

[Note: The printed editions read “we punish”; we follow the manuscripts.]

In the other way, we come into the sight of the Lord when, at the final judgment, we stand before his tribunal. For whenever we bring the power of our Creator back to our awareness, we stand in his sight. Thus it is rightly said now through Elijah, the man of God: “The Lord God of Israel lives, in whose sight I stand.”

### CHAPTER IX.—It is enough for me, Lord; please take my life (1 Kings XIX, 4).

When the discussion concerned the temptations of the elect through a hidden dispensation, in *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XIX (Nos. 9, 10), the following was added: “It is enough for me, Lord; please take my life.” —Holy men who, lifted up by the Spirit, are carried to the heights are restrained by certain temptations as long as they remain in this life, lest they become proud through some form of exaltation; thus they are never able to advance as far as they wish.

But lest they be lifted up by pride, a certain measure of their virtues is established within them. Hence Elijah, although he had advanced to great heights through so many virtues, was held back by a certain measure when he fled from Jezebel, who, though a queen, was nevertheless only a little woman.

I consider this man of extraordinary virtue: drawing fire from heaven; at his sudden request consuming two companies of fifty men with all their men; closing the heavens against rain by a word and opening them again to rain by a word; raising the dead; and foreseeing things to come. And then again his fearful flight before a single woman comes to mind.

I contemplate a man struck with fear, asking death from the hand of God and not receiving it, while fleeing death from the hand of a woman. For he sought death while fleeing, saying: “It is enough; take my life, for I am no better than my fathers.”

Whence, then, was he so powerful that he could perform all those virtues? Whence so weak that he feared a woman so greatly? Only because, by the dispensation of the heavenly will, they are weighed according to a hidden measure of balance, so that these holy men of God may possess great power through God, yet again be moderated by a certain measure through their own weakness.

In those virtues Elijah recognized what he had received from God; in these weaknesses he recognized what he himself was. That power was virtue; this weakness was the guardian of virtue. In those virtues he showed what he had received; in these weaknesses he preserved what he had received. Elijah was displayed in the miracles; he was preserved in his weaknesses.

### CHAPTER X.—Behold, the Lord passes by: a great and strong wind overturning mountains and shattering rocks before the Lord. The Lord is not in the wind. And after the wind, an earthquake; the Lord is not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake, fire; the Lord is not in the fire. And after the fire, the sound of a gentle breeze, and there the Lord is (1 Kings XIX, 11 and following).

When the discussion concerned the vision of the uncircumscribed divine substance, insofar as it is denied to bodily eyes, in *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book V (No. 66), the following was added: “Behold, the Lord passes by,” etc. —The wind before the Lord overturns mountains and shatters rocks, because the fear that rushes upon us at his coming casts down the height of our hearts and melts their hardness.

But the Lord is said not to be in the wind of the earthquake or in the fire; he is not denied to be in the sound of the gentle breeze, because whenever the mind is suspended in the sublimity of contemplation, whatever it is able perfectly to behold is not God. But when it perceives something subtle, this is what it hears concerning the incomprehensible substance of eternity.

For we perceive something like the sound of a gentle breeze when, in sudden contemplation, we subtly taste the savor of uncircumscribed truth. What we know of God is true when we feel that we cannot fully know anything about him.

Hence it is rightly added there: “When Elijah heard this, he covered his face with his cloak and, entering, stood at the entrance of the cave” (ibid.). After the sound of the gentle breeze, the prophet covered his face with his cloak, because in that most subtle contemplation of truth he recognizes how greatly a human being is veiled by ignorance.

To draw a cloak over the face is for the mind not to dare seek higher things; it is to veil oneself through consideration of one’s own weakness, so that one may not rashly open the eyes of understanding beyond oneself, but reverently close them to what one is unable to grasp.

While doing this, he is described as standing at the entrance of the cave. For what is our cave except this habitation of corruption, in which we are still held by our old condition? But when we begin to perceive something of the knowledge of divinity, we stand, as it were, at the entrance of our cave.

For although we cannot proceed fully, yet, longing for knowledge of the truth, we already catch something of the breeze of freedom. To stand at the entrance of the cave is, with the obstacle of our corruption restrained, to begin to emerge toward knowledge of the truth.

Hence, when the cloud descended upon the tabernacle, the Israelites are also remembered as standing at the entrances of their tents, watching from a distance, because those who perceive the coming of divinity in any way are already, as it were, proceeding out of the dwelling place of the flesh.

### CHAPTER XI.—When Elijah heard the voice of the Lord speaking with him, he is described as standing at the entrance of his cave and covering his face (1 Kings XIX, 9, 13).

[Col. 0811C]

[Note: In Michael and Gemeticus this is attributed to Homily 1 on Ezekiel, where it is not found.]

When the progress of the elect through heavenly grace was being discussed, in *Commentary on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 1 (Nos. 17, 18), the following was added: “When Elijah heard the voice of the Lord speaking with him,” etc. —What does it mean that, when the prophet heard the voice of the Lord speaking with him, he stood at the entrance of his cave and covered his face, except that, when through the grace of contemplation the voice of heavenly understanding comes to be in the mind, the whole person is no longer within the cave, because concern for the flesh does not possess the soul?

Yet he stands at the entrance because he is considering how to leave the narrow confines of mortality. But whoever already stands at the entrance of the cave and perceives God’s words with the ear of the heart must cover his face, because, when through heavenly grace we are led to understand higher things, the more subtly we are lifted up, the more we must always press ourselves down in our understanding through humility.

We must not try to understand more than we ought to understand, but understand with sobriety (Rom. XII). We must not go astray by investigating invisible things too closely, nor seek something belonging to bodily light in that incorporeal nature.

To incline the ear and cover the face is to hear the voice of the inner substance through the mind, while nevertheless turning the eyes of the heart away from every bodily form, lest the soul imagine anything corporeal in that nature which is wholly everywhere and everywhere uncircumscribed.

### CHAPTER XII.—I have left seven thousand men for myself who have not bent the knee before Baal (1 Kings XIX, 18).

When the discussion concerned avoiding the vice of self-exaltation, in *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXI (No. 107), the following was added: “I have left seven thousand men for myself who have not bent the knee before Baal.” —It is certain that the person who, while doing what is right, neglects to consider the merits of those who are better extinguishes the eye of his heart through the darkness of self-exaltation.

By contrast, the person who carefully weighs the good deeds of others illuminates himself with a great ray of humility. For when he sees that what he himself has done has also been done openly by others, he suppresses the swelling of pride that attempts to erupt from his inward sense of uniqueness.

Hence the Lord’s voice is said to Elijah, who thought he alone remained: “I have left seven thousand men for myself who have not bent the knee before Baal,” so that, when he recognized that he was not the only one left, he might avoid the glory of self-exaltation that could arise in him from his supposed uniqueness.

He was indeed a prophet and had often learned heavenly mysteries. What difficulty, then, would there have been in recognizing that other faithful servants of God remained in the world? Yet here we should carefully observe how wickedly self-exaltation closes the eye of the heart: the man who, when humble, knew God’s hidden judgments, when exalted did not know even what was obvious.

### CHAPTER XIII.—I saw the Lord seated upon his throne, and the host of heaven stood at his right and at his left; and it was said: “By what means shall I deceive Ahab, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?” One said one thing, and another said something else. Then one came forward and said: “I will deceive Ahab.” And it was said: “By what means will you deceive him?” He answered: “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” (1 Kings XXII, 19 and following).

[Col. 0812B]

When the discussion concerned the ministries of elect and reprobate spirits through the hidden order of divine distribution, in *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book II (No. 38), the following was added: “I saw the Lord seated upon his throne,” etc. —What should we understand by the Lord’s throne except the angelic powers? Presiding more highly over their minds, he disposes all things below.

And what is the host of heaven except the multitude of ministering angels? What does it mean, then, that the host of heaven is said to stand at his right and at his left? God, who is so within all things that he is also outside all things, is enclosed by neither right nor left. Rather, the right side of God signifies the elect part of the angels, while the left side signifies the reprobate part of the angels.

For not only the good, who assist, minister to God, but also the evil, who test. Not only those who lift up people returning from sin, but also those who burden people unwilling to return. Nor does the designation “host of heaven” prohibit our understanding the reprobate part of the angels within it.
