For we call those whom we know to be suspended in the air “birds of heaven.” And Paul says of these same spirits: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI, 12). Naming their chief, he says: “According to the prince of the power of this air” (Eph. II, 2).

Thus the host of angels stands at the right and at the left of God, because the will of the elect spirits agrees with divine mercy, while the mind of the reprobate, serving its own wickedness, obeys the judgment of his strictness.

Hence a lying spirit is immediately described as coming forward, through whom King Ahab was deceived according to the demands of his own deserts. For it is not permissible to believe that a good spirit wished to serve deception when he said: “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.”

But because King Ahab, through his preceding sins, was worthy to be condemned by such a deception, so that he who had often willingly fallen into guilt might at some point be captured unwillingly for punishment, hidden justice grants wicked spirits permission to drag those whom they willingly strangle in the snare of sin, even unwillingly into the punishment of sin.

[Note: These words are not found at the indicated place. They exist in the manuscript of Michael as though separated from what precedes, as may be inferred from the larger initial letter with which the line begins, precisely like those placed at the beginnings of chapters. In Gemeticus, “Likewise, concerning what was said above” is prefixed. In Uticensis, “Likewise, in the same book” is prefixed.]

A person who does not avoid a wicked life and does not turn his mind away from committing sins, when he asks a prophet something, hears, by God’s arrangement, what he deserves to hear as one destined for condemnation.

For behold, to speak of one or two examples among many, the house of Israel had withdrawn from the worship of almighty God into the service of idols, yet it frequently came to the prophets, by whom it was accustomed to be deceived, seeking prosperity. When it heard prosperity from the mouths of prophets while acting perversely, what else were the heavenly judgments doing except capturing the sinful people in their own heart?

Thus, because it had sinned by following faithlessness, it was deceived by the flattering words of its prophets, so that it no longer feared having sinned, and afterward was dragged to punishment all the more harshly because it now lived more securely in guilt.

But now, by the gift of almighty God, the human race has been removed from the worship of idols, publicly professes the true faith, and refuses to submit in worship to wood, stone, or any creature. Therefore anyone established in the faith now consults a prophet securely, since he is going to hear what it is fitting for a faithful person to hear.

I will speak confidently: if he had withdrawn from other impurities and wicked actions, he would be secure. For Paul, that outstanding preacher, cries out: “And greed, which is the service of idols” (Eph. V, 5).

Whoever is still subject to greed is not free from the worship of idols. If, therefore, a person who pants with the fever of greed appears to be established in the faith but seeks to acquire what belongs to others, desires the honors of the world, longs to surpass others in temporal glory, and consults a prophet about that same glory, it is entirely just that, according to the merit of his guilt, he should hear prosperity from the prophet’s mouth.

Thus the person who refused to hear God’s words in the sacred writings, so that he might despise earthly things and love heavenly ones, hears from the mouth of his prophet, by God’s judgment, what will cause him to fall more deeply into bondage: delighted by hope of earthly glory, he is nourished by it and continually led downward by his desires.

For that spirit was not good who desired to become false in the mouths of the prophets. Hence it was stated earlier that the host of heaven stood at his right and left. God, who is uncircumscribed truth, has no left side in that eternal blessedness called his right, because nothing displeasing can exist there; rather, he sees all things together and beholds everything at once.

But the realm in which the good and evil spirit lives is described as having the host of heaven at the right and at the left, so that by the right we understand the elect angels, and by the left the reprobate spirits.

Nor should it trouble us that the rejected angels are also called the host of heaven, because although they have been expelled from the ethereal heaven, they nevertheless still dwell in the aerial heaven, as Paul says: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI, 21).

# BOOK TEN

## Concerning Testimonies on the Fourth Book of Kings

[Col. 0813]

### CHAPTER I.—Concerning Elijah, that he was taken up into heaven (2 Kings II, 11, 12).

[Col. 0813B]

When the Lord’s Ascension, prefigured through the taking up of Elijah, was being discussed, in *Homily 29 on the Gospels* (Nos. 5, 6), the following was added: “Concerning Elijah, that he was taken up into heaven.” —What does it mean that Elijah is said to have been taken up into heaven? Do we believe that, while he was still placed in corruptible flesh, he was brought before the Lord’s resurrection and ascension into the bosom of that highest peace?

But the aerial heaven is one thing, and the ethereal heaven another. The aerial heaven is close to the earth. Hence we speak of the birds of heaven, because we see them flying through the air.

Elijah was lifted up into the aerial heaven, so that he might suddenly be led to a certain hidden region of the earth, where he would live in great peace of flesh and spirit until he returns at the end of the world and pays the debt of death.

By being lifted up, Elijah signified the Lord’s Ascension. He postponed death; he did not escape it. But our Redeemer, because he did not postpone death, overcame it; by rising again he consumed it, and by ascending he revealed the glory of his resurrection.

It should also be noted that Elijah is read to have ascended in a chariot, so that it might plainly be shown that a mere human being needed assistance from another. For these aids were made and displayed through angels, since the one whom the weakness of his nature weighed down could not ascend by himself even into the aerial heaven.

But our Redeemer is not read to have been lifted up by a chariot or by angels, because he who had made all things was evidently carried above all things by his own power. He was returning there where he was and was departing from there where he remained. For when he ascended into heaven through his humanity, by the power of his divinity he continued to contain both earth and heaven.

Just as Joseph, sold by his brothers, prefigured the selling of our Redeemer (Gen. I, 5), so Enoch, translated, and Elijah, lifted up into the aerial heaven, each signified the Lord’s Ascension.

Therefore the Lord had heralds and witnesses of his Ascension: one before the Law and the other under the Law, so that he himself might eventually come who could truly penetrate the heavens.

The order among their two forms of elevation is also distinguished by certain stages of increase. For Enoch is remembered as having been translated, whereas Elijah was carried up into heaven, so that afterward there might come the one who would penetrate the ethereal heaven by his own power, neither translated nor carried up.

To show that he would also grant to us who believe in him the purity of his flesh, and that under him the virtue of chastity would increase through the progression of time, he displayed it both in the translation of those who signified the Lord’s Ascension as servants and in himself, the Lord who ascended into heaven.

Enoch had a wife and children; Elijah, however, is read to have had neither wife nor children. Consider, then, how the purity of chastity increased through the progression of time, as this is plainly shown both by the servants who were translated and by the Lord who ascended.

Enoch was translated, begotten through intercourse and himself begetting through intercourse. Elijah was taken up, begotten through intercourse but no longer begetting through intercourse. The Lord was taken up, begotten neither through intercourse nor begetting through intercourse.

### CHAPTER II.—Concerning the woman who, lest she lose her two sons when the creditor took them away, obeyed the words of the prophet Elisha and poured out what little oil she had into empty vessels; all these were afterward filled to the brim, and through their filling the woman was freed from her creditor’s debt (2 Kings IV, 1, 2).

[Col. 0814C]

When the discussion concerned the faith of the Gentile and Jewish peoples through the Church, through the merit of the Church’s growth, in *Homily 3 on Ezekiel* (No. 6), the following was added: “Concerning the woman who, lest she lose her two sons when the creditor took them away,” etc. —What is signified by this woman except the holy Church?

She is the mother of two peoples, that is, the Jewish and the Gentile peoples, as though of two sons. Through a wicked deed, by the persuasion of the crafty spirit, she had received from the creditor something like a coin of sin, and feared losing the two sons whom she had begotten in faith.

But obeying the words of the prophet—that is, the commands of sacred Scripture—she poured her little oil into empty vessels, because, while many empty minds hear a small measure of the love of divinity from the mouth of one teacher, they are filled to the brim, through overflowing grace, with the ointment of divine love.

Even now many hearts that had previously been empty vessels are full of the Spirit’s ointment, although they appeared to have been filled only from a small amount of oil. As this is given to one person after another and faith is received by the hearers, the woman of Sarepta—that is, the holy Church—is no longer held under the debt of her creditor.

### CHAPTER III.—Concerning the son of the Shunammite, whom the boy sent by Elisha with a staff did not raise; but Elisha himself came, stretched himself over the dead man, drew himself together upon his limbs, walked back and forth, and breathed seven times upon the dead man’s mouth, and immediately through the mystery of compassion brought him to life again (2 Kings IV, 27, 28 and following).

When the discussion concerned the grace of the New Testament manifested through the Mediator, in *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book IX (No. 63), the following was added: “Concerning the son of the Shunammite,” etc. —God, the author of the human race, grieved as over a dead child when, in pity, he looked upon us extinguished by the sting of iniquity.

And because through Moses he brought forth the terror of the Law, he sent the staff, as it were, through a boy. For God held the staff through the Law when he said: “If anyone does this or that, he shall surely die” (Heb. VII, 19).

Therefore the fear of sin was unable to raise us from the death of sin, but the grace of gentleness, breathed upon us, raised us to the state of life. Yet the boy with the staff was unable to raise the dead man, because, as Paul testifies, the Law brought nothing to perfection.

But he himself came in person and humbly stretched himself over the corpse, drawing himself together so that the dead man’s limbs might be made equal to his own, because, although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being (Phil. II, 6).

He walks back and forth, because he calls both Judea nearby and the nations situated far away. He breathes seven times upon the dead man, because, through the opening of the divine gift, he breathes the sevenfold Spirit upon those lying in the death of sin.

Immediately the living man rises, because the one whom the staff of terror could not raise returned to life through the Spirit of love.

### CHAPTER IV.—That, while the sons of the prophets were cutting wood in the Jordan, the ax-head of one of them slipped from its handle and disappeared into the depths. When the wooden handle was thrown in by Elisha, the iron returned to it (2 Kings VI, 4, 5).

When the discussion concerned preserving the gift of understanding in the performance of works, in *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXII (Nos. 9, 10), the following was added: “That, while the sons of the prophets were cutting wood in the Jordan,” etc. —The iron in the handle is the gift of understanding in the heart. To cut wood with it is to rebuke those acting wickedly.

Sometimes, when this is done carelessly, when the fall of vain glory in the knowledge received is not avoided, the iron is lost in the water, because through disordered conduct understanding is made foolish.

We know that this understanding is given so that it may be restored before the eyes of the giver through good action. Hence the one who had lost the iron rightly cried out: “Alas, alas, alas, my lord! And I had borrowed it” (2 Kings VI, 5).

The elect have this distinctive quality: if at some time the guilt of secret vanity slips into their knowledge, they quickly return to their heart and pursue with tears whatever they find in themselves to be condemnable before the eyes of the strict Judge.

In their weeping they carefully examine not only the evils they have committed, but also the good things they ought to have repaid from the gift they received, because they feel themselves all the more sinful insofar as they are held indebted for the good things they could have done but neglected.

The one who lost the iron therefore rightly cried out: “Alas, alas, alas, my lord! And I had borrowed it.” It is as though he were saying: “Through the disorder of negligence I lost what I received from the grace of the Creator so that I might repay it through good works.”

But God never abandons the mind that truly recognizes itself in sins. Hence Elisha immediately comes, throws the wood downward, and brings the iron to the surface, because our Redeemer, looking upon us with compassion, humbles the sinner’s heart and restores to him the understanding he had lost.

He submerges the wood and reveals the iron, because he afflicts the heart and restores knowledge. Hence another translation, the Septuagint translation, says that he broke the wood and threw it in, and thus lifted up the iron.

To break the wood is to crush the heart’s self-exaltation. To throw the wood downward is to humble the exalted heart in the knowledge of its own weakness, as we have said. Immediately the iron returns to the surface, because understanding returns to its former use in practice.

Since the gift of understanding that is received is scarcely preserved amid so many difficulties, we must take great care lest it grow dull through idleness, and lest, in the exercise of work, it vanish through the vice of self-exaltation.

Holy men do not rejoice merely when they know what they are doing, but when they do what they have learned. And if they rejoice in understanding the gift of the giver, they nevertheless consider with sorrow the duty of action, so that through action they may repay what has been bestowed upon them in understanding.

For a debtor is foolish who gladly receives borrowed money but does not consider the time when he must repay it. The joy of receiving is properly moderated when the appointed time for repayment is also considered with diligent foresight.

### CHAPTER V.—This is a day of tribulation, reproach, and blasphemy. The children have come to the point of birth, but the woman in labor has no strength (2 Kings XIX, 3, 4).

When the discussion concerned the difficulty involved in carrying out a work conceived in the mind, the following was added: “This is a day of tribulation,” etc.

[Note: In the manuscript of Michael, this is said to be excerpted from Homily 10 on Ezekiel, although it is not found there. In Gemeticus, Homily 5 on Ezekiel is assigned.]

In the literal sense, we see these things taking place because of sins: when enemies attack, your defenders are prepared, but in no way do the prepared ones grow strong. For it is written: “The spirit of counsel and fortitude will rest upon him” (Isa. XXI).

These two are necessarily joined together, because neither strength without counsel can be useful, nor counsel without strength. What benefit, then, do those prepared through counsel provide when they do not proceed to battle through strength?

Thus King Hezekiah, afflicted and troubled, says: “This is a day of tribulation, and a day of blasphemy. The children have come to the point of birth, but the woman in labor has no strength.”

The children come to the point of birth when suitable counsels proceed as far as the desire to accomplish a work. But the woman in labor has no strength because, while a weak person conceives counsels, he does not bring them through the birth of action to any useful result.

### CHAPTER VI.—Whatever remains of the house of Judah shall send down a root and produce fruit above (2 Kings XIX, 30).

When the discussion concerned the thoughts of the elect that will remain in eternal recompense, in *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XII (No. 54), the following was added: “Whatever remains of the house of Judah,” etc. —What the root is to a tree, a person’s thought is to each human being, because what is seen outwardly is held together by what is not seen outwardly.

Hence it is now said: “He shall send down a root and produce fruit above.” For when we direct our thought toward compassion for a needy neighbor, we send down a root, as it were, so that we may produce the fruit of recompense above.

### CHAPTER VII.—Likewise, concerning what was said above.

In *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book VIII (No. 81). —What do we understand by the name “roots” in this passage except hidden thoughts, which arise secretly but grow openly in the display of works?

To send down a root is to multiply a good thought in hidden places. To produce fruit above is to show through the effectiveness of action what one has rightly thought.

Thus: “He shall send down a root in order to produce fruit above,” as though it were plainly said: “Thought is born in the depths so that recompense may be given in the heights.”

### CHAPTER VIII.—Put your house in order, for you shall die and not live (2 Kings XX, 1).

[Col. 0816D] While, in the preceding section, the order of divine knowledge and the end of human life were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XII (No. 2), the following was added: “Set your house in order, for you shall die, and shall not live.” — Nothing that happens to human beings in this world occurs apart from the hidden counsel of almighty God. For God, foreknowing everything that would follow, decreed before the ages how all things should be ordered throughout the ages. It has indeed already been determined for each person how far the prosperity of this world will follow him, or how far adversity will strike him, lest either excessive prosperity exalt his elect or excessive adversity burden them. It has also been determined how long each person will live temporally in this mortal life. For although almighty God added fifteen years to the life of King Hezekiah, when he permitted him to die he already knew that Hezekiah would die at that time.

Here a question arises: how can the prophet say to him, “Set your house in order, for you shall die, and shall not live,” when, after the sentence of death had been pronounced upon him, life was immediately added in response to his tears? But through the prophet the Lord declared the time at which Hezekiah deserved to die; through the generosity of his mercy, however, he postponed his death until the time that he had foreknown before the ages. The prophet therefore was not false, since he made known the time of death at which that man deserved to die; nor were the Lord’s decrees overturned, since the fact that the years of his life would be increased by God’s generosity had also been fixed before the ages. The span of life outwardly added unexpectedly had inwardly been determined without any increase in divine foreknowledge.

## CHAPTER IX — “I beseech you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart” (2 Kings 20:3).

[Col. 0817B] While purity of heart sought from the Lord was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XII (No. 36), the following was added: “I beseech you, Lord,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0817D] In the printed editions it reads: “Just men sometimes recall their merits without pride.” Gregory’s testimony does indeed have this reading. We, however, follow the manuscripts of Utica, Michael, Gembloux, and others.]

Often the just, afflicted by various necessities, are compelled to acknowledge their own works. But when the unjust hear their words, they think that these have been spoken out of arrogance rather than truth. For they weigh the words of the just by their own hearts and do not think that good words can be spoken humbly. Just as it is a grave fault for a person to claim for himself what he is not, so it is often no fault at all if he humbly speaks of the good that he truly possesses.

Hence it often happens that the just and the unjust have similar words, while their hearts are always entirely different; and by the very words with which the Lord is offended when spoken by the unjust, he is also pleased when they are spoken by the just. For the Pharisee entered the temple and said: “I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess” (Luke 18:12). Yet the tax collector went away more justified than he.

King Hezekiah, too, when afflicted by bodily distress and brought to the extremity of life, said with contrition in his prayer: “I beseech you, [Col. 0817C] Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart.” Yet the Lord neither despised nor rejected this confession of his perfection; rather, he soon heard him in response to his prayers. Behold: the Pharisee declared himself righteous in his actions, while Hezekiah asserted himself righteous even in his thoughts. And where the former offended the Lord, the latter pleased him. Why was this, then, except that almighty God weighs the words of each person according to his thoughts, and that in his ears words spoken with a humble heart are not proud?

## CHAPTER X — “Behold, the days are coming, and everything that is in your house will be carried away to Babylon” (2 Kings 20:17–18).

While avoidance of pride of heart amid prosperity was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book VIII (Nos. 81–82), the following was added: “Behold, the days are coming,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0817D] The sentence is shorter in the commonly printed editions, but we follow the Sagiensis, Utica, Gembloux, and especially the more correct Michael manuscript.]

What does the prophet’s statement against King Hezekiah signify in this passage except the arrogance of hypocrites, who multiply their thoughts in pursuit of human admiration? In everything that hypocrites do, because they seek human praise through hidden thoughts, they are like those who place the roots of a rush in a heap of rocks. While preparing to act, they think about their praises; once praised, they silently turn these praises over in their thoughts. They rejoice that they have shone forth as eminent in human estimation. And when, puffed up by approval, they swell within themselves, they often silently marvel even at their own greatness.

They wish to appear greater to themselves day by day and, through extraordinary efforts, grow beyond themselves in their actions; for just as the virtue of humility weakens every vice, so arrogance strengthens it. Arrogance makes the mind grow young again and become strong beyond its powers, because the love of praise commands what bodily vigor refuses.

Hence, as we have said, they seek witnesses for their deeds. If it happens that witnesses to their work are lacking, they themselves recount what they have done. And when they begin to be carried away by approval, they often add something fictitious to the very deeds they report having accomplished. But even when they speak the truth, by speaking of these things they make them foreign to themselves: having been rewarded with the approval they sought, they empty themselves of the inner reward.

For by making their good deeds public, they show them to evil spirits lurking like enemies in ambush, as though displaying what those spirits may plunder. The well-known fault of Hezekiah clearly prefigured the life of such people. After, through a single prayer and within the space of one night, he had seen one hundred and eighty-five thousand enemies struck down by an angel; after he had brought the sun, which was near its setting, back to the higher regions of the sky; after he had prolonged a life already narrowed by its approaching end into a longer span of time—when he received the envoys of the king of Babylon, he showed them all the good things he possessed.

But immediately he heard from the prophet’s mouth: “Behold, the days are coming, and everything that is in your house will be carried away to Babylon; nothing will be left, says the Lord.” Thus, without doubt, hypocrites, after they have grown through great virtues, neglect to guard against the ambushes of evil spirits and refuse to conceal those same virtues. By displaying their good works, they make an opening, and by betraying them they suddenly lose whatever they have labored for over a long period.

[Note: [Col. 0818D] Sag. reads *praedam faciunt*, “they make them prey.” Other manuscripts read *hostium faciunt*, which admits a double sense: first, “they give them over to enemies”; second, “they open a door.” For in the manuscripts *ostium* (“door”) is written with *h*.]

[Col. 0818B] Hence the Psalmist says: “He delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy” (Psalm 77:61). The strength and beauty of the arrogant are delivered into the hands of the enemy because every good that is displayed through the desire for praise is handed over to the power of the hidden adversary. The person who exposes his riches to the knowledge of his enemies provokes them to plunder. For as long as we remain separated from the security of our eternal homeland, we walk along a road beset by lurking robbers. Whoever fears being robbed on the road must therefore hide the good things he carries.

O wretched people, who, desiring human praise, dissipate within themselves the fruits of their labors! When they desire to display themselves to the eyes of others, they condemn what they do. When evil spirits provoke them to boast, they strip them, as we have said, by taking their works captive.

Hence Truth says through the Gospel: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matthew 6:3–4). Hence the Psalmist says of the Church of the elect: “All the glory of the daughter of the king is within” (Psalm 44:14). Hence Paul says: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12).

The Church is the daughter of the King, generated in good works through the preaching of spiritual rulers. She has her glory within because she does not possess what she does in the boastful display of ostentation. Paul calls the testimony of his conscience his glory because, not seeking the favor of another’s speech, he does not know how to place the joys of his life outside himself.

The things we do must therefore be concealed, lest, carrying them carelessly along the road of this life, we lose them through the attack of predatory spirits.

## CHAPTER XI — “The king of Babylon slew the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes; and he also put out Zedekiah’s eyes” (2 Kings 25:6–7).

[Col. 0818D]

While the enduring innocence of the heart and the need to avoid the most subtle darts of the ancient adversary’s temptation were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book VII (No. 37), the following was added: “The king of Babylon slew the sons of Zedekiah at Riblah before his eyes,” and so forth.

When Sacred Scripture recounts Zedekiah’s captivity, it announces the order of inward captivity. The king of Babylon is the ancient enemy, possessor of inward confusion. He first slaughters the sons before the eyes of the one who is watching, because he often kills good works in such a way that the very person who has been taken captive sees with grief that he has lost them.

The soul often produces good things, yet, overcome by the pleasures of its flesh, it loses through love the good things it has produced and considers the losses it suffers, but still does not raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon. While it is struck by the sight of wickedness being committed, it is eventually brought by the practice of sin to the point that it is deprived even of the light of reason.

Hence the king of Babylon first kills Zedekiah’s sons and then puts out his eyes: the evil spirit first removes good works and afterward takes away the light of understanding. Zedekiah rightly suffers this at Riblah, for Riblah is interpreted as “many things.” At some point the light of reason is also closed to the person who, through evil practice, is weighed down by the multitude of his iniquity.

[Note: [Col. 0819A] After this chapter, the manuscripts of Gembloux and Michael contain another excerpt from book XIV on Job, beginning with the testimony “Flesh and blood,” and ending as follows: “The same according to nature, different according to glory; the same according to truth, different according to power.” These passages have been collected from Nos. 72 and following.]

# BOOK ELEVEN — Testimonies on the Psalms

[Col. 0819]

## CHAPTER I — “And he did not sit in the seat of pestilence” (Psalm 1:1).

[Col. 0819B]

While the avoidance of the operations of perverse zeal was being discussed in the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 34, admonition 33), the following was added: “And he did not sit in the seat of pestilence.”

A judge’s or presiding officer’s seat is customarily called a chair. To sit in the seat of pestilence is to commit evil on the basis of judgment, to distinguish wrongly on the basis of reason, and yet to carry it out after deliberation. He sits, as it were, in the chair of perverse counsel who is raised up by such great elation of iniquity that he tries to accomplish evil even through counsel. And just as those supported by the honor of the chair preside over the crowds standing before them, so sins deliberately pursued surpass the offenses of those who fall through rashness.

## CHAPTER II — “And he shall be like a tree planted beside the streams of waters” (Psalm 1:2).

While the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation was being discussed in homily 2 on Ezekiel (No. 6), the following was added: “And he shall be like a tree,” and so forth.

What are we to understand by the tree planted beside the streams of waters except the Incarnation of our Redeemer? Through the mystery of his Incarnation he deigned to draw near to the human race, which bears the burdens of its sins and flows downward daily toward death from its origin. “He shall be like a tree planted beside the streams of waters.” He was planted beside the streams of waters because he was incarnate beside the falls of peoples flowing downward.

## CHAPTER III — Likewise, in the passage above.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (No. 51): The streams of waters are the daily passages of peoples who are failing away. Truth also says of himself: “If they do this with the green wood, what will happen with the dry?” (Luke 23:31). The tree beside the streams of waters is therefore the one who, bringing forth for us the fruit and protection of his shade, appeared as Creator in the flesh, so that through the resurrection he might make firm the human race, which daily moved toward death through weakness.

## CHAPTER IV — “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you shall break them” (Psalm 2:5).

While the various kinds of blows were being distinguished in the exposition of blessed Job, book VII (No. 19), the following was added: “You shall rule them with an iron rod,” and so forth.

It must be understood that sometimes the adversary crushes us, and sometimes God does. Through the adversary’s crushing we fall away from virtue; through the Lord’s crushing, when broken, we are strengthened in virtue and freed from vices. The Prophet had seen this crushing when he said: “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you shall crush them.”

The Lord rules and crushes us with an iron rod because, in the strength of his ordering providence, he renews us inwardly while afflicting us outwardly. For insofar as he humbles the strength of the flesh, he exalts the purpose of the spirit. Hence this same crushing is compared with a potter’s vessel, as Paul also says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7). Expressing both crushing and rule together, he says: “Although our outward person is being corrupted, yet our inward person is being renewed day by day.”

## CHAPTER V — “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Psalm 2:11).

[Note: [Col. 0819D] This chapter is omitted in the manuscripts.]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XX (No. 8), the following was added: “Serve the Lord in fear,” and so forth.

Holy men are so certain of hope that they nevertheless remain ever watchful concerning temptation. To such people it is said: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling,” so that rejoicing may arise from hope and trembling from apprehension.

## CHAPTER VI — “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4:3).

[Col. 0820C]

While the distinction of meanings in sacred discourse was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (No. 8), the following was added: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?”

It is one thing to be heavy through deliberation, another through sin; one thing to be heavy through steadfastness, another through guilt. The former kind of heaviness has the weight of virtue, the latter the weight of a burden. Souls therefore receive weight so that they no longer leap away from their devotion to God through a light movement, but remain fixed in him with the grave steadfastness of constancy.

That people was still being lightly moved of whom the prophet says: “He went astray, following the way of his heart; I saw his way and abandoned him” (Isaiah 57:17). But a grave counsel of the heart drives out all the instability of wandering. And since there are souls that, through a light movement, desire now one thing and now another, almighty God does not lightly weigh these very light fluctuations of minds; rather, by abandoning the wandering of the heart, he judges it. But when he looks upon it through grace, he fixes the wandering mind in the stability of counsel. For when he mercifully deigns to regard the soul’s light movements, he immediately strengthens it for the maturity of constancy.

## CHAPTER VII — “Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5).

[Note: [Col. 0819D] This is also absent from our manuscripts.]

While the discernment of agitation of mind was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book V (No. 82), the following was added: “Be angry, and do not sin.”

Those who wish us to be angry only with ourselves, and not also with neighbors who commit offenses, do not understand this correctly. For if we are commanded to love our neighbors as ourselves, it follows that we should be angry at their errors just as at our own vices.

## CHAPTER VIII — “With the shield of your good will you have crowned us” (Psalm 5:13).

While the various meanings of things in sacred discourse were being distinguished in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXIII (No. 49), the following was added: “With the shield of your good will you have crowned us.”

[Note: [Col. 0820D] In the manuscripts, *de disserendis* (“on distinguishing”), and so forth.]

Sacred Scripture customarily uses the word “shield” sometimes in a favorable sense and sometimes in an unfavorable one. Often the protection of a shield signifies divine protection; at other times it refers to human resistance.

In the sense of divine protection, the Psalmist says: “With the shield of your good will you have crowned us.” The Lord is said to crown us with a shield because those whom he assists by protecting, he crowns by rewarding.

Again, in the sense of human resistance, the same Prophet uses the shield, as he says elsewhere: “There he broke the horns, the bow, the shield, the sword, and the battle” (Psalm 75:4). In the horns, the elation of the proud is signified; in the bow, the ambushes of those who strike from afar; in the shield, the stubborn hardness of defenses; in the sword, a blow delivered at close range; and in the battle, the mind’s very movement against the Lord. All of this is broken in holy Church when the minds of those resisting God are subdued by the yoke of humility placed upon them.

Again the same Psalmist says: “He will break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (Psalm 45:10). The Lord breaks the bow when he dissolves the hidden schemes of those lying in wait. He shatters the weapons when he crushes the human protections that had been raised up against him. He burns the shields with fire when, through the warmth of the Holy Spirit, he kindles to the fervor of repentance and confession the minds of sinners who defend themselves with stubborn hardness.

## CHAPTER IX — “In the morning I will stand before you, and I will see” (Psalm 5:5).

[Note: [Col. 0821D] Absent from our manuscripts.]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book II (No. 39), the following was added: “In the morning I will stand before you, and I will see.”

The present life is night. As long as we are in it, we remain in darkness under uncertain imagining, even though we perceive inward realities. David, seeing the darkness of this night and awaiting the brightness of the true light, said: “In the morning I will stand before you, and I will see.” The person who longs for the future morning in which he will see God therefore recognizes that he still sees himself only imperfectly in the night.

## CHAPTER X — “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (Psalm 6:2).

[Col. 0821C]

While avoidance of the sentence of the final judgment through the gift of good works was being discussed in homily 16 on Ezekiel (No. 2), or in book II, homily 4, the following was added: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,” and so forth.

The entire span of time is completed in seven days. For the eternal day that follows when the succession of seven days has been completed is the eighth day. Hence, considering the day of the resurrection, and about to speak of the severity of the final judgment, the Psalmist prefaced the psalm with its title: “For the end, a psalm of David, for the eighth.” To show which eighth day he meant, he followed the title at the beginning of the psalm with the day of dreadful terror, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.”

For now, whoever is chastised by scourges and corrected through chastisement is corrected in gentleness, not in anger. But in that strict examination, every rebuke and correction is fury and anger, because there will be no pardon after correction.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] The printed editions incorrectly read *argutia* (“subtlety”).]

## CHAPTER XI — “But in hell, who will confess to you?” (Psalm 6:6).

[Col. 0821D]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book VIII (No. 34), the following was added: “In hell,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] This is absent from the manuscript of Michael and others, nor is it found at the place indicated in the printed editions.]

The name “hell” can signify the despair of the sinner, of which the Psalmist says: “But in hell, who will confess to you?” Hence it is written again: “When the wicked comes into the depths of sins, he despises” (Proverbs 18).

## CHAPTER XII — “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Psalm 6:8).

While the discernment of an agitated mind was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book V (No. 82), the following was added: “My eye is troubled because of anger.”

[Note: [Col. 0822D] This chapter, too, is not found in our manuscripts.]

Anger through vice blinds the eye of the mind; anger through zeal troubles it. For when the mind is shaken even by zeal for what is right, the contemplation that can be perceived only with a tranquil heart is scattered. The zeal itself for righteousness, because it agitates the mind with unrest, immediately obscures its vision, so that in its agitation it does not see higher things that it had previously perceived well in tranquillity.

Yet from the very point at which it is struck so as not to see, it is led more subtly toward higher things. For the zeal for what is right itself, which is eternal, after a little while opens more fully in tranquillity what it temporarily closes through agitation. From the point at which the mind is troubled so that it cannot see, it makes progress so that it may become clearer in seeing truly.

It is like an eye suffering from illness: when an ointment is applied, light is entirely denied to it, but afterward it receives the light more truly from the very point at which it healthfully loses it for a time. Contemplation is never joined to agitation, nor can a disturbed mind perceive what a tranquil one can scarcely aspire to see. The ray of the sun is not visible when agitated clouds cover the face of the sky; nor does a disturbed spring reflect the image of the observer, which it properly displays when tranquil, because the more its wave trembles, the more it obscures within itself the appearance of the likeness.

But when the mind is moved by zeal, one must take the greatest care that the anger assumed as an instrument of virtue does not dominate the mind. It must not go before the mind as a mistress, but, like a handmaid prepared for service, must never depart from the rear of reason. For anger rises more vigorously against vices when it serves in subjection to reason.

However much anger may arise from zeal for righteousness, if it overcomes the mind without measure, it immediately refuses to serve reason. It expands all the more shamelessly because it considers the vice of impatience a virtue. Therefore the person moved by zeal for righteousness must above all attend to this: anger must not pass beyond the mind’s control.

He must consider the proper time and measure for punishing sin, restrain the disturbance rising within him by examining it more subtly, repress his spiritedness, and order his fervent movements according to equity. Thus he will be a more just avenger of another’s fault insofar as he has first proved victorious over his own. In this way he may correct the faults of those who offend so that he himself, the one correcting them, may first grow through patience and judge his own fervor by rising above it; otherwise, excited without restraint by the very zeal for righteousness, he may depart far from righteousness.

## CHAPTER XIII — “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Psalm 6:8).

While the rejection of vices and the pursuit of virtues were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (No. 53), the following was added: “I have grown old among all my enemies.”

[Note: [Col. 0822D] The manuscripts read *studendis virtutibus* (“the cultivation of virtues”) rather than *sectandis virtutibus* (“the pursuit of virtues”).]

It is clear to all who know the truth that vices belong to the old life, while virtues belong to the new. Hence Paul says: “Strip off the old person with his deeds, and put on the new” (Colossians 3:9). And again he says: “Our old person was crucified together with him” (Romans 6:6).

The Psalmist, therefore, speaking as a type of the human race and caught among evil spirits, says: “I have grown old among all my enemies.” For, amid either spiritual enemies or any carnal neighbors, we somehow grow old with respect to the mind’s fervor through the very habitual course of living, and we darken the appearance of the newness we have assumed.

Yet if the practices of vigilance remain alert, we are renewed daily from this old age through prayer, reading, and good living. For while our life is washed by tears, exercised through good works, and stretched toward holiness through sacred meditations, it is continually restored to its newness.

## CHAPTER XIV — “God is a just, strong, and long-suffering judge” (Psalm 7:12).

While the force of divine judgment was being discussed in homily 13 on the Gospel (No. 5), the following was added: “God is a just, strong, and long-suffering judge.”

Before saying “long-suffering,” he first said “just,” so that when you see him patiently bearing the sins of those who offend for a long time, you may know that he will one day judge them strictly. Hence a certain wise man says: “For the Most High is a patient repayer” (Sirach 5:4). He is called a patient repayer because he both bears the sins of human beings and repays them. For those whom he tolerates for a long time so that they may convert, if they do not convert he condemns more harshly.

## CHAPTER XV — “He bent his bow and prepared it, and in it he prepared vessels of death” (Psalm 7:13).

[Note: [Col. 0823D] Here too the manuscripts read *de disserendis* (“on distinguishing”).]

While the meanings of things in Sacred Scripture were being distinguished in the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (No. 55), the following was added: “He bent his bow and prepared it,” and so forth.

What is signified here by the bow except Sacred Scripture? It is itself the bow of the Church; it is the bow of the Lord. From it, as from arrows striking human hearts, come both piercing and terrifying declarations.

The Lord bent his bow because through Sacred Scripture he displayed threats to all sinners. In this bow he prepares vessels of death because, according to the judgment of his word, he condemns as reprobate those who now neglect to be corrected. In it he also makes his arrows fiery, because he sends burning declarations of his words against those whom he corrects through terror.

## CHAPTER XVI — “He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity” (Psalm 7:15).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVIII (No. 36), the following was added: “He conceived pain,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0823D] Chapters 16 and 17 are not found in the manuscripts.]

The name “womb” signifies the hidden and malicious thought of carnal people. This womb does not conceive bodily substance in order to bring forth offspring, but conceives a cause of pain in order to complete wickedness. Concerning this womb of the heart of the wicked it is said elsewhere: “He conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity.” Through this womb the wicked conceive when they think evil; through this womb they give birth when they carry out the evil they have thought.

## CHAPTER XVII — “That you may destroy the enemy and the defender” (Psalm 8:3).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XI (No. 39), the following was added: “That you may destroy the enemy and the defender.”

The enemy and defender is the person who attacks the God whom he proclaims.

[Col. 0823C]

## CHAPTER XVIII — “For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Psalm 8:4).

While the historical and mystical understanding was being discussed in homily 13 on Ezekiel (No. 3), or homily 1, book II, the following was added: “For I shall see your heavens,” and so forth.

In Sacred Scripture, even those things that can be understood according to history are often to be understood spiritually, so that faith may be maintained in the truth of the history while spiritual understanding may be grasped in the mysteries of allegory.

We know this also from what the Psalmist says: “For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars that you founded.” The words of the prayer stand, in the strict sense of the historical reading, because the heavens are works of God, and the moon and stars were created and founded by him.

But if the Psalmist asserts, according to history alone and not also according to mystical understanding, that the heavens are works of God, why, when he is about to mention the moon and stars, did he not also enumerate the sun, which we know to be his work? If he were speaking according to history alone, when he was about to mention the lesser light, he ought first to have mentioned the greater light, so that he would testify that the sun had been founded before the moon and stars.

But because he was speaking according to mystical understanding, so that we should understand the moon as the holy Church and the stars as holy people, he did not wish to name the sun, because he was speaking to that eternal Sun of whom it is written: “But for you who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Malachi 4:2). Concerning him the reprobate will say at the end: “The sun of righteousness did not rise for us” (Wisdom 5:6).

By saying, therefore, “the moon and the stars that you founded,” while remaining silent about the sun that was made, he indicated that he was speaking to that Sun who made not only the sun, moon, and stars bodily, but also the moon—which is the Church—and the stars—which are holy people—spiritually.

## CHAPTER XIX — “The fish of the sea that travel the paths of the sea” (Psalm 8).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XI (No. 5), the following was added: “The fish of the sea that travel the paths of the sea.”

[Note: [Col. 0824D] It is not found in the manuscripts.]

What should we understand by the fish of the sea except the curious people of this age, who lie hidden as though in concealed waves amid their investigations of great matters?

## CHAPTER XX — “You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Psalm 9:15).

While the endeavors of the perfect through the inspiration of divine grace were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (No. 25), the following was added: “You who lift me up from the gates of death,” and so forth.

What is signified by the gates of the daughter of Zion except every good action, through which the soul enters into the assembly of the heavenly kingdom? Hence the Prophet now says: “You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion.”

The gates of death are wicked actions, which draw people toward destruction. Since Zion is interpreted as “vision,” we understand the gates of Zion as good actions, through which we enter our heavenly homeland in order to behold the glory of our King.

## CHAPTER XXI — “The poor shall not be forgotten forever; the patience of the poor shall not perish forever” (Psalm 9).

While contempt for present things and hope for future reward were being discussed in homily 35 (No. 9) on the Gospel, the following was added: “The poor shall not be forgotten forever,” and so forth.

However patient we may be in adversity or humble in prosperity, let us seek no present reward for our good deeds in this life. For the reward of patient labor must be hoped for in the life to come, so that the reward of our labor may begin when all labor has already completely ceased.

Hence the Psalmist says: “There will be no forgetfulness of the poor; the patience of the poor will not perish forever.” The patience of the poor seems to have perished when nothing is repaid to the humble for it in this life. But the patience of the poor will not perish forever, because its glory is received when all laborious things come to an end together.

## CHAPTER XXII — “Under his tongue are labor and pain; he sits in ambush with the rich in secret places” (Psalm 9:7).

While the deceitful minds of the reprobate and the venomous malice of their head were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XV (No. 13), the following was added: “Under his tongue are labor and pain,” and so forth.

The perverse, because they have evil not on their tongue but under their tongue, present sweetness in their words while contriving perverse things in their thoughts. Concerning this head it is therefore written: “Under his tongue are labor and pain.” Since he does not openly display the evils he thinks, he does not bring forth upon his tongue the labor and pain of those whose death he desires, but presses them beneath his tongue.

But whose person did the Psalmist describe here except that of Antichrist? Because of his perverse doctrines, there are labor and pain under his tongue; because of the appearance of miracles, he sits in ambush; and because of the glory of secular power, he sits secretly with the rich. Since he uses both the deception of miracles and earthly power, he is said to sit secretly and with the rich.

## CHAPTER XXIII — “He lies in ambush in secret, like a lion in his den” (Psalm 9:30).

While the operations of the ancient adversary were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXII (No. 25), the following was added: “He lies in ambush in secret, like a lion in his den.”

The prophet testifies here concerning the devil’s final savagery, when he has been released to exercise his power. For open power would have been sufficient for him to be a lion, even if he had not been lying in ambush. Again, secret cunning would have been sufficient for him to steal upon people through ambush, even if he had not been a lion.

But because the ancient enemy is unleashed in all his powers, he is permitted to rage in both ways, so that against the elect he may be released in combat through both deception and strength: through strength by power, through deception by signs. He is therefore rightly called both a lion and one who lies in ambush: he lies in ambush through the appearance of miracles, and he is a lion through secular strength.

To draw those who are openly wicked to himself, he displays secular power; but in order also to deceive the just, he imitates holiness through signs. He persuades the former through the elation of greatness; he deceives the latter by displaying holiness.

## CHAPTER XXIV — “In the Lord I trust; how can you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Psalm 10:1).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXIII (No. 2), the following was added: “In the Lord I trust,” and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] Absent from the manuscripts.]

When it is said that, abandoning the faithful unity of the soul, a heretical preacher trusts in swollen doctrine, he is urged to migrate, as though abandoning the Lord, to the mountain.

## CHAPTER XXV — “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright of heart” (Psalm 10:2).

While the ambushes of the reprobate against the elect were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXI (No. 62), the following was added: “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver,” and so forth.

What is signified by the name “quiver” except the schemes of the wicked? For when the wicked conceal through secret schemes the deceits they devise against the good, they carry arrows as if in a quiver. In the darkness of the present life, as though in darkness, they strike the upright of heart, because their malicious arrows can be felt through the wound, yet cannot be detected as they approach.

## CHAPTER XXVI — “His eyelids question the children of men” (Psalm 10:5).

While the hidden mysteries of divine activity were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVIII (no. 13), the following was added [Col. 0825C]: “His eyelids examine the sons of men.” — By opening certain things to us and closing others, God examines us, as it is said through the Prophet: “His eyelids examine the sons of men.” With open eyelids we see; when they are closed, we see nothing. What, then, do we understand by God’s eyelids except his judgments? These are partly closed and partly opened to human beings, so that people who do not know themselves may become known to themselves: while they comprehend certain things through understanding but are wholly unable to know others, their hearts may secretly examine themselves, asking whether the divine judgments, when closed, fail to spur them on, or, when opened, fail to puff them up.

Paul was tested by this examination. After receiving inward wisdom, after the gates of paradise had been opened, after ascending to the third heaven, and after the mysteries of heavenly speech, he nevertheless says: “I do not consider myself to have comprehended” (Phil. III, 13). And again: “I am the least of all the apostles, and am not worthy to be called an apostle” (I Cor. XV, 9) [Col. 0825D]. And again: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (II Cor. III, 5).

Thus, when God’s eyelids were opened, Paul rightly answered: he had touched the secrets above, yet stood sublimely in humility of heart. Again, when he was discussing God’s secret judgments concerning the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, and was unable to reach their depths, he was examined as though God’s eyelids were closed. Yet he gave a wholly upright answer, knowingly bowing before God in the very midst of his ignorance, saying: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. XI, 33).

Behold: questioned concerning hidden mysteries, as though God’s eyelids were closed, he gave fitting and upright answers [Col. 0826A]. Striking at the entrance to the secret, and unable to be admitted into the interior through knowledge, he stood humbly before the door through confession; and what he could not comprehend within, he praised outside in fear.

## CHAPTER XXVII — Also, from the passage above

Homily 17 on Ezekiel (no. 6). — [Note: [Col. 0825D] This is absent from the manuscripts.] Through those things that are covered over for us in Sacred Scripture, our humility is approved, because whatever we do not understand in it we ought not arrogantly to criticize, but humbly to venerate. Hence it is written concerning the Lord: “His eyelids examine the sons of men.” His eyelids are his judgments, which close some things to us and open others. By opening them, they examine whether we are not exalted through understanding; by closing them, they examine whether we do not despise what we are unable to understand.

Moreover, through those things that we do not say to our neighbors concerning our charity, we are more truly tested in God’s sight. In the mouths of some, charity is feigned; in the hearts of others, it is genuine. Often what is not there is displayed as charity, while what is there is not shown. Therefore our love toward our neighbor is expressed more by good action than by the tongue, so that our neighbor may see in the good work itself that he is loved; and when we cannot accomplish as much as we wish, may the hidden things of our love suffice for almighty God.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — He will rain snares upon sinners, fire, brimstone, and a stormy wind; this is the portion of their cup (Ps. X, 7)

When the force of the more severe judgment was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XV (no. 55), the following was added: “He will rain snares upon sinners,” and so forth. — By saying “snares, fire, brimstone, and stormy wind,” he certainly indicated many sufferings. But because through those sufferings the sinner who is not corrected is summoned to eternal punishments, he called those same sufferings not the whole cup but a portion of the cup, since their affliction begins here through pains but is completed in everlasting retribution.

[Note: [Col. 0826D] In the printed editions, incorrectly: “of zeal.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX — The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire (Ps. XI, 7)

While the operation of the divine word was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book IV (no. 61, at the end), the following was added: “The sayings of the Lord,” and so forth. — The Lord’s saying is called silver tested by fire because, when the word of God is fixed in the heart, it is tested by tribulations.

## CHAPTER XXX — The wicked walk in a circle (Ps. XI, 9)

When the activity of the ancient adversary in what follows was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book II (no. 7), the following was added: “The wicked walk in a circle.” — A circle commonly signifies the anxiety of labor, as it is written in Satan’s reply: “I have traversed the earth and walked through it” (Job II, 2). Satan, laboring, traversed the earth because he scorned to stand at rest on the heights of heaven. And when he indicates that he has not flown across it but walked through it, he shows how heavily the burden of sin weighs upon him in the depths [Col. 0826D]. Thus he walks around the earth in labor: having fallen from the flight of spiritual power and weighed down by the burden of his wickedness, he has come outward into the circuit of toil.

Of the imitators of this leader, that is, of his members, the Psalmist therefore says: “The wicked walk in a circle,” because, corrupted by the foulness of his wickedness, while they do not seek the inner things, they are wearied by labor in outward things.

## CHAPTER XXXI — The fool said in his heart: There is no God (Ps. XIII, 1)

When those who, because of their love of visible things, think perversely about God were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XV (no. 25), the following was added: “The fool said in his heart: There is no God.” — The human mind, poured outward in a wrong manner and scattered among bodily things, is so dispersed that it neither returns inward to itself nor is capable of thinking about him who is invisible [Col. 0827A]. Hence carnal people, despising spiritual commands, sometimes reach the point that, because they do not see God bodily, they even suppose that he does not exist. Therefore it is written: “The fool said in his heart: There is no God.”

People often desire more to serve human beings whom they see bodily than to serve God whom they do not see. In everything they do, they aim at the evidence of their eyes. And because they cannot fix the eyes of the body upon God, they either despise rendering him service or, if they begin, grow weary. As has been said, they do not believe that he exists whom they do not behold bodily.

If they would humbly seek God, the author of all things, they would find within themselves a better understanding of what is not seen from what is seen. They themselves subsist from an invisible soul and a visible body; and if what is unseen were taken away from them, what is seen would immediately collapse. The eyes of the flesh would remain open, but they would be unable either to see or to perceive anything. The faculty of sight has perished because the inhabitant has departed, and the house of flesh remains empty because that invisible spirit has withdrawn, the spirit that was accustomed to look out through the windows of the flesh.

Since invisible things are therefore superior to visible things, all carnal people ought to have reflected upon this in themselves and, through this—as I may put it—ladder of contemplation, to have reached toward God: for he is all the more truly what he is insofar as he remains invisible, and he remains supreme precisely insofar as he can in no way be comprehended.

## CHAPTER XXXII — There they trembled with fear where there was no fear (Ps. XIII, 5)

When the faintheartedness of weak minds was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book VII (no. 32), the following was added: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear.” — It must be understood that many desire to do what is right, but certain things in the present life oppose their weak minds. While they fear suffering adversities in the lowest things, they offend against the rectitude of the heavenly judgment [Col. 0827C]. Thus some, while fearing temporal adversities, expose themselves to the severity of eternal punishment.

The Psalmist therefore rightly says of them: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear.” One person desires to defend the truth freely, but in that very desire he trembles and fears the indignation of human power. When he fears a human being on earth on account of the truth, he endures the anger of that same truth from heaven.

Another, conscious of his sins, now wishes to distribute to the needy what he possesses, but fears that he himself may become poor after giving it away. While trembling, he preserves the supports of the flesh and prepares them for himself; through food withheld from mercy, he kills his soul. When he fears suffering want on earth, he cuts himself off from the eternal abundance of heavenly refreshment.

Those who fear what must be trampled underfoot in the lowest things suffer what must be feared from above; and when they refuse to pass through what they could have trampled down, they encounter a judgment from heaven that they can in no way endure.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — I said to the Lord: You are my God, for you have no need of my goods (Ps. XV, 2)

[Col. 0827D]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVI (no. 2), the following was added: “I said to the Lord,” and so forth. — In everything good that we do, we help ourselves, not the Lord. He is truly our Lord because he is also God, who does not need the goodness of the one who serves him, but bestows the goodness that he receives, so that the goodness offered benefits not him but first those who receive it and afterward those who return it.

For although the Lord, coming in judgment, says: “As long as you did it to one of these, my least brothers, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV, 40), he speaks this with wondrous compassion, out of sympathy for his members. He himself helps us through the fact that he is our head, and he is helped through our good works in his members.

[Note: [Col. 0827D] This is not contained in the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XXXIV — The cords have fallen to me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is pleasant to me (Ps. XV, 6)

[Col. 0828A]

When the various meanings of things were being distinguished in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXIV (no. 18), the following was added: “The cords have fallen to me in pleasant places,” and so forth. — Sacred Scripture customarily uses a cord to signify at one time the lots of allotted dimensions, at another sins, and at another faith.

With reference to the hereditary lots of allotted dimensions, it says: “The cords have fallen to me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is pleasant to me.” The cords fall in pleasant places when, through humility of life, the lots of a better homeland receive us.

Again, since sins are signified by a cord, the Prophet says: “Woe to those who drag iniquities with cords of vanity” (Isa. V, 18). Iniquity is dragged by cords of vanity when guilt is extended through increase. Hence the Psalmist says: “The cords of sinners have entangled me” (Ps. CXVIII, 61). Because a cord is twisted by adding to it so that it grows, sin is not improperly represented by a cord: when it is repeatedly defended by a perverse heart, it multiplies.

Again, faith is expressed by a cord, as Solomon bears witness, saying: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccl. IV, 12). Faith, woven from knowledge of the Trinity by the mouth of preachers, remains strong in the elect but is destroyed in the heart of the reprobate alone.

## CHAPTER XXXV — I cried out, because you heard me, O God (Ps. XV, 6)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXV (no. 4), the following was added: “I cried out,” and so forth. — [Note: [Col. 0827D] Omitted in the manuscripts.] He does not say, “Because I cried out, you heard me,” but “I cried out, because you heard me.” He who had been heard while speaking cried out because he had been heard, with his prayers advancing: “Make your mercies wonderful, you who save those who hope in you.” The Lord’s mercies become wonderful among us—that is, among those who are rescued—when through those same mercies we recognize how grave were the dangers from which we escaped.

## CHAPTER XXXVI — Protect me under the shadow of your wings (Ps. XVI, 9)

[Col. 0828C]

When divine protection over us was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXII (no. 7), the following was added: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings.” — When the Lord protects us as little ones, he nourishes us; and he refreshes us with a protection that is not burdensome or oppressive but light and gentle. When he extends his mercies over us, he spreads wings over us, as birds do.

## CHAPTER XXXVII — I will love you, O Lord, my strength (Ps. XVII, 1)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXII (no. 14), the following was added: “I will love you,” and so forth. — It is certain that the one who understands less of the danger from which he was rescued loves his rescuer less; and he considers the defender’s consolation of little worth when he thinks the adversary’s power weak.

Therefore, rightly attributing his deliverance to the Lord, the Prophet said: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength,” plainly saying: “I love you all the more because, recognizing my own weakness, I understand that you are my strength.”

[Note: [Col. 0828D] Absent from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — Darkness is under his feet; and he ascended upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds and made darkness his hiding place (Ps. XVII, 10)

[Col. 0828D]

When the loftiness of the divine essence was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XVII (no. 39), the following was added: “Darkness is under his feet,” and so forth. — Darkness is under his feet because he is not seen by those below in the brightness in which he rules above.

He ascended upon the cherubim and flew; for “cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” Thus he is said to have ascended and flown above the fullness of knowledge because no knowledge comprehends the height of his majesty. He flew because he has carried himself far above the reach of our understanding. He flew upon the wings of the winds because he transcends the knowledge of souls. He made darkness his hiding place because, while we are obscured by the darkness of our weakness, he is hidden from us through our ignorance, so that we do not yet see him in eternal and innermost brightness.

Hence, in the Song of Songs, the bride says to him: “Flee, my beloved” (Song VIII, 14), “flee.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX — Also, from the passage above

[Note: [Col. 0829D] In Codex Michael this is said to have been taken from a commentary on Ezekiel, a homily. But what homily is this? Certainly nowhere does it occur to us. In book I of the commentary on the Books of Kings, chapter 1, no. 39, nearly similar words are found.]

The Lord ascended upon the cherubim and flew because he deigned to exalt the glory of his incarnation above the fullness of knowledge that could exist in human beings; thus his flying consists in withdrawing the mystery of his power from human understanding.

For however fully the life of spiritual people may shine with knowledge, it cannot grasp how it happened that the one who existed was conceived, that the author of human beings before the ages was born human at the end of the ages, that God was flesh, and that the Word came to be at the end. Hence it is rightly added there: “He flew upon the wings of the winds,” because he transcends all the understandings of souls. We may appropriately understand souls to be represented by winds because of the swiftness of their thought.

## CHAPTER XL — He made darkness his hiding place (Ps. XVII, 12)

While the goodness of repentance through the inspiration of heavenly grace was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book V (nos. 12–13), the following was added: “He made darkness his hiding place.” — Our Creator, because he has withdrawn the light of his vision from us who have been cast into this exile, has hidden himself from our eyes as though in a hiding place of darkness.

When we attentively contemplate these darknesses of our blindness, we stir our mind to lamentation. We weep over the blindness we suffer outwardly if we humbly remember that we have been deprived of the light of inward things. When we look upon the darkness surrounding us, we afflict ourselves with an ardent desire for the innermost splendor; with every effort of our attention we shake ourselves, and, rejected, seek the heavenly light that we abandoned when we were created.

Thus it often happens that, amid those very devout tears, the brightness of inward joy breaks forth, and the mind that had lain blind in torpor, invigorated by sighs, grows strong enough to contemplate the innermost radiance.

## CHAPTER XLI — Dark water is in the clouds of the air. Before his brightness the clouds passed by, hail and coals of fire (Ps. XVII, 12–13)

[Col. 0829C]

When the virtues of the Church’s preachers were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XVII (no. 30), the following was added: “Dark water is in the clouds of the air,” and so forth. — [Note: [Col. 0830D] Also book XXVII, no. 15, and book XX, no. 38.]

What else does dark water signify except the hidden knowledge of the prophets? Before the Lord’s coming, while they were pregnant with hidden sacraments and carrying immense mysteries, their meaning was darkened to the eyes of those who looked upon them.

But “before his brightness the clouds passed by,” because holy preachers traverse all the regions of the world with the brightness of miracles. They are also called “hail and coals of fire,” because they strike through correction and kindle through the flame of charity.

The free rebuke of the saints is also appropriately expressed by the nature of hail. Hail strikes when it falls and waters when it melts. Holy men strike the hearts of their hearers by terrifying them and pour themselves into them by offering consolation.

The Prophet testifies to how they strike, saying: “They will speak of the power of your awesome acts, and they will tell of your greatness” (Ps. CXLIV, 6). And he added how they water by offering consolation: “They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they will rejoice in your righteousness” (ibid., 7).

## CHAPTER XLII — He made my feet like those of deer (Ps. XVII, 34)

When the pursuits of the perfect were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVI (no. 24), the following was added: “He made my feet like those of deer.” — The minds of the strong, fixed immovably in God, despise every adversity all the more because they see that such adversities grow against the commands of the Creator [Col. 0830A].

Awaiting the rewards of eternity, they draw strength from adversities, because they do not doubt that, as the struggle increases, a more glorious victory remains for them. Thus the desires of the elect, when pressed down, advance through adversity, as fire is pressed by the blowing of air so that it may grow; and from the point where it seems almost to be extinguished, it gains strength.

We show how greatly we burn with desire for God if we pass to him not only through calm and gentle things but also through harsh and difficult ones. Therefore the Psalmist rightly says: “He made my feet like those of deer.” When a deer climbs the ridges of the mountains, it leaps over whatever rough things confront it, whatever is entangled with thorns, and rises into the heights without any obstacle to its course.

So also the minds of the elect leap beyond whatever they see opposing and obstructing them in this world through contemplation; like deer, scorning the thorns of earthly things, they raise themselves to the things above. Hence the same Psalmist says again: “In my God I will leap over a wall” (ibid., 30). A wall is everything placed in the way of our journey so that we may not pass to the one we love. But we leap over the wall when, out of love for our heavenly homeland, we trample whatever has been set before us in this world.

## CHAPTER XLIII — The sons of strangers lied to me; the sons of strangers grew old and limped from their paths (Ps. XVII)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (no. 40), the following was added: “The sons of strangers lied to me,” and so forth. — [Note: [Col. 0830D] This chapter and the next two are not found in the manuscripts.] The Israelite people are called lame because they did not have a sound step in their conduct. They refused to use both feet: they accepted one Testament and rejected the other.

## CHAPTER XLIV — The heavens declare the glory of God (Ps. XVIII, 1)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book IV (no. 10), the following was added: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” — What is signified by the name “heavens” except the life of preachers? They are therefore called heavens, and they are also said to be the sun: heavens, because they protect by interceding; the sun, because by preaching they display the force of light.

## CHAPTER XLV — He placed his tabernacle in the sun (Ps. XVIII, 6)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXIV (no. 25), the following was added: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun.” — It is as though he said: “He displayed the mystery of the humanity he assumed in the light of manifest vision.”

## CHAPTER XLVI — For he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber (ibid.)

While the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation was being discussed, homily 38 on the Gospels (no. 3) added the following: “For he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber.” — Our Redeemer came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber: God incarnate, he came forth from the incorrupt womb of the Virgin in order to unite the Church to himself.

## CHAPTER XLVII — You will set them as a furnace of fire at the time of your presence; the Lord in his anger will trouble them, and fire will devour them (Ps. XX, 10)

[Col. 0830D]

When the punishment of the future retribution of the wicked was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XV (no. 35), the following was added: “You will set them as a furnace of fire at the time of your presence,” and so forth. — It must be understood that all the reprobate, because they sinned with soul and body together, will there be tormented in soul and body together.

A furnace burns inwardly; but the one devoured by fire begins to be burned from the outside. Thus, to show that the Sacred Scriptures represent the reprobate as burning both outwardly and inwardly, they testify that they are both devoured by fire and set like a furnace: through fire they are tormented in the body, and through pain they burn in the mind (ibid., book VI, no. 47).
