At the time of the Lord’s presence, therefore, all the unjust are punished both as a furnace and as those devoured by fire: when the Judge appears and the multitude of the wicked is driven away from his sight, their conscience burns inwardly through desire, while Gehenna torments their flesh outwardly.

## CHAPTER XLVIII — My God, I will cry out by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and not for my folly (Ps. XXI, 3)

When the dispensation of the divine gift of mercy toward the elect was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XX (no. 61), the following was added: “My God, I will cry out by day,” and so forth. — During the time of persecution, Holy Church stands firm in faith and cries out in desire. But it grieves as though it were not being regarded when it sees its prayers delayed amid tribulations.

In a profound design, almighty God, when his saints are oppressed by the persecutions of their adversaries and cry out in continual appeals to be delivered, commonly delays the voices of those who ask, so that the merits of those who suffer may increase. Thus they are heard all the more meritoriously because they are not heard so quickly according to their desire.

The Psalmist therefore says: “My God, I will cry out by day, and you will not hear; and by night.” The benefit that comes from delay in being heard is immediately added: “And not for my folly.” What they receive slowly after asking advances the wisdom of the saints: through delay, desire grows; through desire, understanding increases. When understanding is intensified, a more ardent affection for God is opened. Affection becomes capable of attaining heavenly things to the extent that it becomes long-suffering through waiting.

Yet amid all this, pain presses the patience of the saints toward utterance. While they advance through delay, they fear that they may fail and, empty of possessions, be despised and rejected.

## CHAPTER XLIX — Also, from the passage above

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVI (no. 34). — Let no one who is heard slowly believe that he is neglected by heavenly care. Often our desires are heard precisely because they are not fulfilled quickly; and what we urgently ask to be accomplished is brought to a better outcome through that very delay.

Often our voice is perfected by being delayed. When our request is neglected on the surface, our desires are fulfilled more deeply in the root of our thoughts, just as the seeds of crops are strengthened when pressed by frost; the later they emerge to the surface, the more abundantly they rise toward harvest [Col. 0831C].

Our desires are therefore extended by delay so that they may advance; they advance so that they may grow strong enough for what they are to receive. They are exercised in combat so that they may be heaped with greater rewards in recompense. The labor of battle is prolonged so that the crown of victory may grow.

When the Lord does not quickly hear his own, he draws toward himself the one whom he is believed to be rejecting. He is an inward physician: he cuts away the infections of sins that he condemns as rooted in our marrow; he cuts out the poison of corruption with the knife of tribulation. The more he seems to disregard hearing the sick person’s cries, the more he works toward the end of the illness.

Hence the Prophet says: “I will cry out by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and not for my folly” (Ps. XXI, 3). It is as though he said: “It does not advance me toward folly that you continually fail to hear me crying out day and night, because, insofar as you seem to abandon me in temporal tribulation, you thereby instruct me more deeply in eternal wisdom.”

Hence he also says: “A helper in times of opportunity, in tribulation” (Ps. IX, 10). In saying “in tribulation,” he placed “opportunity” first, because we are often crushed by tribulation, yet the opportune time has not arrived for us to be helped according to our desire for deliverance.

## CHAPTER L — Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me (Ps. XXII, 4)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XX (no. 14), the following was added: “Your rod and your staff,” and so forth. — [Note: [Col. 0831D] Chapters 50 and 51 are not found in the manuscripts.] We are struck by the rod and supported by the staff. If, then, there is the severity of the rod that strikes, let there be, correspondingly, the consolation of the staff that supports [Col. 0832A]. Let there be love, but not love that softens; severity, but not severity that exasperates; zeal, but not zeal that rages immoderately; kindness, but not kindness that spares more than is beneficial.

## CHAPTER LI — You have enriched my head with oil (Ps. XXII, 5)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book III (no. 33), the following was added: “You have enriched my head with oil.” — It is as though he said: “You have filled my mind with the richness of charity.”

“My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. XXI, 16). A potsherd is strengthened by fire. The flesh, however, became stronger through its passion: by dying in weakness, it rose from death without weakness.

And again: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd.” His strength dried up like a potsherd because he strengthened the weakness of the flesh he had assumed through the fire of his passion.

## CHAPTER LII — He who has not received his soul in vain (Ps. XXIII, 4)

When the pursuit of good works was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book VII (no. 38), the following was added: “He who has not received,” and so forth. — The Psalmist says of each of the elect: “He who has not received his soul in vain.”

He receives his soul in vain who thinks only about present things and does not consider what will follow forever. He receives his soul in vain who neglects its life and places the care of the flesh before it.

But the righteous do not receive their souls in vain, because in constant intention they refer everything they do bodily to the soul’s benefit, so that, although the work itself passes away, the purpose of the work does not pass away—the purpose that prepares the rewards of life after this life.

The reprobate neglect these concerns because, walking in emptiness, they flee the life they pursue and lose what they find. We are therefore better restrained from imitating the wicked when we weigh their losses according to their end.

## CHAPTER LIII — Deliver me from my necessities (Ps. XXIV, 17)

[Col. 0832C]

When the desires of human weakness were being discussed—desires to be restrained through the practice of good works—in the exposition of blessed Job, book XX (nos. 28–29), the following was added: “Deliver me from my necessities.”

[Note: [Col. 0831D] In the printed editions: “concerning discerning the matter of pleasure and necessity.”]

Human nature, well created but fallen into weakness and calamity through the fault of its own will, was burdened by countless necessities and found in this life nothing except occasions of affliction. But when we commonly serve these necessities of our nature more than is fitting and neglect care of the mind, we add to our weakness, through the misery of negligence, the foulness of guilt.

Natural necessities are often very dangerous because it is frequently impossible to distinguish what is done concerning them through the pursuit of utility and what is done through the vice of pleasure. For, when an occasion for seduction is repeatedly found, while we render what is owed to necessity, we serve the vice of pleasure; and our excuse cloaks itself before the eyes of discernment under the veil of weakness, hiding itself as though under the protection of what utility requires.

To relax the weakness of our nature through negligence is nothing other than to add misery to calamity and, through that same misery, to multiply the foulness of vices.

Hence holy men distinguish with the greatest care everything they do, lest the weakness of their nature demand more from them than is owed to it, and lest the vice of pleasure grow within them under the cover of necessity. They endure one thing from weakness and another from the suggestion of temptation; and, placed like perfectly upright arbiters between necessity and pleasure, they support the one by consolation and restrain the other by pressure.

Thus, although they endure the calamity of their weakness, they do not descend through negligence into the foulness of misery. For it is itself a state of calamity to bear the necessities of nature because of the weakness of still-corruptible flesh. The Psalmist desired to escape these necessities when he said: “Deliver me from my necessities.”

He knew that the sins of pleasure often erupt from the occasion of necessities; and, lest he willingly admit anything unlawful, he strove to have torn out precisely what he unwillingly endured from the root.

By contrast, the wicked rejoice in the necessities of their corruption because they turn them toward the uses of pleasure. When they serve nature by restoring their bodies with food, they stretch themselves through the delight of gluttony into an excess of pleasure. When they seek clothing to cover their limbs, they desire not only what covers but also what elevates them; against the numbness of cold, they seek not only what protects through thickness but also what delights through softness; not only what soothes the touch through softness but also what seduces the eyes through color.

Desiring to be freed from these necessities, the Psalmist says: “Deliver me from my necessities.” For what is it other than joining the foulness of misery to one’s calamity to turn the cause of necessity into the use of pleasure?

## CHAPTER LIV — Test me, O Lord, and try me (Ps. XXV, 2)

When the elect’s pursuit of watchful foresight was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book VII (no. 21), the following was added: “Test me, O Lord, and try me.”

When sudden pain from a scourge or the trial of illness strikes us while we are secure and elated by an abundance of virtues, the exaltation of our mind is immediately cut down from the summit of its position and falls, so that it dares nothing from itself but, struck down by the blow of its weakness, seeks the hand of the one who raises it.

Hence holy men, when they are uncertain about the hidden disposition of God toward them, fear prosperity itself more; they desire to be tested and long to be scourged, so that fear and pain may instruct the unwary mind. Otherwise, on the road of this pilgrimage, when the enemy bursts forth from ambush, its own security may overthrow it all the more disastrously.

The Psalmist therefore rightly says: “Test me, O Lord, and try me.” It is as though he openly said: “First examine my strength, and then permit me to be tested insofar as I am able to endure.”

Hence he says again: “I am ready for scourges” (Ps. XXXVII, 18). Because holy minds consider that the wound of their corruption is not without putrefaction, they willingly prepare themselves for incision under the physician’s hand, so that the poison of sin, which was killing them within beneath healthy skin, may escape through the wound opened.

## CHAPTER LV — The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? (Ps. XXVI, 1)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XIV (no. 41), the following was added: “The Lord is my light,” and so forth. — [Note: [Col. 0833D] Chapters 55 and 56 are missing from the manuscripts.]

It is a punishment of sin to see the good one ought to do and yet be unable to accomplish it. It is again a more serious punishment of sin to be unable to see what one ought to do. Against both conditions the Psalmist’s words are rightly spoken: “The Lord is my light and my salvation.” Against the darkness of ignorance, the Lord is light; against weakness, he is salvation: he both shows what ought to be desired in action and supplies the strength by which what he has shown can be fulfilled.

## CHAPTER LVI — Also, from the passage above

[Col. 0833D]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (no. 39). — Sin is often committed either through ignorance or through weakness, so that a person either does not know what he ought to will or is unable to do everything he wills. In opposition to this the Psalmist rightly says: “The Lord is my light and my salvation.” Because the Lord supplies both knowledge and strength, he is called light against ignorance and salvation against weakness.

## CHAPTER LVII — One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek (Ps. XXVI, 4)

When [Note: [Col. 0833D] In the printed editions: “on preserving tranquility of mind from the tumult of the world.”] the discussion concerned avoiding the desires of the wicked and pursuing the practices of the good, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book IV (No. 57), the following was added:

**“One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek”** (Psalm 26:4).

All who either desire unlawful things or wish to appear to be something in this world are oppressed within their hearts by dense tumultuous thoughts. While they stir up within themselves the crowds of their desires, they trample their prostrate mind beneath the foot of wretched preoccupation (ibid., no. 18). By contrast, holy men, because they desire nothing of this world, are undoubtedly oppressed by no tumult in their hearts. With the hand of holy reflection they drive all the disordered movements of desire from the dwelling-place of the heart; and because they despise all transitory things, they do not suffer the insolences of the thoughts that arise from them. [Note: [Col. 0833D] Michael has “tumults”; Utica presents both readings.] For they desire only the eternal homeland; and because they love nothing belonging to this world, they enjoy great tranquility of mind.

Had he not driven all the tumult of thoughts from himself who said: **“One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord”**? He had fled from the throng of earthly desires and had withdrawn himself into a great solitude, where he would see nothing alien all the more safely because he loved nothing that belonged there. From the tumult of temporal affairs he had sought a great retreat: a quiet mind, in which he might see God more purely, the more he found Him alone with himself.

**CHAPTER LVIII.—“You shall hide them in the hiding-place of your face from the disturbance of men” (Psalm 30:21).**

When the virtues of the elect were being discussed, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book IV (No. 19; and Book IV, No. 9), the following was added:

**“You shall hide them in the hiding-place of your face from the disturbance of men.”**

Each elect person is hidden in the face of the divinity through inward vision, while the outward blindness of the reprobate is shaken and rejected by the strict judgment of justice. Thus holy men do not cease to mortify themselves with the sword of the sacred word: from the importunity of temporal desires, from the tumult of useless cares, and from the clamor of clamorous disturbances. Within, before the face of God, they hide themselves in the bosom of the mind.

Hence the Psalmist rightly says: **“You shall hide them in the secret place of your face from the disturbance of men.”** Although this will be accomplished perfectly hereafter, even now it is carried out in large part, when they are snatched inward from the tumults of temporal desires by delight, so that, while their mind is wholly directed toward the love of God, it is not torn apart by any useless disturbance.

Hence Paul, through contemplation, had seen the disciples as dead and, as it were, hidden in the secret place of divinity, when he said to them: **“For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God”** (Colossians 3:3). Whoever longs to mortify himself rejoices greatly at the rest discovered in contemplation, so that, extinguished to the world, he may remain hidden and conceal himself from all the disturbances of external things within the bosom of intimate love. [Note: [Col. 0834D] The printed editions, together with Michael, have “conceal himself.”]

**CHAPTER LIX.—“I said in my fear: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes” (Psalm 30:23).**

[Col. 0834D] When the progress of the elect through knowledge of their own weakness was being discussed, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIII (Nos. 41–43), the following was added:

**“I said in my fear,”** and so forth.

The holy man, contemplating the eternal homeland [Note: [Col. 0834D] Utica and Gemet have “contemplates.”] and weighing the evils in which he was, as well as considering the good things in which he was not yet, said: **“I said in my fear: I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.”**

Raised up in ecstasy—for what our translators called “fear” was not properly so called—he saw himself cast away from the sight of God’s eyes. After the vision of the inner light, which within the soul shone forth through the grace of contemplation with a ray of brightness, he withdrew from himself; and, having received knowledge, he discovered what evils were present to him here. For no one can see the evils of the present life as they truly are unless he is also able, through a taste of contemplation, to touch the goods of the eternal homeland. Hence he recognized that he had been cast away from the sight of God’s eyes.

Raised up, he saw what he lamented, once released back into himself, that he could not see here. This compunction usually affects the perfect soul in a familiar way, because it disperses all bodily images that intrude upon it presumptuously and directs the eye of the heart to fix itself upon the very ray of unbounded light. Through the weakness of the body, it draws inward to itself the forms of bodily appearances; but when it has been perfectly pierced with compunction, it watches with the greatest care lest, while seeking the truth, the imagination of a circumscribed vision deceive it. It rejects all the images that confront it.

For because it fell beneath itself through those images, it strives to rise above itself without them. And after it has been indecorously scattered among many things, it endeavors to gather itself into one, so that, if it prevails through the great force of love, it may contemplate that which is one and incorporeal. [Note: [Col. 0835D] The remainder is absent from the manuscripts.]

Hence at times it is admitted to an unfamiliar sweetness of inward savor [Col. 0835B] and, suddenly breathed upon in some manner by an ardent spirit, is renewed. The more it tastes what it loves, the more eagerly it thirsts for it. Within itself it desires that which it senses to taste sweetly within, because through love of that sweetness its heart has become contemptible to itself; and after it has been able to perceive it in some way, it discovers what it had formerly been without it.

It strives to cling to it, but is still driven back from its strength by its own weakness. And because it cannot conform itself to its purity, it finds sweetness in weeping and in spreading out before itself, as it falls back upon itself, the tears of its weakness. For it cannot fix the eye of the mind upon that which it had suddenly seen in opposition to itself, because the very habit of its old condition compels it to go downward. Amid all this it pants, burns, and strives to rise above itself, but, overcome by weariness, it falls back into its familiar darkness.

**CHAPTER LX.—Likewise, from the foregoing.**

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XVIII (No. 66). [Note: [Col. 0835D] The manuscripts do not contain Chapters 60, 61, or 62.]

Having contemplated the inward joys of the vision of God and the fellowship of the steadfast angels, he turned his eyes downward. He saw where he lay who had been created so that he might have been able to stand among heavenly beings. He considered where he was and lamented what he was. He grieved that he had been cast away from the sight of God’s eyes, because, in comparison with the innermost light, he had felt more heavily the darkness of his exile, which he endured.

**CHAPTER LXI.—“Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Psalm 30:25).**

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book VII (No. 24), the following was added:

**“Act manfully,”** and so forth.

The strength of the righteous consists in conquering the flesh, resisting their own wills, extinguishing the delight of the present life, loving the hardships of this world for the sake of eternal rewards, despising the seductions of prosperity, and overcoming in their hearts the fear of adversity.

The strength of the reprobate, however, consists in loving transitory things without ceasing, enduring insensibly against the scourges of the Creator, not resting from the love of temporal things even in adversity, attaining empty glory even at the cost of life, seeking increases of wickedness, attacking the life of the good not only with words and conduct but also with swords, placing hope in themselves, and committing iniquity daily without any failure of desire.

**CHAPTER LXII.—Likewise, from the foregoing.**

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXVI (No. 63).

When he said, **“Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened,”** he immediately added something as though he had taken care to fortify the sex of the heart. For the mind of the luxurious is corrupted if it takes delight in transitory things.

**CHAPTER LXIII.—“Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Psalm 30:25).**

When the meaning to be drawn from sacred eloquence was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXVIII (No. 12), the following was added:

**“Act manfully,”** and so forth.

Sacred Scripture is accustomed to call “men” those who follow the ways of the Lord with strong and unwavering steps. Hence Paul also says: **“Raise up the drooping hands and the weakened knees”** (Hebrews 12:12). Hence Wisdom says in Proverbs: **“O men, I call to you”** (Proverbs 8:4). It is as though she plainly said: “I am speaking not to women but to men, because those whose mind is weak are entirely unable to receive my words.”

**CHAPTER LXIV.—“Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1).**

When the efforts of the elect through inward grace were being discussed, in Homily 4 on Ezekiel (No. 6), the following was added:

**“Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven,”** and so forth.

[Note: [Col. 0835D] Codex Michael indicates Book XXXIII on Job. Utica has Book XXXII. This homily exists at the location assigned above.]

Holy men strive before the eyes of God to cover the faults of their speech with the merits of their life. They strive to suppress immoderate words beneath the weight of good works. Hence holy Church, in her elect, daily covers the vice of idle speech with the virtue of good works.

**“Blessed, therefore, are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered”** (Hebrews 4:13).

But again, since it is written: **“All things are naked and open to his eyes,”** how can those things be covered which cannot possibly be hidden from His eyes, to whom all things are naked? Yet because we place beneath what we cover, and bring over it the thing by which we cover it, so that we may cover what has been placed underneath, we are said to cover sins when we place them, as it were, underneath by renouncing them and bring something else over them by then choosing the work of good action, so as to set it before them.

We therefore cover sins when we place good deeds over evil acts. When we renounce the evils we have committed and choose whatever good things we may do, we bring, as it were, a covering over that which we are ashamed to have seen. Whoever therefore abandons his former evils and afterward does good, covers by what he adds the wickedness that has passed, placing over it the merit of a good work.

However holy men may still be in this life, they nevertheless have something that they ought to cover before the eyes of God, because it is altogether impossible that they should never sin either in deed, speech, or thought.

**CHAPTER LXV.—“I turned in my anguish, while the thorn was broken” (Psalm 31:4).**

When the good of repentance was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XX (No. 21), the following was added:

**“I turned in my anguish,”** and so forth.

What is clearly expressed in this passage by “the thorn” except every sin? For while it draws the mind toward delight, it tears it as though by pricking. Hence the voice of the righteous and penitent says: **“I turned in my anguish, while the thorn was broken,”** because the mind is turned toward lamentation so that, through repentance, the prick of sin may be broken.

In another translation, however, the thorn is said not to be broken but to be fixed. This plainly does not differ from the same meaning, because the mind of the penitent is led to mourning when the committed fault is held fixed in memory.

**CHAPTER LXVI.—“I said: I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Psalm 31:5).**

[Col. 0836D]

When the discussion concerned wiping away sins of thought that had not yet proceeded into action, in the *Pastoral Rule*, Part III (Chapter 29, Admonition 30), the following was added:

**“I said,”** and so forth.

Often merciful God washes away the sins of the heart more quickly because He does not allow them to proceed into deeds; and contemplated wickedness is released all the more quickly the more strictly it is not bound by the accomplishment of a deed.

Hence the Psalmist rightly says: **“I said: I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart.”** By adding “of the heart,” he indicated that he wished to declare the injustices of his thoughts. And when he says, **“I said: I will declare,”** and immediately adds, **“And you forgave,”** he shows how readily forgiveness is granted in such matters: while he is still promising that he will ask, he has obtained what he was promising to ask. Thus, because the fault had not reached action, repentance would not reach torment; rather, the distress of thought would cleanse the mind, which only the iniquity of thought had defiled.

**CHAPTER LXVII.—“With bit and bridle bind their jaws, who do not draw near to you” (Psalm 31:9).**

When the usefulness of temporal punishment was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXVI (No. 56), the following was added:

**“With bit,”** and so forth.

Often those who do not listen to the words of one commanding are admonished by the blows of one striking, so that at least punishment may draw toward good desires those whom rewards do not invite. But if they despise even scourges, it is certainly clear that they will then feel the punishments of a more severe vengeance in proportion as here they trample upon the grace of greater providence.

**CHAPTER LXVIII.—“By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their strength” (Psalm 32:6).**

[Col. 0837B]

When the virtues of the apostles through the gift of the Holy Spirit were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XVII (Nos. 48–50), the following was added:

**“By the word of the Lord the heavens were established,”** and so forth.

What are designated by the name “heavens” except the holy apostles? They rain through words and flash with miracles, and their strength is strengthened by the gift of the Spirit. Concerning them the same Psalmist says: **“The heavens declare the glory of God”** (Psalm 18:1).

The Spirit then gave them power when He filled them, as we learn from Luke, who says: **“Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one rested upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in various tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance”** (Acts 2:2; from Homily 30 on the Gospels, nos. 7–8).

From Him, therefore, they received the adornments of strength whom previously an immense disgrace of fear had possessed. For we know that the first of the apostles—that is, of the heavens—before receiving the grace of this Spirit, denied life whenever he feared dying. He was overcome not by punishments, afflictions, or the terrifying power of anyone, but by the sole questioning of one servant.

And, so that the servant might not appear terrifying through a stronger sex, he was tested by a maidservant who questioned him. Again, so that such weakness of sex might be made still more contemptible by the lowliness of the office, he was questioned not merely by a maidservant but by a female doorkeeper.

See how insignificant a person was chosen to test him, so that it might be plainly revealed how greatly the weakness of fear had possessed him—he who could not stand even before the voice of a maidservant doorkeeper.

But now let us see what this man, who shortly before had been fearful, became after receiving the strength of the Spirit. Certainly, as Luke testifies, we learn with what authority he preached the Lord before priests and rulers. When a question arose after a miracle had been performed, and the chief priests, elders, and scribes gathered to persecute the apostles, they set them in the midst and required them to explain by what power they had performed the miracle.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, Peter said to them: **“Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a sick man, by what means this man has been healed, let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, this man stands before you healthy”** (Acts 4:9–10).

When the fury of the persecutors increased over this and the priests and rulers forbade them to preach Jesus, the authority by which Peter had grown against the threats of the rulers is shown when it is immediately added: **“But Peter and the apostles said: We must obey God rather than men”** (Acts 5:29).

But when the commands of those resisting the preachers’ authority could not suppress them, they proceeded to scourging, for it is added: **“Then the chief priests, after having them beaten, ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them.”**

Yet because even scourges could not suppress the strength of the apostles, this is plainly shown when it immediately follows: **“And they indeed went forth from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus”** (ibid., 41).

Soon afterward, what they did following the joy of the scourging is also indicated: **“And every day in the temple and from house to house they did not cease teaching and proclaiming Jesus Christ”** (ibid., 42).

Behold: the man who shortly before had been fearful now speaks in tongues, flashes with miracles, reproves the unbelief of priests and rulers with a free voice, and offers the others an example of authority for preaching Jesus. He is forbidden by blows to speak in the name of Jesus, yet he is not restrained. He who shortly before had feared the words of those questioning him despises the scourges of his attackers; he who had trembled when questioned by a maidservant overcomes the strength of rulers when beaten.

**“By the breath of his mouth is all their strength.”** Already made firm by the power of that same Holy Spirit, he pressed down the heights of this world beneath the foot of freedom, so that he might see as lowly whatever swelled with pride against the grace of the Creator.

This is the firmness of the heavens; these are the gifts of the Spirit, which customarily manifest themselves through various virtues. Paul enumerates them as divided by the gift of hidden dispensation, saying: **“To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the grace of healings in one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of words”** (1 Corinthians 12:8 ff.).

Then, concluding with a general definition, he says: **“But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills.”**

Thus it is rightly said: **“And by the breath of his mouth is all their strength,”** because the holy preachers would have shone with no splendor of strength unless they had received the promised gifts of the Paraclete.

**CHAPTER LXIX.—“Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin” (Psalm 32:7).**

When the discussion concerned the wicked schemes directed against the Church, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XIX (No. 15), the following was added:

**“Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin.”**

The Lord gathers the waters of the sea as in a wineskin when, disposing all things with wondrous restraint, He restrains the threats of carnal people, shut up within their own hearts. For as the persecution of the final age increases, holy Church is compelled to endure the open voices of heretics, when they reveal in the voice of manifest error the movements of their hearts which they now conceal within the folds of their thoughts.

Now, as John says: **“The dragon is held shut in the abyss”** (Revelation 20:3), because diabolical wickedness is hidden in their deceitful hearts. But, as it is said there, **“Let the dragon be brought out from the pit of the abyss,”** because what is now concealed through fear will then be openly revealed against the Church: all the serpent’s venom will be disclosed from the hearts of the wicked.

Now a raging conscience hides itself beneath a flattering tongue, and the malice of cunning conceals itself, as it were, beneath an abyss of pretense. Now the Lord, as the Psalmist says, **“gathers the waters of the sea as in a wineskin.”**

The wineskin is carnal thought; the waters of the sea are therefore gathered in a wineskin when the bitterness of a perverse mind does not burst forth externally in the voice of wicked license.

**CHAPTER LXX.—“Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9).**

When the desire for God, nourished through the experience of good works, was being discussed, in Homily 36 on the Gospels (No. 1), the following was added:

**“Taste and see,”** and so forth.

Spiritual delights always increase desire in the mind while satisfying it, because the more their flavor is perceived, the more fully it is recognized what should be loved with greater eagerness. For this reason things not possessed cannot be loved, because their flavor is unknown. Who can love what he does not know?

Therefore the Psalmist admonishes us, saying: **“Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.”** It is as though he openly said: “You do not know His sweetness if you do not taste it at all. Touch the food of life with the palate of the heart, so that, testing its sweetness, you may be able to love it.”

But man lost these delights when he sinned in paradise, when he closed his mouth to the food of inward sweetness. Hence we too, born into the misery of this exile, come here already with a distaste for it. We do not know what we ought to desire, and the disease of our distaste becomes more severe the more the mind distances itself from eating that sweetness. It no longer desires inward delights because it has long grown unaccustomed to eating them.

Thus we waste away in our distaste and are exhausted by the long disease of famine. And because we do not wish to taste inwardly the sweetness prepared for us, miserable as we are, we love our hunger outwardly.

**CHAPTER LXXI.—“The rich have lacked and suffered hunger” (Psalm 33:11).**

When true and false delights were being distinguished in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XV (No. 9), the following was added:

**“The rich have lacked and suffered hunger.”**

If this were said of the rich person’s want and hunger with respect to outward food, they would certainly not be rich if they needed bodily bread. But because, while they multiply outwardly, they become empty inwardly, they are said to be both rich and needy, since they do not deserve to be filled with the bread of wisdom.

**CHAPTER LXXII.—“Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27).**

When the virtues of the perfect were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book I (No. 3), the following was added:

**“Turn away from evil and do good.”**

The good deeds acceptable to God are by no means acceptable if they are stained before His eyes by an admixture of evil. Hence Solomon says: **“Whoever offends in one thing loses many good things”** (Ecclesiastes 9:18). Hence James bears witness, saying: **“Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all”** (James 2:10). Hence Paul says: **“A little leaven corrupts the whole batch”** (1 Corinthians 5:6).

**CHAPTER LXXIII.—Likewise, from the foregoing.**

[Col. 0839C]

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIII (No. 46). [Note: [Col. 0839D] This chapter and the following one are omitted in the manuscripts.]

To turn away from evil is to rise from the place where one lay. To do good, however, is to prepare works deserving reward in which one ought to rest. For whoever turns away from evil but does not do good has indeed risen from the place where he lay, but has not yet prepared the place where he ought to rest.

**CHAPTER LXXIV.—“The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken” (Psalm 33:21).**

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIII (No. 48), the following was added:

**“The Lord guards all their bones,”** and so forth.

This is certainly said not of bodily bones but of the powers of the mind. For we know that the bones of many people have been physically broken; and the persecutors of the Lord broke the legs of the thief to whom it was said, **“Today you will be with me in paradise”** (Luke 23:43), just as they broke those of the other thief.

**CHAPTER LXXV.—“Let them become like dust before the face of the wind, and let the angel of the Lord afflict them” (Psalm 34:9).**

[Col. 0839D] When the exercise and fall of temptations were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book III (Nos. 62–63), the following was added:

**“Let them become like dust before the face of the wind,”** and so forth.

Whoever is swept away in his heart by the breeze of temptation is lifted up like dust before the face of the wind; and when divine strictness strikes amid these things, what else afflicts him than the angel of the Lord?

But these things happen differently to the reprobate and to the elect. Their hearts are tempted in such a way that they consent; the temptations of the righteous, however, they indeed receive, but resist. The mind of the former is captured delightfully; and although for a time what is wrongly suggested displeases it, afterward, through deliberation, it pleases.

The latter, however, receive the darts of temptation in such a way that they are always wearied by resisting. And if at any time a tempted mind is swept away as far as delight, they nevertheless quickly become ashamed of the intrusion of their own delight and strongly censure whatever carnal thing they discover within themselves. [Note: [Col. 0839D] The Utica and Michael manuscripts have: “whatever carnal thing they discover within themselves through carnal suggestion,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0840D] This chapter is absent from the manuscripts.]

**CHAPTER LXXVI.—“Let their ways become darkness and slippery ground” (Psalm 34:6).**

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XIX (No. 39), the following was added:

**“Let their ways become darkness and slippery ground.”**

That is, through the darkness they may not see where they ought to go; and even if they see the right paths, they cannot stand upon them because of the slipperiness. Thus the former stumble among good things because of slippery ground; the latter, because of darkness, do not know which good things to follow.

**CHAPTER LXXVII.—“All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you?” (Psalm 34:10).**

When the suppression of presumption about oneself through knowledge of the divine and hidden judgment was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book V (No. 55), the following was added:

**“All my bones,”** and so forth.

What is signified by “bones” except strong deeds? Concerning these the prophet also says: **“The Lord guards all their bones.”**

Often people judge the things they do to be of some importance because they do not know how subtle is the judgment of the inner strictness. But when, carried away through contemplation, they behold heavenly things, they melt, in a certain way, from the very security of their presumption; and they tremble all the more in the divine presence the less they consider their own good deeds worthy of the judgment of Him whom they behold.

Hence the one who had advanced by performing strong deeds, raised up by the Spirit, cried out: **“All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you?”** It is as though he said: “My flesh has no word, because my weaknesses are utterly silent before you; but my bones proclaim the praise of your greatness, because even those things which I believed to be strong in me tremble at your judgment.”

**CHAPTER LXXVIII.—Likewise, from the foregoing.**

[Col. 0840C] In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XVIII (No. 79). When the nature of the divine likeness in human beings was being discussed, the following was added:

**“Lord, who is like you?”**

All the saints reach those eternal joys so that they may be able to be like God, as it is written: **“When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is”** (1 John 3:2).

And yet it is written: **“Lord, God of hosts, who is like you?”** (Psalm 88:5). Again he says: **“Who shall be like the Lord among [Note: [Col. 0840D] Some manuscripts have: “among the sons of men.”] the sons?”**

How, then, are they like Him, and how are they not like Him, except because they will be like this Wisdom according to the image, yet will not be like Him according to equality? By looking upon the eternity of God, they become eternal. And while they receive the gift of His vision, through the reception of blessedness they imitate what they see.

They are therefore like Him because they are blessed; yet they are not like the Creator because they are creatures. Thus they possess a certain likeness to God because they have no end. Yet they do not possess the equality of the unbounded, because they are bounded.

**CHAPTER LXXIX.—“I saw the wicked man exalted above measure and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Psalm 36:35).**

[Note: [Col. 0840D] In Gemet, here and thereafter: “above the cedars.”]

[Col. 0840D]

When the progress of merits and the knowledge of the wicked were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book XV (No. 68), the following was added:

**“I saw the wicked man exalted above measure,”** and so forth.

Because the prophet David had already passed in heart beyond love of the present age, he described the glory of the wicked, saying: **“I saw the wicked man exalted above measure and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon.”**

But because he had not subjected his heart to this world, he rightly despised it, saying: **“I passed by, and behold, he was no more.”** The wicked would have been something in his estimation if he himself had not passed beyond this age through the direction of his mind. But to a mind that had passed beyond him, he who would have been something great to one who did not pass by appeared to be nothing, because when eternal recompense is considered, the worthlessness of present glory is recognized.

Hence Moses, when he sought the glory of heavenly contemplation, said: **“As I pass by, I shall see this vision”** (Exodus 3:3). For unless he had moved the step of his heart away from the love of the world, he could never have understood heavenly things.

**CHAPTER LXXX.—“My scars have become putrid and corrupted because of my foolishness” (Psalm 37:6).**

When the abolition of the memory of past transgressions was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book IX (No. 83), the following was added:

**“My scars have become putrid,”** and so forth.

Whoever corrects and mourns sin places a scar over the wound. But when the deceived mind recalls for its own delight that of which it has already repented, the scar of repentance that had been placed over it returns to the putrefaction of the wound, so that perverse delight produces stench after the scar, with its healed skin, had already shown the wound to be safe.

What, then, are scars except healings of wounds? He had seen loosened wickednesses return to the delight of memory who wept over scars. For scars becoming putrid means that the wounds of sins already healed once again creep into temptation, and that after the skin of repentance has been laid over them, the stench of guilt and the pain are felt again from their suggestions, because in reality nothing is done outwardly in deed, while sin is committed inwardly by thought alone. The mind binds itself by strict guilt unless it wipes this away with attentive lamentation.

**CHAPTER LXXXI.—“I have been bent down and humbled exceedingly” (Psalm 37:7).**

When the danger of an evil habit was being discussed, in Homily 13 on the Gospels (No. 7), the following was added:

**“I have been bent down,”** and so forth.

We often see what ought to be done, but do not fulfill it in action; we strive and grow weak. The judgment of the mind sees uprightness, but the strength of action succumbs to it, because it is already part of the punishment of sin that, although one may indeed be able to see the good through a gift, one may nevertheless be driven away by merit from what one sees.

For habitual guilt binds the mind, so that it cannot rise to uprightness. It strives and falls, because where it has long remained voluntarily, there it falls even when unwilling, compelled by force.

Hence the Psalmist aptly speaks of this bending of ours, using the figure of the human race: **“I have been bent down and humbled exceedingly.”**

Contemplating that man had been created to gaze upon the heavenly light but, because sins demanded it, had been cast outside, he carries the darkness of his mind, does not desire heavenly things, fixes his attention on what is below, does not desire celestial things, and constantly turns earthly things over in his mind. What he lamented concerning his race, he cried out concerning himself, saying: **“I have been bent down and humbled exceedingly.”**

If a human being, having lost contemplation of heavenly things, thought only of the necessities of the flesh, he would be bent down and humbled, but he would not be bent down exceedingly. The one whom not only necessity casts down from heavenly thoughts but illicit pleasure also lays low is not merely bent down, but bent down exceedingly.

[Note: [Col. 0841D] Absent from the manuscripts.]

**CHAPTER LXXXII.—“But I am ready for scourges” (Psalm 37:18).**

When the mind of the elect, always ready to receive scourges, was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book VII (No. 21), the following was added:

**“But I am ready for scourges.”**

Because holy men consider the wound of their mind’s corruption not to be free from putrefaction, they willingly prepare themselves under the physician’s hand for cutting, so that, when the wound is opened, the poison may leave which was killing them inwardly beneath healthy skin.

**CHAPTER LXXXIII.—“I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin” (Psalm 37:19).**

[Col. 0842A] When the discussion concerned not abolishing the memory of sin, so that it might be corrected through knowledge of one’s own weakness, in the exposition of blessed Job, Book VIII (No. 37), the following was added:

**“I will declare my iniquity,”** and so forth.

The tribulation of the spirit moves the tongue of the elect, so that the voice of confession may attack the guilt of an evil deed. It must also be known that the reprobate often confess their sins [Note: [Col. 0841D] Utica and Michael have: “but disdain to think upon them.”] but disdain to mourn them. The elect, however, disclose their faults with the words of confession and pursue them with the tears of strict judgment.

Hence, after the prophet had promised that he would declare his iniquity, he added that he would also think upon it. It is as though he openly confessed, saying: “My tongue speaks of guilt in such a way that my spirit does not wander elsewhere, free from the goad of sorrow. In speaking of my faults I open the wound; but by thinking upon my faults for the sake of correction, I seek the wound’s healing through the medicine of sorrow.”

Whoever points out the evils he has committed but refuses to weep over what he has pointed out is like someone who draws back the clothing and exposes a wound, but, with his mind numb, applies no medicine to it.

The voice of confession must therefore be shaken forth by sorrow alone, lest the wound, exposed yet neglected—and now touched more freely because it has become known to others—grow more dangerously putrid.

The Psalmist therefore had not only exposed the wound of his heart but also applied to the exposed wound the medicine of sorrow, saying: **“I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin.”** By declaring it, he exposes the hidden wound; but by thinking upon it, what else does he do except apply medicine to the wound?

Yet in the afflicted mind that carefully considers its own losses, a quarrel arises on its own behalf against itself. For when it urges itself toward the laments of repentance, it tears itself apart through hidden reproach.

[Note: [Col. 0842D] Absent from the manuscripts.]

**CHAPTER LXXXIV.—“I have set a guard over my mouth, when the sinner stood against me” (Psalm 38:2).**
In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXIII (no. 18), the following is added: “I set a guard over my mouth,” etc.—The hearts of the righteous are inflamed when they see the deeds of the wicked increasing without correction, and they believe themselves to share in their guilt because, by keeping silent, they allow them to increase in iniquity. After the prophet David had imposed silence upon himself, saying, “I set a guard over my mouth when the sinner stood against me,” he became mute and was humbled, and kept silent concerning good things; yet in that very silence he burned with the righteous zeal of charity. Immediately he added: “And my pain was renewed. My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire will blaze” (ibid., 3). His heart therefore grew hot within, because the ardor of his love refused to flow outward through words of admonition. The fire burned in the meditation of his heart because the rebuke of the guilty had grown cold through the restraint of his speech. The zeal of charity regulates itself by growing through the marvelous consolation it receives when it flows forth in words of correction against the deeds of the wicked, so that it does not cease to rebuke what it cannot correct, lest through the consent of silence it declare itself an accomplice of the guilty.

## Chapter LXXXV

“I became mute and did not open my mouth, because you did this” (Psalm 38:3).

[Col. 0842D] When the subject of not resisting divine judgments was treated in *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXIII (no. 33), the following was added: “I became mute,” etc.—When a person is scourged and considers that God is greater than he in everything he suffers, he submits himself to the judgment of the one whom he does not doubt to be greater than himself. He should believe that what he suffers from one who is better is just, even if he does not understand the reasons for that justice. For whoever is struck because of sin begins already to be just, unless he resists by murmuring, precisely when he does not accuse the justice of the one who strikes him. Humanity was created under God, and returns to the order of its creation when it places before itself the equity of its judge—even an equity it does not understand—so that, by considering the Creator’s power, the swelling of the mind may subside through remembrance of its created condition.

Hence the prophet David, when the weight of his affliction forced him to break out into an excess of speech, recollecting himself and considering his created condition, said: “I became mute and did not open my mouth, because you did this to me.” He weighed the order of his created condition and found justice in his affliction, because the one who in his goodness created him when he did not exist surely struck him justly when he did exist.

## Chapter LXXXVI

“Nevertheless, every human being is troubled in vain” (Psalm 38:7).

When the frailties of human nature were treated in *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXII (nos. 34–36, in reverse order), the following was added: “Nevertheless, every human being is troubled in vain.”—Although a human being walks in the image of God, he is nevertheless troubled in vain. It often happens that a holy man is outwardly troubled while remaining inwardly undisturbed; and that what can be troubled in vain belongs to the weakness of the flesh, whereas his walking in the image of God belongs to the strength of his mind. Thus he is strengthened within by divine help, yet is still weighed down outwardly by the burden of humanity.

Great indeed is the security of the heart that possesses no worldly desire. For if the heart longs to attain earthly things, it can in no way be secure and tranquil, because it either desires what it does not possess in order to possess it, or, having acquired it, fears that it may lose it. While it hopes for prosperity amid adversity, it fears adversity amid prosperity; it is tossed here and there as if by waves, and is turned about in various ways by the changing fortunes of things.

But if the mind is once firmly fixed in the desire for the heavenly homeland, it is less harassed by the disturbance of temporal things. From all external movements it withdraws its intention as into some most secret retreat; and there, clinging to what is unchanging and rising above all mutable things, it is already, through the very tranquility of its rest, in the world yet outside the world. It surpasses all things below through its intention toward things above; and by a kind of freedom it feels itself superior to all things it does not desire. Nor does it endure inwardly the storm of temporal affairs that it observes outwardly, because all earthly things that, when desired, could oppress the mind now lie beneath it, despised.

Hence the prophet rightly says: “Set up a watchtower for yourself” (Jeremiah 31:21), so that, while each person watches the things above, he may rise above the things below. Habakkuk likewise says: “I will stand upon my watch” (Habakkuk 2:1). He stands upon his watch when, through the diligence of discipline, he does not succumb to earthly desires but rises above them, so that, while he continually desires eternity, which stands firm, everything that passes may be within him.

Yet because a holy man, however greatly he may advance in virtue, is still placed in this life and is pressed outwardly by the weakness of the flesh, Habakkuk again uttered a single statement serving both purposes, saying: “Trembling entered into my bones, and beneath me my strength was troubled” (Habakkuk 3:16). It is as though he were saying: “The strength in which I remain undisturbed when I am lifted above is not my own strength; my weakness is what troubles me below.” He is therefore undisturbed above himself and capable of disturbance beneath himself: above himself, insofar as he had been carried away toward what is highest; beneath himself, insofar as he still bore remnants of himself in what is lowest. He is undisturbed above himself because he had already passed into the contemplation of God; he is capable of disturbance beneath himself because beneath himself he still remained a weak human being.

The prophet David, harmonizing with this statement, says: “I said in the excess of my mind: Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:2). One might reply to him: If everyone is a liar, then you are one also, and the statement you uttered as a liar will already be false. But if you are not a liar, the statement will no longer be true, because, while you are truthful, not every human being is shown to be a liar.

But we must note what precedes: “I said in the excess of my mind.” Through the excess of his mind, therefore, he passed beyond even himself when he pronounced judgment concerning the condition of humanity. It is as though he plainly said: “I uttered a true judgment concerning the falsehood of all human beings from the place where I myself was above humanity.” He is a liar insofar as he is human; but he is not a liar at all insofar as, through the excess of his mind, he is above humanity.

Thus all the perfect, although they still endure something troubled because of the weakness of the flesh, nevertheless already enjoy inwardly, in the most tranquil secrecy of contemplation, such peace that whatever happens outwardly disturbs them inwardly in no way.

## Chapter LXXXVII

“He brought me up from the pit of misery and from the mud of filth; he set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps; and he put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God” (Psalm 39:2–4).

When the growth of good works was treated in book I, homily 9, on Ezekiel (no. 4), the following was added: “He brought me up from the pit of misery,” etc.—When we are still standing upon the summit of pride but have begun to experience something of the fear of eternity, it is fitting that we fall into repentance. When, recognizing our weakness carefully, we lie humbly prostrate, we must rise through the consolation of the divine word to stronger works. And when we already persist in the solidity of good works, it is necessary that we preach and recall others from the very things by which we corrected ourselves.

For one who is lying prostrate is not commanded to proceed to preaching, lest a weak person destroy by his actions what he is able to build by his words. Thus the prophet rightly says here: “He brought me up from the pit of misery and from the mud of filth; he set my feet upon a rock,” etc. After asserting that he had been brought up from the mud of filth and saw his feet set upon the rock, he asserted that a new song had been put into his mouth. He is first brought up from the mud of wickedness, so that his feet may be made firm through faith upon the rock. After the feet and steps of good works have been fixed upon the rock, he then receives the song of preaching, so that he may be able to sing a hymn to God both in works and in words.

Thus Saul, while proceeding proudly toward Damascus, was struck down and lay prostrate by the voice of the Redeemer. Although he was destined to become a preacher, he did not immediately hear that he should preach what he had seen. Rather, while he lay prostrate, he was told: “Enter the city, and it will be told you what you must do” (Acts 9:7). Lying prostrate, he could hear only this: that, once he rose, he might learn what he had heard. Once risen, he learned this: that he should preach what he had learned.

## Chapter LXXXVIII

“You have done many things, O Lord my God; your wonders are many” (Psalm 39:6).

When the Creator’s power was treated through the miracles of created things in *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book VI (no. 18), the following was added: “You have done many things,” etc.—Who could sufficiently explore the wonders of almighty God: that he created all things from nothing; that the very structure of the world has been arranged through the marvelous power of his might; that heaven is suspended above the air and earth balanced above the abyss; that this entire universe exists from invisible things; that he made the human being, so to speak, by gathering another world into a small compass, though a rational one; that, forming this being from soul and flesh, he joined spirit and clay together through an arrangement of power beyond investigation?

From these things, therefore, we know something else, and something else we are; yet we neglect to marvel because those things that are marvelous through incomprehensible investigation have become commonplace in human eyes through familiarity.

Thus it happens that if a dead person is raised, everyone leaps up in astonishment; yet every day a human being who did not exist is born, and no one marvels, although it is certainly evident to everyone that creating what did not exist is greater than restoring what did exist.

Because Aaron’s dry staff blossomed (Numbers 17), everyone marveled; yet every day a tree grows from dry earth, and the power of dust is changed into wood, and no one marvels. Because five thousand people were fed with five loaves (John 6), everyone marveled that food increased beneath their teeth; yet every day scattered grains of seed multiply into the fullness of ears of grain, and no one marvels. When they saw water changed once into wine, everyone marveled (John 2); yet every day the moisture of the earth, drawn up into the root of the vine, is changed through the cluster into wine, and no one marvels.

All things, therefore, are marvelous that people neglect to admire because, as we have said, familiarity has made them dull in their consideration.

## Chapter LXXXIX

“I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Psalm 39:6).

When the steadfastness of the elect and the rejection of the wicked who outwardly maintain the faith within the holy Church were treated in Homily 19 on the Gospels (no. 5) and in *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXV (no. 21), the following was added: “I proclaimed and spoke,” etc.—When the Lord calls, the faithful are multiplied beyond number, because even those who do not attain the number of the elect come to the faith. They are admitted among the faithful through confession, but because of their wicked life they do not deserve to be counted there among the lot of the faithful.

The prophet, therefore, observing so many people outwardly believing in the Church at this time—so many, clearly, as are known to exceed the number and total of the elect—says: “They were multiplied beyond number.” It is as though he were saying: Since many enter the Church, even those who are excluded from the number of the heavenly kingdom enter the kingdom outwardly through faith, because by their multitude they surpass the total of the elect.

[Note: [Col. 0845D] Absent from the manuscripts.]

## Chapter XC

“You have overturned his entire bed in his sickness” (Psalm 40:4).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book VIII (no. 41), the following was added: “You have overturned his entire bed,” etc.—For when the temptation of the flesh shakes us, our trembling weakness also disturbs the bedchamber of the mind.

## Chapter XCI

“You have overturned his entire bed in his sickness” (Psalm 40:4).

[Note: [Col. 0845D] The printed editions read: “Concerning the various disturbances of this pilgrimage, lest the present life delight us more than the future life.”]

When the multiple meanings of things in sacred eloquence were treated in *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXIII (nos. 46–47), the following was added: “You have overturned his entire bed,” etc.—What is understood in this passage by “bed” except temporal rest? When someone, wearied by worldly cares, is moved through divine grace to leave the arduous roads of this world, he usually considers how he may flee the desires of the present life and rest from its labors. He then seeks for himself the order of the desired rest and longs to find, as it were, a bed—a place of cessation from all his labors.

But because a human being, while still placed in this life, cannot live without temptations in any position or in any private retreat, very often greater pain from temptation is found in what is constructed for rest. Hence the prophet rightly says: “You have overturned his entire bed in his sickness.” It is as though he were saying: “Everything he prepared here for himself as rest, by a hidden judgment you have changed into disturbance.”

This occurs by the gracious providence of God, so that during the time of this pilgrimage the life of the elect may be troubled. The present life is a road by which we journey toward our homeland; and therefore, by a hidden judgment, we are frequently worn down here by disturbance, lest we love the road in place of our homeland.

Travelers often, when they see pleasant meadows along the road, delay their journey and turn aside from the straight path they had begun; the beauty of the road slows their steps while it delights them. Hence the Lord makes the road of this world difficult for his elect as they journey toward him, lest, while someone is nourished by the rest of the present life as if by pleasantness, he prefer to travel for a long time rather than arrive quickly; lest, while delighted by the road, he forget what he desired in his homeland.

## Chapter XCII

“My tears have been my bread day and night” (Psalm 41:4).

When the fruit of compunction was treated in *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book V (no. 15), the following was added: “My tears have been my bread day and night.”—The soul feeds upon its own mourning when, by weeping, it is lifted toward the joys above. Within, it endures the groaning of its pain; yet it receives nourishment for refreshment from the very fact that the power of love flows forth here through tears.

## Chapter XCIII

“I shall remember you from the land of the Jordan and Hermoniim” (Psalm 41:7).

When the goodness of humility was treated in *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXXIII (no. 13), the following was added: “I shall remember you from the land of the Jordan,” etc.—What is the Jordan except descent? “Hermoniim,” however, is interpreted as anathema, that is, alienation. He remembers God from the land of the Jordan and Hermoniim when, in casting himself down and becoming alien to himself, he is recalled to the memory of his Creator.

Hence Truth says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9:23). He denies himself when, trampling down the arrogance of pride, he shows himself to be alien before the eyes of God.

## Chapter XCIV

“By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it” (Psalm 41:9).

[Col. 0846B] When the trials of the elect were treated in *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXIII (no. 52), the following was added: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy,” etc.—Each person receives the grace of a heavenly gift in the tranquility of repose, but how much he has received he reveals in the disturbance of adversity. The Lord’s mercy is therefore commanded by day, because it is received by recognizing it in a time of peace; but it is declared by night, because the gift received in tranquility is manifested in tribulations.

## Chapter XCV

“You humbled us in the place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us” (Psalm 43:20).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXVI (no. 54), the following was added: “You humbled us in the place of affliction,” etc.—The place of affliction is the present life. Those who are journeying toward the eternal homeland now cast themselves down temporarily in the place of affliction, so that then they may truly be raised up in the place of joy.

(Ibid., book XX, no. 56.) The souls of the elect are now possessed by days of affliction, because days of joy follow afterward. For it is written: “It will be well with the one who fears God at the end” (Eccles. 1:13). And again it is said of the Church: “She will laugh on the last day” (Proverbs 31:25). The present is a time of affliction for the good, so that exultation without end may eventually follow them.

It continues: “And the shadow of death covered us.” (Ibid., book IV, no. 30.) What is understood in this passage by “the shadow of death” except the death of the flesh? For just as there is a true death by which the soul is separated from God, so there is a shadow of death by which the flesh is separated from the soul.

Through the prophet, therefore, the voice of the martyrs now says: “You humbled us in the place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us.” Since it is clear that they die not in spirit but only in the flesh, they say that they are covered not by true death but by the shadow of death.

(Ibid., book XXXIII, no. 6.) [Note: [Col. 0846D] At this point the manuscripts read: “likewise, whence above.”] What is expressed by “shadow,” which is nevertheless accompanied by the addition “of death,” except the death of the flesh, or perhaps any of the reprobate who imitate the darkness of the ancient enemy through the zeal of wicked action?

Hence the voice of the martyrs says through the Psalmist: “You humbled us in the place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us.” The shadow of death oppresses God’s elect when the death of the flesh, which is an image of eternal death, separates them from this life; for just as eternal death separates the soul from God, so bodily death separates the body from the soul.

Or certainly the shadow of death oppresses them because it is written of the ancient enemy: “His name is Death.” [Note: [Col. 0846D] In several manuscripts: “His name is death.”] The reprobate are therefore the shadow of death because they imitate the wickedness of that enemy’s pride and reproduce his likeness as a shadow, drawing into themselves a resemblance to his evil. They cover God’s elect when, through the cruelty of persecution, they temporarily grow strong against them.

## Chapter XCVI

“My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Psalm 44:2).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXXIII (no. 7), the following was added: “My tongue,” etc.—What we speak passes away, but what we write remains. The tongue of the Father is called the pen of a scribe because from him the Word is immediately generated as eternal and without passing away.

## Chapter XCVII

[Note: [Col. 0847D] Several manuscripts read: “Gird on the sword.”]

“Gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one” (Psalm 44:4).

In the *Commentary on Ezekiel*, homily 8 (no. 26), the following was added: “Gird yourself with your sword,” etc.—What is expressed by “thigh” except the propagation of the flesh? From Abraham’s thigh the virgin Mary came forth; in her womb the Only-Begotten of the Father deigned to become incarnate, and through that incarnation God became known to the whole world.

To him, therefore, the prophet says: “Gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one.” He took up the sword around his thigh because his word of preaching gained strength through his incarnation.

## Chapter XCVIII

[Note: [Col. 0847D] Omitted in the manuscripts.]

“Attend, prosper, advance, and reign, for the sake of truth, gentleness, and justice” (Psalm 44:5).

[Col. 0847B] In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book IX (no. 62), the following was added: “Attend, prosper,” etc.—Through the Law, God had held the rod, saying: “If anyone does this or that, let him die.” But when the Lord became incarnate, he removed the rod because he showed the ways of life through gentleness.

Hence the Psalmist says to him: “Attend, prosper, advance, and reign, for the sake of truth, gentleness, and justice.” He did not wish to be feared as God, but inspired love as a father, so that he might be loved.

## Chapter XCIX

“Likewise, from the passage above.”

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book I (no. 15).—In pursuing truth, he preserved gentleness together with justice, so that he neither lost the zeal for righteousness under the weight of gentleness nor, conversely, disturbed the weight of gentleness through zeal for righteousness.

## Chapter C

“Myrrh, stacte, and cassia are from your garments, from ivory steps, by which daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor” (Psalm 44:9).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXXV (no. 44), the following was added: “Myrrh, resin, and cassia,” etc.—What is designated by the names “myrrh,” “stacte,” and “cassia” except the sweetness of virtues? What is expressed by “ivory steps” except the ascent of those progressing through great strength?

Therefore, when the Redeemer comes, he uses myrrh, stacte, and cassia in his garment, because from his elect, with whom he mercifully clothes himself, he spreads the fragrance of marvelous virtue. In them, the same fragrance is drawn from ivory steps, because the reputation of their virtues arises not from the display of pretense but from the ascent of true and solid works.

He rightly adds: “By which daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor.” For holy souls, raised up from the ancient fathers to knowledge of the truth, delight their Redeemer in his honor, because in whatever good they do, they claim nothing for their own praise.

[Note: [Col. 0848D] The following four chapters are absent from the manuscripts.]

## Chapter CI

“Daughters of Tyre will adore him with gifts” (Psalm 44:13).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXXV (no. 34), the following was added: “Daughters of Tyre will adore him with gifts.”—It is a pleasure to open the eyes of faith and contemplate that final banquet of the holy Church, at which the people of Israel will be received. To that banquet the great Elijah, coming at that time, is appointed as the inviter of the guests. Then relatives and acquaintances come to him with gifts—those who shortly before despised him when he was placed under the scourge.

As the day of judgment approaches, either through the words of the forerunner or through certain signs breaking forth, the power of the Lord who is coming already shines upon them in some manner. Hastening to forestall his wrath, they hasten the time of their conversion.

When converted, they come with gifts, because they honor by offering works of virtue as gifts the one whom shortly before they mocked in his Passion. In their offering they undoubtedly complete what we see already accomplished in large part and still believe will be accomplished perfectly: “Daughters of Tyre will adore him with gifts.” Then the daughters of Tyre adore him more fully with gifts, when the minds of the Israelites, now subject to the desires of this world, at last recognize the one whom in their pride they had killed and bring him the sacrifices of their confession.

## Chapter CII

“All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Psalm 44:14).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XIX (no. 20), the following was added: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within.” But because the Church also preserves exterior things that are irreproachable, he rightly adds concerning her: “She is clothed all around in golden fringes, in varied adornment,” so that she may be beautiful within herself and outwardly before others; advancing herself through inward glory and instructing others through the outward examples of her works.

## Chapter CIII

“Likewise, from the passage above.”

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book VIII (no. 83).—The daughter of kings is the Church, generated in good works through the preaching of spiritual rulers. She has glory within because what she does is not characterized by the boastfulness of display.

## Chapter CIV

“In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44:17).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book IV (no. 61), the following was added: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you,” etc.—He calls the rulers of the holy Church “princes,” whom divine dispensation continually substitutes in the place of the preceding preachers.

## Chapter CV

“Mountains will be moved into the heart of the sea” (Psalm 45:2).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XVIII (no. 50), the following was added: “Mountains will be moved into the heart of the sea.”—What is signified by “mountains” except the height of preachers? Chosen preachers are rightly called mountains of the eternal homeland because, through the loftiness of their life, they abandon the low things of earth and draw near to heaven.

Of these mountains it is now said: “Mountains will be moved into the heart of the sea.” Mountains were moved into the heart of the sea when the preaching apostles, rejected because of Judea’s unbelief, came to the understanding of the Gentiles. Hence they themselves also say in the Acts of the Apostles: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:45).

## Chapter CVI

“Be at leisure and see that I am God” (Psalm 45:11).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book V (nos. 19–20), the following was added: “Be at leisure and see,” etc.—If the contemplative life were not more suitable than the active life for certain minds, the Lord would never say through the prophet: “Be at leisure and see that I am God.”

Those are at leisure who are rightly in control of themselves, when they interrupt and set aside the noise of earthly activities for the love of God, lest, while they continually occupy themselves with what is below, their heart fall completely from what is above. They know that the mind cannot be lifted toward heavenly things if it is continually occupied with lowly matters amid the tumult of cares.

What can an occupied mind obtain concerning God, when even a mind at leisure struggles to grasp something about him? The Psalmist therefore rightly says: “Be at leisure and see that I am God,” because whoever neglects to be at leisure for God hides from himself, by his own judgment, the light of his vision.

Those who are occupied with temporal affairs therefore arrange outward things well when they carefully retreat inward, when they do not love the noise of disturbances outside but rest within themselves in the embrace of tranquility. Small minds, however, do not cease to turn the tumult of temporal affairs around within themselves, even when they are at leisure. They preserve in thought the images of what they love, and although they do nothing outwardly, they nevertheless labor within themselves under the burden of an uneasy rest.

If the administration of those same things is entrusted to them, they abandon themselves completely and pursue fleeting temporal matters through the course of their intention, with the ceaseless steps of their thoughts. Pious minds, however, neither seek these things when they are absent nor bear them heavily when they are present, because they fear leaving themselves through care for outward things.

## Chapter CVII

“God will be recognized in her steps when he receives her” (Psalm 47:3).

In book II, homily 3, on Ezekiel (no. 3), the following was added: “God will be recognized in her steps,” etc.—What is designated by these steps except the merits of virtues? Whether in knowledge of the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Jesus Christ; or in knowledge of divine eloquence; or in the faith that we have received concerning him, we reach higher attainments by certain steps.
