No one suddenly becomes perfect. Rather, in a good way of life each person begins with small things in order to reach great ones. God, therefore, will be recognized in her steps when he receives her. For when the Lord receives the holy Church, he is recognized in her steps, because her glory is declared through her growth. The more the holy Church advances by ascending, the more God becomes known to humanity through her virtues.

Concerning these steps it is written again: “I will declare him by my individual steps” (Job 31:37). He declares the almighty Lord by his individual steps who, through the growth of the virtues he has begun, continually renders him praise for his goodness.

If there were not certain steps in the ascent of the heart, the Psalmist would not say: “They will go from virtue to virtue” (Psalm 63:8). Nor is it surprising that there are steps from virtue to virtue, since each individual virtue itself grows as if through certain steps and is thus brought to the highest things through the progress of merits.

The beginnings of virtue are one thing, its progress another, and its perfection another. If faith itself were not led to perfection through certain steps, the holy apostles would never have said: “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5). A certain man came to the Lord wishing his son to be healed; when asked whether he believed, he answered: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark 9:23).

Consider, therefore, what is said. If he believed, why did he speak of unbelief? But if he knew that he possessed unbelief, how did he believe? Because faith grows through the hidden inspiration of grace by successive degrees of merit, at one and the same time the man who had not yet believed perfectly both believed and was unbelieving.

[Note: [Col. 0849D] The same prophet in the Gembloux manuscript.]

## Chapter CVIII

“Likewise, from the passage above.”

Homily 15 on Ezekiel.—[Note: [Col. 0849D] Assigned in Michael to homily 1 on Ezekiel.] Almighty God is recognized in the steps of his Church because, in each of her virtues and miracles, he demonstrates to everyone how greatly he is to be feared and loved.

He receives this love when she returns from her sins to repentance. His elect are praised when it is said: “For behold, kings are called.” Since they correct their former evils through repentance, the manner in which their repentance takes place is also added: “They saw; then they marveled; they were troubled and shaken; trembling seized them. There were pains like those of a woman in labor. With a vehement spirit you will crush the ships of Tarshish” (Psalm 47:6–8).

They see and marvel, but while marveling they are troubled with trembling. For when, amid the tears of repentance, the light of the heavenly homeland breaks forth into the mind’s awareness, the soul both marvels and is afraid, because it loves what terrifies it. Then pains arise in the soul like those of a woman in labor.

The pain of the penitent is like the pain of a woman in labor, because through tears she expels from herself what she conceived wrongly in pleasure. “Tarshish” is interpreted as “the exploration of joy.” We know that whoever pursues all the pleasures of this world explores temporal joys for himself.

But almighty God crushes the ships of Tarshish with a vehement spirit because, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, he afflicts the minds of the carnal, which previously wandered upon the waves of this world, with the sorrow of repentance. Thus, crushed by pride, they may lie salutarily in humility—those whom previously the wave of their prosperity had lifted upon this sea of the world toward the heights of vanity.

Through this spirit the ships lie crushed, because those who previously thought it a punishment to be despised by human beings later find it grievous to be honored by human beings. And because formerly they were accustomed to perpetrating evil and rejoicing in it, afterward they do not fear even to suffer affliction for the sake of good.

## Chapter CIX

“With a vehement spirit you will crush the ships of Tarshish” (Psalm 47:8).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book IV (no. 35), the following was added: “With a vehement spirit you will crush the ships of Tarshish.”—“Tarshish” is interpreted as “the exploration of joy.” But when the vehement spirit of repentance takes possession of the mind, it disturbs within it every exploration of blameworthy joy, so that it now desires nothing but to weep and attends to nothing except what can make it afraid.

It places before its eyes the strictness of justice; here it sees the merit of its guilt and what punishment it would deserve if the mercy of the one who spares were absent—a mercy accustomed to rescue it from eternal punishment through present lamentation.

The vehement spirit therefore crushes the ships of Tarshish when the powerful force of compunction confounds our minds, devoted to this world as to a sea, with salutary fear.

## Chapter CX

“He will not give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul” (Psalm 48:8).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XII (no. 57), the following was added: “He will not give God his propitiation,” etc.—Whenever we give alms after sin, we give, as it were, a price for our wicked deeds. Hence the prophet says of one who does not do this: “He will not give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul.”

Sometimes proud rich people oppress their inferiors and seize what belongs to others, yet nevertheless give certain things to others as gifts. Although they crush many, they sometimes provide assistance and protection to some, and appear to give a price for iniquities that they never abandon.

But alms free us from guilt as a price only when we mourn and renounce the sins we have committed. For whoever wishes both always to sin and always to give alms offers the price in vain, because he does not redeem the soul that he does not restrain from vices.

To give the price of redemption is to render a good work with grace preceding us.

[Note: [Col. 0850D] The Utica manuscript and others read: “they seek.”]

## Chapter CXI

“He will not see destruction when he sees the wise dying” (Psalm 48:11).

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXVI (nos. 32–33), the following was added: “He will not see destruction,” etc.—The adversaries of the righteous, when they see them visibly dying, do not believe that they can live invisibly; and they increase the guilt of their unbelief precisely when, seeing the death of the faithful, they despair of eternity.

Thus violent people inwardly perish by the very means through which they grow strong outwardly against the lives of the innocent. The inmost truth casts them away from itself all the more as it permits them temporarily to do what they wish against its own servants.

Whoever persecutes the lives of the good is therefore condemned to a worse vengeance when no adversity resists him. He is then subject to the dangers of a more powerful wrath when he successfully accomplishes what he wickedly desires, because the vengeance of the heavenly judgment abandons him by reserving him for future punishments, since it disdained to oppose him here in his evil.

## Chapter CXII

“He will confess to you when you have done good to him” (Psalm 48:19).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII (no. 59), the following is added: “He will confess to you when you have done good to him.” It should be understood that arrogant men praise the rectitude of divine justice when their prosperity raises them up to joy, and scourges chastise others when they see themselves enjoying worldly prosperity and others being worn down by adversity. For while they act perversely yet consider themselves righteous, they believe that the prosperity available to them is owed to their merits; and from this they infer that God does not judge unjustly, since, as though they were righteous, no adversity distresses them. But if the force of heavenly correction touches their life, however briefly, they immediately assail the judgment of the divine tribunal, which shortly before they had extolled while admiring their own security. They deny that the judgment which opposes their conduct is just, dispute divine equity, burst into words of defiance, and, corrected because they have sinned, sin more gravely.

Rightly, therefore, through the Psalmist this is said against the sinner’s confession: “He will confess to you when you have done good to him.” For the voice of confession formed by the delight of prosperity is contemptible. Only that confession possesses great weight of merit which the force of suffering in no way separates from the rectitude of truth, which adversity, the witness of the heart, sharpens even to the point of a verbal judgment:

### CHAPTER CXIII — “He summoned the heavens above and the earth, to judge his people” (Psalm 49:4).

[Column 0851B]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XV (no. 37), the following is added: “He summoned the heavens above,” and so forth. He summons the heavens above when those who, abandoning all that was theirs, have maintained the conduct of a heavenly life are called to sit in judgment and come as judges with him. The earth too is called above when those who had been bound to earthly pursuits nevertheless sought heavenly gains more than earthly ones; to them it is said: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me” (Matthew 25:43).

### CHAPTER CXIV — “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant upon your lips?” (Psalm 49:16).

When the formation of preachers was being discussed in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX (no. 13), the following was added: “But to the sinner God said,” and so forth. A law has been imposed upon preachers: that by living they fulfill what they hasten to urge through speech. For the authority of speech is lost when the voice is not supported by works. Hence the Psalmist says: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant upon your lips? Yet you hate discipline and cast my words behind you.” For a preacher casts the Lord’s words behind him when he refuses to do what he says. When he himself rejects in practice what he preaches in words, how can another obey his sayings, while he refuses by his deeds to hear what he proclaims?

Concerning this law of preaching it is written: “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:19). He calls the present Church the kingdom of heaven, concerning which it is written: “And they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of stumbling” (Matthew 13:41). For in the kingdom above there are no causes of stumbling to be gathered out. Whoever therefore breaks the commandments in practice and teaches them in speech will be least in this kingdom of heaven; in that one, not even least.

### CHAPTER CXV — “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities” (Psalm 50:7).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XI (no. 70), the following is added: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities.” He who alone is pure in himself is able to cleanse the impure. A human being living in corruptible flesh bears within himself the uncleanness of temptations, because he has plainly drawn them from his origin. Indeed, his very conception, because of the pleasure of the flesh, is uncleanness. Hence the Psalmist now says: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins.”

This is why a person is often tempted even unwillingly; this is why he suffers certain impurities in his mind, although he resists by judgment: because, conceived in uncleanness, while striving toward purity he attempts to overcome what he is. Whoever has conquered the movements of hidden temptation and the uncleanness of thought must not attribute his purity to himself, because no one can make pure what was conceived from impure seed except the one who alone is pure in himself. Therefore, whoever has already reached the place of purity in mind should look back upon the path of his conception by which he came, and learn from it that he does not possess purity of life through his own strength, since the beginning of his existence was made from uncleanness.

### CHAPTER CXVI — “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 50:19).

At the end of the Pastoral Rule, part III (chapter 30, admonition 31), the following is added: “A contrite and humbled heart,” and so forth. Whoever mourns his sins but does not abandon them certainly crushes his heart, but refuses to humble it. Whoever has already abandoned his sins but does not mourn them indeed humbles his heart, but nevertheless refuses to crush it.

### CHAPTER CXVII — “The righteous will see, and fear, and laugh over him” (Psalm 51:8).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VI (no. 48), the following is added: “The righteous will see,” and so forth. When the righteous sees all the wicked struck by final punishment, he himself rejoices in the glory of a deserved recompense. He no longer pities the condemned out of human sympathy, because, cleaving to divine justice as it appears, he is made firm by the unshaken strength of inward strictness. For the minds of the elect, raised up in the clarity of heavenly rectitude, are touched by no mercy, since the height of blessedness makes them strangers to misery.

Rightly, therefore, it is said: “The righteous will see, and fear, and laugh over him.” The righteous now see and fear the wicked; then they will see them and laugh. Because they can now slip into imitation of the wicked, they have fear here. But because then they will be unable to benefit the condemned, they will have no compassion there. Those who are set in the justice of the Judge read in that very justice, by which they are blessed, that the eternally punished are not to be pitied. If they wished in the kingdom what they could in no way fulfill, they would diminish the quality of the happiness they have received—a thought which it is not lawful even to entertain.

But whoever directs himself toward the commandments of life tastes here, before receiving eternal rewards, the beginnings of the security that will follow forever, so that he does not fear the ancient enemy and, when the moment of death intervenes, is in no way terrified by his violent assaults. For the beginning of recompense for the righteous is often that very security of mind at death.

### CHAPTER CXVIII — “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Psalm 52:6).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VII (no. 32), the following is added: “There they trembled with fear,” and so forth. There are many who already desire to defend the truth freely, yet in that very desire tremble and fear the indignation of human power. While on earth they fear a human being on account of the truth, they endure the wrath of that same truth from heaven.

There are also some who, conscious of their sins, desire to distribute to the needy the things they possess, but fear lest, once their possessions have been given away, they themselves should suffer want. While tremblingly preserving the supports of the flesh, they kill the soul by withholding the nourishment of mercy. While they fear to suffer poverty on earth, they cut themselves off from the eternal abundance of heavenly refreshment.

Of such people the Psalmist rightly says: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear.” For those who fear what ought to be trampled underfoot in the lowest places suffer what ought to be feared; and when they refuse to pass through what they could have trampled underfoot, they encounter from above a judgment which they can in no way endure.

### CHAPTER CXIX — “Behold, fleeing, I went far away and remained in solitude” (Psalm 54:8).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV (nos. 57–58), the following is added: “Behold, fleeing, I went far away,” and so forth. The one who flees goes far away when he raises himself from the crowd of temporal desires into the heights of contemplation of God. He remains in solitude when he perseveres in the mind’s withdrawn concentration.

For all who either desire what is unlawful or wish to appear as something in this world are confined in the heart by dense tumult of thought. While they stir up crowds of desires outside themselves, they trample their prostrate mind under the foot of wretched preoccupation.

One person submits himself to the rule of lust and forms before the eyes of his mind images of shameful acts. Even when the deed is not carried out, it is enacted all the more frequently in the intention of thought. He seeks the fulfillment of pleasure, and his enervated mind, shaken, anxious, and blinded this way and that, searches out an opportunity for the most wicked gratification. Such a mind suffers, as it were, a certain people within itself, being laid waste by the insolent tumult of thoughts.

Another throws himself beneath the domination of anger, and what does he enact in his heart except quarrels, even quarrels that are not present? He often fails to see those who are present, contradicts those who are absent, utters and receives insults within himself, responds even more harshly to those he has received, and, when no opponent is there, constructs quarrels in his heart with loud outcries. He therefore bears an inward crowd, oppressed by the heavy weight of inflamed thought.

[Note: The Utic and Gemet manuscripts read: “He envies those who are present.”]

Another gives himself over to the rule of avarice, despising his own possessions and desiring those of others. Often unable to acquire what he desires, he turns his days toward idleness and his nights toward thought. He grows sluggish in useful work because he is wearied by unlawful thinking. He multiplies plans and expands the bosom of his mind more widely through inventions of thought; he strives to reach what he desires and seeks certain most secret channels of circumstances by which to obtain it.

As soon as he thinks he has discovered something subtle in the matter, he rejoices as though he had already obtained what he desired. He now considers what he should add to the thing supposedly acquired and reflects on how it ought to be cultivated into a better condition. Since he already seems to possess it and to bring it to a more attractive form, he immediately considers the plots of the envious, weighs what quarrel is being stirred up against him, and searches out what he should answer. Though he possesses nothing, the empty litigant is already laboring in defense of the thing he desires.

Although he has received nothing of what he coveted, he nevertheless already possesses in his heart both the fruit of covetousness and the labor of strife. He is therefore oppressed by a grievous people, laid waste by the tumult of avarice that goads him.

Another subjects himself to the tyranny of pride. While he raises his wretched heart against human beings, he lays it beneath his vice. He desires the insignia of lofty honors, seeks to be exalted by successes, and paints for himself in his thoughts the whole person he wishes to be. Already he presides as though over a tribunal; already he sees the obedience of his subjects; already he towers above others; already he inflicts evils on some and repays others for the evils he has inflicted. Already, surrounded by ranks within himself, he proceeds into public; already he sees by what services he is supported.

[Note: The passage is better read at the place assigned in the Moralia: “alone he crawls.”]

Yet, while thinking these things, he repeats them alone: now he tramples some down and raises others up; now he satisfies his hatred against those he has trampled down; now he receives favors from those he has raised up. What else, then, does one who impresses so many phantoms upon his heart see except a waking dream? Whoever bears so many causes of affairs that he invents plainly carries inwardly crowds born from desires.

Another already flees what is unlawful, but nevertheless fears to lack the goods of the world. He desires to retain what is permitted, is ashamed to appear lesser among people, and takes the greatest care not to be poor at home or despised in public. He seeks what will suffice for himself and what the needs of his dependents require; and, in order to fulfill adequately the rights of patronage toward his dependents, he seeks patrons whom he himself may serve.

But when he joins himself familiarly to these patrons, he is undoubtedly entangled in their causes. He often consents to their unlawful acts and commits for the sake of others what he would not desire for his own sake, because he does not abandon the things that belong to them. Often, while trembling lest his honor be diminished in this world, he approves before more powerful persons what he already condemns by his own judgment. While he anxiously considers what he owes to his patrons and what to his dependents, what increases his own standing and what benefits his affections, he is oppressed by as many crowds as he is torn apart by the importunity of his cares.

By contrast, holy men, who desire nothing of this world, are plainly oppressed by no tumult in their hearts. With the hand of holy reflection they drive all disordered movements of desire from the heart’s dwelling. Because they despise all transitory things, they do not suffer the insolence of thoughts arising from them. They desire only the eternal homeland, and because they love nothing of this world, they enjoy great tranquility of mind.

Hence the Prophet rightly says: “Fleeing, I went far away and remained in solitude.” To remain in solitude is to expel from the heart’s secrecy the tumult of earthly desires and, with a single purpose, to breathe toward the love of inward rest in the eternal homeland.

Had he not expelled every tumult of thought from himself who said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord” (Psalm 26)? He had fled from the crowd of earthly desires into the great solitude of himself, where he would see nothing foreign all the more safely because he loved nothing unsuitable. From the tumult of temporal things he had sought a great retreat: a quiet mind in which he might see God all the more purely because he found him alone with himself.

### CHAPTER CXX — “Cast them down, O Lord, and divide their tongues” (Psalm 54:1).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIV (nos. 8–9), the following is added: “Cast them down, O Lord, and divide their tongues.” Just as it is harmful if unity is lacking among the good, so it is more harmful if it is not lacking among the wicked. For the unity of the reprobate attacks the life of the good all the more harshly the more forcefully it sets itself against them through its cohesion.

Paul had perceived this unity of the reprobate as harmful when, caught in the midst of the Sadducees and Pharisees, he said: “I am being judged concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead.” At this utterance the crowd of his hearers immediately broke apart against itself. When the tumultuous multitude was divided into two parties, a means of escape was opened for Paul: the united crowd of his persecutors had confined him, but its division released him.

The righteous are rescued when the unrighteous are divided, and the desires of the elect reach fulfillment when the ranks of the reprobate are shattered by discord. This is also aptly signified by the division of the Red Sea (Exodus 14). When the wave was divided into two parts, the chosen people proceeded toward the promised land; so, when the unity of the wicked is split, good minds are brought to what they desire.

If the unity of the wicked had not been harmful, divine providence would never have scattered the tongues of the proud in such diversity. Considering this unity of the reprobate against the elect, the Prophet says concerning the enemies of the holy Church: “Cast them down, O Lord, and divide their tongues” (Genesis 11).

### CHAPTER CXXI — “Let them descend alive into hell” (Psalm 54:16).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII (no. 9), the following is added: “Let them descend,” and so forth. The holy Church declares that her enemies aggravate the accumulation of their guilt both by knowing what they ought to follow and by refusing to follow what they know. Of these the Psalmist says: “Let them descend alive into hell.”

Those are alive who perceive what is done to them. The dead neither know nor perceive anything at all. Thus the dead, who do not perceive, are customarily taken for the ignorant; the living, who perceive, for those who know. To descend alive into hell, therefore, is to sin knowingly and consciously. Since the living know and perceive what is done around them, while the dead can perceive nothing, they would descend into hell dead if they committed evil in ignorance. But when they know the evils and nevertheless commit iniquities, the wretched descend into hell alive and perceiving.

### CHAPTER CXXII — “Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days” (Psalm 54:25).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book V (no. 70), the following is added: “Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days.” To halve one’s days is to divide the time of life spent in evil pleasures into the lamentations of repentance and, by apportioning it in this way, restore it to good use. But the wicked do not halve their days at all, because they do not change their perverse mind even at the final hour.

In contrast, Paul rightly admonishes us, saying: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” We redeem time when we restore by weeping the former life which we lost through dissipation.

[Note: This chapter, together with the following one, is omitted in the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CXXIII — “They will watch my heel” (Psalm 55:7).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book I (no. 53), the following is added: “They will watch my heel.” Because the heel is the end of the body, what is signified by it except the end of an action? Whether, therefore, the evil spirits or wicked people, followers of their pride, watch the heel, they do so when they desire to corrupt the end of a good action.

### CHAPTER CCXIV — “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword. He will save the poor man from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the violent” (Psalm 56:5).

[Column 0855B]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VI (no. 35), the following is added: “The sons of men: their teeth,” and so forth. This poor man is the one of whom Paul says: “For your sake he became poor, although he was rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Because the Jews handed the Lord over by accusing him, while the Gentiles killed him after he had been handed over, the sword of the mouth can signify the tongue of the accusing Hebrews, of whom the Psalmist says: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Mark 15). The Gospel also testifies that they cried out: “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke 23:21).

By “the hand of the violent,” however, the crucifying Gentiles themselves are represented, since they fulfilled in action the voices of the Hebrews in the death of the Redeemer. God therefore saved this poor man both from the hand of the violent and from the sword of the mouth, because our Redeemer endured by his humanity the power of the Gentiles and the tongues of the Hebrews in dying, but by the power of his divinity conquered them by rising again.

### CHAPTER CXXV — “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Psalm 57:9).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX (no. 9), the following is added: “Fire fell upon them,” and so forth. Fire falls upon the ungodly, but when the fire falls the sun is not seen, because it blinds to the vision of the true light those whom the flame of Gehenna devours. Thus the pain of burning torments them outwardly, while the punishment of blindness darkens them inwardly, so that those who offended their Author in body and heart may be punished in body and heart together, and those who, while living here, served their perverse pleasures with both may feel punishment in both.

### CHAPTER CXXVI — “The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance of the wicked; he will wash his hands in the blood of sinners” (Psalm 57:11).

[Column 0855D]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII (no. 37), the following is added: “The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance of the wicked,” and so forth. Many people, when they see another’s destruction, are brought back to their senses so that they may consider their own. Thus, from the place where one person is led to torments, another is freed from torment. He sees in another’s punishment what he should fear, and, when he observes the sinner struck in this way, he restrains his own disordered deeds by the force of justice.

Thus it happens that the wicked person who, while living, had drawn many into guilt by the delight of sin, may, when dying, recall some from guilt through the terror of punishment. The Psalmist also testifies that this occurs for the good, saying: “The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance of the wicked; he will wash his hands in the blood of sinners.” The hands of the righteous are washed in the blood of dying sinners, because when their punishment is observed, the life of the observer is cleansed.

### CHAPTER CXXVII — “You are my helper; to you I will sing psalms, for you, O God, are my protector, my God, my mercy” (Psalm 58:8).

[Column 0856A]

In Homily 19 on the Gospels (no. 7), the following is added: “You are my helper; to you I will sing psalms,” and so forth. The Prophet, considering the trials in which human life is established, calls God his helper. And because he receives us from present tribulation into eternal rest, he also calls him his protector.

But when he considers that God looks upon and bears our evils, tolerates our faults, and nevertheless reserves us through repentance for rewards, he did not wish to call God merciful; rather, he called him Mercy itself, saying: “My God, my mercy.” Let us therefore recall before our eyes the evils we have committed; let us weigh the great kindness by which we are tolerated; let us consider the depths of his compassion, so that he not only forgives sins but also promises the heavenly kingdom to the repentant after sin. And from the innermost marrow of our hearts, let each of us say—let us all say: “My God, my mercy.”

[Note: This does not appear in the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CXXVIII — “You have shaken the earth and troubled it; heal its breaches, for it has been shaken” (Psalm 59:4).

[Column 0856B]

In Homily 10 on Ezekiel (no. 28), the following is added: “You have shaken the earth,” and so forth. The earth shaken and troubled is the sinner anxious from knowledge of his guilt and brought to the lamentations of repentance. For it was said to the sinful human being: “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Genesis 3:19). Let him therefore plead that the breach of the earth be healed, because it has been shaken, so that the sinner who is afflicted by his faults may be consoled by the joy of heavenly mercy.

### CHAPTER CXXIX — “You have shown your people hard things; you gave us to drink the wine of compunction. You gave a sign to those who fear you, so that they might flee from the face of the bow” (Psalm 59:5).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX (no. 54), the following is added: “You have shown your people hard things,” and so forth. What is signified here by the bow except the day of final judgment? In a bow, the farther the string is drawn, the more forcefully the arrow issues from it. So, indeed, the farther the day of final judgment is delayed, the more severe the sentence that proceeds from it when it comes.

We are therefore struck now by various calamities so that, corrected here, we may then be found more prepared. Hence it was said beforehand: “You have shown your people hard things”—namely, the scourges of the age that precede the more grievous day of judgment to come. “You gave us to drink the wine of compunction,” so that earthly joys might be turned into tears. “You gave a sign to those who fear you, so that they might flee from the face of the bow.” It is as though he said: This is the time of mercy; that will be the time of judgment. Through the scourges of this present time, therefore, you signify how you will strike then, when you judge without sparing—since you strike so strictly now, while you are sparing.

### CHAPTER CXXX — “Toward Idumaea I will extend my sandal” (Psalm 59:10).

In Homily 7 on the Gospels (no. 3), the following is added: “Toward Idumaea I will extend my sandal.” What is signified by Idumaea except the Gentiles, and by the sandal except the mortality assumed? The Lord therefore declares that he will extend his sandal toward Idumaea, because, when he made himself known to the Gentiles through the flesh, divinity came to us as though shod.

Who does not know that sandals are made from dead animals? Thus, when coming in the flesh, the Lord appeared as though shod: in his divinity he assumed the corpse-like condition of our corruption.

### CHAPTER CXXXI — “Your mercy is better than life” (Psalm 62:4).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII (no. 51), the following is added: “Your mercy is better than life.” Every human virtue is too weak to wash away guilt unless the mercy of the one who spares supports it and the justice of the one who judges rightly does not crush it. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your mercy is better than life,” because however innocent someone may appear, our life does not free us before the strict Judge if the kindness of mercy does not release us from the debt of our guilt.

### CHAPTER CXXXII — “So that my soul may be filled as with fat and rich food” (Psalm 62:6).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII (no. 25), the following is added: “So that my soul may be filled as with fat and rich food.” Fat fills the soul with richness when the infusion of heavenly hope refreshes it against the heat of present desires.

[Note: This chapter, together with the following two, is absent from the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CXXXIII — “Watering its channels, multiply its offspring; in its showers it will rejoice when it rises” (Psalm 64:11).

In Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 10 (no. 4), the following is added: “Watering its channels,” and so forth. The channels are the holy preachers of the Church, who water the soil of our hearts. But when the channels are watered, the offspring of the Church multiply, because when preachers receive a richer grace of the Spirit, the number of the faithful increases.

The holy Church rejoices in its showers. For in a shower, water falls from the roof onto the earth, water which had fallen from heaven onto the roof. The roof of the holy Church is the holy preachers, who protect us by interceding and shielding us with admonitions. But because their hearts are infused by God in preaching, water comes from heaven to the roof, as it were. And because we are watered by their words, water flows from the roof down to the earth.

Thus, when the holy Church rises, it rejoices in its showers, because when it is born in faith and good works, it considers the gifts it has received and exults in the words of the preachers. As the hearers rise toward better things, the grace of their preachers also multiplies.

### CHAPTER CXXXIV — “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness” (Psalm 64:12).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV (no. 37), the following is added: “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness.” The crown of the year is blessed, as it were, when, the time of labor having ended, the reward of virtues is bestowed.

### CHAPTER CXXXV — “And the valleys will abound in grain” (Psalm 64:14).

In the exposition of the Gospels, Homily 10 (no. 3), the following is added: “And the valleys will abound in grain.” For waters flow down from the mountains, because the doctrine of truth abandons proud minds. But springs rise in the valleys, because humble minds receive the word of preaching.

Already we see it; already we behold the valleys abounding in grain, because the mouths of those who had seemed meek and simple, despised by this world, are filled with the nourishment of truth.

### CHAPTER CXXXVI — “Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrible he is in his purposes concerning the sons of men!” (Psalm 65:5).

In the exposition of the Gospels, Homily 4 (no. 1), the following is added: “Come and see the works of the Lord,” and so forth. It must be understood with the greatest care that in everything we do we should fear the hidden purposes of the almighty Lord concerning us, lest, while our mind is poured outward and does not withdraw from its pleasure, the Judge within should terrifyingly arrange adversity against it.

The Psalmist rightly perceived this and said: “Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrible he is in his purposes concerning the sons of men!” For he saw that one person is called mercifully, while another is rejected as justice requires. And because the Lord arranges some things by sparing and others by anger, he was struck with awe at what he could not penetrate. Seeing him not only as unsearchable but also, in certain judgments of his, inflexible, he declared him terrible in his purposes.

### CHAPTER CXXXVII — “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us; and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Psalm 66:8).

[Column 0858A]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX (no. 70), the following is added: “May God bless us,” and so forth. To show that God, the author of all things, is the Trinity, David said: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us.” And lest, by naming God three times, he be thought to have spoken of three gods, he immediately indicated the unity of that Trinity by adding: “And may all the ends of the earth fear him.” By saying not “them” but “him,” he made clear that the three things he had named are one.

Hence Isaiah, when he disclosed the praise of the unity of the Trinity, said through the voice of the Seraphim: “Holy, holy, holy” (Isaiah 6:3). And lest, by naming “holy” three times, he seem to divide the unity of the divine substance, he added: “The Lord God of hosts.” By adding not “the lords, gods” but “the Lord God,” he indicated that the one whom he had called holy three times exists as one.

Hence Paul, to show the operation of the holy Trinity, said: “From him and through him and in him are all things” (Romans 11:36); and, to indicate the unity of that Trinity, he immediately added: “To him be glory forever and ever.” By saying not “to them” but “to him,” he made known that there is one according to nature and three according to persons—the same truth that he had earlier expressed by saying “holy” three times.

### CHAPTER CXXXVIII — “Prepare a way for him who ascends over the setting sun” (Psalm 67:5).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX (no. 6), the following is added: “Prepare a way for him,” and so forth. The Lord ascended over the setting sun because from the place where he set in his Passion, he revealed his greater glory by rising again. He ascended over the setting sun, that is, he trampled by rising again the death that he endured.

He therefore says: “He who ascends over the setting sun—prepare a way for him,” that is, offer a way in your hearts through faith to the risen Lord. We prepare a way for him who ascended over the setting sun when we proclaim his glory to faithful minds, so that he himself, coming afterward, may illumine them through the presence of his love.

Hence it is said to John through the Spirit: “You will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke 1:76). For whoever, by preaching, cleanses the hearts of hearers from the filth of vices prepares a way for wisdom as it comes.

### CHAPTER CXXXIX — “If you sleep among the middle lots, the wings of the dove are silvered, and the hind parts of its back are in the appearance of gold” (Psalm 67:14).

[Note: The homily is not identified in the manuscripts. The final part of this sacred passage is nevertheless expounded in Homily 3, book II, no. 14.]

In the homily on Ezekiel, the following is added: “If you sleep among the middle lots,” and so forth. In Latin, *cleros* means “lots.” Our sleeping is to rest from evil action. Since all the elect restrain themselves from the disturbances of perverse works, abandon earthly things, and desire heavenly things, they sleep among the middle lots: by fleeing temporal things and desiring eternal rewards, they rest from perverse actions.

For in mind they fly upward toward the heights, and hence they are called wings. These are rightly said to be the silvered wings of a dove. The silvered dove is the holy Church, which shines openly with the light of preaching. But this dove is silvered in its wings, while the hind parts of its back gleam in the appearance of gold, because the holy Church, which is now made radiant through the tongues of preachers, will in the reward that follows be adorned not with the gleam of silver but with that of gold.

When it reaches those invisible goods and attains those heavenly gifts “which eye has not seen nor ear heard,” it will no longer need the eloquence of preaching. It is beautiful in its hind parts through the appearance of gold alone, because in what it will receive afterward it shines only with the splendor of glory.

### CHAPTER CXL — “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Psalm 67:10).

In the exposition of the Gospels, Homily 29 (no. 10), the following is added: “Ascending on high,” and so forth. What is declared by these words of the Prophet except the Lord’s ascension? For, ascending on high, he led captivity captive because by the power of his incorruption he swallowed up our corruption.

He gave gifts to human beings because, having sent the Spirit from above, he granted to one the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another the grace of virtues, to another the grace of healings, to another kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of words. He therefore gave gifts to human beings when, through the grace of this Spirit, their power increased in the world.

### CHAPTER CXLI — “The tongue of your dogs is from your enemies, from him” (Psalm 67:24).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XX (no. 15), the following is added: “The tongue of your dogs is from your enemies, from him.” Who are called dogs here except the holy Teachers? They stood as guardians of the faithful in the holy Church; while intent upon vigils for their Lord by day and by night, they gave forth, so to speak, great barkings of preaching.

Some, indeed, were recalled from the worship of idols and became preachers of God. Thus the tongue of the Church’s dogs comes forth from the enemies, because the Lord also makes converted Gentiles into preachers.

Hence the sluggishness of the Jews, who were unwilling to speak for the Lord, is reproved by the condemning Prophet, who says: “Mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isaiah 56:10).

[Note: The remainder of the chapter is lacking in the manuscripts.]

[Homily 40 on the Gospels, no. 2.] In sacred eloquence, preachers are sometimes understood by the name “dogs.” For the tongue of a dog heals a wound while licking it; likewise, holy teachers touch, as it were, the wound of the mind with their tongue when they instruct us in the confession of our sin. And because by speaking they rescue us from sins, they restore us to salvation as though by touching wounds.

Since the tongue of preachers is signified by the name “dogs,” the Psalmist says through the Lord: “The tongue of your dogs is from your enemies, from him.” For from the unbelieving Jews the holy preachers were chosen, and, in asserting the truth against thieves and robbers who came, they gave forth, so to speak, great barkings for the Lord.

In contrast, concerning the rejection of certain others it is said: “Mute dogs, unable to bark.”

### CHAPTER CXLII — “The steps of God were seen; the steps of my God and King, who is in the holy place” (Psalm 67:25).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVI (no. 41), it is added:

“They saw your footsteps, O God,” etc.—For these very works of his that we perceive are, as it were, certain footsteps of God: by them every good and evil person is governed; by them the just and unjust are arranged in their proper orders; by them also each person who is subject is daily led toward better things, while one who falls toward worse things is tolerated. Concerning these footsteps the prophet said: “They saw your footsteps, O God.”

Therefore, when we contemplate the virtue of his patience and compassion, and, in contemplating it, strive to imitate it, what else do we do than follow the traces of his footsteps, since we imitate certain outward aspects of his work? “They saw your footsteps, O God; the footsteps of my God and King, who is in the sanctuary.” When someone perceives that the disordered movements of his mind are restrained within him by the remembrance of divine judgments, he has seen, as it were, the footsteps of the Lord walking within him.

[Col. 0859D]

### CHAPTER CXLIII  
### “Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God” (Psalm 67:32)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVIII (no. 84), it is added:

“Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God.”—The prophet David, seeing that the Lord would come to redeem Judea, but that the Gentiles would believe first and Judea would follow afterward, as it is written, “until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Romans 11:25), says: “Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God”; that is, before Judea believes, the Gentile people, black with sins, offer themselves to the almighty Lord to be saved.

Let us therefore give thanks to the only Son of the supreme Father—we who, gathered from the Gentiles and illumined by his light, have preceded Judea herself in faith, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God.” We were black, therefore, through the merits of our unbelief; but, receiving through the merit of faith the brightness of grace, we have even preceded the Synagogue, through whose offspring we were called to the grace of God.

### CHAPTER CXLIV  
### “I have labored, enduring” (Psalm 68:4)

In Homily 8 on Ezekiel, it is added:

“I have labored, enduring.”—

[Note: [Col. 0859D] In the Mich. manuscript this is assigned to Homily 8 on Ezekiel, where, however, these words are lacking.]

The prophet says this in the person of our Redeemer concerning those who are still living perversely: “I have labored [where we read, ‘crying out’], enduring.” The Lord does not labor by enduring, for no weariness affects the power of his divinity; but, speaking in the language of his humanity, he calls his own patience toward us labor.

### CHAPTER CXLV  
### “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Psalm 68:16)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVI (nos. 65–66), it is added:

“Let not the storm of water overwhelm me,” etc.—Everyone who, abandoning the way of life, casts himself into the darkness of sins plunges himself, as it were, into a pit or ditch. But if, through prolonged practice, he is also oppressed by the habit of iniquity, so that he can no longer rise to higher things, he is constricted as though by the narrow mouth of a pit.

For this reason David, speaking under the figure of sinners, prays: “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me.” The iniquity of an evil deed has shaken someone from good stability, as a storm of water carries him away. But if prolonged habit has not yet prevailed, it has not overwhelmed him. He has already fallen into the pit who has committed what the divine Law forbids. But if prolonged habit does not yet weigh him down, the pit has by no means narrowed its mouth over him. Therefore he emerges more easily, the less he is constricted by habit.

There is, as it were, a certain confinement of a closed mouth: to wish to rise from an evil habit that oppresses one, but to be unable. Already in desire he strives toward heavenly things, but in action he still remains among lower things; he goes ahead in his heart, but does not follow in his conduct; and within himself he endures himself as an adversary.

[Note: Thus it is read in all our manuscripts, although in the *Moralia*, instead of *contradictorem* (“an adversary”), the reading is *contradictionem* (“contradiction”), with all the manuscripts agreeing.]

But when the soul, striving in this way, is helped by the hand of uplifting grace, it passes from the narrow mouth to a place of spaciousness, because, having overcome its difficulties, it accomplishes the good works that it desires. The prophet David had seen the confinement of the narrow mouth when he said: “You have saved my soul from afflictions, and have not shut me up in the hands of the enemy” (Psalm 30:9). He knew that he had been saved in a very spacious place when he added: “You have set my feet in a broad place.”

The feet are established in a broad place when we strive toward suitable good things and are hindered by no difficulty. For we proceed wherever we wish, as though through a broad place, because no obstacles of difficulty constrain us.

### CHAPTER CXLVI  
### “For the sake of my enemies, deliver me” (Psalm 68:19)

[Col. 0860D]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVI (no. 32), it is added:

“For the sake of my enemies, deliver me.”—It often happens that the just, caught in tribulation, receive heavenly assistance even in temporal matters, although they do not implore it for temporal reasons. For they desire to be saved not for their own sake, but for the salvation of their adversaries: so that, when almighty God frees them from immense dangers by some miracle, he may make his power known even to their persecutors and, through the means by which he saves his own temporally, redeem their adversaries for eternity.

Thus the Psalmist, taking up the voices of the martyrs, says: “For the sake of my enemies, deliver me.” As though he were saying: “For my own sake I do not seek deliverance from temporal tribulations; yet I desire to be delivered for the sake of my adversaries, so that, when my life is seen to be marvelously saved, the hardness of my enemies may be converted by the very sight of the miracles.”

Therefore, just as the Lord often delivers the lives of his own temporally for the conversion of their enemies, so he often does not heed the prayers of his own, because of the condemnation of their persecutors—so that they may heap up their guilt precisely by that through which they wickedly rejoice that they have prevailed. Those who despise invisible things can sometimes be moved by visible miracles. But for this reason nothing marvelous is often done visibly for the just: their adversaries do not deserve to be visibly illumined.

[Note: Absent from the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CXLVII  
### “I sought one who would comfort me, and I found none” (Psalm 67:21)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVII (no. 5), it is added:

“I sought one who would comfort me, and I found none.”—The holy Church finds one who comforts her only when she sees many rising within herself to life from that death which her husband endured.

### CHAPTER CXLVIII  
### “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bow their back” (Psalm 68:24)

[Col. 0861B]

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part I, chapter 1, it is added:

“Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see,” etc.—This is spoken by the prophet in the spirit of foretelling concerning the reprobate, not as the wish of one pronouncing a curse. Those who are placed at the very front of high office and undertake the duty of foreseeing the way are called eyes. Those who cling behind them are, naturally, called backs.

When the eyes are darkened, therefore, the back is bent: for when those who lead lose the light of knowledge, those who follow are bent down to carry the burdens of sins. Thus he says: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bow their back,” as though he were saying: Let those who preside over the actions of human life, as though they were foreseeing the way, lack the light of truth, so that those who follow, subjected and bent beneath the burdens of their iniquities, may lose every upright posture (*Moralia*, book XXIV, no. 40).

We undoubtedly know that this happened in Judea, when, at the very coming of our Redeemer, the crowd of Pharisees and priests closed the eyes of their minds to the true light, and the people, walking according to the examples of their leaders, wandered in the darkness of unbelief.

[Note: Not found in the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CXLIX  
### “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ be immediately confounded and put to shame” (Psalm 59:4)

In the exposition of Ezekiel, book I, homily 11 (no. 14), it is added:

“Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ be immediately confounded,” etc.—Flattery, if it is patiently received even for a time, increases and gently caresses the mind, so that it softens from the firmness of its uprightness in the pleasure of speech. But lest it grow, it must immediately and without delay be struck down.

### CHAPTER CL  
### “His enemies will lick the earth” (Psalm 71:9)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XX (nos. 26–27), it is added:

“His enemies will lick the earth.”—It is pleasing to contemplate what is said through the Psalmist: “His enemies will lick the earth.”

There are two kinds of people who serve their ambition. One continually uses the tongue to flatter greed; the other openly applies himself to plunder by force. We gnaw when we wear away something external with strong effort; something is licked when what cannot easily be eaten is tasted by the gentle pressure of the tongue.

Therefore, all who live perversely even under the appearance of faith, who desire what belongs to others but cannot at all seize what they desire, and who attempt to draw it away by flattering words and, as it were, by the softness of sweetness—what do they do other than lick the earth? For they strive by the softness of the tongue to obtain earthly things that they cannot take by force.

But those who are supported in this world by some authority and, desiring what belongs to others, disdain flattering through deceit, because by unjust strength they can accomplish what they wish—these do not lick what they desire but gnaw it. For by the strength of their power, as though by the effort of their teeth, they destroy the lives of their neighbors.

### CHAPTER CLI  
### “But my feet almost slipped; my steps nearly gave way, because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Psalm 72:2)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book VI (nos. 7–8), it is added:

“But my feet almost slipped,” etc.—When the weak see the wicked flourishing, they tremble; disturbed within themselves by the prosperity of sinners, they waver inwardly in the steps of their mind. The Psalmist assumed the appearance of such people when he said: “But my feet almost slipped; my steps nearly gave way; I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners.”

But when the strong behold their glory, they immediately consider what punishment follows glory, and inwardly, with profound reflection, despise what the proud swell outwardly through the vanity of empty inflation.

[Note: At Utica: “with profound reflection.”]

Thus it is said of this contempt shown by the perfect, through blessed Job: “I saw the fool firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty.” To curse the beauty of the fool is to judge his glory in view of his condemnation, because the more highly he is raised in sins, the more cruelly he is overwhelmed in torments; for what is exalted passes away, while what is punished remains. The one who is honored on the way will be condemned upon arrival; and he reaches prison, as it were, through pleasant meadows who advances toward destruction through the prosperity of the present life.

### CHAPTER CLII  
### “You cast them down while they were being raised up” (Psalm 72:12)

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 25, admonition 27, it is added:

“You cast them down while they were being raised up.”—When the reprobate do not repay divine gifts with righteous works, when they abandon themselves entirely here and surrender themselves to overflowing prosperity, they fall inwardly precisely where they advance outwardly.

For this reason it is said to the rich man tormented in hell: “You received good things during your life” (Luke 16:25). The wicked person receives good things here for this reason: so that there he may receive evils more fully, because here he had not been converted even by good things.

He does not therefore say, “You cast them down after they had been raised up,” but “while they were being raised up,” because the very thing that happens to the proud—being raised outwardly by false glory—is their inward fall. For by divine judgment, their guilt here and their punishment here are not different things; rather, their guilt is turned into punishment for them, so that, when they are raised up by the arrogance of pride, the very thing that appears outwardly as advancement is truly an inward fall.

### CHAPTER CLIII  
### “You split open springs and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan” (Psalm 73:15)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXII (no. 20), it is added:

“You split open springs,” etc.—*Ethan* is interpreted as “strong.” And who is this strong one except the one of whom the Truth says through the Gospel: “No one can enter the strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Mark 3:27)?

The Lord therefore split open springs and torrents when he poured out streams of truth in the hearts of his apostles. Of these it is said again through another prophet: “You will draw water with joy from the springs of the Savior” (Isaiah 12:3). For we go thirsting to their teaching, so that we may carry back vessels of our hearts filled with truth.

But Ethan dried up the rivers as his own springs poured forth, when he dried up the teaching of the strong and evil spirit by displaying the ray of his truth.

### CHAPTER CLIV  
### “I said to the wicked, ‘Do not act wickedly,’ and to sinners, ‘Do not lift up your horn’” (Psalm 74:5)

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part II, chapter 30, admonition 31, it is added:

“I said to the wicked,” etc.—Sinners lift up their horn if they do not humble themselves to repentance through recognition of their iniquity. Thus it is said again: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Psalm 50:19).

Whoever mourns his sins but does not abandon them does indeed break his heart, but refuses to humble it. Whoever has already abandoned his sins but does not mourn them does humble himself, but nevertheless refuses to break his heart.

### CHAPTER CLV  
### “You wonderfully illumine from the everlasting mountains” (Psalm 75:5)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVII (no. 16), it is added:

“You wonderfully illumine from the everlasting mountains.”—One who cannot contemplate the east looks upon mountains illuminated by the rays of light and realizes that the sun has risen. God illumines us from the everlasting mountains, because through the admirable life of our forefathers he enlightens us with the ray of his brightness.

Behold, someone is kindled with zeal for devotion to the Lord and for charity; yet in this devotion and charity we are better formed by contemplating these mountains. For who was more devoted than Peter? Who was more loving than John?

The former, through devotion, did not fear to tread upon the fluid surface of the sea (Matthew 14:29); the latter, through love, rested upon the breast of our Creator himself (John 13:21), and, having come for the refreshment of a bodily meal, received spiritual nourishment from the bosom of the Redeemer.

But since we have said that the lives of the preceding fathers are signified by mountains, it is necessary to bring forward also, in the midst of our discussion, examples of earlier fathers.

Behold, when we desire to submit ourselves to heavenly commands through obedience, we are helped by considering the footsteps of the ancient fathers. For who was more obedient than Abraham? At a single command of the Lord he abandoned relatives and homeland (Genesis 12), and, in order to attain an eternal inheritance, did not tremble to strike the one whom, already an old man and almost dying, he had received as heir.

When we strive to grasp the virtue of patience, we contemplate the examples of those who came before us. For who was more patient than Isaac? He carried the wood, asked about the holocaust, was shortly afterward bound, and did not speak (Genesis 22); he was placed upon the altar and did not resist. What man, then, could be called more patient than this one? He is led, as it were, for consolation, and asks a question; he is bound for slaughter, and falls silent; he asks about offering the holocaust, and, destined to be offered as a holocaust, keeps silent.

When we strive to gird ourselves for endurance of labor, we are shaped by the examples of those who came before us. For who was more laborious than Jacob? For such a long time he exercised the work of a servant with Laban, his kinsman by right of relationship (Genesis 39), and served in the place of a household slave in order to enjoy the rewards of an heir.

When we strive to climb the citadel of continence and chastity, we are lifted up by the examples of those who came before us. For who was chaster than Joseph? He could not be pressed beneath the yoke of lust by the desire of a wanton mistress, even when he was a captive (Genesis 39). Indeed, he was a slave to human beings, but against the ruling power of wickedness he was free even in servitude.

When we desire to be filled with gentleness, we are helped by the examples of those who came before us. For who was gentler than Moses? He endured the rebellion of the people entrusted to him, yet he prayed to the angry Lord on behalf of his persecutors and offered himself to the divine anger for them, because in his holy breast charity was inflamed even by persecution.

When we strive to strengthen the steadfastness of our mind against the adversities of the world, we are supported by considering those who came before us. For who was more steadfast than Joshua (Numbers 13–14)? Sent to explore the character of the nations, he did not fear either their great stature or their vast numbers. Hence he struck down in battle the very nations whom he had not feared while exploring them.

When we strive to attain the summit of kindness, we are instructed by the examples of those who came before us. For who was kinder than Samuel? Cast down from the leadership of the people (1 Samuel 10:12), he humbly sought a successor for himself, anointed the one he found as king, and immediately endured the one he had anointed as his persecutor. He trembled lest that man kill him, and yet he prayed that the Lord might not be angry with him.

When he was being sent, he said: “Saul will hear, and he will kill me” (1 Samuel 16:2). And the Truth himself said to him: “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him?” (ibid., 16:1). What man, then, could be called kinder than this one, who did not wish the man by whom he feared being killed to be struck down by God?

When we strive toward the height of compassion and humility, we are lifted up by the examples of those who came before us (1 Samuel 17:18–19). For who could be called more merciful or humbler than David? He received insults from a wicked king for his victories; he bravely rescued the Israelite people from the hand of the enemy, yet fled as though weak lest he himself be killed. He recognized both that he had been chosen by divine judgment and that his persecutor had been rejected, yet he subjected himself to that same persecutor through repeated humble submission.

He took the persecutor’s spear, cut off the edge of his cloak, and immediately hastened to the summit of the mountain; and at one and the same time he displayed that he had possessed the power to kill him and asked that he not be killed (see no. 15).

For this reason it is said through the prophet concerning preachers: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isaiah 60:8) (no. 17). In all the things that we spiritually desire, therefore, we are formed by the examples of those who came before us. We are sheltered by the life of the fathers stretched over us like clouds, so that we may be watered for the fruit of fertile growth. And, as though gazing at the sky, we first look upon the clouds, because we first behold the deeds of the good with admiration; afterward, by experience, we penetrate those things that are heavenly.

### CHAPTER CLVI  
### “All the foolish in heart were troubled. They slept their sleep, and none of all the men of wealth found anything in their hands” (Psalm 75:6)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVIII (nos. 28–29), it is added:

“So that the wealthy may find something in their hands after death, they are told before death in whose hands they should place their riches. ‘Make,’ he says, ‘friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings’” (Luke 16:9).

Therefore, when the rich man sleeps, he will find nothing in his hands (Job 27:19). He would take his possessions with him when he died if, while he lived, he had transferred them to himself at the request of the needy. For all earthly things, which we lose by preserving them, we preserve by giving them away; our patrimony, when retained, is lost, but when distributed, it remains.

We cannot long endure together with our possessions, because either we abandon them by dying, or they, perishing, abandon us while we live, as it were. We must therefore act so that things destined plainly to perish may be compelled to pass into a reward that does not perish.

The rich man sleeps and finds nothing—nothing, certainly, of the possessions that he held. For the guilt associated with those possessions is carried away with him, although all the things for which the guilt was committed are left behind.

Let him go now, then, and swell with the possessions he has received; let him exalt himself above others and glory in having what his neighbor does not have. The time will come when he will awaken, and then he will recognize how empty was what he had held in sleep.

It often happens to a poor man sleeping that he sees himself rich in a dream and exalts his spirit over those same things; he rejoices that he possesses what he did not possess and now seeks to disdain those by whom he grieved that he had been disdained. But suddenly awakening, he regrets that he has awakened, since meanwhile, even while sleeping, he had possessed the image of riches.

He immediately groans beneath the burden of poverty and is pressed by the straits of want—and all the worse because, for the briefest time, he had been rich in vain. Such, precisely, are the rich of this world who swell over the possessions they have received. They do not know how to do good with their abundance. The rich are like sleepers, but they awaken to their poverty, because they carry nothing with them to that judgment which endures; and the more exalted they now are for a brief time, the more grievously they will groan against themselves forever.

[Note: In the Utica manuscript, many other passages are interwoven here; they are excerpts from the place assigned in the *Moralia*.]

These, as Wisdom testifies, are said to speak at the time of their condemnation: “What did our pride profit us, and what did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things passed away like a shadow and like a messenger who runs by” (Wisdom 5:8).

They then recognize that what they had held was worthless and fleeting. While those things were present, they seemed great and lasting to their foolish hearts.

The rich man opened his eyes too late, when he saw Lazarus at rest, whom he had disdained to see lying before his gate (Luke 16:23). There he understood what he had refused to do here, and in his condemnation he was compelled to recognize what he had lost when he had not acknowledged his needy neighbor.

For when the body falls asleep in death, then the soul awakens to true knowledge; and when it dies with the flesh, the soul is compelled to see what it had refused to foresee. Then it perceives that what it feared is present; then it finds itself empty, though it had rejoiced that it was fuller than other human beings in possessions.

[Note: This chapter and the following one are absent from the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CLVII  
### “Those who mounted horses fell asleep” (Psalm 75:7)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXI (no. 43), it is added:

“Those who mounted horses fell asleep.”—By the name “horse,” temporal dignity is understood, as the prophet attests when he says: “Those who mounted horses fell asleep”—that is, those who trusted in the honor of the present life closed the eyes of their minds to the light of truth through the death of the soul.

### CHAPTER CLVIII  
### “Deliver me from the mire, so that I may not cling to it” (Psalm 68:15)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXIV (no. 27, at the end), it is added:

“Deliver me from the mire,” etc.—To cling to mire is to be defiled by the sordid desires of carnal concupiscence.

### CHAPTER CLIX  
### “I refused to let my soul be comforted; I remembered God, and I rejoiced” (Psalm 76:3)

When [Note: Thus it is read in the Gemet. manuscript.] the desires of the perfect within the holy Church were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XVIII (no. 66), it is added:

“I refused to let my soul be comforted,” etc.—Holy men do not admit into their minds any consolation of grace from the present life. For worldly rich people often, when afflicted by weariness of mind, look upon the temporal goods they have received and soothe their sadness. When they feel themselves touched by some grief, they look at their horses, contemplate their vessels of gold and silver, and go around their estates. When they willingly draw their eyes toward these temporal things, they overcome the grief that has arisen in the soul.

Thus the Truth says to them in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation” (Luke 6:24). But the holy man, who grieves because he has fallen from eternal joys, does not accept consolation from temporal things, saying: “I refused to let my soul be comforted.”

As though he were saying plainly: “Since I do not grieve over the loss of temporal things, I cannot at all be comforted by the abundance of temporal things.”

And if we, hearing this, were to say to him, “What, then, do you seek, since you refuse to be comforted by the things that belong to the world?” he immediately adds: “I remembered God, and I rejoiced.”

As though he were saying plainly: “The abundance of earthly things does not refresh me; but the memory alone of my Creator, whom I am not yet able to see, gives me joy.”

### CHAPTER CLX  
### “I exercised myself, and my spirit failed for a little while” (Psalm 76:4)

When the growth of spiritual progress was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XX (no. 46), it is added:

“I exercised myself,” etc.—What does he mean when he says, “my spirit,” except the human spirit—that is, the spirit of pride? Since, through hidden grace, we progress by a measure regulated from above toward the love of God, the more the virtue of God’s Spirit grows within us, the more our own spirit fails.

Because this spirit of error is not suddenly and completely cut off from us, it is rightly said to have failed “for a little while.” We then progress fully in God when we have completely failed in ourselves.

[Note: This chapter is not found in the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CLXI  
### “For your arrows have passed through” (Psalm 26:19)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXIX (no. 47), it is added:

“For your arrows have passed through.”—Concerning the rain of holy preaching it is said elsewhere: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon her” (Isaiah 5:6). But the Psalmist testifies concerning the course of the rain that takes place in the hearts of the elect, saying: “His word runs swiftly” (Psalm 147:15).

Often there is rain, but it does not have a course, because preaching comes to the ears but, when inward grace ceases, does not pass through to the hearts of those who hear. Concerning the words of this preaching, for the sake of the elect, it is said: “For your arrows have passed through.”

The arrows of God pass through when the words of his preaching descend from the ears into the heart. Since this occurs solely through a divine gift, the Lord testifies that he has given the rain its course.

### CHAPTER CLXIII  
### “Attend, my people, to my law” (Psalm 77:1)

When the proper manner of sacred speech was being discussed in the preface to the *Moralia*, chapter 1, no. 3, it is added:

“Attend, my people, to my law.”—It is not David’s law, nor David’s people; rather, assuming the person of the one through whom he was speaking, he speaks with the authority of the one whose inspiration filled him.

We see this happening daily in the Church, if we observe attentively. A lector standing in the midst of the people cries out: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6). He certainly does not truly say that he himself is God; yet, by saying this, he does not depart from the rule of truth, because he presents by his voice the lordship of the one whose ministry of reading he performs.

Thus the writers of sacred speech, because they are filled with the Holy Spirit and lifted above themselves, become, as it were, outside themselves; and so they speak judgments about themselves as though about others.

### CHAPTER CLXIII  
### “The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting their arrows, turned back on the day of battle” (Psalm 77:9)

[Col. 0866C]

When the cowardice of preachers was being discussed in Homily 9 on Ezekiel, it is added:

“The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow,” etc.

[Note: The manuscript codex indicates Homily 9 on Ezekiel, where we sought these passages in vain. A few passages remain in Homily 21, which is the ninth homily of book II.]

Often we who appear to be teachers, while preaching, instruct those who hear us and arm others by speaking, but refuse to go ourselves into the labor of battle. And it is written: “The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting their arrows, turned back on the day of battle.”

For *Ephraim* is interpreted as “fruitfulness.” And what is such or so great a fruitfulness except the tongue of teachers? By sowing the word, they multiply the fruits of souls.

When we prepare to teach and seek out the meaning of sacred Scripture, we bend the bow. When we speak words of correction, we shoot arrows. For in sacred speech the bow sometimes signifies sacred speech itself, which consists of the two Testaments, as it were of horn and cord.

The Old Testament is represented by the horn because of its hardness; the New Testament, which came into being through the incarnate Lord, is signified by the cord. When the cord is drawn, the horn is bent: for when the New Testament is examined, the Old is bent away from the hardness of the letter and turned toward spiritual understanding, because the rigidity of its hardness is not retained.

The arrows are these very words that teachers utter. Hence it is also rightly said through the prophet concerning holy teachers entering among the Gentiles: “With arrows and bow they will enter it” (Isaiah 7:24).

Therefore, when we weigh the sayings of sacred Scripture, we bend the bow when we give words of instruction, and we shoot arrows. But we turn back on the day of battle, because sometimes we refuse to undertake the labor of combat against vices.

### CHAPTER CLXIV  
### “He set the waters as in a wineskin” (Psalm 77:13)

When the machinations of the reprobate against the Church were being discussed, in the exposition of blessed Job, book VIII (no. 39), it is added:

“He set the waters as in a wineskin.”—The waters in a wineskin are the slippery desires of the wicked, because, when they do not find an opportunity for action, they are pressed down beneath the carnal heart.

### CHAPTER CLXV  
### “He remembered that they were flesh” (Psalm 77:39)

When the providence of divine mercy toward the human race was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book IV (no. 8), it is added:

“He remembered,” etc.—Almighty God, just as he was able to make good things from nothing, so, when he willed, restored through the mystery of his incarnation even the good things that had been lost.

He had created two kinds of creatures for the purpose of knowing him: the angelic and the human. Pride struck both and broke them from the condition of their inborn uprightness. But one possessed a covering of flesh, whereas the other bore nothing weak from flesh.

An angel is spirit alone; a human being, however, is both spirit and flesh. Therefore, in his mercy, the Creator, wishing to redeem, had to bring back to himself the one who, in committing the fault, clearly possessed something arising from weakness; and he had to thrust the apostate angel farther away because, when he fell from the strength of perseverance, he bore nothing weak from flesh.

Thus the Psalmist rightly, when saying that the Redeemer had mercy on human beings, also expressed the reason for his mercy, saying: “And he remembered that they were flesh.” As though he were saying: “Because he saw their weakness, he did not wish to punish their sins with strict severity.”

There is still another reason why fallen humanity ought to have been restored while the proud spirit could not be restored: namely, that the angel fell through his own wickedness, whereas another’s fault struck down the human being.

### CHAPTER CLXVI  
### “They turned into a crooked bow” (Psalm 77:57)

[Col. 0867C]

When the vice of pride and the pursuit of true humility were being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVII (no. 75), it is added:

“They turned into a crooked bow.”—A crooked bow strikes the one by whom it is drawn. Hence the tongues of the arrogant in their sayings are like a crooked bow, because, when they speak words against pride, they fix arrows in those who utter them.

Great care must therefore be taken lest received wisdom, when it illumines the darkness of ignorance, remove the light of humility, so that it can no longer be wisdom—although it shines with the power of speech, it obscures the heart of the speaker beneath a veil of pride (no. 70).

Some goods are supreme, others intermediate. The supreme goods are faith, hope, and charity. When these are truly possessed, they cannot be bent toward evil. Intermediate goods, however, are prophecy, teaching, the power of healing, and the like. They are placed between the two alternatives in such a way that through them one may sometimes seek the eternal homeland, and at other times earthly glory.
