We therefore call these virtues intermediate because we incline them toward whatever the mind desires. Once received, they can be used in the same way as earthly riches. Through earthly riches, some grow proud in the display of glory, while others perform works of compassion for the needs of their neighbors.

When external praise is sought through teaching and prophecy, the summit of earthly glory is pursued as though through bodily riches. But when teaching and prophecy are devoted to winning souls, the riches received are distributed to needy brothers.

Therefore, since the unwary mind often withdraws from the hand of the giver through the very gifts whose reception makes it rejoice, we must take vigilant care both to subdue vices beforehand and afterward to hold the gifts with watchfulness. For if the mind carelessly abandons itself in these things, it is not raised up with their help but, as though rewarded for its previous labors, is rejected.

Hence it also happens that a virtue received, when employed in the service of passing praise, is no longer virtue, because it serves vice. Since humility is the origin of virtue, that virtue truly grows in us which remains in its own root—that is, in humility. If it is cut off from this root, it withers, because it loses the charity that gives it life in the depths.

### CHAPTER CLXVII  
### “He delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hands of the enemy” (Psalm 77:61)

When the avoidance of arrogance in good works was being discussed, *Pastoral Rule*, Part IV, adds: “He delivered their virtues into captivity,” etc.—Virtue and beauty are delivered into captivity, into the hands of the enemy, when the ancient adversary gains dominion over a deceived mind through the pride arising from a good work. Yet this pride in virtue, although it does not completely overcome them, nevertheless often tests even the minds of the elect to some degree; but when the one who has been lifted up is abandoned, the abandoned person is recalled to fear. Hence David says: “I said in my prosperity, ‘I shall never be moved’” (Ps. XXIX, 7). But because he had become swollen with confidence in his virtue, he added shortly afterward what he endured: “You hid your face from me, and I was troubled.” It is as though he openly said: “I believed myself strong among the virtues, but when abandoned I recognized how great my weakness is.” Again it is said: “I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice” (Ps. CXVIII, 105). But because it was not within his strength to remain in the keeping he had sworn to maintain, once troubled he immediately discovered his weakness. Therefore he suddenly turned to the help of prayer, saying: “I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; give me life according to your word.”

[Note: [Col. 0867D] The three items that follow are not found in the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CLXVIII.—Likewise, concerning the foregoing

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 8 (no. 82):—The virtue and beauty of the arrogant are delivered into the hands of the enemy, because every good thing displayed through the desire for praise is handed over to the jurisdiction of the hidden adversary. For the one who exposes his riches to their knowledge summons enemies to plunder. As long as we are separated from the security of our eternal homeland, we walk along a road beset by lurking robbers. Whoever therefore fears being robbed on the journey must hide the good things he carries. Wretched are those who, desiring human praise, squander within themselves the fruits of their labors! When they desire to display themselves to the eyes of others, they condemn what they do. When evil spirits incite such people to boastfulness, they strip them bare by taking their works captive, as we have said.

### CHAPTER CLXIX.—“Incursions through evil angels; he made a path for his anger” (Ps. LXXVII, 49)

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 25 (nos. 23–24), there is added: “Incursions through evil angels,” etc.—The Lord justly permits a heart weighed down by former merits to be deceived also by the subsequent persuasions of evil spirits; and when it is worthily drawn into sin, its guilt is increased by punishment. Hence the Lord is said to have made a road for his anger from a path. A road is wider than a path. To make a road for his anger from a path is to enlarge the causes of anger through strict judgment, so that those who, though enlightened, refused to act rightly may, once justly blinded, continue to do what will make them deserving of greater punishment. Sin already deserves punishment, as does the cause of sin; but it is still awaited that sin and the punishment of sin should be added as an increase of punishment. Often one and the same sin is at once sin, punishment for sin, and the cause of sin. We can show this more clearly if we bring the matters themselves forward.

For unrestrained gluttony stimulates the fullness of the flesh toward the heat of lust; and lust once committed is often followed by perjury or homicide, lest the offender be punished by the vengeance of human laws. Let us therefore place before our eyes someone who has loosened the reins of his voracity and, overcome by that voracity, committed the crime of adultery; then, discovered in adultery, he secretly killed the husband of the adulteress, lest he be brought to trial. This adultery, placed between gluttony and homicide—born from the former and generating the latter—is sin, punishment, and the cause of sin. It is sin in itself; it is the punishment of sin because it increased the guilt of gluttony; and it is the cause of sin because it generated the subsequent homicide. Thus one and the same sin is both the punishment of what preceded and the cause of the guilt that follows: it condemns by aggravating what has already happened, and sows what will subsequently be condemned.

### CHAPTER CLXX.—“Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom” (Ps. LXXVIII, 12)

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 22 (no. 32), there is added: “Repay our neighbors,” etc.—Sacred Scripture is accustomed, for the most part, to use “bosom” for “mind.” Thus, through the Psalmist, the voice of the Church speaks concerning our persecutors, who are indeed joined to us by nature but separated from us by their way of life: “Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom.” It is as though it were openly said: “Let them receive in their minds what they inflict while raging against our bodies, so that, while they punish us outwardly in part, they themselves may be perfectly punished inwardly.”

### CHAPTER CLXXI.—“He gave us drink in tears, and by measure” (Ps. LXXVII, 6)

While the practice of worthy repentance was being discussed, *Pastoral Rule*, Part III (chap. 20, admonition 30), adds: “He gave us,” etc.—Those who mourn the sins of their deeds must take care to wash away completed evils with perfect lamentation, lest they be more tightly bound by the debt of the deed committed and pay less through tears of satisfaction. For it is written: “He gave us drink in tears, and by measure,” namely, so that each person, in repenting, may drink as many tears of compunction as he remembers having been estranged from God through his sins.

### CHAPTER CLXXII.—“Take up the psalm, and give the tambourine” (Ps. LXXX, 2)

[Col. 0869C]

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 33 (no. 33), there is added: “Take up the Psalm,” etc.—In the preaching of faith, something like a business transaction takes place, when the word is given and faith is received from the hearers. Those who advance the preaching and receive faith from the peoples conduct something like a business transaction: they impart faith and immediately take from them a holy life. For if the preaching of the righteous were not a transaction, the Psalmist certainly would not say: “Take up the psalm, and give the tambourine.” On the tambourine, leather is dried so that it may sound. What then does it mean to say, “Take up the psalm, and give the tambourine,” except: receive the spiritual song of the heart and return the temporal mortification of the body?

### CHAPTER CLXXIII.—“I heard you in the hiding-place of the tempest; I tested you at the waters of contradiction” (Ps. LXXX, 8)

When the avoidance of those who give wicked counsel against one’s resolve was being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 26 (no. 24), adds: “I heard you in the hiding-place of the tempest,” etc.—The hiding-place of the tempest is when the waves of tempting thoughts swell in a contrite heart, when the tumult of worldly cares crashes against the devotion of holy love. He is therefore heard in the hiding-place of the tempest, because this very fluctuation of tribulation is the cry of one who pleads. Since, however, there are always people who strive to persuade those seeking good things to pursue what is perverse, the waters of contradiction are the resisting peoples. And because a desire is tested when some adversity resists it, it is rightly said: “I tested you at the waters of contradiction.”

[Note: [Col. 0869D] This chapter is not found in the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CLXXIV.—“Their time shall be forever” (Ps. LXXX, 16)

While the ruin of those who perish was being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 4 (no. 5), adds: “Their time shall be forever” (no. 5).—Because time diminishes moment by moment, he called their ruin “their time,” showing that those who are separated from the consolation of the inward vision perish in utter ruin without end.

### CHAPTER CLXXV.—“My God, set them like a wheel, and like stubble before the face of the wind” (Ps. LXXXII, 14)

When the punishment of reprobate minds was being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 16 (no. 79), adds: “My God, set them like a wheel,” etc.—The wicked are set like a wheel because, sent into the circuit of labor, they neglect what lies ahead and follow what ought to be abandoned; thus they are lifted up by what is behind and fall upon what is before. They are also rightly compared to stubble before the face of the wind, because when the breeze of temptation rushes upon them, lacking any support grounded in reason, they are lifted up in order to fall. Often they judge themselves to possess some merit precisely because the breath of error carries them aloft.

### CHAPTER CLXXVI.—“My soul has desired and languished for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII, 3)

[Col. 0870B]

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 8 (no. 45), there is added: “It has desired,” etc.—There are some righteous people who desire heavenly things in such a way that they are nevertheless not at all detached from hope in earthly things. They possess estates granted by God as support for their needs; they retain honors bestowed upon them for a time; they do not covet what belongs to others, and they use their own possessions lawfully. Yet they are detached from the very things they possess, because they are not held by desire for what they have. There are also some righteous people who, girded for attaining the summit of perfection, abandon everything outwardly while desiring greater things inwardly; they strip themselves of possessions and divest themselves of the glory of honor. Through the continual longing for inward things, they subject themselves to the companionship of sorrow; they do not wish to possess consolation from outward things. As they draw near in mind to eternal joys, they utterly kill within themselves the life of bodily pleasure. To such people Paul says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III, 3).

The Psalmist expressed the voices of such people when he said: “My soul has desired and languished for the courts of the Lord.” They desire but do not languish who already seek heavenly things but are still in no way released from earthly pleasures. But the one who desires and languishes in the courts of God is the person who, while desiring eternal things, does not remain in the love of temporal things. Hence the Psalmist says again: “My soul has languished for your salvation” (Ps. CXVIII, 81). Hence Truth itself admonishes through its own voice, saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. XVI, 24). And again: “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 33).

For the soul of the righteous to languish for the salvation of God is to abandon, by a deliberate choice, the goods of the present life for eternity, to seek what will endure, and to place no confidence in temporal things.

### CHAPTER CLXXVII.—“For the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest where it may place its young” (Ps. LXXXIII, 4)

[Col. 0870D]

While the desires of the faithful nurtured in the peace of the Church were being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 19 (no. 48), adds: “For the sparrow has found a house for itself,” etc.—What is expressed by the name “nest” except the tranquil rest of faith, by which every weak person is nourished? For unless holy Church now nourished her weak children in the nest of peace, the Psalmist would not say: “For the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest where it may place its young.”

The sparrow has already found a house, because our Redeemer has entered the eternal dwelling of heaven. And the turtledove has found a nest, because holy Church, filled with love for her Creator, makes use of frequent groanings and builds for herself, as it were, a nest—that is, the most peaceful rest of faith—in which she cherishes her growing children, like fledglings growing feathers, in the bosom of charity until they fly upward to higher things.

### CHAPTER CLXXVIII.—“He has arranged ascents in his heart in the valley of tears” (Ps. LXXXIII, 6)

[Col. 0871A]

When the endeavors of the elect were being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 30 (no. 64), adds: “He has arranged ascents in his heart in the valley of tears.”—The more holy men humble themselves outwardly by despising themselves, the more abundantly they are nourished inwardly by contemplation of revelations. The valley of humility holds them outwardly in weeping, but inwardly the ascent of contemplation lifts them up.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] This is not read in the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CLXXIX.—“Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Ps. LXXXV, 11)

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 20 (no. 8), there is added: “Let my heart rejoice,” etc.—Holy men are so certain concerning hope that they nevertheless remain always wary of temptation. In their voice the Psalmist says: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name.” Here it should be noted that he does not say, “Let it rejoice so that it may be secure,” but, “Let it rejoice so that it may fear.”

They remember that, however much their conduct prospers, they are still in this life, of which the same Job says: “Human life upon earth is a temptation” (Job IX, 71). They remember again what is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind occupied with many thoughts” (Wis. IX, 15). They remember and fear, and do not presume to promise themselves certainty within themselves. Set between the joy of hope and the fear of temptation, they trust and fear, are strengthened and stumble, are assured and remain wary.

### CHAPTER CLXXX.—“They made me an abomination to themselves; I was handed over, and I did not go out” (Ps. LXXXVII, 9)

When the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion were being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 22 (no. 41), adds: “They made me an abomination to themselves,” etc.—Through the prophet our Redeemer intimates this concerning the time of his Passion. He was handed over but did not go out, because, while already suffering the weakness of his humanity at the very hour of his Passion, he did not wish to exercise the power of his divinity.

It would have been as though the Mediator of God and human beings had gone out if, while being held as a man, he had wished to display the power of his majesty and, through the greatness of his divinity, pass beyond the weakness of the flesh he had assumed. In order that the man might die more openly, God remained hidden: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. II, 8).

He therefore did not go out: when questioned by Pilate, he remained silent; among the hands of his persecutors he offered up the body he had assumed for the elect; and to those who resisted him he did not wish to reveal what he was. When he was despised because he appeared to be a man, he would have gone out had he wished to display his hidden majesty. But because he revealed weakness and concealed power, he did not go out to his persecutors, remaining unknown to them. Yet he goes out to the elect, to whom he reveals the sweetness of his divinity when they seek it. Hence it is said to him through the prophet: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones” (Hab. III, 13).

### CHAPTER CLXXXI.—“Free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII, 5)

[Col. 0871D]

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 10 (no. 66), there is added: “Free among the dead.”—Everyone who sins is a slave of sin (John VIII, 35). And because the incarnate Lord became a participant in our nature but not in our guilt, he is called one who was sent forth free, because he is not held under the dominion of sin. He is called “free among the dead” because, assuming our nature, he was in no way held under the yoke of iniquity.

Although the stain of our guilt did not touch him, the suffering of our mortality nevertheless bound him (no. 67). To hunger, thirst, grow weary, be seized, scourged, and crucified was the bond of our mortality. But when, after death had been completed, the veil of the temple was torn, the rocks split, the tombs opened, and the gates of hell disclosed, what else is shown by so many signs of such great power except that the bonds of our weakness were being loosed, so that he who had come to assume the form of a servant, in that very form of a servant freed from the bonds of hell, might return to heaven free, even with his members?

### CHAPTER CLXXXII.—“Your anger passed over me, and your terrors troubled me” (Ps. LXXXVII, 17)

When the fruitful fear of the elect was being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 7 (no. 6), adds: “Your anger passed over me,” etc.—The mind of the righteous considers not only what it endures but also fears what remains. It sees what it suffers in this life and fears that it may suffer more grievous things after this life. It mourns because, in the exile of this blindness, it has fallen from the joys of paradise; it fears that when the exile is left behind, eternal death may follow.

It therefore already endures the sentence in punishment, but still fears the threats of the coming Judge because of its guilt. Thus the Psalmist rightly says: “Your anger passed over me, and your terrors troubled me.” After the anger of the inward judgment has passed over, its terrors also trouble us, because we already suffer one thing from condemnation and still fear another from eternal retribution.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIII.—“I will sing your mercies, Lord, forever” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 1)

While the fear of the elect and the uncertainty of retribution were being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 4 (nos. 71–72), adds: “I will sing your mercies, Lord, forever.”—Often the mind of the righteous already mourns what it remembers having done perversely; it not only abandons its evil deeds but also punishes them with the bitterest lamentation. Yet, while remembering what it has done, it is gravely terrified by fear of judgment.

It has already converted itself perfectly, but still does not raise itself into perfect security, because, while weighing the strictness of the final examination, it trembles anxiously between hope and fear. It does not know what the righteous Judge, when he comes, will reckon concerning the deeds committed or what he will forgive. It remembers what evils it has committed but does not know whether it has mourned them worthily; and it fears lest the enormity of its guilt exceed the measure of its repentance.

Often Truth has already forgiven the guilt, but the afflicted mind, still very anxious about forgiveness, nevertheless trembles. Thus the holy person even here receives mercy but does not know that he has received it: a person abandons his sin by correcting and repenting of it, yet still fears the strict Judge concerning the retribution due for it.

There, therefore, every righteous person freely sings the Lord’s mercies in eternity: there will no longer be uncertainty about the forgiveness of sin; the memory of his guilt will no longer enslave his secure mind; his soul will not tremble under guilt, but will freely rejoice in the Judge’s pardon. But if no memory of sin touches a person there, from what does he rejoice at having been rescued? Or how does he give thanks to the giver for the forgiveness he received, if, because of the intervening oblivion of his past wickedness, he does not know that he was liable to punishment?

For the Psalmist says: “I will sing your mercies, Lord, forever.” How then does he sing God’s mercies forever if he does not know that he was wretched? And if he does not remember his past misery, from what does he offer praises to the giver of mercy?

Yet we must again ask how the mind of the elect can be perfect in blessedness if the memory of its guilt touches it amid its joys. Or how can the glory of perfect light shine brightly when guilt recalled to the mind casts a shadow over it?

We must understand that, just as now we often remember sad things with joy, so then we will remember past wickedness without harm to our blessedness. Often, while in good health, we recall past pains without pain; and the more we remember that we were sick, the more we love ourselves as restored to health.

There will therefore also be, in that blessedness, a memory of guilt—not one that pollutes the mind, but one that binds us more closely to joy. As the mind remembers its pain without pain, it will understand more truly that it was indebted to the physician and will love the salvation it received all the more because it remembers the distress from which it escaped.

In that joy we shall then behold our evils without weariness, just as now, placed in the light, we see darkness with the mind without any darkness of heart. For even if what we perceive in the mind is dark, this is a judgment of the light, not the experience of blindness.

Thus we will also offer eternal praises to our giver of mercy, and the consciousness of misery will in no way burden us. While we look upon our evils without any evil of mind, there will never be anything that pollutes the hearts of those praising God concerning past iniquities; and there will always be something that kindles those hearts to praise the one who delivered us.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIV.—“Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 16)

While the ineffable joy conceived in the minds of the elect was being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 24 (no. 10), adds: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation.”—“Jubilation” is said to occur when an ineffable joy is conceived in the mind—one that can neither be hidden nor disclosed in words, yet is revealed through certain movements, although it cannot be expressed by any precise terms.

Therefore the Prophet David, observing the souls of the elect conceive as much joy as they are unable to disclose in speech, said: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation.” For he did not say, “that speaks,” but “that knows,” because jubilation can indeed be known by understanding but cannot be expressed in words. Through it one experiences what lies beyond sense. And when the consciousness of the one experiencing it scarcely suffices to contemplate it, how could the tongue of the one speaking suffice to express it?

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Absent from the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CLXXXV.—“In the morning, like grass, may it pass away; in the morning may it flower and pass away” (Ps. LXXXIX, 6)

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 29 (no. 52), there is added: “In the morning, like grass, may it pass away,” etc.—In Sacred Scripture, “grass” sometimes signifies the greenness of temporal glory, as the Psalmist says: “In the morning, like grass, may it pass away.” For “in the morning to flower and pass away like grass” means that, amid the prosperity of this age, the beauty of temporal glory quickly withers.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVI.—“You have made his fortifications a source of fear” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 41)

[Col. 0873C]

While the hidden arrangements of divine judgments were being discussed, there is added: “You have made his fortifications a source of fear.”—[Note: [Col. 0873D] It is read in the manuscripts of Michael, Celestine, and Paris that this was taken from Homily 10 on Ezekiel, although we sought it there in vain.]

Often someone remembers his deceit, anger, uncleanness, or pride and hides from the tumult of this world in a place of humility. But when, after his concealment, he is led to govern a people, he is struck by the arrows of sins entering from every side and begins to fear that even this may now be destined for judgment, because he tasted the deep peace of quiet that he was unable to keep.

As it is written: “You have made his fortifications a source of fear.” When we seek a humble place because of uprightness of mind, what else do we hold than the stronghold of a fortification? But when, compelled, we return to the crowds and tumults of the world, caught amid sins rushing upon us, we fear even our own fortification, because, in view of the subtle examination of almighty God, we begin to fear even the state in which we had believed that we had lived well.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVII.—“Who knows the power of your anger, and can number your anger because of your fear?” (Ps. LXXXIX, 11)

[Col. 0873D]

When the fear of the righteous arising from uncertainty concerning divine judgments was being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 5 (no. 16), adds: “Who knows the power of your anger,” etc.—The power of divine anger cannot be grasped by our mind, because its dispensation, through hidden arrangements concerning us, often receives us from the very place where it seems to abandon us, and abandons us from the place where it is believed to receive us. Thus what is called anger is often grace, and what is sometimes thought to be grace is anger.

Scourges correct some people, but lead others into the madness of impatience. Prosperity, because it soothes them, moderates some people’s insanity; but because it exalts others, it uproots them completely from every hope of conversion. Vices drag everyone downward, yet some return from them more easily because they are more deeply ashamed of having fallen into them. Virtues always lift people toward higher things, but sometimes, when they conceive pride from their virtues, they fall along the very path of ascent.

Because the power of divine anger is not at all known, it must necessarily be feared without ceasing in every circumstance.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVIII.—“He himself delivered me from the snare of hunters and from a harsh word” (Ps. XC, 3)

When the exercise of the elect in response to the slanders of the reprobate was being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 6 (no. 45), adds: “He himself delivered me from the snare of hunters,” etc.—Hunters seek nothing except flesh. But we are rescued from the snare of hunters and from a harsh word when, by despising them, we overcome both the snares of carnal people and the insults of mockery.

Their harsh words are those that oppose our good journeys. To escape the harshness of the word is to trample underfoot, by disregarding them, the mockeries of detractors. Thus the holy soul is freed from the harsh word because, while it seeks no honor of praise in this world, it does not feel the insults of detraction.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIX.—“With his shoulders he will overshadow you” (Ps. XC, 4)

When the manner of sacred language was being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 32 (no. 7), adds: “With his shoulders he will overshadow you.”—When shoulders, eyes, or an arm are spoken of in relation to God, the mind must take the greatest care not to imagine anything bodily in him. To fall into the heresy of the Anthropomorphites is to confine within bodily outlines him who fills and embraces all things without being circumscribed.

But almighty God, drawing us toward himself, humbles himself to our level; and, in order to make lofty realities known, he accommodates himself to humble ones, so that the mind of the little ones, nourished by familiar things, may rise to seek what is unknown. Hearing certain things from him who is far above it in terms close to itself, it is moved toward him as though by certain steps.

Thus Scripture sometimes draws from human bodies, sometimes from minds, sometimes from birds, and sometimes from senseless things, certain likenesses in God that are otherwise entirely dissimilar. Often it draws a likeness from human bodies, as when it says through the prophet to the person hoping in him: “With his shoulders he will overshadow you,” although it is certain that, in his own nature, God possesses neither an eye nor shoulders nor the definite outlines of limbs.

But because we see with the eye and bear burdens on the shoulders, God is said to have an eye because he sees everything. And because he tolerates us—and by the very fact that he tolerates us, preserves us—he is said to overshadow us with his shoulders. For he says: “With his shoulders he will overshadow you.” It is as though this were said to a sinful person seeking forgiveness after sin: “The Lord protects you with the same mercy by which he tolerated you.” He overshadows with his shoulders because, while he carries us, he defends us.

### CHAPTER CXC.—“They will still increase in rich old age, and they will be well enduring, so that they may proclaim” (Ps. XCI, 15)

While the gathering of the faithful at the end of time was being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 35 (no. 35), adds: “They will still increase in rich old age,” etc.—The Psalmist foresaw the preachers of holy Church being enriched by the blessing of the final age, when he said: “They will still increase in rich old age.” They increase in rich old age because, as their life is prolonged, their strength is continually brought to greater perfection; and through the increase of time, the gains of their merits also grow for them.

They are well enduring so that they may proclaim, because, preaching heavenly things, they tolerate adversity with greater strength in proportion as, through their endurance, they bring back richer benefits for souls.

### CHAPTER CXCI.—“Wondrous are the swellings of the sea; wondrous is the Lord on high” (Ps. XCII, 4)

When the pride of the reprobate and the divine miracles manifested through the virtue of preachers were being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 9 (no. 11), adds: “Wondrous are the swellings of the sea,” etc.—When the pagan world saw its customs being destroyed by the preaching of a new way of life; when the rich of this world saw the deeds of the poor opposing their pride; and when the wise of the age considered the words of the unlearned to be their adversaries, they immediately swelled into the storm of persecution.

But those who, provoked by opposition in words, rushed into the storms of persecution were restrained by the wonder of signs. Because the world wondrously raised itself into waves of persecution against the life of the elect, the Creator of those above wondrously laid those waves low through the lifted power of the preachers. “Wondrous, therefore, are the swellings of the sea; wondrous is the Lord on high.” For he showed that his ministers could accomplish more through miracles than earthly powers had swollen with anger.

The Lord also fittingly declares inward things through Jeremiah while recounting outward things, saying: “I have set sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting command” (Jer. V, 22).

[Note: [Col. 0875D] This chapter and the following two are absent from the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CXCII.—“Until justice is turned into judgment” (Ps. XCIII, 15)

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 26 (no. 53), there is added: “Until justice is turned into judgment.”—Paul says of himself and his companions: “That we might become the justice of God in him” (1 Cor. V, 21). Justice is therefore turned into judgment because those who now live justly and irreproachably then receive the power of judging.

### CHAPTER CXCIII.—“According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations, Lord, have gladdened my soul” (Ps. XCIII, 19)

[Col. 0875C]

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 35 (no. 22), there is added: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart,” etc.—He indicates that he was consoled in the same measure in which he had been afflicted when he cries that he was gladdened according to the multitude of his sorrows.

### CHAPTER CXCIV.—“You fashion pain through the commandment” (Ps. XCIII, 20)

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 18 (no. 35), there is added: “You fashion pain through the commandment.”—A scourge then washes away guilt when it changes a person’s life. For the scourge does not expiate the deeds of one whose conduct it does not change.

Every divine blow is either a purification of the present life in us or the beginning of a punishment to come. Concerning those who profit from the scourge, it is said: “You fashion pain through the commandment,” because when the wicked person is scourged and corrected, he who refused to hear the commandment hears pain. Pain is fashioned through the commandment for the person who is restrained from evil works by pain, as though pain had taken the place of a commandment.

But concerning those whom scourges condemn and do not free, it is said: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept discipline” (Jer. V, 3). For such people the scourges begin in this life and continue in eternal punishment.

### CHAPTER CXCV.—“The Lord will not reject his people, for all the ends of the earth are in his hand, and he himself beholds the heights of the mountains” (Ps. XCIV, 4)

When the conversion of the powerful of this world through the inspiration of heavenly grace was being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 30 (no. 78), adds: “The Lord will not reject his people,” etc.—The heights of the mountains are certainly the pride of the arrogant, which the Lord is said to behold—that is, to change from their iniquity for the better.

For the Lord converts the one whom he beholds. Hence it is written: “The Lord turned and looked upon Peter; and Peter remembered the word that the Lord had spoken to him: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’ And he went out and wept bitterly” (Luke XXII, 61). And as Solomon says: “The king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters every evil by his gaze” (Prov. XX, 8).

Concerning this height of the mountains, it is said again through the Prophet: “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord” (Ps. XCVI, 5), because, liquefied by divine fear after the hardness of their perversity, they were withdrawn from that formerly rigid swelling.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] This chapter and all the others up to 203 are not found in the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER CXCVI.—“The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord” (Ps. XCVI, 5)

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 33 (no. 2), there is added: “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord.”—Many who had previously swelled with lofty rigidity were melted by great fear through repentance when the Lord appeared in the flesh.

### CHAPTER CXCVII.—“Then all the trees of the forest will rejoice” (Ps. XCV, 13)

[Col. 0876B]

In *Expositions of the Gospel*, Homily 36 (no. 8), there is added: “Then all the trees of the forest will rejoice.”—The trees of the forest are the nations that have been called, because in their unbelief they were always twisted and fruitless.

### CHAPTER CXCVIII.—“The honor of the king loves judgment” (Ps. XCVIII, 4)

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 25 (no. 12), there is added: “The honor of the king loves judgment.”—Namely, the person who already honors the Lord through faith should carefully judge what he owes him in action.

### CHAPTER CXCIX.—“The children of your servants will dwell there” (Ps. CI, 29)

While the despair of the wicked was being discussed, *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 8 (no. 35), adds: “The children of your servants will dwell there.”—The place of the human being, though not a spatial place, was the Creator himself, who created the human being so that he might subsist in him. The human being abandoned that place when, listening to the words of the seducer, he departed from love of the Creator.

But when almighty God, by redeeming the human being, also showed himself bodily, he himself, so to speak, following after the footsteps of his fugitive, came as the place in order to retain the human being whom he had lost. For if the Creator could in no way be called a place, the Psalmist, praising God, would not say: “The children of your servants will dwell there.” We say “there” only when we specifically designate a place.

Yet there are many who, even after receiving the Redeemer’s help, descend into the darkness of despair and perish all the more wickedly because they despise the remedies of mercy offered to them.

### CHAPTER CC.—“For he himself knows our formation” (Ps. CII, 14)

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 13 (no. 27), there is added: “For he himself knows our formation.”—His knowing is his taking us upon himself. For what is surprising if he is said especially to know our formation, when it is clear that there is nothing he does not know? But his knowing our formation means that he mercifully took it upon himself.

### CHAPTER CCI.—“For those who remember his commandments, to do them” (Ps. CII, 18)

In *The Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book 15 (no. 17), there is added: “For those who remember his commandments, to do them.”—Whoever retains his commandments in memory but does not keep them at all holds, in the words of instruction, the judgments by which he will be condemned.

### CHAPTER CCII.—“The mountains rise, and the valleys descend” (Ps. CIII, 8)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXIII (no. 2), the following is added: “The mountains ascend, and the plains descend.” [Col. 0877A] Many of the Lord’s persecutors come against him in pride, but return from him in humility. They ascend mountains through the swelling of power, but descend into plains, having been made level, so to speak, through recognition of their guilt.

## CHAPTER 203.—“Enter his gates with confession; confess to him in his courts with hymns” (Ps. 99:4).

When the matter of worthy repentance was being treated in book II, Homily 4 on Ezekiel (no. 1), the following was added: “Enter his gates with confession,” etc. When we confess our sins with tears, we enter the gate of the narrow life; but when thereafter we are led to eternal life, we enter the courts of our gates with praises of confession, because there will then be no narrowness, when the joy of the eternal solemnity has received us. On account of the narrowness of our confession, Truth says: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. 7:13). And when the Psalmist confidently expected to be received into the spaciousness of eternal joy, he said: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. 30:9).

## CHAPTER 204.—“I was mixing my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101:10).

[Col. 0877B] When the divine judgment upon human beings was being treated in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXV (no. 19), the following was added: “I was mixing my drink with weeping.” It is clear to all who know the truth that, at that final examination, almighty God will conduct a public trial, so that he may consign some to punishments and admit others to participation in the heavenly kingdom. But what will then be made manifest publicly is now accomplished daily through God’s hidden judgment. For, by justly and mercifully examining or ordering the hearts of individuals, he rejects some into outward things and draws others toward what is inward. He kindles in some the desire for inward things, while he abandons others to think about outward things for the sake of their pleasures. He raises the minds of some toward what is above, while through pride he plunges others into the lowest desires.

The hearts of others, however, are closed to human eyes, and it is not known who is being rejected, because what each person thinks cannot be penetrated. For often the deliberation of a perverse heart has not yet proceeded as far as the execution of the deed, and perhaps the person who already wanders outwardly in the mind is still held inwardly by habit. Yet such a person has fallen before the eyes of the interior Judge at the moment when, through desire, he departed from the pursuit of inward things.

Sometimes, however, others suddenly revive to heavenly hope through love after the practice of evil conduct; and those who had scattered themselves in perverse action gather themselves back, reproving themselves, into the bosom of inward reconsideration. [Col. 0877C] People who still despise them, knowing what they were previously like in their conduct, suppose them to remain the same. But they themselves, through the strict examination of reflection, pursue the recollection of what their life had been; and it is known what they were, but it is not known what they have now begun to be.

Thus, among both kinds of people, it often happens that those who appear to stand according to human judgment are already lying prostrate in the sight of the eternal Judge, while those who still lie prostrate before human beings are already standing in the sight of the eternal Judge. For who could have judged that Judas would lose the lot of life even after the ministry of apostleship? And who, on the other hand, would have believed that the thief could find the cause of life at the very moment of death? [Col. 0877D]

But the hidden Judge, presiding and discerning the hearts of both, established the one mercifully and struck down the other justly; he strictly rejected one outwardly, while mercifully drawing the other inward. Hence it is that the prophet, announcing that some would fall at the time of his passion and others rise, says: “I was mixing my drink with weeping.” Drink, certainly, is drawn inward from outward things, while weeping flows outward from inward things. Therefore, to mix the Lord’s drink with weeping is to draw some from outward things inwardly, and to reject others from inward things toward outward things.

[Note: Absent from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER 205.—“But you are the very same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. 101:28).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book IV (no. 8), the following is added: “But you are the very same,” etc. He declares this to be the place of the elect, adding: “The sons of your servants will dwell there.” [Col. 0878A] For God, who contains all things without occupying a place, remains for us, when we come to him, a non-local place; and when we reach that place, we see how great the disturbance of our mind in this life has been. For although the righteous are already quiet in comparison with the wicked, they are nevertheless not at all quiet when measured against the innermost repose.

## CHAPTER 206.—“You have put on confession and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment” (Ps. 103:2).

When the loftiness of the divine essence was being treated in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXII (no. 3), the following was added: “You have put on confession and beauty,” etc. Our Redeemer has put on confession and beauty because he has taken up the choirs of the holy angels, whom he created, for the use of his own beauty; and he presents the Church to himself like a glorious garment, without spot or wrinkle. Therefore he has put on confession and beauty—that is, confession here and beauty there—because those whom here he has made confessing through repentance, there he displays shining through the beauty of righteousness. [Col. 0878B]

He will therefore be clothed with light as with a garment, because he will be clothed in that eternal glory with all the saints, to whom it was said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14). Hence it is also said through the Gospel that, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, “his garments became white as snow” (Matt. 17). What else is announced in this transfiguration than the glory of the final resurrection? On the mountain his garments became like snow, because at the summit of heavenly brightness all the saints will cling to him, shining with the light of righteousness.

[Note: Not found in the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER 207.—“Stretching out heaven like a skin, who covers its upper parts with waters” (Ps. 103:2).

Homily 17 on Ezekiel (no. 4), or book II, Homily 5, adds the following: “Stretching out heaven like a skin,” etc. Heaven is stretched out like a skin because sacred Scripture is explained to us through the mouths of mortals. But there are waters in heaven, namely the higher multitudes—that is, the hosts of angels—in which the upper parts of that same heaven are covered. For the things in sacred discourse that are higher and more obscure are disclosed only to angelic spirits and remain still unknown to us. [Col. 0878C]

## CHAPTER 208.—“Stretching out heaven like a skin, who covers its upper parts with waters” (Ps. 103:2).

When the meaning of sacred discourse, through the dispensation of inward inspiration, was being treated in Homily 9 on Ezekiel (no. 30), the following was added: “Stretching out heaven like a skin,” etc. What is signified here by the name “heaven” except sacred Scripture, from which the sun of wisdom, the moon of knowledge, and the stars of examples and virtues from the ancient fathers shine upon us? It is stretched out like a skin because, formed before our eyes by the language of the flesh through its writers, it is unfolded through the explanatory words of teachers.

What, moreover, is signified by the name “waters” except the most pure choirs of angels? Of these it is written: “And the waters that are above the heavens shall praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:4). The Lord therefore covers the upper parts of this heaven with waters, because the heights of sacred discourse—that is, what it relates concerning the nature of divinity or concerning eternal joys—are still unknown to us and known only to the angels in secret. [Col. 0878D]

Thus this heaven is extended before us, and yet its upper parts are covered with waters, because certain things in sacred discourse are already disclosed to us through the opening of the Spirit, while certain things, which can be made manifest only to the angels, are still kept hidden from us. Nevertheless, of these hidden things we already perceive a portion through spiritual understanding; we have already received the pledge of the Holy Spirit. We do not yet fully know these things, yet we love them from the depths of our being, and in the many spiritual meanings that we already understand, we are nourished by the food of truth.

## CHAPTER 209.—“Who makes the cloud his ascent” (Ps. 103:3).

When the mystery of the divine Incarnation was being treated in Homily 8 on Ezekiel (no. 29), the following was added: “Who makes the cloud his ascent.” [Col. 0879A] What should we appropriately understand by “cloud” in this passage except the flesh of our Redeemer? He made the cloud his ascent because he who is everywhere in his divinity ascended to heavenly things in the flesh.

## CHAPTER 210.—“Who walks upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 103:3).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (no. 8), the following was added: “Who walks upon the wings of the winds.” In sacred Scripture, souls are often signified by the speed and subtlety of the winds, as the Psalmist says of God: “Who walks upon the wings of the winds,” that is, who surpasses the powers of souls.

[Note: This chapter and the following one are not found in the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER 211.—“Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XI (no. 7), the following was added: “Who makes his angels spirits,” etc. Angels, that is, messengers, are sometimes called preachers in sacred discourse, as it is said through the prophet: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7). [Col. 0879B] Almighty God therefore makes his angels spirits because he makes his preachers spiritual.

## CHAPTER 212.—“Likewise, from the passage above.”

Homily 34 on the Gospels (no. 8). It must be understood that “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. For those holy spirits of the heavenly homeland are always spirits, but they cannot always be called angels, because they are angels only when something is announced through them. Hence the Psalmist also says: “Who makes his angels spirits.” It is as though he were saying openly: He makes those whom he always has as spirits also angels whenever he wishes.

Those who announce small matters are called angels, while those who announce great matters are called archangels. Hence it is that Gabriel the archangel, not just any angel, is sent to the Virgin Mary (Luke 1).

## CHAPTER 213.—“The mountains ascend, and the plains descend” (Ps. 103:2).

[Col. 0879C]

When those who were proud and had been brought back to humility through the gift of grace were being treated in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXIII (no. 2), the following was added: “The mountains ascend,” etc. Many of the Lord’s persecutors come against him in pride, but return in humility. They ascend mountains through the swelling of power, but descend into plains, having been made level, so to speak, through recognition of their guilt.

Hence, again, the same Prophet says of these mountains: “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord” (Ps. 95:5), because many who had previously swelled up with lofty hardness were melted, when God appeared in the flesh, by great fear expressed through repentance.

## CHAPTER 214.—“The high mountains are for the deer; the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs” (Ps. 103:18).

When the meaning of sacred discourse according to the merit of its hearers was being treated in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXX (no. 64), the following was added: “The high mountains are for the deer,” etc. [Col. 0879D] What should be understood here by “mountains” except the lofty sentences of sacred Scripture? Those who already know clearly the leaps of contemplation ascend the lofty summits of divine sentences as though they were mountain peaks. Since the weak are certainly unable to reach these peaks, it is rightly added there: “The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs,” because understanding does not exercise the weak sublimely, but humble faith in Christ alone holds them secure.

[Note: Nothing concerning this chapter is found in the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER 215.—“Likewise, from the passage above.”

Homily 9 on Ezekiel (no. 31). Let those possess the mountains of understanding who already clearly [lacuna; surviving ending: “-verunt”] the leaps of contemplation. But let the rock be a refuge for the hedgehogs, because [Col. 0880A] we, who are little ones and covered with the thorns of our sins, even though we cannot understand lofty things, are nevertheless saved in the refuge of our rock—that is, in faith in Christ.

## CHAPTER 216.—“You set darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forests will pass through: the lion cubs roaring to seize and seek food for themselves from God” (Ps. 103:20).

When the rejection of unbelievers through the rectitude of divine judgment was being treated in the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVII (no. 49), the following was added: “You set darkness, and it became night,” etc. The Lord sets darkness when, repaying sins with judgments, he withdraws the light of his understanding; and it becomes night because the mind of the wicked is blinded by the errors of its ignorance. In that night all the beasts of the forest pass through: malignant spirits, lying hidden beneath the shadow of deceit, roam through the hearts of the reprobate, fulfilling their wickedness.

In it also the lion cubs roar, because the ministering spirits of the most wicked yet eminent powers rise up with insistent temptations. Yet they seek food from God, because they plainly cannot seize souls unless they are divinely permitted to prevail by a just judgment. [Col. 0880B]

Appropriately, it is then added: “The sun has risen, and they have gathered together, and have lain down in their dens” (Ps. 103:22), because, when the light of truth appeared in the flesh, they were shaken from the minds of the faithful and returned, as it were, to their dens, since they retained only the hearts of unbelievers.

## CHAPTER 217.—“You will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust” (Ps. 103:29).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXIV (no. 49), the following was added: “You will take away their spirit,” etc. What is meant by “their spirit” except the spirit of pride? Let their spirit therefore be taken away so that they may fail—that is, when the spirit of pride has been withdrawn, may they recognize that they are nothing—and let them return to dust, that is, let them be humbled because of the weakness of their condition.

With reference to this dust, when those who consider themselves are recalled to its remembrance, it is said through Wisdom: “The righteous will shine like the sun, and like sparks they will run through the stubble” (Wis. 3:7). [Col. 0880C] For when holy men are mixed with sinners, they set them ablaze with the fire of their examples, and they reduce to ashes everything that shines, because, consumed by the flame of piety, when they behold the weakness of their condition, they recognize themselves to be nothing other than ash. Thus, released from the hardness of their pride, they say through repentance: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Ps. 102:15).

[Note: Not found in the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER 218.—“Send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:30).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXIX (no. 35), the following was added: “Send forth your spirit,” etc. Thus, indeed, thus the face of the earth is changed by the power of renewal: the mind that was formerly dry is watered when grace comes, and after its former aridity it is clothed, as though with newly produced grasses, in the verdure of knowledge.

## CHAPTER 219.—“Of the word that he commanded for a thousand generations” (Ps. 104:8).

[Col. 0880D]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book IX (no. 3), the following was added: “Of the word that he commanded for a thousand generations.” In sacred Scripture, the number one thousand is customarily understood to signify totality. But since it is clear that, from the beginning of the world up to the coming of the Redeemer, the Evangelist counts no more than seventy-seven generations (Luke 3), what is expressed here by “a thousand generations” except the complete totality of the foreknown generation destined to produce a new offspring?

Hence it is also said through John: “They will reign with him for a thousand years” (Rev. 20:6), because the reign of the holy Church is made firm through the perfection of its totality.

[Note: The three chapters that follow are likewise not found in the cited manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER 220.—“Likewise, from the passage above.”

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXV (no. 42). [Col. 0881A] The number one thousand is also understood as perfect in sacred discourse, because totality is signified by its designation. Hence it is written: “Of the word that he commanded for a thousand generations.” Since it is by no means to be believed that the world extends to a hundred generations, what else is represented by a thousand generations except the totality of generations?

## CHAPTER 221.—“For his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 106:1).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book VIII (no. 30), the following was added: “For his mercy endures forever.” For plainly, the one whom mercy does not rescue now, justice alone condemns after the present age.

## CHAPTER 222.—“Iron passed through his soul” (Ps. 104:18).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XV (no. 30), the following was added: “Iron passed through his soul.” Every necessity is appropriately called iron, because it torments the life of the poor with the wound of sorrow, as it is also written concerning the necessities of the one who, sold by his brothers, led an afflicted life: “Iron passed through his soul.” [Col. 0881B] What, then, are iron weapons except the necessities of the present life, which press harshly upon the poor person and pursue his life?

## CHAPTER 223.—“They ascend to the heavens, and they descend to the abysses” (Ps. 106:26).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book IX (no. 29), the following was added: “They ascend to the heavens,” etc. Often, in order that the soul may be kindled by the fire of divine love and lifted up to behold heavenly and hidden things, it is already carried toward the heights; pierced by perfect desire, it is estranged from what is below. But when it is struck by sudden temptation, it is bent down, pierced by the thoughts that arise, although it had been raised upright toward God with strong purpose. It becomes unable to discern itself and, caught between vices and virtues, does not recognize on which side it is stronger.

Indeed, it is often brought to the point of wondering how it can comprehend such sublime things while an illicit thought pollutes it, and, again, how it can admit illicit thoughts when a powerful spiritual fervor carries it above itself. [Col. 0881C] Observing these alternating movements of thought in the soul, the Psalmist rightly says: “They ascend to the heavens, and they descend to the abysses.” We ascend to the heavens when we penetrate sublime things, but we descend to the abysses when we are suddenly cast down from the summit of contemplation by shameful temptations. Thus, when the movements of the soul alternate between aspirations and vices, they obscure the certainty of being heard.

## CHAPTER 224.—“Contention was poured out upon their rulers, and they led them astray in a trackless place, and not on the way” (Ps. 106:42).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (no. 27), the following was added: “Contention was poured out upon their rulers,” etc. Who are designated here by the name “rulers” except the authors of heretical depravity? For, since they do not fear to interpret God’s dispensation perversely, they lead the peoples subject to them not into the way that is Christ, but into a trackless place. [Col. 0881D]

Contention is rightly said to have been poured out upon them, because they contradict one another through their mutual arguments. Arius, accepting three persons in the Godhead, also believed in three gods. Sabellius, on the contrary, accepting one, believed there to be one person. Between them, the holy Church, holding unwaveringly to the straight path of her preaching, both proclaims one God and asserts three persons against Sabellius; and, asserting three persons, confesses one God against Arius.

Moreover, when Manichaeus discovered that virginity is praised in sacred discourse, he condemned marriage. Jovinianus, on the other hand, because he recognized that marriage is permitted, despised the purity of virginity. Thus it happens that, while heretics are always confused by perverse understanding, their wickedness agrees with itself in guilt but differs in doctrine. [Col. 0882A]

The holy Church, by contrast, proceeds in ordered peace through the conflicts between the two sides. It knows how to accept higher goods while also honoring lower ones, so that it neither equates the highest with the lowest nor, while honoring the highest, despises what is below.

[Note: Omitted in the Michaelian manuscripts and in others.]

## CHAPTER 225.—“Every iniquity has stopped its mouth” (Ps. 106:42).

In the exposition of blessed Job, the following was added: “Every iniquity has stopped its mouth.” Iniquity contracts its mouth. For even now iniquity opens its mouth wide, because it does not cease to assail the Redeemer of the human race with the insults of unbelieving tongues. But it contracts its mouth when it closes through punishment what it refuses to close through deliberate effort.

This can also rightly be understood of persecutors who have been converted. When the poor man has been saved and the needy person has returned to hope, iniquity becomes silent with contracted mouth, because, as the miracle of his resurrection became manifest, a great multitude of unbelievers believed and ceased from insults and reproaches against their Redeemer. [Col. 0882B] Its mouth, which it had opened to mock God, it then contracted through fear.

## CHAPTER 226.—“I was shaken like a locust” (Ps. 108:23).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXI (no. 48), the following was added: “I was shaken like a locust.” What is signified here by the name “locust” except the resurrection of our Redeemer? He endured being held by his persecutors even unto death, but he was shaken like a locust, because he sprang away from their hands in the leap of a sudden resurrection.

## CHAPTER 227.—“Let them be clothed like a double garment with their shame” (Ps. 108:29).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book IX (no. 68), the following was added: “Let them be clothed like a double garment with their shame.” In this life God judges a person in two ways: either he begins, through present evils, to inflict the punishments that follow, or he extinguishes the punishments that follow through present scourges. Unless the just Judge, because their sins demand it, were to strike certain people both now and afterward, the Psalmist would not say concerning the wicked: “Let them be clothed like a double garment with their shame.” [Col. 0882C]

We call a *diploidem* a double garment. Those, therefore, are clothed with shame like a double garment who, according to the measure of their guilt, are struck by both temporal and everlasting punishment. Hence Jude also says: “The second time he destroyed those who did not believe.” Punishment alone liberates from punishment those whom it changes. For those whom present evils do not correct, it leads on to what follows.

But if present punishment did not defend certain people from eternal punishment, Paul certainly would not have said: “When we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Cor. 11:32). Hence the voice of the angel says to John: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Rev. 3:19). Hence it is also written: “For the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. II, 6). [Col. 0882D]

But often the mind of the righteous trembles more deeply, so that it may be more secure; and, when it is beaten with scourges, it is disturbed by uncertainty concerning the heavenly judgment. It fears that everything it suffers may be the beginning of the damnation to come, and, because it doubts the merits of its life under the blow, it questions the Judge in thought. But when the virtue of its life is brought back before the eyes of the mind, consolation, as it were, answers the Judge, because he does not strike to destroy the one whom, by striking, he preserves in the innocence of his conduct.

[Note: This chapter is absent from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER 228.—“The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book VIII (no. 89), the following was added: “The Lord said to my Lord,” etc. This does not mean that the Lord will not sit at the Lord’s right hand after he has struck his enemies and subjected them to his power. Rather, he presides over all in eternal blessedness; and even before he tramples the hearts of his rebels, he reigns in that blessedness—in which, once his enemies are subdued, he assuredly reigns without end thereafter. [Col. 0883A]

## CHAPTER 229.—“He drinks from the torrent on the way; therefore he has lifted up his head” (Ps. 109:7).

A composite passage from Homily 25 on the Gospels (no. 7), the exposition of blessed Job, book XIV (no. 68), and book XXXIII (no. 11), adds the following: “He drinks from the torrent on the way,” etc. Our Creator and Redeemer wished to rise from death quickly, so that our soul would not remain long in the death of unbelief. For from the beginning of the world a torrent of death had flowed through the human race. But from this torrent, as from a certain river of our passion, the Lord deigned to drink not in a dwelling-place but on the way, because he encountered death only temporarily—that is, for three days—and in the death he encountered he did not remain, as we do, until the end of the age. He touched the punishment of mortal life only in a kind of passing. [Col. 0883B]

Therefore he did not remain long in the death to which he had freely submitted; and thus he lifted up his head, because what he had placed in the tomb by dying, he raised above the angels by rising. From the very place where he temporarily permitted the threats of his persecutors to rage against him, he struck down the ancient enemy forever.

[Note: Our manuscripts lack the five chapters that follow.]

## CHAPTER 230.—“Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his purposes” (Ps. 110:2).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book VI (no. 33), the following was added: “Great are the works of the Lord,” etc. His works are indeed so great that, through everything done by human beings, his will is sought out. For what was thought to be prevented often becomes the means by which it is accomplished.

## CHAPTER 231.—“Confession and magnificence are his work” (Ps. 110:3).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVIII (no. 65), the following was added: “Confession and magnificence are his work.” [Col. 0883C] From him, therefore, we receive the ability to confess rightly, from whom we also receive the ability to perform great things.

## CHAPTER 232.—“You have broken my bonds; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115:7).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book IX (no. 94), the following was added: “You have broken my bonds,” etc. The Lord leaves us to lament our sorrow when he both shows us the evils we have committed and helps us to lament the very things we recognize. He places our sins before our eyes and, with the compassionate hand of grace, loosens the bonds of the heart, so that our mind may rise toward the leisure of repentance; and, with the shackles of the flesh released, it may direct its free step toward its Creator through love.

## CHAPTER 233.—“The Lord is my helper, and I will look upon my enemies” (Ps. 117:7).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXIX (no. 25), the following was added: “The Lord is my helper,” etc. The dark gates are called malignant spirits because, while they are not seen through the ambushes of their concealment, they open the way of death to deceived minds. The Lord sees these dark gates because he both observes and restrains the fraudulent malice of unclean spirits. Unless he himself, seeing them, prevented them without our knowledge, our mind would know nothing of their ambushes and would perish after being caught by those same ambushes. [Col. 0883D]

We also see these dark gates when we are illuminated by the rays of the heavenly light. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “The Lord is my helper, and I will look upon my enemies.” He himself sees our enemies when, by his gift, he makes them visible to us.

## CHAPTER 234.—“They surrounded me like bees, and they burned like fire among thorns” (Ps. 117:12).

In Homily 8 on Ezekiel (no. 21), the following was added: “They surrounded me like bees,” etc. Bees have honey in their mouths and a wound in the sting of their tails. [Col. 0884A] All who flatter with their tongue but secretly strike through malice are bees, because in speaking they offer the sweetness of honey, but by striking secretly they inflict a wound.

Those who do this burn like fire among thorns, because the flame of slanderers does not consume the lives of the righteous, but burns up whatever thorns of sins may have existed in them.

## CHAPTER 235.—“The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117:22).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVIII (no. 19), the following was added: “The stone that the builders rejected,” etc. By divine grace it is now clear to all that sacred Scripture calls “the stone that became the head of the corner” the one who, receiving in himself both the Jewish people on one side and the gentile people on the other, joins the two walls in the single structure of the Church.

He is the one of whom it is written: “He made both one,” because he showed himself to be the cornerstone not only in earthly things but also in heavenly things: on earth he joined the nations of the gentiles to the people of Israel, and in heaven he joined both together with the angels. At his birth the angels cried out: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). At the birth of a king they would not have offered the joy of peace to human beings as something great if human beings had not had discord. [Col. 0884B]

King Jechoniah prefigured this stone. When Matthew described the generations in groups of fourteen, he counted Jechoniah in the second group (Matt. 1). He inserted the same person at the end of the second group of generations and again at the beginning of the third. For he was taken into Babylon with the people of Israel; and because he was carried from one place to another, he is rightly counted twice, in view of the side of each of the two walls.

The turn of this migration signifies the cornerstone. Where an order bends away from straightness so that it proceeds in another direction, it forms something like a corner. He could rightly be counted twice because, through both walls, he displayed in himself, as it were, two sides. [Col. 0884C] Thus he also aptly represented the one who, born in Judea and gathering the gentiles, came as if from Jerusalem to Babylon and, in himself, joined together by the craft of love this structure of faith, previously split by the zeal of discord.

## CHAPTER 236.—“Establish the solemn day in the dense gathering, even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. 117:27).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book IX (no. 43), the following was added: “Establish the solemn day,” etc. A person establishes a solemn day for the Lord through constant assembly when he continually afflicts himself in the desire for him. This day of solemnity is commanded to extend even to the horn of the altar, because each person must afflict himself for as long as necessary, until he reaches the height of the heavenly sacrifice and eternal joys.

## CHAPTER 237.—“Then I shall not be put to shame when I look upon all your commandments” (Ps. 118:6).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVIII (nos. 9–10), the following was added: “Then I shall not be put to shame,” etc. It must be understood that whenever anyone disagrees with the Lord’s commandments in conduct, as often as he hears them he is reproved and put to shame by his own heart, because he is reminded of what he has not done. For in whatever matter he considers himself to have erred, his own conscience silently accuses him. [Col. 0884D]

Hence the prophet David prays, saying: “Then I shall not be put to shame when I look upon all your commandments.” For everyone is gravely put to shame when, whether by reading or hearing, he looks upon the commandments of God that he has despised in living. Hence it is said in the words of John: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask, we shall receive from him” (1 John 3:21). It is as though he were saying: If we do what he commands, we shall obtain what we ask.

For these two things necessarily correspond with one another before God: prayer must be supported by conduct, and conduct by prayer. Hence Jeremiah says: “Let us examine our ways and search them out, and let us return to the Lord. Let us lift our hearts with our hands to God in heaven” (Lam. 3:21). [Col. 0885A] To examine our ways is to scrutinize the inner things of our thoughts. A person lifts his heart with his hands when he strengthens his prayer with deeds.

Whoever prays but refuses to act lifts his heart but does not lift his hands. Whoever acts but does not pray lifts his hands but does not lift his heart. Therefore, in accordance with John’s saying, the heart receives confidence in prayer when no perversity of life contradicts it.

## CHAPTER 238.—“I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways” (Ps. 118:15).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVII (no. 9), the following was added: “I will exercise myself in your commandments,” etc. It is as though he were openly promising, saying: I refuse to look at what belongs to me, because I burn with eagerness to proceed along the way of imitation through the steps of a life modeled on you.

For the person who now contradicts the present world continually directs the eyes of his heart toward the ways of his Redeemer, stirred by love, so that his mind may flee prosperity and prepare itself for adversity. Let it desire nothing that charms it; let it fear nothing that is believed capable of deterring it. Let it count sorrow as joy, and regard the joys of the present life as losses that produce sorrow. Let it not fear the losses of degradation, but through these seek a place in abiding glory. [Col. 0885B]

Truth displayed these ways to the eyes of those who follow them when he said: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26). He recalled the swelling hearts of the disciples to these ways when they were already seeking a place in glory but did not know the path to that glory, saying: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20:22). They had sought the height of his confession at his right and left, but they did not see how narrow the path to it would be. Therefore the cup of his passion, which they were to imitate, was immediately set before their eyes, so that, if they were striving toward the joys of exaltation, they might first find the way of humility.

[Note: This is not found in the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER 239.—“Likewise, from the passage above.”

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXV (no. 30). Every action that incarnate Wisdom performed temporally is a way. His ways are the patterns of life that he spread before those coming to him. He offered as many ways to those coming to him as he displayed examples of good living. [Col. 0885C] The prophet had seen the ways of his humility when he sighed, saying: “I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways.”

## CHAPTER 240.—“Do not take the word of truth altogether from my mouth” (Ps. 118:43).

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XI (no. 23), the following is added: “Do not take away…”—When a priest does not do the good things he speaks of, speech itself is also taken away from him, so that he does not dare to say what he does not practice. Hence it is said through the same prophet: “But to the sinner God says: Why do you recount my justifications and take up my covenant in your mouth?” Therefore he now prays, saying: “And do not take away from my mouth the word of truth forever.” For he considers that almighty God grants the word of truth to those who do it, and takes it away from those who do not. Thus, when he asked that it not be taken away from his mouth, what else did he seek than the grace of good works? [Col. 0885D] It is as though he were plainly saying: “Do not let me stray from good works, lest, when I lose the order of right living, I also lose the uprightness of speech.” And often a teacher who dares to teach what he neglects to do, when he ceases to speak of the good things that he disdained to practice, begins to teach his subjects the wicked things he does, so that, by the just judgment of almighty God, he no longer has even a tongue for good, since he refuses to have a good life; and thus, when his mind is inflamed with love of earthly things, he always speaks of earthly things. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart. The good man brings forth good things from his good treasure, and the evil man brings forth evil things from his evil treasure” (Matthew XII, 33). John also says: “They are of the world; therefore they speak of the world” (1 John 4:5).

## Chapter CCXLI—“My soul has languished for your salvation” (Psalm CXVIII, 81)

[Col. 0886A]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV (no. 67), the following is added: “My soul has languished for your salvation.” All who are strong in this world’s power are strong, as it were, without being wearied by their strength. But those who are strengthened by love of their Creator, the more they grow strong in their desired strength in God, the more they fail in their own strength; and the more vigorously they desire eternal things, the more healthfully they are wearied by temporal things. Therefore the Psalmist, wearied by the strength of his love, said: “My soul has languished for your salvation.” For he had languished while advancing in God’s salvation, because, seeing the light of eternity, he panted, already broken in his confidence in the flesh. Again he says: “My soul has desired and languished for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm LXXXIII, 3). When he said, “It has desired,” he rightly added, “and it has languished,” because desire for God is very weak if one’s own failing does not immediately follow it. Whoever is inflamed to desire the courts of eternity ought surely to be wearied by love of temporality, so that he grows as cold toward devotion to the world as he rises more ardently into love of God. If this desire takes hold of him perfectly, he also entirely abandons the world, and dies completely to temporal things in the same measure as he is more deeply animated toward the life above by the breath of eternity.

Had she not found herself wearied in her own strength when she said: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song V, 6)? For when the mind is touched by the inspiration of hidden speech, weakened from the state of its own strength, it melts in the very desire by which it is absorbed; and it finds itself weary within itself precisely because it sees that it has gone beyond itself in the strength it has climbed toward. Hence, when the prophet said that he had seen a vision of God, he added: “I fainted and was sick for many days” (Daniel VIII, 27), because, when the mind is bound to the power of God, the flesh is wearied of its own strength (Genesis XXXII).
