Hence Jacob, who held the angel, immediately limped on one foot, because whoever looks upon exalted things with true love no longer knows how to walk in this world with divided desires. He leans on one foot who is strengthened by the love of God alone, and it is necessary that the other wither, because, as the strength of the mind increases, the strength of the flesh must undoubtedly grow numb.

[Note: [Col. 0886D] This chapter is not found in the manuscripts.]

## Chapter CCXLII—“I opened my mouth and drew in the breath” (Psalm CXVIII, 131)

In Homily 9 on Ezekiel (no. 28), the following is added: “I opened my mouth, etc.”—For he would not draw in the breath unless he opened his mouth; and unless he devoted himself to preaching to his neighbors, the grace of spiritual teaching would not have increased in him.

## Chapter CCXLIII—“The wicked have told me tales, but not like your law, O Lord” (Psalm CXVIII, 83)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VII (nos. 15–17), the following is added: “The wicked have told me tales, but not like your law, O Lord.” Often the words of worldly people, when they thrust themselves importunately upon our ears, give rise to a battle of temptations in the heart. And although reason rejects them and the tongue rebukes them, nevertheless what is judged outwardly with authority is overcome within only with difficulty. Therefore it is necessary that what my vigilant mind repels from the entrance of thought should not even reach my ears.

Thus holy men, when they pant for the desires of eternity, raise themselves to such a height of life that they regard hearing what belongs to the world as a heavy and burdensome weight. They consider whatever does not sound like what they love inwardly to be exceedingly alien and intolerable. But often the mind is already carried upward by desire, already completely separated from the foolish speech of earthly people, yet it is not still girded, for the sake of love of truth, to endure the sufferings of the present life. It already desires heavenly things and already despises the foolishness of what is below. Yet it has not sufficiently directed itself toward enduring adversity; rather, the mind of the just often extends itself to such a summit of virtue [Col. 0887A] that it both presides within itself from the stronghold of inward reason and, by patiently enduring, converts the foolishness of certain people outside.

For when we strive to draw people toward strength, we must necessarily tolerate their weaknesses, since no one raises up the fallen unless, through compassion, he bends from the uprightness of his own position. But when we have compassion on another’s weakness, our own strength is reinforced more powerfully, so that, through love of future things, the mind prepares itself for present adversities and awaits the bodily sufferings it feared. For as heavenly desires increase, the mind is constricted. And when it considers how great is the sweetness of the eternal homeland, it ardently loves the bitterness of the present life for its sake.

By these bonds of divine law—that is, of heavenly commandments—whoever now removes his ear from the suggestions of the wicked raises himself to what is above, suspending his attention in the secrecy of heavenly desire, from which it cannot be torn away.

## Chapter CCXLIV—“Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Psalm CXVIII, 96)

In Homily 14 on Ezekiel (no. 15), the following is added: [Col. 0887B] “Your commandment is exceedingly broad.” Nothing is broader than to receive everyone into the bosom of love and to endure no narrowness of hatred. For charity is so broad that, in the expansiveness of its love, it can contain even enemies. Hence it is commanded: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke VI, 27).

[Note: [Col. 0887D] It is not found in the manuscripts. We say the same about the following.]

## Chapter CCXLV—“I understood more than the elders” (Psalm CXVIII, 100)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XI (no. 24), the following is added: “I understood more than the elders.” The teaching of the elders was taken away after the youthful Church received it from the Gentiles. Because the Church held it by putting it into practice, it showed how it understood more than the elders when it immediately added, saying: “Because I sought your commandments.” Since it devoted itself to fulfilling in action what it had learned, it received understanding of what it was to teach.

## Chapter CCXLVI—“I will rejoice over your words, as one who has found great spoils” (Psalm CXVIII, 162)

[Col. 0887C]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII (no. 25), the following is added: “I will rejoice over your words, etc.”—These are called spoils because, when the Gentiles passed over to the faith of the Lord, the Jews were stripped of the sacred utterances with which they had been clothed.

## Chapter CCXLVII—“Let your hand come to save me” (Psalm CXVIII, 137)

In Homily 2 on Ezekiel (no. 7), the following is added: “Let your hand come, etc.”—The hand or arm of the Lord is called the Son, because through him all things were made. But what does it mean when it says, “Let your hand come”? The hand of God, which through divinity was not made but begotten, was made through humanity, so that it might heal the wounds of the human race.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] It is absent from the manuscripts.]

## Chapter CCXLVIII—“Depart from me, you evildoers, and I will examine the commandments of my God” (Psalm CXVIII, 115)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVI (no. 23), the following is added: “Depart from me, you evildoers, etc.”—Often, when we apply ourselves to the sacred utterances, we endure the snares of wicked spirits more severely, because they scatter the dust of earthly thoughts over our minds, so that they obscure the eyes of our attention from the light of inward vision. The Psalmist had endured this when he said: “Depart from me, you evildoers, and I will examine the commandments of my God,” plainly indicating that he could not scrutinize God’s commandments while he was enduring the snares of wicked spirits in his mind.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] In the Mich. codex it is said to have been taken from a homily on Ezekiel, but the number is not given; nowhere have we seen it. [Col. 0888D]]

## Chapter CCXLIX—“It is vain for you to rise before the light; rise after you have sat down” (Psalm CXXVI, 3)

A homily on Ezekiel adds: “It is vain for you to rise before the light, etc.”—In certain passages of sacred utterance, only the allegory is to be sought, and the words of the literal text are to be set aside entirely. To mention one of many examples, the Psalmist says: “It is vain for you to rise before the light.” If someone wishes to understand this according to the letter, he contradicts the nighttime praises of God. And how does the same Prophet speak when he says: “At midnight I rose to confess to you” (Psalm CXVIII, 62)? If it is vain to rise before the light, why did he rise at midnight to confess to the Lord? But the one rises before the light who, before the day of the age to come, desires to be raised up and make progress in this life, which resembles night.

## Chapter CCL—“The same as above”

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII (no. 80)—To rise before the light means to rejoice in the night of the present life before the brightness of eternal recompense appears. Therefore one must first sit down, so that afterward one may rise rightly, because whoever does not voluntarily humble himself now will by no means be exalted by the glory that follows.

[Note: [Col. 0888D] The next seven chapters are not found in the manuscripts.]

## Chapter CCLI—“When he gives sleep to his beloved, this is the inheritance of the Lord” (Psalm CXXV, 4)

[Col. 0888B]

In Homily 27 on the Gospels (no. 5), the following is added: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, etc.”—Therefore, whoever has already come to know eternal things should regard temporal fruits as worthless in his mind. Let us produce such fruits as remain, which, when death destroys everything, themselves take their beginning from death. For that God’s fruit begins from death is testified by the Prophet, who says: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, this is the inheritance of the Lord.” Everyone who sleeps in death has lost his inheritance. But “when he gives sleep to his beloved, this is the inheritance of the Lord,” because God’s elect, after they have reached death, then find their inheritance.

## Chapter CCLII—“He who trusts in the Lord is like Mount Zion” (Psalm CLII, 1)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIII (no. 2), the following is added: “He who trusts in the Lord, etc.”—For Zion is said to mean “watchtower,” by which watchfulness the Church, contemplating God, is signified.

## Chapter CCLIII—“But coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm CXXV, 6)

[Col. 0888C]

When the barren labor of wicked people was being discussed, the exposition of Blessed Job, book VII (no. 38), adds: “But coming, they will come with rejoicing, etc.”—Those who carry nothing with them from the fruit of their labor walk in vain. One sweats to obtain honors, another burns with eagerness to multiply possessions, another pants to win praise. But since each person abandons all these things when he dies, he has wasted his labors in vain, because he has brought nothing with him before the Judge.

In contrast, the Law rightly says: “You shall not appear empty before the Lord” (Exodus XXIII, 15). Whoever does not provide for the reward of life by doing good appears empty before the Lord. Hence the Psalmist says of the just: “But coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.” Those who carry sheaves to the examination of judgment come bearing within themselves the righteous works by which they may merit life.

## Chapter CCLIV—“Going, they went and wept, sowing their seeds” (Psalm CXXV, 6)

[Col. 0888D]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book X (no. 36), the following is added: “Going, they went, etc.”—Hope in God rises more solidly in proportion as each person has endured more grievous things for him, because the joy of recompense from eternity is not gathered unless it is first sown here through devout tribulation. Since it is now sown through tribulation so that afterward the fruit of joy may be reaped, confidence strengthens the mind all the more as stronger affliction constricts it for the sake of truth.

## Chapter CCLV—“May the Lord guard your entrance and your exit” (Psalm CXX, 6)

In Homily 1, book II, on Ezekiel (no. 16), the following is added: “May the Lord guard your entrance, etc.”—The Lord guards the entrance of each soul, by which it enters into faith, and also its exit, by which it goes forth to the vision, so that neither, upon entering the Church, is it overthrown by errors, nor, when going from this temporal life to the eternal, is it snatched away by the ancient enemy.

Concerning this exit of ours, which we ought daily to meditate upon in our minds, Paul also speaks of our Redeemer, saying: “To sanctify the people through his own blood, he suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we do not have here a lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” (Hebrews XIII, 12).

## Chapter CCLVI—“Sinners have built upon my back” (Psalm CXXVIII, 3)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIII (no. 1), the following is added: “Sinners have built upon my back.” It is usually characteristic of the perverse that they heap their own evils upon the good by reproach before they themselves are truly accused of them. And while they fear being rebuked for what they do, they assert that those who oppose their wickedness do these same things.

Holy men patiently hear even what they do not remember ever having done, although they know that the evils being thrust upon them have been perpetrated by the very people who accuse them. When they cannot correct such people by preaching, they endure them by suffering, so that, if they cannot obtain the fruit of their conversion, they may nevertheless gain from them the reward of long-suffering.

Hence the holy Church says in the words of the prophet David: “Sinners have built upon my back,” because, while it tolerates heretics or any other reprobates whom it cannot correct, it carries the deeds of sinners upon its back.

## Chapter CCLVII—“The same as above”

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part II (chapter 10)—We bear burdens upon our back. Therefore he complains that sinners have built upon his back, as though he were plainly saying: “Those whom I cannot correct I carry as a burden laid upon me.”

## Chapter CCLVIII—“Let them become like the grass of buildings, which withers before it is plucked up” (Psalm CXXVIII, 6)

[Col. 0889C]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII (no. 68), the following is added: “Let them become like the grass of buildings, etc.”—The Psalmist expresses this concerning the person of hypocrites. Grass on a building grows high, but is not at all secured by a deep root; so the hypocrite is seen to do lofty things, but is not strengthened in them by purity of heart. This grass withers quickly even before it is plucked up, because the hypocrite still exists in the present life and already loses, as it were, the appearance of greenness, that is, the works of holiness. Since he strove to do good without the intention of right thinking, by losing these things he shows that he flourished without a root.

[Note: [Col. 0889D] The two following chapters are not found in the manuscripts.]

## Chapter CCLIX—“I have not walked in great things, nor in wonders beyond me” (Psalm CXXX, 1)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII (no. 25), the following is added: “I have not walked in great things, etc.”—He stretches his foot toward a precipice who does not attend to the limit of his capacities. David therefore rightly kept the foot of his heart within the measures granted by divine generosity when he said: “I have not walked in great things, nor in wonders beyond me.” He would walk beyond himself in great things if he sought to appear greater than he could be. He is lifted beyond himself in wonders who strives to appear capable even in things for which he himself is insufficient.

## Chapter CCLX—“Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm CXXXI, 9)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIV (no. 42), the following is added: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.”—Righteousness is the glory of each person. Just as clothing protects from cold, so righteousness protects from death. Therefore righteousness is not inappropriately compared with clothing when the Prophet says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.”

## Chapter CCLXI—“Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments” (Psalm CXXXVI, 2)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIII (no. 11), the following is added: “Upon the willows, etc.”—What is signified here by the barrenness of the willows except the life of sinners? For if this were not so, the Psalmist would never have said in the voice of preachers against Babylon: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments.” Willows are described as existing in the midst of Babylon because all the unfruitful, and those alienated from love of the heavenly homeland, are rooted with all the inward parts of their hearts in the confusion of this world.

Hence holy preachers do not play their instruments among these willows, but hang them up, because when they see unfruitful and reprobate minds, they do not display the power of their preaching but rather, in mourning, keep silent.

## Chapter CCLXII—“Lay it waste, lay it waste, down to its foundation” (Psalm CXXXVI, 7)

[Col. 0890B]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXV (no. 27), the following is added: “Lay it waste, etc.”—Those who disdain to preserve works worthy of faith also lose the faith they appeared to possess. Concerning such people, the prophet, under the figure of Jerusalem, recalls the words of enemies who destroy, saying: “Lay it waste, lay it waste, down to its foundation.”

Paul says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians III, 11). The enemies therefore destroy Jerusalem down to its foundation and lay it waste when wicked spirits, after first destroying the building of good works in the hearts of the faithful, also drain away the solidity of their religion. For just as a structure is built upon a foundation, so works are built upon faith. Therefore to lay waste down to the foundation is, after overthrowing the work of right living, also to dissipate the strength of faith.

## Chapter CCLXIII—“As is his darkness, so also is his light” (Psalm CXXXVIII, 12)

[Col. 0890C]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book V (no. 2), the following is added: “As is his darkness, etc.”—In sacred Scripture, prosperity is sometimes signified by the name of light, while adversity in this world is signified by the name of night. Hence the Psalmist says: “As is his darkness, so also is his light.” Because holy men trample upon the prosperity of the world just as they endure its adversity by trampling upon it, they lay both the world’s adversities and its prosperities beneath them through the great elevation of their minds, saying: “As is his darkness, so also is his light.” It is as though they were saying more plainly: “Just as its gloomy things do not press down the strength of our purpose, so its flattering things do not corrupt it.”

[Note: [Col. 0890D] It is not contained in the manuscripts.]

## Chapter CCLXIV—“And night is my illumination in my delights” (Psalm CXXXVIII, 11)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVI (no. 24), the following is added: “And night is my illumination in my delights.”—When the diligent mind is refreshed by mystical understanding, the darkness of the present life is already illuminated within it by the radiance of the day that follows, so that even amid the gloom of this corruption the power of the future light breaks forth into understanding; and, nourished by the delights of words, it learns by anticipation what it will hunger for from the food of truth.

## Chapter CCLXV—“Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored by me; their rule has been exceedingly strengthened” (Psalm CXXXVIII, 17)

In Homily 27 on the Gospels (no. 4), the following is added: “Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored by me.”—A friend is so called as a guardian of the mind. Since the Psalmist saw that God’s elect were separated from love of this world and guarded God’s will in heavenly commandments, he marveled at God’s friends, saying: “Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored by me.” And as though we might immediately ask him to explain to us the reasons for such great honor, he at once added: “Their rule has been exceedingly strengthened.”

Behold: God’s elect subdue the flesh, strengthen the spirit, command demons, shine with virtues, despise present things, proclaim the eternal homeland by voice and conduct, love it even by dying, and reach it through torments; they can be killed, but cannot be bent. “Their rule has therefore been exceedingly strengthened.” In this very suffering by which they fell into the death of the flesh, see how great was the summit of the mind. Whence did this come, unless because their rule was strengthened?

But perhaps only a few are so great. Therefore he added: “I will number them, and they will be multiplied beyond the sand.” Brothers, look upon the whole world: it is full of martyrs. We who see are now scarcely as numerous as the witnesses of the truth. They are countable to God but multiplied for us beyond the sand, because their number cannot be grasped by us.

But whoever reaches this dignity, that he is called a friend of God, should look upon himself, but regard the gifts he receives as being above himself. Let him attribute nothing to his own merits, lest he break out into enmity.

## Chapter CCLXVI—“Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away over your enemies? With perfect hatred I hated them, and they became enemies to me” (Psalm XXXVIII, 21)

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 22, admonition 23), the following is added: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, etc.”—To hate God’s enemies with perfect hatred means both to love what they have become and to rebuke what they do; to restrain the conduct of the wicked and to benefit their life. For one must consider, when rebuke is withheld, how great a fault it is if peace is maintained with the worst people, since so great a Prophet offered to God as a sacrifice what he raised against himself for the Lord: the hostility of the wicked.

## Chapter CCLXVII—“The labor of their lips will cover them” (Psalm CXXXIX, 10)

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 11, admonition 12), the following is added: “The labor of their lips will cover them.”—Nothing is safer for defense than purity, and nothing easier to say than truth. For while he tries to defend his deceit, his heart is wearied by harsh labor. Hence it is written: “The labor of their lips will cover them.” For what now fills him will then cover him, because what now exhausts his mind through flattering restlessness will then press upon him through harsh recompense.

Hence Jeremiah says: “They have taught their tongues to speak lies; they have labored to act wickedly” (Jeremiah IX, 9). It is as though he were plainly saying: Those who could have been friends of truth without labor labor in order to sin; and, since they refuse to live simply, they compel themselves through labors to die.

[Note: [Col. 0891D] It is not found in the manuscripts.]

## Chapter CCLXVIII—“Shelter my head on the day of battle” (Psalm CXXXIX, 3)

When the nourishment of the word of God was being discussed, the exposition of Blessed Job, book VI (no. 44), adds: “Shelter my head on the day of battle.”—We suffer battle when we are attacked by the temptations of our flesh. Concerning this battle the Prophet says: “Shelter my head on the day of battle.” Since the reprobate, while they waste away from hunger for the word, are also pierced by the sword of battle, the Lord rescues his elect from death in famine and hides them from the sword in battle, because, while he refreshes their minds with the nourishment of his word, he makes them strong against the temptations of the body.

## Chapter CCLXIX—“They will not endure in miseries” (Psalm CXXXIX, 11)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book II (no. 28), the following is added: “They will not endure in miseries.”—The Psalmist testifies here concerning the impatience of the reprobate under scourges, because they would endure in miseries if they bore adversities with equanimity. But after they collapse in mind amid the scourges, they lose, as it were, the steadfastness of enduring amid the miseries inflicted upon them.

## Chapter CCLXX—“The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm CXL, 2)

[Col. 0892A]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XX (no. 3), the following is added: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice.”—Because our Redeemer, near the end of the world, endured the violence of his persecutors, he offered himself for us as an evening sacrifice.

## Chapter CCLXXI—“Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint over my lips” (Psalm CXL, 3)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VII (no. 61), the following is added: “Set, O Lord, etc.”—The tongue must be carefully restrained under the balance of great moderation, not bound insolubly, lest, either loosened, it slide into vice, or, restricted, it grow numb even with respect to usefulness. The Psalmist rightly considered this and embraced it in a brief petition, saying: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint over my lips.”

A door is opened and closed. Therefore, by asking for a door rather than placing an obstacle before his mouth, he plainly taught [Col. 0892B] that the tongue should both be held back by discipline and loosened when necessity requires, so that a discerning mouth may open its voice at the proper time and, in turn, close it with appropriate silence.

Hence a certain writer says: “The wise man will be silent until the proper time” (Sirach XX, 7), so that, when he recognizes the appropriate moment, setting aside the discipline of silence, he may devote himself to saying what is suitable for useful purposes. Solomon likewise says: “A time to be silent and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes III, 7). The times must be weighed with discerning alternation, lest, when the tongue ought to be restrained, it uselessly release itself through words, or, when it can speak profitably, it sluggishly restrain itself.

## Chapter CCLXXII—“But let the oil of the sinner not make my head fat” (Psalm CXL, 5)

In Homily 12 on the Gospels (no. 3), the following is added: “But let the oil of the sinner not make my head fat.”—What is called the head except the mind, which rules the body? The oil of the sinner therefore makes the head fat when the favor of a flatterer caresses the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0891D] Absent from the manuscripts.]

## Chapter CCLXXIII—“Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Psalm CXLIII, 1)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XV (no. 43), the following is added: “Blessed be the Lord my God, etc.”—By the hands he signifies action, and by the fingers, discernment.

## Chapter CCLXXIV—“My protector, and in him I will hope, subjecting my people under me” (Psalm CLIII, 2)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVI (no. 84), the following is added: “My protector, and in him I will hope, etc.”—Peoples are subjected to holy minds when, through the presence of strict severity, foolish thoughts leap away from them, so that they do not carry them off over the precipices of fantasies, but, subjected to reason, rest humbly in the heart.

## Chapter CCLXXV—“Lord, incline your heavens and descend; touch the mountains, and they will smoke” (Psalm CXLIII, 5)

[Col. 0892D]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXX (no. 48), the following is added: “Lord, incline your heavens, etc.”—What is signified by the name of the heavens except the order of preachers? Unless holy preachers descended from that immensity of inward contemplation which they grasp to our weakness through the humblest preaching, as though by a kind of inclination, they would never beget children in the faith.

They could not benefit us if they persisted in the erectness of their own height. For if holy men wished to preach to us the things they grasp while they are intoxicated with heavenly contemplation, and did not temper their knowledge with a certain moderation and sobriety, who could contain, in the narrow bosom of understanding, those streams of the heavenly fountain?

Hence it is rightly said: “Lord, incline your heavens and descend.” For when the heavens are inclined, the Lord descends, because when holy teachers draw themselves down in their preaching, they pour the knowledge of divinity into our hearts. The Lord would in no way descend to us if his preachers remained inflexible in the rigor of contemplation. The heavens are therefore inclined so that the Lord may descend, because, if they did not accommodate themselves to our weakness, they would never raise us to their own height.

[Note: [Col. 0892D] Utic. reads: “they desire.”]

## Chapter CCLXXVI—“You who delivered your servant David from the evil sword” (Psalm CXLIII, 10)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIV (no. 17), the following is added: “You who delivered your servant David from the evil sword.”—What is expressed in this passage by the evil sword except the anger or persuasion of the wicked enemy? The sword of holy preaching is benevolent: we are struck by it so that we may die to sin. But the sword of the devil’s persuasion is evil: each person is struck by it wickedly so that he may be extinguished from the life of uprightness.

For that man, condemned at that time and taken up for the ancient enemy’s service, is his sword. Through the malice of deceit the enemy puts him forward and pierces the hearts of the weak.

## Chapter CCLXXVII—“On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Psalm CXLV, 4)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book X (no. 41), the following is added: “On that day all their thoughts will perish.”—Because they will find that eternal evils were never considered, and suddenly lose the temporal goods which they held for a long time by dwelling upon them.

## Chapter CCLXXVIII—“But he humbles sinners down to the earth” (Psalm CXLVI, 6)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXV (no. 20), the following is added: “But he humbles sinners down to the earth.”—What greater humiliation can there be than, abandoning the Creator, to seek the creature; abandoning heavenly joys, to long for things below? For, having lost heavenly things, everything they thirst for is earthly; and while they try to see more, what they desire is less.

Of such people Jeremiah says: “Those who depart from you will be written in the earth” (Jeremiah XVII, 13). But of the elect: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20).

## Chapter CCLXXIX—“Who brings forth grass on the mountains and plants for the service of human beings” (Psalm CXLV, 8)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX (no. 52), the following is added: “Who brings forth grass on the mountains, etc.”—What is signified here by plants except the sustenance of preachers, when it says: “Who brings forth grass on the mountains and plants for the service of human beings”? Grass and plants are brought forth on the mountains for the service of human beings when the exalted people of this world, called to the knowledge of faith, temporarily supply nourishment to the holy preachers who spiritually serve them on the journey of this life.

## Chapter CCLXXX—“Who gives their food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him” (Psalm CXLVI, 9)

[Col. 0893D]

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXX (nos. 28–29), the following is added: “Who gives their food to the beasts, etc.”—The beasts receive food when minds that were formerly brutish are satisfied with the nourishment of sacred Scripture. Food is given to the young ravens—that is, to the children of the Gentiles—when their desire is refreshed by our way of life.

This raven was food when the holy Church itself was seeking him, but now he receives food because he himself seeks out others for conversion. His young—that is, the preachers sprung from him—do not presume upon themselves but upon the strength of their Redeemer. Hence it is rightly said: “And to the young ravens that call upon him.” For they know that they can do nothing by their own power. And although they hunger for the gain of souls with devout prayers, they nevertheless desire that these things be accomplished by him who works everything inwardly.

For they grasp in true faith that “neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Corinthians III, 7).

## Chapter CCLXXXI—“He will send his word and melt them; his spirit will blow, and the waters will flow” (Psalm CXLVII, 18)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVII (no. 53), the following is added: “He will send his word, etc.”—By these waters he signifies those who run toward him. For waters flow from ice, because many great preachers arise from harsh persecutors. Ice therefore melts into water when the numbness of inward cold is changed into the irrigation of preaching.

Was Paul not ice, who, after receiving letters, was going to Damascus (Acts IX, 2) and sought to restrain the seeds of the word, cast in the hearts of the faithful as in God’s earth, lest they rise to the perfection of works? But this ice returned to water, because those whom he had previously striven to oppress by persecution he afterward drenched with streams of holy exhortation, so that a harvest might arise [Col. 0894B] all the more abundant in the elect as God’s rain also watered it from the mouth of a persecutor.

[Note: [Col. 0893D] In all our manuscripts it reads “[lacuna] exsurgeret”; but “messis” [“harvest”] should be read, as in the designated place in the *Moralia*. [Col. 0894D]]

[Note: [Col. 0894D] The [uncertain: T[lacuna]la] chapters that follow are missing from the manuscripts.]

## Chapter CCLXXXII—“He established a commandment, and it will not pass away” (Psalm CXLVIII, 6)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVI (no. 46), the following is added: “He established a commandment, etc.”—Because once fixed, God’s judgments cannot in any way be changed. Therefore, when the sentence appears to be changed outwardly, the inward plan is not changed, because, concerning each matter, whatever is carried out outwardly in a changeable manner is established inwardly with unchanging firmness.

## Chapter CCLXXXIII—“He will announce the power of his works to his people, to give them the inheritance of the nations” (Psalm CX, 6)

In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII (no. 14), the following is added: “He will announce the power of his works to his people, etc.”—It is as though he were plainly saying: For this reason he reveals the strength of his action, so that the one who hears him may grow rich in gifts.

## Chapter CCLXXXIV—“The saints will exult in glory; they will rejoice in their resting places” (Psalm CXLIX, 5)

In the exposition of blessed Job, book VIII (no. 41), the following is added: “The saints will exult in glory, etc.” —Because, when evils flee from without, they rejoice securely within the secret places of their minds. But then the joy of their hearts will be perfect, when there is no longer any struggle of the flesh from without. For as long as the flesh entices—for it is as though the wall of our house were being shaken—the bedroom too is disturbed.

### CHAPTER CCLXXXV

“Praise him in his mighty deeds; praise him according to the abundance of his greatness” (Ps. 150:2).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book IX (no. 19), the following is added: “Praise him in his mighty deeds, etc.” —We truly accomplish the works of divine strength when we recognize that we cannot accomplish them. We speak more eloquently when, overcome with wonder at these things, we remain silent. For in recounting the works of God, our weakness has a tongue that can express itself sufficiently: what it is not capable of comprehending adequately, it praises adequately by remaining silent. Hence the Psalmist rightly says here: “Praise him in his mighty deeds; praise him according to the abundance of his greatness.” For that person praises God according to the abundance of his greatness who considers himself unequal to completing his praise.

### CHAPTER CCLXXXVI

“Praise him with the tambourine and the choir” (Ps. 150:4).

In Homily 8 on Ezekiel (no. 8), the following is added: “Praise him with the tambourine and the choir.” —The greatness of the virtue of harmony is shown when it is demonstrated that the other virtues do not exist without it. Abstinence is indeed a great virtue; but if someone abstains from food in such a way that he judges others in the matter of eating, and even condemns among the faithful the foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving, what has the virtue of abstinence become for him except a snare of guilt? Therefore the Psalmist, indicating that there is no virtue of abstinence without harmony, says: “Praise him with the tambourine and the choir.” In the tambourine, dry hide resounds; in the choir, voices sing in harmony. What, then, is signified by the tambourine except abstinence, and by the choir except the harmony of charity? Whoever therefore abstains in such a way as to abandon harmony praises indeed with the tambourine, but does not praise with the choir.

### CHAPTER CCLXXXVII

Likewise, on the passage above.

[Col. 0896A]

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 22, admonition 23). —Often some people receive particular gifts, but while they grow proud, they lose the gift of harmony, which is greater. Thus, for example, someone may subdue his flesh more than others by restraining his appetite, yet, through his abstinence, disdain to be in harmony with those whom he surpasses. But whoever separates abstinence from harmony should consider what the Psalmist admonishes; for he says: “Praise him with the tambourine and the choir.” In the tambourine, a dry skin resounds when struck; in the choir, voices agree through fellowship. Therefore whoever afflicts his body but abandons harmony certainly praises God with the tambourine, but does not praise him with the choir.

## BOOK TWELVE: On Testimonies in Proverbs

[Col. 0895]

### CHAPTER I

“With the simple is his conversation” (Prov. 3:32).

[Col. 0895B]

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 11, admonition 12), the following is added: “With the simple is his conversation.” —For God’s conversing is his revealing hidden things to human minds through the illumination of his presence. He is therefore said to converse with the simple because he illumines with the ray of his gift the minds of those whom no shadow of duplicity darkens.

[Note: [Col. 0895] Thus in the manuscripts of Sag., Utic., etc., although at the indicated passage we read “of his visitation.”]

### CHAPTER II

“The path of the righteous proceeds like shining light and grows until the perfect day” (Prov. 4:18).

In Homily 5 on Ezekiel (no. 5), the following is added: “The path of the righteous, etc.” —For in their souls the good desire and understanding of the inner light are already a part of the day. But because they advance in virtue until the end of life, they come to the perfect day when, having been brought to the heavenly kingdoms, they will lack nothing of that light which they desire.

### CHAPTER III

“Guard your heart with every care, because from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4:23).

[Col. 0895C]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (no. 33), the following is added: “Guard your heart with every care, etc.” —When he was about to say “with care,” he first added “every,” so that each person might examine himself carefully on every side. And as long as he is in this life, he should know that he has been placed in battle against spiritual enemies, lest he lose through other actions the reward he gathers through these, lest the enemy block the entrance on one side and open an approach from another. For if a city were strongly fortified against ambushing enemies by a great rampart, enclosed with strong walls, and protected by sleepless watchfulness, but one single opening in it were negligently left unguarded, through that opening the enemy would undoubtedly enter—the enemy who seemed to have been excluded on every side.

### CHAPTER IV

Likewise, on the passage above.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book I (no. 49). —It is therefore fitting that we carefully examine the virtues we practice from the origin of our intention, lest they arise from an evil source, even if what is displayed is right.

### CHAPTER V

“Let your eyelids precede your steps” (Prov. 4:25).

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 15, admonition 16), the following is added: “Let your eyelids precede your steps.” The eyelids precede the steps when right counsels come before our actions. For whoever neglects to foresee through reflection what he is doing advances while closing his eyes. He completes his journey by moving forward, but does not precede himself by looking ahead; and therefore he falls more quickly, because he does not consider through the eyelid of counsel where he ought to place the foot of his action.

### CHAPTER VI

“My son, attend to my wisdom and incline your ear to my prudence, so that you may guard your thoughts” (Prov. 5:1).

[Col. 0896B]

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 14, admonition 15), the following is added: “My son, attend to my wisdom, etc.” —Nothing in us is more fleeting than the heart, which departs from us as often as it flows away through wicked thoughts. Hence the Psalmist says: “My heart has forsaken me” (Ps. 39:13). Returning to himself, he says: “Your servant has found his heart, so that he may pray to you” (2 Sam. 7:27). When, therefore, thought is restrained by watchfulness, the heart, which was accustomed to flee, is found.

Often, however, people who are excessively silent, when they suffer some injustices, fall into sharper pain precisely because they do not speak of what they endure. For if they were to describe the troubles inflicted upon them in the calm speech of their tongue, the pain would flow out from their conscience. Wounds that are closed cause greater torment. When the corruption boiling within is expelled, the pain is opened for healing.

### CHAPTER VII

“Do not give your honor to strangers, nor your years to the cruel one, lest strangers be filled with your strength and your labors be in another’s house; and you groan in the end, when you have consumed your flesh and your body” (Prov. 5:9 ff.).

[Col. 0896C]

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 12, admonition 13), the following is added: “Do not give your honor to strangers, etc.” —Who are those alien to us except the evil spirits, who have been separated from the lot of the heavenly homeland? And what is our honor except that, although we have been formed in earthly bodies, we were nevertheless created in the image and likeness of our Creator? Or who else is the cruel one except that apostate angel who, through pride, struck himself with the punishment of death and, though ruined, did not spare the human race from inflicting death upon it?

Therefore he gives his honor to strangers who, having been created in the image and likeness of God, administers the time of his life according to the will of evil spirits. He gives his years to the cruel one who spends the allotted span of his life according to the will of the wicked ruler, his adversary. Hence it is rightly added: “Lest strangers be filled with your strength and your labors be in another’s house.” Whoever, through the bodily health granted to him and the wisdom bestowed upon him, labors not to exercise the virtues of his mind but to commit vices, multiplies not his own household through his strength, but the dwellings of strangers—that is, of unclean spirits—acting either through lust or through pride, so that, with himself added, the number of the lost may increase.

It is rightly added: “And you groan in the end, when you have consumed your flesh and your body.” Often the health received by the flesh is spent on vices; but when it is suddenly withdrawn, when the flesh is worn down by sufferings, and when the soul is already being compelled to depart, the health long possessed for evil living is sought as though for good living. Then people groan because they were unwilling to serve God, when by serving they can in no way recover the losses caused by their negligence.

### CHAPTER VIII

“Drink water from your cistern and flowing water from your well. Let your springs flow outward, and divide your waters in the streets. Keep them for yourself alone, and let strangers not share them with you” (Prov. 5:15 ff.).

In the commentary on Ezekiel, Homily 13 (no. 12), the following is added: “Drink water from your cistern, etc.” —What he says appears highly contradictory: “Let your springs flow outward, and divide your waters in the streets,” while he immediately adds: “Keep them for yourself alone, and let strangers not share them with you.” For how can he possess the water of knowledge alone if he divides it in the streets? How are strangers not sharers in his waters if his springs flow outward?

But when we preach among the people, we plainly divide waters in the streets, because we spread the words of knowledge among a multitude of hearers. [Col. 0897B] But when, with divine grace helping us, we guard ourselves inwardly, and cautiously watch lest evil spirits—who are truly strangers to us because they have lost the lot of blessedness—steal upon us through elation, we possess alone the waters that we divide in the streets, so that strangers may not share them with us. These are the ones of whom it is written: “Strangers have risen up against me, and the mighty have sought my life” (Ps. 53:5).

Therefore he both divides waters in the streets and possesses them alone who, through what he preaches to many, does not exalt himself in the temporary thought of glory. For a person possesses what he teaches when he rejoices not in becoming known but in being useful.

### CHAPTER IX

Likewise, on the passage above.

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 24, admonition 25). —A preacher drinks water from his cistern when, returning to his heart, he first hears for himself what he says. He drinks the flowing water of his well when he is filled by the irrigation of his own word. Hence it is rightly added: “Let your springs flow outward, and divide your waters in the streets.” It is right that he should drink first himself, and then, by preaching, flow into others.

To make springs flow outward is to pour the power of preaching into others externally; to divide waters in the streets is to distribute the divine words among a great multitude of hearers, according to the condition of each person. And because the desire for empty glory often steals in while the word of God runs to the knowledge of many, after it has been said, “Divide your waters in the streets,” it is rightly added: “Keep them for yourself alone, and let strangers not share them with you.”

He calls evil spirits strangers; of them the voice of a tempted person says through the Prophet: “Strangers have risen up against me, and the mighty have sought my life” (Ps. 53:5). He says, therefore: “Divide your waters in the streets, and yet drink alone.” As though he were saying more plainly: If it is necessary for you to serve preaching outwardly, take care that you do not join yourself to unclean spirits through elation, lest you admit your enemies as sharers with you in the ministry of the divine word. We therefore divide waters in the streets and nevertheless possess them alone when we spread preaching widely outwardly, yet do not strive through it in the least to obtain human praise.

### CHAPTER X

“My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have bound your hand to a stranger; you have been ensnared by the words of your mouth and caught by your own speech. Do therefore what I tell you, my son, and free yourself, because you have fallen into the hand of your neighbor. Run, hasten, rouse your friend; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids” (Prov. 6:6 ff.).

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 4, admonition 5), the following is added: “My son, if you have become surety for your friend, etc.” —To become surety for a friend is to take responsibility for another’s soul at the risk of one’s own conduct. Hence the hand is also bound to a stranger, because the mind is bound to the care of a solicitude that was previously lacking.

He has been ensnared by the words of his mouth and caught by his own speech because, when he is compelled to speak good things to those entrusted to him, he must first keep what he has said himself. He is therefore ensnared by the words of his mouth when, as reason demands, he is constrained not to relax his life into anything other than what he admonishes. Hence before the strict Judge he is compelled to fulfill in his deeds as much as it is clear that he has commanded others by his voice.

Thus the exhortation rightly follows at once: “Do therefore what I tell you, my son, and free yourself, because you have fallen into the hands of your neighbor. Run, hasten, rouse your friend; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids.” Whoever is placed before others as an example for living is admonished not only to remain watchful himself but also to rouse his friend. For it is not enough for him to remain watchful by living well [Note: [Col. 0897] So the Sagiensis and Michaelian manuscripts; but in the Uticensis and Gemetensis: “if he does not also separate the one under his authority from the torpor of sin.”] if he does not also separate from the torpor of sin the person over whom he presides.

It is rightly said: “Do not give sleep to your eyes.” To give sleep to one’s eyes is, when attention has ceased, to neglect entirely the care of one’s subjects. The eyelids slumber when our thoughts, which recognize what ought to be reproved in our subjects, conceal it under the weight of sluggishness. To sleep fully is to be unaware of the actions of those entrusted to us and not to correct them. Not to sleep but to slumber is to recognize what ought indeed to be reproved, yet, because of weariness of mind, not to amend it through appropriate reprimands. Through slumbering, the eye is led to deepest sleep, because when the person in authority often fails to cut away the evil he recognizes, he eventually reaches, through the merit of his negligence, the point at which he does not even recognize what his subordinates are doing wrong.

### CHAPTER XI

“How long will you sleep, sluggard?” (Prov. 6:10).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book VI (no. 20), the following is added: “How long will you sleep, sluggard?” —Therefore every chosen person, when pressed down by the sleep of sin, strives to rise to the watchfulness of righteousness. But often, when he has risen, he perceives that he himself is being lifted up by the greatness of his virtues. Hence, after his virtues, he desires to be tested by the adversities of the present life, lest he fall more grievously through confidence in his virtues. For if he did not know that he could be preserved better through testing, the Psalmist would never have said: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Ps. 25:2).

### CHAPTER XII

“An apostate man, a worthless man, walks with a perverse mouth; he winks with his eyes, rubs with his foot, speaks with his finger, devises evil with a crooked heart, and at all times sows quarrels” (Prov. 6:12).

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 23, admonition 24), the following is added: “A worthless man walks with a perverse mouth, etc.” —Behold: when he wished to call him one who sows quarrels, he first named him an apostate, because unless, in the manner of the proud angel, he had first fallen inwardly from the sight of his Creator through the turning away of his mind, he would not afterwards have reached the point of sowing quarrels.

He is rightly described as winking with his eyes, speaking with his finger, and rubbing with his foot. For inner watchfulness is what keeps the members externally ordered. Therefore whoever has lost the stability of his mind subsequently pours outward into inconsistency of movement and, through external restlessness, shows that he has no inner root by which he remains firm.

Let those who sow quarrels hear what is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9). From this they should infer by contrast that if those who make peace are called sons of God, without doubt those who create confusion are sons of Satan.

All who are separated through discord wither away from the freshness of love. Even if they produce the fruits of good works in their actions, they are certainly nothing, because their works do not arise from the unity of charity. Let those who sow quarrels therefore consider how manifoldly they sin: while committing one wickedness, they uproot all the virtues simultaneously from human hearts. In one evil they accomplish innumerable others, because by sowing discord they extinguish charity, which is plainly the mother of all the virtues.

And because nothing is more precious to God than the virtue of love, and nothing more desirable to the devil than the extinction of charity, whoever, by sowing quarrels, destroys love of neighbor serves God’s enemy more familiarly. For what caused that enemy to fall when he lost it, this person, removing it from wounded hearts, cuts off their path of ascent.

### CHAPTER XIII

“Does not Wisdom cry out, and Prudence give her voice, in the highest and loftiest places, standing above the way in the midst of the paths?” (Prov. 8:1).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXV (nos. 29–30), the following is added: “Does not Wisdom cry out, etc.” —Perhaps we could pass through the way of temporal life in ignorance of it if this same Wisdom had stood hidden at the corners of the path. She would have had to be sought if she had wished to remain concealed. But after she publicly displayed the mysteries of her incarnation, after she offered examples of humility to the proud, she fixed herself before us, as it were, in the middle of the paths, so that we might stumble against the one whom we do not wish to seek and, by stumbling, touch the one whom we neglected to see as we passed by.

### CHAPTER XIV

“O men, I cry out to you” (Prov. 8:4).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVII (no. 6), the following is added: “O men, I cry out to you.” —Men sing of the Lord when either heavenly spirits or perfect teachers make his power known to us. Yet his work remains unknown, because even those who proclaim him reverently acknowledge that his judgments are impenetrable. They therefore know whom they proclaim, yet do not know his works: through grace they know him by whom they were made, but they cannot comprehend the judgments that he carries out even against them.

That the omnipotent God is not clearly perceived in his action, the Psalmist testifies, saying: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. 17:12).

[Note: [Col. 0899D] In this place many additions occur in the Sag., Utic., and Michaelian manuscripts; they are read subsequently in the indicated number of the *Moralia*. Much of what follows in the next chapter is also considerably more extensive in those manuscripts, with many additions at the beginning, middle, or end.]

### CHAPTER XV

“Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars; she sacrificed her victims; she mixed her wine; she set her table. She sent her maidservants to call from the citadel and the walls of the city: ‘Whoever is little, let him come to me’” (Prov. 9:1 ff.).

[Col. 0899C]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVII (no. 43), the following is added: “Wisdom built herself a house, etc.” —The Lord sacrificed victims by offering himself for us. He mixed wine by blending the cup of his commandments from historical narration and spiritual understanding. Hence it is said elsewhere: “The cup in the hand of the Lord is full of unmixed wine mixed” (Ps. 74:9). And he set a table—that is, Holy Scripture—which refreshes us, weary and coming to it from the burdens of the world, with the bread of the word, and strengthens us by its nourishment against adversaries. Hence elsewhere the Church says to him: “You have set a table before me in the presence of those who trouble me” (Ps. 22:5).

He sent his maidservants—namely, the souls of the apostles, weak at the very beginning—to call us to the citadel and the walls of the heavenly city, because, while proclaiming the eternal way, they raise us to the lofty walls of the heavenly city. Surely these walls are ascended by no one except the humble. Hence Wisdom adds there: “Whoever is little, let him come to me.” As though she were saying plainly: Whoever considers himself great in his own eyes narrows the way of access to me, because one reaches me all the more profoundly the more truly each person’s mind is humbled before himself.

But no matter how greatly someone advances in virtue, no matter how much he increases in knowledge, he does not suffice to penetrate where our Creator governs us by the ordering of his judgments.

### CHAPTER XVI

Likewise, on the passage above.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXIII (no. 33). —Wisdom built a house for herself when the only-begotten Son of God, within himself and inside the Virgin’s womb, created for himself a human body through the mediation of a soul. Thus the body of the Only-begotten is called the house of God, just as it is also called a temple. In such a way the one and the same Son of God and of man is himself the one who inhabits and the one who is inhabited.

This can nevertheless rightly be understood in another way if the Church is called the house of Wisdom. She hewed out seven pillars because she raised up, for the support of the structure of that same Church, the minds of preachers separated from the love of the present age. They are designated by the number seven because they are supported by the virtue of perfection.

She sacrificed victims because she permitted the lives of preachers to be slaughtered in persecution. She mixed wine because she proclaimed to us equally the mysteries of his divinity and humanity. She also set a table because, by opening Holy Scripture, she prepared nourishment for us. She sent her maidservants to call us to the citadel and the walls of the city because she chose to have preachers who were weak and lowly, so that they might gather faithful peoples to the heavenly structures of the spiritual homeland.

Hence the Lord praises Nathanael in the Gospel, yet does not count him among the company of preachers, because those who were to come to preach had to be such as possessed nothing of their own praise, so that the more solidly it might be recognized that what they did belonged to the truth, the more clearly it could be seen that they would not have been capable of doing it by themselves. Thus, for wondrous power to shine forth through the tongues of preachers, it was first brought about even more wondrously that those same preachers should have no merit of their own.

### CHAPTER XVII

“Whoever instructs a scoffer does himself an injury” (Prov. 9:10).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book X (no. 3), the following is added: “Whoever instructs a scoffer, etc.” —It often happens that, when they cannot defend the evils of which they have been convicted, they become worse through shame. Thus they grow proud in their defense of themselves and seek out certain vices against the life of the person who corrects them; they do not consider themselves criminals if they impose crimes upon others. When they cannot find genuine faults, they invent them, so that they too may appear to possess something for which they can rebuke him with an unequal standard of justice.

### CHAPTER XVIII

“Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you” (Prov. 9:18).

[Col. 0900C]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book VIII (nos. 67–68), the following is added: “Do not rebuke a scoffer, etc.” —The righteous person need not fear that, when the scoffer is corrected, he will inflict insults; rather, he should fear that the scoffer, drawn into hatred, may become worse.

In this connection it should be known that the good works of the righteous, because they begin in the heart, grow until the end of the present life. But the works of hypocrites, because they are not rooted in secret depths, often fail before the present life ends. They frequently devote themselves to the study of sacred learning, and because they seek it not to prepare merits but to win favor, as soon as they seize the judgment of human praise and thereby obtain the favor of passing advancement, they devote their whole mind to worldly concerns, are completely emptied of sacred learning, and afterwards show by their actions how much they love temporal things—those who previously preached only eternal things.

Often, moreover, they display the appearance of assumed maturity: they are adorned with the quiet of silence, the long-suffering of patience, and the virtue of continence. But when through these they have reached the height of honor they sought, and when reverence is now shown them by everyone, they immediately pour themselves into the wantonness of pleasure. They themselves testify that they did not possess goodness from the heart, since they quickly abandoned it.

Sometimes, however, certain people distribute what they possess and give everything to the needy, yet before the end of life, inflamed by the itch of avarice, they desire what belongs to others—those who had seemed to give away their own—and afterwards, with persistent cruelty, pursue what they had earlier abandoned through feigned piety.

### CHAPTER XIX

Likewise, on the passage above.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XX (no. 47). —If we remain silent rather than rebuke because we fear that the hatred of the scoffer may rise up against us, we are no longer seeking God’s gain but our own. In this matter it should be known that sometimes, when the wicked are reproved, they become worse. We therefore spare them, not ourselves, if we desist from reproving them for their own sake. Hence it is necessary at times for us to tolerate silently what they are, so that by seeing what we are they may learn what they are not. [Note: [Col. 0901] The Gemetensis has “Therefore, since.” Nevertheless, “Since” is read at the indicated passage in the *Moralia*.]

Because the holy Church, which always brings forth its words through charity, sometimes also restrains them out of charity, let it say: “Do not rebuke, etc.”

### CHAPTER XX

“Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasing” (Prov. 9:17).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXIII (no. 49), the following is added: “Stolen waters are sweeter, etc.” —The bread of heretics sometimes signifies preaching, just as in Solomon a woman representing the type of a heretical church, calling the foolish, says: “Eat hidden breads gladly.” Or, as it is written in our translation: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasing.”

There are certain heretics who openly fear preaching what they believe, and they season their words in the minds of the weak all the more strongly because they conceal them with a kind of greater reverence. Hence it is not improperly said: “Eat hidden breads gladly.” The hidden words of heretics taste all the sweeter to wretched hearts because they are not held in common with the rest.

### CHAPTER XXI

“Whoever walks simply walks confidently” (Prov. 10:9).

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 11, admonition 12), the following is added: “Whoever walks simply, etc.” —The simplicity of one’s conduct is the confidence of great security.

### CHAPTER XXII

“Like a passing storm, the wicked man will not be” (Prov. 10:25).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XX (no. 50), the following is added: “Like a passing storm, etc.” —When a weak person sees the wicked flourishing, the wave of miserable imitation plunges him into the sea of wickedness.

### CHAPTER XXIII

“The wicked man will not be innocent hand in hand” (Prov. 11:21).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXV (no. 7), the following is added: “The wicked man will not be innocent hand in hand.” —A hand is accustomed to be joined to a hand when it rests in idleness and no one exercises it in the uses of labor. Therefore the wicked man will not be innocent hand in hand. As though he were saying: Even when the hand ceases from wicked work, the wicked person is nevertheless not innocent because of his thoughts.

Since we know that all things are carefully weighed—not only deeds but also thoughts—what will become of the outward movement of an evil work if God judges the steps of the heart with such subtlety? Behold, no human being sees the hidden paths of our mind, yet we place as many steps before the eyes of God as we set affections in motion; we slip before him as often as we limp away from the right path on the weak foot of thought.

### CHAPTER XXIV

“A golden ring in her nostrils: a beautiful but foolish woman” (Prov. 11:22).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXI (no. 2), the following is added: “A golden ring in a pig’s snout, etc.” —Heretical doctrine appears to shine with the brilliance of eloquence, yet it does not accord with a fitting understanding of wisdom. Therefore he says: “A golden ring in her nostrils,” that is, beautiful and elaborate speech in the thoughts of a foolish mind. Gold hangs from her eloquence, yet, because of the weight of an earthly intention, she does not look upward, in the manner of swine. He explained what follows by saying: “A beautiful but foolish woman,” that is, heretical doctrine—beautiful in its wording, foolish in its understanding.

### CHAPTER XXV

“The expectation of the wicked is fury” (Prov. 11:23).

[Col. 0902A]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book V (no. 79), the following is added: “The expectation of the wicked is fury.” —Thus it happens that a troubled mind senses the greater noise of its own silence, and the flame of enclosed anger consumes it more grievously.

### CHAPTER XXVI

“The soul that blesses will be enriched, and whoever gives others drink will himself also be given drink” (Prov. 11:25).

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 25, admonition 26), the following is added: “The soul that blesses, etc.” —Whoever blesses outwardly by preaching receives the richness of inward growth. And while he does not cease to intoxicate the minds of his hearers with the wine of eloquence, he himself grows intoxicated through the drink of multiplied grace.

### CHAPTER XXVII

“Whoever hides his grain is cursed among the peoples” (Prov. 11:26).

In the *Pastoral Rule*, part III (chapter 25, admonition 26), the following is added: “Whoever hides his grain, etc.” —To hide grain is to retain within oneself the words of holy preaching. Such a person is cursed among the peoples because, through the sole fault of silence, he is condemned to punishment for the many whom he could have corrected.

If those who were not ignorant of medical practice saw a wound that needed cutting and nevertheless refused to cut it, they would certainly commit the sin of a brother’s death through mere torpor. Let those therefore consider how great a guilt ensnares them who, while recognizing the wounds of minds, neglect to heal them by cutting with words. Hence the Prophet rightly says: “Cursed is the one who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. 48:10). To withhold one’s sword from blood is to restrain the word of preaching from killing a carnal life.

### CHAPTER XXVIII

“The foolish will serve the wise” (Prov. 11:83).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XX (no. 52), the following is added: “The foolish will serve the wise.” —Yet we often see the wise subjected and the foolish holding the citadel of dominion; the wise obeying in servile fashion and the foolish ruling with tyrannical pride. How, then, according to the definition of the divine judgment, does the foolish serve the wise, when he often oppresses him by the right of temporal dominion?

But it should be understood that, while the foolish person who is in authority exercises the terror of power against the life of the wise, while he wearies him with hardships and tears him with insults, he actually purifies him by burning away all the rust of vices. The foolish therefore serves the wise even by ruling him, since by pressing him down he advances him toward a better condition. Thus sometimes servants preside over orphan masters for the sake of their discipline; they frighten, oppress, and strike them, yet in no way cease to be servants, because they have been appointed for this very purpose: to serve their advancing masters even by striking them.

Since the evils of the wicked purify the good while afflicting them, the power of the unjust also serves the advantage of the righteous. But often the righteous, caught in tribulation, consider the hand of the one who brings help slow, when the savagery of persecutors constricts them for a little longer. The remedies of deliverance are indeed swift, but what is done more quickly by the deliverer appears slow to the one in pain. And when help is sought for the prayer being made, if it does not immediately follow the voice, it is judged to be absent.

### CHAPTER XXIX

“The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Prov. 12:5).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXV (no. 13), the following is added: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments.” —Each person’s mind ought carefully to examine both his own causes before the Lord and the Lord’s causes against himself. He ought cautiously to weigh both what good he has received from him and how, by living perversely, he has answered his benefits with evil. The chosen certainly do not cease to do this every day.

Hence Solomon rightly says: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments.” They enter the judge’s secret chamber within the breast of the heart and consider how strictly he will one day strike, though he waits patiently for a long time. They fear concerning what they remember having done and punish themselves by weeping for what they understand they have committed. They fear the subtle divine judgments even concerning those things which they perhaps cannot understand in themselves. For they see that, by divine sight, things are seen which they themselves, through human weakness, do not see.

They behold the strict Judge, who, the longer he delays, the more severely he strikes. They also contemplate with him the assembly of the holy fathers seated there, and they reproach themselves for having despised either their examples or their words. In this secret judgment, constrained by the very execution of their own minds, they strike themselves through repentance for what they committed through pride.

There they enumerate against themselves whatever attacks them; there they heap before their own eyes everything they must mourn. There they perceive whatever may be distinguished by the anger of the strict Judge; there they suffer as many punishments as they fear suffering. Nor is any ministry lacking in this judgment conceived in the mind, a ministry that should more fully punish the guilty: conscience accuses, reason judges, fear binds, and pain tortures.

This judgment punishes more certainly the more inwardly it rages, because nothing comes to it from outside. For when each person begins to undertake the examination of this case against himself, he is himself the accuser who presents the case, and himself the defendant who is presented. He hates what he remembers himself to have been; and he himself, through himself, pursues the one whom he was. Thus, from the same person against himself, a kind of conflict arises in the soul, giving birth to peace with God.

### CHAPTER XXX

“Turn the wicked, and they will be no more” (Prov. 12:7).

In Homily 32 on the Gospel (no. 2), the following is added: “Turn the wicked, and they will be no more.” —When the wicked are converted, they will be no more—not because they will not exist at all in essence, but because they will no longer possess the guilt of wickedness. We then abandon ourselves; we then deny ourselves, when we change what we were through oldness and strive toward that to which we are called through newness.

### CHAPTER XXXI

“In the mouth of the fool is the rod of pride” (Prov. 14:3).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXIV (Nos. 40, 41), the following was added: “In the mouth of a fool is a rod of pride.” For he knows how to strike harshly, but does not know how to show compassion humbly. Righteous preachers also commonly correct their hearers by rebuking them; they commonly rage against their vices with stern reproof. Hence it is written: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven firmly in” (Eccles. XII, 11).

## CHAPTER XXXII.—The heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul will not admit a stranger into its joy (Prov. XIV, 10).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book V (Nos. 3, 4), the following was added: “The heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul,” etc. For the hearts of the reprobate are in bitterness, since they are afflicted even by their own perverse desires; but [Col. 0903D] they do not know that same bitterness, because, voluntarily blinded, they cannot weigh what they endure. By contrast, the heart of the good knows its own bitterness, because it understands the misery of exile in which it has been cast and torn apart, and perceives how peaceful were the things it lost and how shameful those into which it fell. But this embittered heart will one day be led back to its joy, and no stranger will share in that joy, because the one who now [Note: [Col. 0903] Utic.: “For this reason, by the error of his heart, he thrusts himself outward toward worldly desires.”] thrusts himself outward from this sorrow of the heart through his desires will then remain excluded from its inward solemnity.

Therefore those who are in the bitterness of soul desire to die completely to the world, so that, just as they desire nothing in the world, they may now also be held by no obligation to the world. It often happens, however, that a person no longer holds the world in his mind, yet the world still binds him through its occupations. He himself is already [Col. 0904A] dead to the world, but the world itself is not yet dead to him. For the world still regards him as though he were alive, while it strives to snatch him away, intent on something else, into its own activities.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—Likewise, from the preceding passage.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book VI (No. 23). The human mind knows the bitterness of its soul when, kindled by desire for its eternal homeland, it recognizes through weeping the punishment of its exile. But no stranger will share in its joy, because the one who is now alien to the sorrow of compunction will then not be a participant in the joy of consolation. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—There is a way that seems right to human beings, but its end leads to death (Prov. XIV, 12).

[Col. 0904B] In the exposition of blessed Job, book V (No. 12), the following was added: “There is a way,” etc. Hence holy men, when they overcome evils, fear even their own good deeds, lest, while they desire to do good, they be deceived by the appearance of their action, lest the poisonous corruption of decay lie hidden beneath the appearance of a good color. For they know that, still weighed down by the burden of corruption, they cannot discern good things subtly; and when they bring before their eyes the standard of the final judgment, they sometimes fear even in themselves those things which they approve. They desire inward things with their whole mind, yet, trembling because of the uncertainty, they do not know where they are going.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—The riches of the wise are their crown; the folly of fools is imprudence (Prov. XIV, 24).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXII (No. 8), the following was added: “The riches of the wise are their crown,” etc. If he had called earthly riches the crowns of the wise, he would undoubtedly have acknowledged poverty rather than imprudence as the folly of fools. But by placing imprudence beneath the folly of fools, he showed that he meant the riches of the wise to be [Col. 0904C] prudence. Contemplating these riches of knowledge within himself, and humbling his contemplation by considering human frailty, Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. IV, 7).

Thus we find many riches within ourselves when, by investigating the sacred writings, we receive the gifts of abundant understanding and perceive many things in them that nevertheless are not mutually contradictory. Yet there is no secure joy in knowing either profound or numerous things in the divine pages, but in preserving what one has learned. For whoever understands well recognizes what he ought to do through understanding. The more widely one is extended through understanding, the more earnestly one is bound to carry out the works.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—In the fear of the Lord there is confidence of strength (Prov. XIV, 26).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book V (No. 33), the following was added: “In the fear of the Lord there is confidence of strength.” Confidence of strength is said to be present in the fear of the Lord because our mind despises the terrors of temporal things with greater strength the more truly it submits to their Creator [Col. 0904D] through fear. Once established in the fear of the Lord, it finds nothing outside him to fear; for when it is joined to the Creator of all things by proper fear, it is raised by a certain power above all things.

Strength, however, is displayed only in adversity; hence patience is immediately set after strength. A person demonstrates more truly that he has progressed in strength the more robustly he endures the evils of others. For one who is overthrown by another’s wickedness has not grown strong enough within himself: unable to bear opposition, he lies pierced by the sword of his own faintheartedness.

Because perfection is born from patience, the perfection of ways is immediately introduced after patience. For the truly perfect person is not impatient with his neighbor’s imperfection. Whoever abandons patience because he cannot endure another’s imperfection is himself a witness [Col. 0905A] that he has not yet progressed toward perfection. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI, 29).

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—The health of the heart is life to the flesh; envy is decay of the bones (Prov. XIV, 30).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book V (No. 85), the following was added: “The health of the heart is life to the flesh,” etc. What is signified by the life of the flesh except something weak and tender, and what by the bones except strong deeds? It often happens that some people, although possessing true innocence of heart, appear weak in [Col. 0906A] certain actions of theirs, while others already perform deeds that seem strong in human eyes but secretly waste away inwardly through the pestilence of envy toward the good of others.

Thus it is rightly said: “The health of the heart is life to the flesh,” because, if innocence of mind is guarded, even those things that are weak outwardly will eventually be strengthened. “Envy is decay of the bones,” because through the vice of jealousy even things that appear strong to human eyes perish before the eyes of God. For the bones to decay through envy is for even strong things to perish. [Note: [Col. 0905A] After these words, the Vatican manuscripts append much material from what follows at the assigned location, up to these words: [Col. 0906A] “There is nothing that contradicts his love toward his neighbor.”]

# BOOK THIRTEEN. D. On Testimonies in the Song of Songs.

[Col. 0905]

## CHAPTER I.—Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth (Song I, 1).

[Col. 0905A]

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XIV (No. 51), the following was added: [Col. 0905B] “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” The holy Church has received as many kisses from his mouth as it has learned commandments from his preaching. She rightly desires the kiss of her Creator, since she prepares herself through love to obey him.

## CHAPTER II.—The young women have loved you (Song I, 3).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXIV (No. 8), the following was added: “The young women have loved you.” Sacred Scripture often customarily uses youth to signify newness of life. Hence it is said to the coming bridegroom: “The young women have loved you,” that is, the souls of the elect, renewed by the grace of baptism. They do not grow weak through the practice of their former life, but are adorned by the conduct of the new person.
