## CHAPTER III.—They appointed me as a keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep (Song I, 5).

In Homily 17 on the Gospel (No. 14), the following was added: “They appointed me as a keeper of the vineyards,” etc. The vineyards are our actions, which we cultivate through the practice of daily labor. But, having been appointed keepers of vineyards, we do not guard our [Col. 0905C] own vineyard at all, because, while we are entangled in the actions of others, we neglect the ministry of our own action.

## CHAPTER IV.—Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie at midday (Song I, 6).

In Homily 33 on the Gospel (No. 7), the following was added: “Tell me,” etc. The Lord is called a fawn of deer with respect to the flesh he assumed, the son of the ancient fathers. The heat burns more intensely at midday, and the fawn seeks a shady place, since the heat afflicts him with its fire. Therefore the Lord rests in those hearts that are not set ablaze by love of the present age, whose fleshly desires do not burn them, and which, inflamed by their own anxieties, do not wither amid the desires of this world. Thus the fawn seeks shady places at midday in which to pasture, because the Lord pastures in minds that, tempered by the regard of grace, are not burned by bodily desires.

## CHAPTER V.—Likewise, from the preceding passage.

[Col. 0905D] In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXX (No. 79). The Lord is fed when he delights in our good actions. He lies at midday when, amid the hearts of the elect, he finds the refreshment of good thought in place of the carnal desires by which the hearts of the reprobate burn.

## CHAPTER VI.—Unless you know yourself, most beautiful among women, go out and depart after the tracks of the flocks, and pasture your young goats (Song I, 7).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVI (chapter 21, near the beginning), the following was added: [Note: [Col. 0905D] The same words are read in book XXX of the same exposition of Job, No. 56.] “Unless you know yourself, most beautiful among women,” etc. That is: unless, by living well, you recognize the dignity by which you were [Col. 0906A] created in the likeness of God, depart from the sight of my contemplation and imitate the life of ignorant peoples. [Note: [Col. 0906D] Here the chapter begins in Michael.] [Col. 0906B] She recognizes herself as the one who is beautiful among women when every elect soul, placed even among sinners, remembers that it was created in the image and likeness of its Author and walks according to the order of the likeness it has received.

If she does not recognize herself, she goes out, because, expelled from the secret place of her heart, she is scattered among outward desires. Once outside, she departs after the tracks of the flocks, because, abandoning her inner life, she is led onto the broad way and follows the examples of peoples. She no longer pastures lambs but young goats, because she aims not to nourish innocent thoughts of the mind but to nurture the perverse movements of the flesh.

## CHAPTER VII.—Until the king is at his resting place, my nard gave forth its fragrance (Song I, 11).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXV (No. 43), the following was added: “Until the king is at his resting place,” etc. It is as though he were saying plainly: As long as the king remains hidden from my eyes with himself in the rest of heavenly secrecy, the life of the elect is exercised in wonderful fragrances of virtue, so that, while it does not yet see the one it [Col. 0906C] desires, it may burn more ardently with longing. When the king is placed at his resting place, the nard gives forth its fragrance: while the Lord rests in his blessedness, the virtue of the saints provides us in the Church with the grace of great sweetness.

## CHAPTER VIII.—Strengthen me with flowers and surround me with apples, for I am sick with love (Song II, 5).

In the Commentary on Ezekiel, book II, Homily 3 (No. 8), the following was added: “Strengthen me with flowers,” etc. What are the flowers except souls beginning a good work and breathing forth a heavenly desire? What are the apples among the flowers except minds already perfected in goodness, which advance from the beginning of a holy resolve to the fruit of a good work?

Therefore the one who is sick with love seeks to be strengthened with flowers and surrounded with apples, because, if she is not yet permitted to see the one she desires, it is a great consolation for her to rejoice in the progress of others. Thus let the soul languishing with holy love be strengthened with flowers and apples, so that she may rest in the good work of her [Col. 0906D] neighbor, since she is not yet able to contemplate the face of God.

## CHAPTER IX.—I am wounded with love (Song II, 5, according to the Septuagint).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book VI (No. 42), the following was added: “I am wounded with love.” The soul was previously unhealthy and prostrate in the blind security of this exile; it neither saw the Lord nor sought to be seen by the Lord. But when struck by the darts of his love, it is wounded in its depths by an affection of devotion, burns with the desire for contemplation, and is wonderfully brought to life through the wound—although previously it lay dead in its well-being.

It burns, pants, and desires even to see the one from whom it used to flee. Through the blow, [Col. 0907A] therefore, it is brought back to salvation; through the disturbance of its love it is recalled from the security of inward repose. But when the wounded mind begins to pant for God, when it despises all the blandishments of this world and stretches out in desire toward the heavenly homeland, whatever previously seemed friendly and pleasing in the world immediately becomes a temptation for it.

For those who had been accustomed to love it when it sinned cruelly attack it when it lives rightly; and the mind that is upright in God endures battles with its own flesh, in which it had previously lain pleasurably while serving its vices. Former pleasures return to memory and afflict the resisting mind with a fierce struggle. But while we are worn down by a passing labor, we are freed from everlasting pain.

## CHAPTER X.—His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me (Song II, 6).

In the Pastoral Rule, part I, in the Royal manuscript (chapter 26, admonition 27), the following was added: “His left hand is beneath my head,” etc. She has placed the left hand of God—that is, the prosperity of the present life—as though [Col. 0907B] beneath her head, pressing it down through the purpose of supreme love. The right hand of God embraces her, because she is held with complete devotion beneath his eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XI.—Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains and bounding over the hills (Song II, 8).

In the exposition of the Gospel, Homily 29 (No. 10), the following was added: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains,” etc. He considered the heights of such great works and said: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains.” In coming for our redemption, he made, so to speak, certain leaps. From heaven he came into the womb; from the womb he came into the manger; from the manger he came to the cross; from the cross he came to the tomb; from the tomb he returned to heaven. Behold, so that he might make us run after him, the Truth made manifest in the flesh performed certain leaps for us.

## CHAPTER XII.—Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the latticework (Song II, 9).

[Col. 0907C] In the exposition of Ezekiel, book II (No. 15), Homily 1, the following was added: “Behold, he stands behind our wall,” etc. He showed to human eyes what he had assumed from mortal nature, yet remained invisible in it to those seeking to see him openly; thus he stood as though behind a wall, because he did not offer himself to be seen in manifest majesty. For he stood as though behind a wall who displayed the nature of humanity that he had assumed and concealed the nature of divinity from human eyes.

Hence it is added there: “Looking through the windows, gazing through the latticework.” Whoever looks through windows or through latticework is neither completely hidden nor completely seen. In this way our Redeemer appeared before the eyes of those who doubted. For if, while performing miracles, he had suffered nothing, he would have appeared to them fully as God rather than as a human being; and again, if, while suffering as a human being, he had performed nothing as God, he would have been thought merely human.

But because he both performed divine acts and endured human sufferings, he looked upon human beings as though through windows or latticework: he appeared as God through his miracles and was hidden through his sufferings; he was seen as human through his sufferings, [Col. 0907D] yet through his miracles he was recognized as being beyond humanity.

[Col. 0907D]

## CHAPTER XIII.—Rise, hurry, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come; for winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed (Song II, 10).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVII (No. 45), the following was added: “Rise, hurry, my beloved,” etc. When winter passes, the rain withdraws, because, when the present life has been completed—the life in which the sluggishness of corruptible flesh had bound us beneath the cloud of ignorance—the whole ministry of preaching ceases. Then we shall see more clearly through ourselves what we now hear less clearly through the voices of the saints.

[Note: [Col. 0907D] This is absent from the Michael manuscript, in which alone we read Paterius’s work on the Song.]

## CHAPTER XIV.—In my bed at night I sought him, and I did not find him (Song III, 1).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book VIII (No. 41), the following was added: [Col. 0908A] “In my bed at night I sought him,” etc. The beloved is sought in bed and at night because the appearance of the invisible Creator, with every image of bodily vision restrained, is found in the chamber of the heart.

## CHAPTER XV.—I sought him, and I did not find him. The watchmen who guard the city found me. Have you seen the one whom my soul loves? When I had passed them a little way, I found the one whom my soul loves (Song III, 3).

In the exposition of the Gospel, Homily 25 (No. 2), the following was added: “I sought him, and I did not find him,” etc. We seek the beloved in bed when, amid a little rest in the present life, we sigh with longing for our Redeemer. We seek him at night because, although the mind is already awake in him, the eye is still dim.

But whoever does not find his beloved must rise and go around the city—that is, must traverse in mind and inquiry the holy Church of the elect. He must seek him through the lanes and in the streets—that is, he must observe those who walk along narrow and broad paths—so that, if he can find anything in them, he may seek his footprints, because there are [Col. 0908B] some who, even while living a worldly life, possess something in their conduct worthy of imitation.

As we seek, the watchmen who guard the city find us, because the holy Fathers, who guard the state of the Church, come to meet our good endeavors and instruct us by either their word or their writing. When we pass them a little way, we find the one whom we love, because our Redeemer, although a human being in humility among human beings, was nevertheless above human beings in divinity.

When the watchmen have been passed, the beloved is found, because, when we see the prophets and apostles as beneath him, we recognize that the one who is God by nature is above humanity. Thus he is first sought as though he could not be found, so that, once found, he may be held more tightly.

[Note: [Col. 0908D] It is not found in the manuscript.]

## CHAPTER XVI.—Likewise, from the preceding passage.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVII (No. 4). The beloved is sought at night in bed because, in the inward chambers of the heart, he is desired amid spiritual tribulation. Yet the bride seeking him does not find him, because every elect soul already burns with the flames of his love, but the sight of the one sought is still denied to it, so that the desire of the lover may increase.

It is as though water were withheld from a thirsty person so that the heat of the thirst might increase. The longer one desires it while thirsting, the more eagerly one will eventually drink it when it is found.

But the watchmen find the bride while she is [Col. 0908C] seeking, wound her, and take away her cloak, because, when diligent teachers find a soul already seeking the appearance of its Redeemer, they wound it with the darts of heavenly love through the word of preaching. If any covering from its former way of life still remains on it, they remove it, so that, the more it is stripped of the burden of this world, the sooner it may find the one it seeks.

## CHAPTER XVII.—Likewise, from the preceding passage.

In the Commentary on Ezekiel, Homily 19 (No. 11). The soul seeks the beloved in bed when, in the very leisure and rest it desires, it already longs to see the [Col. 0908D] Lord, already desires to go out to him, and already pants to be free from the darkness of the present life. But it seeks him and does not find him because, although it desires him with great love, it is not yet permitted to see the one it loves.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—Likewise, from the preceding passage.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book V (No. 6). The bridegroom hides himself when he is sought so that, when he is not found, he may be sought more ardently; and the bride who seeks is delayed so that she may not find him too quickly, lest, made more capacious by delay, she eventually find more abundantly what she was seeking.

## CHAPTER XIX.—Likewise, from the preceding passage.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVIII (No. 80). Whom do we understand by the watchmen who guard the city, except the earlier Fathers or the prophets, who devoted themselves to watching over our [Col. 0909A] protection through the voice of holy preaching? But when the Church sought her Redeemer, she did not wish to fix her hope on those ancient preachers, for she says: “When I had passed them a little way, I found the one whom my soul loves.” She could not have found him if she had not wished to pass them.

The unbelievers fixed themselves upon these watchmen, believing Christ the Son of God to be one of them. Therefore, having found the watchmen through the voice and faith of Peter, the holy Church passed beyond them, refusing to believe the Lord of the prophets to be merely one of the prophets.

## CHAPTER XX.—Likewise, from the preceding passage.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVII (No. 4): “When I had passed them a little way, I found the one whom my soul loves.” Unless the mind eager for his vision passed beyond the estimation of the prophets, the exalted stature of the patriarchs, and the measure of all human beings, it would not find him who is above humanity. To pass beyond the watchmen therefore means to place even those whom the soul admires below him in [Col. 0909B] comparison with him; and then the one who was sought is seen, if he is believed to be human yet nevertheless beyond the measure of human beings.

## CHAPTER XXI.—Who is this that rises through the desert like a column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every kind of perfumer’s powder? (Song III, 6).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book I (No. 54), the following was added: “Who is this that rises through the desert,” etc. The holy Church rises like a column of smoke from spices because, through the virtues of her life, she advances daily toward the uprightness of the inward incense. She does not flow apart, scattered through her thoughts, but binds herself within the hidden places of the heart like a rod of firmness. As she continually reflects upon and reviews what she does, she has myrrh and frankincense in her works, but powder in her thoughts.

## CHAPTER XXII.—All holding swords and most skilled in battle (Song III, 2).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (No. 56), the following was added: [Col. 0909C] “All holding swords,” etc. Paul disclosed what is signified by the sword in divine Scripture when he said: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, 17). Solomon did not say, “All having swords,” but “holding,” because it is not merely wonderful to know the word of God, but to do it.

He has the sword but does not hold it who knows the divine word but neglects to live according to it. He is no longer able to be skilled in battle who does not exercise the spiritual sword he possesses. For one who sets aside holding the sword of God’s word by living badly is entirely unable to resist temptations.

[Note: [Col. 0909D] So the manuscripts and edition read *valet* (“is able”); a variant reads *vellet* (“would wish”).]

## CHAPTER XXIII.—Each one’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night (Song III, 8).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XX (No. 8), the following was added: “Each one’s sword is upon his thigh,” etc. The terrors of the night are the ambushes of hidden temptation. The sword upon the thigh is vigilant protection, restraining the enticements of the flesh. Therefore, lest the terror of the night—that is, a hidden and sudden temptation—creep in, it is always necessary that the sword of guarding, placed upon it, press down our thigh.

Holy men are indeed so certain of hope that they nevertheless remain always suspicious of temptation, for it is said to them: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. II, 11)., in the very leisure and rest it desires, it already longs to see the Lord, already desires to go out to him, and already pants to be free from the darkness of the present life. But it seeks him and does not find him because, although it desires him with great love, it is not yet permitted to see the one it loves.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—Likewise, from the preceding passage.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book V (No. 6). The bridegroom hides himself when he is sought so that, when he is not found, he may be sought more ardently; and the bride who seeks is delayed so that she may not find him too quickly, lest, made more capacious by delay, she eventually find more abundantly what she was seeking.

## CHAPTER XIX.—Likewise, from the preceding passage.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVIII (No. 80). Whom do we understand by the watchmen who guard the city, except the earlier Fathers or the prophets, who devoted themselves to watching over our protection through the voice of holy preaching? But when the Church sought her Redeemer, she did not wish to fix her hope on those ancient preachers, for she says: “When I had passed them a little way, I found the one whom my soul loves.” She could not have found him if she had not wished to pass them.

The unbelievers fixed themselves upon these watchmen, believing Christ the Son of God to be one of them. Therefore, having found the watchmen through the voice and faith of Peter, the holy Church passed beyond them, refusing to believe the Lord of the prophets to be merely one of the prophets.

## CHAPTER XX.—Likewise, from the preceding passage.

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXVII (No. 4): “When I had passed them a little way, I found the one whom my soul loves.” Unless the mind eager for his vision passed beyond the estimation of the prophets, the exalted stature of the patriarchs, and the measure of all human beings, it would not find him who is above humanity. To pass beyond the watchmen therefore means to place even those whom the soul admires below him in comparison with him; and then the one who was sought is seen, if he is believed to be human yet nevertheless beyond the measure of human beings.

## CHAPTER XXI.—Who is this that rises through the desert like a column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every kind of perfumer’s powder? (Song III, 6).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book I (No. 54), the following was added: “Who is this that rises through the desert,” etc. The holy Church rises like a column of smoke from spices because, through the virtues of her life, she advances daily toward the uprightness of inward burning. She does not flow apart, scattered through her thoughts, but binds herself within the hidden places of the heart like a rod of firmness. As she continually reflects upon and reviews what she does, she has myrrh and frankincense in her works, but powder in her thoughts.

## CHAPTER XXII.—All holding swords and most skilled in battle (Song III, 2).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XIX (No. 56), the following was added: “All holding swords,” etc. Paul disclosed what is signified by the sword in divine Scripture when he said: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, 17). Solomon did not say, “All having swords,” but “holding,” because it is not merely wonderful to know the word of God, but to do it.

He has the sword but does not hold it who knows the divine word but neglects to live according to it. He is no longer able to be skilled in battle who does not exercise the spiritual sword he possesses. For one who sets aside holding the sword of God’s word by living badly is entirely unable to resist temptations.

[Note: [Col. 0909D] So the manuscripts and the edition; “would wish.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII.—Each one’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night (Song III, 8).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XX (No. 8), the following was added: “Each one’s sword is upon his thigh,” etc. The terrors of the night are the ambushes of hidden temptation. The sword upon the thigh is vigilant protection, restraining the enticements of the flesh. Therefore, lest the terror of the night—that is, a hidden and sudden temptation—creep in, it is always necessary that the sword placed upon our thigh restrain it through vigilance.

Holy men are indeed so certain of hope that they nevertheless remain always suspicious of temptation, for it is said to them: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. II, 11).

## CHAPTER XXIV.—King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon. He made its columns of silver, its backrest of gold, and its ascent of purple; he paved its midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem (Song III, 9 ff.).

In the Commentary on Ezekiel, book II, Homily 3 (Nos. 13, 14, 15), the following was added: “King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon,” etc. We must not believe that Solomon, a king of such greatness, who abounded in such immense riches that the weight of his [Col. 0910A] gold could not be estimated and silver had no value in those days, made himself a wooden litter.

There is another Solomon, namely our peaceful king, who made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon. The cedars of Lebanon are exceedingly resistant to decay. The litter of our king, therefore, is the holy Church, which is constructed from strong fathers—that is, from minds resistant to decay. It is rightly called a litter because every day it carries souls to the eternal banquet of its Creator.

Silver columns were made for this litter because the preachers of the holy Church shine with the light of eloquence. Along with the silver columns there is a golden backrest, because, through what the holy preachers proclaim clearly, the minds of their hearers find the radiance of clarity—the soul in which they may recline. Through what they hear lucidly and openly, they rest in their hearts upon that which shines.

Its columns are silver and its backrest is made of gold because, through the light of speech, the brightness of rest is found in the [Col. 0910B] mind. The inward radiance of that rest already illumines the mind, so that through its intention it may rest there where the grace of preaching was not sought.

But he adds what kind of ascent leads to what is shown brightly within when, immediately concerning the same litter, he says: “Its ascent of purple.” True purple, because it is dyed with blood, is rightly seen in the color of blood, since a very great multitude of the faithful at the beginning of the nascent Church reached the kingdom through the blood of martyrdom.

Our king made an ascent of purple in the litter because what is seen brightly within is reached through the tribulation of blood. What, then, shall we wretched people do, deprived as we are of all strength? Behold, we cannot be columns in this litter, because in us there is neither strength of action nor the light of preaching. We do not have a golden backrest, because we do not yet behold, as we ought, spiritual rest through the understanding of inward clarity. We are not an ascent of purple, because we are unable to shed our [Col. 0910C] blood for our Redeemer.

What, then, should be done about us? What hope will there be if no one reaches the kingdom except one endowed with the highest virtues? Yet our consolation is also present. Let us love God as much as we can; let us love our neighbor; and together let us hasten toward God’s litter, because, as it is written there: “He paved it with love.” Have love, and without doubt you belong where both a silver column is raised and an ascent of purple is held.

Yet because this is said on account of our weakness, it is shown openly when the passage immediately adds: “For the daughters of Jerusalem.” For the word of God, which says not “sons” but “daughters,” signifies by the female sex nothing other than the weakness of minds. Thus, because love is said to exist among the silver columns, the golden backrest, and the ascent of purple “for the daughters of Jerusalem,” this is represented here among the chambers by five cubits: those who are weak in virtues are not alien to God’s building if they do not neglect to perform with love the good things they are [Col. 0910D] able to do.

## CHAPTER XXV.—Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep ascending from the washing place (Song IV, 2).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXXIII (No. 47), the following was added: “Your teeth are like flocks,” etc. The saints are rightly compared with shorn and washed sheep, because, taking up an innocent life, they laid aside in the washing of baptism the old fleece of their former way of life.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet (Song IV, 3).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book II (No. 82), the following was added: “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon,” etc. A ribbon binds the hair of the head. The lips of the bride, therefore, are like a ribbon, because through the exhortation of the holy Church, [Col. 0911A] all the thoughts diffused in the minds of her hearers are bound together, lest they flow away when loosened, lest they scatter themselves through unlawful things, and lest, once scattered, they cast down the eyes of the heart. Rather, they gather themselves toward a single intention while the ribbon of holy preaching binds them.

He rightly asserts that it is scarlet, because the preaching of the saints burns with the sole ardor of love. What, then, is signified by the head except the mind itself, which is the principal element of each person’s action? Hence it is said elsewhere: “Let oil not fail from your head” (Eccles. IX, 8). Oil in the head is love in the mind, and oil does not fail from the head when love does not depart from the mind.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, feeding among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline (Song IV, 5).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXIV (No. 17), the following was added: “Your two breasts are like twin fawns,” etc. What are the two breasts except the two peoples coming from the Jews and the Gentiles, who are fixed in the body of the holy Church [Col. 0911B] through the intention of wisdom in the secret place of the heart?

From this people, those who are elect are compared with fawns of a gazelle because, through humility, they understand themselves to be small and sinful; but, running through love, they pass over whatever obstacles arising from temporal things confront them, and, taking leaps of contemplation, they ascend to heavenly things. They do this because they behold the examples of the saints who preceded them.

Hence they are also said to feed among the lilies. For what is signified by lilies except the life of those who truly say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God” (II Cor. II, 15)? Therefore the elect, so that they may be strong enough to attain the highest things, are nourished by beholding the fragrant and pure life of the righteous.

They already thirst to see the Lord; they already burn with the heat of love to be satisfied by contemplation of him. But because, placed in this life, they are not yet able to do so, they are meanwhile nourished by the examples of the Fathers who preceded them. Hence the time of this nourishment among the lilies is appropriately defined when it says: “Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.”

For we need to be refreshed by the examples of the righteous [Col. 0911C] until, with the eternal day breathing upon us, we pass beyond the shadows of present mortality. When the shadow of this temporal existence has passed and has been inclined through mortality, because we behold the inward light of that day, we will no longer desire to be inflamed with love for it through the examples of others.

But now, because we cannot yet gaze upon him, it is especially necessary that we be stirred by observing the actions of those who followed him perfectly. Let us therefore contemplate how beautiful is the agility of those who follow, and let us see how ugly is the sluggishness of the lazy. As soon as we look upon the deeds of those who act well, we judge ourselves, with inward shame exacting punishment. Immediately shame shakes the mind; immediately guilt, raging justly, condemns it; and what is still perhaps shamefully pleasing also greatly displeases us.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—You will be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions (Song IV, 8).

[Col. 0911D] In the exposition of blessed Job, book XVII (No. 52), the following was added: “You will be crowned from the summit of Amana,” etc. What else is signified by the name of lions except demons, who rage against us with the most savage cruelty? Sinners, too, were called to the faith, and their hearts had been dens of lions; since the Lord is believed to have conquered death through their confession, he is crowned, as it were, from the dens of lions. For the reward of victory is a crown. Thus the faithful offer him a crown as many times as they confess that he conquered death through his resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—Your breasts are better than wine (Song IV, 10).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XXX (No. 48), the following was added: [Col. 0912A] “Your breasts are better than wine.” Breasts are fixed within the chest’s enclosure and give us milk to drink; thus preachers, clinging to the secrets of supreme contemplation, nourish us through subtle preaching.

## CHAPTER XXX.—Honey and milk are beneath your tongue (Song IV, 11).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book XV (No. 13), the following was added: “Honey and milk are beneath your tongue.” Many righteous people, when they see certain persons acting perversely—persons who must be struck with harsh rebukes—take on harshness in their tongue, but conceal kindness beneath the tongue of their mind. Hence it is said in the voice of the bridegroom to the holy Church: “Honey and milk are beneath your tongue.” [Note: [Col. 0911D] In the manuscript, a chapter begins at these words.]

Those who do not wish to reveal the sweetness of their mind to the weak, but strike them with a certain harshness when they speak, while nevertheless inserting, as though secretly among their harsh words, something sweet—these have sweetness not on their tongue but beneath their tongue. For amid the harsh things they [Col. 0912B] utter, they release certain gentle and sweet words by which the distressed mind may be restored through kindness.

Likewise, all the perverse, because they have evil not on their tongue but beneath their tongue, present sweetness in their speech while plotting perversity in their thoughts.

[Note: [Col. 0911D] This chapter is much longer in the manuscript.]

## CHAPTER XXXI.—Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow (Song IV, 16).

In the exposition of blessed Job, book IX (No. 17), the following was added: “Rise, north wind, and come,” etc. What is signified by the name of the south wind except the fervor of the Holy Spirit? When someone has been filled with it, he burns with love for his spiritual homeland.

Hence it is said in the voice of the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow.” When the south wind comes, the rising north wind withdraws, as the ancient enemy, who had bound the mind in sluggishness, departs when the Holy Spirit arrives and drives him out.

And the south wind blows through the bridegroom’s garden so that its spices may flow, because, [Col. 0912C] when the Spirit of truth has filled the holy Church with the virtues of his gifts, he spreads far and wide from her the fragrances of good works.

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Note: In the manuscript, the exposition of this verse is taken from Homily 14 on Ezekiel: “He sleeps with a watchful heart,” etc., through the words: “And afterward he may attain the glory of his vision.”]

“I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2).

When sleep, understood in three ways in Holy Scripture, was being discussed in the exposition of blessed Job, Book V (no. 54), the following was added: “I sleep,” etc.

It should be known that in Holy Scripture sleep is understood in three ways. Sometimes sleep signifies the death of the flesh; sometimes the torpor of negligence; and sometimes the repose of life after earthly desires have been trampled underfoot. By the name of sleep, or falling asleep, the death of the flesh is indicated, as Paul says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep” (1 Thess. 4:12). And shortly afterward: “So also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (ibid., 13).

Again, sleep signifies the torpor of negligence, as the same Paul says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13:11). And again: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15:34).

Sleep also figures the repose of life after the desires of the flesh have been trampled underfoot, as is said in the voice of the bride in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.” For when the holy mind restrains itself from the tumult of temporal desire, it comes to know inward things more truly; and it keeps watch over the inner realities with greater eagerness, the more it hides itself from outward disturbance.

[Note: This chapter, together with several that follow, is absent from the manuscript, where only four chapters remain.]

## CHAPTER XXXIII

Likewise, concerning the preceding subject.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIII (no. 33):

Those who serve external duties without offense and continually strive to hasten toward the secret places of the heart hear the voice of God as though in a dream, when in the meditation of the mind they are drawn away from carnal movements. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake,” as though she were saying: “While I lull my outward senses to sleep from the cares of this life, with my mind at leisure I come to know inward things more vividly.” Outside I sleep, but within my heart keeps watch, because while I seem not to perceive outward things, I apprehend inward things attentively.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

“My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch” (Song 5:5).

In the commentary on Ezekiel, Book II, Homily 7 (no. 10), the following was added: “My beloved put his hand through the opening,” etc.

The beloved puts his hand through the opening when the Lord strikes our mind through a subtle understanding by his power. And the belly trembles at his touch because our weakness, when touched by an understanding of heavenly joy, is itself disturbed by that very exultation. Thus fear arises in the mind together with joy; and although it already senses what it loves concerning heavenly joy, it still fears that it may not receive what it scarcely perceives.

[Note: The printed editions read “lest it perish,” a serious error which we corrected elsewhere; for Homily 19—or Book II, Homily 7—in the Vatican, Gussanville, and other editions, while the manuscript codices have *recipiat* or *percipiat*, I read here *recipiat* in the Michael manuscript.]

What, then, remains except that all who recognize those joys of the heavenly homeland should direct themselves toward the course of a more perfect life?

## CHAPTER XXXV

“My soul melted away” (Song 5:6).

In the exposition of the Gospel, Homily 25 (no. 2), the following was added: “My soul melted away.”

The human mind that does not seek the appearance of its Creator is wickedly hard, because it remains cold within itself. But if it has already begun to burn with desire, it runs, melted by the fire of love, to follow the one whom it loves.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

“His head is finest gold” (Song 5:11).

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXXIV (no. 26), the following was added: “His head is finest gold.”

In sacred discourse, the designation of gold sometimes signifies the brightness of divinity, sometimes the splendor of the heavenly city, sometimes charity, sometimes the gleam of worldly glory, and sometimes the beauty of holiness.

By the name of gold, the innermost brightness of divinity itself is signified, as the appearance of the bridegroom is described in the Song of Songs: “His head is finest gold.” For nothing among metals is more brilliant than shining gold. The bridegroom’s head is called gold because through his humanity he rules over us by the radiance of his divinity.

Again, by the name of gold the splendor of the heavenly city is understood, as John testifies that he saw it, saying: “The city itself was pure gold, like pure glass” (Rev. 22:12). The gold of which that city consists is said to be like glass, so that by the gold its brightness and by the glass its transparency may be signified.

Again, by the name of gold charity is indicated. The same John saw an angel who spoke with him girded around the breasts with a golden belt (Rev. 1). For the breasts of the heavenly citizens, since they are no longer subject to the fear of punishment and are not loosened from one another by any division, bind themselves together solely by charity. To have a golden belt around the breasts is to restrain all the movements of changeable thoughts by the bond of love alone.

Again, by the name of gold the gleam of temporal glory is expressed, as it is said through the prophet: “Babylon is a golden cup” (Jer. 51:7). For what is signified by the name Babylon except the glory of this world? It is called a golden cup because, while it displays temporal things as beautiful, it intoxicates foolish minds with their desire, so that they seek temporal splendor and disdain invisible beauty.

The first woman, Eve, was intoxicated by this golden cup of her own accord. Concerning her, the truth of the narrative says: “When she desired the forbidden tree, she saw that it was beautiful to look at and pleasing to behold, and she ate” (Gen. 3:6). Babylon’s golden cup, therefore, is so called because, while it displays the appearance of outward beauty, it withdraws the perception of inward uprightness.

Again, by the name of gold the radiance of holiness is understood. Jeremiah laments that the Jewish people were changed from the splendor of righteousness into the darkness of wickedness, saying: “How the gold has become dim, how the finest color has been changed!” (Lam. 4:1). As we said above, gold is darkened when the beauty of righteousness is abandoned amid the succeeding darkness of sins; the finest color is changed when the splendor of innocence is turned into the ugliness of guilt.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

“You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army arranged for battle” (Song 6:3).

In the commentary on Ezekiel, Homily 8 (no. 6), the following was added: “You are beautiful, my beloved,” etc.

Because Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” and by its name the heavenly homeland is expressed, the holy Church is called sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, because her life and desire are already compared with the vision of inward peace. In loving her Creator and desiring to see his appearance—of whom it is written, “Into which the angels long to look” (1 Pet. 1:12)—she is said, through the very desires of her love, to be made like the angels.

The more pleasing she becomes to God, the more she is made terrifying to the evil spirits. How she is terrifying is shown by the comparison that follows: “as an army arranged for battle.” Why is the holy Church to be feared by her enemies like an army in battle? This comparison is not without profound meaning and must therefore be considered carefully.

We know and it is certain that an army in battle appears terrifying to its enemies when it is so closely packed and densely formed that it seems broken at no point. But if it is arranged so that an empty space is left through which the enemy can enter, it is no longer terrifying to its foes.

So, when we set the battle line of spiritual warfare against evil spirits, it is supremely necessary that we always be united and bound together by charity, never found divided through discord. For however many good works there may be in us, if charity is absent, a place is opened in the battle line through the evil of discord, through which the enemy can enter in order to strike us.

[Note: Here this chapter ends, and with it the first part of Paterius’s exposition, in the Michael manuscript.]

The ancient enemy does not fear chastity in us if it is without charity, since he is not weighed down by flesh and cannot be dissolved into its lust. He does not fear abstinence, since he does not use food and is not driven by bodily necessity. He does not fear the distribution of earthly possessions if charity is absent from that work, since he himself has no need of the support of riches.

But he greatly fears true charity in us—that is, the humble love that we show one another—and he is exceedingly envious of our concord, because we hold on earth what he lost in heaven by refusing to hold it.

It is therefore rightly said: “Terrible as an army arranged for battle,” because the evil spirits fear the multitude of the elect to the extent that they see them fortified against themselves and gathered together through the harmony of charity.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

“Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from what is hidden within you” (Song 6:6).

In the commentary on Ezekiel, Book II, Homily 4 (no. 8), the following was added: “Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from what is hidden within you.”

The cheeks are the spiritual fathers of the holy Church, who now shine within her through miracles and appear venerable, as it were, upon her face. For when we see many performing wondrous deeds, prophesying future events, abandoning the world completely, and burning with heavenly desires, the holy cheeks blush like the rind of a pomegranate.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

“Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn?” (Song 6:9).

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book IV (no. 19), the following was added: “Who is this,” etc.

The Church is called dawn because she is changed from the darkness of her sins into the light of righteousness. Hence the Bridegroom marvels at her in the Song of Songs, saying: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn?”

The Church of the elect rises like the dawn: she abandons the darkness of her former wickedness and turns herself toward the brilliance of a new light.

In that light which will be revealed at the coming of the strict Judge, the body of the condemned enemy does not see the rising of the dawn, because when the strict Judge comes for judgment, each wicked person, weighed down by the darkness of his own merits, does not know with how great a brilliance the holy Church rises into the inner light of the heart.

Then the mind of the elect is lifted on high to be illumined by the rays of divinity; and the more it is flooded by his regard, the more it is raised above itself as grace shines forth.

The holy Church becomes full dawn when she utterly loses the darkness of mortality and ignorance. At the judgment, therefore, she is still dawn, but in the kingdom she is day. For although at the judgment she begins to see the light together with the restoration of her bodies, in the kingdom her vision is brought to completion more fully.

The rising of the dawn, then, is the beginning of the Church’s growing brightness, which the reprobate cannot see, because, weighed down by the burden of their evils, they are dragged from the sight of the strict Judge into darkness.

## CHAPTER XL

Likewise, concerning the preceding subject.

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIX (nos. 2–3):

The holy Church, desiring the rewards of heavenly life, is called dawn because, while she abandons the darkness of sins, she shines with the light of righteousness.

Yet there is something subtler that we should consider when we reflect on the nature of the early light, or dawn. Dawn announces that night has passed, but it does not yet display the full brightness of day. While it drives away the night, it receives the day and holds a light mingled with darkness.

What, then, are all of us who follow the truth in this life except dawn or early light? For we already perform certain things that belong to the light, yet in some respects we are still not free from the remnants of darkness.

## CHAPTER XLI

“Your nose is like a tower that is in Lebanon” (Song 7:4).

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXXI (no. 85), the following was added: “Your nose is like a tower,” etc.

What is signified by the nose except the provident discernment of the saints? A tower of watchfulness is placed on high so that an approaching enemy may be seen from afar. Therefore the nose of the Church is rightly said to be like a tower in Lebanon, because the provident discernment of the saints, as it carefully looks about on every side from its elevated place, detects sin before it comes; and the more watchfully it foreknows it, the more strongly it avoids it.

## CHAPTER XLII

Likewise, concerning the preceding subject.

In the commentary on Ezekiel, Homily 11 (no. 7):

What is signified by the nose except the discernment of watchers? This nose is said both to be like a tower and to be of Lebanon, because the discernment of those set over others must always be fortified by circumspection and stand at the height of life—that is, not lie in the valley of weak action. For just as a tower on a mountain is set up for observation so that enemies who are coming may be seen farther off, so the life of a preacher must always remain fixed on high, that, after the manner of nostrils, it may distinguish the stench of vices from the fragrances of virtues, foresee from afar the assaults of evil spirits, and by its prudence make the souls entrusted to it cautious.

## CHAPTER XLIII

“Let us rise early for the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers are bringing forth fruit” (Song 7:2).

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XII (nos. 60–61), the following was added: “Let us rise early for the vineyards,” etc.

The vineyards flower when the minds of the faithful propose good works; but they do not bear fruit if, overcome by certain errors, they are weakened from what they had proposed. Therefore one must not look merely to see whether the vineyards flower, but whether the flowers grow strong for the bearing of fruit. For it is no wonder if someone begins good things; but it is very wonderful if he perseveres in a good work with right intention. Hence it often happens that, if right intention is not retained in a good work, even that work which is believed to be good is lost.

## CHAPTER XLIV

“Who is this who comes up whitened?” (Song 8).

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XVIII (no. 87), the following was added: “Who is this,” etc.

Because the holy Church does not naturally possess heavenly life, but, as the Spirit comes upon her, is fashioned by the beauty of gifts, she is described not as white but as made white.

## CHAPTER XLV

“Set me as a seal upon your heart” (Song 8:6).

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XXIX (no. 12), the following was added: “Set me as a seal upon your heart.”

For a seal is placed upon things so that they may not be violated by the presumptuousness of plunderers. The Bridegroom, therefore, is placed as a seal upon the heart when the mystery of his faith is impressed upon the keeping of our thought, so that the unfaithful servant—namely, our adversary—when he sees hearts that have been sealed, may not presume to break into them by temptation.

## CHAPTER XLVI

“Love is strong as death” (Song 8:6).

In the exposition of the Gospel, Homily 11 (no. 2), the following was added: “Love is strong as death.”

Just as death kills the body, so the charity of eternal life kills us to the love of bodily things. For whomever it has completely absorbed, it renders as it were insensible to outward earthly desires.

## CHAPTER XLVII

“Our little sister is small, and has no breasts” (Song 8:8).

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XIX (no. 19), the following was added: “Our little sister is small,” etc.

Before the holy Church advanced through growth in virtue, she could not offer the breasts of preaching to weak hearers. But the Church is called grown when, united to the word of God and filled with the Holy Spirit, she is made fruitful through the ministry of preaching in the conception of children; and those whom she brings forth by exhorting, she bears by converting.

[Note: In the *Moralia*, the manuscripts read *fetatur*, “is made fruitful.”]

## CHAPTER XLVIII

“You who dwell in the gardens of your friend, listen; make me hear your voice” (Song 8:13).

In the commentary on Ezekiel, Homily 14 (no. 4), the following was added: “You who dwell in the gardens of your friend,” etc.

For every soul dwells in gardens which is green with hope and filled with good works. The hope of this world is dry, because everything loved here withers in haste. And the apostle Peter admonishes us to hasten, saying: “Unto an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled and unfading” (1 Pet. 1:4).

Therefore she who already dwells in the gardens ought to make her Bridegroom hear her voice—that is, to utter the song of good preaching, in which he whom she desires may delight. For the friends listen: namely, all the elect, who desire to hear words of life so that they may return to life in the heavenly homeland.

## CHAPTER XLIX

“Flee, my beloved, flee” (Song 8:14).

In the exposition of blessed Job, Book XVII (no. 39), the following was added: “Flee, my beloved, flee.”

We say that something flees from us whenever we do not retain in memory what we wish to recall. Therefore, after the holy Church has described the Lord’s death, resurrection, and ascension, filled with the prophetic spirit she cries to him: “Flee, my beloved, flee.” As though she said: You who became comprehensible through the flesh, exceed, in your divinity, the understanding of our mind, and remain incomprehensible to us in yourself.

# PART TWO

IN WHICH THREE BOOKS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT ARE EXPLAINED: WISDOM, ECCLESIASTICUS, AND THE PROPHETS

[Col. 0917]

# BOOK ONE

On Testimonies concerning the Book of Wisdom

## CHAPTER I

On temptations from vices or scourges, concerning the words: “God tested them and found them worthy of himself” (Wis. 3:5).

[Col. 0917A]

(*Moralia on Job*, Book XXIII, chapters 25–26, nos. 51–53.)

By the ordering of hidden providence, we are permitted to be tempted in such a way that, while through divine protection we advance in virtue, we may also remember from the recollection of our weakness what we are by our own frailty; and while through receiving the gift we perform works of virtue, we may offer from the recollection of our weakness the sacrifice of humility.

Sometimes, after strength has increased, not only do vices tempt, but scourges also chastise. When we are tempted by vices, kindly providence deals with us lest we be exalted by the virtues through which we advance. But when we are worn down by scourges, we are warned by rebuking evils lest the world’s blandishments deceive us.

While vices tempt us, they humble in us the virtues that are making progress. While scourges tempt us, they root out the pleasures of this world that arise in the heart. Through tempting vices we learn what we are in ourselves; through smiting scourges we learn what we must flee in this world. By the former we are restrained lest we be inwardly exalted; by the latter we are repressed lest we desire anything outwardly.

Therefore, while we are in this life, it is necessary both to be worn down by scourges and sometimes to be tempted by vices. For whether amid the labors of scourges or the contests of vices, not only is our weakness made known to us, but we also recognize how far we have advanced in virtue.

No one recognizes his strength in peace; for if wars are lacking, proofs of virtues do not come forth. The soldier who boasts that he is strong in peace is unwise. Often the merits of strength are disclosed through the adversities of scourges, because, when bodily delight is diminished by rebuking scourges, the strong things of virtue which lay hidden, as it were, under the flesh are disclosed.

No one recognizes how much he has advanced except amid adversities. For when prosperity is present, proofs of strength cannot be seen. Hence elsewhere it is written: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he revealed it” (Ps. 41:9), because each person receives the grace of the heavenly gift in the tranquility of rest, but shows in the disturbance of adversity how much he has received.

Let us therefore be struck by paternal corrections, so that we may recognize how much we are advancing. For by the Lord’s scourges bodily delight is worn down and the strength of our virtues is revealed.

[Note: In Saint Gregory, the reading is “the bones are revealed.” Henceforth these variant readings will be inserted in brackets in the text with the word “Text,” that is, “the text of Saint Gregory.” —Editor.]

Our outward beauty is marred by the adversity of this world itself, but what lay hidden within us is shown. For when the Apostles had been beaten, they were commanded not to speak any more in the name of the Lord [Text: Jesus] (Acts 5); but they rejoiced greatly that they had been considered worthy to suffer insults for his name, and they answered their adversaries confidently: “It is necessary to obey God rather than men” (ibid., 23).

Behold, amid adversities the strength of virtue and faith shone forth more vigorously. Hence it is said of them: “God tested them and found them worthy of himself” (Wis. 3:5). They were tested by the adversity of blows, but were found worthy by the manifestation of virtues [Text: “the uncovering of the bones”].

Thus each person’s strength is disclosed through adversities; and while what is weak is worn down by scourges, what is strong but hidden in us is revealed through this. For in the very adversity of temptation not only is the strength of fortitude uncovered, but also the weakness of humanity is known. Everyone who is tested shows how much he has advanced in God and, amid the afflictions of scourges themselves, learns how weak he is [Text: also] in himself.

## CHAPTER II

That the saints convert sinners by their example, concerning the words: “The righteous shall shine and run to and fro like sparks among reeds” (Wis. 3:7).

(*Moralia*, Book XXXIII, chapter 3, no. 7, and Book XXIV, chapter 22, no. 49.)

“The righteous shall shine and run to and fro like sparks among reeds.” By the reed-bed he means the life of worldly people, who, in the manner of reeds, through temporal glory seem outwardly to rise to great heights, but inwardly become empty of the solidity of truth.

But when holy men are mingled with sinners, they set them ablaze with the fire of their examples and reduce to ashes everything for which they strive. For, consumed by the flame of piety, when they behold the frailty of their own condition, they recognize themselves as nothing but ash, so that, softened from the hardness of their pride, they may say in repentance: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust” (Ps. 102:15).

## CHAPTER III

That we are scourged by insensible things for our sins, concerning the words: “The whole world will fight for them against the senseless” (Wis. 5:21).

(*Moralia*, Book VI, chapter 21, no. 14.)

By the hidden deserts of minds, open scourges of punishments also come forth, and the malice of our perception demands that we be struck by insensible things [Text: “be struck”].

For behold, we see that, for our correction, the awaited rain is withheld from parched earth and the cloudy air is dried by the burning sun. The sea rages with swelling storms and cuts off some who have undertaken the crossing; for others, a wave raised into a mound [Text: heap] obstructs the desired journey. The earth not only diminishes the shoots of fertility but also consumes the seeds it has received.

In all these things one plainly sees what is said of the Lord: “The whole world will fight [Text: with] for him against the senseless” (Wis. 5:12). The world fights with the Lord against the senseless when, in the punishment of offenders, the hostility of the elements does service (*Homily 35 on the Gospels*, no. 1).

For everything that we have received for the use of life we have turned to the use of sin; but all things which we have bent to the use of wickedness are turned to the use of vengeance upon us. We have turned the tranquility of human peace to the use of vain security. We have loved our pilgrimage on earth as the habitation of our homeland; we have reduced bodily health to the use of vices; we have twisted the abundance of plenty not to the need of the flesh but to the perversity of pleasure. We have compelled even the serene allurements of the air to serve our love of earthly delight.

It therefore rightly remains that all things strike us together, because all things [Text: which] had together served our vices after being wickedly subjected to them; so that for as many joys as we formerly had in the world unharmed, we may afterwards be compelled to feel from them [Text: it] so many torments.

## CHAPTER IV

That God is known through visible things, concerning the words: “He shows himself to them cheerfully in the ways, and meets them in every providence” (Wis. 6:17).

[Col. 0918D]

[Col. 0919A] (*Moralia*, Book XXVI, chapter 12, no. 17.)

If we watchfully behold outward things, by those same things we are called back to inward realities. The wondrous works of visible creation are indeed the footprints of our Creator. We cannot yet see him himself, but already we tend toward his vision if we marvel at him in what he has made.

We call creation his footprints because through the things that are from him we go on, by following, to him. Hence Paul says: “His invisible things are understood and seen through the things that have been made, even his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. 1:20). And thus it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “For from the greatness and beauty of the creature the Creator can be seen by understanding” (Wis. 13:5).

God does not yet make himself inwardly known as he is to our mind scattered outward by its sin; but while he displays outwardly the beauty of his creation, he gives us, as it were, certain nods and shows what we should pursue within. In a wondrous way he leads us by these outward forms to inward things. By showing outwardly these wonderful things—which he is not—he intimates in their immense wonder what he is.

Hence it is written of Wisdom: “He shows himself to them cheerfully in the ways, and meets them in every providence” (Wis. 6:17). The ways to the Creator are the works of creation when considered: as we behold what has been made, we marvel at the power of its maker.

In these ways Wisdom meets us in every providence, because the power of the maker is set before us for inquiry in everything that appears to have been wonderfully made. Wherever the soul turns, if it attends watchfully, in those same things it finds God, through which he left traces of his power.

From consideration of the things it loves and serves, it again comes to know them; and through the things by which it fell perversely, it is recalled when converted. For where we fell, there we lean in order to rise; and, as it were, by rising there, we set fast the hand of consideration where, falling through the foot of slippery love, we lay neglected.

Since we fell from invisible things through visible ones, it is fitting that we should lean back toward invisible things by those same visible things, so that by the descent through which the soul came to the lowest things, it may return by a corresponding ascent to the highest, and rise by the same steps by which it fell, while, as was said, things well considered call us back to God just as things wrongly chosen separated us from him.

## CHAPTER V

On the arrogant, concerning the words: “May God grant me to speak these things according to true judgment” (Wis. 7:15).

(*Moralia*, Book XXIII, chapter 17, no. 31.)

Although arrogant people grasp certain hidden matters by understanding, they cannot experience their sweetness; and even if they know how such things are, they do not know how they taste. It often happens that they speak powerfully, yet do not know how to live in accordance with what they say.

Hence a certain Wise Man aptly says: “May God grant me to speak these things according to true judgment” (Wis. 7:15). For *sententia* is named from *sensus*, “perception”; and he who understands rightly desires to speak not from knowledge alone but also from lived perception, desiring to experience by feeling, rather than merely to state by knowing, what he says.

But the mind of arrogant persons does not penetrate the meaning of its own utterances, because from the inward taste it is thrown back, by a right judgment, toward the favors it loves outwardly. True knowledge, however, affects rather than exalts; it makes those whom it fills not proud but lamenting.

## CHAPTER VI

How the Holy Spirit is mobile and stable (Wis. 7:22).

(Book I, Homily 5 on Ezekiel, no. 9.)

The Holy Spirit, God, is coeternal before the ages with the Father and the Son; all things are within him, and there is nowhere that he is not, as it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. 1:7).

Yet, when the praise of Wisdom was being described, it was said: “For in her is a spirit of understanding, holy, one, manifold, subtle, mobile” (ibid., 7:22); and shortly afterward, “human, stable.” These words raise a great question for us: why this Spirit, who fills all things, is said to be at once stable and mobile.

But if we turn to ordinary human usage, we shall more quickly find the speaker’s meaning. A man who moves everywhere throughout the region in which he is, undoubtedly meets one everywhere and is suddenly found where he is not expected.

Therefore the almighty Spirit, in order to signify that he is present everywhere, is said to be at once stable and mobile: stable because by nature he contains all things, but mobile because he meets people everywhere even without their knowing it. Thus, holding all things, he is called stable; showing himself present to all, he is called mobile.

## CHAPTER VII

Why God permitted his sinless Son to be scourged, concerning the words: “Though you are just, you order all things justly” (Wis. 12:15).

(*Moralia*, Book III, chapter 14, no. 26.)

The mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, came to endure the scourges of our mortality in order to extinguish the sins of our transgression. Though equal to the Father in divinity, he came for our sake to scourges in the flesh; for he would not have received scourges unless, in redeeming us, he had taken the form of condemned man.

Unless the first man had sinned, the second would never have come to the reproaches of suffering. For unless the devil had drawn the first Adam, through voluntary vice, into the death of the soul, the second Adam, without vice, would not have come voluntarily into the death of the flesh.

Thus he was afflicted without cause in respect of himself: born in flesh, he had committed no sins of his own, yet he received bodily punishment without guilt. Hence he speaks through the Prophet, saying: “Then I paid what I did not seize” (Ps. 68:6).

Another man was created for paradise and wished in pride to seize the likeness of divine power; yet the Mediator, without guilt, paid the penalty of this pride. Hence a certain Wise Man says to the Father: “Though you are just, you order all things justly; yet you condemn him who ought not to be punished” (Wis. 12:15).

But we must consider how he is just and orders all things justly if he condemns one who ought not to be punished. Our Mediator ought not to have been punished for himself, because he committed no contagion of guilt; but if he had not received an undeserved punishment, he would never have freed us from deserved death.

Therefore, though the Father is just, in punishing the just man he orders all things justly, because by this he justifies all things: he condemns him who is without sin for sinners, so that all the elect might rise to the height of justice by the fact that he who is above all endured the losses of our injustice.

He was afflicted without cause with respect to himself, but not without cause with respect to our deeds; for the rust of vice could not be purged except by the fire of torment. Thus he who came without vice voluntarily subjected himself to torment, so that the punishments due to our iniquity might justly lose their guilty subjects, because they had unjustly held him who was free from them.

He was therefore afflicted both without cause and not without cause: he had indeed committed no sins in himself, but by his own blood he wiped away the stain of our guilt.

## CHAPTER VIII

That the divine word accommodates itself to the character of its hearers, concerning the words: “You gave them bread from heaven, prepared without labor, containing every delight and the sweetness of every flavor” (Wis. 16:20).

[Col. 0920D] (*Moralia*, Book VI, chapter 16, no. 22.)

One person is raised up by pride, another is bowed down by the weight of fear, another burns with lust, another pants after avarice, another casts himself down by laxity, another boils with anger. But through the teaching of sacred discourse humility is given to the proud and confidence offered to the fearful; the lustful person is cleansed of impurity by the pursuit of chastity, the greedy person is moderated from the heat of ambition by self-restraint, the lax person is raised by the uprightness of zeal, and the angry person is restrained from the stirring of his rashness [Text adds: “God waters all things with waters”].

God shapes the power of his word in each person according to the diversity of dispositions, so that in his discourse each may find that by which he may produce the germ of the necessary virtue.

Hence a certain wise man says of the sweetness of manna: “You gave them bread from heaven, prepared without labor, containing every delight and the sweetness of every flavor.” Manna contained every delight and the sweetness of every flavor because it gave, in the mouths of spiritual persons, a taste according to the will of those eating it.

Thus the divine word, both suited to all and not inconsistent with itself, accommodates itself to the character of its hearers; and when each elect person profitably understands it according to his own measure, he turns the manna he has received into a desired flavor [Text: “turns it”].

## CHAPTER IX

That no one can excuse himself on the ground of ignorance of sin (concerning Wis. 17:10).

(Moral. book XXVII, chapter 25, no. 48.) Almighty God the Creator made man a rational creature, distinct from all insensible and irrational beings, so that he cannot be ignorant of what he has done. For by the law of nature he is compelled to know whether what he does is wrong or right. Why, then, does he come to judgment for his action, if he could not be ignorant of what he did? [Text: if he was able to be ignorant of what he did.] Even those, therefore, who, instructed by the Lord’s commandments, despise them—or who disdain to be instructed [Text: erudiri]—know whether the things they do are good or evil. For if they do not know that they are doing good, why do they boast of certain deeds for display? [Text: in display (ostentatione).] Again, if they are ignorant that they are doing evil, why do they avoid the eyes of others in those same actions? They themselves are witnesses against themselves, because they know that what they do is evil, and they fear that it may be seen by others. For if they truly did not believe it to be evil, they would by no means fear that it should be seen by others.

Hence it is rightly said by a certain Wise Man: “Since wickedness is cowardly, it gives testimony of condemnation” (Wisdom XVII, 10). For when fear, striking at the conscience concerning its deed, rebukes it, wickedness itself bears witness that what it does is deserving of condemnation. And whenever anyone commits unlawful acts, he is afraid of what he does; thus fear itself is an open witness to the condemnation of wickedness, because what is done is both feared, and yet the evil that is feared is not overcome.

Let the wicked, therefore, flee human eyes; they certainly cannot flee themselves. Because they know the evil that they do, they have their conscience as a witness and their own reason as a judge. In the sin they commit, therefore, they first encounter the judgment of their own reason against themselves, and afterward they are brought to the strict examination of the eternal court.

Perhaps this is what is said through the Psalmist: “Deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts” (Psalm XLI, 8). For, by the wondrous order of a hidden dispensation, the evil that is done is not permitted to remain unknown; the sinner already condemns himself in his conscience by his own judgment, and after his self-condemnation hastens toward the sentence of the eternal Judge. Thus for deep to call upon deep is to pass from one judgment to another.

Let the holy preachers go forth and rebuke the deeds of sinners; let wicked hearers despise the words of the righteous; let them defend their wickednesses as much as they wish, and, by defending their shameful deeds more shamelessly, multiply them. Certainly, they themselves are witnesses against themselves in their conscience, and they have no excuse. For by the very fact that God made man a rational creature, he seals the hand of every human being, so that each may know his own deeds.

# BOOK TWO. On Testimonies concerning the Book of Ecclesiasticus

[Col. 0921]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the temptations of converts, concerning: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear” (Ecclesiasticus II, 1)

[Col. 0921B]

(Moral. book XXIV, chapter 11, from no. 25 through 34.) We must carefully observe that there are three stages in which each person is afflicted by the anxiety of sorrow and afterward is immediately recalled from sorrow to the security of joy. If we attend to this vigilantly, we find these three stages of sorrow and joy alternating in the mind of every elect person in the following ways: conversion, temptation, and death.

In the first stage, which we have called the stage of conversion, there is deep sorrow, when each person, considering his sins, wishes to break the shackles of worldly cares, to walk along God’s way through the expanse of a secure manner of life, to cast away the heavy burden of temporal desires, and to bear the Lord’s light yoke in free service. For when he reflects upon these things, that familiar carnal pleasure comes before him—the pleasure that, having long since grown old, binds him more tightly the longer it has held him, and permits him to depart from it only more slowly.

What sorrow and anxiety of heart there are when the spirit calls him in one direction and the flesh recalls him in another; when love of a new manner of life invites him one way, while the habit of an old perversity assails him another; when on one side he burns with desire for his spiritual homeland, and on the other he endures within himself a carnal concupiscence that in some way delights him even against his will.

But because divine grace does not permit us to be afflicted by these difficulties for long, it quickly leads us, by consoling us, through the bonds of our sins once broken, into the freedom of a new manner of life; and the joy that follows refreshes the preceding sadness. Thus the mind of each convert rejoices all the more in reaching what it desires, the more it remembers having sorrowfully labored for it. Immense joy arises in the heart, because through the hope of security it is already drawing near to the one whom it desires.

But lest a convert should now believe himself to be holy, and lest security itself afterward overthrow one whom the struggle of sorrow was unable to overcome [Text: lest security, which the struggle of sorrow could not overcome, afterward overthrow him], God’s dispensation permits him, after his conversion, to be wearied by the goads of temptations. Through conversion he has indeed crossed the Red Sea, but in the wilderness of the present life enemies still meet him face to face. We have already left past sins behind us, like Egyptians destroyed, but harmful vices still confront us like other enemies, seeking to block the journey we have begun toward the promised land. Our former faults, like pursuing adversaries, have already been struck down by divine power alone; but the goads of temptations, like other enemies, come against us face to face, and must be overcome by our labor.

Conversion plainly produces security, but security is accustomed to become the mother of negligence. Therefore, lest security give birth to negligence, it is written: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus II, 1). He did not say “for rest,” but “for temptation,” because while our enemy sees that we remain in this life and are rebelling against him more and more, he strives all the more fiercely to conquer us. He neglects to strike those whom he feels he possesses by an undisturbed right. Against us, however, he is stirred with greater violence the more he is expelled from our heart as though from the right of his own dwelling.

The Lord himself prefigured this in his own person under a certain dispensation: he permitted the devil to tempt him only after baptism, so that he might indicate to us a sign of the conversion to come—namely, that his members, after they had advanced toward God, would then endure more dangerous snares of temptation.

After the first stage of sorrow and joy, which each person recognizes through the discipline of conversion, this second stage arises. Lest security be dissolved into negligence [Text: lest the negligence of security be dissolved], the convert is afflicted by the force of temptation. Each person is often received, at the very beginning of conversion, with great sweetness of consolation, but afterward experiences the hard labor of testing.

There are three stages of converts: beginning, middle, and perfection. In the beginning there are found [Text: they find] the caresses of sweetness; in the middle, the struggles of temptation; and at the end, the perfection [Text: completion] of fullness. First, therefore, sweet things receive and console them; afterward, bitter things exercise them; and only then do agreeable and exalted things strengthen them.

A man first cherishes his bride with sweet caresses, but after she has been joined to him he tests her with harsh reproaches; once she has been tested, he possesses her in secure thoughts. Thus the Israelite people, when God called them from Egypt, promising to lead them into the sacred marriage of the mind, first received the caresses of signs as a kind of pledge. Once joined to him, they were exercised by trials in the wilderness; after being tested, they were strengthened in the promised land by the fullness of virtue.

First, therefore, through miracles they tasted what they should desire; afterward they were tested by labor, to see whether they knew how to preserve what they had tasted; and finally they deserved to receive more fully what they had preserved after being tested by labors. Thus the life of every convert is gently delighted by its beginning, tested by the harsh middle, and strengthened by the fullness that follows perfection (Moral. book XXIV, chapter 11, no. 29).

Often the struggles of temptations are as long as the caresses of beginnings had been. Often greater sweetness is given in the beginning and less in the labor of testing; sometimes less sweetness is given in the beginning and greater labor in testing. Yet the labor of temptation is never followed by a perfection of steadfastness that is disproportionate to it, because each person is rewarded with the fullness of perfection according to the measure of the struggle.

Often a convert falls into this error: when he has been received by the sweetness of the beginning through certain gifts of grace, he supposes that he has received the confirmation of perfection and considers himself to possess the fullness of completion, not knowing that these are still merely the caresses of the beginning. Thus, when the sudden storm of temptation strikes him, he imagines himself despised and abandoned by God. If he did not rashly trust his beginning, he would, while still placed in prosperity, prepare his mind for adversity and afterward resist the approaching vices as firmly as he had foreseen them more wisely.

If he foresees these things more calmly, he endures them; nevertheless, even if he foresees them, he does not altogether avoid their struggles, because the course of our journey is never completed without the dust of temptation.

Often a convert is agitated by goads of temptation such as he does not remember having experienced before the grace of conversion—not because the root of that temptation was absent then, but because it was not visible. The human mind, occupied by many thoughts, often remains in some way unknown even to itself, so that it does not know what it is enduring. For while it is scattered among many things, it is removed from inward knowledge of itself.

But if it desires to be free for God alone and cuts off the branches of its many kinds of thought, then it freely sees what proceeds from the innermost root of the flesh.
