When a thistle grows on a road, the feet of travelers trample it, and the constant passage of those who cross it rubs away its surface so that it does not appear. Although the thorns growing above are not visible, the hidden root nevertheless remains below. If the feet of travelers cease to trample and crush it, it soon rises and advances to the surface, and through its thorn brings into public view whatever was living secretly in the root.

So, in the hearts of worldly people, the hidden root of certain temptations often does not readily appear, because, lying as it were on the road of activity, it is trampled by the feet of passing thoughts and pressed down by countless cares, like many travelers, so that it cannot be seen. But if, through the grace of conversion, the crowd of cares is removed from the road of the heart, so that no insolence of action crushes it and no tumult of thoughts presses it down, then what lay hidden is recognized; then the thorn of temptations freely pricks from the root of vices.

Against this thorn the hand of a person living well must act, so that, insofar as possible, what is hidden may not be covered but torn out by the roots. Until this happens, the thorn so troubles the mind of every convert that he often feels himself almost overcome by its sudden blow and fears disastrously that its wound, inflicted to the very marrow, will destroy him.

Often, however, when the goads of temptations become habitual, they spread and become not sharper but longer-lasting. They hurt less but infect more, because the longer they cling to the mind, the less frightening they become through familiarity.

In the midst of these things the mind, caught off guard, is stretched here and there, scattered by the many waves of temptation, and, provoked repeatedly from different directions, often does not know which vice is confronting it or which it should attack first. Hence it frequently happens that, while the vices rising up too fiercely torment it and incline the mind resisting them toward an almost desperate fall, the convert becomes afraid of the lofty path he chose for his remedy. He is like one who, having been led to a height, totters, whereas he had stood firm in a low place.

But because merciful God permits us to be tested by temptations, he does not allow us to be rejected, as it is written: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure it” (I Corinthians X, 13). He quickly comes to our aid through consolation [Text: comes to our assistance], moderates the goads of temptation as they rise up, and calms the movements of thought that assail us with inward peace. Immediately the soul perceives immense joy from heavenly hope when it sees the evil it endured defeated.

After these two stages—namely, confession and testing—have been passed through sorrow and joy, a third remains, in which one still endures sorrow but also attains joy. After the struggles of conversion and the distress of testing, a hard temptation still remains, because no one can come to the joys of perfect freedom unless he has first paid the debt owed by human condition.

Each convert, watchfully and carefully concerned for himself, never ceases silently to consider how strict the eternal Judge will be when he comes. He daily looks toward his own end and reflects what account of his life he will have to render before the severity of such justice. Even if he has avoided all the wrong deeds that he was able to recognize, when he is about to stand before the strict Judge he fears most those things within himself that he does not recognize.

For who can discern how many evils we commit from moment to moment through the very unstable movements of our thoughts? It is easy to avoid perverse actions, but it is exceedingly difficult to cleanse the heart from unlawful thought. Often, even against their will, something steals into the thoughts of the elect; they carefully observe it within themselves and recognize how great its guilt is before God’s eyes.

Although they always fear strict judgment concerning all these things, they fear them most intensely when, coming to pay the debt of human condition, they see themselves drawing near to the strict Judge; and fear becomes sharper as eternal retribution draws nearer. Fear grows as the justice of retribution approaches, and, as the payment required by the flesh presses upon them, the closer the strict judgment seems almost to be touched, the more vehemently it is dreaded.

Even if they remember that they have never knowingly omitted the things they know, they nevertheless fear the things they do not know, because they are altogether unable to judge and comprehend themselves. As their departure presses upon them, they are terrified by a more subtle fear.

Hence our Redeemer, approaching the dissolution of the flesh while preserving the appearance of his members, began, in agony, to pray at greater length. For what could he have been asking for himself in agony, he who, while on earth, bestowed heavenly things with power? But as death approached, he expressed in himself the struggle of our mind, the force of the terror and fear that we suffer when, through the dissolution of the flesh, we draw near to eternal judgment.

Nor is any soul terrified without reason at that time, when after a little while it encounters what it cannot change for eternity. We consider that we have not been able to pass through the way of the present life without guilt. We also consider that even what we have done laudably is not without some guilt of our own if we are judged apart from mercy.

For who among us could surpass or even equal the life of the fathers who came before us? Yet David says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm CXLII, 2). When Paul said, “I am conscious of nothing against myself,” he prudently added, “but I am not thereby justified” (I Corinthians IV, 4). James says: “We all offend in many things” (James III, 2). John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 2).

What, then, will the tablets do when even the pillars tremble? Or how will the movable shrubs stand if even the cedars are shaken by the whirlwind of this fear? [Text: immovable shrubs.] As the dissolution of the flesh approaches, therefore, even the soul of the righteous is sometimes troubled by the terror of punishment; and whatever peace it may have been able to taste in this life is shaken when the moment of death intervenes.

But because the souls of the righteous are often cleansed from lesser defilements by the very fear of death, and from the dissolution of the flesh already begin to perceive the joys of eternal retribution, they frequently grow cheerful through a certain contemplation of eternal reward even before they are stripped of the flesh. While they pay the debt of their former condition, they already enjoy the joy of a new gift.

The mind of each elect person, therefore, is afflicted during these three stages: either by the labor of conversion, or by the temptation of testing, or by the fear of dissolution [Text: is worn down]; afterward it is refreshed by great joys of security.

## CHAPTER II. On hypocrites, concerning: “Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two ways” (Ecclesiasticus II, 14)

[Col. 0925B]

(Moral. book I, chapter 26, no. 3.) “Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two ways” (Ecclesiasticus II, 14). The sinner enters the land by two ways when what he displays in action belongs to God, but what he seeks in thought belongs to the world. For there are some who, in the good things they do, seek not an inward reward but outward approval.

## CHAPTER III. On lovers and despisers of the world, concerning: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclesiasticus II, 16)

(Moral. book VII, chapter 30, no. 45.) Often, when the brevity of the present life is loved as though it were going to last a long time, the soul is broken away from eternal hope and takes delight in present things. When it thinks that the time remaining for it to live is long, it suddenly abandons life and finds eternal realities that it can no longer avoid.

Hence it is said by a certain Wise Man: “Woe to those who have lost endurance.” Those lose endurance who, while imagining that they will remain a long time among visible things, abandon hope of invisible things. When the mind is fixed upon present things, life comes to an end, and they suddenly arrive at unforeseen punishments, which, deceived by their presumptions, they had believed would either never reach them or would come only late.

Hence it is written: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (I Thessalonians V, 2). Because his approach to seize the soul is not perceived, he is compared to a thief in the night. He should therefore be feared as though always coming, precisely because his future arrival cannot be foreseen by us.

Hence holy men, because they constantly consider the brevity of life, live as though dying each day. They prepare themselves all the more firmly for things that endure, the more they continually weigh transient things according to their end. Hence the Psalmist, observing the life of the sinner fleeing at a swift pace, says: “A little while yet, and the sinner will be no more” (Psalm XXXVI, 10).

Hence James rebukes the minds of those who presume, saying: “What is our life? [Text: your life.] It is a vapor that appears for a little while” (James IV, 15). What follows without end is immense, and whatever comes to an end is small. What tends, by the course toward the setting of its time [Text: by the course of its time toward its setting], should not seem long to us, so that it may not be. As it is drawn out moment by moment, those very moments that pass it by drive it onward; and from the place where it is seen to be held, it is driven so that it cannot be held. [Text: those very moments delay it.]

## CHAPTER IV. On good or bad shame, concerning: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory” (Ecclesiasticus IV, 25)

(Book I, Homily 10, on Ezekiel, no. 17.) Just as shame is praiseworthy in relation to evil, so it is blameworthy in relation to good. To blush at evil is wisdom; to blush at doing good is foolishness. Hence it is written: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory” (Ecclesiasticus IV, 25).

Whoever is ashamed of the evils he has committed and repents reaches the freedom of life; but whoever is ashamed to do good falls from the state of uprightness and moves toward condemnation, as it is said through the Redeemer: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty” (Luke IX, 26).

## CHAPTER V. On God’s patience toward sinners, concerning: “Do not say, ‘I have sinned, and what sad thing has happened to me?’” (Ecclesiasticus V, 4)

(Moral. book XXV, chapters 4 and 5, nos. 5 and 6; book I, Homily 13, on the Gospels, no. 3.) Divine severity punishes the wicked person more harshly in judgment precisely because it endured him for a longer time. The sentence is all the stricter in proportion as great patience was extended to the sinner for a longer period.

When the wicked person practices everything he wickedly desires for a long time, and, because he is not struck immediately but his punishment is deferred until the end, he does not believe that God sees his wicked action. He supposes that God does not see the deeds of the unjust because he delays just punishment, and he regards God’s great patience as a kind of negligence. The wicked person himself likewise believes that God does not see him whenever he sins with impunity.

A certain Wise Man says to him: “Do not say, ‘I have sinned, and what sad thing has happened to me?’” (Ecclesiasticus V, 4). He does not wish to correct the wickedness for which he has not yet suffered a fitting punishment. The more mercifully he has been awaited, the more wickedly he has been provoked to sin; and, despising the patience of heavenly forbearance, he has increased the guilt from which that patience should have led him to correct himself.

Often, too, because he does not suddenly receive the punishment he deserves, he does not consider the very fact that he does to be displeasing to God. Let him go on now, therefore, and presumptuously break out into whatever blasphemies he pleases; let him fulfill the wickednesses of his desires [Text: pleasures], seize what belongs to others, and gorge himself on the oppression of the innocent. Because he has not yet been struck, let him suppose either that the Lord does not see his ways or, worse still, that the Lord approves them.

The eternal and sudden blow will surely come—yes, it will come. Then he will know that everything is seen by God, when, through an unforeseen end, he sees himself condemned in recompense for everything. Then he will perceive that the true Judge had observed all things, when he can no longer escape the deserts of his evils.

Let no one, therefore, say that God does not see human deeds when he observes some wicked person freely piling up his wickednesses. Let no one disregard God’s forbearance, because he exercises stricter justice in judgment in proportion to the longer patience he has granted before judgment.

Hence Paul says: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God” (Romans II, 4).

Hence the Psalmist says: “God is judge, just, strong, and long-suffering.” In intending to call him long-suffering, he first called him just, so that you may know that the one whom you see patiently bearing the sins of those who offend for a long time will at some point also judge strictly.

“For the Most High is a patient requiter” (Ecclesiasticus V, 4). He is called a patient requiter because he both endures human sins and requites them: those whom he tolerates for a long time so that they may convert, he condemns more harshly if they do not convert.

## CHAPTER VI. On prayer, concerning: “Do not repeat a word in your prayer” (Ecclesiasticus VII, 15)

(Moral. book X, chapter 15, no. 27, etc.) When the mind lifts itself toward God through the discipline of prayer, it is immediately broken away from confidence in hope if the conscience of its guilt accuses it as it strives upward, or if the memory of sins not yet overcome bites it while it is intent upon prayer. For it distrusts that it can receive what it desires when it remembers that it is still unwilling to do what it has heard from God.

Hence John says: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask from him we shall receive” (I John III, 21). Hence Solomon says: “Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law—his prayer will be accursed” (Proverbs XXVIII, 9).

The heart condemns us in petition when it remembers that it resists the commands of the one whom it beseeches; and prayer becomes accursed when it turns away from the judgment of the law. It is certainly fitting that a person should be excluded from the benefits of one whose commands he does not wish to obey.

In this matter the healthy remedy is that, when the mind reproaches itself from the memory of sin, it should first mourn in prayer the fact that it has erred. Then, when the stain of error has been wiped away with tears, the face of the heart may appear clean before its Creator in petition.

But one must take the greatest care not to fall back again into what one rejoices to have cleansed through tears, lest, when the sin that was mourned is committed again, even the lament itself be made light of in the sight of the just Judge.

We must carefully remember what is said: “Do not repeat a word in your prayer” (Ecclesiasticus VII, 15). By this saying the Wise Man certainly does not prohibit us from repeatedly seeking forgiveness, but from repeating sins. To repeat a word in prayer is to commit, after weeping, what must again be mourned. It is as though he were saying plainly: “When you have mourned your evil deeds, do not again do what you must once more lament in your prayers.”

Before the times of prayer, therefore, whatever can be reproved in prayer should be carefully examined. Let the mind hasten to present itself, even when it is not praying, as it desires to appear before the Judge at the very time of prayer.

Often, when we are free from prayer, we turn over in our minds certain impure or unlawful things. But when the mind has raised itself to the practice of prayer, it suffers the images of those things to recoil from it—things under whose weight it had previously been willingly crushed in its leisure.

Often we are gladly occupied with worldly cares; and when afterward we devote ourselves to prayer, the mind cannot lift itself to heavenly things, because the weight of earthly concern has plunged it into the depths.

Sometimes, however, we shake the heart free from everything and resist even unlawful movements while we are not praying [Text: vertimus, “we turn over,” for versamus, “we turn about/occupy ourselves with”]. Yet because we commit sins less often, we are slower to forgive the sins of others; and the more anxiously our mind fears to sin, the more strictly it abhors what another has done wrong against it. Thus a person is found to be slower to grant forgiveness precisely in proportion as, by advancing, he has become more cautious about committing a fault.

But what could be found worse than this stain of sorrow, which in the sight of the Judge does not defile charity but kills it? Any fault pollutes the life of the soul; but resentment preserved against one’s neighbor destroys it. It is fixed in the mind like a sword, and its blade pierces the hidden parts of the inner being. If it is not first drawn out from the pierced heart, no divine help is obtained through prayers, because medicines of healing cannot be applied to wounded members until the iron has first been removed from the wound.

Hence Truth himself says: “Unless you forgive people their sins, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins” (Matthew VI, 13). Hence, in establishing the form of prayer, he placed the condition of mercy, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (ibid. 12), so that we may first do with our neighbor the good thing that we ask from God when moved to compunction.

We truly pray, then, when we neither commit the evils that are forbidden to us nor, out of personal zeal, retain the wrongs committed against us.

Our mind is weighed down by grave shame at the time of its prayer if either its own conduct still defiles it or the resentment preserved against another’s wickedness accuses it (Moral. book XVI, chapter 20). For just as we are known and visible to human beings through the face of the body, so we are known and visible to God through the inward image. But when we are weighed down by the guilt of sin, we are afraid to lift the face of our heart toward God. When it is supported by no confidence in good works, the highest part of the mind trembles to look upward, because conscience itself accuses it.

But when guilt has been washed away by the tears of repentance, and sins are mourned in such a way that they are not again committed, great confidence arises in the mind, and the face of our heart is lifted to behold the joys of heavenly retribution.

## CHAPTER VII. How crimes are avoided through remembrance of death, concerning: “In all your works remember your last end” (Ecclesiasticus VII, 40)

(Moral. book XIII, chapter 29, no. 33.) “In all your works remember your last end, and you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus VII, 40). Whoever considers what he will be like at death always becomes fearful in his conduct. He desires nothing that passes away, resists all the desires of the present life, and considers himself almost dead because he is not ignorant that he will die.

A perfect life is an imitation of death; while the righteous carefully preserve [Text: practice] it, they escape the snares of sins.

## CHAPTER VIII. On pride, concerning: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclesiasticus X, 15)

(Moral. Book XXXI, chapter 45, no. 87; Book XXXIV, chapter 23, no. 47.) Pride is the root of every evil, as Scripture attests when it says: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclus. 10:15). Its first offspring, however, is vainglory. Indeed, seven principal vices spring from this poisonous root: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. For because he grieved that we had been captured by these seven vices, our Redeemer came, full of the sevenfold Spirit of grace, to the spiritual battle of liberation.

From these seven principal vices, however, other shoots of vices arise. From vainglory come disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, stubbornness, discord, and presumptuous innovations. From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing in one’s neighbor’s misfortunes, and grief at his prosperity. From anger proceed fear of mind [Text: swelling of mind], insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies. From sadness arise malice, resentment, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness regarding the commandments, and wandering of mind toward illicit things. From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, acts of violence, and hardness of heart against mercy. From gluttony are propagated foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding. From lust are generated blindness of mind, lack of consideration, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and dread or despair of the future.

Of these principal vices, therefore, five are spiritual and two carnal. Yet each is joined to the others by such kinship that one is produced only from another. The first offspring of pride is vainglory; when it has corrupted the mind it oppresses, it gives birth to envy, because, while it desires the power of a celebrated name, it wastes away lest anyone else should attain it.

Envy likewise generates anger, because the more deeply the soul is wounded by the inward injury of jealousy, the more it loses the tranquility of gentleness. And because it is as though a suffering limb were touched, the hand of an opposing action is therefore felt as pressing it all the more heavily.

From anger, too, sadness arises, because the more disorderly the disturbed mind agitates itself, the more it confounds itself by yielding to agitation; and when it has lost the sweetness of tranquility, nothing feeds it except the sorrow that follows from its disturbance.

Sadness, in turn, leads to avarice, because when the troubled heart has inwardly lost within itself the good of joy, it seeks outside itself something by which it may be consoled. It desires to acquire external goods all the more eagerly because it has no joy to which it may inwardly return.

After these, the two carnal vices remain: gluttony and lust. It is clear to everyone that lust is born from gluttony, since, in the arrangement of the bodily members, the genitals appear to be supported by the belly [Text: joined to it]. Thus, when one is nourished immoderately, the other is undoubtedly aroused to shameful acts.

Pride, therefore—the root and queen of the vices—once it has begun fully to conquer the heart, immediately drags it away to be ravaged by these seven principal vices. Just as the root is covered beneath the earth while branches spread outward from it, so pride conceals itself inwardly, while open vices immediately sprout from it. No evils would emerge publicly unless it first held the mind captive in secret. Within, what later foams outwardly in action first boils up in elation.

But since the discussion of pride has afforded an occasion for speaking of it, we ought to examine it with greater subtlety and care, and show how great and what kind of thing it comes to human minds, and by what means and in what manner it steals upon them.

Other vices attack only those virtues by which they themselves are destroyed: anger attacks patience, gluttony attacks abstinence, and lust attacks continence. But pride, which we have called the root of the vices, is not satisfied with the extinction of a single virtue. It rises against every member of the soul and, like a general and destructive disease, corrupts the entire body, so that whatever is done while it is invading—even if it appears to be a virtue—is performed not for God but solely in the service of vainglory.

For when pride breaks into the mind, it seizes it like a tyrant taking possession of a besieged city. And the richer the person it captures, the harsher it becomes in its dominion, because the more extensively virtue is practiced without humility, the more broadly pride rules.

Whoever receives its tyranny within himself with a captive mind first suffers this harm: with the eye of his heart closed (cluso; Text: clauso), he loses the equity of judgment. Everything done well by others displeases him, while the things he himself has done—even wrongly—alone please him. He always despises the works of others and always admires what he himself does, because whatever he has done, he believes he has done uniquely. In what he displays, his desire for glory makes him favor himself in thought; and when he supposes that he surpasses everyone in everything, he walks about with himself through the broad spaces of his thoughts and silently proclaims his own praises.

Sometimes the mind is led to such great elation that, in what causes it to swell, it is also unrestrained in the ostentation of speech. But the more shamelessly each person exalts himself in his own eyes, the more easily ruin follows.

Hence it is written: “The heart is exalted before ruin” (Prov. 16:18). Hence Daniel says: “The king was walking in the palace of Babylon; and he answered and said: ‘Is this not Babylon the great, which I built as a royal residence, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my splendor?’” (Dan. 4:26).

Immediately he adds how swiftly vengeance restrained this swelling: “While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: ‘To you it is said, O King Nebuchadnezzar: Your kingdom shall pass from you; and they shall drive you away from human beings, and your dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals; you shall eat grass like an ox, and seven times shall pass over you’” (ibid., 28).

Behold: because the swelling of his mind had extended as far as open words, the Judge’s patience immediately burst forth into sentence. He struck him more severely in proportion as his pride had raised itself more immoderately. And because he had enumerated the good things in which he had taken pleasure, he heard the evils enumerated in which he would be punished.

It must be understood, however, that this very elation of which we are speaking possesses some people through secular goods and others through spiritual ones. One swells with gold, another with eloquence; one with lowly and earthly things, another with lofty and heavenly virtues. Yet one and the same thing is taking place before the eyes of God, although, when it enters human hearts, it is concealed from their sight under different garments.

When someone who formerly took pride in earthly glory later becomes proud of holiness, elation has not at all departed from his heart. It has come to him in its accustomed way, but, so that it might not be recognized, it has changed its clothing.

It must also be understood that pride tempts superiors in one way and subjects in another. To a superior it suggests in his thoughts that he has grown above the rest solely through the merit of his life. If he has ever done anything good, it thrusts this insistently before his mind; and when it suggests that he has been especially pleasing to God, so as easily to persuade him of its suggestions, it summons as evidence the reward of the authority entrusted to him, saying: “If almighty God had not seen that you were better than all these, he would not have placed them under your rule.”

Immediately it raises his mind and shows him that those subject to him are base and useless, so that he now regards no one as worthy of being addressed with equanimity. Thus the tranquility of his mind is soon turned into anger. While he despises everyone and reproves the character and life of all without moderation, he expands into anger all the more uncontrollably [Text: unrestrainedly] because he considers those entrusted to him unworthy of himself.

But when pride incites the hearts of subjects, it strives above all to make them utterly neglect consideration of their own actions and always, in silent thoughts, become judges of their ruler. While they inopportunely scrutinize in him what they ought to reproach, they never see in themselves what they ought to correct.

Thus they perish all the more horribly because they turn their eyes away from themselves: on the road of this life they stumble and fall while looking elsewhere. They do indeed assert that they are sinners, but not so sinful as to have been entrusted to such a harmful person in authority. As they despise his actions and disregard his commands, they descend into such madness that they do not believe God governs human affairs, because they resent being committed to one whom they think they may rightly reproach.

Thus, while they grow proud against their ruler, they also swell against the judgments of the Creator; and while they judge the life of their shepherd, they attack the very wisdom that orders all things [Text: of the one who orders all things].

Often they insolently oppose the words of their ruler and call the same arrogance of speech “freedom.” Thus elation almost presents itself as freedom on behalf of righteousness [Text: thus, indeed, elation presents itself], just as fear often substitutes itself for humility. For just as many remain silent out of fear and nevertheless think that they are silent out of humility, so some speak through the impatience of elation and yet believe that they speak through the freedom of righteousness.

Sometimes, however, subjects do not at all reveal the insolence they feel. Those whose loquacity can scarcely be restrained sometimes fall silent solely because of the bitterness of inward resentment. Withdrawing the words of their impudence through the pain of their mind, they habitually speak badly but remain silent even worse. When, through sinning, they hear something about correction, they indignantly suppress even the words of their response.

When they are dealt with harshly, they often burst forth into complaints about that very harshness. But when their teachers gently anticipate them, they become still more indignant at the very humility with which they have been approached; and their minds are kindled more extensively in proportion as their weakness is judged more thoughtfully.

Because they do not know humility, the mother of the virtues, they lose the benefit of their labor, even if they appear to perform some good works. The sturdy height of a rising structure is not secured when it is not solidified by the strength of a foundation laid upon rock. What they build therefore grows only toward ruin, because they do not first provide the foundations of humility beneath the mass of the structure.

We may rightly expose what they are inwardly if we reveal it briefly in outward matters. In all who swell with proud thoughts about themselves there is shouting in speech, bitterness in silence, dissipation in cheerfulness, fury in sadness, dishonor in conduct, propriety in appearance, loftiness in bearing, and resentment in reply.

Their minds are always strong for inflicting insults but weak for enduring them; slow to obey but importunate in provoking others [Text: in provoking them]; sluggish regarding what they ought and are able to do, but ready for what they neither ought nor are able to do.

They cannot be bent by any exhortations toward what they do not spontaneously desire. But toward what they secretly desire, they seek to be compelled, because, while they fear becoming degraded by their desire, they wish to endure force in the very exercise of their will.

Since, then, we have said that human minds are tempted differently through carnal things and through spiritual things, let those who are tempted by carnal things hear: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6). Let those who are tempted by spiritual things hear what is said to some after miracles: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27).

Again, we have said that superiors and subjects are tempted differently. Let superiors, when they glory in the authority they have received, hear what is said in Abraham’s voice to the rich man in torment: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your lifetime” (Luke 16:2). Let subjects, when they burst forth into complaint against their rulers, hear what is said in the voices of Moses and Aaron to the murmuring people: “Your murmuring is not against us but against the Lord; for what are we?” (Exod. 16:8).

Against this disease of the soul, let us all hear what the Teacher, the Truth, teaches when he says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

For this reason the only-begotten Son of God assumed the form of our humility; for this reason the invisible One appeared not only visible but also despised; for this reason he endured the mockery of insults, the reproaches of ridicule [Text: disgrace], and the torments of suffering, so that humble God might teach human beings not to be proud.

How great, then, is the virtue of humility [Text: humilitatis], for the sake of truly teaching it alone, that One who is great beyond estimation became small even unto suffering? Because the pride of the devil provided the origin of our ruin, the humility of God was found to be the instrument of our redemption.

Our great enemy, created great among all things, wished in his elation to appear above all things. But our Redeemer, remaining great above all things, deigned to become small among all things.

We reveal the cause of elation and disclose the foundations of humility more effectively if we briefly touch upon what the author of death urges and what the creator of life says [Text: commands]. The former teaches minds subjected to him nothing other than to seek the summit of exaltation, to surpass all equals through the swelling of the mind, to rise above the fellowship of all human beings in lofty elation, and to set themselves even against the power of the Creator. Of such people the Psalmist says: “They passed over in the disposition of their heart; they thought and spoke wickedness; they spoke iniquity against the Most High” (Ps. 72:7–8).

The latter, coming to spittle, slaps, blows, a crown of thorns, the cross, the spear, and death, admonishes his members, saying: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26).

Since, therefore, our Redeemer rules the hearts of the humble, while the author of death is king over the proud, we recognize clearly that pride is the most evident sign of the reprobate, whereas humility is the sign of the elect. When it is known which quality each person possesses, it is discovered under which king he serves.

Everyone carries, as it were, a kind of title in his works by which he readily shows under whose rule he serves. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:16).

Those who serve under the king of pride, even if they sometimes assume an appearance of humility, cannot conceal themselves entirely in everything, because their pride, unable to remain hidden for long, is exposed in one action when it is covered by another.

But those who serve under the king of humility are always fearful and watchful on every side. They fight against the arrows of elation and, as though against blows coming at them, guard especially the eye within their own body, while principally protecting humility within themselves.

### CHAPTER IX — That in adversity we ought to remember prosperity, and in prosperity adversity; on the passage: “In the day of good things do not be forgetful of evil things” (Ecclus. 11:27)

(Moral. Book III, 3, chapter 9, no. 16.) Great consolation in tribulation is found when, while suffering adversity, we recall to mind the gifts of our Creator. What confronts the mind through grief does not break it if what raises it up through grace comes more quickly to mind.

Hence it is written: “In the day of good things do not be forgetful of evil things, and in the day of evil things do not be forgetful of good things” (Ecclus. 11:27).

Whoever receives gifts but, in the time of gifts, does not also fear the scourges falls through joy into elation. Whoever, however, is worn down by scourges but, in the time of scourges, does not console himself with the gifts he has happened to receive is destroyed by utter despair of mind.

Thus both must be joined, so that one may be supported by the other: the memory of the gift should temper the punishment of the scourge, while the suspicion and fear of the scourge should bite into the joy of the gift.

### CHAPTER X — On love of God and neighbor; on the passage: “A friend is not recognized in prosperity, and an enemy is not concealed in adversity” (Ecclus. 12:8)

(Moral. Book VII, chapter 24, no. 28.) There are two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbor. Love of neighbor is begotten through love of God, and love of God is nourished through love of neighbor.

For whoever neglects to love God plainly does not know how to love his neighbor. We make fuller progress in love of God when we are first cast by love of neighbor into the embrace of that love [Text: charity].

Because love of God generates love of neighbor, when the Lord was about to say through the Law, “You shall love your neighbor,” he first said, “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:5; 10:12). Thus he might first fix the root of his love in the soil of our hearts, so that fraternal love might afterward bud forth through its branches.

And again, because love of God grows strong through love of neighbor, John bears witness, saying: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20).

This divine love, however, is born through fear, but as it grows in affection it is transformed into love.

Often almighty God, ordering all things with wondrous design so that it may become known how far each person is from charity toward him and his neighbor, or how far he has advanced in it, casts some down with scourges and supports others with success. When he temporarily abandons some, he reveals what evil lies hidden in the hearts of others.

For often those who have honored us without comparison when we were prosperous pursue us when we are miserable. When someone is loved while established in prosperity, it is very uncertain whether prosperity or the person is being loved. The loss of happiness, however, tests the force of love.

Hence it is said [Text: a certain wise man says well]: “A friend is not recognized in prosperity, and an enemy is not concealed in adversity” (Ecclus. 12:8).

Prosperity does not indicate a friend, nor does adversity conceal an enemy, because the former is often hidden by respect for our prosperity, while the latter is revealed by the confidence born of adversity.

Whoever despises his neighbor because of adversity is openly convicted of having not loved him in prosperity. And since almighty God strikes some so that he may both educate those who are struck and offer those who are not struck an opportunity for good works, whoever despises the one who has been struck drives away from himself an opportunity for virtue. He rises all the more wickedly against the Maker (actorem; Text: auctorem, “author”) because he recognizes neither his compassion in the other’s well-being nor his justice in the other’s wound.

### CHAPTER XI — On those who show mercy to others but nevertheless do not abandon injustice; on the passage: “What good is he to whom he is evil?” (Ecclus. 14:5)

(Moral. Book XIX, chapter 23, no. 38.) He performs pious works well who knows first to preserve what is just, so that the stream of mercy poured upon one’s neighbors may be drawn from the fountain of justice.

For many bestow upon their neighbors what seem to be works of mercy but do not abandon acts of injustice. If [quod; Text: qui] they truly desired to show mercy to their neighbors, they ought first to show mercy to themselves by living justly.

Hence it is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30:24). Whoever therefore wishes to show mercy to his neighbor must necessarily draw the origin of mercy from himself. For it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 19:19).

How, then, is one compassionate toward another through mercy who, by continuing to live unjustly, is still impious toward himself? Hence it is said: “Whoever is wicked to himself, to whom will he be good?” (Ecclus. 14:5).

To show mercy fully and outwardly to those in need, two things are necessary: a person who gives and something that is given. But the person is incomparably better than the thing.

Therefore, whoever gives external substance to a needy neighbor but does not guard his own life from wickedness gives his possession to God and himself to sin. He offers to the Creator what is less and preserves what is greater for iniquity.

### CHAPTER XII — That mercy and humility ought to be present in those who give alms; on the passage: “With every gift do not cause sadness by an evil word” (Ecclus. 18:16)

(Moral. Book XXI, chapter 19, no. 29, etc.) Two virtues—namely, humility and compassion—ought to be so joined to one another that they support each other through reciprocal works [Text: that they are always supported by reciprocal action], so that humility, when it honors one’s neighbor, does not abandon the grace of generosity, and compassion, when it gives, does not swell with pride toward the one receiving indulgence.

Thus compassion should support humility toward one’s neighbor, and humility should support compassion, so that, when you see someone in need who shares your nature, you neither cease to cover him through compassion [Text: impiety] nor neglect to honor through pride the one whom you cover.

For there are some who, as soon as needy brothers ask them for what is necessary, first hurl insulting words at them and afterward give the gifts. Although they fulfill the ministry of compassion through their possessions, they lose the grace of humility through their words. Thus they often appear [Text: he appears] to pay compensation for the injury already inflicted when they give gifts after the insults.

What they give when asked is not a great work, because by the very gift they make they scarcely cover the excess of their speech.

To them it is rightly said: “With every gift do not cause sadness by an evil word.” And again: “Behold, a word is above a good gift; and both are with a justified person” (Ecclus. 18:16–17). That is, the gift should be offered through compassion, and a good word should be given through humility.

On the other hand, some do not take care to support needy brothers with material things when they are able, but merely encourage them with flattering words. Holy James’s preaching severely reproves them, saying: “If a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, be warmed and filled,’ but you do not give them what is necessary for the body, what good is that to you?” (James 2:15–16).

The apostle John also admonishes them, saying: “My little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18).

Therefore [Text: indeed], our love must always be displayed both through respectful speech and through the ministry of generosity.

It greatly helps to subdue the giver’s pride if, while giving earthly things, he carefully considers the words of the heavenly Teacher, who says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

If we acquire eternal dwellings through their friendship, those who give must undoubtedly consider that we are offering gifts to patrons rather than bestowing presents upon the needy.

Hence Paul says: “Let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may also be a supply for your need” (2 Cor. 8:14). We should carefully reflect that those whom we now see as needy we shall one day see as abundant, and that if we who are seen as abundant neglect to give, we shall one day be needy.

Whoever now gives temporal assistance to the poor will later receive from it (ea; Text: eo) something perpetual—so to speak, he cultivates the earth for harvest, and the earth returns more abundantly what it has received.

It remains, therefore, that elation should never arise from a gift, since the rich person, from what he gives to the poor, acts so that the poor person may not be poor forever.

Whoever exalts himself through elation over the one to whom he gives anything commits inwardly, through pride, a greater fault than the reward he obtains outwardly through generosity. He himself becomes bare of inner goods when he despises the naked person whom he clothes, because he acts so as to become worse than himself by considering himself better than his needy neighbor.

The person without clothing is less needy than the person without humility. Hence, when we see those who share our nature lacking external goods, we must consider how many interior gifts we ourselves lack, so that our thoughts may not raise themselves above the poor when they carefully see that we are more truly needy because we are needy inwardly as well.

There are some who do not know how to extend the compassion of their hearts even to strangers, but pity only those whom they have come to know through constant familiarity. Among them, familiarity has more force than nature, since they give what is necessary to some not because they are human beings but because they are known.

Yet everyone who is in need is, by that very fact that he is a human being, no longer unknown to us; and in the mind itself nature ought to have greater force than familiarity.

### CHAPTER XIII — On avoiding minor sins; on the passage: “Whoever neglects small things gradually falls” (Ecclus. 19:1)

(Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 33.) “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall.” Whoever neglects to mourn and avoid the smallest sins falls away from the state of justice—not suddenly, indeed, but gradually and altogether.

### CHAPTER XIV — On those who defend their sins; on the passage: “You have sinned; do not add again” (Ecclus. 21:1)

[Column 0934A]

(Moral. Book IV, chapter 21, no. 39.) “You have sinned; do not add again.” He adds sin to sin who even defends what he has done wrongly, who joins to his guilt the protection of a defense [Text: to the darkness of his guilt].

### CHAPTER XV — On those afflicted by the loss of temporal goods; on the passage: “The slothful man is pelted with ox dung” (Ecclus. 20:2)

(Moral. Book XV, chapter 4, no. 5.) “The slothful man is pelted with ox dung.” The joys of the present life, which the unjust consider great goods, the just regard as dung. Whoever is unwilling to follow God grows sluggish in his love of eternal life; and whenever he is struck by the loss of temporal possessions, he is afflicted by those very things that just men despise as dung.

Whoever, then, is worn down by the blow of external [Text: earthly] things—what else is he than scourged [Text: pelted] with ox dung?

### CHAPTER XVI — On hypocrites; on the passage: “Pass on, guest, and adorn the table” (Ecclus. 29:39)

[Column 0934B]

(Moral. Book XXXII, chapter 13, no. 19.) “Pass on, guest, and adorn the table.”

A guest is said to adorn the table by passing on because, if someone placed at God’s altar seeks his own glory through good works, the altar’s praise is extended through the display of his holiness, yet he himself is not counted among the citizens by the Lord. His reputation benefits others, while he himself passes by as a stranger to God.

He adorned the table by passing on, because he wished to remain at the sacred rites [Text: he did not wish to remain], having hastened in mind toward human praise through everything he attempted to do.

For some people are rejected by God [Text: are hay] and yet are counted by human beings as holy, since life displays one thing before human eyes while conscience intends another before the divine judgments.

### CHAPTER XVII — On good and bad superiors; on the passage: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself” (Ecclus. 32:1)

[Col. 0934C]

*(Moral. Book XXIII, ch. 1, no. 8; Book XXIV, ch. 25, no. 22, and ch. 23, no. 50.)* Every spiritual preacher of the holy universal Church carefully considers in all that he says how he may avoid exalting himself through the vice of pride in what he rightly preaches; how his life may not disagree with his tongue; how, while announcing peace in the Church, he may not lose it within himself by speaking well and living badly. Rather, he strives with the utmost diligence, against the malicious rumors of his adversaries, both to defend by his speech the life he leads and to adorn by his life what he says.

In all this he seeks not his own glory but that of the author [Text: auctor, “originator”], and he does not consider that he received all the grace of wisdom which he received in order to speak through his own merits, but through the intercessions of those for whom he speaks. Thus, while he casts himself down beneath others, he rises above them, because it greatly advances his own reward when he attributes to the merits of others the good works he is able to perform; he judges himself unworthy of everyone, even while living more worthily than all.

For he knows that the good things made known to people can scarcely exist without danger. Although he recognizes himself to be wise, he would nevertheless wish to be wise without being seen to be so; he fears in every way whatever is revealed about him through speech, and, if permitted, desires to remain silent, since he sees that silence is safer for many. He considers those happier who, within the holy Church, are concealed by silence in a lower position. Yet, because he is driven by the force of charity to speak in defense of the holy Church, he undertakes the ministry of speech out of necessity, but seeks the leisure of silence out of a great desire: he preserves the latter by his desire and performs the former in his ministry.

The arrogant, however, do not know this manner of speaking. They do not speak because circumstances require it; rather, they wish [Text: seek] circumstances to arise so that they may speak. As we have often observed, they also demand from their subjects an excessive fear of themselves; they wish to be revered not so much for the Lord as in place of the Lord. Within, they exalt themselves through the swelling of their hearts, and they despise all their subjects in comparison with themselves. They do not console them by condescending to them [Text: counsel them], but oppress them by domination, because they raise themselves up in lofty thought and do not recognize that they are equal to those whom it has fallen to them to govern.

Against this swelling of rulers it is said: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. XXXII, 1). Rebuking this swelling in shepherds through the prophet, the Lord says: “But you ruled them with harshness and with power” (Ezek. XXXIV, 4). For the very good things they say to their subjects they utter by domination rather than by counsel, since they imagine that to say anything to them as equals would be to abase themselves. They rejoice in the distinction of their rank, not in the equality of their condition.

Every proud ruler slips into the sin of pride [Text: apostasy] as often as he takes pleasure in governing people and rejoices in the distinction of his honor. He does not consider under whom he stands, and he exults as though he were not equal to those who are his equals.

From what source does this root of vices spring up in the hearts of rulers, unless from imitation of the one who, despising the fellowship of the angels, said: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14)? Therefore, whenever rulers exalt themselves in governing others, they are separated through the fall of pride from the service of the supreme Ruler; and when they despise their subjects as their equals, they do not acknowledge His dominion over them, under whom all are equal.

Because they rule by domination, they draw their subjects toward ungodliness by the example of their pride. They would lead them along the path of piety if they displayed before their eyes examples of humility. An ungodly leader is one who, through swelling pride, strays from the path of truth and, while rushing headlong himself, invites those who follow him toward the precipice. An ungodly leader is one who, through examples of swelling pride, points out the way of error.

Paul feared that he might be an ungodly leader [Text: a leader of ungodliness] when he restrained the exaltedness of his authority, saying: “Nor seeking glory from men, neither from you nor from others, although we could have been burdensome as apostles of Christ; but we became little ones in the midst of you” (1 Thess. II, 6). He had become little in their midst because he feared that, if he claimed the honor of his exaltedness among his disciples, he would display examples of pride. He feared, surely, that while he sought for himself the authority of pastoral power, the flock of his subjects [Text: his subject] might follow him toward the precipice, and that he might lead those who followed him into ungodliness, having undertaken the office of piety.

Therefore, it is necessary that the one who presides carefully consider what examples he offers to his subjects. He must know that he must live for as many people as those over whom he presides, and he must watch attentively lest he become swollen with pride in the fact that he is a ruler; lest he demand the rights of legitimate authority too immoderately; lest the right of discipline be changed into the harshness of pride; and lest, by the very means through which he could restrain his subjects from perversity, he instead pervert the hearts of those who look upon him. Otherwise, as has been said, he may become a leader of ungodliness through the office of piety.

No one should undertake leadership over people who does not know how to precede them by living well, lest the one chosen for the purpose of correcting the faults of others commit himself what he ought to cut away. Therefore, those who preside should look around themselves in every direction [Text: look carefully around], so that they may live for their subjects; so that they may both hide within the bosom of their minds the good they do and, by means of it, offer examples of right action for the advancement of those who follow them; so that, while noticing and correcting the faults of their subjects, they may nevertheless not become swollen through the force of that same correction; so that they may gently tolerate certain matters once corrected, yet not dissolve the bonds of discipline through that gentleness; so that they may overlook certain matters by tolerating them, yet not, by overlooking them, permit them to grow.

These things are burdensome, and unless divine grace supports one, they are difficult to maintain. Therefore, the coming of the Judge is rightly described in the Book of Wisdom: “He will appear terribly and swiftly, for the strictest judgment will be upon those who rule” [Text: judgment will be made against them] (Wis. VI, 6).

Since the power of governance frequently gives rise to the fault of pride, the beginning of pride must immediately be cut away at its very root, so that, when it secretly arises, it may then be watchfully severed; lest it gain strength through advancement and become hardened through habit. For it is difficult for anyone to detect in himself an old and ingrained pride, because the more we suffer from this vice, the less we see it. Pride is generated in the mind just as darkness is generated in the eyes: the farther it spreads, the more intensely it narrows the light [Text: narrows it].

Little by little, therefore, pride grows within the heart; and when it has spread more widely, it completely closes the eye of the oppressed mind, so that the captive soul can both suffer the condition of pride and yet be unable to see what it suffers.

Hence the greatest care must be taken that the one placed over the governance of people preside within himself, in the hidden chamber of his mind, upon the throne of humility. When he is attended outwardly by others as he judges, he must continually look with a watchful eye toward the Judge before whom he himself will one day stand to be judged for these matters. Thus, the more anxiously he now trembles before Him whom he does not see, the more securely he may behold Him when he sees Him.

Let him therefore weigh this: perhaps he scarcely suffices to give an account to the strict Judge for his own soul alone; yet, at the time when he must render an account before Him, he presides over so many subjects to be governed that, so to speak, he alone possesses as many souls. If this thought continually consumes the mind, it suppresses every swelling of pride. Then the prudent ruler will be called neither proud [Text: nor apostate] nor an ungodly leader in proportion as, through anxious reflection, he regards the authority he has received not as an honor but as a burden.

For the one who now wishes to be a judge does not then wish to behold the Judge. The sins committed out of love for possessing authority cannot be counted. Authority is governed well only when it is retained not out of love but out of fear. In order that it may be administered rightly, it must first be imposed not by desire but by necessity. Once received, it must neither be abandoned out of fear nor embraced out of lust, lest one either become more wickedly proud under the guise of humility by fleeing and despising the order of divine providence, or cast off the yoke of the heavenly Ruler because he takes pleasure in private rule over others.

Thus, when authority is received, it must not be loved out of desire but patiently endured through long-suffering, so that it may then be a salutarily light burden at the judgment precisely because it is now recognized as a patiently heavy burden in the ministry.

## CHAPTER XVIII — How the Devil Seeks to Deceive the Just through Their Household, on the Words: “Beware of your children, and pay attention to your household” (Ecclus. XXXII, 26)

*(Moral. Book III, ch. 8, no. 13.)* “Beware of your children, and pay attention to your household.” The ancient adversary strives to bend the state of our mind not only through himself, but also through those who cling to us. When he does not overthrow our heart by his own persuasion, he creeps toward it through the tongues of those who cling to us.

Hence it is said through the prophet: “Let each one beware of his neighbor, and let him not trust in any brother” (Jer. IX, 4). Again it is written: “A man’s enemies are his household” (Matt. X, 36). For when the cunning adversary sees that he is repelled by the hearts of the good, he seeks out those who are greatly loved by them, and speaks flattering words through those who are loved more than the others, so that, when the force of love pierces the heart, the sword of persuasion [Text: his] may easily break into the innermost defenses of uprightness.

## CHAPTER XIX — In How Many Ways the Images of Dreams Affect the Mind, on the Words: “Dreams have led many astray” (Ecclus. XXXIV, 7)

*(Moral. Book VIII, ch. 24, no. 42.)* Sometimes dreams are generated by fullness or emptiness of the stomach; sometimes by deception; sometimes by thought together with deception; sometimes by revelation; and sometimes by thought together with revelation. We all know the first two by experience, while we find the four that follow in the pages of sacred Scripture.

For unless dreams were generally produced through deception by the hidden enemy, the wise man would never have said: “Dreams have led many astray, and vain illusions” (Ecclus. XXXIV, 7). Or again: “You shall not practice divination, nor observe dreams” (Lev. XIX, 26). These words plainly show what detestation is due to them, since they are joined with divinations.

Again, unless dreams sometimes proceeded from thought together with deception, Solomon would not have said: “Dreams follow many cares” (Eccles. V, 2). And unless dreams sometimes arose from the mystery of revelation, Joseph would not have seen himself in a dream as destined to be preferred to his brothers (Gen. XXXVII), nor would Truth [Text: the angel] have warned Mary’s husband in a dream to flee with the child to Egypt (Matt. II).

Again, unless dreams sometimes proceeded from thought together with revelation, the prophet Daniel, interpreting Nebuchadnezzar’s vision, would not have begun from the root of thought by saying: “You, O king, began to think upon your bed what would happen after these things; and He who reveals mysteries has shown you what is to come” (Dan. II, 29). A little later he says: “You saw, and behold, as it were one great statue; that statue was large, and the statue [Text: stature] was lofty and stood before you,” and so forth (ibid., 31).

Thus, when Daniel reverently indicates the dream and its fulfillment [Text: indicates the dream for fulfillment] and makes clear from what thought it arose, it is plainly shown that it is often generated from thought together with revelation.

But since dreams vary according to so many kinds of causes, one ought to believe them with correspondingly greater difficulty, since it is not easy to discern from what impulse they come. Often the evil spirit promises prosperity even to those whom he intercepts while awake through their love of the present life; and those whom he sees fearing adversity he attacks more harshly through images of dreams, so that he may affect the undiscerning mind in different ways and confuse it, either lifting it up by hope or casting it down through fear.

Often, too, he strives to affect the hearts of the holy with dreams, so that they may at least for a moment be diverted from the purpose of firm thought, although they immediately shake the mind free from the image of deception [Text: imagination]. The ambushing enemy attacks them more severely in sleep precisely where he cannot overcome them while they are awake. Yet heavenly providence kindly permits him to act wickedly in this way, lest sleep itself, in the hearts of the elect, be without the reward of suffering.

## CHAPTER XX — On the Sacrifices of the Ungodly, on the Words: “Who offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor” (Ecclus. XXXIV, 24)

*(Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 23, admonition 21.)* It is one thing to show mercy for the sake of sins; it is another to sin for the sake of showing mercy. The latter can no longer be called mercy, because that which has been embittered by the poison of a pestilential root does not advance toward a sweet fruit.

For this reason the Lord also rejects such sacrifices through the Prophet, saying: “I am the Lord, who love judgment and hate robbery for a burnt offering” (Isa. LXI, 8). Again he says: “The sacrifices of the ungodly are abominable, because they are offered from crime” (Prov. XXII, 27).

Often they take away from the needy what they give to the needy. But the Lord shows through a certain Wise Man with what severity he rejects them, saying: “He who offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the sight of his father” (Ecclus. XXXIV, 24). For what can be more intolerable than the death of a son in the sight [Text: before the eyes] of his father? It is therefore shown with what anger this sacrifice is regarded, since it is compared with the grief of a father deprived of his child.

## CHAPTER XXI — On Those Who Repeat Their Sins, on the Words: “He who is baptized by a dead person,” and so forth (Ecclus. XXXIV, 30)

*(Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 30, admonition 31.)* “He who is baptized by a dead person and again touches him, what does his washing profit?” [Text: avail] He is baptized by a dead person who is washed [Text: cleansed] from sin by tears; but after baptism he touches the dead person who repeats his faults after his tears.

## CHAPTER XXII — On the Daily Afflictions of Human Beings, on the Words: “A heavy yoke upon the children of Adam” (Ecclus. XL, 1)

*(Moral. Book XXIV, ch. 4, no. 7; Book VIII, ch. 32, no. 52 and following; Book XI, ch. 49, no. 66; Book VIII, ch. 32, no. 55.)* “A heavy yoke upon the children of Adam from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” [Text: into the mother of all].

When Adam, the first man, departed from the Lord [Text: God], we were driven from the joys of paradise into the misery of this mortal life; and we experience, in the punishment exacted for our guilt, how grave a sin we committed at the serpent’s persuasion. Here, having fallen, we found nothing outside God except that by which we might be afflicted.

And because we followed the flesh through the sight of our eyes, we are scourged by that very flesh which we placed before God’s commands. In it we suffer daily groaning, in it torment, in it death, so that, by a wondrous dispensation, the Lord might turn into punishment for us the very thing through which we committed our guilt. Thus the judgment of punishment would arise from no other source than the cause of sin, so that humanity might be instructed unto life through the bitterness of the flesh by whose pleasure it proudly [Text: through pride] reached death.

For when human beings, captured by the serpent’s persuasion, abandoned the Lord by despising his commands through sin, they deserted the fortress of humility and, through pride, reached the yoke of weakness. By raising the neck of the heart, they placed it beneath the yoke, because the one who refused to be subject to divine commands laid himself beneath his own necessities.

We can show this more clearly if we express first the burdens of the flesh and then those of the mind which the fallen human being endures. To say nothing of the fact that the body tolerates pain and pants under fevers, this very condition of our body which is called health is constrained by a certain sickness of its own. For it wastes away in idleness, fails through work, and, weakened by hunger, is restored by food so that it may continue. Weary from being restored, it is relieved by abstinence so that it may remain vigorous. Water is poured over it lest it dry up; it is wiped with cloths lest it dissolve from being too thoroughly soaked. It is invigorated by labor lest it grow torpid through rest, and it is refreshed by rest lest it succumb to exertion.

It is wearied by vigils and restored by sleep; when weighed down by sleep, it is shaken from sleep by vigils, lest it be wearied still more by its own repose. It is covered with clothing lest it be penetrated by the severity of cold. When weakened by the warmth it has sought, it is refreshed by a breath of air. And when it finds discomfort in the very source from which it sought to flee discomfort, it grows weak, as I might say, from its own medicine, badly wounded.

Therefore, when fevers have been removed and pains have ceased, our very health is a sickness that never lacks the necessity of treatment. For however many comforts we seek for the use of living, we meet, as it were, that many medicines for our sickness. Yet the medicine itself is turned into a wound, because, when we cling somewhat too long to the remedy we have sought, we are more seriously weakened by what we have wisely prepared for our restoration.

Thus presumption ought to be corrected; thus, indeed, pride ought to be laid low. For because we once drew breath in an exalted spirit, behold, every day we carry with us our falling lament [Text: mud]. Our mind itself, excluded from the joy of its inward secret, is now deceived by hope, now harassed by fear, now cast down by the pain of contempt, now lifted up by false happiness.

It obstinately loves transitory things and is continually worn down by their loss, because they are continually changed by the rushing course of time. Subject to mutable things, it is also changed by itself. For, while seeking what it does not have, it receives it anxiously; and when it begins to have what it sought, it is weary of having received it. It often loves what it had despised and despises what it had loved. With labor it learns the things that are eternal, but suddenly forgets them if it ceases to labor.

For a long time it seeks in order to find a little of the highest things; but, quickly falling back into familiar things, it does not persevere even briefly in what it has found. Desiring to be instructed, it scarcely overcomes its ignorance; but once instructed, it struggles more gravely against the glory of knowledge.

It scarcely subjects the tyranny of its flesh to itself, yet still inwardly endures the images of the sin whose outward works it has already restrained by conquering them. It raises itself in the search for its author [Text: originator], but the friendly darkness of bodily things, striking against it, confuses it. It wishes to observe how the incorporeal governs the body, but cannot. It wonderfully seeks what is not sufficient to answer it, and, ignorant, fails beneath that which it seeks wisely.

Considering itself both vast and narrow, it does not know what it truly should judge itself to be. For if it were not vast, it would never seek so diligently to investigate such things; and again, if it were not narrow, it would at least find what it itself seeks.

Since, therefore, fallen humanity endures both bodily troubles and mental questions, it carries a heavy burden in itself. It is pressed on every side by sicknesses and driven on every side by weaknesses, so that the one who, after abandoning God, believed that he was sufficient for his own rest might find nothing within himself except the tumult of disturbance. Having found himself, he would seek to flee from himself; but, having despised his author [Text: creator], he would have nowhere to flee.

If everything that occurs here is also considered carefully, it is the heavy punishment and misery of the expelled human being. The body’s health is guarded with great care, yet even when guarded it is lost; when lost, it is restored with great pain [Text: labor]; and even when restored it is always uncertain. What is this other than the misery of mortal life?

We love our friends, yet fear that they may be offended. We fear our enemies and are not secure concerning those whom we fear. Often we speak to our enemies, and sometimes we receive the sincere words of our neighbors—and perhaps of those who love us greatly—as though they were the words of enemies. Although we never wish to be deceived or to deceive, through our own caution we err more seriously.

What, then, is this other than the grave punishment [Text: misery] of human life? Having been expelled from his heavenly homeland, the human being takes pleasure in exile and is burdened with cares; yet he avoids reflecting on how grievous it is, because there are many things to think about. He has been deprived of inward light, yet wishes to endure his blindness in this life for a long time. What else is this than misery born from our punishment?

Although he desires to remain here for a long time, he is nevertheless driven onward by the very course of mortal life so that he may depart. Contemplating the burdens of this weakness, a certain wise man rightly said: “A heavy yoke upon the children of Adam, from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” [Text: into the mother of all].

## CHAPTER XXXIII — That a discerning person who sins is better than an undiscerning person who acts well, on the Words: “The iniquity of a man is better than a woman doing good” (Ecclus. XLII, 14)

[Col. 0939C]

*(Moral. Book XI, ch. 49, no. 65.)* “The iniquity of a man is better than a woman doing good.” A strong and discerning person is called a man, whereas a weak or undiscerning mind is understood by “woman.” It often happens that even a discerning person suddenly slips into sin, while another who is undiscerning and weak performs a good work.

But the one who is undiscerning and weak is sometimes lifted up more by what he has done well and falls more seriously into sin. The discerning person, however, even from recognizing that he has acted badly, brings himself back more strictly to the rule of discipline and advances more deeply toward justice precisely from the point at which he seemed for a time to have fallen away from justice.

In this respect it is rightly said: “The iniquity of a man is better than a woman doing good,” because sometimes even the fault of the strong becomes an occasion of virtue, and the virtue of the weak an occasion of sin.

## CHAPTER XXIV — On Wisdom, on the Words: “The wisdom of the scribe comes in a time of leisure” (Ecclus. XXXVIII, 25)

*(Moral. Book XVIII, ch. 43, nos. 68 and 69; Book V, ch. 4, nos. 5, 6, and 55.)* “Wisdom comes in a time of leisure, and the one who is less occupied with activity will receive it.” No one fully receives it unless he strives to withdraw himself from all the turmoil of carnal activities.

But what of the fact that we know many of the ancient fathers to have held this wisdom inwardly with vigor while also regularly carrying out the cares of the world outwardly? Shall we say that Joseph was deprived of the reception of this wisdom, when, taking charge of all Egypt’s affairs during the famine, he not only provided food for the Egyptians but also preserved the lives of foreigners who came to him through the exercise of his office (Gen. XLII and following)? Or was Daniel estranged from this wisdom, when, made chief of the magistrates in Babylon by the Chaldean king, he was occupied with still greater cares because he was placed over all in a more exalted dignity (Dan. II)?

Because those who love only their heavenly homeland are sometimes subjected to the cares of an earthly homeland, those who are full of heavenly wisdom discern how they ought to be free for one thing inwardly and occupied with another outwardly. Thus, if by the hidden ordering of God something from the cares of this age is imposed upon them against their desire, they yield to the God whom they love. Out of love for him they desire inwardly only the vision of him; but out of fear of him they humbly fulfill outwardly the task imposed upon them. Thus, they desire to be free for God through the grace of love, while also fulfilling the cares laid upon them according to the condition of servitude.

When outward occupations clamor around them, inwardly they preserve a most peaceful rest in love. The reason that is present within acts as a judge and, with calm moderation, orders the tumult of occupations clamoring outwardly and the matters around it that are less tranquil. Just as the strength of the mind presides over the restraint of the movements of the flesh, so the love of rest often governs well the superimposed tumult of occupation. For if outward cares are not sought through a perverse love, they can be administered by a mind that is not confused but ordered.

Holy men do not seek these cares at all; they grieve that they have been imposed upon them by a hidden order. Although they flee them through a better intention, they nevertheless bear them with a submissive mind. If permitted, they hasten to avoid them as much as possible; but, fearing the hidden dispensations of God, they retain what they flee and perform what they avoid.

They enter into their hearts and there inquire what the hidden will of God desires. Recognizing that they must be subject to the highest ordinances, they humble the neck of their hearts beneath the yoke of divine providence. Whoever is such a person, no matter what turmoil is stirred up outwardly, it never reaches his inner being.

Thus it happens that one thing is held inwardly as a matter of desire and another outwardly as a matter of duty; and through this very wisdom hearts are filled not with turbulence and confusion but with tranquility.

A wondrous act of divine mercy occurs when one who strives with a perfect heart toward contemplation is occupied with human ministries. His perfected mind benefits many who are weaker, and, in that he regards himself as imperfect, he rises from that very awareness to a more perfect height of humility.

Sometimes, from the very source where holy men endure the loss of their desires, they bring greater gains to those whom they convert. For since they are not permitted to devote themselves to contemplation as they wish, they are pleased to carry others along with them, those among whom they live. Thus, by a wondrous dispensation of mercy, they rise richer toward the building of the heavenly homeland precisely from the point at which they judge themselves to have become poorer.

Sometimes they do not reach the desires they have conceived for this very reason: so that, through the delay itself, their minds may be broadened toward those desires with a more expansive capacity. What might perhaps have been diminished if fulfilled is caused, through a great ordering, to grow when refused.

Thus they desire to be mortified so that, if permitted, they may contemplate the face of their Creator perfectly. But their desire is delayed so that it may advance, and it is nourished in the bosom of its delay so that it may grow.

They therefore preserve inwardly the desire for piety, while fulfilling outwardly the ministry of order, so that they may neither depart from perfection through their intention nor, through pride, contradict the ordering of their Creator.

He lives and reigns through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK THREE  
## On Testimonies Concerning the Prophet Isaiah

[Col. 0939]

## CHAPTER I — “The ox knows its owner” (Isa. I, 3)

[Col. 0939D]

*(Moral. Book I, ch. 16, no. 23.)* “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger.” In sacred Scripture, oxen sometimes signify the workers of Judea, while the ass signifies the peoples of the nations [Text: the Gentiles].

Hence, as the Lord was going toward Jerusalem, he is said to have sat upon a young ass (Matt. XXI). For what does it mean for him, sitting upon an ass, to go toward Jerusalem [Text: to come to Jerusalem], unless it means that, by possessing the simple hearts of the Gentiles, he brings them to the vision of peace by governing and presiding over them?
