For who was the ox if not the Jewish people, whose neck the yoke of the Law wore down? And who was the ass if not the Gentile world, which every deceiver found like a brute animal, resisting with no reason, and made subject to whatever error he wished?

Thus the ox recognized its owner and the ass its master’s manger, because the Hebrew people found the Lord whom it worshiped but did not know, while the Gentile world received the nourishment of the Law, which it did not possess.

## CHAPTER II — “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. I, 16)

*(Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 30, admonition 31.)* Those who mourn their sins but do not abandon them cleanse themselves uselessly by weeping, because, by living wickedly, they defile themselves again afterward, cleansing [Text: washing] themselves with tears for the very purpose of returning to their filth.

Hence it is said through Isaiah: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. I, 16). Whoever does not preserve the innocence of life after his tears neglects to be clean after washing. They are therefore washed, but by no means clean, because they do not cease to weep over the sins they have committed, yet commit again sins over which they must weep.

## CHAPTER III — “Take away the evil of your thoughts” (Isa. I, 16)

*(Moral. Book XXV, ch. 5, nos. 7 and 8; Book XXV, ch. 6, no. 11.)* No human being sees the hidden thoughts of our mind, yet we fall before God’s eyes as often as, through weak thought, we turn aside from the right path.

Hence the prophet cries out, saying: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes.” In saying this, he testifies that he cannot, as it were, bear the force of our concealed wickedness. It cannot be concealed from him, because whatever we think unlawfully in our minds [Text: secretly] is thrust importunately into his sight.

For all things, as it is written, are “naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV, 13). He neither fails to know the evils of human beings when they are merely conceived nor forgets them when they have been committed, unless they are erased from his eyes through repentance.

What, then, shall we do about evil deeds, if God carefully weighs everything—not only deeds but even thoughts—and will judge them strictly? Now, while we can, let us erase from the sight of the eternal Judge both the evil things we have thought and the worse things we have committed.

Let us recall before the eyes of our hearts whatever we have done perversely. Let our weakness flatter itself in nothing through the wickedness of presumption; and, in the matters it remembers, let it not fondle itself delicately. Rather, the more conscious it is of having done evil to itself, the more gently yet severely let it act toward itself.

Let it set the future judgment against itself; and whatever it feels must be struck in itself by the sentence of the Judge, let it strike in itself mercifully through the repentance of conversion.

## CHAPTER IV — “Cease to act perversely” (Isa. I, 16)

*(Moral. Book IX, ch. 38, no. 60.)* “Cease to act perversely, learn to do good, come and accuse me.” We confront the one whom we accuse by the authority of reason.

What, then, does the Lord mean when, admonishing us to perform holy deeds, he adds, “Come and accuse me,” unless he openly indicates how much confidence he grants to good actions? It is as though he plainly said: “Act rightly, and confront the movements of my judgment not now through the groaning of supplication but through the confidence of authority.”

Hence John says: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God” (1 John III, 21). Hence the Lord complains through the prophet that he found no one to accuse him, saying: “I sought a man who might interpose a hedge and stand opposite me, lest I destroy it, and I found none” (Ezek. XXII, 30).

Hence Isaiah grievously laments, saying: “Our iniquities, like the wind, have carried us away, and there is no one who calls upon your name, who rises up and takes hold of you” (Isa. LXIV, 7).

## CHAPTER V — “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared” (Isa. II, 2)

*(Moral. Book XXXIII, ch. 1, no. 2; Book II, Homily 1 on Ezekiel, no. 4.)* In sacred Scripture, when “mountain” is placed in the singular, it sometimes signifies the incarnate Lord and sometimes an apostate angel. When mountains are named in the plural, the exaltedness of the apostles and prophets is sometimes expressed.

For the mountain signifies the Lord. Thus Isaiah, foreseeing that he would become incarnate, says, lifted up by the spirit of prophecy: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared upon the summit of the mountains.” The house of the Lord was the people of Israel. Therefore, the mountain of the house of the Lord is called the one who deigned to become incarnate from the people of Israel.

There were holy men among that same people who rightly could be called mountains, because through the merit of their lives they drew near to heavenly things. But the incarnate Lord was not equal to these mountains, for by the nature of his life [Text: because he transcended the nature and life] he surpassed the merits of all through his divinity.

Hence he is rightly called a mountain above the summit of the mountains, because, exalted through his divinity, he was found even above the peaks of the saints. Thus those who had advanced greatly in the Lord [Text: had advanced] could scarcely touch his footsteps from the summit of contemplation.

The mountain upon the summit of the mountains is therefore the incarnate Lord, transcending the exaltedness of the prophets.

Again, the apostate angel is signified by a mountain. Thus, under the figure of the king of Babylon, the same Isaiah later says in his prophecies concerning the ancient enemy: “Raise a signal upon the dark mountain” (Isa. XIII, 2). Holy preachers raise a signal upon the dark mountain when, against the pride of Satan—who often hides beneath a cloud of pretense—they exalt the power of the cross.

## CHAPTER VI — “Enter into the rock; hide in a pit of earth” (Isa. II, 10)

*(Moral. Book XXXI, ch. 27, no. 53.)* The hardness of our heart must be broken by repeated blows of examination, as the Lord says to Isaiah: “Enter into the rock; hide in a pit of earth from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty.”

We enter into the rock when we penetrate the hardness of our sluggishness [Text: our heart]. We are hidden in a pit of earth from the face of the fear of the Lord if, casting out earthly thoughts, we hide ourselves in the humility of our mind from the anger of the strict Judge. For the more earth is thrown out by digging, the lower the floor is always shown to be. Thus, if we cast earthly thoughts out of ourselves with greater diligence, we discover that we are hidden more humbly within ourselves.

Behold, the day of divine judgment is near; its very face of fear already appears, as it were. Therefore, each person must fear it all the more terribly the nearer the glory of its majesty approaches.

What, then, must be done, and where must one flee? For where can anyone hide from the One who is everywhere? Yet behold: we are commanded to enter the rock and conceal ourselves in a pit of earth, so that, breaking open the hardness of our hearts, we may turn aside the invisible wrath precisely by withdrawing ourselves within our own hearts from the love of visible things.

When the earth of wicked thought is cast out, the mind is hidden within itself all the more safely because it is hidden all the more humbly.

## Chapter VII.—“Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils” (Isaiah 2:22)

[Col. 0942D]

(*Moralia*, book XXI, chapter 26, no. 51.) “Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, because he is accounted exalted.” The nostrils signify foreknowledge, because often we apprehend by smell what we do not see, so that some things, even when lying far away, make their quality known to us by their fragrance; and as we draw breath through our nostrils, we often foreknow things that are still unseen. Therefore our Redeemer is said to have breath in his nostrils, so that his knowledge may be signified as foreknowledge: whatever he made known that he knew in the nature of his humanity, this he had certainly foreknown before the ages through his divinity. The prophet adds why he had breath in his nostrils [Text: “why he may have had it”]: “Because he is accounted exalted.” It is as though he said: He foreknows (*praescit*; Text: *praescivit*, “foreknew”) from above the things that are to come below, because he came down from heavenly places to what is lowly.

## Chapter VIII.—“They proclaimed their sin like Sodom” (Isaiah 3:9)

[Col. 0943A]

(*Moralia*, book IV, chapter 27, no. 31; *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 31, admonition 32.) There are some who, after despising God in their minds, scorn human judgments even more. Whatever evil they desire, they do not hesitate to carry out boldly, restrained by no manifest sense of shame. When someone’s wickedness becomes shamelessly known, the more freely he perpetrates every crime, the more he considers it permissible; and what he supposes to be permissible, in this he is undoubtedly immersed all the more deeply. Hence it is written: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and did not hide it.” If Sodom concealed its sin, it would still sin under fear; but it had utterly lost the reins of fear, because it did not even require darkness for its guilt.

## Chapter IX.—“My people, those who call you blessed deceive you” (Isaiah 3:12)

(*Homilies on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 9, no. 15.) In everything that is said about [Col. 0943B] us, we ought silently (*tacite*; Text: *semper taciti*, “always silent”) to return to our own minds and seek the inner witness and judge. For what does it profit if everyone praises us while conscience accuses us? Or what can it harm if everyone disparages us while conscience alone defends us? Hence Isaiah says: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you, and destroy the way of your steps.” So that this people would not attend to words of its own praise and perish more deeply in its sins, it is immediately told whom it should regard and whose judgment it should fear, when he adds: “The Lord stands to judge; he stands to judge the peoples” (Isaiah 3:13). It is as though he plainly said: Why do you follow human judgments, when you know that the heavenly Judge is standing?

## Chapter X.—“On that day the fruit of the earth will be exalted” (Isaiah 4:2)

(*Homilies on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 1, no. 4.) Christ Jesus, the Mediator between God and human beings, was made not only a human being above human beings, but also a human being above the angels. [Col. 0943C] For this reason Isaiah says of him: “On that day the fruit of the earth will be exalted.” Our Creator, because he was incarnate for us, became the fruit of the earth for us. But he is now the exalted fruit of the earth, because the man born on earth reigns over the angels in heaven; for, in the words of David and Paul, “he subjected all things beneath his feet” (Psalm 8:8; Hebrews 2:8). In subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him.

## Chapter XI.—“Woe to you who join house to house” (Isaiah 5:8)

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 20, admonition 21.) To those who desire greatly to multiply the extent of their dwellings, the Lord says through Isaiah: “Woe to you who join house to house and join field (*agrum*) to field [Text: *agro*], even to the limit of the place. Will you alone dwell in the midst of the earth?” It is as though he plainly said: How far do you extend yourselves, when you cannot have companions who share the common world? You oppress those who are joined to you, but [Col. 0943D] you always find others against whom you can extend yourselves.

## Chapter XII.—“Their nobles perished from hunger” (Isaiah 5:13)

(*Moralia*, book I, chapter 21, no. 29; book I, homily 3 on Ezekiel, no. 19.) Holy Scripture is sometimes food for us and sometimes drink. It is food in its more obscure passages, because it is, as it were, broken by explanation and swallowed by chewing; but it is drink in its clearer passages, because it is absorbed just as it is found. The prophet Isaiah saw that food and drink had failed [Text: “been lacking”] Judah when he said: “Its nobles perished from hunger.” It belongs to the few to understand what is profound and hidden, but to the many to perceive the open matters of history. Therefore he says that Judah’s nobles perished not from thirst but from hunger, because those who appeared to preside, while giving themselves entirely to outward understanding, had nothing to chew by examining the inner realities.

[Col. 0944A]

But because, when those of greater stature fall away from inner understanding, the understanding of the little ones also dries up in outward matters, it is rightly added there: “Its multitude dried up from thirst.” It is as though he plainly said: While the common people abandon concern for their life, they no longer seek even the streams of history.

Jeremiah saw Scripture as food that would be broken by explanation when he said: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lamentations 4:4); that is, the weak asked that the stronger sayings of Holy Scripture be broken up by explanation, but no one capable of explaining could be found.

Amid these things, it is worthwhile to consider who we are, since we are raised to investigate the mysteries of sacred speech. Certainly, in our ancient ancestors we were worshipers of idols; but behold, through the Spirit of grace we now search out heavenly words. How has this come about for us? The Redeemer of the human race fulfilled what he said through Isaiah: “And the deserted places turned into fruitfulness; strangers will eat” (Isaiah 5:17). These sayings of the prophets were deserted among the Jews, because they did not wish to cultivate them by seeking their mystical meaning. But for us they have been turned into fruitfulness, because, although spoken according to the historical sense, by God’s generosity they yield spiritual nourishment to our minds; and now we strangers eat what the citizens of the law refused to consume.

## Chapter XIII.—“Woe to those who drag iniquities with cords of vanity” (Isaiah 5:18)

(*Moralia*, book XXXIII, chapter 10, no. 18.) “Woe to those who drag iniquities [Text: ‘iniquity’] with cords of vanity.” Sins are signified by a rope. Thus iniquity is dragged with cords of vanity when guilt is prolonged by increase. For because a rope is twisted by adding to it so that it grows, sin is not improperly represented by a rope, since, when it is defended by a perverse heart, it is often multiplied.

## Chapter XIV.—“In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated” (Isaiah 6:1)

(*Homilies on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 2, no. 14.) We must understand that, as long as one lives in this mortal flesh, no one progresses so far in the power of contemplation that he can fix the eyes of his mind upon the very unbounded ray [Col. 0944C] of light. For the almighty God is not yet seen in his own glory; rather, something beneath that glory is contemplated, by seeing which the soul may progress and afterward reach the glory of his vision.

Thus Isaiah, when he confessed that he had seen God, saying, “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated upon a throne, high and exalted,” immediately added: “And the things that were beneath him filled the temple.” When the proud and presumptuous King Uzziah dies, the Lord is seen, because when the exaltation of this world dies to the mind’s desire, then the mind itself beholds the glory of God.

It should also be noted that the Lord sits upon a throne, high and exalted. For what is his throne except the angelic or human creation, over which he presides through the understanding he has given? He calls this throne high and exalted because human nature, raised to heavenly glory, makes progress; and the angelic creation, having already been established in heaven through the many spirits who fell, has been exalted from the place where it was also confirmed, so that it may not fall. [Col. 0944D]

The temple is the same as the throne, because the eternal King dwells where he sits. We, therefore, are his temple, in whose minds he graciously chooses to dwell. But the things that were beneath him filled the temple, because whatever is now perceived concerning him is not yet he himself, but is beneath him.

Thus Jacob saw an angel and confessed that he had seen the Lord (Genesis 28), because when we behold his mysteries [Text: “ministries,” that is, ministers, namely angels], it is already a great thing that we are raised above ourselves. It should also be noted that it says, “They filled the temple.” Even if an angel appeared, it would satisfy (*satisfaceret*; Text: *satisfecit*, “satisfied”) the desire of a weak mind, so that, if it cannot yet see something greater, it may nevertheless admire the lesser thing it sees.

The things beneath him fill the temple because, as has been said, even when the mind has advanced in contemplation, it does not yet contemplate what he himself is, but what is beneath him.

## Chapter XV.—“Woe is me, because I was silent, because I am a man of polluted lips” (Isaiah 6:5)

[Col. 0945A]

(*Dialogues*, book III, chapter 15.) When we are frequently mingled with the crowds of the world, speaking idle words and sometimes even gravely harmful ones, our mouth becomes that much farther from almighty God as it becomes nearer to this world. For we are dragged far downward when, through continual speech, we mingle with worldly matters.

Isaiah rightly reproached himself and repented [Text: “within himself”] after he had seen the Lord, the King of armies, saying: “Woe is me, because I was silent, because I am a man of polluted lips.” He revealed why he had polluted lips when he added: “I dwell in the midst of a people having polluted lips.” He grieved that he had polluted lips, but he indicated from where he had contracted this pollution when he declared that he dwelt in the midst of a people having polluted lips.

It is exceedingly difficult for the tongue of worldly people not to stain the mind that it touches. For when we usually condescend to them in order to discuss certain matters, we gradually pass from idle to harmful words and from light to serious ones. Our mouth is then heard that much less by almighty God in prayer, the more it is polluted by foolish speech.

## Chapter XVI.—“You have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the scepter of his exactor” (Isaiah 9:4)

(*Moralia*, book XXX, chapter 25, no. 72.) Isaiah says to our Redeemer, who was freeing the Gentiles from the devil’s dominion: “You have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the scepter of his exactor, as on the day of Midian.”

In rescuing the Gentiles, the Lord overcame the yoke of their burden when, by his coming, he freed them from the slavery of demonic tyranny. He overcame the rod of their shoulder when, having redeemed the human race, he restrained the blow by which (*qua*; Text: *quae*) that tyranny had gravely oppressed them through wicked works. He overcame the scepter of their exactor when he destroyed from the hearts of the faithful the kingdom of that same devil, who had been accustomed, through the destructive perpetration of vices, to exact the due tribute of punishments. [Col. 0945C]

But let us hear how these things were accomplished. It follows: “As on the day of Midian.” This war against the Midianites, which the prophet wisely introduced as a comparison with the Lord’s coming, is fully described earlier in the Book of Judges.

## Chapter XVII.—“The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel” (Isaiah 9:8)

(*Moralia*, book II, chapter 35, no. 57.) “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel.” Jacob [Text adds: “indeed”] is called “supplanter,” while Israel is called “a man seeing God.” What is signified by Jacob except the Jewish people, and what by Israel except the Gentile people? For the one whom Jacob strove to supplant through the death of the flesh, the Gentiles saw as God through the eyes of faith.

Therefore the word sent to Jacob fell upon Israel, because the Gentile people, suddenly confessing him whom the Jewish people rejected when he came to them, found him.

## Chapter XVIII.—“The bricks have fallen, but we will build with squared stones” (Isaiah 9:10)

[Col. 0945D]

(*Homilies on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 9, no. 5.) When Isaiah perceived that the Jewish people were perishing from the faith and foresaw the holy apostles rising strong in the Church, through whom many from the Gentiles were established in strength of faith and life, he spoke in great consolation, saying: “The bricks have fallen, but we will build with squared stones.”

A squared stone stands evenly on whichever side it falls [Text: “is turned.”] Whom, then, do we understand as the squared stones except certain saints, whose life knows how to stand firmly in prosperity and adversity and does not suffer collapse under any change?

Thus, seeing apostles, martyrs, and teachers rising in the holy Church, the prophet grieved less over the fall of the bricks—that is, the Jews [Text: “over the destruction of the Jews”], because he saw the building of almighty God, the holy Church, being constructed from squared stones.

## Chapter XIX.—“The yoke will rot before the oil” (Isaiah 10:27)

[Col. 0946A]

(*Moralia*, book X, chapter 15, no. 24; and *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 26, no. 4.) “The yoke will rot before the oil.” By the name of oil the anointing of the Holy Spirit itself is signified. We were held beneath the yoke of demonic domination, but we have been anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit. Because the grace of the Holy Spirit has anointed us, the yoke of demonic domination, by which the necks of our freedom were pressed down, was driven away and rotted; and we were freed from the slavery of our captivity, as Paul testifies when he says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17).

Again, it is written concerning this oil: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn, the son of oil” (Isaiah 5:1). The faithful people are called the son of oil, because they are generated for faith in God through the inward anointing of the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter XX.—“The spirit of wisdom will rest upon him” (Isaiah 11:2)

[Col. 0946B]

(*Homilies on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 7, no. 7.) Through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, the entrance to heavenly life is opened for us. Isaiah, enumerating this sevenfold grace in our Head himself, or in his body, which we are, says: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety will rest upon him, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him” (Isaiah 11:2–3).

Speaking of heavenly things, he counted these degrees by descending rather than ascending: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear. Since it is written, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10), there is no doubt that one ascends from fear to wisdom, not returns from wisdom to fear. For wisdom certainly possesses perfect love, and it is written: “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

Therefore, because God was speaking to us about heavenly things from above down to what is lowly, the prophet began with wisdom and descended to fear. But we, who strive from earthly things toward heavenly ones, ascend by counting from fear to [Col. 0946C] wisdom.

The first step of ascent in the mind is therefore the fear of the Lord. But what sort of fear is it if piety is not present in it? Whoever either does not know or pretends not to know how to sympathize with a neighbor’s tribulation has no fear before God, because such fear is not raised to piety.

Yet piety through disordered mercy [Text adds: “is accustomed to err, if perhaps it spares what ought not to be spared. For sins…”] draws one toward eternal punishment when, for a time, it spares sins that ought not to be spared and that can be struck by the fires of Gehenna [Text adds: “ought to be corrected by the discipline of the scourge. But disordered piety, when…”].

Therefore, in order that piety may be true and rightly ordered, it must be raised to knowledge, so that it may know what to punish according to justice and what to forgive according to mercy.

But what if someone knows what he ought to do, yet does not possess the strength to do it? Our knowledge must therefore grow toward fortitude, so that, when it sees what ought to be done, it can accomplish it through strength of mind and not tremble from fear, nor, having fallen through fear, become unable to defend the good it perceives.

But often, if fortitude [Col. 0946D] is improvident and insufficiently watchful against vices, it falls into ruin through its own presumption. It must therefore ascend to counsel, so that by foresight it may fortify everything it can accomplish courageously.

But counsel cannot exist if understanding is absent. For how can one who does not understand the evil weighing upon the one who acts establish the good that helps him? Therefore, let us ascend from counsel to understanding.

But what if understanding is vigilant with great keenness and does not know how to moderate itself through maturity? Let us therefore ascend from understanding to wisdom, so that wisdom may arrange with maturity what understanding has discovered sharply.

Since, then, through fear we rise to piety, through piety we are led to knowledge, through knowledge we are strengthened for fortitude, through fortitude we advance to counsel, through counsel we make progress in understanding, and through understanding we arrive at wisdom, the entrance to heavenly life is opened for us as we ascend through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0893D] This chapter and the following one are absent from the manuscripts.]

## Chapter XXI.—“The wolf will dwell with the lamb” (Isaiah 11:6)

[Col. 0947A]

(*Homilies on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 4, no. 3.) To hear the word of almighty God, we who appear to be clothed in a religious habit have come together from the world’s various conditions, and, gathered from dissimilar iniquities, have been joined in the concord of the holy Church. Thus what is said through Isaiah concerning the Church’s promise appears to have been plainly fulfilled [Text adds: “now”]: “The wolf will dwell with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the kid.”

The wolf dwells with the lamb because those who were once predators in the world now rest in peace with the gentle and meek. The leopard lies down with the kid because the one who has been marked by the varied stains of his sins consents to humble himself with the one who despises himself and confesses that he is a sinner.

It follows: “The calf, the sheep, and the lion will dwell together.” For one who prepares himself through a contrite heart for a daily sacrifice to God, another who once raged like a lion in cruelty, and another who persists like a sheep in the simplicity of innocence have come together in the folds [Col. 0947B] of the holy Church.

It continues: “And a little child will lead them.” Who is this little child except the one of whom it is written: “A child is born for us” (Isaiah 9:6)? The little child therefore leads us who dwell together, because he who was made a little lower than the angels continually kindles our hearts through inward desire for his love. Through the love he has bestowed upon us, he does not permit us to fix our minds upon this world.

## Chapter XXII.—“The infant at the breast will delight over the hole of the asp” (Isaiah 11:8)

(*Moralia*, book XVII, chapter 32, no. 51.) The ancient enemy now possesses none of the saints by holding them, but persecutes them by tempting them; and because he has lost dominion within, he wages wars outside. The one who expelled him from human hearts of flesh came in the flesh for the sake of human beings.

Hence Isaiah says: “The infant at the breast will delight over the hole of the asp, and into the den of the basilisk the weaned child will put his hand; they will [Col. 0947C] not harm or kill throughout my entire holy mountain.”

Whom does he call the infant at the breast, or the one who has been weaned, except the Lord? What else does he signify by the hole of the asp or the den of the basilisk except the hearts of the wicked?

For the ancient enemy, when he gathered himself entirely into their consent, gathered and coiled the folds of his cunning like a twisting serpent, as though in a hole peculiarly (*proprie*; Text: *proprio*, “its own”). He calls him an asp because he rages secretly, and a basilisk because he strikes openly.

Therefore the Lord put his hand into the hole of the basilisk and the asp when, by divine power, he took possession of the hearts of the wicked and dragged away captive the asp or basilisk—that is, the devil—after seizing him, so that he might not harm the chosen faithful on his holy mountain, which is the Church.

## Chapter XXIII.—“The Lord will lay waste the tongue of the sea of Egypt” (Isaiah 11:15)

(*Moralia*, book XXXIII, chapter 10, nos. 18–19.) Our incarnate Lord destroyed from the hearts of his chosen all the arguments [Col. 0947D] of diabolical deception, and, once his truth was known, every doctrine of error and falsehood fell silent.

Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord will lay waste the tongue of the sea of Egypt.” The tongue of the sea of Egypt is the knowledge of worldly doctrine. Egypt is therefore rightly called a sea, because it is darkened by the obscurity of sin. The Lord lays waste the tongue of the sea of Egypt because, by extending himself through the flesh, he destroyed the false wisdom of this world.

## Chapter XXIV.—“I will sit on the mountain of the covenant” (Isaiah 14:13)

(*Homilies on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 2, no. 9.) “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the North.” The evil spirit who speaks these words held the mountain of the covenant, because he subjected the Jewish people, who had received the law, to himself in unbelief.

When the devil holds the hearts of teachers, he presides on the mountain of the covenant. He also sits on the sides of the North because he possesses minds that are [Col. 0948A] cold. Since the north wind contracts things with cold (Isaiah 14:14), the name “North” appropriately signifies the sluggishness of the evil spirit.

## Chapter XXV.—“Woe to the land of the winged cymbal” (Isaiah 18:1)

(*Moralia*, book XIII, chapter 10, no. 13.) Just as the incarnate Lord chose the poor, the uneducated, and the simple for his preaching, so, conversely, that condemned man whom the apostate angel will assume at the end of the world to preach his falsehood will choose the cunning and double-minded, those possessing the knowledge of this world.

Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to the land of the winged cymbal, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends messengers to the sea and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters.”

The land to which woe is pronounced is principally that condemned man, who is called the cymbal of wings because those who fly upward in the height of their thoughts through pride make that same perverse man resound by their preaching.

This land is rightly said to be beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. Ethiopia produces a black people, and this world, because it produces sinners, brings forth every human being as though Ethiopia were giving birth to a black [Col. 0948B] people.

But the land to which woe is pronounced is said to be beyond the rivers of Ethiopia because that condemned man is so immeasurably wicked that he surpasses the sins of all sinners.

He sends messengers to the sea because he scatters his preachers throughout the world. The manner in which they are sent is rightly added when it says: “In vessels of papyrus upon the waters.” Papyrus produces paper. What, then, is signified by papyrus except worldly knowledge? The vessels of papyrus are therefore the hearts of worldly teachers.

To send messengers in vessels of papyrus upon the waters is to place his preaching in the minds of fleshly wise people and to call peoples who are flowing toward guilt.

## Chapter XXVI.—“Watchman, what of the night?” (Isaiah 21:11)

(*Moralia*, book VI, chapter 19, no. 34; book XVI, chapter 59, no. 72; book II, chapter 31, no. 51.) The Jews, persecutors of our Redeemer, saw in him miracles of divine power and yet doubted his divinity. They were blinded [Col. 0948C] by the error of unbelief in the very presence of the truth, as Isaiah says: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” The watchman said: “Morning has come, and night.”

By “morning,” the advent of the Lord’s incarnation is understood. The watchman came from the night because the protector of the human race appeared openly in the flesh; yet Judea, pressed down by the darkness of its unbelief, did not recognize him at all.

The watchman’s voice rightly adds: “Morning has come, and night,” because through his presence the beginnings of a new light shone upon the world, yet ancient blindness remained in the hearts of unbelievers. The darkness of their unbelief was not wiped away from the hearts of the persecutors; their blindness blazed into cruelty, and their cruelty continued until the open acts of persecution. For, envying the doctrine of truth, they sought an opportunity to hand over the Lord.

Concerning them the Prophet says: “And now fire consumes the adversaries” (Isaiah 26:11). It is as though he plainly said: Fire not only torments the wicked afterward in vengeance, but now also burns them through envy, because those who will later be punished by the penalty of retribution are already afflicting themselves with the torment of envy.

When the flame of envy blazed forth from teachers who appeared to teach the truth, the uneducated people, fearing to endure the hostility of the Pharisees and rulers, were likewise consumed by the burning of unbelief. The flame of envy [Col. 0948D] descended from the leaders and kindled the hearts of the people by overturning them, fulfilling the prophecy that says: “Jealousy has seized an unlearned people” (Romans 10:2).

It is as though he plainly said: Because the people refused to examine the words of the prophets but surrendered their cruelty to the words of the envious, they perished in the fire of jealousy, because they burned themselves in the flame of another’s envy.

## Chapter XXVII.—“You who dwell in the land of the South” (Isaiah 21:14)

(*Moralia*, book XXIII, chapter 25, no. 49.) In Holy Scripture, divine instruction is signified, as Isaiah says: “You who dwell in the land of the South, meet the fugitive with bread.”

Those who dwell in the land of the South are those who, placed in [Col. 0949A] the holy Church, are breathed through by the love of the heavenly Spirit. The fugitive is one who desires to escape the evils of this world.

Therefore, the one who dwells in the land of the South should meet the fugitive with bread; that is, the one who has already been placed within the Church by the Holy Spirit should console through the language of instruction the person striving to escape his evils.

To meet the fugitive with bread means to offer the fearful person the food of sacred teaching concerning eternal punishments, sometimes restraining swelling pride through terror and sometimes reviving fear through exhortation.

Since the nourishment of Holy Scripture may appropriately be understood as bread, the same prophet says to the Jews who observe only the letter: “Why do you weigh out silver, and not for bread?” (Isaiah 55:2). It is as though he said: You weigh sacred words, but not for nourishment, because, while you guard only the outward form of the letter, you lose the richness of inward nourishment through spiritual understanding.

Hence it is plainly [Text: “aptly”] added: “And your labor not for satisfaction” (ibid.).

## Chapter XXVIII.—“Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isaiah 23:4)

[Col. 0949B]

(*Preface to the Moralia*, chapter 2, no. 5; *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 28, admonition 29.) Often the life of those under the law is reproved by the life of the Gentiles, and the conduct of religious people is put to shame by the conduct of worldly people: the former do not keep even what they promise, although they hear it in the commandments, while the latter, by their way of life, keep things to which they are in no way bound by the legal commandments. The former go beyond their assumed religious habit in their deeds, while the latter, according to their proper order, do not rouse their hearts.

This is briefly stated through Isaiah: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isaiah 23:4). In Sidon, the stability of those under the law and of religious people is represented; in the sea, the life of the Gentiles and of worldly people.

Thus Sidon is brought to shame, as it were, by the voice of the sea when, through comparison with the lives of Gentiles and worldly people who are tossed about in this world, the life of Christians and religious people—who appear fortified and, as it were, stable—is reproved.

## Chapter XXIX.—“As the people, so the priest” (Isaiah 24:2)

[Col. 0949C]

(*Pastoral Rule*, part II, chapter 7.) Through Isaiah the Lord threatens in the anger of just retribution, saying: “As the people, so the priest.” The priest is like the people when the person who exercises a spiritual office does what those do who are still judged according to carnal pursuits—when the shepherd of souls occupies himself with earthly business that he ought to have reproved in others.

## Chapter XXX.—“A wall and an outer wall will be placed in it” (Isaiah 26:1)

(*Homilies on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 2, no. 5; same work, part II, no. 5; *Moralia*, book XX, chapter 25.) In sacred speech, the incarnate Lord is often accustomed to be called a wall because of the protection he provides [Text: “because of his protective defense”]. Concerning him, for the building up of the holy Church, Isaiah says: “A wall and an outer wall will be placed in it.”

He himself is the wall for us: he surrounds us on every side by guarding us and prevents the course of evil spirits from reaching [Col. 0949D] our hearts. The outer wall of our wall, however, was all the prophets who, before the Lord appeared in the flesh, were sent by prophesying to construct faith.

They are rightly called an outer wall because, while they proclaimed the Lord who would follow, they stood, as it were, before the wall. In the holy Church, therefore, the Lord has been placed as our wall and his prophets as the outer wall, because the words of the prophets also came to us for the construction of faith, to us whom he himself perfectly protects.

Hence the wall is rightly placed first and the outer wall afterward, because those called from the Gentiles would not have received the sayings of his prophets unless we had first come to know the Lord.

## Chapter XXXI.—“Lord, let your hand be exalted, so that they may not see” (Isaiah 26:11)

(*Moralia*, book VII, chapter 32, no. 47.) The merits of the reprobate now darken their understanding, but on the day of judgment knowledge [Col. 0950A] of their guilt will enlighten it, so that now they do not see the life they ought to follow, while then, after they have lost it, they will behold it.

Concerning them Isaiah says: “Lord, let your hand be exalted, so that they may not see; let them see and be confounded.” Now they neglect to understand eternal things, or, having understood them, disdain to desire them. But then they will see them with understanding and desire, and, although they perceive them, they will be unable to attain them, confounded by shame.

## Chapter XXXII.—“The dead will not live; the giants will not rise again” (Isaiah 26:14)

(*Moralia*, book XVII, chapter 21, no. 30.) “The dead will not live; the giants will not rise again.” Whom does Isaiah call the dead here except sinners, and whom the giants except those who are proud even of their sin?

The former do not live because by sinning they have lost the life of righteousness. The latter cannot rise again after death because, after their guilt, puffed up by pride, they do not return to the remedies of repentance.

## Chapter XXXIII.—“Enter into your chambers” (Isaiah 26:20)

[Col. 0950B]

(*Moralia*, book IV, chapter 26, no. 47.) “Enter into your bedchambers [Text: ‘into rooms’]; close your doors.” The doors are the desires of carnal concupiscence. We enter our chambers when we enter the secrets of our mind; we close the doors when we restrain illicit desires.

## Chapter XXXIV.—“Against the serpent Leviathan, the bar” (Isaiah 27:1)

(*Moralia*, book IV, chapter 9, no. 15.) Describing the apostate angel, the Lord says through Isaiah: “Against the serpent Leviathan, the bar, the twisting serpent.”

*Leviathan* is interpreted as “their addition,” namely, the addition of human beings. He is rightly called their addition because he found them immortal in paradise, but, promising divinity to immortals, craftily promised to add something to them beyond what they were.

He is called the twisting serpent because, in what he promised to add to the human being, he crept [Col. 0950C] toward him with winding coils; for, while he falsely promised impossible things, he truly took away even what was possible.

It must be asked why the one who had called him a twisting serpent, adding a further word, inserted “bar,” unless perhaps the serpent’s twisting signifies flowing softness, while the bar signifies the hardness of rigidity. To designate him as both hard and soft, therefore, he names him both bar and serpent.

He is hard through malice and soft through flatteries. He is called a bar because he strikes even unto death, but a serpent because he insinuates himself softly through ambushes.

## Chapter XXXV.—“Affliction alone will give understanding to hearing” (Isaiah 28:19)

(*Moralia*, book XV, no. 58; book XI, chapter 29, no. 41.) The ungodly person does not know the evils he has committed until he begins to be punished for those same evils. Hence Isaiah says: “Affliction alone will give understanding to hearing.” When he begins to be scourged and afflicted in punishment for despising God’s commandments, then he will understand what he heard.

## Chapter XXXVI.—“That he may perform his work” (Isaiah 28:21)

[Col. 0950D]

(*Homilies on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 4, no. 20.) Contemplating our salvation in the Lord’s Passion, Isaiah says: “That he may perform his work; his work is alien to him.”

God’s work is to gather the souls he created and recall them to the joys of eternal light. But to be scourged, smeared with spittle, crucified, to die and be buried—this is not God’s work in his own substance, but the work of sinful humanity, which deserved all these things through sin.

Therefore, “that he may perform his work,” his alien work is from him, because God became incarnate in order to gather us to his righteousness and graciously chose to be scourged for us like a sinful human being. He performed an alien work in order to perform his own, because, through bearing our evils in weakness, he led us, who are his creatures, to the glory of his strength.

## Chapter XXXVII.—“And your eyes will see your teacher” (Isaiah 30:20)

[The supplied source ends here.]

(Book II, homily 34 on the Gospels, §§16–17; *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 28, admonition 29.) Let us consider, dearly beloved, the charity of our Creator toward us. He sees us sinning and bears with us; and he whom by sinning we despise does not cease, after our guilt, to await us for pardon. We have turned away from him, yet in calling us back he does not turn away. For indeed, through Isaiah, the mercy of his calling is expressed after sin, when it is said to the man who has turned away: “And your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the word [Text: “voice”] of one remaining behind you.”

The Lord warned the human race face to face when, in the paradise he had created, he gave the man standing in the freedom of his will instructions about what he ought and ought not to do. But humanity turned its back on God’s face when, in its pride, it despised his commands. Yet God did not abandon the proud man, for to call humanity back he gave the law, sent angels to exhort it, and appeared in the flesh of our mortality. Therefore he warned us while standing behind us: even after being despised, he called us back to recover grace.

What could be said generally of all must necessarily be understood individually of each person. Each person, as though placed before God, receives the words of his admonition when, before committing sins, he knows the commands of God’s will. He still stands before his face when he has not yet despised him by sinning; but when, abandoning the good of innocence, he desires and chooses iniquity, he turns his back upon God’s face. Yet behold: God, still following behind and warning him, persuades him to return to himself even after his guilt. We hear the voice of one warning from behind us if, at least after our sins, we return to the Lord who invites us. In his patience he awaits those who have proudly turned away, and through his commands he kindly calls them back. May such great mercy of our Creator soften the hardness of our guilt, so that the person who, when struck, might have been made to experience the evil he committed may at least be ashamed when he is awaited.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — “The bridle of error shall be a song for you” (Isaiah 30:28)

(Book II, homily 6 on Ezekiel, §21.) Our ancient parents served wood and stones, but we, through the grace of almighty God, have shaken the necks of our minds free from service to creation. In us has been fulfilled what is said through Isaiah: “And the bridle of error that was on the jaws of the peoples shall be a song for you, like the voice of a sanctified solemnity.” The bridle of error had constricted the jaws of the peoples when the Gentiles, bound by the error of idols, did not know how to offer the true God the praise of confession. But this very bridle of error has now been turned for us into a song, when with joy we sing and chant: “All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Psalm 95:5). Since by singing we say these things to almighty God, we have made the very bridle of our error—which had bound our mouths from praising God—a song for the true Lord.

It is rightly said, “Like the voice of a sanctified solemnity,” because when we render God the praise of confession, we rejoice in a sanctified solemnity. Let us therefore respond in our conduct to the great mercy of our Redeemer, so that we who have recognized the light may avoid the darkness of wicked works.

## CHAPTER XXXIX — “The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion” (Isaiah 31:9)

(Book II, homily 6 on Ezekiel and homily 9, §20.) Isaiah speaks of the love that begins here and is to be perfected through the vision of the Lord in the eternal homeland, saying: “The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.” It is more to be a furnace than to be a fire, because a fire can also be small; but in a furnace a more immense flame is kindled. Zion means “watchtower” or “contemplation”; Jerusalem is called “vision of peace.” Here, for the time being, we contemplate our peace, so that afterward we may see it there in its fullness.

Therefore, in Zion there is the Lord’s fire, and in Jerusalem his furnace: here we burn to some extent with the flames of his love, where we contemplate something of him; but there we shall burn completely, where we shall fully see the one whom we love.

## CHAPTER XL — “Upon the land of my people thorns and briers shall be” (Isaiah 32:13)

[Column 0952A]

(*Moralia* XVII, chapter 17, §23.) If those who already live amid heavenly desires cannot be free from sin, what burdens of sins do those endure who serve the pleasures of their flesh? Hence it is said through Isaiah: “Upon the land of my people thorns and briers shall grow, how much more upon every house of joy of the exultant city?”

The Lord calls the mind of all the elect the land of his people. He declares that thorns and briers grow upon it, because he sees that not even this mind is without the pricks of vices. The house of joy of the exultant city, however, is the mind of the wicked, which, while neglecting to contemplate future punishments, abandons itself to the pleasure of the flesh and rejoices in vain.

Thus he says, “Upon the land of my people,” and so forth—as though he were openly saying: If vices weigh down even the minds of those who afflict themselves out of desire for the heavenly homeland, beneath what faults do those lie who, without any fear, abandon themselves to the pleasure of the flesh?

## CHAPTER XLI — “Blessed are you who sow upon all waters” (Isaiah 32:20)

[Column 0952B]

(*Moralia* XXXV, chapter 16, §§39–40.) “Blessed are you who sow upon all waters, sending forth the foot of the ox and the donkey.” By the ox the Israelite people, subdued under the yoke of the law, is sometimes signified; by the donkey the Gentile people, devoted to pleasures, are indicated. Therefore, to sow upon all waters is to preach fruitful words of life widely to all the peoples through the preachers of the holy Church. To send forth the foot of the ox and the donkey is to bind the ways of the Israelite and Gentile peoples with the bonds of heavenly commandments.

## CHAPTER XLII — “He who walks in righteousnesses shall dwell on high” (Isaiah 33:15)

(*Moralia* XXXI, chapter 51, §102; XXIII, chapter 25, §49; Book I, homily 4 on the Gospels, §4.) It is worthwhile to bring forward Isaiah’s words concerning the active and contemplative life, and to show how they seem to be uttered with one spirit. Speaking of the active life, he says: “He who walks in righteousnesses and speaks the truth; who shakes his hands free from every gift; who stops his ears lest he hear bloodshed; and who closes his eyes lest he see evil.”

It should be known that a gift is sometimes offered through service, sometimes by the hand, and sometimes by the mouth. A gift through service is an undue submission offered in service; one who gives money gives a gift by the hand; but one who offers a word of praise brings forth a gift from the mouth. The righteous person, however, shakes his hands free from every gift because he seeks no repayment in this world for a good work.

What does it mean to stop one’s ears lest one hear bloodshed, except not to give consent to sins arising from the persuasion of blood and flesh? And what does it mean to close one’s eyes lest one see evil, except not to approve anything opposed to uprightness?

After expressing the virtues of the active life, he immediately adds from what stages of that same life one ascends to the heights of contemplation, saying: “He shall dwell on high; the heights of the rocks shall be his fortress; bread shall be given him; his waters shall be faithful; his eyes shall see the king in his beauty; they shall behold the land from afar.”

To dwell on high is to place the heart in heavenly things. Although the flesh is still held below, one already fixes the mind in the heights and in heavenly things [Text: “fixed it”]. The heights of the rocks are our fortresses when we look to the commands of our strong predecessors and fathers, separate ourselves from lowly thoughts, trample underfoot the rejected desires of earthly conduct, and are lifted toward the heavenly homeland by their examples.

The heights of the rocks are our fortresses when in mind we are joined to the choirs and camps of heaven, and, standing in the citadel of the heart, we attack the malicious spirits lying beneath us as though they had been placed below. Then bread is also given to us, because an intention raised toward the heights is refreshed by contemplation of eternity, and through the gift of contemplation we are filled with spiritual grace.

For in sacred speech “bread” sometimes signifies the grace of a spiritual gift, as the Lord says through David concerning the holy Church: “I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Psalm 132:15), because the minds of the humble placed in her are filled with the refreshment of spiritual gifts.

Our waters are faithful because the teaching of God gives there as a gift what it promises here through hope. The wisdom of this world is unfaithful because it does not remain after death. Our waters are faithful because the words of life that they announce before death also reveal after death.

Our eyes see the king in his beauty because our Redeemer will appear in judgment as a man even to the reprobate, but only those who have been chosen are raised up to behold the height of his divinity. To see the king’s ugliness is, as it were, to see only the servile form in which he was despised by the wicked. But the king is seen in his beauty by the elect, because, snatched beyond themselves, they fix the eyes of their hearts upon the radiance of his divinity.

Because, while they are in this life, they cannot see that homeland of the living as it is, it is rightly added: “They shall behold the land from afar.”

## CHAPTER XLIII — “The place of rivers, streams exceedingly broad” (Isaiah 33:21)

(*Moralia* XVIII, chapter 30, §60.) The prophet Isaiah, contemplating the words of the holy Church in their plain meaning, not obscured by the darkness of allegories [Text: “obscure”], exclaimed, saying: “The place of rivers, streams broad and open.” The sayings of the Old Testament had been like narrow and enclosed streams, which confined the immense meanings of its knowledge within very obscure collections. In contrast, the teaching of the holy Church consists of broad and open streams, because its sayings are rich for those who discover them and clear for those who seek them.

## CHAPTER XLIV — “My sword is drunken in heaven” (Isaiah 34:5)

(*Moralia* XXXII, chapter 23, §49.) Let a person consider what one exalted on earth deserves, if an angel who was set above angels is cast down in heaven. Hence the Lord rightly says through Isaiah: “My sword is drunken in heaven.” As though he were openly saying: Consider with what anger I shall strike the proud of earth, since I did not spare even those whom I created beside me in heaven, striking them for the fault of their exaltation.

## CHAPTER XLV — “Thorns and nettles shall spring up in his houses” (Isaiah 34:13)

(*Moralia* XXXIII, chapter 4.) Sinners defend other sinners precisely in what they themselves know they do wrong; shadows protect their shadow, as the more wicked defend the deeds of the utterly wicked through their perverse patronage. They fear that, when the fault in which they too are bound is corrected in others, it may eventually reach them as well.

The Lord reproves this conduct through Isaiah under the figure of Babylon, saying: “Thorns and nettles shall spring up in his houses, and buckthorn in his fortifications.” What do we understand by nettles except the irritations of thoughts? And by thorns except the pricks of vices? In the houses of Babylon, therefore, nettles and thorns spring up, because in the confusion of a reprobate mind desires of thought arise that irritate, and sins of action that prick.

But those who do these things also have more wicked defenders. Hence it is added: “And buckthorn in his fortifications.” Buckthorn becomes so dense through its encompassing thorns that, because of its roughness, it can scarcely be touched. Thus nettle and thorn arise within, but both are guarded externally by buckthorn, because lesser sinners commit various evils, while the more wicked and powerful defend them.

## CHAPTER XLVI — “It shall be a lair of dragons” (Isaiah 34:13)

(*Moralia* VII, chapter 28, §36.) Against a perverse mind, under the figure of Judaea, it is said through Isaiah: “It shall be a lair of dragons and a pasture of ostriches; and demons shall meet onocentaurs, and the hairy one shall cry to the other” (Isaiah 34:13–14).

What is signified by dragons except malice? And what by the name of ostriches except hypocrisy? The ostrich has the appearance of flying but does not have the practice of flight, because hypocrisy presents to all who look upon it an image of holiness, yet does not know how to follow the way of holiness.

In a perverse mind, therefore, the dragon lies and the ostrich feeds, because hidden malice is cunningly concealed, while an appearance of goodness is displayed before the eyes of those who look on.

What else is signified by the name “onocentaurs” except both the lustful and the proud? In Greek, ὄνος means “donkey”; by the designation “donkey” the lustful are indicated, while by the word “bull” the neck of pride is represented. Onocentaurs, therefore, are those who, subjected to the vices of lust and to the pleasures of their flesh, cast off shame, rejoice in shameful deeds, and raise their necks precisely where they ought to humble themselves.

Demons meet the onocentaurs because evil spirits readily serve the desires of those whom they see rejoicing in things over which they ought to weep. “And the hairy one shall cry to the other.” Who are represented by the name “hairy ones” [Text: “others”] except those whom the Greeks call *pans* and the Latins *incubi*? Their form begins with a human likeness but ends in an animal extremity.

By the name “hairy one,” therefore, the harshness of any sin is signified. Although sin sometimes begins under the appearance of reason, it always tends toward irrational impulses. It ends like a human being transformed into a beast when guilt, beginning under the semblance of reason, draws a person on to an irrational result.

Often the pleasure of eating serves gluttony while pretending to serve the needs of nature. When it stretches the belly into greed, it raises the members toward lust. The hairy one cries to the other when one completed wickedness provokes another to be committed, and when, as though by a voice of thought, a guilt already committed invites another guilt still to be committed.

Gluttony often says: “If you do not restore your body with abundant food, you will not persevere in any useful labor.” When it has inflamed the mind through desires of the flesh, lust immediately contributes words from its own suggestion, saying: “If God did not want human beings to unite bodily, he would not have made the very members suited for intercourse.” When it offers these suggestions as though they arose from reason, it draws the mind toward unrestrained desire. Once discovered, lust soon seeks the protection of deceit and denial and does not consider itself guilty if it defends its life by lying.

The hairy one therefore cries to the other when, under some appearance of reasoning, a succeeding sin entangles the perverse mind by taking occasion from the preceding sin. When the hard and harsh weight of sins presses it down, the hairy ones, as though summoned together, rule over it in agreement.

## CHAPTER XLVII — “There the lamia shall dwell and find rest” (Isaiah 34:14)

(*Moralia* XXXIII, chapter 29, §53.) Hypocritical and crafty people avoid confessing their faults all the more vehemently because, in their foolish shame, they blush to appear sinful before human beings; and when they are discovered and reproved, they bring forward defenses.

Hence it is said through Isaiah against Judaea: “There the lamia dwelt and found rest for herself; there the hedgehog had its burrow.” By the lamia hypocrites are signified; by the hedgehog, all malicious people who conceal themselves under various defenses.

The lamia is said to have a human face and an animal body. Thus, in the first appearance that all hypocrites display, there is something resembling the reasonableness of holiness; but what follows is an animal body, because the things they contrive under the appearance of goodness are utterly wicked.

By the name “hedgehog,” the defense of malicious minds is signified. When a hedgehog is seized, its head is seen, its feet are visible, and its entire body can be observed; but once seized, it gathers itself into a sphere, withdraws its feet inward, hides its head, and, between the hand of the person holding it, everything that had previously been visible all at once disappears.

So it is with malicious minds when they are caught in their excesses. The hedgehog’s head and feet are seen because the beginning at which the sinner approached his guilt and the tracks by which his wickedness was committed are recognized. Yet, when excuses are immediately brought forward, the malicious mind draws its feet inward, because it conceals all the traces of its iniquity. It withdraws its head because, through astonishing defenses, it refuses even to show that it began anything wrong.

It remains like a sphere in the hand of the one holding it [Text: “because”]. The person who reproves holds the sinner, wrapped up against [Text: “within”] his conscience, suddenly losing everything he had already recognized; and the one who had seen everything by discovering it is deceived by the perverse defense of evasion and is made entirely ignorant of it.

Therefore the hedgehog had a burrow among the reprobate, because the malicious mind, gathering itself within itself, hides in the darkness of its defense.

## CHAPTER XLVIII — “In the lairs where dragons dwelt” (Isaiah 35:7)

(*Moralia* XXIX, chapter 26, §52; Book II, homily 1 on Ezekiel, §11.) Concerning the holy Church, the Lord promises through Isaiah, saying: “In the lairs where dragons dwelt, the green growth of the reed and rush shall spring up.”

What else is signified by the reed except writers [Text: “preachers”]? And by the rush except small and tender hearers of sacred speech? Just as both the rush and the reed ordinarily grow in the moisture of water, and both flourish from one and the same water—and while the reed is used for writing, one cannot write with the rush—so there is one teaching of truth that irrigates many hearers. Some, watered by it, progress so far in the word of God that they even become writers, like reeds. Others, hearing the word of life, stand like rushes in God’s water and retain the greenness of good hope and upright conduct, but are entirely unable to express letters.

In the lairs of dragons, therefore, the green growth of reed and rush arises, because among those peoples whom the malice of the ancient enemy possessed there accumulates both the knowledge of teachers and the obedience of hearers.

## CHAPTER XLIX — “I will put a ring in your nostrils” (Isaiah 37:29)

(*Moralia* XXXI, chapter 11, §21.) The ancient enemy is restrained from his cunning cruelty by the omnipotence of divine power, so that his craft may not prevail against human weakness as far as he secretly investigates the means of destruction.

Hence, through Isaiah, he is forbidden to harm the Israelites when it is said to the king of Babylon: “I will put a ring in your nostrils.” By the ring the omnipotence of divine power is signified; by the nostrils, ambushes. It is as though it were openly said: You sigh while devising ambushes, but because you cannot accomplish what you desire, you bear the ring of my omnipotence in your nostrils, so that although you eagerly pant for the death of the good, you return empty-handed from their life.

## CHAPTER L — “The voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Isaiah 40:3)

(Book I, homily 7 on the Gospels, §2; homily 20, §§3, 5, 6.) “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.” You know, dearly beloved brothers, that the only-begotten Son is called the Word of the Father, as you recognize from human speech: first the voice sounds, so that afterward the word may be heard.

John the Baptist was therefore called “the voice” by Isaiah because he preceded the Word. The voice is said to go before the Lord’s coming because through his ministry the Word of the Father is heard by human beings. He also cries in the wilderness because he announces the consolation of the Redeemer to abandoned and desolate Judaea.

What he was to cry is made clear when it follows: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Isaiah 40:3). Everyone who preaches right faith and good works prepares a way for the Lord who comes into the hearts of his hearers, so that the power of grace may penetrate them, the light of truth may illumine them, and he may make straight paths for God by forming pure thoughts in the soul through the word of good preaching.

“Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low.” What is signified here by the name “valleys” except the humble? And by “mountains and hills” except proud people? At the Redeemer’s coming, therefore, the valleys were filled, while the mountains and hills were brought low. For, according to his saying, “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 19:11; 18:14).

A filled valley rises, while a humbled mountain decreases. In faith in the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, the Gentiles received the fullness of grace, while Judaea, through the error of unbelief, lost the very thing in which it had swollen with pride.

Every valley shall be filled because the hearts of the humble shall be filled with the grace of virtues through the words of sacred teaching, according to what is written: “You send forth springs in the valleys” (Psalm 104:10). Again it is said: “The valleys shall abound with grain” (Psalm 65:14).

Water flows down from the mountains because the teaching of truth abandons proud minds. But springs rise in the valleys because the minds of the humble receive the word of preaching. We now see the valleys abounding with grain, because the mouths of those who seemed meek, simple, and despised by this world have been filled with the nourishment of truth.

Every valley, therefore, shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, because the humble who persevere in humility of heart receive the gift that those swollen with exalted thoughts reject.

“And crooked things shall be made straight, and rough ways into smooth paths.” Crooked things are made straight when the hearts of the wicked, bent away through sin, are directed toward the rule of righteousness. Rough ways are changed into smooth paths when harsh and angry minds, through the infusion of heavenly grace, return to the gentleness of meekness.

When the word of truth is not received by an angry mind, the roughness of the road, as it were, drives back the step of the traveler. But when an angry mind receives corrections or exhortations through the grace of meekness, the preacher finds a smooth road where previously, because of the roughness of the way, he could not advance—that is, could not set down the step of preaching.

“And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.” “All flesh” means every human being. In this life no human being could see the salvation of God, namely Christ. Where, then, did Isaiah direct the eye of prophecy in this statement except toward the last day of judgment? When the heavens have been opened, the angels are ministering, the apostles are seated, and Christ appears upon the throne of his majesty, all—both the elect and the reprobate—will see him together, so that the righteous may rejoice forever in the reward they receive, while the unrighteous groan eternally in the punishment of vengeance.

## CHAPTER LI — “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6)

(*Moralia* XVII, chapter 8, §10; Book II, chapter 31, §43.) The prophet Isaiah, considering the brief duration of fleshly glory, declares: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass.”

The power of the wicked is compared to the flower of grass, because the glory of the flesh, while it shines, falls; while it exalts itself in its own eyes, it is suddenly cut off and brought to an end. And when the wicked and proud are humbled in death, the glory of the flesh withers in corruption.

Let us look at what kind of corpses of the rich lie in the tombs, what image of death remains in that extinguished flesh, and what decay of corruption. These are the very people who had been exalted by honors, swollen with possessions, and contemptuous of others. Because they did not consider where they were heading, they did not know what they were. But those who swelled with vanity now lie despised in corruption. The decay of corruption proves how much the glory [Text: “power”] of the flesh is worth.

## CHAPTER LII — “Ascend upon the high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isaiah 40:9)

(Book I, homily 11 on Ezekiel, §4.) Whoever is appointed as a watchman over the people ought to stand on high through his life, so that he may benefit them through his foresight. Hence Isaiah admonishes the watchman, saying: “Ascend upon the high mountain, you who evangelize Zion.”

Thus, whoever assumes the position of heavenly preaching must abandon the lowliness of earthly works, ascend to the height of good action, and rise above the works of those entrusted to him. In this way he sees the life of his subjects more subtly, since he does not subject his mind to the earthly things he despises; and he draws his subjects more easily toward better things, since by the merit of his life he cries out from above.

## CHAPTER LIII — “Those who trust in the Lord shall change their strength” (Isaiah 40:31)

[Column 0957A]

(*Moralia* XVIII, chapter 28, §4; XIX, chapter 27, §50.) When the hard and cold heart of someone predestined for life has been touched and softened by the fire of divine love, the person who had previously been hard and strong in love of the world is so changed into true strength, and exercises himself so strongly in the love of God, that what he formerly refused to hear he now begins both to believe and to preach.

Isaiah, contemplating this transformation [Text: “constancy”] of the elect, says: “Those who trust in the Lord shall change their strength; they shall take wings like eagles; they shall run and not grow weary; they shall walk and not faint.”

They change their strength because those who were formerly strong in the flesh strive to be strong in spiritual work [Note: [Column 0957D] These words, printed in italic type, are not found in Saint Gregory; we have already warned that Paterius both removes from and adds to Gregory’s text.]. Once converted, they flee the present world with as much strength as they formerly sought it. They take wings like eagles when they fly through contemplation. They run and do not grow weary because they preach great things with swift speed. They walk and do not faint because they retain the speed of their understanding while accommodating themselves to those who are slower.

## CHAPTER LIV — “I will make the desert into a pool of water” (Isaiah 41:18)

(Book I, homily 20 on the Gospels, §§12–13.) Since there are few who receive spiritual gifts and many who abound in temporal possessions, the rich insert themselves into the virtues of the poor by giving the holy poor consolation from their wealth [Text: “comforting them”].

Thus, when through Isaiah’s voice the Lord promised the abandoned Gentile people—that is, the holy Church—the merits of spiritual virtues as groves in a desert, he also promised the elm, saying: “I will make the desert into pools of water” [Text: “pools of waters”], “and the impassable land into streams of water.”

The Lord made the desert into pools of water and the impassable land into streams of water because he gave the Gentiles, who previously bore no fruit of good works through the aridity of their minds, the flowing waters of holy preaching. The land to which, because of the harshness of its dryness, the way had previously not been open to preachers afterward poured forth streams of teaching.

“I will give in the wilderness the cedar and the thorn, the myrtle and the olive tree” (Isaiah 41:19). By the cedar, because it has a strong fragrance and an imperishable nature, those who display virtues and signs in their conduct are signified—those who can say with Paul: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15). Their hearts are so firmly established in eternal love that no decay of earthly love can corrupt them.

By the thorn are signified spiritual men [Text: “men of spiritual teaching”] who, when they discuss sins and virtues, sometimes threaten eternal punishments and sometimes promise the joys of the heavenly kingdom. They prick the hearts of their hearers and pierce their minds with the pain of compunction, so that tears, like a kind of blood of the soul, flow from their eyes.

By the myrtle, which possesses a moderating virtue, so that by tempering it binds together relaxed limbs, those are signified who know how to sympathize with the afflictions of their neighbors and moderate their tribulation through compassion. When they bring a word or assistance of consolation to afflicted neighbors, they draw them back [Text: “restrain them”] to a state of uprightness, lest they dissolve into despair through immoderate tribulation.

By the olive we understand the merciful. In Greek, ἔλεος (*eleos*) means “mercy,” and, like the oil of the olive, the fruit of mercy shines before the eyes of almighty God.

He adds further in the promise: “I will place in the wilderness the fir, the elm, and the box tree together” (Isaiah 41:19).

Who are signified by the fir, which, growing greatly, rises high into the air, except those who, while still placed in earthly bodies within the holy Church, nevertheless raise the summit of their minds near the heavens through contemplation?

And what is expressed by the elm except the minds of secular people, who, while still serving earthly concerns, bear no fruit of spiritual virtues? Yet although the elm has no fruit of its own, it is accustomed to support a vine with its fruit. So secular people within the holy Church, although they do not possess the gifts of spiritual virtues, nevertheless support through their generosity holy men filled with spiritual gifts. What else do they carry than a vine with its clusters?

The box tree, which does not grow upward and, although it bears no fruit, nevertheless has greenness—whom else does it signify except those who, while still within the holy Church, are unable to produce good works because of the weakness of their age, but, following the faith of believing parents, hold fast to the perpetual greenness of faith?

After all this it is rightly added: “So that they may see, know, consider, and understand together” (ibid., 20).

The cedar is placed in the Church so that whoever draws from a neighbor the fragrance of spiritual virtues may not himself grow sluggish in love of eternal life but may burn with desire for heavenly gifts.

The thorn is placed so that whoever has been pierced by the word of its preaching may himself also learn, by its example, to pierce the hearts of those who follow with the word of preaching.

The myrtle is placed so that whoever has received from the mouth or work of a compassionate neighbor a moderating consolation in the heat of tribulation may himself also learn how to offer the moderation of his consolation to his neighbors.

The olive is placed so that whoever recognizes the work of another’s mercy may learn how he himself ought to show mercy to a needy neighbor.

The fir is placed so that whoever has recognized the power of its contemplation may himself also be inflamed to contemplate eternal rewards.

The elm is placed so that whoever looks upon one who is unable to possess the fruit of spiritual virtues, yet supports those filled with spiritual gifts, may himself also serve the lives of the saints with as much generosity as he can, and may bear, by supporting them, the clusters of heavenly goods that he cannot produce by giving birth to them.

The box tree is placed so that whoever observes many people, still situated in weakness, possessing the greenness of true faith may himself be ashamed to be unbelieving.

Therefore, after the trees have been described, it is rightly said: “So that they may see, know, consider, and understand together,” because within the holy Church human customs and orders are diverse. All must learn together when spiritual men of different qualities, ages, and ranks are seen together in it for imitation.

## CHAPTER LV — “He shall not break the bruised reed” (Isaiah 42:3)

(*Moralia* XXXIII, chapter 3, §7.) The kingdom of the Jews is compared to a reed when, through Isaiah, the Lord appearing in the truth of his flesh is said to be: “He shall not break the bruised reed, and he shall not extinguish the smoking flax.”

What is meant here by the name “reed” except the temporal kingdom of the Jewish people, outwardly gleaming but inwardly empty? Since the royal line had already failed among that people and its kingdom was possessed by a foreigner, he appropriately calls this same kingdom a bruised reed.

What else is expressed by the flax except its priesthood, which used linen garments? Because, at the Lord’s coming, it had lost the ardor of charity, it was like a fire whose flame had already been lost: not burning, but smoking.

The incarnate Lord did not break the bruised reed and did not extinguish the smoking flax, because he did not strike with the power of judgment either Judaea’s kingdom, which had almost already been destroyed, or its priesthood, which did not retain the fire of faith; rather, he endured them with the long-suffering of patience.

## CHAPTER LVI — “I was silent, I was always quiet, I was patient” (Isaiah 42:1)

(*Moralia* IX, chapter 23, §35; X, chapter 31, §54.) God will inflict strict punishments in judgment upon sinners whose sins he long endured silently in this world. He indicates this briefly through Isaiah, saying: “I was silent, I was always quiet, I was patient; like a woman in labor I shall speak.”

A woman in labor painfully expels what she has carried for a long time, hidden and heavy within her. After a long silence, therefore, the Lord speaks like a woman in labor, because the judge who is to come—having long endured human sins without vengeance—will eventually reveal, with the fervor of examination and as though with inward pain, how severe a sentence he has held within himself. What he now tolerates silently within himself, he will one day make manifest in the vengeance of judgment, as though with pain.

## CHAPTER LVII — “I will say to the North, ‘Give,’ and to the South, ‘Do not forbid’” (Isaiah 43:6)

(*Moralia* XXVII, chapter 43, §71.) When the Gentiles had been converted to the faith, Judaea, contradicting them, disdainfully refused to admit to the rewards of heavenly recompense those who had formerly been worshipers of idols. Thus it is said to Peter after the conversion of the Gentiles: “Why did you enter men who were uncircumcised and eat with them?”

Against this, through Isaiah, the Lord says: “I will say to the North, ‘Give,’ and to the South, ‘Do not forbid.’” By the North, the Gentiles are signified, constrained by the cold of sin; by the South, Judaea is signified, warmed as though by the sun at midday, because, when the Redeemer appeared in the flesh, it first received the fervor of faith.
