“To the North, ‘Give,’” is said when the Gentiles are commanded to offer God the gifts of their faith. To the South it is said [Text: “commanded”], “Do not forbid,” because the Hebrews who remain in the faith are instructed not to condemn the life of the Gentiles by rejecting them.

## CHAPTER LVIII — “The beasts of the field shall glorify me” (Isaiah 43:20)

(Moral. XXXI, c. 8, no. 11.) The Lord promises that he will convert both the manifest wickedness of the evil and the pretence of hypocrites, when through Isaiah he says: “The beasts of the field will glorify me, dragons and ostriches.” For whom are indicated by the name “dragons” except minds openly malicious, which continually creep upon the earth through lowly [Text: lowest] thoughts? And whom are designated by the term “ostriches,” which have wings as though for flight [Note: [Col. 0959D] “Should it not read *ad volatum et elevari* (‘for flight and to be lifted up’)?”], but cannot raise themselves from the earth by flying [Note: [Col. 0959D] “Should it not read *ad volatum et elevari* (‘for flight and to be lifted up’)?”], except those who pretend to be good, who retain the life of holiness as though a feather for flight in outward appearance, but do not practice it in their works? [Col. 0959C] Thus the Lord asserts that he is glorified by a dragon or an ostrich, because he often converts both those who are openly evil and those who are falsely good to his service, from the deepest disposition of their thoughts.

Or certainly the beasts of the field—that is, dragons and ostriches—glorify the Lord when the Gentiles, who once were a member of the devil, exalt the faith that is in him. He reproaches them by the name “dragons” on account of their wickedness, and marks them by the term “ostriches” on account of their hypocrisy. For the Gentiles seem to receive wings, but could not fly: they possessed the nature of reason, but did not know the practice of reason.

### CHAPTER LIX.—“They will sprout among the grasses like willows” (Isa. XLIV, 4).

(Moral. XXXIII, chap. 5, no. 11.) Willows are so green that they can scarcely wither, even when they have been cut off at the root and cast away. Hence in sacred speech good people are sometimes signified by the name of willows, on account of their greenness. [Col. 0959D] For unless they expressed the life of the elect through the constancy of its greenness, Isaiah would never have said concerning the sons of the holy Church: “They will sprout among the grasses like willows beside flowing waters.” The sons of the holy Church sprout among the grasses like willows when, amid the withering life of carnal people, they endure both in great numbers and in perpetual freshness of mind. They are rightly said to sprout beside flowing waters, because each of them receives abundance for fruitfulness from the teaching of sacred speech through which he passes for a time.

### CHAPTER LX.—“I am the Lord, and there is no other” (Isa. XLIV, 7).

(Moral. book III, chap. 9, no. 15.) Since evils were not created by the Lord—for they have no existence by any nature of their own—what does Isaiah mean when he says: “I am the Lord, and there is no other, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evils”? [Col. 0960A] The Lord indicates that he creates evils when he turns things well created into a scourge for us who act wrongly, so that those same things are evils for sinners through the pain with which they strike, yet good through the nature by which they exist. Thus poison is death to a human being, and yet life to a serpent.

For through love of present things we withdraw from love of our Creator; and the perverse mind, while submitting itself to love of creation, separates itself from the fellowship of the Creator. Therefore it is from these things that the Creator strikes us which, in our error, we placed before the Creator, so that from the very thing through which a proud person did not fear admitting guilt, he may find punishment and correction, and may return all the more quickly to what he lost, the more he sees that what he sought is full of pain.

Hence it is rightly said: “Forming light and creating darkness,” because when the darkness of pain is created outwardly through scourges, the light of the mind is kindled inwardly through instruction. “Making peace and creating evils,” because peace with God is restored to us when those things that have been well created but wrongly desired are turned into scourges that are evil for us. [Col. 0960B] Through guilt we exist in discord with God. It is therefore fitting that through scourges we should return to his peace, so that whenever something well created is turned into pain for us, the corrected mind may be humbly restored to the peace of its Creator.

### CHAPTER LXI.—“Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. XLVI, 8).

(Moral. XXVI, chap. 33, no. 61.) Hypocrites pour out their hearts outwardly in human praise, and believe themselves to be saints, not because they live in that way, but because they are called so. To these Isaiah rightly says: “Return, transgressors, to the heart.” For if they returned to the heart, they would not pour themselves out through words of outward testimony.

For what is closer to us than our own heart, which is within us? And yet, when it is scattered through perverse thoughts, our heart wanders farther from us. [Col. 0960C] The prophet therefore saw the transgressor as far away when he compelled him to return to his heart [Text: “sends”], because, having poured himself out outwardly, he scarcely finds the place from which he can return to himself. For because he is divided from the single pursuit of eternity, he is laid waste by the flood of countless thoughts.

### CHAPTER LXII.—“Come down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon” (Isa. XLVII, 1).

(Moral. book VI, chap. 16, no. 25; book XIV, chap. 17, no. 21; book VI, chap. 16, no. 25.) Under the figure of Babylon, Isaiah says to the reprobate mind: “Come down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground.” In this passage the human mind is called “virgin,” as I think, not because it is uncorrupted, but because it is unfruitful. And because Babylon is interpreted as “confusion,” the unfruitful mind is rightly called Babylon’s daughter: since it produces no good works and is ordered by no arrangement of right living, it is born, as it were, from a mother who is confusion. [Col. 0960D]

But if “virgin” means not unfruitful but uncorrupted, then, after losing the state of salvation, what she once was is invoked to heighten her confusion. To her the divine voice aptly says, “Come down.” The human mind stands on high when it longs for heavenly rewards, but it comes down from this position when, overcome and shamefully falling, it submits itself to the flowing desires of the world. To her it is added: “Sit in the dust.” What should we understand by dust except earthly thoughts? When they fly about importunately and silently in the mind, they blind its eyes.

Thus she came down and sat in the dust, because, abandoning heavenly things and covered with earthly thoughts, she becomes vile in the lowest places. Then it is added: “Sit on the ground.” What is signified by the ground except earthly action? It is as though the reproach were openly made: “Because you were unwilling to raise yourself through heavenly conduct, prostrate beneath yourself, humble yourself in earthly actions.”

She is therefore ordered to sit first in the dust and afterward on the ground, because the mind of the wicked, having descended from the judgment of inward uprightness, is first cast down into thinking evil things and afterward prostrated into doing them.

It follows: “There is no throne of the daughter of the Chaldeans” (Isa. XLVII, 1). Chaldeans are interpreted as “fierce.” They are indeed very fierce, because, following their own wills, they do not know how to spare even their own lives. [Col. 0961A] Earthly desires are fierce: they make the mind hard and insensible not only against the Creator, but often even against the blows of punishment.

But the daughter of the fierce has no throne, because the mind that is born from evil desires into love of the world and is hardened by those same desires loses the seat of judgment when it subjects itself to earthly cravings. It presides over no throne within itself, because it lacks the judgment of discernment; it is, as it were, driven from the seat of its own judgment because it wanders through outward desires.

For it is clear that the mind that has lost the seat of counsel within scatters itself outward through innumerable desires. And because it pretends not to do what it understands, it is rightly blinded, so that it does not know what it is doing. Often, too, by a just judgment it is abandoned to its own will and released into the most laborious services of the world, beneath the very things it anxiously desires.

Hence it is aptly added there: “Because you will no longer be called soft and tender: take the millstone and grind flour” (ibid., 2). Clearly, the parents of a tender daughter spare her and do not burden her with harsh and servile labors. [Col. 0961B] Almighty God therefore calls each beloved soul a tender daughter when he recalls it from the laborious services of this world, lest, while it is afflicted by outward activities, it become hardened against inward desires.

But the daughter of the Chaldeans is not called soft and tender, because the mind devoted to evil desires is left to the labor of this age in the very thing it anxiously seeks, so that outwardly it serves the world like a slave, while inwardly it does not love God like a daughter.

Hence she is also commanded to take the millstone and grind flour. The millstone is driven in a circle and flour is produced. Every activity of this world is a millstone: while it heaps up many cares, it turns human minds as though in a circle and casts out from itself something like flour, because, once the heart has been led astray, it continually produces the finest thoughts.

Sometimes, however, one who is believed to possess some spiritual merit is exposed when placed in a particular activity. Hence it immediately follows: “Uncover your shame; uncover your shoulder, reveal your leg, cross the rivers” (ibid.). [Col. 0961C]

In the administration of a work, shame is uncovered when a base and degraded mind is recognized in the display of its activity, though previously, in repose, it was considered great. The mind uncovers its shoulder when it displays the work that had been unknown. It reveals its leg because it shows with what steps of desire it longs for worldly profit. It also crosses rivers because it continually pursues the activities of this age, which flow daily toward their end; and while it leaves some behind and reaches others, it is always proceeding, as it were, from river to river.

### CHAPTER LXIII.—“You made the depth of the sea a way” (Isa. LI, 10).

(Moral. book XXIX, chap. 12, 23.) Almighty God, who endured no bonds of sins by which he could be held, came free into hell to release those who were bound, and entered the depth of hell to rescue the souls of his elect. Hence Isaiah says: “You made the depth of the sea a way, so that the liberated might cross.” [Col. 0961D]

If, according to the manner of divine speech, the sea is to be understood as the world, there is no objection to understanding the depth of the sea as the prison of hell. Before the coming of the Redeemer, this depth of the sea was not a way but a prison, because it confined within itself even the souls of the good, although not in places of punishment.

Yet the Lord made that depth a way, because, coming there, he allowed his elect to return from the prisons of hell to heavenly things. Hence it is aptly said: “So that the liberated might cross.”

### CHAPTER LXIV.—“They said to my soul, ‘Bend down, so that we may pass over’” (Isa. LI, 23).

(Book II, homily 31 on the Gospel, nos. 7–8.) We, dearly beloved brothers, give a way through us to evil spirits when we desire earthly things and bend ourselves toward the pursuit of temporal things. Hence Isaiah says concerning unclean spirits: “They said to my soul [Text: your soul], ‘Bend down, so that we may pass over.’”

The soul stands upright when it desires heavenly things and is not at all bent toward what is below; but when evil spirits see it standing in its uprightness, they cannot pass through it. [Col. 0962A] Their “passing through” is to scatter unclean desires in it.

They therefore say: “Bend down, so that we may pass over,” because, unless the soul casts itself down toward the pursuit of what is below, their perversity cannot prevail against it in any way. They cannot pass through the soul that they fear as rigidly set against them in its heavenly purpose.

Let us therefore be ashamed, brothers, to desire earthly things and to offer the backs of our minds to adversaries who are climbing upon them.

### CHAPTER LXV.—“Be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII, 11).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 2.) No ruler who has undertaken the office of cleansing the stains of pollution in others should himself be defiled by any impurity. Hence Isaiah says: “Be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord.”

Those carry the vessels of the Lord who, in the faithfulness of their own conduct, undertake to lead the souls of their neighbors into the inner sanctuaries. Let them therefore consider how greatly they must be cleansed in themselves, since they carry living vessels to the temple of eternity in the bosom [Text: lap] of their own commitment. [Col. 0962B]

### CHAPTER LXVI.—“You will spread out to the right and to the left” (Isa. LIV, 3).

(Moral. XXV, chap. 8, no. 21.) Through Isaiah it is said to the holy Church: “You will spread out to the right and to the left, and your seed will inherit the nations.” As such a multitude of nations enters, the Church is extended to the right when it receives some to be justified; it is also spread out to the left when it admits some who will remain in iniquity.

### CHAPTER LXVII.—“I will lay your stones in orderly courses” (Isa. LIV, 11).

(Moral. book XVIII, chap. 33, no. 52; book II, homily 6 on Ezekiel, no. 4.) Through Isaiah the Lord promises the coming Church, saying: “Behold, I will lay your stones in orderly courses, and I will found you on sapphires, and I will set jasper as your defenses, and your gates in carved stones, and all your boundaries in precious stones: all your children taught by the Lord.” [Col. 0962C]

He laid stones in orderly courses in the holy Church because he distinguished holy souls within it by the diversity of their merits. He founded it on sapphires, which are stones of an airy color and bear within themselves a likeness to the heavens, because the strength of the Church is made firm in souls that desire heavenly things.

And because jasper is green in color, he set jasper as its defenses: for those are set against adversaries for the defense of the holy Church who, green with inward desires, do not wither through the drying barrenness of reprobate sluggishness [Text: lukewarmness; “do not fade”].

He set its gates in carved stones. These are the gates of the Church through whose life and teaching the multitude of believers enters it. Because they are strong in great works and show by their lives what they assert in speech, they are remembered not as plain but as carved stones. In their upright life, right action is visible; in the stones themselves, what they have done is, as it were, engraved.

The gates would be plain rather than carved if they merely uttered the word but did not demonstrate holy works in themselves. But when they show by their lives that they live according to what they say, they are gates because they lead people inward, and carved because, by observing in their lives the holy works they command to others, they display them as though engraved in themselves.

Then, bringing together the whole number of the saints in a general collection, he adds: “All your boundaries in precious stones.” We see all the boundaries of the holy Church set in precious stones when we behold all its faithful strong in faith and charity. And as though we were asking, on hearing these things, that he identify the stones of which he spoke, he added: “All your children taught by the Lord.” [Col. 0962D]

### CHAPTER LXVIII.—“All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. LV, 1).

(Moral. book VI, chap. 5, no. 86.) The minds of the Gentiles who have been converted are now watered by the streams of sacred speech, which the Jewish people had possessed for the display of their pride. Hence Isaiah says to them: “All you who thirst, come to the waters, and you who have no silver, hasten” (Isa. LV, 1). [Col. 0963A]

Because divine utterances are signified by the word “silver,” the Psalmist testifies, saying: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire” (Ps. XI, 7). Those who therefore have no silver are called to the waters, because the Gentiles, who had not received the precepts of sacred Scripture, are satisfied by the flood of sacred speech. They drink it now with all the greater eagerness because they had long thirsted for it in dryness.

### CHAPTER LXIX.—“In place of the thornbush the fir will rise” (Isa. LV, 13).

(Moral. XVIII, chap. 20, no. 32.) Through Isaiah, with the Lord making the promise, it is said to the holy Church: “In place of the thornbush the fir will rise, and in place of the nettle the myrtle will grow.”

In the holy Church the fir rises in place of the thornbush, and the myrtle grows in place of the nettle, when in the hearts of the saints the height of heavenly contemplation is raised in place of the lowliness of earthly thought. The nettle is wholly of a fiery nature; the myrtle, they say, possesses a moderating power. [Col. 0963B]

Therefore the myrtle grows in place of the nettle when the minds of the righteous pass from the irritation and heat of vices to calmness and tranquility of thought: when they no longer desire earthly things and extinguish the flames of the flesh with heavenly desires.

### CHAPTER LXX.—“To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, I will give a place in my house” (Isa. LVI, 4).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chap. 28, admonition 29.) Through Isaiah the Lord promises those who do not know the sins of the flesh, saying: “To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths and choose the things I have willed, I will give them a place in my house and a name better than sons and daughters.”

Eunuchs are those who, restraining the impulses of the flesh [Text: affection], cut off from themselves the accomplishment of evil works. The place they hold with the Father is shown by the fact that in the Father’s house—that is, in the eternal dwelling—they are preferred even to sons.

### CHAPTER LXXI.—“You lied, and you did not remember me” (Isa. LVII, 11).

[Col. 0963C] (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 10.) Some faults of those under one’s authority should prudently be passed over in silence. Yet, because they are passed over, they should be pointed out, so that when the offender knows both that he has been detected and that he is being endured, he may be ashamed to increase the sins that he considers are being silently tolerated in him, and may punish himself as judge—the one whom the ruler’s patience mercifully excuses before him.

With this dissimulation the Lord rightly rebukes Judah through Isaiah, saying: “You lied, and you did not remember me, nor did you consider in your heart that I was silent and as though not seeing.” Thus he both concealed the faults and made them known: he kept silent against the sinner, yet declared that he had kept silent.

### CHAPTER LXXII.—“Cry out, do not cease” (Isa. LVIII, 1).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 4.) Through Isaiah the Lord admonishes the preacher, saying: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet.” Whoever approaches the priesthood undertakes the office of a herald, so that, before the coming of the Judge who follows in terror, he may advance by crying out. [Col. 0963D]

If a priest is ignorant of preaching, what voice of proclamation will a mute herald give?

### CHAPTER LXXIII.—“Your will is found on the days of your fasts” (Isa. LVIII, 3).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chap. 19.) Isaiah says to those who abstain: “Your wills are found on the days of your fasts.” And shortly afterward: “You fast for judgments and quarrels, and you strike with your fists wickedly.”

The will pertains to gladness, and the fist to anger. The minds of those who abstain are sometimes corrupted by anger and sometimes by gladness. The body is therefore worn down by abstinence to no purpose if the mind, abandoned to disordered impulses, is scattered among vices; the good of abstinence is lost precisely because it does not guard itself from spiritual vices.

### CHAPTER LXXIV.—“I will lift you above the heights of the earth” (Isa. LVIII, 14).

(Moral. XXXI, chap. 47, no. 96.) Through Isaiah the Lord promises the soul that follows him, saying: “I will lift you above the height of the earth.” [Col. 0964A]

The lower things of the earth are, as it were, losses, insults, poverty, and humiliation. Its heights are the gains of possessions, the flatteries of subjects, abundance of riches, honor, and the exaltation of offices. Whoever still walks through low desires considers these things high precisely because he regards them as great.

But if the heart is once fixed on heavenly things, it immediately sees how low are those things that had seemed high. For just as, when someone climbs a mountain, he looks down upon the other things lying beneath him the farther he directs his steps toward higher places, so one who strives to fix his purpose on the heights, while by that very effort he discovers that the glory of the present life is nothing, is lifted above the heights of the earth. What he previously believed to be above him while placed in low desires, he recognizes, as he advances by climbing, to be beneath him.

### CHAPTER LXXV.—“They have broken the eggs of vipers” (Isa. LXVI, 5).

(Moral. XV, chap. 15, no. 19.) A person willingly receives the beginning of a hidden suggestion, which an unclean spirit gently persuades the heart to accept through subtle counsels, and afterward, overcome by the violent assaults of its temptation, surrenders himself to it. Hence Isaiah says: “They have broken the eggs of vipers, and woven spiders’ webs. Whoever eats of their eggs will die, and what has been incubated will break forth as a basilisk.” [Col. 0964B]

What are signified by vipers, which are small serpents, except the hidden suggestions of unclean spirits, which first steal into human hearts through a small persuasion? To break open the eggs of vipers for wicked people is to disclose through perverse works the counsels of evil spirits that lie hidden in their hearts.

To weave spiders’ webs is to perform any of the temporal works of this world for the sake of worldly desire. Since these works are established with no stability, the wind of mortal life undoubtedly carries them away.

It is rightly added: “Whoever eats of their eggs will die,” because whoever receives the counsels of unclean spirits kills the life of the soul within himself. “And what has been incubated will break forth as a basilisk,” because the counsel of the evil spirit that is concealed in the heart is nurtured toward complete iniquity.

A basilisk is called the king of serpents. [Col. 0964C] And who is the head of the reprobate except Antichrist? Therefore “what has been incubated will break forth as a basilisk,” because the person who receives within himself the counsels of the viper to be nurtured, having become a member of the wicked head, grows into the body of Antichrist.

### CHAPTER LXXVI.—“Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isa. LX, 8).

(Book II, homily 6 on Ezekiel, no. 15; Moral. book XXI, chap. 2, no. 4.) The earlier fathers used marriage, fathered children, possessed property, and devoted themselves to the concerns of household affairs. But Isaiah, foreseeing by the spirit of prophecy that the preachers of the holy Gospel would abandon their possessions, not desire marriages, and neither desire nor possess anything on earth [Text: *quaerere, et subdit nihil* (“to seek, and it adds ‘nothing’”)], did not call them men walking upon the earth, but said that they flew like clouds, saying: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” [Col. 0964D]

Preachers, and all righteous people, are rightly called clouds because they rain through their words and flash with miracles. They are also said to fly like clouds because, though living on earth, everything they do is beyond the earth (Moral. book XXI, chap. 2, no. 4). Despising earthly things and drawing near to heavenly things in mind, they are lifted above earthly contamination.

They fly who do not touch the earth, because they desire nothing in it; holy preaching and sublime living suspend them above earthly things. They are like doves at their windows because, through the spirit of gentleness, they desire nothing in this world through their eyes, nor do they look upon outward things through all the senses of the body with the intent of rapacity. Carnal desire does not carry them outward; they look upon everything simply.

### CHAPTER LXXVII.—“To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord” (Isa. LXI, 1).

(Moral. IV, chap. 7, no. 12.) “To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” By “year” is understood the multitude of the redeemed. Just as a year is formed from a multitude of days, so that innumerable universal assembly of the elect is completed from the gathering of all the good. [Col. 0965A] The acceptable year of the Lord is therefore proclaimed when the future people of the faithful, who are to be illumined by the light of truth, are foretold.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII.—“Why is your garment red?” (Isa. LXII, 2).

(Book II, homily 1 on Ezekiel, no. 9.) Isaiah, seeing far in advance the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he assumed from the Virgin, stained with blood through the passion of the cross, said: “Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” He himself answered: “I alone have trodden the winepress, and no man from the nations was with me” (Isa. LXII, 3). [Col. 0965B]

He alone trod the winepress in which he himself was trodden, because by his own power he conquered the passion that he endured. For he who suffered even to the death of the cross rose from death in glory.

It is rightly said: “And no man from the nations was with me,” because those for whom he had come to suffer were meant to share in his passion. Since at that time they had not yet believed, he complains in his passion about those whose life was being sought through that very passion [Text: “whose life was being sought in that passion”].

### CHAPTER LXXIX.—“We all fell like a leaf” (Isa. LXIV, 6).

(Moral. II, chap. 44, no. 60.) “We all fell like a leaf, and our iniquities carried us away like the wind.” What is a human being except a leaf—one who fell from the tree [Text: added, “in paradise”]? What is he except a leaf—one who is snatched away by the wind of temptation and lifted by the gusts of desire? [Col. 0965C]

Because what he suffers through temptation is moved and lifted by so many gusts, a human being is rightly compared to a leaf. Iniquity carried us away like the wind because, fixed by no weight of virtue, it lifted us into empty exaltation.

### CHAPTER LXXX.—“A child of a hundred years will die” (Isa. LXV, 20).

(Moral. XVII, chap. 6, no. 8.) Whoever sins and lives is tolerated by divine providence in his iniquity for this reason: that he may be restrained from iniquity. But because he turns the time granted for repentance toward guilt, the strict Judge at the end turns the remedies of mercy that were bestowed toward punishment. [Col. 0965D]

Hence Isaiah says: “A child of a hundred years will die, and the sinner of a hundred years will be accursed.” It is as though he openly warned us, saying: The child’s life is prolonged so that he may be corrected from childish deeds. But if he is not restrained from committing sin even by the length of time, that very length of life which he received through mercy increases for him the accumulation of the curse.

It is therefore necessary that, when we see ourselves being awaited for a long time, we should fear the periods of prolonged mercy as evidence of condemnation, lest the punishment of the sinner increase through the clemency of the Judge, and lest the very means by which someone could have been snatched from death lead him more grievously toward death.

### CHAPTER LXXXI.—“There will be month after month” (Isa. LXVI, 23).

(Moral. XIII, chap. 28, no. 32; book XIX, chap. 10, no. 17.) The more the elect feel themselves drawing near to the final judgment, the more they exercise themselves in good works and tremble more terribly as they examine themselves. If they find in themselves any carnal thoughts or evil works, they consume them in the fervor of repentance.

Because they judge themselves and strike themselves by punishing themselves more carefully, after judgment they will receive eternal rest for their perfect good work, as Isaiah testifies, saying: “There will be month after month” (Isa. LXVI, 23). “Month” is sometimes used for perfection. There will therefore be month after month—that is, perfection in rest for those whose perfection is now found in activity.

### CHAPTER LXXXII.—“Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isa. LXVI, 24).

(Moral. IX, chap. 66, no. 100; chap. 65, no. 97; chap. 64, nos. 96, 101, 104; book XIV, chap. 59, no. 79.) The reprobate, handed over to the fires of hell, will feel pain in their punishments; in the anguish of pain they will be struck with terror; they will always endure what they fear, and without cessation fear what they endure.

Concerning them it is written through Isaiah: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished.” Here the flame that kindles also gives light; there the fire that torments darkens. Here fire both displays light and produces burning, but there the avenging flame of past vices produces burning, not light.

Hence Truth says to the reprobate: “Go, accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41). Again, signifying the whole body of them in one person, he says: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness” (ibid., XXII, 13). If, then, the fire that torments the reprobate could have light, the one who is rejected would not be said to be cast into darkness.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Ps. XXXVII, 9). Fire falls upon the impious, but when the fire falls, the sun is not seen, because the flame of Gehenna, by which it devours them, blinds them from the vision of truth [Text: true light]. [Col. 0966A] Thus the pain of burning torments them outwardly, while the punishment of blindness darkens them inwardly, so that those who sinned against their Creator in body and heart may be punished in body and heart together.

Driven from the sight of the strict Judge, the reprobate will therefore be tormented outwardly by pain, while, separated from the true light, they will be darkened inwardly. They will burn outwardly in eternal fire and be darkened from the inward light. There will be pain with dread, flame with darkness. The punishments will torment them, immersed [Text: submerged] in themselves, beyond their strength, and will preserve them while extinguishing in them the support of life, so that the end of life may punish them in such a way that they live forever in torment without end.

They will hasten toward an end through torments, yet, failing without end, will endure. Thus for the wretched there will be death without death, an end without end, failure without failure: death will live, the end will always begin, and failure will not know how to cease. Death will destroy but will not extinguish; pain will torment but will not drive away fear; flame will burn but will not dispel darkness.

Although the fire there will not shine for consolation, nevertheless, so that it may torment more severely, it will shine for some purpose. For they will see their followers together with themselves in torment, the flame illuminating them [Text: the reprobate illuminating them], in a wondrous order of judgment. They will see those whose disordered love led them into sin, so that those who carnally loved their lives against the commands of the Creator may be afflicted also by the destruction of those very people, to the increase of their own condemnation; and the carnal kinship that they placed before the Creator may intensify the punishment of their own chastisement when it is condemned before their eyes by an equal vengeance. [Col. 0966B]

What wonder is it if we believe that the fire of Gehenna possesses both the punishment of darkness and of light, when experience teaches us that even the flame of torches shines while remaining dark? The fire that will torment the reprobate in darkness must therefore be believed to preserve light for torment. It will not shine as a favor of consolation, yet it will shine for punishment, so that in the eyes of the condemned it neither glows with any brightness nor fails to show, for the increase of their pain, how those they loved are being tormented. [Col. 0966C]

Behold, we have learned what punishment awaits the condemned. Sacred speech instructs us without any doubt how great the fire in condemnation is, how great the darkness in the fire, and how great the terror in the darkness. But what does it profit us to know this beforehand if we do not escape it?

We must therefore take every care that, while we are granted a time of leisure, we may flee the avenging torments of evil through the pursuit of a good life. There are many who know in words that the final judgment exists, but by acting perversely testify that they do not know it. Whoever does not fear it as he ought has not yet understood with what storm of terror it will come.

If he knew how to weigh the burden of the dreadful judgment, he would not do what will be punished in it, and he would certainly forestall the day of wrath by fearing it. The terror of the Judge can be avoided only before judgment. Now he is not seen, but he is appeased by prayers. When he sits at that dreadful tribunal, he can be seen but can no longer be appeased, because he will return all at once, in anger, the deeds of the wicked that he silently endured for so long. [Col. 0966D]

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, it is necessary to fear the Judge now, while he does not yet exercise judgment, while he delays for a long time, while he still tolerates the evils that he sees. Otherwise, when he once stretches out his hand for the repayment of vengeance, he will strike all the more strictly in judgment the longer he waited before judgment. [Col. 0967A]

Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## BOOK FOUR. Testimonies concerning the prophet Jeremiah

[Col. 0967]

### CHAPTER ONE.—“Behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” (Jer. I, 6).

[Col. 0967A]

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chap. 7.) There are two commandments of charity: that of God and that of one’s neighbor. Desiring to benefit his neighbors through the active life, Isaiah sought the office of preaching. When the Lord asked whom he should send, he offered himself freely, saying: “Behold, here I am; send me” (Isa. V, 6). [Col. 0967B]

But Jeremiah, desiring diligently to cling to the love of the Creator through the contemplative life, is sent when he refuses in fear to go; nevertheless, he humbly resists being sent, saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God; behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am a child” (Jer. I, 6).

Thus from both men a voice outwardly different emerged, but it did not flow from a different source of love. What one laudably desired, the other laudably feared: the one feared losing the gains of silent contemplation by speaking; the other feared suffering the losses of diligent work by remaining silent.

But this must be subtly observed in both: the one who refused does not fully resist, and the one who wished to be sent first saw himself purified by the coal from the altar. Thus no one who has not been purified should dare to approach the ministries of sacred preaching, nor should anyone whom heavenly grace has chosen proudly resist under the guise of humility.

### CHAPTER II.—“Behold, I have appointed you today over nations” (Jer. I, 10).

(Moral. XVIII, chap. 10, no. 17; *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chap. 34.) The art of teachers should be to strive first to destroy what is perverse in the minds of their hearers and afterward to preach what is right, lest hearts full of evils be unable to receive the good seed of holy preaching.

Hence it is said to Jeremiah: “Behold, I have appointed you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and destroy, to build and plant.” [Col. 0967C] The foundation of right truth is never laid unless the structure of error has first been destroyed; and unless the preacher uproots the thorns of empty love from the hearts of his hearers, he plants the words of holy preaching in them in vain.

### CHAPTER III.—“I see a boiling pot” (Jer. I, 13).

(Moral. Book XVIII, ch. 20, no. 32; Book XXXIII, ch. 33, 37, no. 66.) The unclean spirit, by the breath of evil suggestion, sets the hearts of the wicked ablaze with earthly desires, as Jeremiah bears witness, saying: “I see a boiling pot, and its face is toward the face of the North.” The boiling pot is the human heart, seething with the fires of worldly cares and the anxieties of desires. The pot is set boiling when the human mind is incited by the persuasions of the malicious enemy and, by consent, is inflamed with the desires of evil persuasion. The pot of the human heart is set boiling from the face of the North when it is inflamed with unlawful desires through the instigation of the opposing spirit, who is commonly called by the name “North” [Col. 0967D]. For he who said, “I will set my throne in the North” (Isa. XIV, 14), kindles the mind he has once seized with the torches of his evil persuasion, like a fire placed beneath it [Text: “with fires placed beneath it”]; and, drawing human minds toward unlawful pleasures, he inflames some with the torches of pride, others with those of envy, others with those of lust, and others with those of avarice.

## CHAPTER IV — “Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest” (Jerem. II, 3).

(Book I, Homily 11 on Ezekiel, no. 1.) “Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest.” The fruits of a good soul are called God’s fruits. For the nations converted to faith later became the Lord’s harvest; but because Israel first believed in the Lord, Isaiah rightly called it the firstfruits of his harvest.

## CHAPTER V — “The sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes have violated you” (Jerem. II, 16).

[Col. 0968A]

(Moral. XXV, ch. 10, no. 27.) Through Jeremiah it is said to Judea: “The sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes have violated you to the crown of your head.” To be violated to the crown of the head means that, after the practice of evil deeds, one is corrupted even in the very height of faith. For when the most wicked spirits entangle each person’s soul in evil works but cannot corrupt the integrity of faith, they pollute its lower members, as it were, but do not reach the crown. Whoever, however, is corrupted in faith is violated to the crown of the head. For the malignant spirit reaches from the lower members to the highest point [Text: “the highest”] when, polluting the active life, he corrupts the chaste loftiness of faith with the disease of distrust [Col. 0968B].

## CHAPTER VI — “A wild ass accustomed to the wilderness” (Jerem. II, 24).

(Moral. Book XVI, ch. 47, no. 60.) “A wild ass accustomed to the wilderness; in the desire of its soul it has drawn in the wind of its love.” In this passage heretics are understood by the name “wild asses”: abandoned to their pleasures, they are alienated from the bonds of faith and reason. Thus the wild ass is accustomed to the wilderness because, while it does not cultivate the soil of its heart by the power of discipline, it dwells where there is no fruit. It draws in the wind of its love in the desire of its soul because the things it has conceived in its mind from the desire for knowledge are able to inflate it, not to build it up.

## CHAPTER VII — “If a man divorces his wife” (Jerem. III, 1).

[Col. 0968C]

(Book II, Homily 33 on the Gospels, no. 8.) Under the figure of Judea, the Lord says through Jeremiah to every sinful soul: “If a man divorces his wife, and she, departing, takes another husband, will he return to her again? Will that woman not be polluted and defiled? Yet you have prostituted yourself with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord.” Behold, he has given the example of a shameful woman. He shows that after disgrace she cannot be received, but he overcomes this very example by mercy when he says that a prostituting woman cannot be received and yet waits to receive the prostituting soul. Consider, brothers, the weight of such great compassion: he says that what cannot happen does happen, and demonstrates that he himself can do this even contrary to custom. Behold, he calls, and he also seeks to embrace those whom he declares polluted—the very ones by whom he complains that he has been abandoned [Text adds *esse*, “to be”]. Behold, heavenly goodness calls us back when we have turned away and prepares the bosom of its clemency for us when we return. Therefore, let no one waste the time of such great mercy; let no one cast away the remedies of divine compassion that are offered. Let each person consider by what debt he is bound, when God waits for him, lest contempt provoke him [Text: “lest he be provoked by contempt”].

## CHAPTER VIII — “Have you seen what faithless Israel has done?” (Jerem. III, 7).

(Book I, Homily 12 on Ezekiel, no. 18.) Often many who are not yet firm in the way of righteousness fall into evil deeds by the example of others. Hence, in the Lord’s voice, it is said through Jeremiah concerning Judah and Israel: “Have you seen what faithless Israel has done? She went up upon every high mountain and beneath every leafy tree, and there she prostituted herself; and I said, after she had done all these things, ‘Return to me,’ but she did not return.” Immediately he adds how Judah too, which seemed to be standing, fell through rivalry with her. For he says: “And her treacherous sister Judah saw that, because faithless Israel had committed adultery, I had dismissed her and given her a bill of divorce; yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear, but went and prostituted herself also.”

Behold, the merciful God is despised, and he calls those who turn away from him [Text: “he opens his bosom to those turning away”]. He opens the bosom of mercy, because he says to the sinner, “Turn back to me,” and yet she did not turn back. But because the Israelite people abandoned God and refused to return, they received a bill of divorce: they abandoned him by sinning, and received a bill of divorce by remaining without punishment amid their iniquities. The soul that sins departs; but if prosperity follows it after sin, no discipline and no rebuke of correction recalls it to its heart. In the separation it has made between itself and the Lord, it also receives a bill of divorce, so that, now abandoned as though alien, it may do whatever evils it wishes and not feel the scourges of God’s jealousy, in order that it may descend more deeply into eternal punishments.

But her sister Judah, because she saw the Israelite people flourishing in their perversity [Text: “because she saw the dismissed Israelite people”], likewise did not fear to withdraw from union with the Lord, as from the bed of a lawful husband. Hence we must regard sinners as all the more wretched when we see them abandoned in their guilt without punishment.

## CHAPTER IX — “How long will harmful thoughts remain within you?” (Jerem. IV, 14).

(Moral. Book XXVII, ch. 26, no. 50.) Through Jeremiah the Lord says to Judea: “How long will harmful thoughts remain within you?” He does not reproach them for coming, but for remaining. Unlawful thoughts also come into good hearts, but they are forbidden to remain, because all who are upright, lest they offer the house of their conscience to captivity, drive the enemy away from the very threshold of the heart. And even if he sometimes enters the minds of the good through sudden suggestions, the help from above prevents him from prevailing as far as consent [Text: “but, when heavenly help resists, he is prevented from prevailing as far as consent”].

## CHAPTER X — “I grieve in my belly” (Jerem. IV, 19).

(Book I, Homily 10 on Ezekiel, no. 6.) In sacred discourse, “belly” is sometimes customarily used for “mind.” Hence it is said through Jeremiah: “I grieve in my belly.” But to show that he spoke of a spiritual, not a bodily belly, he added: “And the senses of my heart are troubled.” It would not have contributed to the salvation of the people if the prophet had proclaimed that his bodily belly was in pain; rather, he grieved in his belly who experienced affliction of mind. Hence the Truth also says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 38). Since holy preaching flows from the mind of the faithful, rivers of living water flow, as it were, from the belly of believers.

## CHAPTER XI — “If Moses were to stand before me” (Jerem. VII, 16).

(Moral. Book IX, ch. 16, no. 23; Book II, Homily 27 on the Gospels, no. 8.) God’s anger can be resisted when he himself who is angry gives assistance; but it cannot be resisted at all when he prepares [Text: “rouses himself”] to take vengeance and himself does not inspire the prayer that is poured out to him. Thus, when Judea had offended God’s justice by sins that demanded punishment, the Lord forbade Jeremiah to pray, saying: “Therefore, do not pray for this people.” And again: “Even if Moses and Samuel were to stand before me, my soul would not be toward this people.”

Here one may usefully ask why, leaving aside so many earlier Fathers, only Moses and Samuel are named for the pouring out of prayer. We readily recognize the reason if we weigh the merits of that charity by which we are commanded to love even our enemies. For that prayer is especially commended to the ears of the Creator which strives to intercede even for enemies. When we review the deeds of the earlier Fathers as sacred discourse describes them, we find that Moses and Samuel prayed for their adversaries. One of them fled the persecution of a raging people and yet intervened for the life of his persecutor; the other, driven from leadership over the people, said to those very adversaries: “Far be it from me to sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you” (1 Sam. XII, 23).

What, then, does it mean, in the difficulty of entreating, to bring forward Moses and Samuel, except to indicate more plainly that not even those men would resist God’s anger if they stood before him—men who could more readily intervene for friends precisely because they were accustomed to intercede with him even for enemies? It is as though he plainly said: “Nor do I now hear them on behalf of friends, whom I know, by the merit of their great virtue, to pray even for enemies.”

## CHAPTER XII — “They have taught their tongue to speak lies” (Jerem. IX, 5).

(In the Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 11.) Nothing is safer for defense than purity; nothing is easier for speech than truth. For while a person is compelled to defend his deceit, his heart is wearied by difficult labor. Hence it is said through Jeremiah: “They have taught their tongue to speak lies; they labored to act wickedly.” It is as though it were plainly said: Those who could have been friends of truth without labor labored in order to sin; and when they refuse to live simply, they impose labor upon themselves in order to die. Hence it is also written: “The labor of their lips will cover them” (Ps. CXXXIX, 13). For the labor which now fills them will then cover them; for what now exercises their mind through flattering unrest will then press it through harsh retribution.

## CHAPTER XIII — “Death has climbed through our windows” (Jerem. IX, 21).

(Moral. XXI, ch. 2, no. 4.) Through the five bodily senses, as through certain windows, the soul looks upon external things and, looking upon them, desires them. Hence Jeremiah says: “Death has climbed through our windows; it has entered our houses.” Death climbs through the windows and enters the houses when desire, coming through the bodily senses, enters the dwelling of the mind. Hence also, speaking in the person of Judea, which by seeing external things had desired them and lost interior goods, the same prophet says: “My eye has plundered my soul” (Lam. III, 51). By desiring visible things, she lost invisible virtues. Thus she who lost interior fruit through exterior sight suffered the plundering of her heart through the bodily eye.

Therefore, in order to preserve purity of heart, discipline must also be maintained over the external senses. For however great the virtue with which the mind is endowed, however great the gravity by which it is strengthened, the carnal senses nevertheless make a childish commotion outside; and unless they are restrained by the weight of interior gravity and by a certain youthful vigor, they drag the enfeebled mind toward every fleeting and trivial thing.

## CHAPTER XIV — “The Lord called your name a fruitful, beautiful olive tree” (Jerem. XI, 16).

(Homily 9 on Ezekiel, second part, no. 16.) It often happens that either certain righteous deeds or words of sacred teaching perish in the judgment of almighty God when someone pursues transient favor through them. Hence Jeremiah says to Judea what an unwary mind may discover within itself if, at least after sin, it carefully examines its thoughts: “The Lord called your name a fruitful, beautiful, fruit-bearing, splendid olive tree. At the sound of a great speech, fire was kindled against it, and all its branches were burned.”

The Lord calls fruitful and beautiful, fruit-bearing and splendid, the olive tree whose effectiveness in action or holy zeal in knowledge of the word he approves. But “at the sound of a great speech fire was kindled against it,” because when someone begins to be praised, he may become ashamed to seem less than he is called and strives to be what he is called. For a great sound of speech is the favor of a flatterer. Thus, at the sound of a great speech, fire was kindled against it, because in the greatness of love [Text: “favor”] a flame is kindled in the heart from love of praise. But all the olive tree’s branches are burned, because in the eyes of almighty God both deeds well done and words spoken with knowledge perish when they are done no longer out of love for the Lord but with the intention of transient praise.

## CHAPTER XV — “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jerem. XI, 29).

(Moral. Book XII, ch. 4, no. 5; Book III, ch. 15, no. 28.) “Let us put wood into his bread” (Latin *in pane*; Text: *in panem*). Here “wood” is understood as the Lord’s cross. To put wood into his bread is to apply the cross to the Lord’s body and, by fastening it to his body, to bring the trunk of the cross against it. “And let us eradicate him from the land of the living.” They imagine that they can eradicate the Lord’s life from the land of the living [Text: “erase it”], since, when they see him as mortal, they suppose that his life will be ended by death.

## CHAPTER XVI — “Gather them like a flock for sacrifice” (Jerem. XII, 3).

(Moral. Book XXVII, ch. 24, no. 45.) When the Lord comes for judgment, the reprobate will perceive that they will not be able to perform holy deeds, and from their punishment (Text: “the punishment of their strength”) they will recognize the righteous path they ought to have followed. Hence it is said through Jeremiah: “Gather them like a flock for sacrifice, and sanctify them on the day of slaughter.” The reprobate are sanctified on the day of slaughter [Text: “for on the day of slaughter”], because then they realize the holy deeds they ought to have performed, when they can no longer avoid the punishments deserved for their wickedness.

## CHAPTER XVII — “The wild asses stood upon the rocks” (Jerem. XIV, 5).

[Col. 0971B]

(Moral. XXIX, ch. 25, no. 52.) “The wild asses stood upon the rocks; they drew in the winds like dragons; their eyes failed, because there was no grass.” In this saying the proud and most wicked persecution of the Jews is prophesied. They themselves are called wild asses because of their elevation of mind; they themselves are called dragons because of their poisonous thought. They stood upon the rocks because they trusted not in God but in the highest powers of this world, saying: “We have no king except Caesar” (John XIX, 15). They drew in the winds like dragons because, swollen with the spirit of pride, they grew inflated with malicious arrogance. Their eyes failed because their hope collapsed from what it had been fixed upon: loving temporal things, it neglected to await eternal things, and because it preferred earthly things to God, it lost them. They feared that they would lose their place if the Lord were not killed, and yet, once he was killed, they lost it.

But he adds why these things happened to the wretched: “because there was no grass”—that is, because the knowledge of eternity was lacking in their hearts, and no nourishment of the verdure of inner teaching refreshed them [Col. 0971C].

## CHAPTER XVIII — “You will be like a settler in the land” (Jerem. XIV, 8).

(Moral. XIV, ch. 41, no. 49.) When our Redeemer was not recognized by the Synagogue, he was like a stranger in his own house. Jeremiah plainly testifies to this, saying: “Why will you be like a settler in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay?” Because he was not heard as Lord, he was believed to be not the owner of the land but a settler. He turned aside like a traveler merely to stay because he took a few from Judea and, proceeding toward the calling of the Gentiles, completed the journey he had begun.

## CHAPTER XIX — “Because of the presence of your hand, I sat alone” (Jerem. XV, 17).

(Moral. Book IV, ch. 30, no. 60.) “Because of the presence of your hand, I sat alone, for you filled me with threat.” The face of God’s hand is the blow of just judgment by which he expelled the proud human being from paradise and shut him out in the blindness of this present exile. His threat is the terror of the punishment still to come. After the face of the hand, therefore, threats still terrify us, because through the experience of judgment he has already struck us with the punishment of our present exile, and, if we do not cease sinning, he still assigns us to eternal punishments.

Let the holy person, then, consider where the human being fell from when cast out here, and where the justice of the Judge still carries the person who sins after these things. Let him drive away from himself every throng of temporal desires and hide himself in great solitude of mind, saying: “Because of the presence of your hand, I sat alone, for you filled me with threat.” It is as though he plainly said: “When I consider what I already suffer through the experience of judgment, I anxiously withdraw from the tumult of temporal desires and seek solitude of mind, because I fear even more intensely those eternal punishments that you threaten.”

## CHAPTER XX — “If you separate the precious from the vile, you will be like my mouth” (Jerem. XV, 19).

(Moral. XVIII, ch. 33, no. 59.) “If you separate the precious from the vile, you will be like my mouth.” The present world is vile to God, whereas the human soul is precious. Whoever, therefore, separates the precious from the vile is called the Lord’s mouth, because through him God utters his words: by speaking what he can, he tears the human soul away from love of the present age.

## CHAPTER XXI — “The same as above.”

(Moral. XXXIII, ch. 17, no. 33.) He also separates the precious from the vile who detaches human minds from the reprobate imitation of the ancient enemy; and he is rightly called the mouth of God, because through him divine utterances are formed.

## CHAPTER XXII — “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus” (Jerem. XVII, 1).

(Moral. XIV, ch. 53, no. 62.) “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, upon an adamantine nail.” The nail is the extremity of the body; the diamond stone is so hard that it cannot be cut by iron. The strong sentence of God is signified by the iron stylus, and the eternal end by the adamantine nail [Col. 0972B]. The sin of Judah is said to be written with an iron stylus upon a diamond point because the guilt of the Jews is preserved by the strong sentence of God for an infinite end.

## CHAPTER XXIII — “And it became in my heart like a burning fire” (Jerem. XX, 9).

(Moral. XXIII, ch. 11, no. 18.) When Jeremiah, because he was not heard by the people, had imposed silence upon himself, saying, “I will no longer speak in his name,” he immediately added: “And it became in my heart like a blazing fire; and I grew weary, unable to endure it, for I heard the insults of many.” Because he saw that he was not heard at all, he desired silence; but when he saw the evils increasing, he did not remain in that silence. For while outwardly he was silent from weariness of speaking, inwardly he bore the fire of zeal for charity. The hearts of the righteous are inflamed when they see the deeds of the wicked increasing without correction; and they consider themselves participants in the guilt of those whom they permit, by their silence, to increase in iniquity.

## CHAPTER XXIV — “Cursed is the man who announced to my father, saying: ‘A male child has been born to you’” (Jerem. XX, 15).

[Col. 0972C]

(Moral. IV, ch. 4, preface.) When Jeremiah saw that his preaching was hindered by the difficulty of his hearers, he cursed, saying: “Cursed is the man who announced to my father, saying: ‘A male child has been born to you.’” If the prophet emerged from his mother’s womb in order to be afflicted in this world, what offense did the messenger of his birth commit? But what is signified by the person of the wavering prophet except the mutability of the human race, which comes through the merit of punishment? And what is expressed by his father except this world from which we are born? And who is that man who announces our birth except the ancient enemy, who, when he sees us wavering in our thoughts, incites the minds of wicked people pre-eminent through the authority of this world to bring about our deception?

When he sees us performing weak deeds, he extols them as though they were strong by means of favor, and speaks of male children being born, when through falsehood he rejoices that we have become corrupters of truth [Text: “of the truth”]. He announces that a male child has been born to the father when he shows this world that the one whom he has persuaded has become a corrupter of innocence. For when it is said to any sinner and proud person, “You have acted like a man,” what else is being declared than that a male child has been born in the world? Rightly, therefore, the man who announces the birth of a male child is cursed, because by that announcement the reprobate joy of our corrupter is revealed [Col. 0972D].

## CHAPTER XXV — “The earth was laid waste by the face of the anger of the dove” (Jerem. XXV, 38).

(Moral. XXXII, ch. 7, no. 9.) The Creator of all things will remain unchangeable in himself at the final judgment and will judge good and evil people with tranquillity. Hence Jeremiah says: “The earth was laid waste by the face of the anger of the dove, by the face of the fury of the Lord.” What he had called the anger of the dove, he then called the fury of the Lord. The dove is an exceedingly simple animal; and because no instability of fury enters into God, he called the Lord’s fury the anger of the dove. To demonstrate the undisturbed force of divine judgment, he spoke both of anger and of the dove. It is as though it were said more plainly [Text: “he said”]: “He brings forth an unshaken judgment with severity, because, remaining gentle, he punishes; yet he will by no means appear in the guise of the same unchangeableness to the elect and the reprobate. For he will appear tranquil to the righteous and angry to the unjust. Prior justice will show him benevolent to the former and guilt will show him terrifying to the latter.”

This happens daily in the conduct of the present life: when two people go to judgment, one innocent and the other guilty, both see the judge still silent before the sentence is pronounced. Yet the guilty person suspects a grave anger of the judge against himself [Text: “that very silence of the judge”]—not because the judge is visibly disturbed, but because he remembers his wickedness. By contrast, the friend of justice rejoices inwardly at the testimony of a good memory; and because [Text: “where”] he has nothing within himself to fear [Text adds: “therefore”], he sees everything concerning himself as kindly disposed.

So, in the dreadful judgment of the Lord, although the righteous and the unjust alike see him tranquil, sinners who are conscious of their evil nevertheless think that he is disturbed and angry toward them [Col. 0973B].

## CHAPTER XXVI — “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel correction” (Jerem. XXX, 14).

(Moral. preface, ch. 3, no. 12; Book XIV, ch. 37.) There are different kinds of blows. Sometimes a sinner is struck so that he may be punished without reprieve, as is said through Jeremiah to doomed Judea: “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel correction.” When God’s scourges go beyond what we can bear and exceed the strength of our patience, we must greatly fear that, because our sins demand it, we are no longer being struck by the Lord as children by a father, but as enemies by the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXVII — “The same as above.”

(Moral. Book XIV, ch. 37, no. 45; preface, ch. 5, no. 12.) Whoever is struck so cruelly that his strength is overcome by the blow [Col. 0973C] is not struck by the Lord as a son for discipline, but as an enemy by anger.

Sometimes a sinner is struck so that he may be corrected, as it is said to someone in the Gospel: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin any longer, lest something worse happen to you” (John V, 14). The words of the Savior indicate that the preceding sins had demanded the force of suffering.

Sometimes a person is struck not to wipe away a past fault but to prevent a future one. Paul plainly testifies to this concerning himself, saying: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me” (2 Cor. XI, 7). For by saying not “because it exalted me” but “lest it exalt me,” he plainly indicates that through that blow he is restrained so that the fault may not occur, not that a fault which has occurred may be cleansed.

Sometimes, however, a person is struck neither for a past nor for a future iniquity, but so that the power of divine virtue alone may be shown through the removal of the blow; and when unexpected healing follows the blow, the power of the one who heals may be known and loved more ardently. When an innocent person is worn down by a scourge, the highest reward of merit is heaped upon him through patience.

Thus, when the disciples said to the Lord in the Gospel concerning the man born blind, “Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?” (John IX, 2), the Lord replied: “Neither did this man sin nor his parents, but that the works of God might be manifested in him.” In this manifestation, what else is accomplished except that the strength of merit is increased through the scourge, and, when no past fault [Text: “iniquity”] is cleansed, great strength is generated through patience [Col. 0973D]?

## CHAPTER XXVIII — “After you converted me, I did penance” (Jerem. XXXI, 19).

(Moral. XXIV, ch. 22, no. 48.) When almighty God changes a person toward the desire for conversion, the person immediately restrains all the fleeting things of the flesh and kills, with a certain sword of discipline, everything in the flesh that was living wrongly. Jeremiah had killed himself with this sword of discipline when he said: “After you converted me, I did penance; and after you showed me, I struck my thigh.” For what is understood by the thigh except the pleasure of the flesh? And what does he mean by saying, “After you showed me, I struck my thigh,” except that, after he had spiritually seen heavenly things, he extinguished everything lower that was living carnally within him? Thus, the more fully heavenly things were revealed [Text: “the highest things”], the less the lower things he had held were set free [the transmitted reading *non liberent* is uncertain]. For the more each person begins to live above, the more he also begins to die below.

## CHAPTER XXIX — “Set up a watchtower for yourself” (Jerem. XXXI, 23).

(Moral. XXXI, ch. 44, no. 85.) Jeremiah admonishes each person’s soul, saying: “Set up a watchtower for yourself; place bitterness for yourself.” To set up a watchtower for oneself is to foresee, through lofty consideration, the future struggles of vices. The mind of the elect places bitterness for itself because, even when established in the peace of virtues, it sees the evils lying in wait and does not consent to rest securely [Text: “whenever it sees them”].

## CHAPTER XXX — “Everyone who eats a sour grape” (Lam. XXXI, 30).

[Col. 0974B]

(Moral. Book XI, ch. 35, no. 45.) “Everyone who eats a sour grape, his teeth will become numb” [Text: “who will eat”]. Food is broken by the teeth so that it may be swallowed. Hence we not improperly understand the inner senses by the teeth: they chew and crush each thing they think about, as it were, and send it on to the stomach of memory.

What, however, is a sour grape except sin? A sour grape is fruit before its time. Whoever desires to be satisfied with the pleasures of the present life hastens, as it were, to eat fruit before its time. Whoever therefore eats a sour grape has his teeth become numb, because the inner senses of the person who feeds on the pleasure of the present life become bound, so that they can no longer chew—or, that is, understand—other things spiritually. For by the things in which they were delighted outwardly, they become numb inwardly. While the soul is fed by sin, it cannot eat the bread of justice, because teeth bound by the habit of sin cannot in any way eat what tastes just within.

That the inner senses are customarily understood by the teeth, the same Jeremiah testifies, saying: “He broke my teeth by number.” He says that his teeth—that is, his senses—were broken by number because, according to the measure of each person’s sin, blindness of understanding is generated in the senses. In proportion to what a person has done outwardly, he becomes numb in that which he could have understood concerning inner and invisible things [Col. 0974C].

## CHAPTER XXXI — “The city will be built for the Lord from the tower of Hananel” (Jerem. XXXI, 38).

(Moral. XXV, ch. 8, no. 21.) “The city will be built for the Lord from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate, and it went beyond the measuring line.” No one is unaware that the holy Church is the city of the Lord. Hananel, however, is interpreted as “the grace of God”; and at a corner a double wall is joined. Therefore the city of the Lord is said to be built from the tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate because the holy Church begins from the height of heavenly grace and is built up to the entrance and reception of both peoples, namely, the Jewish and the Gentile peoples.

But because, as the multitude within it increases, the reprobate too are gathered into it, it is aptly added: “And it went beyond the measuring line,” because it extends even to those who, crossing the measure of justice, do not belong within the number of the heavenly measure [Col. 0974D].

## CHAPTER XXXII — “To lift him from the pit, ropes and old rags are lowered to him” (Jerem. XXXVIII, 11).

(Moral. Book XXV, ch. 7, no. 17.) Aided by divine admonitions and the examples of the Fathers who preceded us, we are freed from the depths of this life. This was signified when Jeremiah was sent into the pit: “To lift him from the pit, ropes and old rags are lowered to him.” What are signified by the ropes except the Lord’s commandments? Because they both convict and rescue us when we are placed in evil action, they bind and draw us out, constrain and lift us, as it were.

But lest a person bound by these ropes be cut while being pulled, old rags are also lowered at the same time. This is because the examples of the ancient Fathers both prevent the divine commandments from terrifying us and strengthen us; by comparison with them, we presume that we can do what we fear because of our weakness. If, therefore, we hasten to be lifted from this depth, let us be bound by these ropes—that is, let us be constrained by the Lord’s commandments. Let the old rags also be present, by which the ropes may be held more securely; that is, let us be strengthened by the examples of those who preceded us, lest subtle commandments wound us, weak and fearful as we are, while they lift us [Col. 0975A].

## CHAPTER XXXIII — “Eighty men came from Shechem” (Jerem. XLI, 5).

(Moral. Book I, ch. 36, no. 52.) When the ancient enemy cannot overcome the intention of a good work, he conceals snares along the way, so that, in the very thing being done well, he may turn the heart aside toward vice by exalting itself. He places himself in the action itself as though in the road, so that, when a person goes forth more confidently because of his intention, he may be killed by a vice secretly attached, as though from ambush.

Jeremiah conveys this more subtly. While he undertook to report external events, he indicated what takes place within us, saying: “Eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, their beards shaved and their garments torn, covered with filth; they had gifts and incense in their hands to offer in the house of the Lord. Ishmael son of Nethaniah went out from Mizpah to meet them, walking along and weeping. When he had met them, he said to them, ‘Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.’ When they had come into the middle of the city, he killed them.”

Those who shave their beards withdraw confidence in their own strength; those who tear their garments do not spare themselves in the rending of their external appearance. They come to offer incense and gifts in the house of the Lord. They promise to present themselves in God’s sacrifice with prayer and works. Yet if they do not know how to look carefully around themselves on the very path of holy devotion, Ishmael son of Nethaniah comes to meet them, because every evil spirit, begotten in the error of pride after the example of his former father, namely Satan, places himself in the way as a snare of deception.

It is rightly said of him: “Walking along and weeping, he went,” because, in order to prevail in striking down devoted minds, he conceals himself, as it were, beneath a covering of virtue. While he pretends to join in sincerely mourning, he is admitted more securely into the depths of the heart and kills whatever virtue lies hidden within. He often promises to raise a person to higher things. Hence he is also said to have spoken thus: “Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam”; and while he promises greater things, he takes away even the lesser ones.

Therefore it is rightly said: “When they had come into the middle of the city, he killed them.” He kills in the middle of the city the men who were coming to offer gifts to the Lord because minds devoted to divine works, unless they guard themselves with great vigilance, lose their life on the very journey while carrying the offering of their devotion, when the enemy steals upon them. No one escapes from the enemy’s hand unless he inwardly turns back to repentance.

Hence it is added: “Ten men, however, were found among them who said to Ishmael: ‘Do not kill us, for we have treasures in the field—of wheat, barley, and honey’; and he did not kill them” (ibid., 18). A treasure in the field is hope in repentance. Because it is not seen, it is kept as though buried within the soil of the heart [Text: “in the earth”]. Those who had treasures in the field were saved, because those who return to lamentation and repentance after the fault of their carelessness do not die after being captured [Col. 0975D].

## CHAPTER XXXIV — “Cursed is the one who performs the work of the Lord negligently” (Jerem. XLVIII, 10).

(Moral. IX, ch. 34, no. 53.) There are two things that must be diligently feared in good works: sloth and fraud. Hence, in the ancient translation, it is said through Jeremiah: “Cursed is everyone who performs the work of the Lord [Text: “of God”] deceitfully and negligently” (Jerem. XLVIII, 10).

But it must be understood that sloth arises from sluggishness, while fraud arises from private love. The former is increased by a lesser love of God; the latter is created by self-love possessing the mind wrongly. Whoever loves himself inordinately commits fraud in God’s work when he hastens, through what he has done rightly, toward transient rewards, and through this fraud desires either the silent approval of the human heart, the breath of favor, or any external possession.

Therefore, the only person who commits no fraud in God’s work is the one who, while devoting himself to good action, does not yearn either for bodily rewards, words of praise, or the favor of human judgment. Often some of our good deeds perish through thieving fraud because earthly desire attaches itself to our righteous actions. Often they fail when sloth intervenes, because, as love grows cold, they wither away from the fervor with which they began.

## CHAPTER XXXV — “Cursed is the one who keeps his sword from blood” (Jerem. XLIII, 18).

(Pastoral Rule, Part III, ch. 25.) Those who recognize the wounds of minds but neglect to heal them by cutting words are entangled in grave guilt. Hence it is said through Jeremiah: “Cursed is the one who keeps his sword from blood” (Jerem. XLVIII, 18). To keep one’s sword from blood is to withhold the word of preaching from killing off a carnal life [Col. 0976B].

## CHAPTER XXXVI — “How the hammer of the whole earth has been broken” (Jerem. L, 23).

(Morals, Book XXXIII, chapter 14, no. 28 and Book XXXIV, chapter 12, no. 23, and chapter 7, nos. 15 and 16.) The ancient enemy maliciously desires to tempt righteous men; nevertheless, the Lord either mercifully brings this about or justly permits it. For he subjects his chosen ones to the tempter in order to educate them, so that those who could have perished through pride may, humbled by temptation, be delivered from destruction. Thus the devil tempts God’s chosen willingly, and by tempting them proves them without knowing it. But in that heavenly homeland, the righteous, enjoying celestial blessedness, will not be permitted to be tempted at all; rather, he will be delivered over to the eternal fires of Gehenna before their eyes, and, together with his own body—that is, with all the reprobate—handed over to avenging flames, he will be tormented without end.

Jeremiah contemplated the force of the final judgment that would come upon the ancient enemy and said: “How the hammer of the whole earth has been broken and shattered!” (Jeremiah 50:23). It is as though he were plainly saying: Who can comprehend with what a whirlwind, when the final judgment comes, the one by whom the Lord strikes his vessels in order to shape them for the use of his ministry will be shattered in eternal damnation? For when the strict Judge arrives, the one who is now endured with extraordinary long-suffering and gentleness will be removed from this world by the anger of judgment. He will be shaken out and swept away with such weight of torment and such a whirlwind of judgment that those who can still be found in bodies—already strong and perfect—will be shaken with great terror amid so immense a storm; and if any light rust of vices could still be present in them, it will be purged away by that fear.

## CHAPTER XXXVII — Babylon is a golden cup (Jeremiah 51:7)

(Morals, Book XXXIV, chapter 15, no. 26.) “Babylon is a golden cup” (Jeremiah 51:7). By the name of gold, the splendor of temporal glory is expressed; but what is signified by the name of Babylon except the glory of this world? It is called a golden cup because, while it displays temporal things as beautiful, it intoxicates foolish minds with desire for itself, so that they pursue attractive temporal things and disregard invisible beauty. Babylon is a golden cup because, while it displays the appearance of outward beauty, it removes the perception of inward uprightness.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — We healed Babylon, but she was not healed (Jeremiah 51:9)

(Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 13.) Jeremiah laments in the voice of those who scourge the life of the reprobate, saying: “We healed Babylon, but she was not healed” (Jeremiah 51:9). Babylon is healed but is nevertheless not restored to health when a mind confused by wicked action hears words of correction, experiences the scourges of correction, and yet refuses to return to the right paths of salvation.

## CHAPTER XXXIX — Weeping, she wept in the night (Lamentations 1:2)

(Morals, Book XIII, chapter 12.) The jaw of holy Church is the holy preachers, as it is said through Jeremiah under the figure of Judea: “Weeping, she wept in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks” (Lamentations 1:2). For those who know how by preaching to break the life of the carnal weep more deeply over the adversity of the Church [Text: “in the adversities of the Church”].

## CHAPTER XL — Her enemies have become her leaders (Lamentations 1:3)

(Morals, Book I, chapter 36, nos. 51 and 53.) The ancient enemy sometimes corrupts the intention behind a good work, so that nothing that follows in the action emerges pure and undefiled, because he disturbs it from the beginning. He corrupts the intention behind a good work because, seeing that human hearts are easy to deceive, he adds to their desires the breath of passing approval, so that in the upright things they do they are bent toward the pursuit of low things by the crookedness of their intention. Hence, under the figure of Judea, Jeremiah rightly says of every soul caught in the snare of a wretched intention: “Her enemies have become her leaders” (Lamentations 1:3). It is as though he were plainly saying: When a good work is undertaken without a good intention, hostile spirits take control of it from the very beginning of the thought; and they possess it more completely the more they hold dominion over it from its beginning. If the heart is once corrupted in its intention, the middle and end of the subsequent action are securely possessed by the crafty enemy. Therefore, we must keep watch with the utmost care, lest a mind serving even good works be corrupted by a reprehensible intention.

## CHAPTER XLI — Her enemies saw her (Lamentations 1:7)

(Morals, Book V, chapter 31, no. 55.)
