There are some who, the more securely they abstain from external actions, the more widely they accumulate within themselves, through idleness, the noise of impure thoughts. Hence, under the figure of Judea, a soul sluggish through idleness is lamented when it is said: “Her enemies saw her and desired her sabbaths” (Lamentations 1:7; [text: “Lamentations”]). By the commandment of the Law, one ceases from external work on the sabbath. Thus the enemies mock when they see the sabbaths, when evil spirits draw the very leisure of inactivity toward illicit thoughts, so that each soul, the more it believes that it is serving God by withdrawing from external actions, the more it serves their tyranny by thinking illicit thoughts.

## CHAPTER XLII — All her people groaning (Lamentations 1:11)

(Morals, Book XXV, chapter 23, no. 49.) When the prophet Jeremiah lamented the corrupt ways of the Synagogue, he said: “All her people are groaning and seeking bread; they gave their precious things for food to revive the soul” (Lamentations 1:11). By “bread,” human enjoyment and delight are sometimes understood. Thus the groaning people seek bread when the wicked multitude of human beings is afflicted, because it is not satisfied according to its desire with the delight of the present life. It also gives all its precious things for food because it inclines the virtues of the mind toward the appetite for passing pleasure and tries to revive the soul because it attempts to satisfy its perverse desires.

Hence, immediately afterward, from the voice of the chosen multitude, it is rightly added [Text: “of that one”]: “See, Lord, and consider, for I have become worthless” (ibid.). The people of God become worthless when, as the number of the wicked increases, they pursue in them not what is supreme and heavenly but what is low and earthly.

## CHAPTER XLIII — O all you who pass along the road (Lamentations 1:12)

(Morals, Book XV, chapter 57.) Jeremiah, asking that the grief of his heart be considered, says: “O all you who pass along the road, pay attention and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (ibid.). Those who do not regard the present life as a road along which they pass but as a homeland do not know how to consider the grief of the elect’s hearts. Therefore, he asks those who have not fixed their minds in this world to consider his sorrow [Text: “the prophet adds”].

## CHAPTER XLIV — Outside, the sword kills (Lamentations 1:20)

(Morals, Book III, chapter 32, no. 62.) Often we are crushed outwardly by scourges and wearied inwardly by carnal suggestion. Hence Jeremiah laments, saying: “Outside, the sword kills, and inside there is a death like it” (Lamentations 1:20). Outside, the sword kills when punishment strikes and pierces us outwardly; but inside there is a similar death because, although one endures the scourges, the conscience within is not clean from the stains of temptation.

## CHAPTER XLV — The Lord has become like an enemy (Lamentations 2:5)

(Morals, Book XI, chapter 16, no. 25.) Looking far in advance upon the fall of the Israelites, Jeremiah says: “The Lord has become like an enemy; he has overthrown Israel, overthrown all her walls, and destroyed her fortifications” (Lamentations 2:5). Walls in cities serve as ornament, while fortifications serve for defense; for some gifts strengthen us, while others adorn us. Prophecy, teaching, kinds of languages, and the power of healings are, as it were, walls of the mind. Even if someone does not possess these, he can stand fortified through faith and justice, though he may not appear adorned with the height of virtues. Hope, faith, and charity, however, are not our walls but our fortifications; if we neglect to possess them, we lie exposed to the ambushes of enemies.

Thus, concerning Judea, because he removed prophecy, teaching, and the signs of miracles, he overthrew her walls. But because, on account of her hardness, he permitted faith, hope, and charity to be taken away, he undertook to remove her fortifications. The proper order is preserved: first the walls, and afterward the fortifications, are said to have been destroyed. For when a sinful soul is abandoned, the gifts of virtue given for the manifestation of the Spirit are first taken from it, and afterward the foundations of faith, hope, and charity are destroyed.

## CHAPTER XLVI — Your prophets saw false things for you (Lamentations 2:14)

(Pastoral Rule, Part II, chapter 4.) Jeremiah says to the sinful people: “Your prophets saw false and foolish things for you, and they did not disclose your iniquity, so as to summon you to repentance” (Lamentations 2:14). In sacred language, “prophets” are sometimes called teachers, who, while pointing out fleeting and present things, reveal what is to come. Divine speech rebukes them for seeing false things because, while they fear reproving faults, they flatter sinners uselessly with promises of security. They do not disclose the iniquity of sinners because they fall silent rather than speak words of reproach. The word of correction is indeed the key of opening, because by reproving it uncovers the fault that often remains unknown even to the one who committed it.

## CHAPTER XLVII — I am the man who sees my poverty (Lamentations 3:1)

(Morals, Book XXXIV, chapter 3, no. 5.) The elect, placed in this sorrowful exile of the present life, know that they are poor. Since they do not at all behold the true riches of the heavenly homeland, they continually sigh for them and groan amid the misery of this poverty. Jeremiah had looked upon this poverty when he said: “I am the man who sees my poverty under the rod of his indignation” (Lamentations 3:1). The rod of God’s indignation is the blow of strict judgment. Man suffered this indignation when, driven from paradise, he lost the true riches of inward joy.

But because each of the elect continually perceives that he has fallen into the poverty of the present life from that innate capacity of power, it is rightly said: “I am the man who sees my poverty.” For whoever still desires visible things does not understand the evil of his pilgrimage and does not know how to see the very thing he suffers. David, seeing this poverty, says: “My strength has been weakened in poverty” (Psalm 30:11). Strength is said to be weakened in poverty because the mind, having fallen into this pilgrimage and battered by the troubles of its corruption, is hindered from contemplating what it has lost.

## CHAPTER XLVIII — He has made my fetter heavy (Lamentations 3:7)

[Col. 0979A]

(Homilies on Ezekiel, Book I, Homily 12, no. 13.) Jeremiah, contemplating the subtle judgment of almighty God, says: “He has made my fetter heavy” (Lamentations 3:7). We have fetters in the very weakness and corruption of our mortality. But when tribulation and groaning are added to us, our fetters themselves become heavier.

## CHAPTER XLIX — He has intoxicated me with wormwood (Lamentations 3:15)

(Morals, Book XX, chapter 15, no. 39; Book VII, chapter 21.) Jeremiah, taking upon himself in lamentation the figure of the whole human condition, complains, saying: “He has intoxicated me with wormwood” (Lamentations 3:15). Anyone who is drunk does not know what he suffers; but whoever is drunk with wormwood both finds what he has taken to be bitter and yet does not understand the very bitterness with which he is filled. Thus the human race, by God’s just judgment abandoned to its pleasures and through those same pleasures delivered over to voluntary tribulations, is drunk with wormwood. The things it endures for love of this life are bitter, yet through the blindness of desire, like the insensibility of drunkenness, it does not recognize that same bitterness.

While thirsting for the glory of the world, it accepts many tribulations for its sake, and what it drinks is bitter. But because it has swallowed this so greedily, it can no longer, because of its very drunkenness, discern the evil of that bitterness. Alienated from rational perception, it considers light whatever it endures for the world and does not recognize the bitterness of the labor it bears, because it is led with pleasure toward everything by which it is painfully wearied.

## CHAPTER L — Let us examine our ways (Lamentations 3:40)

(Morals, Book XVIII, chapter 5, no. 10.) Two things necessarily belong together before God: prayer must be supported by action, and action by prayer. Hence Jeremiah says: “Let us examine our ways and lift our hearts with our hands to God in heaven” (Lamentations 3:40). To examine our ways is to scrutinize the inner movements of our thoughts. One lifts the heart with the hands when one strengthens prayer with works. Whoever prays but avoids acting lifts the heart but does not lift the hands; whoever acts but does not pray lifts the hands but does not lift the heart.

## CHAPTER LI — You have placed a cloud so that prayer may not pass through (Lamentations 3:44)

(Morals, Book XXVIII, chapter 17, no. 37.) Holy men who sympathize even with the negligence of others, and consider themselves to suffer what they perceive others suffering, say to God in prayer: “You have placed a cloud so that prayer may not pass through” (Lamentations 3:44). It is as though they were plainly saying: Against our mind, accustomed to earthly pleasures, you justly set the phantoms of its cares, by which you confuse it in the very concentration of its prayer. You rightly strike down, in blindness, the mind which you know to be devoted to the lowest desires, preventing it from seeing the clarity of your light. Thus, when it is directed toward you, it is turned back from you by the very cloud of its thoughts; and because it constantly thinks about these earthly things willingly, it must also endure them in prayer unwillingly.

## CHAPTER LII — My eye has shed streams of water (Lamentations 3:48)

[Col. 0979D]

(Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 29.) Sinners ought to consider each of their individual offenses, so that, while they mourn the pollution of their error in each one, they may cleanse themselves wholly through tears. Hence Jeremiah says, when he weighed the individual sins of Judea: “My eye has shed streams of water” (Lamentations 3:48). We shed divided streams of water from our eyes when we offer tears apportioned to individual sins. For the mind does not grieve over all things equally at one and the same time; rather, when the memory of one fault and then another touches it more sharply, it is moved concerning all of them in each individual fault and is cleansed.

## CHAPTER LIII — My life has fallen into the pit (Lamentations 3:53)

(Morals, Book XXVI, chapter 36, no. 65.) When Jeremiah saw that Judea had long been buried in iniquities through habitual practice, in his lamentations he mourns himself under her figure, saying: “My life has fallen into the pit, and they have placed a stone over me” (Lamentations 3:53). Life falls into a pit when it is polluted by the stain of iniquity. A stone is placed over it when the mind is also swallowed up in sin by hard habit, so that even if it wishes to rise, it can no longer do so in any way, because the weight of evil habit presses down upon it.

## CHAPTER LIV — How the gold has become dim! (Lamentations 4:1)

(Pastoral Rule, Part II, chapter 7; Morals, Book XXVII, chapter 43, and Book XXXIV, chapter 15; Pastoral Rule, same place.) With great pain of charity, Jeremiah laments the destruction of the Temple, saying: “How the gold has become dim, how the finest color has changed! The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of all the streets” (Lamentations 4:1). What is expressed by gold, which surpasses the other metals, except the excellence of holiness? What by the finest color, except the reverence of religion, beloved by all? What by the stones of the sanctuary, except the persons of the sacred orders? What by the name of streets, except the breadth of the present life? Since in Greek speech πλάθος (*pláthos*) means “breadth,” the streets were evidently named from their breadth.

He mourned that the gold had become dim because he saw in some the brightness of innocence and religion turned into the blackness of guilt. Gold becomes dim when the beauty of justice is abandoned to the darkness of succeeding iniquity, when spiritual life is polluted by earthly actions. The finest color changes when the splendor of innocence is turned into the ugliness of guilt. The finest color changes when the former reputation of certain people who were believed to live religiously is diminished. For when someone, after adopting the habit of holiness, involves himself in earthly actions, his reverence, as though its color had changed, grows pale and despised before human eyes.

The stones of the sanctuary are also scattered through the streets when those who ought to have devoted themselves to the inward mysteries, as though in the secrecy of the sanctuary [Text: “tabernacle”], for the adornment of the Church, seek the broad roads of secular affairs outside. The stones of the sanctuary were made for this purpose: to appear in the Holy of Holies on the vestment of the high priest. But when ministers of religion do not demand from their subjects the honor of their Redeemer on the basis of their way of life, the stones of the sanctuary are not on the priest’s adornment.

Those stones of the sanctuary lie scattered through the streets when persons of the sacred orders, devoted to the breadth of their pleasures, cling to earthly business. It should be noted that he does not say that they are scattered merely in the streets but at the head of the streets. For even when they engage in earthly affairs, they desire to appear eminent, so that they both occupy the broad roads through the pleasure of delight and yet remain at the head of the streets through the honor of holiness.

Therefore, there is no obstacle to our understanding the stones of the sanctuary as those very persons by whom the sanctuary was constructed, who lie scattered at the head of the streets when men of the sacred orders serve earthly actions out of desire, although previously the glory of holiness appeared to stand through their office. Secular affairs are sometimes to be endured out of compassion, but never to be sought out of love, lest, when they weigh upon the mind of the one who loves them, they sink it from heavenly things into the depths, overcome by their weight.

## CHAPTER LV — You will repay them in kind, Lord (Lamentations 3:64)

(Morals, Book XXXIII, chapter 28, no. 49; Book II of the Homilies on the Gospels, Homily 22, no. 4.) Jeremiah speaks of the Jews who arrogantly defended themselves against the Lord’s commandments: “You will repay them in kind, Lord, according to the works of their hands” (Lamentations 3:64). Immediately he expressed the same recompense more explicitly, adding: “You will give them your labor as a shield for their heart” (ibid. 65).

The Lord’s labor, appearing among human beings, was his passible humanity. The Jews, wise in their own arrogance, despised it when they refused to believe in the immortal one whom they saw mortal by nature and subject to suffering. When they saw his humility, hardened by the pride of their arrogance, they took the greatest care to prevent the holy words of the preachers from penetrating their minds.

Thus, when the Lord repaid them for their evil works, he gave them his labor as a shield for their hearts, because by a just judgment he made them obstinately set against him by the very thing through which he himself labored in weakness for us. They repelled the words of the preachers because they disdained the weakness of suffering in the Lord. They therefore made the Lord’s labor a shield of the heart against the same Lord, because he appeared despised to those who were wise in their own arrogance precisely insofar as he was humble for their sake.

So that the darts of preaching might not penetrate their hearts, they disdained the labor of his Passion and held that same labor as a shield, preventing his preachers’ words from passing through to them precisely because they saw him laboring unto death [Text: “because they saw him having labored unto death”].

## CHAPTER LVI — I set sand as a boundary for the sea (Jeremiah 5:22)

(Morals, Book IX, chapter 10, no. 11.) When the Jews, wise in their own arrogance, saw their custom being destroyed by the force of Christ’s commandments through the preaching of his disciples, they rose up remarkably against them in the storms of persecution. But the Creator of heavenly things, by raising up the power of his preachers, struck down those storms still more remarkably, as it is written: “The uprisings of the sea are wondrous; the Lord is wondrous on high” (Psalm 92:4). He showed that his ministers could accomplish more through miracles than earthly powers had swollen with anger.

Hence the Lord, narrating outward things through Jeremiah while announcing inward realities, rightly says: “I set sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting commandment that shall not pass away; they will be moved, but they will not prevail; its waves will swell, but they will not cross it” (Jeremiah 5:22). The Lord set sand as a boundary for the sea because, to break the glory of the world, he chose the despised and the poor. The waves of this sea swell when the powers of the age leap up to stir persecution; but they cannot cross the sand of the sea, because they are broken by the miracles and humility of the despised.

## CHAPTER LVII — Even the lamiae uncover the breast (Lamentations 4:3)

(Morals, Book XIX, chapter 18, no. 27.) At the time of Antichrist, when holy Church is pressed by adversity, permission to speak will be granted to heretics and to all kinds of wicked preachers. Jeremiah saw this far in advance and said: “Even the lamiae uncover the breast; they nurse their young” (Lamentations 4:3). For whom does he call lamiae except heretics, who bear a human face but, through impiety, possess beastlike hearts? They uncover the breast when they freely preach their error. They nurse their young because, by insinuating perverse teachings, they nourish and strengthen the souls of their wicked followers in impiety.

## CHAPTER LVIII — Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven (Lamentations 4:19)

(Morals, Book XXXI, chapter 47.) “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven” (Lamentations 4:19). By the name of eagles, the ambushing spirits are understood. Our persecutors are therefore swifter than the eagles of heaven when wicked people act against us with such force that they seem, by their inventions of malice, to outstrip even the aerial powers.

## CHAPTER LIX — Her Nazirites were whiter than snow (Lamentations 4:7–8)

(Morals, Book XXXII, chapter 22, nos. 46 and 42.) Sometimes those who desire the way of holiness, having fallen into error, are corrected only slowly. They consider what they are doing to be right and therefore serve it more zealously according to their own judgment. Hence, when Jeremiah said: “Her Nazirites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, redder than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphire,” he immediately added: “Their face has become blacker than coal, and they are not recognized in the streets; their skin has clung to their bones; it has dried up and become like wood” (Lamentations 4:7–8).

What is signified by the name of Nazirites except the life of those who abstain and practice continence, which is said to be whiter than snow and brighter than milk? Snow freezes from water that comes from above, whereas milk is pressed from flesh that is nourished below. What, then, is signified by snow except the whiteness of heavenly life? And what by milk except the administration of temporal stewardship?

Because continent men in the Church often perform such remarkable works that many who had maintained a heavenly life, and many who had administered earthly affairs well, appear to be surpassed by them, they are described as whiter than snow and brighter than milk. Because they sometimes seem, through the fervor of the spirit, to surpass the life of ancient and strong fathers, it is rightly added: “Redder than ancient ivory.” For when redness is named [Text: “the name of redness”], the flame of holy desire is signified. We know that ivory is the bone of great animals. They are therefore redder than ancient ivory because they often display before human eyes a more fervent zeal than certain fathers who preceded them.

To show all this together, it is added: “More beautiful than sapphire.” Sapphire is of an ethereal color. Because these people appear, through their heavenly way of life, to surpass many who preceded them and who strive toward higher things, they are said to have become more beautiful than sapphire.

But often, when an abundance of virtues flourishes even beyond what is fitting, the mind is led into a certain self-confidence; deceived by its own presumption, it is suddenly darkened when sin steals upon it. Hence it is immediately and rightly added: “Their face has become black as coal” [Text: “their face is black above coals”]. They become black after their whiteness because, having lost God’s justice, they presume upon themselves and slip even into sins they do not understand. Since after the fire of love they come to the coldness of torpor, they are compared with extinguished coals and found colder than them. For sometimes, when through self-confidence they abandon the fear of God, they become colder even than cold minds.

Of them it is rightly added: “They are not recognized in the streets.” By the logic of the Greek language, a street is called so from breadth. What is narrower for the human mind than to break its own wills? Concerning this breaking, Truth says: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matthew 7:13). What is broader than to resist none of one’s own desires and, wherever the impulse of one’s will leads, to spread oneself without restraint?

Those who follow themselves through confidence in holiness, setting aside the judgment of their superiors, proceed as though through streets. But they are not recognized in the streets because they had displayed something different about their way of life when, by breaking their own wills, they restrained themselves on the narrow path.

And it is rightly added: “Their skin has clung to their bones.” What is expressed by bone except hardness and strength? What by skin except softness and weakness? Their skin is therefore said to cling to their bones because, among those who think perversely, the weakness of vice is regarded as the hardness of virtue. What they do is weak, but, deceived by confidence born of pride, they join it to what they suspect to be strong. The greater their opinion of themselves, the more they refuse to be corrected from their wickedness.

Hence it is rightly added: “It has dried up and become like wood.” Their guilt becomes increasingly insensible insofar as it is regarded by them even as praiseworthy. It is rightly said to be dry because it does not grow green through any knowledge of itself. When error is believed to be virtue, it is corrected with greater difficulty. Their mind abandons its vice more slowly in proportion as, deceived by the appearance of virtue, it seeks a reward for it.

Fault is easily corrected when it is also felt with shame, because it is recognized as fault, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through endless ages of ages.

# BOOK FIVE — Testimonies concerning the prophet Ezekiel

[Col. 0983]

## CHAPTER I — Concerning the appearance of electrum in the midst of fire (On Ezekiel 1)

[Col. 0983A]

(Morals, Book XXVIII, chapter 1, no. 5.) Sometimes God speaks through angels by means of things, when nothing is said in words but future events are announced through an image taken from the elements. Thus Ezekiel, hearing no words, saw the appearance of electrum in the midst of fire (Ezekiel 1), so that, by looking only upon the appearance, he might understand what was to come in the last things.

Electrum is formed from the metals of gold and silver. In this mixture the silver becomes brighter, while the gleam of the gold is tempered. What, then, is represented by electrum except the Mediator between God and human beings? By composing himself for us from a divine and human nature, he made the human brighter through divinity and tempered the divine for our sight through humanity. The fact that his humanity shone with so many miracles through the power of his divinity is like silver increased from gold; and the fact that God could be known through the flesh, and that through the flesh he endured so many adversities, is like gold tempered from silver. This is rightly shown in the midst of fire because the mystery of his Incarnation is accompanied by the flame of the coming judgment. For it is written: “The Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

## CHAPTER II — Concerning the faces of the four living creatures (On Ezekiel 1)

(Morals, Book XXXI, chapter 47, no. 94.) When Ezekiel described the four living creatures he had seen (Ezekiel 1), he testified that the face of a human being, a lion, an ox, and an eagle appeared among them. Although each corresponds to one of the evangelists—one indicating the order of human birth; another, through the sacrifice offered for the world, the death of a calf; another, the strength of power, like the roar of a lion; and another, contemplating the birth of the Word, gazing like an eagle upon the rising sun—these four living creatures can nevertheless signify their own head, of which they are members.

For he himself is a human being because he truly assumed our nature; an ox because he patiently died for us; a lion because, through the strength of his divinity, he broke the bond of the death he had assumed; and finally an eagle because he returned to the heaven from which he had come. He is a human being in being born, an ox in dying, a lion in rising again, and an eagle in ascending into heaven.

## CHAPTER III — The hands of a human being were beneath their wings (Ezekiel 1:8)

(Morals, Book VI, chapter 37, no. 61.) Contemplating the flying creatures, Ezekiel says: “The hands of a human being were beneath their wings” (Ezekiel 1:8). What can we understand by the wings of the creatures except their contemplations [Text: “the contemplations of the saints”], by which they fly toward the heights, abandoning earthly things and balancing themselves in heavenly realities? What do we understand by the hands except works? For when the saints expand themselves in love of their neighbor, they administer bodily even the good things they are able to provide. But their hands are beneath their wings because, through the power of contemplation, they surpass the works of their action.

## CHAPTER IV — Their wings were joined, each to the other (Ezekiel 1:8)

(Morals, Book XXIX, chapter 31, no. 71.) When Ezekiel said that he had seen living creatures of different kinds, he added: “Their wings were joined, each to the other” (Ezekiel 1:8). The wings of the creatures are joined, each to the other, because, although the things they do are dissimilar, the voices and virtues of the saints are joined to one another in one and the same understanding.

Although one is a human being by acting rationally in all things, another is a lion by being strong in sufferings and not fearing the adversities of the world, another is an ox by offering himself as a living sacrifice through abstinence, and another is an eagle by lifting himself high in the flight of contemplation, nevertheless they touch one another with their wings as they fly, because they are joined together by the harmony of their confession and virtues.

## CHAPTER V — They did not turn back as they went forward (Ezekiel 1:9)

(Morals, Book X, chapter 15, no. 31.) In the active life, the mind persists without failure and without weariness; but in the contemplative life, overcome by the weight of its weakness, it grows weary as it descends, and at intervals is restored to it through great efforts. Ezekiel briefly indicates this when he describes the movement of the creatures he had seen, saying: “They did not turn back as they went forward” (Ezekiel 1:9). Shortly afterward he added: “And the creatures went and returned” (ibid. 14).

The holy creatures sometimes go and do not return at all, and sometimes go and immediately return, because when the minds of the elect, through the grace of the active life gathered within them, abandon the way of error, they do not know how to return to the evils of the world that they have left. But when, through the sharpness of contemplation, they withdraw from that same active life, they go and return, because, since they are not at all able to persist for long in contemplation, they pour themselves back into action, exercising themselves in the things near at hand so that they may be refreshed and recover the strength to rise above themselves again through contemplation.

## CHAPTER VI — They were full of eyes all around and within (Ezekiel 1:18)

(Morals, Book XIX, chapter 6, no. 12, no. 20.) All the saints look around themselves outwardly and inwardly, and fear invisibly that they may be reproached outwardly or be seen to be unrighteous inwardly. Hence the creatures seen by Ezekiel are said to be full of eyes all around and within (Ezekiel 1:18).

Whoever arranges his outward affairs honorably but neglects his inward ones has eyes all around. But all the saints, because they watch over their outward conduct so as to offer good examples to their brothers and attentively observe their inward selves because they prepare themselves to be found blameless before the gaze of the inward Judge, are said to have eyes all around and within.

## CHAPTER VII — They stood and lowered their wings (Ezekiel 1:25)

(Morals, Book XXXV, chapter 2, no. 3.) Speaking of the four creatures, Ezekiel says: “When there was a voice above the firmament that was over their heads, they stood and lowered their wings” (Ezekiel 1:25). What is signified by the creatures’ flight except the sublimity of evangelists and teachers? Or what are the creatures’ wings except the contemplations of the saints, lifting them toward heavenly things?

But when a voice comes from above the firmament that is over their heads, they stand and lower their wings. When they hear the inward voice of heavenly wisdom, they lay down, as it were, the wings of their flight, because they recognize that they are less able to contemplate that very height of truth. To lower the wings at the voice coming from above is, once the heavenly power has been recognized, to humble one’s own virtues and, in contemplating the Creator, to think of oneself as nothing but lowly.

## CHAPTER VIII — I heard the sound of the wings (Ezekiel 1:24)

(Morals, Book XXIV, chapter 8, nos. 19–21.) When Ezekiel had described the flying creatures, he added: “I heard the sound of the wings of the creatures striking against one another” (Ezek. 1:24). What are we to understand by the wings of the creatures except the virtues of the saints, who, while they despise earthly things, are lifted up by flying toward heavenly things? Thus the flying creatures strike one another with their wings, because the minds of the saints, in their desire for heavenly things, [Col. 0985A] are mutually stirred when they consider one another’s virtues. Another strikes me with his wing when, by the example of his own holiness, he kindles me to what is better; and I strike a neighboring creature with my wing if I at some time show another a good work to imitate.

For we ought to observe the life of those who are better with great care, because we gird ourselves for the work of our own improvement when we see in others a virtue that we do not possess. We advance toward humility all the more ardently when, considering the good qualities we possess, we weigh them against those who have less than we do; thus we are restrained from elation and kindled to strive for progress. For holy men, while each in turn places others before himself in considering their virtues, touch one another as flying creatures with the striking of their wings, so that they are aroused to fly higher in proportion as each more humbly sees in the other something to admire.

The reprobate, however, consider not the footsteps of the better but the lives and examples of the worse, and, boasting that they are better than these, set themselves above them in pride. Therefore they cannot advance toward what is better, because they believe it sufficient for them that they surpass the worst. [Col. 0985B]

## CHAPTER IX — Concerning the book in which were lamentation, a song, and woe (Ezek. 2:9)

(Morals, Book XX, chapter 16, no. 27.) Since we cannot return to eternal joys except through temporal losses, the whole purpose of Sacred Scripture is that the hope of abiding joy may strengthen us amid these passing adversities. Hence Ezekiel testifies that he received a book in which were written “lamentation, a song, and woe” (Ezek. 2:9). What else is signified by this book except the divine utterances? Since they command us also to shed tears and mourn, lamentation is said to be written in it. It contains a song and woe as well, because it proclaims the joy of hope in such a way that it nevertheless indicates the pressures and tribulations of the present. It contains a song and woe because, although we desire the sweetness of that place, it is first necessary for us to endure bitterness here.

## CHAPTER X — I will make your tongue adhere to your palate (Ezek. 3:26)

[Col. 0985C]

(Morals, Book XXX, chapter 27, no. 82; Book I, Homily 17 on the Gospels, no. 3; likewise, Morals, Book XXX, chapter 27, nos. 82–83.) Often a word is granted to a teacher because of the grace of the hearer, and often speech is withdrawn from a teacher because of the hearer’s fault, as the Lord says to Ezekiel against Israel: “I will make your tongue adhere to your palate, because you are an exasperating house” (Ezek. 3:26). It is as though he plainly said: “For this reason the word of preaching is taken away from you, because, while the people exasperate me by their actions, they are not worthy to receive an exhortation to the truth.”

Sometimes the word of preaching is given on account of both—the teacher, that is, and the hearer—and sometimes it is withdrawn on account of both. Therefore, when a teacher preaches abundantly, let him not exalt himself through any pride, lest perhaps his tongue be filled not for his own sake but for the benefit of the hearer. And when a teacher speaks fruitlessly, let the hearer not become angry, lest perhaps the teacher’s tongue grow sluggish not for his own sake but because the hearer has been rejected. Why, then, should anyone take pride in his teaching, when he does not know, by a hidden judgment, either to whom it is given, or when it is given, or from whom and when it is withdrawn? Since amid these matters we do not know either for whom the word is given or because of whom it is withdrawn, the one healthy remedy is this: neither to exalt ourselves because we have received more than others, nor to mock another because he has received less.

## CHAPTER XI — Take a brick for yourself (Ezek. 4:1)

[Col. 0985D]

(Pastoral Rule, Part II, chapter 10; Part IV; Part II, chapter 10; Morals, Book XXVI, chapter 6, no. 10.) It is the duty of rulers to show their hearers the glory of the heavenly homeland through the word of preaching, to disclose how many temptations of the ancient enemy bark along the road of this life, and to correct with great zeal [Text: “harshness”] the evils of their subjects that ought not to be tolerated gently, lest, if they are insufficiently inflamed against sins, they themselves be held guilty of all sins. Hence Ezekiel is told: “Son of man, take a brick for yourself” (Ezek. 4:1).

It should be noted that whenever the prophet Ezekiel is led to contemplate heavenly [Col. 0986A] things, he is first called “son of man.” It is as though the Lord plainly admonished him, saying: “Do not lift your heart in elation because of what you see; carefully consider what you are, so that when you penetrate the highest things you may recognize that you are a human being. Thus, while you are carried beyond yourself, you may be brought back anxiously to yourself by the bridle of your weakness.”

To Ezekiel, therefore, who represents teachers, it is said: “Take a brick for yourself, and place it before you, and draw upon it the city of Jerusalem.” Teachers take a brick for themselves when, in order to teach, they take hold of the earthly heart of their hearers. They place this brick before them because they guard it with the full attention of their concern. They are also commanded to draw the city of Jerusalem upon it because, by preaching to earthly hearts, they take the utmost care to demonstrate how great is the vision of heavenly peace.

But because the glory of the heavenly homeland is recognized in vain unless people also learn how many temptations of the crafty enemy assail it, the text appropriately adds: “And you shall arrange a siege against it” (Ezek. 4:2). Holy preachers arrange a siege around the brick [Col. 0986B] on which Jerusalem has been drawn when they demonstrate to the earthly mind—which now seeks the heavenly homeland—how greatly the adversity of vices attacks it during this life. Whenever it is shown how each sin lies in wait for the mind [Text: “for those making progress”], a siege is, as it were, arranged around the city of Jerusalem by the preacher’s voice.

But because it is not only explained how vices conquer the mind, but also how guarded virtues strengthen it, the text adds: “And you shall build fortifications” (ibid.). The holy preacher builds a fortification when he indicates which virtues oppose which vices. And because, as virtues increase, the battles of temptation commonly increase as well, it is rightly added: “And you shall bring up a mound, and set camps against it, and place battering rams around it.” Each preacher brings up a mound when he points out the mass of an increasing temptation; he raises camps against Jerusalem when he discloses to his hearers’ right intention the attacks of the crafty enemy and foretells his virtually incomprehensible [Col. 0986C] ambushes. He places battering rams around it when he makes known the goads of temptation that surround us on every side in this life and pierce the wall of the virtues.

But although a ruler may subtly disclose all these things, unless he burns with the spirit of zeal against the sins of individuals, he prepares no lasting absolution for himself. Hence it is rightly added: “And you, take for yourself an iron frying pan” (ibid., 4:3 [printed reference: 30]). By the frying pan is signified the frying and tormenting of the mind; by the iron, the strength of rebuke. What, indeed, fries and torments the teacher’s mind more sharply than the zeal of the Lord? And because whoever is kindled by zeal for God against sinners is guarded forever by strong protection, lest he be condemned for neglecting the care of preaching and governance, it is rightly added: “And you shall place it as an iron wall between you and the city” (ibid.).

The iron frying pan is placed as an iron wall between the prophet and the city because, when teachers now display strong zeal, they later have that same zeal as a strong fortification between themselves and their hearers, lest they then be without protection for punishment if now they have been lax in correction. [Col. 0986D] Teachers must therefore now desire to be seared by the fires of zeal, lest afterward they be compelled to be tortured by the fire of Gehenna because of the torpor of negligence.

## CHAPTER XII — Take a sword for yourself (Ezek. 5:1)

(Morals, Book II, chapter 35.) “Son of man, take a sword for yourself and pass it over your head and over your beard” (Ezek. 5:1). In this action of the prophet the judgment of the Redeemer is expressed. Appearing in the flesh, he shaved his head because he removed the mysteries of his commandments from the Jewish priesthood. He shaved his beard because, abandoning the kingdom of Israel, he cut away its adornment of virtue.

## CHAPTER XIII — A likeness of a hand sent forth seized me (Ezek. 8:3)

(Morals, Book XXXI, chapter 12, no. 19.) When holy men restrain the thoughts of their hearts from the desire for visible things and gather them within themselves, they also detect the hidden sins of others. [Col. 0987A] Hence it is said through Ezekiel: “A likeness of a hand sent forth seized me by a lock of the hair of my head, and the spirit lifted me between heaven and earth and brought me to Jerusalem in a vision of God, beside the inner gate that looked toward the north, where the idol of Jealousy was set up to provoke jealousy” (Ezek. 8:3).

What is the lock of the head except gathered thoughts of the mind, so that they do not flow loosely and disperse [Text: *diffluant*, “flow apart”] but remain bound together by discipline? A hand is therefore sent down from above, and the prophet is lifted by the lock of his head, because when our mind gathers itself through watchfulness, heavenly power draws us upward from the lowest things.

He rightly says that he was lifted between earth and heaven, because every holy person placed in mortal flesh has not yet fully reached heavenly things, but nevertheless has already abandoned what is below. In a vision of God he is led to Jerusalem because each person making progress through the zeal of charity contemplates what the Church ought to be.

It is also rightly added that he was led beside the inner gate that looked toward the north, [Col. 0987B] because holy men, when they look through the entrance of inward contemplation, discover more evil being done within the Church than what is right; and, as though turning their eyes toward the northern quarter—that is, toward the left side of the sun—they kindle themselves by the goads of charity against the coldness of vices.

It is then added that there the idol of Jealousy had been set up to provoke jealousy. When they observe that within the holy Church some people who bear only the outward appearance of believers perpetrate thefts and vices, what else do they see in Jerusalem than an idol? It is called the idol of Jealousy because through it heavenly jealousy is provoked against us; and it strikes sinners with all the greater severity the more dearly the Redeemer loves us.

## CHAPTER XIV — Son of man, dig through the wall (Ezek. 8:8)

(Morals, Book XXVI, chapter 6, no. 7.) Holy teachers often make the vices of wrongdoers appear more serious and probe hidden things from certain public signs, so that from the smallest matters they may learn the greater ones. [Col. 0987C] Hence Ezekiel is told: “Son of man, dig through the wall” (Ezek. 8:8).

Through Ezekiel the person of those set over others is signified; through the wall, the hardness of subjects. What, then, is it to dig through the wall except to open the hardness of the heart by sharp inquiries and severe corrections? When he had pierced the wall, a door appeared, because when the hardness of the heart is split open by questioning and severe rebuke, a kind of door is shown through which all the inner thoughts of the person being corrected may be seen.

Hence it follows: “Enter and see the most wicked abominations that these people commit” (ibid., 9). One enters, as it were, in order to see abominations when, having examined certain outwardly visible signs, one penetrates the hearts of subjects so that everything illicitly contemplated there becomes known.

Hence he adds: “And I entered and saw, and behold, every likeness of reptiles and every abomination of animals” (ibid., 10). By reptiles are signified thoughts [Col. 0987D] that are wholly earthly; by animals, thoughts that have already been raised somewhat above the earth but still seek the rewards of earthly gain. Reptiles cling to the earth with their entire bodies, whereas animals are lifted above the earth by their bellies, yet, through their appetite for food, are always inclined toward the earth.

Thus reptiles are within the wall when thoughts revolve in the mind because they are never lifted from earthly desires. Animals are also within the wall when, although certain just and honorable things are already being contemplated, they nevertheless serve the pursuit of temporal profits and honors. In themselves they are already, as it were, lifted above the earth, but through ambition, as through the desire of the appetite, they lower themselves toward what is below.

Hence it is rightly added: “And all the idols of the house of Israel were depicted on the wall” (ibid.). For it is written: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3:5). Therefore idols are rightly described after the animals, because although some people raise themselves, as it were, above the earth through honorable action, they nevertheless lower themselves to the earth through dishonorable ambition. [Col. 0988A]

It is rightly said that they “were depicted,” because when the forms of external things are drawn inward, whatever is imagined through false images is, as it were, painted in the heart.

It should therefore be noted that first a hole in the wall is seen, then a door, and only afterward the hidden abomination is revealed. For in every sin, signs first appear outwardly; then the door of iniquity is openly displayed; and only afterward is all the evil hidden within disclosed. This is why holy teachers also habitually examine small matters seriously: so that from the outermost signs they may reach the greater hidden things.

## CHAPTER XV — Behold, six men were coming from the way of the upper gate (Ezek. 9:2)

(Morals, Book XXII, chapter 18, no. 44.) The Lord, coming for our redemption, established the New Testament at the end. Ezekiel fittingly announces this, saying: “Behold, six men were coming from the way of the gate above, [Col. 0988B] which looks toward the north” (Ezek. 9:2).

What else is signified by the six men who come except the six ages of the human race? They come by way of the upper gate because, from the creation of paradise—as from the entrance into the world—they unfold from the earlier generations above. The gate looks toward the north because, if the mind of the human race, opened to vices, had not abandoned the warmth of charity and sought the torpor of the mind, it would not have emerged into this broad expanse of mortality.

“And each had the vessel of death in his hand” (ibid.), because every generation, unfolded through its successive ages before the advent of the Redeemer, had in its conduct the source from which it incurred the punishment of condemnation.

“And one man in their midst was clothed in linen” (ibid.), because our Redeemer, who also deigned, according to the flesh, to have parents from the priestly tribe, is said to have been clothed in linen. Or certainly this is because linen grows from the earth, whereas wool does not grow in the same way from corruptible flesh: he who took the garment of his body from a virgin mother, not from the corruption of sexual union, [Col. 0988C] plainly came to us clothed in linen.

“And he had a writer’s inkwell at his loins” (ibid.). The loins are the posterior part of the body. Since the Lord, after dying for us, rose again and ascended into heaven, then wrote the New Testament through the apostles, this man had an inkwell at his loins. He who established the writing of the New Testament after he had departed had an inkwell, as it were, at his loins. [Text: “carried it behind him.”]

## CHAPTER XVI — You have not gone up to confront them (Ezek. 13:5)

(Book I, Letter 25, recent edition.) Often teachers, fearing the loss of human favor, are afraid to speak freely what is right. Hence the Lord rebukes them through Ezekiel, saying: “You have not gone up to confront them, nor have you set up a wall for the house of Israel, so that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezek. 13:5).

To go up to confront them is, in defense of the flock entrusted to one’s care, to oppose any powers of this world with a free voice. To stand for the house of Israel on the day of the Lord and to set up a wall is to resist, out of love for justice, those who contend wickedly, and to vindicate faithful innocents against the injustice of the perverse by the authority of justice. [Text: “To resist those who contend wickedly is [to do so] from love of justice; and to set up a wall is [to vindicate] the faithful innocent, etc.”] For what else is it for a pastor to fear to speak what is right than to offer his back by remaining silent? If he throws himself forward on behalf of the flock, he sets a wall against the enemies for the house of Israel. [Col. 0988D]

## CHAPTER XVII — Woe to those who sew cushions (Ezek. 13:18)

(Morals, Book XVIII, chapter 4, no. 8; Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 8; Morals, same passage.) There are some who, when they exalt people’s evil deeds with praise, increase what they ought to rebuke. Hence it is said through Ezekiel: “Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand and make [Col. 0989A] pillows under every head in order to capture souls” (Ezek. 13:18).

A cushion is placed so that one may rest softly. Therefore, to place cushions under every elbow of the hand is to soothe souls that have fallen from their uprightness and recline in the pleasure of this world with flattering praise. A cushion receives the elbow or a pillow the head of one lying down when the harshness of correction is withdrawn from the sinner and softness of favor is applied to him, so that he may lie comfortably in error, struck by no harshness of contradiction.

Whoever, therefore, flatters those who do evil places a cushion under the elbow or head of one lying down, so that the person who ought to have been corrected for his fault may, supported by praises, rest comfortably in it.

Hence it is written through the same prophet: “He was building a wall, and they were plastering it” (Ezek. 13:10). By the name of the wall the hardness of sin is signified. Therefore, to build a wall is to construct barriers of sin against oneself; but they plaster the wall who flatter those committing sins, so that what the others build by acting perversely, these flatterers make smooth and attractive, as it were.

## CHAPTER XVIII — They put to death souls that do not die (Ezek. 13:19)

[Col. 0989B]

(Book II, Homily 26 on the Gospels, no. 5.) Those who receive the degree of governance assume authority in the Church to bind and loose. Since it often happens that someone occupies the place of judgment while his life does not correspond to that office, it frequently results that he either condemns the undeserving or, himself bound, looses others. Often, in binding and loosing subjects, he follows the impulse of his own will rather than the merits of the cases. Often he is moved toward someone by hatred or favor. Those who follow either their own hatred or their favor in the cases of their subjects cannot judge them rightly.

Hence it is said through Ezekiel: “They put to death souls that do not die, and they brought to life souls that do not live” (Ezek. 13:19). He puts to death one who does not die when he condemns the righteous; and he tries to bring to life one who will not live when he attempts to release the guilty from punishment. The cases must therefore be carefully weighed, and only then should the power to bind and loose be exercised.

## CHAPTER XIX — Concerning the three men who were delivered, namely Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. 14:14)

[Col. 0989C]

(Morals, Book XXXII, chapter 20; and Book II, Homily 4 on Ezekiel, no. 5.) After the apostles, three distinctions followed in the conduct of the Church: rulers, continent persons, and married people. Hence Ezekiel asserts that he heard of three men who were delivered: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. 14:14).

What, then, is signified by Noah, who guided the ark upon the waters, except the order of those set over others, who, while presiding over peoples as an example, govern the holy Church amid the waves of temptation? And what is signified by Daniel, whose remarkable abstinence is recorded, except the life of the continent, who, while abandoning all that belongs to the world, rule with lofty mind over despised Babylon? What is signified by Job except the life of good married people, who, while performing pious works with the worldly possessions they hold, proceed toward the heavenly homeland, as though by way of the earth?

## CHAPTER XX — On the day of your birth your navel was not cut off (Ezek. 16:4)

[Col. 0989D]

(Morals, Book XXXII, chapter 14, no. 20.) The seedbed of lust is contained in the navel of women, as Ezekiel testifies. Rebuking the wantonness of Judaea, under the image of a prostituted woman, he says: “On the day of your birth your navel was not cut off” (Ezek. 16:4).

To cut off the navel on the day of birth is to cut away the lust of the flesh at the time of conversion. Because it is difficult to correct evils once begun and to reform what has once been shamefully formed into something better, Judah is reproved from the time of her birth. Although she was born in God, she retained an uncut navel because she did not sever the flowing excess of lust.

## CHAPTER XXI — Trusting in your beauty, you committed fornication (Ezek. 16:15)

[Col. 0990A]

(Pastoral Rule, Part IV.) The soul that is proud of its virtue under the appearance of Jerusalem is condemned when Ezekiel says: “You were perfect in my beauty, which I had placed upon you, says the Lord; and trusting in your beauty, you committed fornication in your own name” (Ezek. 16:15).

The mind is lifted up by confidence in its own beauty when it gladly boasts in itself with secure complacency concerning the merits of its virtues. But through this same confidence it is led into fornication, because when its captured mind is deceived by its own thoughts, evil spirits corrupt it by seducing it through innumerable vices.

It should be noted that he says, “You committed fornication in your own name,” because when the mind abandons regard for the heavenly Ruler, it immediately seeks private praise and begins to claim for itself every good that it received so that it might serve as a proclamation of the giver. It desires to spread the glory of its reputation and strives to become known to everyone as remarkable. She therefore commits fornication in her own name who, abandoning the lawful union of the marriage bed, submits herself to the corrupting spirit in the pursuit of praise.

## CHAPTER XXII — A great eagle with great wings (Ezek. 17:3)

[Col. 0990B]

(Morals, Book XXXI, chapter 47, no. 94.) “A great eagle with great wings, long in the stretch of its members, full of feathers and variegated, came to Lebanon, took the marrow of the cedar, and tore off the topmost branches of it” (Ezek. 17:3).

What other eagle is signified except Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon? Because of the vastness of his army, he is described as having great wings; because of the length of time, as long in the stretch of his members; because of his many riches, as full of feathers; and because of the countless adornments of earthly glory, as full of variety.

Attacking the height of Judah, he took away the nobility of its kingdom as the marrow of the cedar. And when, by taking them captive, he removed the tenderest offspring of its kings from the height of their kingdom, he tore away, as it were, its topmost branches.

## CHAPTER XXIII — I gave them commands that were not good (Ezek. 20:25)

(Morals, Book XXVIII, chapter 18, no. 41.) The commands that the Lord gave to the inexperienced and newly beginning people of the Jews, he himself criticizes through Ezekiel, saying: “I gave them [Col. 0990C] commands that were not good” (Ezek. 20:25).

Evil things almost cease to be evil in comparison with worse things, and good things are not considered good in comparison with better things. For just as it is said to sinful Judah, in comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah [Text: “and Samaria”]: “You have justified your sisters in all your abominations that you committed” (Ezek. 16:51), so, when the better commandments of the New Testament subsequently appear, the good commandments given to the inexperienced are said not to be good.

## CHAPTER XXIV — The house of Israel has become dross to me (Ezek. 22:18)

(Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 13.) To the Israelite people, taken captive but not converted from iniquity, the Lord reproaches them through Ezekiel, saying: “The house of Israel has become dross to me; all these have become copper, tin, iron, and lead” (Ezek. 22:18). For they burst forth toward vice rather than virtue even in tribulation.

Copper, when struck, produces more [Col. 0990D] sound than the other metals. Therefore, one who, placed in affliction, breaks out into the sound of murmuring has become copper in the midst of the furnace. Tin, when artfully composed, imitates the appearance of silver. Therefore, one who does not lack the fault of hypocrisy in tribulation has become tin in the furnace.

One who lies in wait for the life of his neighbor uses iron; thus iron in the furnace is the person who does not abandon malicious intent to harm even in tribulation. Lead is heavier than the other metals. Lead is therefore found in the furnace in the person who is so weighed down by the burden of his sin that, even when placed in tribulation, he is not lifted from earthly desires.

Hence it is written through the same prophet: “It was sweated over with great labor, and its excessive rust did not come out of it, not even through the fire” (Ezek. 24:6). He applies the fire of tribulation to us in order to cleanse the rust of vices from us. But we do not lose our rust through the fire when, even amid scourges, we do not cease from vice.

Hence the prophet says [Text: “again”]: [Col. 0991A] “The smelter has smelted in vain; their wickednesses have not been consumed” (Jer. 6:29).

## CHAPTER XXV — In Egypt their breasts were pressed down (Ezek. 23:3)

(Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 28.) Under the image of Judah, the Lord recalls through Ezekiel the sins formerly committed by minds corrupted in this world, so that they may be ashamed to be polluted in the future. He says: “In Egypt their breasts were pressed down, and the breasts of their youth were broken” (Ezek. 23:3).

Breasts are pressed down in Egypt when the will of the human mind is subjected to the shameful desire of this world. The breasts of youth are broken in Egypt when natural faculties, still intact within themselves, are corrupted by the destructive force of desire that strikes against them.

## CHAPTER XXVI — Blood is in his midst (Ezek. 14:7)

(Morals, Book XV, chapter 31.) It is more serious if someone harms the righteous rather than sinners. Hence it is said through Ezekiel: “His blood is in his midst; he poured it upon the clearest rock, [Col. 0991B] and not upon the ground, so that it might be covered with dust” (Ezek. 14:7).

By the ground and dust he signifies sinners; by the clearest rock, the righteous person who is not embittered by the grave contagions of sinners. Blood is therefore poured upon the clearest rock when the wickedness of a bloodthirsty mind rages in the affliction of a righteous soul.

Although it is more serious to afflict the righteous than the unrighteous [Text: “unjustly”], it is much more serious still to harm both the righteous and the unrighteous alike.

## CHAPTER XXVII — You are the seal of the likeness of God (Ezek. 28:12)

(Morals, Book XXXII, chapter 23, nos. 47–48.) Concerning the angel who was created first, Ezekiel says: “You are the seal [Col. 0991C] of the likeness of God, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28:12).

As he was about to speak of the angel’s greatness, he encompassed everything in his first word. What good did he not possess if he was the seal [Col. 0991C] of the likeness of God? For an image like this is represented figuratively by the seal of a ring, just as it exists essentially in the seal itself.

Although the human being was created in the likeness of God, the angel is credited with something greater, as it were. He is said not merely to have been created in the likeness of God but to be himself the seal of the likeness of God, so that, the subtler his nature, the more fully the likeness of God may be believed to have been expressed in him.

Hence, still indicating the power of his primacy, the same prophet adds: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, and beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (ibid., 13). He named nine kinds of stones because there are nine orders of angels. For when Scripture openly mentions angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim, it shows the distinctions among the higher citizens.

The first angel is nevertheless described as having been covered with these, because he possessed them as a garment for his adornment; and, since he surpassed their brightness, he was brighter by comparison with them. [Col. 0991D] Concerning him the prophet further adds: “The work of your adornment was gold, and your sockets were prepared on the day when you were created” (ibid.).

Gold was the work of his adornment because he shone with the brightness of wisdom, which he received when he was well created. Sockets are made in stones so that, bound by gold, they may be joined together in the composition of an ornament, and so that those whom the gold poured between them, filling the sockets, binds together may not be separated from one another.

The sockets of this stone were therefore prepared on the day of its creation, because it was created capable of charity. If it had wished to be filled with charity, it could have clung to the standing angels, like stones set in a royal ornament. If it had made itself penetrable to the gold of charity, it would have remained fixed as a stone in the royal [Text: “kingly”] ornament, joined to the holy angels. This stone therefore had sockets, but they were not filled with the gold of charity because of the fault of pride.

Because stones are bound by gold so that they may not fall, this one fell because, although pierced by the craftsman’s hand, it scorned being bound by the bonds of love. [Col. 0992A] Now the other stones that had likewise been pierced are bound together as charity penetrates each of them in turn; and, through the fall of this one, they obtained the gift that they would no longer be loosened from the royal ornament by falling.

Still contemplating the height of his primacy, the same prophet adds: “You were a cherub, extended and protecting, on the holy mountain of God; you walked perfect in the midst of fiery stones” (ibid., 14). Cherub is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” This one is therefore called a cherub because there is no doubt that he surpassed all others in knowledge.

He walked perfect in the midst of fiery stones because he stood glorious in the splendor of his creation among the hearts of the angels inflamed by the fire of charity. He rightly calls him extended and protecting, for whatever we protect by extending ourselves over it, we overshadow. Because he is believed to have overshadowed the brightness of the others by comparison with his own brightness, he is said to have been extended and protecting. He covered the others, as it were, by overshadowing them, because he surpassed their greatness by a greater excellence.

When God was creating all things, he created this one first [Col. 0992B] and made him more eminent than the other angels. Still observing the excellence of his primacy, the same prophet says: “The cedars were not taller than he in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his summit. The plane trees were not equal to his branches; no tree in the paradise of God was like him or like his beauty, for he made him beautiful with many dense branches” (Ezek. 31:8).

Who can be understood by the cedars, fir trees, and plane trees except those ranks of heavenly virtues planted in the verdure of eternal joy, lofty in height? Although they were created exalted, they were neither placed before this one nor made equal to him.

He is said to have been made beautiful with many dense branches because the appearance that placed him before the other legions made him so much more beautiful as the multitude of angels subject to him adorned him. This tree in the paradise of God had as many dense branches [Col. 0992C] as it kindled legions of heavenly spirits placed beneath it. And he was condemned in his sin without pardon because he had been created great beyond comparison.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — However beautiful you are, descend and sleep with the uncircumcised (Ezek. 32:19)

(Pastoral Rule, Part IV; Morals, Book XXIV, chapter 3.) The soul that exalts itself is addressed through Ezekiel: “However beautiful you are, descend and sleep with the uncircumcised” (Ezek. 32:19). It is as though he plainly said: “Because you raise yourself up through the beauty of your virtues, you are driven to fall by that very beauty.”

Everyone who neglects to consider the ugliness of his weakness but attends, through the arrogance of elation, to the glory of his virtue descends precisely from where he is more beautiful. For, exalting himself over his merits, he falls inwardly into the depths [Text: “into destruction”] from the very place where he judged himself glorious. Descending, he sleeps with the uncircumcised because he perishes in eternal death with the other sinners.

## CHAPTER XXIX — There is Assur and all his multitude (Ezek. 32:22)

[Col. 0992D]

(Morals, Book IX, chapter 60, nos. 102–103; chapter 65, no. 97.) The boundless abyss of hell will devour those whom empty elation now exalts. Those who here fulfilled the will of the crafty persuader through any vice will then arrive at torments with their leader as reprobates.

Although the nature of angels and human beings is very different, one punishment nevertheless ensnares those whom one guilt binds together in crime. Ezekiel briefly indicates this when he says: “There is Assur and all his multitude, and around him are his graves” (Ezek. 32:22).

Who else is expressed by Assur, under the name of a proud king, except the ancient enemy who fell through elation? Because he drags many into guilt, he descends with his entire multitude to the prison of hell. Graves cover the dead. And who suffered death more grievously than the one who, despising his Creator, abandoned life? When human [Col. 0993A] hearts receive this dead one, they undoubtedly become his graves.

His graves are around him because he joins to himself through torments those in whose minds he now buries himself through desires. And because the reprobate now receive wicked spirits within themselves by committing unlawful deeds, then their graves will burn with the dead. The devouring flame will then consume those whom the pleasure of the flesh now softens. They will feel punishments in both heart and body, since while they lived here they served their perverse pleasures through both.

Hence it is said through the same prophet: “They went down to hell with their weapons” (ibid., IX, 27 [printed reference]). The weapons of sinners are the members of the body by which they carry out the perverse desires they conceive. Hence Paul says: “Do not offer your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin” (Rom. 6:13).

To descend into hell with weapons is to endure the torments of the eternal Judge with those very members by which they fulfilled their desires for pleasure, so that pain may then overwhelm them on every side—those who, subjected here to their pleasures, now fight on every side against the justice of the Just Judge. [Col. 0993B]

## CHAPTER XXX — What was broken you did not bind up (Ezek. 34:4)

(In *The Book of Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapter 6.) The Lord reproves the shepherds through Ezekiel, saying: “You have not bound up what was broken, and you have not brought back what was cast away” (Ezekiel 34:4). One who has been cast away is brought back when someone who has fallen into guilt is recalled to the state of righteousness through the strength of pastoral solicitude. A fracture is bound when discipline restrains guilt, lest the wound run on to destruction if the severity of correction does not compress it. Yet a fracture is often made worse when it is bound carelessly, so that the tear feels more severe if the bandages tighten it excessively. Therefore, when the wound of sin in those subject to us is being restrained through correction, the discipline itself must also be moderated with great care, so that it exercises the rights of discipline against offenders in such a way that it does not lose the compassion of mercy.

## CHAPTER XXXI — “You ruled over them with severity” (Ezekiel 34:4)

[Column 0993C]

(*Moralia* XXIII, chapter 13.) Arrogant pastors have this particular characteristic: they do not know how to impose humbly what they teach. Seated among themselves, as it were, on a certain summit, they look down upon those whom they teach as though they were far beneath them and at the bottom. They do not deign to speak to them by offering counsel, but scarcely speak except by exercising dominion. The Lord rightly says to such men through Ezekiel: “But you ruled over them with severity and with power” (Ezekiel 34:4). They rule with severity and power because they hasten to correct their subjects not by calmly reasoning with them, but by harshly bending them through domination.

## CHAPTER XXXII — “When you drank the clearest water” (Ezekiel 34:19)

(*The Book of Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chapter 2.) There are certain pastors who diligently investigate spiritual precepts, but what they penetrate by understanding they trample underfoot in their manner of life.

[Column 0993D]

They suddenly teach what they have learned not through practice but through reflection; and what they preach in words they oppose by their conduct. Hence, through Ezekiel, the Lord complains against the contemptible knowledge of pastors, saying (Ezekiel 34:19): “When you drank the clearest water [the text adds: ‘they themselves’], you muddied what remained with your feet; and my sheep drank what your feet had muddied” [the text reads: “and my sheep fed on what had been trampled under your feet, and what …”].

Pastors drink the clearest water when they rightly understand and draw in the streams of truth. But to disturb that same water with their feet is to corrupt the pursuits of holy meditation by living badly. The sheep drink the water muddied by their feet when those subject to them seek, as an example for living, what their superiors pervert by evil conduct.

[Column 0994A]

They do not follow the words they hear, but imitate only the depraved examples they see. Although they thirst for the teaching, they are corrupted by the deeds; as though from polluted springs, they take mud in their drink.

Again, concerning evil pastors, the Lord says through the same prophet: “They have become a stumbling-block of iniquity to the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 44:12). No one harms the Church more than one who acts perversely while possessing the name or rank of holiness. No one dares to rebuke such a delinquent, and the fault spreads powerfully as an example, because the sinner is honored out of respect for his rank. Thus it happens that when the pastor walks over precipices, the flock follows him to destruction.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — “I will take away from you the heart of stone” (Ezekiel 36:26)

(*Moralia* X, chapter 14.) The Lord mercifully says through Ezekiel to certain people: “I will take away from you the heart of stone, and I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). He takes away the heart of stone when he removes from us the hardness of pride; and he gives a heart of flesh when he immediately turns that same hardness of ours into sensitivity.

[Column 0994B]

For the one who bears the compassion of humility is pierced when the arrow of divine fear strikes him. But whoever hardens through the stubbornness of insensibility bears, as it were, a heart of stone [the text reads: “strengthens it”], so that the darts of heavenly fear may not pierce it.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — “Concerning the reed in the man’s hand” (On Ezekiel 40:5)

(*Moralia*, Book XXX, chapter 16, no. 53.) Contemplation is by no means perfected in this world, however ardently it may be begun. This is fittingly expressed through Ezekiel (40:5), who testifies that, as a measure for the city established on the mountain, he saw in the man’s hand a reed six cubits long and a palm. The Church of the elect is situated on a mountain, since it is not founded upon lowly desires.

What is signified by the cubit except action? What by the number six except the perfection of action, since the Lord is remembered to have completed all his works on the sixth day? What, then, does the palm beyond the six cubits signify except the power of contemplation, which already reveals the beginnings of eternal and seventh-day rest?

[Column 0994C]

Since the contemplation of eternal things is by no means perfected here, the measure of the seventh cubit is not completed.

Thus the Church of the elect, because it completes all that must be done, shows itself as a city set upon the mountain in six cubits. But because it still perceives here only the beginnings of contemplation, it touches no more than a palm of the seventh cubit.

## CHAPTER XXXV — “The ground up to the windows, and the windows were closed” (Ezekiel 41:16)

(*Book I, Homily 11 on Ezekiel 41, no. 26.) Ezekiel, seeing the temple set upon a mountain, relates among other things what he saw in it, saying: “The ground up to the windows, and the windows were closed.” The Apostle Paul says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17). In this temple, the windows are priests and watchmen, who pour out the light of holy preaching among the faithful. But when there is ground up to the windows, the windows are closed. For when earthly thought grows in the hearts of priests, the windows do not pour out light, because the priests grow mute in the office of preaching.

[Column 0994D]

To speak about God belongs to a mind that is greatly at peace and free.

## CHAPTER XXXVI — “Show the temple to the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 43:10)

(*Moralia*, Book XXIV, chapter 8, no. 18.) Whoever desires to be led to the heights must necessarily attend to the progress of those who are better, so that the more deeply they see in them what they may admire, the more strictly they may judge their own faults, with inward shame taking vengeance upon them. Hence it is said through Ezekiel: “Son of man, show the temple to the house of Israel, so that they may be ashamed of their iniquities, and measure its construction, and blush for all that they have done” (Ezekiel 43:10).

The temple of God is shown to the children of Israel for their shame when the soul of each righteous person—the soul upon which God breathes by inspiring it—is displayed to sinners in the splendor of its holiness, for their confusion. Thus they may see in it the good they neglect and blush in themselves at the evil they perform.

To measure the construction is to weigh carefully the life of the righteous.

[Column 0995A]

But while we measure the construction, we must blush for everything we have done, because the more carefully we examine the life of the good, the more severely we condemn in ourselves all that we have done wickedly.

The prophet is rightly told to show the temple. Since the sinner refuses to consider the uprightness of the righteous, let him at least recognize it through the voice of one who preaches. To show the temple to sinners is to recount the works of the righteous to those who do not wish to consider them of their own accord.

## CHAPTER XXXVII — “Concerning the trench in God’s altar” (On Ezekiel 43:13)

(*The Book of Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 9.) When patience is abandoned, even the other good deeds that have already been performed are destroyed. Therefore, it is rightly declared [the text reads: “commanded”] concerning Ezekiel that there should be a trench in God’s altar, so that the holocausts placed upon it may be preserved. For if there were no trench in the altar, every sacrifice found upon it would be scattered by a breeze that came upon it.

What should we understand

[Column 0995B]

as God’s altar except the soul of the righteous, which places upon itself, before his eyes, as many sacrifices as it has performed good deeds? What is the trench of the altar except the patience of the good? By enduring adversity, patience humbles the mind and shows it as though placed at the bottom, in the manner of a pit [the text adds: “this”].

Let there therefore be a trench in the altar, lest the sacrifice placed upon it be scattered by the breeze—that is, let patience guard the mind of the elect, lest, shaken by the wind of impatience, it lose even what it has done well.

This same trench is rightly shown to be one cubit in size, because if patience is not abandoned, the measure of unity is preserved. Hence Paul says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). The law of Christ is the charity of unity, which is fulfilled only by those who do not go beyond measure even when they are burdened.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — “The priests going out to the people outside” (Ezekiel 44:17)

(*Book I, Homily 11 on Ezekiel, no. 28.) Nothing is so burdensome in the order of priests as bending the rigor

[Column 0995C]

of the mind through compassion and changing one’s disposition because of persons who come before one; yet this is extremely necessary. For when through his preaching a sinner is restored to the grace of good works, the preacher himself appears ungrateful.

Hence Ezekiel says that the priests who minister within should not wear woolen garments. Concerning them it is added: “And when they go out to the outer court to the people, they shall remove the garments in which they ministered and place them in the treasury of the sanctuary” (Ezekiel 44:17).

Woolen garments are coarser. But when a priest approaches the holy ministry, when he enters within through compunction, he must be clothed, as it were, in a linen garment, through a subtler understanding. But when he goes out to the people, he must put away the garments in which he ministered within and appear before the people clothed in other garments.

For if he remains fixed in the rigor of his compunction, if he continues in the sorrow he possessed during prayer, he will not admit the concerns of external affairs. And what will the flock do about its necessities if the pastor refuses

[Column 0995D]

to hear and consider what the present moment requires?

As he goes out before the people, then, the priest should put on coarser garments, so that, for the benefit of his children, he may also adapt the disposition of his mind to bear earthly matters. Yet one must consider how great a labor it is for a priest to direct his heart toward the heights, suddenly recall it to the depths, refine his mind in the sublimity of inward thought, and, because of the external needs of his neighbors, so to speak, suddenly make his thought coarse.

## CHAPTER XXXIX — “The priests shall not shave their heads” (Ezekiel 44:20)

(*Letter* I.25.)
