The concern that pastors devote externally to their subjects must necessarily be held within a definite measure, lest, while they attend to external care, they be submerged and lost to inward intention. Hence it is rightly said to Ezekiel: “The priests shall not shave their heads, nor let their hair grow long, but they shall carefully trim their heads

[Column 0996A]

” [the text reads: “They shall trim their heads by cutting”] (Ezekiel 44:20).

Those who preside over the faithful are rightly called priests, since they provide sacred leadership. The hairs on the head are external thoughts in the mind. Because they arise imperceptibly over the brain, they signify the concerns of the present life, which, arising from negligent perception, sometimes return inopportunely [the text reads: “emerge”], proceeding as though without our awareness.

Therefore, because all who preside ought indeed to have external concerns but must not devote themselves to them excessively, priests are rightly forbidden both to shave their heads and to let their hair grow, so that they neither cut off entirely the thoughts of the flesh concerning the lives of their subjects nor again allow them excessive freedom to grow.

It is also rightly said: “Let them carefully trim their heads.” Thus the cares of temporal concern should emerge insofar as necessary, yet they should be cut back quickly, lest they grow beyond measure.

While, therefore, the life of the body is protected by the external providence that is administered, and the mind’s lofty attention is not hindered by moderate administration, the hairs

[Column 0996B]

on the priest’s head are both preserved, so that they cover the skin, and cut back, lest they cover the eyes.

## CHAPTER XL — “He measured a thousand cubits” (Ezekiel 47:3)

(*Moralia* XXII, chapter 20, no. 50.) Ezekiel announces in figurative speech concerning the man whom he had seen upon a high mountain: “He measured a thousand cubits and led me through the water up to my ankles; again he measured a thousand and led me through the water up to my knees. He measured a thousand and led me through the water up to my loins. He measured a thousand, and it was a torrent which I could not cross, because the waters of the deep torrent had risen, and it could not be forded” (Ezekiel 47:3–5).

What is signified by the number one thousand except the fullness of a gift bestowed? The man who appeared therefore measures a thousand cubits, and the prophet is said to be led through the water up to his ankles, because when our Redeemer grants us, as we turn toward him, the fullness of a good beginning, he pours into our first traces of action the gift of spiritual wisdom.

[Column 0996C]

For water reaching to the ankles means that, through the wisdom we have received, we already hold to the traces of the righteousness we desire. Again, he measures a thousand, and the prophet is led through the water up to his knees, because when the fullness of good work is granted, our wisdom is increased to this point. Hence Paul says: “Raise your drooping knees and make straight paths for your feet” (Hebrews 12:12).

The water therefore reaches the knees when the wisdom we have received binds us perfectly to the uprightness of good work. Again, he measures a thousand, and the prophet is led through the water up to his loins, because the fullness of work grows within us when the wisdom we have received has extinguished, insofar as possible, every delight of the flesh.

For if the delight of the flesh were not in the loins, the Psalmist would not have said: “Burn my loins and my heart” (Psalm 25:2). The water therefore reaches the loins when the sweetness of wisdom also destroys the incentives of the flesh, so that the fires of delight that could burn the mind grow cold.

He still measures a thousand,

[Column 0996D]

the torrent which the prophet could not cross—of which it is also said that the waters of the deep torrent had risen and could not be forded. For after the perfection of work has been received, one comes to contemplation. In contemplation, when the mind is lifted and drawn upward into the heights, it sees in God that it cannot penetrate what it sees, and it touches, as it were, the water of the torrent which it is unable to cross.

Because it beholds through contemplation what it desires to delight in, yet cannot perfectly behold even that which it desires, the prophet also eventually reaches the water that he does not cross. For when we are finally led to the contemplation of wisdom, its very immensity—which raises the human being above himself—denies the human mind full knowledge of it, so that the mind may love it by touching it, yet may in no way penetrate it by crossing over.

Thus that very wisdom which is accustomed to be the teacher of good works is granted to the yearning mind by degrees, so that one unquestionably ascends to it

[Column 0997A]

by steps of great moderation. This is granted and aided by our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Column 0998A]

# BOOK SIX  
## Concerning Testimonies on the Prophet Daniel

[Column 0997]

## CHAPTER I — “Concerning the harsh life in the king’s house” (On Daniel 1)

(*Moralia*, Book XXX, chapter 10, no. 39.) If we seek the sweetness of inward knowledge but are nevertheless unable to reach its secrets, let us recall Daniel’s life to memory for imitation and grasp the summit of knowledge that is to be desired.

He who was later called by an angelic voice “a man of desires,” because of his longing for inward knowledge, is first remembered to have subdued within himself the desires of the flesh in the royal court. He touched none of the delicious foods, but preferred hard and rough fare to sumptuous and softer food. Thus, by withdrawing from himself the flatteries of external food, he might arrive at the delights of inward nourishment and receive the taste of wisdom within all the more eagerly,

[Column 0997B]

because he had more vigorously restrained the taste of the flesh outside, for the sake of that same wisdom.

If we cut away from the flesh what pleases it, we immediately find in the spirit what delights it. When external wandering is closed off from the soul’s attention, inward retreat is opened. For to the degree that the mind cannot scatter itself outward because of discipline, it can direct itself above itself through progress.

## CHAPTER II — “Concerning the furnace set ablaze” (On Daniel 3)

(*Moralia*, Book XXX, chapter 18, no. 59; Book IX, chapter 66, no. 102.) Charity in Daniel, because it restrained his appetite from the king’s dishes, closed the mouths of the hungry lions for him. And because, while he and his companions were placed in tranquility, it subjected the fires of vice to him, in the time of tribulation it also tempered the flames in the furnace.

For when the king of Babylon ordered the furnace to be kindled, he commanded that a heap of naphtha, tow, pitch, and pinecones be supplied; nevertheless, this fire did not consume the abstaining youths at all [OCR: “minime”].

[Column 0997C]

Similarly, although the ancient enemy places before our eyes innumerable desires for food, by which the fire of lust may increase, the grace of the heavenly Spirit breathes upon good minds, and they remain unharmed by the arts of carnal desire. Thus, even if the flame of temptation burns toward the heart, temptation does not consume them as far as consent.

By a marvelous dispensation of the Creator, therefore, the quality of fire, tempered by different effects, neither touched the clothing nor failed to burn the bonds. For holy men the flame grew cold for the infliction of torment, yet flared up for the work of release.

## CHAPTER III — “Is this not Babylon, which I built?” (Daniel 4:27)

(*The Book of Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chapter 4; Book XXXIV, chapter 23; Book V, chapter 2.) Those who possess power often lose the good things they do because they think of them arrogantly. Because they exalt themselves in thought, they provoke the anger of the judge against themselves. Although what they do inwardly may be hidden from human beings, they sin with God as witness and judge.

The king of Babylon did not first become guilty of pride when he reached the words of pride. Indeed,

[Column 0997D]

even earlier, while he refrained from speaking proudly, he had heard the sentence of rejection from the prophetic voice. He had already wiped away the guilt of the pride he had committed when he proclaimed to all the nations subject to him the almighty God whom he had discovered he had offended.

But sometimes the mind is led to such great arrogance that, through ostentatious speech, it breaks loose in the very thing it fears. Afterward, lifted up by the success of his power and rejoicing that he had accomplished great things, he first preferred himself to everyone in thought, and then, still swollen with pride, said: “Is this not Babylon the great, which I built as a royal residence, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my splendor?” (Daniel 4:27).

This utterance openly bore the vengeance of anger

[Column 0998A]

which hidden arrogance had kindled. For the strict judge first sees invisibly what he publicly exposes by striking it. While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: “To you it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar: Your kingdom shall pass from you, and they shall drive you away from human beings, and your dwelling shall be with the beasts. You shall eat grass like an ox, and seven periods shall pass over you” (ibid., 28ff.).

Behold: because the swelling of his mind extended itself into open words, the patience of the judge immediately burst forth into a sentence. He struck him all the more strictly because his pride had raised itself so immoderately. And because, while enumerating his good works, he had stated the things in which he took pleasure, he heard the evils that were enumerated as the means by which he would be struck.

Thus the judge turned him into an irrational animal, separated him from human society, and joined him, with his mind changed, to the beasts of the field,

[Column 0998B]

so that by a strict and just judgment the man ceased also to be a man because he had judged himself to be great beyond human beings.

He lost what he had been made, because he did not humbly conceal what he had done. And because he had exalted himself above human beings through the pride of thought, he lost the very human understanding that he had shared in common with human beings.

Therefore, if the deeds of anyone who presides are to be more worthy, it is necessary that they should always appear unworthy to him in his own judgment, lest the same good action lift up the heart of the one who performs it and, by lifting it up, cast the agent down through pride more than it benefits those for whom it is undertaken.

## CHAPTER IV — “The throne of God was a flame of fire” (Daniel 7:9)

(*Book I, Homily 5 on Ezekiel, no. 10.) Concerning pastors and preachers it is said through Daniel: “The throne of God was a flame of fire, and its wheels were burning fire” (Daniel 7:9).

Those who are guardians of souls and have undertaken the burdens of feeding the flock are not permitted to change their places. But because, established in one place, they carry within themselves the presence of divinity and burn, the throne of God is called a flame of fire.

[Column 0998C]

Those who run about in preaching out of love for the Lord are his wheels, a burning fire. For when they travel through various places out of desire, they burn themselves and set others on fire from the source of their own burning.

## CHAPTER V — “Thousands of thousands ministered to him” (Daniel 7:10)

(*Moralia*, Book XVII, chapter 13, no. 18; Book II, chapter 3, no. 3.) Concerning the elect angels who serve the sight of the divine majesty, it is said through Daniel: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him” (Daniel 7:10).

To stand before is one thing; to minister is another. Those Powers undoubtedly stand before him who do not go out to announce certain things to human beings. Those minister who come to carry out the duties of messengers. And because there are more who minister than those who principally stand before him, the number of those standing is presented as definite, while the number of those ministering is shown as indefinite.

Concerning these, the Voice of Truth says: “Their angels always see the face of my Father in

[Column 0998D]

heaven” (Matthew 18:10). But Paul says concerning them: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service, for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14).

How, then, can they always stand before him or always see the face of the Father if they are sent out for service on behalf of our salvation? We resolve this more readily if we consider how subtle the angelic nature is. They do not go out from the divine vision in such a way as to be deprived of the joys of inward contemplation. For if, when going out, they lost sight of the Creator, they could neither raise up those who lie fallen nor announce truth to the ignorant; nor could they offer to the blind the fountain of light that they themselves would lose when going out.

In this respect, therefore, [the text adds: “now”] the angelic

[Column 0999A]

nature is distinct from the condition of our nature: we are confined by place and constrained by the ignorance of blindness, whereas angelic spirits are indeed confined by place, but their knowledge is incomparably more expansive than ours. By knowing both inwardly and outwardly, they are extended while contemplating the very fountain of knowledge.

For what can they not know of what is to be known, when they know the One who knows all things? Their knowledge, therefore, is greatly expanded in comparison with ours, yet narrow in comparison with divine knowledge. Similarly, those spirits are spirits in comparison with our bodies, but in comparison with the highest and uncircumscribed Spirit, they are bodies.

Thus they are both sent and stand before him: through being confined by place they go out, and through being present inwardly they never depart. They always see the face of the Father, and yet they come to us, because they go out to us through spiritual presence while still preserving themselves there, through inward contemplation, from which they had not departed.

## CHAPTER VI — “He cast down from the host” (Daniel 8:10)

[Column 0999B]

(*Moralia* XXXII, chapter 15, no. 26; Book XXXIV, chapter 2, no. 2.) Daniel speaks of the Antichrist under the figure of Antiochus, saying: “He cast down some of the host and of the stars, and trampled them; and he was magnified even to the prince of the host, and from him he took away the continual sacrifice, and cast down the place of his sanctuary. And power was given him against the continual sacrifice because of sins, and truth shall be cast down upon the ground; and he shall act and prosper” (Daniel 8:10–12).

He casts down some of the host and of the stars when he breaks certain people who shine with the light of righteousness and are strong in the power of their works. He is magnified even to the prince of the host because he exalts himself against the very author [the text reads: “originator”] of virtue.

He takes away the continual sacrifice because he interrupts the Church’s devotion to its way of life in those whom he captures. Power is given him against the continual sacrifice because of sins, since, unless the merits of those who perish demanded it, the adversary could not overcome those who were thought to be upright.

Truth is cast down upon the ground because then faith

[Column 0999C]

in heavenly realities is inclined toward desire for temporal life. “He shall act and prosper,” because then he will rage with immeasurable cruelty not only in the minds of the reprobate but also in the bodies of the elect, without any obstacle.

Again, through Daniel it is said: “And his power shall be strengthened, but not by his own strength” (ibid., 23). The strength of that man is not strengthened by his own powers, because he is raised up by Satan’s power into the glory of destruction.

Again he says: “He shall destroy the mighty and the people of the saints according to his will, and deceit shall prosper in his hand” (ibid., 24–25). He destroys the mighty when he conquers bodily those who are unconquerable in mind. Or certainly, he destroys the mighty and the people of the saints according to his will when he drags at the command of his will those who were believed to be mighty and holy; deceit prospers in his hand because whatever he contrives cunningly, he also carries out with the power of secular strength.

Deceit is in his hand as fraud is in his power, because whatever he wickedly wishes, he can for a time carry out with force. His deceit is said to prosper because the malice of his fraud is obstructed by no difficulty.

[Column 0999D]

Or certainly, deceit will prosper in his hand because fraud is aided in him through action. Whatever he says by deceiving, he asserts by performing wonders as though it were true. Whatever the lying tongue pretends, the hand of action attempts to display as true through marvelous deeds.

Again, when Daniel described the fourth beast as supported by ten horns, he added: “I was considering the horns, and behold, another little horn arose in the midst of them, and three of the first horns were uprooted from before it; and behold, there were eyes like human eyes in this horn, and a mouth speaking great things” (Daniel 7:8).

This is described as the eleventh horn of the beast because the power of his kingdom is strengthened by dignity. Every sin is an eleven, since, by acting perversely, it passes beyond the Decalogue of the commandment. And because sin is mourned in sackcloth, this is why eleven curtains of goats’ hair were made in the tabernacle.

[Column 1000A]

Peter, fearing that the Apostles would remain at the number eleven and seeing that guilt was signified by eleven, took care to complete the number of the Apostles as twelve by adding Matthias as the twelfth through the casting of lots [the text reads: “he sought”].

Therefore, since transgression is expressed through eleven, the eleventh horn of this beast signifies the author of transgression himself. It arises as a little horn because he is born as a mere human being. But it grows monstrously because it advances as far as the power of angelic strength joined to him.

It uproots the three horns that stand before it because it subjects to its dominion three kingdoms that are located near it. Its eyes are like human eyes, but its mouth speaks great things above all, because a human form is seen in him, but by his words he raises himself above human beings. As Paul says: “He who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped” (2 Thessalonians 2:4).

All the devil’s power will be gathered into that one condemned human being, so that through him he may perform powerful and marvelous deeds all the more to the degree that he incites him with his collected

[Column 1000B]

strength. He will prosper in every arrogance of deceit, strength of power, and exaltation of rank.

Daniel again says concerning him: “He shall rise up against the Prince of princes, and without a hand he shall be crushed” (Daniel 8:25). Paul says the same: “So that he takes his seat in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God” (2 Thessalonians 2:4).

He will be crushed without a hand because he will be struck with eternal death not by angelic warfare or by the struggle of the saints, but by the coming of the Judge, through the spirit of his mouth alone. As Paul says: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the spirit of his mouth and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming” (ibid., 8).

## CHAPTER VII — “And I fainted and was sick” (Daniel 8:27)

(*Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 24; Book I, Homily 8 on Ezekiel, no. 19.) When Daniel had seen a great and terrifying vision, from which he trembled, he immediately added: “And I fainted and was sick for many days” (Daniel 8:27).

The flesh cannot grasp the things that belong to the spirit.

[Column 1000C]

Therefore, sometimes, when the human mind is led beyond itself in order to see, it is necessary that this little vessel of flesh, which cannot bear the weight of such a talent, should become weak.

Or certainly, having seen a sublime vision, he fainted and was sick for many days because those who are strong in virtues become weak and feeble in their own estimation when they behold the higher things of God.

## CHAPTER VIII — “I heard the sound of his words, and when I heard it, I lay terrified” (Daniel 10:9)

(*Moralia* XXII, chapter 20, no. 47.) While the Lord was speaking to him, the prophet Daniel, wishing to show us the position of his body, indicated the stages of his merits. For he says: “I heard the sound of his words; and when I heard it, I lay terrified upon my face, and my face clung to the ground. And behold, a hand touched me and raised me upon my knees and upon the joints of my hands, and he said to me: Daniel, man of desires, understand the words that I speak to you, and stand in your place, for now I have been sent to you.

[Column 1000D]

And when he had spoken this word to me, I stood trembling, and he said to me: Do not be afraid” (Daniel 10:9, 12).

He would by no means have described this position of his body with such care while he was hearing the words of the one speaking inwardly if he had known it to be empty of mysteries. In sacred Scripture, it is not only what righteous men say that is prophecy; often what they do is prophecy as well. A holy man full of inward mysteries expresses the power of his voice also through the position of his body.

By the fact that he first lay prostrate on the ground, by the fact that afterward he raised himself upon the joints of his hands and upon his knees, and by the fact that finally he stood erect and trembling, he makes known to us in himself the entire order of our progress.

We hear the words of God while lying on the ground when, placed in sins and joined to earthly pollution, we learn spiritual precepts through the voice of the saints. We are raised at his commands, as it were upon our knees and upon the joints of our hands, because, withdrawing from earthly contamination, we already lift our belly [the text reads: “mind”] away from

[Column 1001A]

lowly things.

Just as one who lies terrified clings entirely to the earth, so one who bends upon his knees and the joints of his hands, as progress begins, is already suspended from the earth in large part. Finally, we stand upright but trembling at the Lord’s voice when, perfectly lifted above earthly desires, we fear the words of God more as we know them more fully.

For the one who refuses to be raised toward heavenly things through his earthly desires still lies, as it were, on the ground. The one who has abandoned certain contaminations but does not yet oppose certain earthly works still leans upon his knees and hands, as though partially raised. But the one who stands upright at the words of God is the person who perfectly raises the mind

[Column 1001B]

toward heavenly things and scorns to be bent down by impure desires.

He rightly indicates that he stood trembling, because the more fully one progresses toward the inward examination of subtlety, the more that examination is feared. There the divine voice appropriately adds: “Do not be afraid.” For the more we recognize what we ought to fear, the more of God is poured into us through inward grace as what we are to love. Thus our contempt gradually passes into fear, and fear passes into charity.

Because we resist God, who seeks us, through contempt, and flee through fear, we must set aside both contempt and fear and be joined to him through love alone. For little by little we also unlearn fear and cling to him by the force of love alone [the text reads: “we learn to fear him, to whose love alone we cling”].

After setting before us, as it were, certain steps in our progress, we first place the foot of the mind below through fear, and afterward raise it to the heights of love because of charity. Thus we are restrained by what causes us to swell up, so that we may fear; and by what we have already feared, we are lifted up so that we may dare.

## CHAPTER IX — “I came because of your words” (Daniel 10:13)

[The supplied source ends here, with the chapter continuing beyond the text provided.]

*(Morals, Book XVII, chapter 12, no. 17.)* It is worth asking: if supreme peace is maintained in the heights, what is meant by the words spoken to Daniel by the angel: “I came because of your words, but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days. And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (Dan. 10:13)? And shortly afterward: “Now I shall return to fight against the prince of Persia. When I was going out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming” (ibid., 20).

Whom else, then, does he call the princes of the nations but angels who could have resisted him as he departed? What peace, therefore, can exist in the heights if even among the angelic spirits themselves—who always stand in the sight of Truth—there is a contest of battle? But specific angelic ministries have been appointed for the administration of the several nations. When the conduct of those subject to them merits, in turn and in opposition, the assistance of the spirits set over them, the spirits who preside over them are said to come against one another. For the angel who was speaking to Daniel is understood to have been set over the Israelite captives living in Persia. Michael, however, is found to have been appointed over those of the same people who had remained in Judea. Hence, shortly afterward, this same angel says to Daniel: “There is no one who helps me in all these matters except Michael, your prince” (ibid., 21).

Of him also the statement quoted above is made: “Behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me.” Since he is said not to be with him but to come to his assistance, it is clearly recognized that he was set over the people who had been held captive in another region. What, then, does the angel’s statement mean—“I came because of your words, but the prince of Persia resisted me”—except that he announces to his subjects the effects of his own activity? It is as though he plainly said: “The merits of your prayers indeed demand that the Israelite people be released from the yoke of their captivity; but there is still something in that people which must be purged under Persian rule. Therefore the prince of Persia rightly resists me in its deliverance. Yet the tears also of those who have remained in Judea help your prayers.”

Hence he adds this as well, as we have said: “Michael, your prince, came to help me.” And when he goes out to fight against the prince of Persia, the prince of the Greeks appears to him as he comes. By this it is indicated that Judea had also committed something against the Greeks, whose cause was in fact resisting its deliverance. The angel therefore hears the prophet’s prayers, but the prince of Persia resists, because although the life of the righteous man who is praying already demands the people’s deliverance, the life of that same people still opposes it; for since those who had been led into captivity have not yet been completely purified, the Persians still rightly rule over them.

Michael helps, but the prince of the Greeks comes to battle, because the long oppression of the captives could indeed have merited pardon, yet what they had done against the Greeks stood in the way of the benefit of their deliverance. It is therefore rightly said that the angels come against one another, because the merits of the nations placed under their charge oppose one another in turn. For the exalted spirits who preside over those nations do not contend on behalf of those acting unjustly; rather, they examine their deeds by judging them justly. When the guilt or righteousness of each nation is brought before the council of the heavenly court, the prince of that nation is said either to have prevailed in the contest or not to have prevailed. Yet the victory of all of them is one, and so is the supreme will of their Maker over them all. Since they continually behold that will, they never desire to obtain what they are unable to obtain.

## CHAPTER X  
### “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12:4)

*(Book II, Homily 4 on Ezekiel, no. 12.)* We must understand that, as the ages have advanced, the knowledge of the spiritual fathers has increased. Moses was more instructed in the knowledge of almighty God than Abraham; the prophets more than Moses; and the apostles more than the prophets. Daniel bears witness to this when he says: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12:4).

The Lord says to Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; and I did not reveal my name Adonai to them” (Exod. 6:3). Behold, more had been made known to Moses than to Abraham, since God reveals to Moses something about himself that he said he had not revealed to Abraham.

The prophets also were able to grasp more of divine knowledge than Moses, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “How I have loved your law, O Lord; it is my meditation all day long”; and he adds: “I have understood more than all who teach me” (Ps. 118:97–98). And again: “I have understood more than the elders” (Ps. 118:100). By recalling that he meditates on the law and testifying that he has understood more than all who teach him and more than the elders, he makes clear that he had received more divine knowledge than Moses.

The holy apostles were also taught more than the prophets, as the Truth itself testifies when it says: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matt. 13:17). They therefore knew more divine knowledge than the prophets, because what the prophets saw only in spirit, the apostles also saw bodily.

Daniel’s statement has therefore been fulfilled: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied.” For the nearer the world is brought to its end, the more generously the way into eternal knowledge is opened to us, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# BOOK SEVEN  
## Testimonies on the Prophet Hosea

[Column 1001]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### “Behold, I will hedge your ways with thorns” (Hos. 2:6)

[Column 1001D]

*(Book II, Homily 35 on the Gospels, no. 9; Morals, Book XXXIV, chapter 2, no. 3.)* God is the husband of every faithful soul, because through faith it has been joined to him. But it often happens that a soul joined to God, perhaps weakened, falls into illicit desires, still submits itself in its actions to unclean spirits, seeks the glory of the world, feeds on carnal pleasure, and is nourished by carefully sought delights.

Yet often almighty God mercifully regards such a soul and mingles bitterness with its pleasures, so that when strong opposition arises against its desires, it may be corrected by the very impossibility of attaining them. Hence, speaking figuratively of every soul, and of Judea weakened and walking along perverse paths, the Lord says through the prophet Hosea: “Behold, I will hedge your ways with thorns” (Hos. 2:6).

The ways of the faithful soul are hedged with thorns when it encounters the stings of grief in what it desires temporarily. “And I will hedge it with a wall, and it shall not find its paths.” Like a wall placed across its ways, an obstacle confronts it, whose desires are opposed by the difficulty of attaining perfection [Text: “are attacked”]. It cannot find its paths because it is prevented from obtaining what it wrongly seeks. “And it shall pursue its lovers, and shall not overtake them; and it shall seek them, and shall not find them.” It does not at all attain the fulfillment of its desires from the wicked spirits to whom the soul has subjected itself in those desires.

But to show how much benefit arises from this salutary adversity and difficulty, he adds, saying: “I will go and return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now.” The first husband is the Lord, because he joined the chaste soul to himself through the intervening love of the Holy Spirit. The mind of each person desires him when it encounters manifold bitterness, like thorns, in those pleasures that it temporarily craves. For when the soul begins to be wounded by the adversities of the world it loves, then it understands more fully how much better it was for it with its first husband.

Then she who attempted to be an adulteress, though she could not do so openly, decides to be a faithful wife. Thus adversity often corrects those whom wrongful pleasure perverts. Hence it must be greatly feared that prosperity may follow when unjust things are desired, because an evil is corrected with greater difficulty when it is supported by the prosperity of success [Text: “also of perfection”].

## CHAPTER II  
### “I gave them grain, wine, and oil” (Hos. 2:8)

[Column 1003C]

*(Pastoral Rule, chapter 24.)* Those who do not rightly understand the words of sacred law, by generating errors and disagreements, turn the law of God—which was given to humanity for the very purpose of prohibiting sacrifices to Satan—into a sacrifice to Satan itself. Hence the Lord complains through Hosea, saying: “I gave them grain, wine, and oil; and I multiplied silver and gold for them, which they made into Baal” (Hos. 2:8).

We receive grain from the Lord when, in passages of greater obscurity, the covering of the letter is removed and, through the healing power of the spirit, we perceive the inner meaning of the law. The Lord provides us with his wine when, through the lofty preaching of his Scripture, he makes us drunk. He also grants us his oil when, through clearer commandments, he orders our life with gentle kindness. He multiplies silver when he supplies us with splendid words illuminated by the light of truth; and he enriches us with gold when he irradiates our heart with the understanding of supreme splendor.

Heretics offer all these things to Baal, because by corruptly understanding everything in the hearts of their hearers, they pervert it. From God’s grain, wine, and oil, and likewise his silver and gold, they sacrifice to Satan, because they bend words of peace toward the error of discord.

## CHAPTER III  
### “Cursing and lying have overflowed” (Hos. 4:2)

*(Book I, Homily 11 on Ezekiel, no. 25; Morals, Book I, chapter 17.)* The just and almighty God becomes angry with a person because of preceding sins and permits the blinded mind to fall into other sins as well. Hence it is said through Hosea: “Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed; and blood has touched blood” (Hos. 4:2).

For sin is commonly signified by the name “blood.” Hence the one who desires to be freed from sins cries out through repentance: “Deliver me from bloods” (Ps. 50:15). Blood therefore touches blood when one guilt is joined to another. Sin is added to sin, so that, as iniquities are joined together, the soul is stained with blood before the eyes of God.

## CHAPTER IV  
### “They eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4:8)

*(Book I, Homily 17 on the Gospels, no. 8.)* Behold, we live from the offerings of the faithful, but we do not labor for the souls of the faithful. We take as our stipend what the faithful have offered for the redemption of their sins; yet we do not sweat as we ought against those same sins, either through the diligence of prayer or through preaching.

We scarcely rebuke anyone openly for his fault; and, what is more serious, if someone is powerful in this world, we may sometimes praise his actions so that, if he should become angry and oppose us, he may not withdraw the gift he had been providing. But we must constantly remember what is written concerning certain people in Hosea: “They eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4:8).

Why are they said to eat the sins of the people, except because they encourage the sins of those who offend, lest they lose their temporal stipend? And if we who live from the offerings of the faithful—which they offered for their sins—eat and remain silent, then without doubt we eat their sins. Let us therefore consider what a grave crime it is before the Lord to eat the price of sinners’ sins and to do nothing against their sins [Text: “by preaching”].

## CHAPTER V  
### “They brought sacrifices into the depths” (Hos. 5:2)

*(Book I, Homily 4 on Ezekiel, no. 4.)* Woe to those who seek earthly glory through the good things they do. It is said through Hosea: “They brought sacrifices into the depths” (Hos. 5:2).

What else are the tears of prayer except the sacrifices of our offering, as it is written: “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit” (Ps. 50:19)? There are some who afflict themselves with lamentation in prayer for the very purpose of acquiring earthly advantages or appearing holy to others. What do such people do except bring sacrifices into the depths? Since what they seek is below, they place the sacrifice of their prayer downward.

## CHAPTER VI  
### “The spirit of fornication is among them” (Hos. 5:2)

[Column 1004C]

*(Morals, Book XXVI, chapter 17, no. 28.)* The mind must be guarded with every vigilance against the swelling of pride. For God sees within what elevates the mind, and for that reason permits something to grow outwardly that will bring it down. What is first exalted within is afterward struck outwardly by the corruption of lust.

Hence Hosea says against the Israelites: “The spirit of fornication is among them, and they have not known the Lord” (Hos. 5:2). To show that the cause of lust arose from the fault of self-exaltation, he immediately adds: “And the arrogance of Israel shall answer to his face” (ibid., 5). It is as though he said: “The fault that secretly lay hidden through the mind’s self-exaltation answered openly through the lust of the flesh.” An outward blow follows a hidden fault, so that inner things are punished by external evils, and the heart publicly collapses through lust—precisely the heart that was secretly swollen with pride.

## CHAPTER VII  
### “Ephraim has become a cake baked under ashes” (Hos. 7:8)

[Column 1004D]

*(Morals, Book XXXII, chapter 10, no. 12.)* Whoever still desires the things of the world does not appear before the face of the true light, because he lies hidden beneath the dust of earthly contamination [Text: “thought”]. Hence, speaking through Hosea of every soul weighed down by earthly desires under the figure of Ephraim, it is said: “Ephraim has become a cake baked under ashes, which is not turned” (Hos. 7:8).

By nature, a well-formed intention has been given to us that may rise toward the Lord; but from a wickedly accustomed way of life there is a pleasure that presses that intention down in the present world. A cake baked under ashes is cleaner on the side that it conceals underneath and dirtier on the side that carries ashes above. Therefore whoever neglects the intention with which he ought to have sought the Lord presses the cleaner side downward, as a cake baked under ashes. And when he willingly bears the cares of the world, he carries a heap of ashes above him.

The cake baked under ashes would be turned if it cast off the ashes of carnal desires and displayed above the good intention that it had long before oppressed by despising it. But it refuses to be turned when the mind, weighed down by love of worldly cares, neglects to cast away the mass of ashes placed upon it; and, since it does not desire to rise toward a good intention, it presses the cleaner side downward.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it” (Hos. 7:9)

*(Morals, Book XXV, chapter 7, no. 14; Book XXXIV, chapter 3, no. 6.)* To remain in this mortal life is, as it were, to move toward old age. When the mind is left unexamined, it is lulled into a kind of senility of sluggishness. Neglecting its purpose and imperceptibly losing its strength, it grows old without knowing it, moving away from the form of its former vigor.

Hence it is said through Hosea under the figure of Ephraim: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it; and gray hairs also have been scattered upon him, and he himself did not know” (Hos. 7:9) [Text adds: “he himself”]. “Strangers” are commonly understood as apostate spirits. They devour strength when, by perverting the mind’s virtue, they consume it. Ephraim both suffered this and did not know it, because in the temptation of evil spirits he lost the strength of his spirit and did not understand that he had lost it.

## CHAPTER IX  
### “They have reigned, but not from me” (Hos. 8:4)

*(Pastoral Rule, Part I, chapter 1.)* The Lord complains through Hosea against wicked shepherds, saying: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. 8:4).

They reign from themselves and not according to the will of the supreme Ruler who, supported by no virtues and not called by God, seize the summit of government, driven by their own ambition, rather than attaining it. Yet the inner Judge both advances them and does not know them, because those whom he tolerates by permitting them, he certainly rejects by his judgment.

Hence he says to certain people who come to him after performing miracles: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know who you are” (Luke 13:27).

## CHAPTER X  
### “There is no sprout in their standing stalk” (Hos. 8:7)

*(Morals, Book VIII, chapter 43, nos. 70–71.)* Through Hosea it is said to hypocrites who desire human favor: “There is no sprout in their standing stalk, and it produces no flour; and even if they produce it, strangers will eat it” (Hos. 8:7).

A stalk has no sprout when a life lacks the merits of virtue. A stalk produces no flour when one who prospers in the present age understands no subtlety and yields no fruit of good works. But often, even when it has produced flour, strangers eat it, because when hypocrites display good works, the desires of evil spirits are satisfied by them. Those who do not seek to please God through these things feed not the Lord of the field but strangers.

## CHAPTER XI  
### “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing” (Hos. 10:11)

*(Morals, Book XX, chapter 15, no. 39.)* Perverse people willingly serve in every kind of toil for the glory of this world, and most devotedly submit their necks to the yoke of heavy labor. This is well described under the figure of Ephraim, as the prophet Hosea says: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing” (Hos. 10:11).

A heifer accustomed to the labor of threshing, when released, often returns to the same labor even without being compelled. So the mind of the wicked, devoted to the services of this world and accustomed to the exhaustion of temporal affairs, even when permitted to rest freely, nevertheless hastens to subject itself to earthly toil. Through the habit [Text: “use”] of its miserable way of life, it seeks the threshing of labor, so that it does not wish to cease from the yoke of worldly servitude, even when it is permitted to do so.

## CHAPTER XII  
### “I will give you kings in my wrath” (Hos. 13:11)

*(Morals, Book XXV, chapter 16, no. 34.)* No one who suffers under a bad ruler should accuse the ruler whom he suffers, because it was plainly his own merit that caused him to be subjected to the dominion of a perverse ruler. Let him therefore accuse the guilt of his own conduct rather than the injustice of the governor.

For it is written in Hosea: “I will give you kings in my wrath” (Hos. 13:11). Why, then, do we despise those set over us, whose rule over us we receive from the Lord’s wrath? If, therefore, when the Lord God is angry, we receive rulers according to our merits, then in their actions we discern what we should weigh from our own actions [Text: “judgment”].

## CHAPTER XIII  
### “I shall be your death, O death” (Hos. 13:14)

*(Morals, Book XII, chapter 11; Book II, Homily 22 on the Gospels, no. 6.)* When the Lord returned from hell, he did not draw out the elect and the rejected together; rather, he raised from there those whom he recognized as his own in faith and deeds.

Hence through the prophet Hosea he says: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13:14). What we kill, we cause not to exist at all. But from what we bite, we take away one part and leave another. Therefore, because among his elect he completely killed death, he became the death of death; but because he took one part from hell and left another, he did not kill hell completely but bit it.

He therefore says: “I shall be your death, O death.” It is as though he plainly said: “Because I completely destroy you in my elect, I shall be your bite, O hell; because, after removing them, I pierce you in part.” What he promised before his Passion, the Lord fulfilled in his resurrection: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

He removed all the elect; he drew all things, because he left none of his elect among the dead. Jesus Christ our Lord lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK EIGHT  
## Testimonies on the Prophet Joel

[Column 1005]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### “The locust ate what the caterpillar left” (Joel 1:4)

[Column 1005D]

*(Morals, Book XXXIII, chapter 37, no. 63.)* Often the mind of the rejected rejoices over certain vices because it is not subject to them, and neglects to guard against them and grieve over them. For when some desires of wickedness pass away, others take their place—perhaps vices to which the mind submits more wickedly.

Hence it is rightly said through the prophet Joel: “The locust ate what the caterpillar left, and the young locust ate what the locust left, and the rust consumed what the young locust left” (Joel 1:4).

What is signified by the caterpillar, which crawls upon the earth with its whole body, except lust? It so pollutes the heart that it cannot rise through love toward the purity above. What is expressed by the locust, which flies by leaps, except empty glory, which exalts itself through vain presumption? What is represented by the young locust, whose entire body is gathered almost entirely into its belly, except gluttony? What is indicated by rust, which burns when it touches, except anger?

The locust therefore eats what the caterpillar left, because often, when the vice of lust has withdrawn from the mind, empty glory follows. Since the mind is no longer laid low through love of the flesh, it boasts of itself as holy because of charity. The young locust eats what the locust left, because often, when empty glory—which seemed to arise from holiness—is resisted, the belly or various ambitious desires are indulged immoderately. For the mind that does not know God is led toward every kind of ambition with greater violence when it is restrained by no love of human praise.

Rust consumes what the young locust left, because often, when gluttony is restricted through abstinence, the impatience of anger rules more fiercely. Like rust, it consumes the harvest as though by burning it, because the fruit of virtue withers in the flame of impatience. Thus, when vice follows vice, one pest devours the field of the mind while leaving another behind.

It is rightly added: “Awake, you drunkards, and weep” (Joel 1:5). Those who are confused by love of this world, and do not perceive the evils they suffer, are called drunkards. What, then, does it mean to say, “Awake, you drunkards, and weep,” except: Shake off the sleep of your insensibility, and in the devastation of your heart, with so many plagues of vice succeeding one another, meet them with vigilant lamentation?

## CHAPTER II  
### “He made my vineyard a wilderness” (Joel 1:7)

*(Morals, Book VIII, chapter 48, no. 81.)* Hypocrites who seek human praise, when they desire to display themselves to the eyes of others, condemn what they do. When evil spirits provoke them to boastfulness, they strip bare their works by taking them captive.

Hence, indicating the malice of the ancient enemies under the figure of a certain nation, the Truth says through Joel: “He made my vineyard a wilderness; he stripped the bark from my fig tree; he stripped it bare and cast it away; its branches became white” (Joel 1:7).

When spirits lie in wait, God’s vineyard is made a wilderness whenever a soul full of fruits is scattered by desire for human praise. This nation strips the bark from God’s fig tree because, seizing the seduced mind and carrying it away into the desire for favor, it draws it toward display, removes from it the covering of humility, and strips it bare. For as long as the mind hides its good deeds, it is clothed, as it were, in the bark of its own covering. But when it desires that what it has done be seen by others, the fig tree, stripped bare, has lost the bark that covered it.

Hence it is appropriately added: “Its branches became white,” because its works grow bright when exposed to human eyes. It takes a name from holiness when the right action is publicized. But it must be carefully observed that, once the bark has been removed, the branches of this fig tree wither, because the deeds of the arrogant, when displayed to human eyes, dry up through the very means by which they seek to please.

The mind that is brought forth through boastfulness is therefore rightly called a stripped fig tree [Text: “is betrayed”; Text adds: “rightly”], because it is white in what is seen and close to dryness in that it has been stripped of the covering of the heart.

## CHAPTER III  
### “Sanctify a fast” (Joel 1:14)

*(Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 19; Book I, Homily 16 on the Gospels, no. 6.)* The virtue of abstinence is considered small [Text: “is regarded as very small”] when it is not commended by other virtues. Hence Joel says: “Sanctify a fast” (Joel 1:14). To sanctify a fast is, by joining other good works to it, to show an abstinence of the flesh that is worthy of God.

Those who abstain also offer an abstinence pleasing to God when they give to the needy what they take away from themselves in food. We must carefully heed what the Lord rebukes through the prophet, saying: “When you fasted and mourned, did you fast for me? And when you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?” (Zech. 7:5).

A person fasts not for God but for himself if he does not give to the poor what he temporarily withdraws from his belly, but keeps it to offer to his belly afterward. He eats and drinks for himself who consumes the food of the body—which is a common gift of the Creator—without sharing it with the needy.

The Lord therefore approves that fast which raises the hands of almsgiving toward his eyes. The flesh is also afflicted in vain by fasting if the mind is not restrained from its own wicked pleasures, since the Lord says through the prophet: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own will is found, and you exact all your debts” (Isa. 58:3).

For one who demands back from his debtor what he has given does not necessarily act unjustly; but it is fitting that whoever afflicts himself in repentance should also forbid himself what is rightly his. Thus God forgives what we have done unjustly when we are afflicted and repentant, if for love of him we relinquish even what is justly ours.

Through abstinence, therefore, the vices of the flesh are put to death; and so that dead flesh may not putrefy, fasting is practiced. For dead flesh to putrefy is for this mortal body to serve the decay of lust. As it is said of certain people through the same prophet Joel: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:17). For beasts to rot in their dung is for carnal people to end their life in the stench of lust.

We therefore fast well when, through the seasoning of continence and fasting, we preserve this mortal body from the rottenness of lust, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory throughout infinite ages. Amen.

# BOOK NINE  
## Testimonies on the Prophets Amos, Micah, and Nahum

[Column 1007]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### “They cut open the pregnant women of Gilead” (Amos 1:13)

*(Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 24, admonition 25.)* Heretics, in order to extort from the unlearned crowd a reputation for knowledge, strive with all their might both to destroy what others have rightly understood and to strengthen their own perversions. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet Amos: “They cut open the pregnant women of Gilead, in order to enlarge their territory” (Amos 1:13).

Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” And because the entire congregation of the Church together serves the testimony of truth through confession, Gilead appropriately expresses the Church, which through the mouths of all the faithful bears witness to what is true about God.

Those souls are called pregnant which conceive an understanding of the word through divine love and, when the proper time arrives, are destined to give birth to the understanding they have conceived through the manifestation of their works. To enlarge one’s territory is to extend the reputation of one’s name.

They therefore cut open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their territory, because heretics kill, through perverse preaching, the minds of the faithful that had already conceived something of the understanding of truth, and thereby extend their own reputation for knowledge. They cut with the sword of error the hearts of the little ones already pregnant with the conception of the word, and thus create for themselves a reputation for teaching.

## CHAPTER II  
### “Behold, I shall creak over you” (Amos 2:13)

*(Morals, Book XXXII, chapter 5, section 2.)* At times, because of our weakness, the Lord compares himself through profound condescension to insensible things, as it is said through Amos: “Behold, I shall creak over you, as a cart creaks when loaded with hay” (Amos 2:13).

Since the life of carnal people is hay, as it is written, “All flesh is hay” (Isa. 40:6), in bearing the life of carnal people the Lord testifies that he carries hay like a cart. For him to creak under the burden of hay is to endure the burdens and iniquities of sinners with lamentation.

## CHAPTER III  
### “I rained upon one city” (Amos 4:7)

[Column 1008D]

*(Book I, Homily 10 on Ezekiel, no. 23.)* We see fulfilled every day what the Lord recounts through Amos when, being angry, he says: “I rained upon one city, and upon another city I did not rain; one part was drenched, and the part upon which I did not rain [Text: “which was not drenched”] dried up” (Amos 4:7).

When one mind receives the words of holy exhortation and another refuses to receive them, the Lord rains upon one city and does not rain upon another. But when the very person who hears the preaching corrects himself from some vices while refusing to be amended from others, one part of him is drenched because it bears fruit, while the part that is not drenched dries up, because, not fully receiving the word of exhortation, it remains barren of good works.

## CHAPTER IV  
### “Establish judgment at the gate” (Amos 5:15)

*(Morals, Book XXI, chapter 20, no. 32.)* It was the custom among the ancients for elders to sit at the gate and settle the quarrels of disputants through judicial examination, so that those who were at variance would not enter the city in which they ought to live harmoniously. Hence the Lord also says through Amos: “Establish judgment at the gate” (Amos 5:15).

## CHAPTER V  
### “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord” (Amos 5:18)

*(Morals, Book IV, chapter 11, no. 18.)* There are some who destroy by their deeds the faith they display in their words. Either what they do is wicked, or they pursue right works with a wrong heart. For they seek not perpetual rewards for their works but passing favor.

Yet because they hear themselves praised as though they were holy, they believe themselves truly holy; and the more irreproachable they consider themselves according to the judgment of the many, the more confidently they await the day of strict judgment. Concerning them Amos says: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord” (Amos 5:18).

## CHAPTER VI  
### “The Lord called judgment” (Amos 7:4)

*(Morals, Book XXXIII, chapter 6, no. 13.)* Some abandon the world and leave behind the empty things that pass away with earthly goods. Desiring the depths of humility, they rise above the customs of human society through virtuous living. They advance so far in the art of spiritual discipline that they already perform mighty works of signs.

But because they neglect to protect themselves by examining themselves, struck by the weapon of empty glory they fall more disastrously from the heights into the depths of hell. Hence it is said through Amos: “The Lord called judgment upon the fire, and it devoured the great abyss, and consumed a portion of the house” (Amos 7:4).

Judgment is called to the fire when the sentence of justice is shown for the punishment of eternal burning. It devours the great abyss because it burns the wicked and unfathomable minds of human beings, which now hide themselves from others even under miracles of signs. A portion of the house is consumed because Gehenna also devours those who now boast that, through apparently holy actions, they belong to the number of the elect [Text: “the Lord’s house”].

## CHAPTER VII  
### “I am not a prophet” (Amos 7:14)

[Column 1009C]

*(Morals, Book II, chapter 56, no. 89.)* If the spirit of prophecy were always present to the prophets, the prophet Amos, when questioned, would not have said: “I am not a prophet” (Amos 7:14).

But how was he not a prophet who foretold so many true things about the future? Or how was he a prophet who truthfully denied something about himself in the present? Because at the very hour when he was questioned, he sensed that the spirit of prophecy was absent from him, he truthfully said of himself: “I am not a prophet.”

Yet he continued and added: “And now hear the word of the Lord” [Text: “Thus says the Lord”]: “Your wife shall fornicate in the city, and your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword” (ibid., 16). These words of the prophet show that, while he was speaking about himself, he was filled with the spirit of prophecy; immediately he merited to possess the spirit of prophecy, and he humbly acknowledged that he was not a prophet.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### “And when you come to Babylon, there you shall be delivered” (Mic. 4:10)

*(Book I, Homily 10 on Ezekiel, no. 12.)* Those who have fallen from a state of uprightness into wicked action are not to be despaired of, because the Lord says through the prophet Micah: “And when you come as far as Babylon, there you shall be delivered” (Mic. 4:10).

What is called Babylon except confusion? Often, after someone has fallen into the confusion of vices, he returns to repentance, ashamed of the evils he has committed, and raises himself from his falls through good living.

Who, then, is this person except one who comes as far as Babylon? And who is delivered except the one who, after he has committed [evil deeds] in a mind confused by perversity, is ashamed of those very evils he has done, rises up against himself, and returns to a state of uprightness by doing good? He comes to Babylon and is delivered there who, through divine grace, is shown to have been saved even from confusion.

## CHAPTER IX  
### “As thorns embrace one another” (Nah. 1:10)

*(Morals, Book XXXIII, chapter 31, no. 55.)* Concerning the unity of the rejected, the prophet Nahum says: “As thorns embrace one another, so is the banquet of those who drink together” (Nah. 1:10).

The banquet of the rejected is the pleasure of temporal delights. At this banquet those drink together who make themselves drunk in harmony with the enticements of their pleasure.

# BOOK TEN  
## Testimonies on the Prophets Habakkuk and Zephaniah

[Column 1009]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### “I shall stand upon my watch” (Hab. 2:1)

[Column 1009C]

(Moral. Book XXII, chapter 16, sections 35–36.) If the mind is once firmly fixed in the desire for the heavenly homeland, it is less troubled by the disturbance of temporal things; nor does it inwardly endure the storm of temporal affairs which it beholds outwardly, because all earthly things that, when desired, might have overwhelmed the mind now lie beneath it, despised. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Set up a watchtower for yourself” (Jer. XXXI, 21), so that, while each person watches the things above, he may rise above those below.

For this reason Habakkuk also says: “I will stand upon my watch” [Col. 1009D] (Hab. II, 1). He stands upon his watch who, through vigilant discipline, does not succumb to earthly desires but rises above them, so that, while he continually longs for eternity, everything that passes may lie beneath him.

Yet because the holy man, however greatly he may advance in virtue, is still placed in this life and is still pressed outwardly by the weakness of the flesh, as it is written: “Although man walks in the likeness of God, yet he will be troubled in vain” (Ps. XXXVIII, 7), it often comes about that he is troubled outwardly but remains inwardly undisturbed. What can be troubled in vain proceeds from the weakness of the flesh, whereas the fact that he walks in the likeness of God proceeds from the strength of the mind: so that he may be strengthened inwardly by divine assistance and yet still be burdened outwardly by human weight.

Hence Habakkuk fittingly expressed one statement serving both conditions. For he says: “And trembling entered into my bones, and beneath me my strength was troubled” [Col. 1010C] (Hab. III, 16). It is as though he were saying: “The strength in which I remain undisturbed, having been carried above, is not my own strength; and the strength in which I am troubled below is my own.” Thus he is undisturbed above himself and capable of being troubled beneath himself: above himself, because he had ascended insofar as he was carried away toward the heights; beneath himself, because he was still below himself insofar as he continued to bear the remnants of his condition toward the depths. He is undisturbed above himself because in contemplating God he had already passed beyond himself; he is capable of being troubled beneath himself because below himself he still remained a weak human being.

## CHAPTER II.—“Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own” (Hab. II, 6).

[Col. 1010D]

(Moral. Book XXXIV, chapter 15, section 27.) In sacred speech, the name “mud” signifies the multiplicity of earthly things, as it is said through Habakkuk: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own: how long will he load thick mud upon himself?” (Hab. II, 6). To load thick mud upon oneself is to heap up earthly profits together with the burden of sin. For he loads himself with thick mud who, multiplying earthly possessions through avarice, constricts himself beneath the oppression of his sin.

Again, by the name “mud” is signified teaching that has a sordid and earthly character. Thus the Lord is addressed through the same prophet: “You made a way in the sea for your horses, in the mud of many waters” (Hab. III, 15). It is as though he were saying: “You opened a path for your preachers amid the teachings of this age that are sordid and concerned with earthly things.”

## CHAPTER III.—“God will come from Lebanon” (Hab. III, 3).

(Moral. Book XXXIII, chapter 1, section 2.) Sometimes the Testament of God is expressed by a mountain, as Habakkuk says: “God will come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from the shady and dense mountain” (Hab. III, 3). For he who promised that he would come through the pages of his Testament is said, as it were, to come from there, from where he held himself as though beneath a promise. That Testament is rightly called a shady and dense mountain, because it is overshadowed by the very obscurities of its allegories.

## CHAPTER IV.—“His feet stood firm, and the earth was shaken” (Hab. III, 6).

(Moral. Book XXXV, chapter 14, section 26; Book II, chapter 10, section 15.) Because sometimes, when the mind of the sinner is touched by fear of the Truth, it is shaken from its insensibility, Habakkuk rightly says: “His feet stood firm, and the earth was shaken” (Hab. III, 6). When the Lord stands firm, the earth is undoubtedly shaken, because when he impresses the traces of his fear upon our hearts, every earthly thought within us trembles; when the Truth is fixed in the heart, the hardness of the sinful mind is shaken from its obstinate immobility and changed.

## CHAPTER V.—“The abyss gave forth its voice” (Hab. III, 10).

(Moral. Book IX, chapter 25, section 39; likewise Book XXIX, chapter 15; Book IX, section 39; Book XXIX.) “The abyss gave forth its voice from the height of its imagination” (Hab. III, 10). What is the abyss except the human mind? The abyss bears the height of imagination when the human mind, in the darkness of its immense thought, cannot comprehend itself or penetrate itself by examination, and when it lies hidden from itself, like a dark abyss, in all that it is.

But to give forth a voice from this height means that, since it cannot discover itself through the loftiness of its contemplation, it is constrained and narrowed by the very breadth of its searching. It is forced to cry out—that is, to rise in amazement—so that the more it does not dare to scrutinize what is above it, the more, while contemplating its own incomprehensibility, it cannot discover what it is. And by comparison with itself, it praises more humbly the power of the divine nature, which it cannot sufficiently comprehend.

## CHAPTER VI.—“The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. III, 11).

[Col. 1011C]

(Book II, Homily 29 on the Gospels, section 10.) Concerning the glory of the Lord’s ascension, Habakkuk says: “The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. III, 11). For who is signified by the name of the sun except the Lord, and who by the name of the moon except the Church? As long as the Lord had not ascended into heaven, his holy Church greatly feared the adversities of the world in every way. But after it was strengthened by his ascension, it openly proclaimed what it had secretly believed.

Thus the sun was lifted up and the moon stood in its order, because when the Lord sought heaven, his holy Church grew strong, established in the authority of its preaching.

## CHAPTER VII.—“In the light your arrows will go forth” (Hab. III, 11).

(Moral. Book XXX, chapter 2, section 6.) Concerning holy preachers Habakkuk says: “In the light your arrows will go forth” (Hab. III, 11). God’s arrows are the words of the saints, which strike the hearts of sinners. For God’s arrows to go forth in the light means that his words resound with manifest truth.

But because people often despise the words of life even after understanding them, miracles are added. Hence it follows: “In the splendor of the flashing of your weapons” (ibid.). The flashing of weapons is the brilliance of miracles. We defend ourselves with weapons; with arrows we destroy what is hostile. Weapons together with arrows are miracles together with preaching.

For holy preachers strike their adversaries with their words, as with certain arrows; but with weapons—that is, with miracles—they defend themselves, so that by the force of their arrows they may proclaim how greatly they ought to be heard, and through the weapons of miracles they may make clear how greatly they ought to be revered.

## CHAPTER VIII.—“You cut off the heads of the powerful in alienation” (Hab. III, 14).

(Book I, Homily 10 on Ezekiel, section 39; Book XXXI, chapter 24.) Concerning the conversion of the Gentiles, Habakkuk says to the Lord: “You cut off the heads of the powerful in alienation; the nations will be moved in it; they will open their mouths like a poor man eating in secret” (Hab. III, 14).

Almighty God cut off the heads of the powerful in alienation, because by alienating the Jewish people from himself he rejected their pride. In that alienation the Gentiles were moved, because, while the Jews were falling away from the faith, the hearts of the faithful [Text: Gentiles] hastened toward knowledge of the faith. These Gentiles open the mouths of their hearts to the nourishment of sacred reading and eat in secret like a poor man, because they receive the words of life by reading them eagerly and silently.

For what the same Habakkuk says to the Lord concerning them was fulfilled in them: “You sent your horses into the sea, disturbing many waters” (ibid., 15). By the name of horses the holy preachers are understood. The quiet waters had lain still, because the human minds of the Gentiles had long been asleep beneath the lethargy of their vices. But the sea was disturbed by God’s horses, because, when holy preachers were sent, every heart that had grown lethargic through a baneful sense of security was shaken by the impulse of salutary fear.

## CHAPTER IX.—“Behold, the great day of the Lord is coming” (Zeph. I).

(Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 11.) Against the impure and double-minded the prophet Zephaniah threatens the force of divine judgment, saying: “Behold, the great and terrible day of the Lord is coming: a day of wrath, that day; a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and tempest, a day of trumpet and blast, against all fortified cities and against all lofty corners” (Zeph. I).

For what is expressed by fortified cities except minds surrounded on every side by a suspicious and deceptive defense? Whenever their guilt is corrected, they do not admit the arrows of truth into themselves. And what are signified by lofty corners—for a corner always has two walls—except impure hearts? While they flee from the simplicity of truth, they are, as it were, folded back upon themselves by the perversity of duplicity. Worse still, amid their thoughts, in the arrogance of their supposed wisdom, they exalt themselves because of the very guilt of their impurity.

Therefore the day of the Lord, full of vengeance and judgment, comes upon fortified cities and upon lofty corners, because the wrath of the final Judge destroys human hearts closed against the truth by their defenses and dissolves those entangled in duplicity. For then the fortified cities fall, because minds impervious to God will be condemned. Then the lofty corners collapse, because hearts raised up by the cunning of impurity are struck down by the sentence of justice.

# BOOK ELEVEN. Testimonies from the Prophet Haggai

[Col. 1011]

## CHAPTER I.—“You have sown much” (Hag. I, 5).

[Col. 1011D]

(Book I, Homily 10 on Ezekiel, section 7.) Many read and remain hungry despite the reading itself. Many hear the voice of preaching and depart empty after hearing it. Hence the Lord rebukes certain people through the prophet Haggai, saying: “Set your hearts upon your ways: you have sown much and brought in little; you have eaten and have not been satisfied; you have drunk and have not been intoxicated” (Hag. I, 5).

He sows much in his heart but brings in little who learns much from the heavenly commandments, either by reading or by hearing, but produces little fruit by acting negligently. He eats and is not satisfied who, hearing the word of God, desires the profits or favor of the world. He is rightly said not to be satisfied, because he chews one thing and hungers for another.

He drinks and is not intoxicated who inclines his ear to the voice of preaching but does not change his mind. For the understanding of those who drink is accustomed to change through intoxication. Therefore, one who is devoted to learning the word of God but desires to obtain the things of this age drinks but is not intoxicated. If he were intoxicated, he would have changed his mind, so that he would no longer seek earthly things and would no longer love the vain and transitory things that he had loved.

Concerning the elect, the Psalmist says: “They will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house” (Ps. XXXV, 9), because they have been so filled with the love of almighty God that, with their minds changed, they seem to be strangers even to themselves. They fulfill what is written: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. XVI, 24). He denies himself who is changed for the better, begins to be what he was not, and ceases to be what he was.

## CHAPTER II.—“He who gathered wages” (Hag. I, 6).

(Book I, Homily 4 on Ezekiel, section 10; Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 21.) The wicked give many things from their own possessions to the needy; but when they find an opportunity, they devastate by plunder the very people whom they are able to rob. They weigh how much they give, but refuse to consider how much they steal, and decline to ponder how they lose good works through evil practices.

As it is written through Haggai: “He who gathered wages put them into a pierced purse” (Hag. I, 6). From a pierced purse, what is put in from one side goes out from another; and in a pierced purse the money is visible when it is deposited, but invisible when it is lost.

Therefore those who look at how much they give but do not consider how much they steal put their wages into a pierced purse: for they gather them while looking toward them as the hope of their confidence, but lose them because they do not look toward them. The wage acquired from a good work is lost through an evil work.

# BOOK TWELVE. Testimonies from the Prophet Zechariah

[Col. 1013]

## CHAPTER I.—“The angel who spoke in me said” (Zech. I, 14).

[Col. 1013B]

(Moral. Book XXVIII, chapter 1, section 9; Book II, Homily 34 on the Gospels, section 13; Moral. Book IV, chapter 29.) Sometimes, through angels, God pours into human hearts, by their secret presence, the inspiration of his power [Text: “the power of his inspiration”]. Hence Zechariah said: “The angel spoke to me who spoke in me” (Zech. I, 14). By saying that the angel spoke to him but nevertheless within him, he clearly shows that the one who spoke words to him was not outwardly present in bodily form.

Hence a little later he adds: “And behold, the angel of the Lord who spoke in me was going out” (Zech. II, 3). For they often do not appear outwardly; rather, as angelic spirits, they make God’s will known to the senses of the prophets. The subtlety of angelic power, appearing to their minds, raises them to higher things through inward inspirations and shows as present in their original causes the things that are destined to occur.

But let no one think that in the words mentioned above the name “angel” designates either the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, since the text of sacred Scripture never calls the Father or the Holy Spirit an angel, and calls the Son an angel only in the proclamation of his incarnation. Hence it is clearly shown in the words of this same Zechariah that a true angel—that is, a creature—was speaking in him, when it is said: “Behold, the angel who spoke in me was going out.”

Immediately it is added: “And another angel went out to meet him and said to him: Run, speak to this boy, saying: Jerusalem will be inhabited without a wall” (ibid., vv. 3–4). Therefore the angel who is sent is not God, since an angel gives him the words that he is to speak.

But because, in the sight of the Creator, angelic ministries are distinguished by an ordered arrangement of ranks, so that, while all behold their Maker together and rejoice in the common blessedness of happiness, nevertheless some minister to others according to the arrangement of dignity, one angel sends another to the prophet. The angel sees another rejoicing with him in God, and teaches and directs him, because he surpasses him both through superior knowledge in the power of understanding and through more excellent grace in the height of authority.

For we know with complete certainty that the Lord, Creator of all, who sustains everything through himself, governs the beautiful order of the universe by having some things administered through others. Angels are administered through the powers of higher angels, and, to fulfill the ministry from above, some spirits are sent by others.

When an angel says to another angel, “Run and speak,” there is no doubt that one sends the other. If the highest powers did not arrange the least among the offices of the holy spirits, an angel would in no way have known from another angel what he should say to a human being.

We also hold this certainly concerning the very orders of angels: those who are sent are lesser; those who send are greater. Those who are sent, when they come to us, fulfill their ministry outwardly in such a way that they never cease inwardly through contemplation.

## CHAPTER II.—“And he showed me Jesus the high priest” (Zech. III, 1).

(Moral. Book XX, chapter 22, section 48.) In ordinary speech, we say that we regard as “on the right” what we value highly, and as “on the left” what we despise. Zechariah makes this clear, saying: “And he showed me Jesus the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord; and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him” (Zech. III, 1).

To make more evident what he had just stated, he continued: “And the Lord said to Satan: ‘May the Lord rebuke you, Satan, who has chosen Jerusalem. Is this not a brand plucked from the fire?’ And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments” (ibid., v. 2).

Jesus was clothed in filthy garments because, although he was free from every sin, he nevertheless came in the likeness of sinful flesh. When he came, Satan stood at his right hand. For the Lord seemed to regard the Jewish people as something great and the Gentiles as nothing. But after he appeared incarnate, the Gentiles, who had been regarded as being on the left, believed, while the Jewish people turned toward faithlessness.

Therefore Satan stood at the right hand of that people because he snatched from the Lord the people who had formerly been beloved. But because that same Jewish people, now lost, will at the end eventually believe, as the Prophet testifies: “A remnant will be saved” (Isa. X, 21), the Lord removes Satan from its right hand, saying: “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan.” Indicating the liberation of that people, he adds: “For he has chosen Jerusalem.”

Since that people, led by faithlessness, was flowing down toward the fires of Gehenna, but, when it is brought back to the faith, is delivered from the same fire of eternal punishment, the following is immediately said of it there: “Is this not a brand plucked from the fire?”

## CHAPTER III.—“Upon one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. III, 9).

(Moral. Book XXIX, chapter 31, section 74.) When our Redeemer came in the flesh, he possessed simultaneously within himself all the operations of the sevenfold Spirit, as Zechariah says: “Upon one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. III, 9), and again: “And on the golden lampstand were seven lamps” (Zech. IV, 2).

No human being possessed all the operations of the Holy Spirit simultaneously except the one Mediator between God and humanity, whose Spirit is the same Spirit who proceeds from the Father before the ages. For this stone to have seven eyes means to retain in operation all the power of the sevenfold Spirit of grace at once.

## CHAPTER IV.—“What do you see, Zechariah?” (Zech. V, 2).
