(Moral. Book XV, chapter 14, section 18.) Whoever retains God’s commandments in memory but does not complete them by doing them holds, in the words of teaching, sentences by which he will be condemned. Hence it is written in Zechariah: “What do you see, Zechariah?” And I said: “I see a flying scroll; its length is twenty cubits and its width is ten cubits.” And he said to me: “This is the curse that goes forth over the face of the whole earth” (Zech. V, 2–3).

For what is the flying scroll except sacred Scripture? While it speaks of heavenly things, it lifts the intention of our minds upward, because, when we see it as being above us, we avoid attending to or desiring things below.

It is said to have a width of ten cubits and a length of twenty, because the breadth of our work is single, while the endurance of hope extends twofold. For on account of our good work, rest of mind is prepared for us here and eternal joys there, as the Truth testifies when it says: “Whoever has left houses or fields, etc., will receive a hundredfold in this age and will possess eternal life in the future” (Matt. XIX, 29; Luke XVIII, 30).

The number one hundred is made perfect by multiplying ten by ten. He therefore receives a hundredfold who, even if he possesses nothing, nevertheless seeks in this age, through the very perfection of his mind, to possess nothing. Since, therefore, through this we are repaid twofold for what is single, this scroll is rightly extended to a length of twenty cubits while it is broadened by ten.

But because these sacred words bring eternal condemnation upon those who either do not wish to know them or, certainly knowing them, despise them, it is rightly said of the scroll: “This is the curse that will go forth over the face of the whole earth.” And he adds why it is called a curse: “Because every thief, as it is written there, will be judged.”

Therefore the hypocrite, because he refuses to live according to the words of the Law that he knows and seeks favor from teaching, will be judged a thief, because by speaking what is just he steals for himself the praise belonging to the lives of the just.

## CHAPTER V.—“Lift up your eyes and see what this is that is going forth” (Zech. V, 5).

(Moral. Book XIV, chapter 53, sections 63–65.) Through lead, whose nature is heavy in weight, the sin of avarice is especially signified. It makes the mind that it has killed so heavy that it cannot be lifted up to desire higher things.

Hence it is written in Zechariah: “Lift up your eyes and see what this is that is going forth.” And I said: “What is it?” And he said: “This is the vessel that is going forth” (Zech. V, 5). Wishing to show the prophet from what kind of fault the human race chiefly departs from God, the Lord represented, by the image of a vessel, as it were, the open mouth of avarice. For avarice is like a vessel that keeps the mouth of the heart open in the pursuit of gain. And he said: “This is their eye throughout the whole earth” (ibid.).

We see many people dull in understanding, yet we see them shrewd in evil actions, as the prophet testifies: “They are wise to do evil” (Jer. IV, 22). These people are sluggish in understanding, but in what they desire they are roused by the goads of avarice. Because they are blind to seeing good things, they become vigilant in carrying out evil through the rewards that arouse them.

Hence it is rightly said of this same avarice: “This is their eye throughout the whole earth.” And behold, a talent of lead was being carried (Zech. V, 6). What is the talent of lead except the weight of sin proceeding from the same avarice?

“And behold, one woman sitting in the middle of the vessel” (ibid., v. 7). Lest we perhaps be uncertain who this woman was, the angel immediately made it known. For he continues: “And he said: ‘This is Impiety,’ and he threw her into the middle of the vessel” (v. 8). Impiety is thrown into the middle of the vessel because impiety is always held within avarice.

“And he threw the mass of lead into its mouth” (ibid.). The mass of lead is thrown into the vessel’s mouth because, clearly, the impiety of avarice is weighed down by the burden of its sin. For if it did not strive after things below, it would not be impious toward God and toward its neighbors.

To show more fully what he had understood concerning the vision of the vessel, the woman, and the lead, he continued: “And I lifted up my eyes and saw; and behold, two women were going forth, and the spirit was in their wings” (ibid., v. 9). What else do we understand by these two women except the two principal vices, namely pride and empty glory, which are undoubtedly joined to impiety?

They are said to have the spirit in their wings because in their actions they serve Satan’s will. The Prophet calls it the very spirit of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person” (Matt. XII, 43). The spirit is in their wings because pride and empty glory serve Satan’s will in everything they do.

“And they had wings like the wings of a kite.” The kite is always naturally intent on laying ambushes for young birds. These women therefore have wings like the wings of a kite because their actions resemble those of the devil, who is always lying in wait for the life of the little ones.

“And they lifted up the vessel between heaven and earth.” Pride and empty glory have this characteristic: they raise above all other people, in their thoughts, the person whom they have infected. Sometimes through the pursuit of possessions, sometimes through the desire for honors, they elevate the person whom they have once captured as though to the height of honor.

But whoever is between heaven and earth has abandoned what is below and does not touch what is above. These women therefore lift the vessel between heaven and earth, because pride and empty glory elevate the mind captured by avarice for honor in such a way that, despising its neighbors, it abandons what is below and boasts while seeking what is high.

Such people, while they grow proud, mentally pass beyond those with whom they live, yet are not joined to the citizens above. Therefore the vessel is said to be lifted between heaven and earth, because avaricious people, through pride and empty glory, despise their neighbors who are beside them, but do not attain the higher things beyond them.

They are carried between heaven and earth because they neither maintain the equality of brotherhood below through love, nor can they reach the heights by exalting themselves.

“And I said to the angel who spoke in me: ‘Where are they carrying the vessel?’ And he said to me: ‘To build a house for it in the land of Shinar’” (vv. 10–11). *Shinar* is said to mean “their stench.” Just as good odor proceeds from virtue, so, conversely, stench proceeds from vice. “The root of all evils is greed” (1 Tim. VI, 10). Since every evil is generated through avarice, it is fitting that the house of avarice should be built in stench.

It should also be known that Shinar is a very broad valley in which the tower began to be built by the proud, but was destroyed by the diversity of languages. This tower was called Babylon, on account of the confusion of minds and languages. Nor is it without reason that the vessel of avarice is placed there, where Babylon—that is, confusion—is built. Since it is certain that all evils arise through avarice and impiety, it is rightly declared that this same avarice and impiety dwell in confusion.

## CHAPTER VI.—“They will devour and subdue with the stones of a sling” (Zech. IX, 15).

(Moral. Book XXXIV, chapter 9.) Concerning good teachers the Lord says through Zechariah: “They will devour and subdue with the stones of a sling” (Zech. IX, 15). What is signified by the sling except holy Church? When a sling is whirled around, stones come forth from it with which the breasts of adversaries are struck [Text: add. *sic*].

Thus, when holy Church is led through the circuit of tribulations by the revolutions of time, strong men emerge from it, by whose blows, like stones, the hearts of the wicked are battered.

Holy teachers who instruct others in virtue devour their enemies when they transform them within their own body through the power of their way of life. They subdue them with the stones of a sling because, when they train strong men in holy Church, they break through these men the hard breasts of their arrogant adversaries.

Hence the most savage Goliath dies by a sling-stone, because the devil’s loftiness is overcome by the single stone of holy Church.

## CHAPTER VII.—“And it will happen that whoever among them stumbles on that day” (Zech. XII, 8).

(Book II, Homily 8 on Ezekiel, sections 18–20.) Dearest brothers, let us turn the eyes of our minds back toward our past life; and because we remember that we have sinned, let us mourn. Great indeed is the merciful bosom of our Creator for receiving the tears of the humble. Where the tears of countless people have been received, there our own tears too will find a place.

Let us consider what is said through Zechariah: “It will happen that whoever among them stumbles on that day will be like David, and the house of David will be like God” (Zech. XII, 8). For whoever returns to righteousness becomes the dwelling place of his Creator, so that he may be like an angel in his presence, because he distributes to others, by proclaiming it, the mercy that he himself has experienced.

A little later it is also said: “On that day there will be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the cleansing of the sinner and of the menstruous woman” (Zech. XIII, 1).

The hidden fountain is the invisible God, the only-begotten Son of the Father; the open fountain is that same God incarnate. This open fountain is rightly called the house of David, because our Redeemer came to us from the line of David.

Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” Those inhabit Jerusalem who fix their minds upon the inward vision of peace.

The sinner and the menstruous woman signify either one who sins in action or a mind that slips into evil thought. Menstruation is pollution because it is not touched by another’s flesh yet is defiled by its own flesh. So it is with every soul which, even if it does not perform an evil work, is nevertheless stained by polluted thought.

Hence another prophet, speaking under the figure of Judea concerning a soul occupied by unclean desires, says: “All who seek her will not fail” (Jer. II, 24), when they desire to bring about destruction and are not repelled by any uprightness of good thought. They find the soul in its menstruation when they easily draw it, placed amid polluted thoughts, toward perverse action.

Let it therefore be said: “On that day there will be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the cleansing of the sinner and of the menstruous woman,” because the fountain of mercy is now open to us—our Redeemer, who consented to become incarnate in the house of David, so that he might cleanse the sinner from perverse action and wash the menstruous mind from unclean thought.

The fountain is open; let us run with tears and wash ourselves in this fountain of compassion. David himself was washed in this fountain when, after the stain of grave guilt, he returned to the lamentation of repentance. He was seeking to find this very fountain when he said: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Ps. L, 14). For Jesus in Hebrew means “Savior.” What does it mean that he asked for the joy of Jesus to be restored to him, except that before his guilt he had been accustomed to contemplate Jesus, but in his guilt had lost the joys of that contemplation? Hence, after repentance, he rightly sought that the joy of his vision be restored to him.

In this fountain of mercy Mary Magdalene was washed: formerly a notorious sinner, she later washed away her stains with tears (Luke VII). In this open fountain of mercy the Apostle Peter washed away what he had denied, because he wept bitterly (Matt. XXVI). In this fountain of mercy, at the end of his life, the thief was washed, for, reproving himself in death, he was cleansed from his guilt by confessing the truth (Luke XXIII).

Therefore let us not despair of our cleansing, since we know that so many have already washed themselves in this fountain of compassion. We ought to have sought the fountain of mercy even if it had been closed. Now it is open, yet we neglect it and remain sluggish and cold.

Let us cast the eyes of faith upon the whole world. Let us consider how many sinners, day and night, are washed in this fountain of mercy through lamentation; how many return from darkness to light, how many from stains to purity. Let us consider how greatly we have sinned and how greatly we sin each day.

Let us run to the water of life, seeking pardon and possessing confidence with tears. Let us wash ourselves in this fountain of compassion and mercy, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# EXCERPTS in which many verses of the Psalms are explained

[Col. 1017]

[Col. 1017C] (Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 32.) Sins committed through judgment and deliberation, or through design, differ greatly from other sins; the Lord pursues not so much the wrong acts as the deliberate purposes of wrongdoing. In actions, sin is often committed through weakness, often through negligence; but in deliberate purposes it is always committed with a malicious intention.

Against this, the blessed man is rightly described by the Psalmist: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. I, 1).

A judge’s or presiding officer’s place is ordinarily called a seat. To sit in the seat of pestilence is to commit evil by judicial decision. To sit in the seat of pestilence is to distinguish evil by reason and yet carry it out deliberately.

He sits, as it were, in the seat of perverse counsel who is lifted up by such arrogance of iniquity that he attempts to accomplish evil even through planning. Just as those who are supported by the honor of a seat preside over the crowds attending them, so the offenses of those who fall through reckless haste are surpassed by sins carefully devised through deliberate purpose.

Therefore let those who bind themselves to guilt even through planning gather from this what vengeance will one day strike them, since they are now not companions but leaders of the wicked.

(Moral. Book XIX, chapter 28; Book I, Homily 2 on Ezekiel, section 6.) God, the Creator of all, could not be seen in his divinity; he assumed from us that by which he might be seen by us, and through the mystery of his incarnation deigned to appear to the human race, which from its origin flows toward death, as the Psalmist says of him: “And he will be like a tree planted beside streams of waters” (Ps. I, 2).

He was planted beside streams of waters because he was incarnate beside the falls of the peoples who were flowing away. The streams of waters are the daily passages of peoples who are failing, and the Truth says of itself: “If they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?” (Luke XXIII, 31).

The tree beside the streams of waters is therefore the Creator appearing in the flesh, bringing forth for us the fruit and protection of his shade, so that through the resurrection he might establish the human race, which each day was moving toward death through decay.

(Moral. Book XXVI, chapter 27, no. 50.) Concerning the reprobate on the day of judgment: some are judged and perish; others are not judged and perish. Those are judged and perish to whom, by the Lord’s proclamation, it is said: “I was hungry and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25:42), and so forth; to them it is said beforehand: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (ibid., 41). Others, however, are not judged and perish. Concerning them the Lord says: “Whoever does not believe is already judged” (John 3:18), and concerning them Paul says: “Those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law” (Rom. 2:18); and concerning them the Psalmist says: “The wicked shall not rise in judgment” (Ps. 1:6). He calls impious those who are either separated from the piety of faith or contradict by their evil conduct what they faithfully believe.

All unbelievers will indeed rise, but for punishment, not for judgment. Their case is not then examined, for they come before the strict Judge already bearing the condemnation of their unbelief. Those, however, who retain the profession of faith but do not possess the works of that profession are reproved so that they may perish. The former at least hear the words of the Judge, since they at least held the words of faith in him; the latter, in their condemnation, do not even hear the words of the eternal Judge, because they were unwilling to observe his reverence even in word.

The former perish according to the law, because they sinned while placed under the Law; to the latter, in their destruction, nothing is said about the Law, because they made no attempt to possess the Law. For a prince governing an earthly commonwealth punishes in one way a citizen who transgresses within it and in another way an enemy who rebels from outside. In the former case he has regard for his laws and condemns him in words of fitting denunciation. Against the enemy, however, he makes war, employs the instruments of destruction, and returns punishments worthy of his wickedness; but he does not inquire what the law prescribes concerning his evil; nor is it necessary [Text: “by law”] to punish one who could never be held by the law. Thus, at the final judgment, the denunciation of the Law strikes the one who has departed in action from what he held in his profession; but the other is destroyed without judicial denunciation, since he is not held by the law of faith.

(Moral. Book VII, chapter 16, no. 19.) We must know that sometimes the adversary crushes us, and sometimes God crushes us. Through the crushing inflicted by the adversary we fall away from virtue; but, broken through the Lord’s chastisement, we are strengthened in virtue. The prophet had seen this crushing and striking when he said: “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you shall break them” [Text: “crush them”] (Ps. 2:9). The Lord rules and crushes us with an iron rod, because, by the upright strength [Text: “strong uprightness”] of his ordering, he restores us inwardly while afflicting us outwardly. For by humbling the strength of the flesh, he exalts the purpose of the spirit. Hence this same crushing is compared with a potter’s vessel. As Paul also says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). Expressing both crushing and governance together, he says: “Although our outer self is being destroyed, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day” (ibid., 16).

(Moral. Book XX, chapter 3, no. 8.) Holy men are so certain of hope that they nevertheless remain continually wary of temptation; for it is said to them: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11), so that rejoicing may arise from hope and trembling from apprehension. Again the Psalmist says in their voice: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Ps. 85:11). Here we must note that he does not say, “Let it rejoice so that it may be secure,” but, “Let it rejoice so that it may fear.” For they remember that, however prosperously their conduct may proceed, they are still in this life, of which it is said: “Human life upon earth is a trial” (Job 7:1). They remember and fear; placed between the joy of hope and the fear of temptation, they trust and fear, are strengthened and waver, become more certain and remain apprehensive.

(Moral. Book V, chapter 45, no. 82.) We must know that one kind of anger is aroused by impatience, and another is formed by zeal. The former is generated by vice, the latter by virtue. Because Eli did not possess this anger, he aroused against himself the implacable movement of heavenly vengeance. For in proportion as he was lukewarm toward the vices of his subjects, so the severity of the eternal Ruler burned against him. Concerning this anger the Psalmist says: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). Those who wish us to be angry only with ourselves, and not also with our offending neighbors, certainly do not understand this correctly. For if we are commanded to love our neighbors as ourselves, it follows that we should be angry at their errors as at our own vices.

(Moral. Book XXXV, chapter 7, no. 10.) In God’s sight the life of many people is often displeasing, although it also pleases people outwardly. Hence the Psalmist watchfully entreats, saying: “Direct my way in your sight” (Ps. 5:9), because very often a way is considered straight in the sight of men even though it has been distorted from the path of truth: “You have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (ibid., 14). In sacred Scripture, the protection of a shield is often used for divine protection. The Lord is said to crown us with a shield because, protecting us, he assists us, and, rewarding us, he crowns us.

(Book II, Homily 4 on Ezekiel, no. 2; Homily 8, no. 5.) The number eight signifies the day of eternal judgment and the resurrection of the flesh. Thus, considering the day of resurrection, and about to speak of the severity of the final judgment, the Psalmist prefaced the title, saying: “For the end, a psalm of David, for the eighth” (Ps. 6). To show which “eighth” he meant, he followed it at the beginning of the psalm with the day of terrifying dread, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath” (ibid., 1). In the present life each person is corrected through scourges and amended by corrections. He is corrected in gentleness, not in anger; but in that unyielding examination every rebuke and correction is fury and anger, because there is no pardon after correction. Now is the time of mercy; in that judgment it will be the day of wrath. On that day all this period which unfolds through seven days comes to an end; and because it follows the seven days, it is rightly called the eighth. In it, too, our flesh will rise from the dust, so that it may receive from Truth whatever good or evil it has done.

(Moral. Book VIII, chapter 18.) “In hell, who will confess to you?” (Ps. 6:6). The name “hell” signifies the sinner’s despair. Hence it is written: “When the wicked comes into the depth of sins, he despises” (Prov. 18:13).

(Moral. Book XIX, chapter 30, no. 53.) Vices belong to the old life, and virtues to the new. Hence the Psalmist, speaking as a representative of the human race, says, caught among malignant spirits: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6:8). For we somehow grow old away from the fervor of the mind, whether among spiritual enemies or among our various carnal neighbors, through our very manner of living, and are darkened by the appearance of the newness we have assumed. Yet, if the disciplines of vigilance remain watchful, we are daily renewed from this old age by praying, reading, and living well. For while our life is washed with tears and exercised in good works, while it is stretched toward holy meditations, it is continually restored to its newness.

(Moral. Book XIX, chapter 30, no. 55.) Sometimes sacred Scripture is signified by a bow: it is itself the bow of the Church, and it is itself the bow of the Lord. From it terrifying pronouncements come to the hearts of men like arrows that strike. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “He has bent his bow and prepared it; and in it he has prepared instruments of death; he has made his arrows burning” (Ps. 7:13). The Lord has bent his bow because through sacred Scripture he has displayed threats to all sinners. In this bow he prepares instruments of death because, according to the judgment of his word, he condemns as reprobate those who now neglect correction. In it he has also made his arrows burning because against those whom he corrects through terror he sends forth burning judgments of words.

(Moral. Book XI, chapter 28.) Heretics assert things that in no way please the Lord on whose behalf they speak; and when they try, as it were, to defend God, they offend him. Hence the Psalmist says: “That you may destroy the enemy and the defender” (Ps. 8:3). Every heretic is both an enemy and a defender of almighty God, because in the very way in which he tries, as it were, to defend him, he opposes his truth.

(Book II, Homily 1 on Ezekiel, no. 3.) In sacred Scripture, things that are to be understood spiritually can often also be received according to the historical sense, so that faith may be maintained in the truth of the history and spiritual understanding may be gained from the mysteries of allegory. Such is what the Psalmist says: “For I shall see your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you founded” [Text: “whom you founded”] (Ps. 8:4). At the level of outward description, the statement is coherent: the heavens are God’s work, and the moon and stars were created and founded by him. But if the Psalmist asserts this according only to outward works and not also according to mystical understanding, then, having declared the heavens to be God’s works, when he is about to mention the moon and stars, why did he not likewise enumerate the sun, which we know is also his work? But because he was speaking according to mystical understanding, so that we should understand the moon as the holy Church and all the saints as the stars, he did not wish to name the sun, since he was speaking to the eternal Sun himself, concerning whom it is written: “But for you who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. 4:2). For he made not only the bodily sun, moon, and stars, but also, spiritually, the Church as the moon and all the saints as the stars.

(Book I, Homily 8 on Ezekiel, no. 23.) The Father’s only-begotten Son, by becoming human, was made lower than the angels, as the Psalmist says: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6). But when he rose and ascended into heaven, he presides over all angelic powers. As it is written of him there again: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (v. 8).

(Moral. Book XI, chapter 3; Book XIX, chapter 16.) “The birds of heaven and the fish of the sea, which traverse the paths of the sea” (Ps. 9, [lacuna]). By the fish of the sea we must understand the inquisitive people of this age, who lie hidden, as it were, in concealed waves amid their great investigations of things. “You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (ibid.). The gates of death are evil actions that lead to destruction. But because Zion is interpreted as “watchtower,” we understand the gates of Zion as good actions, through which we enter the heavenly homeland so that we may contemplate the glory of our King.

(Book II, Homily 35 on the Gospels, no. 9.) “The patience of the poor shall not perish forever” (Ps. 9:19). The patience of the poor seems to have perished when nothing is repaid to the humble for it in this life. But it shall not perish forever, because its glory is then received when all things that cause labor come to an end together. For good things belonging to the life to come are to be hoped for in return for the labor of patience, so that the reward for our labor may begin when all labor has already ceased.

(Moral. Book XV, chapter 11; Book XXXIII, chapter 27, no. 48; Book XXXII, chapter 15.) “Under his tongue are labor and sorrow; he sits in ambush with the rich in secret places” (Ps. 9:19). This was said about Antichrist. Since he does not openly display the evils he contemplates, he does not bring forth upon his tongue the labor and sorrow of those whose death he desires, but presses them beneath his tongue. Because of his perverse doctrines, there are labor and sorrow beneath his tongue; because of the appearance of miracles, he sits in ambush; and because of the glory of secular power, he sits with the rich in secret places. Since he uses both the deception of miracles and earthly power, he is said to sit both in secret places and with the rich.

This Antichrist, because he is raised up not by power alone but is also supported by the display of signs, is rightly described by the same David: “He lies in ambush in secret, like a lion in his den” (ibid., 30). Since this ancient enemy is unleashed in all his powers, he is permitted to rage through both, so that against the elect he may be released in the struggle through both deceit and force: through force, by power; through deceit, by signs. Thus he is rightly called both a lion and one lying in ambush—lying in ambush through the appearance of miracles, and a lion through secular strength. To drag away those who are openly wicked, he displays secular power; but to deceive even the righteous, he feigns holiness through signs. To the former he persuades an exaltation of greatness; the latter he deceives by displaying holiness.

(Moral. Book XXXIII, chapter 1.) “In the Lord I trust; how can you say to my soul, ‘Flee like a sparrow to the mountain’?” (Ps. 10:1). The Psalmist says this in the voice of the Church. By the mountain, however, any heretic is represented. When the faithful soul is told to abandon unity and trust in the swelling doctrine of a heretical preacher, it is urged to flee, as it were, to the mountain, abandoning the Lord.

(Moral. Book XXXI, chapter 30.) “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright of heart” (Ps. 10:2). The name “quiver” signifies the plotting of the wicked. When the unjust hide through secret schemes the snares they devise against the good, they prepare arrows, as it were, in a quiver. In the darkness of the present life, as though in darkness, they strike the upright of heart, because their malicious arrows can be felt through the wound, yet their approach cannot be detected.

(Moral. Book XXVIII, chapter 4; Book II, Homily 5 on Ezekiel, no. 6.) “His eyelids question the children of men” (Ps. 10:5). With open eyelids we see; with closed eyelids we see nothing. By the eyelids of God, however, we understand his judgments, which in one respect are closed to human beings and in another respect are opened, so that people who do not know themselves may become known to themselves. Thus, while they grasp certain things through understanding but are entirely unable to know others, their hearts may secretly inquire into themselves—if the divine judgments, when closed, do not stimulate them, or, when opened, do not puff them up. By closing, they question us whether we despise what we are unable to understand; by opening, they question us whether we are not exalted by understanding.

(Moral. Book XV, chapter 49.) “He will rain snares upon sinners; fire, brimstone, and the spirit of storms will be the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10:7). Present punishment, which does not change sinners from their evil desires, in no way frees them from eternal punishments. By saying “snares,” “fire,” “brimstone,” and “the spirit of storms,” he certainly indicated many pains. But because the uncorrected sinner is summoned from these pains to eternal punishments, he called those same pains not the whole cup but a portion of the cup, since their portion begins here through pains but is completed in everlasting retribution.

(Moral. Book IV, chapter 31.) “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11:7). What is signified by silver except divine words? The word of the Lord is called silver tested by fire because, when God’s word is fixed in the heart, it is proved through tribulations.

(Moral. Book XXXIII, chapter 10.) “The measuring lines have fallen for me in pleasant places” (Ps. 15:6). Sometimes sacred Scripture customarily uses measuring lines to designate hereditary portions of inheritances. The measuring lines fall in pleasant places when, through humility of life, better portions [Text: “a better portion”] of the homeland fall to us.

[Col. 1022B] (Moral. Book XXXV, chapter 3.) “I cried out, because you heard me, O God” (Ps. 16:6). Whenever good desires attain their fulfillment, they rise toward God in greater number. He does not say, “Because I cried out, you heard me,” but, “I cried out, because you heard me.” He who had been heard while speaking cried out because, through the progress of his desires, he had been heard.

(Book II, Homily 6 on Ezekiel, no. 21.) “Make your mercies wonderful, you who save those who hope in you” (Ps. 16:7). God’s mercies become wonderful to us when our misery is recalled to our memory. For, remembering what we were, we understand to whom we owe what we are. No one understands divine mercy who has not remembered his own misery.

(Moral. Book XXXII, chapter 5.) “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (ibid., 9). Sometimes an image of the Lord is drawn from birds. For, while protecting us, he nourishes us as little ones; and while extending his mercies over us, he refreshes us with a protection that is not heavy or burdensome but light and gentle, as though, after the manner of birds, he spread his wings over us.

(Moral. Book XXXII, chapter 11.) It is certain that the one who understands less of the danger from which he has been rescued loves his rescuer less. Hence, rightly attributing his rescue to the Lord, the Prophet said: “I shall love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps. 17:1). It is as though he said: “I love you the more because, recognizing my own weakness, I understand that you are my strength.” Hence he says again: “Make your mercies wonderful” (Ps. 16:7), because the Lord’s mercies become truly wonderful to us who are rescued when through those same mercies we come to know how grave were the dangers we escaped.

(Moral. Book IV, chapter 16; Book V, chapter 7.) “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. 17:12). Darkness can signify hidden judgments. In darkness we either see nothing at all or grow dim with uncertain sight. Hidden judgments, therefore, are like a kind of darkness before our eyes, because they cannot be searched out. The prophet saw himself surrounded by this darkness when he could not penetrate the inner workings of the divine arrangement, saying: “He made darkness his hiding place.” Our Creator, because he has withdrawn from us, cast down into this exile, the light of his vision, has hidden himself from our eyes as though in darkness’s hiding place.

(Moral. Book XVII, chapter 26, no. 36.) “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17:12). In this passage he calls water knowledge and clouds preachers or prophets. Thus “dark water in the clouds of the air” means hidden knowledge in the prophets, who, before the Lord’s coming, carried within themselves immense mysteries, pregnant with hidden sacraments, while the understanding of them remained dark to the eyes of those who contemplated them.

(Moral. Book XXIX, chapter 20.) “Because of the brightness before him his clouds passed by, hail and coals of fire” (ibid., 13). The clouds pass by because of the brightness when holy preachers traverse the whole expanse of the world with the splendor of miracles. They are also called hail and coals of fire because [Text adds: “and”] they strike through correction and set people aflame through the fire of charity. As hail, when it comes, strikes and, once melted, waters, so they both strike the hearts of their hearers by terrifying them and gently pour refreshment into them.

(Moral. Book XXVI, chapter 24.) “And in my God I shall leap over a wall” (Ps. 17:30). A wall is whatever is placed in the way of our journey so that we cannot pass to the one who is loved. We leap over a wall when, out of love for the heavenly homeland, we trample underfoot whatever obstacles have been placed before us in this world. Hence it is said again: “He made my feet like those of deer” (ibid., 34). When a deer climbs the ridges of the mountains, if rough places arise before it, entangled with thorns, it leaps over them and rises to higher ground without any obstacle to its running. In the same way, the minds of the elect leap beyond through contemplation whatever they see resisting and opposing them in this world; and, like deer, scorning the thorns of earthly things, they raise themselves to what is above.

(Moral. Book XXXIV, chapter 14; Book II, Homily 38 on the Gospels, [Col. 1023B] no. 3.) “He set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18:6). Through the sun the prophet signifies the manifestation of open vision and announces the Lord appearing to the eyes of all. It is as though he said: “He displayed the mystery of the humanity he assumed in the light of manifest vision.” And “he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (ibid.). He came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber because the incarnate Lord came forth from the incorrupt womb of the Virgin in order to unite the Church to himself.

(Moral. Book XI, chapter 42, no. 57.) There is this difference between *scelera* and *delicta*: *scelus* also exceeds the weight of sin, whereas *delictum* does not exceed the weight of sin. For when the Law commands that a sacrifice be offered, it prescribes one for sin as well as for transgression; and *scelus* exists only in an action, whereas *delictum* often exists in thought alone. Hence the Psalmist says: “Who understands transgressions?” (Ps. 18:13). Sins of action are recognized all the more quickly because they are seen outwardly, whereas sins of thought are more difficult to understand because they are committed invisibly.

As for *iniquitas* and *peccatum*, although the apostle John says that they do not differ, saying, “Sin is iniquity” (1 John 3:4), nevertheless, in ordinary usage *iniquitas* conveys something more than *peccatum*. Everyone freely admits that he is a sinner, but a person is sometimes ashamed to call himself wicked.

(Book II, Homily 8 on Ezekiel, no. 17.) There are some who, even while abandoning the world, offer everything they possess to God, yet are not at all moved to compunction by the good things they do. The good they perform is a burnt offering; but because they do not know how to weep and judge themselves, and do not kindle themselves to tears through love, their burnt offering is not perfect. Hence the Psalmist says: “And may your burnt offering be made fat” (Ps. 19:4). A dry burnt offering is a good work that is not watered by the tears of prayer. A fat burnt offering, however, exists when what is done well is also watered by tears from a humble heart. Hence it is said again: “I shall offer you burnt offerings of marrow” (Ps. 65:15). Whoever performs a good work but does not know how to weep out of love and desire for almighty God possesses a burnt offering, but does not possess marrow in the burnt offering. Whoever performs good works, longs for the vision of his Creator, hastens to attain the joys of eternal contemplation, and, through the love by which he is inflamed, immolates himself in tears, offers burnt offerings with marrow to the Lord. We must therefore strive both to abandon evil completely, to perform the good we are able to perform, and, in the very good works we do, to be moved to compunction by love of God [Text: “of eternal light”].

(Moral. Book XV, chapter 29; Book VI, chapter 30.) We must know that all the reprobate, because they sinned with both soul and body, receive retribution in hell in both soul and body, since they were wretched both in thought and in action. For the Psalmist says: “You shall place them like a furnace of fire at the time of your face; the Lord in his anger will trouble them, and fire will devour them” (Ps. 20:10). What is devoured by fire is ignited from the outside, whereas a furnace is inflamed from within. At the time of the Lord’s face, therefore, all the unjust are placed like a furnace [Text: “and a furnace”] and are devoured by fire: for when the Judge appears, their multitude is driven away from his sight, their conscience burns inwardly with pain [Text: “desire”], and Gehenna torments their flesh outwardly.

(Moral. Book XX, chapter 31; Book XXVI, chapter 19; Book XX, chapter 31; Book XXVI, chapter 10.) By a profound plan, almighty God is accustomed to delay the voices of those who ask when his saints are oppressed by the blows [Text: “persecutions”] of their adversaries and cry out with continual pleas to be delivered, so that the merits of those who endure may increase. Hence the Psalmist says: “My God, I shall cry out by day, and you will not hear; and by night” (Ps. 21:3). He immediately adds the benefit that comes from the delay in being heard: “And not to my folly.” It is as though he said: “It does not advance my folly in any way that you do not immediately hear me when I cry out day and night, because, in seeming to abandon me in temporal tribulation, you educate me more deeply in eternal wisdom.”

For the wisdom of the saints is increased by the fact that they receive what they ask for only after delay: desire grows from postponement, understanding increases from desire, and when understanding is intensified, a more ardent affection for God is revealed. Affection becomes all the more capable of attaining heavenly things the more long-suffering it has become through waiting. Hence it is also said: “A helper in tribulations, in times of distress” (Ps. 9:10). Since he was about to speak of tribulation, he first mentioned “times,” because we are often crushed by tribulation, yet the appropriate time has not arrived for us to be helped toward the desire for deliverance. Therefore, let no one who is heard only after delay believe that he is neglected by heavenly care.

(Moral. Book III, chapter 18; Book II, Homily 8 on Ezekiel, no. 6; Moral. Book XXXV, chapter 14, no. 26.) “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21:16). A potsherd is the flesh of our Redeemer, taken from the clay of our substance. Because a potsherd is hardened by fire, the strength of his humanity dried up like a potsherd, since it grew toward the strength of incorruption through the fire of his Passion; and the fire of the tribulation of his Passion strengthened the flesh he had assumed for the glory of the resurrection.

“All who descend into the earth shall fall down before him” (Ps. 21:30). The dead descend into the earth not in spirit but in body. Those who descend into the earth therefore fall down before the Lord, because those who rot in the dust come to judgment by rising again.

“You have anointed my head with oil” (Ps. 22:5), because our ruling faculty is the mind, and the mind is called the head. It is as though he were saying plainly: “You have watered my mind, parched by its thoughts, with the anointing of charity.”

(Moral. Book VII, chapter 29.) “He who has not received his soul in vain” (Ps. 23:4). A person receives his soul in vain when, neglecting its life, he places the care of the flesh first; when he thinks only about present things and does not attend to what follows forever. But the righteous do not receive their souls in vain, because through continual purpose they refer whatever they do bodily to its benefit, so that, although the work passes away, the purpose of the work does not pass away—the purpose that prepares the rewards of life after this life.

(Moral. Book XX, chapter 14, no. 28.) Natural necessities are often extremely dangerous in this respect: it is frequently not discerned what is done concerning them through a concern for usefulness and what is done through the vice of pleasure. For when an opportunity for seduction has been found, while we render what is owed to necessity, we serve the vice of pleasure; and our excuse disguises itself before the eyes of discernment under the cloak of weakness and hides itself, as though under the protection of fulfilling a necessity. The person who wished to escape these necessities said: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. 24:17). He knew that the fault of pleasures often erupts from the occasion of necessities; and, so that he might not knowingly admit anything unlawful, he sought to have uprooted the very thing that, unwillingly, he endured from the root.

[Col. 1025A] Holy men are therefore concerned in everything they do lest the weakness of their nature demand from them more than is due, lest the vice of pleasure grow within them under the cover of necessity.

## Part Three, Containing an Exposition of the New Testament

[Col. 1025]

## Book One: Testimonies on the Gospel according to Matthew

### Chapter One [Note: [Col. 1025D] This chapter is omitted in the Michaeline edition.]

“And after the deportation to Babylon” (Matt. 1:12).

[Col. 1025A]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVIII, chapter 8, no. 19.) By divine grace it is now clear to all whom sacred Scripture calls the cornerstone: namely, the one who, receiving into himself on one side the Jewish people and on the other the Gentile people, joins the two walls in the single structure of the Church; and the one concerning whom it is written: “He has made both one” (Eph. 2:14).

He displayed himself as the cornerstone not only among those below but also among those above, because on earth he joined the nations of the Gentiles to the people of Israel, and in heaven he joined both together to the angels. For when he was born, the angels proclaimed on earth: “Peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). At the birth of a king, they would scarcely have offered the joys of peace to human beings as something great if there had been no discord between them.

Concerning this stone the Prophet says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117:22). King Jeconiah represented this stone. When Matthew described the generations in groups of fourteen, he counted Jeconiah twice: he placed the same person at the end of the second group and again at the beginning of the third generation. He was the one who was deported to Babylon with the people of Israel. Since he was led from one place to another, he is not improperly counted twice as representing the side of each wall; by the turning of his deportation he signifies the cornerstone. For where a straight line bends so as to proceed in another direction, it makes something like an angle. Thus he could rightly be counted twice, because through both walls he displayed, as it were, the two sides joined in himself.

Hence he rightly represented the one who, born in Judea and gathering the Gentiles, came, as it were, from Jerusalem to Babylon and, in himself, wove together by the art of charity the structure of faith that had previously been torn apart by the zeal for discord.

### Chapter II.—“What has been born in her” (Matt. 1:20)

(In the exposition of Job, Book XXIX, chapter 19, no. 36.) “Human beings,” he says, “then begin to exist when they are born in the wombs of their mothers,” for conception itself is also called birth, in accordance with what is written: “What has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 1025D] In the Michaeline edition, *in quid*, perhaps meaning “in something” or “to some extent.” Unless perhaps *d* has intruded in place of *t*. It is certain that manuscripts often have *t* for *d*, as in *Davit* for *David*, but not conversely, *d* for *t*.]

### Chapter III.—“Now the axe is laid at the root” (Matt. 3:10)

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part Three, Admonition 22.) The greedy sometimes say: “We use what has been granted; we do not seek what belongs to others. Even if we do nothing deserving a return of mercy, nevertheless we commit no crime.” They think this because they close the ear of their heart to the heavenly words. For the rich man in the Gospel, who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day, did not seize what belonged to others; rather, he is said to have used his own possessions fruitlessly. Yet avenging Gehenna received him after this life, not because he had done anything unlawful, but because, through immoderate use, he had surrendered himself entirely to lawful things.

Hence John cries out, saying: “Now the axe is laid at the root of the tree; every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). Therefore, those who consider themselves innocent because they do not seize what belongs to others should foresee the blow of the axe drawing near and abandon the torpor of careless security, lest, while they neglect to bear the fruit of good works, they be utterly cut off from the present life, as a tree is cut off from its roots and greenery.

### Chapter IV.—“In whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17)

[Col. 1026B]

(On Ezekiel, Homily 8.) What does it mean that the Father speaks of the Son, saying: “In whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17)? Everyone who corrects through repentance something he has done indicates, by the very fact that he repents, that he was displeasing to himself, since he amends what he did. And because almighty God spoke about sinners in a human manner, insofar as human beings could understand, saying: “It repents me that I made man upon the earth” (Gen. 6:7), he was, as it were, displeased with himself in the sinners whom he had created.

But in his only-begotten Son, our God and Lord Jesus Christ, he alone was well pleased, because he did not repent of having created him as a human being among human beings, in whom he found no sin whatsoever. As the Psalmist says of him: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Ps. 109:4). In our Redeemer alone, therefore, the Father is well pleased, because in him alone he found no fault for which he might reproach himself, as though through repentance.

### Chapter V.—“Jesus was led into the desert” (Matt. 4:1)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXIV, no. 27.) Conversion produces security, but security is usually the mother of negligence. Therefore, lest security give birth to negligence, it is written: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir. 2:1 [Vulgate 2:5]). He does not say “for rest,” but “for temptation,” because our enemy, while we remain in this life, strives all the more vigorously to conquer us the more he sees us rebelling against him. He neglects to strike those whom he feels he possesses by an undisturbed right; but he is stirred against us more vehemently when he is expelled from our heart as though from the right of his own dwelling.

The Lord represented this in himself under a certain dispensation: he permitted the devil to tempt him only after his baptism, so that he might indicate a kind of sign of the future way of life—that his members, after they had advanced toward God, would then endure more violent snares of temptation.

### Chapter VI.—“Opening his mouth” (Matt. 5:2)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book IV, chapter 1, no. 1.) Sacred Scripture indicates that what it adds after introducing it only briefly should be awaited with reverence. Just as we do not know what closed vessels contain within them, but, when the mouths of vessels are opened, we recognize what they hold inside, so the hidden things in the hearts of holy people are disclosed when their mouths are opened. When they reveal their thoughts, they are said to open their mouths, so that with attentive minds we may hasten to recognize what they contain within, as though their vessels had been opened, and may refresh ourselves with their inner fragrance.

Hence, when the Lord was about to speak sublime commands on the mountain, it is first said: “Opening his mouth, he said” (Matt. 5:2). Yet this may also be understood in another way: at that time he opened his mouth in the commandments in which he had earlier opened the mouths of the prophets.

### Chapter VII.—“Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXVI, no. 49.) Sacred Scripture commonly uses the word “poor” to mean humble. Hence, in the Gospel they are named with the addition of “in spirit,” when it says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). For since riches visibly display the powerful, those who are not exalted in their own consciences are poor in themselves.

## CHAPTER VIII — Nor do they light a lamp (Matt. 5:15)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXX, no. 77.) The Lord says in the Gospel: “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand” (Matt. 5:15). By the “bushel,” temporal advantage is understood; by the “lamp,” the light of preaching. To put a lamp under a bushel, therefore, is to hide the grace of preaching for the sake of temporal advantage—a thing [Col. 1027B] none of the elect does. And there it is rightly added: “But on a lampstand.” The condition of the body is signified by the lampstand. The lamp is placed upon it when the care of preaching is set before that same body.

## CHAPTER IX — Let your good works be seen (Matt. 5:16)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book VIII, nos. 83–84.) The Truth says: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). But it is one thing when, in displaying one’s work, the glory of the giver is sought, and another when one privately desires praise for the gift bestowed. Hence, again, the same Truth says in the Gospel: “Take care that you do not perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them” (ibid. 6:1).

When our work is displayed before people, we must first weigh, by an examination of the heart, what is being sought through that display. If we seek the glory of the giver, we keep even our public works hidden in his sight. But if through these works we desire our own praise, [Col. 1027C] they have already been poured out beyond his sight, even if many people remain unaware of them. Yet it belongs greatly to the perfect to seek the glory of the author through a work that has been displayed, while not knowing how to rejoice with private exultation over the praise received. A praiseworthy work is displayed innocently before people only when the praise bestowed is truly trampled underfoot through contempt of self; since the weak cannot overcome it by despising it, they must necessarily conceal the good they do.

Often they seek their own praise from the very beginning of displaying the work; often they wish to reveal the author’s glory through the display of their work, but, caught up in the favor they receive, they are swept away by desire for their own praise. And when they neglect to judge themselves inwardly, scattered outwardly, they do not know what they are doing; their work serves their own pride, while they think they are offering it as a service to the giver.

## CHAPTER X — Likewise as above (Matt. 5:16)

(From the *Pastoral Rule*, admonition 36.) Whoever is already able to trample down the desire for praise [Col. 1027D] commits a fraud against edification if he hides the good he does; and, like one who has sown seed, he removes the roots by which it might germinate if he does not display the work that ought to be imitated. Hence the Truth says in the Gospel: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

There is also that saying which seems to command something very different: “Take care that you do not perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6:2). What, then, does it mean that our work must both be done so that it will not be seen and yet is commanded to be seen, except that what we do must be hidden so that we do not seek human glory, and manifested so that we may increase the praise of our heavenly Father? For when the Lord forbids us to perform our righteousness before people, he immediately adds: “So that you may not be seen by them.” And when he again commands that good works be seen by people, he promptly adds: “So that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

Thus he showed, by the conclusion of the sayings, how they should be seen and how they should not be seen: the mind of the one who acts should neither seek to have its work seen for its own sake, nor hide it when it serves the glory of the heavenly Father. Hence it often happens that a good work is hidden when it is done publicly, and again is public when it is done secretly. Whoever seeks not his own glory but that of the heavenly Father in a public good work hides what he has done, because he had as his sole witness the one whom he strove to please. But whoever desires to be discovered and praised in his secret good work—even if perhaps no one saw what he performed—nevertheless did it before people, because he brought with him as many witnesses to his good work as the human praises he sought in his heart.

## CHAPTER XI — Do not think that I came to abolish the Law (Matt. 5:17)

(In the second part of the *Exposition on Ezekiel*, homily 4.) The lesser commandments were given to the Israelite people through the Law. Hence [Col. 1028B] Moses also spoke to that people on the plain. The Lord gave higher things to the holy apostles, and therefore taught them the commandments of life on the mountain.

When our Redeemer says through the Gospel, “Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the prophets; I did not come to abolish but to fulfill” (Matt. 5:17), he came to fulfill the Law, adding grace to the Law’s righteousness. What the Law commanded in lesser matters, he himself helped to perfect in higher ones; and what it restrained from outward action, he cut away from the heart.

## CHAPTER XII — Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment (Matt. 5:22)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXI, no. 9.) The Lord considers each person’s ways as he counts his steps, so that not even the smallest thoughts or the slightest words—which have become cheap through ordinary use among us—remain unexamined by his judgment. Hence he says: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council. Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:22).

[Col. 1028C] For *raca* in Hebrew speech is an interjection, which indeed reveals the mind of the angry person, but does not yet express a complete word of anger. First, therefore, anger without speech is reproved; afterward, anger with speech, but not yet formed into a complete word; finally, when he says “Fool,” anger is condemned when, with an excess of sound, it is completed even by the fullness of speech.

It should also be noted that he declares the angry person liable to judgment; the utterance of anger, which is “raca,” liable to the council; and the word of the utterance, which is “Fool,” liable to Gehenna. For as the degrees of guilt increase, so does the order of the sentence: in judgment the case is still investigated; in the council the verdict of the case is already determined; and in the fire of Gehenna the sentence proceeding from the council is carried out.

## CHAPTER XIII — You have heard that it was said to the ancients, “You shall not kill” (Matt. 5:27)

(In the second book of the *Exposition on Ezekiel*, homily 3.) The outer threshold rightly signifies the fathers of the Old Testament, because through their preaching perverse actions were punished; through the sayings of the fathers of the New Testament, however, each person’s mind is restrained even from unlawful thoughts, since complete guilt is shown to lie even in the heart’s deliberation.

They took care to prohibit their hearers’ souls from crimes, cruelties, and acts of plunder. But these men, since they cut away not only perverse deeds but also unlawful thoughts, have become for us something like an inner threshold. Hence the Truth itself says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill’; but whoever kills will be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5:27).

## CHAPTER XIV — If you offer your gift at the altar (Matt. 5:23)

(In the first part of the *Exposition on Ezekiel*, homily 8.) That nothing without concord pleases God, the Truth itself demonstrates when it says: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that [Col. 1029A] your brother has sinned against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23).

Behold: he does not wish to receive a sacrifice from those who are at odds; he refuses to accept a burnt offering from them. From this, then, consider how great the evil of discord is, on account of which that very thing by which guilt is loosened is rejected.

[Note: [Col. 1029D] In the Michaelinus manuscript, this chapter is placed after the following one.]

## CHAPTER XV — Likewise as above

(From the third part of the *Pastoral Rule*, admonition 23.) Those who are at odds offer no sacrifice of good work to God so long as they are in disagreement with love of their neighbors. For it is written: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5:23).

From this command, clearly, we must consider whose offering is rejected, since it shows the guilt to be intolerable. For when all evils are washed away by the good deeds that follow, let us consider how great are the evils of discord, which, unless they have been utterly extinguished, do not allow a good work to follow.

## CHAPTER XVI — “You shall not commit adultery”; but I say to you (Matt. 5:27)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXI, chapter 2.) Our Redeemer, coming, transcended the commandments of the Law and abolished among his elect not only the lust of the flesh but also that of the heart, saying: “It is written, ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:27).

Through Moses, lust perpetrated was condemned; by the author of purity, lust conceived was condemned. Hence the first shepherd of the Church says to the disciples: “Therefore, girding up the loins of your mind, being perfectly sober, hope in the grace that is offered to you” (1 Pet. 1:13). To gird the loins of the flesh is to restrain lust from one’s affection; to gird the loins of the mind is to restrain it even from one’s thoughts.

Hence [Col. 1029C] the angel who speaks to John is said to be girded with a golden belt above his breasts (Rev. 1:13). Since the purity of the New Testament also restrains lust of the heart, the angel who appeared in it came girded at the chest; and the golden belt rightly binds him, because whoever is a citizen of the heavenly homeland abandons impurity not now through fear of punishment but through love of charity.

## CHAPTER XVII — Love your enemies (Matt. 5:44)

(Homily 35 on the Gospels, no. 3.) The Truth says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5:44). To endure adversaries is a virtue before people; but before God it is a virtue to love them, because God accepts only that sacrifice which kindles the flame of charity before his eyes on the altar of good work.

## CHAPTER XVIII — Take care that you do not perform your righteousness before people (Matt. 6:1)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XIX, no. 36.) [Col. 1029D] It belongs to holy men to conceal the good things they have done, lest they happen to fall into the pit of pride. Hence the Truth itself says: “Take care that you do not perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6:1).

For this reason, when he gave sight to two blind men sitting beside the road, he commanded them, saying: “See that no one knows” (Matt. 9:30). Immediately afterward it is written that, when they went away, they spread his fame throughout that whole region.

But we must ask what this means: the almighty one, for whom willing and being able are the same, wished his miracles to be kept silent, and yet those who had been enlightened proclaimed them almost against his will. The explanation is that he gave his servants who follow him an example: they should indeed desire to conceal their own virtues, yet, so that others may advance through their example, they should be revealed against their will. By concealing their deeds, they should guard themselves; but when they are revealed against their will, [Col. 1030A] they should transmit good examples to their neighbors.

Let them therefore be concealed deliberately and made public by necessity; let their concealment be their own protection, and their publication another’s benefit. Again, because it is written: “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house. Thus let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works” (Matt. 5:15–16), and so forth, holy men are sometimes compelled to do good before people or to relate to people the deeds they have done.

But they relate their deeds to that end: not that they themselves should be glorified for those works, but that their Father who is in heaven should be glorified. For while they preach holy things, their very preaching may perhaps be despised when their way of life is not known. They are therefore compelled to speak of their life so that they may be able to change the lives of their hearers; and they recount their deeds so that they may be held in veneration. They seek to be venerated so that they may be heard with reverence.

## CHAPTER XIX — Likewise as above

(In the *Pastoral Rule*, admonition 22.) [Col. 1030B] Whenever we provide necessities to the needy, we are returning what is theirs to them, not giving them what is ours; we are paying a debt of justice rather than fulfilling an act of mercy. Hence the Truth itself, speaking cautiously about the exercise of mercy, says: “Take care that you do not perform your righteousness before people” (Matt. 6:1).

The psalmist, echoing this saying, also says: “He distributed and gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever” (Ps. 111:9). For although he had first mentioned the generosity bestowed on the poor, he preferred to call it not mercy but righteousness, because what is given by the common Lord is surely justly used in common by all who receive it. Hence Solomon also says: “The righteous person gives and does not cease” (Prov. 21:26).

## CHAPTER XX — Truly I say to you, they have received their reward (Matt. 6:2)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book IV, no. 18.) Those who present themselves in good action for the sake of human praise hope in vain for [Col. 1030C] the reward of good works when the Judge comes, because, since they do these things for display, they have already received the reward of praise from human lips, as the Truth attests when it says: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2).

## CHAPTER XXI — Likewise as above

(*Pastoral Rule*, admonition 36.) Those who think human approval sufficient as the reward for their good deeds judge their good things to be worthless. When passing praise is sought for a righteous work, something worthy of eternal recompense is sold for a paltry price. Concerning this price that has been received, the Truth says: “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:1).

## CHAPTER XXII — Enter your room (Matt. 6:6)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXII, no. 43.) In the Gospel the Lord says: “Enter your room, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6:6).

He prays with the door shut in his room who, with silent mouth, pours out the affection of his mind in the sight of heavenly mercy. [Col. 1030D] A voice is heard in secret when one silently cries out through holy desires. Hence the psalmist rightly says: “The Lord heard the desire of the poor; your ear heard the desire of their heart” (Ps. 9:17).

## CHAPTER XXIII — Your will be done (Matt. 6:10)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXVII, no. 65.) By “the heavens,” the angelic spirits who were created in heavenly places can be signified. Hence, in our prayer, we are instructed to say aloud: “Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matt. 6:10). In this way, just as God’s will is carried out by the higher creature, so may it also be observed in all things by human weakness.

## CHAPTER XXIV — Our daily bread (Matt. 6:11)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXIV, no. 13.) [Col. 1031A] In the Lord’s Prayer we say: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. 6:11). Behold, we call it “ours,” and yet we pray that it may be given. It becomes ours when it is received; yet it is God’s, because it is given by him. It is therefore God’s by gift, and becomes ours by reception.

## CHAPTER XXV — Forgive us our debts (Matt. 6:12)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book X, no. 30.) Any guilt pollutes the life of the soul, but resentment preserved against one’s neighbor kills it; it is fixed in the mind like a sword, and with its point pierces the hidden parts of the inward being. If it is not first drawn out from the transfixed heart, no benefit of divine assistance is obtained in prayer, because medicines of healing cannot be applied to wounded limbs unless the iron is first removed from the wound.

Hence the Truth itself says: “Unless you forgive people, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your sins” (Matt. 6:15). Hence he admonishes us, saying: “When you stand to pray, [Col. 1031B] forgive if you have anything against another” (Matt. 11:25). Again he says: “Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:38). Hence, in establishing the condition of the petition, he placed the condition of compassion, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). Thus the good we ask of God with contrite hearts, we should first practice in our dealings with our neighbor.

## CHAPTER XXVI — If your eye is simple (Matt. 6:22)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book X, no. 41.) That the name “eyes” expresses the power of intention, the Truth attests through the Gospel when it says: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6:22). For if a pure intention precedes our activity, then, however it may appear to people, the body of the action that follows is shown to be pure in the eyes of the inward Judge.

## CHAPTER XXVII — Likewise as above

[Col. 1031C] (Homily 7 on Ezekiel, no. 2.) Whatever is done must therefore be weighed at the root of its intention, according to the merit it will have in the judgment of the Creator. Hence the same Creator says: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6:22). He calls the intention the “eye,” and the action the “body,” because if our intention is simple before God, our action will not be dark in his judgment.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — Seek first the kingdom of God (Matt. 6:33)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XV, no. 53.) When God is not sought in prayer, the mind soon grows weary in prayer, because when someone asks for things that God perhaps refuses to grant according to his hidden judgment, he also grows displeased with the one who does not wish to give what is loved.

But the Lord wishes himself to be loved more than the things he created, and eternal things to be requested rather than earthly things, as it is written: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). For he did not say “they will be given,” but “they will be added,” clearly indicating that one thing is given as primary and another is added in addition.

Since eternity ought to be our goal in intention, while temporal things ought to serve our use, the former is given and the latter is surely added in abundance. Yet people often ask for temporal goods without seeking eternal rewards: they ask for what is added, but do not desire the place where it is added. They do not count it as gain in their petition if they are poor in temporal things here but live forever rich in blessedness there. Attentive only to visible things, as has been said, they refuse through the labor of prayer to purchase invisible things. If they sought heavenly things, they would already be laboring with profit.

For when the mind, inflamed by divine desires, longs in prayer for the vision of its helper, it is joined to what is above and separated from what is below. Through the fervor of its love it opens itself in order to receive, and by receiving it is inflamed. To love what is above is already to ascend; and while it eagerly desires heavenly things, in a wondrous way it tastes precisely what it seeks to receive.

## CHAPTER XXIX — Do not be anxious about tomorrow (Matt. 6:34)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book IX, no. 105.) Often the mind girds itself for the way of righteousness and shakes off its sluggishness. It is carried away by such desire for heavenly things that almost nothing lower seems to remain in it. Yet when it is brought back to the care of the flesh—without which the journey of the present life cannot be completed in any way—it is held down below as though it had never touched the heights.

When it hears the words of the heavenly oracle, it is raised into love of the heavenly homeland; but when the concern of the present life rises again, it is buried beneath the mound of earthly care. The seed of heavenly hope makes no progress in the soil of the heart, because the thorn of lowly thought grows dense. The Truth itself uproots this thorn with the hand of holy exhortation when it says: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. 6:34). Paul also says against it: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14).

From the words of both guide and soldier, however, we understand that the mind is pierced by a deadly wound from this care when a proper measure is not maintained (no. 106). For those still living in mortal flesh cannot have the care of the flesh cut away entirely; rather, it must be moderated so that it serves the mind with discernment.

Since the Truth forbids us to be anxious about tomorrow, it does not altogether forbid us to have some care for present necessities; it forbids that care from being extended to the time that follows. And when Paul does not allow care of the flesh to be made into desire, he plainly permits it in necessity. The care of the flesh must therefore be restrained by the discretion of great moderation, so that it serves and does not rule.

It must not conquer the mind as a mistress, but, subdued under the rule of the mind, serve like a handmaid: present when commanded, and at the heart’s signal springing away when dismissed; scarcely appearing behind holy thought, and never standing opposed to the face of one who thinks rightly.

[Col. 1032C] ## CHAPTER XXX — Why do you see the splinter? (Matt. 7:3)

[Col. 1032C]

(*Pastoral Rule*, admonition 10.) The Truth says to some who are patient but not loving: “Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam in your own eye?” (Matt. 7:3). The disturbance of impatience is the splinter; malice in the heart is the beam in the eye. The former is shaken by the breeze of temptation, whereas the latter is borne almost immovably by consummate wickedness.

The saying that follows is rightly added: “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye, and then you will see to remove the splinter from your brother’s eye” (ibid. 7:5). It is as though he were saying to the wicked mind that suffers inwardly but displays itself outwardly as holy through patience: “First shake off from yourself the mass of malice, and then condemn others for the lightness of their impatience, lest, while you do not strive to overcome your pretense, it be worse for you to tolerate another’s wrongdoing.”

[Col. 1032D] ## CHAPTER XXXI — Whatever good things you want people to do for you (Matt. 7:12)

[Col. 1032D]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book VI, no. 54.) Another human being is, as it were, the image of a human being. Our neighbor is rightly called our image, because in him we see what we ourselves are. In bodily visitation we approach our neighbor by the movement of our feet; spiritually, we are led not by steps but by affection.

Whoever advances toward one whom he sees to be like himself by nature, on the paths of love, visits his own image, so that, considering himself in the other, he may gather from himself how he ought to condescend to the other in his weakness. He visits his own image who considers himself in another in order to refresh that other through himself.

Hence the Truth, when through Moses it described things that had happened, signified things that were to be done, saying: “The earth brought forth green vegetation and plants producing seed according to their kind, and trees bearing fruit, each having its seed according to its kind” (Gen. 1:12). A tree produces seed according to its kind [Col. 1033A] when our mind gathers from itself a consideration of another and gives birth to the germ of a right action.

Hence a certain wise man says: “What you do not want to happen to you, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16). Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whatever good things you want people to do for you, do the same for them” (Matt. 7:12). It is as though he were saying openly: “Visit your own image in another, and recognize from yourselves what you ought to offer to others.”

## CHAPTER XXXII — What you hate to have done to you by another, see that you never do to another (Tob. 7:12)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book X, no. 8.) Love of God is distinguished in three ways, because the Creator is commanded to be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength. Here it should be noted that, when the divine word commands love, it not only states from what it must be loved but also indicates how completely, when it adds “with the whole.” Thus whoever desires to please God perfectly must leave nothing of himself to himself.

Love of neighbor is derived into two commandments: through a certain righteous man it is said, “What you hate to have done to you by another, see that you never do to another” (Tob. 4:16); and through the Truth itself it is said, “Whatever you want people to do for you, do the same for them” (Matt. 7:12).

By these two commandments of both Testaments, malice is restrained by the one, and kindness is offered by the other: a person ceases from harmful action by not doing the evil he does not wish to suffer; and, by supplying the good he desires to have done to himself, he exercises himself in kindness for his neighbor’s benefit.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — Enter through the narrow gate (Matt. 7:13)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXXII, no. 17.) The word *platea*, “broad street,” takes its name, according to Greek usage, from breadth. But what is narrower for the human mind than to break its own wills? Concerning this breaking, the Truth says: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. 7:13). And what is broader than to resist none of one’s own desires, and to spread oneself without restraint in whatever direction the impulse of one’s will leads?

## CHAPTER XXXIV — Likewise as above
