(In Homily 5 on Ezekiel, nos. 12–13.) It is written concerning charity: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118:96). Again the psalmist says of it: “You set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. 30:9).

But as I speak, the question comes to mind: How is charity broad, if through charity one reaches God, while the Truth itself says, “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. 7:13)? What, then, is broader? Again I hear the psalmist saying: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept to difficult ways” (Ps. 16:4). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

How, then, is charity broad if the gate is narrow? How is the yoke easy and the burden light if the ways kept in God’s commandments are difficult? Charity itself quickly resolves this question for you. The way of God is narrow for beginners, yet God’s burden is light once we have begun to bear it, so that, for love of him, persecution becomes pleasing and every affliction endured for him comes with sweetness to the mind. Thus the holy apostles also rejoiced when they endured blows for the Lord.

The narrow gate itself therefore becomes broad for those who love; the difficult ways themselves become spiritually soft and level for those who run along them. For when the mind knows that it will receive eternal joys in exchange for temporal pains, it begins to love even that by which it is afflicted.

## CHAPTER XXXV — You will know them by their fruits (Matt. 7:20)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XV, no. 66.) A person’s spirit is unknown to another when it is not demonstrated by words or deeds. But since it is written, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:20), whatever lies hidden within is revealed by what is done outwardly. Hence Solomon rightly says: “As faces are reflected in water for those who look, so the hearts of people are manifest to the prudent” (Prov. 27:19).

## CHAPTER XXXVI — Many will say, “Lord, Lord” (Matt. 7:22)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book VIII, no. 66.) Often the wicked perform astonishing works of signs, drive spirits out of possessed bodies, and, through the gift of prophecy, anticipate future events by knowing them beforehand. Yet they are divided from the giver of so many gifts by the intention of their thought, because through his gifts they seek not his glory but their own approval.

When they exalt themselves in their own praise through the good things they have received, they fight against the giver with those very gifts. They grow proud against the one who gives precisely where his apostles ought to have been humble. But afterward a stricter sentence strikes them because the heavenly goodness now pours itself more generously even upon the ungrateful. The greatness of the gift becomes an increase of condemnation, because, watered, they bear no fruit but grow tall and empty beneath the appearance of greenness.

The Truth rightly portrays them in the Gospel, saying: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you workers of iniquity’” (Matt. 7:22).

## CHAPTER XXXVII — Likewise as above

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XX, no. 17.) Sometimes heretics also perform signs and miracles, but they receive the rewards of their affliction and abstinence here—namely, the praises they seek. Hence the voice of the Redeemer says: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, workers of iniquity’” (Matt. 7:22).

What else is conveyed by this sentence except that in human beings [Col. 1034C] the humility of charity should be honored, but signs of power should not be revered? Hence the holy Church now despises even whatever miracles may be performed by heretics, because it recognizes that these are not the appearance of holiness.

The proof of holiness is not to perform signs, but to love each person as oneself; to think truly of God and more highly of one’s neighbor than of oneself. Since true virtue consists in love, not in the display of miracles, the Truth demonstrates this when it says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

He did not say, “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you perform signs,” but said, “If you have love for one another.” He plainly indicates that the true servants of God are proved not by miracles but by God’s love alone. The gift of brotherly love is therefore the testimony of heavenly discipleship.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — Likewise as above

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXXIII, no. 13.) Some abandon the world, leave behind the empty things that pass away, and, seeking the depths of humility, transcend the ways of human society by living well. They advance so far in the skill of their endeavors that they already perform mighty works of signs; [Col. 1034D] but because they neglect to guard themselves by observing themselves, struck by the weapon of empty glory, they fall from a greater height into a worse ruin.

Hence the eternal one who examines the secrets of the heart, foretelling the fall of their ruin, threatens them when he says: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who practice iniquity; I do not know who you are’” (Matt. 7:22–23).

## CHAPTER XXXIX — I do not know where you come from (Matt. 7:22)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXIII, no. 1.) For God’s not knowing is his rejection, just as at the end he will say to some: “I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:22).

## CHAPTER XL — For he was teaching them as one who had authority (Matt. 7:29)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXIII, no. 24.) It is written of the Lord: “For he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. 7:29). Uniquely and preeminently, he alone spoke good things from his own authority, because he committed no evil through weakness. From the power of his divinity he possessed what he supplied to us through the innocence of his humanity.

## CHAPTER XLI — Foxes have dens (Matt. 8:20)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XIX, no. 2.) By “birds,” the powers of the air that oppose the endeavors of the good can sometimes be signified. Hence the Truth says: “The seed fell beside the road; the birds came and ate it” (Matt. 13:4), because, [Col. 1035B] when evil spirits occupy human minds and inject harmful thoughts, they tear the word of life from the memory.

Again, to a certain proud and wise man it is said: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:20). Foxes are exceedingly deceitful animals that hide in ditches or caves. When they appear, they never run along straight paths but through winding twists; birds, as we know, raise themselves into the air on high flight.

By the name “foxes,” therefore, deceitful and fraudulent demons are signified; by the name “birds,” these same proud demons. It is as though he were saying: “Deceitful and arrogant demons find their dwelling in your heart—that is, in the thought of pride—but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head; that is, my humility finds no rest in your proud mind.”

## CHAPTER XLII — Let the dead bury their dead (Matt. 8:22)

[Col. 1035C]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book IV, no. 52.) Our Redeemer raises the girl in the house, the young man outside the gate, and Lazarus in the tomb. For the one who lies hidden in sin is still dead in the house; the one whose iniquity is exposed even to the shame of public perpetration is already being carried, as it were, outside the gate. But the one who is burdened even by the force of habit in the perpetration of wickedness is crushed beneath the mound of the tomb. Yet in his mercy he calls these back to life, because divine grace often illumines with the light of its visitation not only those dead in hidden iniquities, but also those dead in open sins and pressed down by the weight of evil habit.

But the fourth dead man our Redeemer recognizes when a disciple announces him, and nevertheless does not raise him, because it is exceedingly difficult for one whom, after the practice of evil habit, even the tongues of flatterers attend to be recalled from the death of his mind. Concerning him it is said in the same place: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke 9:60). [Col. 1035D] The dead bury their dead when sinners overwhelm sinners with their flatteries. For what else is sinning than falling dead? But those who pursue the sinner with praises conceal the dead man beneath the mound of their words.

Lazarus, too, was dead, but he was not buried by the dead. Faithful women had buried him, and they were announcing his death to the one who gives life. Therefore he immediately returns to the light, because when the soul dies in sin, it is restored to life more quickly if vigilant thoughts are alive above it.

### CHAPTER XLIII — “What have we to do with you, Son of God?” (Matthew 8:29)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book II, no. 43.) The ancient enemy recognized that the Redeemer of the human race had come into the world as his conqueror; therefore, through the possessed man, he says in the Gospel: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matthew 8:29). [Col. 1036A] Yet when he first saw him subject to suffering, when he perceived that his humanity was capable of enduring mortal things, everything he had suspected concerning his divinity came into doubt for him through the arrogance of his pride. For, knowing nothing except pride, when he saw him humble, he doubted that he was God. Hence he turned to the arguments of temptation, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew 4:3). Because he saw him subject to suffering, he believed that one who was not God had been born, but that he had been preserved by grace.

### CHAPTER XLIV — “If you cast us out, send us” (Matthew 8:31)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book II, no. 16.) When Satan desires to tempt a holy man, yet says to God that he must extend his hand, it is very much to be noted that he does not even attribute to himself the power to strike, although he singularly exalts himself against the author of all things. For he knows that he is not sufficient to do anything of himself, since he does not even exist of himself inasmuch as he is a spirit. [Col. 1036B] Hence, when the legion was being expelled from the man, it said in the Gospel: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine” (Matthew 8:31). If he could not go into the swine by his own power, is it any wonder that without the Creator’s hand he could not touch the house of the holy man?

### CHAPTER XLV — “Go to your house” (Matthew 9:6)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VIII, no. 34.) A house is also customarily understood as the dwelling-place of the heart. Hence it is said to a certain man who had been healed: “Go to your house” (Matthew 9:6). For it is fitting that, after receiving forgiveness, the sinner should return to his own mind, lest he again commit something for which he would justly be struck.

### CHAPTER XLVI — “Rise, take up your bed” (Matthew 9:6)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXIII, no. 46.) What else does the Lord say in the Gospel to a certain man who had been healed—“Rise, take up your pallet and walk to your house” (Mark 9:11; John 5:8)—than that [Col. 1036C] bodily pleasure is signified by the pallet? He is commanded, of course, now healthy to carry the pallet on which he had lain sick, because everyone who is still delighted by vices lies sick in the pleasures of the flesh. But, now healed, he carries the pallet on which he had lain sick, because, raised up by divine assistance, he afterward endures the humiliations inflicted by the same flesh whose desires had formerly been his repose.

### CHAPTER XLVII — “New wine in new wineskins” (Matthew 9:17)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXIII, no. 20.) In new wine the fervor of the Holy Spirit is understood. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “They put new wine into new wineskins” (Matthew 9:17). When the apostles were suddenly filled with it and spoke in every language, the Jews—who did not understand, yet nevertheless bore true witness—said: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2:4).

### CHAPTER XLVIII — “When the crowd had been put out” (Matthew 9:15)

[Col. 1036D] (In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XVIII, no. 68.) The hearts of those who love earthly life are battered by the restlessness of their desires; they are pressed down into the depths by crowds of carnal thoughts, so that they are not lifted toward the desire for inward peace. Therefore, when truth comes to the heart through the wondrous work of mercy, it first drives out from it the heat of carnal thoughts and afterward arranges within it the gifts of the virtues.

The sacred history of the Gospel aptly teaches this to us. When the Lord, invited to raise the ruler’s daughter, was being led there, it immediately adds: “When the crowd had been put out, he entered, took her by the hand, and the girl arose” (Matthew 9:25). The crowd is therefore driven outside so that the girl may be raised, because unless the intrusive multitude of worldly cares is first expelled from the heart’s innermost recesses, the soul that lies dead within does not rise again. For while it disperses itself through countless thoughts of earthly desires, it in no way gathers itself together for consideration of itself.

### CHAPTER XLIX — “Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10:16)

[Col. 1037A]

(*Homily* 30 on the Gospels, no. 5.) Neither simplicity without zeal nor zeal without simplicity pleases God. Hence Truth itself says: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10:16). In this matter it must be noted that the Lord did not wish to admonish his disciples concerning the dove without the serpent, nor concerning the serpent without the dove, so that the serpent’s craft might kindle the dove’s simplicity, and the dove’s simplicity might moderate the serpent’s craft.

Hence Paul says: “Do not become children in your understanding” (1 Corinthians 14:20). We have heard of the serpent’s craft; now let us be instructed concerning the dove’s simplicity: “But be children in malice.” Thus, concerning blessed Job: “He was a simple and upright man” (Job 1:1). For what is uprightness without simplicity, or what is simplicity without uprightness?

### CHAPTER L — “The same as above”

(*Pastoral Rule*, Admonition 12.) Truth itself admonishes its elect, saying: “Be wise as serpents [Col. 1037B] and simple as doves” (Matthew 16:16). For in the hearts of the elect the serpent’s craft ought both to sharpen the dove’s simplicity and the dove’s simplicity to moderate the serpent’s craft, so that they may neither become clever through prudence after being deceived, nor grow sluggish through simplicity in the pursuit of understanding.

### CHAPTER LI — “What I tell you in the darkness” (Matthew 10:27)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XI, no. 26.) When believers recognize mystical meanings from the hidden words of the prophets, what else are they than profound things revealed out of darkness? Hence Truth itself, speaking to the disciples in parables, says: “What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light” (Matthew 10:27). When we untie the mystical knots of allegories through explanation, we speak in the light what we heard in the darkness.

### CHAPTER LII — “The same as above”

(*Homily* 6 on Ezekiel.) Truth says to the disciples: “What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light” (Matthew 10:41), that is, explain openly what you have heard in the obscurities of [Col. 1037C] allegories.

### CHAPTER LIII — “Whoever receives a prophet” (Matthew 10:41)

(*Homily* 20 on the Gospels, no. 12.) To show how great a virtue there is in self-restraint and in receiving those in need, our Redeemer said: “Whoever receives a prophet in my name will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matthew 10:41). In these words it must be noted that he did not say, “He will receive a reward from a prophet,” or “a reward from a righteous man,” but “a prophet’s reward” and “a righteous man’s reward.” For a reward from a prophet is one thing, a reward from a righteous man another, and the reward of a righteous man another still.

What does it mean to say, “He will receive a prophet’s reward,” except that the one who supports a prophet by his generosity, although he himself does not possess prophecy, will nevertheless have a prophet’s recompense before almighty God? This man is perhaps righteous; and the less he possesses in this world, the greater is his confidence in speaking on behalf of justice. When he is supported by one who possesses something in this world, and who perhaps still does not presume to speak freely on behalf of [Col. 1037D] justice, the supporter makes himself a partner in that man’s freedom to practice justice, so that he may receive together with him the rewards of justice whom he helped by supporting him, enabling him to speak that same justice freely.

The prophet is full of the spirit of prophecy, but nevertheless needs bodily nourishment; and if the body is not restored, it is certain that the voice itself will be withdrawn. Therefore, whoever supplies nourishment to a prophet because he is a prophet gives strength to that prophet’s voice. He will receive a prophet’s reward together with the prophet who, although he was not himself full of the spirit of prophecy, nevertheless displayed before God what he had done by helping him.

### CHAPTER LIV — “What did you go out to see?” (Matthew 11:7)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIII, no. 7.) By the reed—or, more precisely, the cane—the changeability of the mind is signified, just as the Lord says to the crowds of the Jews in praise of John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see—a reed shaken by the wind?” (Matthew 11:7). The implied answer is, of course, “No.” John was not a reed shaken by the wind, because no breath of human speech could bend his mind, made firm by the Holy Spirit, in different directions.

### CHAPTER LV — “The same as above”

(Book I, *Homily* 9 on Ezekiel, no. 16.) Truth denies that John the Baptist was a reed shaken by the wind, saying: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see—a reed shaken by the wind?” (Matthew 11:7). That he spoke this as a denial, not as an affirmation, is shown by the words that follow. For he says: “But what did you go out into the wilderness to see—a man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses” (ibid.).

A reed shaken by the wind is now raised up by the gusts and now bent down by them. Every weak mind that is cast down by criticism or lifted up by praise is a reed shaken by the wind. [Col. 1038A] John was not such a reed, for amid human praise and criticism he maintained an unbending strength of mind.

### CHAPTER LVI — “From the days of John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:12)

[Col. 1038B] (*Homily* 20 on the Gospels, no. 14.) “From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12). We must examine with the greatest care the meaning of this heavenly pronouncement. For it must be asked how the kingdom of heaven can suffer violence. Who can inflict violence upon heaven? It must also be asked: if the kingdom of heaven can suffer violence, why has it endured this violence from the days of John the Baptist and not also before?

But when the law says, “If anyone does this or that, let him die,” it is clear to all who read that it struck sinners with the punishment of its severity, but did not restore them to life through repentance. When John the Baptist, preceding the grace of the Redeemer, preaches repentance, so that the sinner who is dead through guilt may live through conversion, then certainly from the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence.

What, then, is the kingdom of heaven except the dwelling-place of the righteous? For only the righteous are owed the reward of the heavenly homeland, so that the humble, chaste, meek, and merciful may attain the joys above. [Col. 1038C] But when someone swollen with pride, polluted by sins of the flesh, inflamed by anger, or impious through cruelty returns to repentance after his sins, he receives eternal life as though a sinner were entering a place that did not belong to him.

From the days of John the Baptist, therefore, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it, because the one who prescribed repentance to sinners taught nothing other than how violence should be done to the kingdom of heaven. Let us therefore recall, dearest brothers, the evils we have committed, and let us wear ourselves down by continual lamentation. Let us seize through repentance the inheritance of the righteous, which we did not possess through our life. Almighty God wishes to suffer such violence from us through repentance. He wishes the kingdom of heaven to be seized by our tears, although it is not owed to our merits.

### CHAPTER LVII — “If in Tyre” (Matthew 11:21)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXV, no. 7.) In the Gospel the Lord says to the reprobate city: “If the mighty works that have been done in you [Col. 1038D] had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matthew 11:21). In sackcloth, harshness and the pricking of sins are shown; in ashes, the dust of the dead is shown. For this reason these things are customarily employed in some manner for repentance, so that through the prickling of sackcloth we may recognize what we have done through guilt, and in the dust of ashes consider what we have become through judgment.

Let the vices that prick be considered in sackcloth; let the just punishment of the vices that follows by the sentence of death be considered in ashes. Since after sin the humiliations of the flesh have arisen, let a person see in the harshness of sackcloth what he did through pride, and let him see in the ashes how far he has come by sinning.

### CHAPTER LVIII — “Come to me, all you who labor” (Matthew 11:28)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book IV, no. 66.) In this light, therefore, the wicked cease from tumult, when minds bent toward evil, having recognized the truth, flee the laborious desires of the world and rest in the tranquility of inward love. [Col. 1039A] Does not the light itself call us to rest when it says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28 ff.)?

What heavy burden does he impose upon the necks of our minds, when he commands us to avoid every desire that causes disturbance? What heavy command does he give to his subjects, when he admonishes them to turn aside from the laborious paths of this world?

### CHAPTER LIX — “The same as above”

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXX, no. 50.) The Lord saw the heavy yoke of servitude impressed upon the necks of worldly people when he said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28).

A harsh yoke and, as we have said, [Col. 1039B] the burden of a hard servitude consist in being subject to temporal things, pursuing earthly goods, clinging to what is passing away, wishing to stand amid things that do not stand, desiring things that pass away but refusing to pass away with them. For while everything flees contrary to our desire, what previously afflicted the mind through the desire to acquire things afterward weighs upon it through fear of losing them.

### CHAPTER LX — “He will not break the bruised reed” (Matthew 12:20)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIII, no. 7.) By the cane or reed the splendor of temporal glory is expressed, as Wisdom says concerning the righteous: “The righteous will shine, and like sparks they will run through the reed-bed” (Wisdom 3:7). He calls the life of worldly people a reed-bed because, like reeds, they appear outwardly to rise toward high things through temporal glory, but inwardly become empty of the solidity of truth.

Hence the kingdom of the Jews is compared to a reed when the Lord, appearing in the truth of the flesh, is addressed through the prophet: “He will not break the bruised [Col. 1039C] reed, and he will not extinguish the smoking flax” (Isaiah 42:3). For what is proclaimed under the name of the reed except the temporal kingdom of the Jewish people, outwardly flourishing but inwardly empty? And because the royal line had already failed among that people, while a foreigner possessed its kingdom, he aptly calls that kingdom a bruised reed.

What, then, is expressed by the flax except its priesthood, which indeed used linen garments? Because at the Lord’s coming it had lost the ardor of charity, it was like a fire whose flame had already been lost: not burning, but smoking. The incarnate Lord did not break the bruised reed and did not extinguish the smoking flax, because he did not strike with the power of judgment the kingdom of Judea, which had almost been destroyed, or its priesthood, which did not retain the fire of faith; rather, he endured them with the long-suffering of patience.

### CHAPTER LXI — “Every idle word” (Matthew 12:16)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VII, no. 58.) [Col. 1039D] Truth admonishes us, saying: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36). An idle word is one that lacks either the reason of a just necessity or the intention of pious usefulness. If an account is required even for idle speech, we must carefully consider what punishment follows that loquacity in which one also sins through words of pride.

### CHAPTER LXII — “The same as above”

(*Homily* 6 on the Gospels, final section.) With you I urge that we abstain from idle speech and avoid speaking uselessly. Insofar as we are able to restrain the tongue, let our words not dissipate into the wind, since the King says: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36). An idle word is one that lacks either the usefulness of uprightness or the reason of a necessary judgment.

### CHAPTER LXIII — “When he returns with seven spirits” (Matthew 12:45)

[Col. 1040A]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VII, no. 20.) Often the Lord begins to bring about in us the crushing of vices. But when the mind is lifted up by the very beginning of its progress, and when it already raises itself up as though because of its virtues, it opens a way to the adversary raging against it. Entering the innermost recesses of the heart, he shatters everything he finds there arising from the pursuit of a good beginning; and he displays himself all the more violently in its destruction because he grieves all the more heavily that he had been cast out, even if only for a little while.

Hence, as the Gospel and the voice of Truth testify (Matthew 12), the spirit that went out alone returns with seven spirits to the house of the conscience that had been neglected.

### CHAPTER LXIV — “When the sun rose, they dried up” (Matthew 13:6)

(In *Exposition on Ezekiel*, Book II, Homily 7.) Concerning the seeds that had been sown, the Lord says: “When the sun rose, they dried up” (Matthew 13:6). For when persecution has arisen, the words of preaching dry up in the hearts of the [Col. 1040B] reprobate.

### CHAPTER LXV — “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 13:9)

(Ibid., Book II, Homily 2, no. 2.) It must be understood that bodily eyes and ears are also present in carnal people, and they are used by them for things that they see bodily. But the eyes and ears of the heart belong only to spiritual people, who see invisible things through understanding and hear the praise of God without sound.

The almighty Lord was seeking these ears when he said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matthew 13:9). For who at that time in that people could exist without bodily ears? But when he says, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” he openly shows that he was seeking those ears which not everyone could possess.

### CHAPTER LXVI — “The deceitfulness of riches chokes the word” (Matthew 13:22)

[Col. 1040C] (Ibid., Book II, Homily 6, no. 2.) There are therefore storehouses constructed in the building of the holy Church, because the tongue of teachers abounds in the riches of knowledge. Truth itself declares these to be true riches when, concerning passing riches, it says: “The deceitfulness of riches chokes the word” (Matthew 13:23). The wisdom and knowledge of spiritual teaching are true riches; in comparison with them, things that can pass away are called false.

Concerning these riches Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Proverbs 21:20). Apart from the fact that spiritual riches lead to the eternal homeland, they differ greatly from earthly riches: spiritual riches increase when distributed, whereas earthly riches either are distributed and diminish, or are retained and are of no use.

### CHAPTER LXVII — “Gather the weeds” (Matthew 13:30)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book IX, no. 98.) The punishments that proceed from the scales of justice cannot be inflicted without order. For how could there be no order in [Col. 1040D] punishments, when retribution follows each condemned person according to the measure of his crime? Hence it is written: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments, and a more severe punishment awaits the more powerful” (Wisdom 6:7). Hence, concerning the condemnation of Babylon, it is said: “As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning” (Revelation 18:7).

If punishment is therefore distinguished according to the measure of guilt, it is plainly established that order is preserved in punishments. And unless the deeds of merit determined the degree of torments, the coming Judge would never have said that he would tell the reapers: “Gather the weeds and bind them in bundles to burn them” (Matthew 13:30). For if no order will be preserved in punishments, why are the weeds to be burned bound in bundles?

To bind bundles for burning means to associate those who are to be handed over to eternal fire with their equals, so that those whom a similar guilt defiles may be bound by an equal punishment; and those who have not been polluted by unequal iniquity may not be tormented by unequal [Col. 1041A] punishment. Thus condemnation may crush together those whom arrogance had lifted up together; and a like affliction may constrict those whom ambition had expanded in like manner; and the flame of punishment may torment equally those whom an equal flame of sin had kindled in the fire of lust.

For just as there are many dwelling-places in the Father’s house (John 14), according to the diversity of virtue, so the inequality of crimes subjects the condemned to the fires of Gehenna with differing punishments. Although Gehenna is one for all, it does not burn all with one and the same intensity. For just as we are touched by one sun, yet do not all grow hot beneath it in the same way, since the burden of heat is felt according to the condition of the body, so the condemned are afflicted by one Gehenna, yet it does not burn all with one and the same intensity, because what the unequal health of bodies does here is displayed there by the unequal cause of merits.

### CHAPTER LXVIII — “The kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet” (Matthew 13:17)

[Col. 1041B] (In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIII, no. 34.) “The kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind” (Matthew 13:17). The Church is called the kingdom of heaven; while the Lord lifts its way of life toward heavenly things, it already reigns in the Lord through a heavenly manner of living.

It is rightly compared to a dragnet cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind, because, cast into this age of the Gentiles, it rejects no one. It catches the wicked with the good, the proud with the humble, the angry with the meek, and the foolish with the wise.

### CHAPTER LXIX — “Give them something to eat yourselves” (Matthew 14:17)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book I, no. 27.) Concerning the hungry crowds it is said: “Give them something to eat yourselves.” And again: “I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint” (Matthew 14:17). That is: let them receive the word of consolation through your preaching, lest, remaining hungry for the nourishment of truth, they faint amid the labor of this life.

### CHAPTER LXX — “The same as above”

[Col. 1041C]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXVII, no. 22.) Almighty God first shakes us through his preachers by rebuking our evil action, and afterward nourishes us by consoling us through hope. For if the divine dispensation did not now exercise judgment through these clouds, it would never have said to those same clouds: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20:22).

And again, if it did not feed hungry hearts through these clouds, the Lord would never have said concerning the hungry crowds: “Give them something to eat yourselves” (Matthew 14:16). We believe that this was then done by their hands in such a way that we see it performed daily and without interruption through their words. For what does Peter do when he speaks through his Epistles, except satisfy our hearts, badly weakened by hunger, with the nourishment of the word? What do Paul and John accomplish when they speak through their Epistles, except enable our minds to receive heavenly [Col. 1041D] nourishment and overcome the loathing of their hunger by which they were dying?

### CHAPTER LXXI — “If the blind leads the blind” (Matthew 15:14)

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chapter 1.) The ignorance of shepherds plainly corresponds to the merits of those subject to them. Although, because their own fault demands it, they do not possess the light of knowledge, strict judgment nevertheless decrees that through their ignorance even those who follow them should stumble. Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “If the blind leads the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matthew 15:14).

### CHAPTER LXXII — “You do not understand the things that are of God” (Matthew 16:23)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book X, no. 5.) A person speaks to himself when, through what he perceives, he is by no means separated by the spirit of divinity from the [Col. 1042A] understanding of carnal prudence; when the flesh puts forward its own judgment and, as though summoning the mind to understanding, sends it outward.

Hence Truth says to Peter, who was still thinking in earthly terms: “You do not understand the things that are of God, but those that are of human beings” (Matthew 16:23). Yet to him when he made the correct confession it is said: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 17).

### CHAPTER LXXIII — “If anyone wishes to come after me” (Matthew 16:24)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIII, no. 13.) Truth says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9:23). He denies himself who, having trampled down the pattern of pride, shows before God that he is alien to himself.

### CHAPTER LXXIV — “The same as above”

(*Homily* 10 on Ezekiel, no. 7.) “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew 16:24). He denies himself who, changed for the better, begins to be what he was not and ceases to be what he was.

### CHAPTER LXXV — “His garments became white” (Matthew 17:2)

[Col. 1042B]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXII, no. 8.) He alone is glorious who, while enjoying himself in himself, does not need additional praise. He is clothed in splendid garments because he has taken into the use of his adornment the choirs of the holy angels whom he created; and he presents the Church to himself as a kind of glorious garment, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5).

Hence the prophet says to him: “You have put on confession and beauty, clothed in light as with a garment” (Psalm 103:2). Here, confession; there, beauty: for those whom here he makes confessing through repentance, there he displays shining with the beauty of righteousness. He is therefore clothed in light as in a garment, because he will be clothed in that eternal glory with all the saints to whom it was said: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14).

Hence it is said through the Gospel that, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, his garments became white like snow (Matthew 17). [Col. 1042C] What else is announced in this transfiguration than the glory of the final resurrection? On the mountain his garments became like snow, because at the summit of heavenly brightness all the saints will cling to him, shining with the light of righteousness.

### CHAPTER LXXVI — “Let us make three tents here” (Matthew 17:4)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VIII, no. 92.) The righteous neither receive present good things as something very great nor greatly fear the evils that come upon them. They use present good things while fearing future evils; and while groaning over present evils, they are consoled by love of the good things to come. Thus they are refreshed by temporal assistance, as a traveler uses a bed in an inn: he rests and hastens to depart. He rests in body, but in mind he is moving toward something else.

Sometimes they even desire to suffer adversity and refuse to prosper amid transitory things, lest the pleasure of the journey delay them from reaching their homeland; [Col. 1042D] lest they fix the step of their heart on the road of pilgrimage and at some time arrive at the sight of the heavenly homeland without reward. They rejoice in being despised and do not grieve when they are afflicted by necessities.

Those, therefore, who do not fortify themselves against present adversities are like people who do not wish to have a tent against heat and rain. Hence Peter is rightly rebuked (Matthew 17), because, not yet strengthened by perfection of mind, after recognizing the splendor of truth he attempts to fix a tent on earth.

The righteous therefore neglect to build themselves here, where they know themselves to be travelers and guests. Because they desire to rejoice in what belongs to them, they refuse to be happy in what belongs to another. But the more the wicked are separated from the inheritance of the eternal homeland, the more deeply they fix the foundations of their thoughts in the earth.

### CHAPTER LXXVII — “Elijah indeed is to come” (Matthew 17:11)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XX, no. 66.) Although Elijah is said to have been taken up to heaven, [Col. 1043A] he postponed death; he did not escape it. Concerning him Truth itself says: “Elijah indeed is to come, and he will restore all things” (Matthew 17:11). For he will come to restore all things, since he is certainly restored to this world for the purpose of fulfilling the ministry of preaching and paying the debt of the flesh.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII — “The same as above”

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXV, no. 24.) Truth says in the Gospel: “Elijah comes, and he will restore all things” (Matthew 17:11). Now the Church has lost the Israelites, whom it was unable to convert by preaching; but then, when Elijah preaches, as he gathers however many he finds, it receives more fully, as it were, what it had lost.

### CHAPTER LXXIX — “From whom do the kings of the earth receive?” (Matthew 17:24)

(*Homily* 7, Book I, on Ezekiel, no. 4.) In our good works we must sometimes avoid causing offense to our neighbor, but at other times disregard it as nothing. [Col. 1043B] We learned this from our very Author, who, when tribute was demanded of Peter, first proposed an example by which he showed that he owed nothing, saying: “From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax—from their own sons or from strangers?” (Matthew 17:24–25). When Peter said, “From strangers,” he immediately replied: “Then the sons are free.”

But after showing that he was free, lest he perhaps cause offense to anyone, he added: “Nevertheless, lest we offend them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; and when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you” (ibid., 26).

Again, when he said that everything entering the mouth does not defile a person, those who approached said: “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this word?” But he answered: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Leave them; they are blind leaders of the blind” (Matthew 15:11).

Behold: the Teacher, Truth, gave tribute, so that an offense that ought not to arise would not be generated in certain hearts. [Col. 1043C] Again, when he saw that an offense against the truth was arising in certain hearts, he allowed them to remain in their offense.

From this we must understand that, insofar as we can do so without sin, we ought to avoid causing offense to our neighbors. But if offense is taken at the truth, it is more useful to allow the offense to arise than to abandon the truth.

### CHAPTER LXXX — “Whoever causes one to stumble” (Matthew 18:6)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VI, no. 37.) “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone drawn by an ass be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matthew 18:6).

What is signified by the sea except the world, and by the millstone drawn by an ass except earthly activity? While it binds the necks of the mind through foolish desires, it sends the mind around in the circuit of labor.

There are some who, while abandoning earthly activities and rising beyond the powers of understanding toward the pursuits of contemplation, set humility aside. They not only cast themselves into error, but also separate the weak from the embrace of unity. [Col. 1043D] Whoever causes one of the least to stumble would have been better off thrown into the sea with a millstone tied around his neck, because it would have been more advantageous for a perverse mind to be occupied with earthly business in the world than to devote itself to the pursuits of contemplation to the destruction of many.

### CHAPTER LXXXI — “The same as above”

[Col. 1044A] (*Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chapter 2.) No one does greater harm in the Church than one who acts perversely while possessing the name or rank of holiness. No one dares to rebuke such a delinquent, and the fault is greatly extended as an example when, out of reverence for his rank, a sinner is honored.

Those who are unworthy would flee the burden of so great a guilt if they carefully listened with the ear of the heart to the judgment of Truth, which says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone drawn by an ass be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matthew 18:6).

By the millstone drawn by an ass the circuit and labor of secular life are expressed, and by the depth of the sea the final damnation is signified. Whoever, having been led to the appearance of holiness, destroys others either by word or by example would certainly have been better off if earthly deeds had bound him to death under an outward appearance, than if he had displayed sacred offices in such a way that others could imitate him in guilt. For if he fell alone, the punishment of hell would at least torment him more tolerably.

### CHAPTER LXXXII — “Who owed him ten thousand” (Matthew 18:24)

(Dialogues, Book IV, chapter 60.) It must be understood that the person rightly asks forgiveness for his own offense who first releases the offense committed against him. For an offering is not accepted unless discord has first been driven from the heart, as Truth says: “If you are offering your gift at the altar, [Col. 1044B] and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; and then, when you return, offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23–24). In this matter we must consider: if every fault is absolved by an offering, how serious is the fault of discord, for which even the offering is not accepted? We must therefore go in spirit to our neighbor, however far away and however estranged he may be; we must submit our heart to him and appease him with humility and goodwill, so that our Creator, when he sees such reconciliation of our mind, may free us from sin—the one who accepts the offering for sin.

Moreover, as Truth’s voice bears witness, we have learned that the servant who owed ten thousand talents, when he repented, received remission of the debt from his lord; but because he did not forgive his fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii, he was ordered to repay what had already been forgiven him. From these words it is clear that if we do not forgive from the heart the offense committed against us, then what we rejoiced had already been forgiven us through repentance is again demanded from us. [Col. 1044C]

## CHAPTER LXXXIII.—Not all receive this saying (Matthew 19:11).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, admonition 29.) Truth says of the integrity of virginity in itself: “Not all receive this saying” (Matthew 19:11). He made this known as something of the highest importance because he denied it to all; and while he foretold that it is difficult to grasp, he made known to his hearers with what caution it must be held.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV.—It is easier for a camel… (Matthew 19:24).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XXXV, no. 38.) Since a camel willingly humbles itself in order to bear burdens, it not improperly signifies the grace of the Redeemer, who, because he deigned to bear the burdens of our weakness, willingly descended from the height of his power. Hence he also says through the Evangelist: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again”; and, “No one takes it from me” (John 10:18). Again he says: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:24). What does the name “rich man” signify except anyone who is lifted up, and what does the name “camel” signify except proper self-awareness? The camel passed through the eye of the needle when our Redeemer entered, through the narrowness of his Passion, even unto the acceptance of death. That Passion was like a needle, because it pierced the body with pain. It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven, because unless he himself, first taking upon himself the burdens of our weakness, had shown us through his Passion the pattern of humility, our proud rigidity would never have bent itself toward his humility.

## CHAPTER LXXXV.—In the regeneration, when the Son… (Matthew 19:28).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book IV, no. 46.) The rising of dawn is that new birth of the resurrection by which holy Church, raised even in the flesh, arises to contemplate the light of eternity. For if the resurrection of our flesh itself were not, as it were, a birth, Truth would not have said of it: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty” (Matthew 19:28). He therefore saw this as a rising, which he called “regeneration.” [Col. 1045A]

## CHAPTER LXXXVI.—The same as above.

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book X, no. 52.) Then those who are now unjustly judged on God’s behalf will come as judges with God. Their light will shine more widely in proportion as the hand of their persecutors now constricts them more harshly. Then it will be revealed to the eyes of the reprobate that those who willingly abandoned all earthly things were supported by heavenly power. Hence Truth says to his elect: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28). [Col. 1045B] What then? Will that court within not have more than twelve judges? Indeed, the quantity of the whole is expressed by the number twelve, because whoever, stirred here by the goad of divine love, has abandoned his possessions will undoubtedly there attain the summit of judicial power. Thus the one who now chastises himself through voluntary poverty in consideration of judgment will then come as judge with the Judge.

For this reason it is said through Solomon of the Bridegroom of holy Church: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Proverbs 31:23). Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isaiah 3:14). Truth no longer calls these same elders servants but friends, saying: “I no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15). The Psalmist, looking upon them, says: “But your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored” (Psalm 138:17). As he looked upon the greatness of their hearts, he immediately added how they trample upon the glory of the world: “Their rule has been exceedingly strengthened.” And lest we think that those whom we recognize as advancing toward the heights of such perfection are few, he at once added: “I will count them, and they will be multiplied beyond the sand” (ibid., 18). Thus, as many as now willingly humble themselves for love of truth, so many will then shine as lamps in judgment. [Col. 1045C]

## CHAPTER LXXXVII.—He will receive a hundredfold (Matthew 19:29).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XV, no. 18.) For our good work, rest of mind is prepared for us here, and eternal joys there, as Truth bears witness, saying: “If anyone has left houses or fields, etc., he will receive a hundredfold in this age, and in the future will possess eternal life” (Matthew 19:29). The number one hundred is made perfect by multiplying ten tenfold. He therefore receives a hundredfold who, even if he possesses nothing, nevertheless, by the perfection of his mind, no longer seeks to possess anything in this age.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—The same as above.

[Col. 1045D]

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 6, no. 16.) The number ten, multiplied by itself, rises to one hundred. Hence one hundred rightly signifies great perfection, as it is said of the elect: “Everyone who leaves house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matthew 19:29). No holy person abandons earthly things so that he may possess more of them in this world; for whoever leaves earth out of earthly ambition does not leave earth but desires it. Nor does one who leaves a single wife receive a hundred wives; rather, perfection is signified by the number one hundred, after which eternal life is also promised. Whoever for God’s name despises temporal and earthly things receives perfection of mind here, so that he no longer desires what he despises, and in the age to come reaches the glory of eternal life.

He therefore receives a hundred times what he gave who, receiving the spirit of perfection, has no need of earthly things, even if he does not possess them. For that person is poor who lacks what he does not have. But the person who does not have something and does not desire to have it is rich; poverty lies in want of mind, not in the condition of one’s possessions. For a person who is well reconciled to poverty is not poor. [Col. 1046A]

## CHAPTER LXXXIX.—Can you drink the cup? (Matthew 20:22).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XVII, no. 5.) He was recalling the swollen hearts of the disciples to these paths when they were already seeking a place of glory but did not know the way to that same glory, saying: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (Matthew 20:22). They had sought the height of his confession on the right and on the left, but they did not see how narrow the road to it would be. Therefore the cup of his Passion was immediately placed before their eyes as something to imitate, so that if they were striving toward the joys of exaltation, they might first discover the way of humility.

## CHAPTER XC.—The same as above.

[Col. 1046B]

(Homily 27 on the Gospels, no. 4.) When the sons of Zebedee, through their mother’s intervention, asked that one should sit at God’s right hand and the other at his left, they heard: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (Matthew 20:22). They were already seeking a place of exaltation; Truth calls them back to the way by which they would come to exaltation, as if he were saying: “The place of exaltation already pleases you, but first let the way of labor exercise you; through the cup one reaches majesty. If your mind desires what delights, first drink what causes pain.” Thus through the bitter cup of suffering one reaches the joy of salvation.

## CHAPTER XCI.—You will indeed drink my cup (Matthew 20:23).

(Homily 35, in the same work, no. 7.) There are two kinds of martyrdom: one in the mind, the other in the mind and in action together. We can therefore be martyrs even if we are killed by no sword of our attackers. Death at the hands of a persecutor is martyrdom in open action; [Col. 1046C] bearing insults and loving one who hates us is martyrdom in hidden thought. Since there are two kinds of martyrdom—one in hidden action, the other in public action—Truth bears witness when he asks the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (Matthew 20:22). When they immediately replied, “We can,” the Lord at once answered: “You will indeed drink my cup.” What else do we understand by the cup except the pain of Passion? Elsewhere he says of it: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). The sons of Zebedee—that is, James and John—did not both die by martyrdom, and yet both heard that they would drink the cup. John did not end his life through martyrdom, but he was nevertheless a martyr, because he preserved in his mind the Passion that he did not undergo in his body.

## CHAPTER XCII.—Two blind men sitting beside the road (Matthew 20:30).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XIX, no. 5.) It is written in the Gospel that, as the Lord was leaving Jericho, he was passing by; [Col. 1046D] and two blind men sitting beside the road cried out, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David” (Matthew 20:30). At their voice, as it is written there, “Jesus stopped and restored their sight.” What does it mean that he hears while passing by and restores light while standing, except that through his humanity he had mercy on us, while through the power of his divinity he drove away the darkness of our mind? Because he was born and suffered for us, because he rose and ascended into heaven, Jesus is, as it were, passing by: for this action is temporal. But standing, he touched and illumined us, because the eternity of the Word does not pass away as that temporal dispensation does. Remaining in himself, he renews all things. To stand is proper to God: to dispose all mutable things by an unchanging purpose. Thus he who, while passing by, heard the voices of those who petitioned, restored their light while standing, because although he endured temporal things for us, he nevertheless granted us light from that which knows nothing of the passing away of mutability.

## CHAPTER XCIII.—They spread their garments (Matthew 21:8).

[Col. 1047A]

(Ezekiel, Book II, homily 5, no. 2.) When our Redeemer, seated upon a colt, was heading toward Jerusalem, as the Evangelist bears witness, “Many spread their garments on the road; and those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: ‘Hosanna in the highest; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’” (Matthew 21:8). Our Savior heads toward Jerusalem seated upon a colt when, guiding the soul of each believer—his own beast, so to speak—he leads it to the innermost vision of peace. He also sits upon the beast when he presides universally over holy Church and kindles it with desire for heavenly peace.

Many spread their garments on the road because they discipline their bodies through abstinence, preparing a way for him to the mind or offering good examples to those who follow. Others cut leaves or branches from the trees and spread them on the road, because in the teaching of truth they select words and sayings of the Fathers from their speech, so that, coming along the road of God to the minds of their [Col. 1047B] hearers, they may present them in humble preaching. We too, though unworthy, do this now. For when we take up the sayings of the Fathers in exhortation, we cut leaves from the trees and spread them on the road of the almighty Lord.

“But those who went before and those who followed cried out: ‘Hosanna.’” The Jewish people went before; the Gentiles followed. And because all the elect—whether those who were able to belong to Judea or those who now exist in the Church—believed and believe in the Mediator between God and human beings, those who go before and those who follow cry out, “Hosanna.” In Latin, *hosanna* means “save us.” From him the former sought salvation, the present seek it, and they confess him blessed who comes in the name of the Lord. For there is one faith and one hope of the peoples who precede and those who follow.

Just as the sins of the former were healed by his Passion and resurrection, so we are saved by his past Passion and by his resurrection, which endures forever. The one whom our predecessors from the Jewish people believed in and loved as the one who would come, we believe and love as having come, and we are kindled by desire for him so that we may contemplate him face to face. [Col. 1047C]

## CHAPTER XCIV.—The money of the money-changers… (Matthew 21:12).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XXV, no. 36.) For it was not without reason that the Lord himself poured out the money of the money-changers and overturned the seats of those selling doves (Matthew 21), clearly signifying that through teachers he judges the lives of the people, but through himself he examines the deeds of teachers. Yet the faults of subjects, which are now either concealed from judgment by their teachers or cannot be judged by them, will undoubtedly be reserved for his judgment.

## CHAPTER XCV.—Bind his hands and feet (Matthew 22:13).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XXV, no. 22.) He is then compelled to be sent into the outer darkness who is now voluntarily blinded in his inner self. [Col. 1047D]

## CHAPTER XCVI.—After binding his feet and hands (Matthew 22:13).

(Homily 9, Book I on Ezekiel, no. 34.) Under the figure of one condemned, the entire multitude of the reprobate is expressed when Truth’s voice says: “After binding his feet and hands, cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 22:13). The reprobate then fall into outer darkness because they have now voluntarily cast themselves into inner darkness, refusing to follow the light of truth either by believing or by doing good. They are commanded to be sent there with their feet and hands bound because, while the time for working and running is now at hand, they did not wish to have their hands and feet free for good action.

## CHAPTER XCVII.—They perform all their works (Matthew 23:5).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XV, no. 4.) Often the hypocrite, while pretending to be holy, does not fear to show himself wicked. [Col. 1048A] He is honored by everyone, and the glory of holiness is attributed to him by those who see outward things but cannot perceive inward ones. Thus he rejoices in the first place, brightens at the first couch, swells with pride at the first greeting, is exalted by the reverential voice of those who serve him, and grows inflated with proud thoughts in the service rendered by his subjects.

Thus Truth’s voice says of such people: “They perform all their works in order to be seen by human beings; for they enlarge their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels. They love the first places at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by people” (Matthew 23:5 and following). But what will their joy be when compared with eternity, when, as death suddenly arrives, it is consumed as though it had never existed? The delight of that joy passes away, but the punishment remains; and when the possession is lost, the cause endures.

## CHAPTER XCVIII.—Woe to you, hypocrites (Matthew 23:15).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book I, no. 24.) Even before the Redeemer’s coming, Judea had oxen, [Col. 1048B] because it sent workers to preach, to whom Truth’s voice says: “Woe to you, hypocrites, who travel around sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has been made, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves” (Matthew 23:13).

## CHAPTER XCIX.—You tithe mint (Matthew 23:23).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, admonition 34.) The Pharisees are rebuked by Truth’s mouth when they hear: “You tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have left the weightier matters of the law—judgment, mercy, and faith” (Matthew 23:23). We must not hear carelessly that, when he said they tithed the smallest things, he chose the last items from the herbs, yet mentioned fragrant ones, in order clearly to show that hypocrites, while observing small matters, seek to spread around themselves the scent of a holy reputation. Although they neglect to fulfill the greatest matters, they nevertheless observe the smallest, which by human judgment give off a fragrance far and wide.

## CHAPTER C.—Straining out a gnat (Matthew 23:24).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, admonition 34.) Some bind themselves by grave guilt in more serious sins, yet often sin worse in the small matters they observe, because they act wickedly in the former and use the latter to conceal from people the fact that they are wicked. Thus, when they commit greater evils, they are openly wicked before God; and when they observe small goods, they display simulated holiness before people. Hence it is said to the Pharisees: “Straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel” (Matthew 23:24). It is as though he were saying plainly: “You distinguish the smallest evils but devour the greater ones.” [Col. 1048C]

## CHAPTER CI.—Woe… you are like tombs (Matthew 23:27).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XXVI, no. 59.) All hypocrites grow dark within through wicked action and are whitened on the surface through the display of righteousness. To them the Lord’s voice says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful on the outside to people, but within are full of [Col. 1048D] the bones of the dead and every impurity. So you also appear righteous to people outwardly, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (Matthew 23:27). Thus outwardly they display what they attack inwardly by their lives. Inwardly they magnify the evils they conceal outwardly by placing something else over them. Before the strict Judge they can no longer claim ignorance as an excuse, because, while displaying every appearance of holiness before human eyes, they themselves bear witness that they are not ignorant of how to live well.

## CHAPTER CII.—Iniquity will abound (Matthew 24:12).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XVI, no. 81.) Iniquity is compared to cold because it constricts the sinner’s mind with sluggishness. Hence it is written: “As the cistern makes its water cold, so it makes its wickedness cold” (Jeremiah 6:7). By contrast, charity is heat, because it kindles the mind which it fills. Of this heat it is written: “Iniquity will abound, and the charity of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12).

## CHAPTER CIII.—Unless those days had been shortened (Matthew 24:21).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XXXII, no. 12.) Although savagery expands toward cruelty, heavenly mercy nevertheless confines it by shortening the days. Hence Truth himself says: “Then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor will be” (Matthew 24:21). Again he says: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (ibid., 22). Because the Lord sees that we are both proud and weak, he says that the days he has brought upon us as uniquely evil have mercifully been shortened—certainly to terrify pride through bodily adversity and to sustain weakness through brevity. [Col. 1049A]

## CHAPTER CIV.—Pseudo-Christs will arise (Matthew 24:24).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XXXII, no. 24.) We must carefully consider what happens when this Behemoth lifts up his tail like a cedar and then reveals himself more terribly than [Col. 1049B] he does now. What kinds of punishment do we know that we do not already rejoice have exercised the strength of martyrs? Some were struck down by a sword plunged unexpectedly into the throat; others were fastened to the cross, in which death is both challenged and repelled, and, once repelled, challenged again. Others were ground down by a saw with bristling teeth; others were scattered by a claw armed with iron as it furrowed them; others were crushed by bestial fury, torn limb from limb by bites; others were ripped open from within by the force of blows pressed through the skin; others were buried alive beneath excavated earth; others, thrown from a height, were shattered by a deadly fall; others, cast into water, were swallowed as it filled them; others were consumed by devouring flame, eaten down to ashes.

When, therefore, this Behemoth more wickedly expands his tail at the end of the world, what is it that will then grow more terrible in these torments except what Truth himself says in the Gospel: “Pseudo-Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect will be led into error” (Matthew 24:24)? Now our faithful people perform wonders when they endure perverse things. Then the followers of this Behemoth will perform wonders even while inflicting adversities. Let us consider, therefore, what the temptation of the human mind will be when a devout martyr submits his body to torments, yet the torturer performs miracles before his eyes. Whose mind then would not be shaken from the very depths of its thoughts when the one who torments with whips flashes with signs? [Col. 1049C]

## CHAPTER CV.—The same as above.

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIII, no. 61.) Truth’s mouth says through the Gospel: “Pseudo-Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect will be led into error” (Matthew 24:24). In this matter we must ask carefully how those who are elect can be led into error, or why, if it is possible, the phrase is added as though in uncertainty, when the Lord, foreseeing all things, awaits what is to happen.

But because the hearts of the elect are shaken by anxious thought while their steadfastness is not moved, the Lord embraced both points in this one saying: “So that, if possible, even the elect will be led into error.” For already to err is to be troubled in thought [Note: [Col. 1049D] Alternatively: “to waver.”]; but he immediately adds, “if possible,” because without doubt it cannot happen that the elect are fully caught in error.

## CHAPTER CVI.—They will give great signs (Matthew 24:24).

(Homily 9, Book I on Ezekiel, no. 8.) We must understand that uncertainty in God’s speech arises not from ignorance but from some significance. For who does not know that the one who made and sees all things knows all things? Truth himself says in the Gospel concerning the preachers of Antichrist: “They will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect will be led into error” (Matthew 24:24). Why is this said with uncertainty when the Lord foreknows what will happen?

There is one of two alternatives: if they are elect, it cannot happen; if it can happen, they are not elect. Yet it is said: “So that, if possible, even the elect will be led into error.” This uncertainty in the Lord’s speech therefore indicated the temptation of the elect’s hearts, because those who are elect for perseverance will be tempted by the signs of the preachers of Antichrist to fall. By saying “if possible,” he expresses that the elect will be tempted in their hearts: they waver, but do not fall. It says “if possible” because they will tremble. Yet they are called elect because they do not fall. The uncertainty of the speech from the Lord expresses in the elect a trembling of mind. He calls them elect because he sees that they persist in faith and good works. [Col. 1050A]

## CHAPTER CVII.—As lightning comes out from the East (Matthew 24:27).

(*Commentary on Ezekiel*, Book I, homily 2, no. 17.) “As lightning comes out from the East and appears as far as the West, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew 24:27). Then no one will be permitted to hide from judgment in his mind, because everyone will be penetrated by the lightning of the Judge.

## CHAPTER CVIII.—Who, do you think, is faithful? (Matthew 24:45).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 39.) Matters of great depth ought to be concealed from many hearers and scarcely opened to a few. Hence Truth himself says: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord has set over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?” (Matthew 24:45). By the measure of wheat the appropriate measure of speech is expressed, lest, when something incapable of being contained by a narrow heart is given, it spill outside. Hence Paul says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ; I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3:2). Hence Moses, coming out from the secret presence of God, veils his shining face before the people, because he does not disclose the mysteries of inward brightness to the crowds.

## CHAPTER CIX.—But the five foolish… (Matthew 25:3).

[Col. 1050C]

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XXIII, no. 17.) The foolish virgins are said not to have taken oil in their vessels, because all arrogant people, even when they perhaps restrain themselves from certain vices, cannot possess within their consciences the good of glory. Paul had taken oil in his own vessel when he said: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12). To carry an empty vessel is to seek outside, with an empty heart within, the judgment of the human mouth.

## CHAPTER CX.—Give us some of your oil (Matthew 25:8).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book VIII, no. 76.) The foolish virgins, who had not taken oil in their vessels because they had their glory in the voices of others and not in their own consciences, were troubled by the Bridegroom’s presence and said: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (Matthew 25:8). To ask oil from one’s neighbors is to implore the glory of a good work through the testimony of another’s mouth. For when an empty mind [Col. 1050D] discovers that it has kept nothing within despite all its labors, it seeks testimony outside. It is as though the foolish virgins were saying openly: “When you see us rejected without reward, tell us, in your own work, what you have seen.” But then the hypocrite leans in vain upon this house of praise, because at the judgment no human testimony supports him. The praise that he later demands as testimony he had already received earlier as his reward.

## CHAPTER CXI.—Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day (Matthew 25:13).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book VII, no. 45.) Often, when the brevity of the present life is loved as though it were going to last a long time, the mind is broken away from eternal hope; delighted by present things, it is struck back by the darkness of its despair. And when it thinks that the span remaining for its life is long, it suddenly abandons life and encounters eternal things that it can no longer avoid.

Hence it is said by a certain Wise Man: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclesiasticus 2:16). Those lose endurance who, while they suppose they will linger long among visible things, abandon hope of invisible things. When the mind is fixed upon present things, life comes to an end. Suddenly they reach unforeseen punishments, which, deceived by their presumptions, they believed would either never touch them or would come only late.

Hence Truth says: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matthew 25:13). Again it is written: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2). Because the one who draws near to seize the soul is not seen, he is compared to a thief in the night. It must therefore be feared as something about to arrive all the more because its coming cannot be foreseen by us.

Hence holy men, because they continually look upon the brevity of life, live as though dying each day. They prepare themselves more firmly for what will endure because they constantly consider, from the end, that transient things are nothing. Thus the Psalmist, seeing the sinner’s life flee at a swift pace, says: “A little while, and the sinner will be no more” (Psalm 36:10). [Col. 1051B] Again he says: “A human being is like grass; his days are like the flower of the field” (Psalm 102:15). Isaiah says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6). James reproves the minds of those who presume, saying: “What is our life? It is a vapor appearing for a little while” (James 4:15). [Col. 1051A]

## CHAPTER CXII.—As long as you did it for one of these (Matthew 25:40).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XVI, no. 2.) In everything good that we do, we help ourselves, not God. Hence the Psalmist says: “I have said to the Lord, ‘You are my God, for you have no need of my goods’” (Psalm 15:2). He is truly our Lord because he is God, who does not need the servant’s goodness but bestows goodness; for he receives it so that the goodness offered may benefit not him but rather those who receive it and those who give it in return.

For when the Lord comes to judgment, he says: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:40). He speaks this with wondrous compassion for his members; and through this he himself, because he is our head, helps us, since he is helped in his members through our good works. [Col. 1051C]

## CHAPTER CXIII.—For I was hungry, and you did not give me food (Matthew 25:42).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XV, no. 23.) When the Lord comes to judgment, he will say to the reprobate: “For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me; I was naked, and you did not clothe me,” and so forth (Matthew 25:42). The sentence follows for this fault: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” If, then, one who is convicted of not giving is punished with so great a penalty, what punishment must be inflicted upon one who is accused of taking away?

## CHAPTER CXIV.—My Father, if it is possible (Matthew 26:39).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XII, no. 16.) As the Lord drew near to his Passion, he took upon himself the voice of the weak, saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). Then, to draw away their fear, he again displayed the power of courage through obedience, saying: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.). Thus, when something we do not wish to happen threatens, we should ask through weakness that it not happen, while through courage remaining ready for the will of our Creator to be done even against our will. [Col. 1052A]

## CHAPTER CXV.—Have nothing to do with that righteous man (Matthew 27:19).

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIII, no. 31.) The Lord mocked the devil as a bird (Job 40:24), when, in the Passion of his only-begotten Son, he showed him bait but concealed the snare. He saw what he would take with his mouth, but did not see what would hold him by the throat. For although he had previously confessed him to be the Son of God (Matthew 8), he nevertheless believed him to be merely a human being who would die, and he stirred up the minds of the persecuting Jews to bring about his death.

Yet at the very time of his betrayal he is understood to have realized too late that the devil would be punished by that death. Hence Pilate’s wife was terrified by a dream, so that her husband might cease persecuting the righteous man (Matthew 27:19). But once the matter had been arranged by an inward dispensation, no plot could oppose it. It was necessary that the death of the righteous man, dying unjustly, should undo the death of sinners, who were dying justly. [Col. 1052B]

## CHAPTER CXVI.—They compelled him (Matthew 27:32).

(Homily 32 on the Gospels, no. 3.) Near the body’s abstinence, vainglory sometimes lies in wait, because when leanness is noticed in the body and pallor in the face, the disclosed virtue is praised; and it pours itself outward all the more quickly as it emerges before human eyes through displayed pallor. Often what is believed to be done for God’s sake is done solely for human favor. [Col. 1052C]

This is well signified by that Simon who, found on the road, carries the Lord’s cross under compulsion. Other people’s burdens are carried under compulsion when something is done through the pursuit of vanity. Who, then, are signified by Simon except those who practice abstinence and are arrogant—those who afflict the flesh through abstinence but do not seek inwardly the fruit of abstinence? Simon therefore carries the Lord’s cross under compulsion because, when he is not led to good work by good will, a sinner performs the deed of a righteous person without its fruit. Hence the same Simon carries the cross but does not die: for those who practice abstinence and are arrogant afflict their bodies through abstinence, but live for the world through their desire for glory.

# BOOK TWO: TESTIMONIES ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK

[Col. 1051]

## CHAPTER ONE.—He ate locusts and wild honey (Mark 1:6).

[Col. 1051D]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXI, no. 45.) “He ate locusts and wild honey” (Mark 1:6). John not only proclaims him with prophetic authority but also announces him by the kind of food he eats. In himself he portrayed the Lord whom he preceded.
