When the Lord came for our redemption, because he took for himself the sweetness of the unfruitful Gentiles, he ate wild honey. But because he converted part of the Jewish people into his own body, he took locusts as food.

For the locusts signify them: they make sudden leaps, but immediately fall to the ground. They made leaps when they promised that they would fulfill the Lord’s commandments; but they quickly fell to the ground when, through wicked deeds, they denied that they had heard them. Let us observe in them, as it were, a leap of locusts: “All the words that the Lord has spoken, we will do and we will hear” (Exodus 24:3). But let us observe how quickly they fall to the ground: “Would that we had died in Egypt, and not in this vast wilderness! Would that we might perish, and that the Lord would not bring us into this land!” (Numbers 14:2). They were therefore locusts, because their speech produced a leap, but their actions produced a fall.

## CHAPTER II.—“And it yielded fruit, growing upward” (Mark 4:8).

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book II, homily 5, no. 12.) We say that the number six is perfect because on the sixth day God completed all his works. Since he gave the law to sinful humanity, and it was written in ten commandments, and six multiplied by ten rises to sixty, the perfection of good works is rightly signified by sixty cubits. The Lord also clearly signifies this in the Gospel when, explaining the parable of the sower, he said: “Another seed fell on good soil, and it yielded fruit, growing and increasing; it produced one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one hundredfold” (Mark 4:8).

The good soil bears thirtyfold fruit when the mind conceives the perfection of faith, which is in the Trinity. It bears sixtyfold when it produces the perfection of a life of good works. It bears a hundredfold when it advances to the contemplation of eternal life. For our left hand is the present life, while the right is the life to come. The contemplation of eternal life is rightly signified by the number one hundred, because when, after thirty and sixty, we reach the number one hundred by counting, that same number passes over to the right. Faith and action are still on the left, because while we remain here, we believe what we do not see and act so that we may see it. But when the mind has already raised itself into contemplation of eternal life, the reckoning has, as it were, reached the right hand.

## CHAPTER III.—“So is the kingdom of God, as if…” (Mark 4:26).

[Col. 1053B]

(In Ezekiel, book II, homily 3, no. 3 and following.) If there were not certain steps in the ascent of the heart, the Psalmist would not say: “They will go from strength to strength” (Psalm 83:8). (No. 4.) Nor is it surprising that there are steps from strength to strength, since each individual virtue itself is increased, as it were, by certain steps, and through the growth of merit is brought to the highest things. The beginnings of virtue are one thing, its advancement another, and its perfection another.

For if faith itself were not led to its perfection by certain steps, the holy Apostles would never have said: “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5). And a certain man came to the Lord, wishing his son to be healed; when asked whether he believed, he replied: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark 9:24). Consider what is said: if he believed, why did he speak of unbelief? But if he knew that he possessed unbelief, how did he believe? Yet because faith grows through the hidden inspiration of grace by stages of merit, at one and the same time the man who had not yet believed perfectly both believed and was unbelieving.

(No. 5.) The Lord describes these steps under the figure of a harvest, saying: “So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the ground, and sleep and rise night and day, while the seed sprouts and grows, though he does not know how. For the earth produces fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. And when the fruit has appeared, immediately he sends the sickle, because the harvest has arrived” (Mark 4:26 and following).

A man casts seed into the ground when he plants a good intention in his heart. After he has cast the seed, he sleeps, because he rests in the hope of good work. He rises night and day because he advances amid adversity and prosperity. The seed sprouts and grows while he does not know it, because even when he is still unable to measure his progress, a virtue once conceived is led onward. The earth produces fruit of itself because, through grace preceding it, the human mind rises spontaneously toward the fruit of good work.

But this same earth first produces the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. To produce the blade is to possess, while still tender, the beginning of goodness. The blade reaches the ear when the virtue conceived in the mind draws itself onward to the advancement of good work. It bears full grain in the ear when virtue has advanced so far that it can become a strong and perfect work.

But when the fruit has appeared, it immediately sends the sickle, because the harvest has arrived. For almighty God sends the sickle once the fruit has been produced and cuts down his harvest: when he has brought each person to perfect works, he cuts short that person’s temporal life by an appointed sentence, so that he may bring his grain to the heavenly storehouses.

When, therefore, we conceive good desires, we cast seed into the ground. When we begin to perform what is right, we are the blade. When we grow toward the advancement of good work, we reach the ear. And when we become firmly established in the perfection of that work, we produce full grain in the ear.

(No. 6.) Peter had been the blade. At the time of the Passion, following the Lord out of love, he feared confessing him at the voice of a servant girl (Luke 22). There was already greenness in his mind, because he believed in the Redeemer of all, but it was still very pliable and was trampled under the foot of fear.

The ear had already risen when he saw alive in Galilee, at the angel’s announcement, the one whom he had feared to confess as destined to die. But the full grain in the ear had arrived when the Spirit came from above and strengthened his mind with love for the Lord. He became so firm that, even when beaten, he despised the strength of his persecutors and freely proclaimed his Redeemer amid the blows.

## CHAPTER IV.—“Go home to your own people” (Mark 5:19).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVI, no. 76.) Consciences are signified by the name “houses,” for we dwell in them when, through reflection, we consider what we are doing. Hence the healed man is told: “Go home to your own people, and announce to them how much the Lord has done for you” (Mark 5:19). That is: now secure from the vice of sin, return to your conscience and awaken it to the voice of preaching.

## CHAPTER V.—“Take up your mat” (Mark 2:11).

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book I, homily 12, no. 11.) The Truth itself says to a certain healed man: “Take up your mat and go to your house” (Mark 2:9). By the mat on which the flesh rests, the flesh itself is signified; by the house, the conscience is represented.

When we lie dead in vices with our mind, we rest in the pleasures of the flesh, and, being sick, we are carried on a bed. But once we have been healed in mind so that we resist the vices of the flesh when they assail us, it is necessary that we also endure in our flesh the insults of temptations.

Thus the sick man restored to health is commanded: “Take up your mat,” that is, carry the bed on which you were carried, because everyone who has been healed must carry the insults of the flesh in which he previously lay sick. What, then, does it mean to say, “Take up your mat and go to your house,” except: carry the temptations of the flesh in which you have hitherto lain, and return to your conscience, so that you may see what you have done?

## CHAPTER VI.—“And they reclined in groups of a hundred” (Mark 6:40).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVI, homily 10, no. 68.) In the Gospel, the Lord also signified harmony among those dining with him by distinguishing their places. When he was about to satisfy the crowd with five loaves, he ordered them to recline in groups of fifty or of a hundred, so that the crowd of the faithful might receive its food while separated in place but united in conduct.

The rest of the jubilee is contained in the mystery of the number fifty. Fifty taken twice produces one hundred. Therefore, because one first rests from evil action so that afterward the soul may rest more fully in thought, some are described as groups of fifty and others as groups of one hundred. There are some who already possess rest from evil actions in their conduct, and there are some who already possess rest from perverse thoughts in their minds.

## CHAPTER VII.—“They bring him a deaf and mute man” (Mark 7:32).

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book I, homily 10, no. 20.) We must carefully observe that God’s voice to the prophet instructs him first to hear the Lord’s words and afterward to speak. For we hear God’s words if we do them, and we speak them rightly to our neighbors only when we have first done them ourselves.

Mark the Evangelist confirms this well when he narrates the Lord’s miracle, saying: “They bring him a deaf man who could scarcely speak, and they begged him to lay his hand upon him” (Mark 7:32). He indicates the order of the healing by adding: “He put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue; and looking up to heaven, he groaned; and he said to him, ‘Ephphatha,’ which means, ‘Be opened.’ And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke rightly” [Col. 1055A].

What does it mean that God, the Creator of all, when he wished to heal the deaf and mute man, put his fingers into his ears and, spitting, touched his tongue? What are the fingers of the Redeemer except the gifts of the Holy Spirit? Hence, when he had cast out a demon elsewhere, he said: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke 11:20). For this reason another Evangelist records him as saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28). From this passage it is gathered that the Spirit is called God’s finger.

Therefore, to put his fingers into the ears is to open the deaf mind to obedience through the gifts of the Holy Spirit. But what does it mean that, spitting, he touched the man’s tongue? Saliva for us is wisdom received from the Redeemer’s mouth in divine speech. Saliva flows from the head into the mouth; thus, when the wisdom that he himself is touches our tongue, it immediately forms it for words of preaching.

He looked up to heaven and groaned—not because he himself needed the groan, since he was giving what was requested, but to teach us to groan toward the one who presides in heaven. Thus our ears should be opened through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and our tongue should be loosed by the saliva of his mouth—that is, by knowledge of divine speech—for words of preaching.

Then he says to him, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened,” and immediately his ears were opened and the bond of his tongue was loosed. Here we must note that “Be opened” was said because his ears were closed. But when the ears of the heart have been opened to obedience, the bond of the tongue is undoubtedly also loosed, so that he may speak to others of the good things he himself has done and that they too should do. Hence it is rightly added: “And he spoke rightly.” For that person speaks rightly who first does, by obeying, what he urges others to do by speaking.

## CHAPTER VIII.—“I have compassion on the crowd” (Mark 8:2).

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book II, homily 9, no. 22.) When the people, exhausted and fasting, had gathered to the Lord, he said to his disciples: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away fasting to their homes, they will faint on the way; for some of them have come from far away” (Mark 8:2–3).

The crowd remains with the Lord for three days when the multitude of the faithful, turning away through repentance from the sins it has committed, converts to God in action, speech, and thought. The Lord does not wish to send them away fasting to their homes, lest they faint on the way, because converted sinners faint on the road of the present life if they are sent away into their own consciences without the nourishment of holy teaching. Therefore, lest they grow weary on the journey of their exile, they must be fed with sacred instruction.

The compassionate statement that came from the mouth of the Truth must be carefully considered: “For some of them have come from far away.” There is someone who, having experienced no carnal sin, hastened to the service of almighty God. He did not come from far away, because through purity and innocence he was near. Another, stained by no impurity or disgrace but having experienced only marriage, turned to spiritual service. He too did not come from far away, because, using a permitted union, he did not stray into illicit things.

Others return to repentance after carnal offenses, others after false testimony, others after thefts, others after acts of violence, and others after committing murder; and they turn to the service of almighty God. These truly come to the Lord from far away. For the more deeply each person has gone astray in wicked action, the farther he has withdrawn from almighty God.

The prodigal son, who abandoned his father, also went away into a distant country, where he fed pigs, because he nourished vices. Therefore, food must be given even to those who come from far away. Converted sinners must be supplied with the nourishment of holy teaching so that they may recover in God the strength they lost through their offenses. For doctors must often satisfy people with more abundant nourishment of teaching in proportion to the greater vices from which, exhausted, they have come.

## CHAPTER IX.—“I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark 9:23).

[Col. 1056A]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXII, no. 49.) Faith, which instructs us so that we may perfectly attain other good things, often both wavers and stands firm in its beginnings. It is already possessed with complete certainty, yet its confidence still trembles under doubt. For one part of it is received first, so that afterward it may be perfectly completed in us.

If faith did not advance in the mind of the believer by a definite progression, the father of the child who was to be healed would not have said in the Gospel, when questioned: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark 9:23). He was still ascending toward the faith that he had already received: at one and the same time he cried out that he believed and that he still doubted because of unbelief.

For this reason the disciples also say to our Redeemer: “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5), so that what had already been received in its beginning might come to perfection, as it were, through successive stages of increase.

## CHAPTER X.—“And crying out and tearing him violently” (Mark 9:25).

[Col. 1056B]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book X, no. 50.) Those who die to the desires of this world are considered completely extinguished, so far as earthly minds are concerned. This is well signified by the miracle of our Redeemer when he frees a man from an unclean spirit. It is written of him: “Crying out and tearing him violently, it went out of him; and he became like a dead man, so that many said, ‘He is dead.’ But Jesus, taking him by the hand, raised him, and he arose” (Mark 9:25).

He is shown as though dead when he is freed from the power of the evil spirit, because whoever now subdues earthly desires extinguishes within himself the life of carnal conduct. He appears dead to the world because he no longer has the wicked possessor who was driving him through unclean desires. Many call him dead because those who do not know how to live spiritually consider anyone who does not pursue carnal goods to be utterly extinguished.

## CHAPTER XI.—The same as above.

[Col. 1056C]

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book I, homily 12, no. 24.) As soon as the mind begins to love heavenly things, as soon as it gathers its entire attention toward the vision of inward peace, that ancient adversary who fell from heaven grows jealous and begins to lie in wait more actively. He inflicts temptations sharper than those to which the soul was accustomed, so that often he tests a resisting soul in a way he had never tested it before, when he possessed it.

Hence it is written: “My son, when you come to serve the Lord, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 2:1). Thus the demoniac whom the Lord heals is torn by the departing demon, as it is written: “Crying out and tearing him violently, it went out of him” (Mark 9:25).

What does it mean that the ancient enemy, who had not torn the possessed man while possessing him, tore him when abandoning him, except that often, when he is expelled from the heart, he generates in it temptations sharper than those he had aroused before, when he possessed it in quiet?

## CHAPTER XII.—“Have salt in yourselves” (Mark 9:43).

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book I, homily 8, no. 8.) There are some who, while striving to know more than is necessary, withdraw from peace with their neighbors, despising them as though they were dull and foolish. Hence the Truth itself warns us, saying: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:43). Whoever strives to possess the salt of wisdom must therefore take care never to depart from the peace of harmony.

## CHAPTER XIII.—The same as above.

(In the Pastoral Rule, part III, admonition 23.) Often, when greater knowledge elevates certain people, it separates them from the company of others; and the more they know, the more foolishly they depart from the virtue of concord. Let them therefore hear what the Truth itself says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:43).

Salt without peace is not a gift of virtue but evidence of condemnation [Col. 1057A]. For the more wisely someone knows, the more gravely he sins by abandoning harmony. He will therefore deservedly receive punishment without excuse, because, if he had wished, he could prudently have avoided sin.

To such people James also rightly says: “If you have zeal for souls and contentions in your hearts, do not boast and be liars against the Truth. This is not the wisdom that descends from above, but earthly, natural, demonic. But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable” (James 3:14 and following). Pure, that is, because it understands chastely; peaceable, because it does not separate itself through arrogance from the company of its neighbors.

# BOOK THREE. Testimonies on the Gospel according to Luke

[Col. 1057]

## CHAPTER I.—“They were both righteous before God” (Luke 1:6).

[Col. 1057A]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXV, no. 10.) The statement about the righteous married couple is expressed with very great caution: “They were both righteous before God” (Luke 1:6). It is not a secure commendation to appear righteous before human beings. Human judgment often approves someone as great in God’s sight, as it were, but almighty God, who is apparently being invoked as the basis of that approval, does not know him [Col. 1057B].

For this reason the Psalmist earnestly prays: “Direct my way in your sight” (Psalm 5:9), since often a way is considered straight in the sight of human beings even though it is distorted from the path of truth.

## CHAPTER II.—“And he himself will go before him” (Luke 1:17).

(Homily 7 on the Gospels, no. 1.) The angel says to Zechariah concerning John: “He himself will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). He is said to come in the spirit and power of Elijah because, just as Elijah will precede the Lord’s second coming, so John preceded his first coming. Just as Elijah will be the forerunner of the Judge who is to come, so John became the forerunner of the Redeemer. John, therefore, was Elijah in spirit, but he was not Elijah in person.

## CHAPTER III.—“The angel Gabriel was sent by God” (Luke 1:26).

[Col. 1057C]

(Homily 34 on the Gospels, no. 9.) Gabriel, whose name means “strength of God,” was also sent to Mary. He came to announce the one who deigned to appear in humility in order to defeat the powers of the air. Of him the Psalmist says: “Lift up your gates, princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory will enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.” And again: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Psalm 23:7).

He who is Lord of hosts and mighty in battle was coming to war against the powers of the air; therefore he was to be announced through the strength of God.

## CHAPTER IV.—“And the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, nos. 32–33.) The minds of the righteous pass from the irritation and heat of vices to moderation and tranquility of thought when they no longer desire earthly things and extinguish the flames of the flesh with heavenly desires. (No. 33.) For this reason Mary is also told of the refreshment given from heaven to the mind: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:33).

In this expression, however, the two natures of the incarnate God could both be signified by the word “overshadowing.” For a shadow is formed by light and a body. The Lord is light through his divinity; through the mediation of a soul, he deigned to become a body in her womb through his humanity. Since, therefore, incorporeal light was to become embodied in her womb, she who conceived the incorporeal one is told concerning the body: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you.” That is: the incorporeal light of divinity will receive a body of humanity in you.

## CHAPTER V.—The same as above.

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIII, no. 51.) The Lord’s incarnation, with the truth of the history preserved, is signified by the term “overshadowing,” as the angelic word testifies when it says to Mary: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). Since a shadow is expressed only through light and a body, the power of the Most High overshadowed her because incorporeal light assumed a body in her womb. Through this overshadowing she received refreshment in her mind.

## CHAPTER VI.—“To enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:79).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, no. 30.) Just as death acts by killing what it kills, so that it is no longer in life, so forgetfulness acts by killing what it kills, so that it is no longer in memory. Since John came to proclaim to the Hebrew people the God whom they had forgotten, Zechariah rightly says of him: “To enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:79). To sit in the shadow of death is to grow weary in forgetfulness, away from knowledge of divine love.

## CHAPTER VII.—“To guide our feet into the way of peace” (Luke 1:79).

(Homily 33 on the Gospels, no. 4.) Zechariah says: “To guide our feet into the way of peace” (ibid.). We guide our steps into the way of peace when we proceed along the path of actions in which we do not depart from the grace of our Creator.

## CHAPTER VIII.—“And he laid him in a manger” (Luke 2:7).

[Col. 1058C]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VII, no. 7.) Since the prophet says, “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6), the Creator of the universe, taking flesh from our substance, wished to become grass so that our flesh might not remain grass forever. Hence he is placed, when born, in a manger, signifying that the holy animals, which under the Law were found fasting for a long time, are satisfied with the grass of his incarnation.

He who gave himself as food to the minds of mortals filled the manger at his birth, saying: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57).

## CHAPTER IX.—The same as above.

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXI, no. 3.) The Lord, born, is found by shepherds in a manger because his incarnation, which refreshes us, is recognized in the writings of the prophets.

## CHAPTER X.—“And on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

[Col. 1058D]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVII, nos. 28–29.) What is more difficult than for a human being born on earth, bearing earthly and fragile limbs, to ascend to the heights of heaven and penetrate the secrets of the heavenly spirits? Yet the Creator of those spirits came to us and displayed himself as human even among them, as the prophet says to the Father concerning him: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm 8:6).

Because he found between us and those spirits the scandal of a life at variance with theirs, by marvelous power and even more marvelous compassion he created the highest things, assumed the lowest, and joined the lowest to the highest. Hence, when the same King was born, choirs of angels came forth to announce him and sang a hymn. With the discord of wicked life overcome, they recognized as fellow citizens those whom they had previously despised, proclaiming with one harmonious voice: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

It is as though they plainly said: “Those whom wickedness had separated from us, let goodness now born on earth unite.”

Hence, before his incarnation, a human being is read to have worshiped an angel in the Old Testament, and yet was not forbidden to worship. But after the Mediator’s coming, when John had prostrated himself in worship before an angel, he heard: “See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers” (Revelation 19:10; 22:9).

What does this mean except that previously the angels calmly allowed themselves to be worshiped by human beings, but afterward refused human worship? It means that previously they rightly despised human beings, whom they knew to be more degraded, devoted to carnal corruptions and not yet redeemed from those corruptions. Later, however, they could no longer despise human nature as subject to that condition, because they saw it, in its author, raised even above themselves. For that which has already been subjected in the members ought not to be despised, since in the very head of the members it deserved to be honored as exalted.

## CHAPTER XI.—The same as above.

[Col. 1059B]

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book II, homily 7, no. 5.) Every sluggishness is a constriction caused by tepidity, whereas every kindness of love is a great breadth. Even if the resources that might be given to a needy neighbor are lacking, the substance of good will is abundant and sufficient for the reward of the kingdom, as it is written: “On earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

## CHAPTER XII.—“There appeared with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host” (Luke 2:13).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVII, no. 18.) We rightly call the angelic spirits soldiers of God, because we know that they fight against the powers of the air. Yet they carry out these battles not by labor but by command, because, through the help of the one who governs all things, they can accomplish whatever they desire to do against unclean spirits.

Concerning this army, when our King was born, it is written: “Suddenly there appeared with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host” (Luke 2:13).

## CHAPTER XIII.—“They found Jesus sitting in the temple” (Luke 2:46).

[Col. 1059C]

(In Ezekiel, book I, homily 2, no. 3.) In keeping with the order of reason, the word of teaching is not supplied except at a mature age. Hence the Lord himself, in the twelfth year of his age, wished to be found sitting among the teachers—not teaching, but asking questions. Thus, lest they dare to preach at an immature age, he who through his divinity always teaches the angels in heaven deigned, in the twelfth year of his age, to question human beings on earth.

Because he himself is God and Wisdom, the angels also drink from him, by seeing him, that with which they are satisfied in eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XIV.—“And Jesus himself was beginning” (Luke 3:23).

(In the Pastoral Rule, part III, admonition 26.) Although our Redeemer is the Creator in heaven and, through the power of his manifestation, is always the teacher of angels, he did not wish to become a teacher of human beings on earth before the age of thirty. In this way he impressed upon the rash the yoke of salutary fear, since even he who could not fall preached the grace of perfect life only at a mature age.

It is written: “When he was twelve years old, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem” (Luke 2:42). After his parents sought him, it is shortly added: “They found him sitting in the temple in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them” (ibid.).

We must therefore consider carefully that when Jesus is said to be twelve years old, he is found sitting among the teachers—not teaching, but questioning. By this example it is shown that no one who is weak should dare to teach, if that boy wished to be taught by asking questions—he who, through the power of his divinity, supplied the word of knowledge to those very teachers.

## CHAPTER XV.—“And he entered one of the boats” (Luke 5:3).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVII, no. 37.) Jesus entered Peter’s little boat and asked that it be taken back a short distance from the shore; then, sitting there, he preached to the crowds (Luke 5:3).

What else is signified by Peter’s boat than the Church entrusted to Peter? So that the Lord might preach from it to the crowds flocking together, he ordered it to be moved slightly away from the shore. He did not order it taken out into the deep, yet he commanded it to be removed from the shore, clearly signifying that his preachers ought to preach to inexperienced peoples neither matters too lofty concerning heaven nor merely earthly things.

## CHAPTER XVI.—“And he spent the night in prayer” (Luke 6:12).

(In the Pastoral Rule, part II, chapter 5.) The Truth itself, revealed to us through assuming our humanity, devotes himself to prayer on the mountain and performs miracles in the cities. He thereby lays out the way of imitation for good rulers, so that even if they seek the highest things through contemplation, they may nevertheless mingle with the needs of the weak through compassion.

Love rises wonderfully to the heights when it mercifully draws itself toward the path of its neighbors. And the more kindly it descends to lowly things, the more vigorously it returns to the highest.

## CHAPTER XVII.—“She has not ceased kissing my feet” (Luke 7:45).

(In the exposition of the Song of Songs, chapter 1, no. 5.) Compunction produced by love and kindled by desire is a kind of kiss. The soul kisses God as often as it is pierced by compunction in his love.

There are many who already fear God and already undertake good works, but they do not yet kiss him because they are not at all pierced by compunction for his love. This was well signified at the Pharisee’s banquet. When the Pharisee had received the Lord and inwardly disparaged the woman who was kissing his feet, he heard: “I entered your house; you gave me no kiss. But she, from the moment she entered, has not ceased kissing my feet” (Luke 7:44–45).

Everyone who already gives alms and applies himself to good works receives Christ, as it were, into a banquet and feeds Christ, because he does not cease to sustain him in his members. But if he is not yet pierced by love, he still does not kiss his footprints.

The woman who kisses is therefore preferred to the pastor, because the person who is pierced by inward ardor of mind in desire for the Lord is preferred to one who gives only external things.

It is rightly said: “She has not ceased kissing my feet.” For it is not enough to be pierced by love of God once and then rest; compunction must both exist and increase. The woman is praised because she did not cease kissing—that is, she did not cease to be pierced by compunction.

Hence the Prophet also says: “Establish a solemn day with gatherings, up to the horns of the altar” (Psalm 117:27). A solemn day for the Lord is the compunction of our heart. But the solemn day is established with gatherings when the mind is continually moved to tears by love.

If we were to ask: “How long are we to do these things? How long are we to be afflicted by tribulation?” he immediately adds the limit up to which this must continue, saying: “Up to the horns of the altar.” The horn of the altar is the exaltation of the inward sacrifice. Each person must therefore afflict himself until he reaches the height of the heavenly sacrifice—that is, until he reaches its joys. When we have arrived there, there is no longer any need to make a solemn day for the Lord from our lamentation.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—“Return to your home and declare” (Luke 8:39).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVI, no. 33.) Unless each of the elect had recognized the Lord, he would certainly not love him. Yet it is one thing to know through faith and another to know through sight; one thing to find through belief and another to find through contemplation.

For this reason all the elect, having come to know through faith the one they love, long also to see him by sight. Burning and yearning with love for him, they taste the sweetness of his goodness in the very certainty of their faith.

This was well signified by the man healed from demons in the region of the Gerasenes. He wished to depart with Jesus, but the Master of salvation said to him: “Return to your home and declare how much God has done for you” (Luke 8:39).

A delay is imposed upon one who loves, so that through the desire produced by delayed love the merit of his reward may increase. Thus almighty God becomes sweet to us through miracles, yet remains hidden in his exaltedness, so that by showing us something of himself he may kindle us in his love through hidden inspiration, while by concealing the glory of his majesty he increases the force of his love through the heat of desire.

## CHAPTER XIX.—“The crowds press upon you and hem you in” (Luke 8:45).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XX, no. 43.) Some people in the holy Church suppress rather than venerate the faith they claim to hold, since they desire more to gain their own profits in its name than to attain its benefits. But the elect, while taking care to preserve the merit of faith through right actions, draw near to knowledge of its author even amid the tumult of the reprobate. This is signified in the Gospel by the woman suffering from an issue of blood. When the Lord said of her, “Who touched me?” Peter replied by reasoning: “The crowds press upon you and afflict you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” [Col. 1061B] Immediately he added: “Someone touched me, for I perceived that power had gone out from me” (Luke 8:45). Thus many press upon the Lord, but one touches him, because the carnal among the members of the Church press upon the one from whom they are far away. Yet she deserved to hear the reason for the true answer when the Lord said to her: “Someone touched me, for I knew that power had gone out from me.” Behold, the crowds were pressing upon the Lord, but only she touched him who came to him humbly; for many even in the holy Church press upon the truth by acknowledging it, but neglect to touch it by living well. They press upon it and remain far away, because they follow divine knowledge in their professions but flee from it in their conduct; they press upon it, I say, but remain far away, because by their actions they contradict the very faith that they affirm in speech.

## CHAPTER XX.—“Someone touched me” (Luke 8:46)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book III, nos. 36–37.) While the crowd was pressing upon him, one woman touched our Redeemer. Hence our Redeemer immediately said to her: [Col. 1061C] “Who touched me?” When the disciples replied to him, “The crowds press upon you and afflict you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” he immediately added: “Someone touched me, for I perceived that power had gone out from me” (Luke 8:43). Thus many press upon the Lord, but one touches him, because the carnal among the members of the Church press upon the one from whom they are far away. Only those touch him who truly join themselves to him in humility.

The crowd therefore presses upon him, because the multitude of the carnal is tolerated with greater difficulty the more it is admitted within. It presses and does not touch, because it is importunate in presence but absent in life. Sometimes they pursue us with wicked words; at other times, with nothing but perverse conduct. For sometimes they persuade us to do what they themselves practice; at other times, even if they do not persuade us, they nevertheless do not cease to offer examples of iniquity. Those, therefore, who entice us to evil by words or examples are certainly our persecutors; from them we receive the contests of temptation, which we must at least conquer in our hearts.

## CHAPTER XXI.—“Let the dead bury their own dead; but you, go and announce the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:60)

[Col. 1061D] (In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XIX, no. 42.) We must know that sometimes lesser matters must be left aside for the benefit of greater ones. For who does not know that burying the dead is a meritorious good work? Yet to someone who had asked to be allowed to bury his father, it was said: “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you, go and announce the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:60). The service of this ministry must therefore be postponed to the duty of preaching, because by the former he would bury the dead in the flesh in the earth, whereas by the latter he would raise the dead in soul to life.

## CHAPTER XXII.—“No one who puts his hand to the plow” (Luke 9:62)

(In *Exposition on Ezekiel*, homily III, no. 16.) The Truth says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). To put one’s hand to the plow is, as it were, to open the soil of one’s heart with the plowshare of compunction in order to bring forth fruits. But the one who looks back is he who, after beginning a good work, returns to the evils he had abandoned.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—“Rejoice, however, that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20)

(In *Exposition on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 7, no. 17.) The Truth calls the disciples back from private joy to common joy when, as they return from preaching and rejoice in the subjection of demons, he admonishes them, saying: “Do not rejoice in this, but rather rejoice and exult because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). Not all the elect cast out demons, but the names of all the elect are nevertheless recorded in heaven. The disciples are therefore admonished to lay aside private joy and rejoice in a common and everlasting happiness. Whoever, then, rejoices in what another does not possess has become worse through the very abundance of his own possession and has a private joy.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—“Pouring in oil and wine” (Luke 10:34)

[Col. 1062B]

(*Pastoral Rule*, part II, chapter 6.) Mercy that gives just counsel and discipline that chastises piously ought both to be present in the heart. Hence, when the Truth teaches (Luke 10:33), the half-dead man is brought into an inn through the Samaritan’s care, and wine and oil are applied to his wounds, so that the wounds may be irritated by the wine and soothed by the oil. Whoever is responsible for healing wounds must therefore apply in wine the bite of pain and in oil the gentleness of compassion, so that what is putrid may be cleansed by wine and what is to be healed may be comforted by oil. Gentleness must consequently be mixed with severity, and a certain balance must be formed from the two, so that those under authority are neither ulcerated by excessive harshness nor weakened by excessive kindness.

## CHAPTER XXV.—“But Martha was occupied with much serving” (Luke 10:40)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book VI, no. 61.) Because the contemplative life is lesser in duration but greater in merit than the active life, this is shown by the sacred words of the Gospel (Luke 10), where two women are reported to have acted differently. Mary, listening to the words of our Redeemer, sat at his feet. Martha, however, was devoted to bodily service. When Martha complained about Mary’s leisure, she heard: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (ibid. 10:41–42).

For what is signified by Mary, who sat listening to the Lord’s words, if not the contemplative life? What is signified by Martha, occupied with outward service, if not the active life? Yet Martha’s concern is not reproved, while Mary’s is even praised, because the merits of the active life are great, but those of the contemplative life are greater. Hence Mary’s portion is said never to be taken away, because the works of the active life pass away with the body, whereas the joys of contemplation are strengthened more fully at the end.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—The same as above

[Col. 1062D] (In *Exposition on Ezekiel*, part II, homily 2, no. 9.) Those two women, Martha and Mary, fittingly represented both lives. One was occupied with much serving, while the other sat at Jesus’ feet and listened to the words from his mouth. When Martha complained to her sister that she neglected to help her, the Lord replied, saying: “Martha, you are occupied and anxious about many things; but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:40 ff.).

Behold, Martha’s portion is not reproved, but Mary’s is praised. For he does not say that Mary chose a good portion, but the best, so that Martha’s portion too might be shown to be good. Why Mary’s portion is the best is then added: “which shall not be taken away from her.” For the active life comes to an end with the body. Who, in the eternal homeland, will offer bread to the hungry, where no one hungers? Who will give drink to the thirsty, where no one thirsts? Who will bury the dead, where no one dies? [Col. 1063A]

Thus the active life is taken away with the present age, whereas the contemplative life begins here so that it may advance in the heavenly homeland. For the fire of love that begins to burn here grows more intensely in love when it sees the one whom it loves. The contemplative life, however, is not taken away, because when the light of the present age has been withdrawn, it is brought to perfection.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—“The field of a certain rich man produced abundant crops” (Luke 12:16)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XV, no. 26.) A perverse mind first longs through greed to gather the things it covets; and when, as though in the belly of avarice, it has accumulated many things, it is constricted once it is full. For while it is anxious about how to guard what it has acquired, its very satiety narrows it.

The field of a certain rich man had produced abundant crops. But because he had nowhere to store such great produce, he said: “What shall I do, since I have nowhere to gather my crops?” And he said: “I shall do this: I shall pull down my barns and build larger ones” (Luke 12:17). Thus, constricted by abundance, he said, “What shall I do?” He was feverishly agitated as though weighed down by a great quantity of food. Let us consider with how many desires he sought for his field to produce abundant crops. Behold, his desires were fulfilled, because the field produced abundant crops; but since he did not have sufficient places to store them, the rich man, now richer still, did not know what to do. O distress born from satiety! The miser’s mind is constricted by the abundance of the field; for by saying, “What shall I do?” he clearly shows that, oppressed by the desires of his prayers, he was struggling beneath a kind of burden of possessions.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—“Fool, this night they demand your soul from you” (Luke 12:20)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXV, no. 3.) However late the wicked may be taken from this life, they are taken suddenly and unexpectedly. Because they do not know how to foresee their end by reflection, what they had been unable to consider beforehand comes suddenly upon them. Suddenly the rich man was a fool: he abandoned the barns he was preparing and found the place of hell which he had not foreseen. In thought he was preparing his soul for one thing, but by the sentence of judgment he was sent to another. While he lived, he contemplated one thing; while he died, he experienced another. He left behind the temporal things he had long tested and found the eternal things he had not expected.

Therefore, because of this ignorance arising from his blindness, the divine sentence rightly says to him: “This night they demand your soul from you” (Luke 10:40). It was taken away in the night because it was lost in the darkness of the heart; it was taken away in the night because he did not wish to have the light of reflection by which he might foresee what he could suffer. Hence the Apostle Paul rightly says to the disciples who were thinking about the future: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you like a thief. For you are all sons of light and sons of day; we are not of night or darkness” (1 Thess. 5:4–5). The day of departure overtakes them like a thief in the night when it drives out the souls of fools who do not foresee the future.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXVIII, no. 12.) To gird one’s loins is either to restrain lust in one’s actions or to restrain it in one’s thoughts. The delight of the flesh is in the loins. Hence it is said to the holy preachers: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12:35). Lust is signified by the loins, and the brightness of good works by the lamps. They are therefore commanded to gird their loins and keep their lamps. It is as though they were plainly told: “First restrain lust within yourselves; then display to others examples of good works through yourselves.”

## CHAPTER XXX.—“But the servant who did not know and did things deserving blows” (Luke 12:48)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XV, no. 51.) There are some who, because the Truth says, “The servant who did not know his lord’s will and did things deserving blows shall receive few blows; but the servant who knew his lord’s will and did not act according to it shall receive many blows” (Luke 12:47–48), do not wish to know what they ought to do. They imagine that they will receive fewer blows if they do not know what they should have done. But not knowing is one thing; refusing to know is another. The one who wishes to grasp knowledge but is unable to do so is ignorant. But the one who turns his ear away from the voice of truth so that he will not know is judged not ignorant but contemptuous.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—The same as above

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXV, no. 29.) Often some people not only disdain doing what they reject, but even scorn knowing it. Because it is written, “The servant who did not know his lord’s will and did not do what was deserving shall receive few blows; but the servant who knew his lord’s will and acted according to it shall receive many blows” (Luke 12:47), they consider ignorance a remedy that will grant them impunity for sinning. Such people are darkened by the darkness of pride alone, and therefore they do not discern that not knowing is one thing and refusing to know another: not knowing is ignorance, while refusing to know is pride. They can have all the less excuse for their ignorance, the more that what they ought to know is set before them even against their will.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—“And the servant who knew his lord’s will” (Luke 12:48)

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, admonition 32.) This concerns the hidden retribution of judgment: the mind of certain people is enlightened so that it sees the evil it commits, but it does not strive to overcome it. Thus, the better it sees, the more disastrously it perishes, because it receives the light of understanding while not abandoning the darkness of its wicked action. For when they neglect the knowledge they have received as an aid, they turn it against themselves as a testimony; and they increase their punishments through the light of understanding that they had received precisely so that they might be able to erase their sins.

When their wickedness does the evil that it recognizes, it already tastes the coming judgment, so that, while it is held liable to eternal punishments, it is not meanwhile acquitted by its own judgment. It will suffer more severe torments there insofar as it does not abandon the evil that it itself condemns here. Hence the Truth says: “The servant who knew his lord’s will and did not act according to his will shall receive many blows” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—“Everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required of him” (Luke 12:48)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXII, nos. 8–9.) There is no secure joy in the divine writings from knowing either great or many things, but from guarding what one has learned. For whoever understands well recognizes what he ought to do as a result of understanding; and the more widely he is extended through understanding, the more earnestly he is bound to fulfill works. Hence the Truth says in the Gospel: “To everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and from the one to whom they have entrusted much, they will demand more” (Luke 12:48). Let us regard the understanding given to us as borrowed money, because the more that is entrusted to us through kindness, the more thoroughly we are held debtors in our work.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—“I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49)

(In *Exposition on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 5, no. 8.) The Holy Spirit is customarily represented under the name of fire. Of him the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:49). When the carnal mind receives the Holy Spirit, set ablaze by spiritual love, it mourns the evil it has committed. The earth burns when, as conscience accuses itself, the sinner’s heart is scorched and consumed in the pain of repentance. Hence it is written again: “Your God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24). Because he cleanses the mind he reproves from the rust of sins, our Creator is called both fire and consuming.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—The same as above

(In *Homilies on the Gospel*, homily 30, no. 5.) “I have come to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49). The hearts of earthly people are called earth, because, while they continually heap the lowest thoughts within themselves, they are trampled underfoot by evil spirits. But the Lord cast fire upon the earth when, through the breath of the Holy Spirit, he set the hearts of the carnal ablaze. The earth burns when the carnal heart, previously cold in its perverse pleasures, abandons the desires of the present age and is kindled toward the love of God.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—“When you go with your adversary to the magistrate” (Luke 12:58)

(In *Homilies on the Gospel*, homily 39, no. 5.) “When you go with your adversary to the magistrate on the way, make every effort to be freed from him, lest he perhaps hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison” (Luke 12:58).

Our adversary on the way is the word of the Lord, which in the present life is contrary to our carnal desires. The one who humbly submits to the Lord’s commandments is freed from this adversary. Otherwise, the adversary will hand him over to the judge, and the judge to the officer, because the sinner, guilty on account of having despised the Lord’s word, will be held liable in the judge’s examination. The judge will hand him over to the officer because he permits him to be dragged to punishment by an evil spirit, so that the spirit itself may extract from the body and force into punishment the soul that willingly consented to it in guilt. The officer throws him into prison because he is thrust into hell through the evil spirit, there to remain until the day of judgment, when the spirit itself will then be tormented together with him in the fires of hell.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—“The kingdom of God is like a mustard seed” (Luke 13:19)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XIX, no. 3.) When the Lord announced the likeness of the heavenly kingdom through the mustard seed, he said in the Gospel: “To what is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I compare it? It is like a mustard seed, which a man took and put in his garden; and it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of heaven rested in its branches” (Luke 13:18–19).

He himself is the mustard seed who, planted in the burial place of the garden, rose up as a great tree. He was a seed when he died, a tree when he rose again: a seed through the humility of the flesh, a tree through the power of his majesty. He was a seed because “we saw him, and there was no appearance” [of beauty] (Isa. 53:2); but a tree because he was “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3). The branches of this tree are the holy preachers. Let us see how far they extend. What is said of them? “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5). The birds rest in these branches because holy souls, lifting themselves above earthly thought on the wings of various virtues, breathe again from the weariness of this life in their words and consolations.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—“Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13:24)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XI, no. 68.) The mind, weighed down by its own mutability, is always driven toward something other than what it is; and unless it is held daily in its proper state by upright discipline, it continually slips into worse things. For whoever has abandoned the one who always stands has lost the state he could have possessed. Therefore, when it strives toward better things, it struggles as though against the current of a river; but when it relaxes its intention of ascending, it is brought back to the depths without effort. Because ascent involves labor and descent ease, the Lord admonishes those who are to enter through the narrow gate, saying: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13:24). Since he was about to speak of entering through the narrow gate, he first said, “Strive,” because unless the mind’s striving burns intensely, the wave of the world cannot be overcome—a wave by which the soul is continually called down to the depths.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—“We ate and drank in your presence” (Luke 13:26)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book I, no. 29.) Sacred Scripture is sometimes food for us and sometimes drink. It is food in obscure passages, because it is broken, as it were, by interpretation and swallowed by chewing; but it is drink in clearer passages, because it is imbibed just as it is found. The Prophet saw sacred Scripture as food to be broken by interpretation when he said: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4). [Col. 1066A] That is, the weak asked that the more difficult statements of sacred Scripture be broken down by interpretation, but no one capable of interpreting could be found.

The prophet saw sacred Scripture as drink when he said: “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55:1). If the open commandments were not drink, the Truth itself would not cry out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). The prophet saw food and drink lacking for Judea when he said: “Her nobles perished from hunger, and her multitude dried up with thirst” (Isa. 5:13). For only a few can recognize hidden things, while many perceive the open matters of the narrative.

Therefore he says that the nobles of Judea perished not from thirst but from hunger, because those who seemed to preside, while giving themselves wholly to outward understanding, had nothing to chew upon by examining the inner meanings. But when the more elevated fall away from inner understanding, the understanding of the little ones also dries up in outward matters. Hence it is rightly added there: “Her multitude dried up with thirst.” It is as though he plainly said: “While the common people abandon concern for their life, they no longer seek even the streams of the narrative.”

[Col. 1066B] Those who complain to the judge who condemns them testify that they have understood both the hidden commandments of sacred speech and its open teachings, saying: “We ate and drank in your presence” (Luke 13:26). They add by way of open explanation: “And you taught in our streets.”

## CHAPTER XL.—“I do not know where you are from” (Luke 13:27)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XVII, no. 2.) The Lord considers those whom he punishes, but he does not previously see those whom he does not know. For at the end he will say to certain people: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Luke 13:27). In a remarkable way, therefore, he both observes and forgets the life of the wicked, because those whom he judges by the strictness of his sentence he does not know insofar as concerns the memory of mercy.

## CHAPTER XLI.—“And behold, there was a certain man suffering from dropsy before him” (Luke 14:2)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XIV, no. 14.) For the wicked, to thirst is to desire the goods of this world. Hence our Redeemer heals a man with dropsy before the house of a Pharisee, and when he was arguing against avarice, it is written: “The Pharisees, who were avaricious, heard all these things and mocked him” (Luke 14:12). What, then, does it mean that the man with dropsy is healed before the Pharisee’s house (Luke 16), except that through one person’s bodily illness the illness of the heart is expressed in another? The more a man with dropsy drinks, the more he thirsts; and every avaricious person multiplies his thirst by drinking, because when he has obtained what he desires, he longs still more intensely to desire other things. Whoever desires more by acquiring more has a thirst that grows through drinking.

## CHAPTER XLII.—“Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses” (Luke 14:33)

(In *Exposition on Ezekiel*, book II, homily 3, no. 20.) “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). Some people abandon everything, but many renounce even while possessing, because they retain what they possess for use in such a way that they do not succumb to it through desire.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—“Coming to himself” (Luke 15:17)

(*Homilies on the Gospel*, homily 36, no. 7.) Often a person’s very humiliation brings him back to himself. The one who had left his father and squandered prodigally the portion of property he had received, after he began to hunger, came to himself and said: “How many of my father’s hired servants have an abundance of bread!” (Luke 15:17). He had indeed departed far from himself when he was sinning. And if he had not grown hungry, he would not have returned to himself, because only after he came to need earthly things did he begin to consider what he had lost with respect to spiritual things.

## CHAPTER XLIV.—“Quickly bring out the first robe” (Luke 15:22)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XII, no. 9.) No human being is without sin except the one who came into this world not from sin. And because we are all bound by guilt, [Col. 1067A] we die through the loss of righteousness. The garment of innocence formerly granted in paradise is stripped from us, and we are also consumed when the destruction of the flesh follows. Thus the sinful person dies in guilt, is stripped of righteousness, and is consumed in punishment.

The father deigned to cover the nakedness of this sinful son, and when he returned, he said: “Quickly bring out the first robe” (Luke 15:22). The first robe is the garment of innocence that the well-created human being received, but lost after being wickedly persuaded by the serpent. Against this nakedness it is also said: “Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments, lest he walk naked.” We guard our garments when we preserve the commandments of innocence in our minds, so that when the guilt of judgment strips us naked, repentance may cover us as we return to the innocence we lost.

## CHAPTER XLV.—“And put a ring on his hand” (Luke 15:22)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXIX, no. 12.) The younger son who returned to his father after squandering his property (Luke 15) received a ring as a gift. The Gentile people, who return penitently to God after losing immortality, are fortified by the seal of faith. Hence the Church is also told by her Bridegroom: “Set me as a seal upon your heart” (Song 8:6). A seal is placed on possessions so that they may not be violated by the presumption of robbers. The Bridegroom is therefore placed as a seal upon the heart when the mystery of his faith is impressed upon the keeping of our thoughts, so that the unfaithful servant—namely, our adversary—when he sees hearts sealed with faith, may not presume to break into them by temptation.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—“For what is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God” (Luke 16:15)

(*Homilies on the Gospel*, homily 28, no. 2.) What can be more worthless or more contemptible before God than to preserve one’s honor among human beings and not fear the eyes of the inner witness? Hence the Lord himself says: “You are those who justify yourselves before human beings, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among human beings is abominable before God” (Luke 16:15).

Take note, brothers; take note of what is said. If what is exalted among human beings is abominable before God, then the thought of our heart is as low before God as it is high among human beings; and the humility of our heart is as high before God as it is low among human beings. Let us therefore despise whatever good we do; let no work inflate us, and let neither abundance of possessions nor glory exalt us. For if we swell inwardly from an abundance of good things, we are despised by God. In contrast, the Psalmist says of the humble: “The Lord preserves the little ones” (Ps. 114:6). Because he calls the humble “little ones,” after stating this judgment he adds counsel. For as though we were asking what he himself had done in response to these things, he added: “I was humbled, and he delivered me” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XLVII.—“I ask you, Father, to send him to my father’s house” (Luke 16:27)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book VIII, no. 29.) The eye of the dead does not return to see good things, because once the soul has been stripped of the flesh, it does not return to perform righteous works. Hence the rich man who was tormented by the flames of hell, recognizing that he could not restore himself through action, strove not for his own benefit but for that of his surviving brothers, saying: “I ask you, father Abraham, to send Lazarus to my father’s house. For I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them lest they too come to this place of torment” (Luke 16:27–28).

Hope, even false hope, commonly comforts a sorrowful spirit. But in order that the reprobate may feel their punishment more severely, they lose even the hope of pardon. Therefore, handed over to avenging flames, he desired, as we have said, to help not himself but his brothers; he recognized that he would never be free from the torment of the fires, with the punishment of despair added to it. Hence Solomon says: “Whatever your hand can do, do it with all your strength, because there is neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld to which you are hastening” (Eccl. 9:10).

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—“For I have five brothers” (Luke 16:28)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book IX, no. 101.) The reprobate will see each of their followers with themselves in torment, illuminated by the flames, those for whose love they had sinned. Thus those who had loved their lives carnally against the commandments of the Creator will also be afflicted by the destruction of those very people, increasing their own damnation.

We gather this plainly from the testimony of the Gospel, in which the Truth announces that the rich man who happened to descend into the torments of eternal fire is described as remembering five brothers. He asked Abraham to send someone to instruct them, lest they should later come there and be tortured by the same punishment (Luke 16). Since, to increase his own pain, he remembered absent relatives, it is doubtless clear that shortly afterward he could also see them present, to increase his punishment.

What is surprising if he should see the reprobate burning with him, when, to increase his own pain, he saw in Abraham’s bosom Lazarus, whom he had despised? If, therefore, an elect man appeared to him so as to increase his punishment, why should we not believe that he can also see in torment those whom he had loved against God? From this it follows that those whom the reprobate now love in a disordered way they will then see with themselves in torments, in a remarkable order of judgment, so that the carnal kinship placed before the Creator may intensify the punishment of their own penalty by seeing those relatives condemned to an equal vengeance before their eyes. The fire, therefore, which torments in darkness should be believed to preserve light for the sake of torment.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—“Ten leprous men met him” (Luke 17:12)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book V, no. 28.) Heretics have this distinctive quality: they mix good things with evil so that they may easily deceive the understanding of their hearers. If they always spoke perversely, they would more quickly be recognized in their perversity and would persuade no one of what they wished. Again, if they always held correct opinions, they would certainly not have been heretics. But while they devote themselves to both through the art of deception, they infect good things with evil and conceal evil things within good things so that they may be accepted.

It is like someone who offers a cup of poison and first touches the mouth of the cup with the sweetness of honey. While what is sweet is sampled at the first touch, what is deadly is also undoubtedly swallowed. Thus heretics mix right things with perverse ones: by displaying good things, they attract their hearers to themselves; by presenting evil things, they corrupt them with a hidden plague.

Sometimes, however, corrected by the preaching of the holy Church and by exhortation, they are saved from this deviation of their understanding. The cleansing of the ten lepers in the Gospel (Luke 17) fittingly represents them. In leprosy, one part of the skin is turned bright while another part retains a healthy color. The lepers therefore represent heretics, because, while they mix perverse things with right ones, they spatter the healthy color with stains. Hence, so that they may be saved, they rightly cry out: “Jesus, teacher” (ibid.). Since they signify that they have gone astray in his words, they humbly call him their teacher in order to be saved. When they return to recognition of the teacher, they immediately return to the condition of healing.

## CHAPTER L.—The same as above

[Col. 1068D] (In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XVIII, no. 26.) To be able easily to persuade people of perverse things, heretics mix certain correct things into their statements, so that they may draw the souls of their hearers through correct ideas and strike them with perverse ones. Because in the commandments of God they vary through speech that is partly sound and partly unsound, they are fittingly represented in the Gospel (Luke 17) by the ten lepers. When diseased whiteness is spread over their healthy color, they are disfigured by this excessive whiteness.

Hence we are admonished: “Do not think more highly than one ought to think, but think with sobriety” (Rom. 18:3). Moreover, because they do not yet love God, about whom they think wrongly, nor their neighbor, from whom they are divided, they oppose the commandments of the Decalogue; and for this reason they come as ten to implore the Lord. Because they have mixed what is unsound with what is sound, they are marked by their diversity of color. But because they have offended against his commandments, they call him by the title through which they had offended, saying: “Jesus, teacher” (Luke 17:13). Hence they immediately deserved to be healed.

## CHAPTER LI.—“Wherever the body is, there the eagles will gather” (Luke 17:13)

[Col. 1069A]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXXI, no. 105.) Concerning souls departing from the body, the Truth gives this assurance: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will gather” (Luke 17:13). It is as though he plainly said: “I, the incarnate Redeemer, now preside in the heavenly seat; when I have released the souls of the elect from the flesh, I raise them to heavenly things.”

## CHAPTER LII.—“He neither feared God nor respected human beings” (Luke 18:2)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XIV, no. 31.) There are some who, after despising God in their minds, despise human judgments even more; they are not ashamed to carry out boldly every evil they desire. Hidden iniquity invites them to commit evil, and no outward sense of shame restrains them. Thus it is said of a certain wicked judge: “He did not fear God and did not respect human beings” (Luke 18:2). [Col. 1069B] Hence it was also said of certain people who sinned with shameless faces: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom” (Isa. 3:9).

## CHAPTER LIII.—“When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book I, no. 32.) The Mediator, whose knowledge knows all things, assumes our ignorance in his speech and, by assuming it, teaches us. Sometimes he therefore speaks as though from our uncertainty, as when he says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8).

## CHAPTER LIV.—“I fast twice on the Sabbath” (Luke 18:12)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XII, no. 36.) It often happens that the just and the unjust have similar words, while their hearts are always entirely different. Through the same words God is offended by the unjust and pleased by the just. For the Pharisee entered the temple and said: “I fast twice on the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess” (Luke 18:12). Yet the tax collector went away more justified than he.

King Hezekiah, too, when afflicted by bodily distress and brought to the extremity of life, said in a contrite prayer: “I beg you, Lord; please remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart” (Isa. 38:3). Yet the Lord did not despise or reject this confession of his perfection; rather, he immediately heard him in his prayers.

Behold, the Pharisee asserted that he was justified in action, while Hezekiah asserted that he was also righteous in thought. The very thing by which the former offended was therefore the means by which the latter pleased the Lord. Why is this so, except that almighty God weighs the words of individuals against their thoughts, and that words uttered with a humble heart are not proud in his ears?

## CHAPTER LV.—“How difficult it is for those who have money” (Luke 18:24)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book IV, chapter 3.) It is exceedingly rare for those who possess avarice to move toward rest; [Col. 1069D] for Truth itself says: “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 18:24). For those who here thirst to multiply their riches certainly despise the joys of the other life. Yet, to show that this is exceedingly rare and can come about only through a divine miracle, our Redeemer said: “With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”

## CHAPTER LVI — “And running ahead, he climbed a sycamore tree” (Luke 19:4)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXVII, no. 78.) If, then, we desire to be wise and to contemplate wisdom itself, let us humbly acknowledge ourselves to be foolish. Let us abandon harmful wisdom and learn praiseworthy foolishness. Hence it is written: “God chose the foolish things of the world, to confound the wise” (1 Cor. 1:27). Again it is said: “If anyone among you wishes to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3:18). [Col. 1070A] Hence the words of the Gospel narrative testify (Luke 19) that Zacchaeus, unable to see anything because of the crowd, climbed a sycamore tree so that he might behold the Lord as he passed by. For *sycomorus* is called a foolish fig tree. Thus little Zacchaeus climbed the sycamore and saw the Lord, because those who humbly choose the foolishness of the world contemplate the wisdom of God with insight.

The crowd hinders our smallness from seeing the Lord, because the tumult of worldly cares weighs down the weakness of the human mind, preventing it from directing its attention toward the light of truth. But we wisely climb the sycamore if we deliberately hold fast to the foolishness that is divinely commanded. For what is more foolish in this world than not seeking what has been lost, relinquishing possessions to those who seize them, returning no injury for injuries received, and indeed extending patience even when further injuries are added? He commands us, as it were, to climb the sycamore when he says: “From the one who takes away what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke 6:30). And again: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5:39).

[Col. 1070B] The passing Lord is therefore seen from the sycamore, because through this wise foolishness the wisdom of God, although not yet seen in its fullness, is nevertheless already perceived, as it were in passing, through the light of contemplation. Those who appear wise to themselves cannot see it, because, sunk beneath the elevated crowd of their thoughts, they have not yet found the sycamore tree by which to behold the Lord.

## CHAPTER LVII — “Here is your mina, which I kept stored in a handkerchief” (Luke 19:20)

(*Pastoral Rule*, part I, chapter 9.) Let every faithful person beware lest, binding the money received in a handkerchief (Matt. 25), he be judged for concealing it. To bind money in a handkerchief is to hide the gifts one has received in the idleness of sluggish torpor.

## CHAPTER LVIII — “By your endurance you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book V, no. 33.) That person is perfect who is not impatient with the imperfection of his neighbor. For one who cannot bear another’s imperfection and abandons him thereby bears witness against himself that he has not yet advanced to perfection. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “By your endurance you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

For what is it to possess one’s soul except to live perfectly in all things and to rule over every movement of the mind from the citadel of virtue? Therefore, whoever holds fast to patience possesses his soul, because he becomes strong against all adversities by the very means through which he rules himself by conquering himself. And by breaking himself commendably, he brings himself forth as unconquered with strength, because when he overcomes himself in his pleasures, he prepares himself unconquered for opposition.

## CHAPTER LIX — “Lest your hearts be weighed down by dissipation and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XX, no. 39.) The mind of the wicked, devoted to the service of this world and accustomed to the burdens of temporal affairs, even when it is permitted to be free, nevertheless hastens to remain subject to earthly toil. [Col. 1070D] Through the habit of its wretched way of life it seeks the threshing-floor of labor, so that it is unwilling to cease from the yoke of worldly servitude even when it is allowed to do so. The Lord was loosening this yoke from the necks of his disciples when he said: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down by dissipation and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34). And immediately he added: “And by the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly.” Again he says: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:28).

For what does the Lord mean by saying that he is meek in his teaching and humble, except that, having left behind the difficulties of practicing pride, he shows us level paths for living well?

## CHAPTER LX — “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke 22:43)

(In *Exposition on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 8, no. 25.) The Redeemer of the human race exalted the humanity that he assumed by descending beneath the angels when he ascended above the angels. We say that he was made beneath the angels in the same way that we have heard the Apostle proclaim that he was made under the law. We therefore understand the humanity he assumed to be beneath the angels because of that abasement in which he deigned to appear. For as soon as the Word became flesh, as soon as God became human, he was already in power above the angels.

Concerning him it is written before his Passion: “Behold, angels approached” (Matt. 4:11), “and they ministered to him.” Yet, in order to show the weakness of his humanity, it is again written concerning him: “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke 22:43). Thus, as evidence of both natures, he is described both as being ministered to by angels and as being strengthened by an angel. He is one in both natures, since the one who existed as God before the ages became human at the end of the ages. Yet before his Passion the angels minister to him, and an angel strengthens him. After his Passion and resurrection, the angels can minister to him, but they can no longer strengthen him.

## CHAPTER LXI — “And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly” (Luke 22:44)

[Col. 1071B]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXIV, no. 32.) The elect often fear intensely when, as they come to pay the debt of human existence, they see themselves drawing near to the strict Judge; and their fear becomes sharper in proportion as the eternal recompense draws nearer. At that time nothing empty flies before the eyes of the heart from the imagination of thought, because, with everything else removed, they consider only themselves and the one whom they are approaching. Dread increases as the recompense of justice draws near; and as the dissolution of the flesh presses upon them, the more closely the strict judgment seems already to be touched, the more vehemently it is feared.
