Even if they remember that they have never knowingly neglected the things they know, they nevertheless fear what they do not know. For they are wholly unable to judge and comprehend themselves; and as their departure presses upon them, they are terrified by a subtler fear. Hence our Redeemer, drawing near to the dissolution of the flesh while preserving the appearance of his limbs, entered into agony and began to pray more earnestly. For what could he, while in agony, ask for himself, he who, while on earth, granted heavenly things with authority (Luke 22:44)? Rather, as our death approached, he expressed in himself the struggle of our mind—the force of terror and fear that we experience when, through the dissolution of the flesh, we draw near to eternal judgment.

For no soul is then terrified without reason, when, after a little while, it encounters what it cannot change for eternity.

(No. 33.) We consider that we could not pass through the road of the present life without fault. We also consider that even what we have done praiseworthily is not without some guilt of ours if we are judged apart from mercy. For who among us could surpass or even equal the life of the fathers who came before us? Yet David says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, because no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2). When Paul said, “I am conscious of nothing against myself,” [Col. 1071D] he cautiously added: “But I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4:4). James says: “We all offend in many things” (James 3:2). John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

What, then, will tablets do if columns tremble? Or how will immovable shrubs stand if cedars too are shaken by the storm of this terror?

(No. 34.) Yet the souls of the righteous are often cleansed from every slight contagion by the very fear of death, and from the dissolution of the flesh itself they begin to receive the joys of eternal recompense. Often, indeed, through a kind of contemplation of the inward recompense, they rejoice even before they are stripped of the flesh; and while they pay the debt of their old condition, they already enjoy the gladness of a new gift.

## CHAPTER LXII — “And the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book VIII, no. 30.) The sight of the human being is the mercy of the Redeemer, which softens the hardness of our insensibility when it looks upon us. Hence the Gospel also bears witness: “Jesus looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken. And going outside, he wept bitterly” (Luke 22:61). But once the soul has been stripped of the flesh, the human sight does not look upon it, because after death he does not liberate the one whom grace did not reform unto forgiveness before death.

## CHAPTER LXIII — “For he had long desired to see him” (Luke 23:8)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book X, no. 53.) Herod wished to test the flames of this lamp when he desired to see Christ’s miracles, as it is written: “For he had long desired to see him, because he had heard many things about him; and he hoped to see some sign performed by him” (Luke 23:8). But this lamp emitted no ray of light before his eyes, because it showed nothing marvelous about itself to one who had sought it not reverently but out of curiosity.

The Redeemer, being questioned, remained silent; expected to perform miracles, he disdained to do so. Keeping himself hidden within himself, he left outside, ungrateful, those whom he discovered to be seeking external things. He chose rather to be openly despised by the proud than to be praised with empty words by unbelievers. Hence this lamp was immediately despised, as the text goes on to say: “Herod, with his soldiers, treated him with contempt and mocked him, clothing him in a white garment” (ibid.).

(No. 54.) But the despised lamp that endures mockery on earth flashes forth judgment from heaven.

## CHAPTER LXIV — “And he answered him nothing” (Luke 23:8)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXII, no. 38.) Holy men utterly refuse to display themselves in the trial of agitation; and when they cannot benefit their hearers, they even wish to be despised while remaining silent, lest they glory in displaying their wisdom. When they say something wisely, they do not seek their own glory but the life of their hearers. When they see that they cannot gain their hearers’ lives by speaking, they hide their knowledge by remaining silent.

We run, as it were, toward the life of the Lord as toward a sign set before us for imitation. When he saw that Herod sought not advancement but merely wished to marvel at signs or knowledge, he remained silent when questioned by him. And because he remained steadfastly silent, he departed from him mocked. For it is written: “When Herod saw Jesus, he rejoiced greatly, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard many things about him; and he hoped to see some sign performed by him.” Hence it continues: “He questioned him with many words. But he answered him nothing” (Luke 23:8).

The Lord’s silence is shown to be despised when the text immediately adds: “Herod, with his soldiers, treated him with contempt and mocked him” (ibid.). We who hear this ought to learn from it that whenever our hearers wish to learn what belongs to us, as though it were worthy of praise, but do not wish to change what is perverse in themselves, we should remain entirely silent—lest, if we speak from a desire to display ourselves, their fault, which already existed, should not cease, and ours, which did not exist, should arise.

(No. 39.) Someone may perhaps say: “How do we know with what disposition someone listens?” But there are many things that reveal the listener’s mind, especially when our hearers always praise what they hear but never follow what they praise.

## CHAPTER LXV — “For if they do this with the green wood” (Luke 23:31)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XII, no. 7.) By the wood, the incarnate Wisdom of God is symbolized, as it is written concerning her: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her” (Prov. 3:8). And as she herself says: “If they do this with the green wood, what will happen with the dry?” (Luke 23:31). He called himself the green wood and us the dry wood, because he possesses in himself the power of divinity, whereas we, who are merely human beings, are called dry wood.

## CHAPTER LXVI — “Was not our heart burning within us?” (Luke 24:32)

(*Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 30, no. 5.) Teachers have tongues of fire, because when they preach while loving God, they inflame the hearts of their hearers. The speech of a teacher is idle if it cannot provide the fire of love. Those who said, “Was not our heart burning within us when he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32), had received this fire of teaching from the very mouth of Truth.

When the word has been heard, the soul grows ardent, the coldness of torpor withdraws, the mind becomes anxious in its desire for what is above and alienated from earthly desires. True love, when it has filled the soul, torments it with tears; but while it is tormented by such ardor, it is nourished by those very torments. It delights in hearing heavenly commandments, and with every command by which it is instructed it is, as it were, inflamed by another torch. What previously lay torpid through desire afterward burns through words.

## CHAPTER LXVII — “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones” (Luke 24:39)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XIV, no. 72.) Our Redeemer, to disciples who doubted his resurrection, showed his hands and side and offered flesh and bones to be touched, saying: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

When I was in Constantinople and had presented to Eutychius this testimony of the Evangelist’s truth, he said: “The Lord did this for the reason that he might remove the doubt about his resurrection from the hearts of the disciples.” I replied: “What you assert is a most extraordinary thing: that doubt should arise in us from the very means by which the hearts of the disciples were healed of doubt. For what could be said more disastrously than that we should doubt the reality of his flesh on account of that by which his disciples were restored to faith, free from all doubt? If it is not asserted that he possessed what he displayed, then our faith is destroyed by the very thing through which the faith of his disciples was confirmed.”

He added: “He had a tangible body, which he displayed; but after the hearts of those who touched him had been confirmed, everything in the Lord that could be touched was transformed into some higher condition.”

To this I replied: “It is written: ‘Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him’” (Rom. 6:9). If, therefore, anything in his body could have been changed after the resurrection, then, contrary to Paul’s truthful statement, the Lord returned to death after his resurrection. No one would dare to say this, unless he denied the true resurrection of his flesh.

Then he objected: “Since it is written, ‘Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Cor. 15:50), how is it to be believed that flesh truly rises again?”

I replied: “In sacred Scripture, ‘flesh’ is spoken of in one way according to nature and in another way according to guilt or corruption. Flesh according to nature is meant where it is written: ‘This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh’ (Gen. 2:23), and: ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14).

“Flesh according to guilt, however, is meant where it is written: ‘My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh’ (Gen. 6:3), and where the Psalmist says: ‘He remembered that they were flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return’ (Ps. 77:39). Hence Paul also said to the disciples: ‘You are not in the flesh but in the spirit’ (Rom. 8:9). For those to whom he was sending his letters were certainly not without flesh; but because they had conquered the passions of fleshly desires, they were already, through the power of the spirit, not in the flesh.

“When the Apostle Paul therefore says that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, he wishes ‘flesh’ to be understood according to guilt, not according to nature. Accordingly, he immediately shows that he is speaking of flesh according to guilt when he adds: ‘Nor will corruption possess incorruption.’ In the glory of the heavenly kingdom, therefore, flesh according to nature will exist, but it will not exist according to the desires of passion, because, having conquered the sting of death, it will reign in eternal incorruption.”

## CHAPTER LXVIII — “But you remain in the city until you are clothed” (Luke 24:49)

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, admonition 26.) Truth itself, which could suddenly have strengthened whomever it wished, gave an example to those who would follow, so that the imperfect would not presume to preach. After fully instructing the disciples in the power of preaching, he immediately added: “But you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:39). We remain seated in the city if we confine ourselves within the enclosure of our minds, so that we do not wander outward through speech. Then, when we have been perfectly clothed with divine power, we may go forth from ourselves, as it were, to instruct others.

# BOOK FOUR. On Testimonies from the Gospel according to John

[Col. 1073]

## CHAPTER I — “As of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John 1:14)

[Col. 1073C]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XVIII, no. 12.) In sacred Scripture, “as” and “as if” are sometimes used not for comparison but for truth. Hence also the words: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John [Col. 1073D] 1:14).

## CHAPTER II — “Upon whom you see the Spirit” (John 1:33)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book II, no. 90.) It is written in the Gospel: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33). The Spirit comes upon all the faithful, but in the Mediator alone the Spirit remains continually and in a unique way, because he never abandoned the humanity of the one from whose divinity he proceeds.

The Spirit therefore remains in him who alone can do all things and can always do them. The faithful who receive this Spirit, since they cannot always possess the gifts of signs whenever they wish, rejoice that they have received him as though in a transient manifestation. Yet when Truth’s mouth again says to the disciples concerning this same Spirit: “He will remain with you and will be in you” (John 14:18), what does it mean that, by the divine voice, this same dwelling of the Holy Spirit is declared a sign of the Mediator when it says: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him”? If, then, according to the Teacher’s word, he remains also in the disciples, how will it still be a unique sign that he remains in the Mediator?

We understand this more quickly if we distinguish the gifts of the same Spirit.

(No. 91.) Some of his gifts are those without which one cannot reach life; others are those by which the holiness of life is displayed for the benefit of others. Meekness, humility, patience, faith, hope, and charity are his gifts, but they are gifts without which human beings cannot reach life. The power of prophecy, healing, different kinds of tongues, and the interpretation of speech are also his gifts, but they display the presence of his power for the correction of those who behold it.

In the gifts without which life cannot be attained, the Holy Spirit always remains, whether in his preachers or in all the elect. But in those gifts through whose manifestation not our life is preserved but that of others is sought, he does not always remain in preachers. He always presides over their hearts so that they may live well, yet he does not always display signs of power through them. Sometimes he withdraws himself from them in the manifestation of signs, so that the virtues may be possessed with greater humility precisely because what has been possessed cannot be retained.

(No. 92.) The Mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, has him present in all things, always, and continually, because that same Spirit proceeds substantially from him. Thus it is rightly said that, although he remains in holy preachers, he remains uniquely in the Mediator: in them he remains by grace for some purpose, but in him he remains by substance for all purposes.

Just as our body recognizes only the sense of touch, whereas the head of the body possesses the use of all five senses together—so that it sees, hears, tastes, smells, and touches—in the same way the members of the heavenly Head shine forth in certain virtues, while the Head itself burns with all virtues.

The Spirit therefore remains in him in a different manner, since by nature he never departs from him. His gifts by which one advances toward life cannot be lost without danger. But the gifts by which the holiness of life is demonstrated are often withdrawn, as has been said, without loss. The former are therefore to be held fast for our instruction; the latter are to be sought for the progress of others. In the former, fear should alarm us lest they perish; in the latter, when they are sometimes withdrawn for a time, humility should console us, because perhaps they were lifting the mind toward pride.

## CHAPTER III — “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1:48)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XVIII, no. 59.) In sacred Scripture, “to see” God sometimes means “to choose.” Thus it is written in the Gospel: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1:18), that is, “I chose you when you were placed under the shadow of the Law.”

## CHAPTER IV — “The Spirit breathes where it wills” (John 3:8)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXVII, no. 41.) The voice of God is heard when the inspiration of grace is conceived in the mind, when the insensibility of hidden deafness is broken, and when the heart, awakened to the pursuit of supreme love, is pierced by the cry of inward virtue. Yet the mind itself, enlightened by this voice of the Spirit that comes upon it and insinuates itself into the ear of the heart, cannot investigate it.

For this invisible power cannot be comprehended: by what channels it flows into the soul, by what means it comes toward it, or by what means it departs. Hence John rightly says: “The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes” (John 3:8).

To hear the voice of the Spirit is to rise, through the force of inward compunction, into love of the invisible Creator. But no one knows where it comes from, because it is not known on what occasions it pours itself upon us through the mouths of preachers; and no one knows where it goes, because when many hear the same preaching, it cannot certainly be understood whom it abandons and casts aside and in whose heart it enters and finds rest.

One thing is performed outwardly, but it does not penetrate the hearts of those who behold it in one and the same way, because the one who invisibly orders visible things plants, incomprehensibly, the seeds of causes in human hearts.

## CHAPTER V — “And no one has ascended into heaven” (John 3:13)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXVII, nos. 29–30.) Paul says: “For we know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, an eternal house not made by hands in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1). But if we too, who are from the earth, ascend into heaven, where is what Truth says again: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13)?

The same Truth immediately counters this statement when he says: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:4). His words do not contradict one another; rather, through what appears discordant, he kindles the effort of our minds to seek understanding.

All of us who have been reborn in his faith are certainly his body. Therefore, because the Lord became the head of his members through a wondrous dispensation of mercy, while the multitude of the reprobate is rejected, he is alone and yet also with us. No one, then, has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven, because, since we have already become one with him, he who came alone in himself returns there alone also in us.

And he who is always in heaven ascends daily into heaven, because he who remains above all things in his divinity draws himself daily toward heaven through the structure of his humanity.

## CHAPTER VI — “But whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXVI, no. 50.) There are two groups, namely the elect and the reprobate, and each group contains two orders. Some are judged and perish; others are not judged and perish; some are judged and reign; others are not judged and reign.

Those are judged and perish to whom the Lord’s proclamation says: “I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger and you did not welcome me; naked and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison and you did not visit me” (Matt. 25:42). To them he first says: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41).

Others are not judged at the final judgment, and yet perish. Concerning them the Lord says through the Prophet: “The wicked will not rise in judgment” (Ps. 1:6). And the Lord says concerning them: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). Paul says concerning them: “Those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law” (Rom. 2:12).

All unbelievers do indeed rise, but for punishment, not for judgment. Their case is not examined then, because they depart from the sight of the strict Judge already bearing the condemnation of their unbelief. Those who retain the profession of faith but do not possess the works of that profession are rebuked so that they may perish. But those who did not even hold the sacraments of faith do not hear the Judge’s rebuke in the final examination, because, already prejudged by the darkness of their unbelief, they are not deemed worthy to be rebuked by the denunciation of the one whom they despised.

At least those will hear the Judge’s words who retained at least the words of his faith. The others, in their condemnation, do not even hear the words of the eternal Judge, because they were unwilling to preserve his reverence even in words. The former perish according to the law, because they sinned while placed under the law. To the latter, in their destruction, nothing is said from the law, because they made no effort to possess anything belonging to the law.

A prince ruling an earthly republic punishes differently a citizen who commits an offense within it and an enemy who rebels from outside. In the citizen, he considers his own laws and condemns him with an appropriate verbal denunciation. Against the enemy, however, he wages war, employs instruments of destruction, and repays him with punishments appropriate to warfare. As for the enemy’s wrongdoing, he does not ask what the law says about it; nor is it necessary to destroy by the law one who could never be held by the law.

Thus, at the final judgment, legal denunciation strikes the one who, having professed the faith, avoided its works; but the one who is not held by the law of faith is destroyed without judicial denunciation.

(No. 51.) Among the elect, some are judged and reign: those who wipe away the stains of their life with tears. Redeeming their previous evils through subsequent deeds, they cover whatever unlawful things they have at some time done from the eyes of the Judge by the superimposition of almsgiving.

To those standing at his right hand, the Judge who comes says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me” (ibid., 35). He first says to them: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (verse 34).

Others are not judged and reign: those who transcend even the commandments of the Law through the perfection of their virtues. They are not content merely to fulfill all that the divine Law commands everyone, but, moved by a more excellent desire, they seek to offer more than they could hear commanded by the general precepts.

To them the Lord says: “You who have left everything and followed me, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Concerning them the Prophet says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3:14). And Solomon, speaking of the Bridegroom of the holy Church, says: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31:25).

These, therefore, are not judged at the final judgment but reign, because they come as judges with their Creator. Leaving everything, they carried out with more ready devotion what they had heard commanded generally.

For by a special command addressed to a few more perfect persons, and not generally to all, the young man heard: “Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. And come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). If a general command bound everyone under this precept, it would certainly be a fault for us to possess anything from this world. But one thing is what sacred Scripture commands generally to all, and another is what it commands particularly to the more perfect.

These people, therefore, are rightly not held under the general judgment, because through their way of life they surpassed the general commandments. Just as those are not judged and perish who, persuaded by unbelief, disdain to be held by the law, so those are not judged and reign who, persuaded by devotion, advance even beyond the general precepts of the divine Law.

Hence Paul, also surpassing the particular precepts, displayed more in deed than he had received by the institution of permission. For although he had received permission to live from the Gospel while preaching the Gospel, he both imparted the Gospel to his hearers and nevertheless refused to be supported by the Gospel’s resources. Why, then, should the one be judged so as to reign who received less to preserve but found more to live out?

## CHAPTER VII — “He was the burning lamp” (John 5:35)

[Col. 1077B]

(In *Exposition on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 11, no. 7.) It is not enough for the watchman to live on high unless he also continually draws his hearers toward what is above by speaking and sets their minds ablaze with love of the heavenly homeland through his words. But he acts prudently in this only when his tongue burns from the fire of his life. For a lamp that does not burn of itself does not kindle the object beneath it.

Hence Truth says concerning John: “He was the burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35): burning through heavenly desire, shining through the word.

## CHAPTER VIII — “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:37)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXXV, no. 28.) Truth says in the Gospel: “I will not cast out the one who comes to me, because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:37).

What does this mean? If he had done his own will, would he have cast out those who come to him? Who does not know that the Son’s will does not differ from the Father’s will? But because the first human being, wishing to do his own will, departed from the joy of paradise, the second, coming for the redemption of humanity, taught us to remain within by demonstrating that he did the will of the Father and not his own.

When, therefore, he does not his own will but the Father’s, he does not cast out those who come to him, because by subjecting us to obedience through his example, he closes the road by which we might depart. Again he says: “I can do nothing of myself, but as I hear, I judge” (John 5:30). For obedience is commanded to us until death. But if he judges as he hears, he obeys even when he comes as Judge. Thus, lest obedience appear burdensome to us until the end of the present life, our Redeemer shows that he preserves it even when he comes as Judge.

What wonder, then, if sinful human beings subject themselves to obedience during the brief span of the present life, when the Mediator of God and human beings does not abandon it even when he rewards the obedient?

## CHAPTER IX — “Rivers from his belly” (John 7:38)

(In *Exposition on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 10, no. 6.) In sacred Scripture, “belly” is sometimes customarily used for “mind.” Hence Jeremiah says: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain” (Jer. 4:19). Since he said this about a spiritual rather than a bodily belly, he added: “The senses of my heart are disturbed.” For it would not have contributed to the salvation of the people if the Prophet had proclaimed that he was suffering pain in his physical belly; rather, he suffered in his belly because he experienced anguish of mind.

But why should we produce the Prophet’s example when we have a clearer testimony from God? When Truth itself speaks, the Prophet must be silent, because a lamp has no brightness in the sun: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). Because holy preachings flow from the minds of the faithful, rivers of living water flow, as it were, from the belly of believers.

## CHAPTER X — “And one of you is a devil” (John 6:71)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XIII, no. 38.) The devil and all the wicked are already one body, so that often the body is designated by the name of the head, and the head is called by the name of the body. The body is designated by the name of the head when it is said of a wicked person: “One of you is a devil” (John 6:71). Again, the head is called by the name of the body when it is said of that apostate angel: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. 13:28).

## CHAPTER XI — “When Jesus therefore knew that they were about to come” (John 7:15)

(Regula Pastoralis, Part I, chapter 3.) The Mediator of God and human beings avoided receiving a kingdom on earth—he who, [Col. 1078B] surpassing even the knowledge and understanding of the heavenly spirits, reigns in heaven before the ages. For it is written: “When Jesus knew that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, he fled again to the mountain by himself” (John 6:15). Who could have ruled human beings more blamelessly than the one who would rule those whom he himself had created? But because he appeared in the flesh not only to redeem us through his passion but also to teach us through his way of life, offering himself as an example to those who follow him, he did not wish to become king; instead, he willingly approached the gallows of the cross. He fled the glory of an offered throne and sought the punishment of a shameful death, so that his members might learn to flee the world’s favors, not fear its terrors, love adversity for the sake of truth, and avoid prosperity with apprehension. For the former often stain the heart through pride, while the latter cleanse it through suffering. In prosperity the mind exalts itself; in adversity, even if it had sometimes exalted itself, it is brought low. In prosperity a person often forgets himself; in adversity he is recalled to awareness of himself, even unwillingly and under compulsion. In prosperity even good deeds already accomplished often perish; [Col. 1078C] in adversity, however, the sins of a long period are wiped away.

## CHAPTER XII.—“Let the one among you who is without sin” (John 8:7)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 14, no. 34.) For whoever does not first judge himself does not know what is right to judge in another. And even if he perhaps knows by hearsay what he ought to judge rightly, he is nevertheless unable to judge another’s merits correctly when his own conscience provides no standard for judgment based on innocence. Hence, when certain men were plotting against the adulterous woman and leading her away to punishment, it was said: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7). They were going to punish the sins of others while leaving their own behind. Thus they are recalled inwardly to their conscience, so that they may first correct their own faults and then reproach those of others.

## CHAPTER XIII.—“He spat on the ground and made clay” (John 9:6)

[Col. 1078D]

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 8, no. 49.) By the name “saliva” is understood the flavor of inward contemplation, which flows into the mouth from the head, because from the brightness of the Creator it scarcely touches those who are still placed in this life with a taste of revelation. Hence, when the Redeemer came, he mixed saliva with clay and restored the eyes of the man born blind (John 9): for heavenly grace, by mingling its contemplation with our carnal thought, sheds light upon it and reforms the human being from original blindness to understanding. Since nature, after expelling him from the joys of paradise, brought him forth already into this exile, the human being emerged, as it were, without eyes from birth.

## CHAPTER XIV.—“And it was winter” (John 10:22)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 2, no. 2.) Sacred writings, at the beginning of their narratives, express circumstances and indicate the limits of events. Sometimes they show what they are about to relate by the position of a place, sometimes by the position of a body, sometimes by the condition of the air, and sometimes by the quality of the season. [Col. 1079A] By the position of places, divine Scripture expresses the merits and limits of the events that follow. Thus it says of Israel that the people could not hear the words of God on the mountain but received the commandments in the plain, thereby indicating the people’s subsequent weakness: they were unable to ascend to higher things but, by living carelessly, loosened themselves in what was lowly.

By the position of a body it announces what is to come, as Stephen, in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 7), declares that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of Power. To stand is the posture of one who helps; and he is rightly seen standing who gives aid in the battle of conflict.

By the condition of the air the subsequent event is demonstrated. Thus, when the Evangelist saw that, while the Lord was preaching, no one from Judea would then believe, he prefaced the account by saying: “Now it was winter” (John 10:22). For it is written: “Iniquity will abound, and the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12). He therefore took care to specify the season of winter in order to indicate that the hearts of his hearers contained the cold of wickedness.

Hence, before Peter’s denial, it is stated that [Col. 1079B] “it was cold, and he was standing by the coals and warming himself” (John 18:18). For inwardly he had already grown numb to the warmth of charity, and, with weakness inflaming him, he was warming himself again toward love of the present life, as though at the persecutors’ fire.

The end of an action is also expressed by the quality of the season. Thus Judas, who would not return to forgiveness, is said to have gone out into the night to carry out his treacherous betrayal. As he went out, the Evangelist says: “And it was night” (John 13:30). Hence it is also said to the wicked rich man: “This night your soul is demanded of you” (Luke 12:20). For a soul that is being led into darkness is said to be demanded not in the day but in the night.

Hence Solomon, who received wisdom without persevering in it, is described as having received it in a dream and at night. Hence the angels come to Abraham at midday, but when they are about to punish Sodom, they are said to have come to it in the evening.

## CHAPTER XV.—“No one will snatch them from my hand” (John 10:28)

[Col. 1079C]

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 3, no. 6.) The holy man is handed over to the adversary’s hand, yet inwardly he is held by the hand of his helper. For he belonged to those sheep of whom Truth says in the Gospel: “No one will snatch them from my hand” (John 10:28). Yet to the enemy who seeks him it is said: “Behold, he is in your hand” (Job 2:6). Thus the same person is in God’s hand and in the devil’s hand. For when he says, “He is in your hand,” and immediately adds, “Nevertheless, preserve his life,” the gracious helper plainly reveals himself: he held the one whom he permitted to be seized, and, by giving him over, did not surrender the one whom he concealed while exposing him to the darts of his adversary.

## CHAPTER XVI.—“He groaned in spirit and troubled himself” (John 11:33)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 3, no. 30.) The soul of the Redeemer was not troubled by the necessity of temptation as we are, who are merely human beings and are often shaken when temptation breaks upon us. Our enemy, even though he was permitted to take him up onto a high mountain, even though he claimed that he would give him the kingdoms of the world, and [Col. 1079D] even though he showed him stones that could supposedly be turned into bread, was nevertheless unable to shake the mind of the Mediator of God and human beings through temptation.

For he deigned to undergo all these things externally in such a way that his mind, inwardly clinging to his divinity, remained unshaken. And whenever he is said to have groaned after being troubled in spirit (John 11:33), he himself, by divine ordering, determined the extent to which he would be troubled in his humanity. He presided immutably over all things while showing himself mutable in bearing the weakness he had assumed. Remaining inwardly tranquil, he ordered all that he did, even in turmoil, for the display of the humanity he had taken upon himself.

## CHAPTER XVII.—“And Jesus found a young donkey” (John 12:14)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 1, no. 23.) As the Lord was going toward Jerusalem, he is said to have sat upon a young donkey (John 12:14). What does it mean for him to come to Jerusalem while seated upon a donkey, except that, by possessing the simple hearts of the Gentiles, [Col. 1080A] he brings them to the vision of peace by governing and presiding over them?

## CHAPTER XVIII.—“Unless a grain of wheat falls” (John 12:24)

(*Homily 8 on the Gospels*, no. 1.) Through the prophet it is said: “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6). Having become human, he turned our grass into wheat, who said of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24). Hence he is laid in a manger when born, so that he might nourish all the faithful—holy creatures, so to speak—with the wheat of his flesh, lest they remain hungry for the food of eternal understanding.

## CHAPTER XIX.—“Then a voice came from heaven” (John 17:1)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 28, no. 4.) God speaks words through an angel when he is shown in an image; but the words of heavenly speech are heard, as when the Lord says: “Father, glorify [Col. 1080B] your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1). Immediately the reply is given: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again.” For God, who cries in time without temporal limitation through the force of his inward impulse, did not by his substance produce that voice which he articulated through human words bounded by time. Rather, speaking from the heavenly realm, he formed the words he wished his enemies to hear through the ministry of a rational creature.

## CHAPTER XIX.—“Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands” (John 13:3)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 3, no. 29.) When the Lord handed himself over, for our redemption, into the hands of Satan’s members, what else did he do but permit Satan’s hand to rage against him? Thus, by the very means through which he would outwardly perish, he might free us inwardly and outwardly.

If, then, Satan’s hand signifies power, he endured in the flesh the hand of the one whose bodily power he tolerated through spitting, blows, scourging, the cross, and the lance. [Col. 1080C] Hence, when he came to his bodily passion, he said to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). Yet he inwardly compelled this power, which he had externally granted against himself, to serve his own gains.

For Pilate—or Satan, who had become Pilate’s head—was held under the power of the one over whom he had received power. The one who is above had himself arranged what the persecutor, approaching from below, endured. Thus, although cruelty arose from the evil mind of unbelievers, that same cruelty nevertheless served the benefit of all the elect. He therefore graciously ordered inwardly what he wickedly permitted himself to suffer outwardly.

Hence it is said of him at the supper: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God, rose from supper and laid aside his garments” (John 13:3). Behold: as he was about to go into the hands of his persecutors, he knew that he had taken even his persecutors into his own hand. For since he knew that he had received all things, it is clear that [Col. 1080D] he also held those by whom he was held. Thus he might turn to the use of mercy whatever their malice, permitted against him, might rage.

## CHAPTER XXI.—“And he began to wash the feet” (John 13:3)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 1, no. 31.) The Lord rightly washed the feet of the holy apostles after preaching (John 13), so that it might plainly be shown that even in a good work the dust of sin is often gathered, and that the footsteps of those who speak are stained by the very means through which the hearts of those who hear are cleansed.

For often, while certain people speak words of exhortation, they inwardly exalt themselves, however slightly, because the grace of purification is conveyed through them. When they wash away the works of others by their words, they take up, as it were, the dust of evil thought from the good road.

What, then, did it mean to wash the disciples’ feet after preaching except to wipe away the dust of thoughts from the glory of preaching and cleanse the steps of the heart from inward exaltation?

## CHAPTER XXII.—“One of the disciples reclining” (John 13:23)

[Col. 1081A]

(*Preface to the Book of Morals*, no. 3.) It is indeed the custom of sacred Scripture that those who write it speak of themselves within it as though they were speaking of others. Hence Moses says: “Now Moses was the meekest of all the people who lived on the earth” (Numbers 12:3). Hence John says: “The disciple whom Jesus loved” (John 19:26). Hence Luke says (chapter 24) that two of the disciples were walking on the road, Cleopas and another—an “other” whom, by maintaining such deliberate silence, he showed, as some say, to have been himself.

The writers of sacred speech, therefore, because they are moved by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, offer testimony about themselves within it as though about others. Thus the Holy Spirit spoke through Moses about Moses; the Holy Spirit spoke through John about John. Paul too indicates that he was not speaking from himself when he says: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3).

## CHAPTER XXIII.—“By this everyone will know” (John 13:35)

[Col. 1081B]

(*In the Commentary on Ezekiel*, book 2, homily 5, no. 22.) We often see holy men perform wonders, accomplish many mighty works, cleanse lepers, cast out demons, drive away bodily illnesses by their touch, and proclaim future things through the spirit of prophecy. Yet all these things are not—or are not yet—the palm of victory, but rather a picture of palms. For these things are sometimes granted even to the reprobate.

Hence Truth says through the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them: ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you accursed, who work iniquity’” (Matthew 7:22).

But the one sign of election is steadfastness in charity, as it is written: “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 15:35). When the elect perform these miracles, however, they perform them in a very different way from the reprobate, because what they are inwardly before almighty God is shown outwardly through them.

There will be a palm of victory for them [Col. 1081C] where the struggle with death will already be no more. For the outstanding preacher saw that the true palm would then be given to the victorious, when he foresaw the resurrection taking place. He says: “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When this mortal body has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?’” (1 Corinthians 15:53–55). Perfect victory, therefore, will come when death has been completely swallowed up.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—“In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 4, no. 70.) Because in this life there is a distinction among works, there will undoubtedly be a distinction of dignities in the next, so that just as one person surpasses another here by merit, there one person may surpass another in reward.

Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2). Yet among those many dwelling places there will somehow be a harmonious diversity [Col. 1081D] of rewards, because such great power exists in that peace that each person rejoices in what another has received, even if he has not received it himself.

Hence those who did not labor equally in the vineyard nevertheless all receive the same denarius. There are indeed many dwelling places with the Father, and yet unequal laborers receive the same denarius, because the blessed joy will be one for all, although the exaltation of life will not be the same for everyone.

## CHAPTER XXV.—“The same as above”

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 35, no. 46.) Truth says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2). There are indeed many dwelling places with the Father, because in that life of blessedness each person, according to his unequal merit, receives an unequal place; yet he does not experience the loss arising from this inequality, because what he has received is sufficient for him.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—“And we will come to him” (John 14:23)

(*Homily 7 on the Gospels*, no. 2.) The Lord’s way is directed toward the heart when the word of truth is heard humbly. The Lord’s way is directed toward the heart [Col. 1082A] when life is prepared for obedience. Hence it is written: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

Whoever, therefore, raises his mind in pride, whoever pants in the fever of greed, whoever pollutes himself with the defilements of lust, closes the door of his heart against the truth. And, to prevent the Lord from coming to him, the succession of vices bars the chambers of his soul.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—“I leave you peace” (John 14:27)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 6, no. 53.) In sacred Scripture, complete peace is spoken of in one way and begun peace in another. Truth had given his disciples peace in its beginning when he said: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John 14:27). Simeon had desired complete peace when he prayed, saying: “Now, Lord, you release your servant according to your word in peace” (Luke 2:29).

Our peace begins from desire for the Creator, but it is perfected through manifest vision. It will be complete [Col. 1082B] when our mind is neither blinded by ignorance nor shaken by the opposition of its flesh. Since, however, we touch its beginnings when we subject either the mind to God or the flesh to the mind, the tent of the righteous is said to possess peace, because his body, inhabited by the mind, is restrained from perverse movements of desire under the ordering of justice.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—“The same as above”

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 24, admonition 23.) Tranquility in worldly affairs often tests the focus of our minds more severely, so that, to the extent that what they possess is not troublesome, the things that call them become less lovable, and, to the extent that present things delight them, eternal things are not sought.

Hence Truth himself, speaking and distinguishing earthly peace from heavenly peace, and provoking his disciples from the present toward what was to come, said: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John 14:27). “I leave,” that is, a peace that passes away; “I give,” a peace that remains.

If, then, the heart is fixed upon the peace that has been left behind, it never reaches the peace [Col. 1082C] that is to be given. Present peace must therefore be held in such a way that it is both loved and despised, lest, if it is loved excessively, the mind of the one who loves it be caught in guilt.

Those who are peaceful must also be admonished not to desire human peace so greatly that they fail altogether to rebuke the evil conduct of people and, by consenting to the wicked, separate themselves from the peace of their Creator. Otherwise, while they fear outward human quarrels, they may be struck by the rupture of the inward covenant.

For what is passing peace except a kind of trace of eternal peace? What, then, could be more foolish than to love footprints impressed in dust but not love the one who made them? Hence David, binding himself wholly to the covenants of eternal peace, testifies that he did not maintain concord with the wicked, saying: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become my enemies” (Psalm 138:21–22).

To hate God’s enemies with perfect hatred is both to love what they are and to rebuke what they do: to restrain the conduct of the wicked and benefit their life. [Col. 1082D] We must therefore consider, whenever we refrain from rebuke, how great a fault it is to maintain peace with the worst of people, if so great a prophet offered to God as a sacrifice what he had stirred up against himself for the Lord—the hostility of the wicked.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—“The prince of this world is coming” (John 14:30)

(*Homily 39 on the Gospels*, no. 8.) Among human beings there was one who, before his passion, said in an unrestrained voice: “I will no longer speak much with you. For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

Because he saw this man as mortal, the prince of the world believed that he might at some time [Col. 1083A] find something of his own in him. But the one who came into the world without sin went out from the world’s corruption without any sin.

For it is clear that, among all who are born from the pleasure of the flesh, the prince of this world undoubtedly possesses something of his own in either their speech, their thought, or their deed. Yet he could not seize them afterward or hold them beforehand, because the one who paid on our behalf a debt he did not owe rescued them from the debts they owed.

Thus our debts do not hold us under the authority of our enemy, because Christ Jesus, the Mediator of God and human beings, freely paid what he did not owe on our behalf. Since he paid on our behalf the undeserved debt of bodily death, he freed us from the deserved death of the soul.

He therefore says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” We must consequently take care and think daily, with great tears, how savage and terrible the prince of this world will be when he comes at the time of our departure, demanding his works from us—if he even came to God dying in the flesh and sought something in him in whom he could find nothing.

What, then, will we wretched people say or do, who have committed countless evils? What will we say to the adversary when he demands an account and finds many things of his own in us, except for the one certain refuge and firm [Col. 1083B] hope: that we have become one with him in whom the prince of this world both sought something of his own and was utterly unable to find it? For he alone is free among the dead, and we are released with true freedom from the service of sin because we are united to the one who is truly free.

## CHAPTER XXX.—“This is my commandment” (John 15:12)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 10, no. 7.) What should be understood in this passage as the law of God except charity, through which the commandments of life are always read in the mind so that they may be observed in action? For of this law it is said in the voice of Truth: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15:12). Paul says of it: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Romans 13:10). Again he says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

For what can the law of Christ more appropriately be understood to mean than charity? We truly fulfill it when, out of love, we bear one another’s burdens.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—“You are my friends” (John 15:14)

[Col. 1083C]

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 27, no. 28.) A friend of truth is one who loves right action. Hence Truth himself says to his disciples: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:14). A friend is said to be a guardian of the soul. Therefore, rightly, one who strives to keep God’s will in his commandments is called his friend.

Hence Truth again says to the same disciples: “But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (ibid., 15:15).

## CHAPTER XXXII.—“If I had not come and spoken” (John 15:22)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 25, no. 28.) It must be understood that sin is committed in three ways: through ignorance, through weakness, or deliberately. Sin committed through weakness is indeed more serious than sin committed through ignorance, but sin committed deliberately is far more serious than sin committed through weakness.

Paul sinned through ignorance when he said: “Though formerly I was a blasphemer and a persecutor and insolent, I received mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Timothy 1:13).

Peter, [Col. 1083D] however, sinned through weakness when one voice—that of a servant girl—shook all the strength of faith that he had shown toward the Lord, and with his voice he denied the God whom he held in his heart (Luke 22).

But because the fault of weakness or ignorance is more easily wiped away insofar as it is not committed deliberately, Paul corrected through knowledge what he had not known, and Peter, watering with tears the root of faith that had been shaken and was already, as it were, drying up, strengthened it.

Those about whom the Master said, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22), sinned deliberately. A little later he adds: “They saw and hated both me and my Father” (verse 24).

For it is one thing not to do good things and another to hate the teacher of good things, just as it is one thing to sin through rashness and another to sin through deliberation. Sin is often committed through rashness, yet condemned afterward through reflection and deliberation.

For it commonly happens through weakness that one loves the good but is unable to accomplish it. To sin deliberately, however, is neither [Col. 1084A] to do nor to love the good. Therefore, just as it is sometimes a more serious sin to love sin than to commit it, so it is more wicked to hate righteousness than not to have practiced it.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—“If I do not go away” (John 16:7)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 8, no. 41.) Truth says to those who love him: “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come” (John 16:7). It is as though he said plainly: “If I do not withdraw my bodily presence from the eyes of your attention, I will not lead you to invisible understanding through the Spirit who consoles.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—“The same as above”

(*Dialogues*, book 2, chapter 38.) Truth himself, in order to increase the disciples’ faith, said: “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (ibid.). Since it is clear that the Spirit, the Paraclete, always proceeds from the Father and the Son, why does the Son say that he will depart so that the one who never departs from the Son may come?

But because the disciples, seeing the Lord in the flesh, constantly longed to see him here with bodily [Col. 1084B] eyes, it is rightly said to them: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come.” It is as though it were said plainly: “If I do not withdraw my body, I do not reveal what love of the Spirit is; and unless you cease to see me bodily, you will never learn to love me spiritually.”

## CHAPTER XXXV.—“I will announce the Father to you openly” (John 16:25)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 30, no. 17.) The Lord explains the order of the heavens when he makes known to us how he presides over the elect spirits. He explains the order of the heavens when, after the darkness of our mind has been wiped away, he manifests himself in clear vision.

Hence he says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce the Father to you openly” (John 16:25). He asserts that he will announce the Father openly because, through the manifestation of his majesty then disclosed, he will show both how he arises from the one who begets him without being unequal to him, and how the Spirit, coeternal with both, [Col. 1084C] proceeds from both.

Then we shall plainly see how that which exists by being born is not subsequent to the one from whom it is born, and how the one who is produced by procession is not preceded by those who bring him forth. Then we shall plainly see how the one is three divisibly, and the three are one indivisibly.

The speech, therefore, of God who then announces is the visible brightness that raises us up.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—“The same as above”

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 30, no. 49.) In that contemplation of the joys we have received, we will no longer need to hear the words of teachers, because, escaping the difficulties of the present life, we will no longer need to receive from teachers the preaching of life.

Then what is written will be fulfilled: “No longer shall each person teach his neighbor, or each his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 31:34). Then what Truth says in the Gospel will be fulfilled: “I will announce the Father to you openly” (John 16:25). [Col. 1084D]

For the Son announces the Father openly because, as we said above, by being the Word he enlightens us with the nature of divinity. Therefore, at that time they will not seek the words of teachers, like little streams of human speech, when they are already drunk from the very fountain of truth.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—“I have spoken these things to you so that in me” (John 16:33)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 26, no. 26.) “I have spoken these things to you so that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have distress” (John 16:33). It is as though he said plainly: “Let confidence in me refresh you inwardly through consolation, because outwardly there will be something from the world that will press upon you severely in its rage.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—“My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 8, no. 12.) The Redeemer’s voice says: “My kingdom is not of this [Col. 1085A] world” (John 18:36). All of us, therefore, who are endowed with hope of heavenly things and are worn down by the practice of the present life labor in what belongs to another. Often we are even compelled to serve the reprobate, and we are wearied by labor that belongs to another.

Yet we receive our rewards, and by faithfully administering what belongs to another we arrive at what belongs to us. In contrast, Truth says to certain people: “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16:12).

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—“Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:16)

(*Pastoral Rule*, part I, chapter 5.) The Lord said to Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:16). When he immediately replied that he loved him, he heard: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” If, therefore, the proof of love is pastoral care, whoever, though strong in virtues, refuses to feed God’s flock is shown not to love the supreme Shepherd.

## CHAPTER XL.—“Another will gird you” (John 21:18)

[Col. 1085B]

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 31, nos. 69–70.) If a courageous preacher desires the glory of passion and gladly seeks to undergo the danger of death for the Lord, why does Truth say to that very preacher, Peter—who derived his strength from his name: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:18)?

How can one who is girded by another and does not wish to go where he is led rejoice in passion? But if we consider how the mind is shaken as passion and the fear of death approach, yet still rejoices in the coming reward of the kingdom, we understand how one who wishes to undergo the danger of a glorious struggle does not wish to undergo it, because in death he observes what he fears while enduring it, and [Col. 1086A] in the fruit of death he sees what he seeks while desiring it.

Let us see how Paul loves what he flees and flees what he loves. For he says: “I have the desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23); and, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” Yet he also says: “We who are in this dwelling groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:4).

Behold: he desires to die, yet fears to be stripped of the flesh. Why is this? Because, although victory gives joy forever, the punishment itself nevertheless disturbs him in the present. Although love of the reward that follows prevails, the force of pain still touches the mind without sorrow.

Just as a courageous man, when he is already girding himself with weapons for the battle that is near, both trembles and hastens, both shudders and rages—he seems to fear, as his pallor shows, yet he is driven forward intensely by anger—so the holy man, when he sees that he is drawing near to passion, is shaken by the weakness of his nature and strengthened by the firmness of his hope. He trembles at the approaching [Col. 1086B] death, yet rejoices that by dying he will live more truly.

For he cannot pass to the kingdom unless death intervenes. Therefore he both hesitates as though confident and is confident as though hesitating. He fears while rejoicing, and rejoices while fearing, because he knows that he cannot reach the prize in tranquility unless he crosses with labor what lies between.

So, when we wish to drive illness from the body, we sorrowfully drink the bitter cup of purgation. Yet, confident of the health that follows, we rejoice, because the body cannot otherwise reach health; and so, in drinking, we even take pleasure in what disgusts us.

# BOOK FIVE. Testimonies on the Book of the Acts of the Apostles

[Col. 1085]

## CHAPTER I.—“And while he was eating with them, he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem” (Acts 1:4)

[Col. 1085C]

(*Homily 29 on the Gospels*, no. 1.) To make known the truth of the Lord’s Resurrection, we must also note what Luke reports when he says: “While he was eating with them, he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem” (Acts 1:4). A little later he adds: “As they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts 1:9–10).

Mark the words; recognize the mysteries: he was lifted up while eating; he ate and ascended, so that through the reality of eating the truth of his flesh might be revealed.

## CHAPTER II.—“Behold, two men stood beside them in white garments” (Acts 1:10)

(*Homily 29 on the Gospels*, no. 9.) We must ask why angels appeared when the Lord was born, yet are not read to have appeared in white garments, whereas, when the Lord ascended, the angels sent to him are read to have appeared in white garments.

For it is written: “As they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments” (ibid.).

In white garments, joy and solemnity of mind are signified. Why, then, do they appear not in white garments when the Lord is born, but in white garments when he ascends, except that great solemnity then came to be for the angels, when God in human form entered heaven? At the Lord’s birth, divinity seemed to have been humbled; at the Lord’s ascension, humanity was exalted.

White garments are more fitting for exaltation than for humiliation. Therefore, at his assumption, the angels ought to be seen in white garments, because the one who appeared as humble God in his birth was shown as exalted man in his ascension.

## CHAPTER III.—“There was a crowd of people, almost one hundred and twenty” (Acts 1:15)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 35, no. 17.) Because the number seven signifies temporal things and the number eight signifies eternal things, the Holy Spirit [Col. 1086C] was poured out upon the one hundred and twenty believers residing in the upper room.

For seven and eight make fifteen. And if, counting from one to fifteen, we gradually rise by successive increments, we reach the number one hundred and twenty. This signifies that, through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, they learned both to pass beyond temporal things by enduring them and to desire eternal things with eager longing.

## CHAPTER IV.—“And he acquired a field from the reward” (Acts 1:18)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 9, no. 58.) In accordance with the manner of sacred speech, Peter also says of Judas: “He acquired a field from the reward of iniquity” (Acts 1:18). Judas could not have acquired the potter’s field with the price of blood, for, having returned the thirty pieces of silver, he immediately punished the crime of his betrayal in himself with an even more criminal death. Therefore, “he acquired” was said in the sense that he caused it to be acquired.

## CHAPTER V.—“Therefore, from these men who have been with us” (Acts 1:21)

(*In the Commentary on Blessed Job*, book 32, no. 27.) Every sin is an eleven, because when it is committed perversely [Col. 1086D] it passes beyond the Ten Commandments. And because sin is mourned in sackcloth, it is for this reason that eleven curtains of sackcloth are made in the tabernacle.

Hence the eleventh Psalm says: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed” (Psalm 11:1). Hence Peter, fearing that the apostles would remain at the number eleven, sought a twelfth by casting lots for Matthias (Acts 1:26). For unless he saw that guilt was signified by the number eleven, he would not have been so eager to complete the number of the apostles with twelve.

## CHAPTER VI.—“And suddenly there came from heaven a sound, as of a rushing” (Acts 2:2)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII, no. 2.)* What is written concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent spirit approaching, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues as if of fire appeared to them, and it sat upon each of them” (Acts I)—God appeared indeed through fire, but through himself he effected speech inwardly. For neither was God the fire, nor was that sound he; rather, by what he displayed outwardly, he expressed what he accomplished inwardly.

Because he made the disciples inwardly both inflamed with zeal and instructed by the word, he displayed fiery tongues outwardly. The elements were therefore brought forward as signs, so that their bodies might perceive fire and sound, while their hearts were instructed by invisible fire and a voice without sound. Outwardly, then, there was the fire that appeared; inwardly, the one that bestowed understanding.

## Chapter VII.—The same as above

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book V, no. 65.)* What is signified by “the sound of a gentle breeze” except the knowledge of the Holy Spirit, who, proceeding from the Father and therefore receiving what belongs to the Son, is poured subtly into the weakness of our understanding? Yet when he comes upon the apostles, he is shown through an external sound, as through a mighty wind, when it is said: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty spirit approaching” (Acts II, 2).

When the Spirit insinuates himself into the weakness of human understanding, he is expressed both by the sound of a mighty wind and by the voice of a gentle breeze, because in coming he is both mighty and gentle. Gentle, because he moderates his knowledge for our senses, so far as it can in any way be known; mighty, because however much he moderates it, nevertheless by his coming he disturbs and illumines the blindness of our weakness. By his illumination he touches us gently, but he powerfully shakes our poverty.

## Chapter VIII.—The same as above

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVII, no. 34.)* By “the mouth of God” the Only-Begotten Son may be signified. Just as he is called God’s arm because through him the Father accomplishes all things, so he is also called his mouth, of which the prophet says: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isaiah LVIII, 14). Through him he speaks all things to us, as though by the name “mouth” the Word were plainly indicated.

Just as we also commonly use “tongue” for words, so that when we speak of the Greek or Latin tongue, we indicate Greek or Latin words, so we rightly understand “the mouth of the Lord” itself as the Word. Hence the Bride says to him in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs I, 1). That is as though she said: “Let the sweetness and presence of the Only-Begotten Son, my Redeemer, touch me.”

By “the sound of the mouth,” however, the Holy Spirit of that same Lord may be signified. Hence, elsewhere, in signifying the same Spirit, it is written: “And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty spirit” (Acts II, 2). The sound therefore proceeds from the mouth of the Lord when his consubstantial Spirit, coming to us through the Son, breaks through the deafness of our insensibility. Thus, concerning that same unbounded and incorporeal sound, the mouth of the Lord says: “He shall receive of mine, and shall declare it unto you” (John XVI, 15).

## Chapter IX.—And there appeared unto them divided tongues as of fire (Acts II, 3)

*(Homily 30 on the Gospels, nos. 4, 5, and following.)* The Holy Spirit appeared above the disciples in fiery tongues and gave them knowledge of every language. What, then, is signified by this miracle except that the holy Church, filled with the same Spirit, would speak with the voice of all nations?

Those who attempted to build a tower against God lost the communion of a single language; but among those who humbly feared God, all languages were united. Humility therefore earned virtue for these, while pride brought confusion upon those others.

But we must ask why the Holy Spirit, coeternal with the Father and the Son, appeared in fire; why in fire and simultaneously in tongues; why he is sometimes shown in a dove and sometimes in fire; and why he appeared above the Only-Begotten Son in the form of a dove, but above the disciples in fire—so that he neither came upon the Lord in fire nor was displayed above the disciples in a dove.

Let us therefore return to the four questions proposed and resolve them. The Spirit, coeternal with the Father and the Son, is shown in fire because God is incorporeal, ineffable, and invisible fire, as Paul testifies: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews XII, 29). God is called fire because through him the rust of sins is consumed.

Concerning this fire Truth says: “I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?” (Luke XII, 49). The hearts attached to earthly things are called “earth,” because, while they continually produce within themselves thoughts directed toward what is below, they are trampled by evil spirits. But the Lord sends fire upon the earth when, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he sets the hearts of the carnal aflame. The earth burns when the carnal heart, previously cold in its own pleasures, abandons the desires of the present age and is kindled toward the love of God.

The Spirit therefore rightly appeared in fire, because from every heart he fills he drives away the torpor of coldness and kindles it with desire for his eternity.

He was shown in fiery tongues because the same Spirit is coeternal with the Son, and the tongue has the closest kinship with the Word. The Son is the Word of the Father; and because the Spirit is one in substance with the Word, the same Spirit ought to be shown in a tongue.

Or certainly, because the Word proceeds through the tongue, the Spirit appeared in tongues: for whoever is touched by the Holy Spirit confesses the Word of God, that is, the Only-Begotten Son. Whoever already possesses the tongue of the Holy Spirit cannot deny the Word of God.

Or certainly, the Spirit appeared in fiery tongues because he makes all whom he fills both ardent and eloquent. Teachers have fiery tongues because, while they preach in love of God, they inflame the hearts of their hearers. For the speech of a teacher is idle if it cannot provide the fire of love.

They had received this fire of teaching from the very mouth of Truth, when they said: “Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the Scriptures?” (Luke XXIV, 32). For when a saying has been heard, the spirit grows ardent, the coldness of torpor withdraws, the mind becomes anxious with heavenly desire, and is alienated from earthly cravings.

True love, when it fills the heart, torments it with tears; but while it is tormented by such ardor, it is nourished by the very torments it suffers. It delights to hear heavenly commandments; and with every command by which it is instructed, it is as though inflamed by another torch. What previously languished through desire afterward burns through words.

Hence it is rightly said through Moses: “In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deuteronomy XXXIII, 2). The reprobate are called the left, since they are to be placed on the left; the elect, however, are called God’s right hand. In God’s right hand there is a fiery law because the elect do not hear the heavenly commandments with a cold heart, but burn toward them with the torches of their deepest love. The word is brought to the ear, and their mind, angry with itself, is consumed by the flame of inward love.

The Holy Spirit was shown both in a dove and in fire because he makes all whom he fills both simple and ardent: simple in purity, ardent in zeal. For neither simplicity without zeal nor zeal without simplicity pleases God. Hence Truth himself says: “Be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Matthew X, 16).

Here it must be noted that the Lord wished to admonish his disciples neither about the dove without the serpent nor about the serpent without the dove, so that the simplicity of the dove might be kindled by the serpent’s shrewdness, and the serpent’s shrewdness moderated by the dove’s simplicity.

Hence Paul says: “Do not become children in understanding” (1 Corinthians XIV, 20). Behold, we have heard about the shrewdness of the serpent; now let us be instructed concerning the simplicity of the dove: “In malice be children” (ibid.).

For this reason it is said of blessed Job: “There was a man simple and upright” (Job I, 1). What uprightness is there without simplicity, or what simplicity without uprightness? Since, then, this Spirit teaches both uprightness and simplicity, he ought to be shown both in fire and in a dove, so that every heart touched by his grace may become tranquil through the gentleness of meekness and inflamed with zeal for justice.

Finally, we must ask why he appeared in a dove above our Redeemer, the Mediator between God and human beings, but in fire above the disciples.

Certainly, the Only-Begotten Son is judge of the human race. But who could have endured his justice if, before gathering us through gentleness, he had wished to examine our faults through the zeal of righteousness? Therefore, having become human for human beings, he showed himself gentle toward human beings. He did not wish to strike sinners, but to gather them. First he wished to gather them gently, so that afterward he might have those whom he could save in judgment.

The Spirit therefore ought to appear above him in a dove, since he did not come to strike sins already through zeal, but to tolerate them still through gentleness.

By contrast, the Holy Spirit ought to be shown above the disciples in fire, so that those who were simply human and therefore sinners might be inflamed against themselves by spiritual fervor, and might punish in themselves through repentance the sins that God spared through gentleness. For they could not themselves be without sin, since they adhered to heavenly teaching, as John testifies when he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I, 8).

The Spirit therefore appeared in fire among human beings, but in a dove in the Lord, because the sins that the Lord mercifully tolerates through gentleness we must carefully observe in ourselves through zeal for righteousness and continually burn away through the fervor of repentance.

Thus the Spirit was shown through a dove in the Redeemer, but through fire among human beings: the more the severity of our Judge has been tempered toward us, the more ardent our weakness ought to become toward itself.

## Chapter X.—Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved [by God] (Acts II, 23)

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, admonition 35.)* Concerning Jeremiah, sent to preach, it is said: “See, I have set thee this day over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant” (Jeremiah I, 10).

Unless he first destroyed what was perverse, he could not usefully build what was right; unless he uprooted the thorns of vain love from the hearts of his hearers, he would plainly plant the words of holy preaching in them to no purpose.

This is why Peter first overturned before building afterward. He did not admonish the Jews about what they should now do, but rebuked them for what they had done, saying:

“Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you by mighty works, wonders, and signs, which God did through him in your midst, as you know: him, delivered up by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, you afflicted and put to death through the hands of wicked men; whom God raised, having loosed the pains of hell” (Acts II, 23 and following).

Thus, destroyed by the knowledge of their cruelty, the more anxiously they sought the edifice of holy preaching, the more profitably they heard it.

Accordingly, they immediately replied: “What shall we do, brothers?” And they were at once told: “Repent, and be baptized every one of you.” They would certainly have despised these words of edification unless they had first salutarily discovered the ruin of their own destruction.

## Chapter XI.—Having loosed the pains of hell (Acts II, 24)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, no. 24.)* It must be carefully considered that he declares himself to have walked in the deepest parts of the abyss (Job XXXVIII, 16), for to walk belongs to one who is not bound but free. Whoever is held by chains necessarily has his steps impeded.

Since, therefore, the Lord bore no bonds of sin, he walked in hell: free, he came to those who were bound. Hence it is written: “I am become as a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm LXXXVII, 5).

For the Lord to walk in the deepest parts of the abyss is to find no hold of detention in the pit of condemnation, as Peter testifies when he says: “Having loosed the pains of hell, because it was not possible that he should be held by it” (Acts II, 24).
