## Chapter XII.—Repent, and let every one of you be baptized (Acts II, 38)

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, admonition 31.)* When Peter saw certain people terrified by consideration of their sins, he admonished them, saying: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts II, 38).

For although he was about to speak of baptism, he first introduced the lamentation of repentance, so that they might first immerse themselves in the water of their own affliction and afterward be cleansed by the sacrament of baptism.

With what state of mind, then, do those who neglect to mourn their past sins live secure in forgiveness, when the supreme Pastor of the Church believed that repentance must be added even to this sacrament, which principally extinguishes sins?

## Chapter XIII.—We ought to obey God rather than human beings (Acts V, 29)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII, no. 27.)* Behold, someone fearing either the loss of possessions or bodily affliction dreads the threats of earthly power and does not dare to defend the truth against the force of those who resist it.

Because Peter sees this person cramped by fear, he stretches him toward the breadth of virtue by displaying the line of his own example. For when he had been scourged by the rulers of the people and saw himself released for the very purpose that he should cease preaching, and when he was forbidden to speak in the future, he did not yield even for the present. He immediately replied, saying: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Acts IV, 29); and again: “We cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.”

The person who had previously been weak and afraid of present losses, while contemplating such examples of courage in the authority of the word, now follows Peter’s line; now fears no adversity; now despises the powers of the world that resist God, even when this involves laceration of the body.

Yet the more courageously he destroys the strength of his persecutors by enduring, and the more he yields to no terror amid adversity, the more often he places himself above others even in matters he encounters while situated among the faithful. He chooses his own counsels rather than theirs and trusts himself more than others.

While refusing to yield to unjust objections [variant: “obediences”], he exercises himself in virtue; but by refusing to accept the sound counsels of others, he steps beyond the boundary. Peter recalls him within the line of due measure. After pressing the authority of rulers by the freedom of his speech, Peter nevertheless heard, in humility of heart, Paul’s counsel concerning the Gentiles who were not to be circumcised.

Thus he knew how to raise himself against adversaries through authority, while not trusting himself in matters about which he did not think rightly; he exceeded the powers that swelled with the freedom of courage, while in the humility of gentleness he showed obedience in sound counsel even to lesser brothers. Sometimes he opposed others by himself, and sometimes, together with others, opposed himself.

In Peter’s deeds, therefore, a certain line of authority and humility is stretched before our eyes, so that our mind may neither fail to reach the proper measure through fear nor exceed the boundary through arrogance.

## Chapter XIV.—Whom God raised from the dead (Acts III, 15)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XII, no. 14.)* Because God is Trinity, the Holy Trinity—that is, the Father, the same Son, and the Holy Spirit—raised up the extinguished flesh of the Only-Begotten Son.

## Chapter XV.—May your money perish with you (Acts VIII, 20)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, no. 2.)* When holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, it does not burst forth from a desire for vengeance, but from an examination of justice. Within themselves they perceive God’s subtle judgment, and they recognize what curse ought to strike the evils rising outwardly. They do not sin in that curse because they do not disagree with the inward judgment.

This is why Peter hurled a sentence of cursing against Simon, who offered him money, saying: “May your money perish with you” (Acts VIII, 20). Because he did not say *is*, but *may it be*, he indicated that he had spoken not in the indicative mood but in the optative.

Likewise Elijah said to the two captains of fifty who came to him: “If I be a man of God, let fire come down from heaven, and consume you” (2 Kings I, 10). The outcome of both cases showed with what reason their sentences were confirmed by truth. Simon perished in eternal destruction, and the flame coming down from above consumed the two captains of fifty.

The subsequent effect therefore testifies with what intention a sentence of cursing is uttered. When the innocence of the one who curses remains intact, yet the curse consumes the one who is cursed even unto destruction, it is gathered from the outcome of both parties that the sentence was hurled against the guilty by one and the same inward Judge.

## Chapter XVI.—Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? (Acts IX, 4)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book III, no. 25.)* If the sufferings of our members did not touch our Head, he would certainly not cry from heaven to his persecutor on behalf of his afflicted members: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts IX, 5).

If our sufferings were not his punishments, Paul, converted and afflicted, would not have said: “I fill up those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ in my flesh” (Ephesians II, 6). Yet, already exalted through the resurrection of his Head, he said: “Who hath raised us up together, and hath made us sit together in heavenly places.”

Indeed, the sufferings of persecution had bound him on earth; but, pressed beneath the weight of his punishments, behold, through the glory of his Head he was already dwelling in heaven.

## Chapter XVII.—And immediately there fell from his eyes as it were scales (Acts IX, 18)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIII, no. 51 and following.)* It is said that a dragon’s body is covered with scales so that it may not quickly be pierced by a missile. Thus the whole body of the devil, that is, the multitude of the reprobate, when reproved for its iniquity, tries by every evasion available to excuse itself and casts up, as it were, certain scales of defense so that it may not be pierced by the arrow of truth.

Whoever, when reproved, prefers to excuse his sin rather than mourn it is covered, as it were, with scales, while he is assailed by the sword of the word by holy preachers. He has scales, and therefore the arrow of the word has no path by which to reach his inmost heart. It is repelled by carnal hardness, so that the spiritual sword cannot be driven in.

Saul had hardened himself against God through carnal wisdom when no arrow of evangelical preaching penetrated his heart. But after he had been struck by a powerful rebuke from heaven and blinded by the regard of the Most High—for he lost his sight in order to receive light—he came to Ananias and was illumined.

Because in this illumination he was deprived of the hardness of his defenses, it is rightly written of him: “There fell from his eyes as it were scales” (Acts IX, 18).

The hardness of a carnal covering had oppressed him, and therefore he did not see the rays of true light. But after his proud resistance had been overcome, the scales of his defenses fell away. They fell from the eyes of his body under Ananias’s hands, but they had already fallen from the eyes of his heart under the Lord’s rebuke.

When he lay pierced by the arrow of a lofty reproach, he already sought with a humbled and penetrated heart, saying: “Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?” (Acts IX, 6). Once the scales had been driven away, the arrow of truth had reached the inmost heart, for, having laid aside the arrogance of pride, he confessed as Lord the one whom he had attacked and, not knowing what to do, asked him.

It is pleasant to consider where that fierce persecutor is, where that ravening wolf is. Behold, the one who asks what path of the shepherd he should follow has now been changed into a sheep.

It must also be noted that when he said: “Who art thou, Lord?” (ibid., 5), the Lord did not answer him: “I am the Only-Begotten of the Father, I am the Beginning, I am the Word before the ages.” Because Saul refused to believe that the Lord had become incarnate and despised the weakness of his humanity, he heard from heaven what he had despised: “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom thou persecutest” (verse 8).

It was as though he said: “Hear from me in what is above that which you despise in me as below. You despair that the Author of heaven came to earth. Therefore recognize from heaven the human being who is of earth, so that you may fear in me the mysteries of weakness all the more, the more you perceive that through these they have been brought in the heavenly realms to the excellence of power.”

Therefore, in prostrating you, I do not at all assert to you that I am God before the ages; rather, you hear from me what you disdain to believe concerning me. After he had said “Jesus,” he added “of Nazareth,” further expressing his earthly dwelling.

It was as though he had said more plainly: “Receive the weakness of my humility, and cast off the scales of your pride.”

## Chapter XVIII.—They let him down by the wall (Acts IX, 25)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXI, nos. 56–58.)* Since the holy man opposes himself even to the wicked and evildoers when he is not sought out, it is rightly said of God’s horse: “He goes forth to meet the armed” (Job XXXIX, 21).

It is pleasing to contemplate how Paul, roused by the spurs of his rider against armed enemies, was inflamed by such fervor of zeal when the flame of zeal carried him to break into the crowds in the theater at Ephesus. For it is written:

“They were filled with wrath, and cried out, saying, Great is Diana of the Ephesians. And the whole city was filled with confusion; and having caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul’s companions, they rushed with one accord into the theater. And when Paul would have entered in unto the people, the disciples suffered him not. And certain of the chief of Asia, who were his friends, sent unto him, desiring that he would not venture himself into the theater” (Acts XIX, 28–31).

In these words we recognize with what force he would have rushed against the ranks of his adversaries, had the reins of charity not held him back through his friends and disciples.

But if we ought to confront enemies, voluntarily seek battle, and always put ourselves at risk in the course of our fervor, what does this same outstanding preacher confess about himself when he says:

“The governor under Aretas the king kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desirous to apprehend me: and through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands” (2 Corinthians XI, 32–33)?

What does it mean that this horse sometimes willingly attacks the ranks of the armed, and sometimes, as though frightened, hides himself from armed enemies, except that we must learn in his disciplined virtue both resolutely at times to seek the battle of our adversaries and prudently at times to avoid it?

For in everything we do, we must place the matter on the scales of the mind and weigh the burden on one side and the fruit of our labor on the other. When the burden outweighs the fruit, each person harmlessly avoids the labor, provided that he exercises himself in other matters where the fruit of gain outweighs the burden of labor. But when, in view of the fruit that follows, the measure of labor is either equal to or surpassed by the fruit, the labor is avoided only with grave fault.

Thus the holy preacher, when he saw that the minds of those persecuting him in Damascus were exceedingly stubborn, did not wish to clash with their opposition. He saw that he himself, whom he knew would benefit many, might be wasted there and might benefit either no one or only a few.

He therefore withdrew from the contest and preserved himself for other battles in which he could fight more successfully. It was not virtue that failed him in that place; rather, the place failed virtue. Therefore, as a very brave soldier, he sought the field of battle away from the narrowness of the siege.

But when he saw many necks of adversaries ready to be brought under the yoke of their own King, he did not fear to enter the battle, even at the cost of death. Thus, when he was going to Jerusalem and the disciples, foreseeing his passion through prophecy, tried to restrain him, he testified concerning himself, saying:

“I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. Neither do I count my life dear unto myself” (Acts XXI, 13; and XX, 24).

Thus, the one who here, undaunted even though his passion was foreseen, sought the hostile ranks taught that his flight there arose from prudent administration, not from fear.

## Chapter XIX.—Arise, and make your bed (Acts IX, 34)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIII, no. 46.)* A bed or couch signifies rest in good works. Hence, in the Acts of the Apostles, the apostle Peter says: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; arise, and make your bed” (Acts IX, 34).

What does “Arise” mean except “Abandon the evil things you have committed”? And what does “Make your bed” mean except “Perform the works that earn the reward in which you ought to rest,” so that by arising he may abandon what he did, and by making his bed he may find what he is to do?

The Prophet briefly comprehended both when he said: “Depart from evil, and do good” (Psalm XXXVI, 27). To depart from evil is to rise from that in which one lay. To do good is to prepare the works of reward in which one ought to rest.

Whoever abandons evil but still does not do good has indeed risen from that in which he lay, but has not yet made a bed on which he should rest.

## Chapter XX.—Cornelius, your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended (Acts X, 4)

*(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book II, homily 7, no. 9.)* First we come to faith, and afterward, through the degrees of spiritual gifts, we enter the way to heavenly life. We do not come to faith through virtues; rather, through faith we reach the virtues.

Cornelius the centurion, whose almsgiving was praised before baptism according to the testimony of the angel, did not come to faith through works, but came through faith to works. For the angel said to him: “Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God” (Acts X, 4).

If he had not believed in the true God even before baptism, whom was he praying to? Or how had almighty God heard him, if he was not asking him to perfect him in good things?

He knew, therefore, that God was the Creator of all things, but he did not know that his almighty Son had become incarnate. Nor could he have done good works unless he had believed, for it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews XI, 6).

He therefore possessed the faith through which his prayers and almsgiving could please God. By good action he merited that he should know God perfectly and believe the mystery of his incarnation, so that he might reach the sacraments of baptism.

Through faith, therefore, he came to works; but through works he was established firmly in faith.

## Chapter XXI.—Arise, Peter; kill and eat (Acts X, 13)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIII, no. 15.)* The jaws of the Church are its holy preachers, as is said under the figure of Judea through Jeremiah: “She weepeth sore in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks” (Lamentations I, 2). For in the adversity of the Church, those weep more who know how by preaching to break the lives of carnal people.

Through them the holy Church crushes the wicked from their vices and, as though swallowing them, converts them into her own members. Hence it is said even to the first preacher himself, as to the jaw of the Church: “Kill and eat” (Acts X, 13).

This is also why Samson held the jawbone of an ass and struck down his enemies (Judges XV). Our Redeemer, holding in the hand of his power the simplicity and patience of preachers, killed carnal people with respect to their vices; and when the jawbone had been thrown upon the ground, it afterward poured forth water, because the bodies of preachers given over to death displayed great miracles to the peoples.

## Chapter XXII.—The same as above

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, no. 56.)* “Kill and eat” (Acts X, 13). What is killed is slain with respect to life; but what is eaten is changed into the body of the one who eats it.

“Kill and eat,” therefore, means: “Slay them with respect to the sin in which they live, and convert them from themselves into your own members.”

## Chapter XXIII.—Arise; I myself am also a human being (Acts X, 26)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXI, no. 24.)* When Cornelius worshiped him, the first shepherd of the Church saw that honor was being offered to him beyond what was proper. He quickly returned to the equality of his own condition, saying: “Arise; I myself am also a human being” (Acts X, 26).

Who does not know that a human being ought to prostrate himself before his Creator, not before another human being? Because Peter saw that Cornelius was humbling himself before him more than he ought, he recognized that he was a human being, lest his mind swell beyond the limits of humanity, and thus broke the exaltation produced by the honor shown to him through consideration of the equality of their condition.

For the same reason, when John worshiped the angel, the angel recognized himself to be a creature, saying: “See thou do it not: I am thy fellow servant, and one of thy brethren” (Revelation XIX, 10).

Hence, when the prophet is carried away to behold sublime things, he is called “son of man,” so that, led to heavenly realities, he may remember that he is a human being.

It is as though the divine voice admonished him in clearer words, saying: “Remember what you are, lest you become exalted because of those things to which you are carried away; rather, let the memory of your condition moderate the height of your revelation.”

## Chapter XXIV.—And taking him, he circumcised him (Acts XVI, 3)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII, nos. 28–29.)* If, for the sake of our small good deeds, by which we advance when we perform them but perish if we abandon them, greater evils of labor threaten our neighbors, we must necessarily set aside increases in virtue, lest we cause losses of faith in those who are weaker. Otherwise what we do would no longer be virtue to the extent that, through its occasion, it destroys the foundations of virtue in the hearts of others.

Paul rightly extended this line of discernment before the eyes of those who understood. He prohibited the Gentiles who were coming to the freedom of faith from being circumcised; yet, while passing through Lystra and Iconium, he himself circumcised Timothy, who had been born of a Gentile father (Acts XV and XVI).

For he saw that unless he showed himself to be observing the commandments of the Law, he would arouse the fury of the Jews even against those who were then his companions. He therefore brought forward the force of his assertion and, without damage to the faith, protected himself and his companions from the savagery of persecution.

He did what he had forbidden to be done out of love for the faith, but turned into the service of faith what he had done as though it were not done faithfully.

Often virtue is lost when held without discernment, while, when it is discreetly interrupted, it is held more securely. Nor is it surprising if we understand this in spiritual matters when we see it happen in bodily things.

An archer’s bow is stretched through practice so that at the proper time it may be drawn with benefit. If it receives no period of relaxed rest, it loses the power of striking through the very use of its tension. Thus virtue is sometimes preserved in practice when, through discernment, it is temporarily set aside, so that afterward it may strike vices with greater strength, the more prudently it has ceased inwardly from persecution for a time.

## Chapter XXV.—There was a Macedonian man (Acts XVI, 9)

*(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book II, homily 1, no. 12.)* Our Redeemer held the measuring line and measuring reed in his hand when he deigned to admonish the apostle Paul through the appearance of a Macedonian man, so that this Macedonian man said: “Crossing over, help us” (Acts XVI, 9).

Yet the Spirit of Jesus did not permit the apostles, who wished to preach, to go into Asia. What does it mean that the holy apostles are called to go where perhaps they were not planning to go, while they are forbidden to go where they desired to go, except that the measuring line and measuring reed of hidden judgment are held in the hand, so that some may hear the words of life while others are by no means deemed worthy to hear them?

The measuring line is therefore drawn in one direction and pulled back from another.

## Chapter XXVI.—What does this babbler wish to say? (Acts XVII, 18)

*(Pastoral Rule, part II, chapter 4.)* In the minds of hearers, the quality of speech that has been heard is the seed of the thought that will follow, because, while speech is conceived through the ear, thought is generated in the mind.

Hence the outstanding preacher was called a “babbler” [literally, “seed-picker”] by the wise men of this world (Acts XVII, 18).

## Chapter XXVII.—For we are indeed God’s offspring (Acts XVII, 29)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XX, no. 41.)* “For we are indeed God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man’s device” (Acts XVII, 29).

We are called God’s offspring not because we were brought forth from his nature, but because we were created by his Spirit and will and renewed by adoption. Each person is raised to this nobility in proportion as, through the image he has received, he is renewed in imitation toward God’s likeness.

## Chapter XXVIII.—I testify to you this day (Acts XX, 26)

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book I, homily 11, §§9–10.) O how free from the blood of those entrusted to him was that outstanding preacher who said: “I am clean from the blood of all; for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:26). For if he had not declared it, he would not have been clean from their blood; because he strove to declare the whole counsel to them, he was clean from their blood.

By this statement we are confronted, constrained, and shown to be guilty—we who are called priests. In addition to the evils that are our own, we add the deaths of others, because we kill as many as we see going daily toward death, sluggish and silent. But when it is said, “I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 3:18), if in this passage bodily death is meant by the name “blood,” our fear concerning our silence is greatly increased. For if the one appointed as watchman over his subjects is held so gravely guilty even for the bodily death of one who must eventually die, with what guilt is he bound concerning the death of the souls of his subjects—souls that could have lived forever if they had heard words of correction?

Yet sins may more suitably be signified by the name “blood.” Thus, when someone was lamenting the sins of the flesh, he said: “Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. 50:16). The blood of the dying is therefore required from the watchman’s hand, because the sin of a subject is reckoned as the fault of the superior if he remains silent. There is therefore something he can do so that, even when the subject dies, he himself may be made free: let him rise, keep watch, and oppose evil deeds, as it is written: “Run about, hasten, rouse your friend; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids” (Prov. 6:3).

### CHAPTER XXIX.—The same as above

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, admonition 26.) Paul believed himself clean from the blood of his neighbors because he did not spare their vices when striking at them, saying: “I testify to you this day that I am clean from the blood of all; for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:26).

### CHAPTER XXX.—“Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee” (Acts 23:6)

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, admonition 24.) Whoever therefore unites wicked people in peace supplies strength to wickedness, because good people are oppressed more severely when those who persecute them do so with one accord. Thus the outstanding preacher, seized amid the severe persecution of the Pharisees and Sadducees, sought to divide among themselves those whom he saw united against him and gravely hostile. He cried out: “Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees; concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged” (Acts 23:6).

While the Sadducees denied that there was hope and a resurrection of the dead—things the Pharisees believed in accordance with the teaching of sacred Scripture—dissension arose among the persecutors, and that crowd, which had previously pressed Paul savagely in unity, was divided; Paul came out unharmed.

# BOOK SIX. Testimonies concerning the Catholic Epistles

### CHAPTER I.—“With whom there is no change” (James 1:17)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book II, §38.) Through James it is said: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow caused by turning” (James 1:17). Mutability itself is a shadow that would overshadow the divine light if it altered that light through some change. But because mutability does not belong to God, no shadow of turning interrupts his light.

### CHAPTER II.—Also concerning the same subject

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXII, §9.) A grave error of unbelief is committed if someone fears that, within that substance of divinity, tranquility may be changed by anger. The Creator of all things possesses supreme immortality precisely because he is not mutable in the manner of a creature. Hence it is said of him through James: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow caused by turning” (James 1:17).

### CHAPTER III.—The same, concerning the same subject

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXV, §9.) Every change is, as it were, an imitation of death. For that which changes kills what it was, so to speak, by separating it from what it had been, so that it ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not.

The true light, therefore—namely, our Creator—because it is not darkened by any changeability, is not overshadowed by any defect of its nature. For his being is to shine without mutability; for him not to be is the darkness or shadow of death. Hence it is written elsewhere: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow caused by turning.” The apostle Paul likewise says: “Who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light.”

But since we all know that both the human soul and angelic spirits were created immortal, why is God said by the apostle alone to possess immortality, unless because he alone truly does not die—he who alone is never changed?

### CHAPTER IV.—“If anyone thinks he is religious” (James 1:26)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VII, §58.) That no one who serves excessive talk can preserve the rectitude of justice is attested by the prophet, who says: “The talkative man shall not be directed upon the earth” (Ps. 139:12). Solomon likewise says: “In much speaking sin will not be lacking” (Prov. 1:17). Isaiah says: “The cultivation of justice is silence” (Isa. 37:17), indicating that the justice of the mind is laid waste when one does not refrain from immoderate speech.

James says: “If anyone thinks he is religious but does not bridle his tongue, deceiving his own heart, that person’s religion is worthless” (James 1:26). Again he says: “Let every person be quick to hear, but slow to speak” (ibid., v. 29). He adds further: “The tongue is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison” (James 3:8).

### CHAPTER V.—“For the anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James 1:20)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book V, §78.) “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James 1:2), because when a disturbed mind aggravates the judgment of its reason, it considers everything that fury suggests to be right.

### CHAPTER VI.—“For if anyone keeps the whole law” (James 2:10)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book 19, §§32–33.) When we are clothed in a garment, we are surrounded by it on every side. Thus the person clothed in justice as in a garment is one who protects himself everywhere with good works and leaves no part of his conduct exposed to sin.

For one who is just in some actions but unjust in others is like someone who has covered one side and left the other bare. His works are no longer good, because they are stained by the other evil works that have arisen. Hence it is said through Solomon: “Whoever offends in one thing will lose many good things” (Eccl. 9:18). James says: “Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James 2:10).

He carefully explained this statement of his own when he added: “For he who said, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘You shall not kill.’ Now if you do not commit adultery but do kill, you have become a transgressor of the law” (ibid., v. 11).

With the eyes of the heart therefore extended in every direction, we must maintain watchfulness everywhere. Hence Solomon rightly says: “Guard your heart with every watchfulness, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4:23). In saying “with every watchfulness,” he placed “every” before “watchfulness,” so that each person may examine himself carefully on every side and know that, for as long as he is in this life, he is stationed in battle against spiritual enemies: lest he lose through one set of actions the reward he gathers through others; lest the enemy close the gates on one side and open an entrance on another.

For if a city were fortified by a great rampart against ambushing enemies, surrounded by strong walls, and protected by sleepless watchfulness, yet one single opening were negligently left unguarded, undoubtedly the enemy would enter through it—the enemy who seemed to have been excluded on every side.

# CONCERNING THE FIRST EPISTLE OF SAINT PETER

### CHAPTER I.—“Into which the angels desire to look” (1 Peter 1:12)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, §91.) Through the first preacher of the Church it is said concerning God: “Into whom the angels desire to look” (1 Peter 1:12). Some people consequently suppose that the angels do not see him at all. Yet we know that Truth itself declared: “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18:10).

Does Truth therefore utter one thing and the preacher of Truth another? But when the two statements are compared, it is recognized that they do not disagree. The angels both see God and desire to see him; they thirst to behold him, and they behold him.

If they desire to see him in such a way that they cannot enjoy the fulfillment of their desire, desire without fruit would involve anxiety, and anxiety punishment. But the blessed angels are far removed from every punishment of anxiety, because punishment and blessedness never coexist at the same time.

Again, when we say that they are satisfied by the vision of God—for the Psalmist also says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16:13)—we must consider that satiety is usually followed by disgust. For the two statements to agree rightly, let Truth say, “They always see,” and let the outstanding preacher say, “They always desire to see.” Thus, lest desire contain anxiety, those who desire are satisfied; and lest satisfaction contain disgust, those who are satisfied desire.

They desire without weariness, therefore, because satisfaction accompanies desire; and they are satisfied without disgust, because that very satisfaction is continually kindled by desire.

So too shall we be when we come to the fountain of life itself. Thirst and satisfaction will be delightfully impressed upon us at once, but need will be far from our thirst and disgust far from our satisfaction, because we shall be satisfied while thirsting and shall thirst while satisfied.

### CHAPTER II.—“And you, as living stones” (1 Peter 2:5)

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book II, homily 1, §5.) Through the Psalmist it is said: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. 121:3). Because that inner vision of peace is constructed from the gathering of holy citizens, heavenly Jerusalem is built as a city. Yet, while it is in this land of pilgrimage, its stones are daily squared when it is struck by scourges and battered by tribulations.

This is the city—namely, the holy Church—which will reign in heaven but still labors on earth. To its citizens Peter says: “You also, as living stones, are built up” (1 Peter 2:5). Paul says: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Cor. 3:9).

This city already possesses here a great structure in the conduct of the saints. In a building, one stone supports another, because one stone is placed upon another; and the one who supports another is himself supported by another. For neighbors bear with one another in turn, so that through them the building of charity may rise.

Hence Paul admonishes us, saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2). Proclaiming the power of that law, he says: “The fullness of the law is charity” (Rom. 13:10).

For if I neglect to bear with you in your conduct, and you refuse to tolerate me in mine, from where does the building of charity arise among you—those whom reciprocal love does not join through patience?

In a building, as we have said, the stone that supports is itself supported. Just as I now tolerate the conduct of those who are still inexperienced in a life of good works, so I too have been tolerated by those who preceded me and carried me forward in the fear of the Lord, so that, having been carried, I might learn to carry others. But they too were carried by those who came before them.

The stones placed at the summit and outermost edge of the structure are indeed carried by others, but they carry no others. Those who will be born at the end of the Church—that is, at the end of the world—are tolerated by their elders so that their conduct may be shaped toward good merits. But because they are not followed by those who might advance through them, they carry no stones of the faithful structure above themselves.

Now, therefore, some are carried by us, while we have been carried by others. Yet the foundation carries the entire weight of the structure, because our one Redeemer bears the conduct of us all. Of him Paul says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3:11).

The foundation carries the stones and is not carried by the stones, because our Redeemer tolerates all that is ours, but in him there was nothing that needed to be tolerated.

### CHAPTER III.—“Not in costly clothing” (1 Peter 3:3)

(Homily 6 on the Gospels, §3.) Let no one therefore think that sin is absent from luxury and devotion to clothing. If this were not a fault, the Lord would in no way have praised John for the roughness of his clothing. If this were not a fault, the apostle Peter would certainly not have restrained women through his Epistle from desiring costly garments, saying: “Not in costly clothing” (1 Peter 3:3).

Consider, therefore, how great a fault it is even for men to desire what the Shepherd of the Church took care to forbid to women as well (1 Tim. 2:9).

### CHAPTER IV.—“Always ready to give an answer” (1 Peter 3:15)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIII, §24.) True doctrine flees the vice of arrogance in thought with all the greater force the more ardently it pursues the very teacher of arrogance with the darts of its words. It takes care not, by proud conduct, to preach more highly the very one whom it assails with sacred discourse in the hearts of its hearers.

For it strives both to proclaim humility—the teacher and mother of all virtues—in speech and to display it in life, so that among its disciples it may express the truth more through conduct than through words.

Hence Paul, speaking to the Thessalonians and, as it were, forgetting his own apostolic dignity, says: “We became little ones in your midst” (1 Thess. 2:7).

Thus the apostle Peter, when he said, “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for an account of the hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15), affirmed that a manner of teaching must be preserved even in the knowledge of doctrine, adding: “But with gentleness and fear, keeping a good conscience.”

### CHAPTER V.—“As each has received grace” (1 Peter 4:10)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII, §22.) Our Creator and governor so orders all things that the one who could become proud of the gift he possesses is humbled by the virtue he does not possess.

He orders all things so that, while he raises each person through the grace he bestows, he also subjects one person to another through their unequal gifts. Each should regard the person subject to him as better in another gift; and although he may perceive himself to excel in certain respects, he should nevertheless place himself beneath the one whom he surpasses in other respects.

He orders all things so that, while each gift belongs to everyone through a certain bond of charity, everything belonging to each becomes common to all. Each person should possess in another what he has not received himself, while humbly offering to another for possession what he has received.

Hence Peter says: “As each has received a gift, administer it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Peter 4:10). The manifold grace of God is then well administered when the gift received is believed to belong also to the one who does not possess it, and when it is regarded as having been given for the sake of the person to whom it is devoted.

### CHAPTER VI.—“If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God” (1 Peter 4:11)

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book I, homily 7, §21.) Our good things are not from ourselves; we received them from the one through whom we came into being. Therefore, the more clearly we see that our Creator has given them to us for the common good, the less we should keep them as private possessions.

Hence the apostle Peter rightly adds in exhortation concerning this matter: “As good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Peter 4:10), and further: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God; if anyone ministers, let him do so as from the power that God supplies” (ibid., v. 11).

It is as though he were saying plainly: Humbly devote your good to your neighbors, because you know that what you possess is not from yourselves.

### CHAPTER VII.—“For it is time for judgment to begin” (1 Peter 4:17)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, §90.) From the life and labor of the good we now learn how severely we shall be struck afterward if we do not wish to be corrected while there is still time. We see God’s elect both practicing holy deeds and enduring many cruel things.

From this it follows how severely the strict Judge strikes those whom he rejects, if here he afflicts those whom he loves. Peter bears witness to this when he says: “It is time for judgment to begin with the household of God. And if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the gospel of God?” (1 Peter 4:17).

### CHAPTER VIII.—“And if the righteous scarcely” (1 Peter 4:18)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book V, §22.) It is rightly added: “And indignation came upon me” (Job 3:25). With great skill in teaching, he placed righteous deeds before the words he was about to utter, so that each person might consider what punishments await sinners afterward, if even the righteous are chastised here with such powerful scourges.

Hence Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin with the household of God; and if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear?” (1 Peter 4:17).

# CONCERNING THE SECOND EPISTLE OF SAINT PETER

### CHAPTER I.—“Supply virtue in your faith” (2 Peter 1:5)

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, admonition 20.) If impatience did not often drive the minds of those practicing abstinence from the bosom of tranquility, Peter would not, after saying, “Supply virtue in your faith, and in virtue knowledge, and in knowledge abstinence” (2 Peter 1:15), immediately and watchfully have added: “And in abstinence, patience.”

He foresaw that those practicing abstinence might lack patience and admonished them so that patience might be present in them.

### CHAPTER II.—“A voice having come down to God” (2 Peter 1:17)

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book II, homily 6, §11.) There were some who claimed that the Second Epistle of Peter, in which Paul’s Epistles are praised, was not written by Peter. But if they had carefully considered the words of that Epistle, they might have reached a very different judgment. For it is written there: “A voice of this kind came to him from the magnificent glory: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’” It then adds: “And we ourselves heard this voice when we were with him on the holy mountain” (1 Peter 1:17).

Let them therefore read the Gospel, and they will immediately recognize that, when this voice came from heaven, the apostle Peter was standing with the Lord on the mountain. He therefore wrote this Epistle—the one who heard this voice concerning the Lord on the mountain.

### CHAPTER III.—“And we have the prophetic word made more firm” (2 Peter 1:19)

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book II, homily 3, §17.) So that the holy apostles might believe the mystery of the Lord’s perfect incarnation, the preaching of those who were able both to see and to proclaim it before it happened prevailed.

Hence the first of the apostles, clearly a great pillar of the true tabernacle, rightly says: “We have the prophetic word made more firm, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Peter 1:19).

In these words he indicates that, although the mind has risen to lofty things from the summit, it remains bound there in faith. The lamp of prophetic speech already shines for those who understand, but it remains covered by the obscurities of allegories for those who do not yet understand.

Hence the Psalmist also says concerning the same prophetic words: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 18:12), because knowledge is hidden in the prophets.

### CHAPTER IV.—“And as to a lamp shining” (2 Peter 1:19)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX, §18.) The name “lamp” signifies the light of sacred Scripture. Concerning it the shepherd of the Church himself says: “We have the prophetic word made more firm, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Peter 1:19). The Psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord” (Ps. 118:105).

Because our chief faculty is the mind, the mind is called by the designation “head.” Hence the Psalmist says: “You have anointed my head with oil” (Ps. 23:5), as though he were saying plainly: “You have filled my mind with the richness of charity.”

Now, therefore, the lamp shines over the head of the Church, because sacred utterances illuminate the darkness of our mind, so that, in this dark place of the present life, as we receive the light of God’s words, we may see what ought to be done.

Now it walks by the light amid darkness, because the holy universal Church, although it cannot penetrate the hidden thoughts of another—since it is as though it cannot recognize a face at night—nevertheless sets its steps in good works, guided by the light of the heavenly utterance.

### CHAPTER V.—“As also our most beloved brother” (2 Peter 3:15)

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book II, homily 6, §9.) The first of the apostles, while giving many admonitions to the disciples and recognizing that some people disparaged Paul’s writings, says: “Our most beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you, speaking in them about these things. There are some things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” (2 Peter 3:15).

Behold, Peter asserts in his Epistles that Paul is to be admired in what he wrote. Behold, Paul writes in his Epistles that Peter is blameworthy. Certainly, if Peter had not read Paul’s Epistles, he would not have praised them; but if he read them, he found that he himself was called blameworthy there.

As a friend of truth, therefore, he praised even what had reproved him, and this very thing pleased him: that he had not pleased Paul in those matters in which he had thought differently from what he ought.

Consider, I beg you, dearest brothers, at what height of mind he stood who praised those Epistles in which he found himself described as blameworthy. What great gentleness, what tranquility of spirit, what steadfastness and unshaken composure could there have been?

# CONCERNING THE FIRST EPISTLE OF SAINT JOHN

### CHAPTER I.—“But if anyone sins, we have an advocate” (1 John 2:1)

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book I, homily 7, §24.) It is necessary for us, who are still little ones, always to place before the eyes of our mind both the virtues and the tears of the perfect. Let us imitate what we see in them, so that, when we begin to grow through successive advances, we may be able to cover the evils we have committed from that strict judgment.

In constant tears and in our daily repentance, we have a priest in heaven who intercedes for us. Concerning him it is also said through John: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 2:1).

Our spirit rejoices when we hear of the power of our advocate, but fear again wounds our rejoicing, because the one who is our advocate is called righteous. We do not have righteous causes, for a righteous advocate in no way undertakes unjust causes, nor does he consent to speak in defense of injustice.

What then shall we do, my dearest brothers? But behold, what we should do comes to mind: let us both abandon and accuse the evils we have committed. It is written: “The righteous person is the first to accuse himself” (Prov. 18:17). For any sinner who turns back in tears already begins to be righteous when he begins to accuse what he has done.

Why should the one who now rages through tears against his own injustice not be righteous? Our righteous advocate will therefore defend us as righteous in judgment, because we recognize and accuse ourselves as unjust. Let us therefore trust not in our tears or in our deeds, but in the plea of our advocate.

### CHAPTER II.—“The one who says, ‘I love God,’ and his commandments” (1 John 2:4)

(Homily 30 on the Gospels, §1.) The proof of love is the manifestation of a deed. Hence the same John says in his Epistle: “Whoever says, ‘I love God,’ but does not keep his commandments, is a liar” (1 John 2:4).

We truly love God if we restrain ourselves from our pleasures for the sake of his commandments. For whoever still flows away through unlawful desires certainly does not love God, because in his own will he contradicts God.

### CHAPTER III.—“Do not love the world or the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15)

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book II, homily 7, §17.) John admonishes us, saying: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world” (ibid., v. 15). He immediately supplies the reason: “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”

No one can serve two masters, because he cannot love transitory and eternal things at the same time. If we love eternity, we possess all temporal things for use, not for affection.

He immediately adds the same reason, saying: “For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16). People desire to have something, and more than is necessary, so that they may become proud through possessing it and exalt themselves in their thoughts because someone else does not have it.

### CHAPTER IV.—“If anyone loves the world, the love” (1 John 2:15)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, §16.) Whoever is conquered by love of earthly things can in no way take delight in God. The soul cannot exist without delight; it delights either in lower things or in higher ones. The more ardently it is exercised in pursuit of higher things, the more severely it grows numb with disgust toward lower things; and the more fiercely it burns with concern for lower things, the more damnably it grows cold toward higher things.

The two cannot be loved simultaneously and equally. Therefore the apostle John, knowing that the harvest of heavenly charity cannot grow amid the thorns of worldly loves, first uproots the thorns of worldly loves from the hearts of his hearers with the holy hand of the word, before bringing forth the seeds of eternal love. He says: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:16).

He immediately adds: “For if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.” It is as though he were saying plainly: The two loves cannot be contained in one heart, nor does the crop of heavenly charity spring up in the heart where the thorns of lower delight kill it.

He then enumerates the pricks arising from this lower delight, saying: “For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world passes away, and its desire” (ibid.).

### CHAPTER V.—“His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2:27)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book V, §50.) The hidden word may be understood as the inner address of inspiration, concerning which John says: “His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2:27).

This inspiration, touching the human mind, raises it up; depressing temporal thoughts, it kindles the mind with eternal desires, so that nothing now pleases it except what is heavenly, and it despises everything below that clamors from human corruption.

To hear the hidden word is to conceive in the heart the utterance of the Holy Spirit. This cannot be known except by the one who can possess it. Hence Truth itself says concerning this hidden utterance: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive” (John 14:16–17).

Just as that same Paraclete, after the Mediator’s ascension, is another Consoler of the human race and is invisible in himself, so he kindles everyone whom he fills to desire invisible things. Since worldly hearts love visible things alone, the world does not receive him, because it does not rise toward the love of invisible things.

For the more secular minds expand themselves outward through their desires, the more they narrow the breast of the heart for receiving him.

### CHAPTER VI.—The same as above

(Homily 30 on the Gospels, §9.) Although the voice of the speaker gives general admonition, there is an inner teacher who specially teaches certain persons the meaning of that voice.

Concerning this anointing of the Spirit John again says: “His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2:27). A person is not instructed through the voice when the mind is not anointed by the Spirit.

But why are we speaking about human instruction, when the Creator himself does not speak for a person’s education unless he also speaks to that person through the anointing of the Spirit?

Certainly, before Cain perpetrated fratricide in deed, he heard: “You have sinned; be still” (Gen. 4:7, according to the Septuagint). But because, in accordance with the demands of his guilt, he was admonished by a voice and not by anointing, he was able to hear God’s words but refused to obey them.

### CHAPTER VII.—“We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2)

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book I, homily 2, §20.) After the likeness that is now maintained in conduct, one day we attain the likeness of glory.

Hence John says: “Now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2). He immediately adds how this can happen: “For we shall see him as he is.”

To be God is to remain eternal and unchangeable. For everything that changes ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not. But God’s being means never to be otherwise.

Hence it is said to Moses: “I am who I am.” And: “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14). James also says: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow caused by turning” (James 1:17).

Thus John says: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” By contemplating the essence of his nature, we are freed from our mutability and fixed in eternity. We shall be changed in the one whom we see, because by seeing life we shall be free from death; by seeing the immutable, we shall transcend our mutability; by seeing incorruption, we shall not be held by any corruption.

### CHAPTER VIII.—The same as above

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, §79.) All the saints attain those eternal joys so that they may be like God, as it is written: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Yet it is also written: “Lord, who is like you?” And again: “Who will be like God among the sons of God?” How, then, are they like him, and how are they not like him? They will be like this Wisdom in image, yet they will not be like it in equality.

By contemplating God’s eternity, they become eternal; and while they receive the gift of his vision, through receiving blessedness they imitate what they see. They are therefore like him because they become blessed, yet they are not like the Creator because they are creatures.

They possess a certain likeness to God because they have no end; yet they do not possess the equality of the uncircumscribed, because they are circumscribed.

### CHAPTER IX.—“Whoever has the substance of the world” (1 John 3:17)

(Homily 27 on the Gospels, §3.) Behold, no one persecutes us to the point of death. How then can we prove whether we love our enemies?

Yet there is something that should be done in the peace of the holy Church by which it may become clear whether, in a time of persecution, we would be able to die for love.

John himself says: “Whoever has the substance of the world and sees his brother in need, yet closes his compassion toward him—how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 3:17).

John the Baptist also says: “Whoever has two tunics should give one to the person who has none” (Luke 3:41). If, therefore, someone does not give his tunic for God in a time of tranquility, when will he give his soul in persecution?

For the virtue of charity to remain unconquered in disturbance, let it be nourished by mercy in tranquility, so that it may first learn to devote its possessions to almighty God and afterward itself.

### CHAPTER X.—“Let us not love in word or speech” (1 John 3:12)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXI, §29.) Some people do not strive to support needy brothers with material things, although they are able to do so; instead, they encourage them only with flattering words. The holy preaching of James severely rebukes them, saying: “If a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, be warmed and filled,’ but you do not give them what is necessary for their bodies, what benefit is that?” (James 2:15–16).

The apostle John also admonishes them, saying: “My little children, let us not love in word or speech, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:12). Our love must therefore always be demonstrated both by reverent speech and by the ministry of generosity.

### CHAPTER XI.—“If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence” (1 John 3:21)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book X, no. 27.) Through John it is said: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God; and whatever we ask of him, we shall receive” (1 John 3:18). Hence Solomon says: “Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. 28:9). Our heart does not condemn us [Col. 1103D] in petition when it remembers that it has resisted the commands of the one whom it is asking; and prayer becomes accursed when it turns away from the judgment of the law, because it is certainly fitting that one should be excluded from the benefits of him whose commands one does not wish to obey.

(No. 22.) In this matter, the salutary remedy is that, when the mind reproaches itself from the memory of its guilt, it should first lament in prayer that it has sinned; so that, when the stain of error has been wiped away with tears, the face of the heart may appear clean before its Maker in its petition. But great care must be taken lest it fall again into what it rejoices to have cleansed away with tears, lest, when a lamented sin is committed again in the sight of the righteous Judge, even the lament itself be diminished. For we must carefully remember what is said: “Do not repeat the word in your prayer” (Eccl. 7:15). By this saying the wise man in no way forbids us often to ask forgiveness, but forbids us to repeat our sins. It is as though he plainly said: “When you have lamented what you have done wrongly [Col. 1104A], do not again do what you must once more bewail in your prayers.”

## CHAPTER XII.—The Same Subject

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, no. 9.) For each person is gravely confounded when, whether by reading or hearing, he regards God’s commandments, which he has despised in living. Hence it is said in John’s words: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God, and whatever we ask of him, we shall receive” (1 John 3:21). It is as though he said: “If we do what he commands, we obtain what we ask.” For these two things necessarily correspond before God: prayer must be supported by action, and action by prayer. Hence Jeremiah says: “Let us examine our ways and search them out, and let us return to the Lord. Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God in heaven” (Lam. 3:40). To examine our ways means to scrutinize the interior things of our thoughts. A person lifts up his heart with his hands when he strengthens his prayer by his works. For [Col. 1104B] whoever prays but refuses to act lifts up his heart but does not lift up his hands. Whoever acts but does not pray lifts up his hands but does not lift up his heart. Thus, according to John’s words, the heart receives confidence in prayer when no perversity of life contradicts it.

## CHAPTER XIII.—No One Has Ever Seen God (1 John 4:12)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, no. 88.) Wisdom, which is God, would certainly have been seen by none of the saints if it were hidden from the eyes of all living beings. Yet I hear John agreeing with this statement when he says: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4:12). But when I look again at the Fathers of the Old Testament, I recognize that many of them, as the history of sacred Scripture itself testifies, saw God.

Jacob saw God and said: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved” (Gen. 32:30). Moses saw God, of whom it is written: “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend” (Exod. 33:11). [Col. 1104C] Job saw the Lord, who says: “I heard you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (Job 42:5). Isaiah saw the Lord, who says: “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. 6:1). Micah saw the Lord, who says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and all the army of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left” (1 Kings 22:19).

What, then, does it mean that so many Fathers of the Old Testament testified that they had seen God, and yet it is said of this Wisdom, which is God: “She is hidden from the eyes of all living beings” (Job 28:21)? And John says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). The answer is plainly understood to be this: as long as one lives here in mortality, God can be seen through certain images, but he cannot be seen through the very form of his nature. Thus the soul, inspired by the grace of the Spirit, sees God through certain representations, but does not reach the very power of his essence.

For this reason Jacob, who testifies that he saw God, saw him only in an angel. For this reason [Col. 1104D] Moses, who spoke with God face to face, as a man speaks with his friend, said to him amid the very words of his conversation: “If I have found grace in your sight, show yourself plainly to me, so that I may see you” (Exod. 33:13). Certainly, if the one with whom he was speaking was not God, he would have said, “Show me God,” and not, “Show yourself.” But if he was God with whom he spoke face to face, why did he ask to see the one whom he was seeing?

From this request it is gathered that he thirsted to behold, through the unbounded clarity of his nature, the one whom he had already begun to see through certain images, so that the heavenly essence might be present to the eyes of his mind, and so that no created image, existing temporally, might intervene between him and the vision of eternity.

Thus the Fathers of the Old Testament saw the Lord, and yet, according to John’s words, “No one has ever seen God”; and, according to blessed Job’s statement, Wisdom, which is God, is hidden from the eyes of all living beings, [Col. 1105A] because for those established in this mortal flesh God could both be seen through certain bounded images and could not be seen through the unbounded light of eternity.

(No. 89.) But if some who still live in this corruptible flesh, while nevertheless growing through immeasurable strength, can see God’s eternal brightness through a certain intensity of contemplation, this too is not contrary to blessed Job’s statement, which says: “She is hidden from the eyes of all living beings.” For whoever has seen Wisdom, which is God, dies utterly to this life, so that he is no longer held by its love.

No one who still lives carnally sees her, because no one can embrace God and the world at the same time. Whoever sees God dies by that very act through which, either in the intention of his heart or in the effect of his works, he wholly separates himself from the pleasures of this life. Hence it is also said to that same Moses: “For man shall not see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). It is as though it were plainly said: “No one has ever seen God spiritually and continued to live carnally in the world.”

(No. 90.) It must be understood, however, that there were some [Col. 1105B] who said that God is indeed seen in his brightness in that region of blessedness, but is by no means seen in his nature. These were misled by an insufficiently subtle inquiry. For in that simple and immutable essence, brightness is not one thing and nature another; rather, its very nature is brightness, and its very brightness is nature.

Because this Wisdom of God would one day reveal itself in itself to those who love it, it promises this, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21). It is as though it plainly said: “You who see me in your own nature must finally see me in my nature.”

Again he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Cor. 13:12).

(No. 91.) We shall therefore see God, and he himself will be the reward of our labor, so that, after the darkness of this mortality, we may rejoice when we have approached his light.

(No. 92.) Yet [Col. 1105C] we shall not see him as he sees himself. The Creator sees himself in a manner utterly different from that in which the creature sees the Creator. For, with regard to God’s immensity, a certain measure of contemplation is fixed for us, since we are bounded by that very limitation by which we are creatures.

(No. 93.) Thus we do not behold God as he beholds himself, just as we do not rest in God as he rests in himself. Our vision or rest will in some way resemble his vision or rest, but it will not equal it. For, lest we remain lying in ourselves, so to speak, the wing of contemplation lifts us up, and we are raised from ourselves to behold him. Carried away by the intention of the heart and the sweetness of contemplation, we go in some manner from ourselves into him.

Yet this very going of ours is less than resting; and nevertheless, to go in this way is to rest perfectly. It is therefore perfect rest, because God is seen, yet it is not to be equated with the rest of the one who does not pass from himself into another in order to rest.

There is therefore a rest that is, so to speak, both similar and dissimilar, [Col. 1105D] because what his rest is, ours imitates. To be blessed and eternal forever, we imitate the Eternal; and eternity is great for us—the imitation of eternity. Nor are we excluded from the one whom we are able to imitate, because in seeing him we participate in him, and in participating we imitate him.

This vision begins now in faith, but is perfected then in its proper form, when we drink at its very fountain the coeternal Wisdom of God, which now we receive, as though through flowing streams, from the mouths of preachers.

## CHAPTER XIV.—God Is Love (1 John 4:16)

(Homily 30 on the Gospels, no. 1.) The Holy Spirit [Col. 1106A] himself is love. Hence John also says: “God is love” (1 John 4:8). Whoever desires God with an undivided mind certainly possesses the one whom he loves. For no one could love God if he did not possess the one whom he loved.

## CHAPTER XV.—Perfect Love Casts Out Fear (1 John 4:18)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XI, no. 55.) The Law held the people under the blow of punishment, so that whoever sinned under it was immediately punished by death; and the Israelite people served the Lord not from love but from fear. Yet justice can never be fulfilled through fear, because, according to John’s words: “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

Paul also comforts adopted children, saying: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15).

## CHAPTER XVI.—Every Iniquity Is Sin (1 John 5:17)

[Col. 1106B]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XI, no. 57.) Although the apostle John declares that there is no difference between iniquity and sin, saying, “Iniquity is sin” (1 John 3:4), nevertheless, in ordinary usage the word *iniquity* conveys something greater than *sin*. Everyone freely admits that he is a sinner, but sometimes blushes to call himself wicked.

There is this difference between crimes and offenses: a crime exceeds even the weight of sin, whereas an offense does not exceed the weight of sin. For when the Law commands that a sacrifice be offered, it prescribes one for sin and likewise one for an offense. Sometimes a crime lies in an action, whereas an offense is often found only in thought.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “Who understands offenses?” (Ps. 18:13). Sins of action are recognized more quickly because they are outwardly visible; sins of thought, however, are more difficult to understand precisely because they are committed invisibly.

## CHAPTER XVII.—Whoever Does Not Love His Brother Whom He Sees (1 John 4:20)

[Col. 1106C]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VII, no. 28.) Since there are two commandments of love—love of God and love of neighbor—love of neighbor is generated through love of God, and love of God is nourished through love of neighbor.

Whoever neglects to love God certainly does not know how to love his neighbor. We make fuller progress in the love of God when, within the embrace of that love, we are first nourished by love of neighbor.

Because love of God generates love of neighbor, when the Lord was about to say through the Law, “You shall love your neighbor,” he first said, “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6), so that he might first plant the root of his love in the soil of our breast, in order that brotherly love might afterward sprout through its branches.

And again, because love of God grows warm through love of neighbor, John testifies when he reproves us, saying: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20). [Col. 1106D] Yet this divine reading is born through fear if, as it grows, it is transformed into affection.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—And It Is a Sin unto Death (1 John 5:16)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVI, no. 82.) The sin that is not corrected before the end of the present life through correction and repentance is carried down to hell. Concerning this sin John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5:16).

A sin unto death is a sin extending to death, because forgiveness for a sin that is not corrected here is sought in vain.

# ON THE THIRD EPISTLE OF SAINT JOHN

[Col. 1105]

## CHAPTER I.—We Ought Therefore to Receive Such Persons (3 John 8)

[Col. 1105D]

[Col. 1106D] (Homily 20 on the Gospels, no. 12.) Concerning certain brothers traveling abroad, John says to Gaius: [Col. 1107A] “For they have gone forth for the sake of the name of Christ, receiving nothing from the Gentiles. We therefore ought to receive such persons, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 8). Whoever gives temporal assistance to those who possess spiritual gifts becomes a fellow worker in those spiritual gifts themselves.

For while few possess spiritual gifts and many abound in temporal goods, the rich incorporate themselves into the virtues of the poor by comforting those holy poor with their own wealth.

## CHAPTER II.—The One Who Loves to Hold the First Place (3 John 8)

(In the exposition of Ezekiel, book I, homily 9, no. 17.) When we are following the way of upright action, the matter requires careful inquiry: should we always disregard the words of those who slander us, or should we sometimes restrain them?

Concerning this, it must be known that we should neither stir up the tongues of slanderers through our own [Col. 1108A] efforts, lest they perish, nor should we fail to endure with equanimity those whom their own malice has stirred up, so that our merit may increase. At times, however, we should also restrain them, lest, while they spread evil about us, they corrupt the innocent hearts of those who could have heard us and been led to good.

For this reason John rebuked the tongue of his detractor, saying: “Diotrephes, who loves to hold the first place among them, does not receive us. Therefore, if I come, I will call attention to his works, which he does, prating against us with wicked words” (3 John 9).

Paul likewise speaks to the Corinthians who were slandering him, saying: “His letters, they say, are weighty and forceful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible. Let the one who is such consider that what we are in word through letters when absent, we shall also be in action when present” (2 Cor. 10:10).

# ON THE EPISTLE OF SAINT JUDE

[Col. 1107]

## SINGLE CHAPTER.—Jesus, Saving the People from the Land of Egypt (Jude 5)

[Col. 1107B]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, no. 35.) The elect always take care to return to justice before the judge’s anger is kindled unquenchably, lest, overtaken by the final scourge, their life and their guilt come to an end together.

A scourge dissolves guilt when it changes a person’s life. For if it does not change his conduct, it does not expiate his actions. Every divine stroke is therefore either a purification of the present life in us or the beginning of the punishment to come.

For the sake of those who make progress through the scourge, it is said: “You who fashion pain into instruction” (Ps. 93:20). For when the wicked person is scourged and corrected, he who refused to hear the commandment hears pain. Pain is therefore fashioned into instruction for the one whom pain restrains from evil works as though it were a commandment.

But of those whom scourges condemn and do not deliver, it is said: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept discipline” (Jer. 5:3). For such people, the scourges begin in this life and continue in eternal punishment. [Col. 1107C]

Hence through Moses the Lord says: “A fire has been kindled by [Col. 1108B] my anger, and it shall burn down to the depths of hell below” (Deut. 32:22). With regard to the present stroke, it is rightly said: “A fire has been kindled by my anger.” With regard to eternal damnation, he immediately adds plainly: “And it shall burn down to the depths of hell below.”

Although some customarily say what is written, “God does not judge twice for the same thing” (Nahum 1:9), they nevertheless fail to heed what the prophet says concerning the wicked: “Crush them with a double destruction” (Jer. 17:18). Nor do they heed what is written elsewhere: “Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude 5).

If we grant them that no guilt can be borne twice, this must be understood of those who are struck because of sin and die in their sin: their punishment begins here and is completed there. Thus, in the case of those who are struck, there is one scourge, begun temporally but consummated in eternal punishments; while for those who altogether refuse to be corrected, the blow of present scourges is already the beginning of future torments.

# BOOK SEVEN. Testimonies on the Apocalypse of Saint John the Apostle

[Col. 1107]

## CHAPTER I.—John to the Seven Churches That Are in Asia (Rev. 1:4)

[Col. 1107C]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, no. 13.) By the name of Arcturus—the constellation established on the axis of heaven and shining with the rays of seven stars—the universal Church is signified. In John’s Apocalypse (1:12, 20) she is represented by seven churches and seven lampstands, containing within herself the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, shining with the brilliance of supreme virtue, as though she shone from the axis of truth.

## CHAPTER II.—The Same Subject

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXV, no. 18.) The universality of the holy Church is signified by the number seven. Hence John writes in the Apocalypse (1:4) to seven churches; but what else did he intend to be understood through them except the universal Church? For, to signify that the universal Church is filled with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, Elisha is described as having breathed seven times upon the dead boy (2 Kings 4).

When the Lord comes upon the extinguished people, he breathes, as it were, seven times, [Col. 1107D] because he mercifully bestows upon them the gifts of the Holy Spirit’s sevenfold grace.

## CHAPTER III.—They Are the Angels of the Seven Churches (Rev. 1:20)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIV, no. 14.) Because sacred Scripture often designates the preachers of the Church by the name “angels,” since they proclaim the glory of the heavenly kingdom, we may also understand the angels to be holy preachers.

For this reason John, writing in the Apocalypse (1:4) to the seven churches, speaks to the angels of the churches—that is, to the preachers of the peoples. [Col. 1108B] Hence the prophet says: “The angels of peace shall weep bitterly” (Isa. 33:7). Again the prophet Malachi speaks, saying: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7).

Hence Paul says: “Great is the mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the Gentiles, believed on in the world, and taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16). After saying that the mystery of the dispensation appeared to angels, he added, “It was preached among the Gentiles”; thus he clearly designated by the name “angels” the holy preachers, that is, the messengers of truth.

## CHAPTER IV.—You Have There Those Who Hold the Teaching (Rev. 2:14)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, no. 15.) Cain did not know the time of Antichrist, yet he was a member of Antichrist by his merit (Gen. 4). Judas was ignorant of the cruelty of his persuasion, yet, prompted by avarice, he succumbed to the authority of that [Col. 1108D] cruelty (Acts 8). Simon existed long before the times of Antichrist, yet by perversely seeking the power of miracles he joined himself to Antichrist’s pride.

Thus an evil body is joined to its head, and members to members, when they do not know one another in awareness but are nevertheless united in action.

For Pergamum had neither known Balaam’s books nor his words, yet, following his wickedness, it heard through the voice of heavenly reproach: “You have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel: to eat and to commit fornication [Col. 1109A]” (Rev. 2:14).

The Church of Thyatira was also separated from Jezebel by knowledge, time, and place; but because guilt of a similar life bound her to Jezebel, Jezebel is said to be present in her and to persist in perverse works, as the angel testifies, saying: “I have something against you, because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants, to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols” (ibid., 20).

Behold: because people could be found who followed Jezebel’s life through reprehensible action, Jezebel is said to have been found there. For a perverse body is made one by united conduct, even if places or times divide it.

Hence it comes about that among her perverse imitators, each wicked person who has already passed away remains, and the wicked agent who has not yet come appears in his own practitioners.

## CHAPTER V.—What No One Knows Except the One Who Receives It (Rev. 2:17)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX, no. 4.) To see perfectly the Wisdom coeternal with God [Col. 1109B] is the same as to possess it. Hence concerning the reward of the victor it is said to John: “I will give him a white stone, and upon the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it” (Rev. 2:17).

In this life we can know or see even what we have not received. But to have a new name inscribed on the stone is, in the eternal reward, to possess a knowledge of God unfamiliar to human minds. No one can know it unless he has also received and possessed it.

## CHAPTER VI.—Be Watchful and Strengthen (Rev. 3:2)
