(The Pastoral Rule, part III, admonition 35.) Through Solomon it is said: “Whoever is slack and negligent in his work is a brother to the one who destroys his own works” (Prov. 18:9). For whoever does not strictly carry out the good works he has begun imitates, through negligent laxity, the hand of one who destroys.

Hence to the Church of Sardis it is said by the angel: “Be watchful and strengthen the rest that were about to die; for I have not found your works full before God” (Rev. 3:2). Since his works had not been found full before God, he declared that even the remaining works that had been done [Col. 1109C] were about to die. For if what is dead in us is not kindled into life, what is held as though still alive is also extinguished.

## CHAPTER VII.—The One Who Conquers I Will Make a Pillar in the Temple of My God (Rev. 3:12)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVII, no. 42.) “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God” (Rev. 3:12). Whoever is established with upright intention in God’s work is raised as a pillar in the structure of the spiritual building, so that, placed in this temple, which is the Church, he may be both useful and an ornament.

## CHAPTER VIII.—Would That You Were Cold or Hot (Rev. 3:15)

(The Pastoral Rule, part III, admonition 35.) “Would that you were cold or hot; but because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. 3:15).

The hot person is one who takes up good pursuits and brings them to completion; the cold person is one who does not even begin what must be completed. And just as one passes from cold through lukewarmness [Col. 1109D] to heat, so from heat one returns through lukewarmness to cold.

Whoever, having lost the coldness of unbelief, lives but does not grow beyond lukewarmness so as to burn with fervor, undoubtedly, having abandoned the hope of heat, remains in harmful lukewarmness and acts in such a way as to grow cold.

But just as before lukewarmness coldness exists under hope, so after coldness lukewarmness exists in despair. For the one who is still in sins does not lose confidence in conversion; but the one who has grown lukewarm after conversion has withdrawn the hope that could have existed in his coldness.

Everyone is therefore sought either as hot or as cold, lest he be vomited out as lukewarm: either, if not yet converted, he should still offer hope of conversion, or, if already converted, he should burn with virtue and not be vomited out as lukewarm. For he returns from the heat he had resolved upon through torpor to harmful coldness.

## CHAPTER IX.—Because You Say, “I Am Rich” (Rev. 3:17)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIV, no. 6.) In the angel’s voice it is said to the preacher of Laodicea: “You say, ‘I am rich and have grown wealthy and lack nothing,’ and you do not know that you [Col. 1110A] are wretched and miserable, poor and blind and naked” (ibid., 17).

He declares himself rich who is lifted up through the arrogance of holiness, but he is reproved as poor, blind, and naked. Poor, certainly, because he does not possess the riches of virtues; blind, because he does not even see the poverty he suffers; naked, because he has lost the first robe—and worse still, because he does not recognize that he has lost it.

## CHAPTER X.—I Advise You to Buy Gold (Rev. 3:18)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, no. 61.) What else does he call gold except wisdom, of which Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21:20)?

He saw wisdom as gold, which he called a treasure; and it is rightly signified by the name of gold, because just as gold obtains temporal things, so wisdom merits eternal goods.

If gold were not wisdom, the angel would never have said to the Church of Laodicea: “I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire” (Rev. 3:18). We buy gold when, in order to receive wisdom, we first offer obedience. A certain wise man [Col. 1110B] rightly urges us toward this purchase, saying: “Desiring wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you” (Ecclus. 1:33).

## CHAPTER XI.—Anoint Your Eyes with Eye Salve (Rev. 3:18)

(The Pastoral Rule, part I, chapter 11.) Through the angel it is said: “Anoint your eyes with eye salve, so that you may see” (Rev. 3:18). We anoint our eyes with eye salve so that we may see when, in order to recognize the brightness of the true light, we assist the sharpness of our understanding with the medicine of action.

## CHAPTER XII.—The One Who Conquers, I Will Grant to Sit with Me (Rev. 3:21)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVI, no. 53.) Holy men are rightly called kings in the testimony of sacred Scripture, because, placed above all the movements of the flesh, they sometimes restrain the appetite for lust, sometimes moderate the heat of avarice, sometimes bend the glory of pride, sometimes crush the suggestions of envy, and sometimes extinguish the fire of anger [Col. 1110C].

They are therefore kings because they know not to succumb by consenting to the movements of their temptations, but to rule and preside over them.

Since they pass from this power of governance to the power of reward, it is rightly said: “He sets kings upon the throne forever” (Job 36:7). For they have been wearied for a time by governing themselves, but they are established forever upon the throne of the inner [alternative: eternal] establishment of the kingdom. There they receive the ability to judge others worthily precisely because here they do not know how to wickedly spare themselves.

Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Until justice is turned into judgment” (Ps. 93:15). Paul says of himself and his companions: “So that we might become the justice of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:21). Justice is therefore turned into judgment because those who now live justly and irreproachably then receive the power of judgment.

Hence the Lord says to the Church of Laodicea: “The one who conquers, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat with my Father on his throne” (Rev. 3:21).

The conquering Lord [Col. 1110D] declares that he sat on the throne with the Father because, after the struggles of his passion and after the palm of resurrection, he showed himself more clearly to all as equal in power to the Father, and, having trampled the sting of death, made known that he was not unlike him.

Hence also, to Mary, who had not yet believed, he says that he is like the Father: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” (John 20:17).

For us to sit on the Son’s throne means to judge by the power of that same Son. Because we receive the primacy of judgment through his power, we sit, as it were, on his throne.

Nor does it conflict with the truth that elsewhere he testifies that the disciples will sit upon twelve thrones (Matt. 19), while here he declares that they will sit upon his throne. Through the twelve thrones the universal judgment is shown; through the Son’s throne, the singular summit of judicial power is shown.

What is signified by the twelve thrones is therefore also signified by the one throne of the Son, because the universal judgment is received through the intervention of our Mediator.

## CHAPTER XIII.—And They Cast Their Crowns before the Throne (Rev. 4:10)

[Col. 1111A]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXII, no. 20.) Holy men know that, after the fall of the first parent, they were born from a corruptible stock and were changed toward better desires or works not by their own virtue but by preceding heavenly grace.

Whatever evil they recognize as present in themselves, they attribute to the merit of mortal descent; whatever good they perceive in themselves, they recognize as the gift of immortal grace. They thus become debtors to the one who, by punishing them, gave them the good will that they did not want, and, by following upon it, granted them the power to do the good that they desire.

Hence it is rightly said through John: “They worshiped the one who lives forever and ever, casting their crowns before the throne of the Lord” (Rev. 4:10). To cast their crowns before the throne is not to attribute the victories of their struggles to themselves but to their author, so that they may refer the glory of praise to the one from whom they know they received the strength for the struggle.

## CHAPTER XIV.—I Saw beneath the Altar the Souls of Those Who Had Been Slain (Rev. 6:9)

[Col. 1111B]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book II, no. 11.) In John’s Apocalypse it is said: “I saw beneath the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus that they bore; and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’” Immediately it is added: “White robes were given to each of them. And it was said to them that they should rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be completed” (Rev. 6:9ff.).

What does it mean for souls to utter a request for vengeance except that they desire the day of the final judgment and the resurrection of their extinguished bodies?

Their great cry is their great desire, for each person cries out less the less he desires. And he expresses a greater voice in the ears of the unbounded Spirit the more fully he pours himself into his desire. The words of souls are therefore their desires. [Col. 1111C]

For if desire were not a form of speech, the Prophet would not say: “Your ear will hear the desires of their heart” (Ps. 9:38).

But since the mind that asks is accustomed to be admonished in one way, and the mind that is asked in another, and since the souls of the saints cling to God in the embrace of inward secrecy in such a way that they rest by clinging to him, how are they said to ask when it is clear that they in no way differ from the inner will? How are they said to ask when it is certain that they know both God’s will and the things that are to come?

Because they are placed in him, they are said to ask something from him—not because they desire anything that conflicts with the will of the one whom they behold, but because the more ardently they cling to him in mind, the more they receive from him the capacity to ask him to do what they know he wills to do.

They drink from him what they thirst for from him; and, in a manner still incomprehensible to us, in that for which they hunger by asking, they are satisfied through foreknowledge.

They would therefore conflict with the will of the Creator if, seeing what he wills, they did not ask it; and they would cling to him less if they pressed upon his will with a more sluggish desire.

The answer of the Divinity [Col. 1111D] is said to them: “Rest for a little while longer, until the number of your fellow servants and your brothers is completed.”

To say “Rest for a little while longer” to souls that desire is to breathe the comfort of consolation into the ardor of their desire through foreknowledge itself. The voice of the souls is what lovers desire; the speech of the answering God is what confirms them amid their desires through the certainty of retribution.

His answer therefore means that they must await the gathering of their brothers, and it pours into their minds a willing patience for the delay of waiting, so that, while they desire the resurrection of the flesh, they may also rejoice in the increase of their brothers who are to be gathered.

## CHAPTER XV.—And a Single Robe Was Given to Each of Them (Rev. 6:11)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXV, no. 25.) For the holy Church to receive a double portion at the end means that in each of us she rejoices both in the blessedness of the soul and in the incorruption of the flesh [Col. 1112A].

Hence it is said through the prophet concerning the elect: “In their land they shall possess double” (Isa. 61:7). Hence the apostle John says concerning the saints who await the end of the world: “A single white robe was given to each of them; and it was said to them that they should rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be completed” (Rev. 6:11).

Before the resurrection the saints receive single robes, because they enjoy only the blessedness of their souls. At the end of the world they will have two, because together with the blessedness of the mind they will also possess the glory of the flesh.

## CHAPTER XVI.—And the Sun Became Black Like a Haircloth Sack (Rev. 6:12)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, no. 8.) Sometimes, in sacred speech, the brightness of preachers is signified by the name of the sun. Thus it is said through John: “The sun became like a haircloth sack” (Rev. 6:12).

At the end of time the sun is shown as a haircloth sack, because the radiant life of preachers is displayed as harsh and contemptible before the eyes of the reprobate [Col. 1112B].

## CHAPTER XVII.—Clothed in White Robes and with Palms (Rev. 7:9)

(Homily 5, Book II, on Ezekiel, no. 22.) What else is signified by palms but the rewards of victory? For palms are customarily given to those who conquer. Hence, concerning those who had conquered the ancient enemy in the contest of martyrdom, and who were rejoicing as victors in their homeland, it is written: “Palms in their hands, and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb’” (Rev. 7:7, 9–10). To have palms in one’s hands is to have held victories in one’s conduct; and the palm of that conduct is rewarded there, where one already rejoices without a contest.

CAP. XVIII.—“There was silence in heaven” (Rev. 8:1).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXX, no. 52.) To those who live well, solitude of mind is first granted, so that they may [Col. 1112C] suppress within themselves the rising din of earthly desires; restrain, by the grace of heavenly love, the heart’s cares as they boil up toward lower things; drive away from the eyes of the mind, by the hand of seriousness, all the movements of frivolous thoughts that obtrude themselves importunately, like certain flies flying around; and seek within themselves a kind of secret place with the Lord, where, with outward noise stilled, they may speak silently with him through their inward desires.

(No. 53.) Elsewhere it is said of this secret place of the heart: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8:1). Heaven is called the Church of the elect; when it reaches toward things above through the elevation of contemplation, it suppresses the tumults of thoughts rising from below and creates within itself a kind of silence for God. Yet because this silence of contemplation cannot be perfect in the present life, it is said to have lasted half an hour. For the tumultuous noise of thoughts intrudes upon the unwilling mind, and even when it is intent upon higher things, violently drags the eye of the heart [Col. 1112D] back to regard earthly matters. Hence it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15). Properly, therefore, this silence is described as lasting not a whole hour but half an hour, because contemplation is never perfected here, although it is begun ardently.

CAP. XIX.—The same subject.

(In the Exposition of Ezekiel, Book II, Homily 2, no. 14.) “There was silence for about half an hour” (ibid.). Heaven is the soul of the just, as the Lord says through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1); and, “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1). When, therefore, the repose of the contemplative life is enacted in the mind, there is silence in heaven, because the noise of earthly actions ceases in thought, so that the mind may apply its ear to the innermost secret. But because this repose of mind cannot be perfect in the present life, the silence made in heaven is said not to have lasted a whole hour, but [Col. 1113A] “about half an hour,” so that even the half-hour itself is not plainly perceived when the word “about” is prefixed. For as soon as the mind begins to lift itself up and be suffused with the light of inward quiet, the noise of thoughts quickly returns; the mind is confounded about itself, and in its confusion is blinded.

CAP. XX.—“The power of the horses is in their mouths” (Rev. 9:19).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIII, no. 48.) What, then, will that time of persecution appear like, when some rage against the piety of the faithful with words and others with swords, so that what the former say to them with flattering words is commanded by the latter with striking swords? The activity of both groups—that is, of those who possess power and those who speak—is briefly contained in a sentence of John’s Apocalypse, where it is said: “The power of the horses was in their mouths and in their tails” (Rev. 9:19). In the mouths of the teachers, knowledge is represented; in the tails, secular power. By the tail, which is behind, the temporality of this age—which must be left behind—is signified; concerning it the Apostle Paul says: [Col. 1113B] “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. 3:13). Everything that passes is behind; everything that comes and remains is ahead.

These horses—that is, preachers running everywhere under a carnal impulse—have power in mouth and tail, because they preach by persuading people to what is perverse, but, supported by temporal powers, they glory through the things that lie behind them. And because they themselves may appear contemptible, they demand reverence for themselves from their wicked hearers through those whose patronage supports them.

CAP. XXI.—“The signs which the seven thunders spoke” (Rev. 10:4).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book IX, no. 15.) As the end of the world presses upon us, heavenly knowledge advances and grows more abundantly with the passage of time. Hence it is said through Daniel: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12:4). Hence, in the earlier part of the revelation, the angel says to John: [Col. 1113C] “Seal up the signs which the seven thunders spoke” (Rev. 10:4). Yet at the conclusion of the same revelation he commands him, saying: “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book” (Rev. 22:10). The earlier part of the revelation is commanded to be sealed, while its conclusion is forbidden to be sealed, because whatever lay hidden at the beginnings of the holy Church is disclosed daily by the end.

CAP. XXII.—“But cast out the court that is outside the temple” (Rev. 11:2).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVIII, no. 16.) It is written in the Apocalypse: “The court that is outside the temple, cast out; do not measure it” (Rev. 11:2). What else does the court signify but the breadth of the present life? Those represented by the court are rightly outside the temple; and therefore they are not to be measured, because narrow is the gate that leads to life, and the breadth of the life of the wicked is not admitted to the measures and standards of the elect.

CAP. XXIII.—“These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands” (Rev. 11:4).

[Col. 1113D]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book IX, no. 3.) Those two outstanding preachers have been removed by death being deferred, so that they may be recalled to the work of preaching at the end. Concerning them John says: “These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth” (Rev. 2:4). Of one of them Truth itself promises in the Gospel, saying: “Elijah is to come, and he will restore all things” (Matt. 17:11).

CAP. XXIV.—“A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet” (Rev. 12:2).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIV, no. 25.) When the sun is presented figuratively, it sometimes signifies the Lord, sometimes persecution, sometimes the manifestation of a visible vision concerning some matter, and sometimes the understanding of the wise. For the Lord is represented by the sun, as the Book of Wisdom declares that all the impious, on the day of the final judgment, when they have recognized their condemnation, will say: “We wandered from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not [Col. 1114A] shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. 5:6). It is as though they plainly said: “The ray of inward light did not shine within us.”

Hence John also says: “A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet” (Rev. 12:2). In the sun, the illumination of truth is understood; in the moon, which wanes through its monthly replenishments, the mutability of temporality. But the holy Church, because it is protected by the splendor of heavenly light, is clothed, as it were, with the sun; and because it despises all temporal things, it presses the moon beneath its feet.

CAP. XXV.—“And its tail swept away a third of the stars” (Rev. 12:4).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book IV, no. 17.) By the name of stars, the righteousness of the saints—which shines in the darkness of this life—is sometimes indicated; at other times, the pretence of hypocrites, because they display the good things they do in order to receive praise from human beings. If those who live rightly were not stars, Paul would never say to his disciples: “Among a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. 2: [Col. 1114B] 15).

Again, if among those who seem to act rightly some did not seek the reward of human approval for their conduct, John would never see stars falling from the heavens, saying: “The dragon cast its tail, and swept away a third of the stars” (Rev. 12:4). A portion of the stars is swept away by the dragon’s tail because, through the final persuasion of Antichrist, certain people who seem to shine will be carried off. To drag stars down to earth is to involve, through the love of earthly things, in open error those who seem devoted to the pursuit of heavenly life.

CAP. XXVI.—The same subject.

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXII, no. 25.) Concerning this tail of Behemoth, represented under the figure of the dragon, John says: “And its tail swept away a third of the stars of heaven, and cast them to the earth” (ibid.). Heaven is the Church, which, in this night of the present life, shines with stars radiating from above while it contains within itself the innumerable virtues of the saints. But the dragon’s tail casts the stars to the earth, because that extremity of Satan, raised up through the audacity of the man he assumed, shows certain people whom it found in the Church as though they were God’s elect to be reprobate [Col. 1114C] by gaining them for itself.

For stars to fall from heaven to earth is for some, abandoning the hope of heavenly things, to aspire under his leadership to the pursuit of secular glory.

CAP. XXVII.—“Michael and his angels were fighting” (Rev. 12:7).

(Homily 34 on the Gospels, no. 9.) Michael means “Who is like God?” Whenever something of extraordinary power is accomplished, Michael is said to be sent, so that from the act itself and from his name it may be understood that no one can do what God is able to do.

Hence that ancient enemy who, in his pride, desired to be like God, saying: “I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will sit upon the mountain of the assembly, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13), when at the end of the world he is left in his own power to be destroyed by the final punishment, is said to be about to fight with the archangel Michael. As John says: “There was a battle with Michael the archangel” (Rev. 12:7), so that he who had proudly exalted himself to the likeness of God, being slain by Michael, may learn that no one rises to the likeness of God through pride.

[Col. 1114D]

CAP. XXVIII.—“For the accuser has been cast down” (Rev. 12:10).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book II, no. 15.) The crafty adversary, when he sees that your offspring has acted well amid prosperity, hastens to condemn it before the Judge through adversity. Hence it is rightly said in the Apocalypse, in an angelic voice: “The accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before the presence of our God day and night” (Rev. 12:10).

[Col. 1115A]

Sacred Scripture, moreover, is accustomed often to use “day” for prosperity and “night” for adversity. He does not cease accusing us by day and by night, because at one time he strives to show us blameworthy in prosperity and at another in adversity. He accuses us by day when he teaches that we make bad use of prosperity. He accuses us by night when he demonstrates that we have no patience in adversity.

CAP. XXIX.—“And I saw another beast ascending” (Rev. 13:11).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIII, no. 59.) “I saw another beast ascending from the earth, having two horns like those of a lamb, and it spoke like a dragon” [Col. 1115B] (Rev. 13:11). He had already described the first beast—that is, Antichrist—in the preceding account. After him, this other beast is also said to ascend, because after him his multitude of preachers boasts of earthly power. To ascend from the earth is to become proud of earthly glory.

It has two horns like those of a lamb because, through the hypocrisy of holiness, it falsely claims to possess within itself both the wisdom and the life that the Lord truly possessed uniquely. But because, under the appearance of a lamb, serpentine poison is poured into reprobate hearers, it is rightly added there: “And it spoke like a dragon” (Rev. 13:11). This beast—that is, the multitude of preachers—if it spoke openly like a dragon, would not appear like a lamb; but it assumes the appearance of a lamb in order to carry out the work of a dragon.

CAP. XXX.—“Woe to the earth and to the sea, because he has come down” (Rev. 12:12).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIV, no. 1.) As the time of the world increases with the passing years, it is afflicted by evils that grow more frequent; and from the very source from which it receives an increase of age, it experiences a loss of salvation. For tribulations increase with the times, and life endures its losses more feebly the farther it advances, as it were, toward life. The ancient enemy is released with all his strength against it. Although he has already perished because he lost the blessedness of his heavenly condition, he is then more completely extinguished when, deprived of the permission to tempt, he is bound externally in flames.

Hence he attacks the final period of the world in order to tempt it more savagely, because he becomes more ardent in cruelty the nearer he feels himself [Col. 1115C] to punishment. He considers that the time is near when he will lose the permission of his most wicked freedom; and the more he is confined by the shortness of time, the more he expands himself through multiplied cruelty. Thus an angelic voice says to John concerning him: “Woe to the earth and to the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great anger, knowing that he has only a short time” (Rev. 12:12).

Then he enlarges himself in the fury of great anger, lest he who could not remain in blessedness should fall with the few into the pit of his condemnation. Then he craftily seeks out whatever he can accomplish wickedly. Then he raises the neck of pride still higher and, through the condemned man whom he bears, wickedly displays whatever he can accomplish temporally.

CAP. XXXI.—“So that he might even make fire come down from heaven” (Rev. 13:13).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIII, no. 62.) For then each soul is like a boiling pot, enduring the impulses of its thoughts like the foam of burning [Col. 1115D] waves. The fire of zeal stirs these impulses, while temporal oppression itself keeps them enclosed within the mouth of the pot. Hence John also, when he recounted the signs of this beast, added: “So that he might make fire come down from heaven” (Rev. 13:13). To make fire descend is for the souls of the elect to pour forth from heavenly things the flames of holy zeal.

CAP. XXXII.—“These follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4).

(Pastoral Rule, Part III, admonition 29.) Through John it is said: “These are those who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins; these follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4). And they sing a song that no one can sing except those one hundred forty-four thousand. To sing the song to the Lamb uniquely is to rejoice with him forever, above all the faithful, even in the incorruption of the flesh. Yet the other elect can hear that song, although they cannot sing it, because they rejoice through charity in the exalted state of those others, even though they do not rise to their rewards. [Col. 1116A]

CAP. XXXIII.—“Having a sickle in his hand” (Rev. 14:14).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIII, no. 21.) “I saw, and behold, a white cloud; and upon the cloud one sitting like the Son of Man, having on his head a golden crown and in his hand a sharp sickle” (Rev. 14:14).

The power of divine judgment is called a circle because it closes in upon everything from every side. And because, by cutting through everything, it encompasses all things within itself, it is represented by the name of a sickle. For whatever is cut by a sickle bends in every direction and falls inward.

And because the power of heavenly judgment cannot in any way be escaped—we are within it, however much we may try to flee—it is rightly said, when the coming Judge is shown, that he holds a sickle, because, as he powerfully confronts everything, he surrounds it by cutting it down.

The Prophet saw himself within the Judge’s sickle when he said: “If I ascend into [Col. 1116B] heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings before the light and dwell at the farthest part of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. 138:8–10).

He saw himself within a kind of sickle when he recognized that nowhere could he find a way of escape, saying: “For neither from the east nor from the west nor from the desert mountains” (Ps. 74:7)—that is, a way of escape is open. And immediately adding the all-encompassing grasp of heavenly power, he says: “For God is judge.” It is as though he said: “There is no way of escape anywhere, because the one who judges is everywhere.”

CAP. XXXIV.—“And girded around the breasts with a belt” (Rev. 21:18).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIV, no. 26.) By the name of gold, the splendor of the heavenly city is understood, as John testifies that he saw it, saying: “The city itself was pure gold, like pure glass” (Rev. 21:18). The gold of which it consists is said to be like glass, [Col. 1116D] so that through gold its brilliance and through glass its transparency may be signified.

Again, by the name of gold, charity is indicated. John saw the angel who spoke with him girded around the breasts with a golden belt (Rev. 15:6), because the breasts of the heavenly citizens, since they are no longer subject to fear of punishment and are not separated from one another by any division, bind themselves together solely by charity. To have a golden belt around the breasts is to restrain all the movements of mutable thoughts by the bonds of love alone.

CAP. XXXV.—“And the fourth poured out his bowl” (Rev. 16:8).

[Col. 1116D]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIV, no. 25.) By the name of the sun, the wisdom of understanding is expressed, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “The fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun; and it was given to him to afflict human beings with heat and with fire” (Rev. 16:8). To pour out the bowl upon the sun is to inflict the punishments of affliction upon men who shine with the splendor of wisdom. “And it was given to him to afflict human beings with heat and fire,” because, when wise men are overcome by torments and touched by the error of evil action, all the weak, persuaded by their example, burn with temporal desires. The downfall of the strong increases the destruction of the weak.

Since the sun signifies the acuteness of the wise, Solomon also says by comparison: “The wise man remains like the sun; the fool will change like the moon” (Eccl. 27:12). What, then, is signified here by the sun’s ray except the acuteness of the wise, who in the holy Church seemed to scatter rays of light through the sharpness of wisdom and to shine through the authority of righteousness?

CAP. XXXVI.—“Blessed is the one who watches and keeps” (Rev. 16:15).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book II, no. 81.) For if our works did not cover us before God like garments, [Col. 1117A] an angelic voice would never say: “Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (Rev. 16:15). Our shame is seen when a blameworthy life is not covered before the eyes of the just at the judgment by the protection of subsequent good works.

CAP. XXXVII.—The same subject.

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVI, no. 63.) As garments protect the body, so good works protect the soul. Hence it is said to someone: “Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked” (Rev. 16:15).

CAP. XXXVIII.—“The waters that you saw, where the prostitute is” (Rev. 17:15).

(Homily 8 on Ezekiel, no. 1.) In sacred language, peoples are customarily signified by waters. Hence John says: “The waters are peoples.” The people is signified by waters because in life it makes a sound through the tumult of the flesh and flows away daily through the course of mortality.

CAP. XXXIX.—“Blessed are those who are called to the wedding supper” (Rev. 19:9).

[Col. 1117B]

(Homily 6 on the Gospels, no. 24.) Concerning this final banquet, John says elsewhere: “Blessed are those who are called to the wedding supper” (Rev. 19:9). He reports that they are called not to lunch but to supper because, plainly, a banquet at the end of the day is a supper. Those who, when the time of the present life has ended, come to the refreshment of heavenly contemplation are therefore called not to the Lamb’s lunch but to his supper.

CAP. XL.—“See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant” (Rev. 19:10).

(Homily 8 on the Gospels, no. 2.) Lot and Joshua worship angels, yet they are not forbidden to worship. John wished to worship an angel in the Apocalypse, but that same angel restrains him from worshiping him, saying: “See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers” (Rev. 19:10).

What does it mean that before the Redeemer’s [Col. 1117C] coming angels are worshiped by human beings and remain silent, but afterward refuse to be worshiped, except that they had previously despised our nature, whereas after they saw it assumed above them, they feared to see it placed beneath them? They no longer dared to scorn as weak beneath themselves the nature that they venerate above themselves, namely, in the King of heaven. Nor do they disdain to have a human being as their companion, since above themselves they worship a human being who is God.

CAP. XLI.—“And the armies that are in heaven” (Rev. 19:14).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXI, no. 27.) A horse is each holy soul’s own body, which it knows both to restrain from unlawful things by the bridle of self-control and, again, to release for the exercise of good works through the impulse of charity. Hence the Apostle John, contemplating the Lord in the Apocalypse, says: “And the armies that are in heaven followed him on white horses” (Rev. 19:14).

He rightly calls the multitude of the saints, which had labored in this battle [Col. 1117D] of martyrdom, an army. They are described as sitting on white horses because their bodies shone both with the light of righteousness and with the whiteness of chastity.

CAP. XLII.—“And on his garment and on his thigh he has written: King of kings” (Rev. 19:16).

(In the Exposition of Ezekiel, Book II, Homily 1, no. 9.) John says: “He had written on his garment and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19:16). For what is his garment but himself? Our own garment is also called flesh, yet we ourselves are that flesh with which we are clothed.

Isaiah, seeing his garment long beforehand, bloodstained through the passion of the cross, said: “Why is your garment red, and your vesture like that of those who tread the winepress?” (Isa. 63:2). He answered him: “I alone have trodden the winepress, and no man from the nations was with me” (ibid., v. 8). For he alone trod the winepress [Col. 1118A] in which he was trodden, who by his own power conquered the passion that he endured. For he who suffered even to the death of the cross rose from death in glory.

It is rightly said: “And no man from the nations was with me,” because those for whom he had come to suffer ought to have shared in his passion; yet because at that time they had not yet believed, he complains in the passion about those whose life was being sought through that passion.

The thigh signifies the propagation of the flesh. Since, therefore, through the propagation of the human race—as the genealogical sequences are described by Matthew and Luke—he came into this world from a Virgin, and through the mystery of his incarnation made known everywhere to all nations that he was King and Lord, he had written on his garment and on his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords.” For by the means through which he became known in the world, there he impressed the statement to be read about himself.

CAP. XLIII.—“And he bound him for a thousand years” (Rev. 20:2).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book IV, no. 16.) The spirits of the elect angels now hold this Leviathan [Col. 1118B] shut in the abyss. Hence it is written: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand. And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss” (Rev. 20:1–2).

Yet at the end of the world they recall him to more open combat and release him entirely against us in his own strength. Hence it is written there again: “When the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released” (ibid., v. 7).

That apostate angel, who had been created so as to surpass the other legions of angels, fell so deeply through pride that he is now subjected to the rule of the angels who stand firm, so that, while he is bound by their ministry, he may now lie hidden for our benefit, and, when released by them for our testing, may exercise all his strength against us.

CAP. XLIV.—The same subject.

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, no. 67.) [Col. 1118C]

“I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand; and he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan; and he bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss, and shut him in, and sealed it over him, so that he might no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years were completed” (Rev. 20:1).

By the number one thousand, not a quantity of time but the totality over which the Church reigns is signified. The ancient serpent is bound with a chain and cast into the abyss because, restrained from the hearts of the good and confined within the minds of the reprobate, he exercises a more savage dominion over them.

A little later he is also described as being brought out of the abyss, because from the hearts of the wicked—where he now rages secretly—he will then burst forth into open persecution, having received power against the Church.

CAP. XLV.—The same subject.

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXII, no. 22.) Just as the cedar, growing upward, leaves the other trees behind in height, so then Antichrist, temporarily [Col. 1118D] possessing the glory of the world, surpasses human measures both in the height of honor and in the power of signs. The spirit within him is one that, having been created among the heights, did not lose the power of its nature even after being cast down.

Its power is now not displayed because, by the dispensation of divine strength, it is bound. Hence John says: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand; and he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan; and he bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss, and shut him in, and sealed him over him” (ibid.).

He is said to be bound in the abyss because, shut up in the hearts of the wicked, he is restrained by the power of the divine dispensation, lest, insofar as he prevails, he run wild; so that although he rages secretly through them, he does not burst forth into violent acts of arrogant plunder.

But how he will be released at the end of the world is made known there when it is said: “And after the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out and deceive the nations” (ibid., v. 7). [Col. 1119A] By the number one thousand, because of its perfection, the whole period of the holy Church, however long it may be, is expressed. When it has been completed, the ancient enemy, handed over to his own strength, is released for a short time, but with great power against us.

CAP. XLVI.—“Blessed and holy is the one who has a share” (Rev. 20:6).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIV, no. 19.) “Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection” (Rev. 20:6). The one who will rise happily afterward in the flesh is the one who, while placed in this life, has risen from the death of his mind.

CAP. XLVII.—“And the books were opened, and another” (Rev. 20:12).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXIV, nos. 15–16.) Whoever desires to understand most fully what he is must certainly observe what he is not, so that from the form of the good he may measure how deformed he himself is through having abandoned the good.

From those in whom the good is most fully [Col. 1119B] present, he perceives rightly what is lacking in himself; and in their beauty he sees his own ugliness, which he can suffer in himself but cannot perceive. For one who wishes to judge of darkness must behold light, so that in it he may see what he thinks about the darkness that prevents him from seeing.

If a sinner, unaware of the life of the just, looks at himself, he does not at all understand that he is a sinner. He cannot see himself, because, not knowing the radiance of light, when he looks at himself, what else does he perceive but darkness?

We must therefore contemplate the life of the just in order to recognize our own with precision. Their appearance is set before us as a kind of form to imitate. The life of the good is a living reading. Hence the just are not improperly called books in sacred language, as it is written: “The books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life; and the dead were judged from what was written in the books” (Rev. 20:12).

The book of life is the very vision of the coming Judge, in whom every commandment is, as it were, [Col. 1119C] written, because whoever sees him immediately understands, with conscience as witness, whatever he has not done. The books are also said to have been opened because the life of the just is then seen; in them the heavenly commandments are discerned as impressed by works. And the dead were judged from what was written in the books because, in the displayed life of the just, as in an opened book, they read the good that they themselves were unwilling to do and are condemned by comparison with those who did it.

Therefore, lest each person then weep upon seeing what he did not do, let him now attend to what he may imitate in them.

CAP. XLVIII.—“And I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. 21:1).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVII, no. 11.) Let us distinguish how earth and heaven pass away and how they remain. Both pass away with respect to the form they now possess, yet in their essence they subsist without end. Hence Paul says: “For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. [Col. 1119D] 7:31). Hence Truth itself says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). Hence, by an angelic voice, it is declared to John: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. 21:1). These are not to be created as other things, but these same things are renewed.

Heaven and earth therefore both pass away and will exist, because they are cleansed by fire from the form they now possess, yet are preserved forever in their own nature. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Ps. 101:27).

They now announce this final change of theirs to us through the very alternations by which they continually vary for our use. For the earth loses its winter appearance through dryness and becomes green through the moisture of spring. Heaven is covered daily by the darkness of night and renewed by the brightness of day. From this, then, let every faithful person conclude that these things both perish and are restored through renewal, since they are constantly repaired as though from decline.

CAP. XLIX.—“Having twelve gates, and at the gates” (Rev. 21:12).

[Col. 1120A]

(In the Exposition of Ezekiel, Book II, Homily 2, no. 3.) Each preacher may also be understood by the name “gate,” because whoever opens for us with his mouth the door of the heavenly kingdom is a gate. Hence twelve gates are described either in John’s Apocalypse or in the final vision of this prophecy.

CAP. L.—“The measure of a man, which is that of an angel” (Rev. 21:17).

(Ibid., Book II, Homily 2, no. 15.) The humility of human beings is sometimes brought to equality with that of angels. Hence it is written: “They neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22:30). Hence John says: “The measure of a man, which is that of an angel” (Rev. 21:17). For a human being is brought to that height of glory in which the angels rejoice that they have been made firm.

CAP. LI.—“The city itself was pure gold” (Rev. 21:17).

[Col. 1120B]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, no. 77.) We know that the metal gold shines with greater brilliance than all other metals. It is the nature of glass, however, that, seen from outside, it shines through with pure transparency within. In another metal, whatever is contained inside is hidden; in glass, whatever liquid is contained within is displayed outwardly as it is inside, and, so to speak, every liquid enclosed in a glass vessel is visible.

What else, then, do we understand by gold and glass except that heavenly homeland and the fellowship of those blessed citizens whose hearts both shine toward one another with brilliance and are transparent with purity? John had seen this in the Apocalypse when he said: “The structure of its wall was of jasper; and the city itself was pure gold, [Note: [Col. 1119] Concerning this reading, see note b at the indicated passage of the Moralia, column 593.] like pure glass” (Rev. 21:18).

Because all the saints will shine in it with the highest splendor of blessedness, it is said to be constructed of gold. And because their very brilliance is mutually visible in their hearts, so that when each person’s face is observed, his conscience is simultaneously penetrated, this gold is remembered to be like pure glass.

[Col. 1120C]

There, the corporeal substance of the limbs will not hide each person’s mind from the eyes of another; rather, the mind will be visible, and even the harmony of the body itself will be visible to bodily eyes. Thus each person will then be visible to another in a way in which he cannot now be visible even to himself.

CAP. LII.—“The bright and morning star” (Rev. 22:16).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXIX, no. 75.) “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law” (Gal. 4:4). Born of a Virgin, he appeared like the morning star amid the darkness of our conduct. Having driven away the obscurity of sin, he announced to us the eternal morning. He made himself known as the morning star because at dawn [Col. 1120D] he rose from death and, by the radiance of his light, pressed down the foul darkness of our mortality.

He is rightly called by John “the bright and morning star” (Rev. 22:16). Appearing alive after death, he became for us the morning star because, by providing in himself an example of resurrection, he showed what light would follow.

CAP. LIII.—“And let the one who hears say: Come” (Rev. 22:17).

(In the Exposition of Ezekiel, Book II, Homily 2, no. 4.) Whoever advances by seeing spiritual things ought also to offer them to others through speech. For the one who sees in order to announce is the one who, having advanced within himself, also takes care through preaching for the advancement of his neighbor.

Hence it is written elsewhere: “Let the one who hears say: Come” (Rev. 22:17). When the voice of God calling has already become present in the heart, it is necessary for it to burst forth into a voice for one’s neighbor through the ministry of preaching [Col. 1121A]; and for that reason one calls another, because he himself has already been called.

CAP. LIV.—The same subject.

(Homily 6 on the Gospels, no. 6.) To the extent that you judge yourselves to have made progress, draw others along as well; desire to have companions on the way of God. If one of you, brothers, is going to the marketplace or perhaps to the baths, he invites anyone he sees to be idle to come with him. Let your earthly activity itself admonish you; and if you are making for God, take care not to come to him alone. Hence it is written: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (ibid.). Thus, whoever has already received the voice of heavenly love in his heart should also return to his neighbors a voice of exhortation outwardly.

### CHAPTER LV.—Likewise on the same subject.

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, admonition 26.) John admonishes us with an angelic voice when he says: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (ibid.); so that the person into whom the inner voice insinuates itself may also, by calling out to others, draw them to the place toward which he himself is being carried. Otherwise, even though he has been called, he may find the doors closed if he approaches the one who calls while empty-handed.

# BOOK EIGHT  
## On Testimonies Concerning the Epistles of Saint Paul

## ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

[Col. 1121]

### CHAPTER I.—“Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2:4.)

[Col. 1121A]

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XVII, no. 8.) Whoever sins and continues to live is tolerated by divine providence in his iniquity for this reason: that he may be restrained from iniquity. But whoever is tolerated for a longer time and nevertheless is not restrained from iniquity receives the gift of heavenly patience, yet through that very gift binds himself more tightly in the chains of his guilt. For because he turns the time granted for repentance toward sin, the stern Judge at the end turns the abundant proofs of mercy toward punishment. Hence Paul says: “Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment” (Rom. 2:4–5).

### CHAPTER II.—“The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Rom. 9:18.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXIX, no. 60.) The Lord is said to harden himself—not in the sense that he forms the minds of the wicked for guilt, but in the sense that he does not free them from guilt—as it is written: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Rom. 9:18). Because he did not mercifully wish to soften it, he plainly declared that he would harden it in judgment.

### CHAPTER III.—“To honor God among the Gentiles because of his mercy” (Rom. 15:9.)

[Col. 1122A]

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXVII, no. 58.) The place of God’s mercy is the Gentile world itself. If the stern Judge had dealt with its sins according to justice, it would never have come to reconciliation with grace. Although it possessed no merits before God, it nevertheless received the grace of reconciliation from mercy alone. Hence Paul rightly says: “To honor God among the Gentiles because of his mercy” (Rom. 15:9). Again it is written: “She who had not obtained mercy has now obtained mercy” (1 Pet. 2:10).

### CHAPTER IV.—“For I do not dare to speak of anything” (Rom. 15:18.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXVIII, no. 25.) David had rightly kept the foot of his heart within the measures granted by divine generosity when he said: “I have not walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me” (Ps. 130:1). He would walk in things too wonderful for himself if he sought to appear greater than he was able to be; for the person who strives to seem capable of things beyond his strength lifts himself above himself in matters too wonderful. Paul likewise rightly confined himself within these measures, even in the breadth of his preaching, when he said: “For I do not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through me” (Rom. 15:18).

## ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 1121]

### CHAPTER I.—“For I determined to know nothing” (1 Cor. 2:2.)

[Col. 1121C]

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXI, no. 104.) “Its young ones lap up blood” (Job 39:30). It is as though he were saying openly: The eagle itself is nourished by contemplation of divinity; but because its hearers can in no way grasp the mysteries of divinity, they are satisfied with knowledge of the blood of the crucified Lord. To lap up blood is to honor the weakness of the Lord’s passion. Hence Paul, who, as we said shortly before, had flown up to the secrets of the third heaven, said to his disciples: “I determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). It is as though this eagle were saying openly: I see my food from afar—the power of his divinity—but to you, still little ones, I offer only the blood of his incarnation to lap up. For when, through his preaching, he taught weak hearers only about the blood of the cross, while keeping silent about the sublimity of divinity, what else did he provide for his young but blood?

### CHAPTER II.—“The things that we also speak, not in the learned words of human wisdom” (1 Cor. 2:13.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XVIII, no. 74.) The teaching of wisdom is beautiful in its preaching and conspicuous in pure truth. It does not deceitfully present one thing outwardly and reserve another inwardly; nor does it seek to appear beautiful in its sayings through the polish of speech, but through the integrity of truth. Therefore God’s wisdom in its commandments is not adorned with the dyed colors of India; since it lacks the painted ornaments of eloquence, it pleases like an undyed garment. Paul had rightly despised such cosmetic coloring when he said: “The things that we also speak, not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit” (1 Cor. 2:13). He preferred to display this wisdom through the pure truth alone, rather than to color it with rhetorical ornament.

### CHAPTER III.—“Neither is the one who plants anything, nor the one who waters” (1 Cor. 3:7.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXVII, no. 64.) Teachers should by no means claim for themselves what they see their hearers accomplish through their exhortation. Unless the Holy Spirit fills their hearts, the voice of teachers sounds uselessly upon bodily ears. They can form the teacher’s voice outwardly, but they cannot impress it inwardly: “Neither is the one who plants anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

### CHAPTER IV.—“The wisdom of this world is folly” (1 Cor. 3:19.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XVIII, no. 67.) When an unrighteous mind desires to be carnally wise, it shows itself foolish with respect to spiritual things. For since, as Paul testifies, “the wisdom of this world is folly before God” (1 Cor. 3:19), each person becomes inwardly more foolish the more he strives to appear outwardly wise.

### CHAPTER V.—“Neither fornicators nor adulterers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9.)

[Col. 1123A]

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXI, no. 18.) Although the guilt of fornication is sometimes in no way distinct from the guilt of adultery, since Truth says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). (For, since the Greek word *moechus* means “adulterer,” while what is forbidden to be looked upon is not another man’s wife but simply a woman, Truth plainly shows that adultery is committed by the mere look when even an unmarried woman is shamefully desired.) Nevertheless it is often distinguished by the situation or status of the one who desires. For deliberate desire stains one person in the sacred order just as the guilt of adultery stains another. Yet in persons who are not unlike one another, the same guilt of lust is distinguished. That the guilt of fornication is distinct from the guilt of adultery is testified by the tongue of the eminent preacher, which among other things says: “Neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9). By setting down the sentence with the offence added, he showed how greatly the two differ from one another.

### CHAPTER VI.—“Whoever thinks that he knows something” (1 Cor. 8:2.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXVII, no. 62.) Perfect knowledge is to know everything and yet, in a certain sense, not to know that one is knowledgeable. For although we now know God’s commandments, although we weigh the force of his words with careful consideration, and although we practice what we believe we have understood, we still do not clearly know with what strictness of examination the same things must be scrutinized. We do not yet see God’s face; we do not yet behold his hidden counsels. How great, then, is our knowledge, which, so long as it is weighed down by mortality, is blinded by the very cloud of its uncertainty? Paul rightly says of it: “Whoever thinks that he knows something has not yet known how he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2). Therefore, while we live in this world, we know perfectly what must be known when, advancing toward understanding, we recognize that we know nothing perfectly.

### CHAPTER VII.—The same as above.

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXVIII, no. 11.) The Apostle says: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he has not yet known how he ought to know” (ibid.). Since the first folly of the angel was pride of heart, true wisdom in a human being is humility concerning his own estimation. Whoever abandons this humility through thinking himself wise in great matters is all the more foolish because he does not know himself.

### CHAPTER VIII.—“I discipline my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Cor. 9:27.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XX, no. 9.) Let us see how grace from above already smiles upon Paul, while he himself still seems not to believe it because of fearful suspicion. The Lord had already spoken to him from heaven, opening the eyes within him and closing them outwardly, and had displayed the power of his majesty. He had already said concerning him to Ananias: “He is a vessel of election for me” (Acts 9:15). He had already been caught up above himself into the third heaven; he had already been led into paradise and heard secret words that he could not speak. And yet, still fearful, he says: “I discipline my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27). Behold: while divine grace smiles upon him, he already believes through hope, yet does not believe through security.

### CHAPTER IX.—“Whoever thinks that he stands, let him see that he does not fall” (1 Cor. 10:12.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXV, no. 21.) Let us therefore fear concerning the things we have received, but let us not despair of those who have not yet attained them. We know what we are today, but we do not know what we may shortly become. Those whom we perhaps despise may begin slowly and nevertheless surpass our life through more fervent efforts. We must therefore fear lest, when we fall, the person who is mocked while we stand should rise. Indeed, the one who knows how to mock someone who is not standing no longer knows how to stand. The Apostle Paul instilled this fear of heavenly judgments into the hearts of his disciples, saying: “Whoever thinks that he stands, let him see that he does not fall” (1 Cor. 10:12).

### CHAPTER X.—“He will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Cor. 10:13.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXIX, no. 46.) The high and incomprehensible grace of the Holy Spirit, when it illumines our minds with its light, also regulates the temptations of the adversary, arranging that many should not come at once. Thus only those temptations that can be endured touch the soul already illumined by God; and although their burning contact torments us, it does not consume us in the fire of perfection. Paul bears witness to this when he says: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13).

### CHAPTER XI.—“To one is given, through the Spirit, a word of wisdom” (1 Cor. 12:8.)

[Col. 1124B]

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXVIII, no. 21.) “Who established its measures, if you know, or who stretched the measuring line over it?” (Job 38:5). Who indeed but our Creator establishes the measures of this earth, who, by the secret regulation of inward judgment, grants to one the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another full faith, to another gifts of healing, to another the working of powers, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of words (1 Cor. 12)?

Thus, in the one and the same Spirit, one person may be powerful in the word of wisdom and yet not be supported by the word of knowledge, that is, by learning; for it is enough for him to perceive and discover even what he has not grasped through study. Another may shine in the word of knowledge and yet not grow strong in the word of wisdom; for he is capable of carrying out as much as he has learned, yet does not rise from within himself to perceive anything subtle. One commands even the elements through faith, yet does not heal bodily illnesses through the gift of healing. Another removes diseases through the work of prayer, yet does not return rain to parched earth by a word. One recalls the dead even to the present life through the working of powers, yet, lacking the gift of prophecy, does not know what is to come. Another regards future events as though they were present, yet does not display himself in any working of signs. One subtly perceives minds in their actions through the discernment of spirits, yet does not know tongues of different kinds. Another examines tongues of different kinds, yet does not weigh dissimilar hearts in similar matters. Another prudently examines the force of words by interpreting them in one language that he knows, yet patiently lacks the other good things that he does not possess.

### CHAPTER XII.—“If I deliver my body so that I may burn” (1 Cor. 13:3.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XVIII, no. 41.) The Apostle Paul indicates how worthless is the fire of burning endured outside the Catholic Church, when he says: “If I deliver my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). Some think wrongly about God; others hold right beliefs about the Creator but do not maintain unity with their brothers. The former are divided by error of faith, the latter by the commission of schism. Hence the guilt of both groups is restrained in that part of the Decalogue when the divine voice says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. 6:4–5). It immediately adds: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Whoever thinks perversely about God plainly does not love God; whoever thinks rightly about God but is divided from the unity of the holy Church is clearly not loving his neighbor, whom he refuses to have as a companion.

(No. 42.) Whoever is separated from this unity of Mother Church—whether through heresy, by thinking perversely about God, or through the error of schism, by failing to love his neighbor—is deprived of this grace of charity, of which Paul says what we quoted above: “If I deliver my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.” It is as though he were saying plainly: When fire is applied to me outside its proper place of burning, it tortures me with torment but does not cleanse me by purification.

All lovers of holy peace seek this place with the greatest zeal; seeking it, they find it, and finding it, they hold it—knowing where, when, and for whom the forgiveness of sins is granted. Where, indeed, except in the bosom of the Catholic Mother? When, except before the day of our coming departure? For, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). And: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55:6). For whom, except for those who have been converted, who are formed in instructive humility after the likeness of little children? To them it is said: “Allow the little children to come to me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven.” And: “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:14).

### CHAPTER XIII.—“I am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15:9.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXIV, no. 20.) Paul, by laboring more vigorously in preaching, surpassed the diligence of the other saints. To restrain himself from pride and nourish his strength in the bosom of humility, he did not forget his former cruelty. Considering the innocence of all the apostles, he said: “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9).

## ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 1125]

### CHAPTER I.—“We are the good fragrance of Christ” (2 Cor. 2:15.)

[Col. 1125B]

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXIV, no. 32.) The fragrance of ointments commonly signifies the reputation of virtues. Hence the bride, desiring the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs, says: “We run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3). And the Apostle Paul, not knowing himself to be aflame with the praise of virtues, says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ for God” (2 Cor. 2:15).

### CHAPTER II.—“We have this treasure in vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXII, no. 8.) Contemplating within himself the riches of knowledge, and humbling his contemplation by considering human frailty, Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7).

### CHAPTER III.—“Satan himself disguises himself as an angel” (2 Cor. 11:14.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXIX, no. 58.) Something else lies hidden within him, while he displays something different outwardly: “For he disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14). By the crafty art of deception he often presents what is praiseworthy in order to lead people toward what is unlawful.

### CHAPTER IV.—“What wonder, then, if his ministers” (2 Cor. 11:15.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXIII, no. 44.) His members, when they cannot harm others through open wickedness, often assume the appearance of good action. They do indeed display evil things, but they disguise them under a holy appearance. If the wicked were openly evil, the good could not receive them at all; but they take something from the appearance of the good, so that, while good men accept in them the appearance they love, they also unwittingly take in the poison they avoid.

Thus, observing certain people who, under the guise of preaching, served the interests of their belly, the Apostle Paul said: “Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14). “What wonder, then, if his ministers disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness?”

### CHAPTER V.—“If someone devours, if someone takes” (2 Cor. 11:20.)

[Col. 1125D]

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXIII, no. 24.) We sometimes use *accipere*—“to take”—also in the sense of “to carry off.” Hence those birds that are eager to seize other birds are called *accipitres*, “hawks.” Thus the Apostle Paul says: “For you endure it if someone devours, if someone takes” (2 Cor. 11:20). It is as though he were saying: “If someone robs.”

### CHAPTER VI.—“In whatever anyone dares—I speak foolishly” (2 Cor. 11:21.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XIX, no. 37.) Good preachers flee honor because of pride, yet wish to be honored for the sake of imitation. In this way the Apostle Paul, speaking to his disciples, both flees honor and nevertheless shows how much honor he deserves. When he said to the Thessalonians: “For we were never in a word of flattery, as you know, nor with an occasion for greed; God is witness” (1 Thess. 2:5), he continued: “Nor did we seek glory from human beings, either from you or from others, although, as apostles of Christ, we could have been held in honor; but we became little ones in your midst” (1 Thess. 2:6–7).

Again, fleeing honor, he says to the Corinthians: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. 4:5). Yet when he saw them straying from the path of true faith through the persuasion of false apostles, he showed them with the greatest force how much reverence was due to him, saying: “In whatever anyone dares—I speak foolishly—I dare also. Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I. Are they ministers of Christ? I am even more so”—“I speak as one less wise” (2 Cor. 11:21).

He also adds that the secrets of the third heaven had been opened to him and that he had been caught up and entered the mysteries of paradise. Behold: fleeing honor, he proclaims himself the servant of his disciples. Behold: seeking honor for the sake of his hearers’ benefit, he set the merits of his life above those of the false apostles. The eminent teacher acted so that, when his own character was recognized, both the life and the speech of the wicked preachers might become contemptible by comparison with him (alternative reading: “by his preaching”). He would have commended them if he had hidden himself; and by not displaying himself, he would have given error an opportunity.

Thus, in a wonderful manner, he seeks both the grace of humility and an increase of usefulness: he proclaims himself the servant of his disciples and demonstrates himself superior to his adversaries. He shows his disciples what humility he has received; he shows his adversaries what exaltation he possesses.

### CHAPTER VII.—“Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XIX, no. 18.) Through the entrails of charity, whatever the perfect endure as harm to the little ones grieves their spirit as though they themselves suffered it. The losses of the weak pass through compassion into the hearts of the strong. Hence Paul says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (2 Cor. 11:29). Each person is perfect to the extent that he perfectly feels the pains of others.

### CHAPTER VIII.—“I refrain, lest anyone should think of me above what he sees in me” (2 Cor. 12:6.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XVIII, no. 13.) All who are truly holy not only do not desire glory beyond their measure, but also avoid appearing to be what they have deserved to become. Hence that eminent preacher of truth, speaking against the false apostles, recounted the outstanding works of his ministry for the instruction of his disciples. He described the many dangers he had endured through accumulated persecution and afterward remembered that he had been caught up to the third heaven and again into paradise, where he could have learned such things as he could not possibly speak.

He might perhaps have continued to speak of himself in still more remarkable terms, but, exercising profound restraint from human praise, he added: “I refrain, lest anyone should think of me above what he sees in me or hears from me” (2 Cor. 12:6). He therefore still had something to say about himself, since he refrained from saying it. Yet the eminent teacher accomplished both things: by speaking of what he had done, he instructed his disciples; by remaining silent, he kept himself within the bounds of humility. He would have been extremely ungrateful if he had concealed everything about himself from his disciples, and perhaps extremely careless if he had revealed everything about himself even to his disciples. But, as has been said, he wonderfully accomplished both: by speaking, he educated the life of his hearers; by remaining silent, he guarded his own.

### CHAPTER IX.—“A thorn in the flesh was given to me” (2 Cor. 12:7.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XIX, no. 11.) I see Paul enduring dangers of rivers, robbers, cities, deserts, sea, and land; restraining his body through fasts and vigils; enduring the hardship of cold and nakedness; vigilantly and pastorally laboring for the protection of the churches; caught up to the third heaven; again caught up into paradise; and hearing secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak. Yet he is still handed over to the angel of Satan to be tempted. He prays to be freed, but is not heard.

When I consider the very beginnings of his conversion, I perceive that heavenly mercy opened the heavens to him and that Jesus showed himself to him from on high. He temporarily lost the light of his body but received the light of his heart forever. He was sent to Ananias and called a vessel of election. Yet he later fled from that same city into which he had entered after seeing Jesus, as he himself testifies, saying: “The governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me, and I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall, and so I escaped his hands” (2 Cor. 11:32–33).

I may fittingly say to him: O Paul, you already behold Jesus in heaven, yet on earth you still flee from a human being. You are led into paradise and learn the secret words of God, yet you are still tempted by the angel of Satan. How are you so strong that you are carried up to heavenly things, and how are you so weak that you flee from a human being on earth and still endure adversity from the angel of Satan? It is because the one who lifts you up again moderates you by the most subtle measure: through your miracles you proclaim to us the power of God, while through your fear you remind us of our weakness.

Yet lest this weakness drive us into despair when it assails us, while you were praying to the Lord in hope amid your weakness and were not heard, you also told us what you heard: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

(No. 12.) God’s own open voice therefore shows that weakness is the guardian of strength. We are well guarded inwardly when, by providential arrangement, we are tolerably tempted outwardly, sometimes by vices and sometimes by afflictions. For those whom we know to have been men of virtue were not without temptations and struggles against vice.

Hence, for our consolation, that eminent preacher deigns to disclose certain things about himself, saying: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin that is in my members” (Rom. 7:23). The flesh drags us downward so that the spirit may not become exalted; the spirit draws us upward so that the flesh may not cast us down. The spirit lifts us lest we lie in the lowest places; the flesh weighs us down lest we become exalted from the heights. If the flesh did not tempt us while the spirit lifted us up, the perfection of its temptation would undoubtedly cast us into the depths. Conversely, if the spirit lifted us to the heights without the flesh’s temptation, that very lifting would cast us down more disastrously in the fall of pride.

But by a definite moderation it comes about that, while each of the saints is already carried inwardly toward the heights yet is still tempted outwardly, he falls neither into despair nor into pride. Exterior temptation does not complete guilt, because inward intention draws upward; nor does inward intention lift one into pride, because exterior temptation humbles while it weighs down. Thus, in a great order, we recognize in inward progress what we have received and in outward decline what we are. It is wonderfully arranged that no one should be lifted up by virtue or despair because of temptation: while the spirit draws upward and the flesh draws back, the soul is balanced by the most subtle regulation of inward judgment below the heights and above the depths, in a kind of middle place.

### CHAPTER X.—The same as above.

[Col. 1128B]

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXIII, no. 26.) The pierced jaw of this Behemoth can also be understood in another way: he is said to hold in his mouth not those whom he already involves perfectly in sin, but those whom he still tempts through the persuasions of sin. Thus, for him to chew someone means to tempt that person through the pleasure of sin.

Paul had been given to be chewed but not swallowed when, after so many sublime revelations, the thorn of the flesh afflicted him (2 Cor. 12). At that time, when permission to tempt him was granted, Satan held him in his jaw—but in a pierced jaw. The one who could have been destroyed through pride was tempted so that he would not perish. That temptation, therefore, was not a chasm of vices but a safeguard of merits: this Leviathan crushed him through wearisome affliction, but did not seize and swallow him into guilt.

### CHAPTER XI.—“I have become foolish” (2 Cor. 12:11.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXIV, no. 42.) Paul maintained discipline when he said to the Corinthians: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” (1 Cor. 3:3). Yet he did not lose humility within discipline, because he admonished them by entreaty, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you” (1 Cor. 1:10).

Again, he maintained the form of humility when, speaking to those same Corinthians, he reproved himself somewhat more fully than he perhaps wished, saying: “I have become foolish” (2 Cor. 12:11). But he did not lose discipline in this humility, because he immediately added: “You compelled me.”
