He displayed an example of great humility when he said to his disciples: “For we do not preach ourselves, but our Lord Jesus Christ, and ourselves as your servants through Christ.” Yet he did not lose the justice of discipline in this humility, since he says to those same offenders: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Cor. 4:21). Holy preachers therefore know how to temper the art of teaching by both measures: when they find the guilt of offenders, they know how sometimes to rebuke severely and sometimes to entreat humbly.

## ON THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS

[Col. 1127]

### CHAPTER I.—“Then, after fourteen years, I went up to Jerusalem” (Gal. 1:2.)

[Col. 1127D]

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXV, no. 30.) It must be understood with the greatest care that obedience is sometimes nothing if it contains something of one’s own, and sometimes very small if it contains nothing of one’s own. When worldly success is commanded, when a higher position is imposed, the person who obeys in order to receive these things empties obedience of its virtue if he also longs for them from his own desire. For he does not place himself under obedience who serves the lust of his own ambition in order to obtain the prosperity of this life.

Conversely, when contempt for the world is commanded, when disgrace and insults are ordered, the person who descends unwillingly and reluctantly to what is despised in this life diminishes the merit of obedience unless his spirit also desires it of its own accord. Obedience is brought to ruin when the mind is not accompanied, at least in some measure, by its own wishes in accepting the insults of this age.

Obedience must therefore possess something of its own in adversity, and in prosperity must in every way possess nothing of its own, so that in adversity it may be more glorious insofar as it joins the divine order even through desire, and in prosperity it may be more genuine insofar as the glory it receives from God in the present is completely separated from the mind.

(No. 31.) We can show the weight of this virtue more clearly if we recall the deeds of two heroes of the heavenly homeland. When Moses was tending sheep in the desert, he was called by the Lord, who spoke through an angel in fire, to preside over the whole multitude of Israelites who were to be rescued (Exod. 3). But because he was humble in mind before himself, he immediately feared the glory of such great leadership when it was offered to him, and at once took refuge in pleading his weakness, saying: “I am not eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before. Since you began to speak to your servant, I have become slower and more impeded in speech” (Exod. 4:10). Putting himself aside, he asked that another be sent, saying: “Send the one whom you will send” (v. 13).

Behold: he is speaking with the author of speech, yet, so as not to assume the power of such great leadership, he claims to be speechless.

Paul, too, had been divinely instructed that he should go up to Jerusalem, as he himself says to the Galatians: “Then, after fourteen years, I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus; I went up according to revelation” (Gal. 2:1–2). On the journey, when he encountered the prophet Agabus (Acts 21), he heard how much adversity awaited him in Jerusalem. For it is written that Agabus, taking Paul’s belt and binding his own feet with it, said: “The man whose belt this is will be bound in this way in Jerusalem” (ibid. 11). Paul immediately replied: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of Jesus; for I do not hold my life more precious than myself” (v. 13).

As he went to Jerusalem by command of revelation, he learned of adversity and nevertheless desired it willingly. He heard what he should fear, but he yearned for it more ardently.

Moses, therefore, contributes nothing of his own toward prosperity, since he resists with prayers lest he be placed over the Israelite people. Paul, however, is led toward adversity also by his own will, since he learns of the evils threatening him but, through the devotion of his spirit, grows fervent even toward harsher things. The former wished to decline the glory of present authority when God commanded it; the latter, while God arranged harsh and difficult things, strove to prepare his spirit for still greater hardships.

Therefore, guided by the example of both leaders, we are instructed that if we truly strive to seize the palm of obedience, we must incline toward the prosperity of this age solely because of a command, but toward adversity also because of devotion.

### CHAPTER II.—“My little children, whom I am again in labor” (Gal. 4:19.)

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXX, no. 47.) Holy preachers sow now in tears so that later they may reap a harvest of joys. Now they are like does in the pain of childbirth, so that later they may be fruitful in spiritual offspring. To speak of one among many, I see Paul like a doe uttering cries of great pain in labor. He says: “My little children, whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you, I would like to be present with you now and change my voice, because I am perplexed about you” (Gal. 4:19–20).

Behold, he wishes to change his voice in his labor, so that the speech of preaching may be turned into a cry of pain. He wishes to change his voice because those whom he had already brought forth through preaching he was again bringing forth with groans through reforming them.

What a cry this doe uttered in giving birth when, compelled to shout at those returning to their former ways, she said: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?” and: “Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being completed by the flesh?” Or again: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” (Gal. 3:1; 3:3; 5:7).

What a cry there was in the labor of this doe, who bore sons conceived long before amid so many difficulties, and eventually learned that those whom she had brought forth had returned to the womb of wickedness? Let us consider what pain she endured, what labor, since, after she had been able to bring forth those conceived within her, she was again compelled to raise up those who had died.

## ON THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS

[Col. 1129]

### CHAPTER I.—“Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4:23.)

[Col. 1129C]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXV, no. 14.) It belongs to the elect to examine their actions daily from the very source of thought and to dry up from within whatever flows turbidly. For just as we do not perceive how our limbs grow, our body develops, our appearance changes, and the blackness of our hair turns white with gray—for all these things take place within us without our knowing it—so our mind is changed moment by moment by the very practice of living amid cares. We do not recognize this unless, by vigilant watchfulness, we dwell within ourselves and weigh our progress and our failures every day. Indeed, to remain in this mortal life is, as it were, to move toward old age. And when the mind is left unexamined, it is lulled into a kind of senility of torpor; for, neglecting itself and imperceptibly losing the strength of its purpose, it grows old without knowing it, withdrawing from the form of its former strength. Hence it is said through the prophet, under the figure of Ephraim: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it; indeed, gray hairs have appeared upon him, and he himself did not know it” (Hosea VII, 9).

But when the mind seeks itself and carefully examines itself through repentance, it is washed of this very old age by tears and rekindled by grief; and what had already almost grown cold through age becomes warm again through the supplied attentions of inward love. Hence the Apostle Paul admonishes disciples who are growing old through the practice of mortal life, saying: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians IV, 23).

(Col. 1130C) (No. 15.) To accomplish these things, the examples of the fathers and the precepts of sacred Scripture greatly assist us. For if we look upon the works of the saints and lend our ear to divine commands, some things that we contemplate and others that we hear set us aflame; and our heart is not constricted by torpor while it is stirred to imitation.

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS

[Col. 1129]

## CHAPTER I.—Among whom you shine like great lights (Philippians II, 15)

[Col. 1129D]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVII, no. 22.) By the stars are signified the souls of individuals who live well. Amid the conduct of wicked people, while they stand out through great virtues, they shine as though in the darkness of night. Hence Paul likewise says to the disciples: “Among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Philippians II, 15).

## CHAPTER II.—Brothers, I do not consider myself to have apprehended it (Philippians III, 13)

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXII, nos. 12–13.) Holy men seek sorrow concerning those things which they understand that they have done insufficiently; they consider themselves unworthy, and almost alone fail to see their own good works, which they offer to everyone else to behold as an example. Hence, when Paul set aside the good things already accomplished in himself and thought only of what still remained to be completed, he said: “I do not consider myself to have apprehended it” (Philippians III, 13).

Hence, in order to humble himself concerning the good works he was doing, he strove to bring his former sins back to mind, saying: “I who formerly was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” (I Timothy I, 13). Although he once said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race” (II Timothy IV, 7), “I have kept the faith,” it must be carefully observed that he said these things at a time when he already knew that he was about to depart from this life. For there he first said: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is at hand” (ibid., 6). Thus he recalled the perfection of his work when he already foresaw that no time for labor remained before the time of recompense.

For just as, while we live, we ought to drive our good works from our memory lest they exalt us, so, when our departure approaches, we often rightly recall them to mind, so that they may provide confidence and suppress despairing fear. Although he recounted his good works to the Corinthians by enumerating them, he sought to strengthen them, not to display himself. For he showed that he did not display those same good works in himself when he disclosed the tribulation of his own temptation and then added: “Therefore I am pleased with my infirmities” (II Corinthians XII, 10). Thus, in order to instruct the disciples, he reported the highest things about himself; but in order to preserve himself in humility, he fixed the eye of his consideration not on his virtues but on his weaknesses.

## CHAPTER III.—But our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians III, 20)

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXI, no. 95.) Let us behold the eagle building its nest in lofty places. He says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III, 20). And again: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Ephesians II, 6). Perhaps Paul was then being held in prison when he testified that he was seated together with Christ in the heavenly places; but he was where he had already fixed his ardent mind, not where his sluggish flesh still necessarily kept him. This is ordinarily a distinctive sign of the elect: they know how to travel the road of the present life in such a way that, through the certainty of hope, they know themselves already to have reached the heights; so that they see all transient things beneath them and trample upon everything that rises high in this world through love of eternity.

## CHAPTER IV.—I do not seek the gift, but I seek the fruit (Philippians IV, 17)

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIX, no. 22.) The stipends owed by their hearers are conferred upon holy preachers, and those whom the labor imposed by preaching exhausts are refreshed by the abundance of good works displayed by their disciples—not because they preach in order to be fed, but because they are fed in order to preach; that is, in order that they may continue preaching. The activity of preaching is not to be directed toward the intention of obtaining food; rather, the ministries of support are to serve the usefulness of preaching.

Thus good preachers do not undertake preaching for the sake of food; they receive food for the sake of preaching. And whenever necessities are supplied to preachers by their hearers, they ordinarily rejoice not in the gift of the possessions but in the reward of those who give them. Hence Paul says: “I do not seek the gift, but I seek the fruit” (Philippians IV, 17). (Col. 1132B) The gift is the actual thing that is supplied; the fruit of the gift is that something is supplied with a kindly intention and in pursuit of a future reward. Thus we understand the gift in the thing itself, and the fruit in the heart. And because the Apostle was nourished more by the reward than by the gift of his disciples, he confesses that he seeks not the gift but the fruit. Hence he immediately added: “I have received everything, and I abound” (verse 18).

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS

[Col. 1131]

## CHAPTER I.—Having stripped off the old man with his actions (Colossians III, 9)

[Col. 1131B]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIX, no. 53.) It is clear to all who know the truth that vices belong to the old life, and virtues to the new. Hence Paul says: “Having stripped off the old man with his actions, and having put on the new” (Colossians III, 9). Again he says: “Our old man was crucified together with him” (Romans VI, 6). Hence the Psalmist, speaking figuratively of the human race and discovered among wicked spirits, says: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Psalm VI, 8).

For whether from the ardor of the mind or among carnal enemies, we grow old through the very habitual practice of living and darken the appearance of the newness we have assumed. Yet if the disciplines of watchfulness remain vigilant against this old age each day through prayer, reading, and good living, we are renewed; for while our life is washed by tears, exercised through good works, and stretched toward holy meditations, it is continually restored to its newness.

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 1131]

## CHAPTER I.—We wished to come to you—I, Paul, indeed (I Thessalonians II, 18)

[Col. 1131C]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVII, no. 56.) Holy preachers often wish to exhort certain people but are unable to do so; often they desire to avoid certain people, yet, driven by the impulse of an inward prompting, they are compelled to exhort them with the greatest urgency. Let us behold the cloud of God: how, by the hand of the one who guides it, it is led toward things it does not desire, and how, by that same guiding hand, it is again restrained from its own impulse.

Certainly, when Paul wished to leave the Corinthians after shaking out his garments, he heard: “Do not be afraid, but speak, and do not be silent, because I am with you, and no one will lay hold of you to harm you, because I have many people in this city” (Acts XVIII, 9). Again, when he had wished to go to the Thessalonians, he was held back, saying: “We wished to come to you—I, Paul, indeed, both once and again—but Satan hindered me” (I Thessalonians II, 18). For Satan could not of himself obstruct the paths of so great an apostle; rather, by the motions of a hidden dispensation, while opposing him, he unknowingly served it. Thus, while Paul wished and was unable to approach some, he benefited more suitably those from whom he could not withdraw.

# ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 1131]

## CHAPTER I.—Exalting himself above everything that is called God; but God (II Thessalonians II, 4)

[Col. 1131D]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXIX, no. 18.) The proud exaltation of Antichrist rises above the reprobate minds of human beings through the arrogance of worldly glory, so that the sinful man, while despising the status of being considered merely human, falsely claims to be God over human beings. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “So that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (II Thessalonians II, 4).

To display his swelling pride more fully, he first said: “Who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped.” For a human being can sometimes be called god, in accordance with what is said to Moses: “Behold, I have appointed you as God over Pharaoh” (Exodus VII, 1). But a mere human being cannot be worshiped as God. Because Antichrist exalts himself both above all holy human beings and above the very power of divinity, through the name of glory claimed for himself he attempts to surpass both what is called God and what is worshiped as God.

It must be noted into what a pit of pride he fell: he did not remain within the measure of the fall by which he had fallen. The devil or a human being fell from the status of their own created condition through an uplifted mind, so that the one said: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah XIV, 13), while the other, hearing it, believed: “Your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Genesis III, 5).

Therefore both fell because they desired to be like God not through righteousness but through power. Yet the human being, liberated by grace—the one who had fallen by wrongly desiring God’s likeness—recognizing in the guilt of his sin that he is far from equal to God, cries out: “Lord, who is like you?” (Psalm LXXXVIII, 8).

But the devil, justly abandoned in the guilt of his fall, did not remain within the measure of his ruin. The longer he remained absent from the grace of the Almighty, the more he accumulated the guilt of his crime. For he fell because he perversely wished to be like God; but he was brought to such a point that, entering into Antichrist, he disdains even to appear like God, and, condemned, considers inferior the one whom, in his pride, he could not have as his equal. For when it is said of him, as we have already mentioned, “Exalting himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped,” it is clearly shown that, once desiring the likeness of God, he wished to raise himself as though beside God; but, increasing in the guilt of pride, he now exalts himself above everything that is called God and worshiped as God.

## CHAPTER II.—So that he may be revealed in his own time; for the mystery (II Thessalonians II, 6)

[Col. 1133B]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXIX, no. 15.) John says: “Now many Antichrists have come into being” (I John II, 18), because all wicked people are already his members—members perversely brought forth who, by living wickedly, have gone before their head. Hence Paul says: “So that he may be revealed in his own time; for the mystery of iniquity is already at work” (II Thessalonians II, 6). It is as though he said: “Then Antichrist will be seen openly; for now, while hidden, he already works his secret purposes in the hearts of the wicked.”

To say nothing of more obvious crimes, behold: one person silently envies his brother in his heart and, if he finds an opportunity, strives to undermine him. Whose member is he, if not of the one of whom it is written: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wisdom II, 24)? Another, judging himself to possess great merit and putting himself above everyone through the swelling of his heart, believes that all others are inferior to him. Whose member is he, if not of the one of whom it is written: “He beholds every high thing, and he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI, 25)?

Another seeks the power of this world, not in order to benefit others, but so that he himself may not be subject to another. Whose member is he, if not of the one of whom it is written: “He who said, ‘I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High’” (Isaiah XIV, 13)? For the Most High alone rules over all in such a way that he cannot be subject to another. The devil perversely wished to imitate him when, seeking dominion for himself, he refused to be subject to him.

Thus whoever desires his own power for the reason that he disdains to be subject to the one placed over him by heavenly order imitates the devil. (No. 16.) Moreover, there are very many things that declare certain people to be unbelievers even though they are established within the peace of the Church. For I see some people assume the role of a powerful person in such a way that, when questioned by him, they do not hesitate, out of favor toward him, to deny the truth in a matter concerning their neighbor.

And who is the Truth if not the one who said: “I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life” (John XIV, 6)? John the Baptist did not die after being questioned about confessing Christ, but after being questioned about the truth of justice; yet because Christ is the Truth, he reached death for Christ—and therefore for the Truth. Let us then place before our eyes the case of someone who, when questioned, accepted the person’s authority and, lest he suffer even verbal injury, denied the truth. What, I ask, would such a person do amid the pain of punishments, when he was ashamed of Christ amid the blows of words? Behold, even afterward he is still a Christian in the eyes of human beings; and yet, if the Lord has determined to judge him strictly, he is no longer one.

(No. 17.) But I see others to whom, by virtue of the office of teaching, the duties of exhorting and reproving have been entrusted. They see something illicit being committed, yet, while fearing to offend the favor of certain powerful people, they do not dare to reprove it. Whoever this person is, what else has he done but see the wolf coming and flee? He fled because he remained silent, because, scorning eternal favor, he loved temporal glory more.

Behold, before the face of the powerful man he hides himself within the recesses of his silence; and, just as he would yield a place to open persecution, so he yielded a hidden place to fear. Well is it said of such people: “They loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God” (John XII, 43). Therefore, whoever is such a person—if these matters are judged strictly—even though open persecution was absent, has nevertheless denied Christ by remaining silent.

Thus the temptations of Antichrist are not absent even in the peace of the Church. Let no one, therefore, dread only those final times of persecution as though they alone were to be feared. For among the wicked the cause of Antichrist is enacted every day, because in their hearts, while hidden, he is already at work with his mystery.

## CHAPTER III.—Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the spirit of his mouth (II Thessalonians II, 8)

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXII, no. 12.) “Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the spirit of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming” (II Thessalonians II, 8): he will be struck with eternal death at the coming of the Judge—not through a battle of angels or a contest of the saints, but solely by the spirit of his mouth.

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 1133]

## CHAPTER I.—And dwells in inaccessible light (I Timothy VI, 16)

[Col. 1133C]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, no. 91.) We shall therefore see God, and he himself is the reward of our labor, so that after the darkness of this mortality we may rejoice in access to his light.

(No. 92.) But when we say that his light is accessible, what Paul says stands in the way of our understanding: “Who dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen, nor can see” (I Timothy VI, 16). Behold, again I hear what the Psalmist says: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Psalm XXXIII, 6). How, then, are we enlightened by drawing near if we do not see the very light by which we can be enlightened? But if, by drawing near, we see the very light by which we are enlightened, how is it said to be inaccessible?

In this matter we must consider that he called it inaccessible to every human being, but not to one who is wise in divine things. Sacred Scripture commonly designates all followers of carnal things by the name “human.” Hence the same Apostle says to certain quarrelsome people: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to the human manner?” (I Corinthians III, 3). Shortly afterward he added to them: “Are you not human beings?” And elsewhere he offered this testimony: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of a human being, what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Corinthians II, 9).

And after saying that this had been hidden from human beings, he immediately added: “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit,” distinguishing himself from the human designation, since, caught up above the human level, he already tasted divine things. So also in this passage, when he declared God’s light to be inaccessible, to show to whom he meant this, he added: “Which no human being has seen, nor can see.” In his customary manner, he calls “human beings” all who possess human wisdom, because those who taste divine things are, so to speak, above human beings.

We shall therefore see God if, through a heavenly manner of life, we deserve to be above human beings; yet we shall not see him in the way in which he sees himself. For the Creator sees himself in a manner vastly different from that in which the creature sees the Creator. With regard to God’s immensity, a certain measure of contemplation is fixed for us, because we are bounded by that very limitation through which we are creatures.

(No. 98.) Certainly, we do not behold God in the same way as he beholds himself, just as we do not rest in God in the same way as he rests in himself. Our vision or rest will be, in some manner, like his vision or rest, but it will not be equal to it. For, so that we do not lie prostrate in ourselves, if I may put it so, the wing of contemplation lifts us up; and we are raised from ourselves to behold him. Carried away by the intention of the heart (Col. 1135A) and by the sweetness of contemplation, we go, in some manner, from ourselves into him. And this very movement of ours is less than rest; yet to move in this way is to rest perfectly.

It is therefore a perfect rest, because God is discerned; yet it cannot be made equal to the rest of the one who does not pass from himself into another in order to rest. It is therefore, so to speak, a rest both similar and dissimilar, because what is his rest is imitated by ours. For in order that we may be blessed and eternal forever, we imitate the Eternal. Our eternity is great: it is an imitation of eternity. Nor are we excluded from the one whom we can imitate, because by seeing we become participants, and by participating we imitate.

This vision begins now in faith, but then is perfected in appearance, when we drink at its very source the co-eternal Wisdom of God, which we now receive through the mouths of preachers as through flowing streams.

## CHAPTER II.—Avoiding profane novelties of words (I Timothy VI, 20)

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, no. 39.) Often, when heretics strive to establish their perverse teachings, they bring forward things that are certainly not held in the pages of the sacred books. Hence the distinguished preacher admonishes his disciple, saying: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words” (I Timothy VI, 20). For, wishing to be praised as possessing outstanding intelligence, heretics bring forward certain new things that are not contained in the ancient books of the fathers. Thus it comes about that, while they desire to appear wise, they scatter seeds of folly among their wretched hearers.

# ON THE EPISTLE TO TITUS

[Col. 1135]

## CHAPTER I.—If anyone is without crime (Titus I, 6)

[Col. 1135B]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXI, no. 19.) Sin and crime differ in this respect: every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime. In this life many can be without crime, but no one can be without sins. Hence the holy preacher, when describing a man worthy of priestly grace, did not say: “If anyone is without sin,” but: “If anyone is without crime” (Titus I, 6).

Who, indeed, can be without sin, when John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8)? In this distinction between sins and crimes, it must be considered that some sins defile the soul, whereas crimes extinguish it.

# ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

[Col. 1135]

## CHAPTER I.—And no one shall teach his neighbor any longer (Hebrews III, 11)

[Col. 1135B]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXX, no. 17.) What is meant by the order of the heavens if not the heavenly power of secret things? What is signified by the harmony of heaven if not the harmonious speech of preachers? When our Creator begins to disclose the order of the heavens, therefore, he causes the harmony of heaven to cease, because, when he is already shown to us in appearance, the words of preachers are necessarily withdrawn.

Hence the Lord says through Jeremiah: “No longer shall a man teach his neighbor, nor a man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord” (Jeremiah XXXI, 34). Hence Paul says: “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed” (I Corinthians XIII, 8).

## CHAPTER II.—For the earth, often drinking in the rain that comes upon it (Hebrews VI, 7)

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVIII, no. 20.) If the sinner’s soul is dust—because it is lifted up on the surface and carried away by the breeze of temptation, as it is written: “Not so the wicked, not so; but like dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth” (Psalm I, 5)—nothing prevents us from understanding the soul of the righteous as the earth of which it is written: “For the earth, often drinking in the rain that comes upon it and producing vegetation useful to those by whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing” (Hebrews VI, 7).

## CHAPTER III.—Confessing that they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth (Hebrews XI, 13)

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, no. 48.) What people are strangers in this world if not those who run toward the lot of the elect and know that they have a homeland in heaven, hoping all the more to find there what is their own because here they consider everything that passes away to be alien to them?

The people, therefore, are strangers: the whole number of the elect, who regard this life as a kind of exile and sigh toward the heavenly homeland with the full intention of their hearts. Of them Paul says: “Confessing that they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth” (Hebrews XI, 13). For those who say these things signify that they are seeking a homeland.

The same Apostle also endured this pilgrimage when he said: “While we are in the body, we are strangers from the Lord. For we walk by faith, and not by appearance” (II Corinthians V, 6). He strove to escape the hardships of this pilgrimage when he said: “Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians I, 23). And again: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (verse 21).

The Psalmist felt the heavy burden of this pilgrimage when he said: “Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a long-time sojourner” (Psalm CXIX, 5). He longed to be snatched from it as quickly as possible when, burning with heavenly desires, he said: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm XLI, 3).

## CHAPTER IV.—Enduring the Invisible One as though seeing him (Hebrews XI, 27)

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIX, no. 21.) All the perverse, because they do not desire inward things, pour themselves outward into their thoughts. Hence it is said to them through the Prophet: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isaiah XLVI, 8). And again: “Woe to those who devise useless things” (Micah II, 1).

In their actions people fear those whom they see bodily, but do not consider God to be present to them because they do not see him. In contrast, in praise of the righteous man, when he despised the king of Egypt and obeyed God’s commands, it is said: “Because he endured the Invisible One as though seeing him” (Hebrews XI, 27). He treated the perverse ruler of the earth as though he did not see him, casting him away from the eyes of his heart; but he endured the invisible King as though seeing him, because he did not turn the eye of his mind away from beholding him with fear.

[Col. 1137]

[Note: [Col. 1137C] We explained in the Preface why we append this exposition to the Paterian collection. Concerning Alulf, read what we said in the same place.]

# ALULF’S EXPOSITION OF THE NEW TESTAMENT (S)

Part One, IN WHICH THE FOUR GOSPELS ARE EXPLAINED

## PREFACE. On the Four Evangelists, represented by four animals

[Col. 1137A] (Homily 2 on Ezekiel, no. 18; Homily 3 on Ezekiel, no. 1; Homily 4 on Ezekiel, no. 1.) By the four holy animals shown in a vision to the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel I), the four holy evangelists are represented: namely Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Under the persons of the evangelists, all the perfect are signified together.

Nor is it without good reason that the number of all the perfect is expressed through the four evangelists, since all who are now perfect in the Church have learned the uprightness of their perfection through their Gospel. Ezekiel describes the four holy animals, by which the four evangelists are signified, in a subtle account when he says: “Four faces for one, and four wings for one.” What is expressed by the face if not knowledge, and what by the wings if not flight? For by the face each person is recognized, while by the wing the bodies of birds are lifted on high.

The face, therefore, pertains to faith, and the wing to contemplation. Through faith we are known by almighty God, just as he says of his sheep: “I am the good Shepherd, and I know my sheep, and my sheep know me” (John X, 14). Again he says: “I know whom I have chosen” (John XIII, 18). Through contemplation, however, by which we are lifted above ourselves, we are raised, as it were, into the air.

Thus there are four faces for one: for if you ask what Matthew thinks concerning the Lord’s incarnation, he certainly thinks what Mark, Luke, and John think. If you ask what John thinks, without doubt it is what Luke, Mark, and Matthew think. If you ask what Mark thinks, it is what Matthew, John, and Luke think. If you ask what Luke thinks, it is what John, Matthew, and Mark think.

There are therefore four faces for one, because the knowledge of faith by which they are known by God is one in each and the same in all four. Whatever you find in one, you will recognize simultaneously in all four. And there are four wings for one, because all four unanimously preach our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of almighty God; and, lifting the eyes of their minds toward his divinity, they fly on the wing of contemplation.

The faces of the evangelists therefore pertain to the Lord’s humanity, and the wing to his divinity, because they direct their gaze like a face toward the one whom they behold as bodily. But while they proclaim that, by his divinity, he is unbounded and incorporeal, they are lifted, as it were, into the air on the wing of contemplation.

Since, therefore, there is one faith in his incarnation among them all, and an equal contemplation of his divinity in each, it is rightly said: “Four faces for one, and four wings for one.”

Then these same holy animals are described more subtly, so that the very subtlety of the description may disclose to us that the persons of the evangelists are signified by them, and that the word of God may leave no uncertainty for our understanding. For it is said: “The likeness of their faces was the face of a man, and the face of a lion on the right side of the four of them; but the face of an ox on the left side of the four of them, and the face of an eagle above the four of them.”

That these four winged animals designate the four holy evangelists is attested by the beginnings of each individual Gospel book. Since Matthew began with human generation, he is rightly represented by the man. Since Mark began with a cry in the wilderness, he is rightly represented by the lion. Since Luke began with a sacrifice, he is fittingly represented by the calf. But because John began with the divinity of the Word, he is suitably represented by the eagle.

When he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1), directing his attention to the very substance of divinity, he fixed his eyes upon the sun, as it were, after the manner of an eagle.

But because all the elect are members of our Redeemer, while our Redeemer himself is the head of all the elect, there is no obstacle to his also being signified in all these things by the fact that his members are represented. For he, the only-begotten Son of God, truly became man; he deigned to die in the sacrifice of our redemption, as a calf; through the power of his strength he rose again, as a lion.

The lion is also said to sleep with open eyes, because in the very death in which our Redeemer was able to sleep according to his humanity, he remained immortal and watchful according to his divinity. After his resurrection he also ascended into heaven and was raised on high, as an eagle.

Thus the whole is one for us: by being born he became a man, by dying a calf, by rising again a lion, and by ascending into heaven an eagle. But since we have already said above that the four evangelists, and under their appearance all the perfect together, are signified by these animals, it remains for us to show how each of the elect is expressed by these visions of the animals.

For every elect person who is perfect in the way of the Lord is simultaneously man, calf, lion, and eagle. Man is a rational animal; the calf, however, is accustomed to be slaughtered in sacrifice. The lion is a strong beast, as it is written: “The lion is strongest among beasts and retreats before no encounter” (Proverbs XXX, 30). The eagle flies toward lofty things and directs its unblinking eyes toward the rays of the sun.

Therefore everyone who is perfect in reason is a man. And because he mortifies himself with respect to the pleasure of this age, he is a calf. Because through this voluntary mortification he possesses the strength of security against every adversity, he is a lion. Hence it is written: “But the righteous is confident like a lion and will be without fear” (Proverbs XXVIII, 1). Because he contemplates loftily the things that are heavenly and eternal, he is an eagle.

Therefore, since every righteous person becomes a man through reason, a calf through the sacrifice of his mortification, a lion through the strength of his security, and an eagle through contemplation, each perfect person can rightly be signified by these holy animals. We say this for the purpose of showing that the things said about the four animals also pertain to each of the perfect.

But a great question arises for us concerning these same evangelists and holy preachers: why are the human and the lion said to be on the right of their fourfold group, while the calf is on the left of their fourfold group. For it is not without a remarkable reason that those two are said to be on the right and this one on the left. And again it must be asked why the eagle is remembered as being neither on their right nor on their left, but above their fourfold group.

We have therefore set before ourselves two questions, which we ought, with the Lord opening the way, to resolve. The human and the lion, then, are said to be on the right, while the calf is on the left. For we have joyful things on the right, but sorrowful things on the left. Hence we also call that “left” which we consider adverse. And, as we said earlier, the incarnation is signified by the human, the passion by the calf, and the resurrection of our Author by the lion.

All the elect rejoiced in the incarnation of the Only-Begotten Son, through which we were redeemed; but at his death the first among the elect, the holy apostles themselves, were saddened, and afterward they rejoiced at his resurrection. Therefore, since both his birth and his resurrection brought joy to the disciples whom his passion had saddened, the human and the lion are described as being on the right, while the calf is on the left. The holy evangelists themselves rejoiced in his humanity and were strengthened by his resurrection, though they had been saddened by his passion. Thus the human and the lion are on their right, because the incarnation of our Redeemer gave them life and his resurrection strengthened them. But the calf is on the left, because his death cast them down into unbelief for a brief time.

The eagle, however, is rightly described as having its place not beside them but above them, either because it signifies his ascension, or because it proclaims that the Word of the Father is God with the Father. Through the power of contemplation it rose above the other evangelists: although it speaks together with them about his divinity, it nevertheless contemplates it more subtly than all the others.

But if the eagle, joined with the other three, is remembered as constituting four living creatures, it is strange how it can be described as being above their fourfold group—unless it is because John, by seeing the Word in the beginning, also passed beyond himself. For if he had not passed beyond himself, he would not have seen the Word in the beginning. Therefore, since he also went beyond himself, he was no longer merely above the three; with himself added, he was above the four.

Furthermore, concerning these same holy living creatures, one must ask: since they are described separately by distinct images, so that one thing is said to resemble the human, another the lion, another the calf, and another the eagle, what is meant by the statement made shortly before concerning all of them together: “The likeness of a human was in them”?

But who is this human described here except the one of whom it is written: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being” (Philippians II, 6)?

These living creatures, therefore, if they are to rise to the virtue of holiness, strive toward the likeness of this human. They would not be holy if they did not possess the likeness of this human, because whatever there is in them of the inward parts of compassion, whatever there is of the spirit of gentleness, whatever there is of zeal for uprightness, whatever there is of the guardianship of humility, whatever there is of the fervor of charity—they have drawn all this from the very fountain of mercy, from the very root of God’s gentleness, from the very power of justice, that is, from the Mediator between God and human beings, the Lord God. [Col. 1140B]

The distinguished preacher shows that he possesses the likeness of this human when he says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Corinthians XI, 1). He urges us to rise toward his likeness when he says: “The first human was from the earth, earthly; the second human was from heaven, heavenly. Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who descended from heaven” (I Corinthians XV, 49).

Indeed, every holy person is said to be in the likeness of this human insofar as he imitates the life of his Redeemer. For to disagree with his commands and works—what else is that than to withdraw far from his likeness? The Prophet was hastening to rise toward the likeness of this human when he said: “I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways” (Psalm CXVIII, 15). Whoever silently considers the ways of the Lord in his mind and hastens to exercise himself in his commandments—what else does he reform within himself except the image of the new human?

Because this is ceaselessly accomplished in the hearts of the saints, it is rightly said of the holy living creatures that the likeness of a human is in them. For whatever is holy and wonderful in them comes from the form of this likeness—that is, from the virtue of imitation.

## Preliminary Note on Blessed Matthew

[Col. 1139]

[Col. 1139C] *(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, nos. 43–44.)*

Almighty God, by a hidden purpose, preserves some people innocent from the very beginning of their life and advances them to the summit of virtue; but others he abandons at their beginnings and permits them, as their vices pour forth, to proceed over precipices. Yet often he also regards these people and sets them ablaze with the fire of holy love so that they may follow him; and the habitual irritations of vice in their hearts he turns into the fervor of virtues. They burn all the more intensely with the desire to seek the mercy of God, the more deeply they blush at the memory of their iniquity.

The evangelist Matthew had been such a man. Entangled in earthly business, he served the business of the tax office. But when the Lord saw him sitting at the tax office, in order to call him back to himself, his hard and cold heart was touched by the fire of divine love and set ablaze; he was separated from the earthly activity he had previously pursued and strengthened by the heat of his desires to follow the heavenly life. Thus, just as he had previously been hard in his love of the world, afterward he showed himself strong in the love of God; and what he had formerly refused to hear, he now began to believe and preach.

For he became a strong defender of the holy Church; through the administration of the Gospel, the Lord pierced the hearts of unbelievers by his tongue, as by a very sharp sword. He who had previously been weak and despised because of earthly business afterward became strong for heavenly teaching. Therefore, nothing that he once was should be despised in him who has now begun to be what he was not.

# BOOK ONE. Exposition of the Gospel According to Matthew

[Col. 1139]

## CHAPTER I.—“Abraham begot Isaac; Isaac begot Jacob” (Matthew I, 2)

[Col. 1139D]

*(Homily 25 on the Gospels, no. 8; and exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIII, no. 17.)*

Our Lord Jesus Christ, coming for the redemption of the human race, made, as it were, a hook from himself for the destruction of the devil. For who does not know that on a hook the bait is displayed while the barb is concealed? The bait attracts, so that the barb may enter.

Our Lord therefore assumed a body so that, in it, the devil might desire the death of the flesh as though it were his own bait. When he unjustly desired that death in him, he lost those whom he had held as though justly. He was therefore caught on the hook of Christ’s incarnation: while he desired the bait of the body in him, he was pierced by the barb of divinity. There was humanity to lead the devourer toward itself; there was divinity to pierce him. There was visible weakness to attract him; there was hidden power to transfix the robber’s throat.

He was caught on the hook because he perished by the thing he devoured. In our Redeemer, while through his agents he bit the bait of the body, the barb of divinity pierced him. The hook held the throat of the one swallowing, so to speak: in him the bait of the flesh was visible, which the devourer desired to consume, while the divinity that would destroy him lay hidden at the time of the passion.

In this abyss of waters—that is, in this vast multitude of the human race—this monster moved here and there with open mouth, panting for the death of all and almost devouring the life of all. But for the death of this monster, the hook was suspended in this dark depth of waters by a marvelous arrangement.

The line of this hook is the lineage of the ancient fathers recorded in the Gospel. For when it is said, “Abraham begot Isaac; Isaac begot Jacob,” and when the other successors are described, with Joseph’s name inserted, down to Mary, the betrothed Virgin, there appears to be a kind of line at whose end the incarnate Lord—that is, this hook—would be fastened. The monster, hanging in these waters of the human race with open mouth, would desire it; but after its mouth had bitten through the savagery of its agents, it would no longer have the strength to bite.

For the death of the monster lying in wait for human deaths, the Lord sent his Only-Begotten Son incarnate. While mortal flesh was seen in him and the power of immortality was not seen, the hook held the robber’s throat, bit the one biting it, and destroyed the devourer by the very thing from which it had concealed the sharpness of its power to pierce him. [Col. 1141A]

## CHAPTER II.—“After the migration to Babylon, Jeconiah begot Shealtiel” (Matthew I, 12)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVIII, no. 19.)*

[Note: These words are not found altogether in this form in Saint Gregory; Alulfus also adds or removes much elsewhere. It is sufficient to note this once here.] [Col. 1141D; Col. 1142D]

The Psalmist says concerning the Lord: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm CXVII, 22). The Lord Jesus is called the cornerstone either because, receiving in himself on one side the Jewish people and on the other the Gentile people, he joins two walls, as it were, into the single structure of the Church; or because, on earth, joining the nations of the Gentiles to the Israelite people, he united both of them with the angels in heaven.

King Jeconiah bore the type of this stone. Matthew counted him a second time when he described the generations in groups of fourteen. He inserted the same person both at the end of the second generation and again at the beginning of the third. For he was carried into Babylon with the Israelite people; and because he was led from one place to another, he is rightly counted a second time as representing the side of either wall. The turning of this migration signifies the cornerstone. Wherever a straight line bends so as to go in another direction, it forms something like an angle.

He could therefore rightly be counted twice, because through the two walls he displayed in himself, as it were, two sides. Thus he aptly bore the image of the one who, born in Judea and gathering the Gentiles, came, as it were, from Jerusalem to Babylon; and who wove together within himself, by the art of charity, this structure of faith, previously torn apart by the zeal of discord.

## CHAPTER III.—“Joseph received Mary as his wife; and he did not know her until she bore her firstborn son, and he called his name Jesus” (Matthew I, 25)

[Col. 1141D]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book VIII, no. 89.)*

“He did not know her until she bore her firstborn son.” This should be understood to mean not that he knew her after the birth of God, but that he did not touch her at all, even when he did not know that she was the mother of her Creator. For because he could not touch her at all after he had recognized that the mystery of our redemption was accomplished from her womb, it was necessary for the Evangelist to bear witness specifically to that time about which doubt might have arisen because of Joseph’s ignorance.

Thus the Psalmist also says: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’” (Psalm CIX, 1–2). This does not mean that the Lord does not sit at the Lord’s right hand after he has struck his enemies and subjected them to his power; rather, it means that he presides in eternal blessedness over all even before he tramples the hearts of his rebellious enemies. In this statement, certainly, it is clear that he reigns without end even afterward, when his enemies have been subjected.

## CHAPTER IV.—“And they said to him: ‘In Bethlehem of Judea’” (Matthew II, 5)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXV, no. 26.)*

The Israelites first knew Christ, whom during his passion they afterward despised as though he were unknown. For no one who had thoroughly learned the Law was ignorant that Christ would be born. Hence King Herod, terrified by the arrival of the magi, diligently sought to learn from the priests and rulers where they knew Christ would be born. They immediately answered him: “In Bethlehem of Judea.” Thus they had previously known the one whom, when they despised him at the time of his passion, they did not know.

## CHAPTER V.—“After the Lord Jesus had been baptized in the Jordan by John, he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil” (Matthew IV)

[Col. 1142B]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXIV, no. 27.)*

Our enemy, while we are still placed in this life, strives to attack us more fiercely the more he sees us rebel against him. For he neglects to strike those whom he feels he possesses by an undisputed right. But he is aroused against us with greater violence insofar as he is expelled from our heart as though from the right of his own dwelling.

The Lord represented this in himself under a certain dispensation: he allowed the devil to tempt him only after his baptism, so that he might intimate to us a sign of the conversion that was to come—that his members, after they had advanced toward God, would then endure more savage ambushes of temptation.

## CHAPTER VI.—“If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew IV, 5)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book II, no. 43.)*

The ancient enemy recognized that the Redeemer of the human race, his conqueror, had come into the world. Hence, through a possessed man, he says in the Gospel: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matthew VIII, 29).

Yet when he first saw him subject to suffering and recognized that, in his humanity, he was able to endure mortal things, everything he had suspected concerning his divinity became doubtful to him through the arrogance of his pride. Since he perceived nothing but pride, when he saw him humble he doubted that he was God.

Hence he turned to the arguments of temptation, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.” Because he saw him subject to suffering and did not believe that he was God, he tested him in doubt; but by testing him he could neither penetrate his consciousness nor disturb his mind through temptation.

## CHAPTER VII.—“Again the devil took him to a very high mountain” (Matthew IV, 8)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book III, no. 30.)*

The soul of our Redeemer was not shaken by the necessity of temptation as we are, who are merely human beings and are often thrown into confusion when temptation rushes upon us. For our enemy, doubting that God had become incarnate and wishing to learn this by testing him through the miracles he requested—although he was permitted to take him to a high mountain, although he claimed that he would give him the kingdoms of the world, and although he displayed stones that were to be changed into bread—could not shake the mind of the Mediator between God and human beings through temptation.

He graciously accepted all these things externally in such a way that his mind, inwardly clinging to his divinity, nevertheless remained unshaken. Although he is said, when troubled in spirit, to have groaned (John XI), he himself divinely determined how much he would be troubled humanly. Presiding immutably over all things, he showed himself changeable in the satisfaction of weakness. Remaining quiet within himself, therefore, he arranged everything that, for the display of the humanity he had assumed, he also performed in a state of agitation.

## CHAPTER VIII.—“Behold, angels approached and ministered to him” (Matthew IV, 11)

[Col. 1143A]

*(Homily 8 on Ezekiel, no. 24.)*

After the Only-Begotten of the Father appeared incarnate, having been made for a little while lower than the angels, God as human was, through his humanity, below the angels in power, while even before he was exalted by the glory of the resurrection he was, through his divinity, above the angels.

It is written concerning him before his passion: “Behold, angels approached and ministered to him.” Yet, in order that the weakness of his humanity might be shown, it is again written concerning him: “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke XXII, 34). Thus, as evidence of both natures, he is described as one to whom angels minister and as one whom an angel strengthens.

He is one in both natures, because the one who existed as God before the ages became human at the end of the ages. Before his passion, angels minister to him and an angel strengthens him; after his passion and resurrection, angels can minister to him, but they can no longer strengthen him. For the humanity that he assumed by descending beneath the angels, he exalted above the angels by ascending.

## CHAPTER IX.—“As Jesus walked beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Peter and Andrew casting a net into the sea, and he said to them: ‘Come after me, and I will make you fishers of human beings’” (Matthew IV, 18)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIII, no. 34.)*

The Lord presented weak preachers to the world, and through them conquered the powerful. As Paul testifies: “God first chose the weak things of the world in order afterward to confound the strong” (I Corinthians I, 27). He chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise. For he first gathered the uneducated and afterward the philosophers; he did not teach fishermen through orators, but through fishermen he subdued orators by marvelous power.

## CHAPTER X.—“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V, 3)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVI, no. 49.)*

Sacred Scripture is accustomed often to call the humble “poor”; hence, in the Gospel, they are named with the addition “in spirit.” Those whom visible riches display as powerful are poor in themselves, because they are not lifted up in their consciences.

## CHAPTER XI.—“Blessed are those who mourn” (Matthew V, 5)

*(Homily 2 on the Gospels, no. 8.)*

Let us recall, brothers, the sins we have committed and place them before our eyes. Let us consider how terrible the Judge will be when he comes to punish these things. Let us shape our minds for lamentation; let our life grow bitter for a time through repentance, so that it may not feel eternal bitterness in punishment.

Through weeping we are led to eternal joys, as the Truth promises when it says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” Yet joy leads to weeping, as the same Truth attests when it says: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke VI, 25). If, therefore, we seek the joy of reward at the end, let us hold fast to the bitterness of repentance on the way.

## CHAPTER XII.—“You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew V, 13)

[Col. 1143D]

*(Homily 17 on the Gospels, nos. 10, 13, 14.)*

We must consider, beloved brothers, that because one and the same voice of exhortation is not sufficient to admonish everyone together, each person should strive to instruct individuals as far as he is able and to edify them through private conversations.

We must weigh what the Lord says to the holy apostles and, through the apostles, to us: “You are the salt of the earth.” If, therefore, we are salt, we must season the minds of the faithful.

You, therefore, who are shepherds, consider that you feed God’s animals. Concerning these animals, the Psalmist says to God: “Your animals shall dwell in it” (Psalm LXVII, 11). We often see that a rock of salt is placed before brute animals so that they may lick it and be improved by it. Thus, among brute animals, the priest ought to be a rock of salt among the peoples.

The priest must take care what he says to each person and how he admonishes each one, so that whoever joins himself to the priest may be seasoned, as it were, by contact with salt, with the flavor of eternal life. We are not salt if we do not season the hearts of those who hear us. He truly gives this seasoning to his neighbor who does not withhold the word of preaching.

But we preach what is right to others truly only if we show it through deeds and examples. I do not think, beloved brothers, that God tolerates any greater scandal from others than from priests, when he sees those whom he appointed for the correction of others giving examples of wickedness in themselves; when we ourselves sin, though we ought to restrain sins; when we seek no gain of souls and devote ourselves daily to our own pursuits.

And because, by the very fact that we are placed over others, we have greater license to undertake anything, we turn the ministry of the blessing we have received into an instrument of ambition. We abandon God’s causes and devote ourselves to earthly business. We receive a place of holiness and become entangled in earthly actions.

What Jeremiah, considering and lamenting our death, says has been fulfilled in us: “How the gold has become darkened; how the finest color has been changed. The stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street” (Lamentations IV, 1).

The gold has indeed been darkened, because the life of priests, once bright through the glory of virtues, is now shown to be rejected through base actions. The finest color has been changed, because the habit of holiness has been brought to the dishonor of contempt through earthly and degraded works.

The stones of the sanctuary were kept inside and were not placed upon the body of the high priest except when, entering the Holy of Holies, he appeared in the secrecy of his Creator. We, therefore, beloved brothers—we are the stones of the sanctuary. We ought always to appear in the secrecy of God, and we should never need to be seen outside, that is, we should never be seen in alien activities.

But the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street, because those who ought always to have been inward through life and prayer are occupied outwardly through a rejected life. Behold, now there is scarcely any worldly activity that priests do not administer. Thus, while they stand in a holy habit, they display external things; like stones of the sanctuary, they lie outside.

Because in Greek the word *platea*—“street”—is derived from breadth, the stones of the sanctuary lie in the streets when religious people pursue the broad paths of the world. They are scattered not only in the streets but also at the head of the streets, because they both carry out works through desire for this world and yet seek the height of honor from their religious habit.

They are scattered at the head of the streets because they lie low through the ministry of their works while wishing to be honored on account of the appearance of holiness.

What is written has also been fulfilled in us: “And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest” (Hosea IX, 9). A priest does not differ from the people when he surpasses the conduct of the common people by no merit of his life, though he ought to be their teacher and guide toward eternal life both by the salt of exhortation and by the example of good conduct.

But what shall we call human souls except the food of the Lord? They were created for this purpose: that they might be transferred into his body, that is, that they might advance toward the growth of the eternal Church. But we ought to have been the seasoning of this food. As we have said, it is said to the preachers who have been sent: “You are the salt of the earth.”

If the people are God’s food, priests ought to be the seasoning of the food. But because, when we cease from the practice of prayer and holy instruction, the salt has lost its savor, it cannot season God’s food. For this reason the Creator does not take it, since, because of our foolishness, it is not seasoned at all.

Let us therefore consider who has ever been converted through our tongue; who, corrected by our rebuke, has repented of his perverse conduct. Who has abandoned lust because of our instruction? Who has abandoned greed? Who has turned away from pride?

We should take care of ourselves in such a way that we do not neglect care for our neighbor, so that whoever joins himself to us may be seasoned by the salt of our tongue. Let the one who is already holy be admonished to grow. Let the one who is still wicked be admonished to correct himself, so that whoever joins himself to the priest may return seasoned by the salt of his speech.

## CHAPTER XIII.—“Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V, 16)

[Col. 1145A]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book VIII, no. 83.)*

The good works we do should be concealed, lest, carrying them carelessly along the road of this life, we lose them through the attack of thieving spirits. Yet the Truth says: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

But it is one thing when glory is sought for the giver through the display of the work, and another when private praise is desired from the gift of the giver. Hence, again, in the Gospel the same Truth says: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before human beings, so that you may be seen by them” (Matthew VI, 1).

When our work is displayed to people, we must first weigh in the examination of our heart what is being sought through the desire for that display. If we seek the glory of the giver, then even when our works are made public, we keep them hidden from his sight. But if through them we desire our own praise, they have already been poured forth outside his sight, even if many people do not know of them.

It is, however, a mark of the very perfect to seek the glory of the author by displaying the work in such a way that they do not rejoice in private exultation over the praise brought to them. A praiseworthy work is displayed harmlessly to people only when praise bestowed upon it is truly trampled underfoot through contempt in the mind. Since the weak cannot overcome praise perfectly by despising it, they must conceal the good they do.

## CHAPTER XIV.—“Do not think that I came to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matthew V, 17)

*(Homily 16 on Ezekiel, no. 9.)*

The Old Testament restrained crimes in deeds and commanded that tithes be given. But the New Testament restrained evil thoughts, commanded that everything be abandoned, and ordered that the life of the body be despised together with the present age for God’s sake.

The lesser commandments were given to the Israelite people through the Law (Exodus XIX); hence Moses spoke to that same people on the plain. The Lord gave higher commandments to the holy apostles; hence he taught those same men the commands of life on the mountain.

When our Redeemer says through the Gospel, “Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the prophets; I did not come to abolish but to fulfill,” he came to fulfill the Law by adding the grace of the Law’s righteousness, so that what the Law commanded in lesser matters he might help perfect in greater ones, and what it restrained from action he might cut away from the heart.

## CHAPTER XV.—“Whoever abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V, 19)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIX, no. 13; Homily 12 on the Gospels, at the beginning.)*

The Lord speaks concerning teachers who live badly: “Whoever abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.”

A person abolishes a commandment and teaches others to do so when he proclaims by his voice what he does not fulfill in his life. But he cannot reach the kingdom of eternal blessedness who does not wish to fulfill by his deeds what he teaches.

How, then, is he called least in it, since he is in no way permitted to enter it? The kingdom of heaven therefore refers to the present Church, concerning which it is written: “And they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matthew XIII, 41). In the kingdom above, the scandals that were to be gathered out of it do not exist.

Therefore, whoever abolishes a commandment by his deeds and teaches accordingly by his voice will be least in that kingdom, but in the kingdom above he will not even be least. In the holy Church, however, a teacher who abolishes a commandment is called least, because when his life is despised, it remains that his preaching also be despised.

## CHAPTER XVI.—“Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew V, 22)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXI, no. 9.)*

The Lord will judge the actions of each person in such a way that not even the smallest thoughts or the slightest words—which among us have become cheap through common usage—will remain unexamined by his judgment.

Hence the Lord says: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Racha,’ will be liable to the council; whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.”

*Racha* in the Hebrew language is an interjection, which does indeed reveal the mind of the angry person but does not express a complete word of anger. First, therefore, anger is reproved without a voice; afterward anger with a voice, but not yet formed into a complete word; finally, when “Fool” is said, anger is rebuked when it is completed with an excess of voice and even with the fullness of speech.

It should be noted that he declares the angry person liable to judgment; for the utterance of anger, which is *racha*, liable to the council; and for the word of the utterance, which is “Fool,” liable to Gehenna.

The order of the sentence increased according to the degrees of guilt. In judgment, the case is still examined; in the council, the judgment of the case is already determined; in the fire of Gehenna, the judgment that proceeds from the council is carried out.

Therefore, because the Lord judges human actions with subtle examination, anger without a voice is consigned to judgment; anger in a voice, to the council; and anger expressed in voice and speech is handed over to the fires of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER XVII.—“Likewise, concerning the foregoing”

[Col. 1146B]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book V, no. 17.)*

It must be understood that those who are in authority often break out indiscriminately into insults against their subjects. Through the insolence of their tongue they lose what they gain by serving attentively in government, weighing their words with too little fear of the Judge. For whoever says to his brother without cause, “Fool,” consigns himself to the fires of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—“If you offer your gift at the altar, etc.” (Matthew V, 23)

*(Dialogues, Book IV, chapter 60, at the beginning.)*

It must be understood that the person rightly asks forgiveness from the Lord who first releases what has been done against him. The gift is not accepted unless discord has first been driven from the heart, as the Truth says:

“If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift.”

In this matter we must consider, since every fault is absolved by a gift, how serious the fault of discord is, for which not even a gift is accepted.

We must therefore go in our mind to our neighbor, even if he is far away and greatly separated from us; we must submit ourselves to him and appease him by humility and goodwill, so that our Creator, when he sees such a disposition of our mind, may free us from sin, since he accepts the gift offered for sin.

For, as the voice of the Truth testifies, we have learned from Matthew XVIII that when a servant who owed ten thousand talents repented, he received release from his debt from his master. But when he did not forgive his fellow servant, who owed him one hundred denarii, he was ordered to pay what had already been forgiven him.

From these statements it is clear that if we do not forgive from the heart what is done against us, what we had rejoiced had already been forgiven us through repentance is again exacted from us.

## CHAPTER XIX.—“Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew V, 28)

[Col. 1146D]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXI, no. 18.)*

At times the guilt of fornication is in no way distinct from the guilt of adultery, since the Truth says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

Because the Greek word *moechus* means “adulterer,” while it is not another man’s wife but simply “a woman” whom he forbids one to look upon desirously, the Truth clearly shows that adultery is committed even by sight alone when an unmarried woman is shamefully desired.

Nevertheless, the offense is often distinguished according to the status or rank of the person desiring, since deliberate desire stains one person in sacred orders just as the guilt of adultery stains another. Yet among persons who are not dissimilar, the same guilt of lust is distinguished, in whom the guilt of fornication is distinguished from that of adultery. The distinguished preacher’s words testify that the guilt of fornication is distinguished from the guilt of adultery, when among other things he says: “Neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers will possess the kingdom of God” (I Corinthians VI, 9).

By placing them under separate judgments of guilt, he shows how greatly they differ from one another.

## CHAPTER XX.—“If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you” (Matthew V, 29)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book VI, no. 57.)*

Some people are so sluggish in mind that, if the labor of an occupation overtakes them, they succumb at the very beginning of their work. Others are so restless that, if they have leisure from work, they labor more heavily, because they endure greater disturbances of heart insofar as they have more freedom for their thoughts.

Therefore, it is necessary that neither a quiet mind stretch itself toward immoderate labor nor a restless mind narrow itself toward the practice of contemplation. Often those who could quietly contemplate God have fallen under the pressure of occupations; and often those who, while occupied, could have lived well for human needs have been destroyed by the sword of their own leisure.

This is why some restless spirits, while seeking through contemplation more than they can grasp, burst forth into perverse doctrines. While they negligently refuse to be humble disciples of the truth, they become teachers of error.

Hence the Truth says through itself: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into the fire of Gehenna.”

The two forms of life—namely, the active and the contemplative—when they are preserved in the mind, are like two eyes in the face. The right eye is the contemplative life; the left is the active life.

But there are some, as we have said, who are entirely unable to look discerningly upon sublime and spiritual things, yet undertake lofty contemplation. For this reason they slip, through the error of a perverse understanding, into the pit of unbelief.

The contemplative life, therefore, undertaken beyond their strength, compels those to fall away from the truth whom the active life alone could have humbly preserved in the state of their uprightness. To such people the Truth rightly says what we have quoted: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you.”

It is as though he plainly said: “When you are not adequate for the contemplative life with sound discernment, hold more safely to the active life alone. When you fail even in what you have chosen as something great, be content with what you regard as something small, so that, if through the contemplative life you are compelled to fall away from knowledge of the truth, you may at least enter the kingdom of heaven with one eye through the active life alone.”

## CHAPTER XXI.—“If anyone wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, let him have your cloak” (Matthew V, 40)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXI, no. 21.) The divine voice commands: “If anyone takes your tunic and wishes to contend with you in court, let him have your cloak also.” And again: “If anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back.” Yet hypocritical prelates, having assumed the holy garb of religious conduct, abandon the care of their children and seek to defend every temporal possession even by quarrels. They do not hesitate to ruin the hearts of their disciples by their example, and, as though through negligence, they fear losing earthly patrimonies; they endure the losses of souls with equanimity, but hasten to repel the loss of temporal goods even with agitated spirit [Col. 1147D]. For the more they love earthly things, the more vehemently they fear being deprived of them.

Since we possess something in this world in our mind, we learn what it is only when we lose it: what is possessed without love is lost without pain. But what we ardently love while possessing, we deeply lament when it is taken away. Who, however, does not know that the Lord created earthly things for our use, but created human souls for himself? The one who neglects what belongs properly to God while protecting what belongs to himself thereby proves that he loves himself more than God. Hypocrites do not fear losing what belongs to God—that is, human souls—but fear losing what belongs to them, namely, possessions that pass away with the world, as though they would have to render an account of them before the strict Judge; as though they might find him appeased when, having lost the things they desired—that is, rational beings—they preserve things without sense and without having sought them.

## CHAPTER XXII

“Take heed that you do not practice your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them” (Matthew 6:1).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 35.) Whoever has already learned sufficiently to trample down the desire for praise [Col. 1148A] commits fraud against edification if he conceals the good things he does; and, like one who scatters seed and removes its roots, he hides an action that ought to be imitated. Hence the Truth says: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).
