There is also that saying which seems to command something quite different: “Take heed that you do not practice your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them.”

What, then, does it mean that our work must be done so that it is not seen, and yet we are commanded that it should be seen, except that the things we do must both be concealed, lest we ourselves be praised, and displayed, so that we may increase the praise of our heavenly Father? For when the Lord forbade us to practice our righteousness before people, he immediately added: “In order to be seen by them.” And when he again commanded that our good works be seen by people, he at once added: “So that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.” Thus he showed, by the conclusion of each saying, in what manner they were to be seen and in what manner not seen: the mind of the one acting was neither to seek that its work be seen for its own sake, nor yet to conceal it on account of the glory of the heavenly Father [Col. 1148B].

Hence it often happens that a good work is done secretly while being performed publicly, and again publicly while being done secretly. Whoever seeks in a public good work not his own glory but that of the Father on high conceals what he has done, because he had as his sole witness the one whom he took care to please. And whoever, in his private good work, desires to be discovered and praised has done it before people, even if perhaps no one saw what he offered; for he brought with him into the good work as many witnesses as the human praises he sought in his heart.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“When you give alms, let your left hand not know” (Matthew 6:3).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapters 20 and 35.) The Lord also commands that transient praise not be sought from anyone for a gift expended: “When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing.” That is, the glory of the present life must in no way mingle with the administration of piety [Col. 1148C], but the work of righteousness must be ignorant of the desire for approval. For one greatly devalues his good when he thinks human approval sufficient for its reward. When transient praise is sought for a righteous work, a thing worthy of eternal recompense is sold for a paltry price. Of this price the Truth says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.”

## CHAPTER XXIV

“Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VIII, no. 69.) In all his works the hypocrite seeks the respect of honor, the glory of praise, to be feared by those better than himself, and to be called holy by everyone. But while he thirsts for transient approval, he loses by receiving what he labors for, as the Truth bears witness, saying: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.” Yet this reward cannot be held for long, because honor is bestowed for works displayed, while life is pressed toward its end; praises resound, but time hastens toward its end together with the praises. His mind is by no means fixed upon that glory which is possessed without end [Col. 1148D].

## CHAPTER XXV

“But when you pray, enter your room” (Matthew 6:6).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXII, no. 43.) Within, in the desire of the heart, there is the secret cry of prayer, which does not reach human ears and yet fills the hearing of the Creator. Hence, when Hannah went to the temple, she was silent with her mouth, and yet uttered so many voices of her desire (1 Samuel 1). Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “But when you pray, enter your room; and after shutting the door, pray to your Father; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” With the door shut, one prays in the room when, while the mouth is silent, the heart’s affection is poured out before the sight of heavenly mercy. The voice is heard in secret when one silently cries out through holy desires. Hence the Psalmist rightly says also: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart” (Psalm 9:17).

## CHAPTER XXVI

“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:43).

[Col. 1149A]

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XVIII, no. 7.) In the New Testament, certain actions are prohibited and judged to be grave faults which, under the Old Testament, once seemed to preserve the image of truth and could perhaps have been, and were thought to have been, lesser faults. In that Testament, through the sacrifices of bulls and goats, the sacrifice was not truth itself but the shadow of truth. For in the New Testament, through the higher commandments, we advance in the truth manifested in the flesh, and it is right that we abandon certain actions which, among that people, had served the shadow of truth.

But if anyone wishes to defend some fault by appealing to the Old Testament—for example, lying—because it may perhaps have harmed certain people less there, he must also say that the seizure of another’s property and the retaliation for an injury, which were permitted there to the weak, cannot harm him. How severely the Truth pursues all these things is clear to everyone: now that the shadow of its meaning has been set aside for us, the Truth is revealed in true flesh [Col. 1149B].

## CHAPTER XXVII

“Likewise, concerning the foregoing.”

(Homily 38 on the Gospels, no. 4; Homily 35, nos. 4, 5, 7.) The fathers of the Old Testament had received, by permission of the Law, the right to strike their adversaries with retaliation for hatred, just as it is written in the Law: “You shall love your friend, and you shall hate your enemy” (Leviticus 19:18). At that time the righteous had indeed been granted permission to suppress the adversaries of God and of themselves with all the strength they could muster, and to strike them by right of the sword.

This is undoubtedly restrained in the New Testament, when the Truth herself proclaims: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you”; and elsewhere exhorts his disciples to endure patiently the evils inflicted by them, saying: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). The possession of the soul is therefore placed in the power of patience [Col. 1149C], because patience is the root and guardian of all virtues. Through patience we possess our souls because, as we learn to rule ourselves, we begin to possess precisely what we are.

Patience is to endure the evils of others with equanimity and not to be stung by any grief even against the one who inflicts the evil. For one who bears his neighbor’s evils in such a way that he nevertheless grieves silently and looks for the time of a fitting retaliation does not display patience but only pretends to do so. For it is written: “Charity is patient; it is kind” (1 Corinthians 13:4). It is patient so that it may tolerate the evils of others; it is kind so that it may love even those whom it bears.

Hence the Truth herself says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; pray for those who persecute and slander you.” It is a virtue before people to tolerate adversaries, but it is a virtue before God to love them, because God accepts only that sacrifice which the flame of charity kindles before his eyes on the altar of good works.

It must be understood, however, that we often seem patient because we cannot repay evil with evil. But whoever does not repay evil because he is wholly unable to do so is certainly not patient [Col. 1149D], since patience is not sought in outward display but in the heart.

It must also be understood that it often happens to the patient that, while they are suffering adversity or hearing insults, they are troubled by no grief and display such patience that they take care to preserve even the innocence of their heart. But when, after a little while, they recall to mind the very things they endured, they are goaded by the fire of vehement grief, seek arguments for retaliation, and, judging themselves in their reconsideration, lose the gentleness they had possessed while enduring.

The crafty adversary returns to the victor’s mind when it is at rest and recalls either losses of property or the darts of injuries; exaggerating violently everything inflicted upon him, he makes it appear intolerable. Thus he disturbs the resting mind with such fury that [Col. 1150A] often the patient man is ashamed, even after victory, that he endured those things with equanimity, and grieves that he did not return the insults; and, if an opportunity is offered, he seeks to repay them with worse.

To whom, then, are such people like except those who are victorious through courage in the field but are afterward captured through negligence within the walls of the city? To whom are they like except those whom a severe illness does not remove from life when it first attacks, but whom a returning fever kills when it comes lightly? Therefore, the one who truly preserves patience is he who both endures the evils of others for a time without grief and, when recalling them, rejoices that he endured such things, lest the good of patience, preserved amid disturbances, perish in a time of peace.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

“Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matthew 5:44).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIV, no. 38; *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 44.) The sacrifice of prayer is received more willingly when it is prepared in love of one’s neighbor before the sight of the merciful Judge. Everyone truly makes this sacrifice abundant if he offers it also for his adversaries [Col. 1150B]. Hence the Truth, our teacher, says: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you.” Again he says: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may forgive you your sins.” One therefore makes his prayers more effective for himself when he offers them also for others.

The saints pray for their enemies while they are still able to turn their hearts toward fruitful repentance and save them through that conversion. For what else should be prayed for on behalf of enemies except what the Apostle says: “That the Lord may grant them repentance for knowledge of the truth, and that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will” (2 Timothy 2:25–26)?

But after judgment has taken place, when they see them burning in hell, they will not pray for them, because they will then in no way be able to be changed from iniquity to works of righteousness. The reason, therefore, why prayer is not then offered for people condemned to eternal fire is the same as the reason why prayer is not now offered for the devil and his angels, assigned to eternal punishment; and it is also the reason why holy people do not now pray for unbelieving and impious people who have died: namely, because they shrink from having the merit of their prayer annulled before the sight of the just Judge on behalf of those whom they already know to have been assigned to eternal punishment.

If the righteous who are still living now have no compassion for the dead and unjust who have been condemned [Col. 1150C], although they themselves know that they too must suffer something punishable in their flesh, how much more strictly will they then regard the torments of the wicked, when, stripped of every defect of corruption, they will cling more intimately and firmly to righteousness? For the power of strict judgment so absorbs their minds through their adherence to the most just Judge that they have no inclination whatever toward anything that disagrees with the subtle rule of his inward judgment.

## CHAPTER XXIX

“When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites, who are gloomy. For they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting” (Matthew 6:16).

(Homily 32 on the Gospels, no. 3.) Hypocrites often [Col. 1150D] afflict themselves with extraordinary abstinence; their faces grow pale from fasting, their bodies are shaken by weakness, and their chests are pressed by interrupted sighs. Through abstinence they draw so near to death that they live while dying almost every day. Yet they seek human eyes for these things and desire the glory of admiration.

The abstinence of the flesh is sometimes closely besieged and accompanied by vainglory, because when thinness of body and pallor of face are observed, virtue is exposed and praised; and it pours itself outward all the more quickly because it has emerged into human sight through displayed pallor. It often happens that what is believed to be done for God’s sake is done solely for human approval.

This is well signified by that Simon who was found on the road and carried the Lord’s cross under compulsion (Matthew 27). For burdens belonging to another are carried under compulsion when something is done through devotion to vanity. Who, then, are represented by Simon except those who practice abstinence and are arrogant—who indeed afflict the flesh through abstinence, but do not seek the fruit of abstinence inwardly [Col. 1151A]? Simon carries the Lord’s cross under compulsion when a sinner performs the act of a righteous person without being led to the good work by good will, and without its fruit.

Thus Simon carries the cross but does not die, because those who practice abstinence and are arrogant afflict their bodies through abstinence, but live for the world through their desire for vainglory. They seek from the mouths of their neighbors words of admiration, because through so much labor they think of nothing but human estimation.

## CHAPTER XXX

“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7:15).

(Homily 17 on the Gospels, no. 4.) Many people, when they undertake responsibility for governing, burn with eagerness [Col. 1151B] to tear apart their subjects and display the terror of power; they harm those whom they ought to benefit. Because they do not possess the inward organs of charity, they desire to appear masters and do not recognize themselves as fathers; they change the place of humility into the arrogance of domination. And if at times they flatter outwardly, inwardly they rage. Of such people the Truth says: “They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves.”

Whoever assumes a position of governance ought not to inflict evils but to endure them, so that by his own gentleness he may calm the anger of those who rage, and, himself wounded by afflictions, heal the wounds of sinners in others. Even if the zeal of righteousness sometimes requires him to be harsh toward his subjects, that anger should arise from love, not cruelty, so that he may outwardly display the rights of discipline while inwardly loving with fatherly affection those whom he chastises outwardly as though pursuing them.

## CHAPTER XXXI

“You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:20).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXI, no. 13.) When we see one and the same outward appearance among the good and the wicked, when we see the same form of profession in the chosen and the rejected, where can our understanding find the means [Col. 1151C] to distinguish the chosen from the rejected, the true from the false? Yet we recognize this more quickly if we carefully consider the unimpaired words of our teacher, who said: “You will know them by their fruits.” For we must not weigh what they display in appearance, but what they preserve in action.

## CHAPTER XXXII

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7:21).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXI, no. 12.) After the coming of the Mediator and our Redeemer, the ancient enemy receives many who have been marked with the sacrament of baptism and placed under the Christian name because they neglect to live rightly; after they have known the Redeemer, he takes them; after the water of washing, he pollutes them; after the heavenly sacraments, he drags them into the depths of hell.

They hold the faith, but do not hold the life of faith, because they either openly do unlawful things, or the things they do are wicked because of a perverse heart, even if they appear holy. Since some are believers in confession [Col. 1151D] but not in their manner of life, the voice of the Truth says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 6:46). Again he says: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?” Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). John says: “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4). Hence the Lord complains about his first people, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Mark 7:6). The Psalmist says: “They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him” (Psalm 77:36).

The ancient adversary now rises with all his effort against the death of those whom he begrudges because they will reign against him; and every Christian submits himself to his slavery as often as he runs and slips into iniquity. If, therefore, care in one’s conduct is neglected, it is useless to hold the right path by believing, because the way of faith indeed advances toward the heavenly homeland, but does not bring there those who stumble and neglect to live rightly [Col. 1152A].

## CHAPTER XXXIII

“Let your will be done, as in heaven so on earth” (Matthew 6:10).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXVII, no. 65.) At times, by “heavens” may be signified the angelic spirits who have been created in the heavenly realms. Hence in our Prayer we are instructed by the voice of the Truth to say: “Let your will be done, as in heaven so on earth,” so that God’s will may be observed by human weakness in every respect just as it is done by the higher creation.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

“Likewise, concerning the foregoing.”

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XV, no. 37.) In this prayer, “heaven” may also be understood as the righteous and “earth” as sinners, so that the will of our Creator may be fulfilled in all sinners just as it is perfected in all the righteous.

## CHAPTER XXXV

“Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11).

[Col. 1152B]

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXIV, no. 13.) Behold, we call it “our bread,” and yet we pray that it may be given. It becomes ours when it is received, yet it is God’s because it is given by him. It is therefore God’s by gift, and truly becomes ours through reception.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

(Homily 27 on the Gospels, no. 9.) Our enemy has gravely sinned against us, inflicted losses, harmed those who helped us, and persecuted those who loved us. These things would have to be retained if sins were not to be forgiven us. For our Advocate composed a prayer for us in our case, and he himself is the Judge of that same case—the one who is the Advocate. In the prayer he composed, he inserted a condition, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Since, therefore, the Judge who was the Advocate [Col. 1152C] has come, the one who made the prayer also hears it. Either, then, we say without acting: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” and by saying this we bind ourselves more tightly; or perhaps we omit this condition in prayer, and our Advocate does not recognize the prayer he composed, immediately saying to himself: “I know what I instructed; this is not the prayer I made.”

What, then, must we do except offer true affection of charity to our brothers, leaving no malice in our hearts? Remember what we are instructed: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). Behold, both something is owed to us and we owe something. Let us therefore forgive what is owed to us, so that what is owed by us may be forgiven.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

“Do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XIII, no. 6.) God is said to lead us into temptation when he permits us to be led into it by the adversary [Col. 1152D]. Hence in prayer we ask the Father, saying: “Do not lead us into temptation.” For the Lord does not lead us into temptation, since he mercifully protects his subjects from temptation at all times. Yet to lead us, as it were, into temptation is to fail to fortify us against the enticement of temptation. He does not lead us into the snare of temptation when he does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

“For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your sins” (Matthew 6:15).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book X, no. 30.) Our mind is weighed down by grave shame at the time of its prayer if either its own conduct still defiles it or the pain preserved in the heart against another’s wickedness accuses it. What can be found worse than this stain of grief, which in the sight of the Judge does not merely defile charity but kills it [Col. 1153A]? Any fault pollutes the life of the soul, but preserved resentment against one’s neighbor kills it. It is fixed in the mind like a sword, and with its point it pierces the hidden inward parts.

If it is not first drawn out of the transfixed heart, no help from God is obtained through the petitions of prayer, because medicines of healing cannot be applied to wounded limbs unless the iron is first removed from the wound. Hence the Truth herself says: “Unless you forgive people their sins, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins” (ibid.). Hence he admonishes us, saying: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may forgive you your sins” (Mark 11:25). Again he says: “Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:38). Thus he placed the condition of mercy upon the constitution of the petition, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” so that we should first do toward our neighbor the good thing that, moved by compunction, we ask from God [Col. 1153B].

Then we truly lift our face to God in prayer without stain or shame, when we neither commit the forbidden evils ourselves nor, through personal zeal, retain those committed against us.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

“Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XV, no. 53.) When God is not sought in prayer, the soul soon grows weary in prayer, because when someone asks for things which, according to God’s hidden judgment, he may refuse to grant, he himself becomes tedious to the one who does not wish to give what is loved. But the Lord wishes himself to be loved more than the things he created, and eternal things to be sought rather than earthly things, as it is written: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you.”

For he did not say, “They will be given,” but “They will be added to you,” clearly indicating that one thing is given as the principal gift and another is added. Since eternity should be our concern, while temporality should be our use, the former is given and the latter is indeed added in abundance [Col. 1153C]. Yet often, while people ask for temporal goods and do not seek eternal rewards, they ask for what is added but do not desire the place where it is to be added. Nor do they consider their request a gain if they are temporally poor here but live eternally rich in blessedness there.

## CHAPTER XL

“Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?” (Matthew 7:22).

(Homily 17 on Ezekiel, final section; *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VIII, no. 66.) We often see holy men perform wondrous deeds, do many mighty works, cleanse lepers, cast out demons, drive away bodily illnesses, and proclaim future things through the spirit of prophecy. But these gifts are sometimes granted also to the rejected. There is one sign of election, however: steadfastness in charity, as it is written [Col. 1153D]: “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

When the chosen perform these miracles, they perform them in a way entirely different from the rejected. What the chosen do out of charity, the rejected strive to do through arrogance; and through the gifts they have received from the Lord they seek not his glory but their own approval. They believe themselves to be such as they hear themselves proclaimed outwardly to be.

Hence it often happens that they come confidently even before the heavenly Judge, because they believe themselves before the eternal Judge to be such as they were regarded by people outwardly. But when, in the terror of the strict examination, all confidence in their former holiness has fallen, and they discover that the testimony of other mouths is lacking, they turn in judgment to enumerating their works, saying: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?”

But for these works they by no means receive the reward of recompense, because, when they are rejected in judgment, the Judge immediately says to them [Col. 1154A]: “I never knew you. Depart from me, you workers of iniquity.” The sentence then strikes them all the more strictly because now the heavenly goodness pours its gifts more abundantly even upon the ungrateful. The abundance of the gift becomes an increase of condemnation for them, because by the good things they have received they now exalt themselves in their own praise and grow proud against the giver through the very things by which they ought already to have been more humble before him.

## CHAPTER XLI

“I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXIX, no. 59; Book XXIII, no. 7.) All the arrogant who excel in signs, knowledge, prophecy, or some great works, who through these gifts desire to please people and seek praise from everyone for the virtues they receive, the Lord now tolerates and bears within the bosom of the holy Church. But in the future he will openly cast them out, when he expels them from the heavenly secrets through the final and public judgment.

Yet those who must be rejected will recall their gifts to the Judge who comes and repeat what they have done in his name, saying: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?” (Matthew 7:22). But how the Lord repels such people when he casts them out, he shows by saying to those whom he rejects: “I do not know where you are from; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7).

For God’s knowing is approving, while his not knowing is rejecting. It is as though the Lord plainly said: “I do not know the arrogant,” that is, “I do not approve their life in the power of my wisdom,” because, while they are puffed up by human praises, they are emptied of the true glory of eternal recompense [Col. 1154B].

## CHAPTER XLII

“Likewise, concerning the foregoing.”

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XI, no. 18.) Since God’s knowing is sometimes said to mean recognizing and sometimes approving, he knows the wicked person because he recognizes and judges him—for he would not judge anyone wicked if he did not recognize him—and yet he does not know the wicked person [Col. 1154C] because he does not approve his deeds.

Thus he knows him because he detects him, and does not know him because he does not acknowledge him within the appearance of his wisdom. Similarly, it is said of any truthful man that he does not know falsehood—not because he is unaware of it when others speak falsely, but because he both knows that deception in judgment and does not know it in love: that is, he himself does not do what he condemns when done by others.

## CHAPTER XLIII

“Lord, my servant lies paralyzed at home and is suffering terribly.” Jesus immediately answered him, saying: “I will come and heal him” (Matthew 8:6–7).

(Homily 28 on the Gospels, no. 2.) We should carefully observe here that when a certain royal official, whose son was ill at Capernaum, asked the Lord to come down and heal him, he answered him: “Go; your son lives.” What, then, does it mean that the royal official asks him to come to his son, yet he refuses to go bodily, while the centurion does not invite him to come to his servant [Col. 1154D], and yet he promises that he will go bodily? He does not deign to be present bodily with the royal official’s son, but does not disdain to go to the centurion’s servant.

What does this mean except that our pride is rebuked? For in human beings we venerate not the nature by which they were made in the image of God, but their honors and riches; and while we consider what surrounds them, we entirely fail to attend to what is within. While we consider what is despised in bodily circumstances, we neglect to weigh what they are.

Our Redeemer, therefore, to show that what is exalted among human beings ought to be despised by the holy, and what is despised among human beings is not despised by God, did not wish to go to the royal official’s son, but was ready to go to the centurion’s servant. Our pride, then, was rebuked: it does not know how to weigh people for the sake of people. It considers only what surrounds people, does not look at their nature, and does not recognize the honor of God in human beings.

Behold, the Son of God does not wish to go to the son of a royal official, and yet he is ready to go for the salvation of a servant. Certainly, if the servant of someone were to ask us to go to him [Col. 1155A], our pride would immediately answer us in silent thought: “Do not go, because you demean yourself; your honor is despised; your position is degraded.” Behold, he who came from heaven does not disdain to meet a servant on earth, yet we, who are from the earth, disdain to humble ourselves on earth.

## CHAPTER XLIV

“The blind men who had been given sight spread the report about Jesus” (Matthew 9:31).

(Mixed from *Moralia*, Book XIX, no. 36, and *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 9.) It is characteristic of holy men to conceal the good things they have done, lest they happen to incur the downfall of pride. Hence the Lord Jesus, giving sight to two blind men seated beside the road, commanded them, saying: “See that no one knows.” But it is immediately written of them: “After they went out, they spread the report about him throughout that whole land.”

We must ask what this means: the Lord himself, for whom willing something is the same as being able to do it, wished his miracles to be kept silent, yet those who had been given sight announced them as though against his will. Did the only-begotten Son of the Father, coeternal with the Holy Spirit [Col. 1155B], in this matter will something that he could not accomplish, so that he was unable to conceal the miracle he wished to remain silent?

Rather, our Redeemer provided, through his mortal body, an example of action in everything he did, so that, according to the measure of our strength, following his footsteps with an unimpeded step in our works, we might travel the road of the present life. When performing a miracle, he commanded silence, yet it could not remain silent, so that his chosen ones, following the examples of his teaching, might indeed wish in their intention to remain hidden in the great things they do, but might be revealed against their will for the benefit of others [Col. 1155C]. Thus it would be both a mark of great humility that they desire their works to be kept silent and a mark of great usefulness that their works cannot remain silent.

The Lord therefore did not wish something to happen and find himself unable to accomplish it. Rather, he gave, through the authority of his teaching, an example of what his members ought to will and of what happens to them even against their will. Following his example, then, let them conceal their deeds and guard themselves; but when they are revealed against their will, let them transmit good examples to their neighbors. Let them be concealed by intention, made public by necessity; let their concealment be a safeguard for themselves, and their publication a benefit for others.

## CHAPTER XLV

“Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10:16).

(Mixed from *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book I, no. 2; Homily 30 on the Gospels, no. 5; and *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 11.) The simple ought to labor so that they join prudence to the good of simplicity, so that they may possess the security of simplicity without losing the vigilance of prudence. Hence the Truth herself admonishes her disciples, saying: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves.”

In this matter it should be noted that the Lord did not wish to admonish his disciples either about the dove without the serpent or about the serpent without the dove, but necessarily joined both in the admonition. For in the hearts of the chosen, the simplicity of the dove ought to sharpen and kindle the cunning of the serpent, and the simplicity of the dove ought to temper the cunning of the serpent [Col. 1155D], so that, though deceived, they may not grow crafty through prudence, nor grow sluggish in the pursuit of understanding through simplicity.

Hence Paul says: “Do not become children in your understanding” (1 Corinthians 14:20). Behold, we have heard about the prudence of the serpent; now let us be admonished about the simplicity of the dove: “Be infants in malice” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XLVI

“What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light” (Matthew 10:27).

Source/review notes: The final proposed edit is redundant and should be disregarded; the chapter-LX citation is already correct in the draft. All substantive source content is otherwise represented after the three preceding edits.

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XI, no. 26, and Homily 6 on Ezekiel, no. 1.) When believers recognize certain mystical meanings in the prophets’ hidden words, what else is revealed than profound things from darkness? Hence Truth itself, speaking to the disciples in parables, says: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light”; that is, explain openly what you have heard in the obscurities of allegories. For when we loosen the mysterious knots of allegories through explanation, we speak in the light what we heard in darkness.

## CHAPTER XLVII

“I have come to separate a man from his father, and a daughter from her mother, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household” (Matthew 10:36).

[Col. 1156A]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book III, no. 13.) The ancient adversary strives to incline the state of our mind not only through himself, but also through those who cling to us. For when he cannot overthrow our heart by his own persuasion, he creeps toward it through the tongues of those who cling to us. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Let each one beware of his neighbor, and let him not trust in any of his brothers” (Jeremiah 9:4). Again it is written: “Beware of your children, and pay attention to your household” (Ecclesiasticus 32:26). For when the crafty adversary sees that he is repelled from the hearts of the good, he seeks out those who are greatly loved by them, and speaks flattering words through those who are loved more than the others, so that, when the force of love pierces the heart, the sword of his persuasion may easily break into the innermost defenses of uprightness.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

“Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward” (Matthew 10:41).

[Col. 1156B]

(Homily 20 on the Gospels, no. 12.) Our Redeemer shows how great is the virtue involved in self-restraint and in receiving those in need when he says: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. And whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward.” In these words it should be noted that he does not say, “He will receive a reward from the prophet,” or “a reward from the righteous person,” but “a prophet’s reward” and “a righteous person’s reward.” For a reward from a prophet is one thing, and a prophet’s reward another; a reward from a righteous person is one thing, and a righteous person’s reward another.

What does “he will receive a prophet’s reward” mean, except that the one who supports a prophet through his generosity, although he himself does not possess the gift of prophecy, will nevertheless receive the rewards of prophecy from the almighty Lord? The prophet is filled with the spirit of prophecy, yet he requires bodily nourishment; and if the body is not [Col. 1156C] restored, it is certain that the voice itself will be withdrawn. Therefore, whoever supplies nourishment to a prophet because he is a prophet gives strength to that prophet’s prophecy to speak. Thus, together with the prophet, he receives a prophet’s reward who, although he was not filled with the spirit of prophecy, nevertheless displayed before God what he helped.

That other person is perhaps righteous, and the less he possesses anything in this world, the greater confidence he has to speak on behalf of justice. When someone who possesses something in this world supports him, although perhaps he does not yet dare to speak freely for justice, he makes himself a sharer in that righteous person’s freedom, so that he may receive the rewards of justice together with the one whom he helped by supporting him, enabling him to speak that justice freely.

## CHAPTER XLIX

“What did you go out into the wilderness to see—a reed shaken by the wind?” (Matthew 11:7).

(Mixed from book XXXIII of the exposition of Job, no. 7, and Homily 9 on Ezekiel, no. 16.) The Lord says this in praise of blessed John the Baptist to the crowds of the Jews, denying that the instability of mind—which is sometimes [Col. 1156D] signified by a reed in sacred speech—was present in him. For after the Lord’s question, “No” is to be understood. That he spoke by way of denial and not affirmation is confirmed by the words that follow: “But what did you go out into the wilderness to see—a man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings.” A reed shaken by the wind is raised now by the gusts and bent now by the gusts. Every weak spirit that is cast down by disparagement or exalted by praise is a reed shaken by the wind. John was not such, because he held the summit of his mind unbending amid human praise and disparagement, and no breath of tongues from any direction bent his mind, made firm by the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER L

“What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Indeed, I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matthew 11:9).

(Homily 3 on the Gospels, no. 3.) When John was questioned, he answered, saying: “I am not a prophet” (John 1:21). [Col. 1157A] Because he knew that he was more than a prophet, he denied that he was a prophet. He is called more than a prophet for this reason: it is the prophet’s office to announce what is to come, but not also to point it out. John, however, is more than a prophet, because he pointed out with his finger the one whom he proclaimed in words.

## CHAPTER LI

“From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence” (Matthew 11:12).

(Homily 20 on the Gospels, no. 14.) John admonished the crowds who came to his baptism, saying: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance.” And again: “Whoever has two tunics should give to one who has none” (Luke 3:11). From this it is now plainly understood what Truth means when it says: “From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12).

These words of the heavenly judgment must be examined with the greatest care. For one must ask how the kingdom of heaven can suffer violence. Who can inflict violence upon heaven? Again, if the kingdom of heaven can suffer violence and the violent seize it, why has it endured this violence from the days of John the Baptist and not before?

In the Law it is written: “If anyone does this or that, he shall die.” It is therefore clear to all who read that it struck sinners with the penalty of its severity, but did not bring them back to life through repentance. But when John the Baptist, preceding the grace of the Redeemer, preaches repentance so that the sinner who died through guilt may live through conversion, then indeed, from the days of John the Baptist, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence.

What, then, is the kingdom of heaven except the dwelling-place of the righteous? For the rewards of the heavenly homeland belong only to the righteous, so that the humble, chaste, meek, and merciful may reach the joys above. But when someone swollen with pride, polluted by the sin of the flesh, inflamed with anger, or impious through cruelty returns to repentance after his sins and receives eternal life, the sinner enters, as it were, a place belonging to another. From the days of John the Baptist, therefore, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize [Col. 1157B] it, because the one who imposed repentance upon sinners taught what else but that violence should be done to the kingdom of heaven?

Let us therefore reflect, dearest brothers, upon the evils we have committed, and let us wear ourselves down with continual lamentation. Let us seize through repentance the inheritance of the righteous, which we did not hold through our life. Almighty God wishes to endure such violence from us, for he wishes the kingdom of heaven to be seized by our tears, although it is not owed to our merits.

## CHAPTER LII

“It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person” (Matthew 15:11).

(Book XI, Letter 64, to Augustine, in Response 10.) Just as external works are observed in the Old Testament, so in the New Testament attention is directed more carefully not to what is done outwardly but to what is thought inwardly, so that it may be punished with a subtle judgment. For although the Law forbids eating many things as unclean, in the Gospel the Lord says: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but the things that come out of the heart—[Col. 1157D] those are what defile a person”; and shortly afterward, explaining, he added: “From the heart come evil thoughts.” There it is abundantly shown that what is generated in action from the root of polluted thought is demonstrated to be polluted by almighty God.

Hence the apostle Paul also says: “All things are clean to the clean, but to the polluted and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Titus 1:15); and immediately, announcing the cause of their pollution, he adds: “For their mind and conscience are polluted.” Food, therefore, is not unclean to one whose mind is not unclean.

## CHAPTER LIII

“If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew 16:24).

(Mixed from book XXXIII on Job, no. 13, and Homily 10 on Ezekiel, no. 7.) There are some who, desiring the ways of Truth and longing for eternal things, make themselves entirely strangers to the world. They not only do not desire what belongs to others, but also abandon what is their own; and they not only seek no [Col. 1158A] glory in it, but, when glory is offered, even despise it. They are so filled with love of almighty God that, with their mind changed, they seem to be strangers even to themselves, fulfilling what is said by the voice of Truth: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself.”

He denies himself who, having trampled down the arrogance of pride, demonstrates before God that he is a stranger to himself. He denies himself who is changed for the better, who begins to be what he was not and ceases to be what he was.

## CHAPTER LIV

“See that you do not despise one of these little ones; for I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book II, no. 3; Dialogues, book IV, chapter 33, at the end.) When Paul says of the angels: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to receive the inheritance of salvation?” how can they always see the Father’s face if they are sent outward for our salvation? [Col. 1158B]

We resolve this more readily if we consider how subtle the angelic nature is. They do not go forth from the divine vision in such a way as to be deprived of the joys of inward contemplation. For if, when they went forth, they lost sight of the Creator, they could neither raise up those who lie fallen nor announce the truth to the ignorant; nor could they offer the fountain of light to the blind, since they themselves would lose it when they went forth.

In this respect, then, the angelic nature is now distinguished from the condition of our nature: we are confined by place and constrained by the ignorance of blindness, whereas the spirits of the angels are indeed confined by place, but their knowledge is nevertheless extended incomparably far beyond ours. They are spread inwardly and outwardly through knowing, because they contemplate the very fountain of knowledge. What can they not know among the things that are to be known, when they know the one who knows all things?

Their knowledge, therefore, is greatly extended in comparison with ours, but narrow in comparison with divine knowledge. Likewise, those spirits themselves, in comparison with our bodies, are spirits; but in comparison with the [Col. 1158C] supreme and unbounded Spirit, they are bodies. Thus they always see the Father’s face, and yet they come to us, because they go forth to us by a spiritual presence, while nevertheless remaining there, through inward contemplation, from where they had departed.

## CHAPTER LV

“If the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matthew 11:21).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXV, no. 7.) “If the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes.” In sackcloth are shown the harshness and pricking of sins; in ashes, the dust of the dead. For this reason both are customarily used in repentance, so that in the pricking of sackcloth we may recognize what we have done through guilt, and in the ashes’ embers consider what we have become through judgment.

Let the sins that prick be considered in the sackcloth; let the just punishment of those sins, following through the sentence of death, be considered in the ashes. Since humiliations arose after sin of the flesh, let a person see in the harshness of sackcloth [Col. 1158D] what he did through pride; let him see in the ashes how far he has come by sinning. Sackcloth itself may also signify, through remembrance and repentance, the pricking of sorrow, because the sinner is pricked, as it were, by a kind of sackcloth when he is rubbed by the harsh goads of reproach in his mind. He also does penance in ashes because he carefully considers what he became through just judgment from his first sin.

## CHAPTER LVI

“I confess to you, Father, [Col. 1159A] Lord of heaven and earth, that …” (Matthew 11:25).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVII, no. 4; book XXV, no. 32.) The Lord, appearing to our eyes in the weakness of our flesh, displayed wondrous judgments by rejecting some and calling others—judgments that we can think about but cannot comprehend. For he says: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

Hence, speaking of the cause of this matter, he says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father.” Then, adding as it were a reason for the hiding and revealing, he says: “Because it was pleasing before you.”

From these words we receive examples of humility, so that we may not rashly presume to investigate heavenly counsels concerning the calling of some and the rejection of others. For although he had mentioned both, he did not immediately give an explanation, but said that it was pleasing to God—showing, namely, that what pleased the just one cannot be unjust.

When he says, “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent,” he plainly calls the proud “wise and prudent,” because knowledge of the truth is denied to the proud. For he did not add, “You have revealed them to fools,” but “to little ones,” thereby making it known that he condemned swelling pride, not intelligence.

## CHAPTER LVII

“Come to me, all who labor and are burdened” (Matthew 11:28).

[Col. 1159B]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXI, no. 9.) The Lord commands us to come to him—not with bodily steps, but through progress of the heart. For he himself says: “The hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” And shortly afterward: “True worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such people to worship him” (John 4:21).

He indicates that steps are taken in the heart when he both calls us to come and nevertheless declares that we are not to pass elsewhere through bodily movement. In sacred Scripture, by the designation of steps we sometimes understand movements of the mind or progress in merits. By such steps Truth calls us to itself, saying: “Come to me, all who labor.”

## CHAPTER LVIII

“Take my yoke upon you” (Matthew 11:29).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, no. 66; book XXX, no. 50; book XX, no. 39.) Great is the servitude of worldly affairs, by which the mind is fiercely worn down, [Col. 1159C] although it willingly sweats in them. Prosperity presses like a certain yoke of servitude when it is desired; adversity presses when it is feared. The Lord saw this heavy yoke of servitude impressed upon the necks of worldly people when he said: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you.”

He imposes nothing heavy upon the necks of our minds, since he commands that every desire which disturbs us be avoided. He commands nothing burdensome to those subject to him, since he urges us to turn aside from the wearisome roads of this world: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

For the harsh yoke and, as we have said, the weight of severe servitude consist in being subject to temporal things, pursuing earthly possessions, holding on to what is passing away, wishing to stand amid things that do not stand, desiring things that pass away while refusing to pass away with them. Everything that previously afflicted the mind through the desire to obtain it later presses upon it through fear of losing it, for all things flee against our wishes.

The Lord also loosened this yoke of servitude from the necks of [Col. 1159D] the disciples when he said: “Take heed to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts become weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34), immediately adding, “and by the cares of this life.” For people love even the hardships of labor for the glory of this world, willingly serving it with all their sweat and most devotedly submitting their necks to its heavy yoke. To be free from the condition and yoke of this servitude is now to desire nothing in the world.

But if someone once shakes the neck of his mind free from the domination of temporal desires, he already enjoys a certain freedom even in this life, since he is disturbed by no desire for prosperity and constrained by no fear of adversity.

## CHAPTER LIX

“Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIV, nos. 53, 54, 56.) Against the plague of pride, let us all hear what Truth admonishes the disciples, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.”

For this reason the only-begotten [Col. 1160A] Son of God assumed the form of our humility; for this reason the invisible one appeared not only visible but also despised; for this reason he endured the mockery of insults, the reproaches of derision, and the torments of suffering: so that humble God might teach human beings not to be proud. How great, then, is the virtue of humility, for the true instruction of which alone the one who is great beyond measure became small even unto suffering?

Because the devil’s pride provided the origin of our destruction, the humility of God was found to be the instrument of our redemption. Our enemy, created among all things, wished in his exaltation to appear above all things. Our Redeemer, however, remaining great above all things, deigned to become small among all things.

But we can better expose the cause of pride and disclose the foundations of humility if we briefly touch upon what the author of death and the Creator of life recommend. The former teaches minds subject to him nothing other than to seek the summit of loftiness, to rise above all equals through swelling pride, to pass beyond human fellowship through exaltation, [Col. 1160B] and to raise themselves against the Creator’s power, as the Psalmist says of them: “They have passed over to the purposes of their heart; they have thought and spoken wickedness; they have spoken iniquity on high” (Psalm 72:7).

The latter, coming to spittle, blows, slaps, the crown of thorns, the cross, the spear, and death, admonishes his members, saying: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26).

Since our Redeemer rules the hearts of the humble and the author of death is king over the proud, we clearly recognize that pride is the most evident sign of the reprobate, while humility is the sign of the elect. When it is known whom each person follows, it is discovered under which king he serves. Everyone carries, as it were, a title of his works, by which he easily shows under whose rule he serves.

Hence it is said in the Gospel: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:16). Those who serve under the king of pride, even if they sometimes assume the appearance of humility, cannot conceal themselves [Col. 1160C] in everything, because their pride, unable to remain hidden for long, is exposed in one action when it is concealed by another.

Those who serve under the king of humility, however, always fearful and watchful on every side, fight against the arrows of pride. As though warding off opposing blows, they keep their eye all the more upon their own body, while above all preserving humility in themselves.

When the Lord therefore says to all whom he calls, “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart,” saying that he is meek in his teaching and humble means nothing other than that, leaving aside the difficult exercises of pride, he points out certain level paths for living well.

## CHAPTER LX

“A wicked person brings forth wicked things from a wicked treasure” (Matthew 12:35).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book I, no. 23.) Often a teacher who dares to teach what he neglects to do, when he has ceased speaking the good things he refused to practice, begins to teach his subjects the wrongs that he himself does. Thus, by the just judgment of almighty God, [Col. 1160D] he no longer has a tongue for goodness because he refuses to have a good life, so that when his mind is directed toward love of earthly things, he always speaks of earthly matters.

Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart. A good person brings forth good things from a good treasure, and a wicked person brings forth wicked things from a wicked treasure” (Luke 6:45). Hence John also says: “They are of the world; therefore they speak of the world” (1 John 4:5).

## CHAPTER LXI

“Concerning every idle word that people speak, they will give an account” (Matthew 12:36).

(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 14.) Those who give themselves to excessive speech, because they dissipate themselves through many words, often neglect for a long time to avoid idle words and proceed to harmful ones. First they come to enjoy speaking about the affairs of others; afterward, through their criticisms, they bite the life of those about whom they speak; finally, their tongue breaks out into open insults.

Hence Solomon says: “In much speaking sin will not be absent” (Proverbs 10:19). Hence [Col. 1161A] James says: “If anyone thinks he is religious but does not restrain his tongue and deceives his heart, his religion is worthless” (James 1:26). Again he says: “Let every person be swift to hear, but slow to speak.” Again, defining the force of the tongue, he adds: “It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison” (James 3:8).

Truth itself also admonishes us, saying: “I tell you that for every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment.” An idle word is one that lacks either the reason of just necessity or the purpose of pious usefulness. If, therefore, an account is demanded for idle speech, let us consider what punishment awaits excessive speech, in which one sins even through harmless words.

## CHAPTER LXII

“Gather the weeds and bind them into bundles to burn” (Matthew 13:30).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, no. 98; Dialogues, book IV, chapter 35.) Just as there are many dwelling places in the Father’s house according to the diversity of virtue, so the disparity of crimes subjects the condemned to the fires of Gehenna with differing punishment. Although this Gehenna is one for all, it does not [Col. 1161B] burn all with one and the same intensity.

For just as we are all touched by the same sun, yet do not all grow hot beneath it in the same way—for the weight of the heat is perceived according to the condition of the body—so there is one Gehenna that afflicts the condemned, yet it does not burn all with the same intensity, because what the differing health of bodies does here is accomplished there by the differing causes of merits.

For if the sum of punishments were not distinguished by the deeds of merits, the judge coming to judgment would never declare that he would say to the reapers: “Gather the weeds and bind them into bundles to burn.” The reaping angels bind the weeds into bundles for burning when they join those who are to be handed over to eternal fire—equals with equals—in similar torments, so that the proud may burn with the proud, the lustful with the lustful, the greedy with the greedy, the deceitful with the deceitful, the envious with the envious, and the unbelieving with the unbelieving; and so that those whom a similar fault stains may be restrained by an equal punishment.

When those who are alike in guilt are led to similar torments, [Col. 1161C] because the angels assign them to places of punishment, they bind them, as it were, into bundles of weeds for burning.

## CHAPTER LXIII

“The Son of man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of scandal” (Matthew 13:41).

(Homily 12 on the Gospels, nos. 1, 3, 6.) In sacred speech the kingdom of God does not always mean the kingdom that is to come; sometimes it is called the Church of the present time. For in that kingdom of blessedness, where there is perfect peace, there can be no causes of scandal to be gathered, since the reprobate are certainly not admitted there.

## CHAPTER LXIV

“Likewise, concerning what was said above.”

(Homily 38 on the Gospels, no. 2.) In the holy Gospel the kingdom of God, or the kingdom of heaven, often means the present Church. For the congregation of the righteous is called the kingdom of heaven, because the Lord says through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne” (Isaiah 66:1). Solomon [Col. 1161D] also says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wisdom 7:27). Paul likewise says that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).

We must clearly gather that if God is wisdom, and the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom, then, since heaven is called the seat of God, the soul of the righteous is heaven. Hence the Psalmist says of the holy preachers: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19:1). The kingdom of heaven, therefore, is the Church of the righteous, because, while their hearts desire nothing on earth, the Lord already reigns in them as in heavenly places through their longing for what is above.

## CHAPTER LXV

“The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind” (Matthew 13:47).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIII, no. 34.) The Church is called the kingdom of heaven. When the Lord raises its conduct toward heavenly things, it already reigns in the Lord through a heavenly way of life. It is rightly [Col. 1162A] compared to a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind, because, cast into this age of the gentiles, it rejects no one, but catches the wicked with the good, the proud with the humble, the angry with the meek, and the foolish with the wise.

## CHAPTER LXVI

“The Lord walking upon the sea. The boat in which they were crossing was being tossed about by the waves in the middle of the sea, for the wind was contrary” (Matthew 14:24).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVII, no. 45.) Blessed Job says of the Lord: “By his strength the seas were gathered together” (Job 26:12). What else is designated by the name of the sea than the present age? In it, the hearts of people seeking earthly things swell with diverse waves of thought; stirred by the pride of arrogance, as they strike one another with alternating intent, they collide like waves opposing each other.

But now the seas have been gathered together by the Lord’s strength, because, when the Lord was incarnate, the discordant hearts of worldly people believe in harmony. [Col. 1162B] Now Peter walks upon the sea, because those once-swollen hearts have been subdued to Christ’s preachers by humble hearing. Thus the Gospel rightly also portrayed the gentleness of this world when the stormy water of the sea was trodden down beneath the Lord’s feet, its swelling pressed down.

## CHAPTER LXVII

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

(Dialogues, book II, chapter 23, near the end.) The apostle Peter was still in this flesh when he heard: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.” Those who now hold the place of binding and loosing are the ones who maintain the office of holy governance through faith and conduct. While they still dwell in this corruptible flesh, they can loose souls already placed under that invisible judgment.

But so that a human being might have such power from earth, the Creator of heaven and earth came from heaven to earth. And so that flesh might also judge spiritual matters, God, having become flesh for human beings, graciously [Col. 1162C] bestowed this upon it. Thus our weakness rose above itself from the place where the strength of God was weakened beneath it.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

“Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you” (Matthew 16:22).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book III, no. 38.) It must be understood that carnal people in the Church sometimes strive through fear and sometimes through boldness to persuade the good to do wrong. When they themselves fail either through cowardice or through pride, they endeavor to pour these things into the hearts of the righteous, as though out of love.

Peter retained a carnal mind before the Redeemer’s death and resurrection. The son of Zeruiah had likewise clung to his commander David with a carnal mind. Yet one sinned through fear, the other through pride. The former, hearing of his master’s death, said: “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you.” The latter, unable to bear insults against his commander, said: “Shall Shimei not be put to death for these words, because he cursed the Lord’s anointed?” (2 Samuel 19:21).

To the former it was immediately said: [Col. 1162D] “Get behind me, Satan.” The latter, together with his brother, promptly heard: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Why should you become a Satan to me today?”

Those who advise evil are therefore judged by the designation of apostate angels: through flattering words, as though loving, they draw people toward unlawful things. Those are far worse who succumb to this fault not through fear but through pride.

## CHAPTER LXIX

“The kings of the earth—from whom do they receive tribute?” (Matthew 17:24).

(Homily 7 on Ezekiel, no. 4.) In our good works we must sometimes beware of causing scandal, but sometimes scorn it as insignificant. We learned this from our very author. When tribute was demanded from Peter, the Lord first proposed an example by which he answered that he owed nothing, saying: “The kings of the earth—from whom do they receive tribute or census-tax? From their own sons or from strangers?” He immediately replied: “Therefore the sons are free.”

But after he had shown himself to be free, lest he perhaps [Col. 1163A] cause anyone to stumble, he added: “However, so that we may not scandalize them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you” (Matthew 17:27).

Again, when he said: “Everything that enters the mouth does not defile a person,” the disciples approached and said to him: “Do you know that the Pharisees, when they heard this saying, were scandalized?” But he answered: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Leave them; they are blind and leaders of the blind.”

Behold, Truth the teacher gave what he did not owe as tribute, lest scandal arise in certain hearts. Again, because he saw scandal arising in certain hearts against the truth, he allowed them to remain in their scandal. From this we must consider that, insofar as we can do so without sin, we ought to avoid causing scandal to our neighbors. But if scandal is taken from the truth, it is more useful to allow scandal to arise than to abandon the truth.

## CHAPTER LXX

“Not everyone accepts this saying” (Matthew 19:11).

[Col. 1163B]

(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 28.) Those who are ignorant of sins of the flesh must fear precipitous ruin all the more anxiously the higher they stand, and they must hear what Truth itself says about this integrity: “Not everyone accepts this saying.” It made the matter known as something supreme precisely by denying it to everyone; and, while declaring that it is difficult to grasp, it indicated to its hearers with what caution it must be held once grasped.

## CHAPTER LXXI

“You who have left everything and followed me, in the regeneration, when he sits …” (Matthew 19:28).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book X, no. 52, and *Homily 2 on Ezekiel*, no. 18.) All the saints who have perfectly abandoned the world will come with the Lord for judgment; united to his body, joined to his majesty, and made judges together with him, they will be seen to be those who now follow perfect [Col. 1163C] works according to the precepts of the Gospel. Hence it is said to the holy apostles themselves: “You who have left everything and followed me, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” For that tribunal of the inner assembly will not have more than twelve judges; rather, the number twelve expresses the quantity of the whole, because whoever, stirred by the goad of divine love, leaves his possessions here will undoubtedly obtain there the summit of judicial power, so that the one who now chastises himself through voluntary poverty in consideration of judgment may then come as judge together with the Judge.

Hence it is said through Solomon concerning the Bridegroom of the holy Church: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. XXXI, 23). Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. III, 14). Hence Truth declares that these same elders are no longer servants but friends, [Col. 1163D] saying: “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John XV, 15).

Therefore, on the day of the final judgment, it will be shown with how great a power each just person—now despised—will shine. For then those who are now unjustly judged on behalf of God will come as judges with God. Their light will shine so much more broadly the more harshly the hand of their persecutors now constrains them. Then it will be manifest to the eyes of the reprobate that those who voluntarily abandoned all earthly things were supported by heavenly power. For as many as now willingly humble themselves for love of the truth will then shine like lamps as judges with Christ at the judgment.

All those, indeed, who now surpass the precepts of the Law through the perfection of their virtues—who are not content merely to fulfill what the divine Law has commanded to all, but in a more excellent desire seek to offer more than they have been able to hear in the general commandments—are those to whom the Lord’s voice says: “You who have left everything and followed me, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve [Col. 1164A] tribes of Israel.” At the final judgment these are not judged but reign, because they come as judges together with their Creator. For, leaving everything, they carried out with ready devotion more than they had generally heard commanded.

By a special command, given to a few who are more perfect and not generally to all, the rich young man heard this: “Go, sell what you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21). For if a general command bound everyone under this precept, it would certainly be sinful for us to possess anything of this world. But one thing is what Sacred Scripture generally commands all; another is what it specially orders to the more perfect.

Those, therefore, are rightly not held under the general judgment who have surpassed the general commandments by their manner of life. For just as those who, persuaded by unbelief, disdain to keep the Law are not judged but perish, so those who, moved by devotion, advance even beyond the general precepts [Col. 1164B] of God’s Law are not judged but reign.

Hence Paul, surpassing even the special precepts, demonstrated more by his actions than he had received by the instruction of permission. For although he had received permission to live from the Gospel while preaching the Gospel, he indeed imparted the Gospel to his hearers, yet refused to be supported by the Gospel’s resources. Why, then, should the one who is to reign be judged, when he received the lesser thing to observe but discovered the greater thing by which to live?

## CHAPTER LXXII — “Everyone who leaves house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. XVI, 20).

(*Homily 18 on Ezekiel*, no. 16.) No saint abandons earthly things in order that he may possess more of them in this world. For whoever leaves earth because of earthly ambition does not abandon earth but desires it; nor will the one who leaves one wife receive a hundred [Col. 1164C] wives. Rather, because the number ten, multiplied by itself, rises to one hundred, perfection of great measure is rightly signified by one hundred, through which eternal life is also promised.

Whoever for God’s name despises temporal and earthly things receives perfection of mind, so that he no longer desires what he despises, and in the age to come reaches the glory of eternal life. Thus he who receives the spirit of perfection and has no need of earthly things—even if he does not possess them—will receive a hundred times what he gave.

For the poor person is the one who lacks what he does not have. But the one who, though not possessing something, does not desire to possess it is rich. Poverty consists in the neediness of the mind, not in the quantity of possessions; for the person to whom poverty is a fitting condition is not poor.

## CHAPTER LXXIII — “When the workers of the vineyard came, those who had come about the eleventh hour received a denarius each” (Matt. XX, 10).

[Col. 1164D]

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXXV, no. 42.) The number ten is perfect in Sacred Scripture, because the Law is concluded in ten commandments, and every fault is restrained by no more than ten words. And, as Truth explains, the workers of the vineyard are rewarded with a denarius.

For in the denarius, three are joined to seven. Man, however, who consists of soul and body, is contained in seven qualities: he flourishes spiritually in three and bodily in four. He is spiritually stirred in the love of God by three things, when the Law says to him: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your mind, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matt. XXII, 37). Bodily, however, he is contained in four qualities, since he is composed of hot and cold, moist and dry matter.

Thus man, who consists of seven qualities, is said to be rewarded with a denarius, because in the reception of the heavenly homeland our seven are joined to the eternal three, so that man receives contemplation of the Trinity and lives, perfected in the reward [Col. 1165A] of his work, as though by a certain denarius.

Or certainly, there are seven virtues through which one labors in this life; when the contemplation of the Trinity is given to them as their reward, the life of those who labor is rewarded with a denarius. Yet every perfect person also receives a denarius in this life, when he joins hope, faith, and charity to those same seven virtues.

## CHAPTER LXXIV — “Did you not agree with me for a denarius?” (Matt. XX, 13).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXV, no. 34, and book XXXV, no. 13.) No one should rashly scrutinize heavenly counsels and divine judgments. Rather, let the counsel of the highest and hidden power suffice as a satisfaction to evident reason, since what pleases the just Lord cannot be unjust.

Thus, when he was paying the laborers in the vineyard and made unequal workers equal in their reward—while the one who had labored longer sought more in payment—he said: “Did you not agree with me for a denarius [Col. 1165B]? I wish to give this last one as much as to you. Or is it not lawful for me to do what I wish?”

In everything, therefore, that is arranged outwardly, the cause is openly rational; the justice of the will is hidden. It must be understood, moreover, that the holy Church alone is the vineyard in which good work is carried out; hence only those who labored within the vineyard received the reward of the denarius.

## CHAPTER LXXV — “Two blind men sitting beside the road, when they heard that Jesus was passing by as he went out from Jericho, cried out: ‘Have mercy on us, Son of David’” (Matt. XX, 29).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XIX, no. 5.) Our Lord Jesus Christ, coeternal with God the Father, is said to pass by according to his humanity, but according to his divinity he is as though standing still. For he does not pass by in the respect in which he is eternal, but he passes by in the respect in which he appeared temporal for our sake. Thus it is also written in the Gospel: “As the Lord was going out from Jericho, he was passing by.”

Two blind men sitting beside the road cried out, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.” [Col. 1165C] At their cry, as it is written there: “Jesus stood still and restored their sight.” What does it mean to hear while passing by and to restore light while standing still, except that through his humanity he pitied us, while through the power of his divinity he drove away the darkness of our mind?

Because he was born and suffered for us, because he rose and ascended into heaven, Jesus passes by, as it were, since this action is temporal. But he stood still, touched them, and gave them light, because the eternity of the Word—which remains in itself and renews all things—does not pass away as that temporal dispensation does. For God’s standing still consists in arranging all changeable things through an unchangeable thought.

Thus, when he heard the voices of those asking as he passed by, he restored light while standing still: although he endured temporal things for us, he nevertheless granted us light from that in which he knows no passing into mutability.

## CHAPTER LXXVI — “Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXII, 13).

[Col. 1165D]

(*Homily 9 on Ezekiel*, no. 34.) Whoever still clings in mind to the present age and still delights in earthly pleasures cannot love the eternal joys promised to the just. Let him therefore recognize, in the book of the holy Gospel, the condemnation of the reprobate written there, and drive from his heart through fear what he loves, so that he may be able to love the heavenly glory that he has chosen—or hears proclaimed—in the judgment.

There, under the figure of a single condemned person, the multitude of the reprobate is expressed when Truth’s voice says: “Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Then the reprobate fall into the outer darkness because now they have voluntarily cast themselves into the inner darkness, refusing to follow the light of truth either by believing or by doing good.

They are commanded to be thrown into that darkness with hands and feet bound because, while now it is the time for working and running, they did not wish to have their hands and feet free for good action. It is also written concerning the reprobate: “Their worm [Col. 1166A] will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isa. LXVI, 24).

## CHAPTER LXXVII — “Do whatever they tell you; but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII, 3).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book VI, no. 10.) A foolish person sometimes receives the gift of right understanding, is taught by the sayings of Sacred Scripture, and speaks good things; yet in no way does he practice what he says. He speaks God’s words, but does not love them; by praising them he magnifies them, but by living he tramples them.

The person who yearns for God through holy desires, however, learns what he hears and does what he has learned. Thus Truth admonished his own disciples, when he commanded those who burned with holy desires concerning the Pharisees, saying: “Do whatever they tell you; but do not do what they do.”

## CHAPTER LXXVIII — “They do all their works in order to be seen by people” (Matt. XXIII, 5).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XV, no. 4.) Often, while a hypocrite pretends to be holy and is not at all afraid to show himself wicked, he is honored by people, and [Col. 1166B] the glory of holiness is bestowed upon him by those who see outward things but cannot perceive what is within.
