Thus it happens that he rejoices in the first seat, delights in the first place of reclining, is puffed up by the first greeting, is exalted by the reverent voice of those who serve him, and swells with proud thought in the service of his subjects. As Truth’s voice also says of such people: “They do all their works in order to be seen by people. For they love the first places at banquets, the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by people.”

But the joyful pleasure of their rejoicing will pass away, while their punishment will remain.

## CHAPTER LXXIX — “Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (Matt. XXIII, 24).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book I, no. 21.) The Lord is signified here by the name “camel,” and this is said against the Jews who opposed him. A gnat wounds by buzzing, whereas a camel voluntarily bends down to receive burdens.

The Jews therefore strained out the gnat because they asked for the seditious [Col. 1166C] robber to be released; but they swallowed the camel because by shouting they attempted to destroy the one who had voluntarily descended to bear the burdens of our mortality.

## CHAPTER LXXX — “Woe to you, hypocrites” (Matt. XXIII, 27).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XVIII, no. 13; *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 35.) It is usually the concern of hypocrites both to conceal what they are and to make people know them as what they are not. They avoid being seen as they are and clothe themselves before people’s eyes in a kind of outward respectability of innocence.

Thus they are rightly rebuked in the Gospel by the voice of our Redeemer, when he says to them: “Woe to you, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but within are full of the bones of the dead and of every impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of plunder and iniquity.”

Truth [Col. 1166D] therefore rightly calls hypocrites whitewashed tombs, outwardly beautiful but inwardly full of the bones of the dead, because they conceal the evils of their vices within, while before human eyes they flatter themselves with the mere outward color of righteousness through the display of certain works.

By concealing their faults from people and displaying their virtues, they conceal what ought to bring them punishment and expose what might have brought them reward. For while they place their hidden evils before divine judgment and their righteous deeds before human eyes, the good they perform publicly is without a witness, while what they commit secretly is not without an eternal witness.

## CHAPTER LXXXI — “Likewise, concerning what was said above.”

(*Homily 9 on Ezekiel*, no. 33.) Concerning the saying, “Woe to you, hypocrites,” it must be understood that in Sacred Scripture “woe” is more often understood of eternal lamentation than of the present kind. Hence it is written: “Woe to the wicked in evil; the recompense of his hands will be made to him” (Isa. III, 11).

And blessed Job says: “If I am wicked, woe is me; but if I am righteous, I will not lift up my head, being filled [Col. 1167A] with affliction and misery” (Job X, 15). The affliction of the righteous is temporal. Therefore, by distinguishing the woe he mentioned from temporal affliction, he showed that the righteous have affliction and the wicked have woe.

Truth itself also says: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. XVIII, 7); and: “Woe to you who laugh, for you will mourn” (Luke VI, 25); and: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those nursing in those days” (Luke XXI, 23).

## CHAPTER LXXXII — “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. XXIV, 20).

(*Homily 12 on the Gospels*, no. 7.) We must carefully consider, dearly beloved brothers, lest our time pass away uselessly, and lest we seek to live for doing good only when we are already compelled to depart from the body. We must remember what Truth says: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath.”

For the commandment of the Law does not permit one to walk a long distance on the Sabbath. Winter also impedes walking, because the numbness of the cold constrains the steps of those who walk. Therefore [Col. 1167B] he says: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath,” as though he were openly saying: “See that you do not seek to flee from your sins at the time when it is no longer permitted to walk.”

That time, therefore, when flight is not permitted must now be considered, while it is permitted. That hour of our departure must always be kept in view; this admonition of the Redeemer must always be placed before the eyes of our mind.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII — “If they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the desert,’ do not go out” (Matt. XXIV, 26).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XX, nos. 20, 23.) Blessed Job speaks concerning the heretic: “They gnawed in the wilderness” (Job XXX, 3). What cannot be eaten is usually gnawed. Thus heretics, since they are not helped by heavenly grace but strive to understand Sacred Scripture by their own ability, handle it externally but do not reach its inner spiritual secrets. And because they are separated from the fellowship of the universal Church, they are said to gnaw not in just any place but in the wilderness.

Because false preachers would draw their followers into this wilderness, Truth warned far in advance, [Col. 1167C] saying: “If they say, ‘Behold, he is in the desert,’ do not go out.”

Moreover, heretics gather in secret assemblies among themselves, so that they may give reverence to their error—which they cannot obtain through reason—by means of concealment, and so that the word of depravity may appear more worthy of reverence to weak souls precisely because it is secret.

Hence, through Solomon, a woman representing heresy gives this advice: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Prov. IX, 17). And blessed Job says: “They lived in the deserts of the torrents and in the caves of the earth” (Job XXX, 6).

What else should we understand by “the caves of the earth” than the hidden preachings of heretics? Truth rejects these hidden teachings, saying: “If anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There he is,’ do not believe it.” And again: “If they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the desert,’ do not go out; ‘Behold, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it. For as lightning comes out from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.”

What is called “in the inner rooms” here is called “in the caves” in Job [Col. 1167D]. For heretics live in caves because they usually conceal their error through secret preachings, so that, by not revealing themselves to teachers and wiser people, they may draw the inexperienced to themselves all the more forcefully.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV — “As lightning comes out from the east and appears in the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. XXIV, 27).

(*Homily 2 on Ezekiel*, no. 16.) When the Lord comes to judgment, the shock of the strict judgment will disturb all the elements at once, and on that day the hearts of all who are then found in mortal flesh will be shaken with immense fear.

When what is written begins to be fulfilled—“The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken” (Matt. XXIV, 29)—what human mind will not fear the sentence of the eternal Judge?

Then all sins [Col. 1168A] return together before the eyes; everything done with delight is recalled to memory with fear; and the darkness of miserable thought will arise from the punishment of imminent condemnation. For then the darkness of blindness, arising from the memory of sins, weighs down the sense of the mind, since the reprobate are not permitted to behold the only-begotten Son of God in the form of his divinity.

“For they will see the one whom they pierced” (John X, 37). And: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Zech. XII, 10).

That fire of judgment, moreover, which will burn the aerial heaven and the earth will undoubtedly constrain sinners in the punishment of their condemnation. For “as lightning comes out from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man,” where no one at that time is permitted to hide from judgment in his mind, since he is penetrated by the Judge’s radiance.

Our Redeemer, presiding over the angels and archangels and all the powers, will then be seen in his terror, and the fire of judgment will serve him in vengeance against the reprobate. Hence the Psalmist says: “Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around [Col. 1168B] him” (Ps. XLIX, 3). Hence the apostle Peter says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief; on that day the heavens will pass away with great violence, and the elements will be dissolved by the heat of fire” (II Pet. III, 10).

## CHAPTER LXXXV — “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord appointed over his household?” (Matt. XXIV, 45).

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 39.) The loftier teachings should be concealed by preachers from the many who hear them and scarcely disclosed to the few. Hence Truth itself says: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord appointed over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?”

By the measure of wheat the appropriate measure of the word is expressed, lest something incapable of fitting within a narrow heart be given and spill outside. Hence Paul says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III, 1).

Hence it is said to blessed Job [Col. 1168C]: “Who gave the rooster understanding?” (Job XXXVIII, 36). For the holy preacher, crying out in this dark time, sings like a rooster in the night when he says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. XIII, 11); and again: “Awake, righteous people, and do not sin” (I Cor. XV, 34).

When a rooster is preparing to sing, it first shakes its wings and strikes itself, making itself more alert. Thus those who proclaim the words of holy preaching must first awaken through devotion to good action; first they must rouse themselves through lofty deeds, and then make others attentive to right living.

They must first strike themselves with the wings of their thoughts, correct through strict examination whatever useless thing they discover in themselves, and then, by speaking, shape the lives of others. Before the words of exhortation sound out, everything they are about to say must cry out through their deeds.

A rooster also habitually gives loud cries in the deeper hours of night; but when morning is already near, it produces small and faint voices. Likewise, [Col. 1168D] the person who preaches rightly cries out plainly to hearts that are still obscure, but discloses nothing of the hidden mysteries, so that they may hear more subtle things concerning heaven when they draw near to the light of truth.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI — “The foolish virgins did not take oil with them” (Matt. XXV, 3).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXIII, no. 17.) When holy preachers speak, they do not place the joy of their mind in the display of eloquent speech. Rather, they meditate on the good of knowledge in the secrecy of their heart, and they rejoice where they receive this knowledge, not where they are compelled to become known amid the snares of so many temptations.

When they make known the good they have received, they rejoice through the intervention of charity—not because of their own display, but because of the progress of their hearers.

The arrogant, however, when they receive knowledge, think they have received nothing if it happens that they possess it secretly. They place their joy nowhere except in the mouths [Col. 1169A] of people. Hence the foolish virgins are said not to have taken oil in their own vessels, because arrogant people, even when they perhaps restrain themselves from certain vices, cannot possess the good of glory within their consciences.

Paul had taken oil in his own vessel when he said: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I, 12). To carry an empty vessel, therefore, is to seek outwardly, with an empty heart within, the judgment of human favor; for while glory is sought externally, there is no oil within the vessel.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII — “Give us some of your oil” (Matt. XXV, 8).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book VIII, no. 74.) The hypocrite thinks of nothing else in all that he does except the glory of his reputation. He does not care where he is led afterward by his merit, but what is said about him meanwhile. Yet praise passes away with his life, and human favor fails at the judgment.

Hence the foolish virgins, who had not taken oil in their vessels—because they had glory in the voices [Col. 1169B] of others but not in their own consciences—were troubled by the Bridegroom’s arrival and said: “Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.”

To ask oil from one’s neighbors is to implore the glory of a good work from the testimony of another’s mouth. For an empty mind, when it discovers that it has retained nothing inwardly from all its labors, seeks testimony outwardly.

It is as though the foolish virgins openly said: “When you see us rejected without reward, speak in praise of our work about what you have seen.” But human testimony will provide no support to hypocrites at the judgment, because the praise they then demand as testimony they had already received beforehand as their reward.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII — “At last the other virgins also came, saying: ‘Lord, open to us’” (Matt. XXV, 11).

(*Homily 36 on the Gospels*, no. 10; *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 20.) The Lord calls us, dearly beloved brothers, to the joys of the heavenly kingdom: he calls us through himself, through angels, through the Fathers, through prophets, [Col. 1169C] through apostles, through pastors; often he calls us through miracles, often through scourges; sometimes through the prosperity of this world, sometimes through adversity.

Often, when certain people wish to advance and prosper here, they strive to grasp temporal glory, but the almighty God mercifully looks upon them and does not allow it, because the adversities of this world strike them in their carnal desires. They either waste away through prolonged illness, collapse under injuries, or are afflicted by serious losses. In the pain of the world they see that they ought not to have placed confidence in its pleasure; and, reproaching themselves for their desires, they turn their hearts to God.

Many, therefore, broken by the adversities of this world, return to the love of God who calls them and are corrected concerning the desires of the present life. Let no one despise God when he calls, lest, while refusing to hear and obey when called, he be unable to enter when he wishes.

Hear what Wisdom says through Solomon: “Then they will call upon me, and I will not answer; they will rise in the morning [Col. 1169D], and will not find me” (Prov. I, 28). Hence the foolish virgins, coming late, cry out: “Lord, Lord, open to us”; but then, when they seek entrance, it is said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you, I do not know you.”

Receive this exceedingly fearful sentence, dearly beloved brothers, with attentive ears, so that you may feel it less in the examination than you now hear it fearfully in preaching.

If you cannot leave all the things of this world—which has been granted to few—then hold the things of this world in such a way that you are not held by the world through them; let an earthly possession be possessed, not possess; let what you have be under the dominion of your mind, lest, if your mind is conquered by love of earthly things, it itself be possessed more by its possessions.

Concerning those who either desire more or are able to obtain everything they desire, hear what is written: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world [Col. 1170A] but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI, 26). It is as though Truth openly says: “What does it profit a person if he gathers everything outside himself, if he condemns only what he himself is?”

Let a temporal possession be on the journey, and let eternity be desired at the destination. Let earthly things serve our body without hindering our heart, lest they impede us from reaching the heavenly homeland to which the Lord calls us. Let nothing delay the desire of our mind; let the delight of no thing in this world entangle us.

If something good is loved, let the mind delight in better things—that is, in heavenly things. If evil is feared, let eternal evils be set before the soul, so that, when it sees there is something greater to love and something greater to fear, it may not cling here at all.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX — “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 12).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book VIII, no. 85, and book II, no. 6.) The heavenly dispensation grants hypocrites the good of action but denies them a share in the inheritance. It heaps upon them the gifts of working, yet does not recognize the desires of the one who works [Col. 1170B], because when the gift received is directed toward personal praise, the shadow of pride darkens it before the sight of the inner light.

When, through death, he has been separated from the favors of the present life, the inner Judge denies him and declares that he does not know him. For Truth justly rejects the life of the pretender and does not recognize the good things he did, since he did not produce them from a right intention.

Hence, when he comes to judgment, he will say to the foolish virgins: “Amen, amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” In them, while he considers the corruption of the mind, he also condemns the bodily incorruption.

For God’s not knowing is his rejection. Hence, concerning those whom he rejects, he will say at the end: “I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.”

Likewise, a truthful person who disdains to lapse into falsehood may be said, as it were, not to know how to lie—not because he would be unable to lie if he wished, but because, out of love for truth, he scorns to speak falsehood.

## CHAPTER XC — “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all his angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty; and all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, and he will place the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left” (Matt. XXV, 31–32).

[Col. 1170C]

(*Homily 19 on the Gospels*, no. 5.) How many of us, dearly beloved brothers, have gathered into the holy Church? We fill the walls of the Church, yet none of us can know who will be counted in that flock of God’s elect.

Behold, everyone’s voice cries out to Christ, but not everyone’s life cries out to him. Many follow God with their voices but flee from him in their conduct. Hence Paul says to Titus: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus I, 16). Hence James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James II, 20, 26).

Many, therefore, are mingled with the faithful through their confession, but because of their reprobate life they do not deserve to be counted among the lot of the faithful on the day of judgment.

This sheepfold of the holy Church receives goats together with lambs; but, as the Gospel testifies, when the Judge comes, he separates the good from the evil, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. For those who here serve the pleasures of their flesh cannot there be counted among the sheep. There the Judge separates from the lot of the humble those who here exalt themselves on the horns of pride. Those who here, placed within the heavenly faith, seek earthly things with their whole desire cannot receive the kingdom of heaven.

## CHAPTER XCI — “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXVI, nos. 50–51.) There are two divisions, namely, of the elect and of the reprobate, but within these two divisions there are two orders respectively. Some are judged and reign; others are not judged and reign; some are judged and perish; and others are not judged and perish.

Among the elect, those are judged and reign who wipe away the stains of their life with tears; who redeem former evils through subsequent deeds; and who cover before the eyes of the Judge [Col. 1171A] whatever unlawful things they once did by spreading almsgiving over them. To those standing at his right hand, the Judge who comes says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; I was naked, and you clothed me; I was sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me” (ibid., v. 35).

To these he first says: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

Others are not judged and reign: those who surpass the precepts of the Law through the perfection of their virtues, who are not content merely to fulfill what the divine Law commands all, but in a more excellent desire seek to offer more than they have been able to hear in the general commandments. To them the Lord’s voice says: “You who have left everything and followed me, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28).

The prophet also speaks of them: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. III, 14). And Solomon, speaking of the Bridegroom of the holy Church, [Col. 1171B] adds: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. XXXI, 23).

These, therefore, at the final judgment are not judged and reign, because they come as judges together with their Creator. For, leaving everything, they carried out with ready devotion more than they had generally heard commanded.

By a special command, given to a few who are more perfect and not generally to all, the rich young man heard this: “Go, sell everything you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21). For if a general command bound everyone under this precept, it would certainly be sinful for us to possess anything of this world.

But one thing is what Sacred Scripture generally commands all; another is what it specially orders to the more perfect. These, therefore, are rightly not held under the general judgment who have surpassed the general commandments by their manner of life.

For just as those who, persuaded by unbelief, disdain to keep the Law [Col. 1171C] are not judged but perish, so those who, moved by devotion, advance even beyond the general precepts of God’s Law are not judged but reign.

Hence Paul, surpassing even the special precepts, demonstrated more by his actions than he had received by the instruction of permission. For although he had received permission to live from the Gospel while preaching the Gospel, he imparted the Gospel to his hearers and nevertheless refused to be supported by the Gospel’s resources.

It is therefore just that this person is not judged but reigns: he received the lesser thing to observe but discovered the greater thing by which to live.

## CHAPTER XCII — “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. XXV, 35).

## (Homily 23 on the Gospels, no. 2)

“Brothers most beloved, love hospitality; love works of charity. For this reason it is said through Paul: ‘Let brotherly charity remain among you, and do not forget hospitality; for through it some, having received angels as guests, pleased God’ (Heb. 13:1). Hence Peter says: ‘Be hospitable to one another without complaining’ (1 Pet. 4:9). Hence Truth itself says: ‘I was a stranger, and you welcomed me.’ Since, therefore, the Lord is received before the judgment through his members, when he comes to judgment he will acknowledge those who welcomed him, saying: ‘What you did for one of the least of my brothers, you did for me’ (Matt. 25:40).

“Consider, therefore, brothers, how great is the virtue of hospitality, and do not be slow to show hospitality. Strangers are not merely to be invited into lodging, but even drawn into it. Receive Christ at your tables, so that you may be worthy to be received by him at the eternal banquets. Offer hospitality now to Christ in the stranger, so that at the judgment he may not regard you as strangers, but receive you as his own into the kingdom.”

## CHAPTER 93.—“As long as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me” (Matt. 25:40).

### (Homily 40 on the Gospels, nos. 10 and 12)

“Before the future judgment, brothers most beloved, act diligently; seek intercessors for your sins; procure the poor as advocates for yourselves on the day of judgment. See: the poor present themselves insistently and need those things that, when you are already satisfied, fall daily from your table. See: those who will then come as intercessors for us are now asking us. Certainly, we ought to have been the ones asking, yet we are being asked. Consider whether we ought to refuse what is requested when those requesting it are our patrons.

“Do not, therefore, lose the times of mercy; do not disregard the remedies granted to you; before punishment, think about punishment. Whenever you see people cast down in this world—even if some aspects of their conduct appear blameworthy—do not despise them, because perhaps those whom weakness of character wounds are healed by the medicine of poverty. If they have anything deserving just reproach, turn it, if you wish, to the benefit of your reward, so that from their very faults the increase of your piety may be accumulated for you. In this way give both bread and instruction: bread for nourishment together with words of correction, so that the one who was seeking one kind of nourishment may receive two from you, being satisfied outwardly with food and inwardly with speech.

“Therefore, when a poor person is seen to be blameworthy, he should be admonished but not despised; if he has nothing deserving reproach, he should be honored most highly as an intercessor. But see: you behold many whose merit you do not know. Honor, therefore, all whom you see to be poor, and regard those whom you see despised outwardly by the world as friends of God inwardly. Share with them what you possess, so that one day they may deign to share with you what they possess.

“Consider what is said by the mouth of the teacher of the nations: ‘At the present time, let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may also be the provision for your need’ (2 Cor. 8:14). Consider what Truth itself says: ‘As long as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me.’ You must therefore never be slow to give, since what you extend to one lying on the ground, you give to the One seated in heaven.”

## CHAPTER 94.—“Then he will say to those who are on his left: Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41).

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 26, no. 51)

“The party of the reprobate contains two orders. Some are judged and perish; others are not judged and perish. Those are judged and perish to whom the Lord’s voice says in condemnation: ‘I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.’ To them it is said beforehand: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.’

“Others are not judged at the final judgment, but perish. Concerning them the Prophet says: ‘The impious do not rise in the judgment’ (Ps. 1:5); and concerning them it is said: ‘Whoever does not believe has already been judged’ (John 3:18); and concerning them Paul says: ‘Those who sinned without the law will also perish without the law’ (Rom. 2:12).

“Indeed, all unbelievers will rise, but for punishment, not for judgment; for their case is not then examined, since they come into the sight of the strict Judge already bearing the condemnation of their unbelief. Those who retain the profession of faith but do not possess the works of that profession are rebuked and perish. But those who have held neither the sacraments of faith nor its profession do not hear the Judge’s reprimand in the final examination, because, already condemned by the darkness of their unbelief, they are not deemed worthy to be rebuked by the reproach of the one whom they despised.

“Only those hear the Judge’s words who retained at least the words of his faith. These, in their condemnation, do not hear the words of the eternal Judge, because they were unwilling even in words to preserve reverence for him. The former perish under the law, because, placed under the law, they sinned; to the latter, in their destruction, nothing is said from the law, because they made no attempt to possess anything belonging to the law.

“For a ruler governing an earthly commonwealth punishes differently a citizen who commits an offense within it and an enemy who rebels from outside. Against the citizen he applies his laws and condemns him under the words of a legal indictment. Against the enemy, however, he wages war, deploys instruments of destruction, and inflicts punishments worthy of his wickedness; he does not inquire what the law has to say about the enemy’s wrongdoing. For one who could never be held by the law need not be put to death by the law.

“So, at the final judgment, the legal indictment strikes the person who turned aside in action from what he held in profession, while the one who is not held by the law of faith is destroyed without the indictment of judgment.”

## CHAPTER 95.—“Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41).

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 33, no. 37)

“On the day of the final judgment, when the eternal Judge appears in terror, when legions of angels stand by, when the entire ministry of the heavenly powers is in attendance, and all the elect have been brought to this spectacle, the ancient enemy, the devil, will be led forth captive into the midst. Together with his body—that is, with all the reprobate—he will be consigned to the fires of eternal Gehenna, when it is said: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.’

“What a spectacle that will be, when this most savage beast is displayed before the eyes of the elect—the beast that, if it were seen, could have terrified them greatly during this time of warfare! But by the hidden and wondrous counsel of God it is brought about that now, by his grace, it is conquered by those who fight without seeing it, and then it is seen by the rejoicing victors already captive.

“Then the righteous will fully recognize how much they are indebted to divine assistance, when they see how powerful a beast they, though weak, have now conquered; in the savagery of their enemy they will perceive how much they owe to the grace of their protector. For our soldiers return from this battle then, bearing the trophies of their virtues; and when, having received their bodies, they obtain entry into the heavenly kingdom at that judgment, they first behold the immense powers of this ancient serpent, lest they regard as insignificant what they escaped.

“And before all who see it, it will be hurled down, because the sight of its death then brings joy, whereas its life, endured now, daily wages war upon the righteous amid sufferings.”

## CHAPTER 96.—“I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” etc. (Matt. 25:35).

### (Pastoral Rule, part 3, chapter 20)

“All who are still intent on seizing what belongs to others ought carefully to hear what the Lord says to the reprobate in the judgment. For he says: ‘I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink,’ and so forth. He also says beforehand: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.’

“See: they do not hear that they committed robberies or any other acts of violence, and yet they are handed over to the eternal fires of Gehenna. From this, therefore, it must be inferred how severe a condemnation awaits those who seize what belongs to others, if such punishment strikes those who indiscreetly kept what was their own. Let them consider by what guilt the stolen property binds them, if property not given over subjects a person to such punishment. Let them consider what the injustice inflicted deserves, if kindness not shown is worthy of so great a blow.”

## CHAPTER 97.—“The impious will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46).

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 34, nos. 35–37)

“There are many who neglect to put an end to their sins because they suppose that the judgments to come upon them will one day have an end. To them we briefly reply: if the punishments of the reprobate are someday to end, then the joys of the blessed must also someday end. For Truth itself says: ‘These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.’ If, therefore, what he threatened is not true, neither is what he promised true.

“But they say: ‘He threatened sinners with eternal punishment in order to restrain them from committing sins, because he ought to threaten his creature with eternal punishments, not inflict them.’ We answer them more briefly: if he made a false threat in order to correct them from injustice, he also made a false promise in order to urge them toward justice. Who could tolerate the madness of those who, by asserting that the punishments of the reprobate will end according to his promises, also confuse the rewards and recompenses of the elect by that assertion? Who could tolerate the madness of those who try to establish that what Truth threatened concerning the eternal fire is not true? While they strive to proclaim God merciful, they do not fear declaring him deceitful.

“But they say: ‘A finite fault ought not to be punished without end. Almighty God is just, surely, and what was not committed as an eternal sin ought not to be punished with eternal torment.’ We answer them more briefly that they would speak rightly if the just and strict Judge, when he comes, weighed not the hearts of human beings but their actions.

“For the wicked sinned with an end because they lived with an end; they would have wished to live without end, so that they might have been able to remain in their iniquities without end. For they desire sinning more than living, and therefore wish always to live here, so that they may never cease sinning while they live. It belongs, therefore, to the justice of the strict Judge that those should never be without punishment whose minds in this life never wished to be without sin; and no limit to vengeance should be granted to the wicked, because, for as long as he had the power, he did not wish to have an end to his crime.

“But they say: ‘No just person feeds on cruelty, and a delinquent servant is ordered by a just master to be beaten precisely so that he may be corrected from wickedness. He is therefore beaten for a purpose, since his master does not delight in his sufferings. To what end, then, will the wicked, handed over to the fires of Gehenna, burn forever? And since it is certain that the merciful and almighty God does not feed on the torments of the wicked, why are the wretched tormented if they are not purified?’

“We answer them more briefly that almighty God, who is merciful, does not feed on the torment of the wretched; but because he is just, he is never appeased by vengeance against the wicked. All the wicked, therefore, are punished with eternal punishment—and indeed by their own wickedness—yet they burn for a purpose: namely, so that all the righteous may see in God the joys they receive and may behold in these people the punishments they escaped. Thus they may recognize themselves as eternal debtors to divine grace all the more deeply because they see eternally punished the evils they were able to avoid with his help.”

## CHAPTER 98.—“My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39).

[Col. 1174C]

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 12, no. 16)

“Righteous men often present as though arising from doubt something that they themselves know to be certain and firm, in order to express the words of the weak through themselves. Yet again, by a strong declaration, they wholly contradict the doubt of the weak, so that through the fact that they appear to speak doubtfully they may accommodate themselves somewhat to the weak, while through the certainty of their statement they draw the doubtful minds of the weak toward firmness.

“In doing this they follow the example of our Head. As the Lord approached his passion, he took upon himself the voice of the weak, saying: ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.’ He accepted their fear in order to draw it away. Then again, showing the force of strength through obedience, he said: ‘Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.’ Thus, when what we do not wish to happen is imminent, we should ask in weakness that it may not happen, so that through strength we may be ready for the will of our Creator to be done even against our will.

“Following this example, the words of weakness must sometimes be taken up by the strong, so that afterward, through their strong declarations, the hearts of the weak may be strengthened all the more.”

## CHAPTER 99.—“Judas went away and hanged himself with a noose” (Matt. 27:5).

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 11, no. 12)

“Often some wish to escape from wicked acts, but because they are weighed down by the burden of those same acts, shut up in the prison of evil habit, they cannot escape from themselves. Some, wishing to punish their own sins, turn what they think they are doing rightly into even graver sins. Thus, in a pitiable way, what they suppose to be an escape becomes for them a confinement.

“So it was with the reprobate Judas: when he inflicted death upon himself because of his sin, he reached the punishments of eternal death, and repented of his sin more disastrously than he had committed it.”

## CHAPTER 100.—“My wife has suffered many things today in a dream because of him” (Matt. 27:19).

[Col. 1175A]

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 33, no. 31)

“Although the ancient enemy himself had confessed that the Lord Jesus Christ was the Son of God, he nevertheless believed that he would die as a mere human being, and therefore stirred up the minds of the persecuting Jews to bring about his death. Yet at the very time of the betrayal he is understood to have recognized, though late, that he himself would be punished by that death. Hence he terrified Pilate’s wife through dreams, so that her husband might cease persecuting the just man.

“But what had been arranged by an inward dispensation could not be thwarted by any scheme. For it was fitting that the death of the just man, dying unjustly, should release the death of sinners, who were dying justly.”

## CHAPTER 101.—“And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom, and the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened” (Matt. 27:51).

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 30, nos. 66–67)

“The incarnate Lord, who in the form of God is equal to the Father, in the form of a servant was made less than the Father, because he was also made less than himself. By assuming our nature, he could in no way be held under the yoke of iniquity. Although the stain of our sin did not touch him, the suffering of our mortality nevertheless bound him.

“For he had, as it were, certain bonds consisting of the things that we suffer deservedly because of wickedness—namely, the weaknesses of our mortality. He freely wished to be bound by these even unto death, and he wonderfully loosed them through the resurrection. To hunger, thirst, grow weary, be seized, scourged, crucified: these were bonds of our mortality.

“But when, death having been completed, the veil of the temple was torn, the rocks were split, the tombs were opened, and the prison-bars of hell were exposed, what else is shown by so many signs of such power except that the bonds of our weakness were being loosed? The one who had come to assume the form of a servant was, in that very form of a servant, freed from the bonds of hell and returned even to heaven with his members liberated.

“Concerning these bonds Peter the apostle bears witness, saying: ‘God raised him up, having loosed the pains of hell, since it was impossible for him to be held by it’ (Acts 2:24). His bonds, therefore, were loosed when the weaknesses of his passion were changed into the glory of the resurrection.”

## CHAPTER 102.—“And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose” (Matt. 27:52).

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 14, nos. 69–70; Homily 21 on the Gospels, no. 6)

“We possess hope of our resurrection when we consider the glory of our Head. Yet lest anyone perhaps say, even in silent thought, that he rose from death for this reason: because, being one and the same God and man, he overcame through divinity the death he suffered through humanity, whereas we, who are merely human beings, cannot rise from the condemnation of death—at the time of his resurrection the bodies of many saints also rose. In this way he displayed an example to us in himself and strengthened us through the resurrection of others who were like us in their pure humanity.

“Thus, when a human being despairs of receiving in himself what God made man displayed in himself, he may presume that what he recognizes as having occurred in those whom he does not doubt were merely human beings can also occur in him.

“There are, however, some who, observing that the spirit is separated from the flesh, that the flesh decays, that decay is reduced to dust, and that dust is dispersed into the elements so completely that it is no longer visible to human eyes, despair that resurrection can occur. When they look upon dry bones, they doubt that these can again be clothed with flesh and return to life. If they do not hold the faith of the resurrection through obedience, they ought certainly to hold it through reason.

“For what does the world imitate daily in its elements except our resurrection? At every moment the temporal light itself, as it were, dies when, as the darkness of night comes upon it, what was visible is withdrawn; and it rises again, as though daily, when the light taken from our eyes is restored after night has been suppressed.

“Through the passing moments of time we also see trees lose the greenness of their leaves and cease producing fruit after their abundance has been given. Then suddenly, as though a kind of resurrection were coming from a drying tree, we see leaves burst forth, fruits grow large, and the whole tree be clothed again in renewed beauty.

“We constantly see the small seeds of trees entrusted to the moisture of the earth, and not long afterward we see great trees rise from them, producing leaves and fruit. Let us consider, therefore, the small seed of any tree that is cast into the ground so that a tree may be produced from it, and let us comprehend, if we can, where within that seed’s great smallness such an immense tree lay hidden—the wood, the bark, the green of the leaves, the abundance of the fruit. Was anything of this kind visible in the seed when it was cast into the ground?

“And yet, while the hidden Maker of all things wondrously orders everything, the roughness of the bark lay hidden in the softness of the seed, the strength of its firmness was concealed in its tenderness, and the abundance of fruitfulness lay in its dryness. What wonder, then, if he reforms the tiniest dust—reduced by the elements beyond the sight of our eyes—into a human being when he wills, since he restores immense trees from the tiniest seeds?

“Since, therefore, we were created rational, we ought to gather the hope of our resurrection from the very appearance and contemplation of things. But because the sense of reason has grown sluggish in us, the grace of the Redeemer came to us as an example. Our Creator came, accepted death, and displayed resurrection, so that we who are unwilling to hold the hope of resurrection through reason might hold it through his help and example.

“Blessed Job also spoke of the resurrection: ‘I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth.’ Therefore, whoever despairs that the power of resurrection can occur in him should be ashamed before the words of a faithful man who lived among the Gentiles, and should consider with what weight of punishment he ought to be struck if he still does not believe in his own resurrection, having already learned that the Lord’s resurrection has occurred—if Job, who still hoped that the Lord Jesus’ resurrection would take place, believed that his own would occur.

[Col. 1176C]

“To instruct our ignorance, therefore, and strengthen our weakness, our Lord wished the example of his resurrection to be sufficient for us. He alone died at that time, yet he did not rise alone, since, as was written above: ‘Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose.’

“All arguments for unbelief have therefore been removed. Let no one say that a human being ought not to hope for what the God-man displayed in his flesh. Behold: we know that those whom we do not doubt were merely human beings rose together with the God-man. If, therefore, we are members of our Redeemer, let us presume in ourselves what is known to have occurred in the Head. If we greatly abase ourselves, we ought to hope that we, the lowest members, will possess in ourselves what we have heard concerning his higher members.”

## CHAPTER 103.—“His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow” (Matt. 28:3).

### (Homily 21 on the Gospels, no. 3)

“Matthew the evangelist, describing the angel who appeared to the women as they came to the tomb, says: ‘His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing like snow.’

“In lightning there is the terror of fear; in snow there is the soothing quality of whiteness. Since almighty God is both terrifying to sinners and gentle toward the righteous, rightly the angel who bears witness to his resurrection is shown both in the lightning of his face and in the whiteness of his clothing, so that by his very appearance he might terrify the reprobate and comfort the godly.

“Rightly also did the angel appear covered in snowy garments, because he announced the joys of our celebration. The whiteness of his clothing announces the splendor of our solemnity—or shall we say, his? But, to confess more truly, let us say both his and ours. The resurrection of our Redeemer was our celebration, because it restored us to immortality; and it was the celebration of the angels, because by recalling us to heavenly things it filled their number.

“Thus, at his own celebration and ours, the angel appeared in snowy garments, because while through the Lord’s resurrection we are restored to the things above, the losses of the heavenly homeland are repaired.”

## CHAPTER 104.—“But the angel answered and said to the women: Do not be afraid. For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said” (Matt. 28:5–6).

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 14, nos. 67–68)

“It is pleasing, brothers most beloved, to consider the depths of compassion that our Lord had toward us, and the glory of the resurrection that the angel announced to the women as having taken place. After creating all things, our Creator and Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, appeared incarnate among us in order to redeem us from captivity to the devil, and by his passion freed us from everlasting death.

“For although he was crucified through weakness, ‘he lives by the power of God’ (2 Cor. 13:4). He wished to rise from death quickly, lest, if resurrection were delayed in him, hope in us should altogether fail. He wished to rise quickly from death, lest our soul should remain for long in the death of unbelief. He underwent death temporarily—that is, for three days—and he by no means remained in that death, as we do, until the end of the age.

“The Lord’s body lives after death, but the glory of the resurrection of our bodies is still delayed until the end of the world. Through the death of the flesh we remain in the dust until the end of the world; but he flourished on the third day from the dryness of death, and displayed the power of his divinity through the renewal of his flesh.

“Let us therefore know that our Lord Jesus Christ was scourged, mocked, struck with blows, crowned with a crown of thorns, insulted with spittle, crucified, and put to death. But let us believe with certain faith, proclaim with free voice, that the very one who fell among the hands of the ungodly lives after death, and through his resurrection let us have confidence concerning the resurrection of our flesh.

“For our Lord Jesus Christ, who, rising from the dead, no longer dies and over whom death will no longer rule, promised us that the resurrection which he displayed in himself, our Head, he would one day bring about also in us, who belong to him. ‘For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.’”

# BOOK TWO  
## Exposition of the Gospel according to Mark

[Col. 1177]

## CHAPTER 1.—“John was in the wilderness, baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins; and all the region of Judea and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins. And John was clothed in camel’s hair” (Mark 1:4–6).

[Col. 1177B]

### (Homily 40 on the Gospels, no. 3)

“There are some who do not think that the adornment of delicate and costly clothing is a sin. But if it were not a fault, the word of God would never so carefully state that the rich man who was tormented in hell had been clothed in fine linen and purple. No one seeks costly clothing except for empty glory—that is, so that he may appear more honorable than others. The fact itself bears witness that more expensive clothing is sought solely for empty glory: no one wishes to be clothed in costly garments where he cannot be seen by others.

“We can also gather this fault more clearly from the opposite case, because, if the lowliness of cheap clothing were not a virtue, the evangelist would not carefully say of John the Baptist: ‘He was clothed in camel’s hair.’”

## CHAPTER 2.—“And he ate locusts and wild honey” (Mark 1:6).

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 31, no. 45)

“Under the name of locusts, sometimes the Jewish people are signified, sometimes the converted Gentiles, sometimes the tongue of flatterers, and sometimes, by comparison, the Lord’s resurrection or the life of preachers.

“That locusts signify the Jewish people is indicated by John’s life, of whom it is written: ‘He ate locusts and wild honey.’ John proclaims through the kind of food even the one whom he announces with prophetic authority. In himself he represented the Lord whose coming he preceded.

“When he came for our redemption, because he took up the sweetness of the unfruitful Gentiles, he ate wild honey. But because he converted part of the Jewish people in his own body, he took locusts as food. Locusts signify that people because they give sudden leaps but immediately fall back to the ground.

“They gave leaps when they promised that they would fulfill the Lord’s commandments; but they quickly fell to the ground when, through evil works, they denied that they had heard them. Let us observe in them a certain locust-like leap: ‘All the words that the Lord has spoken we will hear and do’ (Exod. 24:3). Let us also see how quickly they fall to the ground: ‘Would that we had died in Egypt, and not in this vast wilderness! Would that we perish, and that the Lord not bring us into this land!’ (Num. 14:2–3).

“They were therefore locusts, because they had a leap in their speech and a fall in their actions.”

## CHAPTER 3.—“Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee, and was baptized by John in the Jordan. And immediately, as he came up from the water, he saw the heavens opened and the Spirit descending upon him like a dove and remaining in him” (Mark 1:9–10).

[Col. 1178B]

### (Homily 2 on Ezekiel, no. 5; Homily 30 on the Gospels, nos. 5–6)

“In the thirtieth year of his life the Lord came to the River Jordan; and there the heavens were opened, because the Spirit descended in the form of a dove. The Holy Spirit wished to be shown in the form of a dove because he makes all whom he fills simple in purity and peaceful through the gentleness of meekness.

“For this reason he also appeared in our Redeemer, the Mediator between God and human beings, through a dove, because the only-begotten Son is the Judge of the human race. But who could endure his justice if, before gathering us through gentleness, he had wished to examine our sins through the zeal of righteousness?

“Therefore, having become human for human beings, he showed himself gentle toward human beings, and our Judge tempered his severity. He did not wish to strike sinners, but to gather them; he first wished to correct them gently, so that afterward he might have people whom he could save in judgment.

“The Spirit ought therefore to appear over him in the form of a dove, because he did not come to strike sins already through zeal, but still to tolerate them by sparing them through gentleness.

“The Holy Spirit comes in all the faithful, but in Jesus alone he remains in a singular way, because Christ Jesus, the Mediator between God and human beings, possesses him present in all things, always and continually, since the same Spirit proceeds from him according to substance. In him, therefore, the Spirit remains who alone can do all things and always can do them, and he never abandons the humanity from whose divinity he proceeds, from whom by nature he never departs.”

## CHAPTER 4.—“And a voice came from heaven: You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Mark 1:11).

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 28, no. 8; Homily 8 on Ezekiel, no. 21)

“Sometimes God speaks to heavenly beings through angels, as it is written concerning the baptized Lord: ‘A voice sounded from heaven, saying: You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.’ In another evangelist it is said in this way: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’

“What does it mean that the Father speaks of the Son, saying: ‘In whom I am well pleased’? Everyone who corrects through repentance something he has done indicates, by the very fact that he repents, that he displeased himself when he did it. And because almighty Father, as all could understand, spoke in human fashion concerning sinners, saying: ‘It repents me that I made human beings upon the earth’ (Gen. 6:6), he was, as it were, displeased with himself in the sinners whom he had created.

“But in our Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, he alone was well pleased, because he did not repent of having created him as a human being among human beings, in whom he found absolutely no sin. As it is said of him through the Psalmist: ‘The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’ (Ps. 110:4).

“The Father was therefore well pleased in our Redeemer alone, because in him alone he found no fault by which he might, as through repentance, reproach himself.”

## CHAPTER 5.—“Jesus was teaching as one having authority” (Mark 1:22).

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 23, nos. 24–25)

“Teachers rightly teach that what is done comes before what is said. For confidence in teaching is withdrawn when conscience restrains the tongue. Hence it is also written concerning the Lord: ‘He was teaching as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees.’

“He alone, singularly and supremely, spoke from the authority of goodness, because he committed no act arising from sinful weakness. From the power of his divinity he possessed what he supplied to us through the innocence of his humanity.

“We, because we are weak human beings, when we speak to human beings about God, ought first to remember what we are, so that from our own weakness we may consider by what method of teaching we should care for our weak brothers. Let us therefore consider whether we are now like those whom we correct, or whether we once were like them, even if by the working of divine grace we are no longer so. Thus we shall correct with a humble heart all the more gently, the more truly we recognize ourselves in those whom we amend.

“But if we are neither now nor ever were like those whom we still strive to correct, let our heart beware that it does not become proud and fall more disastrously because of that very innocence. In those whose evils we correct, let us bring their other good qualities back before our eyes. If they have none at all, let us turn to the hidden judgments of God. For just as we received the good we possess without any merits of our own, so grace can also pour the power of heaven into them, so that, later awakened, they may even surpass the good things we received earlier.

“For who would have believed that Saul would surpass the stoned Stephen in the merit of apostleship, when he guarded the garments of those who stoned him at Stephen’s death? The heart must first be humbled by these thoughts, and only then should it rebuke the wickedness of sinners.”

## CHAPTER 6.—“What have we to do with you, Son of God? We know who you are, the Holy One of God” (Mark 1:24).

### (Commentary on Blessed Job, book 33, no. 14; book 3, no. 28)

“The ancient enemy knew that the incarnate Son of God had come, but he did not know the order of our redemption. He knew that the Son of God had become incarnate for our redemption, but he did not know at all that the same Redeemer would transform him by dying.

“He also saw before him the one whom, recognizing, he confessed, and whom, confessing, he feared, saying: ‘What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torture us?’ He therefore first recognized whom he should fear, yet afterward he did not fear when, seeing him as it were as his own food, he desired the death of his flesh.

“Our Lord, coming for the redemption of the human race, assumed a body so that the ancient enemy might desire the death of the flesh in him as though it were his own food. When he unjustly desired that death in him, he lost us, whom he had held as though justly.

“Before the malignant spirit desired our Redeemer through death, when he saw him shining with miracles, he cried out, saying: ‘We know who you are, the Holy One of God.’ In saying this, he fears and trembles as he recognizes the Son of God; yet, not understanding the force of heavenly mercy, he sometimes, when he considers him subject to suffering, supposes him to be merely human.”

## CHAPTER 7.—“And Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, saying: Be silent, and come out of the man. And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him” (Mark 1:25–26).

*(Homily 12 on Ezekiel, no. 24.)* When someone begins to despise earthly things and love heavenly things, the ancient [Col. 1180A] adversary inflicts upon him sharper temptations than he was accustomed to do, so that he often tests a resisting soul in a way he had never tested it before, when he possessed it. Hence the demoniac who is healed by the Lord is torn by the departing demon, as it is written: “And crying out and tearing him violently, he went out from him.” For what does it mean that the ancient enemy, when abandoning the possessed man whom he had not torn while possessing him, tore him upon leaving, except that often, when he is driven from the heart, he generates in it sharper temptations than he had previously stirred up when he possessed it undisturbed? Hence it is written: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Eccles. II, 1).

## Chapter VIII

“Rise, take up your pallet” (Mark II, 9).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIII, no. 46; Homily 12 on Ezekiel, no. 11.)* In Holy Scripture, a bed or pallet sometimes signifies carnal pleasure, sometimes repose in [Col. 1180B] good works, and sometimes temporal rest. For what does the Lord’s saying in the Gospel to a certain man who had been healed—“Rise, take up your pallet, and go to your house”—signify, except that the pallet represents carnal pleasure? He is indeed commanded, once healed, to carry what he had lain upon when ill, because everyone who still takes pleasure in vices lies sick in the pleasures of the flesh. But the healed man carries it where he had lain, because, rescued by divine assistance, he afterward endures the insults of that same flesh from whose desires he had previously derived repose.

Thus, by the pallet, in which the flesh finds rest, the flesh itself is signified; by the house, however, conscience is represented. And because, dead in mind, we lie in vices and rest in the delight of the flesh, we are carried as infirm persons upon a bed. But when we have been healed in mind, so that we now resist the vices that assail us, it is necessary for us to endure in our flesh the insults of temptations. Therefore the sick man restored to health is commanded: “Take up your pallet,” that is, carry the bed upon which you were carried [Col. 1180C], because each person who has been healed must carry the insult of the flesh in which he had previously lain sick.

What, then, does it mean to say, “Take up your pallet and go to your house,” except: Carry the temptations of the flesh in which you have hitherto lain, and return to your conscience, so that you may see what you have done? It is as if he said: After the external miracle, return to your mind, and consider what sort of person you ought to present yourself inwardly to God; and after the forgiveness of sins, beware lest you again commit what ought justly to be punished.

## Chapter IX

“The Lord Jesus made the twelve to be with him” (Mark III, 14).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXV, no. 15.)* Among the wise men of this age, the number seven is regarded as perfect according to a certain rationale of its own, because it is completed from the first even number and the first odd number. The first odd number is three, and the first even number is four. Seven consists of these two numbers; multiplied by its own parts, it rises to twelve. For whether we multiply three [Col. 1180D] by four or four by three, we arrive at twelve.

But because, by heavenly gift, we have received the principles of Truth, we trample upon and despise these notions from the height of a firm knowledge, holding without doubt this unwavering faith: those whom the sevenfold Spirit of grace has filled, he perfects, granting them not only knowledge of the Trinity but also the activity of the four virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The Spirit is likewise increased, in a manner of speaking, by its own parts in those whom it enters: through knowledge of the Trinity, the activity of the four virtues is received, and through the activity of the four virtues one reaches the manifest vision of the Trinity.

For us, therefore, the number seven is also perfect, but in a very different way, because it rises fully, not emptily, to twelve: through faith it produces works, and again through works it perfects faith. The holy apostles, who were to be filled with the spirit of sevenfold grace, were chosen as twelve, because they were sent to make known the Trinity, which is God, in the four quarters of the world. Twelve, therefore, were chosen [Col. 1181A], so that the reason for this number itself might also make clear why they were to preach the highest Three through the four lower regions.

## Chapter X

“And he gave Simon the name Peter; and he called James the son of Zebedee and John, the brother of James, Boanerges, which is ‘sons of thunder’; and Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him” (Mark III, 15).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, no. 49.)* Sometimes the incarnate Lord himself is represented by thunder. Through the harmonious prophecy of the ancient Fathers, he was brought to our knowledge, as it were, from the collision of clouds. Appearing visibly among us, he thundered forth fearfully the things that were above us. Hence the holy apostles themselves, born from his grace, were called Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder.” At other times, thunder signifies his preaching itself, through which the terror of heavenly judgments is heard.

## Chapter XI

“He went out sowing to sow. And as he sowed, some fell beside the way, and the birds ate it” (Mark IV, 3).

[Col. 1181B]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX, no. 2.)* In Holy Scripture, birds are sometimes understood in an evil sense and sometimes in a good one, because they signify aerial powers, which are at times opposed to the efforts of the good. Hence Truth says that, when the seed fell beside the way, the birds came and ate it: for malignant spirits, besieging human minds and injecting harmful thoughts, tear the word of life from the memory.

## Chapter XII

“Another fell upon the ground, and when the sun had risen it withered” (Mark IV, 5).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIV, no. 25.)* In Holy Scripture, when the sun is used figuratively, it sometimes signifies persecution, as Truth says in the Gospel that the seed without roots withered when the sun rose. For the words of life, flourishing for a brief time in the hearts of earthly [Col. 1181C] people, dry up when the heat of persecution comes upon them. At other times, the sun signifies understanding and the discernment of the wise, as is said by comparison with Solomon: “The wise man remains like the sun; the fool changes like the moon” (Eccles. XXVII, 12).

## Chapter XIII

“And another fell among thorns, and the thorns choked it” (Mark IV, 7).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VII, no. 39; Homily 15 on the Gospels, no. 1.)* There are many who no longer desire what belongs to others and who, having begun to love tranquility, withdraw from the quarrels of this world. They thirst to be instructed in the sacred writings and long to devote themselves to heavenly contemplation; yet they do not abandon the care of household affairs with complete freedom of spirit. While they often serve these affairs licitly, they also become entangled in the illicit conflicts of this world.

When they eagerly desire to hold on to earthly possessions, they abandon the repose of heart they had sought. And when a perishable substance [Col. 1181D] is protected by continual provision, the word of divine knowledge conceived in the mind is scattered, because, in accordance with Truth’s saying, the thorns choke the seed that has sprung up: worldly anxieties remove the word of God from the memory. Truth says: “The anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.” Riches are deceitful because they cannot remain with us for long. They are deceitful because they do not dispel the poverty of our mind. Only those riches are true that make us rich in virtues.

## Chapter XIV

“And another fell on good soil and produced fruit, thirtyfold” (Mark IV, 8).

*(Homily 17 on Ezekiel, no. 12.)* The number six is said to be perfect because on the sixth day God completed all his works. Since he gave the sinner the Law, which was written in ten commandments, and six multiplied by ten rises to sixty, the perfection of good works is rightly signified by [Col. 1182A] sixty.

The Lord also plainly indicates this in the Gospel. When explaining the parable of the sower, he said: “Another fell on good soil and produced fruit, growing and increasing, and yielded one thirtyfold, one sixtyfold, and one a hundredfold.” Good soil produces thirtyfold fruit when the mind conceives the perfection of faith, which is in the Trinity. It produces sixtyfold when it brings forth the perfected works of a good life. It produces a hundredfold when it advances to contemplation of eternal life.

Our left hand is the present life, while the right is the life to come. The contemplation of eternal life is rightly signified by the number one hundred, because when, after thirty and sixty, we reach the number one hundred, that same number passes over to the right. Faith and action are still on the left, because while we remain here, we believe what we do not see and work so that we may see. But when the mind raises itself into contemplation of eternal life, the reckoning reaches, as it were, the right hand.

## Chapter XV

“Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Mark IV, 9).

[Col. 1182B]

*(Homily 14 on Ezekiel, no. 2.)* We must understand that the eyes and ears of the body are present even in those who are carnal, and that they are used for things perceived bodily. But the eyes and ears of the heart belong only to spiritual people: they see invisible things through understanding and hear the praise of God without sound.

The almighty God was seeking these ears when he said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” For who could then have been present among that people without bodily ears? But when it is said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” it is plainly shown that he was seeking those ears which not everyone could possess.

## Chapter XVI

“So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the ground, and so forth” (Mark IV, 26).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXII, no. 46; Homily 15 on Ezekiel, nos. 5–6.)* Each of the elect, beginning first from the tenderness of his early stage [Col. 1182C], later grows strong and vigorous. The Lord plainly demonstrates this in the Gospel under the image of the harvest, saying: “So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the ground, and sleep, and rise night and day, and the seed should germinate and grow while he does not know it.” Announcing the growth of this seed, he adds: “For the earth produces fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.”

He also sets forth the completion of this growth, saying: “And when it has produced the fruit, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” Behold, through the voice of Truth, the stages of merit’s growth are distinguished by the qualities of the crops. He says: “First the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.”

A man casts seed into the ground when he implants a good intention in his heart. After he has cast the seed, he sleeps, because he rests in the hope of good work. He rises night and day because he advances amid adversity and prosperity. The seed germinates and grows while he does not know it, because, while he is still [Col. 1182D] unable to measure his growth, the virtue once conceived is led toward maturity.

The earth produces fruit of itself because, through grace coming beforehand, the human mind rises spontaneously toward the advancement of good work. Yet this same earth first produces the blade, then the ear, and then the full grain in the ear. To produce the blade is still to possess the tender beginning of goodness. The blade reaches the ear when the virtue conceived in the mind draws itself onward toward the advancement of good work. It produces full grain in the ear when virtue has advanced so far that it is capable of being a strong and perfect work.

But “when it has produced the fruit, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” For the almighty God, once the fruit has been produced, sends the sickle and cuts down his harvest: when he has brought each person to perfect works, he cuts short that person’s temporal life by a sentence sent forth, so that he may bring his grain to the heavenly storehouses.

When, therefore, we conceive good desires, we cast seed into the ground [Col. 1183A]. When we begin to do what is right, we are the blade. When we grow toward the advancement of good work, we reach the ear. When we are made firm in the perfection of that work, we produce full grain in the ear.

Peter was a blade when, at the time of the Passion, following the Lord out of love, he feared confessing him before the voice of a servant girl. There was already greenness in his mind, because he believed in the Redeemer of all; but, still very pliable, he was trampled underfoot by fear. He was already green through devotion, but still tender through weakness, when he was bent by the sudden breath of a single servant girl’s words.

He had already risen into the ear when he saw, at the angel’s announcement, alive in Galilee the one whom he had feared to confess as destined to die. But he had reached full grain in the ear when the Spirit came from above and strengthened his mind in love of him. He was so firmly established that, beaten by the strength of his persecutors, he despised them, freely preached his Redeemer amid scourging, and resisted the rulers who persecuted him [Col. 1183B], saying: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V, 29).

He was found to be full grain when he endured so many blows in the threshing of persecution and yet was in no way diminished like straw, but remained grain. Therefore no one who is still seen to be in the tender stage of a good purpose should be despised, because God’s grain begins with the blade in order to become grain. For a while, so to speak, the moisture of inward grace overflows in each soul, so that the blade may grow into a crop.

Let no one, therefore, despair of a neighbor when he still sees only the blade. The seeds of the crop are made firm as they rise from the leaves of the grasses, which gently bend here and there.

## Chapter XVII

“The kingdom of God is like a mustard seed, which a man took and cast into his garden, and it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of the air rested in its branches” (Mark IV, 31).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX, no. 3.)* He himself [Col. 1183C] is the mustard seed, who, planted in the burial place of the garden, rose as a great tree. He was a seed when he died, a tree when he rose again; a seed through the humility of the flesh, a tree through the power of majesty; a seed because “we saw him, and there was no appearance” (Isa. LIII, 2); a tree because he was “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3).

The branches of this tree are the holy preachers. Let us see how far they extend. For what is said of them? “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5). The birds rest in these branches because holy souls, lifting themselves above earthly thoughts on the wings of certain virtues, find relief from the weariness of this life in their words and consolations.

## Chapter XVIII

“If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine” (Mark V, 12).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXII, no. 50.)* Without the permission of almighty God, the evil spirit has no power against a human being, because, as the Gospel testifies, it is described as having been unable either to remain in [Col. 1183D] the possessed man or, without command, to presume again to invade brute animals.

The legion that held the man said to our Redeemer: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine.” He both expelled them from the man and permitted them to enter the swine and cast them into the abyss. From this it is gathered how weak our adversary is: if supreme power does not grant him permission, he cannot even rage against swine.

When, then, would he dare of his own accord to harm human beings made in the image of God, when it is clear that, without command, he does not even presume to touch swine? We must therefore willingly submit to the one to whom all adverse things are subjected in this life, so that we may be more powerful than our enemies to the degree that, through humility, we become one with the author of all things.

## Chapter XIX

“Return first to your house, and tell how great things the Lord has done for you” (Mark V, 19).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVI, no. 33, and book VI, no. [Col. 1184A] 60.)* It is one thing to know the Lord through faith and another through sight; one thing to find him through belief and another through contemplation. Consequently, all the elect who have known him by faith long also to see him by sight. They burn with love of him because they already taste the sweetness of his goodness in the very certainty of their faith.

But those who desire to hold the summit of contemplation must first exercise themselves in the field of action, because the time of action comes first and contemplation last. Therefore each perfected person must first train the mind in virtues and afterward hide these virtues in the repose of contemplation.

This is why, in the region of the Gerasenes, the man whom the legion of demons abandoned at the Lord’s command sat at the feet of his Savior, received the words of instruction, and desired both to leave his region and to be with the author of his salvation. Yet Truth itself, which had brought him salvation, said to him: “Return first to your house, and tell how great things the Lord has done for you” (ibid., 19).

A delay is imposed upon the one who loves, so that through the longing produced by delayed [Col. 1184B] love the merit of the reward may increase. The almighty God becomes sweet to us through miracles, yet remains hidden in his sublimity, so that by showing us certain things about himself he may kindle us with hidden inspiration in his love, while by concealing the glory of his majesty he may increase the power of his love through the heat of desire.

What, then, is signified by the house to which the healed man is commanded to return, except conscience, in which we dwell while examining what we do? “Return,” he is told, “to your house, and tell how great things the Lord has done”; that is, now secure from the vice of sin, return to your conscience and rouse yourself to proclaim.

For whenever we perceive even a little of divine contemplation, we no longer wish to return to human affairs and refuse to be burdened by the needs of our neighbors. We seek the repose of contemplation and love nothing except what refreshes us without labor. But Truth sends us, once healed, back to our house and commands us to relate what has happened to us, so that the mind [Col. 1184C] may first sweat in work and afterward be refreshed through contemplation.

## Chapter XX

“The crowds press and afflict you” (Mark V, 31).
