*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, no. 43; book III, no. 37.)* The carnal within Holy Church do not exhibit in their lives what they profess to hold, and they press upon the faith they claim to possess rather than honoring it, since they desire, under its name, to acquire their own profits rather than its profits.

The elect, however, while taking care to preserve the merit of faith through right works, draw near to knowledge of their author amid the tumult of the reprobate. This is well signified in the Gospel by the woman suffering from an issue of blood, who, although pressed by the crowd, touched the Lord alone.

When the Lord said of her, “Who touched me?” Peter answered by reasoning: “The crowds press and afflict you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” But he deserved to hear the reason for the true explanation when the Lord said to him: “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me.”

Behold, the crowds were pressing the Lord, yet only she touched [Col. 1184D] him who came to him humbly. For many even within Holy Church press upon the truth by acknowledging it, while they neglect to touch it by living well. They press and are far away, because they pursue divine knowledge in their professions but flee from it in their conduct. They press, I say, but are far away: they affirm the same faith in speech but contradict it in action.

Many therefore press the Lord, but one touches him, because the carnal within the Church press upon the one from whom they are far away, while only the truly humble adhere to him and touch him. The crowd presses because the multitude of the carnal is tolerated with greater difficulty the more it is admitted within. It presses but does not touch, because it is importunate in presence but absent in life.

The carnal, therefore, the more they are in the Church through the words of professed faith, the more gravely they oppress the good by their unreformed conduct. Sometimes they assail us with corrupt speech, and sometimes [Col. 1185A] they do not cease to offer examples of perversity through their wicked behavior alone. At times they persuade others to what they themselves hold; at other times, even if they do not persuade, they nevertheless do not cease to offer examples of iniquity.

Those, therefore, who entice us to evil either by words or by examples are truly our persecutors. From them we receive the struggles of temptation, struggles that we should at least overcome in our hearts.

## Chapter XXI

“Jesus raised the daughter of the ruler” (Mark V).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, no. 68.)* When Truth comes to the heart through the wonderful work of mercy, it first drives out from it the tumult of carnal thoughts and afterward arranges within it the gifts of the virtues.

The sacred history of the Gospel aptly suggests this to us. When the Lord was being led, at the invitation, to raise the ruler’s daughter, it immediately adds: “And when the crowd had been put out, he entered, took her by the hand, and the girl arose.”

The crowd is therefore cast outside so that the girl may be raised, because the soul that lies dead within does not rise unless the importunate multitude of worldly cares is first expelled from the more secret places of the heart. For while it scatters itself among innumerable thoughts of earthly desires, it cannot gather itself together for consideration [Col. 1185B] of its own condition.

## Chapter XXII

“Herod beheaded John the Baptist” (Mark VI).

*(Letter 64, book XI, in the response to inquiries; and in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIII, no. 41, and book III, no. 11; in Ezekiel, book II, Homily 3, no. 21.)* Union with a kinswoman was forbidden because, through the earlier union, she had become the flesh of his brother. For this reason John the Baptist was also beheaded and crowned with holy martyrdom.

He was not told to deny Christ, and yet he was killed for his confession. The reason is that our Lord Jesus Christ had said: “I am the Truth” (John XIV, 6). Since John was killed for the truth, he plainly shed his blood for Christ.

Who would not be astonished that the wicked are permitted to prevail against the innocence of the good, when Herodias, through her daughter’s dance before a drunken king, obtains that the head of the Bridegroom’s friend, the prophet and more than a [Col. 1185C] prophet, should be carried on a platter before the eyes of the banqueters?

I cannot consider without the deepest astonishment that the man who was filled with the spirit of prophecy within his mother’s womb and, so to speak, reborn before he was born—the friend of the Bridegroom, the one greater than whom none had arisen among those born of women, the prophet who was also more than a prophet—was thrown into prison by the wicked, beheaded for a girl’s dance, and that a man of such holiness died for the laughter of the depraved.

Do we perhaps believe that there was something in his life which that despised death might wipe away? But when did he sin even in food, who ate only locusts and wild honey? In what did he offend God concerning the quality of his clothing, who covered his body with camel hair? What fault could he commit in his way of life, who did not withdraw from the wilderness? What guilt of loquacity could stain him, who lived far removed from human beings? When did any fault of silence touch him, who rebuked those coming to him so forcefully, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. III, 7).

What [Col. 1185D] does it mean that John is praised by the voice of God and yet dies for the words of a drunken woman as the reward of a dance? What does it mean that almighty God so severely despises in this world those whom he chose so sublimely before the ages, except what is evident to the devotion of the faithful: that he presses them down so heavily in the depths because he sees how he will reward them in the heights, and casts them outwardly down even to contempt because inwardly he leads them to things beyond comprehension?

From this, therefore, let each person infer what those whom God rejects will suffer there, if here he torments those whom he loves; or how those will be struck who must be accused at the judgment, if the lives of those whom the judge himself bears witness to and praises are so heavily burdened.

If, then, dearest brothers, we resolve to speak freely to the powerful who go astray in this world, let the authority of John be recalled to mind. In reproving Herod’s wickedness, he did not fear to be killed for the uprightness of his word. And because Christ is the truth, he therefore laid down his life for Christ because he laid it down for the truth.

## Chapter XXIII

“Give them something to eat yourselves” (Mark VI, 37).

[Col. 1186A]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVII, no. 22.)* Through holy preachers the Lord feeds the fasting hearts of those subject to their teaching. When the disciples complained about the hungry crowds, the Lord answered them, saying: “Give them something to eat yourselves.”

We believe that this was then done by their hands in such a way that we see it being done every day without ceasing through their words. Peter does this when he speaks through his Epistles, so that our hearts, miserably hungry, may be satisfied with the nourishment of the word. Paul and John do the same when they speak through their Epistles, so that our minds may receive the heavenly mysteries and overcome the disgust of the hunger by which they were dying.

## Chapter XXIV

“And they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties” (Mark VI, 40).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVI, no. 68.)* The various churches established in the different regions of the world make one catholic Church, in which all the faithful who think rightly concerning God live in harmony.

In the Gospel [Col. 1186B], the Lord signified this concord through the groups of people dining and through the distinction of places. When he was about to satisfy the crowds with five loaves, he ordered them to sit down in groups of fifty or one hundred, so that the multitude of the faithful might receive its food, separated in place but united in conduct.

The rest of the Jubilee is contained in the mystery of the number fifty, and fifty is multiplied by two to reach one hundred. Since one first rests from evil work so that afterward the soul may rest more fully in thought, some sit in groups of fifty and others of one hundred: there are some who already possess the rest of work because they have ceased from wicked deeds, and there are others who, having overcome perverse thoughts, already possess the rest of mind.

## Chapter XXV

“He went up into the mountain to pray” (Mark VI, 46).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VI, no. 56.)* A preacher is not perfect if, either because of devotion to contemplation, he neglects what must be done, or because of the urgency of action, he postpones what must be contemplated.

This is why [Col. 1186C] Truth itself, shown to us through the assumption of our humanity, spends the night devoted to prayer on the mountain and performs miracles by day in the cities. Thus he teaches perfect preachers neither to abandon active life entirely out of love for contemplation nor to disregard the joys of contemplation altogether through excessive activity, but, in quiet contemplation, to absorb what they may pour out in speech while occupied with their neighbors.

Through contemplation one rises into the love of God, but through preaching one returns for the benefit of one’s neighbor. Charity rises wonderfully to the heights when it mercifully draws itself down to the lowly needs of neighbors; and the better it descends to the depths, the more powerfully it returns to the heights.

## Chapter XXVI

“They bring him a deaf and mute man, and they begged him to lay his hand upon him” (Mark VII, 32).

*(Homily 10 on Ezekiel, no. 20.)* We hear the words of God when we do them, and we speak them rightly to our neighbors when we have first done them ourselves.

The evangelist Mark [Col. 1186D] aptly confirms this when he narrates the Lord’s miracle, saying: “They bring him a deaf and mute man, and they begged him to lay his hand upon him.” He indicates the order of the healing by saying: “He put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue; and looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him, ‘Ephphatha,’ which means, ‘Be opened.’ And immediately his ears were opened, and the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he spoke correctly.”

What does it mean that God, the Creator of all things, when he wished to heal the deaf and mute man, put his fingers into his ears and, spitting, touched his tongue? What are the fingers of the Redeemer intended to signify except the gifts of the Holy Spirit? Hence, when he had cast out a demon in another place, he said: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has certainly come upon you” (Luke XI, 20). For this reason, another evangelist records him as saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has certainly come upon you” (Matt. XII, 28). From both passages it is gathered that the Spirit is called a finger.

To put his fingers [Col. 1187A] into the ears, therefore, is to open the mind of the deaf person to obedience through the gifts of the Holy Spirit. But what does it mean that, spitting, he touched his tongue? Saliva is wisdom received from the mouth of the Redeemer in divine speech; for saliva flows from the head into the mouth. But that wisdom, who is himself, when our tongue is touched, immediately forms it for the words of preaching.

He looked up to heaven and groaned, not because he himself needed the groan, since he gave what he asked for, but to teach us to groan toward the one who presides over heaven. Thus our ears should be opened through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the tongue should be loosed through the saliva of the mouth—that is, through knowledge of divine speech—for words of preaching.

Then he immediately says to him, “Effeta,” that is, “Be opened,” and at once his ears were opened and the bond of his tongue was loosed. Here we must note that “Be opened” was said because his ears were closed. But for one whose ears of the heart have been opened to obedience, the bond of his tongue will unquestionably also be loosened as a consequence, so that he may speak to others of the good things he has done and of what others ought to do.

It is rightly added [Col. 1187B]: “And he spoke correctly.” For he speaks correctly who first does through obedience what he urges others to do through speech.

## Chapter XXVII

“I have compassion on the crowd” (Mark VIII, 2).

*(Homily 21 on Ezekiel, nos. 21–22.)* Preachers ought to preach to those who are living in sin. When such people have begun to abandon their sins and hasten toward innocence, the preaching spoken by the teacher must necessarily grow in proportion to their progress, and he must insist all the more forcefully in certain words of his instruction as he observes that they have fallen more grievously.

Here it is pleasing to bring forward the words of the Gospel, whose sacred history, by narrating a miracle that occurred, announces wondrous things that happen every day. When the weary and fasting crowds had gathered to the Lord, he said to the disciples: “I have compassion on the crowd, because for three days now they have remained with me and have nothing to eat. And if I send them away fasting to their homes, they will faint on the way; for some of them have come from far away.”

The crowd remains with the Lord for three days [Col. 1187C] when the multitude of the faithful, turning away through repentance from the sins it has committed, turns to the Lord in action, speech, and thought. The Lord does not wish to send them away fasting to their homes, lest they faint on the way, because converted sinners grow faint along the road of the present life if they are sent away within their own conscience without the nourishment of his teaching.

Therefore, so that they may not grow weary on the journey of this pilgrimage, they must be fed by teachers through sacred admonition. As he commanded the apostles elsewhere concerning the hungry crowds, saying: “Give them something to eat yourselves.” And again: “I do not want to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way.” It is as if he said: Let them receive a word of consolation in your preaching, lest, remaining hungry for the nourishment of truth, they succumb beneath the labor of this life.

The compassionate statement that proceeded from the mouth of Truth must be carefully considered: “For some of them have come from far away.” There is someone who, having experienced no deceit and no carnal corruption, hastened to the service of almighty God. He has not come from far away, because through incorruption and innocence he was near [Col. 1187D].

Another, stained by no impurity or disgrace but having experienced only marriage, has turned to spiritual service. He too has not come from far away, because, having used a permitted union, he did not go astray through illicit things.

Others return to repentance after sexual sins; others after false testimony; others after thefts; others after acts of violence; others after committing murder. They turn to the service of almighty God. These have come to God from far away. For the more deeply someone has gone astray in evil conduct, the farther he has withdrawn from the almighty Lord.

The prodigal son, who abandoned his father, also went into a far country where he fed swine, because he nourished vices. Let nourishment, therefore, be given even to those who come from far away, because converted sinners must be provided with the food of holy teaching, so that they may regain in God the strength they lost in their sins. For often it is necessary [Col. 1188A] for teachers to satisfy them with more abundant nourishment of instruction in proportion to the greater vices in which they had become exhausted.

## Chapter XXVIII

“I see people, as it were, walking trees” (Mark VIII, 24).

Some things belonging to the contemplative life are seen for a time through certain images, so that afterward they may be seen as they are in their own power and nature. For Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. XIII, 12). When the blind man had already begun to receive his sight through the laying on of the Redeemer’s hands, he was asked what he saw; and, looking up, he said: “I see people like trees walking.” A human being, of course, is rational by nature, whereas a tree is neither sentient nor alive. And what does this blind man, now illuminated, signify except the human race? When the Lord opens the eyes of its contemplation, it first perceives certain things enigmatically, so that afterward it may behold those true and rational heavenly hosts as they are established. Hence it is added there: “Then he again laid [Col. 1188B] his hands upon his eyes, and he began to see, and was restored, so that he saw everything clearly.” First, therefore, he saw through a mirror and in likeness, so that afterward he might see clearly and perfectly.

### CHAPTER XXIX.—“Jesus took Peter” (Mark IX, 1).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIV, no. 29.)* Those who have recently been converted first experience the sweetness of security and are first nourished by the tranquility of peace. After they have come to know this sweetness, however, they endure the struggles of temptations with greater tolerance, in proportion as they have come to know more deeply in God what they love. Hence Peter is first led up the mountain, first contemplates the brightness of the Lord’s transfiguration, and only then is permitted to be tested when the maidservant questions him (Matt. XXVI), so that, made conscious of his weakness through temptation, he might return through weeping and love to that which he had seen; and when the flood of sinful fear was carrying him into the sea, the anchor of his former sweetness might hold him fast.

### CHAPTER XXX.—“And his garments became white as snow” (Mark IX, 2).

[Col. 1188C]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXII, no. 8.)* The Lord will clothe all the saints to whom it was said, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14), in that eternal glory. Hence the Gospel also says that, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, his garments became white as snow. What else is announced in this transfiguration than the glory of the final resurrection? On the mountain his garments became like snow, because at the summit of heavenly brightness all the saints, shining with the light of righteousness, will cleave to him.

### CHAPTER XXXI.—“Let us make here three tabernacles, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah. For he did not know what he was saying” (Mark IX, 4).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII, nos. 91, 92.)* A tabernacle is built so that the body may be protected from heat and cold. What, then, is expressed here by the name “tabernacle” except the construction of earthly prosperity? Through it the reprobate multiply what will fall upon them, so that they may defend themselves from the necessities of the [Col. 1188D] present life, as from heat and rain. They strive to increase their honors, lest they appear despised; by accumulating earthly possessions they enlarge their wealth, lest they waste away from the cold of poverty. Wherever, therefore, they construct a dwelling for the mind, there undoubtedly they pitch their tabernacles.

The righteous, on the other hand, rejoice to be despised in this world and do not grieve that they are afflicted by necessities. Because they do not fortify themselves against present adversities, they are unwilling to have a tabernacle, as it were, against heat and rain. Hence Paul testifies (Heb. XI) that Abraham dwells in huts because he awaits “the city having foundations, which the heavenly craftsman built.”

Peter is therefore rightly reproved, because, not yet strengthened by perfection of mind, after recognizing the brightness of the truth, he attempts to pitch a tabernacle on earth. That rich man had built himself a seemingly secure tabernacle when he said: “Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat and drink, and feast” [Col. 1189A] (Luke XII, 19–20). But because his tabernacle did not stand upon the foundation of truth, he immediately heard: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and whose will those things be which you have prepared?” (Verse 20). For lovers of the fleeting life, while they zealously try to build themselves up in the present, are suddenly carried away to eternal punishment.

### CHAPTER XXXII.—“Elijah is to come, and he will restore all things” (Mark IX, 11).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XX, no. 66; Homily 12 on Ezekiel; in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XI, no. 24.)* Although Elijah is said to have been taken up into heaven, he postponed death; he did not escape it. For who is the human being who lives and will not see death? He will therefore come to restore all things, because he will certainly be restored to this world for this purpose: both to fulfill the ministry of preaching and to pay the debt of the flesh.

Although the holy Church has now lost the Jews, at the end of this age it receives them twofold, when, after the Gentiles have been fully gathered in, all the Jews who are then found consent to run to its [Col. 1189B] faith. For it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI, 25). Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Elijah has come, and he himself will restore all things.” For now the Church has lost the Israelites whom it cannot convert by preaching; but then, when Elijah preaches, it will gather as many as it finds and receive more fully what it has lost.

For as many as are found from the Jewish people will be converted, and at Elijah’s preaching many of those who then remain in unbelief among the Jews will return to knowledge of the truth. They will rejoice to cling to the divinity of the Lord Jesus, no longer despising him as though he were merely a human being. Before the Lord’s incarnation, the Jews believed and announced that he would come; but after he appeared in the flesh, they denied that he was the one. They despised as present the one whom they had said would come, and they did not follow by believing those things which they remembered their fathers had foretold.

But when Elijah comes, as Malachi says, [Col. 1189C] “He will turn the hearts of the children to their fathers” (Mal. IV, 6), because, when Elijah preaches, the children will begin to understand concerning the Lord what their fathers preached.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.—“I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX, 23).

*(Collected from book XXII, no. 49; the exposition of Blessed Job; and Homily 15 on Ezekiel, no. 4.)* Our faith is led to its perfection by certain steps, because a part of it is first received so that afterward it may be completed perfectly in us. Hence the disciples say to our Redeemer: “Increase our faith” (Luke XVII, 5), so that what had already been received in its beginning might come to perfection, as it were, through successive increases.

For if faith did not progress in the mind of the believer, a certain man who came to the Lord wishing his son to be healed, when asked whether he believed, would certainly not have said: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief.” Consider, I ask, what is being said. If he believed, why did he speak of unbelief? But if he knew that he possessed unbelief, how did he [Col. 1189D] believe? Yet because, through the hidden inspiration of grace, faith grows by successive degrees of merit, at one and the same time the man who did not yet believe perfectly both believed and was unbelieving.

He was therefore still ascending toward the faith that he had already received: he cried out that he already believed, yet still doubted through unbelief.

### CHAPTER XXXIV.—“Jesus threatened the unclean spirit” (Mark IX, 24).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXII, nos. 33, 34.)* When the ancient enemy begins to tempt someone, he first suggests smooth and unlawful things to the mind, as though offering counsel; then he draws the person toward delight; finally, possessing him through consent, he binds him by an inveterate habit of sinning, inseparably to punishment.

Hence some people themselves condemn sins that they have committed for a long time [Col. 1190A] and flee them in judgment, yet cannot avoid them in practice, even while struggling against them. It must also be understood that he often inflicts graver sins upon those whom he has captured when he knows that they are drawing near the end of the present life. Those whom he captured at the beginning through evil, he makes worse at the end, so that the sooner his temptations are to cease, the more forcefully they may be completed.

Because he strives to make their punishment equal to his own, he attempts to intensify all their sins more fiercely before death. Often he already possesses a heart subjected to evil, yet divine grace drives him out and the hand of mercy expels the one whom a captive will introduced. When he is driven from the heart, he tries to implant sharper goads of iniquity, so that the mind attacked by him may feel waves of temptation which, while possessed, it did not know.

This is well expressed in the Gospel when the unclean spirit is ordered by the Lord to leave the man. For when the demon-possessed boy had been brought forward, it is written: “Jesus threatened the unclean spirit, saying: Deaf and mute spirit, I command you, come out of him and enter him no more. And crying out and tearing [Col. 1190B] him violently, it came out of him.”

Behold: it had not torn him when it held him; it tore him as it departed. For clearly it then rends the mind’s thoughts more terribly when, compelled by divine power, it approaches its departure. It had possessed him while mute, but it abandoned him with cries, because often, when it possesses someone, it inflicts lesser temptations; but when it is driven from the heart, it disturbs the person with a more violent assault.

Thus the enemy, while possessing the human heart, always grows in malice through what follows; while abandoning the heart, he strikes it with more violent goads of thought. Everyone must therefore flee the beginning of temptation all the more because he understands that its end cannot quickly be brought to an end. Everything that the enemy suggests at the beginning can indeed be overcome, but from it follows what can scarcely be conquered.

### CHAPTER XXXV.—“And he became as though dead” (Mark IX, 25).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book X, no. 50.)* Carnal people regard as virtually dead those whom they do not think live carnally along with them—namely, those [Col. 1190C] who do not possess the things they possess or love only the things they love.—namely, those who do not possess the things they possess or love only the things they love. For whoever dies to the desires of this world is judged utterly extinguished by earthly minds.

This is well signified by the miracle of our Redeemer when he frees a man from an unclean spirit. It is written: “Crying out and tearing him violently, it came out of him, and he became as though dead, so that many said that he was dead. But Jesus, taking him by the hand, lifted him up, and he arose.”

He appears as though dead when he is freed from the power of the evil spirit, because whoever has now subdued earthly desires extinguishes within himself the life of carnal conduct and appears dead to the world, since he lacks the wicked possessor who was driving him through unclean desires. Many call him dead because those who do not know how to live spiritually consider extinguished anyone who does not pursue carnal goods.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—“Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble” (Mark IX, 41).

[Col. 1190D]

*(Pastoral Rule, part I, chapter 2.)* No one harms the Church more than the person who, while acting perversely, possesses the name or rank of holiness. No one dares to rebuke this offender, and the fault spreads with great force as an example when a sinner is honored out of reverence for his rank.

Yet all who are unworthy would flee the weight of so great a guilt if they carefully considered the sentence of Truth, which says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and that he be plunged into the depths of the sea.”

By the ass’s millstone the circuit and labor of secular life are expressed; by the depths of the sea, final damnation is signified. Therefore, when someone elevated to the appearance of holiness destroys others either by word or by example, it would certainly have been better if earthly deeds had bound him to death under an outward appearance than that sacred offices should display him as an example of guilt for others to imitate. For if he fell alone, the punishment of hell would at least [Col. 1191A] torment him in a more tolerable manner.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—“Likewise, concerning the preceding.”

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VI, no. 57.)* What is signified by the ass’s millstone except earthly action? While it binds the necks of the mind through foolish desires, it sends the mind around in a circuit of labor. What, then, is represented by the sea except the present age?

There are therefore some who, while abandoning earthly actions and rising beyond the powers of their understanding toward contemplation, set humility aside. They not only plunge themselves into error but also divide the weak from the embrace of unity. Whoever, then, causes one of the least to stumble would have been better off with an ass’s millstone tied around his neck and thrown into the sea, because it might have been more advantageous for a perverse mind to be occupied with the world and to conduct earthly business than to be idle through contemplative pursuits to the ruin of many.

For there are restless spirits who, while seeking through contemplation more than they [Col. 1191B] can grasp, burst forth into perverse doctrines. While they negligently refuse to be disciples of Truth in humility, they become teachers of errors.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—“Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark XXIX, 49).

*(Collected from Homily 8 on Ezekiel, no. 8, and the Pastoral Rule, part II, chapter 4.)* There are some who, while striving to know more than is necessary, withdraw from peace with their neighbors, despising them as dull and foolish. Hence Truth itself warns us, saying: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves.”

By salt, words of wisdom are signified. Salt without peace is not a gift of virtue but an increase of condemnation. For the better someone understands, the worse he sins, and therefore he will deserve a much greater punishment without excuse, because, if he had wished, he could prudently have avoided sin.

Whoever therefore strives and labors to possess the salt of wisdom must take care never to depart from the peace of concord. Moreover, [Col. 1191C] when a ruler prepares to speak, he should attend to the great care with which he must speak, lest, if he is carried toward speech without order, the hearts of his hearers be struck by the wound of error and, while he perhaps desires to appear wise, he foolishly sever the bond of unity.

Hence Paul says: “Not to be wiser than one ought to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. XII, 3). Whoever therefore strives to speak wisely should greatly fear that the unity of his hearers may be disturbed by his eloquence, fulfilling what is said: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves.”

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—“Good Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” (Mark X, 17).

*(Homily 37 on the Gospels, no. 6.)* The Lord says through another evangelist: “Who among you, wishing to build a tower, does not first calculate the expenses that are necessary?” (Luke XIV, 26). Behold: according to the voice of Truth, whoever builds a tower first prepares the expense of the building.

If, then, brothers, we desire to construct the tower of humility, we must first prepare ourselves for the adversities [Col. 1191D] of this age. For this is the difference between an earthly and a heavenly building: an earthly building is constructed by gathering expenses, whereas a heavenly building is constructed by dispersing expenses. We incur expense for the former if we gather what we do not possess; we incur expense for the latter if we abandon what we possess.

That rich man could not possess these expenses. Although he possessed many possessions, he asked the Teacher: “Good Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life?” When he heard the command to abandon everything, he departed sadly and was constricted inwardly by what had made him outwardly expansive in possessions. Because in this life he loved the expense of exaltation, he refused, as he journeyed toward the eternal homeland, to possess the expense of humility.

### CHAPTER XL.—“No one is good except God alone” (Mark X, 18).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, no. 46.)* All created things are good, as Moses testifies when he [Col. 1192A] says: “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. I, 31). But that alone is principally good through which all these things that are good exist without being principally good. Concerning this good, Truth says: “No one is good except God alone.”

### CHAPTER XLI.—“How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God” (Mark X, 23).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, preface, chapter 3; Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 20.)* It is exceedingly rare that those who possess gold should advance toward rest, since Truth itself says: “Those who have money will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty.” For those who here yearn to multiply riches, what joys of the other life do they hope for?

Yet, to show that this is exceedingly rare and can occur only through a divine miracle, our Redeemer said: “What is impossible with human beings is possible with God.” Let avaricious rich people therefore listen when they either desire more or are able to obtain everything they desire: “What [Col. 1192B] does it profit a human being if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI, 20). It is as though Truth openly said: “What does it profit a human being if he gathers everything external, if he condemns the one thing that he himself is?”

### CHAPTER XLII.—“It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Mark X, 25).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXV, no. 38.)* By the name “camel,” the Lord is signified in sacred discourse. Because a camel willingly humbles itself to take up burdens, it aptly signifies the grace of our Redeemer, who, in deigning to bear the burdens of our weakness, willingly descended from the height of his power.

Hence he says through the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again; and no one takes it from me, but I lay it down myself” (John X, 18). Again he says: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the [Col. 1192C] kingdom of heaven.”

What is signified by the name “rich” except any proud person? What is signified by the designation “camel” except willing condescension? The camel passes through the eye of a needle when our Redeemer entered, through the narrowness of his passion, even unto the acceptance of death. That passion was like a needle, because it pierced the body with pain.

It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven, because unless he himself first bore the burdens of our weakness and showed us through his passion the form of humility, proud rigidity would never bend itself toward his humility.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—“Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Mark X, 38).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVII, no. 9; Homily 27 on the Gospels, no. 4; Homily 35 on the Gospels, no. 7.)* James and John, the sons of Zebedee, through their mother’s intervention, were seeking from the Lord a place of exaltation and glory, but they did not know the way to that same glory. They were seeking the height [Col. 1192D] of that honor at his right and left, but they did not see how narrow the road to it was.

Their swelling hearts are therefore called back by the Lord to the way by which they would come to exaltation, and the cup of passion, which they were to imitate, is immediately set before their eyes, so that, if they were striving toward the joys of sublimity, they might first find the way of humility.

Jesus therefore said to them: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” It is as though he said: “The place of exaltation already delights you, but first let the way of labor train you; for majesty is reached through the cup. If your mind desires what delights, first drink what causes pain; through the bitter cup of confession, one arrives at the joy of salvation.”

And because there are two kinds of martyrdom—one in hidden action, the other in public action—the Lord himself bears witness. When he had asked, “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” and they had said, “We can,” he immediately continued, saying: “You will indeed drink my cup.”

For what [Col. 1193A] do we understand by the cup except the pain of passion? Concerning it he says elsewhere: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI, 39). The sons of Zebedee—that is, James and John—did not both die through martyrdom, and yet both heard that they would drink the cup.

John did not end his life through martyrdom, yet he was a martyr, because he preserved in his mind the passion which he did not undergo in his body. To die at the hands of a persecutor is martyrdom in open action; to endure insults and love the one who hates is martyrdom in hidden thought.

We too, therefore, even if we are slain by no weapon of our attackers, can be martyrs if we truly preserve patience in our hearts.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—“Jesus, standing, gave sight to the blind” (Mark X).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book V, no. 63.)* Every creature, because it was made from nothing and of itself tends toward nothing, does not possess the power to stand but to flow away. Rational creation, however, by the very fact that it was made in the image of its Creator, is fixed so that it may not pass into nothingness. Irrational creation is not fixed in this way, but, until through its service it fulfills the appearance of the universe, it is delayed in passing away.

For even though heaven and earth remain forever afterward, of themselves they are now hastening toward nothingness; nevertheless, they continue, changed for the better, for the use of those whom they serve.

To stand, therefore, belongs only to the Creator, through whom all things pass without passing away, and in whom certain things are held so that they do not pass away. Hence our Redeemer, because the stability of his divinity could not be grasped by the human mind, showed himself to us, coming to us in the flesh, created, born, dead, [Col. 1193B] buried, rising again, and returning to the heavenly realms—as though passing through.

This was well made known through the blind man who was given sight: while passing by, he gave him hearing, but while standing, he restored his eyes. Through the dispensation of humility he has the power to pass by; through the power of his divinity, by which he is present everywhere, he has the power to stand.

The Lord is therefore said to hear the voices of our blindness while passing by, because, having become human, he takes pity on human misery. But while standing [Col. 1193C] he restores light, because through the power of his divinity he illuminates the darkness of our weakness.

### CHAPTER XLV.—“Jesus, seated upon an ass, came to Jerusalem” (Mark XI).

*(Collected from the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXX, no. 40, and Homily 7 on Ezekiel, no. 2.)* Faithful souls from the Jewish people and from the Gentiles have come together in love of our Creator and Redeemer. Hence, when our Redeemer, seated upon a young ass, was going toward Jerusalem, as the evangelist testifies: “Many spread their garments on the road; others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. And those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Mark XI, 7).

By the name of male or female asses the gentleness of the simple is sometimes signified, and Jerusalem is called “the vision of peace.” What, then, does it signify that the Lord, seated upon an ass, leads it to Jerusalem, except that, while possessing simple minds by ruling over them, he leads them through his holy sitting to the vision of [Col. 1193D] peace?

Our Savior therefore goes toward Jerusalem seated upon a young ass when he leads the soul of each believer—namely, while guiding his own beast—to the innermost vision of peace. He also sits upon the beast when he presides universally over the holy Church and kindles it with desire for heavenly peace.

Our Savior therefore goes toward Jerusalem seated upon a young ass when he leads the soul of each believer—namely, while guiding his own beast—to the innermost vision of peace. The beast is also seated when he presides universally over the holy Church and kindles it with desire for heavenly peace.

Many spread their garments on the road because they subdue their bodies through abstinence, preparing a path to the mind for him or offering good examples to those who follow. Others cut branches, or leafy twigs, from the trees and spread them on the road, because in the teaching of truth they gather the words and judgments of the Fathers from their sayings and, through humble preaching, lay them down on God’s road before the mind of the hearer.

We too, unworthy as we are, do this now. For when we take up the judgments of the Fathers in a sermon of exhortation, we cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road of the almighty Lord.

But those who went before and those who followed cried out: [Col. 1194A] “Hosanna.” The Jewish people went before; the Gentiles followed, because all the elect—whether those who could belong to Judea or those who now exist in the Church—have believed and believe in the Mediator between God and human beings.

Those who go before and those who follow cry out, “Hosanna.” *Hosanna* is said in Latin to mean “save us.” From him the former sought salvation, and the latter seek it; and they confess that he who comes in the name of the Lord is blessed, because the peoples who went before and those who follow have one hope and one faith.

For just as their sins were healed through his passion and resurrection, so we are saved through his past passion, while his resurrection endures forever. The one whom our predecessors from the Jewish people believed in and loved as the one who was to come, we believe and love as the one who has come; and we are inflamed by desire for him so that we may contemplate him face to face.

### CHAPTER XLVI.—“The Lord overturned the seats of those selling doves” (Mark XI, 15).

[Col. 1194B]

*(Homily 17 on the Gospels, no. 13; in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXV, no. 36.)* I speak to you priests in mourning, because we have learned that some of you perform ordinations for payment, sell spiritual grace, and, at the cost of sin, heap up temporal profits from the iniquities of others.

Why, then, does the Lord’s voice, giving the command, not return to your memory: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. X, 8)? Why do you not recall before the eyes of your minds that, when the Redeemer entered the temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves and poured out the money-changers’ coins?

Who are those in God’s temple today who sell doves except those who receive a price in the Church for the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is given from heaven? A dove is therefore sold when the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, is offered for a price.

But our Redeemer overturns the seats of those selling doves because he destroys the priesthood of such traffickers. Hence the sacred canons condemn the Simoniac heresy and command that those who seek payment for conferring orders be deprived [Col. 1194C] of the priesthood.

The seat of those selling doves is therefore overturned when those who traffic in spiritual grace are deprived of the priesthood, either before human beings or before the eyes of God.

There are also many other evils of those in authority that now escape human eyes. Often they present themselves to people as holy pastors, yet in their hidden actions they do not blush to appear disgraceful before the eyes of the inner Judge. What is done secretly can now be denied to human beings; but that Judge will certainly come, and no one can hide from him by remaining silent, nor deceive him by denial.

That day will come—indeed, it will surely come—and it is not far off: the Shepherd of shepherds will appear and bring each person’s deeds into the open. The one who now punishes the faults of subjects through their superiors will then, raging, condemn the evils of superiors through himself.

Hence, when he entered the temple himself, he made a whip, as it were, from cords, and, driving the wicked traffickers from the house of God, overturned the seats of those selling doves. For he strikes the faults of subjects [Col. 1194D] through pastors, but he himself strikes the vices of pastors.

The vices of subjects, too, which are now either concealed from judgment by their teachers or cannot be judged, are undoubtedly reserved for his judgment. Therefore, when the faith remains unharmed, it is a work of virtue if disciples for the time being tolerate whatever in their superior is blameworthy. Yet it should be humbly suggested, if perhaps what is displeasing can be corrected.

Above all, care must be taken lest the disordered defense of justice turn into pride; lest, while rectitude is loved incautiously, humility—the very teacher of rectitude—be lost; lest anyone despise as his superior one whom he happens to criticize in some action.

Against this swelling of pride, the minds of subjects are subdued for the guardianship of humility if they constantly attend to their own weakness. For we neglect to examine our strength truthfully, and because we consider ourselves stronger than we are, we judge those placed over us strictly.

These [Col. 1195A] evils are common, often committed by subjects against superiors and by superiors against subjects. Those who preside consider all their subjects less wise than they themselves are; and those who are subject judge the actions of their rulers, thinking that, if they themselves happened to hold authority, they could act better.

Hence it often happens that rulers see less prudently what ought to be done, because the very cloud of exaltation darkens their eyes. Sometimes the person who, while subject, used to criticize an action will do the same thing when he becomes a superior; and because he now commits what he had judged, he ought at least to blush that he had judged it.

Just as superiors must therefore take care lest the higher position elevate their hearts through an estimation of unique wisdom, so subjects must take care lest the actions of their rulers displease them. And since rulers have a supreme Judge, it is a matter of great caution for subjects not rashly to judge the lives of those who govern.

For, as I said above, it was not without reason that the Lord himself poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned the seats [Col. 1195B] of those selling doves. He signified that, while he judges the life of the people through their teachers, he examines the deeds of teachers through himself.

### CHAPTER XLVII.—“There will then be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world” (Mark XIII, 18).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXII, nos. 22, 23, 24.)* At the end of the age the ancient enemy will enter his own vessel, that lost man—namely, Antichrist—and, handed over to his power, he will be released against us for a short time but with great strength. Although cruelty enlarges him for savagery, heavenly mercy confines him by shortening the days.

Hence Truth itself says: “There will then be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor will be.” Again he says: “If those days had not been shortened, no flesh would be saved.” Because the Lord sees that we are both proud and weak, he mercifully says that the uniquely evil days he has imposed are shortened: to terrify pride by the adversity of the time [Col. 1195C] and to comfort weakness by its brevity.

Yet we must carefully consider in what respect the ancient enemy will then rise more atrociously than now. What kinds of punishments do we not know, which we rejoice have already exercised the strength of martyrs? A sword plunged into one person’s throat by an unexpected blow struck him down; the cross’s gallows afflicted another, where death is both challenged and driven back, and, driven back, challenged again; a saw with bristling teeth crushed another; an armed claw, mocking with iron, tore another; bestial fury mangled another by cutting him apart with bites; the force of blows, pressed from within the entrails through the skin, ripped another apart; dug-up earth covered another alive; another, plunged into the depths, was broken by the precipice of death; water, filling up around another who had been thrown into it, swallowed him; devouring flame consumed another as it fed upon him down to the ashes.

When, therefore, at the end of the world the ancient enemy rises more wickedly through Antichrist, what will then increase the horror of these torments except what Truth itself says in the Gospel: “False christs and false prophets will arise and [Col. 1195D] give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect will be led astray” (Matt. XXIV, 24)?

Now our faithful perform miracles while suffering perversities; but then the satellites of this enemy will perform miracles even while inflicting perversities. Let us consider, therefore, what the temptation of the human mind will be at that time, when the devout martyr subjects his body to torments, yet the torturer performs miracles before his eyes.

Whose virtue will not then be shaken from the very depths of his thoughts, when the one who torments with scourges flashes with signs? The ancient enemy will then be exalted both in the reverence inspired by prodigies and in the harshness of torment, because he will rise not only through power but also be supported by the display of signs.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.—“And they will give great signs, so that, if possible, even the elect will be led astray” (Mark XIII, 22).

*(Mixed from the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIV, no. 27, and Book [Col. 1196A] XXXIII, no. 61, and Homily 9 on Ezekiel, no. 8.)* When the elect see the signs and miracles that the servants and preachers of Antichrist will perform, they will experience a certain cloud of doubt in their hearts, and from their lying wonders a darkness of fear will for a moment arise in their hearts. Hence Truth says through the Gospel: “False Christs and false prophets will arise, and they will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect will be led astray” (Matt. 24:24). This does not mean that God’s elect will fall, but that they will tremble amid great terrors, because wickedness will then rage so fiercely against the righteous that even the hearts of the elect will be struck with no small fear.

In this matter it is very important to ask how those who are elect can be led astray, or why the words “if possible” are added as though in uncertainty, when the Lord, who foreknows all things, awaits what will happen. For there are only two possibilities: if they are elect, it cannot happen; but if it can happen, they are not elect. Yet because the hearts of the elect will be shaken by fearful thoughts, while [Col. 1196B] their steadfastness will not be moved, the Lord embraced both points in this one statement: “So that, if possible, even the elect will be led astray.” For to waver in thought is already, in a sense, to err; but immediately the words “if possible” are added, because it is certainly impossible for the elect to be completely seized by error.

This uncertainty in the Lord’s words therefore indicated the trial that would arise in the hearts of the elect: those chosen to persevere would, through the signs performed by the preachers of Antichrist, be tempted to fall. Thus, by saying “if possible,” he expresses that the elect will be tested in their hearts. They waver, but they do not fall. The words “if possible” are therefore used because they will tremble, while they are called elect because they do not fall. The Lord’s uncertainty of expression thus reveals the agitation of mind among those whom he calls elect, because he sees that they persevere in faith and good works.

## Chapter XLIX — “A young man followed him, clothed in a linen cloth,” etc. (Mark 14:51)

[Col. 1196C]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIV, nos. 54 and 57.)* When the Jewish crowd saw the miracles of our Redeemer, it honored him because of his signs, saying: “This is the Christ.” But when it saw the weakness of his humanity, it refused to believe him the Creator, saying: “No, but he is misleading the crowds” (John 7:12).

But why should it seem remarkable that he suffered these things at the hands of the crowds, when even those who appeared to be teachers of the Law—who declared from the prophetic words that he would become incarnate and who saw him incarnate—were nevertheless separated from him by the persuasion of unbelief and turned away from faith in the truth? The scribes and teachers of the Law, who were accustomed to instructing the peoples toward life, divided many from faith in the incarnate God by their counsels, although previously they themselves had appeared to teach many to believe in the mystery of his incarnation through the words of the prophets.

The crowd of the peoples followed them not only into unbelief but even into persecuting the Lord, and was inflamed with the torches of fury all the way to his Passion. [Col. 1196D] During that Passion the hearts of the disciples were disturbed. When they came to the cross and a great fear of the persecution by the Jews seized them, they all fled individually. The women, however, who had served the Lord by outward ministrations in preparing what was needed for his body, remained with him.

Peter did stand for a while, but afterward, terrified, he denied him. John also stood—the one to whom, at the very time of the cross, it was said: “Behold, your mother” (John 19:27). Yet he could not persevere, for it is also written of him: “A certain young man followed him, clothed in a linen cloth over his naked body; and they seized him. But he, abandoning the linen cloth, fled from them naked.” Although afterward he returned to the cross to hear the words of his Redeemer, he had first fled in fear. The women, however, are reported not only to have neither feared nor fled, but even to have remained standing as far as the tomb.

## Chapter L — “They found a man of Cyrene” (Mark 15:21)

[Col. 1197A]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book VIII, no. 72.)* Hypocrites often afflict themselves with extraordinary abstinence, wear away all the strength of their bodies, and, while living in the flesh, extinguish the life of the flesh completely. Through abstinence they approach death so closely that they live as though dying almost every day. Yet they seek human eyes for these practices and desire the glory of admiration, as Truth testifies: “They disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to be fasting” (Matt. 6:16).

Their faces grow pale, their bodies are shaken by weakness, and their chests are oppressed by sighs that interrupt their breathing. Yet amid all this they seek from the mouths of those around them words of admiration, and think of nothing else after so much labor except human estimation.

Simon fittingly represents such people. At the time of the Lord’s Passion he carried the Lord’s cross under compulsion, and it is written: “They found a man of Cyrene, named Simon, coming toward them; they compelled him to carry [Col. 1197B] Jesus’ cross.” What we do under compulsion, we do not perform out of the devotion of love. To carry the cross of the Lord Jesus under compulsion, therefore, is to endure the affliction of abstinence with an intention other than the one required.

Does he not carry Jesus’ cross under compulsion who subdues his flesh as though in obedience to the Lord’s command, yet does not love his spiritual homeland? Thus Simon carries the cross but by no means dies, because every hypocrite indeed afflicts his body through abstinence, yet through his love of glory lives worse than the world. Often, too, through the appearance of holiness he undeservedly attains a position of authority—one he would not deserve to receive unless he displayed some virtue in himself. But what he obtains with delight passes away, while what follows remains with punishment.

Confidence in holiness is now placed in the mouths of men; but when the inner Judge examines the secrets of the heart, he seeks witnesses from the outward life.

## Chapter LI — “They bring him to the place called Golgotha; it was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark 15:22)

[Col. 1197C]

*(Homily 14 on Ezekiel, no. 6.)* Everything that the Lord, having become incarnate, taught by words, he first demonstrated by deeds, as it is written: “The things that Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1).

Because he came to call us to our heavenly homeland, he taught us to despise transitory goods and not to fear temporal evils. Thus he despised insults, endured injuries, did not fear death, and did not shrink from the punishment of the cross. Yet when they wished to seize him and make him king, he immediately fled. What else does he signify for us by these examples except that we should neither fear the adversities of this world nor pursue its prosperity? For its goods often occupy the mind more than its evils disturb it.

Before his Passion he heard insults, yet did not return insults. He endured his betrayer in silence for a long time and did not refuse to give him a kiss when he came to greet him. He accepted death on the cross so that we would not fear dying. He revealed the resurrection on the third day so that we would believe that we too can rise. After his Passion he also called those who had crucified him to the grace of faith, repaid wickedness with goodness, and instructed us in all things by his example.

## Chapter LII — Likewise, concerning the foregoing

[Col. 1197D]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXI, no. 11.)* Let us therefore direct the eyes of our minds toward the surpassing life of our Redeemer, so that in his life and commandments we may recognize what is lacking in our own life and direct our life according to the examples of his life.

Hence it is written: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow in his footsteps: he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth; when he was reviled, he did not revile; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. 2:21). Hence Paul says: “Let us run with patience the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising its shame” (Heb. 12:1).

The Lord therefore appeared in the flesh to stir [Col. 1198A] human life by admonition, to kindle it by providing examples, to redeem it by dying, and to restore it by rising again.

## Chapter LIII — “He has risen; he is not here” (Mark 16:6)

*(Homily 21 on the Gospels, nos. 6–7.)* There were two lives, one of which we knew and the other of which we did not know. One is mortal and the other immortal; one belongs to corruption and the other to incorruption; one to death and the other to resurrection.

But the Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, came. He assumed one life and revealed the other: he endured the one by dying and revealed the other by rising. If, then, he had promised resurrection of the flesh to us who knew mortal life, but had not visibly displayed it, who would believe his promises?

Having become human, he appeared in the flesh. He willingly consented to die, but rose by his power, and demonstrated by example what he promised us as a reward.

Here again we should recall that when the Son of God was crucified, the Jews insulted him, saying: “If he is the king of Israel, [Col. 1198B] let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.” If he had then come down from the cross, yielding to those who insulted him, he would not have demonstrated to us the power of his patience. But he waited a little, endured insults, bore mockery, maintained patience, and postponed astonishment.

He who refused to come down from the cross rose from the tomb. It was therefore greater to rise from the tomb than to come down from the cross; it was greater to destroy death by rising than to preserve life by descending. But since the Jews did not see him come down from the cross in response to their insults, and saw him dying, they believed that they had conquered him and rejoiced as though they had extinguished his name.

## Chapter LIV — “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15)

*(Mixed from Homily 29 on the Gospels, nos. 1–2, and Book VI of the exposition of Blessed Job, nos. 20–21.)* After the Lord’s death his name spread throughout the whole world, because after his resurrection he sent his disciples throughout the earth to preach his [Col. 1198C] Gospel, saying: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature.”

The name “every creature” signifies the human being, because in humanity the true form and the great communion of the whole creation are displayed. Everything that exists is either existent but does not live; existent and living but entirely without sensation; existent, living, and sentient but lacking understanding and discernment; or existent, living, sentient, understanding, and discerning.

Stones exist, but do not live. Plants exist and live, but do not feel. The life of herbs and trees is called greenness, as Paul says of seeds: “Foolish one! What you sow is not brought to life unless it first dies” (1 Cor. 15:36). Brute animals live and feel, but do not understand or discern.

Human beings therefore have existence in common with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals, and discernment with angels. They are rightly designated by the name “every creature,” since, in a certain respect, every creature is contained in them.

[Col. 1198D]

Thus, when Truth commands the disciples to preach the Gospel to every creature, he wished “every creature” to be understood as the human being alone, with whom he created something in common with all things.

After the resurrection, then, when he had sent his disciples to preach the Gospel, they departed and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the accompanying signs. After their sound went out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world, the Lord’s name spread throughout the world through his death—the death by which the unbelieving crowd had believed that it had extinguished him.

The crowd that had rejoiced at his killing grieved at his death, because it recognized that through punishment he had reached his glory.

If, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, we are members of our Redeemer, let us confidently expect in ourselves the resurrection that has plainly occurred in our Head. Let us love the glory of his resurrection with our whole mind, and let us die for his love. In the resurrection of our Author we have recognized his ministers, the angels, as our fellow citizens.

[Col. 1199A]

Let us therefore hasten to that solemn assembly of these citizens. Since we cannot yet join them by sight, let us be united to them by desire and by the mind. May almighty God assist our desire for life—the God who for us [Col. 1200A] gave his only Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, to death, and who with him lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# Book Three — Exposition of the Gospel According to Luke

[Col. 1199]

## Chapter I — “There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah; and his wife was from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. They were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly” (Luke 1:5)

[Col. 1199A]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXV, no. 10.)* The life of many people is often displeasing to the Lord even though it pleases human beings outwardly. Therefore the evangelist spoke with great care in praising the righteous married couple, Zechariah and Elizabeth: “They were both righteous before God.”

For it is not a secure praise to appear righteous before human beings. Human judgment often approves someone as though he were great before God, but almighty God, who is seemingly approved on his own authority, does not acknowledge him. Hence the Psalmist watchfully prays: “Direct my way in your sight” (Ps. 5:9), because the way that is believed straight in the sight of human beings is often distorted from the path of truth.

[Col. 1199B]

## Chapter II — “The angel Gabriel says to Zechariah concerning the promise of John: Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John; he will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1)

*(Homily 7 on the Gospels, no. 1.)* John is said to come “in the spirit and power of Elijah” because, just as Elijah will precede the Lord’s second coming, John preceded his first coming.

For this reason, when the disciples questioned the Lord elsewhere about the coming of Elijah, he replied: “Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished. And if you wish to know, he himself is Elijah” (Matt. 17:12).

But when John was questioned by the priests and Levites whether he was Elijah, he said: “I am not Elijah.” How is it that what Truth affirms the prophet of Truth denies? But if Truth itself is examined carefully, it is found that what sounds contradictory is not contradictory.

John was Elijah in spirit, [Col. 1199C] but was not Elijah in person. Just as Elijah will be the forerunner of the coming Judge, so John became the forerunner of the Redeemer. What the Lord admits concerning the spirit, John denies concerning the person. It was fitting that the Lord should speak to his disciples of John’s spiritual identity, while John should answer the same carnal crowds not concerning his spirit but concerning his body.

What John said therefore appears contrary to the truth, yet he did not depart from the path of truth.

## Chapter III — “The angel Gabriel was sent” (Luke 1:26)

*(Homily 34 on the Gospels, no. 9.)* The spirits of the heavenly homeland are called angels only when something is announced through them. In Greek, angels are called *messengers*, and archangels *chief messengers*. Those who announce lesser things are called angels; those who announce the greatest things are called archangels.

For this reason it was not just any angel but the archangel Gabriel who was sent to the Virgin Mary. This great mystery required a great angel to come, since he was announcing the greatest of all things.

[Col. 1199D]

Gabriel is said to mean “strength of God.” Gabriel, who is named “the strength of God,” was therefore sent to Mary. He came to announce the one who, in order to conquer the powers of the air, deigned to appear in humility. Of him the Psalmist says: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:9). And again: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory.”

Through [Col. 1200A] the strength of God, therefore, he was to be announced who, the Lord of hosts and mighty in battle, was coming to conquer the powers of the air.

## Chapter IV — “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, no. 33.)* In sacred Scripture “overshadowing” sometimes signifies the Lord’s incarnation, and sometimes the mind’s refreshment from the heat of carnal thoughts. Preserving the truth of the historical account, the angelic word testifies to this when it says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

By the word “overshadowing,” both natures of the incarnate God are signified, for a shadow is formed from light and body. The Lord, through his divinity, is light; through his humanity, assumed in the Virgin’s womb by means of a soul, he deigned to become a body.

Because incorporeal light was to become embodied in her womb, she who conceived the incorporeal is told with reference to the body: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you”—that is, the body of humanity will [Col. 1200B] receive in you the incorporeal light of divinity. From this overshadowing you will receive complete refreshment of mind.

## Chapter V — “The holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, nos. 84–85.)* No saint, however full of virtues, can be compared with him of whom the angel said to blessed Mary: “The holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

For although we are made holy, we are not born holy, since we are bound by the very condition of corruptible nature, so that with the Prophet we say: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. 50:7).

He alone was truly born holy who, in order to conquer the condition of corruptible nature itself, was not conceived through the joining of carnal intercourse.

A certain founder of heresy wished to make himself equal to him when he said: “I do not envy Christ, who was made God, because if I wish, I too can [Col. 1200C] become one.” By this perverse assertion he thought that our Lord Jesus Christ became God not through the mystery of his conception but through an advance in grace: that he was born a mere human being but progressed by merit so as to be God. He therefore judged that both he and any others could be made equal to Christ, since the children of God become so by grace. He did not understand or consider that no one can be made equal to him.

For it is one thing for human beings who are born to receive the grace of adoption, and another for one person uniquely to proceed from conception itself as God through the power of divinity. The glory possessed by the Only-Begotten by nature cannot be equated with what others receive by grace.

The Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, is not, as this heretic foolishly claims, one person in humanity and another in divinity. He was not conceived and born a mere human being and afterward, through merit, received the status of God. Rather, when the angel announced and the Spirit came, immediately the Word was in the womb, immediately within the womb the Word was flesh. While the essence remained unchangeable—the essence that he possesses [Col. 1200D] coeternally with the Father and the Holy Spirit—he assumed within the Virgin’s womb that by which the impassible could suffer, the immortal could die, and the eternal before the ages could become temporal at the end of the ages.

Thus, through an ineffable mystery, by a holy conception and an inviolate birth, according to the truth of both natures, the same virgin was both the Lord’s handmaid and his mother.

For Elizabeth says to her: “And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43). And the Virgin herself, conceiving, [Col. 1201A] said: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (v. 38).

Although he is one thing as proceeding from the Father and another as proceeding from the Virgin, he is not one person from the Father and another from the Virgin. Rather, he himself is eternal from the Father and temporal from his mother; he himself is the one who made and the one who was made; he himself is beautiful in form above the children of men through his divinity, and he himself is the one of whom it was said: “We saw him, and he had no appearance” (Isa. 53:2); “There was in him neither beauty nor comeliness,” through his humanity.

He is the one who existed before the ages from the Father without a mother, and the one who existed at the end of the ages from his mother without a father; he is the temple of the Creator and the Creator of the temple; he is the author of the work and the work of the Author.

Remaining one from and in both natures, he is neither confused by the union of the natures nor divided into two by their distinction.

## Chapter VI — “Blessed are you who believed” (Luke 1:45)

*(Homily 6 on Ezekiel, no. 8.)* At times the mind of a prophet is touched simultaneously by the past, the present, and the future. Thus, when Elizabeth saw Mary coming to her, [Col. 1201B] she recognized that Mary carried the incarnate Word in her womb and already called her the mother of her Lord, saying: “Why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43).

Concerning Mary’s conception, it is also said to Joseph through the angel: “What has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20). Elizabeth says: “Blessed are you who believed, because the things that were spoken to you by the Lord will be fulfilled.”

By saying “Blessed are you who believed,” she plainly indicates that through the Spirit she recognized the angel’s words that had been spoken to Mary. By adding, “The things that were spoken to you by the Lord will be fulfilled,” she foresaw what would follow in the future.

Thus she was touched by the prophetic spirit simultaneously concerning the past, the present, and the future. She recognized that Mary had believed the angel’s promises; by calling her “mother,” she understood that Mary bore the Redeemer of the human race in her womb; and by proclaiming that all things would be fulfilled, she perceived what would follow in the future.

## Chapter VII — “You will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke 1:76)

[Col. 1201C]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIX, no. 6.)* The way of the Lord may appropriately be understood as that which comes to our heart and pours itself inwardly into us. Hence it is said to John through the Spirit: “You will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.”

Whoever cleanses the hearts of his hearers from the filth of vices by preaching prepares a way before the coming Lord.

## Chapter VIII — “To enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:79)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book IV, no. 4.)* In sacred Scripture “the shadow of death” sometimes signifies forgetfulness of mind. For just as death causes what it kills no longer to exist in life, so forgetfulness causes what it seizes no longer to exist in memory.

Since John was coming to preach to the Hebrew people the Lord whom they had forgotten, Zechariah rightly says: [Col. 1201D] “To enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death.”

To sit in the shadow of death is to lie hidden in forgetfulness, away from knowledge of divine love.

## Chapter IX — “To direct our feet into the way of peace” (Luke 1:79)

*(Homily 36 on the Gospels, no. 4.)* Whoever does not turn from the path of truth into the way of scandal walks in the way of peace. Hence Zechariah says: “To direct our feet into the way of peace.”

We direct our steps into the way of peace when we travel along that course of action in which we do not depart from the grace of our Creator.

## Chapter X — “Mary gave birth to her firstborn son and laid him in a manger” (Luke 2:7)

*(Mixed from Book VII of the exposition of Blessed Job, II. 7.)* Before the coming of our Redeemer, all the saints among the elect Gentiles and the Hebrew people groaned [Col. 1202A] as they awaited their redemption for a long time and desired it.

The Gentiles longed for it because the grace of their Redeemer did not yet refresh them; the Jews, because although they possessed the Law, they did not see the author of the Law.

From the life of blessed Job we know enough to believe that many Gentiles also awaited the coming of our Redeemer. When the Lord was born and Simeon came to the temple in the Spirit, we learned with what longing the holy men of the people of Israel desired to see the mystery of his incarnation.

Hence the same Redeemer says to his disciples: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke 10:24). The longing of both peoples, however, was fulfilled and satisfied through the incarnation of the Redeemer.

Because the Prophet says: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40:6), the Creator of the universe, taking flesh from our substance, wished to become grass so that our flesh might not remain grass forever.

Thus the newborn Lord is placed in a manger, signifying that the holy animals, which had long been found fasting under [Col. 1202B] the Law, would be satisfied with the hay of his incarnation. The manger was filled by the newborn Lord, who offered himself as food to mortal minds, saying: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57).

The redemption of the human race, therefore, which came at the end of the world, was believed to be delayed by those who preceded it from the beginning of the world, and was greatly desired by them because for a long period of time they were separated from the reward of heavenly things.

## Chapter XI — “There were shepherds in that region, and behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them and said: Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people: for today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:8)

*(Homily 10 on the Gospels, no. 1.)* We should ask why, when the Redeemer was born, an angel appeared to the shepherds in Judea, while from the East [Col. 1202C] the Magi were led to worship him not by an angel but by a star.

The reason is that the Jews, as rational beings who used reason, ought to receive preaching from a rational creature—that is, an angel. The Gentiles, however, because they did not know how to use reason, were led to recognize the Lord not by a voice but by signs. Prophecy was given to the Jews as to the faithful, not the unfaithful; signs were given to the Gentiles as to the unfaithful, not the faithful.

## Chapter XII — “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:15)
