*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVIII, no. 34, and Book XXVII, no. 29, and Homily 8 on the Gospels, no. 2.)* God the almighty Father revealed in time, for the salvation of human beings, his only Son whom he begot beyond time. This Son, assuming human nature, came down from the heights to the depths.

The elect angels themselves marveled at the mystery of his incarnation, although they were not redeemed by that same mystery. At the end of the world [Col. 1202D] they glorified the abundance of heavenly grace together with the redeemed human beings.

To kindle us to praise the Creator, when the Lord had been born in the flesh they cried out: “Glory to God in the highest.” They praise and glorify the Redeemer’s power because they join their voices of rejoicing to our redemption; for when they see us received, they rejoice that their own number is being completed.

Before our Redeemer was born in the flesh, we were at enmity with the angels, from whose splendor and purity we were far removed through the guilt of our first sin and through our daily offenses. Because by sinning we were strangers to God, the angels, God’s citizens, counted us strangers to their fellowship.

But the Creator of those spirits came to us and displayed himself as a human being even beneath them, as the Prophet says to the Father concerning him: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6).

Because he found between us and those spirits the scandal of a discordant life, he joined the heights and the depths through wondrous power and even more wondrous mercy: creating what was above and assuming what was below.

[Col. 1203A]

Hence, when the same King was born, the choirs of angels came forth at his announcement, sang a hymn, and, once the discord of an evil life had been overcome, recognized as fellow citizens us whom they had formerly despised, proclaiming with harmonious voice: “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will.”

It is as though they openly said: “Those whom wickedness had separated from us, let goodness now born on earth unite.”

He who for our sake became lower than the angels thus made us equal to the angels by the power of his humbling. And because we came to know our King, the angels recognized us again as their fellow citizens.

Because the King of heaven assumed the earth of our flesh, that angelic height no longer despises our weakness. The angels return to peace with us, set aside their former attitude of hostility, and now honor as companions those whom they had previously despised as weak and rejected.

For this reason Lot and Joshua worship angels and are not forbidden to worship them. John, however, wished to worship an angel in the Apocalypse, but the same angel restrained him from worshiping him, saying: “See that you do not do this, for I am your [Col. 1203B] fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers” (Rev. 22:9).

What does it mean that before the Redeemer’s coming angels were worshiped by human beings and remained silent, but afterward they refused to be worshiped? It means that, after seeing our nature—which they had previously despised—assumed above them, they feared to see it prostrate beneath them.

They no longer dared to despise as weak beneath them the nature they venerate above them in the King of heaven. Nor do they disdain to have as a companion the human being whom they worship as God above themselves.

## Chapter XIII — “The shepherds came in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in the manger” (Luke 2:16)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXI, no. 3.)* The manger may appropriately be understood as sacred Scripture, in which holy animals are fed with the nourishment of the word. Of them the Prophet says: “Your animals will dwell in it” (Ps. 67:11).

The shepherds therefore found the newborn Lord [Col. 1203C] in a manger, because his incarnation is recognized in the Scripture of the prophets, by which we are nourished.

## Chapter XIV — “And a sword will pierce your own soul also” (Luke 2:35)

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIV, no. 17.)* In sacred Scripture the sword sometimes signifies holy preaching and sometimes temporal tribulation.

The sword signifies holy preaching, as Paul says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17). The sword signifies temporal tribulation when it is said to blessed Mary concerning the tribulations that would follow: “And a sword will pierce your own soul also.”

## Chapter XV — “His parents found the child Jesus sitting in the temple in the midst of the teachers, listening to them” (Luke 2:42)

*(Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 25.)* Although our Redeemer is the Creator in heaven and is always the teacher of the angels through the display of his power, he did not wish to become a teacher of human beings on earth before the age of [Col. 1203D] thirty, so that he might instill the force of salutary fear in the rash. Even he who could not fall preached the grace of perfect life only at a perfect age.

For it is written: “When he was twelve years old, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem.” When his parents sought him, it is shortly afterward added: “They found him sitting in the temple in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them.”

We should carefully consider that when Jesus is said to have been twelve years old, he is found sitting in the midst of the teachers, not teaching but questioning. By this example it is shown that a weak person should not dare to teach, since the child wished to be taught by questioning—he who through the power of his divinity supplied the word of knowledge to those very teachers.

Hence Paul says to a disciple: “Command and teach these things, and let no one despise your [Col. 1204A] youth” (1 Tim. 4:12).

We should know that in sacred Scripture “adolescence” is sometimes called “youth.” This is shown more clearly if Solomon’s words are brought forward: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Eccl. 11:9). If the two terms did not designate the same thing, he would not call someone “young” while admonishing him in his adolescence.

## Chapter XVI — Likewise, concerning the foregoing

*(Homily 2 on Ezekiel, no. 3.)* In accordance with the use of reason, therefore, the word of instruction is not supplied except at a mature age. No one should presume to preach at an immature age, since he who by his divinity always teaches the angels in heaven deigned, in the twelfth year of his age, to question human beings on earth.

Because he himself is the Wisdom of God, the angels live by seeing him, and by seeing him they are filled with eternal blessedness.

## Chapter XVII — “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Luke 3:8)

*(Mixed from Book XVIII of the exposition of Blessed Job, no. 52, and Book XX, no. 60, and Homily 11 on Ezekiel, no. 19.)* In sacred Scripture stones are sometimes understood in a negative sense and sometimes in a positive one.

When stones signify insensibility, hard [Col. 1204B] hearts are signified through stones. Thus John says in the passage quoted above: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” By the name “stones” he signifies the hearts of the Gentiles, which were then hard and insensible through unbelief.

Through the Prophet the Lord promises: “I will take the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.”

The Gentile peoples are therefore designated by stones because of their very hardness. They had worshiped stones, and the Prophet says of them: “Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them” (Ps. 113:8).

When John saw the Jews exalting themselves in their estimation of their lineage, and foresaw the Gentiles passing by knowledge of faith into the offspring of Abraham, he said: “Do not say within yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham”—calling the Gentiles hard through unbelief “stones.”

Again, however, strong minds are often signified by stones. Hence Peter says to the saints: “You also, like living [Col. 1204C] stones, are being built up into a spiritual house” (1 Pet. 2).

## Chapter XVIII — “The axe has already been placed at the root of the trees” (Luke 3:9)

(Regul. pastor. part III, ch. 21.) Let the avaricious know that they first wrong God in this: although he gives them everything, they return to him no sacrifice of mercy. Hence the Psalmist says: “He will not give God his reconciliation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul” (Ps. XLVIII, 8). To give the price of redemption is to return a good work to the grace that precedes us. Hence John cries out, saying: “The axe has already been placed at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” Therefore, those who consider themselves innocent because they do not seize what belongs to others should foresee the blow of the approaching axe and abandon the lethargy of their heedless security, lest, while they neglect to bear the fruit of good works, they be utterly dried up from the present life, as though from the greenness of their roots.

Let the avaricious also attend carefully [Col. 1204D] to the fact that the gardener complains more severely against the fig tree that has borne no fruit because it has also occupied the ground. The fruitless fig tree occupies the ground when the mind of the avaricious uselessly preserves what could have benefited many. The fruitless fig tree occupies the ground when a fool burdens with the shadow of idleness a place that someone else could have cultivated through the sunshine of good works.

These avaricious people sometimes say: “When we use what has been granted to us, we do not seek what belongs to others; and although we perform nothing deserving a return of mercy, nevertheless we commit no perverse acts.” They think this because they close the ear of their heart to heavenly words. For the rich man in the Gospel (Luke XVI), who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day, is not said to have seized what belonged to others, but to have used his own possessions without fruitfulness. After this life avenging Gehenna receives him—not because he did anything unlawful, but because through immoderate use he gave himself entirely to what was lawful.

## CHAPTER XIX.—“Whoever has two tunics, let him give to one who has none” (Luke III, 8).

[Col. 1205A]

(Homily 17 on the Gospels, no. 3.) In the peace of the holy Church we can test whether we love our friends, and whether, in a time of persecution, we are able to die for love. Certainly John the Evangelist says: “Whoever has the world’s possessions and sees his brother in need, yet closes his compassion against him—how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John III, 17). John the Baptist likewise says: “Whoever has two tunics, let him give to one who has none.” Therefore, if someone does not give his tunic for God in a time of tranquility, when will he give his soul in a time of persecution? The virtue of love, then, so that it may remain unconquerable in disturbance, must be nourished by mercy in tranquility, so that a person may first learn to spend his possessions for almighty God, and afterward himself.

## CHAPTER XX.—“One stronger than I is coming after me” (Luke III, 16).

(Homily 20 on the Gospels, no. 4.) Because the people had seen John the Baptist endowed with marvelous holiness, they thought that he was the Christ, as the Gospel says: “[Col. 1205B] While the people were wondering, and all were considering in their hearts concerning John whether he might be the Christ, whom they were also seeking, saying: ‘Are you the Christ?’” (Luke III, 15). But unless John had remained humble in his own estimation, he would not have been filled with the spirit of grace. To show what he was, he said: “One stronger than I is coming after me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie.” Behold: although, because of the marvelous working of his virtues, he was such that he was thought to be the Christ, he not only replied that he was not the Christ, but also declared himself unworthy to untie the strap of his sandal—that is, to investigate the mystery of Christ’s incarnation.

## CHAPTER XXI.—“His winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor; he will gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire” (Luke III, 17).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVII, nos. 12–13, and book XXVII, no. 54.) Ears of grain emerge together in the spike, but as they grow they gradually separate from one another, becoming bristling and rigid. So, indeed, the wicked rich rise toward the glory of this world: they are joined by the common bond of nature, but as they grow they divide themselves against one another. One despises another, and one burns against another with the torches of envy. Therefore, those who separate themselves from the unity of love through the swelling of their minds stand rigidly against one another, like ears of grain.

What else, then, should I call the wicked rich of this world but ears of grain belonging to the human race? While they grow proud against one another, yet together oppress the life of those beneath them with honors, they are divided against one another, but nevertheless in agreement press the grains downward. Thus the ears now leap upward while the grains remain hidden, because the power of the reprobate rises visibly while the glory of the elect does not appear. The former display themselves in the pomp of honors; the latter abase themselves in humility. But the time of threshing will come—a time that will break the rigidity of the ears without crushing the solid grains.

Then the pride of the wicked will be shattered; then the life of the elect will be revealed in the full splendor of its integrity. When the unjust perish, the very crushing of the ears brings about the appearance of the grains that had been hidden. When the ears are broken, the whiteness of the grains is displayed, because, when the wicked fall into eternal punishments, it is shown with what truth the righteousness of the saints shines.

Hence John rightly says of the Lord: “His winnowing fan is in his hand; he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, and he will store the wheat in his barn, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.” The elect in the holy Church are God’s grain, to be stored in heavenly barns. For now they endure the chaff on the threshing floor, since in this purification of the holy Church they bear the contrary ways of the reprobate, until the inner farmer separates them with the winnowing fan of judgment and, receiving his elect into the heavenly dwellings as already-cleansed grains, consigns the chaff to eternal fires.

## CHAPTER XXII.—“Jesus went up into Peter’s boat and asked him to put out a little from the land” (Luke V, 3).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVII, nos. 36–37.) The apostles took great care to preach to uneducated peoples what was plain and comprehensible, not what was lofty and difficult. For if they poured forth from their mouths the holy knowledge that they drew from their hearts in its full measure, they would overwhelm their hearers by its immensity rather than refresh them. Hence the apostle Paul, nourishing his hearers through the gradual distillation of words, said: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. III, 1–2).

Who could have endured it if, after being caught up to the third heaven and caught up into paradise, hearing secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak, he had opened up the immeasurable expanses of the heavenly homeland? Or whose hearer’s strength would not have been overwhelmed if the immensity of that water which he could drink inwardly had poured outwardly as far as the tongue of the flesh could contain it?

Therefore, so that uneducated hearers may be nourished not by an inundation of knowledge but by the measured distillation of preaching, God moderates the preaching of teachers, so that the weakness of their hearers may grow strong, nourished by the teachers’ dew. [Col. 1206B] This is well narrated in the Gospel through a mystical description, when it says: “Jesus went up into Peter’s boat and asked him to put out a little from the land; and, sitting there, he preached to the crowds.” What else is signified by Peter’s boat than the Church entrusted to Peter? So that the Lord might preach from it to the crowds who were flocking together, he ordered it to be put out a little from the land. He did not command it to be taken into the deep, yet he ordered it to be moved away from the land—clearly signifying that his preachers ought to proclaim to uneducated peoples neither excessively lofty matters about heaven nor merely earthly things.

## CHAPTER XXIII.—“Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke V, 8).

(Homily 9 on the Gospels, no. 3.) There are many in the Church who fear to undertake the paths of a better life, yet do not fear to lie inert in the laziness of their bodies. When they consider themselves sinners, they tremble to seize the paths of holiness, but they do not fear to remain in their iniquities. Peter, while still placed in weakness, aptly represents them when, after seeing the miracle of the fish, he said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.”

Rather, if you consider yourself a sinner, you ought not to drive the Lord away from you. But those who do not wish to grasp the paths of a better way of life and the stronghold of a more upright life because they see themselves as weak confess themselves to be sinners and drive the Lord away. They flee from the one in whom they ought to have been sanctified, and, as though they had no counsel in their distress, they die while fearing life.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—“Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Luke VI, 31).

(Homily 38 on the Gospels, no. 11.) Love is contained in two commandments: love of God and love of neighbor. Love of neighbor itself is divided into two commandments, as a certain wise man says: “Whatever you hate to have done to you, take care not to do to another” (Tob. IV, 16). And Truth himself proclaims: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.” If we impart to others what we rightly wish to have bestowed upon us, and avoid doing to others what we do not wish done to us, we preserve the laws of love unharmed.

But when someone loves another person, let no one immediately suppose that he possesses love unless he first examines the force of his own affection. For if someone loves another but does not love him for God’s sake, he does not possess love, although he thinks that he does. True love exists when a friend is loved in God and an enemy is loved for God’s sake. For the person who loves those whom he loves for God’s sake already knows how to love even those by whom he is not loved.

Love is ordinarily tested through the adversity of hatred alone. Hence the Lord himself says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. V, 44). Therefore, the person who loves securely is the one who, for God’s sake, also loves the person whom he understands does not love him.

Whoever wishes to possess the wedding garment at the marriage feast—that is, in the holy Church—must therefore observe the two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor. Hence, in the prophet Ezekiel, the vestibule of the city gates situated on the mountain is measured at two cubits, because the entrance to the heavenly city is not opened to us unless, in this Church—which is called a vestibule because it is still outside—we maintain love of God and neighbor.

## CHAPTER XXV.—“Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke VI, 37).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXII, no. 27.) Since, according to Paul’s testimony (1 Cor. XIII), love is described as patient and kind, through patience we ought to endure the evils of others with equanimity, and through kindness to offer our own goods mercifully, as the Redeemer of the human race admonishes us, saying: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you.”

Our giving concerns the things we possess outwardly; forgiving concerns releasing the grief that we inwardly contract from another’s fault. But it must be understood that whoever entirely forgives and does not give, although he has not acted fully, nevertheless retains the better part of mercy. Whoever gives but does not forgive performs no mercy at all, because almighty God does not receive a gift from a hand that offers it with a heart bound by malice. The mind that offers alms must first be cleansed, since everything given to God is weighed according to the mind of the giver.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—“Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, etc.?” (Luke VI, 41).

(Pastoral Rule, part III, ch. 9.) The Lord says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you; pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Luke VI, 27). It is a virtue before human beings to tolerate adversaries, but before God it is a virtue to love them, because God accepts only that sacrifice which the flame of love kindles before his eyes upon the altar of good works.

Hence he says again to certain people who endure patiently but do not love: “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye?” The disturbance of impatience is a speck; malice in the heart is a beam in the eye. The former is agitated by the breeze of temptation, while the latter is carried almost immovably by consummate wickedness.

Thus it is rightly added there: “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye, and then you will see to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.” It is as though he were saying to an inwardly grieving wicked mind that displays itself outwardly as holy through patience: “First shake off from yourself the mass of malice, and then rebuke others for the lightness of their impatience, lest, while you do not strive to overcome hypocrisy, it become worse for you to tolerate another’s wrongdoing.”

## CHAPTER XXVII.—“There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous people” (Luke XV, 10).

(Pastoral Rule, part III, ch. 28.) Often some people, returning to the Lord after sins of the flesh, show themselves so much more fervent in good works as they see themselves more liable to condemnation because of their evils. Often others, persisting in bodily purity, because they perceive that they have less to mourn, think that the innocence of their life is fully sufficient for them and kindle themselves with no goads of spiritual fervor.

Thus a life burning with love after sin is often more pleasing to God than an innocence made sluggish by security. Hence the Judge’s voice says: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.” And again: “There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance” (Luke VII, 47).

We can gather this more quickly from ordinary experience if we weigh the judgments of our own minds. We love more the earth that, after being plowed through thorns, produces abundant fruit than the earth that has had no thorns but, when cultivated, produces a barren crop.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—“The Lord summoned the twelve apostles, gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and sent them to preach the kingdom of God and to heal the sick” (Luke IX, 1).

[Col. 1208A]

(Homily 4 on the Gospels, no. 3.) Miracles were granted and added by the Lord to the holy preachers, so that the power displayed might give credibility to their words and those who preached new things might perform new deeds. While the world was flourishing, the human race increasing, people remaining for a long time in this bodily life, and material wealth abounding, who would believe upon hearing that another life existed? Who would prefer invisible things to visible ones?

But when the sick returned to health, the dead rose to life, lepers received cleansing of the flesh, and demoniacs were snatched from the power of unclean spirits—when so many visible miracles had been performed—who would not believe what he heard concerning invisible things? Visible miracles flash forth for this purpose: to draw the hearts of hearers toward faith in invisible things, so that through what is wondrously done outwardly, people may recognize that what is inward is far more wondrous.

Therefore now also, when the multitude of the faithful has grown within the holy Church, many possess the life of virtues but do not possess signs of the virtues, because an outward miracle is displayed in vain if that which works inwardly is lacking. For, according to the words of the teacher of the Gentiles: “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Cor. XIV, 22).

Hence that same outstanding preacher, when he came to Malta and knew that the island was full of unbelievers, healed Publius’s father, who was afflicted with dysentery and fevers, by praying (Acts XXVIII). But he did not heal Timothy, the assistant of the holy preaching, who was weakened by an ailment of the stomach, by a word; rather, he prepared to treat him by medicinal means, saying: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Tim. V, 23).

Why, then, does he save the unbelieving sick man by a single prayer but not free his sick companion by prayer? Because the unbeliever, who was not inwardly alive, had to be healed outwardly through a miracle, so that the inner power might bring him to life through what outward power displayed. But outward signs were not to be shown to the faithful companion who was living soundly inwardly.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—“Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests” (Luke IX, 58).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX, no. 2.) The Lord says to a certain rich man, proud in his wisdom: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to rest his head.”

Foxes are very deceitful animals that hide themselves in pits or caves. When they appear, they never run along straight paths but through winding turns. Birds, as we know, lift themselves into the air on high flight. By the name “foxes,” then, deceitful and fraudulent demons are signified; by the name “birds,” these same demons in their pride. It is as though he were saying: “Deceitful and exalted demons find their dwelling in your heart, that is, in the thought of pride. But the Son of Man has nowhere to rest his head: my humility finds no rest in your proud mind.”

Like a kind of bird in flight, that first one exalted himself when he said: “I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13). See how high he sought to fly in his pride—and he persuaded the first human beings to make the same flight. They too attempted, as though by flying, to rise above themselves when they were told to taste and be like gods. When they desired the likeness of divinity, they lost the gifts of immortality. They would not have gone to the earth through death if they had been willing to stand humbly upon the earth.

## CHAPTER XXX.—“Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke IX, 60).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, passim, from no. 49 to no. 53.) Sin is completed in action in four ways. First, hidden guilt is committed; afterward the crime is openly revealed before human eyes without shame; then it is made habitual; finally it is nourished either by the seductions of false hope or by the wretched obstinacy of despair.

When guilt has become habitual, the mind resists it more weakly, even if it wishes to do so, because as often as it is bound by repeated wrongdoing, it is tied to the mind by as many bonds. Thus, when the enfeebled mind cannot free itself, it turns toward certain consolations of false comfort, promising itself that the coming Judge will show it such great mercy that he will not utterly destroy even those whom he finds deserving of rebuke.

This becomes still worse because the speech of many like-minded people agrees with it, when they even magnify evil deeds with praise, as the Psalmist says: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and when the wicked has acted unjustly, he is blessed” (Ps. IX, 24). Thus guilt continually grows, nourished by approval. The wound that appears worthy of the reward of praise is neglected rather than healed.

Hence Solomon says: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. I, 10). Sinners entice when they either introduce evils to be committed through flattering words or exalt evils already committed through approval.

It must also be understood that the first three kinds of sinners are more easily corrected in the order of their descent; the fourth is more difficult to amend. Hence our Redeemer raised a girl in the house, a young man outside the gate, and Lazarus in the tomb.

The one who lies hidden in sin is still dead in the house. The one whose iniquity has been exposed to the shamelessness of public commission is already being led, as it were, outside the gate. The one who is weighed down in the commission of wickedness and oppressed by habitual practice is pressed beneath the mound of burial.

Yet in his mercy he calls these people back to life, because divine grace often illumines by the light of its regard not only those dead in hidden iniquities but also those dead in open sins and weighed down by the burden of evil habit.

But when the fourth dead man is announced by a disciple, our Redeemer recognizes him but does not raise him, because it is extremely difficult for one whom, after the practice of evil habit, the tongues of flatterers also receive, to be recalled from the death of his mind. Of him it is rightly said: “Let the dead bury their own dead.”

The dead bury the dead when sinners bury sinners beneath the approval they give them. For what else is it to sin than to die, and what else is it to bury than to conceal? Those who pursue the sinner with praise conceal the dead beneath the mound of their words.

Lazarus too was dead, but he was not buried by the dead. Faithful women had covered him, and they also announced his death to the one who gives life. Therefore he immediately returned to the light, because when the mind dies in sin, it is brought back to life more quickly if vigilant thoughts remain alive over it.

Sometimes, as was said above, false hope in divine mercy does not seize the sinner’s mind. Instead, a worse despair pierces the mind, which fears its Maker in a disordered way because of the sins it has committed, and utterly destroys every hope of forgiveness, so that it does not return to correction.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—“But you go and announce the kingdom of God” (Luke IX, 60).

[Col. 1209D]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX, no. 42.) It must be understood that sometimes lesser goods are to be left aside for the sake of greater benefits in our actions. For who does not know that burying the dead is a good work? Yet when a certain man asked the Lord to allow him to depart and bury his father, he was told: “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you go and announce the kingdom of God.”

The service of burial had to be set aside for the office of preaching, because by the former he would lay in the earth those dead in the flesh, while by the latter he would raise to life those dead in soul.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—“No one who puts his hand to the plow, etc.” (Luke IX, 62).

(Homily 3 on Ezekiel, nos. 16–17, 14, 3–4.) God’s elect pass from earthly activities to spiritual ones in such a way that they do not turn back in any manner to what they have left behind. In contrast, it is said of the reprobate: “They turned back in their hearts to Egypt.” And Truth himself says: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

To put one’s hand to the plow is, as it were, through the plowshare of compunction to open the soil of one’s heart so that it may bring forth fruit. But the person who looks back after the plow returns, after beginning a good work, to the evils he abandoned.

This does not happen to God’s elect, because they no longer look back with any desire toward what they left behind, and they continually direct the contemplation of their minds toward the eternal things they desire. Hence that great preacher, who had penetrated into the secrets of the third heaven, said: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. III, 13–14).

The eternal things are before us, while temporal things are behind us, because as we go forward we find the former, and as we withdraw we leave the latter behind us, as though behind our backs. Paul, therefore, stretched toward what lay ahead, had forgotten what lay behind, because he despised temporal things and sought only what is eternal.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—“And he sent them two by two before his face” (Luke X, 1).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXV, no. 41.) When the Lord sent preachers to announce the Gospel, the Gospel testifies that he sent them two by two, saying: “The Lord Jesus appointed seventy-two disciples and sent them two by two before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come.”

They are described as having been sent two by two so that, whether because there are two commandments of love or because companionship cannot exist with fewer than two, the holy preachers might learn from the very character of their mission how greatly they ought to love the harmony of companionship.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—“I was seeing Satan fall from heaven like lightning” (Luke X, 18).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIII, no. 13.) There are four forms in which all the pride of the arrogant is displayed: when they think that they possess a good from themselves; when they believe that it has been given to them from above and suppose that they received it because of their own merits; when they boast of possessing what they do not possess; or when, despising others, they desire to appear uniquely to possess the good that they do possess.

He boasted of possessing good from himself to whom the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. IV, 7).

Again, so that we would not believe that the good of grace was given to us because of our preceding merits, the same apostle admonishes us, saying: “You have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. II, 8). He also says of himself: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy” (1 Tim. I, 13). By these words he plainly declares that grace is not granted because of merits, since he showed from his own case both what he deserved because of malice and what he received because of benevolence.

Again, some boast that they possess what they do not possess, as is said to the angel of the church of Laodicea: “Because you say, ‘I am rich and have grown wealthy, and I need nothing,’ and you do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Rev. III, 17).

Again, some, despising the rest, desire to appear uniquely to possess the good that they possess. Hence the Pharisee descended from the Temple without justification, because he attributed the merits of good works to himself as though uniquely his and placed himself above the praying tax collector.

The holy apostles too are recalled from this fault of elation. When they returned from preaching and, exalted, said: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name” (Luke X, 17), the Lord immediately replied, so that they would not rejoice in this uniqueness of their miracles: “I was seeing Satan fall from heaven like lightning” (Isa. XIV, 13).

He himself, exalted in his uniqueness, had said: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will be like the Most High.” And wonderfully, to suppress elation in the hearts of the disciples, the Lord at once recalled the judgment of ruin that the first teacher of elation had received, so that in the author of pride they might learn what they should fear from the beginning of elation.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—“Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20).

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 7, no. 17; in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIII, no. 13.) Truth recalls the disciples from private joy to common joy when, returning from preaching and rejoicing over the subjection of demons, he admonishes them, saying: “Do not rejoice in this, but rather rejoice and exult because your names are written in heaven.”

Not all the elect cast out demons, but the names of all the elect are nevertheless recorded in heaven. The disciples are therefore admonished to lay aside private joy and rejoice in common and everlasting happiness.

In this fourth form of arrogance, then, the human mind frequently falls, boasting that it possesses what it has as though it alone possessed it. In this respect it approaches most closely to the devil’s likeness, because whoever rejoices in possessing a good uniquely, whoever seeks to appear higher than the rest, imitates the one who, despising the good of the fellowship of the angels, established his seat in the north and proudly sought the likeness of the Most High, striving through an evil desire to break out toward a certain summit of uniqueness.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—“He approached and bound up his wounds, pouring in wine and oil” (Luke X, 34).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XX, no. 14.) Pastoral discipline or mercy is greatly lacking when either is maintained without the other. Rulers ought to possess both toward their subjects: mercy that counsels justly and discipline that corrects with kindness.

Hence wine and oil are applied to the wounds of the half-dead man who was brought by the Samaritan into the inn: the wine bites the wounds, while the oil soothes them. Thus everyone who is responsible for healing wounds should apply in the wine the bite of strictness and in the oil the gentleness of compassion, so that what is putrid may be cleansed by the wine and what can be healed may be soothed by the oil.

Gentleness must therefore be mixed with severity, and a certain balance must be made from both, so that subjects are neither ulcerated by excessive harshness nor loosened by excessive kindness.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—“Jesus entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house; and she had a sister named Mary” (Luke X, 38).

(Compiled from book VI of the exposition of Blessed Job, nos. 57 and 61; homily 3 on Ezekiel, no. 9; and especially book II on Ezekiel, homily 2, no. 8.) There are two lives of the saints: the active and the contemplative.

The active life is to give bread to the hungry, to teach the ignorant with the word of wisdom, to correct the one who errs, to recall the proud neighbor to the path of humility, to care for the sick, to distribute to each person what is useful, and to provide how the responsibilities entrusted to us may be maintained.

The contemplative life, on the other hand, is to retain love of God and neighbor with the whole mind, but to rest from outward action and cling solely to the desire for the Creator, so that one no longer wishes to do anything, but, trampling all cares underfoot, the mind burns with longing to see the face of its Creator. It then knows how to bear the burden of corruptible flesh with grief and to desire with all its longing to participate in the angelic choirs that sing hymns, to be joined to the heavenly citizens, and to rejoice in incorruption before God for eternity.

The active life, however, comes first in time, because one advances from good works to contemplation. Contemplative life is greater in merit than active life, because the latter labors in the practice of present works, while the former already tastes inwardly, through experience, the rest that is to come.

That contemplative life is later in time but greater in merit than active life is shown by the sacred words of the Gospel, in which two women, Martha and Mary, are reported to have acted differently. Martha was busy with extensive service; Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet, was listening to his words.

What else is signified by Martha, occupied with outward services, than the active life? And what else is expressed by Mary, who sat listening to the Lord’s words, than the contemplative life? One was devoted to work, the other to contemplation; one served active life through outward ministry, the other contemplative life through the suspension of her heart upon the word.

Although active life is good, contemplative life is better, because the former comes to an end with mortal life, while the latter grows more fully in immortal life. Thus, when Martha complained to the Lord about the leisure of her sister Mary, because Mary was neglecting to help her, she heard him reply: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.”

Behold: Martha’s part and care are not condemned, but Mary’s part is also praised. He does not say that Mary chose a good part, but the best part, so that Martha’s part too might be judged good, since the merits of active life are great, but those of contemplative life greater.

Why Mary’s part is the best is added when he says: “It will not be taken away from her.” The works of active life pass away with the body, but the joys of contemplative life grow stronger through their consummation. Who will offer bread to the hungry in the eternal homeland, where no one is hungry? Who will give drink to the thirsty, where no one is thirsty? Who will bury the dead, where no one dies?

Active life therefore comes to an end with the body and is taken away with the present age; contemplative life neither ends nor is taken away. It begins here, but when the light of the present age has been removed, it is perfected in the heavenly homeland. The fire of love that begins to burn here burns more intensely in love of the one whom it loves when it sees him.

It must be understood that active life can be held perfectly, and we complete it through works; but, while we remain in this life, we taste only the beginnings of intimate contemplation. Even when we strive for it, we can scarcely touch a small portion of it. However greatly the mind burns with love, however strongly the power of thought reaches toward God, it does not yet see perfectly what it loves, but only begins to see what it is to love, because, as the strongest preacher says: “Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I am known” (1 Cor. XIII, 12).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it travels through waterless places seeking rest, and does not find it, etc.” (Luke XI, 24).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIII, no. 8.) The minds of worldly people, devoted to temporal glory, flow downward toward the desire for outward glory. While they strive to surpass others in the height of honors, they grant the ancient enemy a place where he may find rest within them.

Hence Truth says in the Gospel that the spirit, when it has gone out, travels through dry and waterless places and does not find rest; for it finds the house it had left empty and swept clean, and re-enters it in greater number.

Because earth becomes fluid when it is watered, dry and waterless places signify the hearts of the righteous, which are dried by the strength of discipline from every moisture of carnal desire. Moist places, however, signify the minds of earthly people, whom the moisture of carnal desire fills and makes fluid. Moist places also signify works of pleasure.

A foot does not slip on dry ground, but one fixed on something slippery is scarcely kept secure. Those who cannot stand upright in justice in this life travel along the path of the present life in moist places. In these moist places, that is, in the slippery activity of reprobate people, the ancient enemy finds rest.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—“Then he takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and entering in, they dwell there” (Luke 11:24).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book VII, no. 20.)* The Lord often begins, through scourges, to bring about in us the breaking down of vices; but when the mind becomes elated by the very beginning of its progress, and, as though already rising through the virtues, [Col. 1213A] lifts itself up, it opens an entrance to the adversary raging against it. Penetrating the innermost parts of the heart, he shatters whatever he finds there arising from the zeal of a good beginning; and he displays himself with all the greater violence in its destruction, the more grievously he is pained because he had been cast out, even if only for a short time. Hence, as the Gospel bears witness through the voice of Truth, the unclean spirit who went out alone returns to the neglected house of the conscience with seven spirits.

## CHAPTER XL.—“No one places a lamp under a bushel, but on a lampstand” (Luke 11:33).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXX, no. 77.)* All God’s elect esteem the grace of preaching as something of great importance, but regard the usefulness of the body as something of little importance. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp and places it under a bushel, but on a lampstand.” By the bushel, temporal advantage is understood; by the lamp, the light of preaching. To place a lamp under a bushel, therefore, is to conceal the grace [Col. 1213B] of preaching for the sake of temporal advantage—something none of the elect does. And rightly it is added there: “But on a lampstand.” For by the lampstand the condition of the body is signified; the lamp is placed upon it when care for preaching is set before the same body.

## CHAPTER XLI.—“The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is simple,” etc. (Luke 11:34).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII, no. 30.)* When we undertake anything, we must carefully ensure that what follows in the deed does not become perverse because it was not generated from a rightly ordered intention of thought. Hence the Lord rightly says in the Gospel: “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is simple, your whole body will be luminous; but if your eye is wicked, your whole body will be dark.” For what is expressed by the eye except the intention of the heart that precedes its deed? Before it exercises itself in action, it already contemplates what it desires. And what is designated by the term “body” except each action, [Col. 1213C] which follows its intention as a seeing eye?

The eye, therefore, is the lamp of the body, because through the ray of a good intention the merits of an action are illumined. “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be luminous”: for if we direct our intention rightly through simplicity of thought, a good work is produced, even if it may appear less good; and when something is done with a good intention, the action arising from that intention is not at all darkened before God.

“And if your eye is wicked, your whole body will be dark”: for when something right is done with a perverse intention, even if it is seen to shine before human beings, it is obscured in the judgment of the inward Judge. Hence it is rightly added: “See therefore that the light which is in you is not darkness. If the light which is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be?” (Matthew 6:23). For if we darken through a bad intention what we believe we are doing well, how great are those evils which we do not fail to recognize as evil even while committing them? And if we perceive nothing clearly where we hold what is, as it were, the light of discernment, with what blindness do we stumble over those things we perpetrate without [Col. 1213D] discernment? Therefore, throughout all our works, our intention must be weighed with vigilant care.

## CHAPTER XLII.—“You tithe mint and dill and cumin, and leave aside the weightier matters of the law” (Luke 11:42).

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 33.)* Those who guard themselves from minor sins but are sometimes submerged in grave ones ought to consider that, when they commit greater evils before God, they are openly wicked, while, when they preserve small goods before human beings, they are hypocritically holy. In the former they act wickedly; through the latter they conceal from people the fact that they are wicked.

Hence it is said to the Pharisees: “Straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel” (Matthew 23:24). It is as though he were saying openly: “You distinguish the smallest evils, but devour the greater ones.” Hence again they are rebuked by the mouth of Truth when they hear: “You tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and leave aside the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, [Col. 1214A] and faith.”

Nor should we hear carelessly that, when he spoke of tithing the smallest things, he chose the last examples from herbs, yet mentioned fragrant ones. By this he clearly showed that hypocrites, while observing small matters, seek to spread from themselves the fragrance of a holy reputation; and although they neglect to fulfill the greatest commandments, they nevertheless observe those smallest matters which, in human judgment, spread their scent far and wide.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—“What shall I do, because I have nowhere to gather my crops?” etc. (Luke 12:17).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XV, no. 26.)* Every greedy person first pants to gather through avarice what he has coveted; but after he has heaped up many things, as though in a certain belly of avarice, he is constricted when satiated. For while he is anxious about how to preserve what he has acquired, his very satiety narrows him.

The field of a certain rich man had produced abundant crops; but because he had nowhere to store so much, he said: “What shall I do, because I have nowhere [Col. 1214B] to gather my crops?” And he said: “I shall do this: I shall destroy my barns and build larger ones.” Thus, constrained by abundance, he said, “What shall I do?” As though weighed down by a great quantity of food, he was feverishly agitated.

Let us consider with how many prayers he desired that his field should produce abundant crops. Yet now his prayers have been fulfilled, because the field has produced abundant crops. But since the places for storing them are insufficient, the rich man, overwhelmed by increase, does not know what to do. O distress born from satiety! The mind of the greedy man is distressed by the abundance of the field. For by saying, “What shall I do?” he clearly indicates that, pressed by the desires of his prayers, he was laboring beneath a kind of burden of possessions.

The mind of the greedy rich man, which had first sought rest from abundance, is afterward wearied far more severely by anxiety over its preservation.

## CHAPTER XLIV.—“Soul, you have many good things” (Luke 12:19).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XIV, no. 19; book XXVIII, no. 4.)* We often see certain rich people who could have possessed wealth and honor without guilt, if only they had been willing to possess them with humility. But they are exalted by their possessions, [Col. 1214C] inflated by their honors, disdain others, and place all their confidence for life in the abundance of their goods.

Hence a certain rich man said: “Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast.” Behold, he had fixed his hope upon unstable things, and had placed and secured the confidence of his hope in things that pass away. To despair of the Creator and to place hope in a creature are one and the same thing. For while God remains forever, everything passes away. What, then, is clinging to passing things except fleeing from the One who remains?

Whoever wishes to avoid being swept away must flee what is swept away, lest through what he loves he be compelled to come to what he avoids. For whoever clings to passing things is dragged there, plainly, where the thing he holds is heading.

First, therefore, one must take care not to love temporal things; afterward, one must take care not to place confidence in those same temporal things, which one retains not for pleasure but for use. For the mind joined to things running their course soon loses its own stability: the current of the present life carries away the one whom [Col. 1214D] it raises up.

## CHAPTER XLV.—“Fool, this night they are demanding your soul from you” (Luke 12:20).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXV, no. 3.)* However late the wicked are taken from this life, they are taken suddenly and unexpectedly, because they do not know how to foresee their end by reflection. What could not be thought of beforehand is sudden.

That foolish rich man was suddenly snatched away. He abandoned the barns he was preparing and found the place in hell that he had not foreseen. On that same night he was taken away who had been expecting many years of abundance in his possessions, so that although he had looked ahead by gathering resources for a long future, he did not see even the following day.

In thought he was preparing his soul for one thing, but by the sentence pronounced upon him he was sent toward another. While he lived, he contemplated one thing; while he died, he experienced another. He left behind the temporal things over which he had long deliberated and found the eternal things he had not expected.

Therefore, because of the blindness of his ignorance, he is rightly rebuked by the divine [Col. 1215A] sentence: “Fool, this night they are demanding your soul from you.” It was taken away in the night because it had been lost in the darkness of the heart. It was taken away in the night because he did not wish to possess the light of consideration by which he might foresee what he could suffer.

Hence the Apostle Paul rightly says to disciples who are thinking about future things: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you like a thief” (1 Thessalonians 5:4). The day of departure overtakes a person like a thief in the night when it casts out the souls of fools who do not foresee what is to come.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII, no. 12.)* The Lord says to holy preachers: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands.” To gird one’s loins is to restrain lust in one’s conduct, for the delight of the flesh is located in the loins. Thus lust is signified by the loins, and the brightness of good [Col. 1215B] works by the lamps.

Holy preachers are therefore commanded to gird their loins and hold lamps. It is as though they were hearing openly: “First restrain lust within yourselves, and then display to others examples of good works through yourselves.”

## CHAPTER XLVII.—“But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying,’” etc. (Luke 12:45).

*(Pastoral Rule, part II, chapter 6.)* Those who preside must labor without interruption so that, to the extent that their power is seen to be great outwardly, it may be humbled inwardly among them. Otherwise their minds may be carried away by delight in their authority into exaltation.

Hence Peter says: “Not domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3). Hence Truth itself, calling us toward higher achievements of virtue, says: “Whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave, just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Matthew 20: [Col. 1215C] 26).

For this reason he indicates what punishments await the servant exalted by the authority he has received, saying: “But if that wicked servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to beat his fellow servants, while he eats and drinks with drunkards, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in two and appoint his portion with the hypocrites.”

He is rightly numbered among the hypocrites who, under the pretense of discipline, turns the ministry of governance into an opportunity for domination.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—“The servant who knew his master’s will and did not act according to it will be beaten,” etc. (Luke 12:47).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XV, no. 51.)* There are some who, because Truth says, “The servant who did not know his master’s will and did things deserving blows will be beaten little; but the servant who knew his master’s will and did not act according to it will be beaten much,” do not wish to know what they ought to do. They suppose that they will receive fewer blows [Col. 1215D] if they do not know what they ought to perform.

But not to know is one thing; to have refused to know is another. The one who wishes to grasp knowledge but is unable to do so does not know. But the one who turns his ear away from the voice of Truth so that he may not know is called not ignorant but contemptuous.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—“From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required” (Luke 12:48).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXV, no. 1.)* Because we have closed our eyes to inward and invisible things and feed upon visible ones, we often honor a person not for what he himself is but for what surrounds him. When we do not consider what he is but what power he possesses, our respect of persons is determined not by the persons themselves but by the things attached to them.

Thus it happens that even someone honored outwardly comes to be despised inwardly by us. For while he is considered worthy of honor because of what surrounds him, he is placed below his possessions in our judgment.

But almighty [Col. 1216A] God examines human life solely according to the quality of its merits, and often punishes more severely on account of what he has granted here in greater measure for ministry, as Truth bears witness when it says: “From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required.”

## CHAPTER L.—“I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49).

*(Homily 2 on Ezekiel, no. 12.)* When the name “fire” is used figuratively, it sometimes signifies the Holy Spirit and sometimes the wickedness of the mind. The Holy Spirit is usually represented by fire, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?”

Fire is cast upon the earth when an earthly mind, breathed upon by the ardor of the Holy Spirit, has its carnal desires consumed. [Col. 1216B] When the carnal mind receives the Holy Spirit, set ablaze by spiritual love, it mourns the evil it has done. The earth burns when, as conscience accuses it, the sinner’s heart is scorched and consumed in the pain of repentance.

But concerning evil fire it is said: “And now fire consumes the adversaries” (Hebrews 10:27), because the worst heart wastes away through its own wickedness.

## CHAPTER LI.—“When you go with your adversary to the magistrate along the way, make an effort,” etc. (Luke 12:58).

*(Homily 39 on the Gospels, no. 5; in the Exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, no. 69.)* Because all wicked and perverse people despise God’s commandments in this life, at the end of life they will be handed over to their enemies, with whom they will be joined in an everlasting association of condemnation at the eternal judgment, as it is written: “When you go with your adversary to the magistrate along the way, make an effort to be freed from him, lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison.”

Our adversary along the way is the word of God, which in the present life stands opposed to our carnal desires. The one who humbly submits to its commandments is freed from it. Otherwise, “the adversary will hand you over to the judge, and the judge will hand you over to the officer,” because the sinner, guilty on account of having despised the Lord’s word, will be held liable in the judge’s examination.

The judge will hand him [Col. 1216C] over to the officer because he will permit him to be handed over to an evil spirit for punishment, so that the spirit may exact the soul—which willingly consented to guilt—from the body for punishment.

The officer is understood to be that importunate persuader who once gave the human race the coin of deception and still does not cease daily to demand the debt of death. In paradise he lent money to the sinful human being, but as iniquity increases he demands it daily with interest.

The officer is the devil. By evil persuasion he offered the hope of immortality; by deception he demands the tribute of death. By persuasion he introduced guilt; by raging he demands punishment.

The officer will therefore send the sinner into prison, because through the evil spirit he is thrust into hell until the day of judgment arrives, after which [Col. 1216D] the spirit itself will be tormented together with him in the fires of hell.

## CHAPTER LII.—“Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke 13:24).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XI, no. 68.)* When the human mind strives toward better things, it struggles as though against the force of a river. But when it relaxes its intention of ascending, it is carried downward without effort. Because ascending involves labor and descending ease, the Lord warns those who are to enter through the narrow gate, saying: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate.”

What is the narrow gate except living in this world while possessing nothing of this world’s desire; not coveting what belongs to others; not clinging to what belongs to oneself; despising the praises of the world; loving reproaches for God’s sake; fleeing the world’s glory; pursuing contempt; despising flatterers; honoring those who despise us; dismissing from the heart the evils of those who harm us; and preserving immovably in the heart toward them the grace of love?

Thus, when the Lord was about to speak of entering this narrow gate, he first said: “Strive.” For unless there is struggle in the mind, the wave of the world cannot be overcome; through it the soul is always drawn back downward.

Because of the weight of its mutability, the mind is always driven toward something other than what it is, [Col. 1217A] Unless it is held in its proper state by strict discipline and vigilance, it continually slips into worse things. For it abandoned the One who always stands firm, and thereby lost the stability it could have possessed.

## CHAPTER LIII.—“If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother,” etc. (Luke 14:28).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book VI, nos. 40–41.)* We often see some people who have no desires for the present life and reject the world both in conduct and in profession, yet, because of disordered affections toward their relatives, break into law courts, occupy themselves with quarrels over earthly things, abandon the freedom of inward peace, and restore within themselves the pursuits of the world that they had long since destroyed.

The perfection of life already begun had freed them from the present age, but disordered love of earthly kinship binds them. Those, however, who pursue the reward of an eternal pledge with strict devotion, just as they despise themselves for divine love, so they set aside everything by which they perceive themselves to be hindered. And when it is necessary for God’s sake that they serve everyone within their power, for God’s sake they even refuse private services [Col. 1217B] to their relatives.

For this reason, when someone said, “Permit me first to go and bury my father” (Matthew 8:21), he immediately heard from the mouth of Truth: “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you, go and announce the kingdom of God.”

In this we should note that, when the chosen disciple is restrained from burying his parent, it is not permitted for anyone, out of carnal affection and for the Lord’s sake, to show a dead father the devotion that he ought to show even to strangers for the Lord’s sake.

Hence again Truth says: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.”

Here, when hatred even of our own life is added to hatred of our relatives, it is plainly shown that we are commanded to hate our relatives just as ourselves—not so that we may cease loving them, but so that, when they are dragging us away from eternal things, we may set aside their carnal favor. We must learn, through a measured art of discernment, both to love them appropriately and to hate them beneficially, so that hatred may arise through love, and we may be able to love them more truly [Col. 1217C] through hatred.

## CHAPTER LIV.—“Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

*(Homily 32 on the Gospels, no. 1; in the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXI, no. 22.)* Because our Lord and Redeemer came into the world as a new human being, he issued new commandments to the world. He set the novelty of his life against the old life of ours, which had been nourished in vices.

For what did the old, carnal human being know except to possess something in this world; to gird himself against dangers with immense labor; to defend temporal things through laborious vigilance, even with quarrels? What did he know except to retain what was his, seize what belonged to another if he could, and covet it if he could not seize it?

But when the heavenly and new human being set new commandments before those who followed him, he said: [Col. 1217D] “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple.” It is as though he were saying openly: “You who, through your old life, covet what belongs to others, give away even what belongs to you through the discipline of a new way of life.”

How, then, should the perfect Christian defend earthly possessions by quarrels, when he is now commanded not to possess them? Therefore, when we lose our own possessions, if we follow God perfectly, we have been lightened of a great burden along the road of this life.

When the necessity of this same journey imposes care for possessions upon us, some who seize them must simply be endured; others must be restrained while charity is preserved—not merely so that they do not take away what is ours, but so that, by seizing what is not theirs, they do not destroy themselves.

We ought to fear the plunderers themselves more than we ought to burn with eagerness to defend irrational possessions. For even if they are not seized, we lose these things when we die; but with those people we shall be one both now according to the order of our condition and, if they strive to amend, afterward upon receiving the reward.

Who does not know that we ought to love less the things we use and more [Col. 1218A] what we are? If, therefore, we speak to plunderers for their own benefit, we are now claiming for ourselves not only the temporal things but also the eternal things that belong to them.

In this matter we must carefully observe that, through fear of necessity, desire for possessions does not creep in, and that a prohibition inflamed by zeal, stretched by an excessive impulse, does not burst forth into the disgrace of hateful contention. When peace with one’s neighbor is torn from the heart over an earthly possession, it is plainly evident that the possession is loved more than the neighbor.

For if we do not have the inward compassion of charity even toward a neighbor who is a plunderer, we persecute ourselves worse than the plunderer does. We devastate ourselves more grievously than another could, because, while willingly abandoning the good of love, we lose inwardly from ourselves what we were losing from him only outwardly.

## CHAPTER LV.—“How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread!” (Luke 15:17).

*(Dialogues, book II, chapter 3.)* Whenever we are carried excessively outside ourselves by the movement of thought, we exist [Col. 1218B] yet are not with ourselves, because, failing to see ourselves, we wander through other things.

Can we say that the prodigal son was with himself when he went into a distant region, consumed the portion he had received, attached himself to one of its citizens, fed pigs, saw them eating husks, and himself desired to eat them? Yet later, when he began to think about the good things he had lost, it is written of him: “Coming to himself, he said: ‘How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread!’”

If, then, he was with himself, how did he come back to himself?

It is also written of the Apostle Peter that, after he had been led out of prison by an angel, “coming to himself, he said: ‘Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the people of the Jews’” (Acts 12:11).

We are therefore led outside ourselves in two ways: either we fall beneath ourselves through a lapse of thought, or we are lifted above ourselves through the grace of contemplation. The one who fed pigs fell beneath himself through wandering of mind and uncleanness; but the one whom the angel released and whose mind he carried into ecstasy was [Col. 1218C] indeed outside himself, yet above himself.

Both returned, therefore: the one when he gathered himself from the error of his conduct back into his heart, and the other when he returned from the summit of contemplation to that which he had previously been in ordinary understanding.

## CHAPTER LVI.—“Quickly bring out the first robe and put it on him” (Luke 15:22).

*(Homily 36 on the Gospels, no. 7; book XII on Job, no. 9.)* God chose those whom the world despises, because contempt itself often recalls a person to himself.

The one who left his father and squandered prodigally the portion of property he had received, after he began to hunger, came to himself and said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread! But I am dying here of hunger. I will arise and go to my father.”

He had gone far away from himself when he was sinning; and if he had not grown hungry, he would not have returned to himself. For after he became needy in earthly things, he began to consider what he had lost in spiritual things.

And because he had first been stripped in paradise of the garment of righteousness and [Col. 1218D] innocence that had been granted to him, the father deigned to cover the nakedness of his sinful son. When the son returned, he said: “Quickly bring out the first robe and put it on him.”

The first robe is the garment of innocence, which the human being received when well created but lost after being wickedly persuaded by the serpent.

## CHAPTER LVII.—“And put a ring on his hand” (Luke 15:22).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, no. 12.)* Sacred Scripture commonly calls faith a ring, or a seal. For the younger son, who returned to his father after consuming his property, received a ring as a gift.

The Gentile people, who, after losing immortality, return to God through repentance, are fortified by the seal of faith.

## CHAPTER LVIII.—“Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:9).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXI, nos. 29–30.)* All [Col. 1219A] who give alms to the poor ought to possess two virtues—humility and compassion—so joined to one another that they are always supported by one another’s work. Thus humility must not abandon the grace of generosity while honoring one’s neighbor, nor must compassion become swollen with pride while giving to another’s need.

Let compassion support humility toward one’s neighbor, and humility support compassion, so that, when you see someone in need who shares your human nature, you neither cease to guide him through compassion nor neglect to honor him through pride.

There are some, however, who, as soon as needy brothers ask them for what is necessary, first hurl insulting words at them before giving their gifts. Although they complete the ministry of compassion with their possessions, they lose the grace of humility through their words. They often seem to be paying compensation for the injury they have already inflicted when they give gifts after their insults.

It is not a great work to give what has been requested, since by the very gift of their giving they scarcely conceal the excess of their speech. A benefit should therefore be offered through compassion, and a good [Col. 1219B] word should be given through humility.

Others, by contrast, do not strive to support needy brothers with material things, although they are able to do so, but comfort them only with flattering words. Our love must always be shown together with respectful speech and the ministry of generosity.

Moreover, there are some who do not know how to extend the compassion of their hearts even to strangers, but pity only those whom they have come to know through habitual association. Among them familiarity plainly has greater force than nature, since they give what is necessary to certain people not because they are human beings but because they are known.

In a compassionate mind, therefore, nature ought to be worth more than familiarity, although anyone who is in need is, by the very fact that he is a human being, no stranger.

To tame the pride of the giver, it is greatly beneficial for him, when he grants earthly things, carefully to weigh the words of the heavenly Teacher, who says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.”

If we acquire eternal dwellings through their friendship, we must certainly consider [Col. 1219C] that we are offering gifts to patrons rather than bestowing gifts upon the needy. Hence Paul says: “Let your abundance supply their want, so that their abundance may also be the supply of your want” (2 Corinthians 8:14).

We should carefully reflect that those whom we now see in need we shall one day see in abundance; and we who are seen to abound shall one day be in need if we neglect to give generously.

Therefore, whoever now gives temporal assistance to the poor, from whom he will afterward receive an eternal return, cultivates, so to speak, the earth for harvest: what it has received, it returns more abundantly.

It remains, then, that no pride should ever arise from a gift, since the rich person, by giving to the poor, is working perpetually so that the poor person will not be poor.

Whoever raises himself above the one to whom he has given something through the arrogance of pride commits a greater inward fault through pride than the reward he gains outwardly through generosity. He becomes inwardly naked of good things when he despises the naked person whom he clothes, because he makes himself worse than he was by considering himself better than his needy neighbor.

The one who lacks clothing is less poor [Col. 1219D] than the one who lacks humility. Therefore, when we see those who share our nature lacking outward things, we must consider how many inward goods are lacking in us, so that our thought may not exalt itself above the poor when it carefully sees that we are truly more needy because we are needy inwardly.

## CHAPTER LIX.—“When Jesus had entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the sabbath to eat bread, behold, there was a man with dropsy before him. Taking hold of him, he healed him and dismissed him” (Luke 14:2).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XIV, no. 14.)* Our Redeemer cures a man with dropsy before the house of a Pharisee in order to argue against avarice. It is written: “The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things and mocked him” (Luke 16:14).

What, then, does it mean that the man with dropsy is cured before the house of the Pharisee, except that through one person’s bodily illness the illness of the [Col. 1220A] heart is expressed in another?

A person with dropsy, the more he drinks, the more he thirsts. So too every greedy person multiplies thirst by drinking, because when he has obtained what he desires, he breathes more eagerly after other things he may desire. For the one whose desire increases through acquisition has his thirst increase through drinking.

## CHAPTER LX.—“What is exalted among human beings is abominable before God” (Luke 16:15).

*(Homily 28 on the Gospels, nos. 2–3.)* Because we venerate in human beings not the nature in which they were made according to the image of God, but honors and riches, if some poor person asked us to go to him, our pride would immediately answer us in silent thought: “Do not go, because you degrade yourself; your honor will be despised; your position will become low.”

Behold, the one who came from heaven does not disdain to meet a servant on earth; yet we, who are from the earth, disdain to humble ourselves on earth!

What could be more worthless or more contemptible before God than to preserve honor among human beings and not fear the eyes of the inward witness?

Hence in the holy [Col. 1220B] Gospel he says to the Pharisees: “You are those who justify yourselves before human beings. But God knows your hearts, because what is exalted among human beings is abominable before God.”

Take note, brothers; take note of what is said. If what is exalted among human beings is abominable before God, then the thought of our heart is as low before God as it is high among human beings; and the humility of our heart is as high before God as it is low among human beings.

Let us therefore despise whatever good we do. Let none of our works inflate us; let neither abundance of possessions nor glory exalt us. If we inwardly swell with any good things that flow toward us, we are despised by God.

Therefore, brothers, think about these things; weigh them all with full attention. Do not venerate the goods of this world in your neighbors. For God’s sake, honor this in human beings: that they have been made according to the image of God, although they have not been entrusted to you.

You preserve this truly in your neighbors if you do not first become inflated in your own hearts. For whoever still exalts himself on account of passing things does not know how to honor in his neighbor what endures [Col. 1220C].

Do not therefore consider in yourselves what you possess, but what you are; fix your heart upon love of eternity, so that, while you despise attaining earthly heights, you may reach the glory that you hold through faith.

## CHAPTER LXI.—“He did not fear God and did not respect human beings” (Luke 18:2).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XIV, no. 31.)* There are some who, after despising God in their minds, scorn human judgments even more and are not ashamed boldly to carry out every evil they desire.
