Hidden wickedness invites them to commit evil, and no visible sense of shame restrains them. Thus it is said of a certain wicked judge: “He did not fear God and did not respect human beings,” because he was restrained from perpetrating evils neither by fear of God nor by shame before human beings.

## CHAPTER LXII.—“A certain Pharisee asked Jesus to eat with him. And when he had reclined at table in the Pharisee’s house, behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city brought an alabaster jar of ointment” (Luke 7:36–37).

*(Col. 1220D)*

*(Homily 33 on the Gospels, no. 1.)* We believe that this woman whom Luke calls a sinner and John calls Mary was the Mary whom Mark records as having had seven demons expelled from her. For what is signified by seven demons except all vices?

Because the whole span of time is encompassed by seven days, the number seven rightly represents totality. Mary therefore had seven demons because she was full of every vice.

But behold: when she saw the stains of her degradation, she ran, by washing, to the fountain of mercy; and she was not ashamed in the presence of those reclining at table. For because she was inwardly deeply ashamed of herself, she thought that there was nothing of which she needed to be ashamed outwardly.

## CHAPTER LXIII.—“And standing behind him at his feet, she began to wet his feet with her tears” (Luke 7).

*(Homily 8 on Ezekiel, no. 2.)* Almighty God himself both fills the minds of the saints with heavenly desire and hears those who have been filled. For he creates love in the hearts of the saints, and he himself receives prayer from loving hearts.

Peter wept bitterly over his denial; yet this is stated first: “Jesus looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61).

Mary Magdalene came with tears to the feet of our Redeemer after many [Col. 1221A] stains of guilt. But who inwardly infused her [the object is uncertain] except the one who graciously received her outwardly? Who urged her toward tears through the spirit of compunction except the one who received her outwardly for forgiveness before those reclining together?

Our Redeemer therefore drew the sinful woman’s mind away from guilt when he moved her to compunction; he received her so that he might free her from guilt. For whatever is accomplished in the virtues of the saints belongs to the grace of the one who grants their merits.

## CHAPTER LXIV.—“Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47).

(Homily 25 on the Gospels, §§ 9 and 8, in reverse order.) [Col. 1221B] Everywhere, dearest brothers, heavenly medicine comes to your aid, because God gave humanity the command not to sin, yet to the sinner he gave remedies through repentance, so that he might not despair. Hence Mary Magdalene, who had been a sinful woman in the city, returned to life after her sins by doing penance, and the hand of our Redeemer snatched her from the jaws of the ancient serpent.

Therefore the Lord’s voice rightly says to blessed Job: “Can you catch Leviathan with a hook, or pierce his jaw with a ring?” (Job 40:19). By Leviathan, which is said to mean “their addition,” that ancient serpent, the devourer of the human race, is signified. He promised to add divinity to humanity, but took away immortality; and when he multiplies the guilt of transgression—which he first presented to the first human being—by his most evil persuasion among those who follow him, he heaps punishments upon them without end.

A ring, when placed around something, binds it by encircling it. What, then, is signified by the ring except the divine mercy that surrounds us? It pierces the jaw of this Leviathan when, after we have committed what he forbade, it still shows us the remedy of repentance. The Lord pierces Leviathan’s jaw with a ring, because by the power of his ineffable mercy he so confronts the malice of the ancient enemy that he sometimes even loses those whom he has already captured. Those who return to innocence after committing sins fall, as it were, from his mouth.

For who, once seized by his mouth, could escape his jaw if it had not been pierced? Did he not hold Peter in his mouth when Peter denied the Lord (Matt. 26)? Did he not hold David in his mouth when David plunged himself into so deep an abyss of lust (1 Kings 11)? Yet when both returned to life through repentance, this Leviathan somehow lost them through the opening in his jaw.

But what human being could escape the mouth of this Leviathan so as to commit no unlawful act? From this we recognize how greatly we are indebted to the Redeemer of the human race: he not only prevented us from entering Leviathan’s mouth, but also permitted us to return from it. He did not take hope away from the sinner, because he pierced Leviathan’s jaw in order to provide a way of escape, so that at least the one who had been incautious and unwilling to guard against being bitten might flee after the bite.

The utmost care must therefore be taken lest anyone be seized by the mouth of this Leviathan through the pleasure of sin. Yet if anyone has been seized, let him not despair, because if he mourns his sin perfectly, he will still find an opening in Leviathan’s jaw through which to escape.

Mary Magdalene stands as a witness to divine mercy. This Leviathan held her in his mouth because she had succumbed to the domination of every vice. But she was drawn from his mouth through the opening in his jaw, because she returned through repentance after committing such great wickedness. Loving the Truth, she washed away the stains of her crime with tears. The voice of the Truth is fulfilled in her, for it says: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.” She who had previously remained cold through sinning afterward burned fiercely through love. Our Creator set her before us, as it were, as a sign and example of repentance, since through repentance he made her live after her fall.

### CHAPTER LXV.—“Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7:50).

[Col. 1222A]

(Homily 25 on the Gospels, § 10; Homily 33 on the Gospels, final section.) Every day sinners return to life and, after committing sins, turn back to innocence through the remedy of repentance. Mary Magdalene stands as a witness to divine mercy. When the Pharisee wished to block the fountain of mercy, he said of her: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know what and what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner” (ibid., 39).

But she washed away the stains of her heart and body with tears, and touched the footprints of her Redeemer, having abandoned her sinful ways. She sat at Jesus’ feet and listened to the word from his mouth. She had clung to the Living One; when he had been buried, she sought the dead; she found alive the one whom she had sought as dead. She found such favor with him that she herself announced him even to the apostles, his messengers.

What, then, brothers, what ought we to contemplate in this except the immeasurable mercy of our Creator? He set her before us, as it were, as a sign and example of repentance, since through repentance he made her live after her fall. If anyone, inflamed by the fire of lust, has lost bodily purity, let him look to Mary, who burned out the love of the flesh within herself by the fire of divine love.

Therefore, dearest brothers, turn back the eyes of your minds and place the repentant sinful woman before you as an example for imitation. Love the footprints of our Redeemer, which you despised by sinning; mourn whatever sins you remember committing in adolescence and youth; wipe away the stains of your conduct and deeds with tears. For when we return, the Lord mercifully embraces us, because even the life of sinners, however unworthy, cannot be unacceptable when it is washed by tears.

### CHAPTER LXVI.—“There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, covered with sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave them to him; but even the dogs came and licked his sores” (Luke 16:19 ff.).

[Col. 1222C]

(On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXV, §§ 31–32.) By the rich man feasting splendidly, the Jewish people are signified: they took possession of the abundance of the Law not for the necessity of salvation but for the display of arrogance, and in the words of the commandments they did not orderly nourish themselves but boastfully exhibit themselves.

By Lazarus, however, covered with wounds—his name means “helped”—the figure of the Gentile people is expressed. Divine assistance raises them all the more because they place less confidence in their own strength. He is described as poor and covered with sores because the Gentiles, humble in heart, opened their confession of sins.

For just as a wound draws pus from the depths out onto the skin, so in the confession of sin, when secret things are disclosed publicly, evil humors, as it were, burst outward from the innermost organs. And it is rightly through the rich man living splendidly that the pride of the Jews is signified, and through Lazarus covered with sores—who is interpreted as “helped”—that humility is signified. While the Jews, swollen with pride in the glory of the present life, disdained to understand the height of the Lord’s humility and the lowly deeds he displayed in himself, the Gentiles, confessing their sins, reached God through faith, helped by his grace; and when the Jews fell, the poor—those humble in spirit—were appointed in their place.

Humility opens the light of understanding; pride conceals it. For divine piety is a certain secret, and the more the mind swells, the less it reaches that secret, since it is driven outward precisely in proportion to the madness of its inflation.

We must dread the immense and profound judgments of God. We ought not to scrutinize them by reasoning, but to venerate them with awe. Let no one scrutinize why the Gentiles were taken up and the Jews were lost. Let no one scrutinize why, while the Jewish people stood, the Gentiles long lay prostrate in unbelief, and why, when the Gentiles rose to faith, the Jewish people were laid low by the guilt of unbelief. Let no one scrutinize why one is drawn by gift and another rejected for merit.

Let the counsel of the supreme and hidden power be the satisfaction of manifest reason; and in all that is outwardly ordained, let the manifest cause be the justice of the hidden will.

### CHAPTER LXVII.—“It happened that the beggar died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell” (Luke 16:22).

(Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 21.) This rich man is said not to have seized what belonged to others, but to have used his own possessions fruitlessly; and when avenging Gehenna received him after this life, it was not because he had done anything unlawful, but because, through immoderate use, he had surrendered himself entirely to lawful things.

From these evangelical words we can gather that the soul suffers the fire not only by seeing but also by experiencing it. For the voice of the Truth says that the rich man died and was buried in hell. That his soul is held in fire is suggested by the rich man’s voice, when he begged Abraham, saying: “Send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame” (v. 24).

When, then, the Truth declares that the condemned rich man is in the fire, what wise person would deny that the souls of the reprobate are held in fires? If someone asks how an incorporeal thing can be held and afflicted by a corporeal thing, let us certainly hear what the Truth will say to the reprobate at the end: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

If, then, the devil and his angels, although incorporeal, are to be tormented by corporeal fire, it is not surprising that souls, before receiving bodies, can experience corporeal torments. The soul can also be held by fire, so that in the torment of fire it is both seeing and feeling. It suffers the fire by the very fact that it sees it, and because it sees itself being burned, it is burned. Thus a corporeal thing burns an incorporeal thing, when invisible burning and pain are drawn from visible fire, so that an incorporeal mind is tormented even in corporeal flame by corporeal fire.

### CHAPTER LXVIII.—“Lifting up his eyes while he was in torment, he saw Abraham far away, and Lazarus in his bosom” (Luke 16:23).

(On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book X, § 49; Homily 40 on the Gospels, §§ 3, 7; On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book IV, § 56.) This rich man was punished and struck by the condemnation of hell not because he had oppressed anyone by force or seized another’s property by theft, but because he had not given away his own possessions. Having received material goods, he abandoned himself to evil and raised himself up arrogantly.

There are some whom wealth does not elevate through swelling pride but exalts through works of mercy. And there are some who see themselves abounding in earthly riches, do not seek the true riches of God, and do not love their eternal homeland, because they think that it is enough for them to be supported by temporal possessions.

Wealth itself, therefore, is not a crime, but one’s attitude toward it. Everything God created is good. But whoever uses good things badly acts as though, through the gluttony of greed, he were to die from the very bread by which he ought to live.

The poor man Lazarus had come to rest, while the proud rich man was tormented. Yet Abraham, who held Lazarus in his bosom, had been rich, and in speaking with his Creator he said: “I shall speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18:27). What, then, did this man know about valuing his riches, who reckoned himself dust and ashes? Or how could possessions elevate him who thought so humbly even of himself, their possessor?

Proud and arrogant rich people do not keep the coming Judge before their eyes, while they swell with proud thoughts within themselves. This, then, is what handed the proud rich man over to hell: he was not fearful in his prosperity; he bent the gifts he had received toward the use of arrogance; he did not know the compassion of the heart; and, although he had abundant means, he did not wish to redeem his sins.

Only late did this rich man lift up and open his eyes, when he saw Lazarus at rest—the man whom he had disdained to see lying before his gate. There he understood what he had refused to do here. In his condemnation he was compelled to recognize what he had lost when he failed to acknowledge his needy neighbor.

Because it is said of this rich man, placed in torment, that he saw Abraham and Lazarus in his bosom, we should believe that before the final judgment of retribution the unjust see certain just people at rest, so that when they see them in joy, they are tormented not only by their own punishment but also by the happiness of those others.

The just, however, always look upon the unjust in torment, so that their joy increases when they behold the evil from which they mercifully escaped, and so that they give greater thanks to their Redeemer the more they see in others what they themselves could have suffered had they been abandoned.

Nor does the sight of the punishment of the reprobate obscure such great blessedness in the minds of the just, because where compassion for misery will no longer exist, the joy of the blessed will certainly not be diminished. Although the souls of the just possess mercy in the goodness of their nature, even if they wished to show mercy then they could not at all, because they are bound to the justice of their Creator with such rectitude that no compassion for the reprobate moves them. Already raised up through the justice of judgment, they have no mercy for them.

They agree with the Judge to whom they cling, and they do not bend toward those whom they cannot rescue, even out of mercy, because they will see them as strangers to themselves in proportion as they see them rejected by their beloved Creator.

What wonder is it if, when the just behold the torments of the unjust, this serves the display of their joy, when even in a painting black is placed beneath white or red so that the latter may appear brighter? Yet, as has been said, the joy of the good increases in proportion as the evils of the condemned lie beneath their eyes.

Although their joys fully suffice for their delight, they nevertheless undoubtedly always see the evils of the reprobate, because when they behold the glory of their Creator, nothing occurring in creation can be hidden from their sight.

Moreover, we should know concerning these souls that just as those who are still living do not know where the souls of the dead are kept, so the dead do not know how the life in the flesh of those who come after them is ordered. The life of the spirit is far removed from the life of the flesh; and just as corporeal and incorporeal things differ in kind, so they also differ in knowledge.

This, however, must not be said concerning holy souls, because it is in no way to be believed that those who see the glory of almighty God within do not know something that exists outside. We should also know that after the elect and perfect have departed from their bodies, they are by no means delayed, as were the ancient Fathers, for intervals of time before attaining the heavenly homeland.

As soon as they leave the bonds of the flesh, they rest in the heavenly dwelling, as Paul testifies when he says: “We know that if our earthly house, this habitation, is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, a house not made by human hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1).

Before our Redeemer paid the penalty of the human race by his death, even those who had followed the paths of the heavenly homeland were held after leaving the flesh within the bars of hell—not so that punishment might chastise them as sinners, but so that, while they rested in remote places, the guilt of the first sin might prevent them from entering the kingdom, since the Mediator’s intercession had not yet arrived.

Hence, according to the testimony of that same Redeemer, the rich man being tormented among the dead sees Lazarus resting in Abraham’s bosom. If they were not still in the depths, he, who was placed in torment, certainly would not see them.

Thus our Redeemer, dying for the debt of our sin, entered the regions below, so that he might lead to heaven his own who had clung to him. But to the place where redeemed humanity now ascends, humanity would certainly have reached even without redemption, had it not wished to sin.

### CHAPTER LXIX.—“Father Abraham, have mercy on me” (Luke 16:24).

(On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book I, § 11; Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 19; On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, § 30.) Almost always talkativeness follows feasting, and when the belly is refreshed, the tongue is unrestrained. For unless immoderate loquacity carried away those devoted to gluttony, that rich man who is said to have feasted splendidly every day would not burn more grievously in his tongue, nor would he ask for water, saying: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.”

These words clearly show that he had sinned more frequently with his tongue while feasting every day, since, burning entirely, he especially sought to be cooled in his tongue. First he is said to have feasted splendidly every day; afterward he is remembered as asking for water on his tongue. Since, as we have said, talkativeness commonly pours forth excessively during feasts, the punishment indicates the fault, when the Truth, having said that he feasted splendidly, declares that he burned more intensely in his tongue.

Those who tune the harmony of strings arrange it with such skill that often, when one string is struck, another far away, with many strings lying between, is shaken. When one gives forth its sound, another string tuned to the same song trembles, though the others are not struck.

So Sacred Scripture often treats virtues and vices: while it indicates one thing by speaking, it makes another known by silence. Nothing is specifically mentioned against the rich man concerning talkativeness; but when the punishment is said to be in the tongue, which had been more guilty than the other parts during the banquet, the fault is revealed.

Let us now consider the poverty of the burning rich man, whose abundance at the feast had been so great. He says: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.”

These words do not inform us that, amid such intense heat, a single drop of water was then required to provide sufficient cooling. Rather, they show that the man who had sinned through abundance was there burning amid an extreme poverty. We see in the rich man’s words, through the subtle judgment of God, how great a punishment corresponded to such a fault.

Driven by poverty, he was compelled there to ask for the smallest things—the man who here, driven by stinginess, had gone so far as to refuse the smallest things. What could be distributed more subtly, what more strictly? He who had denied crumbs of bread asked for a drop of water.

### CHAPTER LXX.—“Remember, son, that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke 16:25).

(On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book V, § 1.) Since divine judgments are deeply hidden, it is difficult to know why in this life things are sometimes bad for the good and good for the wicked. They are still more hidden when things are good for the good here and bad for the wicked.

When things are bad for the good here and good for the wicked, this may perhaps be understood: the good receive here whatever they have done wrong, so that they may be more completely freed from eternal condemnation; and the wicked find here the good things they do for this life, so that afterward they may be led only to torments.

Hence the rich man burning in hell is told: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things.”

But when things are good for the good here and bad for the wicked, it is highly uncertain whether the good receive good things so that, moved by them, they may grow toward something better, or whether, by a just and hidden judgment, they receive here the reward for their deeds so that they may be emptied of the rewards of the life to come; and whether adversity strikes the wicked so that, by correction, it may defend them from eternal punishments, or whether their punishment begins here and eventually leads them, when completed, to the final torments of Gehenna.

Thus holy men, when they see worldly prosperity available to them, are disturbed by fearful suspicion. They fear that here they are receiving the fruit of their labors; they fear that divine justice may see a hidden wound within them and, while heaping outward gifts upon them, reject them inwardly.

### CHAPTER LXXI.—“I beg you, father Abraham, to send him to my father’s house” (Luke 16:27).

(On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book VIII, § 29, and Book IX, § 101.) Once the time of the present life has been cut off, the reprobate and sinners will by no means return to the work of earning forgiveness, nor will they be recalled to perform righteous deeds.

This is why the rich man whom the flame of hell tormented, recognizing that he could not restore himself through action, was concerned not for himself but for his surviving brothers, saying: “I beg you, father Abraham, to send him to my father’s house. For I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment.”

Hope, even false hope, commonly sustains a sorrowful mind. But so that the reprobate may feel their punishment more grievously, they also lose hope of forgiveness. Hence, delivered to avenging flames, he desired help not for himself, as we have said, but for his brothers, because he recognized that he would never be free from fiery torment, with the punishment of despair added to it.

We must likewise believe without hesitation that after the wicked have been condemned to eternal punishments, they will think about their parents, relatives, and neighbors whom they left behind. The Truth itself says that the rich man who had been buried in hell was concerned, even while in torment, about the five brothers he had left behind.

Moreover, we should know that the fire in hell does not shine for consolation, yet it shines in some way so that it may torment more greatly. For the reprobate will see all their companions in torment with them, illuminated by the flame—those for whose love they sinned—so that the destruction of those who loved carnal life against the commandments of their Creator may also afflict them by increasing their own condemnation.

We have gathered this from the same Gospel, which reports through the announcement of the Truth that the rich man who descended to the torments of eternal fire remembered five brothers. He asked Abraham to send Lazarus to instruct them, lest they should eventually come there and suffer equal punishment.

Since he remembered absent relatives for the increase of his own pain, it is unquestionably clear that, for the increase of his punishment, he could later also see them present. What wonder is it if he sees the reprobate burning with him, when, for the increase of his pain, he saw Lazarus, whom he had despised, in Abraham’s bosom?

If an elect man appeared to him so that his punishment might increase, why should it not be believed that in his torment he can also see those whom he had loved against God? From this it follows that those whom the reprobate now love in a disordered way, they will then see with themselves in torment, by a wondrous order of judgment, so that the carnal kinship placed before the Creator may magnify their punishment when it is condemned before their eyes by an equal retribution.

### CHAPTER LXXII.—Likewise, concerning the foregoing.

(Dialogues, Book IV, chapter 33.) That the good recognize the good in the kingdom and the wicked recognize the wicked in punishment is demonstrated with the greatest clarity in the Lord’s words.

After it had been said that Lazarus died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom, while the rich man died and was buried in hell, the following was added: “Lifting up his eyes while he was in torment, he saw Abraham far away and Lazarus in his bosom. And crying out, he said: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.’ Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things.’”

The rich man, having no longer any hope of salvation for himself, turned to seeking the salvation of his own, saying: “I beg you, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment.”

These words plainly declare that the good recognize the good and the wicked recognize the wicked. If Abraham had not recognized Lazarus at all, he would certainly not have spoken to the rich man in torment about Lazarus’s former suffering, saying that he had received evil things in his lifetime. And if the wicked did not recognize the wicked, the rich man in torment would certainly not have remembered even the absence of his brothers.

For how could he fail to recognize those who were present, when he took care to plead even for the memory of those who were absent? This also shows that the good recognize the wicked and the wicked recognize the good.

The rich man is recognized by Abraham, who was told: “You received good things in your lifetime.” And Lazarus, the elect, is recognized by the rich reprobate, who asks that he be sent by name, saying: “Send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue.”

Through this recognition on both sides, the fullness of retribution increases: the good rejoice more greatly when they see those whom they loved rejoicing with them; and the wicked, while suffering with those whom they loved in this world while despising God, are consumed not only by their own punishment but also by the punishment of those others.

Something still more wondrous occurs among the elect: they not only recognize those whom they knew in this world, but recognize the good whom they never saw as though they had seen and known them. Since all there behold God in a shared brightness, there is nothing they do not know where they know the One who knows all things.

### CHAPTER LXXIII.—“If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed” (Luke 17:6).

(On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book I, § 9.) Just as perfumes do not spread their fragrance widely unless they are stirred, and just as they expand their aroma only when they are burned, so holy men make known in tribulations everything that they give off as the fragrance of virtues.

Hence it is rightly said in the Gospel: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed.” Unless a mustard seed is crushed, the power of its virtue is not recognized. Uncrushed, it is mild; but if it is crushed, it grows hot and reveals how much sharpness lies hidden within it.

So each holy man, when he is not struck, appears contemptible and mild. But if the crushing of persecution should oppress him, he immediately displays everything that tastes of heat, and whatever previously seemed contemptible and weak in him is turned into the fervor of virtue. Whatever he gladly concealed during times of tranquility, compelled by the agitation of tribulations, he is forced to make known.

### CHAPTER LXXIV.—“Ten lepers met him,” etc. (Luke 17:12).

(On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, § 26.) Heretics have this characteristic: they mix evil with good, so that they may easily deceive the understanding of their hearers. If they always spoke perversely, they would be recognized more quickly in their perversity and would persuade no one of what they wished. Again, if they always thought correctly, they would certainly not be heretics.

Thus they mix what is right with what is perverse, so that by displaying good things they may attract hearers to themselves, while by presenting evil things they may infect them with a hidden disease; they draw them on through right opinions and strike them through perverse ones.

In the commandments of God they vary between sound and unsound speech. Hence, in the Gospel, they are represented under the figure of the ten lepers. When a diseased whiteness is sprinkled over their healthy color, they are defiled by this excessive whiteness.

We are therefore admonished: “Do not think more highly than one ought to think, but think with sober judgment” (Rom. 12:3). Since in leprosy one part of the skin is brought to a shining whiteness while another remains in its healthy color, lepers rightly represent heretics: by mixing perversity with what is right, and unsoundness with what is sound, they sprinkle spots over a healthy color.

They also oppose the precepts of the Decalogue, because they neither love God, about whom they think wrongly, nor their neighbor, from whom they are divided. Therefore they come to beseech the Lord Christ. And because they had stumbled over his commandments, they call upon the one from whose commandments they had stumbled, crying out to be saved and saying: “Jesus, Teacher, have mercy on us.”

By these words they signify that they had gone astray in his teaching; they humbly call him their Teacher, the one who saves. And when they return to knowledge of the Teacher, they immediately turn back to the form of salvation and are deemed worthy to be healed.

### CHAPTER LXXV.—“Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Luke 17:37).

(On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXI, § 105; Dialogues, Book IV, chapter 25.) Before the restoration of their bodies, the souls of certain just people are delayed from the heavenly kingdom in certain dwellings, because they lacked something of perfect righteousness. But the souls of the perfect just, as soon as they leave the confines of this flesh, are received into the seats of the heavenly kingdom.

The Truth itself also bears witness to this, saying: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.” It is as though he were saying openly: “Since I, your incarnate Redeemer, preside over the heavenly seat, when I release the souls of the elect from the flesh, I will raise them to the heavenly places.”

Where, then, our Redeemer is in the body, there undoubtedly the souls of the just are gathered. Paul desires “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). Therefore, whoever does not doubt that Christ is in heaven cannot deny that Paul’s soul is in heaven.

### CHAPTER LXXVI.—“I fast twice in the Sabbath” (Luke 18:12).

(On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIX, § 33; Homily 7 on Ezekiel, § 6; Moralia, Book XIX, § 34.) If a city is surrounded by a great embankment against lurking enemies, enclosed by strong walls, and guarded sleeplessly on every side, but one opening alone is negligently left unprotected, the enemy who seemed to have been shut out everywhere undoubtedly enters through it.

Let us hear with what defenses the Pharisee who went up to the Temple to pray fortified the city of his mind: “I fast twice in the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess.” He prefaced this by saying: “God, I give you thanks.” He rightly gave thanks to God, from whom he had received the good things he had done.

He certainly employed great defenses, but let us see where he left an opening unprotected for the lurking enemy: “I am not like the rest of humanity—robbers, unjust, adulterers—or even like this tax collector.” Behold, through pride he opened the city of his heart to lurking enemies, which he had closed in vain through fasting and almsgiving.

Everything else is fortified in vain when the one place through which the enemy has access is not fortified. He rightly gave thanks, but perversely exalted himself over the tax collector. By exalting himself, he betrayed the city of his heart, which he had preserved through abstinence and generosity.

Through abstinence, gluttony was conquered and the greed of the belly destroyed; through generosity, stinginess was overcome and avarice suppressed. By what labors do we think this was accomplished? Yet how many labors fell, struck down by one vice! How many good things were killed by the sword of a single fault!

Therefore we must always be diligent in doing good and carefully guard ourselves in our thoughts even from those very good works, lest, if they lift up the mind, they cease to be good—serving not their Creator but pride.

In this matter we do not act improperly if we bring forward testimony from books that are not canonical, but were nevertheless published for the edification of the Church. Eleazar struck down an elephant in battle, but he died beneath the one he had destroyed (1 Macc. 6). Whom, then, does this man signify—the man whom his own victory crushed—except those who overcome vices but, by becoming proud beneath the very things they subdue, fall?

For he dies, as it were, beneath the enemy he has felled, who is lifted up by the sin he has overcome. Holy people, therefore, must watch carefully over all their works, lest they either do what is wrong or, after doing the right things that have been commanded, swell with pride in their thoughts once their good acts are complete, and offend more grievously because, in the things they appear outwardly to do justly, they sin more secretly.

Everything that is done perishes if it is not carefully guarded by humility.

### CHAPTER LXXVII.—“Jesus, having gone out, was walking through Jericho; and behold, Zacchaeus was seeking to see him—to see who he was” (Luke 19:4).

[Col. 1228D]

(On the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVII, § 79.) If we desire truly to be wise and to contemplate the very wisdom of God, let us humbly acknowledge ourselves to be foolish. Let us abandon harmful wisdom and learn praiseworthy foolishness.

Hence it is written: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3:18). The words of the Gospel narrative also testify that, since Zacchaeus could not see because of the crowd, he climbed a sycamore tree in order to see the Lord as he passed by.

A sycamore is called a “foolish fig.” Thus little Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore and saw the Lord, because those who humbly choose the foolishness of the world themselves contemplate God’s wisdom subtly.

The crowd obstructs our smallness from seeing the Lord, because the tumult of worldly cares weighs down the weakness of the human mind and prevents it from directing its attention toward the light of truth.

But we climb the sycamore wisely if we hold firmly in our minds that foolishness which is divinely commanded. For what is more foolish in this world than not seeking what has been lost, surrendering one’s possessions to those who seize them, returning no injury for injuries received, and instead adding patience to them?

The Lord commands us, as it were, to climb the sycamore when he says: “Do not demand back what is yours from the one who takes it” (Luke 6:30). And again: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5:39).

The passing Lord is seen from the sycamore, because through this wise foolishness, although we do not yet see God’s wisdom solidly as it is, we nevertheless see it already, as it were, in passing, through the light of contemplation. Those who consider themselves wise cannot see it, because, caught amid the elevated crowd of their thoughts as they try to behold the Lord, they have not yet found the sycamore tree.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII.—“Zacchaeus said to the Lord: ‘Behold, Lord, I give half of my possessions to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold’” (Luke 19:8).

[Col. 1229B]

(Homily 5 on the Gospels, § 2, and Homily 25, § 10.) It has no fixed valuation in money, yet the kingdom of God is worth as much as you possess. It was worth this much to Peter and Andrew when they left their nets and boat; it was worth two small coins to the widow; it was worth a cup of cold water to another; it was worth half of his possessions to Zacchaeus, because he reserved the other half for restoring fourfold whatever he had unjustly taken.

Our outward possessions, however small, are sufficient for the Lord. For he weighs the heart, not the substance, and does not consider how much is offered in his sacrifice but from how much it is offered.

The kingdom of God, then, as we have said, is worth as much as you possess. Consider, therefore, brothers, what is cheaper to purchase and what is more costly to possess.

Moreover, if anyone, panting with the fever of avarice, has seized another’s property, let him look to this Zacchaeus, who restored fourfold whatever he had taken from anyone.

## CHAPTER LXXIX

“Conduct business until I come” (Luke 19:13).

[Col. 1229C]

*(Homily 17 on the Gospels, nos. 16–18.)* Priests ought carefully to consider what profit they are making for God, since they have received a talent from him and have been sent to conduct business. For the Lord himself says: “Conduct business until I come.” Behold, he has already come; behold, he seeks profit from our business. What profit of souls from our trading will we show him? How many sheaves of souls shall we bring before his gaze from the harvest of our preaching?

Let us place before our eyes that day of such strict judgment, when the Judge will come and settle accounts with the servants to whom he entrusted the talents. Behold, in terrible majesty, amid the choirs of angels and archangels, he will appear; in that great examination the multitude of all the elect and the reprobate will be brought forward, and each person’s deeds will be disclosed. There all the shepherds of the Lord’s flock will appear with the profits of souls—those who, through their holy preaching, draw a flock subject to them after them to God.

When so many shepherds, then, come with their flocks before the eyes of the eternal Shepherd, what shall we wretches say, who return to our Lord after our business empty-handed, who have had the name of shepherd but have no sheep to display as having been nourished by us? Here we have been called shepherds, but there we do not lead a flock. Through us, indeed, the faithful come to holy baptism; through our prayers they are blessed; through the laying on of our hands they receive the Holy Spirit from the Lord; and they themselves reach the kingdom of heaven. Yet behold, through our negligence we are heading downward.

The elect, purified by the hands of priests, enter their heavenly homeland, while the priests themselves, through a wicked life, hasten to the punishments of hell. To what, then, to what shall I say that wicked priests are like, except to the water of baptism, which, washing away the sins of those baptized, sends them to the heavenly kingdom, while afterward it itself descends into the sewers?

Let us fear these things, brothers; let our ministry correspond to our conduct. Let us think daily about the remission of our sins, lest our life remain bound by sin, through which almighty God daily releases others. Let us consider our business without ceasing; let us weigh the burden we have undertaken; let us settle daily with ourselves the accounts that we shall have with our Judge; and let us prepare to render to almighty God the fruit of the business we have received.

## CHAPTER LXXX

“Behold your mina, which I kept stored away in a handkerchief” (Luke 19:20).

*(Pastoral Rule, part I, chapter 9.)* He who excels in virtues ought to come to governance even under compulsion; he who is lacking in virtues should not presume to approach it even when compelled. If the former absolutely resists, let him beware lest, binding the money he has received in a handkerchief, he be judged for hiding it. For to bind money in a handkerchief is to conceal the gifts one has received in the idleness of sluggish torpor.

On the other hand, when this latter person desires governance, let him take care lest, after the example of the Pharisees, he become an obstacle to those striving to enter the kingdom by his example of wicked conduct, since, according to the word of the supreme Teacher, “they neither enter themselves nor allow others to enter.”

## CHAPTER LXXXI

“Take the talent away from him, and cast the useless servant into the outer darkness” (Luke 19:24).

*(Homily 6 on the Gospels.)* Each of you, insofar as he is capable and insofar as he has received the grace of heavenly inspiration, ought to call the minds of his neighbors back from wickedness, exhort them to good works, and announce to the erring the eternal kingdom or punishment. Let no one say: “I am not capable of admonishing; I am not fit to exhort.” Offer whatever you can, lest you be required to pay the penalty in torments for the talent you received and kept badly. For the man who took greater pains to hide this talent than to distribute it had not received more than one talent.

And we know that in God’s tabernacle there were made not only bowls but also, at the Lord’s command, cups. By the bowls, overflowing doctrine is signified; by the cups, a small and limited knowledge. One person, full of the doctrine of truth, intoxicates the minds of his hearers; by saying this, he surely offers a bowl. Another is unable to express fully what he understands, but because he announces it in some manner, he surely offers a taste through a cup.

Placed in God’s tabernacle—that is, in the holy Church—if you cannot minister bowls through the teaching of wisdom, give your neighbors cups of good speech, insofar as divine generosity enables you. As far as you judge that you have advanced, draw others along as well; desire to have companions with you on the way of God. If you are striving toward God, take care not to come to him alone. Hence it is written: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation 22:17), so that whoever has already received the voice of heavenly love in his heart may also return outwardly to his neighbors the voice of exhortation.

Perhaps someone does not have bread to offer as alms to the needy, but one who possesses a tongue can give something greater. For it is more valuable to refresh a mind that will live forever with the nourishment of the word than to satisfy with earthly bread the belly of flesh that will die. Therefore, brothers, do not withhold from your neighbors the alms of the word.

## CHAPTER LXXXII

“By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 9; Commentary on Blessed Job, book V, no. 33.)* We have been wonderfully constituted in such a way that reason possesses the soul, and the soul possesses the body. But the soul’s right to possess the body is driven away if the soul is not first possessed by reason.

The Lord therefore showed patience to be the guardian of our constitution, because through it he taught us to possess ourselves. We recognize, then, how great is the sin of impatience, through which we lose even the possession of what we are. Since perfection arises from patience, it is immediately added: “That person is truly perfect who is not impatient with the imperfection of his neighbor.”

Whoever scorns to preserve patience quickly abandons social life through impatience; for harmony can never be preserved except through patience alone. Frequently in human affairs something arises that separates people’s minds from their mutual unity and love. Unless they prepare themselves inwardly to endure adversity, when some adversity occurs that the mind cannot bear, they abandon fraternal harmony.

But whoever abandons another because he cannot endure that person’s imperfection is himself a witness that he has not yet made perfect progress. Hence, as we recalled above, the Truth says in the Gospel: “By your patience you will possess your souls.” For what does possessing souls mean except living perfectly in all things and ruling over every movement of the mind from the citadel of virtue?

Whoever therefore holds fast to patience possesses his soul, because he becomes strong against every adversity precisely by mastering himself through overcoming himself. And what he commendably breaks, he vigorously displays unbroken: when he overcomes himself in his pleasures, he prepares himself unconquered for adversity.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

“Having taken bread, he gave thanks” (Luke 22:19).

[Col. 1231B]

*(Commentary on Blessed Job, book II, no. 61.)* Our Lord Jesus Christ teaches those who believe in him that, when placed under blows, they should know how to bless the Lord and give thanks. For when, as the Gospel testifies, he is said to have been approaching his passion, he is reported to have given thanks after taking bread.

He therefore gives thanks who undergoes the blows of another’s wickedness, and who, although he has exhibited nothing deserving punishment, humbly blesses God while being struck. In this way he shows what each person ought to do under the blows of his own guilt, since he bears with equanimity the blows resulting from another’s guilt; and he shows what a subject should do under correction, if an equal gives thanks to the Father while placed under the blow.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

“Jesus, being in agony, prayed more earnestly” (Luke 22:44).

*(Commentary on Blessed Job, book XXIV, no. 32.)* God’s elect always fear God’s strict judgments concerning themselves. Yet they fear them especially when, coming to pay the debt of human condition, they see themselves drawing near to the strict Judge; and the fear becomes sharper the nearer the eternal recompense approaches.

Dread increases as the judgment of justice draws near. As the dissolution of the flesh presses upon them, the more clearly the strict judgment is seen to be imminent, the more intensely it is feared. Even if they remember that they have never knowingly neglected the things they know, they nevertheless fear what they do not know, because they are wholly unable to judge and comprehend themselves; and as their end presses upon them, they are terrified by a subtler fear.

Therefore our Redeemer, approaching the dissolution of the flesh while preserving the appearance of his members, “being in agony, began to pray more earnestly.” What could he have been asking for himself in agony, he who, while on earth, bestowed heavenly things with authority? But as death approached, while preserving the likeness of his members, he expressed in himself the struggle of our mind, for we suffer a certain force of terror and dread when, through the dissolution of the flesh, we draw near to eternal judgment.

For it is not without reason that anyone’s soul is then terrified, when shortly afterward it encounters what it cannot change for eternity.

## CHAPTER LXXXV

“Friend, for what purpose have you come?” (Matthew 26:50).

*(Commentary on Blessed Job, book III, no. 46.)* We ought to call those who oppose us friends, just as the Lord said even to the traitor himself: “Friend, for what purpose have you come?” And the rich man who is consumed by the fire of hell is called a son of Abraham, because, although through us the wicked neglect to correct themselves, it is nevertheless fitting that we name them not from their wickedness but from our own kindness.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

“When a certain maidservant, the doorkeeper, saw Peter sitting by the light and looked at him, she said: ‘Are you also one of this man’s disciples?’ He denied it and said: ‘I am not’” (Luke 12:56).

*(Homily 30 on the Gospels, nos. 7–8.)* We know what kind of teachers the holy Church had been before the coming of the Holy Spirit, and we see what strength they acquired after his coming. Let the doorkeeper’s maidservant say how great was the weakness and fearfulness of that very shepherd of the Church and first of the apostles, beside whose most sacred body we sit.

Struck by a single woman’s voice, while fearing death he denied life. He was overthrown not by punishments, afflictions, or the terrifying power of anyone, but by the question of a single slave. And indeed, she was a slave: lest the stronger sex appear terrifying, he was tested by a maidservant’s question. Again, so that the weakness of such a sex might be made even more contemptible by the lowliness of her office, he was questioned not merely by a maidservant but by a maidservant who was a doorkeeper.

Behold how lowly was the person chosen to test him, so that it might plainly be revealed how completely fear’s weakness possessed him—he could not withstand even the voice of a doorkeeper’s maidservant. It should also be considered that Peter, when arrested, denied on earth the one whom a thief confessed when hanging on the cross.

But let us hear what this man, once so fearful, became after the coming of the Holy Spirit. An assembly of magistrates and elders is convened, and the apostles are scourged and ordered not to speak in the name of Jesus. Peter replied with great authority: “We must obey God rather than human beings.” And again: “Whether it is right in the sight of God for us to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge. For we cannot refrain from speaking of what we have seen and heard.” And they went away from the council rejoicing, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts 5).

Behold, Peter rejoices in beatings—he who had once been afraid of words; and he who, when questioned by a maidservant, had earlier feared her voice now, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, overcomes the strength of rulers even while being scourged.

We must consider why almighty God permitted the man whom he had decided to place above the whole Church to fear a maidservant’s voice and deny himself. We recognize that this was done through a dispensation of great mercy, so that the one who was to become the shepherd of the Church might learn through his own fault how he ought to show mercy to others.

First, therefore, he showed him to himself, and then placed him over the rest, so that from his own weakness he might learn how mercifully to bear with the weaknesses of others.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII

“And the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61).

*(Commentary on Blessed Job, book VIII, no. 30; book XXXII on Job, no. 10; Commentary on Blessed Job, book XXV, nos. 28–29.)* Each sinner is looked upon by the Lord in two ways: either when he is turned away from sin, or when he is punished for sin.

Regarding the gaze of conversion, it is said that the Lord looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken; and he went outside and wept bitterly. For when the mercy of the Redeemer looks upon the hardness of our insensibility, it softens us for repentance. He certainly does not free after death the one whom grace did not reform for forgiveness before death.

Hence the Psalmist says: “For his mercy endures forever” (Psalm 17:1). For the one whom mercy does not now rescue, justice alone condemns after the present age.

Regarding the gaze of vengeance, it is said: “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Psalm 33:17).

It must be known, moreover, that every sin is committed in one of three ways: through ignorance, through weakness, or deliberately. Sin committed through weakness is more serious than sin committed through ignorance; but sin committed deliberately is far more serious than sin committed through weakness.

Paul had sinned through ignorance when he said: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Timothy 1:13). Peter, however, sinned through weakness when a single girl’s voice shook all the strength of faith that he had shown toward the Lord, and with his voice he denied the God whom he held in his heart.

But because the guilt of weakness or ignorance is more easily wiped away insofar as it is not committed deliberately, Paul corrected through knowledge what he had done in ignorance, while Peter strengthened the root of faith, already shaken and as if withering, by watering it with tears.

If, then, someone perhaps falls in faith, let him look to Peter, who wept bitterly over what he had denied through the weakness of fear.

Those whom the Teacher himself addressed sinned deliberately when he said: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22). And shortly afterward: “They saw and hated both me and my Father.”

For it is one thing not to do good, and another to hate the teacher of good; just as it is one thing to sin through rashness, and another to sin through deliberation. Often sin is committed through rashness, yet afterward condemned through reflection and deliberation. Through weakness it commonly happens that someone loves what is good but is unable to fulfill it; to sin deliberately is neither to do nor to love what is good.

Therefore, just as it is sometimes a graver sin to love sin than to commit it, so it is more wicked to hate justice than not to have practiced it. There are therefore some in the Church who not only fail to do good but even persecute it; and what they themselves neglect to do, they detest in others as well.

Their sin is committed not through weakness or ignorance but through deliberate choice alone. For if they wanted to do good but were unable, they would at least love in others what they neglected in themselves. If they desired these things even by wish alone, they would not hate them when done by others. But because, by hearing, they come to know these good things, by living they despise them, and by observing them they persecute them.

There are likewise some in the Church who scorn even to know the good things they disdain to do. Since it is written: “The servant who did not know his master’s will and did things deserving blows shall be beaten with few blows. But the servant who knew his master’s will and did not act according to it shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47), they regard ignorance as a remedy providing impunity for sin.

Such people are darkened by the blindness of pride alone, and therefore do not distinguish between not knowing and refusing to know. Not to know is ignorance; to refuse to know is pride. And the less excuse they can have for not knowing, the more the deeds of the Lord’s humility and examples of good living are set before them, even against their will, so that they may know them.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII

“Herod questioned Jesus at length, but he answered him nothing” (Luke 23:9).

*(Commentary on Blessed Job, book XI, no. 53, and book XXII, no. 38.)* When holy men cannot benefit their hearers, they willingly choose to be despised even while remaining silent, lest they boast in the display of their wisdom. When they say something wisely, they seek not their own glory but the life of their hearers. When they see that they cannot gain the life of their hearers by speaking, they conceal their knowledge by remaining silent.

For we hasten to imitate the Lord’s life, which is set before us as a kind of sign. Dying on the cross for our redemption, he poured light through the wood like a lamp into our darkened minds. John saw us illuminated by this lamp when he said: “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

Herod wished to examine the flames of this lamp when he desired to see his miracles, as it is written: “When Herod saw Jesus, he rejoiced, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard many things about him and hoped to see some sign performed by him.” Then it is added: “He questioned him at length, but he answered him nothing.”

The lamp shone before his eyes with no ray of light, because it showed nothing remarkable about itself to one who sought it not devoutly but out of curiosity. Thus, when questioned, the Lord remained silent; when expected, he declined to perform miracles, because he saw that Herod sought not progress but wished to marvel at learning or signs.

Keeping himself hidden, he left outside himself, ungrateful, those whom he discovered to be seeking outward things,choosing rather to be openly despised by the proud than to be praised with empty speech by unbelievers.

Because he remained steadfastly silent, he departed from Herod mocked and scorned, as it is written: “Herod, with his soldiers, despised him and mocked him, clothing him in a white robe.”

We who hear this ought to learn from it that whenever our hearers do not wish to recognize our teachings as things worthy of praise, but also do not wish to change their own perverse ways, we should remain completely silent. Otherwise, if we speak the word of God for the sake of ostentation, their guilt—which already existed—may fail to cease, while our own guilt, which did not exist before, may arise.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX

“If they do this with the green wood, what will happen with the dry?” (Luke 23:31).

*(Commentary on Blessed Job, book XII, no. 5.)* In sacred Scripture, the word “wood” sometimes signifies the cross, sometimes a just or unjust person, and sometimes the incarnate Wisdom of God.

The cross is signified by wood when it is said: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jeremiah 11:19). To put wood into the bread is to apply the cross to the Lord’s body.

Again, by the name of wood a just or unjust person is represented, as the Lord says through the prophet: “I, the Lord, have humbled the lofty tree and exalted the lowly tree” (Ezekiel 17:24), because, according to the voice of the same Truth: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

Again, by wood the incarnate Wisdom of God is represented, as it is written of her: “She is a tree of life to those who take hold of her” (Proverbs 3:18). And she herself says: “If they do this with the green wood, what will happen with the dry?”

He called himself the green wood and us the dry wood, because he possessed in himself the power of divinity, whereas we, who are merely human beings, are dry wood.

## CHAPTER XC

“After they came to the place called Calvary, where they crucified the Lord Jesus and the criminals, one on his right and the other on his left” (Luke 23:33).

*(Homily 25 on the Gospels, nos. 7–8.)* Behold, dearly beloved brothers, our Creator came without guilt to the punishment of the cross on behalf of sinners; and for the human race, he who owed nothing to death underwent the punishment of the cross. From the very place where he temporarily allowed the hands of his persecutors to rage against him, he struck down the ancient enemy forever.

The Lord clearly indicates this to blessed Job when he says: “Can you catch Leviathan with a hook?” (Job 40:19). In a hook, bait is displayed while the barb is concealed. Thus the almighty Father caught Leviathan—that is, the ancient serpent, the devil—with a hook, because he sent his only-begotten Son, made flesh, in order to bring about Leviathan’s death. In him the suffering flesh could be seen, while the impassible divinity could not be seen.

When that serpent bit the bait of the body in him through the hands of his persecutors, the barb of divinity pierced him. Earlier he had recognized him as God through his miracles, but he fell from that knowledge into doubt when he saw him subject to suffering.

The hook therefore held the throat of the devourer: in him the bait of flesh was exposed, which the devourer might desire to swallow, while the divinity that would destroy him remained hidden during the passion. He was caught on the hook of the Lord’s incarnation, because, when he desired the bait of the body in him, he was pierced by the barb of divinity.

There was humanity there to draw the devourer toward him; there was divinity to pierce him; there was visible weakness to provoke him; and there was hidden power to transfix the throat of the captor. He was therefore caught on the hook, because he perished through the very thing he bit.

Thus he lost the mortals whom he rightly held, because he presumed to attack through the death of the cross the immortal one in whom he had no right. Behold, the ancient enemy lost the spoils he had seized from the human race and, when our Redeemer died on the cross, lost the victory of his ambush.

## CHAPTER XCI

“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

*(Homily 27 on the Gospels, no. 2.)* The one and highest proof of love is to love even the person who opposes us. Hence the Truth himself both endures the scaffold of the cross and offers affection to his very persecutors, when on the cross he pleads with the Father on their behalf.

What wonder, then, if disciples love their enemies while they live, when the Teacher loved his enemies even as he was being killed?

It must be known that the Lord endured the hands of his enemies without any guilt of his own when he was killed: he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (Isaiah 53). Yet he endured the pain of the cross for our redemption. He alone among all possessed pure prayers before God; in the very pain of his passion he interceded for his persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

For what can be said, and what can be imagined in prayer, purer than this: mercy in intercession is extended to those by whom pain is being endured? Thus it came about that those raging persecutors who had shed our Redeemer’s blood afterward, as believers, drank it eagerly and proclaimed him to be the Son of God.

## CHAPTER XCII

“Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

*(Book XVIII on Job, nos. 63–65.)* When God comes to an unworthy mind, by coming he makes it worthy for himself and creates in it a merit that he may reward—the mind in which he had previously found only what he might punish.

Here I like to turn the eyes of the mind toward that thief who climbed from the jaws of crime to the cross, and from the cross to paradise. Let us observe what kind of man he came to the scaffold, and what kind of man he departed from the scaffold.

He came guilty of a brother’s blood; he came bloodstained, but inwardly he was changed on the cross by grace. The man who had inflicted death on his brother proclaimed the life of the dying Lord, saying: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.”

Nails had fastened his hands and feet to the cross, and nothing in him remained free from punishment except his heart and tongue. Under God’s inspiration, he offered him everything he found free within himself, so that, according to what is written, “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation” (Romans 12).

The apostle testifies that three virtues above all remain in the hearts of the faithful, saying: “But now faith, hope, and love remain” (1 Corinthians 13:13). Filled suddenly with grace, the thief both received and preserved all of them on the cross.

He had faith: he believed that the Lord would reign, although he saw him dying alongside himself. He had hope: he asked for entry into his kingdom, saying: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom.” He also held love vigorously in his death: he rebuked his brother and fellow thief, dying for a similar crime, for his wickedness, and proclaimed to him the life he had not known, saying: “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong” (Luke 23:40–41).

He who came to the cross in such a state because of guilt—behold what kind of man he departed from the cross by grace. He confessed the Lord whom he saw dying with him in human weakness, at the very time when the apostles denied him whom they had seen performing miracles by divine power.

But those who assert that a human being can be saved by his own powers suppose that this confession likewise arose from the man’s own ability. If that were so, the Psalmist would not say in praise of God: “Confession and majesty are his work” (Psalm 110:3). We therefore receive the ability to confess rightly from the one who also grants us the ability to perform great things.

## CHAPTER XCIII

“Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

[Col. 1235D]

*(Homily 20 on the Gospels, no. 15, and homily 25, no. 10.)* That venerable thief offers us, dearly beloved brothers, great confidence in forgiveness—venerable not because he was a thief, but because he confessed. A thief because of his cruelty, venerable because of his confession.

Consider, then, consider how incomprehensible are the depths of mercy in almighty God. This thief, snatched away from the path of crime with bloodstained hands, was hung on the scaffold of the cross. There he confessed; there he was healed; there he deserved to hear: “Today you will be with me in paradise.”

What does this mean? Who could speak of, who could adequately estimate, such great goodness in God? From the very punishment of his crime he reached the rewards of virtue.

If anyone, then, has burned with malicious cruelty against his neighbor, let him look to this thief, who at the very moment of death reached the rewards of life through repentance. Therefore, let no quality or quantity of our evils break our certainty of hope, because almighty God, if we rise toward God with our whole heart, will restore the hope of forgiveness and, through the lamentations of repentance, open for us the way of mercy and compassion.

## CHAPTER XCIV

“On the first day of the week, at very early dawn, certain women came to the tomb; and behold, two men stood beside them in shining garments, who said to them: ‘Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen’” (Luke 24:1 ff.).

*(Commentary on Blessed Job, book XXX, no. 69.)* The Son of God became human among us for this reason: not only to redeem us by the shedding of his blood, but also to transform us by the example he displayed.

In our conversion, therefore, by coming he found one condition and by living he taught another. All those descended from proud Adam’s race were eager to seek the prosperity of the present life, avoid adversity, flee reproaches, and pursue glory.

The incarnate Lord came among them seeking adversity, rejecting prosperity, embracing reproaches, and fleeing glory. For when the Jews wished to make him their king, he refused to become king; but when they plotted to kill him, he came willingly to the scaffold of the cross.

He fled what everyone seeks and sought what everyone flees. By fleeing what everyone seeks and seeking what everyone flees, he did what everyone would marvel at: he himself rose after death and by his death raised others from death.

There are two lives for a human being existing in the body: one before death and another after resurrection. Everyone knew one of these through experience, but did not know the other, and the human race devoted itself only to the one it knew.

The Lord came in the flesh, and by taking one upon himself he revealed the other. By dying, he practiced the life we possess; by rising, he disclosed the life we are to seek. By his example he taught us that this life, which we lead before death, is not to be loved for its own sake but endured for the sake of the other.

Our Redeemer therefore accepted death so that we would not fear dying; he displayed the resurrection so that we might have confidence that we can rise. He also willed that this same death last no more than three days, lest, if resurrection were delayed in him, all hope of it should be lost in us.

He therefore underwent death temporarily—that is, for three days—and did not remain in the death he underwent, as we remain until the end of the age. When he rose on the third day, he showed what would follow in his body, that is, in the Church. By his example he displayed what he promised as a reward, so that just as the faithful recognized that he had risen, they might hope for the rewards of resurrection in themselves at the end of the world.

## CHAPTER XCV

“Two of the disciples were traveling that same day to a village named Emmaus” (Luke 24:13).

*(Commentary on Blessed Job, book XIV, no. 58; book I on Job, no. 3.)* The holy apostles were placed in the body of the Church like teeth for this reason: to bite the lives of carnal people through correction and break them from the hardness of their obstinacy. Hence it is said to the first of the apostles, as to a tooth placed in the body: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13).

But at the time of the Lord’s passion, these teeth lost the bite of correction through fear of death; they lost confidence in their strength and the effectiveness of every kind of action. Thus two of them, walking after his death and resurrection, spoke together on the road and said: “We had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21).

They were still conversing about the Lord, but no longer believed in him at all. They had lost the power of good action and retained only words of conversation about him. They had lost the bite of correction but still possessed the movement of speech: they knew how to converse, but feared either to preach him or to bite the vices of unbelievers.

It should be known that it is the custom of sacred Scripture for the very people who write it to speak of themselves in it as though of others. Hence John says: “The disciple whom Jesus loved” (John 19:26). Hence Luke says that two of the disciples were walking on the road, Cleopas and another. By carefully remaining silent about this other person, as some say, he identified himself.

## CHAPTER XCVI

“Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way?” (Luke 24:32).

*(Homily 7 on the Gospels, no. 5.)* All whom the Holy Spirit fills, he makes both burning and speaking. Therefore holy teachers, when they preach out of love for God, set the hearts of their hearers aflame. A teacher’s speech is idle if it cannot provide the fire of love.

Those who said, “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” had received this fire of doctrine from the very mouth of the Truth. When the speech is heard, the mind catches fire and the coldness of torpor departs. The mind becomes anxious with heavenly desire and alienated from earthly cravings.

True love, when it has filled the mind, torments it with tears; what previously lay sluggish in its desires afterward burns through words, and with every command by which it is instructed it is kindled as though by an equal number of torches.

## CHAPTER XCVII

“Jesus stood in their midst and said to them: ‘Peace be with you’” (Luke 24:36).

[Col. 1237B]

*(Commentary on Blessed Job, book XII, no. 8; Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 25.)* Although our Lord and Redeemer could be killed through suffering, through the glory of the resurrection he returned once more to the freshness of life; and through God’s power his slain flesh returned to life, according to what is written: “Whom God raised from the dead” (Acts 4:10).

Because God is Trinity, the holy Trinity—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—raised the slain flesh of the only-begotten Son.

After celebrating the solemnity of his resurrection, he made known, through certain gradual advances, the incorruptibility of the body he had taken back. From Luke’s testimony we learn that he first sent angels to certain persons seeking him in the tomb; then he himself appeared, though unrecognizable, to those speaking about him on the road; after the delays of exhortation, he showed himself recognizable in the breaking of bread; and finally, entering suddenly, he presented himself not only recognizable but also tangible.

Moreover, the same Truth, who could have strengthened whomever he wished suddenly, gave an example to those who would follow, so that the imperfect would not presume to preach. On the very day on which he ascended into heaven, after fully instructing the disciples in the power of preaching, he immediately added: “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49).

We will remain seated in the city if we confine ourselves within the enclosures of our minds, lest we wander outward by speaking, so that, when we are perfectly clothed with divine power, we may then go forth from ourselves, as it were, to instruct others also.

Because the disciples still bore weak hearts in their understanding of so great a mystery, they had to be nourished by this dispensation: by seeking something for a little while they would find it; by finding it they would grow; and by growing they would hold more firmly what they had learned.

That weakness of the apostles, which had been terrified and had denied at the Lord’s death, and through denial had withered, fell back again into faith through the glory of his resurrection. Through the preaching spread by the apostles among the Gentiles—for the unbelief of the Jews was rejected—because he could be killed in the flesh, the faithful, multiplied through his resurrection, grew far and wide.

## CHAPTER XCVIII

“These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you” (Luke 24:44).

(Homily 24 on the Gospels, no. 2.) After his resurrection the Lord says this to his disciples, and, while present with them, declares that he is no longer with them. For he was not absent from those to whom he appeared bodily in their presence; yet he was already denying that he was with them, since by the immortality of his flesh he had become distinct from their mortal bodies.

## CHAPTER XCIX

“Touch and see: for a spirit does not have flesh and bones” (Luke 24:39).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIV, nos. 68, 74, 75.) [Col. 1238A] Our Redeemer promised us the resurrection that he displayed in himself, and one day he will bring it about in us, because the members follow the glory of their head. But behold, I hear of the resurrection, yet I seek to know its effect. I believe, indeed, that I shall rise again, but I want to hear what kind of resurrection it will be. I must know whether I shall rise in some other, perhaps subtle or airy body, or in the body in which I die. But if I rise in an airy body, I shall no longer be the one who rises. For how can the resurrection be true if the flesh cannot be true? Clear reasoning therefore teaches that, if there is no true flesh, unquestionably there will be no true resurrection. For that cannot rightly be called resurrection in which what fell does not rise again.

We must therefore believe that our body will by no means be, as Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, wrote, intangible in the glory of that resurrection, subtler than winds and air. In the glory of that resurrection our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but tangible through the truth of its nature. For this reason our Redeemer, when his disciples doubted his resurrection, [Col. 1238B] showed them his hands and side and offered flesh and bones to be touched, saying: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.”

When I had presented this testimony of evangelical truth to the same Eutychius while he was in Constantinople, he said: “The Lord did this for the very reason that he might remove doubt about his resurrection from the hearts of the disciples.” I replied: “What you assert is very strange: that doubt should arise for us from the very thing by which the hearts of the disciples were healed of doubt. For what could be said worse than that this should make us doubt the reality of his flesh, when through it his disciples were separated from every doubt and brought to faith? If it is asserted that he did not possess what he displayed, then our faith is destroyed by the very thing through which the faith of his disciples was strengthened.”

He also went on to say: “He had a tangible body, which he displayed; but after he had confirmed the hearts of those who touched him, everything in the Lord that could be touched was transformed into a certain subtlety [Col. 1238C].”

To this I replied: “It is written: ‘Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him’ (Romans 6:9). If, therefore, anything in his body could have been changed after the resurrection, then, contrary to Paul’s truthful statement, the Lord returned to death after his resurrection. Who would dare to say such a thing, unless he denied the true resurrection of the flesh?”

Then he objected: “Since it is written, ‘Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 15:50), how are we to believe that flesh truly rises again?”

I replied: “In sacred Scripture, ‘flesh’ is spoken of in one way according to nature and in another according to guilt or corruption. Flesh according to nature is meant where it is written: ‘This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh’ (Genesis 2:23), and: ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1:14).
