But flesh according to guilt is meant where it is written: ‘My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh’ (Genesis 6:3). And as the Psalmist says: ‘He remembered that they were flesh, [Col. 1238D] a passing spirit and not returning’ (Psalm 77:39).

“Thus Paul also said to the disciples: ‘You are not in the flesh but in the spirit.’ He did not mean that those to whom he sent his letters were not in the flesh; rather, because they had overcome the passions of carnal desires, they were no longer in the flesh through the power of the Spirit, having been set free.

“When the apostle Paul says, ‘Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Corinthians 15:50), he wishes ‘flesh’ to be understood according to guilt, not according to nature. He immediately shows that he was speaking of flesh according to guilt by adding: ‘Nor does corruption possess incorruption.’ In the glory of the heavenly kingdom, therefore, there will be flesh according to nature, but not according to the desires of passion, because, having conquered the sting of death, it will reign in eternal incorruption.”

After these statements, Eutychius immediately replied that he agreed, but he still denied that a tangible body could rise again. In the little book he had written about the resurrection, he had also inserted the testimony of the apostle Paul [Col. 1239A]: “What you sow is not brought to life unless it first dies; and what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain” (1 Corinthians 15:36–37). He was hastening to demonstrate by this that the flesh either would be intangible or would not exist at all, since the holy apostle, speaking of the glory of the resurrection, had said that it was not the body that was to be sown.

But the answer is readily given: when the apostle Paul says, “You sow not the body that is to be, but a bare grain,” he indicates what we see—that a grain is born with stalk and leaves, although it is sown without stalk or leaves. Thus, when speaking of the increase of the resurrection’s glory, Paul did not say that what the seed-grain possessed would be lacking, but that what it did not possess would be added. Eutychius, however, while denying that the true body would rise again, does not say that what was lacking would be added; rather, he says that what existed would be lacking.

After we had been drawn into a long dispute about this matter, we began to withdraw from the bitterest contention between us when the Emperor Tiberius Constantine, of blessed memory, received us both privately and learned what disagreement existed between us. Weighing the arguments of both sides [Col. 1239B], he also refuted with his own arguments the same book that Eutychius had written about the resurrection, and decided that it ought to be burned in the flames.

When we had left his presence, I was immediately overtaken by a serious illness, while Eutychius himself was overtaken by illness and death. After he died, since almost no one remained who followed his teaching, I refrained from pursuing what I had begun, lest I seem to be hurling words into ashes. While he was still alive and I was suffering from very high fevers, whenever acquaintances of mine went to him to offer greetings, I learned from their reports that he held the skin of his own hand before their eyes and said: “[Col. 1240A] I confess that we shall all rise again in this flesh.” As they themselves admitted, he had previously been accustomed to deny this altogether.

But setting these matters aside, and truly believing that the body of our Redeemer was tangible after his resurrection, we confess that our flesh will be both the same and different after the resurrection: the same in nature, different in glory; the same in reality, different in power. It will therefore be spiritual because it will be incorruptible, and it will be tangible because it will not lose the essence of true nature.

There are many who know verbally that the final judgment will follow the resurrection, but by their perverse conduct testify that they do not know it. Whoever does not fear it as he ought has not yet understood with what terrifying upheaval it will come. If we knew how to weigh the dreadful burden of that examination, we would certainly forestall the day of wrath by fearing it, and appease the sentence of strict punishment before it appeared.

The terror of the Judge can be avoided only before the judgment: now he is not seen, but he is appeased by prayers. When he has sat in that fearful tribunal, [Col. 1240B] he can both be seen and no longer be appeased, because he will then return all the wicked deeds that he silently endured for a long time, all at once in anger. It is therefore necessary to fear the Judge now, while he does not yet exercise judgment, while he patiently endures evil, while he still tolerates the evils that he sees—lest, when he has once stretched out his hand for the repayment of vengeance, he strike all the more strictly in judgment because he waits so long before the judgment.

Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# BOOK FOUR

## Exposition of the Gospel according to John

[Col. 1239]

## CHAPTER I

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1).

[Col. 1239C]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIII, nos. 35–36; book XXXII, no. 7.) God the almighty Father begot the Only-Begotten Son, consubstantial with himself, just as Elihu, speaking subtly to blessed Job, says: “God speaks once, and does not repeat the same thing a second time” (Job 33:14). This can be understood more subtly as referring to the Father’s begetting of the Only-Begotten Son, consubstantial with himself. For God’s speaking is his begetting of the Word. To speak once is to have no other Word besides the Only-Begotten. Hence it is appropriately added: “And does not repeat the same thing a second time,” because he begot this very Word—that is, the Son—as the only one.

For this reason John expressed only one Word. The fact that he did not say, “In the beginning was the Word,” but “was,” clearly shows that he was not speaking of an absolute past, since neither past nor future properly applies to God. [Col. 1239D] Thus any tense may freely be used of him precisely because none of them can be used literally. For no tense could be spoken freely if even one were spoken properly. We may therefore boldly attribute any tense to God because no tense can properly be attributed to him.

The Father begot the Word without time. Who could worthily express that ineffable birth: that the one born from the eternal is coeternal; that the one existing before the ages begot an equal; that the one born is not later than the one who begot him? We can marvel at this, but we are wholly unable to contemplate it. To see something of the power of that birth is already, in some measure, to be able to marvel at it; but how do we see what we in no way comprehend?

There is, however, something that we ought to transfer from the experience of the flesh to the understanding of the spirit. If someone were lying in darkness with his eyes closed, and suddenly the light of a lamp burst forth before him, the closed eyes would be struck by the light’s arrival and opened. Why, then, were they disturbed if, while closed, they saw nothing? [Col. 1240C] Yet nothing complete existed that they could see while closed. For if they had seen everything perfectly, why would they open and seek what they might see?

So it is with us when we attempt to contemplate something of the incomprehensible birth. The mind is struck by the radiance of wonder and, as it were, sees what cannot be seen; like someone placed in darkness, it perceives the force of light with closed eyes. The mystery of the divine nature does not easily become known to minds occupied with earthly desires.

Yet he most appropriately said, “was,” a word that includes something perfect and present, because the Only-Begotten Son, the very Word of the Father, is said to have been born in perfection and is also declared, on account of his eternity, always to be being born. In that the Father begot and spoke the perfect Word, he spoke; and in that he always begets, he also speaks continually. Nevertheless, what we have called “perfect” cannot properly be called so. For what has not been made is not properly said to be perfect; rather, we express its fullness through a certain limitation imposed by our language.

[Col. 1240D] We must carefully observe that certain likenesses drawn from inanimate things are sometimes spoken of God on account of the effect of his work, and sometimes to indicate the substance of his majesty. When an eye, shoulders, or foot are attributed to God, a certain effect of his activity is being shown. But when hand, arm, right hand, voice, or word is spoken of God, these terms demonstrate the Son who is consubstantial with him.

He himself is the hand and the right hand, of whose ascension the Father speaks through Moses: “I will lift my hand to heaven and swear by my right hand” (Deuteronomy 32:40). He is the arm of whom the prophet says: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1). He is the voice and the Word, because the Father begot him by speaking him forth, and because John wrote of him: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” David asserts that the Father made all things through this Word, saying: “He spoke, and they were made” (Psalm 32:9).

## CHAPTER II

“Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1:29).

(Homily 1 on Ezekiel, no. 5.) [Col. 1241A] Sometimes the spirit of prophecy touches the mind through the present but does not touch it through the future. Thus, when John saw the Lord coming, he said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” But when he was already near death, he sent disciples to ask: “Are you he who is to come, or should we expect another?” (Matthew 11:3).

These words show that John knew that the Redeemer had indeed come on earth, but he doubted whether he would descend in person to open the gates of hell. He had therefore been touched by the spirit of prophecy concerning the present: seeing the Mediator’s humanity and understanding his divinity, he confessed him to be the Lamb who would take away the sins of the world. But he had not been touched concerning the future, because he did not know of his descent into hell.

## CHAPTER III

“Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining” (John 1:33).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book II, nos. 50, 91–92.) [Col. 1241B] The gifts of the Holy Spirit—prophecy, kinds of tongues, and powers of healing—are not always present in the same way in the minds of those who receive them, because they are sometimes beneficially withdrawn lest the mind be lifted up in presumption.

Hence it is rightly written in the Gospel: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes.” The Spirit comes upon all the faithful, but in the Mediator alone he remains uniquely, because he never abandoned the humanity from whose divinity he proceeds. He therefore remains in the one who alone can do all things and always can do them.

For believers who receive him, when they cannot always possess the gifts of signs as they wish, testify that they have received him as though by a passing manifestation. But when the disciples are told by the mouth of Truth concerning the same Spirit: “He will remain with you and will be in you,” what does it mean that the divine voice declares this same abiding of the Holy Spirit to be a sign of the Mediator by saying: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him”? [Col. 1241C] If, then, he remains in the disciples according to the Master’s word, how is it already a unique sign that he remains in the Mediator?

We understand this more quickly if we distinguish the gifts of the same Spirit. Some are gifts without which one cannot reach life; others are gifts by which the holiness of life is displayed for the benefit of others. Gentleness, humility, patience, faith, hope, and charity are his gifts, but they are gifts without which human beings cannot reach life. Prophecy, the power of healing, kinds of tongues, and interpretation of speech are also his gifts, but they display his presence for the correction of those who behold them.

In the gifts without which one cannot reach life, the Holy Spirit always remains, whether in his preachers or in all the elect. But in those gifts through which he is displayed—not our own life but the life of others being sought—he does not always remain in preachers. He always presides in their hearts so that they may live well, but he does not always display signs of power through them. Sometimes he withdraws the manifestation of signs from them, so that his virtues may be held more humbly because they cannot be retained once possessed.

[Col. 1241D] The Mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, has him present in all things, always, and continually, because the same Spirit proceeds substantially from him. Therefore, although the Spirit remains in holy preachers, he is rightly said to remain uniquely in the Mediator: in them he remains by grace for something, but in him he remains by substance for everything.

Just as our body recognizes only the sense of touch, while the head of the body possesses the use of all five senses at once—seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, and touching—so the members of the heavenly Head shine forth in certain virtues, while the Head himself burns with all virtues. The Spirit therefore remains in him in a different way, since by nature he never departs from him.

[Col. 1242A] The gifts by which one strives toward life cannot be lost without danger; the gifts by which the holiness of life is displayed are often withdrawn, as has been said, without loss. The former are to be held for our instruction; the latter are to be sought for the advancement of others. In the former, fear should terrify us lest they perish; in the latter, when they are withdrawn for a time, humility should console us, because perhaps they lift the mind toward self-exaltation. Thus, when the signs of power granted to us are withdrawn, we truly show that we held them rightly when we endure their temporary removal with equanimity.

## CHAPTER IV

“Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him: ‘Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit’” (John 1:47).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIII, no. 32.) The Only-Begotten Son of God came for our redemption and sent his preachers against the pride of the world. Leaving the wise, he chose the foolish; leaving the strong, the weak; leaving the rich, the poor. He desired to have weak and despised preachers who would gather powerful people and faithful peoples.

[Col. 1242B] This is why he praises Nathanael but does not number him among the preachers, because those who were to come to preach had to be people who possessed nothing of their own praise. Thus the truth of what they did would be recognized all the more firmly, the more clearly it was seen that they had not been capable of accomplishing it by themselves. To make the wondrous power shine forth through the tongues of preachers, it was first brought about even more wondrously that the merit of those same preachers should be nothing.

When Nathanael asked, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered: “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (ibid., v. 48). We should understand that “to see” there means “to choose.” “I saw you under the fig tree” means: “I chose you while you were placed under the shadow of the Law.”

## CHAPTER V

“Fill the jars with water” (John 2:7).

(Homily 6, book I, on Ezekiel, part II, no. 7.) The commandments of sacred Scripture, which are spoken spiritually to the more perfect, correspond literally to the weak. What little ones understand literally, the learned perceive more deeply through spiritual understanding.

[Col. 1242C] Whom among the little ones would the Gospel story itself not refresh by its account of the miracle, when the Lord commanded that empty jars be filled with water and immediately changed that same water into wine? But when those who are more watchful in understanding hear this, they both venerate the sacred history in faith and seek what it signifies inwardly.

He who could change water into wine could also have filled empty jars with wine at once. Yet he commands that the jars be filled with water because, through the history of sacred reading, our hearts must first be filled. He changes water into wine for us when the history itself is transformed for us, through the mystery of allegory, into spiritual understanding. Sacred Scripture therefore accommodates little ones in humble language, yet, by pouring into them what is more spiritual, raises them to a higher level.

## CHAPTER VI

“Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit” (John 3:5).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, in the preliminary preface; book IX, no. 32.) [Col. 1242D] Some are taken away from the present light before they reach the point of earning either good or evil merits through active life. Since the sacraments of salvation do not free them from the guilt of original sin, and since they have done nothing of their own in this life, they nevertheless come to eternal punishment.

Whoever is not released by the water of regeneration remains bound by the guilt of the first bond. What the water of baptism accomplishes among us was accomplished among the ancients either by faith alone in the case of infants, by the power of sacrifice in the case of adults, or by the mystery of circumcision in the case of those who came from Abraham’s stock.

Since everyone is conceived with the guilt of the first parent, the Prophet testifies: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities” (Psalm 50:7). And because the one whom the water of salvation does not cleanse does not escape punishment for original sin, Truth itself openly declares: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not have eternal life.”

[Col. 1243A] Therefore even those who have committed no sin by their own will receive everlasting punishment. No one is clean in the sight of God, not even an infant of one day upon the earth; and whoever adds no personal sin is condemned for original sin alone. Under the strictness of divine judgment it is just that mortal offspring, like a fruitful tree, should retain in its branches the bitterness it drew from its root.

## CHAPTER VII

“The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVII, no. 41.) When the regard of divine grace suddenly strikes with fear a mind numbed by sinners’ carelessness and negligence, the very voice of the Spirit that comes upon it, making its way into the ear of the heart, awakens it; yet the mind illuminated by this voice does not investigate it.

For it cannot weigh by what pathways the invisible power flows into it, by what means it comes to itself, or by what means it departs. Hence John rightly says: “The Spirit breathes where he wills; you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes.”

[Col. 1243B] The Lord’s voice is heard when the breathing of his grace is conceived in the mind, when the insensibility of hidden deafness is broken, and when the heart, awakened to the pursuit of supreme love, is penetrated by the cry of an inward power.

To hear the voice of the Spirit is to rise through the force of inward compunction into love of the invisible Creator. But no one knows where it comes from, because it is not known through what opportunities, by the mouths of preachers, he pours himself into us. No one knows where it goes, because when many hear the same preaching, it cannot be understood whom it abandons and casts away, or in whose heart it enters and rests.

One thing is outwardly done, but it does not penetrate the hearts of those who observe it in one and the same way, because the one who invisibly orders visible things plants, incomprehensibly, the seeds of causes in human hearts.

Thus, after Lazarus had been raised, many believed, but many of the Jews were nevertheless moved by that very resurrection to zeal for persecution (John 11). One and the same miracle therefore gave the light of faith to some, while through the darkness of envy it blinded others to the light of the mind.

[Col. 1243C] Thus both thieves saw the same death of the Redeemer, a death like their own, yet one did not fear to provoke him with insults in pride, while the other honored him in fear. Their thought was not the same regarding one and the same event, because the inward Judge distinguished it by invisibly ordering it.

The modes of hidden inspiration therefore cannot be grasped by our thought, nor can the mind’s eye comprehend the ways in which divine grace pours itself into us; by it the mind’s intention is changed for the better.

## CHAPTER VIII

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVII, nos. 29–30.) Our Lord Jesus Christ, who for our sake was made lower than the angels, made us equal to the angels through the power of his abasement. By dying he taught us not to fear death; by rising, to trust in life; by ascending, to glory in the inheritance of the heavenly homeland. Thus, when the members see where the Head has gone before, they may rejoice that they will follow him there.

Hence our same Head rightly says: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matthew 24:28). [Col. 1243D] Paul says: “For we know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).

But if we too, who were born on earth, ascend to heaven, what becomes of the statement that Truth makes again: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven”? This same Truth immediately answers the apparent difficulty when it says: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

These statements do not disagree with one another; rather, they kindle the effort of our mind to investigate what seems discordant. Since we were all born in faith in him, we are unquestionably his body. Therefore, by a wondrous dispensation of mercy, the Lord became the Head of his members. With the multitude of the reprobate rejected, he alone is also with us.

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven,” [Col. 1244A] because, since we have already become one with him, he who came alone in himself returns there alone also in us. And the one who is always in heaven ascends to heaven each day, because he who remains above all things in divinity daily draws his humanity to the heavens through the bond of his humanity.

Human frailty should not despair. Let it consider the blood of the Only-Begotten and see in its price how great it is, since it is worth so much. Let it carefully weigh where the Head has gone before; and in the commandments by which it is bound to live, let it find strength through his example to hope.

Let it trust in heaven, hope for the heavenly homeland, know itself to be the companion of angels, and rejoice that in its Head it has been exalted even above the angels.

## CHAPTER IX

“The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXII, no. 41.) [Col. 1244B] Just as the Law was transmitted through a servant to a people that still feared, so the grace of the Gospel was bestowed through the Lord upon sons who love. He came for our redemption and established the New Testament for us; yet, when he examines us according to the commandment of that same Testament, he will also come as Judge.

The one who is now the Author of the Gospel will then be the Author of judgment, so that he may strictly demand what he now commands and enjoins with gentleness. We see this happening daily: teachers gently impose the rudiments of letters upon children, but later demand them from the children with severity; what they give with gentleness, they require with blows.

The commandments of divine speech now sound gentle, but in action they will be felt as harsh. The admonition of the one who calls is gentle now, but then the justice of the Judge will come with strictness, because it is certain that not even the least commandment will be overlooked in the examination. Thus it is clear that the one who gave the Gospel is the one who judges.

For this reason Truth itself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

## CHAPTER X

“He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29).

[Col. 1244C] (Homily 20 on the Gospels, nos. 4–5.) The holy Church of the peoples was believed to be the bride of blessed John the Baptist by those who thought that he was the Christ. But he himself said: “He who has the bride is the Bridegroom; but the friend of the Bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the Bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is fulfilled.”

It is as though he said: “I am not the Bridegroom; I am the friend of the Bridegroom.” He declared that he rejoiced not because of his own voice but in the Bridegroom’s voice, because he was not glad that he was heard speaking humbly by the people, but because he heard inwardly the voice of Truth so that he might speak it outwardly.

He rightly says that his joy is fulfilled, because whoever rejoices in his own voice does not possess full joy. Hence he adds: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

[Col. 1244D] In this matter we must ask in what way Christ increased and in what way John decreased. The answer is that, when the people saw John’s abstinence and observed that he kept himself apart from human beings, they thought that he was the Christ. But when they saw Christ eating with tax collectors and walking among sinners, they believed him to be not the Christ but a prophet.

As time passed, however, Christ—who had been thought to be a prophet—was recognized as Christ, and John—who had been thought to be Christ—was recognized as a prophet. Thus what Christ’s forerunner had foretold was fulfilled: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” In the estimation of the people, Christ increased because he was recognized as what he was, while John decreased because he ceased to be called what he was not.

## CHAPTER XI

“I do not seek my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 5:30).

(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 18.) Stubborn people think more highly of themselves than they are, and therefore do not yield to the counsels of others. If they did not consider themselves better than the rest, they would never place the advice of everyone else beneath their own deliberation.

[Col. 1245A] Stubbornness is born of pride. Stubborn people should therefore recognize the arrogance of their own judgment and strive to conquer themselves, lest, while they disdain being outwardly overcome by the sound admonitions of others, they be held captive inwardly by pride.

They should also carefully observe that the Son of Man, whose will is always one with the Father’s, in order to give us an example of breaking our own will, says: “I do not seek my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me.” To commend further the grace of this virtue, he foretold that he would preserve it even at the final judgment, saying: “I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge.”

With what conscience, then, does a human being disdain to yield to another’s will, when the Son of God and man, coming to display the glory of his power, testifies that he does not judge from himself?

## CHAPTER XII

“Jesus, knowing that they were about to come and seize him,” and so forth (John 6:15).

(Pastoral Rule, part I, chapter 3.) [Col. 1245B] Whoever is unequal to sacred governance should not dare rashly to undertake it or, through desire for high office, undertake a leadership that leads to destruction. James piously forbids this, saying: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers” (James 3:1).

For this reason the Mediator of God and human beings himself avoided receiving kingship on earth, although he reigns in heaven before the ages and surpasses even the knowledge and understanding of the heavenly spirits. It is written: “When Jesus realized that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, he fled to the mountain by himself.”

For who could have ruled over human beings so blamelessly as the one who would rule those whom he himself had created? Yet because he appeared in the flesh not only to redeem us through his passion but also to teach us through his conduct, giving an example to those who follow him, he did not wish to be made king.

He willingly came to the gallows of the cross; he fled the offered glory of high office; he sought the punishment of a shameful death, so that his members might learn to flee the world’s favors, not fear its terrors, love adversity for the sake of truth, and avoid prosperity through fear. [Col. 1245C] The former often pollute the heart through pride, while the latter cleanse it through suffering. In prosperity the mind exalts itself; in adversity, even when it has exalted itself, it is thrown down. In prosperity a person forgets himself; in adversity he is unwillingly and even forcibly recalled to awareness of himself.

## CHAPTER XIII

“You seek me because you ate of the loaves” (John 6:26).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIII, no. 49.) In sacred Scripture “bread” sometimes signifies the Lord himself, as he says in the Gospel: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51).

Sometimes bread signifies the grace of a spiritual gift, as the Lord says through David concerning the holy Church: “I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Psalm 131:15), because the minds of the humble who are placed in her are filled with the refreshment of spiritual gifts.

Sometimes bread signifies the support of the present life, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel to the crowds following him: “You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.” They had been satisfied with seven loaves.

[Col. 1245D] Through their person the Lord condemns those within the holy Church who, approaching the Lord through the sacred orders, seek in those orders not the merits that belong to them but the supports of the present life. They do not consider what they ought to imitate by living, but what advantages will satisfy them when they receive them.

To follow the Lord after being satisfied with bread is to receive temporal nourishment from the holy Church. To seek the Lord not for the sake of signs but for the sake of bread is to aspire to the office of religion not in order to increase one’s virtues, but in order to obtain its material supports.

## CHAPTER XIV

“The one who comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6:17).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXV, no. 12.) [Col. 1246A] Obedience alone is the virtue that implants the other virtues in the mind and preserves them once implanted. Thus the first human being received a commandment to observe; if he had willingly submitted himself in obedience, he would have reached eternal blessedness without labor.

For this reason Truth says in the Gospel: “Whoever comes to me I will not cast out, because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.”

For what would have happened if he had done his own will? Would he have rejected those who came to him? Who does not know that the Son’s will does not differ from the Father’s will? But because the first human being wished to do his own will and therefore departed from the joy of paradise, the Second, coming for the redemption of humanity, showed that he did the Father’s will and not his own, and taught us to remain within.

When, therefore, he does not his own will but the Father’s, he does not cast out those who come to him because, by subjecting us to obedience through his example, he closes the way by which we might depart.

Again he says: “I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge” (John 5:30). We are commanded to preserve obedience even unto death. But he, when he judges according to what he hears, obeys even when he comes as Judge.

[Col. 1246B] So that obedience might not seem burdensome to us until the end of the present life, our Redeemer shows that he preserves it even when he comes as Judge. It is therefore no wonder if sinful human beings submit themselves to obedience during the brief span of the present life, when the Mediator of God and human beings does not abandon obedience even when he rewards those who obey.

## Chapter XV

**“Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, no. 58; Book XI, no. 14; Homily 10 on Ezekiel, no. 6; in the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XII, no. 8.)*

Blessed Job says of the Lord that he “cut channels in the rocks,” that is, that he opened streams of preaching in the hard hearts of the Gentiles. The prophet likewise speaks of watering the arid land of the Gentiles: “He made the wilderness into a pool of water, and the dry land into channels of water” (Psalm 160:30). In the Gospel, too, the Lord promises, saying: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” We heard this promise at that time.

[Col. 1246C] For behold, among the holy preachers who were not descended from Judah, throughout the Church spread across the whole world, streams of heavenly commandments flow abundantly from Gentile mouths. When he opened channels in the rocks, a river of holy preaching likewise flowed from hard hearts.

Water sometimes signifies the knowledge of preaching, in accordance with what is written: “Deep water is the word from the mouth of a man, and an overflowing stream, a fountain of wisdom.” In the language of Sacred Scripture, the belly is also sometimes used for the mind. Since holy preachings flow from the minds of the faithful, rivers of living water flow, as it were, from the bellies of believers.

Water also sometimes signifies the irrigation, grace, or infusion of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst” (John 4:13). Again the Lord says: “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The evangelist then adds: “He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive.”

## Chapter XVI

**“Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIV, nos. 33–34; Book I, no. 16.)*

[Col. 1246D] We must rise up against ourselves in order to correct ourselves: recognizing our own evils, we must strike ourselves with the strict punishment of repentance and, yielding to no flattering allurements of our thoughts, by no means spare ourselves in our sins.

If we first pursue our own evils strictly within ourselves, it is also right that we rise up usefully against the evils of others, so that by reproving in others what we punish in ourselves, we may overcome it. But the wicked do not know this way of rising up for correction. They abandon themselves and attack the good; bending themselves inwardly through the softness of flattering self-adulation, they rise up against the lives of the good with harsh severity. They leave themselves to be reproved while reproving others with severe judgments.

[Col. 1247A] Whoever does not first judge himself does not know what is right to judge in another. Even if, perhaps, he knows by hearsay what he ought to judge rightly, he is nevertheless unable to judge another’s merits rightly, because the innocence of his own conscience provides him with no rule of judgment. Hence, when certain men laid snares and brought forward an adulterous woman to be punished, it was said to them: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.” They were going to punish another’s sins while leaving their own behind. Thus they are recalled inwardly to their conscience, so that they may first correct their own faults and then reprove those of others.

The proper order of correction is this: first we rise up against ourselves, and afterward against those who need to be corrected. For whoever rises up against the good is puffed up by pride.

It should also be considered that the incarnate Lord maintained simplicity together with uprightness, because in gentleness he neither lost the strictness of justice, nor again, in the strictness of justice, the virtue of gentleness. Therefore, when certain men, as has been said, brought forward the adulterous woman in order to test him, hoping to make him fall into either harshness or injustice, he responded to both, saying: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.”

[Col. 1247B] He gives the simplicity of gentleness when he says, “the one who is without sin”; he gives the zeal of justice when he says, “let him be the first to throw a stone at her.” Frequently, when we pursue the uprightness of justice, we abandon gentleness; and when we wish to preserve gentleness, we turn aside from the uprightness of justice.

## Chapter XVII

**“Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” (John 9:2).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Preface, no. 12.)*

There are various kinds of blows. One kind is the blow by which a sinner is struck so that he may be punished without reprieve. Another is the blow by which a sinner is struck so that he may be corrected. Another is the blow by which someone is sometimes struck, not so that he may correct past sins, but so that he may not commit future ones. Yet another is the blow by which someone is often struck, through which neither past guilt is corrected nor future guilt prevented.

But when unexpected healing follows a blow, the power of the one who saves becomes known and is loved more ardently; and when an innocent person is worn down by the scourge, the fullness of his merits is increased through patience.

[Col. 1247C] Sometimes a sinner is struck so that he may be punished without reprieve, as it is said to doomed Judah: “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel chastisement” (Jeremiah 30:14). Again: “Why do you cry out over your wound? Your pain is incurable” (ibid., 15).

Sometimes a sinner is struck so that he may be corrected, as it is said to someone in the Gospel: “See, you have been healed; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14). The words of the one who healed him show that his preceding sins had demanded the force of suffering.

Sometimes someone is struck not to wash away past guilt, but to prevent future guilt. Paul openly testifies to this concerning himself, saying: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (1 Corinthians 12:7). For he does not say that he was exalted, but “lest he should be exalted,” clearly indicating that this blow restrained what might otherwise occur; it did not cleanse a fault that had already occurred.

[Col. 1247D] Sometimes, however, someone is struck neither because of past nor future iniquity, but so that the power of divine virtue alone may be displayed through the removal of the blow. Thus, when it was said to the Lord concerning the man born blind, “Did this man sin, or his parents, that he was born blind?” he answered: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but that the works of God might be manifested.”

What takes place in this manifestation except that the strength of merit is increased through the scourge? When no past iniquity is cleansed, great strength is produced through patience.

## Chapter XVIII

**“The Lord made mud from spittle and anointed my eyes with it” (John 9:6).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book VIII, no. 49; Homily 10 on Ezekiel, no. 6.)*

Saliva descends into us from the head; from the mouth it is carried to the belly when it is swallowed. What, then, is our head except divinity, through which we receive the beginning of existence so that we may be creatures? Paul bears witness to this when he says: “The head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

[Col. 1248A] What, then, is our belly except the mind? When it looks toward its heavenly food—that is, understanding—having been nourished, it undoubtedly governs all the members of our actions. For unless Sacred Scripture sometimes expressed the mind by the name “belly,” Solomon would certainly not have said: “The lamp of the Lord is the spirit of man, searching all the hidden places of the belly” (Proverbs 20:27). For when the grace of heavenly regard illuminates us, it also reveals to us everything hidden within our mind.

Hence it is also said through Jeremiah: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain” (Jeremiah 4:19). Because he had spoken of a spiritual, not bodily, belly, he adds: “The senses of my heart are troubled.” It would not have concerned the salvation of the people if the prophet had proclaimed that he was suffering pain in his bodily belly. He suffered in his belly because he felt affliction of mind.

[Col. 1248B] But why should we bring forward the prophet’s example when we have a clearer testimony from the Lord? When Truth itself speaks, the prophet must be silent, because a lamp has no brightness in the sun. The Lord says: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). Since holy preachings flow from the minds of the faithful, rivers of living water flow, as it were, from the bellies of believers.

What is meant by the name “spittle” except the taste of intimate contemplation? It flows from the head to the mouth because, from the brightness of the Creator, only a faint taste of revelation touches us while we remain placed in this life.

Therefore, when the Redeemer came, he mixed spittle with mud and restored the eyes of the man born blind. For heavenly grace illuminates our carnal thought through the admixture of its contemplation and reforms man from original blindness to understanding. Since nature brought forth the man who had been expelled from the joys of paradise into this exile, he came forth, as it were, from birth without eyes.

## Chapter XIX

**“Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 3:34).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book IV, no. 71.)*

[Col. 1248C] Whoever submits himself to wicked desire places the neck of a mind that was once free beneath the dominion of iniquity. We oppose this dominion when we resist the iniquity that has begun to dominate us; when we violently resist habit and, trampling perverse desires beneath our feet, assert against it the right of our inborn liberty; when we strike down guilt through repentance and wash away the stains of defilement with tears.

Often the mind remembers that it has acted perversely and, mourning, not only abandons its wicked deeds but also punishes them with the bitterest lamentation. Yet it still does not raise itself fully into security. It remembers what evils it committed, but does not know whether it has mourned its deeds worthily; and it fears that the enormity of its guilt may exceed the measure of its repentance.

Often Truth has already forgiven the guilt, but the afflicted mind, still extremely anxious about pardon, continues to fear between hope and dread, because it does not know what the just Judge will reckon concerning its deeds and what he will forgive when he comes.

[Col. 1248D] Thus the slave already flees from the Lord in this life, but is not free. A person has already abandoned his sin by correcting and repenting of it, yet still fears the strict Judge and what recompense he will assign for it. In the other life, therefore, the slave will be freed by the Lord: there will be no longer any uncertainty about the forgiveness of sin; the memory of guilt will no longer enslave the secure mind; the spirit will not tremble beneath accusation, but, freed by his indulgence, will rejoice.

## Chapter XX

**“If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John 8:36).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, no. 72.)*

The eternal Wisdom of God was sent to redeem the human race—not holy angels or righteous men—but came in visible manifestation through himself. No angel, no righteous man, was sent so that the human race might be redeemed from guilt, because it was necessary that God’s creature be liberated by the Creator, as Truth itself says: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free.”

[Col. 1249A] Since the eternal Wisdom of God, remaining with the Father throughout the ages, was to be incarnate at the end of the ages, righteous and holy men were sent for this purpose: to prepare the way for this Wisdom in human hearts by preaching. They could not have been holy in any way unless they recognized themselves as servants of this Wisdom.

Because it was certain that, as time advanced and the age declined, its diseases would increase, it was brought about that the eternal Wisdom of God would come in person at the end of the ages to this great sufferer, afflicted with immense weakness—that is, to the human race, lying sick throughout the whole world. Preachers were first sent, like physicians making visits, so that afterward the power of the physician might appear all the greater as the illness of the sick man had grown worse.

## Chapter XXI

**“You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIII, no. 38, in reverse order.)*

[Col. 1249B] The ancient enemy, prince of all the wicked, has some as his companions and others as his children. Who are his companions except those apostate angels who fell with him from the seat of their heavenly homeland? And whom else does he have as children except wicked men, who, through his evil persuasion, are generated in the practice of malice?

Hence Truth’s voice says to unbelievers: “You are of your father the devil.” The devil and all the wicked are so truly one body that often the body is designated by the name of the head, and the head is called by the name of the body.

The body is designated by the name of the head when it is said concerning a wicked man: “One of you is a devil” (John 6:71). Again, the head is called by the name of the body when it is said concerning that apostate angel himself: “An enemy has done this” (Matthew 13:28).

## Chapter XXII

**“Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the gate, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber; but whoever enters through the gate is the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10:1).**

*(Homily 13 on Ezekiel, no. 8, and especially Homily 13, no. 1.)*

[Col. 1249C] If the good shepherd enters through the gate, and he himself is the gate and the shepherd, then undoubtedly he enters through himself. We must therefore ask how he enters, and how he enters through himself.

For our Lord and Redeemer is, according to the flesh, one substance with the holy Church that he redeemed, as Paul bears witness when he says: “I fill up what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh for his body, which is the Church” (Colossians 1:24). The Church is the body of this head, and Christ is the head of this body.

The body rejoices in its head, that is, the holy Church, with the Psalmist saying: “But now he has exalted my head above my enemies” (Psalm 26:6). Since the Church itself is also one day to be exalted, it already rejoices in heaven that its head has been exalted above its enemies.

When the elect reach life, therefore, because they enter through him as his members, he enters through himself into himself. For he himself is in his members who enters: he is the head to which the entering members attain.

## Chapter XXIII

**“If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).**

*(Homily 1, Book II, on Ezekiel, no. 16; and Homily 14, Book I, on the Gospel, no. 5.)*

[Col. 1249D] We must always turn the eyes of our hearts toward our departure and meditate without ceasing on when we shall leave this present life and attain eternal joys. For this reason the Only-Begotten of the Father became incarnate: to bring us into the faith of the holy Church and lead us to the vision of his appearance.

Hence he says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture.” He will enter, that is, into faith; he will go out from faith into vision, from belief into contemplation; and he will find pasture in eternal refreshment and satisfaction.

Whoever follows the Lord Jesus with a simple heart is nourished by the food of eternal verdure. What are these pastures except the eternal joys of ever-green paradise? The pasture of the elect is the present face of God: while it is contemplated without failing, the mind is satisfied forever with the food of life.

[Col. 1250A] Concerning this departure of ours, which we ought daily to meditate upon in our minds, Paul also speaks of our Redeemer, saying: “To sanctify the people through his own blood, he suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach; for we have no lasting city here, but we seek the one that is to come” (Hebrews 13:12–14).

## Chapter XXIV

**“I have power to lay down my life” (John 10:18).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXIV, nos. 2–5, sometimes in reverse order.)*

That hostile persuasion had polluted the whole human race with the contagion of guilt from its very root. There was no one who, interceding with God for sinners, could appear free from sin, because the same guilt enveloped all alike, born from the same mass.

Therefore the Only-Begotten of the Father came to us. He assumed a nature from us without committing sin. He who could intervene for sinners had to be without sin, because he could not cleanse the contagion of another’s pollution if he himself bore his own.

[Col. 1250B] Thus the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, interceding for sinners, showed himself to be a righteous man who could merit forgiveness for others. Our physician came to us from above and, finding us weighed down by so many illnesses, applied to us something similar and something contrary.

He came as a human being to human beings, but as a righteous man to sinners. He agreed with us in the truth of nature, but differed from us in the truth of righteousness. A vicious human being could not be corrected except through God; yet the one who corrected him had to be seen, so that by providing a model for imitation he might change his former way of life.

But he could not be seen by man unless God became man, so that he could be seen. Thus the just and invisible God appeared as a visible man like us, so that, while he healed through what was similar, he might heal through what was just; and while he agreed with our condition in the truth of his human lineage, he might counter our sickness through the power of his art.

[Col. 1250C] When the Lord came in the flesh, he did not assume our guilt from corruption, nor our punishment from necessity. Since he was stained by no sin, he could not be held under the condition of our guilt; therefore, having trampled down every necessity, he freely assumed our death when he willed.

He was not born as we are, nor did he die as we do, nor was he raised as we are. He was conceived not through human intercourse, but when the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin. His mother’s womb, in giving birth, was both fruitful and remained undefiled.

Again, we all die unwillingly, because the condition of our guilt constrains us to pay the debt of punishment. But since no guilt was mixed with him, he did not succumb to punishment by necessity. Because he subjected our guilt beneath his dominion, however, he assumed our punishment in compassion, as he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again.” He had also said beforehand: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.”

[Col. 1250D] Again, he was not raised as we are, because our resurrection has been deferred until the end of the age, whereas his was celebrated on the third day. We rise through him; he rose through himself. Since he was God, he had no need to be raised by another, as though he could not rise as we do.

His resurrection therefore differs from ours in that we do not rise through ourselves as he did. Because we are simply human beings, we require assistance from above in order to rise. But he, as God together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, displayed the power of resurrection, though he alone experienced it in his humanity.

The Lord, therefore, was truly born, truly dead, and truly raised. In all things he differs from us by the greatness of his power, but in the sole truth of nature he agrees with us. Although in all his works he surpasses us by immeasurable power, in one respect—that is, in the truth of his form—he does not differ from us.

Since, as has been said, there was no one whose merits could have induced the Lord to be merciful to us, the Only-Begotten of the Father assumed the form of our weakness and appeared alone as the righteous one, interceding for sinners. By enduring our punishment in dying, he changed our corruption by rising again.

[Col. 1251A] In the very flesh that he assumed, he showed free the flesh that he redeemed. This redeemed flesh is, of course, us: we are bound by the knowledge of our guilt, but we are freed by the righteousness of so great a Mediator, as he himself says: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John 8:36).

## Chapter XXV

**“The Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter” (John 10:22).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book II, no. 2.)*

While preserving the truth of the historical account, divine words sometimes indicate causes that they do not disclose in explicit speech by the position of a place, sometimes by the position of a body, sometimes by the quality of the air, and sometimes by the quality of the time.

They indicate something by the position of places, for example, when Scripture says concerning Israel that it could not hear the words of God on the mountain, but received the commandments in the plains (Exodus 19; 24; 34). This indicates the people’s subsequent weakness: they were unable to ascend to higher things, but by living carelessly they let themselves sink into the lowest places.

(Numbers 36.) [Col. 1251B] Thus, when Moses descended from the mountain, the Law was given to the carnal Israelite people in the plains. But the Lord, seated on the mountain, spoke lofty and spiritual commandments to the holy apostles (Matthew 5), so that the locations might show that the former, as carnal people, received lesser commandments in the valley of the earth, while the latter, as spiritual and holy people, heard heavenly commandments on the mountain. It was thereby clearly shown that those who ascend in heart to heavenly things leave behind what is low and stand upon the summit of the mind.

Through the position of a body, divine Scripture announces future events. Thus, in the Acts of the Apostles, Stephen declares that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of Power (Acts 7). To stand is the posture of one who gives assistance; and rightly he is seen standing who offers help in the battle of conflict.

The quality of the air reveals what follows, as when the evangelist, saying that none of the Jews would then believe while the Lord was preaching, first stated: “It was winter.” For it is written: “Iniquity will abound, and the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12).

[Col. 1251C] He therefore took care to specify the time of winter so that he might indicate the coldness of wickedness in the hearts of his hearers. Among the mysteries that Truth was proclaiming, why was the word “winter” added except to show, through the quality of the season and the air, the coldness of the heart? For while they were receiving the words of Truth, the hearts of the Jews remained cold.

Hence it is also said beforehand concerning Peter, who was to deny the Lord: “Because it was cold, and he stood by the fire warming himself” (John 18:18). Already he had grown numb within from the warmth of charity, and, as weakness burned within him, he warmed himself toward the love of the present life as though toward the fires of his persecutors.

[Col. 1251D] The quality of time also expresses the end of an action. Thus Judas, who would not return to forgiveness, is said to have gone out at night to the treachery of betrayal. As he went out, the evangelist says: “And it was night” (John 13:30). Hence it is also said to the wicked rich man: “This night they demand your soul from you” (Luke 12:20). A soul being led into darkness is said to be demanded not in the day but in the night (1 Kings 3).

Hence Solomon, who did not persevere in the wisdom he received, is described as having received it in a dream and at night. Hence the angels come to Abraham at midday, but are said to have come in the evening to punish Sodom.

## Chapter XXVI

**“Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXII, no. 31; Homily 26 on the Gospel, no. 6.)*

When a sinner, reproved for his vice, flees beneath words of defense and excuse, refusing to let what he has done be known, he hides not himself from the Lord but the Lord from himself. He acts so that he may not see the one who sees everything, not so that he himself may not be seen.

[Col. 1252A] By contrast, for every sinner the beginning of illumination is the humility of confession. A person already refuses to spare himself when he is not ashamed to confess the evil he has done; and the one who could have been accused by defending himself very quickly defends himself by accusing himself.

Therefore, when Lazarus was dead and weighed down by a great mass, the Lord did not say, “Come back to life,” but “Come out.” In the resurrection that took place in his body, the manner in which we are raised in heart is signified: the dead man is told, “Come out,” so that the person dead in sin and already buried beneath the mass of evil habit, lying hidden within his conscience through wickedness, may come out from himself through confession.

“Come out” is said to the dead man so that he may be summoned to leave the excuse and concealment of sin and come forth with his own mouth to accuse himself. Thus the prophet David, reviving from the great mass of such a crime, came forth, as it were, at the Lord’s voice, when, corrected by Nathan, he accused himself of what he had done.

After confession, therefore, those who have received authority to bind and loose must weigh the case; only then is the power of binding and loosing to be exercised. It must be considered what the guilt was and what repentance followed the guilt, so that the pastor’s judgment may absolve those whom almighty God visits through the grace of compunction.

[Col. 1252B] The superior’s absolution is true when it follows the decision of the eternal Judge. This is well signified by the resurrection of the dead man who had been four days in the tomb. It shows that the Lord first called and gave life to the dead man, saying: “Lazarus, come out”; afterward, the one who had come forth alive was released by the disciples, as it is written: “When the one who had been bound came out, he said to the disciples: ‘Unbind him and let him go’” (John 11:45).

Behold: the disciples release the one who was already living, whom the Master had raised while dead. If the disciples had released Lazarus while he was dead, they would have displayed stench rather than power.

From this consideration it must be understood that we ought, through pastoral authority, to release those whom we recognize our Creator to have brought to life through his reviving grace. This life-giving work is already recognized in the confession of sin, before the work of righteousness.

Therefore, even to this dead Lazarus the Lord did not say, “Come back to life,” but “Come out.” Every sinner who hides his guilt within his conscience lies concealed inwardly and hidden in his own depths. But the dead man comes out when the sinner willingly confesses his wickedness.

[Col. 1252C] Lazarus is therefore told: “Come out.” It is as though every dead person were openly told: “When you hide your guilt within your conscience, come out through confession—you who lie hidden inwardly within yourself through denial.” Let the dead man come out, that is, let the sinner confess his guilt; and let the disciples release the one who comes out, so that the pastors of the Church may remove the punishment deserved by the one who was not ashamed to confess what he had done.

## Chapter XXVII

**“I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (John 12:28).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVIII, nos. 3–5 and 7–8.)*

When the Lord makes his will known through an angelic creature, he sometimes reveals it in words, sometimes through images presented to the eyes of the heart, and sometimes through heavenly substances.

[Col. 1252D] He speaks through an angel in words when nothing is shown in an image, but the words of heavenly speech are heard. Thus, when the Lord says: “Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you,” the response immediately follows: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”

God, who cries out without time through the force of his inner impulse, did not utter that voice in time through his own substance and distinguish it through human words bounded by time. Rather, speaking from heavenly things, he formed the words he wished human beings to hear through the agency of a rational creature.

Sometimes God speaks through images, with the eyes of the heart extended, through angels: Jacob, sleeping, saw a ladder resting upon heaven; Peter, carried away in ecstasy, saw a sheet full of reptiles and quadrupeds. Unless Peter had seen these things with bodily eyes, he would not have been in ecstasy. Likewise, in a nighttime vision a Macedonian man appeared to Paul and begged him to cross over into Macedonia.

[Col. 1253A] Sometimes God speaks through heavenly substances. Thus, when the Lord had been baptized, it is written that a voice sounded from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

## Chapter XXVIII

**“Isaiah said this when he saw his glory” (John 12:41).**

*(Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 8, nos. 30–31.)*

However intensely the human mind stretches itself—even if it restrains every fantasy of bodily images from its thought and removes all bounded spirits from the eyes of the heart—while it remains placed in mortal flesh it cannot see the glory of God as it is. Whatever of that glory shines in the mind is a likeness, not the glory itself.

Hence the prophet Ezekiel said: “This was the appearance of the brightness round about, and this was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord” (Ezekiel 1:28; 2:1). The preacher who had been caught up to the third heaven likewise said: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

[Col. 1253B] This gives rise to a question that should not be dismissed: how is it that the evangelist John, after describing the Jews’ unbelief concerning the miracles of our Redeemer even from the words of the prophets, adds: “Isaiah said this when he saw his glory, and spoke of him”? If Ezekiel saw it, what does it mean that one is said to have seen the likeness of the glory and the other to have seen his glory?

When the evangelist John first narrated the miracles of our Redeemer and afterward added the unbelief of the Jews, he showed that Isaiah had seen the glory of that same Redeemer which appeared in the world. Everything miraculous that is divinely accomplished on earth is the glory of almighty God, and his glory is seen in all his works.

Isaiah therefore saw his glory on earth. Ezekiel, however, could not see his glory in heaven as it truly is, because his glory is one thing in created works and another thing in himself. The glory that exists in created things can be seen; the glory that exists in him cannot now be seen except through a likeness.

## Chapter XXIX

**“Whoever serves me must follow me” (John 12:26).**

*(Homily on the Gospel, no. 8.)*

[Col. 1253C] Our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, admonishes us to follow him. Therefore, dearest brothers, since we believe in him, let us strive to follow him through good works. Let us look where he walks and hold fast to his footsteps by imitating him.

For the one who imitates Jesus follows him. Hence he said: “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead” (Matthew 8:22). “Follow” means “imitate.” Let us therefore consider where he walks, so that we may deserve to follow him.

Behold, although he is Lord and Creator of the angels, when he was about to assume the nature he had created, he came into a virgin’s womb. Yet he did not wish to be born in this world through the wealthy; he chose poor parents. When the lamb to be offered for him was lacking, his mother found a pair of turtledoves and young pigeons for the sacrifice.

He did not wish to prosper in this world. He endured mockery and reproach; he endured spittle, scourges, blows, a crown of thorns, and the cross. Because we had fallen from inward joy through the delight of bodily things, he showed with what bitterness we must return there.

What, then, ought a human being to endure for his sake, if God endured so much for human beings?

[Col. 1253D] Whoever has believed in Christ but still pursues the profits of avarice, is lifted up by the honor of pride, burns with the fires of envy, pollutes himself with the filth of lust, and desires to prosper in the things of this world, refuses to follow the Jesus in whom he has believed.

He walks and proceeds by a different road if he seeks joys and pleasures while his guide has shown him the way of bitterness.

## Chapter XXX

**“If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).**

*(Homily 22 on the Gospel, no. 6.)*

Through the resurrection of our Redeemer, all the elect who, although in a place of tranquility, were nevertheless held within the prison of hell were brought back to the pleasant places of paradise.

[Col. 1254A] The Lord fulfilled in his resurrection what he had promised before his Passion. He drew all things to himself because he left none of his elect among the dead; he took away all that was elect. For by rising again the Lord did not restore unbelievers, who had been condemned to eternal punishments for their crimes, to pardon. Rather, he snatched from the prison of hell those whom he recognized as his own in faith and conduct.

## Chapter XXXI

**“The Lord washed the feet of the disciples” (John 13:4).**

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIX, no. 22.)*

[Col. 1254A] Hardly any preaching passes without some fault being committed. Therefore, rightly, after preaching the Lord washed the feet of the holy apostles, showing that often even in a good work the dust of sin is contracted; and the footprints of those who speak become soiled precisely where the hearts of those who hear are cleansed.

For often, when certain people speak words of exhortation, they are honored by their hearers to some degree and rise inwardly, however slightly, because the grace of purification is conveyed through them. While they wash away the works of others by their words, they take up, as it were, the dust of evil thought from the good road.

[Col. 1254B] What, then, did it mean for him to wash the disciples’ feet after preaching except to wipe away the dust of thought after the glory of preaching and cleanse the steps of the heart from inward elation?

The apostles’ feet were therefore washed so that they might be cleansed from whatever small contagion had been contracted during the preaching itself, as from dust gathered on a journey.

## Chapter XXXII

**“By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).**
(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XX, section 17; book XXII on Job, section 23.) Only the keeping of charity proves that we are disciples of almighty God. The outstanding preacher testifies that the power of works performed without charity is worthless, saying: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

Concerning heretics also who perform signs and miracles, but receive as the rewards of their affliction and abstinence the praises that they love, the voice of the Redeemer says: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name drive out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you who practice iniquity’” (Matt. 7:22). What, surely, is conveyed by this judgment except that charity and humility ought to be honored in human beings, rather than signs of power? The proof of holiness is not to perform signs, but for each person to love another as himself, to hold true views concerning God, and to think better things of his neighbor than of himself.

Since true virtue consists in love, not in the display of miracles, the Truth demonstrates this when it says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” For he did not say, “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you perform signs,” but said, “If you have love for one another.” He thus clearly indicates that true servants of God are proved not by miracles but by charity alone. Therefore the testimony of heavenly discipleship is the gift of heavenly love.

This love, if it truly fills our heart, is ordinarily shown in two ways: namely, if we love both our friends in God and our enemies for God’s sake. But it must be understood that love of an enemy is truly preserved when we are neither saddened by his advancement nor delighted by his downfall. Often the mind is deceived by the appearance of love toward an enemy and thinks that it loves him if it does not oppose his life; but the strength of love is truly tested by the enemy’s advancement or by his fall.

Indeed, in this matter the human mind does not fully know itself unless, when the person it considers its adversary changes in misfortune or prosperity, it finds that it has changed the manner of its own disposition. For if it is saddened by his prosperity and rejoices at the calamity of the one who hates it, it is clear that it does not love him: it does not want him to become better than itself, and even while he stands, it pursues him in its desire—the very man whose downfall it celebrates.

Yet amid these considerations it must be understood that it often happens, without charity having been lost, that our enemy’s ruin makes us glad, while his success troubles us without any fault of envy. This occurs when we rightly believe that, as he falls, some people are raised up, and fear that, as he prospers, many are unjustly oppressed. In such a case our mind is raised neither by his downfall nor saddened by his advancement, if our sound judgment considers not what is happening in him but what is being done because of him to others.

For preserving this attitude, a very careful examination of discernment is necessary, lest, while carrying out our hatred, we deceive ourselves under the appearance of another’s advantage. But if one ought never to rejoice at the death of an enemy, the Psalmist would not say: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees the vengeance upon the wicked” (Ps. 57:11).

Yet it is one thing to suffer a wicked person and another to suffer an enemy. There are many enemies who are not wicked, and some wicked people who do not appear to be our particular enemies. The human mind, however, considers everyone whom it endures as an enemy to be wicked and unjust, because the resentment accusing him in its thoughts magnifies his faults. However burdened by whatever crimes, a person is considered less unjust if he is not perceived as an adversary.

In this matter we must distinguish between what our enemy does to us and what he does harmfully to himself and to others. For if he is good to others, perhaps he cannot be bad to us without fault on our part; nor should we rejoice at the ruin of one whose adversity we alone are certain to have endured. But when our enemy and the enemy of many is punished, the mind must rejoice rather in the deliverance of those near us than in the death of the enemy.

For when an adversary perishes, we ought carefully to weigh both what we owe to the sinner’s ruin and what we owe to the justice of the one who strikes. When almighty God strikes someone perverse, we must both grieve over the misery of the one who perishes and rejoice with the justice of the Judge, so that for us the punishment of our neighbor who is dying may be a source of mourning, while the equity displayed by God the Judge may again become a source of joy. Thus we may neither become adversaries to the human being who perishes nor be found ungrateful to God who judges.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2)

[Col. 1255C]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, section 76; book II on Ezekiel, homily 4, section 6.) Since in this life there is a distinction among God’s chosen in the quality of their works, there will undoubtedly also be a distinction of dignities in the next life, so that just as one person here surpasses another in merit, there one will excel another in reward.

Although the dignity will not be the same for everyone, the life of blessedness will nevertheless be one for all. Hence the Truth itself says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places.” For if there were no differing rewards in that eternal blessedness, there would be one dwelling place rather than many. There are therefore many dwelling places, in which the distinct orders of the good rejoice together because they share in their merits.

Those who came to the vineyard after being summoned at different hours, although they had not labored equally, nevertheless all received the same denarius equally. In what way, then, do many dwelling places accord with one denarius, except that the dignities of the blessed citizens will indeed be different, while the rest of eternal reward will nevertheless be one?

For if the quality of the reward resulting from different works will be unequal, the blessedness received there by those distinguished in many dwelling places is nevertheless one. And although the merit of individuals will differ, there will not be a diversity of joys, because, even if one rejoices less and another more greatly, one joy in the vision of their Creator gladdens them all. There is one blessedness and joy for all, although the exaltedness of their life is not the same for everyone.

The Truth therefore says that in his Father’s house there are many dwelling places, because in that life of blessedness each person receives, according to differing merit, a different place without receiving an unequal blessedness; and he does not feel the loss arising from that difference, because whatever he receives is sufficient for him.

In those many dwelling places the very diversity of rewards will somehow be harmonious, because the power of love in that peace unites us so greatly that each person rejoices to have received in another what he himself has not received. Paul aptly indicates that these dwelling places are distributed according to merits when he says: “There is one glory of the moon and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15:41).

## CHAPTER XXXIV — “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14:16)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book V, section 50.) The breath of the Holy Spirit raises the human mind by touching it. Depressing temporal thoughts, it inflames the mind with eternal desires, so that it now desires nothing except what is above and scorns all the things below that clamor through human corruption.

Hence the voice of the Truth also says: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive.” For just as this same Paraclete—that is, another Comforter of the human race after the Mediator’s ascension—is invisible in himself, so he kindles everyone whom he fills to desire invisible things. Since worldly hearts love visible things alone, the world does not receive him, because it does not rise toward love of invisible things.

For the more worldly minds expand themselves outward through their desires, the more they narrow the bosom of their heart for receiving him. Very few in the human race are found who, cleansed from the filth of carnal desires, are enlarged by that very purification for receiving the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXV — “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father” (John 14:21)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, section 90.) There were some who said that God is indeed seen in his glory in that region of blessedness, but is not at all seen in his nature. A lesser subtlety of inquiry misled them. For in that simple and unchangeable essence, glory is not one thing and nature another; rather, its very nature is its very glory, and its very glory is its nature.

God himself promises that this divine Wisdom will at some time show itself to those who love him, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him.” It is as though he plainly said: “You who see me in the flesh must still see me in the nature of my divinity.” Again he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

## CHAPTER XXXVI — “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23)

(Homily 7 on the Gospels, section 2.) We make a way for the Lord who comes to our heart when we prepare our life for the commandment. We prepare a dwelling in our heart for the Lord who comes when we humbly hear the word of the Truth and keep it with love.

But whoever raises his mind in pride, whoever pants with the fever of greed, whoever pollutes himself with the defilements of lust, closes the door of his heart against the Truth and bars the Lord, lest he come to him and make his dwelling there, with the bolts of vices.

## CHAPTER XXXVII — “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John 14:27)

[Col. 1256D]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VI, section 35.) In Sacred Scripture peace is called complete in one way and begun in another.
