The Truth had given the disciples peace that had begun when he said: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace.” Simeon had desired complete peace when he prayed, saying: “Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant according to your word in peace” (Luke 2:29).

Our peace begins from desire for the Creator; it is perfected by manifest vision. It will be complete when our mind is neither blinded by ignorance nor struck by the opposition of its own flesh.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — “Likewise, concerning the foregoing”

(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 22.) Those who are peacefully settled must carefully ensure that, while they love the peace they possess more than is necessary, they do not cease to desire reaching the everlasting peace.

For tranquility in worldly affairs often tests the mind’s attention more severely: the less troublesome the things they possess are, the less they love the things that remain unpossessed; and the more present things delight them, the less they seek eternal things.

Hence the Truth itself, distinguishing earthly peace from heavenly peace and urging the disciples from the present toward what was to come, says: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace”—that is, “I leave a passing peace; I give an abiding one.” If the heart is fixed on the peace that has been left, it never reaches the peace that is to be given. Present peace must therefore be held in such a way that it is both loved and despised, lest, if it is loved immoderately, the mind of the one who loves it be caught in guilt.

## CHAPTER XXXIX — “For the prince of this world is coming” (John 14:30)

(Homily 39 on the Gospels, sections 8, 9, 10.) Evil spirits seek their own works not only when they enter the souls of the wicked, in order to drag them to punishments; they also come to the elect and seek something of their own in them, if they can prevail.

Yet there was one among human beings who, before his Passion, said openly: “I will no longer speak much with you, for the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” Because he saw him as a mortal human being, the prince of the world believed that he could find something belonging to himself in him. But the one who came into the world without sin departed from the world’s corruption without any sin. No one else could say this of himself against the prince of the world.

For when the prophet says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. 50:7), no one who came into the world could be without guilt, since he came into the world with guilt. It is certain that the prince of this world possessed something of his own in all who were conceived through the pleasure of the flesh—undoubtedly in their actions, words, or thoughts.

But he could not afterward seize them or previously hold them because the one who paid the debt of death for us, though owing none himself, rescued them from their debts. Thus our debts do not keep us under the law of our enemy, because Christ Jesus, the Mediator between God and human beings, freely paid on our behalf what he did not owe.

For by paying the undeserved death of the flesh on our behalf, he freed us from the deserved death of the soul. He therefore says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.”

Accordingly, we must take care and think each day with great tears how swift and terrifying the prince of this world will be on the day of our departure, seeking his works in us. If he came even to God dying in the flesh and sought something in him, though he could find nothing, what will we wretched people say or do, who have committed innumerable evils?

What will we say to the adversary when he seeks and finds much of his own in us, except the one thing that is certain refuge and solid hope for us: that we have become one with the one in whom the prince of this world both sought something of his own and could find nothing? For he alone is “free among the dead,” and we are released from the service of sin in true freedom because we are united to him who is true freedom.

We cannot deny, but truly confess, that the prince of this world has much in us. Nevertheless, at the time of our death he can no longer seize us, because we have become members of him in whom he has nothing.

But what does it profit us to be joined to our Redeemer by faith if we are separated from him in our conduct? For he himself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21).

Right works must therefore be joined to right faith; the evils we have committed must be washed away by continual lamentation; and we must offer our brothers the good things we are able to offer. For we do not become members of our Redeemer in any other way than by clinging to God and suffering with our neighbor.

Compassion for a brother is very powerful, and the inward mercies of compassion unite us to almighty God. We draw near to the one who is above all precisely from the place where, through compassion for our neighbor, we lower ourselves even beneath ourselves. In bodily matters no one touches high things unless he stretches upward. In spiritual matters also, it is certain that the more we are drawn downward through compassion, the more truly we approach what is high.

## CHAPTER XL — “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5)

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 9, section 1.) By the grace of almighty God we can indeed strive toward good works, but we cannot accomplish them unless he who commands also helps us.

Thus Paul, when admonishing the disciples by saying, “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2:12), immediately added who works these very good things in them, saying: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good will.”

This is why the Truth itself says to the disciples: “Without me you can do nothing.” But in this we must consider: if our good works are gifts of almighty God in such a way that nothing in them belongs to us, why do we seek eternal reward as though it were owed to our merits? If, however, they are ours in such a way that they are not gifts of almighty God, why do we give thanks to almighty God for them?

We must understand that our evil deeds are ours alone, but our good deeds belong both to almighty God and to us. For he precedes us by inspiring us to will, and follows us by helping us, so that we do not will in vain but are able to accomplish what we will.

When grace precedes and good will follows, that which is the gift of almighty God becomes our merit. Paul explains this well in a brief statement: “I labored more than all of them” (1 Cor. 15:10). And lest he appear to attribute what he had done to his own virtue, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.”

It is as though he said: “I labored in a good work—not I, but also I.” Insofar as I was preceded by the Lord’s gift alone, it was not I; insofar as I followed that gift by my will, it was also I.

These remarks are made briefly against Pelagius and Caelestius.

## CHAPTER XLI — “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:15)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVII, section 28.) A friend of the Truth is one who loves right action. Hence the Truth itself says to the disciples: “You are my friends if you do what I command you.”

A friend is called a guardian of the soul. Therefore, not undeservedly, one who strives to guard God’s will in his commandments is called his friend. Hence the Truth says again to the same disciples: “But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (ibid., 15).

## CHAPTER XLII — “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26)

(Homily 26 on the Gospels, section 2.) The Son promises that he will send the Holy Paraclete from himself to the disciples, while elsewhere he also asserts that he himself was sent by the Father, saying: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John 20:21).

Although in these words “sending” may be understood as his incarnation—for the Father sent the Son when he ordained that he become incarnate for the redemption of the human race—it can also be understood according to the nature of his divinity. For the Son is said to be sent by the Father precisely insofar as he is begotten by the Father.

Likewise, the Son says that he sends the Holy Spirit, who, although coequal with the Father and the Son, was not incarnate: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father.” If being sent were understood only as becoming incarnate, the Holy Spirit would certainly not be said to be sent, since he was by no means incarnate. Rather, his sending is the procession by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Thus, just as the Son is appropriately said to be sent because he is begotten, so the Holy Spirit is said to be sent because he proceeds.

## CHAPTER XLIII — “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John 16:7)

(Dialogue, book II, chapter 38; and in the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII, section 41.) Our Lord, in order to increase the disciples’ faith, said: “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you.”

Since it is established that the Spirit, the Paraclete, proceeds always from the Father and from the Son, why does the Son say that he will depart so that the one who never departs from the Son may come?

But because the disciples, seeing the Lord in the flesh, desired always to see him with bodily eyes, he rightly says to them: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come.” It is as though he openly said: “If I do not remove my body from the sight of your attention, I will not lead you to invisible understanding through the Spirit, the Comforter. If I do not remove my body, I do not show you what love of the Spirit is; and unless you cease to see me bodily, you will never learn to love me spiritually.”

## CHAPTER XLIV — “Truly I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16:20)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VI, section 23.) All who, inflamed by desire for our Redeemer, flee prosperity, suffer adversity, endure the tortures of their persecutors, and chastise themselves through lamentation receive a joy all the higher in the future the more devotedly they now die to all the joys of the world.

Hence the same Truth says: “So you now have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (ibid., 22). All who are now despised for the love of God and afflicted temporally for his sake will be consoled eternally by true joy in heavenly glory.

## CHAPTER XLV — “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name” (John 16:23)

(Homily 27 on the Gospels, sections 6, 7.) If the Father gives us everything we ask in the Son’s name, how is it that Paul asked the Lord three times and did not merit being heard, but was told: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9)?

Did that outstanding preacher not ask in the Son’s name? Why did he not receive what he asked? How, then, is it true that whatever we ask in the Son’s name the Father gives us, if the Apostle asked in the Son’s name that the angel of Satan be taken away from him and nevertheless did not receive what he asked?

But since the Son’s name is Jesus, and Jesus means “Savior,” or is also called “salutary,” the person who asks in the name of the Savior is the one who asks for what pertains to true salvation. For if someone asks for what is not beneficial, he is not asking in the name of Jesus.

Hence the Lord says to the same apostles while they were still weak: “Until now you have asked nothing in my name.” It is as though he openly said: “You have not asked in the name of the Savior, because you do not know how to seek eternal salvation.”

This is why Paul was not heard: it would not have benefited him for salvation to be freed from temptation. Therefore, dearest brothers, when you come together in church, consider, I beg you, your petitions. See whether you ask in the name of Jesus—that is, whether you ask for the joys of eternal salvation.

In the house of Jesus you do not seek Jesus if, in the temple of eternity, you importunately pray for temporal things. Certainly, when these things are lacking, they should be requested from almighty God; but we must immediately remember what we have received by the command of that same Redeemer: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33).

It is therefore not wrong to ask Jesus for these things also, provided they are not requested excessively.

## CHAPTER XLVI — “I will proclaim the Father openly to you” (John 16:25)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXX, section 17.) Because of our weakness, the Lord speaks to us not in the open appearance of his majesty but through the voice of his preachers. He strikes hearts that are still carnal with the language of the flesh, so that they may receive unfamiliar things more readily when they hear them through the sound of a familiar voice.

But after the flesh has been dissolved into dust through death and the dust has been given life through resurrection, then we will not seek to hear words about God. We will already see in direct vision God the Word himself, the one who fills all things, and we will no longer require instruction from teachers of life.

Then what the Lord says through Jeremiah will be fulfilled: “A man will no longer teach his neighbor, nor a man his father, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all will know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord” (Jer. 31:34).

When the Lord is shown to us after the resurrection through vision, he will then disclose to us how he presides over all creatures. With the darkness of our mind wiped away, he will manifest himself in clear vision. Then what the Truth itself says in the Gospel will be fulfilled: “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will proclaim the Father openly to you.”

The Son proclaims the Father openly because, by being the Word, he enlightens us with the nature of divinity. He says that he will proclaim the Father openly because, through the appearance of his majesty then revealed, he shows both how he is born from the Father without being unequal to his Begetter and how the Spirit of both proceeds, coeternal with both.

Then we will clearly see how the one who is begotten is not later than the one from whom he is begotten, and how the one produced through procession is not preceded by those who produce him. We will clearly see how the one is three distinctly (*divisibiliter*) and the three are one indivisibly.

## CHAPTER XLVII — “Jesus, knowing what was about to happen to him, went out and said, ‘Whom do you seek?’” (John 18:4)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, section 17.) How incomprehensible and beyond consideration will be that greatness with which the Lord will come at his second manifestation is well understood if we carefully weigh the weight of his first coming.

Certainly, the Lord came to die in order to redeem us from death. He endured in his body the weakness of our flesh and its punishments. Before he reached the gibbet of the cross, he allowed himself to be seized, spat upon, mocked, and struck with blows.

See to what insults he consented to come for our sake. Yet before allowing himself to be seized, he questioned his persecutors, saying: “Whom do you seek?” They immediately answered: “Jesus of Nazareth.” When he suddenly said to them, “I am he,” he uttered only the voice of a most gentle reply, and at once struck his armed persecutors to the ground.

What, then, will he do when he comes to judge, who, when he came to be judged, struck down his enemies with a single word? What will that judgment be which the immortal One exercises, when even as he was about to die he could not be endured in a single utterance? Who can endure his anger when even his gentleness could not be endured? No one will be able to bear the terror of his majesty when the power of his second coming, exercising judgment through fire, shines forth in the majesty of his authority.

## CHAPTER XLVIII — “They therefore brought Jesus from Caiaphas into the praetorium, to Pilate” (John 18:28)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVII, sections 49–52.) Against the ancient enemy, the prophets’ words promise that the holy Church will be restored to its former state: “The evil beast will not ascend through it” (Isa. 35:9).

The ancient enemy is understood under the name “beast.” In his savagery he attacked the first human being through deception and tore apart the integrity of that life by evil persuasion. This beast possesses the hearts of all the reprobate; through hidden malice it holds them as its own den, and whenever it desires to harm the good, it hides itself in their obscure minds.

Were not the hearts of the persecuting Jews the den of this beast? For a long time it lay hidden in their counsels, but suddenly burst forth in their cries: “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6). And because, in its attempts, it could not reach the wounding of the mind, it thirsted for death in our Redeemer.

This beast also held the hearts of the elect, but the Lamb, by dying, shook it off them. Hence the Gospel says: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31). It can enter the minds of the good, but it cannot remain in them, because the heart of a righteous person is not this beast’s den.

Overcome by a sudden impulse of fear, Peter opened the door of his heart to this beast by denying the Lord; but he quickly resisted it through recognition and closed the door through weeping.

But the beast not only entered the hearts of the persecuting Jews and held them; by holding them and remaining in them, it possessed them. It first led their thoughts to wicked desires, and then their wicked desires to the most evil deeds.

We learn how long it remained in their minds when we hear, in the testimony of the Gospel narrative, their counsels: how, while they saw our Redeemer raise the dead to life, they raged with the anxiety of cruelty over his death; how fervently they wanted to fulfill their evil desires against him, yet feared the people; how they sought opportunities to kill him and could not find them; and how they used the hands of foreigners to accomplish the purpose of their wickedness.

Because they themselves could not legally put him to death, they handed him over to the Gentiles to be struck down, so that the Roman governor might carry out by his own authority what they themselves desired from pure malice and what they wanted to have done.

They were full of the malice of envy; when they saw the miracles, they envied him and said: “Look, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19). They observed the signs and saw the miracles performed through his ministers, and already foresaw the whole world following the teachings of the faith.

Thus from the envious Jews arose the persecuting malice, and from the Gentiles the oppressive power. The precepts of the Law had not forbidden miracles to be performed, yet the Jews sought to kill the Redeemer of the human race because of those very miracles.

Therefore, unable to complete what they had begun, they hastened to Pilate’s praetorium so that he might kill the one whom no law prevented them from killing unjustly. What Judea demanded out of envy, the Gentile judge carried out by Roman authority.

## CHAPTER XLIX — “Pilate entered the praetorium and said to Jesus, ‘Where are you from?’ But Jesus gave him no answer, etc.” (John 18:33)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXII, sections 40 and 41.) In this life, whoever desires no prosperity undoubtedly fears no adversity. The outward number of people does not terrify one whom the inward multitude of vices does not devastate.

Hence our Redeemer did not fear the enormous crowd. When his persecutors came with swords and clubs, he struck them down with a single reply, saying: “I am he” (John 18:6). Nor did the contempt and scorn of his relatives terrify him; in order to free us from eternal punishments, he calmly received blows upon the face.

He remained silent and did not reveal who he was. Although, at that very hour of his Passion, he was enduring the weakness of his humanity, he did not wish to exercise the power of his divinity.

The Mediator between God and human beings would have revealed who he was if, when being seized as a human being, he had wished to display the power of his majesty and pass beyond the weakness of the flesh he had assumed through the greatness of his divinity. In order that he might die more openly as a human being, God remained hidden: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

When questioned, he offered the body he had assumed for the elect to suffering; he did not reveal to those resisting him what he was. He displayed weakness to his persecutors but concealed the power of his majesty and divinity.

## CHAPTER L — “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11)

[Col. 1261D]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book III, sections 28–29.) All who are joined to Satan by living perversely are members of Satan. Pilate was his member, for he did not recognize the Lord who came to the extremes of death for our redemption.

The chief priests were his body, for by persecuting the Redeemer of the world they attempted to drive him from the world even to the cross. His members were those who, in the words of the prophecy, say: “Let us put wood into his bread and wipe him from the land of the living” (Jer. 11:19).

To put wood into his bread is to apply the wood of the cross by fastening it to his body. They think they can wipe his life from the land of the living; when they see him as mortal, they suspect that death will bring him to an end.

When the Lord therefore handed himself over for our redemption into the hands of Satan’s members, what else did he do than permit Satan’s own hand to rage against him, so that by the very means through which he outwardly perished, he might free us outwardly and inwardly?

He endured the power of Satan’s body through spitting, blows, scourges, the cross, and the spear. Hence, as he came to suffer, he says to Pilate, who belonged to that body: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11).

Yet the power that had been given to Pilate against him externally, he compelled to serve his own gains internally. Pilate—or Satan, who was the head of that same Pilate—was held under the power of the one over whom he had received power. The superior had himself arranged what he tolerated from the persecutor when the latter approached from below, so that although it arose from the evil mind of unbelievers, that very cruelty would nevertheless serve the benefit of all the elect.

Thus inwardly he was piously arranging what he wickedly feared to suffer outwardly. Hence it is said of him at the supper: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God, rose from supper and laid aside his garments” (John 13:3).

Behold: as he was about to go into the hands of his persecutors, he knew that he had taken even the persecutors themselves into his own hand. For since he knew that he had received all things, it is clear that he held those by whom he was being held, so that he himself might turn to the service of mercy whatever their malice was permitted to rage against him.

## CHAPTER LI — “They therefore took Jesus, who had been handed over to them by Pilate, and led him out to the place called the Place of the Skull, where they crucified him” (John 19:17)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XI, no. 30; book IX, no. 44.) That ancient people of the Jews, who seemed to be faithful to God but was reprobate at heart, was cast away, so that, deceived by its own faithlessness, it might afterward rise up against the very one whom it had previously proclaimed. For the chief priests and elders of the people were attempting, by their counsel, to oppose the one whom they had earlier proclaimed would come. And when, by persecuting him, they endeavored to extinguish his name, deceived by their own wickedness they vainly tried to proceed along a pathless way, because no path could lie open to their cruelty against the Author of all things.

They were indeed terrified [Col. 1262C] when they saw so many miracles of the Author of all things and witnessed his mighty works; but, refusing to believe, they still demanded signs, saying: “What sign, then, will you perform, that we may see it and believe you? What work will you do?” (John 6:30). At times they even appeared to believe, when they said: “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing” (John 9:33). At other times they denied that he was from God, despising him and saying: “Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas? And are not all his sisters here with us?” (Matthew 13:55).

They saw him raise the dead, and yet saw that he was mortal. Who would not believe him to be God when they saw him raise a dead person? But again, when they saw him to be mortal, they despised believing that this mortal man was the immortal God. Thus, because almighty God displayed himself to their eyes as one who could both reveal divine things and suffer human things, he made them, as it were, drunk with confusion. For everyone who is in error is led now here, now there, so that their pride—which preferred to despise the mystery of his incarnation rather than follow it—might exalt itself against his humanity while inwardly marveling at the power of his divinity.

At last, therefore, they became the servants and instruments of the devil, because they raged against the death of our Redeemer. For the ancient enemy was unable, by tempting him directly, to corrupt the Redeemer’s mind; but, through his agents, he was permitted to destroy his flesh for three days, and unknowingly served the dispensation of heavenly mercy precisely through this permission. For when he assaulted our Redeemer with three temptations, he could not violate the heart of God; but when he stirred Judas’s mind to bring about the death of his flesh, and handed over to him the cohort and the servants from the chief priests and Pharisees, surely the devil himself extended his hands against his flesh.

For his agents and servants—the priests and rulers, Pilate, and the soldiers—were mockers. He covered and blinded their faces and hearts, and veiled them in a cloud of wickedness so that they would not recognize their own Author [Col. 1263A]. Their faces were covered, because the minds of those persecuting him, who could hold the God whom they were able to seize in the flesh, did not recognize him even through his miracles. Hence Paul says: “To this very day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart” (2 Corinthians 3:15). He says again: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

CAP. LII.—“And Jesus, bowing his head, gave up his spirit” (John 19:30).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book IV, no. 31.) Just as true death is that by which the soul is separated from God, so the shadow of death is that by which the flesh is separated from the soul. But the Mediator of God and human beings assumed for us only the death of the flesh, and by the shadow of his death he abolished the true death of sinners. He came to us, for we were held in the death of spirit and flesh; he brought to us one death of his own and released the two deaths that he found in us. For if he had assumed both, he would have freed us from neither; but he mercifully accepted one and justly condemned both of ours. He applied his single death to our double death, and by dying subdued our double death. Hence, not without reason, he lay one day in the tomb and two nights, because he joined the light of his single death to the darkness of our double death.

He therefore who accepted for us only the death of the flesh endured the shadow of death and hid from God’s eyes the guilt that we had committed. Thus, in order to rescue us, debtors as we were to the death of flesh and spirit, the Lord, though not himself indebted to death, paid the death of the flesh.

CAP. LIII.—“Christ had to rise from the dead” (John 20:9).

(Book II, on Ezekiel, homily 4, no. 2.) All this present time unfolds through seven days, whereas the eternal day is the eighth, which follows after the succession of the seven days has been completed. For by the number eight, the resurrection and the joy of future blessedness are signified. The reason for this number eight is that after the Sabbath the Lord willed to rise from death [Col. 1263C]. The Lord’s Day, which is the third from the Lord’s death, is counted as the eighth from the creation of the days, because it follows the seventh.

Hence the true passion and true resurrection of our Redeemer also represented something concerning his body through the days of his passion. He suffered on Friday, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose from death on the Lord’s Day. The present life is still a Friday for us, because it is spent in pains and afflicted by troubles; but on the Sabbath we rest, as it were, in the tomb, because after the body we find rest for the soul. On the Lord’s Day—that is, on the third day from the passion, but, as we have said, the eighth from creation—we shall rise bodily from death and rejoice in the glory of the soul together with the flesh.

Thus what our Savior wondrously accomplished in himself he truly signified in us, so that pain might receive us on the sixth day, rest on the seventh, and glory on the eighth.

CAP. LIV.—“They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him” (John 20:2).

[Col. 1263D]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book III, no. 22.) Sacred Scripture sometimes customarily puts the whole for a part, as when Mary, at the tomb, complains here, saying: “They have taken away my Lord.” Only the Lord’s body had lain in the tomb, and she had come seeking only it. Therefore, while she lamented as though the whole Lord had been buried together and sought not the Lord’s body but the Lord who had been taken away, she signified the part by reference to the whole.

CAP. LV.—“When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them” (John 20:19).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXX, no. 26.) After the Lord’s passion, the apostles remained behind closed doors because of the tenderness of their minds and the weakness of their fear. For since they did not yet rise up against the members of the devil with the free voice of preaching, and since, after the Lord’s passion, they had not yet been strengthened by the infusion of the Holy Spirit to proclaim their Redeemer with firm authority, they still lay in ambush against their adversaries, as though in caves.

With the doors closed, these young hounds of his, as it were, lay in their hidden dens, preparing to tear apart the world, so that afterward they might seize the prey of souls; for at that time it is certain that they feared the assault of the world even while hiding from it. With those doors closed, these young hounds sought to ambush and destroy the death of our death, so that they might kill guilt and put to death every life of sin in us.

To the first of them, that hungry but already vigorous young hound, the gentiles were shown through the linen cloth as though prey had been displayed, and it was said: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). To these young hounds, still seemingly weak and therefore commanded to lie in their dens, it is said by the Lord’s voice: “Remain here in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). For the apostles may rightly be called the young hounds of the holy Church: born within the Church, they tore apart the hostile world with their mouths and their preaching.

CAP. LVI.—“Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:23).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXVII, no. 34; homily 26 on the Gospels, no. 4.) Those whom the grace of the Holy Spirit fills, he first terrifies concerning earthly conduct and afterward consoles with the hope of heavenly things, so that afterward they may rejoice in rewards through confession to the same extent that earlier they feared when they saw only punishments.

Since, therefore, the holy apostles did not yet dare to rise against the members of the devil with the free voice of preaching, and had not yet been strengthened through the Lord’s passion by the infusion of the Holy Spirit to proclaim their Redeemer with firm authority; and since, because of the tenderness of their minds and the weakness of their fear, they were afraid to go out, remaining behind closed doors on the first day of the week because of fear of the Jews, the Lord came and stood among them, breathed upon them, and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive [Col. 1264C], they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained.”

Behold, the terror of those who had been converted is changed into power, because, by doing penance, they punish their own sins and rise to the exercise of judgment, so that they receive from God the ability to exercise what they had previously feared concerning God. Those who perfectly feared the heavenly judgment become judges, and those who earlier feared that their own sins might be retained now begin to forgive the sins of others.

It is pleasing, dearest brothers, to contemplate to what a height of glory the Lord’s disciples, called to such great burdens of humility, have been led. Behold, they not only become secure concerning themselves, but also receive power to release another’s bondage. They receive a share in the authority of the heavenly Judge, so that in God’s place they may retain sins in some and release them in others. Thus it was fitting that God should raise up those who had consented to humble themselves so greatly for God.

Behold, those who fear God’s strict judgment become judges of souls, so that they may condemn or free others, although they had feared being condemned themselves.

CAP. LVII.—“Come and eat” (John 21:12).

[Col. 1264D]

(Homily 24 on the Gospels, no. 6; homily 14, nos. 5–6; homily 24, no. 6; homily 25, nos. 9–10.) The risen Lord is described as appearing at last and eating with seven disciples, because those who are now perfected in him are satisfied through him with eternal nourishment. Peter and Thomas, Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples are mentioned as having been with him.

Why, then, does he celebrate a final meal with seven disciples, unless because he declares that only those who are full of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit will be with him in eternal nourishment? This whole time also unfolds through seven days, and perfection is often signified by the number seven.

Those, therefore, feast at the final meal upon the presence of truth who now transcend earthly things through their pursuit of perfection; the love of this world does not bind them, and although it may in some way disturb them through temptations, it does not blunt their desires once begun [Col. 1265A].

Concerning this final meal, John says elsewhere: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). He says that they are invited not to a lunch but to a supper because, plainly, at the end of the day a meal is a supper. Those who, when the time of the present life has ended, come to the nourishment of heavenly contemplation are invited not to the Lamb’s lunch but to his supper.

This supper is represented by that final meal at which the seven disciples are said to have been present, because, as we have said, at that time an inward nourishment restores those who, now filled with the sevenfold grace, yearn in the love of the Spirit. The good Shepherd promises this nourishment to his sheep who hear his voice and follow him, saying: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture” (John 10:9).

He will enter into faith, but he will go out from faith into vision, from belief into contemplation; and he will find pasture in eternal nourishment. His sheep will find pasture because whoever follows him with a simple heart is nourished by the food of eternal green pastures.

[Col. 1265B] What, then, are the pastures of these sheep except the inward joys of the paradise of eternal life? The pasture of the elect is the present face of God: when the mind beholds it without failing, it is satisfied forever with food. In these pastures all who have already escaped the snares of temporal pleasure rejoice in the fullness of eternity.

There are the hymn-singing choirs of angels; there is the fellowship of the heavenly citizens; there is the sweet solemnity of those returning from the sad labor of this pilgrimage; there are the watchful choirs of the prophets; there is the ordered company of the apostles as judges; there is the victorious army of innumerable martyrs, all the happier there because they suffered more harshly here; there is the steadfastness of confessors, consoled by receiving their reward; there are faithful men whom worldly pleasure could not soften from the strength of their manhood; there are holy women who conquered both the world and their sex; there are children who here surpassed their years in conduct; there are old men whom age here made weak but did not deprive of the strength of good works.

Let us seek these pastures, brothers, so that, while we rejoice there amid the solemnity of so many citizens, that very celebration of those rejoicing may invite us. Behold, in heaven the joy of the elect citizens is celebrated; all rejoice with one another in their assembly. Yet we, lukewarm in our love of eternity, burn with no desire and do not seek to be present at so great a solemnity. We are deprived of its joys, and yet we are happy.

Let us therefore kindle our spirit, brothers. Let faith grow warm in what it has believed; let our desires blaze toward heavenly things. To love in this way is already to go. Let no adversity call us back from the joy of the inward solemnity; let no flattering prosperity seduce us. Let the soul therefore yearn with its whole desire for the heavenly homeland; let it desire nothing in this world that it plainly must soon abandon. Thus, if we are truly sheep of the heavenly Shepherd, because we are not fixed in the delight of this life, we shall be satisfied upon arriving at the eternal pastures.

Let us therefore, brothers, practice these things with one another. Let us desire to be filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit; let us consider from the present what may follow us into the future. Let us examine whether we are full of the Holy Spirit, and thus learn whether we can reach the pastures of eternal nourishment, whether we can arrive at that final meal.

Whoever he may be whom this Spirit does not now restore is surely fasting from the nourishment of that eternal banquet. We must remember what the apostle Paul says about this same Spirit: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9). This Spirit of love is, as it were, the mark of divine possession.

Does the person whose mind is scattered by hatred, puffed up by arrogance, sharpened by anger even to division of mind, tormented by greed, and weakened by lust have the Spirit of Christ? We must consider what the Spirit of Christ is. Surely it is the Spirit that makes us love friends and enemies, despise earthly things, burn with longing for heavenly things, subdue the flesh because of its vices, and restrain the mind from its desires.

If, then, we wish to know the possessions of God, let us consider the character of our possessor. For Paul proclaims with truthful voice what we have said: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (ibid.). It is as though he openly said: “Whoever is not now ruled by God dwelling within him will not afterward rejoice in the vision of divine glory.”

Yet we who are weakened by the things just mentioned and have not yet reached the summit of perfection should daily set our steps along the path of holy desire on God’s road. The Truth consoles us through the Psalmist, who says: “Your eyes saw my imperfect state” (Psalm 138:16). Our imperfection will not be wholly harmful to us if, established on God’s path, we neither look back toward what has been completed nor cease hastening toward what remains.

For our Lord Jesus Christ at times strengthens unto perfection the person whom the desires of the imperfect ardently inflame. He assumed flesh without sin for sinners, descended from heaven to earth, and, for the human race—which because of the guilt of its first parent had been subject to everlasting death—died, although he owed nothing to death.

Hence we return daily to life after our sins, because the guiltless Creator descended to our punishment. Behold, the ancient enemy has now lost the spoils that he had taken from the human race, and has lost the mortals whom he held by right, because he presumed to attack with death the immortal one in whom he had no right.

Sinners return to life daily, and after committing sins turn back to innocence through the remedy of repentance. Mary Magdalene stands as a witness to divine mercy. When the Pharisee wished to close the fountain of mercy, he said: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know what sort of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner” (Luke 7:39).

But she washed away the stains of her heart and body with tears and wiped the feet of her Redeemer, abandoning her former wicked ways. She sat at Jesus’ feet and listened to the word from his mouth. She had clung to him while he was alive; she sought him when he was dead; she found him alive whom she had sought dead. And she found such a place of grace with him that she herself announced him alive even to the apostles, his messengers.

What, then, brothers, what should we see in this matter except the immense mercy of our Creator? He has set before us, as in a sign, an example of repentance in those whom he caused to live again after their fall through repentance.

I consider Peter, I contemplate the thief, I look upon Zacchaeus, I behold Mary, and I see in them nothing other than examples of hope and repentance placed before our eyes. Perhaps someone has fallen in faith: let him look upon Peter, who wept bitterly over what he had denied through fear (Matthew 26). Another has burned against his neighbor with the wickedness of cruelty: let him look upon the thief, who at the very moment of death reached the rewards of life through repentance (Luke 23). Another, panting with the fever of greed, has seized what belongs to others: let him look upon Zacchaeus, who, if he had taken anything from anyone, restored it fourfold (Luke 19). Another, inflamed by the fire of lust, has lost the purity of the flesh: let him look upon Mary, who burned away in herself the love of the flesh through the fire of divine love (Luke 7).

Behold, almighty God everywhere places before our eyes those whom we ought to imitate; everywhere he sets forth examples of his mercy. Let the evils we have experienced now displease us. God willingly forgets that we were guilty; he is ready to count our repentance as innocence.

Let us therefore, once stained, be reborn from tears after the waters of salvation. Thus, according to the voice of the first Shepherd: “Like newborn infants, desire the milk” (1 Peter 2:1), return as little children to the bosom of our mother, eternal Wisdom; suck the abundant breasts of God’s mercy. And if you mourn what has passed, avoid what is coming. For our Redeemer will console our momentary weeping with eternal joy.

CAP. LVIII.—“Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:15).

(*Pastoral Rule*, part I, chapter 5; homily 26 on the Gospels, nos. 5–6.) There are some who receive exceptional gifts of virtue and are exalted with great responsibilities for the training of others. They are pure through their devotion to chastity, strong through the power of abstinence, filled with the nourishment of doctrine, humble through the endurance of patience, upright through the authority of courage, kind through the grace of compassion, and strict through the severity of justice.

If such people, when called, refuse to accept the summit of governance, they often deprive themselves of the very gifts that they received not only for themselves but also for others. When they consider their own gain rather than that of others, they deprive themselves of the good things prepared for them, though they desire to possess them.

Hence the Truth says to the disciples: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house” (Matthew 5:15). Hence he says to Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” When Peter immediately replied that he loved him, he heard: “If you love me, feed my sheep.”

If, then, care for the flock is the testimony of love, whoever is strong in virtues but refuses to feed God’s flock is proved not to love the supreme Shepherd.

Therefore our good Shepherd, the Lord, gave blessed Peter, the first shepherd, the keys of the heavenly kingdom before his passion, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16:19). After his resurrection, he entrusted the same power of binding and loosing jointly to the disciples with blessed Peter, saying: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:23).

The bishops and other shepherds in the Church now hold their place; those who receive the office of governance take up the authority to loose and to bind. Great is the honor, but heavy is the burden of this honor. It is difficult for one who does not know how to govern his own life to become the judge of another’s life.

It often happens that someone holds the place of judgment whose life in no way corresponds to that office. It also often happens that he either condemns the undeserving or, himself bound, looses others. He is frequently moved toward various people by hatred or favor, and in loosing and binding his subjects follows the movement of his own will rather than the merits of their cases. Thus he deprives himself of the power to bind and loose by exercising it according to his own will and not according to the conduct of his subjects.

Therefore, under great restraint, the pastors of the Church should strive either to loose or to bind. But whether a pastor binds justly or unjustly, the pastor’s sentence must nevertheless be feared by the flock [Col. 1267C], lest the subject who is unjustly bound perhaps deserve, through another fault, the very sentence of his binding.

The pastor, therefore, should fear either to absolve indiscriminately or to bind. But the person who is under the pastor’s authority should fear being bound, even unjustly, and should not rashly criticize his pastor’s judgment, lest, although he has been unjustly bound, the fault that did not previously exist be created by the pride of his rash criticism.

CAP. LIX.—“When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you” (John 21:18).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXXI, no. 69; homily 3 on the Gospels, no. 3; *Exposition on Blessed Job*, book XXXI, no. 70; homily 3 on the Gospels, no. 4; homily 26 on the Gospels, no. 10, often with the order reversed.) Every courageous preacher, when he considers that the struggle of passion is approaching, rejoices in the exercise of virtue. He is not frightened by the danger of battle, because he rejoices in the triumph of victory.

But if a courageous preacher desires the glory of passion, if he gladly seeks to undergo the danger of death for the Lord, why does the Truth say to that very courageous preacher, Peter, who drew virtue from a strong heart in the Lord’s name: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go”? How can one who rejoices in passion be unwilling to go where he is led when another has girded him?

But if we consider how the mind is shaken when passion and the fear of death draw near, and yet rejoices in the reward of the coming kingdom, we understand how one who wishes to undergo the danger of glorious combat may nevertheless be unwilling to do so. In death he considers what he fears while enduring it; in the fruit of death he sees what he seeks while desiring it.

For if Peter had been completely unwilling to suffer for Christ, he could not have suffered. But he loved through the strength of the spirit the martyrdom that he did not desire through the weakness of the flesh. While he trembled before punishment through the flesh, he rejoiced in glory through the spirit. Thus it came about that, though unwilling, he willed the torment of martyrdom, just as we too, when we seek the joy of salvation, drink the bitter cup of purification.

The bitterness displeases in the cup, but the salvation restored through bitterness pleases. Let us see how Paul loves what he shrinks from and shrinks from what he loves. He says: “Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ; for me, indeed, to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Philippians 2:23). And yet he says: “We who are in this dwelling groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:4).

Behold, he desires to die, and yet fears to be stripped of the flesh. Why is this? Because although victory makes one rejoice forever, the punishment itself nevertheless troubles one in the present. Although love of the reward that follows prevails, the blow of pain still touches the mind without sorrow.

Just as a courageous man, when he is girding himself with weapons for the battle that is already near, trembles, hastens, fears, and rages—he appears to fear through his pallor, yet is driven forward vehemently by anger—so the holy man, when he sees passion approaching, is shaken by the weakness of his nature and strengthened by the firmness of his hope. He trembles before the death that is near, and yet rejoices that through dying he will live more truly.

He cannot pass to the kingdom unless he crosses through death. Therefore, by confessing, he seems to doubt; by seeming to doubt, he trusts; rejoicing, he fears; fearing, he rejoices, because he knows that he cannot reach the prize of rest unless he crosses with labor what lies between.

So too, when we wish to drive illnesses from the body, we take the bitter cup of purification with sadness, as we have said above, but rejoice because we are certain of the health that follows. Since the body cannot otherwise reach health, even what is distasteful in the drink becomes pleasing. When the mind sees that life lies within bitterness, it grows cheerful even while troubled by sorrow.

Therefore the Lord rightly foretold to blessed Peter, his most courageous preacher, concerning his future passion after his resurrection: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” For although, as a human being, he trembled before the violence of persecution and death, nevertheless, through the certainty of hope, he rejoiced in the reward of recompense, because there was within him a force of love that would overcome the pain of the flesh.

Therefore, dearest brothers, knowing that our Redeemer, who suffered and died for us, truly rose again, and firmly believing that we too will rise in the future and give him an account of our deeds, let us imitate blessed Peter and, as far as we can, endure the adversities and persecutions of this world patiently and joyfully for the glory of eternal life.

Let us despise all present things, for nothing in this world can remain. It is shameful to love what plainly perishes quickly. Let not the love of earthly things overcome us; let not pride inflate us; let not anger tear us apart; let not lust defile us; let not envy consume us.

Our Redeemer died because of his love for us, dearest brothers; let us learn through our love for him to conquer ourselves. If we do this perfectly, we shall not only escape the punishments that threaten us but also receive, together with blessed Peter and the other martyrs, a common glory as our reward.

For although the occasion of persecution is lacking, our peace nevertheless has its own martyrdom. Even if we do not submit the necks of our flesh to the sword, we nevertheless kill carnal desires in the mind with the spiritual sword.

Therefore order your lives and your conduct, brothers. Consider in advance how the one who rose gentle from death will come strict in judgment. Certainly, on the day of his dread examination, he will appear with angels, archangels, Thrones and Dominions, principalities and powers, while heaven and earth burn and all the elements are shaken in terror to serve him.

Place this Judge of such great terror before your eyes; fear his coming, so that when he comes you may see him not timidly but securely. He must indeed be feared, so that he need not be feared; let his terror train us for good works, and let fear of him restrain our lives from wickedness.

Believe me, brothers: we shall then be as secure concerning his sentence as we now strive to be wary concerning our guilt. If the judgment of any powerful person—who is destined to be a worm after being a human being, and after a worm the most despised dust—is feared with such care, with what earnestness must the judgment of such majesty be considered, and with what dread must it be anticipated?

Fear this, therefore, dearest brothers, with your whole attention; consider it among yourselves with an anxious mind. Behold, we celebrate annually the solemnities of the Lord’s resurrection, but we must live in such a way that we may deserve to reach the eternal festivals.

Everything celebrated temporally passes away. You who attend these solemnities, take care that you are not separated from the eternal solemnity. What does it profit to attend human festivals if it happens that we are absent from the festivals of the angels?

The present and temporal solemnity is a shadow of the solemnity to come [Col. 1270A]. We celebrate this one annually so that we may be led to that which is not annual but continual. Since this is performed at an appointed time, our memory is renewed toward the desire for that other solemnity.

Therefore, through the repeated joy of temporal celebration, let the mind grow warm and burn toward eternal joys, so that in the truth of joy it may enjoy in its homeland what it contemplates of the shadow of joy on the way. This is granted by our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, who, rising from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over him; who, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity, for ever and ever. Amen.

**Part Two. In which the Acts of the Apostles, the Epistles of Blessed Paul, the Catholic Epistles, and the Apocalypse are expounded.**

[Col. 1269]

**BOOK FIVE. Exposition on the Acts of the Apostles.**

**CHAPTER ONE.—** “I made the first account, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began to do and teach until the day on which, after giving commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up; to whom also he presented himself alive after his passion by many proofs, appearing to them for forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God, and so forth” (Acts 1:1).

[Col. 1269B]

(Homily 26 on the Gospels, especially no. 7, and homily 29, at the beginning and nos. 5–6.) The resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ was demonstrated to the doubting disciples by many proofs. When we recognize these as we read, what else do we do except become strengthened by their doubt? The fact that they believed the Lord’s resurrection slowly was not so much their weakness as, so to speak, the future strengthening of our faith.

Thomas’s unbelief benefited us more for faith than the faith of the believing disciples, because while he is brought back to faith by touching, our mind, setting aside every doubt, is made firm in faith. After his resurrection, the Lord permitted the disciple to doubt, but did not abandon him in his doubt, so that, while he touched the wounds of the flesh in his Master, he might heal in us the wounds of unbelief; and while by doubting he touched the scars of the wounds, he might cut away the wound of doubt from our hearts.

To make the truth of the Lord’s resurrection known, we should also note what Luke adds when he says: “And while he was eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem.” And shortly afterward: “While they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes.” Observe the words; mark the mysteries. He was lifted up while eating: he ate and ascended, so that the reality of his flesh might be revealed through the act of eating.

In the Old Testament we learn that Elijah was seized and lifted up into the aerial heaven, which is nearest to the earth, so that he might suddenly be led into a certain hidden region of the earth, where he would live in great repose of flesh and spirit until he returns at the end of the world and pays the debt of death. For he postponed death; he did not escape it.

But our Redeemer, because he did not postpone death, overcame it; by rising again he consumed it, and by ascending he revealed the glory of his resurrection. We should also note that Elijah is read to have ascended in a chariot, so that it might plainly be shown that a mere human being needed the assistance of another.

For through angels those forms of assistance were made and displayed, since the one burdened by the weakness of his nature could not ascend even into the aerial heaven by himself. Our Redeemer, however, is not read to have been lifted up by a chariot or by angels, because he who had made all things was plainly carried above all things by his own power [Col. 1270B].

He was returning to where he was and departing from where he remained, because, while through his humanity he ascended into heaven, through his divinity he continued to contain both earth and heaven.

Just as Joseph, sold by his brothers (Genesis 37), represented the selling of our Redeemer, so Enoch, who was translated, and Elijah, who was lifted up into the aerial heaven, each signified the Lord’s ascension. The Lord therefore had heralds and witnesses of his ascension: one before the Law and the other under the Law, so that in due time he himself might come who could truly penetrate heaven.

For the order itself is distinguished by certain stages of increase in their being lifted up into the heavens. Enoch was both begotten through intercourse and, himself begetting through intercourse, was translated; Elijah was begotten through intercourse but did not beget through intercourse, and was carried up into heaven. Afterward he would come who neither begot through intercourse nor was begotten through intercourse, and who, neither translated nor carried up, would penetrate the aetherial heaven by his own power.

He, in those of us who believe in him, would also bestow the purity of his flesh, and under him the power of chastity would increase through the succession of the ages [Note: [Col. 1270D] This passage is mutilated. Supply what is missing from the assigned homily.].

CAP. II.—“And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments” (Acts 3:10).

(Homily 29 on the Gospels, nos. 9–11.) We must ask what it means that, when the Lord was born, angels appeared, yet are not recorded as appearing in white garments, whereas, when the Lord ascended, the angels sent to him are recorded as appearing in white garments. White garments signify joy and solemnity of mind. What, then, does it mean that, at the Lord’s birth, the angels appeared not in white garments, but at his ascension in white garments, except that a great solemnity then came to the angels, when the God-man penetrated heaven? At the Lord’s birth, divinity seemed humbled; at the Lord’s ascension, humanity was exalted. White garments are more fitting to exaltation than to [Col. 1270D] humiliation. At his assumption, therefore, the angels ought to be seen in white garments, because he who appeared in his birth as humble God was manifested in his ascension as exalted man.

But this must be considered very carefully by us, brothers, in the Lord’s ascension: the bond recording our condemnation has been erased, and the sentence of our corruption has been changed. For that nature [Col. 1271A] to which it was said, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19), went into heaven with the ascending Lord. Because of this very lifting up of our flesh, blessed Job figuratively calls the Lord a bird. When he saw that Judea did not understand the mystery of his ascension, he pronounced judgment on its unbelief, saying: “The bird has not known the path” (Job 28:7). The Lord is rightly called a bird, because he carried his fleshly body aloft into the heavens. Whoever has not believed that he ascended into heaven has not known the path of this bird.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we both believe that our Lord ascended into the heavens, and have heard what the two angels standing beside those who watched him going into heaven said in white garments. “Men of Galilee,” they said, “why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.” Therefore we ought to follow him in our hearts to the place where we believe he has ascended in his body. Let us flee earthly desires; now let nothing delight us in lowly things, since we have the Father in [Col. 1271B] heaven.

We must also weigh this very carefully: he who ascended peacefully will return terribly, and whatever he commands us with gentleness, he will demand from us with severity. Let no one, therefore, regard the time granted for repentance as insignificant; let no one neglect to care for himself while he has the ability to do so. For our Redeemer will come in judgment with severity proportionate to the great patience he has shown us before judgment.

Do these things, then, with me, brothers; turn them over in your minds with attentive reflection: we believe that the Lord has ascended into heaven. And although we are still held here by bodily weakness, let us nevertheless follow him with the steps of love.

## Chapter III.—He acquired a field from the reward of iniquity (Acts 1:18).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book 9, no. 58.)* Concerning Judas the betrayer, the blessed apostle Peter says: “He acquired a field from the reward of iniquity.” Judas [Col. 1271C] certainly could not acquire the potter’s field with the price of blood; after returning the thirty pieces of silver, he immediately punished the crime of his betrayal by an even more criminal death inflicted upon himself. But “he acquired” means “he caused to be acquired.”

## Chapter IV.—The lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles (Acts 1:26).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book 32, no. 27.)* Every sin is “eleven,” because, by doing what is perverse, it passes beyond the Decalogue. And because sin is mourned in sackcloth, it is for this reason that eleven curtains of sackcloth are made in the tabernacle. Hence, in the eleventh Psalm, it is said: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed” (Psalm 11:1). Hence Peter, fearing that the apostles would remain at the number eleven, sought Matthias as the twelfth by casting lots. For unless he had seen that guilt was signified by the number eleven, he would not have been so eager to complete the apostolic number by twelve.

## Chapter V.—Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a mighty rushing spirit (Acts 2:2).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book 5, no. 65.)* The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and receiving from what belongs to the Son, [Col. 1271D] is poured gently into the weakness of our understanding. Yet, when he comes upon the apostles, he is manifested through an external sound, as through a mighty spirit, when it is said: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together in the same place, and suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a mighty rushing spirit.”

For when the Holy Spirit makes himself known to human weakness, he is expressed both by the sound of a mighty spirit and by the voice of a gentle breeze, as it is written in the Book of Blessed Job: “And I heard a voice like that of a gentle breeze” (Job 4:16). What is signified by the voice of a breeze except knowledge of the Holy Spirit? The Holy Spirit, then, when he comes, is gentle and mighty: gentle, because he adapts his knowledge to our senses, insofar as it can in some way be known; mighty, because, however much he accommodates himself, by his coming he nevertheless illumines and shakes the blindness of our weakness. By his illumination [Col. 1272A] he touches us gently, but he violently disturbs our poverty.

## Chapter VI.—And he filled the whole house where they were sitting (Acts 2:1).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book 35, no. 17.)* In Holy Scripture, the number seven sometimes signifies the totality of the present age, which is completed in seven days; the number eight signifies everlasting life, which the Lord revealed to us by his resurrection, when he rose on the Lord’s Day. Because of this number seven, signifying temporal things, and eight, signifying eternal things, the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the one hundred and twenty faithful sitting in the upper room.

For seven and eight together make fifteen; and if, counting from one to fifteen, we rise gradually by successive increments, we reach the number one hundred and twenty. Through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit they learned both to pass beyond temporal things by enduring them and eagerly to desire eternal things. [Col. 1272B]

## Chapter VII.—And there appeared to them divided tongues, as if of fire, and it rested upon each of them (Acts 2:3).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book 28, no. 2.)* It must be understood that either the Lord himself speaks, or that words from him are formed for us through his angelic creature. But when he speaks through himself, only the power of inner inspiration is opened to us. When he speaks through himself, the heart is taught by his word without words or syllables, because his power is recognized in a certain innermost elevation. The mind is lifted up when it is full of him, and weighed down when it is empty; for he is a kind of weight that lifts every soul he fills.

He is incorporeal light that fills the interior and surrounds what it has filled externally. He is speech without sound, which opens the hearing but does not know how to produce a noise.

For what is written concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit—“Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a mighty rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were [Col. 1272C] sitting; and there appeared to them divided tongues as if of fire, and it rested upon each of them”—shows that the Lord appeared through fire, but spoke inwardly through himself. The fire was not God, nor was that sound God; rather, through what he presented externally he expressed what he accomplished inwardly. Because he made the disciples inwardly ardent with zeal and instructed by the word, he displayed fiery tongues outwardly.

The elements were therefore brought forward as signs, so that bodies might perceive fire and sound, while hearts were taught by invisible fire and a voice without sound. Outwardly there was the fire that appeared; inwardly, the fire that imparted knowledge.

When the eunuch of Queen Candace, sitting in charge of her chariot and traveling along the road, was carrying Isaiah in his hands without understanding him, the Spirit had certainly said in Philip’s heart: “Go near and join yourself to the chariot” (Acts 8:23). And when Cornelius had sent soldiers who feared God to summon Peter, Peter undoubtedly heard in his mind from the Spirit: “Behold, three men are seeking you. Rise, go down, and go with them” (Acts 10:19).

For the Spirit of God speaks words to us, as it were, when by a hidden power he makes known what must be [Col. 1272D] done and, without the noise or delay of speech, suddenly renders the ignorant human heart knowledgeable concerning hidden things.

## Chapter VIII.—And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in various languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance (Acts 2:4).

*(Homily 30 on the Gospels, nos. 4–6; Homily 26 on the Gospels, no. 3.)* You have heard, brothers, that the Holy Spirit appeared over the disciples in fiery tongues and gave them knowledge of all languages. What did this miracle signify except that the holy Church, filled with the same Spirit, would speak with the voice of all nations?

Those who attempted to build a tower against God lost the communion of one language. In those, however, who humbly feared God, all languages were united. In the one case humility earned power; in the other, [Col. 1273A] pride brought confusion.

But we must ask why the Holy Spirit, coeternal with the Father and the Son, appeared in fire; why in fire and at the same time in tongues; why he is sometimes shown in a dove and sometimes in fire; why he appeared over the only-begotten Son in the form of a dove, but over the disciples in fire; and why he neither came over the Lord in fire nor was shown over the disciples in the form of a dove.

Let us answer these four questions in order.

The Spirit, coeternal with the Father and the Son, is shown in fire because God is incorporeal, ineffable, and invisible fire, as Paul attests: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29). God is called fire because through him the rust of sins is consumed. Concerning this fire, the Truth says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49). Earth signifies earthly hearts, which, continually piling up the lowest thoughts within themselves, are trampled by evil spirits.

The Lord casts fire upon the earth when, through the breath of the Holy Spirit, he inflames the hearts of the [Col. 1273B] carnal. The earth is kindled when the carnal heart, previously cold in its wicked pleasures, abandons the desires of the present age and burns with love of God. The Spirit therefore rightly appeared in fire: he drives the torpor of coldness from every heart he fills and kindles it with desire for his eternity.

He was shown in fiery tongues because the same Spirit is coeternal with the Son and has a very close kinship with the Word, since the Son is the Word of the Father. Because the substance of the Spirit and the Word is one, the Spirit ought to be shown in a tongue. Or, certainly, because a word proceeds through the tongue, the Spirit appeared in tongues because whoever is touched by the Holy Spirit confesses the Word of God, that is, the only-begotten Son of God. He cannot deny the Word of God, because he already possesses the tongue of the Holy Spirit.

Or, certainly, the Spirit appeared in fiery tongues because he makes all whom he fills both burning and speaking. Teachers have fiery tongues because, while preaching out of love for God, they inflame the hearts of their [Col. 1273C] hearers. A teacher’s speech is idle if it cannot provide the fire of love.

Those who said, “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32), had received this fire of teaching from the very mouth of the Truth. When the word is heard, the soul is inflamed, the coldness of torpor departs, the mind becomes anxious in its desire for heavenly things, and estranged from earthly desires. The true love that fills it torments it with tears. Yet, when it is tormented by such ardor, it is nourished by those very torments. It delights to hear heavenly commandments, and as it is instructed by each commandment, it is kindled as though by so many torches. What previously lay inert through desire afterward burns through words.

Hence Moses rightly says: “In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deuteronomy 33:2). The wicked, who are to be placed on the left, are called the left; the elect are called God’s right hand. The law is therefore fiery in God’s right hand, because the elect do not hear heavenly commandments with a cold heart, but burn toward them with the torches of inward love. The word is brought to their ear, and their mind [Col. 1273D], angry with itself, is consumed by the flame of inward sweetness.

The Spirit was shown in a dove and in fire because he makes all whom he fills both simple and ardent: simple in purity, ardent in zeal. Neither simplicity without zeal nor zeal without simplicity would please God. Hence the Truth himself says: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10:16).

In this matter it must be noted that the Lord wished to admonish his disciples neither by the dove without the serpent nor by the serpent without the dove, so that the serpent’s shrewdness might kindle the dove’s simplicity, and the dove’s simplicity might temper the serpent’s shrewdness. Hence Paul says: “Do not become children in understanding” (1 Corinthians 14:20). We have heard of the serpent’s prudence; now let us be instructed concerning the dove’s simplicity: “Be infants in wickedness” (ibid.).

Hence it is said of blessed Job: “He was a simple and upright man” (Job 1:1). What uprightness is there without simplicity, [Col. 1274A] or what simplicity without uprightness? Because this Spirit teaches both uprightness and simplicity, he ought to be shown both in fire and in a dove, so that every heart touched by his grace might be made tranquil through the gentleness of meekness and inflamed with zeal for justice.

Finally, we must ask why, in our Redeemer himself, the Mediator between God and human beings, the Spirit appeared through a dove, but in the disciples through fire.

Certainly, the only-begotten Son is the judge of the human race. But who could endure his justice if, before gathering us through gentleness, he had wished to examine our sins through the zeal of uprightness? Made human for human beings, therefore, he showed himself gentle toward human beings. He did not wish to strike sinners but to correct them; he first wished to correct them gently, so that he might have people whom he could later acquit in judgment.

The Spirit ought therefore to appear over him in a dove, because he did not come to strike sins already through zeal, but still to bear with them through gentleness. By contrast, the Holy Spirit ought to be shown over the disciples in fire, so that those who were simply [Col. 1274B] human and therefore sinners might be inflamed by spiritual fervor against themselves and punish within themselves through repentance the sins that God mercifully spared through gentleness.

They could not be without sin, even though they adhered to heavenly teaching, as John testifies when he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). He came in fire among human beings, but appeared in a dove in the Lord, because we must carefully observe through the zeal of uprightness the sins that the Lord mercifully tolerates through gentleness, and continually burn them away in the ardor of repentance.

Thus the Spirit was shown in the Redeemer through a dove, but in human beings through fire, because the more the severity of our Judge has been tempered toward us, the more our weakness ought to be inflamed against itself.

Having completed the reasoning of these four questions, let us consider, dearest brothers, what our preachers were like when the Holy Spirit found them and what he made them. Certainly, while they were residing in one room out of fear of the Jews, [Col. 1274C] each of them knew his native language, yet they did not dare openly to speak of Christ even in the language they knew. The Spirit came and taught them in their mouths through the diversity of languages, while strengthening them inwardly through authority. They began to proclaim Christ in foreign languages, although previously they had feared to speak of him in their own.

Let us further consider what solemnity there is in the coming of the Holy Spirit after the incarnation of the only-begotten Son. Just as the first event was honorable, so also is this one. In the first, God, remaining what he was, created himself as man. In the second, human beings received from above the God who was coming; in the first, God naturally became man, while in the second, human beings became gods by adoption.

If, then, we do not wish to remain carnal in death, let us love this life-giving Spirit, dearest brothers. But because flesh does not know the spirit, someone may perhaps say to himself in carnal thought: “How can I love one whom I do not know?” Yet, since we cannot see God, there is something we can do, a path by which the eye of [Col. 1274D] our understanding may come to him. Certainly, we cannot see him in himself at all, but he has made himself visible to us in his servants. When we see them doing wonderful things, we know that the Lord dwells in their minds.

Let us therefore love God and our neighbor with an undivided mind. For God is not truly loved without the neighbor, nor is the neighbor truly loved without God.

This is why the same Holy Spirit is read to have been given to the disciples twice: first by the Lord dwelling on earth, and afterward by the Lord presiding from heaven. He was given on earth so that the neighbor might be loved; from heaven, so that God might be loved. But why first on earth and afterward from heaven, except that it is plainly shown, in accordance with John’s words: “Whoever does not love the brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20).

Let us therefore love our neighbor, brothers; let us love the one who is beside us, so that we may be able to reach the love of him who is above us.

## Chapter IX.—These men are full of new wine (Acts 2:13).

[Col. 1275A]

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book 23, no. 20.)* When the Lord’s disciples were speaking in various languages, some Jews mocked them, saying: “These men are full of new wine.” New wine signifies the fervor of the Holy Spirit, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “They put new wine into new wineskins.” Since the apostles were suddenly filled with it and spoke in every language, the Jews, ignorant but nevertheless bearing true witness, said: “These men are full of new wine” (Matthew 9:17).

## Chapter X.—Peter rebukes the Jews (Acts 2:14).
