*(Pastoral Rule, part 3, chapter 34.)* Those who have not yet begun to do good works should not first be given instruction in what they rightly love, but should first be torn down from the things in which they wickedly involve themselves. Thus Peter first overturns in order afterward to build. He did not initially warn the Jews about what they should do, but rebuked them for what they had done, saying:

“Jesus the Nazarene, a man approved by God among you through mighty works, wonders, and signs that God performed through him in your midst, as you yourselves know: [Col. 1275B] this man, delivered up by the predetermined plan and foreknowledge of God, you killed by the hands of wicked men, afflicting him, whom God raised, having loosed the pains of hell” (ibid. 2:22ff.).

Thus, when they had been cast down by reflection on their cruelty, the more anxiously they sought the construction of holy preaching, the more profitably they heard it. Hence they immediately replied: “What then shall we do, brothers?” They were promptly told: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized” (ibid. 2:37–38). They would certainly have despised these words of construction unless they had first salutarily discovered the ruin of their own destruction.

This is why, when a light sent from heaven shone upon Saul, he did not hear what he should now rightly do, but what he had done wrongly. For when he fell down and asked, saying, “Who are you, Lord?” the answer immediately came: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.” And when he suddenly added, “Lord, what do you command me to do?” it was immediately said: “Rise and enter the city, and there you will be told what you must do” (Acts 9). [Col. 1275C]

Behold, the Lord speaking from heaven rebuked the deeds of his persecutor, yet did not immediately show him what had to be done. Behold, the entire structure of his pride had already collapsed, and after his ruin he humbly sought to be built up. When pride is destroyed, however, the words of construction are retained, so that the savage persecutor might lie long in ruins and afterward rise more firmly in good works, the more thoroughly he had first fallen from his former error.

Those, therefore, who have not yet begun to do any good works must first be overturned from the rigidity of their perversity by the hand of correction, so that afterward they may be raised up to the condition of right action.

## Chapter XI.—Repent (Acts 2:38).

*(Pastoral Rule, part 3, chapter 30; Homily 9 on Ezekiel, no. 6.)* Sinners who abandon their offenses but do not mourn them should not yet consider their sins forgiven. Although they no longer multiply them by committing them, they do not cleanse them with any tears. For one who has uttered insults has not made satisfaction merely by becoming silent, since it is plainly necessary [Col. 1275D] that the words of the humility that follows should oppose the words of the pride that preceded them.

So also, when we sin against God, we do not make satisfaction merely by ceasing from iniquity, unless we also pursue, with added lamentation, the pleasures that we loved. Hence Paul says: “And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified” (1 Corinthians 6:11). His statement evidently corrects those whom a more reformed life sanctifies, after the affliction of tears has cleansed them through repentance.

Hence, when Peter received certain people terrified by consideration of their evils, he admonished them, saying: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized.” Since he was going to speak of baptism, he first mentioned the lamentation of repentance, so that they might first immerse themselves in the water of [Col. 1276A] their own affliction and afterward be washed by the sacrament of baptism.

With what mindset, then, do those who neglect to mourn their past sins live securely concerning forgiveness, when the supreme shepherd of the Church believes that repentance must be added even to the sacrament that principally extinguishes sins?

God is not nourished by our torments; rather, he cures the diseases of our offenses with contrary remedies, so that we who departed from him, delighted by pleasures, may return embittered by tears; and we who fell by flowing into unlawful things may rise by restraining ourselves even from lawful things.

Human beings depart from God in two ways, and in two ways they become apostates from God. Each person departs from his Creator either in faith or in conduct. Therefore, just as one who departs from the faith is an apostate, so one who returns to the wicked deed he had abandoned will undoubtedly be judged an apostate from almighty God, even if he appears to retain the faith. For faith is worthless without works (James 2:20).

## Chapter XII.—Peter healed a lame man (Acts 3).

*(Homily 5 on Ezekiel, no. 15.)* Holy men perform miracles before unbelievers in order to draw them to the faith. Yet they do not attribute what they have done to themselves; they ascribe it to the power of almighty God and return glory and praise to their [Col. 1276B] author, through whom they know that they can do such things.

Thus Peter performed a sign with the man who had been lame from his mother’s womb. When all who knew him were greatly amazed, he said:

“Why do you marvel at this, or why do you look at us as though by our own power or piety we had made this man walk? The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Son Jesus.”

A little later he added:

“Through faith in his name, his name has strengthened this man whom you see and know” (Acts 3:12).

By performing the sign, he struck the eyes of those looking on with the light of a miracle; but, preserving humility, he returned praise to its author. Holy men always return praise to the Creator for every good they do, so that they may remain steadfast in the virtue they have received.

## Chapter XIII.—We must obey God rather than human beings (Acts 5:29).

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book 17, nos. 48–50; [Col. 1276C] book 7, nos. 53–54.)* From the Holy Spirit who came upon the disciples they received the adornments of virtue, although previously an immense ugliness of fear had possessed them. We know that the foremost of the apostles, before receiving the grace of this Spirit, denied life whenever he feared death. He was overthrown not by punishments, afflictions, or the terrifying power of anyone, but by the single question of a servant.

Indeed, so that the stronger sex might not appear terrifying, he was tested by a female servant making the inquiry. And, so that the weakness of such a sex might be further degraded by the lowliness of her office, he was questioned not merely by a servant but by a servant-girl who was a doorkeeper.

Behold how lowly was the person chosen for the test, so that it might plainly be revealed how greatly the weakness of fear possessed him, since he could not withstand even the voice of a servant-girl who kept the door.

But let us now see what this man, timid shortly before, became after the coming of the Spirit. Certainly, as [Col. 1276D] Luke testifies, we have learned with what authority he preached the Lord before priests and rulers.

When a dispute arose after a miracle had been performed, and the chief priests, elders, and scribes gathered to persecute the apostles, they placed them in their midst and demanded to know by what power they had performed the miracle. Filled with the Holy Spirit, Peter said:

“Rulers of the people and elders, if we are examined today concerning a good deed done to a sick man, by what means this man has been saved, let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, this man stands before you whole” (Acts 4:8).

When the fury of the persecutors increased over this, and the priests and rulers forbade them to preach Jesus, Peter’s authority in opposition to the anger of the rulers is shown when it is immediately added:

“But Peter and the apostles said: ‘We must obey God rather than human beings.’”

When the commands of those resisting the authority of the preachers could not suppress them, they proceeded to scourging. For it is added: [Col. 1277A]

“Then the chief priests had them beaten and ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and they dismissed them” (Acts 5:40).

But that even scourging could not suppress the apostles’ strength is plainly shown by what follows:

“And they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts [5:41; printed: XLI]).

Immediately afterward, what they did following the joy of the scourging is indicated:

“Every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and evangelizing Jesus Christ.”

Behold, the man who had been timid shortly before now speaks in tongues, shines with miracles, rebukes the unbelief of priests and rulers with a free voice, and offers the others an example of authority in preaching Jesus. He is forbidden by blows to speak in his name, yet he is not restrained. He who shortly before had feared the words of those questioning him now despises the blows of those who strike him; he who had trembled at the strength of a servant-girl now, after being beaten, overwhelms the strength of rulers.

Already made firm by the power of the Holy Spirit, he trampled beneath the foot of freedom the heights of this world, recognizing as lowly whatever swelled upward against the grace of the Creator.

These are the adornments of heaven; these are the gifts of the Spirit, which customarily become manifest through various virtues. Paul enumerates them as gifts divided by the dispensation of the hidden purpose:

“To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings in one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues” (1 Corinthians 12:8–9). [Col. 1277B]

Concluding these with a general definition, he says:

“But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each one as he wills” (ibid.).

Unless holy preachers received the promised gifts of the Paraclete, they would not have shone with any splendor of courage. But because the holy apostles were adorned with the grace of virtues, the preaching of their life grew strong against the hearts of unbelievers. Therefore they spare no power opposed to the truth; those whom they see lifted up through pride they press down through the authority of the Holy Spirit.

Hence, when priests [Col. 1277C] and rulers were raging even with scourges and forbidding Peter to speak in the name of Jesus, he immediately replied with great authority:

“Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves. For we cannot fail to speak of what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:19).

Hence, when Paul saw that the chief priest was resisting the truth and a minister of that priest had struck him on the cheek, he did not, disturbed, utter a curse; rather, filled with the Holy Spirit, he prophesied in a free voice, saying:

“God will strike you, whitewashed wall! And you sit judging me according to the law, while contrary to the law you order me to be struck” (Acts 23:2).

Hence, even while dying, Stephen did not fear to exercise the authority of his voice against the force of his persecutors, saying:

“Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you” (Acts 7:51).

But because holy men rise to words of such greatness through zeal for the truth, not through the vice of pride, they themselves plainly reveal this by other deeds and words, showing both how powerful they are in humility [Col. 1277D] and how ardently they love those whom they rebuke. Pride generates hatred; humility generates love. Thus words sharpened by love certainly flow from the fountain of humility.

How, then, could Stephen have delivered his rebuke through pride, when he prayed on bended knees for the very people whom he had rebuked, as they increased in evil and stoned him, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them”?

How could Paul have uttered harsh words proudly against the priest and ruler of his own people, when in humility he subjected himself even to the service of the disciples, saying:

“We do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ the Lord; and ourselves as your servants through Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:5)?

How could Peter have resisted the rulers through arrogance, when, pitying their error, he seemed to excuse their guilt, saying:

“I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your rulers. But God, who foretold through the mouth of all the prophets [Col. 1278A] that his Christ would suffer, has thus fulfilled it” (Acts 3:17)?

He mercifully draws them to life, saying:

“Repent, therefore, and turn back, so that your sins may be blotted out” (verse 19).

When Peter was scourged by the rulers of the people and saw that he had been released for the purpose of making him cease preaching, since he was forbidden to speak in the future, he nevertheless did not yield even for the present. He immediately replied:

“We must obey God rather than human beings.”

And again:

“We cannot fail to speak of what we have seen and heard.”

After pressing down the authority of the rulers by the freedom of his speech, he afterward, through humility of heart, accepted Paul’s counsel that the Gentiles were not to be circumcised. Thus he knew how to raise himself against adversaries through authority, yet not to trust himself in matters where he did not think rightly; through freedom from fear he surpassed swelling powers, while through the humility of gentleness he showed obedience in a right judgment even to lesser brothers, sometimes opposing others by himself and sometimes opposing himself together with others.

In Peter’s deeds, therefore, an example of authority and humility [Col. 1278B] is placed before our eyes, so that, fearing no adversity, we may condemn the powers of the world that resist God, even at the cost of bodily suffering; and so that, in matters we may perceive while placed among the faithful, we may not put ourselves above the others, nor, preferring our own counsels, trust ourselves more than others.

## Chapter XIV.—You have always resisted the Holy Spirit (Acts 7:51).

(Homily 18 on Ezekiel, no. 14; Homily 29 on the Gospels, no. 7.) Blessed Stephen the martyr, seized for the name of his Creator and brought into the midst of persecutors, stood undaunted, taught confidently, and boldly reproached his persecutors out of zeal for the truth, saying: “You always resist the Holy Spirit.” When they ran at him with stones and killed him by stoning, he knelt and prayed for those same persecutors, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59).

What, then, is this virtue: to burn with zeal in such a way that he confidently reproached those by whom he was threatened for their faithlessness, [Col. 1278C] and yet to love in such a way that even in death he prayed for those by whom he was being killed? Thus he blazed with zeal as though he possessed no gentleness at all, and thus he remained gentle in his love for them as though he possessed no fervor against them. Let us consider, in all this, where the guilt of our own conscience lies. For which of us, if he has received even a verbal insult from his neighbor, does not immediately return the insult, become utterly agitated, break out into hatred, and forget the commandment of love? But blessed Stephen was able to do this through the grace of almighty God.

When he was full of the Holy Spirit, he gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand, and said: “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55). We must consider what Mark means when he says: “He sat at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19), while Stephen says: “I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” Why does Mark testify that he saw him sitting, while Stephen testifies that he saw him standing?

But you know, brothers, [Col. 1278D] that sitting belongs to one who judges, while standing belongs to one who fights or gives assistance. Since our Redeemer, taken up into heaven, now judges all things and will come at the end as Judge of all, Mark describes him after his ascension as sitting, for after the glory of his ascension he will be seen as judge at the end of the world. Stephen, however, placed in the contest of suffering, saw him standing as the one who assisted him, because, so that Stephen might overcome the unbelief of his persecutors on earth, Christ’s grace fought for him from heaven.

## CHAPTER XV — “And the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man called Saul, and they were stoning Stephen” (Acts 7:57).

(Homily 19 on the Gospels, no. 6; Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXIX, nos. 38–39.) Let no one, brothers, exalt himself because of his work; let no one exalt himself because of the time he has spent; let no one place himself above another on account of his works. For he does not know how many workers of righteousness and [Col. 1279A] defenders of the true faith the Lord will make from those whom he sees still cold through guilt. We see many cold people within the holy Church, dearly beloved brothers, but we must neither imitate nor despise them. We see what someone is today, but we do not know what each person will be tomorrow. Often the one whom we see coming after us surpasses us through the vigor of good works, and tomorrow we scarcely follow the one whom today we seemed to precede.

Certainly, when Stephen was dying for the faith, Saul was guarding the garments of those who were stoning him. Thus it was he himself who stoned Stephen with the hands of all the stone-throwers, since he made them all ready to stone him; yet in the holy Church he later surpassed in labors the very man whom, by persecuting him, he had made a martyr. O what a soldier, prepared for the day of battle and combat, almighty God possessed in him as a hidden treasure! While he was still cold in life and set among the lives of the wicked, God had already chosen him and secretly concealed him for a long time within the bosom of his foreknowledge. O against how many breasts of adversaries did he bring forth this champion of his when he willed, so that through his words and rebukes [Col. 1279B] he overthrew so many hearts resisting him!

Let no one, therefore, exalt himself because of his works; let no one despair of those whom he still sees cold, because no one can see and distinguish, among the wicked, who are destined to become servants of God. For who would have believed that, through the grace of apostleship, the man who would surpass the stoned Stephen was the one who, at Stephen’s death, guarded the garments of all those who were stoning him? If, then, we turn to these hidden gifts of the Judge, let us never despair of anyone, nor in our hearts place ourselves above those over whom we are for a time set, because even if we now see how far we have gone ahead, we do not know by how far we will be surpassed when they begin to run.

There are therefore two things that we must carefully consider. First, no one should presume on himself in the least, because even if he has already been called to the faith, he does not know whether he is worthy of the eternal kingdom. Second, no one should dare to despair of his neighbor, whom he perhaps sees lying in vices, because he does not know the riches of divine mercy.

## CHAPTER XVI — “Give me this power,” etc. (Acts 8:19).

[Col. 1279C]

(Homily 4 on the Gospels, no. 4.) After granting the power of preaching and granting miracles of power, our Redeemer said to his disciples: “You have received freely; give freely” (Matthew 10:8). For he knew beforehand that some would turn this very gift of the Spirit they had received into an instrument of business, and divert the signs of miracles into the service of greed.

Hence, when Simon Magus saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, saying: “Give me also this power, so that whoever receives the laying on of my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” Desiring the miracles performed through the laying on of hands, he wanted to obtain the gift of the Spirit, so that he might sell more wickedly what he had wickedly acquired.

When the prophet was describing a righteous man, he said: “He shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isaiah 33:15). He does not say, “He shakes his hands free from a gift,” but adds “every,” because one gift comes from service, another from the hand, and another from the tongue. A gift from service is submission improperly rendered; a gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favor.

That person, therefore, shakes his hands free from every gift who, in divine matters, seeks not only no money but also no human favor; who does not bestow sacred orders for the sake of human favor, nor seek any return of praise for that bestowal; who seeks no small measure of favor for any holy service he has performed; and who confers the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, for the merit of life and not for a reward.

## CHAPTER XVII — “Let your money be with you for destruction” (Acts 8:20).

(Exposition of Blessed Job, Book IV, no. 2.) When holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, they do not burst forth from a desire for vengeance, but from the justice of judgment. Within themselves they perceive the subtle judgment of God and understand that the evils rising outwardly ought to be struck by a curse; and they do not sin in cursing because they do not disagree with the inward judgment.

Hence Peter hurled a sentence of cursing at Simon, who had offered him money, saying: “Let your money be with you for destruction.” For by saying not “is,” but “let it be,” he showed that he had spoken these words not in the indicative but in the optative mood. Thus Elijah said to the two captains of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men” (2 Kings 1:10). The outcome of both cases showed with what force of justice the sentence had been confirmed. Simon perished in eternal destruction, and flame coming down from above consumed the two companies of fifty.

The subsequent deed, therefore, testifies with what intention a sentence of cursing is pronounced. For when the innocence of the one who curses remains intact, yet the curse consumes the one who is cursed even unto destruction, it is gathered from the end of both parties that the sentence against the guilty has been hurled by one inward Judge.

## CHAPTER XVIII — “Saul, still breathing threats,” etc. (Acts 9:1).

[Col. 1280B]

(Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXI, nos. 29–30.) The Lord says to blessed Job: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you, or will it remain at your manger? Will you bind the rhinoceros to plow with your rope?” (Job 39:9).

This rhinoceros, which is also called *monoceros* in the Greek copies, is altogether of an untamable nature, so that if it is ever captured, it cannot be held in any way; for, being impatient, as is said, it immediately dies. It is also said to possess such great strength that it cannot be captured by any skill of hunters. But, as those assert who have labored with painstaking investigation to describe the natures of animals, a virgin girl is placed before it; when it approaches, she opens her lap, and it lays down its head there, setting aside all its ferocity. Thus it is suddenly found defenseless by those who seek to capture it.

It is also described as being the color of boxwood; and when it engages elephants in combat, it is said to strike the bellies of its adversaries with the horn that it bears singly on its nose, so that when it wounds the softer parts, it easily lays low those attacking it. Its name, interpreted in Latin, means “horn in the nose.” And what else is signified by the nose except folly? What else by the horn except pride?

Although through this rhinoceros—or certainly monoceros, that is, unicorn—the Jewish people as a whole may be understood, of whom the Lord, foretelling his Passion while the Prophet sang, says: “Deliver me from the mouth of the lion, and my humility from the horns of the unicorns” (Psalm 21:22),—for there were as many unicorns, or certainly rhinoceroses, in that people as there were those who, relying on a singular and foolish pride upon the works of the Law, opposed the proclamations of the truth—nevertheless, let Paul be brought forward from this people in particular: first in pride, and afterward as an outstanding witness in humility.

When he ignorantly exalted himself against God on account of his observance of the Law, he carried a horn in his nose. Later, bending this very horn of the nose through humility, he said: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy, because I acted ignorantly” (1 Timothy 1:13). He carried a horn in his nose when he confidently believed that his cruelty would please God, as he later rebukes himself by saying: “I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers” (Galatians 1:14).

Every hunter feared the strength of this rhinoceros, because every preacher was terrified by Saul’s savagery. For it is written: “Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to Damascus, to the synagogues, so that if he found any men or women belonging to this way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem” (Acts 9:1–2).

When breath is drawn in order to be expelled through the nose, it is called inspiration. Often, too, we detect by smell through the nose what we do not see with our eyes. [Col. 1281A] This rhinoceros, therefore, carried a horn in his nose with which to strike, because, breathing threats and murder against the Lord’s disciples, after killing those who were present, he sought those who were absent. But behold, every hunter hides before him; every human being—that is, every rational creature—is driven away by fear of him.

To blessed Job, therefore, who represents the holy Church, it is said: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?” (Job 39:9). As though it were plainly said concerning blessed Paul: “Will you bend Saul, whom you see growing proud in the slaughter of the faithful through his foolish pride, beneath the authority of your preaching?” The implied answer is: “I, who see him lifted up against me with a singular horn, nevertheless subdue him to myself immediately whenever I will.”

Thus, to capture this rhinoceros, let the virgin—that is, the Wisdom of God, inviolate in the flesh—open her lap, her secret, by herself. For it is written: “As he was going toward Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven shone around him at midday, and a voice was made, saying: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.’ He, falling to the ground, answered: ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to him: ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.’ Trembling and astonished, he said: ‘Lord, what do you want me to do?’ And the Lord said to him: ‘Rise and enter the city, and there you will be told what you must do’” (Acts 9:6–7).

The virgin opened her lap to the rhinoceros when incorrupt Wisdom revealed to Saul from heaven, by speaking, the mystery of its incarnation. And the rhinoceros lost its strength, because, prostrate on the ground, it lost everything with which it had been swollen in pride. It is pleasing to observe where that savage persecutor is, where that ravenous wolf is. Behold, he has now been changed into a sheep, asking about the shepherd’s path that he should follow.

It should be noted that when he said, “Who are you, Lord?” the Lord did not answer him: “I am the Beginning; I am the Word before the ages; I am the only-begotten Son of the Father.” Because Saul had refused to believe that God had become incarnate and had despised the weakness of his humanity, he heard from heaven what he had despised: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.”

It was as though he were saying: “Hear from me concerning what is above what you despise in me concerning what is below. You despise the Creator of heaven because he has come to earth; therefore recognize from heaven the human being from earth, so that you may fear the mysteries of my weakness all the more, the more you prove that these, having been carried into heavenly things, have been brought to the excellence of power.”

Thus, prostrating you, I do not at all assert to you that I am God before the ages; rather, you hear from me what you disdain to believe concerning me. For after saying “Jesus,” he immediately added, in an expression of earthly dwelling, “the Nazarene,” as though he were saying more plainly: “Receive the weakness of my humility, and lay aside the hardness of your pride.”

## CHAPTER XIX — “Rise and enter the city” (Acts 9:4).

(Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 34; Homily 9 on Ezekiel, nos. 4–5.) It should be noted that in this prostration of Paul, those who have not yet begun to do any good must first be overturned from the rigidity of their former wickedness by the hand of correction, so that afterward they may be raised to the upright state of right action. For this is why we cut down a tall tree of the forest: so that we may raise it into the roof of a building. Yet it is not immediately placed in the structure, because its defective greenness must first dry out; and the more moisture is boiled out of it below, the more solidly it is raised to the heights.

Hence, when a light sent from heaven shone over Saul, he did not yet hear what he ought rightly to do, but what he had done wrongly. For when, prostrate, he asked, saying, “Who are you, Lord?” (Acts 9:6), he was immediately answered: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.” And when he suddenly added, “Lord, what do you command me to do?” the answer immediately followed: “Rise and enter the city, and there you will be told what you must do” (ibid., 7).

Behold, the Lord, speaking from heaven, reproved the deeds of his persecutor, yet did not immediately show him what had to be done. Behold, the entire structure of his pride had already collapsed, and after his ruin he sought to be built up in humility. And although pride is destroyed, the words of construction are nevertheless retained, so that the savage persecutor might lie long in his destruction and afterward rise more solidly in good works, in proportion as he had first fallen from his former error and been utterly overthrown.

Paul, therefore, while traveling proudly toward Damascus, was cast down by the voice of the Redeemer; and although he was destined to become a preacher, he did not immediately hear that he should preach what he had seen. Rather, as he lay there, he was told: “Rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you must do” (Acts 9:7). Lying down, he could hear only this: that, once risen, he should declare what he had heard. Once risen, he was told to preach what he had not known.

The one lying down is told to rise; the one standing is commanded to set out for preaching. So also, when we lie in the confusion of weakness, the authority to preach ought not to be given to us. But when we already rise in good work, when we have already begun to stand upright, it is fitting that we should be sent in preaching to win others.

We must also ask why Paul and Ezekiel fall on their faces, while it is written concerning the Lord’s persecutors: “They went backward and fell to the ground” (John 18:6). What does this mean—that the elect fall forward, while the reprobate fall backward—except that everyone who falls backward undoubtedly falls where he does not see, whereas one who falls forward falls where he sees? The wicked, therefore, because they fall in invisible things, are said to fall backward, since they collapse where they cannot now see what will follow them. The righteous, however, because they voluntarily cast themselves down in visible things so that they may be raised in invisible things, fall, as it were, on their faces, because, pierced by fear, they humble themselves while seeing.

## CHAPTER XX — “Now there was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord said to him in a vision: ‘Ananias.’ And he said: ‘Here I am, Lord.’ And the Lord said to him: ‘Rise and go to the street called Straight, and seek in the house of Judas a man named Saul of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying’” (Acts 9:10 ff.).

(Exposition of Blessed Job, Book I, no. 34.) Let us consider, brothers, what Saul had been: from his youth he had been an assistant to those who stoned Stephen; he devastated other places of the Church and, having received letters, sought others to devastate; no death of the faithful was sufficient for him, but, after others had been killed, he always thirsted for the destruction of still others. We certainly recognize that none of the faithful at that time would have believed that God would bend the force of such great pride beneath the yoke of his fear.

Thus Ananias, on hearing the Lord’s voice concerning him after his conversion, was afraid and said: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem.”

## CHAPTER XXI — “Go, for this man is a vessel of election for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts 9:15).

(Exposition of Blessed Job, Book IX, no. 54.) When blessed Job says to the Lord: “I feared all my works, knowing that you would not spare the one who sins” (Job 9:28),

[Note: [Col. 1282D] Perhaps it should be read as in the cited passage of the *Moralia*: “What follows causes the heart great perplexity: ‘knowing that …’”]

if the sinner is not spared, who is rescued from eternal death, since no one is found free from sin? Does God spare the penitent but not spare the sinner? For when we mourn our sins, we are no longer sinners in the same way.

But what does it mean that Peter, when he denies him, is looked upon, and through the gaze of the Redeemer whom he denied is called to tears? What does it mean that Paul, when he was attempting to extinguish the Redeemer’s name on earth, was deemed worthy to hear his words from heaven? Yet in both cases the guilt was punished, because concerning Peter it is written, as the Gospel testifies: “Peter remembered the word of Jesus, which he had spoken; and going out, he wept bitterly” (Luke 22:61).

Concerning Paul, the Truth itself, which called him, says: “I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts 9:16). The Lord therefore by no means spares the sinner, because he does not leave sin without punishment. Either the person himself punishes it in himself through repentance, or God strikes it while taking vengeance together with the person. Sin is therefore not spared, because it is never released without punishment.

## CHAPTER XXII — “Ananias went and entered the house; and laying his hands upon him, he said: ‘Saul, brother, the Lord Jesus has sent me, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, so that you may see and be filled with the Holy Spirit.’ And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight; and rising, he was baptized” (Acts 9:17).

(Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIII, nos. 51–52.) Whoever, when reproved, desires more to excuse and defend his sin than to mourn it is, as it were, covered with scales when he is struck by the sword of the word by holy preachers. He has scales, and therefore the arrow of the word has no path by which to pass to his innermost heart. For he is repelled by carnal hardness, so that the spiritual sword cannot be driven into him.

Saul had hardened himself against God through carnal wisdom when no arrow of evangelical preaching penetrated his heart. But after he had been struck by a powerful rebuke from heaven and blinded by the regard of the Most High—for he lost the light so that he might receive it—he came to Ananias and was enlightened.

In this enlightenment, because he was rid of the hardness of his defenses, it is rightly written of him: “Something like scales fell from his eyes” (ibid.). The hardness of carnal covering had pressed upon him, and therefore he did not see the rays of the true light. But after his proud resistance had been overcome, the scales of his defenses fell away.

They fell from the eyes of his body under Ananias’s hands, but they had already fallen from the eyes of his heart under the Lord’s rebuke. For when he lay pierced by the dart of a lofty reproach, he already asked with a humbled and pierced heart, saying: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (ibid.). When the scales had been driven away, the arrow of truth had already reached the inward parts of his heart: having laid aside the exaltation of pride, he confessed the Lord whom he had attacked, and, not knowing what he should do, he asked.

## CHAPTER XXIII — “But Paul grew much stronger and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus, affirming and teaching that this is the Christ” (Acts 9:22).

[Col. 1283C]

(Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXI, nos. 30–31, 34–35.) While Paul, after the light of his eyes had been taken away, was led by the hand to Ananias, it became clear by what ropes of God this rhinoceros was bound: at one and the same time he was bound by blindness, baptism, and preaching.

He also remained at God’s manger, because he did not disdain to ruminate upon the words of the Gospel. For he says: “I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also. I went up according to a revelation, and I conferred the Gospel with them” (Galatians 2:1–2).

Having earlier heard, while still fasting, “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:5), he afterward, pressed by the marvelous power of the one who presided over him, gained strength from the food of the word and lost the kick of pride. Bound by God’s ropes, he is not merely restrained from ferocity; what is more wondrous, he is bound for plowing, so that he not only no longer attacks human beings with the horn of cruelty, but also, serving their refreshment, draws the plow of preaching.

He himself says of those who evangelize and of those who plow: “The one who plows ought to plow in hope; and the one who threshes ought to thresh in hope of sharing in the harvest” (1 Corinthians 9:10).

The man who had formerly inflicted dreadful things upon the faithful and afterward willingly carried whips for the faith; who, even in written letters, humbly and as one despised preaches what he had once attacked with terror—he certainly labors well beneath the plow, sweating over the field, although he had formerly been wickedly free from fear in the field.

Suddenly changed from an enemy into a preacher, he makes the name of his Redeemer known throughout all the regions of the world. He endures punishments for the truth; he rejoices to suffer what he had inflicted; he calls some by gentleness and recalls others to the faith by terrors. To these he promises the kingdom of the heavenly homeland; to those he threatens the fires of Gehenna. Some he corrects with authority; others he draws toward the way of uprightness through humility. In every respect he bends himself beneath the hand of his Ruler, and with as much skill he gathers God’s threshing floor as he had previously scattered it through pride.

Nor is it inconsistent with Paul that the rhinoceros is said to be the color of boxwood and to strike the bellies of elephants with its horn. For what is expressed by the color of boxwood except the pallor of abstinence? Paul testifies that he adhered firmly to this, saying: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection” (1 Corinthians 9:27).

Endowed with knowledge of the divine Law, he strikes the elephants in the belly with his horn when, rebuking the gluttony of others, he says: “Many walk—of whom I often told you, and now tell you even with weeping—that they are enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Philippians 3:18). And again: “Such people do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly” (Romans 16:18).

This rhinoceros, therefore, now strikes not human beings but beasts with his horn, when Paul, through the strength of his teaching, does not attack the humble, who are not to be destroyed, but kills the proud worshipers of the belly.

## CHAPTER XXIV — “He was lowered down through the wall” (Acts 9:25).

[Col. 1284B]

(Dialogues, Book II, chapter 3.) When many days had passed, the Jews took counsel to kill him. Their plot became known to Paul. They guarded the gates day and night so that they might kill him. But his disciples took him by night and lowered him down through the wall, letting him down in a basket.

It often happens in the minds of the perfect—and this must not be passed over in silence—that when they see their labor to be without fruit, they move elsewhere to labor with fruit. Thus this outstanding preacher, who desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for whom “to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21), and who not only sought the contests of suffering himself but also exhorted others to endure them, when he suffered persecution at Damascus, sought a wall, a rope, and a basket in order to escape, and wished to be lowered down secretly.

Are we to say that Paul feared the death which he himself testifies that he desired for the love of Jesus? But when he saw that in that place there was less fruit for him, he preserved himself through severe labor for labor elsewhere where there would be fruit. For the brave preacher of God did not wish to be held within confinement; he sought the field of combat.

## CHAPTER XXV — “Paul was entering and leaving with them in Jerusalem, acting boldly in the name of the Lord; he also spoke to the Gentiles and disputed with the Greeks, but they sought to kill him” (Acts 9:28).

(Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XI, nos. 15–16; Dialogues, Book III, chapter 17.) If the grace of the Holy Spirit, infused as a heavenly gift, touches the heart of a sinner who remains immovable in his wickedness, the hardness of the sinful mind is immediately changed from its obstinate immobility. Then, moistened by the dew of the divine gift, he willingly endures the injuries that he formerly inflicted with violence; afterward he gives away his own possessions, whereas previously he seized those of others; afterward, by abstinence, he chastises the flesh that previously melted away in deadly pleasures of shame through the satisfaction of the flesh; afterward he also loves his persecutors, whereas previously he had refused to love even those who loved him.

It is pleasing to bring forward Paul as one example among many of this matter. When he was traveling toward Damascus with letters received against Christ, the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured into him on the way, and he was immediately changed from his former cruelty. Later he received blows for Christ that he had been coming to inflict upon Christians.

While formerly living according to the flesh and striving to deliver the Lord’s saints to death, he afterward rejoiced to sacrifice the life of his flesh for the life of the saints. He had formerly been a blasphemer and persecutor, but afterward became a humble and devout preacher. He had considered it the greatest gain to kill Christ in his disciples; now he considered his own life to be Christ and death to be gain.

The mind of Paul, therefore, as soon as it received the grace of the Holy Spirit, changed its former state of immobility and cruelty. In his conversion we can judge that it is a greater miracle to convert a sinner through the word of preaching and the help of prayer than to raise a dead body. In one case flesh is raised again only to die; in the other, a soul is raised to live forever.

The Lord raised Lazarus bodily, whom we believe had already begun to stink; but he raised Saul in mind. And indeed, after the resurrection of Lazarus’s flesh, nothing is said about his virtues; for after the resurrection of the soul our weakness cannot grasp how much is said in sacred Scripture about Paul’s virtues:

that through his preaching the most savage nations were changed into the tender inward parts of piety;

that he desired to die for the brothers whose death he had formerly rejoiced in;

that, full of knowledge of all Scripture, he judged himself to know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2);

that he was willingly beaten with rods for Christ, whom he had pursued with swords;

that, exalted by the honor of apostleship, he nevertheless willingly became little in the midst of the disciples;

that he was led into the secrets of the third heaven, and yet turned the eye of his mind through compassion toward arranging the bed of married couples, saying: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Corinthians 7:3);

that he was admitted into the contemplation of the companies of angels, and yet did not disdain to think about and arrange the actions of those who live according to the flesh;

that he rejoiced in weaknesses and was pleased with insults directed against him;

that Christ was his life and death his gain;

that he was already wholly outside the flesh in the very fact that he lived in the flesh.

Behold how he lives who returned from the hell of the mind to the life of piety. It is therefore a lesser thing for someone to be raised in the flesh, unless perhaps, through the revival of the flesh, he is restored to the life of the mind, so that an outward miracle may be performed for him in such a way that he is inwardly brought to life through conversion.

## CHAPTER XXVI — “Aeneas, may the Lord Jesus heal you” (Acts 9:34).

(Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXIII, no. 46.) In sacred Scripture, a bed sometimes signifies rest in good works. Hence the apostle Peter says: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ the Lord heals you; rise and make your bed.” What does “rise” mean except: “Abandon the evils you have committed”? And what does “make your bed” mean except: “Perform the works that provide the grounds for the reward in which you ought to rest,” so that by rising he may abandon what he did, and by making his bed he may find what he will have done?

The prophet briefly expresses both, saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27). To turn away from evil is to rise from that in which one lay; to do good is to prepare works of reward in which one ought to rest. For whoever turns away from evil but does not yet do good has indeed risen from that in which he lay, but has not yet made a bed in which he ought to rest.

## CHAPTER XXVII — “Peter raised Tabitha” (Acts 9).

(Dialogues, Book II, chapter 30.) Those who cling to God with devoted mind, whenever necessity requires, usually display signs in two ways: sometimes they perform miracles through prayer, sometimes through authority. For when John says: “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12), what is surprising if those who are children of God through authority are able to perform signs through authority?

That they display miracles in both ways is testified by Peter, who raised the dead Tabitha by praying, but by rebuking handed Ananias and Sapphira, who were lying, over to death. For it is not recorded that he prayed for their destruction, but only that he rebuked the fault they had committed. It is therefore clear that they sometimes display these things through authority and sometimes through petition, since he took life from the former by rebuking and restored it to the latter by praying.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — “Your prayers and almsgiving have ascended into the presence of God” (Acts 10:4).

(Homily 19 on Ezekiel, no. 9.) There was a certain man in Caesarea named Cornelius, religious and fearing God. One does not come to faith through virtues; rather, through faith one reaches virtues. For Cornelius the centurion, whose almsgiving was praised by the testimony of an angel before baptism, did not come to faith from works; rather, he came from faith to works. For the angel says to him: “Your prayers and almsgiving have ascended into the presence of God.”

If he had not truly believed in God even before baptism, what did he pray for? Or how had almighty God heard him, if he was not asking God himself to perfect him in good things? He therefore knew God, the Creator of all, but did not know that the Son of almighty God had become incarnate. For he could not have done good works unless he had first believed; for it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6).

He therefore possessed faith, since his prayers and almsgiving could please God. Through good action he merited to know God perfectly and to believe the mystery of his incarnation, so that he might reach the sacraments of baptism. Through faith, therefore, he came to works; but through works he was made firm in faith.

## CHAPTER XXIX — “Now send men to Joppa and summon Simon, who is called Peter; he will tell you what you must do” (Acts 10:15 ff.).

(Homily 9 on Ezekiel, no. 6.) Neither faith without works nor works without faith is of help, unless perhaps the works are done in order to receive faith, as Cornelius, before he became a believer, merited through good works to hear [the preaching of faith].

From this it is gathered that he performed good works in order to receive faith. For to the one to whom the angel says: “Your prayers and almsgiving have ascended as a memorial in the presence of God” (ibid., 4), and immediately, because of that ascent, commands him to send to Simon, who would come and preach to him, it is clear that he asked for the very thing through which he merited to be heard.

## CHAPTER XXX — “Peter went up to the upper room to pray, about the sixth hour; and when he was hungry, he wanted to taste something. While they were preparing food, an ecstasy of mind came over him; and he saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending, like a great linen cloth, lowered from heaven to earth by its four corners. In it were all four-footed animals, reptiles of the earth, and birds of heaven, etc.” (Acts 10:9 ff.).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXX, no. 26; Book XXXIII, no. 33.) The apostles may rightly be called the whelps of Holy Church: born within the Church, they seized the hostile world with their mouths. These whelps, not yet strengthened after the Lord’s Passion by the infusion of the Holy Spirit, lay ready to seize the world behind closed doors, [Col. 1286C] as though in certain hidden caves, so that afterward they might boldly seize the spoils of souls and kill our guilt, destroying within us the whole life of sin.

To that first, hungry but already vigorous whelp, the gentiles—shown as prey displayed in a linen cloth—are said to have been presented with the words: “Kill and eat.” Under the figure of the strong woman, Solomon says of Holy Church: “She made and sold a linen cloth” (Prov. XXXI, 24). What is signified by the linen cloth except the finely woven fabric of holy preaching, in which one rests softly, because the mind of the faithful is refreshed within it by heavenly hope? Hence animals are also shown to Peter in the linen cloth, because the souls of sinners, mercifully gathered together, are held within the gentle repose of faith. Therefore the Church made and sold this linen cloth: she gave by speaking the faith which she had merited by believing, and received from unbelievers a life of upright conduct.

### CHAPTER XXXI.—“And a voice came to Peter: Rise, Peter, kill and eat” (Acts X, 13).

[Col. 1286D] (In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XI, no. 45.) Holy Church kills those who live wickedly in their vices through the mouth of holy preaching. For the holy apostles and the other pastors have been placed in the body of the Church like teeth for this reason: to bite the life of carnal people through correction and to break it of the hardness of its obstinacy. Hence it is said to the first apostle and pastor, placed like a tooth in the body of the Church, when the gentiles are shown in figure: “Kill and eat.” What is killed is taken from life; what is eaten, however, is changed into the body of the one who eats. Therefore “Kill and eat” means: Crush their former state, kill them from the sin in which they live, and convert them into the body of the Church—that is, into your members.

### CHAPTER XXXII.—“Behold, the men sent by Cornelius, seeking Simon’s house, stood at the door” (Acts X, 17).

(Homily 1 on Ezekiel, no. 11.) Sometimes the spirit of prophecy [Col. 1287A] touches the mind in part while not touching it in part. This is attested by the history of the apostle Peter, when soldiers sent by Cornelius were announced to him through the Spirit. For it is written: “The Spirit said to him: Behold, three men are seeking you” (v. 19). He went down to them and, asking, said: “What is the reason for which you have come?” His words show that through the Spirit he had not heard the same reason that he was asking from the soldiers. Thus, at that moment, the Spirit had touched Peter’s mind in part and had not touched it in part: it told him that the soldiers were present but was silent about the reason for which they had come.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.—“When Peter had entered, Cornelius came to meet him; and falling at his feet, he worshiped” (Acts X, 25).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXI, no. 22; Book XXVI, no. 45.) Power is good in its proper order, but it requires the cautious life of the one who governs. He exercises it well who knows through it how to rise above faults and knows how, together with it, to place himself [Col. 1287B] on an equal footing with others. Thus holy men who preside, when there is no vice to correct, rejoice not in the excellence of their power but in the equality of their condition; and they not only avoid being feared by their subjects but also shrink from being honored more than necessary. For they do not consider the damage done to humility slight if, perhaps because of the dignity of their office, they are esteemed more highly.

When, therefore, the ministry of temporal power is undertaken, one must watch with the utmost care, so that each person may know both how to regard himself as equal to others in relation to that power and how, in zeal for punishment, to place himself above sinners. We recognize this discernment more fully if we observe the example of the chief shepherd. Peter, holding the primacy of the Church by God’s authority, refused excessive veneration when the good Cornelius humbly prostrated himself before him; he rejected the honor offered to him and quickly returned to the equality of his condition, recognizing himself as like Cornelius and saying: “Rise; do not do this, for I myself am also a man” (Acts X, 26).

Who does not know that one must prostrate oneself before one’s Creator, not before [Col. 1287C] a human being? Since Peter saw that his fellow man was humbling himself before him more than he ought, he recognized himself as a man, lest his mind swell beyond the limits of humanity, and thus he broke the exaltation produced by the honor offered to him by considering the equality of their condition.

But when he discovered the fault of Ananias and Sapphira, he immediately showed how much power he had acquired over the others: by his word he struck down their life, which he had detected through the Spirit’s searching. He recalled that within the Church he stood above sins, although before brothers acting rightly he had not recognized this when honor was lavishly offered to him. There, the holiness of their conduct earned the fellowship of equality; here, zeal for punishment disclosed the right of authority.

Paul did not regard himself as superior to brothers acting rightly when he said: “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy” (II Cor. I, 23). Immediately he added: “For by faith you stand,” as if he were saying: “We do not lord it over your faith because you stand by faith.” We are equal to you wherever we recognize that you stand.

He likewise did not regard himself as superior to the brothers when he said: “We became little ones in the midst of you” (I Thess. II, 7). [Col. 1287D] And again: “We are your servants through Jesus Christ” (II Cor. IV, 5). But when he found a fault that ought to be corrected, he immediately remembered that he was their teacher, saying: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (I Cor. IV, 5).

A position of authority is therefore well governed when the one who presides lords it over vices rather than over brothers. Rulers ought to rise above vices, for the sake of which they are placed in authority, and to strike faults lawfully through the power of discipline; but by guarding humility they should recognize themselves as equal to the very brothers whom they correct, and in silent thought should place those brothers above themselves. For the vices of their subjects are struck by the rigor of discipline exercised through them, whereas the faults committed by the rulers themselves are not torn apart by even a word of reproach from anyone. Thus they are all the more bound before the Lord the more freely they sin among human beings.

[Col. 1288A] The discipline of superiors, however, renders their subjects all the freer in the divine judgment insofar as it does not leave their faults here without punishment. Humility must therefore be preserved in the heart and discipline in one’s actions. At the same time, one must carefully ensure that, while the virtue of humility is guarded without measure, the rights of governance are not dissolved; and that, while a superior abases himself more than is fitting, he does not become unable to restrain the lives of his subjects under the bond of discipline.

Let us therefore maintain outwardly what we undertake for the benefit of others; let us maintain inwardly what we think about our own estimation. Yet, through certain appropriately emerging signs, let even those entrusted to us understand what we are within ourselves, so that they may see what they ought to fear in our authority and recognize what they ought to imitate in our humility. While preserving the authority of governance, let us continually return to our heart and constantly consider that we were created equal with others, not that we have been placed above others temporarily.

### CHAPTER XXXIV.—“God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts X, 34).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVIII, no. 38.) All [Col. 1288B] the apostles are doors of the Church when they hear from the voice of their Redeemer: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX, 22). It is as though it were plainly said to them: “Through you those will enter to me to whom you open yourselves, and those will be repelled to whom you close yourselves.” They are rightly called doors, because they open an entrance to the faithful and, in turn, oppose themselves to the faithless so that they may not enter.

Let us consider what sort of door of the Church Peter was. He received Cornelius, who was investigating the faith, and repelled Simon, who sought miracles for a price. To the former he said: “In truth I have discovered that God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts VIII, 20), and he opened the secrets of the kingdom kindly. To the latter he said: “May your money be with you unto perdition,” and by the sentence of strict condemnation he closed the entrance to the heavenly court.

### CHAPTER XXXV.—“Paul is stoned” (Acts XIV).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXI, no. 68.) The holy man and brave preacher of the Lord is urged all the more vigorously to preach the truth the greater the persecution that [Col. 1288C] oppresses him; and while he patiently endures his persecutors, he hastens eagerly to draw his hearers to himself.

Let us see Paul, inflamed by zeal for the Holy Spirit, and how he is not at all afraid of the threats of his persecutors. How, placed amid torments, he hastens to draw sinners to himself, as it is written: “Some Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, supposing him to be dead. But when the disciples surrounded him, he rose and entered the city; and on the following day he departed with Barnabas for Derbe. And when they had evangelized that city and taught many, they returned to Lystra and Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples” (Acts XIV, 18).

Let us therefore consider what threats could restrain this preacher when death itself cannot prevent him from pursuing his purpose. Behold, he is overwhelmed by stones, yet he is not removed from speaking the truth. He can be killed, but he cannot be overcome. He is thrown outside the city as though dead, but on another day he is found unharmed within the city as a preacher.

[Col. 1288D] O how strong is the weakness present in this man! O how victorious is his punishment! O how dominant is his patience! Rejection provokes him to reproof; blows raise him up to preach salvation; punishment refreshes him so that he may drive away the weariness of labor. No adversity, therefore, can overcome the man whom punishment sustains.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—“Paul circumcised Timothy” (Acts XVI).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVIII, nos. 28–29.) We depart from the line of discretion within one and the same virtue if we do not know how sometimes to practice it and sometimes to postpone it. For the same thing is not always a virtue, since the merits of actions often change with the moments of time.

Thus, when we do something good, it often happens that we should cease from doing it, and that what the mind held laudably in its proper time should be abandoned for a time even more laudably. For if, because of the small good things by which [Col. 1289A] we advance when they are done, we should not perish when they are interrupted, while greater evils of labor threaten our neighbors, we necessarily set aside the increase of our virtues lest we generate a loss of faith in weaker neighbors; lest what we are doing cease to be a virtue precisely insofar as, through the occasion it provides, it destroys the foundations of virtue in the hearts of others.

Paul clearly showed us this force [Text: lineam] of discretion. He forbade gentiles coming to the freedom of faith to be circumcised, yet, passing through Lystra and Iconium, he himself circumcised Timothy, who had been born of a gentile father. Seeing that, unless he showed himself to observe the commands of the Law, he would stir up the fury of the Jews even against those who accompanied him, he set aside the force of his own assertion and preserved himself and his companions, without harm to the faith, from the violence of persecution.

He did what he had forbidden through love of the faith, but he turned to the service of the faith what he had done as though he had acted unfaithfully. Often virtue is lost when it is held without discretion; when it is discreetly interrupted, it is held more firmly. Yet profound consideration is needed, lest one cease from practicing virtue not for the sake [Col. 1289B] of the common good but through personal fear or the ambition of some sort. When this is done, one is serving not dispensation but guilt.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—“The Spirit of Jesus forbade them” (Acts XVI, 6).

(Homily 12 on Ezekiel, no. 16; Homily 4 on the Gospels, no. 1.) On account of wicked hearers, speech is taken away from good teachers, as it is said to Paul: “Hasten and go out quickly from Jerusalem, because they will not receive your testimony concerning me” (Acts XXII, 18).

And when the apostles wished to preach in Asia, it is written that “the Holy Spirit forbade them” (for when the apostles wished to preach to the gentiles in Asia, they are recorded to have been forbidden through the Spirit). Yet he himself who first forbade the preaching later poured it into the hearts of the Asians, for it is long since all Asia came to believe.

He therefore first forbade what he later accomplished because at that time [Col. 1289C] there were in Asia people who were not to be saved, people who had not yet merited restoration to life. Nevertheless, the ministry of preaching was usefully withdrawn from them, lest they deserve to be judged more severely for despising the preaching. Thus, by a subtle and hidden judgment, holy preaching is withdrawn from the ears of some because they do not merit being raised up by grace.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—“I am pure from the blood of all” (Acts XX, 26).

(Homily 11 on Ezekiel, no. 9.) The sins of subjects and superiors are closely connected, because where a subject dies through his own fault, the one who presides is held guilty of death because he remained silent.

Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, consider that the fact that we are not worthy pastors is also partly your fault, since such men have been placed over you. And whenever you fall into iniquity, it is also part of our guilt that you do not have us opposing and protesting against your wicked desires. You spare yourselves and us if you desist from wicked action; we spare you and ourselves when we do not remain silent about what [Col. 1289D] displeases us.

O how free from the blood of those entrusted to him was that excellent preacher who said: “I am pure from the blood of all, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God”! For if he had not declared it, he would not have been free from their blood; but because he strove to declare to them the whole counsel of God, he was free from their blood.

In these words we too are summoned, we are bound, and we are shown to be guilty—we who are called priests—because, in addition to the evils that are our own, we add the deaths of others, killing as many as we see going daily toward death while we remain sluggish and silent. Thus we are held guilty of the death of the souls of our subjects, who might always have lived if they had heard words of correction.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—“The man whose belt this is, they will bind in Jerusalem” (Acts XXI, 11).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXV, nos. 30–31.) Since [Col. 1290A] adversity in this world is sometimes commanded to us, we must recognize above all that obedience is very slight if, at such a time, it contributes nothing of its own. For when contempt for this world is commanded, when disgrace and insults are ordered, unless the mind desires these things of its own accord, it diminishes the merit of its obedience, because it descends unwillingly and reluctantly to what is despised in this life.

Obedience is brought to harm when the mind’s own desires do not in any way accompany it in accepting the disgrace of this age. Obedience must therefore contribute something of its own in adversity, so that it may be more glorious insofar as it is joined to the divine order even by desire.

We show this weight of virtue more clearly if we recall what happened to blessed Paul. Paul had been divinely warned that he ought to go up to Jerusalem, as he himself says to the Galatians: “Then after fourteen years I again went up to Jerusalem, taking Barnabas and Titus with me; I went up according to revelation” (Gal. II, 1).

When he encountered the prophet Agabus on the journey, he heard what [Col. 1290B] adversity awaited him in Jerusalem. For it is written that Agabus took Paul’s belt and bound his own feet with it, saying: “The man whose belt this is, they will bind in Jerusalem.” Paul immediately replied: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of Jesus; for I do not make my life more precious than myself.”

Thus, going to Jerusalem at the command of the revelation, he learns of the adversities, yet willingly desires them. He hears what he should fear, but he longs for it more ardently. Paul therefore, while God was arranging harsh and difficult things, prepared himself for things still more severe; he was led to adversity even by his own desire, because he perceived the knowledge of the evils that threatened him, yet through devotion of spirit he burned for still harsher things.

Therefore, with the unbroken virtue of blessed Paul going before us, we are instructed that, if we truly strive to seize the palm of obedience, we must also serve amid the adversities of this age out of devotion.

### CHAPTER XL.—“Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged” (Acts XXIII, 6).

[Col. 1290C]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXIV, nos. 8–9; and in the Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 23; Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 24; and in the book of the Morals, at the place cited above. Homily 26 on the Gospels, no. 12.) Just as it is harmful if unity is absent among the good, so it is more harmful if it is not absent among the wicked. For the unity of the reprobate hinders the life of the good all the more harshly insofar as it presents itself against that life in a more forceful combination.

Thus, when the excellent preacher Paul was caught amid the severe persecution of the Pharisees and Sadducees, he recognized that their unity would be harmful to him. Seeing them united against him, he sought to divide them among themselves and cried out: “Men, brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of Pharisees. Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged.”

At once, struck by this declaration, the crowd of his hearers split apart against itself. While the Sadducees denied that there was hope and a resurrection of the dead, which the Pharisees believed according to the teaching of the sacred word, dissension arose within the unanimity of the persecutors. When the tumultuous crowd was divided [Col. 1290D] into two parties, a way of escape was opened for Paul. The united crowd that had bound him as it pursued him released him when divided; and Paul emerged unharmed from the divided crowd that had previously oppressed him savagely when united. For the righteous are rescued when the unjust are divided, and the desires of the elect reach fulfillment when the ranks of the reprobate are thrown into confusion through discord.

But since there are some who are uncertain about the resurrection of the flesh, and since we teach this more rightly when we also respond to the hidden questions of our hearts, we must say a few things about faith in the resurrection itself.

Many people—for we ourselves were once among them—observe flesh reduced to corruption and bones to dust in the tombs, and doubt that flesh and bones can be restored from dust. Reasoning within themselves, they say: “When is a human being brought back from dust? When does it happen that ashes are given life?”

We answer them briefly: for God it is far less to restore [Col. 1291A] what once was than to create what did not exist. What wonder is it if he restores a human being from dust, when he created all things together from nothing? It is more wondrous to establish heaven and earth from things that did not exist than to restore a human being from earth. Yet people look at the ashes and despair that they can return to flesh, seeking to comprehend the power of divine action as though by reasoning.

They say these things in their thoughts because daily miracles of God have become cheap to them through constant familiarity. For behold, within one tiny grain of seed lies the entire mass of the tree that will grow. Let us place before our eyes the wondrous size of any tree, and consider from what beginning arose the tree that reached such a great mass by growing. Without doubt, we find its origin in a very small seed.

Let us now consider where, in that small grain of seed, there lies the strength of the wood, the roughness of the bark, the abundance of flavor and fragrance, the richness of fruits, and the greenness of leaves. When handled, the seed is not strong; from where, then, did the hardness of the wood arise? It is not [Col. 1291B] rough; from where did the roughness of the bark break forth? It is not flavorful; from where did the flavor in the fruits come? When smelled, it gives off no scent; from where does fragrance [Col. 1292A] spread through the fruits? It shows nothing green within itself; from where did the greenness of the leaves emerge?

All these things therefore lie together in the seed, although they do not all emerge from the seed together. From the seed the root is produced; from the root the shoot is produced; from the shoot the fruit arises; and from the fruit the seed is also produced. Let us add that the seed itself lies hidden in the seed.

What wonder, then, if God restores bones, sinews, flesh, and hair from dust, when every day he restores wood, fruits, and leaves in the great mass of a tree from a small seed?

When a doubting mind seeks a reason concerning the power of the resurrection, there should be introduced into it questions about those things that occur constantly but nevertheless cannot be comprehended by reason. Thus, when it cannot penetrate through the sight of what it observes, it may believe, from the promise of divine power, what it hears—with the help of the Mediator between God and human beings, our Lord Jesus Christ, who has already shown the glory of the resurrection accomplished in his own body and promised its future fulfillment in his members.

He lives and reigns with God the Father, [Col. 1292B] in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## BOOK SIX

Here begin the Extracts on the Epistles of Blessed Paul the Apostle.

### PREFATORY NOTE ON THE EPISTLES OF BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE

[Col. 1291]

[Col. 1291B] (In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXV, nos. 42 and 47, in reverse order.) Although the apostle Paul wrote fifteen Epistles, Holy Church nevertheless accepts no more than fourteen. This number consists precisely of two perfect numbers: ten and four.

The number ten is perfect in that the Law is contained in ten commandments, and every fault is restrained by no more than ten [Col. 1291C] words; and, as the Truth declares, the workers of the vineyard are rewarded with a denarius (Matt. XX).

The number four is recognized as especially perfect [Col. 1292B] because every good and perfect work is known through the four books of the holy Gospel. Rightly, therefore, does Holy Church, guarding both Testaments and living according to both the Decalogue of the Law and the four books of the Gospel, extending herself toward the summit of perfection, hold no more than fourteen Epistles of blessed Paul the apostle, so that even from the number of his Epistles she might show [Col. 1292C] that the excellent teacher had searched out the secrets of the Law and the Gospel.

## EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE ROMANS

[Col. 1291]

### CHAPTER I.—“Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts” (Rom. I, 21).

[Col. 1291C]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXVI, no. 28; Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 11, no. 24; and in the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXV, no. 22; Book XVI, no. 71; Book XXV, nos. 22–23; Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 11, no. 25.) If we attend vigilantly to maintaining both humility of mind and chastity of the flesh, we quickly recognize that one is guarded by the other. For pride has often been the seedbed of lust, because while the spirit lifted them up on high, the flesh plunged them, as it were, into the lowest depths.

Such people are first secretly exalted, but afterward fall publicly, because while they swell inwardly through hidden movements of the heart, they fall through manifest lapses of the body. They were rightly struck with a just retribution, so that because they exalt themselves above human beings through pride, they might fall through lust to the likeness of beasts.

“For man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish [Col. 1291D] beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII, 13). Beasts are those who seek the lowest things through the practice of a carnal life. For whoever slips through the flesh is cast down by the appetite of beasts. Thus pride in knowledge had lifted up those of whom Paul said: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts.”

But how they fell into the pleasure of beasts, or rather into something worse than that of beasts, he added, [Col. 1292C] saying: “Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their own bodies among themselves” (v. 24). Behold, they fell beyond the appetite of beasts, and the flesh plunged down those whom proud knowledge had lifted up; they were prostrated beneath themselves precisely where they had seemed to rise above themselves.

The mind must therefore be guarded with every care from the swelling of pride. For God sees inwardly what raises the mind, and therefore allows outwardly to grow strong what will bring it down. What is first exalted inwardly is afterward struck outwardly by the corruption of lust. Hidden guilt is followed by open punishment, so that inward things may be punished by outward evils, and the heart that secretly swelled may publicly collapse.

Accordingly, purity of chastity must be preserved through the guarding of humility. For if the spirit is devoutly held beneath God, the flesh is not unlawfully raised above the spirit.

In the words of the Apostle just mentioned, we must consider that a sin which is not quickly erased through repentance is either the cause of sin, or the punishment of sin, [Col. 1292D] or both the cause and the punishment of sin.

Everything committed at first is sin. But if it is not quickly cleansed through repentance, almighty God, in a just judgment, binds the mind already burdened with sins and permits it to fall into another guilt, so that what it refused to cleanse by weeping and correction, it begins to heap up with sin.

A sin that is not dissolved by the lament of repentance is therefore both sin and the cause of sin, because from it arises that by which the sinner’s mind is bound still more [Col. 1293A] deeply.

But the sin that follows from sin is both sin and the punishment of sin, because, as blindness increases, it is generated as retribution for the earlier guilt, so that the very growth of vices becomes, as it were, a punishment within the sinner.

It sometimes happens, however, that one and the same sin is at once sin, punishment of sin, and cause of sin. Let us place before our eyes someone who coveted his neighbor’s property and, because he could not seize it openly, stole it; then, when accused of the theft, denied under oath that he had taken it.

For this man, covetousness was sin and the cause of sin, because through it he came to robbery.
