The theft itself, by which he seized the property he had coveted, became both sin and the punishment of sin, because, as retribution for his covetousness—which had not been restrained—it caused him to come to theft, and the guilt of his heart grew into an act and into the punishment of blindness.

But because he sought to cover the theft with perjury, he again generated sin from sin. The theft, therefore, which proceeded from covetousness and resulted in [Col. 1293B] perjury, became sin and the punishment of sin in relation to the preceding guilt, but sin and the cause of sin in relation to the subsequent guilt: born from the former, it gave birth to the latter.

The apostle Paul aptly indicates this concerning certain people who understood God but did not honor him, saying: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts.”

Here is sin and the cause of sin. He adds what followed: “And their foolish heart was darkened; for while claiming to be wise, they became fools; and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents” (vv. 22–23).

Here is sin and the punishment of sin. But it would be only sin and the punishment of sin if nothing further followed from the sin. After their unbelief, however, he adds: “Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their own bodies among themselves” (v. 24).

Since, [Col. 1293C] therefore, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, through that sin and its consequence they were also led to fall into the worship of serpents and birds. But because through this blindness they fell still further into impurity and dishonor of the flesh, their very blindness of unbelief was both sin and punishment of sin in relation to the preceding understanding, while in relation to the subsequent impurity it became sin and the cause of sin.

We must consider this with trembling: how the just and almighty God, when he is angered by preceding sins, permits a blinded mind to fall into other sins as well; so that those who were previously rebellious through knowledge are afterward blinded so that they may not know.

Thus, concerning the same unbelieving and lustful people who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God, it is added shortly afterward: “God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting.” Because they did not wish to glorify the one whom they knew, they were handed over to a reprobate mind and left so that they would not even know how to weigh the evils they were doing.

Those who knowingly [Col. 1293D] committed the sin of pride by understanding are also blinded so that they do not understand what they are admitting. The pit of subsequent sins is therefore covered over by the merit of the preceding sin, so that whoever knowingly commits evil may afterward justly fall into other evils without knowing it.

This is done so that sins may be punished by sins, so that the growth of vices among sinners may itself become punishment. In a just judgment, guilt is permitted to increase so that it may one day be accumulated for a deeper blow.

Again Paul says concerning certain people: “So that they may always fill up their sins” (I Thess. II, 16). Hence the angelic voice says to John: “Let the one who harms continue to harm, and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy” (Rev. XXII, 11). Hence David says: “Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness” (Ps. LXVIII, 28).

Hence the Lord says through Moses: “From the vine of Sodom is their vine, and their shoot is from Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is bitterness [Col. 1294A] in them; the wine of dragons is their wine, and the fury of asps is incurable. Are these things not gathered up with me and sealed in my treasures? On the day of vengeance I will repay them” (Deut. XXXII, 32).

He recounted many of their evils, yet immediately added: “At the time when their foot slips.” Behold, their most atrocious crimes are described, yet a subsequent fall is still awaited until the day of vengeance, by which their guilt may be heaped up. They already possess enough to deserve punishment, but sin is nevertheless allowed to grow further, so that a more atrocious punishment may torment the sinners. Sin already deserves punishment and is already the cause of sin, but it is still awaited that an increase of punishment may introduce sin as its own penalty.

### CHAPTER II.—“Their women exchanged natural use for that use which is against nature” (Rom. I, 26).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXIII, no. 5.) Everything that is said can be distinguished according to four qualities: whether evil things are spoken evilly, good things well, evil things well, or good [Col. 1294B] things evilly.

An evil thing is spoken evilly when a wicked act is urged, as it is written: “Bless God and die” (Job II, 9). A good thing is spoken well when what is right is rightly proclaimed, as John says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (John IX, 28).

An evil thing is spoken well when a vice is expressed through the mouth of the speaker for the purpose of condemning it, as Paul says: “Their women exchanged natural use for that use which is against nature.” In this passage he also added the detestable crimes of men, but he narrated dishonorable things honorably, so that by narrating dishonorable deeds he might recall many people to the form of honorable conduct.

A good thing is spoken evilly when something right is not expressed with a right intention, as the Pharisees are reported to have said to the man who had been blind and received sight: “You be his disciple” (John IX, 28). They said this with the intention of cursing, not from a desire to pray. Or as Caiaphas said: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people, so that the whole nation may not perish” (John XI, 50). He spoke a good thing, but not [Col. 1294C] well, because while he desired the cruelty of death, he prophesied the grace of redemption.

### CHAPTER III.—“Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?” (Rom. II, 4).

(Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 11, no. 25.) It often happens that while heavenly mercy waits for sinners, they rush into a greater blindness of heart. The sentence that follows them is all the stricter insofar as great patience has been shown toward their sins, because divine severity punishes the wicked more sharply the longer it has tolerated them.

In his mercy, God grants us sinners time for repentance. But when we turn the patience of his grace into an increase of guilt, he turns the very time which he mercifully arranged for sparing us into a stricter occasion for striking us. Thus, when someone refuses to return even after receiving an interval of time, he increases his evils to his own guilt through the very means by which he could have cleansed them, had he wished to be converted.

Hence it is written: “Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to [Col. 1294D] your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God.”

By the kindness of almighty God, the reprobate therefore stores up the wrath of almighty God for himself on the day of wrath, because while time is granted for repentance, it is used for sinning, and he turns the very remedy of grace into an increase of guilt.

Thus almighty God, seeing that the remedies he has granted are being turned into an increase of guilt, turns the kindness he bestowed into the severity of judgment, so that from the very thing by which he now waits longer, he may afterward strike more severely. And because a person does not wish to abandon evil in order to live, he increases what will bring about his death.

### CHAPTER IV.—“Who will repay each person according to his works” (Rom. II, 6).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII, no. 31.) Just as some structure rests upon columns, and columns upon bases, so our life rests upon virtues, while virtues subsist upon the inmost intention. For the intentions of each soul are its bases. And since it is written, “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. III, 11), the bases are upon the foundation when our intentions are strengthened in Christ. Indeed, we perform even the greatest works in vain if the intentions of our hearts do not seek the rewards of the true life that is in Christ. Hence, when Paul was describing the strict Judge and recounting good actions, saying, “Who will repay each according to his works: to those indeed who, by perseverance in good work, [Col. 1295A] seek glory and incorruption,” because, having named perseverance in good work, he had seemed to speak of the whole structure of the chosen action, he immediately and subtly inquired where the bases of that same structure stood, saying: “Seeking glory and honor and incorruption, eternal life.” It was as though he said openly: Even if some display perseverance in good work, they do not receive glory and incorruption if they do not fix the intentions of their hearts—that is, the bases of the structure—upon the foundation; for God evidently does not inhabit the edifice of an honorable life that he himself does not sustain because it has been placed outside him.

**CHAPTER V.—That he himself might be just, and the one who justifies (Rom. III, 26).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, no. 81.) All the elect of the heavenly homeland are customarily called “light” through participation in the true light, which is God: but he is illuminating light, while they are illuminated light, as it is written, “There was the true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I, 9). But to these alone it is said, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V, 14). Through participation in the righteousness that is God, they are called “righteousness”; but he is justifying righteousness, while they are justified righteousness. For it is said of God, “That he himself might be just, and the one who justifies” (II Cor. V, 21); whereas they say, “That we might become the righteousness of God in him.” Thus illuminating light must be revered in one way, illuminated light in another; justifying righteousness in one way, justified righteousness in another.

**CHAPTER VI.—Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more (Rom. VI, 9).**

[Col. 1295C]

(Dialogue, book IV, chapter 57.) We must believe that the sacred offering of the saving victim greatly benefits not only the living but also the dead, if they have not been bound by sins that cannot be absolved, and that it contributes much to their release—so much so that sometimes the souls of the departed themselves seem to seek it. Yet we must know that the sacred victims benefit those dead who, while living here, obtained that the good things done here on their behalf by others should also help them after death. Among these matters, however, we must consider that the safer course is for each person to do himself while alive the good that he hopes will be done for him after his death by others. For it is more blessed to depart free than to seek freedom after chains.

Therefore, since we already see the present age slipping away, we ought to despise it with our whole mind, offering God daily sacrifices of tears and immolating daily the victims of his flesh and blood. For this victim alone saves the soul from eternal destruction, restoring to us, through mystery, the death of the Only-Begotten. Although, rising from the dead, he dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him, nevertheless, living in himself immortally and incorruptibly, he is again immolated for us in this mystery of the sacred offering. For there his body is received, his flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people, and his blood is poured not now into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of the faithful.

From this, then, let us consider what kind of sacrifice this is for us, which perpetually imitates, for our absolution, the passion of the Only-Begotten Son. For what believer could doubt that, at the very hour of the immolation, at the priest’s voice the heavens are opened; that in this mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that the highest and lowest are joined, earthly things united with heavenly things, and that from visible things one single reality is made? Yet while we do these things, we must also slay ourselves before God in contrition of heart, because we who celebrate the mystery of the Lord’s passion must imitate what we do. For then the victim offered to God on our behalf will truly be acceptable, when we have made ourselves a victim.

**CHAPTER VII.—He who died to sin died once for all (Rom. VI, 10).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, no. 41.) Since we have withdrawn in mind from God and in the flesh return to dust, we are bound by the punishment of a twofold death and are daily worn down by the scourge of vengeance for our sin. But he came to us who, for our sake and without sin, would die once in the flesh alone, who would join his single death to our twofold death and free us from both; concerning this Paul says: “He who died to sin died once for all.”

**CHAPTER VIII.—Let sin not reign in your mortal body (Rom. VI, 12).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIV, no. 21.) A person placed in this life cannot be without the temptation of sin. But it is one thing to resist sin when it tempts, and another to serve sin when it rules. The Apostle was driving the dominion and reign of this sin from the hearts of the disciples when he said, “Let sin not reign in your mortal body.” For he did not say, “Let it not exist,” but “Let it not reign,” because its nonexistence is impossible, whereas it can refrain from reigning in the hearts of the good.

**CHAPTER IX.—I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh (Rom. VI, 19).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX, no. 49.) The righteous are by no means strong in earthly pursuits and weak in heavenly ones; rather, they show themselves more devoted to God, and more intensely so, than they remember having been to the world. For when our blessed preacher Paul says to certain people, “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh: just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness for sanctification,” he plainly accommodates himself to their weakness, as though he said to them more openly: If you can no longer do more, at least be such in the fruit of good works as you once were in the practice of vices, lest holy freedom have as its heirs those whom the habit of earthly pleasure possessed as strong in the flesh.

**CHAPTER X.—To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good (Rom. VII, 18).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, nos. 62–63.) Seed cast upon the earth is pressed down by frost after the rain: the more quickly it is driven back from appearing outside, the more fruitfully it takes root within; and the more it is prevented from advancing, the more it is compelled to multiply, because, when it is restrained from premature growth, it is loosened by the delay of its conception and filled more abundantly for fruitfulness.

So the Lord, in a wondrous manner, first moistens our breast for receiving the seeds of the word through the rain of hidden grace, and afterward, lest it should flow forth too immoderately in the virtues it has conceived, presses it down with the discipline of inward governance, as with frost. Thus what the rain of received grace irrigates, the rigor of discipline also binds, lest, if it brings forth its conceived virtues either before the proper time or more than necessary, it turn the crops into mere grass.

For if righteous people advance before they ought or more than they ought, through the greatness of their advancement they fall into the failure of exaltation. Let us see how Paul, the earth that has been watered, is pressed down by the frost of discipline when he says, “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good.” By asserting that he possesses the will, he already shows, through the infusion of grace, what seeds lie hidden within him. But by saying that he does not find how to accomplish the good, he clearly indicates how greatly the frost of heavenly governance presses upon him.

Had this frost not pressed upon the hearts of those to whom he said that they should not do whatever they wished (Gal. V, 17)? It was as though he said openly: The hidden seeds of your hearts already seek to emerge as fruit, but they are pressed down by the frost of heavenly moderation, so that they may emerge all the more fruitfully later, the more patiently they bear the pressing weights of divine judgment.

**CHAPTER XI.—I see another law in my members (Rom. VII, 23).**

[Col. 1297A]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX, no. 12.) We are well guarded inwardly when, through God’s governance, we are tolerably tested outwardly, sometimes by vices and sometimes by afflictions. For even those whom we know to have been men of virtue were not without temptations and struggles against vices. Thus, for our consolation, the blessed Paul, that outstanding preacher, deigns to disclose certain things of this kind about himself, saying: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members.”

The flesh drags downward, lest the spirit become exalted, while the spirit draws upward, lest the flesh be cast down: the spirit lifts us so that we do not lie in the lowest places; the flesh weighs us down so that we do not become exalted from the heights. If the flesh did not test us while the spirit raised us up, it would doubtless cast us down to the depths through the very perfection of its temptation. Again, if the spirit did not raise us to the heights while the flesh tested us, that very elevation would cast us down more disastrously in a fall into pride.

But this happens according to a measured order, so that while each of the saints is indeed already carried inwardly toward the heights, yet is still tested outwardly, he may fall neither into despair nor into exaltation. For outward temptation does not complete guilt, because inward intention draws upward; nor does inward intention raise one into pride, because outward temptation humbles while it weighs down. Thus, by a great ordering, we recognize what we receive in inward advancement and what we are in outward decline. And wondrously it is brought about that no one should become exalted because of virtue or despair because of temptation, since, while the spirit draws and the flesh pulls back, the soul is balanced by the most subtle moderation of inward judgment between the heights above and the depths below, in a kind of middle place.

**CHAPTER XII.—But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit (Rom. VIII, 9).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIV, no. 72.) The righteous place their joy in heaven, and their manner of life is in heaven; and although they are in the flesh, they are already, as it were, no longer in the flesh, because they are nourished by no pleasure of the flesh. Hence it is said to certain people, “But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit.” For those who received the letters and words of exhortation from the teacher were not actually outside the flesh; rather, to be as though already no longer in the flesh means to possess nothing of the love of carnal things.

**CHAPTER XIII.—If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him (Rom. VIII, 9).**

(Homily 24 on the Gospels, no. 6.) We must remember what the blessed Paul says about the Holy Spirit: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.” This Spirit of love is, as it were, the title deed of divine possession. Does the person whose mind is scattered by hatred, inflated by pride, embittered by anger even to the point of division of mind, tormented by greed, and weakened by lust, have the Spirit of Christ?

Consider what the Spirit of Christ is: certainly the one who causes friends and enemies to be loved, earthly things to be despised, heavenly things to be ardently desired, the flesh to be chastised because of vices, and the mind to be restrained from desires. If, then, you wish to know the right of God’s possession, consider the person of our possessor. For behold, Paul cries out in truthful speech what we have said: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.” It is as though he said openly: Whoever is not now governed by God dwelling within him will not afterward rejoice in the vision of divine brightness.

**CHAPTER XIV.—You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear (Rom. VIII, 15).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XI, no. 55.) The Jewish people were slaves: they obeyed the Lord not with the love of a son but with servile fear. For the Law held the people under the threat of punishment, so that whoever sinned under it was immediately punished by death; and the Israelite people served the Lord not out of love but out of fear. Yet righteousness can never be fulfilled through fear, because, in the words of John, “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John IV, 10).

Therefore Paul consoles the children of adoption, saying: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” For no one can be righteous in God’s sight who serves him not through love but through dread.

**CHAPTER XV.—The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory (Rom. VIII, 18).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII, no. 14.) Whenever the elect suffer such adversities—when they endure dishonor, insults, loss of possessions, and bodily torments—they consider the things by which they are exercised to be grievous. But when they direct the eye of their mind toward consideration of the eternal homeland, they discover, by comparison with the reward, how light is what they suffer. What pain shows to be extremely unbearable is lightened by careful consideration of the recompense.

This is why Paul always rises against adversity stronger than himself, because he awaits the end of his labor. He considers what he endures grievous, but weighs it as light through consideration of the reward. He himself indicates how grievous what he suffers is: he testifies that he was in prisons more abundantly, in beatings beyond measure, and frequently in deaths; that from the Jews he received five times forty lashes less one; that he was beaten with rods three times, stoned once, suffered shipwreck three times, and spent a night and a day in the depths of the sea; that he endured dangers from rivers, from robbers, from his own people, from the Gentiles, in the city, in the wilderness, at sea, and among false brothers; that he labored in toil and hardship, in many fasts, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness; that he endured battles outside and fears within (II Cor. XI, 23 ff.); and that he asserts he was burdened beyond his strength, saying, “We were weighed down beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were weary even of living” (II Cor. I, 8).

But how he wipes away the sweat of such great labor with the cloth of recompense, he himself declares when he says: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us.” He therefore awaits the end of his labor and, while considering the profit of the reward, regards as insignificant what he labors at while almost failing.

**CHAPTER XVI.—Creation was subjected to futility, not willingly (Rom. VIII, 20).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book V, no. 69; book VIII, no. 13.) Apart from those troubles that the elect of God suffer inwardly in the mind, they are outwardly bound by the heavy necessities and chains of corruption. To hunger, thirst, and grow weary are bonds of corruption, which cannot be broken until our mortality is changed into that glory of immortality.

We replenish the body with food so that, weakened, it does not fail; we weaken it through abstinence so that, when filled, it does not oppress us; we invigorate it through movement so that it does not perish through the stagnation of inactivity. Yet we more quickly bring it to rest so that it does not succumb through that very vigor; we cover it with the aid of clothing so that cold does not kill it, and we remove the aids we have sought so that heat does not burn it.

Confronting so many variations, what are we doing except serving corruptibility, so that at least the multiplicity of our devoted care may sustain the body that the anxiety of frail mutability burdens? Hence Paul rightly says: “For creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope; because creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.”

Creation is subjected to futility unwillingly because the human being, who willingly abandoned the state of his innate steadfastness, pressed down by the weight of just mortality, unwillingly serves the corruption of his mutability. But this creation is then freed and rescued from the slavery of corruption when, rising incorruptibly, it is lifted up into the glory of the children of God. Having received the dignity of freedom, it is transformed into the glory of the children of God, because, united to God through the spirit, it shows that it has, as it were, passed beyond and subdued the very condition of being creation.

Now the elect are weighed down by the punishment of corruption, but then they will be exalted by the glory of incorruption. As far as the burdens of present necessity are concerned, nothing of freedom is now displayed in the children of God; but with regard to the glory of the freedom that follows, then nothing of slavery will appear in the servants of God.

**CHAPTER XVII.—Creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. VIII, 21).**

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 3, no. 13; homily 8, no. 3.) While corruption still struggles against us in the present age, we can by no means attain perfect freedom of mind for praising or contemplating God; but after the present age we shall arrive at true freedom. For true freedom will be in us when our adoption reaches the glory of the children of God.

All the elect will eventually be gathered into the heavenly homeland and will be changed in the God whom they will see. Then the whole multitude of the saints will perfectly become the body of the Redeemer, and, seeing incorruption, will be held by no corruption, in accordance with Paul’s words: “Creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” Then they will cling to him, so that nothing of the corruption conquered through the resurrection will any longer oppose their holy love; rather, united to the glory of their Redeemer, they will become one with it.

Then, therefore, all the elect, lifted into heavenly things and united to the omnipotent Lord, their head, will freely offer and resound with the praises of the liberator of all, when they see without end the one whom they will praise.

**CHAPTER XVIII.—The Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings (Rom. VIII, 26).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book II, no. 58; Homily 30 on the Gospels, no. 3.) In Greek usage the Holy Spirit is called *Paraclete*, which in Latin is interpreted as “comforter” or “advocate.” He is called an advocate because he intervenes for the error of sinners before the Father’s justice. He is called a comforter because, while preparing the hope of forgiveness for those who grieve over the commission of sin, he lifts their minds from the affliction of sadness.

Although he is of one substance with the Father and the Son, he is said to plead for sinners, because he makes those whom he fills into people who plead. Hence Paul also says: “The Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings.” But the one who pleads is inferior to the one to whom he pleads. How, then, is the Spirit said to plead, when he is not inferior? The one who is equal does not plead in the ordinary sense; rather, he is said to plead because he inflames those whom he has filled so that they may plead.

**CHAPTER XIX.—Those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. VIII, 29).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XX, no. 62.) In Sacred Scripture certain things unworthy of God are said of him, drawn from human qualities when speech descends to the level of our weakness. For he is called “foreknowing,” as the Apostle says of him: “Those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son,” although foreknowledge cannot exist in God.

One is said to foreknow when one sees a thing before it comes and foresees what is going to be before it becomes present. How, then, can God be foreknowing, when nothing is foreknown except what is future? We know that nothing is future for God, before whose eyes there are no past things, present things do not pass away, and future things do not arrive. Indeed, everything that was and will be for us is present in his sight, and everything that is present can be known rather than foreknown.

Yet because he sees those things that are future for us, although they are always present to him, he is said in human fashion to foreknow, even though he does not foresee as future what he sees as present. For even things that have existed from his eternity are not seen because they exist; rather, they exist because they are seen. In God, therefore, neither past nor future can be found; instead, all mutable things endure immutably. Things that cannot exist simultaneously in themselves all stand simultaneously before him, and nothing passes away in him that passes away in time. For in his eternity, in an incomprehensible manner, all the passing ages remain as they pass, and all that runs stands still.

**CHAPTER XX.—Who also intercedes for us (Rom. VIII, 34).**

[Col. 1300A]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXII, no. 42.) The Only-Begotten Son of God, having become human for us, assumed human nature in himself, so that, since a way of returning to God was not open to a mere human being, the way of return might be made through the God-man.

We were very far from the just and immortal one: we were mortal and unjust. But between the immortal and just one and us, mortals and unjust, there appeared the Mediator of God and human beings, mortal and just, who would possess death with human beings and justice with God. Thus, because through our lowest condition we were very far from the highest, he joined the lowest to the highest in himself, so that through him the way of return to God might be made for us, through whom he united our lowest condition to his highest.

Concerning him the Apostle John says: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the just; and he is the propitiation for sins—not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world” (1 John XXI, 2). The Apostle Paul says of him: “Christ Jesus, who died for us—or rather, who also rose, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.”

For the Only-Begotten Son to intercede for humanity means to show himself human before the coeternal Father. To have pleaded for human nature means to have assumed that same nature in the height of his divinity. Therefore the Lord intercedes for us not by voice but by compassion, because, by assuming what he did not wish to be condemned in the elect, he set it free.

**CHAPTER XXI.—I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor any other creature, will be able to separate us from the love of God (Rom. VIII, 38).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book X, no. 29.) Whoever is fixed upon the sole desire for eternity is neither raised up by prosperity nor shaken by adversity. Since he has nothing in the world to desire, he fears nothing that belongs to the world. Hence Solomon says: “Whatever happens to him will not grieve the righteous” (Prov. XII, 21). Again he says: “The righteous, confident as a lion, will be without terror” (Prov. XXVIII, 1).

The more truly each person conquers the desire for the world within himself, the more fully he casts away from himself the fear that comes from the world. Paul rested in his heart without terror when he said: “For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things future, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

For the love of God completely kills the love of the world in the mind it has once begun to possess, and raises that mind into authority with all the greater strength as it renders it insensible to terrors.

**CHAPTER XXII.—Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever (Rom. IX, 5).**

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 3.) In Sacred Scripture, God is sometimes spoken of nominally and sometimes essentially. He is spoken of nominally when he says to Moses, “Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exod. VII, 4). He is called God essentially when he says to the same man, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. IV).

Hence the blessed Apostle Paul distinguishes between these nominal and essential usages of the word “God” when, speaking of the Antichrist, he says: “Who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped” (II Thess. II, 4). For a human being can sometimes be called “god,” but a mere human being cannot be worshiped as God.

Again, elsewhere, wishing to distinguish the nominal name “God” from the essential one, the same Apostle, speaking of our Redeemer, said: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. IX, 5). He who is called God nominally is God among all things, whereas he who is God essentially is God over all. Thus, to show that Christ is God by nature, he did not merely call him God, but declared him to be God over all. For even each of the elect, placed either as an example or for the propagation of righteousness, can be called “god,” but only among all things, since he is God nominally. Christ, however, is God over all, because he is God by nature.

**CHAPTER XXIII.—O human being, who are you to answer back to God (Rom. IX, 20)?**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, nos. 21–22.) When the omnipotent God strikes us with harsh blows and adversities, a person, considering himself, falls silent and fears examining the divine judgments, because he knows himself to be dust. Hence Paul says: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” The one who is called a human being is shown to be unable to answer God, because, having been taken from the earth, he is not worthy to examine the heavenly judgments.

Hence this too is fittingly added: “Or who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’” (Job IX, 11). The works of the Creator must always be revered without examination, because they can by no means be unjust. To seek a reason for his hidden counsel is nothing other than to act proudly against his counsel.

When, therefore, the reason for his deeds cannot be discerned, it remains that one should keep silent with humility beneath his deeds, because the understanding of the flesh is by no means sufficient to penetrate the secrets of majesty. Whoever, then, does not see the reason in God’s deeds sees the reason for not seeing it when he considers his own weakness.

Hence it is subsequently added: “Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me this way?’” (Rom. IX, 20). For in distinguishing itself as a thing fashioned by divine workmanship, the thing formed reproves itself, lest it resist the hand of the one who works, because the one who benevolently made what did not exist does not unjustly abandon what exists.

Therefore, when struck, let the mind return to itself and not seek what it cannot grasp, lest, if the cause of divine anger is investigated, that anger be provoked all the more by the investigation, and pride kindle inexhaustibly what humility could have appeased.

**CHAPTER XXIV.—Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Rom. X, 4).**

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 4, nos. 14–15.) The Old Testament announced to us one Mediator of God and human beings, and the New Testament announces that the same one will come to us in eternal glory—the one whom we have already known as incarnate for us.

Christ is the end of both Testaments, because the one whom the Law foretold appeared in the flesh, and that same one of whom the New Testament now speaks will appear in the glory of his majesty. The end of both will come when, seen in the power of his divinity, he fulfills everything that has been foretold.

For it is written: “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” “End” here means not one who brings to an end by destroying, but one who brings to completion. He also fulfilled it when, as the Law had foretold, he appeared incarnate. Yet the New Testament still speaks much about his judgment and still recounts much about his kingdom that we do not yet see fulfilled.

Behold, the Gospel is read daily and the life to come is proclaimed. The end of the New Testament, therefore, will also come when he fulfills what he promised concerning himself. The New Testament will then be ended because it will be completed. For when the one of whom it speaks has been seen, the words of that same Testament will cease.

Just as our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns in heaven with the Father and the Holy Spirit, fulfilled the Law through the mystery of his incarnation and perfect humanity, so he will fulfill the promise of the New Testament through the manifestation of the glory of his splendor.

**CHAPTER XXV.—Blindness has occurred in part in Israel (Rom. XI, 26).**

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, no. 9.) The holy preachers, when they proclaim what is right to sinners, illuminate the darkness of our night like stars. Thus, while the Jewish people remained in the night of their unbelief, the Lord, by silence, held back his preachers within themselves and hid the heavenly light from the blind senses of the wicked.

But, as the sacred word bears witness, we have learned that Judaea, which is now being abandoned, will at the end be gathered into the embrace of faith. Hence Isaiah says: “Though the number of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Isa. X, 22). Hence Paul says: “Blindness has occurred in part in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI, 25).

The one who now withdraws his preachers from the eyes of Judaea but afterward reveals them hides his stars, as it were, so that, through the rays of the spiritual stars first hidden and afterward flashing forth, Judaea may neither see the night of its unbelief and present rejection nor fail to recognize it when illuminated.

The Israelite people, which will be gathered abundantly at the end, is cruelly hardened at the very beginnings of the holy Church: it rejected the preachers of truth and despised the words of help. Yet this is brought about by the Creator’s ordering, so that the glory of the preachers—which, received by one people, might have remained hidden—might be spread among all the Gentiles after its rejection.

When Judaea raged with the force of persecution, the Lord spread the lives of the apostles throughout the knowledge of all the Gentiles. Judaea, through judgment, is scattered captive throughout the world, while the life of the apostles, through grace, is extended everywhere in honor.

For who among the Gentiles would have known Peter if he had remained solely in the preaching of the Israelite people? Who would have recognized Paul’s virtues if Judaea, by persecuting him, had not sent him into our knowledge? Behold, those who were rejected by the Israelite people with blows and insults are now honored throughout the ends of the world. Through a wondrous secret ordering of his counsel, the Lord permitted his preachers to be oppressed in one nation, and from there caused them to spread to the ends of the world.

**CHAPTER XXVI.—God confined all things in unbelief (Rom. XI, 30).**
(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, no. 56, and in the Dialogues, book II, chapter 16.) “How unsearchable are the judgments of God and how inscrutable his ways” (ibid., 33)! The incomprehensibility of divine judgment cannot be penetrated by the eye of the human mind. Why did Judaea believe first, while the whole Gentile world remained in the obstinacy of its unbelief; but afterward the hearts of the Gentiles were softened at the end, while the unbelief of the Jews was hardened? When the merciful God drew the Gentiles to himself, he rejected Judaea in anger; [Col. 1302C] and those tender and penetrable Jewish hearts were changed into the insensibility of the Gentiles. It came about that, just as the Gentile world had formerly been hardened against receiving the faith, so afterward, when the Gentiles had embraced the faith, the people of Judaea became hardened by the strength of unbelief.

Hence the Apostle Paul says to those same Gentiles: “Just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief, so they too have now not believed because of the mercy shown to you, so that they themselves also may obtain mercy. For God has enclosed all things in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. XI, 30–32). Considering this statement of his first with regard to the calling of the Jews and the rejection of the Gentiles, and afterward with regard to the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews, and recognizing that he could not comprehend God’s hidden judgments, he added with an exclamation: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways” (Rom. XI, 33)! Therefore let no one seek to investigate [Col. 1302D] why, when one is rejected, another is chosen, or why, when one is chosen, another is rejected, since, as Paul testifies, his judgments are inscrutable.

Yet a question arises from these words of the Apostle. For the prophet David speaks to the Lord, saying: “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth” (Ps. CXVIII, 13). Since knowing is less than declaring, what does it mean that Paul asserts God’s judgments to be incomprehensible, while David testifies that he not only knew them all but also declared them with his lips?

We must understand that holy men, insofar as they are one with the Lord, are not ignorant of the Lord’s mind. All who devoutly follow the Lord are with the Lord through their devotion; yet, while still weighed down by the burden of corruptible flesh, they are not with the Lord. Thus they know God’s hidden judgments insofar as they are joined to him, but insofar as they are separated from him, they do not know them. Those who have not yet perfectly penetrated his secrets testify that his judgments are incomprehensible; but those who cling to him in mind, and [Col. 1303A] by clinging to him recognize them—so far as they receive them—either through the words of Sacred Scripture or through hidden revelations, both know and declare them. Therefore they do not know the judgments that God keeps silent; they know those that God speaks.

Hence, after the prophet David had said, “With my lips I have declared all the judgments,” he immediately added, “of your mouth.” It is as though he said openly: “I have been able both to know and to declare those judgments which I have recognized you to have spoken. For those which you yourself do not speak, you undoubtedly conceal from our knowledge.” The prophetic and apostolic statements therefore agree: God’s judgments are incomprehensible, and yet those which have proceeded from his mouth are declared by human lips, because what has been uttered can be known by human beings and made public, whereas what is hidden cannot be made known.

Again another question arises. If the spirit that clings to the Lord becomes one spirit with the Lord, as it is written, “He who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17), what does the same outstanding preacher Paul mean when he adds: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor” (I Cor. II, 16)? It seems wholly incongruous [Col. 1303B] to be ignorant of the mind of one with whom one has become one.

But we must understand that, as was briefly stated above, holy men, insofar as they are one with the Lord, are not ignorant of the Lord’s mind. For the same Apostle also says: “Who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one has known what belongs to God except the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II, 11). To show that he knew what belongs to God, he added: “But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is from God.” Again he says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him—God has revealed to us through the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. II, 9–10).

## CHAPTER XXVII.—From him, through him, and in him are all things (Rom. XI, 36).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, nos. 69 and 70.) Abel, Isaiah, and John appeared at different times; they were separated in time, but not in preaching. [Col. 1303C] Abel, signifying the passion of our Redeemer, offered a lamb in sacrifice. Concerning that passion Isaiah says: “Like a lamb before its shearer he will be silent, not opening his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7). John also says of him: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I, 29).

Behold: although they were sent at different times, and yet agreed in their testimony concerning the innocence of our Redeemer, John spoke of the same Lamb by pointing him out, Isaiah by foreseeing him, and Abel by offering him. The one whom John held forth by pointing him out, and whom Isaiah held forth in his speech, Abel held in his hands by signifying him.

David, Isaiah, and Paul likewise appeared in this world at different times; nevertheless, none of them held a view different from the others, because, although they did not know one another face to face, they had nevertheless learned one thing through divine knowledge.

David, wishing to show God, the author of all things, in the Trinity, said: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us” (Ps. LXVI, 8). And lest, by naming God three times, he should seem to have spoken of three gods, he immediately indicated the unity of that Trinity [Col. 1303D] by adding: “And may all the ends of the earth fear him.” By saying not “them” but “him,” he made known that the three things he had mentioned are one.

Isaiah likewise, when he was proclaiming praise of the unity of the Trinity and expressing the voices of the seraphim, said: “Holy, holy, holy.” And lest, by naming “Holy” three times, he should seem to divide the unity of the divine substance, he added: “The Lord God of hosts” (Isa. VI, 3). By adding not “the lords gods” but “the Lord God,” he indicated that the one whom he had three times called “Holy” exists as one.

Paul too, wishing to show the operation of the holy Trinity, said: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things.” And, to indicate the unity of that same Trinity, he added: “To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.” By saying not “to them” but “to him,” he made known that there is one according to nature and three according to persons—the same reality that he had previously expressed three times.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—I beseech you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice (Rom. XII, 1).

[Col. 1304A]

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 10, no. 19.) There are many placed within the holy Church who, mindful of their sins, wash themselves with tears, mortify the flesh through abstinence, and involve themselves in none of the affairs of this world. What they have, they give to the needy, and they do not desire to possess what they do not have. Mindful of eternal judgment, they sacrifice themselves daily to God through the lamentation of compunction.

For this reason they discipline their bodies, so that they may fulfill what is said by the teacher of the Gentiles: “To present your bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God.” A sacrifice is killed in order to be offered. But a living sacrifice is a body afflicted for the Lord; it is called a sacrifice and living because it lives in virtues—that is, it has been killed with respect to vices. It is a sacrifice because it is already dead to this world’s wicked deeds, but living because it performs all the good works of which it is capable.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—Not to think more highly than one ought to think (Rom. XII, 3).

[Col. 1304B]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XX, no. 18.) Heretics often speak boldly about the nature of divinity, although, in their misery, they do not know themselves. They do not seek those things from which they might learn humility, order their character in tranquillity, preserve patience, and display long-suffering; instead, they desire to investigate what lies beyond them. While they strive toward what they cannot comprehend, they neglect to learn the things from which they could have been instructed.

How well the outstanding preacher restrains their boldness when he says: “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety.” Hence Solomon says: “Set a limit to your prudence” (Prov. XXIII, 4).

## CHAPTER XXX.—Do not be wise in your own eyes (Rom. XII, 16).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XIII, no. 45.) Those who are deceived by confidence in [Col. 1304C] their false wisdom cannot attain true wisdom. Of them it is written: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. V, 21).

[Col. 1304D] Therefore the outstanding preacher, when he found people who were wise according to the flesh, sought that they should first become fools in order to receive true wisdom, saying: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool so that he may be wise” (I Cor. III, 18). It is as though he said openly to them: “Learn to be fools in your own eyes, so that you may be able to be truly wise in God.”

Again he says: “Do not be wise in your own eyes.” It is as though he said: “Those who are wise in their own eyes cannot attain true wisdom.” And Truth itself says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI, 25).

## CHAPTER XXXI.—If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people (Rom. II, 18).

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 22.) If those who love peace come forward with words of reproach, they should not [Col. 1304D] fear disturbing temporal peace for themselves. Nevertheless, they must inwardly preserve with complete love that same peace which, by the forcefulness of their speech, they appear outwardly to disturb for themselves.

Hence Paul says: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people.” Since he was about to urge his disciples to have peace with everyone, he prefaced the exhortation by saying, “If possible,” and added, “so far as it depends on you.” It was difficult for them to be at peace with everyone if they reproved evil deeds. But when temporal peace is disturbed in the hearts of the wicked by our rebuke, it must nevertheless be preserved inviolate in our own hearts.

He therefore rightly says, “so far as it depends on you,” as though he were saying: “Because peace rests upon the agreement of two parties, if it is driven away by those who are reproved, let it nevertheless remain whole in the minds of you who reprove.” Hence he again admonishes the same disciples, saying: “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of him and do not [Col. 1305A] associate with him, so that he may be ashamed” (II Thess. III, 14). Immediately he adds: “And do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother” (v. 15).

It is as though he said: “Break exterior peace with him, but preserve interior peace toward him in the depths of your hearts, so that your discord may strike the mind of the sinner in such a way that peace does not depart from your hearts without being renounced.”

## CHAPTER XXXII.—Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it (Rom. XIII, 3).

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 38.) When two vices are involved, one of which cannot in any way be extinguished unless the other is nourished, the one that oppresses more dangerously must be attacked more ardently.

Often someone does not restrain himself at all from gluttony, and is already almost overcome by the goads of lust. Terrified by the danger of this struggle, while he tries to restrain himself through abstinence, he is tormented by the temptation of empty glory. It must therefore be tolerated that, through the virtue of abstinence, arrogance temporarily grows against the person who is living, lest lust, through gluttony, completely destroy him from life.

This is why Paul [Col. 1305B], perceiving that his weak hearer either still wished to act wrongly or rejoiced in receiving human praise as a reward for a right action, said: “Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it.” Good deeds are not to be performed so that the authority of this world may not be feared at all, nor so that the glory of passing praise may be gained through them. But because the outstanding preacher judged that the weak mind could not rise to such strength as to avoid wickedness and praise at the same time, he both offered something by his admonition and took something away.

By granting what was less serious, he removed what was more dangerous. Since the mind would not rise to abandon everything at once, he allowed it to remain familiarly attached to one of its vices, so that it might be taken away from another without pain.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—The night has passed, but the day has drawn near (Rom. XIII, 12).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, nos. 3–4.) All of us who follow the truth in this life may be called [Col. 1305C] dawn or daybreak. Dawn and daybreak announce that night has passed away, but they do not yet display the full brightness of day. While they drive night away, they receive day and hold a light mixed with darkness.

Similarly, we already perform certain works that belong to the light, yet we are not free from certain remnants of darkness. Through the prophet it is said to God: “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII, 2). Again it is written: “For we all offend in many things” (Jas. III, 2). Paul also says: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin that is in my members” (Rom. VII, 23).

Where, then, the law of sin contends with the law of the mind, it is certainly still dawn. It is still dawn because the light that has already appeared has not yet completely overcome the darkness that is passing away. It is still dawn because, while the law of the flesh strikes against the law of the mind and the law of the mind against the law of the flesh, light and shadow struggle with one another in turn.

Hence, when Paul again said, [Col. 1305D] “The night has passed,” he did not simply add, “The day has come,” but “the day has drawn near.” By indicating that, after the departure of night, the day had not yet come but had drawn near, he clearly shows that after the darkness he is still before the sun, in the dawn.

The holy Church of the elect will then fully be day, when the shadow of sin is no longer mixed with it. It will fully be day when it shines with the perfect fervor of inward light. It will fully be day when, enduring no troubling memory of its evils, it hides from itself even all remnants of darkness.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires (Rom. XIII, 14).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXX, nos. 62–63.) A disciplined and temperate person refreshes the stomach only so far as necessary to moderate need, and restrains it from pleasure. We must understand, however, that pleasure so disguises itself under necessity that scarcely anyone, however perfect, can distinguish it.

[Col. 1306A]

When necessity demands that a debt be paid, pleasure supplies the fulfillment of desire; and it drags the appetite headlong all the more securely because it conceals itself under the respectable name of satisfying necessity. Often, while one is eating, pleasure secretly follows after what has been added; sometimes, shamelessly and without restraint, it even tries to go ahead.

It is easy to detect when pleasure anticipates necessity, but it is very difficult to discern when, during the necessary act of eating itself, pleasure secretly attaches itself to it. Because it follows the appetite of nature that goes before it, it appears slower, as though coming from behind. At the time when the debt owed to necessity is being paid, pleasure is mingled with necessity through eating, and it is not known what necessity demands and what, as has been said, pleasure supplies.

Often we do discern this; but because we know by experience that the two are joined together, when we are carried beyond the limits, we take pleasure in knowingly allowing ourselves to be deceived. While the mind flatters itself with the thought of necessity, it is deceived by pleasure, as it is written: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires.” What is forbidden when done from desire is permitted [Col. 1306B] when done from necessity.

Yet often, when we carelessly yield to necessity, we serve desires; and sometimes, when we try too severely to resist desires, we increase the misery of necessity. Each person must therefore hold to the art of self-restraint in such a way that he kills not the flesh but the vices of the flesh.

Often, when the flesh is restrained more than is right, it is also weakened for the practice of good works, so that it is not sufficient even for prayer or preaching, while it hastens to suffocate the incentives of vices completely within itself. We have, after all, as an assistant to our inward purpose this human being whom we bear outwardly; and in him are movements of wantonness, while from him also come the powers for good action.

Often, while pursuing the enemy in him, we also slaughter the fellow citizen whom we love; and often, while sparing the fellow citizen, so to speak, we nourish the enemy for battle. For the vices grow strong on the same foods by which the virtues are nourished and live. When virtue is nourished, the strength of the vices is often increased as well; but when excessive restraint weakens the strength of the vices, even [Col. 1306C] virtue, as it declines, gasps for breath.

Therefore our inward person must preside as a fair judge between himself and the one whom he bears outwardly, so that his outward person may always be sufficient to serve him in the required ministry and never resist with an arrogantly unrestrained neck. Let it not disturb him if the outward person mutters suggestions, provided that he always keeps him pressed down under the heel of his mastery.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—Again, concerning the foregoing.

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, nos. 105–106.) Often the mind is kindled toward the path of righteousness, shakes off sluggishness, and is carried upward by such a desire for heavenly things that almost nothing lower seems to remain in it. Yet when it is brought back to the care of the flesh, without which the journey of the present life cannot in any way be completed, that care holds it pressed down below, as though it had never touched the heights.

When it hears the words of the heavenly oracle, it is raised into love of the heavenly homeland; but when the concern of the present life rises again, it is buried beneath the mound of earthly care. [Col. 1306D] In the soil of the heart, the seed of heavenly hope does not prosper, because the thorn of lowly thought grows dense.

Truth itself uproots this thorn by the hand of holy exhortation, saying: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matt. VI, 34). Through Paul also it is said against it: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII, 14).

From the words of both leader and soldier we recognize that the mind is then pierced by a deadly wound from this care when it is not held within the measure of equity. Care for the flesh is not entirely cut away from those still living in mortal flesh; rather, it is moderated so that it may serve the mind in a disciplined way.

Since Christ forbids us to be anxious about tomorrow, he does not deny us some care for present necessities; he forbids that care to be extended into the time that follows. Likewise, when Paul does not permit care for the flesh to arise from desire, he plainly permits it when it arises from necessity.

Care must therefore be taken that the care of the flesh neither exceeds the limits of necessity [Col. 1307A] nor presumes upon itself in what it carries out moderately. Often the mind is deceived, so that it supposes what it desires voluptuously to be necessary, and considers everything it likes to be required for life. Often, too, because success follows foresight, the mind is lifted up in self-confidence. When it possesses what it sees lacking in others, it silently rejoices at the greatness of its own promise; and it becomes farther from true foresight precisely because it does not recognize even the pride it suffers.

Therefore, with the vigilant attention of constant watchfulness, we must always weigh both what we do outwardly and what we turn over in our hearts, lest earthly care multiply outside and impede the mind, or at least the thought within become exalted over its management. Thus, while we fear divine judgments with temporal prudence, we may escape the punishments of eternal dread.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—One person judges one day to be different from another, etc. (Rom. XIV, 5).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book I, no. 28.) Just as the obscurity of ignorance [Col. 1307B] is without doubt the night of the heart, so understanding is rightly called day. Hence Paul says: “One person judges one day to be different from another; another judges every day.” It is as though he said openly: “One person understands certain things while leaving some aside; another recognizes all things capable of being understood as they ought to be seen.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—The Gentiles glorify God because of his mercy (Rom. XV, 9).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVII, no. 58; book X on Job, no. 7.) God’s judgments are secrets of wisdom: although the Gentile world possessed no merits before God, it nevertheless received the grace of reconciliation solely through mercy. Hence Paul rightly says: “The Gentiles glorify God because of his mercy” (I Pet. II, 10). Again it is written: “That which had not obtained mercy has now obtained mercy.”

The Gentile world itself is therefore the place of God’s mercy. If the strict Judge had justly punished its sins, [Col. 1307C] it would never have come to the reconciliation of grace. Few are able to investigate the secrets of his wisdom, but no one can discover them, because what immortal Wisdom justly disposes concerning us above our understanding is rightly hidden from us, who are still mortal.

Yet to behold, however imperfectly, these very secrets of his wisdom is already to see something of the power of its incomprehensibility. Although we fail in the investigation of his counsels, through that failure we learn more truly whom we ought to fear.

Paul was reaching toward these secrets of that wisdom. As he examined God’s hidden judgments concerning the rejection [Col. 1308A] of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, and could not reach them, he said: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor” (Rom. XI, 33–34)?

Earlier, exhausted by the very act of investigating them, yet advancing through that exhaustion toward knowledge of his own weakness, he had prefaced this by saying: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me thus?’” (Rom. IX, 20).

Because he could not reach God’s judgments, he returned to knowledge of his own weakness and, through failing, recalled himself to his own instruction. Thus, so to speak, he found the secrets of wisdom by not finding them. When he had grown weary in seeking the heavenly counsels, he learned to fear more humbly. His weakness drove him away from intimate knowledge, but humility joined him more truly to the one whom he could not know.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—I wish you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil (Rom. XVI, 19).

[Col. 1308B]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book I, no. 2; *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 11.) It is written of blessed Job that he was simple and upright. Some people are so simple that they do not know what is right. They abandon the innocence of true simplicity precisely by failing to rise to the virtue of uprightness. Since they do not know how to be cautious through uprightness, they cannot remain innocent through simplicity.

The simple must therefore be admonished always to join prudence to the goodness of simplicity, so that they may possess the security of simplicity without losing the circumspection of prudence. Hence the teacher of the Gentiles, Paul, admonishes his disciples, saying: “I wish you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil.”

Again he says: “Do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in wickedness” (I Cor. XIV, 20). Truth itself likewise commands the disciples, saying: “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matt. X, 16). [Col. 1308C] He necessarily joined both qualities in his admonition, so that the simplicity of the dove might be instructed by the cunning of the serpent, and again the cunning of the serpent might be tempered by the simplicity of the dove.

Hence the Holy Spirit revealed his presence to human beings not only in a dove but also in fire. Through the dove simplicity is signified; through fire, zeal. The Holy Spirit is therefore shown in both dove and fire, because all who are filled with him serve the gentleness of simplicity while also being kindled by the zeal of uprightness against the faults of sinners.

# EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST LETTER OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 1307]

## CHAPTER I.—You have been enriched in everything (I Cor. I, 4).

[Col. 1307D]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIV, no. 41, and especially book I on Ezekiel, homily 11, nos. 17–19.) If modest minds have perhaps committed some faults, they should be reproved gently, because if they are rebuked too harshly, they are broken rather than instructed.

Therefore, when righteous preachers correct certain people, if they are able to find in them, on another side, something of good conduct, they should descend to the same words of reproof with great tact. We learn this well from the outstanding preacher, blessed Paul. When he knew that the Corinthians had been divided by schism out of partiality for particular persons, he took care of their modesty and began his address to them with thanksgiving and praise, saying: “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God that has been given to you in Christ Jesus, because you have been enriched in him in everything.”

He certainly praised greatly those whom he called rich in everything in Christ. Behold, he multiplies his words of affection still further, saying: “In every word and in every knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed [Col. 1308C] in you” (v. 5). He said, “The testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you,” as though they had accomplished in their works [Col. 1308D] what they had learned through teaching.

Then, as the culmination of his praise, he added: “So that you lack nothing in any grace, awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 7).

I ask you, Paul: if they lack nothing, why do you weary yourself by writing to them? Why do you speak while placed at such a distance? Let us consider, dearly beloved brothers, how greatly he praises them. He says that the grace of God has been given to them; he calls them rich in everything; he declares that the testimony of Christ—that is, what Christ testified concerning himself by dying and rising again—has been confirmed in their life in every word and in every knowledge; and he testifies that they lack nothing in any grace.

Who, I ask, would believe that shortly afterward he would rebuke those whom he praises in such terms? For after other matters he adds: “I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you” (II Cor. I, 10). How could schism have crept in among people so perfect and so praiseworthy?

“For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those of Chloe’s household, that there are contentions among you” (v. 11). Concerning these contentions he shortly afterward added: “When there is jealousy and [Col. 1309A] contention among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human standards?” (I Cor. III, 3).

He continues: “I mean that each one of you says: ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I to Apollos,’ or ‘I to Cephas,’ or ‘I to Christ’” (I Cor. I, 12).

Behold: those whom he had praised for every word and every knowledge, of whom he had said that they lacked nothing in any grace—speaking for a little while and gently approaching his rebuke—he reproved for being divided among themselves. He had first described their health and afterward exposed their wounds.

A skilled physician, seeing a wound that needed to be cut but observing that the patient was timid, [Col. 1309C] stroked him for a long time and then suddenly struck. First he applied praise with a gentle hand; afterward he drove in the instrument of rebuke. Unless modest minds are reproved through such soothing, so that from other matters they may hear something they can take as consolation, they immediately fall into despair under rebuke.

But did Paul lie when he first said that they lacked nothing in any grace, although he would afterward say that they lacked unity? Far be it from anyone, even a foolish person, to believe such things about him. Rather, because among the Corinthians [Col. 1309B] there were some filled with every grace, while others were cut off by partiality toward particular persons, he began with praise of the perfect so that, by a moderate attack, he might reach the correction of the weak—drawing here also upon the practice of bodily medicine for the medicine of the heart.

When a physician sees a wound that must be struck, he first touches the healthy members around the wound, so that afterward he may reach the wounded members by gentle touching. Thus, when Paul praised the perfect among the Corinthians, he touched the healthy members beside the wound; but when he rebuked the weak for their division, he struck the wound in the body.

## CHAPTER II.—We speak the things granted to us by God, not in words taught by human wisdom (I Cor. II, 13).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, no. 74.) The words of God’s commandments differ from those of the wise people of this world. While such people devote themselves to eloquence, their statements appear beautiful; and because they lack the power of reality, they falsely present themselves as something other [Col. 1309C] than they are, as though covered with a superficial color through the arrangement of words.

By contrast, the teaching of God is beautiful in its preaching and conspicuous in its purity. It does not fraudulently present one thing outwardly while reserving another inwardly; nor does it seek to appear beautiful in its sayings through the brilliance of language, but through the integrity of truth.

Paul had rightly despised the adornments of eloquence when he said: “We speak the things granted to us by God, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit.” He preferred to display the wisdom of God through the sheer purity of truth rather than to embellish it through verbal composition.

## CHAPTER III.—Who knows what belongs to a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? (I Cor. II, 11).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XV, no. 66.) The human spirit is unknown to another person when it is not demonstrated by words or deeds. Since it is written, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII, 16), whatever is hidden within is disclosed through what is done outwardly. [Col. 1309D]

Hence Solomon also rightly says: “As faces are reflected in water for those who look into it, so the hearts of human beings are manifest to the prudent” (Prov. XXVII, 19).

## CHAPTER IV.—But we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles (I Cor. I, 23).

(Homily 6 on the Gospels, no. 1.) In our Lord Jesus Christ the minds of unbelievers suffered a grave stumbling block when they saw him dying after all the miracles he had performed. It seemed foolish to human beings that the author of life should die for human beings; and from the very fact by which he ought to have been honored, because of it they took offense against him and became still more indebted to him.

For God deserved to be honored by human beings all the more greatly the more he accepted unworthy things on behalf of human beings.

## CHAPTER V.—For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (I Cor. II, 2).

[Col. 1309D]

[Col. 1310A]

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 9, no. 31.) The things that Sacred Scripture tells us about the nature of divinity and about eternal joys, while we still do not know them, are known only to the angels in secret. In sacred speech, the strong are nourished by more hidden and sublime statements, while we, the little ones, who cannot understand lofty things, are nourished by more accessible commandments and are saved in faith in Christ.

Hence blessed Paul says to the Corinthians: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” It is as though he said: “Because I judged that you could not grasp the mysteries of his divinity, I have spoken to you only of the weakness of his humanity.”

## CHAPTER VI.—Because the world did not know God through the wisdom of God, it pleased God to save those who believe through the foolishness of preaching (I Cor. I, 21).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, no. 1.) Our Lord [Col. 1310B] Jesus Christ, who is the power of God and is wisdom, born from the Father before the ages, could not be known by the human race in that birth. Therefore he came in humanity so that he might be seen; he wished to be seen so that he might be imitated.

This birth in the flesh appeared contemptible to the wise of the world. They despised the weakness of his humanity, judging these things unworthy of God, although humanity was all the more indebted to him because God accepted even unworthy things for humanity’s sake. To save humanity, he assumed the foolishness of preaching.

For it is written: “Because the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God to save those who believe in him through the foolishness of preaching.” The Word of God is wisdom. But his foolishness was called the flesh of the Word, so that, because all fleshly people could not reach the wisdom of God through the prudence of their flesh, they might be healed through the foolishness of preaching—that is, through the incarnation of the Word.

It is as though he said: “Since the world could not find God, who is wisdom, through its own wisdom, it pleased God that it should recognize God made human through the foolishness of humility [Col. 1310C], so that his wisdom might descend to our foolish things, and our blindness, illuminated by the clay of his flesh, might see the light of heavenly understanding.”

Therefore, born from the Father without time, he deigned to be born from his mother in time.

## CHAPTER VII.—What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings (I Cor. I, 2).

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XX, no. 41; book IV, no. 71.) Within the holy Church, those who despise the wisdom of the flesh and the foolish wisdom of the world, and who eagerly desire and seek the foolishness of God, which is wise and profitable for them, are called fools—but nevertheless they are noble. For it is written: “What is foolish in God is wiser than men.” Paul admonishes us to grasp this foolishness when he says: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise” (1 Cor. III, 18).

Those who followed this foolishness perfectly deserved to hear the voice of Wisdom: “You who have followed me, in the renewal, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28). Behold: by abandoning temporal things, they purchased the glory of eternal power. What, then, is more foolish in this world than to abandon one’s own possessions? And what is nobler in eternity than to come as judges with God?

The nobility of these judges is recalled with Solomon as witness when it is said, in the passage already mentioned: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. XXXI, 23). He considers them exceedingly noble, for he calls them elders. Paul had perceived this nobility in himself when, joined to the knowledge of the Creator through the Spirit, he said: “Since, then, we are the offspring of God, we ought not to suppose that the divine nature is like gold, silver, or stone, the product of human art and imagination” (Acts XVII, 29).

We are called the offspring of God—not because we were brought forth from his nature, but because we were created by his Spirit and, through adoption, restored to life. Each person is raised to this nobility in proportion as, through the image he has received, he is renewed into God’s likeness by imitation.

On the other hand, those are foolish and ignoble who flee from heavenly wisdom by following themselves. They lie dormant in their ignorance as though in the degradation of an outcast offspring; and because they do not understand the purpose for which they were created, they also lose the kinship of the nobility they received through the image.
