Foolish and ignoble are those whom slavery of mind excludes from sharing in the eternal inheritance.

For it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII, 34). Indeed, whoever submits himself to an evil desire places the formerly free neck of his mind beneath the dominion of iniquity. But we oppose this dominion when we resist the iniquity that had taken us captive, when we withstand violent habit, and, trampling upon perverse desires, assert against it the right of our innate freedom—when we strike down guilt through repentance and wash away the stains of uncleanness with tears.

Moreover, concerning the foolish and ignoble, the outstanding preacher says: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. III, 19). Therefore those who, while savoring earthly things, have been rejected from their inward nobility are both foolish and ignoble before God.

## CHAPTER VIII — “God chose the foolish things of the world” (1 Cor. I, 27)

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXI, no. 1; book I, no. 25; book XXXI, no. 1.) In paradise, the devil, envying a sound man, inflicted upon him the wound of pride, so that the one who had been created without having received death might, through exaltation, deserve it. Against this wound inflicted by pride, the medicine of God’s humility appeared among human beings, so that those who had fallen through imitation of the enemy might rise through the example of their Creator’s humility.

Against the proud devil, therefore, God appeared among human beings as a humble man: God made man. Coming for our redemption and sending his preachers against the pride of the world, he chose the foolish instead of the wise, the weak instead of the strong, and the poor instead of the rich. For the foolish of the world were first gathered to the knowledge of faith, so that afterward its shrewd ones too might be called, as Paul attests when he says: “Not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world, to confound the wise” (1 Cor. I).

The beginnings of the holy Church are said to have been unlearned in letters, so that the Redeemer might show all his preachers that it is not speech but the cause that persuades believing peoples unto life.

Moreover, “God chose the weak things of the world, to confound the strong” (1 Cor. I, 27); and it came about that the poor accomplished what the proud rich afterward marveled at. For when they saw new virtues in the poor, they were subsequently astonished at the miracles of those whose life they had previously despised. Thus, soon returning fearfully to their senses, they came to dread the holiness manifested in miracles, which they had despised in commandments. Through the weak, therefore, the strong were confounded, because as the life of the humble rose into veneration, the pride of the arrogant fell.

## CHAPTER IX — “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal?” (1 Cor. III, 3)

[Col. 1311D]

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXIV, no. 42.) Often righteous preachers, with a certain becoming moderation, disclose their faults before their disciples, so that those who hear them may learn how to reprove themselves subtly for their own actions. They regulate themselves with such careful discipline that, when they elevate themselves inwardly, they are not harsh, nor, when they humble themselves, are they lax outwardly; for they preserve humility in discipline and discipline in humility.

Paul maintained discipline when he said to the Corinthians: “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal and walking according to man?” But he did not lose this humility within discipline, because he prefaced his words with a plea, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, through the mercy of God, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you” (1 Cor. I, 10).

Again, he maintained humility when, speaking to the same Corinthians, he reproved himself—perhaps more extensively than he had intended—saying: “I have become foolish” (2 Cor. XII, 11). Yet he did not lose discipline in this humility, for he immediately added: “You compelled me” (2 Cor. IV, 5).

He displayed an example of great humility when he said to his disciples: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord; and ourselves as your servants through Christ” (2 Cor. IV, 5). Yet in this humility he did not lose the justice of discipline, for he says to those same offenders: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” and so forth.

Holy preachers therefore know how to temper the art of teaching with both forms of moderation. When they discover the guilt of offenders, they know at one time to rebuke severely and at another to plead humbly. Yet when, prompted by justice, they correct them severely, they do not lose the grace of inward sweetness and charity toward them. They burn with love for those against whom they rage with harsh correction, and inwardly, in the secret of their hearts, they humble themselves before those whom they chastise outwardly with the hard goads of reprimand, as though despising them.

Often, too, they despise without despising, and despair without despairing, so that they may make them return and spring back from their guilt all the more quickly by displaying, as though it were already near, the pit of death.

## CHAPTER X — “I planted, Apollos watered” (1 Cor. III, 6)

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXVII, no. 43; book XVII, no. 27.) The Lord makes his preachers and teachers resound outwardly with his voice, but inwardly he himself illuminates the hearts of those who hear, as Paul attests when he says: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.”

Teachers should therefore by no means attribute to themselves the fact that, through their exhortation, they see their hearers advance toward higher things. For unless the Holy Spirit fills their hearts, the voice of teachers sounds uselessly in bodily ears. They can form the teacher’s voice outwardly, but they cannot cause it to be expressed inwardly.

Yet amid these things it must be understood that we sometimes humbly assist even God, who is not weak. Hence Paul says: “For we are God’s assistants” (1 Cor. III, 9). When we join by the voice of exhortation with him whom God himself fills through inward grace, we assist outwardly, through the ministry of the voice, what he accomplishes inwardly through the Holy Spirit.

Our exhortation is brought to perfection only when God is in the heart to assist. Hence Paul also says: “Neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (ibid., 7). To plant and to water is to assist; both forms of ministry will be empty if God does not give the growth in the heart.

But those who think lofty thoughts from their own understanding do not wish humbly to be God’s assistants, because, while they consider themselves useful to God, they estrange themselves from the fruit of usefulness. Hence the voice of Truth says to the disciples: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke XVII, 10).

## CHAPTER XI — “No one can lay another foundation” (1 Cor. III, 11)

[Col. 1312D]

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXVIII, no. 14.) In sacred Scripture, preachers are understood by “foundations.” Hence the prophet David, when he saw that the holy Church was established and built upon the exalted minds of the apostles, said: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1).

But when sacred discourse speaks not of foundations in the plural but of “the foundation” in the singular, no one other than the Lord himself is signified. Through the power of his divinity, the wavering hearts of our weakness are made firm. Concerning him Paul says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.” He himself is the foundation of foundations, because he is both the beginning of those who commence and the steadfastness of those who are strong.

## CHAPTER XII — “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold and silver,” etc. (1 Cor. III, 12)

(*Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 39.) We must believe that, before judgment, there is a purifying fire for certain light faults, because Truth says: “If anyone speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” In this statement it is made clear that certain faults can be remitted in this age and certain others in the age to come. Since one kind is denied, the corresponding inference is evident: some other kinds are permitted.

Nevertheless, as I have said, this should be understood as applying to small and very minor sins, such as persistent idle talk, immoderate laughter, or the sin involved in managing household affairs—which scarcely anyone, even those who know how they ought to avoid sin, can carry out without fault—or an error of ignorance in matters that are not serious. All these things continue to burden a person even after death if they have not been remitted while he still remained in this life.

For when Paul says that Christ is the foundation and adds: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is. If anyone’s work that he built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire”—although this may be understood of the fire of tribulation applied to us in this life, nevertheless, if anyone accepts it as referring to the fire of future purification, it must be carefully considered that Paul says he can be saved through fire who builds upon this foundation not iron, bronze, or lead—that is, greater sins, which are consequently more severe and by then insoluble—but wood, hay, and straw, that is, the smallest and lightest sins, which the fire can easily consume.

This, however, must be understood: there no one will obtain purification even from the smallest faults unless, while still in this life, he earns through good works the right to obtain it there.

## CHAPTER XIII — “I will catch the wise in their craftiness” (1 Cor. III, 19)

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book V, no. 27; book VI, no. 2.) I see that it must be asked why Paul uses the statements of the friends of blessed Job with such authority, if their statements are annulled by the Lord’s rebuke, when it is said: “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” (Job XXXII, 7).

The words are Eliphaz’s that Paul brought to the Corinthians, saying, as it is written: “I will catch the wise in their craftiness.” How, then, shall we reject as wrong what Paul establishes on authority? Or how shall we regard as right, on Paul’s testimony, what the Lord himself declared to be wrong?

We recognize more readily that these two things are not contradictory if we weigh more carefully the words of that same divine judgment. For when he said, “You have not spoken rightly before me,” he immediately added, “as my servant Job has.” It is therefore clear that some things they say are right, but that they are surpassed by comparison with what is better.

For among the many irrational things they say, they utter many strong statements to blessed Job. But when compared with stronger statements, they lose the force of their strength. Many of the things they say are remarkable, except that they are spoken against the holy man. In themselves they are great, but because they seek to pierce the righteous man, they lose the weight of their greatness. Even a very strong spear, when thrown against hard rocks, is useless; the more forcefully it is hurled, the farther it rebounds blunted.

Thus, although the sayings of blessed Job’s friends are in some respects very strong, when they strike against the strong life of the holy man, they blunt the entire edge of their sharpness. Since they are great in themselves but should by no means have been employed against blessed Job, Paul, weighing them for their strength, brings them forward with authority; while the Judge, because they were uttered rashly, rebukes them in view of the dignity of the person against whom they were spoken.

We therefore do not reject the friends of blessed Job in all respects in their statements, since when the heavenly judgment is spoken against them—“You have not spoken rightly before me” (Job XLII, 7)—it immediately adds, “as my servant Job has.” It is plainly evident that what is rejected by comparison with the better is not wholly despised.

They go astray, however, in their rebuke because they speak rashly. Nevertheless, because they are friends of so great a man, they learned many things of a mystical kind from their association with him. Hence, as we have said, Paul also uses their words, taking them as support for his own assertion and testifying that they were spoken from the Truth. Yet the Truth rightly rebukes them, because however strong a statement may be, it should not have been brought forward against a holy man.

## CHAPTER XIV — “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day” (1 Cor. IV, 3)

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book V, nos. 21 and 56; and book I of the *Commentary on Ezekiel*, homily 9, no. 14.) The righteous, fearing not human judgments but the examination of the eternal Judge, regard with contempt not only the evils that the reprobate and perverse inflict upon them, but also the words of those who disparage their actions.

Thus Paul said to the Corinthians who were disparaging him: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day.” Finding nothing even in his own heart by which he could reprove himself, he added: “But I do not even judge myself; for I am conscious of nothing against myself.” Yet seeing that his own judgment was insufficient for the perfection of holiness, he added: “But I am not thereby justified.”

He explained why he was not justified and why he did not trust his own judgment about himself when he continued: “He who judges me is the Lord.” It was as though he were saying openly: “I remember that I have acted rightly, yet I do not presume upon my merits.” For precisely because I am conscious of nothing against myself, I refuse to declare myself justified, nor do I think that my own judgment concerning me should be trusted, since I am brought before the examination of one whose judgment I cannot comprehend, and I know that I shall be examined by him who will judge me more subtly.

Often our righteousness, brought before the examination of divine justice, is unrighteousness; and what shines in the estimation of the one who acts is filthy in the strict judgment of the Judge. Contemplating, therefore, the strictness of divine justice, we must fear even concerning those works that we consider strong and holy. For when our rectitude is brought to the eternal standard, if it encounters a strict judgment, it strikes against inward rectitude with the many crooked folds of its apparent uprightness.

Blessed Job also, when he suffered the arrows of words amid the pain of his wounds, hurled through the tongues of his disparaging friends, immediately returned in thought to his conscience. He looked to see where his mind stood alone and said: “For behold, my witness is in heaven, and my confidant is on high” (Job XVI, 20). He added: “My verbose friends—my eye drips tears to God” (ibid., v. 21).

Blessed Job, standing with his mind bowed amid the tongues of those who disparaged him, saw that he was attacked on earth by false words and therefore sought a witness in heaven. In everything that is said about us, therefore, we should always return silently to the mind, seeking the inner witness and judge. It is of no benefit if everyone praises us while conscience accuses us; and it can do no harm if everyone disparages us while conscience alone defends us.

## CHAPTER XV — “Fornication is heard of among you” (1 Cor. V, 1)

[Col. 1314D]

(*Pastoral Care*, part III, chapter 8.) Sometimes insolent people, when corrected and aware that they have not committed the fault in question, can be brought more quickly to correction if they are shamed by the reproach of another more evident fault, sought out from elsewhere, so that from what they cannot defend they may recognize the wickedness of what they are defending.

Thus, when Paul saw the Corinthians insolently puffed up against one another—one saying that he belonged to Apollos, another to Paul, another to Cephas, another to Christ—he brought forward the incestuous offense that had both been committed among them and remained uncorrected, saying: “Fornication is heard of among you, and such fornication as does not occur even among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst?”

It was as though he were saying openly: “Why do you insolently claim to belong to this or that person, when through the dissolution of negligence you show yourselves to belong to no one?” We correct insolent people more effectively when we show that those things they believe they have done well were done badly, so that useful shame may follow from the very source from which glory is believed to have been gained.

## CHAPTER XVI — “If you have secular judgments” (1 Cor. VI, 4)

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XIX, no. 42; *Pastoral Care*, part II, chapter 2.) Subordinates should attend to lower matters, while rulers should think upon higher things, so that the eye appointed to watch over the steps may not be obscured by concern for dust. All who preside are, as it were, the head of those subject to them; and so that the feet may be able to take the right paths, the head must undoubtedly survey them from above. Otherwise, when the head bends itself toward the earth with the body’s uprightness bent down, the feet grow sluggish on the path of their progress.

Hence Moses, who spoke with God, was judged by the reproach of Jethro, a foreigner, because he devoted himself through foolish labor to the earthly affairs of the people (Exod. XVIII). He was soon given the counsel to appoint others in his place to settle disputes, so that he himself might more freely learn the mysteries of spiritual instruction for the people.

Hence Paul, by his admonition—and indeed by his injunction—restrains the minds of religious people from association with the world, saying: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. II, 4).

Hence he both commands the rulers of the Church to devote themselves to leisure for study and points out a remedy for dealing with affairs, saying: “If, then, you have secular judgments, appoint as judges those who are contemptible in the Church” (1 Cor. VI, 4–5), so that those whom spiritual gifts do not adorn may serve in earthly administration.

It is as though he were saying more openly: “Let those who have lesser merit in the Church, and who possess none of the powers of great gifts, judge earthly matters, so that the lesser goods may be supplied by those who cannot accomplish great things. Since they cannot penetrate inward things, let them at least perform outward necessities.”

He calls them contemptible, yet calls them wise when he says: “Is there no one wise among you who can judge between his brothers?” What, then, is gathered from this except that those who have acquired wisdom in external matters should examine earthly cases? But those who have been enriched with spiritual gifts certainly ought not to be entangled in earthly affairs, so that, while they are not compelled to arrange lesser goods, they may be practiced in serving higher goods.

For it must be understood that sometimes lesser goods must be neglected in our actions for the sake of the usefulness of greater ones. Who does not know that burying the dead is a good work deserving merit? Yet when one man asked to be allowed to bury his father, he was told: “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you go and announce the kingdom of God” (Luke IX, 60).

The service of this duty had to be placed after the office of preaching, because the former would bury men dead in the flesh in the earth, while the latter would raise men dead in soul to life.

Yet amid these things it must be understood that when there is no one suitably able to serve the external needs of one’s neighbors, those who are full of spiritual goods must also condescend to their weakness and, insofar as they can appropriately do so, serve their earthly needs with charitable condescension.

The mind should not be wearied if, always intent upon the contemplation of spiritual things, it is sometimes bent down, as though diminished, to administer small matters. For the Word through whom all created things endure, in order to benefit human beings, assumed humanity and willed to be made a little lower than the angels. What wonder, then, if a human being brings himself down for the sake of another human being, when the Creator of human beings and angels assumed the form of a human being for the sake of human beings (Heb. II)?

The mind is not thereby diminished when it is thus drawn down, because the more subtly it penetrates higher things, the more humbly, for love of the Creator, it refuses to despise lower things.

## CHAPTER XVII — “Why do you not rather suffer wrong?” (1 Cor. VI, 7)

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXI, nos. 21 and 24.) The apostle Paul, wishing his disciples to despise external things so that they might preserve inward things, admonishes them, saying: “It is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather endure it?”

Yet the hypocrite, having assumed the appearance of holy conduct, abandons the care of his children and seeks even through quarrels to defend whatever is temporal. Loving earthly things more than heavenly ones, he inflames himself with savage hatred inwardly against the one who takes away temporal possessions.

It must be understood, however, that there are some whom Mother Church, nourishing them in the bosom of charity, tolerates until she brings them to the growth of spiritual maturity. Sometimes they maintain the appearance of holiness but cannot carry out the merit of perfection. They do not rise to spiritual gifts and therefore serve those joined to them in protecting earthly possessions; sometimes they exceed the bounds of defense through anger.

We should not believe that such people belong to the number of hypocrites, because it is one thing to sin through weakness and another to sin through malice.

The difference between these people and hypocrites is this: the former, according to the measure of their understanding, serve God’s causes even in worldly matters, whereas the latter serve the purposes of the world under the pretense of serving God’s causes. For even amid the holy works they appear to perform, the latter do not seek conversion in others but the breezes of human favor. The former do not fear displeasing wicked people even through a good action, provided they please only the heavenly judgments; the latter never consider what they are doing, but only how they may please people through whatever action they undertake.

Therefore, when we see men of respectable conduct angrily or excessively defending earthly things, we ought to reprove this in them through charity, yet we must not despair of them when reproving them. For often, in one and the same person, there are both certain visible faults that deserve judgment and great things that remain hidden; while in us, great things often appear openly, and what deserves reproof is sometimes concealed.

Our mind’s pride must therefore be humbled: their weaknesses are public, while ours are secret; and, conversely, their strengths are hidden, while ours are displayed publicly. When we reprove them for open weakness, it remains for us to honor them in recognition of their hidden strength. And if our mind rises up because of our own visible weakness, let it press itself down in humility by considering its hidden faults.

## CHAPTER XVIII — “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient” (1 Cor. VI, 12)

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book V, no. 17.) Often those who possess power, because they do not know how to restrain themselves even from lawful things, fall into unlawful and disorderly actions. No one avoids falling into unlawful things except the person who sometimes carefully restrains himself even from lawful things.

Paul shows that he was bound by this restraint when he says: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient.” And, to show through this very restraint how freely his mind ranged, he immediately added: “All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything.”

When the mind follows desires it has conceived, it is shown to serve the things by whose love it has been overcome. But Paul, for whom all things were lawful, brought himself under the power of nothing, because by restraining himself even from lawful things he rose above, as despised, those things that had given him pleasure and oppressed him.

## CHAPTER XIX — “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Cor. VII, 2)

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXII, no. 19 and following; and *Pastoral Care*, part III, chapter 27.) When the mind is constrained between lesser and greater sins, if no path of escape entirely without sin is open, the lesser things should always be chosen. For when someone is enclosed on every side by walls and cannot escape, he flees wherever he finds the shorter wall.

Thus Paul, when he saw that some in the Church were incontinent, permitted lesser things so that they might avoid greater ones. As a physician skilled in heavenly medicine, he did not so much instruct the healthy as show remedies to the weak, saying: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (1 Cor. VII, 1–2).

By prefacing his words with the fear of fornication, he plainly did not give a command to those who were standing firm, but showed a bed to those who might perhaps fall to the ground, lest they should fall. Hence he adds to those who are still weak: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.”

And because married partners are free of fault in intercourse only when they unite not to satisfy lust but to receive offspring, he showed that even what he had permitted was not entirely without fault, however slight. After granting something of pleasure within the great honor of marriage, he immediately added: “But I say this by way of concession, not by way of command” (ibid., v. 6).

What is forgiven but not commanded is not without fault. He clearly saw a sin in what he foresaw could be forgiven. For what is said to be forgiven is thereby indicated to be a fault, though one that is all the sooner released because no unlawful act is committed through it, but what is lawful is not maintained with due moderation.

Married partners must know that they were joined for the sake of receiving offspring. When, by serving immoderate intercourse, they turn the means of procreation into an instrument of pleasure, they should consider that, although they do not go beyond the bounds of marriage, they nevertheless overstep the rights of marriage within marriage itself.

They must therefore lament in frequent prayers the fact that, by mingling pleasures with it, they defile the beautiful appearance of marital union.

But when we are constrained by doubtful matters, we rightly submit to lesser things, lest we sin in greater matters without pardon. Thus the strategy of the ancient enemy is often undone when one advances to the greatest virtues through the commission of lesser things.

## CHAPTER XX — “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. VII, 9)

(*Pastoral Care*, part III, chapter 27; in the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XII, no. 27; *Pastoral Care*, part II, chapter 5.) Those who are not bound by marriage should by no means suppose that they can mingle with unmarried women without fear of condemnation.

When Paul inserted the vice of fornication among so many abominable crimes, he indicated its guilt, saying: “Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. VI, 9 and following).

If, then, they endure the storms of temptation with difficulty and at the risk of salvation, let them seek the harbor of marriage. For it is written: “It is better to marry than to burn.” They come to marriage without guilt, provided that they have not already vowed something better. For whoever has resolved to undertake a greater good makes the lesser good unlawful for himself.

It is written: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX, 62). Therefore, whoever had been intent upon a stronger course of discipline is shown to look back if, abandoning greater goods, he turns back toward lesser ones (1 Cor. VII, 28).

“Such people will have tribulation in the flesh.” Those who live spiritually can also suffer tribulation in the flesh. Why, then, is tribulation of the flesh said to exist in married people as though it were something spiritual, when it is known not to be absent even from the life of spiritual people? It is because those who delight in and devote themselves to the pleasures of the flesh frequently receive greater tribulations from the flesh.

Pastors and rulers should also consider that Paul, who was taken up into paradise and examined the secrets of the third heaven, nevertheless, while suspended in contemplation of invisible things, brings the gaze of his mind back to the bed of carnal people and administers instruction concerning how they ought to conduct themselves in their hidden relations, saying: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (2 Cor. XII, 3). And shortly afterward: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (ibid., v. 5). And again: “Return to the same union” (ibid.).

Behold, he is already incorporated into heavenly secrets, yet through the entrails of condescension he examines the bed of carnal people. The one whom, lifted up, he raises to invisible things, he mercifully bends the eye of his heart toward the hidden matters of the weak.

He transcends heaven through contemplation, yet does not abandon the condition of carnal people through concern for them. Likewise, rulers and teachers who seek lofty things through profound contemplation should not despise the weaknesses of their neighbors; nor, while accommodating themselves to the weaknesses of their neighbors, should they abandon lofty things.

## CHAPTER XXI — “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord” (1 Cor. VII, 25)

(In the *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XV, no. 22; book XVI, no. 10.) Those chosen people who are practiced in good works sometimes strive to do more than the Lord has deigned to command them. For bodily virginity was by no means commanded, but merely praised. If it were owed as a duty, marriage would already be considered a fault.

Nevertheless, many are distinguished by the virtue of virginity, so that they may offer more in service than they have received in commandment.

It must also be understood that there are certain heretics who devote themselves so zealously to bodily virginity that they condemn marriage. There are likewise some who praise abstinence so excessively that they detest those who consume necessary food. Concerning them Paul writes: “Those who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful” (1 Tim. IV, 3).

## CHAPTER XXII — “Those who have wives should be as though they had none” (1 Cor. VII, 29)

[Col. 1318B]

(Care of Pastors, part 3, chapter 27.) Few are given to leave everything, set aside the cares of the world, and yearn only for eternal desires. Therefore, brothers, we do not dare tell you to leave everything; nevertheless, if you wish, you may leave everything even while retaining everything, if you handle temporal matters in such a way that with your whole mind you still strive toward eternal things.

Hence the Apostle Paul says: “The time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep, as though they did not weep; those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice; those who buy, as though they did not possess; and those who use this world, as though they did not use it; for the form of this world is passing away.” The man who has a wife but is as though he did not have one is he who, seeing that all things are transitory, endures the care of the flesh from necessity but awaits the eternal joys of the spirit from desire; he knows how to discharge the obligations of the flesh without thereby being compelled to cling to the world with his whole mind.

For when the same outstanding preacher again says, [Col. 1318C] “He who has a wife thinks about the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (I Cor. VII, 33), that man has a wife as though he did not have one who strives to please his spouse without displeasing his Creator; who uses her for carnal consolation in such a way that her love never bends him from the uprightness of a better purpose toward evil works.

He also weeps but is as though he did not weep who is afflicted by temporal losses in such a way that he always consoles his mind with regard to eternal gains. To weep without weeping is to lament outward adversities while nevertheless knowing how to rejoice in the consolation of eternal hope.

He rejoices, but is as though he did not rejoice, who takes pleasure in temporal goods while continually considering everlasting torments; and, while joy lifts his mind, immediately presses it down with the weight of prudent fear.

He buys, but is as though he did not possess, who prepares earthly things for use while cautiously foreseeing that he will soon leave them behind.

He uses the world with a pure heart, but as though he did not use it, who brings all necessary things outwardly into the service of his life, yet does not allow these same things [Col. 1318D] to rule his mind, so that what is subject serves outwardly and never breaks the purpose of the mind striving toward higher things. There he also plainly adds: “For the form of this world is passing away” (Ibid., v. 31), as though he were openly saying: “Do not love the world steadfastly, since even it cannot remain—the world that you love. In vain do you fix your heart as though upon things that remain, while the very object of your love is fleeing.”

Those, therefore, whom necessity binds to this world, so that they cannot be stripped of the world in every respect, ought to hold the things of the world in such a way that they do not know how to succumb to them through the breaking of their minds. And when they cannot leave everything that belongs to the world, they will act well outwardly if inwardly they hasten fervently toward eternal things.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### “But he who is with a wife thinks about the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (I Cor. VII, 33)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXVI, no. 44.) In the conduct [Col. 1319A] of mortal life, some things are harmful in themselves, while others become harmful through what surrounds them. Some things are harmful in themselves, such as sins and crimes; others sometimes harm us through what surrounds them, such as temporal power or marital union. Marriage itself is good, but the things that arise around it from care for this world are evil.

Therefore Paul, persuading certain people toward what is better, calls them away from marriage, saying: “I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but for what is honorable and what may enable you to serve the Lord without impediment” (Ibid., v. 35). Thus, while what is not harmful is retained, what is harmful is often committed through the things placed nearby. It is as when we travel along a straight road through the world, yet are caught by our garments on thorns that have grown beside the way. We do not stumble on the clean road itself, but something grows at its side by which we are pricked.

Temporal power is also great, and before God it has its own merit [Col. 1319B] when government is administered well; yet sometimes, besides other evils, it swells with arrogance of thought precisely because it rises above others.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### “I say this for your benefit” (I Cor. VII, 35)

(*Care of Pastors*, part III, chapter 27.) When Paul was instructing certain people toward the grace of celibacy, he did not despise marriage; rather, he rejected the worldly cares arising from marriage, saying: “I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but for what is honorable and what may enable you to entreat the Lord without impediment.” Earthly anxieties arise from marriages, and therefore the teacher of the nations persuaded his hearers toward better things, so that they would not be bound by earthly concern. Thus the man whom the impediment of worldly cares hinders from celibacy, though he has not submitted himself to marriage, has nevertheless not escaped the burdens of marriage.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (I Cor. VIII, 1)

[Col. 1319C] (*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book VIII, no. 72.) The mind of hypocrites, occupied with outward desires, is not warmed by the fire of divine love. Therefore they cannot inflame their hearers toward heavenly desire, because they speak words from a cold heart. A thing that has not itself burned cannot set others aflame.

Consequently, the sayings of hypocrites often neither instruct their hearers nor make those very men who utter them better; instead, being puffed up by praise, they make them worse. For Paul testifies: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” When love does not raise a person by building him up, knowledge perverts him by puffing him up.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he has not yet known how he ought to know” (I Cor. VIII, 2)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXVII, no. 62; book XXVIII, chapter 3.) Perfect knowledge is to live in this world while possessing nothing of the desire for this world; not to covet what belongs to others; not to cling to what is one’s own; to despise the praises of the world; to love reproaches for God’s sake; to flee the world’s glory; [Col. 1319D] to pursue contempt; to despise flatterers; to honor those who despise; to dismiss from the heart the evils of those who do harm; and to retain immovable in the heart the grace of love toward them.

Perfect knowledge is diligently to practice all these things and to know that one is nothing because of one’s own merits. Thus the Lord’s disciples themselves are taught this perfect knowledge when the Voice of Truth says to them: “When you have done all these things that have been commanded you, say: ‘We are useless servants’” (Luke XVII, 10).

Perfect knowledge is to know everything and yet, in a certain sense, not to know oneself to be learned. Of this Paul rightly says: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he has not yet known how he ought to know.” Therefore, while we live in this world, we know perfectly what must be known when, advancing in understanding, we recognize that we know nothing perfectly.

Since the first folly of the angel was pride of heart, the true wisdom of a human being is humility concerning his own estimation. Whoever abandons this humility through thinking himself wise in great matters [Col. 1320A] is all the more foolish because he does not know himself.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### “See to it that your freedom does not become a stumbling-block to the weak” (I Cor. VIII, 9)

(*Care of Pastors*, part III, chapter 35.) When a wrongful opinion, insofar as it can exist without sin, is not removed from the minds of those who observe, an example offers guilt to all who believe evil. Thus it often happens that those who carelessly allow others to think badly of them commit no wrongdoing themselves, yet through those who imitate them they cause sins to multiply.

Therefore Paul says not to those who eat certain clean foods without pollution, but to the imperfect, who through this eating of theirs provoke the scandal of temptation: “See to it that perhaps this freedom of yours does not become a stumbling-block to the weak.” And again: “The weak brother will perish because of your knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died.” Thus, by sinning against the brothers and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (I Cor. IX, 11)

[Col. 1320B]

(*Homily 17 on the Gospels*, no. 7.) It is fitting that preachers receive earthly support from those to whom they offer the rewards of the heavenly homeland, because, as the Wisdom of God itself says: “The laborer is worthy of his wage” (Luke X, 7).

The very provisions that sustain life are already the wage of the work, so that here the reward for the labor of preaching begins, while there it is perfected through the vision of truth. In this matter it must be considered that two rewards are owed for one work of ours: one on the way, the other in the homeland; one that sustains us in our labor, the other that rewards us in the resurrection.

The reward received in the present must act in us so that we may strive more vigorously toward the next reward. Therefore a true preacher should not preach in order to receive a reward in this present time; rather, he should receive a reward in order to continue preaching.

Whoever preaches in order to receive here the reward either of praise or of [Col. 1320C] payment undoubtedly deprives himself of the eternal reward. But whoever desires what he says to please people for this reason—that, while what is said pleases, the Lord rather than the speaker himself may be loved—or whoever receives earthly support for preaching so that he will not be exhausted by lack and cease from preaching, for him nothing undoubtedly prevents the reception of a reward in the homeland because of the expenses he incurred on the way.

Thus, accepting these expenses from the Corinthians to whom Paul preached as a very small matter, he says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?”

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### “I became as a Jew to the Jews, that I might win the Jews” (I Cor. IX, 20)

(*Care of Pastors*, part II, chapter 5; *In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book VI, no. 54.) A ruler ought to be lifted above all others by contemplation and near to each person through compassion, so that by the height of contemplation he may transcend even himself in desiring invisible things, and through the inward organs of pity may transfer the weakness of others into himself. [Col. 1320D]

Hence blessed Paul, joined by the bond of love to both the highest and the lowest, is at once carried upward in himself by the power of the spirit soaring toward higher things, and in others is compassionately weakened with equanimity, saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (II Cor. XI, 29).

Again he says: “I became as a Jew to the Jews, that I might win the Jews; and to those who are under the law, as though I were under the law (although I myself was not under the law), that I might win those who were under the law; and to those who are without the law, as though I were without the law (although I was not without the law of God, but was under the law of Christ), that I might win those who were without the law.” A little later: “I have become all things to all people, that I might save all.”

He did this not by abandoning faith but by extending compassion: taking upon himself the person of unbelievers, he learned from himself how he ought to have mercy on others, so that he might bestow upon them what he himself, if he were in their condition, would rightly wish to have bestowed upon him.

For the outstanding preacher did not erupt into treachery in order to become as a Jew; nor did he return to carnal sacrifice in order to be as one under the law; nor, in order to become all things to all people, did he change simplicity of mind into a variety of error. Rather, by condescending he drew near to unbelievers, not by falling; so that, receiving each person into himself and transforming himself into each person, he might gather them through compassion: if he himself were as they were, he would rightly wish others to bestow upon him what he bestowed upon them; and he would come to the aid of each person who was wandering all the more truly because he had learned from his own reflection the way to that person’s salvation. [Col. 1321A]

Again he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (II Cor. V, 13), because he knew how to transcend himself in contemplation and to temper that same self for his hearers by condescending to them.

## CHAPTER XXX  
### “So I run, not as uncertainly” (I Cor. IX, 26)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXX, no. 59.) Some lose everything they do courageously because the vice of gluttony [Col. 1321B] rules them. When the belly is not restrained, all the virtues are simultaneously overwhelmed by the desire of the flesh.

Therefore Paul was withdrawing strength from the prince of cooks—that is, the belly, which is served by cooks—who was fighting against the walls of Jerusalem and wished to destroy the virtues of the soul striving toward the vision of peace, when he said: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (I Cor. IX).

For this reason he had also said beforehand: “So I run, not as uncertainly; so I fight, not as one beating the air” (Ibid., 27). For when we restrain the flesh, by the very blows of our self-control we strike not the air but unclean spirits. And when we subject what is within us, we deliver blows against the adversaries stationed outside.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection” (I Cor. IX, 27)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXIX, nos. 32–33.) Every day we see many who shine with the light of righteousness and yet, at the end of their lives, are darkened [Col. 1321C] by the obscurity of wickedness. We also see many wrapped in the darkness of sins who, near the end of their lives, are suddenly restored to the freedom of the light of righteousness.

Thus it is said to some who have been converted from the wickedness of sins: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. V, 8). The name “light” signifies righteousness; through “darkness,” iniquity is designated.

We also know many who, having once found the way of righteousness, have kept it undefiled until death; and we have seen very many accumulate, without ceasing, the crimes they once began until their end. But amid these clouds of hidden judgments, who can send the ray of his mind so as to discern by any consideration whether someone will persevere in evil or remain in goodness; whether someone will turn from the lowest things to the highest, or return from the highest to the lowest?

These things are hidden from human understanding, and nothing concerning anyone’s end can be known, because the abyss of divine judgments cannot in any way be penetrated by the eye of the human mind. We see, indeed, that the pagan nation hostile to God has been filled with the light of righteousness, [Col. 1321D] while Judea, once beloved, has been blinded by the night of unbelief.

We also know that the thief passed from the cross to the kingdom, while Judas fell from the glory of apostleship into Tartarus. Again, since sometimes the lots that have begun do not change, we know that another thief reached punishment, and we know that the apostles received the kingdom they had desired and been appointed to attain.

Moreover, I see Paul called from that fury of persecution to the grace of apostleship; yet, amid hidden judgments, he fears so greatly that he fears he may be rejected even after he has been called. For he says: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (Acts IX, 15).

Certainly it had already been said of him by the Lord’s voice: “He is a vessel of election for me”; yet, still chastising his body, he fears that he may be rejected. Woe to us miserable people, who have not yet heard any word of God concerning our election, yet already grow sluggish in idleness as though secure!

There ought indeed to be security in hope and fear in one’s conduct, [Col. 1322A] so that the former may encourage those who are striving and the latter prick those who are sluggish. He presumes upon hope in vain who refuses to fear God in his works.

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXXI, no. 97.) In sacred Scripture, when “rock” is placed and named in the singular, whom other than Christ should we understand? Paul bears witness to this when he says: “The rock was Christ” (I Pet. II, 5).

But when rocks are called in the plural, his members are signified—namely, holy men who have been made firm by his strength. The Apostle Peter calls them stones, saying: “You, as living stones, are being built together into spiritual houses” (I Pet. II, 5).

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### “Do not become idolaters” (I Cor. X, 7)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book X, no. 21.) We act vainly whenever we think about transitory things. From vanity we are led [Col. 1322B] to iniquity when we first slide through slight offenses and, because habit smooths everything over, no longer fear afterward committing even graver offenses.

When the tongue neglects to restrain idle words, once seized by the customary habit of laxity it bursts forth boldly into harmful speech. When one devotes oneself to the appetite of the belly, one immediately proceeds to the madness of frivolity. And when the mind refuses to subdue the pleasure of the flesh, it often plunges into the abyss of unbelief.

Therefore Paul, observing the losses of the Israelite people, took care to recount in order what had happened, so as to restrain the evils threatening his hearers, saying: “Do not become idolaters, as some of them did, as it is written: ‘The people sat down to eat and drink, and they rose up to play’” (Exod. XXXII, 6).

Eating and drinking impelled them toward luxury; play dragged them toward idolatry. For if the fault of vanity is not carefully restrained, the unwary mind is immediately devoured by iniquity, as Solomon testifies when he says: “He who despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclus. XIX, 1). If we neglect to care about small matters, then, being led astray imperceptibly, [Col. 1322C] we also commit greater ones boldly.

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X, 12)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXV, nos. 20–21.) You must strive with utmost care to guard your heart with every form of vigilance, because from it life proceeds, and as it is written: “Out of the heart come evil thoughts” (Matt. XV, 18).

Let us therefore fear amid the good things we have received, and let us not despair of those who have not yet attained them. We know what we are today, but we do not know what we may shortly become. Those whom we perhaps despise may begin late and yet, through more fervent efforts, surpass our life.

It must therefore be feared that, even when we fall, someone may rise whom we mock while we stand; although one who does not know how to mock someone who is standing does not yet know how to stand. The Apostle Paul instills this fear of heavenly judgments into the hearts of the disciples when he says: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.”

The proud may [Col. 1322D] lose the good things of which they are proud, and the humble may receive those things which they are despised because they do not possess. We must therefore keep watch within; within, let us guard everything we do outwardly, lest, if the mind exalts itself, we fall.

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### “Let no temptation seize you except what is human” (I Cor. X, 13)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXI, no. 7, and *Care of Pastors*, part I, chapter 11, shortly before the end.) It must be understood that one thing is what the mind suffers from the temptation of the flesh, and another is what happens when it is bound by consent to pleasures.

Often the mind is struck by an evil thought but resists; often, however, when it conceives something perverse, it turns it over within itself even through desire. An unclean thought does not defile the mind when it strikes it, but when it subjugates it to itself through pleasure.

Hence the outstanding preacher says: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human.” It is human to suffer temptation in the heart; [Col. 1323A] it is demonic to be overcome by the contest of temptation and in action.

Human temptation is that by which we are often touched in thought even against our will, because the fact that unlawful things sometimes come to the mind is something we possess within ourselves through the burden of corruptible humanity. But it is demonic, and not human, temptation when the mind binds itself by consent to what it suggests in corruptible fashion.

Again he says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI, 12). He did not prohibit sin from existing in the mortal body, but from reigning there, because in corruptible flesh it can fail to reign, but it cannot fail to exist.

Indeed, even being tempted by sin is itself sin; and because, as long as we live, we are wholly without sin at no time, holy preaching, since it could not completely expel this, took away its kingdom from the dwelling-place of our heart, so that unlawful desire, although it often secretly inserts itself into our good thoughts like a thief, at least may not rule if it enters.

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear” (I Cor. X, 13)

[Col. 1323B]

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book IX, no. 71, and book XXIX, no. 35.) Since evil spirits cannot return to life, they cruelly seek companions for death. They therefore continually devise plans against the good, so that those whom they see serving God innocently in tranquility may, when harassed by adversities, be dragged into the abyss of guilt.

But the sharpness of their counsel is destroyed because the Creator first moderates the scourges according to their strength, lest punishment exceed strength and human weakness be overcome by the cunning of the mighty. Hence Paul rightly says: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; but with the temptation he will also provide a way of escape, so that you may be able to endure it.”

Our Creator knows when to allow the storm of persecution to rise and when to restrain what has risen. He knows how, for our protection, to restrict what he permits to go forth against us for our training, so that the raging storm may wash us but not drown us.

He knows how to regulate the temptations of the adversary by his providence, [Col. 1323C] so that many do not come at once, or so that only those temptations that can be endured touch the soul already illumined by God; thus, while they torment us with the burning of their touch, they do not consume us in the fire of perfection.

For unless merciful God moderates temptations together with the blows, no one could bear the snares of evil spirits without falling. If the Judge does not provide a measure for temptations, he immediately casts down the one who was standing precisely by placing burdens upon him beyond his strength.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### “If anyone seems to be contentious” (I Cor. XI, 16)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book VIII, no. 4.) Heretics do not strive to attain the truth through their inquiries, but to appear victorious. While they seek to display themselves outwardly as wise, inwardly they are bound by the chains of their own foolish pride.

Thus they seek out contests of disputation and do not know how to speak peacefully [Col. 1323D] about God, who is our peace; instead, from the business of peace they become inventors of quarrels. To them Paul rightly says: “If anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI, 31)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XII, no. 20; *Care of Pastors*, part III, chapter 29.) Who can measure the generosity of divine mercy? Almighty God carefully observes each and every evil and sin we have committed, yet through the grace of his kindness mercifully releases the repentant from them.

He sees hardness in sinners, yet by prevenient grace softens it toward repentance, and turns us to mourn each of the faults we have committed. He mercifully releases these faults because, while we punish them ourselves, he does not judge us for them at the final examination.

Sinners who lament the sins of their deeds ought therefore to presume upon the mercy they request, lest they perish through excessive severity of [Col. 1324A] affliction. The Lord would not mercifully set sins worthy of tears before the eyes of the guilty if he intended to strike them strictly by himself.

For it is clear that he wished to hide from his judgment those whom, in his mercy, he anticipated and made judges of themselves. Hence it is written: “Let us come before his face in confession” (Ps. XCIV, 2). Hence Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
### “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 6)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XI, no. 8; book XXVIII, no. 21; *On Ezekiel*, book II, homily 6, no. 2; *In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXVIII, nos. 21–25.) Almost no one is unaware that there are five senses of our body: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.

These senses draw from the brain the power of discernment and sensation for everything they perceive and distinguish. Although there is one judge of the brain—the sense that presides inwardly—through their own channels it distinguishes the five senses, God [Col. 1324B] working wondrously so that the eye does not hear, the ear does not see, the mouth does not smell, the nose does not taste, and the hand does not smell.

Although everything is arranged through the one sense of the brain, none of these senses can perform another’s function, except what it has received from the Creator’s arrangement. From these bodily and outward things, therefore, we must gather inward and spiritual things, so that through what is public in us we may pass to what is secret within us and hidden in ourselves.

We must observe that, although there is one Wisdom, it dwells in one person less and in another more, granting one person this and another that. And, as though after the manner of the brain, it uses us as certain senses, so that although it is never unlike itself, through us it always performs diverse and unlike works: one person receives the gift of wisdom, another of knowledge; one receives kinds of tongues, another the grace of healings.

Our almighty Creator and God, by the secret ordering of inward judgment, according to the words of blessed Paul, [Col. 1324C] grants “to one the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another complete faith, to another the grace of healings, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of words” (I Cor. XII, 8).

There are some who, through the gift of grace, understand even those things which they have not heard explained by teachers. These have received the word of wisdom. There are others who cannot understand by themselves what they have heard, but retain what they have read in commentators and knowingly produce what they have learned through reading. These are full of the word of knowledge.

Thus, in one and the same Spirit, one person is powerful in the word of wisdom but is not supported by the word of knowledge—that is, by teaching—because he is capable of perceiving and discovering even what he has not grasped through the labor of learning. Another shines in the word of knowledge but does not grow strong in the word of wisdom, because he is capable of completing what he has learned but does not rise by himself to perceive something subtle.

One person commands even the elements through faith but does not heal bodily illnesses [Col. 1324D] through the grace of healings. Another removes diseases through the aid of prayer but does not bring rain by his word upon parched earth.

One, through the working of miracles, even restores the dead to the present life, yet, lacking the grace of prophecy, does not know what is to come. Another regards future events as though they were present, yet does not exercise himself in any working of signs.

One, through discernment of spirits, subtly perceives minds in their deeds, but does not know different kinds of tongues. Another examines different kinds of tongues, but does not weigh dissimilar hearts in similar matters. Another prudently examines, by interpreting, the meanings of words in one language that he knows, yet patiently lacks the other good things that he does not possess.

Thus our Creator and Disposer orders everything, so that whoever might be lifted up by the good he possesses may be humbled by the virtue he lacks. He orders everything so that, while he raises each person up through an abundant gift, he also subjects one person to another through unequal gifts; and each person may recognize that the person subject to him is better in another gift, and, although he may feel that he surpasses others in one respect, may nevertheless place himself below the one whom he surpasses in another.

He orders everything so that, while each thing belongs to all through a certain intervening bond of love, everything becomes the possession of each individual; and each person possesses in another what he has not received himself, while humbly offering to another for possession what he has received. [Col. 1325A]

Hence Paul says: “Through love serve one another” (Gal. V, 13). Love frees us from the yoke of guilt when it subjects us to one another in loving service, when we believe another’s goods to be our own and offer our own things to others as though they were theirs.

Again the same Paul says: “The body is not one member, but many. [Col. 1325B] If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body,’ is it therefore not of the body? And if the ear should say, ‘Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body,’ is it therefore not of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If it were all hearing, where would smell be?” A little later: “If all were one member, where would the body be? But now there are many members, yet one body” (I Cor. XII, 14 ff.).

For what is the holy Church except the body of its heavenly Head? In it one person is an eye by seeing high things; another is a hand by doing what is right; another is a foot by running toward what has been commanded; another is an ear by understanding the voice of the commandments; another is a nose by discerning the stench of evils and the fragrance of good things.

Following the pattern of bodily members, while they mutually perform the duties entrusted to them, they make one body out of themselves all together. And while they perform diverse tasks in love, they prevent diversity from dividing the place in which they are contained.

But if all were to do one thing, they would not be a body, which is composed of many parts, because it would not exist as something joined together in many ways if this harmonious diversity of members did not hold it together.

The Lord therefore distributes gifts of virtues to the holy members of the Church, assigning them to each as he wills and, as it were, setting measures within boundaries for them. When, therefore, our Author and Disposer, by a marvelous plan, grants one person [Col. 1325C] what he denies to another and denies another what he grants to this one, whoever attempts to do more than he has received strives to exceed the measures set for him.

Perhaps the person to whom it has been given only to explain the hidden things of the commandments will attempt also to shine through miracles; or the person whom the gift of heavenly power strengthens for miracles alone will also strive to disclose the hidden things of divine law.

Often the person who rashly hastens to seize what he cannot attain loses what he possesses. We also use the services of our bodily members properly only when we preserve their distinct functions. We see light with our eyes, but hear a voice with our ears.

If someone, reversing the order, applies eyes to a voice and ears to light, both are open to him in vain. If someone wishes to distinguish smells with his mouth or taste flavors with his ear, he destroys the service of both senses because he has perverted them.

While these members are not adapted to their proper uses, they abandon their own functions and do not rise to foreign ones. Thus Paul rightly confined himself within the measures received from divine generosity, even in the breadth of his preaching, when he said: [Col. 1325D] “I do not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through me” (Rom. XV, 18).

Almighty God therefore imposes a measure upon our progress, so that we may possess certain good virtues which we never sought, and seek certain others without being able to possess them. In this way, while our mind cannot possess what it desires, it understands that of itself it does not possess even what it does possess; through the things that are present, the things that are absent are considered, and through the things that are usefully absent, the good things that are present are humbly preserved.

## CHAPTER XL  
### “Our unseemly members have greater honor” (I Cor. XII, 23)

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XIII, nos. 6–7.) When a powerful and insolent person is known to have committed something wrong, the preacher [Col. 1326A] waits for an appropriate time to rebuke him for the evil he has done. Unless the preacher waits until he can suitably deliver correction, he increases the evil he is pursuing, because it often happens that such a person will accept no words of rebuke.

The art of preaching must therefore be practiced with great skill, so that those who become worse through open correction may return to salvation through a certain moderation of correction. Hence Paul also says: “Those members of the body that we think less honorable, we surround with greater honor; and our unseemly members have greater honor, while our seemly members have no need of it.”

Just as there are unseemly members in the body, so within the holy Church there are certain powerful and insolent people who, because they cannot be struck by open denunciation, are, as it were, covered by a cloak of honor.

We are speaking here, however, of the hidden offenses of the powerful. For when they sin in ways recognized by others, they must also be rebuked before those who know, lest, if the preacher is silent, he appear to have approved the fault, and lest the growing fault become an example that the shepherd’s tongue does not cut away.

## CHAPTER XLI  
### “You are the body of Christ, and members from member” (I Cor. XII, 27)

[Col. 1326B]

(*In the exposition of Blessed Job*, book XXXIV, no. 8.) All who are joined to the reprobate when they act perversely are members of the reprobate, just as Paul says, by contrast, concerning the Lord’s body: “You are the body of Christ, and members from member.”

A member of the body is one thing, and a member of a member another. A member of the body is a part in relation to the whole; a member of a member is a portion in relation to a part. A member of a member is a finger in relation to the hand, and the hand in relation to the arm; but a member of the body is all these together in relation to the entire body.

Thus, in the spiritual body of the Lord, we call members from member those who are governed by others in his Church. Likewise, in the reprobate congregation of the ancient enemy, those who join themselves through wicked deeds to people even more wicked are members from members.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels” (I Cor. XIII, 1)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIV, nos. 29–30.) The ministers of Antichrist sometimes display the sweetness of their tongues in order to deceive their hearers, since thorns too produce flowers: what gives off a pleasant scent is indeed apparent in them, but what pricks lies hidden. They mix sweet things with bitter and soothing words with harmful ones; by the art of deception, through relaxed conversation and humble speech, they insinuate about themselves what they deny by their conduct. These men, plainly, have—as though they were insensible metal—the sound of speaking well, but they do not have the sense of living well; for, speaking as though humbly, they assert what by their proud way of life they despise. Hence Paul rightly says: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.” Speaking good things, but not pursuing those same good things through love, he gives back a sound like bronze or a cymbal, because he himself does not feel the words that he himself produces.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—“Charity is patient, it is kind” (I Cor. XIII, 4).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VIII, no. 2; Book X, no. 10.) In this battle of temptations, the mind of the saints, fortified by the shield of patience and girded with the swords of love, gathers strength to endure evils and displays kindness in returning good, so that it may powerfully receive the weapons of hatred and vigorously send back the darts of love. The soldier of God, caught in the war of adversity, must hold up the shield of patience lest he perish, and, ready for preaching, must launch the darts of love in order to conquer. Paul briefly indicates the sum of this armor when he says: “Charity is patient, it is kind.” When one of the two is lacking, charity is not present: if someone endures the wicked without kindness, he does not love them; or, again, if he shows himself without patience, he neglects to endure those whom he loves. Therefore, if true charity is to be maintained by us, it is necessary that patience support kindness, and, in turn, kindness support patience; so that, building a great structure in our heart, patience may strengthen the citadel of kindness, and kindness may adorn the buildings founded upon patience.

But although charity is one and the same, it is nevertheless called manifold, because, when it fully takes possession of the mind, it kindles it in many different ways for countless works. Paul rightly enumerates the variety and multiplicity of this charity, saying: “Charity is patient, it is kind; it does not envy, it is not puffed up, it does not act improperly; it is not ambitious, it does not seek what is its own, it is not provoked, it does not think evil, it does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth.”

Charity is patient because it endures injuries with equanimity. It is kind because it generously supplies good things in return for evils. It does not envy because, desiring nothing in the present world, it does not know how to envy earthly successes. It is not puffed up because, while it anxiously desires the reward of inward recompense, it does not exalt itself over external goods. It does not act improperly because, as it extends itself solely to the love of God and neighbor, it ignores whatever departs from uprightness. It is not ambitious because, as it ardently strives inwardly for what is its own, it in no way covets what belongs to others outwardly. It does not seek what is its own because it disregards as alien whatever it possesses here temporarily, recognizing that nothing is properly its own except what remains with it. It is not provoked because, even when challenged by injuries, it does not rouse itself to any movement of revenge, while it awaits greater rewards after great labors. It does not think evil because, strengthening the mind in the love of purity and uprooting all hatred from its roots, it does not know how to turn over in the mind what defiles it. It does not rejoice over iniquity because, longing only through love for everyone, it does not exult over the destruction of those who oppose it. But it rejoices with the truth because, loving others as it loves itself, it rejoices as though at an increase of its own progress whenever it sees what is right in others.

Thus manifold charity confronts, with the protection of its instruction, the dart of each individual fault that attacks the mind in order to destroy it. Since the ancient enemy surrounds us with varied assaults, charity itself fights him off from us in many ways. Charity in Peter both resisted strongly the threats of rulers who terrified him and humbly listened to the words of the lesser brethren concerning the removal of circumcision. Charity in Paul both humbly endured the hands of his persecutors and yet, in the matter of circumcision, boldly rebuked the opinion of his predecessor, who was far his inferior.

### CHAPTER XLIV.—“Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XVII, no. 38.) It is fitting that the one who preaches should consider the capacity of the hearer, so that the preaching itself may grow along with the progress of its hearer. Every preacher ought to act in this way, just as God deals with him, so that he may by no means disclose to the weak everything that he himself understands; for, so long as he himself is weak in mortal flesh, he too does not understand everything that is above. A preacher therefore ought not to proclaim to beginners how much he knows, since he himself is unable to know how great the heavenly mysteries are. Hence the Apostle Paul, after he had entered into heavenly mysteries, says: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face.”

### CHAPTER XLV.—“Then I shall know, even as I have been known” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

[Col. 1327D]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XIII, no. 30.) Our very weakness is a great barrier before the eyes of our heart when we contemplate the subtlety of God. But then we shall behold clearly him whom we now behold with subtle perception, when, having laid aside this weakness, we come to the grace of inward contemplation of which Paul says: “Then I shall know, even as I have been known.”

### CHAPTER XLVI.—“Tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (II Cor. XIV, 22).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXVII, nos. 36–37.) There are some who, when they hear of the wonderful works of the apostles—that, having received the Holy Spirit, they raised the dead by their word, drove demons from the possessed, removed illnesses by their shadow, foretold all future events by prophecy, and preached the only-begotten Word of God while speaking in the languages of all nations—suspect that heavenly grace has now been withdrawn from the Church because they do not see these powers in the Church today. They do not know how to weigh what is written: “A helper in times of need, in tribulation” (Ps. IX, 10). For the holy Church needed the help of miracles when the retribution of persecution weighed upon her. After she had subdued the pride of unbelief, she no longer required signs of powers but only the merits of works, although she still displays those signs through many people whenever necessity demands it.

For it is written: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers.” Where, then, all are believers, what need requires signs to be displayed? We can answer this more readily if we recall something about the apostolic dispensation itself. When the distinguished preacher Paul came to Malta, knowing that the island was full of unbelievers, he saved Publius’s father, who was afflicted with dysentery and fevers, by praying. Yet he instructed Timothy, who was ill, saying: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (I Tim. V, 23).

What is this, Paul? You restore a sick unbeliever to health through prayer, yet you care for the sick man Timothy, a great helper of the Gospel, like a physician, through nourishment. What else does it mean but that external miracles are performed in order to lead human minds to inward things, so that, through what is visibly shown as wonderful, invisible things still more wonderful may be believed? Publius’s father had to be healed by a sign of power so that he might come alive in mind, returning to health through a miracle. But Timothy, who was already wholly alive inwardly, did not need an external miracle to be applied to him. It is therefore not surprising if, once the faith has been propagated, miracles are not frequently performed, since the apostles themselves did not perform them for certain people who were already believers.

### CHAPTER XLVII.—“But if all prophesy,” etc. (I Cor. XIV, 24).

(Book I, *On Ezekiel*, Homily 1, no. 1.) It must be understood that prophecy is sometimes concerned with the present, as the Apostle Paul says: “But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all, he is judged by all; the secrets of his heart are made manifest. And so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.” When it is said, “The secrets of his heart are made manifest,” it is clearly shown that, in this form of prophecy, the spirit does not foretell what is going to happen but reveals what is.

But in what sense is it called the spirit of prophecy when it indicates nothing future but relates what is present? Here it must be observed that something is rightly called prophecy not because it foretells the future but because it exposes what is hidden. Just as the passage of time conceals any future event from our eyes, so in the present the cause conceals a thought from our eyes. A future event is hidden in future time, while a present thought is concealed in the secrecy of the heart.
