There is also a prophecy concerning the present when some matter is concealed not in the mind but by its being in a distant place, and yet is unveiled through the spirit. The mind of the prophet is present there where his body is not present. Gehazi, too, had gone far from the prophet when he received the gifts of Naaman the Syrian; yet the same prophet said to him: “Was not my heart present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you?” (IV Kings V, 26).

### CHAPTER XLVIII.—“I am the least of the apostles” (I Cor. XV, 9).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXIV, nos. 19–20, and Homily 10 on Ezekiel, no. 33.) Whoever desires to be led to the highest things must always attend to the progress of those who are better, so that they may judge their own faults more strictly in proportion as they see more profoundly in others what they should admire. A wonderful dispensation is at work among us: through what one person has and another does not have, one is shown to be better than the other, so that each person may advance more ardently toward humility insofar as, on the basis of the good things he does not have, he considers himself inferior to those who possess them.

Thus it comes about that, while one sees in the other what he should admire, and the other in the first, their distinct virtues both restrain them from the height of pride and kindle them toward the pursuit of progress. Therefore Paul, when through laboring more vigorously in preaching he surpassed the concern of the other saints, sought to suppress pride in himself and nourish his strength in the bosom of humility. Not forgetting his former cruelty, and contemplating the innocence of all the apostles, he said: “For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.” Yet the foremost of all those apostles, as though forgetting the primacy he had received, and as though he himself understood little, admires wisdom in Paul, saying: “As also our most beloved brother Paul wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters, speaking in them about these matters, in which there are some things difficult to understand” (II Pet. III, 15).

Behold: Paul admires innocence in the apostles; behold: the chief of the apostles admires wisdom in Paul. What does this mean except that holy men, by considering virtues, mutually place others before themselves, so that each may be raised more greatly toward heavenly things by being stirred more profoundly when he sees in another, with greater humility, what he should admire?

From this, then, we must gather with what great care we ought to contemplate the life of those who are better, we who lie in low places, if even those who are already exalted by such holiness that they advance to greater things by the steps of humility still seek in others what they may admire and imitate.

### CHAPTER XLIX.—“By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV, 10).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XVI, no. 30, and Book XXIV, no. 24.) Since it is written concerning God: “For he will repay each according to his works” (Prov. XXIV, 29), the one whom his mercy here frees from unclean works is saved in the final judgment by the justice of the eternal Judge. Therefore, whoever is believed to be saved here through the purity of his hands, as though he had become innocent by his own strength, is certainly in error. For if heavenly grace does not go before the guilty person, it never finds someone whom it can reward as innocent. Hence Moses’s truthful voice says: “No one is innocent before you” (Exod. XXXIV, 7).

Heavenly mercy therefore first accomplishes something in us without us, so that afterward it may also accomplish with us, through our free will, the good that we already desire. Yet at the final judgment grace rewards this in us as though it had proceeded from us alone. Because divine goodness goes before us in order to make us innocent, Paul says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV, 18). And because our free will follows that same grace, he adds: “And his grace in me was not empty, but I labored more abundantly than all of them” (ibid.). When he saw that he was nothing in himself, lest he appear to attribute his labors to himself, he immediately added: “Yet not I.” But because he found himself to be something together with grace—for he himself had followed the prevenient grace of God through free will—he appropriately continued: “But the grace of God with me,” so that he would neither be ungrateful for the divine gift nor remain outside the merit of free will.

For he would not say “with me” if, together with prevenient grace, he did not also have a free will that followed. Thus, to show that without grace he was nothing, he said: “Yet not I.” But to demonstrate that he had worked together with grace through free will, he added: “But the grace of God with me.”

It must therefore be held with complete certainty that in every good work, when divine grace goes before, our free will follows; and whoever is here preceded by the gift that makes him innocent is rewarded according to merit when he comes to judgment. Through the grace of almighty God we can indeed strive toward good works, but if he himself, who commands, does not also help us, we cannot fulfill them.

Thus Paul, when he admonished his disciples, saying: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling,” immediately added who was working these very good things in them: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Phil. II, 12). Almighty God goes before us by inspiring us to will good things; he also follows by helping us, so that our willing may not be fruitless but that we may be able to fulfill what we will.

When grace goes before and good will follows, what is the gift of almighty God becomes our merit. Paul explains this well in a brief statement, saying: “I labored more than all of them.” Lest he seem to have attributed what he had done to his own service, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of the Lord with me.” It is as though he said: “I labored in a good work—not I, but I also.” Insofar as I was preceded by the Lord’s gift alone, it was not I. But insofar as I followed the gift by my will, it was I also.

### CHAPTER L.—“Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV, 33).

(Book I, *On Ezekiel*, Homily 9, no. 23.) There is one reason why the company of the wicked must be avoided: if they perhaps cannot be corrected, they may draw others to imitate them, and, while they themselves are not changed from their wickedness, they may corrupt those who have been joined to them. Hence Paul says: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals.”

By listening daily to the words of our neighbors, we take them into our minds just as, by blowing and breathing, we draw air into our bodies. And just as foul air, drawn in through continual breathing, infects the body, so perverse speech, heard continually, infects the mind of the weak, so that it withers through delight in evil deeds and through the persistent wickedness of speech.

Therefore, just as perfect men ought not to flee from their perverse neighbors—for they often draw them toward uprightness, while they themselves are never drawn into perversity—so all who are weak ought to avoid the company of the wicked, lest they take pleasure in imitating the evils that they frequently hear and see but are unable to correct.

### CHAPTER LI.—“As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (I Cor. XV, 49).

(Book I, *On Ezekiel*, Homily 2, no. 19.) All the saints, in order to be able to rise to the virtue of holiness, strive toward the likeness and image of the Mediator of God and human beings, Jesus Christ. They would not be saints if they did not possess the likeness of this new and second human being.

Whatever there is in them of compassionate affection, whatever of gentleness of spirit, whatever of zeal for uprightness, whatever of guardianship of humility, whatever of fervor of charity, they have drawn from the very source of mercy, from the very root of gentleness, from the very power of justice—that is, from the Mediator of God and human beings, the Lord God.

The distinguished preacher shows that he bears the likeness of this human being when he says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. IV, 16). He urges us to rise to his image and likeness when he says: “The first human being was from the earth, earthly; the second human being was from heaven, heavenly. As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of him who descended from heaven” (I Cor. XV, 47).

Every saint is led toward the likeness of this human being insofar as he imitates the life of his Redeemer. For to disagree with his commandments and works: what else is it than to withdraw far from his likeness? The Prophet was hastening to rise to the likeness of this human being when he said: “I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways” (Ps. CXVIII, 15). Whoever silently considers the ways of the Lord in his mind and hastens to exercise himself in his commandments reforms in himself the image of the heavenly and new human being.

### CHAPTER LII.—“But this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV, 50).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XIV, no. 72; Book II, *On Ezekiel*, Homily 5, no. 22.) In sacred Scripture, “flesh” is spoken of in one way according to nature and in another way according to guilt or corruption. Flesh according to nature is meant, for example, where it is written: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. II, 23); and: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14).

Flesh according to guilt is meant where it is written: “My spirit will not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI, 3); and where the Psalmist says: “He remembered that they were flesh, a passing spirit and not returning” (Ps. LXXVII, 39).

Hence Paul also said to his disciples: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit” (Rom. VIII, 9). Were those to whom he was sending his letters not in the flesh? But because they had conquered the passions of carnal desires, they were already, through the virtue of the spirit, free from being in the flesh.

When the same Paul says: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God,” he wishes “flesh” to be understood according to guilt, not flesh according to nature. Therefore, immediately afterward, since he was speaking of flesh according to guilt, he makes this clear by adding: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

In the glory of the heavenly kingdom, therefore, there will be flesh according to nature, but not according to the desires of passion; for, once the sting of death has been conquered, it will rejoice in eternal incorruption. There the Lord will repay his faithful with the palm of victory for good works, where there will now be joy without struggle and without end. There will be the palm of victory where there will be no contest with death.

For the distinguished preacher foresaw that the palm would then be given to the conquerors when he anticipated the resurrection of the dead, saying: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. But when this mortal has put on immortality, then the saying will come to pass that is written: Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (I Cor. XV, 55). Perfect victory, therefore, will exist when death has been completely swallowed up.

## EXPOSITION ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS

### CHAPTER ONE.—“Not that we lord it over your faith” (II Cor. I, 23).

[Col. 1331]

[Col. 1331B] (In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXVI, nos. 45–46.) Nature brought all human beings into existence equal. But that some are entrusted with governing others is not nature’s doing; rather, guilt places some beneath others. Therefore, the one who knows how to rise above faults through the power of governance, and knows how through that same power to remain joined to others in equality, exercises authority well.

For the human mind is often lifted up even when it is supported by no power; how much more does it raise itself on high when power is also joined to it? Yet it is then prepared, through suitable execution, to correct the faults of others. Hence Paul also says: “For he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath” (Rom. XIII, 4).

Paul did not regard himself as superior to brothers who were doing well when he said: “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy”; and he immediately added: “For by faith you stand.” It is as though he said: “For this reason we do not lord it over your faith: because you stand by faith. We are your equals wherever we recognize that you stand.”

He did not regard himself as superior to the brothers when he said: “We became little ones in the midst of you” (I Thess. II, 7); and again: “But we are your servants through Jesus” (II Cor. IV, 5). But when he found a fault that needed correction, he immediately remembered that he was a teacher, saying: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?”

The highest position, therefore, is governed well when the one who presides rules over faults rather than over brothers, because rulers ought to rise above the faults on account of which they are placed in authority.

### CHAPTER TWO.—“This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I, 12).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXVI, nos. 42–43; Book VIII, no. 82.) We are not at all secure before the subtle examination of truth, even if, in human judgment, we have no action of ours that ought to be condemned. For often, when we think carelessly, we are driven by pride, although we suppress it by remaining silent. But unless, through self-examination, the hidden swelling is quickly suffocated in the very chamber of the heart where it arises, all the merit of our action is extinguished before the strict Judge.

From this it must be considered with what punishment that pride of heart will be condemned which is nourished all the way to the boldness of speech; for without such speech, the pride that secretly arises in the heart is at least excusable. It must also be considered what kind of pride reigns inwardly when it has been preserved to such an extent that it is not even ashamed to burst outward.

Therefore, dearest brothers, the good things we do must be kept inwardly if we expect to receive from the inward Judge a return for our work. Hence the Psalmist says concerning the Church of the elect: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is from within” (Ps. XLIV, 14). The wise virgins are also reported to carry oil in their vessels.

Therefore, through Paul, the voice of the saints says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience.” The arrogant, because they do not have the testimony of their conscience before God, seek before human beings the testimony of another’s voice. Since what they desire is outward, they cannot perceive what is desirable inwardly. Paul, however, calls the testimony of his conscience his glory because, not seeking the favor of another’s speech, he does not know how to place the joys of his life outside himself.

### CHAPTER THREE.—“Have I used fickleness? Or do I think according to the flesh what I plan?” (II Cor. II, 17).

(Curae pastoralis, Part III, chapter 18.) The inconstant must strengthen their mind with steadfastness. The shoots of mutability dry up within them when they first cut off the root of fickleness from the heart, because a strong structure is built when the solid place where the foundation ought to be laid is first prepared.

Unless fickleness of mind is guarded against beforehand, inconstancy of thought cannot be overcome. Paul declared himself to be free from this when he said: “Have I used fickleness? Or do I think according to the flesh what I plan, so that with me there may be ‘yes’ and ‘no’?” It is as though he openly said: “For this reason I am not moved by the breeze of mutability: I do not yield to the vice of fickleness.”

### CHAPTER FOUR.—“To whomever you have forgiven anything, I also forgive” (II Cor. II, 10).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIII, no. 15; Book I, *On Ezekiel*, Homily 7, no. 3.) Often the ancient enemy circles around the ways of good people with cautious skill, seeking through the things he knows they have done well an entrance into wickedness. When he sees one person giving generously, he uses that as an occasion to set another ablaze with the fire of discord. When he sees one showing mercy, he persuades another to become angry, so that, by suggesting that the good was not done communally, he may sever harmonious minds from the good of their shared grace.

Because he cannot break the minds of the righteous by persuading them to do evil, he strives to sow evil among their good actions. But holy men overcome these plots all the more quickly because they detect them all the more subtly.

We can show this more clearly if we summon Paul, one among the many defenders of the truth, as a witness. When a certain Corinthian had committed the crime of incest, the distinguished teacher handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that he might be brought to penitential satisfaction, while preserving his spirit safe for the day of the Lord. With great skill in teaching, he was handed over to the one to whom he had voluntarily submitted in guilt, but under compulsion as punishment, so that the one who had been the author of wickedness might himself become the instrument of discipline.

When Paul learned that the Corinthians, after this well-performed repentance, had already been moved to mercy toward him, he said: “To whomever you have forgiven anything, I also forgive. For what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, was for your sake, in the person of Christ.”

Considering the grace of communion, he said: “To whomever you have forgiven anything, I also forgive.” It is as though he said: “I do not dissent from your good action. Whatever you have done, let it be mine as well.” Then he immediately added: “And if I have forgiven anything, it was for your sake.” It is as though he said: “I have added to your actions whatever good I have mercifully done for your sake. My goodness, therefore, is your benefit; your goodness is my benefit.”

Then, joining to this the very bond of hearts by which it is held together, he added: “In the person of Christ.” If we should presume to ask him, as it were: “Why do you join yourself so carefully to your disciples? Why do you conform either yourself to their actions or them to yours with such attentive concern?” he immediately added: “So that we may not be outwitted by Satan.”

Satan, as we know, is accustomed to produce evil from good and to turn what is done through charity toward discord. Paul indicates with what acute understanding he cuts through Satan’s subtle plots when he adds: “For we are not ignorant of his thoughts.” It is as though he were saying in other words: “By the Lord’s authority, we have perceptive minds, and by carefully observing them we penetrate the crafty plots of the ancient enemy, lest he turn what the mind begins well into an evil end. For he habitually introduces the evil of quarrels into one person’s heart precisely where he sees another carrying out an act of mercy.”

Since the man who had fallen and been cast out of the Church, but had already repented of the crime he had committed, ought to be spared, the distinguished teacher joined himself with great humility to the will of the disciples, so that neither he himself might appear divided from the disciples nor the disciples from him in the matter of compassion.

With the attentive eye of foresight, he considered that often, when one person forgives, another becomes angry. And what kind of sacrifice of mercy is it when it is offered together with discord toward one’s neighbor? The good is imperfect when it is done without attention to whether something evil might secretly enter it from another side.

### CHAPTER FIVE.—“To some we are the odor of death unto death, to others the odor of life unto life” (II Cor. II, 15).

[Col. 1333B]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXIX, no. 76.) The word of God is one and the same in the mouth of the preacher. While some hear it with joy and others with envy, the former humbly receive the voice of holy preaching, whereas the latter, envying the one who speaks well, seek not the cause of salvation but the glory of pride.

Thus, through the holy exhortation by which the good return to life, the wicked die more grievously in their guilt. Hence Paul rightly says: “We are the good odor of Christ for God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some indeed the odor of death unto death, but to others the odor of life unto life.”

He saw that his word was simultaneously the odor of life and of death to his hearers: through it some were raised from iniquity, while others, conversely, were lulled to sleep in iniquity. Since this occurs through God’s hidden judgments, which human beings cannot comprehend in this life, he rightly added there: “And who is sufficient for these things?” It is as though he said: “We are indeed sufficient to consider what happens, but we are not sufficient to investigate why it happens.”

### CHAPTER SIX.—“We are not like the many, adulterating the word of God” (II Cor. II, 17).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXII, nos. 38–39; Book XVI, no. 74; Book XXII, no. 12.) Whenever our hearers wish to have our own qualities recognized as worthy of praise, but do not wish to change their own perversity, we ought to remain completely silent, lest, if we speak the word of God from a desire for display, their fault, which existed, should not cease to exist, while our own fault, which did not exist, comes into being.

Someone may perhaps say: “How do we know with what disposition someone listens?” But there are many things that reveal the mind of the hearer—especially if our hearers always praise what they hear but never follow what they praise.

The distinguished preacher had fled from this empty glory of speaking when he said: “For we are not like the many, adulterating the word of God, but from sincerity, as from God, before God, we speak in Christ.”

To adulterate the word of God means either to think about it otherwise than it truly is, or to seek from it not spiritual fruits but adulterous offspring of human praise. An adulterer in carnal intercourse seeks not offspring but pleasure. Likewise, every perverse person who serves empty glory is rightly said to adulterate the word of God, because through sacred speech he desires not to beget children for God but to display his own knowledge. Whoever is drawn to speak by the lust for glory devotes himself more to pleasure than to begetting.

To speak from sincerity means to seek nothing in speech beyond what is appropriate. One speaks as from God when one knows that what one says is not possessed from oneself but received from God. One speaks before God when, in everything one says, one seeks not human favor but fixes one’s attention on the presence of almighty God; one seeks not one’s own glory but the glory of the Author.

But whoever knows that he has received from God what he says and yet seeks his own glory by saying it speaks as from God but not before God, because, while preaching, he regards as absent the one whom he does not set before his heart.

Holy men, however, speak both as from God and before God, because they know that what they say comes from him, and they consider him present in their words as judge and helper. They speak as from God and before God when they understand both that they have received the word of preaching from God and that through it they seek to please God, not human beings.

Hence, when they recognize that they are despised by their neighbors and that their words do not benefit the lives of their hearers, they conceal how great their virtue is, lest, if a word spoken without usefulness should disclose the secret of the heart, it break out into empty glory.

### CHAPTER SEVEN.—“We have such confidence toward God, not because we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (II Cor. III, 5).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIII, no. 38.) We have contributed nothing to God so that divine grace might follow us. For if we precede God by doing good, where is what the Prophet says: “His mercy will go before me” (Ps. LIII, 11)? If we have offered some good work of our own so as to deserve his grace, where is what Paul says: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves, for it is God’s gift, not from works” (Eph. II, 8)?

If our love preceded God, where is what the Apostle John says: “Not because we loved God, but because he first loved us” (I John IV, 10)? Where is what the Lord says through Hosea: “I will love them freely” (Hos. XIV, 5)?

If we follow God by our own strength without his gift, where is what the Truth declares through the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5)? Where is what he says: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him”? Where is what he says again: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (ibid., 16)?

If at least we precede, by the power of our own virtue, the gifts of good works through good thinking, where is what Paul again says so beneficially that every confidence of the human mind in itself is cut off from the very root of the heart: “Not because we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God”?

We therefore do not precede God by our merits. Rather, every good that we do under the inspiration of his grace belongs both to God and to us: to God through prevenient grace, and to us through the free will that follows. For if it does not belong to God, why do we give him eternal thanks? Again, if it does not belong to us, where do we hope that rewards will be repaid to us?

Because, then, we rightly give thanks, we know that we are preceded by his gift; and again, because we rightly seek recompense, we know that, with free will following, we choose the good things that we are to do.

### CHAPTER EIGHT.—“Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (II Cor. III, 17).

(Curae pastoralis, part III, chapter 13.) Those who fear punishments and therefore live innocently, if they truly desire to be free from evils, should dread eternal punishments; yet they should not remain in this fear of punishments, but should grow toward the grace of love through the nourishment of charity. For it is written: “Perfect love drives out fear” (1 John 4:18). And again it is written: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15). [Column 1334D] Hence the same teacher says again: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17). If, then, fear of a punishment still prevents someone from an evil action, clearly no freedom of the Spirit possesses the soul of one who fears. For if he did not fear the punishment, he would undoubtedly commit the offense. The mind, therefore, does not know the grace of freedom when it is bound by the slavery of fear. Good deeds ought to be loved for their own sake, and not performed under compulsion from punishments. For whoever does good because he fears the evils of torment wishes there to be nothing for him to fear, so that he may boldly commit what is unlawful. Thus it is perfectly clear that innocence is lost before God, in whose sight sin is committed even by desire.

**CHAPTER IX.—Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16).**

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book VI, nos. 14–15; *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 37, no. 1.) [Column 1335A] Great care must be taken that, when we are afflicted by the weight of sorrow in outward circumstances, we strive toward what is above through hope, so that the mind may reach higher things in the same measure as outward punishment chastises us. For it is exceedingly impossible for us to pass through the times of our pilgrimage without groaning. Hence Paul, when he enumerated his tribulations to his disciples, added: “You yourselves know that we are destined for this” (2 Thessalonians 3:3). Yet while the flesh is afflicted by blows, the mind is raised to desire higher things, as Paul again bears witness when he says: “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.” The mind, therefore, soars upward and is renewed precisely where the flesh labors longer and is worn down in lowly things.

It must also be considered that great rewards cannot be attained except through great labors. Hence the outstanding preacher Paul says: “No one will be crowned unless he competes lawfully” (2 Timothy 2:5). No tongue can express, nor understanding fully grasp, [Column 1335B] the rewards God has promised to those who labor for him: the joys of the heavenly city; participation in the choirs of angels; standing with the blessed spirits in the glory of the Creator; seeing the face of God present; beholding the boundless light; suffering no fear of death; and rejoicing in the perpetual gift of incorruption. Whoever, therefore, desires to stand there where he hopes to rejoice without end—if the greatness of such rewards delights his mind—must not be deterred in this world by the contest of labors.

It must be known, however, that the lofty dispensation of God’s judgments often drives deserving servants forward by threats, presses them with blows, burdens them with certain imposed loads, or entangles them in laborious occupations, because in his wondrous power he foresees that, if they were to remain undisturbed and free in tranquility, they would be unable to withstand the adversary’s temptations and would lie prostrate, wounded in mind. Therefore, while he occupies them outwardly with blows or burdens that must be endured, he hides them inwardly from the darts of temptations that they might otherwise receive. It is characteristic of medical treatment that the heat of wounds is often drawn toward an itching of the skin, [Column 1335C] and that what heals inwardly frequently does so by wounding outwardly. In the same way, divine providence sometimes acts through outward pains to remove an inward wound, and through the incisions of blows to drive away the inward decay of vices that might have occupied the mind.

Yet often, when people are not conscious of any manifest fault in themselves and are either tormented by pains or crushed by labors, they break out in complaint against the just and almighty Judge, paying too little attention to how powerful an adversary they are fighting. If they carefully considered his intolerable strength, they would never murmur about what they suffer outwardly. But these things seem burdensome to us because we do not wish to weigh the greater battles of the hidden adversary. From those battles, as we have said, we are often defended while we are scourged and concealed while we are afflicted.

Before our flesh is strengthened by the incorruption of the resurrection, if it is touched by no sorrow, it runs wild in temptations. Who does not know that it is far better to burn with the flame of fevers [Column 1335D] than with the flame of vices? Yet when we are seized by fever, because we neglect to consider the heat of vices that might have taken possession of us, we murmur about the blow. Who does not know that it is far better to be subjected to harsh human masters than to be enslaved to flattering demonic spirits? Yet when, by the deep judgment of God, we are worn down under the yoke of human condition, we break out in complaint—plainly because we pay too little attention to the fact that, if no condition of servitude oppressed us, our mind might, in its freedom, serve many iniquities even worse.

We therefore believe the things we endure to be burdensome because we do not see how harsh and intolerable against us are the battles of the crafty enemy. The whole weight of our mind would become insignificant if it weighed the battles of the hidden adversary that could overwhelm it. For what if almighty God lifted the burdens we suffer, but withdrew his assistance from us and abandoned us amid the temptations of the ancient enemy? When so great an enemy rages, where shall we go if we are not protected by the defenses of [Column 1336A] our Creator? Therefore, when by God’s correction we endure harsh blows or labors, we must recall our enemy, so that we may bear these things with equanimity and not overstep into the vice of murmuring. We must not consider anything we suffer harsh while we are being freed from inward suffering through outward torments.

**CHAPTER X.—We groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be further clothed (2 Corinthians 5:4).**

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXI, no. 70.) When a preacher considers that the contest of suffering is approaching him outwardly, he wishes to undergo the danger of a glorious struggle, and yet he trembles, because in death he sees what he fears to endure, while in the fruit of death he sees what he desires. Let us see how Paul loves what he avoids and avoids what he loves. For he says: “My desire is to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). And: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” Yet he also says: “While we are in this dwelling, we groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be further clothed [Column 1336B], so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.”

Behold: he desires to die, and yet he fears to be unclothed of the flesh. Why is this? Because although victory rejoices him forever, present punishment nevertheless disturbs him; and although love of the reward that follows prevails, the pain of being driven out still touches the mind with sorrow. Just as a brave man, when he arms himself for a battle that is already near, both palpitates and hastens, trembles and rages—as though he could be seen to fear by his pallor, yet is violently driven on by anger—so the holy man, when he sees suffering approaching, is shaken by the weakness of his nature and strengthened by the firmness of his hope; he trembles at approaching death and yet rejoices that, by dying, he will live more truly. For he cannot pass to the kingdom except through death; therefore he fears while rejoicing and rejoices while fearing, because he knows that he will not reach the prize of rest unless he crosses with labor what lies between.

**CHAPTER XI.—So that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (2 Corinthians 5:4).**

[Column 1336C]

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book IV, no. 45.) However brightly God’s elect may shine through the splendor of their works, and however greatly they may kindle themselves with the fire of compunction, it is nevertheless certain that, while they are still burdened with corruptible flesh, they cannot see the eternal light as it truly is. Yet often their minds are so kindled that, although they are situated in the flesh, they are snatched up into God, with every carnal thought subjected to him.

Nevertheless, they do not see God as he is, because, as has been said, the weight of the first condemnation presses upon them in corruptible flesh. It often desires to be swallowed up in this manner, so that, if it could happen, it might reach eternal life without the intervention of bodily death. Hence Paul, when he ardently sought the inner light but nevertheless feared, to some extent, the losses of outward death, says: “While we are in this dwelling, we groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.”

Holy men, therefore, desire to see the true light, and, if it were granted, they would even wish [Column 1336D] to reach the innermost secret of that light while still in the body. But however ardently they leap forward in their intention, the ancient night—that is, the consent of the first parent—still burdens them with guilt; and the just Judge restrains from the sight of his inner radiance the eyes of this corruptible flesh, which the crafty enemy opened to desire.

**CHAPTER XII.—He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 5:5).**

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XVI, no. 6.) In Sacred Scripture the gift of the Holy Spirit is sometimes called a pledge, because through it our soul is strengthened toward certainty of inward hope. Paul therefore rightly says: “He who has given us the pledge of the Spirit.” We have received this pledge so that we may hold firm certainty concerning the promise made to us.

**CHAPTER XIII.—While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:6).**

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XVIII, no. 48.) The pilgrim [Column 1337A] people are the whole number of the elect, who regard this life as a kind of exile and sigh toward the heavenly homeland with the full intention of their hearts. Of them Paul says: “They confess that they are strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13). Those who say this signify that they are seeking a homeland.

The same apostle also endured this pilgrimage when he said: “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; for we walk by faith, and not by sight.” He strove to escape the hardships of this pilgrimage when he said: “My desire is to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). And again: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (ibid.).

**CHAPTER XIV.—The old things have passed away, and new things have come to be (2 Corinthians 5:17).**

(*Book I on Ezekiel*, homily 10, nos. 8–10.) We have often seen certain people, apparently moved to compunction by the voice of preaching, change their clothing but not their mind. They put on religious dress but do not [Column 1337B] trample their former vices; they eagerly seek the profits of the present world and place their confidence in holiness merely because of the outward garment they have assumed.

What else should be said to such people but what the outstanding Teacher says to those who observe the outward aspects of the law: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but a new creation” (Galatians 5:6)? It is not a matter of great merit if something outwardly is done with regard to our body; what must be weighed with the greatest care is what is done in the mind.

To despise the present world; not to love transient things; to lay the mind deeply in humility before God and one’s neighbors; to preserve patience in response to insults inflicted upon us; and, with patience guarded, to drive the pain of malice from the heart; to give one’s own possessions to the needy; not to covet what belongs to others; to love a friend in God and for God; to love even those who are enemies; to grieve over a neighbor’s affliction; and not to rejoice over the death of one who is an enemy—this is the new creation that the same teacher of the nations seeks among other disciples with watchful eye, saying: “If [Column 1337C] anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: the old things have passed away; behold, everything has become new.”

To the old person belong: loving the world; loving transient things out of desire; raising the mind in pride; having no patience; thinking maliciously, out of envy, about a neighbor’s injury; not giving one’s possessions to those in need; seeking to multiply what belongs to others; loving no one purely for God’s sake; repaying enemies with enmity; and rejoicing over a neighbor’s affliction. All these things belong to the old person, which we draw, so to speak, from the root of corruption.

But whoever now overcomes these things and changes the mind toward kindness in accordance with the Lord’s commandments is rightly told: “The old things have passed away, and behold, new things have come to be.” New things therefore come to be in our minds when the vices of the old person pass away from us.

**CHAPTER XV.—We entreat you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20).**

(*Homily on the Gospels*, homily 32, no. 5.) If it happens that we have perhaps quarreled with a neighbor, we are ashamed to be the first to make [Column 1337D] satisfaction. The carnal heart, while it seeks the glory of this life, rejects humility; and often the very person who is angry desires to be reconciled with the one who is at odds with him, but is ashamed to go first to make amends.

Let us weigh the deeds of Truth, so that we may see where the actions of our wickedness lie. For if we are members of the supreme Head, we ought to imitate the one to whom we are joined. What example of our instruction does the outstanding preacher Paul give? “Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making his appeal through us. We entreat you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20).

Behold: by sinning, we created discord between ourselves and God, yet God first sent his ambassadors to us, so that we who had sinned might come, when entreated, to God’s peace. Let human pride therefore be ashamed and let each person be confounded if he does not make satisfaction first to his neighbor, when, after our fault, God himself—the one who has been offended—entreats us through ambassadors that we should be reconciled to him.

**CHAPTER XVI.—Through glory and dishonor, etc. (2 Corinthians 6:8).**

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXII, no. 17.) It must be known that, so that we may not be lifted up by excessive praise, our Ruler often, through his wondrous moderation, permits us also to be torn by detraction. Thus, when the voice of one who praises us raises us up, the tongue of one who detracts from us may humble us. For a tree that is sometimes driven by the force of one wind so violently that it seems almost capable of being uprooted is raised upright by a blast coming from the opposite direction; and the tree that has suffered bending from one side returns to its position through the other.

Thus that deeply rooted tree stood firm, fixed amid opposing winds, which said: “Through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute.”

**CHAPTER XVII.—Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians, etc. (1 Corinthians 6:11).**

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXVI, no. 42.) When righteous people see that they cannot be understood by weak hearers, they often even praise the good things they say; [Column 1338B] not because they themselves are eager for their own praise, but so that they may kindle their hearers’ attentiveness to listening, so that, while these things are uttered by their voice, the hearts of the hearers may be seized by them with more ardent affection.

Hence Paul, after saying many remarkable and important things to the Corinthians, added: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged.” When holy teachers exalt the praise of preaching, they raise the hearts of their hearers, as though by the hand of their voice, from the depths of their thoughts, so that, once shaken free, they may swiftly meet the words that follow as though on a journey and embrace them with an understanding all the tighter because they had already loved them in the voice of the one praising them, even before they saw them.

**CHAPTER XVIII.—You are not restricted in us (2 Corinthians 6:12).**

Those who hear the words of preaching ought to receive them in the broad bosom of charity. A spacious place for the teacher to dwell ought to be in the hearer’s heart—a breadth of goodness. Hence Paul says to certain people: [Column 1338C] “Make room for us. We have wronged no one; we have corrupted no one. You are not restricted in us; you are restricted in your own affections” (2 Corinthians 7:2). It is as though he were saying openly: “Make a spacious place in your minds for receiving instruction, but remain narrow in thinking about carnal things.”

**CHAPTER XIX.—When we came to Macedonia, our flesh had no rest (1 Corinthians 7:5).**

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book V, no. 55.) A man who is well subject to God is not broken by adversity, just as he is not lifted up by prosperity, because adversity does not cast down the one whom prosperity does not corrupt. Often, moreover, because he knows that he is more usefully exercised by the labors of his own contrition, he rejoices in adversity. While he steadfastly suffers for the truth, he rejoices that the merits of his virtue are increased.

Hence we read that the apostles rejoiced when it happened that they endured blows for Christ, as it is written: “They went away from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus [Column 1338D]” (Acts 5:4). Hence Paul, when he had been oppressed by harsh persecutions in Macedonia, shows that, while indicating that he was afflicted, he also experienced joy, saying: “When we came to Macedonia, our flesh had no rest.” It is as though he were saying openly: “Our spirit had rest, while, for the advancement of the soul, our flesh endured the punishments of persecution.”

**CHAPTER XX.—Outwardly conflicts, inwardly fears (2 Corinthians 7:6).**

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book III, nos. 39–40.) Holy men, caught in the battle of tribulations, when at one and the same time they endure some people striking them and others persuading them, oppose to the former the shield of patience and hurl at the latter the darts of instruction. They wisely teach those who give perverse advice, and bravely despise those who inflict adversity outwardly. They correct the former by teaching and restrain the latter by enduring; by suffering, they disdain enemies who rise against them, while by compassion they restore weakened fellow citizens to salvation.

[Column 1339A] Let us see the soldier of God’s camp fighting on both fronts. He says: “Outwardly conflicts, inwardly fears.” He enumerates the battles he endures outwardly, saying: “Danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from the Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger among false brothers” (2 Corinthians 11:26). In this battle he adds what weapons he hurls against the adversary: “In labor and hardship, through many vigils, in hunger and thirst, through many fasts, in cold and nakedness.” Yet, caught amid so many contests, let him say by what protection of vigilance he also guards the camp, for he immediately adds: “Besides these external things, there is my daily pressure, my concern for all the churches.”

Behold: he bravely accepts battles upon himself and mercifully expends himself in protecting his neighbors. He recounts the evils he suffers and adds the good things he bestows. Let us therefore consider what labor it is to endure adversity outwardly and weakness inwardly at the same time. Outwardly he suffers conflicts because he is torn by blows and bound with chains; inwardly [Column 1339B] he endures fear because he fears that his suffering may harm not himself but his disciples.

Hence he writes to them: “Let no one be shaken by these tribulations; for you yourselves know that I am destined for this” (2 Thessalonians 3:3). He feared the downfall of others in his own suffering, lest, when the disciples saw him afflicted and beaten for the faith, they should refuse to profess themselves believers.

O bowels of immense charity! He despises what he himself suffers and takes care that the heart of a disciple suffer no harm from perverse persuasion. In himself he disregards wounds of the body; in others he heals wounds of the heart. The righteous have this characteristic: while placed in the pain of their own tribulation, they do not abandon concern for another’s benefit. While suffering adversity for themselves, they foresee what is necessary for others by teaching them.

It is much less labor either to teach when one endures nothing or to endure when one teaches nothing. Hence holy men diligently extend themselves to both, and yet they may perhaps be struck amid tribulations. They accept outward battles while carefully [Column 1339C] considering that the inward parts of their neighbors should not be torn.

**CHAPTER XXI.—Not that others should have relief while you have tribulation (2 Corinthians 8:13).**

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XX, nos. 68–69.) It is necessary to know that the one who gives perfectly is the one who, together with what he offers to the afflicted, also takes upon himself the afflicted person’s state of mind, so that he first transfers the sufferer’s pain into himself and then contends against that pain through his service. For abundance of possessions often makes someone generous in gifts, rather than the virtue of compassion.

Whoever perfectly sympathizes with the afflicted often gives the needy even something by which the giver himself is constricted. The compassion of our heart is complete when we do not fear accepting the evil of poverty as something very great, in order to free the other person from suffering.

The Mediator of God and humanity gave us this form of piety. Although he could have helped us without dying, he nevertheless wished to assist humanity by dying, because he would have loved us less if he had not also taken upon himself our wounds. [Column 1339D] Nor would he have shown us the power of his love unless he himself had temporarily endured what he tolerates from us.

He found us capable of suffering and subject to death; and he who brought us into existence from nothing could have recalled us from suffering even without his own death. But, to show how great the virtue of compassion was, he deigned to become for us what he wished us to be, so that in himself he might temporarily receive the death from which he would free us forever.

Could he not, remaining invisible to us in the riches of his divinity, have enriched us through wondrous powers? Yet, so that humanity might return to inward riches, God deigned to appear outwardly as poor. Hence the outstanding preacher, in order to kindle our compassionate hearts toward the grace of generosity, said: “You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: although he was rich, he became poor for your sake” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

He also says: “Not that others should have relief while you have tribulation, but that, by equality, your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may also supply your need” [Column 1340A] (2 Corinthians 8:13–14). He certainly said this by accommodating himself to the weak, lest those who gave very much and afterward were unable to endure poverty should break out into impatience.

For when the mind of the giver does not know how to endure poverty, if he takes much away from himself, he seeks an occasion for impatience against himself. The mind must first be prepared for patience, and then either much or everything may be given, lest, when the poverty that descends is borne with insufficient equanimity, both the reward of the generosity already offered perish and the mind be further destroyed by the murmuring that follows.

For those unable to endure poverty, it is more tolerable to give less than, after their generosity, to murmur under the distress of poverty. Yet, to kindle the minds of his hearers toward great generosity, he shortly afterward added: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Corinthians 9:6).

We sometimes say that compassion from the heart is greater than giving, because whoever perfectly sympathizes with the needy regards whatever he gives as insignificant. Unless the good will of the giver [Column 1340B] had prevailed, the outstanding preacher would not have said to the same disciples: “You began not only to do something but also to desire it from the previous year” (2 Corinthians 8:10). It is easy even for one who is willing to obey in a good work, but this was a great virtue in the disciples: they had first desired the good thing that had been commanded them.

We therefore say that compassion is greater than what is given because almost anyone, even one who does not sympathize, may give some possession; but one who truly sympathizes never denies what he sees to be necessary for his neighbor.

**CHAPTER XXII.—His letters are weighty, but his bodily presence is weak (2 Corinthians 10:10).**

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book X, no. 51.) It must be known that every righteous person either possesses no temporal glory or breaks it beneath himself if he possesses it, so that he may stand free above his honor and not, conquered by its delight, succumb to it. Hence the outstanding preacher humbled the glory of his apostleship before human eyes when he said: “We did not make use of this authority, although as apostles of Christ we could have been a burden, [Column 1340C] but we became gentle among you” (1 Thessalonians 2:7).

Before his hearers he was held in contempt when he said: “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible.” Those who knew him to say such things judged that someone who lived commonly among them could not be like that. When they saw him humble in his life yet considered him lofty in speech, their own pride compelled them to despise in words of his presence the one whom they had feared in his writings.

Paul therefore received insults of pride from inexperienced disciples precisely where he had displayed the teaching of humility. In a terrible manner, the weakness of the proud grew precisely where it ought to have diminished, when the elevated mind of carnal people rejected as contemptible what the teacher had shown to be worthy of imitation.

**CHAPTER XXIII.—When I was with you and in need, I was a burden to no one (2 Corinthians 11:9).**

(*Book II on Ezekiel*, homily 6, nos. 12–13.) Let us consider the gentleness of blessed Paul, [Column 1340D] and, if we can, weigh it properly. He possessed such ardor in the zeal of preaching that he did not spare even the first of the apostles; yet how great was his gentleness in the practice of long-suffering?

Let us say nothing of the fact that he was beaten with rods three times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times, in the depths of the sea night and day, and received from the Jews five times “forty lashes less one” (1 Corinthians 11). Evils inflicted upon us by open adversaries move the mind to anger less; what we suffer from our own people usually causes more pain. Hence Truth itself speaks through the Psalmist against his betrayer: “If an enemy had reproached me, I could have endured it; but you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food” (Psalm 54:13).

Let us therefore consider, if we can, the apostle Paul, who was as patient among persecutors as he was gentle among disciples. Certainly, when he came to Corinth, he drew the Corinthians away from the [Column 1341A] service of idols, made known to them who the true God was, and preached to them the joys of eternal life. After gathering a great multitude of people into the faith, he endured such poverty there that he suffered severe need for his daily food, and did not receive earthly bread from the disciples to whom he had preached the bread of heaven.

He devoted himself to the word for the life of his hearers and to the labor of his hands for the life of his body. Disciples from other lands also sent him support so that he could preach to the Corinthians. For afterward he says to these same Corinthians in a letter: “When I was with you and in need, I was a burden to no one; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked.” To them he had prefaced this as a great reproach: “I robbed other churches, receiving support for serving you.”

Let us consider, if we can, how much gentleness it showed to preach spiritual bread and not receive bodily bread; to instruct the hearts of hearers in eternal riches and to suffer hunger among those same faithful and wealthy disciples; to endure poverty among the satisfied, [Column 1341B] yet neither to mention what he suffered nor to grieve over it; to see the hard hearts of his grasping hearers and nevertheless not cease preaching.

For, as the Acts of the Apostles testify, he preached continually in that same city for a year and six months (Acts 18). After he had departed from those Corinthians, he later wrote to them about what he had endured while among them. Why had he never told them this while living among them? So that what had not been done toward him from good will would not be done from command, and so that, when their poverty became known, their good will might remain unknown.

Why, then, did he write this to them later, when he was far away? So that the disciples would not remain entirely without correction, and so that, having been grasping toward their teacher, they would not become such toward other brothers as well.

In this too Paul was truly the teacher of the nations: neglecting his own interests and caring for those of others, he fulfilled what he had preached: “Let no one seek his own good, but that of the other” (1 Corinthians 10:24); and: “Let each of you look not to his own interests, but to those of others.”

[Column 1341C] How great, then, was this virtue of gentleness! How great the tranquility of spirit! Which one of us, if he had converted one rich man of this world to the service of almighty God, and then saw himself in need while that man did not provide him the means of life, would not immediately have despaired of that man’s life? Who would not say that he had labored in vain? Who would not fall silent in exhorting one whom he did not see first bearing the fruit of a good work in himself?

But Paul, made firm at the summit of virtue through gentleness, remained, preached, loved, and completed the good work he had begun. By bearing with them and persevering, he led the hearts of the disciples to mercy. For later, indicating that he knew of their progress, he writes in the same Epistle: “Concerning the ministry for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know your readiness, about which I boast of you to the Macedonians: that Achaia has been ready since the previous year, and your zeal has stirred up very many” (2 Corinthians 9:8).

Of them he says again: “You began not only to do something but [Column 1341D] also to desire it from the previous year.” In this he sought not so much their deeds as their pious intentions, and plainly praises their pious intentions more than their deeds. Yet it must be noted that this very consolation contains a reproach when he says “from the previous year.” They had done a good thing, but late; and therefore the teacher praised it not without correction.

He is a physician who applies medicine to a wound—medicine that both soothes what has been cleansed and bites what is found to be rotten. By enduring and preaching these things, he completed what he had begun, and the virtue of extraordinary patience softened the hardness of the disciples into the depths of mercy.

**CHAPTER XXIV.—Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14).**

(*Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XXXIII, no. 44.) The ancient enemy tests the religious minds of human beings in one way and those devoted to this world in another. He openly sets before the wicked the evils they desire; but he secretly lies in wait [Column 1342A] for the good and mocks them under the appearance of holiness. To the former, as though they were his intimates, he openly reveals himself as wicked; to the latter, as though they were strangers, he cloaks himself under a pretext of apparent respectability, so that he may insinuate evils he cannot openly display, hidden beneath a covering of good action.

Hence his members often, when they cannot cause harm through open wickedness, assume the appearance of good action. They perform what is evil in their deeds but pretend to be holy in appearance. If the wicked were openly evil, they could not be received by the good; but they take something from the appearance of the good, so that, when good people receive in them the appearance they love, they may also unwittingly receive the poison they avoid.

Thus the apostle Paul, observing certain people who, under the cloak of preaching, served the interests of their belly, says: “Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.” What wonder, then, if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness?

Joshua feared this disguise when, seeing an angel, he asked whose side he was on, saying: “Are you for us, or for our adversaries?” (Joshua 5:13). If he belonged to the hostile power, then, by recognizing [Column 1342B] that he was suspect, Joshua would recoil from the deception.

**CHAPTER XXV.—They are ministers of Christ—and so am I (2 Corinthians 11:23).**

(*Book I on Ezekiel*, homily 9, no. 19; *Commentary on Blessed Job*, book XIX, no. 37.) The righteous and perfect, while fleeing the glory of praise and seeking the gain of souls, sometimes proclaim their own virtues and recount the good things they have received from God—not so that they themselves may advance among human beings through self-display, but so that, by their example, they may draw those to whom they preach toward life.

Hence the apostle Paul tells the Corinthians how often he was beaten with rods, how often he was stoned, how often he suffered shipwreck, and how much he endured for the truth; he tells them that he was caught up to the third heaven and taken into paradise (2 Corinthians 11:2), so that he might turn their understanding away from false preachers. By making known what kind of man he was, he caused those whom he knew they were perversely venerating to become contemptible to them.

To these same Corinthians, therefore, while fleeing honor, he says: “We do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, [Column 1342C] and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake” (2 Corinthians 4:5). Yet, seeing them straying from the path of the true faith through the persuasion of false apostles, he shows them with great care how worthy of honor he is, saying: “Whatever anyone dares to claim—I am speaking foolishly—I also dare. Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I. Are they ministers of Christ? I am speaking as one out of his mind—I am more” (2 Corinthians 11:21–23).

He adds that the secrets of the third heaven had also been opened to him and that, having been caught up, he had entered the mysteries of paradise. Behold: fleeing honor, he proclaims himself the servant of the disciples; seeking honor for the benefit of his hearers, he sets the merits of his life above those of the false apostles.

The outstanding teacher acted so that, when his own character became known, the life and speech of the evil preachers would become contemptible by comparison. If he had concealed himself, he would have commended them; by not showing himself, he would have given error room to spread.

Thus, in a wondrous way, he seeks the increase of humility: he proclaims himself a servant to his disciples and demonstrates himself superior to his adversaries. He shows his disciples what humility he has received; [Column 1342D] he shows his adversaries what sublimity he possesses. Against his adversaries he makes known what he has received as a gift; to his disciples he makes known what his inward disposition remains before himself.

Therefore, when holy men are compelled to recount the good things they do, they serve not self-exaltation but usefulness.

**CHAPTER XXVI.—The governor of the nation of King Aretas at Damascus (2 Corinthians 11:32).**
(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXI, nos. 56–60.) If our spirit has been inflamed with the desire for eternal life, if it now looks inwardly upon the true light, if it kindles within itself the flame of holy fervor, then, insofar as the occasion permits and the matter requires, we ought to expose ourselves in defense of justice and oppose those rushing into injustice—even when they do not summon us. For when they strike the justice that we love in others, they pierce us no less by their blow, even if they seem to be showing reverence.

It is pleasing to consider [Col. 1343A] how great a fervor inflamed Paul when at Ephesus the flame of zeal carried him toward breaking into the riotous crowd in the theater. For it is written: “They were filled with anger and cried out, saying, ‘Great is Diana of the Ephesians!’ And the city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s companions.” And immediately afterward it is added: “But when Paul wished to enter among the people, the disciples would not permit him; and some of the leading men of Asia, who were his friends, sent to him, asking him not to give himself up to the theater” (Acts 19:28 ff.). In these words we recognize with what force he would have rushed against the opposing ranks, had the restraints of charity not held him back through his friends and disciples.

But if we ought to confront enemies, seek battle of our own accord, and always abandon ourselves to the course of our fervor, what are we to make of the same outstanding preacher’s confession about himself: “The governor of Damascus under King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me; and through a window I was let down in a basket by the wall, and so I escaped [Col. 1343B] his hands”? What does it mean that now he willingly attacks armed ranks, and now hides from armed enemies as though fearful, except that through his skillful courage we must learn both steadfastly to seek battle with our adversaries at times and prudently to avoid it at others?

For in everything we do, it is necessary to weigh on the scales of the mind, on one side the burden and on the other the fruit of our labor. When the burden outweighs the fruit, each person may harmlessly avoid the labor, provided that he exercises himself in other matters in which the profit of the fruits surpasses the burden of the labor. But when the measure of the labor is equaled or surpassed by the resulting quantity of fruits, the labor may be avoided without grave fault.

Thus the holy preacher, seeing that the minds of his persecutors at Damascus were exceedingly obstinate, wished to engage their opposition, because he saw that he himself—whom he knew would be useful to many—might fail, and that he would benefit either no one there or only a few. He therefore withdrew from the conflict and preserved himself for [Col. 1343C] other battles, where he could fight more successfully. It was not that courage was lacking in the place, but that the place for courage was lacking; and therefore the strongest soldier sought a field of battle beyond the narrow confines of the siege.

But when he saw many necks of his adversaries ready to be subjected to their own King, he did not fear to enter the battle, even with death, as when he was going to Jerusalem and the disciples, having foreseen through prophecy his coming passion, tried to stop him. He himself testified, saying: “I am ready not only to be bound, but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus; for I do not hold my life more precious than myself” (Acts 21:13). Thus he who here, despite having foreseen his passion, fearlessly sought the hostile ranks, showed that his flight there had arisen from prudent dispensation, not from fear.

In this matter we must consider that the person who commendably avoids certain labors by a judgment of prudent dispensation is the one who bravely endures other, greater labors for God. Often, however, weak fear is called prudent caution by human beings, and they claim to have prudently avoided an attack when, in shameful flight, they are struck from behind. Therefore, [Col. 1343D] when a matter of prudent dispensation is being conducted in God’s cause, fear of the heart must be weighed with the subtlest balance, lest fear creep in through weakness and disguise itself as reason under the appearance of prudent dispensation; lest guilt call itself prudence, and the mind no longer return to repentance when it names virtue what it has done wickedly.

Therefore, whenever someone is caught in uncertainty and some adversity threatens him, he must first fight within himself against both fear and rashness, so that he neither withdraws in cowardice nor presents himself rashly. For the person who always throws himself against adversity is exceedingly rash, and the one who always hides is exceedingly timid.

We learn these things more clearly in spiritual battles if we draw the pattern of our training from bodily wars. A commander is not wise if he rashly drives his army against hostile ranks, nor is he brave if he always withdraws it by avoiding the enemy’s face. A commander must know how at one time cautiously to withdraw his army from the enemy’s attack, and at another to [Col. 1344A] hem in the enemy by surrounding him with his wings.

The perfect preachers carefully display this very conduct: at one time, while avoiding the rage of persecution, they know how to yield wisely but not weakly; at another, while disregarding the attack of persecution, they know how to confront it bravely but not rashly.

### CHAPTER XXVII

“But I refrain, lest anyone should think of me above what he sees in me” (2 Corinthians 12:6).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XVIII, no. 13.) Those who are truly holy not only do not seek glory beyond their measure, but also avoid being seen as what they have deserved to become. Thus that outstanding preacher of truth, speaking against the false apostles, recounted the exceptional works of his ministry for the instruction of his disciples; he described the many dangers he had endured amid accumulated persecutions; and after this he recalled that he had been caught up to the third heaven and again into paradise, where he could have learned things so great that he could not speak of them at all. [Col. 1344B] He might perhaps have said even more extraordinary things about himself, but, restraining himself from human praise through profound reflection, he added: “But I refrain, lest anyone should think of me above what he sees in me or hears from me.”

He therefore still had something to say about himself, since he refrained from saying it. Yet the outstanding teacher accomplished both things: by speaking of what he had done, he instructed his disciples; by remaining silent, he kept himself within the bounds of humility. For he would have been exceedingly ungrateful if he had concealed everything about himself from his disciples, and perhaps exceedingly careless if he had disclosed everything about himself even to his disciples. But, as has been said, he wonderfully accomplished both: by speaking, he educated the life of his hearers; by remaining silent, he guarded his own.

### CHAPTER XXVIII

“There was given to me a thorn for my flesh, an angel of Satan,” etc. (2 Corinthians 12:7).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XIX, no. 11; Book XXXI, no. 71.) As long as God’s elect remain in this life, they are restrained by certain temptations so that they do not grow proud through any presumption and are unable to advance as far as they [Col. 1344C] wish. Yet, lest they become arrogant, no fixed measure of virtues is established in them.

I see Paul enduring dangers from rivers and robbers, from cities and solitude, from the sea and false brothers; curbing his body with fasts and vigils; bearing the hardship of cold and nakedness; devoting himself vigilantly and pastorally to the guardianship of the churches; caught up to the third heaven; again caught up into paradise; and hearing secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak. Yet, when he is permitted to be tested by the angel of Satan, he prays to be delivered from him and is not heard, as he himself says: “And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn for my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. For this I besought the Lord three times, that he might depart from me.”

When I consider the beginnings of his way of life, I reflect that heavenly goodness opened the heavens to him and that Jesus showed himself to him from on high. He temporarily lost the light of his bodily eyes but received the light of his heart forever. He was sent to Ananias and called a chosen vessel; yet he withdrew as a fugitive from that same city into which he had entered after [Col. 1344D] seeing Jesus, as he himself testifies: “The governor of Damascus under King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me; and through a window I was let down in a basket by the wall, and so I escaped his hands” (2 Corinthians 11:32).

I may fittingly say to him: “O Paul, you already behold Jesus in heaven, yet you flee a human being on earth; you are led into paradise and learn the secrets of God, yet you are still tempted by an angel of Satan? How are you so strong that you are carried up to heavenly things? How are you so weak that you flee a human being on earth and still endure adversity from an angel of Satan?”

For behold: the one who lifts you up also restrains you again with the most precise measure, so that in your miracles you may proclaim to us the power of God, and again, in your fear, make us remember our weakness. Yet, lest this weakness drive us to despair when it strikes us, while you were praying to the Lord in your weakness and were not heard, you also told us what you heard: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in [Col. 1345A] weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Thus, by God’s open utterance, it is shown that weakness is the guardian of power. We are well guarded inwardly when, by God’s dispensation, we are tolerably tested outwardly—at times by vices, at times by afflictions and the adversities of persecution.

But whoever wishes to prepare his mind for battle before the battle of temptation must foresee through reflection the adversities that are still far away, lest perhaps they overcome him because they are unexpected. Hence Paul admonished the disciples when he said: “Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves” (2 Corinthians 13:5). As though he were openly commanding them: “Bring the struggles of persecution back to mind, and, weighing the innermost and hidden things of your heart, discover what sort of people you will be able to remain amid torments.”

Thus the outstanding preacher Paul, who had been caught up to the third heaven and had entered the secrets of paradise, wished to remain tranquil and free from temptation after his revelation. But because almighty God has established boundaries for human beings that cannot be passed, he both raised Paul to know sublime things and brought him back [Col. 1345B] again to endure lowly ones. Thus, as Paul looked upon the limits appointed to him and tried to attain security but could not, he was prevented by humility from going outside himself and compelled always to return within his own boundaries.

Sometimes, therefore, God’s elect strive to advance in virtues and receive certain gifts. At other times, driven back, they lie in the depths. No one attains as much virtue as he desires, because almighty God, discerning the inner person, sets a measure even upon spiritual progress, so that, because a person strives to grasp something and cannot, he may not exalt himself in those things that he can attain.

### CHAPTER XXIX

“I have become foolish” (1 Corinthians 12:11).

(Book I, in Ezekiel, Homily 9, nos. 19–20.) The just and perfect never reveal their good deeds unless either the benefit of their neighbors or [Col. 1346A] some extreme necessity compels them. Thus the apostle Paul also recounted many courageous deeds about himself for the edification of his disciples, but in recounting them he did not sin at all, since he did not depart from the path of truth, certain testimony, and humble heart.

Whoever speaks truthfully about his own good deeds when necessity compels him is joined to humility all the more because he is also joined to truth. Was Paul not such a person when, out of zeal for truth, he recounted so many courageous deeds about himself to the disciples against the false apostles? He would have been an enemy of truth if, by hiding his own virtues, he had allowed preachers of error to prevail.

Thus, after listing his virtues to the Corinthians, he added: “I have become foolish: you compelled me.” Yet it sometimes happens that, compelled by necessity, people seek not the benefit of others but their own in the good deeds they report about themselves. Thus blessed Job lists his deeds, saying: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and when I did not know the case, I investigated it most carefully” (Job 29:15); and many other things that he often [Col. 1346B] recalls having done.

But because he was placed in the wound of grief and was being accused by his reproving friends of having acted wickedly, of being violent toward his neighbors, and of oppressing the poor, the holy man, caught between God’s blows and the words of human reproach, saw his mind violently shaken and driven toward the pit of despair. He was on the point of falling, unless he recalled his good deeds, so that he might be brought back to hope and not perish in despair, overwhelmed by words and wounds.

Therefore, when he lists his good deeds, he does not desire to make them known to others as though seeking praise; rather, he restores his spirit to hope. Thus the just are not blameworthy when they speak of the virtues they possess to the weak, because through the life they recount they seek the life of other souls.

## EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE GALATIANS

[Col. 1345]

### CHAPTER I

“If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10).

[Col. 1345C]

(Pastoral Rule, Part II, chapter 8.) It must be understood that good rulers ought not seek to please human beings, but should draw their neighbors into affection for the truth through the sweetness of their reputation—not desiring to be loved for themselves, but making their love like a road by which they may lead the hearts of their hearers into love of the Creator.

For it is difficult for a preacher, however rightly he may proclaim, to be willingly heard if he is not loved. Therefore the one who presides should strive to be loved, so that he may be heard; yet he should not seek their love for himself, lest he be found secretly to resist, through the tyranny of his thoughts, the one whom he is seen to serve by his office.

Paul aptly indicates this when he reveals to us the hidden purpose of his endeavor, saying: “Just as I also please everyone in everything” (1 Corinthians 10:33).
