Yet he says again: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.” Paul therefore both pleases and does not please, because in that which he seeks to please, [Col. 1345D] he seeks not himself, but to please human beings through himself by means of the truth.

### CHAPTER II

“I make known to you the Gospel,” etc. (Galatians 1:11).

(Book I, in Ezekiel, Homily 1, no. 9.) Sometimes the spirit of prophecy touches the mind concerning the past but does not touch it concerning the future, as is clearly shown in the apostle Paul, who says to the disciples: “I make known to you the Gospel that was preached by me: for it is not according to man. For I neither received it from man nor learned it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 3:5).

Thus he also says to other disciples: “According to revelation the mystery was made known to me.” Yet, when he was going up to Jerusalem to preach the very Gospel that he had learned through revelation, he said: “And now, behold, bound in spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there” (Acts 20:22).

This is the mystery of the Gospel [Col. 1346C]: that the Only-Begotten of the Father became incarnate and was made perfect man; that, crucified, dead, and buried, he rose on the third day; that on the fortieth day he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.

Therefore, when he learned the Gospel through revelation, he was touched by the spirit of prophecy concerning the past. But because he did not know what he would suffer for that same Gospel, he was surely not touched concerning the future. For he says: “Except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city, saying that bonds and tribulations await me in Jerusalem” (verse 23).

From this it is plainly shown that what was going to happen to him was revealed to others concerning him, but not to him concerning himself, as it is said of him through Agabus: “The man whose belt this is must be bound in Jerusalem” (Acts 21:11).

### CHAPTER III

“O foolish Galatians” (Galatians 3:1).

(Book I, in Ezekiel, Homily 11, no. 20.) Harsh and shameless minds, if they are reproved gently, are provoked by that very gentleness to [Col. 1346D] greater sins. Hence the outstanding preacher Paul rises up very harshly against the Galatians, who had departed from the faith.

Without first showing any modest patience or preceding his words with any sweetness of speech, he rebukes from the very beginning of his Epistle those whom he knew had departed from the faith. For, after his greeting, he began in this way: “I am amazed that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from him who called you into the grace of Christ” (Galatians 1:6).

After other words, he adds to them in open rebuke: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?” For unless hard minds are struck by open reproof, they will in no way recognize the evil they have done. Often those who are shameless do not perceive that they have sinned to the extent that they are not reproved for the sins they have committed. Thus they judge their lesser faults by the lesser rebuke that corrects them, and recognize that those for which they see themselves vehemently rebuked are greater.

Therefore the preacher’s speech must always be shaped according to the character [Col. 1347A] of his hearers, lest he speak harshly to the modest or gently to the shameless.

### CHAPTER IV

“I live, yet no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

(Homily 23 on the Gospels, no. 2.) The Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9:23). A person leaves and denies himself when he abandons and avoids what he was through oldness and strives toward that to which he is called through newness.

He denies himself not because he does not exist at all in his essence, but because he is no longer what he was in the guilt of impiety. He is himself by nature, but he is not himself in wickedness.

Let us consider how Paul had denied himself when he said: “I live, yet no longer I.” That savage persecutor had been extinguished, and a devout preacher had begun to live. For if he had remained himself, he certainly would not have been devout. But since he denies that he himself lives, let him say from whom it is that he cries out holy words through the teaching of Truth. He immediately adds: “Rather, Christ lives in me.”

As though he were openly saying: “I have been extinguished from myself, [Col. 1347B] because I do not live according to the flesh; yet I am not dead in essence, because I live spiritually in Christ.”

### CHAPTER V

“My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19).

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXX, nos. 47–48.) Just as does a doe that bends down toward childbirth, gives birth, and emits cries, so holy preachers cry out when, through their bending down in the conduct of the light, they give birth to the souls of their hearers. For they cannot remove them from eternal punishments except by weeping.

Now they sow in tears so that afterward they may reap a harvest of joys; now, like does, they are in the pains of childbirth so that afterward they may be fruitful in spiritual offspring.

To speak of one among many, I see Paul, like a doe in labor, emitting the cries of great pain. For he says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you. I wish that I could be present with you now and change my voice, because I am [Col. 1347C] perplexed about you.”

Behold, he wishes to change his voice in his labor, so that the speech of preaching may be changed into a cry of pain. He wishes to change his voice because those whom he had already brought forth by preaching he was again bringing forth with groans by reforming them.

What kind of cry did this laboring doe utter when, compelled to cry out to those same people who had turned back from him, he said: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?” (Galatians 3:1); and: “Why are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being completed by the flesh?” Or certainly: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?”

What a cry there was in the labor of this doe, who had given birth with so many difficulties to children conceived long before, and eventually discovered that her offspring had returned to the womb of wickedness! Let us consider what pain she endured and what labor she suffered—she who, after being able to bring forth those whom she had conceived, was compelled once more to raise the dead.

It must be especially noted that does bend down in order to give birth, for if they stood upright they could not give birth. Likewise, unless holy preachers descended from the immensity of the inner contemplation that they grasp, through the most humble preaching of a kind of bending down, to our [Col. 1347D] weakness, they would never beget children in the faith.

They could not benefit us if they persisted in the uprightness of their own height. But let us see the doe bending down in order to give birth: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal—as little ones in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3:1–2). Immediately afterward he explains the reasons for this bending down, saying: “For you were not yet able, and indeed even now you are not able” (ibid.).

But let us see this doe, who bent down for our sake, standing upright. He says: “We speak wisdom among the mature” (1 Corinthians 2:6). And again: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (2 Corinthians 5:13). But when he is beside himself for God, we do not receive his ecstasy at all. Therefore, in order to win us, he bends down to us; hence he suitably adds there: “Whether we are of sound mind, it is for you.”

### CHAPTER VI

“Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh” (Galatians 5:24).

[Col. 1348A]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book VIII, nos. 72–73.) Every hypocrite afflicts his body through abstinence, yet through his love of glory he lives for the world. In contrast, Paul rightly says of the elect: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.”

We crucify the flesh with its vices and desires if we restrain the appetite in such a way that we seek nothing from the glory of the world. For the person who mortifies his body but pants after honors has brought the cross to his flesh, yet through desire lives for the world. Often, indeed, someone who is unworthy attains a position of leadership under the appearance of holiness—a position he would not have deserved to receive unless he had displayed some virtue in himself. But what he obtains with delight passes away, while what follows remains with pain.

### CHAPTER VII

“If a person is overtaken in any offense” (Galatians 6:1).

[Col. 1348B]

(Pastoral Rule, Part II, chapter 10.) When a person sins not through malice but through ignorance alone or weakness, the correction of the offense must certainly be tempered with great moderation. As long as we remain in this mortal flesh, we are all subject to the weaknesses of our corruption.

Therefore each person ought to gather from himself how he should show mercy toward another’s weakness, lest, if he is carried too fervently into reproof against the weakness of his neighbor, he appear to have forgotten himself. Hence Paul rightly admonishes us, saying: “If a person is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted.”

As though he were openly saying: “When what you observe in another’s weakness now displeases you, consider what you are, so that the spirit may moderate its zeal for reproof while fearing for itself the very thing it reproves.”

### CHAPTER VIII

“Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2).

[Col. 1348C]

(Book II, in Ezekiel, Homily 1, no. 5; Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 27.) Just as in a building one stone bears another, because one stone is placed upon another, and the one that bears another is itself borne by another, so in the holy Church each person bears another and is borne by another.

For neighbors mutually tolerate one another, so that through them the structure of charity may rise. Thus Paul admonishes us, saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”

What else should the law be understood as meaning here except charity, through which the commandments of life are always read in the mind, so that they may be observed in action? The law of Christ is charity, because he both generously bestowed his good things upon us and patiently bore our evils.

We therefore fulfill the law of Christ by imitating him when we also generously contribute what is ours and piously endure the evils of our own people, bearing fraternal burdens out of love.

Paul again declares the power of this law, saying: “The fullness of the law is charity” (Romans 13:10). For if I refuse to bear with you in your conduct, and you disdain to tolerate me in mine, from where does the structure of charity arise among [Col. 1348D] you, whom reciprocal love does not join through patience?

Now, therefore, some are borne by you, while we have been borne by others. Those who will be born at the end of the Church—that is, at the extremity of the world—are indeed tolerated by their elders, so that their conduct may be shaped toward good merits. But since they do not follow those who may advance through them, they bear no stones of a faithful structure above themselves.

The foundation, however, bears the entire weight of the structure, because our one Redeemer bears the conduct of all. Of him Paul says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

Our Redeemer therefore bears all our burdens, but there was no evil in him that needed to be borne; and he alone bears your sins who carries the entire structure of his holy Church. Through the prophet’s voice he says of those who are still living perversely: “I am weary, bearing it” (Jeremiah 6:11).

### CHAPTER IX

“The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

[Col. 1349A]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book V, no. 4.) God’s elect desire utterly to die to the world, so that just as they desire nothing in the world, so they may no longer be held by any obligation to the world.

Often it happens that a person no longer holds the world in his mind, yet the world still binds the person through its occupations. He himself is already dead to the world, but the world itself is not yet dead to him. For the world, as though still alive, continues to desire him, striving to draw him, intent upon something else, into its own activities.

Thus Paul, who himself perfectly despised the world and saw that he had become such that he could no longer desire this world at all, says, freed from the bonds of this life: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

The world had been crucified to him because he no longer loved it, since it had died to his heart. But he had also crucified himself because he strove to present himself to the world in such a way that, as though he were dead, he could not be desired by it.

Paul therefore, who testified that he was wholly [Col. 1349B] dead to this world, was not content to say, “I have been crucified to the world,” unless he also added, “The world has been crucified to me,” so that he might testify not only that he was dead, but also that the world was [Col. 1350A] dead to him, and that neither he desired the world nor the world desired him.

If, for example, two people are in one place, one alive and the other dead, although the dead person does not see the living person, the living person nevertheless sees the dead one. But if both are dead, neither sees the other. Likewise, someone who no longer loves the world but is nevertheless loved by it, even unwillingly, does not see the world, as it were being dead; yet the world, still not dead, continues to see him.

But if he neither retains the world in his love nor is retained by the world’s love, then each is extinguished for the other, because, while one does not desire the other as though dead, he pays no attention to the dead.

Since Paul therefore neither sought the glory of the world nor was sought by the glory of the world, he boasts that he was crucified to the world and the world to him.

To show that, through the rejection by which he had humbled and cast himself down, he had become such that neither he desired the world nor the world desired him, he not only said that he had been crucified to the world, so that, as though dead, he would not see the world’s glory that he might desire [Col. 1350B]; he also asserted that the world had been crucified to him, since he had cast himself down in such profound humility that the world itself, as though dead, could no longer see humble and despised Paul.

## EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE EPHESIANS

[Col. 1349]

### CHAPTER I

“He purposed to restore all things in Christ” (Ephesians 1:9).

[Col. 1349B]

(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, Book XXXI, no. 99.) The most powerful choirs of angels, although not complete but remaining fixed in their own state when the devil fell with his angels, may nevertheless be called broken and diminished, because part of them fell and part remained.

They stand complete in the quality of their merit, but they are broken and diminished in the quantity of their number. The Mediator came to restore this breach, so that, when the human race had been redeemed, he might repair the angelic losses and perhaps enrich even more abundantly the measure of the heavenly homeland.

Because of this breach it is said of the Father: “He purposed in him, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth, in him.”

In him the things on earth are restored when sinners are converted to righteousness. In him the things in heaven are restored when humbled human beings return there, [Col. 1349C] where the proud apostate angels fell.

### CHAPTER II

“The Father raised Christ from the dead, setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, authority, power, and dominion” (Ephesians 1:21).

(Homily 34 on the Gospels, §§7–8, etc.) The Lord created the nature of angels and human beings in order that they might know him; and since he willed that it should endure unto eternity, he undoubtedly created it in his own likeness. There are nine orders of angels; but, so that the number of the elect might be completed, the human being was created as the tenth. Humanity was indeed created in the image of God, but by sinning withdrew from the likeness of its Creator. Nevertheless, it did not perish after its fault, because the eternal Wisdom of God appeared in human nature and, shining forth through the flesh in miracles, restored it.

Now nine orders of angels are found to exist. Hence the prophet says even to that angel who was created first:

[Col. 1349D]

> You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God (Ezek. 28:12).

Here it must be noted that he is said not to have been made “in the likeness of God,” but “the seal of likeness,” so that, the more subtle his nature is, the more subtly the image of God may be understood to have been expressed in him. Immediately afterward the passage continues:

> Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, and jasper; chrysolite, onyx, and beryl; sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald (ibid.).

Behold, he names nine kinds of stones, because there are certainly nine orders of angels. [Col. 1350B]

That first angel was adorned and covered with these orders because, being placed above all the angelic ranks, he was more splendid by comparison with them.

Thus, as the sacred word bears witness, we know of angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. Nearly all the pages of sacred Scripture testify to the existence of angels and archangels. The books of the prophets, as is well known, frequently speak of cherubim and seraphim. The Apostle Paul also enumerates the names of four orders in this Epistle to the Ephesians, saying:

> Above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion (Eph. 1:21).

Of thrones he writes to the Colossians:

> Whether thrones, or powers, or principalities, or dominions (Col. 1:16).

It must be understood, however, that “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. For those holy spirits of the heavenly homeland are always spirits, but they cannot always be called angels, because they are angels only when something is announced through them. [Col. 1350C] In the Greek language, *angeloi* means “messengers,” while *archangeloi* means “chief messengers.” Those who announce lesser things are called angels; those who announce greater things are called archangels.

“Virtues” are the spirits through whom signs and miracles are more frequently performed. “Powers” are those who have received this more powerfully than others in their order, so that hostile virtues are subjected to their authority and restrained by their power from tempting human hearts as much as they wish. “Principalities” are those who preside even over the good spirits of the angels and, being set over others, exercise authority over them while arranging what must be done in the performance of divine ministries. “Dominions” are those who transcend even the powers of the principalities by a lofty distinction. To exercise principality is to stand first among others; to exercise dominion is also to possess those who are subject. Those angelic ranks, therefore, which excel in wondrous power are called dominions because the others are subjected to them for obedience.

[Col. 1350D]

In that supreme city, certain properties belong especially to individuals, yet they are common to all; and what each possesses in part, another order possesses in its entirety. They are therefore not all designated by one and the same common name, so that the order which has more fully received a particular gift may be called by the special name of that gift. We have said that the seraphim signify burning; yet all alike burn with love of their Creator. The cherubim signify the fullness of knowledge; yet who there is ignorant of anything, [Col. 1351A] where all together behold God himself, the source of knowledge? Those ranks are called thrones upon which the Creator presides in order to exercise judgments; yet who can be blessed unless his Creator presides over his mind?

What is given to all in part is therefore given by a special name to those who have received it more fully. Although some there possess things in such a way that others cannot possess them—for example, certain ones are called dominions and principalities by a special name—everything there belongs to each, because through the love of the Spirit the gifts possessed by one are held by others. Since that heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, and since we believe that as many human beings will ascend to it as the number of the angels who remained, it follows that those human beings who return to the heavenly homeland must imitate something of those angelic ranks, so that by similarity of conduct they may be assigned to their lot.

There are some who grasp only small things, yet do not cease piously to announce these same small things to their brothers. Such people run among the number of the angels. There are others who, [Col. 1351B] filled with the gift of divine generosity, can both grasp and announce the greatest heavenly secrets. Where, then, are such people assigned except among the number of the archangels? There are others who perform wonders and powerfully work signs. To what place, then, do these belong except to the lot and number of the heavenly virtues? There are others who drive evil spirits from possessed bodies and cast them out by the power of prayer and the force of the authority they have received. To what rank, then, do these attain their reward except among the number of the heavenly powers?

There are others who, having received virtues, even surpass the merits of elect human beings. Since they are better than the good, they also preside over their elect brothers. Where, then, have they received their lot except among the numbers of the principalities? There are others who so rule over all vices and desires within themselves that, by right of their purity, they are called gods among human beings. Hence it is said to Moses:

> Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh (Exod. 7:1).

To what place, then, do such people run except among the numbers of the dominions?

[Col. 1351C]

But, most beloved brothers, as I speak of these things, turn inward and return to yourselves; examine the merits and thoughts within you. See whether you already practice any good inwardly with yourselves; see whether, among the number of those ranks that we have briefly touched upon, you find the lot of your calling. Woe to the soul that recognizes nothing of these goods we have enumerated within itself. An even greater woe threatens it if it understands that it is deprived of these gifts and yet does not grieve. Whoever is such, my brothers, must be deeply mourned, because he does not mourn.

Let us therefore consider the gifts received by the elect, and, with whatever strength we possess, let us pant after the love of so great a lot. Let the one who recognizes no grace of gifts within himself grieve; but let the one who recognizes lesser gifts within himself not envy greater gifts in others, because those distinctions among the heavenly good spirits have been established in such a way that some are placed before others.

## CHAPTER III — He made us sit with him in the heavenly places (Eph. 2:6)

[Col. 1351D]

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book VI, §24; book III, §25.)* When the elect humble themselves in this life, they pass beyond all temporal things by the judgment of a lofty mind; and when they consider themselves unworthy in everything, they trample underfoot the glory of this world by the scrutiny of right thought. Let them observe the humble Paul saying to his disciples:

> For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord; and ourselves as your servants through Christ (2 Cor. 4:5).

Let us observe the humble man, already placed on high, saying:

> Do you not know that we shall judge angels? (1 Cor. 6:3)

And again:

> Our citizenship is in heaven.

And once more:

> He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places.

Paul does not wish the mind to be cast down into the depths; he does not wish to dwell in lowly places through the degradation of human conduct. Perhaps Paul was then being held in prison when he testified that he was seated with Christ in the heavenly places. Yet he was there [Col. 1352A] where he had already fixed his ardent mind, not where his still sluggish flesh necessarily held him. Perhaps a chain then bound him outwardly, but in his mind he had been placed on high, because through the certainty of his hope he was already seated in the heavenly places.

Holy men are therefore despised outwardly and endure everything as though unworthy, but, confident that they are worthy of the heavenly seats, they await the glory of eternity with certainty. When they suffer outwardly under the adversity of persecution, they return, having been admonished, to the fortress of the mind; from there they look down upon everything beneath them and see that they themselves are also passing bodily through these things. They do not fear threats, because even while suffering torments they despise them. Hence Solomon says:

> The righteous is confident as a lion and will be without fear (Prov. 28:1).

Again it is written by him:

> Nothing that happens will sadden the righteous (Prov. 12:21).

Because all the upright are situated on the summit of their lofty purpose, and because they do not perceive death when dying, the arrows of the wicked wonderfully both strike them and do not touch them. For from the very point at which they despise themselves in everything, [Col. 1352B] they become more secure against everything.

Our Lord still suffers many things through the body that we are, and already his body—that is, the Church—glories in heaven from its head, namely the Lord. If the torments of our head did not touch him, he would never have cried out from heaven to his persecutor on behalf of his afflicted members:

> Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:5)

If our sufferings were not his suffering, afflicted Paul would certainly not have said:

> I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ (Col. 1:24).

And yet, exalted already by the resurrection of his head, he says:

> He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places.

The torments of persecution had indeed confined him on earth; but, pressed beneath the weight of his punishments, behold, through the glory of his head he was already dwelling in heaven. We therefore know and believe that head and body are united in all things by a bond of glory.

## CHAPTER IV — You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves (Eph. 2:8)

[Col. 1352C]

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIII, §13.)* When arrogant people do something good, they either judge that they possess it from themselves or, if they believe that it has been given to them from above, think that they received it on account of their own merits. The one who was boasting that he possessed goodness from himself is addressed through the Apostle:

> What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it? (1 Cor. 4:7)

Again, lest we think that the good of grace is given to us because of our preceding merits, the same Apostle admonishes us, saying:

> You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast.

He also says of himself:

> I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy (1 Tim. 1:13).

By these words he plainly declares that grace is not bestowed on account of merits, since in his own case he showed both what he deserved because of his wickedness and what he received because of divine benevolence.

## CHAPTER V — I ask that you not lose heart in my tribulations for you (Eph. 3:13)

[Col. 1352D]

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXI, §17.)* True teachers possess toward their disciples the inward compassion of fear arising from the power of love; hypocrites, however, fear those entrusted to them all the less because they do not even perceive what they ought to fear for themselves. How tender was the compassion Paul bore when, burning with such great love for his children, he said:

> We live, if you stand firm in the Lord (Phil. 1:8).

And:

> God is my witness, how I long for you all in the compassion of Jesus.

Indicating his love also to the Thessalonians, he says:

> But we, brothers, having been separated from you for a short time, in presence but not in heart, hasten all the more eagerly to see your face, with great desire (1 Thess. 3:8).

Pressed by harsh persecutions and yet anxious for the salvation of his children, he added:

> We sent Timothy, our brother and God’s minister in the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and exhort you concerning your faith, so that no one might be shaken by these tribulations; for you yourselves know that we have been appointed to this (1 Thess. 3:2).

He also says to the Ephesians:

[Col. 1353A]

> I ask that you not lose heart in my tribulations for you, which are your glory (Eph. 3:13).

Behold: placed in tribulation, he exhorts others; and by what he endures, he strengthens them. He had not forgotten his children, but was exceedingly afraid that his disciples, seeing so many reproaches of persecution in their preacher, might despise the faith in him, against which the countless insults of his sufferings might prevail. Therefore he grieved less over his own torments, but feared more that his children might be tempted by the sight of those torments. He regarded bodily wounds inflicted upon himself as little, while fearing wounds of the heart in his children. He himself received the wounds of torments by suffering, but by consoling his children he healed the wounds of their hearts.

Let us consider, then, what love it was to fear for others amid his own sufferings; let us consider what love it is to seek the salvation of one’s children amid one’s own losses, and to preserve the state of mind in one’s neighbors even through one’s own humiliation.

## CHAPTER VI — That you may comprehend with all the saints, etc. (Eph. 3:18)

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book I, §15.)* The outstanding [Col. 1353B] teacher presents the power of almighty God to us very well when he briefly says:

> That you may comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth.

God possesses breadth because he extends his love even to the gathering in of persecutors. He possesses length because, patiently enduring us, he leads us to the homeland of life. He possesses height because he surpasses even the understanding of those who will be received into the heavenly assembly. He possesses depth because, below, he incomprehensibly exercises the judgment of his strictness upon the condemned.

He exercises these four things individually for us who are placed in this life: breadth by loving, length by enduring, height by surpassing not only our understanding but also our desires, and depth by strictly judging the hidden and illicit movements of our thoughts. Yet no one recognizes how unsearchable are his height and depth except one who either begins to be raised to the heights by contemplation or, [Col. 1353C] resisting hidden movements, begins to be troubled by the persistence of temptations.

## CHAPTER VII — Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:3)

[Col. 1353C]

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 22.)* However great the virtues with which the quarrelsome may be endowed, they can in no way become spiritual if they neglect to unite themselves with their neighbors through concord. For it is written:

> The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace (Gal. 5:22).

Therefore whoever does not care to preserve peace refuses to bear the fruit of the Spirit. Hence Paul says:

> Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal? (1 Cor. 3:3)

Again he says:

> Pursue peace with everyone and holiness, without which no one will see God (Heb. 12:14).

Again he admonishes us, saying:

> Be eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling.

We cannot reach the one hope of our calling unless we run toward it with a mind united to our neighbors.

## CHAPTER VIII — Be renewed in the spirit of your mind (Eph. 4:23)

[Col. 1353D]

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXII, §7.)* The mind that strives through daily renewal of fervor always to begin again through desire does not know how to grow old through sluggishness. Hence Paul says:

> Be renewed in the spirit of your mind.

Hence the Psalmist, who had already reached the summit of perfection, spoke as though beginning:

> I said, “Now I begin” (Ps. 76:11).

For if we do not wish to grow weary of the good things we have begun, it is very necessary that we believe ourselves to begin anew each day.

## CHAPTER IX — Let all bitterness and anger be taken away from you (Eph. 4:31)

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 10.)* The patient must strive to love those whom they are obliged to tolerate, lest, if love does not follow patience, the virtue displayed be transformed into the worse fault of hatred. Hence, when Paul said:

> Love is patient (1 Cor. 13:4),

he immediately added:

> It is kind,

showing, clearly, that those whom it tolerates through patience [Col. 1354A] it does not cease to love through kindness.

Hence the same outstanding teacher, when urging patience upon his disciples, says:

> Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be taken away from you.

As though, after setting all outward things in order, he then turns to the interior and adds:

> With all malice.

For indignation, shouting, and blasphemy are removed from outward behavior in vain if malice, the mother of vices, rules within. Wickedness is cut away from its branches outside to no purpose if it is preserved in the root, where it will secretly multiply.

It is a virtue before human beings to tolerate adversaries, but before God it is a virtue to love them. The impatient should know that, when they do not resist their own agitation, they confuse even whatever good they may have accomplished with a tranquil mind and, by an unforeseen impulse, destroy whatever they perhaps built through long and careful labor. For through the vice of impatience the virtue of love is lost, although love itself is the mother and guardian of all virtues. It is written:

> Love is patient (1 Cor. 13:4).

Therefore, when it is not patient, it is not love. Of this same love Paul says:

> Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. 6:2).

The law of Christ’s unity is love, and only those fulfill it who do not go beyond proper bounds even when they are burdened.

## CHAPTER X — Let us not be carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. 4:14)

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XX, §23.)* Just as running water carries along very small stones, so teachers of perverse doctrines carry along human minds that are not fixed, but mobile, and not solidified by any stability of weight. Like streams, they continually lead such minds from place to place through the rivers of error. Hence the outstanding preacher, wishing his hearers not to be led about temporally but to be solidified by firm gravity, admonished them, saying:

> So that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro, nor carried about by every wind of doctrine.

## CHAPTER XI — That he might present to himself a glorious Church (Eph. 5:27)

[Col. 1354C]

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XX, §58; book XIII, §§10–12.)* The holy Church is Christ’s garment, as Paul testifies when he says:

> That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle.

For through sin it does not have a spot, nor through duplicity a wrinkle, because it is clean through righteousness and stretched smooth through singleness of purpose. Since it has been washed so that it might have no spot and stretched so that it might have no wrinkle, it is certainly a garment.

What is signified by wrinkles except duplicity? The wrinkles of the holy Church are therefore all those who live doubly within it, who proclaim faith with their words but deny it by their actions. The holy Church does not have these wrinkles in its elect, because they do not know how to display one thing outwardly and possess another inwardly. Hence, as was said above, the outstanding preacher rightly says:

> That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle.

The Church has neither spot nor wrinkle when it is free both from the shamefulness of deeds and from duplicity of speech.

Those who live in duplicity within it, however, when they see in times of peace that the Christian faith is honored by the powers of this world, pretend to be faithful. But when a sudden storm of adversity disturbs the holy Church and the time of persecution blazes forth, they immediately reveal what they are plotting with their faithless minds. Those who now slander through fear come forward to oppose, because they resist the true faith with openly expressed words.

[Col. 1354D]

It must be understood, however, that when we suffer these things from carnal people, it is not so much they themselves who rage against our death as the evil spirit that rules their minds, as Paul says:

> Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age (Eph. 6:12).

For what else are all the wicked than members of the devil? Through them, therefore, he himself does whatever he places in their hearts for them to do.

## CHAPTER XII — Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the Church (Eph. 5:25)

[Col. 1355A]

*(Homily 37 on the Gospels, §§1–3.)* The Truth says to those who come to him:

> If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, he cannot be my disciple.

Behold: the disciple proclaims that a wife must be loved, while the Master says:

> Whoever does not hate his wife cannot be my disciple (Luke 14:26).

Does the judge announce one thing and the herald proclaim another? Or can we hate and love at the same time?

But if we weigh the force of the command, we can do both through discernment: we can love our wife and those joined to us by kinship of flesh, whom we recognize as our neighbors; yet those whom we suffer as adversaries on the way of God we must know neither by loving nor by following them. Someone who is carnally minded is loved, as it were, through hatred when, while pressing evil things upon us, he is not obeyed.

[Col. 1355B]

In the same way, we rightly hate our own soul when we do not consent to its carnal desires, when we break its appetite and resist its pleasures. What is disregarded and led toward something better is loved, as it were, through hatred.

Thus, precisely, we must show our wife and our neighbors the discernment of hatred, so that in them we may love what they are and hate what obstructs us through them on the way of God.

When Paul was traveling to Jerusalem, the prophet Agabus took his belt, bound his own feet with it, and said:

> The Jews will bind the man whose belt this is in Jerusalem (Acts 21:11).

But what did the man who perfectly hated his own soul say?

> I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus; nor do I make my life more precious than myself (ibid., v. 13).

Behold how he hated his soul by loving it—or rather, by hating it he loved it. He desired to hand it over to death for Jesus, so that he might raise it to life from the death of sin.

[Col. 1355C]

Let us therefore draw from this discernment of our hatred a pattern for hating our wife and our neighbor. Let each adversary in this world be loved, but let no one who is opposed on the way of God be loved—whether spouse, neighbor, or any other relative.

## CHAPTER XIII — Everything that is exposed is made manifest by the light (Eph. 5:13)

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book VI, §40.)* The first virtue is to ensure that sins are not committed, but avoided. The second is at least to correct sins once committed. Yet often we not only fail to avoid impending faults, but [Col. 1356A] do not even acknowledge those already committed; and the sinner’s mind grows darker the more it fails to understand the harm caused by its blindness.

It therefore often comes about, through the generosity of divine mercy, that punishment follows fault and blows open the eyes of the delinquent, which security had kept blind amid vices. The sluggish spirit is touched by a blow so that it may be aroused; so that the person who, secure in himself, lost the state of his uprightness may, when afflicted, consider where he lies.

Thus the very harshness of correction becomes the source of light. Hence Paul says:

> Everything that is exposed is made manifest by the light.

The force of pain is an indication of salvation. Hence Solomon says:

> Healing will put an end to great sins (Eccles. 10:4).

Again he says:

> The Lord disciplines the one whom he loves and scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12:6).

Again, the Lord speaks to John with an angelic voice, saying:

> Those whom I love, I expose and discipline (Rev. 3:19).

Paul also says:

> No discipline seems at the time [Col. 1356B] to be joyful but sorrowful; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it (Heb. 12:11).

Therefore let every elect person rejoice to be worn down here by continual blows, so that, escaping eternal punishments, he may be found purified at the judgment. By the very weight of our weakness we are daily dragged downward unless we are lifted up by the helpful blows of the craftsman’s wondrous hand. Yet by the fact that the sinner is corrected and pressed by the pain of blows, he is eventually instructed for the blessedness that exists without the intervention of pain.

## CHAPTER XIV — Redeeming the time, because the days are evil (Eph. 5:17)

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book V, §70.)* At every time, from the beginning to the end of their lives, the reprobate persevere in committing iniquity and increasing their wickedness; they do not change their perverse minds even at the final hour. In contrast, Paul rightly admonishes us, saying:

> Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.

We redeem time when, by weeping, we restore the former life that we lost through wantonness. [Col. 1356C] In contrast, the Psalmist says of the reprobate:

> Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days (Ps. 54:25).

To halve one’s days means to divide the time of life spent in pleasures by the lamentations of repentance and to restore it by assigning it to good use. But the wicked do not halve their days because, as has been said, they do not change their perverse minds even at the final hour.

# EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS

[Col. 1355]

## CHAPTER I — I desire to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1:23)

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, §68.)* God’s elect are bound in this life by harsh bonds of distress, because they are still weighed down by the punishment of their corruption. To hunger, [Col. 1355D] thirst, and grow weary are bonds of corruption; but when we are stripped of corruptible flesh, we are released, as it were, from the bonds of distress by which we are now constrained.

We already desire to be presented to God, but we are still hindered by the obligation of a mortal body. We must therefore rightly be called bound, because we do not yet have free movement of our desire toward the Lord. Hence Paul, desiring eternal things but still carrying the burden of his corruption, cries out while bound:

> I desire to depart and be with Christ.

He would not seek to depart unless he clearly saw himself to be bound. Since he had perceived with complete certainty that these bonds would be broken in the resurrection, the Prophet rejoiced as though they had already been broken when he said:

> You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise (Ps. 115:7).

## CHAPTER II — Considering one another superior to yourselves (Phil. 2:3)

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIV, §43; Homily 10 on Ezekiel, §32.)* This is usually the distinctive mark [Col. 1356C] of the elect: they always think less of themselves than they are. Hence Solomon calls the little ones to wisdom, saying:

> If anyone is little, let him come to her (Prov. 9:4).

For whoever does not yet despise himself does not grasp the humble wisdom of God. Hence the teacher of the nations says:

> We became little ones in your midst [Col. 1356D] (1 Thess. 2:7).

Admonishing his disciples, he says:

> Considering one another superior to yourselves.

Because every wicked person considers everyone whom he thinks about to be beneath him, the righteous, by contrast, strives to regard every neighbor as superior. And lest, while one humbles himself, the other fall into exaltation, he rightly admonishes both sides, saying:

> Considering one another superior to yourselves,

so that in the thoughts of the heart I may prefer him to myself and, in turn, he may prefer me to himself; thus, when the heart is pressed down from both sides, no one is lifted up by the honor bestowed.

It often happens to the elect that, although they abound in the grace of many virtues, one very slight vice afflicts and assails them severely. Thus, when they see themselves weakened in one respect, they do not become proud of those virtues in which they excel; and while they tremble over their weakness, they preserve even the place where they are strong with greater humility.

Moreover, not all virtues are given to one person, lest he fall into pride when exalted. One person receives what is not given to you, and you receive what is denied to him, so that, when he considers the good that you possess and he does not, he may prefer you to himself in thought. Again, when you see that he possesses what you do not, [Col. 1357A] you may put yourself below him in your own thought, and what was said above may come to pass:

> Considering one another superior to yourselves.

By a wondrous dispensation, almighty God arranges his gifts among his elect in such a way that he gives one what he denies to another, and grants a greater gift to one and a lesser gift to another. Thus, when either one sees that the other possesses what he himself does not, or the other considers that the first has received more and judges that he himself has less, each admires God’s gifts in the other—that is, all admire them reciprocally. From this admiration one humbles himself before the other and considers the one whom he sees possessing what he does not have to be preferred to himself by divine judgment.

## CHAPTER III — Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized (Phil. 2:6)

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, §1; Homily 25 on the Gospels, §6.)* Our Lord Jesus, insofar as he is the power [Col. 1357B] and wisdom of God, was born from the Father before all times—or rather, because he neither began nor ceased to be born, let us more accurately say that he is eternally born. We cannot say “he is always being born,” lest he appear imperfect. But, so that he may be designated as eternal and perfect, let us say both “always” and “born.” “Born” pertains to perfection, and “always” to eternity. In this way, by whatever means, that timeless essence may be designated in temporal speech, although by the very fact that we call it perfect we depart greatly from expressing that truth, since what has not been made cannot be called perfect.

Nevertheless, the Lord, accommodating himself to the words of our weakness, says:

> Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect (Matt. 5:48).

Our Lord Jesus Christ, born from the Father outside time, was willing to be born from his mother in time. We must firmly and truly believe him to be the Son of God, coeternal and coequal with the Father in the eternity of substance.

[Col. 1357C]

Someone may perhaps be troubled by a silent question: how can the Son be equal to the Father? In this matter, what human nature cannot comprehend with wonder must learn to regard as credible from another wonder; for it has a brief answer to give itself. It is established that he himself created the mother in whose virginal womb he was to be created in human nature. Why, then, is it surprising that he is equal to the Father who existed before his mother?

With Paul as witness, we have learned that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24). Whoever therefore considers the Son lesser specifically dishonors the Father, whose wisdom he confesses to be unequal to him. What human being could calmly endure someone saying to him: “You are indeed great, but your wisdom is less than you are”?

The Lord himself also says:

> I and the Father are one (John 10:30).

And again he says:

> The Father is greater than I (John 14:28).

It is also written of him:

> He was subject to his parents (Luke 2:51).

It is therefore not surprising if, [Col. 1357D] in his human nature, he asserts that he is lesser than the Father in heaven, since in that same nature he was subject even to his parents on earth. In Paul’s heart, therefore, Jesus was equal to the Father by faith; Paul said the same:

> Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.

## CHAPTER IV — But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6)

*(In the Exposition of Blessed Job, book II, §42.)* The Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, came among human beings to provide them with an example of life. No one on earth is like him, because every human being is merely human, whereas he is God and human. Although each adopted son progresses toward receiving divinity, he did not receive it in such a way that he might naturally be God.

When God therefore took the form of a servant, the humility of the assumed flesh did not injure his majesty. He assumed it in order to save it, without changing what he already possessed; he neither diminished the divine through the human nor consumed the human through the divine. For, as Paul says:

> Although he was in the form of God, [Col. 1358A] he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.

For him to empty himself means to make himself visible from the greatness of his invisibility, so that the form of a servant might conceal what, by his divinity, penetrated all things without being circumscribed.

## CHAPTER V — A Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee according to the law (Phil. 3:5)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII, no. 44.) Holy men know with absolute certainty that they can by no means have rest in this life, and therefore subject themselves to hanging, because, abandoning earthly desires, they raise their minds to what is above. For everything that is suspended is undoubtedly lifted up from below. Thus the elect of God, suspended aloft, inflict death upon the strength of their flesh; girded by love of the heavenly homeland and devoted to the pursuit of virtues, they pursue through the bond of humility what they had previously been strong in possessing within the world.

It is pleasing to consider how Paul had suspended his soul, when he said: “I live, yet it is no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20). And again: “Having the desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23). And: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (ibid.). Recalling and enumerating the deeds of his earthly strength, he said: “A Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the law a Pharisee, according to zeal persecuting the Church of God.” But the suspension of the soul that immediately kills these strengths in him is expressly affirmed by what he adds: “But whatever things were gains to me, these I considered losses for Christ.” He further indicates that these strengths had been extinguished in him even more completely when he continues: “For whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and consider them as refuse.” Yet he shows how lifelessly he hangs after these strengths have died when he immediately adds: “That I may gain Christ and be found in him, not possessing that righteousness which comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Jesus Christ” (Phil. III, 9).

Behold: by bringing together his testimonies, we have shown Paul suspended aloft and dead to the world, because, while he lifted the intention of his mind to what is above, he killed within himself every strength belonging to exterior life.

## CHAPTER VI — “I do not consider myself to have apprehended” (Phil. III, 13)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXII, nos. 11–13.) There are some who, when they do anything good, immediately forget their sins. They fix the eye of their heart upon consideration of the good works they perform and now consider themselves holy, precisely because, amid the good things they do, they avoid remembering the evils in which they are perhaps still entangled.

If such people attentively considered the strictness of the Judge, they would fear their evils more than they would rejoice in their imperfect good works; they would look more closely at what they remain obliged to do than at the fact that, by performing certain deeds, they have already paid part of their debt. For a debtor is not discharged who repays much, but one who repays everything. Nor does someone reach the prize of victory who runs swiftly through most of the spectacle if, arriving near the goal, he fails in what remains.

We must therefore consider more carefully the good things we have not yet done than those we are already glad to have done. Often even the elect are tempted by this fault: their heart is frequently prompted to recall the good things they have done and to exult already in the joy of security. But if they are truly elect, they turn the eyes of their minds away from what pleases them. They suppress within themselves all joy over the good works they have completed and seek sorrow over those they understand themselves to have done inadequately. They consider themselves unworthy, and almost alone fail to see their own good works, which they offer to everyone else as an example to behold.

Hence, when Paul set aside the good things accomplished in him and thought only of what still remained to be completed, he said: “Brothers, I do not consider myself to have apprehended.” Hence also, so that he might humble himself concerning the good things he was doing, he took care to recall his former evils, saying: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” (I Tim. I, 13).

Although he once said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (II Tim. IV, 7), we must carefully observe that he said this at the time when he already knew that he was about to depart from the body. For there he first said: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand” (ibid., v. 6). Thus he recalled the perfection of his work when he had already foreseen that no time for further labor remained before the time of divine generosity.

For just as, while we live, we ought to drive our good works from our memory lest they exalt us, so, when our end approaches, we often rightly recall them to mind, so that they may provide confidence and suppress despairing fear. Although Paul also recounted his good works to the Corinthians, he did so in order to strengthen them, not to display himself. Since he regarded those same good works not in himself but in the Lord, he made this clear by disclosing the tribulation of his own temptation, when he expressly added: “Therefore I am pleased with my weaknesses” (II Cor. XII, 10).

Thus, in order to instruct his disciples, he recounted the highest things concerning himself; but, in order to preserve himself in humility, he fixed the eye of his consideration not upon his virtues but upon his weaknesses. Holy men therefore have this characteristic: they see the good things they do, yet, once they have completed them, they turn their eyes away from remembering them.

## CHAPTER VII — “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. III, 13)

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily III, no. 17.) The elect of God no longer look back with any desire upon what they have abandoned, but continually direct the contemplation of their minds toward the eternal things they desire. Hence that great preacher also said that he had flown up to the secrets of the third heaven. “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the prize of the heavenly calling.”

The eternal things are before us, while temporal things are behind us: we find the former as we proceed, and, as we withdraw from the latter, we leave them behind us as though at our backs. Paul, therefore, had stretched himself toward what lay ahead and had forgotten what was behind, because, scorning temporal things, he sought only what is eternal.

## CHAPTER VIII — “I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound” (Phil. IV, 12)

[Col. 1359C]

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 7, nos. 15–20.) All who are making their way toward the heavenly homeland ought to possess strength on both the right and the left: on the right, lest prosperity exalt us; on the left, lest adversity cast us down. Paul was strong on both sides when he said: “Through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful” (II Cor. VI, 7).

Adversity did not break him, nor did prosperity raise him up in mental pride. He remained strong in adversity and humble in prosperity. Confidence in adversity and fear in prosperity ought therefore always to be present in our minds, lest adversity drag us into despair or prosperity raise our spirit into confidence in itself.

Hence that same outstanding preacher said: “I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. Everywhere and in all things I have been instructed, both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me.”

Is it really some kind of skill to be brought low and to abound, to be filled and to hunger, to abound and to suffer want, so that so great a preacher declares that he knows these things as something extraordinary? It is an altogether profound and marvelous knowledge of discipline, which we must learn with the full exertion of our hearts.

Whoever is not broken by his poverty, is not turned away from thanksgiving, and is not inflamed with desire for temporal things knows how to be brought low. In this passage the Apostle means “to be brought low” as “to suffer want,” for immediately he adds the opposite: “I know how to abound.”

Whoever is not exalted by possessions received, does not turn them toward the use of empty glory, and does not possess alone what he has received, but mercifully distributes it among the needy, knows how to abound. Whoever uses food received not to stuff his belly but to restore his strength, and grants the flesh no more than necessity requires, knows how to be filled.

Whoever endures scarcity of food without murmuring, and does nothing on account of the necessities of sustenance by which the soul might fall into the snare of sin, knows how to hunger. Whoever is raised neither by pride in abundance nor provoked by greed in need knows how to abound and how to suffer want.

When Paul immediately adds, “I can do all things,” lest we think these words arise from exaltation, he adds: “In him who strengthens me.” Behold, a branch has grown upward; but because it remained in the root, it has continued green. It would dry up as it rose upward if it had separated itself from the root. For he attributes nothing to himself who confesses that he can do all things, not in himself but in him who strengthens him.

Thus, on both sides, the outstanding preacher proves himself strong: abundance does not draw him into pride, nor poverty into avarice. Let us therefore learn, brothers, to give thanks not only in prosperity but also in adversity.

In his compassion the Father became our Creator; he also nourishes us, his adopted children, for the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. He not only restores us through gifts but also instructs us through scourges. Let us learn, then, how to abound, so that we may share with the needy everything we receive from him; let us ensure that abundance does not raise our minds up, lest we perhaps rejoice because we possess what another lacks and rejoice no longer in the common good but in our own.

For this reason everyone desires to possess something, and more than is necessary: they become proud in possessing it and exalt themselves in their thoughts because another does not have it. Whoever is such has not yet learned how to carry abundance.

Often what avarice suggests out of desire he considers necessity. When lesser things would suffice, he grieves that greater things are lacking; and the unwary mind suffers a kind of necessity which it itself has produced. When what he desires is excessive, he somehow excuses his avarice to himself.

Abundance is therefore close to pride. If desire also seizes it, then, so to speak, a foreign captivity has invaded it. If we wish to know the art of abundance, we must flee not only the vices that are near at hand but also those that come from afar.

Let us learn to suffer want, lest we seek, even with guilt, to possess what we do not have, and lest we consider happy those whom we see weighed down with possessions. The things they prepare for themselves as though for the expenses of the present life are exceedingly numerous. They carry much, but on the short road of this journey poverty is a great companion for us: when earthly substance is absent, it does not constrict the soul, since we must render an account of that substance to the eternal Judge. We make our way to the homeland more freely because, as on a road, we are free from burdens.

Let us learn to be satisfied when taking bodily nourishment, lest we serve gluttony more than necessity. Desire often asks for more than necessity, and while we take care to satisfy the deficiency of the flesh, pleasure often slips in and exceeds the proper measure of refreshment. Thus one fault passes into another, because another temptation of the flesh often arises when the flesh is served too immoderately in refreshment.

Because nature was weakened by the sin of the first man, we are born into this world with its temptations. The flesh is sometimes our helper in good work, but at other times it leads us into evil. If, therefore, we give it more than we ought, we nourish an enemy; and if we do not give it what we owe to its necessity, we kill a fellow citizen. The flesh must indeed be satisfied, but only to the point at which it is able to serve in good work.

It is therefore a great art to be satisfied, lest anyone, through the satiety of the flesh, break out into the wickedness of shameful conduct. Let us learn to hunger, so that, because of the abundance that follows, our present want may please us. Let not the necessity of the belly draw us into sin, lest need itself suggest sin to the mind; lest, while the flesh is afflicted by hunger, the soul be provoked to desire and seek, with guilt, some means by which it may satisfy the flesh in its need; lest the heart leap into indignation and inflame the tongue with the bitterness of murmuring.

Whoever, therefore, in the want of his flesh looks around on every side and guards himself from the snare of sin knows how to hunger. Let us therefore, dearest brothers, flee anger and avarice in adversity, avoid exaltation and immoderate joys in prosperity, and maintain strength on both sides.

It is pleasing to recall to mind another citizen of the heavenly homeland and to show how strong he was in both conditions. Blessed Job, though he was richer than the men of the East, though every prosperity was available to him, his sons flourished, his household increased, and his flocks multiplied, nevertheless remained in such great fear of almighty God that, amid his vigilance in discipline, his practice of righteousness, and his many acts of humility, he devoted himself to works of mercy and to offering sacrifices. He offered a burnt offering to the Lord for each of his sons, lest any of them might have sinned at least in his heart.

Let us consider how great was the vigilance of his good work, since by sacrifices he expiated the sins of the heart in his sons. Yet his righteousness had become known in prosperity; it was entirely unknown whether he could persevere as a righteous man amid scourges. That holy man therefore had to be struck with a blow while prosperous, so that he might be tested by adversity; and the one known to almighty God might become known through scourges to us and to himself.

By the Lord’s arrangement, therefore, the flocks were destroyed, the servants killed, the house overturned, the sons slain, and his flesh struck from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. His wife alone remained unharmed, so that she might increase his wounds by the darts of her words. But the holy man, sound amid his wounds, wisely instructed her in the temptation and answered her, saying: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not receive evil things?” (Job II, 10).

His friends also came to console him, but broke out into insults, adding wounds of words to the pain of his injuries. They called him merciless, named him a robber, declared him violent, and accused him of oppressing the poor.

What, then, was the soldier of God to do, crushed beneath painful wounds and bitter words? Behold, the scourges of God and the words of human beings together pressed his afflicted soul toward despair. But, full of spiritual strength, lying amid wounds of the flesh yet standing firm in the strength of his mind, he recalled the good things he had done against the assault of despair.

Because he had been merciful, he said: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame” (Job XXIX, 15). And again: “I was a father to the poor” (v. 16). Because he had been both a guardian of discipline and kind, he said: “When I sat as a king, with the army surrounding me, I was nevertheless a comforter of the mourners” (v. 25).

Because he had been humble, he said: “If I despised entering into judgment with my servant or with my maidservant when they disputed against me” (Job XXXI, 13). Because he had been hospitable, he confessed: “If I disregarded a passerby because he had no clothing” (v. 19). Because he had been generous in gifts, he said: “If his sides did not bless me, and he was warmed by the fleece of my sheep” (v. 20).

Because he had not been violent, he testified, saying: “If I raised my hand against the orphan when he saw me as superior at the gate” (v. 21). Because he had never rejoiced at the danger of an enemy, he said: “If I rejoiced at the ruin of one who hated me” (v. 29). Because he had been patient and had endured even the malice of his own people with equanimity, he said: “If the men of my tent did not say, ‘Who will give us some of his flesh, that we may be satisfied?’” (v. 31).

Why, then, does the holy man enumerate so many of his virtues amid the scourges? Why does he praise with his own mouth the works he had done? Surely it is because, amid wounds and words that could have drawn him into despair, he reshapes his soul toward hope. He had been humble in prosperity; by recalling his good works to mind, he remained unbroken in adversity.

For whose soul would not those words, amid so many scourges, have driven him into despair, unless he had recalled to mind the good things he had done? The holy man therefore saw his mind shaken toward despair when it heard so many evils, and marvelously took care to strengthen it in certain hope through his good deeds.

Thus what is written is fulfilled: “In the day of good things, do not be forgetful of evils; and in the day of evils, do not be forgetful of good things” (Eccles. XI, 27). For if, when we are in good circumstances, we remember the evils we have either suffered or may still suffer, the good things we have received do not raise the mind, because fear of the evils remembered weighs down their joys. And if, when we have evils, we remember the good things we have either already received or still hope to receive, the burden of evils does not depress the soul into despair, because the memory of good things lifts it toward hope.

Thus, dearest brothers, let us walk by the commandments of the Lord and by the examples of the saints, so that prosperity may not raise us up, adversity may not break us, and we may show ourselves to possess strength both in prosperity and in adversity.

## CHAPTER IX — “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII, no. 74.) Just as the house of exterior dwelling is the building inhabited by the body, so the house of thought is whatever reality the soul inhabits through love. For whatever we love, we inhabit as though resting in it.

Therefore Paul, because he had fixed his heart on things above, said, though placed on earth yet a stranger to the earth: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

## CHAPTER X — “From there also we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Phil. III, 30)

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 2, no. 21.) After the resurrection there will be a likeness to our Lord Jesus Christ in our hearts, and our bodies too will receive his likeness through conformity. For then the bodies of the elect will be conformed to the glory of the Lord’s body. Although by nature they will not possess equality with his glory, by grace they will possess the likeness of conformity.

## CHAPTER XI — “I do not seek the gift, but I seek the fruit” (Phil. IV, 17)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX, no. 22.) The stipends owed to holy preachers ought to be conferred by their hearers; and those whom the labor of preaching assigned to them exhausts should be refreshed by the good work displayed by their disciples—not so that they preach in order to be fed, but so that they may be fed in order to preach, that is, so that they may continue preaching.

The activity of preaching should not pass over into an intention to obtain food; rather, the services of sustenance should serve the usefulness of preaching. Thus good preachers do not undertake preaching for the sake of obtaining food, but receive food from others for the sake of preaching. Whenever necessities are supplied to preachers by their hearers, they usually rejoice not in the gift of the possessions but in the reward of those who give them.

Hence Paul says: “I do not seek the gift, but I seek the fruit.” The gift is the thing itself that is offered; the fruit of the gift is that something is offered with a benevolent mind for the sake of a future reward. Thus we receive the gift in the thing, but the fruit in the heart.

Since the Apostle was nourished by the reward of his disciples rather than by their gift, he declared that he sought not the gift but the fruit. Therefore he immediately added: “But I have everything, and abound” (Phil. IV, 18).

Holy preachers, exhausted by preaching itself, ought therefore to be refreshed by the good works of their hearers, as did the one of whom it was said: “The hearts of the saints have found rest through you, brother” (Philem. 7). He had been refreshed by good work who, bound in chains, said: “May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, who often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain” (II Tim. II, 16).

# EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE COLOSSIANS

[Col. 1361]

## CHAPTER I — “Whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers, all things were created through him and in him” (Coloss. I, 16)

[Col. 1361D]

(Mixed from Homily 14 on the Gospels, no. 7 and following, and Book I on Ezekiel, homily 8, no. 20.) When speaking earlier to the Ephesians, the Apostle Paul had described dominions, principalities, and powers; but, intending to speak of these things also to the Colossians, he prefaced them with thrones.

Those angelic powers are called thrones which surpass even the angels themselves in the dignity of their higher station. For although angels are called messengers, and angels often come to announce various things to human beings, thrones are nowhere read to have been sent on a mission of announcement, since the Creator of all presides over them in a far more exalted manner.

Thus the Apostle Paul, describing the ranks of the hosts that he had seen when he was caught up to the third heaven, says: “Whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers.” He placed thrones before the other orders of angels because he knew that they were set above those others.

Those hosts are therefore called thrones over which almighty God continually presides in order to exercise judgment. Since in Latin we call thrones *sedes*, that is, seats, the thrones of God are said to be those who are filled with so great a grace of divinity that the Lord sits in them and through them decrees his judgments. Hence it is also said through the Psalmist: “You sit upon the throne, you who judge equity” (Ps. IX, 5).

Often, however, the orders of the blessed spirits take the names of the orders nearest to them. We have said that thrones, that is, the seats of God, are a distinct order of blessed spirits; yet the Psalmist says: “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear” (Ps. LXX, 2). This is because, while the cherubim are placed above the thrones within the distinctions of the hosts, the Lord is also said to sit upon the cherubim because of the equality of the neighboring host.

It must also be understood that there are certain human beings who, while ruling themselves with vigilant care, while examining themselves with attentive purpose and continually clinging to the fear of God, receive this gift of virtue: that they are able to judge rightly even concerning others. Since divine contemplation is present to their minds, the Lord presides in them as upon his throne, examines the deeds of others, and wonderfully dispenses all things from his seat.

What, then, are such people except thrones of their Creator? To what else are they counted except among the number of the heavenly seats? Through them the holy Church is governed, and often even the elect are judged concerning some of their weaker deeds.

## CHAPTER II — “From whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its bonds and connections...” (Coloss. II, 19)

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 6, no. 8.) The Redeemer of the human race advances daily in his members, who are us, through blows, because, while we are struck and afflicted so that we may deserve to be his body, he himself advances.

Concerning his body it is written: “From whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its bonds and connections, grows with the increase of God.” We are all his body. Through bonds and connections the body is joined together: the chest is joined to the head, the arms to the chest, the hands to the arms, and the fingers to the hands; the members cling to the other members, and the whole body is perfected.

Thus the holy apostles, because they stood close to our Redeemer, adhered to him as the chest adheres to the head. Since martyrs followed them, they were like arms joined to the chest. When pastors and teachers were added to them, their good works adhered to the arms like hands.

This whole body of our Redeemer is daily supplied in heaven through bonds and connections, because, when the souls of the elect are led there, his members are joined to him. Concerning this it is rightly said: “Supplied and constructed, it grows with the increase of God” (ibid.). Almighty God, our Redeemer, who has no need to advance in himself, nevertheless receives daily increase through his members.

Hence it is written again: “Until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV, 13).

## CHAPTER III — “For although I am absent in body...” (Coloss. II, 5)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXX, no. 31.) Holy preachers, while they desire to gather peoples into the bosom of the Church, burn with great ardor and send their longing now to one group, now to another, in order to gather them. For the sake of bringing souls together, they run with hungry minds through different modes, numbers, and divisions.

This very agitation of thought is a kind of wandering. The outstanding preacher Paul moves from place to place all the more restlessly the more powerfully he burns with charity. He desires to pass from one place to another because the charity that fills him impels him.

Although he was far from the Romans, he wrote: “I always make mention of you in my prayers, asking whether somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come to you. For I long to see you” (Rom. I, 9–10).

While detained at Ephesus, he wrote to the Corinthians: “Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you” (II Cor. XII, 14). Again, while staying at Ephesus, he said to the Galatians: “I would that I were with you now and could change my voice” (Gal. IV, 20).

Also confined at Rome by the custody of imprisonment, and unable to go personally to the Philippians, he promised to send his disciple, saying: “I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly, so that I too may be encouraged when I learn what concerns you” (Phil. II, 19).

Even bound in chains and detained at Ephesus, he wrote to the Colossians: “For although I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit” (Coloss. II, 5).

Behold how he wanders through holy desire: here he is held in body, there he is led in spirit. He displays the affection of a father to those who are present and shows it to those who are absent. To those who are physically present he gives his work; to those who hear him he expresses his wishes. He is effectively present with those among whom he is, yet he is not absent from those among whom he is not.
