We understand his wandering more clearly if we consider further what he says to the Corinthians: “I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia. For I will pass through Macedonia; but I may remain with you, or even spend the winter” (I Cor. XVI, 5).

Let us consider, I ask, what kind of wandering this is. Behold, for the moment he remains in one place, says that he will go to another, and promises to turn aside to a third. What makes him endure such anxious movement through so many places except that he is bound to everyone by one charity? Charity, which ordinarily unites what is divided, compels Paul’s one heart to be divided among many. Yet it gathers him more tightly into God the more widely it scatters him through holy desires.

Thus, by preaching, Paul wishes to speak to everyone at once; by loving, he wishes to see everyone at once. By remaining in the flesh, he wishes to live for everyone; and, by departing from the flesh through the sacrifice of faith, he wishes to benefit everyone.

## CHAPTER IV — “These things indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility...” (Coloss. II, 23)

[Col. 1364C]

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 19.) If the thoughts of those who practice abstinence were not sometimes pierced by the fault of pride, Paul would certainly not have said: “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Rom. XIV, 3).

Again, speaking to others and touching upon the instruction of those who gloried in the virtue of abstinence, he added: “These things indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility, and not in sparing the body, nor in any honor for the satisfying of the flesh.”

Here we must note that, in his argument, the outstanding preacher joins an appearance of humility to superstition. When the flesh is worn down through abstinence beyond what is necessary, humility is displayed outwardly, but inwardly there is serious pride in that very humility.

And unless the mind sometimes swelled through the virtue of abstinence, the arrogant Pharisee would never have deliberately counted it among his great merits, saying: “I fast twice a week” (Luke XVIII, 12).

## CHAPTER V — “Having love above all things” (Coloss. III, 14)

[Col. 1364D]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII, no. 46.) Every good of the virtues is easily destroyed when temptation bursts upon the heart, unless it is made firm from within by firmly rooted love.

Thus Paul, in his preaching, while setting certain virtues against temptations, immediately joined love to those same virtues as a kind of strength, saying: “Above all these things, having love, which is the bond of perfection.”

Love is called the bond of perfection because through it every good that is done is bound together lest it perish. Any work is more quickly torn away by the tempter if it is found detached from the bond of love.

But if the mind is bound by love of God and neighbor, then, whenever the movements of temptation suggest anything unjust to it, love itself opposes a barrier to them. It breaks the waves of evil persuasion against the gates of virtue and the garment of inward love, and through the strength of inspired charity it restrains and suppresses the assaults of vices as they arise.

## CHAPTER VI — “You have died, and your life is hidden” (Coloss. III, 3)

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book VIII, no. 45; book V, no. 9.) There are some righteous people who, girded to attain the summit of perfection, abandon everything outward while seeking higher things inwardly. They strip themselves of possessions, divest themselves of the glory of honor, and afflict themselves through continual sorrow from longing for what is within. They refuse to receive consolation from outward things.

As they draw near inward joys in mind, they utterly kill within themselves the life of bodily pleasure. They do not cease to mortify themselves with the sword of the sacred word amid the tumult of useless cares, and inwardly they hide themselves before the face of God in the bosom of the mind.

To such people Paul says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” We cannot die perfectly to the world unless we are hidden from visible things within the invisible realities of our mind.

Just as a tomb is the place where the body is hidden, so divine contemplation is a kind of tomb of the mind in which the soul is hidden. We live, as it were, for this world when we wander outwardly through it in our minds; but we are hidden as dead in a tomb when, having been put to death outwardly, we are concealed in the secret place of inward contemplation.

Thus Paul saw his disciples dead through contemplation and hidden as though in a tomb, when he said to them: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

# EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 1365]

## CHAPTER I — “Nor were we ever in flattering speech” (I Thess. II, 5)

[Col. 1365B]

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIX, no. 36.) Since it is written: “Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house”; and: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 15), holy men are sometimes compelled to do good before human beings or to recount their deeds to human beings. Yet they refer everything to this end: that not they themselves, through those works, but their Father who is in heaven should be glorified.

For while they preach holy things, their preaching may perhaps be despised because their life is unknown. They are therefore compelled to make their life known, so that they may be able to change the lives of their hearers. They recount their deeds so that they may be held in reverence; they desire to be revered so that they may be heard with respect.

For it is written: “When the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up together with them” (Ezek. I, 19). When the minds of hearers receive the life of preachers, they necessarily also admire the force of their preaching.

Thus good preachers flee honor on account of exaltation, yet wish to be honored for the sake of imitation. In this way the Apostle Paul, speaking to his disciples, both flees honor and shows how much he ought to be honored.

When he said to the Thessalonians: “For we were never in flattering speech, as you know, nor in an occasion for greed—God is witness,” he continued: “Nor seeking glory from human beings, neither from you nor from others, although we could have been burdensome to you as apostles of Christ; but we became little ones in your midst.”

## CHAPTER II — “We became little ones in your midst” (I Thess. II, 7)

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXIII, no. 24; Book XXIV, no. 53; Book XXIII, no. 24; Book XXIV, no. 54.) [Col. 1365D] True teachers both endeavor to proclaim humility—which is the teacher and mother of all virtues—and strive to demonstrate it by their lives, so that among the disciples of Truth it may speak more through conduct than through words. Hence Paul, speaking to the Thessalonians, after restraining the height of his authority by saying, “Nor seeking glory from human beings, neither from you nor from others, although we could have been burdensome as apostles of Christ” (I Thess. II, 6), immediately added, as though descending from the summit of his apostolic dignity: “But we became little ones in the midst of you.”

He had become little in their midst because he feared that, if he claimed for himself the honor of his exalted position among the disciples, he would display an example of pride. He clearly feared that, while seeking for himself the authority of pastoral power, the flock entrusted to him might follow him over precipices, and that he who had undertaken the office of piety might lead those who followed him into impiety. The apostle Peter likewise, when he said, “Always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you” (I Pet. III, 15), asserted that a proper manner of teaching must be preserved even in the knowledge of doctrine, saying: “But with gentleness and fear, having a good conscience.”

When Paul says this to his disciple Titus: “Command these things and teach with all authority” (I Tim. IV, 11; Tit. II, 15), he recommends not the domination of power but the authority of life. That is taught with authority which is practiced before it is spoken. For teaching loses its confidence when conscience restrains the tongue. He therefore conveyed not the power of arrogant speech, but the confidence of good conduct.

It is therefore necessary that the one who presides carefully consider what examples he offers to those subject to him, recognize that he must live at the same level at which he presides, and watch vigilantly lest he become swollen with pride in the position he has received, or demand the rights of due authority without measure. Otherwise the right of discipline may be changed into the harshness of pride, and the very means by which he could restrain his subjects from perversity may instead pervert the hearts of those who look to him. He must not become, through his office, a leader into impiety.

For an impious leader is one who, through arrogance, strays from the path of truth; and while he himself plunges headlong, he invites those who follow him toward the precipice. By the examples of his arrogance he shows his followers the way of error.

## CHAPTER III — “We wished to come to you, but Satan hindered us” (I Thess. II, 18).

[Col. 1366C]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXVII, no. 55.) Often holy preachers wish to exhort certain people but cannot; often they desire to withdraw from certain others, yet, driven by the impulse of an inward prompting, they are compelled to exhort them with the greatest urgency. Thus, when Paul wished to leave the Corinthians, shaking out his garments, he heard: “Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent, because I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you; for I have many people in this city” (Acts XVIII, 9).

Again, when he wished to go to the Thessalonians but was detained, he said: “We wished to come to you—I, Paul, indeed, both once and again—but Satan hindered us.” Satan could not of himself obstruct the paths of so great an apostle. Rather, while opposing him for the purposes of a hidden dispensation, he unknowingly served it: namely, so that while Paul wished to approach some people but was unable to do so, he might more suitably benefit those from whom he could not withdraw.

Thus holy preachers are led by the hand of God, who governs them, toward things they do not desire, and by that same governing hand they are again restrained from their own impulse. Subject to divine motions, they cannot accomplish what they wish, and they can go only where the will of the One who governs them leads.

## CHAPTER IV — “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord?” (I Thess. II, 19).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XI, no. 22.) The uprightness of those subject to them is the great glory of priests. As the outstanding preacher rightly says to his disciples: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord?”

But when priests neglect the lives of their disciples and bring no fruit of their progress before the Lord, what else can they be called but inglorious? For before the strict Judge they will then find no glory, because now, through the zeal of preaching, they do not seek it in the conduct of those subject to them.

## CHAPTER V — “Let no one be shaken by these tribulations; for you yourselves know that we have been appointed to this” (I Thess. III).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XIII, no. 18; Book III, no. 40.) The ancient enemy continually attacks the faithful of the holy Church with his blows and afflicts them with his strikes. Hence the outstanding preacher Paul, while enduring the evils of beatings and groaning under the persecutions of his adversaries, feared that his suffering might harm not himself but his disciples. Consoling their tender minds concerning his afflictions, he wrote to them: “Let no one be shaken by these tribulations; for you yourselves know that we have been appointed to this.”

It is as though he said openly: “Do not at all be astonished at our wounds in this present time, for if we seek eternal joys, we have come here for this purpose: to be struck. If we are striving toward eternal goods, it is not surprising that we suffer temporal evils.” He had carefully contemplated these goods when he endured the evils inflicted upon him with equanimity, saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

He therefore feared the downfall of others in his own suffering, lest, when the disciples recognized that he was afflicted with blows for the faith, they should refuse to profess themselves believers. O the bowels of immeasurable charity! He despises what he himself suffers, and takes care that his disciples should suffer no wound of corrupt persuasion in their hearts. In himself he disregards the wounds of the body, while in others he heals the wounds of the heart. Like some great physician who has been struck and is ill, he bears the lacerations of his wound himself while offering medicines of healing to others.

The righteous have this distinctive quality: when placed in the pain of their own tribulation, they do not abandon concern for another’s welfare. They know how to endure adversities outwardly while also knowing how to correct adversities within.

## CHAPTER VI — “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep” (I Thess. IV, 12).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book V, no. 54; Book XII, no. 12.) In Holy Scripture, sleep sometimes expresses the sluggishness of negligence, as blessed Paul says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep.” And again: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (Rom. XIII, 11).

At other times, under the name of sleep or falling asleep, the death of the flesh is signified. Thus the same Paul, giving admonition, says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep” (I Cor. XV, 34).

Speaking of the death of the flesh, he preferred to call it not death but sleep and falling asleep. For the name of death is greatly feared by weak minds, whereas the term “sleep” does not inspire fear. What, then, is the reason that the outstanding preacher calls the Lord’s death death, but names the death of the Lord’s servants not death but sleep? He does so because, observing the weakness of his hearers’ hearts, he composes the medicine of his preaching with marvelous skill. He does not hesitate to present as dead the One whom he already knew to have risen, while he calls those who had not yet risen not dead but sleeping, so as to instill hope of resurrection.

He did not fear calling dead the One whom his hearers knew had already risen, but he feared calling dead those whom they scarcely believed would rise. Because he does not doubt that those who have died in the flesh will awaken again to life, he calls them sleeping rather than dead, clearly conveying the hope of resurrection: just as a person awakens quickly from sleep, so at the command of the Creator he rises promptly from bodily death.

## CHAPTER VII — “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (I Thess. V, 2).

[Col. 1368B]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VII, no. 45.) While the reprobate believe that they will long remain among visible things, they abandon hope of invisible things; and when the mind is fixed on the present, life comes to an end. Suddenly they arrive at unforeseen punishments, which, deceived by their own presumption, they had believed would either never touch them or would come only late.

Hence Paul says: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.” Because its approach to seize the soul cannot at all be seen, it is compared to a thief in the night. Thus Paul rightly says to disciples who are thinking about the future: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you like a thief” (I Thess. V, 4).

The day of departure overtakes people like a thief in the night when it drives out the souls of fools who do not foresee what is to come. It ought therefore to be feared by everyone as though it were always coming, precisely because we cannot foresee its arrival. Alternatively, the day of the Lord may be understood as the day of judgment, which steals upon us in such a way that it cannot be foreseen when it comes.

# EXPOSITION ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 1367]

## CHAPTER I — “Your faith grows exceedingly” (II Thess. I, 3).

[Col. 1367C]

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 8.) We often lead fainthearted people more effectively back to the path of good conduct if we recall their good deeds. And if they have done anything improperly, we do not rebuke it as something already committed, but forbid it as something that must not yet be committed. In this way, the favor bestowed on what we approve increases it, while, against what we criticize, a modest exhortation grows stronger among the fainthearted.

Thus Paul, recognizing that the Thessalonians had persevered in the preaching they had received but had been disturbed by a certain faintheartedness concerning the supposedly imminent end of the world, first praises in them the strengths he sees, and afterward, by careful admonition, strengthens what has become weak.

For he says: “We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith grows exceedingly, and the charity of each one of you toward one another abounds, so that we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God for your patience and faith” (II Thess. I, 3).

After prefacing these flattering praises of their life, he shortly afterward added: “But we ask you, brothers, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, that you not be quickly shaken from your understanding, nor terrified, either by spirit, or by word, or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were at hand” (ibid., 1).

The true teacher acted so that they might first hear themselves praised for qualities they recognized, and afterward hear what they were urged to follow. Thus the preceding praise might strengthen their minds, so that the subsequent disturbance would not shake them. He knew that they had been disturbed by suspicion of the approaching end, but he did not rebuke them as already disturbed; rather, as though unaware of what had happened, he forbade them to become disturbed. In this way, while they believed that their preacher did not know of their very instability, they would become all the more blameworthy, because they feared that he might discover it.

## CHAPTER II — “You endure as an example of the just judgment of God” (II Thess. I, 4, 5).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book V, no. 22.) Everyone ought to consider what punishments later await sinners, if even the righteous are chastised here by such severe scourges. Hence Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the household of God; and if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the impious and the sinner appear?” (I Pet. IV, 17–18).

For this reason Paul, after saying many things in praise of the Thessalonians, immediately added: “So that we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God for your patience and faith, in all your persecutions and tribulations that you endure as an example of the just judgment of God.”

It is as though he said: “While you endure so many hardships, you who act so rightly, what else are you doing than providing examples of God’s just judgment? For from your punishment one must infer how he strikes those with whom he is angry, if he permits you to be afflicted in this way, you in whom he rejoices. He will strike much more severely those to whom he displays his just judgment, if he also torments you in this way, whom he lovingly corrects and cherishes.”

## CHAPTER III — “He will sit in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (II Thess. II, 4).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIV, no. 7; Book XXIX, no. 18; Book XXXII, no. 25.) By a terrifying order of hidden arrangement, before the ancient enemy appears in that condemned man whom he will assume—that is, in the Antichrist—the signs of power will be withdrawn from the holy Church. Prophecy will be concealed, the grace of healings will be taken away, the virtue of prolonged abstinence will be diminished, the words of teaching will fall silent, and the signs of miracles will be removed.

The heavenly dispensation will not altogether withdraw these things; rather, it will not display them openly and abundantly as in former times. This will nevertheless be accomplished by a marvelous dispensation, so that through one and the same event both divine mercy and justice may be fulfilled.

For while the holy Church appears more despised, deprived of the powers of signs, the reward of the good increases: they honor it for the hope of heavenly things, not because of present signs. At the same time, the minds of the wicked are revealed more quickly against it, because they neglect to follow the invisible things it promises when they are not held by visible signs.

Thus, while the humility of the faithful is deprived, as it were, of the multitude and manifestation of signs, the terrifying examination of the hidden dispensation grants mercy to the good through the very means by which just anger is heaped upon the wicked.

Before that time, therefore, signs of power and miracles will for the most part be withdrawn from the faithful in the holy Church. Then, against them, the ancient enemy will appear conspicuous and manifest in that condemned man, the Antichrist, through open prodigies, so that the more he exalts himself through signs, the more robustly and gloriously he may be conquered by the faithful without signs.

Signs will not, however, be lacking to the faithful in their struggle against him. His signs will be so great that ours will appear few or nonexistent. Yet the power of our signs becomes stronger than all signs, because everything that is terrifyingly seen to be done by him is crushed beneath the heel of inward steadfastness.

The malignant enemy will therefore display himself against them with a cruelty all the more savage because he will grieve at being despised even while miracles are becoming evident. He will gather his entire force for their destruction and will inflame all the reprobate with one mind and cruelty toward the death of the faithful.

The proud exaltation of the Antichrist will therefore be raised over the reprobate minds of human beings through the arrogance of worldly glory, so that the sinful man, though still a man and despising the thought that he should be regarded as merely human, will falsely claim to be God. Hence the apostle Paul says: “So that he will sit in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God.”

To make his terror more fully apparent, Paul had prefaced this by saying: “He who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped.” For a human being can sometimes be called “god,” as is also said to Moses: “Behold, I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exod. VII, 1). But a mere human being cannot be worshiped as God.

Because the Antichrist exalts himself above every holy human being and above the very power of divinity, he attempts, by claiming for himself the precise title of glory, to surpass both what is called God and what is worshiped as God.

It should be observed into what a pit of pride he has fallen, since he did not remain within the measure of the ruin into which he had fallen. The devil and human beings alike fell from the status of their proper condition through an exalted mind: the devil saying, “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13), and the human being believing what he heard: “Your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Gen. III, 5).

Each therefore fell because he desired to be like God, not through justice but through power. Yet the human being, liberated by grace, who had fallen perversely by desiring likeness to God, recognizing in the guilt of his crime that he is far inferior to God, cries out: “Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. XXXIV, 10).

The devil, however, justly abandoned in the guilt of his fall, did not remain within the measure of his ruin. The longer he remained distant from the grace of the almighty One, the more he accumulated the guilt of his crime. He fell because, in perverse order, he wished to be like God; but when he came in the Antichrist, he was brought to the point of disdaining even to appear like God, and, in his pride, he judged inferior the One whom he could not possess as his equal.

For when it is said of him, as already mentioned, “Exalting himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped” (II Thess. II, 4), it is openly shown that, once desiring the likeness of God, he wished to raise himself up as though beside God; but, growing in the guilt of pride, he now exalts himself above everything that is called God and worshiped as God.

Yet this pride of his will be struck down at the coming of the strict Judge, as it is written: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming” (II Thess. II, 8).

Concerning this lost man, Daniel says: “He will rise up against the Prince of princes, and he will be broken without a hand” (Dan. VIII, 25). What is said through Daniel—“He will rise up against the Prince of princes”—is said through Paul as: “So that he will sit in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God.” And what Daniel adds—“He will be broken without a hand”—Paul expresses as: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming.”

He will be broken without a hand, that is, not by an angelic battle or by the struggle of the saints, but by the coming of the Judge; by the breath of his mouth alone he will be struck with eternal death.

## CHAPTER IV — “So that he may be revealed in his own time; for the mystery of iniquity is already at work” (II Thess. II, 6–7).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXIX, nos. 15–16.) There are some who truly believe the eternal things they hear, yet neglect to live according to the preaching of faith. By living badly they contradict the same faith which they hold while venerating it outwardly.

Because they love earthly things more than heavenly things, and visible things more than what they hear, when the moment of persecution strikes, they lose what they appeared to believe rightly. This occurs most abundantly at that time when, with the very head of the wicked arising, his strength will rage with unrestricted force in the final persecution of the holy Church.

Then the heart of each person will be revealed; whatever lay hidden will be brought into the open. Those who are now pure in speech but impious in heart will fall when their wickedness is exposed, and they will lose the faith they had held only outwardly.

Hence Paul says: “So that he may be revealed in his own time; for the mystery of iniquity is already at work.” It is as though he said: “Then the Antichrist will be seen openly, because even now, hidden in the hearts of the wicked—that is, of his members—he secretly works his own mysteries.”

To say nothing of more open crimes, consider: one person silently envies his brother in his heart and, if he finds an opportunity, strives to undermine him. Whose member is he, if not the one of whom it is written: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wis. II, 24)?

Another, believing himself to possess great merit, places himself above everyone through the swelling of his heart and considers all others inferior to himself. Whose member is he, if not the one of whom it is written: “He sees every high thing, and he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI, 25)?

Another seeks worldly power, not in order to benefit others, but so that he may not be subject to anyone else. Whose member is he, if not the one of whom it is written that he said: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13–14)?

The Most High alone rules over all in such a way that he cannot be subject to another. The devil perversely wished to imitate him when, while seeking his own lordship, he refused to be subject to him.

Therefore, whoever desires power for himself precisely because he resents being subject, by heavenly ordinance, to the one set over him, imitates the devil.

There are also many other things that declare certain people, even while established in the peace of the Church, to be unbelievers. I see some people show partiality to a powerful person in such a way that, when questioned by him, they do not hesitate, for his favor, to deny the truth in a matter concerning their neighbor.

And who is the Truth, except the One who said: “I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life” (John XIV, 6)? John the Baptist did not die because of a confession about Christ, but because he was questioned about the truth of justice. Yet because Christ is the Truth, he reached death for Christ precisely because he reached it for the truth.

Let us place before our eyes a person who, when questioned, showed partiality to a powerful person and denied the truth so as not even to suffer an insult in words. What, then, would this person do amid the pain of punishments, if he was ashamed of Christ amid verbal blows?

Behold, even after this he is still a Christian in the eyes of human beings; yet if the Lord has resolved to judge him strictly, he is no longer one.

I also see others to whom, through the office of teaching, the duties of exhorting and rebuking have been entrusted. They see something unlawful being committed, yet, fearing to offend the favor of certain powerful people, they do not dare to rebuke it.

Whoever this person is, what else does he do except see the wolf coming, abandon the sheep, and flee (John X, 12)? He flees because he remains silent, because, disregarding eternal favor, he has loved temporal glory more.

Behold, before the face of the powerful person he hides himself within the recesses of his silence; and, just as he would to public persecution, so he has yielded ground to hidden fear. Whoever is such a person, if these matters are judged strictly, even if public persecution was absent, has nevertheless denied Christ by remaining silent.

The temptations of the Antichrist are therefore not absent even during the peace of the Church. Let no one fear only those final times of persecution as though they alone were to be dreaded. Among the wicked, the affairs of the Antichrist are enacted daily, because he already works his mystery secretly in their hearts.

And although many who are established within the Church only outwardly now pretend to be what they are not, at the coming of the Judge they will be exposed as what they are. Concerning them Solomon rightly says: “I saw the wicked buried, even while they were still living; they were in the holy place, and they were praised in the city as though they had performed righteous works” (Eccles. VIII, 10).

## CHAPTER V — “Do not regard him as an enemy” (II Thess. III, 15).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 22.) When temporal peace is disturbed in the hearts of the wicked by our rebuke, it is necessary that inviolable peace be preserved in our own hearts. Hence he admonishes the disciples, saying: “If anyone does not obey our word through the letter, take note of him, and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame.” And immediately he adds: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother.”

It is as though he said: “Break external peace with him, but preserve inward peace toward him in the depths of your heart, so that your disagreement may strike the mind of the sinner in such a way that peace does not depart from your hearts, nor is it denied by them.”

# EXPOSITION ON THE FIRST EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 1371]

## CHAPTER I — “I obtained mercy because I acted in ignorance” (I Tim. I, 13).

[Col. 1371B]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XVIII, nos. 62–63.) No one can say that, by the recompense of his own actions, he has gone beforehand in coming to know God, or that he has offered some merit of worthy work as a price by which he might receive Christ, the power and wisdom of God. We give a price for this purpose: so that we may possess in exchange the thing we desire.

But what did we give in order to deserve to receive Wisdom, who is Christ? We were redeemed by grace. The only works we gave were those of an evil life; if a just recompense had been assigned to them, they would have received not Christ but punishments.

A person has therefore deserved one thing by justice and received another by grace. Paul testifies to the thorns of error that oppressed him before his mind received the seed of gratuitous truth: “I was formerly,” he says, “a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy because I acted in ignorance, in unbelief” (I Tim. I, 13).

He also testifies for what sort of people Christ deigned to die: “While we were still sinners,” he says, “at the appointed time Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. V, 8).

When Christ, the power and Wisdom of God, came, we were found to be ungodly. What good work, then, did we offer by which we deserved to receive him? Paul understood that no one had been saved by his own merits, and he knew that no one had offered any good work in order to come to faith. Thus he said: “Who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him?” (Rom. XI, 35).

Again it is written: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. II, 8). Again he speaks about himself, saying: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV, 10).

Since, through the inspiration of this grace, works of virtue are immediately generated in the heart, so that action may also follow from free choice and eternal recompense may correspond to it after this life, he immediately added: “And his grace toward me was not fruitless.”

## CHAPTER II — “Women are to adorn themselves in well-ordered dress, with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing” (II Tim. II, 9).

[Col. 1371D]

(*Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 6, no. 3.) Let no one suppose that there is no sin in luxury and in the desire for costly clothing. If this were not a fault, the Lord would never have praised John the Baptist for the roughness of his clothing. If this were not a fault, Paul would never have restrained women through his letter from desiring costly clothing, saying: “Not in costly clothing.”

The blessed apostle Peter likewise says: “Let women be subject to their husbands. Their adornment should not be external, consisting of braided hair, or the wearing of gold, or the adornment of clothing” (I Pet. III, 3).

Consider, then, what kind of fault it is for men to desire what the pastor of the Church and outstanding teacher took care to forbid even to women.

## CHAPTER III — “But the woman will be saved through the bearing of children” (I Tim. II, 15).

[Col. 1372B]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XII, no. 26.) In Holy Scripture, the name “children” sometimes signifies works. Thus Paul says concerning a woman: “She will be saved through the bearing of children.”

He does not mean that a woman who pursues continence and does not bear children will not be saved. Rather, she is said to be saved through the bearing of children because through the production of good works she is joined to everlasting salvation.

## CHAPTER IV — “It is necessary for a bishop to be blameless,” etc. (I Tim. III).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chapter 8; *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXI, no. 19.) Instructing Timothy concerning the office of the episcopate, Paul says: “If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work.”

Yet, while praising the desire, he immediately turns what he praised into a source of fear, when he adds: “But it is necessary for a bishop to be blameless.” As he subsequently enumerates the virtues required, he makes clear what blamelessness is. Thus he encourages through desire and terrifies through command.

It is as though he said openly: “I praise what you seek, but first learn what you are seeking, lest, while neglecting to measure yourselves, your blameworthiness appear all the more shameful because you hasten to be seen by everyone at the summit of honor.”

The great master of governance urges people forward by praise and draws them back by fear. By describing the height of blamelessness, he restrains his hearers from pride; and by praising the office they seek, he shapes them for a good life.

The office of the episcopate itself is also defined by the expression “good work,” when it is said: “If anyone desires the episcopate.” Therefore, the person who does not desire the episcopate is his own witness: he seeks through it not the ministry of good work but the glory of honor.

Concerning this same episcopal office, he teaches: “It is necessary for a bishop to be without crime.” The difference between sin and crime is this: every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime. In this life many can be without crime, but no one can be without sins.

Thus the holy preacher, when describing a man worthy of priestly grace, did not say, “If anyone is without sin,” but, “If anyone is without crime.” No one can be without sin, since John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8).

## CHAPTER V — “Great is the mystery of piety” (I Tim. III, 16).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIV, no. 14.) Holy Scripture commonly designates the preachers of the Church by the name “angels,” because they announce the glory of the heavenly homeland. Hence the prophet Malachi says: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II, 4).

Hence Paul says: “Great is the mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory.”

After saying that the mystery of the dispensation appeared to angels, he added that it was preached among the nations. By the name “angels,” therefore, he clearly designated holy preachers, that is, messengers of the truth.

## CHAPTER VI — “Let no one despise your youth” (I Tim. IV, 12).

(*Book I on Ezekiel*, Homily 2, no. 3; *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 25.) When the years of our adolescence or youth are still beginning, we should refrain from preaching and ought not to preach in an immature age, because the discourse of teaching is not available except in mature age.

For as long as we are weak, we must contain ourselves within ourselves, lest, while displaying tender virtues too early, we lose them. Only what is firm should therefore be displayed as an example.

Hence it is also said by a certain Wise Man: “Young man, speak scarcely in your own cause; and if you have been questioned twice, let your answer begin” (Ezek. XXXII, 10).

When Paul says to the disciple Timothy: “Command and teach; let no one despise your youth,” we must understand that in sacred speech “youth” sometimes means young adulthood. We can show this more quickly if we cite Solomon’s words, who says: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Eccles. XI, 9).

If he did not understand the two terms to refer to one and the same stage, he would not call the person whom he admonished in adolescence a young man.

Those whom either immaturity or age prevents from undertaking the office of preaching, yet whom rashness impels to do so, lose even what they could eventually have accomplished at the proper time when they prematurely seize what they cannot bear. Before their wings are fully developed, they are plunged into the depths from the heights toward which they desire to fly.

## CHAPTER VII — “Lay hands quickly on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (I Tim. V, 22).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book V, no. 74.) It is customary in Holy Scripture that, when it narrates something, it inserts a statement concerning another matter and then immediately returns to what came before. We can show this custom of sacred speech more clearly by providing an example of it.

When the apostle Paul was admonishing his beloved disciple concerning the establishment of the offices of the Church, lest he should improperly promote anyone to the sacred orders, he said: “Lay hands quickly on no one, nor share in the sins of others; keep yourself chaste.”

Then, immediately turning his words to Timothy’s bodily weakness, he said: “Do not continue to drink water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (v. 23). At once he added: “The sins of some people are manifest, preceding them to judgment; but those of others also follow afterward” (v. 24).

What connection, then, does the prohibition against drinking water by a sick man have with what he added concerning the hidden and manifest sins of certain people? The connection is that, after inserting a statement about Timothy’s infirmity, he returned at the end to what he had said above: “Lay hands quickly on no one, nor share in the sins of others.”

To show with what great care these same sins had to be investigated, he inserted an admonition concerning discernment in response to the burden of infirmity, and immediately added that in some people sins are evident while in others they remain hidden, saying: “The sins of some people are manifest, preceding them to judgment; but those of others also follow afterward.”

In this statement, therefore, Paul does not use words that correspond to the statement he had added while speaking about Timothy’s infirmity; rather, by interrupting his narrative, he returned to what he had previously been discussing.

## CHAPTER VIII — “While I come, attend to the reading” (I Tim. IV, 13).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapter 11.) Every prelate and ruler ought daily to meditate diligently on the commands of sacred eloquence, so that the words of divine admonition may restore in him the force of care and the prudent vigilance directed toward heavenly life—qualities that the practice of human society continually destroys.

The one who is led toward the old age of life through association with worldly people should continually be renewed by the aspiration of compunction toward love of his spiritual homeland.

The heart flows away greatly amid human words, since it is unquestionably true that, driven by the outward tumult of occupations, it falls away from itself. It must therefore strive without ceasing to rise again through the study of instruction.

Hence Paul admonishes the disciple who presides over the flock, saying: “While I come, attend to the reading.” Hence David says: “How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day” (Ps. CXVIII, 97).

## CHAPTER IX — “The desire for money is the root of all evils” (I Tim. VI, 10).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XX, no. 21.) When avarice, that is, covetousness, dominates someone, that person is undoubtedly shown to be subject to every evil, because all evils arise from avarice, and the thorns of every sin are produced from it. Through Paul it is said: “Covetousness is the root of all evils” [Col. 1374B]. It secretly arises in the mind, but openly produces the pricks of every sin in action. The distinguished preacher immediately discloses these pricks arising from this root when he adds: “By desiring it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.” In saying “many sorrows,” he made known that the pricks arise as though born from this root.

## CHAPTER X.—Who alone possesses immortality (I Tim. VI, 16).

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXV, nos. 9–10.) Every change is, as it were, an imitation of death. For that which is changed is, as it were, killed by what it was, so that it ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not. But the true light—namely, our Creator—is darkened by no alteration of mutability and is overshadowed by no defects of his nature. His being shines without change, as it is written: “With whom there is no alteration, nor shadow caused by turning” (James I, 17). Hence the Apostle Paul says again: “Who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light.”  

But since we all know that the human soul and angelic spirits were created immortal, why does the Apostle assert that God alone possesses immortality, unless because God alone truly does not die, since he alone never changes? The human soul would never fall into ruin if it were not mutable. And when it was expelled even from the joys of paradise, it would never have returned to life if it were not mutable. Yet in the very fact that it strives to return to life, it is compelled, through its ever-alternating mutability, to endure its defects. Since it was created from nothing, it tends of itself no less downward, unless it is held by the hand of its Maker in the condition of good desire.

Because it is a creature, therefore, it is inclined to go downward. It recognizes that by its own strength it can rush headlong; but by the hand of love it holds fast to its Creator, lest it fall, until it passes into immutability [Col. 1374D] and lives truly immortally insofar as it lives unchangeably.

The angelic spirits, too, were created mutable by nature, so that they could either fall of their own accord or stand by their own choice. But because they humbly chose to cling to him by whom they were created, they have now overcome in themselves this very mutability through the immutability of their standing. Thus by this merit they have transcended the fact that, according to the order of their nature, they could have been subject to mutability. Since, then, our Creator suffers no mutability, Paul rightly says of him: “Who alone possesses immortality.”

## CHAPTER XI.—And dwells in inaccessible light (I Tim. VI, 16).

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XVIII, no. 92.) When we come to the very fountain of life, our Creator, thirst and satisfaction will be delightfully impressed upon us together; yet necessity will be far from that thirst, and weariness far from that satisfaction, because we shall thirst when satisfied and thirst again when satisfied. We shall therefore see God himself, who will be the reward of our labor, so that after the darkness of this mortality we may rejoice in the light we have entered.

But when we say that we have entered his light, the saying of Paul presents an obstacle to the mind: “Who dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen, nor can see.” Yet I hear again what the Psalmist says: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII, 6). How, then, are we enlightened by drawing near, if we do not see the light itself by which we can be enlightened? But if, by drawing near to him, we see the very light by which we are enlightened, how is it said to be inaccessible?

In this matter we must consider that he called it inaccessible not to every human being, but to human wisdom. Holy Scripture commonly designates all followers of carnal humanity by the term “human.” Thus the same Apostle says to certain quarrelsome people: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to human ways?” (I Cor. III, 3). Elsewhere he also gives this testimony: “What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9).

And when the Lord had called this hidden, he immediately added: “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit” (ibid.), distinguishing himself from the designation “human,” because he who had been caught up above humanity was already tasting divine things. So also here, when he declares God’s light inaccessible, he adds, to show to whom it is inaccessible: “Whom no human being has seen, nor can see.” In his customary manner he calls all who are wise according to human standards “human,” because those who taste divine things are, in fact, above human beings.

We shall therefore see God through a heavenly way of life if we are found worthy to be above human beings. This vision begins now through faith, but then is perfected in its visible reality, when we shall drink at its very source the Wisdom coeternal with God, which we now receive through the mouths of preachers as though through flowing rivers.

## CHAPTER XII.—Command the rich not to be high-minded (I Tim. VI, 17).

[Col. 1376A]

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 2.) We must instill fear of pride in the rich who are proud, just as Paul says to his disciple concerning the rich: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of their riches.” Here it is especially noteworthy that the teacher of humility, when mentioning the rich, does not say “Ask,” but “Command,” because although compassion must be shown to weakness, honor is not owed to pride. The more swollen they become with the height of their thoughts over transitory possessions, the more rightly such people are commanded what is right.

The Lord says of them in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation” (Luke VI, 24). Because they do not know what eternal joys are, they are consoled by the abundance of the present life. Preachers must therefore offer fear to the rich whom the consolation of temporal glory exalts, so that they may recognize that they cannot in any way retain the riches they see.

## CHAPTER XIII.—O Timothy, guard the deposit (I Tim. VI, 20).

[Col. 1376B]

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XVIII, no. 39.) Whoever prepares himself for the words of true preaching must take the foundations of his arguments from the sacred pages, so that everything he says may establish within him the structure of his discourse. Heretics often, while striving to support their perverse ideas, bring forward things that are certainly not contained in the pages of the sacred books. Hence the preacher admonishes his disciple, saying: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words.” For while heretics desire to be praised as possessing exceptional intelligence, they bring forward certain novelties that are not contained in the old books of the ancient Fathers. Thus it happens that, while they wish to appear wise, they scatter seeds of folly among their wretched hearers.

# EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO TIMOTHY II

[Col. 1375]

## CHAPTER I.—No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs (II Tim. II, 4).

[Col. 1375C]

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book V, no. 55.) Holy men withdraw themselves completely from the restless desire of this world, abandon the tumult of earthly activities, and, ceasing from outward works through their devotion to quiet, strive to penetrate inward things. They are not brought to contemplate inward realities unless they are carefully withdrawn from those things that entangle them outwardly.

Hence Truth itself says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI, 24). Hence Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself.” Hence through the Prophet the Lord admonishes us, saying: “Be still and see that I am God” (Ps. XLV, 11). Inner knowledge cannot be perceived unless one ceases from outward entanglement, and our mind is in no way carried away into the power of inward contemplation unless it is first carefully quieted from the tumult of earthly desires [Col. 1375D].

## CHAPTER II.—Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season (II Tim. IV, 1).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapter 4.) Rulers must carefully attend to how much they say, so that they may bring forward not only nothing wrong, but not even what is right in excess or without order. For the force of what is said is often lost when, through the importunity of unwary speech, it is made trivial in the hearts of the hearers.

Hence Paul, admonishing his disciple about persistence in preaching, said: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, by his coming and his kingdom: Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season.” When he was about to say “out of season,” he first said “in season,” because, plainly, in the mind of the hearer even importunity destroys its own usefulness if it does not know how to possess suitability.

## CHAPTER III.—Convict, exhort, rebuke with all patience and teaching (II Tim. IV, 2).

[Col. 1376C]

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 16; Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 11, no. 15.) Gentle rulers should strive also to possess zeal for justice, while irascible rulers should add gentleness to the zeal they believe they possess. For this reason the Holy Spirit was shown to us in the dove and in fire: he makes all whom he fills both gentle with the simplicity of the dove and burning with the fire of zeal. No one, therefore, is full of the Holy Spirit who either abandons the fervor of zeal in the tranquility of gentleness or, conversely, loses the virtue of gentleness in the ardor of zeal.

We may perhaps show this more clearly if we bring forward Paul’s ministry, who bestowed different forms of preaching assistance upon two disciples endowed with the same love. Advising Timothy, he says: “Convict, exhort, rebuke with all patience and teaching.” He also admonishes Titus, saying: “Speak these things, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority” (Tit. II, 15).

Why does he distribute his teaching with such art that, in presenting it, he proposes authority to one and patience to the other, unless because he saw Titus as possessing the gentler spirit and Timothy the more fervent one? He therefore inflames the former through zeal and tempers the latter through patient gentleness. He adds to one what he lacks and removes from the other what he has in excess; he strives to fill the one with a goad and moderates the other with a bridle. Severity of speech had to be imposed upon the gentle person through the authority of command, while the one fervent in spirit had to be tempered through patience, lest, if he burned more than was proper, he should not return to heal the wounds of his subjects but instead wound those who were healthy. For words that often recall one person to healing wound another.

## CHAPTER IV.—From now on a crown of righteousness is laid up for me (II Tim. IV, 8).

[Col. 1377A]

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book X, nos. 36–37; Homily 37 on the Gospels, no. 1.) Because holy men faithfully serve the Lord’s commands, they await his coming with certain hope. They desire the final judgment to come, the heavenly homeland to be revealed, and rewards to be paid to the righteous. We must know that the minds of the blessed hope more certainly for the rewards of eternity the harsher the things they endure for the truth, and that hope in God rises more firmly in each person the heavier the things he has endured for God.

The saints, considering their labors, seek the reward of recompense; knowing the merit of their cause, they long for the Judge’s presence. They desire with the greatest ardor that he come in a flame of fire, inflicting vengeance on the ungodly and bringing to the godly the vision of himself as their reward.

Considering his labors, therefore, the distinguished preacher says: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is at hand. I have fought the good fight; I have finished the race; I have kept the faith. From now on a crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will give me on that day.” Because he had fought without failing against passing evils, he confidently anticipated joys that would endure. He openly adds: “And not only to me, but also to those who love his coming.”

It is as though he said: “And likewise to all who are conscious of good works in themselves.” For they do not love the Judge’s coming unless they know that they possess the merit of righteousness in their own cause. No joy or crown of recompense is gathered from eternity unless it is first sown here through devout tribulation and labor.

Hence Paul says: “If we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him” (II Tim. II, 11). Hence, revealing the glory of the saints to John, the angel says: “These are they who have come from great tribulation” (Rev. VII, 14). Hence Paul again admonishes the disciples, saying: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV, 21). Again he says: “He will not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (II Tim. II, 5). One cannot reach the crown and great rewards except through great labors. Whoever, therefore, delights in the greatness of heavenly rewards must not be deterred by the struggle of labors.

# EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE HEBREWS

[Col. 1377]

## CHAPTER I.—He did not take hold of angels at all (Hebr. II, 16).

[Col. 1377B]

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book IV, nos. 9–12.) Almighty God, just as he was able to make good things from nothing, so, when he willed, also restored what had been lost through the mystery of his incarnation. He had made two creatures capable of knowing him: the angelic and the human. Pride struck both and cast them down from the state of uprightness implanted in them. But one possessed the covering of flesh, while the other bore nothing weak from flesh. An angel is spirit alone, whereas a human being is spirit and flesh.

Therefore, in his mercy, the Creator had to bring back to himself the one he was redeeming, since it is clear that, in committing the offense, that one possessed something arising from weakness. He had to drive the apostate angel farther away, because when the angel fell from the strength of perseverance, he bore nothing weak from flesh.

Hence it is written: “He did not take hold of angels at all, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham.” For this reason our Redeemer became not an angel but a human being: undoubtedly, he had to become that which he redeemed, so that, by not taking hold of the fallen angel, he would leave him, while by taking hold of the human being in himself, he would restore him.

There is another reason as well why fallen humanity had to be restored while the proud spirit could not be restored: the angel fell through his own wickedness, whereas another’s wickedness overthrew humanity. The human race is therefore brought back to repentance through the Redeemer’s coming; but the apostate angel is recalled to restoration by no hope of pardon and by no correction through conversion. The blindness of the pride he committed weighs upon him so heavily that he cannot thereafter rise to the light of repentance through remembrance of divine regard, nor return to pardon with the elect, nor again to those heavenly ranks of inward glory.

## CHAPTER II.—Through Abraham Levi was tithed, for he was still in his father’s loins (Hebr. VII, 10).

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXXII, no. 20.) The term “loins” expresses the succession of mortality, because the generative seeds are said to be present in men’s loins and in women’s navel. Hence Truth says to the disciples: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII, 35). And when Peter was restraining lust from the heart, he admonished them, saying: “Girding the loins of your mind” (I Pet. I, 13).

For this reason it is also said of Levi: “He was still in his father’s loins when Melchizedek met Abraham.” When Paul declared through Abraham’s sacrifice that Levi’s priesthood had been tithed at the time of Melchizedek, he showed where Levi was then hidden in Abraham’s body, saying: “For he was still in his father’s loins.”

## CHAPTER III.—The word of God is living and effective (Hebr. IV, 12).

[Col. 1378B]

(Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 9, nos. 16–17.) In the sight of almighty God, both deeds well performed and words knowingly spoken perish when they are done no longer out of love for the Lord but with the intention of transitory praise. For a sinister thought is often joined to a good thought in such a way that scarcely does the mind itself, which generates these thoughts, recognize them.

Hence the distinguished preacher, speaking subtly, said: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit”; and immediately he adds: “Of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” The word of God distinguishes joints and marrow because it discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

Through joints, bones are joined to bones. Often, when we do something with a right thought but suddenly turn aside in the love of praise, doing for praise what we had begun to do for the sake of truth, thoughts are joined to thoughts and become, as it were, joints. But the bones joined in a joint also have marrow. The holy preacher explains this more clearly when he adds: “Discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (ibid.). Our thoughts are the joints, while the intentions are the marrow.

For we think one thing, while our intention through that thought is something else. If someone, for the sake of a promised payment, defends the case of an orphan or widow, and perhaps, entering a church, says to God in his prayers, “You see that I am defending the case of an orphan and a widow,” he certainly knows what he is thinking, but his thought does not reveal what he intends. He thinks one thing but intends another: he is not seeking the defense of the orphan or widow, but payment in money. Remove the temporal reward, and he will not defend the orphan or widow.

The word of God is therefore the discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart, because it does not look at what you are thinking within yourself, but, through the marrow of the joint—that is, through the intention of the thought—what you seek to obtain [Col. 1378D].

## CHAPTER IV.—It is necessary that the copies of heavenly things be cleansed by these (Hebr. IX, 23).

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XVII, nos. 46–47.) Although in the simple nature of divinity it is not one thing to exist, another to be wise, and another to be strong—for it is itself strength, which is wisdom, and itself wisdom, which is the essence of divinity—the Lord nevertheless overcame the devil, as far as outward appearance is concerned, not by power but by reason.

For the devil, without overthrowing us through any root in our first parent, held the human race, as it were, justly under his captivity, since humanity, created with free choice, consented to him when he offered an unjust suggestion. Created for life in the freedom of its own will, humanity voluntarily made itself liable to death.

Such guilt therefore had to be erased, but it could not be erased except through sacrifice. A sacrifice had to be sought, but what sort of sacrifice could be found for absolving human beings? It was not just that victims of brute animals should be slaughtered for a rational creature, that is, for a human being. Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore it is necessary that the copies of heavenly things be cleansed by these, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these.”

If brute animals, then, were not worthy victims on behalf of a rational animal—that is, a human being—a human being had to be sought who should be offered for human beings, so that a rational victim might be slaughtered for the rational sinner. But what of the fact that a human being without sin could not be found? Once the victim had been offered for us, how could it cleanse us from sin if that victim itself were not free from the contagion of sin? What was defiled could not cleanse the defiled.

Therefore, for the victim to be rational, a human being had to be offered; but for the human race to be cleansed from sins, that human being had also to be without sin. Yet who could be a human being without sin if he descended from the commingling of sin?

Accordingly, for our sake the Son of God came into the Virgin’s womb; there he became human for us. He took a nature from her, not guilt. He made his body a sacrifice for us and presented for sinners a victim without sin, one that could both die through humility and cleanse through righteousness.

When the ancient enemy saw him after his baptism, he immediately attacked him with temptations. He tried to creep into his inward being through various approaches, but was defeated and overthrown by the very unconquerable integrity of his mind. Since he was unable to reach his inward being, he turned to his outward parts, so that, having been defeated by the power of his mind and unable to deceive him through temptation, he might at least seem to overcome him through the death of his flesh. As stated above, he was permitted to act against that which the Mediator had received from us mortals.

But where he was able to do something, there he was defeated in every respect. From the very place where he received outward power to kill the Lord’s flesh, the power by which he held us was inwardly killed. He was defeated inwardly while seeming to conquer outwardly. And he who had held us as debtors to death by right lost by right his claim of death over us, because he sought to destroy through his agents the flesh of the one in whom he found nothing subject to the debt of guilt.

Our Lord therefore paid for us an undue death so that the death due to us would not harm us. But the ancient enemy, through the excess of his presumption, also lost the one whom he had possessed by the law of an unjust persuasion. While he boldly attacked one over whom he had no claim, he rightly lost the one whom he had held as though justly.

He was therefore defeated by prudence, not by power. When he was released to tempt God, he was restrained from possessing the human being, so that he lost the one who was subject to him precisely because he had presumed to contend with the one who is above him.

## CHAPTER V.—Not abandoning your gathering (Hebr. X, 25).

[Col. 1379D]

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book V, no. 7.) Those who fully desire their own mortification display themselves as more fervent in action the nearer they come to the end. They do not fail through labor; rather, they grow more practised in their labors, because the nearer they see the rewards, the more joyfully they toil in their work.

Hence the Apostle Paul rightly says to certain people seeking the eternal homeland: “Not abandoning your gathering, as is the custom of some, but comforting one another; and all the more as you see the day approaching.” To comfort one who is laboring is to persist together in labor, because the visit of a fellow worker lightens labor; just as when a companion joins someone on a journey, the road is not removed, but the burden of the journey is nevertheless lightened by the companion’s company.

Thus, while Paul sought people to comfort one another in labor, he added: “All the more as you see the day approaching.” It is as though he said: “Let labor increase in proportion as the rewards of labor draw near.”

## CHAPTER VI.—We had the fathers of our flesh as instructors and revered them; shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? (Hebr. XII, 9–10).

[Col. 1380A]

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 12.) All whom the Lord scourges in this present time ought to recognize themselves as God’s children precisely when the discipline of scourging corrects them. For if he did not intend to give them an inheritance once corrected, he would not care to instruct them through hardships.

Hence the Lord says to John through the angel: “Those whom I love, I reprove and chastise” (Rev. III, 19). Again it is written: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are reproved by him; for the Lord reproves the one he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. III, 10). Hence the Psalmist says: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII, 20). Blessed Job, too, crying out in his anguish, says: “If I am righteous, I shall not lift up my head, being filled with affliction and misery” (Job X, 15).

We should also consider how severely the blows of discipline chastise children of the flesh for the sake of receiving earthly inheritances. What punishment of divine correction, then, can be grievous to us, by which both an inheritance never to be lost is received and punishments destined to last forever are avoided?

Hence Paul says: “We had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them; shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? And they indeed instructed us for a few days according to their own will, but he does so for what is useful, so that we may receive his sanctification.”

Those whom the Lord scourges should therefore diligently strive to preserve the virtue of patience. They must continually consider how many evils our Redeemer endured from those he had created: how he endured so many contemptuous insults; how, daily snatching the souls of captives from the hand of the ancient enemy, he received the slaps of those who insulted him; how, washing us with the water of salvation, he did not hide his face from the spittle of the faithless; how, freeing us from eternal punishments through his call, he silently endured blows; how, while granting us everlasting honors among the choirs of angels, he endured blows to the face; how, saving us from the pricks of sinners, he did not refuse to submit his head to thorns; how, while intoxicating us with eternal sweetness, he accepted the bitterness of gall in his thirst; how he who, though equal to the Father in divinity, worshiped the Father for our sake, remained silent when worshiped in mockery; and how he who prepared life for the dead, being himself life, proceeded even to death.

Why, then, should it be thought harsh for a human being to endure scourges from God for evils, if God endured such evils from human beings for good? Or who of sound understanding would be ungrateful for his chastisement, if the one who lived without sin did not depart from this life without a scourge?

## CHAPTER VII.—The blood of sprinkling speaks better than Abel (Hebr. XII, 24).

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XIII, no. 26.) Concerning Abel’s blood, the Lord said to Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.” The blood of redemption that is received is itself also the cry of our Redeemer. Hence Paul says: “And the blood of sprinkling, speaking better than Abel” (Gen. IV, 10).

The blood of Jesus speaks better than Abel’s, because Abel’s blood sought the death of the fratricide, whereas the Lord’s blood obtained life for his persecutors. Thus it came about that those who in their fury shed the blood of our Redeemer afterward licked it as believers and proclaimed him to be the Son of God.

## CHAPTER VIII.—I will shake not only the earth but also heaven (Hebr. XII, 26).

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXI, no. 35.) When a storm arises at sea, light waves are stirred first, then larger masses; finally the waves rise into the heights and, by their very height, overturn the sailors. In this way that final storm of souls which will overthrow the whole world is surely hastening upon us.

For now it shows us its beginnings through wars and calamities, as through certain waves. The nearer we come to the end each day, the more grievous masses of tribulation we see rushing upon us. Finally, when all the elements have been shaken, the heavenly Judge comes and brings the end of all things, because at that time the storm raises its waves to heaven.

Hence it is also said: “Yet a little while, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Hag. II, 7). Holy men watch this storm attentively; from the tribulations that strike the world they foresee what follows. Considering in their minds the coming of the final judgment amid such great things, they fear; and when they consider the power of the heavenly Majesty coming to judgment and the terror of so great an examination, they tremble.

How will God’s judgments crush those who exalt themselves, if they sometimes temporarily depress even those who always fear these judgments in humility? We must therefore fear with the utmost care that examination of such strictness.

It is clear, however, that in this life, when correction follows chastisement, it is the discipline of a father, not the anger of a judge; it is the love of one correcting, not the severity of one punishing. From this present scourging, therefore, we must weigh the eternal judgments. We should thereby consider how severe that judgment which condemns will be, if the anger that purifies can scarcely now be endured [Col. 1381B].

## CHAPTER IX.—Jesus suffered outside the gate (Hebr. XIII, 12).

(In the *Exposition on the Seven Penitential Psalms*, on Psalm L, no. 9.) The Lord commanded Moses that the red heifer brought by the children of Israel be handed over to Eleazar the priest, who was to lead it outside the camp and sacrifice it in the Lord’s presence.

What is signified by the red heifer except the weakness of the Lord’s assumed incarnation, destined for sacrifice and reddened by the blood of the Passion? What does it mean that this heifer is handed over to the priest for sacrifice except that the incarnate Lord, who made himself a sacrifice for our redemption, is delivered into the hands of the Jewish people?

He was also sacrificed outside the camp in the Lord’s presence, because he suffered outside the gate. Hence Paul says: “Jesus, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate. Let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we have no abiding city here, but we seek the one that is to come” [Col. 1381C].

He suffered outside the gate in order to lead us out from the way of life in the present, as though out of a city, and to persuade us to tear our hearts away from earthly habitation. He was sacrificed in the presence of the Father because what was punishment before the eyes of human beings was sacrifice before the eyes of the Father.

## CHAPTER X.—He endured as though seeing the Invisible One (Hebr. XI, 27).

(In the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XIX, no. 21.) By faith Moses left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger, “for he endured as though seeing the Invisible One.” The perverse fear human beings whom they see bodily in their actions, but do not consider God, who is present to them though unseen.

By contrast, Moses is praised because, while despising the king of Egypt and obeying God’s commands, “he endured as though seeing the Invisible One.” He regarded the perverse earthly ruler as though he did not see him, having cast him away from the eyes of his heart. But he endured the invisible King as though seeing him, because he did not turn the eye of his mind away from contemplating his fear.

## CHAPTER XI.—Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen (Hebr. XI, 1).

(Homily 26 on the Gospels, no. 8, and Homily 32 on the Gospels, no. 7.) When the Apostle Paul says this, it is entirely clear that faith is the proof of those things that cannot appear. For things that appear no longer possess faith but recognition. What is visibly presented to human sight and can be seen is more properly said to be known than believed.

## CHAPTER XII.—I have written to you with very few words (Hebr. XIII, 22).

(Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 11, no. 16; in the *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book V, no. 25.) Pastors must take care how much they say, lest, if they extend the word of exhortation or rebuke too far for those unable to bear much, they lead their hearers to weariness. Hence the distinguished preacher says: “I ask you, brothers, to bear with the word of consolation, for I have written to you with very few words.”

This applies especially to the weak: they should hear few things, indeed, and only those they are able to grasp, but such things as prick their minds with the pain of repentance. If the word of exhortation is delivered to them at one time in many forms, they cannot retain much and lose everything at once.

If at times a longer discourse exceeds its proper measure, this is not dangerous for the hearers. It should be noted, however, that when Paul was wonderfully admonishing the Hebrews, he humbly regarded the great things he had said and called his words words of consolation. He had said many things humbly to his hearers, but he tried to placate them even more humbly concerning that humble exhortation.

When taking leave of the Ephesians at Miletus, he likewise recalls his humility to those afflicted and weeping, saying: “Keep watch, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not cease admonishing each one of you with tears” (Acts XX, 31) [Col. 1382C].

Let the disciple therefore learn from this how humbly he ought to speak to his teacher when he feels something rightly: the teacher of the Gentiles himself so humbly entreats disciples in the things he preaches with authority. Let each person also learn how humbly to say what he rightly understands to those from whom he receives examples of good living, since Paul submitted himself in humble speech to those whom he himself had raised to life.

When, therefore, certain actions of better people displease those who are worse, what disturbs the mind should by no means be left unspoken, but should be expressed with great humility, so that the intention of the one who thinks devoutly may truly preserve the form of righteousness by walking along the path of humility. What we feel must therefore be spoken freely, but what we say must be sought with profound humility, lest, by expressing proudly what we rightly intend, we fail to act rightly.

# EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE JAMES

## CHAPTER I.—Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no alteration or shadow caused by turning (James I, 17).

[Col. 1381D]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XII, no. 38.) All the saints by nature possess within themselves a proper mutability; but while they always earnestly desire to cling to immutability, by clinging to it they act so as to become immutable.
