And when they hold fast to this with their whole affection, they are sometimes granted, carried above themselves, to conquer that by which they had been mutable within themselves. For what is mutability but a kind of death? When it changes anything into something else, it seems to kill what had existed, so that what had not existed may begin to be.

Of the Author of all things it is written: “He alone possesses immutability” (1 Tim. 6:16), because He alone is immutable in Himself. Of Him James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning” [Col. 1382D]. For mutability itself is a shadow which would, so to speak, darken the light if it altered it through any changes. But because mutability does not enter into God, no shadow of change interrupts His light.

## CHAPTER II.—Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all (James 2:10).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XIX, no. 32.) When we are clothed with a garment, we are surrounded by it on every side. Therefore, the person who clothes himself well in every righteousness as in a garment is the one who protects himself on every side with good works and leaves no part of his conduct bare to sin. For one who is righteous in some actions but unjust in others has, as it were, covered one side and exposed another; nor are works good any longer when they are defiled by other wicked works that have arisen alongside them.

Hence Solomon says: “Whoever offends in one thing will lose many good things” (Eccl. 9:18). [Col. 1383A] Hence James says: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all.” He himself carefully explained this judgment when he added: “For the one who said, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘You shall not kill.’ Now if you do not commit adultery but do kill, you have become a transgressor of the law.”

Therefore, with the eyes of our hearts extended in every direction, we must maintain vigilance on all sides, lest we lose through other actions the reward that we gather through these actions; for good things cannot profit us if we do not guard against the evils that steal them away.

## CHAPTER III.—But if a brother or sister is naked (James 2:15).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXI, nos. 29, 31.) There are some who, when needy brothers ask them for what is necessary, do not, although able, endeavor to support them with material aid, but seek only to encourage them with flattering words. Holy James’s preaching sharply reproves such people, saying: “But if a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, be warmed and filled,’ but you do not give them what is necessary for the body, what benefit is that to you?” [Col. 1383B]

The apostle John likewise admonishes them, saying: “My little children, let us not love in word or with the tongue, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18). Our love, therefore, must always be displayed both in respectful speech and in the service of generosity.

There are, however, some who do not know how to extend the compassion of their hearts even to strangers, but show mercy only to those whom they have come to know through constant association. Among such people familiarity evidently counts for more than nature, since they give what is necessary to certain persons not because they are human beings but because they are known to them. But in a devout mind nature counts for more than acquaintance. For anyone who is in need is not a stranger, precisely because he is a human being.

## CHAPTER IV.—Faith without works is dead (James 2:26).

(*Homily* 26 on the Gospels, no. 9.) The person who believes is the one who puts into practice what he believes. Conversely, concerning those who retain faith only in name, Paul says: “They profess [Col. 1383C] to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). Hence John says: “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4). Hence James says: “Faith without works is dead.”

Hence also the Lord says to blessed Job concerning the ancient enemy of the human race: “He will swallow [Col. 1383D] the river and not be astonished, and he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job 40:18). For what is signified by the river except the course of the human race? This race flows from its beginning to its end and, like water, runs on from the fluidity of the flesh until its appointed limit.

What is signified by the Jordan except the figure of the baptized? Because the Author of our redemption graciously consented to be baptized in the river Jordan, the multitude of those held within the sacrament of baptism is rightly expressed by the name “Jordan.”

The ancient enemy of the human race therefore swallowed the river, because from the beginning of the world until the Redeemer’s coming, with scarcely a few of the elect escaping, he dragged the human race into the belly of his malice. Of him it is rightly said: “He will swallow the river and not be astonished” (ibid.), because he does not regard it as a great thing when he seizes unbelievers.

But what follows is very grave: “And he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.” For after he had seized all unbelievers from the beginning of the world, he still presumes that he can deceive the faithful. With the mouth of his deadly persuasion he daily devours those whose reprobate life is at odds with their confession of faith.

Whoever, therefore, understands through faith the hidden things that are right, yet refuses to maintain the works of faith, is convicted of unbelief, because by his manner of living he rejects what he professes to believe.

## CHAPTER V.—The wisdom from above is first chaste (James 3:17).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 22.) Often, when greater learning exalts certain people, it separates them from the fellowship of others; and the more they seem to know, the more foolishly they depart from the virtue of concord. To such people James rightly says: [Col. 1384A] “But if you have bitter jealousy and contention in your hearts, do not boast and become liars against the truth. This is not the wisdom that descends from above, but earthly, natural, demonic. But the wisdom from above is first chaste, then peaceable.”

It is chaste because it understands chastely; it is peaceable because it does not, through arrogance, separate itself in the least from fellowship with its neighbors.

## CHAPTER VI.—You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly (James 4:3).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXI, no. 25.) In Holy Scripture the humble are often called poor, because those are truly poor who are not inflated by the spirit of pride. The Truth clearly describes them when it says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3).

Without doubt, whatever they request with humility ought to be given to them without hesitation—that is, whatever they ask not from desire but from necessity. For it is extreme pride to desire something beyond the limits of one’s need. Hence James’s voice says to those who ask proudly: [Col. 1384B] “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your passions.”

## CHAPTER VII.—Our life is a vapor, appearing for a little while (James 4:15).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VII, no. 45.) Because holy men constantly contemplate the brevity of this life, they live as though dying every day. They prepare themselves all the more firmly for what will endure, the more they continually reckon transient things as nothing, considering their end.

Hence the Psalmist, seeing the sinner’s life fleeing swiftly, says: “A little while, and the sinner will be no more” (Ps. 36:10). Again he says: “Man’s days are like grass” (Ps. 102:17). Isaiah says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6).

Hence James reproves the minds of those who presume, saying: “What is our life? It is a vapor appearing for a little while.” For what follows without limit is immense, while whatever comes to an end is small. What hastens toward the setting of its own time, so as not to exist, ought not to seem long to us [Col. 1384C]. As it is carried along moment by moment, those very moments that delay it drive it onward; and from the fact that it is seen to be held, it is shown that it must not be held.

## CHAPTER VIII.—Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God (James 4:4).

(*Homily* 1 on the Gospels, nos. 3, 5, and *Homily* 37 on the Gospels, no. 10.) Those who love God ought to rejoice and be glad at the world’s afflictions and at its end, because they will soon find the one whom they love when what they have not loved passes away.

Far be it from any faithful person who desires to see God to mourn over the world’s afflictions, since he knows that the world will be ended by those very afflictions. Whoever, therefore, does not rejoice as the world’s end approaches testifies that he is its friend, and is thereby proved to be an enemy of God.

God’s friends ought to desire to depart from this world sooner and to reach by a shorter road the joys of the heavenly homeland that they love. For by what evils is the world not oppressed? [Col. 1384D] What sadness, what adversity does not distress us? What is mortal life except a road? And consider, my brothers, how strange it is to grow weary from the labor of the journey and finally not wish that the same road should end.

The world ought to be trampled underfoot and despised, my brothers. In earlier years, as though in its youth, it flourished; it was strong for propagating the human race, vigorous in the health of bodies, and rich in the abundance of possessions. But now it is weighed down by its own old age and, as though death were near, is pressed by troubles that continually increase.

Therefore, my brothers, do not love what you see cannot remain long. Set in your hearts the apostolic commands by which he admonishes us, saying: “Do not love the world or the things in the world. For if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15–16).

Let the one who can leave everything do so. Whoever cannot leave everything should wash away the stains of sins with tears, cleanse them by almsgiving, and expiate them through the sacred offerings. For the sacrifice of the sacred altar, offered with tears and kindness of heart, gives singular assistance toward our absolution [Col. 1385A], because the one who, having risen from the dead in himself, no longer dies, nevertheless suffers again for us through this sacrifice in his mystery.

For as often as we offer him the sacrifice of his passion, so often we renew his passion for our absolution. Therefore, my brothers, do not possess through desire what you have not yet abandoned in practice. Fix your hope in the Redeemer alone; pass in spirit to the eternal homeland. For if you possess nothing in this world by loving it, then even while possessing everything you have abandoned it all.

## CHAPTER IX.—Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins (James 5:20).

[Col. 1386A]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XIX, no. 31.) Blessed Job says: “The blessing of the perishing came upon me” (Job 29:13). The blessing of the perishing comes upon someone who, anticipating the sinner’s destruction, brings him back from the pit of guilt through holy exhortations.

For if it is a great reward to rescue a body that will eventually die from death, it is a far greater merit to free a soul from death, a soul destined to live without end in the heavenly homeland.

# EXPOSITION ON THE FIRST EPISTLE OF BLESSED PETER THE APOSTLE

[Col. 1385]

## CHAPTER I.—He regenerated us unto a living hope, etc., into an incorruptible inheritance (1 Pet. 1:4).

[Col. 1385A]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXX, no. 80.) Human hearts wither when they are planted in the perishable hope of this age and have no confidence in eternity. But those hearts flourish which cling to that inheritance of which the apostle Peter says: [Col. 1385B] “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, kept in heaven.”

The more truly people flourish, the more firmly they fix the root of their thought in the unfading inheritance. Therefore, whoever fears withering inwardly should flee the withering desires of this world outwardly and, desiring the eternal homeland, grow vigorous in the eternal planting of the heart.

## CHAPTER II.—Into whom the angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1:12).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XVIII, no. 91.) Since the first preacher of the Church says of God: “Into whom the angels desire to look,” there are some who do not suppose that the angels see God at all. Yet we know that the Truth has said: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” [Col. 1385C] (Matt. 18:10).

Does the Truth, then, suggest one thing and the preacher of the Truth another? But when both statements are considered together, they are found not to disagree. The angels both see God and desire to see Him; they thirst to behold Him and do behold Him. For if they desired to see Him in such a way that they never enjoyed the fulfillment of their desire, desire without fruit would bring anxiety, and anxiety would bring punishment. But the blessed angels are far removed from every punishment of anxiety, since punishment and blessedness can never coexist.

Again, when we say that they are satisfied by the vision of God, since the Psalmist also says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16:13), we must consider that satiety is usually followed by weariness. Therefore, so that both statements may rightly agree, let the Truth say: “They always see”; and let the distinguished preacher say: “They always desire to see.”

So that there may be no anxiety in desire, they are satisfied while desiring; and so that there may be no weariness in satisfaction, they desire while satisfied. Thus they desire without labor, because satisfaction [Col. 1385D] accompanies their desire; and they are satisfied without weariness, because that very satisfaction is continually kindled by desire.

## CHAPTER III.—Therefore, girding up the loins of your mind, etc. (1 Pet. 1:13).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXI, no. 5.) The evil of lust is committed either in thought or in deed. Through Moses, lust committed in deed is condemned; by the Author of purity, lust conceived in thought is condemned.

Hence the first shepherd of the Church says to the disciples: “Therefore, girding up the loins of your mind, being perfectly sober, hope in the grace that is offered to you.” To gird the loins of the flesh is to restrain lust from action. To gird the loins of the mind is to restrain it even from thought.

## CHAPTER IV.—Let none of you suffer as a murderer (1 Pet. 4:15).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXXIV, no. 41.) When holy [Col. 1386A] men suffer persecution outwardly and inwardly, they not only do not exceed the bounds of propriety when God is insulted, but they do not even hurl insulting words against their adversaries.

Peter, the leader of the good, rightly admonishes this, saying: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or a reviler.” A reviler suffers as such when, during the time of his suffering [Col. 1386B], he becomes unrestrained even to the injury of his persecutor.

## CHAPTER V.—As each has received grace, administering it to one another, etc. (1 Pet. 4:10).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXVIII, no. 22.) Each person ought to share with others the virtues he has received, and ought to devote to another the good that he possesses.

Thus, the person who has received earthly substance should relieve the poverty of a needy neighbor. Whoever is full of the grace of teaching should illuminate the darkness of an ignorant neighbor by the word of his preaching. Whoever is supported by temporal power should rescue the oppressed from their troubles. Whoever is full of the spirit of prophecy should turn impending evils away from the life of a neighbor by urging what is good. Whoever has received the grace of healing should, through his intercession, piously and humbly provide health to the sick. Whoever has been freed from earthly affairs and has been granted the privilege of devoting himself to God alone should pray for neighbors who are at fault.

It often happens, however, that the person who is excessively occupied with earthly possessions does not devote himself to prayer as he ought [Col. 1386C]. And it often happens that the person who, stripped of all the burdens of the world, is free to entreat the Lord has no means of sustaining his life.

Therefore, let the rich provide food and clothing to the poor, and let the poor offer their prayer to the soul of the rich. One person offers me the word of preaching and drives the darkness of ignorance from my heart with the light of truth. But I, because perhaps he is oppressed by the powerful of this world, offer him the support of my protection and rescue him from violent hands.

Hence the first shepherd rightly admonishes us, saying: “Be prudent and watchful in prayers, above all maintaining constant mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins; be hospitable to one another without grumbling, administering to one another the grace each has received.”

For our Creator and Disposer regulates all things in such a way that, while each thing belongs to everyone through a certain bond of charity, everything becomes the possession of each individual. Each person thus possesses in another what he himself has not received, while humbly offering to another for possession what he has received [Col. 1386D].

Hence Paul says: “Through charity serve one another” (Gal. 5:13). Charity then frees us from the yoke of guilt when, through love, it subjects us to one another in mutual service; when we believe that the goods of others are ours and offer our own as though they belonged to others.

Because our goods do not come from ourselves, but we received them from the one who made us exist, we ought not to keep them private to ourselves in proportion as we see that our Creator gave them to us for the common good.

Therefore Peter rightly added in his exhortation concerning this matter: “As good stewards of the manifold grace of God.” The manifold grace of God is then well administered when the gift that has been received is believed to belong also to the one who does not possess it, and when it is considered to have been given for the sake of the person to whom it is devoted.

Hence Peter further added: “If anyone speaks, as [Col. 1387A] the oracles of God; if anyone serves, as from the strength that God supplies” (ibid.). It is as though he openly said: “Humbly devote what is good to your neighbors, because you know that what you possess does not come from yourselves.”

## CHAPTER VI.—If anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God (1 Pet. 4:11).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 24.) Those who do not speak God’s words humbly ought to consider what is written by the first shepherd: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the oracles of God.”

If, therefore, they do not possess from themselves the words they utter, why do they swell up as though they did? Again it is written: “We speak as from God, before God, in Christ” (2 Cor. 2:17). The person who speaks as from God, before God, understands that he has received the word of preaching from God and seeks through it to please God, not human beings.

Again it is written: “Everyone who is arrogant is an abomination to the Lord” (Prov. 16:15), because, while seeking his own glory in God’s word, he seizes the right of the giver and is not afraid to place Him beneath his own praise [Col. 1387B]—the One from whom he received the very thing for which he is praised.

## CHAPTER VII.—It is time for judgment to begin with the household of God (1 Pet. 4:17).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book IX, no. 35.) From the life and labor of the elect we can now learn how severely we shall be struck afterward if we do not wish to be corrected while there is still time. We see God’s elect both doing what is devout and enduring many cruel things.

It belongs to the elect to be crushed here, so that they may be trained for the rewards of the eternal inheritance. It belongs to the elect to receive scourging here, by which they are preserved so that they may rejoice in eternity.

Hence it is said to John: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Rev. 3). Hence Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin with the household of God.” Immediately he added in wonder: “And if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God?”

From this, therefore, we gather [Col. 1388A] how severe the Judge will be in striking those whom He rejects there, if here He so torments those whom He loves.

## CHAPTER VIII.—Feed the flock of God that is among you (1 Pet. 5:1–2).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapter 7.) [Col. 1388A] Some undertake the care of a flock but, while entirely neglecting bodily needs, do not come to the aid of their subjects’ necessities. Their preaching is often despised, because when they rebuke the deeds of sinners but do not provide them with what is necessary for the present life, they are by no means heard willingly.

The word of doctrine does not penetrate the heart of a ruler if the hand of mercy does not commend it to his mind. Hence the first shepherd carefully admonishes us, saying: “The elders among you I exhort, as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and as one who shares in the glory that is to be revealed: feed the flock of God that is among you.”

He made clear whether in this passage he was urging the feeding of the heart or of the body [Col. 1388B] when he added: “Exercising oversight, not under compulsion but willingly according to God, and not for shameful gain but eagerly” (ibid.).

These words expressly warn shepherds not to kill themselves with the sword of ambition while satisfying the poverty of their subjects; not to refresh their neighbors through them with bodily provisions while they themselves remain hungry for heavenly bread.

Paul arouses this concern in shepherds, saying: “If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:3).

Therefore, the ruler must be able to pour out inward things while, with an innocent thought, also providing for outward things. Shepherds should burn with concern for the inner life of their subjects in such a way that they do not neglect in them the provision required for outward life as well.

For, as we have said, the mind of the flock is rightly broken away from receiving preaching if the shepherd neglects the outward care of material assistance.

# EXPOSITION ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF BLESSED PETER THE APOSTLE

[Col. 1387]

## CHAPTER I.—Supply self-control in knowledge, and endurance in self-control (2 Pet. 1:5–6).

[Col. 1387C]

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 19.) Those who practice abstinence must always carefully consider whether, while fleeing the vice of gluttony, they may generate even harsher vices from what they regard as virtue; whether, while mortifying the flesh, they may break out into impatience of spirit.

Hence Peter admonishes them, saying: “Supply virtue in your faith, knowledge in virtue, self-control in knowledge, and endurance in self-control.”

The minds of those who practice abstinence are often shaken from the bosom of tranquility by impatience. Therefore, after saying, “Self-control in knowledge,” he immediately added with vigilance: “Endurance in self-control.”

He foresaw that those practicing abstinence would lack endurance and admonished them so that it might be present in them, because it is no virtue to conquer the flesh if the spirit is overcome by anger.

## CHAPTER II.—We possess the prophetic word made more certain (2 Pet. 1:19).

[Col. 1387D]

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 3, no. 17; Book I on Ezekiel, homily 6, no. 1.) In the construction of the tabernacle, bronze pegs fixed outside held the ropes by which the silver columns were fastened so that they might stand immovable within. The Fathers of the Old Testament and the prophets were like those pegs: before the time of the holy Church they were fixed outside. They bound and fastened the columns standing within it—that is, the holy apostles and preachers—with the ropes of their words, securing them in the firmness of faith.

While they proclaimed the heavenly mysteries that were to come, they made these mysteries credible to all after they had been revealed. Through their preaching, the holy apostles firmly and perfectly believed the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

Therefore the first of the apostles himself, clearly a great column of the true tabernacle, rightly says: “We possess the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place” [Col. 1388C].

By these words he indicates how far he has risen to higher things from the summit where, tied fast, he remains in faith. The Scripture of the prophetic word has become for us a lamp and the light of our journey amid the darkness of the present life.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, Lord, and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:105). Yet this lamp of the prophetic word already shines for those who understand, while it remains veiled by the obscurities of allegories for those who do not yet understand.

Hence the Psalmist also says of those same prophetic utterances: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17:12), because knowledge is hidden in the prophets.

## CHAPTER III.—God did not spare the angels when they sinned (2 Pet. 2:4).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VIII, no. 39.) In relation to the height of heaven, the space of this air may rightly be called hell. Thus, when the apostate angels [Col. 1388D] were plunged from their heavenly dwelling into this darkened air, the apostle Peter says: “God did not spare the angels who sinned, but thrusting them into the dark prisons of hell, he delivered them to be kept for judgment and punishment.”

Therefore, in relation to the height of heaven, this darkened air is hell. Likewise, in relation to the height of that same air, the earth, which lies below it, can be understood as hell and as a deep abyss.

The evil spirit, therefore, cast down from the higher regions into these lower ones, is restrained by the weight of his punishment, so that he cannot fly up to heavenly things. He is confined here as though in a prison, because he is prevented from tempting the good as much as he desires. The severity of the heavenly judgment constricts him so that he cannot accomplish the evils he seeks.

## CHAPTER IV.—Lot was righteous in sight and hearing (2 Pet. 2:7).

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book I, no. 1.) It is not especially [Col. 1389A] praiseworthy to be good among the good, but to be good among the wicked. For just as it is a more serious fault not to be good among the good, so it is an extraordinary distinction to have been good even among the wicked.

Hence Peter praised Lot more highly, because he found goodness among the reprobate, saying: “He rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the unjust conduct of the wicked. For he was righteous in sight and hearing while living among those who day after day tortured the soul of the righteous man through wicked deeds.”

He could not have been tortured unless he both heard and saw the evil deeds of his neighbors. Yet he is said to have been righteous in sight because the life of the wicked touched the righteous man’s ears and eyes not by delighting the righteous man’s ears and eyes, but by striking them.

Hence Paul says to the disciples: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. 2:15). Hence it is said to the angel of the Church of Pergamum: “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; and you hold fast my name and did not deny my faith” (Rev. 2:13).

Hence the holy Church is praised in the voice of the bridegroom when it is said to her in the Song of Love: “As a lily among thorns [Col. 1389B], so is my beloved among the daughters” (Song 2:2). Therefore Lot is rightly said to have lived among the wicked, so that, in accordance with the bridegroom’s praise, a lily might be shown to have grown among thorns.

## CHAPTER V.—The she-ass rebuked Balaam (2 Pet. 2:16).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 12.) Bodily distress is a great remedy for the heart. It recalls the mind to knowledge of itself, and the memory of infirmity restores it when health has often cast it aside, so that the mind carried outside itself into exaltation may be reminded, through the flesh it suffers being struck, to what condition it is subject.

This is rightly signified by Balaam, if only he had been willing to follow God’s voice in obedience, in the very delay of his journey. Balaam was pressing on toward his intended destination, but the animal over which he presided hindered his desire.

For while the she-ass delayed because of the prohibition, it saw the angel whom the human mind did not see. Often the flesh, made sluggish through distress, points out by its blows the God whom the mind itself, presiding over the flesh, did not see. Thus it impedes the anxiety of the spirit that desires to advance in this world, as though proceeding on a journey, until the invisible one becomes known to it because he stands in its way [Col. 1389C].

Hence Peter rightly says: “He received a rebuke for his madness from a mute beast of burden, which, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s folly” (2 Pet. 2:15–16).

A mad person is rebuked by a mute beast of burden when an exalted mind is reminded by afflicted flesh of the good of humility that it ought to preserve. But Balaam did not obtain the benefit of this rebuke because, while proceeding to curse, he changed his voice but not his mind.

## CHAPTER VI.—Paul wrote to you according to the wisdom granted to him (2 Pet. 3:15).

[Col. 1389D]

(Ezekiel, homily 6, nos. 9–11; *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book X, no. 9.) Whoever wishes to act wickedly and yet wants others to remain silent about it is his own witness that he desires to be loved more than truth, since he does not want truth defended against him.

No one lives in such a way as not to fall into some fault. Therefore, the person who wants no one to spare him against the truth desires truth to be loved more than himself.

Although we can perceive certain things as just and right, we comprehend one matter as it is and remain ignorant of another. Peter had shone with such great faith and such great miracles, yet when the Gentiles were converted and he imposed the burden of circumcision, he took care to say what was right.

Because Peter did not want himself to be spared against the truth, he willingly accepted Paul’s rebuke. Paul says that he had died to the Law through the Law, because the Law itself had prepared the way for him to believe in Christ. Burning with great zeal for faith, he did not want the precepts of the Law to be observed in a carnal manner and forbade circumcision among the Gentiles.

When the apostle Peter still wished the custom of observing the Law’s circumcision to be maintained, Paul opposed him to his face and says that Peter was blameworthy in this matter. Speaking of his conduct to the disciples, Paul calls it not only a fault but, what is more serious, hypocrisy—that is, pretense—saying: “When Peter came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was blameworthy” (Gal. 2:11) [Col. 1390A]. A little later he adds: “And the other Jews joined him in his pretense.”

The first of the apostles, while admonishing the disciples on many matters and learning that Paul’s writings were being disparaged by some, said: “Our most beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you, speaking in them of these matters, among which there are certain things difficult to understand, which the ignorant and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.”

Behold, Paul writes in his Epistles that Peter was blameworthy. Behold, Peter in his Epistles asserts that Paul is admirable in what he wrote. Certainly, if Peter had not read Paul’s Epistles, he would not have praised them. But if he read them, he found that Peter himself was called blameworthy in them.

As a friend of truth, therefore, he praised even the fact that he had been rebuked, and he was pleased by this very thing: that he had not been pleasing in those matters in which he had thought differently than he ought. He also yielded to a lesser brother in agreement and, in the same matter, became the follower of his inferior, so that he might even lead in this respect; so that the one who was first in the summit of the apostolate might also be first in humility [Col. 1390B].

Consider, therefore, dearest brothers, at what height of mind stood the man who praised Epistles in which he found himself described as worthy of blame. What great gentleness was that? What peace of soul? What firmness of mind and tranquility of thought?

Behold, he is rebuked by his lesser brother and does not disdain to be rebuked. He does not recall that he was called first to the apostolate; nor that he received the keys of the heavenly kingdom; nor that whatever sins he loosed on earth would be loosed in heaven; nor that he walked upon the sea; nor that he had raised paralytics by commanding them in Jesus’ name; nor that he had healed the sick by the shadow of his body; nor that he had struck liars dead by a word; nor that he had raised the dead through prayer.

Thus, so that he would not disdain to hear words of rebuke, he thrust all the gifts he had received away from his memory, as it were, so that he might hold firmly to the one gift of humility.

Who among us, then, if he had performed even some small sign, would patiently hear words of rebuke after being rebuked by a lesser brother [Col. 1390C]? We have performed no sign at all, and if someone perhaps criticizes our conduct, we immediately swell up. Silently we imagine ourselves to be great; we bring our virtues to mind, including even those we do not possess.

Peter, on the contrary, remained humble in rebuke despite his virtues.

There are some, however, who understand not Peter, the chief of the apostles, but another person named Peter as the one rebuked by Paul. If they had read the words of the apostle Paul more carefully, they would not say this.

For when Paul was about to say, “When Peter came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face” (Gal. 2:11), he first stated at the beginning of his account whom he meant by Peter, saying: “The Gospel of the uncircumcision was entrusted to me, just as the Gospel of the circumcision was entrusted to Peter. For the one who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked in me among the Gentiles” (ibid. 7–8).

It is therefore clear which Peter Paul is speaking about: the one whom he calls an apostle and whom he relates to have presided over the Gospel of the circumcision.

There were also some who said that the Second Epistle of Peter [Col. 1390D], in which Paul’s Epistles are praised, was not written by Peter. But if they had weighed the words of that Epistle, they could have thought very differently.

For in it we read: “A voice came to him from the magnificent glory: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (2 Pet. 1:17). It then adds: “And we ourselves heard this voice when we were with him on the holy mountain.”

Let them read the Gospel, and they will immediately recognize that when this voice came from heaven, the apostle Peter stood with God on the mountain. Therefore, the one who wrote this Epistle is the one who heard this voice from the Lord on the mountain.

Love in Peter firmly resisted the threats of terrifying rulers, and in the removal of circumcision humbly heard the words of his juniors. Love also in Paul humbly endured the hands of persecutors, yet boldly rebuked, concerning the matter of circumcision, the opinion of one who was his superior in rank.

# EXPOSITION ON THE FIRST EPISTLE OF BLESSED JOHN THE APOSTLE

[Col. 1391]

## CHAPTER I.—If we say that we have no sin, etc. (1 John 1:8).

[Col. 1391A]

(In *Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XVIII, no. 71.) Although just men shine forth in this life with the great splendor of righteousness, they are nevertheless by no means free from the stains of sin altogether, as the Apostle John testifies, saying: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” James likewise affirms this, declaring: “For in many things we all offend” (James 3:2). The Prophet also entreats, saying: “Enter not into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no living person will be justified” (Psalm 142:2). For as long as just men live mortally in this corruptible flesh, they may indeed be just, but they cannot entirely lack the contagion of guilt, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9:15).

## CHAPTER II.—“We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous,” etc. (1 John 2:1).

[Col. 1391B]

(*Book I on Ezekiel*, Homily 7, no. 24.) It is necessary that we who are still little ones should always place both the virtues and the tears of the perfect before the eyes of our mind. Let us imitate what we see in them, so that when we have begun to grow through successive advances, we may be able to conceal from that strict judgment the evils we have committed. For in continual weeping and in our daily repentance we have a Priest in heaven who intercedes for us; of him it is also said through John: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ; and he himself is the expiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2).

Behold, the spirit rejoices when we hear of the power of our advocate; yet fear again wounds our joy, because he who is our advocate is said to be righteous. We have causes grounded in injustice, whereas the righteous advocate in no way accepts unjust causes, nor does he consent to plead on behalf of injustice. What, then, are we to do, my dearest brothers? But behold, what we should do comes to mind: let us lament and accuse the evils we have committed. It is written: “The righteous person is the first accuser of himself” (Proverbs 18:17). For every converted sinner begins already to become just in his tears when he begins to accuse what he has done. Why should the one who now rages against his own injustice through tears not be just?

Our righteous advocate, therefore, will defend us as righteous in judgment, because we both recognize and accuse ourselves as unjust. Let us therefore place our confidence not in our tears, nor in our deeds, but in the pleading of our advocate.

## CHAPTER III.—“Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4).

(*Homily 29 on the Gospels*, no. 3.) True faith is that which is not contradicted in conduct by what it says in words. Hence Paul says to certain false believers: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). Hence John says: “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar.”

Since this is so, we must recognize the truth of our faith by examining our life. For we are truly faithful when we fulfill in our actions what we promise in words. On the day of baptism we promised to renounce all the works of the ancient enemy and all his pomps. Therefore let each of you turn the eyes of his mind back upon himself; and if, after baptism, he keeps what he pledged before baptism, let him rejoice, already certain that he is faithful.

But suppose that he has by no means kept what he promised, and has fallen into practicing evil deeds and desiring the pomps of the world. Let us see whether he now knows how to mourn that he went astray. Before the merciful Judge, even the one who returns to the truth after lying will not be considered deceitful, because almighty God, when he willingly receives our repentance, conceals by his judgment the error into which we fell.

## CHAPTER IV.—“Do not love the world” (1 John 2:15).

[Col. 1392A]

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XVIII, no. 16; *Book II on Ezekiel*, Homily 7, no. 17.) The soul can never exist without delight, for it takes delight either in what is low or in what is high. The more intensely it is exercised in striving toward the highest things, the more intensely it grows sluggish toward the lowest; and the more sharply it burns with concern for the lowest things, the more culpably it grows cold toward the highest. For these two things cannot be loved simultaneously and equally.

Thus the Apostle John, knowing that the harvest of heavenly love cannot germinate among the thorns of worldly loves, first uproots the thorns of worldly loves from the hearts of his hearers with the holy hand of the word, before bringing forth the seeds of eternal love, saying: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world.” He immediately added the reason why: “Because if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.” It is as though he were saying openly: The two loves cannot both be contained in one heart, nor does the crop of heavenly love spring up in one where the thorns of lowly pleasure destroy it.

He immediately gives the same reason and enumerates the stings that arise from this lowly pleasure, saying: “Because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, and the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16). This is why everyone desires to possess something, and more than is necessary: so that by possessing it they may grow proud, and because someone else does not have it, they may exalt themselves in their thoughts.

Whoever, therefore, is conquered by love of earthly things takes no delight in God. “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24), because one cannot love transitory and eternal things at the same time. If we love eternity, we possess all temporal things for use, not as our ultimate end.

## CHAPTER V.—“Many antichrists have arisen” (1 John 2:18).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXIX, no. 15.) When the Antichrist, the head of the wicked, rises in persecution of the holy Church, many who are now pious in speech but impious in heart will fall once their wickedness has been made public, and will lose the faith they had outwardly maintained. Yet no one should therefore consider himself safe from such a fall because he does not expect to reach the storm of that temptation.

How many have not seen the times of that temptation, and yet are caught up in the storm of its temptation! Cain did not see the time of the Antichrist, yet by his merits he was a member of the Antichrist. Judas did not experience the cruelty of that persecution, yet, persuaded by greed, he succumbed to the force of its cruelty. Simon lived far removed from the times of the Antichrist, yet by perversely desiring the power of his miracles he joined himself to his pride.

Thus the wicked body is joined to its head, and members are joined to members. Although they do not know one another in understanding, they are nevertheless joined to him by wicked action. Hence it comes about that the Antichrist, the author of the wicked, already appears in his agents, although he has not yet come.

Thus John says: “Little children, it is the last hour; and just as you heard that the Antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have arisen; therefore we know that it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). For now many antichrists have arisen, since all the wicked are already his members; by their wicked deeds they have gone ahead of their head, living badly.

Amid all this, each one of us must return to the secret place of his heart and fear the losses caused by his conduct, lest, as his merits demand, he run by the strict justice of God’s judgments into the number of such people.

## CHAPTER VI.—“His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2:27).

(*Homily 30 on the Gospels*, nos. 3, 8.) Unless the Holy Spirit is present in the heart of the listener, the teacher’s speech is useless. Therefore no one should attribute to the human teacher what he understands from the teacher’s mouth, because unless there is one within who teaches, the teacher’s tongue labors outwardly in vain.

Behold, you all hear one voice speaking, yet you do not all receive the meaning of the voice you have heard in the same way. Since the voice is not different, why is the understanding of the voice different in your hearts, unless there is an inner teacher who, through what the speaker’s voice commonly urges, teaches certain people in a special way about the meaning of the voice?

Of this anointing of the Holy Spirit John says: “As his anointing teaches you about everything.” A person is therefore not instructed through the voice when the mind is not anointed by the Holy Spirit.

It is a pleasure to raise the eyes of faith to the power of this craftsman and to consider separately the Fathers of the New and Old Testaments. Behold, with those same eyes of faith I look upon David, Amos, Daniel, Peter, Paul, and Matthew, and I wish to consider what kind of craftsman this Holy Spirit is—but in the very act of considering I fail.

He fills the boy who plays the lyre and makes him a psalmist. He fills the herdsman who tends sycamores and makes him a prophet. He fills the abstinent boy and makes him a judge of elders. He fills the fisherman and makes him a preacher. He fills the persecutor and makes him a teacher of the nations. He fills the tax collector and makes him an evangelist.

O what a craftsman this Spirit is! No delay is required in learning whatever he wishes; as soon as he touches the mind, he teaches it. His touching alone is his teaching. For as soon as he illuminates the human mind, he changes it: suddenly he makes it cease to be what it was and suddenly presents what it was not.

## CHAPTER VII.—“We shall be like him” (1 John 3:2).

(*Book I on Ezekiel*, Homily 2, nos. 20–21; *Book XVIII on Job*, no. 78.) All the saints, in order to rise to the virtue of holiness, strive toward the likeness of the Mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ. They would not be saints if they did not possess the likeness of this human being. Each saint is led into the likeness of this human being insofar as he imitates the life of his Redeemer.

After this likeness, which is now held in conduct, the likeness of glory will one day be attained. Hence John says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him.” He immediately adds how this can happen, saying: “Because we shall see him as he is.”

To be God is to remain eternal and unchangeable. For everything that changes ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not. God’s being, however, is never to be otherwise. Hence it is said to Moses: “I am who I am”; and, “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3:14). James likewise says: “With whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning” (James 1:17).

Thus John says: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” By beholding the essence of his nature, we are freed from our mutability and fixed in eternity. We shall be changed into the one whom we shall see, because by seeing life we shall be free from death; by seeing immutability we shall transcend our mutability; and by seeing incorruption we shall be held by no corruption.

At that time there will also be a likeness of the human being in our bodies. For Paul says: “Our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our humiliation, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3:20–21; the supplied reference reads “Phil. V, 20”).

The bodies of the elect, therefore, will then be conformed to the glory of the Lord’s body. Although by nature they do not possess equality with his glory, they nevertheless possess the likeness of his configuration by grace. For just as the likeness of his life is now drawn in the conduct of the elect, so in the resurrection the likeness of eternity will follow in the mind, because “we shall see him as he is.”

All the saints will reach those eternal joys so that they may be like God; yet it is written: “Lord, who is like you?” (Psalm 88:9). And again: “Who will be like God among the sons of God?” How, then, will they be like him and not like him? They will be like him in image, yet not like him in equality.

By gazing upon God’s eternity they become eternal; and while they receive the gift of his vision, from their reception of blessedness they imitate what they see. They are therefore like him because they become blessed, yet they are not like the Creator because they are creatures. They possess a certain likeness to God because they have no end, yet they do not possess the equality of the unbounded, because they are bounded.

## CHAPTER VIII.—“If our heart does not condemn us” (1 John 3:21).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book X, nos. 27–28.) We must know that whenever anyone disagrees in action with the Lord’s commandments, every time he hears them he is reproved and confounded by his own heart, because he is reminded of what he has not done. For in whatever he considers himself to have gone astray, conscience itself secretly accuses him.

The mind is immediately broken in its confidence of hope if, while intent upon prayer, it is still bitten by the memory of an unconquered fault. For it distrusts that it can receive what it desires when it remembers that it is still unwilling to do what it has heard from God.

Hence John says: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God; and whatever we ask from him, we shall receive” (1 John 3:21–22; the supplied text prints “I Joan. XXXI, 21”). Hence Solomon says: “Whoever turns his ear away from hearing the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Proverbs 28:9).

The heart reproves us in our petition when it remembers that it resists the commandments of the one it asks; and prayer becomes accursed when it turns away from the law’s judgment. For it is certainly fitting that anyone should be excluded from the benefits of the one whose commands he does not wish to obey.

In this matter the wholesome remedy is that when the mind reproves itself from the memory of guilt, it should first mourn in prayer the fact that it went astray. Thus, when the stain of error has been wiped away with tears, the face of the heart may appear clean before its author in its petition; and then, as John says, “having confidence before God, whatever we ask from him, we shall receive.”

If we do what he commanded, we shall obtain what we ask. According to John’s saying, the heart receives confidence in prayer when no perversity of life contradicts it. For these two things necessarily belong together before the Lord: action must support prayer, and prayer must support action.

## CHAPTER IX.—“No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4:12).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XVIII, no. 88.) When I contemplate the Fathers of the Old Testament, I recognize from the testimony of the history of sacred speech itself that many of them saw God. Jacob saw the Lord, for he said: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my life has been preserved” (Genesis 32:30). Moses saw the Lord, concerning whom it is written: “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend” (Exodus 33:11).

Behold, the Fathers of the Old Testament testified that they had seen God, yet John says: “No one has ever seen God.” What does this mean except that it is plainly shown that, as long as one lives mortally here, God can be seen through certain images, but cannot be seen through the very appearance of his nature? The soul, breathed upon by the grace of the Spirit, sees God through certain figures, but does not reach the very power of his essence.

Hence Jacob, who testifies that he saw God, saw him only in an angel. Hence Moses, who spoke with God face to face as a man speaks with his friend, says to him in the very course of his speech: “If I have found favor in your sight, show yourself to me openly, so that I may see you” (ibid. 33:13).

Certainly, if the one with whom he was speaking was not God, he would have said, “Show me God,” and not, “Show yourself to me.” But if it was God with whom he spoke face to face, why did he ask to see the one whom he was seeing? From this request it is gathered that he thirsted to behold him in the splendor of his unbounded nature, whom he had already begun to see through certain images, so that the heavenly essence might be present to the eyes of his mind, with no created bodily image intervening in the vision of eternity.

The Fathers of the Old Testament therefore saw the Lord, yet, according to John’s saying, no one has ever seen God. For those who remain in this mortal flesh could see him through certain bounded images, but could not see him through the unbounded light of eternity.

But if some who still live in this corruptible flesh, yet grow through immeasurable virtue, can see God’s eternal splendor through a certain sharpness of contemplation, this too does not conflict with blessed John’s statement, “No one has ever seen God.” For whoever sees Wisdom, which is God, dies utterly to this life, so that he may no longer be held by love of it.

No one sees him who still lives carnally, because no one can embrace God and the world at the same time. Whoever sees God dies precisely insofar as he is wholly separated from the pleasures of this life, whether in the intention of his heart or in the devotion of his deeds. Hence it is also said to that same Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (ibid. 33:20). It is as though it were said openly: No one ever sees God spiritually while living carnally in the world.

## CHAPTER X.—“Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God?” etc. (1 John 4:20).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book VII, no. 28.) How can one love God, whom one does not see? There are two commandments of love: love of God and love of neighbor. Through love of God, love of neighbor is born; and through love of neighbor, love of God is nourished.

For whoever neglects to love God certainly does not know how to love his neighbor. We advance more fully in the love of God when, within the embrace of that same love, we are first nourished by love of our neighbor.

Because the love of God generates love of neighbor, when the Lord was about to declare through the Law, “You shall love your neighbor,” he first said, “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 6:5), so that he might first fix the root of his love in the soil of our breast, in order that brotherly love might later germinate through its branches.

Again, because the love of God grows warm through love of neighbor, John testifies, rebuking us: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God, whom he does not see?” Yet this divine love is born through fear, and as it grows it is transformed into affection.

## CHAPTER XI.—“Whoever loves God loves his brother also” (1 John 4:21).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book X, no. 8; *Book II on Ezekiel*, Homily 9, no. 2.) Love expands into every virtuous deed. It begins with two commandments, but extends itself into countless others. The beginning of this law is love of God and love of neighbor. Of this love John says: “We have this commandment from God, that whoever loves God should love his brother also.”

The love of God, however, is distinguished in three ways, because the Creator commands that he be loved with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all one’s strength. Here we must note that when the divine word commands that God be loved, it not only states from what source, but also teaches to what extent, when it adds “with all,” so that whoever desires perfectly to please God should leave nothing of himself for himself.

Love of neighbor, on the other hand, is derived into two commandments. Through a certain just man it is said: “What you hate to have done to you, take care not to do to another” (Tobit 4:16). And the Truth himself says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matthew 7:12).

Through these two commandments of both Testaments, malice is restrained by one, and kindness is bestowed by the other. Thus, by not doing the evil that one does not wish to suffer, a person ceases from the work of harming; and again, by bestowing the good that he desires to have done to himself, he exercises himself in kindness for the benefit of his neighbor.

When these two things are considered with attentive intention, the heart is directed toward countless ministries of virtue, so that the restless mind may neither burn with desires to inflict what it ought not to inflict nor grow slack through idleness in displaying what it ought to display.

For when one takes care not to do to another what one in no way wishes to endure from another, one attentively examines oneself:

- lest pride lift one up and, casting the mind down into contempt for one’s neighbor, exalt it;
- lest ambition tear the thought apart and, when it expands it toward desiring what belongs to others, constrict it;
- lest lust stain the heart and corrupt it when subjected to unlawful desires;
- lest anger embitter it and inflame it even to the utterance of insult;
- lest envy bite it and, jealous of others’ happiness, consume itself with its own fire;
- lest excessive talkativeness drag out the tongue and extend it even to the wantonness of slander;
- lest malice stir up hatred and provoke the mouth even to the dart of a curse.

Again, when one considers doing to another what one expects another to do to oneself, one carefully weighs how to answer evils with good and good things with better things:

- to show the bold the gentleness of patience;
- to bestow the grace of kindness upon those weakened by the plague of malice;
- to unite the divided in peace and bind the united to the desire for true peace;
- to provide necessities for those in need;
- to show the way of uprightness to those who have gone astray;
- to soothe the afflicted with word and compassion;
- to restrain by reproof those inflamed with desires for this world;
- to mitigate the threats of the powerful by reason;
- to relieve the distress of the oppressed with whatever help one can;
- to oppose patience to those resisting outwardly;
- to offer disciplined patience to those who are proud inwardly;
- to temper zeal for the errors of subjects with gentleness, so that it does not weaken the pursuit of justice;
- to make zeal for punishment burn without allowing it, in burning, to cross the limit of mercy;
- to provoke the ungrateful to love of God through benefits;
- to preserve the grateful in love through service;
- to keep silent about the faults of neighbors when one cannot correct them, yet to fear that silence may become consent when they can be corrected by speaking;
- to tolerate what one keeps silent about without concealing the poison of grief in the heart;
- to offer the gift of kindness to the malicious without, through favor, departing from the rule of uprightness;
- to give one’s neighbors everything one is able to give, without fearing to do so;
- to fear the precipice of pride in the good things one displays, without therefore growing sluggish in the practice of good;
- to distribute what one possesses, while considering how great is the generosity of the one who rewards;
- and, when distributing earthly goods, not to dwell more than necessary upon one’s own poverty, lest sorrow obscure the light of cheerfulness in the offering of the gift.

When love fully takes possession of the mind, it kindles it in manifold ways toward countless works. Therefore faith and life must necessarily be maintained in the love of God; while in the love of neighbor, patience and kindness must be guarded with the utmost care.

Faith and life are necessary in the love of God, since it is written: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:26). The proof of love, therefore, is the manifestation of works. Hence John says in his epistle: “Whoever says, ‘I love God,’ and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 4:20; 2:4). We truly love when we constrain ourselves away from our pleasures toward his commandments. For whoever still flows away into unlawful desires certainly does not love God, because in his pleasure he contradicts him.

Patience and kindness must be preserved in the love of neighbor, because it is written of this same love: “Love is patient, love is kind” (1 Corinthians 13:4)—patient, so that it may bear calmly the evils inflicted by neighbors; kind, so that it may willingly bestow its own good things upon neighbors.

## CHAPTER XII.—“There is a sin unto death” (1 John 5:16).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XVI, no. 82; *Book II on Ezekiel*, Homily 9, no. 3.) That sin leads to hell which is not corrected before the end of the present life through reproof and repentance. Of this sin John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it.”

A sin unto death is a sin extending unto death, because forgiveness is sought in vain for the sin that is not corrected here. The difference between sin and fault is this: sin is to do evil, whereas fault is to abandon good things that must be held above all. Or, certainly, sin lies in action, while fault lies in thought.

# EXPOSITION ON THE THIRD EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE JOHN

[Col. 1397]

## CHAPTER I.—“Therefore we ought to receive such people, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 1:7–8).

[Col. 1397A]

(*Homily 20 on the Gospels*, no. 12.) Although secular men within the holy Church do not possess the gifts of spiritual virtues, when they nevertheless support by their generosity holy men filled with spiritual gifts, they become fellow workers in those spiritual gifts, displaying before God what they assist.

Hence John says to Gaius concerning certain brothers who were traveling: “For they have gone out for the sake of the name of Christ, receiving nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to receive such people, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth.”

Whoever gives temporal support to those who possess spiritual gifts becomes a fellow worker in those spiritual gifts. For since few receive spiritual gifts while many abound in temporal possessions, the rich attach themselves to the virtues of the poor by comforting those holy poor from their own wealth.

## CHAPTER II.—“Diotrephes does not receive us” (3 John 1:9).

[Col. 1397B]

(*Book I on Ezekiel*, Homily 9, nos. 17–18.) When we hold to the right path of conduct, great inquiry is needed to determine whether we should always disregard the words of those who slander us, or whether we should sometimes restrain them.

Concerning this, we must know that just as we should not stir up the tongues of detractors by our own efforts, lest they perish, so, when those tongues have been stirred up by their own malice, we should endure them with equanimity, so that our merit may increase. Sometimes, however, we must restrain them, lest, while they spread evil about us, they corrupt the innocent hearts of those who could have listened to us for their good.

Hence John rebukes the tongue of his detractor, saying: “Diotrephes, who loves to hold the primacy among them, does not receive us. Therefore, if I come, I will call attention to his deeds, which he performs by babbling malicious words against us.”

Hence Paul speaks to the Corinthians who were slandering him, saying: “His letters, they say, are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible.” Let the person of this kind consider that just as we are in word through letters when absent, so we are present in action (2 Corinthians 10:10).

Those whose life is set forth as an example for imitation ought, if they can, to restrain the words of those who slander them, lest those who could have listened to their preaching fail to hear it and, remaining in evil conduct, disdain to live well.

But in this matter the mind must investigate itself with subtle inquiry, lest perhaps it seek the glory of its own praise, while our thought pretends that it is seeking the gain of souls. Often the mind feeds on praise of its own name, and, as though under the pretext of spiritual gain, rejoices when it learns that good things are being said about it.

Often, too, it becomes angry with detractors in defense of its own glory and invents for itself the claim that it is doing this out of zeal for those whose hearts the detractor’s speech disturbs from good fervor.

Therefore those who find, through carefully examining their conscience, that they possess nothing in it of love for private glory must take the greatest care that the words of detractors do not prevail against their reputation.

# EXPOSITION ON THE APOCALYPSE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE JOHN

[Col. 1397]

## CHAPTER I.—“John to the seven churches that are in Asia” (Revelation 1:11).

[Col. 1397B]

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXIII, no. 6.) The number seven ordinarily signifies universality. Hence John writes in this Apocalypse to seven churches. But what else did he wish to be understood through them except the universal Church?

This universal Church, moreover, is represented as being full of the sevenfold spirit of grace when Elisha is described as yawning seven times over the dead boy (2 Kings 4:35). For when the Lord comes upon the dead people, he yawns, as it were, seven times, because the gift of the Spirit’s sevenfold grace mercifully breathes upon them.

The Apostle John therefore writes to seven churches in order to signify the one catholic Church, filled with the sevenfold Spirit of grace. We also know that Solomon said of the Lord: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars” (Proverbs 9:1). To make it known that he had said this concerning the seven churches, he carefully added the mysteries themselves, saying: “She sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set her table.”

By the seven pillars we appropriately understand all the churches, which together make one catholic Church spread throughout the whole world.

## CHAPTER II.—“I, John, was on the island called Patmos, because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ. I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet saying: ‘What you see, write in a book and send it to the seven churches that are in Asia: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.’ And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me. And when I had turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the seven lampstands one like the Son of Man, clothed in a long robe and girded around the breasts with a golden belt” (Revelation 1:9–13; the supplied text prints “Apoc. X, 11 seq.”).

[Col. 1397D]

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXI, no. 5; Book XXIV, no. 26.) The evil of lust is committed either in thought or in deed. Through Moses, lust committed in deed was condemned; by the author of purity, lust conceived in thought was condemned, as he himself says: “It is written: ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you: Everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:27–28).

Our Redeemer came and, transcending the commandments of the Law, ordered that, so that he might abolish in his elect not only lust of the flesh but also lust of the heart, they should gird not only the loins of the flesh—that is, restrain lust from being carried into action—but also the loins of the mind, that is, restrain it from thought as well.

Hence the angel who speaks to John exiled on the island of Patmos is said to be girded with a golden belt around his breasts. Gold ordinarily signifies charity. Because, therefore, the purity of the New Testament also restrains lust of the heart, the angel who appeared within it came girded around the breast.

The golden belt aptly restrains him, because whoever is a citizen of the heavenly homeland abandons impurity no longer out of fear of punishment but out of love of charity. Or the angel appeared to John girded with a golden belt around the breasts because the breasts of the heavenly citizens, since they are no longer subject to fear of punishment and are not separated from one another by any division, are bound together by charity alone.

To have a golden belt around the breasts is to restrain all the movements of changeable thoughts by the bonds of love alone.

## CHAPTER III.—“And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write” (Revelation 2:12).

[Col. 1398D]

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XIV, no. 14.) Sacred Scripture often designates the preachers of the Church by the name of angels, because they announce the glory of the heavenly homeland. Hence, when John writes to the seven churches, he speaks to the angels of the churches—that is, to the preachers of the peoples.

Hence the Prophet says: “The angels of peace will weep bitterly” (Isaiah 33:7).

## CHAPTER IV.—“I know where you dwell, where the seat of Satan is” (Revelation 2:13).

(*Exposition on Blessed Job*, Book XXI, no. 10.) The Lord God considers the ways of all with such careful examination that in each of us he neither overlooks the good things he rewards nor leaves without reproof the evils that displease him.

Hence the Lord praises the angel of the church in Pergamum in some respects and rebukes him in others, saying: “I know where you dwell, where the seat of Satan is; and you hold fast to my name and have not denied my faith” (ibid., v. 13). And shortly afterward: “But I have a few things against you, because you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam.”

To the angel of Thyatira he says: “I know your works, your love, your faith, your ministry, and your wisdom, and your latest works are full in comparison with the earlier ones; but I have a few things against you, because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophet, to teach and seduce my servants, to commit fornication, and to eat food sacrificed to idols.”

Behold, he recalls the good things, yet does not release the evils requiring correction without repentance. For he examines the ways of individuals in such a manner and weighs their steps as he enumerates them, so that by subtle examination he may determine both how much each person advances in good and how much, by turning toward evil, he contradicts his own progress.

The increase of merits gained through the practices of a good life is often held back by an admixture of evil; and what the mind builds by acting well, it overturns by committing other deeds.

## CHAPTER V.—“You have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam” (Revelation 2:14).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXIX, no. 15.) Cain, Judas, Simon, and many others lived long before the times of Antichrist, and yet by living perversely they joined themselves to him. Thus an iniquitous body is joined to its head, and members are joined to members, when they do not know one another in person and yet are united by their wicked conduct. For Pergamum had not known Balaam’s books or words, and yet, following his wickedness, it heard the voice of heavenly rebuke: “You have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication.” The Church of Thyatira was likewise divided from Jezebel by knowledge, times, and places; but because a guilt equal to hers bound it, Jezebel is said to be present in it and to persist in perverse works, as the angel testifies, saying: “I have some things against you, because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants, to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed to idols” (v. 20). Behold: because people could be found who had followed Jezebel’s life through reproachable conduct, Jezebel is said to have been found there; for associated ways of living make one perverse body, even if places or times divide it. Hence it happens that in his perverse imitators every wicked man who has already passed away remains present, and in their works the author of the wicked appears already, although he has not yet come. Therefore John says: “Now many Antichrists have arisen” (1 John 2:18), because all the wicked are already his members; by their perversely performed deeds they have anticipated their head through evil living.

## CHAPTER VI — “I will give you a white stone” (Rev. 2:17).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XIX, no. 4.) To see perfectly the wisdom of God, coeternal with him, is what it means to possess it. Hence concerning the reward of the victor it is said to John: “I will give you a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.” In this life we can know or see even something that we do not receive. But the new name written on the stone signifies, in the eternal reward, a knowledge of God unfamiliar to human minds, which no one can know except the one who receives it and possesses it.

## CHAPTER VII — “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest” (Rev. 3:2).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 34.) Those who do not complete the good things they have begun must consider with careful vigilance that, while they fail to finish what they have undertaken, they also tear down what they had begun. For if what appears to be done does not grow through diligent application, even what was done well diminishes. Hence the angel says to the Church of Sardis: “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die; for I have not found your works complete before my God.” Since, therefore, its works had not been found complete before God, he foretold that the remaining things already accomplished were also about to die. For if what is dead in us is not kindled to life, what is held as though still alive is also extinguished.

In this world the human soul is, as it were, like a ship striving against the force of a river’s current: it is not permitted to remain in one place, because unless it strives toward the heights, it slips back to the depths. If, therefore, the strong hand of the one who acts does not raise begun good works toward perfection, the relaxation of his activity itself fights against what has been accomplished. Hence Solomon says: “Whoever is slack and negligent in his work is a brother to one who dissipates his works” (Prov. 18:9). For whoever does not carry out begun good works with strictness imitates, through the dissolution of negligence, the hand of one who destroys.

## CHAPTER VIII — “Whoever conquers, I will make him a pillar” (Rev. 3:12).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XVII, no. 42.) The foremost preachers of the Church, upon whom the whole structure of the spiritual building rises as it grows in the heavens, are called pillars, as John’s Apocalypse testifies, saying: “Whoever conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God.” Whoever is firmly established in the work of God with right intention is raised as a pillar in the structure of the spiritual building, so that, placed in this temple—which is the Church—he may be both useful and an adornment. Concerning such pillars the Apostle says: “Peter, James, and John, who were regarded as pillars, gave me their right hands” (Gal. 2:9).

## CHAPTER IX — “Would that you were cold or hot” (Rev. 3:15).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 34.) Those who begin good works but do not complete them must consider that it would actually be more tolerable not to take up that straight path than, after taking it up, to turn back. For if they did not look behind them, they would not grow faint through any torpor in their undertaking. Let them therefore hear what is written: “Would that you were cold or hot; but because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I am about to vomit you out of my mouth.”

The one who is hot both takes up good pursuits and brings them to completion; the one who is cold neither begins the things that must be completed. Just as one passes from cold through lukewarmness to heat, so from heat through lukewarmness one returns to cold. Whoever, therefore, after losing the coldness of unbelief, does not overcome lukewarmness and blaze up so as to burn, unquestionably, having despaired of heat while lingering in harmful lukewarmness, acts so as to grow cold.

But just as before lukewarmness there is cold under hope, so after cold there is lukewarmness in despair. One who is still in sins does not lose confidence in conversion. But one who has grown lukewarm after conversion has taken away the hope that could have been held concerning the sinner. Everyone is therefore required to be either hot or cold, lest he be vomited out while lukewarm: either, if not yet converted, he should still offer hope of conversion in himself, or, if already converted, he should burn with zeal in the virtues. Otherwise the lukewarm person who returns from the heat he had resolved upon, through torpor, to harmful cold will be vomited out.

## CHAPTER X — “You say, ‘I am rich’” (Rev. 3:17).

[Col. 1400D]

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXXIV, no. 6.) The poverty of the reprobate is properly so called because, while they are filled with vices, they are emptied of the riches of virtues. It often happens to them that, lifted up through the madness of pride, they fail to consider the losses of their own ruin and do not recognize that they are also lacking in good works. Hence, through the angel’s voice, it is said to the preacher of Laodicea: “You say, ‘I am rich, and have grown wealthy, and lack nothing’; and you do not know that you are wretched, poor, blind, and naked.”

He asserts himself to be rich who exalts himself through arrogance, but he is exposed as poor, blind, and naked. Poor, certainly, because he does not possess the riches of virtues; blind, because he does not even see the poverty he suffers; naked, because he has lost his first robe—and worse still, because he does not recognize that he has lost it.

## CHAPTER XI — “I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire” (Rev. 3:18).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book IV, no. 61.) Gold signifies wisdom, concerning which Solomon says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21:20). He saw wisdom as gold, which he called a treasure. It is rightly signified by the name of gold, because just as temporal things are purchased with gold, so eternal goods are purchased with wisdom.

Since, therefore, wisdom is sometimes signified by gold, the angel says to the preacher of Laodicea: “I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire.” We buy gold when, in order to receive wisdom, we first offer obedience.
