A certain Wise Man urges us to this transaction, saying: “If you desired wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will give it to you” (Sirach 1:33).

## CHAPTER XII — “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, so that you may see” (Rev. 3:18).

(*Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chapter 11.) One is bleary-eyed when his intelligence flashes toward knowledge of the truth, but the perverse activity of carnal life nevertheless obscures it. Nature sharpens the understanding, but the perversity of one’s conduct confounds it. To such a person it is rightly said through the angel: “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, so that you may see.”

We anoint our eyes with eye-salve so that we may see when we assist the sharpness of our understanding with the remedy of good works, in order to recognize the brightness of the true light.

## CHAPTER XIII — “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3:19).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XVIII, no. 35.) Every divine stroke is either a purification of our present life or the beginning of a punishment to come. Concerning those who advance through scourging, the Lord himself says through the angel to John: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise,” as it is said elsewhere: “Whom God loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

On the other hand, concerning the scourge of condemnation, the Lord says through Jeremiah, when he sees peoples sinning incorrigibly—whom he regards no longer as sons under discipline but as enemies under strict punishment: “With the wound of an enemy I have struck you, with cruel chastisement” (Jer. 30:14). These scourges condemn and do not liberate; for them the scourges begin in this life and persist in eternal punishment.

Hence the Lord says through Moses: “A fire has been kindled by my anger, and it shall burn down to the depths of the underworld” (Deut. 32:22). Insofar as this concerns present punishment, it is rightly said: “A fire has been kindled by my anger”; insofar as it concerns eternal condemnation, what follows is suitably added: “And it shall burn down to the depths of the underworld.”

Although some are accustomed to say what is written, according to the Septuagint interpreters, in the prophet Nahum: “God will not take vengeance twice for the same thing” (Nah. 1:9), they do not attend to what is said through the prophet Jeremiah concerning the wicked: “Crush them with a double destruction” (Jer. 17:18), nor to what is written elsewhere: “Jesus, who saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude 5).

Yet if we grant them agreement that no fault can be struck twice, this must be understood of those who are struck in sin and die in their sin: their punishment begins here and is completed there. Thus for the uncorrected there is one scourge, which begins temporally but is completed in eternal torments, so that for those who wholly refuse correction the stroke of present scourges becomes the beginning of subsequent torments.

Hence the elect always foresee this: that they should return to righteousness before the Judge’s anger kindles itself unquenchably, lest, overtaken by the final scourge, their life and their guilt come to an end together. For a scourge then washes away guilt when it changes one’s life; but when it does not change a person’s conduct, it does not expiate his deeds.

## CHAPTER XIV — “Whoever conquers, I will grant him to sit with me” (Rev. 3:21).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXVI, no. 53.) Holy men who now live justly and irreproachably will in the future obtain the power to judge. Hence the Lord says to the Church of Laodicea: “Whoever conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, just as I conquered and sat with my Father on his throne.”

The conquering Lord asserts that he sat on the throne with the Father because, after the contests of his passion and the palm of his resurrection, he showed more clearly to all that he was equal in power to the Father, and, having trampled down the sting of death, made it known that he was not unequal to him. Hence he also says to Mary, who did not yet believe in him: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17).

For us, to sit on the throne of the Son is to judge by the power of that same Son. Since we receive the primacy of judgment through his power, we sit, as it were, on his throne. Nor does it conflict with the truth that elsewhere he testifies that the disciples will sit on twelve thrones, while here he declares that they will sit on his throne. Through the twelve thrones, universal judgment is signified; through the throne of the Son, the singular summit of judicial power is indicated. What is designated by the twelve thrones is therefore also designated by the one throne of the Son, because universal judgment is received through the intervention of our Mediator.

## CHAPTER XV — “And behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one seated upon the throne. And in the midst of the throne, and around the throne, were four living creatures full of eyes in front and behind” (Rev. 4:2 ff.).

[Col. 1402B]

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXXI, no. 94.) The prophet Ezekiel, describing how he saw the four evangelists under the form of living creatures, testifies that the face of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle appeared in them. John himself certainly does not differ from this prophetic statement in his revelation, saying: “The first living creature was like a lion, the second living creature like a calf, the third living creature had the face of a man, and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle” (ibid., v. 7).

These four living creatures properly correspond individually to each evangelist: one indicates the order of human birth; another, through the immolation of the sacrifice for the world, as it were the death of a calf, indicates it; another signifies the strength of power, like the roar of a lion; and another, gazing upon the birth of the Word, looks upon it like an eagle gazing at the rising sun.

In Holy Scripture, the word “eagle” sometimes represents either the subtle understanding of the saints and their lofty contemplation, or the incarnate Lord, swiftly flying across the depths and soon returning to the heights. Thus, through the fourth living creature—that is, the eagle, which surpasses the sight of all birds in sharpness, so that the ray of the sun, fixed upon it, cannot make its eyes close by any flashing of its light—John is signified. He left the earth in flight because, through subtle understanding, he penetrated the inner mysteries of the Word by seeing them.

Moreover, these four living creatures can signify their own head, of which they are members. He himself is man, because he truly assumed our nature; he is a calf, because he patiently died for us; he is a lion, because through the strength of his divinity he broke the bond of the death he had assumed; and finally he is an eagle, because he returned to heaven, from which he had come. He was therefore called man in being born, calf in dying, lion in rising again, and eagle in ascending to heaven.

The saints, too, can be signified through these living creatures: one becomes man by acting rationally in all things; another, strong in sufferings and unafraid of the world’s adversities, becomes a lion; another, through abstinence and offering himself as a living sacrifice, becomes a calf; another, lifting himself into the heights on the wings of contemplation, becomes an eagle.

## CHAPTER XVI — “And each of the four living creatures had six wings, and around and within they were full of eyes” (Rev. 4:8).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XIX, no. 20.) All the saints look around themselves externally and internally, and invisibly fear either that they may be found blameworthy outwardly or that they may be seen to be wicked inwardly. Hence the living creatures seen by John are said to be full of eyes around and within.

Whoever arranges his outward conduct honorably but neglects his interior life has eyes around him but not within. All the saints, however, because they look carefully upon their outward conduct so that they may offer good examples to their brothers, and because they watch attentively over their interior life, preparing themselves to be irreproachable before the gaze of the inward Judge, are said to have eyes both around and within.

## CHAPTER XVII — “And they had no rest day or night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who is and who is to come” (Rev. 4:8).

[Col. 1403A]

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 4, no. 7.) It must be considered that the faith of the ancient and the new Fathers was one, and that they believed the almighty God to be a Trinity. Behold, John says in his revelation that four living creatures in heaven cried out: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord almighty.” In order to show the Trinity of persons, “Holy” is said three times. But to make it clear that the Trinity is one in substance, he is said to be not “Lords God” but “Lord.”

David, likewise holding this view, says: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us” (Ps. 66:8). Although he had said “God” three times, to show that this one God exists, he added: “And may all the ends of the earth fear him.” Paul likewise says: “For from him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:36): “from him,” namely, from the Father; “through him,” through the Son; “in him,” in the Holy Spirit. Having thus said “him” three times, he made the distinction clear and added: “To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.” For by not saying “to them” but “to him,” he distinguished the persons by saying “him” three times, and by adding “to him be glory,” he did not divide the substance.

## CHAPTER XVIII — “And when the four living creatures gave glory and honor and blessing to the one seated upon the throne, who lives forever and ever, the twenty-four elders fell before the one seated upon the throne and worshiped the one who lives forever and ever, and they cast their crowns before the throne of God” (Rev. 4:9–10).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXII, no. 20.) Holy men recognize that whatever good they see in themselves is a gift of immortal grace. They become debtors for the gift they have received: grace, going before them, gave them the good will they had not possessed; following after, it granted them the ability to do the good they desire.

Hence John rightly says: “They worshiped the one who lives forever and ever, casting their crowns before the throne of God.” To cast their crowns before the throne of God is not to attribute the victories of their contests to themselves but to their author, so that they may refer the glory of praise to the one from whom they know they received the strength for the contest.

Whoever attributes to himself what he accomplishes is convicted of denying the grace of his author; he denies God because, despising his grace, he arrogates to himself the strength for good works. Every sin that arises from weakness does not altogether destroy hope, because it seeks pardon from the heavenly Judge. But the presumption of one’s own virtue is all the more grievous in despair the farther it is from humility. When a person attributes the strength of his work to himself, he does not return to the help of its author; and thus the sinner perishes more grievously because he is unaware even that he is a sinner.

## CHAPTER XIX — “And I saw in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne a book written within and on the back, sealed with seven seals” (Rev. 5:1).

(Book I on Ezekiel, homily 9, nos. 30–31.) The book in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne signifies the page of Holy Scripture, which is closed by the depth of its meanings, so that it is not easily penetrated by everyone’s understanding.

This book of sacred speech is written within through allegory and without through history; within through spiritual understanding, but without through the simple meaning of the letter, suited to those who are still weak. It is written within because it promises invisible things; without because it orders visible things through the rectitude of its commandments. Within because it promises heavenly things; without because it commands how earthly and contemptible things are either to be used or avoided through desire. For it speaks one way about heavenly secrets, but commands another way in external actions.

The things it commands outwardly are evident, but those it relates concerning inward realities cannot be clearly grasped. What it tells us about the nature of divinity or about eternal joys is, while we still lack knowledge of these things, known secretly to the angels alone. Yet of these hidden realities we already perceive a portion through spiritual understanding and have already received the pledge of the Holy Spirit, because we do not yet know them fully, but nevertheless love them from the depths, and are nourished by the food of truth in the many spiritual perceptions we already possess.

Let it therefore be said that the book was written within and without, because in sacred speech the stronger are filled by its more hidden and sublime sayings, while we little ones are nourished by its more open commandments.

## CHAPTER XX — “And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice: ‘Who is worthy to open the book and break its seals?’ And no one was able, in heaven or on earth or under the earth, to open the book or look upon it. And I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book” (Rev. 5:2).

(*Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 42.) John later says that this book sealed with seven seals was opened by the Lion of the tribe of Judah. What else, indeed, is signified by this book but Holy Scripture? Our Redeemer alone opened it: by becoming human, dying, rising again, and ascending, he disclosed all the mysteries that had been closed within it.

No one in heaven was found worthy, because there was no angel; no one on earth, because there was no living human being in the body; and no one under the earth, because no souls separated from the body could open for us the secrets of sacred speech apart from the Lord. Moreover, when it is said that no one under the earth was found worthy to open the book, I do not see what prevents us from believing that hell is under the earth.

## CHAPTER XXI — “And one of the elders said to me: ‘Do not weep. Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so as to open the book and break its seven seals’” (Rev. 5:5).

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 4, no. 19.) The depth of Holy Scripture is like a well, which almighty God has provided for the watering of the mind. And, so that we might reach an understanding of Scripture, the humility of the Only-Begotten’s passion became for us the way by which what the streams of Holy Scripture had previously spoken secretly was opened to us.

For unless the Only-Begotten Son of God had become incarnate, been tempted, seized, struck with blows, smeared with spittle, crucified, and killed, the depth of this well—that is, of Holy Scripture—would not have been opened to us. What, then, did the humility of his passion become for the faithful, if not the key of opening, through which we find the well of God’s mysteries so that we may drink the water of knowledge from its depths?

The pages of sacred speech speak of his incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension. Because we know that these things have occurred, we now understand what we have heard. They could indeed have been read earlier, but because they had not yet happened, they could not be understood. Hence it is said through John: “The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered, so as to open the book and break its seals.” He opened the book and broke its seals who, by being born, dying, rising again, and ascending to heaven, disclosed to us the mysteries of Holy Scripture.

## CHAPTER XXII — “And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain. And he came and took the book from the right hand of the one seated upon the throne. And when he had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell before the Lamb and sang a new song, saying: ‘You are worthy, Lord, to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us for our God by your blood’” (Rev. 5:6).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXX, no. 66.) No one should judge the incarnate Lord unworthy of being represented by a lamb, since it is evident to all that, by a certain signification, Scripture also uses “worm” and “beetle.” For it is written: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21:7). Or, as it is said through the prophet according to the Septuagint interpreters: “The beetle cried out from the wood” (Hab. 2:2).

When he is therefore represented by things so lowly and contemptible, what is said of him insultingly, when it is clear that nothing is said of him in a merely literal sense? He is called a lamb because of his innocence; he is called a lion because of his power; at times he is also compared with a serpent because of death or wisdom. Through all these images something can be said of him figuratively, because nothing of all these things can be believed to belong to his essence.

For if he essentially existed as any one of these things, he could no longer be called by another. If he were literally a lamb, he could no longer be called a lion; if he were literally a lion, he could not be signified by a serpent. We therefore speak of all these things in him figuratively, the more broadly the farther they are from his essence.

## CHAPTER XXIII — “And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne and the living creatures and the elders; their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice: ‘Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing’” (Rev. 5:11).

[Col. 1405B]

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book II, nos. 8 and 10.) God speaks one way to the angels, and the angels another way to God. God speaks to the angels when his inward will is manifested to them through their life. The angels speak to the Lord when, by looking above themselves, they rise into a movement of wonder. They speak to God, as John says: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity and wisdom.”

The voice of the angels in praise of the Creator is itself the inward wonder of contemplation. To say that they have been astonished at the miracles of divine power is to say that, when a great movement of the heart is aroused with reverence, its cry of voice reaches the ears of the unbounded Spirit. This voice expresses itself as though through distinct words, while taking shape through innumerable forms of wonder.

## CHAPTER XXIV — “And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and because of the testimony they held. And they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, Lord, holy and true, will you refrain from judging and avenging our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’” (Rev. 6:9).

[Col. 1405C]

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book II, no. 11.) God speaks one way to the souls of the saints, and the souls of the saints speak another way to God. What does it mean for souls to express a request for vengeance except that they desire the day of the final judgment and the resurrection of bodies that have died? Their great cry is their great desire. Each person cries out less in proportion as he desires less; and he gives forth a greater voice into the ears of the unbounded Spirit in proportion as he pours himself more fully into that desire.

The words of the souls are therefore their desires. For if desire were not a form of speech, the prophet would not say: “Your ear has heard the desire of their heart” (Ps. 9:17). But since the mind that asks is accustomed to be moved one way, and the mind that is asked another way, and since the souls of the saints cling to God in the bosom of inward secrecy so that they may rest by clinging to him, how are they said to ask when it is clear that they in no way differ from the inward will?

How are they said to desire vengeance when it is certain that they know both the will of God and the things that are to come? Yet because they are placed in him, they are said to ask something from him—not because they desire anything that conflicts with the will of the one they behold, but because the more ardently they cling to God in mind, the more they receive from him that they may ask of him what they know that he wills to do.

They therefore drink from him what they thirst for from him, and, in a manner still incomprehensible to us, they are satisfied in advance by what they hunger for in asking. They would conflict with the will of the Creator if they did not ask for what they see him willing; and they would cling to him less if they pressed upon him, with more sluggish desire, what he wills to give.

## CHAPTER XXV — “And white robes were given to them” (Rev. 6:11).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book II, no. 11, and Book XXXV, no. 25.) John, who in his revelation saw the souls of the saints crying out before the resurrection of their bodies, observed that they had received individual robes. Before the resurrection, the saints are said to have received individual robes because they still enjoy only the blessedness of soul and mind.

At the end of the world they will receive two robes, because together with blessedness of mind they will possess the glory of the flesh; and together with the perfect joy of their souls they will be clothed in the incorruption of their bodies. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “In their land they shall possess double” (Isa. 61:7). The saints possess double in the land of the living because they rejoice in blessedness of mind and body together: they will have not only the joy of souls but also the blessedness of bodies.

## CHAPTER XXVI — “And it was said to them that they should rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers was complete” (Rev. 6:11).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book II, no. 11.) To say “Rest a little longer” to souls that desire is to breathe the consolation of comfort into the ardor of desire from the very presence of the one who speaks, so that the voice of the souls may be what lovers desire, while the speech of the responding God may be what confirms them amid their desires through the certainty of their reward.

His response therefore means that they must await the gathering of their brothers, instilling willingly bearable delays into their minds; and when they long for the resurrection of the flesh, they should also rejoice in the increase of the brothers who are to be gathered.

## CHAPTER XXVII — “And when he had opened the sixth seal, behold, a great earthquake occurred [the supplied text reads: *terrae radius factus est magnus*], and the sun became black like a sackcloth garment” (Rev. 6:12).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book IX, no. 8.) Sometimes in sacred speech the name “sun” signifies the brightness of a preacher. At the end of time the sun is shown as being like a sackcloth garment, because the shining life of preachers is displayed as harsh and despised before the eyes of the reprobate.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — “After this I saw a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation and tribe and language and people, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands” (Rev. 7:9).

[Col. 1406C]

(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 5, no. 22.) What is signified by palms except the rewards of victory? They are customarily given to those who conquer. Therefore, for those who had overcome the ancient enemy in the contest of martyrdom and rejoiced as victors in their homeland to have palms in their hands means that they had held victories in their works. The palm of that work will be rewarded there, where joy is already experienced without struggle.

## CHAPTER XXIX — “And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8:1).

(In *Exposition of Blessed Job*, Book XXX, nos. 52–53, and Book II on Ezekiel, homily 3, no. 14.) Bodily solitude is of no benefit if solitude of heart is lacking. Whoever lives removed in body but, through thoughts of earthly desires, inserts himself amid the tumult of human society is not in solitude. If someone is physically pressed by crowds, yet suffers no tumult of worldly cares in his heart, he is not in the city.

Therefore, for those who live well, solitude of mind is first granted, so that they may suppress the inward noise of earthly desires, restrain the cares boiling up from below through the grace of heavenly love, and drive away from the eyes of the mind, with the hand of gravity, all the movements of frivolous thoughts that present themselves intrusively, like certain flies buzzing around. They seek within themselves a kind of secret place with the Lord, where, when outward noise has ceased, they may speak silently with him through inward desires.

Concerning this secret place of the heart it is said: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour.” Heaven is the soul of the righteous, as the Lord says through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1), and: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1).

When the soul of the righteous directs itself toward eternal heights through the elevation of contemplation, it suppresses the rising tumult of thoughts from below and creates within itself a kind of silence for God. When the repose of contemplative life takes place in the mind, there is silence in heaven, because the noise of earthly actions ceases in thought, so that the mind may apply its ear to the innermost secret.

But because this silence of contemplation and this repose of mind cannot be perfect in this life, the silence in heaven is said to last not for a full hour but for about half an hour. It is not even fully experienced as half an hour, since the word “about” is added: as soon as the mind begins to lift itself up and be suffused with the light of inward repose, the movement of thoughts returns, and the mind, stunned, is ashamed of itself; in its shame it is blinded.

For tumultuous noises of thoughts intrude upon the unwilling mind, and forcibly drag the heart’s eye, already intent upon sublime things, back to look upon earthly realities. Hence it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15).

It is therefore rightly described that this silence lasted not a full hour but half an hour, because contemplation is never perfected here, although it is begun with ardor.

## CHAPTER XXX — “And I saw horses in the vision, and their heads were like the heads of lions; and a third of humankind was killed by the fire, the sulfur, and the smoke that proceeded from their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails” (Rev. 9:18–19).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIII, nos. 46–47.) When Antichrist comes, he will also seize the highest powers of this age. Raging with a twofold error, he will endeavor to draw human hearts to himself both by sending preachers and by bending the authorities he has stirred up. The preaching of his ministers could easily be despised by their hearers; but the terror of secular powers, joined to it before human judgment, exalts it. For many of the powerful will strive, by raging and afflicting, to terrify those whom the others seek to seduce by their words.

What, then, will that time of persecution look like, when some rage with words and others with swords [Col. 1407C] to pervert the devotion of the faithful? For what weak person would not despise the preachers of Antichrist if the terror of secular powers did not fortify them all around? Yet a twofold cunning will be employed against them, because what is said to them by some who flatter with words will be commanded by others who strike. The action of both groups—that is, of the powerful and of those who speak—is briefly comprised in a sentence of John’s Apocalypse, where it says: “The power of the horses was in their mouths and in their tails.”

In sacred Scripture, the preacher is sometimes understood by the name “horse.” In the mouth of the teachers, therefore, there is knowledge; in the tail, the power of secular authorities is represented. For by the tail, which is behind, is signified the temporality of this age, which must be left behind; concerning it the apostle Paul says: “But one thing: forgetting what is behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. 3:13). Everything that passes is behind; everything that comes and remains is ahead.

These horses, then—that is, these most wicked preachers running everywhere under a carnal impulse—have power in their mouth [Col. 1407D] and in their tail, because they preach by persuading people to what is perverse, but, supported by temporal authorities, exalt themselves through the things that are behind. And because they themselves can appear contemptible, they demand reverence for themselves from their wicked hearers through those whose patronage supports them. They will employ many terrors so that, in their perverse preaching, even if the judgment of truth is not feared, at least temporal power will certainly be feared.

**CHAPTER XXXI.**—“And I saw another angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow was upon his head; and he had in his hand an open book” (Rev. 10:1).

(*Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 42.) This book, which is here said to have been seen open, appears shortly before as sealed with seven seals. Concerning it, the blessed John is also told: “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so as to open the book.” What else, indeed, is signified by this book except sacred Scripture? Our Redeemer alone opened it: by becoming human, dying, rising again, and ascending, he disclosed all the mysteries that had been closed within it [Col. 1408A].

**CHAPTER XXXII.**—“And the angel raised his hand to heaven and swore by him who lives forever and ever, that there would be time no longer” (Rev. 10:6).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, no. 5.) The time of our mutability will one day pass away in such a manner that it will utterly cease to be, as the angel bears witness in the sacred utterance, saying: “By him who lives forever, because time will be no more.” For although the Prophet says, “Their time will be forever” (Ps. 80:16), because time gradually fails, he called their failure “their time,” showing that those who are separated from the intimate consolation of the vision fail utterly and without end through every kind of deprivation.

**CHAPTER XXXIII.**—“And I went to the angel, saying that he should give me the book” (Rev. 10:9).

[Col. 1408B] (*Book I on Ezekiel*, homily 18, no. 3.) And he said to me: “Take the book and devour it.” Sacred Scripture is food and drink. Hence, through another prophet, the Lord also threatens: “I will send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord” (Amos 8:11). By saying that he wears us down with hunger and thirst when he withdraws his utterance, he shows that his words are both our food and our drink.

But it must be observed that Scripture is sometimes food and sometimes drink. In obscure matters, which cannot be understood unless they are explained, sacred Scripture is food, because whatever is explained, so that it may be understood, is somehow chewed in order to be swallowed. In clearer matters it is drink, for we swallow drink without chewing. We therefore drink the clearer commandments, because we can understand them even without explanation.

Since John was about to hear many obscure and perplexing things, he is by no means told concerning the sacred book, “Drink,” but “Devour and eat” (Amos 8:11). It is as though he were told: “Examine and understand; that is, chew first and now swallow.”

**CHAPTER XXXIV.**—“And I took the book from the hand of the angel and devoured it; and it was sweet as honey in my mouth” (Rev. 10:10).

[Col. 1408C] (*Book I on Ezekiel*, homily 10, nos. 11–12.) We devour the book when we receive the words of life eagerly. What else is reproved by this expression “devouring” than the sluggishness of our laziness? We neither seek the words and mysteries of the Lord for ourselves, nor listen willingly when they are spoken by others.

We therefore devour and eat the book when we read the word of God. Many read but remain fasting from the reading itself; many hear the voice of preaching but leave empty and fasting after hearing it, because, although they receive an understanding of the sacred utterance in their minds, by forgetting and not observing what they have heard they do not store it in the depths of their hearts. Those, however, are not fasting from their reading who understand and preserve what they have labored to grasp.

We have often seen certain people devote themselves wholeheartedly to the study of sacred reading. Recognizing, amid the words of the Lord, how greatly they had sinned [Col. 1408D], they slaughtered themselves in tears, afflicted themselves with continual sorrow, and took no pleasure in any prosperity of this world, so that the present life became a burden to them and the light itself a weariness. They scarcely allowed themselves to engage in ordinary conversation and found it difficult to relax their spirit from the strictness of discipline; for love of the Creator, they rejoiced only in mourning and silence.

Such people devour and eat the holy book and are not fasting, because their memory has not lost the precepts of life that their understanding could grasp. Rather, their spirit, gathered into God, has preserved these precepts by reading and recalling them.

It often happens that such people, through the gift of heavenly grace, also receive the word of teaching; and from the nourishment of truth, which they themselves have sweetly received and inwardly ruminated, they gently feed those near them. Their preaching is sweet to their hearers precisely because their conduct is not contrary to their preaching: from their own life they draw what they impart to their neighbors through their tongue. Hence it is rightly said: “And I devoured it, and it was sweet as honey in my mouth” [Col. 1409A].

The book that is eaten and devoured becomes sweet in the mouth like honey, because those who have learned to love the omnipotent Lord truly in the secret of their hearts know how to speak of him sweetly. Sacred Scripture is sweet in the mouth of the person whose inner life is filled with its commandments, because it is pleasant for him to speak what has been impressed upon him inwardly for living. The word of God has no sweetness for one whose wicked life gnaws at his conscience.

It is therefore necessary that the person who speaks the word of God first strive to know how he should live, so that afterward he may gather from his life what he should say and how he should say it. For in preaching, the consciousness of holy love builds up more than practice in speaking, because by loving heavenly things the preacher reads within himself how to persuade others that earthly things should be despised.

The person who examines his life inwardly and, by admonishing others outwardly through his example, builds them up is as though he dipped the pen of his tongue in his heart when he writes outwardly for his neighbors with the hand of the word. Hence the remarkable preacher, after giving his disciples many exhortations, added—because he bore no contrary testimony within himself in his conscience: “If there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline, think on these things, which you have both learned and received and heard and seen in me; practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you” (Phil. 4:8–9) [Col. 1409B].

**CHAPTER XXXV.**—“And when I had devoured the book, my belly became bitter” (Rev. 10:10).

(*Book I on Ezekiel*, homily 10, no. 6.) In sacred Scripture, “belly” is sometimes customarily used for “mind.” Hence Jeremiah says: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain” (Jer. 4:19). His belly was in pain because he felt the affliction of his mind. Here too the Truth says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). Since holy preachings flow from the minds of the faithful, rivers of living water pour forth, as it were, from the belly of believers.

But when it was written above concerning the book he had received, “It was sweet as honey in my mouth,” how can it afterward be said, “When I had devoured the book, my belly became bitter” [Col. 1409C]? It is very astonishing if sweetness and bitterness occur together. Yet it must be understood that when the word of God begins to be sweet in the mouth of the heart, the soul of that person undoubtedly becomes bitter against itself. The more subtly he learns from it how he ought to rebuke himself, the more harshly he chastises himself through the bitterness of repentance, because he displeases himself all the more the more he sees in the sacred book what he ought to love concerning the omnipotent God.

**CHAPTER XXXVI.**—“And the angel said to me: You must prophesy again concerning peoples, nations, languages, and many kings” (Rev. 10:11).

(*Book I on Ezekiel*, homily 10, no. 3.) In the words of the sacred utterance, this order of our endeavor must be maintained: we should learn these things so that, pierced with compunction for our iniquity, we may avoid the evils we have committed and not commit others. And when, through long practice in tears, confidence concerning the forgiveness of sins begins to arise, we should also draw others to life through the words of God that we understand [Col. 1409D].

They are to be understood for this purpose: that they may benefit us and be imparted to others through spiritual intention. Hence, after the angel said to the blessed John, “Take the book and devour it,” he added shortly afterward: “You must prophesy concerning peoples, nations, languages, and many kings.” It was as though he were told concerning the sacred food: “Eat and feed others; be satisfied and belch forth; receive and scatter; be strengthened and make strong” [Text: “labor”].

**CHAPTER XXXVII.**—“And a reed like a rod was given to me, saying: Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar and those who worship in it; but cast out the court that is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the nations” (Rev. 11:1–2).

(*Book II on Ezekiel*, homily 1, nos. 14 and 13; and in the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVIII, nos. 15–16.) When the Lord came in the flesh to the Church, he established measures for that same Church and distinguished its boundaries by the subtlety of hidden judgment. Within them some are retained as called, while others are kept away so that they may not approach [Col. 1410A].

Sacred Scripture is the reed of measurement, because in the sacred utterance of God, which has been circumscribed for us, we recognize that his dispensations are hidden. For through his incomprehensible judgment, in the gathering of human beings, he leads some out of their iniquities and abandons others in their iniquity. One is brought within the measure of the elect, while another is left outside, so that he may in no way deserve to belong to the number of the elect.

As the holy Gospel bears witness, we have learned that when someone said, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go,” the same Teacher answered: “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:19). To another who said, “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father,” the same Teacher answered: “Let the dead bury their dead; but you, go and announce the kingdom of God” (ibid., 21).

Behold: one promises that he will follow, and is rejected; another asks to be released, and is retained. The former is not received; the latter is not released from service even for an hour [Col. 1410B].

Preachers, too, were called to go to various parts of the world according to their knowledge, nation, and spirit, while they were restrained from other regions so that they would not approach them. When the apostle Paul was neglecting to preach in Macedonia, a Macedonian man appeared to him in a vision and said: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us.” But, on the contrary, as it is written: “The apostles attempted to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” (Acts 16:9).

Thus, while the holy preachers are called to Macedonia, where perhaps they had not been planning to go, and are prohibited from Asia, where they desired to go, this reed of hidden measures is extended there and drawn back here. It is extended there so that Macedonia may be gathered within the bounds of the holy Church; it is drawn back here so that Asia may remain outside the boundaries of the faith. There were then in Asia people who were not to be gathered; when they had been lost according to their deserts, Asia has now, by God’s generosity, been received within the measures of the Church.

Within these measures, therefore, are all the elect; outside them are all the reprobate, even if they appear to be within the boundary of the faith. Hence it is rightly said to the holy John: “Cast out the court that is outside the temple, and do not measure it.” For what else does the court signify except the breadth of the present life? Those who are designated by the court are rightly outside the temple, and therefore must not be measured, because narrow is the gate that leads to life (Matt. 7:14); the broad way of the life of the wicked is not admitted to the measures and standards of the elect [Col. 1410C].

**CHAPTER XXXVIII.**—“And the temple of the Lord was opened in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple; and a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet” (Rev. 11:19; 12:1).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIV, no. 25.) When the sun is used figuratively in sacred Scripture, the Lord is sometimes designated by it. Thus, in the Book of Wisdom, it is reported that all the wicked, when they recognize their condemnation at the final judgment, will say: “We went astray from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine for us; and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. 5:6) [Col. 1410D]. It is as though they plainly said: “The ray of inward light did not shine upon us.”

Hence John also says: “A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet.” In the sun, the illumination of truth is understood; in the moon, which wanes through its monthly replenishments, the mutability of temporality is understood. Since the holy Church is protected by the splendor of the heavenly light, she is clothed, as it were, with the sun; but because she despises all temporal things, she presses the moon beneath her feet.

**CHAPTER XXXIX.**—“And another sign appeared in heaven: behold, a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and upon its heads seven diadems; and its tail dragged a third of the stars of heaven and cast them upon the earth” (Rev. 12:3–4).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXII, no. 25; book IV, no. 17; book XXXII on Job, no. 25.) This is said concerning Antichrist under the figure of the dragon. Heaven is the Church, which, in the night of the present life, while it contains within itself countless virtues of the saints, shines with the stars radiating above [Col. 1411A].

In sacred Scripture, by the name “stars” the justice of the saints, which shines in the darkness of this life, is sometimes demonstrated; at other times, the pretense of hypocrites is signified—those who display the good things they do in order to receive praise from human beings. If those who live rightly were not stars, Paul would never have said to his disciples: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. 2:15).

Again, if among those who seem to act rightly some did not seek a reward of human favor for their actions, John would never have seen stars falling from the heavenly places, saying: “The dragon sent out its tail and dragged a third of the stars and cast them upon the earth.” That extremity of Satan, raised up through the audacity of the man he assumed, by gaining possession of certain people whom it found in the Church as though they were God’s elect, revealed them to be reprobate; and through the final persuasion of Antichrist, some who seem to shine will be carried away.

To drag stars to the earth is to entangle in the love of earthly things, through open error and iniquity, those who seem devoted to the life of heaven. For stars to fall from heaven to earth is for some, abandoning hope of heavenly things under his guidance, to yearn for the pursuit of secular glory [Col. 1411B].

**CHAPTER XL.**—“And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she had given birth he might devour her child” (Rev. 12:4).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIV, no. 12.) Sacred Scripture sometimes so mingles past and future time that it sometimes uses the future for the past and sometimes the past for the future.

It uses the future for the past when John is shown a woman about to bear a male child who will rule the nations with an iron rod. Since this had already happened at that time, when the incarnate Lord came, the event was being announced as something accomplished.

Again, it uses the past for the future, as the Lord speaks through the Psalmist, saying: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 21:18) [Col. 1411C]. In these words the form of the Lord’s Passion is described as though it had already taken place, yet it is announced as something that would occur much later.

**CHAPTER XLI.**—“And there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon. And the dragon fought, and his angels, and they did not prevail; nor was their place found any longer in heaven. And that great dragon was cast down” (Rev. 12:7).

(Homily 34 on the Gospels, nos. 8–9.) The ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan and who deceives the whole world, was cast down to the earth, and his angels were sent down with him.

The spirits of the heavenly homeland are designated by individual names so that their capacities in their activity may also be indicated through their names. And when they come to minister something to us, among us as well they derive a name from their ministries. Michael is called “Who is like God?”; Raphael is called “the medicine of God.”

Whenever something of marvelous power is accomplished, Michael is said to be sent, so that from the deed itself and from his name it may be understood that no one can do what God is able to do [Col. 1411D]. Hence that ancient enemy who, in his pride, desired to be like God, saying, “I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13), when at the end of the world he is left to his own power, destined to be destroyed at the final judgment, is said to fight with the archangel Michael. Thus the one who had raised himself up in pride toward the likeness of God may, after being destroyed by Michael, learn that no one should rise through pride toward the likeness of God.

Raphael, as we have said, is interpreted as “the medicine of God,” because when he touched Tobias’s eyes as though in the performance of a healing service, he wiped away the darkness of his blindness. Since he is sent to heal, it was fitting that he should be called the medicine of God.

**CHAPTER XLII.**—“And I heard a loud voice saying: Now salvation and power and the kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ have come, because the accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before the presence of our God day and night” (Rev. 12:10).

[Col. 1412A] (In the exposition of Blessed Job, book II, no. 15.) When the crafty adversary observes that a holy man has behaved well amid prosperity, he hastens to condemn him before the Judge through adversity. Sacred Scripture, moreover, often customarily uses “day” for prosperity and “night” for adversity. He therefore does not cease accusing us by day and by night, because he strives to show us blameworthy now in prosperity and now in adversity. He accuses us by day when he suggests that we use prosperity badly; he accuses us by night when he demonstrates that we do not possess patience in adversity.

**CHAPTER XLIII.**—“Woe to the earth and to the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has only a short time” (Rev. 12:12).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIV, no. 1.) At the end of the world, the ancient enemy attacks with greater ferocity, for he becomes all the more fervent in savagery the nearer he feels himself to punishment [Col. 1412B]. He considers that the time is near when he will lose the license of his wicked freedom, since, withdrawn from the license of tempting, he will be bound over to eternal fires.

And to the extent that he is confined by the shortness of time, he expands through multiplicity of cruelty: “having great wrath, knowing that he has only a short time,” as the angelic voice says to John concerning him. Then he stretches himself out in the heat of great wrath, lest the one who could not stand in blessedness should fall with the few into the pit of his condemnation. Then he cunningly seeks out whatever he can accomplish wickedly; then he raises the neck of pride higher; and through the condemned man whom he carries, he wickedly displays everything that he can achieve temporally.

**CHAPTER XLIV.**—“And I saw another beast rising from the earth, and it had two horns like those of a lamb, and it spoke like a dragon; and it exercised all the authority of the first beast in its presence, and it performed great signs, even making fire descend from heaven to earth in the presence of human beings” (Rev. 13:11).

[Col. 1412C] (In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIII, nos. 59, 61–62.) The preachers of Antichrist will claim for themselves an appearance of holiness, yet they will practice works of iniquity. They will be conspicuous through a pretense of justice but obscure through the perpetration of wickedness.

John has comprised the malice of their pretense in a brief description. He had already described the first beast—that is, Antichrist—in the preceding account. It is said that this other beast rose after him, because after him the multitude of his preachers takes pride in earthly power. To rise from the earth is to become proud of earthly glory.

It has two horns like those of a lamb because, through hypocrisy of holiness, it will falsely claim for itself the distinctive wisdom and life that the Lord truly possessed in himself. But because, under the appearance of a lamb, serpentine venom is poured into the ears of reprobate hearers, it is rightly added there: “And it spoke like a dragon.” This beast, then—that is, the multitude of preachers—if it spoke openly like a dragon, would not appear like a lamb; but it assumed the appearance of a lamb in order to carry out the activity of a dragon [Col. 1412D].

At that time what is said through the Gospel by the mouth of Truth will be fulfilled: “False Christs and false prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect” (Mark 13:22). For when the elect see their signs and, while despising their way of life, shudder at such great miracles performed by the ministers of Antichrist, they will experience a certain cloud of doubt in their hearts. As their wickedness raises itself up through wonders, the clearer sight of these people will become somewhat darkened.

Thus, from the signs and lying wonders of the preachers of Antichrist, doubt will for a moment arise in good minds; and, when terrifying signs are seen, obscure thought will gather in the hearts of the elect. Then every soul of the elect will endure the rush of its thoughts like the foam of waves boiling in a pot. The fire of zeal will stir these thoughts, while the temporal oppression itself, like a pot, will keep them enclosed within [Col. 1413A].

Hence, when John described the signs of this beast, he added: “So that he might make fire descend from heaven.” For fire descending from heaven is for the flames of holy zeal to pour forth from the heavenly souls of the elect.

**CHAPTER XLV.**—“I saw the Lamb standing upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand. And they were singing as though a new song, and no one could sing the song except those one hundred and forty-four thousand” (Rev. 14:1).

(*Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 28.) This is said by John concerning virgins who have no knowledge of the sin of the flesh. To sing the Lamb’s song uniquely, together with him forever, is to rejoice before all the faithful even in incorruption of the flesh.

The other elect, however, can hear the song, although they cannot sing it, because through charity they rejoice in the exalted state of those people, even though they do not rise to their rewards. Concerning this incorruption and integrity of the flesh, the Truth says of itself: “Not all can receive this word” (Matt. 19:11). By this he made it known that it is supreme, in that he denied it to all; and by declaring that it is difficult to receive, he indicated to his hearers with what caution what has been received must be held [Col. 1413B].

**CHAPTER XLVI.**—“I saw a white cloud, and upon the cloud one seated like the Son of Man, having upon his head a golden crown and in his hand a sharp sickle” (Rev. 14:14).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIII, no. 21.) The power of divine judgment is signified by the name “sickle,” because it encompasses all things within itself by cutting them down. Whatever is cut by a sickle falls inside it, however it may be bent in any direction. And because the power of heavenly judgment cannot in any way be avoided—for we are within it, no matter where we try to flee—when the Judge who is to come is shown, he is rightly said to hold a sickle, because, powerfully confronting all things, he surrounds them by cutting them down.

**CHAPTER XLVII.**—“And the fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was given to him to afflict human beings with heat and fire” (Rev. 16:2).

[Col. 1413C] (In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIV, no. 25.) By the name “sun,” the understanding of the wise is expressed. To pour out the bowl upon the sun is to inflict the punishments of persecution upon men shining with the splendor of wisdom.

“And it was given to him to afflict human beings with heat and fire,” because when wise men, overcome by tortures, are touched by the error of doing evil, the weak are inflamed with temporal desires, persuaded by their example. The downfall of the strong provides increase for the destruction of the weak.

Because the sun signifies the keenness of the wise, Solomon also says by comparison: “The wise man remains like the sun; the fool changes like the moon” (Eccl. 27:12).

**CHAPTER XLVIII.**—“Behold, I come like a thief” (Rev. 16:8).

(Homily 13 on the Gospels, nos. 5–6.) To shake off the sluggishness of our mind and awaken the spirit to watchfulness over itself, the Lord speaks by way of comparison in the Gospel, saying: “But know this: if the householder had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have watched and would not have allowed his house to be broken into” (Luke 12:39) [Col. 1413D].

From this comparison already given, an exhortation is also added when it is said: “You also, be ready, because at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man will come.” Without the householder’s knowledge, the thief breaks into the house, because while the spirit sleeps, neglecting its own watchfulness, sudden death comes and breaks into the dwelling of our flesh; and kills the person whom it finds sleeping as the master of the house. For when the spirit does not foresee the coming losses at all, death carries it away unawares to punishment.

He would resist the thief if he were awake, because by anticipating the coming of the Judge, who secretly seizes the soul, he would meet him through repentance, lest he perish unrepentant. Our Lord therefore wished the final hour to remain unknown to us, so that it could always be feared; so that, while we cannot foresee it, we may prepare for it without interruption [Col. 1414A].

Since we do not know the time of coming death and cannot act after death, it remains for us to seize the time granted before death. Death itself is conquered in this way—yes, in this way—if it is always feared before it comes.

**CHAPTER XLIX.**—“Blessed is the one who watches” (Rev. 16:15).

(Homily 13 on the Gospels, no. 3.) The person watches who keeps the eyes of the mind open to the sight of the true light. The person watches who preserves through action what he believes. The person watches who drives away from himself the darkness of sluggishness and negligence. Hence Paul says: “Awake, righteous people, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15:34). Again he says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13:11).

**CHAPTER L.**—“Blessed is the one who keeps his garments, lest he walk naked” (Rev. 16:15).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XII, no. 9, and book XVI, no. 63.) Just as garments cover the body, so good works protect the soul. The first human being, when rightly created, received the garment of innocence; deceived by the serpent, he wrongly lost it. And because, having first been granted the garment of innocence in paradise, we have been stripped naked, it is said against this nakedness: “Blessed is the one who keeps his garments, lest he walk naked.”

We keep our garments when we preserve innocence in our minds, so that when the guilt of judgment strips us naked, repentance may clothe us as we return to the innocence we lost [Col. 1414B].

**CHAPTER LI.**—“And they may see its shame” (Rev. 14:15).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book II, no. 81.) Our shame is then seen when a blameworthy life is not at all veiled before the eyes of the righteous at the judgment by the covering of subsequent good works. With our God, our works cover us like garments.

**CHAPTER LII.**—“As much as Babylon glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much torment give her” (Rev. 18:7).

[Col. 1414C] (In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, no. 98.) The omnipotent God, who rightly punishes evil, by no means permits punishments to be disordered in any way, because the penalties that proceed from the balance of justice cannot themselves be inflicted without order.

For how could there be no order in punishments, when retribution of vengeance follows each condemned person according to the measure of his crime, as was said above concerning the condemnation of Babylon? If punishment is distinguished according to the measure of guilt, it is plainly evident that order is preserved in punishments.

**CHAPTER LIII.**—“Blessed are those who are called to the wedding supper of the Lamb” (Rev. 19:9).

(Homily 24 on the Gospels, no. 6, and homily 36.) By this wedding supper of the Lamb, the eternal and final banquet is signified, and whoever enters it once will never leave again. This final banquet of God is called not lunch but supper because supper follows lunch, whereas after supper no banquet remains. Since God’s eternal banquet will be prepared for us at the end, it was right that it should be called not lunch but supper.

John therefore says that they are called not to lunch but to supper, because at the end of the day a banquet is supper. Those who, when the time of the present life has ended, come to the refreshment of heavenly contemplation are called not to the Lamb’s lunch but to his supper.

At that final banquet they will feast upon the presence of truth—those who now transcend earthly things through the pursuit of perfection, whom the love of this world does not bind. Although that love may in some way assail them through temptations, it does not blunt their desires once begun. Then inward refreshment will restore them, because now, filled with sevenfold grace, they pant with love of the Spirit.

Therefore, brothers, let us desire to be filled with the presence of this Spirit. For if we are full of this Spirit, we shall be able to reach that banquet. Whoever is not now restored by the Holy Spirit surely fasts from the refreshment of that eternal banquet [Col. 1415A].

**CHAPTER LIV.**—“And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse; and the one sitting upon it was called Faithful and True. He was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood, and his name is called the Word of God. And the armies that are in heaven followed him on white horses” (Rev. 19:11 and following).

(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXI, no. 27.) He rightly calls the multitude of the saints who had labored in this battle of martyrdom an army. They are reported to sit upon white horses because their bodies shone both with the light of justice and with the brightness of chastity. For each soul’s body is its horse, which it knows how to restrain from illicit things by the bridle of continence and again to release, through the impulse of charity, for the practice of good works.

**CHAPTER LV.**—“And he had written on his garment and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19:16).

[Col. 1415B] (Book II on Ezekiel, homily 1, no. 2.) The garment of the Lord Jesus Christ is the body that he assumed from the Virgin; yet his garment is not one thing and he himself another. For our garment, too, is called flesh, yet we ourselves are our flesh with which we are clothed.

Isaiah, seeing this garment of his long beforehand, stained with blood through the suffering of the cross, said: “Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” (Isa. 63:2).

By the thigh, the propagation of the flesh is meant. Since, through the propagation of the human race—as the lines of the generations are described by Matthew and Luke—he came into this world from the Virgin, and since through the mystery of his incarnation he made known to all nations everywhere that he was King and Lord, he had written on his garment and on his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords.” For where he became known in the world, there he impressed the knowledge of himself upon the reading [Col. 1415C].

**CHAPTER LVI.**—“I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand. And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might deceive the nations no longer, until the thousand years were ended. After this he must be released for a short time” (Rev. 20:2 and following).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IV, no. 16; book XXXII, no. 22.)* The ancient enemy is called both dragon and serpent. He is called “dragon” because he inflames us toward the malice of doing harm and maliciously desires to harm us. He is called “serpent” because he always insinuates his snares gently. By “the abyss,” however, he means the hearts of human beings, which are both fluid through their falling and dark through the obscurity of duplicity. [Col. 1415D] Thus the ancient serpent, bound with a chain, is cast into the abyss, because, restrained from the hearts of the good and shut up in the minds of the reprobate, he dominates them more savagely, while by the power of divine providence he is held fast, so that, insofar as he is able to harm, he may not run wild. Thus, although he secretly rages through them, he does not break out into the violent plunderings of pride.

That apostate angel, therefore, who had been created so as to surpass the other legions of angels, fell through pride so completely that he is now subjected to the dominion of the angels who stand firm. Thus either he now lies hidden, restrained while they minister for our benefit, or later, when they release him for our testing, he will be loosed and exert all his strength against us. The elect spirits of the angels therefore now confine the proud apostate, shut up in the well of the abyss, since those who would not follow him in pride have overcome him. Through their administration it is ordained that he will eventually be recalled for the purpose of open combat, in order to be utterly destroyed.

### CHAPTER LVII

“Blessed and holy is he who has a share in the first resurrection” (Revelation 20:6).

[Col. 1416A]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XIV, no. 19.)* Death is sin, which kills the soul by separating it from the inner life. Therefore he afterwards rises happily in the flesh who, while placed in this life, has risen from the death of his mind.

### CHAPTER LVIII

“And over these the second death has no power, but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years” (Revelation 20:6).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, no. 3.)* In Sacred Scripture, the number one thousand is customarily understood to signify totality. Hence the Psalmist says: “The word which he commanded for a thousand generations” (Psalm 104:8), although it is plainly established that, from the beginning of the world up to the coming of the Redeemer, no more than seventy-seven generations are counted by the Evangelist. What, then, is expressed by the number one thousand except the complete totality of the foreknown generation, destined to bring forth a new offspring? Hence John says: [Col. 1416B] “And they will reign with him for a thousand years,” because the reign of the holy Church is consolidated in the perfection of its totality.

### CHAPTER LIX

“And when the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison; and he will go out and deceive the nations” (Revelation 20:7).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, no. 67; book XIX, no. 15; book XVIII, no. 67; book XXXII, nos. 23, 27.)* By the number one thousand he designated not a quantity of time but the universality in which the Church reigns; and by that number he expressed the entire span of the holy Church, whatever its duration may be, in accordance with its perfection. When this has been completed, the dragon will be brought out from the well of the abyss, because the devil’s malice, which is concealed in the deceitful hearts of the wicked, will then be revealed; and what is now concealed through fear will then disclose publicly, from the mouths of the wicked against the Church, every kind of serpentine venom.

For now the raging conscience hides itself beneath a flattering tongue, and the malice of cunning covers itself, as it were, with an abyss of pretense. At the end of the world, however, the ancient enemy will enter his own vessel—that lost man who is specially called Antichrist. He will be permitted to rise above the measure of human beings, sometimes through the height of worldly honor, sometimes through signs and wonders of pretended holiness, swelling with power.

For he will be that spirit who, created among the heavenly beings, did not lose the power of his nature even when cast down. His power is now not displayed at all for this reason: by the ordering of divine strength, he is restrained from the hearts of the good; and by the spirits of the elect angels he is now confined and suppressed in the well of the abyss, that is, in the minds of the reprobate. At the time of Antichrist he will come forth from the well of the abyss—that is, from the hearts of the wicked in which he now rages secretly—and then, having received power, he will break out against the Church with the force of open persecution.

Truth itself says: “Then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor will be” (Matthew 24:21). Then [Col. 1416D] the ancient enemy, handed over to his own powers, will be released for a short time, indeed, but with great strength against us, as it is written above: “After this he must be released for a short time.” Although his ferocity will give him scope for cruelty, heavenly mercy will constrain him by the shortness of the days, as Truth itself says: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved.” Because the Lord sees that we are both proud and weak, he says that the days he has brought upon us as exceptionally evil are mercifully shortened: thus he both terrifies pride through the adversity of the time and comforts weakness through its brevity.

The proud exaltation of Antichrist will therefore rise over the reprobate minds of human beings through the arrogance of worldly glory, so that sinful man—yet one who despises being regarded as merely human—will falsely claim to be God over human beings. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “So that he takes his seat in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (2 Thessalonians 2:4). But this pride of his will be struck down by the coming of the strict Judge, as it is written: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2:8).

Of this lost man it is also said through Daniel: “He will rise up against the Prince of princes, and without a hand he will be crushed” (Daniel 8:25), because he will be struck with eternal death not by an angelic battle or by a contest with the saints, but by the coming of the Judge and by the breath of his mouth alone. John likewise continues in this revelation, saying: “And fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them” (Revelation 20:9)—namely, Antichrist, his ministers, and his preachers.

### CHAPTER LX

“And the devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet will be tormented day and night forever and ever. Amen” (Revelation 20:9–10).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXXIII, no. 37.)* When the eternal Judge appears in terror, with legions of angels standing by, with the entire ministry of the heavenly powers attending, and with all the elect led forth for this spectacle, that cruel and powerful beast will be brought captive into the midst. Together with his body—that is, with all the reprobate—he will be handed over to the eternal fires of Gehenna, when it is said: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

What a spectacle that will be, when this most savage beast is displayed before the eyes of the elect! If it were seen now, it could terrify them exceedingly during the time of this battle. But by the hidden and wondrous counsel of God it is brought about that, by his grace, it is now defeated by those who fight against it without seeing it, while then it will be seen by the victorious elect already taken captive.

Then the righteous will recognize more fully how much they are indebted to divine assistance, when they see so powerful a beast defeated by those who are now weak; and in the savagery of their enemy they will perceive how much they owe to the grace of their defender. Our soldiers will then return from this battle, bearing the trophies of their virtues. After receiving their bodies, when at that judgment they are already taking possession of entry into the heavenly kingdom, they will first behold the enormous strength of this ancient serpent, so that they will not consider insignificant what they escaped. When his death is seen, it will bring joy—his life, endured now, daily wages war against the righteous amid their torments.

### CHAPTER LXI

“And I saw a great white throne and the one seated upon it; from whose presence earth and heaven fled. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne; and the books were opened. And another book was opened, which is the book of life; and the dead were judged from what was written in the books, according to their works” (Revelation 20:12).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIV, no. 16.)* Whoever wishes to discern his own life precisely ought to observe the life of the righteous. The life of the good is a living reading. Therefore the righteous themselves are not inappropriately called “books” in sacred eloquence, as John says: “The books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life.”

The book of life is the very vision of the coming Judge, in whom every commandment is, as it were, written, because whoever sees him immediately understands, with his conscience bearing witness, everything that he has not done. The books are also said to be opened because the life of the righteous is then seen, in whom the heavenly commandments are discerned as expressed through their deeds.

“And the dead were judged from what was written in the books,” because, in the life of the righteous displayed as in an open book, they read the good which they themselves refused to do, and they are condemned by comparison with those who did it. Therefore, lest anyone then mourn upon seeing what he did not do, let him now attend to what he should imitate in them. Their likeness is set before us as a kind of pattern for imitation.

For whoever desires to understand most fully what he is ought plainly to observe those who are what he is not, so that from the form of the good he may measure how disfigured he himself is through abandoning the good. From those in whom goodness is fully present, he rightly assesses what is lacking in himself; and in their beauty he sees his own ugliness, which he can suffer and yet cannot perceive in himself.

### CHAPTER LXII

“And I saw a new heaven and a new earth; for the first heaven and the first earth passed away” (Revelation 20:1).

[Col. 1418A]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVII, no. 11.)* When Solomon says, “One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever,” one may ask why blessed John asserts that heaven and earth have passed away. We can readily resolve this if we distinguish how earth and heaven pass away and how they remain.

Both pass away with respect to the form they now possess, yet in their essence they endure without end. Hence Paul says: “For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:31). Hence Truth itself says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35). Hence the angelic voice says to John: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth.” These will not be created as other things, but these same things will be renewed.

Heaven and earth therefore pass away and will remain, because they will be cleansed by fire from the appearance they now possess, yet will always be preserved in their own nature. Hence the Psalmist says: “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Psalm 102:27).

They now announce this final transformation of theirs to us through the very changes by which they continually alternate for our use. The earth loses its form through winter’s dryness and becomes green through spring’s moisture. The heaven is daily covered with the darkness of night and renewed by the brightness of day. From this, then, let every believer infer that these things both perish and yet are restored through renewal, since they are constantly repaired as though from decay.

### CHAPTER LXIII

“And one of the seven angels came and carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city, the Church, descending from heaven from God and possessing the glory of God. It had a great and high wall, having twelve gates; and the structure of its wall was of jasper, while the city itself was pure gold, like pure glass” (Revelation 21:17–18).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XVIII, no. 77, and book XXXIV, no. 26.)* In sacred eloquence, the name “gold” sometimes signifies the splendor of the heavenly city. The gold of which that city consists is said to be like glass, so that gold signifies brightness and glass transparency.

We know that the metal gold shines with greater brilliance than all other metals; the nature of glass, however, is such that what is seen from outside shines through with inward purity and transparency. In another metal, whatever is contained within is hidden; in glass, however, any liquid contained within is displayed outwardly as it is inwardly, and, so to speak, every liquid enclosed in a glass vessel is visible.

What else, then, do we understand by gold and glass except that heavenly homeland, that society of blessed citizens whose hearts shine toward one another with brightness and shine through with purity? Because all the saints will shine with supreme brightness in eternal blessedness, the city is said to be constructed of gold. And because their brightness is mutually visible in one another’s hearts, so that when one person’s face is observed his conscience is simultaneously penetrated, this same gold is remembered as being like pure glass.

There, the corporeal substance of each person’s members will not conceal his mind from another’s eyes; rather, the spirit will be visible, and even the harmony of the body will be apparent to bodily eyes. Thus each person will then be visible to another as he cannot now be visible to himself.

Now, while we are in this life, our hearts cannot be seen by one person in another; they are enclosed not in glass vessels but in vessels of clay. The Prophet feared clinging to this clay through the suffering of the mind when he said: “Rescue me from the clay, lest I cling to it” (Psalm 68:15).

Paul calls this dwelling of the bodies an earthly house, saying: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, an eternal house not made by hands in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1). In this earthly house and corruptible flesh, therefore, for as long as we live, we cannot in any way penetrate with the eye of the mind the wall of our corruption, so to speak; nor can we see one another’s thoughts and secrets.

Hence again Paul says: “Who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him?” (1 Corinthians 2:11). And again: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Corinthians 4:5).

That city, therefore, in which all the saints shine with such brightness and shine through with such transparency, revealing their hearts to one another, is said to be like pure glass made of gold, so that it is designated as bright through gold and transparent through glass.

### CHAPTER LXIV

“The length, breadth, and height of the city are equal. And the angel measured its wall with a human measure, which is also an angel’s” (Revelation 21:16–17).

*(Book II on Ezekiel, homily 2, no. 15.)* The holy city Jerusalem, which God inhabits, is perfected from both angelic and human nature.
