Because the angelic creature is above while the human creature is still below, these two creatures can be signified in the city by its breadth and height: the one still dwells in the depths, while the other remains in the heights.

But its breadth and height are equal, because human humility will eventually be brought to equality with the angels. Hence it is written: “They will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but they will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matthew 22:30). Hence it is also said through John: “A human measure, which is also an angel’s,” because the human being is brought to that height of glory at which the angels rejoice that they have been established.

The breadth of the city is therefore as great as its height, because each of the elect, who now labor in the depths, will eventually not be unequal to those most blessed spirits.

### CHAPTER LXV

“And I, John, who heard and saw these things, after I had heard and seen them, fell at the feet of the angel who was showing me these things, to worship him; and he said to me: ‘See that you do not do this. I am your fellow servant, and one of your brothers the prophets, and of those who keep the words of this book’” (Revelation 22:9).

[Col. 1419C]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXVII, no. 29.)* Before the Lord’s incarnation, a human being is read to have worshiped an angel in the Old Testament, and yet he is not forbidden to worship. But after the Mediator’s coming, when John had prostrated himself in worship before an angel, he is forbidden.

What does it mean that angels once calmly allowed themselves to be worshiped, but afterward refused to be worshiped by a human being? It means that formerly they more justly despised human beings, whom they knew to be given over to carnal corruptions and not yet redeemed from those same carnal corruptions, and therefore more abject. But afterward they could no longer endure to have human nature subjected in this way, since they saw that, in its Author, it had been raised even above themselves.

For that which had merited honor in the very Head of the members ought no longer to be despised as subjected in his members.

### CHAPTER LXVI

“And he says to me: ‘Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near’” (Revelation 22:10).

[Col. 1419D]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book IX, no. 15; book XX, no. 66.)* As the end of the world presses near, heavenly knowledge advances and grows more abundantly with time. Hence it is said through Daniel: “Many will pass through, and knowledge will be multiplied” (Daniel 12:4).

Hence, in the earlier part of the Revelation, the angel says to John: “Seal up what the seven thunders have spoken” (Revelation 10:4). Yet at the conclusion of the same revelation he commands him, saying: “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book.” The earlier portion of the revelation is ordered to be sealed, while its conclusion is not, because whatever lay hidden at the beginnings of the holy Church is revealed daily as the end approaches.

To seal means, as it were, to close with a seal. Hence blessed Job says of the Lord: “He closes up the stars as though under a seal” (Job 9:9). Just as the names “heavens” and “clouds” signify the heavenly life of preachers, who pour the rains of holy preaching over the parched earth of the human heart—of whom the Psalmist says, “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:1)—so the preachers themselves are also represented by the brightness of the stars, because when they preach what is right to sinners, they illuminate the darkness of our night.

Hence, when preachers are withdrawn, it is said through the prophet: “The stars were prohibited from giving their rain” (Jeremiah 3:3). If the word of preaching were not rain, Moses would certainly not have said: “Let my speech be awaited like rain” (Deuteronomy 32:2). Nor would Truth itself have said through Isaiah: “I will command the clouds not to rain upon it” (Isaiah 5:6).

The Lord therefore closes the stars under a seal, because, while he holds his preachers within themselves through silence, he hides the heavenly light from the blind senses of the wicked. We must consider that we close something under a seal for the purpose of bringing it forth when the proper time arrives.

Hence those two eminent preachers, Enoch and Elijah, were removed after their deaths had been deferred, so that they might be recalled for the work of preaching at the end. Of them it is said through John: “And I will give power to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for twelve hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth. These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth” (Revelation 11:3).

They have power to shut heaven, so that it does not rain during the days of their prophecy. One of them Truth itself promises in the Gospel, saying: “Elijah will come, and he will restore all things” (Matthew 17:11). Although Elijah is said to have been taken up into heaven, he deferred death; he did not escape it. He will come to restore all things, because for this purpose he will be restored to the world: to fulfill the ministry of preaching and to pay the debt of the flesh.

John continues concerning both of them—that is, Enoch and Elijah—saying: “And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the abyss will make war against them, and will conquer them, and will kill them.” Enoch and Elijah, therefore, are like stars closed under a seal: they are now hidden so that they do not appear, and afterward they will appear so that they may be of benefit.

### CHAPTER LXVII

“Let him who does harm do harm still; and let him who is in filth become filthy still” (Revelation 22:11).

[Col. 1420C]

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXV, no. 23; book V, no. 35.)* When almighty God grants time for repentance, but human wickedness turns that time toward the practice of its iniquity, then, by a just judgment, guilt is permitted to increase, so that it may eventually be heaped up more highly for punishment.

Hence the Apostle Paul says of certain people: “That they may always fill up their sins” (1 Thessalonians 2:16). Hence David says: “Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness” (Psalm 68:28). For, as it is written: “The Lord is patient, but he is also a requiter” (Sirach 5:4).

Often he long tolerates those whom he condemns forever, both so that the life of the righteous may be purified more thoroughly and so that he may reveal to those who consider it the judgment for which he preserves them. Sometimes, however, he strikes swiftly, and by confirming the hearts of the innocent through the destruction of the guilty, he comes to the aid of their weakness with consolation. He also shows that he does not abandon many evils.

For if he struck down all who do evil now, for whom would he reserve the final judgment? But if he struck down no one at all, who would believe that God cares for human affairs?

### CHAPTER LXVIII

“And the Bridegroom and the bride say: ‘Come.’ And let him who hears say: ‘Come’” (Revelation 22:17).

*(Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 25; Matthew 25.)* Let all those who, although they are able to preach worthily, withdraw through excessive and immoderate humility because they are afraid, hear the divine sentences against them with terror, so that fear may drive fear from their hearts.

Let them hear that the person who refused to distribute his talent lost it together with the sentence of condemnation. Let them hear that Paul believed himself clean from the blood of his neighbors precisely because he did not spare their vices when they needed to be struck, saying: “I testify to you today that I am clean from the blood of all, for I did not shrink from announcing to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:26).

Let them hear that Isaiah, who had been silent concerning the ministry of God’s word, reproached himself in a loud voice of repentance after being illumined by heavenly light, saying: “Woe is me, because I was silent” (Isaiah 6:5). [Col. 1421A]

Let them hear that David offered this to God as a gift: that he did not hide the grace of preaching which he had received, saying: “Behold, I will not restrain my lips, Lord; you know it. I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation” (Psalm 39:10–11).

Let them hear what is said to the bride in the Bridegroom’s address: “You who dwell in the gardens, friends are listening to you; let me hear your voice” (Song of Songs 8:13). The Church dwells in gardens because it preserves cultivated plantings of virtues for inward greenness. For the elect to listen to her voice means that they desire her word of preaching.

The Bridegroom desires to hear this voice because through the souls of his elect he longs for her preaching. John is admonished by an angel’s voice, which says: “Let him who hears say: ‘Come.’” For whoever has already received the voice of God calling in his heart must necessarily burst forth in voice toward his neighbor through the ministry of preaching, and for that reason call another, because he himself has already been called.

Indeed, whoever perceives the inward voice ought, by crying out, to draw others there where he himself is being drawn, lest, although called, he find the doors closed if he approaches the one calling while empty.

### CHAPTER LXIX

“I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches. I am the root and offspring of David, the bright and morning star” (Revelation 22:16).

*(In the exposition of Blessed Job, book XXIX, no. 75; book II on Ezekiel, homily 8, nos. 5, 6, 7, 8, 10; homily 4, nos. 19, 20.)* After creating all things, our Creator and Redeemer appeared among us, incarnate from the line of David, in order to redeem us from captivity; and through his passion he freed us from everlasting death.

Though scourged, mocked, struck with blows, crowned with a crown of thorns, smeared with spittle, crucified, dead, and buried, he rose on the third day. By displaying in himself the resurrection, he promised us the resurrection that is to come, since the members follow the glory of their Head.

Born from the Virgin, he appeared like the morning star amid the darkness of our night, because, dispelling obscurity, he announced to us the eternal dawn of freedom from sin. He made himself known as the morning star because he rose from the dead at dawn, and by the radiance of his light he pressed down the foul darkness of our mortality.

He is therefore aptly called by John “the bright and morning star.” Appearing alive after death, he became the morning star for us because, by providing in himself an example of resurrection, he showed what light would follow. In his resurrection he first displayed to us the glory of the eternal homeland. “Rising from the dead, he dies no more, and death no longer has dominion over him” (Romans 6:9); and he gave us an example, so that we might believe that what happened to his flesh on the day of resurrection will also happen to our flesh on the last day.

But since the subject of the resurrection of the flesh has presented itself to us, it is exceedingly sad and grievous that we know some people standing in the Church who doubt the resurrection of the flesh. The ancient Fathers most certainly believed that it would come, even when they still possessed no example of that resurrection.

[Col. 1421D] Since those deserve condemnation who have received both the example of the Lord’s resurrection and yet still distrust the resurrection—they hold the pledge but have no faith; they fill the Church but, because they doubt their own resurrection, stand empty in mind—Blessed Job says concerning this: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I will rise from the earth; and again I will be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I will see God, whom I myself will see, and my eyes will behold” (Job 19:25).

Hence the Psalmist says: “Take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust” (Psalm 103:29). Immediately he adds concerning the resurrection of the flesh: “Send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.”

Hence it is said through the prophet Ezekiel: “Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I will bring spirit into you, and you will live; and I will place sinews upon you, and cause flesh to grow over you, and stretch skin over you, and give you spirit, and you will live” (Ezekiel 37:4).

Hence another prophet saw the human race raised up at the end through the Lord’s resurrection and said: “He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we will live in his sight” (Hosea 6:3).

Hence, when the Lord was speaking about himself, he added: “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28).

Hence Paul says: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 4:14). Again he says: “Christ, the first fruits of those who sleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). For if we do not rise from the sleep of death, how can we have the Lord’s resurrection as first fruits?

The ancient and the new Fathers therefore agree with one spirit concerning the resurrection of the flesh. Truth itself first taught by word what it afterward demonstrated by the work of the resurrection of the flesh. Yet still the weakness of some has no faith, even while standing in the house of faith; they are accustomed to wonder how flesh can come to life again from dust.

Let them wonder, then, at the vastness and mass of the earth, at the abysses of the waters, at all the things that are in the world, and even at the angels created from nothing. It is far less to make something from something than to have made everything from nothing.

The elements themselves and the forms of created things proclaim to us an image of the resurrection. The sun dies daily before our eyes and rises daily; the stars likewise set for us in the morning hours and rise again in the evening. We see trees full of leaves and fruits during the summer seasons; in winter they remain stripped of flowers and fruits, as though dry, but when the spring sun returns, after moisture has risen from the root, they are again clothed in their beauty.

Why, then, do people distrust what appears to take place in trees? Often they look upon the dust of decaying flesh and say: “From where can bones and marrow, flesh and hair, be restored here?” While asking such questions, let them observe the small seeds of enormous trees. If they can, let them say where in those seeds lies such a mass of strength, such a variety of branches, such an abundance and greenness of leaves, such a display of flowers, such richness of flavors, and such fragrance of fruits.

Do the seeds of trees possess the fragrance or flavor which the trees afterward produce in their fruits? If, therefore, something invisible can be produced from the seed of a tree, why distrust that from the dust of human flesh the form that is not seen can be restored?

People often raise a pointless little objection, saying: “A wolf ate a human being’s flesh; a lion devoured the wolf; when the lion died, it returned to dust. When that dust is raised, how will the human flesh be separated from the flesh of the wolf and lion?”

What should we answer them except that they should first consider how they came into this world, and then discover how they will rise? Surely you, human being who speak, were once foam of blood in your mother’s womb. There you were a small and liquid mass from your father’s seed and your mother’s blood.

Tell me, I ask, if you know, how that fluid of the seed hardened into bones, how it remained liquid in the marrow, how it solidified into sinews, and how it was differentiated into hair and fingernails—so that the hair was softer than the flesh, while the nails were more delicate than the bones but harder than the flesh.

If so many and such diverse things were differentiated from one seed and yet remained joined together in form, what is surprising if almighty God can, in the resurrection of the dead, distinguish human flesh from the flesh of beasts, so that one and the same dust does not rise insofar as it is the dust of a wolf or lion, yet rises insofar as it is human dust?

Consider, then, human being, how you came to life, so that you may never doubt how you will return to life. Why do you wish to understand by reason how you will return, when you do not know how you came? Grant to the power of your Creator what you cannot understand concerning yourself.

Certainly, since you were made from earth, and earth from nothing, you were created from nothing. Therefore do not despair of the resurrection of your flesh; wisely consider that it is less for God to restore what existed than to make what did not exist.

If you cannot comprehend by reason the effect of the resurrection, consider how many things there are whose nature you do not understand, yet whose existence you do not doubt. Tell me, if you know: where do the circuit of the heavens, the hinges of the earth, and the abysses of the waters end? Where are they suspended?

We know that what was made from nothing hangs upon nothing. But if there is something called “nothing,” then it is no longer nothing. If it is nothing, the mass of the world hangs nowhere, nor is there any place where that which was created to exist can be. How, then, is that nowhere which we know exists?

But perhaps these matters are too much for you. Human being, return to yourself. Certainly you were created from spirit and clay: one invisible, the other visible; one perceptible, the other imperceptible. How, then, could spirit and clay be mingled in you, and from different things become something not different, so that spirit and clay were mixed in such harmony that when the flesh is worn down, the spirit withers, and when the spirit is afflicted, the flesh wastes away?

But perhaps you are not yet able to examine yourself. Consider, then, if you are able, how the Red Sea was divided by a rod (Exodus 14); how the hardness of a rock poured forth waves when struck by a rod (Numbers 20); how Aaron’s dry rod blossomed (Numbers 17); how the Virgin who came from his lineage conceived, and how she remained a virgin in childbirth; how a man dead for four days was raised at a command and came out of the tomb bound hand and foot, whom the Lord afterward ordered his disciples to release (John 20); and how that same Redeemer of ours, rising in flesh and bones, entered to his disciples through closed doors.

You cannot investigate these things, and yet you believe them. Why, then, do you hesitate by arguing and examining the glory of the resurrection, when you have believed so many mysteries without examination? Yet if you do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh, you have believed everything in vain; for in this spectacle of the angels you seem indeed to run swiftly, but after completing the race you oppose yourself, so as not to receive the prize. Hence Paul says: “Run in such a way that you may obtain it” (1 Cor. 9:24). He says again: “If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Cor. 15:19).

The mysteries of divine power, however, which cannot be comprehended, are not to be examined by the understanding but revered by faith. We must therefore know that whatever can be comprehended by human reason can no longer be wondrous; in miracles, the sole principle is the power of the one who performs them.

Behold, while speaking about the resurrection of the flesh, we have lingered for a little while in treating it. But it is worthwhile to consider who we are who discuss these matters. Certainly, we have come from the Gentiles; certainly, our ancestors were worshipers of wood and stones. How, then, has it come about that we can recall such profound mysteries of the Scriptures? Let us give thanks to the One who fulfilled in deed everything written about him in the sacred word, so that what could not be understood when heard might be disclosed when seen. For there are contained there his incarnation, his passion, his death, his resurrection, and his ascension.

But who among us would have believed these things when heard, unless we had recognized them as accomplished? Therefore, as we read in this Apocalypse of John (ch. 5), when no one could open and read the sealed book, the Lion from the tribe of Judah opened it, because he disclosed all his mysteries to us through his passion and resurrection. By enduring the evils of our weakness, he showed us the blessings of his power and glory.

For he became flesh in order to make us spiritual; he graciously bent down in order to raise us up; he went out in order to bring us in; he appeared visibly in order to reveal invisible things; he endured scourging in order to heal; he bore insults and mockery in order to free us from eternal disgrace; he died in order to give life.

Let us therefore give thanks to him who gives life and who died—and therefore gives life all the more because he died—who, by becoming weak and enduring our evils, brought us, who are his creatures, to the glory of his strength, in which he lives and reigns with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Acies. What it means for a Jew to flee from the battle line, 132.
