The perfect knowledge of God is consummated vision, 8. It can be attained only by the citizens of heaven, ibid. To appear continually in God’s sight is always to have him present in good conduct, 24. Knowledge of God must be held not only by faith but also by confession, 25. Ignorance of God is exceedingly harmful to salvation, 82. To know God by faith is one thing, and by love another, 102. The first is compared with report, the second with presence, ibid. The Lord is known by some to whom the word of the Lord is not revealed, ibid. A mind empty of works of virtue does not attain to knowledge of God, 144. Whatever the human mind can think about God, God is not, 234. The face of God is his knowledge, 235. This knowledge does not know how to satisfy the desires of the elect for light, but rather to arouse them, ibid. The truth of that light itself usually both satisfies and arouses, ibid. Knowledge of God in this miserable life is exceedingly imperfect, 537. By what steps the sublimity of God is reached, 6. God is known through a mirror and through himself, 235.

God, without changing himself, both withdraws promises and relents from threats, 109. How God’s Majesty is said to be angered, 179. How God’s repentance is to be understood, 352, 565. God is not subject to change, 367, 522, 534. The unchanging God makes changeable things, 565. God alone is immortal, 533.

God is inaccessible light, 234. In this life one does not reach the vision of God himself, ibid., 537. Nor does one reach the light that God is, but rather the light in which he dwells, ibid. Moses had reached the light on the mountain and was seeking the light that is God, ibid. Moses did not see God intuitively while he lived, 235, 537.

How God is said to have sought a man, 290. God is all in all, 88. The image and likeness of God are engraved on a coin so that it may be recognized as belonging to him, 92. The image and likeness of God consist in hating evil with renowned hatred and loving God with perfect love, ibid.

God’s eternity is explained, 534. When “is” and “is not” apply to God, 400. True eternity exists only in the Godhead, 533. What the years of God are, and why they do not fail, 534. Who will dwell in God’s eternity, ibid.

What uncertain and hidden matters of God’s wisdom were revealed to David, 498. For God to know is to approve, 487. All things are naked and open to the eyes of God, 496. One who turns away from his commandments hides himself from his eyes, 552. God kills the one whom his divine foreknowledge knows to be unchangeable, 73. With God, things that he has ordained beforehand are already accomplished, 290. The certainty of divine foreknowledge, 328, 426.

God’s antecedent will is to save all; his consequent will is to condemn the wicked, 73. The priests of the Jews, by raging against Christ, fulfilled God’s plan, 13. We are in accordance with God’s will when we recognize it through understanding and preserve it through love, 290. Constant meditation is necessary in order to investigate the divine will, 322, 555. God’s repentance is his not having a will toward the reprobate, 352.

God is affirmed to be mighty because he transfers the dust of our flesh into the glory of perpetual incorruption, 56.

God’s holiness sanctifies us on the way, 56. God alone is holy, 44. God alone is without sin, 321.

God cannot fail his faithful in tribulation, 63. God has predetermined how much harm evils may do, 373. The Church establishes nothing except what it knows to have been preordained by God, 374. God fixes his eyes upon one who walks on the way of salvation, 479. Why God allowed a king to be chosen whom he knew would be rejected, 179. God provides good things from evils, ibid.

God, when angry and threatening extreme punishments, [Col. 1445] is moved to mercy, 108. God sometimes grants temporal things in anger, 179. The sentence of infinite condemnation is called God’s fury, 468, 472, 482. God’s anger signifies the passing correction of purgation, 482. Fury signifies eternal condemnation, ibid.

How holy men always stand before God’s presence, 486. What it means to be in the presence of the Lord, 65. What it means to be expelled from the presence of the Lord, 66. One ought always to see oneself in God’s presence, 80. Some ministers are in the presence of God, not of human beings, 81. What it means to pour out water in the presence of God, 166. What it means to stand in the presence of the Lord, 275. No one is perfectly righteous in the presence of God, 547. The sinner lies bound in the tomb and cast away from God’s presence, 548.

God speaks through himself only to the perfect, 100. What it signifies when the soul says to God, “Speak, Lord,” 104. God speaks to the elect not only through Scripture but also through hidden revelation, 115. What it means to hear God speaking, 120. When God is full daylight to holy men, 214. God speaks through riddles to the blind and cold, 397. One who hears God’s voice is his friend, 461.

God’s work in rejecting Judea and choosing the Gentiles is to be venerated, not investigated, 50. For God to predestine is to accomplish, 290. The certainty of divine predestination, 328, 413. Its immutability as well, 565. See *Reprobation*, *Reprobates*.

God gives life to the Gentiles through mercy and brings them back from the underworld, 50, 61. He enriches the chosen Gentiles, ibid. Divine compassion helps those for whom no human being was sufficient, 73. Disordered confidence in God’s mercy, 108. God’s mercy is reached through the grief and humility of repentance, 149. God sometimes punishes mercifully, 179, 469. God’s mercy is greater than our merits, 468. Here God always reproves in mercy, ibid. God’s mercy must be summoned by tears and groans, 469. God’s mercy toward the righteous, 480. If the elect fall through weakness, they find divine mercy all the sooner the more bitterly they afflict themselves, 489. God’s mercy, by which he grants pardon to penitents without preceding merits, 503. God’s mercy, by which he calls even those who have turned away, 512, 551. How great God’s mercy is, 522. Toward Jews and Gentiles, 523, 527. The name of the Lord is “mercy,” 528. Without divine mercy, no one should expect salvation, 539. The law of God is mercy, 540. Christ fulfilled this law, and the Teacher commanded us to keep it, ibid. God’s infinite mercy in the incarnation and passion of his Son, 544. God’s mercy toward penitents, 551.

Through his justice God puts the Jews to death and leads them down to the underworld, 50, 61. He makes the rejected Judea poor, ibid. In mercy he wishes to save through justice; unwillingly he condemns, 73. When the strictness of divine justice is heard, both ears tingle, 106. The truth by which he punishes the sins of the unrepentant, 503. The justice of God is faith, 504. Who proclaims God’s justice with exultation, ibid. Who can glory in God’s justice, 546.

The worship of God: it belongs to the perfect man to devote himself to God alone, 30. To turn others away from the worship of God is a sin scarcely erased by repentance, 69. After idols have been rejected, we are commanded to serve God alone, 164. Fearing God is not enough unless he is served, 273. How God is to be sought, 557, 422. The mind is stripped of the beauty of its devotion by idle words, 57. Demons are frightened by the devotion of the elect and struck down by their works, 170. The sacrifice of the people is the devotion of the chosen people, 210. Great devotion in hearing the word is a sacrifice [Col. 1446] before it has been offered, 211. Greater devotion arising from the word is called an offered sacrifice, ibid. The affection of devotion is food for the mind, ibid.

The right hand of God consists of the elect who are separated from those on the left, 400. What it means to turn aside to the right, 153. Eternal life is represented by the right hand, 302, 417, 455, 531. What the works of the right hand are, 203.

The Devil, the worst tree, did not produce good fruit, 10. The Devil is represented by the name Pharaoh, 149, and by the name Philistines, 165. It also designates devils, 171. The devils were driven out because they were cast down from the heavenly sanctuary through pride, ibid. The Devil is called “the strong armed one,” 517. How Christ took away the Devil’s weapons and distributed the spoils, ibid.

The Devil fell from heaven, 10. The Philistines are humbled when the demons are sent into the fires of eternal fire prepared for them, 172. They do not set out again to come into the territory of Israel, that is, they do not go forth to tempt the hearts of the elect, ibid. The progress of the elect is an increase and accumulation of the Devil’s condemnation, 196. Who are freed from the Devil’s power, or need to be freed from it, 165. By desiring unlawful things, the Devil lost what he had acquired, 517. The Devil can do nothing unless permitted, 265. By what arts the Devil deceives us, 547, 554. The Devil’s severe persecution, 548, 554. By what arts the Devil’s schemes are overcome, 261, 554. The perverse intention of the Devil, who seeks to destroy souls, 548.

The Devil cast down the strong Adam in paradise, 6. He was defeated by Christ in a weak human nature in the wilderness, ibid., 7. The Devil was caught by the Redeemer on a hook, 261. The enemies of the chosen mind are evil spirits, 55. The impious are silent in darkness while God guards the feet of his saints, 63. Even the fugitive spirits fear us when they see that we have been taken up into the strength of divine grace, 64. By his help we shatter the strength of our adversaries, ibid. Demons are more hostile toward those making greater progress, 167, 554. Not one Devil alone but countless devils attack in order to test the patience of the elect, ibid. When the time of our victory is affirmed, a stone is said to have been placed between us and them, 171. Evil spirits are servants of holy men, 196. Our enemies attack us in a threefold array, 293. How much we must ascend and strive in order to defeat the devils, 302, 330. The battles of the fallen angels are directed toward dragging human beings into earthly desires, 411. They prepare more grievous stings of temptation for the stronger, 554. How the Devil is to be conquered, 282, 293, 297. The Devil is overcome by the light and fire of grace, 265.

Those under the Devil’s rule, 413, 554. Those who do not obey spiritual fathers become imitators of apostate spirits, 82. Those who here put on the image of the fallen angel will be ignoble and will be joined to him in eternal punishment, 87. Here they already have the Devil as father, 88.

What the diadem signifies, 427. By what diadem Christ was redeemed by his mother, ibid.

What the appointed days signify, 11, 32. The days on which we are commended to the Lord signify the periods of the present life, 29. The days of spiritual virtues are their brightnesses, ibid. How we ascend on the appointed days, 32. What the days of ascent are: we resolve to adore and sacrifice on them, but neither adore nor sacrifice on them, 35. What that other day is on which we sacrifice, ibid. What that day is which kills, 90. What it means to be called by the Lord in the day, 97. The day of the sinful soul is hope of obtaining pardon, 166. The springlike days of the good Teacher [Col. 1447] are rays of shining eternity, 172. The days of every Teacher’s life are the brightnesses of spiritual virtues, 173. The heavenly conduct of the good Teacher is called “day,” 212. The life of the righteous is called “day,” 214. The days of the reprobate mind are evil pleasures, 235. What it means for a sinner to reflect upon all his days, ibid. One who walks in the day sees the level ground on which to walk and the precipices from which to turn away, 246. A preacher is recognized in two days; on the third he possesses what is unknown to others, 248. This is the day of the leaping spirit, ibid. The shepherds’ exhortation is called “day,” 264. Tomorrow is the coming of divine visitation, ibid. The first day is the light of preaching, ibid. The day of the serpent’s appetite is the day of abstinence, 265. The day of the mind is the splendor of instruction, 318. “Day” is the thought of the mind, 322. Saul’s days are called works of light, 339. What it means to fight in one’s own day or in another’s, ibid. The solemn day of the Lord is the compunction of our heart, 404. “Day” signifies the light of good actions, 475. What the day of the perverse soul is, 514. The day of sinful Jerusalem, ibid. What the day of a human being is, ibid. A human being’s days fade like smoke, ibid. What the days of grace are, 521. These days decline within us like a shadow, ibid. Half of the days signifies the imperfection of life, 530, 531. In this life we receive only half of our days, ibid. What the multiplicity and scarcity of days signify, 531. Length of days signifies perpetual life, ibid. The saints are signified by the name “day,” 534. What the ancient days were, 549. Day signifies eternal life; night signifies the present life, 552.

The finger signifies the Holy Spirit, 257, 346, 532. The various fingers of the hand signify various virtues distinguished through discernment, 438.

The heights of dignities are dangerous to humility, 109, 162. The danger of those who raise relatives to ecclesiastical dignities, 86. Many who are religious in a lowly place, once raised to the height of dignity, abandon their former works, 109. The merit of dignity is observance of the divine word, 362. How one should approach ecclesiastical dignities, 253, 254, 290. The misery of those who seek them, 279. See *Height*, *Prelacy*.

The three degrees of love, 116. What it means to love with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s strength, ibid. Through the degrees of love we are raised to the highest things, ibid. How those three degrees of love are acquired, 117. Perfect love is free from fear, 408. Christ is nourished and strengthened by a twofold love, or by two breasts, 415. The Church’s twofold beauty consists in its twofold love of God and neighbor, ibid. Christ delights in the breasts of the bride, that is, in doubled love, 431. The fragrance of the good works performed from this love, ibid. Love, which is strong as death, must be impressed upon the heart, 456. See *Love*.

The flood of waters is the multiplicity of doctrines, 477. God forgives not only past sins but also protects from future ones, 478. We ought to choose the director of our conduct after mature deliberation, 412. One must learn before teaching, 543.

In arranging ecclesiastical affairs, although people may err, ecclesiastical discipline must nevertheless not be abandoned, 175. The mind of the chosen disciple is the teacher’s fruitful land, 293. Christ’s disciples ought not to be ordinary human beings but above human beings, 399.

The measure of discernment is signified by the bushel, [Col. 1447] 26. The shepherd’s discernment in moderating burdens according to the weakness of his subjects, 83. The discernment of that same shepherd and of preachers in concealing high and profound matters from the inexperienced, 117. The preacher’s lack of discernment in preaching divine mysteries to unbelievers and despisers, 142. One must walk along the right path with discernment as guide, 153. Discernment of spirits is necessary for prelates, 156. How much discernment the saints show in concealing or revealing their virtues, 220, 299. The discernment of ecclesiastical censure, 258. The virtue of discernment is expressed by the name of the three-pronged hoe, 296. The power of discernment orders what must be done, thought, and said, ibid. The lack of discernment of those who run not after Christ but before him, 406. Torpor and indiscriminate fervor must alike be avoided, ibid. Discernment sets a measure for the various virtues, 438. The discernment of preachers is signified by the bride’s nose, 450. Discernment is signified by the hooves of calves, 510. How one ought to investigate spiritual matters, 188.

Dispensation is salutary in many affairs of the Church, 381. Dispensation in promoting an unworthy person to primacy is deadly, ibid.

When the splendor of the Godhead is seen, 16. Perishable riches are dung, 62. God enriches by offering heavenly goods, 61. The wretched consolation of an evil conscience received from riches, 557. Riches are thorns that choke the seed of the word, ibid.

The teacher has a twofold task: to convert sinners and to preserve the righteous, 26. A teacher accomplishes nothing by teaching us unless what sounds outwardly is poured inwardly through divine grace, 28. Samuel’s sleep signifies the teacher’s perfect contempt for the world in his mind, 114. The teacher ought to devote himself through sacred eloquence to contemplating inward mysteries, 118. Only one who knows perfectly, not one who merely examines and tests, may teach, 119. The teachers’ singular radiance in glory, 172. The teacher should judge, having the days of his life renowned, 173. One who desires to teach others should be teachable by God, 174, 300. What a teacher can do in order to be perfect, ibid. A teacher’s study is useless if the heavenly building is not increased by what he does on earth, 176. The teacher of the holy Church should rarely be in public and frequently in private, 210. It belongs to the teacher to disclose to the faithful everything that is in their hearts, 220. If the teacher lies sick through weariness of mind, he cannot heal the sick or raise those who lie prostrate, 225. Teachers who disclose hidden things and reveal the future, 238. The sacred teachers of both Testaments, illuminated from heaven, announce Christ, 239. In order to be understood by us little ones, they had to descend, ibid. What it means for teachers to depart and return when they wish, 256. The teacher who climbs to the Philistine outpost by crawling on his hands, 307. The teacher fights while preaching and conquers while persuading through his works, 329. What the chief virtues of the Church’s teachers are, 333. The teacher fights powerfully when he teaches others nothing that he himself does not complete in practice, 339. Those who teach correctly but act badly are traitors in Christ’s army, 340. Teachers err when, while living badly, they flatter themselves about the progress of their disciples, 354. When teachers lead the way toward evil, their subjects rush more foolishly into ruin, 369. The spiritual horn is the teacher’s conduct, 375. A teacher who speaks good things with his mouth and shows them in his works has a calf in his hand, 377. When he speaks and acts while persuading, he is a victim on the altar, [Col. 1448] ibid. With what splendors of virtue a teacher ought to be adorned, 382. What false teachers must be avoided, 412. The teachers of the Church are watchmen, 423. When the bride busily seeks to find the Beloved, the teachers find and instruct her, ibid. How the bride questions them, ibid. The teachers of the Church are signified by the name “heavens,” 532. The power of binding and loosing has been granted to them, 533. They are works of God’s hands, ibid. The Lord sits in them, ibid. Rash teachers are rebuked, 121.

The doctrine of the word is signified by measures of flour, 27. Sound doctrine should accompany the pursuit of good works, 163.

Sudden pains are sudden afflictions of death arriving without warning, 136. There is deceit in the spirit of one who desires more to appear righteous than to be righteous, 475. Blessed is the one in whose spirit there is no deceit; otherwise, he is wretched, ibid.

The dwelling signifies the Jews, 517. The duties of masters toward servants, 468. It belongs to masters to show mercy, 528. The signs of a lord’s anger toward his servant, 551.

The house of the Lord designates the eternal homeland, 40. It is also called the house of the faithful, 80. This house is now being built through the actions of a devout life, ibid. For this building, human work is worthless unless it is accomplished through the grace of the merciful God, ibid. The house of the condemned is hell, 88. What the priest’s house is, 91. What is called the house of the unbeliever, ibid. What the doors of the house of God, that is, of the Church, are, 122. The house of the willing people is the fortification of holy love, 161. Why it is said to be situated at Gibeah, ibid. The preacher’s house is said to be the place in which he dwells through love, 176, 217, 222. One house belongs to the king, another to the subject people, 256. The king’s house at Gibeah, that is, in a lofty place, ibid. The impious are called a useless house, 285. The house of anger is a mind serving a contentious tongue, 293. The house of the transgressor is the habit of evil conduct, 372. The house of the proud person is the measure of his wickedness, 373. The reprobate remains as if in a house because he can never leave his punishments, ibid. He ascends to the house who fills up his sins, ibid. No one can build a house for Wisdom unless he possesses peace within himself toward the enemies subject to him, 510.

“Until” is said of a time about which there was doubt; concerning the future, however, it neither denies nor affirms, 423.

A gift from a wicked person should not be accepted, 17. God’s gifts must be requested with fear, 205. We merit God’s gifts through knowledge of our sins and humility, 252. Certain gifts of spiritual grace are, as it were, breasts, 408.

To sleep with women is to sin without fear of future vengeance, 84. Sleeping is one thing, lying down another, 99. “To sleep” is sometimes understood in a favorable sense, ibid., 225. To sleep in the temple is one thing, and to sleep in the place where the ark of God is another, 99. To sleep is to rest in the desire for eternal life, 102. Why we are commanded to sleep three times, 103. What it means to sleep until morning, 106. What it means to sleep all night, 107. What Samuel’s threefold sleeping signifies, 117. One cannot sleep who does not prepare a bed for himself, 225.

The lost tenth drachma signifies the fellowship of the angels, diminished by a tenth and incomplete without our restoration, 185.

The sweetness of God, unknown to those who fear God, should be known to those who love him, 408.

## E
## E

Spiritual drunkenness of the Church, by which the heart is changed and the mind alienated, 18. Another meaning of the Church’s drunkenness, 19. Who are called “mighty to drink wine” and “strong to mix drunkenness,” 197. Ivory signifies incorruption, 441. The Church is prefigured by Hannah, the wife of Elkanah, 10, 41. The Church is the spouse of death and heir of the cross, 14. Why the Church is called a woman, and exceedingly unfortunate, 19. The Church’s husband is the Redeemer of the human race, 21. The house of the Lord is called the Church, 27, 122, 422. How the holy Church is said to be perfected through fault, 30. The Church is signified by the name “world,” 51. The Church is called the kingdom of Christ, 54. It is signified by the name “cart,” 149. The Church is called Israel, that is, “in whom God is” and “seeing God,” 208. The land of Benjamin is the holy Church, 214. The Church is called the bride, 402. The bride of Christ joined to him through the Incarnation, 507. The devout desires of the Church awaiting the coming of Christ the Bridegroom, 402. The Church, the royal house, 407. Its door is faith, its hope the ascent, and its dining room charity, ibid. The Church is marked by the name “turtledove,” 420. It is figured by the fig tree producing its early figs, ibid. By the she-goat, 422. The Church is called Jerusalem, 426, 443. Why the Church is like a pomegranate, 428. The enclosed garden is the Church, 432. It is called a garden of pomegranates, 433. It is called Zion, 446. Why the Church is compared with dawn and the sun, 447. The Church is called the daughter of a prince, 449. Christ calls the Church his sister, 458. Having received the Holy Spirit, the Church became a wall, ibid. And was fortified with defenses, ibid. Why the Church is called a door, 459. Why it is compared with doves, 485. The Church is signified by the name “stable,” 494. The Church is Christ’s vineyard, 519, 520. Various names of the Church, 529. Why the Church is called earth, 532.

Who closes the womb of the holy Church is the Lord, 14. How many children the Church gives birth to, and how it desires them to be strong, 16. In contemplation of God, the Church learns how earthly things are to be ordered, 22. The fruitfulness of the Church comes from the grace of heavenly love, ibid. The Church’s purpose proceeds not from human judgment but from divine judgment, 25. Without Christ the Bridegroom, the Church can do nothing, 27. Which sons are commended to the Lord by Mother Church in this life, 29. The Church’s exultation over the conversion of the Gentiles, 41. From where the Church’s joy comes, 42. When the Church is to be raised to the summit of eternal joy, 54. Christ withdrew his bodily presence from the Church, yet remains invisibly present to it until the end, 65, 124. At times he was present to it through the grace of a gift; at times he withdrew through the dispensation of testing, ibid. God alone could build the Church, 80. God revealed the future construction of the Church to the prophets, 118. Christ will remain in the Church until the end of the world, 120. From the fullness of Christ the head, his members receive divided portions of grace, 196. The Holy Spirit, poured out upon Christ’s disciples, remains in the Church, 242. Why the Church is called both black and beautiful, 409. The Church is black through merit, beautiful through grace, 410. Through the harshness of repentance it is like Solomon’s skins, ibid. The Church gathered from the Gentiles was once also despised by the faithful, ibid. What kind of wine the Church produces, 415. With what kind of water it washes us, ibid. From where the Church’s twofold beauty comes, ibid. With what flowers and fruits the Church seeks to be supported, 417. The Church, enduring temporal things of necessity, presses on toward eternal things, 417. The Church’s sighs are heard in heaven, 420. The Synagogue was the mother of the Church, 423. The Church, washed from sins in baptism, receives the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1449] 430. By what merit the Church comes from Lebanon to the crown, ibid. The Church is chiefly fortified by three virtues, ibid. Its crown is woven from the converted mighty of this world, ibid. With what benefit Christ visits the Church, 443. The Church is joined to Christ through faith, hope, and charity, ibid. The happiness of the Church, which is fed with the flesh of its Bridegroom, washed with his blood, and nourished with his word, 446. Strengthened by these foods, what the Church does and what it hopes for, ibid. The Church is destined to share in the glory of its head, 447. Within the body of the Church, the weak are strengthened by the perfect, and the wicked are converted by the good, 448. The fraternal concord of Jews and Gentiles born in faith, 450.

Christ is the head of the Church, 451. Why the Church is called Carmel, ibid. What the hairs of this head signify, ibid. Christ and his bride the Church are concerned for the salvation of their neighbor, 453.

The Church, having kissed Christ the Bridegroom, is no longer despised, 454. At the end of the world the Church will preach Christ to the Synagogue, ibid. To it she will offer the excellent wine of the New Testament, ibid. When Christ will address the Church as a little sister, 458. The Church, having received the Holy Spirit, became a wall, ibid. The faithful within the body of the Church are members of Christ, 487. Christ and the Church are one person, 511. The Church possesses the life-giving Spirit, ibid. Christ, our head, sits at the right hand of God and still suffers in his body, 512. The Church was built from both peoples, 524, 526. God rejected the Synagogue and chose the Church, 525. Christ, who was seen in weakness in the Synagogue, is seen in his glory in the Church, ibid. The Church, a virgin, generates children for God, 527. How the Church corresponds to God on the path of virtue, 529. The earth, that is, the Church, was founded in Christ, 531. The earth, that is, the Church, stands forever, 532. The Church is founded upon the rock, that is, Christ, ibid. The gates of hell, that is, heresies and the hostile powers of this world, will not prevail against the Church, ibid. The Church has attained fruitfulness through the rains of apostolic preaching, ibid. Joshua and Caleb alone, that is, the head and body of the Church, signify those who will enter the land of the living, 535.

The Church is founded upon the sacred Scriptures, 27. The Church is spread throughout the whole world, 42. Fruitfulness was granted to the formerly barren Church, 49. Christ is sometimes present to the Church and sometimes withdraws from it, 65. The Church’s growth, 123, 403. In order that it might grow, it received increase from Christ’s presence, ibid. The youth and old age of the Church, 190. From where it has grown old, ibid. Although its vigor has been dissolved, the Church nevertheless prophesies and teaches rightly, ibid. The younger Church was weak in charity, 458. The Church will remain until the end of the world, 531.

In the Church there are several orders of prelates, 150. In the Church there are lower ministers, who share in the labor of their superiors, 257, 279. The priests of the first and second orders are signified by two oxen, 308. Jonathan and his armor-bearer are also signified by them, ibid. Saul and Jonathan likewise, 310.

By giving birth through preaching to those predestined for eternal life, the Church never removes their temporal goods, 18. The Church’s steadfastness and freedom, 19. Joined with gentleness, ibid. And with contempt for earthly things, ibid. The Church’s innocence, 20. Outside the Church there is no place where the merits of virtues increase, 27. In the Catholic Church alone divine love is bestowed upon the elect, 30. The Church is exalted both in the intention of vision and in the excellence of its conduct, [Col. 1450] ibid. The Church’s conduct, patiently enduring the hardships of its exile for the winning of souls, 41. The holy Church, loving and venerating divine benefits, remembers, proclaims, and prays, ibid. In the conduct of the Church, its horn is exalted in its God, 42. The Church’s spices are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, 403. How much these surpass the spices of the Law, ibid. The Church prefers the humble wisdom of the incarnate Word to the empty wisdom of proud philosophers, ibid. In exile here, the Church, as in a desert, rejecting all things, longs for the heavenly homeland, 424. Why the Church is compared with smoke exhaled from spices, ibid. Its spices are the fragrance and progress of virtues, 433. The Church’s shoes are the examples of the fathers who went before, 449.

For the Church to be terrifying to its enemies, it must fortify itself with peace and bind itself together with unity, 443. Christ suffered death to strengthen unity among the Church’s members, 431. Converted Jews will suffer under Antichrist for the unity of the faith, 444. The elect support one another in the unity of charity, 446. Outside the body of the Church the Spirit does not give life, 511. The Church is one from many and diverse members, 529. Outside it no one praises God and no one proclaims him, ibid.

The Church prepared itself to preach to those predestined for life from the Jews and to Gentiles converted to the faith, 16. What it means for the Church to put on shoes for preaching, 450.

The power of the Church bestowed by Christ, 41, 518. The Church appoints no one except one whom it knows to have been preordained by God, 374. The Church’s authority vanishes without mercy, 384. The Church’s royal dignity is neither harsh nor proud, 387. What weapons the Church uses and with which it fortifies itself, 429. The Church subjected kings and emperors to Christ through repentance, 431. It subdued lions and leopards, ibid. Christ gave the Church the power of binding and loosing, 521.

What the heart of the Church signifies, 18. For the benefit of its little ones, the Church willingly endures the delay of glory, 24. What the weaning of the Church’s little ones means, ibid. Doing good benefits only the Church’s children, 31. Most people within the Church bear no fruit, ibid. Jerusalem, that is, the Church’s multiplied children, 60. In the Church not only the perfect but also the weak attain salvation, 70. In the Church there are perfect men joined to Christ, the supreme stone, through the perfection of charity, 159. Whoever within the Church rebels against God through wicked action must be admonished to remove foreign gods from his midst, 164. The Church’s last order, that of penitents, 222, 227. The weak are not to be taken for the defense of the Church, 279. Others assist the faithful by the examples of a higher life, ibid. Others by humility and contempt for earthly things, 280. Who are the Church’s strong workers, 292. Some in the Church are learned in sacred Scripture but irreligious, 354. When the Synagogue is left in blindness, the Holy Spirit is directed toward the Church’s elect, 392. The Church enters the king’s chamber, 407. The Church’s eyes are preachers, 415, 427, 428. The Church’s hair is its peoples, ibid. The Church’s teeth are holy preachers, 428. And its lips, ibid. And the Church’s cheeks are those same preachers, ibid. In holy preachers, the things that are visible are great, but those hidden are greater, ibid. How the Church’s neck is like David’s tower, ibid. The Church’s fruits are its children, especially martyrs, 433. Within the Church there are two orders of those living perfectly, 435. In the Church some shine like dawn, 447. Others like the moon, ibid. Others like the sun, ibid. Some in the Church are like nuts: beneath outward lowliness they conceal inward wisdom, as a kernel is hidden in its shell, 448. The two women of the bride signify the Church’s two peoples, gathered from circumcision and uncircumcision, 450. The Church’s members are adorned with various virtues, 459. As one soul gives life to many members, so the Holy Spirit animates the whole Church, 511. Christ suffers again in his members, 512.

The Church’s discipline must always be maintained together with mercy, 381.

The Church’s bridehood to Christ has temporal affliction as its sole portion, 13. The Synagogue is the Church’s rival, 14. The Synagogue rages against the Church, ibid. Amid adversities the Church is refreshed by the sweetness of inward consolation, 15. From where the Church’s joy and grief amid persecutions arise, 16. From where the Church’s sorrow comes, 20. In more severe persecutions the Church always stands firm, 28. The Church is crowned from the lairs of lions and the mountains of leopards, 431. The persecutions of a Christian king against the Church, 518, 532. The persecutors tried in vain to prevail against the Church, 532.

By what path the Church’s stages are to be reached, 253, 254, 290. Edom is interpreted as “red,” 330. Edom suggests an excessive fervor for sinning, ibid. How the needy is raised from the dust and lifted from the dung heap, 62. And how he sits with princes, 63. Pride and gluttony, the ancient weapons of the devil, 6. By the sight of the condemnation of others like himself, the mind is restrained from pride over gifts it has received, 105. We must beware lest, while growing in virtues, we fall through pride, 109. Pride must be feared by those advanced to contemplation, 117. We have already become so corrupt that we can scarcely be seen as good, even by our own pastors, without pride, 299. Since we cannot perfectly avoid pride, the good from which it can arise must be hidden from everyone, 300, 302. It is the custom of the proud that, when an alien tongue is silent concerning their praises, their own estimation is not silent, 319. To become proud over one’s good works is to become guilty of theft, ibid. To bring an ox by the hand means to erase the sin of pride through repentance, 320. Often those who grow in rank decline through pride, 357. See Vain glory.

Eleazar is interpreted as “God is helper,” 161. Eleazar, sanctified to guard the ark of God, whom he signifies, ibid. Why he is called the son of Amminadab, 162. The unchangeability of divine election, 120, 446, 563. A person bears the sign of election when he is concerned both for another’s salvation and for his own, 232. The mystery of election and reprobation is a deep abyss, 520. Unless God had made vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath, no one would be distinguished from that mass of perdition by a holy life, 553. See Reprobation.

The merits of the elect are unequal, and their rewards are not equal, 13. God himself is the reward of the elect, 15. Christ never abandons his elect through his spiritual presence, 21. The elect are weaned so that they may become worthy of the Lord’s presence, 24. Through wisdom and charity bestowed by God, the elect overcome their enemies, 55. From this they rejoice in the salvation of God, 56. The order of the humble elect is received among the choirs of angels, 89. The groaning and tears of the elect in this exile, 209. It is often beneficial for the elect that wicked rulers are appointed, 215.

The elect receive grace in such a way that they persevere in it to the end, 386. The number of the elect is established by God, 446. Only those who remain in simplicity and unity are elect, ibid.

The elect are called the fruits of Christ’s tree, 10. No one of the elect exists except in Christ, 44. All the elect are priests, 94. The maidens signify the minds of the elect, pure through innocence and beautiful through the radiance of virtues, 209. The souls of the elect are called young women, 405. The elect are figured by incorruptible cedar and cypress, 416. The elect are called “raised up like palms,” 410. Why they are called black like a raven, ibid.

The elect, admonished by negligent and proud teachers, obey humbly, 89. Those who fail at the end did not, with God as their author, attain their withdrawal, 152. The elect walk by one road, 153. Those are called the children of the elect who imitate their virtues, 182. The elect know both how to hide and how to reveal the good things they possess, 220. Every elect person is humble and not barren, 382. The Church of the elect is foul through ignorance and beautiful through faith, 412. Many enter the Church with the elect who do not belong to their lot, 445. The conduct of the elect, 446.

The elect themselves cannot be without sin, 59. Every elect person is strong in good work, humble in self-estimation, and afflicted through the contrition of repentance, 235. The elect deal individually with each of their sins, chastising themselves through repentance, 513. Why God sometimes permits his elect to stumble, 283.

The days of the elect’s life are virtues, 17. The hand of the elect signifies the power of inward freedom, 54. The elect person carries his soul in his hands, ibid. The elect person advances through preaching the truth, 61. The elect have a twofold movement: one by which they turn away from temporal things, and another by which they turn toward eternal things, 150. The saving fear of the elect, 167. The flocks of the elect are multitudes of spiritual virtues, 185. What each elect person’s sword upon his thigh signifies, 425. Amid the bitterness of the world, the minds of the elect taste the sweetness of future blessedness by contemplating it, 478.

The progress of the elect is an increase and accumulation of the devil’s condemnation, 196. The hearts of the elect are filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, 242.

The intention of the elect is raised to high things, while that of the reprobate is pressed down to low things, 55. Not all human beings, but only the elect, are led to eternal joys, 60. The more children the barren Jerusalem gives birth to, the fewer Babylon’s children become, ibid. By hearing the word of God, the elect are accustomed to be kindled to good works, unlike the reprobate, 166. The elect fear the face of the Philistines, that is, demons, so that they may not at some point fear their rear, 168. The reprobate, however, will experience the horror of this rear, ibid. The elect are signified by Israel, and the reprobate by the Amorite, 173. How peace between the two will be made at the final judgment, ibid. While God punishes the reprobate, he instructs the saints, 179. Even the reprobate speak the divine utterances, 206. The elect alone both speak and act, ibid. The elect, under the name of the poor, eat and are satisfied; the rich, that is, the reprobate, cannot be satisfied, 207. God’s judgments concerning the elect and the reprobate in this life differ from human judgments, 413. As the number of the elect in heaven increases, the reprobate are cut off from the Church like useless branches, 420. The reprobate often confess their sins but disdain to weep over them; the elect amend what they confess with tears, 491, 505.

Almsgiving. Whoever does not cease to sustain Christ in his members feeds Christ, 404. He contracts his hands who does not heed the voice of the poor, 550. The raising of the eyes signifies the practice of discerning spirits, 156. Eliab is interpreted as “My God is father,” 379. He signifies those who do good and are learned, but arrogant, ibid. What Eliab’s rejection from the preeminence signifies, ibid. Elijah, lifted into heaven in a fiery chariot, is a figure of a prelate seeking eternal joys, 192. Elijah fasted for forty days in order to escape Jezebel’s hands, 266. Elijah, praying on Carmel, obtained rain, 451. Elijah did not depart from God’s sight, 486. Why Elizabeth conceals that she is pregnant for five months, 245. The divine utterances are signified by the name “silver,” 206. Eugaddi is interpreted as “the spring of the kid,” 415. The sword signifies the subtlety of the understanding of prelates, 297. With the sword of understanding he strikes the neighboring enemy who sends wicked suggestions, ibid. Strictness of conduct is signified by the sword, 425. What it means to carry the ephod before God, 75, 76. The linen ephod signifies the whiteness of continence, 82. The ephod signifies the chosen order of the Gentile people, 69. Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitful,” or “bearing fruit,” 8, 30. Mount Ephraim signifies heaven, ibid. “From Mount Ephraim” and “Ephrathite” refers to one who is not barren in fertile land, 31. The way of Ephraim, that is, of the fruitful heart, is good thought, 293.

A bishop should shine with the light of faith and good works, 214. He who is placed over the Church ought to be perfect, ibid. Often the one who assumes primacy is useful to others in speech but, swollen in mind, harms himself, 215. Shepherds are kings who free us from servitude, 230, 256.

When choosing persons for sacred orders, whoever honors men rather than God by choosing them for the love of kinship rather than for honorable conduct, 86, 377. How easy it is to err in choosing sacred ministers, 176. Chosen imitators of the holy fathers, useful to others through teaching and to themselves through conduct, 202. The one to be chosen should stand out above the whole people from the shoulder upward, ibid. He should excel in life, speech, and contemplation, 203, 206. The one to be chosen should display signs of brotherly charity, ibid. The Holy Spirit makes them bold so that they may presume, and timid so that they may not grow proud, 206. A good shepherd is often rightly chosen by a good flock, 214. The life of those to be promoted to govern the Church must be examined, 216, 380, 381. He should be more exalted in merit than those over whom he ought to be superior in dignity, 223. Those who are to be raised to the summit must be chosen after great reconsideration, 224. A person bears the sign of election when he is concerned both for another’s salvation and for his own, 232. The election of a good bishop must be made not by human but by divine judgment, that is, by sacred Scripture, 252, 374. With what mature deliberation the leaders of the Church should be chosen, ibid. Samuel, in choosing Saul as king, provided a model for choosing the Church’s leader, 253. Even when chosen by God’s authority, they avoid this dignity, ibid. The Lord brings forward those who flee, 254. Before ascending the height of the ecclesiastical summit, let him ascend the summit of virtue, ibid. To find the person to be chosen as bishop, the prophetic electors consult the sacred Scriptures, 374. Who and what sort of persons are to be chosen for pastoral care, 375. What sort of bishops sacred Scripture shows should be chosen or rejected, 251, 269, 379. In their election, neither knowledge nor good works should be considered without humility, ibid. They are not to be chosen for expertise in secular affairs, 380. The model for choosing bishops, 290. The one to be chosen must be according to God’s heart, ibid. He is to be taken from a community in which religion flourishes, 375. God must be consulted in choosing shepherds, 377. Not carnal affection, ibid. Merits must be discerned, not personal connections accepted, ibid. The one pointed out by the Lord is chosen, who is commended through sacred Scripture, 378. Unskilled but humble men are to be rejected from preeminence, 380. Those suitable for the care of souls must be sought with tireless labor, 381. Who are to be placed over the pastoral office, ibid.

A bishop is ordained either for himself and for the people; or neither for himself nor for the people; or for himself but not for the people; or for the people but not for himself, 215, 216. For whom exterior sacraments benefit priests, 214. Priests are anointed when, through the ministry of those ordaining them, they receive an increase of grace, ibid. Those ordained to govern others receive greater charisms, by which they may benefit them, ibid. Those promoted should enter through the gate of humility, 216. The pastor to be ordained for the Church is commanded to consider how great his strength must be, 224. What the highest men should teach those whom they place at the summit of the Church through ordination, 225. Both those who ordain pastors and those who are ordained must rise, 226. They rise together because a sublime office is given and received, ibid. He who is placed at the summit receives the sacraments of anointing, 228. The Truth first kisses those whom he ordains, then sends them to free others, 229. Having been kissed, he is appointed over the Lord’s inheritance, ibid. Those whom God ordains to the summit of rule he sends to endure the battles of the ancient enemy, 230. Strengthened by God, who ordained them, they conquer, ibid. Two loaves are given to the one being ordained, teaching him to mourn both his own sins and those of others, 236. Those ordained by the ministers of the Church are inwardly strengthened by God through the power of the sacraments, 246. The power of the sacrament is the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, ibid. A person should recognize by clear signs that he has been anointed for the leadership of the Church, 247. Those who do not recognize these signs in themselves should be afraid, ibid. How many sins are incurred by those who entrust the government of the Church to carnal men, 274. The chosen men who come to the honor of primacy do not come from ambition but are led there under compulsion, 290. Those who wish to ordain others at the summit of the Church must be prophets, 374. What the anointing of bishops signifies, 375. Those called to the episcopate should burn with love, ibid. Let them rejoice in a fullness of graces from which others may receive, ibid. Bishops should be anointed with a full horn, ibid. It belongs to God to indicate the person to be ordained; it belongs to the ordainer to provide the anointing, 377. Several wise and religious men must be summoned to ordain a bishop, 379. The minister of the Church must never act precipitately in ordaining, 381. The ordination of an unworthy pastor is a deadly evil for the Church, ibid. How many and how great evils proceed from the ordination of an unworthy prelate, ibid. An ill-considered ordination of pastors is censured, 384. Contemplation and charity must meet in the one ordained, ibid. The mysteries of priestly anointing, ibid. Whoever is anointed should possess a full horn in his anointing, ibid. Why he is anointed in the midst of his brothers, 385. Outwardly it is a man, inwardly God works, not man, ibid. Great is the burden of the Order; great is the frailty of the flesh, ibid.

The bishop’s position is supreme, yet unless supreme grace is present it is not well governed, 296. “The speech of the kingdom” is the honorable dignity of a shepherd, 251. Those chosen to govern the Church must be seriously examined, 269. The dignity of a bishop must consist not in ambition for the summit but in the highest virtue, ibid. Let the bishop recognize his dignity and exercise the power of his dignity, 385. Let him surpass all in virtue, 254. Whether he is a shepherd in merit, as he is in rank, is not known unless it is demonstrated by the strength of his works, 269. The action of a good prelate must be distinguished by virtue, 292.

The virtues of bishops are signified by the virtues of oil, 228. The danger facing prelates who are not perfect in love of God and neighbor, ibid. Bishops should be strong in teaching and virtues, 269.

A bishop should seek another’s salvation in such a way that he does not neglect his own, 252. Bishops strike the horn when, by rebuking, they join sharp words to sinners, 375.

A bishop appointed to govern the Church should be directed by the Holy Spirit, 213. Anointed over the Lord’s inheritance, he should seek only that which Christ sought, 229. He should be so devoted to contemplation that he nevertheless bears concern for the Church, 230. The affairs of the Churches are exceedingly high and would crush the weak and inexperienced, 269. For the defense of the Church, not the weak but strong warriors should be appointed, 279. Bishops should use the counsel of lesser and learned ministers in ecclesiastical affairs, 314. In doubtful matters they should consult those whom they clearly know not to lack spiritual gifts, ibid. Matters are better handled by consulting about what is uncertain and carrying out what is clear, ibid. In doubtful and important matters God must be consulted, 322, 325. Those placed at the summit must be prophets, 374. When spiritual affairs press urgently, one must cease from other things, 382.

Bishops must not enrich their relatives with ecclesiastical goods, 86. The pastor concerned with heavenly things should not care for secular matters, 225. What bishops ought to fear from the enemies surrounding them, 229. A mind filled with secular cares finds sacred reading distasteful, 4. Those occupied with external cares are driven away from contemplation of heavenly things, 247. Prelates should preside as equals, 272, 385.

Horsemen are called those exalted in dignity and fierce in power, 182. Hard horsemen signify harsh rulers, ibid. They are horsemen when they restrain the pleasures of their flesh, 192. Like one raised upon a horse, free and swift through the virtue of chastity, a person either flees from or attacks the enemy, ibid. The horsemen who come to battle against us, 282. What the violent assault of a horseman, violent through the strength of the horse, signifies, ibid. Horses are swift for running and strong for assault, 282. Horses signify evil thoughts, ibid. One horse is seen raging against us, but it is not alone, ibid. Who are Pharaoh’s horses and who are God’s, 413. God’s hidden judgments concerning them, ibid. Those are like a horse who admit riders other than God, 480.

Teachers of errors who beget children, 136. The children encourage their teachers to die securely in error, ibid. Who are the king’s eunuchs, to whom the tithes are given, 184, 197. Eunuchs are those who by strength of spirit have crushed within themselves all the fuel of lust, ibid. Eve’s temptation in Paradise, 259. The preaching of the Gospel among the Gentiles bore much fruit, 21. The astonishing effects of Gospel preaching, 140. The ark carried around among the Philistines prefigured the Gospel to be preached and carried among the Gentiles, ibid. The preaching of the Gospel is taken away from the unbelieving and barren, 141, 142. The Gospel is commanded to be preached to every creature, that is, every class of human beings is called to the faith, 331. At times the four Gospels are to be devoutly venerated by the Synagogue imitating the Church, 443. By following them in works, it will become beautiful like Jerusalem, ibid. Three Evangelists wrote little about Christ’s divinity for the faithful, [Col. 1454] giving milk to little ones, 25. John, however, delivered lofty matters about that same divinity as solid food to the mature, ibid.

Bold recipients of the Eucharist, after first being filled, take their place for the bread, 59. They receive the sacrament with the mouth but are not filled by the power of the sacrament, ibid. The more diligently we are cleansed by the lament of repentance, the more abundantly we are filled at the sacramental feast, 60. What punishment those deserve who handle Christ’s body and blood unworthily, 160. True believers fear the dignity of so great a sacrament, 161. Through receiving Christ’s life-giving body and blood, the Church is fed and given drink, washed and sanctified, 544. We are fed and given life by Christ’s body and blood; we are nourished and filled, 556. No one receives the fruit of the Eucharist unless he fasts from vices, 59.

Evilat is interpreted as “giving birth,” 348. It signifies desire, ibid. Indications of being heard that are pleasing to the one who asks, 539. Whoever glories in himself is not heard, 546. Whoever, after praying, murmurs if he is not heard enters into judgment with God, 547. The devil is heard by an angry God, while the apostle is not heard by a merciful God, ibid. God hears those who cry out from the heart, 551.

**High places.** What it means for the mind to stand in a high place, 39. The one to whom the divinity of the Redeemer is revealed is set upon high places, 52.

Excommunicated sinners, because of disobedience: what they should do, 292. The penalty of excommunication is justly decreed against the impenitent, 373. An excommunicated person does not live by the Spirit of Christ, 511. The empty excuses of one refusing authority, 288. Saul’s excuse, like that of other sinners, concerning his disobedience, ibid.

How much an example of devout conduct contributes to the conversion of others, 83. How much the wicked examples of pastors harm, 86, 340, 369. The elect subjects do not allow themselves to be led astray by the evil examples of pastors, 89. Those who imitate a condemned teacher close at hand fall into the same precipice, 90. Whoever praises the examples of the righteous in words is bound to imitate them, 193. The gifts of the elect become examples for others to imitate, 197. The worst sinners are those who give others examples of sinning, ibid. We must follow the examples of good pastors and flee those of bad ones, 208. Whoever wishes to advance should place the examples of the saints before his eyes, 232. Those commonly devoted to a penitential life should encourage one another by good examples, 236. A pastor should teach more people by example than by word, 251. Those tested are helped by a pastor through the good examples of the strongest fathers, 264. The faithful should be urged to virtue by the examples of the saints, 281. Here we are constrained externally by the examples of the wicked, 285. A repentant sinner benefits both himself and others by his example, 309. How much the bad example of teachers harms the weak, 340. Examples of chastity are the traces of the heavenly soldiers imprinted upon the earth, 345. Good external examples of hypocrites often benefit those who do not know the evil within, 368, 369, 372. How much the good and bad examples of the powerful of this world benefit or harm peoples, 369. The pastor is commanded to scatter examples of virtue everywhere, 385. The good examples of the Church are the fragrance of the vineyards, 420. Christ draws us to himself both by his commandments and by the examples of the saints, ibid. The fragrance of the sons signifies good examples, 421.

Strong men, that is, the perfect, fortify the holy mind by words and examples, 425. When a holy soul offers examples to sinners, it shines like the moon in the night, 447. The usefulness of the saints’ examples, 449. We must be fortified by the examples of the saints, 450. The Synagogue must be strengthened against the persecutions of Antichrist by the examples of the martyrs who went before, 454. The example of a converted sinner is powerful for bringing about the conversion of others, 504. Everyone ought to rouse himself to good works by the example of the saints, 550.

Who the army of almighty God is, 12. The traitors in Christ’s army are those who teach rightly but act wrongly, 340. By the name “army” the examples of the fathers and the precepts of Scripture are signified, 342. A song of exhortation and testimony, 400. Here in exile the Church, as in a desert, rejecting all things, longs for the heavenly homeland, 424. Hannah sang a song of exultation, 400. “For the entrails to rot” means that the passage of sin has completely perished from the customary discharge of its foulness, 141. Who the stranger is, 38. What the ends of the earth signify, 51. Hezekiah, afflicting himself with the tears of repentance, escaped the death threatened to him, 109. He promises that he will torment himself with royal pleasures, 235. The prophet Ezekiel came harshly against those hardened in evil, 201. Although he was about to announce harsh things to the harsh, he was not lenient toward himself, ibid. The good shepherd Ezekiel was placed over the wicked, 215. Why and when he was called “Son of Man,” 407.

## F
## F

The name “blacksmiths” signifies secular learning and the liberal arts, 295. What it means to forge a chariot, 183, 194. What weapons must be forged against the enemy, ibid. What it means to fear the face, or to fear from the face, 167. Everyone is recognized by the face, 199. The king’s face signifies the conduct and learning of a good preacher, ibid. Why those who sought the king cry out from before the king’s face, ibid. The face of God is his knowledge, 235. Moses is said to see face to face: he asks that the face be shown to him, ibid. When sinners do evil, they flee from the face of the Lord, 275. What it means for Jonathan’s face to be seen by the Philistines, 307. Those who fall as sinners before the face of the shepherd, ibid. The face signifies outward glory of moral excellence, 382. What the beauty of the face signifies, ibid., 390, 391. The face of Christ is perfect knowledge, 390. The face signifies faith, 420. He is cast away from the face of God to whom hope of pardon after sin is denied, 501. The face of anger signifies recognition of condemnation, 521. The face of God is a certain brightness of knowledge of him, 552.

Who the hungry were who were satisfied, 48, 59. Until the end of the world the hungry are satisfied, 60. Who are the king’s servants to whom tithes are given, 184, 197. Servants are those who, while still devoted to the disciplines of the active life, serve under another’s care, ibid. What it means to serve as a servant for six years and to go out free in the seventh year, ibid.

What flour signifies, 26. What offering a calf without flour represents, 40. What it means to give flour to calves and to mix wine with flour, ibid. What a honeycomb trampled by a satisfied soul signifies, 4. Why preachers are compared with a honeycomb, 432. What Christ eats the honeycomb with honey, 435.

Where happiness is to be hoped for and where it is to be desired by the righteous, 19. That eternal happiness, which is repaid according to works, is granted from the mercy of God, 552. To those who are given the grace of fruitfulness in this life, the grace of eternal happiness is given in the next, [Col. 1455] 553. See *Beatitude*, *Eternal life*.

The two women signify the two peoples of the Church, 450. Through the joining of the thighs the concord of preachers is signified, ibid. The thigh signifies the appetite of the flesh, 425.

### Window

What it means to look through windows and lattices, 419.

Why the human being is compared with hay, 515. Christ’s litter is the Church of the elect, 426. Its silver columns signify preachers, ibid.

The fervor of the ancients reproves our lukewarmness, 323. In the fervor of faith and charity Christ the Bridegroom reclines, 411.

What the command that the fig tree be cut down signifies, 31. What the fig tree producing its large figs represents, 420. No one possesses faith without the grace of God, 550. All classes of human beings are called to faith and to eternal life, 331. Through faith one goes to Christ, God and man, and Christ is said to be brought by each of the faithful, 390. The face signifies faith by which we are known by God, 420. Faith is signified by the name of clothing, 516. It is also signified by the name of the neck, 431, 528.

Those who hear the faith but do not receive it are rejected as perverse, 141. When these refused to believe, others received the faith, ibid. Those who pretend to repent think that they are saved by faith alone, 364. Let no one, having received faith through grace, presume upon immunity from sin, 473. The world gathered into the unity of faith not only announces the works of God but also praises him by its life and works, 529. Testing comes first, knowledge follows, and certainty and confession of faith come afterward, 138.

The faith of the rejected, shattered, is cast away, 31. Most people within the Church bear no fruit, ibid. God’s threats against them, ibid. Faith must be preached in such a way that it is confirmed by good works, 420. All the faithful are called flocks, 413. In what way the faithful are free, 256. The faithful who hold peace are terrifying to their enemies, 444. All the faithful are called the locks of Christ, 440.

Disordered confidence in the mercy of God, 108. He trusts in the mercy of God in an ordered manner who corrects by repentance what he has done wrong by sinning and wipes it away with weeping, ibid. Repentance should accompany trust in God, 166. Those who think little of themselves have trust in God, 478. God the Father acted confidently in Christ, whom conscience accused of nothing, 502.

The minds of the weak are signified by the name of daughters in the Church, 183. What is to be understood by the daughters of Jerusalem, 195, 426. Sons are those who are attached to spiritual fathers for instruction, 82. The sons of great men, in the flesh, are the Jews, who lost the nobility of their faith and virtues, 129. Who is called “son,” not from affection of love but from the cunning of flattery, 133. Who the sons of Belial are, 82, 257. The sons of Eli represented the Israelites, 66. On the prodigal son, 549. The sons of God are those who are joined to him by charity, 249, 527. Christ has the Father as God in a far more perfect manner, ibid. The Son of God in heaven is the altar of the saints, 509. The Son of God is called the Word and Splendor of the Father, 523. It belongs to sons to love, not to fear, 527. We cannot be sons of God unless, observing God’s law and mercy, we love our enemies, 540. Who are called the sons of the elect, 182.

The golden fringes are splendors that never fail from the mind, 346. Through the golden fringes perseverance in virtue is signified, ibid.

Why Christ is our end, 466. The Psalms are inscribed “unto the end,” that is, “unto Christ,” ibid.

He is corrected with scourges and reproved with gentleness, 468. God’s scourges against the rejected, 480. Scourges often open the eyes of wrongdoers, which the darkness of insolence and security had closed, 491. He accuses God’s judgment who thinks that he has been struck unjustly, 546. For what purpose God’s scourges benefit us, 491. See *Affliction*, *Tribulation*.

Weeping arising from compunction, 38. The flowers of eternal fruits are the works of the saints, 232. Flowers signify the tender and the beginners, 417, 421, 448. What it means that flowers have appeared on the earth, 419. What the rushing of the river that gladdens the city of God signifies, 434. Rivers are commonly called living waters, 457. They signify the greatest tribulations, ibid.

The “cooks,” the daughters of a carnal superior, are weak subjects who serve tyrants by flattering them, 184. The cooks prepare on fires what kings eat, ibid. The cooks are those who, through services intended to gain favor, kindle swelling of heart in a carnal superior, ibid. What it means for the daughters of Israel to become the king’s cooks, 195.

What it means to make a covenant with death, 353. Christ shows our ugliness to us all the more clearly the nearer he comes to us, 409. What the sealed fountain signifies, 433. Who is the open fountain in the washing away of sins, 544. Let us draw from Christ, the open fountain of mercy, and wash ourselves in him, ibid. The fountain and the well signify Sacred Scripture, 433.

The spirit of fornication is driven away by the virtue of continence, 302. Why the greater part of humanity rushes headlong into fornication, 297. These have a spear or sword, but not in their hand, ibid. Many virtues are necessary to overcome the spirit of fornication, 331, 341. Why the spirits of fornication are called destroyers, 332. The great struggle of fornication, which is overcome with such difficulty, 341. Its remnants in the mind, mouth, and deed must by no means be spared, 343. The devil drives some into open fornication and deceives others through fraud, 344.

The resolve of strength is signified by calves, 27. Strength is the man’s moderating of the movements of his soul, 474. One kind of strength is laid aside, another is newly begun, 508. The strength of the saints, ibid.

A pit is the height of the world, 231. Spiritual men leap over pits when, moved by heavenly desire, they despise earthly things, ibid. They leap over pits at midday, that is, from the fervor of charity, ibid.

By pious deceit, without the danger of lying, evil people are sometimes to be deceived, 376. He hardens his forehead like a prostitute who heaps sin upon sin, 473.

Fruit must always be borne, 460. In this life we are together on the threshing floor as grain and chaff, 171. It belongs to one who fears to flee, 132. For a Jew to flee from the battle line is to separate himself from the error of the faithless, 132. The actions of holy men fleeing earthly things are not flight but glorious victory, 268.

The Church is compared with smoke rising from aromatics, 424. What the slender column of smoke signifies, ibid.

Those who have not laid Christ as their foundation are to be reproved in anger, 469. Those who have built wood, hay, and straw upon the same foundation are to be rebuked in wrath, [Col. 1457] ibid. What fury is attributed to the unchangeable God, 468. God will reprove the rejected in fury, ibid. The distinction between fury and anger, ibid., 482. Fury signifies eternal condemnation, 469, 482.

He is guilty of theft who attributes anything from good works to himself, 319. The small fork in the boy’s hand signifies the persecution inflicted upon Holy Church by the Jewish people, 67. Who the three teeth of the small fork are, ibid. Whatever the small fork lifted, the boy carried away for the priests, ibid.

## G

Gabaa is interpreted as “high,” 161, 256, 279. The king’s house is said to have been situated at Gabaa, ibid. What it means to go with the king to Gabaa as part of the army, ibid. Gabaa of Benjamin is interpreted as “hill of the son of the right hand,” 291, 299. The hill of the son of the right hand is the eternal height of the Redeemer, ibid.

Galaad is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” 427. This heap of testimony signifies the multitude of martyrs, ibid.

Galgal is interpreted as “wheel,” 174, 244, 269, 291. Galgal signifies the order of married people, 174. Galgal can signify Sacred Scripture, ibid., 291. What it means to establish the king before the Lord at Galgala, 269.

Joy over the promise of the eternal inheritance is expressed by the lyre, 240. Tribulation is the entrance into heavenly joy, 286. Only the righteous can truly rejoice, 481. Through tears one reaches joys, and through joys one reaches weeping, 493. The joy of the saints, immeasurable in the final judgment, 499.

A twin son is one who imitates the negligent person in caring for himself and in the example of his neighbor, 222. The groaning of the devout soul recalling the presence of the Bridegroom, 439. What the voice of groaning is, 516. God would not hear the groaning of those in fetters unless he had given us the Son as mediator, 528.

Gems signify works, 414. The modesty of the cheeks reveals purity of heart, 414.

The other generation is understood spiritually, distinct from the carnal generation of the Jews, 526. In this spiritual generation the divine promises were fulfilled, ibid. This generation is divine and heavenly, ibid. The present life arises from successive generations, 530. From the succession of generations there comes one generation, the divine generation, which is not succeeded by another, ibid.

The faithful multitudes of the nations are God’s army, 12. How great God’s mercy is toward Jews and Gentiles, 523, 524. The nations feared the name of God when they accepted the institutions of Christian teaching, 524. The conversion of the Gentiles consoles the Church for the rejection of the Jews, 15. The preaching of the Gospel bore much fruit among the nations, 21. The completed calling of the nations is the prophets’ fulfilled vision, 22. The word to be fulfilled is the predestined conversion of the Gentiles, 26. The Church’s exultation over the conversion of the Gentiles, 41. The unspeakable joy of the nations over the Redeemer rejected by the Jews and received by the Church, 43. Why the Gentiles are called hungry, 48. The Gentiles raised from the dust and lifted from the dungheap, 50. The boy Samuel represents the people of the Gentiles who believe, 65. The Gentile people were devoted to hearing the Church and ready to act, ibid. The Gentile people were children in the generation of faith, ibid. After the Jews had been rejected, the Gentiles alone ministered before God, 66. The prophets formerly foresaw the ministry of the preachers of Holy Church, [Col. 1457] the conversion of the Gentiles, and their service toward Christ, ibid. The Ark of God was brought into the temples of idols when faith was implanted in the minds of the Gentiles, 137. The progress of preaching and faith in their hearts, ibid. The hand of God, made heavier upon the Gentiles, brought about their conversion, 138. For the Gentiles to die meant to be separated from unbelief, 139. What it means for the Gentiles to be slain by the hand of the Lord, ibid. The nations are signified by the name “peoples,” 140. The conversion of the Gentiles was their killing and striking down, ibid. The whole converted world sings God’s praises, 143. In the salvation of the Gentiles it was not the will of the wicked that was fulfilled but God’s dispensation, ibid.

Geth is interpreted as “winepress,” 172.

One person’s sword is turned against his neighbor when converted people, by exhorting others, turn sinners toward the Lord, 312. When the elect strengthen one another in Holy Church and inflame one another with love of the heavenly homeland, ibid.

The sword signifies the word of God, 425. The hands by which swords are held represent works, ibid.

The Lord glorifies the one who glorifies him, 77, 87. How God is glorified by shepherds, and how he himself glorifies the shepherds, 87, 88. Concerning zeal for good work and humility: one must glory not in oneself but in the Lord, 148. What it means to give glory to God, 148. He who here despises empty glory from good works will eventually enjoy eternal glory, 314. Often those who are great in word and deed do not sufficiently guard against empty glory, 316. All glory is within; for what is outside alone is not within alone, 346. He who glories in himself is not heard, 546. He does not stretch out his hands to God who seeks human glory from good works, 550.

### Goliath

What David, about to fight against Goliath, laying aside all military equipment, represents, 83.

### Gomorrah

What offspring proceeds from it, 195.

What the fifteen steps by which one ascended to the temple represent, 535, 536, 537. The steps by which one ascends to God, 553, 554.

The grace necessary by which a man may love what is highest and despise what is lowest, 31. The grace of the Holy Spirit is rightly called strength, 47. Who were under the law and who under grace, 49. How much the latter surpass the former, ibid. Without God’s help we cannot stand, 64. The devil fears the saints who have been taken up into the strength of divine grace, ibid. We fall as often as the Lord, who holds our inner footsteps, abandons them, ibid. A man does not possess a condition of strength in himself but a weakness prone to falling, ibid. We are heavenly when we are raised up to the height of divine grace, ibid. By its help we crush the strength of our adversaries, ibid. God sometimes withdraws himself so that, in his absence, we may experience how weak we are, 65. In building the house of the Lord, human strength fails unless it is divinely assisted, 80. Whatever good is accomplished by us must be attributed to divine grace, 171. The effect of grace is a change of heart, 246. The nearer we approach grace, the more we acknowledge ourselves to be sinners, 409. Those intoxicated with grace despise all things, 455. The soul trusting in Christ’s help alone is transferred from exile to the homeland, ibid. It is from God both to understand rightly and to do what has rightly been understood, 479. Grace poured into human minds is demonstrated in works, 532. That we may do good comes from God, 550. Earth without water is a soul without grace, ibid.

The effect of prevenient grace, 32. Divine grace sometimes anticipates one who is contemplating; suddenly the contemplative is flooded with ineffable love, [Col. 1458] 35. Every human virtue is weak without God’s help, 52. God alone can rouse minds by grace, 116. We are prepared to receive grace through the quieting of the mind, ibid. Grace is present to those who are tested, by which it helps them endure, 288. Just as water washes the body from filth, so grace cleanses the soul from sins, 499.

The exposition of Saint Gregory the Great on the *Song of Songs* is asserted, 393.

Let us look inwardly toward Christ so that our footsteps may be straight, 92. The flock of the prophets signifies the pastors of the Church under one supreme shepherd, 241. Who are the flocks to be tithed by the appointed king, 185, 198. Our flocks are the crowds of innocent thoughts, ibid. What harms threaten the flock because of the faults of its shepherd. See *Example*, *Shepherd*, *Prelate*.

Gluttony and pride are the devil’s ancient weapons, 6. The three kinds of the sin of gluttony, 82. The vice of gluttony represented by the serpent, 259. How much must be feared from the vice of gluttony, ibid. Gluttony creeps in under the pretense of legitimate necessity, ibid. Gluttonous people are weighed down by innumerable cares out of concern for their stomach, ibid. How foreign the vice of gluttony is to perfected men, 260. Those who would restore the flesh according to their desire, if possible without the incitement of lust, seek an alliance with gluttony, ibid. Through this vice the right eye, by which we contemplate eternal things, is torn out, ibid. By what art gluttony is to be overcome, 261, 265. Innumerable things proceed from the single vice of gluttony, 266. Gluttony is broken by abstinence, 302.

The throat of the Bridegroom signifies Christ’s Testament, 442, and preaching, 452.

## H

The Lord’s inheritance is the multitude of the faithful, 229. The fruit of sacred anointing is the cultivation of the divine inheritance, ibid.

The first heresy in the Church was simony, 518. Heresies are signified by the gates of hell, 532. The leaders of heresies and false teachers—Arius, Sabellius, and Montanus—seemed to be God’s companions; but when examined, they appeared to be enemies, 412. A heretic does not live by the Spirit of Christ, 511. Heretics are signified by little foxes, 421. Heretics are to be driven from their hiding places by preachers, or dogs, ibid. How much danger threatens the weak from them, ibid. The perfected are not endangered so greatly by their breath, ibid. Why the speech of heretics is said not to have come, 112. Heretics destroy the vineyards, that is, the Churches, 421. These are captured by holy preachers, ibid. The reproaches of heretics against the Church, 518. For heretics to eat a lamb cooked in water is to empty, through human wisdom, the mysteries of the incarnation of the Word, 67. Heretics deceived by false contemplation are struck down, 160. Heretics are deceived in their understanding of Sacred Scripture, 238. Heretics contradict Christ set up as a sign, 239. Proud heretics do not find a suitable time for prayer, 477. They do not approach God, 478. Heretics perish: some deceived by error alone, others perverted also by wicked action, 160.

The devil was caught on a hook by the Redeemer, who offered him the flesh while concealing the divinity, 261.

What the two wives of Elkanah signify, 2, 10, 31. Elkanah represents Christ, 5. Christ’s Passion is represented by Elkanah’s sacrifice, 13. Elkanah knew his wife Hannah; God joined the Church to himself through the grace of love, 23. What Elkanah’s solemn sacrifice is, 25. What Elkanah and his wife Hannah signify when they sacrifice a calf, 28.

Eli is interpreted as “my God,” 301. What the conduct of Eli the priest and the cause of his death signify morally and allegorically, 2. His two wicked sons, nevertheless priests of the Lord, 12. What Eli the priest sitting on a chair represents, 15. Eli thought Hannah drunk, and the Apostles were believed to be drunk, 18. What Eli’s command that Hannah digest the wine signifies, 19. Eli signifies not only teachers but also teaching, 28, 70. The sons of Eli signify the Israelites according to the flesh, 66. In the person of Eli the good teachers of the ancient people are represented, 69, 111. What Eli as a young man, and afterward as an old man—indeed a very old man—represents, 71. The crimes of Eli’s sons signify the corruptions of the Jews, ibid. What Eli’s sons sleeping with women represent, ibid. What Eli’s sharp reproof and gentle admonition of his sons signify, 72. He honored his sons more than God, 77. Eli’s face signifies the exercise of free choice in every teacher, 81. Eli is condemned for the fault of his sons, although no personal sins of his are recorded, 83. The sons of Eli signify those who are promoted to sacred orders by carnal relatives, 90. What it means for both sons of Eli to die on one day, ibid. Let those who resemble Eli’s sons hear this, ibid. What Eli’s blindness represents, 97. Eli lying in his place signifies a reprobate shepherd resting in the seat of a just man, 98. The feigned humility of Eli’s humble reply, 108. The imitators of Eli put the threats of divine indignation after human enmities, ibid. When Eli neglected what he heard, he incurred what he deserved, ibid.
