The place of Eli, that is, of the Jewish preacher, is the sacred law, 113. Eli sitting on a chair signifies the teachers of the law in the Synagogue, 131. What the father sitting on the chair after the death of his sons represents, ibid. What the two years lacking for Eli to reach the perfect age of one hundred years signify, 132. What Eli’s falling beside the doorway and dying in that fall represents, 134. What it means that Eli broke his neck by falling, 135. Eli’s daughter-in-law signifies the Jewish people subjected to reprobate priests, ibid. What this daughter-in-law being pregnant represents, ibid. To spare them is to disclose by speaking the wickedness conceived by the Synagogue to others, 136. Eli was just in his own life but lax in pastoral authority, 327. He was struck for his laxity but regarded for his former conduct, ibid.

Why Christ escaped Herod’s sword, 11. Herod swore rashly and fulfilled his wicked oath, 328.

Hesebon is interpreted as “belt of mourning,” 450. What the pools in Hesebon represent, ibid.

Hilarity is necessary in vows offered to God, 27.

Goats signify sinners, 235. He carries three goats who, in repentance, considers that he has sinned in mouth, heart, and deed, ibid. Goats are our carnal movements and unlawful temptations, 413. What it means to feed goats, ibid. A goat was formerly sacrificed for sins, 415. What the fountain of the goat signifies, ibid.

A burnt offering is called something burned, 157. Burnt offerings are made by cutting up the wood of a cart and placing it above the cows, ibid. What it means to add victims to a burnt offering, 158. In the offerings of the perfected, burnt offerings and victims must be present together, ibid. Who offers a burnt offering without victims, ibid. Let a burnt offering of love be offered on the altar of the heart, 176. Why the burnt offerings of the elect are acceptable to God, 509, 510.

A human being is called “flesh” when reason is subjected to the perception of the flesh, 349. A human being is called one subjected to carnal passions, 367. A human being is called a tree, either fruitless or bearing fruits unsuitable for human use, 416. He is called hay, 515. Fallen humanity could not prevail over the victorious enemy if Christ had not assumed condemned nature, 6. Ministers of the Church are called for the destruction of the old human being and the building up of the new, 120. To tear one’s garment and sprinkle dust upon one’s head is to strip off the old human being and put on the new, 131. From the old the new human being is made through the Spirit who leaps in, 242. The transformation of the old state is effected by love, ibid. The life of sin belongs to the old human being; the life of righteousness belongs to the new, 405. What belongs to the new and what to the old human being, 501. The image of the heavenly human being must be borne just as we bore the image of the earthly, 522. Christ, born from the Virgin, restored the human being made carnal, 526. The old human being cannot reach the heavenly kingdom; the new, made a son through love, can, 535.

The virtue of every human being is weak without God’s help, 52. From the fallen angels let humanity learn what it must fear, 58. Humanity lost through sin, 204. Our nature was so condemned through the fall of the first human being that, failing daily, it grows old, 242. The condition of humanity before original guilt, 370. From that guilt come the shameful sensations of the flesh, ibid. Humanity’s blindness and sluggishness after the fall, 397. Its weakness, 406, 503. Whatever is in a human being apart from God is deadly, 416. From how great a happiness the first human being fell through sin, 481, 482, 549. We are overwhelmed in body and soul by the heaviest burden of sin, 485. Subject to death and corruption by the sentence of a just condemnation, 515. The human being placed in honor was cast down through sin, 520. His grievous crushing, 521. The dryness of the human being who withdraws from God, 522. To avoid this, we must cling to Christ, ibid. The arrows fixed in us are mortality and vulnerability, 482. The same human being does not remain the same for a single day, being subject to continual change, 522, 534.

The pain of the human being who considers from what great happiness he has fallen into what great misery, 482. Human weakness, unless strengthened by God’s power, 503. The frequency of miseries is signified by the hand of the Lord being confirmed over humanity, 482.

What the renewal of the inner human being is, 93, 212. A human being cannot free himself from sin by his own power, 186. The human being was anointed with the oil of gladness when he was created, 403. Through creation humanity was raised above all the animals, 521.

The honor of dignity is in itself a great burden upon the mind, 253. Honor offered by a subordinate is accepted so that preaching may be commended, ibid. Few withdraw from the honors of the Church’s ministry; many thrust themselves into them, 254. Reverence due to honor and the humility of submission are great gifts to be offered to prelates, 258. How foreign the desire to be honored is to true repentance, 367. Those who eagerly seek ecclesiastical honors are rejected by God, 87.

The gardens of the Bridegroom are the hearts of the saints, fortified by watchfulness and flowering through chastity, 332. The enclosed garden of the bride signifies the virtue of chastity fortified by continence, ibid. The enclosed garden is the Church and the devout soul, 432. For the Bridegroom’s garden to bear flowers and fruits, it needs the breath of the Holy Spirit, 434. Christ feeds in the gardens, 443. The gardens are the hearts of the saints, 448. What it means for the Bridegroom to descend into the garden of nuts, to see not nuts but fruits, ibid.

The sacrifice of the solemn offering is the offering of the love of Holy Church, 23. Another interpretation of the solemn offering, 25. The offering of the mind is its devotion, 211. Who blesses the offering, ibid. Sins are cleansed through the offerings of sacrifices, ibid. What the pure and cleansing offering is, ibid. What it means to offer an entire offering, 168.

We have enemies all around us, and in everything we think, speak, and do we suffer battles from them, 230. The multitude and ferocity of our enemies, 282. In how many ways they attack us, ibid. Why the mass of enemies is compared with the sand of the sea, 283. Our enemies attack us in a threefold battle line, 293. How much strength we need in order to overcome them, 330. A fallen enemy rises again if we act too leniently, 342.

The dignity of the human condition inclines toward the service of Christ, 524. In sacred eloquence “humble” often means a lack of virtue, 284, 318. When raised up, the soul is lofty; when bent down, it is humble, ibid. Our words and works are plain and humble when they are worldly, ibid. Whose life is humbled on earth, 548.

The elect obey humbly when admonished by proud and negligent teachers, 89. Those called humble, condescending to fraternal love, do not withdraw themselves from Christ, 161. The little ones are called humble, 216. When a humble person hears great things about himself, let him remember his weakness, 222. The elect are great in merit and humble in their own estimation, 227. To behold God here through a mirror is granted only to the humble, 235. The higher they are in merit, the flatter they are through the virtue of humility, 244, 250. From the gift of contemplation one must advance in humility, 41, 407. God cherishes the humble because of his own mercy toward them, 448. Access to God is open to the humble, 478. Trust in God belongs to the humble, ibid. The soul is dearer to God the more despised it is in its own eyes, 484. God hears the prayers of the humble, 526.

Those who join the virtue of humility to a store of merits truly make progress, 95. The infusion of heavenly grace comes to minds prepared through humility, 155. Through humility spiritual sight is sharpened, ibid. By the merit of humility one rises to contemplate the true light, 236. The gifts of humility are signs of signs, 244. How pleasing humility is to God, 379. Humility is better than knowledge, 408. Whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind, as it were, 483. Humility ensures that those who pray are heard, 551. The fruit of humility, 362. Humility must be guarded among the great gifts of the virtues, 38. We are humbled in the estimation of our exile, 62. Let humility accompany contemplation, 41. Humility is necessary for those who speak lofty things, 57. How harmful it is to be exalted after humility has been lost, 70. The remembered shamefulness of one’s past life contributes greatly to humility, 148. To overcome fornication, humility must be added to abstinence, 331. It must be attributed to God’s grace that we are humbled, 551. The gifts of humility are produced by the movement of the Holy Spirit, 243. Obedience shown to superiors should be evidence of humility, 244. Every elect person is humble, and is not fruitless, 382. Signs of true humility, 491, 550.

The feigned humility of Eli, whose reply appears humble, 108. He would truly have been humble if he had offered himself for correction of the fault for which he was reproved, ibid. The simulated humility of the proud, 363. Why the elect preachers accept the false humility of the rejected, 368. In the election of prelates, primary consideration must be given to humility, 379. Humility commendably conceals great actions, 299. The gains of the humble and the losses of the proud, 362. The proud are bold in despising the righteous but cannot despise honors, [Col. 1461] 363. The humble are ready for the commands of their superiors and secure when high things are lost, ibid. Who God humbles and raises up, 62. The humble are exalted when the obedient are granted eternal glory, 363. What grace is given to the humble, 382. How great is the height of the humble, 383. The humble hide themselves in silence and reveal themselves through examples, 251.

Hur is interpreted as “fire,” 342.

Winter was driven away by Christ’s coming, 419. The austerity of the Law is represented by winter, ibid. And the present life, ibid.

The virtues of hypocrites are false, 212. There are two things in hypocrites: inwardly pure evil, outwardly simulated good, 368. How greatly one must beware of hypocrites and false teachers, 412. Let us turn continually to God so that he may indicate whom we must avoid, ibid. The deceitful counsels of hypocrites, 518. Hypocrites must be rejected and abandoned, 365. Hypocrites are compared with leopards, 431.

Hyssop is a humble herb, 498. What its virtue is, ibid. Christ’s humility is signified by hyssop, ibid. A bundle of hyssop dipped in the blood of the red heifer cleansed the defiled, ibid.

## I
Idolatry’s head and arms are crushed, 138. Whoever avoids striking Dagon’s head and hands is shown, in a certain sense, to be an idolater, ibid. The priests of Dagon insinuate that they are themselves Dagon, since they do not tread upon the threshold, ibid. Why the disobedient resemble idolaters, 361. Idols are called vanities, 276. Those whom the spiritual fire does not examine here, it tests by fire at the future judgment, 567. Terror of the judgment is expressed by fire, 111. No ignorance is worse than not knowing what we ought to know while falsely thinking that we know it, 82. The ignorant person is in the night; when enlightened, in the day, 226. We ought to believe not ourselves but those who are better than we are, 231. Vast is the sea of human ignorance, 324. Those who do not know themselves devote themselves to feeding kids—that is, to carnal impulses, 413. Whoever acknowledges the darkness of his ignorance begins to possess the light of understanding, 487. The devil deceives us in many ways, 485. In what does the image of God consist? 92. What it means to sacrifice a victim, 67. Who sacrifices while adoring, 34. The chosen mind that consecrates itself to God, as though to a spiritual sacrifice, ibid. The soul that stands before God with supreme reverence nevertheless sacrifices and does not adore, 35. The crime of uncleanness is hidden from human beings, but is not concealed from God, who sees all things, 359. Nothing is unclean by nature; but what is forbidden to be eaten defiles a person, 566. The Lord often grants to the impatient what they ask, in anger, 547. Pagan emperors—Nero, Diocletian, and others—are called the gates of hell, 532. Impiety is the intention of a wicked act, 477. The impious are silent in darkness, 52. The impious are a useless house, 285. Why God permits the impious to prosper, 492. The impious cries out when he adds sin to sin, 511. Every impious person is a sinner, but not conversely, 566. What God threatens the impenitent, 500. The penalty of excommunication is justly decreed against the impenitent, 373. The supreme shamelessness of those who do not blush at their sins, 472. We must continually keep watch against the deceits and stratagems of unchastity [Col. 1461], 342. To overcome unchastity, the examples of the saints should be brought forward, 344. Who are well-equipped soldiers against unchastity, 345. They should care no less for guarding the heart than for bodily continence, ibid. The unchaste falsely believe that their disgraceful acts remain hidden, 355. They are made public by the voice of rumor, ibid. Sin is to be imputed to no one but oneself, 476. Let us punish our sins so that they may not be imputed to us, 474. What it means to burn incense, 75. The remedy for incontinence is confession, 356. Unless God gives growth, a person plants or waters in vain, 550. Reproof is signified by the name “goad,” 297. When a prelate reproves faults, reproof pricks the mind, ibid. What those who bow down and those who do not bow down produce, 136. To promote the unworthy is to honor them more than God, 86. The unworthy are not to be promoted to the governance of the Church under any dispensation, 381. The unlearned who presume to contemplate heavenly things go astray rather than grasp the truth, 154. The wonderful swiftness of divine mercy toward the repentant sinner, 476. Hell, the house of the damned, 88. In hell there are no counsels of salvation, ibid. God leads people to hell by terrifying them with consideration of eternal torments, 61. He brings them back from hell by consoling them with the hope of forgiveness, ibid. The person led to hell and brought back from hell is the one who dies to the world and lives for heaven, ibid. See Damnation.

There is no one more incurable than the sick person who thinks himself well, 494. To sin through weakness belongs to one who is unequal to the strength of sin, 363. Human weakness must be strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit, 503. The shepherd should become weak with the weak through the sympathy of his mind, not through an inner sickness of soul, 225. The weak should not be appointed to the defense of the Church, 279. The weak should not presume to undertake things above them, 280. The weak should have recourse to the indulgence of marriage, 348. Through consideration of the perfect, the weak are raised to hope for mercy, 408. Secular learning sharpens the blunted edge of the intellect, 296. A blunted intellect penetrates spiritual obscurities only slowly and with difficulty, ibid. A peaceful entrance occurs when the presence of peace has come, 389. The enemies of the saints are called malignant spirits, 314. Duties of charity are to be shown even to enemies, 15, 277, 540. The person truly possesses charity who loves both a friend in God and an enemy for God’s sake, 472. What it means for iniquity to sit in a talent of lead, 483. If God observed human iniquities, no one would be able to endure, 540. Why God permits the wicked to live long, 492. The stratagems of the wicked against the just, ibid. What behaviors are characteristic of the wicked, ibid. We need God’s help in order to defeat the stratagems of the wicked, ibid. See Impious; Reprobate.

**Injury.** Whoever schemes to harm another first strikes himself with his own weapon, 495.

Samuel’s innocence in government, 270. From where the crime of disobedience arises, 287, 288. The devils lie in ambush like bandits for those walking along the road of salvation, 479. What benefit we can gain from remembering the devil’s ambushes, 147. Divine inspirations and revelations must be submitted to the judgment of superiors, 103. [Col. 1462] Sometimes God speaks to the elect through hidden inspiration, 115. By the name “islands” are signified minds surrounded by the waves of temptations, 376. Which islands rejoice, ibid. The strong heart of a subject, unmoved by temptations, is called an island, ibid. What the Lord’s breathing upon the face of the disciples signifies, before he gave them the power to forgive and retain sins, 167. By humility in confession we recover the light of understanding lost through sin, 478. The virtue of a good intention is the love of God, 26. The intention of charity is signified by a jar of wine, 27. Who is “one in intention,” 30. The intention must be pure and simple, 153. From a right intention arises the light of action, 214. A person who does good publicly does not stand firm through the strength of the deed if the intention lacks uprightness, 254. God gives a right intention and the discernment necessary for action, 479. The interpreter of sacred Scripture is like a watchman, 3, and like a traveler, ibid. A question does not always presuppose ignorance but indicates the gravity of guilt, 288. The sinner is questioned so that through lamentation he may be led back to his heart, ibid. We neglect to discover our sins and, once discovered, to weigh them, 325. The person afflicted by envy is a punishment to himself, 88. The fire of envy cannot be carried without burning its bearer, 457. Everyone who is dragged unwillingly is dragged either because he is unable or because he is unwilling, 406. To invoke the Lord’s name is one thing, and to repeat it is another, 564. The good invoke him by pleasing him in all things; the wicked repeat the words while destroying them by their conduct, ibid. Many call upon God but do not invoke him—that is, they pray with their lips and not with the affection of the heart, 513. How greatly the anger of superiors is to be feared, 263. Anger is conquered by love of heavenly things and contempt for earthly goods, 303. Isaac represented natural life by digging wells, 401. What Jesse and his sons, sanctified by Samuel and invited to the sacrifice, signify, 389. The seven sons are all the perfect members of the Synagogue, ibid. Isaiah touched upon the tambourine of Christ’s mortification, 241. Isaiah, more eloquent than the other prophets, was nobly instructed, 295. What Isaiah means when he declares that his lips are unclean, 501. The Israelites according to the flesh are represented by the sons of Eli, 66. They did not know the Lord because they rejected him who came in the flesh, ibid. Nor did they exercise the priestly office toward the people, since they did not proclaim that Christ had come but, in persecuting him, raged madly, ibid. What are the prosperities of Israel according to the flesh? 78. Israel is interpreted as “seeing God” and “in whom God is,” 88, 208, 264, 307. Israel signifies the blessed multitude of angels, ibid., 221. Israel’s prosperities are the everlasting joys of the blessed spirits, ibid. For Israel according to the flesh to go out is to pass beyond the boundaries of right faith, 126. What it means to camp Israel beside the stone of help, ibid. Why Israel turned its back, ibid. The Israelites flee so that they may not die; and because they flee, they die, ibid. The carnal Israelites engage in battle against Christian preachers, ibid. Why the Israelites are said to have been slain in the fields of battle, 127. What it means for some to return to the camp after others have been slain, ibid. Why the Israelites, especially the elders, defeated by the Philistines, are struck dumb with amazement, ibid. They chatter vainly against the Christians, 128. Their chatter and futile efforts are mocked, ibid. What it means that the ark of the Lord came into the camp and the Philistines feared and groaned [Col. 1463], ibid. The carnal Israelites are despised by the teachers of the Church, 129. They are defeated and put to flight by them, ibid. When the ark was captured, Israel’s glory did not perish but was transferred to the Church, 136. The person who is said to rest after the Lord is declared to be Israel, 164. Those who obey God are rightly called sons of Israel, 166. Israel’s boundaries are the heavens, 172. The evil spirits, confined in the depths of hell, will not be able to advance any farther into these boundaries, ibid. The elect are designated by the name Israel, 173. We are more stubborn than the Israelites who do not obey God, 180. Israel’s best things are the gifts of eternal recompense, 221. What is signified by the fact that not the Israelites who crossed the sea, but their sons, were brought into the promised land? 535. A journey. The person who performs a good work with a right intention walks along one road, 153.

## J

Jabesh is interpreted as “dried up,” 259. Who the inhabitants of Jabesh are, 260. What is signified by the citizens of Jabesh waiting seven days for help, 261. To lie down belongs to one who is resting, 98. To lie down pertains to negligence in a more relaxed way of life, ibid. The eyes of one lying down grow dim, ibid. Sleeping is one thing, lying down another, 99. “To lie down” is almost always taken in a bad sense, ibid. Jacob serves for Rachel, but Leah is substituted for her, 32. Why he obtained Rachel as wife only after a doubled course of prolonged labor, ibid. Who failed to know that God was in the place where Jacob had slept, 102. What the road by which he went to his wife signifies, ibid. What it means for Jacob to sleep on the road, ibid. Jacob led the contemplative life, 401. After Jacob saw the Lord, he limped on one foot, 537. James, the Lord’s brother, as the man carrying the kids, 235. The spirit of gluttony attacks more sharply those weakened by fasting, 259. Some people often plan to fast, but, overcome by gluttony, decide that they must eat that day and postpone the fast to the future, 261. By what examples fasting should be commended to us, 266. Jerusalem becomes a citizen through the love of God, 507. Why barren Jerusalem is called our mother, 60. Jerusalem, the city of the saints, is the one that is above, 161, 508. Its citizens are perfect men, separated from the love of the world, ibid. Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” 410, 426, 443, 507, 544. Jerusalem signifies the holy soul, 507. The walls of Jerusalem signify virtues, ibid. Who build Jerusalem, 507. The construction of this city is represented by the building of Solomon’s Temple, 508. It is called a city, a Temple, and a Tabernacle, 509. Who inhabit Jerusalem, 544. Jesse is interpreted as “relief of the islands,” 376. Jesui is interpreted as “plain” or “my desire,” 333. Jesus is “God’s Salvation,” God, the Savior, 42. The Jews call Jesus the Father and await a Savior who is not the Son, ibid. Jesus is anointed in the tomb when the glory of his Resurrection is proclaimed, 387. Why John the Baptist is described as going before the face of the Lord, 82. Why John sent disciples to Christ as though he did not know, 118, 231. John was harsh toward others but not indulgent toward himself, 201. John the Baptist was not a prophet with respect to exaltation; he was more than a prophet with respect to ministry, 220. When John came to preach, he held a calf in his hand—that is, he sacrificed his own flesh to God, 388. John’s parents were just before God, 435. John the Evangelist, a young man, fled naked after leaving behind the linen cloth, 366. What it signifies to flee naked after leaving behind the linen cloth, ibid. Why John wrote the Gospel, 25. Job seems to accuse God when he questioned whether his persecution had been just, 546. As though contending with God, he readily became quiet after hearing the life of the saints, ibid. The people, sharply rebuked by Joel’s voice, prostrated themselves before God and, pierced with lamentation, lessened his anger, 148. Jonah is born as a fugitive, perhaps, 325. He cried out to God from the belly of the sea creature, and his prayer reached God’s ears, 537. Jonathan represents those who serve as assistants to teachers in the ministry of preaching, 279. Jonathan is interpreted as “gift of a dove,” ibid., 333. What the thousand men with Jonathan at Gibeah signify, 279. Jonathan’s weapons are a teacher’s exhortations, 298. What Jonathan and his armor-bearer signify, 308. What Jonathan’s eyes, illuminated by tasting honey, signify, 316. Why Jonathan did not reign after his father, 317. Jordan is interpreted as “their descent,” 286. Those who bend down to perpetrate the crimes of the flesh cross the Jordan, ibid. So do those who begin to sin and surpass the wickedness of others, 287. Those who dwell beyond the Jordan become worse than the wicked through habitual sinning, ibid. Joshua of Beth-shemesh, in his very name and dignity, signifies the Redeemer, 156. The field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh is the pleasantness of the contemplative life, ibid. The cart comes into Joshua’s field when the chosen mind, divided from the love of the world, directs itself solely toward heavenly things, ibid. The cart stood in the field, ibid.

**Jews.** The corruptions of the Jews are signified by the crimes of the sons of Eli, 71. The sin of the Jews could be forgiven by no human prayers, 72. Therefore divine mercy came to their aid, 73. To the crime of the Jews against Christ was added contempt for preaching, 74. The justice of the judgment pronounced against the Jews, 75. The food of the Scriptures was taken away from the Jews, 48. It was offered to the Gentiles, ibid. The madness of the Jews who await a Savior who is not God, 43. The Jews should not despise Christ because he died, but should marvel because he rose again, 48. How greatly they attempted to harm those who believed in Christ, 67. The persecution inflicted by the Jews upon the Church is signified by the trident-shaped fork of the priest’s servant, ibid. The Jews thought they could overthrow Christ’s confessors before they were united to God through perfect charity, 68. They suggested to the faithful that they should deny the Redeemer’s divinity, ibid. In wishing to kill Christ, the Jews were sinning against God, 73. The Church openly refutes the Jews’ faithlessness, 43. The Jews remain in the tabernacle of faithlessness by fighting against the Redeemer, 45. Christ triumphed over their savagery by rising again, 47. By asserting that Christ was a sinner, they denied that he was God and a just man, 68. They rejected the victim of God—that is, the preaching of the holy Church—solely through the force of their ferocity, 76, 123. Some Jews, abandoning their faithlessness, fled to Christ, 131. The faithlessness of the Jews who fortified the tomb with guards, 541. The faithlessness of the Jews who mocked the threats of the Church, 123. They falsely thought that they were fighting against the devil, 125. They are deceived by the vain expectation of the future Christ, 126. They go out to battle against Christian preachers, 126. Defeated by them, they are struck dumb with amazement, 127 [Col. 1464]. Especially the elders, ibid. The plans of the Jews who opposed their ancient law to us, 127. They chatter vainly against the Christians, 128. Their chatter and futile efforts are mocked, ibid. They boast in vain of the ancient fathers, from whose faith they have departed, 129. Having lost the succession of their ancestral virtues, they become ignoble, ibid. How despised they are by the teachers of the Church, ibid. Defeated by them and put to flight, ibid. Returning to the hiding places of their error, they have a heart surrounded by faithlessness, 130. Their spiritual wound, ibid. The blindness of the Jews, 132. The darkness in which they lie, 52. Their terror when they behold the majesty of the crucified one, 52. And they stood beside the apostles as judges, 53. Although the Jews boasted of their knowledge of Scripture, Christ, hidden in the Scriptures, was unknown to them, 66. They suggested that the Redeemer’s divinity should be denied, 68. The Church rejects this, ibid. The Jews are enemies of the Church, 42, 67, and elsewhere. With what intention the Jews approached Christ, 488. How much those converted from Judaism suffered at the hands of others, 409. Christ’s victory over the Jews, 490. Their insults against Christ, 518. God’s mercy toward the Jews, 523, 524, 527. Christ is the Redeemer not only of the Jews but also of all the nations, 12. We are worse than the Jews, 180, 181, and elsewhere. When the Jews alone ascend, they perish, 238. Who ate but were not satisfied, 49. The principal order of Jewish teachers brought death upon Christ for the sake of profit, 77. Therefore the rights of the first fruits, which they wished to retain for themselves, were taken away from them, ibid. The temple, tabernacle, and priesthood were also taken away, 78. These passed to their rivals, ibid. Nevertheless, many Jewish priests were exempted from this rejection, 79. Most of them withered after losing the grace of the Holy Spirit, ibid. The pride of the Jewish teachers, 131. Their uproar and shouting, 132. What they lacked for true faith, ibid. The Jewish teachers were held not by a zeal for knowing the truth but by curiosity, 133. What Paul taught them, 134. When Christians grasped the knowledge of the Jewish sacraments, the Jewish teachers were cast down and fell, ibid. In falling, they stumbled against Christ, ibid. The letter of sacred Scripture is a stumbling block to them, 135. The Jewish priests, raging against Christ, fulfilled God’s plan, 13. They marveled at the apostles’ works but were nevertheless not converted, 18. The twofold order of the Jewish priests, 79. What the Jewish priesthood and teaching were like, 15. Some Jewish priests obeyed the faith while others opposed it, 21.

—**The rejection of the Jews.** The Jews were cast away so that they neither see nor be able to see, 114. They carry the light of sacred Scripture for us and remain ignorant of it, ibid. The rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles were foreseen by the prophets, 66. The rejection of the Jews and its causes, 120. The conversion of the Gentiles consoles the Church concerning the rejection of the Jews, 15. The justice of the divine judgment rejecting the Jews, 75. The rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles are mysteries not to be debated, 50. Once the Jews were rejected, the Gentiles alone minister before God, 66. The Church won many from among the Jews, 16. The Jews will one day return to God and preach the true faith, 80. They will also imitate Christ’s Passion, 81. They will desire to be joined to true priests and to eat heavenly bread, ibid.

—**The Jewish people.** The Jewish people were conquered and rejected by the teachers of the Church before they were destroyed by the Roman army, 130. Why, when God willed it, the ancient people lost the city, the temple, and the ark of the covenant, ibid. The Jewish people are signified by Phinehas—that is, “mute mouth”—601. Why this people was formerly “mouth” but is now called “mute mouth,” ibid. Phinehas is also interpreted as “sparing the mouth,” because this people disdain to blush piously by confessing, ibid. The Jewish people are represented by the figure of the elder son who refuses to enter the house of the Church, 545.

**Judge.** Christ is judge not only of the tongue but also of the heart, 47. What it means that the Lord judges the ends of the earth, 64. Those who will judge spiritual matters should remove carnal considerations, 188. The Church follows divine judgment, not human judgment, 25, 178. God’s judgments must not be scrutinized with excessive curiosity, 178. God’s incomprehensible judgment in the rejection of the Synagogue is to be revered, 22. Who contends with God in judgment? 546. God’s judgments are hidden, 413. The keeping of God’s judgments, 542. By God’s judgment it happens that the one who was unwilling to avoid evil when able later cannot avoid it even if he wishes, 186. God’s judgments must be feared in such a way that hope of forgiveness is not lost, 275. What the demons will bring against us at the judgment, 284. God’s judgments cannot be changed, 366. By God’s judgment wicked shepherds are permitted to rise to the governance of the Church, 189. In their judgments the saints are not rash, 177. They follow God’s will, 178. At the judgment God leaves nothing either unpunished or unrewarded, 52. Not only words but also thoughts are judged by God, 58. Who will be judged on the day of judgment, 568. God’s yoke must be borne from youth, 542. The younger Church was weak in charity, 458. An oath must be carefully avoided, 328. Oaths sworn rashly are not to be fulfilled, 328.

**Right.** What should be understood concerning the king’s right as Samuel sets it forth, 181. The history of Ahab proves that kings are not permitted everything contained in it, 182. David’s example proves the same, ibid. Carnal prelates usurp this right, ibid. What this right contains, ibid., 254, 255. The rights of the king are imposed upon those who despise God’s rights, 180. The former are harsh and intolerable; the latter easy, ibid.

No one is just in God’s sight, 547. The just should fear being held and ensnared by their own praises, 365. They should not allow themselves to be led away from the rigor of justice, 366. Whoever rages against his subjects out of zeal for justice should spare neither himself nor his own, 324. Christ was granted to the desires and prayers of the just, 525. Only the just are permitted to rejoice, 481. It is the teacher’s duty to guard the just, 26. We are kindled to the love of God by the examples of the just, 157. Thus a holocaust should be offered, ibid. Those whom God terrified by the threat of justice he consoles by showing mercy, 110. The weapons that were formerly weapons of iniquity should become weapons of justice, 147. Who are the excellent young men devoted to God? 197.

## L

How God opens the lips, 504. The reward is repaid to the laborer, not to the rank, 221.

**Tears.** The devout soul is refreshed by tears, 35. Tears arising from remorse, 38. God gives the drink of tears according to measure, 146. The tears and groans of the elect in this exile, 209. From where spiritual tears arise, 237.

Only the just are permitted to rejoice, 481. Carnal joy arising from consciousness of virtues is condemned, 319. What delights arise from contempt for earthly joy, 36. Exterior joy must be cast away so that we may experience interior joy, 38 [Col. 1465]. The bridegroom’s left hand is the present life, 417.

**Bottle.** What is signified by a man carrying a bottle of wine, 235. Who possesses prepared lamps, 169. The stone of help, 137. Christ is the stone of help for the elect; he crushes and shatters the reprobate, 171. The great stone is understood as the Redeemer, 157. Christ is the cornerstone, 524. The apostles are the stones of the Church, 523. The cypress-panelled ceilings signify peoples, 416.

**To wash.** Those who washed their feet fear high office and love leisure, 437. Let the penitent continue to wash himself in mourning, 471.

**To praise.** Many praise God with another’s mouth, 505. How it is permissible to praise oneself, 573.

**Praise.** The person makes the best use of praise who presents himself as the kind of person others praise him as being, 317. The blessed never cease from praising God, 63. Lazarus, buried in the tomb and raised by Christ, is a figure of the sinner whom Christ restores to life, 548. The bride’s little bed signifies the repose of holy leisure, 415. The soul’s little bed is flight from and seclusion from every disturbance, 422. Christ’s little bed is a mind free from the world’s cares, 425. Who should be appointed to this little bed as watchmen and guardians, 425. A lenticula is a small vessel, 228. The lions’ dens, 431. Levites is interpreted as “those who have been taken up,” 157. Who the Levites are, ibid. The Law is signified by wine, the Gospel by breasts, 402. Both the elect and the reprobate see in their members a law opposed to God’s law, 563. The evangelical Law is more perfect than the Mosaic, 17. Knowledge of the old and new Law is necessary, 28. The old Law is carnal; the new, spiritual, 69. The harshness of the Law and the grace needed to fulfill it both arise from the one God, 338. The freedom and constancy of the Church, 19. From where the soul’s freedom comes, 54. Who are freed from the power of demons, or need to be freed, 165. We are freely delivered by Christ, ibid. In how many ways lust entices the mind, 351. If we confront wicked thoughts, it is easily conquered, ibid. Its remedy is confession, 356. How subtly the vice of lust creeps in and infects the mind, 350. The movements of lust cannot be removed from the flesh, 266. We should grieve over them, ibid. They must be mitigated by fasting, ibid. To conquer them, we must never allow an impure thought and a natural movement of the flesh to remain together, 267. See Luxury.

Lust kills every good work, 371. It destroys all good thoughts and virtues, ibid. By what art the fire of lust should be extinguished, 371. Thoughts by which it is kindled must immediately be rejected, 372. What diligence should be employed against each of lust’s ambushes, ibid. The counsel of teachers is necessary, ibid. The lustful falsely believe that their disgraceful acts remain hidden, 355. They are made public by the voice of rumor, ibid. Their blindness, 357.

**Lily.** Lilies are chaste souls in whom Christ delights, 421. The devout soul imitates the lily’s whiteness and fragrance, 416. The mind melts at the Bridegroom’s word, 438. Humanistic letters do not furnish us with weapons, but divine letters do, 295. Nevertheless, they aid understanding of sacred Scripture, ibid. The devil is responsible for our ignorance of secular letters, ibid. Their usefulness is proved by the examples of Moses, Isaiah, and Paul, ibid. They are useful not only to preachers but also to those living a private life, 296. Especially for perceiving the depths of the sacred word [Col. 1466], ibid. They sharpen the blunted edge of the intellect, ibid. A high position is not governed well unless supreme grace is present, 246. What it means to speak in God’s ears, 187. Those who desire outward profits do not consider the inward losses they suffer, 186. The Church’s mourning and joy, 16. The mourning of the perfect is indescribable, 318. Light in contemplation is dispensed according to measure, 39.

**Moon.** How some in the Church shine like the moon, 447. The light that is God and the light in which God dwells, 234. Divine light precedes heavenly love, 313. The light of action comes from a right intention, 214. Let the light of a good work advance toward higher knowledge, 220. When the soul receives the morning light, 542.

The vice of luxury must not merely be struck down but also uprooted, 339. It must especially be torn from the heart, 341. God’s grave hatred of luxury, ibid. How greatly it obstructs those hastening toward perfection, ibid. It obstructs not only novices but also men endowed with great virtue, ibid. Luxury is scarcely overcome, ibid. Once this enemy has been thrown down, it rises again if we act too laxly, 342. We must continually keep watch against its deceits, ibid. Its remnants must not be spared, 343. What must be done for it to be completely subdued in the flesh and uprooted from the mind, ibid. The futile arguments by which it defends itself, 344. The examples of the saints should be brought forward to overcome it, ibid. Who are the well-equipped soldiers against it, 345. What weapons are to be used, 346.

## M
Machinations of the wicked against the just, 492. Masters must examine whether disciples left to themselves use that freedom of life for greater progress, 152. How long they ought to devote care to educated disciples, 158. What Jewish teaching was like, 15. “Magmas” signifies humility, 279, 284. And the modesty of the continent, 280. Great men often do not guard sufficiently against vainglory in word and deed, 316. What “Magron” signifies, 299. How greatly the anger of superiors is to be feared, 263. The apple tree designates Christ, in whom we find the food of salvation, 416. “Apples” signify the perfect faithful, 417. Especially martyrs, 433, 452. Why the Church is likened to a pomegranate, 428. What it means for pomegranates to germinate, 448. How, in the pomegranates, the bride gives her breasts to the Bridegroom, 412. Under the pomegranate the king sits: that is, the preacher rests in the shade of the Redeemer, 300.

**Evil.** How great an advantage it is for the wicked to watch those who are perishing and to follow them, 181. From the evils he permits to occur, God provides good things, 179. He turns one away from evil even while allowing it to occur, 180. Goods mingled with evils are not acceptable to God, 474.

**The wicked.** When their measure is full, the wicked are seized for eternal punishments, ibid. The wicked may sometimes be deceived by a pious stratagem without danger of lying, 376.

One must remain in him who remains forever, 540. The Church’s meekness, 19. To stretch out one’s hands toward God is to perform good works for God, 550. The description of Christ’s hand, 441. Mary, a mountain higher than all the angels, 9. Martyrs, the fruit of the Church, 433. Christ’s cheeks, 440. The martyrs who will suffer under Antichrist, 444. The multitude of martyrs, a heap of testimony, 427. The lips of the praising martyrs drip with myrrh, 441. The martyrs conquered through charity, 457. The twofold kind of martyrdom, 528. “Masphath” is interpreted as “contemplation,” 166. What “Matini” signifies [reading uncertain], 3. Matthew, apostle and preacher of Ethiopia, 198. Matthias is found worthy by lot of apostolic eminence, 325. Healing derived from the virtues of the perfect, 453. Those devoted to inward meditation fight more successfully against the enemy, 170. Preachers offer honey and milk to others in such a way that they reserve them for themselves, 432.

**Mind.** The beauty of the divine majesty sometimes strikes the chosen mind with wondrous fear, 105. The chosen minds are called daughters of Israel, 195. How they become the King’s perfumers, cooks, and bakers, ibid. God alone can rouse the mind, 116. A mind empty of works of virtue does not attain knowledge of God, 144. How the thoughts of the mind ought to be subject to Christ, 198. The minds of the elect are whole through innocence and beautiful through the splendor of virtues, 209. What the seven months during which the ark of God was in the land of the Philistines signify, 143. A meretricious use of intercourse is forbidden to married couples, 347.

**Noon** signifies the fervor of charity, 231. There must be discernment of merits, not partiality toward persons, 328. What “Merob” signifies, 334. What “Michal” signifies, 334.

**Soldier.** Innumerable vices serve under the devil as leader, 282. The strength of soldiers in spiritual warfare must be weighed, 281. Who become Christ’s soldiers, 257. What the number one thousand signifies, 279.

When the number of ministers increased, 74. Which sacred ministers please God and human beings, ibid. Some ministers are [approved] in God’s sight, not in the sight of human beings, 81. The twofold office of ministers of the Church, 120. The consecration of ministers of the Church before they undertake the ministry of offering, 161. The manner of choosing them, 290.

**Ministry.** By what sign someone may know that he has been taken up by God for sacred ministry, 231. Flight from ministry should be attributed to the virtue of humility, not to the boastful vaunting of office, 254. Those who have been defiled by earthly crimes must abstain from sacred ministry, 368. Humility should gird itself for sacred ministry, 59. Chastity should gird it about, 82. These are God’s helpers, 162. The destruction of those who approach sacred ministry unworthily, 89. How seriously those approaching it must be examined, 269. Let them be strong in doctrine and virtues, ibid. Those who choose carnal men: to how many sins they become liable, 274. To minister to the Lord is to go forth into the labor of preaching, 112. The twofold office of ministers of the Church, 120. What punishment sacred ministers of the altar deserve when they handle the body and blood of the Lord unworthily, 160. Those who humbly avoid sacred ministries, considering themselves unequal to so great an offering, 161. Called in humility, and accommodating themselves to fraternal love, they do not withdraw themselves from Christ, ibid. The consecration of the Church’s chosen ministers, ibid. How few minister worthily to God, 162. There are hours for ministering and hours for contemplation, 210. What monks especially must observe, ibid.

Miracles of divine compassion, 543. Mercy, the law of God that we are bound to keep, 540. Mercy, the name of God, 528. How great God’s mercy is, [Col. 1467] 522. God’s mercy even in calling those who have turned away, 512. God’s mercy toward the just, 480. Toward penitents, 551. The difference and definition of mercy and compassion, 494. From God’s mercy comes eternal happiness, although it is bestowed according to works, 552–553. Singular mercy shone forth in David, not the harshness of the law, 387. God sometimes punishes out of mercy, 179.

“Moab” is interpreted as “from the father,” 330. It signifies desire, 330. What it is, ibid. The modesty of pastors who take care of their reputation, 271. The modes and limits of contemplation, 231.

**Monk.** Why monks are so called, 30. The monks’ pledge and written bond, 200. What sort of pastor should be appointed over monks, 201. Let him be strict, so that he does not speak soft words to sinners, ibid. Strong through the virtue of the Holy Spirit, not through exaltation and arrogance, ibid. Let him seek the profits of others in such a way that he suffers no losses of his own, 202. Let him surpass the others, ibid. Those who are lukewarm in monasteries should not be cast off as dead, but treated as sick, 200. They are sometimes liable to negligence, and hence to many evils, 286.

**The monastic life.** Monks devote themselves not so much to converting the wicked as to inviting those already converted to a more perfect life, 313. Religious men may sometimes be instructed by the examples of those serving in the world, 315. The works of monks are good when they do not conflict with the conscience of their superiors, 360. Other things must be postponed to the good works that are commanded, ibid. Monks, having cast aside the burdens of the world, make a chamber for the Bridegroom, 424. The holiness and duties of the monastic life, 435. Sleep joined to vigilance, ibid. Christ sometimes rouses them from sleep so that they may attend to the salvation of others, ibid.

**The monks’ zeal.** In a monastery, each person’s sword is turned against his neighbor, 312. They are killed as though by mutual wounds when each strikes the other with the word of God and extinguishes whatever lives carnally within himself, ibid. And not only superiors, through the word of preaching, but also the multitude of subjects win others through both words and examples, ibid. It is praiseworthy for those devoted to the solitary life to labor intensely for the winning of souls, 313. Provided that they are not weak and imperfect, ibid. It is usually their custom to speak the word rather to those who consult them than to those who oppose them, ibid.

The mountains of God are the highest men, 105. Perilous is the death of those who are held by love of the present life, 630. Death is twofold: one by which we die to righteousness through sin, the other by which we die to sin through repentance, 139. The Church is the spouse of death, 14. What it means for an arm to be cut off in death, 88. Christ’s mortality joined to immortality, 441. The mortification of the flesh must never be abandoned, 438. How God's killing and making alive, descending into hell, etc., are to be understood [text uncertain], 50, 61. The elect have two movements: one by which they turn away from temporal things, the other by which they turn toward eternal things, 150. How the movements of the heart ought to be subject to Christ, 198. Unlawful impulses cannot be removed from the flesh, 267. We must grieve over them, ibid. Moses did not see God intuitively, 235. He is a figure of the perfect, ibid. Christ is far greater than Moses and Abraham, 43. Whatever virtue Moses displayed was not his own but God’s, 45.

**Woman.** The sinful woman received Christ as a guest and proclaimed his resurrection, 198. Harlot women signify worldly desires, 84. The women who came to the tomb to anoint Jesus [Col. 1468] figure the contemplative life, 336. They have their work on the journey and their intention in rest, ibid. Three women come with spices to anoint Christ in the tomb, 357. Why they did not find Jesus in the tomb, ibid.

The multitude and savagery of our enemies, 282. In how many ways they attack us, ibid. **Mule.** Those who are like a mule, 480. How the heart must be cleansed, 501. We must die to the world in order to be made alive, 60–61. The fortifications of the soul necessary for it to stand on high, 38. **Gift.** What gifts should be offered to our superiors, 258. Necklaces are fastened around the neck with chains, 414. What the chains signify, ibid. Why they are called golden and embroidered with silver, ibid.

**Mouse.** What it means to be bitten by mice, 139, 143. What the likenesses of mice signify, 146–147. What the new wine of pomegranates is, 454. The saints will undergo a twofold future transformation, 534. Myrrh with which the bodies of the mortified are seasoned, 414. Christ harvests myrrh by bringing the saints perfected through mortification into heaven, 435.

## N

“Naas” signifies a serpent, 264–265. And the desire of gluttony, ibid. By what method it must be conquered, ibid., 266. Innumerable things proceed from this vice, 266. The bride’s nard gave its fragrance when Christ ascended into the heavens, 414. The captivity of human nature in this life, 294. The vice of gluttony insinuates itself under the guise of necessity, 259. The negligent are rash, inquisitive, and impatient of spiritual warfare, 286. Such people are sometimes found in monasteries, ibid. Great and obscure undertakings must not be begun without consulting God, 322. When spiritual matters press urgently, one must take a break from other affairs, 382. “Ner” signifies a lamp, 337. **Not knowing.** The worst ignorance of those who do not know themselves, 82. The nobility of those who serve God resolutely, 205. The name of the Lord: mercy, 528. **Knowing.** To know God through love is one thing, and through faith another, 102. The razor signifies desire, 17. Night is the present life compared with the eternal one, 321. It is night now; when will it be day? 422. What it means to offer a coin to God, 92. The night raven foreshadows carnal people, 516.

## O

The blindness of those who refuse to fulfill the good that they know, 96. The blindness of the lustful and proud, 357–358. Christ, obedient and humble, as an example for the elect, 11. The people’s obedience toward the pastor, 322. The pattern of perfect obedience in Jonathan’s armor-bearer, 304. Life comes through obedience alone, because death comes through disobedience alone, ibid. Labor and rest prepare life for us if the obedient person considers nothing but the good of obedience, ibid. A commandment must be weighed only in this respect: that it is the commandment of a superior, ibid. In obedience, the mortification of one’s own will and the execution of another’s will are produced, 101. Nothing is insignificant that can prepare the obedient for eternal life, ibid. A meal imposed by charity has greater merit than a fast undertaken by one’s own decision [Col. 1469] 101. The commands of superiors must be revered, even if they live less laudably, ibid. Obedience must be rendered to superiors in two ways, 107. The blind hearts of proud disobedient people, cast away by divine judgment, 187. Nothing must be done apart from the authority of superiors, 198. Obedience strengthens the other virtues, 199. It is never permissible to shake off the yoke of obedience, ibid. Those who make good progress should strive above all to hold fast to the good of obedience, 244. The order of the chosen manner of life is that one should not impose obedience on others when one has not cared to render it to others oneself, 244. The wheel signifies the life of the obedient, 244. What the obedient do below, they raise upward, ibid. What they have above, they bend toward the earth, ibid. The form of perfect obedience, ibid. Perfect obedience, which we show to human beings, is a gift of the Creator, 245. Obedience is the Lord's offering, but, when offered to human beings, it is received from God, ibid. The services of the obedient are sacrifices, ibid. The notable victory of the obedient, ibid. Nothing should be avoided more diligently than pride and disobedience, 287. What is commanded must not be considered at all, ibid. It is easier to obey than to command, 257. In order to command others correctly, one must obey God perfectly, 290. Some obey while they are inexperienced; once educated, they recoil from obedience, 95. This is proved by the example of Hagar, ibid. Saul’s rejection for a slight fault against obedience should terrify us, 287. Through obedience we consecrate ourselves to God; through the other virtues, our possessions, 360. Everything must be done with the knowledge of the superiors, ibid. Obedience is better than holocausts and sacrifices, ibid. Those who place their own will before the commands of their superiors are struck down, ibid. Obedience is preferred to great fasts and compunction, 361. Why the disobedient are like diviners and idolaters, 361. The word of God is rejected by the disobedient, 362. Therefore he is rejected by God himself, ibid. A person did not have his flesh obedient to him when he himself did not obey God, 370. How serious a crime it is not to obey God, 288. The vain excuses of those who refuse to obey, 288.

Let our offering be made from devotion, 27. **Obscenity.** Married couples must beware of every obscenity, 334, 347. God threatens those who act otherwise with eternal punishment, ibid. Those who hear obscene things risk becoming inflamed by them, 350. The eighth signifies eternal life, 467. How it is understood that the eyes are opened through sin, 303. The good odor of works performed from charity, 431. From the virtues of the perfect, 453. In how many ways “to offer a lamb” can be explained, 168. The virtues of oil are explained, 228. A burden must not be taken upon oneself, 200. A burden arising from honor, 253. Grace precedes good works, 553. The path of good works by which one ascends to contemplation, 154. Christ is fed by good works, 435. We must answer God with works, 529. The light of a work comes from right intention, 214. Lust kills good works, 371. Great men often do not guard sufficiently against vainglory in work and word, 316. Which tithe of good works must be gathered, 196. Good works must be concealed, 302. We are helped by the good works of others, 327. Concerning zeal for good work and humility: one must glory not in oneself but in the Lord, 148. Sound doctrine must accompany zeal for good works, 163. The elect are customarily stirred to good works by hearing the word of God; the reprobate react otherwise, [Col. 1469] 165–166. Good works benefit only the sons of the Church, 31. Whoever attributes anything from a good work to himself is guilty of theft, 319. The higher one ascends in contemplation, the more diligently one must pursue good works, 35. More perfect things should not be set before the weak, but plain ones, 83. Those who might have conquered through lesser works often fall amid great ones, 83. **To work.** That we work well comes from God, 550. Who the strong workers in the Church are, 292. Although Hophni was wicked, he was nevertheless the Lord’s priest, 12. The sins of the eminent must sometimes be tolerated, 369.

What it means to pray without interruption, 37. What is required for this, ibid. Christ and the Church pray for the perseverance of the just and for the conversion of sinners, 546. Every saint prays for his own sins, because no one is free from sin, 477. Now is the opportune time for prayer, 477. For prayer to reach God, it must ascend from the depth of humility, 537. Prayer must accompany good works, 432. In prayer the saints ask for nothing transitory, 477. The prayers of the saints are never without fruit, 187. Yet those praying for the reprobate cannot be heard, 188. One must persevere in prayer, 538. How prayer and supplication differ, 539. The eloquence of orators is not to be sought in interpreters of sacred Scripture, 5.

**World.** The Church is spread throughout the entire world, 42. Horeb, the mountain of God, 266. The order of conversion and integrity, 164. Order must be maintained in judgments, 323. The order of our victory against the enemy, 170. The order of those who are to be saved, 227. The reward is paid not to the highest rank but to the greatest labor, 221. The final order of the Church: penitents, 222. The hypocrisy, avarice, and unjust judgments of those aspiring to sacred orders, 190. Those ordained by the ministers of the Church are strengthened inwardly by God through the power of the sacraments, 246. By what signs it may be examined whether the person being ordained has been anointed by God, ibid. Let whoever does not recognize those signs in himself be afraid, 247. And let him not be lifted up by the height of pre-eminence, 248. Let the others marvel at him, transformed by the power of the Holy Spirit, 248. From this it is proved that he has been begotten by God, 249. The ill-considered ordination of pastors is censured, 384. In the ordained person, contemplation and charity must come together, 384. See **Pastor**.

Original sin is propagated through carnal desire, 497. It is the reason why we do not stand firm in righteousness, 520. Original guilt, 370. From it come the shameful sensations of the flesh, ibid. The sins and vices of desire, ibid. He kisses Christ who is pierced with compunction through love, 404. The kiss of Christ the Bridegroom is the perfection of inner peace, 405. The display and boasting of certain teachers, 354. What the gates of the house of God are, 122.

## P
Palms of Dagon cut off: what they signify, 138. Christ, ascending the palm—that is, the cross—offered us its fruit, 452. What is the bread of man? 515. Eating the bread of one who forgets evils, 515. To hire oneself out for bread means to search the sacred Scriptures for the mysteries of the coming Redeemer, 49. Paradise closed before Christ, 42. [Col. 1470] God spares the one who weeps for sins, 472. The mountains of leopards, 431. What it means to obey the mind and conceive, 53. Wall. Behind the wall God lay hidden, concealed in the flesh, 419. For the sake of little ones, the Church patiently endures the postponement of her glory, 24. What the offering of the little ones of the Church is, ibid. Thus weaned, they are continually set before the sight of God, ibid. They must not presume to climb too high, 25.

The Passion of Christ prefigured in the sacrifice of Elkanah, 13. The pastor’s office, 29. Let no one trust that he can fulfill it by his own strength, ibid. Continuous prayers are necessary for it, ibid. — The pastor must excel in life, word, and contemplation, 203. He must imitate Christ, to whom no one was harsher than he was to himself, ibid. He must be sent by Christ himself, ibid. How long pastors ought to devote care to educated subjects, 158. With what zeal one must watch over the correction of subjects, 164. For subjects under trial, pastors provide the support of prayer and sacrifices, 168. Suspended in the highest contemplation, pastors must descend to teach their subjects, 209, 255. They have one place for themselves and another for their subjects, ibid. They must leave their own places in order to arrange common affairs, ibid. While ascending through love of their own perfection, they must descend through compassion for another’s weakness, 225. Pastors must have compassion on subjects under trial, 262. They must strengthen them with exhortations, 268. With great cries pastors must seek the salvation of the faithful, 274. At their cry the Lord gives a voice, ibid. The pastor must possess such great charity that, in his urgent desire, he feels himself to be not the petitioner but the petition itself, 280. In correcting the faults of subjects, the pastor must rise and ascend, 291. Pastors must not delay to bring help to subjects under trial, 298. Let them place some in safety and lead others with them into battle, ibid. While summoning them to battle, let them themselves fight first, ibid. They are a shelter for their subjects, protecting them by exhortations from the heat of concupiscence, 300. “Shelter” is expressed diminutively, so that no one may be compared with Christ, 301. Pastors must learn to have great compassion for sinners, 307. When pastors investigate the faults of subjects by divine judgment, they must ask that those same faults be covered by divine mercy, 325. Let them examine the weakness or strength of each individual, ibid. The pastor holds the lots of individuals when he observes the conduct of each of his subjects, 326. He should appear to belong to each individual, 333.

— Pastors ought to possess the highest perfection, 223. And strength in good works, ibid. In order to reign, they must be crucified, 224. They must arrange what is to be done with mature deliberation, ibid. They must be chosen only after extensive reconsideration, ibid. While ascending through love of their own perfection, they must descend through compassion for another’s weakness, 225, 236. They must be strict with themselves and moderate with their subjects, ibid. They must not concern themselves with worldly affairs, so that they may be solicitous for heavenly things, ibid. They must rest in spiritual matters, 226. Both those who appoint pastors and those who are appointed must rise, ibid.

— The pastor “goes out” when he comes from the secrecy of meditation to public action, 226. He must not go outside before dawn, 227. He is ordained for sinners rather than for the just, ibid. He must not yield to his own opinion or follow his own judgment, ibid. The pastor is a mediator between God and humanity, 229. In freeing God’s people, he must beware of the enemy’s yoke, ibid. What the Lord’s inheritance is, which he is bound to seek, ibid. What he must fear from the surrounding enemies, [Col. 1471] 229.

— The humble pastor, trembling at the ministry he has undertaken: what signs of divine calling he should possess, 230. — He must be so devoted to contemplation while also carrying responsibility for the Church, ibid. He bears the sign of election when he is concerned both for another’s salvation and for his own, 232. Whoever wishes to make progress should set before himself the examples of the saints, 232. He should seek refreshment in the shade of a more secluded life, 233. He should weep not only for his own sins but also for those of others, 236. Sacred Scripture is the mirror of elected pastors, 251. With what mature deliberation they ought to be chosen, 252. Even those chosen by God’s authority flee, 253. Who the assistants of pastors are, 257. The pastor’s foresight should guard against future sins, 297. He must not delay to bring help to those under trial, 297. Let him place some in safety and lead others into battle, ibid. Let him himself fight first, ibid.

The pastor must possess holiness of life and instruction in wisdom, 144. The faithful readily trust that they can be governed by him and willingly consult him, ibid. A good pastor is often rightly chosen by the people, 214. Many pastors have the means both to fall themselves and to raise others up, 214, 215. A pastor is sometimes ordained for himself and for the people, 215. Sometimes neither for himself nor for the people; sometimes for himself and not for the people, ibid. Sometimes for the people and not for himself, 216. In what manner he ought to feed and be fed, 218. And to experience the delights of the mind, ibid. The distinction between the uneducated and the educated, 221. The pastor should be sharp in reproving and gentle in showing mercy, 384. He is commanded to scatter examples of virtue everywhere, 385. He must live not for himself but for his own people, ibid. By doing what he says, the pastor persuades effectively, 377. Whoever speaks and does not act is slaughtered by the sword of his own mouth, ibid.

— The pastor should rarely be seen in public, 378. He should awaken great admiration not only in the uneducated but also in the perfect, ibid. The divine will should be sought from him, ibid. What harms threaten because of a pastor’s fault, 329. Through the satisfaction of repentance, they must immediately be raised to higher things, ibid. And they must crush the enemies, ibid. They must be the salvation of the people, 376. They must strengthen and confirm those who waver, ibid. The pastor must fight against the enemy by life and doctrine, 330. Pastors should be afflicted by the fall of their subjects, 353. They should mourn them with hidden compassion and strike them with open rebuke, ibid. What rule they should observe in governing souls, 354. Some pastors live wickedly and imagine that they please God through the progress of others, 354. How greatly they err, 355. Who and what sort of persons should be chosen for pastoral care, 375. God must be consulted in choosing pastors, 377. Not fleshly affection, ibid. What their anointing signifies, ibid. Let them rejoice in the fullness of graces, from which others may receive, ibid. Let them be taken from a congregation in which religious observance flourishes, ibid. What sort of persons sacred Scripture shows should be chosen or rejected, 379. In their election, neither learning nor good works should be considered without humility, ibid. They must not be chosen for expertise in secular business, 380. The unskilled, though humble, must be rejected, 380.

— Pastors must go out freely to their subjects and return to the secrecy of the mind, 255. Weighed down by their own weakness, they cannot pursue the vices of others, 328. When pastors are silent, who perish, ibid. In temptations one must flee to the counsels of pastors, 262. Pastors must have compassion on those under trial, ibid. Whatever is done against the best pastors is attributed to an injury against God, 179. God is despised in pastors, 352. With what modesty a pastor ought to care for his reputation, 271. What he may freely avoid and rebuke in others, ibid. While asking that the faults of subjects be revealed to him, he should pray that they be covered by divine mercy, 325. He should examine the weakness and strength of each individual, ibid.

— What assistance pastors provide to subjects under trial, 168. With great cries they must seek the salvation of the faithful, 274. What rains they should thereby call forth, ibid. God reserves pastors for his own judgment, 96. Therefore they ought to fear more, ibid. The pastor is the eye of the Church, 98. He sometimes grows dim, ibid. The source of this dimness, ibid. He lies where he ought to stand, ibid. He not only does not see but cannot even see, ibid. In such pastors only the shell of the lamp remains, without light, 98.

The greed of evil pastors signified by the razor, 17. Their faults are punished more severely, 85. Evil pastors are permitted by God’s judgment to rise to the governance of the Church, 189. The plundering and avarice of evil pastors, 270. In pastors, the fall of the flesh is especially serious, 349. The ordination of an unworthy pastor is a deadly evil for the Church, 381. Punishment is heaped upon a reprobate pastor when his subjects make progress, 89. To one who exercises pastoral care wisely, God multiplies the gains of conversions, 83. Those suitable for the care of souls must be sought with tireless labor, 381. Who should be appointed to pastoral office, ibid.

Patience is superior to strength, 268. Patience must be learned from Christ, 489. Incentives to patience, 490. Christ suffers again in his members, 512. Christ has God as Father in a more perfect manner, 249. The command to Christ to die was imposed by the Father, 12. Presenting himself to the Father in the flesh, Christ prays for us, 26. The agreement of the ancient Fathers and the New Testament, 69. By what rule the ancient Fathers should be followed by us interpreters of Scripture, 5. Fathers must be admonished by their children cautiously and humbly when necessity requires it, 316. The eternal homeland signified by the house of the Lord, 40.

How lofty Paul’s teaching is concerning future blessedness, 293. How great a miracle Paul’s conversion was, 250. Paul’s writings. His letters proceeded from the neck of the apostle Paul, 203. Wise men, making daily progress in his learning, cannot reach the top of his neck, ibid. Through the support of humane letters, Paul perhaps surpassed the other apostles in learning, 295. Paul laments the law in his members that resists the law of his mind, 267. How Paul crawled on his hands toward sinners, 307.

Who is called the God who makes poor and enriches, 61.

Peace. What boundaries God sets for the peace of the Church, 173. What fruits should be produced in time of peace, 193. In this life there is no peace with the ancient enemy, 194. In peace of mind the eye is cleansed, by which one gazes toward the homeland, 444. We cannot attain perfect peace here, 459. What peace the apostles preached, 523. The abundance of peace is found only in the land of the living, 555. What the peace of Christ is, ibid. Christ is our peace, 64. The abundance of peace in heaven, 555. The perfection of inner peace, 405.

Restoration of sinners through repentance, 172. See Penitents, Repentance. Whom God wishes to kill while they sin, 73. No sin has existence, 306.

— What it means to be gnawed by the conscience of sin, 139. Some are struck only toward recognition of their sins, but do not die, 142.

— Sin must be recalled in the mind so that we may be stirred to repentance, [Col. 1472] 146. How carefully one must guard against falling back into sin, 159. Past sins should be mourned in such a way that future sins are avoided, ibid.

— The punishment of sin is that the reprobate are permitted to do what they desire, 178. Through sin the human being is lost, 203. He is found when he confesses it, 204. Sins wiped away by tears lose their ugliness, 150. They must be recalled to memory in such a way that they do not hinder contemplation of heavenly things, 151. Confession of sins must be made to a priest, 166, 369. He must impose a penalty proportionate to the crime, ibid. What qualities are necessary for him to bind and loose rightly, ibid.

— Confession of sin. Sin must be disclosed in confession, not increased by a lie, 326. The vain evasions of those who conceal their sins, 355. Sins are killed when, by apostolic authority, they are remitted to those who confess them, 356. The devices by which sinners conceal their sins, 358. Confession before God is made to priests, 359. Sins must not only be confessed but also wiped away by the austerity of repentance, 359. The faults of repentance and confession, 364. Sin that is loved is not erased by confessing it, 367. What confession of the mouth brings salvation, ibid. The sign of true confession is found in the affliction of repentance, ibid. We cover sins by exposing them through confession, 474. The face of the Judge must be anticipated by humble confession, after the example of the Publican, 475. For perfect confession, all the circumstances of the sin must be recounted, 476. Sins both of omission and commission must be declared in confession, ibid. Confession of sin must be made before God and priests, 359. Confession of hidden sins of the heart, 275. The most perfect model of confession of sins, 326. Those who receive the confession of sins risk becoming inflamed by the obscene things they hear, 350. How it is to be understood that sin opens the eyes, 303. Not even the elect can be without sin, 59, 60. We cannot avoid all sins, even though we can avoid all crimes, 421. Those who do not avoid sins when they can later cannot do so, even though they may seem willing, 351. Sins must be confessed and amended, 559. The weight of sin, 383. We are overwhelmed by this weight, 485. By what waters sins are washed, 495. How God protects from future sins, 479. Christ alone was without sin, 440. Original sin. See Original guilt. The sinner is like ashes, 519. The sinner who is silent and cries out, 475. The sinner is like one gravely wounded, 494. It is permissible to pray for adversities for sinners, that they may be restrained, 480. Sin is committed in three ways, 489. The unhappy condition of the sinner, 548. How he is recalled to life, 548. The sinner’s house, in which evil habit rests, 372. Unrepentant sinners are rightly excommunicated, 373. Thus rejected, they must be mourned by pastors, ibid. Sinners must be shown both the good they have received from God and the evils they have perpetrated against him, 252. To convert sinners is the duty of a teacher, 26. Sinners are signified by goats, 235. The sin of those who turn others away from the worship of God is scarcely erased by repentance, 69. If we are condemned because of another’s sins, how much more because of our own? 106. Sinners attempt to break the steadfastness of pastors by flattery, 356. One must not yield to them, 357. They must be rebuked in such a way that no avenue of escape is left, ibid. The highest degree of sin is to become proud of sin itself, 353. The vain evasions of those who conceal their sins, 355. Sins live as long as they are not erased through repentance, 356. They are killed when, by apostolic authority, they are remitted to those who confess them, [Col. 1473] ibid. Those who abandon their sins but do not mourn them are rebuked, 358. Not only greater but also lesser sins must be mourned, 359.

— Sin is admitted in three ways, 575. How sins should be reproved, 577. The worst sinners are those who give others examples of sinning, 197. The first wound of sinners is conversion, the second condemnation, 308. Converted sinners sometimes kindle others to conversion, 309. In their conversion God accomplishes some things by himself and some through human beings, ibid.

Snare. What it means for a snare to be hidden as though in the earth, 547. The elect are figuratively represented by the name of foot soldiers, 345. The sea of human ignorance, 324. The pelican prefigures the carnal, 516. Christ is like the pelican, 517.

Three degrees of perfection, 248. — What counsels should be given to those who seek perfection, 157. One must strive toward the summit of perfection, 170, 26. Even to the end of life, 171. Perfection befits pastors, 223. The privileges, characteristics, and duties of perfect men, 30, 70, 100, 151, 152, 210–213. Treachery must be abandoned before the true faith is preached, 132. This is demonstrated from the history of Paul’s conversion, ibid. What dangers surround those who walk on the way of salvation, 554. What must be done so that we may be rescued from them, 554. What perishes in the saints? 533. In persecutions the Church always stands, 28. The usefulness of persecutions, 491. Perseverance in virtue signified by golden fringes, 346. — God gives perseverance to one who weeps for sins, 472. The perseverance of the elect, 386. We do not know who will persevere, 386. One must persevere by conquering carnal desires, 153, 154. There must be no partiality toward persons, but discernment of merits, 328. Human beings must be passed by in order to reach God, 423.

Peter is not only a prophet but also the supreme patriarch, 391. He saw Christ’s glory imperfectly, ibid. What Peter’s threefold questioning signifies, 383. The holes in the rock are Christ’s wounds, 410. Those who refuse conversion are like Pharaoh and Egypt, 149. Peninnah, Elkanah’s wife, 13. What the Philistines signify, 125. What satraps are, 140. The carrying of the ark among the Philistines signified that the Gospel would be carried among the Gentiles, 140. Although Phinehas and Hophni were wicked, they were nevertheless priests of the Lord, 12.

The lazy must be compelled to good works by fear, 263. They must afterward be led to perfect charity, 160. Christ chose fishermen in order to subjugate kings, 524. To please God and human beings is perfection, 85. We should seek to please God alone by our tears, 166. One must please human beings in matters not forbidden, 571. What it means to seek Christ through streets and alleys, 423. The distinction between the common people and the people, 160. What a willing people is, 161.

One must ask insistently of God, 538, 539. The power of the Church bestowed by Christ, 41. Some precepts are common and others particular; violating the latter is more serious, 289. What it means to offer the beginnings of spoils, 355. For God to predestine is for him to act, 290. What God predestined, he accomplishes, 576. The certainty of God’s predestination and foreknowledge, 328. The preaching of the Gospel bore many fruits among the nations, 21. Contempt for this preaching is the crime of the Jews, 74. The progress of preaching, ibid. It is one thing to know what should be preached, another the manner of preaching, and another when to preach, 121. The astonishing effects of evangelical preaching, 147. One must return from preaching to contemplation, 204.

— Preaching is a kind of sacrifice, 69. The preacher must fulfill in action what he teaches, 243, 306. He must sometimes ascend and sometimes descend, 250. He should teach more by example than by word, 251. How great his charity must be, 280. When holy preachers ascend, they encounter the preachers of the Church, 238. And the ancient prophets, ibid. They agree with them, 239. They have before them what they preach; the reprobate have it behind them, 241. They must excel both in action and in contemplation, 239. They must feed and be fed with heavenly food, 300. What sort of fellow ministers of the word they should have, ibid. They are a shelter from the heat of concupiscence, ibid. Those who despise the admonitions of preachers gnaw at their lives, 303. What must be preached about Christ, 241. What was foretold by the prophets, ibid.

— Preachers are oxen who plow the field of the Church, 308. They should not be fed merely on praises, so that they may eventually enjoy eternal glory, 314.

— The vain preacher fails when he is not fed with praise, 317. He has received an imitation of light, not the truth, 318. The humble example of Christ must be set before him, 320. It is the preacher’s duty to rebuke faults committed and teach how future faults may be avoided, 319. Preachers must unite humility with purity of life, 131. The preacher gives to God those whom he has begotten, claiming nothing for himself from their generation, 17. He must not seek the temporal goods of his subjects, ibid.
