The preacher must return by hastening back to contemplation, 22. The order of preachers is understood under the name of Samuel, 23. By what their life must be proven, 110. Some preachers were chosen from the Gentiles and raised to the summit of apostolic authority, 51. They may be called the hinges of the earth, ibid. They perform the ministry of the prophets, 124. God is manifested more clearly to them; they are compared with the Philistines, 126. Through the zeal of preachers, those who serve the flesh are made servants of God, 197. Preachers suspended in the highest contemplation should descend to teach their subjects, 209. They should leave their own things in order to arrange common affairs, ibid. According to the capacity of their hearers, they should teach sometimes plain and sometimes lofty matters, ibid., 210. They should rarely be in public, ibid. In the secrecy of contemplation they should be enriched with heavenly treasures, ibid.

— The preacher’s duty is to declare war on the pleasure of the flesh, the concupiscence of the mind, and the pretense of good works, 195.

— Preachers who are free from crime should be chosen, 150. Yet they must not flatter themselves about their holiness or be secure, ibid. With what zeal a preacher must watch over the correction of subjects, 164. The singular brightness of preachers in glory, 172. They should put forward by example the light of justice that they display in words, 173. From the saints of every order and condition they should also borrow examples to propose for imitation, [Col. 1474] 174. They should be so instructed in reading sacred Scripture that inwardly they are taught by God through contemplation, 174. So that they are not overwhelmed by labor, they should seek the fellowship of the saints, 175. On the altar of the heart they should offer the holocaust of love, 176. The highest reward of the best preachers, 221. A great incentive to the labor of preaching, ibid. The reward is given not to the highest rank but to the greatest labor, ibid. Hearing great things about himself, the preacher should remember his weakness, 222. Great marks of virtue are attributed to preachers, 230. They are kings who free us from servitude, strengthened by God, who appointed them, ibid. By despising the heights of the world, the preacher leaps over them as over pits, 231. He does so from the fervor of charity, ibid. He should work in alternating turns and rest from labor, so that he may have time for himself, 232. What sign he has of election, ibid. Whoever wishes to make progress should place the examples of the saints before his eyes, ibid.

— The duty of preachers. It is the duty of preachers to rebuke faults committed and teach how future ones may be avoided, 319. The pious stratagems of preachers, 374. What must be learned by one who preaches Christ, 388. Whoever wishes to show Jesus by preaching must imitate his sufferings through mortification, 388. The danger of a preacher who acts badly, ibid. It belongs to preachers to catch foxes—that is, heretics—for Christ, 421. By explaining Scripture, preachers chew bread for little ones as mothers chew it for their children, 428. They bear twin offspring in the two precepts of charity and preach a twofold love, ibid. They do not cease to beget both Jew and Gentile, ibid. In preaching they are like a dripping honeycomb, 432. They offer honey and milk to others while also keeping some for themselves, ibid. Through renunciation of outward things they acquire the word of God, 437. Through divine inspiration they rise to the labor of preaching, ibid. By word and example they prepare a place in minds for the Bridegroom, ibid. How the soul may be healthfully wounded and stripped by its guardians—that is, by preachers, 439. They remove the cloak when, by preaching, they reveal what lay hidden within, 439. What preachers offer to others, they taste more abundantly than the rest, 450. What, how much, when, and to whom the preacher should speak, 305. He must first carry out what he teaches, 306. Those who leave their hiding places for the sake of preaching should not be judged lightly, ibid.

— The preacher’s life must not be inferior to his reputation, 212. The preacher’s proper place is contemplation, ibid. He should go forth from the secrecy of contemplation to preach, ibid. He must have experience of the Spirit speaking within him, in the sudden revelation of truth, 218. Whoever does not love the things he preaches fasts while feeding others, 209. Preachers are the pillars of the Church, 426. The preachers of Christ are its eyes, 440, and its lips, 441. The vigilance and strength of a holy preacher, 428. — The conduct of preachers. The preacher should put forward by example the light of justice that he displays in words, 173. Preachers should rarely be in public, 210. The preacher’s house is his spiritual conduct, 217, 222. The distinction between carnal and spiritual preachers, 250. Preachers should be fed with heavenly food and feed others, 300. Preachers are signified by two oxen, filled with the grace of twofold charity, 308. Preachers should not be fed merely on praise for brave deeds, [Col. 1475] 314. The ministry of preaching should not be undertaken except by those distinguished for chastity, 346. One must not consider what the preachers of the Church once were, but what they have become, 411. Preachers should shine with wisdom and religion, 414. Why they are called dogs, 421. The eyes of the Bride, 427, and its lips, 428. The preacher begets children from good will, or right intention, 337. The pious stratagems of preachers, 347. The ministry of preaching should not be undertaken except by those distinguished for charity, 345. What must be learned by one who preaches Christ, 388. What must be done, ibid. No one should dare to preach Christ’s glory unless he is raised toward heavenly things, 392.

— The names of preachers, 399. Holy preachers are cows, 150. Why they are two in number and feminine in gender, ibid. They are called flying clouds and doves at the windows, 263, 299. In sacred Scripture, “gods” sometimes means the elected preachers, 301. Preachers are called oxen because they plow by preaching, 308. Why the preacher is called a king, 333. Why he is also called salvation, ibid. The lofty preachers are called heavens, 382. Preachers are the breasts of the Bride, 408. They are the Bride’s neck, 414. Why they are called the eyes of doves, 415, 427. The cedar beams of the Bride’s houses signify preachers, 416. They are called dogs, 421. The silver columns of Solomon’s litter, 426. The teeth of the Church, 423. They are the lips of the Church, 428, 432, 441. And a scarlet ribbon, ibid. Scarlet signifies the flame of charity by which they themselves burn and kindle others, ibid. The cheeks of the Church, ibid. They are called a fragment of a pomegranate, ibid. The neck of the Church, ibid. And the tower of David, 429. The two orders of preachers are represented by the two breasts of the Bride, ibid.

Evil preachers are like concubines, 445. The faith must be preached in such a way that it is proved by good works, 420. What should be offered to prefects, 258.

Spiritual preeminence is transferred into secular domination, 177. The burden of preeminence, 162, 176. Most of those who lived as subjects die as prelates, 162. Because they are carried away by ambition, not led by charity, ibid. Countless people seek the honor of preeminence; few seek its labors, 237. — The care of prelates is to raise those withdrawn from earthly things toward heavenly things, 192. They must teach by words and works, 193. Whom they appoint as tribunes and centurions, 183. Who their fields, plowmen, and reapers are, ibid. Who their armorers and chariot-makers are, ibid. Their tongues become perfumeries of flatterers, 183. These fatten their pride by their flatteries, 184. How many evils carnal prelates inflict upon themselves and their subjects, 184. Under a reprobate prelate even the good deeds of the elect are not whole, ibid. The virtues lie exposed as prey, 185.

— Nothing must be done apart from the authority of a prelate, 199. He must be perfect, 214. He must shine with the light of faith and good works, ibid. Anointed with spiritual grace, he can save others, ibid. Before he is promoted, his life must be examined, 216, 269. He must enter through the gate of humility, ibid. The danger of prelates who are not perfect in charity, [Col. 1475] 228. One must not rush easily to rebuke prelates, 107. Obedience must be rendered to them in two ways, ibid. Even carnal prelates must be honored when they exceed the measure of reason, 37. The inconsiderate severity of some, 324. Yet it must be borne humbly, ibid. Prelates should sometimes consider themselves subject, 51. Nothing must be presumed apart from the judgment of prelates, 82, 198. We must not judge them, 96. For prelates who are not held by their own sins, there must be fear on account of the sins of others, 83. If they rebuke the sins of their subjects too gently, 84. He should surpass all in virtue, ibid. His power derives from Christ, 301.

— Prelates should preside as equals, 272. It is their task to free us from the servitude of Egypt, 272. Yet they must attribute the grace of liberation to God, ibid. They must be free from the evil movements of the mind that they heal in others, 290. They should look upon the defilements of others in such a way that they are not themselves stained, 291. The condition of faithful subjects must not be compared with the exalted state of prelates, 243.

Our battles with vices and the enemy of the human race, 259. Those who prepare their heart for the Lord and serve him alone, 164. The preparation of the mind necessary for contemplating higher things, 217. Whoever is appointed to the care of souls must follow a harsh life, 338. The spiritual presence of Christ is never absent from the elect, 21. From it the Church received the means to grow, 123. God is always present to the Church, 124. The presumption of those who think they can change the commands of their superiors for the better, 359. This often happens in monasteries, ibid. It must be regarded as disobedience, ibid. There are several orders of prelates, 150. One who cannot atone by his own prayers may be atoned for by the prayers of others, 92. The apostles are princes, 51.

The proof of abstinence is chastity, 266. The characteristics, degrees, and manner of the progress of the elect, 95, 119, 196, 147, 148, 153. The progress of faith and preaching in the minds of the Gentiles, 137. How the promise of the eternal inheritance is signified, 240. The certainty of the divine promises fortifies against distrust, 543. Whoever hastens toward the love of Christ must cast away the fervor of the flesh, 419. Prophecy and the prophets, 175, 238, 239, 241, 242, 248, 249, 257, 545. What it means to prophesy from the heart, 568. The danger of raising relatives to ecclesiastical dignities, 86. We are more useful to our neighbors when we are suspended higher in contemplation, 205. A teacher should benefit his neighbors in such a way that he remains attached to God, 26.

The Psalter signifies the preaching of eternal joys, 240. What sort of instrument the Psalter is and what it signifies, 466. What the Psalter is, 240. What the sons of the priests who seized portions of the sacrifice signify, 68.

On spiritual battle, 263, 364, 338, 339, 346, 340. The ancients were accustomed to fight from a chariot, 192. Spiritual battle is described, 192. Who fight from the chariot in it, [Col. 1476] ibid. Who the horsemen are, ibid. Who follow or precede the king’s quadrigas, ibid. Who the foot soldiers are, 193. Who the tribunes and centurions are, ibid. What weapons must be forged against the enemy, 194. What chariot must be prepared, ibid. In this way the elect become victors, ibid. One must fight continually, 323. Why God always leaves some enemies surviving for us, ibid.

The Bride’s true beauty: whence does it come? 415. What is the Bride’s greater beauty? 427. Whence comes the Bridegroom’s beauty? 415. That the Bride is wholly beautiful, 429.

Dust. Those raised from dust and from dung, 50, 62. Dust is illicit thought; dung is wicked action, ibid. God has mercy when he punishes here, 469. Purgatorial fire is a sign of God’s anger, 469. The punishment of purgatory, after which one reaches life, 94. Whoever wishes to escape it should afflict himself through repentance, ibid. The purple ascent to heaven, 426. The time of pruning, 419.

Ramatha: what it signifies, 8, 65. The golden reclining couch: what it signifies, 426. The ease and difficulty of obtaining reconciliation from God, 148. Rest prepared for us after death; securely we await death, 56. [Col. 1477] The Resurrection, the foundation of hope, 541. Before the resurrection, blessedness is granted to the saints, 499. What Sabaa signifies, 296. Many priests lose the chastity they had cultivated when they were clerics, 358. Their devices for concealing their sins, ibid. In Samuel, a model of perfect obedience, 99. What Samuel’s being led to the tabernacle with three calves signifies, 39, 40. The boy Samuel signifies the believing Gentiles, 65. He who is ready to hear and to act, ibid. He who, after the rejection of the Jews, ministers alone before God, 66. What his threefold calling signifies, 116. Samuel who became victorious, 186. Although not heard by the people, he deserved to be heard by God, 187. The first two books of Kings are attributed to Samuel, 4. What Samuel’s dreams signify, 121. His humility when he says that he sees, 217. Samuel, the author of the First Book of Kings, 4, 219. Why he speaks in the third person, ibid. What Samuel’s taking Saul signifies, 222. Those who are unworthy die when they see holy things—how much more when they handle them! 160. How much the flower of former holiness has withered, 207. The holiness of the apostolic assembly, 75. We are sanctified by God, led to rest, and glorified, 56. Holy men are unknown to most people, 216. They desire to appear contemptible outwardly, but do not cease doing venerable things, 217, 257. The spiritual way of life of the saints is disclosed only to the devout, ibid. With what discernment the saints both conceal and reveal their virtues, 220. Holy men greet us when they announce to us the eternal goods of salvation, 236. We rightly admire the virtues of the saints when we ascribe them to the Creator’s goodness, 249. How cautious and circumspect saints must be against the darts of enemies, 283. Why saints are permitted to succumb to lighter temptations after gaining victory in great ones, ibid. God hides his treasures, that is, holy men, 381. Holy men are the breasts of the Bridegroom, 408. Christ reclines in the heart of saints burning with charity, 411. Here the saints are like myrrh in a desert, 424. — Jerusalem is the city of the saints, 161. The rest of the saints in heaven will be disturbed by no temptations of the enemy, 172. They do nothing without counsel, 204. The deeds of earlier saints are consolations to later ones, 175. Even their weakness strengthens us, ibid. Saints are not rash in their judgments, 177. Their judgments accord with the divine judgments through the power of charity, 178. The prayers of the saints are never without fruit, unless they pray for the reprobate, 187, 188. — Saints are outwardly circumspect and inwardly provident, 207. They can scarcely find their own hearts, 325. How much less can the imperfect! ibid. Holy men are the breasts of Christ’s Bride, 408. The saints are to be sought as intercessors, 439. The saints will undergo a twofold future transformation, 534. Why the saints are called God’s garments, 534. Those wishing to make progress should place the examples of the saints before their eyes, 232. The faithful are to be exhorted to virtue by the examples of the saints, 281. The hearts of the saints are gardens of the heavenly Bridegroom, 332. The saints rage outwardly but love inwardly, 374. Through wisdom and charity bestowed by God, the elect overcome their enemies, 55. Who does not know how to be satisfied? 573. [Col. 1478] Saul, relying on bodily strength, is defeated, while Samuel, lacking it, becomes victorious, 186. Saul’s evil omens concerning the future kingdom, 188. What is to be learned from Saul’s history—he began well but did not persevere, 348. May Saul’s death terrify disobedient rulers, 2. His rejection because of slight disobedience should make us afraid, 287. Saul, the persecutor of the Church, 14. See Paul. How grave the sin of scandal is, 84. Knowledge of the Old and New Law is necessary, 28. Who is the Lord of knowledge? 57. The reefs we must avoid, 304. Holy Scripture is a shady mountain, 399. Those devoted to carnal impulses do not approach it, ibid. It is like a painting, 398. Fire, 399. A spring and a well, 433, 434. The letter of Scripture covers the spirit as straw covers grain, 399. It belongs to animals to feed on straw, and to human beings to feed on grain, ibid. From Sacred Scripture come the light of understanding and the oil of charity, 337. The interpreter of Sacred Scripture is like a watchman, 3. And like a traveler, ibid. Why Jews and heretics are deceived in understanding it, 237. Sacred Scripture is not to be evaluated according to the measure of interpreters and commentators, 3. It is like a neck, 237. It is divinely inspired, 3. In knowledge of it no one is so perfect that he cannot progress further, 4. It deserves veneration even when it is not understood, ibid. The more it is learned each day, the more gratefully it is read, ibid. Sacred Scripture is a ladder to God, 6. It supplies us with as many weapons as it has precepts and counsels, 10. It is the foundation of the Church, 27. In Scripture one hears not the voice of prophets and patriarchs but the voice of God, 115. By the sayings of Sacred Scripture we are kindled to love of God, 157. Thus the holocaust is to be offered, ibid. Sacred Scripture is the mirror of chosen shepherds, 251. Sacred Scripture is fire, 399. What the three books of Solomon signify, 401. What their order signifies, ibid. The *murenulae*—little chains—signify Sacred Scripture, 414. Why they are golden and embroidered with silver, ibid. Sacred Scripture is represented by the wine cellar, 417. How charity is ordered through Sacred Scripture, ibid. What the strength of bread and the strength of water in Scripture are, ibid. With what force its waters flow, 434. The two orders of those who read Holy Scripture profitably, 435. The streams and fullest-flowing waters are called Sacred Scripture, 440. No one is dear to Christ unless he delights in the Sacred Scriptures, 451. The soul intent on meditating upon Sacred Scripture overflows with delights, 455. Those who read the word of God with a corrupt intention do not find the truth, 461. Sacred Scripture is represented under the name of a wagon, 162. Sacred Scripture is signified by Galgal, 174, 291. Through reading Sacred Scripture the preacher should be instructed so that inwardly, through contemplation, he may be taught by God, ibid. He who receives the word of Scripture not in love but in knowledge receives from its fullness not the fullness of the word but of the book, 219. John or Paul wrote the letter; but the Word, speaking in them, inspired it, ibid. The letter of Scripture, without the spirit, is not only dead but also kills, ibid. The letter is the body, but the Spirit is the life of this body, ibid. Samuel, the author of the First Book of Kings: why he speaks in the third person, ibid. Those who do not close the gates of their eyes, heart, and mouth to that life are less suited to it, ibid. God is revealed in secrecy, 244. From there one ascends to God, ibid. Who are called the elect’s harvest being tithed, 196, 197. Our enemies lie in ambush through all the senses, 329. We have sinned through all the senses; let us be moved to compunction, 147. The proud cannot be filled with the divine gift, 59. The blinding of the proud and lustful, 357. The devices of the proud for attaining the summit of honor, 365. Even if they are good, those who pray on their behalf ought not to be heard, ibid. The hand of God is heavy over the proud, 475. Our progress should be subjected to the judgment of our superiors, 40. Carnal people are forbidden to awaken the soul sleeping in the Bridegroom’s bosom, 418. Christ raised up the Church by dying on the cross, 456.

The Synagogue, a rival of the Church, 14. He rages against it, ibid. It did not give birth to a male, 17. Prayers of the Church against the Synagogue lying in wait for her, 18. The rejection of the Synagogue, 41. The Synagogue’s boast is blunted, 45. The elect of the Synagogue raised by Christ to heavenly things, 23. The barrenness of the Synagogue, while the formerly barren Church rejoices in fruitfulness, 49. Its unhappy childbirth, 135. Bent down by the pains of childbirth, it is killed, 136. The Synagogue had grown old, and was blind amid such great light from Christ, 71. When God came to the Synagogue, he did not remain, 119. He who will remain in the Church until the end of the world, 120. From where the Synagogue of the Jews derives its beauty, 443. At the end, the Synagogue repents of its former darkness, 449. What it means that the Synagogue is disturbed because of the chariots of Aminadab, ibid. The Synagogue is summoned by the Church to conversion, ibid., 454. Once converted, the Synagogue will fight vigorously for the faith, ibid. The Church will lead the Christ whom she has apprehended into the house of the Synagogue, her mother, 454. How great the perfection of certain converts from the Synagogue will be at the end of the world, 445. The Synagogue, nailing Christ to the wood, defiled itself by an unspeakable crime, 455. It is called the vineyard of the Peaceful One, 455, 459.

## T

Tabernacles. What it means to be dismissed into the tabernacles, 280. Let discernment teach whether to be silent about or reveal the good things we do, 299. Sins are to be covered by clothing them with good works, 474. The great darts of bitterness suffered by converts, 370. The devil’s ancient weapons are gluttony and pride, 6. Our body is the temple of God, 509. The temple of God is profaned by unclean thoughts, 350. The ark of God was brought into the temples of idols when the faith of the Gentiles was implanted in their minds, 137. [Col. 1481] God grants certain temporal things to the brethren, 179. Lovers of temporal things make little of their own souls, 191. No vice imposes thicker darkness than lust, 358. The devil is not always permitted to tempt, 574. When the enemy brings more serious temptations against us, 169. Through the help of divine grace they are rendered ineffective, ibid. Why, after overcoming great temptations, we are permitted to succumb to lighter ones, 283. The rest of the saints in heaven will be disturbed by no temptations, 172. When temptation presses, one must not abandon one’s position, 264. We are tempted inwardly by unclean spirits and outwardly by wicked people, 285. When we are tempted, grace is near to help, 288. What temptations we are liable to after conversion, 311. To subjects who are tempted, pastors should supply the aid of prayers and sacrifices, 168. What hiding places we should seek when tempted, 285. Let pastors not delay in bringing help to those who are tempted, 298. The fervor of the ancients condemns our tepidity, 323. The Bride comes to Christ three times, 430. The end: by “the end,” the end of our life is understood, 294. Demons strive to prevent a good work from being carried through to the end of life, ibid. What the boundaries of Bethshemesh signify, 151. The earth made fruitful by the preaching of the apostles, 532. Contempt for earthly things in the Church, 19. Those who delight in earthly things are turned in the wheel of transient things, 63. Truth is hidden from those who love earthly things with their whole heart, 97. To draw people away from earthly things and lift them to heavenly things is the concern of prelates, 192. God terrifies us in order to make us solicitous, 123. Demons do not fear the imperfect desires of Christians, 169. In what way the Church is terrible to her enemies, 443. The two Testaments are two wheels, 149. What is to be learned from both Testaments, 454. Thabor. What the oak of Thabor signifies, 247. Treasures. The saints are God’s treasures, which he hides, 381. Those who will sit on the throne with Christ, 62. What the tibia signifies, 240. Cedar beams designate preachers, 416. It is not enough to fear God unless one serves him, 273. By doing good out of delight in grace, ibid. Those who fear but do not love are not upright, 408. By fearing God we avoid evil; by serving him we do good, 277. What a human being should fear from the fallen angels, 58. How much the reprobate who do not fear now will have to fear in the future, 168. The twofold fear of God, 557. Perfect love is free from fear, 408. From fear one must ascend to contemplation, 34. Yet sometimes fear follows contemplation, ibid. Sometimes it neither precedes nor follows it, ibid. Conversion begins with fear, 309. The salutary fear of the elect, 167. The weak and carnal are to be pierced with fear, 273. Gifts are to be requested with fear of God, 205. What the bells of the high priest’s garment signify, 251. *Geth* is interpreted as “winepress,” 172. Human torpor after the fall, 397. It is transgression of the prohibition, not the thing itself, that defiles a person, 566. Tribulation accompanies true repentance in the Spirit, 505. The time of tribulation will seem short, 531. Tribulation is the entrance into heavenly joy, 286. The number thirty designates those who hold the faith that works through love, 223, 263. The dining room is the beauty of the spiritual life, [Col. 1481] 223. Those to whom the breadth of charity is shown are brought into the dining room, ibid. The twofold sadness, 562. The last trumpet on the day of judgment, 575. He strips off his tunic who rejects all outward things, 437. The holy soul imitates the love and lament of the turtledove, 414. The voice of the turtledove is the Church’s lament, 420. The tambourine signifies mortification of the flesh, 240. Why the author preferred the typical sense in his commentary on First Kings, chapter VI. In a typical interpretation, correspondence is not to be sought with excessive precision, 122. Anna is a type of the Church, 41 and passim.

## U

Breasts. The breasts signify evangelical preaching, 402. God’s breasts brought near to us in the Incarnation, 403. God’s breasts are the condescension of his most humble Incarnation, ibid. What the Bridegroom’s breasts are, 405, 408. Why Christ, the bundle of myrrh, dwells among the Bride’s breasts, 415. The Bride’s two breasts are the two peoples, 450. Why the Bride’s two breasts are called two fawns, twins of a she-goat, 450. The Gospel is designated by the Bride’s breasts, 402. Why the Church’s breasts are compared with ropes, 459. — He who has a saleable discourse and doctrine is not a man of God, 207. We are refreshed by the shadow of the Holy Spirit, 417. Those who protect us from the heat of desire by their exhortations are a shelter for us, 300. The sacraments of anointing in the Church, 228. The fruit of sacred anointing, 229. What is signified by the priests’ anointing, 375. The mysteries of priestly anointing, 384. The anointing that is accompanied by the grace of the Holy Spirit, 385. It flees the proud and hypocritical, ibid. No one is brought to life unless he has died to the world, 60. The ointment of Christ is the Holy Spirit, 403. The unity of the Church. Christ suffered death to strengthen unity among the members of the Church, 431. So that it may be terrible to its enemies, the Church must arm itself with peace and bind itself together in unity, 443. Converted Jews will suffer under Antichrist for the unity of the faith, 444. In unity the elect support one another, 446. Outside the body of the Church the Spirit of charity does not give life, 511. The Church is one from many and diverse members, 529. Outside it no one praises God and no one proclaims him, ibid. He died to strengthen unity among the members of the Church, 43. The one thing necessary, 336. What the grape of the reprobate mind is, 173. Desire is a grape in appearance and beauty, but gall in taste, 196. Elkanah’s two wives prefigure the Synagogue and the Church, 10. The active and contemplative life, 31. The quarrels of those two wives, 36. While the barrenness of the contemplative life is reproached, ibid. Let humility accompany the contemplative life, 41.

## V
The bride most willingly accepts the opportunity to devote herself to God, 418. The cows bearing the ark that went straight onward—what they signify, 153. What a valley signifies in Sacred Scripture, 155. In the valley of humility, a foretaste of heaven’s delights, 155. What “vain things” signify literally, 276. How great the promises are to those who do not turn aside after vain things, ibid. Golden vessels placed upon a great stone, 157. If God did not spare the golden vessels, what will happen to the bronze ones? 58. The hope of forgiveness must not be abandoned, 275. Let us rejoice over forgiveness received in such a way that we always fear on account of our guilt, 502. We obtain forgiveness by imitating humility and Christ’s Passion, 498. The word of faith to be preached to the elect to the end of the world, 207. The word of God is the soul’s food, 218. By the sword of the divine word, we ought to strike one another with mutual blows, 312. Those who are great in word and deed often do not guard sufficiently against vainglory, 316. The incarnation of the Word foreseen by David, 496. How rich in wisdom the word of Christ is, 442. The worth of the word of God, 113. It is one thing to utter the word of God, another to understand it, 206. With what zeal the word of God should be received and guarded, 97. The word of God is revealed to some so that it may be loved, and to others so that it may also be preached, 102. The divine word falls upon the earth when it becomes despised because of the preacher’s life, 109. The word of God must be understood before it becomes evident to us, 111. The seed of the word of God must not be entrusted to sterile soil, 142. Truth is hidden from those who love earthly things, 97. Those who read the word of God with a wrong intention do not find the truth, 461. What it means for the old things to depart from the mouth, ibid. The fervor of the ancients reproves our lukewarmness, 323. The way to heaven is not level and broad, 535. The way of life is the affliction of repentance, 95. Why not every good way is straight, 277. One must walk on the straight way with discretion as guide, 153. One must not turn to the right by denying the necessities of the flesh, nor to the left by indulging the flesh too much, ibid. On this way, the intention must be pure and simple, ibid. One must always proceed and persevere by conquering carnal desires, ibid. and 154. What it means to seek Christ through the alleys and streets, 423. What victims and offerings we ought to present to God, 85. What it means to add victims to a burnt offering, 158. Christ’s victory over the Jews, 490. The order of our victory, 170. Victory must be ascribed to God, not to us, 307. The praise of victory consists not in words but in deeds, 354. “He who conquers” will sit with Christ on the throne, 62. To see. Through contemplation we see in God both what causes fear and what gives delight, 33. To see God through a mirror is granted here only to the humble, 235. How a human being can see God, 577, 578. What “seeing” signifies, 217. The sleep of the saints is joined to vigilance, 436. Christ kept vigil in the Resurrection, 517. The teachers of the Church are watchful, 423. God leaves no sin without vengeance, 497. What the peaceful vineyard of Christ is, 459. The vineyard of Christ, the Church, 519. The fragrance of the Church’s vineyard is good examples, 420. What it means for the vineyards of the elect to be tithed, 196, 197. Wine signifies the Old Law, 402. The best wine is preaching, 452. “Man” is so called from virtue, 5. Why Christ is called one man, 7. Manhood is the time for administering the priesthood, 89. The rod signifies a word of correction, 316. What the rod in Jonathan’s hand signifies, ibid., 327. What the tip of the rod dipped into the honeycomb represents, ibid. Jonathan’s rod signifies the teaching and discipline of preaching, 327. Virginity must be preserved through great labors, 383. What the example of virgins provides, 279. The titles of victory owed to virgins, 281. The choir of virgins is most powerful against the enemy, 293, 345. Virgins should care no less for guarding the heart than for bodily continence, 345. Who ascend like a little column of smoke? 424. Many virtues are necessary for conquering the spirit of fornication, 331.

[Col. 1483] See Abstinence, Humility. Frequent prayer, ibid. Guarding the mind against lustful thoughts; an escort of chaste thoughts, ibid. The excellence of the four cardinal virtues in Christ, 9. Humility must be guarded amid the great gifts of virtue, 38, 109. Every virtue is weak without God’s help, 52. Those nourished by contemplation are adorned with the splendor of virtues, 163. Increases in virtue are granted to the elect according to the merit of their work, 213. The poor, humble, and simple, advanced by the Holy Spirit to the summit of virtue, 250. From virtues comes a good fragrance, 405. The fragrance and progress of virtues, the Church’s spices, 433. What the virtues of the Church’s teachers should be, 433. The consummated vision is perfect knowledge of God, 8. It can be obtained only by the citizens of heaven, 8, 234. Whether Moses saw God intuitively, 235. One must advance little by little in the splendors of the eternal vision, 32. That which is beyond human capacity, ibid. From this comes contempt for earthly things, 33. In this vision the mind rejoices all the more because the appearance of no creature can retain it in love of itself, 53. Christ visits the Church—with what benefit? 443. In what order? 447, 448. Spiritual sight is sharpened through humility, 155. The present life is night; the future life, day, 552. The distinction between the present and eternal life, 530. The temporal life must be used to prepare for the eternal one, 519. What sort of banquet is eternal life? 94. In the present life the ears of grain are gathered; afterward the bread will be eaten, 155. God is the life of the soul, 470. Some are drawn from every kind of human being to eternal life and to faith, 331. Whoever is placed in charge of souls must follow an austere life, 338. The stages of the worst life, 330. What virtue we need in order to overcome them, ibid. The pursuit and manner of the more perfect life, 164. The more secluded life. See More secluded life. The life of the good is secure and most cautious, 286. Compared with eternal life, the present life is night, 321. One must devote oneself to the active and contemplative life, 31. The former is compared to severe labor, 32, 334. Lest what is easily obtained become despised, 32. One must sometimes flee from the active life to the contemplative, 70. In the contemplative life, elation must be feared, 117. The pleasantness of the contemplative life, 156. It is Christ’s field, ibid. Its delights and labors, ibid. We would fail in them unless Christ provided help, 157. The active and contemplative lives are two sisters; both are fruitful, 334. Few devote themselves to contemplation, ibid. One must reach it through the labors of good works, ibid. The younger sister is so not in dignity but in time, ibid. The active life belongs to all the sons of the Church, ibid. Both are represented by Martha and Mary, 335. And by Leah and Rachel, ibid. Prelates are rarely admitted to the embrace of contemplation, ibid. In what respects the active and contemplative life agree or differ, ibid. Christ is anointed in the tomb by contemplatives, 336. These are rare in public, ibid. They think it fornication to withdraw from Christ even for a moment, ibid. Those serving the active life pray only not while sitting, but while standing or walking, ibid. Yet those who are perfect workers in it pray to God with greater confidence the more laboriously they serve him, ibid. Excessive anxiety must be avoided in the active life, ibid. One must devote oneself to the one necessary thing, ibid. To understand the brevity of life is a gift of grace, 530. The labors of temporal life, 536. The happiness of eternal life, 558.

[Col. 1484] The vices propagated from greed, 191. An innumerable multitude of vices serves under the leadership of the devil, 282. What is necessary for overcoming vices? 268. Those who declare war on the vices of the flesh should excel in courage and teaching, 346. Appropriate remedies must be applied to each individual vice, 302. Why God permits the wicked to live long, 492. Those who have lost innocence and humility do not live, 278. To be made alive. It is one thing to be made alive in righteousness, another to be made alive for righteousness, 556. God alone avenges sins justly, 496. Converts who are sinners call others to repentance, 503. The signs of a divine calling, 230. What signs of his calling Paul sought, 231. What signs John’s disciples sought, ibid. What every preacher ought to investigate, ibid. God calls when he awakens someone through the force of greater grace, 99. What Samuel’s being called three times signifies, 116. Why he was called by God, not by Eli, ibid. The love and joy of the soul hearing God calling it, 104. Things that cannot be explained in words, ibid. Those who place their own will before the commands of their superiors are struck down, 360. “Heart” is understood in place of “will,” 290. Married people cannot avoid the impulse of pleasure, but restrain it within the bond of honor, 348. The wounds of Christ, the openings in the rock, 420. What it means for the bride to be wounded and stripped by the watchmen, 439. The sinner is like one gravely wounded, 494. The little foxes are heretics, especially those who feign humility, 421. Through their breath the weak are endangered, 421. The perfect are not endangered in the same way, 421.

Z

Zeal for souls is a sacrifice most pleasing to God, 504. To whom it belongs, 504.
